## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library,** containing all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition from the first twelve centuries of the Church, based on the most accurate editions, very diligently corrected by comparison with one another and with several manuscript codices; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or each author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever any Father has written on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be determined which Fathers commented on the individual texts of each book of Scripture, and in which passages of their works they did so. An extremely accurate edition, easily preferable to all others if the following are taken into account: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—which for the first time in our library brings together six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, drawn from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

**Second series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology was printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. — The 1,200 volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; the 1,300 volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for eight hundred francs. — The purely Latin edition indeed embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

## In the year of the Lord 1100. Goscelin, monk of Canterbury

[Col. 0009]

### Historical notice

(Oudin, *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers*, II, 961.)

[Col. 0009A] Gotsennus, or Goscelin, a monk of Saint Bertin in Artois, believed to have been a Frenchman by birth and of the Order of Saint Benedict, first professed monastic life in the monastery of Bertin and was later summoned to England, to the monastery of Saint Augustine of Canterbury, on account of his exceptional gifts in regular observance and every kind of learning. After Bede, who discusses the matter in Book I, chapter 23 and following, and in Book II, chapters 2 and 3 of his *History of the English*, he most diligently wrote the Life of Saint Augustine, archbishop of Canterbury, in two works, a greater and a lesser, as he explains in his preface, no. 4.

One of these was found published after the works of Lanfranc, without the author’s name, by Dacherius in 1648 at Paris, in folio. The other, namely the greater work, never before published, was issued in the first century of the *Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, p. 499, together with a Book of Miracles composed by the same Gotselinus. The prologue of the greater work begins, “To the dearest lords,” etc. The little book itself begins, “The most powerful victor,” etc.

William Cave reports that he flourished by [Col. 0009B] the year 1096 in his *History of Literary Scholarship*, century XI, p. 629; Gerard John Vossius places him in the year 1110, Book II, chapter 48 of *On Latin Historians*, p. 398 in my edition. Both statements may be true.

Moreover, this Gotselinus composed a History of the Translation of Saint Augustine in two books dedicated to Saint Anselm, bishop of Canterbury. They are in manuscript in the possession of Jean Mabillon, who will publish them in the sixth century of the *Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*. He also commended in writing the Life of Saint Swithun, bishop of Winchester, which exists, or at least an epitome of it exists, in Laurentius Surius, volume IV, under 11 July.

He also wrote Lives of Saint Lawrence, archbishop of Dublin; Abbot Grimbald; Bishop Erkenwald; Edith, Milburga, and Withburga, virgins. Likewise, a book *On the Origin of Saint Ivo* and another *On His Translation and Miracles*, concerning which Vossius speaks in the place cited. The *Acts of the Saints* contain these under 10 June, volume II, p. 287, where they discuss Saint Ivo, bishop of [Col. 0009C] Persia, and his three holy companions in England.

Goscelin, a monk of Ramsey, wrote this work and dedicated it to his abbot Herbert, who was appointed in 1087 and after four years became bishop of Norwich; his eulogy is found in the *Monastic History of England*, p. 1003. Goscelin later became a monk of Canterbury at Saint Augustine’s and wrote the Life of Saint Augustine, archbishop of Canterbury, assigned to 26 May, together with several other Lives of saints. He was regarded as second after Bede in celebrating the praises of the saints of England, as Malmesbury testifies concerning him in Book IV, chapter 1 of *On the Deeds of the Kings of England*.

Below, in the prologue, he explains what he received from Andrew Leucander, abbot of Ramsey and the first author of this Life, and what he himself added from the report of others. The material found in chapter 4 was added by the same author while Herbert, bishop of Norwich, was still alive; Herbert died on 22 July 1119.

No one describes the works of Gotselinus, monk of Bertin or Canterbury, more fully than Henry Wharton, a most learned student of English affairs, who published several of his minor works recovered from manuscript codices in volume II of *Anglia Sacra*. He writes as follows in the preface, no. 3, p. 6:

[Col. 0010A] “Gocelinus, or Gotselinus, commonly called Bertinianus, was, according to Bale, century XIII, chapter 17, from the region of Morini and a monk at the shrine of Saint Bertin. Later, as his reputation for learning increased, he was summoned to England by Archbishop Anselm. First at Ramsey under Abbot Herbert, and later at the monastery of Saint Augustine of Canterbury, he led a monastic life and committed to writing several Lives of English saints.

“Vossius says much the same in Book II, chapter 48 of *On Latin Historians*, except that he reverses the order and wishes him to have been first a monk of Canterbury and afterward of Ramsey. Both are wrong. For if Gotselinus was summoned to England by Archbishop Anselm, he could in no way have lived among the monks of Ramsey under Abbot Herbert, who left the abbacy in 1091.

“William of Malmesbury gives more certain information about Gotselinus. In Book IV of *On the Deeds of the Kings of England*, at the end, he says: ‘Goscelin, a monk of Saint Bertin, had formerly come to England with Herman, bishop of Salisbury’—Herman, after spending three years at Saint Bertin, returned to England in 1058—‘a man distinguished by his knowledge of letters and song. Traveling through many bishoprics and abbeys over time, he left monuments of outstanding learning in many places; in celebrating the praises of the saints of England he was second to none after Bede, and in music he gained the palm after Osbern. Finally, he elevated innumerable Lives of saints by his style and more elegantly renewed the works of earlier writers, whether lost through hostility or issued in an inartful form. He also polished the account of the translation of this Saint Augustine so thoroughly that he seems to have shown it with his finger to those present and placed it before the eyes of those to come.’

[Col. 0010B] “Gotselinus himself testifies in both prefaces to the Life of Saint Augustine that he was a monk of Saint Augustine’s at Canterbury. For he wrote two Histories of the same saint’s Life. ‘We made,’ he says in the preface to the greater History, ‘two books on the same subject, a greater and a lesser.’

“Jean Mabillon published the greater one in the first century of the *Acts of the Benedictines*, p. 499, adding there also his greater Book of the Miracles of Saint Augustine, p. 535. A shorter History of the Life and another still shorter work on the Miracles of Saint Augustine, inscribed to Gotselinus, are found in a Lambeth Palace Library manuscript.

[Col. 0011A] “From this manuscript we copied the shorter Life and arranged for it to be published in print in this second volume, p. 55, so that the first preacher of the Christian faith among the English might not lack his due praise among the English, although Goscelin knew very little about him that Bede had not written earlier.

“The greater History is far more extensive; nevertheless, if one omits its stories and empty verbal embellishments, it leaves nothing in the shorter History untouched. Dacherius had previously published the shorter one in an appendix to the works of Lanfranc, Paris, 1648, p. 57, but without the author’s name and without the entirety of chapter 36.

“Many works of Gotselinus are found in a very ancient and elegant Cotton manuscript, Vespasian B. 20, in the following order:

[Col. 0011B] “A shorter History of the Life of Saint Augustine, archbishop of Canterbury.

“A shorter History of the Miracles of Saint Augustine.

“A greater History of the Life of the same Saint Augustine.

“A greater History of the Miracles of Saint Augustine.

[Col. 0011C] “A Sermon on the Feast of Saint Augustine. It begins: ‘The splendid solemnity of the present day.’

“Two books to Anselm on the translation of Saint Augustine, which took place on 6 September 1091. The learned Mabillon promises to bring these to light in the sixth Benedictine century. The sixth century of the saints of the Order of Saint Benedict—which extends from the year 1000 to 1100—was begun by Dom Luca D’Achery, a monk of the Congregation of Saint Maur; Dom Jean Mabillon and Théodoric Ruinart of the same congregation completed and published it with the necessary indexes, in two folio volumes, Paris, 1701, at the press of Charles Rebustel. In these books the Life of Saint Petard follows in continuous sequence.

“A Life of Saint Mildred.

“The Translation of Saint Mildred and the foundation of her monastery.

“Lives of the saints Lawrence, Mellitus, Justus, Honorius, Deusdedit, and Theodore, archbishops of Canterbury. In these, whatever is historical is taken from Bede in almost exactly the same words, with Bede’s statements merely expanded in grand style and many miracles added at the end of each. In the Life of Saint Lawrence, the author makes a lengthy digression in an attempt to win credence for the miracles of his own time.

“A Life of Adrian, abbot of Saint Augustine’s, whom he reports to have died in 708.

“A History of his translation, which took place in the time of King William.

“A little book against the empty claimants of Saint Mildred, proving that her body is not kept in the parish of Saint Gregory of Canterbury, in a church called by the fabricated name of Miltrudis, but in the monastery of Saint Augustine, to which it was translated by Abbot Aelstan in the time of King Canute. Thus far the Cotton manuscript.

[Col. 0012A] “Besides these works, Bale records that Gotselinus wrote Lives of Saints Swithun, Grimbald, Erkenwald, Edith, Milburga, Withburga, and Ivo, and a History of the Translation of Ivo.

“Moreover, he is said by Usserius, *British Antiquities*, chapter 2, p. 15, to have translated into Latin an ancient catalogue, written in Saxon, of the saints buried in England. Many copies of this translation are found in our libraries.

“William Thorn praises his Chronicle in his *History of Saint Augustine*, col. 1783. Nor do I think that the following passage from the ancient register of the Church of Ely, chapter 10, should be understood of anyone else. In the time of Abbot Symeon of Ely, who presided from 1082 to 1094, there was among the monks a certain man named Gocalinus, most eloquent, who transformed the Lives, miracles, and deeds of the male and female saints gathered from throughout England into histories and prose compositions dedicated to them.

“He wrote a prose work on Saint Etheldreda, whose opening is: ‘To Christ the King be glory.’ The obituary of Saint Augustine of Canterbury records his death as follows: ‘On the Ides of May died [Col. 0012B] Gezelinus, monk and priest.’

“Goscelin’s Life of Saint Wereburga, virgin, was published by Godefridus Henschenius under 3 February, volume I, p. 386; in the preliminary commentary to the Life, paragraph I, no. 2, p. 384, he attributes it to him.

“Also in 1688, at Antwerp, by Michel Cnobar, Daniel Papebrochius published in the approved Lives of the Saints, volume VI for the month of May, under 26 May, pp. 375 and following, all of Gocelinus’s minor works relating to the Life of Saint Augustine, bishop of Canterbury—namely, two books *On His Life and Miracles* and two books *On His Translation*, preceded by a commentary beginning on p. 373 and extending to p. 443.

“In the same Cotton Library, under the image of Vibellius, letter c, manuscript 8, no. 15, there is a Life of Saint Kentigern the Confessor, also called Ingalschu, by Joscelinus.”

Guillelmus of Malmesbury praises this Goscelinus highly in Book IV, final chapter, of *On the Kings of England*, and in his book *On the Archbishops of Dorobernia*.

Caesar Baronius, in his *Annals* under the year 862, calls this Gotselinus “the Morinian”; others call him a Bertinian monk. These descriptions do not conflict with the foregoing, since he was summoned to England by Saint Anselm from the town of Saint-Omer, or from the abbey of Saint Bertin.

Jean Mabillon says more about him in the preliminary observations to the Life of Saint Augustine, archbishop of Canterbury, in the first century of the *Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, p. 498; that volume was printed in folio at Paris in 1668 by Charles Sarreux. See also Gerard John Vossius, Book II, chapter 48 of *On Latin Historians*, p. 398; and Valerius Andreas, *Belgian Library*, under “Gotselinus,” p. 298, edition of 1643, Leuven, quarto.

[Col. 0011]

# History of the Translation of Saint Augustine, Bishop and Apostle of the English, and of the Other Saints Who Rested in His Monastery at Canterbury

By Goscelin, a monk of that same place and a contemporary.

(Mabillon, *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, volume IX.)

## Preliminary Observations

### 1

Gotselinus, or, as the manuscript reads, Gocelinus, a monk transferred from Bertin to the monastery at Canterbury, devoted himself entirely to writing the histories of the saints, so that most authors regard him as the principal writer after Bede the Venerable on the deeds performed by holy men in England.

We previously published his Life of blessed Augustine, apostle of the English, in the first Benedictine century, under the year 607. We reserved until the present time the history of the translation of that saint and of the other saints resting in the monastery outside Canterbury, because it contributes greatly to illuminating the affairs of our Order carried out in England during this present eleventh century.

It would be superfluous to collect more information about the same author here, since he ought already to be sufficiently and more than sufficiently known from what we presented about him in the place cited in the first century, where we also said more about the saints mentioned in this history of the translation. It is not useful to repeat that material here.

### 2

It remains only to say a little about the other translations of Saint Augustine that took place on various occasions afterward, as we learn from William Thorn, who wrote the Chronicle of the Augustinian monastery in which he lived and brought it down to the year 1397.

This author says that Abbot Wido, in the year 1091, immediately after the solemn translation of the holy relics described by Gocelinus had been completed, concealed most of blessed Augustine’s bones in the wall of the church, lest, if the Danes, or Northmen, or other barbarians should invade—as happened frequently in England at that time—the bones of the blessed pontiff be violated.

The abbot’s precaution was not useless. For in the year 1168, as the same author attests, on the day of the beheading of Saint John the Baptist, when almost the entire Augustinian church was burned, the bier of the blessed pontiff was so disfigured and afterward so neglected that shortly thereafter it became entirely unknown where the relics of the holy bishop were kept.

At last the Augustinian monks were distressed by this. Therefore, in the year 1221, at the urging of John, prior of that place, they resolved, together with the other elders of the monastery, to devote themselves to fasts, vigils, prayers, and other pious exercises until God should grant them knowledge of the whereabouts of so great a treasure.

God granted their request. The prior, following the advice of several brothers who claimed that this had been revealed to them by God, ordered the wall beside Saint Augustine’s altar to be broken through. There a stone coffin was discovered which, as the inscription indicated, contained the body of blessed Augustine.

### 3

At that time Hugh, the abbot of the place, was away as envoy to Louis, king of the French. When he returned, many abbots and other nobles of England having been summoned for the solemnity, the relics of the holy man were placed in suitable locations, except for the head, which was enclosed in a vessel adorned with gold, silver, and various extremely precious stones, so that it might be exposed for the people’s veneration on appointed days.

Twenty years later, in the year 1240, after the monastery’s sanctuary had been restored, the body of Saint Augustine was placed in its center, with the bodies of the other patrons of that place arranged in a circle on either side. In subsequent years two altars were added, one on each side.

All this is magnificently represented in an engraved copperplate that you will find in volume I of the *Monastic History of England*, and which Papebrochius arranged to have inserted in volume VI of the Bollandist *May*, under 26 May. Thus the memory of so illustrious a monument of English devotion might not perish—a memory which the apostasy of Henry VIII would otherwise have erased by overthrowing the sanctuary.

The holy man’s chin escaped this catastrophe; it is reverently preserved in the monastery of Saint Saviour of the Cistercian Order at Antwerp, a celebrated city of Belgium. The Reverend Lord Franciscus Dierick, abbot of that place, published a special book on this matter, which was printed in 1624.

### 4

Although, at the end of Saint Augustine’s Life in the first Benedictine century, we had promised to present here his entire history of the translation, nevertheless, since we later communicated it to the distinguished Daniel Papebrochius, who published it under 26 May in the Bollandist *May*, it seemed sufficient here to present only those matters that could contribute more substantially to illuminating the history of this Benedictine century, leaving aside the miracles and other acts of lesser importance, which anyone wishing to know more will find among the Bollandists.

# The Prologue of Lord Gocelinus

To Anselm, venerable archbishop of Canterbury, on the translation of Saint Augustine, apostle of the English, and of his companions.

Leader Anselm, Father of Fathers, and strength of the churches,

Whom the Roman and English world celebrates with titles,

Do not disdain the humble gift of Gocelinus.

In the citadel of wisdom, at the table of heavenly philosophy, my heart eagerly desires, O ecclesiastical prince who presides in chief, to bring you a golden dish—not precious through my own efforts, but through the resources of the supreme Augustine; filled with his virtues, seasoned with his charisms, and fashioned from the gold and gems of him and his holy companions.

It is a little book of the recent translation and of the signs of Augustine himself and of his companions, which, in various places, during nearly the seven years since the translation itself, are known to have been clearly accomplished before the eyes of faithful witnesses present.

Blessed are the times of your pontificate, in which, after the earth of the saints had given birth to what had been enclosed for so long, this angelic pearl shone forth for us together with its gems! etc.

# Book One

## Chapter I. The feast of this translation is shared with the other saints

[Col. 0015A]

After the ancient solemnities of Augustine, the evangelical first parent of the English, which we recently celebrated with festive praise and which heaven has crowned in triumph, a new glory, a new joy, a new solemnity arises for us.

It is the new translation of Augustine himself and of his holy companions, which now shines in his new church, after nearly one hundred [Note: [Col. 0015C] He died in the year 707.] lustres.

## Chapter II. A new and larger church is built

The more exalted presbytery of the new church of Augustine embraces in its entirety, together with its spacious porticoes, the whole area formerly occupied by the oratory of the holy Mother of God, adjoining it on the eastern side and illustrious through its continual solemnity and the signs of heavenly virtues.

The remaining nave of the old monastery, ordered to yield to the rising building, already weakened and threatened with collapse, is demolished lest it overwhelm the new structure. Before this, however, the entire crowd of saints, dispersed throughout all the chapels, is rescued from destruction and placed under new roofs, just as Lot and his companions are delivered by the Lord from the ruin of the world.

Thus Augustine’s apostolic hall was advancing toward its appointed goal, but the portico of his burial stood in the way. What, then, should the devoted abbot Scolland, the builder, do? He did not dare move those holy inner chambers, untouched for so many ages, yet the work already begun could not proceed unless the obstacles were removed—especially since his predecessor had paid with his death for demolishing the aforesaid basilica of the Mother of God.

But while these events were taking place, Scolland was removed from earthly cares by heavenly judgment, and Abbot Wido succeeded him [Col. 0015C] [Note: That is, in the year 1091.]. In Wido’s fourth year [Note: [Col. 0015D] Scolland, as is said below in the final chapter of Book II, died one day before King William, that is, on 8 September 1087. William the Conqueror died at Rouen on 9 September of the same year, according to Orderic Vitalis and other authors. William Thorn should therefore be corrected, since he recorded Scolland’s death on 3 September. Wido succeeded Scolland, having been taken from within the monastery.] the translation in question took place.

The king, having been consulted and approving, had ordered him to conduct the solemnity with the greatest decorum, amid an influx of bishops, abbots, and peoples. He himself also wished to be present, but at that time he was setting out [Note: [Col. 0016D] This was William Rufus, who, having returned from Normandy in August of that year, marched against Malcolm, king of the Scots, who was ravaging Northumbria.] on an expedition to Scotland.

But the head of the monastery, after raising a tower above the aforementioned porticoes to a lofty height, while eagerly extending the remaining nave of the church, caused that chamber of the blessed—impatient of delay until the saints should be brought out—to be overturned by a powerful battering ram. It buried so many princes of the heavenly kingdom, sleeping in long peace, while the hastened deed excused the negligence.

Before this, however, he solemnly had the fragrant relics of the worthy saints Adrian the confessor [Col. 0016A] and Mildred, virgin of Christ, carried out; flourishing with wondrous sweetness, they thus escaped the impending collapse.

## Chapter III. The relics of the saints remain unharmed amid the ruins

But when the foremost saints themselves—Augustine, Laurence, Mellitus, Justus, Honorius, and Deusdedit—had been left in the aforementioned collapse, divine protection, as though extending a hand beneath them, caused the stones and timbers to spare them, although the harsher obstinacy of human beings had not spared them.

For when the great masses of stones, roof beams, and lead-covered roofing that had overwhelmed the sacred bodies had been removed, all their little sepulchral structures, although fragile and made of brick, together with the sculptures and angelic images wonderfully fashioned above the tomb of the magnificent Augustine with the majesty of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0016D] That is, of the Holy Trinity or of Christ.], appeared unharmed, while all proclaimed the miracles of God [Col. 0016B].

## Chapter IV

Meanwhile the southern wall remained, on the side where the gracious Augustine and the holy Deusdedit rested. At last, after being loosened by many blows of the battering ram, when it was believed that with a certain inclination it would crush the saints, it was immediately hurled out with immeasurable force from God, as though into a leap, and fell in its entirety southward, with its solid structure intact, contrary to those who were driving it.

As vast and high as it had been, so much space did it occupy as it lay fallen. The attackers would scarcely have escaped unharmed had heavenly mercy not spared them for the merits of the saints.

Then all raised a loud cry of praise at so evident a sign. For the one who had preserved his beloved saints when they were buried above now forbade that they be buried here.

Thus the wondrous maker of saints often protected some in the midst of fires and drove the fires away from others; he carried these across the depths of the sea with dry feet and caused others to run upon the waves.

## Chapter V. Left in the open air

Those heavenly remains then lay for nine weeks under the open sky, as though they were ordinary corpses exposed to view, and were open to every assault of weather and filth.

Alas, how the indignity of earthly neglect concealed the dignity of those whom we believe angels, their fellow citizens, had frequently guarded. Nevertheless, the devotion of the brothers did what it could to prepare special protection for Augustine, their own chief.

## Chapter VI. The negligent man is rebuked

They constructed a hut from thin boards [that is, small planks], and one or two men in turn kept watch, according to the narrowness of the place, with lights and sacred songs.

Once, when someone was overcome by heavy sleep, a voice was heard rebuking him: “This place,” it said, “is suited not to sleep but to prayer.” By this correction the brother was made more vigilant in prayer.

## Chapter VII. The ornaments are wonderfully preserved

Next, a candle that had been offered and negligently fixed in a candlestick fell upon the saint’s tomb, solemnly adorned with linen cloths and coverings. There, marking a three-foot trail with its glowing ash—for the guards were absent—it caught fire.

At last someone came upon the scene. The candle was removed, the embers shaken off, and the linen cloths and coverings shone completely untouched. At this miracle all joyfully gave thanks to God.

## Chapter VIII. Bishop Gundulf of Rochester performs the translation

[Col. 0017B]

The appointed day of the sacred translation had now dawned most welcome. The venerable Gundulf, bishop of the church of Rochester, was present; he then exercised authority in place of the deceased archbishop [Note: [Col. 0017D] The see of Canterbury was vacant from the year 1089, when Lanfranc died, until Saint Anselm’s ordination in 1093. Gundulf had been a monk at Bec in Normandy under Abbot Herluin. His Life was published in volume II of *Anglia Sacra*, p. 273.].

He proceeded with the abbot, the Fathers, and the liturgical officials to that Holy of Holies, that sanctuary and propitiatory of the Lord.

He first ordered the tomb of the great Augustine to be opened; no one dared approach it, and fear deterred them all. You would have seen the workmen trembling like criminals before judges and investigators, as though before a thunderbolt.

They had previously seen an outstanding young craftsman of the monastery struck down by sudden death. At the abbot’s command he had first attacked this sacred portico; nor [Col. 0017C] could he, although he had obeyed his superior, escape punishment for his presumptuous service.

But the most confident bishop, after the brothers had first undertaken a three-day fast, armed with faith, prayer, and devotion, himself boldly seized the tool, struck the front of the tomb, and by his example and encouragement animated the others to the work.

## Chapter IX. Sweet fragrance from Saint Augustine’s tomb

First Blitherus, the foremost master of the craftsmen and the distinguished director of the church, after requesting the bishop’s blessing, approached trembling, in tears, and prostrate. He cleared away the altar above the head of the great Augustine down to the pavement.

There he encountered a smooth, shining square stone of Parian marble set into the floor. When it had been raised slightly, a fragrant vapor, flowing with the scent of spikenard, burst forth and struck the seeker in the face, answering the man who was knocking that the one being sought was present [Col. 0017D].

The prudent man understood that the one whom he had feared would scarcely be found after deep digging and arduous searching had offered himself freely. Astonished and trembling, he replaced the stone and closed this marvelous incense chamber, wisely recognizing that it was not his duty to proceed farther.

He immediately withdrew, humbly testifying that the sought-for relic was present. Meanwhile the unceasing psalmody did not fall silent.

At once, by order of the abbot, the brothers’ hands removed the stone mentioned above. Then a great breath of exceedingly sweet spices, as though from the breast and mouth of the sleeping Augustine [Col. 0018A], sprang forth and, wafted far around, filled everyone with a sweetness as wondrous as it was previously unknown.

The more this balsamic storehouse was opened, the more abundantly the heavenly fragrance shot forth. Immediately the place was surrounded with curtains, both for the glory of the Father and because of the press of the people, and within, the most eagerly desired treasure was examined by the faithful members of the household.

## Chapter X. The tomb is opened
With the doorway now open, bright lamps are brought in, and behold: the chief founder of the Christianity of England, hidden for so many centuries, so greatly desired, displayed with joy as immense as it was unexpected, is seen after nearly five hundred years. Indeed, through so many storms of war, so great a flood of pagans, the extermination of peoples, and the overthrow of cities and churches, by God’s remarkable protection the Augustinian vestibule [Col. 0018B], like Noah’s ark, always remained unharmed. Thus, where and as he had originally been buried with his blessed companions from the day of his death, in that same place and in the same manner he was found entirely undisturbed. The form and size of the body, the pious character and condition of its ancient clothing, and the arrangements of its first burial were visible. He was seen with chasuble, alb, stole, staff, sandals, and the other pontifical instruments, so that he might have been thought still to possess bodily integrity, unless touch had proved his mortal condition—which nevertheless serves to increase immortal glory.

Therefore, at the wish of all, suitable brothers entered with the utmost trembling and reverence into that cave, the treasury of an inestimable treasure, with prayer and Davidic praise. [Col. 0018C] They gathered into linen-lined and gold- and gem-covered reliquaries those pledges, duly arranged in bodily composition and harmony. One of them also asserts with truthful firmness that among that pigment-like dust he actually touched with his hand solid flesh of one who had been buried five hundred years, and reverently cherished it. Hence this sacred earth is rightly judged to have endured for a long time in incorruption, under the guardianship of heavenly grace.

**CHAPTER XI. A great solemnity is held. The body of Saint Augustine is transferred.**

Meanwhile, after the bishop had proclaimed a festival to be celebrated with supreme and every kind of splendid joy, the whole monastery was adorned as though with Paschal dignity. At once the distant crowd smelled from afar the fragrance of so great a novelty; the entire city streamed together, [Col. 0018D] Kent overflowed, and swarms of people hastened from every direction. They rejoiced immeasurably in their Augustine, now restored, as it were, from death, etc.

He was therefore carried out with every ornament, in a procession and with the rejoicing of ecclesiastical celebration, amid the harmony of voices and cymbals, amid the shared congratulations of those above and below; and with this high-sounding glory he was placed before the authentic altar of the chief apostles, like a heavenly deposit, until he could be laid in a suitably prepared bier. So many gifts of Christ’s grace were poured out upon the people from the sweetness of so great a Father that, like incense, they seemed everywhere to drip with tears [Col. 0019A] of joy, through which that day of the Father’s presence might have shone forth as an occasion of immeasurable worth.

**CHAPTER XII. The sick are healed.**

Meanwhile that place of his former rest, that little bed of his long sleep, was not without the work of salvation: it grew warm from the reclining of its great inhabitant, exuded healing balsams, and by its fragrance cured the sick. The ill, the weak, the infirm, and the crippled came in the evening and returned healthy in the morning, etc.

**CHAPTER XIII. Enemies are reconciled.**

The miracles of bodily healings then wrought through Augustine’s protection were great, but greater still were the healings of hearts. We saw irreconcilable enemies come together here, and they were reconciled in the presence of the saint, etc.

At so new and splendid a festival the bishop celebrated Mass while the white-robed choir rejoiced together; and after the Gospel [Col. 0019B] he delivered a sermon to the people concerning the triumph of so great a patron. He faithfully proclaimed the mystery of so great a light, together with the hope of his blessed resurrection, vision, and perpetual dwelling with them. Finally, in the place and with the authority of that first bishop and founder of theirs, he gave the whole assembled people absolution from sins, remission to the penitent, and his blessing, and confirmed everlasting peace in Christ.

**CHAPTER XIV. The angels rejoice with them.**

The heavenly ranks also seemed to rejoice with these solemnities. This celebrated translation took place on a Saturday, followed on the third day by the Nativity of the holy Mother of God. On that Saturday and the following Sunday night, Augustine, ever-watchful guardian of his people, awaited the preparations for his resting place before the apostolic altar together with those who kept vigil, singing psalms. [Col. 0019C]

There was then a priest, a well-known citizen of Kent, of proven faith and truthfulness, who happened at that time to be staying at Winchester (Wincester). On that Sunday night, near dawn, he was preparing to return home. But behold: amid sleepiness or ecstasy—as he attests under oath—he saw from a distance the heavens opened above the Augustinian church, and a ladder radiant with fiery brilliance extending from the very heavenly gate to the top of that church, where the Lord’s saint was reclining, like a balanced column. He saw a choir of angels, dressed in the whitest and most splendid garments, descending along it to the very apostolic hall.

The entire monastery, moreover, was enveloped like an immense globe by so great a ray of flame-emitting brightness at the lower end of the ladder that, his gaze being struck by the reflected light, he was unable to discern what was happening within or around those places, etc. [Col. 0019D]

**CHAPTER XV. The offerings of the peoples.**

Then, after those recent Saturday festivities, when Sunday shone upon them, another glory of celebration followed for Augustine. With the whole company again dressed in white and purple, amid the rushing stream of the peoples and the high-sounding rejoicing of praise, he was solemnly placed in the adorned shrine. There he now keeps watch in his golden little shrine, as a vigilant observer from the front and face of the church and as guardian of the house, the city, and all his England. He is duly venerated by all and worshiped as the intercessor of all. [Col. 0020A]

Who, indeed, has ever seen so great an offering in gold, silver, wax, candles, and the other little gifts of the faithful? The unfamiliar abundance was a marvel to everyone. The altars could not contain it, nor could the efforts of those collecting it suffice. Night and day the crowd of offerers did not rest, etc.

**CHAPTER XVI. The other saints are also transferred.**

They then wished to transfer his blessed companions as well, so that the celebration of one day might unite the members of the same company in a single spirit. But both on that day and on the following day—which, as has been stated, was the Nativity of the Mother of the Most High, the Word-Bearer—they devoted their hands to arranging Augustine alone, and, because of the continual gathering of crowds, they were wholly unable to complete the work.

Only on the third day, that is, Tuesday, did they scarcely finish the small shrine and covering of the reclining leader. Finally, on the fourth day, Wednesday, as though their arms had been freed for action, they approached his most blessed companions and successors, Laurence and Mellitus, in order to carry them to the same prince.

Laurence came first with the leader Augustine. With him he was the first to break the line of the devil, and he was the first archbishop ordained by Augustine while he was still alive, just as Saint Clement once succeeded the living Peter. Mellitus, most select, was sent after Augustine by the most excellent Gregory as an auxiliary, vigorously serving as Christ’s reserve force in the campaign.

It would be pleasant to relate of blessed Laurence how he raised a dead man, ran on foot across the waves of the sea, and, having called down fire from heaven by the power of Elijah, burned the impious; how he brought forth a spring in arid places and poured it into an everlasting stream; and by what punishment every approach of women is barred from the church built and consecrated for his apostolate in Scotland. Thus, recently, when the renowned queen of Scotland, Margaret [Note: [Col. 0019D] the wife of Malcolm, who shone so greatly in piety that she deserved a place among the saints. She died in the year 1097, on 10 June.], dared to attempt entry with offerings, she was suddenly struck and repelled, but was restored through the prayer of the clerics. But, excluded by the narrowness of this place, I pass over these matters, to be unfolded elsewhere if God grants the opportunity.

The most approved holiness of the exceedingly sweet Mellitus, third archbishop after the first Augustine, is recorded in the history of the most faithful Bede. When the city of Dorobernia was burning, he saved it by opposing himself to the flames; he drove the fire backward with a storm and violent whirlwind, and from his face the winds and fires fell away and perished more quickly than their terror. [Col. 0020D]

Of this first bishop and illuminator of London it is also read, as a merited account, how on the Sunday night when he was to dedicate the famous church of Westminster in honor of the Prince of the Apostles, he himself, the key-bearer, anticipated the lofty work; carried across the River Thames (la Tamise) by a fisherman, he performed the entire office and solemnity of the dedication according to ecclesiastical order. This was evident through clear signs, and, as a token of the event, he sent the bishop a splendid fish as a gift.

**CHAPTER XVII. The order in which the holy bodies were arranged.**

It is also pious for posterity to hear what it is no longer possible to see: the arrangement in which the saints formerly rested here. Augustine first occupied the southern side of his portico and touched the eastern wall with his sacred remains. On his left, his first successor and companion, Laurence, extended himself, as stated above, at a similar distance, removed only by the amount of space occupied by the altar of his most blessed founder Gregory, which extended between them and touched each on either side.

The remaining northern portion of the width received Saint Adrian on the left of the gracious Laurence. The virgin of Christ, Mildrith, the unique jewel among the fathers, stood opposite Augustine from the northern wall toward the south, in harmonious alignment; we have spoken above of those who were transferred. At her head stood the altar of blessed Augustine; over the sacred head of Laurence, Mellitus, as his nearest successor, was positioned in the extended area of the church. [Col. 0021B]

Mellitus placed the righteous Justus at his head according to the order of succession. At Justus’s right was blessed Honorius, Justus’s successor; and to the right of Honorius, Saint Deusdedit, given by God, was placed according to the order of his succession. He earned the bed at the head of the supreme Augustine along that same southern wall; only the central doorway, through which one entered, separated them. Yet all those mausoleums of God’s angels were so arranged that there was a passage between each one.

**CHAPTER XVIII. The tomb of an unknown saint. He is called Deonotus.**

When, therefore, the body of blessed Laurence was being brought out, and it was judged necessary first to remove the pavement that lay before Gregory’s altar, between it and the distinguished Augustine, so that a more convenient exit might be prepared for the saint by breaking through the tomb from the side, something marvelous to relate occurred: the hardness of the bricks mocked all the tools and devices. Indeed, this exceptionally solid structure revealed a treasure hidden from our age.

But since labor conquers all things—or rather, faith that persists in God—they dug beneath and drove in an iron bar of the greatest strength at the front edge. At last the rebellious resistance yielded to repeated blows; yet the extremely secure fabric of the little bricks did not come apart. But, marvelous to behold, an intact grating was lifted up for the width of a broad doorway, as though it were a wooden floor fastened with nails.

As the grating, torn out with the pavement thus scraped away, was raised, the little sepulchral crypt that lay concealed before or beneath the altar itself was likewise breached when its stone was removed. Thus, once a small opening had been made, an immense vapor of unprecedented sweetness immediately boiled forth. It struck not only those standing nearby in the face like a violent blast, but also permeated the entire cloister of the monastery and the brothers living there with a new power of aromas. [Col. 0021D]

At this unexpected miracle those present said, “Who is this?” Those absent said, “What is this?” Thus he, unknown to all in person and in name, became known to everyone, present and absent alike, through the grace of his merits. For he had been so completely erased from the memory of our entire age that no one suspected anything more than earth lay beneath that level pavement.

Thanks be to God, giver of all good things! In place of the known patron Laurence whom we were seeking, we have found an unknown companion; and our joy increases twofold while we possess both. Yet here our unworthiness wastes away in a single sorrow: although we know what it is that we possess, we do not know who he is, except that we suppose him to have been one of the closest companions of Father Augustine, since he deserved to be buried in such a place.

Because we had lost his ancient name, we faithfully bestowed upon him a new and familiar one, so that until the day of his revelation he might be called Saint Deonotus by us. Accordingly, beneath Gregory’s altar, the sacred earth of his burial lay contiguous with the eastern wall, extending as had that of Augustine and Laurence. Like the son between twin fathers, he stood equally in the middle, as though sheltered by the wings of both.

When that storehouse of aromas had been opened, it increasingly refreshed the eager crowds with divine fragrance. One person therefore applied some of the dust he had snatched to his nostrils and judged it to possess the delight of paradise. And, more astonishing still, when he immediately replaced the dust, his hand continued to smell of it for a long time.

Because on that day they could not proceed on account of the crowd’s pressure, they transferred the most sacred earth of Deonotus, enclosed in a leaden case, to the new church in the morning—that is, on Thursday—and suitably placed it behind the new altar of the new portico of the much-mentioned Pope Gregory.

We have among the monastery’s elders a man of such well-known probity that it would be unjust not to believe his testimony. He declares that on the following night, in sleep, he saw with extraordinary clarity what seemed to be the face and form of this saint, appropriate to his tall stature and monastic appearance. The figure addressed him [Col. 0022C] as follows:

“I give friendly thanks and invoke everlasting reward,” he said, “upon your brotherly devotion, for the care and labor you displayed yesterday in transferring and arranging my body. But in truth I am not the one you thought me to be.”

For the brothers had been discussing among themselves whether he was that Rufinian whom blessed Pope Gregory had once sent, together with the blessed Mellitus and Justus, to assist the most sacred Augustine in preaching the Gospel, or someone from that holy company.

“You do not know,” he said, “who I am, nor will you know yet; but later you will know, according to the command of heavenly providence.”

**CHAPTER XIX. Saints Laurence and Mellitus are transferred. A soldier is healed.**

Since this event anticipated—or, as I may more pleasantly say, displaced—the translation of the former Laurence [Col. 0022D] and Mellitus, let us return to them in our account. Their tombs were opened from the side, and they poured out their cinnamon and balsams upon the advancing crowd no less than we have described above.

Laurence, now prepared, awaited his worthy companion Mellitus. After both had been arranged in suitably adorned coffers, the first was carried out and the other followed. As the white-robed assembly proceeded, the Lord was glorified in a loud hymn amid his saints.

Laurence had already entered the doorway of the new church, while Mellitus was still outside. There a pious and memorable miracle of God stirred the people toward good understanding. A certain soldier was present whose right eye had been so completely possessed by a carbuncle—a disease which the French, by antiphrasis, call *Bonum-malannum* (“good evil”)—that he was in danger not only of his sight but of his life. The eyeball itself, the eyebrows, and the space around the nose had extended beyond their proper dimensions from the swelling; his entire face bulged greatly.

He pressed forward, pushed, and panted, striving to reach his one remedy, Augustine. But the crowd, as in the Gospel’s case of the blind man who cried out, obstructed him, and by closing ranks prevented his approach. Yet perseverance, as usual, prevailed; he prevailed as best he could and seized salvation by force.

Thus, pushing and breaking through the dense wedges of people, he extended his raised arm and, leaning above, touched with his fingertips the end of the pole by which the bier of blessed Mellitus was being carried. He rubbed that touch into his diseased eye as though it were an eye-salve, a plaster, or the finest ointment, and at the same time cried out, “O Saint Augustine, help me!” [Col. 0023B]

O power of God! O grace of the saints! O confidence of the man! When the tyranny of that disease, irritated by some injury, threatened destruction even more fiercely, immediately at the sacred touch it burst like an enchanted serpent; the poisonous discharge flowed away, sight and face returned from their swelling, and sudden health and light drove away all pain and darkness, etc.

**CHAPTER XX. A blind woman receives sight.**

Meanwhile, after the saints had been placed before the altar of the bishop Augustine, a most celebrated Mass was celebrated for them, as was fitting for the holy priests of the Lord. During it, a sermon was delivered to the people in which their illustrious merits were expounded.

As a result, an old woman who was present, long deprived of worldly light, was illuminated by faith. While she faithfully called upon the most merciful fathers, her eyes were immediately opened, and she clearly received the light of day, etc.

After the Masses, worthy fellow bishops were placed beside Augustine: Laurence, the first, on his right; Mellitus, the second, on his left.

**CHAPTER XXI. The remaining saints are transferred: Deusdedit, Justus, Honorius, and Nothelm.**

After these had been arranged on Thursday, Friday was allotted for bringing the remaining saints, Justus, Honorius, and Deusdedit [Note: [Col. 0023D] Justus is commemorated on 10 November, Honorius on 30 September, and Deusdedit on 15 July.].

But divine providence evidently intended Saturday for these matters. It was already the eighth day of Augustine’s translation, so that the grace of these saints might be renewed more fully, and that the festive day might be consecrated to all those transferred on their respective days; and so that this one day might unite and solemnize them all together, as one charity.

Accordingly, on Friday they went to the aforementioned saints [Col. 0023D], as though they could be brought away very easily and quickly. They approached the most sacred Deusdedit, who, as noted above, occupied the southern wall behind Augustine.

We shall relate something incredible but true. They spent the entire day and the whole following night, with their strength exhausted, breaking into or opening his mausoleum. Finally, on Saturday morning, with breathless labor, they broke through his little crypt. Then they worked carefully until the first hour on the crypt of blessed Justus and scarcely succeeded in opening it. Finally, the crypt of Saint Honorius, who lay between these two, was pierced at the side and gave the saint an exit.

Therefore, ask the life of the gracious Deusdedit: the remarkable grace of sweet fragrances bursting from his tomb will tell you. Inquire who Justus is: the house of heavenly aromas will explain it to you. The abundant fragrance of his own shrine likewise speaks eloquently of the virtues and merits of Honorius. Thus the single paternal heart and breast of all these patriarchs proclaims their common paternal affection through the privilege of divine nards.

These three radiant candlesticks were therefore transferred before the Supreme Trinity on this eighth day of Augustine. We believe that heavenly benevolence delayed and postponed this event for the purpose that, as we have said, this same day might be consecrated and solemnized more fully in honor of so many hierarchs; that the entire week, completed in festivity, might make the eighth day the first; and that the mystery of resurrection might already operate in these saints, so that after the seven ages of the world, an unending eighth age might be born.

Nor do we separate from them the archbishop of blessed memory and his companion Nothelm, who had earlier been buried among them within Saint Gregory’s altar and was now transferred with them for the second time. Bede, the historian of the English, praises him as the author and source of their history [Note: [Col. 0023D] In the prologue to the *History*. Nothelm is nowhere celebrated as a saint in the martyrologies; Godwin says that he died on 17 October 741.]. The most solemn procession and sonorous praise led these leaders, as it had the earlier ones; and before the altar of their bishop Augustine, festive Mass was celebrated for them until they were enthroned in their own seats.

**CHAPTERS XXII–XXIII**

On this day also, heavenly goodness deigned to favor its saints, illuminated by clear miracles, etc.

**CHAPTER XXIV. The new arrangement of the relics.**

[Col. 0024C]

Now these senators and conscript fathers of ours rest together, arranged as they were at first, as one spirit, one faith, one charity, one religion, and one grace existed among them.

Augustine, the chief steward, occupies the front and principal portico of the church, together with Laurence, his first successor, crowned with honor and placed nearest to him on the left, and the honey-sweet Mellitus, his second successor, set beside him on the right. He gently inclines his principal head toward the adjacent altar of the Holy Trinity.

After Laurence, the most just Justus and Deusdedit, given by God and taken up among the saints, are placed on the left; the most honorable Honorius and the contemplative Theodore (*theorito*) answer them on the right. These are the seven eyes of the Lord, through whom he looks favorably upon us. These are the seven stars in his right hand and the seven golden lampstands shining before him, by which he illuminates his Church sevenfold with the sevenfold grace of his Spirit. [Col. 0024D]

Mildrith, in the northern outer wing, and Adrian, in the southern, hold their own porticos and altars at their heads, like Augustine. Mildrith shines before the altar of the holy Innocents, whom she cherishes all within her virginal embrace; with them she plays the zither and sings a new song to her Bridegroom and the Lamb, following him wherever he goes. Adrian, holding the altar of the Protomartyr Stephen, as well as those of the martyrs Laurence and Vincent, bears witness through a martyr’s life to the fellowship of martyrs. [Col. 0025A]

Likewise, each of those situated in the northern region greets his successor to the south opposite him: Laurence greets Mellitus, Justus greets Honorius, Deusdedit greets Theodore, and Mildrith, beside her temporary bier, greets her father Adrian. All exalt their bishop Augustine.

**CHAPTER XXV. Eulogy of Justus. The letter written by Pope Boniface to Saint Justus.**

Since three of these confessors of the Most High Trinity—Justus, Honorius, and Deusdedit—by their own translation lay claim to first place in this present octave of Augustine, we think it an injustice to pass over their dignity.

Although the Venerable Bede declared fewer of their miracles in his manifold history, their merits as such great men should not therefore be erased from our faith. Was it not enough for the slowness and hardness of our understanding that he described Augustine and these companions of his as imitating the apostolic life and virtues with innumerable signs, and as ready to die for the faith they preached?

Is it a small testimony to holiness, among the other praises, that the most sacred Pope Boniface, the fourth after the principal Gregory [Note: [Col. 0025D] It should be read “the fifth,” for this was Boniface V, who was also the fifth pope after blessed Gregory; and below Honorius is said to have succeeded this Boniface, in the following number. Indeed, this Boniface could not have been Boniface IV, who was third after Gregory and died in 614. Justus was transferred from the see of Rochester to Canterbury in 625, the year in which Boniface V died in October. Honorius, who died in 634, succeeded Justus.], praises blessed Justus in an apostolic letter and attributes the conversion of the nations to his merits and heavenly rewards. This will become clearer and more pleasing from the letter itself, partly noted here:

“To our most beloved brother Justus, Boniface. How devotedly and vigilantly your brotherhood has labored for the Gospel of Christ was indicated not only by the tenor of the letter sent by you, but also by the perfection bestowed from above upon your work,” etc.

The complete letter is found in Bede, Book II of the *History*, chapter 8.

**CHAPTER XXVI. Eulogy of Honorius.**

The apostolic letter of blessed Pope Honorius, successor of the aforementioned Boniface, likewise celebrates as a most powerful champion of Christ, crowned with victory, Honorius, the most holy successor of Justus (in the year 634), fifth after the first Augustine.

How beautifully, and in pleasing harmony with divine grace, this man of the same holiness and the same name encounters that man at the same time, so that the Roman world may have its Honorius and the English world likewise its own. Beautifully, I say, the one sends to the other this gift of love, united by the same name and privilege:

“To our most beloved brother Honorius, Honorius. Among the many gifts of good things which the mercy of our Redeemer deigns to bestow upon his servants, his kindness has also graciously granted this through the munificence of his compassion: whenever, through brotherly affection, he represents unanimous love in a certain contemplation through reciprocal regard,” etc.

Bede gives the complete letter in Book II, chapter 18.

Nor is it a small glory or commendation for him that through Saint Felix [Note: [Col. 0026D] Concerning him, see the Bollandists on 8 March.], whom he himself ordained bishop of the East Angles, he also converted that people to Christ.

We shall insert here a small but great monument of faith concerning his recent revelation. Someone who envied this saint disparaged him, preferring to him a certain bishop of worldly wealth who had built up the Church of God with many riches and ornaments, since there was no evidence that this man had accomplished anything of comparable usefulness in his life.

When a prior, a member of that place, heard this report and took it badly, on the following night a most distinguished person appeared in a vision to a certain elder venerable in age and character. He appeared so clearly that the elder still remembers what figure he could compare him to. Astonished at so impressive and magnificent a person, the figure said:

“Why did that man yesterday wish to tear apart Saint Honorius, the Lord’s bishop, with abusive slander, by exalting another bishop? Why, when this was reported, did the prior not respond from the holy Gospel that, in the judgment of the just Judge, two small coins of a poor woman were worth more than all the golden and abundant gifts of the rich?” [Col. 0026B]

**CHAPTER XXVII. Deusdedit, etc., praised by Bede.**

We also join blessed Deusdedit [Note: [Col. 0026D] He succeeded blessed Honorius in the year 653 and presided over the Church of Canterbury until 664.] to them in comparable holiness. He was worthy to be placed sixth after the apostolate of blessed Augustine and to be buried very near him.

These, then, are all the men of mercy, whose righteousness has not been forgotten. Because the historian mentioned above, Bede, thought it too much to describe the deeds of each individually, he concluded the merits of them all at the end in this way:

“Of all these it can rightly and truthfully be said that their bodies were buried in peace, and that their names live through generations and generations.”

As for the others—that is, the kings, bishops, abbots, and other saints transferred—our account must now pause. They have already been discussed elsewhere, or are to be discussed in their proper time, when, after the temple has been prepared, they receive the bier appointed for them.

**CHAPTER XXVIII. Sweet fragrance from the tomb of Saint Mellitus.**

After this Saturday, when on the following Sunday the coverings that protected the broken and emptied monuments of the saints’ bodies had been stained by rain and mud, their venerable custodian was uncertain whether he should attempt to remove them or allow them to be spoiled in the service of the saints, who could repay it with better things. Again he reflected that their glory would not seek the church’s loss of its ornaments. [Col. 0026D]

At last, approaching timidly with the incense of psalmody, he slightly drew back the pallium from the opening of blessed Mellitus’s little crypt, which had likewise been broken into and emptied. Behold: the heavenly fragrance whose power he had experienced the day before struck him again with the freshness of spring. Struck by the prodigy, he said:

“What is this, Lord God? What is this? From where does this grace breathe? Does the empty tomb, four days later, still exude balsams even in their absence?”

As the elder turned such thoughts over in his astonished heart, he replaced the coverings over the nard-flowing opening, burning to discover more certainly whose grace this was. Immediately the obstructed fragrance vanished like a ray of light shut out. Again he uncovered it; again, when a path had been opened, the released fragrance gave off its scent, etc.

**CHAPTER XXIX. Likewise from the tomb of Saint Augustine.**

On the following Monday, when the space had been opened, construction of the church’s nave proceeded. A broad column was founded in the northern row, at the very place from which the exceedingly rich treasure of Augustine’s body had been taken. The capacious hollow of that tomb or little crypt embraced the sacred bricks in place of the holy pledges.

The bricks of the underlying pavement on which the most blessed earth had lain—red, bright, joined in a level flooring, and smoking with yellow nard—were eagerly scraped up and deposited in the previously mentioned altar of the new portico of blessed Gregory. [Col. 0027B]

Beneath these bricks there was found a layer of exceptionally clean earth, half a foot thick, spread over a foundation that projected from the old wall of Augustine’s portico. This earth, penetrated by the fragrance of Augustine’s bricks, also gave off a marvelous sweetness.

They judged that this earth, excavated down to the stones of the aforesaid foundation, should be distributed and preserved among the sacred tombs of Laurence, Mellitus, and Justus, which had escaped the destruction caused by the church’s construction.

So that our descendants—those who may be the children of love for so great a father—may not grieve that they do not know the location of his ancient monument as described here, let anyone who wishes note this column, which we designated a little earlier, as containing his brick tomb, and let him count and know that it is the third from the column arched toward the eastern tower. What, indeed, would not seem sweet to pious heirs to know about so great a forefather? What would not be grievous about remaining ignorant of his grace?

But concerning those balsam-scented bricks, the aforementioned most faithful elder, who denies that he wishes his possession of this grace to become known, secretly removed one—indeed, I should say, stole one. This is a praiseworthy fault, adorned by faith and justified by charity, because he was providing through this pious sacrilege a remedy for the sick. For the subsequent miracles prove that, by divine inspiration, he had preserved this sacred object.

**CHAPTERS XXX–XXXII. Miracles.**

The province of the East Saxons knew a distinguished Frankish inhabitant whose wife, after a long illness, had already despaired of health and life. At last it was revealed to him in a dream that he should quickly send to Saint Augustine at Canterbury and request that a brick which had lain beneath Augustine’s healing body be washed with water; that she should drink from it and trust in Augustine’s power, because she would receive a remedy of certain health. [Col. 0028A]

This was done. Chapters 2 and following relate other miracles as well.

**CHAPTER XXXIII. Dust and bricks from the tomb of Saint Augustine as relics.**

Many people sought relics from Augustine’s precious body, but no one—such and so pious was the avarice with which the paternal treasure was guarded—could obtain even a single hair from it.

Yet the miracles still compel us to speak of the benefits granted through the brick mentioned above. Its aforementioned guardian, while staying at the monastery of Ramsey [Note: [Col. 0027D] More is found concerning the monastery of Ramsey in the *Life of Saint Oswald*, who was its founder, in the preceding century, under the year 992, p. 727.], was speaking about the powers of that most excellent patron. He also related that the incense-bearing bricks on which the saint had lain were overflowing with the grace of healings.

When the brothers therefore asked him for relics, on the condition that his translation should be commemorated perpetually, he brought with him a suitable brother from that community. He sent him ahead with a sign to the appropriate elder, named Ælfwine, a great friend of this faith at Saint Augustine’s, while he himself awaited his return at Barking, carefully pretending that he knew nothing of any sacred secret about to be taken away.

That man sent back with the aforesaid brother a small portion of dust which he had drawn from Saint Augustine’s sepulchral crypt and two fragments of the bricks on which the saint had slept, so that the brother might divide equally between the churches of Barking [Note: [Col. 0027D] Perhaps “Barking” (*Berkingense*) should be read, since a nunnery of that name existed not far from London in Essex. Certainly below the bearer of the relics is said to have spent the night in the church at Rochester, which lies precisely midway between Canterbury and Barking.] and Ramsey the gifts of both graces.

The bearer of these sacred objects, fearing either that he would be discovered as a thief or that, as a treasurer, he would be plundered, hurried from Saint Augustine’s to Christ’s church [Note: [Col. 0028D] That is, from the suburban monastery of Saint Augustine to the cathedral church dedicated to Christ the Savior. Both churches belonged to Benedictine monks until the time of Henry VIII.]. There he was received with the brothers’ customary kindness and rested with them that night.

His satchel, which guarded the sacred mystery, remained outside with the servants. But the servants, growing insolent and ignorant of the presence or reverence due to such power, were tormented that night by such terror and shuddering as they had never experienced in their lives. They thought they were about to die or pass into madness, though they had no idea at all what caused this fear, where it came from, or what it foretold.

The brother himself also heard a divine voice rebuke him in sleep:

“Why, brother,” it said, “have you exposed the pledge entrusted to you so carelessly?”

Nevertheless, on the following night, when he was staying in the church at Rochester, the satchel containing the sacred treasures was again left with the servants. Once more the former dread struck their brutish minds, untrained in divine matters, and occupied much of the night, leaving them senseless with fear. [Col. 0028D]

On the third day he displayed the Augustinian relics at Barking to an Augustinian monk. The monk received them with great joy and, as night approached, kept them with him.

**CHAPTER XXXIV. The monk’s vision and that of the abbess.**

That very night the keeper of the sacred treasury was visited by great mysteries of visions, etc. When dawn had come, he brought those dusty but miraculous relics into the church and related the entire matter of the vision and the prodigies in order to the abbess, the woman beloved by God, whose gracious sincerity had led the fathers to call her *Chara-gratia* (“Dear Grace”).

While she marveled at his account, she entered into even greater wonder and began to tell, at approximately the same time, the vision that had been revealed to her, etc.

**CHAPTER XXXV.**
Therefore, with the priests and clerics vested, and the sisterhood also festively dressed for the procession, its half of the sacred side and of the perfumed dust was received by the most devout church with melodious praise; the other half was reserved for the other church mentioned above. This treasure was gathered into a splendidly decorated reliquary, carried around the cloister by the priests as a blessing amid rejoicing, while the virginal assembly accompanied it with praises befitting a father. A most solemn Mass was celebrated in blessed Augustine’s memory, angelic song providing the melody, while the virgins’ melody surpassed the bronze organs. They contended in triumph so greatly that it was as though they had held Augustine in bodily form. An Augustinian monk, the most faithful guardian and distributor of his sacred relics, sang the Mass. When the sacred preface had ended with the angelic hymn consecrated to the Most Holy Trinity, a great portent appeared, as astonishing and unfamiliar to our age as it was wonderful.

### CHAPTER XXXVI. Augustine himself appears.

An older sister, who was serving at the altar, while standing there intent upon the psalms and prayers, openly beheld the priest previously described, as he stood assisting at the celebration of the Lord’s sacraments, and so forth. With the same solemnity of procession, music, and vestments, and with the same Masses, the other half of the aforesaid side and dust, which had fallen to the monastery of Ramsey, was received. Thus it was promised and confirmed that the translation of the most worthy father Augustine should be celebrated perpetually at Ramsey just as at Berting.

### CHAPTER XXXVII. The feast of the Translation.

This festive translation of the saints, therefore, always to be commemorated, was most gratefully consecrated in our age on 6 September in the year 1091 of the incarnate Savior, when the younger William was king of England and Wido was abbot, the bearer of this Augustinian feast; Gundulf, the memorable bishop of Rochester, kindly cooperated with him as archbishop. At that same abbot’s wish, the most excellent archbishop Anselm and the other bishops approved that this octave should be observed perpetually as the foremost and most celebrated feast, so that it might be consecrated collectively both to Augustine the leader and to his other companions—the fosterlings and legates of the Roman Church—and to the princes of the English and all their successors. In it the translation of all of them, as mentioned above, is confirmed. The miracles that follow at the end of this book we have omitted.

## BOOK TWO

[Column 0029]

Our first father Augustine, although he was translated later together with those who lay beside him, is placed first in the sequence of the narrative; the other friends of his, translated before him, are reviewed after him. The order is reversed, but necessarily rearranged. Why? Because primacy is owed to the one for whom this solemnity is chiefly prescribed, and because it is better to minister promptly to those who hunger for their father’s banquets, lest, through the long suspension and prolonged winding of the journey, the sickly expectant diner perish before reaching the dining room. Now, therefore, since the agreeable opportunity of the renewed church has produced for us, through the elevation of Augustine and the other chief men, this triumph, it seems fitting to support the same text by recounting the deeds of the earlier fathers who brought it forth, and, with miracles interspersed, to celebrate the grace shown both to them and to our own days. Thus, [the narrative] will make up for the delays caused by gathering flowers from the Elysian meadows, and we shall relate the various translations of the saints who preceded Augustine, already translated, to his shrine.

### CHAPTER I. Almerus, abbot of Saint Augustine’s. Also Elfstan.

First, then, Almerus, abbot of Augustine’s monastery—[Note: Or Elmerus; he succeeded Wulfric in 1006 and became bishop of Sherborne in 1022. William Thorn says of him that, although he is believed to have been piously holy, his feast nevertheless cannot be celebrated without the authority of the Apostolic See.]—as though by a kind of vow and foreknowledge of the future translation, removed the arches and columns solemnly built with Roman elegance above the bodies of the saints, and, as far as he dared, prepared a way for them to rise. From those columns and arches he decorated the cloister of his monastery.

From the abbacy Almerus was remarkably raised, though strongly resisting, to the bishopric of Sherborne; the worthy Elfstan succeeded him and translated the most blessed Mildred to his Augustine. But Almerus himself, by God’s judgment and mercy—God chastising those whom he loves—was struck with blindness. He willingly abandoned the episcopate which he had accepted unwillingly, returned to the fatherly embrace of Augustine, and, living in the infirmary, occupied his leisure with psalmody and prayers.

Nor should the remarkable vision concerning him be omitted. His servant, an honorable man, was lying in the church of Saint Maurice, adjoining the infirmary. One night, as he lay there fully awake, he saw two venerable persons bringing the bishop from the very cell in which he was resting into the basilica of the martyrs of Thebes. There they seated him familiarly between them, and held a long conversation with him, which the observer plainly heard, and so forth.

### CHAPTER II. The Emperor Henry desires relics of Saint Augustine.

The most distinguished abbot Aelstan, traveling to Rome, was magnificently received by the most excellent Emperor Henry for the sake of the famous father Augustine. [Note: This seems to have happened at Rome, or in Italy, where Saint Henry was staying in the very year in which Aelstan became abbot and went to Rome.] When they were solemnly discussing so great a bishop, the emperor exclaimed:

> “If only I might deserve to obtain even the smallest joint, or some hair, or at least the tiniest particle of dust from so great a treasure, at what price in worldly goods I would buy it! What a prize of immeasurable splendor! As much as England rejoices that it has gained, so much would Rome mourn that it had lost him, unless faith led both places to believe that he is present there and beneficial everywhere from the heavenly kingdom.”

As he said this, the most devout prince pressed the venerable abbot insistently to transfer to him that precious glory of the Roman Empire and of the human race, and to bestow upon him something from so sacred a relic. If he obtained it, he would magnificently grant him whatever he wished on earth—in vineyards, gold, and silver; moreover, he himself would surround the reliquary of so great a treasure in imperial fashion with the purest gold and the most precious gems.

But the abbot, although he valued access to the father’s presence—which our age had merited—above all the wealth of the earth, nevertheless did not dare, for any worldly riches, to comply either with his own desire or with the emperor’s. Returning home, after he had energetically governed the advancement of his monastery for four years, while he was growing weak shortly before his death, he had the outstanding ram of his flock, Wulfric—[Note: Wulfric, the second of that name, is said to have succeeded Aelstan in 1047.]—a man distinguished by secular, ecclesiastical, and literary learning, ordained abbot for him at the apostolic altar of Saint Peter, according to the ancient custom of Roman privilege and freedom, first confirmed by apostolic authority.

### CHAPTER III. Concerning Wulfric the abbot.

Wulfric strove to equal all his predecessors in expanding the commonwealth entrusted to him, but in the restoration of his own church he struggled to surpass them all. Yet he feared rashly to undertake an enterprise that others had not presumed to attempt, and to violate without public authority that ancient and primary dwelling of innumerable saints.

Meanwhile, that most splendid and holy radiance of our age, Pope Leo—[Note: Leo IX, who pursued the Simonians at the Council of Reims in 1049, attended by Abbot Wulfric and Duducus from England. The acts of that council, and the history of the dedication of the basilica of the great monastery of Reims in which it was held, may be found in Part I of this *Century*]—was overthrowing the Simoniacal heresy in Gaul, overturning the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves, and driving every commerce of avarice from the temple of the Lord.

Wulfric himself, the vicar of Augustine, prince of the English Churches, was sent to him by King Edward to answer for the ecclesiastical authorities and people of his nation. He was as accustomed and as qualified to be sent to overseas kingdoms and to conduct the highest affairs. Distinguished companions were added to him: Duducus, bishop of Somerset, and Aelfeuvinus, abbot of Ramsey.

At that time the great priest, Leo IX, was dedicating the church of Saint Remigius at Reims and displaying the faithful steward of Christ through miracles. After examining the sacred orders—who had entered through the door and who had climbed up by some other route—the counselor of Christ found the English more innocent than the others, and received the English, especially the Augustinian legate, with greater kindness, in view of the dignity of so great a name.

For earlier, the bishop Hermann of Salisbury, of venerable memory—[Note: At that time Hermann was bishop of Wilton; but since he transferred his see to Salisbury in 1078, our author names him from his later see.]—to whom we who lay beside the relics were attached, had argued clearly before the most blessed Leo in the broad senate of bishops at Rome—[Note: Apparently at the Roman council of 1049, shortly before Leo came to Gaul to dedicate the Remigian basilica]—about the English people’s hospitality, beyond excuse toward all kinds of people, whether foreigners or citizens; about England itself, everywhere filled with churches, with new ones added daily in new places; about the innumerable distribution of ornaments and images throughout the oratories; and about the exceedingly generous gifts of kings and rich men for Christ’s inheritance.

Leo, the supreme friend of the Lord, rejoiced so greatly that he raised his hands and gave thanks to God. The bishop mentioned above also proceeded to explain the nobility of the English hierarchy: namely, that the archbishop of Canterbury, by apostolic authority, ought to sit at Rome beside the bishop of Saint Rufina—[Note: He was one of the seven cardinal bishops; his see was united with the bishopric of Porto]—while the Augustinian abbot ought to sit beside the abbot of the fortress of Monte Cassino.
