The matter was sought in the decrees and found there, and was strengthened by the assent of the pope and everyone present.

Because of these favors, the same most blessed pope treated the English more familiarly. He became especially devoted to Wulfric on account of Saint Augustine and Wulfric’s own excellence. He listened most lovingly as Wulfric recalled everything concerning that saint and his worthy companions; he most gladly approved and blessed Wulfric’s proposal to restore his monastery.

Thus Nathan favored King David’s desire to build the temple. But since both were prophets, each nevertheless erred here, as a human being, against God’s plan; and no one can accomplish anything unless and until God has decreed it.

The desirous abbot failed to consider this. Striving in vain to undertake a work not granted to him, after completing his embassy he demolished his church from the front. He transferred the most blessed virgin Mildred, buried before the principal altar, into the portico of Father Augustine and placed her opposite Saint Augustine beside the northern wall. He also demolished the western part of the oratory of the holy Mother of God, together with the porticoes surrounding it. After clearing the space between the two churches and the adjoining cemetery of the brothers, he appropriated the entire area for construction, raised walls, and assembled columns and arches.

Kent rejoiced in the new work, although the incompetence of the craftsmen had produced something unsuitable for monastic habitation.

### CHAPTER IV. Wulfric is punished for demolishing the church of Saint Mary.

But the Queen of Heaven was offended by the injury done to her temple. This was her shrine; this, according to the English inscription, was her wardrobe; this was the bosom and lap of many saints. Here, as will become clear in what follows, the choir of angels was heard; here the organs of virgins; here the power of miracles was continually present.

This Lady of all things deigned to appear in a vision to a certain old woman:

> “Go,” she said, “and tell Abbot Wulfric that he will be punished with death for destroying my oratory.”

The woman was warned once, again, and a third time. At last, because she feared him, she communicated the heavenly commands to him through the abbot’s very devout sister. He feared the majesty of so great a Lady, but refused to believe the message, treating it as an old woman’s tale because of the messenger’s lowly status. He held to his intended course and neglected to make satisfaction for the heavenly complaint.

For human impulse often rushes on irrevocably, in accordance with what Naso says:

> Every impulse has difficult approaches.

Thus the guilty man fell under the divine sentence. He was struck by the deadly arrow of illness around the Lord’s Supper. Nevertheless, every day—and on the Lord’s Supper itself, on Good Friday, on Holy Saturday, on Easter Day, and also on the second and third days of the week—he completed the greater Masses in the congregation, stronger than both the illness and himself. On the following night, however, he died suddenly before the brothers could arrive, and turned his feast days into mourning for them. His work, frustrated after innumerable expenses and labors, he left to others to demolish. Yet no one should judge that so great a man was deprived of God’s mercy after the divine vengeance, or emptied of the fruit of his good will. The lion punished the prophet’s disobedience, but, as though the dead body had already been purified and justified, he did not dare eat it or harm its little donkey.

### CHAPTER V. Egelsinus the abbot is granted a privilege.

[Column 0033D]

After him, Lord Egelsinus was raised to the office of head of the monastery and consecrated in the king’s palace. He went to Rome, where Pope Alexander granted him a mitre and priestly sandals and ordered him to use them in the manner of a bishop.

> “We decree,” he said, “that the Augustinian rector shall perpetually possess this distinction, on account of the dignity of Augustine himself, the fosterling of the Romans and the apostle of the English.”

Egelsinus therefore brought this prerogative home and held it during his rule over Augustine’s monastery. But when he exchanged the abbacy for another office, he left to his Augustinian successor those rights that he had claimed elsewhere.

### CHAPTER VI. Concerning Scotland the abbot.

Meanwhile William, duke of the Normans, by God’s providence for the instruction of his people, became king of the English. [Note: In 1066 William seized England. When Egelsinus, abbot of Augustine’s monastery, incurred the king’s displeasure and failed to appear, Scotland, a Norman, was appointed in his place.]

The house of Augustine received Lord Scotland, a good and exceptionally learned man, as a suitable Father. Like his predecessors, he was ordained in his own monastery. When he extended his ambition generously toward lengthening the building of his church, he was grievously troubled by the obstructive extension of the work already undertaken; he was also troubled by the narrowness of the space allotted to the structure. He feared the judgment of the Mother of God concerning his church, which had been torn down; he feared the danger of collapse in the old monastery, consumed by prolonged decay.

In these anxieties he was carried to Rome on a royal embassy to Pope Alexander. There, after delivering the king’s replies, he received from the pope counsel and a blessing concerning the translation of the saints and, according to his wishes and the will of heavenly generosity, the destruction and rebuilding of his basilica.

Then the reverend apostolic carefully investigated that same outer church, which rose nearest to the walls of the city, asking in which part of the church the eminent Augustine and his most worthy companions rested, in what order, and whether in adjoining or separate porticoes. The distinguished abbot satisfied all his wishes. The pope said:

> “This is the city’s most preeminent citadel and the most splendid royal palace of the entire kingdom, where that leader of the propagation of the churches, the prince of the company of the blessed—the prince, that is, of princes—and Augustine, the saint of saints in his apostleship, placed his bed and his triumph, raised up toward the heavens. How splendid a house of so many and such great stars of heaven! How venerable a court for the entire English people! How blessed a homeland, illuminated by the rays of its patron saints!”

### CHAPTER VII. He reluctantly demolishes the oratory of Blessed Mary, in which holy abbots and kings were buried.

Then the faithful abbot, astonished at the testimony of so great a man and giving thanks, hurried home and overturned the massive beginning of the new work. But the remaining part of the virginal oratory of the exalted Mary delayed his assault; it likewise delays the progress of our subsequent narrative.

The heavenly praises of this shrine came before him, as did the miracles of the saints lying in its lap. Here the exalted Mother of the Most High was often seen, and here she was heard with the sweet choir of virgins, in the ineffable delight of heavenly harmony. It is known that Saint Dunstan, the angel of the Lord of hosts and, after Augustine and his companions, the brightest glory of the English, was present at this most pure fellowship more familiarly and more frequently. [Note: His life is given in the preceding *Century* under the year 988.] Like a thirsty stag at the springs of water, he was inexhaustibly constant in this paradise of the saints, captivated by the sweetness of the heavenly music.

So that our own times might not lack an experience confirming this faith, Scotland himself, guardian of the Lord’s flock, was awakened from sleep one night before the nocturnal vigils. As he lay in a cell adjoining the church, a choir of singers was heard alternately, wondrously sweet in tone, like the most pleasing harmony of men and boys producing an octave: sometimes they sang together in joined melodies, and sometimes the little boys answered the men with distinct musical parts.

He remained transfixed by the unfamiliar melody. Yet, not recognizing that the songs were heavenly, he thought that the brothers, having completed the matutinal offices, had held a procession in that church, as they used to do at that time, day and night. He asked his awakened companions whether they had heard the signals for Matins; all denied it. He asked whether they heard the songs he heard; all, both monks and laymen, firmly asserted that they clearly heard them.

He sent the most faithful brother, named Sinvold, to investigate the truth of the matter. Sinvold went and found the doors locked; he saw no one there and heard no sound any longer. Returning, he went around all the brothers’ beds and found them all asleep.

When he reported this to the Father, Scotland reclined on his bed and slept lightly. At once the vocal signal for Matins rang out. Then, astonished, he understood without hesitation that the Olympic hosts had truly gathered in that place in the hearing of everyone who had listened, and that the miracles related earlier had been made most clearly certain to him by experience. He understood that the heavenly citizens truly inhabited those dwellings.

For this place was especially illumined by the most powerful relic of the beloved Father of God and of all ages, and our best teacher after the supreme Augustine, Adrian. [Note: He was sent to England by Pope Vitalian together with Archbishop Theodore. Concerning them, see the Second *Century*, under the year 690, from Bede and elsewhere. He is commemorated on 9 January.] It was also illumined by the venerable bodies of Saint Albinus, his disciple and successor—[Note: He was the first Englishman to preside over the Augustinian monastery, toward the end of the eighth century. He was the source for Bede’s writing of his history. He is nowhere commemorated among the saints, nor is John the abbot, mentioned below, who was the second abbot of the same monastery. He is said to have died in 618]—and of blessed John, an earlier abbot.

In addition, many holy bishops and numerous abbots, as well as four kings with their royal wives and children and a long genealogy of grandchildren, illuminated and ennobled the Lord’s court by their repose.

### CHAPTER VIII. Concerning Edbald.

The first of these kings is known to have been Edbald, son of Aedelbert, the third king of the English but the first worshiper of Christ. Emerging from the error of idolatry as though from Acheron, he fled into the embrace of Christ through the blessed archbishop Laurence, after the Apostle Peter had beaten the shepherd on account of the lost sheep. As an imitator of his father’s piety, he founded and dedicated this church to the exalted Mother of God. There he rested until now, inheriting what he had made and possessing what he had given, together with the righteous whom he had received in the name of Justus.

He devoutly arranged for the church to be incorporated, with its abbot and monastic order, into the Augustinian monastery. He endowed it most abundantly with royal ornaments and wealth, lands, and the necessities of life, and added to it the royal estate called Northbourne. Moreover, he showed himself a devoted helper and fellow worker of the blessed Fathers in spreading the Christian faith.

### CHAPTER IX. Concerning Lotharius.

The second was Lotharius, grandson of King Edbald, son of King Erconbert, and uncle of the God-beloved virgin Mildred. His most holy mother, Queen Sexburga, first founded a monastery of the Mother of God on the island of Sheppey and established there a choir of nuns. There, exchanging the royal diadem for the sacred veil, she joined herself to the handmaids of Christ, with the support of her son, who royally added lands and riches sufficient for the place.

Later she succeeded her precious virgin sister Etheldreda in the governance of the monastery of Ely. [Note: The Life of Etheldreda, written by Thomas, a monk of Ely, is found in the Second *Century* of the Benedictines under the year 679, p. 738. It contains further information about Sexburga and Mildred, mentioned here, as well as about the monastery of Ely.]

After reigning for twelve years following his brother Ecgberht, founder of the monastery of Reculver, Lotharius was attacked in battle by his nephew Eadric, son of his brother Egbert, among the South Saxons. Wounded there, he died while being treated. After Eadric was removed following a year and a half of rule, foreign and uncertain kings dominated for some time. [Note: Ceadwalla, king of Wessex, and Wulf, his brother, called Mul by some.] One of them, named Mul, was buried here, third in order among those mentioned above.

### CHAPTER X. Concerning Withred.

The fourth was the legitimate king Withred, the other son of the earlier King Ecgberht. Powerful in virtue and religion, he rescued his father’s kingdom from foreign tyrants. At the command of blessed Martin, who appeared to him in a vision, he was the first to establish a monastery at Dover in Martin’s honor, and he enriched the servants of God there perpetually with royal gifts.

Among other gifts, he granted to Augustine’s church of Mary and to its most blessed inhabitant Adrian, as a gift worthy of a prince, the royal residence called Listleburna, forever. Thus, in that house, he inherited rest, having increased it by his wealth.

### CHAPTER XI. Saint Adrian is translated.

Since so many saints, together with exalted persons, had to be translated before the church itself was demolished, the illustrious abbot first approached reverently to overturn the altar and tomb of Father Adrian, after appeasing the exalted Mother of the supreme King through his own fasts, prayers, and tears and those of the devout brothers.

The working area was leveled, and the saint’s burial stone was cleaned with the greatest care. The treasure to be taken up, as though already lifted into hand, was postponed until night, lest an inexperienced hope should somehow be harmed.

At night they returned with lights prepared to carry away the joy of their light. They removed the burial stone and, with the saint’s body prosperously rising like a wall from its foundation, found it. At once night of grief seized their confused hearts, and a chill trembling ran through their very bones, as everyone thought that they had been deprived of the presence of so great a Father.

But, at the abbot’s command, the stone obstruction was overturned. As they dug deeper, a small crypt appeared on the left. When it was pierced, Saint Albinus was revealed, heavenly fragrance bursting forth as a messenger. On the right they saw a huge sarcophagus of white marble, and at once their spirits and joy returned at the discovery of the Adrian they had so greatly desired.

As they dug around it and struggled in vain to remove the lid, they saw a stone placed over the sarcophagus at the feet. When this was removed, the witness and herald of their longed-for desire suddenly sprang forth, breathing the fragrance of the Lord’s paradise.

But they were again tested with sadness amid their greater joy when a certain brother, looking timidly inside, cried out that the tomb was empty. The more attentive observation of the others replied that it was instead truly full, filled with the true substance of the saint’s body. It looked so beautiful that they thought he still lay there with his flesh intact, just as he had originally been placed.

At last the leader of the flock himself looked in and saw it. Immediately, with great exultation, he cried:

> “Glory to you, Christ!”

“Truly,” he said, “this is the most precious pearl of blessed Adrian’s body, to be raised again in the splendors of the saints.”

At this, one of the brothers, named David, a Briton by birth, rashly extended his finger toward the holy body, curious to test whether it was still solid. He experienced the power of the one whose condition he had dared to test. His finger was pierced as though by a needle, or struck by a burning iron or poisonous serpent; not only the finger but the whole hand swelled with intolerable pain.

When the abbot asked him, as he cried out in anguish, what had happened, he showed the punishment of his presumptuous hand, swollen with inflammation. The Father replied that this had rightly happened to one so rash. The man then dragged out the rest of the night with sleepless lamentation.

The head of the monastery was consequently tormented by a twofold burden of cares. It was neither safe to touch the holy body nor did it seem possible to carry it out with so great a weight of stone. The presumptuous man had deterred even those for whom touching the saint would have been beneficial.

He therefore set guards over the treasure until daybreak: brothers praying inside, vigilant soldiers outside. He immediately ordered the entire monastery to shine with hangings, cloaks, purple, gold, and every kind of ornament, in Paschal splendor.

At that time Odo, bishop of Bayeux, the king’s brother and, in the king’s absence, governor of England, was at Canterbury. The abbot summoned him at dawn. Odo heard and saw the saint’s power. When consulted, he urged the abbot not to remove Adrian from his ancient resting place, but to carry out the sarcophagus with him, just as he had first been placed there by the holy attendants.

The prudent listener followed this counsel. When everything had been prepared, a white-robed and purple-clad company of brothers, together with the people rushing forward in eager competition, proceeded in splendid array to that holy-of-holies sanctuary.

The entire desirable Adrian, with his stone mass beautifully adorned, was lifted by the strongest beams. He was carried out amid sweet musical instruments of praise striking the stars, and placed in the portico of the most desired Father Augustine as his most welcome companion. There, among his most blessed companions and beside his first successor, the most holy archbishop Laurence, he was buried with a holiness worthy of him.

Great rejoicing arose among both the French—that is, the Normans—and the English. Everyone eagerly pressed forward to approach and look; tears ran from joy.

The saint added a dance of mercy to the miracle, having terrified them earlier with the miracle of punishment. When the Mass celebrating his glory had been completed with the greatest splendor and purity, the aforesaid tempter came running in misery with his swollen hand. With mournful repentance, and through the intercession of the brothers standing by, he offered a candle whose measure encircled Adrian’s tomb.

O power of the most merciful Father! Immediately all pain vanished, the hand subsided, and health and joy returned more pleasingly after the anguish.

Having thus experienced the saint’s twofold power, severe and serene, the man asked for something from these life-giving relics. He swore over the holy relics that, if he obtained even the smallest fragment, which he could carry to his monastery of Saint Savior at Redon in Brittany, he would arrange for the saint’s feast to be celebrated annually in copes, as the monastic custom calls it.

When the abbot’s kindness agreed and he ordered a small fragment to be taken and handed to him, the man recoiled from what was offered with such trembling that he could not be persuaded by any means to receive it. You would have seen [Column 0038C] a man terrified by a blazing torch aimed at him, fearing that his right hand would be struck more severely if he dared touch it.

When the giver asked why he so fearfully rejected what he had so eagerly begged for, he replied:

> “The promise of the whole world would not now impose this upon me.”

Thus, when the petitioner had been deterred, the sacred gift was returned to its reliquary, the saint evidently deigning to preserve it intact in the chosen place.

[Note: The monastery of Saint Savior at Redon in Brittany Minor, commonly called Rhedon, is still famous today under the Congregation of Saint Maur.]

### CHAPTER XII. A girl is healed.

When the repository of the fragrant body had been closed, a girl came from the suburb. For many years she had been worn down by an incurable intestinal disorder. After praying, she asked the brothers for a remedy for her illness.

They washed the hand of the brother who had touched the saint’s fragment and gave the sick girl the washing to drink.

O faith powerful for everything! O confessor of Christ, powerful for everything on behalf of those who believe in Christ! The touch of the holy body, just as it harmed the presumptuous man, so, through a dutiful act, brought benefit to others. As soon as the sick woman had tasted the washing of that touch, she immediately received complete health.

### CHAPTER XIII. Other bodies are translated.

Thus, after the most excellent Adrian had been translated and glorified, and after the aforesaid solemn Masses, while during those same Masses all the others who were to be translated were lifted from their crypts and prepared for removal, the steward of the household of the Lord returned with a most pure procession. Carrying the relics of the bishops, abbots, and other saints, amid the loud reverberation of voices and cymbals, he arranged them all in the western tower of the monastery before the altar of the holy Mother of God, until the new church should be rebuilt and they could be reburied with new honor.

The four kings mentioned above were not absent from this translation, having been carried there with their wives and descendants.

### CHAPTER XIV. The altar of Blessed Mary is demolished; unknown relics are found there.

Then the principal altar of the virginal church was demolished. There too the work was extended, and our subsequent narrative is likewise prolonged.

There appeared sacred relics of saints, suffused with ivory whiteness and redness and fragrant with every sweetness. They had once been placed there most suitably by the most holy archbishop Mellitus, when he consecrated this altar together with the church. Their names and identifying marks had been written on little sheets and separately placed in a stone hollowed in the form of a cross. These were found to have been consumed by flames at some time.

We grieve that the knowledge of these saints, and of so many others, has been erased from the earth, since this loss reproves our negligence: we do not rise either to praise worthily those whom we know or to reread the deeds of so many people, and so forth.

### CHAPTER XV. The body of a little child.

After the relics mentioned above had been taken up, other treasures and other pearls were encountered before the very altar that had been uprooted.

There emerged a sacred crypt containing the snowy, milk-white limbs of a little child. They were so tiny that they could scarcely be held, yet so hard that they could be broken only with the greatest difficulty.

While everyone marveled at their unfamiliar smallness, solidity, and whiteness, one of the bystanders, already advanced in age, burst into this account:

> “When I was a boy, my fellow boys and I were learning sacred songs in this church. Meanwhile, one night, after Matins had been completed and we were singing together according to custom, it happened that one of us, more advanced in age and spirit, suddenly collapsed as though in a convulsion and lay senseless, like a dead man, without feeling or voice.
>
> “At last, when he began to breathe and sigh, we anxiously asked what he was suffering. He said: ‘Did none of you see the miracle that appeared to me?’
>
> “Everyone denied it. ‘I saw,’ he said, ‘at the entrance of the choir a little child standing, shining white like snow, with his little hands extended toward heaven in prayer. After praying, he turned southward along the path toward the altar and hurried there, and then vanished between Saint Adrian and the principal altar.’”

When that observer had related these things, trembling and pale, we were all so terrified—the teacher and the pupils alike—that, led and urged on by the teacher, we fled headlong from the church together, and so forth.

But you, O child, whom we have described and whom we suppose may have been angered by undisciplined boys—we assign you in faith, though we do not know your name, to the Bethlehemite Innocents by your merits.

### CHAPTER XVI. The crypt of Blessed Mary is built.

Thus, after the aforesaid church had been emptied of its relics, it was overturned to the ground and leveled. Soon a new façade of the hall was raised directly at the front where it had been struck down, and it enclosed the entire womb of the old space with greater capacity.

In its original and most excellent place, the exalted Virgin obtained a new crypt. The chamber of Augustine and the house of the chief apostles were crowned above it. The accessible resting place of the exalted Mary was then revealed by the signs that follow.

### CHAPTERS XVII–XXII. A blind woman is given sight.

The royal crypt was not yet complete when the grace of our Queen smiled upon it. It was the holy day of Palm Sunday, on which the world celebrated the triumph of the Son of God and of his Mother. The Church made a festive procession, flourishing with flowers and palms, receiving its King, together with the ancient people of Jerusalem: seated on a donkey among human beings, yet reigning in heaven above the cherubim.

Meanwhile, an old woman afflicted with blindness and a long illness had remained alone in the crypt with Mary, the Mother of the Savior and the salvation of the world. The Mother of Mercy pitied the wretched woman’s calamity. Before the procession had ended, she restored the blind woman’s sight and granted complete health to her weakened body, and so forth.

Several further miracles follow, which may be found in the Bollandists.

### CHAPTERS XXIII–XXIV.

Another brother also, venerable in age and character, named Gregory, was still asleep one night before the nocturnal hymns when, from that same crypt, a melody of wondrous heavenly harmony was clearly heard, so that he awoke from sleep at the sweetness of the sound. At that time, as to this day, he was lying ill in the infirmary adjoining the front of the monastery and the crypt itself. He sat up on his bed and listened: the office was being sung which the brothers’ devotion performs there daily in honor of the Virgin:

“Salve, holy Mother, who, having given birth, bore the King,”

and so forth to the end, “world without end.”

He supposed that, once Matins had ended, the community of brothers was celebrating the customary Mass, except that the previously unheard sweetness of the song left him bewildered. He hastened to attend Mass, came to the door of the crypt, and found it secured by lock and bar. He searched through the brothers’ quarters: a deep sleep held them all, and by then the unfamiliar melody had fallen silent. The fact that nothing had yet been moved, together with the later ringing of the Matins bells, gave him certain proof that, while mortals slept, he had heard a heavenly concert. It must therefore be observed with the utmost devotion that, in response to our songs, a choir of the heavenly beings resounds, and that the Queen of Heaven has deigned to give this sign: she deigns to be saluted and praised by the songs of those above in the manner of our own service, etc.

## CHAPTERS XXV–XXVI. Saints Transferred from the Old Church. The Virtues and Miracles of Lambert, Bishop of Canterbury

When the basilica had been rebuilt and prepared over the crypt, and had received the brothers into their choir for the divine praises, the aforementioned abbot Scollandus prepared to demolish the remaining part of the ancient church, which was already about to collapse lest it crush someone. First, however, he took care to remove the bodies of the saints, with which the whole church was filled. From among the many, five exceptionally distinguished archbishops of Canterbury were transferred first, like five stewards of the Lord’s palace: the most illustrious and holy Theodore, and his holy successors Britwald, Tatuwin, Nothelm, and Lambert.

[Note: [Col. 0041D] In some copies, Jambertus; formerly abbot of St. Augustine’s, he became archbishop in the year 763. We gave Theodore’s Life under the year 690. We treated the others in the following century, under the year 732, p. 528.]

It would take too long to speak of each individually, since at the elevation of each, the fragrance from above and the manifest evidence of their virtues proclaimed the merits of each. Grace, however, permits us to say a little about the first and the last.

Lambert, taken from the abbacy of St. Augustine’s and appointed archbishop of Canterbury, suffered many persecutions for the sake of justice. Among other things, Offa, king of the Mercians, had begun transferring the archbishopric of Canterbury, Dorobernia, as the primacy of his kingdom to the Church of Lichfield, so that henceforth it might be the head of the churches of England—contrary, of course, to the perpetual authority of the original institution of blessed Pope Gregory. Lambert, Christ’s warrior, resisted in the spirit of Elijah. Amid repeated threats and rebuffs from kings, and frequent journeys to Rome to appeal to the Apostolic See, he at last brought back the palm of the rightful primacy to its proper seat.

Among these and his other outstanding virtues of holiness, he possessed such a treasury of humility that he ordered himself to be buried after death in the brothers’ capitolium, near the primicerius Augustine, judging himself unworthy to be admitted into the church of the saints and among so many of his most holy predecessor-bishops. Thus, after his death, although he had been buried in the capitolium, as though in a more despised place, a column of heavenly light often poured down from above and proved by celestial honor that he was worthy of the saints.

When at last, because of these and other miracles, they opened his tomb and carried him out to be reinterred in the church, the entire cloister all around was wonderfully fragrant with incense flowing like nard. There, too, when the abbot of that time reverently placed him on the right side of the altar, the customary signs accompanied him with supreme favor; these we now pass over, to spare the reader tediousness. We append only one brief revelation of his, by which we may prove his continual watchfulness over the dwelling of his repose, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0041D] Papebrochius substitutes *capitulo* for this word; but medieval authors commonly used *capitolium*.]

## CHAPTER XXVII. St. Theodore

When the lid of the tomb of the aforementioned Theodore was removed during the translation, the fragrance he emitted gave full satisfaction to everyone, so that this delight also spread into the brothers’ cloister. He lay just as he had been placed there from the beginning, whole in form, clothed in the pallium of metropolitan priesthood and covered only with a monastic cowl. Such was the grace surrounding him that one might think his flesh still firm and living, and the brothers, placing their hands upon him, attempted to lift him as though he were intact. Yet the motionless dust had previously presented an image of wholeness; touch proved the truth of dissolution, and dissolution added a more venerable grace of holiness. For that most precious ash, destined for the glory of the blessed resurrection, exhaled such a powerful fragrance when touched that, when ground, it smelled altogether like spices.

The leaden casket therefore received those most sacred relics, gathered with the greatest care as though they were precious gems. He was clothed in the finest ornaments and placed upon a bier by two brothers with little difficulty—but he was not carried away with equal ease. The proclamation of the responsory rang out; the solemn company proceeded; four chosen brothers took up the bier bearing the light. The mass clung to the ground as though rooted there. More help was added. They exerted all their strength with prayers, and only with difficulty, on eight shoulders, was it lifted. It was carried out with the greatest exertion and, only after immense labor, reached the steps of the presbytery.

There, at last, the effort and strength of all who carried or assisted collapsed. The overpowering weight fixed everyone in place; the more men took their turn, the more it left them panting in vain, as though lifeless. They were already about to be crushed beneath their burden when, turning finally to prayers and tears, they began to beat their breasts, accuse themselves of unworthiness, ask forgiveness, and promise amendment of life. They begged only that the saint permit himself to be carried out.

Pleased by these vows, he immediately became light, and a few men carried him to the principal altar and prepared place—though shortly before he could not have been moved by everyone. They marveled joyfully that the temple of God and dwelling of the Holy Spirit had proved so heavy to the empty-hearted and so light to the devout. He was therefore placed in the tomb prepared on the right side of the altar; only two brothers deposited him there together with the leaden casket.

When the other four saints mentioned above, his successors and fellow bishops, were likewise transferred, the quality of their merit was revealed by the power of the fragrance. The incense of their sarcophagi, stirred into motion, proclaimed that the Lord had made a perpetual dwelling among them and had kindled the incense of his love.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. King Æthelbert. Letardus. Berta. The Praises of King Æthelbert. He Founds Churches. The Monastery of St. Augustine. The Holiness of Abbot Peter. The Praise of His Monastery. The King’s Death. His Veneration among the Saints

The holy and God-beloved King Æthelbert was also transferred. As the first founder of the apostolic church, so he was its perpetual heir and possessor: third among the kings of the English, but the first to ascend the kingdom of heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0041D] He received Augustine, as everyone knows, when Augustine came to England, and was brought by him to the faith. See Augustine’s Life, chapter 16, etc., in the eleventh century, p. 511.]

The blessed bishop Letardus was also transferred. His sacred bones had long before been taken by Abbot Wulfric into a golden shrine, while the rest of his body had remained in a sarcophagus.

[Note: [Col. 0042D] More about him below. He had been bishop of Silvanectum in Belgica II; when Berta, daughter of Charibert, king of the Franks, came with him to England to marry Æthelbert, she brought him along. His feast is later said to be celebrated in May.]

The pious translation of the venerable Queen Berta was also carried out. With her, and for the sake of preserving the faith of Christ, that athlete of God, Letardus, had not feared to wander and remain amid the immense barbarism of paganism.

They lay in the portico of the most blessed bishop Martin: the king on the right side of the altar, against the southern wall; the bishop opposite, on the left, toward the north; and the queen behind the king. They had their own altars at the head of their tombs. The miracles of blessed Letardus, not to be passed over, will be related later.

For now, the manifest merits of Æthelbert throughout England demand our attention: England belongs to Christ because it believes in him. Whatever the teacher Augustine and his fellow evangelists accomplished in the Lord’s vineyard and harvest, apart from Christ’s prevenient grace, is owed first to this king, etc.

Through Augustine he built a church of the Lord and Savior and an archbishopric in his royal metropolis, where Augustine and all his successors would preside in the principal seat. He also built the principal monastery outside the city walls, on the eastern side, in honor of the chief apostles Peter and Paul, where the king and bishop, together with all their successors, would rest forever.

Among the East Saxons, the most blessed Mellitus emerged as the first teacher and first bishop. Augustine, the founder of that people’s faith, gave and consecrated him to them; afterward, he became the third to succeed Augustine in his apostolate.

This Æthelbert, friend of God, also founded in the metropolis of that province, London, the church of the Apostle Paul, commonly called Paul’s-Berig, and established and endowed an episcopal see there in royal fashion. Likewise, the see of Rochester, together with the basilica of the blessed Apostle Andrew, was first founded and adequately endowed by that prince. It received Justus—most just and most worthy of his name—whom the metropolitan church of Canterbury later took from there as its fourth bishop after Augustine.

He is also recorded in ancient charters as the founder of the monastery at Ely, although the blessed virgin Æthelthryth likewise deserves primacy there after its long desolation. It is unnecessary to explain how many other illustrious churches, whether episcopal or monastic, this most generous king and devoted worshiper of the heavenly kingdom elevated along with the lesser oratories, since the reality shines forth more clearly to this day.

He took care to ennoble that apostolic dwelling—where, as previously stated, he was to inherit repose by decree of blessed Pope Gregory together with his apostle Augustine and the entire succession—so much more splendidly because he recognized that this privilege had been specially granted to him by God together with so many holy and exalted men. On the outside he enlarged it with royal possessions; within, he adorned it with royal ornaments; and, with royal freedom and apostolic authority, he confirmed it by perpetual decrees.

There are charters and privileges of his, attested by the testimony of so many of the first founders. He appointed as the first abbot of this sacred community Peter, elected by its holy founders.

[Note: [Col. 0043D] About him, Bollandus under 6 January.]

After he had been drowned as a martyr while carrying out the obedience of a sacred mission, a ray of heavenly light, poured down from above every night, revealed him as a citizen of heaven until he could have a tomb in a more worthy place. He is solemnly honored at Boulogne in the church of the canons, where a recent prodigy seems worth recording as an example for those who disparage unknown saints.

The custodian of the place cast the saint’s body out of the church into the cemetery, indignant that a man whom he himself did not know should be honored in the church—although he also did not know how great was the man whom he had dishonored. Believing that his predecessors, who had honored the saint in this way, had been mistaken, he was instead seized by his own error.

For on the following night, while he was lying in bed and congratulating himself extravagantly for having done such a great deed by cleansing the church of so ignoble a corpse, the abbot suddenly appeared to him visibly, wearing a cowl and carrying a crozier. Rebuking him with a terrifying and threatening look, he said:

“Are you really pleased that you have thrown me out of the church?”

The terrified custodian asked who he was.

“I am Abbot Peter,” he replied, “who stand holy among the saints in heaven with God. Hence you will now learn whom you took pains to cast out before knowing him.”

A succession of savage threats followed. He struck him again and again with the pastoral staff he held in his hand; he hit his head, beat his sides, and shook all his limbs. Finally, leaving him half-dead and motionless, the divine avenger departed.

Meanwhile, until sunrise, the Matins bell remained silent under its condemned ringer, and no one came to open the door for those knocking and shouting. At last they broke down the doors, rushed in upon the crushed man, heard from him the cause of his complaint, carried him out wrapped in linen, and the next day buried him dead in the cemetery, mourning for their brother. But they honorably recovered the saint from that same cemetery and placed him in the church, rejoicing over the prodigy by which his holiness had been revealed.

The recently deceased Abbot Scollandus, who was present when these events had recently taken place and were being recounted, is a witness to the truth of this account.

[Note: [Col. 0043D] This city once had another seat of the bishop of the Morini. Today, with the bishopric of Terouanne divided into three dioceses, Boulogne has its own bishop, who is a suffragan of the archbishop of Reims.]

I have recalled these things in honor of the blessed King Æthelbert, so that no one may prejudice his merits, even if his miracles are unknown. Let discourse now solemnize the rest concerning him and the monastery of his dwelling.

He reigned in the neighboring metropolis; here he rests. Likewise, his evangelical father Augustine has his see there and his repose here. There is his throne; here, his bridal chamber. Thus, under Christ, he presides over both churches: he governs the one and inhabits the other, etc.

Here too, after many years, his most sacred co-heir Dunstan came frequently by night, like a stag to springs of water, and repeatedly experienced his customary visions and heard the hymns of the citizens of heaven. He is also said to have stated with complete confidence that wherever one set foot, whether in the church or in the cemetery, one would tread upon some saint, so full was the place of saints.

Nor is it without profound significance that the divine Augustine chose a place outside the gate together with his companions, as though at the exodus from the world and, like Israel’s exodus from Egypt, so that he might go forth with the Lord who suffered outside the gate.

Æthelbert, however, departed to the Lord, exchanging his kingdom for the heavenly one, on the twenty-fourth day of February, in the fifty-sixth year of his reign, the twenty-first after the arrival of blessed Augustine among his people and their acceptance of Christianity, and in the six hundred and sixteenth year of the Lord’s Incarnation.

“To quote Bede’s words: ‘Among the other good things which, in caring for his people, he contributed to them, he also established, with the counsel of wise men, judicial decrees modeled on those of the Romans. These were written down in the language of the English and are preserved and observed by them to this day. In them he first laid down how the person who secretly took away any property belonging either to the church, or to a bishop, or to any other order, ought to make restitution, wishing thereby to provide protection for those whose faith and teaching he had received.’”

The same venerable historian continues with the king’s lofty genealogy; we refer the reader to him.

The antiquity of his sanctity is its witness, together with the favorable authority of the ancient saints: namely, that from the beginning his solemnity was celebrated among the saints. We may believe that no one, amid so many wise and religious men, would have presumed to do this out of affection, error, or rashness unless he had been proved worthy by purity of life and heavenly signs. For his sons and other successors—good kings and men of great virtues—are merely recorded among the faithful departed; nor would the faithful Bede have written that he was the first of the kings of the English to ascend the kingdom of heaven unless he had learned of his merit. England has produced and venerates many kings of renowned holiness after him, etc.

## CHAPTER XXIX. The Holiness of Letardus

Now let us turn to blessed Letardus for a while. Letardus, a bishop worthy of God, appeared as the forerunner and doorkeeper of the Augustine who was to come. He preceded him as Lucifer—the morning star—precedes the sun; he prepared for him the way, the entrance, and the place, so that Augustine might prepare them for the Lord.

Generous in spirit beyond measure, he did not fear the beast-like barbarism of the pagans, terrifying as it was to the princes of the world. When the Christian queen Berta, daughter of the Frankish royal house, was sent from her father’s kingdom to the still-pagan Æthelbert, he was her guide, companion, teacher, protector, and instigator of every form of piety, etc.

Who could worthily estimate how many miracles he displayed after so many merits during his life, when so many miracles have multiplied in our own times, after so many centuries since his death? It would be wrong not to record some of them.

## CHAPTER XXX. He Gives Sight to a Blind Woman

Under the previously mentioned Abbot Wulfric, a girl blind from birth was brought by her parents to the tomb of this saint, as he himself was a reliable witness. God’s light-bringer bestowed on her a light previously unknown and gave the world, together with the sun, to her who had been enveloped in the darkness of her birth.

## CHAPTER XXXI. He Raises a Cripple

During a certain Lent, a woman placed at his tomb her son, crippled with his heels twisted backward from birth. At the urging of a devout nun who guarded the place, she abandoned the unfortunate child and departed.

[Note: [Col. 0045D] By this term even the laws of the English designated a religious woman.]

Meanwhile, at Vespers, the hymn of the Mother of God, “My soul magnifies the Lord,” was being sung, and the boy, released from his natural bonds, began to cry out. His inverted heels were straightened; his bent legs extended; blood flowed abundantly from the congealed flesh and stained the pavement. The boy stretched out his arms and tried to grasp the saint’s tomb; then he stood upright on his feet.

The people rushed in at the boy’s cries, but the nun barred the door until the brothers arrived and sang a hymn of praise for the miracle. The boy returned home on his own feet, though he had arrived on another’s.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Through His Help a Lost Ring Is Found

We know an outstanding craftsman, Speraver by name, abbot of Abbendon, highly skilled in painting, sculpture, and goldsmithing.

[Note: [Col. 0046D] The oldest monastery of the county of Berkshire, at the confluence of the Thames and the Ock.]

He had lost Queen Edith’s most precious ring. After searching for it everywhere in vain, he had also lost all hope of finding it. At last he fled to St. Letardus—for at that time he was working at St. Augustine’s, invited there by Abbot Ælstan—and implored his mercy with prayers and tears wrung from him by the distress of having lost a powerful person’s property.

The event was astonishing: immediately the ring shone before him where he was praying, although he could swear in good faith that he had never placed or lost it there. At once he seized it with as much amazement and joy as he had previously experienced despair and distress. Nor did he rejoice alone; by relating so great a miracle he also filled all the brothers with festive joy.

He did not merely remain mindful of so great a favor; he also worked to ensure that its memory would endure longer. He had images of the saint and of the venerable Queen Berta, the crown of his pilgrimage, fashioned on a colossal scale and with great beauty, and solemnly erected them above the saint’s tomb.

Other miracles follow, which we have omitted until chapter 40.

## CHAPTER XLI. Abbot Scollandus Dies

After everything had been removed from the old church and placed in a more suitable location for the translation, the frequently mentioned Abbot Scollandus demolished the church itself, which already threatened destruction and was preparing to collapse. There he raised new buildings as far as the portico and the translation-site of the most illustrious Augustine and his companions. But divine providence prevented him from proceeding farther by sending death to meet him.

He went before the face of the Lord through the pious performance of almsgiving and other good works. With the most renowned archbishop Lanfranc fulfilling every duty of service, he died a peaceful death while many mourned him. He died one day before King William, who left behind a worthy son as heir to his name and kingdom. The son fulfilled his father’s zealous desire to advance the church and its saints—a desire which, through God’s free generosity, would have sufficed for his reward even if it had already been completed—as the first book has explained.

# LIFE OF SAINT SWITHUN, BISHOP AND CONFESSOR OF WINCHESTER IN ENGLAND, BY GOSCELINUS

In Bollandus, *Acta Sanctorum*, July, vol. I, 2 July, p. 321.

[Col. 0047]

## PRELIMINARY COMMENTARY

### § 1. The Cult of St. Swithun, the Translation of His Body, Miracles, Relics, and Proper Prayers

[Col. 0047A]

1. I would not wish to seem excessively long-winded here in collecting the praises of St. Swithun. Other authors have already run this course before me: namely, William of Malmesbury in book II of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English*; John Pitseus in the fourth century of his *Appendix on Illustrious Writers of England*; and Cardinal Baronius, briefly, in volume X, under the years of Christ 847 and 862.

Yet, lest I say nothing about his praises, I shall at present gather from the Martyrologies a few items relevant to the subject. The *Roman Fasti* offer this brief praise of St. Swithun under 2 July:

“At Winchester in England, St. Swithun, bishop, whose grace shone forth through miracles.”

In the larger Antwerp codex, about which see the preface to the new edition of Usuard’s Martyrology, the praise of St. Swithun is briefly concluded as follows:

“Among the West Saxons, in the city of Venta, the deposition of St. Swithun, a man of wondrous holiness.”

The Altemps codex, discussed in the preface just mentioned, commemorates our saint on 30 October—or rather, his ordination:

“On this day, the ordination of our most holy bishop and patron, Swithun.”

Brief also is the distich on Swithun which Rudburnus cites from Lantfredus:

“You give the poor food and clothing to the naked,

And, pious, distribute generous gifts to the wretched.”

But no one will deny, if he has examined the end of the cited Life, printed by Mabillon in *Annales Benedictini*, century V, p. 634, that these verses were composed by Wulstan, a monk of Winchester, and inserted into Swithun’s metrical Life, although they were pronounced in praise of St. Æthelwold, bishop of Winchester, about whom discussion will return below.

2. I should also briefly instruct the reader that even the Protestants whom we call such, living in England, have always thought of St. Swithun and esteemed him so honorably and highly that, after the schism had been introduced and the Church and its saints had been attacked with canine fury, they nevertheless wished some traces of their veneration for him to survive by leaving his name written in the calendar of their reformed liturgy, as I find observed by a more recent author.

3. We shall present in full the history of the translation, whose outline Mabillon gives in abbreviated form in *Acta Benedictina*, century IV, from a very old Bigotian codex; perhaps the author mentioned above also drew his account from a copy of that manuscript, or at least from a similar one.

But elsewhere we shall say somewhat more about the author of the aforementioned history of the translation. In support of it, Mathew cites in volume II of the *Benedictine Trophies*, under 15 July, these words from the Sarum Missal and Breviary:

“The translation of St. Swithun and his companions.”

The author just mentioned probably thinks that by “companions” all the bishops and confessors of the aforementioned church or city are designated, although it may have happened that their bodies were transferred on different days.

Meanwhile, this is a convenient and opportune place to discuss the humble and neglected tomb to which this bishop ordered his body to be taken after death, until, after an interval of more than a hundred years—namely, in the year of Christ 971, in the fourteenth indiction—it was later discovered and found by divine prompting and solemnly transferred to a more honored place.

What Mabillon collected from Wulstan concerning the present subject I transcribe here:

“There was a certain very great tower, crested with cupolas,

Before the most beautiful thresholds of that sacred temple,

Consecrated to God in honor of the same hierarch.

Between it and the temple’s sacred and noble hall,

The holy man of God rested buried in body,

Though at that time his name was still hidden from us.

There were scarcely more than a few who could reveal

Either the name or the merit of the man, since a long time

Had passed after that sacred priest had been buried there.

For the same bishop, illustrious though he was, was so humble in mind before himself,

As all the faithful who knew him testify,

That after death he absolutely refused to allow his body

To be placed within the inner sanctuary of Christ’s church,

Nor among the chosen and various burial places

Where the ancient Fathers lay buried,

Where the rising golden sun sends its rays across the world

And burns through the middle of the day with fervent heat.

Rather, he entrusted himself to the western region

Of that illustrious hall which we have often mentioned,

Testifying with tears that his body was not to be placed

In the sacred house of the Lord, nor splendidly among

The monuments of the ancient Fathers. By Christ’s governance

It happened that this holy man, who had humbly despised himself,

Was buried outside the temple like a base and unworthy man,

Although renowned by countless signs, virtues, and radiant wonders,

Until he was transferred to the apostolic hall.”

4. This is what Wulstan writes in Mabillon, after Wulstan had prefaced it with certain verses that run as follows:

“Seek with diligent zeal

The lofty tomb of one holy bishop,

The small burial chapel which you will find placed above,

Built with walls and covered with a roof,

Set in the form of a sarcophagus, with a double pair of fronts.

Between it and the sacred stone cross which stands there,

Gradually seek your sleep-filled rest.”

Nor was this translation without its own signs and prodigies. Rather, glorified by the one who casts down the powerful from their seat and exalts the humble (Luke 1:52), it shone forth with a great multitude and variety of miracles. Surius summarized them as follows from Gotselinus, and Mabillon after him.

5. “On the same day, that is, on the Ides of July, he healed a boy crippled from birth; restored sight to three women deprived of the light of their eyes; freed a woman shackled in prison by breaking her iron bonds; cured a paralytic; restored sight to a noble but blind matron; completely restored twenty-five people afflicted with various diseases in a single day; cured several blind people and two crippled women within one day; cured thirty-six people who came from different places and suffered from illnesses of different kinds within the space of three days; and not long afterward cured one hundred and twenty-four people within fourteen days.”

So far the account there.

“Mabillon adds one more,” as he recorded in writing, “with William of Malmesbury as an eyewitness, in these words:

‘I saw—strange though it may seem—a man whose eyes had been gouged out by the violence of robbers receive, through Swithun’s merits, those very eyes or others—for the original eyes had been thrown some distance away. The indication of his former calamity was that the eyelids were disfigured by the points of the punctures.’”

The Winchester Annals, in Wharton’s *Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 295, give us this account of the most famous translation of St. Swithun:

“In the year 1093, in the presence of almost all the bishops and abbots of England, the monks came with the greatest rejoicing and glory from the old Winchester monastery to the new one, on 8 April. On the feast of St. Swithun, however, a procession was made, and they carried the bier of St. Swithun from the new monastery to the old; from there they brought it back and placed it honorably in the new monastery.”

Since the occasion of the translation also required treatment of the miracles, the copy from the very old Bigotian codex mentioned above was of great assistance to us in this part, as was another copy taken from the most ancient parchment of the Queen of Sweden. The latter came into our hands only mutilated, with its beginning and end cut off.

[Col. 0049C]

6. From the frequently praised Mabillon I extract certain materials that may in some measure make good this deficiency, since they contribute wonderfully to the glory of the Saint and to our purpose. Thus he himself speaks in *Acta Benedictina*, century IV, part I, p. 71:

“After the preceding translation, the church of Winchester took its title from his name. Ælfwold, a monk of Winchester who became bishop of Wilton, placed an image of the most holy Swithun at Sherborne and raised, as William of Malmesbury says in book II of *The Bishops of the English*, a torch of veneration. According to Gotselinus, remarkable miracles regularly occurred before this statue; among them, a leper was cleansed of leprosy.

Finally, when Queen Emma, mother of King Edward, had been accused by Earl Godwin of violating her chastity and had been confined in the monastery of Warewell, she underwent, at her son’s command, the ordeal of the red-hot iron in the church of St. Swithun at Winchester, to prove her own innocence and that of Ælwin, bishop of Winchester, who was said to be her lover.”

[Col. 0049D]

7. “Emma kept vigil all the following night at the tomb of St. Swithun. When day had come and the church floor had been swept, nine red-hot plowshares were placed in a row. After they had been briefly blessed, the queen’s shoes were removed. Then, after her veil had been put on and with two bishops girding her on either side, she walked unharmed over the nine plowshares, to the amazement of the king and the astonishment of all who were present, as is read at greater length, especially in the *Anglican Monastic Register*, from p. 33 onward.

On that same day, she herself gave her deliverer, St. Swithun, nine manors in offering for the nine plowshares, with King Edward’s approval, and he added two manors from his own possessions. Finally, in the year 1052, Queen Emma departed this world and was buried at Winchester in the church of St. Swithun.”

8. The posthumous fame of St. Swithun, confirmed and spread by signs and miracles, also contributed substantially to advancing the apostolic labors of St. Æthelwold, his successor in the bishopric of Winchester. This is declared in honorable words in the Life of Æthelwold, composed, as Mabillon thinks, by Wulstan, a monk and his disciple, and printed by Mabillon in *Annales Benedictini*, century V, p. 616, where we read:

“The preaching of this Æthelwold was greatly aided by the holy bishop Swithun, who at the same time was manifested by heavenly signs and most gloriously transferred beneath the temple’s royal roof and most fittingly placed there. Thus two lights shone together in the house of God, set upon golden lampstands: what Æthelwold preached through the wholesome exhortation of words, Swithun wonderfully adorned through the glorious display of miracles, to the praise of Christ’s name.”

You will find certain miracles written in bound verse in the following paragraph, where the writers are discussed.

We must also speak of the relics of our holy bishop. Edmerus, or Eadmer, the inseparable companion of St. Anselm, archbishop, described the ancient crypt of the church of Canterbury. From that description, omitting other matters irrelevant here, I extract a few passages pertinent to our subject:

“Moreover, another altar stood at a suitable distance before the aforementioned altar. It was dedicated in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the divine mysteries are celebrated there daily. Upon this altar blessed Ælfheah had solemnly placed the head of blessed Swithun . . . together with many relics of others.”

See part II of the June supplement, p. 114. As for the relics, this is all that has so far been said.

9. For the proper prayers or collects, reader, take from our manuscript codex “the following items, excerpted from a most elegant Missal given for the use of the English Church to the monastery of Jumièges by Robert, formerly its abbot, then bishop of London around the year 1050, and finally archbishop of Canterbury, etc. The Missal’s Easter table runs from the year 1000 to the year 1005.”

Thus it reads there:

“God, who have deigned to reveal to the world in these present times the heavenly radiance, Bishop Swithun, we humbly implore your omnipotence: through the glorious merits of this Saint, whom you cause to shine with signs and miracles, grant us, your servants who beseech you, an increase of every virtue and the rejoicing of everlasting happiness. Through, etc.”

There is no preface. The prayer for completion, or postcommunion, reads:

“God, who through your holy confessor, Bishop Swithun, heal the ailments of the sick, grant us your help, that we who implore his intercession may enjoy the well-being of the present life and the fellowship of the citizens of heaven. Through our Lord,” etc.

I took the following verses, together with the prayer, from a manuscript containing collects and antiphons of various saints of England:

“O Father Swithun, our most gentle bishop,

Through whom the Lord God performs wondrous signs,

We, frail in spirit, ask you to defend us as a father;

Protect us by your holy merits.

With you as our patron interceding for us,

May we be able to ascend to everlasting life.

Pray for us, etc.

God, who grant us to celebrate this most sacred day in the deposition of blessed Swithun, your confessor and bishop, be graciously present to the prayers of your Church, so that she who glories in his merits may be protected by his intercessions. Through Christ our Lord.”

## § II. On the Writers of the Life, Miracles, and Translation of St. Swithun
10. We have three sources available to us for illuminating the subject of Saint Swithun: namely, his life, his miracles, and his translation. What writers have committed to writing about these matters for the memory of posterity, we shall present in its proper place and, wherever necessary, elucidate with notes, first giving a brief account of their authors.

His life is found described in the *Legenda*, printed in old type, which is commonly and generally attributed to Capgrave. There are those who consider the author of this *Legenda* to have been John of Tynemouth, a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict at Saint Albans. John flourished in the year 1366; after examining the libraries of ancient monasteries, he devoted himself to composing an ecclesiastical history and the Lives of the Saints. It is said that from his *Sanctilogium*, or *History of the Saints of Both Sexes*, John Capgrave transferred either everything or most of it into the aforementioned *Legenda* and used it as his own. Consult the note of John Bollandus, February, vol. II, p. 308, letter a.

11. The same life, which we shall also present here, with only a few alterations and with its style corrected in places, was printed by Surius on 2 July under the name of Goscelin, of whom presently. The life published by Capgrave and the one we have mentioned agrees too closely with the version which, as we have said, the aforementioned Surius polished in his own manner for them to have been drawn from different sources, as is established by the collation I made of the two texts with one another.

It will be useful to hear what John Mabillon wrote in commentary on the author of the Life in the *Benedictine Acts*, century IV, p. 69:

> “This Life,” he says, “Goscelin the monk at last attempted to bring forth from darkness at the turn of the eleventh century. He had been transferred to England from the monastery of Sithiu together with Herman, bishop of Salisbury. Goscelin, according to William, a monk of Malmesbury, in book IV of *The Kings of the English*, at the final chapter, raised innumerable Lives of the Saints to the dignity of literary style: those either lost through hostility or published in crude form he renewed with greater elegance. From this author William himself borrowed what he reported about Swithun when treating of the bishops of Winchester. Harpsfield followed in the footsteps of both, and after him Thomas Maihew and other more recent writers.”

Vossius speaks of Goscelin in book II of *On Latin Historians* as follows:

> “He flourished in the year 1110. He wrote the Life of Saint Swithun, bishop of Winchester, which exists either in its entirety or at least in an epitome in Surius, vol. IV, 2 July.”

Since, then, scholars are in substantial agreement that the often-mentioned Goscelin committed the Life of Saint Swithun to writing, and since, so far as I judge, no author who had traversed this stage of literary activity before his time can be identified, it remains that whatever John of Tynemouth or Capgrave published in later times should apparently be referred to this one Goscelin as its first source.

Unless, perhaps, Lantfred—and possibly also Wulstan, whom we shall now discuss—had themselves shed some light before Goscelin.

12. Consider these words, which the author of the translation of the body of our holy bishop inserted into the history he composed:

> “We saw it happen in the manner which this present little book demonstrates;”

and, in addition, these words which he says in the same place:

> “He who in our time deigned to glorify his saint through signs and miracles.”

From these words, I say, it is clear that the aforesaid author was contemporary with the translation of the body of Saint Swithun, indeed even an eyewitness. Now, since scholars generally agree that Lantfred recorded in prose the history of the aforementioned translation—or the miracles performed after the saint’s death—and since it is established with no less certainty from other evidence that he flourished around the year 980, I do not see to whom this manuscript of ours, which we are publishing in print, could more plausibly and with greater probability be attributed than to Lantfred—at least in the sense that our text was taken and extracted from his writings, with other miracles omitted. That he wrote a larger number will become clear from what is later reported from Mabillon.

Why should this very text not be identical, or at least drawn from the same sources, as the work Mabillon refrained from publishing, content merely to give a brief account of Saint Swithun’s miracles? He says:

> “I judged that the works of Lantfred and Wulstan, which we possess, were not of such importance as to deserve public light. In them I find only a few things worthy of observation, which I shall report at the end of this summary.”

13. With all due respect to that learned man, we hold the contrary view: it is entirely consistent with the work of an investigator of antiquity, and by no means foreign to his purpose, to bring venerable monuments of the distant past out of darkness into public light, and also to offer for publication whatever of this kind—provided it is sincere and genuine—can be transmitted to posterity. Its sole and often its only value may be its candid, ancient, and primitive simplicity.

Perhaps this manuscript of ours coincides with that other one which, as a more recent author writes, “is found in the Cottonian Library, in a codex of exceptional antiquity and beauty, under Nero E. I.”

For attributing the aforementioned history of the translation and miracles, as it appears in our copy, to Lantfred as its author, these words of the same copy provide considerable support:

> “Yet the life and ancient conduct of this remarkable bishop are unknown to us, because no writings concerning them are available.”

From this it appears that what is said of Lantfred and Wulstan by Mabillon agrees with the author of our copy. Mabillon says that they

> “complain that, through the negligence of writers, nothing about his [Saint Swithun’s] life has been transmitted to posterity.”

I cannot understand how these statements can be made consistent with the opinion of Pitseus, who, according to Mabillon, “in his book on the ecclesiastical writers of the English attributes to Lantfred two books on the life and miracles of Saint Swithun,” although, Mabillon says,

> “I find only one concerning the translation and miracles, and he appears to have written none concerning his life. Lantfred complains that Saint Swithun’s deeds were unknown because of the scarcity of writers.”

14. It remains finally that I present here those miracles which Mabillon excerpted from the writings of Wulstan and Lantfred.

The first concerns a parricide who, for nine years, had been bound in iron fetters on account of that crime, and who was released from his chains. “This miracle,” as the aforementioned Mabillon reports, “Lantfred recounts in chapter 24” (and it is reported among us as miracle no. 32, taken from the ancient manuscripts of the Queen of Sweden).

Wulstan describes this kind of penance, which, he says, he had often observed elsewhere, in the following verses, book II, chapter 7:

> Meanwhile it happened that a certain man committed a crime,  
> For he killed his own parent by a cruel death.  
> Therefore the bishop of the city immediately ordered the guilty man  
> To have an iron circle fasten his entire belly tightly,  
> And his arms likewise to suffer a similar punishment.  
> For nine continuous years, tormenting himself,  
> He was often to walk through the courts of holy places  
> And visit the most beautiful threshold of holy Peter,  
> So that he might deserve to receive pardon for so great a crime.

The aforementioned Mabillon continues:

> “Likewise, in the following chapter another event is reported concerning the servant of a certain Flodoald, a very wealthy merchant of Winchester. The servant, accused before Eadric the magistrate of an unspecified crime, is ordered to  
>   
> Carry with his naked hand glowing coals  
> And red-hot iron: if he continued unharmed, he would be innocent;  
> But if he were guilty, the executioner would punish him  
> With the sword upon his exposed neck.”

15. “The third [miracle] is in chapter 11: the sight of Birferth, a monk of Abingdon, was restored. At that time Otgar was abbot of Abingdon; he was succeeded by Wulfgar, who was flourishing when Wulstan wrote these things.

“The fourth is in chapter 12: a blind man was given sight. On a day of fasting, when he came to Winchester, he considered it religiously proper not to break his fast before the solemn hour of None.

“The fifth concerns a certain Gallic woman who, when she yawned one night without making the sign of the cross, was suddenly struck with an affliction of the jaw.

“The sixth concerns the law established by King Edgar against robbers: whoever was discovered guilty of this crime was to be tortured for a long time, with his eyes blinded, his hands cut off, his ears torn away, his nostrils slit, and his feet removed; finally, with the skin of his head stripped away together with his hair, he was to be left almost dead in the fields, to be devoured by beasts, birds, and nocturnal dogs. Lantfred mentions this last punishment in his final chapter.”

Anyone who compares these recently mentioned miracles of Saint Swithun with those we are about to present will easily observe that nearly all the miracles listed here are also described there. We thought it would be of interest to the reader to include here everything Mabillon excerpted from the writings of Wulstan and Lantfred. These accounts may not provide information about miracles found elsewhere, but they may nevertheless contribute to their fuller confirmation.

16. Regarding our copy, which treats of the miracles of our Saint and was extracted from the most ancient manuscripts of the Queen of Sweden, I have no certain or established information either about the author who wrote it or about the time when it was written. Thus I have nothing ready to say except for the few remarks which we made on that occasion in the preceding paragraph, to which I refer the reader.

This is also the appropriate place for Lantfred’s letter, which is published under his name as author in Wharton’s *Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 322, under the title: “Lantfred’s letter prefixed to the history of the miracles of Saint Swithun, bishop of Winchester.”

I hope that it will be inserted here on a second reading. Although it has no great affinity with the matters treated intermittently throughout this paragraph, and although it offers little new historical illumination or learning, it may nevertheless serve as a prologue to the history of the miracles performed by Saint Swithun. The letter runs as follows:

> To the most beloved brothers dwelling at Winchester in the monastery of Saint Peter, called the Old Minster: may unbroken concord, salvation and everlasting glory, indescribable joy, splendor without end, everlasting peace, and continual charity here and in heaven be multiplied by the Lord.
>
> Although, dearest and most gracious brothers, the miracles which the all-powerful author of miracles deigned to bestow upon the peoples of the English through the merit of Saint Swithun have been thoroughly spread throughout almost the whole of Europe, nevertheless, lest such great benefits of God remain hidden from succeeding posterity, I—the most wicked of all men in my evil deeds, possessing no prerogative of divine knowledge and supported by no authority of goodness—yet obedient to your commands and trusting in your prayers, trembling, approached so vast a sea and, like a drop from the waves of the ocean, plucked a very few accounts from the multitude of the Saint’s miracles.

17. “Therefore I beseech the Creator of all things to regard not my merit but the affection of those who command. I also ask you, my beloved ones, to pray for me, lest the spirit of falsehood deceive me. A mind entangled in earthly cares can devise nothing true unless the spirit of knowledge and piety has first expelled the deceptive darknesses of error.

“And since we know very little about the miraculous signs, wonders, and works of power which this Saint performed by his prayers during his life—for, as Priscian, that most skilled author of the grammatical art, says, literary studies pass into neglect through the scarcity of writers—let us come to those things which were unquestionably accomplished after his death at the tomb of the man of God.

“We have therefore approached especially the task of unfolding this Saint’s miracles, because just as it is most fitting to praise the benefits of God and most just to proclaim them to those who do not know them, so it is most impious to deny them by keeping silent and most wicked not to recount them to those ignorant of them.

“The human mind is of such a nature that whenever, by reading or hearing, it learns the sacred deeds of the ancients or the conduct of the fathers, it abandons the hardness of its heart, relinquishes the obstinacy of the mind that follows vices, and inclines toward mercy and follows humility, the teacher of virtues.”

As you have seen, reader, the aforementioned letter supplies no new illumination and no new information. Nevertheless, I judged that it should be inserted here, lest some learned person perhaps miss it here.

§ III. Answers to Certain Questions Concerning the Life and Death of Saint Swithun

18. Where our blessed bishop was born, from what family he came, and what way of life he professed before he wore the sacred insignia of the bishopric of Winchester, I do not think is defined distinctly anywhere in the ancient records.

“Florence of Worcester writes that he was born of a noble line of parents in the year of Christ 827,” as can be seen in Maihew. I do not investigate where he derived this chronological anachronism.

Regarding his way of life before the episcopate of Winchester, Mabillon replies:

> “Harpsfield and Maihew believe that he was a monk at Winchester in the Old Minster. Their position, therefore, is that the cathedral church of Saint Peter at Winchester was served by monks in the middle of the ninth century and subsequently passed to secular canons, whom King Edgar replaced with monks after the middle of the tenth century. Maihew explains his view so explicitly that he even supposes the principal church of Winchester, later called the Old Minster, to have been subject to Benedictine monks from the time of its foundation by Saint Birinus the bishop. We shall discuss this matter more fully in the following century.”

From the Life of Goscelin, which we shall later publish, we learn of his childlike simplicity, innocence of conduct, clerical status, priesthood, and education of Adulph, or Ethelwulf, the son of King Egbert. Beyond this, it gives us nothing that would provide a more distinct or detailed account of the deeds performed by Saint Swithun before his episcopate.

Pitseus indeed asserts, on the authority of Leland, that Swithun was a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict; but he would deserve greater belief if he proved this assertion as plausibly as he makes it categorically.

19. Despite these considerations, his monastic profession before the episcopate is not obscurely inferred and asserted by Mabillon in the *Benedictine Annals*, vol. III, p. 98, on the basis of a document which he certainly did not yet possess when he was composing the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, but which he acquired later, when he undertook to compose the aforementioned *Annals*.

That document is published in the larger history of Winchester, vol. I of *Anglia Sacra*, mentioned above, pp. 201 and following. There the profession of our Saint is cited, made into the hands of Celnot, archbishop of Canterbury, before Swithun was consecrated bishop of Winchester. Among other things it explicitly states that he had previously been a monk:

> “I, Swithun,” he says, “a monk, servant of the servants of God, though unworthy, elected to the episcopal seat of the Church of the city of Winchester, first of all confess to you, most reverend Father, Archbishop Celnoch, my continence, which I previously expressed in my monastic profession, and my love toward you—something free from every scruple of ambiguity and every invention of falsehood. I believe in God the Father,” etc.

There can therefore be no doubt that before his episcopate Saint Swithun followed a monastic way of life. But whether that way of life was Benedictine or some other, the ancient sources do not state. Mabillon seems tacitly to suppose that he was a monk of the Benedictine order, since in the *Benedictine Acts* he assigns him a place alongside the other previously mentioned followers of that order.

20. It may also be asked in what year our Saint assumed the administration and possession of the Winchester see. The authors agree sufficiently that this occurred in the ninth century, but there is greater disagreement and controversy among them as to the particular year.

I take it as certain and beyond doubt that he had not yet been promoted to bear the pastoral staff in the year 833. I establish my assertion as follows.

In the year 833, Withlaf, king of the Mercians, while, as our Alford relates, he was living as an exile in retreat at Crowland, established by royal charter that, if he recovered his kingdom, he would do good to that place.
