He fulfilled this promise fully and abundantly and subscribed at the Council of London a public document, reported by Ingulf, abbot of that monastery, which can be seen in Alford and other writers.

The royal privilege was subscribed first by Cenwulf, archbishop of Canterbury, and then by the other archbishops, bishops, and abbots in their proper order; after them by King Egbert himself, his son Ethelwulf, and three dukes. Finally, after all these, Swithun also subscribed in these words:

> “I, Swithun, priest of King Egbert, was present.”

Therefore, in the year 833 Saint Swithun was merely priest of King Egbert and was not yet a bishop.

I further assert that he did not hold episcopal dignity before the year 837; this is clear from the fact that Helmstan, his predecessor in the episcopate, died only in the year 837.

21. The following passage from the aforementioned Alford’s *Annals of the Church* under that year is relevant:

> “In this year Helmstan, bishop of Winchester, died after having governed the church for five years. Godwin says the following about him in his catalogue: ‘Helmstan died in the year 837 and lies buried above the northern wall of the presbytery.’”

Alford then continues:

> “The Worcester writer records the same year of his death, which should be noted because there are also distinguished historians who think that after Helmstan’s death Ethelwulf succeeded him as king of the West Saxons. But since he entered upon the kingdom on 4 February, he could not have occupied the episcopal see for seven years, as certain authors seem to wish. Godwin therefore wrote correctly.”

> “Around this time,” they say, “many of our historians maintain that Athulf, or Athelwulf, who later became king, was made bishop of Winchester—namely, Symeon of Durham, Henry of Huntingdon, Roger Hoveden, and others—and that he presided over this see for seven years. This is in no way convincing to me.”

Thus Alford follows Godwin.

22. Let it therefore remain fixed that Helmstan’s Winchester see was not occupied before the year 837. Helmstan was succeeded not by Athelwulf, as certain otherwise highly respected historians have fancifully maintained, but by Saint Swithun. This occurred either in the following year, namely 838, which the highly praised Alford says is recorded in the annals, or in the preceding year, 837, as Maihew states in the *Benedictine Trophies of England* under 2 July:

> “All agree that, when Ethelwulf was already established as king, and therefore after the beginning of his reign, which occurred in 837, he was placed over that episcopal see.”

William of Malmesbury agrees in book II of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English*:

> “Ethelwulf,” he says, “taking Swithun as his tutor and teacher—for that is what he called him—did not desist until he had honored him with the bishopric of Winchester, with the consent of the clergy and the ordination of Ceolnoth, archbishop of Canterbury.”

Florence of Worcester also agrees, writing under the year 837:

> “While Ethelwulf was reigning as king, Saint Helmstan the bishop departed this life; by the king’s command, blessed Swithun succeeded him.”

23. Thomas Rudburn, mentioned above, does indeed assert that Saint Swithun’s ordination took place “after the death of Helmstan, bishop of Winchester,” while Athulf, or Ethelwulf, was reigning; but he removes and postpones it until the year 852. On what foundation he relied, I do not sufficiently understand.

Indeed, the same author shortly beforehand presents a privilege, or charter of donation, which “was written in the year 844 of the Lord’s incarnation, in the fourth indiction” (which is the seventh), in which Swithun is named as bishop in these words:

> “Then it pleased the bishops Alstan of the church of Sherborne and Swithun of the church of Winchester, together with their abbots and servants, to enter into the said agreement.”

Wharton, the commentator or scholiast on the cited Rudburn, considers that Rudburn correctly placed Swithun’s accession to the episcopal see in 852, but that an error entered the aforementioned diploma, or charter of donation, and that 855 should be substituted for 844. The fourth indiction recorded there agrees exactly with that year—although that year had the third indiction, not the fourth—and conflicts with 844, which fell under the ninth indiction, or seventh according to the stated computation.

Wharton likewise charges Godwin with an error arising from carelessness because he records Helmstan’s death under the year 837. But should his judgment in this matter carry such weight that it outweighs the authors cited earlier? The contrary is evident even from the errors concerning the indictions.

24. Usserius committed a still greater and more obvious error when, in his chronological index, he stated that Swithun succeeded Helmstan in the episcopal see in the year 937, in these words:

> “937. Swithun succeeded Helmstan in the bishopric of Winchester. They hold that he had been professor of sacred theology in the university of Cambridge; Bonagracia of Villa Dei, his contemporary, attests this in a letter to the Black Monks of England.”

Usserius wrote this in the index after saying the following in his *History of the Beginnings of the British Churches*, p. 340:

> “The Swithun who follows appears to be the same person whom Florence of Worcester records in his chronicle as having succeeded Helmstan in the bishopric of Winchester in the year 937.”

Yet the year is plainly given there as 837, and there is no mention of either Helmstan or Swithun in the year 937.

The aforementioned Usserius then continues:

> “For they also hold that he was a Cambridge man, on the authority of Bonagracia of Villa Dei. From his letter to the Black Monks in England, Thomas Rudburn, in book III, chapter 2 of the *Larger History*, and the author of the short history of the Church of Winchester, produce the following words:
>
> ‘When, exiled from my own country, I was living in England among the most holy and religious monks of your entire kingdom, in the city of Winchester, the venerable Helmstan, abbot of the cathedral church, and the venerable Swithun, provost of that same church and professor of sacred theology, installed in a chair at the university of Cambridge, sustained me amid the hardships of exile with special kindness, as though offering me a reward of consolation.’”

25. Wharton comments on these words as follows:

> “I fear that the elder Swithun, also bishop of Winchester, a companion of Saints Dubricius and David and most celebrated for his literary reputation, may have been wrongly confused with the younger Swithun. Concerning him, see Geoffrey of Monmouth, *History of Britain*, book IX, chapter 12, and Gerald of Wales, *Life of Saint David*.”

Rudburn had embellished the antiquity of the university of Cambridge with a splendid fiction in his shorter history, using these words:

> “In the year of the Lord 871, the University of Cambridge was burned. It had been built in the year 4815 from the creation of the world by the duke Cantaber, and had been frequented by philosophers for 314 years before the incarnation of Christ.”

So he writes.

When these matters are carefully weighed and considered, it follows that in these and similar matters, as also in the chronology mentioned above, too much weight should not be given to Rudburn’s authority. Accordingly, concerning the provostship of Winchester and the professorship at the University of Cambridge which the aforesaid author claims Saint Swithun held, I shall not be readily persuaded unless I see this established and supported by older and more reliable evidence.

26. “Furthermore, what Rudburn reports about monks inhabiting the Church of Winchester from the year 169 onward is mere nonsense,” as Wharton says in his *Succession of the Priors of the Church of Winchester*. From this it may be inferred that Rudburn inserted more than one fiction into his writings.

But what are we to make of the fragment of the letter cited above and attributed to Bonagracia of Villa Dei? Accept this answer.

To say that the fragment is entirely spurious and adulterated seems a somewhat difficult assertion to digest. What, then? Perhaps certain passages were inserted here by an interpolator out of personal affection and inclination. Or, if that does not seem likely, the confusion of the elder Swithun with the younger could readily have been the mother who gave birth to the story in question.

Yet this last explanation does not seem sufficient to settle the present controversy, because the name “Helmstan, venerable abbot of the cathedral church” is included, and this Helmstan lived at the same time as the younger Swithun. Unless perhaps there were also two Helmstans, the first merely abbot of the cathedral church, and the second bishop of that same church and contemporary with our Swithun. This is not a matter we have leisure to investigate.

But enough of these matters. Let us now hurry on to others.

27. Let the final task now be to determine in what year the holy bishop departed this life. The authors agree sufficiently about the time, with only a difference of one year remaining among them.

Mabillon says in the frequently cited summary of the Life of Saint Swithun:

> “Goscelin, Matthew of Westminster, Florence of Worcester, and Cardinal Baronius with them assign his death to the year of Christ 862. William of Malmesbury in his *Bishops*, Symeon of Durham in book [*On the Deeds of the Kings of the English*], and Roger Hoveden prefer the following year. Goscelin, together with the Roman Martyrology and other more recent sources, assigns the sixth day before the Nones of July. Egilward, in his book *On the Life of Saint Burchard, Bishop of Würzburg*, is far astray when he calls Burchard the full brother of this same Saint Swithun, since Burchard preceded Swithun by one hundred years.”

29. Mabillon adheres to the authors last enumerated, who assign Swithun’s death to the year 863; he likewise records that year in the passage immediately cited.

I confess that I do not know what compelled him to depart from the opinion of Goscelin, whom Mabillon himself praised at greater length above in section 11. Nor do I sufficiently see any reason why, abandoning Goscelin’s view, which places the death of our Saint in 862, I should conform myself to the judgment of other more recent authors, who attach that death only to the immediately following year, namely 863.

I therefore consider the year 862 preferable, following our predecessors, who long ago, under 11 April, p. 54, in the notes, letter l, held the same opinion:

> “Saint Swithun … occupied the see from the year 838 to 862.”

From what has been said, Baillet—so often hypercritical of others—is shown to have fallen into error and deserves criticism when, in the Life of Saint Swithun, he asserts that Swithun spent almost forty years in episcopal office.

By way of corollary I add what the scholiast noted on the *History of Winchester* in part I of *Anglia Sacra*, edited by Wharton. On the words of that history, “Saint Swithun died in the year 863 of the Lord’s incarnation,” he comments as follows:

> “So indeed say Hoveden, the writer of Melrose, and several others. But he actually died in the year 862, on the sixth day before the Nones of July, on a Thursday; this is established from the Worcester and Westminster writers. So too the short manuscript history of Winchester records that Swithun died in 862, in the third year of King Ethelberht. The brief Winchester Annals are grossly mistaken: they extend Swithun’s birth to the year 826 and his death to 872.”

With these remarks, offered for the reader’s instruction concerning matters relating to the Life and miracles of Saint Swithun, I conclude and append our copies.

[Col. 0057]

# LIFE OF SAINT SWITHUN

(*Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists, as above, from Surius and Capgrave.)

1. While the glorious king of the English, Egbert, was reigning—he succeeded King Kinegilph, who had been converted from idolatry by the blessed Birinus, and was the eighth in the administration of the kingdom—blessed Swithun, destined to become father and shepherd in the Church of God, by the ordering of divine mercy received the beginning of his course through the race of this world.

[Note: King of the East Saxons. He began to reign in the year 800 and ceased to reign at the beginning of the year 837, on 4 February, as Alford relates in the *Annals of the English Church*, vol. III, where there is further information.]

[Note: Alternatively, Kinegilsus. He began his reign in 612 and died in 642; see the aforementioned Alford, vol. II, for further information.]

[Note: He departed to heaven in the year 650. He is honored on 3 December as the apostle of the West Saxons; there will be occasion to discuss him more fully elsewhere, on the same day.]

[Note: According to Alford’s chronological index, found at the end of vol. III of the *Annals of the English Church*, Egbert is numbered the eleventh king after Kinegils.]

After spending his childhood years in devout simplicity, he wished the yoke of the Lord’s service to be placed upon his shoulders; once he had accepted it, he carried it humbly and courageously. Thus, admitted into the clergy and ascending from rank to rank and from virtue to virtue, with God directing his steps in all things, he was advanced to the dignity of the priesthood under Helinstan, bishop of Winchester.

[Note: There is considerable discussion of Helinstan, or Helmstan, in the preceding commentary.]

Moreover, he took care always to show himself to God as a suitable and worthy minister; to handle the word of truth correctly and in accordance with Catholic teaching; to cultivate kindness and gentleness; to practice works of mercy above all; to correct those who did not live rightly or orderly with the rod of discipline; and to serve all humbly.

2. When his reputation reached the ears of the king, he was summoned by him and counted among his chief friends. The king entrusted to him his son Adulph for education in the liberal disciplines and instruction in holy conduct; Swithun later ordained him subdeacon.

[Note: Alternatively, Ethelwolfus, Ethelvulphus, or Alidulphus.]

Nevertheless, when his father died without an heir, and no other heir existed besides him, he took a wife with the dispensation of Pope Leo.

[Note: The frequently mentioned Alford reports that Leo III, Roman pontiff, granted the dispensation, vol. III, p. 54; thus this occurred before the year 817, since that pontiff died in the preceding year, 816.]

When Bishop Helmstan died, Swithun was elected by the unanimous vote of all. Moved by his prayers and exhortations, King Adulph generously gave to the churches of God the entire tithe of the land of his kingdom and granted them permission to claim it freely for themselves.

The same holy bishop built the Winchester bridge which lies to the east. While he was diligently supervising its construction, a poor woman came to him one day carrying eggs for sale in a vessel. The playful and mischievous workmen seized her and greatly distressed her, not by taking all the eggs away but by breaking them.

As she complained tearfully and wailing before the bishop about the injury inflicted and the damage suffered, the holy man, moved by compassion, seized the vessel in which the eggs had been placed, made the sign of the cross over it with his right hand, and restored the eggs unbroken and whole.

3. He was accustomed to build churches zealously in places where none existed and to restore those that were ruined and broken down. When he was about to dedicate sacred buildings, he did not ride proudly on horseback or surround himself with the trappings of worldly pomp; instead, accompanied by his clerics and household, he walked humbly with bare feet.

To his banquets he invited not the wealthy but the needy and poor. His mouth was always open to exhort sinners to undertake penance. He warned those standing to take care lest they fall, and those who had fallen to rise again.

He did not take food to fill his belly but consumed it sparingly and moderately for the support of his body. After many vigils and many labors, so that he would not fail, he allowed himself a little sleep, always intent upon psalms and spiritual songs.

To those nearest to him, just as to himself, he proposed in modest and humble speech whatever was useful, honorable, pious, and holy. The blessed man lived until the end of his life in the true observance of God’s commandments, guarding his heart in all purity and spiritual cleanness; he was an upright guardian of Catholic and apostolic doctrine, an ever-watchful teacher of his spiritually regenerated children, instructing them in the practice of holy conduct.

He pursued humility and gentleness with particular care. Finally, following peace and holiness, he thirsted for the fountain of life and eternal blessedness. Thus he happily departed from this world to the heavenly dwellings on the sixth day before the Nones of July, in the year of salvation 862.

[Note: We stated in the preceding commentary, section 28, that this year should be assigned rather than the following one.]

He ordered that he be buried not inside the church but outside its enclosure, in an unworthy and lowly place.

[Note: See the preceding commentary for further information.]

4. After his death he shone forth through many miracles. Among them, he appeared to a certain man [Note: [Col. 0060D] Concerning this and the miracles that follow, see those given below.] suffering from an incredible infirmity of all his limbs, and admonished him to visit Ethelwold, bishop of Winchester, and tell him that divine providence had determined that his body should be lifted from the place where it had been buried and reinterred more honorably within the church, in a worthier place. If he should doubt and hesitate, he would have as proof the recovery of his health: at that very hour he would immediately regain it, once the illness from which he had long suffered had been driven away. He also added that he should come to the place of burial, where he would pull out, without damaging the stone at all, one of the iron rings that could still be seen fixed into it, and then replace it in its original position with equal ease, without damaging the stone. The man arose perfectly healthy, found everything as had been foretold, and recounted all of it to the bishop.

He restored to health and safety a certain bent man who, like cattle, kept his face lowered toward the ground. A certain noble and wealthy man, while walking beside the river at midday, suddenly saw three women appear before him, horrifying beyond measure and of immense stature. Seizing him as he fled, tormenting him in many ways, and nearly suffocating him with their pestilential breath, they reduced him, overwhelmed by incredible terror, to the likeness of a madman. When he had been brought to the church, Saint Swithun appeared to him during the night and, removing all his suffering, restored him to health.

5. When Bishop Ethelwold raised the blessed man’s body from the earth, an extraordinary fragrance of perfume pervaded everyone; a blind woman recovered her sight, and many afflicted by various illnesses were healed through his merits. This translation occurred in the one hundred and tenth year after his death, but in the year 971 of the Lord’s Incarnation, on the Ides of July. On that same day he healed a boy who had been miraculously crippled from birth; restored sight to three women deprived of the light of their eyes; freed a woman chained in prison with iron bonds, breaking her fetters; cured a paralytic; gave sight to a noble but blind matron; completely restored in one day twenty-five people afflicted with various diseases who had come from different places; healed several blind people and two crippled women within one day; healed thirty-six people who came from different places and suffered from illnesses not all of one kind within three days; and, not long afterward, one hundred and twenty-four people within fourteen days.

6. King Edgar enacted a law to restrain theft: anyone caught in theft was to be deprived of his eyes, have his ears, hands, and feet cut off, have the skin of his head stripped away, and then be exposed to be torn apart by wild beasts and birds. It happened, however, that an innocent man, punished by that penalty, nearly lost his hearing because the passages of his ears were blocked with blood. His relatives carried him to the oratory of Saint Swithun so that his hearing alone might be restored; but he obtained not only that, but also other things he had not requested.

A certain woman, sleeping with the door open in a village of the city of Winchester, was carried from her bed into the forest by a wolf, which summoned other wolves to itself with a dreadful howl. The woman, weakened both by hunger and by age, did not know what to do. She turned to prayer, implored divine aid, and called upon Saint Swithun. When the wolf heard his name, it fell asleep, and the woman slipped away. When the wolf awoke, it pursued her with its companions, but could not harm the woman whom the mercy of God and of the blessed bishop had undertaken to save.

7. The Bishop of Sherborne honorably placed in his church a statue of Saint Swithun that he had obtained from the brothers, where splendid miracles frequently took place. A certain leper came to this statue not to obtain healing, but to receive alms from those who offered prayers there. After he had fallen asleep there for a short while, it seemed to him that Saint Swithun was present, wiping away his leprosy with his hand and suddenly driving the whole disease from him. On waking, he gladly loosened his belt before everyone and showed that he had been cleansed.

[Col. 0061]

THE HISTORY OF THE TRANSLATION AND MIRACLES, by Lantfred, apparently, [Note: [Col. 0061D] In the preliminary commentary we touched upon matters relating to this.] a monk of Winchester in England.

From the very ancient Bigot manuscript.

CHAPTER ONE. Saint Swithun’s body divinely revealed, and miracles.

[Col. 0061B]

1. In the time of the most fortunate King Fabgar [Eadgar], [Note: [Col. 0061D] Elsewhere he is written Edgar. Our Alford, in volume [of the] Annals of the Church of England, places his birth in the year 943, on the basis of earlier authorities, and his death in 975; he also discusses him in various places in the cited volume.] king of the English and most glorious emperor of the entire island of Albion, [Note: [Col. 0061D] That is, Britain. Aristotle’s translator, in Cellarius, book III of Ancient Geography, chapter 4, page 280, said that Albion and Jerna—that is, Britain and Ireland—[are meant], as is established from Cellarius himself in the same work, page 254.] in the year 971 of the Incarnation of our Lord and Savior of the world Jesus Christ, in the fourteenth indiction, almighty God deigned to reveal to the English Saxons [Note: [Col. 0062D] The part of England in which Winchester lies is designated here. Malmesbury, book I of On the Deeds of the Kings of the English, chapter 1, discusses the arrival of the English and Saxons in Britain.] the holy body of the blessed Bishop Swithun. Through his merits, with God’s favor, so many sick people were restored to their former health that no living person had ever heard by report, seen with bodily eyes, or learned by reading that such numbers had been healed at the tomb of any saint. Nevertheless, the life and former conduct of this miraculous bishop are unknown to us, since no writings about them exist; but the mercy of almighty God deigned to make his merits most clearly manifest through the miracles that shone forth.

2. Three years, therefore, before the sacred remains of the aforesaid bishop were taken from the mausoleum in which they had once been buried by the most reverend bishop of that place, Athelwold, and his brothers, the saint himself appeared in sleep to a truthful smith, radiant with an angelic appearance, and said to him:

“Do you recognize that canon who was recently expelled from the old monastery [Note: [Col. 0062D] For elucidation of this passage, consult what was said near the beginning, no. 18, in the preliminary commentary.] together with the other men living wickedly? So that you may recognize him clearly, his name is Eadsin.”

The smith replied: “I once knew him, Father, but now I do not know where he is.”

The bishop said to him: “He is now living at Wincelcumbe.” [Note: [Col. 0062D] The place is unknown to me. Perhaps it was some village or a small town of little distinction.]

And he added: “I ask you, and command you in the name of Christ, to go to him quickly and tell him my orders:

“‘This is what Bishop Swithun commands you, Eadsin: hasten to the city of Winchester, and tell the bishop who now at last governs the diocese over which I once presided to raise my body from the grave and place it in the church, since it has been granted to him from heaven that I am to be revealed in his time.’”

3. But the smith said to the saint: “Lord, he will in no way believe my words.”

The holy man replied: “So that he may believe your words, tell him to go to my tomb and pull out one ring from among these three that are fixed into the cover of my sarcophagus. If he immediately follows through on this, let it be truly evident to him that I sent you to him. But if he cannot pull it out from here, then he ought in no way to believe you.

“Afterward you may confidently tell him that, if he desires to enjoy the well-being of both lives, he must change his ways and actions for the better and hasten without ceasing toward the blessedness of the heavenly homeland. Moreover, proclaim prophetically to everyone that, as soon as they open my burial place, they will find treasures so immeasurable and precious that everything in the world consisting of gold and jewels will seem worthless in comparison with them.”

After the holy prophet had delivered such commands to the smith, he flew upward to heaven. But the smith, initially afraid of appearing deceitful, did not dare to tell anyone living of this vision at all the first time.

[Col. 0062D]

4. When he had been warned a second and a third time, the same holy bishop sharply rebuked him for refusing to obey his commands. At last he approached the tomb of the gracious bishop and, taking hold of one of the rings mentioned above, said in these words to the Lord, creator of all things:

“Lord God, creator of every creature, grant me, a sinner, that if this saint who rests here in body appeared three times before my eyes in the sleep of night, I may now pull out this little iron sphere, just as the same man of God recently took pains to disclose it to my ears in a dream vision.”

As soon as he pulled the steel ring, the stone mass followed it, as though it had been fixed in sea sand. When he placed it back in its own crevice, it remained fixed, having been pressed a little with his heel, so that afterward no one could pull it out from there.

5. On that same day, while he was crossing the marketplace, he encountered a certain little servant of the aforementioned cleric who was coming to Winchester for an urgent purchase. He told him what he had seen in his dreams and humbly begged him to relate it to his master. After a long interval of time, when the servant reached his own master, he remained silent, having forgotten the matter; but later, moved by penitence, he carefully told his master everything he had heard from the smith.

At that time the cleric so detested not only the bishop of the Winchester diocese but also all the brothers living there, because of the expulsion of the canons—men who practiced abominable and utterly filthy ways, for which the venerable Athelwold had expelled them from the aforesaid monastery—that he refused to hear the message, rather than making any effort to fulfill the commands of the holy Father. But after the course of two years had been completed, through the favor of the mercy of the heavenly Creator, who freely draws to his grace all those whom he has summoned to labor in the Lord’s vineyard, the same cleric who shortly before had been [lacuna] became a venerable monk. For we ourselves saw that it happened just as this little book now shows. Blessed be almighty God, who justifies sinners, saves those who hope in him, humbles the proud, and exalts the humble!

6. Thus, two years before the discovery of the sacred body, a certain hunchbacked man, extremely bent because of a huge goiter, heard in a dream that he should come to Winchester and there receive health through the merit of Saint Swithun. Rising in the morning, he supported his hump with two camburta, [Note: [Col. 0063] Camburta means a support or staff.] as best he could, and reached Winchester. After remaining there for a long time, he was again admonished by an angelic visitation to go to the tomb of the holy Bishop Swithun. Kneeling, he begged the Lord that he might be healed there through the merits of that saint, just as he had heard in his dream. As soon as he rose from his prayers, he was so divinely healed that nowhere did any deformity of a hump appear.

As the day of the most sacred solemnity approached, on which the venerable bishop of God, Swithun, freed from bodily bonds, departed from this world to the Lord, a certain man was miserably weakened in all his limbs by demonic deceptions. After he had been tormented for a long time, his neighbors and relatives brought him to the tomb of God’s saint, and spent that night in vigil with their suffering friend, persevering in prayers. In the morning the sick man, overcome by sleep, dozed off for a short while, and it seemed to him that certain people approached him and removed one of his shoes from his foot. Immediately afterward he returned home healthy with his friends. His slipper, however, was searched for intensely but found nowhere. Eight other infirm people were healed at the holy man’s mausoleum before his bones were raised from there.

CHAPTER TWO. The translation of the body and other miracles.

7. When these things had taken place, on the Ides of July the venerable Bishop Athelwold, together with his fellow bishops and abbots and with many monks, raised the sacred relics from the tomb by order of the glorious King Fabgar [Eadgar] and placed them with great reverence in the basilica of the apostles Peter and Paul. There benefits are granted to all who ask in true faith.

Afterward, four sick people received healing at his tomb over a period of three days. Then, for a period of five months, there was scarcely a day on which the sick were not healed at the honorable relics of that saint—sometimes three, sometimes five, sometimes seven, sometimes ten, now twelve, and now fifteen. We saw more than two hundred sick people healed through the saint’s merit in ten days, and, over the course of a year, numbers that cannot be counted. Therefore let the unbelieving come to God’s saint, so that they may acknowledge the Creator’s benefits and praise the Creator.

8. Let the faithful know, finally, that our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, who at the beginning of this age, veiled in the garment of flesh, himself gave sight to the blind, granted the lame the ability to walk, restored hearing to the deaf, healed paralytics, raised the dead, and walked upon the sea with dry footsteps—in our own times likewise bestows the benefit of healing upon the bodies of the sick, innumerable beyond counting like the sands of the sea, in order to glorify the omnipotence of his majesty and manifest the merit of the outstanding priest Swithun.

Blessed be almighty God, who in our time has deigned to make his saint wonderful through signs and powers; who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages. Amen.

9. At the time when the Lord of all things was revealing his saint Swithun to humanity, it happened that twenty-six sick people came to Winchester on a single day to recover their health. Some of them were blind, some deaf, some mute, and some paralytic. When they had approached the monument of the holy bishop and poured out their prayers before God, they were all healed through his intercession within three days, and so returned home joyfully, with great gladness, magnifying and praising the Lord.

Not long afterward, one hundred and twenty-four infirm people came to the same saint from various regions of the English and Saxons, afflicted with many different illnesses. All of them, by the merit of the holy bishop and by God’s will, were healed of their various diseases within the course of two weeks, and returned safely to their homes, blessing the Lord, though they had come there weak.

A certain man was blinded during the Greater Litanies because of theft. But since he had been blinded while innocent, he came on the Epiphany of the Lord to the mausoleum of Saint Swithun and humbly poured out his prayers. His eyes, which had been extinguished and completely torn out by iron, were illumined. Afterward he possessed clear eyes for the whole of his life.

Therefore, since we are wholly unable to enumerate all the miracles that the Lord has deigned to perform through Saint Swithun, let us ask the holy bishop to deign to heal the illnesses of our souls by interceding for us with the Lord, with whom he merited to remain forever because of his good works.

Thus, when the Savior of the world had decided to display so many signs at the tomb of the venerable Father Swithun, Bishop Athelwold, of blessed memory, ordered the brothers living there always to go immediately to the church and glorify God with hymns and praises whenever anyone received healing through the merit of the holy man.

10. It happened, however, that after several days certain men began to complain bitterly that they were sometimes awakened four times during the night, sometimes three, and began to persuade the others wickedly to abandon what their bishop had piously commanded them. When this had been carelessly neglected for a period of fifteen days, Saint Swithun himself appeared in a dream to a certain faithful man and said to him:

“Go to the old monastery and tell the brothers that their murmuring greatly displeases almighty God, because every day he performs many miracles before them, while they act so unjustly that they do not give him thanks but put transitory concerns before divine works. Add also that, if they cease from their praises, the great works of God will immediately cease; but if they do not cease glorifying God, he will perform so many wonders there that no living person remembers such things ever having been done anywhere.”

After the aforesaid man awoke following the saint’s departure, he hastened to Bishop Athelwold and reported to him everything that God’s saint had commanded. The bishop, angered that the brothers had not acted according to the saint’s order, again sent word to the monks, with a grave warning, that whenever healings took place at the saint’s tomb, all should go together to the church at the ringing of the signal and sing praises to almighty God in hymnic voices.

We have heard that this has been observed from then until now. To him be glory and praise, almighty God, who has deigned thus to glorify his saint, who lives and reigns throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

MIRACLES OF SAINT SWITHUN

From the most ancient parchment leaves in the codex of the Queen of Sweden, no. 769.

[Col. 0065]

CHAPTER ONE. First part of the miracles.

[Col. 0065C]

1. After the body of the most holy bishop had been placed within the church, as was stated above, four or five sick people received healing at his tomb over a period of three days. When the three days had passed, for nearly five months there was scarcely a day on which the sick were not healed in the basilica where the relics of the holy man had been deposited—sometimes as many as sixteen or eighteen, sometimes fewer, five or three, and very frequently seven, eight, ten, twelve, or fifteen. We saw more than two hundred people healed through the saint’s merit in ten days, and, over the course of a year, numbers beyond counting.

[Col. 0065D]

2. We also saw the streets around the aforementioned [Note: [Col. 0065D] That is, the aforesaid monastery. The author is evidently assumed to have been referring to it; what we give here is not a complete history but a fragment, mutilated at least at its beginning and end.] monastery so filled on both sides with crowds of sick people that a traveler could scarcely find a path by which to walk to it. After several days, by God’s favor and through the saint’s merits, they were so healed that scarcely five sick people could be found even inside the basilica.

Therefore let the envious and the reprobate be silent—those who either deny the glorious miracles of this saint or, unable to deny them, twist them into an evil interpretation. Let the unbelieving also come to the holy servant of God, so that they may acknowledge the Creator’s benefits and praise the Creator.

Finally, let the faithful know that our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, who at the beginning of this age, veiled in the garment of flesh, himself gave sight to the blind, granted the lame the ability to walk, restored hearing to the deaf, healed paralytics, raised the dead, and walked upon the sea with dry footsteps, likewise in our times, to glorify the omnipotence of his majesty and manifest the merit of the outstanding priest, grants the benefit of healing to the bodies of the sick, innumerable beyond counting like the sands of the sea, whose number cannot be reckoned.

[Col. 0067A]

3. In those days three blind women lived on the island of Wight. One had never seen bodily light with her eyes; the other two had been blind for a period of nine years. When they heard that the blind were given sight at the tomb of the holy bishop and that the sick also were healed through the power of the Lord Jesus Christ, they asked their relatives and kinsmen to lead them as quickly as possible across the island [Note: [Col. 0067D] To lead them across the island. The island of Wight, in the British Sea and in the province of Hampshire, where Winchester is situated, lies almost adjacent to it and is separated from it by only a narrow strait.] surrounded on every side by the waves of the Ocean, so that they might more easily reach the place where the bishop of Christ rested in body. [Note: [Col. 0067D] That is, in body. From Greek σῶμα, “body.” The manuscript Life of Saint Magnobodus, bishop of Angers, chapter 51: “Where the bodies of many of the faithful, held worthy of veneration, rest.”]

When they had been put ashore outside the island and were drifting without a guide, wholly unaware of what they could do, the merciful Creator of creatures, taking pity on their helplessness, gave them [a certain young man mute from birth] [Note: [Col. 0067D] The words in brackets were supplied in his own hand by P. Papebrochius, who added in the margin: “It seemed that this should be read thus, the letters having been almost entirely erased by accident.”] about twenty years of age.

When they had reached the same place, the women began with one voice to beg him to lead them to the city of Winchester, where the holy bishop was powerful through miraculous signs. By God’s marvelous design, moved by their prayers, he led the aforesaid blind women along a winding road to the place. On the very night when they entered the basilica in which the bones of God’s servant rested, the three blind women, through the merit of the holy bishop, were deemed worthy to receive the light of their eyes from the true light, God.

4. At the dawning of the light of morning, the young man who had guided the women was able to speak correctly whatever he wished. He immediately signaled to the custodian to come outside the church, so that he might speak with him. The custodian, wondering what he wished to say, came to him and asked why he had summoned him.

The young man said to him: “Know for certain that I can now speak properly.”

The custodian replied: “Could you speak before?”

He answered: “I had never spoken before, and you have now heard the first words that have come from my mouth. Yesterday I was mute, but I brought three blind women here; with God’s help they can now see. Therefore go and call the brothers, so that they may give thanks in the customary manner.”

5. At the same time, a certain little servant girl had been bound by her own master at Winchester in iron fetters and accursed shackles for a small offense. She was being kept until the next day to be tortured with dreadful beatings and some stripes. All night long she did not cease to plead with God, her face wet with tears, that through the intercession of the holy bishop he might free her from the worst torturer.

When the hour of day brightened at which she was to suffer severe torture, amid prayers and groans, the fetters fell from her feet. Immediately escaping the danger, she fled, while her masters slept, to the tomb of the sacred bishop, still bound in shackles on her hands.

Then certain people informed her master that the aforesaid servant girl had fled to God’s holy servant and, through his benefits, had been freed from her fetters. When he heard this, he was stirred by anger and went there with the utmost haste. Not of his own will but compelled by God, he retained the hand-shackles, allowed the girl to depart unharmed, and inflicted no harm upon her for that deed.

6. A certain man had lived for many years as a paralytic in an English province called Hamme in their language. He was so weakened in all his limbs that he could not possibly rise from the support on which he reclined.

When he heard of the miracles that the Lord performed at Winchester through the merits of the holy prophet, he began thoughtfully to consider that it would be more pleasant for him if he could spend at least one night in vigil before the life-giving remains of the man of God. He summoned his relatives and friendly neighbors and earnestly begged them to saddle their horses and place him on a bier, [Note: [Col. 0068D] It is a litter on which the dead are carried out; elsewhere bacapulus or baccapulus, as in Du Cange.] and carry him to the body of the holy bishop.

His friends obeyed his instructions and quickly did what he had commanded. But before the sick man had finished speaking, through the compassion of the glorious bishop he was healed: rising from his bed, he set out on foot and outran all the mounted companions who were traveling with him. With swift steps he reached the place where the relics of the gracious bishop were venerated, safe and sound, while his companions were still far behind, even though horses and supports were aiding them.

7. A powerful matron also lived in another English province called in their language Bedfordshire. [Note: [Col. 0068D] The county of Bedford, a province of England, situated in its central region, quite small and extending from north to south. To the north it borders the counties of Northampton and Huntingdon; to the east, Cambridge and Hertford; to the west and south, Buckingham. Its principal town is called Bedford.] She had been blind for three years, so that she could not behold even the brightness of the sun’s light.

While she was being tormented by great pains, she promised the holy Bishop Swithun that she would give him many gifts if through his merit she received the light of her eyes. When her servants had brought her to the bones of the most blessed man, she gave God and Saint Swithun a certain garment. As she placed it beneath the altar, she immediately merited to receive the light that she had long since lost.

With devout heart she gave praise to God and, after receiving health, took food; then she returned home in the greatest joy. She had approached the tomb of the holy bishop in deepest sorrow, but departed through the power of God, creator of all, and of our Savior Jesus Christ in gladness.

8. Another housewife also began to fall ill with a serious disease at the same time. Her relatives and servants therefore approached her one after another, groaning and urging her to arrange her possessions before the end of death arrived, since they thought she would die soon.

As the unbearable illness grew worse each day, and she had been placed in despair of this life because death was near, she promised God and the holy Bishop Swithun that, if through his intercession she should receive any relief from her illness, she would come to his mausoleum with many gifts as soon as she was able and spend one night in vigil before the most sacred body of God’s servant.

As she made this promise, she obtained bodily health, but lost the strength of her mind: she forgot God’s benefits, failed to keep the promises by which she had bound herself, and did not render the thanks due to God, as was fitting.

9. After some time, while she was planning to ride with her husband to a certain wedding, she ordered her servants to prepare the best horses. After they had been magnificently adorned with trappings, her husband went ahead with a few retainers, and she followed more quickly with a larger company.

When she mounted the caparisoned horse and rode behind her husband, she felt no pain at all and no discomfort from any illness. But when she reached the aforesaid wedding, where many counts and numerous powerful royal retainers were present, the illness from which she had recently been cured through God’s holy servant suddenly seized her again.

Only then did she understand that she had acted unjustly: although she had been healed by God through the saint’s merit, she had not given glory to the Creator. Immediately, insofar as she was able, she repented and summoned her servants. As best she could speak, she humbly begged them to carry her as quickly as possible to the place where the holy man rested, so that through God’s mercy she might again receive health.

When she had been carried there with the help of her servants, she was healed again during the following night. The next day she returned safely to the aforementioned wedding, rendering the most just thanks to almighty God.

10. While the illustrious Lord and Savior of the world was making his saint wonderful through prodigies and powers, the venerable Bishop Adelwold, who presided over the diocese of Winchester, ordered the brothers living there in those days that whenever anyone received the desired bodily healing through the power of the Lord and the merit of the holy bishop, all the brothers of that place should immediately leave whatever tasks were necessary or whatever they held in their hands, go to the church, and worthily glorify God.

It happened, however, that certain men, enticed by the deceits of demons, complained bitterly that they were so often roused from their nightly rest—sometimes three times, sometimes four times in a single night—and persuaded the others wickedly to abandon what their bishop had piously commanded them.

11. When this had been carelessly neglected for a period of fifteen days, God’s holy servant grieved that the aforesaid brothers considered a good work of little value, did not obey the commands of their bishop, and did not offer God his due praises, but had fallen into Satan’s destructive traps. One night he appeared in a dream [Note: [Col. 0069D] This apparition is given above, more briefly, in the History taken from the Bigot manuscript, with some changes in the accompanying details.] to a certain venerable matron, dressed in a snow-white melote and a long garment, wearing on his head a golden crown appropriately adorned with precious gems and beautifully decorated with Indian pearls, and shod in very beautiful sandals.

He said to her in the gentlest words:

“As soon as you see the Bishop of Winchester, beloved of God, tell him to order the monks living there not to cease glorifying almighty God whenever any sick person receives healing at the tomb of Bishop Swithun. For it greatly displeases almighty God, the author of miracles, that he performs innumerable miracles daily before the eyes of the saints while they act so unjustly that they do not give God praise, but put fleeting and evil pursuits—an offense even to mention—before divine works.

“Let it not, I beg, be burdensome for them to glorify the Author of all virtues for each of the virtues of the King who created all things, lest they experience the anger of the Judge of the living and the dead. What more is there to say?”

12. Henceforth, if anyone ceases from praise, filled with the stain of envy, sluggishness, and pride, unless he wipes away this offense through repentance, he will by no means escape the deceit of his vices.

Indeed, for this reason God offers the world so many and such unheard-of miracles in these latter times: so that the stony hearts of men may soften, the hearts of the wicked may come to their senses, and they may hasten through good works toward heavenly joys. Signs are to be given to unbelieving peoples, but they are by no means necessary to the faithful.

Do those who treat his benefits as worthless obey God, the creator of all things? Do they not provoke the Lord to anger who deny his magnificence through silence? Add also this: if the brothers cease from praises, the great works of God will immediately cease.

13. But if they do not cease to magnify the heavenly King, the Lord of all will perform there so many and such great miracles as no living person remembers ever having been performed anywhere on earth, after the divinity that joined a twofold mighty nature in the one person of Christ—God and man, servant and Lord, creature and Creator—raised our humanity to the heavens.

As soon as God’s holy servant had gloriously delivered such commands to the matron in the vision of sleep, he turned away his angelic face and, with flashing light, ascended Olympus.

The matron, however, waking from the heaviness of sleep after the saint’s departure, began to grieve deeply because she was deprived of the ineffable radiance that she had seen in her dream. As soon as she was able, she rose from the support on which she lay, summoned the venerable bishop, and endeavored to tell him everything that she had received in sleep from the angel of Christ.

[Col. 0071A]

14. He was somewhat moved, as befit a wise man, by the fact that the brothers had not acted according to the saint’s command. He again sent instructions to the monks from the king’s palace, where in those days they served God, the almighty, for the common good of the kingdom: if anyone were present who did not give praise to God and immediately hasten to the church whenever any sick person received health through the power of the Holy Trinity, that person was to perform penance for seven days, eating and drinking nothing except water and bread.

From that time onward, whenever any miracle occurred at the body of the blessed man, whether by day or in the middle of the night, it was never neglected that the sacristan should ring a small bell, so that the brothers might not go to the monastery to glorify almighty God—to whom belong honor, power, and dominion, glory [Note: [Col. 0071D] That is, glory; in Greek δόξα, “glory.”], majesty, peace, and rejoicing throughout immortal ages of ages.

### 15

Finally, a certain man from London was at that time so weakened in all his limbs that he could no longer hope for any remedy at all. When he heard of the reputation of the miracles that were being performed at the prophet’s tomb through the piety of the Savior of the world—*cosmi* [Note: That is, “world,” in Greek *κόσμος*.]—his relatives carried him to Winchester, according to his desire. He longed to approach the little body of Christ’s servant and spend one night keeping vigil there, but he was entirely unable to do so because of the severity of his pain.

When he was carried there after several days, he was healed from heaven that same night. The man himself had been struck by such a grave illness that his hands and feet could be seen turned backward behind him. But almighty God, merciful and compassionate, who does not abandon all who hope in him, took pity on his creature through the merit of holy Swithun, restoring to the sick man the former vigor of his body, for the glorification of his name. Thus, once restored to health, he magnified the Lord, who alone performs great wonders, throughout all his days.

### 16

Finally, sixteen blind people of both sexes once came together from the aforesaid city to Winchester. Of these, fifteen were divinely given sight on the first day; but the sixteenth, when the following morning dawned, together with many other sick people, merited receiving healing through the merit of the holy bishop. [Col. 0071D] Thus they later returned joyfully to London, giving God the most fitting thanks, those who had recently come blind now seeing.

There was also a lame man in that same city of London, disabled in both feet. By seeking healing through various provinces, he had nearly exhausted all his resources. At length he was carried on horseback to the holy Augustine, archbishop of Canterbury, [Note: He is treated at length on 26 May.] and through Augustine’s intercession he merited recovering the health of one foot. After a short interval, when he heard of the reputation of the miracles at Winchester, [Note: In our manuscript I repeatedly find *Pintoniam* written instead of *Wintoniam*; I have substituted *Wintoniam*.] he came there and approached the little body of the holy man. On that very day he was healed in the other foot, and he immediately returned home joyfully on his feet, magnifying the Lord in words.

### 17

At one time twenty-five sick people came to the holy servant of God from various provinces of the English, afflicted by different illnesses: namely, blind, lame, deaf, and mute people. Within the space of a single day, through the glorious intervention of the outstanding priest, all of them merited receiving healing from the Lord.

A certain very wealthy count also had a son who, from birth, enjoyed bodily sight for five years. When that period had passed, he lost it and remained blind for another five years. While his mother kept vigil over him one night, together with a very large crowd of dependents, in the church where the relics of the venerable man rested, as dawn brought in the day the glaucoma departed from his eyes, and, by God’s will, he was able to see clearly.

## CHAPTER II  
### The Second Part of the Miracles

### 18

It must not be passed over in silence that, before the discovery of the most sacred body of Bishop Swithun, a certain man born of noble lineage and possessing very great wealth lived in the same region of England. He became blind through an accident.

Accordingly, he went to Rome with complete devotion of mind, so that he might be healed there through the blessed bodies of the saints, of which innumerable ones rest there. He remained for nearly five years in prayers, but obtained no cure for his blindness.

While he was staying there, he heard from pilgrims who were coming to Rome from the lands of the English to the thresholds of the apostles that the Lord healed innumerable illnesses of the sick through the merit of Saint Swithun. He therefore quickly left the aforesaid city and, returning to the region from which he had been born, sought out the tomb of the holy bishop before he sought that part of the kingdom from which he was born—or rather [*imo eum*], “him” (the bishop). When he arrived there, he merited receiving his former sight that same night. Illuminated by the Lord, the creator of the world, he returned home unharmed, glorifying the King of heaven and praising God, the creator of all.

### 19

In those days a certain man lived in a city called by its proper name Brofeceaster. He was blind and paralyzed on both sides. His relatives led him to Winchester, where he received healing through the omnipotence of the Holy Trinity.

Indeed, after he approached the church in which the limbs of the holy man rested, he persevered there in vigils and prayers for three days and nights. When these had been completed, his eyes were opened, and the former strength returned to his arms and hands. He immediately departed from there healed, blessing God.

### 20

A man also lived in a province of the English called *hunum* [lacuna]. He had been blind for seven years. As is customary for those deprived of sight, he had a guide who led him either to church or wherever he needed to go, and brought him home again whenever he wished.

At a certain time the guide, in anger, left the blind man a great distance from his lodging. Since he had no idea how to return home, he prayed to God, the ruler of all things, with earnest cries, asking him to look upon him mercifully. He poured out prayers such as these:

“O Lord, ruler of angels and of human beings, I know that nothing can be hidden from your providence. You see me deprived of light, far removed from my own dwelling, and abandoned by a stubborn guide. Look upon my humility; dispose my actions according to your will, direct my steps toward you, and grant me, most wretched as I am, everlasting light in the heavenly dwelling with the saints and the elect.

“Have mercy on me, Lord, according to your will, and deal with me according to the clemency of your compassion. Do not abandon me any longer, Lord, into the hands of the wicked. Either receive my soul from this little body, or, through the merits of Saint Swithun, restore clear light to my blindness.

“I also beg you, most compassionate bishop, through whom the magnificent Author of all things grants healing for the various illnesses of the sick: come to my aid through your holy prayers. For I believe that you will obtain immediately whatever you ask from the Lord. Therefore ask the Prince of light to restore the light of my eyes to me.”

### 21

When that blind man had poured out such prayers with profound groaning, his eyes were immediately opened in that very place. He was able to see the brightness of the air, which he had been unable to see during the previous seven years, and he returned home safely without a guide.

His neighbors and relatives were astonished beyond belief at how their kinsman, who had departed from there shortly before deprived of sight, had plainly been illuminated by the Lord. When they learned that their friend had recovered his health through the venerable bishop of God, they glorified the Lord with one voice—he who alone performs great wonders, whose name and dominion remain forever throughout the ages of ages.

### 22

In those same days four people of both sexes lived in a part of the British region called Eastsexan. [Note: Commonly Essex, in Latin *Essexia*, a province in the eastern part of England.] For many cycles of summers they had been tormented by pains and various illnesses: two men were blind, while two women were weak in both hands and lame in their feet.

When they heard of the benefits of God, which almighty God had deigned to bestow through his servant upon those suffering in their limbs, they came to the tomb of the holy bishop, beseeching in humble prayer the triune and one God of heaven and earth.

When they had arrived together, the eyes of the blind were immediately opened, and sound health was at once restored to the women’s hands and feet. They began to walk before all who stood around, and with their hands to imprint the sign of the holy cross upon their foreheads, and to perform everything that was necessary. Thus they returned home blessing the Lord, the author of healings.

### 23

At that same time, a female servant belonging to a certain man had been stolen in the northern districts of England. Greedy traffickers led her to the city in which the holy bishop’s body rested, and sold her to a certain man of that city, Urbanus.

After she had remained there under another master for a long period, it happened that the man from whom she had first been stolen came to Winchester to purchase things he needed. When the servant girl heard this, she boldly went to speak with her former master without the permission of the man whose authority then held her subject.

When the mistress whom the servant served learned that she had been speaking with a man from another province, she ordered her to be bound in fetters, in great anger, so that she could not in any way return to her former master.

### 24

The next day it happened that this same woman went out at daybreak on some business useful to herself, leaving the servant girl fettered at home. As soon as she could, the girl went outside and sat miserably beside the threshold of the house.

Then, with the whole attention of her mind, she began to implore the all-creating God to free her from the terrible bonds of her wicked mistress. Turning toward that church in which the body of the holy bishop was honored with fitting reverence, she diligently begged God’s aid through his intercession, and immediately obtained the assistance she desired.

### 25

Meanwhile, a priest venerable for his gray hair, clothed in garments of dazzling whiteness, hurried to the chained woman and gently asked why she was sorrowful—*elegam*. [Note: That is, “sad”; a Greco-barbarous word from the Greek *ἔλεγος*, “mourning, lamentation.”]

Taking her right arm in his hand, he carried her to the tomb of the saint with a swift, piercing motion. Among the innumerable crowd of people who surrounded the monastery entrance like a fortification, he set her down beside the sacred altar, still bound below the entrance by a fetter. The holy man was resting bodily upon that altar.

It was astonishing and wondrous that none of those standing around saw her, nor the priest who brought her there, until she had been set down in the chapel. The people present then saw the chapel locked with a key by its guardians. Her mistress, for her part, followed the servant’s tracks as rapidly as she could.

### 26

When the monk who guarded the saint saw her—the monk who possessed the little key to the chapel where the bishop’s body rested—he was exceedingly astonished and said to himself:

“Who shut this woman inside the saint’s chamber, which I see? Perhaps he found the door open, although shortly before I myself closed it with the bolt.”

Approaching the chapel door, he said to her, with the people listening:

“Tell me, woman, who brought you inside this venerable little place where you now appear to be standing? With what presumptuous boldness did you dare to enter the enclosure where the bishop of Christ rests bodily? How could you remain hidden? I certainly did not see you when I closed the door.”

Then she saw a certain young cleric standing behind her outside the balcony. [Note: In Italian *balconi*, in French *balcons*, are projecting recesses. On this word Acharisius, in Du Cange, writes: “Some say that it is a word proper to the Venetians, others to the Genoese.”]

She replied to the beadle, saying:

“Although I resisted, this cleric lifted me upon his shoulders, carried me to his place, and just now set me down before the saint.”

The cleric, on the contrary, replied under oath:

“I have never before seen you with my eyes.”

### 27

The woman said: “But you yourself brought me here.”

The cleric replied: “I would rather nocturnal dogs had torn you apart with dreadful bites than that I should have placed such a dishonorable burden upon my back.”

Coming to herself, she then related the following:

“A certain priest, gray-haired and greatly venerable, dressed in brilliantly shining garments, found me weeping at my mistress’s threshold. He consoled me with words sweeter than any I can describe. Taking hold of the right sleeve of my garment, he immediately carried me to this basilica, with such speed and bodily ease that I cannot express it in words. Since, after he set me down at this entrance, I saw no other cleric standing around except this young man, I therefore thought that he was the one who had brought me here.”

### 28

When the crowds of people who were present from various parts of England heard these things, they were exceedingly amazed and glorified the Lord, the king of all and the Savior of humankind, who had deigned to perform such unheard-of miracles through the glorious merits of his holy priest.

To him be glory, praise, and dominion; with the Father and the holy Spirit—*Pneumate* [Note: That is, “spirit,” from the Greek *πνεῦμα*.]—he lives as one God and reigns throughout infinite ages.

### 29

At that time two women came from the distant western regions to the tomb of the man of God with prayers. One could not see light with her own eyes; the other had been mute from birth, almost until old age.

The mute woman guided the blind woman throughout the entire journey, asking passersby to show her the path along which she should walk. When they came together to the place where the holy bishop rested, the blind woman received sight and the mute woman the ability to speak.

Healed from heaven through the merit of the glorious man, they immediately returned home, glorifying almighty God.

### 30

Then thirty-six sick people came to Winchester to recover their health. Some were blind, some deaf, some mute, and some paralyzed. When they approached the monument of the holy bishop and poured out prayers before God, they were all healed within three days through his intervention. Thus they returned home joyfully and with great happiness, magnifying and praising the Lord.

### 31

Not long afterward, one hundred and twenty-four people came to the same holy man from various regions of the Anglo-Saxons, afflicted by many different illnesses. Through the merit of the holy bishop, all of them, by God’s will, were healed of their various diseases within the course of two [days], and they returned safely to their homes, blessing the Lord—those who had come weak and sick.

### 32

I consider it unworthy to pass over in silence that a certain man had been most harshly bound in iron for a parricide that he had committed unlawfully [lacuna]. He bore nine rings of iron upon his body, tormenting himself for the crime for as many years in a foreign land.

When news spread and he heard of the famous wonders of God that were being performed in the English province through the merit of his saint, he came to Winchester from overseas lands by divine guidance.

While he prayed to God for a long time with humble entreaties, asking that through the healing intervention of the holy bishop the unbearable pain of his torment might be relieved, by God’s favor the iron ring that cut into his belly—so deeply that it had already penetrated to the innermost vital organs—burst apart and sprang out from the man’s viscera, from which it had inflicted an immense torment.

Finally, another ring that grievously tortured the man’s arm fell immediately at his feet, since the flesh wound had swollen and was already entirely covered with pus and blood. At once the sharp torment of pain departed from him.

That ring had been so tightly fastened that it scarcely appeared capable of admitting three fingers. It was therefore a wonder that it sprang intact from the man’s arm. As a testimony to this miracle, it was hung in the same monastery.

### 33

In the times just mentioned, a certain merchant named Flodoaldus, a man prudent in secular affairs and possessing abundant wealth, had a servant whom he loved greatly.

The servant was arrested for a certain crime by the king’s governor and ordered to be held by the royal attendants until his master arrived. He was then to carry a piece of iron heated among coals with his bare hands. If he were innocent, he was to be released unharmed; if he were found guilty, he was to be punished by death.

When the servant’s master heard that he was being held in chains under savage guards, he hurried there as quickly as he could. He begged the king’s prefect to abandon the judgment and to allow him to retain his servant, under the condition stated above, unharmed.

[Note: *Senior* is a barbarous form derived from the French word *seigneur*, “lord.” See Du Cange’s Glossary.]

### 34

The prefect, however, was not at all swayed by his promises. Exceedingly proud of his worldly office, he ordered the servant to carry a red-hot mass of iron for the sake of his secular authority.

When the servant’s master heard this, he grieved deeply for the servant, who seemed destined to perish. He again promised the royal governor a pound of pure silver and likewise agreed to let him keep the servant mentioned above, begging him to abandon the unjust judgment. He could not endure the loss and disgrace of having his slave slaughtered for a petty offense and crime.

The friends and relatives of the accused man also promised enormous gifts to the king’s *gastaldus*. [Note: This was the name given to the governors of regions and cities, whose duties included administering justice to the people and presiding over the trials of humbler subjects. Du Cange provides more information.] They eagerly desired above all to free their kinsman from a dishonorable death.

### 35

Nevertheless, the prefect rejected their entreaties and compelled the aforesaid man to carry in his bare hand an iron object of extraordinary size, burning hot and glowing with much charcoal.

When that man, forced by the governor, timidly carried it in his hand, an enormous burn immediately filled his palm and scorched the skin. His hand was sealed in the customary manner until the third day.

On the following day Flodoaldus summoned the man and found him condemned and guilty. Indeed, overcome with grief for the man’s impending death, he summoned his brother and the companions who were present and prepared to return home, since, as we have said, he could not bear to see the afflicted man undergo the capital sentence.

### 36

Why say more? The master, together with his entire company, implored the Author of all things in humble prayer to free that man from a dishonorable death through the intercession of Saint Swithun. He turned his prayers to the Savior of the world, saying with all the effort of his mind:

“Almighty Lord God, free this slave through the intervention of the glorious bishop, and I shall give him to that saint through whose merit you heal the dreadful diseases of the sick, if from heaven you rescue him from the wicked hands of those who seek to kill him.”

After the second day had passed from the time he carried the iron, and when Phoebus was beginning the third day—*hymeram* [Note: That is, “day,” in Greek *ἡμέρα*.]—he was led before the governor, so that the attendants standing around might see whether he was free from the crime charged against him.

What more can I say in a lengthy account?

### 37

When they had come before the judges, the hostile accusers themselves judged the man innocent and asserted that he should remain unharmed, although his own master had seen him as deserving punishment and his friends had believed that he would immediately be condemned to a cruel death.

Thus the grief of his friends was changed into joy. It was astonishing beyond measure: his supporters saw the burn and swelling, while the accusers saw his palm so sound that it seemed the iron had not touched the servant at all.

When the companions saw this, they all gave praise to almighty God and glorified Jesus the Savior. They returned rejoicing to the place from which they had come in sadness, firmly believing that their kinsman had been divinely freed, and all confessing with one voice that through the prayers of the holy bishop Swithun, which are heard . . .

The man whose servant had been mentioned above then handed him over to the aforesaid blessed bishop, who rescued him from the dreadful danger of a death that would have brought pestilence.

### 38

The provost of the monastery of Abundon [Note: I think *Abendoniensis* should be written; concerning it, consult William of Malmesbury, book II of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English*.] became blind for a period of fifteen years.

While he was tormented by excessive blindness, after many medicines had been tried, his head was cauterized with twelve burnings. These did him no good at all; rather, they harmed him even more.

At last, when he heard what great and merciful miracles the Author of all things had deigned most kindly to provide through his servant for suffering people, he came to Winchester barefoot and approached the bishop’s holy body with constant prayers.

When he arrived there and kept vigil in that place that same night, at dawn on the following day he merited seeing light with his eyes. Returning home safely, he devoted himself to glorifying almighty God.

### 39

In that same year, a blind man from the distant regions of England, hearing of the reputation of the miracles, was hastening with a boy as his guide to seek healing from the saint.

As he approached the city of Winchester, he came to a certain place where, exhausted from the journey, he began to rest for a while. Where they rested there was a great stone cross, situated nearly three miles from the aforesaid city.

When they had rested there for a little while, the hungry boy said to the blind old man:

“Let us eat something, father, because I am suffering great hunger now, and we are near the city. When we arrive there, we shall have no opportunity to eat.”

The blind man replied:

“Son, the appropriate time has not yet come.”

The boy said:

“Indeed, father, the hour for dining has already passed.”

The blind man replied:

“How much of the road still remains from here to the city?”

The boy said to the sick man:

“We shall soon come to the saint. Therefore let us take food before we enter the city wall, because there is a great crowd.”

### 40

The sick man replied to the boy:

“The ninth hour has not yet sounded. I ask you, therefore, let us wait until the ninth hour, and after we have come to the little body of the man of God, let us break our fast there with the blessing of Christ the Lord.”

The guide again, importunate, began to ask—

While they were making such arrangements in conversation, the blind man heard people hurrying to the saint to keep vigil. He immediately asked the guide where they were going.

The boy replied:

“They are directing their steps to Winchester to venerate the tomb of blessed Swithun, so that through his intervention those sick people may receive the medicine of healing.”

The old man said:

“What is this place where we are sitting?”

The boy replied:

“This is a stone cross, shining, large, and very lofty, set up in praise of Christ.”

He rose quickly and prayed to Christ, asking that through the merit of the great man he might be healed from heaven.

### 41

“Almighty Lord God, hear my prayers,” he said. “Restore light to my eyes, through the interceding merits of the holy bishop Swithun. O, if only I might someday deserve to see the city with clear light, rejoicing!

“O glorious confessor of Christ, Swithun, pray for me, the most wretched of sinners, so that it may not be a grave offense for me to break my fast before the proper hour.”

When the blind man had poured out this prayer with groaning, he was illuminated there through the intervention of the holy priest. As soon as the glaucoma fell from his eyes, he saw Winchester not far away—the city he had desired to see a little earlier with all the ardor of his mind.

Without eating, as he had wished, he hurried to the relics of the holy prophet and approached them, magnifying the omnipotence of the Savior.

When he arrived, he told the brothers of that place how he had been healed through the servant of the Creator of the world. They gathered in the church and praised the Author of miracles with hymn-singing voices.

[Note: *Glaucoma* is an eye disorder in which the eye becomes bluish contrary to nature, because the crystalline humor is transformed into a blue-green color. See the medical definitions of John Gorraeus.]

### 42

In those days a certain weak man came to the holy servant of God. He was lame in both feet and so bent by illness that he could not move himself from the spot at all unless he was supported by two crutches.

As soon as he approached the saint’s tomb, he recovered bodily health. In mind, however, he remained weak, because he did not give thanks to God the Creator as the other sick people had done.

Indeed, scarcely had he been divinely straightened when, leaving the saint, he immediately fled as quickly as he could, and afterward was seen by no one in that monastery.

The crutches by which he had been supported nevertheless revealed his illness, showing that he had departed healed through the merit of Saint Swithun. The crowds standing around, all who were present there, steadfastly affirmed that everything had happened exactly as it is written on this page.

### 43

At that same time a certain royal councillor, greatly loved and powerful in perishable affairs, was riding hurriedly with a large retinue, as is customary among the Anglo-Saxons, toward a certain village where an abundant feast had been lavishly prepared for the needs of dining.

During the journey it happened that a boy of exceptional character, whom the count loved more than the others, fell from his horse as it rushed forward. As soon as he fell, he broke his leg and arm and was so shattered in all his limbs that everyone present believed him immediately dead.

### 44

When the master of the household saw the boy he loved dying, and grieved deeply over the misfortune of his friend, he implored the Lord with earnest prayers to have pity on the dying boy through the venerable intercession of the glorious bishop:

“Holy Swithun,” he said, “ask the Redeemer of the world with humble prayer to grant life and health to this boy. If he grants this request, he shall find me more faithful to him throughout all the days of my life.

“For I shall also bring the innocent child, supreme priest, to the life-giving tomb of your body, so that through your healing intercession he may experience the benefit of Christ.”

### 45

When that man was entreating God with such words, the boy suddenly leapt up healthy—the boy who shortly before had been lying there, overtaken by the ruin of death.

When the councillor saw this, he became happier than words could express and began with complete devotion of mind to glorify God, who does not despise a contrite and humbled heart.

### 46

Miracles were performed not only in the lands of the English but also in the province of the Franks through the merits of this saint.

In that region, as those who witnessed the event report, a certain *cleptes*—that is, a thief, from the Greek *κλέπτης*—caught in a most monstrous crime was being held in a dark prison, bound with wicked chains and a dreadful fetter, until the following day, when he was to be suspended on the rack for such a crime.

He had heard from merchants crossing the Ocean for the sake of trade that a saint had been discovered in lands across the sea, through whose intervention the sick were healed of many different illnesses.

Remembering this in the darkness of the obscure night, he prayed to the incomprehensible divinity of almighty God that . . .

*The rest is missing.*

---

# THE LIFE OF SAINT YVON, BISHOP

## THE LIFE OF SAINT YVON, A PERSIAN BISHOP BURIED IN ENGLAND, AND OF HIS THREE COMPANIONS, BY GOSCELIN

*(In the Bollandists, Acts of the Saints, June, volume II, 10 June, p. 287.)*

## PRELIMINARY COMMENTARY  
### On the Saint’s Date and the Two Writers of His Life
