William Camden, describing in his *Britannia* the county of Huntingdon—named from its principal town, Huntingdon, situated in the middle of England on the northern bank of the river Ouse—writes:

“From here,” he says, “the Ouse, as it is now about to reach Cambridge, spreads out beside a very handsome town amid the most pleasant meadows. It was formerly called Slepe in Anglo-Saxon, but is now called Saint Yves, after Yvo the Persian bishop, who, as they write, traveled through England around the year 600 after Christ with a great reputation for holiness; diligently sowed the word of God; and left his name to this place, where he departed this life. Nevertheless, religious men soon transferred his body to Ramsey.”

So far Camden. Ramsey is an abbey in the same county of Huntingdon, toward the north, five leagues from the town of Saint Yves. Under its first abbot, Eadnoth, this translation was carried out in the year 1001, on this day, 10 June, on which his solemn feast has continued to be celebrated.

### 2

When Eadnoth was appointed bishop of Dorchester in the year 1008, Wlsius was made abbot in his place. After Wlsius was killed by the Danes, he was succeeded by the third abbot, Andrew Withmannus, or Andrew Leucander, in 1016.

In the fourth year of his rule, Andrew set out for Jerusalem. Returning the following year, he found Ethelstan as abbot. Ethelstan wished to yield the office to him, but Withmannus refused and chose a solitary life at Narthæje, where he lived for more than twenty years.

At the same time, the same Withmannus—as Molanus also testifies in the *Auctarium* of Usuard for this day—“carefully wrote the Life of Yvo, bishop of the Persians, buried in England; Goscelin the Bertinian later made it somewhat more elegant.” We have not yet obtained that earlier Life; we give the later one, in which Yvo is always written *Yvo*, as it was sent to Maclovius by the Reverend Father Leander Prichard, Benedictine.

Goscelin, or Goscelinus, then a monk of Ramsey, dedicated this Life to his abbot Herbert, appointed in 1087 and made bishop of Norwich four years later. His eulogy is found in the *Monasticum Anglicanum*, p. 1003.

In the prologue Goscelin explains what he received from the aforesaid Abbot Andrew, the first author of the Life, and what he himself added from the reports of others. The material found in chapter four was added by the same author while Herbert was still bishop of Norwich. Herbert died on 22 July 1119, during the reign of Henry I, who became king in 1101 and died on 3 December 1135.

### 3

John Capgrave also published another Life in his *Legend of the Saints of England*. From it, in an appendix, we give the miracles performed through the intercession of Saint Yvon. Goscelin seems to have added these miracles, or at least some of them, but the copyist of our manuscript omitted them.

We note the remaining matters concerning Capgrave’s Acts in the annotations. The memory of Saint Yvon the Persian is also celebrated by other writers of English history who lived after Goscelin, such as Florence of Worcester, William of Malmesbury, Henry of Huntingdon, Matthew of Westminster, John Brompton, and others. Among more recent writers are the William Camden mentioned above, Nicholas Harpsfield, Michael Alford, and others, some of whom are cited in the notes that follow.

Finally, the memory of the same Saint Yvon is celebrated in a manuscript Martyrology that we found at Rome among the ancient codices of the Duke of Altemps. It reads:

“In England, at Ramsey, the translation of Saint Yvon the archbishop, with his three companions. Above his sacred relics a most white dove flew for seven miles, until they were carried into holy ground.”

In the Martyrology of Richard Wilford, printed in English at London in 1526, we find the following:

“In England, the feast of Saint Yvon the archbishop. He was born in Persia and of royal family. After enduring many labors, he came to England and lived in a place called Slepe, now called Saint Yvon, near Huntingdon, eight miles from Ramsey. Having been transferred from there through a revelation, he shines forth through great miracles.”

Molanus and others followed this account.

The three companions and their twofold translation are discussed below in the Acts; for that reason we include their memory in the title. One of them was a Roman of patrician rank, the son of a senator, and is therefore called a patrician in section 3. The others are also considered Persians. We doubt whether they are correctly called Sithius, his nephew, and Inthius, his kinsman, in Capgrave; for that reason we name only the three companions.

We suppose that their arrival took place around the beginning of the seventh century, when England began to be converted to the faith of Christ. Thus they may be reckoned as approximately one hundred lustrums (five hundred years) before the translation of the body, although six or eight lustrums (thirty or forty years) may be lacking.

In any case, do not suppose that the name Yvon is Persian or was brought from Persia. Rather, it may have been assumed while traveling through Italy or Gaul to make concealment easier, perhaps because of some similarity of sound to his native name.

# THE LIFE BEGINS

## PROLOGUE
1. Brother Goscelin to Rector Herebert.

What is related concerning the life of blessed Yvo is known to have been celebrated by the venerable Abbot Andrew. Having made a pilgrimage from England to the Lord’s city of Jerusalem, he practiced so arduous a life that no faithful person would have doubted believing him. In Greece, he testified that Yvo’s name and life were regarded as exceedingly renowned through many deeds and miracles, and that the praises of his good Christian fragrance were widely and famously known. From the discovery of his body onward, the revelations and wonders which the predecessor records here—seen with the eyes as well as confirmed by the testimony of the faithful—have remained written more memorably in the hearts of nearly all the brothers of Ramsey and of some of the Foresters than in the book; and they recall in writing some things passed over [Col. 0081B] here.

Therefore, at the request of this most holy Father and of the whole beloved and venerable Community, I have collected these matters somewhat more briefly, so that what is sought may be found more easily in a small portion than amid many things; that one may reach the destination more quickly by a shorter road than by a long circuit; that food may be served more readily from a prepared table than from a granary; and that one may drink more pleasantly from a little spring than from a river. Yet I have not made such poverty out of abundance that understanding could complain that this slight seasoning of ours lacks what overflows from the other, richer dish. Rather, a measure has been preserved by which neither the more eager nor the more fastidious reader will take offense.

This work, most honorable abbot, we have deposited for your loving and everlasting memory in the sacred Father Yvo, whom we have received as the venerable prince of your salvation together with the principality of Ramsey, so that, just as you have honored and cherished him here, so may he receive you at the end into the joys of his light.

# CHAPTER ONE  
## The Life of Saint Yvo, Bishop

[Col. 0082B]

2. [Note: [Col. 0081B] What Capgrave relates concerning the city of his birth, his bishopric there, his parents, and then his archbishopric [Col. 0082B], we omit together with Goscelin, since these matters have not been sufficiently established for us. They may be read in Capgrave and in Alford [Col. 0083D], under the year 600. Florence of Worcester preferred, under the same year, to transcribe this beginning of the Life as presented by Goscelin; it was also subsequently inserted in Capgrave.]

An apostolic teacher and messenger of the true sun, the renowned Bishop Yvo arose in Persia like a star of the East, destined by the Lord for the western borders of Britain. He left his sweet homeland as an exile, a fellow citizen of the heavenly virtues; and, a pilgrim of Christ throughout the world, he pressed onward toward the eternal kingdom.

Wherever he went, he shone forth with his rays. He filled all things with the Gospel as a sower of the word; by instruction, example, and innumerable miracles he drew peoples and nations to the Savior. After great Asia, after Illyricum, after Rome, [Note: [Col. 0083D] In this author it reads: “When he had reached Rome, by the counsel of the pope he entered Britain.”] after passing through innumerable cities and peoples, he entered Gaul. There likewise he flashed forth with such great signs that extraordinary wonders proclaimed his heavenly life and angelic teaching.

[Note: [Col. 0083D] This may have been Chlothar II, who began to reign in 584, became sole ruler in 613, and died in 628.]

When the king of the Franks and the nobles and peoples of the kingdom tried to retain him with fitting honors as an angel of God, he—who had fled the ancestral glory of the world by living as an exile and was striving through many tribulations to enter the kingdom of God—could not be held by any earthly favor.

3. [Note: [Col. 0083D] William of Malmesbury, *On the Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, book IV, p. 292: “Yvo,” he says, “wearied of the pleasures administered by his very great bishopric, secretly left everything behind and undertook an extremely long pilgrimage with only three companions. After traversing a journey of many years, and disguising himself before those who saw him as a rustic in ragged clothing, he finally sailed to England. He was greatly delighted by the barbarism of the unknown language, because he was laughed at by everyone as though he were a fool; and he settled in a muddy province, where he spent his life, whatever its extent.”]

Thus, having confirmed all peoples in the faith, he crossed over with his worthy companions and associates into Britain, the fair Albion. Taking pity on the fair-skinned people with paternal compassion, he freed them from the error of idolatry by signs and preaching, insofar as the Lord granted, and made them truly fairer through baptism.

The youth Patricius, of patrician rank and the son of a senator, also followed this most beloved father. Out of love for Christ, who called him through Saint Yvo, he not only set aside his sweet birthplace and ancestral honors, but also abandoned untouched the virgin betrothed to him, together with his entire hope in this world. By love and imitation he clung inseparably to his sweet teacher. Blessed is he who attained the example of John, Christ’s intimate and bosom friend.

4. Then the life-giving newcomer Yvo advanced into the province of the Mercians, to a town called Huntedun, and to the nearby village called Slepe. [Note: [Col. 0084D] Harpsfield, century XI, chapter 22, has this concerning Saint Yvo: “He came to a certain place called in English Slepe (that is, if you translate it, ‘Sleep’), near the town of Huntingdon and the monastery of Ramsey. There too he fell asleep in Christ, and there he was buried.”] When he understood that he had been led by the Lord to a definite place, he remained there for many years until the end of his life. Here he embraced the heavenly way of life with such fervor as though he were only then beginning it, and as though, after a long thirst, he had found the fountain he had sought.

Here, I say, by continually watching over his own salvation and that of everyone else, here by awaiting the Lord until the end, with the lamps of his virtues burning and the belt of chastity around him, he finally opened the door with joy to the One who came and knocked. And Yvo went from the Lord to the Lord, who came forth from the Father and entered the world, and who, after triumphing over the world, carried back the triumph of the elect.

Here also his place was established in peace, and in peace he was buried. Although for approximately five lustres of a hundred years—as is calculated from the revelation that follows—he lay hidden from human knowledge, his name lives forever.

How greatly he shone throughout his whole life in charity, kindness, piety, gentleness, humility, modesty, constancy, patience, continence, service, almsgiving, fasting, vigils, prayers, preaching, and every radiance of virtue; how many signs he performed either at the place of his repose or anywhere throughout the world—one who is faithful will more readily believe it to be indescribable than attempt to gather it into words.

Let our land bless the Lord, who sent such a luminous Father to our western world, like the sun from the East to the West and like an angel flying through the midst of heaven.

# CHAPTER TWO  
## The Discovery of the Body of Saint Yvo

5. While the Lord teaches endurance for a time but repays endlessly with infinite rewards, when at last it pleased him to reveal to human beings the heavenly treasure hidden in the field, so that they might possess what was precious, and to place the lamp from beneath the bushel on a lampstand, a peasant, plowing the earth with the impressed blade of his plow, struck this most holy sarcophagus.

Immediately astonished and raised up by the hope of gain, he called back the halted oxen and cleared the place with all his strength. But when he had taken in with his eyes a human burial, he summoned his fellow plowmen. After removing the cover, they found venerable remains worthy of priestly estimation. They were seized by the radiant splendor of the chalice standing there. Thinking it silver, they vied with one another to break it apart. They snatched the bishop’s brooches, transparent with a glassy brightness, which the men of Ramsey later inherited together with the holy body and the fragments of the chalice.

A monk, the provost of the village, came running with the village smith. [Note: [Col. 0084D] In Capgrave he is called Elnothus the provost; but because no mention is made of Abbot Ednoth, who was then summoned by him, the names seem to have been confused.] Then the nearby Ednoth was summoned by a swift message, and he had the remains of this admirable servant of God carefully washed, carried into the church, and placed beside the altar. The people came running and, with minds alert, hoped that the Lord who had granted that he be found would also grant that his identity be recognized.

6. So that it might become clear that this discovery had been made not by chance but by divine prompting, on the following night glorious Yvo appeared in sleep to the smith of the same village—an innocent and simple man [Note: [Col. 0084D] He is said to have been “a smith called Ezi.”] [Col. 0085A] of the kind to whom the Lord speaks mouth to mouth, entrusts his secrets, and reveals to little ones what is hidden from the wise.

Yvo appeared tall in stature, fair of face, lively in appearance, with eyes bright as flame, wearing a bishop’s mitre and holding a staff, with an archiepiscopal cross extended before him. He soothed the astonished man with an unfamiliar, honey-sweet voice and said:

“Whoever has just been found in such a place and whom you marvel at—I am Yvo the bishop, who until now have lain buried here with my blessed companions. Come in the morning and measure eight feet from the right side of my mausoleum; you will find the tomb of one of my holy companions. Another companion, buried with us, will likewise be found not far away by one who seeks him; they triumph with me in glory.

“Once you have been assured by these signs, tell the provost on my behalf that he himself is to announce to Abbot Ednoth [Col. 0085B] that he should transfer me with these same companions of mine to the monastery at Ramsey.”

But while this poor man in spirit feared to report the heavenly commands, on the following night his negligence was rebuked, and he was instructed with the same authority. On the third night, while he was still hesitating, the same teacher appeared to him in his earlier sleep and now reproved the disobedient man more sternly. When the trembling man asked that a sign be given him, the bishop struck him with his staff:

“And this sign,” he said, “you will have, and you will by no means be without it unless you announce what has been commanded.”

7. Awakening from this, he felt such pain in the place where he had been struck that it was as though he had been pierced by iron. When he reported the commands together with the sign of pain, he himself recovered. [Col. 0085C] Yet, for the greater manifestation of the Saint, the same provost refused to believe him and drove away the peasant as though he were telling ghost stories.

“Are we then,” he said, “to transfer and honor as saints every worthless ash of some shoemaker?”

As he spoke these words of rejection, sleep seized him at night. The holy bishop appeared in a sterner manner and attire and roused him severely:

“Rise,” he said; “rise as quickly as possible. For I am the one whom yesterday you mocked as a shoemaker, and I have prepared durable boots for you. You will put them on, and wearing them you will ride home in memory of me.”

At this, as the sleeper rose and sat up, the just chastiser fitted the boots most tightly around his legs. Thus shaken, he awoke; already the most constricting pain had gripped both his shins from the feet upward, and he had no ability either to stand or to walk.

He rode to the monastery on someone else’s conveyance. When he entered, he reported everything in due order, suffering the punishment he had refused to believe through another’s account. By both his illness and his true words he proclaimed what he had rejected as though it were ghost stories.

[Col. 0085D] [Note: The Westminster writer, under the year 1001, attributes this punishment to the abbot and, not distinguishing him from the provost, says: “Since the abbot of Ramsey had not received the discovery with due reverence, he was severely punished.”]

8. Then Abbot Ednoth, gladdened by the unexpected gain of the heavenly treasure and by its evident sign, offered the most devout thanks to the lavishly generous Lord, with the great joy of the entire community, although they sympathized with their brother’s suffering. He then assigned everyone the support of prayers and hurried to the revealed bodies of the Saint and his companions, in the very village of Slepe, eight English leagues from Ramsey and three from the town of Huntedun, situated above the River Ouse.

The horses seemed slow to him as he hurried, and his desire flew ahead of them all on wings. When the leading men came to meet him, along with the common people displaying their joy, he went down into the field, the treasury of the Saints. He knelt with his brother-monks, worshiped the help of God, and himself seized the digging tool. Working in the manner Saint Yvo had indicated, he quickly found the object of his search.

Then, perceiving that there was further hope, he found both Saints, in accordance with the true indication of the divine bishop, together with the holy patrician mentioned above. He carried them from there into the church and, together with blessed Yvo himself, arranged them there until a more fitting translation.

9. But the provost, so that he might remain a lasting example of not despising heavenly things, and so that his enduring weakness might proclaim the man whom he had rejected with precipitous disbelief, remained weak and fettered by the bonds of that blessed Father for fifteen years and until the very end of his life. Yet the grace of God, spread abundantly among the Saints, increased the fruit of salvation for him.

For seven days before his death, that serene consoler appeared to him with a radiant face and in splendid attire, rejoicing with him, and said to him in a most encouraging voice:

“Now the time is near for the blows with which I chastised you to pass over into a remedy for your health; and, in place of the long night of your sojourn, for you to possess the most joyful day of eternal happiness. For seven days from now, only be prepared: I shall come to receive you from this prison of the flesh into our light.”

When he had explained this to his brothers, hastening to meet the face of the Lord in confession and departing on the appointed day, he made them all fully certain of the promised grace.

So that the matter might also become better known through the distinction of his lineage, he was the nephew of the very close and illustrious Archbishop Oswald of York. [Note: [Col. 0085D] Saint Oswald died in the year 992, on the last day of February, the date on which we have edited his Acts.] He also had a brother of equal name, Oswald, a learned monk and prior, as his verse-book bears witness; he was so devout in the Lord that he refrained from accepting the bishopric offered to him. [Note: [Col. 0086D] Saint Edward the Confessor and king, at the prompting of Oswald, the monk and nephew of Saint Oswald, gave various gifts to the Church of Ramsey in 1047, as explained in the *Monasticum Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 240. We regret that the versified book cited here cannot be found.]

Thus the order of the manifestation of the most sacred Yvo stands forth clearly to all. Whoever explains these matters less fully is not a copious writer.

10. This discovery of his body took place in the year of the Lord 1001, during the reign of King Ethelred, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the month of April. April is called almost *Aperilis*, “the opening month,” because the sky opens more brightly to the summer suns, the world is enlivened with flowers and offspring, and then every field, every tree, gives birth. Then the forests put forth leaves; then the year is most beautiful; then the green places are filled with flowers, the birds with songs, [Col. 0087A] and all the joys of creation resound in response to Christ’s resurrection and the days of Easter.

At such a season, therefore, it was fitting that these blessed remains should be found, since they must be raised to eternal glory in a new heaven and a new earth.

11. With equal appropriateness, God’s provident grace, after revealing so great a light, gladdened the brothers on the same day on which, ten full years earlier, the death of the famous Duke Ethelwin, founder of the monastery at Ramsey, had bereaved them. It is fitting to recall him here, if only briefly, for the benefit of the Church.

Among his other services, he began and completed this monastery with the consent of the most blessed Archbishop Oswald of York. He raised it up through the wealth of estates and furnishings, as its glory remains evident to this day, established a community of monks, [Col. 0087B] and ennobled it with the bodies of the twin martyr brothers Ethelred and Ethelbrict. [Note: [Col. 0087D] These martyrs are commemorated on 12 October; they were buried at Ramsey and killed within the year 668.]

He was now being summoned by illness to the highest King. Saint Elfegus, then bishop and afterward a martyr, [Note: [Col. 0087D] Elfegus was then bishop of Winchester and later archbishop of Canterbury; he was killed in 1012, on 19 April, the day on which we edited his Acts.] released him from confession, anointed him with oil, and refreshed him with divine Communion. As his end approached, he humbly asked those standing by to sing the seven penitential psalms.

When these were finished, he added the final instrument of the Psalter, “Praise the Lord.” As they sang the final words of this last hymn, he, with mind and eyes directed toward heaven, sang the psalm with them and repeated three times: “Let every spirit praise the Lord.” Thus, signing himself with the Lord’s cross with his right hand and closing his eyes with his left, he gave up his spirit in faith in the Trinity and in mercy.

He was buried in the same monastery that he had built for the holy Father Benedict. Just as Benedict prepared a dwelling for him on earth, so he is believed to have been received by him into his heavenly dwelling, among the company of monks, in accordance with the Savior’s merciful saying: “Whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive the reward of a righteous person” (Matthew 10:41).

Thus the illumination of blessed Yvo wiped away the grief of his funeral on those same Kalends, as has been said.

# CHAPTER THREE  
## The Translation of the Body of Saint Yvo to Ramsey

12. After it pleased God, through divine inspiration, that the most holy body of blessed Father Yvo, previously revealed by God, should be transferred to Ramsey, the famous Abbot Germanus was summoned. [Note: [Col. 0087D] Aimoin, in the *Life of Saint Abbo*, abbot of Fleury, who was killed in 1004 on 13 November, mentions this Germanus as having been “taken from the holy monastery of Fleury”; but he incorrectly makes him abbot of the monastery of Ramsey, perhaps having been led into error by this translation.]

He was formed in the institution of Fleury and had long adhered to the aforementioned Archbishop Oswald. The most glorious King Edgar had placed him over the monastery of Saint Kenelm at Winchcombe, [Col. 0088A] and Edgar’s son and successor, Ethelred, had appointed him over the monastery at Celesige. [Note: [Col. 0088D] The text has *Celesige*, but the margin has Shepton, or Shaftesbury in Dorset; that this is correct may be inferred from the Edward mentioned immediately afterward, the martyr king, and from the extensive discussion of him and that monastery under the Acts for 18 March.]

At the suggestion of Archbishop Siricius, [Note: [Col. 0088D] Siricius is said to have held the see among the people of Canterbury from 989 to 995. At that time Ethelred was reigning, namely after Saint Edward, his brother, who was killed in 978, until the year 1016; therefore he is called “Long-lived” by Henry of Huntingdon in *The Lives of the Saints of England*, where he says that Saint Yvo’s body was revealed under him.] he had ordered it to be built and dedicated to monks with paternal devotion, for the sake of the royal martyrdom of his holy brother Edward and as a bulwark of the kingdom.

With this excellent companion, Germanus, the excellent Father Ednoth, after prayer and fasting, and with the favor of the king and bishops, transferred Saint Yvo to his dwelling at Ramsey. These two abbots, like Christ’s twin oxen, carried the ark of God’s covenant, Bishop Saint Yvo. The other brothers who had assembled carried the remaining Saints who had been found with him.

An immense crowd followed. People from the countryside and towns streamed together toward the place; the open fields could scarcely contain the converging multitudes. Prayers and hymns resounding with praise delighted the air. Heaven itself seemed to favor the Saints, and the sun to rejoice with all its rays, so sweet was the hour and so serene the day that had dawned.

13. Many faithful people also assert that throughout the entire route of this festive translation, an exceedingly white dove flew above the earth containing the most blessed Yvo. This was such a visible miracle to many that everyone testified that it had come from heaven as a favor to the Saint.

The people of Ramsey came to meet it with the rest of the crowd, whitened with white garments and crowned with purple ornaments. They carried the cross-bearing banners of Christ, golden Gospels, splendid shrines of the Saints, lights in candelabra, fragrant incense in thuribles, and everything that votive devotion could provide.

The entire island resounded with songs, cymbals, and little bells. Forests and rivers shone. Thus, while angels rejoiced above together with the human choir, precious pearls were brought in devotion to the temple.

Then they sang the Ambrosian hymn of praise, with Abbot Ednoth gratefully beginning, “We praise you, O God” (*Te Deum laudamus*). Solemn Masses followed, and the day of Saint Yvo’s translation, consecrated on the fourth day before the Ides of June, was decreed for perpetual celebration.

14. Since they were earnestly concerned to store him in a more suitable place, Yvo, the ever-watchful intercessor, appeared by night to a devout brother and instructed the Father of the monastery to place him in such a location that he would be accessible to everyone who came to pray.

Thus, after the sacred remains had been transferred and wrapped in precious cloth, [Col. 0088D] he was placed at the ascent of the presbytery, where he still shines forth and may be touched by eyes and kisses. He plainly appears to be a citizen of heaven who does not seek a more exalted place here, but only the salvation of human beings. For what does the lowest glory of the world contribute to Saints who despised earthly things while dwelling on earth and now reign in heaven?

15. This also seems to belong to the ancient knowledge of our Patron: near the village called Hirst, a meadow is called Yvo’s Meadow.

Before these events, in Rome, an aged man addressed someone who had come from England to pray. When he learned that the man was from England, he carefully asked whether he knew the village called Slepe. When the visitor replied that he knew it very well, the old man continued:

“Believe this, and preserve it in unwavering memory: not far from the ford of the neighboring river, very bright lamps lie hidden, which in their own time will be raised up into clear public knowledge.”

When the Englishman returned to his homeland, he joyfully proclaimed this in faith; the truth revealed afterward has confirmed it for us to this day. There also remained until these events a certain faithful cleric named Durandus, who often foretold what we now see accomplished.

16. Since these matters had now been proved by their fulfillment, Abbot Ednoth, at the request of all the brothers, built a church in honor and memory of blessed Yvo, in the very place of his tomb and discovery. It was so constructed that the life-giving tomb extended halfway within the wall and halfway outside it, so that, whether the door was locked or open, the water of grace would not be lacking to those who came.

For, since the Lord is wondrous in his Saints, and brings rivers out of rock, the mausoleum itself pours forth a stream of sweet water. [Note: [Col. 0089D] Malmesbury, in the place cited above, describes this as follows: “From the winding recesses of the mausoleum itself a stream burst forth, exceedingly rich in fleeting bubbles. To this day a spring flows, sweet to drink and suited to the health of all. The multitude healed through that blessed man cannot be estimated in number, much less comprehended in writing; so that no saint in England is either easier to implore or more effective in result than Yvo. I have seen what I say. A certain monk suffered from dropsy. His swollen skin had risen high; his heavy breath drove away those standing by; he seemed about to drink whole rivers and drain full casks. Warned in a dream, he went to Saint Yvo; and there, after drinking the water three times, he expelled from his mouth the flood of superfluous fluid. His belly subsided, his legs shrank; and, not to say more, the whole man grew green again into health. At last he boasted that, after so health-giving a vomit, he might at some time be satisfied with drink.” These are Malmesbury’s words; he was somewhat later than Goscelin and died in 1142.] This surge of the river gladdens the city of God among the faithful. It is rightly evident on the sepulchral stone that from the innermost depths of his compassion rivers of living water once flowed, a spring gushing up into eternal life, which through teaching and assistance poured out his paternal stream upon all.

We therefore record here a few of the many cures performed by this water and of the many signs and revelations of merciful Yvo, following the most certain testimony, witnessed by the eyes or heard by the ears, of the earlier writer; these things also continue in the memory of the faithful.

[Note: [Col. 0090D] These matters are absent from our account; some are given in the Appendix from Capgrave. The following chapter, however, bore this specific title: “How the sacred relics of the companions of Saint Yvo, after a three-day fast had been observed, in the reign of King Henry, on the fifth day before the Ides of August, were carried back by the brothers of Ramsey to the church of their discovery.” Henry I reigned from 1088 to 1100.]

[Textual lacuna.]

# CHAPTER FOUR  
## The Translation of the Companions of Saint Yvo to This Church; Their Relics, in the Reign of King Henry, Are Carried Back to the Church of Their Discovery

[Col. 0089D]

17. At the estate belonging to the Church of Ramsey, also, called Slepe, where the bodies of Saint Yvo and his companions were once found through the glorious revelation of Saint Yvo himself and transferred to Ramsey by the brothers with due honor, frequent signs of healing are divinely performed for people suffering from various infirmities.

Some inhabitants of the same village also testify that on many nights they clearly saw a beam of flashing light extending from that place all the way to Ramsey and sometimes directed upward as far as heaven. The village itself is not far from Ramsey, but is separated from it by approximately seven thousand paces.

18. At the urging and counsel of certain distinguished men, the brothers of Ramsey decided to return the relics of the three blessed companions of Yvo, who had once clung inseparably to his side, to the church of the same estate, constructed in their honor. The relics had been decently placed together in a silver shrine. They wished both to make the church more honored and famous because of the Saints’ reverence, and to have it visited more abundantly and devoutly by peoples streaming together from every direction through the intercession of its present patrons.

They added that it seemed just that the master should honor the greater place of translation by his presence, while the disciples should honor the lesser place of discovery by theirs.

Yet, lest they appear by rash presumption to oppose the divine arrangement or detract from the excellence and veneration of the Saints, they resolved to consult their will concerning this matter through vigils, prayers, and a three-day fast.

While these things were being done, a certain girl, half-paralyzed on the left side of her body, received in a dream that she was to be healed at the memorial of blessed Yvo and his companions. When she arrived there and had prostrated herself in prayer for a while, she obtained the fulfillment of her dream in the sight of the brothers.

Made more joyful and confident by the judgment of this sign, after completing the fasts and prayers they transferred the holy shrine, filled with heavenly manna, to the aforesaid church on the fifth day before the Ides of August, with praises, hymns, and fitting honor. Brothers were appointed there, whose vigilant diligence would guard the heavenly treasure and perform the divine office devoutly by day and night.

19. To show clearly that divine mercy had approved their pious action and sincere devotion, and to demonstrate how acceptable to it were the exalted merits of its Saints, on the day when these things were being done it restored fifteen people weakened by various illnesses to health. From then onward, through the intervention of his Saints, it has not ceased in that place to grant the help of its mercy to those who seek it.

[Col. 0091]

# APPENDIX OF MIRACLES  
## From John Capgrave’s *New Legend of England*

[Col. 0091A]

20. A young man from Venice, of consular rank, killed his pregnant sister at the instigation of the devil. Moved to repentance, the bishop bound him with iron chains: he fastened iron from his shoulders to his loins and girded his belly and arms with iron. Thus bound, he traveled through the regions of the world, seeking the aid of the Saints.

At last, when he reached Saint-Denis, one of the bonds was broken through the Saint’s prayer. He crossed the sea and arrived at the tomb of Saint Yvo. While the *Magnificat* was being sung at Vespers, and this verse was being recited—“And his mercy is from generation to generation”—he was seized by an invisible power, lifted completely from the ground, and quickly set down again. The iron chains broke, and the bonds were immediately shattered.

Four others, likewise bound with iron by bishops as a penance, were freed from their chains at the tomb of Saint Yvo.

21. He comforted a woman who had been abandoned by her husband because of the affliction of blindness by restoring her sight.

He rendered a young man who mocked the miracles of the holy bishop and reviled the Saint incapable of walking until death, with his knees bent and rigid.

When a monk compelled his servants to engage in servile labor on the Saint’s feast and heaped insults upon the Saint, Yvo appeared to him and said:

“Do you know me?”

Trembling, the monk replied, “No.”

“I am Yvo,” he said, “whom you recently said you did not know and whom you prevented those who wished to celebrate my feast from honoring.”

He gave him a belt and said:

“Gird yourself with this belt and from now on retain knowledge of me.”

After girding him with it, he departed.

When the monk awoke, he felt as though he had been tightly bound all around with an iron chain. Internally he was tormented by the cutting of his vital organs; externally he suffered from poisonous corruption and swelling, while his flesh flowed away into putrefaction.

At last he tearfully confessed the offense he had committed against the Saint. After devoutly visiting his tomb, he returned healed.

22. When a certain monk, abhorring the rule, attempted to flee, an evil spirit seized him. Around midnight, when he had begun to feel somewhat better, he saw two hideous men coming toward him. They said:

“Because you wished to flee from this place, we will seize you and lead you away to the gates of hell.”

On hearing this, he sprang up and fled to the monastery, crying, “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”). He was taken into the infirmary. When Saint Yvo appeared to him and made the sign of the cross over him, he was restored to health.

From the tomb of Saint Yvo a clear water bursts forth, pleasing to the eye, sweet to the taste, and health-giving to those who drink it. It gives hearing to the deaf, sight to the blind, and health to the desperate and those at the point of death. Two lepers, bathed with the same water, are healed, and three blind people are restored to the light of their eyes.

23. A certain boy, diligently carrying out the kitchen duty assigned to him by his merchant masters, drew water from the Saint’s tomb, poured it into a pot, and kindled a strong fire. Yet the meats served to the diners were found raw and full of blood.

When the matter was revealed as it had occurred, the water in the pot was found to be completely cold. For the water of Saint Yvo always remains in the same condition. It knows no setting and never suffers eclipse. If at any time it is taken too eagerly in a large quantity, it never causes harm to the one who drinks it, nor does it swell the drinker’s stomach.

24. A certain woman was so enslaved to the devil’s power that the evil spirit repeatedly had intercourse with her in the form of a hare. During the intercourse, that unhappy woman—horrible to relate—would vomit the flow of semen through her mouth, to her still greater shame.

At last she confessed her offenses with tears to the prior of the place. Receiving from him a small vessel containing water from Saint Yvo and trusting in God’s mercy, she saw the demon standing nearby in an unusual form but daring in no way to approach. Nevertheless, he threatened and rebuked her because she had wished to raise up a wall of water against him.

The woman, however, freed from the devil’s power and suffering none of her former shame, returned home unharmed and joyful.

[Col. 0092C]

25. A certain woman who had been blind from birth visited the shrines of the Saints throughout England. Returning from Saint Thomas the Martyr and intending to seek the intercession of Saint Yvo, she approached a small hill near that village. Weary, she sat down and began to sleep for a short while.

Two distinguished men in episcopal dress stood beside her, one coming along the road by which she had arrived, the other along the road by which she was to travel. They carried in their hands two exceedingly bright eyes, as it seemed to her. One fitted the eye he held into one side of her head, and the other fitted the other eye into the other side.

When the woman awoke, she realized that she had received eyes and sight, and she rejoiced. No one doubted that this miracle should be attributed to blessed martyr Thomas and Saint Yvo.

26. Three men swollen with dropsy drank the Saint’s water; their swelling subsided, and they returned to health.

[Col. 0093]

# LIFE OF SAINT WEREBURGA, VIRGIN, DAUGHTER OF THE KING OF THE MERCIANS  
## By the Author Goscelin

*(In the Bollandists, February, vol. I, day 3, p. 384, from the manuscript of William Camden.)*

## Preliminary Commentary

### § I. The Royal Descent of Saint Wereburga; the Life Written; the Period of Her Monastic Governorship

[Col. 0093A]

# Life of Saint Wereburga, Virgin, Daughter of the King of the Mercians

## Preliminary Commentary

### § I. The Royal Descent of Saint Wereburga; the Composition of Her Life; the Date of Her Monastic Superintendence

1. Saint Wereburga was born to Wulfhere, the most Christian king of the Mercians, the Middle Angles, and the southern kingdoms, and to his most devout wife, Saint Ermenilda, whose sacred feast is celebrated on 23 February. On that day, together with the Acts of Ermenilda, we shall discuss the notable deeds accomplished by Wulfhere her husband, as well as the location and circumstances of the kingdom of the Mercians, founded by his great-grandfather Crida, or Creadda, and of the other regions subsequently annexed to it, along with the various kings who succeeded from that same family of Crida and Wulfhere. We shall also investigate how some regard Saint Wereburga as the only child of Saint Ermenilda, while nevertheless certain writers report that King Ceonred, or Coenred—between whom and Wulfhere reigned Saint Ethelred, his brother—was Wulfhere’s son.

Above all, however, we shall here remove the fabulous story of parricide by which even men otherwise learned in the ancient history of the Anglo-Saxons have believed that Wulfhere—either the fiercest enemy of the Christians from the beginning of his reign, or an utterly disgraceful apostate who had relapsed from the faith and baptism he had previously received into idolatry—killed his own sons with his own hand out of hatred for the Christian religion. We shall demonstrate that Saints Wulfhad and Ruffinus, who are venerated as martyrs because they were killed for the faith of Christ, were not brothers of Saint Wereburga born to the said Wulfhere and Saint Ermenilda.

We shall explain below, in the Acts themselves, the remainder of Saint Wereburga’s maternal lineage, descended from the kings of Kent, together with the royal family connected with them by legitimate marriages, and the royal families of the East Angles and of the Franks across the sea. In the same Acts are described Weduna, Saint Wereburga’s birthplace, distinguished by her miracles; the monastery of Ely, where she first embraced the monastic life; Tricingham, commonly called Trentham, the second monastery made famous by her death; and the third, Hamburg, where her body was buried and for a long time remained incorrupt through divine power.

[Col. 0093C] 2. We present the Acts of Saint Wereburga from a very ancient manuscript sent from England by William Camden to Rosweyde. The author’s name is not supplied. In our judgment, he is that Goscelin, or Gotzelin, who, according to William of Malmesbury, *De gestis regum Anglorum*, book IV, chapter 1, “brought forth innumerable Lives of the saints in a polished style, or more elegantly revised those that had been roughly composed, being second after Bede in recounting the praises of the saints of England.”

He flourished around the year of Christ 1100, having been summoned to England from Belgium by Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, and others on account of his exceptional learning and piety. Previously he had been a monk of Saint Bertin at Saint-Omer, where he had illuminated various Lives of the saints and among them had also revised, in a more cultivated style, the Life of Saint Amelberga the virgin. We possess that Life in manuscript and shall publish it on 10 July, her feast day. Here, in chapter 6, he acknowledges that he has reworked that Life in his own style and thereby reveals himself to be its author. Moreover, both Lives are divided in the same manner into chapters bearing their own titles.

Furthermore, although Molanus, in his *Catalogue of the Writers of Britain*, cited by Usuard on 8 July, and Valerius Andreas, following him in the *Bibliotheca Belgica*, observe that Goscelin wrote the Life of Saint Witeburga the virgin, we suspect that it was rather the Life of Saint Wereburga, whose great-aunt she was—that is, the sister of Saint Sexburga, Wereburga’s grandmother. As we shall say below, Witeburga is confused with Wereburga because of the similarity of their names. Nevertheless, just as Goscelin wrote the Lives of very many saints, he may also have composed the Acts of both Saint Witeburga and Saint Wereburga, since he was living at Ramsey, not far from the monastery of Ely, where Saint Wereburga had lived and where at that time the body of Saint Witeburga was resting. Witeburga had been transferred there from Dereham in the county of Norfolk, where she had led a holy monastic life after founding a monastery; her relics had been placed beside those of the two holy sisters, Saint Etheldreda and Sexburga, and of Sexburga’s daughter, Saint Ermenilda.

Finally, just as Saint Anselm persuaded Count Hugh—of whom we shall speak below—to give the church and monastery of Chester to monks, so he could easily have induced Goscelin to compose this Life of Saint Wereburga. John Capgrave, in the *Legend of the Saints of England*, and a manuscript codex of the monastery of Rood Valley near Brussels possess an abridgment of this Life, retaining Goscelin’s very words. From this one may infer that many of Capgrave’s other abridgments were likewise taken from Goscelin. We make this observation in the Life of Saint Ermenilda, her mother, and in that of Saint Laurence, archbishop of Canterbury, on 2 February, where we provide further information about Goscelin.

3. The following passages are read partly from the same Life and partly from elsewhere in the manuscript *History of Ely*:

“Werburga, daughter of Saint Ermenilda, after the death of her father, entered the monastery of Saint Etheldreda at Ely, as is read in her Life, before her mother entered that same monastery. When her uncle, King Ethelred, learned of her holiness, he took her from there and entrusted to her the governance of the monasteries and religious women throughout his kingdom. Thus Werburga, the bride of the Lord, while presiding over certain churches, after the death of her beloved mother also assumed, by right of superintendence, the monastery of Ely. Since, therefore, burning with excessive charity, she desired to be present with all the household and monasteries entrusted to her, while on the other hand no one could bear to be deprived of her sweet presence, she chose, with divine foreknowledge, to rest bodily in the monastery of Hehamburg. For this reason she ordered the household of Hehamburg that, wherever she should depart this life, they were to come without delay and carry her body to their monastery . . .

“It is read in English that Sexburga received from Archbishop Theodore, in the church at Sheppey which she had built, the veil of holiness; and that her daughter Ermenilda, under her authority, later undertook there the discipline of religious life, rejecting the height of royal power. When Ermenilda had prepared to journey to Ely, she appointed her daughter Werburga abbess in her place at the monastery, as she had long desired.”

Sheppey is an eastern island of Kent. Because a monastery for religious women was then built there, the settlement is still called Minster.

4. Nothing has been transmitted anywhere concerning the time when Wereburga was placed over the other monasteries or when she departed this mortal life to receive the reward of her labors. Saint Etheldreda began to build the monastery of Ely in the year 673. King Wulfhere died in the year 675; after his death, under Saint Etheldreda, who died in 679, Wereburga assumed the habit of sacred religion at Ely. Saint Sexburga was then appointed abbess there as her second successor; William of Malmesbury, in book IV of *De pontificibus Anglorum*, says that she grew old under the religious rule and title of abbess.

But by then she was entirely aged, and her granddaughter through her daughter, Saint Wereburga, had long before rejected the suitors who, while her father Wulfhere was still alive, pressed her to marry. Hence Edovard Maihew, in his chronological index to the *English Trophies of the Benedictine Order*, gives the following under the year 680:

“At the same time Saint Sexburga, queen and abbess, flourished. Likewise Saint Ermenilda, her daughter, first queen and afterward abbess.”

This suggests that Saint Sexburga did not long survive and that Saint Ermenilda succeeded her as the third abbess at Ely. This seems more plausible to us than what we read in Wion’s notes on 13 February: that Saint Ermenilda became abbess in the year of Christ 703, when we believe that she—or even earlier—had already departed this life.

At the time when Ermenilda migrated to Ely, she would have appointed her daughter Saint Wereburga over the monastery at Sheppey in Kent, if the English record cited by the people of Ely is trustworthy. From there Wereburga would have been summoned by her uncle, Saint King Ethelred, and appointed abbess by right over the monasteries of religious women in his kingdom, as the Worcester historian explains under the year 676. At the same time, after the death of her mother Saint Ermenilda, she would have become the fourth abbess of Ely.

Camden, after Ranulf of Chester, writing about the county of Northampton; Harsfield, in the seventh century, chapter 23; and Edovard Maihew, in his treatise on the Life of Saint Wereburga, report that Saint Wereburga converted Weduna, the royal seat of her father Wulfhere, into a monastery.

Saint Ethelred, having abandoned his kingdom, became a monk in the year of Christ 704, at which time Saint Wereburga was still alive. But to what old age she lived, or in what year she died, we nowhere read. Some write that Saint Ermenilda, her mother, survived until the year 710; we would prefer to say this of her daughter, provided that she did not live longer still.

## § II. The Translation of Saint Wereburga’s Relics to Chester and Her Public Veneration

5. Among the Britons there are two cities called City of the Legions, commonly Caerlegion or Caerlion, from the winter quarters or permanent camps of the legions.

One was in Britannia II among the Silures: in ancient times Isca, then Legio II, assigned by Ranulf of Chester, *Polychronicon*, book I, chapter 48, to Demetia, or South Wales. It stood in that part beside the River Usk which is enclosed by the county of Monmouth. In the early period of the Christian Britons it possessed an archiepiscopal see, later transferred to Llandaff and afterward to Menevia, which we call the city of Saint David.

Gildas, the most ancient of the British writers, reports in his book *On the Ruin of Britain* that Saints Aaron and Julius, crowned with the palm of martyrdom during the persecution of Diocletian, were citizens of this City of the Legions. Giraldus Cambrensis, *Itinerary through Wales*, book I, chapter 5, and Geoffrey of Monmouth, *History of the Britons*, book IX, chapter 12, state that the Britons erected a church there for both of them. We shall discuss them on the Kalends of July.

The other City of the Legions remained no less famous. To the Britons it was Caer-Legion or Caer-Leon-Vaur; to the Saxons, Lege-cester; in English, Chester; and, from its location, Westchester. In Latin it is called Cestra and Cestria, and it gave its name to the adjoining county. The Romans are believed to have called it Deva, Deunana, or Divana. It was developed by the Cornovii and assigned to the province of Flavia Caesariensis.

According to Ranulf, who composed his history there, it “was in the time of the Britons the capital and metropolis of Venedotia and North Wales, and afterward stood on the border of the English, within sight of Wales, situated between two arms of the sea, or two rivers, the Dee and the Mosey.”

It is believed to have remained in the hands of the Britons at the beginning of the seventh century. Its bishop, together with other Britons, is said to have attended the conference held with Saint Augustine, archbishop of Canterbury, in the territory of the Wiccians and the West Saxons. Bede discusses this in book II, chapter 2, while Ussher debates various matters concerning the British bishops in chapter 5 of *On the Origins of the British Churches*.

Ranulf of Chester, *Polychronicon*, book V, chapter 18, reports:

“Saint Wereburga lay buried at Hamburg until the arrival of the Danes. Then, while the Danes were wintering at Repton and the Mercian king Burhred had been driven out—which, as we read in the Saxon Chronicle, occurred in the year 884—the citizens of Hamburg, fearing for themselves, fled with the coffin containing the Virgin’s body, which by then had been reduced to dust, to Legecestria, now called Chester, as to the safest place against barbarian slaughter.”

6. Camden and Speed, writing about Chester, maintain that in the meantime it had been miserably disfigured by the Danes but splendidly restored by Aethelflaed, Lady of the Mercians and sister of King Edward the Elder, who ruled the English from 901 to 925. Under him Aethelflaed ruled with her husband Ethelred until 912 and, as a widow, ruled the Mercians for another seven years.

Edward was succeeded by Aethelstan. From his time, according to Ranulf, “until the arrival of the Normans, secular canons, contributing their possessions in turn, served the praises of the Virgin.” But William of Malmesbury, book IV of *De pontificibus Anglorum*, adds incorrectly that it had been an ancient monastery of religious women, “among whom Saint Werburga, professing celibacy, had shone with good virtues for a very long period.”

In the year of Christ 973, Chester saw King Edgar triumphantly arrive with magnificent pomp. Having placed the kings Kenneth of the Scots, Malcolm of the Cumbrians, and Maccus of the many islands, together with five Welsh sub-kings, at the oars, Edgar himself took hold of the rudder and sailed from the palace to the monastery of Saint John. After praying, he returned to the palace, as the Worcester historian and others relate at greater length.

Edgar was succeeded by his son Saint Edward, later a martyr, and afterward by another Saint Edward, the confessor. We shall discuss the former on 18 March; the latter we celebrated on 5 January, where chapter 7 of his Life states:

“Count Leofric saw Christ standing upon the altar, extending his right hand over the king and portraying him with the sign of the holy cross as he blessed him. This Count Leofric, and his noble wife, Countess Godiva, a worshiper of God and devoted lover of Saint Mary ever-virgin, built the monastery of Coventry from its foundations. They also enriched with precious ornaments the abbeys of Leominster and Winchcombe, the monasteries of Saint John the Baptist and Saint Werburga the virgin situated at Leicester, and the church of Saint Mary at Stowe. They enriched the monastery of Worcester with lands, and that of Evesham with buildings, various ornaments, and lands. Leofric died in a good old age on 31 August 1057,” as the Worcester historian, Hoveden, the Westminster historian, the Chester historian, and others assign it to that year.

Camden adds that “Leofric founded the church at Chester in honor of Saint Wereburga.”

Under William the Conqueror, Bishop Peter transferred his see from Lichfield to Chester, as William of Malmesbury observes; afterward, according to the Worcester historian, it was transferred to Coventry in 1102. Lichfield and Coventry are cities of Staffordshire, and later bishops often take their title from these several sees.

This King William I created Hugh Lupus hereditary palatine and earl of Chester; six earls succeeded him in hereditary order. This is the Hugh through whom, according to William of Malmesbury in *De pontificibus Anglorum*, book IV, “the monastery of Chester, in place of a monastery of religious women, was filled with monks of Saint Wereburga.” The Chester historian, however, prefers to say that “regular monks succeeded the secular canons,” whom William of Malmesbury, in book II of *De gestis regum Anglorum*, chapter 13, describes as having been expelled—few in number, and living in a shameful and impoverished manner—whether they had been alone there or had been added to the religious women so that the divine office might be celebrated more suitably.

Camden adds that “the church of Saint Wereburga was restored by Count Hugh and granted to the monks through the authority of Saint Anselm.” Nearly everyone writes, together with the *Annals of Stowe* and the first edition of the *English Martyrology*, that this occurred in 1092 under King William Rufus.

In the later edition of the *Martyrology*, it is said that at that time the bones of Saint Werburga were solemnly transferred from the church at Hamburg to Chester, and that Hugh built a church dedicated to her together with a monastery, now honored as a cathedral. The sacred relics had rested among the people of Hamburg for approximately three hundred years, which the Chester historian also noted.

Yet although the account above describes her body as having been transferred to Chester after “the Mercian king Burhred had been driven out”—that is, in the year 884—it appears that, through some error of the copyists, 170 years may have been inserted in place of 300. Indeed, since the translation is said to have taken place under William II, approximately eighty years beyond the stated three hundred would have elapsed. And if we believe the same *Martyrology*, which says that she died around the year 676, more than four hundred years would have passed since her death.

7. At the end of the manuscript history of the monastery of Peterborough it is noted that “Saint Werburga rests at Legecestria.”

On this same day, 3 February, besides the *English Martyrology*, the Carthusians of Cologne, in the *Auctarium* of Usuard, record her in these words: “Likewise, Wereburga the virgin.” Ferrarius, in his *General Catalogue*, writes: “In England, Saint Wetereburga the virgin,” whom he calls Wereburga in his notes.

Menard, in the Benedictine *Martyrology*, writes: “At the monastery of Chester, Saint Werburga, virgin and abbess, daughter of Wulfhere, king of the Mercians.”

Edovard Maihew, in the *Trophies of the English Benedictines*, writes: “At Tricingham, commonly Trentham, in the county of Stafford, Saint Wereburga, virgin and abbess, renowned for the splendor of her lineage and the holiness of her life”; and he recounts her deeds from various sources.

On this day Jerome Porter, in *The Flowers of the Saints of England*, gives an abridgment of her Life and says that she died “around the year of the Lord 676,” when she may have begun the monastic life after her father Wulfhere’s death in the preceding year.

Arnold Wion confuses her with Saint Witeburga, her great-aunt, and celebrates her on 8 July:

“In England,” he says, “Saint Witeburga the virgin, daughter of Wulfer, king of the Mercians, and religious woman of Ely, renowned for holiness and miracles.” In his notes he adds that she was also called Wereburga and Vereburga and that “she was offered to God by her mother, Queen Ermenilda, in the monastery of Ely around the year of the Lord 670.”

The manuscript *Florarium* has the following under 19 February: “In England, Saint Wicburga the virgin.” Thus it may be uncertain whether the author is speaking of Saint Witburga or of Wereburga.

Could Saint Wereburga also have been confused by some with Saint Walburga, virgin and abbess, and could this have given rise to the belief that she was the daughter of a king and that her father was Saint Richard, king of England? We shall investigate this on 7 February in the Life of Saint Richard and on 25 February, the feast of Saint Walburga.

8. Finally, Florentius of Worcester, under the year 675, and the Westminster historian, under 676, speak of Saint Wereburga. They say that she was “a virgin of great virtues, who, with God’s cooperation, performed many miracles; that she was placed over certain monasteries of virgins devoted to God, living with them according to the rule and piously advising them in all things; and that, until the end of her life, she served Christ the King. Thus, departing from this world, she entered into the embrace and marriage feast of her heavenly Bridegroom.”

William of Malmesbury, book II of *De gestis regum Anglorum*, chapter 13, says:

“The merits of Saint Ermenilda at Ely, and especially those of her daughter Wereburga in the City of the Legions, are praised, and their miracles exalted. Since they are unfailingly favorable to every petition, they most especially reach the prayers of women and children with the aid of one who is near and at hand.”

Nearly the same words are read in Vincent of Beauvais, *Speculum historiale*, book XXV, chapter 32, and in Peter de Natalibus, *Catalogue*, book II, chapter 67. Polydore Vergil, book IV of *Anglica Historia*, Harsfield, seventh century, chapter 23, Andrew du Chesne, book VI of *Anglica Historia*, and many others are also illustrious heralds of her virtues.

9. The following Life was divided in the manuscript codex into the chapters listed below; it is sufficient to place them here in advance, with a new division made according to our custom:

**Chapter I.** Genealogy of Saint Wereburga.  
**II.** Her life in the monastery at Ely.  
**III.** Her mother’s life in the same monastery.  
**IV.** Wereburga is placed by her uncle, King Ethelred, over the monasteries of religious women. The same king, following the example of her holiness, becomes a most blessed monk.  
**V.** As she is a pious mother, so Wereburga becomes the servant of all rather than their mistress.  
**VI.** At her command she captures and releases flocks of birds.  
**VII.** Her humility. She rebukes an executioner who has turned his neck backward while it remains whole, and reforms the suppliant.  
**VIII.** Her death on 3 February.  
**IX.** While the people of Tricingham guard her body, they fall asleep; the people of Hamburg take it away after the doors are miraculously opened.  
**X.** After nine years, when it is raised, it is found entirely fresh in body and garments, as though alive.

# The Life Begins

[Col. 0097]

## Chapter One. The Illustrious Descent of Saint Wereburga from Four Royal Families

1. Werburga, daughter of kings and most worthy bride of Christ, rests in the city of Chester, glorious in the signs of her merits. She is renowned throughout England for pure holiness, royal dignity, the testimony of her virtues, and the fame of the histories of the English.

She shines sublimely from the earliest kings of the English, and especially from the most powerful king of Dorobernia, that is, Canterbury, Aethelberht, who, through his principal teacher Augustine, made it possible for the first of the English kings to be consecrated to Christ. Indeed, her noble and holy lineage is traced through four kingdoms. It seems pleasing to set it out here in the following order, so that the jewel of God may be valued more highly and this morning star may be seen more clearly, as it were among the stars that precede it.

Aethelberht, therefore, begot Eadbald by Queen Berta, daughter of the king of the Franks. He left Eadbald, together with his daughter Aethelburga, as the excellent heir of his piety and kingdom.

Aethelburga, after the killing of her own king, Edwin of Northumbria, returned to her brother Eadbald at Lyming. There she built a monastery, in which Saint Aeadburga rests with her. Eadbald also begot, by Emma, daughter of another king of the Franks, Eormred and Ergombert, princes, and the holy virgin Answyth, who is venerated at Folkestone, where she was buried.

Eormred, by his illustrious wife Oslava, had Aethelred and Aethelberht. When they had been innocently slaughtered, a radiant column of light from heaven revealed them as martyrs of Christ. He also had four holy daughters: Domneva, Aermenberga, Aermenburga, and Aermengida, who shone forth like the four branches of a river from the fountain of paradise.

To his brother, King Ergombert, was born by the daughter of King Anna, Saexburga, the sister of the perpetual virgin Aetheldretha. United in royal marriage, Saexburga bore kings worthy of heaven, Aegbricht and Lotharius, and queens worthy of heaven, Eormhilda and Eorkengoda.

Eormhilda, given in marriage to Wulfhere, king of the Mercians and son of King Penda, gave birth to the most illustrious Werburga, in whom this ancestral purple blossoms.

2. Her most blessed maternal aunt, the virgin Eorkengoda, traveled across the sea out of love for sacred religion and rests there. She showed through many virtues that she had been received by the Lord as his guest and stranger.

But the blessed and royal Domneva, married to Merwala, the royal brother of Wulfhere, bore to the grace of the most holy Trinity a threefold crown of virginity: namely, the most holy sisters Mildburga, Mildryda, and Mildgyda, who, in the distinct foundations of their monasteries, illumine their homeland. She also bore a son, Merevin, who, having been baptized, was snatched away as a little child and numbered among the holy innocents.

The noble birth and holiness of life-giving Wereburga are also closely adorned by her most holy paternal aunts, the daughters of King Penda, Kyneburga and Kynewida, who, together with their kinswoman, the most blessed Tibba, illumine the church of the heavenly gatekeeper Peter at Burgh.

Their father and the kings who were their uncles—namely Peada, Aethelred, and the aforementioned Merwala, brothers of the women mentioned above—were not merely worshipers of Christian teaching but its first and most zealous propagators. Just as Aethelberht first extended Christianity in Dorobernia, so Wulfhere first extended it among the Mercians.

Thus, as we stated earlier, from four kingdoms and ancient kings Christ’s rose, Werburga, flourishes: from Aethelberht, prince of the Kentish, who first received the faith; from Berta or Emma of the Franks; from King Anna and grandmother Sexburga of the East Angles; and from her father, she became most resplendent among the Mercians.

These things are prefixed to the praise of the virgin, so that holiness may fittingly proceed from a holy root; indeed, so that greater glory may be ascribed to her because of the excellence of royalty, which she despised. It remains now to explain her holy manner of life and her worthy end in the Lord.

## Chapter Two. Saint Wereburga’s Life in the Monastery at Ely and Her Superintendence of Various Monasteries

3. From the tender dawn of her life, when the beauty of her appearance remarkably corresponded to the nobility of her birth, she began, with a beautiful face and a most beautiful mind, to strive toward him who is “beautiful beyond the sons of men.” When she was able to taste in advance his inestimable sweetness, she immediately burned for his love with longing heart; and, like a deer for springs of water, her virginal soul thirsted for him.

The Spirit of the Lord, proceeding from the Father of love, was so sweet and gentle that he drew her to himself, kindled heavenly desires in her heart, and extinguished earthly ones. Through love of perpetual virginity she flew toward the Bridegroom of eternal purity. With angelic chastity she rejected royal suitors and lovers; indeed, Christ, dwelling in his chosen one, snatched her away from all who desired her.

Her most holy mother never ceased, through constant admonitions, to water the garden of the Lord, plant in it the unfading shoots of paradise, and kindle her lamp with the oil and flame of unquenchable charity. She trained her daughter for that life toward which she herself, still under the yoke of marriage, sighed with inexpressible groanings.

Yet the most high providence of God, mercifully ordering all things, established the mother as the refuge of all the poor and of all who were in need. At the same time, it arranged that she should bear to God, through her pious maternal heart, a pledge most acceptable to him, and that she should eventually receive a greater crown for her long-deferred desires.

Riches had become worthless to both mother and daughter. They regarded the palace as a monastery. Gold, gems, garments woven with gold, and everything that the pompous vanity of the world displays were more burdensome to them than glorious. If royal dignity ever compelled them to use such things for a time, they grieved that they were subject to vanity as though to captivity.

4. But the virginal freedom of Blessed Werburga, as soon as she was able, cast off these chains and went to the monastery of Ely, offering herself to God with the dignity of her exalted parents.

There Saint Aetheldreda, her blessed and undefiled maternal aunt, first presided; afterward Sexburga, the sister of that virgin and therefore, as stated above, Wereburga’s grandmother, presided there.

At once the adornment of earthly splendor was cast aside. She put on the habit of sacred religion: a dark garment instead of the glory of ornament, and a humble veil upon her head instead of the diadem of a kingdom. Thus the illustrious virgin strove to trample upon worldly arrogance; in mind and conduct, like a pilgrim here below, to journey toward the heavenly homeland; and with complete submission of spirit to show herself the most humble handmaid of Christ, whom he might deign to exalt as his bride.

She anticipated every service of the monastery. She showed herself inferior to everyone. For the needs of all she lavished the tender compassion of love wounded by charity.

### Editorial Notes Preserved from the Source

- [Col. 0097D] King Saint Ethelbert, her great-great-grandfather, died in 616; he is commemorated on 24 February, on which day we shall treat of his ancestors.
- [Col. 0098D] Saint Augustine is commemorated on 26 May; his companion and successor in the archbishopric, Saint Laurence, on 2 February.
- [Col. 0099B] Berta, called Adilberga by Saint Gregory, was the daughter of Charibert, king of Paris, Saint Wereburga’s great-great-grandfather, who died in 570. Chlothar I, her great-great-great-grandfather, died in 562; Clovis I, father of that great-great-great-grandfather, in 509.
- [Col. 0099B] Eadbald, her great-grandfather, reigned from 616 to 640. According to Bede, book II, chapter 6, having “anathematized every worship of idolatry,” into which he had relapsed after his father’s death, and having “renounced an unlawful marriage,” contracted with his stepmother, “he embraced the faith of Christ and, being baptized, took care, as far as he was able, in every respect to provide for and favor the affairs of the Church.” Bede discusses his death in book III, chapter 8.
- [Col. 0099B–C] Saint Ethelburga is commemorated on 8 September. Bede, book II, chapter 9: “Ethelburga, otherwise called Tate, was by her marriage the occasion of the Northumbrian people’s receiving the faith.” Pope Boniface V sent her a letter, which Bede reports in chapter 11.
- [Col. 0099C] Saint Edwin, the first Christian king of the Northumbrians, reigned seventeen years and was killed on 12 October 633. Bede treats of him in chapter 9 and, with a few intervening matters, through chapter 20.
- [Col. 0099C] “King Eadbald gave his sister Ethelburga the estate of Lyming, where she built a monastery; consecrated with the veil by Blessed Honorius, archbishop of Canterbury, she became the mother of many virgins and widows.” Thus Capgrave in the Life of Saint Honorius. Camden places Lyming in the district, or lathe, of Shepway, near Elham, not far from the sea and the port of Dover.
- [Col. 0099C–D] Eadburga, or Edburga. In his separate Life Capgrave calls her daughter of Saint Ethelbert; thus the text here should read: “rests with her sister Eadburga.” This better suits the author. But Capgrave confuses that Edburga with another, younger woman, who lived as abbess of Saint Mildred’s monastery on the Isle of Thanet and transferred its body to a new church dedicated by Archbishop Cuthbert. The Worcester historian writes that Cuthbert succeeded Nothelm, who “died on 17 October 741.”
- [Col. 0099D] We nowhere read who this king was. When Emma married, Chlothar II was monarch of the Franks; she may have been his daughter, sister, or a kinswoman descended from the kings of Austrasia or Burgundy.
- [Col. 0099D] Elsewhere he is called Ercomred and Ermenred; in the manuscript History of Peterborough he is called a saint.
- [Col. 0099D] Ercombert, Saint Werburga’s grandfather, reigned from 640 to 664. According to Bede, book III, chapter 8, he ordered idols to be destroyed throughout his kingdom and the Lenten fast to be observed.
- [Col. 0099D] Saint Eanswith, or Enswida, is commemorated on 12 September.
- [Col. 0100B] “Folkestone,” says Camden in his account of Kent, “was famous among the Anglo-Saxons for religion because of the monastery which Eanswith, virgin daughter of Eadbald king of Kent, dedicated for virgins; it is now a village, and the Ocean has washed away its greater part.” It lies near Dover, toward the west.
- [Col. 0100B] These brothers, Ethelred and Ethelberht, are commemorated on 17 October, the day on which they were translated to Ramsey monastery under King Ethelred.
- [Col. 0100B] “A ray of prolonged and immeasurable light, like a blazing torch, appeared to the king to stretch from the summit of the royal hall,” where they had been buried that very night, “up to heaven.” Manuscript Life.
- [Col. 0100B–C] In the same Life the four daughters are called Dompnena, Ermenburga, Etheldritha, and Ermengitha; of these, Ermenburga is commemorated on 19 November.
- [Col. 0100C] Anna, her other great-grandfather, king of the East Angles, was killed in 654. Among his royal predecessors was his cousin, Saint Sigebert the martyr, whose feast is 17 September. Bede, book IV, chapter 29, calls Anna “a very religious man, excellent in every respect in mind and deed”; the manuscript History of Ely also calls him a saint.
- [Col. 0100C] Saint Sexburga, her maternal grandmother, is commemorated on 6 July; her sisters Saint Withburga and Ethelburga are commemorated on 8 and 7 July respectively.
- [Col. 0100C] Saint Etheldreda, Ethelreda, or Etheldryth, first married to Prince Tondbert and afterward for twelve years to Egfrid, later king of the Northumbrians, preserved her virginity. Bede treats of her in book IV, chapters 19 and 20. She is commemorated on 23 June. Egfrid began to reign in 670.
- [Col. 0100C] Egbert, her maternal uncle, reigned in Kent from 664 to 673.
- [Col. 0100C–D] Lothair, another maternal uncle, reigned after his brother until 685.
- [Col. 0100D] Saint Ermenilda, her mother, is commemorated on 13 February.
- [Col. 0100D] Earcongota, or Erkengotha, lived under her great-aunt Saint Ethelburga as abbess in the monastery of Saint Fara in the diocese of Meaux, not far from Paris. Saint Earcongota is commemorated on 25 February and Saint Ethelburga on 7 July. Bede treats of them in book III, chapter 8.
- [Col. 0100D] Wulfhere, her father, reigned from 657.
- [Col. 0100D] Penda, her paternal grandfather, reigned from 626 to 655; he was succeeded first by his other son Peada, and then by Wulfhere.
- [Col. 0100D] This agrees with Capgrave’s Life of Saint Milburga and with the manuscript Life of the brothers Saints Ethelred and Ethelberht. On the other hand, William of Malmesbury, book I of *De gestis regum Anglorum*, chapter 4, the Worcester historian under 675, and the Westminster historian under 676 write that Saint Ermenburga married Merwala, or Merewald.
- [Col. 0100D–0101D] Saint Milburga is commemorated on 23 February, Saint Mildred, or Milthryth, on 13 July. We treated of Saint Milwida on 17 January, where much was said concerning the boy Merevin; we shall discuss Merewald’s kingdom on 23 February.
- [Col. 0101D] Saints Kyneburga and Kynewida, also called Chineburga and Chineswida, are commemorated on 6 March. They are also joined in the Life of Saint Tibba, which says that they died on 13 December.
- [Col. 0101D] Their bodies are said to have been translated in 1005 “to the monastery of the Borough of Saint Peter,” commonly Peterborough, built by Wulfhere with his brothers and these sisters. We treat of it in the Life of Saint Ermenilda.
- [Col. 0101D–0102D] Saint Ethelred is commemorated on 4 May. In the Appendix to the Worcester historian another brother, Mercelmus, is added; there Merewald, here Merwala, is also called a saint.
- [Col. 0102D] Capgrave and the manuscript of Rood Valley read “ascend.”
- [Col. 0102D] Ely, in Bede, book IV, chapter 19; elsewhere Elia and Eli. Formerly a monastery and now a town, it is on an island of the same name, so called, according to Bede, from eels, beside the River Granta in Cambridgeshire among the East Angles.
- [Col. 0102D] She founded that monastery in 673 and died in 679.

5. Her father Wlferus, now beloved of God, builder of many churches, and a supreme lover and promoter of the Christian faith—for he even drew subject kings to the worship of Christ by granting them provinces as their reward [Note: [Col. 0102D] We discuss this fully on 13 February]—passed from his temporal kingdom to the everlasting one in the seventeenth year of his reign [Note: [Col. 0102D] In the year 675]. Then the most blessed queen Eormenilda, after devout tears, rejoicing that she had been released from the worldly chain, took up the way of life she had long desired and, together with her blessed daughter, submitted to the Lord’s easy yoke in the monastery at Ely. From that time onward she lived there indefatigably in such ardor of virtue, holiness, and religious observance that she was an example of chastity and every virtue even to the virgins [Col. 0102D]. Mother and daughter strove with one another in devotion, each asking who could be humbler and more submissive: the mother placed before herself the virginity of the daughter whom she had borne; the virgin, her mother’s authority. Both rejoiced both to conquer and to be conquered [Col. 0103A]. Now, at the same monastery, beside the conspicuous tomb of that most kindly parent, it shines forth how generously she poured out the compassion of her heart upon everyone while she lived bodily, so much so that those who experienced her benefits dare faithfully assert that no believing petitioner was ever disappointed of her help.

6. Accordingly, the uncle of the gracious Werburga, King Aethelred, who had succeeded her brother Wlferus, was most gentle in every holiness and possessed a holy mind.
