Seeing divine prudence and sanctity shining more deeply in his blessed niece—and being one who could love virtue even beyond kinship—he entrusted her with authority over the monasteries of religious women flourishing in his kingdom. This was most beautifully brought about by heavenly providence [Col. 0103B], so that she who was a perfect disciple of sacred discipline might become its most fitting teacher for the salvation of many.

7. The king, meanwhile, began to grow increasingly weary of ruling, considering himself amid secular affairs like an animal bent toward the earth, while she, on the wings of her merits like a dove, flew toward heaven. And why say more? The heat of his spirit did not rest until, in the twenty-ninth year of his reign [Note: [Col. 0103D] He began to reign in the year 675, after Wulferus’s death; the twenty-ninth year was 704], in the monastery at Bardney [Note: [Col. 0103D] Bardney, also Beardena and Peartaneau, commonly Bardneg, in Lincolnshire, not far from the town, on the left bank of the Witham], he was made a monk from a king; and he is now proved, by heavenly favor, worthy of veneration for his merits.

8. Werburga, most beloved of God, was such a teacher to those under her authority that she seemed rather their servant. She equaled herself to the lowest, or rather subjected herself to them, preferring, if it were permitted, the lowest place to a position of authority. She carried everyone as though they were her own entrails, cherished them as though they were children of her own womb, and instructed them more attentively by example than by command. Love, kindness, peace, and cheerfulness wholly possessed her. She was most ready in generosity toward the needy and most compassionate in piety toward the afflicted. With the greatest compassion, patience laughed at adversity [the text is evidently corrupt here]; confidence conquered it, and heavenly joy trampled it underfoot. For the use of divine wisdom, she received prosperity; she regarded abstinence as delicacies, vigils as sleep [Note: [Col. 0103D] The manuscript of Cambden: “solemnities”], labor as pleasure, and sacred readings and prayers as banquets. In body she dwelt on earth, but in spirit she lived in heaven.

## CHAPTER III. The obedience of wild geese; the punished disobedience of a steward

9. But perhaps we are already tiring the reader by delaying the miracles. Merits are greater than the miracles themselves, because miracles arise from them: merits can be perfect without signs, whereas signs are nothing without merits. Nevertheless, the most worthy virgin is proved to have shone with many wonders, both in the monastery at Ely and wherever she lived. In the region of Weduna [Note: [Col. 0103D] Weduna, which Cambden believes to be Banavenna in the Itinerary of Antoninus, commonly Wedon, on the river Ausona [Col. 0104D], which from there flows toward Northampton; the chief town of the province here called Hamtuna], which was part of her own estate in the province of Hamtuna [Col. 0104A], the whole local population has handed down this pleasant and celebrated miracle from generation to generation.

10. While the royal virgin was staying at her estate at Weduna, an enormous multitude of untamed birds, ordinarily called geese [Note: [Col. 0104D] Capgrave and the manuscript of Ruberval have “wild geese,” that is, geese], was ravaging her fields. A household peasant reported this damage to his mistress. Then, with courageous faith, she ordered him to bring them all in and shut them up, as one does with animals that graze on another’s crops.

“Go,” she said, “and bring all these birds in here.”

He went away, deeply astonished, wondering whether the command was a joke or madness. For how could a suspect outsider force so many flying creatures, which could escape through the sky, to go on foot into captivity? “How,” he said, “shall I turn them here when they flee into the air at my first approach?”

Then the virgin, pressing her command, said: “Go as quickly as possible, and by our order bring them all into our custody.”

Fearing that he might neglect even a seemingly pointless command from the holy mistress, he went after them all and said to them: “Go, go to our mistress.” He drove them all before him as though they were captive animals. Not a single bird among that great gathering lifted a wing; rather, like featherless chicks or birds whose wings had been cut off, they moved slowly on foot, approaching with bowed necks as though out of shame for their offense. Thus they gathered, trembling and subdued like condemned prisoners, within the court of their judge, and there [Note: [Col. 0104D] “There they are shut up”] they were confined as captives—or rather preserved for mercy [Col. 0104C].

11. The daughter of light spent that night, as was her custom, in heavenly hymns and unceasing prayers. In the morning all the newcomers cried out loudly to their mistress, as though asking pardon and permission to depart. But she, being most kind toward every creature of God, ordered them to be released, warning them not to dare return to that place again.

One of them, however, had been secretly taken away and hidden by one of the servants. When all the others had risen into the air on lifted wings and, looking about, had searched for her, they recognized the loss of their companion because one was absent [Note: [Col. 0104D] “There they perceive it”]. Immediately the entire army gathered above the virgin’s house [Note: [Col. 0104D] “There they assemble”] and, with an immense clamor, complained of the wrong done to their community. The sky was covered on every side by their widespread host, so that they seemed by this voice to be invoking the judgment of their compassionate mistress in human words:

“Why, mistress, when your mercy has released all of us, is one of our number being held captive? Can such wickedness remain hidden in your holy house, and can shameful robbery prevail under your innocence?”

The divine virgin therefore went out to the murmuring and complaint of so great a multitude [Col. 0105A]. She understood the cause as though she had heard it expressed in the words just given. Immediately she investigated the matter, and the guilty servant himself publicly confessed the theft [Note: [Col. 0105D] Malmesbury, *De gestis pontificum*, book IV, adds a new miracle, in which he wishes “that goose” to have been “eaten by a rustic. Saint Wereburga therefore ordered its bones to be gathered up; and at once, through the healing sign of the virgin’s hand, skin and flesh grew over the bones, and the skin began to sprout feathers, until the bird, restored to life, first sprang up joyfully and then balanced itself in flight through the air.” These details are less credible; and Cambden, speaking of Northamptonshire, says that “credulous writers have sung of her miracles in driving away geese.”]. The bird having been recovered, she reunited it with its own kind as a merciful conciliator and ordered them all to depart together under the condition already stated. As they rejoiced in this, she said kindly:

“Bless the Lord, birds of the air.”

Without delay, the whole assembly flew away, so that, as the famous account records, no little bird of this kind was ever again found in the land belonging to gracious Werburga. Thus the animal creature obeyed her well, since she continually obeyed the Creator of all things with complete devotion. Precisely such a miracle is read in the *Life of the most blessed virgin Amelberga* [Note: [Col. 0105D] She is commemorated on 10 July. In her manuscript Life the same miracle is narrated; the birds are also called geese. One is said to have been taken away and hidden by a young servant, and on the following day to have been restored, as though at the request of the others], which we are reissuing in our own style, so that the same faith of both women may be demonstrated in the same work, although they lived at different times and in different places [Col. 0105B].

12. How great was her humility, and how great also her exaltation before God, is confirmed by other evidence in the same region of Weduna. She had a herdsman named Alnotus, a man of pious conduct and, insofar as was possible under human servitude, of holy life; the fame of his merits is perpetuated and celebrated in his own places [Note: [Col. 0105D] In the earlier edition of the *English Martyrology* he is listed on 27 February, but in the later edition on 25 November].

When the steward of his mistress happened to be flaying him with a most bloody beating, while he endured everything with the greatest gentleness in the name of God, the gracious virgin, unable to bear his suffering, threw herself at the feet of the unworthy butcher, crying out with prayer and reproach:

“Spare him for the love of God. Why are you tearing apart an innocent man, who is more acceptable, as I believe, to the Most High, the Inspector of us all?” [Col. 0105C]

When the man, whether because of rage or pride, was slow to bend, at once his hard neck and grim face were twisted backward by heavenly indignation [Note: [Col. 0106D] Cambden’s manuscript has “whole,” as above in the heading, “whole”; Capgrave and the manuscript of Ruberval have the better reading]. At last, as he should have done earlier, he fell at his mistress’s feet and tearfully begged pardon for his own offense—the pardon he had denied the innocent man. Immediately, through the intervention of the virgin’s mercy, he was restored to his former condition.

The man of God just mentioned lies at Stow [Note: [Col. 0106D] Commonly Stow or Stowe, between Weduna and Buccabrive, elsewhere Bugbrok and Biabroock; in the manuscript Uccabrue], one league from Buccabrive. While leading the life of a hermit in the forest, he was martyred by bandits and, as is celebrated, manifested divine signs showing that he was acceptable to God [Note: [Col. 0106D] More probably, “revealed” them].

## CHAPTER IV. The death, burial, and translation of Saint Werburga

[Col. 0105D]

13. Moreover, there is no doubt that Werburga, most beloved of God, shone forth through many other signs and, by heavenly grace, healed various sick and weak persons. By divine inspiration she was also able to foresee and foretell many things; nor could she remain unaware that the final day, which she always kept before her eyes and watched from afar with complete vigilance and a burning lamp, was already near.

Since, then, she continually desired, out of her excessive charity, to be present to all her household and to the monasteries entrusted to her, while, conversely, no one could bear to be deprived of her sweet presence, divine foreknowledge and will nevertheless chose that she should rest bodily in the monastery at Heamburga [Note: [Col. 0106D] Commonly Handbury in southern Staffordshire], while she would always be present to all in spirit. Therefore she ordered the community at Heamburga [Note: [Col. 0106D] Capgrave and the manuscript of Ruberval read: “all her own people”] that, wherever she departed from this light, they should come without delay and transport her body to their monastery [Col. 0106B] [Note: [Col. 0106D] “That they should transfer her body to the monastery at Heamburga and bury it without delay.”].

14. Thus the long-desired end of earthly labors and sorrows came to the heavenly virgin, and she entered into heavenly and eternal joys. The night of immortality passed forth, and the day of eternity dawned; darkness passed away, and the true light shone, and the sun of everlasting joy rose for her.

The blessed soul rejoiced as though invited to a banquet: she was passing from exile to her homeland, from prison to the kingdom, from death to life, from captivity to triumph, and from the tyranny of the world to the everlasting Bridegroom of glory, whom she desired. Accordingly, after she had been placed in the monastery called Tricengeham [Note: [Col. 0106D] Also Tricingham; commonly Trentham in Staffordshire, not far from the source of the Trent, after the river Lyma had flowed into it], through the illness and death of her body she was taken up by angelic choirs [Col. 0106C] into immortal ceremonies, and was celebrated with heavenly songs in the court above. Her deposition is commemorated on the third day before the Nones of February.

15. The sacred body was carried into the church and guarded with the greatest care in the midst of the people of Tricengeham, the doors having been securely locked. Everyone strove in vain to exclude the people of Heamburga, so that by their own service or defense they might defeat the command of the prophetic virgin and retain the sacred treasure forever in that place.

But there is neither wisdom nor counsel against God. While they kept especially vigilant watch that very night, a profound sleep suddenly overcame them all. Immediately a large multitude from Heamburga arrived with God’s ministers. At once all the doors of the monastery were opened for them, the locks and bars falling to the ground [Col. 0106D]. They rushed in while the entire crowd of guards lay buried in sleep, seized the virgin’s body without anyone from the opposing party stirring [Col. 0107A] [Note: [Col. 0107D] Others read “the body”], and carried it away. With immense joy and songs of praise mingled with thanksgiving, they led it to the monastery at Heamburga, while the rebels were confounded.

16. Who could adequately reckon with what solemnity her soul was received by God, since he transferred her body to its predestined rest through so great a marvel? Buried in this sacred place with due reverence and solemn rejoicing, the pearl of God proved by many signs that she lives in the heavenly kingdom: health is restored to the sick, light to the blind, hearing to the deaf, and speech to the mute; lepers rejoice in their cleansing, and those oppressed by various illnesses rejoice after receiving healing. Thus, after her death, she restores so many to life—she who had lived so holily.

[Col. 0107B] 17. After this, the Lord’s ineffable grace also deigned to show clearly, through the virgin flesh that remained incorrupt for a long time, how pleasing to him had been her undefiled chastity together with the most pure mind by which she saw God.

Nine years after her burial, at the urging of the people of Heamburga, it pleased King Ceolred [Note: [Col. 0107D] Ceolred, son of Saint Aethelred, became king after Ceonred had been tonsured as a monk at Rome in 709; he died in 716 and was buried at Lichfield], who then ruled the Mercians, that her sacred body should be raised from the tomb, since everyone cried out that it was unworthy for so great a light of many people to be hidden beneath a bushel of earth.

When the cover of the burial chamber had been removed, everyone supposed that, according to the human condition, all the flesh had decayed and that only bare bones remained. Instead, the virgin was found entirely intact, as though sleeping on a soft bed. Her garments appeared completely bright and sound, just as when she had first put them on; her face was white and her cheeks rosy, as in the first bloom of life, when her covering was reverently removed [Col. 0107C].

A cry of thanksgiving rose to heaven, and the wonder of so great a grace kindled the gathered people into praise of the Lord. She was therefore taken up by priests solemnly arrayed, amid supplicating prayers and the melodious rhythms of the Church’s choirs. When they examined her still more carefully, no injury at all and no corruption whatsoever was found in her. At last she was placed in a suitably prepared shrine, where she visibly enlightens the faithful people with her splendid lamp.

18. This honor of her uninjured body endured for a long time under angelic protection, until the time of the pagans [Col. 0107D] [Col. 0108A] [Note: [Col. 0107D] Others read “Danes.” They began ravaging England in 832; in 851 they put Beortulf, king of the Mercians, and his army to flight. Under King Burrhed, the Mercians made treaties with the Danes, who refused to depart, in the years 868 and 872. When King Burrhed went to Rome in 874, a certain thane administered the kingdom, part of which was granted in 877 to King Ceolwulf. Under him the kingdom of the Mercians completely withered away. Later, when the heptarchy of the English coalesced into a monarchy, King Eadward freed the Mercians at the beginning of the tenth century, appointing Ethered, husband of Aegelfleda, as earl of the Mercians; under her, as we said above, Chester was restored after being handed over. Finally, in 942 King Eadmund invaded Mercia and occupied the cities of Lincoln, Nottingham, Stamford, Derby, and others, reducing all Mercia to his power, as the Anglo-Saxon chronicler, who wrote in that tenth century, reports in nearly these words. The Danes returned to England in 991 and ravaged the provinces of Mercia, especially from 1010 to 1016, when Canute, king of the Danes, received the northern part of England and in the following year gained rule over all England], and the day of calamity, when by God’s most just dispensation this land of the English was delivered into the swords of the heathen.

Then at last the life-giving body chose to yield to mortal law and dissolve, lest enemies—unbelievers in God’s miracles and ungrateful for his benefits—should touch it with impious hands. [Note: [Col. 0108D] Capgrave, together with Saint Ruberval, concludes the *Life* here as follows: “Her bones were then transferred to Chester, where they rest to this day, and frequent miracles are performed through her merits.”]

Certainly, God’s omnipotence could have protected his beloved even in the day of calamity, just as he preserved many saints of this land from wicked contamination. Even now, after more than four hundred years, they flourish with bodies whole and incorrupt, and unquestionably they may endure to the end according to the divine will.

Yet God is wonderful and glorious in his saints. In marvelous and immeasurable providence, he dissolves some for a time into the greater glory of the resurrection [Col. 0108B], while he preserves others in perpetual incorruption as an example of his promise. So many of the noblest martyrs and highest priests of the Lord have been consumed by beasts, birds, or fire.

“As the Psalmist says: ‘They have given the dead bodies of your servants, O Lord, as food to the birds of the air, the flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth’ (Psalm 78:2).”

The greater the disgrace, the greater will be the glory. Stephen, the chief standard-bearer of the martyrs, is read to have performed many signs during his life, but it is not read there that he raised the dead. After the triumph of his death and the dissolution of all his members, however, he is described as having restored many dead people to life, so that from the injury of death a greater power of life might arise. Thus God’s great grace was present in the solid body of blessed Werburga, but a greater hope of eternal renewal remains in her body now consumed [Col. 0108C].

19. Let us therefore celebrate her most sacred feast with the readiest devotion, because all its celebration belongs to the honor of Christ the Lord, who made her worthy of celebration through such fitting merits. He has provided her for us as an intercessor before him, so that through the veneration of his beloved we may deserve his favor, since we have no merits of our own to put into effect.

For he will hear her praying for us all the more kindly the more ardently we offer praises to God through her. May the Crowned One, Werburga, ever worthy of remembrance, grant that through her holy intercessions we may obtain both the desires that will profit us here [Col. 0108D] and, forever, the fellowship of blessed vision [Col. 0109A] and of his resurrection. May the Savior himself grant this—I mean he who reigns and rules with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages. Amen.

[Col. 0109]

# LIFE OF SAINT EADGITHA, OR EDITH, DAUGHTER OF EADGAR, KING OF THE ENGLISH, AND RELIGIOUS WOMAN OF WILTON, BY GOTSELINUS

(Edited by Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Benedicti*, vol. VI, p. 636, from volume IX of Surius, who altered the style somewhat.)

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

[Col. 0109]

1. Gotselinus, or Goscelinus, the monk whose work on Saint Augustine, apostle of the English, we presented above, is said—among several other Lives of saints—to have written the *Acts of Saint Eadgitha the Virgin*, according to the *Catalogue of Writers of Britain* and according to Wion and Possevinus.

I do not doubt that this is Eadgitha, or Edgitha, or Editha, daughter of Eadgar, king of the English, whose Life Surius published with its style somewhat altered. We present the same work here, adding passages or testimonies from William of Malmesbury, who praised the same virgin more than once: both in book II, chapter 13, of *On the Kings of the English*, and in book II, chapter 4, of *On the Bishops of the English*. Harpsfeld also celebrates her in *Century X*, chapter 10, in addition to John Bromton, Maiheuvius, and other writers of English history.

2. Eadgitha professed the monastic life in the monastery at Wilton among the West Saxons. “Wilton,” according to William of Malmesbury in *On the Bishops of the English*, book II, chapter 4, “is a fairly large village situated above the River Wile, so famous that the whole district is named after it,” and it was formerly an episcopal see. Asser, in his book *On the Life of Alfred*, names the hill “Wilton, which is on the southern bank of the River Guilou.”

Eadgitha lived there most piously among religious women and received burial there. “In the same church,” says the same William, “lies her mother Wilfrith, whom popular opinion describes [another reading: “imagines”] not as a religious woman but as one veiled solely by the king’s private decision, under sudden fear of the king, after being taken from the royal bed and subjected to it. For touching a woman who had been, even if only outwardly, a religious woman, he was rebuked by Saint Dunstan and was required to perform penance for seven years. After giving birth, she too did not cling to the repeated pursuit of pleasure; rather, she grieved and rejected it, and she is asserted and believed to have been holy in truth.”

It is said in the following Life that, after the king had used force against her, she assumed the monastic habit at Wilton.

3. William’s testimony in the passage mentioned above does not allow us to doubt Eadgitha’s sanctity. “Her venerable feast,” he says, “is therefore held in many places in England, and no one should dare profane it with impunity.”

When King Cnut, a Dane among the English, irreverently treated the saint in jest and ordered her tomb to be opened, he scarcely escaped death, as the same author records there together with the writer of her Life. Theodoric, who had been punished from heaven along with others because he had violated the religious observance of the Nativity of the Lord through sexual misconduct and dancing, was restored to health at the tomb of the holy virgin. Harpsfeld records the event at length from Bruno, bishop of Toul, who was later called Pope Leo IX.

4. In the same period, three other royal virgins named Edith are said to have lived in England, apart from Edith, wife of Otto the Great. One was the daughter of King Ethelwluf and sister of King Alfred, who was entrusted to Saint Modwenna, the abbess discussed among the omitted saints of the fourth century. Another was Edith, daughter of Eadward the Elder and sister of Aethelstan. The third was the daughter of King Edmund and sister of Eadgar. All were saints and, indeed, religious women in the monastery at Pollesworth, which lies near the Forest of Arden in the diocese of Chester.

The first is praised in the *Acts of Saint Ositha* under 7 October and in the *Life of Saint Modwenna, Abbess of Streneshal*, by Capgrave. Modwenna is said to have placed Edith, the sister of King Alfred, in charge of the Pollesworth monastery she had founded. The place was later called Saint Edith’s Pollesworth, or Pollesworda, as the old records in volume I of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, p. 179, establish.

The second Edith, daughter of Eadward, was given by her brother Aethelstan in marriage to Sithric, king of the Northumbrians, but was later repudiated by him. She withdrew to Pollesworth and spent the remainder of her life there in religion, as Matthew of Westminster testifies under the year 925.

The third is Edith, daughter of King Edmund, sister of Eadgar, and niece of Eadward the Elder, whose daughter we have said the second Edith was. Thomas Maiheuvius, under 15 July, where he discusses all three together, suspects that the second and third are not distinct persons and that there was no other Edith than the daughter of Eadward the Elder; for no Edith who was the daughter of Edmund and sister of King Eadgar can be found. Yet in chapter 1 of the following Life, Edith is praised as the sister of King Eadgar.

5. Nevertheless, the solution to this difficulty does not depend so entirely upon the following Life that no doubt remains. For if its author was Gotselinus, who flourished at the beginning of the eleventh century, we cannot, on his authority, settle the matter with certainty. According to William of Malmesbury in book IV, chapter 1, of *On the Kings of the English*, he was:

“A monk of Saint-Bertin, who had come with Hermann, bishop of Salisbury, distinguished by remarkable skill in letters and song. Traveling for a long time through many bishoprics and abbeys, he left monuments of outstanding learning in many places in praise of the saints of England, second only to Bede. In music, moreover, he won the palm after Obernus. Finally, he raised innumerable Lives of recent saints into literary form; those of earlier times, lost through hostility or poorly edited, he renewed more elegantly. Happy the tongue that served so many saints; happy the breast that uttered so many melodious voices, especially since in his conduct the integrity of his learning was matched by his character.”

Thus far William.

## THE LIFE BEGINS

[Col. 0111]

### 1. Edith’s parents. The establishment of the monastic life under her mother

The blessed virgin Editha was the daughter of King Edgar and Wlftrudis, the daughter of a royal duke. The king had decided to join Wlftrudis to himself permanently in royal partnership, but, after she had been delivered of a child, she preferred to live thereafter in continence rather than serve sensual pleasures, being invited to this by the love of Christ.

Accordingly, at Wilton, she received the habit of a nun from the hands of Saint Ethelwold, bishop. Advancing through examples and virtues, she was placed over the virgins as their spiritual mother.

The blessed Editha, meanwhile, was left under her mother’s care. At last, with the king’s consent, she put on the monastic garment in the same monastery. Her mother equipped her not with gold, necklaces, or multicolored adornment, but with the splendor of learning and virtues.

Among the many examples of holy men that she both read repeatedly in books, saw before her with her own eyes, and learned through hearing, she was especially inflamed by the most holy crown of virginal integrity belonging to her mother’s dear friend Edith, who was the full sister of King Edgar, her father. In the monastery at Pollesworth in the province of Warwick, that Edith shone through signs of merit just as Eadgitha herself did at Wilton.

### 2. Her virtues

To her sisters she presented herself as Martha, but to Christ as Mary; toward everyone she devoted herself to service by performing helpful offices. She embraced all guests with the compassion of Christ. She was so devoted to abstinence as though she were attending banquets, and when she approached banquets, she did so without turning aside from the pursuit of frugality.

Entirely avoiding worldly favor, she devoted herself to the sick [Col. 0111C] and to those lacking human assistance, and she preferred lepers to the king’s children. The more disfigured anyone seemed by disease, the more humane she became toward that person through the greater compassion of her heart and the more ready to serve.

She could rightly be called the eye of the blind, the support of the weak, the clothing and nourishment of the needy, and the comfort of all the desolate.

### 3. Hair shirt and clothing

She wore an extremely rough hair shirt against her naked flesh, while outwardly dressed in bright clothing. Once, when blessed Ethelwold saw her entering in more ornate attire, he said to her:

“My daughter, one does not go to Christ’s bridal chamber in such garments, nor is the heavenly Bridegroom pleased by the body’s external adornment.”

But she, conscious of the inhabitant within, replied:

“Believe me, Father: with God’s help, my mind under this covering is in no way worse than it would be beneath a goatskin. I have my Lord, who regards not so much the clothing as the mind” [Note: [Col. 0111D] Surius rightly notes here that Editha did and said this in order to conceal the roughness of the hair shirt beneath her outer clothing. William of Malmesbury records the event both in book II, chapter 13, of [Col. 0112D] *On the Kings of the English* and in book II, chapter 4, of *On the Bishops of the English*.]

The man of God therefore perceived the authority of grace in the virgin and did not dare grieve God, the supreme Judge, in her. Rather, he rejoiced that the Lord governed all things in his saints according to his will, and that a pure mind pleased God both in purple and in sackcloth [Col. 0112A].

### 4. Love of the cross. Refusal of the dignity of abbess. Foreknowledge of her brother’s death

Wherever Editha went, the cross of Christ accompanied her. She bore the cross on her forehead, on her breast, on her journeys, and in all her works.

Once, as she was carrying food in a dish according to her custom, to be placed in the bosom of a poor person, a boy ran up from the side asking for alms. She extended it to him with the customary sign of the cross. Immediately the boy disappeared, so that she could no longer see him at all.

When she was fifteen years old, her father, King Edgar, appointed her abbess over three monasteries of nuns: Winchester, Barking, and a third. But she could not be drawn away from the house in which she had begun to serve God. She arranged that spiritual mothers, as more suitable persons, should be placed over each of those monasteries, preferring to be subject to her mother rather than to preside over others, and to fear her mother rather than command others [Col. 0112B].

After her father Edgar died and his son Edward, still a child, succeeded him, the holy woman saw in a dream that her right eye had fallen out. She reported the matter to the sisters and explained it at the same time:

“I seem to see this vision foretelling the fall of my brother Edward.”

Not long afterward, while Edward was wishing to visit his brother Ethelred, he was killed by the sons of iniquity, as may be seen in his history.

When the nobles of the kingdom wished to draw the holy virgin out of the monastery and place her on her father’s throne, as women rule among many peoples [Col. 0112C], and at last even attempted to use force, she gave no consent. She seemed to make it easier to turn stones into lead than to draw Christ’s virgin away from her purpose and the service of God.

### 5. Dunstan’s prophecy of Edith’s death

When she had built a church in honor of Saint Dionysius and had invited Saint Dunstan [Note: [Col. 0112D] William reports this very event in the two passages mentioned above, though the *Acts of Dunstan* omit it] to its dedication, the holy bishop saw the sacred virgin repeatedly extend her right thumb and trace the sign of the cross upon her forehead.

Delighted by this, he took the virgin’s right hand and said:

“May this finger never decay.”

Shortly afterward, during the celebration of Mass, the most holy man burst into tears. When his deacon asked why he was weeping, he sighed and drew his voice from the depths of his heart:

“This soul beloved of God, this starry jewel, will be carried away from the filth of the earth and this sorrowful life to the homeland of the saints. For this shameful world is not worthy of the presence of so great a light. On the forty-third day from now, this brilliant star will set for us. Behold, from our prison the lights of the saints are departing, while we sit in darkness and the shadow of death. Our sluggish old age is condemned by her untimely youth, while, as we slumber, she penetrates the heavens.”

### 6. Edith’s death in the year 984

As the hour approached when she was to depart from the world to the Lord, Saint Dunstan was present. Strengthening her soul with exhortations and prayers, he commended her as she departed from the body into the hands of the Lord.

Meanwhile, a frightened sister ran from the church of Saint Dionysius, where the holy virgin had died, to the monastery. She heard there a great crowd, as though singing psalms in choir. As she hesitated, a man of elegant appearance and distinguished dress met her and said:

“Do not come any nearer. The holy angels are about to carry the girl GODA (“Good”)—for they called her by this name as a greater grace, while in the language of her homeland she was called BONA (“good”)—from here with them to everlasting joys, so that with this melody the heavenly army may enter the palace of perpetual delight.”

Thus, in the twenty-third year of her age, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, she departed to Christ, around the year of the Lord 984. Blessed Dunstan buried her in the church of Saint Dionysius, which she herself had built.

The holy virgin had often visited this place in prophetic anticipation, saying:

“This is the place of my rest.”

She watered it continually with a shower of tears. In the very courtyard of the monastery she established a hospice in which thirteen poor people are still fed today.

## 7. Her Apparition. Brithgina’s Baptism

On the thirtieth day after her death, the holy virgin appeared to her mother Wlftrud, exceedingly beautiful and cheerful, clothed and radiant in light as though in a garment. She told her that she was very dear to her King in everlasting glory; that she had accused Satan himself before Him, but through the patronage of the holy apostles had crushed his head, and by the cross of the Lord Jesus had struck him down and triumphed over him.

On that same thirtieth day, a little girl was born to very illustrious parents. Before Edith’s death, the blessed woman had been asked to receive the child from the sacred font, and had replied that she would do so as the Lord saw fit. But since she herself had been born into heaven before the girl was born into the world, the child was brought to the church. As Saint Elphege was baptizing her and presenting her with a candle, he said: “Receive, girl, the lamp with which you may enter the marriage-feast of the Lord.” Suddenly, as though the holy Edith herself were holding the girl, a very tender little hand reached out, received the candle, and held it.

At once Saint Bishop Elphege understood that this was a wondrous omen of divine election, and he said to the child’s parents: “Raise this infant as one betrothed to God alone, and after she has been weaned, hand her over to a monastery.”

This girl was called Brithgina [Note: Harpsfeld calls her Brithina in *Saeculi X*, chapter 10, where he records, from Bruno, Bishop of Toul, who later became Pope Leo IX, the healing of a certain Theoderic at the tomb of Saint Edith under this abbess.] and later became abbess at Wilton; she ended her life in holiness.

## 8. The Elevation of Edith’s Body

Thirteen years after the death of Saint Edith, she appeared to the blessed Archbishop Dunstan and said:

“Remembering His mercies, the Lord has taken me to Himself, and it pleases His ineffable goodness that among human beings I should be honored for the salvation of His faithful, just as He has honored me among the angelic citizens in heaven. Go therefore to Wilton, and, carrying out the divine command, raise my body from the earth. Do not doubt, nor suppose that you are being deceived by any phantom; for this will be the sign of the truth: apart from those members which, in youthful frivolity, I misused—the eyes, hands, and feet—you will find the rest of my body as intact and incorrupt as it was. For I was always free from lust and drunkenness. You will also see the thumb of my right hand, with which I continually impressed upon myself the sign of the holy cross, unharmed, so that the Lord’s mercy may be seen in the part preserved and His fatherly chastisement in the part taken away.”

While Dunstan was spending the night at Sarum, near Wilton, he was carried in a vision to the church at Wilton, as far as the tomb of the holy virgin. And behold, he saw Saint Dionysius standing beside the altar in angelic splendor, and the virgin Edith, conspicuous for her light and radiance, addressing her beloved patron in these words:

“Do you know, Father, what the divine grace has willed concerning me? You, therefore, interpreter of the supreme counsel and messenger of the divine will, explain to this stranger with what faith and authority I have invited him here.”

Saint Dionysius said:

“Understand, brother, that the vision you recently saw is true concerning the revelation of this beloved lady. She is worthy to be venerated by those born on earth, since she deserved to be crowned among the citizens of heaven. This body is worthy of honor, this temple of virginal chastity, in which the Lord, the King of glory, the lover of virginity, reigned. Her intercessions, moreover, most pleasing to Christ, are necessary for mortals.”

Thus, on the third day before the Nones of November, the holy body was raised from the earth, and everything was found as had been foretold.

## 9.

A certain monk of Glastonbury, named Edulfus, rashly cut away a tunic from the holy body in a fold, and at the same time struck the sacred body with iron. Immediately a great quantity of blood burst forth, just as it usually does from a cut vein, and flowed over the garments and the pavement. Terrified, the reckless brother threw down the iron together with the sacred spoil, fell on his face, and tried to expiate his crime with tears. Then, rising, he saw no blood at all.

Likewise, when a certain sister attempted to cut away a piece from the band of the sacred head, she was wonderfully prevented: the living head raised itself and, with threatening indignation, frightened away her rash attempt.

## 10.

The clerics of the Picts were carrying Saint Juvinus the confessor around in a chest. They were honorably received in the monastery of the holy virgin and placed the sacred relics on the altar of Blessed Edith. When they wished to depart, those relics clung to the altar with such weight that they could not be removed by any means. The visitors therefore wept, wailed, tore their garments, and pulled their hair. At last, when all hope was abandoned, they received two thousand solidi from Wlftrud the abbess and departed sadly to their own country.

## 11. King Cnut’s Laughter Punished. Aldred’s Invocation

During the sacred feast of Pentecost at Wilton, King Cnut repeatedly burst into laughter while eating and declared that he would never believe that Edith, daughter of King Edgar, was a saint, since her father had always been devoted to lust and tyranny. Archbishop Ednotus, who was present, contradicted him and immediately opened the virgin’s tomb. She then seemed to raise herself as far as the girdle and to make an assault upon the insulting king. The king, overwhelmed with fear, collapsed upon the ground as though lifeless.

At last, recovering his breath, he blushed with joy, begged forgiveness for his rashness, and thereafter held the holy virgin in great honor. Once, when a storm arose at sea, he invoked her; and when calm was restored, he reached the desired harbor.

Aldred, likewise, Archbishop of York [Note: Formerly a monk and Bishop of Winchester, and at the same time Archbishop of York, according to William in Book III of *The Bishops of the English*. He flourished in the middle of the ninth century.], having been cast into great danger in the Adriatic Sea, invoked the holy virgin. She immediately appeared to him visibly and said: “I am Edith.” Tranquillity was restored at once.

### A Robber Pays the Penalty

A certain man had usurped land belonging to Saint Edith and, overwhelmed by death, had departed this life without repentance. Shortly afterward, however, he rose and said:

“Help, friends; assist me, all you faithful of God. Behold, the intolerable indignation of Saint Edith excludes this wretched soul from every region of heaven and earth; she permits the invader of her property to settle nowhere, and neither allows me to remain in this body nor lets me die.”

When the land he had taken was restored, he immediately breathed out his soul.

---

# Historical Eulogy of Saint Laurence, Bishop of Canterbury

*(Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, Second Century, p. 60.)*

## 1. Bede and Gotselinus Wrote about Laurence

Besides the Venerable Bede, the monk Gotselinus of Bertin described the Life of Saint Laurence, just as he did that of his predecessor Augustine. Summoned to England by Saint Anselm, Bishop of Canterbury, he lived first at Ramsey and then at Canterbury, where he wrote various Lives of the saints. Since Gotselinus’s work on Laurence cannot be found, it is useful to insert here what the same author recorded about him in chapter 16 of the *History of the Translation of Saint Augustine*.

### Laurence’s Deeds, from Gotselinus

“Finally, on the fourth day, which is Wednesday, they approached, as though now ready, to convey their most blessed companions and successors, Laurence and Mellitus, to that chief man, Augustine. Laurence came first with that leader Augustine; with him he was the first to break the battle-line of the devil, and he was the first to be ordained by Augustine while the latter was still alive as archbishop, just as Saint Clement once succeeded the surviving supreme Peter.”

And farther on:

“It would be pleasant to recount concerning blessed Laurence how he raised a dead man, ran on foot over the waves of the sea, summoned fire from heaven by the power of Elijah and burned up the impious, and caused a spring brought forth in arid places to pour out into an everlasting stream; and how every approach of women to the church which was built and consecrated for his apostolate in Scotland is prevented by punishment, so that recently the illustrious Queen Margaret of Scotland, daring to attempt entry with offerings, was suddenly struck and driven back, but restored through the prayer of the clerics. But because of the narrowness of the place I deliberately omit these matters for now; with God’s help they are to be unfolded elsewhere.”

## 2. The Life of Saint Laurence Promised Here by the Author

The Life of Saint Laurence which the author promises here was undoubtedly published, as William of Malmesbury attests in his *Book of the Bishops of the English* in these words:

“Laurence succeeded Augustine and ruled for five years. His virtues, and those of the others—concerning whom Bede, in his brief account, touches on everything, fearing the offense of tediousness—were written by a certain Gotselinus, who, as far as he could learn from the reports of the ancients, added deeds altogether remarkable and worthy of praise, which he had himself observed with eyewitness faith.”

Molanus had read this offspring of Gotselinus, and reports its opening in his additions to Usuard on 2 February: “To the most beloved lords and to the paternal …,” and so forth. John Capgrave reduced Gotselinus to an abridgment. What we have excerpted above from Gotselinus is sufficient.

## 3. Laurence a Priest and Monk

Some doubt whether Laurence came from Italy with Augustine or was summoned by Augustine from Gaul to Britain. They also doubt whether he was a monk, since Gregory everywhere calls him a priest (Gregory, Book IX, Letters 52, 55, 56), as does Bede.

The first question appears to be settled both by Gotselinus above and by Augustine’s own action. Bede says in Book I, chapter 26 of his *History*:

“When he had been ordained archbishop for the English people, he immediately sent Laurence the priest and Peter the monk to Rome, to report to the blessed Pope Gregory that the English people had received the faith of Christ and that he himself had been made bishop.”

He would certainly not have sent men whom he had not brought with him from Rome and whom Gregory did not know. From this it also appears that Laurence was a monk, since Gregory sent no others from Italy to England except “monks fearing God” (Bede, Book I, chapter 25). Since priests were then rarer in monasteries, however, they were accustomed to call such men priests rather than monks; Bede accordingly habitually celebrates Laurence under the title “priest.” Add that, in the Church of Canterbury, from Augustine’s time for many years, no bishops except monks presided.

Let us hear Bede speaking about Laurence.

## 4. Laurence, Designated Successor by Augustine, Faithfully Performs His Office

“Laurence succeeded Augustine,” he says in Book I, chapter 4, “in the episcopate. Augustine had ordained him while still alive for this reason: lest, after his death, the condition of the Church, still so undeveloped, should begin to waver, deprived even for an hour of a shepherd. In this he followed the example of the first pastor of the Church, namely the most blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, who, after the Church of Christ had been founded at Rome, is said to have consecrated Clement as his helper in evangelizing and as his successor.”

Possidius records in chapter 8 of his *Life of Augustine* that Valerius of Hippo also did this “against the custom of the Church,” to the great benefit of Augustine.

“Once Laurence had obtained the rank of archbishop, he worked with the greatest vigor to enlarge the foundations of the Church, which he saw nobly laid, and to advance them toward the perfection of their proper culmination by frequent exhortation and continuous examples of pious works. Finally, he cared not only for the newly gathered Church, which was from the angels, but also for the peoples of the ancient inhabitants of Britain, and likewise for the Scots, who inhabit Ireland, an island neighboring Britain, striving to provide pastoral care for them.”

## 5. He Tries to Bring the Scots to Catholic Rites and Writes Them a Letter

“When he learned that the aforesaid native life and religious practice of the Scots, as also that of the Britons in Britain itself, was in many respects less ecclesiastical—especially because they did not celebrate the solemnity of Easter at its proper time, but thought, as we explained above (chapter 2), that the day of the Lord’s Resurrection should be observed from the fourteenth moon up to the twentieth—he wrote, together with his fellow bishops, an exhortatory letter to them. He entreated and adjured them to maintain the unity of peace and of Catholic observance with the Church of Christ, which is spread throughout the whole world. The beginning of that letter is as follows:

“‘To our most beloved lords and brothers, the bishops or abbots throughout Scotland: Laurence, Mellitus, and Justus, bishops, servants of the servants of God.

“‘When the apostolic see, in accordance with its custom, sent us—as throughout the whole world—to these western regions to preach to the pagan peoples, and it happened that we entered this island which is called Britain, before we understood the facts, believing that they followed the custom of the universal Church, we held both the Britons and the Scots in great reverence for their holiness. But after learning the truth, we thought the Britons better than the Scots. As for the Scots, through Bishop Dagan, who came to this island mentioned above, and through Abbot Columbanus, who came to Gaul, we learned that in their conduct they differed in nothing from the Britons. For Bishop Dagan, when he came to us, was unwilling not only to eat with us, but even to take food in the same lodging in which we were eating.’

“Laurence, together with his fellow bishops, also sent letters to the priests of the Britons, appropriate to their rank, striving to strengthen them in Catholic unity. But how much he accomplished by doing these things, the present times still make clear.”

The remainder of the letter is missing. That letter was not without fruit, as is evident from a fragment of the Life of Saint Laurence written by Gotselinus, which Usserius renders in his notes on Letter 7 to the Irish:

“Saint Terenanus, archbishop of Ireland, came to him. He was a man of such holiness that he is said to have raised three dead persons. When he heard Blessed Laurence discussing, in a mutual meeting, the observance of Easter and other apostolic institutions, he yielded to the truth. He corrected his disciples, who were indignant that so divine a man should submit to such a stranger, bringing them back by his example, together with his people, to the rule of truth”—that is, he reproved them.

This question was settled and almost put to rest through the agency of Saint Wilfrid in the year of Christ 664. Read Bede’s *History*, Book III, chapters 25 and 26.

## 6. As He Is About to Abandon His Flock, He Is Rebuked by Saint Peter

“But when Laurence,” says Bede in chapter 6, “was about to leave Britain, following Mellitus and Justus, he ordered a bed to be prepared for him that very night in the church of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, of which we have already spoken frequently. After pouring out many prayers and tears to God for the condition of the Church, he placed his limbs down to rest and fell asleep. Then the most blessed prince of the apostles appeared to him and, for a long time during the secrecy of the night, inflicted severe blows upon him. With apostolic severity he asked why he was abandoning the flock which he himself had entrusted to him, or to what shepherds he was, in his flight, abandoning Christ’s sheep, placed amid wolves.

“‘Have you forgotten my example?’ he said. ‘For the little ones of Christ, whom He had entrusted to me as a pledge of His love, I endured from unbelievers and enemies of Christ bonds, blows, prisons, afflictions, and finally death itself—the death, moreover, of the cross—so that I might be crowned with Christ.’”

## 7. By Displaying His Wounds, He Brings the King Back to the Faith

“Strengthened by these blows and exhortations of blessed Peter, Christ’s servant Laurence came early in the morning to the king—that is, Eadbald—and, opening his garment, showed him how grievously he had been beaten. The king was greatly astonished and asked who had dared to inflict such wounds on so great a man. When he heard that, for the sake of his salvation, the bishop had suffered such tortures and wounds from Christ’s apostle, he was exceedingly afraid. He renounced every form of idolatrous worship, abandoned an unlawful marriage, received the faith of Christ, and, once baptized, took care in every way he could to support and favor the interests of the Church.”

## 8. He Recalls Mellitus and Justus from Gaul

“He also sent to Gaul and recalled Mellitus and Justus, ordering them to return and freely establish their Churches. They returned after a year from their departure. Justus returned to the city of Rochester, over which he had presided. The people of London, however, refused to receive Mellitus as bishop, preferring to serve idolatrous priests. For Eadbald did not possess the same royal power as his father, so that even against the will and opposition of the pagans he could restore a bishop to his Church.

“Nevertheless, from the time he was converted to the Lord, he and his people devoted themselves to the divine commandments. Finally, in the monastery of the most blessed prince of the apostles, he built a church of the holy Mother of God, which Archbishop Mellitus consecrated.”

## 9.

The same author shortly afterward summarizes Saint Laurence’s death in these words:

“For while this king was reigning, the blessed Archbishop Laurence ascended to the heavenly kingdom, and was buried in the church and monastery of Saint Peter the Apostle, beside his predecessor Augustine, on the fourth day before the Nones of February.”

That was in the year 619, as may be gathered from Bede at the end of this chapter, where he says that Mellitus, Laurence’s successor, died after five years of governance in the year 624.

Laurence, buried near Saint Augustine in the suburban basilica of Saint Peter, deserved this epitaph, if we believe Harpsfeld:

> Here, Laurence, are the sacred signs of your monument.  
> You too, cheerful Father and second bishop,  
> Gave your shoulders and back for Christ’s people;  
> With limbs, alas, lacerated, you heal many wounds.

These verses, however, have the character of a much later age, and perhaps should be assigned to the end of the eleventh century, when his sacred body was raised together with those of others.

# In the Year of the Lord 1100. Lupus the Protospatarius

## Historical Notice

*(Muratori, *Writers of Italian Affairs*, vol. V, p. 36, Preface to Lupus the Protospatarius.)*

This author, Apulian by origin, and almost wholly occupied with the affairs of that region, has been considered by some a citizen of Matera. They were persuaded to this by the form of expression he used in the Chronicle under the year 1093: “Pope Urban came to Matera.” I do not know why, on the same reasoning, they did not make him Antiochene, since under the year 1098 he says: “The Christians, fighting, came as far as Antioch.” Yet in very correct Latin, *venire* used for “to go” is common; less so is what Salmasius observed in his notes on Hadrian of Spartianus: *redire* for “to go,” just as *reddere* is used for “to hand over.” Even among present-day Italians, children know that those first two words are often confused.

Others believed Lupus to have been from Bari, because under the years 886 and 890 he simply, almost as though by antonomasia, calls the ruler of Bari “the prince.” I would hardly dissent from them; for Lupus is very much concerned with Bari’s affairs, if the Ajo whom he describes in both places had been prince of Bari rather than of Benevento. “Then,” you will say, “he must have been Beneventan.” Let him be so, for those to whom that reasoning is convincing; and he will also be Greek by origin, because he often uses Greek expressions and repeatedly shows himself devoted to the Greeks.

For me, however, he is an Apulian. That people, long subject to and intermixed with the Greeks under varying fortunes, used many of their words even in everyday speech; and, as commonly happens through factional allegiance, many Apulians continued to preserve love of the Greeks in their hearts even after centuries. Whether he was called *Protospata* from an office or by descent, and whether the name of his people was derived from the Greek office of *protospatarius*, I have discovered nothing certain.

This much I know: on a stone column belonging to a very ancient work at Brindisi, according to Scipione Ammirato, where the *logothete* and *protonotary* are mentioned, there is inscribed in letters of a later age this epigram: “Protospata Lupus”—unless it should be read in the reverse order, “Lupus Protospata,” since it is written on a circular surface, on which it is not easy to say what comes first and what second. If this was our Lupus, he must certainly be regarded as a man of Brindisi, whether by birthplace, residence, or some other connection.

So much concerning the author’s origin. For his date, see under the year 1088.

# Chronicle of Lupus the Protospatarius, with the Barense Annals Added

*(Most recently edited by D. Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Writers, vol. V, p. 51.)*

## Prefatory Notice

The nineteen-year cycles in the Church of Bari, enlarged by various annotations, gave rise to several little works derived from them. We possess the Barense Annals, which Muratori first published from Vatican Codex 1, among the Urbinate manuscripts numbered 983 and written around the year 1490, transcribed with the help of Nicolaus Aloysius, in volume I of his *Antiquities*, under the title *Chronicle of Bari* [Note: Reprinted by Pratillo in *History of the Princes of Lombardy*, IV, 348 ff.]. We now present them in a much more corrected form, after the distinguished Dr. Heyse had compared them with the manuscript.

For this purpose we also used:

**2)** Royal Codex Matritensis V. 83, on parchment, from the fifteenth century, which translated a large part of our Annals, inserted into the Chronicle of Lupus the Protospatarius, into Italian. It was derived from an older manuscript, the source of the Urbinate copy. Although it is unknown by what fate it reached Madrid, it is at least certain that it had previously been copied in Italy, as seems to have happened with the Lupus manuscript once preserved by the Duke of Andria [Note: See Peregrinius in the preface to Lupus.].

Several notices also flowed into **3)** the Chronicle first published by Peregrinius under the name of an unknown man of Bari [Note: For example, under the years 1026, 1034, 1035, 1040, and 1042.]. You may readily believe that the final portion of the Annals was added around the years 1040–1043.

The Barense Annals were also used by the author of the Chronicle which, since the seventeenth century, has been cited under the name of Lupus the Barense Protospatarius. Antonius Caracciolus published it in 1626 at Naples, in the *Four Chronologists*, p. 93, from a badly made copy of the Urbinate manuscript, using the Italian version of the Duke of Andria. His edition was repeated by Muratori [Note: *Scriptores Rerum Italicarum*, V, 37 ff.], Burmannus [Note: *Thesaurus of Italy*, IX, 1, 411], Carusius [Note: *Sicilian Library*, I, 35], and Pratillus [Note: *History of the Princes of Lombardy*, IV, 17.].

Whoever the author was—for none of the manuscripts claims the name of Lupus [Note: Concerning Lupus the Protospatarius of Brindisi, see Peregrinius’s preface.]—he seems to have been from Bari and to have written, using the ancient cycles and the Annals mentioned above [Note: Compare the years 901, 924, 926, 927, 947, 994, 1002, 1010, 1019, 1040, 1042, and 1043], toward the end of the eleventh century, perhaps in the years 1082–1090, unless one should attribute the history of 1091–1102 to him rather than to some continuator from Matera.

He either used sources of less accuracy or misused good ones, since, for example, he assigns Otto I’s victory over the Hungarians to the year 945, Otto II’s battle with the Saracens to 981, and Otto III’s death to 1000; he writes Conon in place of Henry III and Robert in place of William I the Conqueror. Sometimes he begins the year, as do the people of Salerno, from the Incarnation of the Lord on 25 March [Note: Under the year 1067 he assigns to that year the comet which appeared on 24 April 1066, and under 1099 he assigns the Synod of Bari.].

It has been possible to establish a new recension of the work with the help of several materials brought together for our purpose. First among them is:

**1)** Vatican Codex among the Urbinate manuscripts, no. 983, mentioned above, written around the year 1490, which the distinguished Dr. Heyse compared for our use with the printed editions [Note: Vatican Codex of Queen Christina, no. 378, is a recent copy of Caracciolus’s edition, with readings from the Urbinate manuscript added.].

It is closely followed by the Italian version, namely:

**1a)** Madrid Codex V. 83, on parchment, fifteenth century, copied by our colleague F. Heinrich Knust of Hanover, of blessed memory, who was recently—alas—taken by a premature death; I mentioned above that this manuscript had been interpolated from the Barense Annals. The translator generally expressed a text that he sometimes misunderstood, but on the whole rendered it well. It is entitled:

> HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF THE ANNALS OF THE DEEDS DONE IN ITALY FROM THE YEAR OF THE LORD 600 TO THE YEAR 1100.

**2)** Royal Parisian Codex no. 6061, on paper, octavo, from the beginning of the sixteenth century. In several respects it agrees with the Urbinate manuscript, but in others it departs from it together with the remaining witnesses. Our Bethmann compared it with the printed editions.

**3)** Neapolitan Codex of the Bourbon Library, on paper, quarto, from the sixteenth or beginning of the seventeenth century, marked V. F. 52. I mentioned it in our Annals, vol. V, p. 157; I myself compared it with the printed editions in 1822. On the whole it agrees with the preceding witnesses, and with them derives from a corrupt source.

**4)** It departs from the text of the printed editions. I have not thought it proper to repeat each individual fault, since the printed text is readily available to everyone. I have added a few readings.

**5 and 5b)** The Chronicle mentioned above under the name of the unknown man of Bari, whose author had ours before his eyes but added much which, as foreign to our subject and corrupted by the carelessness of copyists, I decided should be omitted.

The brief Norman Chronicle of the years 1041–1085, edited by Muratori in *Scriptores*, vol. V, pp. 278–279, derives for the most part from the Annals of Lupus.

[Note: The following two divisions should be read in parallel.]

# Barense Annals

## 605

The death of Saint Gregory the Pope. Phocas reigned for eight years [Note: The edition adds: “In 612 Domitian reigned for fifteen years.” This belongs under the year 80, as is shown by the system of the double cycles and by the notes of the first major cycle written on the same page; compare below, under the year 931.].

## 782

In this year King Charles celebrated Holy Easter at Rome, and his son Pippin was baptized by Pope Adrian.

## 902

In this year Habraam, king of the Saracens, came down into Calabria and died at Cosenza, in the church of Saint [Note: In another hand in manuscript 1.] Pacratius [Note: In another hand in manuscript 1.].

## 925

In this year Oria [Note: In the province of Otranto.] was captured by the Saracen people in the month of July, and Eusebius died at Clauso.

## 928

In this year Michael [Note: “Itachael” in the manuscript.] king of the Slavs captured the city of Siponto in the month of July, on the day of Saint Felicity, Monday, in the fifteenth indiction—that is, 10 July 926 [Note: 10 July 926 fell on a Monday.].

## 929

In this year Taranto was captured by the Saracen people in the month of August, on the solemnity of Saint Mary, 15 August.

## 949

[Note: The edition adds under the year 931: “In this year Ambrose, Bishop of Milan, died.” The system of the double cycles demonstrates that this belongs under the year 399.] In this year the Hungarians entered Italy and came as far as Otranto, and there was a slaughter [of oxen [Note: It is clear from Lupus that this must be supplied.]]. And Placipodi besieged Conversano.

## 979

Here the monastery of Saint Benedict at Bari was begun by Lord Jerome, the venerable abbot.

## 981

In this year the people of Siponto and Ascoli fought a battle at Vado Somilo.

## 996

In this year Matera [Note: Matera in Basilicata, not far from Taranto.] was besieged for three continuous months by the wicked Saracen people. In the fourth month, that is, December, they captured it by force; and in it a certain woman ate her own son.

## 1003

In this year the city of Bari was besieged by Saphi the apostate and the *caiti* [Note: The name of a military office among the Saracens.], and the siege continued from the month of May until the tenth day before the Kalends of October. It was liberated by Peter, Duke of Venice, of blessed memory.

## 1011

In this year Longobardia [Note: The part of Apulia formerly subject to the Lombards.] rebelled, together with Mele, against Curcua on the ninth day after the beginning of May. They fought a battle at Betete [Note: Perhaps Bitecto near Bari. Pratillo.], where many men of Bari fell. Ismael fought a battle on Mount Pelosus with the Greeks, and Pasiano fell there.

## 1013

In this year Bari was besieged by Basil, the *catepan* [Note: That is, commander.], surnamed Sardonti, on the eleventh day after the beginning of April. After sixty-one days had been completed, he made peace with them, and he himself entered the fortress of Bari, where the seat of the Greek nobles now is [Note: Bari was captured by the Normans in 1071.].

## 1021

Here Basil Vulcano [Note: “Vulano” in manuscript 1; see below under the year 1027.] fought with the Franks and defeated them in the city of Cannae.

## 1027

In this year Ispo the *chitoniti* [Note: That is, Greek κοιτωνίτης (*kōitōnitēs*), “chamberlain.”] came down into Italy with a great army—namely, Russians, Vandals, Turks, Bulgarians, Vlachs, Macedonians, and others—to capture Sicily [Note: “Having captured it, Reggio was …” in witness 2.]. And Reggio was restored by Vulcano the *catepan*. But because sins stood in the way, the emperor Basil died in the second year [Note: Basil died in 1025; Constantine in 1027.]. All those men returned in vain [Note: “On the vigil of Saint Martin. And while he was alive he renounced the empire in favor of Romanus, and gave him his daughter Zoe in marriage.” Compare Lupus under the year 1029.].

## 1035

Here, on the Epiphany of the Lord, Bishop Bisantius died. He had been a most pious father of orphans, founder of the holy church of Bari, guardian and defender of the whole city, and terrible and fearless against all the Greeks. Romualt the protospatarius was elected to the episcopate by the entire people. In the month of April the emperor summoned him into exile, and on the fifth day before the Ides after the beginning of August Nicolaus was elected.

## 1040

Here, on the ninth day after the beginning of January, Nichiforus, also called Dulchianus, *catepan* in the city of Ascoli, died. On the fifth day after the beginning of May, Michael Criti [Note: I correct it thus; manuscript 1 has “cati,” from “Cato” in witness 2.]—called Kirosfactes—was killed beneath the fortress of Motola by his fellow citizens [Note: Manuscript 1 has “conterati”; witness 2 reads “cive rocti e vinti.”] [Note: That is, by his fellow citizens.]. On the seventh day after the beginning of the month, everyone came to the city of Bari with Argyrus, son of Mele. Then Argyrus himself wounded Musondus [Note: Witness 2 has “musando.”], who was first among them, and, binding his hands, sent him to prison with John Stonensis. All the fellow citizens dispersed.

## 1041

Here Michael the protospatarius and *catepan*, also called the younger Dulkianus, came from Sicily into Lombardy [Note: “And then into Apulia” in witness 2; incorrectly.]. In the month of November he entered Bari. He also ordered four men to be hanged from a gallows [Note: “Four leading citizens of Bari” in witness 2.] above the wall of Bitonto.

On the seventeenth day after the beginning of March, a battle was fought between the Normans and the Greeks beside the river Dulibentus [Note: Pratillo conjectured “Olibenti.”] [Note: It seems to refer to the Aufidus, indicating the stream Olivento near Venosa.]. Many Russians and Obsequians fell there [Note: Witness 2 has “many Greek Russians and Obsequians.”] [Note: They appear to have been auxiliary troops.].

Dulkianus himself, with the remaining army that had survived the battle, fled to Mount Pelosus [Note: Mount Pilosus east of Venosa.]. Then, in the month of May, all the Greeks were gathered together at Mount Maior beside the waters of the Aufidus, and battle was begun on the fourth day after the beginning of the month. There very many Natulichi [Note: That is, *Anatolici*: Anatolics, or easterners.] and Obsequians [Note: Witness 2 has “obsequani.”], Russians, Thracians [Note: That is, Thracians.], Calabrians, Lombards, and Capitinates perished.

The priest Angelus, Bishop of Troia, and Stephen, Bishop of Acherontia, were also killed there. For, as was said by everyone who knew these events, there were no more than two thousand Normans [Note: Witness 2 has “four thousand.”] [Note: Witness 2 reads: “Two thousand Normans were killed.”], but eighteen thousand Greeks, excluding the servants.

From there Michael returned in confusion with a few men, leaving behind those who were half-dead from fear of the raging Normans. He wrote to Sicily, and those wretched Macedonians, Paulicians, and Calabrians came. After they had been gathered together with the survivors in the *catuna* of Mount Pilosus [Note: *Catuna*, still called *Catojo* in the vernacular among the Calabrians, is a cavernous, marshy place situated below a mountain, in which herds are kept. [Col. 0128D] Pratillo.], the *catepan*, the son of Budianus, then came down into Apulia. Michael returned to Sicily at the emperor’s command, from where he had come.

1042. In this year, on the third day beginning the month of September [Col. 0127C], the army of the Greeks descended from Mount Piloso, and the Normans from the castle of Siricolo. Between the two mountains they entered into a very great battle, in which all the wretched Macedonians fell, and only a few of the remainder of the army survived. There Bugiano was captured alive and carried through all Apulia as far as the territory of Benevento. For, as those who were present at that battle truthfully report, there were seven hundred Normans and ten thousand Greeks.

After the third battle just mentioned had been completed, the people of Matera and Bari made a treaty with those Franks [Col. 0129A], since there was no one who could rescue them from their hands. Then, in February, the Normans and the citizens of Bari chose Argiro, also called Meli, as their prince and chief.

In April Manichi descended upon Tarentum. He was also called “the master,” assembled the entire Greek army, and built a *suda*—that is, a rampart or fortress [Col. 0129D]—in the place called Tara. Then Argiri wrote to the Normans at Aversa and Melfi, and they all came, nearly seven thousand [the first witness reads *quas*, “as if”], to Mutula. Then that wicked Manichi, together with the whole host of the enemy, terrified by immense fear, fled by night and shut themselves up in Tarentum. But the Normans, standing before the landward gate and seeking battle, found no one at all who would answer them; so they plundered the entire territory of Oria [Col. 0129B] and thus returned to their own places.

In July the wretched inhabitants of Giovenazzo [Col. 0129D: inhabitants of the city of Giovenazzo], having made a treaty with those Greeks who were staying at Trani [one witness reads *mantibus* for *manentibus*], were besieged by the prince Argiro together with the Normans and the people of Bari. On the third day of their siege, that wretched Giovenazzo was taken by force and stripped of all its possessions; the Greeks, and others as well, were killed there. But the prince himself rescued many people, men and women, from the hands of the Normans.

Afterwards, when the people of Trani were unwilling to inflict harm upon the people of Bari, in the last week of June the prince himself, together with the Normans and the people of Bari, besieged it for thirty-six days [one witness omits “with the Normans and the people of Bari”]. He afflicted it severely with battles and other calamities. For he had a tower constructed there out of a heap of timber such as human eyes had never seen in modern times. But Argiro, after receiving imperial letters granting him the honors of patrician and either catepan or vestes [Col. 0129D: a certain palatine dignity], ordered the siege-engines to be burned. He returned to Bari and offered it, for the sake of praise, to the holy emperor Constantine Monomachus together with his fellow citizens [the source has an uncertain or defective phrase here].

Thus far, such things have been done; now I shall return to the episode concerning the impiety of Maniachi. Therefore, after the Normans had, as I have said, been removed from his territories, and after the army had been gathered into one body, in June Maniachi set out by night toward the city of Matera. There, before the eyes of the people of Matera, the impious man had more than two hundred men killed—how many he captured among the crops and from every direction. Similarly, on a second expedition to Monopoli, the wicked man did not fear to act in the same way.

1043. In this year, in September, Tubachi the protospatharius, Pardus the patrician, and Nicolaus the archbishop came down to Otranto with Chrysubulus [one witness reads *chyrisubulo*] and Simpatia. Then that wicked Maniachi, going out to meet them under the pretense of peace, immediately ordered Pardus to be killed by the sword, and Tubachi to be thrown into custody; in October he likewise had Tubachi killed.

## LUPUS THE PROTOSPATHARIUS

[Col. 0124A]

From the passage of Saint Gregory the pope: year 252, A.D. 855, indiction 3.

[Note: The first witness repeats annotations from the Annals of Bari for the years 605, 612, and 782.]

In the year 860, indiction 8. In this year [the annual notices begin in the form “In the year …, indiction …, In this year,” apparently derived from nineteen-year cycles; the editor has chosen to omit the formula here] the city of Bari [one witness has *bari*] was captured by the emperor [witnesses 3 and 4 add “the Constantinopolitan emperor”].

861 [A.D. 867]. The emperor Michael died, and Basil the *parakoimomenos*, his son, rose to power; he alone ruled for twenty-one years, and for nine [witness 1: eight] years with his sons [witnesses 3 and 4: “with his own sons”]. The words “his son” are absent from witnesses 1 and 1a. The name appears as *parascenumenus*, *parast.*, and *parascensu*.

866. The emperor Louis entered Benevento.

867. Matera was burned by the emperor Louis, and the same emperor Louis entered the city of Oria [one witness reads *oriem*; Oria is in the province of Otranto].

868. The Saracens left the city of Bari through the Franks, on the third day beginning the month of February [witness 3 reads “September”]. In that same year the aforesaid Louis was captured at Benevento [compare the *Chronicle of Salerno*, chapter 107; Symeon the Master, concerning Basil, chapter 20, Bonn edition, pp. 694 ff.; Cedrenus, ibid., II, p. 221; Zonaras XVI.9, Paris edition, II, p. 170].

875. The Greeks entered Bari in December, on the day of the Nativity of the Lord, on the third feria [some witnesses omit “feria”; others read “the third” or “III”]: Gregory the *stratēgos*, who was also called the *bajulus*.

880. The Saracens left Tarentum [compare Theophanes Continuatus V.66, Bonn edition, p. 306; Cedrenus II, p. 233].

884 [witness 1 has 883]. Aio rose to power as prince in October [all the manuscripts consistently read *Alo*; one witness has *priceps*, “prince”].

885. The emperor Basil died, and Leo and Alexander [one witness has “Alexius”], his sons, began to rule: alone for twenty-six years and with him for nine years [one witness omits “died”; another omits “and with him for nine years”].

886. A disaster occurred in Bari in June, when the prince fought with the *stratēgos* of Trapezus and the Greeks. The Greek phrase is Κωνσταντῖνος ὁ τῆς τραπέζης, “Constantine of the table” [see Symeon, Bonn edition, p. 701; compare George the Monk, ibid., p. 852; Theophanes Continuatus VI.5, Bonn edition, p. 356; Cedrenus II, p. 253; also Erchempert, chapter 76]. Other witnesses read “treachery,” or “disaster and slaughter”; one has “when” rather than “that.”

890. Aio the prince died, and his brother Ursus rose to power [one witness has *urso*; another adds “indiction 4”].

[Col. 0124C] 891. The Greeks entered Benevento in October, and the *stratēgos* Sabbatichi entered Siponto in June [one witness has *Sabbathici*].

894. The Greeks left Benevento in August through the Franks.

900. Melisiano the *stratēgos* descended into Apulia [one witness reads *Meclitanus*].

901 [one witness has 902, indiction 5; another says that this entry is taken from the Annals of Bari]. Abrami, king of the Saracens, descended into Calabria, went to the city of Cosenza, and was struck by lightning.

912. Five hundred years were completed since the death of Saint Martin [one witness spells out “five hundred”; another has “five”; another “fifty-one”; some omit the phrase].

913. Constantine, emperor and son of the aforementioned Leo, was crowned; he ruled for forty-seven years.

916. The Saracens left Garigliano, and 350 years had passed since the Lombards entered Italy under their king Alboin [the place appears as *Garaliano*, *Gariliano*, and *Carigliano*].

919 [some witnesses have 916; another adds “and in that same year”]. Eighty years were completed since the Saracens entered Italy [one witness omits the phrase; other witnesses read “forty years”].

920. The Hungarians, that is, the Huns [one witness has *Hunnii*], entered Italy in February.

921. Ursileo the *stratēgos* fell in battle at Ascoli in April, and Nadulfus seized Apulia [the name appears as *Nandolfus*, *Andulfus*, and *Pandulfus*]. That is, Landulfus seized Apulia [Cedrenus II, p. 355].

924 [one witness has 925, taken from the Annals of Bari]. Oria was captured by the Saracens in July, and they killed all the males; the rest they led away to Africa and sold them.

926. Michael Sclavus captured Siponto in July [one witness has June].

927. The destruction of Tarentum was accomplished, and all who fought bravely were killed; the survivors were carried away to Africa. This happened in August, on the feast of Saint Mary [some witnesses read “This was done”; others add “the year”].

929. The princes Nandolfus and Guaimarius entered Apulia [compare the *Chronicle of Salerno*, chapter 158].

936. The Hungarians came to Capua.

[Col. 0126C] 939. The sun was darkened and stars appeared in July, on the third day, Tuesday, at the third hour, with the moon twenty-nine days old.

940. The Hungarians entered Italy in April. In that same year a battle was fought at Matera by the Greeks against the Lombards, with the *stratēgos* Imogalaptus [the name appears as *Imo Galacto*]. It is uncertain whether this Greek commander’s name derives from ὀμογάλακτος, “foster-brother,” or whether it is an epithet meaning “one who was suckled together”; I do not decide the matter. And he killed Pao at sea [one witness reads “denied him”; another has *Laeo*; an Italian note reads, “Paul seized him and threw him into the sea”].

942. Nandolfus the prince died on the tenth day of April [the name also appears as *Nadolfus*, *Nadulfo*, and *Pandulphus*].

945. Romanus and Ubo fell in December, and the Hungarians perished at the hands of King Otto [Romanus was the Greek emperor, deposed in December 944 and dead in July 948; Ubo was Hugh, king of Italy, in 947. Some witnesses omit “and”; other forms are *Romano*, *Romani*, *Octone*, and *Othone*].

946. A homicide took place in Bari in December [some witnesses add “among the citizens”].

947. The Hungarians entered Italy and advanced as far as Otranto. Platopodi besieged the city of Conversano [some witnesses read *Cupersani*]. That same year there was a destruction of cattle throughout the whole land [one witness reads *interritus*; witnesses 3 and 4 read *bonus introitus*, “a good entry”).].

950. The Greeks besieged Ascoli [some witnesses add “and captured it”].
