951. Malachiano fought a battle in Calabria with the Saracens and fell [some witnesses add: “In the year 955 Marianus the patrician descended into Apulia”; compare Cedrenus II, p. 358].

956 [compare Theophanes Continuatus VI.30, p. 453]. Marantius Clemeri and Excessula were burned in Bari [the names appear in various forms, including *Demerus*, *Cremerus*, *Clerus*, and *Thessula*].

960. The emperor Constantine died, having ruled for forty-seven years, and his son Romanus rose to power. There was a battle between Adralistus and Ismael.

961. The island of Crete was captured by the Greeks under Romanus in March [compare Leo the Deacon II.6–8]. Trabomen was captured by the Saracens, and the sun was darkened [one witness adds *tertio*, “third”; the name appears as *Titabomen* and *Trabomen*].

963. The emperor Romanus died, and Nicephorus was elevated; he ruled for seven years. King Otto entered Rome, and the sun was darkened.

965. Manuel the patrician entered Sicily and died there [the name appears as *Manuli*, *Manuelis*, and *Manuyci*; compare Leo the Deacon IV.7–8; Cedrenus II, pp. 353, 360; Zonaras XVI.24].

966. Nicephorus the *magister* entered the city of Bari, and 400 years had passed since the Lombards entered Italy [one witness omits “the *magister*”].

967. Otto the elder, father of King Otto, descended; he fought with Bulchassinus, king of the Saracens, and killed him [one witness adds: “and forty thousand pagans were killed”; compare below, year 982].

969. King Otto entered Apulia in March and besieged the city of Bari [some witnesses add “with an unsuccessful attempt”]. In the following year he entered Calabria in October, and the sun was darkened in December [a note identifies the eclipse as occurring in A.D. 968, on December 22].

970. Simischi killed the emperor Nicephorus, and he was elevated in his place [the name appears as *Simihi* and *Simichy*].

972. Atto, son of Transamundus, marquis of Spoleto, fought with 40,000 Saracens. Their *caytus*, that is, commander, was called Bucoboli. Atto prevailed with his 60,000 men, pursuing the Saracens as far as Tarentum [the names appear as *Apto*, *Acto*, *Actho*, *Asto*, and *Octo*; *Transamundus* also appears as *Transmundus*].

973 [one witness has 977]. Passarus the protospatharius died [some witnesses have *protosphatha*].

975. Ismael was killed, and Zacharias took Bitonto [the place appears as *Botuntum*, *Butontem*, and *Botritum*].

976. The Saracens besieged Gravina, and Simischi the emperor died—he was also called John. Basil and Constantine, brothers, began to reign [some witnesses add “with an unsuccessful attempt”].

977. The Saracens burned the city of Oria and led all the common people away to Sicily [one witness has *Horiae*].

978 [the entire year is absent from one witness]. John the bishop died, and Pao became archbishop, in indiction 6 [witness 5b reads *Paulus*, “Paul”].

979. Porfirius the protospatharius killed Andrew, bishop of Oria, in August [the names appear as *Profreus*, *Oretanus*, *Horetanus*, and *Oratanus*].

[Col. 0130B] 981. King Otto fought a battle with the Saracens in Calabria, in the city of Colonna, and 50,000 pagans died there together with their king, whose name was Bullicassinus [the place appears as *Colupna* and *Cotruna*; some witnesses read *poenorum*, “Punics,” rather than *paganorum*, “pagans”; the king’s name appears as *Bullicassimus* and *Bulcassinus*. One witness refers here to a note under the year 982 in the Annals of Bari].

982. Bari was handed over to the patrician Calochirus, also called Dalfina, by two brothers, Sergius and Theophylact, on June 11. King Otto died at Rome.

983. The aforementioned Dalfina the patrician captured the city of Ascoli in December [one witness calls him “Delfinus of the Franks”].

985. The patrician Romanus descended into Apulia with his son.

986. The Saracens captured the holy city of San Chiriaco and devastated Calabria [one witness adds “the whole of Calabria”; the city appears as *S. Chiriaco*, *Kyrathy*, and *Chirachi*].

987. Sergius the protospatharius was killed by the people of Bari on February 15. In that same year Andralistus was killed by Nicolaus Criti on August 15, and the sun was darkened [the name appears as *Andraliscus*].

988. The Saracens ravaged the villages and farmsteads of the people of Bari and carried men and women captive to Sicily [one witness specifically reads “villages and farmsteads”].

989. John the patrician, also called Ammiropolus, descended and killed Leo Cannatus, Nicolaus Critis, and Porfirius [the names appear as *Canutus*, *Cretis*, and *Porfirius*].

990. Bubali and Petrus the *exubitus* were killed in March [another witness reads “Bubali descended.” An *excubitor* was an office in the Byzantine court].

[Col. 0130D] 991. Atto the count fought a battle with the Saracens at Tarentum, and he fell there together with many men of Bari [the name appears as *Apto*, *Actho*, and *Octo*].

992. A great famine occurred throughout all Italy [some witnesses add “and a scarcity of grain”].

993. Paul the archbishop died, and Chrysostom was elevated [the latter phrase is absent from one witness].

994. Matera was besieged by a Saracen force for three months, and in the fourth month it was captured by them.

997. Theodore the *marco* and *exubitus* was killed in the city of Oria by Smaragdus and Petrus, brothers [the first term is variously *nearco*, *marco*, *marcus*, and *marcho*; *exubitus* is also written *excubitus*].

998. Busitu the *caytus* came with the aforementioned Smaragdus to Bari in October. The aforesaid Smaragdus, on horseback, entered Bari by force through the western gate and went out again; then Busitu, having learned of the deception, departed [the title appears as *kaitus* and *chaitus*].

999. Trachamoti the catepan, also called Gregory, descended and besieged the city of Gravina, and captured Theophylact.

## LUPUS THE PROTOSPATHARIUS

[Col. 0131]

[Col. 0131B] In the year 1000 from the incarnation of the Lord, indiction 13, the aforementioned Smaragdus was captured by Trachamoti on July 11. In that same year King Otto died at Rome [one witness reads “Smaragdus in Trachamotus”].

1002. The *caytus* Sapi besieged Bari from May 2 until Saint Luke’s day in October; then it was liberated by Peter, duke of the Venetians.

1003. The Saracens besieged Monte Caveoso in March [some witnesses add “and accomplished nothing”].

1005. Durazzo returned to the hands of the emperor through Theodore [one witness has *Eraclius*].

1006. Siphea the catepan descended in July [the name appears as *Xyphea*].

1007. The aforementioned catepan died in the city of Bari.

1008. The patrician Curcua descended in May [one witness has *Curcira*].

1009. A very great snow fell, from which the olive trees dried up; fish and birds also died. In May a rebellion began, and in August the Saracens, after breaking the treaty, captured the city of Cosenza in the name of the *caytus* Sati [one witness has “named Sati”; other witnesses omit the phrase identifying the *caytus*].

1010. Curcua died, and Basil the catepan of Macedonia descended in March. Sillictus burned the people themselves in the city of Trani [the designation attached to the catepan appears as *Marsedonici*, *Marcedonico*, *Mascedoniti*, *Macedonia*, and *Mesardoniti*; Trani appears as *Trane*].

1014. The emperor Henry came to Rome in February, and Cassano was burned in August [the place appears as *Cassanus*; some witnesses read “Cassano was burned”].

[Col. 0132B] 1015. A comet appeared in February. King Samuel died, and his son reigned.

1016. The aforesaid Samuel’s son was killed by his cousin, the son of Aaron, and the latter himself reigned. The city of Salerno was besieged by the Saracens by sea and by land [some witnesses add “and they accomplished nothing”; one adds “king of Africa”].

1017. The catepan of Macedonia died at Butrint, and in November Leo, the brother of Argiro, was killed. In this year Turnichi the catepan descended in May. Leo Patiano the *exubitus* fought with Mele and the Normans. Again, on June 22, the aforesaid Turnichi the catepan fought a battle and defeated Mele and the Normans; Patiano died there [several witnesses omit the concluding words]. Condoleo descended in that same year.

[Col. 0132C] 1018. Basil the catepan, also called Bugianus, and the patrician Abalanti descended in December. Ligorius Tepoterici fought a battle at Trani; Joannatius the protospatharius was killed there, and Romoald was captured and carried away to Constantinople [the names appear as *Ababanti*, *Abalautius*, *Tepoteriti*, *Romoala*, and *Romoal*].

1019. The aforementioned Bugianus fought a battle in October with the Franks and defeated them. Mele fled with some Franks to the emperor Henry.

1020. The Saracens descended with Rayca, besieged Bisignano, and captured it. The *amira* himself and Melis, duke of Apulia, died [the title appears as *admira*, *ammira*, *amira*, and *amita*].

1021. Dactus was captured and entered the city of Bari riding on a donkey on June 15 [the name appears as *Dictus*, *Dattus*, and *Dactus*].

1022. The emperor Henry came to Benevento in March and besieged the city of Troia [one witness adds “in the Capitanata”].

1023. Rayca came with Jaffari Criti to the city of Bari in June and besieged it for one day. Then, having been driven away from there, they captured the town of Palagiano and built the castle of Mutula [Palagiano is now Palesciano; the names appear as *Bayca*, *Taffari*, *Saffari*, and *Zaffari*; one witness has *Disutile* for Mutula].

1024. A great sign occurred in the episcopate of Acherontia, under Bishop Stephen II of Matera, on the holy day of Easter [witness 2: “the second day”]: a great silver crucifix was shaken three times—at the head, the arms, and the feet—with everyone looking on. In this year a great snow also fell. In this year Bugianus crossed over to Croatia and captured Patrocissa, the wife of Cismigi, and sent her to Constantinople. In this year the emperor Henry died, and his nephew Conus rose to power [the names appear as *Chorvatia*, *Curbathia*, *Curbachia*, and *Corbatia*; Patrocissa also appears as *Patricissa* and perhaps *Principissa*; Cismigi appears as *Cosmigi*, *Cormici*, *Cosmici*, and *Cosmizi*].

1028. Orestes the *chetonites* descended in April [compare Cedrenus II, p. 479]. Then John, the bishop of Bari, died, and Bisancius became archbishop [the title appears as *Chetonici*, *Ketoniti*, and *Chetensi*].

1029. Eustachius came with his sons Basiliscus and Mandatora, and brought the honor of catepan to Christophorus. The aforementioned Orestes descended to Constantinople with Bugianus. In this year the emperor Constantine died on the eve of Saint Martin’s day; while still alive, he installed Romanus in his seat and gave him his daughter Zoe as wife. Finally, Raycha and Zaffari besieged the castle of Obbianum; the people of Obbianum, handing over outsiders, made peace with them. In July Potho the catepan came and fought with Raycha at Bari [one witness has “August”]. In this year Guaimarius, prince of Salerno, died [a marginal note in another hand reads: “This year—at Salerno”].

1031. In June the Saracens captured the city of Cassano. On the third day beginning July, Potho fought a battle with the Saracens, and the Greeks fell [one witness calls him the *protocatepan*].

[Col. 0134A] 1032. Hychiacon the *ketonites* descended and brought with him the Anatolici. The manuscripts vary considerably. One version reads: “Michael the *protospatarius*, *kritēs* of the *bēlon* and of the Hippodrome, descended, and brought the Anatolici under Hychiacon the catepan.”

1033. On the first day of May, Constantine the protospatharius, also called Opo, descended as catepan of Italy [according to the editor, this is apparently the same person whom Cedrenus II, p. 503, calls Λέων ὁ λεγόμενος Ὦπος, “Leo called Opos”].

1034. On April 11, the emperor Romanus died, and the emperor Michael rose to power. Argiro of Bari also died at Constantinople [one witness has a marginal note that Argiro died; other witnesses omit the statement].

1038. Michael the patrician and duke, also called Sfrondili, descended and crossed over to Sicily with the patrician Maniachi [Cedrenus II, p. 512, calls him Γεώργιος πατρίκιος ὁ Μανίακης, “George the patrician, Maniaches”; compare ibid., pp. 520, 522, 545; Zonaras XVII.15].

1039 [one witness has 1038]. In February, Nicephorus the catepan descended; he was also called Dulchianus [the name appears as *Nikiforus* and *Dulkyanus*]. Cedrenus, p. 545, calls him Μιχαὴλ πρωτοσπαθαρίος ὁ Δοκειανός, “Michael the protospatharius Dochianus”; William of Apulia calls him Michael Dochianus.

1040. The aforementioned Dulchianus expelled 201 *conterati* from Apulia, and those *conterati* killed Chirisfactira, the imperial *kritēr* (“judge”), and Romanus of Matera beneath Mutula in May; the source also prints the unexplained numeral 204 immediately before “beneath Mutula” [the manuscripts read *conteratos* or *contractos*; the name Chirisfactira appears as *Kyrifactora*, *Christophorus*, and Greek κειρισφακτῆρα]. In the same month Argiro, son of Melis, besieged the city of Bari, struck Musandus, bound him with fetters, and entered Bari with him. The *conterati* were scattered [some witnesses read “bound him” or “bound him with chains”].

1041. Dulchianus descended from Sicily and went to Ascoli. In March the Lombard Arduinus summoned the Normans to Apulia, in the city of Melfi [witnesses 1 and 2 omit “the Normans”]. The aforementioned Dulchianus fought with the Normans—nearly three thousand [witnesses 2–4 omit the number]—and the Greeks fell. In May the Normans again fought with the Greeks on Wednesday, and Dulchianus fled to Bari [one witness reads “four hundred Normans”; compare Cedrenus I, p. 546].

1042. Exaugustus descended and fought a battle with the Normans on the third day beginning September, and he was captured there and carried to Melfi. The manuscripts read *Exaugusto*, *Exagusto*, or “Exaugustus the catepan, son of Bugianus. He fought again.” Cedrenus calls the Greek patrician captured in battle Boiannes [II, p. 546]. William of Apulia, book I, and the bishop of Ostia, book II, chapter 67, call him Exaugustus, a surname perhaps imposed because of the circumstances. One witness adds: “and with Atinolfo, their duke, from Benevento, beneath Mount Piloso.”

In December the emperor Michael died, and his nephew, the Caesar Michael, was elevated as emperor [several witnesses omit the intervening words]. In February Argiro of Bari became prince and duke of Italy. In April Maniaki the *magister* descended upon Tarentum [the same man is mentioned under 1038; compare Cedrenus I, pp. 541, 545, 547]. In June he carried away the city of Monopoli, then went to the city of Matera and perpetrated a great slaughter there.

In September William was chosen count by the people of Matera [the name appears as *Guilelmus*, *Guidelmus*, *Guidelmo*, and *Gulielmus*]. In this year the aforementioned Caesar Michael was deposed from the kingdom, blinded at the command of Zoe and her sister Theodora, and Constantine Monomachus was made emperor. On the third day beginning July, Giovenazzo was captured by the duke Argiro. In August the aforementioned Argiro went to besiege Trani and sat before it for one month [the place is identified in a note as Giovenazzo].

1043. Bari returned to the hands of the emperor. In September Pardus the patrician came down with much gold; Maniaki had him killed and caused everyone to call him emperor. In October he came to Bari, but it did not receive him at all. In February, however, Theodore Canus the *magister* and catepan came down, and the aforementioned Maniaki proceeded to Durazzo [compare Zonaras XVII.22].

1044. William, son of Tancred, descended with the prince Guaimarius into Calabria, and they made Stridula into a fortress [the place appears as *Inedula*, *Squillaci*, and *Scridula*; one witness specifies “Tancred of Sicily”].

1046. The patrician Argiro went to Constantinople, and the catepan Palatinus, also called Eustachius, recalled all the exiles to Bari; he then proceeded to Tarentum. On the eighth day beginning May [some witnesses read “at Trani”], he engaged in battle with the Normans, and the Greeks fell. In this year Conus, king of the Germans, came to Rome because there were three popes there: Sylvester in the church of Saint Peter, Gregory in the Lateran, and Benedict in Tusculum. After expelling them, the aforementioned emperor consecrated Clement; then the emperor came to Benevento. The people of Benevento, to insult him, cut off the straps of his horse [that is, the stirrups]. In this year William died, and his brother Drogo became count.

1047. The town of Stira was captured by the Guarangi in October [the names appear as *Garangi* and *Guaragnis*]. In December they ravaged Lecce, and in June the aforementioned Pope Benedict killed Pope Clement with a cup of poison [the place appears as *Scyra*, *Stita*, and *Liceum*].

1050. The empress Zoe died, the sister of Theodora; both had been daughters of the emperor Constantine. Zoe had three husbands: first Romanus, second Michael, and third Constantine Monomachus. She reigned with these three husbands for twenty-two years. After the death of the aforementioned Zoe, the emperor Constantine himself reigned with Theodora, his kinswoman, for nine years already [some witnesses read “the emperor Constantine had already reigned nine years”].

1051 [one witness has 1052]. Argiro the *magister*, *vestes*, and duke of Italy, son of Melis, descended in March and went to Bari. Adralistus and Romoald, together with his brother Peter, did not receive him. But not long afterward the people of Bari received him without the consent of Adralistus and the others, and Adralistus fled. Romoald and Peter, however, were captured by Argiro, bound in chains, and carried away to Constantinople. In this year Drogo was killed on Mount Ilari by his godfather Concilio, and his brother Umfreda became count [the name appears as *Umfredus*].

1053. On Friday in June, the Normans fought with the Germans whom Pope Leo had hired, and they defeated them [one witness reads “whom the pope had brought in”]. In this year there was a great famine.

1054. Sico the protospatharius of Matera died [one witness reads “of Mantua”].

1055. The emperor Constantine, also called Monomachus, died [one witness has *Monachus*].

1056. The aforementioned Theodora Augusta, sister of the empress Zoe, began to reign. Umfreda died, and his brother Robert became duke. In this year Peter, archbishop of Cosenza, died.

1057. The Augusta Theodora died, and Michael Bringas became emperor [one witness has *Brinza*].

1058. The patrician Trombi had Scribones killed in the city of Crotone [witnesses 2 and 4 read *Scribonem*].

[Col. 0136C] 1059. Michael Bringas died, and Isaac Comnenus became emperor [the source has the particle *o*, identified editorially as an article; the name appears as *Comni*, *Komni*, and *Coni*].

1060. The emperor Constantine Ducas was elevated [some witnesses omit “emperor”; one has *Ducas*].

1061. The duke Robert captured the city of Acherontia.
### Canonical apparatus register

This register preserves the printed source forms that the English annalistic translation would otherwise normalize. A numeral adjacent to a witness marker remains a source notation unless the source identifies it as a count.

- **928–929:** retain the alternate personal-name spellings exactly as printed, including the Hychiacon forms, with each treated as a name-form rather than silently regularised. The apparent differences do not license a new identification.
- **972:** *caytus* is retained as the printed, uncertain title/name; Atto is a distinct reading, not an English gloss of *caytus*. The troop-number notation is reproduced as a manuscript notation, not expanded into a troop count. *persequens* means “pursuing,” while *prosequens* means “following/escorting.”
- **978:** *Pao* is the source form for the man who became archbishop; 5b reads *Paulus*, “Paul.”
- **997:** *nearco*, *marco*, *marcus*, and *marcho* are the actual competing forms; *exubitus/excubitus* denotes the excubitor, an imperial guard official.
- **999:** retain *catapanus*, “catepan/governor,” as the supplied office reading rather than replacing it with an unmarked generic official.
- **1032:** retain the forms *Hychiacon* and *ketoniti* with their witness scope. The mixed Greek–Latin witness reading is preserved as a source form and glossed only where its wording supplies a meaning; it is not flattened into a generic statement that the manuscripts vary.
- **1033–1034:** *qui Ropo* is retained as the defective printed form with no invented referent; *cerigo* is retained as the source’s name/place form rather than emended silently.
- **1038:** the Maniachi-name variants are retained as alternate spellings of the source form; they do not establish separate people.
- **1042:** the defective phrase after *ad laudem dedit* is rendered “gave [text defective] in praise,” without an invented object or referent.
- **1043:** retain *Manachi* and *sicque*: *Manachi* is the printed name-form; *sicque* means “and thus.”
- **1046:** retain *Eustasius* and *Palatinus* as the alternate supplied forms/titles, rather than treating them as interchangeable English names.
- **1051:** retain each printed personal-name form for Adralistus and Drogo; the orthographic variants are witness readings, not separate people.

The 201 and 204 adjacent to the Dulchianus notice are left as unexplained printed numerals/notations. They are not converted into a troop count. *conteratos/contractos* remains an uncertain source designation; *kritēr* is Greek for “judge,” and κειρισφακτῆρα is preserved as the supplied Greek name-form.

1062. Alexander of Lucania became pope. In this year Robert the duke entered the city of Oria, and again seized Brindisi and the miriarch himself [Note: “the miriarch herself,” 3.].

1063. Taranto was seized by the Normans.

1064. Matera was seized by Robert in April.

[Col. 0136D] 1065. Robert the duke entered Sicily, killed a multitude of Agarenes, and took hostages [Note: “the siege,” 4, 1a.] from the city of Palermo.

1066. Count Lofredus [Note: “Loffredus,” 4.], son of Petronius, wished to go to Romania with a large force, but a certain Greek commander named Mambrita opposed him. In this year also Prince Richard entered the territory of Campania [Note: “Capitaniae,” 3.], besieged Ciperanum, captured it, and, devastating the country, reached Rome.

1067. In the month of May the emperor Constantine Ducas died, and Michael, his son, assumed the empire. In this year a comet appeared; and the Norman count Robert made war with Harold [Note: “Arnold,” 1, 1a, 4.], king of the English, and Robert won [Note: omitted in 2 and 3.], and he became king over the English people.

1068. On the sixteenth day of February Robert the duke [Col. 0137B] besieged a city named Montempillosum. Making no progress there, he departed with a few men for Obianum and captured it. Then, through the treachery of a certain Gotifred, the duke himself entered the aforesaid city of Montispillosum.

1069. In the month of September the aforesaid duke Robert [Note: omitted in 2–4.] besieged the city of Bari. Romano Diogenes, who held the empire together with the aforesaid Michael, his stepson, was seized and blinded through the treachery of the aforesaid stepson Michael at a certain city of Armenia [Note: “Arthemia,” 1; “Arthenia,” 2; “Arteria,” 3; “Arctenia,” 1a.] [Note: He was defeated at the Armenian city of Zarah in 1071, on 24 August. See also Nicephorus Bryennius I.25; Zonaras XVIII.14–15.].

1070. In the month of January a great slaughter took place in the city of Brindisi. For when the Normans wished to seize it, forty of them, together with forty-three of their other attendants, were captured, and [Note: the remainder of the year is missing in 1 and 1a.] the heads of all the aforesaid men were carried to the emperor [Col. 0137C].

1071. Robert the duke entered Brindisi, having previously abandoned the siege of Bari. For the duke himself had a bridge built in the sea so that he might close the harbor of the aforesaid city of Bari. In this year also, through the treachery of a certain Argirichus [Note: “Arzerizi,” 1; “Argirigi,” 3.], son of Joannacius, Bisantius, surnamed Guirdeliku [Note: “Girdeliku,” 1; “Guirdelithum,” 3; “Guinderlichus,” 4; “Guirdeliku,” 1a.], was killed at Bari. And [Note: “and … Bari” is missing in 1a.] on the fifteenth day of April Robert the duke captured the city of Bari; and in the month of July the aforesaid duke crossed the expanse of the Adriatic Sea and proceeded to Sicily with fifty-eight ships.

1072. On the tenth day of January [Note: “June,” 4.] Robert the duke entered the city of Palermo in Sicily.

1073. The Normans first entered Trani [Note: “Bari,” 1a; “Trane,” 2; “Taranto,” 3; “Trano,” 4.] on the octave of Epiphany with Count Petronus [Note: “Peter,” 1.]. [Col. 0138A] But Robert the duke, having expelled Petronus [Note: “Patronus,” 1.], entered that city on the Purification of Saint Mary.

1076. A certain nephew of the African king was captured by Roger, brother of the duke Robert [Note: omitted in 2, 3, and 4.], who governed Sicily, with 150 ships at the city of Mazara [Note: “Marzaia,” 3.]. In this year also the aforesaid duke gave his daughter [Note: Helena was betrothed to Constantine Ducas. See Anna Comnena, Paris edition I, pp. 23, 27, 28 (Zonaras XVIII.17).] as a daughter-in-law [Note: “wife,” 3.] to the emperor of Constantinople.

1077. The city of Salerno was besieged by Robert, duke of the Normans, and was captured by him.

1078. Naples was besieged by Prince Richard but was not captured. Robert the duke besieged Benevento, but his siege was dispersed by Count Rodulfus Pipinus. In this year the aforesaid Prince Richard died.

[Col. 0138B] 1079. Petronus entered Trani; and Bari rebelled, after the duke’s garrison had been expelled from it. Bajalardus, son of Umfreda [Note: “Umfredus,” 1.], captured Ascoli. In this year also the aforesaid emperor Michael was expelled from the kingdom, and a certain Botoniates [Note: “Botamites,” 1.] became emperor. He took the aforesaid Michael’s wife and violated her [Note: Nicephorus Bryennius III.24–25; Anna Comnena, Paris edition III, p. 73; Zonaras XVIII.18–19.]. In this year there was a mortality among the people of Matera.

1080. The body of blessed Canion was discovered at Acherontia [Note: “Acheronta,” 1.] by Archbishop Arnaldus, and that same archbishop began to construct a new episcopal church, that is, a church of Saint Mary, Mother of God. In this year the city of Bari returned to the power of Duke Robert; and the same duke besieged the city of Taranto and captured it in April. He [Note: “and … it” is missing in 1a.] then besieged Castellaneta [Note: “Castelaneta,” 1.] again and captured it. In this year the emperor [Col. 0138C] Michael came down into Apulia, seeking aid from Duke Robert against Botaniates [Note: “Bocthamates,” 1.] [Note: Anna Comnena I, pp. 28–29, states that he was not truly the emperor but a certain monk who had fabricated these claims; Michael, appointed patriarch of Ephesus, died.]. On 26 July [Note: “27 July,” 2.] of that same month the illustrious Count Robert died [Note: “the magnanimous and illustrious count,” 1a.], and the Normans were expelled from Matera for the second time. His son, Count Lofredus, began to rule in his place at Matera on the vigil of Saint Mary in the month of August.

1081. Robert the duke entered Tricarico in the month of October. In April Archiricus went to Michael, king of the Slavs, and gave him his daughter as wife to the king’s son. Robert the duke then proceeded with the aforesaid Emperor Michael to Otranto. Having sent ships ahead to the island of Corfu [Note: “Corfu,” 1.], which captured it, he himself crossed over shortly afterward [Note: “beforehand,” 3.] together with the emperor. In the month of July they placed Durazzo under siege by sea and land [Col. 0139A] [Note: Anna I.1, I, pp. 37–40; III, pp. 92–97 and following; IV, p. 103 and following.]. A Venetian fleet came and broke up the siege, and the sea-route to Durazzo was opened [Note: Ibid., p. 105 and following.]. In this year Botaniates [Note: “Bothimatini,” 1.] became a monk, and Alexius became emperor. King Henry of the Germans [Note: “Enrichus,” 2.] came to Rome to expel Pope Gregory from it.

1082. In this year there were 6,281 years from the beginning of the world and 1,824 years from the founding of the City [Note: “824,” 2–4.]. In this year also the emperor Alexius, having gathered a large army, entered into battle with Duke Robert not far from Durazzo [Note: “that is, not”], and fled with his back turned; more than 6,000 of his men fell in that battle. His army, however, numbered 70,000 men [Note: See Anna IV, p. 3 and following (Zonaras XVIII.22).]. [And [Note: omitted in 1, 2, and 1a.] while this Alexius was emperor, the bishop of Rubi, named [Col. 0139B] Guislibertus [Note: “Guisbertus,” 3.], gave to the prior of Montispillosum the church of Saint Sabinus [Note: “Sabbino,” 3.], which is in the city of Rubi. The prior was bound each year, on Holy Saturday, to provide four pounds of wax and to send one mounted man at his own expense whenever the bishop of Rubi went to the city of Bari [Note: “to Bari,” 4.] or to Canosa.]

In the month of January Duke Robert captured the city of Durazzo [Note: “Dirachium,” consistently in 2.] through the treachery of certain Venetians [Note: Anna V, p. 125.]. At this time the aforesaid King Henry besieged Rome so that he might enter it and make the archbishop of Ravenna pope there [Note: “but he was quite unable to do so,” added in 4.]. Duke Robert [Note: omitted in 2–4.], returning from Epidaurus and leaving his son Bohemond there [Note: “thus,” 1, 3.], went to Rome, bringing aid to Pope Gregory, while the king was staying in the region of Liguria [Note: “Lombardy,” 4, 1a.] to wage war against the province of Matilda [Note: “Matilda,” 1.], which Matilda held with Pope Gregory. In this year Bajalardus went to the emperor Alexius of Constantinople for assistance. In the same year, on the sixteenth day of May, a new church was consecrated at Matera in honor of Saint Eustace [Note: “Eustasius,” 2, 4.] by Archbishop Arnaldus, under Lord Stephen the abbot, the founder [Note: “and lord,” 3.] of that church.

1083. In this year 517 years were completed since the Lombards entered Italy [Note: “617,” 1.]. In this year the solar cycle was 28, the lunar cycle 17, and the first nine-year cycle; and the lunar epact was zero [Note: “epacts,” 3.]. At this time the Romans, withdrawing from Pope Gregory’s fellowship [Note: “following Pope Gregory,” 1; “humbling themselves in submission,” 3.], sent envoys to the aforesaid king [Col. 0139D] so that he might send him to Rome [Note: “who might send him,” 3; “that they might send him,” 2, 4; “to send him,” 3.]. But the duke, anticipating this, sent the Romans more than 30,000 solidi so that he might reconcile them to himself and to the pope; and this was done.

Nevertheless, when the king came to Rome, he seized the entire district across the Tiber, in which the church of the prince of the apostles stands out. In the month of June, leaving there his garrison and his son in the fortress that he himself [Note: “he,” 2, 3, 4.] had constructed there, to wage war against Pope Gregory, who was confined in the Lateran [Note: “Latium,” 3.] and on the Caelian Hill, he withdrew into the region of Tuscany, taking forty hostages with him from Rome. In May the duke placed the city of Canne [Note: “Canna,” 1; “in” is absent in 3.] in Apulia under siege, and in June [Note: “July,” 2, 4.] he captured it.

1084. Duke Robert, having gathered a multitude of Normans, Lombards, and other peoples, [Col. 0140B] went to Rome to free Pope Gregory, who was being held under a harsh siege [Note: “retained,” 1.]. This was accomplished. For when he came to Rome, he captured most of the City and, courageously extracting the pope from it, brought him with him to Salerno.

1085. The aforesaid duke came to Brindisi with a great naval equipment and an innumerable army of men [Note: “with a large equipment of ships and men,” 2–4.]. Having arranged a naval apparatus there, he entered the Adriatic Sea and proceeded to an island called Cassopi [Note: “Casopi,” 1; “Casoppi,” 3; “Cassiopi,” 4.]. There a Venetian fleet and the son of the duke of Venice, with very many [Note: omitted in 1 and 1a; absent in 3.] ships, were hostile to Duke Robert. But after a battle had been fought between them at sea, victory fell to the Normans. More than a thousand men were killed in that battle [Col. 0140C] [Note: “more than five thousand,” 2–5.]. In addition, five ships were captured; two were sunk with their men, so that those who were able to escape the warrior’s sword were swallowed by the sea’s abyss [Note: “with ‘horse’ written above ‘sea,’” 1.] [Note: Anna VI, pp. 159–161.].

In this year, in the month of May, while the aforesaid Pope Gregory was staying at Salerno [Note: “while he was at Momuretum of Salerno on the third day,” 1.], he died. At his death, it is said, there arose such a storm of hail and thunder that all who were there thought that they would perish in a storm of this kind [Note: “thought that they would perish in such whirlwinds,” 2, 4.].

In the month of July, while the aforementioned Duke Robert [Guiscardus [Note: omitted in 1 and 1a.]] was staying in a place called . . . . . . [Note: “the Venetians were defeated on the fifth day”; the place is absent in 2 and 3.], and while his army was staying on the island of Cephalonia to capture a certain city [Note: “for its capture,” 1; omitted in 3.], he himself was stationed in the aforesaid place with part of the army, preparing himself [Col. 0140D] so that [Note: omitted in 1 and 2; “he prepared a ship with three …,” 4.] with a great fleet and an innumerable multitude of soldiers [Col. 0141A] he might sail toward the royal city [Note: “Constantinople.”], by order of the most merciful almighty God, who disperses and rejects [Note: “governs,” 3.] the thoughts and counsels [Note: omitted in 3.] of princes [Note: “proceeding from the stream of the belly, he died,” 3.], not proceeding from His own will [Note: omitted in 1, 2, and 1a.], he was extinguished by a discharge of the bowels [Note: this entire phrase is omitted in 1, 2, and 1a.] [Note: 1 adds here the words that are read there and in the following year: “the son of the aforesaid duke Robert became duke”; likewise 1a and 2.] [Note: Anna VI, p. 162.].

1086 [Note: everything for this year is missing in 2.]. Roger, son of the aforesaid Duke Robert, became duke.

1087. In the month of May the body of the most blessed Nicholas, bishop of Myra, was taken by certain men of Bari from Myra itself and transported to Bari, the chief city of Apulia. In this year Abbot Desiderius of Saint Benedict of Monte Cassino, with the consent of certain Roman nobles, became Roman pope while Pope Clement was still alive; he had been [Col. 0141B] archbishop of Ravenna.

1088. In the month of September a great earthquake occurred throughout Apulia, so that it is said to have destroyed towers and houses in certain places. For at that time war began between Duke Roger and his brother Bohemond. In this year Syracuse, formerly the capital of Sicily [Note: “once,” 4; omitted in 3.], was captured by Count Roger. It is said that, because of the length of the siege, people and children were eaten there [Note: “consumed,” 2? 4.].

1089. A synod of all the bishops of Apulia, Calabria, and Bruttium [Note: “Briezium,” 1; “Briczium,” 2; “Brutium,” 3, 4; “Abruzzi,” 1a.] was held in the city of Melfi [Note: “Melfia,” 2.]. Duke Roger and all the counts of Apulia, Calabria, and the other provinces were also present. It was established that God’s holy truce [Note: “trevia,” 2, 4; “trecia,” 3; likewise below.] should be observed [Note: “detained,” 3; “retained,” 4.] by all who were subject to them.

[Col. 0141C] In this year Ursus, archbishop of Bari, died. Pope Urban by name came to the city of Bari and there consecrated the confessio of Saint Nicholas and Archbishop Elias [Note: “while the pope was still alive,” 2–4; “while he was still alive” is omitted in 1a; space left blank.], who had previously come with the aforesaid Pope Clement. The aforesaid Pope Urban also consecrated the church of Brindisi.

1090. In the month of August Acherontia burned itself in a remarkable manner [Note: added in 4.]. In this year Prince Jordan died [Note: “Jordanus,” 3.].

1091. God’s truce was sworn by the Normans. There were 6,291 years from the beginning of the world, and the epact was 29.

1092. While the city of Oria was being besieged by Bohemond, certain men of Oria, with assistance, broke up his siege [Col. 0141D]; and Bohemond himself, taking flight, they captured all his equipment and standards [Note: “insignia,” 3; “the banners,” 1a.].

[Col. 0142A] 1093. Abbess Eugenia of the monastery of Saint Benedict at Matera died in the month of October [Note: “December,” 1a, 2.]. In the same month of that year Pope Urban came to Matera and reached the monastery [Note: “the monastery of,” 2? 4.] of Saint Eustace with a great multitude of his people.

1095. In the month of April, on the night of the fifth feria (Thursday) [Note: “on the night of Wednesday,” 2, 3; “on the night of the fourth day,” 4.] little fires were suddenly seen falling from heaven like stars throughout Apulia, and they filled the entire surface [Note: “the whole earth,” 1.] of the earth. From that time the peoples of Gaul began to travel—or rather, those of all Italy—to the Lord’s tomb with weapons, carrying on their right shoulder the banner of the cross [Note: “the sign,” 4; “segno,” 1a.].

1096. Count Roger of Sicily, with 20,000 Saracens and an innumerable [Note: “an excessive,” 1.] multitude of other peoples, and all the counts of Apulia besieged Amalfi [Note: “Amalfici,” 1, 2]. While they persisted there, suddenly, by God’s inspiration [Note: omitted in 1.], Bohemond, with other counts and more than 500 horsemen, making for themselves the sign of the cross over their garments on the right shoulder, abandoned the siege [Note: “the besiegement,” 1.]. Crossing the sea, they proceeded to the royal city so that, with the aid of the emperor Alexius, they might go to wage war against the pagans [Note: “waging war,” 2–4.] and proceed to Jerusalem [Note: “Iherusalem,” 1; consistently so.] to the holy sepulcher of the Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer.

1097. Bohemond, with the Count of Saint-Gilles, the Count of Normandy, and other counts of the West [Note: “others,” 1.], moved from the royal city in April with an innumerable multitude, crossed the sea, and captured the lands that the Turks had taken from the emperors [Col. 0142C] [Note: “all the land which,” 4.]. They fought a battle with the Turks, and Christ granted victory to his Christian people. It is said that there were 140,000 pagans [Note: “one hundred forty thousand,” 1; “140,000,” 1a; “150,000 and 40,000,” 2; “100,000 and 40,000,” 3; “150,000,” 4.]. This took place near the city of Nicaea.

1098. In the month of October a comet appeared, and the Christians, fighting, came as far as Antioch and besieged it. In April they captured it and killed more than 60,000 men there [Note: “more than …,” omitted in 1.]. When battle was joined again, the Christians won and captured much booty from the Turks. In this year also Capua was captured by Count Roger in the month of May.

1099. In the month of October Pope Urban convened a universal synod [Note: “the year 1098,” Col. 0142D.] [Note: “universal” is omitted in 3; “the whole,” 4.] in the city of Bari, at which 185 bishops were present. In this year, in the month of June, on the feast of the holy apostle Peter, the city of Jerusalem was captured by the Christians in battle; and they killed everyone whom they found there. It is said that 200,000 people were killed there. Then the Christians raised up as their king Gotifredus, who had been duke of the Swabians. In the month of July the aforesaid Pope Urban died, and Paschal was elected [Note: “raised up,” 3.] pope.

1100. The aforesaid Gotifredus died from a bear [Note: “a she-bear,” 3.] while emerging from a woodland [Note: “from a height,” 1.], which he had previously [Note: “before,” 1.] struck forcefully [Note: “he himself,” 2? 4.] [Note: “had struck,” 2? 4.].

1101. Caesarea was captured by the Christians and brought down to the ground. In this year, in the month of September, Count Goffridus died; and Alexius [Note: “Alexander,” 2, 4; “Alexius,” 3.], his son, entered Matera, and the upper parts [Note: “above it,” 1; “the upper parts,” 2; “above,” 3; absent in 4; “and the upper parts of the city began to be inhabited,” omitted in 1a, with space left.] began to be inhabited [Note: “to inhabit,” 1.] by the men of Monti [Note: “the men of Monti,” 1; “the Amantines,” 3.]. In this year Arnaldus, archbishop of Acherontia, died, as did Count Roger of Sicily [Note: omitted in 1.] in the month of June [Note: “July,” 4.].

1102. In the month of November Stephen, abbot of Matera, died, and Abbot Symeon succeeded him. In May Peter of Acherontia was elected archbishop [Note: “End,” 3; “The End of Lupus Protospata,” 4.].

## In the Year of the Lord 1100. The Encyclical Letter of the Monks of the Major Monastery of Tours on the Death of Abbot Bernard

(Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, V, 668.)

[Col. 0143]

### Note

At the Major Monastery, in this turbulent life, the most devout Abbot Bernard migrated this year (1100) to heavenly rest, after governing this holy place for more than fifteen years amid various disturbances and vigorously preserving its regular discipline and liberty. As is customary at the Major Monastery, the brothers wrote an encyclical letter concerning his death, in which they testify to the intolerable grief of their bereavement.

[Col. 0143]

### Encyclical Letter

[Col. 0143B] To all the sons and daughters of the Church of God spread throughout the world, dedicated to the service of the Lord, and to his fellow servants and fellow sharers in the hope that is in Christ, the brothers of the Major Monastery send participation in mutual charity in all good things.

Since, as the Apostle teaches, we have learned that all of us who confess the Lord Jesus, provided that we do not kill our faith by evil living, are members of his body, which is the Church; and since, as the same Apostle indicates, we know that when one member suffers, the other members ought to suffer with it, we announce to you, our fellow members, so that you may suffer with us as the law of charity demands, the unbearable pain of our bereavement.

For we have been bereaved of our father Bernard, a most venerable man, truly—and this is the first thing to say—a Catholic, gentle, wise, and pious; and, so that we may briefly reveal what you ought to think of him without error, worthy of reverence in the practice and appearance of true religion and holiness. Therefore, without hesitation or doubt, we trust that a glorious place of rest has been prepared for him in the blessed dwelling of the saints.

But because we know from the examples of the most approved saints and from the testimonies of divine Scripture that no one lives so watchfully or so purely amid this sorrowful mortality of the flesh that no worldly contagion clings to him, we fear that some measure of carnal rust remained attached to him, to be expiated by purgatorial punishments. For this reason we ask—and in this we seek from you the aid of devout compassion—that, lest the gate of the rest due to him have been closed for a time of purification because of some stain of carnal weakness, you may obtain that it be opened more quickly by the keys of your prayers and the force of pious offerings.

We also ask you to pray to the common Creator of all on our behalf, that he may cause the successor of our deceased Father [Col. 0144C] to live according to his good pleasure and to govern us. And because our pious Father was a man of holy severity, and hated not only sinful words but also empty and clownish speech and whatever was useless in any way, rejecting such things from his hearing as far as he could, we entreat your holiness to remove from this letter the songs and mockeries of verse which, rather than benefiting the deceased, add condemnation to those who make them. Instead, simply record the names of your places and what you have done for our deceased Father and for us, so that we may also know what we ought to do for you. Thus, fulfilling the command of the Apostle James—“Pray for one another, so that you may be saved”—let us draw one another by mutual prayers to our Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with [Col. 0146A] the Father and the Holy Spirit, one blessed God who makes blessed, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

This most devout Father of ours died in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1100, in the eighth indiction, with epact 7 and concurrent 7, on the Ides of April, in the very week of Easter, on the Saturday that is called in albis, at the rising of that very day—like one passing from darkness into light.

## In the Year of the Lord 1100. Bruno

[Col. 0145]

### Historical Notice Concerning Bruno

(Oudin, *Ecclesiastical Writers*, II, 958.)

[Col. 0145B] A certain Bruno flourished in this year, 1100 or 1110, about whom it has not been possible to learn more. He seems to have been of the same generation as Alulfus, at the beginning of the twelfth century. Both wished to restore the *Paterian Collection*, compiled from the writings of Saint Gregory on books of Scripture and lost through the injury of time.

Concerning Alulfus, Hermannus says the following in the *History of the Restoration of the Monastery of Saint Martin of Tournai*, volume XII of the *Spicilegium*, no. 38, pp. 395 and following:

> “He was first a cleric, then a monk in the aforesaid monastery, and held the office of keeper of the books or cantor for forty-seven years. Reading through all the books of blessed Gregory repeatedly, and imitating Paterius, he excerpted from Gregory all the passages he had expounded from both the Old and the New Testament. From these he composed three volumes and added a fourth concerning very useful passages, giving them the name *Gregorial*.”

This is what Hermannus says about Alulfus, who, in composing the *Gregorial*, wished to imitate Paterius and repair the loss of that work, of which only the first part remained. The other man who devoted his labor to repairing Paterius’ loss was the Bruno of whom we are speaking. When he saw that Paterius’ *Collection*, written from Gregory’s books into books of the Old and New Testaments and lost through the injury of time, had perished, he wished to repair the same loss.

Since only the first part of Paterius’ work, or *Collection*, on the books of Scripture had survived, this Bruno added to that first part of the ancient Paterius a second and a third part, while retaining even the name Paterius. Hence it has happened that in all the manuscripts of the libraries these parts are believed to belong to Paterius, because they are marked with his name. Nevertheless, these second and third parts belong to Bruno, as is clear from a letter of Bruno to a certain Werner, which the Benedictine monks published in the latest edition of all the works of Pope Saint Gregory, produced at Paris in four folio volumes in 1705, volume IV, part II, near the end of the preface that they prefixed to their edition of the Paterian work.

[Col. 0146C] From this letter, therefore, it is clear that the Paterius whom the French Benedictine monks presented as genuine and complete is mutilated, and that only the first part belongs to Paterius; the second and third parts, however, belong to this Bruno, who around the year 1110 supplied the deficient Paterius and added to it the two parts that had perished through the injury of time.

[Col. 0145]

### Bruno’s *Gregorial*

(See *Patrologia*, volume LXXIX, *Works of Saint Gregory the Great*, volume V, column 681.)

## In the Year of the Lord 1100. Bernard of Toledo

[Col. 0145]

### Historical Notice

(Fabricius, *Library of Medieval and Late Latin Literature*, I, 234.)

Bernard, archbishop of Toledo, took part in the councils of León, Nîmes, and Girona in the years 1091, 1096, and 1097. He was the author of four sermons on the antiphon *Salve, Regina misericordiae*, published among the works of Saint Bernard of Clairvaux.

[Col. 0147]

### Bernard’s Sermons

(See the works of Saint Bernard, in the volumes of *Patrologia* soon to be published.)

## In the Year of the Lord 1100. Manegaldus

[Col. 0147]

### Historical and Literary Notice

(Fabricius, *Library of Medieval and Late Latin Literature*, IV, 12.)

[Col. 0147A] Manegaudus, Manegaldus, or Manegoldus, concerning whom the Anonymous of Melk says in chapter 105:

> “Manegoldus the priest, teacher of modern teachers, was a vigorous champion of truth, from which neither promises nor threats could bend him, although made by the schismatic king. Indeed, in that dispute which arose between Gregory VII and Henry IV, he labored in defense of justice even unto imprisonment.”

There survives a certain exhortatory letter of Ivo, bishop of Chartres, written to him—the fortieth among the Ivonian letters. This man divided the text of the prophet Isaiah into page-length sections. On Matthew, however, he wrote continuous glosses. He also wrote on the Psalter, a most excellent work, “more precious than topaz and refined gold.”

As it seems, this man wrote a little work in support of Gregory VII, though after Gregory’s death and after 1080 but before 1101, against Wolfelmus of Cologne; the highly esteemed Muratorius published it in the fourth volume of his *Latin Anecdotes*, Padua, 1713, quarto. The work that he promises to write against Wenericus, however, exists nowhere.

Without doubt, this is the same Manegundus whom Henry of Ghent says in chapter 28 left to posterity monuments of his intellect in an exposition of the Psalms and Paul’s Epistles. Some have attributed to this Manegold the German commentaries on the Psalms published at Cologne in 1536, folio. Miraeus, citing John Molanus, noted them; nevertheless, the common conviction is that they belong to Remigius, bishop of Auxerre.

The illustrious Muratorius also thought it likely that this same man is mentioned in Ptolemy of Lucca’s *Annals* under the year 1090:

> “At this time there flourished in Germany a certain philosopher named Menegaldus, whose wife and daughters were highly accomplished in philosophy.”

The Anonymous, in André du Chesne, volume IV, *On the Affairs of the Franks*, p. 89:

> “At this time, in both divine and human philosophy, there flourished Lanfranc, bishop of Canterbury; Guido the Lombard; Maingaudus the German; and Bruno of Rheims, who afterward led an eremitical life.”

This was Master Manegold of Lautenbach, among the first canons and provost of the regular canons of Murbach in Alsace. Berthold of Constance speaks of him in the appendix to Hermann the Lame under the years 1093 and 1098, and an uncertain author under the year 1090, in Urstius, volume II, p. 83.

He was therefore different from two other men of the same period: Manegold, abbot of Saint George in Swabia, whom Berthold reports under the year 1100 to have been killed by his monks [Note: *Acts of the Saints*, volume III, February, p. 52.]; and Manegold, dean of Raitenbuch, whose book composed in defense of Gregory VII—written while Gregory was still alive, though not approved by Gregory himself—is mentioned by Gerlach, provost of Reichersberg, in the illustrious Pez, volume II of the *Anecdotes*, part II, p. 491. See also the same author’s prolegomena to that volume, [Col. 0148B] p. XXIX and following, and the *Journal of the Learned Men of Italy*, volume XV, p. 32 and following.

[The little work published by Muratorius is of a very different subject from what Fabricius believed. Its entire purpose is to demonstrate that the writings of the ancient pagans should not be approved so readily that everything in them is admitted indiscriminately, since it proves that they contain many things opposed to the doctrines of our faith. These matters are argued against Wolfelmus through chapter 23; then, in only two chapters, it treats the cause of Gregory VII. The author states in the preface that he added this discussion because he knew that Wolfelmus had attacked Pope Gregory with a polluted mouth; therefore, he says: “I thought that something about him ought to be appended.” Mansi.]

[Col. 0147]

## L. A. Muratorius’ Prefatory Notice to the Following Little Work

(*Latin Anecdotes* IV, 163. Padua, 1713.)

This little work was copied from manuscript codex 305, letter S, of the Ambrosian Library. Its author is known to me only by his name and his position as a master; otherwise he is unknown, since the more celebrated writers of literary history provide no information about him. Nor do I have either enough leisure to investigate or enough books to discover any fuller information about him and about Wolfelmus of Cologne, perhaps.

I remember having read long ago that a certain Manegaudus, who seems to have lived and written some works around the year 1150 of Christ, is mentioned in the illustrious Baluze’s *Miscellany*, volume IV. In my own manuscript notes I also find a brief catalogue of unpublished books once shown to the highly learned Holstenius, later prefect of the Vatican Library, in which the following appears:

> “Menegaldus or Menengaldus, a Latin historian: *Ecclesiastical History*. He seems to have transcribed much from Trogus Pompeius and Justin regarding secular matters. The beginning of the work is as follows: ‘Ninus was once the most powerful of the Assyrian kings. When he brought war against neighboring kings, etc.’”

A note follows. Lucas Holstenius:

> “I believe that it is a certain Manigoldus [lacuna], an author of no judgment or value, of whom hundreds are found everywhere in the libraries of monasteries, such as Peter Comestor, Vincent of Beauvais, and other compilers of that sort. Since they could find no beginning for their histories, they traced them back to the beginning of the world, as bad poets begin the Trojan War from the twin egg. Perhaps toward the end he descends to the particular history of some people and to his own times; these portions could be useful for understanding those periods. But this is to be despaired of in the near future and at present.”

I am uncertain, however, whether these matters belong in any part to our Manegaldus or Manegaudus.

It is not difficult to determine approximately when this author flourished. He discusses the very famous controversies of Pope Gregory VII with the emperor Henry IV, and does so in such a way as plainly to indicate that the matter was not ancient but recent, and that the disputes had been conducted only a few years earlier. For in chapter 22 he censures the contentions and dissensions of Wolfelm and his associates, “in which you, workers of the flesh, have been engaged throughout all these years.” Then, in the following chapter, he speaks more openly about these matters, defending Gregory VII’s cause, and writes among other things:

> “At that time there were not lacking great and religious men to whom such iniquity was displeasing; and even today there remain in that same kingdom [of the Teutons] very many who, by God’s mercy, have not yet bent the knee to Baal,” etc.

A little farther below he adds:

> “The discreet men established around you, who openly attack your schism with free condemnation, ought at least to have been sufficient for your shame,” etc.

The Germans who favored Henry were therefore still separated from the Apostolic See by the schism; and, as he himself says, scarcely any city in the whole of Latin Christendom remained that did not have a population divided into various parties, some fighting for the memory of Gregory VII, who had already died, and others, as I suppose, fighting for Henry IV, who was still alive. Manegaudus further adds:

> “To provoke the Most High, and to increase profanation, in your sacrifices you implore the divine clemency for Wipert as the Father and pontiff of your souls.”

All these things seem to suggest that the antipope Guibert was still alive when Manegaudus wrote this. Let the other passages that the same author has in his first and last chapters be read; and then, unless I am mistaken, it will be established that this little work was composed before the year 1101 of Christ (the year in which it is more probable that the pseudopope Guibert died), or at least not far from that time. I therefore incline to the view that the author of this little work was none other than Manegaldus, whom I may perhaps have shown to be mentioned in the Annals of Ptolemy of Lucca, p. 952, vol. XXV of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. That historian writes as follows under the year 1090 of Christ:

> “At that same time there flourished in Germany a certain philosopher named Menegaldus, whose wife and daughters were very distinguished in philosophy.”

From this it will also be useful to learn, in chapter 4, the reason why the ancient Christians thought that the antipodes had to be denied. Those who posited them imagined the earth divided into four habitable regions, at least two of which were so cut off from the others by the intervening torrid zone that no intercourse between human beings could take place. Once this had been assumed, the most certain doctrine, handed down by God, concerning the propagation of the human race from Adam and the proclamation of the Gospel throughout the whole world was undermined. But Columbus and the other first explorers of America and the Indies removed both the hypothesis of the pagans and the entire Christian fear concerning this matter.

Then, in chapter 23, you will learn that a history of the deeds performed by Pope Gregory VII was composed by the archbishop of Salzburg, whom I believe to have been Gebhard or Gebehard, mentioned in Baronius’s *Annals*. Whether this history is the same as the letter of Saint Gebhard, archbishop of Salzburg, to Hermann of Metz, which was published by Tengnagel at Ingolstadt in 1612 among the *Ancient Monuments against the Schismatics*, etc., others may investigate.

Again, in chapter 24, you will find that the author of a certain highly deceitful and calumnious letter against Gregory VII was Wiricus, a master of Trier, who assumed the person of the bishop of Verdun. Consider the remaining matters relating to theology and philosophy for yourself.

[Col. 0149]

# The Little Work of Master Manegaldus against Wolfelm of Cologne

[Col. 0149A] When we recently met in the gardens at Lutenbach, and, as scholars commonly do, a discussion arose between us concerning the Scriptures that were then under consideration, after much conversation we came upon something like a knot and began to pull at the rope of controversy. You maintained that the philosophers—and Macrobius in particular, in his *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, which was then under discussion—had said only a few things that displeased you; whereas I asserted that I had found in them a great many things contrary to our faith and salvation.

The course of our words proceeded so far that it could easily have become clear either that you were insufficiently instructed in the divine writings and, through inborn harshness and a passion for contradiction, wished to defend what you did not know, or that, if you really held the views you expressed, you had plainly departed from the reasoning of sincere faith.

Since it often happens that some people attend to the noise of words and the surface of a narrative without weighing the meaning and intention of the writer—like those who, lacking taste and smell, recognize indeed the root of things but cannot distinguish the force of their flavor and odor—while others investigate the hidden meanings through the sound of speeches and, just as they separate cold things externally from hot, so internally distinguish good from evil, rejecting the latter more vigorously in proportion to the delight they have taken in the good, I therefore drew nearer and came to know your illness through you yourself.

I asked you under oath whether you assented to the meaning of those statements in such a way that you did not understand them to be harmful to those who believed them. You replied quite rashly that you knew of nothing in them that your mind strongly rejected. Thus, after being assailed by many insults from you, I left you raging and threatening.

I therefore propose to write something to you about this, so that you may clearly recognize that heretical depravity is contained in the books and opinions of those whose error you pretend not to notice. I have also thought it appropriate to append something concerning Lord Pope Gregory, whom you lacerate with your polluted mouth, so that you may reflect that a preceding sin is often the cause of a greater sin.

## Table of Contents

**Chapter I.** That not all philosophical opinions should be rejected, but only those in which the philosophers were deceived and by which they deceive others; and concerning the exceedingly detestable opinion of Pythagoras about the soul.

**Chapter II.** Concerning Plato and his figurative formulations, by which he shows of what the soul consists and that it penetrates the body at a distance.

**Chapter III.** Concerning the various philosophical opinions about the soul.

**Chapter IV.** That, in measuring the sun and moon and in determining the habitable regions, the philosophers were deceived; and that anyone who believes Macrobius on these matters will easily suffer shipwreck in the faith.

**Chapter V.** That, according to the Apostle, such things must be tested [Col. 0151C] and cut away in accordance with the sobriety of Christian discipline.

**Chapter VI.** Concerning their unsound confession and the fall of Origen, who devoted himself excessively to their doctrines.

**Chapter VII.** Concerning the Holy Spirit and his sound and moderate teaching: that he abandons the proud and permits them to be cut apart by the unclean Spirit.

**Chapter VIII.** That the philosophers, deprived of the blessings of the patriarchs, were not worthy to form any worthy conception of the mystery of the Trinity.

**Chapter IX.** That such things arose from the evil Spirit, and that the author of division constructed idolatry through many arguments.

**Chapter X.** That they are the Egyptians whom we are to despoil, and that they prepared for us treasures and adornments of eloquence [Col. 0151D].

**Chapter XI.** Concerning God, whom we have as the subject of our speech; concerning right confession; and concerning the creation of angels and human beings, with regard to whose fall the Lord’s judgment was mercifully tempered.

**Chapter XII.** Concerning the commandments of obedience by which the contemptuous human being is restored, and concerning the fact that this restoration was signified in many ways, so that the falls of the fathers of old were permitted to signify the greatness of grace—such as the fall of David, from whose line the Author of forgiveness was born.

**Chapter XIII.** Concerning the prophets who foresaw and desired the two advents.

**Chapter XIV.** That, once all necessary arrangements had been made, God was born of a Virgin, thereby destroying the philosophical chain of reasoning [Col. 0152A].

**Chapter XV.** With what result he was born.

**Chapter XVI.** Concerning God who was born: that all the truth of the Scriptures was disclosed by him; and concerning the raising of souls and the teaching of humility.

**Chapter XVII.** Concerning the simplicity of the apostle Peter and the merit of his faith.

**Chapter XVIII.** Concerning the two sacraments of regeneration and nourishment instituted before the Passion at the Supper.

**Chapter XIX.** That on the cross of Jesus Christ there is forgiveness of sins and redemption for all, including the saints of earlier times.

**Chapter XX.** Concerning the glory of the resurrection, and that the disciples were called not to philosophize but to proclaim eternal life [Col. 0152B].

**Chapter XXI.** Concerning the coming of the Spirit, what he accomplished in them, and the fact that perfection is not present in this life but that the beginning of blessedness is.

**Chapter XXII.** That these matters have been stated briefly to show how great a danger it is to assent to the writings of those who know nothing of the resurrection of bodies; and that their definition has been overthrown, while the spirit subject to the flesh cannot grasp this.

**Chapter XXIII.** That certain Germans have fallen away from obedience to and unity with the Roman Church, saying that they have no pontiff except the emperor.

**Chapter XXIV.** Concerning the letter composed by them against Saint Pope Gregory, and that this letter must be answered by the grace of God.

# Chapter One

[Col. 0152C]

We wish first to warn the discernment of our readers that we have undertaken this work by no means in order to regard all philosophical opinions as condemnable. Some of them, because of their subtlety, we scarcely have the capacity to penetrate; and we are not unaware that certain others have been accepted by holy men.

Rather, I wish to restrain your rashness, since you praise their subtleties in such a way that you pay no attention to the manifold errors entangled in those fabrications. For the guilt of our first parent had not condemned the endowment of nature to such an extent that they could not, according to human reasoning, distinguish with sufficient care and appropriateness the common features and differences of certain things—so far as a human being could presume upon his own powers.

But because they were without the Spirit who teaches all truth, whose wisdom reaches powerfully from end to end and orders all things gently, it was necessary that, as human beings and therefore liars, they should sometimes exceed the bounds of truth and, once they had undertaken the defense of falsehood, be dragged through various arguments of deception.

This was what happened to Pythagoras, one of the earliest leaders of this tradition. After discovering and handing down certain useful things, he finally began to investigate the mystery of the rational animal. He attempted to pursue and comprehend by mortal reasoning that nature which cannot be rightly known without the Author of nature. His intellect was thereby emptied and ultimately reduced to such bestiality that he falsely claimed that the human soul, which had been endowed with perpetual rationality, could at some time become irrational [Col. 0153A].

He held that, in this way, once the will had been removed from its own simplicity, it would fall into a desire to become embodied in these lowest things. If it had lived badly in its first body in the present age, or in some future age—for he promised an infinite succession of ages—it would receive a worse body. Thus, as its crimes multiplied, it would eventually reach the point at which one who had previously been a human being would be thrust into a horrible prison in order to give life to some utterly filthy body.

Behold the outcome to which that sublime meditation led, and the kind of necessity which, according to the folly of his heart, he did not shrink from imposing upon the creature formed in the image and likeness of the Creator of all things.

Tell me, please: if you do not dissent from this opinion, what hope of honor can you conceive, or what do you expect concerning the blessedness of those who, in the perfect resurrection of bodies and souls, will receive the double robe, according to those things that meanwhile the eye is not sufficient to see and the ear to hear—those things that God prepares, in the abundance of his grace and glory, for those who love him?

For according to this philosophical view, you and the rest of your accomplices established in the kingdom of Germany, who have disagreed with the Apostolic See and the obedience owed to holy Pope Gregory and have incurred a sentence of condemnation for countless crimes, will, after being separated from your present bodies, enter in the future age a more shameful body. When you have again polluted it with bestial contagion and have been driven through endless kinds of bodies to be animated, you will finally be shut up in the bowels of the earth and in filthy places and be deprived of eternal salvation forever.

# Chapter Two

[Col. 0153C]

Yet this cruelty [read: credulity] was not approved even in that period by the philosophers who succeeded them and who held a more dignified opinion of themselves; rather, it was moderated through lighter insanities. Among these was Plato, who investigated the beginnings of things more keenly than the others but burdened the composition of the soul with certain figurative formulations. He affirmed that it consisted of an indivisible and a divisible essence, of a nature both the same and different, and he imagined that heavenly and earthly bodies were brought to life through it, so that the force of perpetual fire would suffer a diminution of its own power in accordance with the nature of the bodies it vivified.

Macrobius testifies that Cicero, Virgil, and other followers of philosophical discipline held this view. This may be understood more clearly by anyone who takes care to examine his treatise *On the Dream of Scipio* [Col. 0153D].

There, as he relates through his introduced pupil Timaeus, he wished, by means of certain quasi-delirious arguments derived from numerical speculation, to show that the same soul penetrates and vivifies every animated body without distinction. Speaking of God as the maker of the soul, and calling the commixture of the aforementioned essences a “ferment,” he says:

> “From the whole ferment he took the first part; from this he took a double part of the first; a third part, one and a half times the second,”

and certain other things that we would recall to memory for no purpose, since by the very extravagance of their obscurity they dull the mind of the listener. If anyone wishes to hear them, he may examine them in Plato himself, or in Macrobius, who undertook in some manner to elucidate those same darknesses [Col. 0154A]. It will nevertheless be surprising if, once heard, he does not despise them.

# Chapter Three

In the same place you have Pythagoras, Plato, Xenocrates, Aristotle, Posidonius, Hippocrates, Heraclitus, Zeno, Democritus, another Heraclitus, Chrysolaus, Hypantus, Anaximenes, Empedocles, Parmenides, Xenophon, Boethus, and Epicurus gathered together. Many of them, led astray by various spirits of error and puffed up by the perception of their flesh, as though scattered through various precipices, produced discordant and contradictory opinions concerning the soul in the judgment of their own minds.

Of these, Plato—who seems to come sufficiently close to the truth—defined the soul as an essence that moves itself [Col. 0154B]. Another defined it as a number that moves itself; another as an *entelechy*, which they interpret as the form of the body; another as harmony; another as an idea; another as the exercise of the five senses; another as a subtle spirit; another as light; another as a spark of stellar essence; another as a spirit compacted with the body; another as a spirit inserted into atoms; another as something derived from the fifth essence; another as fire; another as air; another as blood; another as composed of earth and fire; another as composed of earth and water; another as compounded from air, fire, and spirit.

Consider, then, amid so great a variety of division, whether you can accommodate yourself to all of them with sound judgment. And if you can agree that your soul may rightly be called blood, tell me, I ask, what kingdoms of heaven do you expect? For in this condition, being blood and flesh, you cannot possess the kingdom of God.

# Chapter Four

As for what is asserted concerning the sphere, the orbits, and the harmony of heaven; concerning the deceptive measurement of the sun and moon and of the terrestrial globe; concerning the four habitable regions established around the earthly point according to the doctrine of your Macrobius; and concerning the antipodes, or *Antoeci*, arranged through those regions so that passage between them is impossible—you seem not to have considered sufficiently the danger involved in saying such things.

Once you have assumed that there are four human habitations, with absolutely no natural possibility of travel from one to another, tell me, come now: how will it be true that the holy and apostolic Church reasonably confesses that the Savior—foreshadowed by the first fathers, so to speak, from the very cradle of this world, then prefigured by the patriarchs [Col. 0154D] and prophets in many different and evident ways, and finally made known and glorified in the fullness of time through the ineffable works of his humility and charity—came for the salvation of the entire human race, if there are three races of human beings besides this habitable region which we inhabit, according to the temperate arrangement of the zones of heaven and earth, and which the aforementioned Macrobius maintains may exist, but to which knowledge of such great salvation could not have reached?

Where is the statement of that faithful man whom the Lord found to be a man after his own heart, who cries out in the Spirit of truth: “God has revealed his righteousness in the sight of the nations”? And likewise: “All the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God,” if there are certain ends of the earth uninhabited by human beings, to which the sound of our prophets [Col. 0155A] and apostles could not cross because nature blocked the way through inaccessible distances of waters, cold, or heat?

# Chapter Five

Indeed, I read these matters with you and, as I recall, I used often to say that they ought to be understood in such a way that one should possess only knowledge of the sphere, not believe that it was supported by truth, because, according to the Apostle’s command, everything must be tested and examined with a pure gaze of the mind.

For, just as in things subject to the senses, so also in intellectual matters, especially in the sciences, there are so many and varied forms that, unless the Spirit of piety is present to guide us by its rule, the human heart—perverse and inscrutable—is easily led astray by plausible reasoning. And unless it is restrained by a certain sobriety of understanding, it will sometimes be lifted too high and finally burst when the swelling itself grows to immense proportions; at other times, sinking too far in a perverse direction toward the depths, it will be submerged in the darkness of foolishness.

The Apostle’s mind, illuminated by the grace of the Holy Spirit, foresaw this. Among the rules of faith that he set before us for imitation, he gave the strongest warning that we should not be wiser than we ought to be, but should be wise unto sobriety.

Accordingly, when something presents itself to our mind that delights us by its sublimity and plausibility, we possess the square of Christian teaching, which we must place alongside it once we have understood and recognized it. If anything in our meditations exceeds that standard, we must cut it away by a prompt judgment according to its rule.

In this way, both the danger of condemnable errors may be avoided and the expertise of the philosophers—which, like a kind of superfluous immensity, is suitable for our studies—may be made to serve us appropriately and beneficially.

But so that you may recognize without evasion how destructive it is to imitate the faith of those whose intellect we admire, consider what the assertion presented in the first part of their philosophical confession claims. Macrobius took it from them and inserted it in his book in these words.

# Chapter Six

[Col. 0155C]

> “God, who both is and is called the first cause, is the one ruler and origin of all things that are and that appear to be. This God, through the superabundant fecundity of his majesty, created mind from himself. This mind, which is called *nous* (νοῦς), gazes upon the Father and preserves the complete likeness of its author; but the soul creates what comes later from itself, looking backward. Again, the soul is clothed with the *nous* by which it gazes upon the Father; and, as its gaze gradually turns back toward the construction of bodies, it degenerates into corporeal things.”

If you assent to the meaning of these words, do you not seem to be reviving many errors that, in the first age of the Church, were refuted and suffocated by the vigilant diligence of the Fathers?

Among these, Arius introduced inequality among the persons within the simplicity of the Godhead. Mani, moreover, asserted that a degenerate part of the Godhead was the devil and that the same being was the creator of evil creatures. No one who has read the histories of the Church is unaware of how many devastations these abominable perversions inflicted upon the faith and how much fruit they produced for wickedness.

Origen, a great man in the Church and a remarkable interpreter of the divine utterances, did not deserve to escape the snare of this philosophical trap through the fearful judgment of God. After publishing many treatises usefully and excellently for the honor of the holy Church, he finally turned to the interpretation of the *Song of Songs* and asserted that the Father is not seen by the Son, nor the Son by the Holy Spirit.

Saint Jerome indicates this in his letters, and, deeply lamenting the fall of so great a teacher, says:

> “Origen, though he had surpassed others in other matters, surpassed himself in the *Song of Songs*.”

As long as his praiseworthy intellect was warmed under the guidance of charity and did not depart from the light of apostolic teaching, he proceeded along a straight path and beneficially supplied others with the height of spiritual understanding. But when he attempted to mingle the incomprehensible depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God—comprehensible to a human being foolish in himself not by power but by divine condescension—with the profane doctrines of the Greeks, by which perhaps he had previously indulged himself too much, he fell miserably.

Thus, when treating of the resurrection, he denied the solidity and reality of the bodies that are to rise. This distinguished man, lofty in contemplation, fell with terrible force, like one who had slipped from a very high watchtower, through the pitiable lot of human weakness. He became an example to later generations, showing with how much reverence and fear of the divine counsel the height and depth of God’s mysteries must be approached, and teaching each person to understand that the swifter the movement of his soul, the more ready its fall, unless it moves with caution and heavenly protection.

The Savior indicates this to his disciples when he prepares them to stand before the powers of the world, through fear or love of which they could easily have fallen away from the Holy Spirit, as witnesses of the faith:

> “Do not consider how or what you are to speak; for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.”

# Chapter Seven
