This is the Spirit who flees from fictitious discipline, whom a body subjected to sins does not deserve, who departs wherever he wishes and comes without difficulty of place or time to wherever he wishes, and who brings with himself, when he comes, the seal of his presence.

What he suggests is upright and devout; what he sends forth is strong and sound; what he makes fruitful is sweet and pleasing. In him is the grace of truth; through him we have the hope of life and virtue. When he enters the dwelling of infants, he makes them eloquent; and when he comes upon a cold and dark heart, he turns the seat of vices into a tribunal of purity.

In his presence nothing can be foolish or useless. He loves nothing singular or discordant; he loves nothing immoderate. For he himself is both measure and immeasurable measure. Every gift is sufficient for him, because even if what I deserve seems little in relation to my desire, nevertheless, possessing the whole in the fullness of the body of the Church—which God himself gives life to—I am not confounded by the loss of any necessity.

When this Spirit therefore sees a mind presuming upon itself, he despises the place of pride, because he is a lover of humility. And because he is one and the same, he multiplies the gifts of his graces in such a way that, through that distribution, he nevertheless makes one simple and true body of indissoluble charity [Col. 0157A], detesting divisions and scandals.

The result is that the unclean spirit invades a soul devoted to divisions, fashions it according to its own qualities and powers, miserably tears it apart, and, rending it through various errors, brings it to destruction and perdition.

# Chapter Eight

This happened to those about whom we are speaking, whom an earlier age called the philosophers of the Gentiles. Their fathers, descended from the stock of the patriarchs of the Israelite people, were deprived of hereditary blessings and lacked true knowledge of the Lord our God; they left the same loss of ignorance to their children until the blessed seed came, to whom the inheritance of the nations was owed.

Meanwhile they began to be tormented by natural hunger. Just as people who seek bread in a rock, or gold in flint, or the sun in caves beneath the earth, so, in investigating the nature of things and learning the underlying structure of the whole fabric of the world and the harmonious discord of the elements, some occupied themselves with these matters, while others tried to discern the outcomes of causes that they supposed were indicated to them by a fatal necessity through the conjunction of planets and stars. Divided among such wandering paths, they went astray around the highest good after expending much effort in vain.

Yet if among them there arose some whom a purer and freer reason urged to insist that there must be something more ancient and better than the creature itself—something whose power encompassed the whole universe of creation and whose providence bound together, according to fixed weights and numbers, the sequence of all existing things and of those that pass away contingently—nevertheless, when they reached that inaccessible light which surpasses every firmament and every height of the heavens, they were in no way worthy to apprehend the venerable and worshipful simplicity of the ineffable Trinity or the threefold mystery of that simple majesty.

Hence it happened that they posited three principles for themselves: the artificer, forms, and intelligible matter. They placed the world in the divine mind, where, as the model of this sensible world and according to the rational order of numbers, it would contain intelligibly within itself all things destined to fall under the senses. In these principles they diminished the omnipotence of God, decreeing that nothing could be made from nothing.

These are the matters in learning which you boast of having spent much effort. I read them with you and took care to reject most of what I read because of its very nature. They possessed great difficulty, little usefulness, and no salvific value.

Yet when, for the sake of testing them, I followed them to see where they would end, I marveled at where they finally wished to settle, since they seemed to be wrapped in immense coils, as though in circles of smoke—unless, indeed, I suspected that they promised no outcome in truth.

# Chapter Nine

Such, assuredly, are the seeds of that one who, through pride, desired to be like his own God. When he was once permitted to invade the minds of the Gentiles, he made lofty promises, led them upward, and prepared their fall.

Mortal hearts could not suffice to guard against his deceit and his thousand arts of harming, because at times, by introducing impiety, he assumes the appearance of piety. He relaxes the laws of authority so that his supporters may raise themselves toward virtue in one respect, while in another he presses them down so that they remain subject to the corruption familiar to him. At the proper time he infects their good and, through a pitiable exchange, covers the baseness of his own confusion with what he has taken from another.

Neither narrowness of place nor length of time resists the darts of his incitements. The secrets of nature lie readily open to him; he fears entering only that citadel over which presides the Spirit who loves holiness.

When this adversary, so powerful and effective, saw the mass of that earlier generation prostrate and lying fallen, he began to rage among the ruins he had made. As the author of division, he divided the animal human being into various doctrines and opposing sects. Hence the Socratics, Pythagoreans, Platonists, and countless other schools went astray along different paths and assisted their errors with ingenious inventions.

As the devil’s seed advanced and grew strong, there followed a crowd of poets. Like entertainers rushing to the wedding feast of idolatry, they delighted the souls of those who pursued vanity with fabrications and immoderate praises.

For the sake of profit they were ready both to flatter and to slander. They deified wicked rulers and violent plunderers, serving useless memory and empty glory with the jingling of inflated words and the ornament of opinions unsupported by any purity of truth. They adorned obscene and shameful things with various coverings. As the nature of each one flourished, some became comedians, others lyric poets, satirists, or tragedians, and through many phantoms they deceived the souls of sinners [Col. 0158C].

They also bent the simpler people—who, under the deep night of ignorance, did not understand the honor of their own condition—down to the cultivation of stones and disgraceful things, making them comparable, or rather inferior, to beasts of burden.

# Chapter Ten

These are the Egyptians whom God’s providence exposed for the Holy Church to plunder. With their spoils we adorn the face of the Lord’s temple, and the natural gift that they themselves retained in pride and abuse for their own condemnation we, as lovers of humility, turn back to its proper uses.

Presuming nothing upon their rights, attributing nothing to themselves, and seeking not their own interests but proclaiming the glory of the eternal kingdom, they—simply wise and wisely simple—transferred the armor of faithlessness into the service of faith and gave life, through the spirit of charity, to knowledge that had been inflated and dead.

These are the people concerning whom it was said to us: “Others have labored, and you have entered into their labors.” All their wisdom was swallowed up in the deepest wells of questions. Those who searched them did not find in them the fountain of water springing up into eternal life; but abundant riches of words and treasures of eloquence were most usefully prepared for us, to whom knowledge of salvation has been granted in the forgiveness of sins through the mercies of God.

Accordingly, breaking through the snares and deceptions of meaning that they, like a decaying spider wasting away and draining its own inward parts, foolishly spread before those who imitated them, as though they were the devil’s net, we left bare the corpse of idolatry [Col. 0159A]. We offered to the Savior and Liberator of our souls the adornment of speeches and of certain practices by which the vessels of dishonor had for a long time concealed their putrid remains.

# Chapter Eleven

The subject matter around which we expend our store of words is that same one concerning whom nothing that is said can ever be sufficient: namely, the Wisdom of God the Father, consubstantial and coeternal with him and with the Holy Spirit; the one immortal and invisible God, to whose honor and glory alone all things heavenly, earthly, and infernal serve, willingly or unwillingly.

When he had done everything whatsoever he willed in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses, he turned toward the pitiable human race with merciful prudence, bending the justice of his will and tempering the strength of his power with charity.

He does not degenerate in any part of himself in any way, as the foolish confession of the philosophers persuaded them; he never fails, nor does he essentially receive anything by which he begins to be what he previously was not. He is wholly present everywhere and suffers no limitations of place. He always exists, yet he is the creator of times, the sure measurer of all numbers and weights.

A rational person thinks rightly about him when he recognizes the greatness of the One who is at once greatly to be feared and greatly to be praised. Through his wisdom and providence, tirelessly and without error, he links together in an admirable sequence not only the distinction of the elements but also the causal outcomes of things composed from the elements.

This is our Lord, and there is no other beside him. Although he was perfect in himself and had no need of another’s favor or praise, the Lord of all, according to the good pleasure of his will, created heaven, earth, and all the things contained within the circuit of heaven from nothing.

Among these he created the rational angel and the human being—not equal to himself, certainly, but similar—so that in heaven eternal praise might be offered to the invisible God by countless hosts of attending spirits, while on earth the human being might likewise offer thanksgiving according to his transitory capacity. The offering of praise itself would be pleasing to the praised Lord in proportion to the devotion of those praising him, insofar as it benefited them in attaining the reward of eternity.

From the continual offering of this praise the one who had been made higher than all the rest withdrew. It was not because the Creator compelled him, but because he abused the abundance of his free choice and was lifted up in pride. He lied to himself, desiring to seize an immoderate robbery of equality with God.

Therefore, because by the highest counsel of the Creator his fall had become irretrievable, he began to range throughout the whole creation, seeking someone whom he might associate with his ruin. He passed over the angelic legions, whose stability he distrusted; he neglected irrational creation, whose end he perceived to be swift.

Against the human being alone, whom he saw as destined for eternity whether he stood or fell, he directed all the arguments of his wickedness. With all his strength he strove to erase in him the image of the Maker, so that, having been made like himself, he might be punished by an irrevocable judgment of condemnation.

He therefore persuaded, and was heard; he fought, and conquered. And although the merciful Lord had granted his creature, in addition to the freedom of choice by which it could refrain from sinning, the protection of a commandment, he nevertheless knew that the deceptive clay had received elsewhere the counsel to become proud.

Accordingly, toward the deceived and wretched creature he tempered the sentence of his severity in such a way that, through his commandment, the necessity of mortality might be imposed, while at the same time, through the merit of obedience, the capacity to rise again might be acquired beneath the debt of death. This capacity was to be granted meanwhile to the soul; but when the span of the present life had ended, it was to be restored equally to body and soul.

# Chapter Twelve
Obedience, therefore, he prescribed as a lesson to the first fathers before the Law; and, to dispatch great matters briefly, he ordained beforehand through Melchizedek the sacrifice, through Abraham circumcision and the offering, and through Jacob the erection of the pillar as a figure of the high priesthood and the true sacrifice, which were to be presented to the Church through his Son at the appointed time. Through Moses as well, his servant, he burdened the carnal people with precepts and legal institutions, containing mysteries of such profound depth that in all of them the Wisdom of God the Father marked, in manifold ways, the sacraments of human salvation and of his coming, and that people’s actions concluded, through mystical proclamation, the truth of what was to be done in the last times. For the whole description of the tabernacle and the burnt offerings, and the worship of the Lord’s temple, points to nothing else than the figuration of the state of the present Church and of the future one.

Moreover, how greatly God cared to raise man up to know and understand the mystery of his restoration—not to pry into the secrets of the servant creature or weary the mind with sterile meditation—may also be seen from the falls of the men of the former people. Among them, especially, our holy men, considering David’s fall with deeper insight, judged that it contained a great proclamation of grace to be revealed; and they understand that it did not happen without cause or without commendation of the faith that shone gloriously in the patriarchs: after the crime of adultery, for which no remission was granted in the wording of the Law, he was preserved as an example of mercy.

For it was fitting that the Lord, who is not the instigator but the ordainer of evils, should providentially arrange that he who by the merit of faith had risen from the lowest depth to the height of the kingdom should, through the guilt of lust, be cast down from the height to the lowest place; and that the Lord’s chosen one, a special herald of approaching grace, should experience in himself, miserable man that he was, how much he needed the help of the merciful God. He who sinned with his own flesh endured the fruit of his flesh—Absalom, namely—as his persecutor; and he who had been glorious in obeying God, following the wantonness of his proud flesh, became so dishonored that, assailed with stones by servants and provoked by insults, he lost his royal dignity as a fugitive.

But after he had returned to himself from the grievous hell to which he had drawn near, humbled, he raised his shamefaced eyes to the fountain of mercy from which he had often drunk before, and from the depth of his heart cried out to the abundance of God’s mercies. Since he perceived that no hope had been granted him by the Law, he promises—as though made the standard-bearer of the Savior who was to follow, offering grace to sinners—that he would give a draught to those who sinned: “I will teach the unjust your ways,” he says, “and the impious shall be converted to you.” Thus, coming toward the Lord’s prophecy, the guilty man became all the more fervent because, redeemed from legal severity, he was neither deprived of the kingdom as an infamous man nor of life as an adulterer.

Indeed, the humble king is crowned with so great a privilege of dignity that, by an astonishing miracle of divine condescension, the stock of the confessor, justified by an abundance of faith and cleansed by the grace of the Holy Spirit—which the same prophet had sincerely asked to renew his inward parts and his heart—became fit to minister the virginal creature whom Aaron’s rod, blossoming and bearing fruit without earthly nourishment, had designated by an extraordinary miracle; and whom Isaiah was shortly afterward to display beforehand in an evident oracle: she would, through the ineffable working of the Spirit, conceive the source of all propitiation. Thus all this served grace: that the author of forgiveness should be born from the seed of a penitent man.

This good word, this holy work, this new song, the harpist who had escaped the punishment of the Law, as though already joined to the people who were to come and dancing spiritually before the bridal chamber of the perpetual Virgin, sang beforehand with spiritual rejoicing: “We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple,” and many other passages that seem rather to indicate that he had attained complete joy than the longing of one who desires.

## CHAPTER XIII

The holy prophets are not content merely to foretell the time of remission; turning their faithful eyes alternately toward the two comings of the Son of God, they indicate one as a coming of humility and the other of sublimity, the first of gentleness and the second of power. And because human pride is accustomed to despise what is humble, they show with what reverence the former coming ought to be received by the magnificence of the latter, so that whoever has despised the time of indulgence may, without any excuse, deserve the terrible sentence on the day of wrath.

Isaiah, proclaiming this good news, and Jeremiah, lamenting, first signify the calling of the nations and the walls joined together into one corner-stone; then, lamenting the destruction of the people and of the city of Jerusalem and the common hardships of captivity, they seek the enduring city in which we behold the Lord of majesty, already seated with our flesh. This is the land of promise and the region of the living—not that land in which many thousands repeatedly fell and in which they watched their sons and grandsons perish through the violence of kings, hunger, swords, and other forms of death, but that land of which the aforementioned David, among others, marvels with clear truth, saying:

“How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts. And blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you.”

And he exhorts his soul to turn toward him after the Lord has done him good—a thing he understands as destined to occur when he is delivered from death, his feet from falling, and his eyes from tears. They looked toward it, I say, and sighed for it with the greatest desires.

But when, placed in the land of the earthly promise, they saw the world as a desert full of bitterness and a valley of tears lying between, they implored a stronger and better Moses with continual groans, crying: “Come, O Lord, and do not delay; stir up your power, O Lord and ruler.” Nor did that venerable company of fathers cease crying out until, when the birth of Jesus the great leader drew near, they exulted in pressing joys and said: “Behold, the Lord and ruler has arrived, and the kingdom is in his hand, and power and dominion.”

By these and similar signs, the truthful forerunners prepared the minds of carnal people to receive the Savior’s humble birth, and by definite signs and indications of his power they marked the greatness of him who was to be born for the salvation of all, lest the faithless Jew and the empty-minded gentile pretend not to recognize the one whom they saw indicated by so many prophecies. If you take care to savor the writings of these prophets according to their inner meaning, you will certainly discover that it is the height of madness to devote oneself to worldly knowledge in such a way that the salutary depth of the spiritual Scriptures is neither honored nor loved.

## CHAPTER XIV

When, therefore, everything that had to be placed beforehand figuratively to announce the birth of the new man had been ordered and completed, according to the predestination held before all ages in the counsel of the merciful God, in the fullness of time God sent his Son, made on earth from a woman, made under the Law, so that he might redeem not only those who were under the Law but, because he wished no one to perish, might exclude no one from salvation.

When you hear “God sent,” do not understand a superiority in the one who sends, or a change in the one who is sent, since divinity admits no alteration; rather, understand the Father’s good will and the Son’s devoted obedience, accomplished through the cooperation of the consubstantial Spirit.

If you ask about the manner of this incarnation, I do not know what can suitably be said except what is perceived from the Virgin who inquired and the archangel who answered: namely, that when the Spirit came upon her and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, divinity was united with virginal flesh with such sanctifying efficacy that the Son of God—God begotten from God before all times—was born from a Virgin in time; he became flesh, credibly though ineffably, not with the substance confused, but as one person of God and man.

Thus teaches the Vessel of Grace after the scales of unbelief had fallen from his eyes—he who, caught up to the third heaven, heard even those secret things that it is not lawful for man to speak. To indicate the utterly simple, natural, and inherent unity of the Father and the Son, he called the Son the form of the Father, where no robbery intervenes because of equality in the same majesty. Nor, on account of the word “form,” which among human beings signifies something distinct from the thing formed, should you make the Son anything distinct from the one whose form he is. In the passage that follows, the preacher of truth extends our understanding and, through the word adapted to sensible things, leads the mortal intellect toward the ineffable Word, so that by faith we may grasp what cannot be explained in human speech.

To disclose the mystery of the Incarnation for the salvation of believers, he consequently added: “He emptied himself.” And so that you might understand the word “emptying” in relation to the immutable deity not as a word of diminution but as expressing condescension, he carefully added: “taking the form of a servant.”

Both births, therefore, are marvelous. In both, the resources of human invention fail. The first, because of the unity of the Trinity, surpasses the understanding of angels and men; the second, because of its extraordinary manner of birth, empties the foundation of all philosophical reasoning. For they consistently proposed: “If she gave birth, she had intercourse with a man.” But a strong child was born, the Angel of Counsel, the philosopher of chastity, and by his venerable birth from a perpetual Virgin he overturned that proposition, since he was born from a mother who had not known a man and therefore had intercourse with no man by any reasoning.

## CHAPTER XV

But let us return to the teacher of the nations to see with what result this new event took place upon earth. Showing the effect of this birth, he says: “The grace of our Savior God appeared to all men, instructing us to deny impiety and worldly desires and to live temperately and justly in this present age, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God.”

Thus, at the birth of the new man, we are instructed to deny the desires of the age—which cannot be loved while piety remains unharmed—and, just as the holy fathers of the former people yearned under the desire for the first coming, so we, for whom truth has now arisen from the earth, should groan in expectation of the second, patiently enduring the blessed glory.

Before the coming of grace, the human race, devoting itself solely to vanity and pride, lived in a false security, apart from the few Israelites who had been granted a foretaste of the mystery of the kingdom of God. But since the King of humility appeared, we are commanded with great earnestness to follow his gentleness and embrace chastity, so that, with our limbs continually fastened to his cross—our limbs that under the old man had served impurity—we may preserve them immovable for sanctification, and oppose to every pride the sign of God’s humility as the banner of victory.

And although the foolishness of the gentiles and the unbelief of the Jews oppose this sign—ignorant of God’s immeasurable goodness and therefore ungrateful merely because God became so humble for their sake—we, who hear with the Apostle what he himself speaks in us, oppose the tree of life to pride, answering the Jew with Paul, that chosen one from the Jews: “Christ became obedient for us unto death, even the death of the Cross.” But to the gentile who boasts of empty knowledge we answer: “We judge that we know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.” For this reason God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at his name every knee should bend. For the end of humility is exaltation, just as the end of the proud is a fall.

## CHAPTER XVI

When, therefore, the King of Jews and gentiles had bowed himself down and had been born from a Virgin in a manner fitting to God, he declared by the privilege of a singular work that he was the one foretold by the Law and the prophets. First, he underwent legal circumcision, so that he might be shown not a destroyer but the accomplisher of the preceding covenant, and so that the murderous Jew, pursuing the letter that kills, might be profitably drawn through outward observance toward the inner life.

Therefore he endured what was written, so that he might present the sentence; he fulfilled the letter, bestowed the Spirit, removed the figure, and opened the truth. And just as two natures had come together in the Mediator, so, in freeing human beings and snatching them from darkness into light, he preserved a certain order: the Law is fulfilled so that grace may be introduced; the dead are restored to life so that the souls of the living may be raised; and it might be established on both sides by the strongest proof that, through subjection to the Law, he was true and just man, while through teaching and action he was God, omnipotent Wisdom.

The resurrection of three dead persons distinctly signifies this raising of souls. For every soul condemned by the death of sins is either still within, like the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, so that, as though delivered over to death nearby, it may easily be restored to life; or it has gone out through the doors of a good conscience and is carried forth dead amid the surrounding crowds; or, shut in under the stone of hardness, it has already become fetid through a more prolonged death.

But when the omnipotent physician approaches, the girl’s hand is taken and she rises; the bier of the young man is touched, and the dead man, called, comes back to life; the buried man is called forth amid the preceding tears of compassion and comes out. No condition of a soul that is completely dying surpasses the power of the Savior who heals, for he is the one who forgives all your iniquities, who heals all your infirmities, who also redeems your life from destruction.

He is the propitiator because he wills it; he is Lord because he is able. He used his power in raising the dead, so that, when you see what was done in the whole man, you may not despair that it can be done in a part. This is why he did it in a few cases: so that, before you are buried, you may hasten.

Let the wretched man not fear because of his unworthiness or weakness, for no one who approaches seems unworthy to God of being healed—God who, so that all might have access to him, deigned to become a poor man. This is the Father’s will; this is the Son’s obedience: that in the flesh he had assumed he might teach true and voluntary humility, of which he had come as the special teacher, and bring back to himself the proud man, drunk with the world’s vanities and delirious amid the corruptions of carnal desires.

This was effected by his birth from a poor and humble Virgin; by his being placed in a narrow manger; by the performance of circumcision and the legal offering; by his receiving baptism from the Forerunner; by his encounter with the evil spirit; by the sanctification of fasting; and finally by the choice of disciples. This choice was made so entirely with regard to humility and charity that every opportunity for pride was utterly cut off from his discipleship, since those were chosen especially who could never boast of the dignities or riches they had abandoned.

In this, too, the great providence of the chooser took care that they should not consider others unworthy of sharing the same grace because of earthly poverty, since in them nothing was found of human glory by which they might have deserved to be chosen.

## CHAPTER XVII

Simon Bar-Jonah was also chosen, the teacher of the gentle assembly. Raised to that sublime contemplation by the prerogative of simplicity and love for Christ, and not by flesh and blood but by the revelation of the Father of lights, he promptly expressed, while his companions hesitated, the pure confession concerning the Savior that all the faithful must hold: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God, who came into this world.”

Therefore, the solidity of so penetrating a faith was made by the Son of God himself the foundation of the Church, upon which the structure of the entire edifice would rise. Peter himself, blessed by divine testimony, received the office of keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, with such fullness of power that whatever he binds is bound, and whatever he looses is loosed, equally in heaven and on earth.

Since, therefore, God the Father made that revelation in Peter through the Holy Spirit, the power of loosing and the authority conferred—which proceeds from the merit of his confession—must be assessed chiefly according to its inner meaning; only one who applies the eye of faith can experience it, although the punishment of binding sometimes broke out in certain cases, as with Ananias and Sapphira, even into bodily condemnation.

Accordingly, if you believe with a pure heart, you will be absolved; if you confess with your mouth, you will be saved. For “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” In this way, built upon the foundation of the apostolic confession, you are justified, and, justified by faith, you live.

The foremost of the apostles is plainly the precursor of this justifying faith. Among his fellow elect, the abundance of his faith conferred on him the primacy of heaven and earth, with this exceptional dignity: whoever does not preserve the obedience of this key-bearer is altogether unworthy to obtain the Lord’s grace and is not permitted to enter the kingdom of God, since Peter’s key does not grant him entry. For whose sin he retains, it is retained; and whose he forgives, it is forgiven.

This heavenly gift and spiritual power, although bestowed by the generosity of the Redeemer upon all the apostles, nevertheless seems to shine more specially in him who was repeatedly tested as to whether he loved the Lord more than the other disciples and who was more particularly admonished concerning the care of feeding the sheep.

## CHAPTER XVIII

After the disciples had been chosen and adopted as sons into the kingdom, and after signs of miracles had also been abundantly displayed—miracles that no mere man could ever perform and that, by undeniable truth, proved the bodily presence of the divinity at work in the Son of Man—when the hour was approaching in which he would pass from this world to the Father, he preserved the purpose of the humility and charity he had assumed. So that he might leave his coheirs a sure hope of their inheritance, he established in himself a new Testament, according to which the old man, destined to be changed into a new creature, would be washed through the bath of regeneration and afterward nourished from Christ’s body, which had been taken from the Virgin.

Although this body was already immortal and incorruptible before the resurrection, it is extended by divine power, so that when you hear that the Lord ascended bodily into heaven, you should not therefore think that his faithful are deprived of so great a gift. Although he sits irrevocably at the right hand of the Father, the faithful still receive on the altar, by the same power, that very body which he then gave to the disciples while he still appeared mortal among them.

For just as in baptism you are buried with Christ into death, while the hands of the baptizer serve outwardly as certain instruments, and he stands in the middle of it all of whom it is said, “This is he who baptizes”—whom the faithful sees and the unbeliever does not, and who brings about the effect of salvation—so at Christ’s table you are nourished by his very, not figurative, body, insofar as you grasp it by faith visibly. The invisible priest is present as the transformer and taker-up of the offered creature, with such efficacy of sanctification that, when the priest speaks the words of the Lord, which are living and sanctifying, what must be attended to and received is, as Blessed Ambrose testifies, “not what nature formed, but what blessing consecrated.”

## CHAPTER XIX

After this sacrament had been celebrated and instituted with the disciples, and after the discourse containing, with incomparable sweetness, the mysteries of the love and unity of the head and the body, as the narrative of Saint John the Evangelist indicates, he wished to use the power by which he had taken up his soul in order to lay it down and take it up again. Though his flesh was weak, his spirit was ready, and he proceeded to the cross, so that, when the blood of the testator had been poured out, the Testament might be made firm.

Concerning the pouring out of this blood—what salvation it contains and what it deserves from those for whose redemption it was poured—we must hold this: every human act of thanksgiving is inferior to the repayment it calls for. Yet it is a devout presumption of the Christian to celebrate continually in memory the life-giving death that is the price of his redemption and, inwardly applauding his Lord God, to embrace so great a benefit with unshaken firmness of faith, remembering that the one whom every rational creature worships as risen by the power of God and seated at the Father’s right hand died for him.

Let him humble himself before the cross of his Lord, fastening his flesh with fear of him; and if perhaps he is weighed down by the multitude of his crimes or by the narrowness of time, let him raise his eyes to the thief who hung there.

For that blood always washes us from our sins. Even when it was being poured out, it was not without the effect of salvation: under the very punishment of condemnation and at the moment of death, it absolved iniquities accumulated over a long time. To the one whose present life was being closed by crime, the repose of eternity was opened through the merit of confession based on faith.

Christ also sanctified his own torment. The cross, which had previously been the disgrace of the condemned, became, through his action, terror to unclean spirits and glory to the Savior, before whom the dreadful impurity of a blaspheming conscience is judged.

Whoever desires to follow Jesus will carry this cross after denying himself. Through it we are initiated into life and strengthened for battle; carrying it before us against the world’s dangers, we are to trample down pride, so that where the master was offered, the disciple may be fortified.

When the Lord descended to the underworld to free his own, breaking the gates of death and defeating the prince of darkness, the vessels of faith recognized this sign of his offering: the ancient saints who sat in darkness and the shadow of death, awaiting the restoration of the way of peace that had been closed to them by Adam who brought death, through him who brings life. Insofar as faith was concerned, nothing had been lacking for them to receive the inheritance; whatever is certain for us concerning the past was certain for them as a firm hope concerning the future.

But those who had formerly been placed under a pedagogue and burdened by the servile yoke of the Law were held back from the kingdom, shut up under sin, until that true Lamb was raised upon the cross. Through his blood the Israelite people, marked with the sign, would be freed; and under that Son, as the most powerful King of all, the same capacity and grace of rising again would be granted to the elder and the younger people.

That this had already occurred in some of those who came before is confirmed by the testimony of the Gospel: when the signs of the dying Savior revealed his power to created beings, the sun was darkened, the rocks were split, and, when the tombs had been opened, many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose and came into the holy city of Jerusalem and appeared to many.

## CHAPTER XX

After the disgrace of the dead man had thus been glorified through the glory of the one who rose, only then did what he had said while still subject to suffering begin to be fulfilled: “When I have been lifted up, I will draw all things to myself.” For not only were the former fathers, as we have said, who had desired the first coming, called forth from darkness, but the gentiles as well, who had lain in the pit of misery and the depths of vices, soon after the coming of the Spirit received the light of faith. When the apostles announced the powers of the one who, in his risen body, had most clearly declared what the bodies of the faithful would be, they firmly hoped concerning themselves what was evidently shown to have preceded in the same nature.

For God the Word had assumed a body and our soul for no other reason than that he might raise each of them at its proper time. Therefore, although the sentence of the first curse still dominates mortal man, by which he pays the debt of death, the mercy of God did not delay the resurrection of the human soul—the soul to which, because of its dignity, help had to be brought more swiftly. Rather, most mercifully, both before the Law and under the Law, through the faith of Jesus Christ, which is life, he raised the souls of the elect. Once they had been vivified, they would suffer no loss even if the flesh of believers were dissolved, since according to his predestination the resurrection of the dead would unquestionably take place at the end of the ages.

The Son of God prepared the truth of this resurrection for us with such certainty that he presented to his disciples an incorruptible body tangible against the nature of incorruptible things. By a twofold demonstration he made himself both visible and not visible to those who doubted, so that by the one they might be strengthened in faith, and by the other conceive the desire to hasten toward that life in which, with their eyes changed for the better, they would always enjoy the most joyful vision of the Lord’s body—a body which here, at times glorified by immortality, mortal eyes could not see.

In displaying himself in this way, he did not refuse even the touch of the holy women. Whether by being touched or by eating with them, the Lord, in his accustomed humility, continued until the day on which he was taken up to stir the minds of his intimates, by speaking about the kingdom of God, to seek that homeland in which male and female would encounter one another, their vice indeed changed but the truth of their nature preserved, attaining the measure of the fullness of their age.

In him we have here the beginning of that kingdom, since in him the first fruits of those who rise were made; and it will be perfected in us when the crown of the saints begins to exist.

Therefore, when the disciples, still inexperienced, heard from him about the baptism of the Spirit and thought that Israel’s temporal kingdom was to be restored by its power, they asked: “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” He replied: “It is not for you to know the times or moments that the Father has placed in his own authority. But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.”

The Creator of time was not calling lovers of eternal life to measure the regions of heaven, distinguish the conjunctions or movements of the planets and stars, or pursue the study of worldly philosophy, which is almost entirely concerned with things that perish. Rather, he said: “You will receive the Spirit who comes upon you to bear witness to my name.”

It was as though he were saying to the poor in spirit and despisers of the world: “Do not investigate the sun’s winding courses or the moon’s wandering, to which the philosophers of the world have devoted themselves excessively. Still ignorant of what it is most useful for you to seek and love, await the promise of the Father, which you heard from my mouth, and sit until you are clothed with power from on high. For when the Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth, and he will announce to you the things that are to come.”

## CHAPTER XXI

After Christ had been lifted up into heaven before their eyes and placed at the Father’s right hand above every height, they received this promise after the completion of the days of Pentecost: suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a mighty wind, appearing to them in the form of tongues and fire.

What he accomplished in them is not for our smallness to explain; may he himself be present also to us and teach our infancy, so that we may be able to think and speak things worthy of him. For who would be capable of conceiving how, when the Holy Spirit came upon them, he baptized them and, cleansing away the rust of every iniquity, filled them with the gift of all virtues—so that suddenly they became strong instead of fearful, wise instead of foolish, fervent instead of lukewarm—unless rivers of living water were flowing from his belly?

Such was the abundance of their devotion that they had one heart and one soul, through the love of God poured into their hearts by the divinity of the same Spirit, who was given to them abundantly.

Then, when God’s work had at last been confirmed in them and they had been endowed with true freedom, they offered to Christ the Lord the voluntary gifts of faithful hearts. Those who had previously feared like servants, now brought to life by the Spirit, taught by the mighty works of God, gave invincible testimony to the resurrection entrusted to them before the sight of the hostile assembly.

Then truly the heavens declared the glory of God. When the apostolic firmament announced the work of the Spirit, the voice of majesty thundered, shaking the desert, in power and magnificence. Nor were there nations among whom their voices could not be understood. Thus, as the divine fire flashed and sparked, their sound went out into all the earth; and, since the Spirit contained all things and thereby filled the whole world, knowledge of the voice was also conveyed to many nations.

Here the Spirit distributed his gifts as he willed: to some he gave kinds of tongues, to others the grace of healings, to some discernment of spirits, and to all who believed in the Savior the forgiveness of sins; and, greater than these, unfailing love of God and neighbor. He inflamed the tongues of those who taught and softened the hardness of those who listened. He filled the mouths of the speakers and went before the hearts of the learners to receive the word of life, so that there might be teaching without delay, discipline without difficulty, and a true and joyful reception of salutary doctrine.

Then the outpouring began to be fulfilled which the Lord God had foretold through Joel, saying: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh,” and the sons of the Jews—namely, the holy apostles—would prophesy the life to come.

From this side, the Synagogue lost the blood of animals; from the other, gentility lost the worship of idols. For the Spirit who had marked his coming through the hiding places of the prophets, sent forth by the Father and the Son, came into the open after the veil of the Law had been removed, so that, through a new creation, he might renew the face of the earth; and, after the filth of idolaters had been removed, might unite walls previously separated into one house of the Lord. Thus there would be a holy nation, a people for possession, an elect race, a royal priesthood, all called into the marvelous light of the Lord Jesus Christ.

With the Paraclete suggesting all these things and accomplishing them through the laying on of apostolic hands, the sacrament of the institution of the sacred orders and the pious gathering of the venerable council were established. The fathers were to follow and imitate this pattern, so that, enlightened by the same Spirit, they might avoid creeping heresies and, according to the needs of times and places, enact rules with gentle moderation.

Animated by this same Spirit, both the apostles and apostolic men steadfastly overcame the torments of transitory kings. Glorifying God in themselves by faith, words, and conduct, they scorned the burning of their bodies in the stronger heat of love, possessing their holy souls in patience and preserving the treasure of faith in earthen vessels until the end of this life and the crown of martyrdom.

His inspiration is what the Catholic confession of priests everywhere acknowledges; and whoever has spoken soundly concerning the incarnate Word, whether for the instruction of others or for his own consolation, has drawn from no other source than him. For no one loves the Lord Jesus Christ except in the Holy Spirit, who, coming into the hearts of the elect, kindles them with love for the Word coeternal with himself and makes them ask with unutterable groanings, and with the Psalmist to groan:

“Make known to me, O Lord, my end, and the number of my days,”

—that is, so that I may know what is still lacking for me, who remain here beyond the debt of death.

The Spirit of devotion sometimes makes us leap across this infinite number of remaining days. By his anointing, through which he teaches concerning all things, he warns us not to imagine that we have comprehended everything; but, initiated into the present sacraments, we should, with the Apostle, stretch forward toward what is to come, toward the prize of God’s heavenly calling, mindful of that inheritance in which, delivered from the hand of all invisible and visible enemies, and presented bodily before him in holiness and righteousness, we shall serve him at all times.

For just as the former things signify the present, so these things are indeed effective for salvation but are the presentation of what is to come. For “by hope we have been saved,” and now “we see through a mirror,” but then we shall see “face to face,” when Christ our life appears and it begins to appear what we shall be.

## CHAPTER XXII
Briefly, we have touched upon the long succession of God’s works and set before your eyes the condition of the Church, so that from this you might judge how incompatible and discordant, in many respects, are heavenly institution and the crafty inventions of men. For although, in moral discernment—apart from those matters that all pertain to sanctifying faith—philosophical reasoning often does not differ from Catholic understanding, as in their description of the virtues, which they call political, purgative, and purified, and in many other matters from which ecclesiastical rulers and governors of the divine commonwealth have adopted certain principles, nevertheless, when they came to discuss our bodies, they lamentably lost their reason. They established for themselves pernicious opinions that contradict the mystery of the resurrection, around which the riches of God’s goodness and humiliation are chiefly displayed—something they neither deserved to comprehend under nature’s guidance nor to know through divine inspiration.

For, supposing that the body was composed of the elements, they thought that, because it was heavy, it necessarily had to return to the earth, so that, while the spirit returned to its kindred star, each of the elements from which the body had been formed might be disentangled back into its elemental substances. Hence they regarded the body as nothing other than the prison and tomb of the penitent soul.

Therefore, whoever accepts as true the meaning of those writings that assert the restoration of bodies in eternal life to be impossible—regarding as more truthful what the pagans have decreed, namely, that all weights are carried to the earth at its command—is without doubt an enemy of himself and ungrateful to the Author of the elements, who made everything whatever he willed. Certainly, it is as easy for him to place one thing in the highest realm as it was in the first creation to establish the joined chaos by distinguishing the elements.

And in this, I think, you agree with me: that God can do everything he wills. But perhaps you will object: Although he does everything he wills and does not do one thing while willing another, but wills even those things that he does—for no one compels his will—nevertheless, for the philosopher it remains doubtful whether he willed what the blessed simplicity of the faithful believes him to have willed and done.

This knot of the question is difficult for the unbeliever but easy for the believer; and, so far as human capacity is concerned, I consider it insoluble unless the key of David is present, the one that shuts and no one opens, and opens and no one shuts.

For us, however, this has been resolved in faithful Abraham, in whose seed even the believing philosopher is blessed; in the pillar of cloud and fire in the time of Moses; in the division of the Red Sea; and in the other matters we have set forth above. In these, nature’s customary order was so often defeated that nature itself can now place little confidence in itself.

Finally, God was born as man from a perpetual Virgin, and that same man, after being buried, was raised forever with a true body. Earlier, as proof of his power, he had truly restored the stinking corpse of Lazarus to mortal life.

The philosopher therefore lies when he declares that every human being is a mortal rational animal, because Christ, having risen from the dead, no longer dies; death will no longer rule over him. Accordingly, one man became an immortal animal, who grants this saving doctrine to his imitators and assists them in debate, so that, resisting manfully the devil—the destroyer of faith—and his members, they may believe and swiftly proclaim that the time will come when, once immortality has been granted to man—the quality by which God differed from him—he will remove mortality, by which wretched man was estranged from God. Thus, through Christ’s wisdom and grace, those whom the mortal philosopher divided by a foolish prudence according to transitory qualities will meet under a single definition.

This is not understood once the spirit has become subject to the flesh. For when the flesh lusts against the spirit, if the spirit, having rejected its fruits—which, according to the Apostle exhorting the Galatians, are charity, joy, peace, faith, temperance, chastity, and other such things not subject to a coercive law—passes under the flesh’s dominion, and the most shameful servant, oppressed by the command of his wanton mistress, becomes accustomed to bearing the yoke of sensuality, then at once, having cast aside the patience by which lasting goods are endured, he becomes entangled and confused in the works of the flesh.

These are fornication, uncleanness, and avarice, which is slavery to idols and includes idolatry; the crime of disobedience; and contentions and dissensions, to which you, workers of the flesh, have devoted yourselves with all your strength especially in these times. Those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God. Thus, deprived of God’s grace, which is eternal life, he serves under the pay of sins, which are the unending torments of everlasting death.

For just as the spirit, through the instruction of virtue and the practice of holy conduct, ought to have trained and advanced the flesh toward receiving the robe of immortality, so the flesh, having blinded and suffocated the spirit, drags it down with itself to receive the punishments of hell.

From this, finally, faith perishes—the strongest proof of future goods, faith that works through love—and unbelief succeeds, the creator of despair. With the eyes of reason extinguished, by which the true, the honorable, and the purely useful are ordinarily distinguished, one lives in servitude to the senses, so that whatever is dishonorable and shameful may be desired, whatever is harmful may be loved, and man, created for the honor of God, may be reduced to bestial disgrace, like foolish beasts of burden.

For without distinction one passes from vice to vice, where even the preceding sin becomes the cause of the next. The constant pleasure of sinning drags the reprobate mind into the depths of sins, until no remission of offenses appears possible to it. Then the good of obedience, which is preferable to every sacrifice, is despised: when the fear of God has died, obedience is given only to the ruling lust.

## CHAPTER XXIII

It seems that persons whom you call archbishops and bishops have prepared for you and for themselves an abyss of such confusion—unless God’s greater mercy deigns to come to the aid of your destruction—that they are not ordinary persons. Their fury, in the midst of abundant iniquity, became so deranged that they did not hesitate to despise the salutary admonitions and canonical decrees of the holy man Gregory VII, bishop of the Roman See, and to tear themselves away from the heart of the apostolic Church, the mother of all.

When the same Gregory pressed them concerning their crimes according to canonical principles, and when, whether condemned or fearing condemnation, they saw no means left by that prudent and persistent man by which they could escape their impiety, they involved their king, Henry, in the same condemnation. Just as they had made him the agent of their heresy, so they also made him its defender.

The madness of the Teutonic kingdom grew immeasurably, and, sinning beyond all measure, you became imitators of Jewish unbelief. For when those who stood on the Catholic side objected to you that it was not right to act in this way against the teacher of the entire Church, the bishop of the supreme see, while setting aside all reverence for divine worship, you often did not blush to cry out: “We have no pontiff except the Caesar.”

Yet, so that Satan’s body might preserve its integrity, you asked that a murderous man be given to you—namely Wibert, the archbishop of Ravenna—whom the Roman Church had previously condemned for definite and publicly known crimes in a plenary synod presided over by that same pontiff Gregory.

As far as lay within your power, you demanded by wicked vows and actions that the disciple of Jesus, who devoted himself entirely to restoring the holy Church to its proper honor and necessary freedom, be expelled and crucified.

But because the Lord knows those who are his, and in every nation chooses men acceptable to him who fear him and practice justice, there were at that time great and devout men who were not pleased by such great iniquity. Even today many remain in that same kingdom who, by God’s mercy, have not yet bent the knee to Baal. They did not make illustrious dignities more precious than their own salvation; rather, regarding everything as dung in order to gain Christ, they went to the chief of the apostles and to his successor Gregory in defense of the faith.

How impiously action was taken against him even according to secular laws—and the entire conduct of the affair, over which for ten years and more they labored, not without grave shaking of the holy Church, as described in *The Life of the Holy Pope*—will be made clearer from the history said to belong to the archbishop of Salzburg, a man illustrious in those regions and especially wearied in that same matter on behalf of justice.

From this it is even more astonishing to observe your imprudence, and that of the others who, in the Church’s cause, wage such frequent and empty battles of words against the arguments of faith, knowing nothing at all of what you say or of what you affirm.

If the sacred Scriptures—which your hardness does not deserve to understand—satisfy you less, and if the Savior’s words, testifying that the disciple is not above the master, do not satisfy you; if the authority of the Holy Spirit, by which it has been established that no one may judge the supreme pontiff, does not satisfy you; and if, beyond this, the harmony of the decrees—which have not only wrested from your impious hands the sword of judgment with which you intend to slaughter the patriarch of Christendom, but have in every way subjected your obstinacy to the yoke of his obedience—does not satisfy you, then at least the discreet men around you, learned in the law of the Lord, and the lawful rulers who honor God, and finally monks, hermits, and religious persons of every calling, who openly attack your schism with abhorrence, ought to have sufficed for your shame.

For the fact that you set canons against canons is the act of senseless ignorance, especially when no ambiguity obscures the matter and it can be demonstrated by true judgment wherever you wish. But where the will is measured by force, where judgments are evident, there is the conduct of violent men who have despaired of justice.

Thus, to this very day, the two cities—one belonging to Christ, the other to the devil—have remained distinct in their citizens from the beginning of this affair. There is scarcely any city in all Latinity that does not have defenders on opposing sides of this cause. Some, with murderous Cain, offer before God ears of grain as offerings of bitterness; others, with righteous Abel, offer in a simple lamb the innocence of truth.

Hence also, in order to provoke the Most High and increase profanation in your sacrifices, you implore divine clemency on behalf of Wibert as the father and pontiff of your souls.

We utterly execrate that same heretical man who, while our father and lord was alive, attempted through the bloody hand of a criminal and excommunicated king to usurp and pollute the most holy See of the apostles, imposing bonds of sin.

There is no middle position here: either you, if we speak the truth, are held under an inescapable condemnation as men who most perniciously worship the devil in place of Christ; or we, if we lie, are led astray by an intolerable and excessively hateful presumption concerning an innocent man.

It remains, therefore, that, once what we allege has been proved, either God’s fury and indignation correct you if you persist, or his mercy look upon you if you repent.

But, as we suppose [the reading is uncertain], none of you who have undertaken his defense will be so brazen as to dare deny what is said about the invasion, since almost the entire Roman world bears witness to it as to something already notorious and established by public knowledge.

When, therefore, you feel your insolence most powerfully constrained in this matter, you bring forward another means of escape, like thieves caught in the act, who deny everything they foresee will harm them but invent whatever they think will help them. You falsely claim that he was never pope—the man whom that same Church, in whose bosom he had been raised from childhood in holiness and devotion, appointed as its rector and governor of all regenerated in Christ, at a time of need when, amid advancing vices, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit had to be chosen to revive the canons, through the celebrated election of all those who, because of the urgency of the time, ought and were able to be present.

Not only the Gallican Church but also the Teutonic and Spanish Churches, and finally the Greek and Latin Churches, accepted him without contradiction and with due reverence. To this very day they remember, not without thanksgiving, that they had so great a pontiff.

The canons had taught them such things. The Spirit who proceeds from the Father commanded his dove—the Church that desires to be without wrinkle or stain—to preserve this inviolably: that the successors of the one whom the Lord called Barjona, that is, “son of the dove,” should be regarded as supreme pontiffs. Just as the power once received by that same apostle was transferred successively to them, so the honor of ecclesiastical eminence and the burdens of other affairs were to be referred to them. Nor, in judgments concerning apostolic dignity, should the inferior life of a successor diminish anything, when through Catholic ordination both the grace of the Holy Spirit and the merits of the presiding Peter were present.

Whether you ever received this same man as supreme pontiff is shown by the satisfaction rendered by your king in Italy after his first excommunication. Driven by despair over his circumstances, he saw no way out of your misery except absolution from the man whom, despite your faithless minds, you nevertheless recognized as Shepherd and Lord.

We omit writing more about these matters, since they have all been fully and clearly arranged in the history of the aforementioned man.

## CHAPTER XXIV

We could not by any means omit what your malignity fabricated concerning a certain letter composed against the same holy Gregory in order to corrupt those of lesser understanding and to persuade and implant your crime in the minds of the simple—as though what you are doing proceeds from zeal for equity rather than from the falsity of hatred. The letter was sent through various parts of the kingdom so that undiscerning people, who do not consider whether something is as it is said but believe that what is written in such a way must be true, might assist your party and, moved by horror at the unprecedented cruelty of the lies you are pursuing, consider your conduct excusable.

To anyone who judges rightly it is clear that you, through whose mouths the father of lies spoke from his own resources, are of your father the devil, who did not stand in the truth. He compelled you to say and write such things about Christ the Lord and the blessed apostles’ successor that it is scarcely believable that they could have befallen even any common person.

But because, in the entire assembly of the wicked—where, as we have heard, a council was held at Trier to crush the just man—none of those who sat in the seats of pestilence was found capable of composing words with which to rebuke the innocent, overturn justice, and ornament slander with the language of truth, the responsibility for this affair is said to have been assigned to a certain grammarian, Wirricus, a teacher at Trier.

Under the persona of Eliphaz the Temanite—namely, the bishop of Verdun—he was to increase by fraudulent words and deceitful questioning the suffering of holy Job, sitting upon the dungheap of worldly tribulation and scraping away with the compassionate hand and potsherd of truth the worms of vice streaming from the body of the Church.

That grammarian, chosen from the Philistine assembly to reproach the living God, gladly undertook the task. Following the practice of school rhetoricians, who, once they have taken up a theme, pay no attention to what has or has not actually happened but sharpen their tongues in invented cases and say as much as anyone might either inflict as an injury or endure himself, he composed a letter overflowing with insults against the holy Church.

We have resolved to answer it promptly, with the grace of the one whose gift enables us to distinguish pride from obedience, shamefulness from chastity, truth from falsehood, and the angel of Satan when he transforms himself into an angel of light.

Thus, in the words of that letter, the introduced bishop pretends to be a friend, while under the guise of an inquirer he pours out all the venom of the enemies. If he were a true friend, he would not permit the blasphemies of sacrilegious men to be published under his name, since, had he cared to do so, it would have been easy for him to refute the slanders alleged.

But the excellent friend preferred to chant the fabricated insults of his lord and teacher rather than offend the consent of the impious. If he had judged piously, he would have burned these insults in the appropriate flames rather than accept them for transmission.

And that aforesaid servant of the Lord, Gregory, hidden in the hiding-place of God’s face from your disturbance and protected in his tabernacle from the contradiction of your tongues, enjoys the beauty of the house of God. He loved, preached, and taught its honor and freedom in the word of truth and in the power of God.

Walking before men with his predecessor, Blessed Paul, armed with righteousness through ill repute and good repute, as a deceiver and yet truthful, as dying—and behold, he lives—saddened for an hour but henceforth always rejoicing, he has attained the dwelling-place of the glory of God. He is intoxicated with the abundance of God’s grace and drinks from the torrent of eternal delight, experiencing with faithful David how great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you.

Therefore, while your tongues still crawl upon the earth, he blesses the Lord, who has shown him his mercy wondrously in a fortified city—namely, the heavenly Jerusalem—to which your folly and curses cannot aspire. There the truth of the Father presides, and from his holy place he exposes all who speak lies; but he unquestionably strengthens the defenders of equity and the protectors of his Christianity, so that they may be confident, because he has conquered the world.

For even if he delays, he does not fail; rather, he always communicates the present help of his omnipotence to those to whom it is said: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age.”

## In the Year of the Lord 1100: Paul, Monk of Saint Peter of Chartres

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*Literary History of France*, vol. VIII, p. 254.

Paul was a monk of Saint-Père-en-Vallée at Chartres. He testifies that he lived there with Ardfaste, or Arefaste, a Norman lord, a man of integrity, sound counsel, and eloquence, whom Richard II, duke of Normandy, frequently employed in negotiations with the king of France and other rulers.

This provides a basis for fixing the beginnings of our author’s history. In 1022 Arefaste discovered that sect of Manichaeans who became famous in history (*MAB. Annals*, book LV, no. 2). After the council of Orléans, held concerning them, he withdrew to the abbey of Saint-Père, where he embraced the monastic profession and was still living in 1029 (*ibid.*, book LVI, no. 56).

Paul, who was already a monk there, could consequently have been born after the early years of the eleventh century, and he did not die until a very long time afterward, as will be shown below.

He was a man of intelligence and merit, extremely studious, who made it his particular occupation to preserve for posterity the historical monuments he was able to discover, together with the events of his century, especially those concerning his monastery and the city of Chartres, which may have been his birthplace.

His candor, sincerity, and good faith earned him the confidence of his abbots. In 1038, Abbot Landri sent him to Blois to carry a sum of money to a certain Rahère, to induce him to abandon the claims he had upon the royal chapel given to Saint-Père.

He had a servant named Tescelin, as we learn from a monument of that period. This might suggest that for some time he was cellarer or procurator of the abbey. The supposition is strengthened by the statement that he planted boundary markers to indicate the limits of the monastery’s territory: *magnis lapidibus a Paulo monacho solo infixis*, “with large stones set in place solely by the monk Paul.” This took place under Abbot Landri (*MAB.*, same work, book LXII, no. 83), and therefore before 1065, the year in which that abbot died.

It is at least certain that Paul performed for several years the functions of chancellor or secretary of the house of Saint-Père, which at that time were expressed by the term “notary.” Proof is found in several charters that he himself records, in which the following statements occur: *Scripsit Paulus monachus*, “the monk Paul wrote”; *Paulus monachus scripsit*, “the monk Paul wrote”; *Paulus monachus exstitit notarius*, “the monk Paul served as notary.”

When he was absent and another took his place, that person took care to indicate that he had acted by order of the abbot. For example, under Abbot Landri, whose trusted man Paul was, we read: *Robertus monachus scripsit hanc chartam jubente Landrico abbate*, “the monk Robert wrote this charter at the command of Abbot Landri.”

When Paul himself wrote, however, he simply indicated that he did so under such-and-such an abbot. Charters of this kind exist from at least 1040 through 1077, inclusively.

Paul himself confirms through several facts, which he incorporated into his work, the period during which he has just been shown to have flourished. He expressly says that he lived under the episcopate of Agobert, who died around 1060, and mentions the bishops who succeeded him, Robert and Geoffrey.

He reports an event that occurred in 1075 and in which he took part (*MAB.*, same work, book LXIV, no. 2). Bishop Robert, who was from Tours, wished to appoint as abbot of Saint-Père the monk Hubert, who was accused of following the heresy of Berengar. But he could not succeed, our writer adds, because of the protest we made aloud and the strong opposition we offered: *nobis acriter renitentibus, ac viva voce refutantibus*, “we resisting fiercely and rejecting it by our spoken words.”

Nevertheless, Hubert continued for the rest of his life to bear the title of abbot, although Eustace, whom Paul also mentions, had been substituted in his place.

Another fact proves what has just been established and shows that our author did not live beyond this century. Paul tells us that Count Rotrou gave the monastery of Saint-Denis of Nogent to the abbey of Saint-Père, and that it enjoyed possession of it until the count’s death—that is, until 1079 or, at the latest, 1084.

But then Beatrice, his widow, took the monastery away from Saint-Père and gave it to Cluny. This became the subject of disputes between the two abbeys, which ended only at the beginning of the following century through an agreement between them. Our writer does not mention this agreement, although his purpose would have required him to do so if he had written at that time.

Finally, among the titles of the priory of Léoncourt, which then belonged to the abbey of Saint-Père, one finds that in 1088 Ibert of Erigny gave the tithes to that priory, and that he showed them to the monk Paul mounted on a white steed. There is no appearance that Paul lived beyond this period.

Let it be remembered that he was a monk before 1029 and that, from 1038 onward, he was managing the affairs of his house. We have dwelt somewhat on his history because until now it was not known, and because those who have undertaken to discuss it—particularly the author of the *Chartres Library*—fell into several errors that it would be useless to detail. What we have just said is drawn from the writing of our author himself.

The only work of the monk Paul that remains to us is a celebrated cartulary, known to several scholars of the last century, who drew useful material from it. Among these were Sainte-Marthe, Dom Hugues Ménard, Dom d’Achery, and Dom Mabillon. In citing it, they slightly altered its true title, calling it *Liber Aganonis* or *Haganonis*, “The Book of Aganon” or “Haganon,” and sometimes *Apotheca*, “Repository,” because it is a collection of various documents.

It comprises 138 vellum leaves in quarto, written in an eleventh-century hand, so that there seems to be no doubt that it is the author’s original. Nor is there any doubt that it belonged to the monk Paul. This has already been partly proved by the account of his history and is confirmed by another cartulary also preserved at the abbey of Saint-Père, ordinarily called the *Cartulary of Argent*.

The author of that cartulary, who lived approximately a century later, copied a passage from the first cartulary and explicitly attributed it to Paul by placing the following inscription at its head: *Scriptum Pauli monachi*, “The writing of the monk Paul.”

Paul begins his collection by giving an account of his purpose. He explains that, having undertaken it at the urging of his brothers, he intends to gather in it all the charters and privileges of his monastery that had escaped fires and other misfortunes of the times and that he had been able to recover, so as to preserve them for posterity and to ensure that those interested in the matter might find in it the history of the abbey of Saint-Père.

The author divided his work into two books. To the first he gave the title *Liber Agani*, “The Book of Agani,” because it contains donations made under the episcopate of Aganon, bishop of Chartres. Since the second book contains those made under Bishop Ragenfroi, the restorer of the monastery, he titled it *Liber Ragenfredi*, “The Book of Ragenfroi.”

But it is from the first title that the cartulary took its designation. It is ordinarily called only *Vetus Aganus*, “Old Aganus,” from which the title *Liber Aganonis* was formed, as has been said, and as it is even read at the end of the book.

Nevertheless, despite this established arrangement, the first part contains a charter belonging to the episcopate of Ragenfroi. The author takes care to explain this by saying that he placed it in the first class because it concerns the canons who were then established at Saint-Père, and that this class is intended for all charters of this kind, just as the second is intended for those concerning the monks.

The cartulary should not, moreover, be regarded as a dry compilation devoid of historical features beyond those scattered through, as though drowned in, the charters that partly compose it.

The author took care to make it interesting by incorporating a large number of events that had occurred in his century or even preceded it, most of which are found nowhere else. He calls these “digressions,” which, he says, should not be displeasing to the reader.

Far from that, he deserves great gratitude for interrupting the sequence of his original documents in this way, thereby varying his work so agreeably. If he had feared less the jealousy of certain persons—who in every age too often obstruct the praiseworthy enterprises of others—and had presumed somewhat more upon his own ability, he would have given us a formal and continuous history.

That was initially his intention, but he was restrained by the reflections just mentioned. He was so afraid of returning to it that, after describing certain events, he immediately stopped himself with the thought that he might appear to exceed the limits of a compiler and assume the role of a historian.

All these precautions did not prevent our writer from giving us an abbreviated history of his monastery, according to what he had learned from the ancients or read in the monuments they had left to posterity.

There we see the abbey’s ancient location outside the city walls; a description of its territory and boundaries; details of its repeated destruction by the Normans; the defeat of those barbarians through the power of the holy shirt, which is still displayed at Chartres; the zeal of Bishop Aganon in restoring the monastery; and the efforts of Ragenfroi to compensate it for what Bishop Elias had taken from it.

Several other memorable events concerning the abbey of Saint-Père are found there as well. A new value is added to this piece of history by the author’s description of the city of Chartres, its enclosure, its gates, and most of its streets.

Paul did not restrict himself to domestic events. He was also careful to inform us of several facts belonging to public history. One such fact is the discovery of the heretics on account of whom the Council of Orléans was assembled in 1022.

The author of the *Chartres Library* had not read this account in the original and therefore believed it to have been written by Arefaste. But Paul learned its history from Arefaste, the discoverer, with whom he lived for some time, and wrote it for posterity on the basis of his testimony.

Another such event is the discovery of the head of Saint Romanus, which took place at Brou while foundations were being dug for a stone church to replace an earlier wooden one. Finally, without entering into greater detail, there is the abbreviated account of the miracles of Saint Sigismund, a canon of Chartres.

To convey the full merit of this collection, one should not omit that the author is careful to present things as they are and carries his impartiality so far as not to conceal the faults of his brothers.

He doubts where he thinks there is reason to doubt. Hence such frequently occurring expressions as: “I do not know,” he says, “what the outcome of such an event was; I know only . . . . I do not know such-and-such a place, but I do not doubt that it exists, because I find it written in this way.”

At times he even indicates the first source from which he learned the events he discusses. For example, when speaking of the discovery of Saint Romanus’s head, he explains that neither he nor the person who recounted it to him had witnessed it, but that the latter had learned it from the archpriest Agobert, later a bishop, who had been present.

At other times he retraces his steps when he realizes that he has made some digression, and he is not ashamed to retract what he had stated contrary to the accuracy of the facts.

It was from this collection that Dom d’Achery drew the history of the new Manichaeans discovered at Orléans at the beginning of the eleventh century (*Spicilegium*, vol. II, pp. 670–676). This history was later incorporated into the general collection of the Councils (*Councils*, vol. IX, pp. 838–842), and nowhere else is it found in such detail.

From the same source, the authors of *Gallia Christiana* (II, 483–487; IV, 720–724) drew everything most well attested that they say about the bishops of Chartres and the abbots of Saint-Père in the ninth century and the two following centuries.

It was also from the work of our writer that Dom Mabillon took the entire substance of the eulogies of the venerable abbots Alevée and Arnulf (*Mabillon, Acts*, vol. VII, pp. 279–285; vol. VIII, pp. 315–319).

Abbot Landri (*MAB. Annals*, book LXII, no. 83), under whom the monk Paul spent most of his life, died in 1065—or, according to others, only two years later—and was buried at Saint-Père.

An epitaph of sixteen elegiac verses was composed for him. It has been preserved and is somewhat less dull than the other pieces of this kind from the same century. We mention it only because there is considerable reason to believe that it was composed by the author of the *Cartulary*.

## OLD AGANUS
