Edited by Dom Guérard, *Collection of the Cartularies of France*, vol. I, part I, p. 1. The *Codex diplomaticus of the monastery of Saint Peter* consists of three parts; we reprint only the first, which acknowledges the monk Paul as its author.

## NOTICE

From Dom Guérard’s Prolegomena to the *Chartulary of Saint Peter of Chartres*, p. cclxvii.

[Col. 0179D] The collection written by the monk Paul is known by the name *Vetus Agano*, or the Cartulary of Aganon. In its preface, which he calls the *epilogus*, he announces that he has given the name *Liber Hagani* to his first book, which comprises the donations made to the abbey of Saint-Père during the episcopate of Haganus or Aganon, bishop of Chartres; and the name *Liber Ragenfredi* to his second book, because it was the bishop Rainfroi, Aganon’s successor, who made this abbey flourish and established it on firm foundations. As for the following books, they are not mentioned, and it is we who have distinguished them by giving each the name of the abbot under whom the acts contained in them were written. Nevertheless, we were compelled to bring together in Book VII the acts [Col. 0180D] relating to the periods of the two abbots Landri and Hubert, because these acts are intermingled with one another without regard to chronological order. This book also contains charters of the abbots Gisbert, Magénard, Arnou, and Eustache, which belong to Books IV, V, VI, and VIII. It even contains a charter from the year 954, whose proper place would be in the second book. Moreover, in Aganon’s book we encounter acts assigned to the time of Rainfroi, his successor. Finally, although the author warns that he will transcribe only the acts from the first eight years of Abbot Eustache, ending at the latest in 1087, one of these acts is dated to the year 1096 and precedes charters of more recent date; it must therefore be regarded as an [Col. 0181A] addition made to the work. This lack of chronological order among the charters is, moreover, nothing that should surprise us: in the majority of cartularies, the documents are arranged less according to their dates than according to the rank of the persons from whom they originate, and according to the times or places with which they are concerned [Note: Paul himself says that he brought together the acts concerning the land of Jusiers.].

## Purpose of the author of the Cartulary of Aganon

The author, as he declares in his preface, consented to publish (*edere*) a collection of the charters of the abbey of Saint-Père, preserved in their originals in that abbey’s archives, only at the repeated and urgent insistence of the monks. His inadequacy, he says, and the rusticity of his style advised him rather to keep silent than to expose himself [Col. 0181B] to the poisoned darts of the envious, who take pleasure in pouring blame upon the most praiseworthy actions of good men. Thus it was solely to obey the religious, his brothers, and not out of vanity, that he decided, against his inclination, to collect their privileges that had escaped the fire of the monastery (1078), forming them into a small work easy to save from fire and other accidental dangers, and convenient to consult when deciding the affairs of the convent. He also proposed, insofar as he had the leisure and ability, to describe the villages, lands, and other places given to the brothers for their support, so that they might have knowledge of their possessions as exact as that possessed by the persons charged with administering them. Finally, it seemed appropriate to him [Col. 0181C] to report, as he had learned them from the accounts and writings of the ancients, those facts demonstrating that his abbey deserved, through its distinction and through the richness of its ornaments and other possessions, one of the foremost places among the most celebrated abbeys of Gaul.

## Composition of the work

Accordingly, the work of the monk Paul, instead of being a simple cartulary, contains at once a collection of charters, a land register, and a mixture of narratives. He composed his work from documents left by earlier generations, from the accounts of the old men whom he consulted, and from his direct knowledge of the events of his own time. Most of the [Col. 0181D] documents he used were kept in the archives of the abbey of Saint-Père. For the description of the ancient possessions and rights of this abbey, he used two volumes or rolls, *rotuli*: as for the original title-deeds, he was unable to find them, either because they had perished through age, because they had been burned by enemy fire, or even because they had never been drawn up for lack of persons capable of writing them. He copied all the charters issued under the administration of the abbots Wibert, Gisbert, Magénard, Landri, and Hubert that he found in the archives.

[Col. 0182A] Having reached the period of Abbot Hubert’s expulsion, he warns that Abbot Thierry of Vendôme, who temporarily replaced him, has so far left only one charter to posterity, and announces that after transcribing it he will likewise transcribe those made by the monks during the time when they were without an abbot [Note: A charter of 1077 is classified among those drawn up during the vacancy of the abbatial office.].

As for the charters from the time of Abbot Arnou, he transcribed only those that still seemed to him to have some usefulness for the abbey; he replaced the others with an abbreviated account of the misfortunes that this abbot had to endure in his old age. Finally, from Abbot Eustache, as we have said, he reported only the acts issued during the first eight years of his administration. It was from a writing of Fulbert, later bishop of Chartres, that he took the history of Magénard’s appointment to the dignity of abbot of Saint-Père.

Among the old men who supplied information for his work, he names the monk Robert, former abbot of Saint-Maur-les-Fossés, who informed him about an agreement concluded between Odo II, count of Blois, and the monks of Saint-Père. He also names the archpriest Agobert, later bishop of Chartres, who told him how the head of Saint Romanus was brought from Rome to the castle of Brou.

Besides the ravages of the Normans, the destruction and then restoration of the abbey of Saint-Père, and generally the ancient history of this abbey, [Col. 0182C] the heresy of the new Manichaeans, and the other events he recounts in his work, he also makes known several particulars concerning the counts of Blois, and many others concerning the disturbances in the abbey caused by the bishops of Chartres, Thierry, Robert, and Arrald. The first expelled part of the monks from the abbey; they withdrew with their abbot Arnou at their head to their land of Jusiers. Robert placed the monastery under interdict for three months on account of a monk of Marmoutier, a follower of the famous Berengar, whom he unsuccessfully attempted to put at the head of the monastery. His successor continued to mistreat the monks.

In the descriptions he gives of the monastery’s possessions, he reports several details concerning ancient events, and very often places, after the charters he transcribes, explanatory notes about their contents.

After being forced to interrupt his work because of the disorders that prevailed in the abbey for three years, caused by the indomitable rivalries of persons deprived of leaders, he took up his pen again, so that no one might say of him that he had begun to build but had been unable to finish.

## Manuscripts of the Cartulary of Aganon

He must have written at the end of his book an account of the [Col. 0183A] recent events concerning his abbey; but the mutilation suffered by the manuscripts has deprived us of the final fruits of his labor. Only two ancient manuscripts of his work exist, belonging to the library of the city of Chartres. They are from the twelfth century [Note: The Benedictines (*Hist. litt.*, vol. VIII, p. 257) judge that the older of the two, the one containing 138 folios, goes back to the eleventh century, and that it is even the author’s original manuscript. But I examined the manuscript, and I do not believe it to be so old, if it is permissible to express an opinion different from theirs. D. Muley considers this manuscript to be from the twelfth century, and the other from the thirteenth.], on parchment and in quarto format. One is less detailed than the other, of which it even seems to be merely a somewhat abridged copy; but it contains parts or passages lacking in the latter, notably the eighth book and the end of the seventh [Note: In Book I, chapters 6 and 8, paragraphs drawn from the second manuscript will be found. They are enclosed in brackets.]. The one that may be regarded as the original of the two has 138 folios; the copy has 110.

## The monk Paul, compiler of this Cartulary

The monk Paul, the actual author of the book or [Col. 0183B] Cartulary of Aganon—for the title of the first book became the title of the entire collection—is often named in his work. The oldest securely dated act in which he appears is from 1060, and the latest from 1088. In both he is described simply as a monk. Another, issued in 1079 and 1088, gives him the title *edituus*; another, from 1086, calls him *monachus et edituus, notarius*: this tells us that, at least in his later years, he was the doorkeeper, or rather treasurer, of the abbey of Saint-Père. In most of the acts that mention him, he is designated as the notary or compiler of those very acts. Thus, among the charters copied by him, there were several whose originals he himself had written. The persons named [Col. 0183C] Ernulfus Niger and Tescelinus, who appear in the acts among the witnesses with the designation *famulus Pauli monachi* (“servant of the monk Paul”), were apparently a kind of lay brothers attached to his service.

Paul’s collection bears witness to his zeal for the interests of his abbey and to the care he devoted to investigating the possessions and rights that it had or could claim. He suffered greatly, together with the other monks, from the disturbances that afflicted the convent, and he speaks of them only with sorrow.

Perhaps it was in his capacity as doorkeeper or treasurer that he was entrusted with several matters on behalf of [Col. 0184A] his abbey. On the commission given him by Abbot Landri, he traveled to Blois and, in the town of Vienne on the Loire, delivered to Raherius, Berthe’s son-in-law, a sum of forty sous as the price of an arrangement concluded with him by the abbot [Note: P. 124. The Benedictines, in the *Hist. litt.*, vol. VIII, p. 255, suppose that Paul’s journey took place in 1038; but this date is very doubtful, since the charter that alone informs us of Paul’s journey is undated. It is merely in the name of Abbot Landri, and it designates Thibaut [III] as then count of Chartres. Now Abbot Landri did not die until 1069, and Thibaut did not become count until 15 November 1037, the day of the death of Count Odo II, his father (Doyen, I, 139). Paul’s journey, therefore, which could scarcely have taken place before 1038, very probably occurred several years later, but no later than 1069.]. In 1088 he went to the land of Liancourt, where, mounted on a white palfrey, he identified the lands whose tithe had just been ceded to the monks by the knight Ilbert of Érigni. It was also he who planted large stones to serve as boundary markers for lands situated west of the city of Chartres. This is more or less what is known of the author’s life, and what we might have passed over in silence without harming history, had we had something more remarkable [Col. 0184B] to put in its place.

## Qualities of his writings

His work, in the portions that properly belong to him, is distinguished neither by the order of its subject matter, nor by the connection of its ideas, nor by its diction. The sentence is often obscure, and the Latin generally lacks not only elegance but also correctness. Nevertheless, allowance must be made for the barbarism of the age in which he flourished, and it must be recognized that, although he is far below writers such as the celebrated bishops of Chartres, Fulbert and Yves, who lived in the same century, he wrote better than most authors of his time. Moreover, he displays judgment, candor, and good faith, and does not conceal even facts that are not honorable [Col. 0184C] to his brothers.

## The period in which he lived

It is in any case impossible to establish the time of his birth or of his death. The *Histoire littéraire de la France* says [Note: Vol. VIII, p. 254. Apart from a few minor inaccuracies, the article devoted by the Benedictines to the monk Paul and his work (pp. 254–260) is very well done and worthy of the authors of the *Hist. litt.*] that he must have been very old in 1088, having been born around the beginning of the eleventh century; but this is an opinion lacking proof, and perhaps plausibility as well. Since we see him traveling on horseback in that very year, we must suppose that he was not then extremely advanced in age [Note: From the fact that Paul calls himself a contemporary of Aréfaste, p. 109, and that the latter was still living in 1029 in the abbey of Saint-Père, where he had embraced the monastic life, the Benedictines concluded that Paul likewise was already a monk in 1029, and that he might therefore have been born at the beginning of the eleventh century. But Aréfaste prolonged his life much further, since he appears among the witnesses in a charter of Abbot Landri (p. 191), consequently drawn up between 1033 and 1069 if one follows the calculations of the *Gallia christiana*.].

## Spelling of place-names

It is unnecessary to point out that we made it a rule to publish the texts in all their ingenuousness—one might sometimes say, in all their barbarism [Col. 0185A]. Even in reproducing proper names, we followed the variety of spelling given by the manuscripts. But we must observe, concerning the words *villa*, *villare*, *curtis*, *mons*, and other similar terms when written in isolation, that we adopted the rule of printing with a capital letter the word that formed an integral part of the name; whereas, in the opposite or doubtful cases, the word was printed with a lowercase initial.

[Col. 0186A] Thus, for example, we wrote *Manus Villare*, Mainvilliers; *Fracta Vallis*, Fréteval; *Campus Fauni*, Champhol; *Germinionis Villa*, Germignonville, because the words *Villare*, *Vallis*, *Campus*, and *Villa* enter into the composition of the name. On the contrary, we printed *Cruciacum villa*, Crucé; *villa Lereti*, Léri; *Gesiaci cella*, Jusiers; *villa Condatum*, Condé; *Lupiniacus villa*, and so forth, because the words *villa* and *cella* remained outside the name.

# TITLE OF AGANON IN THE BOOK OF THE CHARTERS OF SAINT-PETER

[Note: That is: “Prologue to the book entitled Agano, in the chartulary of Saint-Peter.” At the top of the page is written in a more recent hand: “The old Book of Aganon.”]

[Col. 0185]

[Col. 0185B] I. Until now, although very frequently urged by the brothers, I have postponed collecting and publishing in orderly fashion the contents of this little work from the privileges that I was able to find in the sacred chests of our monastery. For, because of the dullness [Note: Thus the manuscripts, for *hebetudinem*.] of my intellect, or the rusticity of my uncultivated speech, I thought it more useful to conceal what was better hidden by silence than to expose its nakedness by babbling, through the office of an unskilled style, to those who do not know it [Note: Thus the manuscripts, as elsewhere, for *ignotis*.]. I was also deterred by the poisoned darts of the envious, who, following their customary practice, continually gnaw at and condemn the praiseworthy deeds of good men, and, whenever they see in others the good that they do not acknowledge in their own consciences, hasten to obscure it with the deceptive coloring of a serpentine tongue, so that the innocence of the upright may not be exalted with its due praises. Thus, with patience as my companion, the virtue of integrity, oppressed by the schemes of the wicked, appears in the opinion of the crowd to lie in the lowest depths, like a weakling.

Now, however, at the command of brotherly authority, not with the brow of presumption, setting aside the goads of ignorance and the canine barking of mockers, I have endeavored in this little work, as in a small vessel, to gather in the style of a foolish speech the privileges that were rescued, not without danger, from the burning of our church and our buildings, so that they may more easily be protected from fire and other accidental dangers, and also so that, whenever—as often happens—some question arises concerning the possessions recorded in the monastery, it may be resolved more quickly by reading what has been found. In the end, I preferred, with an unshaken brow, to obey your commands rather than, by refusing obedience, to remain idle and silent out of fear of detractors who, regarding the efforts of simple men as worthless, themselves sleep amid their pleasures while wishing to appear wise among men without producing any good work.

[Col. 0185C] I have also decided, if leisure or ability should be granted me, to distinguish from outsiders by their proper boundaries or natural limits the individual villages, settlements, fields, woods, and other places given through the generosity of religious men for their maintenance. Thus those who by voluntary vow have enclosed themselves within the paradisiacal folds [Col. 0186B] of the most holy sheepfold, dead indeed to the world but living to God, who continually mortify the desires of the flesh and adorn their souls with good morals, may have at hand knowledge of their possessions, like those who oversee them. For everyone ought to know the goods by which their food and clothing are supplied, so that they may repel the ambition of sacrilegious men, which always frightens simple persons with lawsuits and threats in order to extort something from them. In legal cases, the assertion of many is stronger than that of one.

It has also seemed fitting to insert into this little page the fact that this place, as we have learned from the statements or writings of the ancients, stood among the nobly founded royal establishments throughout Gaul, distinguished by august titles and adorned with gold or silver, with a vast abundance of ornaments, and with all the worldly goods by which human frailty is exalted.

[Col. 0186C] Yet because it often happens that where riches abound, there, with impunity as their companion, enormous sins are heaped up—sins in which wretched men become entangled while, in their blindness, neglecting the giver of their possessions—and while they sleep in the slumber of sin and follow the enemy, destined to be punished with everlasting penalties, nevertheless almighty God often both shows mercy to sinners by afflicting them and afflicts the sons whom he receives by showing them mercy.

## II

Accordingly, the aforesaid place, properly situated not far from the walls of the city of Chartres, shone with a considerable company of monks who, in the love of Christ, restrained themselves by mortifying the vices of the flesh. Serving the blessed apostle Peter, it then radiated upon all like Lucifer with the light of virtues [Col. 0186D]. The city mentioned above, exceedingly populous and most wealthy among the cities of Neustria, was regarded as especially famous for the size of its walls, the beauty of its buildings, and the study of the liberal arts.

## III

At a certain time, a pagan people boiling over from overseas regions in beaked ships [Col. 0187A], with the sword of their wickedness drawn, was cruelly devastating almost the whole of Neustria. Plundering several holy places, they consigned them to voracious flames; captured cities they razed to the ground, and Christians they either tore apart with unsated iron or led into captivity and sold under an irrevocable sentence.

Their fury grew so fierce that they rowed up the Seine River, laying waste to every place around them, and finally reached the city of Chartres, which they longed, with panting breast, to overthrow. By devastating everything in the city’s vicinity that they could reach, they rendered it uninhabitable.

## IV

When the city, because of the inhabitants’ deserts, had been afflicted by such hardships through many years, its citizens were at last killed, its wealth carried away, and all its strength broken; then, unexpectedly, it was captured one night. All the Christians were butchered like sheep by various forms of death. The city that had once resisted Julius Caesar’s siege for ten years, remaining unconquerable, and had tirelessly repelled Roman forces and Argolic [Greek] phalanxes—for it had been built of squared and enormous stones, fortified with lofty towers, and therefore called the “City of Stones,” made pleasant by aqueducts and cheerful with underground passages through which all necessary supplies were conveyed—was now, by God’s permission, overthrown to the ground by a people destitute of divine virtue and burned with fire [Note: B: Yet the wisdom of God, which corrects the insolence of his own so that they may not perish in the future, subdued the cruelty of the most impious barbarians; when the fugitives and remnants of the people returned, he restored worldly peace to them. Unable to rebuild the entire city after its overthrow, they chose for habitation a corner of the city still enclosed by a wall, and strove to fortify themselves from the ruins of the walls by setting stone upon stone there, without mortar, in the manner of a wall, as is still visible.].

Yet the patience of God, which corrects the insolence of his own so that they may not perish in the future, did not permit the cruelty of the most impious people to return home unpunished. For the Franks, gathered together from every direction [Note: Alberic gives a different account of Hasting’s flight (under the year 904). In his chronicle, Theobald threatens the Norman duke with the imminent attack of the emperor Charles the Fat; “out of fear,” Alberic says, “he sold the city of Chartres to Theobald, secretly departed, and was never afterward seen in France.” This Theobald, the son-in-law of Robert the Strong, duke of France, had a son named Theobald the Trickster, who is regarded as the first count of Blois and Chartres.], hastening to reach the anchorage of the ships, encountered them as they returned with much booty and immediately engaged them boldly. At their first assault the barbarians began to fall in such numbers as leaves in mature winter when the north wind blows through the woods.

You could see them, at last, having laid aside their former ferocity, some throwing themselves into the river called the Diva in order to drown themselves, others fleeing vainly to the ships and being miserably trampled under the feet of horses or pierced by the swords of their pursuers, so that from that great multitude scarcely a few were found to have escaped to be led into captivity.

## V

Their duke was called Astingus [Note: Here Codex B transposes several passages, postponing the entire account of Astingus below, with some variation and omission in the text, apparently for the sake of brevity.]. We have thought it useful to demonstrate what a man of deceit he was by recounting one deed of his [Col. 0187D]. Sailing the sea and laying waste to many lands, he reached the city of Luna [Note: D. Muley conjectures the year 858.]. Having examined it on every side and seeing that it was very strongly fortified, he conceived a deceitful plan: he undertook to capture it not by force but by a trick.

Pretending, therefore, to be ill, he summoned the bishop of the city and, in a subdued voice, asked him to wash away his sins in the waters of holy baptism and to become his godfather, since he was about to die. For this reason, he said, he repented in his inmost heart of the evils he had committed and was turning to Christ with all his heart; he wished to renounce the Devil and his pomp, so that, having received holy baptism even in death, he might escape the punishments of hell.

The bishop, immediately believing his words, catechized him without delay and washed him with baptismal water, as one of the dying [Note: A: *babtismatis*.], and raised him from the sacred font [Note: Dudo of Saint-Quentin, p. 64c, adds that Astingus was godfather, together with the bishop, to the count.].

Because of this, the citizens, secure in their false hope together with their bishop, made a treaty with the barbarians and opened the city gates. They granted them the opportunity to buy inside and outside the city every kind of merchandise, as though they were allies and friends.

Once they had obtained this opportunity, the barbarians spent the entire week going from door to door through the city and making familiar to themselves the streets previously unknown to them. On the eighth day, while the citizens were occupied in the forum, groups of four or six barbarians gradually and silently entered the city’s streets, stationing guards at each gate, while sending many others back to the forum as though they wished to buy something.

When this had been done, Astingus was placed, armed, in a coffin, as though dead, and was carried by his men into the church. With feigned weeping he was presented to his godfather the bishop, so that the customary final rites for Christians departing from this world might be performed for him.

When the bishop had devoutly performed this act of human kindness and ordered the corpse, as it was believed to be, to be placed in the tomb according to custom, the barbarians began to shout with immense voices; curses resounded, and the whole church, stunned, rose together in an uproar. What more need be said? That deadly henchman suddenly sprang from the bier and, drawing his sword, set about carrying out the crime he had conceived.

First he raised his sword against his own godfather, the bishop, who stood there wearing his mitre in order to commend Astingus’s soul to God its maker, and, more cruel than cruel, made him a martyr by cutting off his head.

His soldiers then carried out slaughter of every kind throughout the church, sparing neither age nor sex. Just as the burning Sirius scorches a field of sheaves, so their sword, thirsting for blood, covered the pavement with the corpses of the dead; they even caused the courts to run with a stream of blood.

When their accomplices throughout the city heard their voices spreading [Col. 0188D], they slaughtered like sheep all whom they encountered. Forgetting every form of humanity and pity, they killed old men and young, married women and virgins, little children, and infants hanging at their mothers’ breasts with their wicked blade.

In the same way, wandering through the *rostrum* [Note: Here *rostrum* seems to be used for “forum,” unless the word is corrupt.], they drenched in blood with their cruel sword those buying and selling alike, those going and returning, and they carried away to the ships the merchandise they found in the *rostrum*.

Those who had overrun the city plundered the gold and silver and various riches found there, burned the city, and likewise carried them away aboard the ships. Returning quickly to the city, they razed its walls to the ground and left the corpses of the dead, reduced to ashes, among the ruins as though buried [Note: A: *urs*.—B: *ubrs* [sic].].

Then, setting their sails at the tops of the masts [Note: Thus the manuscript, for *supparis*, namely the sails of ships.], they turned the ships’ prows toward the west. With the southwest wind blowing, they traveled the sea routes like pirates, laying waste to islands and coastal places, and slaughtering with the sword whatever people they found [Col. 0189B].

[Note: Dudo of Saint-Quentin tells at much greater length than anyone else the deceit of Astingus and the capture of Luna in the first chapter of his work *On the Customs and Deeds of the Normans* (*Ancient Historians of Normandy*, p. 63 ff.). William of Jumièges follows him in chapters IX and X (ibid., p. 220 C–D), adding that the barbarian leader took possession of Luna while believing that he had captured Rome. We find the first mention of the capture of Luna in an old chronicle by an uncertain author, apparently a monk of Fleury, published by André Duchesne. It says nothing of the Norman’s deceit and reports no more about the city of Luna than these few words: “Alstagnus, proceeding from the land of the Franks across the ocean toward Italy, reached the harbor of Luna and immediately captured the city itself.” (*Ancient Historians of Normandy*, p. 32 B.) There the Norman duke is called Alstagnus; by Jumièges he is called Astingus. But in Dudo of Saint-Quentin, with greater variation, we find Anstinnus and Alstignus, then Adstignus and Astelmus, and more often Anstignus, as the name of this barbarian duke, of whom we have found no trace in the Italian historical writers collected by Muratori. Perhaps for this reason the more recent historian of ancient Normandy, Théodore Licquet, a learned and discerning man who was rightly held in high esteem at Rouen, his native city, did not hesitate to declare that everything the old chronicles have handed down about that ancient leader of the northern barbarians was mere fable. See Th. Licquet, *History of Normandy from the Earliest Times to the Conquest of England in 1066*, vol. I, p. 58, note 2.]

## VI

Yet the creator of all things, who is accustomed to have mercy on his faithful by chastising them and to train the wicked for the confines of hell by enduring them, did not wish the enormity of this host’s crime to reign for long. Rather, having corrected the Christian people for their sins with a just scourge, he wished them to breathe again for a little while and determined to put an end to the evil works of the wicked people, intending to avenge the blood of his faithful in the everlasting, fire-spewing flames of Etna [Note: Read *Etnae*.].

Accordingly, when the host had reached the borders of the Armoricans by rowing, and had put in near the bridge of the River Diva, it began to restore its exhausted bodies from so much labor without any fear. Then, abandoned by God, whom it had angered in many ways by evil deeds, and utterly hated by land and sea, it was surrounded on every side by the Franks [Col. 0189C] and, as we said above, was so devoured by swords that, from such a multitude, I do not remember reading that anyone escaped, nor that anyone was led into captivity except one [Note: What Paul relates here about Hasting’s invasion of the Chartres region and the defeat of the Northmen at the mouth of the River Diva must be relegated among the fables.].

The sands, soaked and thirsty with their blood, as though disgusted with it, vomited that blood back through the waves of their river and, over a long stretch, stained the adjoining sea with unclean gore.

But since the heat of speaking compelled me to make a digression [Col. 0190A], I shall now return to the task of making my first journey. Whatever I can first find that was given or possessed either by the clerics of the aforesaid church or by the monks established in our own time by the venerable bishop Ragenfroi through divine providence, or that was donated by other religious men for the salvation of their souls, I shall endeavor to transcribe with the true work of the pen, as it can be found in the writings of our archive.

## VII

Beforehand, however, I have wished briefly to summarize, with the truthful testimony I learned from our elders, how the aforesaid place fell from its ancient nobility and highest honor through a certain Bishop Elia [Note: From 840 to 846. D. Muley.]. He, having obtained royal authority, which he may perhaps have purchased with money, did not fear to usurp it by force of arms. Much blood was shed at the very threshold of that church [Col. 0190B] while the monks maintained their former order and rejected the bishop [Note: Codex B, instead of “while the monks,” etc., has: “He displayed his mournful and initial entrance and inflicted irreconcilable divisions upon the inhabitants. Hence it came to pass that …”].

As a result, very many of the monks abandoned the place to which they had devoted themselves, and, dwelling in the regions of Burgundy near blessed Germanus of Auxerre, completed the course of their present life there.

The aforesaid bishop, having found a precious opportunity, carried away and sold the ornaments and various vessels of gold or silver that he found there and coveted. He also did not fear to subject to his own uses and financial support the sanctuary lands that the generosity of religious men had given, wherever he was able to lay hands on them, and, with reckless audacity, presumed to distribute them as benefices among his own household.

The weak band of monks who remained there, not knowing where to go, was fed sparingly and without mercy by the bishop. Meanwhile, the once-famous and most distinguished place gradually declined; deprived of its former dignity and customary office, it was regarded by the people as deserving of no veneration.

After not much time had passed, Bishop Elia died. He had brought to nothing this place, distinguished by royal titles, being inflamed by the torch of the demon; he had also utterly destroyed another nunnery, elegantly situated on Mount Leugarus [Col. 0191A], not far from the city of Chartres. Then a hostile force captured the city under siege and, as we have already stated, set it ablaze [Note: Codex B adds: “And the Christians were butchered like sheep by various deaths.”]. At that time, the often-mentioned place was profaned by the enemy and also consumed by fire.

## VIII

When peace had been restored through divine mercy, a certain bishop rebuilt the place, at God’s prompting, though on a small scale [Note: B: “The church is rebuilt and, with the offices of clerics and a modest income, is said to have been handed over to them; then, when times improved, the monastic order was introduced.”], and it is said to have been entrusted to the services of clerics with a modest income.

IX. Nevertheless, because the faults of the citizens demanded it, the city was again devastated by pagan raiders from overseas, and the place itself was utterly destroyed. It remained in this condition until the time of Hagano, the glorious bishop. Noble by birth, rich in worldly possessions, and distinguished by good virtues, he felt compassion for [Col. 0191B] a place once revered by men but now utterly neglected and reduced to solitude. Inflamed by zeal for divine virtue, he summoned stonecutters and masons, supplied the expenses, and ordered them with great diligence to restore the place [Note: [Col. 0191D] About the year 930. D. Muley.]; and, once it had been restored, he resolved to consecrate it with pontifical blessing.

He also established a succession of clergy who would render there the praises owed to God day and night. For necessary uses he granted it a vineyard enclosure and adjoining land, which his predecessors had sacrilegiously seized from it; he also bestowed in perpetual donation the estates that he believed sufficient for the number of clerics. As long as he lived, he wished to watch over them with attentive concern, devoted to the welfare and advancement of the place.

After his happy death [Note: [Col. 0191D] The year 950. D. Muley.], when angels had transferred him from the sea of this world to the company of the saints, the venerable Ragenfred succeeded him in the bishopric. How greatly he loved the place can easily be recognized from the work that follows.

For through the prudent ingenuity and persistent urging of this bishop, Alveus, distinguished in birth and in conduct, abbot of the same place, wishing—together with the canons whom he appeared to govern—to enter the narrow way that leads to God, adorned the succession of the clergy at the monastery of Floriacum with the habit of religion. For three years he diligently learned the Rule of blessed Benedict through the practice of obedience. Then, recalled by the oft-mentioned Bishop Ragenfred, he returned to his own place at Chartres, instructed with his companions in the disciplines of the Rule. He also brought with him twelve other monks, [Col. 0191D] whom he had preferred to choose from the community of the aforementioned monastery, so that he might have them as helpers against the ancient enemy, like very strong recruits in a new battle.

During the entire three-year period in which they were being trained in holy religion, therefore, the bishop built with assiduous labor dwellings for them and a cloister suitable for monks. When they had been received with great joy, and with the consent of the whole people, and when the aforementioned Alveus had been consecrated abbot, he generously provided them with food and everything necessary. He also withdrew from himself the churches and estates that his predecessors had wrongfully usurped, excluding every uncertainty and “bithalapso” [Note: [Col. 0192D] Read *bithalasso*.], and gladly restored them to the revived order for its support. He likewise willingly surrendered, in exchange for a great silver censer, a garden situated beside the monastery and the adjoining land, which bishops in former times had unjustly retained.

Since neither from Elias nor from the other bishops who succeeded him could he recover the lands without regard to any restitution, he assigned to the monks, for perpetual possession, twelve prebends in the greater church—lands that had been given to soldiers as fiefs [*casamentum*]. He struck with the throat of anathema anyone who might attempt by deceit to annul the gift of this donation or by any unlawful encroachment to diminish it.

Thus, by strengthening the monks who lived in complete peace, he never ceased to support them as long as he lived. He repeatedly exhorted them with fatherly admonition to persevere with firm step in holy religion; to root out the vices of the negligent with the hoe of correction; continually to instruct the good so that they might advance toward better things through unceasing praises; to teach the inexperienced and ignorant through the oracles of the Holy Scriptures; and to yearn with all their hearts for the joys of the heavenly homeland.

After his happy death, when he passed from the shipwreck of this fluctuating world to the heavenly homeland [Note: [Col. 0192D] The year 960.], his bodily remains were buried with due honor in the aforementioned monastery, before the altar of blessed Peter the Apostle, amid choirs of those singing psalms [Col. 0192C] and those mourning. At his left rests in the body Guantelmus, a venerable bishop, who by his personal intervention and by displaying the inner tunic of Mary, ever Virgin, drove away from the siege of the city the hated forces of the Normans.

Next comes Bishop Fulbertus [Note: [Col. 0192D] The year 1007.], worthy of remembrance; how great his wisdom was is conveyed to readers by his hagiographical writings, glowing with remarkable sweetness. On the right lies Bishop Theoderic, whose wealth of ambrosia flows like a torrent, fills the splendid fabric of the shrine of the Lord’s gracious Mother, and continually relieves the hunger and thirst of the poor, making him worthy of sacred praise [Note: [Col. 0192D] *Peredia*, eagerness to eat; *bibesia*, eagerness to drink, according to the interpretation of Dom Muley.] [Note: [Col. 0192D] So the manuscript reads, perhaps instead of *obviantes*, which would have the same meaning as “providing for.”].

X. Finally, after the death of the oft-mentioned Bishop Ragenfred [Col. 0192D], his brother Arduinus became bishop [Note: [Col. 0192D] The year 960.], possessing his position but not his religion. Inflated by the arrogance of pride, he pursued secular ambition beyond measure. Consequently, he came to hate the monks and considered whatever benefited them to be a great loss to himself.

For whatever the outstanding bishop had granted for the monks’ use, he lamented as though it had been stolen from him. He therefore burned with such greed that, of the twelve prebends which his brother had given, as we have said, he did not fear to extort and seize half. Several bishops who succeeded him followed the path of this sacrilege: wasting what was their own, desiring what belonged to others, harassing the monks with various pretexts, and presenting accusations and deceptions, they did not hesitate at all to take things away with sacrilegious audacity. The abundant charity of the faithful had bestowed very many gifts; although these bishops ought to have been their protectors, blinded in mind they became tyrants and plunderers.

XI. Among these I have taken care to record in this little work:

Robert of Tours, who, on account of a monk of the Greater Monastery who followed the sect of Berengarius, as we heard from truthful reporters, was unable to thrust him upon us in the abbot’s seat because we vigorously resisted and refuted him aloud. He caused the sacred altar of the apostles to be deprived, contrary to canon law, of the celebration of the mystery of Christ’s body and blood for three months and more. He also publicly declared, in profane language and breathing threats against all, that the monks—who were praying for the help of God and his mother—should be removed far from him. Despite the opposition of the legate of the Roman Church, he likewise forbade them the divine office and dared publicly to excommunicate them in the principal church.

Next there was Arrald, abbot of Braim, who possessed such great deceitfulness that, unless the charm of his speech obscured it, he would not merely have appeared to possess the character of deceit, but would himself have seemed to be deceit. It had such power in him that, through the blindness of flattery [Note: [Col. 0193D] D. Muley thinks *aurariae* should be read, which he interprets as “flattery.”], he very quickly deprived even the eyes of good men of the light of truth by his sacrilegious speech.

Thus, in a paltry period [*crocotillo*] [Note: [Col. 0193D] *Crocotillus*, according to Festus, means “thin, small.” *Crocotula* is a type of garment used by women; Plautus, *Epidicus* II.2.47.], he deprived the place of its abbot and expelled the better part of the monks. He unexpectedly made a former monk abbot and took forty times twenty pounds for himself. Had the unheard-of cruelty of death not soon brought his evils to an end, he would, true to his name, have scraped away everything inside and outside the monastery. For he used to say that gold, silver, and the precious ornaments of the church were fuel for the monks’ pride and incitements to wantonness.

He also said that it was a cruel deed for monks to eat fish or fat, allowing them [Col. 0193D] only bare vegetables to eat and urging them to persist as *xyrophagi*, without any accompaniment [Note: [Col. 0193D] For *xerophagi*, Greek Ξηροφάγους, that is, “those who eat dry or arid things.”]. Yet he ordered great fish and exotic foods to be served to himself, always keeping *gastrimargia*—gluttony [Note: [Col. 0194D] For *gastrimargia*, French *gourmandise*]—as a handmaid to his belly.

XII. But since I realize that, in the service of my writing, I have digressed from the path I began far more than enough, I wish to return. I confess that I did this because the matters I have woven in are in no way unrelated to our work and ought not to become burdensome to readers, especially since they have not always been illuminated but have been covered by the very dark cloak of oblivion.

Nevertheless, we have forged certain matters at the end of the work so recently that even childhood is not unaware of them. But because they acted upon us with such insolence and cruelty, and because it is known that we endured them somehow or other, I did not wish our successors to remain ignorant of them. Otherwise, when the evil of the times requires them to endure lesser or similar things, they might wish to bear them intolerably, keeping before their eyes the fact that we were once entangled in these evils for three years and more through the deceptions [Note: [Col. 0194D] So the manuscript reads; D. Muley thinks *offuciis* should be read, which he interprets as “tricks, deceptions, frauds.”] of certain people among us, and that afterward, through God’s gracious regard, we were freed and restored to prosperity.

Finally, leaping toward the conclusion in the manner of an epilogue, I have taken care to make known to the reader that the matters I am first about to write appear very different from present practice. For the rolls written by the ancients and now found in our archives do not show that the peasants of that time had, in matters of revenue, the customs that modern peasants are known to have today; nor do modern peasants have the names for things that vernacular speech then possessed.

Therefore, leaving behind the inner light of its proper subject, my mind is shaken by excessive dullness because it cannot determine for itself whether these usages belonged to the monks in ancient times or arose later, in the period of the clerics whom the venerable Bishop Hagano established in the restored place to serve almighty God. Whichever they belonged to, I leave it to readers to investigate, lest I be found by the most learned or wiser men to be a circumlocutor or a babbler [Col. 0194C] speaking foolishly.

**THE END.**

**ALSO.**

XIII. Since, in the epilogue written above, I remembered that I had written that this place had twice been entrusted to the service of canons, after it had been corrupted by the insatiable ambition of Elias, I therefore took as evidence a document of Bishop Aimericus, found in our archives, who is known to have lived long before the venerable Hagano.

From this document and from the writings of the outstanding Ragenfred, his successor, we have also learned that he completely restored the monastery, which had been destroyed to the ground by raiders from overseas, and handed it over to the canons with food and provisions for their support.

But because the gifts of the faithful, owing to the scarcity of written records at that time, were either not recorded or, if recorded, have through the negligence of the chief archivists been erased by excessive age, I have been unable to find among the ancient charters any other than this one. It indicates below that the place, deprived of royal dignity and stripped of its former condition, was handed over to the canons.

Thus begins the document of Bishop Aimericus [Note: [Col. 0194D] In Codex B, the same document of Aimericus, published in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, instruments, col. 287, is followed by these words: “I have placed the following document of the venerable Bishop Haimericus in the execution of this work so that the prudent reader may understand that, after the desolation of this place began under Bishop Elias, it was twice entrusted to clerics and an equal number of times to monks.” It proceeds as follows: “When the most Christian [Col. 0195C] …”]:

“Since the most Christian [Col. 0195A] and Catholic, most invincible emperor Augustus, with the aid of divine moderation, desired to raise the condition of the holy and universal Church to the dignity of a higher rank, lest it appear stained in any part of its character, by the shared resolve and assent of the magnates of his empire he issued an edict that all canonical cloisters existing within his kingdom should henceforth remain free from the obligation of tribute, so that, endowed with liberating freedom, they might through successive ages render to the Lord a more sincere service of divine worship.

His illustrious offspring as well, namely King Charles [Note: [Col. 0195D] Charles the Bald, son of Emperor Louis.], following his father’s example, ordered under the authority of his command that this should be observed perpetually.

I therefore, in the name of God, Aimericus, humble bishop of the Church of Chartres—not because of any preceding merits of service, but solely through the favor of divine mercy—mindful of the sacred constitution of the aforementioned princes, wish it to be known to all the faithful of holy Mary, the mother church, and to our own people, how a certain deacon and canon of ours, named Frotgingus, nobly brought up from infancy by that same church, came into our presence and humbly requested that we choose to draw up and confirm in our name a charter of security concerning a certain plot of land which a certain priest and canon of Saint Peter, named Winemarus, is known formerly to have sold to him as he went the way of all flesh [Note: [Col. 0195D] Here the superscript reads: “to have left behind.”].

With the consent of our canons and faithful, we judged this worthy to be done.

The plot itself lies in view of the city of Chartres, within the cloister of Saint Peter, toward the south. It measures thirty-six perches in length, with eight perches and one foot at one end, and seven perches and one foot at the other. On one side and one end it is bounded by the land of the brothers of Saint Peter; on the other side by a public road; and at one end by an exit [Note: [Col. 0195D] Perhaps read: “and at the other end, an exit.”] into the cloister.

Within these boundaries, we grant him the aforesaid plot, together with the vineyard that appears to be situated upon it, to hold perpetually by this charter. This is provided, however, that, in accordance with the decrees of the aforesaid princes, he may hold it without payment of tribute and serve the Lord in the worship of freer service; he shall pay no tribute whatsoever to anyone from it, except that which appears to belong to the service of divine worship.

Moreover, we grant him permission, without prejudice to pontifical right and in accordance with what is contained in the royal command, to have the power to grant or sell it to whomever he wishes among those serving the Lord in that canonry.

In order that this charter may retain inviolate and unshaken validity through the course of succeeding ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and decreed that it be strengthened by the hands of our canons.

Given successfully in the second year of the reign of King Odo [Note: [Col. 0195D] The year 889 or 890.]. Ingelgaldus, an unworthy priest, wrote this.”

I would have listed in silence the names of those who confirmed it, if I knew that this would provide any advantage to those now living or to those yet to come. But since I perceive in these names neither loss nor benefit, let the pen [Note: [Col. 0195D] Codex B: “the little pen.”] turn to the writings of Lord Hagano.

He restored the place, which had been destroyed by pagans, decently with the help of divine grace, and installed there a succession of clergy who would serve God. He assigned to it a small portion of the goods formerly belonging to the place, so that it might supply what was needed for bodily necessities and, with the concern for external affairs driven far away, the clergy might devote themselves to divine praises in free contemplation.

Therefore [Note: [Col. 0195D] Codex B: “Therefore I judged it fitting, at the end of this epilogue, to write out charters issued by the bishops—namely Hagano and Ragenfred—and by Gradulfus, abbot of Saint Caraunus, concerning the goods given, restored, and granted by them to Saint Peter while they were still serving as canons at the place. Next, I shall record the possessions held by them that I found written in two rolls, together with the customs they received from the cultivators, which differ greatly from the customs of our own time. I have not found the charters of these possessions, or the names of those who bestowed them. I do not know whether they were destroyed by age, burned by the fire of enemies, or never written down because of the scarcity of scribes.] we judged it fitting that a book compiled from the little parchments containing the gifts that he himself and other most devout men bestowed upon the place, up to the time when the venerable Ragenfred raised that same place to a more dignified condition and a more religious form of worship, should be called **The Book of Hagano**. In it the diligent reader will find nearly everything that appears to have been bestowed or granted by the faithful during the interval between those two outstanding bishops.

Let the work that follows be called **The Book of Ragenfred’s Hagiography**, because, through divine mercy, the place began under his care to advance in two ways; and because the foundation he laid, although it often suffers shipwreck amid the stormy sea of this world, will nevertheless remain victorious and unconquerable forever through patient endurance.

# BOOK ONE [Note: [Col. 0197C] Codex: “Here begins the Book of Hagano.”]  
## OR, THE BOOK OF BISHOP HAGANO  
*(From the year 931 to the year 954.)*

[Col. 0197]

## CHAPTER I. A document of Hagano concerning the enclosure of vineyards and concerning land restored not far from the monastery  
*(About the year 930.)*

[Col. 0197A]

### § 1

“[Note: [Col. 0197C] Charters previously published are distinguished by an asterisk. This document of Bishop Hagano concerning the rebuilt monastery of Saint Peter appears to be slightly earlier than the charter of the following chapter, chapter III, dated on the Nones of June in the year 931; it may therefore be assigned approximately to the year 930.] In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

The words of the divine books, full before and behind with eyes, teach each person carefully to avoid past evils and to look ahead more desirably toward good things. It is therefore very fitting that the prerogative of pontifical reverence, which is established upon the watchtower of the Lord, should, by watching more clearly, consider the ways of equity and direct the people entrusted to it to walk along them; should correct what has been corrupted, gather together what has been scattered on the day of cloud and darkness, restore what has been taken away, strengthen what has been broken, bring back what had been cast aside, [Col. 0197B] loosen oppressive bundles, and break every burden according to the rule of justice.

Moved, therefore, by these exhortations of divine admonition [Note: [Col. 0198C] The preceding material was still neglected by the editors in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, instruments, col. 288.], I, Hagano, Bishop of the Church of Chartres—not because of any existing merits, but solely through the Lord’s gratuitous goodness—felt compassion for a certain monastery of ours, almost entirely ruined and dedicated in honor of Saint Peter, which lies not far from that city. We ordered it to be rebuilt from its foundations and, according to canonical institution, to be served there by clerics of every rank who would practice holy religion.

In former times of peace that place flourished splendidly, with canons serving God and striving well in the exercises of good works. But when pagan attacks and other subsequent pressures came upon it, [Col. 0197C] we found it almost deserted.

Now, with God’s grace assisting us, we desire to renew its former religious practices, so that the praise of God may perpetually be celebrated there according to the authentic canonical rite, in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, to be observed in perpetual practice.

Meanwhile, there is a certain piece of land lying apart, belonging to Saint Peter and not far from that monastery, where there was formerly a vineyard enclosure under the direct lordship of the brothers of the same monastery. But one of our predecessors removed it from their sustenance and, through foolish greed, retained it under episcopal control.

It is bounded on one side by the public road leading to the monastery of Saint Martin; on another side by land belonging to the same estate; at one end by land belonging to the same estate and to Saint Piatus; and at the other by the road leading to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Peter.

I, therefore, Hagano, established as bishop, to whom the balance of judgment and equity has been divinely entrusted, together with the consent and entreaty of our faithful, give and justly restore this land of the enclosure under direct lordship, so that the aforementioned brothers of Saint Peter may safely have it, hold it freely, and perpetually possess it for their own support, without any accusation of repossession; and so that, secure in this grant, they may build, plant, and construct upon it with Christ’s help, without any disturbance opposing them.

We have likewise given, in another place, to those same canons, land near the city extending from the place where the land of Saint Anianus ends to the gate of the same monastery of Saint Peter, together with the ascent and descent of the valley. It is bounded on one side by the public road leading from the city to the aforementioned monastery. Thus, with no barrier obstructing them, they shall have free power, with Christ’s help and our permission, to build and develop it above, and to improve it in whatever way they can.

But if any of our successors, which God forbid, should be so unsound of mind as to attempt to remove anything from the gift of this donation [Note: [Col. 0198C] So the manuscript reads instead of *quidpiam*, “anything at all.”], as long as he persists in this intention, struck by the rod of anathema and separated from almighty God, let him be punished with the death of Ananias and Sapphira.

To make this charter remain more firmly established, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and delivered it for confirmation by the hands of both our clerics and our faithful.

Enacted at Chartres, publicly in the house of the mother church.

Aganus, humble bishop.  
Graulfus, subdeacon.  
Alcharius, priest.  
Ganzo, priest.  
Suggerius, canon.  
Lambertus, canon.  
Bernardus, priest.  
Giroardus, viscount.  
Aymo, Burchardus, laymen [Note: [Col. 0198C] Codex B omits what follows and inserts here a brief commemoration: “After his happy death, when he had been transferred by angels from the sea of this world to the company of the saints, his body was buried in the monastery of Saint Peter. In it rests in the body Guantelmus, a venerable bishop; and the venerable Bishop Ragenfred succeeded him. How greatly he loved the place can be recognized from the work that follows.”].

It seemed tedious to set down the others as well.”

### § 2

“But I judged it worthwhile to insert this: the land that the aforementioned Bishop Hagano gave now extends as far as the land of Saint Martin, enlarged by the gifts of the faithful [Col. 0199A] [Note: [Col. 0199D] So the manuscript reads; read *progreditur*, “advances.”].

The lands are divided by a certain road that descends from the royal highway and runs above our enclosure toward the village of Saint Martin, as far as the gate of our village. There the land of Saint Martin is enclosed on the right of those entering the village, extending as far as Guestraud’s well [Note: [Col. 0199D] Guestraud’s well (*Puteus Guestraudi*, so in the manuscript), French *le puits Guestrand*, was situated in the parish of Saint Brice, on the road called *rue des Basbourgs*. In Dom Muley’s time it was already enclosed by a fragment of stone.]. It continues, as the stones placed there indicate, as far as the Audura.

The land of Saint Peter crosses the river as far as the land of Saint Launomarus, which extends only to the public road; from that road the land of Saint Peter begins again, now filled with fruitful vineyards, and extends almost as far as the cross in the churchyard of Saint Bartholomew.

The venerable Bishop Ragenfred therefore wished to grant this land to Saint Peter as freely as possible for the monks’ support, so that no collector might cause the monks any disturbance by demanding tribute or a tithe from it. In it the bishop, together with his brother Arduinus, planted nearly thirteen *aripennis* of vineyard.

When Alveus became abbot, he and the other monks gradually planted the whole area, so that the vineyards appear to contain twenty-seven *aripennis* in all. The land is bounded from the cross we mentioned by the road descending to Morard’s gate; on another side by the land of Saint Launomarus, at which boundary it is enclosed in one place as far as the Audura. On the south it is enclosed by the vineyards of many people. On the eastern side it is bounded by two *aripennis* of vineyard that we gave [Col. 0199C] to two of our carpenters, together with other vineyards.

Now let the pen turn to the land of the Borough. It begins again at the road that runs from Audura to Morard’s gate, leaving at the fork the land of the sons of Belial [Note: [Col. 0200D] D. Muley explains that the author’s “land of the sons of Belial” was the place situated beyond Saint Hilary’s bridge, with the river and the road to Morard’s gate on the right and the road of La Grenouillère on the left.]. From that gate it extends as far as the crossroad leading to the back gate called Trievitulus [Note: [Col. 0200D] Hence the present name of the road, *Tireveau*.], and from there returns on the left as far as the Audura.

It crosses the river by the bridge of Mergentis Pediculus [Note: [Col. 0200D] Today, the Taillard bridge.], runs beside the river as far as the lane that leads from the river to the road of Merdosa [Note: [Col. 0200D] Later, the *rue aux Fumiers*.].

The road that begins at the aforementioned bridge and runs to the back gate of Fulcherius Nivelonis divides the land of Saint Peter from the land of Saint Anianus and Saint Piatus. For those going toward the market it lies on the right, while Saint Peter’s land lies on the left; it appears to extend from the Audura river as far as the road of Saint Michael, which leads to the monastery of Saint Martin. Where it ends need not be repeated [Col. 0200A] here, since it was stated above.

But let us go to the gate of Benedict the Locksmith and trace the land lying on the left of those entering the village, through the churchyard of Saint Hilary, along the public road leading to the Cinerosa gate [Note: [Col. 0200D] This gate, in French *porte Cendreuse*, near the Cross of the Beautiful Place, was formerly an entrance to the city.].

When one reaches the narrow road that descends from the projection and cemetery of Saint Anianus, beside the land of Saint Piatus, as we said above, the land of Saint Peter lies both above and below as far as the Audura. Within the city as well, from the gate called Aquaria [Note: [Col. 0200D] D. Muley likewise teaches that the Aquaria gate, long since destroyed, stood between the William and Morard gates.] to the Cinerosa gate, the land belongs to Saint Peter.

The ancient monks, and the canons after them, possessed by hereditary right all the land beside the wall, as the road divided it, running from one gate to the other. But after a tower was built in the city by the count who had been introduced there, he seized the tribute and other customary dues in the surrounding valley [Col. 0200B]. Nevertheless, for this very reason the count ordered one measure of wine to be given to the monks each year, on the western side, in the Field of the Smith, although they are negligent in possessing the vineyard.

Again, from the Cinerosa gate began the land of Saint Hilary of Poitiers, which occupied nearly a quarter of the city. It was bounded by the road running through the middle of the city to the tower.

A certain knight therefore possessed this land by a certain right; but, aflame with love of God, he granted it to Saint Peter, giving it on the condition that the monks build a church in honor of Saint Hilary in the churchyard of Saint Peter. This was indeed done.

But the land itself, which they received from the knight, was so held by them through the force of powerful men and their own weakness that scarcely a sixth part of the tribute is returned to them by the inhabitants [Col. 0200C].

The knight of whom we spoke also gave Saint Peter, from the same estate, a considerable extent of land at Manu Villare, where the monks built a second church in honor of Saint Hilary.

There is also land belonging to Saint Peter in many places around the city, both in the Borough and outside the Borough. On the western side there is half the land of Pendentis Pediculus, granted to Saint Peter in our own time in exchange for a certain knight who became a monk. It pays twelve coins on the feast of Saint Maurice, for it appears to belong to his estate.

Fulcherius, whose benefice it had been, received forty solidi in coin; Gungerius, who held it from him, also received thirty [Col. 0200D] solidi, with our consent. We receive twenty-one solidi from its cultivators on the feast of Saint Remigius. From the portion that is nothing but bare soil we receive only bundles of grain [Col. 0201A].

This land is bounded by two public roads, running on the right toward the wood—not merely by the road but also by large stones fixed into the ground by the monk Paul [Note: [Col. 0201D] He is the author of this work; see *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. VIII, p. 225.]. On the eastern side it is bounded by cultivated and uncultivated lands belonging to the estate of Saint Mary.

Next comes Manu Villare, most of whose land is divided by a certain road that appears to mark the boundary between the land of Saint Peter and that of Saint Maurice.

At one end it is bounded by the public road leading to the Perticana gate; at the other by the road leading to the gate of Saint John of Valais. On the eastern side it reaches the goldsmiths’ house; then, along the furrow of the vineyards, it runs transversely—not far from the church of Saint Hilary—to the public road of which we spoke above [Col. 0201B], and there ends not far from a certain winepress.

Likewise, thirty *aripennis* of vineyard at Luciacus follow. At one end they are bounded by the road running from the church of Luciacus to the church of Manu Villare; at another by the road leading to Seras; and at a third by the road that bounds Manu Villare and also bounds these vineyards. The side facing the city is bounded by other vineyards.

These vineyards were given by Bishop Ragenfred to the monks for planting, with every exaction from them removed.

To the south there is a certain church among the vineyards, built in honor of Saint Leobinus, which is known once to have been an abbey. A certain matron named Ermentrudis, wife of Nivelo, left this church to Saint Peter by vow when she died, for the sake of her soul, together with the lands and tithes belonging to it. She gave her necklaces and golden bracelets for his consent; the church was indeed part of her patrimony.

But when she had gone the way of all flesh, her husband, setting aside his wife’s request and forgetting his own promise, preferred to retain everything for his own use. As long as he was able to enjoy worldly possessions, he never repented.

When he saw himself being brought to his end, he wished to become a monk in the monastery of Saint Peter. What he had refused to do while healthy, he urged his sons to do through an empty request [Note: [Col. 0201D] Corrected to “his son.”].

After his death, his son Paganus enjoyed his father’s benefice for a short time. For while he was fighting the fortress called Fracta Vallis, which had been taken from his father by Gausfridus Martellus, he was killed by the enemy with swords at the very entrance of the fortress.

On his account his brother Fulcherius, already a cleric but girded with worldly arms, followed a secular military career. The venerable Abbot Landricus, recalling the mother’s vows and the father’s request, obtained from him the church of Saint Leobinus together with several *aripennis* of vineyard, from which we receive tribute and a tithe.

At that time he also remitted the tribute from the vineyards of blessed Siemundus, retaining only the tithe.

[Col. 0202A] We still have certain vineyards in the territory of the count, not far from the church mentioned above. They had formerly been given to someone as a benefice and were later, under pressure of poverty, sold to Countess Berta with our consent, on the condition that after the countess’s death the monks should recover them without any exaction, for their own support, without any delay. Her brother, Count Theobald, later acknowledged this before his faithful men.

Now let the pen turn to the northern side. There, above the ditch and not far from the Drocensis gate, the son of Gerald the merchant holds as a benefice land belonging to Saint Peter that yields ten solidi in coin.

In the village of Saint Andrew, Saint Peter possesses in direct lordship two solidi in coin from tribute, not far from the bridge that faces the gate of Ainboldus [Note: [Col. 0201D] We learn from D. Muley that the ancient gate called *la porte Ambaud* stood near Saint Andrew’s bridge, later called the Massacre bridge, between the Drocensis and William gates.]. Not far from that gate is Joliannus’s house with a vineyard that yields three solidi in coin.

How the Field of Faunus is bounded will be stated in its proper place. But now let us return to the matters indicated by the chapters.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning an *aripennus* of land given by the canons for planting a vineyard in the enclosure under direct lordship  
*(1 October 940.)*
“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. We, the canons of the monastery of Saint Peter, which is in the suburb of the city of Chartres, devoted to divine praises, wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, that a certain man named Theoderic came before us and humbly requested that we grant to him and to his wife, named Dominica, and to their daughter Geroisa, one arpent of land under a firm tenure for planting a vineyard there, in the brothers’ demesne enclosure, which had been withdrawn from their uses for many years but now, as in ancient times, has been justly restored; it lies near the church of Saint Michael.

“Considering his request valid, we kindly assented to and granted whatever the aforesaid Theoderic had asked of us: namely, to Theoderic, his wife Dominica, and their daughter Geroisa, the same arpent of land for planting and [Col. 0202D] constructing a vineyard there, with the consent and permission of Lord Aganus, the bishop who appears to have the governance of the same monastery. It is bounded on one side by the land of Saint Piatus and on the other by the land of Saint Peter; on one end by the public road leading to the monastery of Saint Martin; and on the other side and end by the land of that enclosure itself. We gave it to them under this condition: that every year, on the feast of Saint Peter, which falls on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, they should diligently pay one solidus as a census to the brothers. If they should thereafter be late or negligent in this census, they are to make legal amends, but in no way lose what they appear to hold. We also gave them permission to give or sell it, as might be convenient for them, to whomever they wished, provided only that the proceeds of the sale should come to the brothers’ uses.

“Moreover, so that this charter might be believed all the more truly and kept all the more firmly throughout all time, we asked that it be strengthened by the hand of the aforesaid senior, Lord Bishop Aganus, and we likewise confirmed it with our own hands.

“Aganus, humble bishop of the people of Chartres. Alveus, humble priest and chief keeper of the keys. John, priest. Majenfredus, priest. Airmandus, priest. Bernoardus, priest. Benedictus, priest. Odelricus, acolyte. Lambertus, acolyte. Galcherius, acolyte. Hardradus, cleric. Warengaudus, cleric.

“Given on the Kalends of October, in the fifth year of the reign of King Louis. [Col. 0203B] Aregarius, acting in the place of Clement, wrote this.”

I do not know how this matter afterward passed away. This, however, I do know: Lord Abbot Landricus, while he was presiding over the place of Saint Peter, bought this arpent of vineyard from a certain cleric named Albuinus, for an agreed sum of money. He also bought another arpent of vineyard farther down in the same enclosure from the priest of Saint Aignan, named Dominicus; the arpent of vineyard still retains his name.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the miller’s site at Lupchiacus, granted to two brothers. (5 June 931)

“In the name of the eternal God and of our Savior Jesus Christ. We, the brothers and canons of the monastery of Saint Peter, which is in the suburb of the city of Chartres, devoted to sacred [Col. 0203C] praises, wish it to be known to all the faithful of this monastery, present and future, that a certain man named Adremarus came before us and humbly begged that we grant, under a firm tenure and subject to a census, to himself, to his brother Ebbo, and to their sister Eldesind, a certain site beside the River Eure, with a mill newly built there by him, not far from the village called Lupchiacus, from our demesne.

“We unanimously gave our assent and kindly agreed; and by this authority we granted the same site, so that they might securely build upon it, construct, and strive to improve it; on the condition that every year, on the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter, which falls on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, they should promptly pay four solidi as a census to the canons of this monastery serving the Lord. If they should be found late or negligent in paying this census, they are to make legal amends, but not lose the aforesaid mill during their lifetimes. No further census is to be demanded from them beyond what is written above. They are also to have permission to sell or give it to whomever they wish, saving ecclesiastical right, as is the custom of the district or as is contained in the archive of this church.

“So that this firm grant may remain inviolate for long ages, we presented it for confirmation by the hands of our senior, Lord Bishop Aganus, and we likewise signed it beneath with willing hearts, no one objecting.

[Col. 0204A] “Done publicly in the city of Chartres, in the house of the mother church. Aganus, humble bishop of the people of Chartres. Sanson, priest. Aimo, dean. Deotimus, priest. Adelveus, priest. Frodgingus, priest. Cleotinus, priest. Aregarius, deacon. Arduinus, deacon. Ansoldus, subdeacon.

“Given on the Nones of June, in the eighth year of the reign of Rodulfus, most serene king. Ragenfredus, humble deacon, acting in the place of Clement the priest and chancellor, wrote this.”

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning Germinionis Villa, restored and granted to the canons by Bishop Ragenfredus; also, in the same place, the two adjoining estates of Plaiseni Villa and Moirollum Villare; likewise, in the same place, the church of Ursi Villare; in the same place, the church of Immonis Villa with eight holdings; in Ginnonis Villa, two holdings; the church of Bodasi and land within the city walls. (Around 954)

[Col. 0204B]

“The divine grace of God beneficially inspired the hearts of orthodox fathers and preceding faithful people, especially bishops, from the beginning of the Christian religion’s birth, so that they might found throughout the various regions of the earth the bride of Christ, namely the most holy Church, whom the same mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus, joined to himself with an unbreakable bond, and might strive to honor and exalt her with temporal goods.

“Therefore, although these pious examples ought to be undertaken and faithfully imitated in common by all Catholics and religious people, it is undoubtedly especially incumbent upon us, the stewards of that same holy mother Church, to provide with the most vigilant [Col. 0204C] care that, out of veneration for her bridegroom, namely the spotless Lamb, we adorn her with fitting honors and enlarge her resources with appropriate goods, according to our knowledge and ability.

“Instructed by such examples of the fathers and stirred by the teachings of the holy Scriptures, I, Ragenfredus, by the free mercy of the Lord humble bishop of the church of Chartres, desiring that the holy places belonging to our church and adjoining the city, which had been ruined by invading evils, should be rebuilt, first of all resolved to restore the monastery of Saint Peter to the state of its former honor, in which it had flourished in ancient times. It had been restored during the time of our predecessor, Lord Aganus, reverend bishop, at his command and through the many gifts he bestowed for carrying out that work, while Alveus, provost of the same place, took charge of everything. We also resolved to provide with temporal and stipendary goods the canons serving the Lord and his holy apostle Peter there, seeking to remove from them the poverty which they appeared to suffer in the necessities of daily sustenance.

“Therefore we wish it to be known to all our successors and to the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, how we hand over and grant to the canons of the aforesaid monastery a certain estate from our demesne, called Germinionis Villa, together with its two adjoining estates, namely Pleseni Villa and Moirollum Villare, with their boundaries, situated in the district of Dunois; and how we transfer it from our lordship into their possession, assigning it to their stipendary uses and decreeing that they shall hold it perpetually.

“We also grant them, for the same uses, in the same district and parish, the church of the village called Ursi Villaris, with its tithes and other revenues. In the district of Chartres we likewise grant them another church in the place called Ymonis Villa, with eight holdings of land.

“Again, in the same district, in Bodasi Villa, we restore to them a third church, which the aforesaid Alveus, provost of that monastery, holds, on this condition: that he hold it for as long as he lives, and after his death it return to their uses without opposition from any claimant or resister.

“In Ginnonis Villa, likewise in the district of Chartres, we grant them two holdings of land. Furthermore, in order to carry out this desire of ours, we wish to bring fully to the memory and knowledge of all our successors and the rest of Christ’s faithful that we restore to the aforesaid canons a certain piece of land which they repeatedly claimed for themselves, asserting that it had been possessed by their predecessors in ancient times and later taken from them unjustly, so that they may possess it justly and completely, just as the testimony of many confirms that their predecessors held it.

“That land lies within the walls of our city of Chartres, beside the Cinerosa Gate. On one side or end it is bounded by the public road leading to the aforesaid gate; on the other side it adjoins the city wall; and on its second end it is bounded by the land of the church of Saint Peter of Poitiers.

“All these things mentioned above, both the lands and the churches named above, with their tithes and other revenues, we grant and restore to the brothers of the aforesaid monastery, on this condition: that from this day forward no debt or service whatsoever be exacted from them there—whether in circuit duties, synods, censuses, or any kind of payment—and that no claim be made by any successor against these canons, who are devotedly to commemorate us and our successors in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, and to labor more freely in divine praises.
