“Moreover, so that the authority of this act of ours may in no way be violated by our successors or other persons, we forbid it in every manner, and we strive to place the barrier of anathema before any attempt to divide what has been gathered together, given, and restored by us.

“If, therefore, any rash plunderer and wicked violator of ecclesiastical sanctions should despise the provisions of this donation or restoration and attempt to annul them, may he be unable to vindicate what he has presumed to claim; but, condemned with Dathan and Abiron, may he perish in eternal damnation, and with the Devil and his angels endure forever the flames that avenge crimes.

“So that this page may be strengthened by the anchor of greater firmness, [Col. 0206A] we have signed it beneath with our own hand and have delivered it for confirmation by the hands of the venerable bishops and of the other faithful clerics.

“Hildemanus, archbishop of Sens. Joseph, archbishop of Tours. Constantius, bishop of Paris. Ragenfredus, bishop of Chartres.”  
[Note: [Col. 0205D] Compare this charter with another of the same Ragenfredus, col. 219.]

Finally, the land in Ymonis Villa that was given and restored by the aforesaid bishop, as we mentioned above, is not fully possessed by us; nor do we possess the city land on which the count’s tower and other buildings have been constructed. For it, the count, builder of the tower, gave the monks one measure of wine every year in the field of Fabri as a census.

But those possessing the vineyard are negligently insolent in making the payment, since there is no judge to pursue justice and restrain [Col. 0206B] the violence of the usurpers [Note: [Col. 0206D] Read: violence], nor anyone possessing the balance of equity to avenge the injury done to the holy Church. For the bishops are lulled by the sleep of sloth, swollen with the glue of pride, driven from the path of uprightness by the wind of flatterers; like mercenaries, they disregard the losses of the holy churches. As Pope Gregory says: “They flee the approaching wolf, not by changing their place but by withdrawing their support; of them it is said through the prophet: ‘Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who were unwilling to stand in opposition, nor set themselves as a wall for the house of the Lord.’”

By these and other means the holy Church, daily diminishing, is stripped of her honors, and there is neither king nor prince who sympathizes with her or who grants any relief from her sobs or daily tears. Therefore all the wicked, relying on impunity and envying the worshipers of God, obtain temporal profits for themselves from their losses; and, devising tricks colored by lies, they seize their goods and, through insatiable greed, devastate what they cannot take away.

But because it would be lengthy to recall all the evils that our church has suffered at Satan’s prompting, I shall add a very few from among the many: for example, the church of Baliolis Villa, which Bishop Radulfus, turning it from the monks’ lordship to his own uses along with other goods, offended by showing contempt for the blessed apostle Peter.

Agobertus also, bishop in our time [Note: [Col. 0206D] From the year 1052 to the year 1053], gave the canons his assent to usurping a considerable part of the land of the field of Faunus toward the east, which our predecessors without any claim, and we modern monks through long possession, had held.

Finally, Gauslinus of Leugis stubbornly retains for himself the census that ought to be paid to us each year from certain vineyards left to him by Bishop Hugh, not far from the River Eure.

Herveus of Gualardone has also usurped, not far from his residence, a certain piece of land belonging to our rights, said to be sufficient for one ox.

But leaving these matters aside for now, let the little pen turn to assigning the properties which by divine providence remain and will remain ours forever.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning twelve arpents of vineyards given to the canons by the venerable Bishop Ragenfredus. (13 June 949)

[Col. 0207A]

[Note: [Col. 0207D] The charter is published for the most part in Gallia Christiana, vol. VIII, instruments, col. 289.]

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. If, by the institution of the Creator of all things, human beings are born for labor, they must undoubtedly labor with the greatest effort at that by which they may attain a twofold benefit. Likewise, by prudent reasoning, one must reasonably devote oneself to both kinds of labor, so that through what one accomplishes by laboring one may obtain the name and reward of blessedness, nourishing oneself inwardly and outwardly; and it may rightly be said to such a person in the prophetic words: ‘You shall eat the labors of your hands. You are blessed, and it shall be well with you.’

“But even if, as labor advances, riches flow outwardly, one must not set one’s heart upon them, since in acquiring worldly goods anxiety must be removed and labor undertaken. Whoever therefore desires to be the true possessor of both kinds of good must not be bound by love of temporal goods, lest he appear not to become their master but their servant; for one bound by love of earthly things does not possess but is possessed. Nor should we give what we acquire temporally to our flesh, but rather to our soul, [Note: [Col. 0208D] So it reads, but afterward we find it corrected], since, as it is written, ‘the redemption of a man’s soul is his wealth.’

“Instructed by these and other teachings of the holy Scriptures, and kindled by the fire of heavenly love, I, Ragenfredus, humble bishop of the church of Saint Mary the Mother, wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, and also to our successors, how we hand over and grant for perpetual stipendary use to the canons of the monastery of Saint Peter, situated in the suburb of the city of Chartres, a certain vineyard enclosure planted and constructed by us at our own expense and labor, for the remedy of our soul and for obtaining from God the forgiveness of the sins of our parents.

“To confirm the cause of this donation, we deemed it fitting to have a charter made from the aforesaid vineyard for the said canons, with the consent and petition of Graulfus, who is seen to hold the abbey of Saint Caraun by the authority of our generosity.

“The vineyard itself lies near the cemetery of that same Saint Caraun, toward the northern side of that place. In all it contains twelve and a half arpents, each measured at fifty perches. It is bounded on two sides by land belonging to the same lordship and on its two ends by public roads.

“Within these boundaries we granted the aforesaid vineyard to them, at the repeated petition of Abbot Graulfus, so that they might build securely upon it and construct it well, and that they should have permission to sell or give the same vineyard to whomever they wished.

“We arranged this gift also with complete devotion of spirit so that, with earthly sustenance abundantly available to the aforesaid canons, they might more freely strive toward the heavenly [Note: [Col. 0208D] Read: toward the heavenly], and that in the aforesaid church of Peter, prince of the apostles, the duties of divine service might be more fully performed, while rewards of recompense might be returned to us a hundredfold in heaven.

“If any of our successors or any other person should presume to violate this page of donation, may he incur the wrath of God; may blessed Peter become his adversary, and may he be an enemy together with all the other apostles; may he not deserve to enter the sheepfold of the heavenly kingdom, whose keys he is known, by the Lord’s gift, to hold; may the rashness of the claimant be utterly frustrated; and may this present authority remain strengthened and inviolable.

“So that this page may possess the stronger force of firmness, we have signed it beneath with our own hands, [Col. 0208B] and have decreed that it be confirmed by the canons of our church, by the brothers of the aforesaid monastery, and by our other faithful.

“Ragenfredus, bishop of Chartres, made and confirmed this page of donation. Graulfus, abbot. Waracco, priest. Bernardus, priest. Ragenbaldus, priest. Arduinus, deacon. Alcarius, deacon. Aimericus, deacon. Malbertus, deacon. Ebroinus, deacon. Wido, deacon. Ardradus, priest. Isaac, priest. Ardradus, deacon. Lambertus, subdeacon. Gauslinus, subdeacon. Hunbertus, cleric. Heirveus, cleric. Dodo, cleric.

“Done in the city of Chartres, in the house of the mother church. Given on the Ides of June, in the thirteenth year of the fortunate reign of King Louis.”

## CHAPTER VI. Also concerning the same matter: the charter of Abbot Graulfus, for the monks already established in the monastery of Saint Peter. (Year 949)

[Col. 0208C]

“In the name of Christ. We, Graulfus, who appear to hold the abbey of Saint Caraun, which is in the suburb of Chartres, wish it to be known to all our successors and to the other faithful of Christ how we willingly grant to the monks of the same place certain vineyards planted by Bishop Ragenfredus and his brother Arduinus, as well as by Abbot Alveus, and donated and left to the monastery of Saint Peter, situated in the suburb of Chartres, with the consent of the faithful of Saint Mary, the mother church of Chartres.

“These vineyards are situated in three places. One enclosure consists of twelve and a half arpents, beside the monastery of Saint Caraun, which Ragenfredus and Arduinus gave; there are also four arpents and two parts of a fifth arpent, not far from the place called At the Cross of Saint Caraun.

“The aforesaid enclosure is bounded on two sides by the same lordship and on its two ends by public roads. The four arpents given by Alveus are bounded on one side by the same land, on the other by the land of the brothers of Saint Caraun, on one end by the road leading to the city, and on the other end by the land of Saint Martin.

“Those two parts of one arpent are bounded on one side by the land of Saint Mary, on the other by the lordship of the brothers of Saint Caraun, and on their two ends by public roads.

“Within these boundaries we grant the aforesaid vineyards to be held perpetually, so that they may build securely upon them and have permission to sell or give them to whomever they wish.

“So that this charter may be the firmer, we have confirmed it with our own hands and presented it for confirmation by the canons of Saint Mary and Saint Caraun.

“Done publicly at Chartres. Sign of Graulfus, abbot. Sugerius, dean. Arduinus, chief keeper of the keys. Marinus, priest. Alcarius, priest. Theodericus, priest. Algerius, priest. Josbertus, priest. Odbertus, priest. Leobinus, priest. Girardus, deacon. Evrardus, deacon. Adelardus, deacon.”

[Col. 0209B] [Note: The matters enclosed in brackets are found only in codex B.] Finally, the properties which I found written down and which appeared to belong to the canons, and afterward the properties assigned to the church’s lights and to the sustenance of the doorkeeper, as well as those later added by the bishops, namely Aganus and Ragenfredus, the monks now possess none of them.

For I found certain places written down whose names are now so obliterated and unknown that they are entirely ignored by human beings, much less possessed. Some are known but nevertheless not held, such as the land of Odulfus at Verno, which Bishop Ragenfredus promised would be held after Odulfus’s death; and Gundrevilla with its copse and meadows, of which they appear to be deprived; and Imonis Villa, where eight holdings were given but are not possessed at all.

There are also properties that are possessed and have been possessed from ancient times, but whose written record has perished, such as Bosco Medio in the district of Dunois, and the land of Saint Peter of Poitiers that lies within the city of Chartres. A certain knight possessed it under some right and granted it to Saint Peter of Chartres on the condition that they build in the atrium of Saint Peter a church in honor of Saint Hilary. This was done, but through the force of powerful men and knights living there, the census from that land is withheld, so that scarcely a sixth part is paid.

The aforesaid knight also gave Saint Peter, from that lordship, a large expanse of land at Manu Villare, for which the monks built a second church in honor of Saint Hilary.

Now that the charters and properties of the canons have been completed, we must turn to the charters and properties of the restored order, namely the monks who were reformed in the monastery of Saint Peter under the venerable Bishop Ragenfredus.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the properties of the brothers of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres

### 1. Concerning the vineyards beside the bishop’s vineyard

In ancient times, since the use of vineyards was rare at Chartres, the brothers had only three arpents of vineyard beside the bishop’s vineyard, given to them by a certain man named Bernoinus.  
[Note: [Col. 0209D] Codex B adds: “If I had found a charter concerning them, I would not have been reluctant to write it down.”]

### 2. Concerning four mills

They had four mills, [Col. 0210A] whose keeper paid the brothers every year, for the two better mills, one hundred measures of mixed grain, two of wheat and twelve of oats for making beer; one hundred eels, four fat pigs, six hens with eggs, and twice each month two eulogies. The other two mills ground the brothers’ provisions and supplied wood for baking bread.

### 3. Concerning Bodasi Villa

In Bodasi Villa there was a demesne house with a granary and garden, enclosed in modern times by the monk Ursone with a new wall. Beside it, toward the east, was a vineyard enclosure containing five arpents. There was also a church of the blessed martyr Lawrence, built of stone and cement.

The same estate, in four separate locations, had fifteen bonuaria of land and five cultivators: Teogrinus, Ragenbaldus, Frodoardus, Teotradus, and Riculfus. Each performed two perches of plowing for the winter crop, one and a half perches for the spring crop, and the same amount in corvée labor. For that plowing each gave two measures of wheat; for the army expedition, one solidus; he performed fifteen days of caplim [uncertain term], and carting labor, manual work being imposed upon him.

He paid one measure of the required oats and three chickens with eggs. Riculfus alone gave four measures of wheat for plowing [Note: [Col. 0210D] Later superscribed: one measure of plowing] and corvée labor, two solidi for the army expedition, six chickens, and two measures of the required oats; he performed caplim. There was also one and a half holdings there, free from obligations.

### 4. Concerning Domani Villa and Moris Villa, which appear to lie beside Bodasi

In Domani Villa there was one [Col. 0210C] holding, which Frogaudus held at that time. He performed four perches of winter plowing and the same amount in corvée labor. For that plowing he gave four measures of wheat; for the army expedition, four solidi; eight denarii for the sheep tax; for pasturing, one measure of wheat and one measure of barley; and two cartloads of wood.

He enclosed the court or supplied one perch of ditching. He performed manual labor; he paid 220 scintuli [uncertain term], three clothed chickens [Note: [Col. 0210D] A “clothed chicken” seems to be one to which, although Du Cange is silent here, eggs—usually five in number—are added], one measure of the required oats, and performed caplim; he rendered vineyard service of half a cartload.

In Moris Villa the cultivators Balduinus, Vintharius, Areharius, Fulcherius, and Adalgrimus rendered payments in the same manner.

### 5. Concerning Cavannis

In Cavannis Villa these were the cultivators: Teotradus, Winebertus, Amalbertus, Godulbertus, Archenarius, Godefredus, Beneventus, Madalgaudus, [Col. 0210D] Beraldus, Hildeboldus, Sadrius, Petrus, Guaningus, Raduinus, Adalcarius, Ricbrannus, Odoenus, Electeus, Ingeraldus, Bernardus, and Guinebertus. They all paid like the others written above.

### 6. Concerning Cipedo

In Cipedo the cultivators were Adelardus, Erchenarius, Petrus, Agifredus, Guineboldus, Angenbertus, Gandremarus, Bernegarius, Goduirleus, and Huncbertus. They paid like those written above.

In modern times this estate was transferred by the monk Ursone to the place called Nova Villa, because the vicariate oppressed it severely. It lies not far from Bodasi Villa, toward the east.

### 7. Concerning Comonis Villa

In Comonis Villa, Albuinus, who held five bonuaria of land, paid three measures of wheat and the other customary dues, as stated above. Rainaldus paid the same. Adalveus held six bonuaria of land and gave four measures of wheat [Note: [Col. 0211D] The codex reads: “gave four measures of wheat, four measures of wheat”] and the other customary dues. Gindbertus did likewise.

### 8. Concerning Moenis Villa

In Moenis Villa lived three people: Erembertus, Benedictus, and Amaltrudis. They paid two measures of wheat and the remainder as above.

### 9. Concerning Abbonis Villa

In Abbonis Villa there was a demesne barn; in various places there were fifteen bonuaria of land. I do not know what bonuaria are, but, as I learned in this estate, there are nine plowlands of land.

I am also surprised that, in a manner differing from those written above, the cultivators of this estate numbered thirty-three in rendering revenues: Bertegaudus, Leobinus, Garnuinus, Godulgarius with Dado, Rainaldus, Leotardus, Radfulsus, Johannes, Sigaldus, Godobaldus, Gualterius, Rainarius, Adalmarus, Electrudis, Gaurembertus, Guido, Christianus, Adoardus, Remedius, Guillelmus, and Watraldus. Each paid one solidus.

Municarius paid three solidi; Agedardus and Radoardus paid one and a half solidi. Godoardus likewise. Benedictus paid two solidi; Raincarius and Benedictus eight denarii; Godovertus one solidus and four denarii; Goduinus eight denarii; Natalis, Aloinus, and Raduinus six denarii.

The tithe of this estate is ours, although they go to another church, since they have no church of their own.

### 10. Concerning Ahildulfi Villa

In Ahildulfi Villa, whose location I do not know, the countrymen were Teodoaldus, Municharius, Adalgaudus, and Adalguinus, each of whom paid one solidus; Frodegis paid two solidi.

All these held three bonuaria of land and performed six days of corvée labor in the grain fields. They gave three chickens with eggs, half a measure of the required oats, and one denarius.

In the place called Absa there were only three hospitia [lodgings or holdings]. I know nothing at all of this place; but, since I find it written down, I have no doubt that it existed.

### 11. Concerning Buxetum

In this place, which we now lack and whose location I also do not know, there was a woodland belonging to the brothers for fattening five hundred pigs. Of demesne land there were three bonuaria of meadow between two locations, from which three cartloads of hay were supplied.

The cultivators were Teodardus, Bernardus, Teodbaldus, Mammenus, and Adalgis. They performed three perches of winter plowing, the same amount for the spring crop, and corvée labor. They paid one solidus and one denarius, caplim every year, one cartload and carting labor, and three chickens with eggs.

Rada paid one solidus; Teotardus four denarii; Leotrannus the same. For winter plowing, one and a half solidi. At Mount Cenose there were two holdings of arable land.

### 12.

All these properties that I have set forth, and many other places, were possessed and held by the ancient monks; but concerning those whose written record has perished or which negligence has consigned to oblivion, I thought it worthless to write. Only those about which the sequence of documents made me certain, or which have always been possessed by substitute clerics, have I endeavored, according to the modest measure of my limited intellect, to insert into these pages, lest perhaps the reader should judge that this place had once been poor in revenue, through a deceptive opinion.

Finally, the place called Bosco Medio, bounded on its northern side by a considerable woodland and on its southern side by the stream of the Eure, is said always to have been held by those known to have possessed it.

They also held in the district of Vexin one-third of Genet Villa, which the most holy queen named Balthildis divided into three parts and bestowed one part upon this church of the blessed apostle Peter, prince of the apostles, for the glory of attaining eternal life; another she assigned to the use of the brothers of the venerable church of Gemmeticum, dedicated to the Mother of the Lord; and the third to the basilica of the blessed Remigius, archbishop of Rheims.

The portion given to Saint Peter is known to have been granted under a firm tenure by Abbot Guibertus, once imprudently, to a certain knight and his two heirs. From it, five solidi of money were customarily paid each year.

But after those people had departed from this world, a certain noblewoman of their family named Addela, relying upon force and power, did not fear to hold it by violence until old age, until, bound by a long sentence of excommunication and fearing the fire of Gehenna, she restored it to blessed Peter with the charter, with all her kindred consenting.

After the church had possessed it by hereditary right for nearly five years, a certain knight named Gaubertus [Note: [Col. 0211] After “Gaubertus named,” codex B adds: “of Calidus Mons”], who had as his niece the aforesaid noblewoman, took it away from the use of the servants of God and did not fear to enslave it with impunity for his own uses.

Not only this, but many other properties passed from our uses into the uses of others: for example, Gundre Villa with its eight holdings, its copse, meadows, and all its appurtenances. A certain abbot of this place gave it as an increase to a boy whom he had taken from the sacred font; his descendants appear to hold it to this day, despite the brothers.

Finally, in Normandy, beside the sea, Count Robert took Tedis Villa from Saint Peter and gave it to a certain knight.

Many other properties were taken from us in that same region, both churches [Col. 0212D] and fisheries, which the renowned Count Richard gave away. He royally exalted the church of the Holy Trinity and regularly established the monastery of Saint Michael on the Peril of the Sea, providing the necessary expenses. His goodness, acquiring praise forever, happily obtained the glory of eternal life with all the saints.

## CHAPTER VIII. The properties of the doorkeeper of Saint Peter follow

### 1. Concerning the mill near the city

A mill belonging to the doorkeeper of this church, near the city, paid every year, according to the larger measure, thirty measures of grain, one measure of wheat, thirty eels, one pig or five solidi in place of the pig; every month, two fogatiae [uncertain term] and a sextary of wine; and three chickens with eggs.

### 2. Concerning Giaco

There was a small meadow from which two cartloads of hay were gathered. The four cultivators—Elisardus, Acculfus, Gualbertus, and Salomon—paid five solidi with eulogies at the mass of Saint Peter, performed fifteen days during harvest time, supplied fifteen sextaries of the required oats, and paid five denarii.

### 3. Concerning Cortrone

The inhabitants of this place were Walterius, Aclardus, and Aclulfus. They paid four solidi and eight denarii as a census.

Each of them, during harvest time, performed twelve days or redeemed them for six denarii; he paid four chickens with eggs and gave the required amount—four denarii.  
[Note: [Col. 0213] Codex B: “the required oats and four denarii”; and likewise below.]

[Col. 0213B]

### 4. Concerning Gereni Villare

There were, according to estimation, thirty bonuaria of land in the demesne, beside four bonuaria of woodland. The cultivators Adelulfus, Godeneus, and Hernes paid two solidi as a census.

Each gave four clothed chickens per hearth; he gave one measure of the required oats, according to the market measure, and two denarii.

### 5. Concerning Tilidum

Quintinus and Adalbertus, living there, paid four solidi as a census. Each of them paid two clothed chickens, gave half a measure of the required oats according to the market measure, and four denarii.

### 6. Concerning Pincionis Villa

Adrevertus, living there, paid two solidi as a census and gave the required due and two denarii.

[Col. 0213C]

### 7. Concerning Monticelli

One mill paid fifteen solidi every year. Gislarius and Guauzelmus paid three solidi as a census. A certain little vineyard held by Hildegildis paid one solidus.

### 8. Concerning Haireni Villa

The cultivators Electeus and Ercatringa paid two solidi and two denarii as a census, and two chickens with eggs.

### 9. Concerning Seresii Villa

There was arable land there from which eight denarii issued.

### 10. Concerning the land at Berqvu

[Note: [Col. 0213D] So written.]

From the land in the same place two denarii issued.

### 11. Concerning the land at Duabus Casis

There is arable land there from which six denarii issued.

12. **Wadriacum.** There was there a *mansus* that paid five solidi in rent. Concerning this *mansus*, the canons of the same church claimed that their fellow canon Wenilo had left it to them at his death for the salvation of his soul. There is also there one small *mansus* that paid one solidus.

13. **Cintriacum.** There was there arable land paying eight denarii.

14. **Felcherola Villa.** There was there one *mansus* which a certain man named Lanto gave to Saint Peter; from it his son Hermarus paid two solidi annually as rent.

15. **Mitanis Villare.** The church of Saint Mary Magdalene, founded there in her honor, belonged there for the lighting of the church of Saint Peter, and the priest of that church paid three solidi each year. In the same estate Capitiarius held two *bonuaria* of arable land.  
[Col. 0214A]

16. **Walardone.** Beside the same estate is land belonging to Saint Peter, which used to yield one solidus. But now Herveus, lord of that place, trusting in his own strength and setting aside the fear of God, is unwilling to pay either the customary solidus or any customary due.

17. **Nidus Corbinus.** From a certain piece of arable land there came eight denarii for the church lighting and four denarii for the work of the brothers.

18. **Joiri Villa.** There was there one small *mansus*, held by Adalbert, which paid three solidi; the brothers claimed it, just as they did the one at Wadriacum.  
[Col. 0214B]

19. **The benefice of the canon Winemarus.** The benefice which Winemarus, while alive, held as a canon and at his death left to Saint Peter for the preparation of the church lights had been granted at that time. From this benefice, beside Saint Peter’s atrium, there were seven plots, paying seven solidi. It would have been laborious to add the names of their inhabitants to the page, especially since it would have served no useful purpose, nor could sons or grandsons have been identified by their names.

Beside the lord’s fishpond, from the same benefice, there were two and a half *aripennia* of vineyard, with a small meadow adjoining them, from which five solidi used to be yielded. From the same benefice, before the brothers’ gate, above the River Audura, there was one *aripennis*  
[Col. 0214C] paying one solidus. In another place, belonging to the lighting of the altar itself, there were two *aripennia* of excellent vineyard.

20. **The head-tax payers.** All those listed below paid four denarii each from their own persons: Banegildis, Ansgundis, Christianus, Flodegarius, Saxenildis, Rainburgis, Laubertus, Godenildis, Dominica, Frotlandus, Acchildis, Isentrudis, Berta, Bertranna, Bertingus, Dominicus, Ermenaldus and his sister, Widlegis, Aintrudis, Dominicus, Agenardus, Wandalgis, Lambertus, Leodoardus, Anstrudis, Landrada, Anstrudis, Bracca, and Savera.

21. What I have taken care to weave into these new pages up to this point  
[Col. 0214D] I received from the exceedingly ancient charters of the canons of this place. In them I also found the usufruct due each year from the peasants to the clergy, and I wished to consign it to the knowledge of posterity, so that a prudent reader might observe that, if its quality or quantity differs from the practice of the present time, the land, already weary with age, is growing numb: while returning, all too often, the seeds entrusted to it with a sparing hand, it deceives those who reap by frustrating them with empty hope.

I also preferred to record the estates and rural properties which, according to written evidence, the canons themselves have always been seen to possess, so that I might silence the tongues of those who babble.  
[Col. 0215A] Some of them assert in mad voices that Bodas Villa and its dependencies came from episcopal donations; others likewise claim that they came from the largesse of counts. But they are mistaken. For almost all the bishops, following Helias—who, with reckless boldness and insatiable madness, was the first to seize this place and, without regard for goodness, having expelled religion, strip it bare—suffered from the same disease; and, except for a few, with blind intention they turned to their own uses whatever they could.

Among them the munificent bishop Gislevertus shone forth. Seeing that in the oft-mentioned monastery of Saint Peter there was only a small number of monks, who, from the meager resources left to them by Helias and ravaged by the frequent attacks of pagans, could scarcely satisfy the necessities of nature, he wisely strove to dispel, or at least in some measure alleviate, their poverty. He transferred to them the properties listed below, so that they might serve the Lord more willingly  
[Col. 0215B] and become more devoted.

For the treasury of that place and for the lighting of its church, as I found in a charter written by him, he assigned one *mansus* near the monastery in the same village; two *mansi* at Maslaicum; three *mansi* at Calnacum; three *aripennia* of vineyard at Campiniacum; and, beside the church, two-thirds of an *aripennis* of vineyard. Likewise, in other places, ten *aripennia* of vineyard and arable land. But since they have long been abandoned by cultivation and are known to be deserted by human beings, we judged it pointless to record their names in writing.

For the annual observance of the anniversary of certain of his relatives: two *mansi* at Maslacum and, in other places, eight *aripennia* of vineyard.

For the chamber: four and a half *mansi* in a certain place; one and a half *mansi* at Paridum; two *mansi* in another place; one *mansus* at Planca; at Campiniacum, one *aripennis* of vineyard and one vineyard beside the wall.

For the house of the sick: one *mansus* in the village and one mill; at Campiniacum, one *aripennis* of vineyard; in another place, four *aripennia* of vineyard; and three small guesthouses above Aurosa.

For the hospital: one *mansus* at Saliniacum; at Guarenna, one *aripennis* of vineyard and fifteen *anzingae* of arable land; at Gerilla, whatever he possessed.

For the cellar: three and a half *aripennia* of vineyard.

For the garden: half a *mansus*.

At Maslacum: one small guesthouse.

At the end of the charter, the following was written: “These things,” he said, “apart from those which they already had, we have granted to the brothers who asked for assistance. And so that they might possess them more securely in our own time and in that of our successors, we have confirmed them with our own subscription; and, entreating our brothers and fellow bishops to deign to do the same, we readily persuaded them to provide the same benefit. We beseech all our successors that what has been done kindly by us may also be preserved by their goodwill, so that in the divine recompense they may become participants in our generosity.”

We have omitted from the document the name of the archbishop of Sens, which had been worn away by age.

“Gislebertus, humble bishop of the Carnutes, have subscribed this decree made by us. Hildegarius, bishop of the church of Meaux. Aeneas, bishop of Paris. Folchichus, unworthy bishop of Troyes. Cristianus, unworthy bishop of Auxerre, *egrapsi* [Greek: ἔγραψα, ‘I wrote’].”  
[Note: Instead of *ἔγραψα*. On the distinctive mark of this Greek-writing bishop, see Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, book VI, plate 57.]

“Aius, bishop of Orléans. In the name of God, I, Lupus, abbot of the monastery of Ferrières.”  
[Note: From the period in which the subscribers lived, the charter appears to belong approximately to the year 860.]

This charter was written at the end of the book because it was found only late, on a little document used as a cover.  
[Col. 0216B]

22. Finally, after the death of Bishop Gislevertus, pagans from overseas came with a great fleet and devastated almost the whole of Europe with fire, plunder, and the sword’s cruelty. For, as I have already written at length above, after capturing the city of Luna by deceit, they slaughtered both sexes with the bloody sword. Then, having overturned the city, raising their sail and with the African wind blowing, they returned and ravaged with plunder and unjust slaughter the region of Aquitaine and the coastal territory adjoining Poitou. Sailing into the regions of Neustria, they put in at the harbor of the River Dives.

Then, feeling secure, they left their ships and the various spoils of their plundering there and reached this city at a swift pace. Finally, at night, after surrounding the city and unexpectedly besieging its citizens, the barbarians burst in through the walls, which had often been destroyed by enemies, and through the gates. They killed with the sword everyone who met them, without distinction. Within the mother church they slaughtered with bloody swords, like sheep, a considerable number of the populace together with their bishop, named Frodboldus, as well as the church’s canons and the monks who had taken refuge in that church.

After plundering and burning the city, they rejoiced and exulted as though they had attained the object of their desire, thinking that they would return with great forces to the ships they had left behind. But, through the intervention of blessed Mary, Mother of God—whose displeasure they had thought little of offending—they descended in a single day, by a deserved death, through the mouth of the gatekeeper of hell into the pit of mercilessness. For before the Franks could reach their ships, they engaged them in battle; and, with God’s help, winning victory over them, they left their slaughtered bodies scattered across the fields to be gnawed by birds and beasts.

[Note: Codex B gives a fuller account of this victory of the Franks: “For the Franks, gathering from every direction, engaged them before the barbarians could reach the ships they had left behind. Under God’s protection, they won victory over them and, as is still evident today, left their slaughtered bodies scattered across the fields to be gnawed by birds and beasts. Finally, the people who were able to escape the barbarians’ sword returned to the burned city, gathered the ashes of those who had been cremated, and threw them into a certain well situated within the church itself. For this reason the citizens still call that well the Strong Place, where, through the cooperation of God, many miracles continually occur on behalf of those whose ashes await resurrection with Christ and reign with him in heaven.”]  
[Col. 0216D]

23. [Note: This digression concerning Rollo, which we have enclosed in brackets, is found only in Codex B, which is later than Codex A.] I considered it worthwhile to insert into this account the siege that took place in the time of Bishop Gancelinus, both because of the recency of the event and because of the memorable miracle that the Lord Jesus Christ deigned to perform during it through the intervention of his mother, the blessed Virgin Mary.

For overseas pagans, commanded by a leader named Rollo, crossed the sea and, invading a great part of the territory of Neustria by force of arms, had already seized seven cities; from their name the same land received its designation. They are called Normans from the blowing of the north wind.  
[Note: Instead of *northi*, meaning “the north.”]  
From this name the land is called Normandy.

Thus, burning with insatiable avarice, they sailed along the River Seine and sought to seize the city of Paris. When they saw that, through a prolonged siege and the exercise of arms, they were laboring in vain, they turned the prows of their ships back and abandoned the siege. Then they directed all the ambition of their hearts toward the city of Chartres.

Rowing along the Seine toward it, they landed at Givaldus’s ditch. There they left their ships and came swiftly to the city, surrounding it with a siege on every side. But the aforesaid bishop, learning by divine revelation that the siege was approaching, sent word to the count of Poitou to come to his aid, as well as to the duke of Burgundy and two very powerful counts of France. On the day appointed by the bishop, they arrived prepared, with a very large army, to bring aid to the Christian people.

When the pagans, confident in their strength and weapons, pressed on fiercely and hastened to capture the city, the bishop, on the day when he knew that the aforementioned counts were coming to his aid, ordered all his men, very early in the morning, to arm themselves and go to the gates.

He then drew the inner garment of the Mother of God, Mary, across the gate called the New Gate, displayed it before the eyes of the pagans, opened the city gates, and ordered the Christians to fight boldly.

Then the Christians, receiving strength from almighty God, fought bravely. But the pagans, abandoned by God and deprived of the strength of all their limbs, were slaughtered on one side by the citizens and on the other side were felled like hay in the fields by the army that arrived. So great was the slaughter that the river’s water was blocked by the corpses of the dead, and all of them alike would have been struck down by the avenging sword on that very day, had not the last survivors, together with their leader, been able to escape death by the protection of flight.

Thus it happened that, when evening had come, they reached the mountain of Leugara. There they encamped and fortified themselves on every side with animal hides.  
[Note: Codex A reads *animalium*.]

But the Christians followed them and surrounded the mountain, intending to attack them as they fled on the following day. [Note: Thus the manuscript, for *quod* (“which”), apparently incorrectly even in this very low Latin style.] When the pagans saw this, they were terrified and contrived a way to save themselves from the danger of death. Finally, they chose three very brave men to leave the camp secretly and, at a distance from the camp, sound trumpets.

When they had gone away and were sounding the trumpets, the Christians heard them and feared that the pagans’ allies might be coming to their assistance. They then gathered together on one side and awaited the outcome.

But when the pagans saw an opportunity for escape, they gradually and silently left the camp, abandoning all their baggage. At a swift pace they returned to their ships and from there to their own country. Remembering their disgrace and defeat, they never again attempted to return to the city of Chartres.

Leaving these matters aside, let the little pen turn to the writings of Bishop Aganus, who, with the assistance of divine Grace, restoring suitably the place destroyed by the pagans, installed there a body of clergy to serve God. He assigned a small portion of the properties formerly belonging to the place, so that it might provide supplements for the needs of the body and, with concern for external matters driven far away, the clergy might devote themselves freely to divine praises.

Therefore I considered it fitting, at the end of this epilogue, to write out the charters issued by the bishops Aganus and Ragenfredus, and by Gradulfus, abbot of Saint Caraunus, concerning the properties which they gave, restored, or granted to Saint Peter while they were still serving the place as canons.

After that, I record the properties possessed by them which I found written in two rolls, as well as the customary payments they received from the peasants, which differ greatly from the customs of our own time. As for the charters of those properties, or the names of those who donated them, I found none at all. Whether they were destroyed by age, burned in the fires of enemies, or never written down because of a shortage of scribes, I do not know.

**Here ends the Book of Bishop Haganus.**

# BOOK TWO, OR OF BISHOP RAGENFREDUS  
*(From the year 954 to the year 960.)*

[Col. 0219]

## HERE BEGINS THE PREFACE OF THE BOOK OF RAGENFREDUS

[Col. 0219A]

In the following little work, I seem to see that it is sufficient merely to write down separately the writings of each of the bishops and abbots, so that a prudent investigator may easily recognize, by reading, by what stages this place gradually grew and with what diligence each of them labored for its interests.

If anyone finds that the things which, in the earlier work of Bishop Ragenfredus, were given or granted without chapter headings have been repeated here, this has been done because in the first work those same things were written chapter by chapter as having been given or granted once more by that bishop to the canons.

**HERE ENDS THE PREFACE OF THE BOOK OF RAGENFREDUS.**

[Col. 0219B]

**[Concerning the properties which Bishop Ragenfredus gave or restored to Saint Peter.]** *(Around the year 954.)*  
[Note: This charter is published, though not without omission, in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, instruments, cols. 289–291.]

*“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Ragenfredus, bishop raised to the holy see of Chartres, though no merits are present to warrant it. Whenever the examples of our preceding fathers are brought before us, they are incentives to virtue for sound minds, instruction in a better life, and unhindered progress along the way of God’s commandments.

Since many divine things are beyond the capacity of reason and wonder, contemplative thoughts sometimes arise. Therefore I, Ragenfredus, called bishop, when I had for a little while freed my mind from the tumult of secular affairs, in which I am held entangled more by necessity than by choice, gathered my whole self within myself and began to contemplate with wonder the benefits of divine mercy toward the salvation of the human race: how he heals those whom he loves by wounding them with his healing right hand, and, striking them with fatherly affection, supplies the prosperity of salvation and health.

Although the greatness of his clemency graciously extends itself throughout all the lands, it seemed to me that he judged the diocese of our see worthy of his love above the others. For, because of the burden of the sins of his children, he subjected it to the blows of corrective discipline, permitting a savage people to rage throughout it in slaughter, fires, and devastation without restraint.

No honor was shown to the holy places, as voracious flame licked them all indiscriminately; no dignity, age, or sex received the relief of mercy, as the sword of most impious cruelty mowed everything down. At that time all the properties of this bishopric were destroyed by fire, the monasteries consumed, and almost all the churches demolished down to their foundations.  
[Note: Thus in both manuscripts; but *funde tenus* should be read, “down to the foundations.”]

Whatever escaped their hands nevertheless suffered the losses of domestic oppression, whether from private persons or from the powerful.

At last, the heavenly mercy looking down from on high, grieved over the tears of the afflicted and the lamenting complaints of the wretched. As the heavens let fall the dew of mercy upon the city, almost crushed by the siege, divine assistance granted relief; after the most powerful oppression of those wars, it allowed the joys of the long-desired peace to smile upon us.

Meanwhile, not long afterward, Aganus, an illustrious man, having obtained the episcopate of this eminent church, strove to direct the whole purpose of his mind toward rebuilding monasteries and reconstructing churches.

“There was in the suburb of the aforementioned city of Chartres a monastery famous from ancient times, dedicated in honor of the chief of the apostles and accustomed to regular discipline. But after the devastation described above, it had been neglected and had scarcely been converted into a canonical institution within a small church. In our time the venerable man Alveus presided over it, although under the outward form of a canon. A lover and cultivator of religion, he often began discussing with the aforesaid bishop how he might bring to completion in action what he had resolved in his mind.

With the assent of heavenly Grace and the favorable support and encouragement of the bishop, he achieved the fulfillment of his desire. Having prepared the necessary expenses, he laid the foundations of a considerable building; and, as time progressed, he placed upon them a large basilica of elaborate beauty, as can easily be seen at the present time. Immediately afterward, by episcopal authority, he assigned the services of canons there.

When these matters had taken place and the bishop had reached the final day of his calling, I, Ragenfredus, although raised to the throne of this see without any distinction of merit, was installed in this episcopal seat. Once enthroned, I began, in watchful meditation, to consider whether I could offer anything acceptable to the eyes of the divine Majesty and what might be beneficial for the remedy of my soul.

For this purpose, I think, material was not hard to find. I saw that the clergy of the aforesaid church of Saint Peter were behaving carelessly, abandoning the exercises of spiritual warfare and pursuing earthly and transitory things in mind and deed, and that they were already committing things too wicked to mention. In consultation with the aforementioned Alveus, of blessed memory, I summoned Vulfaldus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict, in whom, without compromising the good of discretion, everyone declared that the discipline of religion was maintained more strictly and perfectly.

When he arrived with several companions of the same order, we reformed the aforesaid place together with him according to the observance of ancient monasticism.

“Lest the monks be presented with an occasion to wander outside through the poverty of an indictable want, we strove to restore whatever appeared to have been unjustly taken from that place by the invasions of our predecessors and others, both from military benefices and from our own demesne, as circumstances permitted. Moreover, while life remains, if opportunity is supplied, my mind urges me to restore still more; some of these matters we have decided to include in this episcopal privilege and some in other documents.

“We therefore restore to them a certain parcel of land possessed by their predecessors in ancient times and later taken away by improper means, so that they may possess it fully, just as it is proved by the testimony of many that their predecessors held it. This land lies within and outside the walls of the city of Chartres, beside the Cinerosa Gate.

On one side the land is bounded by the road that leads out of the city; on the other side it is bounded by the land of Saint Peter of Poitiers and of Saint Aignan. The land of Saint Peter of Poitiers, however, lies within the city walls, while the land of Saint Aignan lies both within and outside them.

On one frontage it is bounded by the land of Saint Peter of Chartres and by the road that runs through the middle of the city to the wall; on the other frontage, by the road outside the gate that leads to the monastery itself.

“We also exchanged for the land they possessed at Belmont the allod of Oidolo, beside the land described above in the city itself, before the gate of the cloister of Saint Peter, on the road commonly called Merdosa. We restored to them as much land as yielded eighteen solidi; not far from the ditch of Algis, eight *aripennia* of vineyards; and, for planting, according to the assessment, eight *bonuaria*.

In the site of the monastery itself we gave them a garden with fifteen *aripennia* of vineyards, and not far from Luceiacum an empty field for planting, thirty *aripennia*.

“An exchange was also made between the canons of Saint Mary and the monks of Saint Peter. From their churches the canons of Saint Mary gave them the church of Ursi Villaris, with one *aripennis* of land belonging to that church, and received in return the church at Cintriacum, together with its endowment.

We also gave them from the estate of Saint Mary, in the aforesaid parish of Ursi Villaris, Germinionis Villa in the pagus of Duno, with thirty cultivated and uncultivated *mansi*.

In the pagus of Chartres we also gave the church called Immonis Villa, with nine and a half *mansi*; likewise the church of Alona, with the three and a half *mansi* belonging to it; also the chapel of Saint Victor in the estate called Vernus, with one mill, and, after Odulfus’s death, the whole estate; and also the chapel at Mitani Villare.

We restore all these churches to them, granting them the tithes and remitting the synod and the *circada* payments. We likewise restore to them the church at Bodas Villa, which they have held at all times, so that neither we nor our successors may ever demand anything from them concerning it in any way.

“We also restore to them in the pagus of Chartres, in the estate called Britiniacum, eight *mansi* of land, together with their dwelling plots and cultivated and uncultivated lands; at Campchiacum, one *mansus* with its dwelling plots and cultivated and uncultivated lands; at Cosentiacum, one *mansus*; at Emprani Villa and Concrecia, whatever is known to be held from that estate; at Saint Mary’s, above the highway, one *mansus*; at Spotmeri Villa, one *mansus*; at Magneriae, three and a half *mansi*; at Gondri Villa, eight *mansi*, with woodland and meadows; at Cepidum, one *mansus*; at Fontinidum, one *mansus*, together with two *aripennia* of meadow lying at Villeta; at Levesi Villa, one *mansus*; at Wadreium, one quarter-*mansus*; at Teuvasium, one *mansus*; at Vallis, one *mansus*, with meadows—namely, nine *aripennia*; at Mount Otricus, one mill, with ten *aripennia* of meadow; at Mandri Villa, one *mansus*; at Lotdreium, one *mansus*, with one mill; at Bertoni Villare, one quarter-*mansus*; at Saxna Villa, in the same pagus, two *mansi* of land; in the pagus of Étampes, in the estate called Malaredus, one *mansus*; and in the pagus of Duno, in the estate called Alpedagnus, one church with all the land belonging there to that estate.

“Moreover, under the authoritative threat of episcopal excommunication and the unavoidable condemnation of anathema, we forbid both those now living and all future generations that no bishop, no cleric, and no layman may harass them in any matter whatsoever: neither by demanding tithes or *circada* payments, which others call the prepared dues; nor by any secular ambition to invade their lands; nor may anyone presume to exercise coercion over the people of that estate; nor to exact tolls or fines; nor to inflict upon them or their servants any injury, however great or small.

Rather, free from the disturbance of anxiety, let them lead a tranquil life in God’s service and in the monastic vocation, remembering us and the church entrusted to us at all times in their prayers, both private and common.

But if anyone should presume to oppose these episcopal decrees or render them void, let him be pierced by the arrows of eternal malediction and, together with Judas the betrayer, Annas and Caiaphas, Pilate, and their head, the devil, pay the penalties of everlasting condemnation, assigned to the flames of Gehenna, unless he repent and turn his mind away from this purpose.

“So that the authority of this privilege may possess perpetual and unshaken firmness, we have decreed that it be confirmed below by both our own hands and those of our fellow bishops.

“Done publicly in the city of Chartres. Ragenfredus, bishop of the city of Chartres, confirmed and strengthened this charter of authority. Hildemannus, archbishop of Sens. Graulfus, abbot of Saint Caraunus. Arduinus, chief chancellor. Teodericus, priest. Arcarius, priest. Adelandus, priest. Gauzzo, deacon. Ardradus, subdean. Radulfus, priest. Bernardus, priest. Gerardus, deacon. Lambertus, canon. Aymo, Walleranus, and Burchardus, the knights subscribed below, later confirmed it. Joseph, archbishop of Tours. Constantius, bishop of Paris. Gunhardus, bishop of Évreux. Mainardus, bishop of Le Mans. Mabbo, bishop of the Breton see of Aleth. Nordoardus, bishop of Rennes. Count Tedbaldus.”  
[Note: Tedbaldus I, surnamed “the Trickster,” son of that Tedbaldus who is said to have bought the city of Chartres from Hastingus, died in the year 978, having lived almost an entire century; hence he was also called “the Old.”]

“Hugo, archbishop, son of Count Tedbaldus. Count Odo. Hugo, duke of the Franks. Hugo, his son.”  
[Note: Hugo Capito, son of Hugo Magnus.]

“Countess Ledgardis.”  
[Note: Wife of Tedbaldus I.]

“—At a later time: Odo, bishop of Chartres. Ottho, count of Burgundy. Suggerius, dean.”*

[Col. 0223B]

Finally, after the death of the illustrious Bishop Ragenfredus,  
[Note: He died around the year 960.]  
who labored with devoted affection to restore this place to its ancient status and strove to establish it in holy religion, his brother Arduinus succeeded him in the episcopate. But, as we have said, he neither cared for the place nor wished to enrich it; rather, he did not hesitate to withdraw certain things that had been granted by his brother.

Therefore, since I have nothing else to insert concerning him into these pages  
[Note: Read *paginis* or *paginae*.]  
apart from what I have inserted, I have only the lamentable deed that I learned from the account of earlier generations: namely, that he had the entrance to the episcopate closed against him, and, in order to make it passable, he removed the abbey of Saint Martin from episcopal control and handed it over permanently to the power of the counts.

Leaving him aside, we must pass with Arembertus—whom, after the death of blessed Alveus, he appointed father over the community—to the venerable Widbertus, whom Bishop Vulfaldus ordained abbot. What a man he was in learned knowledge is shown by the Passion of Saint Emanus, which he composed in a polished style; and what a man he was in religion is demonstrated by the donations of many faithful, recorded in the charters written below. For many, recognizing his holiness and enriched by the salt of his wisdom and the abundance of his words, despising earthly riches, exchanged them for entry into the kingdom of heaven.

# BOOK THREE  
## OR OF ABBOT WIDBERTUS  
*(From the year 965 to approximately the year 980.)*

[Note: The following books lack numbers and names in the manuscript; we have supplied them from the chapter lists, which begin again with each new abbot. Therefore, after the first two books dedicated by the author to Bishops Aganus and Ragenfredus, we judged that the names of the abbots should be assigned to the following six books, since the author himself clearly divides them in this way.]

[Col. 0223]

## CHAPTER ONE  
### Concerning the church of Saint George given to Saint Peter  
[Note: Without doubt an apocryphal diploma. First, Count Walter gives a property that belongs not to him but to Richard; second, Richard subscribes after the count, as though he were a vassal; third, Richard was never called “duke,” but “margrave of the Normans,” as can be seen in the diplomas of King Lothair and Pope John XIII.]  
*(Year 965.)*

[Col. 0223C]

“With the help of Christ our Lord and Savior, Walter, count of the county of Dourdan and of Vexin.”  
[Note: Manuscript A: *Auxiante* (“With the help”).]  
[Note: Walter I, count of Dourdan and Vexin, son of Count Waleran and advocate of Saint-Denis. He is not mentioned in history before this charter, but later gave other gifts to various monasteries and was still living in 987.]

“We wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy church, both present and future, that the noble vassal Teodfredus came into our presence, asking that we give him our consent concerning a certain church belonging to his benefice, namely one consecrated in honor of Saint George, which he intended to transfer to the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, where the humble abbot Guibertus appears to preside.  
[Note: See *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. VI, pp. 406–421, under GUIBERTUS, abbot.]

Indeed, all the monks of Saint Peter collectively requested that he transfer the same church to them in perpetual donation, according to the terms and agreement that had been deliberated among them.

Considering, therefore, that his petition was salutary, I most willingly assented to his wish, especially for the remedy of my soul, of the souls of my parents, and of my predecessor Count Landricus.  
[Note: That Landricus, count of Dourdan, was the father of Eva, Walter I’s wife, through whom Walter held the county of Dourdan, while through his father he was already count of Vexin and through his mother, Eldegardis of Amiens, count of Amiens.]

For a similar reason Teodfredus likewise confirmed that he would do this, for the sake of obtaining pardon for the sins of himself and his parents.

To prevent the calumny of subsequent enemies—which we certainly do not expect—we establish, as a recognition payment, that each year, at the Mass of Saint Remigius celebrated on the Kalends of October, they are to pay a pension of three solidi.

If anyone at any time should attempt to oppose this donation and transfer or wish to bring any calumny against it, let him be condemned by ecclesiastical authority and struck by the anathema of episcopal excommunication. To us and our successors, compelled by the associated treasury, let him pay five pounds of refined gold as compensation. But from the monks, at no time until the end of the age, shall anything else be demanded concerning it except what is written above.

Therefore, so that these written records may possess stable and unshaken firmness, we have decided to confirm them below with our own hand, with that of Duke Richard, in whose county he appears to be situated, and also with those of the noble laymen.

“Done publicly in the county of Évreux. The sign of Count Walter, author of this charter. The sign of the soldier Teodfredus. The sign of Duke Richard.

“In the year 965 from the Incarnation of the Lord, indiction 8, in the eleventh year of the reign of King Clotharius. This donation was written by the Levite Germanus.”  
[Col. 0225B]

## CHAPTER TWO  
### Concerning the exchange of lands between the monks of Saint Peter and Ingelerius  
*(8 March 967.)*

“In the name of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. It was pleasing and agreed between the monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, over whom Abbot Wibertus appears to preside, and a certain man named Ingelerius that they should exchange their lands; and so they did.

The monks therefore gave the aforesaid Ingelerius whatever they appeared to possess at Piei Villa, Sirei Villa, Adorlei Villa, Atellei Villa, and Abassinei Villa.

In return, Ingelerius gave the monks of Saint Peter the estate called Septem Modioli, with its woods, fields, and everything belonging to it. The land itself is bounded on one side by the land of Saint Mary, on the other by the land of Saint Martin, on the third side by the land of Saint Peter himself, and on the fourth by the land of Tetmarus.

This exchange was made on the condition that from this day forward each party might do whatever it wished with the properties just mentioned. And so that the exchange might remain firm and stable, it was agreed that this charter should be drawn up and confirmed with their own hands.

“Done publicly at Chartres. The sign of Abbot Wibertus. The sign of Hermanus, dean. The sign of Gisbertus. The sign of Norboldus. The sign of Germanus. The sign of Warengaudus. The sign of Ebertus. The sign of Durandus. The sign of Alveus. The sign of Odo. The sign of Bernardus. The sign of Aimo. The sign of Fulcuinus. The sign of Tedbertus, monks.

“Given on the eighth day before the Ides of March, in the thirteenth year of the reign of King Lothair.

“Waldricus, notary, wrote this at their request.”

## CHAPTER THREE  
### Concerning the plot of land of two mills at Falesia, purchased by the canon Ardradus for rent  
*(12 May 768.)*
[Note: This charter is absent from manuscript B.] In the name of Christ, Eirveus, who appears to hold the abbey of Saint Caraun through the generosity of Lord Odo the bishop. We wish it to be known to all our successors and to the other faithful Christians [Col. 0226A] how we grant by firm tenure, subject to a rent, to a certain canon of Saint Mary, named Ardrad, and to his two brothers Benedict and Magenfred, with the consent of our lord Odo, a site for two mills, together with the mills themselves, built by Alcarius, their uncle.

The area lies in the county of Chartres, on the river Audura, in the place called Faliza, together with one manse of land, which lies in the valley of Saint Caraun, and in another place called Lupo Vulto. We grant them this area, therefore, together with the mills and the aforesaid manse of land, on lease and firm tenure, so that they may safely build upon it and pay annually, on the feast of Saint Caraun, which falls on the fifth day before the Kalends of June, ten solidi as rent. If they should be negligent in this matter, let them make legal restitution, [Col. 0226B] but let them not lose the mills or the land; rather, let them have permission to sell or give them to whomever they wish, provided that the sale and the rent come to the lord, and that no further rent be demanded from them beyond what is written above. In order that this charter might be more firmly established, we confirmed it with our own hand and presented it to our lord and his faithful men for their confirmation.

“Enacted at Chartres. Sign of Odo, the bishop. Sign of Suggerius, the dean. Sign of Eirveus, who ordered this charter to be made. Sign of Alcherius, priest. Sign of Otbaldus, priest. Sign of Evrardus, priest. Sign of Wido, deacon. Sign of Teduinus, deacon. Sign of John, deacon. Sign of Roger. Sign of Dolio, the mayor.

“Given on the fourth day before the Ides of May, in the fourteenth year of the reign of King Clothar. Grimuinus wrote it, in place of Suggerius.”

## CHAPTER IV. How the same area came to the monks of Saint Peter (27 June 971)

[Col. 0226C]

“In the name of Christ, Odo, by the grace of God humble bishop of the people of Chartres. We wish it to be known to all our successors and to the other faithful of Christ how we grant by firm tenure, subject to a rent, to a certain canon of Saint Mary and of our church, named Rodbert, an area belonging to the abbey of Saint Caraun, together with the mills themselves, which he purchased from Ardrad at his own expense.

The area lies in the county of Chartres, on the river Audura, in the place called Faliza, together with one manse of land, which lies in the valley of Saint [Col. 0226D] Caraun, and at Dorulfus Mons, and in another place called Lupo Vultus. We grant this area, therefore, together with the mills and the aforesaid land, to the aforesaid Rodbert on lease, so that he may build upon it securely and pay annually, on the feast of Saint Caraun, ten solidi as rent. If he should be negligent in this matter, let him make legal restitution and not lose the area, but let him hold it for as long as he lives. After his death, moreover, let him leave these same mills to the brothers and monks of Saint Peter, so that they may continually pray to God for his soul and that of his mother Ermentrudis, and pay ten solidi to the lord of that abbey, as stated above. In order that this charter might be more firmly established, we confirmed it with our own hand [Col. 0227A] and presented it to our faithful men for confirmation. Sign of Odo, bishop of Chartres. Sign of Suggerius, dean. Sign of Evrardus, priest. Sign of Roger, deacon. Sign of Ardrad. Sign of Teduinus. Enacted publicly at Chartres. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, in the seventeenth year of the reign of King Clothar.”

## CHAPTER V. Concerning the vineyard land given by Bishop Odo beside the episcopal grove, and concerning Placentiacum Villare (5 February 974)

*“The venerable and God-beloved Odo, bishop of the church of Chartres, while seated in an assembly of noble clerics and laymen, began, with prudent reasoning and canonical authority, to discuss the condition of the holy church entrusted to him, and to admonish with shrewd exhortation the ministers to whom responsibility for the churches entrusted to him had been transferred, so that in the churches committed to them they might keep the most diligent watch and perform the worship of the holy religion with irreproachable service.

When he had spoken at length on this and many other matters, the discussion at last came to the monastery of Saint Peter, situated in the suburb of the city of Chartres. It had formerly been corrupted, for certain reasons, in its monastic observance and reduced to canonical governance, but very recently had been restored by his episcopal predecessors to its former rank of monastic religion. They had also offered to that place, as circumstances dictated and opportunity allowed, provisions for the monks from which they are still supported, as alms; and their deliberation would have been to contribute more, had they not been taken away by the funeral of envious death.

When these and certain other benefits bestowed upon that place by those same predecessors had been made known to the holy bishop’s ears, he, stirred by their examples—or rather touched by the grace of divine mercy—replied to those who told him that he too had long been held by no less strong a desire for the same monastery, and that he would have brought other plans to fulfillment had not those obstacles arisen which are known to all.

Meanwhile, so that this intention of his deliberation might become known in part to everyone, he gave to the same place twenty solidi-worth of vineyard land, near the city of Chartres, situated toward the north, beside the episcopal grove. It is bounded on one side by land belonging to the same estate, [Col. 0227D] on another by the canons’ land, on the third by the land of Saint Maurice, and on the fourth by the public road leading to the city. [Note: The word “land” appears to be an interpolation and should probably be deleted.]

He also gave a certain small estate situated wholly in the Belsia, named Placentiacum Villare, so that they might possess both properties forever, provided only that they remember him in their sacred prayers. But if anyone should wish to invalidate or annul this donation, may he incur, from him and from his fellow bishops, the perpetual punishment of excommunication, joined to the devil and his angels and to those who are to be cast into the lake of eternal fire, where the worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished. May his destruction be with Judas the betrayer; may he experience condemnation with Dathan and Abiron, whom the earth swallowed alive; may that perpetual indignation of divine vengeance remain upon him by which those will be condemned to whom it will be said at the judgment: ‘Depart, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.’ Amen.

In order that this donation might possess perpetual and unshakable firmness, it seemed right that it should be confirmed below both by the hand of the lord bishop and by that of the whole church. Odo, bishop of the church of Chartres, confirmed it. Suggerius, dean. Salico, subdean. Suggerius, key-bearer. Lambertus, archdeacon. Rodulfus, precentor. Wido, archdeacon. Alcarius, provost. Alto, provost. Bernardus, provost. Erembertus, archdeacon. Hilduinus, subdeacon. [Col. 0228B] Waracco, priest. Ardrad, priest. Ebroinus, priest. Isaac, priest. Wenilo, priest. Humbertus, deacon. Winemandus, deacon. Hildegarius, deacon. Eirveus, deacon. John, deacon. Teudo, deacon. Gauzbertus, knight. Fulcarius. Romaldus. Ucbertus. Hugo. Albertus. Salo. Gilduinus. Grimvinus, unworthy priest, wrote it. Given on the Nones of February, in the twentieth year of King Lothar.” [Note: The charter was published in the *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, instruments, col. 292.]

[Note: This brief note is absent from manuscript B, where only the following is read: “Later Bishop Rodulfus extorted this donation for himself.”] Let the prudent reader consider where the vineyard land is which Bishop Odo gave beside his grove, since none of our people knows of any such land, nor is any other grove known except the one that appears to have been beside the village of Baliol.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the church of the village of Baliolis, sold to the canon Geraldus (before 977)

[Col. 0228C]

“In the name of the Lord, Odo, humble bishop of the people of Chartres. We wish it to be known to all the faithful of Christ how a certain canon of ours, named Geraldus, came into our presence and requested that we graciously grant by a written charter of security to him and to one heir the church from our estate called Baliolus, dedicated in honor of Saint Stephen and situated in the county of Chartres.

Accordingly, granting assent to his petition, with the common counsel and consent of our faithful clerics and laymen, we grant them the aforesaid church, so that, with God presiding, in our time and in that of our successors they may possess, govern, and administer it as though they had been ordained in it through all the grades; and let no one presume to disturb or remove them from it, unless—which God forbid—they should have departed from the path of truth. Nevertheless, in accordance with canonical authority, let them govern and administer it with free power, and let them pay them annually, on the feast of Saint Mary, which falls on the sixth day before the Ides of September, five solidi as rent; and let no further rent be demanded from them beyond what is written above. And so that this authority may remain firm, we confirmed it with our own hand and delivered it to our faithful men for confirmation. Enacted at Chartres, in the church of Saint Mary.”

## CHAPTER VII. Likewise, how the same church came to Saint Peter [Note: B: “Concerning the church of the village of Baliolis, which Bishop Rodulfus took away from Saint Peter.”] (February 977)

[Col. 0229A]

“We believe that no one of orthodox faith and Catholic profession can be wholly unaware how greatly, both in the present and in the future, those prosper who, for the name of Christ, cheerfully offer from their own resources some gift to his saints and faithful, since the Lord says: ‘Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness,’ and again: ‘Give, and it will be given to you.’

Instructed by these and other teachings, and inwardly illumined by the breath of the Holy Spirit, I, Godeleva, and my companion, equal to me in age and grace, named Clementia, purchased from a certain canon called Geraldus, at a fixed price and with the consent of the distinguished bishop, Lord Odo of the city of Chartres, a certain church, and we give and wish it to be given to Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, for the remission of our sins, a power which God has rightly granted him both on earth and in heaven, and for the salvation of our souls, from this day and for all time.

The aforesaid church is called Baliolus, is dedicated in honor of Saint Stephen, and is situated in the county of Chartres, so that the monks serving the Lord and Saint Peter there according to the regular path may hold and possess it. The aforesaid bishop granted it in pious devotion on this condition: that his memory should perpetually be celebrated both in prayers and in the solemn services of the Mass, and that they should pay twelve denarii annually as rent, without synod or circada.

But if any of his successors, inflamed by the heat of greed, should attempt to act against this donation and invalidate it, let him, without prejudice to his episcopal rank, render an account to God and Saint Peter on the day of the final judgment for so great a presumption. And so that this donation may remain firm, we confirmed it below and presented it to the faithful of the same church, both clerics and laymen, for confirmation. Enacted publicly at Chartres. I, Odo, by the grace of God bishop of Chartres, confirmed it with my own hand. Odo, count. Suggerius, chief key-bearer. Rodulfus, precentor. Salico, subdean. Atto, provost. Wido, provost. Alcarius, provost. Vitalis. Teudo. Romoldus. Rodbertus, and others. Given in the month of February, in the twenty-third year of the reign of King Lothar. Grimvinus, deacon, wrote it.”

[Note: The following is absent from manuscript B.] As long as this venerable man, Bishop Odo, lived, the monks firmly possessed the aforesaid church, which pious women of the religious life had purchased for themselves. But when he departed this life and Bishop Rodulfus was appointed in his place, inflamed by the heat of greed, he did not hesitate to appropriate for his own uses both the church and the other possessions which he found had been given by the bishop to the Apostle [Col. 0230A].

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning Greseicum [Note: A, in the index, Giseicum. B, Jesiacum.], a royal seat, and Fontinidum and Limaeum, given to Saint Peter by the most noble Countess Ledgardis (5 February 978)

*“The provident dispensation of our Creator, wondrously praiseworthy and ever praiseworthily wondrous, from the world’s first beginning, having redeemed men at the price of his blood and cleansed them from original sin by the washing of holy baptism, foreseeing and foreknowing that after all this no one could live, even for the space of one day, free from any sin or escape the stain of human corruption, bestowed many remedies for the soul’s salvation, by which not only the diseased conditions of vices are healed, but also the joys of blessed immortality are acquired. [Note: This text appears, with some omissions, in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, instruments, col. 7, and in Ph. Labbe, *Alliance chronologique*, vol. I, p. 579.]

Among these remedies the generosity of almsgiving is especially powerful. It is supported not only by the authority of many fathers, but is also praised by the blessed voice of the Lord himself, who says: ‘Forgive, and you will be forgiven,’ and ‘Whatever you do for one of my least, you do for me.’ A certain wise man also says: ‘A man’s redemption is his own wealth,’ and again: ‘Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you.’ Many similar and especially exhortatory passages concerning the giving of alms are found, but it would be lengthy to go through them individually.

Instructed by such exhortations and by the commendable devotion of our predecessors, who, as sons of the Church, endowed the same church with many revenues from their estates and bestowed many things upon it for its various needs—things by which it is adorned throughout the four quarters of the world, enriched with abundance of possessions, and rejoices and exults—I, Ledgardis [Note: Daughter of Herbert, count of Troyes; in her first marriage she had William Longsword, duke of Normandy, as her husband, and in her second Theobald the Trickster, count of Chartres. Among the princes who enriched the monastery of Saint Peter by their piety, this countess easily holds the first place.], following their examples and admonished by divine prompting, resolved in the secret chamber of my heart to make the holy church of God an heir to possessions from my estates.

But because the power of binding and loosing was specially granted by the Lord to the blessed apostle Peter, so that whatever he should bind or loose on earth would immediately be bound or loosed in heaven, I judged that no one would be a better counselor for me, nor a more merciful intercessor for my sins, than the one whom God loved with so great a love.

Therefore, both to obtain forgiveness for my crimes and for the soul of my most noble lord and glorious count Theobald, so that the Lord may grant both of us remission of all sins, with the consent of the most honorable men, namely Archbishop Hugo and the excellent Count Odo, my sons, I cede to the church of Saint Peter at Chartres a church consecrated in honor of Peter, prince of the apostles and keeper of the heavenly kingdom, in the place commonly called Gizei, together with the estate called Gizei, with sixteen manses, cultivated and uncultivated lands, lodgings, meadows, vineyards, waters and watercourses.

In another place, I also cede an estate called Fontenedum, with the church situated in that estate, with *masingili* [Note: *Massingelum* appears to be the same as *Masgnellum*; see Du Cange, *Glossarium*, under that word.] and vineyards, and with everything belonging to it in its entirety. Likewise, in another place, in the estate which in the rustic language is called Limais, I cede whatever appears to belong to me.

The aforesaid possessions lie in the county of Vexin, on the river Seine. All these things, as prescribed above, I transfer and wish to be transferred in perpetuity.

But if anyone should attempt to act against this donation of ours—which God forbid—or to violate it, or to bring any accusation against it, let him incur the irrecoverable indignation of Almighty God unless he quickly repents, and let him be eternally thrust into infernal torments, where the worm that never dies will gnaw his flesh and the fire that never goes out will always feed upon his sufferings.

To ensure that this donation should possess inviolable firmness, we confirmed it with our own hands and decreed that it be strengthened by the hands of our faithful men. At the end of this document I also wished to make clear that, just as I have granted all the aforesaid possessions to Christ, to the blessed apostle Peter, and to the monks serving there, for the sake of my soul, so I have done this for the soul of my father Herbert, count of Troyes, who gave and granted me the aforesaid possessions as an inheritance.

“Odo, count. Hugo, archbishop of the holy church of Bourges. Odo, bishop of Chartres. Ledgardis, countess, who made this gift. Emma, countess of the city of Poitiers. Landricus. Hilgaudus. Suggerius. Rotrocus. Arduinus. Ucbertus. Fulcherius. Teudo. Widgerius. Erembertus. Hugo of Aloia. Gelduinus. Avesgaudus. Isaac.

“To this maternal donation I, Hugo, first of the foremost archbishops, and Odo, the wealthiest count, gave our consent for this reason: that every day, except on ferial days, the psalm ‘Incline your ear, O Lord,’ should be sung for us by the brothers of the aforesaid place, and that our memory should continually be kept in the morning offices for as long as we live; but after our death, our anniversary should be celebrated with the utmost diligence, with antiphons and responsories, with the customary readings interspersed and with the solemn services of the Mass.
