Let there also be, for the brothers laboring on our behalf, an abundant provision of food and drink on that same day. And let this memorial of ours not be erased by any forgetfulness, so long as two brothers survive, from generation to generation, before God and Saint Peter, the guardian and perpetual protector of that place. Given on the day of the Nones of February, while King Lothar reigned, in the twenty-fourth year, by the Lord’s favor.”

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning an allod at Probata Villa purchased from religious women (16 August 979)

[Col. 0232A]

“I, Ledgardis, in the name of God, most devout and faithful among the servants of God, make known to all the faithful of the orthodox and Catholic Church that I myself, together with another woman consecrated to God, named Godeleia, joined to me in body and soul, purchased by agreement from a certain man named Othbertus an allod in its entirety, everything that had been left and transferred to him by hereditary right from both his grandfathers and his great-grandfathers, in the estate commonly called Probata Villa, at a price fixed as appropriate, namely in the county of Chartres.

The transaction was made on this condition: that from his person and right it should pass into our lordship and power from this day and for the remainder of the age. This purchase was made with the following provision and devotion: as long as we survive, it shall remain at the disposition of our will; but after our deaths, it shall pass and be transferred, in its entirety and without any opposing person bringing a claim against it, into the power and lordship of Saint Peter, established in the suburb of Chartres, and of the brothers serving God there.

To make this charter more firmly and truly credible, we caused it to be confirmed with our own hand and by the hands of the faithful of the holy church of God. Enacted publicly at Chartres. Odo, count. Conamus, count of Brittany. Landricus. Arduinus. Rodbertus. Erchembaldus, cleric. Teduinus. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the twenty-fifth year [Col. 0232C] of the reign of King Clothar.”

## CHAPTER X. Concerning six *aripennis* of the vineyard of the blessed priest Sigemundus (February 981)

[Note: It appears in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, instruments, col. 293.]

“In the name of the All-Powerful. I, Fulcherius, who appear to hold the abbey of Saint Leobinus, situated in the suburb of Chartres, through the generosity of my lord Count Odo, wish it to be known to all my successors how we granted by firm tenure, subject to a rent, six and more *aripennia* of vineyard belonging to the estate of the aforesaid Saint Leobinus to the priest Sigemundus, together with two monks of Saint Peter, Peter and Durandus.

It is bounded on two sides by land belonging to that estate and on the other sides by public roads. By this grant we lease it to them on the following condition: that they hold and possess this land firmly and pay annually, on the feast of Saint Leobinus, which falls on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, three solidi and five denarii as rent. If they should be negligent in this matter, let them make legal restitution, but let them not lose the vineyard; rather, let them have permission to sell or give it to whomever they wish, provided that the sale and the rent come to the lord.

In order that this charter might be more firmly established, I confirmed it with my own hand and presented it to my lord and his faithful men for confirmation. Enacted publicly at Chartres. Odo, count. Fulcherius, abbot. Vivianus. Rodbertus. Teudo. Evrardus. [Col. 0233A] Odo. Given in the month of February, in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of King Clothar.”

Here the most blessed man Siemundus [Note: A: thus.] wished to place two monks of Saint Peter with himself in the aforesaid firm tenure so that, if death should happen to overtake him before he could fulfill the vow of his gracious desire, Saint Peter would at least possess the vineyard for as long as these men survived.

But because God always looks favorably upon the pious vows of those who please him, and brings them to fulfillment so that he may reward them with a worthy recompense [Note: Thus in the manuscripts.], this illustrious man, before he departed from the world, acted—as is clear in what follows—so that the blessed apostle might become the perpetual heir of the same vineyard. How great the man’s goodness was, and how holy his life, adorned with every virtue, became known to everyone more clearly than daylight, both among the clergy and among the [Col. 0233B] people. For he was fiery in faith, cheerful in speech, outstanding in chastity, eminent in humility, prudent in counsel, generous in almsgiving, devoted to reading, constant in prayer, and distinguished in every moral excellence.

I have undertaken to weave into this little work the miracles which he performed while living in the body, as well as those which I learned from truthful narrators, lest in the future I be reproved by the Lord as a lazy and wicked servant concerning the talent entrusted to me and hidden away. But, lest I seem to overstep the limits of a notary and enter upon the broad road of historians, I shall tell only two miracles concerning the same blessed priest.

One day, as he was customarily present with the clergy in the church of the holy mother of the Lord and waiting for the conclusion of the Mass that had begun, his steward hurried there and quietly announced to him that not only had the provisions for his household entirely run out in his storerooms, but that nothing at all remained to give to the needy. For it was the custom of the blessed man throughout his life that no poor person ever left his house empty-handed.

When the work of God had been completely finished, he knelt before the altar of Mary, the Mother of God, and prayed silently to the Lord for a little while. Then, fortifying himself with the sign of the cross and rising from prayer, he returned home. After summoning his steward, he said: ‘Go, open for me all the storerooms of the house.’

When they had been opened and signed with the sign of the cross by him, they were immediately found, by the Creator’s command, to be as full as though they had been filled in the present autumn [Note: B: “autumn”]. Then, summoning the steward, he said: ‘Do not be anxious in giving. For those who fear God lack nothing. Rather, distribute generously among the hands of the poor what the Lord has graciously bestowed freely upon us sinners. These supplies will not fail until, when the new year returns and new provisions arrive, you throw out the old.’

In this deed he appears not unlike that prophet who foretold that the jar of oil and the handful of flour would not diminish until the Lord poured his blessing upon the earth [Note: *Kings*, book III, chapter XVII, §§ 12, 14, 16.].

Again, when Odo, count of the city, most famous far and wide, was preparing to dine on one occasion and his cupbearers were searching throughout the town for excellent wine, they learned from certain people that an honorific wine was being sold in the cellar of the blessed Siemundus. Filled with joy, they hastened to the holy man’s house, entered the cellar with reckless boldness, and hurried to fill all their wineskins from the wine; once filled, they carried them back to the court.

Meanwhile the man of God returned from the church. While the master of the cupbearers was still in the cellar with some others, he mockingly questioned the man of God as he entered, saying: ‘My lord, tell me whether this wine is very excellent or not.’

The blessed man replied to him in gentle speech: ‘Brother, you have it ready at hand. You need not learn through someone else what, with you as master, you can test for yourself as quickly as possible.’

When the man asked that a cup be given him from which to drink, the blessed man answered him again: ‘By no means will you find it better in any other vessel than in the one from which it is drawn.’

When the wretched man placed the pitcher to his mouth to drink, he was immediately struck by paralysis, so that he fell foaming to the ground and was entirely deprived of the use of all his limbs. At once he was carried by the hands of the armor-bearers to the court, surrounded by soldiers and mourned by many. The matter was then reported to the count.

When the count learned why this had happened to him, he had the blessed Siemundus summoned. When he arrived, the count ordered that, as punishment for the injury done to him, the eyes of those who had violently carried away the wine from his house should be torn out, and that the wine should immediately be returned to the house.

But when the blessed man saw that the count’s spirit was greatly inflamed with anger, he did not leave him until he had recalled the count from anger by gracious words, freed the guilty men from punishment, obtained the wine as a gift of charity for the count to drink, and restored the cupbearer struck by paralysis to his former health through extended prayer.

When these things had been accomplished, he was raised up by great praise from everyone; and my little pen, having strayed somewhat from its course, returns to its path by this slight embellishment.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the aforesaid six *agripennia* of vineyard given by the canon Siemundus to Saint Peter (before 986)

“In the name of the All-Powerful. I, Fulcherius, who appear to hold the abbey of Saint Leobinus, situated beneath the city of Chartres, through the generosity of my lord Count Odo, wish it to be known to all my successors, present and future, that we grant by firm tenure, subject to a rent, six and more *agripennia* of vineyard to the priest and canon Siemundus, and after his death to Saint Peter of Chartres and his monks.

They are bounded on two sides by land belonging to the same estate and on the other two sides by public roads. By this grant we lease the land to them on the following condition: that they hold it firmly as far as the cross and possess it perpetually, and pay each year, on the feast of Saint Leobinus, which falls on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, three solidi and five denarii without delay to the administrator of that land. If they should be negligent in this matter, let them make legal restitution, but let them not lose the vineyard; rather, let them have permission to sell or give it to whomever they wish.

In order that this charter might be more firmly established, I confirmed it with my own hand and presented it to my lord Count Odo and his faithful men for confirmation. Enacted publicly at Chartres.

“Odo, count. Fulcherius, abbot. Vivianus—who later became a monk and gave Pomereta with its dependencies, cultivated and uncultivated lands, groves, shrublands, and thickets; he also gave in Lovis Villa whatever he appeared to possess there, and whatever he gave appeared to be free from every evil custom. Harduinus. Teduinus. Alcharius. Ebrardus. Guauslinus. Rodbertus.”

While Abbot Landricus was alive, Fulcherius, son of Nivelon, remitted the rent of the aforesaid vineyard to Saint Peter for his own well-being and for the souls of his parents, together with the church of Saint Leobinus and a certain piece of land beside that church’s cemetery, as well as ten solidi in coin on the solemnity of the blessed Leobinus.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the exchange made between the canons of the church of Saint Mary of Chartres and the monks of Saint Peter, built in the southern suburb of the same city (before 986)

In the name of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who is one in power and three in persons. An exchange was made between the canons of the church of Saint Mary of Chartres and the monks of Saint Peter, built in the southern suburb of the same city, formerly constructed with great elegance and nobility, and no less so, as far as the present age is concerned.

The aforesaid canons gave to the place of the holy virgin Mary Moris Villa and whatever they appear to possess in Subritana and in Uni Villa, with an equitable and willing spirit, as befits holy men who have resolved to act with venerable and godly conduct. In return, by mutual exchange, they received from us, the monks of Saint Peter, under their authority, everything that we appeared to have possessed from ancient times in Ginone Villa and Petripertusa.

The sites of these estates are known to lie in the county of Chartres. Let both present and future faithful of the holy church of God know that this was done so that the inviolable and ever-beneficent protection of charity may be preserved between both orders, as time and circumstances, with God as guide, shall dictate.

In order that this might possess unshakable firmness, we presented it to the hands of the clerics for exact confirmation.

“Odo, bishop. Suggerius, dean. Salico, subdean. Lambertus, archdeacon. Rodulfus, provost. Atto, provost. Humbertus, deacon. Aimo, subdeacon. Hilduinus, deacon. Isaac, priest. Warnerius, deacon. Guido, archdeacon. Gauzbertus, deacon. Adelmus, dean, jul. [Note: Thus.]. Morandus, deacon. Erbertus, subdeacon. [Col. 0236A] Arembertus, subdeacon. Suggerius, key-bearer. Ailbertus, subdeacon. Romoldus, subdeacon. Gauzbertus, knight.”

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the allod given to Saint Peter by Lambertus in the estate formerly called Guadresigia (before 986)

“Having for a little while set aside the biting cares of this age, in which the flesh rejoices and the spirit is saddened, and having been touched inwardly by a certain breath of inspiration, I, Lambertus, hearing the divine voice that says, ‘Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness,’ and, ‘Give, and it will be given to you,’ wishing in every way to have a share with those who have striven to fulfill this command of the Lord with a perfect and excellent heart, reflected and immediately bound myself by a better vow to contribute, from the things I appear to possess in this present age, something out of love and reverence for Almighty God to the place of Saint Peter and to his servants dwelling there under the light yoke of the Lord and under the regular profession of Saint Benedict, under the authority, as it appears, of the venerable abbot Widbertus.

I do this without any delay, lest, if the crisis of death should steal upon me by chance, I be found guilty of this incomplete intention. Therefore, from this day onward, for the salvation of my soul and of my wife and children in succeeding generations, I transfer and wish to have transferred, cede and desire to have ceded without any claim, to the aforesaid place, an allod in its entirety, situated in the estate formerly called Guadresigia, so that they may have, hold, and possess it for all time.

An agreement has been made that, as long as I live, I shall hold it and pay twelve denarii annually as rent on the feast of Saint Peter, which falls on the third day before the Kalends of July. But after my departure and the death of my body, as this present document testifies, it shall return to the aforesaid monastery with every improvement and in its entirety, so that Peter, the first and merciful shepherd of the Church, may immediately come to the aid of my soul and deem it worthy to assist it.

I wish this, therefore, to be known to all worshipers of the orthodox and apostolic faith. But if anyone should attempt by some act of daring to act against this donation, let him immediately receive the curse of Judas the apostate and betrayer of the Lord in both heart and body.

I have therefore resolved that this donation be confirmed by the hand of my excellent count and lord Odo and by the hands of his faithful men, together with my own hand. Enacted publicly at Chartres. Odo, count. Rotrocus. Arduinus. Teduinus. Alcharius. Gauslinus. Lambertus, who made this donation.”

But whether we possess it or not, or whether it is now called by another name after the former name was abandoned, or where this estate may be, we are entirely ignorant.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the church of Ermenteria and all the land which the monks of Saint Peter purchased from a certain knight named Archinulfus (before 986)

«In the name of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0237A] Count Walter makes known to all, present and future, that the monks of Saint Peter of Chartres came into our presence so that permission might be granted them, on our behalf, to purchase from the benefice of our faithful man Archinulf a church belonging to him by right of benefice, called Ermenteria, together with everything belonging in that village and to the benefice of the same Archinulf. Since he consented to this and also requested it, we willingly assented.

That land is bounded on one side by the River Arve, on the other by the public road, at one end by a stream commonly called the Berlo, and at the fourth end by the land separated from it that belongs to Evrold’s Villa. Within these boundaries we grant everything contained there: cultivated and uncultivated lands, including the portion that appears to be woodland, for the price agreed upon between Archinulf and the monks. The arrangement is that every year, on the feast of Saint Martin, which falls on the third day before the Ides of November, the monks shall pay Archinulf, and after his death his heirs, two solidi as a token of goodwill and for the protection of the place. No other payment whatsoever shall be demanded of them; and they shall possess and hold the church and all the land described by perpetual right, without any claim being brought against them, and shall never lose it.

We have also granted them the other church nearby, called Roheria, for the remedy of my soul and at the voluntary wish of my wife Eva. Archinulf, who held a share in that church, likewise follows our example and makes the same grant, together with his son Roscelin.

[Col. 0237C] So that these grants may remain firm and stable forever, at the monks’ request we caused a written charter to be made for them and took care that it be confirmed below by our hand and by those of our faithful men. If anyone should wish to invalidate these donations, destroy them in any way, demand anything more than what we have set out above, or burden the inhabitants by any wrongful custom, let him incur the wrath of almighty God and, with Dathan and Abiram, Judas the traitor, and the Antichrist himself and his angels, suffer eternal damnation in the flames of everlasting fire.

“Executed publicly at Dreux.

“Count Walter. Countess Eva. Erchenulf and Roscelin, his son, who were the sellers and donors of the aforesaid properties. Albert. Baldwin. [Col. 0237D] Urso. Marquard. Salico. Hadebrand. Gosfred. Nanter. Anseius. Rainard, priest. Anfred. Erenbert. Haimo. Gislebert. Hubert. Hugh. Emmo. Magenard. Hilgald. Evrard. Alo. Hugh.”»

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning land beside Buxedulo, given by the knight Arduin to the monks of Saint Peter at a census-rent. (Before 986)

I, Odo, count of the people of Chartres, make known to all, present and future, [Col. 0238A] that the noble man Arduin, our faithful servant, came into our presence and explained that the monks of Saint Peter of Chartres, whose abbot appears to be Wibert, had come to him asking that he grant them, at a census-rent, a certain piece of land from his benefice. Considering their request reasonable, I gave my consent, with the agreement of Arduin himself and of the other faithful men, both clerical and lay, on the condition that every year, on the feast of Saint Mary, which falls on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September, they—or whoever holds that benefice—shall pay one solidus as the census.

If they are late or negligent in this payment, let them make legal compensation, but on that account let them not lose the aforesaid land. Rather, let them hold, cultivate, and possess it [Col. 0238B] for all succeeding time without anyone’s opposition.

The land lies in the county of Dunois, beside a certain watercourse called the Edera, near a little village called Buxidulo. It measures two hundred perches in length and fifty across. On three sides it is bounded by land belonging to the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, and on the fourth by the aforesaid stream.

[Note: [Col. 0237D] Thus in two manuscripts, in the nominative case.]

So that this donation may remain firm and stable, we ordered these letters to be made for them and deemed it fitting that they be confirmed by my hand and by those of others, both clerics and laymen.

Executed publicly at Chartres.

Odo, count. Arduin, knight, donor of this land. [Note: [Col. 0238D] So in the manuscripts.] Suggerius, chief key-bearer. Fulcher. Teduin. Archebald. Aldric, provost. Stephen, vicar.»

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning an estate in Erminulf’s Greater Villa, sold to the monks of Saint Peter by a certain man named Heldebert. (Before 986)

[Col. 0238C]

«In the name of Christ, it was agreed between me, Heldebert, and the monks of Saint Peter of Chartres, whose abbot appears to be Wibert, that I should sell them an estate belonging to me by right, which had come to me by inheritance from my parents; and I did so with the advice of my parents and friends.

It lies in Erminulf’s Greater Villa. On one side it is bounded by Corbo’s land, on the other by the estate of my parents, at one end by the public road, and at the other by the land of Saint [Col. 0238D] Maurice. I received five solidi as the purchase price, and I transferred that land to them forever, so that from the present day onward they should have the firmest authority to do with it whatever they wished, without any opposition. I transferred it to them under the authority of this charter and confirmed it with my own hand, with a stipulation clause attached.

If anyone should attempt to act against this sale or transfer, or bring any claim against it, we impose upon him a fine of one pound of gold; and let the present sale remain valid forever.

Executed publicly at Chartres.

The sign of Heldebert, the seller. The sign of Solomon. The sign of Amalbert. The sign of Theodulf.»

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning lands returned to the monks of Saint Peter by Bishop Odo. (Before 986)

[Col. 0239A]

«In the name of Christ, I, Odo, raised to the episcopal see of the church of Chartres, make known to the sons of our holy church, present and future, that a company of monks came into our presence. Their humble abbot Wibert appears to preside over them; they are established in the suburb of the same city and were asking our mildness for certain reasonable concessions.

For these monks were claiming certain lands near the aforesaid city, intermingled with the property of our bishopric, and earnestly demanding that our religious authority restore them to them. But, following as far as we were able the example of the bishops who preceded us in this see—men who preferred to exalt that place and, insofar as possible, enrich it with possessions—we resolved not only to restore what was under dispute, but also to grant what adjoining land of ours was situated there. This would provide them with sustenance, while for us and for the entire condition of our church a daily recompense of prayers would be offered by them.

The land of which we speak lies partly in a village called Manus Villaris. On two sides it is bounded by land of Saint Mary, from the property of the brothers of this see; on one side by the land of the bishopric and of the brothers; and on the other by the road leading to the village of Amiliacum.

We also granted them, in another place called [Col. 0239C] Campus Follis, the lands that appeared to be held by us in part under our jurisdiction. This land is bounded on one side by the public road; on the other, extending as far as the precarial grant held by Hervé; at one end by the land of Saint Piatus and by episcopal property; and at the other end near the valley called Saint Cauraunus.

All these lands, therefore, exactly as set out above, we grant to them by our authority and with the consent of our church, both clerical and lay. We unanimously decreed that they should possess perpetual stability; and, so that they might be preserved with unimpaired force, we confirmed them by the subscription of our own hand and by the signatures of all our faithful men.

If anyone should wish to oppose this gift of our beneficence or attempt to violate it, let him be pierced by the anathema of perpetual malediction and, cast into everlasting fires, share the lot of those who said to the Lord God: “Depart from us; we do not wish to know your ways.”

The sign of Odo, bishop. The sign of Suggerius, dean. The sign of Hugh, archbishop. The sign of Fulco. The sign of Fulcher. The sign of Helgald. The sign of Girald. The sign of Wido. The sign of Aimeric. The sign of Rodulf. The sign of Atto. The sign of Alcher. The sign of Wiger. The sign of Gelduin. The sign of Arembert. The sign of Hilduin. The sign of John. The sign of Heriveus. The sign of Adam. The sign of Ardrad. The sign of Lambert. The sign of Bernard. The sign of Dodo. The sign of Fulco. The sign of Odilard. The sign of Romald. The sign of Alo. The sign of Isaac. The sign of Vulgis.»

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the place called Aurion, but commonly Evron, given to Saint Peter under the jurisdiction of the abbots of the monastery of Chartres. (985)

[Col. 0240A]

«The succession of many signs bears witness that the end of the world and the passing away of all things contained within its structure are drawing near. Therefore no one should delay or procrastinate; while he has the opportunity, no one should neglect to hasten his conversion for the sake of his salvation, nor, indeed, despair miserably of the innate goodness of our Creator.

For this reason, let the universal Church of God, present and future throughout the perpetuity of succeeding ages, consider how and with what resources I, the unworthy Rodbertus, deeply entangled in wanton deeds, have labored, with God’s favor, to the best of my ability, for the removal of my faults and the attainment of rewards. Within a place dedicated in honor of the perpetual Virgin and exalted Mother of God, situated in the county of Maine, called Aurion, though commonly known as Evron, which I appear to hold as a benefice from my lord Count Odo, together with other much greater properties, I resolved to establish a monastery for those serving God there under the direction of Father Benedict, as it had existed from ancient times.

As I pondered these matters anxiously in my mind, and as I reconsidered them in deliberation, I determined that it was impossible for me to accomplish this according to the resources of my property. I therefore judged it worthwhile to seek quickly and humbly the monastery of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, divinely ordered according to the institutions of the contemplative life, in the suburb of the city of Chartres. To its abbot and administrator, the venerable lord Wibert, who then presided over—and rather benefited—the chief monastery, and to his brothers who were striving cheerfully there, living for God and not for themselves, I disclosed from the depths of my heart my long-standing and heartfelt desire.

It therefore pleased the eternal and unchangeable counsel of our almighty Lord Jesus Christ that my lord Odo, together with his mother Ledgarde, and likewise my lady Berta, his wife, should favorably consent and join in this wish and deliberation of mine. Together with me, they subjected and granted to the aforesaid monastery, under the perpetual dominion of the highest apostolic privilege, the chapel of the aforesaid place of Haurion, together with the hospice already mentioned.

[Note: [Col. 0239] Hospice.]

It was also agreed that the aforementioned abbot of blessed memory, after taking common counsel with the brothers, should send some of his fellow-monks, according to the rule of their profession, to serve God and more devotedly attend upon his undefiled and perpetual Mother.

For the recovery of that place, for the sustenance and clothing of the brothers, for the reception of guests, and for the fulfillment of whatever needs might arise, I have at present restored what I could to that little monastery, and I hold, shall hold, and have held the vow of restoring it.

After that abbot had been received into the bosom of the peaceful region, I nevertheless humbly and devoutly petitioned his successor, the lord Gisbert, an abbot of exemplary life, to appoint one of his monks as abbot of the aforesaid little chapel by blessing him. At first he refused; but finally, overcome by the petitions of my lord and of my fellow soldiers as well as by my own, since he was benevolent and open to entreaty, he kindly granted what I had humbly requested.

This was done under the following condition promulgated by my lord at my petition, with the additional protection of royal consent, the solemn prohibition of the bishops, and the decree of both ecclesiastical and secular authorities, together with the judgment of the whole people: the aforesaid place of Haurion, for the conferring of blessings and the appointment of abbots, should remain perpetually under the authority of the chief monastery of the apostles, the supreme apex, and of the administrator of that place, since from him it receives the substance and beginning of its recovery and restoration.

The father of the abbots of Chartres shall appoint as successor to the abbot of the aforesaid little monastery of Haurion whomever he chooses, with the consent of the brothers of both places assembled as one, together with the election of the defender or advocate of the same little place, provided that he is zealous for God.

The man so appointed, in the presence of his ordainer or father, shall seek not the position of prior, equality, or parity, but the humility of a junior and disciple. In accordance with the rule of Saint Benedict, he shall offer every submission to him with a ready foot of obedience; he shall obey, I say, the one who commands and comply with the one who orders.

If, therefore, he should wish to become a turncoat or an opponent—may this never happen!—imitating the devil, and insolently shake from his neck the yoke of due subjection, let him be excommunicated. If he should nevertheless persist shamelessly in his obstinacy, let him be deposed and another be appointed in his place, better equipped with the splendid and victorious arms of obedience.

But whoever, of whatever order, sex, or rank, should dare to persist as one who tears away or breaks this security, shall in the present life receive a share with Gehazi, the trafficker in fraud, and in eternity be handed over to the dark gloom with Dathan and Abiram; let him obtain forgiveness only when the devil shall obtain it.

I therefore beseech the mercy of all kings and of all persons of rank in Christ: if, in a succeeding age—may this never happen, and, as is believed, it shall not—some abbot should arise in the monastery of Chartres who, driven by godless greed and seeking what belongs to himself rather than what belongs to Jesus Christ, wishes to desolate the monastery of Haurion described above, let him achieve no effect in his prosecution, and let the oft-mentioned little monastery remain permanently established.

So that the cause of this security may remain unshaken forever, with every dispute arising from fraud or claim marked by penalties, I presented it to my lord, to the duke, and to the other nobles in Christ, for confirmation. Finally, it was agreed that it should be written and preserved in both places in one wording and under the same arrangement.

The sign of Hugh, duke. The sign of Odo, count. The sign of Hugh, archbishop of the holy [Note: [Col. 0241C] Church.] of Bourges. The sign of Letgard, countess. The sign of Berta, countess. The sign of Gauzfrid, viscount. The sign of Hugh of the village of Aloya. The sign of Hubert. The sign of Avesgaud. The sign of Fulcher. The sign of Landric. The sign of Helgaud. The sign of Rodbert, who ordered this charter to be made. The sign of Suggerius. The sign of Rotroc. The sign of Harduin. The sign of Theudon. The sign of Gelduin. The sign of Isaac.»

[Col. 0242C] I have written in order, in this little work, as many charters as I was able to find that were written during the time of Abbot Wilbertus. Now I shall undertake to write those that appear to me to have been issued during the time of Abbot Gisbertus. [But I wish the reader to know that the blessed man Wibertus, when dying, ordered that his body be placed in the common cemetery, saying that, when the bodies of sinners are placed within the church, the punishments of their souls are increased in hell.]

# BOOK FOUR, OR THE BOOK OF ABBOT GISBERTUS  
*(From the year 984 to approximately the year 1001.)*

[Col. 0241]

## CHAPTER I. Concerning the privilege confirmed by King Lothar. (985)

[Col. 0241D]

«In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Lothar, by the favor of God king.

Just as, for those who contemplate the glory and beauty of God’s tabernacle in the present age, access to the house of his eternal life is opened, so without doubt for those who violate it the entrance to everlasting death will lie open in the abyss of hell; faithfully adhering to this hope, we rejoice in invisible truth, and clinging to it we are made firm. Therefore may the pious discernment of the universal Church of God and of all our faithful, both present and future in the age to come, know that our kingdom’s faithful men—namely Odo, bishop of Chartres, and the most illustrious count, our faithful man Odo, especially beloved among the others, together with his wife Berta, [Col. 0242D] our sweetest granddaughter—humbly approached the knees of our majesty. The illustrious duke and our faithful man Hugh also added his favorable entreaty, asking that we might deem it worthy to adorn with some gift of our serenity a certain monastery nobly founded, by God’s favor, in the suburb of the aforesaid city of Chartres, in honor of the most blessed chief apostles, Peter and Paul, where a considerable flock of monks was reputedly dwelling, practicing contemplative life according to a praiseworthy rule.

It is an excellent distinction, and by Christ’s favor it will remain so through generations of ages: the height of that monastery will always be in rejoicing, the glory of the monks in triumph, and the spiritual exultation of the people in jubilation. For [Note: [Col. 0243D] We have taken the words enclosed in brackets from a copy made by Dom Muley, who added in the margin of manuscript A: “The author passed over several lines here, which I inserted in my copy of 1774, having the original before my eyes.” Since these lines are likewise omitted in manuscript B, it is evident—as often elsewhere—that that manuscript was copied from manuscript A.] [the aforesaid faithful men earnestly desire that it be established forever by the foundation of our serenity. They have approached the suppliability of our highness with prayer and humble petition, being chiefly and especially inspired by a wondrously ardent love for the beauty of God’s house. The prayers of our aforesaid faithful and beloved count Odo, in whose town the aforementioned monastery is known to be situated, and likewise of his aforesaid wife Berta, our granddaughter, were also benevolently favorable, so that, for the eternal memorial of ourselves and of them, the cloister of the aforesaid chief monastery, with the full integrity of its appurtenances—namely, those things which, within the rights of the benefices or counties of our aforesaid faithful count Odo, whether near or far, appear to belong or pertain to the possession of the same monastery, or which in future may be bestowed there through the devotion of the faithful—might, by the advance of our firmness, be made free and exempt, as though protected by a wall and a kind of outer defense, from every exaction that earthly justice appears to demand.]

Therefore, piously considering the cause of God and the reverence due to that place, at the entreaty of our aforesaid faithful men, and especially at the humble petitions and likewise the benevolent consent of the above-mentioned faithful count Odo and his aforesaid wife, whose watchful solicitude, as has been said, has humbly devoted itself to the present anchor of our authority granted to the aforesaid monastery, we have, according to royal custom, decreed and established that the aforesaid oratory, with all its lands and possessions in every county or benefice adjacent to the properties of our often-mentioned faithful count Odo, shall remain universally free and inviolate from every jurisdiction of judges, as the order of the world proceeds.

This is on the condition that, from this day forward, with every power removed, no prince, ecclesiastical or secular, bishop, duke, count, vicar, or official of any kind may at any place or time impose on the cloister of the aforesaid monastery, or on all the things adjoining it as decreed above, any exactions whatsoever—whether ban, distraint, or anything else that may be called by any title of earthly justice.

Let both ecclesiastical and secular highness, present and future generations, with pious and prudent care, see to it that what we grant to the apostles of the highest rank—for the Savior’s most desirable love, for the complete removal of sins, and for the perpetual attainment of blessed hope—be preserved chastely and inviolably forever, with every malicious conception of claim entirely silenced, and defended for eternity by strengthening goodness. For the servants of God will devote themselves to prayer more attentively and freely if their hearts are not disturbed by lawsuits.

So that, in God’s name, this edict of our authority may rest on stronger force through the succession of ages, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it to be authenticated and ennobled by the impression of our ring.

—In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 987 [Note: [Col. 0244D] This should be corrected to 985, in agreement with the authors of Gallia Christiana, vol. VIII, instruments, col. 295.], in the thirty-first year of the reign of our lord Lothar, most glorious king. Executed at the palace of Compiègne. I, Arnulfus, notary acting in place of Lord Adalbero, archbishop and chief chancellor, have reviewed it.

The sign of Count Odo. The sign of Gelduin. The sign of Fulcher. The sign of Alcher. The sign of Theudon. The sign of Hubert and of his son Hubert. The sign of Odo. The sign of Hugh. The sign of Rainald. The sign of Erchembald. The sign of Gilo. The sign of Guascelin. The sign of Adrald. The sign of Hervé. The sign of Haimo. The sign of Nivelon. The sign of Rodbert.»

## CHAPTER II. Concerning Pomereda and Lovis Villa, given by Vivianus, brother of Fulcher. (988)

[Col. 0244D]

«The cause of divine mercy is singular and especially pre-eminent, because, in his kindness, our Savior, Lord, and God was pleased to provide and, by providing, to care for the frailty of human nature in such a way that in the divine books he has dispensed ornaments suitable to the healthy and remedies appropriate to the sick. Since it is impossible for anyone to escape the stain of corruption or to live free from sin in this corruptible condition, the pious and merciful one provided certain occasions or opportunities by which, through his favor, we might readily redeem our sins.

Among all of these, two remedies sweetly fragrant and especially familiar to the sick soul are those concerning which the voice of blessed Truth proclaimed: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven.” Obediently receiving the truth of so splendid a promise, and burning with zeal for the house of God, the immeasurable devotion of the faithful—most worthy of praise and imitation—has enriched the Church, as sons of the Church, by the most abundant generosity of their estates and has exalted it with many of their properties. Through these gifts, living by faith in the course of this age and awaiting with patience the stability of the eternal dwelling, the Church fully dispenses all that is holy, just, and pleasing to God, useful for various purposes.

They therefore already rejoice within themselves in hope of a more excellent glory, having fulfilled the apostle’s saying: “God loves a cheerful giver”; and that of the wise man: “The redemption of a man’s soul is his riches”; and: “He who gives to the poor shall never lack.” Also the Lord’s saying: “Nevertheless, give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you”; and: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin”; and: “Whoever does this for one of the least of mine does it for me”; along with many other examples of pious exhortation, of which, for the sake of brevity, we have mentioned only a very few out of countless examples.

Therefore I, Vivianus, desiring with all my strength that such great benefits and such splendid remedies of the most merciful Creator be granted to me, following the examples mentioned above, proposed in my heart and, by proposing, deliberated that from the resources of my estates I should appoint the holy Church as my heir, in faithful devotion, by the favor of Christ.

But because blessed Peter and Paul, brothers joined by the merit of glory in the citadel of holiness, are believed to shine with special brilliance and to gleam more splendidly than others, I entrusted myself to them wholeheartedly and placed myself entirely under their protection, since I could find no greater power for absolving crimes nor any more merciful soul for appeasing the anger of divine justice.

Therefore, for the redemption of my sins and for the repose of both my parents, namely my father and mother, with the consent of my brother Fulcher and of our faithful men, I cede to the monastery of Chartres, the place of the most blessed apostles of the highest rank, Peter and Paul, a certain estate of mine called Pomeraria, situated in the county of Chartres, with cultivated and uncultivated arable lands, woods, and pastures, together with everything that is known to be under my lordship there, both what has been discovered and what may be discovered, belonging or pertaining to the aforesaid estate, namely Pomeraria.

I also hand over to the aforesaid place, in the territory of Dreux, all of my share in Lovis Villa, whatever there appears to be in my possession or under my lordship. The condition is that, from this day forward, the monks serving God in the aforesaid monastery may hold and possess the aforesaid land and, with Christ’s favor, have entirely free power to do with it whatever they wish.

If anyone should rise against this charter of donation or attempt to bring any claim against it, let him be struck by the royal disease, punished with blindness of the eyes, and bring his present life to an exceedingly swift end in the most miserable death. Let him undergo everlasting damnation with the Devil, where, bound in chains of fire, he shall groan eternally; let the worm that never dies gnaw his flesh, and let the fire that cannot be extinguished remain forever his fuel and food.

So that knowledge of this transfer may rest on a perpetual anchor in Christ, for the redemption of my sins and for the repose of my father Fulcher, my mother Anstrud, and my brother Rodulf, already deceased, and for the safety and eternal reward of my brother Fulcher, I subscribed it with my own hand and presented it for confirmation by the hands and signatures of other noble men.

The sign of Odo, bishop of Chartres. The sign of Rodulf, dean. The sign of Solomon, subdean. The sign of Gerold, archdeacon. The sign of Count Odo. The sign of Countess Berta. The sign of Fulcher, Vivian’s brother, who made this donation. The sign of Gelduin. The sign of Teduin. The sign of Erchenold. The sign of Alo. The sign of Albert. The sign of Rotroc. The sign of Baldwin, cleric. The sign of Rodbert. The sign of Theudon. The sign of Einard. The sign of Arduin. The sign of Atto. The sign of Gradulf. The sign of Segenfred.

In the year 988 of the Lord’s Incarnation. Executed publicly at Chartres, in the presence of Lord Odo, bishop, and of the most noble Odo, [Col. 0245D] patrician. [Note: [Col. 0245D] Odo the First, count of Blois, son of Theobald the Trickster (978–995).] Also present were their faithful men of various orders and ages.»

## CHAPTER III. Concerning Bon Villa, given by Fulcher the standard-bearer. (Before 1002)

«Royal authority and the laws grant their assent that whoever wishes to assign something of his property to a house of God for the remedy of his soul should arrange to make the transfer publicly.

Therefore I, Fulcher, recalling that I have committed many offenses in the sight of God and his saints, for the redemption of my soul and that of my wife, my children, and my parents, hand over and [Col. 0246D] grant to the power of Saint Peter of Chartres, for the support of the monks over whom Abbot Gisbert appears to preside, the estate that I appear to possess in the village called Bon Villa, within or outside it, so that from this day forward they may have free power to do with it whatever they wish.

If either I myself, or any of my relatives, or any other interposed person should wish to violate this donation of my transfer or bring a lawsuit against the monks serving there, let him first be pierced by the anathema of malediction and excommunication, and moreover, compelled by public authority, let him pay fifty [Col. 0247A] pounds of gold.

So that this transfer might be strengthened with firmer force, I subscribed it with my own hand, with a stipulation clause attached.»

[Note: [Col. 0245D] This charter should be placed before the year 1002, as is shown by the name of Abbot Gisbert, who died in 1001.]

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning land given in the village called Thevas by Rotroc of Nogent. (Before 996)

«In the name of God, I, Rotroc, devoted to secular military service and faithful to Count Odo, make known to all, present and future, that Gisbert, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, and the entire congregation entrusted to him, asked me to grant to that place the land belonging to the church of Saint Hilary, which is in Thevas and pertains to the abbey of Saint Martin.

The land lies below the hill of the same little village and excludes the water. Therefore I agreed to their request, on the condition that every year, on the feast of Saint Remigius, which falls on the Kalends of October, they pay twelve denarii as the census. If they are negligent in this matter, let them make legal compensation, but let them not lose the aforesaid land.

So that this charter might obtain the support of my lord Odo and of all his nobles, I presented it for confirmation. Executed publicly in the city of Chartres.»

## CHAPTER V. Concerning Gunherius Villa, given by Countess Eldegard. (Before 987)

[Note: [Col. 0247D] Thus in the manuscripts; below, however, Guntherius Villa, today Gondreville.]

«The ineffable mercy of our Creator is worthy of praise and exceedingly worthy of proclamation. He redeemed us at the price of his blood and cleansed us from original sin by the water of sacred baptism. Foreseeing and foreknowing that, after all this, no one could live even for the space of a single day free from every sin, nor could anyone escape the stain of human corruption, he bestowed many remedies of salvation for the soul. By them not only are the diseased conditions of vices healed, but the joys of immortality are also acquired.

Among these, the generosity of almsgiving is of great value. Not only does the authority of many fathers attest to it, but it is also praised by the blessed voice of the Lord, who says: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven,” and: “Whatever you do for one of the least, you will do for me.” A certain wise man also says: “The redemption of a man’s soul is his own riches,” and: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you.” Many similar and especially important exhortations concerning the giving of alms are found elsewhere; it would be lengthy to go through them one by one.

Instructed by such exhortations, the praiseworthy devotion of preceding fathers—sons of the Church—endowed the same Church with many revenues from their estates and bestowed upon it many things useful for various needs. By these she is adorned throughout the fourfold world, her wealth is enlarged, and she rejoices and exults.

Following their examples, I, Eldegard, resolved in my heart to make the holy Church of God the heir to possessions from my estates. But because the power of binding and loosing was specially conferred upon the blessed apostle Peter, I judged that no one could offer me better counsel and that, for my sins, I should mercifully seek the intercession of him whom the Lord loved with so great a love.

Therefore, both to obtain pardon for my crimes and for my lord Walerannus, so that the Lord might deign to grant remission of sins to us both, with the consent of my son Count Walter, I cede to the place of Saint Peter of Chartres an estate belonging to me by right. My aforesaid lord, according to Salic law and according to the custom by which men endow their wives with property, had granted it to me as my own. It is called Guntherius Villa. From my lordship I perpetually transfer and copy it into the lordship of the monks serving there.

There are eight manors, each containing twenty bonuarii. If anyone should attempt, God forbid, to act against this donation, violate it, or bring any claim against it, let him incur the indignation of almighty God irrecoverably unless he quickly repent; and let him be thrust eternally into infernal torments, where the worm that never dies shall gnaw their flesh and the fire that never goes out shall forever feed upon their torments.

So that this donation might obtain inviolable firmness, I deemed it fitting to have it confirmed by the hands of Lord Hugh, duke of the Franks, and of the noble men sitting with him, with a stipulation clause attached.

Executed publicly at the castle of Pont-Isère.

The sign of Hugh, duke. The sign of Walter, count.»

[Note: [Col. 0248D] The Benedictine Annals, vol. IV, p. 3, assign the year 981 to this charter.]

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning Vileta, given by the knight Teduin. (984)

[Col. 0248C]

“By the gratuitous kindness of Christ’s clemency, desiring that the whole human race should come to knowledge of him, he is accustomed to touch their hearts in diverse and inscrutable ways—sometimes, namely, by granting them many prosperous things for a time, but now by changing their prosperity into different circumstances. For in one respect we are of heaven, in another of earth: insofar as we are earthly, we conduct earthly affairs; insofar as we are heavenly, we contemplate heavenly things in our minds. But, alas! in sorrow, weighed down by the wickedness of sins and the mire of filth, we forget the homeland toward which we ought to strive without end; and, in the pilgrimage of our sojourn, by continually adding iniquity upon iniquity, [Col. 0248D] we await the end of mortality while living badly.

“Struck by this fear in body and heart, I, Teduinus, resolved in my mind that, from the property that comes to me by maternal right, for the salvation of my father Adelard and my mother Eldegardis, and for the remission of the sins of my parents, I should solemnly donate and publicly hand over to blessed Peter of the monastery of Chartres—where the venerable abbot Gisbertus appears to preside—with the consent of my relatives, a certain alod called Vileta, and another in a different place called Duplex Curtis, together with everything belonging to them, including woods and meadows; and everything that up to this day I seem to have acquired or not yet acquired there.

“On this condition, however: that as long as I survive, they shall remain under my lordship, and every year, at the Mass of Saint Peter, I shall not neglect to pay the aforesaid monks twelve denarii as recognition; but after my death, without any contradiction, the aforesaid monks shall hold and possess them with all improvements. This donation of mine is in the county of Wastina, not far from Soisy castle. If anyone should presume to bring any action against it, let him first incur the anger of almighty God and be subject to perpetual malediction; moreover, let him be compelled publicly to pay a pound of gold to the person against whom he has brought the suit, and let his claim obtain no effect.

“But so that this charter may be believed the firmer and truer, I have confirmed it below with my own hand and delivered it to be strengthened by the hands of my lords and friends. Acted publicly in the city of Chartres. [Sign] of Hugh, archbishop of the church of Bourges. [Sign] of Odo, count. [Sign] of Gausfridus, count of Wastina. [Sign] of Rodulfus, knight. [Sign] of Adelard, Teduinus’s father. [Sign] of Teduinus, Teduinus’s maternal uncle. [Sign] of Hunbaldus, the same Teduinus’s maternal uncle.”

### CHAPTER VII. Concerning the meadows of Teuvas given by the knight Arnaldo. (Before 996.)

“ In the name of God. Arduinus, devoted to secular knighthood and faithful to Count Odo. Let it be known to all, present and future, that Gisbertus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, came into my presence with certain brothers, requesting that all the meadows and the water which a certain vassal of mine, named Arnoldus, appears to possess in the village called Teubas, from the estate of Saint Martin, be granted to him and to the aforesaid place. Considering their petition reasonable, I assented to their will, on the condition, however, that every year, on the feast of Saint Remigius, which falls on the Kalends of October, whoever holds the benefice shall pay two solidi as rent. If they should be negligent in this matter, let them make legal amends and not lose what has been granted.

“But so that this charter may be held firmly, I have delivered it to be strengthened by my hand, by that of my lord Count Odo, and by the attestation of his faithful men. Acted solemnly at Chartres, in the citadel. [Sign] of Count Odo. [Sign] of Arduinus. [Sign] of Arnoldus, from whose benefice the aforesaid gift proceeded.”

It must by no means be omitted that the rent written above was later remitted in its entirety to Saint Peter by Arnoldus’s successors, as were many others entered in ancient charters and later commuted by the successors of those to whom they had formerly been paid, for the reward of eternal life and on sound advice.

### CHAPTER VIII. Concerning Haimo and his two sisters, granted freedom, and concerning two arpents of land given by them. (1000–1001.)

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Gisbertus, by the mercy of God abbot of the monastery of Chartres. We wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy church that a certain man subject to our authority, named Haimo, came to us humbly asking that, after accepting from him a certain estate which he possessed in the village called Pinus, we should grant freedom to him and to his two sisters—one called Ermengardis, the other Roscelina—and to their children, remitting the head-tax owed by them.

“Because certain relatives of his were bringing a claim against this estate, we have taken care to commit to this present charter how it came freely into his possession, after they had amicably released it to him, and how, when he handed it over, we began to possess it. The aforesaid Haimo, born of a free father and a mother descended from our household, was being challenged by them concerning the share of the inheritance that his father had left him. At last, at his request, they were brought to this agreement: that if, after handing over the estate, he could be made a freedman, no further complaint would be brought against him on their part.

“Accordingly, we accepted in the aforesaid village two arpents of land, and in another place one; granting the aforesaid man and his two sisters, together with their children, freedom, firmly in such a way that from this day forward both he and his sisters, with their own children, shall be released from every servile obligation and payment of the head-tax. And so that no slanderer might presume to usurp anything against this arrangement, we caused the names of our brothers to be inserted.

“[Sign] of Gisbertus, abbot. [Sign] of Herbertus, abbot of Lagny. [Sign] of Durandus, dean. [Sign] of Arnulfus. [Sign] of Vivianus. [Sign] of Mainardus. [Sign] of Herbertus. [Sign] of Bernardus. [Sign] of Beringerius. [Sign] of Walterius. [Sign] of Gualdrus. [Sign] of Richerius. [Sign] of Marcuinus. [Sign] of Rodbertus. Acted at the monastery of Saint Peter, in the city of Chartres, while King Robert was reigning, in his fifth year. Alveus the monk wrote this.”

I have not refused to write out as many charters made under Abbot Gisbertus as I was able to find in our archives. Now my little pen attempts to proceed to those acquired during the time of Abbot Magenardus.

## BOOK FIVE, OR THE BOOK OF ABBOT MAGENARDUS

*(From the year 1001 to the year 1023.)*

[Col. 0251]

### CHAPTER I. Concerning the church of Rescolium given to Saint Peter by Count Richard. (Before 1024.)

“God, creator of all things, is wondrous in his works, since from some things he brings forth others, namely greater things from lesser ones. [Note: In Codex A, the words “vel perpetrat” are written above the line.] By considering this matter sincerely within ourselves, we owe him no small thanks for it, and in that matter—in heart, voice, and deed—the greatest thanks we can offer, because, as we have already indicated, he not only nurtures the eternal from temporal things, but also, by disposing of them rationally, mercifully advances them toward eternal things.

“To strengthen faith in this perfect and most desirable joy, among the other things that instill in mortals hope of holy eternity, Truth herself says through her own mouth: ‘Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.’

“Understanding this as his gift, and by his same will, I, Richard, count of the Normans, among the other things that, under his inspiration, I returned to him from his property, gave to the monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres a certain church situated in the county of Évreux, in a village called by the name Rescolium. I have entrusted this matter to these written lines so that it may serve the generous as an example and the rapacious as a warning. If anyone should make opposition to the aforesaid gift, then, as long as he persists in this intention, let him be punished by human and divine malediction.

“[Sign] of Count Richard. [Sign] of Archbishop Rodbertus [Note: Brother of Count Richard, archbishop of Rouen.]. [Sign] of Countess Gunnor. [Sign] of Richard, the count’s son. [Sign] of Rodbertus, the count’s son. [Sign] of Unfridus [Note: Codex B adds: ‘of Vetulabus.’].”

The aforesaid village was once called Rescolium because of the collection of goods: for there the goods of the fisc were collected or assembled. In it, not far from the river Arva, beside a certain spring, there stood a small wooden church dedicated to Saint Remigius. As time passed, however, both the village and the church were nearly destroyed by continual wars. Then, with the consent of Count Richard, the parish itself was joined to the parish of Saint George, whose church was not far away; and the altar of Saint Remigius was transferred by the monks into a wing of that church, where it remained [Note: B: “Until in modern times it was built larger, of cement and stone, by a monk named Hubertus.”], until it was built larger, of cement and stone, by the modern monks.

### CHAPTER II. Concerning the church of Wadonis Curtis given to Saint Peter by Rajenarius. (Before 1024.)

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Richard, duke of the Normans, wish it to be known to present and future generations that my vassal, named Rajenarius, came into my presence with the consent of his wife, named Wandelburgis, humbly asking that, for the salvation of my soul, or for the soul of his son, whose name was Rodbertus, or for the remission of his own sins, I should grant to the monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres a church in the county of Évreux called Wadonis Curtis. Considering the just petition of so important a man, I gave my assent, and further decreed that from this day and in succeeding generations none of his people, nor anyone else, should attempt with rash insolence to impose any right of lordship or any violence of intrusion upon the terms of this compact of our confirmation.

“And so that this charter might rest upon firmer authority in the name of God, I subscribed it with my own hand and delivered it to my faithful men for confirmation.

“[Sign] of Count Richard. [Sign] of Archbishop Rodbertus. [Sign] of Bishop Herbertus. [Sign] of Abbot Theodericus. [Sign] of the cleric Rodbertus. [Sign] of Rajenarius, who made this donation. [Sign] of Hunfridus of Vetulabus.”

Whether the monks of that time possessed or held the aforesaid church, I have no knowledge at all; for I have neither heard from the ancient monks that they possessed it, nor ever heard any mention of it from the modern monks.

### CHAPTER III. Concerning Blidun Villare, given to Saint Peter by the knight Teduinus. (Before 996.)

“[Note: This charter should apparently be assigned either before the year 996 or to the year 996 itself, in which Odo died.]

“In the name of God. I, Teduinus, with my wife, named Adalais, acknowledging that we have committed many offenses before the eyes of the Lord and his saints, for the remedy of our sins and of our parents’ sins—from whom we hold these possessions by right—, hand over and grant to the authority of Saint Peter of the monastery of Chartres an alod named Blidum Villare [Note: B: Blumvillare.], together with the enclosed grove; and, in addition, whatever we appear to possess there by hereditary right. Thus, after the death of either one of us, it shall pass by perpetual right into the possession of the monks of the aforesaid monastery who serve God there, and no one shall cause them disturbance on account of sons or relatives.

“If anyone should do so, let him be condemned by perpetual malediction and, moreover, compelled by public authority to pay fifty pounds of gold. But so that this charter may remain unshaken in the future, with the consent of the count and the nobles of that county, we have subscribed it with our own names.

“[Sign] of Count Odo. [Sign] of Countess Berta. [Sign] of the knight Teduinus, who made this donation. [Sign] of Gerardus, his son. [Sign] of Adalais, his wife, with their two daughters. [Sign] of the knight Fulcherius. [Sign] of Arduinus. [Sign] of Gelduinus. [Sign] of Rodbertus. [Sign] of Rodulfus, cleric.”

### CHAPTER IV. Concerning the alod of Sclusella, given by Gausfridus and his son Joscelinus. (Before 1024.)

“Since it remains written and sanctioned in the decrees of the ancients that, if any noble layman honors a church or monastery from his own inheritances, or makes a donation, he may under no circumstances reclaim it either through a son or through any successor [Note: Thus in the manuscript.], I, Joscelinus, son of Gausfridus, wish it to be known to all, present and future, how and for what reason, concerning the things that had been left and handed over by my father to Saint Peter of the monastery of Chartres, after his death I came to Lord Abbot Magenardus and the whole congregation of that place.

“My father Gausfridus, for the salvation of his sins, assigned to Saint Peter an alod named Exclusella, in the county of Dourdan, on the river Auvre, while I was a child and my mother was alive. I sought this alod, not because I wished to withdraw it from the venerable place to which it had been given, nor in order to possess it by any fraud, but on these terms and under this agreement: that as long as I lived I should pay two solidi as rent at the appointed time and render the required service; and that it should never be lawful for me either to sell it or to hand it over to anyone—whether to a son or to any of my relatives—but that, as long as I breathed, it should remain in my hand and under my lordship.

“After the end of my life, so that my father’s memory may be greater and I may have a share in his good deed, not only what my father donated, which I now hold, by the gift of Lord Abbot Magenardus and the other lords, but everything together with what is in it—namely, mills, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, and woods—shall pass to the same place from which I received it, for the use of Christ’s servants.

“And so that this might occur without any claim or contradiction, I have taken care to commit it to writing, especially so that none of my successors, nor even a son, if I should have one, might claim it for himself. I have also delivered it to my lord, the illustrious Count Odo, and to his nobles, to be confirmed, so that what has been inserted may remain firm and unshaken forever.

“[Sign] of Count Odo. [Sign] of Berta, his mother. [Sign] of Agnes, her daughter. [Sign] of Count Walterius. [Sign] of the knight Gausfridus. [Sign] of Herveus, viscount. [Sign] of Rodulfus. [Sign] of Gausbertus. [Sign] of Albertus. [Sign] of Wascelinus. [Sign] of Sulius. [Sign] of Joscelinus, who arranged for this charter to be confirmed. [Sign] of Gausfridus, his knight.”

### CHAPTER V. Count Odo’s agreement concerning Bosco Medio. (Before 1024.)

“Let it be known to present and future generations that an agreement was made between Count Odo [Note: Odo II, count of Chartres, married his first wife, Mahildis, in 1005; his second wife was Ermengardis of France, daughter of Robert I, count of Auvergne, whom he married in 1020.] and the monks of Saint Peter.

“For the aforesaid monks possess a certain land in the county of Dunois called Bosco Medio. A dispute had arisen concerning part of it between the men of that count and the men of Saint Peter, and that part was divided between them by oaths and judgments. Concerning the portion that belonged to Count Odo, the aforesaid count, for the salvation of his soul, made an agreement with Abbot Magenardus and the monks of that place that he would return it to them—on the condition, namely, that the aforesaid count should hold it only during his lifetime, and that the monks should have one tenant in vestiture; but after the death of the aforesaid count, the aforesaid land should remain with the same place.

“And so that this agreement might be firm between them, the count ordered this document to be made; and so that it might remain valid and firm forever, he strengthened it with his own hands and delivered it to be strengthened by the hands of his faithful men.

“[Sign] of Count Odo. [Sign] of Ermengardis, his wife [Note: In Gallia Christiana, vol. VIII, col. 1220, Abbot Magenardus is conjectured to have died in 1013; but from the subscription of Countess Ermengardis, and also from the fact that Adrefastus withdrew into the monastery of Saint Peter after the council held at Orléans in 1022, while Magenardus was still abbot, it appears that this abbot’s administration should be extended to the year 1023.]. [Sign] of Queen Berta. [Sign] of Agnes. [Sign] of Ivo. [Sign] of Rainoldus, vicedominus. [Sign] of Nivelo. [Sign] of Wascelinus. [Sign] of Landricus the Generous. [Sign] of Gilo. [Sign] of Tedbaldus, layman. [Sign] of Odo. [Sign] of Gausbertus. [Sign] of Siebodus. [Sign] of Walterius. [Sign] of Tedbaldus, cleric.”

This agreement was not carried out at all. For, killed by the sword of the Lotharingians, he was unable to fulfill the agreement, and his sons are not known to have possessed the aforesaid land for their own use. The knights who possess it also assert that the same land, together with the adjoining woodland, was given by Count Odo to Walterius of Alogia [Col. 0255A] in the battle of Pontlevoy [Note: That battle was fought at Pontlevoy, in Touraine, on the day before the Nones of July in the year 1016.], where he fought unsuccessfully against Fulk [Note: Byname Nerra.], count of Anjou.

“Whether they speak truthfully or not, I am not certain. Yet I know that the tenant who, as stated above, was given by the count to the monks for their investiture remains under their authority to the present day.

“The land of which I am speaking is bounded on the eastern side by a great woodland, of which we appear to possess as much as a bow can shoot, together with those who share the same land with us. On the western side it is divided by a certain road; beneath that road, as far as the water called Edera, the entire land has from ancient times been subject to the authority of the monks; and as far as the spring called Meidlai, from which no woman can draw water without going unpunished—for it is said that one woman once dared to do so rashly and immediately lost her sight. On the other side lies the land of Buxedulus, which is also known to have been subjected by the modern monks to their authority by right of purchase.

“Nevertheless, I cannot keep silent about the aforesaid agreement and what I have often heard from the account of Lord Rodbertus, formerly our monk and abbot of the monastery of Fosses. For when the furnace of his heart was greatly kindled by the fire of indignation, it was necessary for the smoke of that fire to leave by some opening, so that it might rise to the heights. Therefore I shall openly report what I remember hearing from that man.

“For he related that at that time the monks possessed a certain village not far from the castle called Provinus, and that it itself was called Guuiz. In the aforesaid agreement, Abbot Magenardus, together with all the brothers, immediately gave it to the count so that, after the count’s death, they might possess the portion of the land mentioned above, joined to the remaining land that was theirs by hereditary right.

“In this matter, abandoning the rest as uncertain, they followed the habits of a dog holding a morsel of meat in its mouth. Its greed is seen to be so great that, while crossing the water of a river, when it sees the shadow of meat on the riverbed, it runs with open mouth toward the shadow that it will never be able to seize, and loses the morsel, which is carried away by the flowing water.”

### CHAPTER VI. Concerning Tesneriae and Grossus Testiculus given to Saint Peter. (Before 1024?)

“[Col. 0255D] In the name of Christ. I, Ermentrudis, first the wife of Erchembaldus and afterward of Bernardus, wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy church, present and future, how I hand over and perpetually transfer for possession to the same Saint Peter—namely, to the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres—the alods that I possessed in the county of Chartres, near Pomeriata, the land of the monks of Saint Peter, at the request of my knight Hunverus, for the soul of my son Solio, for my lord Bernardus, and for myself.

“These are the alods of which we speak, near Pomeriata, the land of the monks of Saint Peter: one is called Tesneriae, and the other, adjoining it, has an obscene name, yet is commonly called Grossus Testiculus. On one side they are bounded by the aforesaid land of Saint Peter, namely Pomeriata; on another by Saint Martin of Chartres; on the third side by the land of Sigenfredus, the man of Fulcherius; and on the fourth by the land of the sons of Guazo.

“Within these boundaries I grant the alods to Saint Peter on this agreement: that every year, on the feast of Saint Maurice, they shall pay two solidi in denarii as rent to the aforesaid Unverus, or to those to whom the benefice shall pass. If they are negligent in paying, let them make legal amends and not lose what we give; but let them build securely above it and possess it forever.

“And so that this record may be firmer for all ages, I have confirmed it with my own hand and delivered it to be strengthened by the hands of my knights.

“[Sign] of Ermentrudis. [Sign] of Ermentrudis, her niece. [Sign] of Unverus. [Sign] of Erma, his wife. [Sign] of Raherius, his son. [Sign] of Aremburgis, his daughter. [Sign] of Adalais, his daughter. [Sign] of Ebrardus, his nephew. [Sign] of Hugh. [Sign] of Odo. [Sign] of Giroldus. [Sign] of Drogo. [Sign] of Osmundus. [Sign] of Bernardus. [Sign] of Teudo, son of Unverus. [Sign] of Solio. [Sign] of Rorigo. [Sign] of Gerardus. [Sign] of Rainerius. [Sign] of Roger. [Sign] of Guido. [Sign] of Berio. [Sign] of Germundus.”

This rent, written into the charter, is known to have been remitted, since it is now neither paid nor demanded by anyone.

### CHAPTER VII. Concerning Jerani Villare granted by precaria to the knight Gradulfus, and Palisiacum given by him in compensation. (Before 1024.)

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity—that is, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Fulbertus, by the grace of God bishop of Chartres, and Magenardus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter, and the congregation of the brothers.

“We wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy church, present and future, how a certain knight named Gradulfus came before us and humbly requested that we make him a precaria of a certain piece of land belonging to our aforesaid monastery, while he, in compensation, would assign one of his alods for our use—on this condition, namely, that as long as he and his wife, named Oda, in whose dowry the aforesaid alod lies, lived, they should hold both; but after their death, both should remain with the brothers.

“We willingly assented to his requests, with the consent of Count Odo, in whose county both lands of which we speak are situated. Our land, which he asks to hold by precaria, lies in the county of Chartres and is called Jerani Villare; the alod that he gives in compensation lies in the county of Dourdan [Note: Thus. B: Dorcasini.], on the river Blesis, and is called Palisiacum.

“Accordingly, we grant our land of Jerani Villare by precaria to the aforesaid Gradulfus on these terms: that as long as he and his aforesaid wife Oda live, they shall hold both; but after their death, both the land that we give and the aforesaid alod shall pass peacefully and securely to the use of the brothers.

“It was further agreed that this agreement of ours should be written in two charters, one of which the aforesaid knight should have, while the other should remain with us. And so that this record may remain firm, we have set down our names and subscribed the names of Count Odo and of those who took the greatest part in this transaction.

“[Sign] of Bishop Fulbertus. [Sign] of Count Odo. [Sign] of Abbot Magenardus. [Sign] of Durandus, dean. [Sign] of Arnulfus. [Sign] of Marcuinus. [Sign] of Richerius. [Sign] of Beringerius. [Sign] of Waldricus. [Sign] of Letaldus. [Sign] of Christophorus. [Sign] of Gausbertus. [Sign] of Guinefredus. [Sign] of Otbertus. [Sign] of Hubertus. [Sign] of Rodbertus, and of the others.”

After Gradulfus and his wife Oda died, the monks suffered many wrongs from the relatives of the aforesaid persons, who said that what their parents had formerly been seen to hold belonged to them by right. Therefore, after paying an immense sum of money, the monks finally, with God’s help, recovered the lands for their own use.

### CHAPTER VIII. Concerning Agneis Villa. (Before 1024.)

Concerning Agneis Villa, I was unable to find any documents in our archives apart from those transcribed below. Hence, as I infer, no others were made; but through these, the persons to whom the land had been exchanged by Count Odo made a gift to Saint Peter and the monks, and these documents have been preserved to the present day as evidence of the land given. The documents are as follows:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Odo, count of Chartres. We wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy church, and to our successors, present and future, that a certain cleric named Ledbertus, together with his brother Heribertus, petitioned us to exchange for them a certain alod in place of the inheritance they possessed in the county of Sens, and requested that we have the security of written documents strengthened for them. I did so.

“The aforesaid alod is in the county of Dunois, in a place called Agneis Villa. Two fields with a well belong to it; in another place, two fields, and two arpents of arable land; in a third place, at the well of Sichardus, one arpent; and in a fourth place, called Budelea, one arpent.

“The aforesaid alod is bounded on one side by the alod of Ragenardus; on another by that of Hugh; on the third by the public road; and on the fourth by the land of Saint Florentinus. We have also given the aforesaid persons the right to sell or give it to whomever they wish.

“If anyone—which we believe will by no means happen—should wish to rise against or violate this authority, let him incur the anger of God, and let him fail to prevail in what he claims; but, compelled by judicial authority, let him pay a pound of gold to the person against whom he has brought the action.

“But so that this charter may be firmer, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and the sign of the cross, and offered it to our faithful men for strengthening.

“[Signs:] Odo, count; Ledgardis, countess; Rotrocus; Gelduinus; Rotbertus; Hugh; Landricus the Generous; Albertus; Gilo; Nivelo.”

Among the charters issued during the time of Abbot Magenardus that I found written [Note: This epilogue is absent in Codex B.], I have taken care to insert at the beginning of this work the account written by Lord Fulbertus, afterward bishop, so that it may be clear to all that not only simple but even highly learned men are often deceived by ambition for fleeting goods.

[Note: This writing of Fulbert is found in Bouquet, *Recueil des Historiens de France*, vol. X, p. 444.]

While the abbot of Saint Peter was seriously ill, though still in possession of his mind and speech, the monk Magenardus—previously not a little dear to me—secretly slipped away from the cloister at night and hurried to Count Tedbaldus, who was then staying at Blois, in order to seek the abbacy. The next day the count sent him back to us with envoys who announced that he was to be received with honor, as abbot, by the canons and monks.

But to almost all of us this matter seemed equally strange and horrifying. We therefore replied that it appeared to us quite otherwise: he could not legitimately become abbot, nor ought he to be received—one who, while another abbot was still alive, sought his abbacy out of ambition; who was not elected by the brothers and yet attempted to rule over them; and, finally, who was neither our monk nor our cleric and had more witnesses for conducting courtly affairs than for living the monastic life.

Receiving this unfavorably, he rode back to the count and violently inflamed the young man’s anger against us. But on the fifth day after he had publicized his ambition, the aforesaid abbot brought his illness to an end by death.

Our monks and certain canons whom reason required to be admitted assembled in the chapter. We asked whether any of the brothers favored Magenardus’s undertaking. Each denied it; all denied it. We decided that some of them should be sent to the count—who had been designated our bishop—to announce the death of Father Gisbertus and ask for permission to elect another according to the rule.
