When these men had been sent, behold, two others, Vivianus and Durandus—one uneducated, the other ill-versed in letters—both provosts, pretending that for the sake of the common good they wished to go out to their obediences, followed Magenardus, although the monastery’s dean had forbidden them to go elsewhere. They had secretly persuaded him to pursue the undertaking he had begun, and at Blois, in the presence of Lord Tedbaldus, they deceitfully claimed that Magenardus had been requested and elected by the brothers.

Delighted by their support, the count immediately and publicly presented him with the pastoral staff. When the brothers who had remained in the cloister heard this, armed with zeal for divine law against the fraud, they composed and subscribed the following document of rejection:

“Let every church know that we do not elect Magenardus to become our abbot; we do not approve him, we do not want him, we do not consent; rather, we reject him, repudiate him, [Col. 0259A] and altogether oppose him—namely, we whose names are subscribed, of the monastery of Saint Peter.

“Durandus, dean. Genesius. Isembertus. Alveus. Richerius. Herbertus. Benedictus. Rodbertus. Evrardus. Arnulfus. Marcuinus. Warinus. Walterius. Guarnerius. Beringerius. Waldricus. Bernardus.”

All these men either subscribed their names or ordered them to be subscribed, in my presence.

On the following day Count Tedbaldus returned, but sent ahead word that he was to be received into the monastery in procession. The monks replied that they would gladly do this if he did not bring that usurper with him. Although he was again angered, he endured it that day; but on the next, amid the din of those accompanying him, he forced his Magenardus into the monastery of Saint Peter.

At his violent entrance, the holy brothers, fearing contamination through association with him, saluted the Lord’s sanctuary with tears and went out; knowing no other refuge, they fled to the threshold of the principal church. There too, deprived of both shepherds, the sheep consoled themselves with sorrowful cries. But the holy Mother of God received them with her customary compassion. Dean Rodulfus received them with gentle kindness. From there they went to the monastery of the holy father Herbertus, whose abundant charity, from its poor revenues, supplied them with whatever necessities it could.

Meanwhile, that brother whose importunity had driven them away was, as they say, made a pretended abbot by a certain Hervise, bishop of the Breton region, on the fourth day before the Nones of February, in the suburbs of Chartres, in the absence of the clergy, to the indignation of the people, while the archbishop’s legate openly opposed the act and some of the monks who had remained in the place also protested, with true expression, living voice, and canonical authority.

Even now that man, relying on secular power and exulting in the victory he has achieved, occupies the foremost place on the abbatial seat, relying on secular power, and, by courting abbots, bishops, and even the pope, works by every means to prevent any more serious sentence from being imposed upon him.

Meanwhile the humility of the expelled brothers lies defeated and confounded, and there is no prelate in Gaul whose heart compassion moves or whose zeal for sacred law inflames him to rise up to break the assaults of error and to restore the hopes of those wasting away in grief. For the strength of Dionysius has died; the compassion of Martin does not appear. You too have abandoned us, holy Father Hilary, who once defended the unity of the church with the sword of the Holy Spirit.

“O abandoned, sorrowful, desolate church of Gaul! What hope of further salvation will there now be? Where will the afflicted Christian soul breathe freely again? This alone, or at least chiefly, seemed to comfort us: that if it should happen that we could not repair the ruins of your walls, we might at least take refuge in the still-secure citadel of the monastic life. But if even that may be entered by thieves or invaded with impunity by any ambitious persons, alas! you have fallen utterly.

“Therefore, returning now to you, venerable father, whom I believe—and see—to have been provided by the Lord as our helper, together with my lord and your faithful servant Rodulfus, I beseech and implore you, by the holy spiritual gifts of wisdom granted to you, by the sweetness of fraternal charity: if you can do anything, attack the enemies of the Lord, cherish the stricken brothers, and do not allow those for whom you believe Christ’s blood was shed to perish through lack of your consolation.”

Meanwhile the count went to Rome for the sake of prayer [Note: In the year 1004.]. Returning from there, he died on the journey as a pilgrim and was carried by wagon to Chartres, where, with great weeping, he was laid in the chapter house of Saint Peter at the feet of his brother Theodericus.

Then, after Dean Rodulfus had been elevated to the episcopate by King Robert, the zeal of bitterness—shortly before suppressed by fear of the count—was vehemently inflamed against Abbot Magenardus, and proceeded so far that they wrested the pastoral staff from him by force of authority and made him remain for several days in the bishop’s house.

But after they observed him spending the night in vigils and prayer, lucid in speech, and powerful in learning, they set aside the dispute and, with joyful hearts, returned to him both the pastoral staff and the abbatial office. As long as the breath of life accompanied him, he fed the sheep entrusted to him abundantly with a twofold nourishment.

After his death, before he was restored to his mother, Arnulfus, the sacristan, was appointed in his place by Bishop Fulbertus. Let our truthful pen therefore turn to the charters enacted in his time, so that, gathered together chapter by chapter, the diligent investigator may quickly find whatever he seeks.

## BOOK SIX, OR THE BOOK OF ABBOT ARNULFUS

*(From the year 1023 to the year 1033.)*

[Col. 0259]

### CHAPTER I. Concerning the *guerpum* of the church of Ursi Villaris. (Before 1028.)

[Col. 0259D]

* “[Note: [Col. 0259] This charter appears in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, instruments, col. 491.] Established in my time under the eternal rule and supreme priesthood of Christ, [Col. 0260D] I, Odolric, bishop of Orléans, wish the manner and outcome of the case written in this charter to be known to my contemporaries and successors.

[Col. 0261A] The monks of the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres had long possessed a certain church in the county of Dunois, in a place called Ursi Villaris. But one of our casati, named Hilduin, together with his relatives, brought a claim against them concerning that church, saying that it belonged to our casamentum and to his benefice. He also asserted that, in the time of my predecessors, he had pursued this claim diligently but had been unable to obtain justice.

We therefore summoned Lord Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, and Arnulf, abbot of Saint Peter, so that they might grant us a hearing concerning this case. They did so once in the same village called Ursi Villaris, and again in the village called Castanetus. When the dispute had been examined on both sides, we found that [Col. 0261B] the monks’ claim was supported by written evidence, witnesses, and long possession to such an extent that, under no law of Christians, could the aforesaid church be taken from their possession.

Therefore, unwilling to contend against right and justice, I, Odolric the bishop, my brother Isembard, and the aforesaid Hilduin, together with his sons and other relatives, have wholly renounced—*gurpivimus*—the claim begun against the monks of Saint Peter, consenting that they possess their church of Ursi Villaris securely and peacefully forever, as we have found to be just.

I have also forbidden, by the episcopal authority entrusted to me by God, that any of our successors should thereafter disturb the aforesaid monks of Saint Peter through any such sacrilegious claim. If any rash person should presume to violate this prohibition, [Col. 0261C] let him make lawful satisfaction for the sacrilege of his presumption and, once punished, desist from what he has begun. But if he should stubbornly prefer to persist in his hateful claim, let him be struck by the anathema with which God, when angered, condemns the incorrigible. So be it, so be it.

We who have renounced the aforesaid claim caused our names, and those of our faithful who were present, to be recorded in this charter for remembrance.

Sign of Odolric, bishop of Orléans.  
Sign of Fulbert, bishop of Chartres.  
Sign of Albert, abbot.  
Sign of Isembard, layman.  
Sign of Erfredi, cleric.  
Sign of Salo, cleric.  
Sign of Bovo, dean of Saint Martin of Tours.  
Sign of Tescelin, cleric.  
Sign of Tedoin, cleric, son of Alberic.  
Sign of Hilduin, layman.  
Sign of Hilduin, his son.  
Sign of Odolric, his son.  
Sign of Pontelin, his nephew.  
Sign of Godefrey, layman.  
[Col. 0261D] Sign of Adrold, viscount.  
Sign of Frederick, layman, brother.  
Sign of Hugh Radoard.  
Sign of Gualo, layman.”

## CHAPTER II. Concerning the possessions that Count Richard gave to Saint Peter. (Before 1028)

* “[Note: [Col. 0261D] Published by Mabillon, *Saecula Benedictina* VI, part I, p. 282.] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Richard, most humble count of the Normans, while listening to the Scripture of the Catholic faith expounded through words of exhortation, silently considered with myself the condition of this transient and perpetual acquisition—that is, of the secular and heavenly kinds—and which of them was more excellent and more secure. Then, through the illumination of divine [Col. 0262A] grace, I understood that in the one there is the movement of wandering, while in the other there is the calling to stability.

Likewise, it became clear that my elevation to dominion of such authority was not a concession of human but rather of divine power, and that it had been granted for no other reason than the defense of holy mother Church and the establishment of the rule of public justice.

Having learned these things through rational inquiry, I feared that the Gospel saying, ‘Every tree that does not produce good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire,’ might be applied to me as an unfruitful man, if I did not deserve to become an inheritor of heavenly acquisition through the production of the fruits of good works, and if I did not recall the congregation of holy Church to better things by the example of integrity.

Mindful also of what is said—‘Having gifts [Col. 0262B] according to the grace that has been given to you’—I resolved to give to God a portion of the possession divinely granted to me, since one who stores up treasure in Christ does not fail to know for whom he will gather it.

Therefore let it be known to all Christ’s faithful how I, the aforesaid Richard, for the remedy of my soul and those of my parents, gave to Saint Peter of the monastery of Chartres and to the monks serving there a certain hospitable reception-house, with its land and other furnishings, in the village of Lereti, in the county of Coutances, called Techvilla, together with its church, mills, and all its appurtenances, to remain perpetually according to the customary arrangement in place of the former provisions.

In the county of Lesuin I also gave a fishery in the river Tolca, from Saturday evening through the whole of Sunday; and in [Col. 0262C] the Seine, continuously by day and night, from first light on Saturday until the same hour on Monday, eight stretches of my fishing-weirs—namely, two at the port of Danes, four at the port of Guellebod, and two in the ditch of Helluin.

Furthermore, so that in all commercial transactions conducted anywhere under my authority they should pay no toll, I have perpetually remitted that payment for the love of Christ.

In the village of Cadon I also gave the monks of the aforesaid monastery a certain dwelling with all its internal and external appurtenances, on the condition that, from these and the other possessions mentioned above, they should have free power to retain them without the harassment of any opposition.

Sign of Count Richard.  
Sign of Countess Gonnor.  
Sign of Richard, her son, count.  
Sign of Robert, the same count’s son.  
Sign of William, his son.  
Sign of Rolderic, cleric.  
Sign of Robert, archbishop.  
Sign of Herbert, bishop.  
Sign of Theoderic, abbot.  
Sign of Hunfrid.”

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the possessions that the monk Arefastus gave to Saint Peter. (Before 1028)

“In the name of the Lord. I, Arefastus, wish it to be known to all Christians that I grant the possessions of my inheritance to Saint Peter of the monastery of Chartres, for my salvation and that of my ancestors, and also for the salvation of Count Richard [Note: [Col. 0262D] This concerns Count Richard II, who died in the year 1027.] and his mother Gonnor, and [Col. 0263A] of the sons of both of them, with whose counsel and favor I do this.

These possessions are in the county of Coutances, in the province of Normandy, divided among various places, whose names are written below.

In the village called Hams, a sixth part of all the revenues that issue from it, namely from the churches, the woodland, the open land, and the marsh, excepting the mill and the weir that Roger had constructed. Nevertheless, whenever the brothers to whom I grant these things wish, they may grind at that mill without restriction, provided that the mill’s lord has not found his customary grain there; they shall pay no profit from it.

I also grant two fisheries in the water of the same village, whose name is Uldra [Note: [Col. 0263D] Perhaps the Orne, as Dom Muley conjectures.]. In the same village I grant three resident knights with their benefices, [Col. 0263B], whose names are Rollo, Angoht, and Unbeina, so that they may render free service from them.

I also grant a third part of Torgis Villa, except for the two tenants, Suedan and the black Anschetil, together with their two salt-pans, whom I granted to my nephew Bosolin so that from this he might render free service to Saint Peter. The salt-pans of the other tenants, with their holdings, which they possess in that third part of Torgis Villa, shall belong to Saint Peter.

I also grant one fishery at sea to Saint Peter, and one mill in the village called Barna Villa.

If anyone belonging to the aforesaid monastery, whether abbot or administrator, should sell or give away any part or the whole of this donation, he shall be compelled to render an account to Saint Peter, to whom I give it and from whom he takes it. Amen.”

[Col. 0263C] It must be made known both to those now living and to those to come that we, Arefastus’s contemporaries, neither possessed nor knew of the three knights whom he says were to serve us in Ham Villa, except for one alone, named Roger, who, as I believe, holds seven acres of land as a benefice from the monks.

His nephew Bosolin, whom we knew well, also held in Turgis Villa what appeared to be held from us and had been given by his uncle. But he became so burdened with thefts and other wickedness that he abandoned the whole benefice to us and lived for a considerable time with his entire household in a certain hut—*croto*—beside the enclosure that the venerable Abbot Landric built around the monastery, dependent upon the monks’ provision.

Again [Note: [Col. 0263D] This account of the Manichaeans is absent from manuscript B. It was published in *Scriptores Francorum*, vol. X, p. 536.] I have considered it worthy of being committed to memory [Col. 0263D] how the aforesaid man, Arefastus, through divine aid and the salutary sharpness of his own intellect, detected and completely suppressed in the city of Orléans a heretical depravity that was secretly springing up and already distributing the deadly poisons of a criminal error throughout the provinces of Gaul.

He was of the family of the Norman counts, polished in speech, prudent in counsel, and adorned with good morals; consequently he was very well known in the office of ambassador both at the court of the Frankish king and among the nobles.

It is said that this man had in his household a certain cleric [Col. 0264A] named Herbert, who had decided to go to the city of Orléans for the sake of study. But while he diligently sought teachers of the truth, he fell blindly into the abyss of complete heresy. For at that time two clerics in the same city, Stephen and Lisoius [Note: [Col. 0264D] Or Lisovis, since the manuscripts offer both readings], were considered by everyone distinguished for wisdom, eminent in holiness and religion, generous in almsgiving, and highly esteemed by the common people.

The aforementioned cleric sought them out, and within a short interval, as a teachable pupil, he was intoxicated by them with the sweetness of the divine word, but with the deadly breath of wickedness. Seized by madness and diabolical error, deprived of all divinity, he believed that he had climbed the citadel of wisdom.

Returning to his homeland, he gradually tried, [Col. 0264B], by subtly admonishing his master with skillful words, to draw him along with himself into the path of error. He testified that the city of Orléans shone above all other cities with the light of wisdom and the lamp of holiness.

From his words his master perceived, with intellectual discernment, that he had strayed from the way of justice. He quickly made the matter known to Count Richard and asked him to reveal by letter to King Robert the pestilence still lurking in his kingdom before it spread, and to ask the king not to deny Arefastus suitable assistance for expelling it.

Thus the king, astonished by this unexpected matter, ordered that the same man, together with his cleric, should promptly direct his steps to the city of Orléans, promising him every kind of assistance in this affair.

As he traveled at the king’s command, he came to Chartres to consult the venerable Bishop Fulbert about the matter. Fulbert happened at that time [Col. 0264C] to be absent, for he had gone to Rome for the sake of prayer.

Arefastus then made the purpose of his journey known to a certain learned cleric named Ebrard, keeper of the archives of the church of Chartres, asking for the help of his counsel: how he ought to stand in the battle line and with what weapons he should arm himself against the many arts of diabolical deceit.

Using wise counsel, Ebrard instructed him to visit the church devoutly every day at first light to seek the aid of the Almighty, to devote himself to prayer, and to fortify himself with the most holy communion of the body and blood of Christ. Then, protected by the sign of the holy cross, he should go confidently to hear the heretical depravity. He was not to contradict anything he heard from them, but, adopting the appearance of a disciple, was to commit everything silently to the chamber of his heart.

[Col. 0264D] When Arefastus arrived at Orléans, he followed the instruction he had received. Every day, fortified by holy communion and humble prayer, he came to their teaching and, like an inexperienced disciple, sat inside the house of the heretics in the last place.

When they had first instructed him with examples from the divine books and with certain comparisons, and saw that, like a perfect disciple, he listened attentively with bowed ear, among their other comparisons they presented him with the likeness of a woodland tree.

‘You must be treated by us,’ they said, ‘like a woodland tree which, transplanted into a garden, is watered for so long [Col. 0265A] until it takes root in the soil. Then it is cleansed of thorns and superfluous growths, so that afterward, cut down to the level of the earth with a hoe, it may be grafted onto a better shoot, which will later become fertile with honey-sweet fruit.

‘In the same way, transplanted from the wicked world into our holy fellowship, you are watered with wisdom until you are formed. Then, through the sword of God’s word, you will be able to rid yourself of the thorns of vices. Once the tasteless teaching of your heart has been expelled from its cavern, you will be able to receive with a pure mind our teaching, handed down by the Holy Spirit.’

For his part, he always gave thanks to God for every word they spoke. Thus they thought that he had been converted to their error, and, secure in this belief, they opened the cesspool of their wickedness, previously covered over with words from the divine books.

They said that Christ had not been born of the Virgin Mary [Col. 0265B], had not suffered for humanity, had not truly been placed in the tomb, and had not risen from the dead. They added that baptism brought no washing away of crimes, and that, in the priest’s consecration, the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood was not present. They considered it worthless to invoke holy martyrs and confessors.

When these lost and most wretched men were vomiting forth these and other abominable things from their foul hearts, Arefastus is said to have spoken to them as follows:

“‘If, as you say, there can be no salvation for human beings in any of the things you have listed, I earnestly ask you to reveal to me in what things salvation may be hoped for, lest my mind, placed in uncertainty, quickly fall into the ruin of despair.’

“‘Without doubt, brother,’ they replied, ‘until now you have lain with the unlearned in the Charybdis of false opinion. But now, [Col. 0265C] raised to the summit of complete truth, you have begun to open the eyes of an undivided mind to the light of true faith.

“‘We open to you the doorway of salvation. Entering through it, you will be cleansed of every stain of sin through the laying on of our hands and will be filled with the gift of the Holy Spirit, who will teach you without hesitation the depth and true divinity of all the Scriptures.

“‘Then, nourished with heavenly food and refreshed through inward fellowship, you will often see angelic visions with us. Sustained by their consolation, you will be able to go with them, wherever you wish, to any place without delay or difficulty. Nothing will be lacking to you, because God, the companion of all, will never be lacking to you; in him are the treasures of wisdom and riches.’”

Meanwhile, King Robert and Queen Constance, as the aforesaid man had [Col. 0265D] instructed, came to the city of Orléans with a college of bishops. On the following day, at his own suggestion, the entire most wicked congregation was dragged out by the royal officials from the house where they had gathered and brought into the church of the Holy Cross before the king and the assembly of bishops and clerics.

But before we come to the confrontation, I shall explain to those who do not know by what art that food which they called heavenly was prepared.

On certain nights they gathered in the designated house, each holding a lamp in his hands, and, in the manner of a litany, they recited the names of demons until suddenly they saw a demon descend among them in the likeness of some small animal.

As soon as [Col. 0266A] that visible apparition appeared, all the lights were extinguished, and each man seized the woman who came to hand, as quickly as he could, in order to abuse her, without regard for sin. Whether she was regarded as a mother, sister, or nun, they esteemed intercourse with her to be an act of holiness and religion.

From this most filthy intercourse a child was conceived. On the eighth day, after a great fire had been kindled in their midst, it was purified through fire in the manner of the ancient pagans, and thus burned in the flames.

Its ashes were gathered and guarded with such veneration that Christian religious practice ordinarily accords to the body of Christ, to be given as viaticum to the sick who are about to depart from this world.

For such was the power of diabolical deceit in those [Col. 0266B] ashes that whoever had been imbued with the aforesaid heresy and had tasted even a small amount of those ashes could scarcely ever afterward direct the step of his mind from that heresy onto the path of truth.

Let it suffice to have said little about this matter, so that worshipers of Christ may guard themselves from such a wicked practice, not so that they may imitate it by following it. But since I seem to have made a digression, let the narrative now return to the matters I left aside, and let it briefly run through the cruelty of the unbelievers, lest a lengthy discussion of the controversy produce weariness for the delicate reader.

Accordingly, when they had been brought before the king and the assembly of bishops, Arefastus first addressed the king, saying:

“‘My lord king, I am a knight of Richard, your most faithful count of Normandy, and undeservedly I am held bound and chained before you.’”

[Col. 0266C] The king replied:

“‘Quickly tell us the reason for your coming, so that, once it is known, you may either be held in chains as guilty or, if innocent, released from your bonds and sent away.’”

He answered:

“‘Having heard the wisdom and religion of these men who stand bound with me before you, I wished to come to this city so that I might return improved by the example of their good works and their teaching. This indeed is the reason why I wished to leave my homeland and seek this city. If I am held guilty of any offense on account of this undertaking, let the bishops assisting you see and judge.’”

Then the bishops said:

“‘If you present us with the manner of wisdom and religion that you learned from them, our judgment will easily discern the matter.’”

He replied:

“‘Let the royal majesty and your authority order them to state before you the things they taught me, so that, when you have heard them, they may either be judged worthy of praise or consigned as unworthy to oblivion.’”

[Col. 0266D] When the king and the bishops ordered them to reveal the standard of their faith by explaining it, those enemies of all truth, saying one thing in place of another, refused to enter by any opening into the filth of their heresy. But just as a serpent slips away all the more the more tightly it is held in the hands, so these men, the more they were hemmed in by the discourse of truth, appeared to escape all the more precariously.

Then Arefastus, seeing that they were buying time and hastening to obscure the error of their faith with a shield of words, turned to them and said:

“‘I thought that you possessed teachers of truth, not of error, when I saw you steadfastly teaching me the doctrine that [Col. 0267A] you proclaimed as saving, and when you promised that, even under the infliction of punishments and in the face of death, you would never deny it.

“‘But now, as I see, having forgotten the faith you promised, you wish, through fear of death, to distance yourselves completely from that doctrine, and you think little of leaving me, still an inexperienced disciple, in danger of death.

“‘Therefore the king’s command must be obeyed, and it is right to submit to the authority of such great bishops, so that, if anything I learned from you is contrary to the Christian religion, I may recognize through their judgment what must be followed and what must be rejected.

“‘You taught me, indeed, that no forgiveness of sins is obtained in baptism; that Christ was not born of the Virgin; that he did not suffer for humanity; that he was not truly buried; that he did not rise from the dead; and that the bread and wine which, through the operation of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0267B], appear to be made a sacrament by the hands of priests upon the altar cannot be converted into Christ’s body and blood.’”

When Arefastus had spoken these words aloud, Guarinus, bishop of Beauvais, asked Stephen and Lisoius, who appeared to be the teachers of this error, whether they thought and believed what Arefastus had recounted.

But they, already having a dwelling prepared for themselves with the devil in hell, firmly asserted that what had been recounted was true and that they thought and believed it so.

When the bishop said to them that Christ had wished to be born of a virgin because he was able to do so, and to suffer in human nature for our salvation, so that on the third day, having conquered death, he might rise again in his divinity [Col. 0267C] and teach us that we too would rise again in the renewal of our nature, they replied with viperous mouths:

“‘We were not present, nor can we believe that these things are true.’”

But [Note: [Col. 0267] So in the manuscript, for *ad haec*.], the bishop questioned them, saying:

“‘Do you believe that you had human parents, or not?’”

When they asserted that they did believe this, the bishop replied:

“‘If you believe that you were begotten from parents, although you did not previously exist, why do you refuse to believe that, before the ages, God was begotten from God without a mother, and that at the end of time he was born from a virgin through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit?’”

They answered:

“‘Whatever nature denies is always at variance with the Creator.’”

The bishop replied:

“‘Before anything came into being through nature, do you not believe that God the Father, through the Son, made all things from nothing?’”

Alienated from the faith, they said:

“‘You may tell these things to those who think and believe earthly things, and who believe the fictions of carnal men written on little pieces of animal parchment [Col. 0267D]. But to us, who have the law written in the inner person by the Holy Spirit and think of nothing except what we have learned from God, the creator of all, you present useless things that deviate from the Divinity.

“‘Therefore bring your words to an end and do whatever you wish to us. Already we see our king reigning in the heavens, who lifts us with his right hand to immortal triumphs and grants us heavenly joys.’”

From the first hour of the day until the ninth [Col. 0268A], everyone labored in many ways to recall them from their error, but they, harder than iron, did not repent at all.

They were ordered to put on sacred vestments according to their respective orders, and immediately the bishops deposed them from their proper honors. At the king’s command, Queen Constance stood before the doors of the basilica so that the people would not kill them inside the church. Thus they were expelled from the bosom of holy Church.

As they were being expelled, the queen gouged out the eye of Stephen, once her confessor, with the staff she was carrying in her hand.

Then they were led outside the walls of the city and, except for one cleric and one nun, were burned in a certain hut after a great fire had been kindled, together with the wicked powder of which we spoke above. The cleric and the nun, however, repented by divine prompting.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the church of Fontinido, which Archbishop Robert made free. (In the year 1033)

[Col. 0268B]

* “[Note: [Col. 0267] Published in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, instruments, col. 297.] With God and our Lord Jesus Christ presiding, we decree—I, Robert, by the grace of God archbishop of Rouen, and our fellow bishops Herbert of the city of Lisieux, Robert of Coutances, Radbod of Sées, and Hugh of the city of Évreux—we decree, I say, and establish that, from this day forever, the church of Fontinido shall be removed from every disturbance by either bishop or archdeacon, for the love and honor of Saint Peter, prince and teacher of the apostles.

“In the same manner as the cell of Gesiacum belonging to the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres is subject together with that church, so it shall remain secure [Col. 0268C] from every exaction and disturbance, with only these three exceptions: namely, the reconciliation of that church, the reception of oil and holy chrism, and the reconciliation of penitents.

“All these things, whenever necessary, shall be requested from the bishop in whose diocese it lies, and shall be provided by him freely and without any demand for or payment of a reward, for the honor of Saint Peter, so that the power and mercy of our aforesaid teacher may deign to absolve both us and our successors from every yoke of sin.

“And so that this notice may remain unshaken, we have strengthened it with our hands, and have confirmed it by our sign and names. We have also presented it to Guascelin, the archdeacon who was directly responsible under me, [Col. 0268D] to be sealed and confirmed, and to our other clerics and laymen.

“But if any Antichrist should attempt to violate this work of piety, which we have fashioned in the name of God, let him be slain by the sword of anathema from the mouth of the true Christ and of all of us whom he has deigned to call his Christians.

“We decree that this mark—or, so to speak, this seal—be subscribed by the individual names of each of our fellow bishops.

“Robert, archbishop, who began and completed this work of piety.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning Abbot Arnulf’s recompense. (In the year 1033)

* “[Note: [Col. 0269D] This charter is published in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, instruments, col. 298.] In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. I, Brother Arnulf, abbot—although unworthy—of the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres, [Col. 0269B] together with the brothers entrusted to me, wish it to be known to our successors that, in return for the charity and great kindness which the archbishop of Rouen, Lord Robert, worthy of cherished memory, has shown to our place and to us for the honor of Saint Peter, we have established the following.

“He removed forever from the church of our monastery all violence by the archdeacon and his successors, as is contained in our archive: namely, a written document which the frequently mentioned Archbishop Lord Robert caused to be written in his presence and gave to us to preserve forever.

“For this benevolent charity, then, we wish it to be known that we have gratefully established and decreed that, for the sake of his soul, from this day forever, one poor person shall have his feet washed every day, [Col. 0269C] be fed, cared for while alive, and buried when dead.

“On appropriate days, the psalm ‘May the Lord answer you in the day’ shall be sung for him in the full community; every week a Mass shall be celebrated especially for him with the full community.

“For he bestowed many other benefits upon us besides these, and may the one God who lives and reigns in perfect Trinity repay them all to him with his most benevolent hand.

“And so that this recompense may remain firm forever, we have confirmed it with our hands and names, and have ordered it written for our successors in our golden Gospel book, as an inviolable testimony.

“Arnulf, abbot.  
Ebrard, monk.  
Beringer, dean.  
Richerius, monk.  
Marchuinus, monk.  
Gausbert, monk.  
Robert, monk.  
Hubert [Col. 0269D], monk.  
Letald, monk.  
Roger, monk.  
Guinefred, monk.  
Berard, monk.”

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the allod of Hot Mountain (*Calidus Mons*) [Note: [Col. 0269D] B: “Concerning the allod of Beautiful Mountain (*Bellus Mons*).”]. (Around the year 1020)

* [Note: [Col. 0270D] This charter has been made publicly available in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, instruments, col. 295.] “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, namely, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Among Christian peoples, praise of the Catholic and true mother Church always flourishes and shall flourish forever.

“This most worthy and just fact is evident: she is our mother and the bride of Christ our Lord, whom he acquired with his precious blood. [Col. 0270A] In her we are reborn through the washing of baptism; in her we rise from the death of the soul through the grief of repentance; and after the end of life our corpses are buried in her atrium.

“Christ founded her upon the faith which the most faithful Peter confessed when he said to the Lord: ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.’ For no one can lay another foundation except that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus.

“Blessed are those who dwell there by living as Catholics, as David sang: ‘Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they will praise you.’

“Instructed and admonished by these and many other sayings, by the words of the saints and the mysteries of sacred Scripture, I, Hildegard, viscountess of Châteaudun, give to Saint Peter [Col. 0270B] of the monastery of Chartres my allod at Beautiful Mountain (*Bellus Mons*), with its cultivated and uncultivated lands, and the woods and fisheries belonging there, with the consent and approval of my son Hugh, archbishop of Tours.

“I give it on this condition: after my death, I shall be buried in the monks’ cloister, so that those who pass by my tomb may always pray continually for me.

“The nobles of Châteaudun whose names are written below saw this and gave their consent.

“But if anyone from my lineage, or any other invader, goaded and pierced by the devil’s spurs or arrows, should use force against the monks and in any way take away the alms which I gave to Saint Peter, let him, condemned by eternal condemnation, perish with Dathan, Abiron, Annas, and Caiaphas; and by the authority of my son, Archbishop Hugh, let him remain anathematized. [Col. 0270C]

“Hugh, archbishop.  
Gausfrey, his nephew.  
Hubert.  
Godescalc, his son.  
Hubert, treasurer of Le Mans.  
Radulf, learned in law.  
Fulcald.  
Gathon.  
Odo Brunel.  
Hubert Brunel.  
Helgaud, the archbishop’s son.  
Helgaud the Black.  
Gradulf.  
Firmatus, canon.  
Frederick.  
Hugh, vicar.  
Bernard of Buslo.  
Junanigus, by command of the archbishop, made this charter.”

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the mill-weir rights of Anet. (Before 1034)

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, namely, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I, the knight Urso, son of Germund of Aisy, wish it to be known to all Christians, present and future [Col. 0270D], that I relinquish from this day to Saint Peter the half-share in the weir-rights—*exclusatio*—of the mills of the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres which are at Anet.

“My grandfather had given this share to Saint Peter and my ancestors had confirmed it, but through evil counsel I had brought a claim against it. I now leave it quiet to Saint Peter, so that I too may have a share in the alms of my ancestors.

“And so that this notice may remain firm, you, lords of the castle of Évreux, in whose presence I do this, are witnesses to Saint Peter. I have confirmed it with my own hand and presented it to those to whom it belonged for strengthening.

“Sign of Urso, [Col. 0271A] son of Germund, who ordered this charter to be made.  
Sign of Germund, viscount.  
Sign of Hugh, clerical provost.  
Sign of Gervin.  
Sign of Aitard, Germund’s brother, who made this charter.  
Sign of Odo, son of Ascelin Bordet.  
Sign of Hugh, his brother.  
Sign of Bodo.  
Sign of Odo, son of Ragenad.  
Sign of Borgeret.  
Sign of William, son of Guascelin, properly named Achard.”

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning land given in the village called Pinus. (Before 1034)

“In the name of Christ. I, the knight Guarinus of the castle of Dreux, son of Alberic, knight of Ragenold the viscount, wish it to be known to all Christians, present and future, that I give to the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres, presided over by the venerable Abbot Arnulf, for the sake of my soul and those of my parents, my allod in the county of Dreux, at the village called Pinus, [Col. 0271B] as much as is sufficient for two oxen for all sowings.

“This is on the condition that, as long as I live, I shall hold that land, while Saint Peter shall have the investiture, a share of the fields, and the tithe from me as from an outsider.

“And so that this notice may be firmer in every respect, I placed this charter with my own hands upon the altar of Saint Peter, in the presence of those whose names are written below and many others.

“Afterward, at Dreux, in the presence and with the consent of my lords Ribald and Ansold and of my kinsmen who were present, I had it read aloud; and I installed a monk of Saint Peter in the allod on Saint Peter’s behalf, while he put me out, as is customary.”

In the aforesaid village, after many years had passed, a certain monk of Saint Peter named Hildegarius bought a considerable portion of land from the farmers there.

That most famous Guaszo also bought from them, with money paid, the sites of houses and small courtyards of the village, because of their shortage of food; he gave them to Saint Peter for the salvation of his soul and caused the farmers to live at Saint George’s.

[Note: [Col. 0271D] This account is absent from manuscript B.]

Finally, having finished writing the charters that I knew would be useful, I thought that those should be omitted in which, by recalling them, no present benefit seemed to be gained. But concerning the blessed man, namely Abbot Arnulf, under whose rule we know that the aforementioned charters were made, I deemed it worthwhile to record the evils that he suffered from members of his own household in his old age.

He had been a monk from childhood and had been thoroughly educated in monastic studies. Conducting his youth chastely and daily adorning it with good works, he deserved, after Abbot Magenard, to be consecrated and appointed to govern the abbey by Lord Bishop Fulbert. His life and innocence shone so brightly at that time that he was greatly loved by Odo, the palatine count, and became the confessor of Richard, count of Normandy, whose honors he often enjoyed. Among these, Richard gave him the church of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, with its dependencies. But afterward Arnulf lost it through the insatiable greed of certain monks whom he had placed there. The church itself is situated not far from the walls of the city of Rouen.

Since each day the monks mentioned above received in the count’s kitchen a tenth of the fish [Col. 0272A] from the cooks, or from the fishermen on the bank of the Seine, they considered it unworthy either to eat the fish or to send it to their brothers at Chartres; instead, publicly receiving its price from the buyers, they put it into their own purses. As a result of this conduct, the reputation of the Osi [reading uncertain] spread throughout all the people of the city to the count, by whom they were ordered to leave the place because of this disease of avarice.

The abbot, however, as long as he lived, permitted no one in any way to deviate from the path of the Rule. With him leading the way, all followed the Rule as their mistress and daily abounded in various works in the Lord. Hence the devil, always envious of the most prosperous actions, frequently stirred up undeserved injuries against the blessed and simple man through certain of them whose minds were easily influenced.

But since it would be lengthy to go through them individually, I wish to bring one of these into the open: the injury that the enemy of the human race inflicted upon him through Walter, the monastery’s dean. Although Walter was regarded as honorable in ecclesiastical studies, in worldly affairs he readily followed the inclination of his heart. Together with his supporters, he arranged with Theodoric, then bishop, that the devout and excellent monks should be expelled from the monastery: namely Ebrard, abbot of the castle of Bréteuil, who was then present there and for certain reasons had left his abbey at that time; and Guinefred, Durand, Arefast, and Ernald.

These men, above all, wished to uphold the strength of the Rule with the abbot, and the abbot used their counsel wherever and whenever it was needed. When matters had finally reached this point, the bishop [Col. 0272C] came to the monastery with a large crowd of clergy and laymen. Sitting before the altar of blessed Peter the Apostle, he ordered the church’s golden vessels, silver vessels, and other ornaments to be recorded on wax tablets; then he commanded the aforementioned monks to leave the monastery.

The abbot, following the footsteps of the pious shepherd, declared that if the bishop expelled them, he himself would depart with them and endure all their hardship. But the bishop, paying little attention to his words, returned to his own house.

Accordingly, on the eighth day, the abbot left the monastery with the aforementioned monks. All the people followed him with weeping, and, relying on no small degree of equity, he withdrew to the cell at Gizy. After remaining there for three months, he returned to his abbey through Odo the count and was received with due honor. Living happily there for nearly three years afterward, an old man and full of days, he deserved to receive from Christ the Lord the reward of his labors, one that would endure without end.

When they were digging the ground inside the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle, namely before the altar of the martyr Laurence, on the left of Robert, son of Count Richard, having no sarcophagus, they found one there, as I believe, prepared by God—of marvelous beauty, as though it had been polished by stonemasons that very day and fitted to the blessed man’s body. His limbs rest there, secure in the hope of the glory of the resurrection.

On the third day after he died, he appeared in a vision to Lord Abbot Ebrard, who had already returned to his own abbey, and said to him:

“Dearest brother, know that I have been rescued from the storms of this world and now enjoy blessed rest; but know also that those who hated me will not rejoice for long.”

And so it happened. For some of them departed this life in that same year, while those whom the world retained alive were always treated harshly and cruelly by the disturbed vicissitudes of time.

Nevertheless, since I have shed little light on the life of the blessed man, my pen must now turn to the charters made under Abbot Landricus [Note: [Col. 0273A] In manuscript B the scribe corrupted this passage and added it at the end of the book of Abbot Landricus; moreover, he changed “under Abbot Landricus” to “under Abbot Hubertus”; [Col. 0274A] and between “unless” and “hinder” he added “under Bishop Arraldus.”], the successor, that is, of the aforementioned Abbot Arnulf. How diligently he watched over the growth of the place entrusted to him through additions of property during his tenure will be shown by the large number of charters, unless the altered vicissitudes of time obstruct it—vicissitudes that displeased us, drove the abbot from the place, disturbed us all, and, installing in the monastery certain men expelled for particular reasons, raised them over us against our will. But since this must be endured with equanimity, although by a slow and winding path, as I am far away and receive these materials from ignorant men in disorder, I shall try to write them out as best I can.

# BOOK SEVEN, OR OF ABBOTS LANDRICUS AND HUBERTUS

(From the year 1033 to the year 1069; from the year 1069 to the year 1079 [Note: [Col. 0273D] We gathered into one book the charters issued during the times of these abbots, which are reported in the manuscripts in confused and disordered sequence.])

[Col. 0273]

## CHAPTER I. Concerning the Royal Chapel

(Before 1070.)

[Col. 0273B]

“In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. I, Landricus, abbot of Saint Peter of Chartres, and the entire community entrusted to me, wish it to be known to those present and to those to come that we approached the presence of the lady Berta and her sons Walter the cleric, Hervé, Hugh, Tedbald, Sigebod, and Engucia, asking that, for the redemption of her soul and those of her sons and daughters, she grant us the land of the Royal Chapel, which is next to our land of Bois-Moyen, together with the church and two mill-sites and everything belonging there.

“She most willingly consented, together with her sons and daughters [Col. 0273C], on the condition that they obtain the consent of our lord Count Tedbald, from whose grant it appears to derive, and that they make it free from all claims that might arise there. And this was done in the presence of those whose names are subscribed below.

“Our lord Count Tedbald consented that this should be done, for the salvation of his own soul and that of his father, and with his own hand and the names of his faithful men he confirmed this little document.

“Signature of Count Tedbald. Signature of Gilduin the viscount. Signature of Hugh the vice-count. Signature of Hervé the viscount. Signature of Ivo the cleric. Signature of Fulcher, son of Gradulf. Signature of Ilbert, son of Nivelon. Signature of Albert, abbot of Saint Martin. Signature of Richer, abbot of Saint Launomar. Signature of Viger of Castanet. Signature of William. Signature of Warin. Signature of Herbert the cleric of Imonis Villa. Signature of Hermuin [Col. 0273D], mayor of Bois-Moyen. Signature of Berner, priest. [Col. 0274B] Signature of Walter of Bodacis Villa. Signature of Hubert, stepson of Adventus. Signature of Girard the cook. Signature of Morard. Signature of Hugolin the servant.”

## CHAPTER II. Concerning the Altar of the Royal Chapel

(Before 1048.)

* “[Note: [Col. 0274D] Published in Gallia Christiana, vol. VIII, instruments, col. 298.] If it is acknowledged to be an act of piety and religion, for the praise and glory of the highest and eternal King, to show honor to churches established by the faithful in honor of martyrs or confessors, how much more should honor be shown to those established in memory of him upon whom the catholic Church was founded, to whom also the authority of binding and loosing is known to have been entrusted by the heavenly Creator, when the keys of heaven were committed to him?

“Therefore, for the acquisition of eternal happiness—which, through the intercession of the prince of the apostles, we hope more easily to obtain from the liberator of souls—I grant the altar situated in the church called the Royal Chapel to the church of Chartres, established in memory of the aforesaid apostle, for the support of the monks serving God there [Note: [Col. 0274D] B: ‘I, Bishop Theodoricus, grant.’]. It is granted on this condition: from this day forward and throughout succeeding time, it shall remain free from every obligation and payment, from the synodal dues, from every debt or levy, so that neither we nor our successors may ever presume to demand, receive, or reclaim any of these things from the Royal Chapel.

“And so that the generosity of our liberality might be known to all the faithful of holy Mother Church, we order it to be written out with the greatest care and diligence, so that what we have established with our own hand, impressing the sign of the cross, [Col. 0275A] may remain firm and unshaken through the course of succeeding time.

“And if anyone should attempt to violate any small portion of this alms—may it not happen!—let him incur the wrath of God; and, convicted by our authority and that of all our successors, let him depart. For his unlawful presumption, let him grieve forever, pierced by the sentence of the Judge who is to come at the end of the ages and cast into the lower hell under perpetual anathema.

“Bishop Theodoricus, who gave this donation. Arnulf, precentor. Agobert, succentor. Fulcher, archdeacon. Hildegarius, subdeacon. Hugh, provost. Guiddo Rubeus. Robert. Berner. Ingelrannus.”

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the Claim against the Same Royal Chapel

(Before 1070.)

[Col. 0275B]

“We, Landricus, abbot, and the entire community of our brothers, wish it to be known to all Christians, present and future, that we had purchased the Royal Chapel from the matron Berta and her sons and daughters for a fixed sum of money, as the document written above shows; afterward her son-in-law Raherius, namely the husband of Engucia, brought a claim against it.

“For this reason we summoned him to Chartres before Count Tedbald. At the urging of the count himself and his nobles, we promised him forty Chartrain solidi in coin, so that he would withdraw the claim that he was bringing before the count. He willingly did so.

“Afterward, through the monk Paul, we sent him forty solidi in coin [Col. 0275C]. He received them at the castle of Blois, in the village of Vienne on the bank of the Loire. Within the castle, before the church of the Mother of the Lord, he publicly renounced the claim, together with his wife Engucia, their only son named Rainald, and their two daughters, namely Berta and Adelina. There he ordered this document to be drawn up and wished to confirm it with his own hand and with the hands of all his people, in the presence of his neighbors and kinsmen.

“Raimund of Vienne. Theodoric of Saint-Brice. Gausfrid, son of Archembald. Pila de Lupo. Rainald of Calidus Mons. Hervé. Burchard. Haimeric the dean. Hubert, son of Gislard. Gunter, son of Andrew. Herbert, son of Teduin. Robert the cleric. Hubert. Bernard. Ernulf Niger, servant [Col. 0275D] of Paul [the monk who wrote this charter].”

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the Ban of Bermerii Villa

(Before 1038.)

“With the Lord Jesus Christ, creator of all things, presiding, I, Odo, by the grace of God palatine count, following the generosity and kindness of my parents—which their many properties and great gifts bestowed upon the place of Saint Peter of Chartres attest that they held toward it—wish it to be known to all the sons of holy Church, present and future, that, among the other benefits that I have conferred, with the consent of my faithful men I also grant to the same place the ban of Bermerii Villa, which I restore, and likewise any other customary dues belonging to me, if it is ever recalled that they existed there.

“Now, on the fifth day before the Ides of July, I preferred publicly to place a branch of savin as a gift upon the altar of Saint Peter the Apostle, for my salvation. And so that this charter might remain unshaken, I ordered it to be confirmed in my name and in the names of my faithful men, so that, if anyone should ever attempt to oppose this gift of mine, they may stand against him and force him, troubled and confounded, to depart without accomplishing anything.

“Odo, palatine count. Sansgualo, seneschal. Hugh of Melius. Hilduin of Ramerud. Hugh Tronellus. Fulco the vice-count. Hugh of Versailles. Ingelger of Islar.”

## CHAPTER V. Concerning the Restoration of Villula

(Before 1061.)

[Col. 0276B]

* “[Note: [Col. 0275] Published in Gallia Christiana, vol. VIII, instruments, col. 302.] In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. I, Landricus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, together with the brothers entrusted to me, wish it to be known to the worshipers of holy Church, present and future, that I approached the presence of Gausfrid, count of Anjou, surnamed Martel, lodging with him a complaint concerning his nephew Gausfrid, count of the territory of Gastinois. The latter had unjustly given to one of his knights the land called Villula, formerly given to Saint Peter by the knight Teduin, and had taken it away from Saint Peter by usurpation.

“When the aforesaid count heard this, he was displeased and, correcting the matter that had been wrongly handled, immediately restored the aforesaid land to Saint Peter. He ordered this document to be confirmed in his own name and in the names of his leading men.

“Gausfrid, count of Anjou. Bartholomew, archbishop of Tours. John of the castle of Chinon, brother of the archbishop. Ivo Mala Corona. Theodoric, son of Unberga. Rainald of the castle of Gunter. Richard of the castle of Landon. Guidbert. Godefrid, son of Ansgard. Ralph of Malli Villa.

“From our side: Gausfrid Bicotus. Gilduin, mayor. Landricus, mayor. Walter the cleric.”

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the Vicariate of Ermenteria Villa

(Before 1070.)

[Col. 0276D]

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, creator of all things. I, Landricus, by the grace of God abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, and all the brothers over whom I appear to preside, wish it to be known to all the faithful of the present and future age that, after our predecessors had purchased from a certain knight, the father of Roscelin, the village of Ermenteria, then uninhabitable, together with its church, free from every customary due—as is written in our archives—except for two solidi in coin for custody and pasnage, the same Roscelin, overcome by an irreverent and foolish disposition, was not ashamed, after the sale, to usurp the vicariate of that village.

“Eventually, coming to his senses at his death, he restored it to Saint Peter, with the consent of his household, for the remedy of his soul. His son Teduo afterward, on the wicked advice of his men, again seized the same vicariate at the sound of the church bell.

“Nevertheless, after many prayers by the monk Warin, he was persuaded to abandon the vicariate that he had unjustly seized, having received ten solidi in coin for it. Hugh of Manselaria and Walter Cristallus of Senunches were with him.

“Then Lord Albert, son of Ribald, taking advantage of an opportunity, appropriated to his own use the aforementioned two solidi, together with the pasnage, and the vicariate itself. After holding it for several years, he restored this same vicariate to Saint Peter the Apostle, to be possessed in perpetuity for the salvation of his soul [Col. 0277A], and donated the aforementioned two solidi, with their pasnage, to a certain faithful man, Isnard of Mori Villare.

“The witnesses of this matter are: Guado, Hugh of Drocais, Herbert of Burseries. Dodo, seneschal.”

Below we shall speak of the possessions added to our place by a most noble man named Albert.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the Possessions and Church Given to Saint Peter by Albert, with the King’s Consent and Charters

(Before 1061.)

* “[Note: [Col. 0277] Edited in Gallia Christiana, vol. VIII, instruments, col. 301.] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Henry, by the grace of God king of the Franks. Although the royal throne of dignity is adorned by the manifold cultivation of virtues, liberality and generosity nevertheless hold a pre-eminent place among them, since their effects stoop to the needs of many and satisfy the petitions of the just.

“Let it therefore be known to all the faithful of holy Mother Church and to our own people, present and future, that one of my faithful men, named Albert, namely the son of Ribald, a most noble man, approached the presence of our serenity, asking and earnestly requesting that, by graciously lending an ear to his prayers through the royal piety of our generosity, we might deign to incline ourselves to his petitions, so that what he was preparing to fulfill under divine inspiration might be brought to completion with the consent of our liberality.

“Specifically, he wished that a certain church, which his father, our faithful Ribald, had built in the village of Bruerolis in honor of Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, through the work of masons and for the salvation of his soul, might, by royal will, be given by him to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to the monks serving him in the monastery situated not far from the walls of the city of Chartres. He also wished that both he and his faithful men might freely enrich the aforesaid church, for the love of God, with possessions that he appeared to hold from our grant.

“Judging his petition to be just and acceptable to God, we considered it fitting, for our salvation and the integrity of our kingdom, to grant his request, together with Bishop Agobert, in whose diocese that church lies, and with our nobles who were present with us.

“We therefore give him permission both to enlarge the aforementioned church from the property that he possesses by our grant [Col. 0278A] and to make whatever donation or grant he wishes to it, so that it may be free and exempt from every judicial authority, just as our faithful Albert has hitherto held it free and exempt from us. Thus the monks serving God there may lead a peaceful life, without disturbance from any secular person, devoting themselves night and day to prayers and other good works.

“It has therefore pleased our serenity, by royal authority, to prohibit anyone at any time from presuming rashly to oppose this work of our generosity, which we have set down in writing; nor may anyone dare to diminish, whether greatly or slightly, the possessions that our faithful Albert has already given or will give to the aforesaid church, or those that other people have given. Let no one burden the people of this church with corvées, or with a ban, toll, vicariate, or any exaction, or harass them in any way. Rather, free from every customary due owed to secular men, let them dwell securely and freely, serve the monks of the aforesaid church, and pay their due obligations.

“If any presumptuous or mad person should rashly attempt to do anything against this authority of ours, let him pay fifty pounds of gold, and let his attempt remain ineffective.

“It has also pleased our piety to add to this work and subscribe this charter, made at the command of our faithful Albert, concerning the possessions that he has already given to the aforesaid church and that he has decided to leave to it after his bodily death, as well as the other gifts that his faithful men have bestowed with his consent, so that, confirmed at the end with our name, the names of our leading men, and the seal of royal dignity, they may remain valid and inviolate forever.

“Scripture in the divine books bears witness that all secular things are rushing toward destruction, while heavenly things endure eternally in the opposite direction. It therefore commands the faithful, redeemed by Christ’s blood, to attain nobler things by giving up lesser ones.

“Therefore I, Albert, son of the most noble Ribald, desiring to obtain a share in heavenly things, with the favor of my beloved wife Adelaisa, grant to Saint Peter of the monastery of Chartres, for our souls and those of our parents, the church in the village of Bruerolis, free from every claim by all men, which my father built in honor of Saint Germanus the bishop, together with its churchyard and burial ground [Col. 0278D] and the tithe of that church, which appears to be in my possession. From this day forward, let the monks of that monastery have, hold, and possess the same church forever.

“I had always held the altar of the same church in fief from the bishop of Chartres. My lord Bishop Agobert, together with the consent of the canons who were with him at Drocais, in the king’s court, has added it to this gift of mine, persuaded by the petition of Abbot Landricus and by ours.

“Likewise, I grant the customary due of the village together with the market-tithe, and everything of every kind of vegetable or fruit that may be received by market right, as well as the handful of salt collected from each salt-worker [Col. 0279A].

“Likewise, two parts of the oven in that village, apart from which there is no other oven in the whole village.

“Likewise, beyond the head of that church, I grant two agripennia of land and meadows that I appear to have held under that village, and the land of Walter Costatus, which he held while he was provost. I also grant the adjoining wood.

“As for the land that is cultivated for me, together with the adjoining wood, when I leave this wicked age alive or depart from it in bodily death, let the monks of the aforementioned monastery possess it as their own and cultivate it by possessing it, dwelling there and praying for all of us in the aforesaid church.

“Finally, in the wood called Saint Remigius, I annually grant the monks the pasnage for their pigs, and one agripennium where the monks’ swineherds, when they sleep there with their pigs, may have a domestic lodging [Col. 0279B].

“I also grant all my men permission to enrich and adorn the aforesaid church, for the sake of their souls, from the possessions that they appear to hold from my grant, just as Walter, surnamed Palardus, has already done [Note: [Col. 0279D] Concerning Walter’s grant, see below, chapter XIV, col. 284]. He granted half the land of Bulfiniac for the support of the monks for the sake of his soul; after his death he will add to that half, in the same way, the other part of the land that he retains while alive, as is written elsewhere.

“Likewise, Robert of Fossatis granted the land of one plow at Fontanis.

“Likewise, a certain widow named Hersindis gave to Saint Peter and Saint Germanus, at a place called Juris Vena, the land that she held from our grant, together with half of the church of the village of Cruciacus and all the holdings that she had there from me, for the remedy of her soul, adding herself to the monks’ provision.

“I approve the purchases, exchanges, and transactions that the monks have made or will make. Likewise, I grant the monks of Saint Peter free passage through all my land, so that no customary due may ever be demanded from them for fish, hides, or any other things that prove to belong to the monks.

“I could add other things that my faithful men have given to the aforesaid place; but since they have been written elsewhere, and since I hasten to bring this charter to an end and confirm it with the seal of my lord the king and the names of his nobles, I wish this alone to be made known to all at the end of this work: just as I have hitherto held freely from my lord the king, so may the monks freely hold the things that I have given for the salvation of my soul and the souls of my parents, and those that others have likewise given for their souls. Thus neither from the monks nor from the people of their land may any customary due be demanded by anyone—not vicariate, not ban, not corvée, not military expedition. Rather, as stated above, let the monks devote themselves to prayer, and let their people pay their dues to the monks alone.

“If any of my heirs or any other person should wish to oppose this work, unless he comes to his senses and flees to the remedy of satisfaction, let him be thrust into hell and suffer everlasting punishments with Anna and Caiaphas, Ananias and Sapphira, and Judas the betrayer.

“Signature of Count Ralph. Signature of Count Walter, son of Ralph. Signature of Count Hugh. Signature of Albert, who made this gift. Signature of Teduo, Albert’s brother. Signature of Guarin, his brother. Signature of Frederick. Signature of Baldwin. Signature of Simon. Signature of Bishop Agobert. Signature of Hugh the dean. Signature of William the provost. Signature of Sigo. Signature of Ascelin. Signature of Gencelin the dean.”

After the death of King Henry, in the second year of his reign, King Philip, together with his queen mother, confirmed this charter with his own hand at Drocais, in his chamber, at the request of Lord Albert, and handed it over to be confirmed by the hands of his own men.

“Baldwin, count of Flanders. Simon, son of Count Ralph. Tedbald of Montmorency. Hugh, the butler. Adelard, the chamberlain. [Col. 0280B] Ingelrannus, the king’s tutor. Hugh Dublellus. Robert Rufus.”

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the Land of Walter Costatus

(Before 1080.)

“In the name of the Lord Jesus, creator of all things. I, Hubertus, abbot, successor of Abbot Landricus, and all the monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, wish it to be known to all Christians, present and future, that a certain piece of land, which the venerable Albert had given to Saint Peter and Saint Germanus of Bruerolis, and which is known to have formerly been given to a certain man named Walter Costatus [Col. 0280C] when he was provost, was subsequently given again to Provost Richard; but, as we have said, it was given by Lord Albert to the Apostle Peter and Saint Germanus.

“As long as he lived, both Provost Richard and the heir of Walter Costatus remained silent concerning that land. But when Lord Albert had died, Walter’s son, named Guinebert, arose and brought a claim against the land, which included the adjoining wood and lay in sight of the aforesaid village.

“After struggling over this matter for a long time, he finally received from us, for that land, as we had mutually assessed it, twenty solidi in coin. He publicly placed a renunciation upon the altar, in the presence of the witnesses subscribed below.

“Then Provost Richard, Walter’s successor, brought a claim; to him also we gave seven solidi in coin and caused him to renounce the claim [Col. 0280D], before all these men: Robert, formerly abbot of the monastery of Fosses; Gausfrid Guiscard, a monk, who delivered the seven solidi; Robert the provost; Hugh of Famis; Bernard of Lameri Villa; Ingenulf; Richer the baker; Ernulf; Wimund the boy; Robert the miller; Hubert; Robert Canarnus; Adelelm; and many others.

“Whoever wishes to oppose this charter or to reclaim the land itself shall pay one hundred solidi in coin to the judge, and his attempt shall remain ineffective. Unless he comes to his senses, let him be thrust into the abyss of hell with the devil and burn there without end.”

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the Land Purchased by the Monk Warin

(Before 1070.)

[Col. 0281A]

“In the name of Jesus Christ our Lord. I, Landricus, abbot, and all the monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, wish it to be known to all who belong to the Christian faith, present and future, that one of our monks, named Warin, with the consent of the most noble man Albert, purchased not far from the village of Bruerolis a certain piece of land with its adjoining wood from a certain man named Mascelin, namely the son of Gerald of Rest. For it he paid the aforesaid Mascelin three pounds in coin, with the consent of his lord Herbert, from whose grant the land derived.

“His wife Hildeburg also gave her consent, as did their sons, namely Hervé and Hugh [Col. 0281B]. For this consent we gave Herbert twenty solidi in coin and his aforementioned wife ten solidi; to the sons we gave suitable gifts.

“Then all of them came together to Chartres and publicly placed the gift of the aforesaid land upon the altar of Saint Peter. We included them there in our prayers.

“We wished this document to be made for the following reason: if anyone should ever wish to oppose this gift, struck by the sword of excommunication and convicted by the testimony of those whose names we have subscribed, let him depart in shame and without accomplishing anything.

“Lord Albert, whose gift was the beginning of the many donations that follow. Herbert of Burseries. Robert of Fosses. Rainerius Finemundus. Richard the provost. [Col. 0281C] Sulpicius. Walter of Ungena. Also Walter ‘Pungens Asinum.’ Haimeric. Robert Mischinus. Guinebert. Tescelin, servant of the monk Paul. Ralph, servant of the monk Warin.”

## CHAPTER X. Concerning Half of the Church of Cruciacus and the Land Given to Saint Peter by the Matron Hersindis

(Before 1080.)

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I, Hubertus, abbot, unworthy of any merit, and the entire community of monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, wish it to be known to the faithful of holy Church, present and future, that a certain woman named Hersindis, whose husband had already died and who had been bereft of sons, had long been living in the territory of the castle of Drocais, namely at a place called Cruciacus.

“When she was compelled to serve according to military custom because of the benefice that she held from Lord Albert, son of the illustrious man Ribald, and when, as a fragile woman, she was greatly burdened by the weight of that service, she chose a salutary course. She approached the presence of Lord Abbot Landricus, my predecessor, earnestly asking him to obtain through his plea from her aforementioned lord Albert that, for the sake of her soul and the souls of her parents, she be given permission to give half of her land to Saint Peter, retaining the other half for her own use, without service, as long as she lived.

“Since the aforesaid Albert was most generous, devoted to God, and a great friend of our place, he most willingly consented, on this condition: after the woman’s death, the part retained by her, together with all the knights belonging to that fisc, and half of the church of the village of Cruciacus that she held, should return to Saint Peter.

“After this had been done, and after the deaths of both Abbot Landricus and the frequently mentioned Lord Albert, the aforementioned matron, struck by an incurable illness, approached our presence. She transferred to blessed Peter the Apostle half of the church of the village of Cruciacus, which she held by perpetual right, as well as the other things mentioned above. This was on the condition that she be provided for while alive, buried by us after death, and that her soul, and the soul of her only daughter Alpes, and of Alpes’ husband Gauslinus, as well as the souls of all her parents, might, through the Apostle Peter and the support of our prayers, be freed from every bond of sins and deserve to enter the gate of eternal life.

“With her intervening, her aforementioned daughter Alpes consented to this gift, together with her husband Gauslinus and their nephews Simon and Ralph. Their sisters Emmelina, Eva, and Elisabeth subscribed, and at Saint Clodoald they confirmed this charter together with their mother.

“If anyone should ever wish to oppose this gift, let him first pay one hundred pounds of gold to the judge; and unless he comes to his senses, let him fall into hell and suffer everlasting punishment with those who crucified the Lord.

“This charter was made at Chartres on the eighth day before the Kalends of October and publicly placed upon the altar of blessed Peter the Apostle by Gauslinus, the husband of Alpes, who also confirmed it with the sign of the cross. Present with him were Alberic, cleric of the castle of Mantes, and Nivard, son of Hugh.

“With us were Ernulf Niger, Rainald the groom, Gilduin the mayor, Stephen Galoius, Fulchard, Frodo, Adventus, Tescelin, Leodegarius, Girard, Rainald, Laurence, and another Laurence.

“At Saint Clodoald, where Alpes, wife of Gauslinus, confirmed this charter together with her sons and daughters, the following were present: Oger, dean of Saint Clodoald; Teduo; Othger; Ralph; Albert, son of Ingenulf; Ernulf; and Gunher, son of Ernald of Vallo.

“The sons of Waszo also confirmed this charter, namely Hugh, heir of Lord Albert, and Guaszo, his brother.

“At the end it also seemed good to place the names of those from whose benefice the aforesaid gift descended, so that prayers might continually be offered for them: Maingotus, [Col. 0282D] husband of Hersindis, who gave this gift; and Ingenulf, whose son Albert we mentioned above.”

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the Mill of Mala Poena

(Before 1070.)

«In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. We wish it to be known to all the faithful of Christ’s Church, both present and future, that I, Landricus, abbot, and the monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, since the church of Brueroles had been granted to us by the most noble man Albert, judged it beneficial to construct a pond beneath that church. Since this could not be done unless the site [Col. 0283A] of a mill, formerly called Mala Poena, was purchased from a certain knight, Walter of Ungena, whose that site was, we ordered that one excellent horse and forty solidi of coins be given to him. These were paid by Warinus the monk, administrator and builder of that place. We purchased the site on the condition that, with no one ever contradicting it, we should possess and hold it forever, and that each year, for that site, we should pay the aforesaid Walter and his heirs two solidi of coins on the feast of Saint Remigius. If we should be negligent in making the payment, let legal compensation be made, and let the site nevertheless remain in our possession. But if anyone should at any time attempt to oppose this work, may he suffer eternal punishments with Judas the traitor in hell, unless he should repent after making satisfaction. We have taken care that the witnesses to this matter subscribe their names: Teudo, son of Roscelinus. [Col. 0283B] Richard of Bairo. Rodbert of Fossatis. Ivo of Regemalasto. Sulpicius, son of Hadebert. Richard the provost. Rainerius Finemundus. Rodbert Mischinus.»

### CHAPTER XII. Concerning the exchange of the land covered by the pond. (Before 1070.)

«In the name of Christ. I, Abbot Landricus, and all the monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, wish it to be known to those present and to those to come, namely, to the worshipers of the Christian faith, that, with the assent of the illustrious man, namely Lord Albert, in exchange for a certain piece of land covered by the water of the pond constructed within the village of Brueroles, we gave two brothers, namely Guauscelinus and Sulpicius, [Col. 0283C] another piece of land not far from the village. On one side it is bounded by a certain pear tree, and on the other by a stream of water called the Medua. We also gave Sulpicius, for this same transaction, five solidi of coins and one house. The wife of the aforesaid Sulpicius, named Roscelina, and his son Rodbert assented to this exchange. We have also subscribed the names of the witnesses, so that, should opponents arise, their ineffective attempt might fail once they had been convicted by reason. Walter of Ungena. Richard the provost. Rainerius Finemundus. Rodbert. Guinebertus. Radulfus. If any rash person should attempt to contradict this charter, let him pay ten pounds of silver; and, if he remains obstinate, let him be anathema until, by repenting, he comes to amendment. [Col. 0283D]»

### CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the land and grove purchased from Guarnerius Gazellus. (Before 1080.)

«In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. We, the monks of Saint Peter of Chartres, living under Abbot Hubert according to the rule, wish it to be known that a certain knight named Guarnerius, surnamed Guazellus, sold us a small portion of his grove adjoining our grove, as well as arable land in front of the grove, toward that land which the monk Warinus had purchased from Mascelinus, son of Gerald. The aforesaid Guarnerius received the assessed sum of money for both the grove and the land from Lord Ernaldo the monk, who was then living in the village of Brueroles and enrolled him in our prayers, fed him while he lay ill, and buried him when he died. [Col. 0284A] After his death, his brother Vitalis laid claim to the land and grove; and, since he persisted in his claim, he received ten solidi of coins for the matter from the monk Gausfridus. Together with Guarnerius’s son, he placed a quitclaim upon the altar of Saint Germanus, in the presence of the witnesses subscribed below: Walter of Ungena. Lambert of Lammeri Villa. Rodbert Mischinus. Sulpicius, his son. Ernulf the shoemaker. Wineberbus. If anyone should wish to oppose this purchase and bring the matter to court, let him first pay a pound of gold; and for as long as he persists in obstinacy, let him be anathema, by the mouth of God and of all the saints, male and female.»

### CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the land of Bulfiniacus given to Saint Peter by Walter Palart. (Before 1070.)

[Col. 0284B]

«In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.
