We wish it to be known, I, Landricus the abbot, and the entire congregation of monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, to all, present and future, worshipers of the holy Church of God, that after the renowned and honorable man, Lord Albert, as circumstances permitted, had granted our place and us the church of Saint Germanus of Brueroles, together with other possessions, he observed the land of one of his knights called Bulfiniacus, in the parish of the estate of Cruciacus. Since that land was then uninhabited, he repeatedly urged the knight to give it to blessed Peter the apostle and Saint Germanus for the sake of his soul. After delaying for a long time, this same knight, named Walter and surnamed Palart, happened to be severely wounded before the New Castle in the war that had lasted for a long time between Lord Albert and Guaszo. Fearing that he would die, he summoned his lord Albert and his fellow soldiers and, with the consent of his lord, granted half of the aforesaid land to Saint Peter and Saint Germanus; he sent the gift upon the altar of Saint Germanus, on the condition that, while he lived, he should retain the other half for his own use. After his bodily death, however, his half, which he had retained, was to be joined to the other half and return to the aforesaid apostle and to Saint Germanus. And so it happened: for when he died, at the command of Lord Albert, we possessed the land in its entirety, and we placed this same Walter among our prayers, together with all our benefactors; for his soul we rang the church bells and poured forth the prayers owed to God and to be poured forth by us forever. In the aforesaid gift, the often-mentioned Lord Albert, as in the other gifts made by himself and by his faithful, added this provision: if the land had previously been burdened by any customary due, after it had been given it should in no way be burdened by vicaria, bannum, or toll. This devoted man also gave it to Saint Peter and Saint Germanus, wishing that the monks might always live there peacefully and serve God. He also wished a curse to be subscribed, so that, if anyone should at any time wish to oppose this good work, he might find God himself and all the saints opposed to him, unless he repented, and might grieve to be tormented with the devil and his angels by eternal sufferings in hell. We have taken care that the witnesses to these matters subscribe their names: Herbert of Burseriis. Rodbert of Fossatis. Tedbald of Valle Grinnoso. Ebrard, son of Walter. Dodo the seneschal. Walter of Ungena.»

### CHAPTER XV. Concerning the church of Castellariorum. (Before 1080.)

«With our Lord Jesus Christ, creator of all things, presiding. We wish it to be known to all the sons of the holy Church of God, I, Hubert the abbot, and the convent of monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, [Col. 0285B] that a certain knight named Rodbert of Fossatis, and Agnes, his venerable wife, for the salvation of their souls and those of their parents, in honor of blessed Peter the apostle, granted to our place in the Perche, not far from Mori Villare, the church of Castellariorum, built with cement and stone by a religious woman named Hadvisa—namely, the mother of the aforesaid Agnes—with the consent and willing affection of this religious woman and likewise of her sons and daughters. And lest their gift should appear to be the only one, in the same place they added, for cultivation, land sufficient for one plow and two aripennia of meadow. May their souls, placed in the bosom of Abraham the patriarch, receive from Christ the reward of eternal life. But if anyone should at any time presume to bring a claim against this good work of theirs, let him be thrust into hell with Nero, who killed the apostle Peter upon a stake of the cross and put his fellow apostle Paul to death by the sword; unless he repents, let him be tormented by perpetual fires and gnawed without end by worms that never die.»

### CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the tithe of Finemundus. (Before 1080.)

«In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. We wish it to be known to the present and future worshipers of the Church of God that a certain knight named Rainerius, commonly called Finemundus, when ill, requested the monastic habit at the point of death, [Col. 0285D] in order to obtain forgiveness for his sins. He received it from our monks, who were then serving God and Saint Germanus at the place of Brueroles. The aforesaid Rainerius gave to Saint Peter the apostle and Saint Germanus, for the support of the brothers serving God there, with the assent of his lord Hugh, the tithe that he held in the mansus called Cantante Pica, so that from that Judge who at the end of the age will give each of us the reward of eternal life according to what each has done, whether good or evil, he might deserve to receive it. This tithe is in the masura called Monticulorum, and also in another masura described as ante lucem (“before the light”; sense uncertain), called Grandis Campus. [Col. 0286A] If anyone should ever wish to oppose this gift, let him be placed in the fire of hell with Annas, Caiaphas, and Judas the traitor; unless he repents and flees to the remedy of satisfaction, let him grieve to be tormented by eternal punishments. We have taken care to subscribe the names of the witnesses to this matter: Richard the provost. Rodbert Mischinus. Guinebertus. Walter of Ungena. Hubert of Cantante Lupo.»

### CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the church of Fessonis Villare. (Before 1070.)

«In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, who personally is threefold and essentially one God. We wish it to be known, I, Landricus the abbot, and the entire assembly of monks of the monastery of Saint Peter [Col. 0286B] of Chartres, to all worshipers of the holy Church of God, present and future, that a certain knight named Guado, wishing to put an end to the allurements and pleasures of this world, devoting himself to God’s service and holy works, earnestly desired for himself the habit of holy religion. Under the protection of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, he sought from us the monastic habit, intending to follow the rule of the excellent father Benedict. From the possessions that he had held in the world, with the assent of his son Baldric, surnamed Jhotard, he granted to Saint Peter half of the church of Fessonis Villare and its churchyard, for the use of the brothers. He further gave one plowland, bounded on one side by the church’s churchyard, and on the other by the public road leading to Tegularias; on its remaining sides it is bounded by pear trees and other trees. If some false accuser should attempt to nullify this charter, let him be brought to judgment and pay six pounds of gold to the judge, and let his attempt remain ineffective. But if he persists, pierced by the sword of anathema, unless he repents, let him suffer punishment in hell with the devil and his angels, obtaining forgiveness when the devil obtains it.»

### CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning half of the church of the estate of Cruciacus. (Before 1102.)

«[Note: [Col. 0285] This charter is to be transferred to the book of Abbot Eustachius.]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. We wish it to be known, I, Eustachius the abbot, and the entire convent of monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, [Col. 0286D] to all worshipers of the Christian faith, present and future, that a certain cleric named Hugh, son of Gauscelinus of Vernogilum, voluntarily came into the presence of certain monks of ours, namely Rodbert, formerly abbot of Fossatis, and Gausfridus, then administrator of the place of Brueroles, offering to sell them half of the church of the estate of Cruciacus. It had entirely fallen into ruin and been reduced to a deserted place, with no inhabitant and no income whatever. His aforesaid father had left this church to him by hereditary right, leaving the other benefits to his other brothers. Since the monks already possessed the other half of this church, with the consent of Lord Hugh, nephew of the most illustrious man Albert, they also purchased the other half from the aforesaid cleric, without any human claimant opposing them. They gave him first seven solidi of coins, then five solidi, and again three solidi; and whenever he returned to them, they gave him small gifts necessary for him. The reader can see the witnesses to this matter listed below: Balduin the priest. Walter of Ungena. Baldric Bucellus. Rodbert Mischinus. Guimundus and Sulpicius, brothers. Osmundus. Stephanus. Morardus. Richard the provost. Rodbert the carpenter.

«We also wish it to be known to all the faithful through this charter that one agripennus of land was purchased by the monk Gausfridus from a certain knight named Rodbert, thirty solidi of coins being given for it. Bardulfus, son of Bertrannus, later claimed this agripennus as his own. Therefore Lord Hugh, with his faithful men, and Lord Gislebert of Tegularias met concerning the land, and by certain reasoning determined that what Bardulfus asserted was not true. Then those lords and all the other knights granted the aforesaid agripennus of land to Saint Peter and Saint Germanus with common assent. But since everyone, small and great alike, from the village was present, I considered it unnecessary to subscribe the names of the witnesses; Guarinus of Islo, whose land lay nearer to that little plot, also gave his assent there. In the same place the matron Milesindis, formerly the wife of the now-deceased knight Gualdinus, for the soul of her lord and for her own, gave beside our land—which the monk Warinus purchased—a small portion of her land, having been entreated by the monk Gausfridus. Below, this portion begins at a certain thorn tree, which also marks the boundary of the land mentioned above, which that same Gausfridus purchased from the knight Rodbert; above, it is bounded by the road that leads to the woodland, passing through the middle of our land.

«Finally, we wish it to be known by all that a certain knight named Hugh of Famis, for his salvation, gave Saint Peter, beyond the pond and between two roads, a small piece of his land adjoining the pond, so that the breach caused by the force of the water might always be repaired, with no one ever opposing it. After he had been killed by the sword of the Normans, his wife, named Hildeburgis, for his soul, with the consent of her faithful men, gave Saint Peter and Saint Germanus a certain rocky and uncultivated piece of land between the road leading to Fontanas and the road leading to the estate of Matonis Villaris. It begins at a transverse rock situated beside the cross of Osanna and descends between the two roads as far as the place where they join and form a single road. Many people from the village were present for its delimitation and showing, among them Herbert the provost, Richard, Rodbert Mischinus, the knight Hunbaldus, Rodbert, and Albert.»

### CHAPTER XIX. Concerning the vicaria of Ermenterias. (Before 1080.)

[Col. 0288A]

«Almighty God, among his other admonitions concerning salvation, urges us to give so that we may receive—namely, earthly things so that we may receive heavenly ones—and again, to give alms, so that all things may be clean for us. Therefore, in the name of him who gives such admonitions, I, Rodulfus, for the salvation of my soul, the remission of my sins, and those of my wife and my sons, Teudo and Ingenulfus, as well as of my parents and successors, grant to Saint Peter of Chartres and to the monks serving there the vicaria and commendaticia that I possess in their land, namely, in the village called Ermenterias. And so that this grant may endure forever, [Col. 0288B] I confirmed this document before witnesses, as did my wife and the sons named above. If anyone, inflamed by the fire of greed, should attempt to destroy the aforesaid alms, let him be erased forever from the book of life.

«The sign of Rodulfus, who ordered this charter to be made. The signs of Teudo and Ingenulfus, his sons. The sign of Agevertus the archpriest. The sign of Erardus. The sign of Herveus. The sign of Oda, wife of Ragenoldus the vice-lord. The sign of Huncboldus.»

You may wonder, reader, that you have found another charter concerning the same vicaria, drawn up earlier; the impossibility of obtaining this one brought that about. Nevertheless, I published that other charter, which is found to have been written first, just as I learned it from a truthful informant. The earlier one differs from this one in that it names Roscelinus as the usurper of the vicaria, whereas this one names Radulfus. This perhaps happened because he had two names: among the common people he was always called Roscelinus, while at the baptismal washing his godparents imposed the name Radulfus. Whatever the case may be, I wished to subscribe this one just as I found it written, lest my weariness or laziness impose any inconvenience upon the brothers.

### CHAPTER XX. Concerning the church of Nantiliacus. (Before 1070.)

«We believe that no one professing the orthodox Catholic faith can be unaware of how greatly, both in the present and in the future, those prosper who, for Christ’s name, cheerfully offer from their own resources some gift to his saints and faithful. Since it is impossible for any human being to escape the stain of corruption and live free from sin amid this corruption, the compassionate and merciful one has provided certain occasions or opportunities by which we may readily redeem our sins. Among all these, two remedies, familiar to the sick soul, give off the sweetest fragrance; concerning them the voice of blessed Truth resounds: “Give, and it will be given to you”; and again: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness”; and: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you”; and: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin.” Therefore I, Bernard, knight of the castle of Évreux, considering in my mind these many admonitions of divine Scripture, with the consent of my lord Rodbert and of his son Rodbert, from whose benefice it derives, cede to the place of Saint Peter of Chartres and to the monks serving God there a certain church, together with all the tithe that was in my demesne. This church is situated in view of the castle of Évreux, in the village called Nantiliacus, and is consecrated in honor of Peter the key-bearer. I likewise grant my knights permission, if they should wish to grant from the tithes they hold from me, to give them to the same place without any opposition. To make this gift firm, when struck by a serious illness I received the monastic habit there from Abbot Landricus. But if anyone—God forbid!—at the devil’s instigation should attempt to violate this gift of our smallness, let him incur God’s wrath; let blessed Peter, together with all the other apostles, become opposed and hostile to him; let him not deserve to enter Christ’s sheepfold, whose keys he is believed to have received from the supreme Shepherd. The witnesses to this matter are those whose names we have subscribed: Rodbert the knight, with Albereda his wife, Rodbert his son, and Hildeburgis his wife. Rodbert the monk and Richard, brothers. Gualterius the priest. Urricus the cleric. Bernard the brother. Radulfus and Richard, brothers, with their sister Emma. Isnardus. Radulfus Thick-Tongue. Girardus. Tiberius. Of the men of Saint Peter: Arnulfus, Rainaldus, Gualterius, Giraldus. Of the monks: Odo, Strabo, Gervasius, Herbert the priest, Arnulfus Rufus.»

### CHAPTER XXI. Concerning a certain piece of land at Capella Regia. (Before 1070.)

[Col. 0289C]

«In the name of Christ. I, Gualterius, stepson of Ansgotus, and my mother Pleitrudis, wish it to be known to those present and to those to come that Abbot Landricus of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres came to me very often, asking that I give Saint Peter a certain piece of land situated at Capella Regia. At first I refused to do so, but when he persisted in his request, after receiving money from him I gave the land to Saint Peter, with the assent of my lord Hubert, from whose benefice I had held that land. The census of the land is four denarii, payable on the Kalends of September, at the Nativity of Saint Mary. To make this charter firm, I impressed it with the sign of the cross by my own hand. But if anyone—whether I, my heirs, or any opposing person—should attempt to come against this charter or violate it, let him pay one hundred gold solidi together with the enforcing fisc, and let him be unable to vindicate what he claims; rather, let this present charter remain firm and unshaken for all time, strengthened by stipulation. The sign of Erveus. The sign of Bernaldus. The sign of Hubert, son of Magnon. The sign of Huncbert of Firmitas. The sign of Ernulfus, son of Ansgotus. The sign of Ingelbaldus. The sign of Laurentius. The sign of Martinus. The sign of Rainaldus. The sign of Giraldus.»

### CHAPTER XXII. Concerning the land of Brogili Amari. (Before 1080.)

«In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. I, Rodbert, son of Guillelmus, and my wife, named Adelina, wish it to be known to those present and to those to come that a monk of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres named Guarinus came to us, asking that we grant him, by census, the land—namely, one hundred aripennia—which we appeared to hold in our demesne at Brogilo Amaro. We willingly granted it for a census, as he requested, for the salvation of the souls of my father and mother and of ourselves. We granted the land for the sustenance of the brothers residing at the place of Saint Peter of Chartres, so that from now on they might hold it perpetually and build upon it securely, without any debt or return, except for three solidi, which they should pay as census on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; and if they should be negligent in this matter, let them make legal compensation and retain the land. So that this gift might remain firm forever, we confirmed this charter with our own hands, as did all my men, who are witnesses to this matter. If anyone should wish to falsify this gift, let him pay a pound of gold; and unless he repents, let him perish condemned. The sign of Rodbert, giver of this gift. The sign of Adelina. The sign of Willelmus of Plancis. The sign of Ernaldo, son of Ansgui. The sign of Osbert of Orgulium. The sign of Lancelinus, son of Willelmus. The sign of Rodbert, son of Aszo. The sign of Fulbert, son of Bertrannus. The sign of Hubelinus, our man. The sign of Herbert, brother of Morinus of Curba Villa.»

### CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning the church of Plancis. (Before 1067.)

«In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father [Col. 0290C] and Son and Holy Spirit, amen. The Lord Jesus Christ, creator of all, sent by God the Father into the world so that he might restore what had been lost and preserve what had been restored, living in the flesh among us, incarnate from the ever-Virgin Mary, taught us what would be beneficial and useful for the salvation of our souls. Among other things, he urged us to give for his sake from what we possess, so that we might receive it back a hundredfold in the future. Then, through his apostle, among other things he urged us to pray for one another so that we might be saved. Moved by these and many other exhortations and admonished by these addresses, I, Guidmundus, and my wife Emma, with our offspring, so that the burden of our sins might be lightened and prayers for us might not be lacking day by day, with kind hearts and ready will, grant to Saint Peter of the monastery of Chartres the little estate of Saint Mary of Plancis, together with the tithe belonging to that place, and the suburb, toll, and fair (fera); namely, the portion belonging to me; and one mill, with three leagues of water for fishing, namely in the Risle, the Moira, and the Iton; and one fishery at Terciacus, and the tithe from the other fisheries and from the weirs there belonging to me. I also give three aripennia of meadow before the church, and as much cultivated land as is sufficient for two plows. From my castle of Molinis I grant the tithe of the entire year’s market and of every tax belonging to that castle. Let the monks of Saint Peter adorn and build up the aforesaid little estate as their own property, [Col. 0291A] so that through them God may be glorified in it and above it.

So that this gift of the estate may remain firm forever, I, my wife, and our sons have confirmed this charter with our own hands; and I gave it to my lord, Count Guillelmus, from whose benefice I appear to hold it, for confirmation, and also to our bishop Ivo and to all my neighbors and nobles who are subscribed below. Thus, if at any time, with the devil’s instigation, any of our successors—God forbid!—should wish to violate this gift and grant, the undersigned confirmers should be witnesses and defenders in the place of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles. But if anyone should attempt to violate this gift, unless he repents, let him perish condemned forever. The sign of Count Guillelmus [Note: [Col. 0291D] Guillelmus the Conqueror.]. The sign of Guillelmus, son of Osbert. [Col. 0291B] The sign of Guimundus, who made this gift. The sign of Emma, his wife. The sign of Rodulfus, his son. The sign of Rodbert, his son. The sign of Antonius, his son. The sign of Guimundus, his son. The sign of Hugh, his son. The sign of Alannus, his son. The sign of Guillelmus, his son. The sign of Toresgaudus, his son. The sign of Guillelmus of Plancis. The sign of Fulbert the cleric. The sign of Radulfus the chaplain. The sign of Guillelmus the toll-collector. The sign of Fulbert, son of Bertrannus. The sign of Guiddo the cleric.»

### CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning the land of Girardus Caper and of Paganus the provost. (In the year 1077.)

«[Note: [Col. 0291D] We have assigned this charter to the year 1077, whose indiction is XV and which falls within the reigns of Kings Philip and Guillelmus and the abbacy of Hubert.]

Although irrevocable death continually devours all mortals with an insatiable throat, nevertheless the diligence of the ancients wisely determined that it would be most useful for the examples of human posterity to commit to writing not only the pious deeds of faithful men for the memory of those to come, but also to place them on pages, so that their mind, traveling through many things and forgetting past events because of present ones, might know not only what it remembers having seen but also, rereading what was done from the beginning, might recognize it as though it had seen it.

Therefore I, Gausfridus, a monk of Saint Peter of Chartres, with the consent of the entire congregation and by the command of Abbot Hubert, having been appointed guardian and administrator of the possessions that appear to belong to us in the regions of Normandy, wish it to be known to all, present and future, faithful of the holy Church of God, that a certain man named Girardus, surnamed Caper, for the redemption of his soul and likewise for that of his parents, granted freely, with the consent of his mother Emmelina and of his brothers Guarinus and Hubertus, a certain piece of land not far from the land of Saint Mary of Plancis to Saint Mary and to Saint Peter the apostle, whose cell that Saint Mary appears to be. Since he was prevented by a certain war from carrying out the gift himself, he sent it upon the altar of Saint Mary through his brother Guarinus. Guillelmus of the castle of Molinis and his wife Albereda assented to this act.

I also insert in this page the land of Paganus, which he gave to Saint Mary in exchange for eleven pounds of coins that he owed us from the toll of the aforesaid castle. Paganus himself had pledged this land for twenty solidi of coins, which we also returned. In addition, for consent, we gave Gauscelinus, the lord of Paganus, twenty solidi of coins and an additional three solidi; finally, to Willelmus, lord of both men, namely Girardus and Paganus, because of the customary dues he appeared to hold in those lands and which he remitted, we gave thirty solidi, and to his wife Albereda five solidi. Those who were present, saw, and heard are listed below: Guillelmus the priest. Guiddo the priest. Gauscelinus, son of Ricuardus. Rodbert Lupeculus. Fulco of Tedis Villa. Hugh of Chira. Herimannus, son of Hugh Tronellus. Ebrardus of Rugia. Gualterius of Asperis. Paganus the provost. Richard, servant of Girardus and Warinus. Willelmus, servant of the monks.

Done at Plancis publicly, while Willelmus, the most invincible duke of the Normans and king of the English, was alive; in France, the most serene King Philip was reigning; indiction XV. Paul the monk served as notary.»

There are also other gifts belonging to the aforesaid little estate that are recorded despite the scarcity of scribes, such as the church of the martyr Lawrence, which was given to the aforesaid place by Odo Rufus. This church lies beyond the little river that runs before the church of Saint Mary, beneath the monks’ buildings.

### CHAPTER XXV. Concerning the church of Saint Romanus, given beneath the castle of Braiai. (Before 1070.)

«In the name of the holy Trinity and the one Godhead, namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. We wish it to be known that, by common counsel and with equal devotion, I, Airardus of Buslo, and Landricus of Toriello, together with our most devout fellow townsmen, approached Gausfridus our fellow soldier, asking him to grant to the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, for the salvation of his soul and those of his family, the little estate in which a church dedicated to the holy martyr Romanus stood. Since it is not far from the castle of Braiai, but at that time was considered among us worthless and uncultivated, although it is believed to possess splendid sanctity in the sight of the divine Majesty, the aforesaid knight accepted our requests, followed our counsel, gave something of his own there, and thus entrusted the whole matter to Abbot Landricus, so that it might be held in as much honor as previously it had been despised. The abbot voluntarily and out of kindness gave the knight fifty solidi of coins. Therefore, what we had done by divine inspiration we made known in words to our lord Gausfridus and to our lady Mahildis. They praised it most devotedly and promised to enrich the place from their own resources; they also gave permission that whoever wished to grant there to God and the saints anything from his own right, as a better recompense, should be freely allowed to do so.

Accordingly, we requested that this charter of the deed be made, so that, with the names of the witnesses subscribed, it might always remain firm as both witness and index of the truth. If anyone should presume to contradict this, or should attempt in any way, however slightly—God forbid!—to rescind or reclaim any part of this gift, let no consent be given to him; but, placed under anathema, let him pay one hundred pounds of gold to the prince of the land. The names of the witnesses: Lord Gausfridus, with whose consent this was done. Mahildis, his wife. Willelmus, his son. Airardus of Buslo. Bernardus, his brother. Landricus of Toriello. Willelmus the provost. Odo of Domicilium. Gausfridus. Guarinus. Gausfridus. Raiardus, who made this gift. Rainaldus the forester.»
There are [Note: [Col. 0293D] What follows is absent from manuscript B.] other gifts as well, which, through the negligence or scarcity of scribes, still remain recorded. Since, however, the place and the leisure provide a suitable opportunity for writing, I do not think it should be passed over how the head of the blessed martyr Romanus was brought from the city of Rome to the aforementioned place and deposited there, [Col. 0293B] remaining unknown to men for a long time.

But after, in our own time, as we said above, the aforesaid place began to be improved under the authority of Abbot Landricus, and was frequently visited by the people for the sake of prayer, the monks living there, wishing to rebuild that little wooden oratory in better condition, began to dig the ground so that they might strengthen the foundations of a larger oratory with cement and stone.

Before I explain the discovery of the head of the Roman martyr, however, it is necessary to begin with how and on what occasion the holy martyr wished his own head to be carried there by a certain Breton. Once there was, in this nearer part of Brittany, a wealthy man, born of noble parents, who, by divine favor, had been marked with the title of Christian. Having renounced the pomp of the devil in the bath of baptism and been cleansed from every stain of sin by the illumination of the Holy Spirit, he was called Paulinus.

Burning with zeal for divine love, he was considering having one of his estates made into a church in honor of some martyr, if he could somehow obtain relics of that very martyr from elsewhere. While his mind was occupied with this matter, he heard from many people that the city of Rome, more than other cities, was adorned with the bodies of countless martyrs. Without delay, he sent there one of his faithful men, named Maurus, a most Christian and simple man, to bring back from there, by whatever means, the body of some martyr.

When he reached Rome, he remained there for three seasons of the year without revealing the secret of his heart to anyone, and he was unable by himself to fulfill his lord’s desire. When he began to be anxious within himself and his supply of money had almost run out, and when he was hastening to undertake the journey back to his homeland, his host noticed that his spirit was unusually troubled. He carefully inquired into the cause of his distress, and, having discovered it, comforted him with the remedy of friendly consolation and offered him every form of assistance, as one friend to another guest.

The host promptly bought from a certain archimandrite the venerable head of the blessed martyr Romanus. Carefully, in the pilgrim guest’s *psistarchia*—that is, his travel bag—he placed the most sacred treasure, wrapped in a clean cloth, together with the written slips; then, after giving him the kiss of peace, he ordered him to leave the city of Rome at a swift pace.

When, by God’s will and with a prosperous journey, he reached the village of Braiaum, crossing the Osana River, he was detained there by bodily illness. In accordance with God’s plan, when he was dying, he instructed the Christians dwelling there, by entreating them, to place his body, together with the treasure he had brought, beside the wall of the church that then stood there.

Thus the treasure, and so incomparable a gift bestowed by God, remained unknown to men through the passing of many years, until, by the favor of divine mercy, the monks mentioned above were performing the offices of divine service there, the place was held in esteem by the entire populace, and, gradually increasing, its fame spread far and wide on flying wings.

Then, with the assistance of the people, as they were laying the greater foundations of the church, they discovered an unexpected treasure: the body [Col. 0294B] of the aforesaid pilgrim and, beside his body, his *psistarchia* intact, containing the head of the martyr mentioned above.

When an unworthy man rashly wished to lift it from the ground, he immediately received, deservedly, the punishment for his presumption by divine retribution. For the wretched man lost the sight of his eyes before his hand touched the object toward which he had stretched it.

After this, the people of that place, gathered together in a single company with religious persons and singing praises with due honor, lifted that case containing the sacred relics without difficulty. They found that the martyr’s head and the written slips were undisturbed, demonstrating that it was the head of the blessed martyr Romanus.

When it was lifted from the ground, such an exceedingly sweet fragrance was present that all who were there believed they sensed the perfumes of fragrant Paradise.

Meanwhile, the martyr’s power was not absent. The one who did not disdain to illuminate the man blind from birth himself illuminated this man, through the merits of the Roman martyr, with a brighter light, to the praise and glory of his illustrious name.

I myself, nor even the man who reported this to me, was present at these events. But, as he affirmed, Agobertus, archpriest and later bishop of the city of Chartres, was present; and he himself learned it from Agobertus. Now let the little pen turn to what follows.

### CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning the church of Buxet in the Perche, given by the knight Isnardus to Saint Peter of Chartres. (Before 1080.)

“ Our Lord Jesus [Col. 0294D] Christ, our Creator and Savior, who wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, exhorts us piously and mercifully, saying: ‘Honor the Lord from your substance’; and likewise: ‘Give alms, and all things are clean for you.’

“Therefore I, Isnardus, one of the Christians, son of Sulpicius, wishing to obey the voice of that most merciful Lord of mine, Jesus Christ, grant to Saint Peter, the key-bearer of heaven, and to his monastery situated in the suburb of Chartres, my church which is in Buxet, with its churchyard, for the salvation of the soul of my father and mother, of my ancestors, and of my lords, with the consent of my lord Teudo, son of Boso, who holds it as a benefice from the king.

“I also give the land beside the church, as much as one plow can till. In my own demesne I do not hold all the tithes, but my men hold many of them from the fisc. I have granted them permission that whoever wishes to give anything to Saint Peter may have license to do so on my behalf.

“I also grant pasture in my woodland, without pannage, for all the pigs of the monks of Saint Peter’s monastery of Chartres. Likewise, I give the tithe of one mill situated at Alnetum; and I give the tithe of the money that I receive from the pasturing of pigs; and I give the tithe of the money from the market of Mort-Villare.

“And so that this donation of mine may remain most firmly established, I delivered it for confirmation to my lord Teudo, from whose benefice I hold it. My son Isnardus and both my daughters, together with their mother Albereda, approved all that I have given by their consent, and consent to it by their approval, and with their own hands [Col. 0295B] confirmed this document. The following men are witnesses to this:

“Teudo, from whose benefice it derives. Isnardus, who made this donation. Albereda, his wife. Isnardus, his son. Columba, his daughter. Aremburgis. Rodbertus Rufus. Hugo of Mort-Villare. Baldricus. Mascelinus of Curba-Villa. Gausfridus of Longa-Luna. Guarinus of Puteus. Arroldus of Croto. Richardus, his brother. Rodulfus of Calloet.

“From our men: Bernardus, son of Vulmarus; Albertus; Frodo; Stephanus; Gualoius; Ernulfus Rufus; Rainaldus, his son; Fulchardus; Tescelinus, son of Hildegarius; Arnulfus Niger; Giraldus the cook.”

### CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning the land of Gausberti-Villa. (29 August 1060.)

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. We wish it to be known to all the faithful of Christ, present and future—I, Landricus, by the grace of God abbot, and the whole community of monks of Saint Peter’s monastery of Chartres—how the land which we appear to possess at Gausberti-Villa was given to our place by a certain knight of distinguished lineage, named Richardus, and how it was granted by the most noble count of Normandy, William, and by the brothers of the aforesaid knight, namely William [Col. 0295D] and Baldwin.

“In the year in which the internal war that had long endured between King Henry and Count William is known to have ended, the aforesaid knight Richardus had been sent by the count, with other Normans, to guard the castle of Tedmarus. At that time the castle and its inhabitants were under an anathema.

“While he was there, having been struck by an illness of the body from which he also died, he carefully fearing the loss of his soul summoned a certain Nigellus, who had his sister in marriage, and other friends. He asked them to have one of our monks, Gausfridus, who happened then to be present, hasten to the bishop of the city, and to have both himself and the others absolved, and to have him carried to the monastery for burial.

“The condition was that, from that day and forever, the monks of our place should possess a third part of Gausberti-Villa, excepting the knights—that is, whatever he himself had possessed in houses, lands, meadows, waters, the church, and oxen.

“After he had obtained absolution and, according to the custom of holy religion, had been buried among the leading men of the city, we entered his name in our memorial, and shall do so every day, together with the others by whose benefactions our life is sustained.

“The glorious count William, so often mentioned, confirmed this gift as a reward for heavenly life in the village commonly called Curtis Dominicus, not far from the castle of Drocis, in the presence of his nobles, whose names are these: William, son of Osbertus; Walter Gifardus; Fulco of Alnetum; Hubertus of Rigia; Rodbertus Bertrannus; William Marmio; Rainaldus Darsellus; Radulfus Falchemandus; Hunfridus; Turoldus; William, son of Corbucio; Bencelinus of Schoht; Raberius and William of Vernon; Hugo, son of Gerelmus.

“The deceased man’s brothers also confirmed it, in the presence of all those mentioned above, namely William and Baldwin, so that they too might deserve to share with their brother in the recompense.

“From our men there were present: Bernardus, son of Vulmarus; Warinus the cook; Walterius the mayor; Oydelerius the stableman.

“If anyone wishes to contradict this charter, let him be struck by the throat of perpetual anathema and, frustrated in his purpose, let him pay three pounds of gold to the judge.

“This donation was granted and confirmed on the day before the Nones of August, the day on which Henry, king [Col. 0296C] of France, died [and was written by Paul, a monk].”

### CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning the serf Raimbertus and Frodburga. (Before 1061.)

“In the name of God. I, Odo, son of Count Manasses, with the consent of my brother Hugo and our sister Eustachia, make known to the present and future people that I have given to the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres and to the cell of Jociacum belonging to the aforesaid monastery, from our household, a male serf named Raimbertus and a female serf named Frodburga—brother and sister, together with their sons and daughters—for the salvation of the soul of our father and our mother.

“If any of our heirs should at any time wish to oppose this gift, may he, together with the traitor Judas and those who crucified the Lord, be anathematized by blessed Peter, to whom the Lord Jesus Christ granted the power of binding and loosing, and, excluded beyond the gates of Paradise, be handed over to the devil in the lower flames, to be tortured for all time.

“I therefore ask all who read or hear this document of our largesse to strive to pray for the mercy of God on behalf of our father Manasses, our mother Constantia, and ourselves, so that, after the course of this world, through the holy apostle Peter, to whom we have bestowed the gift mentioned above, the almighty Lord may open to us the gate of eternal life.

“Wishing this charter always to remain inviolate, on the fifth day before the Ides of August, in the palace of the castle of Meledunum, in the presence of our lord King Henry, [Col. 0297A] we confirmed it with our own hands and entrusted it for confirmation by the hands of many who stood there. We subscribed it again and added our names, making the sign of the saving cross and setting down the names of witnesses from both parties.

“Sign of Odo, count, who made this donation. Sign of Hugo, count, Odo’s brother. Sign of Eustachia, sister of both counts.

“The following are witnesses: Count Walterius; Droco of Conflans; Gualerannus of Paris; Teduinus the viscount; Oidelardus; Hugo, son of Richardus of Bistisiacum; Guaszo of Pissiacum; Hugo, son of Lipericus; Rodbertus Budicus; Fulcuinus; Baldwin, the king’s archchaplain; Guiscelinus and Richardus, chaplains; Albertus, provost of the cell of Jociacum; Rodbertus of Fraxinum; Hulgerius the mayor.

“Johannes the chamberlain dictated this charter. Droco, archdeacon of the Vexin.

“But whoever, prompted by the devil, wishes to oppose this matter shall pay one hundred pounds of refined gold to the king’s fisc, and his attempt shall remain without effect.”

### CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning the cell of Saint Gauburgis. (Before 1061.)

“Since faith holds primacy in the bosom of holy mother Church, mercy—which in Greek is called *elemosina*, ‘almsgiving’—because it proceeds from the fountain of charity, is not considered the least among the other virtues. When it is distributed to Christ’s least ones, it obtains the remission of sins; the kingdom of heaven is opened to those who practice it. Hence the saying: ‘The merciful man does good to his own soul,’ and many similar statements.

“For our Savior, the Lord of the universe, although he himself is powerful, does not reject the powerful, because he wishes no one [Note: [Col. 0297D] So also above, chapter 26.] to perish, but to come to the knowledge of the truth; and through the fruits of good works he calls all the faithful to himself. In the Gospel he also terrifies lovers of the world: ‘Every tree,’ he says, ‘that does not produce good fruit shall be cut down and thrown into the fire’; and many similar passages that have not been entrusted to this style.

“Therefore I, Ivo, entangled in the snares of worldly conduct and, above all, weighed down by the burden of sins, nevertheless, relying unworthily on the multitude of the Lord’s mercies, undertake a good work believed praiseworthy: I commit and give to Saint Peter of Chartres the little establishment of Saint Gauburgis, situated in the territory of Belesme, together with everything belonging to that place, so that a monastic order may be maintained there in the service of God.

“And so that this gift may remain stable and unshaken, I wish it to be known to all, present and future, throughout succeeding times, that I delivered it for confirmation to my lord King Henry, from whose benefice it derives.

“But if anyone, prompted by diabolical wickedness, should oppose this deed—which God forbid!—may he incur the wrath of God; may blessed Peter become his opponent and enemy, together with all the others; and, confounded by his own presumption, may he pay one thousand pounds of gold to the king of the Franks for the rashness of his insult.”

[Col. 0298A] This aforesaid little establishment is known to have first been given by Count William to a certain monk of Bonneval, named Beringarius. But after he had been consecrated abbot, unable for a long time to endure the frequent wars and the poverty of the place, which was increasing day by day, he voluntarily returned to his own monastery, where he later spent his life.

After the death of Count William and his son Rodbertus, whom his enemies killed with an axe while he was imprisoned, Ivo, William’s brother, succeeded to the honor. He asked Abbot Landricus to receive the aforesaid place for Saint Peter to possess perpetually and to send his monks there to serve God.

The abbot complied with his request and sent some of his men, who held the place for nearly three years. It happened, however, that a certain [Col. 0298B] young monk named Solo, called Deodatus from the sacred font, was said to be committing certain abominable acts there and, prompted by the devil, was plotting to commit still greater crimes. He was stripped by his accomplices; escaping by means of flight, he took refuge in Brittany, leaving us a great stench from his deeds. He estranged us from the place and the place from us.

### CHAPTER XXX. Concerning the church of Saint Dionysius at Nogent. (Around 1078.)

“[Note: [Col. 0297D] This charter is published in *Gallia Christiana*, [Col. 0298D] vol. VIII, instruments, col. 304.] Since faith holds primacy in the bosom of holy mother Church, mercy—which in Greek is called *elemosina*, ‘almsgiving’—because it proceeds from the fountain of charity, [Col. 0298C] is not considered the least among the other virtues. When it is distributed to Christ’s least ones, it obtains the remission of sins; the kingdom of heaven is opened to those who practice it. Hence the saying: ‘The merciful man does good to his own soul,’ and many similar statements.

“For our Savior, the Lord of the universe, although he himself is powerful, does not reject the powerful, because he wishes no one to perish [Note: [Col. 0298D] *Vult*—‘he wishes’—is omitted.], but to come to the knowledge of the truth; and through the fruits of good works he calls all the faithful to himself. In the Gospel he also terrifies lovers of the world: ‘Every tree,’ he says, ‘that does not produce good fruit shall be cut down and thrown into the fire’; and many similar passages that have not been entrusted to this style.

“Therefore I, Rotrocus, entangled in the snares of worldly conduct, girded with the arms of military service, and, above all, weighed down by the burden of sins, nevertheless, relying unworthily on the multitude of the Lord’s mercies, undertake a good work believed more praiseworthy: namely, I desire further to adorn and enlarge the monastery which my father Gausfredus began to build in honor of Saint Dionysius, in a territory not far from a castle called Nogent.

“For the abbot Landricus, of venerable memory, came to me and earnestly begged me to give that same monastery to Saint Peter of Chartres, for the remembrance of me, my wife, and my children, and for the soul of my aforesaid father and my mother. I gladly consented, so that that pastor and prince might come to the aid of me and their souls, opening to us the gates of the heavenly kingdom, which, having received authority from the Lord, he opens to all the faithful.

“And so that this may remain stable and unshaken, I wish it to be known to all the faithful, present and future, throughout succeeding times, that I delivered it for confirmation by the hands of all my faithful men.

“But if anyone, prompted by diabolical wickedness, should oppose this deed—which God forbid!—let him be anathema and thrust into the lowest hell, where the worm that never dies shall gnaw his flesh, and the fire that is never extinguished shall forever feed upon his torments.”

This place was held by our monks for several years, as long as Count Rotrocus lived, [Col. 0299B] until they were ordered to leave by Gausfredus’s wife, named Beatrix. She found as her pretext the fact that our former abbot, Lord Hubertus, could not exercise the office of abbot. While Rotrocus was alive, he had entrusted the governance of the church to him through Abbot Eustachius and had given him the pastoral staff; and, when he died, he left everything he possessed in gold and silver, wine and grain, entirely for the use of the monks.

After his death, his sons borrowed all the grain and wine, having a moneylender as an enemy whenever he demanded what he had lent. Beatrix too, the wife of the elder son, having gold and silver within her fortress and considering herself the closer heir, absolutely refused to return anything except a single chalice that she had made of gold.

When she was repeatedly and sharply urged by the aforesaid administrator of the place to return the dead man’s alms for the purchase of lands and construction of buildings, she became so enraged that she expelled our monks from the place and installed Cluniac monks there.

Once expelled by the sword of anathema, they returned again, fleeing the hunger of the Allobroges to every land. Like gyrovagues, they cross dry places and seas in order to find food.

### CHAPTER XXXI. Donation of certain colliberti by Count Tedbaldus. (Before 1080.)

“Whoever, for the love of God, releases from a debt of service a man bound to him may confidently expect to receive from him, without doubt, a reward in the future, as he himself says through the prophet: ‘Set the oppressed free, and tear apart every burden.’ Then you shall call, and the Lord will answer; you shall cry, and he will say: ‘Here I am.’

“Therefore I, Count Tedbaldus, in the name of God, for the remedy of my soul, hand over to the monks of that place certain male serfs of my jurisdiction, born from my male and female serfs belonging to Saint Peter of Chartres, together with one free male serf of mine, so that from this day they may render the service owed.

“I agree to this arrangement on the condition that, at all times except feast days, in the full convent, after the litany, the same brothers shall sing a psalm for me.

“And so that the charter of this donation may remain firm forever, I myself strengthened it with the sign of the cross made by my hand and proposed it for confirmation by my son.

“Sign of Count Stephanus. Sign of Gausfridus of Calidus-Mons. Sign of Wido of Breina. Sign of Hainricus the steward. Sign of Wido of Mount Leodoricus. Sign of Alcherius, son of Guauslinus. Sign of Hugo, son of Tedbaldus.”

### CHAPTER XXXII. Donation of colliberti by Viscount Ebrardus. (Before 1070.)

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the Most High God. I, Ebrardus, viscount of the people of Chartres [Note: [Col. 0299] This viscount Ebrardus, having set out for the Holy Land with the army of the crusaders, was killed during the siege of Antioch in the year 1097.], wish it to be known to those present and to those yet to come that monks of Saint Peter of Chartres came before me, asking me, for the remedy of my soul, to relinquish the claim that I had brought against the sons of Girbertus, my serf, from Ymon’s Villa, who were born from a female serf of Saint Peter of Chartres.

“This I did, receiving from them one hundred solidi of coin and one ounce of gold. I granted to Saint Peter of Chartres and to the monks serving there, free from any claim, those sons of Girbertus and Beringerius, their kinsman, together with his wife, sons, daughters, and the descendants of that Gisbertus, who dwells within the boundaries of Ymon’s Villa, for the remedy of my soul and those of my parents, my wife Hunberga, and my sons, so that from this day forward they may serve the monks without any opposition or claim.

“But if anyone should wish to condemn this charter and donation, may he perish eternally, condemned.

“Sign of Ebrardus the viscount, who made this donation. Sign of Ebrardus, his son. Sign of Hugo, his son. [Col. 0300C] Sign of Hunberga, his wife. Sign of Odo, son of Guaszo. Sign of Guarinus, son of Guarinus of the Tower. Sign of Walterius, son of Loscelinus of Curte-Entismum. Sign of Gunterius, son of Haimo. Sign of Guido Apostolus and Gausbertus, his brother.

“From our side: Arnulfus Bigotus; Stephanus, son of Dodo; Gausfridus Tosardus; Teduinus the mayor; Hubertus Bovardus; Gualteriolus of the Monastery.

“Rodbertus the monk wrote this charter at the command of Abbot Landricus.”

### CHAPTER XXXIII. Acknowledgment concerning the land of Rodbertus Cornus. (Around 1028–1037.)

“Acknowledgment of how the land that Abbot Magenardus gave to Rodbertus Cornus was restored to the brothers’ sustenance.—When Rodbertus Cornus had died, the monks wished to recover the land itself. But his wife caused a judicial case to be brought, because it had been given to her lord under the arrangement that she should possess it as long as she lived.

“A certain knight named Sulio took this woman in marriage. He offered service to Abbot Arnulfus on many occasions, but the abbot always rejected and never accepted that service. While Sulio was living with the aforesaid woman, the sons of the aforementioned Rodbertus died.

“After the woman’s death, the nephews of that same Rodbertus claimed the land. But the monks firmly resisted them. Then they came to the court of Count Odo and Bishop Teodericus, and a hearing was held there.

“The nephews of Rodbertus maintained that the woman had caused the judgment to be brought under the agreement that, after her death, Rodbertus’s heirs would hold the land from the abbot as a fief. To contradict this, we had sufficient witnesses.

“Then Count Odo judged that a judicial combat should take place—specifically, that the heirs of Rodbertus should be sent into judgment concerning what they claimed, namely the judgment that Rodbertus’s wife had caused to be brought. But the witness for Saint Peter said that no one had been sent except the woman herself.

“Then Rodbertus, one of the aforesaid nephews, gave a pledge to the count. Teodericus, a man of Saint Peter and by then the mayor, likewise gave his pledge to the count in order to oppose it.

“Afterward, while the combat remained pending, an agreement was made as follows: at the request of Bishop Teodericus, Abbot Landricus gave forty solidi to Rodbertus and his brother Sancelinus, and remitted two *aripennia* of vineyard, which Rodbertus Cornus had given to Saint Peter when he received that land from Abbot Magenardus.

“The brothers Rodbertus and Sancio themselves relinquished the land and gave as sureties themselves and two of their men, Gilduinus and Emalricus, so that, if at any time the land were claimed by anyone on their behalf, they would restore it free and would erase the entire claim in the count’s court.

“This agreement was made in the bishop’s court, and many people were present, some of whom are subscribed here: Nivelo; Albertus of Gualardone; Rogerius Podardus; Haimo Barbatus; Girogius the cleric; Herbertus of Chartres.

“From our side: Dodo; Herbrannus; Adventus; Teduinus; Lambertus; Labaddon; Gausfredus, stepson of Osbertus.”

### CHAPTER XXXIV. Donation of the customary dues of the borough by Viscount Gilduinus. (29 April 1046.)

“Since it is certain and established by eternal law that nothing born endures, it is fitting that all who bear the Christian name and are placed in this sea of fortune should not trust in fleeting goods. We must therefore consider how, through a worthy fruit of repentance and almsgiving alike, we may deserve joy without end when the final day carries us away.

“For this reason I, Gilduinus, viscount of the city of Chartres, and my wife, named Emmelina, together with our dearest children, gladly grant to Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, the customary dues of his suburb that belong to our jurisdiction, so that the monks devotedly serving him in the monastery situated beside the aforesaid city may have the right to pray for our salvation and, each year after the bodily death of each of us, celebrate our anniversaries.

“We also give one small oven, free from every customary due except the rent, and a most flourishing orchard.

“We confirmed this charter through the testimony of those whose names we have subscribed, strengthening it with the sign of the cross.

“Gilduinus the viscount, who made this donation. Harduinus the viscount, his son. Elisabeth, his wife. Johannes the physician. Guiszo the physician. Girbertus the priest. Goscelinus the priest. Rodbertus of Villa-Pali. Herbrannus of Trans-Grand-Pont. Rodulfus Musculus. Guarinus, the viscount’s chief cook. Durandus, the count’s cupbearer. Teduinus, prior of Saint Peter’s. Ernulfus. Durandus the cellarer. Hugolinus the cook. Tedbaldus Boldardus. Ericus the boy.

“This was augmented on the third day before the Kalends of May, while the invincible King Henry was reigning, in the second year after the war in which Tedbaldus, count palatine, was captured by Count Gausfridus Martellus of Anjou.”

### CHAPTER XXXV. Purchase of the land of Walterius and Guarnerius. (Before 1070.)

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I, Landricus, by the grace of God abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, which was honorably and fittingly situated in ancient times not far from the gate of that city called Cinerosa—in which a considerable congregation of monks, living piously according to the rule of Saint Benedict and the examples of the earlier fathers, keeping watch with the innermost devotion of their hearts amid hymns and spiritual songs and adorned with the bright insignia of the other virtues, strives day and night, under Peter the bishop, through the never-quiet sea of this world toward the ever-pleasant harbor of the eternal homeland, and earnestly implores Christ in prayer for all the Catholic people, but especially for those by whose benefactions and gifts it is sustained while living in this fragile hut of flesh—

“With this community, then, I, the aforesaid abbot, wish it to be known to all the faithful, present and future, that one of our monks, named Warinus, administrator of one of our cells built in honor of Mary, the Mother of God, in the territory of Normandy, in a village commonly called Plancas, bought in perpetuity from a certain priest named Fulbertus the land of Walterius of Vico and the land of Guarnerius.

“For one of these he paid twenty solidi of coin, and for the other three pounds of coin. To obtain their consent to this sale, he gave twenty solidi to the lords of the aforesaid priest, two brothers—namely William of Fagetum and Guimundus—and the same amount also to their lord, Guimundus Felix, who at that time held the castle of Molinis, from whose benefice the aforesaid two brothers had held that land.

“Thus, both by the aforesaid priest and by his aforesaid lords, the gift was placed upon the altar of the gracious Mother of the Lord, in the sight and hearing of those whose names we have ordered to be written below.

“First, however, we thought it necessary to record that Giraldus, the son of the aforesaid priest, attempted to claim for himself a share of the aforesaid land. But, defeated in the court of the castle of Molinis before the lady of that castle, Albereda, daughter of Guimundus Felix, he too placed the gift upon the altar, receiving fifty solidi for it.

“The witnesses to this matter are: Guido the priest; Fulbertus of Plancas; Herbertus of Melicurte; Seirannus of Plancas; Restaldus the mediator; Corbellus; Guillelmus the vinedresser; Turoldus the servant; [Col. 0303A] William Canutus; William of Aspris; William, son of Milo; Ebrardus of Ruga.”

### CHAPTER XXXVI. Concerning the church of Villa-Villon and the land given there. (In the year 1059.)

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Odo, son of Guazzo, wish it to be known to all present and to those who shall follow that, mindful of the divine word which says, ‘Give, and it will be given to you,’ I myself, for the salvation of my soul and that of my wife, from the benefices which I appear to possess temporarily, grant to Saint Peter, Abbot Landricus, and his monks, to possess by right, the church formerly situated in the place called Villa-Villon, but now, because of impending evils, reduced to nothing, together with the land and tithe belonging to the church, and another piece of land sufficient for one plow.

“This is done with the consent of Agobertus, the venerable bishop, and of my most noble lady Mahildis and her son William, from whom I possess these things.

“A certain knight named Richerius had until now held this church from me. But, having recently received money from me, he returned it to me in the presence of many men, of whom I shall subscribe a few as witnesses: Bernardus of Buslo; Rodulfus, son of Hunger; Gausfridus of Braia; Guillelmus the provost; Radulfus, son of Leodegarius.

“On their advice also I made the aforesaid donation, so that I myself and my wife, named Ermengardis, might from this day forward receive the assistance of the monks’ benefactions and prayers.

“But if they should later judge it better to rebuild the aforesaid church elsewhere, I shall gladly grant, wherever they wish, three *aripennia* of land in the same village for the work of the church or cemetery, reserving for them the site of the church in its new location.

“Since I hear that it is written by the Apostle, ‘God loves a cheerful giver,’ I add to this gift one of my knights, named Stabilus, together with the land or tithe that he held from my benefice in that place.

“The abbot and monks, in return for these things, gave me fifty solidi of coin as a gift of charity.

“But if anyone hostile to our welfare should at any time attempt to disparage this charter, confirmed by its proper names, let him be subjected to the fires of Gehenna with Dathan and Abiron.

“It was written while King Henry was reigning, in the same year in which he appointed Philip, his son, as his successor in the kingdom.

“Sign of Odo, who made this donation. Sign of Ermengardis, his wife. Sign of Avesgaudus, his nephew. Sign of Erveus. Sign of Hugo of Barzilleriae. Sign of Herbertus of Teon’s Villa.

“From our side: Stephanus; Ernulfus; Fulchdus; Tescelinus; Gauscelinus of Fragante-Villa.”

### CHAPTER XXXVII. Concerning the church-rent of Saliciolum and the land given. (Before 1080.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. It is fitting that all who have been reborn in Christ, and all who wish to live devoutly in him, should always be intent upon mourning through repentance the stains of earthly contamination that have clung to them through the pleasure of the flesh, guarding against what is to come, joining themselves to good works through sincere willingness, and following with all their effort the command of the Creator, who says: “Whoever has left a field or a house, or anything else in this world, for my sake, will receive a hundredfold in the future and will possess eternal life abundantly.”

I, Urso by name, hearing this most sweet praise of Christ with open ears, with the consent of my lord Walter, son of Vivian, whose benefice I appear hitherto to have held—namely, the dues of the church of Saliciolus, and also twenty-three jugera of land situated beside that church, on its eastern side—grant these to Saint Peter of the monastery of Chartres as a direct donation, for the salvation of my soul and of the souls of my parents, so that never at any time, in any manner, may they be reclaimed for any of my heirs.

I also add the consent of my wife Ausindis, my only son Gislebert, and my daughters, so that they may be able to share with me in the recompense in eternal life. And if life remains with me, and I should wish to draw nearer to that monastery in order to live there as a monk, I will increase the aforesaid gift as far as God grants me the means, and, as the Psalmist says: “I will please my Lord during my life; I will sing psalms to my God as long as I live.”

But so that this charter may remain inviolate, I wished the guarantors or witnesses to subscribe: Richard the cleric; Adrald and Bernard, his brothers; Walter, my nephew, surnamed Postellus; and Marcuard of Givriacum. I wished certain of those who heard and saw this to subscribe, so that, if perchance—which God forbid!—anyone should wish to oppose this donation, they might all rise against him and, for God’s sake, see to it that his attempt should not prevail.

Urso, who made this donation.  
Ausindis, his wife.  
Gislebert, his son.  
Walter Domnus, son of Vivian.  
Vivian, his son.  
Hildeburg, wife of Walter.  
Fulco the provost.  
Herbert of Burseriis.  
Rodulf of Calliolus.  
Amalric.  
Guido the priest.  
Herbert the priest.  
Girald the dean.  
Isengrius.  
Rainald of Harei Court.  
Radulf Gruellus.  
Ivo, son of Fulco.  
Radulf of the Market.  
Walter Postellus.  
Rodbert, keeper of the infirm.  
Walter of Groslu.  
Leodegarius, son of Hildegarius.  
Gauscelin of Villaris.  
Otrannus, his son.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII. Concerning the vicariate of the churchyard of the church of Anetis and of the mills. (Before 1080)

[Col. 0304D]

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Adelina, born of parents of distinguished rank according to the dignity of this world, nobly joined in a second marriage to a certain illustrious man named Rodbert—I, I say, wish it to be known to all worshipers of the holy Church of God that, for the salvation of my lord Rodbert, who, struck by a serious bodily illness and mindful of the divine word that says, ‘Whoever loves father or mother or wife or children more than me is not worthy of me,’ abandoned everything that he temporarily possessed in this world and, under Abbot Landric, in the monastery of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, namely that of Chartres, cutting the hair of his head and intending to live as a monk, strove to give himself to his Maker—for his sake, I grant, for the salvation of his soul and likewise of the soul of my father Ingenulf and of John, my first husband, to the holy community of monks dwelling there, that vicariate which appeared to be mine by right through my parents, both in the churchyard and in the mills and in their land, so that they may possess the vicariate and all the customs of judicial authority by perpetual right and hold them without any challenge.

“But so that this charter may have firmer validity in this matter, I have confirmed it with my own hand and delivered it to be confirmed by the hands of many witnesses, whose names are also subscribed:

Andreas of Moncello.  
Guido, son of Girelmus Malum Auxilium.  
Adrald of Croto.  
Frodelinus.  
Walter the priest.  
Girald the cook.  
Rainald the groom.  
Frodo.  
Adventius.  
Richard the cleric, and others.”

### CHAPTER XXXIX. Concerning the upper church of Croto. (In the year 1061)

“Serving the Creator of all things, I, Adrald, together with my two brothers, Richard the cleric and Bernard the layman, willingly and perpetually grant to Saint Peter of the monastery of Chartres the upper church of Croto, with four hospites, for my own soul and for the souls of my parents, so that, just as we are included in the prayers of the monks of the Greater Monastery, to whom I had first sold it, so may we be included in the prayers of these men who afterward bought it from them.

“Therefore let the monks of Saint Peter have that church and possess it by eternal right from this day forward, with no opposing claim. Let it be served by whatever priest they wish, notwithstanding the earlier agreement by which we stipulated that a monk should always be present there. For this matter, having received ten solidi of coin, at the request of Ascelin the monk, my cousin, I have confirmed this new charter with my own hand and delivered it for confirmation by the others written below: Gencelin the dean, Gerard the priest, Rainald the cleric, Godefrid son of Raherius; Isnard, Urso, Postellus, Odo, Fulbert, Beringer, Walter, and Rodbert.

“This charter was made in the second year of the reign of King Philip and was read aloud and confirmed before the doors of the church of Saint Stephen at the castle of Dreux.”

This aforesaid church had been bought from a certain monk of the Greater Monastery, named Ascelin. But when he saw that it contained little benefit and could scarcely endure the long-standing wickedness [Note: Codex B adds: “and insatiable rapacity.”] of Adrald, from whom he had bought it, he turned to Abbot Landric [Note: The same codex adds: “by stratagem.”] and asked him to buy it from him, so that it might be joined to the churches of Saint Peter, among which it was located. Accordingly, the abbot, foreseeing the future advantage, set aside the man’s present importunity, which would end with his flesh, gave the monk sixteen pounds of coin, and, with the consent of the entire chapter, returned to us the charter that the monks of Saint Martin had made for him; it is preserved among us to the present day together with the other sacred documents.

### CHAPTER XL. Concerning seven acres of land given to Saint Peter. (Before 1070)

“In the name of Christ. I, Landric, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, and our entire congregation of monks, wish it to be known to all worshipers of the Christian faith, both of the present age and of the future, that a certain man of Norman origin, named Herbert of Meli Court, gave seven acres of land in the territory of the castle of Meulan to Saint Peter, for the sake of his soul, together with every customary due, and placed the gift upon the altar of Saint Peter with his own hand.

“For this matter, before that altar, through the silver missal, we wished him to be clothed with the prayers of both the brothers present and those who would succeed them, in the presence of these witnesses: Hugh, priest of Bonneval; Arnulf the Black; Warin the cellarer; Hilduf and Gausfrid, brothers; Oidelerius; Ainerius the laundryman; and Engelbert the cook.

“But if anyone should wish to oppose this gift, by the authority of the apostle Peter, to whom it was given, let him be excommunicated; and, unless while alive he seeks satisfaction, let him, dead in hell, suffer the eternal punishments he deserves.”

### CHAPTER XLI. Concerning the customs of Broillamat [Note: The table of chapters reads “Broidlamart.”] (Before 1067)

[Col. 0306C]

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, in whose kingdom the quiet of perpetual peace flourishes. To all who dwell in my county, I, William, count of Normandy, make it known that the following account will clearly show what was done among us.

“There is in our region a certain village called Broillemat, given of old by its founders to the monastery of Saint Peter the apostle at Chartres; that monastery of Saint Peter is situated in the suburb of the city of Chartres. A certain monk of this monastery, named Gausfrid, came to us and asked that the judicial authority over the aforesaid village be given to Saint Peter. By God’s gift, I had until now possessed this authority, among many other things, by hereditary succession.

“Therefore, hoping that my sins might one day be forgiven me through the power of granting release bestowed upon Saint Peter by the Redeemer, I assent to the petitions of Landric, abbot of that monastery, and of all the brothers, which the aforesaid monk presented to us at their command. Whatever I appear to possess in the aforesaid village, I now transfer perpetually to Saint Peter from this day onward, because I firmly believe that in the future life he must repay it to me.

“This is confirmed by the subscribed names of suitable men who were present at this transfer, so that none of my successors may afterward dissolve it.

“William, count, who made this donation.  
Rodbert, his brother.  
William, son of Osbert.  
Corbution of Falaise.  
Gislebert, provost of Usmes.  
Baldwin of Gacé.  
Herbert of Meli Court.”

When the storm of persecution had subsided and the flames of anger that the insatiable zeal of the acephali’s bitterness vomited forth had been extinguished, the mind was again kindled with its innermost love for writing charters, which I had abandoned, wasting away in the horror of the most savage tempest. I desired to bring the work I had begun to its conclusion, so that, with divine mercy favoring me, I might remain free from that detestable saying: “This man began to build, and was unable to finish.”

Now, therefore, since I have the charters of the cell of Gisiacum before me, I am pleased to weave them together.

### CHAPTER XLII. Concerning the firm grant made by Abbot Gisbert. (29 September 986)

[Col. 0307B]

“[Note: This document is to be transferred to the book of Abbot Gisbert, above, cols. 241–242.] In the name of Christ. Gisbert, by divine favor abbot, and the entire flock of the Chartres monastery of the highest summit of the apostles Peter and Paul, to all faithful members of the present or future order.

“Although eternal law establishes that nothing created remains unchanged and that nothing that will exist in due course lasts forever, it is nevertheless clear that memory of past events cannot be restored by any better means than by the testimony of written documents.

“Accordingly, let the diligence of all the faithful, both present and future, consider that a certain knight named Ubert came to us, earnestly requesting the unanimous consent of our devotion that we grant to him, to his wife named Aiga, and to their one heir, in the county of Vexin, from the abbey of blessed ever-virgin Mary—which the inhabitants of that place call Avanglia—at a place called Altera Villa, one mansus in demesne, with all the appurtenances of that mansus, under an annual payment or rent.

“Therefore, agreeing to his petition with unanimous hearts, we grant the aforesaid mansus to him, to his aforementioned wife, and to their one heir, as stated, on the condition that they pay six solidi each year on the feast of Saint Remigius. If they should prove negligent or rebellious concerning this rent, let them make lawful amends and not lose the aforesaid land.

“But so that this charter may obtain firmer force, it has been handled by our hands and marked and confirmed by the names of many.

“Odo, count.  
Walter, count.  
[Note: Walter I, count of Duras and Vexin; see above, chapter I.]  
Abbot Gisbert.  
Durand the dean.  
Erbert the monk.  
Alveus the monk.  
Tedbert the monk.  
John the monk.  
Benedict the monk.  
Magenfred the monk.

“Done at the estate of Gisiacum, on the third day before the Kalends of October, in the first year of the reign of Louis, in the fourth indiction. [Note: A numeral X appears to have been omitted here in the codex, since the third day before the Kalends of October in the first year of Louis V corresponds to 29 September 986, which falls in the fourteenth indiction.] Erbert, monk and deacon, wrote this.”

This transaction brought us great loss, as we have already indicated. For, after those to whom the aforesaid charter had granted the right of possession had died, their survivors, through force and the presumptuous audacity of unpunished wrongdoing, wished to retain it for many years. One of them, a woman named Adela, supported by secular powers, endured the blow of daily excommunication for almost three lustrums. At last, worn out by old age and terrified by irrevocable death, she unwillingly relinquished it, fearing to bear the bonds of excommunication.

For this matter thirty pounds of coin were given to her two daughters and their husbands, so that in this way at least their immoderate greed might be extinguished—a greed that had allowed us, silently, to enjoy the produce of the estate for five years. But now, revived and boiling over, weighing right and wrong in an equal balance, it unjustly seizes what it had abandoned, while the blessed apostle Peter looks on and still holds vengeance back with merciful hand.

### CHAPTER XLIII. Concerning the custom granted by Count Walter [Note: The date of this charter is conjectured from a charter given by the same Walter, count of Vexin, to the monastery of Jumièges in the year 1006, concerning the same toll collected from vessels traveling along the Seine. See *The Art of Verifying Dates*, vol. II, p. 682.] (Around 1006)

“[Note: This charter belongs in the book of Abbot Magenard.] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. We judge it wholesome, useful, and profitable for our soul that, from the things granted to us by God in the present age, we should make grants to those who serve God for the salvation of souls. For whatever we see in this world we recognize as altogether fleeting, transitory, and unstable.

“Therefore I, Walter [Note: Walter II, surnamed the White, son of Walter I.], by the grace of God count, for the advancement and salvation of my soul, of the soul of my wife Adelidis, and of the souls of my sons, have granted to that place, at the request of Abbot Magenard and the other brothers, whatever temporal custom appears to belong to us from the ships of Saint Peter of Gisiacum passing along the Seine near our castle, commonly called Mantes; and this on the condition that neither I, nor my sons, nor any of our officials, may receive anything from it in time to come.

“But if anyone should attempt to rise against this gift of our largesse, bound by the bond of curse and anathema, let him be subjected to perpetual damnation; and because he did not wish to share with benefactors, let him perish forever with the blasphemers and persecutors of the Lord, and with Judas the traitor, and also with Dathan and Abiron, whom the earth swallowed alive.

“And so that this command of our authority may remain unshaken, we have confirmed it with our own hand and subscription and delivered it to be strengthened by the hands of our sons and faithful men.

“Walter, count.  
Rodulf, his son.  
Drogo, his son.  
Walter the knight.  
Rorigo.  
Hugh.  
Sanson.  
Ubert.  
Hugh.  
Addo.  
Guadso.”

### CHAPTER XLIV. Concerning the female serf given by Count Walerannus. (Before 1071)

“ In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. I, Gualerannus [Note: Gualerannus or Walerannus II, count of the castle of Meulan; he died either around 1069 or in the following year], count of the castle of Meulan, wish it to be known to the faithful of the holy Church of God, both present and future, that a certain man born from the household of Saint Peter of Gisiacum—a place known to be a cell of the monastery of Chartres—called Walter, had taken one of my female serfs as his wife.

“When I learned of this, I resolved to subject both the man and the woman to my jurisdiction. But when Landric, abbot of the aforesaid monastery, intervened together with certain monks, for love of almighty God, who in his free goodness provides all that his faithful require, and with the consent of my sweetest wife, my sons, and my faithful men, I relinquished that subjection and granted to Saint Peter the woman who had been mine by right, together with her husband, so that from this day forward he may possess them perpetually, as well as those who are to be born from them.

“But if any of my heirs should wish to oppose this small portion of my gift, may Saint Peter close the gate of Paradise against him and, unless he repents, hand him over to be punished in the bolts of Gehenna.

“But so that this charter may be firmer, I marked it with the sign of my assent before the church of Saint Nicaise and delivered it to be confirmed by my sons and faithful men.

“Gualerannus, count.  
Hugh, the firstborn.  
Adelidis, his wife.  
Gualerannus, his son.  
Fulcois, his son.  
Teduinus, the viscount.  
Heluisus, the cleric.  
Drogo of Conflans.  
Ansold the Parisian.  
Hilduin, son of Hermer.  
William the Bald.  
Warner, the provost.  
Odo of the Gate.  
Bernard White Saddle.  
Guarin the cleric.  
Vitalis.  
John.”

### CHAPTER XLV. Concerning the wrongful custom usurped by the viscount Hilduin. (Before 1080)

“ In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Hilduin the viscount, a hearer of the one who says that there is joy among the angels of God over one sinner who repents, wish it to be known to the faithful of the holy Church of God, both present and future, that I restore the pastures of my land, according to ancient custom and perpetual right, to all the beasts of the land of the cell of Saint Peter of Gisiacum, both in the woodland and outside the woodland, so that from now on they may have and graze them without any contradiction, in summer and winter alike.
