“I do this for the salvation of my soul and for the remedy of the soul of my father Hugh, who, in the absence of justice, introduced this wrongful custom: he forbade the grass that God ordered the earth to produce for all beasts, and did not fear to extort from men, as though by custom, a payment of a plow or of oxen for the grazing of that grass.

“For this evil custom, which I myself usurped after him until now, I confess that I have sinned gravely; and with the consent of my brother Hugh, as I have resolved, I relinquish it publicly for our souls.

“I confirm this charter with my own hand and the sign of the cross, and order my name and the names of our faithful men to be subscribed. But if any madman should at any time wish to oppose this act, unless he quickly repents, may he be swallowed alive by the earth with Dathan and Abiron; and may he be handed over to the fires of Gehenna with Herod, the slayer of the innocents, and Judas, the betrayer of the Lord.

“Hilduin the viscount, who relinquished this custom.  
Hugh, his brother.

“Names of the witnesses: Gualerannus, monk and provost, who for this matter gave the viscount thirty solidi of coin; Paul the monk, who wrote this charter; Roscelinus; Odo of Roseto; Aimard, son of Guntard; Adam of Buscheledo; Walter, son of Hugh of Aincourt; William, his nephew; William Folding-the-Mountain; Hugh Cutting-the-Willow; Hubert of Roseto; Urso the merchant; Turold, his son; Hubert Donzellus; Gauslin the Norman; Gambard; and Garnerius Bultio.”

### CHAPTER XLVI. Concerning the fair usurped by Count Drogo. (Before 1036)

“Truth, who is the Son of God and who said, ‘I am the truth,’ exhorts and teaches us not to seize what belongs to another and to give away what is our own.

“Therefore I, Drogo [Note: Drogo, count of Amiens, poisoned to death in Bithynia toward the end of 1035], count of Amiens, for love of the Son of God and the salvation of my soul, entirely relinquish the custom that I claimed to possess at the fair of Saint Peter of Gisiacum, which falls on the third day before the Kalends of July, and the *brennaticum* that I unjustly received at Calderiacum, Saint Ciricus, and Drogo’s Court.

“And so that this remission may remain firm forever, I have confirmed these letters with my own hand, together with my wife, sons, and faithful men.

“Drogo, count.  
Ehtde, countess.  
Fulco, the count’s brother.  
Rodulf, the count’s son.  
Walter, his other son.  
Sanson.  
Hugh Cutting-the-Willow.  
Arnulf the provost.  
Agard Fortis.  
Walter of Gronniacum.  
Rodbert of Viri.  
Othmund.  
Guido, son of Sansgualo.  
Ivo Guespa.  
Walter the Frank.  
Hubert of Roseto.  
Urso the archdeacon.  
Hugh Bascodelis.”

### CHAPTER XLVII. Concerning Rainbert and Frodburga, given by Count Odo. (Before 1061)

“In the name of God. I, Odo, son of Manasses, wish it to be made known to the people of the present and of the future that, with the consent of my brother Hugh, I have given to the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres and to the cell of that monastery at Gisiacum one male serf from our household, named Raimbert, and one female serf, named Frodburga, brother and sister, together with their sons and daughters, for the salvation of the soul of our father and of our mother.

“If anyone should wish to oppose this gift, let him be enveloped in infernal flames with Judas, the betrayer of the Lord; and, anathematized by him to whom the Lord Jesus Christ granted the power of binding and loosing, let him remain outside the gates of Paradise, tormented by the devil forever.

“I therefore beg all who read this document to strive to implore God’s mercy for our father Manasses, for our mother Constantia, and for ourselves, so that, after the course of this world, through the blessed apostle Peter, to whom we have bestowed the aforesaid gift, the Lord Christ may open for us the way to eternal life.

“Odo, count.  
Hugh, his brother.

“This charter was confirmed on the fifth day before the Ides of August, at the castle of Melun, in the palace of King Henry, by the hands of the two brothers aforesaid and of very many other men. Selecting a few of them, we have subscribed their names as testimony to both parties:

“Oidelard; Hugh, son of Richard of Bistisiacum; Hugh, son of Liperic; Rodbert Budicus; Fulcuin; Albert, monk and provost; Baldwin the archchaplain; Richard and Guiscelin, chaplains; Ulger the mayor; and John the chamberlain.

“Drogo, archdeacon of the Vexin, dictated this charter. If anyone should wish to oppose it, may his attempt remain ineffective, and may he pay the king one hundred pounds of gold.”

### CHAPTER XLVIII. Concerning the custom relinquished by Viscount Hugh. (Before 1034)

[Col. 0311C]

“[Note: This too is to be placed among the charters of Abbot Arnulf.] In the name of Christ. I, Arnulf, humble abbot of Saint Peter of Chartres, wish it to be known to all, present and future, concerning Hugh, viscount of the Vexin.

“For that same viscount had violently claimed for himself a certain vicariate in the land of Saint Peter of Gisiacum, in the estates called Droun Court, Saint Ciricus, and Calderiacum, belonging to the jurisdiction of Fontenay. Because he relinquished it in the presence of many of his companions, whose names we have subscribed, with the consent and command of his lord Count Drogo, from whose benefice he admitted that he held it, the aforesaid Count Drogo and the aforementioned Viscount Hugh first relinquished it upon the altar of Saint Peter of Gisiacum.

“The witnesses who heard and saw this matter are: Gualerannus, the viscount’s brother; Richard of Nielfa, his kinsman; Sanson, viscount of Mantes; Walter, son of Odo of Longue-Essé; Odo Morellus; Rodbert Friscus; Grurengarus; Walter the statue-maker [Note: In Codex A, this is superscribed, “or statuerus”]; Addo; Guaszo; Ivo Guespa; William; Guido Jerusalem; Gualerannus and Richard, his brother; Arnulf the provost; Fulcuin the Lame; Hugh of Aincourt; Hildebert of Gronniacum; and Mascelin of Gresiacum. These are from Mantes.

“From Meulan: Teduinus the viscount; Amelius, his brother; Warner the provost; Hervisus the cleric; Hildegarius Bodinus; William the Eloquent; Odo; Bernard; Hervisus the layman; Fulco the dean; Ernald; Walter, son of Bebo, and Achard, his brother; Rodulf Delicatus; Ivo of Arcura; Hubert of the Island; Hubert of Dunois; and Rainard the Younger.

“From our men: Hilduf; Rainbold; Stephen; and Gualonius.”

### CHAPTER XLIX. Concerning the toll of Andeliacum given by Archbishop Malgerius. (Before 1056)

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. It is highly suitable and altogether necessary for every faithful person who fears God and wishes to have a share in the land of the living to strive to honor, enrich, and exalt God, his saints, and their places from the things he possesses temporarily, so that in exchange for temporal things he may acquire eternal ones and in exchange for earthly things obtain heavenly ones.

“From the beginning of the Church’s birth there have been devout men who feared God and desired to merit true goods; they honored and exalted the Church of God from their possessions, and therefore received from Christ a worthy reward.

“Reflecting upon this and often considering it with a vigilant mind, I, Malgerius [Note: Archbishop Malgerius died around 1035], by the grace of God archbishop of the church of Saint Mary of Rouen, for divine love, for the remedy of my soul, and for the redemption of the souls of my parents, have forever forgiven to Saint Peter of the monastery of Chartres and to the monks serving there the toll dues that my officials collect at Andeliacum, so that henceforth they may pay no toll on the goods of Saint Peter brought by the river Seine to Rouen.

“This too I have forgiven at the intervention of Landric, abbot of the aforesaid monastery. But if any invader of the Church’s property should wish to destroy this donation, may God destroy him, so that he may have no share in the kingdom of Christ and of God.

“And so that the authority of this donation may remain firm, I have confirmed it with my own hand and the sign of the cross, and ordered my faithful men, whose names are written here, to confirm it with me.

“Malgerius, archbishop.  
Osbern the dean.  
Hugh the archdeacon.  
Fulbert the chancellor.  
Radbod the canon.  
Rodbert the deacon.  
Gislebert the deacon.  
Gerard, master of the cupbearers of Count William [Note: the Conqueror].  
Heribert the layman.  
Stephen the layman.  
Albert, monk and provost of Gisiacum.  
Rainerius, monk and sacristan.  
Magenard, monk and steward of Abbot Landric.  
Gausfrid the layman.  
Haimeric the layman.  
Roscelin of Rouen.  
Oduin the mayor.”

### CHAPTER L. Concerning the same toll, given again by Archbishop Maurilius. (Before 1068)

“I, Maurilius [Note: Archbishop Maurilius died in 1067], by the grace of God archbishop of Rouen, for the alms of my lord William, count of the Normans, and for the salvation of my soul and of my predecessors and successors, forgive to the monastery of the church of Chartres, situated in the suburb of that city in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the toll on its own wine, which previously used to be collected at a place belonging to us whose center is Andeliacum, so that from now and forever the officials of the aforesaid monastery may travel safely through that place without paying any toll.

“Done at Rouen, on the day before the Ides of October, in the presence of Lord Maurilius the archbishop, with the canons standing by and giving their approval: Benedict the archdeacon, Stigand the cantor, Godbert the canon, Landric the canon, Walchelin the canon, and William; also the monks Walerannus, provost of Gisiacum, and Teduinus, his brother; and the laymen Gelduin the mayor, Deodatus, and Goisbert.”

### CHAPTER LI. Concerning the pastures that Viscount Teduinus used to forbid. (Before 1070)

“In the name of God. I, Teduinus, viscount of the castle of Meulan, wish it to be known to all, present and future, that I have relinquished before the altar of that Saint Peter at Gisiacum, in the presence of many people, together with my son Walter, surnamed Pagan, that custom which I had until now unjustly held in my land—namely, the prohibition of pasture to the animals of Saint Peter of Gisiacum—which I held unjustly.

“Afterward I asked the monks of that place to go to Chartres and tell the abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter, namely Landric, and all the brothers, to grant me absolution for having held that custom unjustly for so long a period. They fulfilled this willingly.

“But if anyone should wish to revive this custom, let him, anathematized and convicted by the witnesses, go to destruction with Annas and Caiaphas.

“And so that this charter may remain inviolate, I confirmed it before that altar with my own hand and with the hand of my aforementioned son, in the presence of the following witnesses:

“John the provost; Adelelm of Feluix; Odo of Montmorency; Teduinus, son of Vivian; Walter of Anetis; and Rainald the seneschal.

“From our men: Gausfrid Bicotus; Oduin the mayor; Odo and Bernard, brothers; Brunellus; Stephen, son of Aitrudis; Hubold; Gislebert; Bernerius; Gausbert the baker; Herbert the baker; Herbelin of the Rock; Warner; Constantius; Roscelin, surnamed Foal; Teduinus, son of Rodbert; and Ernulf, son of Oduin.”

### CHAPTER LII. Concerning the toll of the castle of Vernon. (Before 1061)

“In the name of God. I, Hugh the monk, together with my son William, still a boy, wish it to be known to all worshipers of Christ, present and future, that, for the remedy of our souls and of the souls of our parents, we perpetually grant to Saint Peter of the monastery of Chartres and to the cell of Gisiacum, and to the monks serving God there, the toll custom that until now has been collected at our castle of Vernon, so that henceforth they may pay no toll on the goods of Saint Peter brought to Rouen or brought back from there by the river Seine or by land.

“We granted this at the preaching of Landric, abbot of the aforesaid monastery, from whom in return we received the prayers of the place and one excellent horse.

“But if any invader of the Church’s property should attempt to rise against this gift of ours, bound by an unbreakable bond of curse, let him be handed over with the devil to everlasting punishments.

“We have confirmed this charter with our hands and signs and delivered it to be confirmed by others whose names are subscribed.

“Hugh the monk.  
William, his son.  
Richard the viscount.  
Roger.  
Schroc.  
William.  
Raherius.  
William the provost.  
Godefrid.  
Osmund.  
Girelmus.  
Letald the chaplain.

“These are witnesses on Hugh’s side, the donor of this matter.

“On the abbot’s side: Albert, monk and provost; Magenard, monk and steward; Gausfrid Bigotus; Bernard, son of Vulmar; Hubelinus; and Guiddo the cleric.

“This was done in the castle of Vernon, on the feast day of Saint Clement the martyr, while the fearless King Henry was reigning and the illustrious Count William held the sovereignty of Normandy.”

### CHAPTER LIII. Concerning a male serf and a female serf given by Gameno. (Before 1071)

[Col. 0314C]

“In the name of Christ. I, Gameno, wish it to be known to all, present and future, what agreement I made with the monks of Saint Peter of Gisiacum, under whose supervision that place was then held—namely, concerning one of my male serfs, named Reinerius, and his wife and children.

“For the aforesaid monks petitioned me concerning the aforementioned serf, asking me to hand him over to Saint Peter. I willingly consented to their request. Therefore I handed him over to Saint Peter, together with his wife and children, on this condition: that both he and all his descendants should remain perpetually in the service of that place.

“And so that this agreement may remain firm, I ordered these letters to be made on parchment, confirmed them with my own hand, and placed upon them the sign of the holy [Note: The word “cross” is omitted.] cross, together with my wife and sons. I also presented them to my lord, named Walerannus [Note: This is the count of the castle of Meulan, Walerannus II, mentioned above, chapter XLIV], for confirmation.

“If any of my relatives or successors should contradict them or attempt to destroy the agreement, let him be subject to the dart of eternal curse with Judas the traitor.

“We have also subscribed as witnesses, having heard and seen this: Hilduard; Ricuard; Milo; Guinemund; John; Alhaldus; and Warner.”

### CHAPTER LIV. Concerning Letald, his wife, and his brother, given by Hugh. (Before 1061)

“Let it be known that whoever, whether faithful or Christian, releases a person subjected to him by the bond of servitude, for love of almighty God, should know that the gracious Lord will repay him with an everlasting reward in due time. For Truth himself, who is Christ, instructs his faithful to do good, saying in the Gospel: ‘Release, and you will be released; give, and it will be given to you.’

Therefore I, Hugh, in God’s name, together with my son Hugh and my daughter Beatrice, transfer this half-free man subject to my jurisdiction, Letald, with his wife Amalberga and his brother Rannulf, together with the sons and daughters who shall be born from them, to the place of Saint Peter of the monastery of Chartres, so that they may remain free in the service of that place. But if anyone should wish to oppose this donation [Note: So in the manuscripts], he shall be compelled by the king’s treasury to pay a pound of gold. And so that this donation of mine may remain unshaken, I have confirmed it with my own hand and delivered it to be strengthened by the hands of my faithful.

The mark of Hugh Brustans Salicem, who made this donation.
The mark of Hugh, his son.
The mark of Beatrice, his daughter.
The mark of Ralph Malus Vicinus.
The mark of Amalric.
The mark of Hescelin.
The mark of Hugh of Arculus.
The mark of Robert, son of Landric.
The mark of Geoffrey.
The mark of Hubert of Rosetum.
The mark of Ansfrid Gabardus.
The mark of Constantius.
The mark of Benedict.
The mark of Wido.
The mark of Tedald the priest.

This was publicly enacted at Gisiacum, while the most serene King Henry was reigning.”

## CHAPTER LV. Concerning a customary due relinquished by Hugh the viscount. (Before 1061)

[Col. 0315C]

“I, Hilduin, son of Hugh the viscount, make known to those present and those to come that I have abandoned the claim which I was unjustly bringing against the land of Saint Peter of Jociacum. My grandfather, Hilduin the viscount, bestowed it upon Saint Peter as he himself possessed it—that is, all the customary dues that he held there, namely the right of billeting and the provision of dog food, and, in addition, everything belonging to the viscountcy.

The name of this land is Calciacum, and the name of the other land is Berneacum. I confess that I have abandoned the claim to these customary dues which I was unjustly making. I placed the gift and relinquishment of these things upon the altar [Col. 0315D] of Saint Peter, together with my brother Hugh. I solemnly confess that I sinned gravely through this claim.

Therefore, whoever wishes to invalidate this document shall suffer torment in hell with Judas, the betrayer of the Lord. The hearers and witnesses of this matter are those whose names are recorded here:

Droco, archdeacon; Hilduin, who relinquished this claim; Hugh; Teduin; Walter the constable; Odo Rufinus; Hugh Brustans Salicem; William of Bacelmont; Odo, son of Aluzo; Berard; Norman of Guadon’s Court; John the provost; Raimer; Nicholas of Jutogilum; Walter Statuerius; Odo Rufinus; Hugh Brustans Salicem; William of Bacelmont; Odo, son of Aluzo; Berard; Norman of Guadon’s Court; John the provost; Raimer; Nicholas of Jutogilum; Warner of Medanta; Hugh of Fagetulum; John the chamberlain; Hulger the elder [Col. 0316A]; Gamelin the elder; Hoduin the elder; Odo, son of Constantius; Rainald Cossardus; Alberic the oxherd; Hilduin Tirellus; Ralph of Beaumont [Note: B: “of Mollemont”]; Bernerius; Germund; Guiard, son of Roscelin.

Sienfred wrote this, while King Henry was reigning.”

## CHAPTER LVI. Concerning the toll of the Rock, which Guido and Richard gave. (Before 1080)

“In Christ’s name. I, Guido of the Rock, together with the consent of my brother Richard, wish it to be known to all Christians of the present and future age that, for love of our Creator and for the salvation of our souls, as well as for the repose of the souls of our parents who have passed from this fleeting [Col. 0316B] world, and of those who will arise in the flesh from our descendants, I willingly grant to Saint Peter of the monastery of Chartres and to the brothers serving Christ there—for whom the cell of Gisiacum supplies what is due through obedience—the right to collect the toll, for all succeeding time, from the ships of Saint Peter that pass under the protection of our Rock along the Seine to Rouen and return from there.

Both my brother and I have publicly confirmed this charter with our own hands, invoking the destruction of Dathan and Abiron and the punishments of Judas the betrayer upon all who may wish to oppose this gift of our generosity.”

## CHAPTER LVII. Concerning customary dues given by Hugh Pirarius. (Before 1080)

[Col. 0316C]

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

I, Hugh, surnamed Pirarius, and my wife Ledgardis, and our son Fulcoisus, having heard the voice of the Apostle Paul, who says, ‘While we have time, let us do good to all,’ and wishing to fulfill the meaning of this saying, now relinquish, for the honor of God and of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, all the customary dues which my predecessors held and which I have until now held, against right and divine law, in Droco’s Court, that is, in the land of Saint Peter of Gisiacum.

May he deign to lead my soul, and the souls of my wife and my son, into the kingdom of heaven, with the assent of Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever.

The mark of Hugh Pirarius.
The mark of Ledgardis, his wife.
The mark of Fulcoisus, his son.

On their side were these: Albert the priest; John the knight; Walter, surnamed Joscelin; Bernard, son of Ernulf; Gauslin of White Way; Ernulf, son of Ermenfred Croculus.

On our side: Hugh, viscount of Domicilium; Hugh of Aiga Court; Guiard, son of Roscelin; Ralph of Heri Villa; Ulger the elder; Anscher, his son; Girelmus, his nephew; Odo the elder; Bernard, his brother; Elvis the knight; Teduin and Bernard, brothers; Brunellus and Morellus, brothers; Warner, son of Germund; Warner, [Col. 0317A] son of Hilduin of Ablainmont; Bernard of the Meadow; Hubold, son of Martin; Gausbert the elder; Boldard, son of Rainard.

Paul the monk wrote this.”

## CHAPTER LVIII. Concerning Aiga Court, given by Geretrude. (In 1062)

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Since an irreversible fate awaits everyone at the hour appointed, each of us must beware lest he follow the left-hand path leading toward the punishments of hell, but must carefully guard the path of justice leading to the pleasant dwellings of eternal life. Anyone can guard it if he wishes to obey the Lord’s commandments diligently.

It is also the Lord’s command that each person give away what is his for the love of God. For he says: ‘Give, and it will be given to you’; and, ‘Whoever gives only a cup of cold water in my name, amen I say to you, shall not lose his reward.’

Obedient to these and other sayings of almighty God, I, the sinner Geretrude, born, according to the dignity of the world, from parents of no low standing, strive most willingly to obey as far as my weakness permits. I grant to almighty God and to Saint Peter of Gisiacum, that is, to the cell of the monastery of Chartres, to be possessed after my death by hereditary right, a certain allod which I seem lawfully to possess at Aiga Court.

Thus may he to whom the Lord said, ‘Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven,’ loosen the bonds of my sins and those of my husband Hilduin, son of Hermar, and of my parents, lest the most just Judge, at the final judgment, send us with the reprobate to infernal punishments; but may he speak to us that honey-sweet voice with which he will comfort the righteous, saying: ‘Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.’

I grant, then, the cultivated and uncultivated land of this allod, irrigated and dry land, meadows and woodland, its entrances and exits, and two portions of the church which are my right.

As long as I wish to hold it while alive, I shall invest Saint Peter with only two tenants from the aforesaid allod: one by my own will and the other at the request of my aforesaid husband.

We wish to confirm this charter with our own hands and names, and we have judged it worthy to have it confirmed by the names of others, so that, if anyone should ever attempt—which God forbid!—to violate this written donation of ours, he may be struck by the sword of anathema, severely punished before the judges according to the law, pay three pounds of gold, and may his attempt have no effect.

This was enacted in the second year of the reign of King Philip, still a very young boy, while Abbot Landric governed our house.

Paul the monk wrote this.”

Before leaving this world through death, this noblewoman Geretrude left the aforesaid allod to Saint Peter and to us. We possessed it for many years, not only while she was alive but also after she had died and been buried before the doors of the atrium of the church at Gisiacum [Col. 0318A]. Then, at the devil’s instigation, one of her nieces, named Hildeburg, the wife of Robert, a knight from the castle of Évreux, seized by force and secular power everything that her maternal aunt had bestowed upon Saint Peter for the sake of her soul. Both she and her aforesaid husband disinherited the Lord and his apostle Peter, preferring to make worldly men their heirs. We leave their crime for now in silence, to be examined by God, the most equitable judge.

## CHAPTER LIX. Concerning the restoration of Geneth Villa. (In 1066)

“In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

I, Adela, formerly wife of Hubert, a knight from the castle of Medanta [Col. 0318B], wish it to be known to the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, that the father of my aforesaid husband humbly approached the presence of Abbot Gisbert and the monks of the monastery of the holy apostles Peter and Paul at Chartres, earnestly requesting that they grant him, his wife, and their sole heir, under a secure tenure, the land called Geneth Villa, which lies in the territory of the Vexin. It appeared to be the third part of a village whose ancient name, since it is unknown to those now living, we have judged would be of no benefit to record for those to come.

While they lived, the heirs appeared to possess this land lawfully and not unjustly. Those who seized and held it after them undoubtedly lost paradise because of it, to the detriment of their souls.

I myself, a sinner adding sins to sins, did not fear to retain it unlawfully for more than twenty years after my husband’s death, under the bond of anathema. But now, since I am an old woman and am setting foot upon the boundaries of this life, I wish by salutary counsel to draw it back from this evil beginning. The ordinary judgment of reason shows how I can do this: namely, by asking pardon for this monstrous crime and relinquishing what I wrongly held.

Therefore, I now first restore the secure tenure before our lord Count Ralph and his son Walter, while retaining the land as necessary for my very brief life. After I have died, let the monks [Col. 0318D] of Saint Peter possess that land forever, with no one opposing them.

My son-in-law Anscher and his daughters also consented to this restoration. Their names are: Havisa, Matilda, Avicia, Adela, and Helvisa, who is already married to her husband Statualis.

Since we could not gather them all in one place, we took care to insert into this charter the individual places where each separately gave her consent.

Thus, before Count Ralph and his son Walter, there were: Geoffrey of Gummeth; Simon of Montfort; Mainer, his brother; Ralph Malus Vicinus; Robert, his son; Arrald; Sansgualo; Waszo; Urso of Fontaines; Alberic of Blara Church; Walter of Montiacum; Guiard of Étampes; Hubert d[.....] [Col. 0319A]dus; Odo, son of Cuscha; Odo, brother of Frohard; Eric; Roger the Norman; Ulger the elder; Odo the elder; Bernard and Arnulf, brothers; Gausbert the elder; Walter and Rainer, brothers; Hubert; John; Letald; Odard of Alto Monte; Hilduin and Warner, his son; Roscelin the colt-rider; Rainard; Odo, son of Ogis.

In the village called Ri, Anscher, Adela’s son-in-law, consented together with his daughter named Advisa. The witnesses to this were: Gislebert; Eustace, son of Hugh of Ansellis Villa; Rodulf; Girard, son of Hugh of Dorlech; Adelelm, son of Alfred; Gerard of Alleatum.

At Noviomum, Matilda and Avicia, sisters and daughters of Anscher, consented. The witnesses were: Gislebert; Auscher, son of Guantelm; Guenelann, son of Gislebert [Col. 0319B] of Portus; Roger, son of Alfred; Girard, son of Hugh of Dorlech.

Hugh Statualis in the castle of Medanta consented together with his wife Helvisa. The witnesses were: Sansgualo; Odo, brother of Frohard; Amalric Sine Pilo; Tedbald of Bishop’s Mount; Geoffrey Cocardus; Gadelo; Teduin and John, brothers; Ascelin; Ebrard; Odo the elder; Ulger the elder; Gausbert the elder; Robert of Boton’s Court; Maurice; Bernard; Roger the baker; Herbert; Tedbald; Hilduin; Brunellus; Garner; Hilduin Tirellus; Hubold; Fulchard.

I confirmed this charter with my own hand and delivered it to be strengthened by the hands of Counts Ralph and his son Walter, and also by those of their leading men. If any of my heirs should wish to oppose this work, may he perish in hell forever with Judas [Col. 0319C] the betrayer.

This was enacted in the sixth year of King Philip, in the seventh indiction [Note: Indiction VII corresponds to the year 1069, not to 1066. Art de vérifier les dates.].

Paul the monk wrote it out, and the monk Walerann gave thirty pounds in coin for this very matter, besides small gifts.”

## CHAPTER LX. Concerning the customary due of the vineyard of Guarinus the cleric and Walter the Frank. (Before 1070)

“Let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, that I, Walter, surnamed Paganus, son of Teduin and viscount of the castle of Mellent, in order to obtain the rewards of our eternal homeland, from the possessions which I seem to hold in the present world, together with my wife Rainsuinde, for the soul of my father and my mother, relinquish to Saint Peter—that is, to the cell of the monastery of Chartres at Gisiacum—the customary due which I claim in the vineyard of Guarinus the cleric.

I also give the customary due of Walter the Frank’s vineyard, which he himself had given to Saint Peter, so that none of my heirs may henceforth dare to claim any customary due in these vineyards.

These vineyards are in the territory of Maisiacum, my village. At the request of the monk Walerann, I have finally placed stone markers dividing the land of Saint Peter from mine, so that there may no longer be a dispute between me and the monks of Saint Peter, or between my servants and theirs.

So that this charter may remain more firmly established, after the confirmation by my own hand and by the hands of the witnesses subscribed below, I ordered the penalty of excommunication to be written beneath it: whoever wishes to oppose this charter shall perish in hell with Judas the betrayer, with Dathan and Abiron, whom the earth swallowed alive; with Herod, the murderer of the innocent; and with Nero, the killer of Peter and Paul.

Paganus, viscount.
Rainsuindis, his wife.
Joscelin of Botignac.
Hugh Comedens Rusticum.
Odo of Vernugilum.
Ebrard, son of Ernald.
Joscelin the younger.
Fulco the provost.
Teduin, son of Otold.
Fulcolin of Nielfa.
Herbert the vicar.
Guibert of Maisi.
Ansold.
Ralph and Odo, brothers.
Teduin Vivanda.

On the side of the monk Walerann: Ulger the elder; Odo the elder; Bernard, his brother; Oduin; Arnulf, his son [Col. 0320B]; Rainald Cossardus; Herbert Illuns; Germund and Berner, brothers; Hilduin and Amalric, brothers; Hilduin Tirellus; Odo of Alto Monte; Warner, son of Germund; Teduin, son of Robert; Brunellus and Morellus, brothers; Sansgalo; Otold; Hubald.”

## CHAPTER LXI. Concerning the fourth part of Guairiacum. (Before 1070)

“Truth, who is Christ, commands his followers not to seize what belongs to others and to give away what is theirs. Therefore, for love of the Redeemer, I, Hugh, surnamed Brustans Salicem, grant to Saint Peter—that is, to the cell of the monastery of Chartres at Gisiacum—a certain piece of land belonging to me, for the salvation of my soul, my wife’s soul, and my son’s soul: namely, a fourth part of the church and village called Guairiacum, and a fourth part of the woodland, mill, and meadows, excepting the orchard and the cultivated fields.

So that this charter may remain firm, I have confirmed it with my own hand, with the hand of my lord Count Walter, in whose county it lies, and with the hands of my faithful. If anyone attempts to do anything against this donation, let him be sent into the lowest hell, where the fire that is never extinguished shall burn him and the worm that never dies shall gnaw his flesh.

In addition to this gift, I grant to Saint Peter a certain half-free woman named Ingelburg, daughter of Walter Capra. Of both things I publicly placed the gift upon the altar of Saint Peter.

The witnesses to this are: Hugh, my son [Col. 0320D]; Beatrice, my daughter; Adelelm; Frodmund; Odo Donzellus; Ansfrid Imbardus; Hubold the elder; Hubelin; Bernard; Hugolin.

On the monks’ side: Geoffrey Bigot; Arnulf, his brother; Oduin; Rannulf the priest; Rainald Cossardus; Adventus; Gausbert; Fulchard; Robert of Gizecium and Arnulf, his son.”

This man was one of the leading men of the castle of Medanta, according to the dignity of the world. For love of God he abandoned estates and earthly riches, cut the hair of his head and his beard in this monastery under Abbot Landric, and, taking the monastic habit, gave himself entirely, stripped of the wicked world, to be shaped by good works [Col. 0321A].

Ascending to the highest summit of obedience and humility, he was appointed by the aforesaid abbot administrator and guardian of the place at Gisiacum. When he governed it successfully without deceit or ambition, a prudent reader can infer from this single story how great was his simplicity and chaste shrewdness [Note: What follows concerning Hugh is absent from manuscript B.].

On one occasion he had eaten with the abbot in the village called Fontinidus and hurried back to the monastery. When the brothers asked him whether he had eaten that day, he came to himself, hesitated inwardly for a while, and thought, saying to himself: ‘If I say that I ate, perhaps I shall be criticized as having violated the fast; but if I deny the truth, I shall depart marked by the stain of lying.’

Then, when the brothers questioned him, he is said to have replied: ‘If the lord abbot ate, so did we; but if the lord abbot did not eat, neither did we.’

After he had departed from the present world, his son—sharing his name, serving under the military belt, and differing from his father in no way in good conduct—granted to Saint Peter in the aforesaid village, Guairiacum, another fourth part of the village, just as his father had done. He placed the gift upon the altar before witnesses, retaining for himself from that same portion only the tenure of one tenant; and after the course of this life, let the entire portion remain intact, so that from then on his heirs may possess half the village, while Saint Peter may have an equal amount for the entrance into the heavenly homeland.

## CHAPTER LXII. Concerning Gibuin and Waland, and their wives. (In 1061)

[Col. 0321C]

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Let it be known to all the faithful, present and future, concerning a certain man named Gibuin, who lived freely for eighteen years on the land of Saint Peter. My father, the viscount Teduin, seized him for himself by force and power under the law of servitude. This indeed happened so that the highest right became the highest injustice.

Thus my father held this man, and afterward I held him for several years. But since from one wrongly possessed thing much wealth is often forfeited, moved by fear of eternal torments and also by love of almighty God, who says, ‘Loosen the bundles that weigh down and break every burden,’ I, Walter, surnamed Paganus, the viscount, and my wife Raisindis, through whom I had possessed the aforesaid man’s servitude, now in turn release from the yoke of servitude Gibuin, his brother Waland, their wives, all their offspring, and all their descendants. I also relinquish the vineyards which that same Gibuin had sold to Arnulf of the castle of Medanta.

So that this freedom, once granted, may remain firm forever, we have confirmed this charter with our proper names and the marks of our hands, and delivered it to be confirmed by others. If anyone of unsound mind should ever wish to oppose it, let him be convicted according to law and excommunicated by God’s authority; let him pay a pound of gold to the judge, and let his attempt remain ineffective.

The witnesses to this matter are: Ralph, son of Gualo the priest; Gualdric of Rangisport; Sigismund, son of Ernald of Brugilum; William the zither-player.

Witnesses for Gibuin, on behalf of Saint Peter, to whom he voluntarily submitted himself: Ulger the elder; Gausbert the elder; Rainald Cossardus; John; Ralph; Amalric Bornus; Alelm; Ernulf.

This freedom was granted in the second year of the reign of King Philip, still a very young boy.”

Now let us turn our pen to the charters that remain, because we have written out those at Gisiacum that we had in hand.

## CHAPTER LXIII. Concerning the vineyards and house given by Firmatus, canon of Saint Leobinus. (Before 1049)

[Col. 0322B]

“[Note: We assigned this charter to the time of Theoderic, bishop of Chartres, who died in 1048.]

In Christ’s name. I, Firmatus, priest of Saint Leobinus in the castle of Dunum, wish it to be known to those present and those to come how, for the salvation of my soul and that of my brother Elbert, I give to Saint Peter of Chartres my house situated in the castle of Dunum, not far from the monastery of holy Mary, Mother of God.

The arrangement is this: as long as I live, I shall guard it by the will and command of the monks of Saint Peter, and they shall possess it perpetually as its rightful lords. If anyone, warned on by the devil, attempts to inflict a claim or violence upon Saint Peter—which I do not at all expect—let him know that he will be condemned forever by pontifical authority [Col. 0322C], unless he performs worthy penance.

Therefore, so that this may remain firm, I offered it for confirmation to my shepherd, the lord Bishop Theoderic, in whose time I carried this out.

I also give to blessed Peter, near Saint Albinus, in the territory of the aforesaid castle, three *quartarii* of vineyard without any customary due, and likewise half an *aripennus* of vineyard beside the vineyards of my brother Ailbert.

The witnesses to this are: Odo the archdeacon; Odo the dean; Frederick the priest; Dago the priest; Godescaudus the knight; Ascelin the knight and Hugh, his son; Odo Brunellus; Engelbald the knight and Rainald, his son; Dodo, canon of Saint Peter; Elbert; Hildier, the cleric.”

## CHAPTER LXIV. Secure tenure at Trunniacum. (Before 1070)

[Col. 0322D]

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

I, Abbot Landric, and all the monks of the monastery of Chartres, wish it to be known to everyone, present and future, that a certain man named Roszo came to us, asking that we give him a certain small piece of our land which he claimed through his predecessors. The land is divided into two parts, one situated at Trunniacum and the other at Gomma.

He also asked that we grant it to his brother, named Alcher, and to one heir of theirs. We did so, on the condition that on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, which is in the month of July, they pay twelve denarii in rent. If they pass beyond that deadline, let them make good the default and retain the aforesaid land.

So that this charter may remain inviolate, we have judged that it should be confirmed by our hands.

The mark of Landric, abbot.
Rainer, prior.
Marcuin.
Robert.
Arefast.
Agenard.
Durand.
Raymond.
Ernald.
Albert.
Magenard.
Martin.
Paul.
Rainald.”

## CHAPTER LXV. Concerning two plots redeemed by Landric. (Before 1061)

“Let it be known to those present and those to come that I, Abbot Landric, and all the monks of the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres, on the third day before the Nones of November, received from Walter, surnamed Fugans Lupum, together with his wife Unberga and his stepchildren Simon, Milesind, and Oydela, with the consent of his lord Guarinus and his wife Adelaide, two plots of land with two inhabitants, to be held by Saint Peter forever. In return he received from us one horse worth three pounds, together with the benefits of our prayers.

The land itself lies above our enclosure, in the street facing the gate beside Saint Michael’s. It had once been granted temporarily by Abbot Arnulf to Teudo, predecessor of Guarinus of the Tower.

The witnesses to this are: Ansold of Mungervilla; Walter of Munhervilla; Gausfrid, his son; Landric, son of Hunger; Stephen and Adventius, his son; Hugh the priest; Fulco the Eunuch; Oideler; Girogius, son of Gauscelin; Ermenold; Stephen; Teduin; Warinus the baker.

This was publicly enacted at Chartres, in the church of Saint Peter, while King Henry was reigning.

Paul the monk wrote it.”

## CHAPTER LXVI. Concerning Saint Germanus of Alogia. (Before 1070)

“In Christ’s name. I, Landric, by the grace of God abbot of the monastery of Chartres, and the entire congregation of monks entrusted to me, wish it to be known to all our successors, present and future, that a certain priest of the church of Saint Germanus of Alogia, named Natalis, showed such affection and love toward us and our house that, sound in mind and body, he asked his lords—from whom he held the aforesaid church and other possessions as a benefice—to grant him the power to transfer everything he appeared to possess from them into the authority of Saint Peter and his monks, for love of God and for the redemption of their souls.

Thus they might possess and hold perpetually, without any claim against them, the aforesaid church; the land belonging to the altar; the offerings and burial rights; the small tithes that he held; half of one mill; and the land of one plough; also two *aripennos* of vineyard at Alto Pedaneo.

The condition was that, if at any time he wished to come to the monastic habit in [Col. 0324A] our monastery, he would be received in return for the aforesaid possessions given; but if death overtook him in the clerical habit, his body would be buried in the cemetery.

His lords, namely Bernard of Buslo and Walter of Monte Mirabili, gladly consented to this. They also preferred to increase the aforesaid gift from their own possessions, as will be stated in their proper places. They ordered it to be publicly placed upon the altar of the apostles Peter and Paul, in the presence of the entire congregation and of many people, and commanded that it be made known in writing to all their successors. They bound all who attempted to oppose it with the bond of excommunication and invoked that their souls, unless they repented and sought the remedy of satisfaction, should fall into hell, where they would have forgiveness and rest with the devil.

Gausfrid [Col. 0324B] of Medena also gave his consent, for at that time he held the whole honor of Alogia. His wife Matilda, Gausfrid’s stepson William, and his son Walter also consented. I would subscribe other witnesses if that did not seem superfluous.”

## CHAPTER LXVII. Concerning land given by the noblewoman Matilda. (Before 1070)

“Whatever good is done is done in the name of the one by whom a person is inspired to desire the good and raised up to perform it; and, perfected through perseverance to the end, he is rewarded forever.

Therefore Lady Matilda, for the redemption of her soul and of the souls of her lords, namely William and Gausfrid, and of her parents and children, gave to Saint Germanus a piece of land which, lying beside the cemetery of that same church, is bounded by the road leading from that basilica to Colummeries, and is terminated by that same land; on this side by Monte Canori and Algunni Villa; and on the other side by Ulsiaca, the land of the Island, and the land of Baldwin.

She placed this entire land, together with the meadow, just as she had held it in demesne, as a gift upon the altar of Saint Germanus.

The witnesses to this are: Algrin; Adelelm and Natalis, priests; Guido, son of Guarinus; Robert, son of Lambert.

Lord William, her son, willingly granted this same gift, just as his mother had made it. The witnesses to this are: Walter, brother of Hugh; Eirard of Busto Loco; Walter of Munhervilla; Hamelin Livarecus; Briccius of the castle of Laetum; Gausfrid; Hugh of Barzilleries; Rainald, son of Gausfrid; Bernard of Abon’s Villa.”

## CHAPTER LXVIII. Concerning a road given by the same Matilda. (Before 1070)

“In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

I, Matilda, who by hereditary right appear, by divine favor, to be lady of the honor of Alogia, wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, that, for love of God, from whom I have everything necessary for human life and to whom I owe everything, and for the honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom, among other gifts, we grant the church of Saint Germanus in the area of Alogia itself, I now remove the public road which has until now appeared to run beside the wall of that church, for the salvation of my soul and of my parents.

From this day forward, let that road run outside, far from the church, so that the monks dwelling there may be free from travelers and from collectors of the customary toll, without any disturbance.

I ordered this charter to be made, and through it placed the gift of the aforesaid road upon the altar of the apostles Peter and Paul, impressing the sign of the cross with my own hand. I likewise ordered this to be done by those present with me: Warinus the provost, Eirard, Bernard of Barzilleries, and David.”

## CHAPTER LXIX. Concerning the vicariate purchased at Mitanis Villa. (Before 1080)

[Col. 0325B]

“Since, according to the saying of Truth, iniquity abounds and the charity of many grows cold, the possessions bestowed upon churches by the faithful of old are seized and plundered by unbelievers with insatiable greed. And, in accordance with the prophecy, one is rarely found who rises in opposition and sets up a wall for the house of Israel. It is therefore very useful for the guardians of churches, to refute the claim of usurpers, to draw up and preserve a written record concerning the possessions delivered to those churches.

For this reason we, the monks of blessed Peter of Chartres, have taken care to commit to writing the gift made by Fulcher, son of Girard, to the apostle Peter, for the sake of his soul and those of his parents, concerning the vicariate which he held at Mitanis Villa and throughout the land of blessed Peter.

He himself, and all those whose names are written below who appeared to possess anything through him in the aforesaid land, gave blessed Peter whatever was legally theirs. They received in return, as a charitable payment from Geoffrey the Black:

- Lord Fulcher: forty solidi in coin;
- Ingelrann of Nociacum: ten solidi;
- Hilduin, son of Fulcher of Scriniololis: ten solidi;
- Hervé of Caletulum: twenty-five solidi;
- Hugh, his brother: five solidi and fellowship;
- Roger, surnamed Cochin: ten solidi;
- Fulco, his son: five solidi;
- Rainald, his other son: half a *modius* of oats.

All those whom we have mentioned placed the gift of the aforesaid vicariate upon the altar of blessed Peter, in the presence of those whose names we have wished to commit to memory:

Gauscelin of Fragani Villa; his son Roscelin; Gerogius; and Walter, his nephew; Robert Adoratus; Gunter Gruem Ad Suam Sellam; Walter, son of Archenold; Udo of Scriniolis.

These were on their side.

On our side: Walter the money-changer; Bernard, son of Vulmar; Berner the priest; Landric the elder; Walter the elder; Durand, son of Gualdric; Laurence the chamberlain; Gerogius the canon; Girard the chief cook; Herbert the chief cook; Guarinus the steward; Oideler the stablemaster; Tescelin, son of Hildegarius; Frodo; Gislebert, son of Lorin.”

## CHAPTER LXX. Further concerning the same vicariate. (Before 1080)

“Let it be known to all of Christian profession, present and future [Col. 0326A], that we, the monks of Saint Peter, after we purchased the vicariate of Mitanis Villa, as we stated above, from all those to whom it appeared to belong, were opposed both verbally and with all their might by the sons of Fulcher of Scriniolis, namely Hilduin and Walter, who, at the devil’s instigation, inflicted various injuries upon us.

At last they came to their senses and asked pardon for their sin. Voluntarily placing upon the altar of Saint Peter the relinquishment of the vicariate which they had claimed, and obtaining the pardon they requested, they began to share with us in the benefits of our prayers.

The witnesses to this matter on our side were: Frodland and Gunbaud, his son; Stephen the elder; Laurence the chamberlain; Herbert and Warinus, bakers; Walter the tailor; Hubert the registrar [Col. 0326B].

On their side: Girard, Walter’s squire.

If anyone should attempt to oppose this charter, unless, coming to repentance, he takes refuge in making amends, let him be wounded by the sword of anathema and suffer punishment without end in hell with Ananias and Sapphira, slain for their sacrilege.”

## CHAPTER LXXI. Concerning half the burial right, bread, and candle of the church of Alogia, given by Walter of Monte Mirabili. (Before 1080)

«We wish all our successors to know that we, the monks of the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres, after Bernard of Buslo had given the church of Saint Germanus at Alogia, while Landricus was abbot, for the salvation of his soul, a certain cleric named Walter of the Castle, whose place-name is Mont Mirellus, began in that same church to claim half of the burial fees, bread, and candles. At last, moved by our petitions and by money, he decided voluntarily to grant to Saint Peter, for the use of the brothers, whatever he said he possessed in the aforesaid church, for the remedy of his own soul and those of his parents. He ordered his son Walter, already a cleric, to come to this city and publicly place the renunciation of the aforesaid rights upon the altar of the apostle Peter, in the presence of us and our servants, so that from that day forward we might possess and hold them without any disturbance from any claimant. The son fulfilled what his father had ordered, and, after we had given him twenty-two solidi, returned to his father.

Because we did not wish knowledge of this matter to be delivered to oblivion, we preferred to insert it in this work. If any heir of the aforesaid persons should attempt to bring a claim, let the money given for this purpose be set against him, and let the judges before whom he brings suit against anyone exact from him a pound of gold; let his attempt also remain ineffective, and let him remain excommunicated for as long as he persists in this obstinacy.

These are the witnesses to the gift made by Walter, surnamed Infant, and by his son, whose names we have taken care to subscribe. On his side were: Droco of Domicile, Nihardus, and Hubert of Mont Mirellus. On our side: Tedaldus, brother of Hubert, formerly abbot; Fulcardus; Oidelerius; Gausfridus and Hildulfus, brothers; Gilduinus, mayor of Sesni Villa; Durandus the younger, the barber; Durandus the smith; Harduinus and Gaudius, brothers; Rainaldus the stableman; Haldricus the shoemaker; Herbertus the baker; Rainaldus the advocate. These men and others saw him place the renunciation upon the principal altar.»

## CHAPTER LXXII. Concerning land given at Corbonensis by Girvardus. (Before 1070.)

«We wish it to be known to all worshipers of the Christian faith, present and future, that I, Landricus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, together with all those entrusted to me, record the following. A certain knight named Girvardus once bought an allod in the territory of Corbonensis from a man named Ansbertus and from certain others, whose names are given below. A charter was made concerning it and confirmed by Duke Hugo and by the count of the aforesaid territory. Girvardus possessed and held it for as long as he wished. Later, Abbot Gisbertus granted it by a rent-holding arrangement, with secure tenure, to two relatives of the aforesaid Girvardus and to one heir of theirs, on the condition that the rent be paid at the appointed time and day; if they were late in paying it, they were to make lawful compensation but were not to lose the land.

A charter was made concerning this and confirmed by all the brothers [Note: Thus in the manuscripts]. After some interval of time, it was consumed by a destructive fire in the castle of Mauritania. In our own time, when I sought it in order to inspect it, they confessed that they did not have it, earnestly begging that our clemency renew it for them and that I grant it, in the same manner as it had previously been set down in another charter, to two persons and to one heir of theirs. This I did, establishing that they were to pay, without delay, on the feast of Saint Remigius, a rent of five solidi in coin. If they were negligent in paying, they were to make lawful compensation but were not to lose the land until the third heir failed.

It also pleased us to insert in this document Girvardus’s charter, which, while giving the aforesaid land, he placed upon the altar of Saint Peter.»

## CHAPTER LXXIII. Concerning an allod bought from the knight Girvardus. (25 June 954.)

[Note: This charter was drawn up in the time of Ragenfredus, bishop of Chartres.]

«In the name of God. We wish it to be known to all the faithful, present and future, that I, Lambertus, son of Ansbertus, together with my sister Girberga, and also with our kinsman Guaningo and his sons Gadilo and Ingo, and his daughter Girberga, sell and transfer our allod—which until now we have possessed by hereditary right in the territory of Corbonensis—to the knight Girvardus and his brother Gertrannus, and also to Odo and Ildegarius, receiving from them twenty-three solidi in silver coin.

The allod that we sell is in a village called Condatus, with cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows and pastures, and the site of a mill on the river Odanus, together with all its boundaries belonging to that allod. In the village of Rovredus there is also one mansus, with lands and meadows, belonging to the aforesaid allod.

Therefore, with all our kinsmen consenting together, we transfer and sell our allod to the aforesaid men on this condition: from today forward they shall possess the same allod and shall have the power to sell or give it to whomever they wish, without any claim being brought against them. It is bounded on one side by the river Odanus; on the second side by the public road; on the third by the land of Saint Launomarus; and on the fourth by the allod of Ruinnaldus.

If any of our heirs should attempt to invalidate or claim this sale, let him incur the wrath of God and fail to establish the thing he seeks to reclaim; moreover, let him be compelled to pay a pound of gold to the person against whom he has brought suit.

So that this charter might remain more firmly established, we have confirmed it with our own hands and submitted it for confirmation by Duke Hugo and by noblemen, whose names we have ordered to be subscribed:

The sign of Duke Hugo. The signs of his sons, Otho and Hugo. The sign of Count Odo. The sign of Hugo, count of Maine. The sign of Herveus, count of Mauritania. The sign of Lambertus, viscount. The sign of Willelmus, advocate. The sign of Siefridus. The sign of Aimo. The sign of Gualerannus. The sign of Erlandus, vicar.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, in the first year of the reign of King Chlotharius.»

Our predecessors, believing this charter sufficient for themselves, took care to preserve it in the church archives. For the information of posterity, however, they neglected to write another document concerning this matter, apart from the secure-tenure grant which, as we stated above, was made by Abbot Landricus.

Now, therefore, let the pen hasten toward the cell of Ledon’s Court. After writing only the two charters that were issued in the time of Abbot Landricus, let us bring this section to an end, and so let our little pen run on to the charters of Abbot Hubertus.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. Concerning the cell of Ledon’s Court given by Count Walter. (February, before 1055.)

[Note: It exists in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, instruments, col. 302.]

«It is supremely necessary for each one of us, from the things granted to us by God in this world, to enrich with gifts the churches built throughout the world in memory of the saints, for the honor of the Almighty. It is fitting, therefore, to appease the apostle Peter with the finest gifts, since by the Lord he holds the highest power of binding and loosing the bonds of sins on earth and in heaven.

For this reason I, Count Walter, for the salvation of my soul and the remedy of the souls of my predecessors, with the approval of my faithful men, grant and submit to the brothers of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres the upper church of Ledon’s Court, at the repeated request of Abbot Landricus. The monks of that monastery shall have and possess it freely, just as I and my father, Count Droco, have held and possessed it, with every customary claim and disturbance by the archdeacon removed.

I also grant the land within the valley, where there appears once to have been a castle; likewise the tithe of sheep and beasts of burden, a candle and bread, and the burial rights of the people living there. Below, I grant one oven, together with the land on which it stands, which shall be the sole oven for all the inhabitants above and below. If it alone is not sufficient for everyone, no one shall have the power to build another, either below or above, except the monks, to whom the oven’s profit will belong.

I also give, in the fields, as much land as their plough can plough, together with the tithe; not far from the church, I grant half of one mill and one fishing-right at Villa Nova.

Finally, I give all my faithful men permission concerning the property which they appear to hold from our benefice, both lands and tithes, to give it to Saint Peter, so that the aforesaid place, whose foundation we have begun, may be served by monks day and night, and may be increased not only by me but also by my faithful men. Thus, through the intercession of the blessed apostle Peter, having been freed from the bonds of sins, may we deserve to become companions of all the saints in the heavenly kingdoms, having obtained the blessings of eternal glory.

If any profane person, instigated by the devil, should attempt to annul this charter by opposing it, let him remain excommunicated by the mouth of God and of all the saints unless he repents by making satisfaction, and let him pay ten pounds of gold to the king’s treasury; let his attempt remain ineffective.

It also pleased us that this charter, so that it might remain unshaken, should be confirmed by my own hand with the sign of the cross. We also judged it ratified to deliver it for confirmation by the hands of my faithful men, whose names are subscribed below.

On the Sunday called the seventieth, in the twenty-fourth year of the reign of King Henry, we publicly placed it upon the altar of Saint Peter at Gesiacum, which is the aforesaid cell of the monastery:

Teduinus, viscount of the castle of Mellentum; Gualo, viscount of the castle of Calidus Mons; Nivardus of Mons Fortis; Radulfus Malus Vicinus; Gualterius of Pensiacum; Drogo of Cuflantum; Guarnerius and Amalricus of the Bridge of the Isera; Radulfus Delicatus; Walter the Frank; Ericus and Ingelerius, brothers.»

## CHAPTER LXXV. Concerning land given by Droco at Loconis Villa. (Year 1060.)

«We wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy church of God, present and future, that I, Droco of the castle of Cuflantum, situated within the river Seine, for the remedy of my soul and for the souls of my parents, with the consent of my faithful men and at the request of Landricus, abbot of the monastery of Chartres, freely give and grant to Saint Peter of Ledon’s Court—which is known to be a cell of the monastery of Chartres, given by Count Walter—at Loconis Villa seven full hospites, together with a certain part of the woodland, as the public road to Beauvais divides it on the left, and half of the toll of Calceda, as the river Trenna runs.

Although these may seem to be very small gifts, nevertheless, because I perform this act with full faith and complete devotion, I shall by no means be an unbeliever in the saying: “Whoever gives even a cup of cold water in the name of the Lord shall receive a reward.” For as Scripture says: “The kingdom of God is worth as much as what you possess.”

It also pleased us that this charter should always remain unshaken, confirmed by the hand of my lord Count Walter, by mine, and by the hands of all our faithful men present, and that it be placed among the other gifts in the monastery archives. Thus the monks of the aforesaid monastery may possess the things given by me, holding them as long as the world endures and having them through possession, and may always entreat God for our offenses, so that, even at the final judgment, we may deserve forgiveness for our sins from God, the righteous judge.

If any profane person should ever attempt to violate this charter, unless he quickly repents and seeks the remedy of satisfaction, let him be handed over to the fires of hell and to worms that never die, with Dathan and Abiron, whom the earth swallowed alive because of the merit of their presumption, and with those who crucified the Lord.

We have also taken care to display below, for the reader to inspect, the names of those who confirmed the charter, so that no opportunity for any claimant may be found in our work:

Count Walter; Droco, who made this gift; Guarnerius of the Bridge of the Isera; Rodbertus Calvus; Balduinus; Amalricus of the Bridge of the Isera; Ericus of Medanta; Abbot Landricus; Albertus the monk; Gislemarus the monk; Rodbertus; Gausfridus Bigotus; Bernardus, son of Vulmarus; Oduinus, mayor; Bernardus, nephew of Gislemarus.»

## CHAPTER LXXVI. Concerning the agreement of Gauscelinus of Fraganis Villa. (Before 1070.)

«Agreement of Gauscelinus Gausfridus of Fraganis Villa with Abbot Landricus of the monastery of Saint Peter: while he lived, the abbot was to grant him one aripennis of land at Manu Villare for the construction of a granary there. The condition was that whatever he stored there while alive he should leave to Saint Peter at his death; in addition, he was to leave his own allod in the village called Hulsetum, whose cultivator was the peasant Suggerius.

The abbot not only granted this but also gave one house, which stood at Luciacum above a certain winepress, for the construction of a granary, together with ten solidi in coin.

As soon as this Gausfridus, whose forename was Gauscelinus, obtained what he had requested, he and his wife and children placed the gift of the allod upon the altar of Saint Peter, and established that, while he lived, an annual rent of four coins should be given to Saint Peter. After his death, his sons and many of his grandchildren, for the soul of the deceased and for their own salvation, publicly placed the gift of the aforesaid allod upon the altar of Saint Peter a second time.

For this they received from the monks the benefit of their prayers. It also pleased us, according to ecclesiastical custom, to subscribe the names both of the sons and grandchildren who were present and of certain other men, so that if anyone of unsound mind should ever attempt to rise against this gift, overcome by the testimony of these witnesses, his attempt might perish and his soul suffer punishment in hell.

Roscelinus, Gerogius, Hugo, and Fulco, brothers, the sons of the deceased man who made this gift; Guidbergis and Hersindis, sisters of the deceased; Gerogius, Gualterius, Stephanus, Ansoldus, and Guarinus, his grandchildren.

On the monks’ side: Gauslinus of Leuges; Ingelrannus of Nociacum; Gualterius the table-servant; Gualterius, son of Gandebertus; Hildulfus and Gausfridus, brothers; Gunbaldus; Tescelinus; Adventius; Laurentius.»

[Note: Here Codex A ends, its final leaves having been torn away. What we have added to this first section is taken from Codex B.]

## CHAPTER LXXVII. Concerning the allods of Mesliacum. (Before 1070.)

«The present church, through which one travels to that heavenly church which does not know how to come to an end, is always accustomed to be enlarged and strengthened by the gifts of Christ’s faithful. Although the devil hastens to assault it through the deceits and attacks of his minions, nevertheless, supported by the stability of faith and the firmness of charity, it will remain immovable and unconquerable until the end of the age.

Therefore its children, rooted in faith and charity according to their capacity, offer earthly estates and worldly riches to their mother, so that in exchange for perishable and earthly things they may purchase heavenly ones. Since their names are written in the register of heaven, it is fitting that they be entrusted in writing to the memory of the faithful, so that the faithful may always pray to God for them, and so that, raised among the saints in the glory of the resurrection, they may breathe again.

Therefore I, Landricus, abbot of the monastery of Chartres, and the whole flock of monks entrusted to me, have ordered the names of those who gave their own estates to Saint Peter for their souls to be set down in this document, at the place called Mesliacum.

We first ordered Germundus the priest to be recorded. After receiving the monastic habit, he left both his estate and everything he possessed to Saint Peter.

Second, Radulfus, father of Walter the moneyer, who, when he died, left his estate to Saint Peter.

Third, the same Walter, who left to Saint Peter whatever estates he was able to purchase in that same place, for the soul of his son Gausfridus the cleric, so that his anniversary might be celebrated each year with the ringing of bells. He also redeemed for us two aripennes of vineyard in our enclosure, beside Saint Bartholomew’s, toward the south, for the soul of his uncle Hato, so that his anniversary might be celebrated each year with the ringing of bells.

Fourth, Herveus, father of Fulcherius, canon of Saint Martin, who left his estate there, amounting to two modii of seedland, to Saint Peter.

Fifth, Ansoldus, with his wife Ermengardis, who left his allod in the same place to Saint Peter.

If any profane person should attempt to remove anything from these gifts, struck by the sword of excommunication and thrust into hell with the devil, let him suffer punishments destined to last without end.»

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. Concerning the vicariate of Hunis Villa and the churchyard of Reclamantis Villa. (Before 1080.)

[Note: We have already published several charters of Abbot Hubertus among those of Landricus, and above, at the beginning of Book VII, we noted that the chronological order in the manuscripts is confused.]

«In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Hubertus, by the grace of God abbot, and the whole congregation of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, wish it to be known to the faithful of the holy church of God, present and future, that Walter, son of Fladaldus, has granted to Saint Peter in perpetual right half of the vicariate of Hunis Villa, as well as the churchyard of Reclamantis Villa and all the land belonging to these two villages, for the salvation of his soul and that of his wife and for the souls of his parents. In exchange he received one aripennis of vineyard called Radfredus, for which twenty-five pounds in coin had been offered to us.

Walter of Alnetum, through whose benefice the aforesaid Walter had held this vicariate, also gave his consent to this gift; and his sons Gunherius, Gauslinus, and Gualterius gave their consent together with their father.

We have also subscribed the names of Walter’s relatives and of those who were with him when he placed the renunciation of this matter upon the altar of Saint Peter, as well as the names of our servants whom we had there, so that if anyone should ever attempt to bring a claim against this transaction, having first been separated from the thresholds of the holy church of God and struck at the throat by excommunication, he might be driven away by the staff of vengeance held by one of these witnesses, and, unless he repented, be cast into the lowest hell.

Rajenaldus, brother of Walter; Fredesindis, his wife; Beliardis, his sister; Rajenaldus, his son; Adelina, his daughter; Gislebertus of Britiniacum.

With us: Gerogius and Fulco, brothers and canons; Erardus the canon; Gualterius the moneyer; Gilduinus, mayor; Girbertus, mayor; Stephanus, mayor; Goscelinus and Rodbertus, toll collectors; Guarinus the baker; Teodaldus; Fulchardus; Aventius; Lorinus; Gislebertus; Gunbaldus; Oydelerius; Laurentius; Rainaldus the stableman; Ragenfredus of Reclamantis Villa.»

[Note: In the manuscript called the Silver Codex, the following is added after the names of the witnesses: “This was publicly enacted at Chartres, while King Philip was reigning, in the ninth year.”]

## CHAPTER LXXIX. Concerning a garden bought beside the river Audura. (Before 1080.)

«I, Abbot Hubertus, and all the monks of the monastery of Chartres, wish it to be known that a certain woman named Roscelina had held a garden situated in our land beside our garden for twenty years and more, having received it by right of dowry from her first lord, Gausfridus. She had no offspring from it.

Now, receiving from us the sum of money assessed for it, she relinquished it to be possessed perpetually. Together with her present lord Hubertus and the three sons whom she had by Frodo, she placed the gift, or renunciation, upon the altar of the apostles Peter and Paul, in the presence of us and our servants, whose names we have subscribed:

Bernardus, son of Vulmarus; Stephanus, mayor, and Salomon, his brother; Dodo, mayor; Oydelerius; Alcherius the miller; Belod, his son; Fulchardus; Rainaldus the stableman; Ascelinus, mayor; Hugo Berbellus; Gislebertus.

On the woman’s side: Walter of Alnetum and Sugerius, the former of whom had first been appointed guarantor of the transaction’s validity.»

## CHAPTER LXXX. Concerning a mill given by Rogerius at Haraca Villa in Normandy. (Before 1080.)

«Let it be known to all the faithful that Rogerius, formerly a knight and afterward a monk, left to Saint Peter one mill in Normandy, together with land for one plough, with the consent of Eunardus, the viscount, through whose benefice he held it. Through Mainerius, son of Anselmus, the viscount himself ordered this gift to be placed upon the altar of Saint Peter, for it lay outside the church.

The witnesses to this matter are: Willelmus Paganus; Ivo, son of Norbertus; Bernerius of Britogilum; Stephanus of Britiniacum; Odo Sanglarius; Haimericus Bobinus; Gausfridus the physician; Rodbertus, his brother; Guiddo of Mulcetum.

On our side: Rainaldus, mayor; Stephanus, mayor; Hildulfus and Gausfridus, brothers; Fulchardus; Rodbertus the furrier; Gunbaldus the younger; Frotlandus; Sugerius.»

## CHAPTER LXXXI. Concerning the woodland of Monticuli granted by Haimericus of Vileretum. (Before 1080.)

«Let it be known to all Christ’s faithful, present and future, that on the Kalends of August, at the feast of Saint Peter called “in Chains,” Haimericus of Virellum placed upon the altar of Saint Peter his consent concerning the woodland of Monticuli, at the request of Gualterius the table-servant. Gualterius held that woodland as a royal holding from the sons of Avesgaudus, and they held it from Haimericus.

He made this act of consent by means of a rod, or by the handle of a blessed hoe, in the presence of Abbot Hubertus and the whole congregation, with the following witnesses, whose names we have subscribed:

Fulcherius, son of Gerardus; Gualterius the table-servant, who gave the woodland with all its appurtenances; Ribaldus of Fraxinum; Salvisus, son of Odo, the falconer.

On our side: Frotlandus and Gunbaldus, his son; Fulchardus; Sugerius; Gislebertus and Laurentius, brothers; Tescelinus, son of Hildegarius; Martinus; Roscelinus; Rodbertus, son of Gausfridus; Stephanus and Salomon, brothers; Adelandus; Rotbertus the furrier.

Vulferius, son of Haimericus, also consented to this matter, receiving from it one shield-worth of ten solidi.»

## CHAPTER LXXXII. Concerning the vicariate of Abonis Villa. (Before 1080.)

«Let it be known to all the faithful of the holy church of God that Gualterius, son of Fledaldus, and his wife Fredesindis, with the consent of Gualterius of Alnetum, whose holding it was, just as Berardus, his father-in-law, had formerly given it, for the souls of their father and mother and of their brother Guaningus, who had been killed, during the life of Abbot Landricus, and afterward, during the life of Abbot Hubertus, renounced to Saint Peter the vicariate of Abonis Villa and the entire territory of that village, together with the allod of Picati Villaris, concerning what he had unjustly usurped after the death of the aforesaid Guaningus.

The witnesses to this matter are: Gualterius of Alnetum and his son Gualterius; Evrardus of Levois Villa; Gualterius Blancardus; Gislebertus, brother of Beringarius; Rainaldus, son of Hugo of Reclamantis Villa; Hugo of Treijonum; Gunbertus of Raschin Villa; Germundus of Saint Albinus; Gerogius of Haimulfi Villa; Gilduinus, mayor; Stephanus, mayor; Bernardus; Fulchardus; Ernulfus and his son Rainaldus; Tealdus, brother of the abbot; Gislebertus and Laurentius, brothers; Adventius; Oydelerius and Rodbertus, brothers; Gualterius and Adventius, tailors; Teduinus and Gaudius, brothers; Gausfridus the carpenter; Ingelbertus and Gausfridus, cooks.»

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. Concerning the burial right and tithe of Gerardus of Buxetum. (Before 1080.)

«I, Abbot Hubertus, and all the monks of Saint Peter of Chartres, wish it to be known that, for the remedy of his soul and those of his parents, on the second day before the Ides of August, Girardus of Buxetum publicly placed upon the altar of Saint Peter a gift consisting of the burial right of his household and of his entire land, which lies in the parish of the church of Buxetum.

At the dedication of this church he also gave half of his tithe, with the consent of Isnardus, his lord, and of his son, who was present, as well as of Gerogius, brother of the same Girardus, and Albereda, mother of Isnardus.

The witnesses to the burial right are: Stephanus, mayor; Rotbertus the toll collector; Hubertus of the church; Gaudius; Theodaldus; Frotlandus; and Gunbaldus. The witnesses to the tithe are all the neighbors who were present at the dedication.»

## CHAPTER LXXXIV. Concerning the gift of Fulcandus of Arro. (Before 1080.)

«In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

I, Fulcandus, wish it to be known to all the faithful, present and future, that, with the assent of my lords Gausfridus and Willelmus, his stepson, and also of Mahildis, Willelmus’s mother, I have granted to Saint Peter of the monastery of Chartres one third of the church of Arro, together with the altar land customarily held by the priests, and half of the offerings of the four feasts, which I had retained; also land for one plough for the three seasons of the year, wherever the monks choose; two aripennes of meadow; six denarii from the rent of Odo’s mill; the burial fee of four denarii, namely, for infants in white garments; the entire burial right of Buxetum, which is Saint Peter’s land; half of the archpriest’s share of that church; half of the burial right of the entire churchyard which they cause to be inhabited; and half of the rent, oven, churchyard, and every customary due demanded by human custom.

I also grant the tithe of Buxedulum, which appears to be held from my benefice, if the monks should at some time be able to buy it from him.

This was enacted at Capella Regia, while King Philip was reigning and Abbot Hubertus was governing the monastery of Saint Peter, with Hubertus the monk, surnamed Querco, and my mother Sufficia taking part in this matter.

I wished to make this gift for the soul of my father and mother, for my own salvation, for that of my wife and sons and daughters, and for all my relatives. If anyone should wish to oppose this gift, let him pay three hundred pounds of gold, and let his will remain ineffective; unless he comes to make amends, let him be subjected to the punishments of hell with Judas the traitor.

We have also subscribed the names of the witnesses from both sides who witnessed this gift:

Herbertus, brother of Fulcandus, confirmed it; Suffitia, their mother; Fulcaldus, giver of this gift; Lizinia, his wife; Joannes, Rotrocus, and Herbertus, his sons; Milesindis, his daughter; Aremburgis, his sister; Hugo Palestellus; Durandus the priest; Lambertus; Odo; Ascelinus; Bernardus.

On our side: Hermoinus, mayor of Bosci Medii; Herbertus Canis Parvulus; Ernaudellus; Austasius; Guarinus; Lorinus, son of Gualo; Rainaldus of Saint Romanus.»

## CHAPTER LXXXV. Concerning the vicariate of Abonis Vittae given by Fulco. (Before 1080.)

«We wish it to be known to the faithful of the holy church, present and future, that I, Hubertus, unworthy abbot, and the whole congregation of monks of the monastery of Saint Peter, record the following.

A certain knight named Fulco, when dying during the life of Abbot Landricus, with the consent of his sons, namely Hugo and Guarinus, who were still children, and of his sister Richildis, granted to the apostle Saint Peter and to the monks serving him half of the vicariate which he held at Abonis Villa, for the remedy of his soul, the souls of his parents, and the safety of his children. He sent the gift upon the altar of Saint Peter through the hands of his sons and relatives.

After his death, his son Hugo, now grown, overcome by greed and setting aside his father’s gift, seized the vicariate. But afterward, having received from us thirty solidi in coin, he relinquished the vicariate which he had unjustly seized and, together with his brother Guarinus, publicly placed the renunciation upon the altar of Saint Peter, in the testimony of those whose names we have taken care to subscribe.

With Hugo were: Girogius, his cousin; also Girogius of Haimulfi Villa; Herbertus Corbonensis; Siguinus.

With us: Stephanus Gualoius and his son Adventius; Stephanus, mayor; Oydelerius; Teduinus and Gaudius, brothers; Gunbaldus; Laurentius; Isembertus, son of Goscelinus; Fulchardus; Ernulfus and his son Rainaldus; Rodbertus, brother of Frotlandus.»

## CHAPTER LXXXVI. Concerning the vineyards bought by Countess Berta. (12 May 1069.)

«Let it be known to all that Radulfus, surnamed Calculus, wishing to sell certain vineyards which he held in the count’s territory from our benefice, came to an agreement with us and with the count’s sister, named Berta [Note: Bertha, wife of Alan V, count of Brittany, and sister of Theobald III, count of Chartres, gave this charter in the year in which Abbot Landricus and Bishop Rodbertus died, and in that same year, though it had not yet ended, Abbot Hubertus was elected—that is, 1069].

But since this was not lawful, the countess came into the presence of Abbot Landricus so that they might grant the vineyards to her on the condition that she hold them as long as she lived and leave them to us after her death. Later, she acknowledged this agreement before her brother, Count Theobald, and, at the request of that same brother, confirmed it—for the soul of her father, her mother, her brother, and herself—on the fourth day before the Ides of May, in the presence of these men:

Gualerannus the monk; Otbertus the monk; Gausfridus of Calidus Mons; Girardus, their cook; and Radulfus, provost.

This was publicly enacted at Chartres, between the tower and the Ashen Gate, in the countess’s chamber, of which we are speaking, in the year in which Rodbertus, bishop, died abroad; at that time the city was also without a bishop, and Hubertus, whom we had elected abbot, was still alive.»

Here the limits of the charters of Lord Hubertus must be set down.
