For, when the wind of wickedness blew and the whirlwind of deceit shook everything, almost all his own men, alienated from him and bound in an inextricable knot, violently expelled him from his office. In his place they accepted Theodericus of Vendôme from Bishop Arraldus, willingly or unwillingly. Retaining only the vigor of the rule, he exterminated many of those who had made his predecessor an exile. During the period in which he lived and held office, he was finally very inept in external affairs and has so far left to posterity scarcely one charter, and that of little use to us. Having written this, let us turn our pen to the charters issued while the monks were suspended without an abbot.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII. Concerning the church of Saint Mary of Alogia. (Year 1069.)

«In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who is one in essence and three in power.

We wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy church of God, present and future, that I, Theodericus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, and the whole congregation of monks over whom I appear to preside, record that Gualterius, surnamed Infant, for the sake of his soul and those of his wife, parents, and lords, has granted to Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, in perpetual right the presbytery of the church of Saint Mary, which is situated not far from the river of the village of Alogia, and everything known to belong to that presbytery, both the altar and the offerings, burials, and tithes, so that we may have and possess them without any contradiction.

With the consent of his lady Mahildis, from whom he held this benefice, he placed the gift of this grant upon the altar of Saint Romanus the martyr, who is sought and venerated not far from the castle of Braia (the printed word *apostolo* is uncertain).

Later his son Gualterius the cleric went to Chartres and placed a gift concerning the same matter upon the altar of Saint Peter. From us he then received thirty solidi in coin and carried five solidi to his mother in a cloak purchased for her.

Whoever wishes to withdraw this gift, unless he repents, let him be excommunicated by all the saints of God and perish in hell with all those who crucified the Lord and with Judas the traitor.

This was publicly enacted in the castle of Braia, inside the granary of Saint Romanus, in the ninth year of King Philip, in the presence of those whose names we have subscribed:

Bernardus of Buslo; Landricus of Toriellum and Odo, his brother; Gualterius Infant, who made this gift; Radulfus, provost; Gausfridus; Raiardus; Rainaldus the forester.

On our side: Girvardus, mayor; Laurentius, chamberlain; Bernardus, son of Vulmarus; Frollandus.»

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII. Concerning the juniorate of the church of Saint Leobinus of Châteaudun. (Before 1080.)

Formerly, when the outstanding men of the Christian religion flourished in every kind of abundance and most devoutly honored the churches built nobly throughout the world, far and wide, in honor of God and in memory of the saints, they wished to enrich them with various titles of donations. Their privileges are preserved, and shall be preserved, in those very churches together with their memorials, Christ the Lord consenting.

Therefore I, Albert, son of Hugh, vicedominus of the holy church of Chartres, wish it to be known to those now living and to those yet to come—namely, to my successors—that concerning the church of Saint Leobinus, which was founded in Braiao castle above the River Osanna and which I appear to hold from my lord William, lord of that castle, together with other possessions [Col. 0337D]: concerning this church, I say, with the consent of my dearest brother Guerric, who is now vicedominus after the death of my father, I annually grant and, by granting, confirm to Saint Peter and to the monks serving him in his monastery, which is suitably situated in the suburb of the aforesaid city, the juniorate, for the souls of our parents and also for the salvation of both myself and my aforesaid brother, in perpetuity.

The arrangement is this: the priests of that church shall in no way be appointed by me or by my successors, but from this day forward they shall be sent by those monks to that church; they shall exercise authority there and, should they happen to deserve it, be expelled. Nevertheless, from the tithe of the church that we retain, they shall receive each year two measures of wheat, without any payment [Col. 0338A] of money. They shall also have the altar and the offerings throughout the year, except on four feast days, on which we still retain for our own use two parts of the offerings.

We also relinquish the claim against the church of Saint Romanus, which lies beyond the aforesaid river, so that none of our heirs may ever dare to exact anything from it; rather, the monks shall possess it wholly, build upon it, and hold it securely. We wished this charter of our donation, written at our command, to be confirmed by our hands and names, so that it might remain forever inviolate and unshaken.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX. Concerning the Church of Saint Leobinus of Castrum Dunum. (Before 1080.)

[Col. 0338B]

“Earthly riches lead those who squander them according to the will of the flesh and the luxury of their desires to the punishments of hell; but those who distribute them to the needy for the love of God, they lead to eternal rewards. Therefore I, William, lord of the honor of Alogia, distinguished in lineage insofar as worldly rank is concerned, but exceedingly darkened by evil conduct, amid the storms of this tempestuous world, girded with military arms and entangled in worldly affairs, since I cannot by my merits—which are small, or rather nonexistent—wash away the countless crimes I have committed, attempt to redeem them by the largesse of donations.

Thus I have judged it right to take as my intercessor blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom the Lord entrusted the care of His Church and granted power to bind and loose souls, and to render him propitious to me from my own possessions. For so the Lord’s gracious teaching commands: ‘Give, and it will be given to you’; and elsewhere: ‘Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.’

Accordingly, with the assent of my venerable mother Mahildis, together with my dearest wife Eustachia and our still infant children Hugh and William, for the redemption of the souls of our ancestors and for our own welfare, I grant and, by granting, bestow upon the blessed apostle Peter and his monks, who serve him according to the monastic rule in the monastery situated not far from the walls of the city of Chartres, the church of the most blessed confessor and bishop Leobinus [Col. 0338D] of the aforesaid city.

This church appears to have been suitably built from ancient times within the enclosure of Castrum Dunum, and it was possessed by our fathers by hereditary right. Accordingly, on the eighth day before the Ides of December, with the consent of my faithful men who were then with me at Chartres and whose names we have recorded at the end of this document, I placed its donation upon the altar of that apostle.

From this day forward, therefore, let the aforesaid monks possess that church by hereditary right, with all its furnishings and with every possession belonging to it, both within and outside it, which appeared to be under my authority. I also grant the plots adjoining the church called Arnulf’s; likewise the knight Bovo, with his fief, which is known to belong to the aforesaid church [Col. 0339A]. If he himself should nevertheless wish to turn [or alter his status; uncertain], I freely grant also the tithes and rents belonging to the aforesaid church, so that the monks may redeem them, either by lease or by payment, from the very knights who appear to possess them by our benefaction.

All these things are very small indeed: they are earthly and passing away. For the heavenly and eternal things are higher and better, and, with Christ as our guide, we shall receive them in the future in exchange for these gifts. For it benefited the widow of whom we read that she offered two small coins in the temple; and it benefited the giver of a cup of cold water.

Therefore, so that this gift of my largesse might remain firm and unshaken, I resolved to strengthen it with the sign of the cross and my own hands, and I entrusted it to be strengthened by the hands of my faithful men, whose names are also found written below. If anyone should ever attempt, at the devil’s instigation, to oppose this largesse of mine, unless he quickly repents and seeks pardon for his presumption, let him be thrust into hell with Dathan and Abiron, whom the earth swallowed alive; with Herod, the slaughterer of the innocent; with Judas the betrayer; and with those who crucified Christ the Lord. There let him suffer punishment, where the ravenous serpent does not die, the devouring fire is not extinguished, the shades of death are not absent, and the darkness of gloom remains.

Sign of Mahildis, William’s mother. Sign of William himself. Of Eustachia, his wife. Sign of his sons Hugh and William. Sign of William of Montboon. Of Gausfrid. Warin. Osmund. Guarnerius. Anisard. Hugh, son of Burchard. Rainald, son of Gausfrid. [Col. 0339C] Radulf, son of William. Gausfrid of Salmeredo. Odo Craton. William of Montmirable. Girard Brunel. William. Berner. Gauslin. Helgot. Walter, son of Burchard. Hildegarius the archdeacon. Rainald the dean. Vitalis the priest. Bernard of Buslo. Radulf Noth. Landric of Toriellis. Odo Radulf. Gausfrid. Letald.”

## CHAPTER XC. Concerning the Church of the Village of Treion. (Before 1080.)

“Solomon, admonishing every person to care for his soul while he lives, says: ‘Whatever your hand is able to do, perform it diligently, because there is neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom in the underworld, where you are hastening’ [Note: [Col. 0339D] Ecclesiastes 9:10.].

Therefore I, Wenricus, together with my brother Albert, fulfilling in our father’s place the vow which our father had delayed to discharge during his lifetime, transfer to Saint Peter, for the remedy of the soul of that same father and of our ancestors and ancestresses, the church of Treion, dedicated in honor of the holy Mother of God.

Because we possessed it free from every episcopal exaction, except the provision of chrism and the reconciliation of the church, so too, with such matters removed as an impediment, we assign it free to Saint Peter, to the abbot, and to the brothers serving God there. In addition, we grant a courtyard for constructing the monks’ workshops, a garden for planting trees and herbs, and land for one plow; also the mill of Spina and half a vineyard enclosure. Whatever our men may wish to add from the same benefice, we approve.

The witnesses to this donation are: Ingelrannus the dean; Adelardus the subdean; Ascelinus Britto; Gausbertus, schoolmaster; Bernerius the canon; Gerogius the canon; Fulcherius, son of Nivelo; Gauslinus of Leugis and his son Gauslinus; Rainaldus, son of Flealdus; Gauslinus, son of Gausfridus; Ingenulfus, son of Norbertus; Ansoldus of Mungeri Villa [Note: [Col. 0339D] Two charters concerning the vicarage of Mittanis Villa follow in this codex B; we have published them above, pp. 194 and 195.].”

## CHAPTER XCI. Concerning the Vicarage of Imonis Villa and the Claim to Two Agripennos of Vineyard beside Saint Bartholomew’s. (26 November 1077.)

[Col. 0340B]

“We, the monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy church, present and future, that in the year when a devouring flame consumed the roofs of our monastery and buildings, namely on the sixth day before the Kalends of December [Note: [Col. 0340D] As will be stated below, chapter 104, this fire occurred in the first year of Gausfridus, bishop of Chartres, but in the second year before the election of Abbot Eustachius—that is, in 1077.], Robert, surnamed Aculeus, relinquished to Saint Peter the vicarage of our land at Imonis Villa, which he had unjustly possessed, and publicly placed the abandonment of his claim upon Saint Peter’s altar.

He also settled his claim to two agripennos of vineyard beside the cemetery of Saint Bartholomew, at the head of our enclosure, receiving in return the prayers of the brothers and one horse worth six pounds. Ansoldus of Mungeri Villa was present with him [Col. 0340C], as were Rainaldus and his brother, sons of Walter. With us were Laurentius the chamberlain, Laurinus the groom, Gaudius and Teduinus, brothers, Stephanus the elder, and others.”

## CHAPTER XCII. Concerning the Church of Upper Croto. (Around 1080.)

“We wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy church that a certain church situated in Upper Croto above the River Audura had formerly been purchased by Abbot Landricus from the monks of Saint Martin of the Greater Monastery, with the approval of the brothers from whose patrimony it had come—namely Arraldus, Richardus, and Bernardus, who had sold this same church to Saint Martin—with the approval of the lords from whose benefice the three aforesaid brothers had held it.

But because poverty always limps, Arraldus, overcome by want, frequently retained the church’s revenues for his own use, against our will, alleging that by agreement we were obliged to build that church for him in cement and stone. For this reason he was excommunicated by us many times and then absolved again, outwardly, after relinquishing the things he had usurped. At last, acting on wise counsel and coming to his senses, he came to the threshold of Saint Peter [Col. 0341A] with his wife, Adelida by name, and his daughter Badehildis. Before the altar he sought pardon for his offenses and placed the donation of that church upon the altar, saying under oath, in place of a written pledge, that from that day forward he would never bring any claim against us concerning it, nor exercise any customary right in it or in the land belonging to it; nor would he take any milling charge from the grain that was to be placed in the church, as he had previously done, nor accept anything else whatsoever. Rather, he would henceforth leave it as free to us as the church of Saint George and the church of Saint Cyricus at Anet.

Afterward he caused his sons—Walter and Gislebert—and his younger daughter, Milesinde by name, to approve the matter. This was enacted publicly at Chartres on the fifth day before the Kalends of June.

We also thought it appropriate to subscribe the names of those who were present from both sides: Marcuardus; Walter and Albert, brothers; Walter, White-Eye. From our side: Gilduinus the elder, Walter the cleric, Richerius the elder, Stephanus the elder, Laurentius, Gislebertus, Adventius, Oydelerius, Rotbertus the nosochomiarius [uncertain title], Radulfus, Gilduinus, and Gaudius.”

## CHAPTER XCIII. Concerning Five Plowlands of Land Given to Saint Peter at Nantilliac. (Before 1080.)

“We wish all who will read this document to know that a certain knight named Herluinus, accompanied by Germundus of Raschiniac [Col. 0341C] and his squire Isenbardus, came to the monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres. Seeking the support of their prayers, so that from that day forward he might become a participant with those monks in their benefits, he gave five plowlands of land, not far from the church of Saint Peter at Nantilliac, to Saint Peter in perpetuity.

He placed the donation of this land upon the altar of that apostle on the octave of the apostles Peter and Paul, on the condition that, just as he had freely held those five plowlands from his ancestors, so the aforesaid monks should have, possess, inhabit, or otherwise dispose of them as they wished, without disturbance by anyone.

If any of his heirs or anyone else should wish to oppose this gift of his largesse [Col. 0341D], let him receive condemnation in hell with Dathan and Abiron, unless he repents and has recourse to the remedy of satisfaction.

The witnesses from our side were: Gausfridus the cook; Johannes the doorkeeper; Herveus and Durandus, smiths; Teduinus, Gaudius, and Harduinus, brothers; Laurentius the chamberlain; Laurinus the driver; Adventius Sophia; Engelbaudus; and Gislebertus.”

## CHAPTER XCIV. Concerning the Church of the Village of Spelterolis. (Before 1080.)

“In the name of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ. The entire community of monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres wishes it to be known to all worshipers of the Christian faith that a certain knight named Hugh of Dreux, with Abbot Hubert supporting this monastery, gave Saint Peter half of the church of Spelterolis village and land for two oxen, receiving from us in return the prayers of the brothers and other works of mercy.

But because the property then seemed to us small and unproductive, and the sons of the aforesaid knight were making claims against it, we did not possess it at all. After a long time, however, the aforesaid knight became a monk in the monastery of Bourgueil. Later, returning to us to visit us, he was severely afflicted by illness and died among us. After commending his soul to Christ according to custom, we buried his body with our brothers with suitable honor.

His wife, Olisia by name, whom he had left in the world with his sons, Gausbert and Guarinus, was also present there. Together with their mother, after burying their father, they hastened before the altar of the apostles Peter and Paul and publicly transferred, by unanimous agreement, the aforesaid church, with its churchyard and half the tithe, for their father’s soul; they also gave land for one plow and placed the donation upon the altar, invoking the curse of Annas and Caiaphas, Ananias and Sapphira, upon all who opposed this largesse.”

## CHAPTER XCV. Concerning the Allod Given by Haimericus Vibrans Lupum. (In 1081 or 1082.)

“In the name of Christ. I, Girardus the prior, together with all the brothers of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, wish it to be known to all our successors [Col. 0342C] that at the time when the lord Abbot Eustachius was staying at Rome with Gausfridus, bishop of Chartres, and the bishop of Paris, so that together they might demonstrate that the excommunication pronounced unjustly at the council of Étampes by Hugh, bishop of Die, against Gausfridus, bishop of Chartres, had been invalid—namely, in the presence of the lord Pope Gregory VII, whom Emperor Henry was then also fighting with the Alamanni and Lombards—at that time, I say, a certain knight named Haimericus Vibrans Lupum, suffering from the illness of which he subsequently died, became a monk among us to escape the punishments of hell.

With the consent of his son Paganus, he left to Saint Peter and to us the estates that he possessed by hereditary right near the place called Miseriacus, together with three knights who held fiefs from that estate [Col. 0342D]. His son publicly placed the donation of the estate upon the altar of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, receiving there in return the prayers of the brothers. If anyone, I say, should attempt to oppose this gift, unless he repents, let him be accursed.”

## CHAPTER XCVI. Concerning the Allod Given by Baldwin within the Borough of the City of Chartres. (Before 1080.)

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. So that those now living may not lose sight of this matter and those yet to come may know it, this document shall be preserved in our archives.

A certain knight named Baldwin came into our presence, that is, into the presence of the monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, humbly asking that we make him a monk [Col. 0343A]. We consented. For this reason he gave Saint Peter and us, with his own exemption, the land where vineyards once existed and where there are now gardens belonging to many people. It yields in rent seven solidi and ten denarii on the feast of Saint Remigius, and it is entirely free from every vicarial charge, every seizure, and all customary dues.

His wife and son approved this transaction. To make them consent most willingly, we gave them from our own resources three measures of wheat and two measures of oats. Baldwin himself requested that, if any claimant should arise concerning this matter, he should be excommunicated by God and Saint Peter.

To make this matter more secure, we have written below the witnesses from his side and ours: Ermengardis [Col. 0343B], Baldwin’s wife; Hugh, son of both; Ingenulfus; Otbertus; William; Hamelinus, son of Herbrannus. From our side: Guarnerius the elder; Guarinus and Laurinus, bread-makers; Laurentius and Gislebertus, brothers; Walter and Adventius, tailors; Joscelinus, son of Gilduinus; Arroldus the groom; Radulfus, son of Hildegarius the porter.”

## CHAPTER XCVII. Concerning the Land Given by Roscelin at Pendent Pediculus. (Before 1080.)

“We wish it to be known to the faithful of Christ, both of the present and of the future age, that when the monk Roscelin entered the religious life, his brother Gerogius gave half of the land of Pendent Pediculus to Saint Peter for the support of the brothers, with the approval of Teudo, surnamed Caput Perri, to whom twelve denarii are owed annually in rent from our portion.

Afterward that land was seized through the ambition of Fulcherius, son of Girardus, and Gerogius of Curba Villa, since it appeared to belong to their benefice. To secure their approval, we gave Fulcherius fifty solidi of denarii and Gerogius thirty. They then placed the abandonment of their claim upon Saint Peter’s altar and granted the land to be possessed, provided only that the aforesaid rent be paid on the feast of Saint Remigius.

This was enacted publicly in the church of Saint Peter, in the presence and hearing of those whose names we have written below: Walter the moneyer; Gerogius the cleric; Stephanus the elder [Col. 0343D]; Arnulfus Rufus; Fulchardus; Stephanus, Aventius, and Laurentius, brothers; Ascelinus the elder; Teduinus, Gaudius, and Harduinus, brothers; William; Arraldus; Hildegarius; and Radulfus, his son [Note: [Col. 0343D] The charter following this one bears the title ‘Concerning the Tithe of Rainerius Finemundus’ and has been published above, p. 138.].”

## CHAPTER XCVIII. Concerning Property Given for the Boy Ernaldus. (Before 1080.)

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. I, Landricus, devoted to secular military service, together with my wife Ermelina and my firstborn son Hugh, wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy church, present and future, that I entrust my eight-year-old son, Ernaldus by name, to almighty God and to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and deliver him to the monastery of the aforesaid prince of the apostles, so that there he may serve God and His saints all the days of his life and pour forth prayers day and night for us and for all God’s faithful.

For delivering him to the aforesaid monastery, we grant, at the place called Baliolus, land for two animals together with a homestead. To this gift we add the fourth part of the brennagium which we have hitherto held in the village of Saint Romanus, beside Braiao castle, so that from this day forward the monks of the aforesaid monastery may have and possess it forever [Col. 0344B].

We also grant the juniorate of the church of Saint Peter, as Rainaldus the dean appears to hold it, and everything that he possesses from us in that village. We wish to confirm this charter of our largesse with our own hands and to impress upon it the sign of the saving cross, so that no opponent may ever have the right to lay claim to it.

+ Of Landricus. Sign of Ermelina. Of Hugh. Of Rainaldus the dean. Of Odo [Note: [Col. 0343D] A charter entitled ‘Concerning Land Given at Saint Germanus of Alogia’ follows; we have already published it, p. 194.].”

## CHAPTER XCIX. Concerning Property Given for the Boy Hugh. (Before 1080.)

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. I, Hildegardis, surnamed Franca, formerly the wife of a certain knight named Gausfridus Niger, wish it to be known to all the faithful, present and future, that my husband, scorning all the fleeting and perishable things of this world, laid aside the military belt in the sacred monastery of the blessed apostle Peter of Chartres, intending devotedly to serve as a soldier of God. Leaving behind, according to the Lord’s command, his wife and children, fields, houses, and everything he possessed in the world, and following Christ Himself in the steps of obedience, he longs to journey toward the palace of heaven.

Thus widowed by him, I was bereft of the two sons whom I had borne him, while they were advancing in the flower of adolescence, as they went to unknown lands in Apulia [Note: [Col. 0344D] So the text reads. The sense, however, requires: ‘I was bereft of two sons …’]. One of them, Fulco by name, left with me in the cradle a small son whom he had had by a certain girl. I raised him as a son and, while he was still a child, entrusted him to be instructed in sacred letters. Then, when he was already eight years old, I entrusted him in the aforesaid monastery, where both his grandfather and his kinsman, also named Fulco, serve God, so that, with the consent of Prior Rotbertus and the other monks, he might pray there for my soul and for the souls of all my parents and serve God under the monastic rule [Note: [Col. 0344D] Read: ‘I entrusted him.’]

For him I gave in Belsia, in the village called Pantaginis Villa, certain land formerly granted in firm tenure to two brothers, Frogerius and Fulco, and to one of their heirs; from them it was sold to a certain knight, Heribrannus, whose son Haimericus, now a cleric, possesses it and pays seven solidi of denarii on the feast of Saint Caraunus.

Likewise, in the territory of Dunum, in the parish of Saint Ebrulfus, in the village called Torellelis, I gave one measure of land, free from every exaction and customary due, with a house and barn. Likewise, in Bahardi Villa, one field in which one and a half measures are sown.

I, Hildegardis, publicly placed this charter upon the altar of the apostles Peter and Paul at Chartres, impressing upon it the sign of the cross. If anyone should wish to oppose it, let him be accursed [Note: [Col. 0345D] We have presented the following charter, ‘Concerning Half of the Church of Saint Germanus,’ above, chapter 71.].”

## CHAPTER C. Concerning the Allods of Guntardus. (Before 1080.)

[Col. 0345B]

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I, namely Rotbertus the prior, and all the monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy church, present and future, that a certain knight named Guntardus of Garenceriis sent to us, earnestly asking that we quickly send one of our brothers to him.

When the brother had come to him and asked what he wanted, he replied: ‘I am weighed down by an illness of which I fear I shall die. With the Lord’s approval, I desire to become a monk; and, so that I may deserve to obtain pardon for my sins, from the earthly possessions that I have hitherto held I grant and, by granting, bestow upon Saint Peter, by direct donation, my allod—namely, the one in the territory of Abbonis Villa [Col. 0345C]—and likewise another in the parish of Imonis Villa, at the place called Rosetus.

I make this donation with the consent of my son Walter, in the presence of many people, and I invoke a curse upon all who strive to oppose the aforesaid donation, so that, unless they repent, they may suffer punishment in hell with Judas the betrayer.’

After he had spoken these words, before he could put on the monastic habit that was being brought to him from the monastery, that man entered upon the way of all flesh. The brother who had gone to him took up his body and carried it to the monastery, and we took care to bury him honorably among the brothers of the monastery.

We have wished to subscribe the names of the witnesses to the aforesaid donation, for the memory of posterity and to repel the disturbance of claimants: Harduinus, Guntardus’s nephew; Martinus, his squire; Herbertus the priest; Albertus the elder; Hildegarius; Johannes; Mainerius; Guarnerius of Poponis Villa; Vulgrinus of Saint Scubilius; Albertus of Segetis Villa [Note: [Col. 0346D] After this comes a charter, ‘Concerning Land Given by Mathildis,’ which you already have above, chapter 67.].”

## CHAPTER CI. Concerning the Allods of Herbertus. (Before 1080.)

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. We, the monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, wish it to be known to all worshipers of God’s holy church, present and future [Col. 0346A], that a certain knight named Herbertus of Galardon castle, coming to conversion under Abbot Hubertus, for the redemption of his soul and with the consent of his sons, Herveus and Fulcherius, and his only daughter, Guiburgis by name, granted to Saint Peter and his monks the allods that he held in the territory of Castrum Dunum.

He also granted one house within the castle; in Premetis Villa, the allod possessed by his mother Rotrudis, together with the firm tenure; likewise, in Marlai Villa, on the right side of the road to Dunum, six agripennos of land, and on the left side of the same road five agripennos; likewise, in Angeliacum, three and a half agripennos; in Boardi Villa, whatever he possessed by hereditary right; and in Isiginiacum, the land cultivated by Constantius, father of Vitalis, or which his mother Rotrudis appears to have held while she lived.

Sign of Herbertus, who gave this gift. Of Herveus. Of Fulcherius. The witnesses to this matter are: Ebrardus; Gauscelinus Lupulus; Normannus; Amalguinus; Frotlandus; Tescelinus; and Gaudius. If anyone should wish to annul this, unless he repents, let him be thrust into hell under anathema.”

## CHAPTER CII. Concerning the Allod of Piei Villaris, Huni Villa, and Argentela. (Before 1080.)

“In the name of Jesus Christ our Savior. I, Walter, son of Fledaldus, together with my wife and her sister, wish it to be known to all our successors, present and future, that we abandon our claim to the allod of Piei Villaris, which Berardus, my wife’s father, gave for the soul of his brother Guaningus [Col. 0346C], and to the allod of Huni Villa, and to the allod of Argentela, which my wife’s parents, the nephews of the monk Fulco, gave to Saint Peter.

Whatever I had seized by invasion in these allods, for the remedy of our souls we relinquish; we place the abandonment of our claim upon Saint Peter’s altar; and we have caused these letters to be made so that the witnesses subscribed below may stand against all who, at the devil’s instigation, wish to oppose this transaction.

The witnesses from our side are: Rainaldus, my brother; Fulcherius; Hugh of Treion; Gislebertus of Britiniacum; Haimericus, son of Heribrannus. The witnesses of the monks are: Walter the moneyer; Odielardus the money-changer; Hugh Berbellus; Baldwin; Arnulfus Rufus; Fulchardus; Arnulfus Niger [Col. 0346D]; Rotbertus, his brother; Stephanus the elder; Tescelinus, son of Hildegarius; Stephanus, son of Dodo; Bertrannus the cleric.

If anyone should bring a claim against this transaction, unless he quickly repents and seeks the remedy of satisfaction, struck down by the sword of anathema, let him suffer endless punishment in hell with Judas the betrayer.”

## CHAPTER CIII. Concerning the Property Given by William, Provost of Alogia. (Before 1080.)

“In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. We, the monks of Saint Peter of Chartres, wish it to be known that a certain knight named William, formerly provost of Braiao castle, afflicted by an illness of the body [Col. 0347A] from which he later departed this life, fearing the punishments of hell, took the monastic habit among us and appointed Saint Peter and us heirs to the worldly possessions that he had held in Alogia.

Although these possessions appeared very small to us, perhaps they are great before God. Therefore we have taken care to record them in this little document: one agripennus of land, namely, before the doors of the church of Saint Germanus; likewise, in Agonis Villa, the entire tithe; and similarly in Luetum and Fola Villa. His surviving son William granted all these things.”

## CHAPTER CIV. Concerning Six Agripennos of Allodial Land. (Before 1080.)

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. We, the entire community of monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, wish it to be known to all the faithful of Christ, present and future, that, for the soul of a certain Gausfridus, who was killed by men of Alonis Villa during harvest time and buried by us, his brothers and other relatives gave Saint Peter six day-plots of allodial land situated not far from Inpregni Villa.

They publicly placed the gift upon the principal altar on the fourth day before the Ides of October, while we were celebrating Mass, in the presence of those whose names are written below: Rotbertus, priest of Alona; Siguinus, horse dealer; Herbertus the baker; Guarinus the cellarer; Gausfridus the woodworker; Martinus Baiardus. The murdered man’s brothers were: Girbertus, Walterius, and Gislebertus. His relatives were: Girbertus and the woman Ledgardis. Let the opponent of this crocotilla alms-gift [term uncertain] be accursed.”

Not driven by the breath of pride, nor kindled by the fire of a flame-spewing intellect, but undertaking with an obedient foot a long journey through byways, and disregarding the hissing and mockery of readers, I have, as I promised the brothers, obeyed their commands. Lacking literary skill and using unpolished speech, I have explained in detail how this place ceased to be in its splendid and noble condition, and how it gradually grew back toward its former state of religion and pious activity through the efforts of venerable bishops, the donations of counts, and the gifts of many of the faithful.

Then I gathered together in sequence the names of the abbots and their writings that were found in our archives, up to the time when, because our excesses demanded it, a devouring flame burned this church together with its buildings [Note: [Col. 0347C] On 30 July 1077.]. At that time, by God’s providence, Bishop Gaufridus and Abbot Eustachius each attained his rank: the bishop before the fire, on the third day before the Kalends of August [Col. 0348B], and the abbot in the second year after the fire, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September.

In the work mentioned above, therefore, the prudent reader can observe that this place was destroyed by enemies more than once, since he reads three times that it was assigned to monks and twice to canons.

Now, having freed myself from the ancient writings that seemed worth committing to memory, I have taken care to inform the reader of five charters [Note: [Col. 0348C] See chapters 67, 71, 97, and 102 of this book], because they came to my attention late and were not in the places where they ought to have been: one charter of Abbot Landricus, concerning land given by Mahildis; and four of Abbot Hubertus—concerning the land of Pendent Pediculus, half of the church of Saint Germanus, the allods of Herbertus, and the allod of Picati Villaris, Huni Villa, and Argentela. I have inserted this so that I may not appear to have defrauded anyone.

Now I shall hasten, girded for writing, to the deeds accomplished by Abbot Eustachius over the past eight years.

# BOOK EIGHT, OR THE BOOK OF ABBOT EUSTACHIUS. (From 1079 to 1088.)

[Col. 0347]

## CHAPTER I. Concerning the Wrongful Custom Usurped by Fulco of Vadis at Ermenteriis. (Before 1088.)

[Col. 0347D]

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Let it be known to all the faithful sons of holy mother Church, present and future, that Fulco of Vadis was usurping an unlawful customary due at Ermenteriis, a village of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres.

Therefore, through the justice of Lord Isnardus, he came to court against Lord Eustachius, abbot of the aforesaid place, and a judicial combat was arranged at Dreux. Since Fulco could not demonstrate his right in the aforesaid custom [Col. 0348D], he and his son Godefridus relinquished it forever to God and blessed Peter, and for this reason they received seven pounds of denarii from Saint Peter’s property.

The witnesses were: Hugh of the Castle; Gislebertus of Tegulariis; the aforesaid Isnardus; Chotardus; and Rotbertus Rufus. From the abbot’s side: Arroldus of Croto; Laurentius the chamberlain; Fulchardus; Lorinus the driver; Johannes the cook; Durandulus the servant; and Adventius.”

## CHAPTER II. Concerning Property Given for the Boy Widdo. (Before 1088.)

«In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, creator of all things. I, Eustachius, abbot, and the entire congregation of the monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, wish it to be known to the faithful sons of God’s holy Church, both present and future, that a certain twice-married woman, named Gila of Pertico, came into our presence. She had two sons by her first husband, Hubert: namely Vivian and Wido. She offered the younger of them to God and Saint Peter, to serve there for as long as he lived in the profession of holy religion and monastic habit.

She also gave Saint Peter half of the woodland of Bustello and two arpents of meadow; she remitted the census that we used to pay for the land called Mala Cultura; and in her own woodland she granted, every year, pannage for our pigs. She ordered that our houses and barns in that same woodland be rebuilt as necessity required, and that the fire of our house be tended every day.

All these things Vivian, her aforementioned son, approved, and together with his mother he placed the gift upon the altar of Saint Peter. The sureties and witnesses of this transaction were these: Fulbert, priest of Roheria; Amalguinus; Sulpicius, cleric; Rodbert of Bodvers; and Durandus Ketellus. From our side: Teduinus and Gaudius, brothers; Stephanus and Salomon, brothers; Oydelerius and Rodbert, brothers; Fulchardus, Aventius, and Lorinus, brothers; Laurentius, chamberlain; Gilduinus, cook; and Guarinus, cellarer.

For the aforesaid properties we gave Willelmus of Baindis Terris, from whose benefice they had come, ten solidi in coin and the prayers of the community; and he gave his consent. But if any profane person should at any time wish to oppose this arrangement, unless he quickly repents, let him, plunged into Vulcan’s cauldron together with the profane King Theoderic, suffer everlasting punishments.»

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the church of Monasteriolus. (Before 1088.)

«In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. I, Eustachius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, together with the whole congregation entrusted to me, wish it to be known to all the faithful sons of God’s Church that there was a certain church called Monasteriolus, which the venerable abbot Landricus is known formerly to have acquired from a certain knight named Radulf, on this condition: that the monks should have half of the church for their own use, while Radulf should retain the other half for as long as he lived; and after his death both the church and the property that he appeared to possess in the aforesaid place, both on land and in water, should wholly return to Saint Peter.

When they had thus possessed the aforesaid church jointly for many years, a certain knight named Vitalis, a kinsman of the aforementioned Radulf, arose and asserted his right in the same church, obtaining half of it. As long as he lived, he retained for himself the portion bought from the monks. After the death of both men, their lord, Baldric, surnamed Chotardus, together with a certain young son named Eustachius, whom he dedicated to God’s service in monastic habit, gave the church to Saint Peter and granted whatever appeared to belong to him in that place, with the consent of Hugo, son of Guaszo, and of all those whose names we have written below:

Isnard of Mori Villare; Rodbert Rufus; Walter, son of Nivard; Guarinus, son of Josbert; Simon of Monte Pincionis; Ranald of Bello Puteo; Guarinus of Islo; Simon, his son; Rainald Corbulus; Aventius; Laurentius; Fulbert the elder.

The aforementioned Baldric wished this charter to be made so that, if anyone should ever—God forbid!—wish to oppose it, once convicted in court he should pay a pound of gold to the judge; and, wounded by the sword of anathema, unless he repented and sought the remedy of satisfaction, he should be plunged into hell and suffer punishments with the devil.»

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the evil customary exactions renounced by Willelmus at Plancis. (Before 1088.)

[Col. 0350B]

«In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I, Gausfridus, surnamed Niger, namely a monk of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres and, under Abbot Eustachius, administrator of the place of Plancis, wish it to be known to all worshippers of the Christian faith, present and future, that Lord Willelmus of the castle of Molinis, moved by many entreaties, wholly remitted to God, his virgin mother Mary, and the blessed apostle Peter, with the consent of his son Rodbert and for the salvation of his soul, the evil customary exactions that had gradually arisen through wicked servants in the place of Plancis during his time. He publicly placed the gift upon the altar of Saint Mary at Plancis.

The condition was that henceforth none of his successors should ever demand any customary exaction in the aforesaid place: neither toll, nor ban, nor the levy for fire, nor the levy of a thief, nor carts. Rather, the place should be entirely free from every exaction and customary due, except for one thing, namely the fortification of the aforesaid castle. When necessity required it, the inhabitants of the aforementioned place were to fortify the site shown to them in the said castle.

He also remitted in full the toll which we had omitted, both for the inhabitants of the place and for outsiders, except only the townsmen of the castle of Molinis. Therefore we wished this charter to be made, so that if any profane person should ever attempt to violate or oppose this grant, unless he quickly repented and sought the satisfaction of amendment, he might suffer in hell the punishments of Judas the betrayer and of those who crucified Christ.

The witnesses of this donation were written below: Gualterius of Asperes and his brother Ingenulfus; Balduinus of the castle of Mellente; Rotgerius, steward; Willelmus, priest; Wido of the castle of Medante and Stephanus; Rodbert, his arms-bearer; Rotgerius and Tescelinus of Scagiolis; Joscelinus, son of Ricoard, and Rodbert, his son.

From the side of Abbot Eustachius: Guarinus, priest; Ernulfus, cleric; Rainoldus Rufus; Rogerius, son of Wido the priest; Corbellus and Beroldus, his son; Richerius and Gualterius, elders; Fulchardus, Gunbaldus, Laurentius, Rodbert of Jesiaco, Raimundus, Johannes Brustinus, Leodegarius, Odelinus, and Guarinus.»

## CHAPTER V. The renunciation of Hugh’s customary food due. (Before 1088.)

«In the name of Him through whom all ages were created. I, Eustachius, abbot, and the whole congregation of the brothers of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, wish it to be known to all worshippers of God’s holy Church that, in the time of Abbot Hubert, our monk Gausfridus Niger bought from Herveus, Hugh’s brother, the vicariate of Mittanis Villare, with the consent of Fulcherius the primicerius, from whose benefice that vicariate itself came. Hugh therefore received five solidi for his consent.

In our time, however, he claimed that this customary right had been granted to him: whenever he came to the monastery with six or four knights accompanying him, bread, wine, and sufficient meat were customarily to be given to him, and likewise oats and wine for his horses. Since we were unwilling to submit to his importunity and denied him the custom he demanded, on one occasion he took our donkeys, which had been inspected; for their ransom we gave thirty solidi. On another occasion he took them again, but through Willelmus, the count’s provost, he reluctantly returned them.

Finally, through Countess Berta and the aforementioned provost, he abandoned that evil custom. While we were celebrating the feast of Saint Firminus, he placed the renunciation upon the altar of Saint Peter and received twenty-five solidi from us. If he should ever wish to become a monk, he is to be received with whatever property he possesses; but if death should overtake him, he is to be buried by us, with his property likewise left to us.

The witnesses of this matter, from his side, were Dodo, Guarinus, Godefridus, and Geraldus. From our side: Stephanus the elder; Gilduinus the elder; Laurentius, chamberlain; Teduinus, registrar; Johannes, cook; Gislebertus, the boy; Oydelerius; and Rodbert, his brother.»

[Note: [Col. 0351D] Perhaps read: “And when we were unwilling to submit to his importunity.”]

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the guardianship claim at Argentela. (Before 1088.)

«In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Eustachius, by divine appointment abbot, and the entire congregation of monks of Saint Peter, wish it to be known concerning a certain guardianship claim that Rodbert the swineherd of Curba Villa said he possessed over the land called Argentela. For this he inflicted no small loss upon us and, moreover, did not fear to commit homicide.

At last, coming to this agreement, we gave him fifty solidi in coin and the benefice of this place, so that he would relinquish to Saint Peter the land that he held in the aforementioned Argentela, together with the guardianship he claimed. He willingly agreed and did so, placing the gift upon the altar of the blessed apostle Peter, while a crowd of monks and a throng of servants stood present. We have taken care to record their names:

Stephanus and Salomon, brothers; Girogius, cleric; Teudo and Gaudius, brothers; Oydelerius and Rodbert, brothers; Aventius and Lorinus, brothers; Laurentius, chamberlain; Ingelbertus and Gausfridus, cooks; Gislebertus, the boy; Fulchardus; Hildulfus and Gausfridus, brothers.

From Rodbert’s side: Mainfredus, provost; Richerius and Gauslinus.

This was publicly enacted at Chartres, in the monastery of Saint Peter, before the altar, while King Philip was reigning. Paulus, the church custodian, wrote it.»

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning Lord Germanus. (1081.)

«With our Lord Jesus Christ, creator of all things, showing favor. I, Willelmus of Sumbone, girded with the weapons of knighthood, exceedingly wealthy in earthly possessions, and, at the instigation of the Devil, entangled in snares of evil deeds, wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church, present and future, that a certain faithful man of mine, named Sulpicius, had made a vow at the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres to strip himself of this deceptive world and dedicate himself to the service of the true God, and to leave to the chief key-bearer and the monks serving there, as their support, the benefice that he held from me in the territory of Chartres.

But, held back by a false love of the world, he was not permitted to fulfill his vow completely, for sudden death, seizing him with greedy jaws, carried him away. Nevertheless, while still retaining his soul within his dying breast, he ordered his faithful men and his wife to carry his body to the monastery, to be buried in the brothers’ cemetery, and to place before everyone upon the altar of Saint Peter the gift of the benefice that he had vowed should be given for him.

His son Ascelinus afterward gave his consent to this gift. Not long afterward he too died from a certain wound and was buried beside his father on account of this matter. Gausbert of Evroldi Villare, and Rainerius and Guaszo, their knights, were witnesses of this gift.

Then Winebertus, Sulpicius’s brother, from the territory of the Vexin, brought by Hubert Querculus, placed his consent upon the altar of Saint Peter and was included in the prayers of the brothers.

We have deemed it appropriate to describe what that benefice consisted of: namely, whatever he appeared to hold from me in the parish of Lord Germanus—in the church itself, in tithes, in cultivated and uncultivated lands, in woods and knights, and in all possessions already discovered or still to be discovered. All this the aforementioned Sulpicius left for his soul to the prince of the apostles and his monks.

Moved by the prayer of Abbot Eustachius and the monks, I too, together with my wife Ermengardis and my only son, named after me, wished this to be done for the redemption of our souls. On the day of the Purification of the gracious mother of the Lord, I placed my consent upon the altar of the apostle Peter and publicly confirmed this charter by the sign of the cross.

For this I received from the aforementioned abbot one hundred solidi of Chartres coin; my wife received two ounces of gold; and my son one variegated cloak.

The witnesses from my side were: Rodbert of Bello Monte; Jhotardus; Willelmus; Renaldus of Gaudena; and Gualterius. From the monks’ side: Stephanus and Salomon, brothers; Oydelerius and Rodbert, brothers; Teduinus and Gaudius, brothers; Guarinus, cellarer; Tescelinus, son of Hildegarius; Laurentius, chamberlain; Aventius and Lorinus, brothers; and others.

If anyone should oppose this charter, may the gate of heaven be closed to him; and, unless he repents, may he suffer without end with Judas the betrayer in the fires of Gehenna. This was publicly enacted at Chartres in the twenty-first year of the reign of King Philip.»

[Note: [Col. 0352D] So printed.]

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the church of Stilion. (Before 1088.)

«In the name of Christ, creator of all things. I, Willelmus, together with my wife Ermengardis and my only son Willelmus, wish it to be known to all the faithful and future sons of God’s holy Church that, for the redemption of our souls, we grant and divide to almighty God and Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, in whose monastery at the city of Chartres I am taking up the habit of holy religion, a certain church founded in honor of the mother of the Lord, in a place in Pertico called Extiliolus [Extiliolus, Stilio, Steliones; today Les Étilleux], so that they may possess forever half of the tithe, the archdeaconry dues, and the burial rights, the whole altar, half of the churchyard, land sufficient for two oxen, and one arpent of meadow.

I ordered the gift of these things to be placed upon the altar of blessed Peter and wished the names of the witnesses to be written below. If any of my heirs should ever attempt to oppose this gift, let him first incur the penalty of excommunication; then let him pay eight ounces of gold to the person against whom he brought the dispute, and let his attempt remain ineffective.

The mark of Ermengardis, his wife, who placed the gift of this grant upon the altar. The mark of Willelmus, his son. Of Hugo, Gausfridus the cook’s maternal uncle.»

[Note: [Col. 0353D] Extiliolus, Stilio, Steliones; today Les Étilleux.]

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the tithe of Caletulus. (Before 1088.)

«In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Eustachius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, together with all the brothers serving God there, wish it to be known to all worshippers of the orthodox faith that a certain knight named Guinebertus, brother of Sulpicius—who, when he died, left to Saint Peter, for our use, the church of Lord Germanus with all the property that he appeared to hold there from the benefice of Willelmus of Sumbone, namely tithes, lands, woods, knights, as stated above—after he himself had placed his consent upon the altar of Saint Peter and had been received into the prayers of the brothers, sold a portion of the aforesaid tithe to a certain woman for twenty-five solidi.

When summoned to court concerning this matter, he said that the tithe belonged to the fief of Guaszo, brother of Hugo of the Castle, and that therefore his consent was worthless without his lord’s approval. We therefore gave Guaszo one horse worth forty solidi, twenty solidi in coin, one shield, and the prayers of our community.

He too, through the arm of his arms-bearer, placed the renunciation of the tithe, or his consent, upon the altar of Saint Peter through Hubert Querculus and a monk, in the hearing and sight of those whose names we have written below: Radulf, Willelmus, Rodbert, Philippus, Hugo, Huberto, Tetardus, Ledfredus, Fulbertus, Rainaldus, Guarnerius, Fulco, Raimboldus, Rodbert, Laurentius, and Aszo.

The tithe itself is in the place called Caletulus. This was publicly enacted at the castle of Drocae.»

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the toll granted by Mainerius at Agili Villa. (Before 1091.)

[Col. 0354B]

«We, I, Eustachius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, wish it to be known to all the faithful sons of God’s holy Church that, while I was at the court of King Philip near the castle of Étampes and had appealed to the king for the benefit of our community, I met there Mainerius, brother of Simon of Monte Forti, and asked him, for the soul of his father and mother and for the safety of himself and his offspring, to grant freely to God and Saint Peter passage both for salt and fish and for our goods that were carried through Agili Villa from Chartres for the use of the brothers.

With willing heart, on the sixth day before the Ides of February, he released the passage freely from every customary charge, so that from that day forward neither he nor his successors might demand any toll or customary due for goods of Saint Peter passing through the aforesaid village. Just as his father Amalric had granted free passage throughout his entire territory for the goods of Saint Peter, so the aforementioned Mainerius granted it, in the presence of Bishop Gausfridus [Gausfridus, or Godefridus I, bishop of Chartres, was condemned for simony and deposed from the episcopate in 1091], and of his brother Simon, count of Beaumont.

In like manner Lord Simon decided that the consent of his father and brother should willingly remain valid throughout all the land under his authority in the aforementioned castle, in the presence and with the consent of his son Amalric and of Hugo of the castle of Puteolus.

But if anyone should ever wish to oppose this consent, as long as he remains obstinate let him continually be struck by the staff of excommunication; and unless he repents and seeks the remedy of satisfaction, may the worm that never dies consume his soul forever in the darkness of hell.»

[Note: [Col. 0353D] Gausfridus, or Godefridus I, bishop of Chartres, was condemned for simony and deposed from the episcopate in 1091.]

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the tithe of Ledonis Curia, which the monks of Bec claimed. (Before 1088.)

«In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. We, the monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres—namely Guarnerius and Joscelinus, serving under Abbot Eustachius at Ledonis Curia, which is a cell of the aforementioned monastery—wish it to be known to all those of the Christian religion, present and future, how the dispute and accusation that the monks of Bec were bringing against us came to an end in the chamber of the house of Paganus, son of Hugo Franco, at the castle of Chaumont.

Anselm, abbot of the monastery of Bec, was present there, and with him, from among his monks, Gislebertus, descended from the family of the Crispini, and Eustachius, surnamed Paganus. Also present were the leading men of that castle, holding a court concerning the priest of the church of Saint Mary, situated below, not far from Ledonis Curia. They wanted either to dispossess him of his wife or to take away the church, which belonged to them.

In the middle of the proceedings, certain letters were sent to us by the archbishop of Rouen [Guillelmus I governed the church of Rouen from 1078 to 1110], asking that, for love of the archbishop, we return to the monks of Bec the tithes of the goods and the burial rights of our church, which we received from our people living within the Fossés.

When the men of the castle, both clerics and laymen, heard this, the demand seemed strange to them: that what Count Gualterius had granted to Saint Peter nearly thirty years earlier, or more, with the consent of his leading men, should now unjustly be taken from us by monks who had only recently acquired the little church in question.

Then all gave testimony with one voice and undisguised countenance that, in their sight and hearing, Count Gualterius had given Saint Peter the burial rights and the tithe of the people living within the Fossés—namely the tithe of oxen, sheep, asses, and horses; also the tithe of the land that the monks plowed; and likewise the tithe of one arpent where an oven had formerly stood.

When the monks and their abbot heard this, they abandoned their unjust accusation and thereafter remained silent.

We also took care to have the witnesses of this matter written below: Manasses, archpriest; Herbertus, Genricus, Gualterius, and Sanson, canons; Odo, viscount; Herbertus, cupbearer; Rodbert, provost; Rogerius, knight; Givelinus; and Rodbert, a knight of the coast.»

[Note: [Col. 0355] Guillelmus I governed the church of Rouen from 1078 to 1110.]

## CHAPTER XII. Likewise, the gift of Godefridus’s woodland. (Before 1088.)

«In the name of Christ. I, Guarnerius, together with Joscelinus, of the monastery of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, at Chartres, and under Abbot Eustachius, administrators of the place of Ledonis Curia in the territory of the castle of the Vexin—which Count Gualterius, son of Count Drogo, while King Henry was reigning, granted to Saint Peter to possess forever during the lifetime of Abbot Landricus—wish it to be known to the faithful of God’s holy Church, present and future, that a certain knight named Godefridus of Floriacum, seized by the illness from which he died, sent through his son Hugo and his wife Adela the gift of his woodland to be placed upon the altar of Saint Peter, so that the monks of the aforesaid place might possess it perpetually and by right, without any accusation.

The condition was that from it they might build their church, houses, and barns whenever necessary, enclose their fields and court, and supply all their necessities.

After his death, his body was buried in the cemetery of Saint Peter on the fifth day before the Ides of April. Then his wife and his remaining sons once again placed the gift of the aforementioned woodland upon the altar for their father’s soul.

The names of the witnesses of this matter are written below: Gerelmus, priest; Milo, priest; Urso, knight; Odo, knight; Ivo, knight of Fai; Hilduinus, his brother; Givelinus; Rainaldus, his son; and Godefridus, knight.»

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the vicariate of Belsia. (Before 1091.)

[Col. 0356B]

«In the name of Christ. I, Walterius, son of Flealdus, moved by the prayers of Abbot Eustachius of Saint Peter and of the congregation entrusted to him, permanently relinquish to the church of Saint Peter, with the consent of my lord Gunherius, every vicariate that I held in all the lands of Saint Peter, together with my wife Fredesindis and my son Rainaldus, with his brothers and sisters, and also with Lisiardus consenting, for the redemption of our souls and those of our parents.

In exchange, I receive from the aforementioned abbot and monks three arpents of vineyards in the valley of Saint Bartholomew, in the enclosure called Ingelbaudus. The aforementioned monks also give my wife two ounces of gold and my son a horse purchased for six marks of silver; they add five solidi for the aforementioned Lisiardus.

Desiring to make this known to our descendants and to have it remain valid through succeeding ages, we wished it to be committed to written memory. We confirmed it by marking it with our own hands and offered it to our lords and friends to touch in confirmation.

The mark of Gualterius, son of Flealdus; of Fredesindis, his wife; of Rainaldus, their son; of Helias; of Hugo; of Lisiardus; of Adeline, his daughter; and of Elisabeth.

From Gualterius’s side: Rodbert, son of Rodulf; Hugo, son of Lambert; Ivo, son of Norbert; Oydelardus, Gualterius’s nephew; Einardus; Raimbaldus, priest; and Lambertus, priest.

From our side: Gausfredus, bishop; Ingelrannus, dean; Adelardus, subdean; Gauslinus, archdeacon; Guerricus, cleric; Hilbertus of Gurzeis; Gerogius, cleric; Guerricus, vicedominus; Willelmus, provost; Tedbaldus, his brother; Tedbaldus Farsit; Willelmus Mordens; Jhotardus; Gunbaldus; Laurentius, chamberlain; Fulchardus; Teduinus and Gaudius, brothers; Hildulfus and Gausfredus, brothers; Aventius, Stephanus, and Salomon, brothers; Ingelbertus, Johannes, and Gausfredus, cooks; Gualterius, tailor; Ribaldus of Frausino; Stephanus, son of Dodo; and Radul, son of Hildegarius.»

## CHAPTER XIV. Gunherius’s gift of the vicariates. (Before 1088.)

[Col. 0357A]

«In the name of the Creator of all things. I, Eustachius, abbot, and the entire congregation of the monks of Saint Peter of Chartres, wish it to be known to all the faithful, present and future, that Gunherius of Monte Letardi, namely son of Gualterius of Alneto, gladly gave his consent concerning the vicariates in Belsia that Gualterius, son of Flealdus, sold to us, both at Abonis Villa and in other places, and placed his gift upon the altar of Saint Peter.

Not only concerning those already given or sold, but also concerning those to be given or sold, he gave us firm assurance that we might receive them from his knights. He consented that we should possess not only the vicariates known to come from his benefice, but also the lands that his knights might wish to give or sell to Saint Peter.

Therefore we have included him in our prayers and in all our good works, so that he may share the reward with us in the kingdom of heaven. We wished, according to ecclesiastical custom, to have the witnesses of his grant sign this document.

From his side: Ansoldus of Mungerii Villa.

From ours: Balduinus, the abbot’s brother; Wibaldus and Rainaldus, son of Ernulfus Rufus; Fulchardus; Laurentius; Durandus; Richerius; Rodbert, furrier; Stephanus; Isenbardus; and Gualterius of Ver.»

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the vicariates redeemed from Viscount Hugo. (1096.)

[Col. 0357C]

«In the name of Christ. I, Eustachius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, and the entire congregation of monks entrusted to me by God, wish it to be known to the sons of God’s holy Church, present and future, that, under Count Tedbald, both our predecessors and we had bought all the vicariates that were in our land, or guardianship rights throughout Belsia, from those to whom they belonged, by giving more suitable and better properties.

But when Count Stephanus succeeded to his father’s dignity, Hugo the viscount, claiming those same vicariates by hereditary right, received them from that count. Desiring to live secure from disturbance, we moved the viscount by our entreaties to grant those same vicariates to Saint Peter, with the consent of Count Stephanus, as we had bought them, so that he, together with his wife and three sons and daughter, might be included in our prayers.

He placed the gift upon the principal altar of Saint Peter with his wife and children, in the sight and hearing of those whose names we have written below: Adelidis, the viscount’s wife; their sons Ebrardus, Hugo, and Wido; and their daughter Unberga.

Their faithful men: Ernulfus of Domicilium; Gausfridus Boviculus; Petrus Aper; Gerogius of Fraganis Villa; Guarinus of Alona; Adelardus, provost; Gausfridus of Novale; Ansoldus Infans; Rodbertus Paganus; and Gualterius of Alneto.

From our side: Laurentius, chamberlain; Aventius; Gunbaldus; Fulchardus; Stephanus and Salomon, brothers; Teduinus, Gaudius, and Harduinus, brothers; Radulfus and Richardus, brothers; Leodegarius; Stephanus; Martinus; Rodbert, furrier; Gualterius, Aventius, and Durandus, tailors; Engelbertus and Gausfridus, cooks; and Durandus, baker.

This was publicly enacted at Chartres in the church of Saint Peter, in the year 1096 of the Lord’s incarnation, while Philip was reigning as king in France.»

## CHAPTER XVI. Donation of the vicariate of Domna Maria. (Before 1088.)

«We are instructed not only by the pages of the New Law but also by those of the Old, because by the faith or merit of the good, pardon for their sins is granted to sinners. Thus the Lord says to Abraham: “If ten good men are found, the others will be saved on their account” [Note: [Col. 0357D] See Genesis 18:32].

Having cited this testimony from the Old Law, let us take a second from the Gospel, where the evangelist speaks of the paralytic lowered through the roof tiles into the house before Jesus. For he says: “When he saw their faith, he said to the paralytic: Son, your sins are forgiven. Take up your bed and walk in peace” [Note: [Col. 0357D] Luke 5:20 and 24].

Supported by these and many other testimonies, I, Ansoldus the knight, together with my beloved wife Hildegardis, all our offspring, and with the consent of my lord Gunherius, give and grant—and in granting give—the vicariate and the bannum, or any other exaction that I have hitherto appeared to hold from the benefice of my aforementioned lord, in the land of Saint Peter situated at Domna Maria.

For the remedy of the soul of my son Willelmus, struck down by death through the sword, I give it by perpetual right to the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to the monks serving night and day in his monastery, situated not far from the walls of the city of Chartres, so that, freed through their prayers from every bond of sin, placed at the right hand of the Lord, and raised among his saints and elect in the glory of the resurrection, he may breathe again.

We wished to place the gift of this grant upon the altar of blessed Peter by this charter on the third day before the Ides of July, invoking that if anyone should ever wish to oppose this charter, unless he quickly sought the remedy of amendment, he might be thrust into hell with Judas the betrayer, to be burned in the fires of Etna.

In order that this charter might remain unshaken as long as the present age endures, we wished it to be confirmed by our own hands and by the names of all the others standing around.

The mark of Ansoldus, who made this donation; of Rainaldus; of Gauscelinus and Arnulfus, his sons; of Gualterius, their maternal uncle; of Gausfridus, their paternal uncle; of Hilbertus, their cleric and kinsman, who placed this donation upon the altar in place of their father and mother; of Gausfridus of Monte Boonis; of Gausfridus “who does not drink water”; of Teudo Tronellus; of Guerricus, cleric, nephew [Note: [Col. 0358D] So printed] of Fulcherius the primicerius of Saint Mary; and of Tedbaldus of Vidicis.

From our side: Aventius and Lorinus, brothers; Stephanus; Laurentius; Frodo; Dodo the elder; Stephanus the elder; Oydelerius; Durandus; and Gislebertus.

This was publicly enacted at Chartres, while Philip was reigning as king in France.»

[Note: [Col. 0357D] See Genesis 18:32.]

[Note: [Col. 0357D] Luke 5:20 and 24.]

[Note: [Col. 0358D] So printed.]

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the church of Lord Peter. (Before 1088.)

«In the name of Christ. We wish it to be known to all our successors that I, Landricus, together with my sons, following the words of the Gospel, which says, “Give, and it will be given to you,” not deaf hearers but as far as our poverty permits, for the souls of ourselves and our parents, and also for the safety of Willelmus, our lord, and of his mother Mahildis, with their consent, gave long ago to Saint Peter, namely to the monastery of Chartres, the presbytery of the church of Lord Peter and the land belonging to the altar.

This was done at the request of Rainaldus the dean, who in old age preferred to serve God in the aforementioned monastery under the monastic habit.

Now we also give half of the tithe of the aforementioned church, which appears to belong to the church in our demesne, as well as half of the archdeaconry dues and burial rights. We also grant the property belonging to the altar, and the land of Ernaldus the mediator, which my father Teduinus granted during his lifetime, together with the meadow above it, and the fishpond of Mota free of charge.

If a mill can ever be built there, half shall belong to my sons, unless by their own will they consent to give their share to Saint Peter.

On the outer side of the church we freely give the land where the monks’ dwelling, their barn, and their other necessities may stand. We give it so freely that neither burial rights nor any other customary due may be demanded there by my sons or by any person.

We likewise give half of the kiln [Note: [Col. 0359] Three lines follow, the writing of which has been completely erased and cannot be read]. [lacuna]

If any of our faithful men should wish to give Saint Peter and the monks a portion of the benefice that he holds from us, let him be free to do so.

We made this gift on the fourth day before the Kalends of March—I, Landricus of Toriellum, and my sons Gausfridus, Hugo, and Landricus—publicly; and they sent the gift to Saint Peter through Abbot Eustachius, while Philip was reigning as king.

We also wish everyone to know that, whenever necessary, my sons will give twenty solidi for the vicariate.

The witnesses of this matter are: Gilduinus of Lord Peter; Gausfridus, smith; Odo of Floriacum; Rainaldus, his brother; Rodbert the elder and Willelmus, his brother; Odo, son of Ingilsindis; Ernaldus, son of Bernard; Rainaldus, dean; Odo, priest; Frogerius, the dean’s mediator; Willelmus, juggler; Gualterius, his companion; and Rainaldus, furrier.

From our side: Gilo and Elias, his son; Tedbaldus; Dolardus; Herbertus, son of Fulcadus; Vitalis, priest; Richerius the elder; Laurentius, chamberlain; Rodbert, elder of the Royal Chapel; Rainaldus, nephew of the monk Majenardus; Tescelinus, son of Hildegarius; Aventius; Beringerius, horseman; and Johannes, cook.

If any profane person should oppose this charter, unless he repents and makes satisfaction, may the earth swallow him alive, as it did Dathan and Abiron, and may he suffer punishments with the devil in the lowest hell.

We also wish it to be known at the end of this charter that, just as we gave the aforesaid properties, so we also gave the entire orchard situated beside the head of the church. We also consented that Odo, our knight, gave the tithe of the newly cleared lands that he held from us.»

[Note: [Col. 0359] Three lines follow, the writing of which has been completely erased and cannot be read.]

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the alods of Bernard of Buslo. (Before 1088.)

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. We wish it to be known to all our successors that I, Eustace, and the entire community of monks of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres [Col. 0360B], declare that a certain nobleman, highly renowned throughout this region, weakened in his entire body by wounds received in war, lay in bed for many years, unable either to sit or to place one foot before the other; nevertheless, by counsel and the wholesome assistance of his words, he was never lacking to anyone who sought him. He greatly loved our house and, while living in the body, benefited us as much as he could. Under Abbot Landricus, he gave to Saint Peter the church of Saint Germanus of Alogia; and, departing this life, he left to Saint Peter the allodial lands he possessed in Belsia: one, namely, in the village of Fontinidi; another in Marchesi Villa; and, near Braia, one arpent of meadow. He ordered his faithful men that, after his death, they should bring his body to Chartres to be buried among the brethren. This was done on the ides of November; and his relatives publicly placed upon the altar of Saint Peter the gift of the aforesaid properties. Their names we have written below [Col. 0360C]: Ernaldus, son of Eva; Widdo of Barzilleries; Alcherius; Hugo the cleric. On our side: Stephanus and Salomon; Laurentius; Adventius; Stephanus; Oydelerius; Martinus; Gunbaldus; Fulchardus; and the others.”

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning the freedom of the church of Bruerolis (7 May 1084)

“In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, amen. I, Gausfridus, although unworthy, bishop of the church of Chartres, make known to my successors and to the other faithful of our church that Brother Eustace, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, humbly entreated my smallness with prayers to give him and the congregation of monks serving there [Col. 0360D] the altar of Bruerolis, to be held thereafter without any redemption payment.

Since this petition appeared suitable both to their advantage and to my honor, I therefore give them the aforesaid altar, with the consent of Brother Gauslinus, in whose archdeaconry it lies, sound and free from every sale, from synod-fees, from circada, from every customary due, and also from every disturbance or exaction of justice by the priest serving in that place.

So that this gift may remain firm and stable through succeeding times, I have committed it to writing here, strengthened it by the sign of the cross made with my own hand, and handed it over to be confirmed by the hands of my faithful men.

Sign of Gausfridus, bishop. Hilduinus, precentor. [Col. 0361A] Gauslinus, archdeacon. Frodon, succentor. Morinus, priest. Landricus. Willelmus, the bishop’s nephew. Ernaldus, Morinus’s nephew. Rogerius. Engelrannus, dean. Adelardus, subdean. Ernaldus, provost. Hilgotus. Guerricus. Guarinus, brother of Robert, the succentor. Frodon, son of Algisus. Stephanus, son of Odilardus. Durandus.

Given on the nones of May, in the seventh indiction, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1084, and in the twenty-fourth year of the reign of Philip.”

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning Herbert’s vineyards, granted by King Philip at Area Braca (1086)

“In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, of the Father [Col. 0361B] and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Although the royal throne of dignity is adorned by the manifold cultivation of virtues, liberality and munificence nevertheless hold the foremost place: their effect stoops to the needs of many, and their power satisfies their petitions.

Therefore I, Philip, by the grace of God king of the Franks, wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy church of God and to our own people, present and future, that Eustace, abbot namely of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, came into the presence of our serenity, earnestly asking that, in royal piety, we might deign to incline the ear of our munificence to his prayers, so that, for our safety and the stability of our kingdom, we might grant the assent of our liberality to a certain Herbert and his wife, named Ingelburgis [Col. 0361C], enabling them, with our permission, to bring to completion what, inspired by God, they had long been preparing to fulfill.

That is, from the property they possessed at Area Braca, they might make Saint Peter and his monks their heirs: specifically, of two and a half arpents of vineyard, of their house, granary, and oven, and of all their household goods.

Judging their petition to be just, and together with our faithful men who were present with us, we considered it worthy, for the soul of my father King Henry and for our salvation, to grant assent to the donation of the aforesaid man and his wife.

It also pleased our serenity to forbid by royal authority that anyone at any time in the future should presume with any rashness to oppose this work of our munificence which we have fashioned, or dare to diminish anything, great or small, from the aforesaid property already granted. Nor shall anyone burden or oppress the guardian whom the monks place there [Col. 0361D] with any corvée or exaction; rather, free from every customary due owed to secular men, he shall remain there securely and serve the monks.

Only, at the appointed time, fifteen denarii, four cantari of wine, a mina of oats, bread, and one hen shall be rendered to our office for us to receive. If the monks are late in rendering these, let them make compensation, but let them not lose the named properties.

We have therefore commanded this charter to be strengthened in our name, in the names of our leading men, and with the seal of royal dignity, so that it may remain valid and inviolate forever.

Sign of Philip, king. Gausfridus, bishop of Chartres. [Col. 0362A] Amalricus, cleric. Frogerius of Châlons. Robert of Rochefort. Gausfridus, count of Maritaniae. Gervasius, the king’s steward. Philip, chaplain. Tedbaldus, the king’s stable-master. Lancelin, the king’s cupbearer. Gislebertus of Tegularies. Hugo of Courte-Sexaudi. Fulco, cupbearer. Odo, the bishop’s steward. Wibaldus, cleric. Adventius. Johannes Brustinus. Arroldus. Richerius and Girardus of Saint George.

This was publicly enacted at the castle of Drocis, before the gate of Saint Vincent, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1086, in the ninth indiction, while King Philip was reigning in his twenty-sixth year. I, Gislebertus the notary, acting in the place of Gaufridus, bishop of Paris and the king’s supreme chancellor, have subscribed after rereading it.”

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning the freedom of the five churches situated in the Perche (4 March 1086)

[Col. 0362B]

“In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, namely of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from both. I, Gausfridus, although unworthy, bishop of the church of Chartres, wish it to be made known to my successors and to the other faithful of our church that Brother Eustace, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, humbly entreated my smallness to give him and the congregation of monks serving there several altars, to be held thereafter without any redemption payment: namely, the altar of Ermenteriis, of Roheria, of Buxsetum, of Castellaria, and of Cruciacum.

Since this petition appeared suitable both to my honor and to their advantage, I give them the aforesaid altars, with the consent of Brother Gauslinus the archdeacon, settled and free from every sale, from synod-fees and circada, from every customary due, and from every exaction of justice, while our brother Gauslinus retains only this for himself for as long as he lives: namely, justice over the priests serving in those places [Col. 0362C].

So that this gift may remain firm and stable through succeeding times, I have committed it to writing here, strengthened it by the sign of the cross made with my own hand, and handed it over to be confirmed by the hands of my faithful men.

Sign + of Gausfridus, bishop. Adelardus, dean. Hilduinus, precentor. Widdo, abbot of Saint John. Hilbertus of Gurzeis. Rainbaldus of Calniacum. Ernaldus of Curba Villa. Giraldus, priest. Mainardus, priest. Garinus, deacon. Durandus. Sign of Willelmus, archdeacon. Gauslinus, subdeacon and archdeacon. Frodon, succentor. Fulco, archdeacon. Hilduinus, son of Girardus. Landricus. Odo, Ernaldus’s nephew. Morinus, priest. Gausfridus, priest. [Col. 0362D]
