This charter was delivered by Gauslinus the chancellor on the fourth day before the nones of March, in the ninth indiction, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1086, and in the twenty-sixth year of the reign of King Philip.”

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning the remission of wrongful customary dues at Saint George (1086)

“In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, [Col. 0363A] namely of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. All who believe in Christ are called living stones, as the Apostle says: ‘You are living stones built up into spiritual houses’ [Note: See 1 Peter 2:5.].

Therefore, if we wish Christ to dwell in us and us in him, we ought to kill our enemies—that is, our vices—following the example of the prophet Samuel, who, taking a sword, cut Agag, the very fat king, into pieces [Note: 1 Samuel 15:32–33], showing us by this deed that those who fight against the vices of the flesh ought to spare no one at all, but kill them all, lest we fall into the guilt of death, like King Saul, who, contrary to the Lord’s command, spared King Agag [Note: Ibid., verse 9], and therefore the Lord departed from him and an evil spirit seized him.

Fully instructed by this and many other examples of Holy Scripture [Col. 0363B], we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy church of God, present and future, that I, namely Hanricus, and my youngest brother, named Morinus, both girded with the military belt, because we have driven away from ourselves the wicked ambition which, when we were adolescents, had hitherto deceived us, and because, at the humble entreaty of Eustace, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, we have been brought to this point, for the love of God and our salvation, wholly to renounce the wrongful and intolerable customary dues which we unjustly received at the place of Saint George, situated not far from the river called Arva.

We retain only those dues which our father Rainbertus is said to have held by precarious tenure for the protection of the men: namely, the peasants’ oxen, three times a year, for cultivating the land in that place. Similarly, once a year and at a suitable time, if there are any rams and lambs, the monk who governs the place, when asked, shall provide them to us without burdening the inhabitants [Col. 0363C], so that we may willingly defend, to the best of our ability, against all men both the place and all its property, within and without.

If a dispute arises among the men of that place which cannot be settled without violence, it shall be settled in our court in the presence of the monk. The meal which, with shameless boldness, we used to demand on the feast of Saint George, we wholly renounce, because one celebrates a solemnity badly if one does not restrain oneself from unlawful acts.

And, as we have already said, we now and henceforth remit all the detestable customary dues which we used to usurp at the aforesaid place [Col. 0363D], except those which many say our father possessed; these are to be requested from the monk by precarious tenure, not extorted from the men by force.

We have strengthened this document, which we ordered to be made, by publicly impressing the sign of the holy cross at the castle of Drocis, and have handed it over to be confirmed by the hands of our peers and faithful men, whose names we ordered to be written below as witnesses.

But if any profane person wishes to oppose this gift of ours, unless he repents, may he suffer endlessly in hell with the betrayer Judas and with those who crucified the Lord Jesus [Col. 0364A].

This charter was publicly given at the castle of Drocis, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1086, in the ninth indiction, in the twenty-sixth year of the reign of King Philip. Paul, monk and sacristan, acted as notary.”

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning the church of Puteosa Villa (1086)

“In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, who is three in persons and one in essence. To the desolate Gentile people—that is, to the church gathered from the nations—the Lord, through the voice of the prophet Isaiah, promised the gifts of spiritual virtues. Among fragrant trees I placed the elm and the boxwood [Note: Read: ‘he placed.’], saying: ‘I will place in the desert the fir, the elm, and the boxwood together’ [Note: Isaiah 41:19].

Now, leaving aside the fir in this exposition—for by it holy men are signified, whose minds, through continual meditation and holy desire, are raised to contemplate heavenly things—we who are frail and weighed down by the mass of our iniquities ought to be instructed by lesser things, so that we may appear to bear either the significance of the elm or of the boxwood [Col. 0364B]. We are sluggish in good works and serve the honors of this frail and fleeting world.

The elm indeed grows tall but bears no fruit; it doubtless signifies those who, thoroughly entangled in worldly affairs, are empty of the fruit of spiritual works. Yet, just as the elm often supports the vine with its clusters, so the powerful of this world support God’s servants throughout the churches far and wide with distinguished benefactions. In this way they make their spiritual works their own and are rewarded with them by an eternal recompense in the world to come [Col. 0364C].

Finally, the boxwood, retaining only its greenness, reveals those who preserve the perfection of true faith with an unimpaired vow.

With these matters prefaced, I, Isnardus of the Perche, girded with the military belt and wishing to join myself to them, for the salvation of my soul and out of every affection for my beloved mother Albereda, give, with her, to him to whom the power of binding and loosing has been granted by God, who opens the gate of the heavenly kingdom to the faithful and closes it to the unbelieving—namely to Saint Peter of the monastery of Chartres—I say, both I and my dearest mother willingly give, in the Perche, the church dedicated to Saint John, situated in the village which the inhabitants call Puteosa [Col. 0364D], together with its churchyard, tithe, and all revenues belonging to us.

We also grant one mansus of land and its customary dues, so that from now on the monks may possess it as we ourselves have possessed it until now.

We have also decreed that, if any of our men wishes to give Saint Peter anything from property which he holds from our benefice [Note: “which he holds” is omitted in the manuscript], he may give it confidently, with no one resisting, just as my faithful men Bernardus and Rogerius have already done, having become monks in the aforesaid monastery. The first of these gave, at the place called Manseleria, one mansus as freely as he held it from me; the other likewise gave one mansus, not far from the aforesaid church which we have given [Col. 0365A].

My mother, recently confined by illness, also gave one hospes beside the church of Buxetum, which my father, while living, gave to Saint Peter; and I likewise gave another at the dedication of that church.

With my lord Simon, son of Gaucherius, consenting—for all these things belong to his benefice—I publicly gave these properties to Abbot Eustace, in the place of Saint Peter, in the very church which I had given; afterward, at Chartres, with the approval of our faithful men, I placed the gift upon the altar of Saint Peter.

This charter was given in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1086, in the ninth indiction, and in the twenty-sixth year of the reign of King Philip.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning the claim against the forest of Munticuli (1086)

[Col. 0365B]

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. I, Eustace the abbot, together with all the brothers of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy church of God, present and future, that while Abbot Hubert governed this place, the forest of Munticuli, with all its appurtenances, was given to Saint Peter by Gualterius the money-changer, with the consent of the lords to whom it belonged, for the use of the brethren; and it was possessed by the brothers for nearly fifteen years without a claim.

In our time, however, a certain young man named Mainerius, namely the son of Germundus, from whose benefice the aforesaid forest [Col. 0365C] had come, began, after his father’s death, to bring a claim against it. We finally extinguished his claim by giving him twenty-five solidi in coin and by the prayers of the brothers.

Accordingly, he came on the third day before the Kalends of August and publicly placed a quitclaim upon the altar of Saint Peter, before those whose names we have written below.

On his side: Archenaldus and Savericus. On our side: Gauscelinus, brother of Carnalis; Gumbaldus; Stephanus and Salomon; Gausfridus and Hildulfus, brothers; Gislebertus; Teduinus; Gaudius and Harduinus; Robertus, the hospitaler.”

[Note: “This was enacted in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1086, in the ninth indiction, in the twenty-sixth year of the reign of King Philip.” Codex Argentoratensis.]

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning the claim against the church of Spelterol, remitted by Gualterius of Aulnay (Before 1088)

[Col. 0365D]

“In the name of Christ. I, Eustace the abbot, and all the brothers of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, wish it to be known to all our successors that, after the church of Spelterol had been given to us by Hugo of Drocis and his sons, Gausbertus and Guarinus, and also by their mother, named Osilia, the brother whom we had sent there frequently suffered injuries and losses from Gualterius of Aulnay, until we gave the aforesaid Gualterius fifty solidi in coin [Col. 0366A], on the condition that he allow that brother to live in peace and withdraw the claim which he was making against the church itself.

Gladly agreeing, he publicly placed at Chartres upon the altar of Saint Peter a quitclaim of the claim, taking with him Rainbaldus the cleric.

With us were Georgius the cleric; Stephanus and Salomon, brothers; Teduinus, Gaudius, and Harduinus, brothers; Oydelerius and Robertus, brothers; Hildulfus and Gausfridus, brothers; Adventius; Fulchardus; Stephanus; Tescelinus; Ingelbertus and Gausfridus, cooks; Herbertus and Guarinus, bakers.”

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning the toll granted by Bishop Gausfridus (14 November 1087)

[Col. 0366B]

“In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, namely of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Let all who share the Christian religion, future and present, and especially the successors to my episcopal see, as well as the other faithful of our church, know that Brother Eustace, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Chartres, petitioned me, Gausfridus, although unworthy bishop of the church of Chartres, with the greatest humility and an abundance of prayers, that I might grant perpetually to him and to the brothers serving God there the portion of the toll from the suburb of the aforesaid prince of the apostles which belonged to me by episcopal right.

I, assenting to his petition, providing for their advantage, and consulting my own honor, grant them in full and without any reduction the aforesaid toll, hitherto held by my predecessors and by myself [Col. 0366C], with such permanence that no successor of mine at any time may presume to invalidate this blessing.

So that this gift may remain firm and unshaken through the course of succeeding times, I have committed it to writing here, confirmed it with my own hand by the sign of the cross, and handed it over to be strengthened by the hands of my canons and faithful men.

Sign of Gausfridus, bishop. Sign of Adelardus, dean. Willelmus, archdeacon. Widdo, abbot of Saint John. Ebrardus, treasurer. Giraldus, priest. Warinus, deacon. Warinus, succentor, son of Durandus the canon. Gauslinus, subdean. Odo, archdeacon. Hilduinus, son of Girardus. Morinus, priest. Gausfridus, priest. Guerricus, canon. Gislebertus, canon. Rainbaldus, canon [Col. 0366D].

This charter was given by Gauslinus the chancellor on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of King Philip [Note: Over the words “King Philip,” a later hand wrote “of Louis the Younger”; we do not know why, since it is clear that this charter was given by Gausfridus I, bishop of Chartres, who died in 1090, and whose episcopate corresponds with the reign of King Philip, not by Gausfridus II, whose episcopate began in 1115 and therefore cannot in any way fall within the time of Abbot Eustace, who relinquished the government of the abbey in 1101.]. It was placed by the aforementioned bishop upon the altar of Saint Peter on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the presence of those whose names we have written below: Hilduinus the cantor; Hugo the viscount; Gauslinus of Leugis; Nivelon; Philip; Bartholomew; Willelmus, formerly provost; Waffridus kissing Aculon; and many others, both his men and ours [Col. 0367A].”

## CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning the oven of Bruerolis (Before 1088)

“In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. I, Landricus, son of Gislebertus, together with my wife Hildeburgis, my sons and my daughters, wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy church of God, of the present and future age, that I once pledged for twenty-five solidi in coin to Arnold the monk the half of the oven situated in the village of Bruerolis.

Now, I say, for the sake of my soul and of the souls of my ancestors and successors, with the consent of my lord Warinus of Islo, from whose benefice I appear to hold this same part of the oven, and also with that of Simon, his son, I grant it in perpetual right to Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, of the monastery of Chartres, governed by Abbot Eustace, and to Saint Germanus, so that the monks of Saint Peter may have, hold, and possess it from this day forward without any claim [Col. 0368A].

For this property I received from Gausfridus the monk, surnamed Wischardus, fifty solidi in coin; my wife, named Hildeburgis, one teristrum worth two solidi; and each of my sons, Isnardus and Radulfus, one shoe; my daughter Adelina, whom I gave in marriage to the knight Rainaldus, to whom I had also given the aforesaid part of the oven, received a gold ring; Warinus, my lord, received ten solidi, and his son the same amount.

I wished this document to be made for the memory of posterity, and at the castle of Drocis, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, I publicly agreed that it should be confirmed. If any of my heirs should ever attempt to contradict these provisions, he shall first be compelled to pay thirty pounds of gold to the king’s treasury, and thereafter his attempt shall remain ineffective; and if he persists, let him be struck with the rod of excommunication [Col. 0368B] until he repents.

May we and our relatives, together with our lord Guarinus, deserve always, for this deed, to enjoy the prayers of the brothers. We have also taken care that the witnesses of this matter subscribe.

Sign of Lord Hugo. Sign of Gislebertus of Tilerias.”

[Note: “This charter is incomplete; its ending will be found in Part II, Book IV. In this Codex B, after the scribe had copied this charter, he filled the page with subscriptions belonging to another charter, which run as follows:

‘These are the witnesses to the gift of the mill which G., son of N., gave to Saint Peter: G. himself; Adelina, his wife; Amalricus and Simon, his sons; Philippa, his daughter; Gualterius of Trotto; Gualterius of Bociacum; Urso of Tinniacum Valley; Erchenbaldus of Geremari Villa; Radulfus of Sibriacum; Bernerius of Ebriacum; Milo the priest; Ernaldus the abbot; Johannes of Saliciolum; Raimbaldus.

On our side: Marcoardus the priest; Algerius, his brother; Bodo; Richerius; Adventus; Laurentius; Berengerius and Johannes, his brother; Herlebaldus; Richardus …’”]

[Col. 0367]

## EPITAPH OF ABBOT LANDRICUS

By Paul, a monk, apparently

(Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. IV, book LXII, no. 83, p. 668.)

Here bend your eyes and pause a little, traveler,

And learn who he was whom this tomb covers.

This small urn contains the body of Landricus,

Our shepherd and outstanding Father.

While he was able to live, he ruled his subjects well,

Showing by his deeds what he taught by his admonitions.

He was gentle, compassionate, pious, and kind;

He scorned the proud and bravely restrained them.

A good and prudent man, he raised to great honor

This Church entrusted to him, worthily,

For three times ten and three times two years.

Then, after being like a widow, this Church raised its head.

Here he departed this life, holy like Leobinus,

Whose feast-day March shows to be approaching.

May peace and everlasting rest be yours, Father Landricus;

May joys with all the saints now be yours. Amen.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1100. GODEFROY OF BOUILLON, DUKE OF LORRAINE, FIRST KING OF JERUSALEM

[Col. 0369]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(*Literary History of France*, vol. VIII, p. 598.)

### § I.—History of his life

[Col. 0369A]

Godefroy, who has furnished the subject of so many French [Note: There are in fact at least three or four old romances of Godefroy of Bouillon in our old French language. One also knows the *Jerusalem Delivered*, or *Godefroy*, the finest poem of Tasso, and the *Syriade*, or *The Expeditions of Godefroy of Bouillon in the Holy Land*, in twelve books, by Pierre Ange de Barga, another Italian poet.] and Italian romances, and whom almost all the writers of the First Crusade have taken as their hero, has nevertheless so far had no single author who has given his complete history. The little that the Abbé Fleury, the Abbé de Choisy, and Father Maimbourg have written about him incidentally is suited only to make one wish to see so rich a subject treated with due breadth by some skillful pen. May God grant that what we are about to say in our turn may give rise to such an undertaking, and that its execution may closely follow.

If the life of this incomparable hero presents memorable events for military, ecclesiastical, and civil history, it also offers events for literary history. It is with the latter that we shall be especially concerned [Col. 0369B].

[Note: William of Tyre, book IX, no. 5; Orderic Vitalis, book IV, 9, pp. 508–509, 743, 757; *Miracles and Notices of the Churches of Belgium*, pp. 257–259, 262–263; Bollandists, 13 April, p. 142, no. 4.]

He was the eldest son [Note: His mother Ida, in one of her charters, calls him the first of her three sons; but in another she names Eustace, his brother, before him.], according to William of Tyre and Orderic Vitalis—or only the younger, according to others—of Eustace II, count of Boulogne and Lens, one of the most powerful lords and bravest captains of his age, who earned as much reputation through the practice of Christian piety as through the profession of arms.

His mother, named Ida, who became no less renowned for her virtue than the count her husband, was the daughter of Godefroy the Great, or the Bearded, duke of Lower Lorraine and Bouillon, who took Beatrix, marchioness or countess of Tuscany, as his second wife. Ida was thereby the niece of Pope Stephen IX and the sister of Duke Godefroy the Hunchback, who married the illustrious Matilda, only daughter and heiress of Countess Beatrix [Col. 0370A].

[Note: *Spicilegium*, vol. VII, pp. 584–585; *Miracles*, cited above, pp. 262–263.]

Through Matilda, his paternal grandmother, daughter of Gerberga and granddaughter of Charles, first duke of Lower Lorraine and brother of Lothair, king of France, our hero was descended from the Carolingian kings; and through his maternal grandmother, from the kings of Lombardy. On this basis Orderic Vitalis and the historian of Blessed Ida attest that Count Eustace, his father, was of the race of Charlemagne [Note: Orderic Vitalis, book IV, p. 508; Bollandists, cited above, p. 141, no. 3.].

[Note: William of Tyre, book VIII, no. 24; book IX, nos. 5–6; *Miracles*, cited above, p. 259; Bollandists, cited above, p. 145, no. 17.]

Godefroy was born at Boulogne-sur-Mer, at the extremity of Picardy, or rather at Baisy, in French Brabant, and had two brothers: Baldwin, who later succeeded him in the kingdom of Jerusalem, and Eustace, who inherited their father’s states and married Mary of Scotland. By her he had an only daughter, named Matilda, who married Stephen of Champagne, later king of England, after the death of Henry I [Col. 0370B].

[Note: William of Tyre, book IX, no. 5; *Miracles*, donation codex, p. 225.]

William of Tyre and several other writers also give Godefroy a third brother named William, whom the genealogists count as the ancestor of the later dukes of Lorraine.

[Note: *Miracles and Notices of the Churches of Belgium*, pp. 262–263; donation codex, pp. 223–224, 229–230.]

But a genealogy written around the year 1095 recognizes only three sons of Count Eustace and Countess Ida: Eustace, Godefroy, and Baldwin. Likewise, neither Countess Ida, when she had occasion to speak of her children, nor Godefroy, when speaking of his brothers, ever names this William. Whatever the truth about this fourth son of Count Eustace may be [Note: Orderic Vitalis, book IV, 7, pp. 509, 639; Berthold’s chronicle, year 1095; Dodechin’s chronicle, years 1093 and 1097], Godefroy had a sister named Praxedes-Adelaide, who married Henry IV, king of Germany and afterward emperor.

[Col. 0370C]

Providence, which destined Godefroy for great things, caused him to be born with every necessary disposition of heart, mind, and body [Col. 0371A].

[Note: Robert the Monk, *Deeds of the Franks*, book IX, p. 76; Ralph of Caen, *Deeds of Tancred*, pp. 121–122, no. 14; Mabillon, *Museum Italicum*, part II, p. 133; William of Tyre, book IX, no. 5; Orderic Vitalis, book IX, p. 757; Malmesbury, *On the Kings of England*, book IV, pp. 133, 142; the Ursperg Chronicle, year 1097.]

Soon there appeared in him natural inclinations toward virtue: a rich store of goodness, generosity, compassion even for the guilty, gentleness, modesty, humility, and fear of God; an uprightness of morals free from cloudiness and changeability; an easy, lively, penetrating, elevated mind, capable of the greatest undertakings; a greatness of soul for which there are few examples; an intrepid courage, supported by a robust constitution and great skill in military exercises [Col. 0371B].

These happy dispositions gave him more than one trait of resemblance to Charlemagne, from whom he was descended—*cui vere plurimus inerat Carolus*, “in whom Charles was truly present in great measure,” both in blood and in mind.

Nothing is more worthy of praise than the admirable union he knew how to make of two professions apparently incompatible in the eyes of most people.

[Note: Ralph of Caen, cited above; Mabillon, cited above.]

Was the question military art? He shone in it as much as his father the count, who had earned a brilliant reputation in it. Was the question the worship of God? Godefroy practiced it with the same piety as his mother, who herself already enjoyed a great reputation for holiness.

[Note: Martène, *Anecdotes*, vol. I, p. 261.]

As he himself explains, he regretted that the profession of arms prevented him from applying himself to divine matters as much as he wished. To make up for this, and to have a greater share in the good works of God’s servants, he willingly devoted himself to helping them and doing them good. He had received this example from his ancestors, who are recognized as founders or benefactors of several monasteries [Col. 0371C].

[Note: *Miracles and Notices*, cited above, pp. 195, 199, 223, 226; Meyer, *Annals*, year 1090; Bollandists, 13 April, p. 141, no. 2.]

Blessed Ida had been too well instructed in letters in her youth to neglect having her children instructed in them as well [Col. 0371D].

[Note: Orderic Vitalis, book VII, p. 639.]

Baldwin became skilled in them, according to the testimony of a historian close to his time. But Godefroy surpassed him in this respect as in so many others.

[Note: Guibert of Nogent, *Deeds of the Franks*, book II, chapter 7.]

It is evident from his letter to Prince Bohemond [Note: William of Tyre, book II, no. 10.] and from one of his speeches preserved for us by William of Tyre [Note: Ibid., book II, no. 10.] that he spoke Latin more purely than any other writer of his age [Col. 0372D]. If he himself dictated the charters that survive from him, they provide another proof of what we assert here.

To his knowledge of Latin he added that of the old French language and of the Teutonic language. This knowledge served him more than once during the Crusade to calm disputes that arose between the French and the Germans [Col. 0372A].

[Note: Otto of Freising, *Chronicle*, book VII, chapter 5; the Ursperg Chronicle, year 1099; Albert of Aachen, *Chronicle*, year 1099, part II, p. 180.]

The solidity of his piety likewise leaves no room to doubt that he was thoroughly instructed in his religion. We have another indication of this which, although drawn from rather ordinary matters, nevertheless gives favorable grounds for judging what took place in more important matters.

[Note: William of Tyre, book IX, no. 2.]

Godefroy never saw images or figures in churches without wishing to know what they represented. For this purpose he approached clerics and other persons who seemed to him more learned, and asked them to instruct him. The brilliant role he played on so many occasions—whether in battles or encampments, at the sieges of cities or in negotiations, and finally in the government of the kingdom of Jerusalem, although his reign was very brief—all this shows that he possessed all the knowledge necessary for a great captain, a skillful statesman, and a wise sovereign [Col. 0372B].”

Thus was Godfrey [Note: [Col. 0372D] Lamb. Schab. an. 1076; Spic. vol. XII, p. 284; Mir. Not. ib., pp. 257–258; Cal. Hist. de Lor. vol. I, p. 1125] in 1076, the year in which Duke Godfrey the Hunchback, his maternal uncle, died and left him the duchy of Bouillon. He immediately assumed the title Duke of Bouillon, by which he is better known and which he immortalized. He was also to succeed his uncle in his other possessions, since the latter, having no children, had adopted him as his son and designated him as his heir. But King Henry IV, considering the fiefs of [Col. 0372C] this inheritance to have devolved upon him, invested Conrad, his own son, with the duchy of Lorraine and gave the young Godfrey the marquisate of Antwerp as a kind of compensation. Later, however, when Conrad gave his father the king cause for displeasure, that prince took Lorraine from him and restored it to Godfrey, to whom it rightfully belonged and who had moreover well deserved it through the outstanding services he had rendered Henry, as will be seen below [Note: [Col. 0372D] Malm. ib. p. 143].

At that time Upper and Lower Lorraine were distinguished. Upper Lorraine, however, was scarcely known except by the name of Mosellana; and by the designation Lorraine people understood only the lower region, which was none other than the duchy of Brabant. Subsequently, the name Lorraine passed to Mosellana. This seems to have begun as early as the time of Jacques de Vitry, who, praising our hero, calls him Duke of Brabant, although all the historians who preceded him give him the title Duke of Lorraine [Note: [Col. 0372D] Mart. ibid. vol. III, p. 282].

[Col. 0373A] One of the first occasions on which Godfrey distinguished his courage [Note: [Col. 0373D] Will. Tyr. ib. no. 7] was a single combat that he was compelled to undertake against another young lord of the country, his relative. They were at odds over a considerable estate, and the dispute had to be settled by this murderous method, which at that time was only too common, especially among the nobility. When the day appointed for the contest arrived, the two champions entered the lists in the presence of Henry, King of Germany, and his entire court. After several passes, Godfrey struck his opponent’s shield with such force that the sword broke in his hand. The spectators, seeing that the contest was no longer equal, wished to stop the combat. But both men refused. Godfrey, then using as best he could the fragment of sword that remained to him, struck his opponent so violently on the left temple that he knocked him half dead to the ground and immediately disarmed him. But seeing that he had his enemy’s life in his power, instead of taking it, he asked the lords present to persuade him to accept an honorable settlement. The generosity and courage that Godfrey displayed on this occasion won him immortal glory.

[Note: [Col. 0373D] Malm. ib.; Wil. Tyr. ib. no. 8.] He subsequently joined King Henry’s armies, the king who later became emperor, and served that prince with great bravery and success. He took part in the battle fought in Saxony in 1080, and no one was judged more worthy than Godfrey to carry the imperial eagle [Note: [Col. 0373D] Berth. Chr. an. 1080; Ursp. ib.]. Fortune initially seemed to favor the Saxons, [Col. 0373C] and the king already saw his army fleeing before its victorious enemies, when Godfrey turned their victory into defeat by killing with his own hand King Rudolf [Note: [Col. 0373D] Will. Tyr. ibid.], the cause of the war. Three years later, King Henry, still angered against Pope Gregory VII, having laid siege to Rome and lost much time there, Godfrey finally found a way to enter the city first and opened its gates to the besiegers. This notable service enabled Henry to carry out the long-standing plan of having himself crowned emperor, which took place at Easter of the following year [Note: [Col. 0373D] Berth. ibid. an. 1082; Malm. ib.; Hug. Fl. Chr., pp. 227–228].

It nevertheless happened that the man who had served this prince so advantageously found himself obliged to declare war on him. When Henry insulted [Col. 0373D] the Empress Praxedes, Godfrey’s sister, this hero, being extraordinarily sensitive to matters of honor, did not believe that he should leave such an affront unavenged [Note: [Col. 0373D] Berth. ibid. an. 1095; Dod. ibid.]. He therefore took up arms against the emperor and was fortunate enough to defeat and put him to flight [Note: [Col. 0374D] Ord. Vit. bk. VII, p. 639].

Taking advantage of this war, Thierry, surnamed the Great, Bishop of Verdun [Note: [Col. 0374D] Spic. vol. XII, p. 284], attempted to remove from the dependence of the duchy of Bouillon the county of Verdun, which in fact depended upon it, as is shown beyond doubt by the statutes of our hero’s maternal grandfather [Note: [Col. 0374D] Mart. Anec. vol. I, pp. 189–190], in order to keep the advocates of that church in their proper obedience. To improve his chances of success [Note: [Col. 0374D] Spic. ibid.], Thierry persuaded the emperor to appoint Albert, Count of Namur, as viscount of Verdun—a powerful lord known to be Godfrey’s enemy. Supported by the troops of the Bishop of Verdun, Albert came to besiege Bouillon. At the news, Godfrey hastened there with his army and forced him to raise the siege, after killing many nobles. Then, in retaliation, Godfrey freed Henry, Count of Grandpré, whom the Bishop of Verdun was holding prisoner, released him upon the bishop’s lands, and [Col. 0374B] for his part built a fortress at Stenay, on the borders of the same diocese. War broke out again, and Thierry, assisted by Count Albert and other auxiliary troops, came to lay siege to Stenay. The two sides fought with great courage, and victory remained uncertain. Godfrey sent his brothers Eustace and Baldwin to raise troops in France and Germany; with these reinforcements he hastened to relieve Stenay, and the Bishop of Verdun was forced to raise the siege. This occurred in the fortieth year of Thierry’s episcopate, around 1086; and matters remained in this state until the proclamation of the crusade.

[Note: [Col. 0374D] Malm. ib. p. 144.] Then Godfrey, animated by a spirit of piety, decided to turn his arms against the enemies [Col. 0374C] of the Christian name, and bound himself to do so by a vow. From that moment he was delivered from the lingering fever left him by the hardships of the siege of Rome, and his health steadily grew stronger, inspiring him with fresh zeal for the holy war. To undertake it with greater success, he generously made peace with Richer, Bishop of Verdun, Thierry’s successor. Not only did he cede to him the county of his episcopal city—which Richer, out of gratitude, immediately transferred to Baldwin, Godfrey’s brother, and which Baldwin, upon his departure for the crusade, returned to the bishop in an even greater act of generosity—but he also razed the fortress of Montfaucon, which he had built in the diocese of Verdun, and gave the places of Stenay and Mouzay to that [Col. 0374D] church. In compensation, the bishop and clergy of Verdun gave the duke considerable sums, which he used to pay the expenses of his journey. Since this still did not suffice for his expenditure, he alienated his beautiful duchy of Bouillon to the church of Liège for three marks of gold and three hundred marks of silver [Note: [Col. 0374D] Ibid.; Mart. Amp. Coll. vol. IV, p. 1079].

[Col. 0375A] [Note: [Col. 0375D] Ursp. Chr. an. 1066, 1097; Mart. ib.; Malm. ib., p. 133.] After these preparations, Godfrey, relying even more on God’s assistance than on his own strength, departed in the spring of 1096 with his brothers Eustace and Baldwin, at the head of more than two hundred thousand crusaders: Frisians, Saxons, and Germans, as well as Lorrainers and, above all, Frenchmen [Note: [Col. 0375D] Will. Tyr. bk. II, no. 3]. He took the route through Hungary, having obtained the king’s permission, and was treated by him with great honor. Godfrey, for his part, kept his army under such strict discipline that it caused no damage there. The same was not true near Constantinople. The duke learned that the emperor Alexius, a deceitful and crafty prince, was holding Hugh the Great, brother of Philip, King of France, and several other crusading lords captive there. He wrote to him, asking that they be released. [Col. 0375B] Alexius refused and continued to make the crusaders feel the effects of his hatred of the Latins. Matters came to blows; and when the troops of this badly advised prince were defeated, he feared for his states and understood the consequences of his false policy. He therefore made peace with the duke and sent him away laden with gifts.

Godfrey, having given proof on this occasion of his fearlessness and greatness of soul, had another opportunity to display his gentleness and moderation [Note: [Col. 0375D] Tud. ib.; Ges. Fr., bk. II, p. 781]. The Count of Saint-Gilles arrived almost immediately near Constantinople with the crusaders he led and, having received further cause for resentment from the same emperor, wished to take revenge for his treachery. But Duke Godfrey [Col. 0375C] represented to him that it was not fitting for them to turn their arms against Christians, as Alexius’s subjects were, and persuaded him to go to this wicked prince in order to prevent any hostilities.

After the various crusading armies had united to act against the infidels, even if Duke Godfrey was not formally elected their principal leader, together with Adhemar, Bishop of Le Puy, who, as papal legate and lieutenant, held the first rank, it is at least certain that he was regarded as such [Note: [Col. 0375D] Will. Tyr. bk. IV, no. 22]. Indeed, no better choice could have been made [Note: [Col. 0375D] Ord. Vit. bk. IX, p. 757; Malm. ib.], since, as has been said, he united in his person every Christian, civil, and military virtue. He had learned to wage war in the French manner and had already won great glory in it. He also possessed extraordinary strength, of which several examples will be given below; and for a long time no commander had appeared who possessed either greater courage or greater valor. He therefore fully deserved to lead this innumerable multitude of Christians armed against [Col. 0376A] the enemies of the Christian name. Accordingly, he bore the entire weight of command. “Who, of the whole army,” says William of Tyre, one of his most faithful historians, “was almost its solitary pillar” (*qui totius exercitus quasi singularis erat columna*). Under such a leader the Christian army would have accomplished wonders if the crusaders had been more amenable to discipline and greater harmony had prevailed among the lords who commanded them.

The operations of the holy war began with the siege of Nicaea in Bithynia [Note: [Col. 0375D] Willelm. Tyr. bk. III, ch. 1; Tud. ib., bk. II, [Col. 0376D] p. 781; Raim. de Ag., p. 141]. Godfrey was the first, together with the Count of Flanders, to attack it, and he played a major part in the capture of the city, which surrendered by agreement [Note: [Col. 0376D] Will. Tyr. bk. IV, nos. 1, 5, 9, 13]. Baldwin, our duke’s brother, having separated from the main army with some troops and been recognized as prince of Edessa, [Col. 0376B] where he founded a powerful state, the other crusaders advanced into Syria and went to besiege Antioch [Note: [Col. 0376D] Raim. de Ag. p. 147]. It was during this expedition, which cost the Christians many men and much hardship, that Godfrey displayed as much endurance as courage: “there the Duke of Lorraine shone greatly” (*claruit ibi multum dux Lotharingiae*). As he approached the city, he distinguished himself by a heroic deed that deserved not to fall into oblivion. While accompanied by only twelve of his men, he encountered a band of one hundred and fifty Turks. Anyone else would surely have trembled, and perhaps succumbed, in such circumstances; but the fearless Godfrey, whose courage surpassed this kind of danger, charged the infidels with such vigor that he killed thirty of them on the spot, took thirty others prisoner, and put the rest to flight; they perished in the marshes and the neighboring river.

One is not surprised by so extraordinary an exploit when one reads in the historians of the time several selected examples of the extraordinary strength that nature had bestowed upon this hero [Note: [Col. 0376D] Tud. ibid. bk. III, p. 780; Malm. ib. p. 144; Will. Tyr. bk. V, no. 6]. Having encountered an armored Turk on the bridge of Antioch during the siege of the city, Godfrey, with a single blow of his scimitar, cut him through the middle of his body, so that the upper part fell onto the ground while the other was carried away by the horse ridden by the unfortunate man. On another occasion, with a single blow of his scimitar, he cleft another Turk in two from the head to the saddle of his horse; he even cut the horse and wounded it along the spine. [Note: [Col. 0376D] Will. Tyr. bk. III, no. 17.] Once, while hunting for recreation with other crusading lords, he found himself in a wood at some distance from them and encountered an enormous bear that was about to devour a poor man gathering dry wood. Godfrey, naturally compassionate, urged his horse [Col. 0377A] forward to rescue the unfortunate man. Seeing him approach, the bear abandoned its first prey and turned all its fury against him. On this occasion our hero needed all his strength and skill. Forced to abandon his wounded horse, he managed to seize the beast with his left hand while piercing it with his sword in the other. He himself received serious wounds that brought him to the brink of the grave. It is William of Tyre, that most truthful historian, who has preserved this memorable event for us.

William of Malmesbury also reports it, for his part, as having learned it from an eyewitness. But instead of a bear, he says that it was a lion.

[Note: [Col. 0377D] Will. Tyr. bk. V, nos. 4–6.] Meanwhile, discouragement was taking hold of the [Col. 0377B] crusaders, who had been held before Antioch for six months, and they were seriously considering raising the siege. Godfrey, whom the renown of his recent exploits had won new confidence, noticed this, restored their courage, and urged them to make renewed efforts. He himself performed prodigies of valor there, followed by a victory over the enemy and the capture of the city on 3 June 1098. [Note: [Col. 0377D] Will. Tyr., bk. VI, nos. 7, 10, 13, 14, 19–22.] A few days later he was of even greater assistance to them, when they themselves were besieged by an innumerable Turkish army and reduced to such extremity that even the Christian leaders were resolved to abandon everything and withdraw during the night. Godfrey, who knew no fear under God’s protection, had recourse to his eloquence; aided by Bishop Adhemar, he succeeded through his moving admonitions in holding them back. Only Stephen, Count of Chartres, abandoned the enterprise. The others recovered their courage and, revived by new confidence in God through the discovery of the holy lance, made such an effort that on the twenty-eighth of the same month, after suffering terribly for twenty-five days from lack of provisions, they put the enemies to flight, captured their camp, and took immense booty from them.

[Note: [Col. 0377D] Will. Tyr., bk. VIII, no. 5; Raym. de Agil., p. 177.] After everything had been restored to order at Antioch, the Christian army marched toward Jerusalem and arrived there on the seventh. But the army now numbered only twenty thousand fighting men and at most fifteen hundred horses, [Col. 0377D] whereas, it was said, the city contained forty thousand well-armed men supplied with every kind of ammunition [Note: [Col. 0377D] Tud. ibid. bk. V, p. 809; Alb. Aq. bk. VI, p. 274]. Godfrey undertook, with Tancred, to attack it at its strongest point, while the Count of Saint-Gilles, the Duke of Normandy, and the Count of Flanders would attack it from two other sides [Note: [Col. 0377D] Malm. ibid.]. Although several experienced, courageous, [Col. 0378A] and fearless commanders were among the crusading lords, none surpassed Duke Godfrey in the assaults [Note: [Col. 0378D] Tud. ib. p. 811; Will. Tyr. bk. VIII, nos. 18, 24]. He advanced against Jerusalem with such success that he was the first to enter the city, which was captured on the following 15 July [Note: [Col. 0378D] Alb. Aq. ibid., pp. 281–282]. Godfrey, who had abstained from slaughter after the victory, left his companions to indulge in the excess of their joy and, followed by three servants, went unarmed and barefoot to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. This act of devotion edified the entire army and reminded it of the duties of piety.

After the capture of Jerusalem, attention turned to restoring its kingdom. Four equally illustrious men—Godfrey, Raymond, Robert, Duke of Normandy, and Tancred—could claim the crown. Ten Christians, chosen from among the most distinguished figures of the clergy and army, were called upon to elect the King of Jerusalem. The electors proclaimed Godfrey’s name, and the army received the decision with the liveliest joy. The duke was led in triumph to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, where he swore to respect the laws of honor and good faith. His inauguration ceremony was limited to this formality, for he would never wear the insignia of royalty, saying that it was not fitting for a golden crown to be seen upon his head in the very place where Jesus Christ had worn one of thorns for the salvation of mankind. He likewise refused to take the title of king, contenting himself with that of duke and advocate of the Holy Sepulchre. All [Col. 0378C] the historians who have discussed this election, most of whom had personally known Godfrey, applaud it with the highest praise [Note: [Col. 0378D] Alb. Aquens. p. 284; Will. Tyr. bk. IX, nos. 1–2; Rob. ib. p. 76; Bald. Gest. Fr. bk. IV, p. 135; Malm. ib., pp. 142, 144; Ord. Vit. bk. IX, p. 757; Fulch. Gest. Fr. bk. I, p. 836; Spic. vol. XII, p. 293]. “It was just,” says one, “that on this occasion Godfrey should have precedence, since he stood above all the princes of the army both through his heroic exploits and counsels and through his faith and virtues.” He deserved it, adds another, because he was better suited to enhance the dignity of kingship than to receive distinction from it. For it was not honors that made him illustrious; on the contrary, it was he who heightened the splendor and brilliance of honors. Thus it came about that, for a duchy he had abandoned out of piety, Providence gave him a kingdom in return.

[Col. 0378D] This kingdom, it is true, was then of little account, yet it nevertheless continued for eighty-eight years. The cities dependent upon it were few and separated from one another by vast deserts. During the short time Godfrey reigned, he thought less about undertaking operations against the enemy than about preserving the Christians’ conquests and establishing good administration there. Nevertheless, an occasion arose that caused the new king to be greatly feared and respected far and wide. [Note: [Col. 0379D] Will. Tyr. ib., nos. 10–12; Alb. Aq. ib., p. 288; Dod. chr. an. 1100, p. 464; Sig. Chr. an. 1099; Tud. ib. pp. 813–814; Raim. de Ag., pp. 182–183.] The sultan of Egypt, angered by the capture of Jerusalem, assembled an innumerable army of Turks, Arabs, and Saracens and marched with the King of Babylon to retake it from the Christians. According to various authors, and even according to Godfrey’s own admission in his letter to Pope Paschal II, his forces amounted to four hundred thousand infantry and one hundred thousand cavalry. When the king was informed of this, he ordered public prayers to be offered to implore the Lord’s assistance and went with the other crusading princes to meet the enemy. They found him encamped in the plains of Ascalon; and although the Christian army numbered only five thousand cavalry and fifteen thousand infantry, it attacked that multitude of infidels, [Col. 0379B] killed one hundred thousand of them on the spot, put the rest to flight, and took immense booty from them. This was on 4 August, only a few days after Godfrey’s election; from that time onward, the emirs or princes of Ascalon, Caesarea, and Ptolemais sought his friendship and even became his tributaries.

After this triumphant expedition, most of the crusading lords returned to their own countries, and Godfrey devoted all his attention to the sound government of his new state. His piety led him to begin with spiritual matters. He established a patriarchate, founded and richly endowed two chapters of canons—one in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, the other in the Church of the Temple—and a monastery in the Valley of Jehoshaphat. [Col. 0379C] He placed in this monastery the monks he had brought with him, after taking them from the best-regulated religious houses. He then worked to provide his subjects with a fixed code to serve as their rule in civil affairs. This is what are called the Assizes, or Good Usages, of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, which will be discussed in greater detail below.

Not quite a full year had passed since this excellent prince began to reign when God, wishing to reward his labors and crown his virtue, called him to a kingdom that shall have no end. Godfrey, fearless in battle, was equally so as death approached. This fearlessness, however, arose only from a firm confidence in God’s mercies, quite different from that of those supposedly strong-minded men and vain philosophers. Since his illness lasted five weeks and people were already mourning the loss they were about to suffer, he took care himself to console the afflicted. When consulted about his successor, he replied simply that it should be the one who was worthy of it. Finally, feeling the illness worsen, he confessed with great contrition and tears; and after receiving the holy viaticum, he fell asleep in the Lord. His death, which occurred on 18 [Col. 0380A] July 1100 [Note: [Col. 0379D] An error has slipped into Father Maimbourg, where “eighth” is printed instead of “eighteenth.” Orderic Vital (bk. X, p. 777) makes an even more serious error by giving Godfrey a reign of three years], was mourned by all the Christians and even by many of the infidels among the Turks, Arabs, and Saracens. His body was buried with suitable pomp in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, which thereafter became the burial place of the kings who succeeded him.

Foucher, a cleric of Chartres, chaplain and historian of Baldwin, Godfrey’s brother and successor, composed an epitaph to adorn the tomb of this pious king. But it is so insipid that it does not deserve to be quoted. Another, common to both brothers, is found among the works of Philip, abbot of Bonne-Espérance in Hainaut. But here is a third, which seems to us original and better than the other two.

[Col. 0380B] EPITAPH

*Mirificum sidus, dux hic recubat Godefridus:*  
Here lies Duke Godfrey, a wondrous star;

*Aegypti terror, Arabum fuga, Persidis horror.*  
The terror of Egypt, the flight of the Arabs, the dread of Persia.

*Rex licet electus, rex noluit intitulari,*  
Although elected king, he did not wish to be called king,

*Nec diademari, sed sub Christo famulari:*  
nor to be crowned, but to serve beneath Christ;

*Cujus erat cura Sion reddere sua jura,*  
For it was his care to restore Zion’s rights,

*Catholiceque sequi sacra dogmata juris et aequi:*  
and to follow, in Catholic fashion, the sacred doctrines of law and justice;

*Totum schisma seu [teri] circa se jusque fovere*  
to cherish all schism—or [teri]—around him and likewise to foster [the text is uncertain];

*Sic et cum superis potuit diadema mereri:*  
thus, together with the heavenly beings, he was able to merit a crown;

*Militiae speculum, populi vigor, anchora cleri.*  
A mirror of knighthood, the strength of the people, the anchor of the clergy.

This epitaph, together with all that has been said of Godfrey in the history of his life, is sufficient to make him known as he was. He eminently united in his person all Christian, [Col. 0380C] civil, and military virtues, unmixed with any defect. We may add that he was taller than average, with a majestic appearance and bearing, and possessed extraordinary strength. He lived without entering into a marriage alliance and died without children. None of the writers of his time, or of those who followed closely after them, has told us the age at which this incomparable hero died. Father Maimbourg is the only modern writer known to us who fixed it at forty years [Note: [Col. 0380D] Mir. Cod. don. p. 230; Boll. ib. p. 141, note]. It is certain that he did not die old, since his mother was still living in 1098 and did not die until 1113. According to this calculation, he would have been born in 1060 or 1061. It is said that he came into the world with the figure of a sword imprinted on the outer part [Col. 0380D] of his right arm, from the shoulder to the wrist [Note: [Col. 0380D] Andr. Bib. Belg. p. 291].

William of Tyre, concluding his eulogy, assures us that he died in penitence and gives him the title of confessor of Jesus Christ. Molanus, Fisen, and the successors of Bollandus make some mention of him. Several monasteries, including the abbeys of Saint-Hubert, Afflighem, and Gorze, and the priory of Saint-Dagobert of Stenay, honor him as their [Col. 0381A] benefactor [Note: [Col. 0381D] Mart. am. Coll., vol. IV, p. 996; Anec. vol. I, pp. 261–262; Mit. Cod. don., p. 224; Spic. vol. X, p. [Col. 0382D] 605]. The churches of Liège and Verdun are equally entitled to regard him in that capacity, on account of the great benefits he conferred upon them. We shall conclude what we have to say about this Christian hero with the fine portrait that the Abbé de Choisy gives of him in a few words [Note: [Col. 0382D] Journ. des savants. 1712, p. 119]:

“Never did fabulous antiquity imagine a hero as perfect in every respect as historical truth represents Godfrey of Bouillon. His birth was illustrious; but it was his merit that raised him above others, and one may say of him that his greatness was the work of his virtue.”

Horstius and Picard, both editors of Saint Bernard, give our hero Mathilda, founder of the abbey of Saint-Satur, as his wife. [Col. 0381B] But it is certain, from the course of his history, that he never entered into a marriage alliance. These writers may therefore very well have confused him in this respect with Godfrey the Hunchback, his maternal uncle.

## § II.—His Writings

As for Godfrey’s writings, one should not expect them to be numerous or lengthy. Nevertheless, there are enough of them to earn him the title of author.

1. The most famous, as well as the most substantial, are the Assizes, or Good Usages, of the Kingdom of Jerusalem. One need only read the following inscription, which stands at their head, to have no doubt that they were originally his work. Here it is in the same terms in which it is written:

“Here begins the book of the Assizes and the Good Usages of the kingdom of Jerusalem, which were established and put into writing by Duke Godfrey of Bouillon, who was elected king and lord of the said kingdom, and with the counsel of the other kings, princes, and barons who came after Duke Godfrey, and by order of the Patriarch of Jerusalem.”

In the manuscript possessed by René Choppin, they are entitled: “On the Assizes, Usages, and Pleas of the High Court of the Kingdom of Jerusalem”; and in William of Tyre: “The Customary Law according to which the Kingdom of the East was governed.”

Godfrey, having conceived the plan of drawing up this Code, [Col. 0381D] or collection of statutes, laws, usages, and customs, which would serve as a rule both for his subjects and for all foreigners who might come into his states, whether to settle there or merely to reside temporarily, took all the measures of a skillful politician to accomplish it. After the famous victory won near Ascalon and the departure of most of the crusading princes, those who had remained in Syria and Palestine, together with almost all the Christian inhabitants, assembled at Jerusalem for the feast of Christmas in that same year, 1099. The king took advantage of this gathering to set forth his plan, which was applauded there; [Col. 0382A] and, on the advice of the patriarch, the princes, the barons, and the others who were more enlightened, capable persons were chosen and charged to make the necessary inquiries among the people of the country in order to learn what the usages and customs of their lands were. They were further instructed to put in writing everything they could learn or discover and to bring their memoranda to the king. Having received them, Godfrey assembled the patriarch, the princes, and the barons and communicated them to them. Then, in consultation with them, he selected what seemed most suitable to him and formed it into his Code. It was given the title Assizes because it was drawn up in the assembly, or sitting, of the great men of the kingdom. It was written in capital letters, the first of which was in gold and the table of contents in red.

It appears that there were two copies, each signed by the king, the patriarch, and the viscount, and sealed with their seals. One of these copies was for the use of the high or sovereign court, in which the king was the chief judge or president; the other was for the use of the court of the burgesses, presided over by the viscount. These two copies were kept in a chest at the Holy Sepulchre and were removed from it for consultation only with great precaution. This had to take place in the presence of the king, or of one of his high officials acting in his place; two of his liegemen or vassals; the patriarch, or, in his absence, the prior of the Holy Sepulchre; two canons; the viscount; [Col. 0382C] and two jurors of the court of the burgesses. The place where this code was kept sometimes caused it to be called the Letters of the Holy Sepulchre.

Godfrey begins it by invoking the help of the Holy Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and declaring the motives that led him to undertake it and the purpose he had in carrying it out. What he says at this point, which formed the first chapter of the original version and is the fifth chapter of the version we possess, is entirely worthy of his tender piety and reveals a prince attentive to the spiritual and temporal welfare of his subjects.

From there he proceeds to describe the qualities that the lord of Jerusalem must possess, whether he bears the title of king or any other title; here one recognizes the language of Duke Godfrey. He then discusses the barons and other lords of the kingdom who possess the right of administering justice. Among these qualities he does not forget to specify that they must know jurisprudence and be attentive to governing their lordships well. Then, turning to the judges charged with administering justice, he describes their essential obligations very well, though in few words, recommending above all that they fear God more than men and show greater regard for the salvation of their souls and their own honor than for their temporal interests. He proceeds [Col. 0383A] in the same way concerning the qualities and duties of those who plead the parties’ cases. Next come the instructions concerning the preliminary stages of procedure.

It would be very difficult to determine, from the printed exemplar of these Assizes, what originally belongs to Godfrey [Note: [Col. 0383D] It follows from the recent work of M. Beugnot on the Assizes of Jerusalem that the primitive titles have been lost and that we possess only a text later by a century than Godfrey of Bouillon, the work of two lay jurists. See *Assises de Jérusalem*, [Col. 0384D] by M. Count Arthur Beugnot. Paris, 1841, folio, Royal Printing Office. EDIT. PATROL.], because, in the form in which we have them, they were corrected, enlarged, and perhaps altered in certain respects by the kings who succeeded him. Thus, the passage of time produced different recensions. John of Ibelin, count of Jaffa and Ascalon, who died in 1266, made one around 1250. After more than a century, in 1369, there was another, made on the orders of John of Lusignan, prince of Antioch and bailiff of [Col. 0383B] Peter of Lusignan, king of Cyprus, his nephew. John of Lusignan employed sixteen persons chosen from the assembly of the kingdom’s Estates; their recension was deposited in the treasury of the church of Nicosia, in a chest sealed with four seals. It was apparently in this last recension that material concerning the kingdom of Cyprus was added—substantial additions filling the final twenty-two chapters, besides numerous passages on the same subject intercalated into the preceding chapters.

Nevertheless, one can clearly perceive, through all these foreign additions, that the original recension began with the fifth chapter of the version that has come down to [Col. 0383C] us. It is no less evident that this chapter and the following ones, through chapter nineteen, were treated with the greatest respect and are as Godfrey drafted them. The only alteration made in them was to polish somewhat the Romance language in which these Assizes were written from the first recension onward. Even so, this language retains more of its former roughness in these chapters than in the remainder of the work. As for the first four chapters, it is clear that they were added either by John of Ibelin or by the final redactors.

It does not appear that either the former or the latter touched the order Godfrey had established there. [Col. 0383D] It is also a just and sufficiently natural order. He divided his Code into chapters, the first of which concern procedure and everything related to it, beginning, as we have seen, by characterizing judges and other officers of justice. He devoted the subsequent chapters to appeals, *appeaux* or *appels*, the pledges of battle, and duels. This section is noteworthy because it displays all the ceremonies and other circumstances of single combats between champions. Another section was intended to establish [Col. 0384A] what concerned leases and guardianships; another to discuss feudal matters, chiefly the services owed by vassals in war, in court, and in marriage. This particular portion shows that the substance of these Assizes is drawn from our French jurisprudence and that they are one of the oldest and purest sources of our customary law. In a fifth section, Godfrey treated various matters not included in the preceding ones; and in a sixth, the rights of the king and the great officers of the crown.

The same order was retained in the recensions that followed the first; today they comprise three hundred and thirty-one chapters, including [Col. 0384B] the additions. These Assizes were long famous in the East, where they had the force of law. Baldwin, the first French emperor of Constantinople, in 1204, had them brought from Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0384D] *Journal des Savants*, 1690, p. 309] and ordered that they be observed in the lands under his authority. This was therefore before John of Ibelin made his recension. In France, the jurists of recent centuries and other writers—especially Du Cange, in his fine edition of *The Life and Establishments of Saint Louis*—made extensive use of them. It nevertheless appears that the ancient manuscripts of this Code are extremely rare, and that there is no copy other than the one in the Vatican Library, from which all the copies seen in France were made. There was [Col. 0384C] a copy among the manuscripts of John Selden in England [Note: [Col. 0384D] *Ang. Bib. ms.* par. I, no. 3457.], but it is impossible to determine whether it is ancient or recent. If it went back to the twelfth century and represented the work as it existed before John of Ibelin’s recension, it would be precious. In any event, it does not appear that we possess a manuscript of this kind, although the use made of this Code in the Byzantine Empire at the beginning of the thirteenth century ought to have multiplied its copies. The manuscripts of the last recension are no longer of great value, since that recension has been printed.

The edition is due to the care of M. Gaspar Thaumas de la Thaumassière, an advocate in Parliament, [Col. 0384D] who appended to it the lineages from overseas; the ancient Customs of Beauvaisis by Philippe de Beaumanoir; those of Riom and Orléans; together with learned notes and observations on the Assizes of Jerusalem and the Customs of Beauvaisis, and a Glossary explaining most of the old words. All these pieces together form a folio volume, printed at Bourges and sold in Paris in 1690.

Before this edition, the original text of the Assizes [Col. 0385A] had been translated into Italian, printed at Venice as early as 1535, and not put on sale there until 1543. In this translation, however, the original division of the work was changed. Two parts are distinguished: one entitled *l’Alta Corte*, the other *la Bassa Corte*. Moreover, its chapters do not correspond to those of the original text. Father Labbe, who incorporated a great deal of material from the Assizes of Jerusalem into his *Royal Epitome of the Chronological Alliance of Sacred and Profane History*, took care to mark there the other differences found between these same Assizes in Romance and their Italian translation.

2. There are several letters under the name of Duke Godfrey, some belonging specifically to him and others shared with other crusading princes and prelates. Although the latter were apparently not products of his pen, more than one reason nevertheless requires us to discuss them. On the one hand, they bear his name and therefore belong to him in some respect, since he had some part in them, perhaps the principal part, in his capacity as first general of the Christian army. On the other hand, they deserve to be known because they concern the adventures of the crusaders, and we could have no more suitable occasion than this to make them known.

The first of these letters in chronological order, and the one specific to our hero, was written from the vicinity of Constantinople in May 1096, when the emperor Alexius Comnenus was making [Col. 0385C] the author feel the effects of his hatred of the Latins [Note: [Col. 0385D] William of Tyre, book II, no. 10.]. It is a reply to the letter that Prince Bohemond had written to Godfrey before departing on the crusade, to acquaint him with the emperor’s duplicity and deceit and to warn him to beware of them. Godfrey, who had already learned too much of him through his own experience, confirms in his letter everything his friend had told him. It is well written in every respect and was preserved for us by William of Tyre, who included it in his *History of the Holy War*.

Fulk of Chartres [Note: [Col. 0385D] *Fulc. Ges. Fr.*, book I, no. 15, pp. 830–831.], another historian of the Crusade, transmitted to us another letter addressed to Pope Urban II. This one was written at Antioch on 11 September 1098, and its heading bears the names of Bohemond, named first because he had been recognized as prince of Antioch; Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles; Godfrey, duke of Lorraine; Robert, count of Normandy; Robert, count of Flanders; and Eustace, count of Boulogne. The first part of this letter deals chiefly with the manner in which the crusaders captured the city of Antioch, what they suffered there when, three days after becoming its masters, they found themselves besieged by an innumerable multitude of infidels; the discovery of the Holy Lance, which they regarded as a pledge of God’s protection [Col. 0386A] over them; and the notable victory they won over their enemies after twenty-five days, counting from 3 June, when they had taken the city, to the twenty-eighth of the same month, when the infidels raised the siege and were defeated.

The other part of the letter announces to the pope the sad news of the death of Adhemar, bishop of Le Puy, whom he had appointed his vicar for the Crusade, and urges him to come and replace him. To persuade him to do so, the crusading princes employ the most powerful arguments and conclude by praying God to bring this praiseworthy design to completion.

M. Baluze, apparently unaware that this letter is embedded in Fulk’s history, reprinted it in his *Miscellanea* [Note: [Col. 0386D] Volume I, pp. 415–419.]. [Col. 0386B] His edition, based on an ancient manuscript from the King’s Library, is not entirely without value. It contains an addition, or postscript, absent from Fulk’s copy, which gives us the letter’s precise date. The addition complains that the pope, who had been the preacher and principal author of the Crusade, nevertheless granted certain crusaders dispensation from undertaking the journey to which they had committed themselves—something highly damaging to the execution of the projected enterprise. It also informs the Roman pontiff that the emperor of Constantinople had not kept what he had promised the crusaders. Only one person speaks in this addition, *mihi quidem relatum est* (“I have indeed been informed”), although the letter is in everyone’s name and all speak collectively, except in the passage concerning Bohemond’s agreement with a Turk to surrender the city, where that prince relates the event alone and speaks in his own name.

For the rest, the differences between the two copies of this letter are not very significant. Fulk’s copy, when giving the day on which Antioch was taken, says the third day before the Nones of July, which would be the fifth of that month; this is an error, as is clear from the testimony of William of Tyre and other historians. “June” must be read instead of “July,” as it appears in Baluze’s copy. [Col. 0386D] In the latter, the prince of Antioch at the time of its capture is called Cassian, and Gratian in Fulk. Here the city’s fortress is always called *Castrum*, whereas in Baluze it is *Asylum*. Likewise, the emir or commander who surrendered it to the crusaders is called *Admiratus* in Fulk and *Admirabilis* in Baluze, which is an error. Finally, the original address of the letter is more complete in Fulk’s copy than in Baluze’s.

Dom Martène and Dom Durand gave us another letter from the crusading princes [Note: [Col. 0386D] *Anec.*, vol. I, pp. 272–273.]; but its heading bears only the names of Bohemond, Raymond [Col. 0387A] count of Saint-Gilles, Duke Godfrey, and Hugh the Great. It is circular, being addressed generally to all Catholics, to inform them of the Crusade’s progress. Although much shorter than the preceding letter, it nevertheless contains more facts, though only in general terms and without their circumstances. It goes back to the agreement that the crusading princes made with the Greek emperor in May 1096, and touches upon the engagement between the Christian army and that of the Turks at the end of the same month, in which the crusaders lost three thousand men and killed thirty thousand of the infidels. It then proceeds to the capture of Nicaea and that of Antioch, adding no other circumstances except that the latter city [Col. 0387B] had cost the Christians ten thousand men and the Turks seventy thousand. The letter ends by informing the faithful to whom it is addressed that the king of Persia was preparing to give battle to the crusaders on the following All Saints’ Day, and by imploring them to obtain the Lord’s aid for the crusaders through their prayers, fasts, and almsgiving. To move them more powerfully, it adds that this prince had declared that, if he won the victory, he would continue, together with the king of Babylon and several other pagan kings, to wage war against the Christians; whereas, if the Christians were victorious, he himself and all whom he could bring over would embrace the faith of Jesus Christ.

The editors had already published this letter from [Col. 0387C] a manuscript of Saint-Aubin of Angers, assigning it to the year 1097. When they found it in another manuscript from Saint-Thierry near Reims, they published it again [Note: [Col. 0387D] *Am. coll.*, vol. I, pp. 568–569], assigning it to the following year, to which it belongs. Indeed, although it is undated, there is every appearance that it was written and sent to Europe at the same time as the preceding letter, to Pope Urban II. This cannot even be doubted when one sees that it mentions the capture of Antioch, which took place on 3 June 1098, and speaks of no subsequent events except those expected to occur at the following All Saints’ Day.

In this latter copy, the letter is accompanied [Col. 0387D] by a note from Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, to the archbishop of Tours and his canons. Hugh says that, since this letter had been brought to him at Grenoble, he was sending them a copy so that they might communicate it to everyone who would gather for the feast—apparently the feast of Saint Martin, then celebrated with an extraordinary throng of people—and so that these people, in turn, might make it known in the various places where they lived. As this pious prelate expressly declares, his aim was thereby to increase the number of crusaders and obtain for them the spiritual assistance they requested.

Dodechin, in his continuation of the Chronicle [Col. 0388A] of Marianus Scotus [Note: [Col. 0387D] Dodechin, *Chronicle*, year 1100, pp. 463–465], preserved for us another letter from King Godfrey, who nevertheless assumes in it, out of humble modesty, only the title of advocate of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. This letter is joint with Daimbert, archbishop of Pisa and established patriarch of Jerusalem, and Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles. It is addressed to Pope Paschal II, Urban’s immediate successor, and was written shortly after the famous victory that the Christian army won over the infidels near Ascalon on 4 August 1099; it gives a somewhat detailed account of that victory. The pope, however, received it somewhat late, since he did not reply until 4 May of the following year—a delay doubtless caused by the measures he had to take [Col. 0388B] in order to send a legate to the crusaders. It appears that the authors intended the letter to be circular. This is suggested by the address, in which they join to the pope all the bishops and all the faithful of the Christian world. Besides the account of the day at Ascalon already mentioned, the letter contains a brief recapitulation of the crusading army’s conquests, from the capture of Nicaea until the departure of the duke of Normandy and the count of Flanders to return to their own states, which occurred shortly after the victory at Ascalon. It ends by imploring those to whom it is addressed to show every possible consideration to the crusaders returning to Europe—who were presumably its bearers—and to help them pay their [Col. 0388C] debts.

Dom Martène and Dom Durand, having found this letter in a manuscript of the abbey of Signy in the diocese of Reims, published it again [Note: [Col. 0388D] *Anec.*, ibid., pp. 281–283.]. The text in their edition is somewhat more complete than in Dodechin’s copy. One error has nevertheless slipped into it and deserves notice. After the opening lines, it reads *ut de ariete nummus*, whereas it should read *ut de ariete minimus*. The absence of dots over the *i*s in ancient manuscripts gave rise to this error.

Valère-André [Note: [Col. 0388D] *Andr. Bib. Belg.*, p. 291] testifies that there was still another letter of King Godfrey, one belonging specifically to him. In this bibliographer’s time [Col. 0388D] it was preserved by the regular canons of Tongeren. Godfrey addressed it to the pope—no indication is given of which pope, whether Urban or Paschal II—and treated there of his wars in Palestine. If Valère-André examined the matter closely, and if this letter really was specific to Godfrey, it must differ from the other two, one addressed to Urban and the other to Paschal, which have been discussed. In that case it would deserve to be sought out and presented to the public, which might perhaps find in it facts or details of facts not recorded in the others, though concerning the same subject.

Of all the speeches, remonstrances, or exhortations [Col. 0389A] that Godfrey delivered, whether to the crusaders in his capacity as general of their army or to his subjects in his capacity as sovereign, only the one he gave at the siege of Antioch has been preserved for us. At that time, when everything seemed desperate for the Christian army, it was on the point of raising the siege. We owe it to William of Tyre, who took care to include it in his fine *History of the Crusade* [Note: [Col. 0389A] William of Tyre, book V, no. 5]—an honor he did not grant to so many others reported by other historians. This speech is brief but impassioned, powerful in its arguments, and full of expressions of piety and greatness [Col. 0390A] of soul. It achieved its effect by inspiring the crusaders with renewed courage and leading them to make fresh efforts, which were followed by the defeat of the infidels and the capture of the city.

The style of this piece, and that of the letter specific to Godfrey, show that their author spoke Latin fairly purely and even with a certain elegance for his century. The same is evident from three or four charters of his that we possess, in favor of an equal number of monasteries—assuming, nevertheless, that he himself dictated them.

[Col. 0389]

## LETTERS OF KING GODFREY

### FIRST LETTER. THE PRINCE OF ANTIOCH TO GODFREY: BOHEMOND TO GODFREY  
*(Year 1096, May.)*  
**That he should beware the Greeks’ cunning.**

[WILLIAM OF TYRE, book II, no. 10.]

[Col. 0389B]

Know, best of living men, that you have a task before you against a most savage beast and a wicked man, whose purpose is always to deceive and to persecute the entire Latin nation by every means until death; and that your own judgment will someday confirm that I have formed a correct opinion of him. For I know the Greeks’ malice and their persistent, obstinate hatred of the Latin name. Therefore, if you please, withdraw from the city and go toward Adrianople or the region around Philippopolis, and order the troops entrusted to you by the Lord to rest and recover in fertile places, with provisions and leisure. For my part, God willing, I shall arrive hastily around the beginning of spring, to provide counsel and aid, in fraternal charity, as though to my lord, against the impious prince of the Greeks.

### SECOND LETTER. GODFREY TO BOHEMOND  
*(In the same year and month.)*  
**A reply to the preceding letter.**

[Col. 0389C]

I know, dearest brother—and I was informed of it long ago by report—that the Greeks, driven by an implacable hatred, have always striven with the utmost zeal to persecute our people through their cunning. If previously I lacked anything in my knowledge, I learn it more fully every day through experience. Nor do I doubt that you are moved against them by righteous zeal and hold a correct opinion of their wickedness. But, keeping the fear of God before my eyes and considering my purpose, I fear to turn the weapons owed to the infidels against a Christian people. Nevertheless, the army, which is with us and beloved of God, eagerly awaits your desirable arrival and the presence of the other princes devoted to God.

### THIRD LETTER. BOHEMOND, RAYMOND OF SAINT-GILLES, GODFREY, ROBERT COUNT OF NORMANDY, ROBERT COUNT OF FLANDERS, AND EUSTACE COUNT OF BOULOGNE TO POPE URBAN  
*(Year 1098, September.)*  
**On the siege and capture of Antioch.**

[Col. 0390B]

[See under Urban II, *Patrologia*, vol. CL, col. 551.]

### FOURTH LETTER. BOHEMOND, RAYMOND COUNT OF SAINT-GILLES, GODFREY THE DUKE, AND HUGH THE GREAT TO ALL THE FAITHFUL OF CHRIST  
*(Year 1098.)*  
**On the peace concluded with the emperor of Constantinople and on the victories won by the Christian army over the Turks.**

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, p. 568, from the manuscript of the monastery of Saint-Thierry.]

[Col. 0390C]

Bohemond, son of Robert, and Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles, together with Godfrey the duke and Hugh the Great, wish everlasting life to the great and the humble worshipers of the Catholic faith throughout the whole world.

So that it may be known to all how peace was made between us and the emperor, and what happened to us in the land of the Saracens after we arrived there, we are sending you this messenger of ours, who will carefully explain to you, in order, everything that took place among us. First, it must be said that in the middle of May the emperor gave us assurances and security under oath, also giving us hostages—namely, his nephew and his son-in-law—and adding that he would not again attempt to inflict an insult upon any pilgrim of the Holy Sepulchre. Afterwards he sent his own [text incomplete] throughout all his territory, directing him as far as Durazzo, and ordered that no one dare harm any pilgrim. If anyone violated this order, he was immediately to suffer the penalty of hanging deservedly. What more need be said? Let us now turn to those matters with which your hearts ought to be filled with the greatest joy. At the end of May we arranged to fight a battle with the Turks. Thanks be to God, we defeated them. Of them, without doubt, thirty thousand died in that battle; of our men, three thousand died in peace, and without any doubt rejoice in eternal life. There we all recovered an incalculable abundance of gold and silver, precious garments, and weapons. We also captured the great city of Nicaea by force of arms and acquired beyond it camps and cities extending over ten days’ journey. Afterwards we fought a great war at Antioch, which we defeated with great valor, so that sixty-nine thousand of them were killed [Col. 0391B], while ten thousand of our men died in peace.
