Who has ever seen such joy? For whether we live or whether we die, we belong to the Lord (Romans 14:8). Furthermore, know for certain that the king of Persia has announced that he will fight us on the feast of All Saints, asserting that, if he defeats us, he will never cease, together with the king of Babylon and several other pagan kings, to wage war against the Christians. But if he is defeated, he has promised that he and all whom he can bring over will become Christians. Therefore, we earnestly ask you to undertake there, continually and devoutly, fasts, almsgiving, and Masses. In particular, observe devoutly, with almsgiving and prayers, the third day before the feast, which is Friday, on which, with Christ triumphing, we shall engage in battle with strength.

I, the bishop of Grenoble [Note: [Col. 0391B] This was Saint Hugh, who, consecrated by Pope Gregory VII in 1081, received Saint Bruno and his companions a few years later and entrusted to them the solitude of Chartreuse, so that they might establish there a new way of life. At that time Radulf II presided over the Church of Tours.], am sending these letters, which were brought to me at Grenoble, to you, the archbishop and canons of the holy Church of Tours, so that through you they may become known to all who will gather for the feast, and so that through them others in the various regions of the world to which they will return may assist their just petitions with prayers and almsgiving, while still others hasten to their aid with arms.

### FIFTH LETTER. DAIMBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF PISA, GODFREY OF BOUILLON, AND RAYMOND, COUNT OF SAINT-GILLES, TO POPE PASCHAL  
*(Year 1100.)*  
**On the victories won by the Christian army in the Holy Land.**

[Col. 0392B]

[See under Paschal, at the year 1118.]

[Col. 0391]

## KING GODFREY’S SPEECH TO THE CHRISTIAN SOLDIERS

**That they should remember their former valor and persist in the siege of Antioch.**

[WILLIAM OF TYRE, book V, no. 5.]

[Col. 0391C]

If, as we have been informed, because our sins demanded it and the Lord permitted it, the enemies of the Christian name and faith have triumphed over our lords and brothers, I see nothing else remaining, illustrious men, than either to die with them or to avenge the great injury inflicted upon the Lord Jesus Christ. Believe me: neither life nor safety is dearer to me than death or any kind of affliction, if the blood of so many princes has been shed upon the earth with impunity, or if the slaughter of so great a people devoted to God has not found a fitting vengeance. It seems to me, therefore, that [Col. 0392C] the enemy, somewhat elated by his present victory, will conduct himself imprudently; and, trusting in his own strength, will not fear to return to the city through us and carry off booty and spoils. Therefore, if this seems right to you, let us remain prepared here; and, supporting a just cause, let us place our firm hope of obtaining victory in him whom we believe we serve as soldiers. If the enemy attempts to return through us, let us receive him at the edge of the sword, as enemies deserve, mindful of the injury inflicted and not degenerate from the virtues of our fathers.

[Col. 0391]

## DIPLOMAS OF KING GODFREY

### Decree of Duke Godfrey for the cell of Satanacum  
[Note: [Col. 0391D] Stenai.]

He restored to the monks of Gorze the church of Saint Dagobert the Martyr, situated at Satanacum and seized by Count Arnulf. *(Year 1093.)*

[MARTÈNE, *Anecdota*, vol. I, p. 162.]

[Col. 0391D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, of the Father [Col. 0392D], and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Godfrey, by the favor of divine grace, duke and margrave.

We ought to know and consider that, since we are occupied with the business of secular warfare and are wholly unable to devote ourselves to divine matters as we ought, we may at least, by offering our counsel [Col. 0393A] and aid to God and to the saints, who are served more particularly in monasteries devoted to God, thereby become, with God himself granting it, participants in their beneficence and likewise in their reward. Therefore, we wish it to be known to the faithful sons of the holy universal Church, both present and future, that Duke Godfrey, my grandfather, together with his wife Beatrice, established monks from the monastery of Saint-Gorgon at Satanacum, a village belonging to him, in the church of Saint Dagobert the Martyr, for the salvation of their souls; and among other things, as an addition to their food and clothing, legally granted them the church of the village of Mosacum, which was undisputedly his property. The monks themselves possessed it peacefully and without disturbance throughout the life of my grandfather and of his son, my uncle. But after both had died and their lordship had come into our hands by succession [Col. 0393B], and almost the entire region previously subject to them had conspired out of hatred for us and gratuitous hostility, those who were then our enemies, because of the hatred they had taken up against us, also rose against the monks and, with the utmost injustice and violence, took that church from their hands and granted it as a benefice to another. For many years, until they returned to favor with us, they thus inflicted upon God and his holy servants an injustice they had begun.

When a dispute over this matter arose at Satanacum in our presence, and those who had carried out the violence were also present, the assembly of monks began to appeal to us concerning it. They declared that they had already lodged a complaint about it before the synod of Trier; that by synodal judgment [Col. 0393C] the church had been adjudged to their right; that by pontifical authority they had been ordered to possess it in peace and quiet; and, at the same time, they emphatically affirmed that witnesses who had attended my grandfather’s aforesaid donation still survived. We therefore caused those witnesses to be summoned from every direction and gathered before us, and, when they testified, we found in every respect that what the monks asserted was true. After hearing and carefully considering all these matters, it seemed appropriate to us to adjure Count Arnulf, who had been the principal of those who had seized the church, under the obligation of oath and good faith, asking whether he knew all this to be true or whether he would or could truthfully challenge it. Without requiring the adjuration, he confessed that these events had taken place as we have said, and that he had been present, heard, [Col. 0393D] and seen them, and, when my grandfather made this donation, [Col. 0394A] had approved it. Having received this confession, we next admonished him to do toward the saint and toward us what he ought in law to do thereafter: to make amends before God and the saints for this seizure, to abstain perpetually from that church and everything subject to it. Since he could not lawfully resist, he restored the church to us in full, for the work of God and of Saint Dagobert and the monks serving him, without any future claim whatsoever; he renounced it formally, and when we restored the gift of that church to Saint Dagobert upon the altar, he himself was voluntarily present and approved it. Therefore, so that the memory of these events may remain firm and unshaken through the succeeding ages, we ordered this memorial record to be made and decreed that it be confirmed by the impression of our seal and [Col. 0394B] by the attachment of suitable witnesses.

The sign of Godfrey, duke and margrave by the grace of God. The sign of Amalric. The sign of Simon, his brother. The sign of Walter. The sign of Atto. The sign of Dudo. The sign of Gerard. The sign of Hembard. The sign of Helbert. The sign of Arnulf. The sign of Aleran. The sign of Simon. The sign of Ursion; the sign of Heribert; the sign of Hagner; the sign of Oilard; the sign of Guigfrid; the sign of Francon; the sign of Hugh; the sign of Herman.

Enacted at Bouillon in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1093, indiction 1, in the thirty-seventh year of the reign of Henry IV, the tenth of his empire, while Lord Fulbert, archbishop of Trier, was presiding, in the tenth year of his pontificate [Note: [Col. 0393D] Miraeus published this charter in his *Notice of the Churches of Belgium*, but in a very mutilated form and with several errors. Here we give it complete and accurate from the Gorze cartulary.].

### II. Godfrey of Bouillon, duke of Lorraine and later king of Jerusalem, enriches more generously the small monastery, or priory, of Saint Peter in the district of Bouillon, founded by Godfrey the Bearded, duke of Lorraine.  
*(Year 1094.)*

[MIRAEUS, *Opera diplomatica*, I, 76.]

[Col. 0394C]

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

I, GODEFROY, legitimate successor and heir of Duke Godefroy the Bearded, [Note: Godefroy, surnamed the Bearded, was appointed successor to his father Gozelo, while the latter was still alive, in the duchy of Moselle, according to Hermannus Contractus. He was later deprived of that duchy by King Henry IV because of rebellion, withdrew to Italy, and married Beatrice, widow of Boniface, margrave of Italy, and daughter of Frederick II, duke of Moselle. Thereafter he obtained the duchy of Lower Lorraine and, dying in 1070, was buried at Verdun. He left children: Godefroy, surnamed the Hunchback, or the Struma, or the Just— as he is called by William of Tyre, book IX, chapter 5—and Ida, mother of Godefroy of Bouillon.] and of his son, the most powerful and most just Duke Godefroy, [Note: Godefroy, surnamed the Hunchback, or the Struma, or the Just, as he is called above in this charter, succeeded his father in the duchy of Lower Lorraine and at the same time held the margraviate of Antwerp. His wife was Matilda, the most powerful marchioness of Italy, daughter of the Beatrice mentioned shortly before; she bequeathed extensive possessions to the Roman Church in her testament and died in 1115. Godefroy the Hunchback was stabbed by an assassin at Antwerp in 1076 and buried at Verdun beside his father. Dying childless, the Hunchback appointed his nephew through his sister Ida, Godefroy of Bouillon, heir to all his patrimony—including Bouillon, according to Gomicurtus. William of Tyre, book IX, chapter 5, regarded Bouillon as having long belonged on his mother’s side to his ancestors; hence Godefroy is also called “of Bouillon.” Gom[icurtus], from Sigebert.] my maternal uncle, representing him, and also reflecting upon the benefits that divine grace had bestowed upon me, resolved to return some of these gifts of his for the increase of His service.

And since my aforesaid grandfather Godefroy had established religious brothers from the monastery of Saint Hubert the Bishop, with the permission of the venerable Abbot Theoderic, at the church of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, situated before the castle of Bouillon, for the remedy of his soul, [Col. 0394D] and had caused this establishment, with the revenues named therein, to be confirmed by the authority and privilege of Pope Alexander, [Col. 0395A] it also seemed just to me, as the result of divine inspiration, that I who shared in his honor should also share in his devotion.

When I had communicated this intention of mine to my mother Ida, daughter of the aforesaid duke, and to my brothers Baldwin and Eustace, then, with their counsel and willing consent, we assigned and donated our church of Baseio, held by our own hereditary right, to be given perpetually to Saint Peter and Saint Hubert as an increase of the aforesaid alms of my grandfather Godefroy.

To make this gift valid and firm, I brought the same mother and my brothers to Bouillon, [Col. 0395B] and in the presence of my nobles we together placed upon the altar of Saint Peter, without any claim or contradiction, the investiture of the aforesaid church at Baseio. I myself, who was the lawful advocate of the Church—or monastery of Saint Hubert—accepted it there, in the presence of Abbot Theoderic, to defend it by law.

[Note: Baseio. Godefroy of Bouillon was born and raised at Baisu near Genappe, as is recorded in the Nivelles manuscript genealogy of the dukes of Brabant; in the great chronicle of Belgium it is said to be near Villers in French Brabant, on the Thyle.]

Publicly enacted at Bouillon in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1094, indiction II.

## III. Godefroy of Bouillon, Duke of Lorraine, and his brother Baldwin—who later became kings of Jerusalem in succession—arrange for a further endowment of the church of Saint Dagobert, situated in the Lorraine town of Sathanacum. (Year 1096.)

[MIRAEUS, as above, p. 365.]

[Col. 0395C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, GODEFROY, by the grace and mercy of God duke and margrave.

Since we are detained sufficiently and more than sufficiently by secular affairs and cannot attend to divine matters as necessary, and since, while pursuing temporal profits, we do not fear neglecting the condition of our souls—which is something greatly fearful to us—it is worthwhile for us at least to provide for the needs of those who regularly serve God, so that, while they pray for us, we may be able to share in some measure in their reward with God.

Therefore I and my brother Baldwin make known to all the sons and faithful of Holy [Col. 0395D] Church, present and future, that the church at Sathanacum—formerly a village, now a castle—built in honor of Saint Dagobert the martyr, had in ancient times been donated, with all its appurtenances, by our grandfather Duke Godefroy the Bearded and his wife Beatrice [Col. 0396A] [Note: Beatrice, daughter of Frederick II, duke of Lorraine and Moselle, first married Boniface, margrave of Tuscany, and afterward Godefroy the Great, or the Bearded, duke of both Lorraines. By Boniface she had Matilda, and by Godefroy the Great she had Godefroy the Hunchback, duke of Lower Lorraine, and Ida, wife of Eustace II, count of Boulogne and mother of Godefroy of Bouillon. Matilda, a woman of manly spirit, donated various towns of Tuscany and Liguria to the Holy Roman Church in 1077 and 1102; these are today called the patrimony of Saint Peter. She died in 1115. She was married first to the above-mentioned Godefroy the Hunchback and afterward, in 1089, to Welf, son of Welf IV, duke of Bavaria and grandson of Azzo, margrave of Ferrara; yet she always remained untouched, as Berthold, Donizo, Leo of Ostia, and the author of the Chronicle of the Welfs, vol. II of Canisius, relate.] to Saint Gorgonius of Gorze and to the venerable Henry, abbot of that place, and his monks. It had also been commended throughout his life by his son Godefroy, likewise duke and our maternal uncle. But afterward, when we succeeded them in their inheritance and many serious and burdensome wars were stirred up against us, on the one hand it was plundered and devastated throughout its circuit by our enemies, on account of their hatred toward us; on the other, while we were occupied by such storms, it was not provided for and defended as was fitting and necessary.

Therefore, since the monks who had been assigned there were suffering considerable privations, and certain respectable men had moreover brought a complaint concerning this before our hearing, we resolved to summon to us Lord Warner, abbot of Gorze and successor of the aforesaid Henry, together with his brethren. After conferring counsel among ourselves, it seemed just and useful that, through a donation from us and from him, the substance of those brothers living at Sathanacum should be multiplied and increased, so that, while they were less occupied with the concerns of temporal things, they might be encouraged to devote themselves more effectively to the studies of divine service.

Accordingly, the aforesaid abbot, with the counsel of his brothers, for the supplementation of their substance, transferred whatever the Church of Gorze possessed at Gaudiacum, a village situated on the Moselle River, and confirmed it by a valid donation for perpetual possession: namely, the church, tithes, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, lands, and all its appurtenances; reserving, however, the passage by boat there and back, which runs between the monastery and the city.

But whatever our aforesaid grandfather Godefroy the Bearded and his wife Beatrice had originally contributed to that church and to the support and benefit of the monks serving God there, and whatever afterward had either been taken away by the presumption of enemies or, because of our occupation and need of assistance, had been violently retained by our own men against them, we, namely I, Duke Godefroy, and my brother Baldwin, restored wholly and unconditionally, with hands extended together. And so that thereafter, perpetually and peacefully, the brothers serving at the aforesaid place might hold it without anyone’s [Col. 0396D] disturbance, we caused the gift to be placed upon the altar of Saint Gorgonius through the hands of free guarantors and confirmed by lawful investiture: namely, the church of Saint Dagobert, with the house commonly called the cell and with all its ancient appurtenances—tithes, meadows, woods, cultivated and uncultivated lands, orchards, mills, waters, fisheries, things acquired and to be acquired, and all appurtenances that can in any way be named—together with the church of Mosacum and all its revenues, and everything that my aforesaid grandfather added to it, with the donations previously mentioned.

Moreover, lest anyone ever dare to oppose this our ordinance and lawful investiture, we prohibit and forbid it by our authority and ban, and whoever should presume to do anything of the kind, we summon before the divine judgment.

[Col. 0398A] So that these our enactments might also remain valid and unshaken, we ordered this memorial record to be made and have marked it with the impression of our seal and the affixing of suitable witnesses.

The sign of Godefroy, duke, who caused this charter to be written.

The sign of Baldwin, his brother; the sign of Walter, advocate; the sign of Henry, count; the signs of Amalric, Richer, Otto, Ludo, Heribert, Everard, Albric, Leudo, Sihard, Sozfrid his brother, Helgaud, Francon, and Hugh.

Enacted at Sathanacum in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1096, indiction IV.

[Col. 0397]

# THE ASSISES OF JERUSALEM

[Note: We give only some rubrics and excerpts, together with the editor’s preface. See, if desired, *Assises et bons usages du royaume de Jérusalem*, taken from a manuscript of the Vatican Library, with the notes and observations of Gaspard Thaumas de la Thaumassière, esquire, lord of Puy-Ferrand, advocate in parliament—Bourges, 1690—or the excellent edition of this Collection most recently published by the illustrious Count Arthur Beugnot, Paris, 1841.]

## Preface to the Bourges Edition of 1690

[Col. 0397B]

The Assises of Jerusalem are the laws, statutes, usages, and customs granted to the kingdom of Jerusalem by Godefroy, duke of Bouillon, in the year 1099, with the advice of the patriarch and his barons, after he had been elected king. They are called *Assises* because they were made at the *assise*, or assembly, of the great men of the kingdom, just as the celebrated ordinance of Godefroy, count of Brittany, and his barons, of the year 1185, concerning noble partition, is called the *Assise of Count Godefroy*. Likewise in Houeden: *Assisae Henrici regis factae apud Clarendonum*—“the assizes of King Henry made at Clarendon”—in the *Regiam Majestatem*, book III, chapter 27, §2: “By virtue of the constitution of the kingdom, which is called an assise.” The assise of King Baldwin, chapter 117; the assise of King Amalric, chapter 273; the assise of King Amalric and his son King Baldwin, assise, chapter 288; the assise of King Hugh, chapter 309. Spelman, folio 53, under the word *ASSISIA*.

These Assises were written at the command of Godefroy of Bouillon and sealed with his seal, those of the patriarch, and that of the viscount of Jerusalem. They were called the “Letters of the Sepulchre” because they were kept in a chest in the Church of the Sepulchre, from which they were taken, in the presence of the king or of his representative, the patriarch—or, in his absence, the prior of the Sepulchre, two canons, and the viscount—whenever there was a dispute concerning any article of these customs.

But since they had been corrected and enlarged on various occasions by Godefroy and his successors, the kings of Jerusalem, they were written down and arranged by John of Ibelin, count of Jaffa and Ascalon, lord of Beirut and Ramla, around the year 1250. He was the son of Balian of Ibelin and Eschiva of Montbéliard, and died in 1266.

They were reviewed a second time on 3 November 1369, after the death of Peter of Lusignan, king of Cyprus, by order of John of Lusignan, prince of Antioch and regent for Peter of Lusignan, king of Cyprus, his nephew. This was done by sixteen men named and chosen at the assembly of the estates of the kingdom. They were afterward placed in the treasury of the Church of Nicosia, in a chest sealed with four seals.

Through Monsieur d’Herouval I recovered [Col. 0398C] a copy in the library of the late Monsieur Brodeau, transcribed from the manuscript of the Vatican Library, and another in that of Monsieur Colbert. The Assises were translated into Italian and printed at Venice in 1543.

Rhamnusius says that Baldwin I, emperor of Constantinople, had them brought from Jerusalem so that they might be observed in the Empire and regulate the services of fiefs and vassals.

It is certain that they were drawn from the customs and usages of France, as chapters 294 and 295 demonstrate, together with William of Tyre, book XVI, chapter 2, and book XIX, chapter 2.

[Col. 0399A]

The Italian Assises are divided into two parts. The first is entitled *The High Court: The Assises and Good Usages of the Kingdom of Jerusalem*.

The second part is *The Low Court: The Assises and Good Usage of the Kingdom of Jerusalem*. The table of chapters begins with these words:

“These are the rubrics of the book of the Assises of the High Court of the Kingdom of Jerusalem in pleading, that is, in the form of litigation, composed by the good John of Ibelin, count of Jaffa and Ascalon and lord of Ramla.”

Before chapter 163—which corresponds to chapter 147 of our Assises, “What is the assise when someone alienates all or part of his fief otherwise than by the assise”—there is the title “Of fiefs.” At the end of the first part it says:

“The Assises of the High Court of the Kingdom of Jerusalem and Cyprus, translated from French into the Italian language by order of the Most Serene Ducal Lordship of Venice, by me, Florio Bustron, thus commanded by the most illustrious Lords Rectors of this kingdom of Cyprus, as notary of the distinguished deputies for the said translation.”

At the end it is stated that the printing was completed in March 1535.

Father Labbe, the Jesuit, in his *Royal Abridgment of the Chronological Alliance of Sacred and Profane History*, printed at Paris in 1651, p. 560, noted the difference between the French Assises and the Italian version. In the same work he extracted the thirty genealogical tables that he gives from pages 351 to 420, from the genealogy of Outremer, which forms part of these Assises. [Col. 0399C] He also printed the genealogy of Outremer from pages 422 to 461, the beginning of these Assises from chapter 1 through chapter 8, and the table of chapters from chapter 9 through chapter 281; he ended the first book at chapter 281.

He began the second book at chapter 282, which he made the first chapter of the second part, and ended it at the fiftieth chapter. He began the second book of these Assises with chapter 282, “How the lord and governor of the land and people should be,” and continued through chapter 308, “How Sir Hugh of Lusignan demanded the kingdom of Cyprus from Sir Guy of Ibelin,” and so forth. He omitted the four following chapters and then gave the subsequent chapters concerning the services of the kingdom of Jerusalem [Col. 0399D] through chapter 330, “Of the aids that the churches and burgesses owe,” and so ended the second book of the Assises. But because I did not find this division in the manuscripts communicated to me, I have confined myself to numbering and arranging the chapters in the order in which I found them, without changing anything. Father Labbe also printed the Book of the Lineages of Outremer, consisting of thirty chapters, which are at the end of the Assises in the manuscript I followed.

This is the order followed by the author of these Assises.

The first eighty-one chapters concern procedure.

[Col. 0400A] Chapters 82 and following, through 112, treat of appeals, pledges of battle, and duels.

Chapters 113 and following, through 137, treat of assises on different matters.

Chapters 138 and following, through chapter 175, concern fiefs.

Chapters 176 through 181 concern leases and guardianships.

In chapters 182 and following, through 274, he returns to feudal matters, especially the services owed by vassals in war, in court, and in marriage.

Chapter 275 and following, through 281, contain assises on different matters.

Chapter 282 and following, through 292, speak [Col. 0400B] of the rights of the king and of the great officers of the crown.

Chapters 293 and following, through 308, concern the disputes over the bailiwick and succession of the kingdom between Hugh of Lusignan, the count of Brienne, and Marie of Beaumont.

Chapters 309 and following, through 313, contain new ordinances and assises.

Chapters 314 and following, through chapter 330, the last, concern the services owed to the king by bishops, the great men of the kingdom, nobles, and communities.

Monsieur Du Cange mentions these Assises in his preface to the *Establishments of Saint Louis*. He says that he read the manuscript in one of the volumes [Col. 0400C] of the papers of Monsieur de Peiresc, copied from the Vatican manuscript, from which most of the copies in the libraries of Paris were made. In the same place he says that he does not despair that, in time, some sufficiently inquisitive person may be found to give these Assises and other ancient customs to the public and undertake a work so glorious and useful to the public and to those who practice French jurisprudence. He quotes several passages from them in his learned *Glossary* and in his notes on the *Establishments of Saint Louis*. Chopin cited them in his *Custom of Anjou*, as did Monsieur Julien Brodeau concerning the title “Lineal Retraction” in the *Custom of Paris*, and in other places in his works.

[Col. 0400D]

I wish that these learned and scholarly authors had taken the trouble to have them printed with their notes and observations. But since their extensive occupations did not allow them to do so, I thought I would please the curious and all who love the origins of our French jurisprudence by having them printed with my notes and observations. This may perhaps encourage someone else to give to the public the other ancient French doctors and practitioners who have not yet been printed and who deserve to be.

# THE ASSISES OF JERUSALEM

[Col. 0401]

## I. RUBRICS

[Col. 0401A]

1. Here begin the rubrics of the book of the Assises and good usages of the kingdom of Jerusalem, which were established and put into writing by Duke Godefroy of Bouillon, who was elected king and lord of that kingdom, and by the counsel of the other kings, princes, and barons who came after Duke Godefroy, and by order of the patriarch of Jerusalem.

2. Here it is stated how Duke Godefroy established two secular courts: one is the High Court, of which he was governor and judge; the other is the court of the burgesses, which is called the court of the viscount.

3. Here it is stated how the assises and usages of the aforesaid kingdom of Jerusalem were amended several times by Duke Godefroy and by the other kings and lords who came after him.

[Col. 0401B]

4. Here it is stated how the Syrian people came before the king of the kingdom of Jerusalem and begged and requested him to be governed according to the usage of the Syrians.

5. Here it is stated how the lord of the kingdom of Jerusalem, and the barons who have coinage, court, and justice, ought to know the assises and usages of the aforesaid kingdom.

6. Here it is stated what sort of chief lord the kingdom of Jerusalem ought to have, whether king or another, and concerning all the barons and lords of the aforesaid kingdom who have court, coinage, and justice.

7. Here it is stated how pleading ought to be conducted.

8. Here it is explained how, concerning what matters, and why one ought to request the advice of the court.

9. When someone requests the advice of the court, what he ought to ask his counsel.

[Col. 0401C]

10. How one ought to request advice, so that the person from whom advice is requested cannot advise his adversary concerning that dispute.

11. Why one may request the advice of the court by judgment.

12. Why one may request the advice of the court without judgment.

13. From whom a man may not request the advice of the court if his adversary objects.

14. To what persons the lord may not and ought not to give the advice of the court.

15. To whom the lord ought to give the advice of the court when it is requested.

16. What difference there is between the lord holding a man to his counsel and holding him to keep his word.

[Col. 0401D]

17. How the lord ought to retain a man for his counsel and to keep his word.

18. How and why the lord ought to retain a man to keep his word.

19. How one ought to plead in the High Court [Col. 0402A] of the kingdom of Jerusalem or in that of Cyprus.

20. Why a man may plead in the High Court.

21. The matters concerning which one ought to plead in the High Court.

22. Why one may plead against one’s lord and against one’s man.

23. What a good pleader ought to be, what he must do, and what he must avoid in the plea.

24. What those who undertake to plead in the High Court of the kingdom of Jerusalem and that of Cyprus ought to know.

25. What someone who is giving counsel to another must do when he wishes to state the force of his argument and sit for judgment.

26. If someone wishes to bring a claim against a man or woman who is present in court, how he ought to do so.

[Col. 0402B]

27. When the man or woman against whom a claim has been made is not in court, how one ought to claim against that person.

28. What the right-minded and loyal person must do when something is demanded of him against his will, or when a claim is made against him.

29. How many days one has to answer a new claim when the assise does not occupy the whole day.

30. How many principal delays there are in a plea, and what they are in the kingdoms of Jerusalem and Cyprus.

31. How one ought to delay a plea by the first principal delay of a plea.

32. How one ought to delay a plea by the second principal delay of a plea.

33. How one ought to delay by the third delay.

[Col. 0402C]

34. How one may delay a plea for a long time.

35. How one ought to defend oneself when the dispute concerns an inheritance situated within a town.

36. Here it is stated what tenure is to be made of an inheritance of *mermiau*.

37. No tenure of an inheritance outside the spoken jurisdiction harms him.

38. How one ought to request a day when one wishes to delay a plea.

39. How the claimant ought to guard against the person delaying having several judgments and then another day.

40. If someone wishes to delay a plea, how he ought to request a day concerning the claim, for which the assise occupies the whole day.

41. How the claimant ought to guard against the person delaying prolonging his plea by requesting a day.

[Col. 0402D]

42. How the claimant ought to shorten the plea.

43. What someone who wishes to bring his plea to an early conclusion must do.

44. If someone wishes to bring the plea to an end, how he ought to plead when the person delaying delays by the first principal delay of the plea.

[Col. 0403A]

45. How one ought to bring a plea to an end when the person delaying delays by the second principal delay of the plea.

46. If the person delaying delays by the third principal delay of the plea, how one ought to bring it to an end.

47. How one must request a day for all claims made against him in court, except for those concerning which he has been reached and to which he does not answer without requesting a day.

48. When one person claims against another and requests a day, and receives it from the court, why both parties must put the claim in writing exactly as it was made.

49. When the parties are summoned by the court, how and why each must ask the lord where he commands him to keep his day.

50. When the parties are summoned by the court and properly keep their day as they ought, how the claimant must renew his claim.

51. When one keeps the day received from the court and the claimant claims as he had claimed previously, how the person delaying must answer.

52. When one of those summoned by the court keeps his day as he ought and the other does not keep it or does not countermand it as he ought, what the person who keeps it must say and do.

53. When someone comes to keep his day at the place where he was summoned by the court and finds neither the lord nor anyone whom the lord has appointed in his place, what he must say and do.

54. When people are summoned by the court and keep their days as they ought, but do not find a man before whom the defendant is bound to answer, and the claimant claims on another day, exactly as he had claimed previously, what the claimant must answer.

55. When people are summoned by the court and keep their day as they ought, but the lord or the person acting in his place does not wish to hear the plea that day, what they must say and what must be answered to them.

56. If someone is summoned by the court and wishes to countermand his day, how he must countermand it, and through whom and by what men.

57. If someone is summoned by the court and comes at the proper hour and time to keep his day, but encounters such an impediment on the road [Col. 0403D] that he cannot keep it, how and through whom he may countermand it.

58. Why a man against whom a claim is made in court, where he is present, must not leave the court without answering the claim or requesting a day.

59. Why the person accused of some wrongdoing in court, or from whom something is demanded there, must answer or deny it if he is offered the opportunity to prove it.

60. How and why, when the person accused of wrongdoing in court denies it and is not offered the opportunity to prove it before the court disperses, the person who accused him cannot afterward demand anything from him.

61. Here it is stated that every wise man ought to avoid litigation as much as he can, and above all with his lord more than with anyone else.

[Col. 0404A]

62. What one must say and do when one wishes to recover seisin of something of which one has been dispossessed.

63. In what case force brings back all seisin, and in what case it does not bring it all back.

64. When the pleader must take the proof upon himself and when he must give it to his adversary, and how one must prove a negative.

65. How one must defend himself against taking the proof upon himself when his adversary wishes him to prove as his own what he has and holds as his own.

66. How, by what means, and on whose behalf one must prove in the High Court.

67. How one must be furnished with a privilege or a record of the court.

[Col. 0404B]

68. If someone wishes to prove by guarantors, what kind and which guarantors they must be.

69. What persons cannot give guarantee in the High Court of the kingdoms of Jerusalem and Cyprus.

70. What the person against whom one wishes to prove by guarantee must do.

71. When someone wishes to prove something by a record of the court, what the person against whom one wishes to prove must say and do.

72. How one must object to guarantors, how to reject them, and how to turn the matter.

73. When a knight gives guarantee against a man who is not a knight, how the latter may reject him and how he may turn the matter.

74. What period one has for bringing one’s guarantors, according to the place where one summoned them.

75. When one has brought one’s guarantors to court, what one must say and do, and what the guarantors must say and do when giving the guarantee.

76. Why a living guarantor may give guarantee for the dead, and how he must give it.

77. When someone acknowledges before witnesses that he owes a debt to some person, or that he is that person’s pledge, or that he has other obligations, and the person to whom he says he is bound by one of these things is present, whether that acknowledgment avails him.

78. When someone acknowledges before witnesses that he owes a debt to a person, or that he is that person’s pledge, or that he has other obligations, and the person to whom he says he is bound by one of these things is not present, whether that acknowledgment avails him.

If a man is summoned for the service he owes the lord, and wishes to surrender his fief to the lord, or deliver it up to be returned, for any of the reasons stated above for which a man may sell his fief, the lord is not required to receive the fief and cause it to be sold, nor to accept its surrender, once he has already summoned the man for service, until that summons has expired; rather, he may reasonably refuse it.

## II. Certain Excerpts

[Col. 0419]

### CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0419C]

Here begins the Book of the Assizes and Good Usages of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, which were established and put into writing by Duke Godfrey of Bouillon, who was elected king and lord of that kingdom, and by the counsel of the other kings, princes, and barons who came after Duke Godfrey, and by order of the patriarch of Jerusalem.

When the holy city of Jerusalem was conquered from the enemies of the Cross, in the year of the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ 1099, on a Friday, and was restored to the power of the faithful of Jesus Christ by the pilgrims who had set out to come and conquer it at the preaching of the Cross—which was preached by Peter the Hermit—and when the princes and barons who had conquered it [Col. 0419D] had elected Duke Godfrey of Bouillon king and lord of the kingdom of Jerusalem, and he had received the lordship, he did not wish to be consecrated or crowned king in that kingdom, because he did not wish to wear a crown of gold where the King of Kings, Jesus Christ the Son of God, had worn a crown of thorns on the day of his Passion.

He devoted himself to putting the kingdom into good order and good condition, so that his men and his people, and every kind of person traveling through, coming to, or dwelling in that kingdom, might be protected and governed, held and maintained, and brought to justice, right, and reason. With the counsel of the patriarch of the holy city and Church of Jerusalem, and with the counsel of the princes and barons and of the wisest men he could find, he chose wise men to inquire into and learn from people of various lands the usages of their countries. Everything that those whom he had chosen for this task could learn or discover, they put, or caused to be put, into writing, and they brought that writing to Duke Godfrey.

He assembled the patriarch and those mentioned above, showed it to them, and had the writing read aloud before them. Afterwards, by their counsel and agreement, he gathered from those writings whatever seemed good to him, and made from it assizes and usages that were to be observed, maintained, and followed in the kingdom of Jerusalem. By these means he, his people, and every other kind of person traveling through or dwelling there might be governed and led according to right and reason in the said kingdom.

### CHAPTER V. Here it states how the lord of the kingdom of Jerusalem and the barons who have court, coinage, and justice must know the assizes and usages of that kingdom.

[Col. 0421A]

Because it seems to me right and reasonable that the chief lord of the kingdom of Jerusalem, and the barons and other wealthy men who have court, coinage, and justice, should know the assizes and usages of the said kingdom—which the chief lord swears, before he is received as lord, anointed, or crowned king, to uphold to the best of his power and to cause to be upheld in his kingdom, and which all his men and the men of his men must likewise swear—and because their men, who are to be judges in their courts, should know well and justly how to give the judgments that they must give according to these assizes and usages, I now begin this book.

Although I know well that I have neither the wisdom nor the knowledge by which I ought to have undertaken to make it, I rely on and hope in God, in the power of God the Son, and in the blessedness of the Holy Spirit, who gives me understanding and grace to do well according to what I have learned and retained from those whom I have heard speak, and who were the wisest men of my time: those whom I have heard speak of the assizes and usages of the said kingdom and of the pleas of that court.

Because I have seen them do and apply these things, I have undertaken to make this book. I therefore pray the Holy Trinity to send me the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that I may bring this book to such perfection as will be to the honor of God, to the benefit [Col. 0421C] of my soul, and to the proper governance of the people of the kingdom of Jerusalem, according to the rightful assizes and rightful usages of that kingdom, and to the benefit of the arms and bodies of all those who will read it.

I pray, request, and adjure them on God’s behalf not to use anything in it wickedly, to take away or diminish another’s right, or to draw near to and defend another’s right according to whatever need may arise. For my intention in making this book has not been, nor is it, anything other than to teach those who will need it, who have a right and will claim it, how to approach and enforce it; and to teach those from whom what is another’s right is demanded how to withdraw from it and defend themselves.

Therefore it seems to me that, before I speak in this book of the assizes and usages, or of the pleas of the high [Col. 0421D] court of the said kingdom, I ought first to speak of the king, who is the chief lord of that kingdom, even if he is not crowned, and of the other wealthy men and barons who have court, coinage, and justice in that kingdom. I shall also speak at the beginning of my book of the judges, the pleaders, and their courts. This is what I have undertaken to say about the king and those mentioned above.

### CHAPTER LXXXI. On what matters one may not defend oneself by the assize or usage of judicial battle

These are the matters concerning which, under the assize or usage of the kingdom of Jerusalem, there is battle, and in which one may defend oneself by the judgment or recognition of the court without battle.

[Col. 0422A]

Of manifest murder, murder in court; of manifest treason; of homicide, manifest murder in court; of a claim involving one mark of silver or more; of attracting against one’s lord something that does not belong to his fief; and of every other matter for which one would lose life or limb, or one’s honor, if convicted or proved guilty in the high court.

### CHAPTER LXXXII. What persons may bring an appeal of murder, and to whom one is bound to answer

Because murder has been divided earlier in this book from the other matters concerning which one may bring a claim under the assize and obtain justice, and because there is no fixed day for such a claim, while the assize or usage of the kingdom of Jerusalem provides turns of battle, I shall speak of it first. I therefore wish to set out what kinds of people may bring an appeal of murder, against whom one cannot refuse to answer for the murder under the assize or usage of the kingdom of Jerusalem.

The wife of the murdered man. The husband of the murdered woman. All male and female blood relatives. All male and female relatives by affinity. All godfathers. All godmothers. All godsons. All goddaughters. All *compères* (co-godfathers). [Col. 0422C] All *commères* (co-godmothers). All men and women from the country of the murdered person, if he is a foreign pilgrim. All men and women who came on the crossing on which he came, if he is from overseas. All men and women who have been with the murdered man or woman for a year and a day, as stated above. All men and women who owe fealty to the murdered man or woman, whether man or woman, lord or lady. All men and women who belong to the commune of the murdered man or woman, if that is the custom. All men and women who belong to the brotherhood of the murdered man or woman, if he or she belongs to a brotherhood. [Col. 0422D] A woman, if she was caring for the murdered man. A man, if he had the murdered woman in his care.

But a woman who has a husband cannot bring an appeal of murder except with her husband’s permission. The reason why this kind of person may bring the appeal and others may not is that it is quite apparent that love leads them to bring the appeal, because of the affection that existed between them and the murdered man or woman, and not because of hatred, greed, or malice.

### CHAPTER CI. How champions of every kind must be armed when they go to offer to fight the battle in court

Here is the manner in which people of every kind—champions, knights, and others—must fight; how they must first come to offer themselves to the lord, where and how; what arms they must wear; and how they must come to court to offer themselves for battle. It also states how and with what armor they must be armed in the field and in battle on horseback, and how and with what the horses must be covered.

### CHAPTER CII. How knights who fight for murder must be armed, how they must be armed for another quarrel, and how, where, and at what hour they must come to offer themselves

Knights who fight for murder or homicide must fight on foot and without a coif; they must be tonsured round, and dressed in red tunics or shirts, or short padded garments reaching from the elbow to the knee, with the sleeves cut off above the elbow. They must have red cloth hose for the stirrup, and nothing more, and a shield called a *harasse*, which is half a foot, or a full palm, larger than the man himself. It must have two ordinary-sized openings, placed so that he can see his adversary through them.

He must have one lance and two swords, one belted on and the other attached to his shield, so that he may have it when he needs it. There are only three days’ respite for such a battle once the pledges have been given and received.

When the champions who have pledged themselves to such a battle wish to offer themselves on the day of battle, they must come on foot, between Prime and Terce, to the lord’s residence, the appellant first, dressed and shod as described above. They must have several *harasses*, several lances, and several swords carried before them, so that they may choose at the entrance to the field whichever they wish. For if each presented only one, and it were broken, split, or damaged in any way before he reached the field, he could have no other thereafter, but only the one he had presented to the lord and the court.

The appellant must come forward to offer himself and say this when he has come into the lord’s court:

“Lord, I present myself and my arms to you and to the court. Here are my arms”—and he must show them—“and I present myself to offer and fulfill what I have undertaken to do, and to fulfill the battle that I have pledged against this man,” naming him.

Then the lord must have all his arms displayed before the court, to see whether they are as they ought to be. He must then deliver the arms to his men and command the champions to go to the field, together with those who carry their arms.

The defendant must afterwards come to offer himself, as stated above concerning the appellant. The lord must likewise do and say to him what he did and said to the appellant. If one of the lances is longer than the other, the lord must shorten it to the larger measure. He must have the two champions carefully guarded on the way to the field, so that neither of them flees or turns aside, and so that no one does them bodily harm or shame, or speaks or commits any insult or annoyance against them. The lord must have them protected from all this, since they are in his keeping.

When they are in the field, the lord must place some of his men there to guard them. One of these men must say before the others to each champion: “Choose from your arms whichever you wish to have for the battle.” They must do so and retain those arms in the field, while the others are removed from the field.

Afterwards each champion must be made to swear that he carries no charm, talisman, witchcraft, or sorcery; that he has not had any made for this battle, nor had another make any for him to his knowledge; that he has not given or promised anything to any person whatsoever in any manner for a charm, spell, talisman, or sorcery that could help him in that battle or harm his adversary; and that he has no other arms upon him than those which the court has seen.

Then the champions must be led together into the middle of the field, where there must be a Gospel book. The defendant must first kneel, place his right hand on the Gospel, and swear upon the saints, saying: “So help me God and these holy Gospels, I did not commit this murder,” naming it.

The appellant must say that he is lying. He must be raised as a perjurer and seized by the fist, and swear: “So help me God and these holy Gospels, he committed this murder,” naming it.

After this, the guards must lead each champion to one side of the field. The ban must be proclaimed at the four corners of the field, declaring that no one, however bold or of whatever language, may say or do anything by which either of the two champions might in any way be helped, seen, or made visible to another; and that if anyone did so, his body and property would fall under the lord’s mercy.

If the murdered person is present, he must be on one side of the field, entirely uncovered. If a man or woman who has brought the appeal through a champion is present, that person must remain beside the body, in such a way as neither to harm nor help either party by word, deed, or gesture, except by praying to God in a manner that the champions cannot hear.

The arms of the defeated man, and those of the victor that fall, whether broken or intact, belong to the lord; and, if there is a constable, to the constable. If peace is made after they have been allowed to go together, any arms of either man that are broken or have fallen in the field belong to the lord, or to the constable if there is one.

Then the guards of the field must divide the sunlight so that it is not more in the face of one than of the other. One of the guards must say to the lord: “Lord, what do you command? We have done everything we ought to do.”

The lord must then say to them: “Let them go together, draw aside to one part of the field, and let them meet.” If a champion carries or brings another weapon than the one provided by the court, and wishes to use it to harm his adversary, and the guards of the field notice it, they must seize him at once, and the lord must have him treated as a murderer.

If one takes hold of the other and they throw each other down, the guards of the field must move toward them and come as close as they can, so that if one says the word of surrender, they can hear him. If he says it and they hear him, they must immediately say to the other: “Let go; you have done enough.” They must then seize the man who surrendered and leave him to the lord’s command. The lord must immediately have him dragged to the gallows and hanged by the throat, even if the man who was killed did not say the word of surrender.

Anyone who wishes to bring an appeal of murder but is not a knight must do everything stated above, except that the champions must be armed differently, in the manner and with the arms set out in this book for champions other than knights. Foot sergeants fight in all quarrels with one set of arms.

### CHAPTER CIV. How the champions must offer themselves on the day of battle

[Col. 0425B]

On the fourth day, the champions must come to offer themselves at the lord’s residence between Prime and Terce, the appellant first and the defendant afterwards. Each must have several covered horses, as specified above, and several of each of the arms mentioned earlier brought before him. For if he brought only one and had only one horse led along, and that horse died or became lame, or any of the arms were badly fitted or damaged, he could neither have nor obtain another after he had presented it at court.

When the appellant comes before the lord, he must say to him:

“Lord, I have come on the day for which you and the court have given me a guarantee and provision of whatever I may need to complete my battle. I offer to carry out in deed the battle that I have undertaken in words, and I ask and request you to command that I go to the field to fight my battle.”

The lord must say: “Wait until I command you.”

He must then withdraw to one side of the lord’s residence. When the defendant comes before the lord, he must do as has been set out above concerning the appellant.

When they have thus come to offer themselves, the lord must first command the appellant to go to the field, and afterwards the defendant. He must assign to each of them some of his men to accompany them to the field and guard them so that neither turns aside, and so that no one speaks to them, harms them, commits shame, or assaults them. When they come near the field, each must have tents pitched or shelters made outside the field, where they may arm themselves.

The lord, or his men, must come there and appoint some of his best men to guard the field. He must have enough armed men around the field to ensure that no wrong, force, or outrage is committed against his lordship or either of the champions.

When they have arrived there, the lord must have the champions brought before him and say to each: “Which horse do you wish to have for fighting? Which are the arms with which you wish to fight?” They must show them, and the lord must have them taken and displayed before his court, to see whether they are as they ought to be for such a deed.

[Col. 0426A] The court must then measure the lances, and if one is longer than the other, shorten it so that they are of equal length. If one of the swords, or the point of one of the lances, is such that it can pass through the mail of the hauberk without breaking and cutting the mail, it must be replaced, so that they do not have arms other than those they are required to have as stated above.

When this has been done, the lord must tell the champions to go and arm themselves with all their arms except the helmet and lance. The lord must command his men to take them into the field, lead their horses before them, carry their shields, lances, and helmets, and enter the field on foot, leading each man separately to one side.

When this has been done, those whom the lord appointed to guard the field must carry a Gospel book and make each champion swear separately that he carries neither upon himself nor upon his horse any arms by which he could harm the other, other than those that the court has seen; and that, to his knowledge, he carries neither upon himself nor upon his horse any charm, written spell, talisman, sorcery, or anything else intended for him.

After this oath, they must bring the two champions into the middle of the field. One of the field guards must hold a Gospel book and say to the defendant: “Come forward and swear what you must.” He must kneel, place his hand on the Gospel, and say:

“So help me God and these holy Gospels, I did not commit the treason of which this man accuses me,” naming it.

The appellant must immediately seize him by the fist and say: “You are a perjurer, and I raise you as a perjurer.” He must swear: “So help me God and his holy Gospels, you committed the treason of which I accuse you.”

Then the field guards must lead each champion to one side of the field and command that the ban be proclaimed in the four parts of the field. Each champion must mount his horse, lower his helmet, and take his shield in his tent. The guards must hold each champion by the bridle of his horse. The others must divide the sunlight.

When the sunlight has been divided and the ban proclaimed, they must say to the lord, who must be outside the field on horseback: “Lord, we have done all that we ought to do. What do you command?”

The lord must say to them: “Let them go together.” Then those holding them must let them go, and each must move against the other and do the best he knows.

If either champion carries an arm and draws it in order to harm his adversary, he must be treated as stated in the passage concerning murder and homicide.

The man who is killed or surrenders in the field must be dragged and hanged by order of the lord. The horse and arms of the defeated man belong to the constable; those of the victor that are broken or fall in the field also belong to the constable. If peace is made after the champions have been allowed to go together, all arms that have fallen in the field, broken or intact, belong [Col. 0427A] to the constable; and if there is no constable, they belong to the lord.

If the man accused of treason is defeated, he is convicted of treason, since it has been proved against him as it ought to be. His heirs must therefore be disinherited as the heirs of a traitor convicted and proved guilty of treason.

If the lord wishes to have the fief, and the man convicted and proved guilty of treason, as stated above, has had the fief granted to him and justice has been done, the lord must assemble the court and say how that man was accused of treason, and that he was convicted as one against whom the charge was proved by battle and who was defeated in battle. He must ask his court to recognize whether his heirs are disinherited from the fief of the man convicted of treason because the charge was proved against him in the field by battle.

The court must decide whether his heirs are disinherited from the fief that he held, and from everything that came to them through him, as heirs of a manifest traitor convicted and proved guilty of treason.

Then the lord may seize his fief, take possession of it, cause it to be held, and do with it all that he wishes, as with his own property, since he has acquired it by the judgment or recognition of the court.

### CHAPTER CVII. What persons may defend themselves by champion

These are the persons who may defend themselves by champion: a woman; a maimed man; a man who has passed the age of sixty; and, if their champion is defeated, the same shall be done to them both as stated above.

### CHAPTER CIX. How all other kinds of people besides knights who wage battle must be armed for battle

[Col. 0428A]

All kinds of people other than knights, whatever their quarrel, must fight on foot in a bliaut, or in red tunics, and in stirrup hose and breeches, and with a belt such as foot champions customarily wear. They must be tonsured round and have canvas and champions’ staffs. Whoever cannot have these may have other staffs of equal length.

The arms of the defeated and of the victor shall be dealt with in the manner stated above. An appeal made for murder or homicide has only three days’ respite between the day on which the pledges are given and received [Col. 0428B] and the day of battle. For all other quarrels, the period until the day of battle is forty days.

On the day on which the lord or the court grants them battle, they must come and offer themselves at the lord’s residence, prepared in the manner stated above in this book. The lord must do as described, and when they are in the field, the field guards must arrange the oaths, proclamations, and other matters mentioned above, in the manner set out earlier in this book.

### CHAPTER CX. What lords must do when a father and son, or two brothers, pledge battle against one another

It is an assize of the kingdom of Jerusalem that the lord must not accept pledges of battle between father and son, between son and father, or between two brothers.

# HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF THE LINEAGES FROM OVERSEAS

[Col. 0427]

### CHAPTER I. Here it speaks of the kings of Jerusalem

[Col. 0427C]

The holy city of Jerusalem, where it pleased our Savior to suffer death and Passion in order to redeem us from the pains of hell, was conquered from the enemies of our faith on a Friday, at the hour of None, on the fifteenth day of June, in the year of the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ 1099, and was restored to the power of the faithful of Christ.

The barons and pilgrims elected Godfrey of Bouillon, duke of Lorraine, king and lord. He did not wish to be crowned or to wear a crown, for he said that in the city where our Savior had worn a crown of thorns on the day of his Passion, he would not wear a crown of gold; and that the crowning which our Savior received in his Passion for our redemption was sufficient for all the kings who would rule that holy kingdom.

This Godfrey of Bouillon reigned only one year and died without an heir of his body. After the death of the said Godfrey, his brother Baldwin became king of Jerusalem. He had been count of Edessa and gave the county to a cousin of his named Baldwin of Bourcq, who was the son of Count Hugh of Rethel and of Countess Melisende.

The aforesaid King Baldwin was a very worthy man and died without an heir. These verses were written on his tomb, and they say as follows:

> King Baldwin, another Judas Maccabaeus, hope of his country, guardian of the Church, whom Caesar feared, to whom Egypt and Damascus gave gifts and tribute—  
> alas, that one so great should be confined in so small a tomb!

After the death of the aforesaid King Baldwin, Baldwin of Bourcq, count of Edessa, became king of Jerusalem. He was the son of Count Hugh of Rethel and Countess Melisende, as has been said. He gave the county of Edessa to a relative of his named Joscelin of Courtenay.

The aforesaid King Baldwin married the daughter of a wealthy Armenian, lord of Melitene, whose name was Gabriel. Her name was Morphia, and by her he had four daughters: Melisende, Alice, Odoart, and Joy.

Melisende married Fulk, count of Anjou. Alice married Bohemond, prince of Antioch. Odoart was the wife of Count Raymond of Tripoli. Joy became a nun, and for her the abbey of Saint Lazarus of Bethany was endowed.

After the death of the said King Baldwin, Fulk, his son-in-law and the husband of his daughter Melisende, became king of Jerusalem. He had two sons, Baldwin and Amalric.

King Fulk was hunting a hare on the plain of Acre when his horse fell upon his body, and he died. After his death, his son Baldwin became king of Jerusalem, and Amalric became count of Jaffa.

King Baldwin sent to Greece to obtain a wife and married Theodora, the niece of the Emperor Manuel, but they had no heir.

After the death of King Baldwin, his brother Amalric became king. But the patriarch would not crown him until he separated from Agnes, the daughter of Count Joscelin of Edessa, who was his cousin. This Agnes had been betrothed to Hugh of Ibelin. As she was coming to the kingdom, she arrived at Jaffa; Count Amalric, on the advice of his men, took her by force and married her. He had by her a son and a daughter, Baldwin and Sibyl.

For this reason the patriarch would not crown him until he left her. She then went to Hugh of Ibelin and said that he was her husband, and he took her.

King Amalric married a woman from Greece, Maria, the niece of the Emperor Manuel, and they had a daughter named Isabella.

After the death of King Amalric, his son Baldwin, whom he had had by the aforementioned Agnes, became king of Jerusalem. He was called the Leper. His sister Sibyl was the wife of the marquis of Montferrat, and they had a son named Baldwin. After the death of the said marquis, she married Guy of Lusignan.

Isabella, the daughter of King Amalric and Queen Maria, married Geoffrey of Toron.

After the death of King the Leper, his nephew Baldwin became king of Jerusalem. He was the son of the marquis, as you have heard. His uncle, King the Leper, had had him crowned at the age of seven. He was called the child king and died as a child.

Then Guy of Lusignan, the husband of the aforementioned Sibyl, became king of Jerusalem. Although the barons offered to make Geoffrey of Toron king—he was the husband of Isabella, the daughter of King Amalric and Queen Maria—he was so timid that he did not wish it. Instead, he went to King Guy and paid him homage.

In the time of that King Guy, the land was lost. Afterwards, during the siege of Acre, Queen Sibyl, his wife, died. Her sister Isabella became queen. She was the wife of Geoffrey of Toron, then married Conrad, the marquis of Montferrat, and they had a daughter named Maria, who was called the Marchioness.

The Assassins killed the aforementioned marquis. Queen Isabella married Count Henry of Champagne, and they had two daughters, Alice and Philippe.

Alice married King Hugh of Cyprus. Philippe married Gerard of Brienne and had five daughters and one son. One daughter was lady of Hauteville, another was lady of Montmorency, the third was countess of Grandpré, the fourth was lady of Bievres, and the fifth became abbess of an abbey in Champagne, in a town called Nerru. That abbey is called La Pitié. The son was named Gerard, like his father.

The aforesaid Count Henry of Champagne fell from a window of the castle of Acre into the moat and died. The aforementioned Queen Isabella married King Aimery of Cyprus, and they had two daughters, Sibyl and Melisende.

Sibyl married King Leo of Armenia. Melisende was the wife of Prince Raymond of Antioch, who was called the One-Eyed.

[Col. 0430C] After the death of the aforementioned Queen Isabella, the kingdom passed to her daughter Maria, whom she had had by the marquis of Montferrat, as stated above. Maria married John of Brienne, who was King John of Acre. They had a daughter named Isabella, who married the Emperor Frederick. They had a daughter and a son named Conrad. This was King Conrad, who was the father of Conradin, whose head King Charles had cut off at Naples.

## APPENDIX ONE. LIFE OF BLESSED IDA, COUNTESS OF BOULOGNE, MOTHER OF KING GODFREY

*(Bolland, Acta Sanctorum, April, vol. II, day 13, p. 139.)*

[Col. 0431]

### PRELIMINARY COMMENTARY

#### § I. The marriage of Blessed Ida. Her and her husband’s royal descent. Their children

[Col. 0431A]

1. Boulogne, or Bononia, a city of lower Picardy situated among the Morini on the Strait of the British Ocean, appears to have been called by the ancients Gessoriacum, the naval station of the Morini; and the surrounding region was called the district of Gessoriacum.

Saint Vulmar, abbot, was born there and died in a monastery that he himself had built, in the seventh century after Christ, on July 20. His monastery is called Saint Vulmar in the Forest, or in Silviacum, or in the Wood.

Moreover, the city of Boulogne contains two towns: the upper town, with a castle of some kind, and the lower town. In the upper town, besides the cathedral church, which recognizes the Virgin Mother of God as its patroness, there are other churches and monasteries. Among them was [Col. 0431B] the abbey of Saint Vulmar of the Order of Saint Augustine, in which the Fathers of the Oratory of Our Lord Jesus Christ now reside.

Blessed Ida, countess of Boulogne and a widow, formerly built this monastery of Saint Vulmar within the walls, and restored another Saint Vulmar in the Forest, which had fallen into ruin.

2. Andrea Du Chesne, in his *Probationes* for the genealogical history of the families of Guînes, Ardres, Ghent, and Coyeques, cites on page 5 an extract from an ancient genealogy of the counts of Boulogne, written in the time of Saint Louis, king of France. From it we transfer the following:

“Guy, it says, count of Boulogne, had three sons. The firstborn was called Baldwin, to whom his father gave Boulogne and Lens. The middle one was called Hugh, to whom his father gave Saint-Pol, and he was the first count who ever existed at Saint-Pol. The third was called William, to whom his father gave Guînes; he was the first count of Guînes. That count Guy, after these things had been accomplished, died and was buried at Saint-Vulmar in the Forest. Later his son Baldwin, count of Boulogne, was buried there also; apart from Fulk the bishop, Baldwin’s sons were Geoffrey, count of Boulogne, and Eustace, count of l’Oeul. Both were buried at Saint-Vulmar in the Forest.”

Such is the account given there, although some regard it as not entirely certain. It is reported that the county of Boulogne came to William, count of Ponthieu, from whom his son Ernuculus, or Arnulf, received the county of Boulogne in the year 972. His son Baldwin succeeded him and transmitted it to his son Eustace I, the father-in-law of Blessed Ida, who married Eustace II, son of the aforesaid Eustace I and of Matilda, daughter of Lambert, count of Leuven, and Gerberga. Through her this family is known to have descended from Charlemagne: namely through the emperors Louis the Pious and Charles the Bald, the kings of the Franks Louis the Stammerer, Charles the Simple, and Louis IV of Overseas, and Charles, duke of Lower Lorraine, whose daughter was the aforementioned Gerberga, grandmother of Eustace II, whom Blessed Ida married.

Orderic Vitalis, in Book IV of his *Ecclesiastical History*, under the year 1067, says the following about these spouses:

“Eustace was a count of great nobility, descended, that is, from Charlemagne, the most vigorous king of the Franks. He was also a man of great power, being a lofty prince of three counties—Boulogne, Guînes, and Thérouanne—and he had as his wife the noble and religious Ida.”

This is what Orderic says. Yet he is mistaken in attributing two counties to Eustace. At that time the counts of Guînes were independent; they are accurately described by Lambert, priest of Ardres, in his *History of the Counts of Ardres*, which he completed in 1181 and which survives in manuscript. Andrea Du Chesne published most of it in the *Probationes* mentioned above.

As for the county of Thérouanne, Miraeus and others believe it to have been the same as the county of Saint-Pol. This county was at one time joined to the county of Boulogne, but was later separated from it and given to Hugh, the son either of Guy or of William. Whether, however, Eustace bore the title of both counties, we do not wish to conjecture.

It was stated above that the county of Lens was transferred together with Boulogne. It was later given to Lambert, brother of Eustace II; when the latter died without children in 1054, Eustace II obtained that same county as well. This will become clear below from the foundations made there.

3. Blessed Ida inherited this nobility from her husband, and she herself brought him no lesser distinction, being likewise descended from the line of Charlemagne through the emperors Louis the Pious, Lothair, and Louis II. Ermengard, daughter of this last Louis, who was also king of Italy, married Boso, king of Provence, and bore Cunegund, mother of Godfrey of the Ardennes, commonly called the Captive. He, count of Verdun and of Étampes, fathered Godfrey the Childless and Gothelon the Great, duke of both Lotharings and grandfather of Blessed Ida. Gothelon died in 1044.

Gothelon was succeeded by two sons: Gothelon, called the Slothful, who survived him only a short time; and Godfrey the Bearded, called the Bold and the Great. The latter rebelled against the emperor because the full succession was denied him; at length he was reconciled with the emperor and obtained the duchy of both Lotharings.

He had two wives. The first was Doda, mother of Blessed Ida and of Godfrey the Hunchback. The second was Beatrice, widow of Boniface, margrave of Tuscany, by whom she had Matilda, the marchioness so famous among writers for her noble character.

Andrea Du Chesne, at the beginning of his preface to the *Genealogical History of the House of Dreux*, asserts that “Godfrey’s first wife had as her paternal great-grandmother Cunegund, daughter of Ermengard,” whom we stated above to have been married to Boso, king of Provence.

4. Blessed Ida seems to have been born around the year 1040. She could therefore have been given in marriage in 1057, as James Malbrancus writes in Book VIII, chapter 49, of his work on the Morini, or at least in 1059, which some assign as the date.

It is certain that she bore her husband three sons. The ancient *Acts* place them in the following order. The firstborn was Eustace III, so named after his father and grandfather and later made count of Boulogne. The second was Godfrey, later called the Bouillonese, a name borne by his maternal uncle and grandfather. The third was Baldwin, whose name represented his paternal great-grandfather. These last two died as kings of Jerusalem.

Blessed Ida lists them in this same order in a charter of donation made in 1098 for the monastery of Saint-Bertin. But in a diploma for the monastery of Affligem, dated 1096, Saint Ida first names Godfrey, then Eustace and Baldwin. They are listed in the same order in the second *Life*, which will be presented below from the manuscript *Hagiologium* of Roodendael; in Alberic’s *Chronicle* under the year 1096; in the *Great Belgian Chronicle*; and by later historians.

The aforementioned Orderic Vitalis lists them in this order: Godfrey, Baldwin, and Eustace. Lambert of Ardres, in chapter 18, calls Blessed Ida the mother of Godfrey and Baldwin, kings of Jerusalem, and of Eustace, the most noble count, referring to royal dignity. Yet in the most ancient *Life* of Blessed Ida, Eustace is placed first, as he is also in an ancient genealogy written before the other two had been elected kings.

We possess this genealogy in an illustrious codex communicated to us from the Bruges library of the Society of Jesus. It followed the *Chronicle of Hugh of Fleury*, and was subsequently printed by Miraeus in Book I, chapter 30, of the *Belgian Donations*. From it we give the following:

“Eustace, count of Boulogne, took as wife Matilda, daughter of Gerberga, as we said above, and begot by her two sons, Eustace and Lambert. Eustace took as wife Ida, daughter of Godfrey the duke, noble by birth and character; and by her he begot three sons: Eustace, Godfrey, now duke of Lorraine, and Baldwin.”

This was copied from that source into a manuscript codex of Nivelles, with the word “now” omitted.

This Godfrey, having become heir to the patrimony of his maternal uncle Godfrey the Hunchback, who died without children in 1076—and especially to the lordship of Bouillon—was called Godfrey of Bouillon. In 1076 Henry III, emperor and Henry IV, king of Germany, conferred upon him the Mark of Antwerp; in 1089 he added the duchy of Lower Lorraine, as indicated in the genealogy.

5. A certain question is raised here: whether Blessed Ida, besides the three sons mentioned, bore other children to her husband, specifically a son called William and one or two daughters.

William, archbishop of Tyre, writing in Book IX of the *Sacred Expedition* around the year 1174, speaks as follows of Godfrey of Bouillon:

“This Godfrey had three brothers by both parents. Their nobility of character and excellence of virtue made them worthy to be brothers of so great a prince: namely, Lord Baldwin, count of Edessa, who afterward succeeded him in the kingdom; and also Lord Eustace, count of Boulogne, who, succeeding to his father’s possessions after his father’s death, obtained the county. The third was Lord William, an illustrious man, not degenerate from the honor and vigor alike of his father and his brothers. The first two followed their lord and brother on the expedition, while the third remained at home.”

This is what Tyre says; Saint Antoninus followed him in the fifteenth century, as did other later writers. Yet because none of the ancient writers who were flourishing in learning in Europe at that time mention William, and because Ida herself does not list him among her sons in her diplomas, Tyre has not been regarded as sufficiently reliable by Louis Chanterel Faber, in Book II of *Historical Considerations on the Genealogy of Lorraine*, and by others. They judge that Tyre counted among Godfrey of Bouillon’s brothers the brother of another prince who had gone to the Holy Land.

Orderic Vitalis, in Book IV, page 509, makes no mention of William. After listing the other three sons of Blessed Ida, he adds a daughter who married Henry IV, emperor of the Germans. Aubert Miraeus, in the *Belgian Chronicle*, page 263, says that she was called Agnes or Adelaide, married Henry IV, king of the Romans, and was repudiated shortly afterward.

The same Orderic, in Book IX, page 755, lists among the distinguished men who went to the Holy Land a certain Conon, a German count, an upright and wise man. Miraeus states that the counselor who had married a sister of Duke Godfrey was Conon, count of Montaigu, and that Lambert was descended from them.

In the manuscript history of the monastery of Brogne, in the county of Namur, it is said that Godfrey, duke of Bouillon; Baldwin, king; and Eustace, count, had a sister whose son was Manasses. He possessed a castle and a certain town called Hirgia, together with villages and revenues quite modest for a man of such distinction.

Whether all this should be attributed to one sister or to several is not equally clear. Miraeus believes that they had two sisters. Hirgia, called Herca by others, is a town in the Liège region near Brabant, situated in the ancient Hasbaye.

6. When William, duke of Normandy, sailed to that island in 1066 with a large army to receive the kingdom of England, he was forced to engage the English army. Among those who took part in this battle and secured victory for William, Orderic Vitalis, in Book III, names Eustace, count of Boulogne, first.

Later, as Orderic says in Book IV under the year 1067:

“When the English, provoked to rebellion by the various oppressions of the Normans, sent envoys to Boulogne and ordered Count Eustace to hasten with a fleet carefully equipped with soldiers and weapons to receive Dover. When this expedition did not succeed, Count Eustace was reconciled with King William not long afterward and subsequently enjoyed his friendship for a long time.”

How long he lived afterward is not known. We shall discuss below the restoration of the church of Lens and its confirmation by privileges in the year 1070.

There exists a charter of Baldwin, count of Guînes, in the *Chronicle of the Monastery of Andres*, concerning the foundation of that monastery, reported by Andrea Du Chesne in the *Probationes* for the genealogical history of that family of Guînes, page 25. Among the witnesses, after Geoffrey, bishop of Paris, Blessed Ida, countess of Boulogne, is the first named. The charter was made in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1084. How long she had then been a widow is not known.

That she lived until the year 1106 will become clear from various diplomas presented below.
