§ II. Death of Blessed Ida. The various Lives written. Her title of saint and blessed.

7. The *Acts* relate that Blessed Ida died on Sunday, the Ides of April [13 April]. Lambert, bishop of Arras, testifies below, in a diploma for the church of Lens and its college of canons, signed on the seventh day before the Ides of June [7 June] of that year, that she survived until 1106. After that year, Sunday fell on the Ides of April in 1113, in the twelfth lunar cycle, the second solar cycle, with dominical letter E, when Easter was celebrated on 6 April and the following Sunday in Albis fell on the Ides of April. Blessed Ida was then more than seventy years old by some years; thus she does not seem to have prolonged her life to a still greater old age, of which her *Acts* make no mention.

[Col. 0436A] 8. We have three versions of her *Acts*. We give the oldest from a very ancient manuscript codex of the Jesuit college at Bruges, composed, so far as we can ascertain, by a monk of the monastery of Wast, founded by Ida herself in the territory of Boulogne and where she was buried. The author himself, an eyewitness, testifies that her body was found intact with its garments after many days. Some miracles, confirmed by the testimony of others, are then added. Among them, nearly the last is one granted to a granddaughter of Blessed Ida through her son Eustace; the said *Acts* seem to have been written while she was still alive, after 1130, when Blessed John, bishop of Thérouanne, died, whom the author honours with the title “of pious memory.”

As they stand in the said copy, these *Acts* are divided into various lessons, and at the end is added the customary conclusion of the lessons: “But thou, O Lord, have mercy upon us. Thanks be to God.” The following title is prefixed: “The Life of Blessed Ida, countess of Boulogne, widow.” In the text she is called saint, most holy, blessed, most blessed, most venerable, and venerable; and many are said to have hastened to venerate her after her death.

9. A second *Life* is given from a manuscript codex of the monastery of the Regular Canons of Roodendael near Brussels, from the first part of the *Hagiology of Brabant*, collected and written by John Gillemans. Two hundred years ago he gathered several lives of saints with great industry and labour, and before his preface to this *Life* placed the following title: “Life of Saint Ida, widow and countess of Boulogne, of the stock of the Carolingians.” It adds certain deeds done in Brabant which were omitted in the earlier *Life*.

We have another abridgment from a manuscript codex of Saint Saviour’s at Utrecht, under this title: “The Life of Saint Ida, Countess of Boulogne.” We omit the rest, since it is abridged from the first *Life*. Throughout both these Lives, not only in the title but also in the narrative itself, Ida is called saint and blessed. Gerbrand of Leiden and the author of the *Belgian Chronicle* likewise call her Saint Ida. The author of the manuscript *Florarium of Saints* adorns her with this encomium for 13 April: “The deposition of Saint Ida, widow, countess of Boulogne, mother of the brothers Godfrey and Baldwin of Boulogne, later kings of Jerusalem, of Carolingian stock.” Molanus celebrates her in the *Nativities of the Saints of Belgium*, Miraeus in the *Belgian and Burgundian Fasti*, Ferrarius in the *General Catalogue*, and more recent writers frequently do the same.

Malbrancus, in his history of the Morini, regularly calls her blessed and, in Book IX, chapter 35, asserts that he had been at the place of her burial and had “seen her monument of white stone, five feet high, in the church of Saint Michael; and that the inhabitants maintain that she there received a magnificent tomb from her son Eustace, and even now point out the upper marble with that monument or statue, which lies neglected after the destruction of that church.”

[Col. 0437]

# THE LIFE OF BLESSED IDA, BY A CONTEMPORARY MONK OF WAST

*(From the Bruges manuscript of the Society of Jesus.)*

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0437A]

1. As the age of the world grows old, according to the testimony of the Scriptures, and now, as its decline shows, is almost falling to its end, it must be assisted by the merits of the past because it is destitute of present merits. For the sin of the first man appeared at the beginning of the world together with the death that had been promised; and thereafter death, not without sin, held it under foot. When sin had multiplied, the Lord saw that the earth was corrupt and filled with iniquity, and that all were bent toward evil; therefore he first brought judgment upon the world by water. Yet the merit of the righteous who then existed, though they were not many, benefited the world, lest everything should perish.

Abraham’s entreaty, however, did not in the least free unrepentant Sodom from the danger of fire. Why? Because they were unwilling to imitate Abraham’s faith or believe the admonitions. After the Law, which, as it were through clouds, aided the world, the holy Fathers promised salvation to come to the world and sustained its recurring affliction by their merits. For the salvation that had been proclaimed, as it drew near, revealed to the declining world the various assaults of the devil which it suffers. But even now, as it were bending and hanging, it is aided by the merits and prayers of the saints.

Therefore let us always faithfully place beneath the falling world the merits of those past persons whom we believe to have power. Once the merits of both sexes, now translated to glory, have been celebrated and invoked, strengthened steadfastly and bravely, we go forth to meet and oppose the wicked world. For no rank has been omitted of which there is not testimony to holiness: some were saved from the flood in the ark, some sanctified through circumcision, some justified through the Law, and some worthily reborn through baptism. It has been granted to them that they might benefit the world by the merits of that benevolence which they always possessed. For example, if those blessed women who did not bear children are so called by the testimony of truth, then surely the mothers of the persons mentioned above are inscribed in the book of life by their own merits and those of their children. And if virginity is preached as good, chastity after bearing children—without which the work is not good—is proved great. For by the precept of the Law fruitfulness in offspring rejoices, and a posterity that does not appear is cursed. It is better to marry than to burn, so that the fall of the world may be sustained.

Now let the subject begun descend to that woman, and let it be made known by true testimony who she is. Therefore let the voice and hand of the writer agree, so as to show that this is indeed the truth, in order that readers and hearers may glorify God because of it without doubt.

# CHAPTER I. The lineage, education, marriage, children, and virtue in marriage of Blessed Ida

2. Thus, after the passage of many years, there arose a certain most noble maiden of distinguished lineage, named Ida. Her father, surpassing the powerful and those greater in renown, held before the emperor of the Germans a higher rank and, as it were, a prerogative of dignity and power; his name was Godfrey. [Note: [Col. 0437B] This Godfrey was surnamed the Bearded, the Bold, and the Great; he was the son of Gothelon the Great, duke of Lorraine, and died in 1070. We have said the rest above.] Her mother was called Doda, no less distinguished. [Note: [Col. 0437B] Doda was Godfrey’s first wife. After her death his second wife was Beatrice, then widow of Boniface, margrave of Tuscany, and mother of the celebrated Matilda, as indicated above.] They had one son, called, like his father, Godfrey, admirable in martial bearing and deeds, and older than the venerable Ida by birth. [Note: [Col. 0438B] This is Godfrey the Hunchback, called by others the Swollen; wounded by Sicarius, he died without children in 1076.]

While they ordered high and low matters according to their station, the aforesaid girl was instructed in letters throughout the suitable years of her childhood. Enriched with honourable manners, she did not give her attention to the wantonness of the present life, but sighed more and more for love of the heavenly country; from this it is sufficiently apparent and known with how great and what kind of grace she was filled.

3. One night, when she had given herself to sleep while thinking on things above, she saw in a dream the whole sun descending from heaven and, as it were, making a single moment in her bosom. This dream showed that something great was to happen, since there would proceed from her persons who would possess for a time kingdom and empire [lacuna]. Divine providence indeed ordains certain signs, showing future events to some by inspiration and to many by vision before they occur. And because all things have their season, the matters signified by the vision of the venerable maiden now under discussion were made known at the fitting time predestined by God.

We shall try to explain to the charity and benevolence of faithful persons both present and future how and on what grounds these things came about. In the time of the aforesaid Duke Godfrey there was a certain hero, most noble by birth, closely related by blood even to King Charles, [Note: [Col. 0439D] Charles the Great seems to be meant, whose grandfather was Charles Martel and whose grandson was Charles the Bald; the latter’s grandson in turn was Charles the Simplex. These three were kings of the Franks. The grandson in turn of the last Charles was another Charles, duke only of Lorraine, and great-grandfather of Count Eustace, husband of Blessed Ida.] exceedingly powerful in body, mind, and secular action, renowned far and wide, and mighty in name: Eustace. [Note: [Col. 0439D] Eustace is also written Eustachius, and without aspiration, Eusthacius.] He was count and lord of Boulogne, a city then famed for great lordship and power.

It is said—and it is true—that reputation joins together followers of virtue, and a man of whatever rank, if he is good, seeks one like himself. Count Eustace, therefore, having heard from the most truthful reports of many people about the manners, deeds, beauty, and dignity of birth of the aforesaid maiden Ida, sent envoys, equipped with intelligence and eloquence, to the aforesaid Duke Godfrey, asking him to give his daughter Ida to him in marriage, so that an enduring bond of their shared nobility might exist between them. [Note: [Col. 0439D] Malbrancus, Book VIII of *On the Morini*, chapter 47, states that Eustace came to Blessed Ida and that the marriage was celebrated at Cambrai in 1057. Contrary to this contemporary author, that assertion of a modern writer would need proof stronger than a simple assertion before we could give it credit.] Thus, after counsel had been taken about the request, and since heavenly grace was not lacking, her parents gave the honourable maiden Ida to the men who had come for her, accompanied by certain worthy persons. As they approached the territory of Boulogne, the whole city came out to meet them with great joy.

4. Received honourably, as was fitting, she was joined in marriage to Eustace, count of Boulogne, according to the custom of the Catholic Church. When the wedding had been solemnly celebrated, the venerable Ida faithfully loved, beneath consular dignity, the things that belonged to God; but she did not stubbornly seek the things that seemed to belong to the world. Keeping her marriage chaste, according to the Apostle’s command, and using her husband as one duly ought, yet as though she had no husband, she bore three sons before God’s mercy, as had been foretold, corresponding to the prophecy of the vision above.

The first of her sons was Eustace, [Note: [Col. 0439D] Count Eustace also went to the Holy Land with his brothers, but returned from it in 1102 and survived his mother for a long time as count of Boulogne.] a powerful man in all secular affairs and outstanding in lay piety. Imitating his father’s nobility, he stoutly held his inheritance, as is known. The second was Godfrey, called duke after his grandfather’s name and possession; [Note: [Col. 0440D] Godfrey, duke of Boulogne and thereafter also of Lorraine—namely Lower Lorraine—and margrave of Antwerp.] by God’s favour, after triumphing over the Turks, he was the first appointed king in Jerusalem under the new dispensation. [Note: [Col. 0440D] After Jerusalem was captured on 15 July 1099, he was by universal agreement made king of Jerusalem.] The third, younger than he in age but no less powerful in deed and authority, was Baldwin of blessed memory, governor and lord of the city of Acre and the lands subject to it; and finally, after the death of his brother Godfrey, [Note: [Col. 0440D] When Godfrey died on 19 July 1100, Baldwin was installed as king until 1118, when his brother Eustace, elected in absentia, yielded to his kinsman Baldwin of Bourcq.] he was enriched with royal honour in order to discharge the office of king. When the venerable Ida was the mother of such great sons, [Note: [Col. 0440D] Whether there were more children has been examined above.] while they still lay in their cradles, she did not permit them to be fed at another woman’s breasts but at her own, fearing that they might be contaminated by corrupt morals.

5. When the count saw that she was lovable to all, gracious to everyone, and praiseworthy in every respect, he not only endured this without displeasure, but even urged her to persevere and advance in every way toward better things. Then the handmaid of God, with her husband’s assent and will—indeed, filled with heavenly grace and divine compassion—frequented churches and, with great and devout humility, prepared with willing diligence what was useful and suitable for the divine service and its ministers.

While Ida, beloved by God and humankind, was doing this, hidden within the city walls beneath the cloak of her own mind, she burned to found churches outside them, carrying or sending gifts of lavish charity. For she had heard that the Lord commands the observer of the Law: “You shall not appear before me empty-handed, and you shall not delay to pay to God the vows of your heart.” Understanding this well, the Psalmist says: “Vows are upon me, O God; I will render praises unto thee” (Psalm 55:12). Hearing and observing these things, the most blessed Ida, with heavenly grace favourable to her, received in her tranquil mind the vows, pleasing to him who had granted them, which she was to pay.

Humility shone forth in her, such as Queen Esther is said to have possessed, who regarded royal ornaments before God as though they were menstrual garments (Esther 14:12). Therefore, not despising the devout humility of so powerful a queen whom she imitated, she scorned in every action of her life the superfluous prosperity of this present life. She carefully attended to the poor, awaiting future recompense; she aided widows, orphans, and the sick everywhere, especially those of the household of faith, by prayers and continual gifts. The venerable lady endeavoured to treat the powerful with chaste familiarity, the aged with pious consolation, and the innocent with humble speech.

# CHAPTER II. Her virtues in widowhood; monasteries founded; miracles performed

6. While she excelled in these and similar pursuits, her noble husband Eustace was deprived of the light of this life by the intervention of inevitable death. [Note: [Col. 0440D] He died after 1070, but we have been unable to ascertain the precise year.] Then the most venerable Ida, released from the bond of marriage, did not abandon the good works she performed but multiplied them. Though deprived of her husband’s consolation, she was continually enriched by heavenly love and rejoiced in the nobility of her sons. First building in her mind, taught by divine prompting, what afterwards appeared in the number of three, she pondered these things in her devout heart so that her holiness might be made manifest. Charity brought her into the Germany of her kinsfolk. [Note: [Col. 0441C] By *parents*, according to French usage, blood relatives are meant. Malbrancus believes that her stepmother Beatrice was still living in these parts of Lower Lorraine, which the author calls Germany according to French usage. But Beatrice, not long after her husband’s death—that is, after 1070—went to Italy and died at Pisa on 18 April 1079, as Domnizo, a contemporary author, testifies in *The Deeds of Matilda*, her daughter. How then did Malbrancus defer the death of her husband Eustace as late as 1090? The argument he drew from Ypres is rejected below.]

While she was making the journey, she came to a church built in honour of Saint Walburga the virgin. [Note: [Col. 0441D] We have treated Saint Walburga’s *Acts* at length on 25 February, the day on which she died, and have listed various churches dedicated to her which Ida might have visited on this journey. The first is the principal collegiate church of the city of Veurne in Flanders, where another church of hers stands in the suburb. At Bruges in the same Flanders, Saint Walburga is among the older parish churches. A third principal church in Flanders, at Oudenaarde, is spacious and magnificent. Moreover, at Antwerp, where her son Godfrey held the margraviate, there is a church of Saint Walburga with a crypt in which it is piously believed that she lived or was received as a guest. Finally, there was formerly a church of hers at Liège, from which a city gate took, and still retains, its name.] As she entered the church, a double miracle presented itself for performance through her great grace. There was there a sick woman unable to walk and afflicted throughout her body with dropsy. The most gentle Ida raised her from the ground with her own hands and touched her swollen limbs. Thus healed of the infirmities which held her, the woman quickly rose and entered the church with her, safe through the merits of the woman who had healed her, lifting up her voice all the more in praise.

Having visited relatives near to her by blood and marriage, the excellent Ida exchanged for silver the estates which she had there by paternal inheritance. Having done this, she returned home in order to accomplish what she had long contemplated. On her return, with the counsel and assistance of her son, then count of Boulogne, she honourably built a monastery of Saint Vulmar [Note: [Col. 0442C] Saint Vulmar is venerated on 20 July; we have spoken above of his two monasteries.] still standing within the city walls, where she also established servants of God and the means by which they might live.

7. Then the most venerable Ida, instructed by God’s grace and always intent with cheerful mind and devout heart upon accomplishing better things, sought with great and devout prayers a certain place in the territory of Boulogne. [Note: [Col. 0442C] The monastery of Saint Vulmar in the Forest or Wood seems to be indicated, its name omitted because her husband was buried there with other great persons.] The pious mother obtained its consent and assistance and came, as it were, to restore that place to life. That place had formerly been renowned for antiquity and prosperity in temporal matters, but, as the weight of sins required, had been reduced almost to nothing.

Coming there, the venerable Ida, strengthened by the assent and counsel of the most pious Gerard, bishop of Thérouanne, [Note: [Col. 0442C] Gerard governed the church of Thérouanne from 1083 to 1099.] redeemed the properties of that place which had been challenged; she repaired the ruined church and adorned it with ornaments and books, so that with the Psalmist she might say to God, “Lord, I have loved the beauty of thy house” (Psalm 25:8). She also rebuilt the cloisters and dwellings, enriched them with revenues and many resources, and moreover adorned the place itself by dwelling there in person. [Note: [Col. 0442C] The small Saulmerium, joined about the year 1098 as an appendage, seems to be meant; we shall speak of it below.]

Meanwhile she earnestly entreated Saint Hugh, abbot, [Note: [Col. 0442D] Saint Hugh is venerated on 29 April; he died in 1109 after having been abbot for sixty years.] to send some brothers of the church of Cluny to establish monastic observance at the place called Wast. [Note: [Col. 0442D] Wast is in the county of Boulogne, where Blessed Ida is buried. Malbrancus errs in writing that it was established for Regular Canons. Others erred more seriously in understanding either the monastery of Wastines on the Lys between Ypres and Lille, or Watten between Saint-Omer and Brouckerque, founded in 1071 by Robert the Frisian, count of Flanders. Those were houses of Regular Canons and lay outside the county of Boulogne. We shall speak again below of Wast in Boulogne.] With multiplied and devout prayers she prevailed upon him to redeem her as a daughter of adoption and make her a spiritual heir among the brothers. Hearing this, Saint Hugh, beloved of God, and knowing her holiness and devotion, satisfied the desire and request of the devout lady. She then received the brothers who had been sent with tranquil countenance and joyful spirit, and showed herself toward them with diligent care and willing heart.

8. While the most blessed Ida was thus solicitous, [Note: [Col. 0442D] We suppose that some lordships were granted to her husband Eustace by William the Conqueror in return for services rendered.] a suitable reason caused her to cross into England. There, as she entered a certain church, a lame man asked her for alms. When the poor man had received in his hands from her—who denied charity to no one—the alms, he stood upright on his feet, sound and whole. Those who knew him marvelled and asked how such sudden health had happened to him. He replied: “A lady, unknown to me but most venerable and illustrious, gave me the charity for which I asked, together with the health of which I had despaired.”

The blessed lady, indeed, declined the people’s praises for this miracle and emphatically denied having done it. To many sick persons she restored health from various infirmities, not by fabricated incantation but by pious prayer and the laying on of her hand; these miracles are not recounted.

9. As religion increased in this place through the instruction of the Cluniac brothers, and likewise through the perfection of the merits of the most holy Ida, that renowned place was held in esteem far and wide while Ida, the most perfect widow and most pleasing to God, was still alive. And although the most blessed Ida appeared to have been widowed of a mortal husband, she was believed to have married an immortal spouse through a chaste and celibate life, filled with pious acts and good works. Nevertheless, she did not seek the boastfulness of a good reputation or human praise, but stored up in the shrine of her heart the grace given from heaven. For, wise through holy desires directed toward the things above, and wishing to build for their glory, she constructed a place commonly called Capella [Note: [Col. 0443D] Below, in the *Analecta*, we discuss this foundation at length, since Iperius and others attribute it to her husband Eustachius.]. Founded in honor of Mary, Mother of God and perpetual Virgin, she enlarged it with her own resources and revenues, and moreover enriched it with the most precious relics of the saints.

Since the place appeared suitable and well adapted to the monastic order, she appointed Abbot Ravagerus [Note: [Col. 0443D] Others write *Ravengerus*; this is also how he subscribes in the charter of Manasses, count of Guînes, issued in 1097.] and a community of brothers who, with the counsel and consent of John [Note: [Col. 0443D] We published the life of Blessed John on 27 January, in which it is said that he was ordained bishop in 1099 and died in 1130. Hence it seems that this counsel was initially given by Blessed John while he was not yet bishop, and later approved.] of pious memory, bishop of the Morini, were to observe, as far as possible, the rule of Saint Benedict. She loved this place with all the strength of body and spirit; she diligently cared for the nourishment of the brothers and the poor, and, intent upon the divine services, sang the psalms humbly and moderately with the brothers.

## CHAPTER III. A deaf and mute girl repeatedly healed. The pious death and burial of Blessed Ida.

10. And because the holy person strives to descend from virtue to virtue in order to be sanctified, Ida is truly reported to have done the same. At the time when she frequently stayed within the monastery, keeping watch day and night and performing the service of the monks, she came to accomplish an admirable prodigy. There was there a little girl deaf and mute from birth, and also greatly deprived of the necessities and comforts of temporal life. Venerable Ida was accustomed to extend toward her the hand of charity for her daily sustenance (Psalm 67:36).

For God, who is always wonderful in his saints, had given this girl that doubled infirmity so that he might show her healed of both infirmities, for the praise of his name and to reveal the merits of the most holy Ida. It happened that one night, when the brothers were present for the celebration of the morning praises, Ida, most beloved of God, was also there. Her mother brought the aforementioned infirm girl to the church that same night to be healed, not without God’s prompting—for it was then the celebration of a great feast.

When the sick girl was overcome by the cold, she trembled throughout her body. The sweet-speaking lady, recognizing this, beckoned her to come to her and kindly received her beneath her cloak. When the girl sensed the fragrance of the most blessed woman’s garments—or rather, the grace of her merits that was to be displayed—she immediately acquired a new power of hearing, which she had not possessed; and, having been granted speech, which she had not known, she heard the voices and melody of the singing brothers and uttered this first word: “Mother, mother.” Her mother therefore hurried to hear the daughter whom she had never before heard speak.

When this became known, Abbot Ravagerus began the *Te Deum laudamus* again; and on the following day the healed girl was granted a provision by the abbot. Many marvelous things indeed occur, so that still more marvelous things may appear at the proper time. For this girl of whom we are now speaking, not long after her healing, conceived and gave birth after losing her virginity; and she fell pitifully back into the infirmities from which she had been healed, and through this manifest lapse lost the provision that had been granted to her.

It happened, however, that her mother again brought the wretched girl to the church on the night of a certain great feast [Col. 0444B]. Through the merits of the most holy Ida she once more obtained mercy. Then the brothers who had witnessed it joyfully gave praise and thanks to God for the double miracle. Alas! The wretched girl again fell into the same sin and the same infirmities, and lost the church provision that she had possessed. But because God is merciful—he who commanded Blessed Peter to forgive the sinner not merely seven times but seventy times seven (Matthew 18:22)—he restored this sinner to health a third time, through the faith and holiness of his servant Ida. Once healed and again possessing her provision, she preserved chastity to the end.

But the most noble Ida, endowed with great devotion and merit, was solicitous toward the places she had built, clinging to them with all her heart, caring entirely for each one, abandoning neither in any way, and faithfully serving both.

11. Blessed Ida, her bodily strength evidently weakened by fasts, vigils, and constant prayers, and by the concerns for the brothers and the poor that she carried in her heart, was happily approaching the end, as though it were already near. She did not fear her death but awaited eternal recompense from the Lord. Gradually weakened, as her illness grew worse, she came to a bed of prolonged sickness. [Note: [Col. 0444D] Nothing is said here of decrepit old age, which those who maintain that she lived until 1122 or 1127 ought to recognize.]

Then, strengthened inwardly according to Paul’s saying, she performed good works with greater devotion and more abundant charity, especially toward those who belonged to the household of faith (Galatians 6:10). Stripped of worldly possessions and having given to widows, orphans, and the needy every garment that she used, as the Apostle commands, she asked the brothers, with tears and pious affection, for the holy anointing and the true and life-giving Communion.

When the monks of Wast heard that the most blessed Ida was at the point of death, they came to attend upon her rites. Having received the sacraments in the Catholic manner, holy and venerable Ida, in the spirit of prophecy, said to the brothers who had come, in a suppliant voice: “Go, knowing for certain that on the next Sunday, alive or dead, I shall remain in the church at Wast.”

When inevitable death came to her, at the predestined hour to receive its due, at midnight on Sunday, on the Ides of April [Note: [Col. 0445D] Above we said that she seems to have died in the year 1113, at more than seventy years of age; it was the Sunday called *in Albis*], the spirit of the most holy Ida departed from the prison of the flesh and from the present life; and, taking possession of eternal life, she put on the garment of joy.

12. Then, as was right, her body was reverently and with great honor prepared and brought by the brothers into the church before the altar, amid tearful lamentations and indescribable sighs. The mournful voices of widows and orphans, and of those whose care she had undertaken, grew louder; they moved the tears of many who heard them.

Very swift rumor also proclaimed everywhere that the most venerable Ida had died [Col. 0445B], and brought crowds of both sexes to her dead body. For the abbot and monks of Saint Vulmar, since her husband Eustachius [Note: [Col. 0445D] Eustachius, although the son of Count Eustachius I, is called “the Elder” in relation to Eustachius III, his son, who appears still to have been alive when this Life was written.] the Elder had been buried among them, sought by quasi-hereditary right to have the body of his wife beside her husband.

Likewise, the canons of the city of Boulogne, out of reverence for her son Count Eustachius—and also because he had first rebuilt their monastery—demanded that the body of the most holy Ida be buried among them. But the brothers of the church where she had died [Note: [Col. 0446D] The church of Blessed Mary at Capella.] asserted that she ought justly to be buried there.

Yet neither petition prevailed, nor did the reasons they presented, against the prophecy that the blessed woman had uttered: that, alive or dead, she would certainly remain at Wast on the next Sunday. Her body was therefore removed and, the saint’s prophecy having been fulfilled, carried to the place where it lies. After several religious persons and a great crowd of the common people had gathered there, it was committed to burial worthily and honorably, after excessive tears had been shed by those standing around, with lamentations and many cries.

While alive, the servant of God loved this place with heart and mind, and promoted its growth in every way she could. Now, even after death, she protects and strengthens it by her merits and by the miracles that proclaim them. The weak and the sick, coming to her tomb on account of various illnesses, are healed if they do not waver in faith, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER IV. The incorrupt body. Miracles after death.

13. After the most blessed Ida had been buried in the place that is still commonly called Wast, as divine decree had promised her, some people of each sex began to be healed of various illnesses; unwavering faith brought them to her tomb. The fame of the miracles, spreading not only through the surrounding region but also far and wide, made known the merits of the most holy Ida.

Fame does not remain silent but cries out, because proven truth compels it. Thus the sweet-smelling report of the saint’s miracles flew even to Alemannia, to people near her kinsfolk. Glorifying the Lord for what they had heard, they nevertheless considered how they might transfer the body of Blessed Ida there. They resolved to send certain men more experienced in such matters to the place where she lay; but they accomplished nothing against God’s decree.

When the brothers of the place learned of their deceitful cunning, they took greater care to guard the treasure. Then, at a suitable time, as reason required, the brothers of that place, after taking the counsel of prudent men, appointed a day to inspect the body. When many people from the region had gathered, the tomb was opened, and those present were permitted to see the body of the most holy Ida intact and her clothing perfectly clean [Col. 0446B].

No stain or defilement had been able to corrupt her, although she had lain dead there for many days, and none has corrupted her to this day. No foul odor issuing from her offended those standing nearby; rather, a sufficient sweetness filled the place. We testify that this ought rightly to be believed by the faithful as a great miracle.

14. Meanwhile, among the signs that attest the excellence of her life, she was also granted after death the power to drive out demons, as the emphatic testimonies of certain people affirm. A wicked spirit appeared to a certain young man from a village called Vertum in the likeness of an ox, and, taking away his senses, entered into him. The demon made the unfortunate young man’s face exceedingly savage, his voice hollow and terrifying, as is its custom; it made him look around with fierce and dreadful eyes, emit foul spittle from his throat, utter hiccups, and gnash his teeth.

When his parents had taken him to certain relics of the saints without obtaining any benefit, they finally brought him to the tomb of Blessed Ida. The Lord, looking upon him from on high through the merits of the saint, restored him after three days healthy and unharmed, and lacking nothing in the faith that the enemy had taken from him.

15. Another miracle, not unlike this one, is also asserted by many to have been performed through the merits of the same beloved servant of God, and is rightly recalled with honor as a great event. A certain village, whose name is . . . . . [Col. 0446D], lies not far from the monastery, where blessed Ida still bestows many benefits of healing upon the sick. A demoniac from the aforementioned village was brought bound before her tomb, while his parents and friends tearfully and suppliantly begged the most blessed woman’s aid for him.

The merciful and compassionate Lord, accepting their devotion and faith through the merits and intercessions of venerable Ida, just as he healed the paralytic lowered before him through the roof tiles, so freed this man from the oppression of the demon and, reconciled to himself, sent him home amid the rejoicing of those who had brought him.

16. Another miracle worthy of admiration and remembrance must be made known to the faithful: through divine clemency, for the praise of his name and the veneration of the most holy Ida, he performed it through her merits, equal to the miracles mentioned above.

The same enemy of the human race, who always prowls about like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour (1 Peter 5:8), attacked a certain woman from the territory of Boulogne. He expelled her good spirit and established a seat for himself within her. After her parents had traveled with her to many holy places without obtaining any benefit, they returned home.

The wretched woman was tormented by the demon more fiercely than before. Having lost the powers of soul and body, she lay bound, tearing and rending herself. Her mother, remembering the holiness and power of the most holy Ida in such illnesses, came with her daughter and several relatives to the church of Saint Michael, where the most holy Ida performed many healings. These relatives rejoiced in advance at the girl’s liberation and recovery.

After they had kept vigil with the sick woman for three days before the presence of an altar, they prayed with great devotion that the monks of the church would allow the sick woman to be carried before the tomb of Saint Ida. This was done. It was then the Vigil of Blessed John the Baptist. After the evening offices had been completed, through the merits of Saint Ida the girl obtained both forms of healing: she began to call her mother and declared herself healthy and unharmed [Col. 0447C].

Thus, through this woman, the grace of God’s customary compassion shone forth through the intervention of blessed and venerable Ida, just as it is said in the Gospel of another person: “The deaf hear, the mute speak, and the one possessed by a demon is freed” (Matthew 11:5). In the morning, because of the miracle that had been heard of, not only the parents but also many people from the neighboring area came with offerings and presented praises and thanks to God and Saint Ida; they departed rejoicing.

17. Blessed Ida therefore did not abandon after death the love of God, which is first and gives birth to love of neighbor, and which she is known to have possessed while alive. Through this love she is proved to have healed various illnesses in relatives and also in certain people far away by nationality.

It happened that a grievous and wretched fever seized violently the daughter of her son, the countess of Boulogne, named Matilda [Note: [Col. 0447C] Machtildis or Mathildis, born to Eustachius III and Mary, daughter of Malcolm, king of Scotland. She married Stephen, count of Blois and Mortain, and through her he became king of England, being crowned not long afterward, namely on the Kalends of January in the year 1136. Queen Matilda survived until the year 1153 and was buried in the royal villa of Faversham, where she herself had established a community and residence of monks, as John, prior of Hexham, who was then living, writes in his appendix to Simeon of Durham. Since the author of this Life does not mention the marriage, we suppose that he wrote before that time.].

After she had been worn down for some time by excessive suffering, she finally, trusting and relying upon the holiness of the most blessed Ida and also upon the blood relationship from which she had descended, presented herself with many others at the venerable tomb to be healed. While she sought the merits of the most blessed woman with devout and repeated prayers, after a short delay she departed healthy and unharmed.

Thus venerable Ida, the servant of God, fulfilled the commandment in the Law that enjoins one to love a neighbor (Leviticus 19:13). She also fulfilled that saying of Wisdom: “I love those who love me” (Proverbs 8:17), by granting the grace of healing to those who served her and to strangers also, if they supplicate her from the heart.

18. To a certain monk named Hugh, who served her most devoutly night and day and was severely afflicted by fever, she granted the grace of an unexpected recovery because of the intimacy and service that he had offered to the saint while she was alive and after her death.

But you, O Lord, have mercy on us. Thanks be to God.

[Col. 0447]

# ANOTHER LIFE. BY JOHN GUILLEMANS, REGULAR CANON

*(From a manuscript of the Abbey of Rouge-Cloître.)*

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0447D]

1. As we review the festivals of holy widows through the swiftly passing seasons of the year, we ascribe the immense praises of divine virtues to God alone. Nevertheless, by their examples we strive to hasten toward love of our heavenly homeland, so that, with the supreme Author’s help, we may be able to proceed with perpetual efforts along the narrow path that leads to life, and attain through them and with them the sixtieth fruit, arriving at the dwelling of perpetual beauty where the light of supreme brightness shines forth. There we shall hear that delightful voice of the Lord saying: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34), in return for the labors in which you diligently contended; and there you shall receive unfading crowns from him who says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you; for my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30).

And the Apostle says: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or hunger, or cold, or death, or life, or danger, or the sword?” (Romans 8:35). And again the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I will except that it burn?” (Luke 12:49).

Comforted by these sacred supports, let us trample underfoot the snares of the ancient enemy, so that, with the most blessed Ida, a most noble lady—whose deeds we shall briefly insert here, both because they are virtuous and because they suit our purpose, and because she, who is mentioned here, sprang from the stock of the Carolingians—we may reach the flower-bearing seat, there to reign with her forever in the heavenly realms. Amen.

## HISTORICAL ACCOUNT OF HER LIFE

2. There was a certain virgin, a distinguished young woman sprung from a most noble lineage, named Ida. Her father, named Godfrey, stood first before the emperor and was renowned as count of Ardennes; her mother, no less noble, was called Doda. At that time there was a famous count of Boulogne named Eustatius, son of Eustatius and Matilda, countess of Brussels. Saint Ida, having become the wife of this second Eustatius, bore him three sons, namely Godfrey, Baldwin, and Eustatius.

She educated these sons in every discipline and in the fear of God, taught them to perform deeds worthy of princely status, and formed them in holy and good conduct. Of these, Godfrey, after the death of his uncle Godfrey the Hunchback, possessed the greater part of Brabant and was afterward elected king and prince in Jerusalem, after the Holy Land had been recovered by the Christians; after him came his brother Baldwin. They became renowned for many victories against the treacherous people of the Saracens. And although Blessed Ida was the mother of such sons, she did not allow them to be suckled by others but nursed them at her own breasts.

3. When Count Eustatius, her husband, saw that she was lovable to all, agreeable to everyone, and praiseworthy in every respect, he did not endure this with displeasure; rather, he urged her, as she persevered in goodness, to strive toward what lay ahead and toward better things. When holy Ida learned of the good will toward her of her husband, Count Eustatius of Boulogne, she began to build churches, refresh and enrich the poor, and show herself perfect in every work of charity and mercy.

While she excelled nobly in these devout pursuits, her husband, Count Eustatius, died in the Lord [Col. 0449D]. After his burial she returned to her parents. Blessed Ida lived most holily after her husband’s death, and shone with miracles both during her life and after her death.

At length she first came to a certain church dedicated in honor of Saint Walburga the virgin, in order to pray. Seeing at a distance a woman oppressed throughout her body by dropsy, she raised her from the ground with her own hands; and, praying and healing her, allowed her to return home.

4. When the venerable Blessed Ida came to the brothers of the Cluniac church, she earnestly and devoutly begged Saint Hugh, the most reverend abbot of that church [Note: [Col. 0449D] She seems rather to have accomplished this through letters or messengers sent to Saint Hugh.], to send some of his disciples whom he had rigorously trained in regular discipline to the place called Wast. With urgent prayers she implored him that she might be given an inheritance among the brothers. The holy and God-beloved Hugh, hearing this, fulfilled her request, sending brothers to construct a new monastery.

5. After this it happened that the most blessed Ida sailed to England. When she entered a certain church, she encountered a poor lame man asking alms from her. She not only gave him a monetary gift, but also extended her hand to him, raised him up, and healed him.

Afterward, returning from England, she established her residence at Brussels, the most noble city of Brabant, or in its vicinity, for a large part of her life. Near Genappe [Note: [Col. 0450D] We shall discuss below Genappe and the nearby village of Baisy, the allod of Blessed Ida.], she lived honorably with her sons. A sacred baptismal font is still shown there, in which her firstborn, Godfrey, is said to have been initiated.

6. It happened afterward that one night, when the most holy Ida was present with the brothers at the morning praises, a certain woman came to her in supplication, bringing with her her deaf and mute daughter. The blessed lady restored the girl to her former health and obtained that on the following day the abbot of that place should grant the healed girl a provision.

Not long afterward, however, the girl, at the instigation of the enemy of the human race, conceived and gave birth by a certain man, and consequently fell back into her former infirmities and lost the provision obtained for her. But at length, through the merits of venerable Ida, she again obtained mercy, and the brothers then gave thanks to almighty God for the double miracle.

After a short time the aforementioned girl relapsed again, conceived, and gave birth; and on this account she fell a third time into her former infirmities. Blessed Ida took pity on her a third time and, after prayer, restored her to her former health.

7. At length venerable Ida, having continually disciplined her weak and delicate body with vigils, fasts, and prayers, began to grow ill and to fail markedly from day to day; thus she was approaching the end as though it were already near. When the monks of Wast heard that their most holy spiritual mother was at the point of death, they began to grieve greatly over her death.

At midnight on Sunday, on the Ides of April, the spirit of the most sacred Ida left the prison of the flesh and laid aside the vesture of the present life; and, possessing eternal life, she was worthy to put on the garment of joy.

8. At length, as was right, the glorious lady’s body was brought by the brothers before the altar amid tearful lamentations and was honorably buried there. While alive, the servant of God loved this place; now, even after death, she strengthens and protects it by the miracles that proclaim her merits.

For the weak and sick, afflicted by various illnesses, come to her tomb and, if they do not waver in faith, carry away health. The body of the most blessed Ida was found intact after a long period and untouched by every form of corruption. At her tomb a certain possessed man was likewise freed from a demon, as was also a certain possessed woman. To a certain man named Hugh, who served that most devout lady and was severely afflicted by fever, she granted the grace of health because of the familiarity and service that he had offered her so often during life and after death; through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, the triune and one God, throughout infinite ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0451]

# ANALecta on the Deeds of Blessed Ida from Various Authors

## CHAPTER I. Benefits Granted to the Church of Lens and the College of Canons

[Col. 0451B]

1. Lens, or Lendium, which Baldric called the castle of Lens in Book II, chapter 22 of his *Chronicle of Cambrai*, is a town of present-day Artois, four leagues from Douai and five from Arras, with an extensive territory belonging in ancient times to a county that formerly pertained to the jurisdiction of the counts of Boulogne. Count Eustachius I gave it to Lambert, his second-born son. When Lambert died childless in 1055, this county came into the power of Eustachius II and Blessed Ida his wife, who endowed the college of canons of Lens with estates and privileges; whether they also founded it appears disputed.

Jacques Meyer, in Book II of his *Annals of Flanders*, under the year 1028, writes as follows. The church of Lens began to have priests who were canons, whence you may read this inscription there:

> In the thousandth year, thirty less two,  
> The company of canons began to enter this choir.

Georgius Colvenerius follows Meyer in his notes on Baldric’s *Chronicle*, adding: “It is still a collegiate and parish church at the same time, in which there are a dean and twelve canons.” Baldric merely writes that “there is a monastery of canons, where Saint Vulganus rests,” concerning whom we shall treat on 2 November.

Colvenerius proves in many ways that Baldric wrote Books I and II of his *Chronicle* toward the end of the life of Gerard I, bishop of Cambrai, around the year 1040. Malbranc did not consider these matters when, in Book VIII, chapter 49 of *De Morinis*, he wrote that a church dedicated to the Virgin Mother of God and likewise to Vulganus had been built by Blessed Ida, and that a college of canons had been established. It is worthwhile to quote his words.

2. Ida, the wife of Count Eustachius, observed that the town of Lens was served by a very modest church. Therefore, she gently complained to her husband Eustachius and said that she intended to build there a magnificent church in honor of the Mother of God. Eustachius readily agreed—indeed, he declared that his foreign-born wife’s intention was most pleasing to him, since she was moved to increase her husband’s own territories with such pious monuments. What marriage could be imagined more Christian than one in which the wife, having left her own homeland, adorns her husband’s towns and dominion with churches and priestly offices?

Thus the Marian basilica arose. When Saint Liethertus, prelate of Arras and Cambrai, came to consecrate it after its completion, Ida and Count Eustachius decided to join Saint Vulganus, whose body they possessed, as a second patron of the church. There was also another considerable incentive for this: that the great former archbishop of Canterbury in England, having abandoned his overseas possessions, had crossed the sea to the Morini at the prompting of an angel and had cultivated the people of Boulogne excellently for seven years. He would not have abandoned them had not fear of the hospitality that arose from the excessive fame of his miracles driven him to seek another desert.

Hence it is not surprising if his sacred body passed from the men of Arras to the town of Lens, as though to the county of the prince of Boulogne. Indeed, it may perhaps have happened by divine providence that the lordship of Lens passed to the people of Boulogne.

Thus Malbranc writes at length concerning the basilica erected in honor of the Virgin Mother of God and Saint Vulganus, the archbishop, whom others rather call a confessor. If he was indeed a bishop, he should be numbered among those who, while Britain was still held by the Anglo-Saxons in idolatry, fled to Cambria or Wales and from there crossed into these regions. We discussed this more fully on 4 February in the Life of Saint Lietphard, likewise a bishop of Canterbury among the said Welsh, who later came to Belgium and was crowned with martyrdom.

But let us return to the institution of the canons, which Malbranc continues as follows.

3. “The distinguished splendor of the Church invited Ida to greater and better things, and to adorn it with a notable college of canons. Having drawn up charters, she assigned estates and rich revenues, establishing several priestly offices over which a dean would preside, to be chosen by the canons themselves for the integrity of his life and the necessary qualifications for that office.

“At Lens there were two smaller sanctuaries, looking to Saints Laurence and Leodegarius the martyrs as their patrons. Bishop Lietbert converted their episcopal revenues to the use and administration of the canons.

“Moreover, the verses formerly read in the church of Lens, which indicate the time of the institution’s founder, should be punctuated as follows:

> In the thousandth year, thirty twice, less one,  
> The company of canons began to enter this choir.

“For I find that in the printed books this is referred to the year 1028, with the words *ter deno, bis minus uno*—“thirty, less by two”—and incorrectly. For it is sufficiently clear that in that year Ida had not yet enjoyed the use of this light, and that twice thirty years above a thousand must necessarily be understood. By counting one year less, you will arrive at the year 1059; namely, Ida entered her marriage chamber in 1057 and, on her honorable arrival, adorned Lens, ordering that the basilica be built and, two years later, introducing the college of canons.”

Thus Malbranc rather subtly twists those ancient verses. We think instead that the church had been founded long before, and that Eustachius I, count of Boulogne and Lens, and his wife Matilda established the college of canons in 1028.

A charter of donation by Eustachius II and Blessed Ida, printed by Miraeus in Book I, chapter 38 of the *Belgian Diplomas*, and in a more condensed form in the *Notice of the Churches of Belgium*, chapter 101, moves us to this opinion. We give here what pertains to the matter, as follows.

4. “I, Eustachius, count of the people of Boulogne, and my wife Ida, especially desire to exalt the church in this place called Lens, honorably established by our predecessors. At the beginning of its foundation it was endowed with lands, books, and liberal provision. But the presumption of rashness and the envy of the devil, burning the church together with its books and the privilege together with its seals, thought to destroy everything. But what envy destroyed, with God and our lord Bishop Lietbert favoring us, we wish to repair through goodwill.

“We therefore grant the canons free power to assume whichever advocate they wish, who shall preside over their property and causes for as long, and no longer, as they please. We also declare that the altars of Saint Mary and Saint Laurence are free from every form of servitude. And so that our church might be equal to the others that enjoy the endowment of liberty, namely Saint Mary of Arras and Saint Gaugericus of Cambrai, we labored greatly and, thanks be to God, with the approval of Bishop Lietbert brought the matter to completion . . . In the year 1070 from the Incarnation of the Lord, indiction VIII, we accomplished these things in the basilica of Saint Mary.”

From these words it is clear that the church had been established by their predecessors, but was burned through the envy of malevolent persons; that it was repaired and restored by Eustachius and Blessed Ida, and dedicated anew. Saint Lietbert indicates this in the following charter in these words:

“I, Lietbertus, by the grace of God bishop of Cambrai, in response to the just petitions of Count Eustachius and his wife Ida, countess, permit the church that, with God’s merciful cooperation, we consecrated at Lens in honor of the holy Mother of God, and the support or administration of the canons of that place, to be free from every exaction of the bishop and his officials, namely from tax or revenue, from this time forward.

“And if the church of Saint Gaugericus of Cambrai, or rather the church of Saint Mary of Arras, is known to possess any greater liberty, let the canons of Lens possess it in similar peace. Acted at Lens in the basilica of Saint Mary in the year 1070, indiction VIII.” [Col. 0454A]

The rest, with the subscriptions, may be read in Miraeus, especially the confirmation of the revenues and possessions belonging to the said church.

## CHAPTER II. Monasteries Built and Restored in the County of Boulogne; the Monastery of Capella Founded

5. We have already discussed the monastery of Saint Vulmar within the walls of Boulogne, erected by Blessed Ida when she was already a widow, and another monastery of Saint Vulmar restored in the Wood. A third, the monastery of Wast, is added to these: she built it and dedicated it to Saint Michael, and there she was also committed to burial.

Malbranc, in Book IX, chapter 35 of *De Morinis*, says that he himself was there and that it was two leagues from Boulogne, “toward Wisant and Wasconvillare,” as it was formerly called; but he is mistaken when he writes that it was a college of canons. It was a Benedictine monastery following the Cluniac reform, with monks sent from Cluny itself by Saint Hugh the abbot, as the author of the Life—who seems to us to have been from Wast—explains at length:

6. The fourth monastery constructed by the same woman, likewise while she was a widow, was the monastery called Saint Mary of Capella, in which she laid aside this mortal life in order to depart for a better one. John Iperius, in his *Chronicle of Bertin*, chapter 39, paragraph 2, attributes this foundation to Eustace and Blessed Ida, as though Eustace had still been alive in the year 1090. His words are these:

“In the year of the Lord 1090, Eustace, count of Boulogne, and his wife Ida, parents and progenitors of that most renowned and illustrious Godfrey of Bouillon and Baldwin, later kings of Jerusalem, founded the monastery of Blessed Mary of Capella in the land of Merck, near Calais, in a place formerly called Brocham, and established monks from Ham there. There the countess Ida herself offered eleven hairs of Blessed Mary the Virgin, which she had obtained from Hastulf the Iberian king through great supplication, together with other relics of the saints.”

Thus John Iperius, created abbot of Saint Bertin in 1369 and deceased in 1380. Lambert of Ardres, however, who was two hundred years his senior, attributes this foundation to Blessed Ida the widow in his *Chronicle of Guînes*. Its previously unpublished chapter 31 is headed as follows: “How Ida, countess of Boulogne, founded the monastery of Blessed Mary of Capella.” Since chapter 30 had dealt with the monastery of Ardres, restored by Baldwin, count of Guînes, the following matters are related in the said chapter 31.

7. Therefore, in imitation of so pious an undertaking, Ida, daughter of Godfrey, formerly duke of Lotharingia, at one time widow of Eustace, count of Boulogne, mother of Godfrey and Baldwin—who, in the kingdom of Judaea, in the holy city of Jerusalem, after Antioch had been bravely conquered and completely liberated from the Arabs, Saracens, and other foreign and unbelieving peoples by a strong hand and outstretched arm, became kings of Jerusalem—and mother of the most noble Eustace, count of Boulogne, a woman venerable in name and holiness of life, founded, in the territory of Merck, in a village formerly called Brocham, a church in honor of the blessed, glorious, and ever-virgin [Col. 0455A] Mary, and established a distinguished monastery of religious life.

In that same church she deposited and placed, more precious than gold and precious stone, eleven extremely precious hairs of the same blessed Virgin Mary, which she had sought out and obtained from the Iberian king Anstulf, not without the greatest labor and diligent effort. Together with countless other relics of the saints, offered to that holy place, she established that these should be honored above all. At the same time, she established there a holy community of monks, taken from the monastery of Ham, recently built by Engelram, lord of Lillers, together with the venerable man Ravenger, its abbot, and other brothers of honorable and religious life, so that they might perpetually and continually serve the everlasting God, for the memory of the holy Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, and for the perpetually increasing honor due her; and she introduced them into God’s prepared dwelling.

Indeed, this most celebrated place of Saint Mary, while the new and tender infancy of holy religion was still sprouting there, distinguished for its virtues, glorious for the frequency of its miracles, most holy in charity and religion, exceedingly enriched by abundance of goods, and exceptionally well supplied with persons worthy of every honor and promotion through the discipline of their morals and their instruction in the liberal arts no less than in theological Scripture, stood out and surpassed all neighboring places in the proclamation of its fame—may every stain of envy be absent. For God continually illuminated it with his divine presence, visited it with that heavenly grace with which the blessed Virgin had formerly been suffused, and there granted innumerable benefits to those who piously sought them.

8. “That place is therefore believed to have been of such great renown and veneration that certain nobles of the surrounding land, and other faithful people of Christ, if they possessed little churches, or any other ecclesiastical benefices, or even small estates, strove either to confer them upon that place entirely and in full, or to bind and subject them to it under some title of subjection. They thought and reconsidered—or rather, they firmly believed and recognized—that their little churches would stand and serve with freer revenue if they were subjected by some bond of subjection to so holy and venerable a place than if they remained and persisted in whatever freedom had been assigned to them. For in this way, since they themselves also adjudged this to them, they would serve under a better name and shine with the title of greater authority.

“That place is known to be entirely free from every imputation of disgrace, exaction, and improper custom. Hence it is called a *capella*—a chapel, I say, of the supreme pontiff, namely, the lord pope, constructed in honor of Blessed Mary the Virgin. In recognition and memory of this freedom, the church of that free place owes the Roman Church twelve denarii each year. Collected together over five or ten years, these are sent to Rome by the abbot of that most holy place, as an acknowledgment, as we have said, of its freedom.

“The abbot of that place also possesses such dignity in the Roman Church that, if it happens that the abbot himself is present in the Roman Church at the lord pope’s Mass, he must hold the subdeacon’s book while that same subdeacon pronounces the Epistle. But, lest we prolong our words to the detriment of our soldiers, who are murmuring, let it suffice to have said this very little about this most holy place and the religious monks who inhabit it. At a more suitable place and time, with greater and more fervent zeal, we shall turn our writing pen to insert certain other matters concerning them.”

Thus far Lambert. Immediately afterward, in chapter 32, he treats of the construction of the church of Ardres and places before it, as its model, “the monastery of Blessed Mary of Capella, built by Ida, countess of Boulogne.” Near the end he says: “The church of Blessed Mary of Capella was founded in the year 1091.”

9. This is a very ancient and noble monastery of the order of [Col. 0456B] Blessed Benedict, situated in the march of the district of Poitou, Charroux of Saint Saviour, from which the aforementioned Engelram, lord of Lillers, brought monks and placed them in the monastery of Ham, constructed around the year 1084 between Lillers and Aire. From there Ravenger was brought with several monks and was first appointed abbot of Saint Mary of Capella. He subscribed to the donation made by Manasses, count of Guînes, to the monastery of Andres in 1097, in the previously cited Du Chesne, page 38, from the account of William, abbot, in his *History of Andres*.

Among his successors was Theodoric, who in 1144 received from Baldwin, lord of Ardres, the church of Ardres with its college of canons, on the condition that whenever one of the canons or clerics of that church died, a monk would be substituted in his place. Then he also purchased from the same lord Baldwin the mill of Bramis with the adjoining lands, where he established a monks’ cell and appointed Caradoc its first prior, later making him abbot in the church of Saint Mary of Capella.

Lambert, son of the aforementioned lord of Ardres and priest of the church of Ardres, describes all these matters at length in his *History of Guînes*, chapters 137 and the following three chapters; Du Chesne draws upon him on pages 1609 and following. These matters had to be set out more accurately against Iperius, whose errors Meyer, Miraeus, Malbranc, and others reproduced. The authority of the writer also had to be confirmed, since in the *Life* above he asserts that the monastery of Blessed Mary of Capella was constructed by Blessed Ida the widow.

The gift of eleven hairs of the Virgin Mother of God donated by Blessed Ida to the church of Capella was said by Iperius to have been received from the Iberian king Ansculf, by Malbranc, book VIII, chapter 80, from “Haistulf, king of the Irish.” At that time several kings still ruled in Ireland; later, around the year 1172, they were conquered by the English. The name, however, is so clearly Gothic that it seems much more advisable to understand it as referring to some petty king of that nation in Iberia, that is, Spain.

Malbranc states that the monastery of Capella was situated “between Mark and Escalles, called Calais in the following century, on an estate under the jurisdiction of Boulogne called Broucham, in the territory of Mark.” Lambert of Ardres, however, places it on the borders of Merck.

In the general register of the benefices of the Gallican dioceses, in the diocese of Boulogne, [Col. 0457A] page 10, there are mentioned “eleven collations or presentations of parish priests, and nine chaplaincies dependent upon the abbot of Capella.” Among these are the chaplaincies of the churches of Ardres, Oye, and Mark. From this it may be very clearly inferred that the ancient site of this monastery was changed by the continuous wars between the English and the French.

## CHAPTER III. Various Benefits Granted to the Monasteries of Bouillon, Affligem, Saint Bertin, and Lens. A Vision in Ecstasy of the Capture of Jerusalem

10. Godfrey the Bearded, duke of Lotharingia and father of Blessed Ida, had formerly founded the priory of Saint Peter in his town of Bouillon, receiving monks from the monastery of Saint Hubert. Godfrey of Bouillon added a certain endowment, by a charter of donation sealed at Bouillon in the year 1094, published by Miraeus in his *Book of Donations*, chapter 67, and in his *Notice of the Churches of Belgium*, chapter 11. In it Godfrey says:

“When I had reported this intention of mine to my mother Ida, daughter of the aforesaid duke, and to my brothers Baldwin and Eustace, then, with their counsel and willing consent, we assigned and donated our church of Baisy, held by our own hereditary right, for the increase of the aforesaid alms, to be perpetually given to Blessed Peter and Blessed Hubert. In order that this gift might be valid and firm, I brought the same mother and my brothers with me to Bouillon, and in the presence of my nobles we together placed upon the altar of Blessed Peter, without any accusation or contradiction, the vesting of the aforesaid church at Baisy.”

Baisy is a village in French Brabant, toward the county of Namur, commonly called Basy, in the territory of Genappe, on the river Thyle. Above we said that the inhabitants believe Godfrey of Bouillon was born and raised in this village. Genappe itself, or Genapium, situated between Nivelles and Gembloux, is a sufficiently notable town with an ancient castle, where there is a marketplace or tribunal commonly called the high court of Lotharingia. Justice is customarily administered there in civil, capital, and feudal cases, and the place still represents something of Lower Lotharingia.

Blessed Ida granted the tithes of this place to the monastery of Affligem, situated in the same Brabant between Brussels and Aalst. Miraeus published the charter of this donation in his *Book of Donations*, chapter 68, and in his *Notice of the Churches of Belgium*, chapter 119. From it we excerpt the following.

11. “I, Ida, countess of Boulogne, humble servant of Christ, wish it to be known to those present and to those who will come after, as a sign of my affection toward my lords and brothers, namely the monks of Novum Monasterium, which the ancients called Hafflingem.

“Since their fellowship and devotion to religion have pleased me and many others, I have considered it worthy to commend myself to the prayers of such men, and not to place my hope in uncertain riches, but rather to share these riches with them. Therefore, in my allod and in the village called Genappe, for the salvation of my soul, and also for the soul of my father, Duke Godfrey, and of my lord Count Eustace, I have given to the aforesaid brothers, to be held in perpetuity, the church with its tithes and all its revenues, my sons Godfrey, Eustace, and Baldwin cooperating with me in this matter.

“My son Duke Godfrey also donated five holdings of land in the same village of Genappe to these brothers. I later granted them, in addition, certain surrounding portions amounting plainly to a sixth holding, free and exempt from every comital charge and tributary census. Moreover, whatever they claimed for themselves, since they had possessed it from the time of the earlier donation—whether in woods, pastures, or arable lands—I granted them with the same freedom with which I had held it. I also granted them every share in the woodland and in the remaining common usufruct, my sons likewise consenting to this with me.

“This was done at Utrecht, in the church of Saint Servatius the Confessor, with the relics of Saint Gertrude also present, having been brought there at that time for a similar matter, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1096, in the year of the departure of the Christians against the pagans toward Jerusalem.”

12. As Blessed Ida gradually became burdened by advancing age, she did not cease to devote herself to pious works. Rather, increasing her merits, she endowed the monastery of Saint Bertin. Miraeus published the charter of this offering in his *Book of Donations*, chapter 70, and in abbreviated form in his *Notice of the Churches of Belgium*, chapter 121. From the former we insert the following:

“Since everyone recognizes that death is uncertain and imminent, the daily decline of worldly affairs clearly shows how necessary it is for us to provide for our salvation by persevering in good works and gifts of alms. Therefore I, Ida, by the grace of God countess of the people of Boulogne, make known to all, present and future, that for the salvation of my soul, and also for the soul of my lord Count Eustace, and for the safety of my sons Eustace, Godfrey, and Baldwin—who have departed for Jerusalem against the attacks of the pagans at the apostolic command—I have granted to Lord Lambert, abbot of the monastery of the same confessor of Christ, Bertin, and to the brothers serving God there, to possess in perpetuity, all the customs and the comital jurisdiction, and whatever belonged to me, of the land which Ondigir and Berewoldus gave to God and Saint Bertin as alms for the poor.

“This was done on the following condition: that none of the heirs of the aforesaid men should dare thereafter to usurp anything from that land, nor should the count of Boulogne, nor anyone on his behalf, exact anything from its customs or comital jurisdiction. Rather, it should remain forever free and undisturbed for the use of the poor.

“Done in the village of Merck, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1098. Sign of Ida, glorious countess…”

13. The arms of her sons prevailed in the Holy Land, “while Blessed Ida, their mother, commended their military undertaking to God with the most ardent prayers and watched from the territory of the Morini,” as Malbranc explains from the records of the monastery of Saint Vulmar, book IX *On the Morini*, chapter 6, in his own words:

“What has been intimated concerning Ida, that most holy mother, must be explained more fully. After she had built the little Saulmerium, as they call it—that is, a small monastery, almost an appendage to the larger monastery of Saint Vulmar—and had endowed it splendidly with monks taken from that monastery, she arranged, for the latter part of the preceding year or the first months of this year, 1099, through Gerard, bishop of Thérouanne, for it to be consecrated to the lamenting or sorrowful Virgin.

“Thus Blessed Ida spent her days in prayer in that special shrine of the Sorrowful Virgin. Before the divine Mother and Saint Vulmar, protectors of the place, she most ardently pleaded the military cause of her son Godfrey. They did not disappoint the woman’s good purpose. Rather, while she was praying and had been carried away in ecstasy, they caused her in a certain manner to see her son Godfrey encouraging his men from a wooden fortress, hurling a dense shower of weapons against the enemy, and, with heroic assault, climbing the walls before all others. In short, one might say that images of all the events that took place there concerning her offspring had been presented to her from heaven across so great a distance.

“For, when I had already been staying at Boulogne for several years, I discovered in that shrine of the divine Virgin and Saint Vulmar a panel on which the following had been written:

‘Here Ida, while attending the sacred mysteries, saw her son Godfrey invading Jerusalem by an extraordinary stratagem and with heroic strength, and also crowned king of Jerusalem.’”

“Since these events took place at different times, it appears that the intervening events and circumstances also fell beneath the eyes of her mind.”

Then, in chapter 8, after discussing Godfrey’s coronation as king, he adds concerning Blessed Ida:

“Although this took place within the precincts of the temple of Jerusalem, that royal display and the pious rejection of the royal diadem were conveyed to the eyes of Ida, that most holy mother, while she was attending the sacred rites of Mass in that new monastery of the ascetics of Vulmar, who served the sorrowful Virgin, at the farthest limits of the Morini.”

14. When King Godfrey died in the year 1100, Baldwin, another son of Blessed Ida, was appointed in his place. Then the third son, Eustace, returned to his mother Blessed Ida and to the county of Boulogne. He arranged for the college of canons of Lens to be confirmed by Lambert, bishop of Arras, with the support of his mother, Blessed Ida. Malbranc printed the bishop’s diploma from the manuscript records of Lens in his notes to chapter 16 of book IX, beginning as follows:

“I, Lambert, by the mercy of God bishop of Arras, yielding to the just and honorable petitions of the distinguished Count Eustace and of his noble wife Mary, countess, and also of the mother of the aforesaid count, Ida, a religious countess, wish it to be known to all our sons, present and future, that what they demand from our ministry, at the request of the aforesaid persons, we have confirmed as ratified and stable for all time by the privilege of our authority, in the freedom of the spirit, for the Church of Lens and the canons of that church…

“Given at Arras, in the year of Christ 1106, on the seventh day before the Ides of June, in the fourteenth indiction, in the twelfth year of the pontificate of Lord Lambert, bishop of Arras, while Philip was reigning as king in France, Robert the Younger was count of Flanders, and Eustace was count of the people of Boulogne and Lens.”

[Col. 0459]

## ECCLESIASTICAL DONATIONS OF BLESSED IDA

(See above, columns 453, 454, 457, 458.)

[Col. 0459]

## LETTER OF OSMUND, BISHOP OF ASTORGA, TO IDA

(Published by Mabillon, *Analecta*, new edition, page 433.)

### NOTICE

This letter was written around the year 1059, when Ida, wife of Eustace, count of Boulogne, built a church for the Virgin Mother of God in the castle of Lens, in the district of Arras—the later Lens—and established a college of canons there. She also sought relics from every quarter and brought them into the basilica she had built, namely the relics of Saint Vulgan, whose body Balderic testifies to be resting in the monastery of the canons of Lens in book II, chapter 22, of his *Chronicle*. I therefore believe that Ida obtained from Spain, through Bishop Osmund, the hairs of Blessed Mary discussed in this letter. See Jacob Malbranc, *On the Morini*, book VIII, chapter 48, where he treats of the Church of Lens.

[Col. 0461A] Osmund, by the grace of God bishop of Astorga, to Ida, noble countess of Boulogne, greetings in Christ.

Since your supreme prudence desires to investigate, and moreover to discover, how the city of Astorga came to possess so many relics of the hairs of Saint Mary, Mother of God, and from where it obtained them, we have decided, with the greatest devotion, to attend to your holy request and investigation, as far as we have found in the statements of our books, and to do so briefly.

We have found that, when the persecution of the pagans was pressing hard, seven disciples—Torquatus and Iscius together with five others—sailed from Jerusalem to Spain, carrying these and many other relics, and brought them as far as Toledo. The king of Spain and all his people received them honorably and, rejoicing, held them in great reverence, as was fitting.

When the race of the Saracens once again pressed hard upon Spain, the bishops and all religious men fled to our mountains, namely those of Astorga, which take their name from Astorga. They carried away whatever they considered especially precious and stored everything in our city of Astorga and in Oviedo.

We, their successors, retaining them in this manner and not resisting the command of our king, namely Alfonso, sent you a large portion of the better and more distinguished relics, entreating you to remember the Church of Astorga.

I, King Alfonso, saw and read this charter, and whatever is written in it I confirmed with my own hand.

[Col. 0461]

## GENEALOGY OF THE COUNTS OF BOULOGNE, EDITED BY L. C. BETHMANN

(In Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, *Scriptores*, volume IX, page 299.)

### [NOTE]

The genealogy of the Carolingian house did not, in its earliest period, ascend beyond Ansbert. But after the Carolingians had obtained the kingdom, there were those who derived them through Blithild from the Merovingians, so that they might appear to possess by legitimate hereditary right what in reality they possessed as a kingdom only through force and the consent of the people. Genealogies of this kind are set out below on page 296 and in *SS.* II, 308. Several manuscripts likewise present the genealogy of those who, after this lineage had been deprived of the kingdom of the Franks, descended from it through Duke Charles. Although these manuscripts differ greatly among themselves, they can all nevertheless be reduced to one form.

A. The primary form, composed around the year 1096, which descends from Priam to Godfrey of Bouillon. It is contained in:

1. Brussels manuscript no. 9823, twelfth century, formerly belonging to Pamelius, then to the Society of Jesus at Bruges.
