It contains the histories of Robert and Fulcher, a description of the Holy Land, catalogues of the bishops of Jerusalem, kings, and popes, a description of the Lateran sanctuary, a miracle in Saxony, the seven wonders of the world, a genealogy of the kings of the Franks, a poem on Muhammad, and our genealogy.

2. Vatican Christina manuscript no. 236, which has a genealogy after the letters of Hildebert; it is perhaps of the same type.

B. We call those manuscripts copies of the second family which placed after the genealogy of Charlemagne the account entitled “How the kingdom of the Franks was separated” from that genealogy. They are:

1. Marchiennes, now Douai manuscript no. 838, twelfth century; concerning it, see Pertz, *Archiv*, VIII, 430. It contains nearly the same material as A1 and B4.

2. Brussels manuscript no. 9837, twelfth century, after Bede’s *Chronicle*.

3. Vatican Christina manuscript no. 596, twelfth century, after the catalogue of the popes.

4. Vatican Christina manuscript no. 712, parchment, containing the histories of Robert and Fulcher; R., a description of the Holy Land; catalogues of the bishops of Jerusalem; a description of the Lateran sanctuary; a catalogue of the popes; this genealogy; a description of the sanctuary of Constantinople; and a lament for Charles of Flanders.

5. Vatican Christina manuscript no. 637, paper, seventeenth century, containing Einhard’s *Life of Charles*, the *Life of Louis*, and this genealogy.

6. The manuscript of Saint Medard of Soissons, greatly interpolated and continued to the year 1241, published by D’Achery, *Spicilegium* II, 493.

C. The third family consists of the manuscript of Saint-Quentin, later belonging to Pamelius and then to the Society of Jesus at Bruges, now Brussels, written in the year 1227 by Peter the monk. It begins with Charles the Bald and ends with Eustace. It follows Hugh of Fleury; see Pertz, *Archiv*, VII, 531. From it the genealogy was published by Miraeus, *Diplomata Belgica* I, 363; Le Roy, *Balduinus Avesnensis*, part 2; and Butkens, *Trophées*, I, proofs 5.

D. The manuscripts of the fourth family begin it with Charlemagne and bring it down to Baldwin VI, or approximately to the year 1172.

1. Orval, now Luxembourg manuscript no. 22; concerning it, see *Archiv*, VIII, 593. It contains Freculf, John’s work on the king and the seven sages, Turpin, and our genealogy.

2. Lobbes, published by Martene, *Thesaurus* III, 1431, and from him by Brial XIII, 585.

3. A Parisian seventeenth-century copy among the Baluzians, shelf II, page 1, no. 3.

L. C. Bethmann.

This is the genealogy of King Charles, who was called the Great, from whose lineage sprang King Godfrey and his brother King Baldwin [Note: [Col. 0463] So A and B3. “This is the lineage from which sprang King Charles, who was called the Great,” B2. “Here begins the genealogy from which sprang Charles the Great, king of the Franks and emperor of the Romans,” B6.].

[Col. 0463]

[Col. 0463A] Priam begot Faramund. Faramund begot Clodio. Since Clodio was without a son, his nephew Merovech succeeded him in the kingdom. Merovech begot Childeric. Childeric begot Clovis, whom Saint Remigius baptized; at his baptism, his name being changed, he was called Louis. Louis begot Lothar and his brothers. Lothar begot Chilperic and his brothers. Chilperic begot the great Lothar by Fredegund. Lothar begot Dagobert and his sister Blithild. [Note: [Col. 0463] The following material through Blithild is absent in B6.]

Dagobert begot Clovis and Sigebert. Clovis begot Lothar, Childeric, and Theuderic. Theuderic begot Clovis and Childebert. Childebert begot the younger Dagobert. The younger Dagobert begot Lothar. When this Lothar was seven months old, he was entrusted for upbringing at the royal estate called Kala, and the mayors of the palace, Ragenfrid and Chilperic, invaded the kingdom.

Blithild, sister of the elder Dagobert, begot Arnold by Ansbert, an illustrious man. Arnold begot Arnulf, later bishop of Metz. Duke Arnulf, who afterward became a bishop, begot Aistulf, bishop of Metz, and also Chlodulf, Qualchis, and Ansigis. Duke Ansigis begot the elder Pepin by Begga, daughter of Pepin, mayor of the palace. Pepin [Note: [Col. 0463] Much interpolated material is found in B6.] the elder and duke begot Charles Martel. Duke Charles begot Pepin the Short, king. King Pepin begot Charles the Great, [Col. 0464A] king. [Note: [Col. 0463] “Who, summoned to Rome by Pope Adrian I to defend the affairs of the Church, received from the aforesaid pope and from 153 religious bishops and abbots assembled there in council the right and power to elect the pontiff and to order the apostolic see. In addition, he granted him the dignity of the patriciate and decreed that archbishops and bishops in each province should receive investiture from him, and that no bishop should be consecrated by anyone unless approved and invested by the king; and he bound anyone who acted against this decree with the chain of anathema. Later, Pope Leo III, successor of the aforementioned Adrian, anointed King Charles emperor in the church of Saint Peter on Christmas Day.” Added by A. Here D begins, with what precedes omitted.]

Charles the Great begot Louis the Pious Augustus. Louis begot Lothar, Pepin, and Louis by Ermengard, and Charles the Bald by Judith. Charles [Note: [Col. 0463] C begins here.] the Bald begot Louis, of whom it was said that he did nothing, because he lived only two years after his father’s death. Louis, son of Charles, [Note: [Col. 0463] I have corrected the text thus; “son of Louis” in B1, B6, and C.] begot Charles the Simple and Carloman.

Charles the Simple was captured by Heribert. This Charles begot Louis by Ogiva. Louis begot King Lothar and Duke Charles by Gerberga. King Lothar begot the young Louis, [Note: [Col. 0463] “King Louis the Young died, and his maternal uncle, namely Duke Charles, brother of Lothar, succeeded him in the kingdom. But because Hugh Capet, duke of the Franks, prevented it, he was not anointed king; rather, the aforesaid Hugh captured the aforesaid Charles and drove him from the kingdom, as is written above.” Added by B6.] and Duke Charles, brother of King Lothar, begot Ermengard and Gerberga.

Ermengard begot Albert, count of Namur. Albert begot the Albert who is now living, [Note: [Col. 0463B] The third, who died around 1105.] [Note: [Col. 0463] Thus B6; “who is now dead” in C. The words “who is now living” are absent in B1, B3, and D2. The words “and his brother Henry, count of Durbuy” are absent in B6 and C, which instead has: “from whom four sons were born: Frederick, provost of Saint Lambert, Godfrey, Henry, and Alberic.”] and his brother Henry, count of Durbuy. [Note: [Col. 0463B] Durbuy, in the duchy of Luxembourg.]

Gerberga, sister of Ermengard, begot [Note: [Col. 0463B] “Of Lambert the Bearded, count of Leuven, who died around 1015.”] Henry the Elder of Borsella. Henry the Elder begot [Note: [Col. 0464B] False. Henry the Elder was not the father of Lambert and Matilda, but their brother.] Count Lambert, his brother Henry, and their sister Matilda.

Count Eustace of Boulogne married this Matilda, and she bore him two sons, Eustace and Lambert. Eustace took as his wife Ida, daughter of Duke Godfrey, [Note: [Col. 0464B] The fourth, or the Bearded, duke of Lotharingia.] a woman noble in birth and character; and she bore him three sons, Eustace, [Note: [Col. 0463] B1 adds “count of Boulogne.”] Godfrey, who is now duke of Lotharingia, [Note: [Col. 0463] Thus B6: “Godfrey, now duke of Lotharingia,” C, and perhaps B2. The words “who is now duke of Lotharingia” are absent in A, B, and D (printed abbreviation *p. n. e. d. L.*, referring to *qui nunc est dux Lotharingiae*).] [Note: [Col. 0464B] He died on 18 July 1100.] and Baldwin. [Note: [Col. 0463] A, B1, B3, and C add “kings of Jerusalem,” undoubtedly added in another hand in the original manuscript. B6 has the whole passage as follows: “And she bore him four sons, William, Godfrey, who is now duke of Lotharingia, Baldwin, and Eustace. Godfrey and Baldwin became kings of Jerusalem. Eustace begot a daughter named Matilda, whom Stephen, king of the English, later married.” After this, B adds: “Whoever wishes to know how the kingdom of the Franks was separated from the genealogy of Charlemagne may learn it from this point onward,” and so forth. These brief additions concern only French history. B ends with the words “Louis. This man is of the lineage of Charlemagne”; B2 ends with “Philip begot Louis”; B3 ends with “Philip begot Louis, Louis begot Louis, Louis begot Philip,” to which someone else added: “Philip begot Louis, Louis begot the good Louis, Louis begot Philip.” B5 ends with “through her he possessed Poitiers and all Aquitaine.” B6 continues as far as “Dagobert had already died; the year was 1241.” In place of all these, D proceeds immediately after Godfrey and Baldwin as we have set out above.]

[Col. 0465A] D adds:

Eustace, brother of Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, married Mary, daughter of the king of Scotland, and begot Matilda. Matilda, married to Stephen, son of Stephen, count of Blois, begot Mary, an abbess. When the legitimate heirs in Boulogne had died out, Matthew, son of Theoderic, count of Flanders, unlawfully married the abbess, and revived the hereditary line by begetting two daughters, and restored her to her position.

Albert [Col. 0466A] of Namur [Note: [Col. 0465A] The third.] begot Godfrey and Henry, count of La Roche, [Note: [Col. 0465A] La Roche in the Ardennes.] father of Matilda, who bore James of Avesnes, [Note: [Col. 0465A] Killed in 1192.] Godfrey, however, his brother, begot Henry, count of Namur, who had no children, [Note: [Col. 0465A] Male children; for he had two daughters.] and his sister Alithia, [Note: [Col. 0466A] Alice, or Adelicia, Adelaide.] who, married to Baldwin, count of Hainaut, [Note: [Col. 0466A] The fourth.] bore Baldwin. He married Margaret, daughter of Theoderic, count of Flanders, and begot a son bearing his own name. [Note: [Col. 0465] After this, D1 and D2 repeat only the names Charles the Great, Louis Augustus … Mary the abbess, as published by Martene on page 1432. We have omitted these, since they are entirely without value.] [Note: [Col. 0466A] Baldwin VI, born in 1171.]

# SECOND APPENDIX: MONUMENTS CONCERNING THE HOLY WAR

[Col. 0465]

## LETTER OF THE EMPEROR OF CONSTANTINOPLE TO ROBERT, COUNT OF FLANDERS, AND TO ALL CHRISTIANS, ASKING THEM TO SEND HIM AID AGAINST THE PAGANS

(Year 1095.)

[Martene, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum* I, 267, from two manuscripts, one belonging to the monastery of Saint Albinus, the other to the monastery of Saint-Evroul.]

[Col. 0465B] [Note: [Col. 0465B] It appears to have been written in the year 1095, when Alexius sent an embassy to Urban II, who was celebrating a council in the city of Piacenza, and earnestly implored him and all the faithful of Christ to provide him with some aid for the defense of Holy Church against the pagans. The pagans had already destroyed that region and, as Bartholomew of Coutances says, had occupied it as far as the walls of the city of Constantinople.]

To the lord and glorious Robert, count of the Flemings, and to all the princes of the entire kingdom, lovers of the Christian faith, both laymen and clerics, the emperor of Constantinople sends greetings and peace in the same Lord Jesus Christ, and in his Father and the Holy Spirit.

O most renowned count and greatest consoler of the faith, I wish to make known to your prudence how grievously the most holy empire of the Christian Greeks is daily afflicted by the Pincinaoi [Note: [Col. 0466C] Alternatively, Pincinates], how it is continually plundered and seized without respite, and how various massacres and unspeakable killings and mockeries of Christians [Col. 0466B] are perpetrated.

But since there are many evils that they commit and, as we have said, evils beyond telling, let us mention a few of the many, though they are nevertheless horrible to hear and disturb even the air itself. For they circumcise Christian boys and young men upon Christian baptismal fonts, pour the blood of the circumcision into those same fonts in contempt of Christ, and compel them to urinate upon them. Thereafter they lead them violently around the church and compel them to blaspheme the name and faith of the Holy Trinity. Those who refuse they afflict with various punishments and finally kill.

As for noble matrons and their daughters, after plundering them, they mock them by committing adultery with them one after another like animals. Others, having shamefully corrupted virgins, set their mothers before their faces and compel them to sing wicked and lustful songs until they have completed their own abominable acts of sexual violation. For thus we read that it was done in ancient times among the people of God, when the impious Babylonians, after their various profanations, mocked them, saying: “Sing for us one of the songs of Zion” (Psalm 136:3). So now, during the violation of their daughters, they compel the mothers to sing wicked songs, whose voices, as we believe, sound not like singing but rather like lamentation, as it is written concerning the death of the innocent: “A voice was heard in Ramah, mourning and great wailing: Rachel weeping for her children, and she would not be comforted because they are no more” (Matthew 2:18).

But although the mothers of the innocent, represented by Rachel, were unable to be comforted over the death of their children, they were nevertheless able to be comforted over the salvation of their souls. These women, however—and this is worse—can in no way be comforted, because they perish both in body and in soul.

But what more? Let us come to worse things. They abuse with the sin of Sodom men of every age and rank—that is, boys, adolescents, young men, old men, nobles, slaves, and, what is worse and more shameless, clerics and monks—and, alas, woe!—bishops: something that from the beginning had neither been said nor heard of. They have already burst one bishop under this abominable sin.

They pollute and destroy the holy places in innumerable ways and threaten them with worse things. And at this, who does not weep? Who does not sympathize? [Col. 0467C] Who does not shudder? Who does not pray?

For nearly the whole land from Jerusalem to Greece, and all Greece with its upper regions—namely, Lesser Cappadocia, the other, Greater Cappadocia, Phrygia and Bithynia, and Lesser Phrygia, that is, Troy, Pontus, Galatia, Libya, Pamphylia, Isauria, Lycia, and the principal islands of Chios and Militene, together with many other regions and islands that we cannot now enumerate—up to Thrace, has already been invaded by them. Almost nothing remains except Constantinople, which they threaten to take from us very soon unless the help of God and of the faithful Latin Christians comes swiftly to our aid.

For they have also invaded the Propontis, also called the Aridus, which flows from the Pontus beside Constantinople itself into the Great Sea [Col. 0467D], with two hundred ships. The Greeks captured these ships from them and built them; and they compel the Greeks, willing or unwilling, to man them at the oars. They threaten to seize Constantinople swiftly, as we have said, both by land and across that same Propontis.

These few examples of the innumerable evils committed by this most impious people we have told and written to you, count of Flanders, lover of the Christian faith. Let us leave the rest aside, lest we weary the readers.

Therefore, for the sake of God’s name and out of devotion to all the Christian Greeks, we ask that you bring here, for my aid and that of the Christian Greeks, as many faithful warriors of Christ as you can gather in your land—great and small, together with those of middling rank [Col. 0468A]—and that, just as last year they somewhat freed Galicia and the other western kingdoms from the yoke of the pagans, so now they may attempt to free the kingdom of the Greeks, for the salvation of their souls.

For although I am emperor, I know of no remedy or suitable counsel for myself; instead, I am always fleeing from the presence of the Turks and the Pinemaci [Note: [Col. 0467D] Alternatively, Pincinates.], and I remain in each individual city only until I sense their arrival nearby. I would rather be subject to your Latins than to the pagan shrines.

Therefore, before Constantinople is captured by them, you must fight with all your strength, so that you may joyfully receive in heaven a glorious and ineffable reward. For it is better that you possess Constantinople than that the pagans do, [Col. 0468B] because it contains the most precious relics of the Lord: the statue to which he was bound; the scourge with which he was flogged; the scarlet cloak with which he was clothed; the crown of thorns with which he was crowned; the reed that he held in his hands in place of a scepter; the garments of which he was stripped before the cross; the greater part of the wood of the cross on which he was crucified; the nails with which he was fastened; the linen cloths found in the tomb after the resurrection; twelve baskets of fragments from the five loaves and two fish; the intact head, with hair, and the beard of Saint John the Baptist; and the relics or bodies of many innocents, of certain prophets, apostles, martyrs, and especially Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, as well as confessors and virgins. Because of their great number, we have omitted listing them individually.

All these things ought nevertheless to be possessed by Christians rather than by pagans, and they will be a great defense for all Christians if they possess them; but their loss will be a disaster and a judgment. If they will not fight for this reason and prefer gold, they will find more gold there than in the whole world. For the treasures alone of the churches of Constantinople—in silver, gold, gems, precious stones, and silk fabrics, that is, pallia or vestments—could suffice for all the churches of the world.

Yet all these treasures are immeasurably surpassed by the treasure of the mother church, namely Holy Sophia, that is, the Wisdom of God; and without doubt it can be compared with the treasure of Solomon’s Temple. What more shall I say about the infinite treasure of the nobles [Col. 0468D], when no one can estimate the treasure of the merchants and peasants? What is found in the treasures of former emperors? I say with certainty that no tongue will be able to recount it, since not only the treasure of the emperors of Constantinople is kept there, but the treasure of all the ancient Roman emperors has also been transferred there and hidden in the palaces.

What more shall I say? Whatever is plainly visible to human eyes is nothing in comparison with what is hidden there. Run, therefore, with all your people, and fight with all your strength, lest such a treasure fall into the hands of the Turks and the Pincinates, because, although they are innumerable, another sixty thousand [Col. 0469A] are still expected each day. I fear that, through that treasure, they may gradually seduce our greedy soldiers, just as Julius Caesar once did, when he invaded the kingdom of the Franks out of greed, and as the Antichrist will act when he is to capture the whole world at the end of the world [Col. 0470A].

Act, therefore, while you have the opportunity, lest you lose the kingdom of the Christians and, what is greater, the Lord’s sepulchre, and lest you receive judgment rather than a reward in heaven. Amen.

[Col. 0469]

## LETTER OF THE PATRIARCH OF JERUSALEM AND OTHER BISHOPS TO THE WESTERNERS

They report a victory won over the pagans and request further assistance against them. (Year 1097.)

[MARTEN, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 271, from a manuscript of Saint Ebrulfus.]

[Col. 0469B] The patriarch of Jerusalem, and the bishops, both Greek and Latin, together with the entire army of the Lord, offer to the Western Church fellowship in the heavenly Jerusalem and a share in the reward for its labor.

Since we know that you rejoice in the growth of the Church and believe that you are eager to hear both adverse and favorable news, we therefore make known to you the success of its expansion. Let it be known, then, to your charity that God has triumphed for his Church in eleven principal cities and two hundred fortresses, both in Romania and in Syria, and that we still have one hundred thousand armored men besides the common people, although many were lost in the first battles.

But what of this? What is one against a thousand? Where we have one count, the enemy has eleven kings; where we have a troop, the enemy has a legion; where we have a soldier, [Col. 0469C] they have a commander; where we have an infantryman, they likewise have a count; where we have a fortress, they have a kingdom.

Yet we, trusting neither in numbers nor in strength nor in any presumption, but protected by the shield of Christ and by justice, with George, Theodore, Demetrius, and blessed Basil—true soldiers of Christ accompanying us—have entered and continue to enter the enemy’s ranks without fear. In five major pitched battles, with God granting the victory, we have conquered.

But why say more? On behalf of God and ourselves, the patriarch and bishops and the entire order of the Lord earnestly command and pray, [Col. 0470B] and our spiritual mother cries out:

“Come, my dearest sons, come to me; receive the crown destined for you from the beginning of the world from the sons of idolatry who rise up against me. Come, therefore, we pray, to serve in the army of the Lord, to that same place where the Lord fought, where Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example so that you might follow his footsteps. Did not the innocent God die for you? Let us therefore die also—not for him, but for ourselves—so that, by dying to the world, we may live for God.

“Yet we need not die, nor fight very much. We have endured what was more difficult, although the camps and cities that we must hold have greatly reduced our army. Come, therefore; hasten to receive your reward. Behold, the roads are everywhere marked by the shedding of our blood. Bring nothing with you except what is necessary to reach us. Let only men come; women should for the present be left behind. Of a household in which there are two men, let the one more fit for war come, especially those who have made vows. Unless they come and fulfill their vows, we excommunicate them and remove them from communion with the Church. Let the patriarch, the apostolic representative, and the bishops do the same, so that such men may not even have burial among you unless they have a definite reason for remaining.”

Farewell.

[Col. 0469]

## LETTER OF ANSELM OF RIBEMONT TO MANASSES, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

On the expedition to Jerusalem.

### NOTICE

(*Literary History of France*, VIII, 496.)

Anselm, count of Ribemont and lord of several other lands, already known for his pious generosity toward churches and for his extraordinary valor in the holy war, deserves to be known also among the writers [Col. 0471] of his time. He descended from the ancient counts of Valenciennes and brought into the world excellent qualities suited to sustain his birth. He was praised above all for his great courage, generosity, magnificence, and marvelous aptitude for arms: *in regenda militia mire industrius*, “remarkably diligent in directing military affairs”; or, as William of Tyre expresses it [Note: [Col. 0471] Book VII, chapter 17], *vir in armis strenuus*, “a vigorous man in arms.”

The famous expedition for the liberation of the Holy Land having been resolved upon at the Council of Clermont in 1095, Anselm wished to take part in it, like so many other Christian lords. The Chronicler of Andres, listing those from Second Belgium who joined the journey, names him before all the others (p. 375), immediately after Godfrey of Bouillon, who was its leader. All the historians of this war bear witness to the heroic valor displayed there by Anselm [Note: [Col. 0471] Ray. de Ag., p. 164; Mab. *Mus. It.*, p. 204, no. 97; Guib. de Nov., *Ges. Fr.*, p. 643; Will. Tyr., ibid.; Du Ches., vol. IV, pp. 807–808.]. But after escaping the dangers of the sieges of Nicaea and Antioch, he met his end before the castle of Archos, or Arcas, two leagues from Tripoli. The Crusaders, unable to take it at once, resolved, without necessity, to besiege it. The siege lasted three months less one day, from the fourteenth or fifteenth of February 1099 until the following thirteenth of May. Anselm, one of the most zealous commanders in advancing it, performed new feats of valor there and lost his life from a stone that struck him in the head. His death, regarded as a kind of martyrdom in accordance with the idea then formed of this sort of warfare, occurred in February or March, since he is named among the first who were killed there.

All the besiegers mourned him greatly; and after taking away his body, they buried it with due honor [Note: [Col. 0471] Mab. ibid., p. 211, nos. 104–105.]. On the night preceding his death, Anselm had foreseen it in a vision, reported differently by the historians, but of which he took advantage to prepare himself seriously [Note: [Col. 0471] Ray. de Ag., ibid.; Mab. ibid., pp. 210–211, no. 104.]. Almost all these same writers speak of him only with high praise, some calling him an illustrious hero, others a man worthy of eternal remembrance, *perpetua dignus memoria* [Note: [Col. 0471] Will. Tyr., ibid.].

Among the praises that Guibert, abbot of Nogent [Note: [Col. 0471] Guib. de Nov., *Ges. Fr.*, book VI, chapter 8], gives Anselm of Ribemont, he emphasizes above all the service he had rendered to all men of letters by teaching them what had taken place most memorably during the Crusade while he himself was bearing arms there. Guibert regarded this service as an outstanding mark both of the hero’s lively faith and of his ingenious attentiveness. From the account given by this writer, two different reports by Anselm on the subject can clearly be distinguished. One gave the details of the Crusaders’ capture of Nicaea in Bithynia and of everything that had happened to them as they passed through Romania and Armenia. The other contained an account of the siege and capture of Antioch and what followed from them, as well as of the various battles that the Christian army had had to sustain against the emirs, princes, or governors of Galapia, Damascus, and Jerusalem. These two reports were addressed to Manasses II, archbishop of Reims, to whom the author had entrusted his land of Ribemont.

Unfortunately, only the second of these two writings has been preserved; and it shows that the notice given of it by Guibert is entirely accurate. Anselm composed it a few days after the feast of Saint Peter—that is, at the beginning of July—after the Christians had become masters of the citadel of Antioch, and consequently in the year 1098 [Note: [Col. 0471] M. Fabricius assigns this report only to 1099; but the author, as has been seen, had already lost his life in February or March of that year.]. He provides fairly detailed information about the principal events, but treats them in a manner that is too precise and too concise. His narratives, moreover, are agreeable, lively, and animated; and one can readily feel that an eyewitness, indeed one of the participants, is speaking. In general, Anselm’s style is at once simple and noble, natural, and interwoven with pious touches that give it new distinction.

Distance from his homeland and the tumult of arms did not make him forget what he owed to his vassals. For this reason, he asks the prelate to whom he addresses his writing to maintain peace in his lands and prevent the churches and the poor from being oppressed. In speaking of the Christian army’s successes, he attributes them less to the merits and valor of the Crusaders than to the prayers offered for them. He takes this occasion to implore Manasses to continue rendering them this good service, to induce others to do the same, and not to forget those whom death had taken from them. The charitable care Anselm had shown in having prayers offered for these men was extended to him himself after his death. The same archbishop, announcing his death to his fellow bishops, exhorted them to commend to God the repose of the soul of this brave lord.

At the beginning of this account, Anselm reminds Manasses of the one he had already sent him concerning the capture of Nicaea and the Crusaders’ passage through Romania and Armenia. Abbot Guibert, who had both reports in his hands and drew much from them for his History of the Crusade, valued them so highly for the certainty of their facts that he preferred their authority to that of all the other writers on the holy war, who were already numerous when he himself undertook to write about it.

## IN THE NAME OF THE LORD

Here begins the letter sent by the holy pilgrims who, out of love for God, journeyed to Jerusalem in the year 1099 from the Incarnation of the Lord, during the pontificate of Pope Urban, in the seventh indiction.

[Col. 0471]

[Col. 0471A] To his lord and father, M., by the grace of God venerable archbishop of Reims, A. of RIBEMONT [Note: [Col. 0471A] Ribomontium, Riburgismons, Ribodium, but best of all Ripemontium, situated on a mountain [Col. 0472A] beside the banks of the Isara as it flows past, two leagues from Augusta.], his faithful man and humble servant, sends greetings.

[Col. 0472A] Let your sublimity know, reverend father and lord, that although we are not physically present, nevertheless, while absent, we ask your help daily in our hearts; [Col. 0473A] and not only yours, but also that of all the sons of the holy mother Church of Reims, in whom we place very great confidence. Since you are also our lord, and since the counsel of the entire kingdom of France depends especially upon you, we make known to your fatherhood some of the favorable and adverse events that have happened to us. Let the rest be made known through you, so that you may likewise sympathize with us in adversity and rejoice with us in prosperity.

We informed you how we besieged and captured Nicaea and, departing from there, traversed the whole of Romania and Armenia, and how we fared. Now it remains for us to speak briefly of the siege of Antioch, of the many dangers endured there, of the countless battles fought against the king of Galapia, against Damascus, [Col. 0473B] and finally against that one at Jerusalem.

Antioch was besieged by the army of the Lord with a courage and boldness beyond description. What unheard-of clashes you would have witnessed there at a certain western gate! How wonderfully you would have seen them leaping forth daily through six gates, had you been present! Both sides—that is, they and our men—were fighting for freedom and life.

In those days our princes, wishing to press the city more and more closely, first besieged the eastern gate. After strengthening a fort there, Bohemond placed part of his army in it. But when our princes had then grown somewhat confident, God, who chastises every son whom he loves, punished us so severely [Col. 0473C] that scarcely seven hundred knights could be found in our army—not because good and courageous men were lacking, but because almost all the horses had perished either from lack of food or from excessive cold.

The Turks, however, abounding in horses and every necessity, surrounded our camp daily. A certain river lay between us and them and served us as a wall. Their castle was also nearly eight miles away; those entering and leaving it killed men from our army every day. Our princes went out against them and, with God’s help, put them to flight and killed many of them.

Seeing, therefore, that he had been harmed, the Antiochene summoned Damascus to his aid. By God’s providence, Damascus encountered Bohemond and the count of Flanders, who had gone with part of our army to seek provisions [Col. 0473D]; with God’s help preceding them, Damascus was defeated and driven to flight by them.

Still concerned for his safety, the Antiochene sent to the king of Galapia and, promising him a very large sum of money, stirred him to come with all his forces. When he arrived, our princes left the camp and, with God’s help, defeated and routed fifteen thousand Turks with their king that day, with seven hundred knights and a few infantrymen, killing many of them. Thus, having recovered not a few horses in that battle, our men returned rejoicing in victory.

From that day onward, therefore, growing stronger and recovering their strength, they took counsel about besieging the western gate, which cut us off from the harbor, wood, [Col. 0474A] and pasture. By common agreement, Bohemond and the count of Saint-Gilles went to the harbor to attack those who were staying there [printed *addicturi*; corrected in the source to *adituri*]. Meanwhile, those who had remained behind with the baggage, wishing to win a reputation for themselves, went carelessly after lunch one day to that western gate, from which they were disgracefully repulsed and put to flight.

On the third day afterward, Bohemond and the count of Saint-Gilles returned and sent to the army’s princes that they should come to meet them, so that together they might besiege the gate. While the others delayed for a short time, Bohemond and the count of Saint-Gilles were defeated and routed by the Turks. Thus our men, grieving and likewise lamenting their disgrace—for a thousand of our men had fallen that day—after arranging their affairs, defeated the Turks, who were resisting and holding back the soldiers [source reading uncertain: *militum multum*], and put them to flight. On that day nearly one thousand four hundred of the enemy perished, some by weapons and some in the river, which had been swollen by the winter rains [Col. 0474B].

After these events, our men began to strengthen the fort. Having furnished it with a multiple rampart, a very strong wall, and also two towers, they stationed there the count of Saint-Gilles with crossbowmen and archers. Oh, with what danger and what labor we strengthened it! One part of our army guarded the eastern fort, another the camp, while all were engaged in strengthening the fort. Among those there, the crossbowmen and archers guarded the gate. The rest, including the princes themselves, did not cease casting up the embankment, carrying stones, and building the wall.

Who could count the many tribulations [Col. 0474C], which are sufficiently apparent even without being spoken of—hunger, inclement weather, and the flight of fearful soldiers? The harsher these hardships were, the more eagerly our men endured them. Nevertheless, we think that one event must not be passed over in silence: one day the Turks pretended that they would surrender the city, and deceived us so thoroughly that they received some of our men among them, while many of theirs came out to us.

While these things were happening, since they possessed no faith whatever, they laid an ambush for our men. There Wallo, the constable, was killed. Many others, both of theirs and of ours, also fell.

A few days after this had passed, it was announced to us that Corbaran, commander of the army of the king of Persia, had conspired for our destruction and had already crossed the great river Euphrates with an innumerable army [Col. 0474D]. But God, who never abandons those who hope in him, did not abandon his own. Instead, he mercifully gave us the city of Antioch on the Nones of June, when three citizens handed it over to us. After the city had been devastated, we killed all the pagans in it that same day, except for certain men defending themselves in the city’s castle.

On the following day Corbaran arrived with the king of Damascus, the duke of Baldach, the king of Jerusalem, and many others, and besieged the city. We, besieged by them while besieging the few men mentioned above in the city’s castle, were compelled to eat the flesh of horses and donkeys.

On the second day after their arrival, they killed Roger of Barnonisvilla among us. [Col. 0475A] On the third day they attacked the castle that we had fortified against the Antiochenes, but achieved nothing. They did, however, wound Roger, castellan of the island, and he died from the wound.

Seeing that they were accomplishing nothing on that side, they climbed into the mountains. We went out against them, but were defeated and routed by them. They themselves entered the walls with us, and we remained together throughout that day and the following night, separated from one another by about the distance of a stone’s throw.

At dawn on the following day, they invoked Baphomet in loud voices. We, praying to our God in our hearts, attacked them and drove them all from the city walls. Roger of Bithiniacavilla died there. Then, moving their camps that same day, they besieged all the city gates, hoping to compel us to surrender through lack of food [Col. 0475B].

When God saw his servants placed in such tribulation, he stretched out his helping right hand, and by divine revelation mercifully revealed the lance with which Christ’s body had been pierced. It had been hidden in the church of Saint Peter beneath the pavement, at a depth of nearly two men’s heights.

After this precious pearl had been found, the hearts of all our men revived. On the vigil of the Apostles Peter and Paul, having taken counsel among themselves, they sent messengers to Corbaran to say:

“Thus says the army of the Lord: ‘Withdraw from us and from the inheritance of blessed Peter; otherwise you will be driven away by arms.’”

When he heard this, Corbaran drew his sword and swore by his kingdom and throne that he would defend himself against all the Franks [Col. 0475C]. He said that he possessed the land and would always possess it, justly or unjustly. For he ordered them not to hear another word from him until, abandoning Antioch, they denied Christ and professed the law of the Persians.

After hearing this, the Christians, cleansed by confession and firmly armed through receiving the body and blood of Christ [Col. 0476A], prepared for battle and went out through the gate. Hugh the Great with his Franks went out first of all. Then came the count of the Normans and the count of Flanders. After them came the venerable bishop of Le Puy and the line of the count of Saint-Gilles. After him came Tancred. Last of all came Bohemond, utterly unconquerable.

When the lines had been arranged, with the Lord’s lance and the Lord’s wood leading the way, they began to fight with the greatest confidence. With God’s help, they put the aforementioned Turkish princes to confusion, completely defeated them, and drove them to flight, killing countless numbers of them.

Returning in victory, we gave thanks to the Lord and celebrated the feast of the Apostles with the greatest joy. That same day the castle was surrendered to us, after the son of the king of Antioch had been put to flight with Corbaran. The king himself, on the day the city was surrendered, had fled into the mountains and had been killed by peasants [Col. 0476B].

We have sent these matters to your fatherhood so that you may rejoice in the deliverance of the Christians and in the freedom of Antioch, the mother Church, and so that you may pray to God more devoutly for all of us. For we place great confidence in your prayers, and whatever progress we make we attribute not to our own merits but to your prayers.

We therefore now ask you to preserve our lands in peace and defend the churches and the poor from the hands of tyrants. We also ask you to take counsel concerning the false pilgrims, so that they may either once again take up the sign of the life-giving cross with repentance and complete the Lord’s journey, or be subjected to the danger of excommunication [Col. 0476C]. Know for certain that the gateway to the land is open to us; and among our other favorable developments, the king of Babylonia, having sent messengers to us, said that he would obey our will.

Farewell. We beseech you in the Lord Jesus that all to whom this letter comes pray to God for us and for our dead.

[Col. 0475]

## CHARTER OF ODO, BISHOP OF BAYEUX

By which he grants the monastery of Saint-Vigor of Bayeux to Jarenton, abbot of Saint-Benignus of Dijon. (Year 1096.)

[Dom PLANCHER, *History of Burgundy*, vol. I, documents, p. 32, from the archives of the abbey of Saint-Benignus of Dijon.]

[Col. 0475D] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, Odo, bishop of Bayeux, considering the enormity of my sins and also weighing the investigation that the strict Judge will make into my deeds, for the remedy of my soul and of the souls of my parents, and for the repose of the bishops of this holy see of Bayeux, and of the canons who have fallen asleep, who now are, and who shall be, establish and give to God and Saint Benignus, to Jarenton, abbot of Dijon, and to his successors and to the brothers, future and present, of that same monastery [Col. 0476D], the monastery of Saint-Vigor of Mont Chrismat with its appurtenances, namely the full tithe of the entire village in which the monastery is situated and of everything belonging to that same village; and whatever belonged to the church that had previously stood there, together with its priest and all its customary dues; and, in addition, half of that entire village, both in people and territory and in its other revenues, together with half of the annual market [Col. 0477A] held there on the feast of All Saints; and four burgesses, two at Campo Florido and two at Olibert’s Bridge, with their land and customary dues; and at a certain village called Fisherman’s Harbor, the land on which they dwell, together with its ship and customary dues.

I also give the full tithe of the entire village of Chricea, with the land and everything belonging to the church; and the church of Detor; and those of Crusseium, Ulferes, and Colgrino, with the full tithes and lands belonging to those churches, and the lands of the priests.

All these possessions, just as the aforesaid Church of Saint-Vigor has appeared to possess them long ago, including in the time of William, my brother, king of the English and count of Normandy, and whatever I myself give, I transfer, approve, and grant to the Church [Col. 0477B] of Dijon, with the consent and approval of the canons and of our faithful men, while preserving the reverence and due obedience owed to the holy mother Church of Bayeux.

I also establish that the burial of my body and of the bodies of my successors and of the canons shall take place there in perpetuity, with the approval of those same canons. But if the place should grow so greatly that an abbot could rightly be appointed there—that is, if its revenues should become sufficient to support this—then the abbot of Dijon and the bishop of Bayeux shall deliberate together and jointly judge that it is expedient. The abbot of Dijon shall make an election from among his own men in the chapter of Dijon and shall assign the person elected to the bishop of Bayeux. Once ordained, he shall remain under that abbot, and the abbot of Dijon shall possess in the aforesaid monastery over him and over the others the same authority that he previously possessed [Col. 0477C].

This gift was confirmed with the approval and consent of my lord Robert, count of Normandy. He also granted to the same monastery of Saint-Vigor complete liberty—namely, freedom from all customary exactions throughout his entire land that pertained to him from his demesne possessions, whether in passage dues, tolls, or other revenues—and, from his own property, for the daily use of the brothers serving God there [Col. 0478A], four ass-loads of green wood from his forest of Verneuil. He also granted that if anyone from his land should give anything of his own to the aforesaid monastery, it would be ratified for him and could not in any way be revoked on the pretext of his legal right, so that the same monastery might be possessed by the Church of Dijon by perpetual right.

Therefore, if anyone should attempt to violate this charter of donation, may the anger of God come upon him; may he be erased from the book of the living and not be written with the just; and may he be anathema, Maranatha, until the day of the Lord, unless he repents. But upon whoever approves these things and approaches as a faithful collaborator, may peace and blessing rest until he sees the God of gods in Zion.

And so that this charter may remain firm and unshaken, I have confirmed it with the impression of our seal and delivered it to be strengthened by witnesses [Col. 0478B].

+ I, Odo, bishop of Bayeux, confirm and subscribe to this charter, having read and reread it.

+ Sign of Robert, most noble count of Normandy.

+ Sign of William, dean.

+ Sign of Ralph, archdeacon.

+ Sign of Helgold, archdeacon.

+ Sign of Robert of the Three Mountains.

+ Sign of William of Arques, monk.

+ Sign of Eugebrannus, son of Hilbert.

+ Sign of William of Bretuil.

+ Sign of William of Similiacum.

+ Sign of William of Columbers.

[Col. 0478C] In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1096, indiction IV, concurrent II, in the nineteenth year of the rule of Lord Robert, son of William, king of the English and duke of Normandy, this charter was confirmed and signed with his seal.

Done publicly at Bayeux, in the month of May, on the twenty-fourth day of that month, the ninth day before the Kalends of July, on the twenty-seventh day of the lunar month, on Saturday, in a leap year.

[Col. 0477]

## LETTER OF HUGH, ARCHBISHOP OF EDESSA

To R., archbishop of Reims, and the canons of the Holy Apostles and Saint Symphorian. He sends relics of Saint Thaddeus and King Abgar.

(MARLOT, *Metropolis of Reims*, II, 241.)

[Col. 0477D] To R. [the remainder of the name is absent in the supplied text], by the grace of God venerable archbishop of Reims, and to the canons of the Holy Apostles and of blessed Symphorian, Hugh, by that same grace archbishop of the city of Edessa, sends greetings and brotherly love in Christ.

E [lacuna], chaplain of the king of Jerusalem and of you, came with the aforesaid king to the city of Edessa after the capture of Count Joscelin. Finding there in your Church certain of his friends from your regions, men of great probity, he consulted with them concerning the Church of the Apostles and blessed Symphorian, over which you appointed him, and which in ancient times had also been an episcopal see. He informed them that no body of the aforesaid saint lay there, and announced that he wished to make a request; what he devoutly requested, he truly obtained.

Accordingly, at last, by God’s will, with the king’s assistance, and also with our permission, he received from our Church a most precious treasure, namely relics [Col. 0479A] of Saint Thaddaeus the Apostle and Saint Abagar, king and confessor. That this is true we confirm by the testimony of ourselves and of persons of our Church [Col. 0480A]—Gerard the archdeacon, Stephen the dean, and Theson the treasurer—and we authenticate it by the impression of our seal. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0479A] Attached to this letter is a lead seal with red silk threads, bearing on one side the likeness of the archbishop with a staff; on the other is the following Latin inscription around the edge: “Hugo, archbishop of Edessa by the grace of God.”]

[Col. 0479]

## Pious Gifts of Fulk, Count of Anjou

### I. He grants certain estates to the Church of Saint Maurice of Angers. (Year 1096.)

[Gal. Christ., first edition, vol. II, p. 128.]

[Col. 0479B]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, Fulk, count of Anjou.

Among the various concerns of his solicitude by which a person ought to provide remedies for his sins and for human misery, this is not the least: that, in accordance with the saving admonition of our Lord Jesus Christ, we should strive, by giving alms from the transitory goods of this world, to acquire everlasting gains. This may indeed be approached by many paths of mercy, but the shorter way is thought to be that, through the hand of the holy Church, mother of all the faithful, possession of temporary earthly goods may be transferred into an eternal possession, thereby undoubtedly providing support both for the perpetual praises of God and for the needs of Christ’s poor.

This matter can especially at the present time be both a great example and a great merit, since dangerous times are pressing upon the world, which has fallen so deeply into evil; since there are wicked people who, as they suppose, love themselves, but who in truth hate themselves; and since, as though ready to plunder God, they are innumerable, while those who support others are scarcely found at all.

Therefore, in the name of God, Savior of the world, I, Fulk, by the dispensation of divine mercy count of Anjou, not despairing of the mercy of our Creator, wish it to be known to all present and future to whom this matter may come, that I desired by divine deliberation to establish something, with God’s approval, for Saint Maurice and Saint Maurilius and their servants; and at last, with God’s favor, and with the consent and confirmation of my sons—namely Geoffrey and Fulk the Younger—and of my daughter Ermengard, I brought this desire to completion.

I therefore give to God and to Saint Maurice, the Mother Church of Angers, over which Lord Geoffrey of Meduana presides as bishop by God’s appointment, everything that I possess on the island of Calonna, free and quit, as I possess it, to have, hold, sell, or give forever to whomever he or his successors may wish; and also all the water flowing nearby on the northern side, called the Meduanilis, as I possess it [Col. 0480B], in its entirety, together with everything belonging to that island or water.

The following exception applies: if my men, while crossing that same water, should in any way stir up a disturbance among themselves, the forfeiture shall belong to me; if the bishop’s men should stir up a disturbance among themselves, the forfeiture shall belong to the bishop; but if my men and the bishop’s men, or the bishop’s men and mine, should stir up a disturbance, the forfeiture shall be divided between me and the bishop. The bishop or his provost shall distrain them and shall receive eleven and a half solidi from the distraint.

Thus, as stated above, we give this property and wish this gift to remain firm forever, both I and my sons and daughter, having nevertheless received five thousand Angevin solidi from the bishop himself, Geoffrey. And so that this gift [Col. 0480C] and grant may possess firm and inviolable strength forever, in the presence of advocates both from my side and from the bishop’s, and of lawful and reputable persons who saw and heard the matter, whose names are written below, we made the gift with our own hand by means of a knife upon the Lord’s altar, ordered it to be written down, and confirmed this charter beneath with the sign of the Holy Cross.

If any of my successors or heirs—God forbid!—trusting either in force or in wicked cunning, should at any time attempt to annul this charter, let him be condemned to pay one hundred pounds of the purest gold; let his attempt have no effect; let him stand before Christ’s tribunal to render an account; and let him be condemned by a perpetual and indissoluble anathema as the companion of Judas Iscariot and of all who laid impious hands upon the Lord [Col. 0480D].

Done at Angers, in the bishop’s chamber, on the ninth day before the Kalends of July, the vigil of Saint John the Baptist, in the year of the Lord 1096, indiction IV, epact XXIII, in the year when an innumerable multitude was going to Jerusalem to drive away the persecution of the treachery of the Pincenati—namely, in the second year after Pope Urban visited Angers—while Philip was reigning over the Franks and Fulk the Younger was ruling over the Angevins, in the twenty-ninth year of his rule, under Geoffrey of Meduana, bishop of Angers, in the first year of his ordination. The following canons and clerics were present and heard it:

On the bishop’s side: Gosbert the dean; Hubert the cantor; Bernard, abbot of Saint Sergius; Peter the monk; [Col. 0481A] William Transligerensis, archdeacon; Warner Transmeduanensis, archdeacon; Eudo the archpriest; Geoffrey Girbanei; William of Saint-Laud; Ralph of Valle; Richald; Geoffrey Guid Gedeon; William Musca; Bernerius Macondus, canon and cellarer; Alberic, the bishop’s chaplain; William of Camiliacum; Juhellus; Geoffrey of Château-Gontier; Benedict the priest; Gosbert, canon of Saint Maurilius; Laurence, canon of Saint Maurilius; Geoffrey Cosin; Ralph the cleric; Roscelin the priest; and John of Ramorfort, canon of Saint John.

The following laymen were also present: Geoffrey, son of Eudo of Calonna; Pagan, his brother; Eudo, his son; and Americ the cleric.

On the count’s side: Leo of Brioledo; Fulk, son of Urso; Segebrand, count of the stables; [Col. 0481B] Peter Rubiscallus; Gerald the provost; Ceric, his son; Hervé Rosondelli; Richard of Saint-Quentin; Geoffrey Trevis; Hugh of Vado; and Ranulf of Craon.

Sign of Fulk the count; sign of Geoffrey his son; sign of Fulk his son; sign of Ermengard his daughter.

### II. Charter of a gift for the monastery of Saint Nicholas

(*Brief account of the foundation and succession of abbots of Saint Nicholas of Angers*, by Laurence Lepelletier, p. 5.)

In ancient times certain kings and princes took care to build churches in the name of Christ. I also, Fulk, count of Anjou, although one of the least and most negligent of men, resolved, in the name of God and of Christ’s supreme prelate Nicholas, to build a church in sight of the city of Angers. In the year 1020 from the Incarnation of the Lord, I had it consecrated by Lord Hubert, bishop of the aforesaid city.

Not long after its consecration, I appointed as abbot one of the monks of the great monastery of Saint Martin, named Baldric, and took care to enrich it from my own possessions for the support of the brothers and of the poor. I gave that church, on the bank of the Brionel, vineyards and my mother’s garden, together with lands of my own which I had cleared and levelled; and I gave it at Lupellus twelve arpents of meadow and more. All these were free from rent and tithe, free and quit like royal allodial land.

The triumphal road leading to the city divides these cultivated lands and the land belonging to them. On the bank of the Brionel, on the southern side, is the dwelling of our dogs. On the southern side there is also the dwelling of our oxherds, and there the land descends into the river.

I also gave that church the land of Accisoria, free and quit, namely the vicariate, the fodrum, and all the customary dues that the land usually yields. Guido, treasurer of Saint Maurice, exchanged this land with me; he held it from Alberic of Mount John, formerly one of our nobles. The exchanges that I gave him in return for the land were these: half of a church; a vineyard enclosure between the Meduana and the Brionel; and, across the river, other vineyards.

If vineyards with their wine dues are given to the monks or purchased by them, they shall be free and quit. If I sell my wine under the ban, my officer shall not cross the little stream of Barra in order to seize the monks’ wine vessels. If a dispute arises between the men of the estate, let it be settled there; likewise if it arises between one of those men and an outsider. The provost, nor the vicar, shall interfere with the man of that estate, enter their land, or administer justice over their man until he has received a complaint made twice to the abbot.

At the estate of Lanaria I gave cleared land in a corner. But it must not be left unmentioned that I granted to the church that, if my army should go into the land of my enemies to ravage it or build a fortress, no man of that church should go, unless war should arise; and the carts, oxen, and donkeys of that church must not be seized by my officers [Col. 0482B]. Let everything belonging to them be free and quit.

I made this gift in the twenty-seventh year of King Robert, son of Hugh the Great. After Abbot Baldric had left the monastery, secretly sought the wilderness, and finally returned to the greater monastery, he ended his life at the monastery of the Thebans. After him, Lord Albert restored the monk Reginald in his place. Before receiving his blessing, however, Reginald fled to my son Geoffrey and assumed, without the permission of his own abbot, the governance of the newly founded monastery of Vendôme.

When I saw that I had been deceived by two abbots, I became very angry and ordered the other monks to return quickly to their monastery. Then I asked Lord Walter, abbot of Saint Albinius, to grant Lord Hildinus, the prior of that church [Col. 0482C]. Appointed in the year 1032 from the Incarnation of the Lord, on the feast of the Nativity of blessed Mary, which is the third year of King Henry, he governs the monastery according to the rule.

I ordered the aforesaid possessions of the church to be written down by Lord Berengar and Lord Reginald; and before I went to Jerusalem for the last time, I confirmed them with my own hand.

### III. Another gift for the same monastery of Saint Nicholas

(Ibid., p. 7.)

As far as the human intellect and understanding can consider with an acute mind and weigh by diligent investigation, nothing among the fleeting joys of this age is more effective for deserving eternal reward than taking care to spend our own possessions for the sustenance of places prepared for divine worship, so that Christ himself may receive earthly goods through the hand of the poor, and we may fashion eternal merchandise from perishable substance.

Therefore, in the name of God, I, Fulk, count of Anjou, and my wife Hildegard, and our son Geoffrey, wish it to be known to the faithful of the holy Church how, with God as author, we founded a monastery in honor of blessed Nicholas the Confessor, in sight of the city of Angers, established there the monastic order according to the rule of blessed Father Benedict, and assigned that place possessions from our own estate.

Accordingly, for the honor of the divine Majesty, in hope of eternal reward, for the remission of sins and the salvation of souls, [Col. 0483A] by this charter of grant we give, and wish to be given forever, to the monastery of Saint Nicholas and to the congregation of monks living there, from our possessions, the following:

In the county of Anjou, not far from the city, the whole land called Accisarias, in its entirety and free and quit, just as it is established that Guido, sacristan of Saint Maurice, held it from Alberic, our lord's vassal, and that we exchanged it with Guido the treasurer by means of exchanges.

In another place near the monastery, with only the Brionel River flowing between, twelve measures of arable land, together with two arpents of garden and vineyards.

Likewise, at the place called [Col. 0484A] Lupellus, twelve arpents of meadow on the bank of the Meduana.

Likewise, at the estate of Lanaria, between the wood of Captia, three measures of land.

In the land of Saint Peter, eleven arpents of vineyard, subject to rent and tithe.

Sign of confirmation, placed by Count Geoffrey with his own hand. So that the authority of this settlement or gift may, in the name of God, retain through succeeding ages a firm power of remembrance and preservation, we marked it with the sign of the cross with our own hands and asked our faithful men to confirm it.

[Col. 0483]

## Charter of Raymond of Curamonta, who, departing for Jerusalem, pledges certain estates to the monks of Tulle. (Year 1096.)

[Baluze, *History of Tulle*, p. 411.]

[Col. 0483B]

Let those living now and those to come know that I, Raymond of Curamonta, when I wished to go to Jerusalem with Raymond, viscount of Turenne, pledged to Abbot William and the monks of Tulle a fourth part of the church of Brancels, namely a fourth part of the tithe and offerings and the priest’s fief, [Col. 0484B] as well as my tower and other houses, etc.

This was done in the year 1096 of the Incarnate Word, indiction IV, in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban II, while Philip was reigning as king, the see of Limoges was without a bishop, and William, abbot of the monastery of Tulle, was exercising pastoral care.

[Col. 0483]

## Diploma of Raymond, Count of Saint-Gilles

### Concerning the gift of half the town of Gibelet to Saint Victor of Marseille. (Year 1103.)

(Edited by Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 600. D. Furnerius recovered it from the archives of Saint Victor of Marseille.)

[Col. 0483C]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, I, [Note: [Col. 0483C] Baluze published this charter in his proofs for the history of the house of Auvergne, but so mutilated and interpolated that it necessarily had to be reprinted.] Raymond, by the grace of God count of Saint-Gilles and marquis of Provence, and, with God’s help, leader of the Christian army on the journey to Jerusalem, considering the enormity of my sins and the weakness of the very small body of Christians that is with me amid various excesses, and at the urgent and persistent request of Lord Richard, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and abbot of Marseille, who expends his labor and solicitude in my service, I give and grant [Col. 0484C] to the only-begotten Son of God, and to his venerable mother Saint Mary, and also to the precious martyrs Victor and his companions, and to the others whose relics rest in honor at the monastery of Marseille in Christ, half of the city called Gibelet, which is fortified with high walls and strong towers on the shore of the Great Sea between Tripoli and Beirut, together with everything belonging to it by sea and land: namely, churches, estates, castles, villages, cultivated and uncultivated lands, the harbor and shipwreck rights, and all appurtenances everywhere [Col. 0485A].

All these things I, Raymond, count by the grace of God, confirm and strengthen by an unchangeable gift to the Lord God, to the aforesaid saints, and to the monastery, and also to the present abbot of that place, Raymond, or to his monks, both those now present and those who will serve God there in the future, without fraud, deceit, or any evil design, so that they may possess them honorably forever, hold them with authority, and enjoy them happily and honorably.

I did this at the counsel—or rather at the urging—of my venerable fellow soldiers: namely William, count of Auvergne; B., viscount of Béziers; and finally [Note: [Col. 0485C] Baluze wrote “Aicard, most reverend bishop of Marseille,” and from this took occasion, in the index to volume II, to make Aicard a bishop of Marseille, as though the title “most reverend” could belong to no one other than a bishop. But apart from the fact that this title, “most reverend,” is foreign to the original of this charter, the word “fellow soldier,” which is applied to him here, should have diverted him from that opinion; for the very reading of this passage shows that all those mentioned here were illustrious soldiers marked with the cross. Baluze’s [Col. 0486C] opinion led the author of the new *Gallia Christiana* into error. In order to make room for Aicard, a supposed bishop of Marseille, among the bishops of Marseille, he divided Raymond, who then occupied that see and lived for a long time afterward, into two persons, placing Aicard between the two Raymonds.] Aicard of Marseille, and Berengar of Narbonne, so that almighty God may deign, through the intercessions of the congregation of the aforesaid saints, to be propitious to my iniquities and to oppose the adversities of the very small body of Christians which chose me, after him, as its head and leader.

Both I and the nobles of our aforesaid army wish this charter of gift to be firm, ratified, and inviolable, and by our will we decree it so. By the authority of the heavenly Judge, of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose obedience and fidelity we now bear arms, of all the saints, and of ourselves, we prohibit any king, any prince, or any person of whatever rank or order, whether clerical or lay authority, from presuming to inflict any violence upon it by violating it.

But if—God forbid!—after my death, since we are subject to the laws of mortality, or before it, since the judgments of God are a great abyss, anyone endowed with power should, with God’s permission, attempt to exercise the tyranny of his greed over this labor of ours, our alms, or our gift by violating it, let him in the future be subjected to the penalties of divine vengeance [Col. 0486A]; and in the present let him be dishonored and condemned by public judgment like Ahab because of the field of Naboth the Jezreelite, which he wickedly desired to possess; let him be deprived of all honor, unless he takes care to amend what he has unjustly presumed to do by an adequate satisfaction, restoring it to its former dignity and honor, and paying the monastery one thousand pounds of the finest gold for the damage he has inflicted. This charter and gift shall nevertheless remain stable and unchangeable forever.

This charter of gift was made in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1103, in January, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February, on the fifth day of the moon, indiction XI, in the castle called Pilgrim’s Mount, which stands before the gate of Tripoli, while Philip was also reigning as king in [Col. 0486B] France, with epact XI concurrent.

+ Count Raymond confirms. + Sign of William, count of Auvergne, confirms. + Sign of Bernard, viscount, confirms. + Sign of Aicard, confirms. + Sign of Berengar of Narbonne, confirms. Sign of William son of Hugh. § Sign of Peter, [Note: [Col. 0486C] This bishop, hitherto unknown, is absent from the published lists of the bishops of Glandes, where he should be placed between Pontius and Imbert.] bishop of Glandensis, confirms. § Sign of Arbert, abbot of Saint Evrard, confirms. Sign of Pontius Grillonensis, confirms. Sign of William son of Peter, confirms. Sign of Berengar William, confirms. Sign of Aicfred, confirms.

In the presence of Durand and Raymond, who made this charter for the monks, and of Bernard and Stephen, clerics.

[Col. 0485]

## Itineraries or Exhortations of a Certain Dermatius the Irishman Departing for Jerusalem

(Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 340.)

[Col. 0485D]

I, Dermatius, an Irishman by birth, say to all who recognize that they have no lasting city here: seek the city to come, leave Babylon, and go or return to Jerusalem.

[Col. 0486D]

By the name Babylon, dearest friends, we wish you here to understand this world, which is indeed “placed in wickedness” (1 John V), so that nothing is more confused, nothing more turbulent, and nothing at all is more uncertain in its certainty or more certain in its uncertainty.

Here no one now builds a tower, for although he strives to ascend toward holy things, even if not by holy merits, he digs pits, cisterns, and wells, and sets traps and snares by which, if possible, he attempts even to make heavenly beings earthly. He has reached such a point and has come so deeply that what is said of the sinner now almost suits him: “When the sinner has come into the depths, he despises” (Proverbs XVIII).

For who is there who reflects? Who, ascending to the tribunal of his own mind, thinks about judgment before the judgment? Yet that pious Father in heaven does not cease to admonish us—now, indeed, more frequently than usual, in proportion as he sees us pursuing the crookedness of our hearts more stubbornly.

You saw this year, dearest friends—namely, the year 1117 from the Incarnation [Col. 0487B] of the Lord—how often he seemed to descend and come to us, now with a rod, now with a staff. What? Have you ever seen rains falling with such force? Have you ever heard thunderclaps of such violence? Have lightning bolts ever raged in such numbers across the sky?

Earthquakes too were so great in various places that they not only overthrew cities, as we have sometimes heard, but even, by a new and astonishing miracle, tore mountains from their very foundations. The terrors and signs from heaven that an earlier age remembers also appeared at night in the northern region: part of the sky glowed as though it were a burning furnace, while part of it shone with an exceedingly bright light almost until midnight, as though it were broad daylight.

These, dearest friends, these were the voices the Most High gave us; by them he both admonished us terribly and frightened us mercifully. For although, by multiplying flashes of lightning, he once so disturbed us that even in the churches themselves he struck certain people down with bodily death—as we saw happen when we were then at Liège—yet in this he did not prove cruel toward us, but displayed his compassion. By the severity of discipline, he punished the crimes committed with deaths of the body far milder than the eternal punishments of Gehenna.

“For by deaths of the body,” says Augustine, “we read that some died, not because of their own sins but because of the sins of others; and there the wound of the living in the sorrow of the heart is greater than the pain of the dying in the dissolution of the flesh, while the souls leaving their bodies have their own causes, whether good or bad, and are not burdened on that account [Col. 0487D] because they have been stripped of them.” Augustine says this in the first book *Against the Marcionites*.

In the second book he says: “Who knows what God grants them after death as a good recompense, whose deaths corrected or terrified the living? For God often punishes the sins of some, in order to produce in the minds even of those who did not commit them a greater pain and terror of punishment, not by spiritual but by bodily deaths, so that the condition by which they are soon to die may in this way also serve God’s providence and contribute to our discipline.”

Behold, dearest friends: taught not by me but by Augustine, you have learned that, in avenging the sins of others, God often strikes some people here; that this does not harm those who are struck; and that it greatly benefits those who are not struck. For God deals more gently with those whom he strikes temporarily, and those whom he corrects and reforms here through the deaths of others are not left without protection.

Therefore, receiving this correction from God with thanksgiving—not as indignation, but as paternal and pious chastisement—do not, dearest friends, do not neglect him when he corrects you, lest he perhaps make his hand heavier, lest he perhaps trouble you in his fury, lest he perhaps cast you down in his anger.

Leave Babylon, as I said; leave it; go, or return, to Jerusalem. Gather again the stones of the sanctuary that have been scattered; rebuild the walls that Nabuzardan, the commander of Babylon’s army, destroyed.

But what do you think? Perhaps you suppose that I mean this earthly Jerusalem, to which you see me going or returning. You think that I am speaking of that, although it is praiseworthy to go to this Jerusalem for the sake of the other about which I am speaking here. Yet I am not referring here to this one. I am speaking of the spiritual Jerusalem, dearest friends, the heavenly Jerusalem, which “is built as a city” (Psalm CXXI), and in whose building each person offers, as it were, stones in the form of whatever virtues he has acquired.

When I urge you to leave Babylon—that is, the world—and come to this Jerusalem, I summon you to its building or rebuilding; by this modest exhortation of mine I stir you up toward it. To this city, you who are pilgrims upon earth, to this city that “remains” and “has foundations” (Hebrews XIII; XI), I call you from this house of clay.

This city is situated in the mountains, and therefore no one burdened with weight can ascend to it. Whoever wishes to climb these mountains must first be unburdened. Let him cast away this worldly load—namely, desire and worldly anxiety; let him deny himself; let him go out with Christ beyond the gate; let him take up his reproach; let him crucify his flesh with its vices and desires.

As for goodwill and fellowship, there is abundant reason to exhort those to whom, as the Apostle teaches, it has become known that God is pleased by such sacrifices (Hebrews XIII). This is that good which, according to the same Apostle, we ought to work toward all, but especially toward those who belong to the household of faith (Galatians VI).

Consider, then, how great and of what kind this good is, from which no one belonging to the human condition is excluded. Show it all the more generously to me and to the other members of the household of faith, in proportion as you would act more inhumanely by denying us what you owe to everyone.

You see that I have made myself an exile for God. You see that I bear not merely this cross which is on my cloth, but that I bear Christ’s cross. You see that I flee to God not only in Jerusalem but everywhere, because he is everywhere.

Therefore, through him, I urge you: take care, as far as lies within you, that I do not fail on this road. There is certainly a way to God: for those who are on God’s road, it is necessary to serve God. Hold to this way; do not turn aside from it; walk upon it continually, if only with the steps of your will.

This truly is the way that leads back from exile to the homeland; this is the way that leads to the city that remains and has foundations; this, I say, is the way that rightly leads from Babylon and brings one back to Jerusalem.

Therefore, dearest brothers, if, as we said at the beginning, you do not recognize that you have a lasting city here, and if you seek one that is to come, seek it by this way and you will find it; walk by this way and you will arrive; strive to see by this way, and you will see the God of gods in Zion.

Do not be surprised that this way belongs to me. For although I am Irish, although I am Scottish, I am nevertheless a fellow member of your household in the sacraments of the Church and in your faith.

Therefore, as I have already often said, do not forget this member of your household in faith when it comes to kindness and fellowship. For unless the Apostle is lying, God is pleased by such sacrifices (Hebrews XIII).

While you are still on the road, strive to be among those to whom the Son of Man will say: “As long as you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me” (Matthew XXVI). If you do not act in this way, do not be angry with me or take offense: this Scot tells you the truth, that you will go into the eternal fire “which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid.).

Therefore, dearest friends, take care rather that it may be said to you: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid.). You will be able to attain it in this way, if, for God’s sake, you prove most generous toward Christ’s poor from what you possess.

Farewell. And when, with God’s assent, I have experienced this generosity of yours, pray also, I ask, for Raimbald of Liège, who provided and wrote this letter for me as I was departing, as provisions for my journey.

[Col. 0489]

## Deeds of Tancred in the Jerusalem Expedition, by Ralph of Caen, His Companion

(Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, III, 107, from a manuscript of Gembloux.)

### Preliminary Notice

The following history of Tancred is an appendix to the *Chronicle of Sicily*. Tancred was related to that outstanding warrior Roger, surnamed “Guiscard,” who freed the Sicilian people from the yoke of the Saracens; and under Bohemond, Roger’s son, in the Jerusalem expedition, Tancred served almost as commander under the king and second to him.

Although this history does not encompass the whole course of his life, but only what that illustrious commander accomplished under so great a prince during a period of five years, it is nevertheless a great and remarkable monument to his valor, and will commend him to the furthest posterity as the greatest commander of his age.

It will show that in recovering the Holy Land he labored with the utmost vigor and success, that he far surpassed the other commanders of the Christian army whom antiquity has praised so highly, and that he earned nearly the same praise for the liberation of the Church of Palestine as Roger Guiscard earned for Sicily.

The events testify to this: what he accomplished at Nicaea, Tarsus, and Mamistra while they were being captured; at Antioch, before and after its most difficult conquest; at Jerusalem; during the crossing of the Bardal River; before the Emperor Alexius; and, finally, everywhere that his deeds are recorded. For nothing undertaken in this war, unless it was trivial, was successfully completed without Tancred displaying outstanding examples of exceptional valor, singular wisdom, and counsel.

The author of this history devotes himself entirely to recounting all these events, and expressly declares that he had proposed nothing else in this work, in article 53, in these words:

“Let Normandy celebrate its Roberts; let the rest of the West celebrate its other commanders; for me, one Marchiside is enough, though I am not enough for him in my entirety.”

Who this author was, from what people he came, and in what age he lived—his name, character, manner of life—it is worthwhile to investigate from the history itself, for these matters can contribute greatly to the commendation of that same history.

The author’s name was Ralph, as the first heading, *Tancred of Ralph*, reveals. His homeland was Normandy, as we gather from article 57, where, describing the capture of Antioch—which began in 1097 and continued through the entire following year—he says of himself in passing:

“That sign, when I was still a young man living in my father’s house at Caen, was not yet seen or known to me except by name—Antioch; nor was Rome.”

He was therefore born at Caen around the year 1080 and was educated in that same city. From childhood he devoted himself to the best disciplines under the celebrated Arnulf, who had been chaplain to the count of Normandy in the holy war and, after the death of Adhemar, bishop of Le Puy, had been placed in charge of the Christian army and obtained the see of Jerusalem. Ralph dedicates his book to him and calls him his teacher.

“I have chosen you,” he says in the preface, “Arnulf, most learned patriarch among teachers, to cut away what is superfluous from my page and fill its gaps . . . Your correction, whatever it may be, will be gentle toward me, if I obtain you as my corrector now that you are an old man, having received you as my teacher when I was a boy and young man.”

Let the fair-minded reader judge from Ralph’s manner of writing what sort of progress, and how great a progress, he made in his studies under such a teacher. He acquired this learning within a very short period. For he had not yet passed beyond adolescence when he was called into military service.

Around the year 1107 he took the cross and served under Prince Bohemond; two years later, in the expedition to Edessa, he fought under Tancred’s standards [Col. 0491].

The role he then played in the army the most modest of writers thought best to leave unmentioned. But we believe that he held an important position, since, as he sufficiently suggests in the preface already cited, he obtained the particular favor of both princes.
