A strong conjecture also moves us to believe that this is the same Ralph of Acre whom Walter the Chancellor, in the book entitled *The Antiochene War*, says was a vigorous commander of that city under Roger, Tancred’s nephew, and during Roger’s rule of Antioch; for otherwise we have no certain knowledge of who that Ralph was.

Whom could Tancred have appointed to this office—both to advise himself and Roger and to strengthen Roger’s rule in a foreign land—unless it were certainly a soldier whose loyalty and integrity he could trust completely, whose keenness of mind, experience in war, and valor had been tested?

Although Radulfus had chiefly set out to describe what Tancred had accomplished on the Jerusalem expedition, he did not consider it wholly contrary to his purpose occasionally to treat matters relating to the general history of that expedition. Following the practice of the ancient historians, if a famous battle, the capture of a city, a victory, or any other notable deed had been splendidly accomplished under Tancred’s or Bohemond’s command—or, in their presence, under another’s command—and had also been recorded by others, he did not omit it, so that from the comparison of their merits a fresh brilliance might accrue to the virtue of his own hero. Thus this history is not so exclusively and distinctively Tancred’s that it cannot also be called a concise and orderly account of the Jerusalem war. Indeed, it seems to us more complete and accurate than all the accounts of the same subject that have so far been published. For almost all their authors, eager to narrate the deeds of individual princes without exercising any discrimination, piled together much that was useless; unable, amid such a diversity of events, to investigate and examine anything more deeply, they produced a bare history stripped of its circumstances. Our Radulfus, however, keeping within definite limits, undertakes only the principal matters; he investigates their causes, recounts their beginnings and progress, searches out their consequences, and, moreover, as one thoroughly versed in the art of war, judges each matter soundly and honestly, speaking not rashly but with knowledge.

Who, for example, has described the evil stratagems of the emperor Alexius so fully and extensively? What snares he contrived; what he attempted in order to entrap the Christian princes, turn them away from their holy purpose, or bind them to himself through the onerous obligations of an unowed dependence—terrors, threats, flatteries: nothing has been omitted. All this is related in sections 9, 10, and 12, which I do not remember ever having read elsewhere. More than one author has recorded that Baldwin and Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles, repeatedly stirred up hostile dissensions against Tancred, and not without grave danger involving the shedding of blood. But our author, as though deliberately, related the causes of this hatred, which the others scarcely touched upon; these causes reveal and explain the grounds of certain important events. As for what the same author wrote about the capture of Jerusalem, it is owed to him alone, if it has not been entirely erased by oblivion. For what that anonymous writer, published by Mabillon in volume I of the *Museum Italicum*, reported on this subject, he took from our Radulfus, suppressing his name.

That this may be beyond doubt, the manuscript codex that we used provides evident proof. It breathes the age of its author through its script, and, if our conjecture does not deceive us, it is in his own hand. This is sufficiently demonstrated by the frequent additions, transpositions, corrections, and rearrangements of periods, written in the same hand—features which no one even slightly acquainted with antiquity can fail to recognize as the marks of the original exemplar. The codex lay hidden in the distinguished library of Gembloux, which, to the greatest loss of letters, was almost entirely reduced to ashes with the monastery thirty years ago. Rescued from the fire along with a few books of the same character, it was kindly shared with us by the monastery’s excellent abbot. It appears to be entirely intact; yet I can scarcely believe that it contains Radulfus’s complete history. For it is hardly probable that he finished writing as early as 1105, when he had scarcely entered military service, since, when speaking of the capture of Antioch, he promised that he would treat at greater length the events that had taken place in his presence, in these words: “Pardon me, Gaul, rich in writers: I am glad to devote myself to the prince of Antioch; what took place in my presence I shall set forth more freely.”

Whatever the case may be, to conclude briefly: Radulfus wrote in an elegant and ornate style, whose majesty and splendor far surpass those of all the writers of his time; but he was no less truthful, since he always adhered to Tancred and Bohemond and committed to writing events as he had received them from them or had himself witnessed them. He also reports many circumstances of various events that cannot be found at all in other writers of the age. We therefore hope that his work will be held in high esteem by everyone.

# PREFACE

[Col. 0491A] It is a noble undertaking to recount the worthy deeds of princes. The generosity of this service leaves no period of time untouched: it celebrates the buried, delights survivors, and prepares instruction long in advance for those yet to come. While it recalls what has passed, while it brings victories forward, while it pays tribute to victors, it removes sluggishness, brings integrity, transfers vices, introduces virtues, and contributes greatly to all things. We must therefore strive with all our strength both to read what has been written and to write what should be read, so that by reading ancient works we may satisfy our own need from antiquity, and by writing new ones, once satisfied, nourish the needy posterity.

As I considered these matters repeatedly and attentively, that fortunate pilgrimage came to mind, that glorious labor which restored to our mother Jerusalem her inheritance, extinguished idolatry, and repaired the faith. Thus one who applauded these deeds might not unreasonably say: “Behold, your sons, Jerusalem, have come from afar, and your daughters”—namely, Joppa; and many others, crushed by ruin, rose again at her side.

It happened that I served among the fellow-workers in this great and splendid labor: with Bohemond when he was besieging Dyrrhachium, and shortly afterward with Tancred when he liberated Edessa from the siege of the Turks. The daily conversation of both men recalled the flight of the Turks, the advance of the Franks, enemies now slain, cities now captured, Antioch taken by night through stratagems, and Jerusalem by day through arms. Amid these recollections they would exclaim, “Good heavens! How our sluggishness destroys us, when the ancient prophets found the writing of such things their greatest pleasure!” And they would add: “Why do they devise fabulous inventions? The writers of today are silent about the victories of Christ’s army—truly a cowardly herd, fit to be augmented by drones.”

As they voiced these complaints publicly, they seemed often to turn their eyes particularly toward me, I know not under what omen, as though indicating: “We are speaking to you; we trust in you.” Thus both men, but especially Tancred, inflamed my zeal. No lord was kinder, none more generous, none so gracious as he. To him, I say, as he pressed me more urgently, my silent mind replied: “What you ask, while alive, you shall receive if I survive; but buried, you shall receive it from me. I shall not praise you during your life; I shall praise you after death; I shall magnify you after your completion. For then neither the praised nor the praiser rises into self-exaltation or falls into flattery.”

Moreover, the envious man will be silent, and the whisperer will be mute, when, after your death, the gifts cease by which, while you are alive, you continually rewarded me, and through which poisonous tongues would make me out to be a seller of tales and you their buyer.

Delay had another cause as well: distrusting my own abilities, I was meanwhile waiting to see whether someone more skillful would apply his pen to these matters, or whether someone more deeply indebted to Tancred’s gifts would hasten to do so. But I discovered some neglecting the task, others growing sluggish, and others—shame upon them!—resisting, the whisperers that they were. Good heavens! Where was reverence? Where liberty? Where the gifts by which that glory of princes so often illumined the obscure, released the indebted, and enriched the poor?

I therefore undertook the labor left to me—not because I was worthy of undertaking it, but because those who were worthy disdained it, and I was indignant.

Nevertheless, since

> It is something to have advanced so far, if one is not permitted to go farther,  
> **HORACE**

I shall transmit even an unadorned work [lacuna] to posterity. A kindly future age, I predict, will adorn what the writers of today have left unadorned for me. Therefore, reader, we must each make a concession to the other: I must entreat you, and you must forgive me, because sometimes my speech is meager and sometimes, as they say, “rich in Minerva,” yet it has fallen far below the grandeur of its subject. For these matters scarcely reach the heights of Maro, while an almost useless tongue stammers them out.

I feel myself weak in this respect; but I depend wholly upon the strength of him—that is, Christ—whose standard-bearer and triumphs I intend to describe. From him, in turn, I have chosen you, most learned patriarch Arnulfus, as teacher: cut away what is superfluous from my page, fill its cracks, illuminate what is obscure, and pour moisture over what is dry. We have recognized you as lacking no liberal science. Above all, your correction will be sweet to me, whatever form it takes, if, having received you as my teacher when I was a boy and young man, I now obtain you as my corrector in old age.

# HERE BEGINS RADULFUS’S *TANCRED*

[Col. 0493]

## I. Tancred’s Parents

[Col. 0493C]

Tancred, a most illustrious shoot of a noble lineage, had distinguished parents, Marchisus and Emma. On his father’s side he was the son of no ignoble man; through his mother’s brothers he was a nephew of far greater eminence. For the earlier members of that family were content to have their renown praised by the neighboring peoples, who were sufficiently close to them; but his mother’s brothers carried the glory of their military service beyond and above their homeland, that is, Normandy.

For who would not approve the valor of Guiscard, whose victorious standards, as they say, caused both the Greek and German emperors to tremble on a single day? In person, he liberated Rome from the German; and by defeating the king of the Greeks in battle, he subdued that region. [The wording of the preceding sentence is materially uncertain.] His remaining brothers, eleven in number, were content to conquer Campania, Calabria, and Apulia.

Roger must be excepted: the subjugation of the Sicilian people won him, among the brothers, a glory second to Guiscard’s. But the same narrative that brought me into this digression does not permit me to linger longer over these matters.

### Tancred’s kingly character; he prepares for the holy war

I now return to Tancred. Neither his father’s wealth drew him into wantonness, nor the power of his kinsmen into pride. While still a youth, he surpassed young men in agility with weapons and old men in gravity of character, presenting now to one group, now to the other, a new spectacle of virtue.

From that time he was a diligent hearer of God’s commandments. He made every effort both to recall what he had heard and, as far as the company of his contemporaries allowed, to fulfill what he had recalled. He would not disparage anyone, even when he himself was being disparaged. Indeed, he was a herald of hostile valor and used to say that an enemy should be struck, not gnawed at.

He himself said nothing about himself, yet thirsted insatiably to be spoken of. Accordingly, he put sleep after wakefulness, rest after labor, satiety after hunger, leisure after study, and, finally, all superfluous things after what was necessary. The only glory that stirred the young man’s mind was the glory of praise. In purchasing daily titles to it, he regarded the loss caused by frequent wounds as easy to bear; thus he spared neither his own blood nor that of the enemy.

His prudent mind debated with itself each day, and a more frequent anxiety consumed him: he saw that the contests of his military life conflicted with the Lord’s commandment. The Lord commands one whose cheek has been struck to offer the other cheek to the striker; secular military service, however, requires one not to spare even kindred blood. The Lord teaches that one must give one’s tunic to the person who takes it, and one’s cloak as well; military necessity requires that, once both have been stripped away, whatever remains must also be taken.

This conflict, whenever he was permitted to indulge in rest, lulled the wise man’s boldness. But after the decree of Pope Urban assigned remission of all sins to all who would conquer the pagan nations, only then did the man’s valor, as though previously asleep, fully awaken: his strength was gathered, his eyes opened, and his boldness doubled. Before this, as has been stated, his mind was divided in uncertainty at a crossroads, wondering whose footsteps it should follow, those of the Gospel or those of the world. But the experience of arms, recalled to the service of Christ, inflamed the man beyond belief, since he now had a double occasion for military service.

Accordingly, he set about obtaining provisions, and within a short time the necessities were prepared. The man, who from childhood had made it his practice to transfer things to another’s ownership before they came into his own, was not forced to incur great expenses. Nevertheless, he adequately equipped himself with military arms, horses, mules, and other such things according to the number of his fellow soldiers.

## II. Bohemond’s Eulogy

At that time there was a hero of great renown, whose youth has been mentioned above: Bohemond, son of that distinguished warrior Robert Guiscard, and a vigorous emulator of his father’s boldness. Apostolic preaching had stirred his spirit, as it had those of the other princes throughout the world, to free Jerusalem from the yoke of unbelievers.

Under his rule, all the towns and cities from Siponto to Otranto along the coast, and practically all those in the mountains and plains, were entirely subject to him. In addition, the Apulian mountains and much of Calabria sustained both his cities and his towns.

Twice, under his father, he had put the Greek emperor Alexius to flight: first, in his father’s presence, beneath the walls of Dyrrhachium; and a second time, after his father had returned to Rome, when Bohemond had been left as his father’s deputy with the paternal army at Larissa. Just as this victory had doubled his glory, so now, although victorious, it tormented him more sharply because he was about to cross under the name of peace. For the Greeks’ treachery was feared: they make it their practice, even when they have invited those who have served them well to receive gifts, to thrust them back into punishment.

What, then, would the embittered and repeatedly defeated Greeks attempt? What hope did they offer their victorious enemies concerning themselves? Would they inflict destruction upon the wretched, or desist before the power of those who terrified them?

This anxiety therefore delayed Bohemond’s voyage. Consequently, wisely consulting his own interests, he decided to fortify himself with the strength of every capable man, while for the time being denying the ports an exit. When Tancred was reported to have been inflamed by the same desire, this both diminished and increased Bohemond’s anxiety: it diminished it because he believed that strength had been added to strength; it increased it because it compelled the unwary man to prepare prudently for the journey.

## III. Tancred Enters into an Alliance with Him

After many gifts and flatteries had been sent in advance, Tancred was induced to serve under Bohemond, as a duke serving second to a king. Besides the flatteries and the wealth offered to him, two other considerations pressed him: kinship and the difficulty of the crossing. The former and the latter alternately offered him the cup of affection and the cup of fear. For unless he complied with Bohemond’s requests in these matters, he could easily be accused of envy and might appear worthy of being repelled from the shore. Thus a request heaped with prayers and gifts earned an easy path to fulfillment.

The two Guiscardids, therefore, allied with each other, descended into Epirus with the entire outstanding valor of their family, their ship moving under loosened reins. Tancred, having found an opportunity to exercise his virtue, sometimes confronted ambushes lying ahead, and at other times kept brigands away from the army’s trail. Whether ahead or behind, he was always useful and always armed, and rejoiced to expose himself to danger.

While the others lay buried in wine and sleep, he kept watch wide awake at the crossroads, tempering snow and hail with his shield. Fortunate was the old woman whom Tancred found either faint from hunger or about to wade across the bank of a rushing river: for the starving woman food was immediately supplied; for the woman about to wade, a horse served in place of a boat, and a horseman in place of a ferryman—the horseman, I mean, being Tancred himself, who willingly supplied the service.

## IV. He Crosses the Bardal River with His Men and Defeats the Greeks

With such a blessed safeguard, that people was successfully brought to a river called the Bardal. There they spent several days encamped and delayed. A rushing river obstructed their crossing, and the hostile threats filling both banks terrified many. For those who advanced in crossing seemed to face Turcopoles in front, while those who lagged appeared to have the enemy behind them.

When Tancred saw the army hesitating, he exposed his life to danger. He crossed the whirlpool, with only a few following him—those whom, I say, he compelled to do so, while he himself went voluntarily. They were afraid that a hostile multitude would attack such a small troop; Tancred, on the contrary, feared that, while he was crossing to the battle, he might terrify them into flight. Thus boldness might indeed produce victory, but at the price of depriving them of the spoils of victory.

Once the river had been crossed amid this anxiety, the omens of both fears yielded to the outcome desired by both sides. For when a small number was offered to a plural enemy lying in ambush, it seemed that the prey of the nation had come to battle—men ignorant of hiding places, not men aware of them. Bursting from their concealment, the arrows formed a cloud as they flew, hail as they fell, and a field of grain as they stood fixed.

The Franks had not yet been reached, yet every mode of fighting was already being encountered—not at a run, not rapidly, not by leaps, but step by step. Tancred endured the missiles sent from a distance until they had advanced so far that the arrows fell behind his men. For he had often experienced that people’s method of fighting in close engagement and had learned the manner in which they could most easily be defeated. Thus, through prudence, he restrained their naturally unbridled spirits.

When the engagement could be conducted at close quarters, the abundance of the ensuing action redeemed the delays of patience. They loosened the reins, applied the spurs, brandished their lances, and leaned into the thrusts. The Greeks’ bucklers could not withstand the men leaning upon them. Their arrows, formerly their protection, were turned into baggage under the pressure of the lances: once swords were reached, the arrows had lost their use.

Thus deprived of both shield and missile, the Greeks merely received wounds and returned none. Wretched men! Everything, without doubt and without respite, threatened them with immediate death or flight. Wretched men—but, just as they had shown mercy to no one, so no one pitied them.

The helpless multitude was cut down and taught no longer to presume upon the scarcity of the Franks, but to fear a hundred men in one. Tancred opened a path with his sword, and as many as he attacked to be slain, so many corpses did he pass. The tracks of those following him easily showed wherever he had turned. Half-dead trunks filled the banks on right and left amid a channel of blood. There was no license to wander here and there; they could run only along the path made by the one who had shed the blood.

From this it was evident who the shedder was—not merely the one who had poured it out, but the one who had produced it. So drenched and bloodstained was Tancred that the color of his appearance denied him, but his deeds did not deny him. In the same way, his allied young men, putting the enemy to flight, cutting them down, and throwing them to the ground, each bloodied the fields according to his strength.

## V. The Greeks Attack the Part of Bohemond’s Army That Had Not Yet Crossed the River

Bohemond’s army, which had remained sluggishly on the nearer bank of the river and had sent Tancred ahead, saw the Greeks turned to flight, broke its delay, and crossed. Some swam the river; others, skilled in rowing, carried boats across; still others, ignorant of both arts, used the tails of their horses as oars.

Thus, when the whole multitude had been transported within a short time, about six hundred remained to be carried over. They were neither soldiers nor armed men, nor people capable of rushing against the enemy or repelling an attack: an unarmed crowd, except for those whom age or illness had weakened despite their weapons.

Then the Greeks who had been sent to follow the Latins’ trail found an opportunity to dip their iron in blood and fell upon those who had been left behind, like wolves slaughtering a sheepfold deprived of its shepherd and dogs. A cry arose; both banks mourned, and on either side there was no lack of lamentation or groaning. Some grieved over their delay, others over their haste: the former were ashamed because they were not permitted to attack; the latter were even more distressed because they were not allowed to escape.

Meanwhile Tancred, still pressing the fleeing Greeks, received the report of the urgency of those who followed him: no one was resisting; no one was coming to their aid; the armed men had rowed across the river voluntarily; the unarmed remained on this side, already almost scattered as though by biting.

When this became known to the most pious commander, ever ready for every form of valor, he turned fearlessly from one group to the other, like a lion that, having found prey, looks back at an ambush prepared on the opposite side after leaving its cubs; immediately turning against the raiders, it leaves its prey with dry throats.

## VI. Tancred Leaps into the River and Puts Them to Flight

[Note: [Col. 0497] Robert the Monk agrees with this in Book II of his *History of Jerusalem*, adding that two thousand horsemen charged into the river with Tancred.]

Tancred therefore returned to the river. Rejecting a boatman, he leapt into the whirlpool, with his horse supplying both the service of a boat and the service of a rower. For delay seemed sluggishness to the man and akin to fear, if, while he prepared a vessel, he had to wait for the soldiers preparing to follow him.

Accordingly, as has been stated, he entered the river headlong as though it were a field. The swift current caught him and submerged him, but soon restored him unharmed to the opposite bank. The ranks of his fellow soldiers, following the footsteps of their advancing lord, used the same kind of rowing.

[Col. 0497D] The Greek phalanx was terrified both by Tancred’s arrival and by his name. For this was all that echoed along both banks: fearing slaughter, they ceased to slaughter and devoted themselves to their customary refuge, flight. They fled through precipices, pathless places, and everything that seemed to promise concealment to the defeated and deny access to the victors.

Yet the victor continued to press the fugitives, thirsting all the more for the blood of the man whose feet carried him more swiftly through inaccessible places. No defeated man remembered to turn his face, unless flight, once discovered, compelled someone to beg at the victor’s knees. Their ardor had grown so cold, their fury had subsided, and all hope had passed from their weapons into the speed of their feet.

Thus it remained their greatest consolation for preserving life to throw away their bows, loosen their quivers, drop their bucklers, and strip off their breastplates. Accordingly, much equipment, polished by great skill, purchased at great expense, and produced through long exertion, enriched the roads and pathless places alike, awaiting victorious hands that would seize everything without price or contest.

Nor was there any lack of people to take it up or to follow the fleeing crowd when they heard Tancred’s name. Those survivors of the slaughter described above—those, I mean, whom the arrival of reinforcements had saved—fled without order and followed without order: the unburdened followed the laden, the naked the armed, the unwearied the weary. Many who were being led into slavery, freed when their bonds broke, in turn bound their own captors.

Others, while looking for the spoils taken from them, found both what the raider had thrown down and what was theirs. There were even some who, while searching for the things mentioned above, found what they sought and carried it away; they discarded what they had picked up in order to take better things. Whether bearing another’s burden or their own, no one returned to camp without being heavily laden.

## VII. Tancred’s Victory Is Proclaimed

Tancred therefore avenged the wounds of his companions, acquired spoils, and, blessed by favor, sent everyone across the river ahead of him, while he himself followed last of all.

O how many praises greeted him! How great he appeared, and how much greater still he seemed destined to become in the hearts of everyone! With how much reverence he was honored at once by both nobles and commoners!

All had one mind and one story. O where, and when, and in whom among the sons of men was there ever your equal, Tancred? From what place was sluggishness so far removed from you? How entirely was rest separated from you, fear alien to you, pride polished away, and luxury expelled? Who was swifter when summoned, more obliging when asked, more easily reconciled when offended?

Happy were your ancestors in possessing such a pledge, your descendants in possessing such an ancestor, the Calabrians in possessing such a fosterling, and the Normans in possessing such offspring! Happy those to whom you came as their glory—and we far happier, for whom your boldness is a wall.

Your boldness is our shield against those who attack us, and bow and sword against those whom we must fight. If danger advances, you are sent ahead against it; if it follows, you are placed behind to cut it down. Blessed is God, who preserved you as a safeguard for his people; and blessed are you, who protect it with the arm of your valor.

With such praises, and many others still greater, everyone congratulated the victor’s return, repeatedly echoing these words and following him along the roads and through the tents all the way to Tancred himself.

From that time, being in Tancred’s company seemed to make one secure; being in the army without him seemed, because of one’s loneliness, almost the same as not being in the army at all. Consequently, many, inferring greater things from the great deeds they had witnessed, subjected both themselves and their possessions to his rule.

He gathered the boldness and strength of young men by payment, attracted them by merit, and earned them by example. When he had plenty, no one serving under him was in want; when he was in want, he borrowed from richer companions, distributing the money so as to enrich the need of the poorer. Again, if what he had borrowed was demanded back, he sought other creditors. Thus he begged from some on behalf of others, whether booty or war had made him wealthy.

So prudent was the man that he showed himself generous to some, truthful to others, and indeed truthful to everyone.

## VIII. Alexius the Emperor Is Informed of Bohemond’s and Tancred’s Arrival and Victory

Meanwhile, a messenger sent to investigate the emperor Alexius—whether with this or a similar report—returned and threw him into confusion:

“Bohemond, son of Guiscard, has crossed the Adriatic and now possesses Macedonia. You have already often experienced the greatness of his forces, but today’s forces surpass those of the past no less than an eagle surpasses a sparrow.

Formerly Normandy supplied him with soldiers and Lombardy with infantry. The Normans came to win victories; the Lombards came to increase the numbers. One people had come for war, the other to serve. Now, however, both are warriors: two peoples only, but few of two peoples.

Moreover, they served for pay, compelled by an edict, not voluntarily and not eager for glory. Now, by contrast, a people stirred up from all Gaul has come and joined to it all Italy as well. Beyond and on this side of the Alps, from Illyricum to the Ocean, there is no region that has denied Bohemond its arms.

Soldiers, archers, and slingers, by their great numbers, have left no place in the army for an unarmed crowd. The bread of this side of the sea is not enough for the armed men; it is dug out from the very caverns of the earth—much less for the unarmed common people, who must turn from leisure and abundance to labor and hunger.

Everyone who serves in the camp of the Guiscardid is armed, warlike, and laborious. Add the Guiscardids Tancred, William, and Robert, whose boldness, like that of Punic lions, is akin to Bohemond’s both by family relationship and by zeal for war.

He compels none of them, as he himself was once compelled; rather, he crossed because the entreaties of all compelled him. Hence those whom one will, equal purpose, and the same zeal have joined in harmony will rarely be torn apart.”

## IX. Alexius Sends a Letter to Bohemond

Struck by these reports, the crafty emperor turned new deceits over in his heart and new plans in his breast. He sought to entangle in nets the lions whom he did not dare to provoke with a hunting spear.

Accordingly, he burdened messengers with snares and instructed them to meet the approaching Bohemond with flatteries such as these:

“King Alexius sends greetings to Bohemond.

[Col. 0499D] I have been informed of your arrival, which I received with a father’s affection upon hearing of it. You are now undertaking an enterprise worthy of your character, since you have turned your zeal for war against the barbarians. As I see, God has favored the undertakings of the Franks, whom he foresaw must be protected by so great a companion.

Your arrival also promises singular effectiveness for my own desires. To say nothing of everything else, even the Turkish prophets themselves assign triumphs to you from their own people. Come, then, and hasten, my son, and by your arrival release the leaders who are awaiting you here from their delay. The leaders sigh for you, the nobles sigh for you, and the whole people sigh for you.

There are Latin heroes with me, and they too have been presented with great gifts; but the better known you are to me than the others, the greater gifts you have yet to receive. Here are cloaks, here gold, here horses; here an abundance of every kind of treasure awaits you. Whatever you have seen anywhere is nothing compared with what is here with me.

Know that all these things have been prepared for you, as for a son, provided that you make yourself kind to me; as a son, provided that you make yourself faithful to me. You will therefore find a fountain of gold, so that whenever you have exhausted what you seek, you may seek again what is to be spent, and take what you have requested without difficulty.

To enable you to undertake the journey with a lighter step, if you come content with a few companions, you will hasten your arrival more freely. The rest of the multitude, however, leaving the leaders behind, should take the road all the more conveniently because it is to be traversed more slowly.”

## X. Deceived by Alexius’s Promises, Bohemond Reluctantly Pays Him Homage

The ambassadors, equipped with these deceptions in addition to their own, set out, approached, met him, and spoke. Bohemond, therefore, intoxicated by the honeyed surface of their words, did not sense the hidden poison beneath. The wealth of Constantinople, offered to him without solicitation, deceived him—the wealth for which he had long sprinkled land and sea with much blood.

He was also pleased that what he had done wrong against the Greeks during his prolonged campaign had been so readily forgiven. It was therefore decided that he should go ahead with a few companions to the place to which he was summoned, while Tancred followed more slowly with the remaining multitude.

This decision did not displease the ears of Marchisus’s son when it reached them. For just as a hawk fears snares and a fish fears the hook, so he dreaded the fraudulent familiarity of the Greeks. Therefore, scorning the king’s gifts, he had already decided to evade his presence.

When Bohemond had determined whom he would honor by taking with him and whom by sending away, he departed from a town called Chympsala. While the promises wearied his mind, his mind drove the horseman, the horseman drove the horse, and within a few days they reached Constantinople.

There Bohemond was presented to Alexius and submitted to the yoke commonly called *hommagium*—homage. He did so under compulsion, but was nevertheless granted so great an extent of Romania that a horse would require fifteen days to cross it lengthwise and eight days to cross it from side to side.

Before long, flying rumor revealed and added the new event to Tancred: “A similar submission awaits you, who are following, and it will be the more disgraceful the smaller the reward.”

## XI. Tancred Secretly Laments Bohemond’s Downfall

When Tancred heard this, he grieved for Bohemond and was anxious for himself. Seeing, as it were, the neighboring wall already aflame, he did not doubt that the fire threatened his own house.

He therefore turned the matter over in his mind, considered it, and reflected on what path he could use to pass by, by what arts he could deceive, and by what strength he could punish the treacheries of the faithless king. Here he weighed forces, there deceits; here boldness, there power; here soldiers, there wealth; here small numbers, there a multitude.

What should he undertake? Should he fight? But the enemy was stronger. Should he plead? But the same man was inexorable. Should he cross? But the sea raged between them.

Seeing, then, the Frankish leaders entangled by gifts, Bohemond by deceits, and himself by difficulties, he persisted and revolved these thoughts in his heart:

“Shameful crime! Where is faith? Where prudence? O human hearts! This man is faithless, that one improvident; this one shameless in doing harm, that one imprudent in recognizing it.

A man went out, summoned by the name of his son to be embraced with a father’s affection. He came to a kingdom and found a yoke. He came to become more exalted, but was compelled to exalt another, becoming himself the lower. Certainly, ignorant of fraud, he believed fraudulent flatteries.

Yet he was ordered, leaving the army behind, to go ahead with a few companions, as though he were being released from the burden of the multitude. Was this one decision alone not enough to dissolve the unjust coils of the entanglement? If his mind had not been perverse, that single decision would both have excluded the snares and closed the roads.

Nevertheless, they went with a few companions, as though unarmed hands could serve as protection. For what should I say about the leaders of Gaul, whose very multitude ought not merely to have withdrawn them from the yoke of homage, but also to have subdued all rebels?

I pity the men and am ashamed for them, although they themselves have felt neither shame nor pity for their own situation. I seem already to see the outcome, when expenditure will be followed by punishment, want, and repentance. They will indeed repent when they see themselves being compelled to unjust actions, burdened because they were compelled, and unable to free themselves once burdened.

Then, I say, they will repent. But what place is there for repentance when there is none for correction? For what correction remains now? Can what has once been sworn be forsworn? Can those who voluntarily subjected themselves to another’s authority become their own masters? Can those be free who have been sold?

For who serves more justly: the man purchased by the very seller of himself, or the man brought to market by a robber’s violence? They will therefore rightly pay the penalties of what is to come, secure in the present and content with it.”

## XII. He Avoids Approaching Alexius

Having lamented Bohemond’s downfall, Tancred wisely resolved to escape the yoke of Gaul, to console Bohemond, and to punish Alexius’s wiles.

Accordingly, when he came to Constantinople, he did not, like the others, turn toward the king; he sent no trumpets ahead, sounded no horn, but passed secretly. For after stripping off his military identity, he assumed the appearance of a foot traveler, so that rustic clothing might conceal Tancred and deceive Alexius.

Thus, with the vessel, the rower, and the north wind driving the sail, Europe receded behind him while Asia hurried to meet him. Meanwhile the Guiscardid invited the sailors to the oars and himself moved the blue waters of the Hellespont with an oar.

Before long the stern reached the desired shore, the shortness of the journey aiding the travelers’ hopes. Once he had gained the Asian beach, the son of Marchisus, now safer, resumed his clothing and name; and when the other leaders departed for Nicaea, he joined them as a companion.

Bohemond, however, had not yet left the Thracian shore. He had delayed at the request of Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles. The necessity that compelled the count to delay and intercede was this: the king wished to impose upon the count the law that he had imposed upon the others who had gone ahead.

The count replied that it would be far more agreeable to him to cut short this condition by the shortcut of death; Bohemond’s arrival was therefore extremely necessary for settling the matter.

When Alexius learned from his scouts that the Guiscardid had secretly crossed, he grieved at having been outwitted and demanded the absent man from those who were present. He attributed Tancred’s escape to their deceit. His eyes turned especially toward Bohemond, and his anger made them like those of a stepmother.

As they thundered at him, while his throat simultaneously roared threats, Bohemond, whether he wished to or not, swore that he would surrender Tancred into the king’s hands by homage. Otherwise, it had not been safe either to remain or to depart.

## XIII. He Sends Envoys to Bohemond
While these events were taking place, Tancred sent two soldiers, Atropius and Garinus, back to Constantinople, to rebuke Bohemond for his delays and to report that the Turks’ forces were approaching; unless he hastened, his hopes would have to be abandoned, since the enemy would be defeated without him. This was reported to Alexius as well, who therefore summoned the messengers to him, intending to deal with their master and, as though to extort something new from them through fear of his presence.

When the envoys were asked who they were, where they were from, and for what purpose they had been sent, they confidently replied that they were Normans sent by Tancred [Col. 0502B] to draw Bohemond out. Seeing that the fearless men did not falter, the emperor dismissed them unpunished, for he saw that punishing them would be useless.

When Tancred had learned all this both from the envoys, who had preceded him on their return, and from Bohemond, who had followed them, it is difficult to say—and difficult to believe—how bitterly he bore it, and how deeply he grieved that his vigilance had been deceived by another’s sleepiness. Nor could the blazing furnace contain its flames, as the whirlwind of swift rumor fanned them into surging fire. Accordingly, he is said to have poured forth his inward groans in the following complaint:

> “Alas, how blind are mortal minds concerning the future! When they think they have completed their task, they must begin again from the start. Vain is prudence when hostile fortune opposes it; and conversely, it is vain to oppose one whom the gods favor. I had thought that sufficient provision had been made for me, and that I had left no room either for sluggishness or negligence. I had rejected gifts, escaped alone, eluded the guards, avoided the ambushes, and accomplished what I had scarcely been permitted even to attempt.
>
> “Alas, how great a thing it was to pass unharmed through the snares which even the innocent are not permitted to escape unharmed! I had seen noble men—some descended from commanders, others from kings—voluntarily exchange kingdoms for exile; I had seen them come peacefully, immense regions and barbarian kingdoms bowing before their arrival. Neither land nor sea had stood in their way. Yet when we reached the point at which no monster was more savage than the three-formed Chimera, there was no Pegasus to free those entangled, no [Col. 0502D] one to carry away the stunned. All were compelled to pass as though beneath a mistress’s spear; all were forced to swear everything they were ordered to swear.
>
> “To return to myself: having deserved a strict exactor, I feared an even stricter avenger. Therefore, the greater the zeal for vengeance that had blazed up against me, the more vigilant I ought to have been in rescuing myself. For that reason I had cast aside both command of the camp and myself, lest I be bent down like the others and so avenge the anger of others more freely.
>
> “For what purpose is there in complaining about a man who has returned me to the fetter I had broken? He is not satisfied to have bound his own neck unless he also binds mine. Perhaps his mouth denies that he begrudged my prosperity; but the fact that this oath flowed from the fountain of envy is plain even to bleary eyes, and the outcome proves it. It is indeed uncertain whether greater laziness [Col. 0503A] or incompetence threw me into this misery. Both were great, and both were stepmothers to my prosperity.
>
> “Yet he swore under compulsion to my ruin, as though by these words he might conceal his envy, moderate his indignation, excuse his deed, and absolve its author; and by this other device, proclaim his innocence. But delays do not make the innocent innocent, nor do they defend the sleeper from guilt.
>
> “Very well: I shall preserve my vow; I shall redeem the perjury—at my own, I say, at my own peril I shall redeem another’s. I was deceived, but not overcome through my own negligence; overcome, but through another’s weakness; captured, but through the liberation of a kinsman. Indeed, if I live, the victor in this contest will regret having fostered hatred and not having deserved reconciliation. For I consider it a small matter to annul what I did not willingly desire to swear, but submitted to unwillingly under the violence of a tyrant’s command [Col. 0503B]—especially since observing that promise brings public harm, whereas contempt of it brings general advantage.”

XIV.—On the siege of Nicaea, and first on the commanders conducting it. Godfrey of Bouillon.

Now, having unfolded what Marchisides either has complained of or could have complained of, let him himself breathe for a little while, as we recall the encirclement of Nicaea, measure out the camps, and remember the names, lineage, and character of the princes by whom that city was attacked and compelled to surrender. These matters are such that they neither conflict with the praises already prescribed nor fail to provide material for those still to be written.

The commanders of the greatest renown—those from whom the others descended, not those who received “Martiatic” honors from certain persons—were these. First was Duke Godfrey, son of the aged Eustace, count of Boulogne; the same man who had sent him gave him the dignity and name of duke of Bouillon. Bouillon is a town in the kingdom of Lothair, the chief place of the neighboring duchy, which had been left to Godfrey, the duke’s nephew, by his uncle, the elder Godfrey.

The younger Godfrey’s nobility was enriched by many virtues, both secular and divine: divine virtues in his generosity toward the poor and his mercy toward offenders. Moreover, he was distinguished by humility, gentleness, sobriety, justice, and chastity; he appeared more the light of monks than the leader of soldiers. Yet he also knew how to handle worldly affairs: to fight, arrange battle lines, and extend the Church by arms. He learned to strike the enemy first, or among the first, as a boy; he made it his practice as a young man; and he did not cease from it in old age.

So devout was he, the son of a warlike count and a most religious countess, that even when observed by a rival he deserved to hear: “For the pursuit of war, behold the father; for devotion to God, behold the mother.” Countless warriors followed this commander of such character to the walls of the aforesaid city, where he was the first besieger.

XV.—Robert, count of Normandy; Bohemond; Hugh the Great; Stephen, count of Blois; Robert, count of Flanders; Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles.

Robert, count of Normandy, followed him. He was the son of William, king and conqueror of England; in birth, wealth, and eloquence he was not second but superior to the duke; in the things belonging to Caesar, his equal; in the things belonging to God, his inferior. His piety and generosity would have been greatly admirable, had he observed moderation in either; but because he observed it in neither, he went astray in both.

Normandy experienced his merciless mercy while he governed: through the impunity granted to robberies, he spared neither man nor God from the license of plunderers. The count considered that assassins’ hands, robbers’ throats, and adulterers’ lascivious tails owed him the same reverence as his own men. Consequently, no bound prisoner was dragged before him in tears without immediately obtaining from him, once released, reciprocal tears. Thus, as I have said, Normandy complained that at that time no crime had a bridle; rather, a spur had been added to them all.

It is clear that generosity was the little sister of this piety, since it would purchase a hawk or a dog for any amount of silver. Meanwhile, the count’s table had only one refuge: the plunder of the citizens, and even that within his own country. But once he had crossed his native borders, he largely mastered the luxury to which he had previously succumbed through the abundance of his great wealth.

Bohemond shines third in this order. To repeat his genealogy here would be superfluous, and to record his character and spirit seems premature, especially since the preceding page has dealt with his lineage. The following page, however, will turn almost entirely upon the fortunes and misfortunes of this same man as upon a hinge.

Hugh the Great, brother of Philip, king of France, and son of Henry, holds fourth place: great by birth, great by surname, great in integrity, and great and powerful both through his own military force and that of his brother’s kingdom. Yet he was more venerable for the glory of royal blood than for abundance of wealth, exceptional numbers, or triumphal achievements.

Fifth was Stephen, count of Blois, himself close to kings, being a great-grandson of the Franks [Col. 0504C] and a son-in-law of the English. If generosity had been illumined by cheerfulness, and boldness by ardor, to the extent they deserved, nothing would have been lacking in him for a commander, nothing for a most vigorous soldier.

After him came Robert, count of Flanders—Flanders, nurse of knights; Flanders, fertile in horses; Flanders, land of Ceres; Flanders, land of dangers—which, excelling even in maidenly beauty, had deserved the French, English, and Danish kings as sons-in-law. The count, now a lofty kinsman of these, disdained popular rule, while he himself was praised above all other commanders of armies for sword and lance. Hence it later happened that he was celebrated as possessing far more soldiers than the other dukes, but, because he neglected the care of command, much less of a duke.

Last of all, Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles, shines forth as a besieger. Last, I say, in time—not in wealth, power, counsel, or military numbers. In all these he had been distinguished among the foremost from the beginning; and soon, when the money of the others had ebbed away, his wealth flowed in and surpassed theirs. His people were frugal rather than extravagant, serving thrift rather than reputation. Terrified by another’s example, they did not, like the Franks, labor to diminish their substance, but always worked to increase it. Thus that prudent people, with a divine foresight of the future, did not allow their count to suffer want: a man who cultivated justice and punished injustice; a lamb to the timid, a lion to the arrogant.

XVI.—The city is surrounded. Tancred is the first of all to kill a Turk and put others to flight.

Thus France strove to surround Nicaea with these conquerors, to subdue it, and finally to compel it to surrender; Greece assisted, and God accomplished it. But while the last, as I have said, Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles, was pitching his tents before the eastern gate—for that space alone remained vacant, since the others had already been occupied—behold, a Turkish army appeared descending by the shortcuts of the nearby mountain, as though about to enter the city through that same gate, eager to come to the aid of the besieged in a swift attack.

A shout arose. The count, being nearest the place, was the first to meet them; soon the other commanders followed. Some came armed, others half-armed, each hastening forward as the ardor of battle had roused him. Tancred, farther away, came racing up on horseback, burning with anger that the place had denied him the glory of the first wound [Col. 0505B]. Thus what the place had taken away, courage restored. In his absence, flight and attack had distributed the turns of hope and fear now to one side, now to the other; but when the man who was regarded—and truly was—as one standing for a multitude, a soldier for an army, arrived and charged, a Turk’s neck was immediately severed; Christ’s soldiers were made fierce, and the enemy effeminate.

The Turks, therefore, their spirits extinguished, turned their faces toward the mountains, their backs toward the Franks, and their efforts toward flight. But the count’s courage, the enemy’s flight, and the shame of delay drove the Franks against the fugitives. Had the refuge of the nearby mountain not suddenly received the retreating men, barbarian blood would somewhat later have quenched the thirst of Latin spears to satiety. But once fear of the mountain’s nearness—fear that gives wings to the feet—suddenly intervened, the men easily escaped by ascending where they had invaded by descending, leaving behind only that life which Tancred had sent beneath the underworld as a herald of his courage.

Many, nevertheless, carried home dishonorable wounds in their backs. The worshipers of Christ returned joyfully to camp, some marked by bloody spears, others by bent spearheads, others by shafts broken off, and some by blunted swords. The sight of the Turk’s head was displayed publicly. Through all the peoples, tongues, ages, sexes, and professions of the entire army, Tancred was celebrated as the first to cut off one Turkish head and put countless others to flight.

Anyone who considers the matter carefully will discover that this deed was not without some prophetic foreshadowing of the future Tancred. Such first fruits, offered from heaven, suited the man who already from that moment—or rather from eternity—had been chosen to undertake war as the most unconquerable of all and to be overcome in no peril.

XVII.—The city is surrendered. Tancred is brought before Alexius. Tancred’s words to the emperor.

When the besieged saw that the strength of the besiegers had increased while their own forces had been deprived of the reinforcements long awaited, and when they were further terrified because Count Raymond, having dug beneath the walls last of all, was shaking their foundations more violently through his deeper excavations, they surrendered the city on terms allowing them at least to destroy what they were not permitted to purchase, provided that they themselves remained unharmed.

Both sides approved the arrangement, and a message was sent to the emperor. The emperor, informed by that fortunate report, sent reinforcements and himself followed the messengers as far as the inlet commonly called the Arm of Saint George. From there, with the city secured, Bohemond was adjured by the terms of the treaty, by joined right hands, and by the faith of his homage to sail to him, bringing back Marchisides with him as he had promised.

When Alexius saw Marchisides’ homage, he was more frightened than reassured and far more cast down than uplifted. He intensified his anger but did not obtain reverence. For the prudent man, as though instructed by a divine oracle, measured the outcomes that thereafter followed. The kingdom of the Greeks did not reach Jerusalem across the immense extent of its territory. Cities captured from the Turks across so great a distance would have to be dedicated to Christian worship. Yet cities taken from the Greeks ought not to be returned to such guardians. The Franks alone were sufficient for this kind of guardianship; otherwise, to restore cities and towns to the Greeks was to restore them to the Turks. He could not serve two masters at once—namely, the commonwealth and the king of Greece.

Turning these matters over in his mind, the prudent man is said to have filled the royal ears with a complaint much like this:

> “Bohemond, your blood kinsman, compelled by your power, forced me, O emperor, to return here. If your promises, gifts, or intimacy had captured me, there were approaches by which I might have been allowed to burst in. But once those things had displeased me, your arrival would have pleased me in vain. Considering this, I took care to pass you by more freely; though I had freed myself by vigilant care, your force has driven me back here against my will. You should therefore know that you cannot trust me if today I make any agreement under compulsion.
>
> “Having been warned of this, you must also consider what follows. Behold, the time has come for me to discharge the oath of our kindred compact. Yet this condition will intervene: you must seek Jerusalem with my assistance, and the treaty will soon collapse when you either begrudge their successes or fail to relieve their misfortunes. Let anyone who abandons their loyalty never expect me to remain loyal.
>
> “If, therefore, you desire to rule, strive to serve, assured of Tancred’s obedience whenever you have assured yourself of Christ’s army. I do not refuse to serve you, as the servant of all, on behalf of all. Let a concise statement define the sum of these matters: whatever devotion you show first toward the Franks, such devotion may the Greeks expect from me toward themselves.”

These words, drawn from the fountain of prudence, the tabernacle of his secret heart, the dwelling-place of wisdom, won praise for a spirit that both interceded so faithfully for the commonwealth and so steadfastly feared neither for his household nor abandoned justice. A Gallic shout arose; the Greek murmurs likewise did not refuse him the favor he deserved.

XVIII.—He asks for the emperor’s tent. The emperor is indignant.

When Alexius saw that the man despised money and could not be caught, like the others, in a golden chain, and that he could not draw him after himself, he followed the man who was leading him and assented to his repeated words.

They joined right hands, although Marchisides inwardly seethed and outwardly grew fierce with grim eyes. After the ceremony that princes observe for such treaties had been completed, Tancred was invited to ask the king for whatever he wished, with no refusal to be suffered concerning his request. It was assumed that he would ask for gold, silver, gems, robes, and similar things—necessary support for the journey and a blandishment for a greedy spirit.

But the spirit that despised money and rivaled royal grandeur scorned ordinary things. What other commanders would have refused because of the burden of the honor offered, he desired; and he said that he preferred only royal possessions.

The king had a tent remarkable both for workmanship and for its natural qualities, offering the spectator a double wonder. Its courtyards were towered like those of a city; twenty camels could scarcely carry its heavy burden; its capacity was suitable for accommodating a multitude; and its summit rose above all the rest.

> “As cypresses customarily rise among the pliant viburnums.”  
> *(Virgil, First Eclogue.)*

This gift, therefore, alone captured the mind of the great-hearted son of Wiscard. He designated this hall as suitable for himself: a burden indeed useless at present, but no insignificant sign of the future.

When Alexius learned of this, he is said to have seethed against the petitioner as Delian Apollo once did against Phaethon—except that there paternal affection trembled, whereas here hostile indignation raged. Phoebus groaned over the danger of his son; Alexius over the lofty spirit of the man. Phoebus urged his son to desire safer things. Alexius refused Tancred’s request in these words:

> “So Alexius refuses what Marchisides desires, and after refusing it rebukes him: ‘Is Marchisides, then, comparing himself with me by asking for royal insignia? Do common things seem mean to him unless he seeks my one palace, unique throughout the world? Once he has obtained that, what remains except for him to remove the diadem from my head and place it on his own? But, I suppose, he lacks halls spacious enough to accommodate the clients he has gathered, and such a great multitude of soldiers cannot be enclosed within domestic walls.
>
> “‘Therefore he asks for a royal residence which, immense in its dimensions, might suffice for so magnificent a lord. Yet, if the thing he requests is to be ceded to him, where are the mules, where the muleteers, where the vehicle suited to so great a mass? Surely, once he has obtained it, the only thing left is for him to follow on foot, as though following divine beings, the residence loaded onto others.
>
> “‘Let him remember the ass disguised as a lion, who suffered harm from the lion’s hide: having put it on to frighten others, he deserved to experience the terrifying rustic. Warned by this example, let him not try to frighten the ignorant with the shadow of my name, lest, when finally recognized, Tancred be exposed.
>
> “‘Let him measure himself according to his own measure and foot, and provide himself with a tent suited to himself; but let him abandon all hope of this one. If he continues to be angry at the refusal, I shall make light of his anger—and of his threats, however great they may be. For his foolish ambition has now revealed his mind to me more and more. While he remained silent, he could be thought a philosopher; but once he opened his mouth, he proved himself mad.
>
> “‘Come, then, whatever fraud, cunning, anger, and fury you possess, Marchisides, hurl them against my head. I shall receive your burning rage. I do not deem you worthy either to be my enemy or my friend.’”

Alexius spoke thus, dictated by anger and cunning. In part he concealed his fear; in part he softened the swelling of his most savage bile. But Tancred, as though imitating that jesting image, seized upon the final words of the lengthy speech and, replying to no one ever more willingly, said:

> “I deem you worthy to be my enemy, not my friend. We have parted from one another, and shall meet no further.”

XIX.—Tancred and Bohemond escape from his hands.

Tancred returned to the shore, where, with a rower prepared, fortune was at once invoked and present. He crossed without delay, he to whom nothing was so displeasing as delay.

Bohemond, however, having departed somewhat later, nearly awaited and encountered the king’s ambushes. But secretly informed, he turned to flight; otherwise he would have been taken in chains. Then the king’s messenger followed those who had departed, shouting and calling them back. But, having been granted their discharge, extricated from knots, and emerged from storms, they were unwilling to expose themselves again to the same whirlwinds.

They despised the recall of one absent, whose person had been scorned when present; and, since they were not going to approach the cradle of the highest king, they did not listen to the perfidy of the one calling them back like Herod. Having put their hand to the plow, they did not turn their eyes backward, having once learned how harmful that backward glance can be.

Even those women—one of whom looked back upon the chaos of Sodom, and the other of whom was looked back upon by her Treician husband—prevent those who have emerged into the light from being plunged again into darkness. Warned by so many examples, they seemed to themselves to have escaped all these torments by passing this one torturer by.

After a long stretch of delays had afflicted the Latin commanders, they overcame their weariness and loaded the pack animals with provisions necessary both for themselves and for the beasts that carried them. For many days, a sterility that removed all fertility confronted those making the crossing; no relief from crops would lighten their want.

On its frontier, the Turkish king Solyman was waiting for their arrival, so that the prudent might fall upon the unsuspecting, the well-provisioned upon the hungry, the lively upon the exhausted, and the strong upon the weak. But, as though by divine providence, provision was made for the faithful people: a supply of food was transported across the uncultivated wilderness, and, once carried there, it in a way carried its own carriers.

XX.—The Christian army is divided at a fork in the road.

When the day before the last had passed, near the end of that arid region, fortune’s game almost turned its favor from the worshipers of Christ to the worshipers of Muhammad, and dared to favor Tancred excessively. As they resumed their daily—or, so to speak, nightly—road, as they habitually did, the route divided into two, and Christ’s army became a traveler at a fork.

Most people attributed this error to deliberate policy: the land would serve the wealthy people more generously if they spread out across its breadth than if they remained packed together in a confined mass. It also happened that the count of Normandy, Bohemond, and Tancred were separated from the crowd, as though the three of the same stock might, by one plan, anticipate one glory for their homeland.

Others asserted that the division had not been voluntary but accidental, neither planned in advance nor desired by those who had turned aside—an opinion that mercifully excused fortune and softened envy. This view stood more firmly supported because the commanders mentioned above had not removed their baggage after subduing the common people; because they enjoyed the company of foreign soldiers; and because, finally, they had not fortified their own force, the greater part of which was absent.

XXI.—In their mutual encounter, the Latin and barbarian lines clash in battle.

When the Norman standards therefore announced the threat of war to the Turks—for tireless Tancred, maintaining his custom of pressing ahead, had been the first to hasten both to see and to be seen—it was arranged on both sides that the more rapid troops should be prevented from cutting off the slower by the river flowing between them.

Evening twilight had begun to yield when the Latin and barbarian lines discovered one another’s approach. They spent the ensuing night partly in rest and, from midnight onward, in labor. The more ready part of the faithful reached the banks of the specified river around the first hour, before the unbelievers did. The diligent surveyor had scarcely fixed the first camp when the cry arose: “The enemy! The enemy!” It was repeated sharply, and the troops advanced boldly.

Those who had come to be armed put on their arms; those already armed were carried into battle. The hand powerful with arrows was blunted, now pierced by lances, now severed by swords. It was blunted, I say, so that what had been the first line had to be brought into the middle, while what had been in the middle was compelled, for protection, to become the front.

When the Normans had pressed upon the fleeing enemy to that point, the dense wedges recovered their strength, and those who had just driven the others to flight were themselves turned to flight.

Meanwhile the count of Normandy and Bohemond had each drawn up only one battle line of his own; already they were advancing step by step, eager to enter the fight. As the Turks pressed on and the Christians came to their aid, the battle was fought with great force on both sides. The bow did little; the lance somewhat; the sword most of all.

The Turks were defended by a multitude lacking numerical order; our men by their armor, shields, and helmets. Much blood was shed on both sides, more among the barbarians. Their slaughter did not cease; but, like the regenerating heads of the Hydra, whenever a few fell, countless others took their place.

XXII.—The Christians are turned to flight. Count Robert of Normandy rallies their courage.

But the faithful legion shared a common downfall with these men, not a common reinforcement. Exhausted as it struck, shaken as it resisted, and weakened as it thinned, it turned its back; and what it had never learned anywhere before, it learned in an instant: to flee.

O miserable battle! O mournful flight! O loss upon loss! O wound upon wound! The force of the military flight trampled the slowness of the foot soldiers, while the thick forest of infantry spears alternately impeded and extinguished the flight. The disaster became pitiable even to the enemy: the backs bristled with arrows, while the others were pierced by lances like spits for roasting.

Since neither those who drove them with bows nor those who were driven with spurs spared them, the fugitives withdrew to the camp—the least consolation, but the only one.

There at last the royal blood of the son of William, remembering who he was, of what lineage, and for whom he served, uncovered his head, called upon Normandy, and rebuked Bohemond, his comrade—or rather his fellow fugitive:

> “Ho, Bohemond, where are you fleeing? Apulia is far away, Hydruntum is far away, and every hope of Latin territory is far away. Here we must stand. Here awaits us either glorious punishment as the defeated or a glorious crown as victors. Both fates are glorious, I say, but one is also the happier, inasmuch as it makes men blessed more quickly. Come, young men: let us die and rush into the midst of the weapons.”

Warned by these words, the rest of the young men gathered around the commanders, henceforth readier for death than for flight. They stood unafraid, like a lion covering itself against hunting-spears in fury, recently roused from a long, sluggish rest in its lair and gradually roused to anger by the barking, trumpet, shouting, and darts that harass it. As though each man’s anger did not run separately from one to the other, but the anger of both were a single thing, the more fiercely the lion’s anger is kindled, the more the hunter’s sluggishness grows cold.

In the same way, as the faithful people grew fiercer, the unbelievers relaxed, and no longer dared to attack men who had begun to fear nothing. Both sides therefore drew breath, one held back by courage, as has been said, and the other by fear.

XXIII.—A great slaughter of the faithful.

Meanwhile a messenger was sent to report the outcome to the army, which knew nothing of it, and to hasten away so that those men might hasten to be present. But the adversaries sent others for another purpose: scouts to inflict destruction, not petitioners for assistance and safety.

That band of Turks, therefore, sweeping past our horsemen, leapt upon the common people—greatest in number, but weak in strength. These stragglers were following the tracks of the hastening army, believing that they had opposed walls to the dangers, when suddenly the Turks rushed upon them, raging first with arrows and then with swords. They obtained booty beyond their hopes and victory without a battle.

The old were slaughtered; the children were dragged away; those of middle age, whether of one side or the other, displayed the face of their condition and suffered its fate. Yet the sword most often and most savagely claimed the underage as well, the abundance of booty making the robber more ferocious than the most ferocious creature. When the hands of Briareus were not enough for plundering, he persisted in slaughter, so that by this means at least he might fill his ravenous spirit.

Thus it happened that, among so great a number, scarcely anyone escaped either wound or bondage. Never, in all the disasters of wars that had preceded or were yet to come, was so much Latin blood granted to a Gentile sword.

What more is there to say? Their rage for slaughter exhausted but not yet satisfied, the victorious enemy pursued the vanquished to the camp, burdened with their own baggage or that of their companions. It was a spectacle sufficiently pitiable to our army, but no one pitied its courage sufficiently: for their hopes clung to this alone, that they might resist their attackers, not that they might in turn attack them at all while they paused.

XXIV.—Tancred resists fiercely.

Tancred, on the opposite side of the camp, was subduing the enemy who had climbed the hill separating the tents; from there they could more easily inflict harm and more difficultly suffer it. Having cast these men down in one swift and rapid attack, the brave man occupied the ascent, attacking many with the help of only a few.

Bohemond, unwilling—indeed, forbidding him to do so—could scarcely induce a few companions to join the undertaking. He forbade it because the enemy army, spread out around ours in a kind of theatrical display, had enclosed it, signifying death on every side. Therefore the prudence of the Christians denied the young men, whose spirits were burning for combat, permission to go out, lest the rashness of a few should disrupt the whole order of affairs.

XXV.—His brother William also cuts down the enemy.

William Marchisides, however, while fearing for his brother, forgot himself. He did not fear Bohemond, who was calling him back, nor the strength of the hostile multitude; he burned to become the companion of his brother’s boldness.

Oh, wretched and blessed in the same deed—the man who rushes to death in order to pass over into life! For when the crowd had been driven back from the hill, as described above, it had not so much retreated from those whose swords it had sensed as from those whom it had vainly feared would follow.

When he looked back and saw how many he had driven away, rather than which men, weighing their number, his courage did not return. His ardor grew sharper, for grief heaped upon his labor and shame upon his grief. They therefore rushed forward, having cast aside their bows, intending to rage more boldly with drawn blades.

This battle was now thought to be not a battle but a punishment; they were not fighting enemies but taking a second vengeance, as though upon men condemned in capital matters. Yet the strength of the very small number set against them displayed a wall of courage that would not yield, even if King Solyman himself should rage against them with all his forces [Col. 0511B].

There was a crash. These men brandished their lances; those, as has been said, drew their swords. These applied armor to their chests, shields to their armor, and helmets as protection; the others had bucklers. The attack of the former descended from above; that of the latter strove upward from below.

The former were spurred on by grief mingled with shame; the latter, as though standing on a theater’s viewing platform, were pressed by as many goads as there were eyes watching them. Thus, for some, the position of the ground, the advantage of their weapons, and even their small number served as protection; for the others, everything worked to their disadvantage, including the very multitude in which they trusted.

Indeed, as the Turk climbed, an ash spear met him from a distance; and when struck with force, it either finished him or threw him down. When one had been finished or thrown down, as the spear was swung it attacked several others with a similar fall. Yet when one fell, as happens in a vast multitude, many immediately took his place, and again other, equally numerous men succeeded those many.

Thus it happened that those who had come to fight in fury, indignation, and contempt first matched the height of the mound by the piled-up ruin of their own men before they could trample it; whereas Christ’s number was neither diminished nor wounded. So lavish was the ash spear with its abundant assistance that it simultaneously supplied the functions of both shield and sword.

What could a blade do against this? A blade, I say, whose function is to strike what is near and spare what is distant; to plunge in at close quarters and threaten from afar. To summarize its capacity briefly: because the limits of its effectiveness are equal to the bounds set by its length, once drawn it could threaten, but even when thrown it could not inflict a wound.

The experienced battle line therefore realized that its assault upon the bold was broken and that boldness was not safe. It no longer attempted to match strength against strength, but resumed the arts and bows it had cast aside. Had it continued for some time, as it had begun, to join foot to foot, hand to hand, boss to boss, surely the savage slaughter inflicted by the great-hearted men would have yielded; its only consolation would have been that it had one warrior, while these had all their fierce fighters.

XXVI.—William falls.

But once they had resumed their bows, the flying hail—those swords had spared—did not spare. Those whom the swords had not reached, the arrows pierced; where the swords had not climbed, the arrows descended. Until then, armor, shields, and helmets had been only a heavy burden; now they became a most welcome barrier, dividing the boundaries of life and death.

Even so, they were burdensome only insofar as they were troublesome, since their lightness, which the men sought, repeatedly turned the skillful hands back toward the threshold.

As the Turks’ bowstrings rained wounds, our men endured while the hail of arrows abated, hoping that some whirlwind blowing from elsewhere might scatter so great a cloud of weapons. The kindred battle lines were close by; the enemy was everywhere; assistance nowhere. Meanwhile the wounded groaned.

One man had his hand pierced, another his eye torn out; some had their feet pierced through, others their heads struck through from above. O compassion! O grief! O mourning! The Marchisides was the shield of some, and William himself was pierced along with the others. The pain of the others remained in the wound; his wounds continued to hurt until death.

His noble body slipped down. His companions carried it into the camp, while the poor man, because of the war, was left behind as a mound. What did you feel, Tancred, when you watched such things? What groans did you utter—you whose breast had just been surrounded by strength and triple bronze? Now your manly features softened into womanly tears; your lips cried out a woman’s wail; your fingers tore at your chin, cheeks, and head. Finally, whatever parts arm a human being tore the remaining unarmed parts apart in cruel rebellion.

Many of the heroes of the faithful likewise dissolved into the same lamentation and mourned over the Marchisides. They pitied Tancred’s tears no less than William’s death.

While these events were taking place, the hill had scarcely been subdued and had received the Turks when, behold, dust testified that Christian cohorts were arriving. Spirits that had been cast down were raised; those that had been raised were cast down in turn.

The cry “God wills it!” was shouted, for our men interjected this joyfully. The adversaries, murmuring “Alas!” and “But—ah, but!” repeated their cries, trembling not so much because their hopes had been taken away as because fears had been brought upon them.

XXVII.—Hugh the Great presses on.

Before the others there raced forward the most illustrious offspring of kings,

Great Hugh, supported by scarcely three hundred helmets.

He rushed into the midst not like one who fights against enemies,

But like one who pursues backs fleeing after battle.

So swift, so fearless, so secure on every side,

He attacks, tears apart, routs, pursues, presses, confines,

Hurls thunderbolts, exults, roars, cries out, rages, burns.

King Solyman sends against him a steel-clad battle line,

Immense in number, valor, threats, and ferocity,

Surpassing in number your harvests, O Gargara;

Equaling in valor Etna’s valleys;

Claiming the whole world for itself in ferocity and threats;

Glad to endure heavy blows and return them.

Thus from one side came so great a cohort, so many weapons, so many bows;

From the other, the great count, as great in character as in name,

Met them with equal encounter, relying on unequal numbers.

They entered battle. One part stood opposite the Gauls,

Shields joined to shields and swords to swords;

One part occupied the circuit of the right flank, another the left,

And on both sides they sent their swift arrows.

Surrounded everywhere by weapons and by the enemy,

The Gallic courage did not know toward whom it should turn

Unless it turned toward all: now it turned against these, now against those,

Like a boar surrounded by a vast crowd of hounds,

Lightning-swift, now tearing these with its teeth, now disemboweling those;

Now biting from behind, and now threatening from the front.

In this way the great-hearted man and the youth relying upon his leadership

Fiercely wheeled around in countless circles,

And wherever it rushed, the enemy fell as it struck and was struck.

XXVIII.—He puts the Turks to flight.

Thus the fresh battle line, already stained red by much slaughter,

Now met the count, already weary, and the cruel anger
