Of the enemy increased the man’s labor and sweat.

It wounds before, behind, to the right and left, and no …

That gives rest to the weary, burdened by no exertion.

After no force can recall the countless men to their ranks, and the enemy returns in greater number than he has fallen, the great count, pitying the deaths of the small band, turns his face toward the rear—the sole appearance of one who fears. In every other respect he was the victor: tearing, overthrowing, and putting the fugitives to flight. His spear was aimed at their fleeing backs; his sword cleaved them; his fiery horse and blazing right hand pursued them. Indeed, the enemy who had killed while retreating now himself retreated, for as soon as he saw the turned face and threatening gaze—the man fleeing death only to encounter it—he hoped it safer to meet unknown multitudes than to remain exposed to the blows of that hand, once experienced.

The commander drives the terrified onward, and heavy pressure is brought to bear upon the driver; he both flees and follows, and alike puts to flight and is put to flight.

### XXIX.—And with him Robert, Count of Flanders

Robert of Flanders, terrible with spear and sword, rushing to battle at full speed, meets them. He lightens the losses and delays, while [the reading is uncertain: *dum quam ultimus hauserat aure*] he is the first to kindle the battle and fatten it with blood.

Thus he confronts the rout and presses on into the very fugitives; wherever he sees dense ranks seething with arrows and hissing threats, there he makes them seethe and hiss still more. The Turks rush upon the count; the fierce count rushes upon them. The Flemish phalanxes, nearly equal in number and valor, kindled by the same fire, follow with footfall, slaughter, and din.

The bow-bearing line is struck down, and the bows are scattered. Quivers are broken; arrows are trampled like seaweed. Shields and cuirasses, like threads of linen before swords, become burdens rather than protection for the Turks.

Thus the mighty count makes those who had been following the backs of the Gauls once again present their backs; and, the positions reversed, compels the Gauls to turn their breasts. By striking down and killing the initially outnumbered ranks, he brings the armies back into numerical balance.

Yet the Turks inflict no wounds at all, whether few or many. Their hope, ignorant of an iron spur, depends wholly upon the lash of the backward-turning rein. Nevertheless, according to their ancestral custom, they wound while fleeing by means of the bow; but the trembling arrow, striking in fear, does not wound. So great a terror has penetrated to their innermost marrow.

“Ah! What trembling the Flemish fire has produced!”

While the unconquered count subdues the enemy and scatters their dense ranks—cutting apart what he has scattered, crushing what he has cut apart, and trampling what he has crushed—he is accompanied by the great-hearted Hugh.

The slaughter does not cease until allied arms receive the fugitives, delaying them and preventing their flight. Once again they find new strength, fresh courage, an encounter, eager hands, and everything else suitable for war—everything new and fresh among our men. Though already wearied by much slaughter, they receive blows fiercely and return them fiercely.

You might say that Roland and Oliver have been reborn, if you watched these counts raging—this one with his spear, that one with his sword.

### XXX.—Godefridus rushes upon the enemy

Duke Godefridus, a man wholly devoted to war and to God, whose ardor, strength, and spirited courage yielded nothing to those of Hector, took command of the arms and appeared joyfully.

Oh, what battle lines, what iron-clad breasts accompanied the duke! How long a strip of tempered steel [*calybem*] could be seen protecting the left side! What a snorting of horses, what a roar of men, what glory of the Lotharingians!

The duke therefore presses the Turkish ranks and pursues them—not aided by watchful cunning, not by advantageous terrain, nor by any art that turns even cowards into brave men, but by throwing the enemy into confusion through all the very advantages of cunning, terrain, and deception by which they had been assisted.

### XXXI.—He takes the rampart; he pursues the fugitives, while the neighboring mountain favors the enemy

A rampart stood before the duke, and a field beneath it separated the retreating mountain from the rampart.

When the people who trusted in stratagems more than in arrows fled here for refuge, thinking that he intended to seize the rampart, the duke—ignorant of their deceit and unjust tactics—turned the face of the battle against them. In a swift attack he first freed the mound, which had been burdened by the enemy; then, driving their flight across the level ground toward the mountain, he pressed them with great slaughter—of both the enemy and his own men.

For that people, armed with deceit, pierces the cuirass of the pursuer no less than that of the fugitive. And unless a swift horse had brought the spears within reach of the fleeing men, the farther they escaped, the more terrible the wounds they would have scattered. Thus the flight of the Turks achieved what victory had achieved for the Franks.

The troop, having taken refuge on the mountain and being unburdened by bronze and arms, easily escapes the men, weighed down by bronze and arms, who rush after them; with an easy, downward arrow it wounds them, while from afar scorning the hurled spear.

Anxious and gnashing his teeth at the obstacle before him, the duke returns to the plain at the foot of the mountain, so that if the mountain were concealing any enemies, they might be drawn out; and so that the empty fields and the rampart might again be reached by the duke.

At this the enemy rejoices, descends, and challenges him voluntarily, continually ranging about and continually scattering wounds. Trusting in his swift horse and in the favor of the neighboring mountain, the duke again and again pursues them, receives many blows upon his breast, and returns still more upon their backs.

Yet the mountain always curtailed his deserved triumphs, sheltering the defeated in its hollow while opposing the victorious standards. It was like a hawk wheeling through the air in a circle, or like one which, seated before a flock of complaining birds, drives them about and fills the thickets with varied cries.

Then, if some insolent crow, flying nearer, displayed its swollen body, the hawk, indignant and aflame, hurled itself with all its force against the airy flock. The crow fled on trembling wings, returning to its nest, while the predator—where rocky cliff or earthly hiding place confined its prey—stretched out its claws. Yet it brought back feathers in its claw, tokens of victory; having gained its perch, it mourned, wings spread, beak gaping, eyes aflame, breast panting, gazing upon the feathered barrier of its escaped prey. [The corrupt phrase *similem hesuro* is not securely recoverable.]

In the same way anger troubles the duke, while the Turk, driven from the fields, possesses a safe hiding place along the mountain’s edge.

### XXXII.—Hugh the Great comes to the duke’s aid and crosses the mountain with Count Raymond; terror seizes the Turks

But when Hugh the Great, attacking the battle from another direction, had easily crossed the accessible and enemy-free side of the mountain, soon neither ridges nor steep paths restrained the horses, whose loosened reins allowed them to snatch the Turks—fugitives—across level ground and rugged heights.

Thus, while the hostile throng was fleeing from the count on one side and from the duke on the other, Count Raymond hastens forward, fearing that neither he nor his men might lack an enemy with whom to fight. His own infantry and other foot soldiers and horsemen accompanied this leader of war and disposer of the legions, enriching him with such numbers, defenses, and standards that one might believe that none of those whose absence had been noticed was absent, and that none of those believed to have survived remained alive.

Therefore, fearing that he might himself be formidable, he attacks the broken battle line, cutting off fear. If the fury of Ida were to carry oaks to the depths of the Sigean shore, let all Ida’s neighboring mountain and valley tremble, and let Phoebus hide beneath the dust; if you were to remove the light from the helmets or add foliage to them, the appearance would be this, the aspect similar, the roar alike, the trembling the same.

Such was the state and appearance of the count’s allied throng and of those allied with the throng. What a din struck the astonished ears of the Turks, and what a flash their eyes perceived! They feared that all Europe was rushing upon them, with no commander, consul, or king left behind.

At first they stand uncertain. Then, as soon as Raymond’s spear wheels whatever meets it, collides with it, and the sword enters, neither Arab trusts his javelin nor Turk his bow; neither horse feels the bridle, nor horseman the road, nor flight any turning—so completely did they regard flight as the hope of safety.

Thus each seeks, in his scattering, some familiar hiding place: Cylix, Tarsus; the Aetherian groves, Coatra; the Syrian, Antioch; the Phoenician, the walls of Sidon; Artasium, Jacob’s; the towers of the Elamite, Caleph. They flee toward countless known refuges, each by an irregular and disorderly path.

### XXXIII.—The commanders measure out a route toward Antioch after dispersing the enemy; Tancred’s boldness

The enemy had been defeated, slain, and dispersed; the victor had returned, enriched and rejoicing. The road, now safer, recalls the traveler to his customary route, and the safer it is, the more widely he spreads out. The commanders arrange for their infantry companies a longer but easier circuit toward Antioch, measuring out and surveying the cultivated plain.

Tancred, however, chooses the path through the trackless woods, the steep mountains, and the rivers of Cilicia that must be crossed; by this route he hastened more directly toward the aforesaid city. O astonishing warrior, to whom toil is pleasure, war security, idleness difficult, every difficulty easy, and finally nothing sweet unless seasoned with sweat!

Meanwhile let us be astonished at the man who was never astonished, and let us fear for him because he feared nothing. Ah! What is this boldness—or rather, madness—Tancred? You are about to plunder Antioch, yet you are content to join a hundred cuirasses; the number of your bows scarcely reaches two hundred. With these [few] hundreds you attack Syria? You employ few men: increase the number. Your enemy is numerous; many swords are arrayed against you. Your enemy arms more peoples than you have men.

The towns and cities that await an adversary are calling you to protect them, yet you lead only a few guards. Let the total number of citizens, I beg, rise fivefold, so that the multitude of the towns may not at least be without guards. Otherwise, summoned as protector, you will not suffice for their protection, since you would need to distribute one defender to every people.

Above all, Antioch is a city fortified with arms, crowded with armed men, accustomed to wars, proud of triumphs. It has grown old in ruling and does not know how to be ruled. Rein in the headlong course of your spirit, and use as a bridle the judgment of some wise man.

The experienced man—both commander and soldier—has reported what belongs to a commander and what to a soldier. He says: “Before you begin, deliberate; and when you have deliberated, carry the deed out promptly. What belongs to deliberation is to be referred to the commander; what belongs to the soldier is to fight.” This is clear even to the simplest. Nevertheless, each sometimes bears both duties, or each one the other’s; indeed, both duties often fall upon both.

The glory of both titles inflames you, but you seek pride from the lower one all the more recklessly because you would have obtained it more effectively from the higher. You burn to be called fearless, and so prudent will you be that you will be said to rage imprudently. While you release this slight breath of fame, you throw away your life, waste your labor, win hatred, and incur disgrace.

Return, then, to yourself; restore yourself to the commander. Deliberate first, and when you have deliberated, deploy your cohort. Otherwise, when danger has arrived, you will deliberate too late and grow weary too soon; you will wish to have come to battle after deliberation, not to have deliberated by fighting.

### XXXIV.—He besieges Tarsus and prepares an ambush

While such a recall, perhaps even more eloquent, was deafening Tancred’s ears, he himself, hardened like a deaf asp—or like an asp shutting out the charmers who serve as its warners—flew across Bithynia, swifter than the flames of heaven and than a tigress that has given birth; he traversed the Taurus Mountains and the valleys of Buteotis, the latter reaching toward Baritis, the former toward the sky. Having seized Cilicia, he besieged Tarsus.

Indignation seized the Turks, exultation the Greeks, exhortation the Armenians, and amazement everyone. For at that time the Turks happened to rule, the Greeks to serve, and the Armenians to preserve their freedom through the steepness of the mountains.

Yet when he had viewed the city from afar, admired the heights of its towers, the extent of its mountains, and the magnificence of its houses, he hastened to test the strength of its inhabitants. Having therefore arranged an ambush, when [lacuna; the source is materially incomplete] the things that had to be prepared had been prepared, the bowmen of Marnys the Turcopole were sent ahead, supported by a few of our own cuirassiers. They were positioned in advance, after cattle had been drawn out to pasture, in whatever order and dispersal the herds had taken, so that the enemy, rushing upon the prey, would not discover the ambush before the ambushed men themselves had paid the penalty.

The plan was spoken and done. The raiders were sent out; they flew forward and ravaged the suburb, repeatedly retreating beneath a feigned appearance of fear wherever they had been ordered. The city roused whatever arms and strength it possessed and sent them after the fugitives, meanwhile leaving scarcely more than the number of men required to guard the gates.

Thus these hasten, and those hasten, seized by [lacuna]. Soon those who flee hasten toward safety, while those who pursue hasten toward death; the fugitives prevail in such a way that the pursuers are defeated. Meanwhile, as [lacuna] was taking place, pressure was applied. The pursuer repeatedly pierces the fugitive; a swifter rescuer arrives; and the fleeing spearman, unable to withstand the pressure, turns and overturns him. As Fortune played these reversals, some escaped and others were overwhelmed.

Then, when a signal had been given from the watchtower, the valley, pregnant with arms, openly poured forth the armed men it had conceived. At first the iron-tipped spears began to bristle; soon oaks and ash trees rose into a forest, helmets rushed forward in equal fashion, shields grew up, then cuirasses, and finally horsemen and horses—a sight closely resembling the offspring of Cadmus.

When the bold fury of the Turks discovered them, it turned of its own accord and sent the iron-clad city forward in its accustomed manner, first with the armed men and then with the winged cavalry.

### XXXV.—He slays and puts the enemies to flight

When Tancred saw those whom he had drawn into battle, relying as they did upon the great superiority of their own numbers and upon the small number of our men, he himself first brought the fight into their midst, dividing each man he met with his sword or fixing him with his spear. The faithful young men of the Turks first strike their breasts, then their backs: some have no protection on the left, others no protection over the chest. [lacuna]—they all cannot withstand helmets, shields, and cuirasses, and the clothing embraces them.

Thus the gate, which had been spacious when it led them out a little earlier, now receives them back through a narrow entrance. So confused, terrified, senseless, and massed together, they enter the threshold [lacuna] under the pressure of the victor’s sword.

Had not the defenders of the wall, raining down a stony hail, broken apart the interlocked barrier of shields, both the walls and the citizens would have been entered in a single assault by the enemy. Some were therefore admitted, while others, repulsed, returned over the fallen corpses, giving thanks to Christ.

Within the walls there was sorrow; outside, joy. Within, hope is turned into fear; outside, it does not know how to be turned, but only to increase. Meanwhile the day closes, and night, opportune for deliberating and planning, falls.

### XXXVI.—He attacks the city

As soon as the sun’s radiance arose, Tancred hastened to break the gates, fill the ditch, apply the ladders, and climb the towers; already he called the night’s delay a year. He had no sleep, or, if he had any, it was very brief. Yet even with his eye closed, through omens of the coming day’s action, he troubled his Turks [lacuna]. Indeed, by this [lacuna] he terrifies enemies and citizens alike, distrustful of both, with the image of a long battle; and Tancred, hurling [lacuna] from no one, [lacuna] and into the minds of each.

Thus he [lacuna]. The sun [lacuna], and [lacuna] is entrusted with flight. [lacuna extending through twelve lines; the lines cannot be read.] And may you have those whom you can defeat and those whom you can spare, [lacuna] granted liberty to the people of Tarsus; here still such great walls of Tarsus [lacuna], [lacuna] to their own homes as a sign of victory [lacuna].

### XXXVII.—Balduin is terrified by the unexpected arrival; a eulogy of Balduin

The banner was waving from the taller tower when suddenly—an astonishing and terrifying sight and sound—the lookout cried that arms were being born from the womb of the mountains and that the fields were already bubbling over with armed men as they ranged across them.

Roused by this uproar, the Marchiside [lacuna] summoned his allied soldiery; soon, having called for his horse, he himself flew out first, while his companions followed behind.

The same ardor for extending his reputation that had moved the Marchiside had also stirred the multitude that had set out from a dangerous concentration of men. By chance, the same footsteps had been taken by one who, after departing from Duke Godefrid and Count Eustace, Eustace’s son [lacuna], had won for himself several thousands of companions. Among them Count Conon was especially prominent, while Norman soldiery increased his forces; under Count Robert he himself held the chief command. Moreover, his own young men were not lacking [lacuna]. Eager for arms, they had chosen this man, the most eager of all, as their commander.

He was generous with money, devoted to military service, humble in speech, great in strength, and exalted in piety. When I contemplated the tall form of his body from sole to crown, I thought: behold, you would say that Nature herself had sculpted him by her own hand into a soldier.

[lacuna] to be adorned with so many intervals of life, beginning with light under the scepter of the Franks and destined to end under that of the Jerusalemites; and, so that the matter might shine more clearly, he was drawing his lineage from that great King Charles and was being divinely drawn toward sitting upon David’s throne.

Rightly and deservedly he lived as an Alexander: Charles illuminated his rising, David his setting. Nor ought the sword to degenerate whose cradle and tomb would shine in this way.

Inflamed by these torches of nobility, he had separated from the great army those companions whom he recognized as the more ardent. His force numbered about five hundred cavalry and two thousand infantry. When they had already advanced from the mountain into the street, the Marchiside saw Frankish arms, believed them auxiliary forces, did not know that they were our men, did not know the ambush, the battle, or the victory of the previous day. He displayed the spoils, brought them back, exhibited what had been brought, divided what had been exhibited for presentation, [lacuna] sending back unharmed those who followed, which the man who went ahead had resisted.

### XXXVIII.—Balduin’s injustice toward Tancred

But the commander of the well-protected column, still more secure, argues that either the shields should be distributed individually and then assigned, or that everything should fall into the hands of the stronger, unarmed men; that the flight of the enemy should be attributed not to the swords of the men who went before but to the terror of those who followed.

Tancred, certainly, had fought, but the palm of victory had fallen to Balduin. The Marchiside was no less angered by this than Telamonian Ajax was when he took for himself the arms denied to Achilles. He seethed, raged, and grieved that he had not taken the fleece for himself, the honey, the vein of gold dug out of the lowest caverns of the earth, so that an ungrateful plunderer might transfer it into his treasury. What need is there to speak of the pitiable division that had been proposed?

The very division that had just pleased him as voluntary would now displease him if forced. For once the title to his victory had been transferred, he would seem less a spontaneous giver than an obligated restitutor.

What then should he do? Fight? The enemy is a fellow citizen. Tear him apart? The blood is Christian. Enter Tarsus? It is shameful to be shut inside Tarsus. Stir up the barbarians to fight against a brother? That is apostasy. Thus it is bad to be defeated, but much worse to conquer.

After searching out a path by a thousand tracks, he finally sits down to disdain the defeated and hasten to defeat others—like an eagle and a hawk, like a cedar, a leopard, and a lion; so the greater may lawfully press upon the lesser.

The Marchiside departs groaning that the servitude of the people of Tarsus had not been freed by the arrival of the Latins but made heavier. He departs, I say, to where greater men call him, lest the mere sound of his name impoverish a rich land by driving away its inhabitants.

### XXXIX.—Nevertheless, heralds are sent to Tancred concerning the restoration of the city

But a swifter report had already run ahead, concealing nothing from the people of Adana about the character of so great a man: how great a defender he would be of the Christian name, how powerful a conqueror of the unbelieving flock, how gentle toward subjects, and how harsh toward rebels.

Therefore the city, rejoicing in gratitude, voluntarily sends its heralds, who would lead the man in with hymns and drums.

For Christ, having pitied his people, had recently shaken the yoke from their necks, expelling their rulers while retaining in chains the Turkish prince himself—a man, or rather a dog, whose anger could not be calmed and whose drunken revels could not be enjoyed except when a Christ-worshipper had been shot and fastened to a stake before his eyes.

Therefore He who looks upon the lowly and recognizes the lofty from afar reserved for him, through Tancred as dispenser, the same measure by which he had measured others. This was indeed divine; for no law is more equitable than that the craftsmen of death should perish by their own craft.

### XL.—And this was accomplished through the ingenuity of Ursinus, whose history is told here

At that time Ursinus, a Christian and an Armenian, governed the city. As has been stated, he had sent envoys to invite the Marchiside. He himself went out to meet the arrival of so great a guest, greeting him with his right hand and in good faith; he promised allied—or rather, subordinate—forces and invited him to plunder Mamystana, which was as near in location as it was easy to capture.

Nor did he himself receive less in return for what he deserved; indeed, from the seed scattered there arose a harvest a hundredfold greater. Among those who entered the walls, the entire people applauded and sang.

When the horse had yielded to carpets, hunger to banquets, and care to Bacchus, Ursinus, being asked how the city’s present condition had endured, and by what strength he had been able to protect its citizens while surrounded by so many thousands of enemies, began:

“You see me, a new inhabitant, sent to restore ancient liberty. For while the fields and valleys had long served miserably under Turkish rule, I lived in the mountains, free indeed, but lamenting the servitude of the Christian people no less than those who endured it. And when many saw that this condition had already been imposed and endured for many years, although they had attempted many desperate measures, at last one sure road to freedom became clear.

“The meadows had yielded their harvest; their tresses, having endured the sickle of the earth, had dried into hay. Daily labor pressed to bring it here on carts. At that time, however, the countryside was inhabited by those whom you have just seen snorting on horseback and gleaming in purple.” (He had seen many Turks shortly before riding about in purple garments. When they repeatedly returned as solitary men driving carts, they surpassed the oxen only in this respect: their oxen were weighed down by guards, whereas they themselves were not.)

“Thus opportunity produced suspicion, suspicion counsel, counsel boldness, and boldness freedom. When they were loading hay onto carts, free of guards, they thought that the carts could likewise be loaded with armed men, and war concealed inside; while peace hung all around, armed men could be brought within the town, and the Turks easily killed or driven back.

“While they were considering these matters, they came to me where, as I said, I was staying in the mountains. Once I had learned the reason for their arrival, I rejoiced, advised, and urged them not to delay and not to withdraw themselves from the grace that was urging them from heaven.

“‘Hasten your return,’ I said; ‘take care of the carts, and I shall provide you with warriors to carry inside.’

“They hastened to carry out my orders; I fulfilled my promises. The guards were buried in the hay, while I pretended on the other side to be carrying off plunder, so that, drawn out into an external battle, they would have left the townsmen an easy victory upon entering.

“As had been foreseen, so it happened. For when those who rushed in behind me had stripped the city, the carts brought war to the walls, prudently clothed in peace and hay. Once the armed men had been brought within the walls, they stripped off peace, barred the gates, killed the guards, and took their places.

“All this was done secretly. The present colonnade had provided hidden ambushes for the concealed slaughter. From there they rushed everywhere through the streets, palaces, and towers. Woe to the Turk who was found, whether on horseback or on foot, with a bow or without one, boy or old man! No consideration was shown for age, appearance, or sex. All fell by the sword, low and great alike. In a single victory he punished every wound that he had suffered from ancient days, in the manifold slaughter of a kindred servitude.

“Yet one Turk was preserved alive, the prince no less of crimes than of criminals. Bound with a very heavy chain in a dovecote, he awaited tortures in his temporal life and eternal tortures thereafter. But since the sword had left nothing untouched of the rest of the unbelieving crowd, mice climbed the drums and filled the whole surrounding region everywhere with joyful thunder.

“For I had given orders that, once the slaughter was complete, they should applaud us and sing together. When I had heard the towers resounding with joyful sounds, I cried: ‘Ho, companions! Let us turn our faces toward the rear.’ I took up the trumpets, messengers of joy. The city was calling us back as citizens. Pretending that we had captured plunder, and feigning a return because of the pressure of the enemy, we had turned our backs; but turning toward the horns and trumpets, we boldly attacked those from whom we had prudently been retreating.

“Astonished by our unprecedented boldness, they hesitated. Then, for a little while, they returned our reversal of flight, while we pressed them all the more confidently as the city drew nearer and nearer. Ignorant of what had happened, the enemies thought that the clanging bronze, the booming drum, and the echoing town were instruments of their expected relief. Thus it happened that our advantage doubled beyond hope, and the punishment of the enemy beyond fear.

“The same sound—marvelous to say—was truthful for us and deceptive for them. It brought back the true inhabitants and led us in, while it misled those whose retreat was already rejoicing in the nearness of the suburb. They discovered that the deceitful sound had tricked them when they saw Armenians running about upon the walls.

“What could they do? Hope had escaped them from the walls; swords pressed them from behind. Outside they could neither stand nor be received within the gates. There was neither room for flight nor room for battle. Nevertheless all attempted flight, but it was favorable to not one of them. Confused by thoughtlessness and unexpected chance, those who had just fled along the very paths by which they expected to escape and live soon returned by those same tracks to perish.

“They had eyes but did not see, as profaners of God’s church. Their hands, bows, and swords had likewise grown weak in their proper uses. Everything, by a sad fortune for them and a joyful one for us, doubled our strength against theirs.

“But lest my prolixity offend you: we attacked the confused and senseless crowd, and the sword left not one survivor. The deaf man amid the slaughter does not hear money, though it repeatedly offers itself as hostage for the wretched. From that time the cry “Allachibar” [Arabic: “God is greatest”], which unbelief shouts in prayer, fell silent in that city; and in its place resounded: “Christ conquers, Christ reigns, Christ commands,” as though returning by right of restoration.”

Thus Ursinus spoke. When he uttered his final word, Tancred sang back, “Thanks be to God.”

### XLI.—The citizens meet Tancred

In these circumstances they extend the night into the day, until sleep relieves those weighed down by the day’s labor and sends them, refreshed, into the following day. For Phoebus had not yet worn down the chariot of the morning star when Tancred’s helmets, hastening to enclose the Mamystans, appeared faintly gleaming around Mamysta.

The Turks, for whom the delay had long indulged the city—too long for justice, too long for length, too rapacious for delicacy, too delicate for security—had withdrawn from the feared battle of Tarsus, fortified by the very silence of the night.

When the citizens learned this at sunrise, they went out to make a treaty, so that they might deserve to follow Tancred’s footsteps and, scarcely recovering from their agitation, undertake the sweet yoke and light burden. Rescued from the most impious servitude, they thought that they were reigning by serving their rescuer.

They therefore easily obtained favor with him, from whom even one who had not deserved it would not have returned empty-handed. Tancred and the city thus gained one another in reciprocal exchange: Tancred gained the city’s filial obedience, and the city Tancred’s paternal rule.

### XLII.—Balduin departs; after measuring out a camp in the suburbs, he seeks peace, obtains peace from Tancred, and establishes commerce

Meanwhile Count Balduin’s army, laden with spoils, empty of mercy, and abusing its licence, had left Tarsus, exchanging Tarsus, to its own loss, from Frankish thousands for hundreds [lacuna]. Abhorring the count’s wrongs, it moved toward greater objects [lacuna], which it had seen occupied by certain light forces [lacuna]. Its eager inviter was the Euphrates, whose present embassy kept promising Edessa on the left bank while troubling him on the right bank of the river. Neither place deemed the other its equal: neither this town, among all the towns of nearer Syria, nor that city beyond the Euphrates in the land called Mesopotamia. Each rejoiced to rule a rich, fertile territory through the service of many towns and cities.

Frequently rehearsing these matters—the messenger to his superior, and the superior to the people subject to him—Balduin had left Tarsus. Having scarcely forded, one by one, the rivers of Adana and Mamysta, he pitched his tents near Tancred.

Indignant at being trodden down by a rustic foot, the riverbanks had granted bridges only to the cities. Yet access had not been open across them, because Tancred had ordered that they prevent those who followed. He no longer wished to call as a brother one who was expelling him as an enemy.

Count Balduin therefore measured out a camp in the suburb and sought peace from the city. Provisions were now obtained not freely or by force, but by agreement and payment. He knew that the man’s mind was still disturbed by the recent injury and that he himself, having inflicted it, was hateful to him.

Moreover, the city, fortified with towers, capable of containing a population, and filled with arms, gave no weakness of its own to strengthen the plunderer’s hope. In addition, the Count Conon whom the preceding page celebrated had been confined to his bed by serious illness. Balduin therefore neither wished to proceed while leaving him behind, nor to take him away, nor to remain there without being granted commerce. So many cares made him anxious to seek peace.

The event is remarkable—and as unknown to other princes as it was, through a singular intimacy, bound up with the Marchiside. Though inflamed by the damage, insult, and abuse of the day before yesterday, he immediately grants and proclaims the peace requested by Balduin.

Whether joyful or offended, the man never limps when invited toward what is right. To bend him toward pardon was to appeal to pardon. Asked, therefore, as stated, to promise peace mutually, he responds in both directions and does not refuse commerce, provided that the goods feel no force.

They go and return, sell and buy back, from city to camp and from camp to city. Armed men mingle with the unarmed, while those whom outdoor exposure had weakened and whom Phoebus had scorched are kept between the shade and the walls, swifter in their hope of relief.

This arrangement lasted only a few days. For, as yesterday and the day before yesterday, disputes arose when commerce was renewed, as happens when the buyer’s and seller’s valuations disagree about the price or quantity of the goods for sale.

### XLIII.—The peace is broken; single combats

A camp follower from a tavern porch began the matter, and in this fashion the war overflowed to the princes themselves. The one who had suffered the injury thought that the present offense had grown out of the former one in the ordinary course of events; the one who had inflicted it feared that retaliation had been reserved for him. Thus differing opinions deceived both, while each charged the other with the offense in which he himself had sinned four times.

On both sides men rose to their swords. Fury seized the arms. Those found within the walls from the camp were handed over to custody if weak; if strong, they were beaten with fists and clubs. The common crowd was expelled, while the nobles were kept in bonds. Similar measures were taken outside against similar townsmen found in the suburb.

Even this seemed too little military action unless the outer party battered the city gates with an assault, while the inner party, shaken into war, went out and opened them. Once no barriers obstructed either side, with only the field between them and standards arrayed on both sides, the commanders finally hesitated to commit themselves to so great a danger, their forces being evenly balanced against those of the enemy.

As stated earlier, Balduin’s number was great and his forces very powerful. He had therefore withdrawn somewhat farther, intending to draw the smaller enemy away from the aid of the walls. Tancred’s force was much smaller; for that reason he had armed the towers with missiles, so that they might meet the war first and the descent of missiles might support the inferiority of his fighting force.

Trusting and distrusting such sources of support and desolation, each commander awaited the other’s attack. Neither wished to strike first rather than be struck, but each preferred the reverse.

There were several reasons for this. The chief was that whoever first wickedly rushed upon the wall would sound more guilty. Yet during this delay, as military custom dictates, some young men from both sides entered into single combat. From them it might have been determined which side had taken up the defense of the more just cause, if only one side’s attackers had fallen and the other side’s had prevailed.

But since both sides gained and both suffered losses, both fell and both overwhelmed others, it is impious to know who had put on arms with the juster cause.

Among those who were staging this martial game in the middle was Richard, inferior neither in rank nor in lineage nor in courage. He encouraged the related parties at once with his speech and with his spear. He was the son of Count William, grandson of Guiscard. Leaving Syracuse to his brother Tancred, he had followed his maternal uncle Bohemond and joined Tancred.

As he flew between them, passing one and trampling another, a treacherous spear from the side pierced his unwary flank, and a foot soldier soon took the place of the horseman. What good does a whirling sword, once drawn, do for a fallen man? A hostile crowd rushed upon him because he had left the support of his companions somewhat rashly and was nearer to his adversaries.

Thus, alone and surrounded by so many encircling men, he was captured, dragged away, disarmed, and kept safe.

The same fate had degraded many on both sides from horse and saddle to their feet. It seemed to the wisdom of their superiors that men who had unanimously gone out against hostile arms had turned their own weapons against themselves through discord, and that it was madness. A wealthier multitude must necessarily be employed against the barbarians rather than impoverished by a small force.

### XLIV.—Peace is renewed

Carefully weighing many such matters, the wise men exchange war for peace. Yet this proposal, though most difficult and one which the offended Marchiside would have rejected with deaf ears, was accepted because his maternal nephew Richard, returning, softened the spirits which his capture had embittered. The same man alone now became the cause of hatred, now of peace.

Likewise, the aforesaid Count Conon, lying ill in the city, restored his mind to his companions and was to be restored by the commerce of peace.

They therefore return alternately to their own positions: hero for hero, knight for knight, foot soldier for foot soldier. Losses and gains remain entirely undisturbed in the order in which they began, so that the common lament may rightly be applied here: “He who has it, has it; he who lost it, lost it.”

They do not remain together longer. One departs to acquire; the other remains and enjoys what he has. Yet that remaining is neither sluggish nor long, for what was a brief rest according to the man’s judgment would have been prolonged idleness.

Accordingly, after a short stay, he sets out toward the Syrians—having prosperously taken possession of Cilicia, but about to take possession of Syria much more prosperously.

Before that, however, he exacts punishment from the wicked Turk whom Adana had imprisoned, and imposes upon the people of Mamysta penalties more paternal than princely.

When these matters were completed, he climbed the mountains that separate Alexandriola from the little town of Guasto—a difficult road, but the most direct of all routes toward the Syrians.

After crossing the highest summit there, he is said to measure with eye and mind at once the cliffs of Antioch, its plains, its roads and trackless ways, its marshes and dry ground. From there he traverses the entire plain, because the rivers, towns, and cities of Sepchet, Spitachchet, Domith, and Commith lie between.

### XLV.—Tancred comes to Artasium and frees Balduin, surrounded by the Antiochenes; he is attacked by the enemy at Artasium
When Artasium is reached, Count Baldwin is found there, the fortunate expeller of the Turks from Artasium, but miserably shut in by the Antiochenes. When Marchisides appeared before them, he ordered a withdrawal, gathering together some baggage and sending some ahead. At the arrival of one man, it was thought that all the commanders of so great an army would come to meet him; such terror and uproar followed the man. Yet one part of his army had been left behind among the Cilicians, and he had reduced it from a hundred men to fifty. But Fame, herald of truth, had proclaimed a single Marchisides as equal to many soldiers.

The new guest entered Artasium, but the return offered for his hospitality was far below the magnitude of his merits. He was excluded from the inner city; permission was nevertheless granted him to occupy the outer wall, either so that he might defend the city against those stationed opposite, or so that the narrowness of the interior might not renew quarrels, or certainly because the root of the contempt recently cut off had not yet entirely withered. Whatever the sufficient reason, whoever exposed Tancred to danger enclosed himself within an adamantine wall.

When Antioch understood that the Latins’ forces had increased—forces which its own men had experienced, felt, fled from, and reported—it reinforced weakness with abundant strength and made up for small numbers; then it sent men out a second time, and, if it sent them out seven times, it would send them out to be overcome seven times. They, so that no method of testing the defenders might be left untried, even devised stratagems, trusting little either to their weapons or to themselves.

By night they entered the shadows of the thicket commonly called Saint Palladius’s Grove. At daybreak five men were sent ahead to provoke the horsemen at Artasium; but war lay hidden among the branches and leaves. Those who had been sent did not delay, but displayed sudden threats to Artasium: just as sheep are to shepherds, so the shepherds became a protection to the sheep. Both the men and the animals were dragged away together; nothing escaped the faces of the raiders. A cry went up from the watchtower; shepherds and swineherds howled before the gates. This was the sole complaint of them all: that, to their own disadvantage, the Franks had come against the Turks as their protectors.

They were tormented all the more because they had hoped for freedom through the protection of the newcomers. When Tancred heard this, he hurried out, suspecting that the city was surrounded for battle. But when he saw the situation outside, he immediately understood that their courage depended on hidden forces, and that their boldness was greater than his own. To make this clear, however, he sent three Turcopoles to meet them, so that if they yielded, their timid isolation might be exposed; if they resisted, the hope of reinforcements might be discovered. But the five not only did not yield to those who attacked them; they also struck down the attackers who had turned to flee. Then, when what had been hidden became more clearly understood, battle was prepared, the lines were arranged, and they went out to meet one another.

## XLVI.—Mars Favors the Turk

[Col. 0525A]

For the enemy, an archer and monstrous in his great numbers, when he saw our men, scorned concealment and came out openly; he was ashamed to have hidden, though he had attacked our individual spears with ten or more bows. Thus the Turks engaged the Latins, natives fought foreigners, men familiar with the region fought those ignorant of both the people and the land.

At the first clash the spear was strong: the spear pierced, the spear threw down. Soon, however, weakening under such a burden, it could no longer penetrate shields, breasts, or iron helmets intact. Pack saddles splitting apart weakened one spear; a broken point shortened another; a Turk’s sword cut a third in half. Thus the spearman seemed rather to have come armed with a wooden staff on foot than as a soldier with a lance.

But the bow was far more economical and richer in wounds: it was always shooting, frequently wounding; it was never shot at and was wounded only rarely. Near or far, before or behind, it was energetic; even when it missed through its own aim, chance often served as its assistant and did not allow it to miss. While fortune consoled some and devastated others, and while one of the commanders, Baldwin or Tancred, listened little to the other, they became divided against themselves and were routed; they were driven back as far as the walls.

The Turks then encamped before the city and continued their sleepless watch through the night.

## XLVII.—Artasium Is Entrusted to Baldwin

The following day was shining when, after the enemy had returned to Antioch, fear was removed. Then Marchisides, ordered to leave—for the kingdom’s companions are never to be trusted—was expelled from the very outer wall called the Barbican. Eustachius handed the government of Artasium to Baldwin, under whose long administration Edessa later flourished. He himself departed for Edessa with the other counts, Airard and Conon.

Tancred, knowing that a man’s life consists in military service and having nothing safer than war, occupied the nearby mountains. With a small force he attacked great companies, and the barbarian hills were roused by so great a name. Some hurried to flight, others to meet him, while some remained fearless: the same faith consecrated certain of them to the Franks, while fanatical error separated the rest.

Accordingly, those who knew Christ received the Christians as they came. But those to whom this name was either unknown and unspoken or despised when heard were persuaded by fear to abandon the towns of Barisan and Hersen, and flight filled them. Once they had been abandoned, they summoned Marchisides and enriched him, when he entered, with a great abundance of provisions.

[Col. 0525D]

Now, therefore, having changed his residence, the exile was more fortunate than the city’s guest. He suffered no losses, slaughter, or imprisonment. While the enemy practiced his customary return and ambushes, he buried the war among the foliage; but he displayed as an urban spectacle the captured mules, muleteers, wagons, and wagon drivers. The beasts groaned beneath straw as though beneath blankets, and moved knowingly through danger as though unaware of danger.

When they had come near the river that irrigates the fields of the town of Balena, almost at the same time visible to the city, they were seized and captured, so eagerly did the companions of the spoil strive to outstrip one another. Alas, wretched men! Why do you divide the spoil when you are soon to be divided as spoil? Why do you strike, bind, and constrict—when you will soon be constricted, soon bound, soon struck?

The gates had scarcely poured them out when they barely repelled, suddenly, the ambushing crowd that was hastening to break in.

## XLVIII.—Antioch Is Besieged, and Its Situation Is Described

Thus, when the city had been besieged and the return route blocked, the Turks overtook and killed with bonds or sword whatever Latin blood had gone out. Yet heaven took pity on the affliction of the besieged, so that, when the Franks hurried to besiege Antioch, the Antiochenes yielded their role as besiegers.

That venerable army of kings passed through the cities and neighboring towns, and across the intervening river Farfar, until at last it encamped in the suburb of Antioch, for which it had longed. Mountains constrict the sides of the central plain, one from the south and the other from the north; the sea strikes its front from the west. But the farther this region withdraws from the shore toward the east, the wider and wider the rock extends.

Descending from the south, the Damascene Farfar washes it, flowing in a winding course across the level ground toward the sea. It runs between the mountains, nearer the southern one. Indeed, at times it bends so far into its shadow that only a path lies between them. But where the slope begins to descend into those narrow places, the city is situated, extending lengthwise with the river on one side and the mountain on the other.

It also joins the side of the mountain to itself as though to a hospitable neighbor, raising its walls to the summit and constructing the municipal buildings there. Yet in the same way it descends toward the river, so that from its middle it runs westward together with the river, then withdraws slightly from it at the western horn, while to the east it remains far removed as far as the middle. On that side, however, the double walls are more securely defended by a marsh, whose own trembling softness provides a stronger protection than any hardness of stone.

Thus the only front of the city exposed to the rising sun permits access as far as its middle—that is, from the gate called Jusum.

[Note: [Col. 0525] Porta Jusum is the lower gate; Porta Susum is the upper gate.]

For from the gate called Susum, the precipice of the sheer rock is open only to human eyes for looking, not to human feet for approach.

## XLIX.—The Order of the Besiegers

Opposite this, the nearby rock held Bohemond’s standards all the way to the descending road that led out from the gate. It raised the nearest mound beside the gate; Tancred placed his camp there, closer to the city than the others by the distance a sling can cast. Behind him were Count Northmannus and those who adhered to him, with the count of Flanders between Northmannus and Tancred.

On the other side were the counts of Blois, Boulogne, Albamar, Montaigu, Saint-Paul, and Hugh the Great; all these were bound by obligations to Count Northmannus, and some also by homage. From them to the river, the camps of the heroes held the plain in the order in which their names appear on the page: Duke Godfrey, the bishop of Le Puy, and Count Raymond.

This, then, was the first arrangement of the camps. It besieged the city’s fourth corner, while the others were left vacant, since this one was convenient because of the neighboring plain, whereas the others were inaccessible because of the river, ditch, or mountain.

Later, however, on the following day, the necessity of resisting an invading enemy sometimes compelled them to alter this arrangement, and at other times the desire to attack the enemy compelled them to do so.

Indeed, the rock that towered over Bohemond’s camp, although it seemed exceedingly difficult to approach, was convenient for the Turks, who could descend from the mountain to shoot arrows. After carrying out a slaughter, they could retreat to the walls in their light armor, where the heavy equipment of those following them could find no ascent.

To resist these incursions, therefore, the mound above Bohemond’s rock was enclosed by a wall, defended by the strength of Hugh the Great. Moreover, two northern gates were accustomed to pour out the Turks, and the army on this side of the river was left exposed to their attacks. Duke Godfrey attacked the nearer of them and at last restrained the enemy’s exit, though in the first encounter he was desolated by the death of the marquis Guarnerius.

The more distant gate, however, customarily sent the enemy across the adjoining bridge. Count Raymond decided that it should be blocked, for the broad plain beyond the river, empty of camps, had allowed the wandering Turk freer rein. Therefore a bridge of floating construction was extended across the river; its superimposed latticework was weighted by the burden of beams woven together and laid upon the supporting boats.

This continuation of the banks, serving to cross the riverbed, brought the count across in order to restrain the exit from the gate mentioned above. The situation of the place itself also aided the besieger, serving usefully to strengthen the siege. The earth had risen into a modest hill, on whose summit stood a stone shrine commonly called Mahummaria. Opposite and near the river gate, it invited the count by its advantageous position.

The count supplied what remained for the defense of the camp: namely, a ditch carried around it, providing a double strength through the depth of its hollow and the steepness of the thrown-up embankment. A wall was also founded upon this, low in itself but proud in the courage of its protector.

Now, with the Turks increasingly confined by these restrictions, they were able to inflict less and less harm, since their customary freedom to roam had been removed. Yet on the western side there remained a gate effective for causing harm but difficult to besiege.

## L.—The Difficulty of the Siege

The narrowness between the mountain and the river hindered the siege. These same barriers denied a ford on one side and a descent on the other: the unfamiliar newcomers were shut out, while the natives, familiar with the terrain, crossed the river. Watching the road that descended to the harbor, they frequently stained it with Christian blood.

Thus it was possible to pass from the harbor to the army or from the army to the harbor only in battle—and even then sometimes with little safety—so effectively did the freedom granted by the one gate redeem the blocked exits.

Tancred would have found a remedy for this evil, as the later outcome showed; but, being closer to the walls, he was the first to meet the raging Turks. Therefore he spent the day fasting beneath the sun and the night keeping watch beneath the dew. Alone, and still with only a small force, he sustained the attack of the entire war.

At last, repelled by the man’s great exertion, the enemy ceased to provoke him and contented themselves with towers and hiding places. But, you may object, Tancred’s courage, having conquered the east, immediately turned toward the unconquered west. There, where he encountered the enemy, he claimed that a walled enclosure was a town prepared for him, though scarcely begun to be prepared.

O love of glory! O courage! O rashness! In other matters I would call you, Tancred, energetic; here, rash. In other matters steadfast; here, obstinate. Other circumstances could excuse the rest—either the advantage of the place, the hope of assistance, pressing necessity, or whatever other prudent path might be open. But here everything accuses rashness: the old ruined wall, the powerful marauder, the proximity of the enemy, and the distance of the allies. Even if everything else favored you, crossing the Farfar separated you from assistance; and, if—God forbid—you had fallen into the hands of the Turks and been overcome, you would have passed more quickly, cooked, into the bellies of the enemy than, as a captive, to the ears of your allies.

Yet you remain; you remain, fight, hold the gate, shake the gate—now you the enemy’s, now the enemy yours. The entire West, vast as it is, fights in the East; you alone fight in the West. You rejoice in a few comrades-in-arms, but they are brave. The prescribed fortification, however, was too narrow to admit a multitude and scarcely held a few.

## LI.—Tancred Destroys Seven Hundred Turks Who Had Gone Out to Plunder

To return to the beginning: Tancred first tried to carry out his plan secretly, so that the inhabitants—who, without missing a day, were accustomed to go out into that region to cut grass—would remain unaware. For this reason he entered that enclosure by night. But they, led by some omen I do not know, were brought to suspect this very thing. On the first day they sent out a few reapers from a distance, to determine by this test whether they needed to fear new ambushes.

When our men saw them, they immediately hid themselves, and no one came out. Thus the Turks who had gone out returned within the walls, disturbed by no attack of arms. The next day they went out in the same way, but in greater numbers and nearer the fort. The previous day, which had passed safely and brought the grass-cutters safely out and back, had made them more confident.

Then Tancred could scarcely restrain his lions when he saw the sheep standing nearby.

“Wait,” he said, “for this one little day, brave men. Tomorrow, unless I am mistaken, richer prey will fall into our nets.”

As he foresaw, so it happened. After the approach had already been tested twice, and after the shortage of grass had been endured for two days, on the third day they went out—safe on the one hand, compelled on the other. Because they had cut the meadows nearer the city, and because they still hesitated over the Franks, many went out and passed beyond them.

Then Tancred burst through the enclosure and suddenly showed what prudence joined with courage could accomplish. Breaking into their midst, he swallowed them all more eagerly with the sword, the more fiercely their entrails burned with the three-day thirst that had sustained them between their drinking vessels.

Not to prolong the account: after about seven hundred had been killed, Tancred sent their heads to the bishop of Le Puy—seventy as a tithe of the triumph. When these were presented, the bishop was struck by a double joy: first, by his friend’s victory; second, by the honor and glory bestowed upon him through the offering of the gift.

He rewarded the victor with as many marks as he himself had received from the necks of the slain. At that time Tancred owed a great deal of money to his comrades and had nothing in his purses. Joy and celebration therefore accompanied the money, which immediately freed the commander from debt and relieved the soldiers’ poverty when the silver was distributed.

It also happened by chance that another messenger outran the one sent by the bishop, though he had not been sent. When this was heard, what did not yet exist was immediately scattered: soon it enriched others, while the man who had still been in need was left so. For he said in his heart:

“Let my soldiers be my treasury. Let me be poor while they abound; I do not care to possess, but to command those who possess. Let them load their purses with silver; let me load them with cares, arms, sweat, trembling, hail, and rain.”

Yet he himself gently supported those whom the battles by day and watches by night had exhausted, taking upon himself the debts of the needy and excusing any wound or illness. But reverence for his authority never made him idle; he always fulfilled his own duty and not only, as prescribed, supplied what was lacking, but also anticipated the duties of others.

## LII.—In Single Combat Tancred Pierces Three Turks

While he was doing this repeatedly, it happened that he went out to keep watch accompanied by Achates. Without cuirass or helmet, he rode girded with a sword, while the boy carried a spear and shield. Three Turks, likewise armed, were keeping watch; the gate of Antioch had sent them out. They wandered about without knowing of one another, for the camps were separated from the city by a considerable distance, with bushes, hillocks, and hollows providing hiding places suitable for ambushes.

When the three discovered the two, they rushed upon them, uncertain which of the two they should attack. Yet, poor men, flee! Flee, I say, from the ash tree of Castor, Cyllarus, and Achilles; from the right hand of Meleager; from the courage of Tydeus; from the triple-knotted club of Hercules; from the sevenfold shield of Ajax. All these arm this one warrior. He is challenged in vain; armed with all these, he himself advances against them. It is prudent to flee him, foolish to await him, mad to attack him.

Nevertheless, since the man who preserves an unwilling victim does the same thing as the one who kills him, rush forward more quickly, so that you may fall more quickly. Fall suddenly, so that Marchisides may remain forever.

When he saw the madman advancing, he seized an ash spear—as often happens—and pierced the one who was rushing upon him. A shield and breastplate usually protect the others, but here they were exposed to the one who pierced them. This piercer leaves no cuirass trustworthy and none not deceptive. This striker turns a helmet into a cap, a shield into a cloak, a breastplate into an undergarment. In short, he pierces wood as though it were linen, steel as though it were hemp, and a metal plate (*lamma*) as though it were wool.

But the one in the middle of the first group became slower when he saw the death, so that he might be supported by the help of the last, who was slower. Unhappy man, who just now envied the faster one for getting ahead! Now you prefer the blessed slowness of the slower one—and yet in vain. The swift and the slow alike belong to one right hand: attacking both, he cuts through the forehead of the one still advancing to meet him and stops the flight of the other by piercing his back.

Yet there is something at which I am amazed and cannot sufficiently cease to be amazed. When this man, so precious a purchaser of glory, had accomplished such a deed, why did he immediately seal it in silence by binding his arms-bearer with an oath? I do not know at all whether shame, religious scruple, or distrust of the oath’s reliability was the reason. For if shame: what will anyone ever call honorable, if he considers it shameful to kill three armed men in a single charge? If religious scruple: they say it is like a monster for fish to swarm beneath a plow; but I regard it as far more monstrous for one so eager for glory to flee glory.

Finally, so distinguished a warrior, having undertaken so many difficult tasks, endured so many hardships, and overcome so many combats, could easily obtain belief—especially since the slaughter was witnessed by the nearby weapons, and above all by his own tongue, which was trusted more than any other. Nevertheless, although the cause remained hidden, the result was evident. The cause—namely, the reason for the silence—was revealed by the outcome of the slaughter long afterward, when the sworn arms-bearer completed the appointed day of silence.

## LIII.—The Endurance of the Christians During This Harsh and Protracted Siege

[Col. 0530B]

Time urges me to return to the interrupted siege, so that those who endured such sweat may receive at least some small reward for their labor. For in its army, after almost eight months of delay, many men of distinction had performed many brave deeds, and the greatest men had accomplished the greatest things. As companions, however, the highest, the middling, and the lowest endured severe hardships: famine, earthquake, floods, various terrors of the air, and attacks now of the falling sky, now of advancing war. There were also portents and visions: the visions shone forth from heaven secretly to many, the portents openly to all.

If I were to explain each of these in its proper order, manner, and dignity, Tancred would meanwhile be too greatly silenced—just as he is the writer of repose, yet unworthy of silence. Moreover, if I undertake to plow through so many storms of the sea, our little boat will reach harbor late. Who, indeed, would dare to speak of the astonishing strength of Godfrey, whose sword made one Turk into two, so that one half rode into the city while the other, an archer, floated in the river?

Or who could worthily admire what Raymond did: how he alone so often stood against Antioch when it came out to meet him, how he bravely repelled it when it sometimes crossed the ditches and sometimes surmounted the walls; indeed, how, relying on no assistance from the absent army, he besieged the bridge?

Does not Robert the Fleming’s single lance alone demand a writer of its own? While he enriched Antioch with daily deaths, his daily companion, the horse, grew poor, so that at one point the great prince would have been without a horse unless one had been procured through begging from house to house. A broad basin was carried through the taverns, and pitying contributions supplied the count with a horse—one butcher’s shop from the tavern.

What comparable deed has our age seen, when approximately two hundred men, almost unarmed, most of them mule-drivers and horse-boys, drove fifteen thousand armed men, the majority cavalry, into flight? Count Stephen of Blois is said to have been the leader of this victory, joined with Godfrey and Bohemond. Hence more than seven hundred heads were carried away and displayed as a mournful spectacle to Antioch. Among them, one was fixed separately upon a stake. Imagine how much glory this brought to the sword of the count of Blois, since the distance between the eyes was half a foot.

As I said, the hundred-branched path of these events calls me back again; if I linger wandering among individual deeds, I shall stray from the path I began. Let Normandy, Flanders, and the rest of the West celebrate their own Roberts and other commanders. One Marchisides is enough for me, though I am not enough for him even in my entirety.

Forgive me, rich Gaul, with your historians. I am glad to devote myself to the Antiochene prince; in his presence I shall more freely discharge the debt I owe to my creditor. Nevertheless, lest my silence repay those who have deserved well with no reward at all, I shall try to touch briefly upon something that posterity may be able to explain at greater length with a fuller style.

## LIV.—The Severe Distress of the Besiegers

Thus, with the city besieged on three sides, the southern side was traversed by no besieger. On that side there was nothing moist and nothing level. This disadvantage benefited the citizens: it excluded those who would have closed them in and released those who were closed in. On one side were ambushes; on the other, difficult encounters for travelers, whether a Frank was going out to seek provisions or returning with what he had found.

So great a population, so many peoples, so many thousands required much livestock and much grain. Syria, Cilicia, Rhodes, and Cyprus, extremely wealthy, fed the army, though sparingly; so did Chios, Samos, Crete, Mytilene, and almost innumerable other islands of lesser renown. There was also a herald of the emperor Alexius, who pressed the peoples to transport grain by land and sea.

The siege had begun with winter, through which the entire army endured the horrors of winter: floods of rain, now sudden and now continuous, and such great convulsions of heaven and earth that, as though the pact between the elements had been dissolved, one seemed to rise to the heights and the other to collapse into the depths.

For what shall I say of whirlwinds, what of the fury of the winds? When they raged, neither tent nor covering stood; scarcely a palace or tower remained standing. Nobility endured beneath the open sky beside the common people; winter spared neither. Yet it was harsher to the nobility in proportion as the peasant is hardier than the soldier and the laborer than the delicate man.

Famine accompanied so many storms, and death accompanied famine. Death, with loose reins, ran everywhere ahead of both men and the horses that provided the consolation of war. A stable was rare in the camp that famine, after taking nine horses, had left a tenth.

Whatever iron and steel there was in the weapons, rust had seized. Nails and leather had come away from the shields. The wooden material of spears and saddles was intact for only a few, repaired in many, shining for none, and entirely absent for some. Bows stood idle without strings, and arrows without shafts. There was poverty everywhere, disaster everywhere, desolation everywhere.

## LV.—The Astonishing Confidence of the Christians

[Col. 0531D]

These hardships and sorrows were already excessive when suddenly grave burdens were piled upon grave burdens, spring succeeding winter under Pisces and Aries—the spring whose grass restores the horses of the Medes and Persians for war.

Unexpectedly the Turks appeared in great numbers, with forces prepared for battle. They were already near, about to attack the walls that same day or break into the camp, when a preceding rumor flew in and revealed the matter to the Christians as it was. As usual, it added to the truth and spoke of great things as greater still.

Roused by this, the Latin nobles prepared to meet them. Yet this was so difficult that it could almost be considered a rush into death, as though they were weary of life. For, from the great number and the great forces of soldiers who had besieged the city, scarcely two hundred were gathered to go out on horseback to meet the enemy.

Even among these, however, asses supplied a considerable part of the horses’ place. Our people, not expecting anything of the kind, had perhaps sent the horses far away to obtain grain.

Thus so small a number went out to fight fifteen thousand, as I learned from those who were present. What astonishing courage, worthy to be proclaimed through every age! The commanders in this expedition are said to have been Godfrey, Bohemond, and Stephen of Blois. When they came to the place that the common people corruptly call the Bridge of Iron instead of Farfar, they saw the enemy far away on the opposite side. They did not remain like frightened men; they crossed like men to be feared. Bohemond went first, Godfrey followed, and Stephen served as support.

## LVI.—A Few Men Attack the Enemy and Put Them to Flight

[Col. 0532B]

A hillock rises across the river, near the bridge, in the plain. Our men waited beneath it, while the Turks came rushing across the broadest part of the plain. They had seen our men from a distance and wondered with what confidence so small a force crossed the bridge.

That crossing, as prudent as it was bold, cast great terror into the enemy and magnified the small number of our men through the belief that their multitude was much greater. Therefore, when the Turks approached, they halted, fearing that the hill mentioned above might display a few and conceal many. The Christians pretended precisely this.

They armed their spears with standards, attaching one to each, as though there were as many troops hidden as there were standards displayed. Then, without hesitation, with their spears raised, they disturbed the enemy with such an attack as if a flock of falcons had fallen upon coots.

Dust arose, weapons clashed, hooves thundered, trumpets blared, eyes grew dim, ears were stunned, and the hearts of the enemy were paralyzed, so that they feared that more thousands of Franks might rise from hiding than they saw standards.

It is marvelous to say, and almost contrary to belief: they turned their backs and fled as quickly as possible. So great a multitude was routed by a few, with only a small number of the Christians lost—among them chiefly Count Gunano the Breton, who, with a heart aflame, had dared to attack the Persian army first, content with a single companion.

Much later, near the bridge, I was shown his mound beside the road. As far as was possible, and in keeping with the piety of his people, it was adorned with a stone and a cross.

The Franks, having won the victory, pursued the fugitives; but the scarcity of horses, the slowness of the horses, and the hunger of both men and animals soon prevented a prolonged pursuit. They carried back to the camp, as a sign of victory, seven hundred heads from the slaughter. First, however, they buried the count mentioned above and his companions in martyrdom, as the circumstances permitted.

If I remember correctly, this happened on the day when the Latin people are accustomed to indulge diligently in food and the eating of meat, intending on the following day to sprinkle their heads with ashes.

## LVII.—The Author’s Homeland; Famine in the City

The following night covered the sky with a dreadful redness, so that those positioned in the west, when they saw it, immediately cried out that the east was at war. I myself saw that sign when, still a young man, I was living in my father’s house at Caen, while Antioch was not yet known or seen by me except by name—nor Rome either.

Many were astonished when they saw it; with one voice they all declared war and bloodshed. But when the victors returned to their allied arms, the heads that had been brought were fixed upon stakes. The stakes were planted in the earth before the walls, in rows, in the sight of the enemy.

Among the others, one head was found with a distance of half a foot from eye to eye. Those who fixed them cried out to the citizens watching from the walls:

“Behold your hope; behold your threats; behold the forces gathered against the Franks. We reserve the same rewards for you. A similar end awaits similar men. You are shut in; flight has been taken from you; Ceres has been consumed; famine has been brought in; assistance has been removed; everything is against you.”

When the Franks’ deed had been seen and heard, and these words had been spoken, the city trembled. It no longer opened its gates as before; it wasted away in famine and mourned in fear. They spent that spring amid continuing misery, relieving the lack of bread with the spring abundance of leaves and grasses, after the manner of cattle.

Then Cassianus—this was the name of the besieged ruler—issued an edict and sent men to search out whose house among the citizens contained grain. Half of it was to be sent to the court; from the remainder each person was to sustain life as best he could.

When the city heard this, it took the measure heavily but endured it. They divided the grain in half, one portion for the court and one for life. Habit itself softened the loss of the losses, especially because that expenditure had to feed the hand that fought.

## LVIII.—Many Commanders Withdrew from the Siege

Meanwhile, weary and disgusted with the hardship, the count of Blois had departed from the camp for Cilicia, and Count Northmannus for Laodicea; the man of Blois went to Tarsus to remedy his want, while Northmannus went to the English in the hope of ruling.

At that time the English held Laodicea, sent there as its protection by the emperor. A wandering army was ravaging its territory and attempting to break violently into the city itself. In this danger the English summoned the count mentioned above, seeking faithful and prudent counsel.

It was an act of loyalty to take as their lord a faithful man, to whom they could entrust themselves. They had withdrawn from the Norman yoke, but now submitted themselves again. This was an act of prudence: having experienced that people’s loyalty and gifts, they easily returned to where they had come from.

Thus, when Count Northmannus entered Laodicea, he devoted himself to sleep and leisure. Yet he was not useless, for having obtained wealth, he distributed it generously to others in need. For Cyprus, its fellow servant, abounding in wine, grain, and much livestock, had filled Laodicea—its needy neighboring fellow Christian and, as it were, foster sister—with supplies. For it alone on the Syrian shore both worshiped Christ and served Alexius.

Yet even with this excuse for leisure, the count mentioned above was recalled to the camp once and again in vain. Summoned a third time under threat of anathema, he returned unwillingly, for the transport that had to come from Laodicea to supply the count had a difficult passage.

## LIX.—The Stations of the Besieging Commanders

The other princes had occupied the nearer towns and were therefore easily fed by the more convenient advantages of their positions. The duke of the seat had obtained a populous city abundant in provisions and wine.

The count of Flanders held a nearby valley containing the towns of Balena, Barthemolin, Corsehel, Barsoldan, and several others besides. Hence it is still called the Count’s Valley, just as the duke’s city is also so called.

Emma and Harenc served Tancred, together with many other places near the camp and exceedingly fertile. Tancred himself had arrived first of all, as I mentioned above, as a forerunner. This precedence is confirmed by the popular saying that “the first born is the first fed.” When famine increased, he was prosperous and excluded none of his household from his table; he received and nourished many who had been excluded from the tables of others.

The Valley of Doxa fed Bohemond. It deserved such a name, since among the other valleys it abounded in the glory of harvests, vineyards, trees, and streams, so that in ancient times it might have deserved to be called Daphne—a name that among the Greeks signifies pleasantness. Lying next to Antioch on the south, it greatly needed a protector capable of keeping the citizens’ hunger away from its abundance of food.

The other princes also possessed other towns, whose memory long days have erased. Yet they have not erased the fact that Rubea, Rufa, Arcican, and Belmesyn served Count Raymond as municipal towns.

## LX.—Severe Famine in the Army

Thus the chief men had occupied the province. But the others, though of lesser renown, were afflicted by great want and much deprivation. Death did not permit them to go out, nor famine to remain: these twin forms of distress left the people no middle course.

The long delay and the countless population had brought on famine. Moreover, scarcely a day passed without news of the death of those who had gone out for provisions terrifying the ears of the besiegers. The princes nevertheless brought protection to the travelers, now one and now another in turn, and sometimes they themselves needed protection.

For the southern gate mentioned above, always open to ambushes, never ceased pouring out troops that blockaded the narrow roads and thus confronted travelers who were ignorant of the danger.

But the other and sharper evil—famine—now prevailed. Disregarding death, it sent the army wandering here and there like swarms of bees. What does famine not disdain? What does it not compel? Whom does it allow to feel shame?

It was also the reason for the departure of Guido Rubeus and William, surnamed Carpentarius—illustrious men and not obscure among the palatines of the king of France. As they were preparing to leave, Bohemond appeared.

“What kind of rest are you seeking?” he said. “Are you unconcerned about the common labor? You are nobles; the way is open. Here your tents will remain forever, reserved for the public sewer of your name, indeed of your family.”

They departed, indifferent to disgrace; famine, driven by its goads, disdained disgrace. They followed Count Stephen, who, as has been written above, had gone to rest within the borders of Cilicia.

The men were of one generation and one character. With one accord they hated labor and pursued leisure, though they were warlike—accustomed, however, amid wars to the pleasures of luxury.

## LXI.—The Customs of the Provincials
The chief excellence of this people is its eye, its bold spirit, and its right hands ready for arms; in everything else they are lavish in scattering and sluggish in gathering.
