In these qualities the provincials differed from them as much as a duck from a hen [uncertain comparison in the text]: in their customs, their dispositions, their dress, and their food they lived peacefully, investigated carefully, and were industrious—but, not to conceal the truth, less warlike. They say that bodily adornment is something womanly and reject it as contemptible; yet they diligently attend to the adornment of horses and mules.

Their diligence during the time of famine helped much more than did that of many peoples readier for war. When bread was lacking, they endured contentedly on roots and did not disdain pods; their right hands carried long iron rods with which they probed the earth’s entrails for provisions. Hence the children’s song still chants: “The Franks for war, the provincials for provisions.”

There was, however, one thing they committed too eagerly and disgracefully: they sold dog’s flesh to other peoples as hare, and donkey flesh as goat; or, if they were able to approach a fat horse or mule without being noticed, they drove wounds into its entrails through the rear opening, or excretory passage, and the animal died. All were astonished who, unaware of the fraud, had just seen the animal fat, lively, strong, and playful: no trace of the wounds appeared, and no sign of death was visible at all. The spectators, terrified at the sight of the strange thing, said: “Let us stand far away; the spirit of a demon has breathed upon this animal.” When they had gone, those who knew of the killing approached as though ignorant of it, but, forbidden to touch the animal, they said: “We would rather die from eating this food than remain fasting.”

The man who had suffered the loss pitied the one who had caused it; the culprit repaid him with laughter. Then, like ravens, that people flew upon the corpse, and each dragged away whatever pieces he could, putting them either into his belly or into the butcher’s shop.

### LXII. — Cassianus’s harshness toward the Armenian

But now Christ, having tested and pitied His athletes, leads their struggle toward a joyful conclusion. After scorching the people with the sun, He opens the city—and its shade—in this way.

Among those whose grain Cassianus had halved was a wealthy Armenian who, having renounced the Christian doctrine, followed the errors of the pagans. He had a very large household, and grain in proportion to the size of his household. When this became known to Cassianus as the famine grew worse, he halved again what had earlier been left as a small consolation for miserable life. The first act had been a general robbery carried out house by house and family by family; this was a particular robbery, and therefore more grievous, as though insult had been added to injury.

Stripped of the means of sustaining life, the man, mournful and distraught, kissed the ruler’s footsteps, seeking back the consolation that had been taken from his needy children. Who could remain unmoved by a flood of tears and a cry striking the heavens?

“Woe to you, my children, no longer to be called, as before, dear pledges, but dreadful wounds! Your hunger consumes mine; yours penetrates my heart, and I do not feel my own. What benefit was there in feeding you with delicate foods, when now bread is denied to you—the bread that is given to useless slaves? It would have been better for your wretched father to see you slaughtered than afflicted by starvation. May a spear pierce your father first; may lightning burn him first; may the seas engulf him first, before I behold that end of yours which my soul recoils from seeing.

“Woe! So it will be. This one consolation alone remains to me: my death will go before yours and free me from the sight of you—either the sword or the noose. But have pity, citizens! Intercede for the innocent; or at least let me be punished as a guilty man, so long as my household is not tortured by the torment of hunger.”

### LXIII. — The city is betrayed

[Col. 0536A]

After pouring out many such words, piteously but uselessly, he is despised, mocked, and driven away. From the beginning of the siege, the custody of one tower had been entrusted to him. It stood far from the army, in a corner of the city toward the west wind, above the mountain. Cassianus had entrusted the neighboring lower tower to his brother, so that one might say that two sisters had been committed to two brothers. Yet this had not been done carelessly or by chance: guards who had once been Christians had prudently been assigned far from the Christians. This had been foreseen and carried out.

But when the rejected brother saw himself insulted, with no one interceding and no one showing pity, he took thought for his own safety, intending to avenge his injuries through the general destruction of the citizens. When the watches had been lulled in the dead of night, he lowered a rope from the wall beside which he guarded the tower. Accompanied by his two sons, his pledges, he descended by it and, exhausted by the long circuit, at last reached Boamundus.

That eastern people regarded Boamundus among the others as the chief of princes, because long ago, when Wiscardus was conquering Greece, the fame of Boamundus had terrified the Greeks and won glory through many conflicts. From that time he had become renowned throughout Asia and was now thought to be lord of all.

When the Armenian was ordered to explain why he had come, he agreed to open the city’s entrance. He fixed the day and the hour and indicated a place suitable for the entry. Then, after voluntarily offering his sons as hostages and handing them over, he alone returned to the rope. Anger, boldness, hope, and fear accompanied and urged him, yet he flew upward with ease.

### LXIV. — Boamundus informs the bishop of Puy. The bishop of Puy’s address to the soldiers

[Col. 0536C]

At this, Boamundus, never stirred by equal joy before, went at sunrise to the bishop of Puy, the man whom Pope Urban had placed over the army as his second self, and entrusted this secret to his faith. The bishop promised faithfully both to conceal the matter and diligently to advance what had been concealed. He therefore immediately summoned the commanders of the armies and the leading men among the people. When they had assembled, he spoke as follows:

“Brothers, our present labor has afflicted us for a long time and, unless the Lord’s eye is upon us, will afflict us for a long time still. We built siege engines; the enemy openly resisted. We dug at the walls; we were repulsed. We fought, and this alone turned out favorably. But we must fear that the battle which they say is imminent may be more difficult because it will be larger.

“The number of those enemies was fifteen thousand; these, they say, are four hundred thousand. The enemy’s strength does not cease increasing, nor ours diminishing. But consider the city’s strength and its position. Ditches surround three of its sides, making them inaccessible; the fourth is protected by a marsh and a river. No place in the world could furnish equal defenses around its circuit of walls. Springs well up within; they have been able to gather sufficient supplies for the necessities of life, and among them a year has passed under the threat of our arrival.

“O Antioch, either may you never have existed, or may you never have stood in our way! Jerusalem is the reason for our journey: what have Antioch and we to do with one another? If we leave this city behind us, if, repulsed from it, we proceed farther, nothing has been accomplished and nothing remains to be hoped for. If, I say, we leave it, it will not leave us. It will always follow as a companion—or, more truly, as an adversary. It will block the roads; it will fight from behind and from in front. By resisting, it will give others hope of resistance; if captured, it would have wrapped all the others in fear.

“O walls! Would that you had either never risen or stood far from our eyes and ears! But let us deliberate, my lords. Let us discuss the matter openly and propose a reward for courage. I hope that, once the highest rewards have been heard, we shall rouse men’s hearts.

“Consider what Saul did, and let us take examples from ancient times. Among the Hebrews there was no one who would rise against Goliath, until the king’s daughter and the freedom of his homeland were promised to David and stirred him to action. Many say to themselves, and even openly: ‘Why should I labor? Why torment myself? Why receive wounds? Shall I give my life as the price of Antioch? Some ungrateful nobody will rule.’ Let me not weep so that another ingrate may laugh through my tears.

“Come, therefore; let not the ambition to rule move you, but rather the completion of the journey begun. Let the city itself better fall as a reward to the man by whose aid we shall recover it, than that courage should grow numb, deprived of reward, while offering the excuse you have heard.

“This is what my mind can devise, investigate, and imagine as soundest, most effective, and most excellent. Let your discernment, my lords, supply anything I have said too little; remove anything I have said too much; change anything wrongly said; and, if it is well said, approve it.”

### LXV. — Sovereignty over the city is promised to the man through whom entry into it is to be gained

[Col. 0537C]

At this, the whole council gave its support. First those of highest rank, then each of the others in due order, voiced their assent. No one failed to approve; all agreed that the city should belong to whoever opened the entrance.

Then Boamundus said: “A promise bound by an oath is already almost a gift, so that what is future passes, in a manner, into the present, and hope into joy. But if these are merely words released from this bond, what does that accomplish? Anyone may be rich in promises. Therefore, if you want what you promise to become ratified and stand firm, swear together.”

There was no delay and no withdrawal. As they had been instructed, they swore; even had he instructed them to promise greater things, they would not have found it difficult to comply in hope of a remedy. Thus Boamundus, now more confident and alert, disclosed his plan to several leading men and made it more openly known that everyone must prepare to enter. He promised timely assistance under such a firm hope.

Then, having exchanged farewells, they returned to their own quarters and set about preparing ropes. The man in particular who intended to seize the prize among all the runners hastened, reflected, and depended entirely upon the arrival of the coming night, which seemed sluggish to him—more so than to one awaiting a beloved or those in need of work.

### LXVI. — The city is handed over

At last, when that night arrived and silence held everything in its midst, Boamundus approached the tower promised to him on foot, not without much exertion; the ruggedness of the place did not admit horses. As he went, however, he sent ahead a messenger to keep watch and determine whether the approach to the walls was sufficiently safe.

That holy traitor had given this sign as he departed: “When you come, my lord, send a messenger ahead to the foot of my tower. I shall keep careful watch upon the walls. If everything is favorable, I shall lower one stone after another; if danger is present, one stone will indicate it.”

The watchman was therefore sent ahead to distinguish these conditions. As he approached the tower, he was immediately recognized; once recognized, he received the sign of success and returned to report what he had heard.

Boamundus accordingly proceeded as he had begun and reached the walls. He found the rope hanging outside, tied his men to it, and the Armenian pulled. When he had made the knots sufficiently firm, the swift young men, their winged bodies girded with swords, flew up the ropes. Gouel of Chartres was first, like an eagle calling its young to fly and hovering above them. That noble man, who from childhood had hungered for nothing except praise, thirsted to be praised not for the sake of life, but to live for the sake of praise.

At first there was silence, while the few feared the multitude. But when the multitude had been brought in, it expelled fear. The spirit of those whom the ascent had made like eagles now turned them into lions.

### LXVII. — The slaughter of the citizens

They ran to the gates, and whoever encountered them fell. The first to experience their swords was the brother of the Armenian who had brought them in—the guardian of the first tower into which they descended. The brother who knew the secret had left him ignorant, lest informing him should be to build a gallows for himself and his family.

After that man and his fellow guards had been slaughtered by the sudden sword, a shout arose, at which the other towers trembled. The guards fled wherever they could; for others, the towers themselves became tombs, preserving buried those by whom they had just been guarded.

Thus our men descended to the gates. They cut through the bars and opened to Boamundus the nearer gate on the western side, and to Raymond the other, which faced north and the bridge. Boamundus had descended to the first through steep and trackless places; Raymond had long besieged the second from nearby, and, hearing the uproar from within, immediately arrived without hesitation.

That had been the greatest of their anxieties and the great fear: that, once our men were brought in, the city might confront them, guard the gates, and shut out assistance. But while these men came, the others fled, Christ having pity on His people. The gates, left without guards, easily opened while the opposing axes labored to destroy the central beam.

Until then the night had favored the Christians. Dawn reddened, and the day, hastening on, envied the night its joy. At first light, therefore, the Christians burst into the palaces, exulted over the captured city, searched hiding places, and seized gold, children, matrons, girls, and whatever else each man found. They slaughtered whatever males were capable of war and kept those who were not.

But the citizens fled to the mountain—whoever was ready for flight, whoever was swift of foot—abandoning everything. A wounded father did not wait for his son, nor a son for his aged father.

### LXVIII. — Cassianus, prince of Antioch, saves himself by flight

The castle situated on the summit of the cliff received many, while very many were shut out, turned back by the Christian sword that met them. Some fell onto the mountain; others climbed the walls by interior steps and leapt outside—a fatal leap for some, a life-restoring one for others.

That side of the city, as stated above, was free of besiegers, and so those whom permission to leave released saw it as a suitable avenue of escape. The prince Cassianus himself, wounded in the crown of the head by a sword, in the back by a spear, and in the thigh by a javelin, escaped by this route. As much as night, dawn, spur, and horse had helped him, he had already drawn far away, almost to the town of Rubea.

There, deprived of his horse and concealed by darkness in a thicket, he hoped either for a helpful traveler in the present daylight, or at least for the darkness of the coming night to assist his flight. In this hope the wretched wounded man, as I have said, panting and thirsty, his ears pricked and his eyes fixed upon the roads, hid in the bushes like a little hare which thorns conceal after it has been snatched from the jaws of hounds.

Alas for the glory of the world! What was more wretched than he now? Only yesterday he had been prince of Antioch, ruler of Syria and Phoenicia, terror of Assyria, the most powerful of the eastern kings, second only to Solidanus, who had ruled Persia. But while the wretched man was being harassed by such great distresses, a fiercer thirst scorched his entrails. He saw a peasant carrying a pitcher of water, signaled to him, approached, and drank.

The rustic looked at his clothing and contemplated his face. Astonished at his downfall and wounds, he said: “Alas, my lord prince, who has been permitted to do so much to you, and against whom has such audacity arisen?”

For he had recognized him, just as the eyes of the common people are always fixed upon royal majesty. He was therefore astonished, ignorant of the still recent event.

### LXIX. — He is killed by a peasant

[Col. 0539C]

Then Cassianus, trusting the man who pitied his misfortune, and at the same time fearing that, if he concealed the truth, the man would distrust him and seem to be taking the enemy’s side, said:

“Antioch is lost; the Franks hold it. As you see me, I have barely escaped with three wounds. But I beg you not to make this public. In the evening, of course, I shall undertake my flight. If I escape, expect from me the greatest reward.”

The common crowd follows fortune. When she smiles, it will count many friends in that man; when she frowns, they scatter when the casks have been drained to their dregs, all alike treacherous in bearing the yoke.

Stunned by so great and sudden a reversal, the peasant was beside himself. He growled inwardly, was astonished, and at last deliberated what ought to be done at such a turning point. Immediately he considered the death of the man whose wounds he had just pitied, weighing two things: the ease of access and the usefulness of the outcome.

If he killed him, a reward was ready—royal clothing and a horse, and, beyond these, the favor of the Franks. Yet more important than these should have been Christ his friend, whose enemy he would kill, and the immortal praise arising from the death of so great a prince—a praise that has driven many mortals to their deaths. But such thoughts were foreign to the peasant’s mind, which noticed nothing noble; thus he considered only the advantage.

He saw a man exhausted, bloodless, half-dead, alone, and unarmed, and easily judged that what remained of his life could be extinguished. What more need be said? Forgetful of honor and neglecting pity, the servant tore apart his master with a raised club and scattered his brains, carrying off the rather meager spoils in preference to the great promises.

### LXX. — Tancredus complains that he had not been informed of this expedition

Meanwhile Tancredus, unaware of everything that had happened, [Note: [Col. 0539D] By contrast, Baldric, book II, says: “For Tancred and his advisers had known the whole affair from its origin.” But greater credit is due to our Ralph.] was, as usual, blockading the roads far from the city—roads that had often allowed the townspeople both entry and exit. When he learned from fugitives who had left by that route what had happened, he cried out repeatedly:

“Alas for me! Alas for me! In such great and unspeakable joy, I alone am forced to grieve. Shame! Who labored while I rested? Who kept watch while I snored? O Boamundus, Boamundus! You made it known to others openly, but secretly to me. O blood of my kinsman! Was this what kinship meant? You kept me away, although you knew that in this great campaign I would not decline the leading role.

“You knew that, had I been present, I would have run first to the walls, seized the ropes first, flown over first, and cut down the enemy first. You begrudged me this glory, although strength, age, and perhaps courage denied it to you. O fortunate man, whoever he is, who offered these first fruits to the Lord our God! But let us hurry, my companions. We have lost the advance; at least let us follow.

“For he who made you poor and me inglorious will not also take this from you. But let Him who fashioned human hearts individually and understands their works judge and avenge.”

After saying this, he came to Antioch and found joy. He who had just been weeping with those who wept now rejoiced with those who rejoiced; for shared joy expelled private grief from his noble heart.

A small addition was nevertheless made to the common happiness: some of the troops who had been left to guard the castle, hearing the sound of the disturbances, had entered with Boamundus and prepared a splendid palace for their absent lord. When all those who held authority had entered, only the count of Blois was absent—whether modestly excluded by the deserved anger of heaven or by the envy of fortune.

### LXXI. — A marvelous event

[Note: [Col. 0539D] The events contained under this number appear in a document appended to the deeds of Tancredus, whether sewn on by the same author or added later by another. They nevertheless seem to interrupt the sequence of the narrative.]

At that time an unexpected and unprecedented accident occurred, of a kind such as neither ancient nor present ages remember having preceded or followed it as a prodigy.

The counts invited by Boamundus to dinner were seated: the Fleming on his right, the Boulonnais on his left. A large crowd of common people was present in the same palace, some reclining at table and others serving, as happens when three such great princes meet at a meal.

Food makes people silent; drink, as someone prudent has said, makes them talkative. After dinner, Boamundus was balancing a knife in his right hand when the count of Flanders, joking, said:

“What does this balancing mean? I see clearly that it is a sign of anxiety. This is no time for cares; it is an hour of joy, not of anxiety.”

“Indeed,” Boamundus replied, “my lord count, it is something else. Your presence does not permit me to be anxious. I am preparing a game while I balance the knife. This candle, whose thickness surpasses the others”—and a candle thicker than the rest was burning before him upon a candlestick—“this candle I shall divide into two with a single stroke.”

The counts thought his speech delirious and incapable of producing any result. Therefore the Fleming added:

“Attempt what you boast, prince, and I shall give you my cloak as the reward of your success. But you, unable to do it, must not refuse to give me yours.”

The wager was accepted. Boamundus immediately struck the standing candle with the knife and cut it in two. Descending obliquely from the right, he achieved an easy and careful cut.

Thus one candle became two—a marvel to relate—both burning while burning. The upper portion, which had fallen, continued to burn; the lower portion, which remained fixed upright, also caught fire by itself, without anyone bringing flame near it.

The minds of those looking on were stunned; moved by the omen, the performer himself was terrified. When news of the event flew through the people, everyone came running from every hall and workshop; they were astonished and could not satisfy their hearts by looking. While they were still astonished and wondering, the flame that had suddenly ignited was suddenly extinguished: a sad omen.

If the wax and flame had preserved an undivided partnership of remaining and perishing, a long inheritance and a long succession would have been promised, to be carried down to the final day of the world. But because the little flame that had grown disappeared as soon as it arose, the diviners promise hope for offspring, but offspring soon to pass away.

“The fates will show him to the world only,” they say, “and will not allow him to live longer”—and the other things that the Mantuan added. We saw these fulfilled in the death of the younger Boamundus.

The novelty of the prodigy defended the count. Not a fragment of the pledged cloak was demanded; rather, wealth and poverty surrounded the prince and the count respectively. Thus not only was what was owed not exacted, but the count was heaped with a very generous gift.

### LXXII. — Having gained the city, the Christians are besieged by countless unbelievers

That day was a day of joy, but the next was one of sorrow. Corbozan, commander of the king of the Persians, arrived with four hundred thousand cavalry, besieged the city, and threatened those enclosed within it with death and imprisonment.

Hearing this, the count of Blois hastened his flight as quickly as possible, considering it almost a victory if he could escape while his companions were given over to imminent death. Returning toward Greece, he met the emperor Alexius at the city of Cuthai in Lycia. The emperor was hastening with one hundred thousand Greeks to aid the Franks. Guido, Boamundus’s brother, came with him, along with certain other Frankish nobles, about ten thousand armed men.

When the emperor heard from Stephanus the report concerning the besieged Franks and the Persian besiegers, it is said that he first wished to come to their aid but, recalled by the words of the man who ought to have encouraged him, ceased from the attempt.

When consulted about the number of the Persians, Stephanus is said to have replied: “My lord, if this entire army of yours were given to them as food, it would not suffice for each man to receive even a little.”

Terrified by these words, the emperor fled back into Greece and devastated by fire the towns, fields, and huts through which he returned, dragging the populations behind him, lest he himself should feed the approaching enemy with his own provisions.

Guido wished to bring aid to the Christians enclosed within, and was scarcely restrained, although deprived of Greek assistance; but, discouraged by the same man who had dissuaded the emperor, he was drawn back.

### LXXIII. — They are afflicted by dreadful famine

Meanwhile the Franks, hemmed in by hostile soldiers,

shut within the walls and exposed to Persian arrows,

are tortured by dreadful famine—a hard condition, but hope is harsher.

There is no rest for the wretched: on one side the mountain rains down arrows,

on the other the plain; a wall and a river confine this side.

The mountain is subject to none of these things; passable, it urges on the enemy.

Thus day excites battle, and dark night excites battle.

The Turks hold the heights; the Latins defend the lower ground.

A few spears stand against countless arrows—

an unequal contest in number, strength, position, and weapons;

all these advantages belong to the Turks.

Yet the Franks, surpassing in courage,

drive away all sadness. They overcome those whom all advantages favor;

they take counsel concerning the means by which they may

skillfully avoid their hardship and bring light sleep to their eyes.

### LXXIV. — They resist and construct defensive works

They prepare cement, stones, plumb lines, craftsmen,

ropes, vessels, and mattocks. When everything is ready,

they build by night—a good thing, though it hates the light.

The work goes out into the night; by daylight the arrows return.

A spear stands against them, and while it presses forward,

the construction rises.

While the enemy withdraws, the work ceases. Thus fortune is balanced between the two.

A wall is built, a barrier against the Turks’ descents.

If wood is needed, so that fire may seek its material,

send sixteen teams there to gather the scattered arrows;

you will receive the returning draft animals, streaming with sweat.

No one returns empty, ready to fill the quivers.

Thus, having found some—but scarcely any—rest,

only later do they drive their Parthian arrows into the Franks;

now they turn their cares from one danger to another,

the people overwhelmed by every kind of tear, anxiety, and labor,

by wounds, hunger, cares, cold, and heat.

Whatever sleep they could greedily snatch,

they seized at night.

In place of bread, that sleep nourished their empty bellies.

### LXXV. — While they indulge in sleep, the enemy presses upon them

While the people snored, the wall was without a guard.

For, as the common saying goes, he guards badly who snores well.

The herald, whose lofty palace had hidden recesses,

went through the streets crying out:

“Rise, rise! The enemy is here; he has climbed the towers;

he already holds the city.

Why this sluggish rest? Wretched men, come to your own aid!”

While he shouted this, they rose at the cries as though

Ismarus and Rhodope, the rocks that Thrace preserves,

had been ordered to rise, commanded by those same cries.

Then the leaders resolved to burn their hiding places and dwellings:

once the houses were kindled, the wall would have guards.

### LXXVI. — Robertus sets the city on fire so that the soldiers may soon come

Robertus, born of Flanders, was urged to attend this undertaking.

He himself, active, quickly roused the sluggish, and by this means the slow,

lest great things perish while little men prolong their leisure.

What was said was done: Robertus ravaged the city with fire,

and, while saving the walls, saved the townspeople.

If I remember correctly, Provence had sent those whom shadow made sluggish

and the added flame made swift.

That quarter lay beside the mountain, though not at the foot of the mountain.

But the people near the foot had very large halls,

having received the first entrances through opened gates.

At first they had chosen the highest houses that seemed suitable;

the palace of Raymond also fell to the prince there.

From that place one part of the people, sickly, and another, proud,

were enjoying rest. But when Vulcan consumed the rooftops,

those who had been sluggish rose, regretting that they had indulged in rest.

They ran to the walls and set up tents beside them.

Some made coverings. Thus, although close to destruction,

the walls were preserved; thus losses were relieved by losses;

thus a general evil, when it ceased, established in a particular case

the saying that is read everywhere:

“Pain is the medicine of pain.”

### LXXVII. — Fire consumes the temples and palaces

The city, once kindled, burns more and more—and, alas!—

the remedy exceeds its proper measure. When the harmful fire

had roamed through the houses, harmless temples were burned:

temples at whose sight the Achaean painter,

the Arab caster of gold, and the Scottish and English sculptors

would have stood amazed.

O what quantity of material, what beauty, that ornament concealed!

For there was a row of columns cut from Parian rocks;

the pavement was fashioned like a glassy sea, equal to crystal;

fragrant cedar beams from the forests of Lebanon;

Coatus fashioned timbers from woods that touched the heavens.

Atlas supplied the marble, Tyre the glass, Cyprus the bronze,

and England the iron.

Each kingdom strove to send its own treasures.

And although a hidden Antiochene furnace smelts lead,

they say that Amathus sent it to cover the temples;

the mother possessed the worship of another lord.

One was Jacob’s—whether he was killed by the sword

or bound to wood and thrown down from the temple is uncertain.

Such materials and such beauty perished in this fire.

### LXXVIII. — Though the walls are saved, the enemy nevertheless presses on

But now, although the walls had been saved at such great cost,

the enemy still presses on. He attempts to deceive the guards.

The night fears ambushes; the daylight scorns to learn that they must be feared.

Those who look down from the high rocks

see everything openly: who sleeps and who keeps watch,

which places lack a guardian and which enjoy a defender.

The people of the Alemanni, whose front faced the east wind,

guarded by night and rested in sleep by day.

The Turks, seeing them so often from the summit of the rock,

conceived the hope that they could climb beneath them while they slept.

They therefore prepared ladders and came secretly to the walls.

At once they climbed; no one prevented them.

The wretched guards lay there as though released from death by sleep.

Many had already climbed into the towers, carrying bows and swords,

when such things were seen from the distant wall.

A shout arose. At last the city, sunk in sleep, awoke.

The crowd was astonished to see Turks moving close beside it.

Some drew their swords; others fled in bewilderment.

Those who drew their swords struck; those who fled were struck.

The Christians pressed forward; the Persians fled toward the walls.

Fortunate was the man to whom the use of ladders or ropes fell;

unfortunate he to whom neither was available.

The bold man leapt from the high walls onto the flints;

the timid fled the drawn swords.

While the awakened Alemanni at last rose and pressed forward,

the crowd of Latins—shame!—as the Greeks themselves testify,

cried through the streets, “Caco Alemanni!” (“Bad Germans!”).

### LXXIX. — Pressed by famine, the besieged compel certain nobles to leave the city

Nor did fortune then cease to challenge Christ—or Christ’s servants.

The defeated eagle attempts to rise again;

having fallen while climbing and entered the walls,

it prepares a descent and an escape, leaving nothing unattempted.

Now it works with the right hand, now with weapons in the left,

saying: “If I cannot move heaven, I shall move Acheron.”

The Christians shut within, enduring a harsh day

and a harsh night, are afflicted, torn, consumed, and wasted

by hunger more cruel than every enemy.

Cruel yesterday, now more cruel, tomorrow and the day after still fiercer,

it advances ever more savagely as food recedes.

In such wasting, amid such weariness of life,

without assistance, part of the army begins to consider flight:

good, noble, war-renowned youth,

worthy of praise until this moment—

William and his brothers, Alberic, and Ivo.

These three bear the surname of Grentemesnil;

Radulphus bears that of Fontenelle, and he is the man from Tours.

But, alas, shame! alas, shame! Normandy sent the brothers.

That race is everywhere victory and the glory of the world:

the people victorious over the English, victorious over the Sicilians,

victorious over the Greeks, the Capuans, and the Apulians;

to whom the Cenomans and Calabrians are subject,

to whom the African is subject,

to whom Japix is subject—

and from their stock that race endures shame.

Many of them were addressed by the voice of others,

so that they might become companions in so great a league of disgrace.

But God and His Arnulfus restrain those ready to obey

and call them back from the shameful arrangement.

Yet that youth, forgetful of God, country, and itself,

the initiator of that disgraceful path and author of the shameful plan,

persists in its undertaking, recalled by no voice,

thinking it an outstanding deed and a splendid story

if, after the others have been slaughtered,

it alone withdraws from the enemy.

Therefore it constructs ropes. Once they have been constructed and tied,

a flying owl is made to hang from the wall by night.

Thus she flees by night; her flight is revealed at sunrise,

and soon an order is issued that no one dare untie the ropes—

so that they may remain a monument of disgrace for posterity.

### LXXX. — The besieged consume deadly foods

When the winnowing basket and the wind had driven away the chaff,

the pure grain that remained—gold tested by fire,

cleansed of earth—the steadfast, unafraid people,

though torn apart by hunger, pitiable and restless,

ran to whatever resources offered hope of life,

and ate deadly morsels that promised death:

salvinca, hemlock, hellebore, lapan, darnel, and tares.

While the wretched men ate these things to remain alive,

they died.

Moreover, they boiled the soles of shoes wherever they had been put away,

and whatever pieces of leather they found discarded anywhere.

Thrown into a cooking pot, these softened in flames and water.

From them they prepared feasts. Fortunate was he to whom fate granted such food;

but fate denied it to others and left them death and disease.

That noble and illustrious stock of leaders, counts, and kings,

pressed by misfortunes though accustomed to good things,

such as no walls had enclosed before or would enclose afterward,

was terrified by hunger. In place of nectar, it scarcely possessed a stream.

Hence came intestinal flux, fever, and watery pestilence;

there was no consolation, and everywhere they saw the death they had brought forth.

### LXXXI. — They ask the Persians for a single combat through Peter the Hermit

They ponder, investigate, devise, and explore many things:

by what force, in what way, by what reason or skill

they might avoid death and call back their fleeing life.

Whether night or day, they consider it. They made the matter public

and, after taking counsel, decided to send envoys to

the Persian satrap whom they dared to call Corbozan.

They sent five, among whom was Peter the Hermit—

Peter, whose complexion was dark, whose spirit was fierce,

whose foot was bare, whose stature was short,

and whose face was emaciated.

Like a little donkey among horses, he had only a donkey’s trappings.

Peter was clothed in a most wretched cloak, after the manner of the desert.

In such a guise, the trabeated man [trabeatus] approached the tyrant’s presence.

When the Persians saw their clothing, their faces, and the rest,

they rejoiced and hoped that the poor man wished to fall

before the prince’s feet, so that, bending,

he might bend the prince’s knees and come beforehand as a herald of peace.

Not so, impiety, not so; rather, as the wind casts away dust,

so you too shall be cast away.

Then Peter began in this fashion, his head held upright:

“While the Frankish nobility, pilgrims of Christ,

seek the tomb, they have taken possession of this splendid city,

fearing nothing. Peter, leader of the apostolic army,

rules here; he shelters it as a guest and rejoices to have fellow servants.

“You ravage its territories and shut the Christians in by siege.

In the name of Christ, in the name of Peter, I order you:

withdraw quickly from his territories.

Or, if you follow justice, if the Persian kingdoms care about what is fair

and what is right, let ten, or six, or at least three armed men

come out from your side.

Let an equal number of Christians meet them.

Let whichever people wins have the Antiochene serve it;

whichever is defeated must depart from Antioch.

“Or, if this condition seems too difficult and displeases you,

hear what follows and what we propose. Another alternative remains,

perhaps more serious. When tomorrow’s Dawn has shone,

know without doubt that a war has been prepared for you.

“These are the words that the Latin people command me to say to you.”

### LXXXII. — The Persians’ response

While Peter proposed such things in the midst of the Persians,

the crowd of commanders laughed, and the common people also laughed.

They mocked the wretched man for speaking in the manner of men in robes.

At last the supreme commander answered with a swollen throat:

“I have found prey: a foreign people ravaging the kingdom of the Persians

and offending the god Muhammad and, next to him,

the sole Solidanus. I was sent to seek it out and destroy it;

but the walls close it in—I shall break them.

I shall give your bodies to the jaws of dogs and lions.

Go and report these words of mine to your Latins.

For what answer shall I find to Peter, or to your Christ?

As Peter is worth so much, so much is Christ worth to me.

Neither concerns me; both alike are a laughing matter.”

After Peter had heard such great breaths of threats,

he returned to his companions and reported in due order the commander’s rage.

At once the bold-hearted Gauls girded themselves for battle—

but their flesh had been consumed by hunger, leaving only bones.

### LXXXIII. — The faithful plan a sortie

A broad area lies close beneath the wall beside the gate,

which opens toward the north, adjoining the bridge and the river.

[Col. 0546B]

There they assemble. There the unarmed man measures himself—
That sacred people determine who shall be first against the enemy,

and who, following first, shall raise the standards second;

thus the rest arrange the battle in a fixed order:

where the javelins shall stand, where the spear, and where the arrows;

from where the cavalry, from where the infantry, shall charge against the enemy or stand their ground.

When they had arranged everything in its proper order,

the sun sank, and the battle was postponed until the following day.

The night of Byssa had passed; the third part of the night remained,

when Arnulf’s teacher, hurrying with breathless run,

simultaneously struck the doors of the halls with voice and hand:

“Rise, come, rise quickly! Why do you delay the standards and the heavens?

[Col. 0546C] Look: victory is flashing in the sky; look up at the stars.

The star that was just following now leads the way, while that

which now moves backward, Arnulf, was previously leading the way.

Rise, summon the leaders, and drive them into battle. If there is any danger,

let me be held hostage; let me be burned or crucified—

and your wife, and both your parents, and both your sons;

for he had both parents, both sons, and a wife.

From childhood this man had been taught the order in which the stars move,

what they signify, whether a comet alters kingdoms,

whether the icy old man threatens frost and rain,

whether the chariots of Phaethon, the savage lion, and fires,

or Orion’s sword-bearing flank, excessively heated,

portend war, or whatever each one may threaten.

[Col. 0546D] The supreme teacher had instructed many in this art,

among them Arnulf, and had shown him two stars

that revealed omens at the beginning of the war.

One star was giving its destiny to the Christians, the other to the Turks;

then, running in a different order from before, those stars

were foretelling destruction for the Persians and rejoicing for the Franks.”

LXXXIV.—They Charge Against the Enemy.

Therefore, when Arnulf’s lynx-like eye and ear perceived

the signs of the heavens through his teacher’s speech and gesture,

he quickly went out to the chief leaders and roused them to arms;

and, with the order of their courses reversed, he explained the meaning of the omen:

now all was favorable, because the earlier signs had passed over.

Meanwhile night had yielded to Phoebus; therefore the illustrious people,

hungry for battle, sprang out through the opened gates.

[Col. 0547A] Now there is need of help, now there is need of action, now, fostering Spirit, bring aid to the one who calls;

tell the poet which was the first battle line, which the second,

which were the remaining lines, and inspire the singer who thirsts for you.

LXXXV.—The Order of the Leaders in the Assault upon the Enemy.

First, great Hugh leads the Franks out of the city:

he shines foremost in advance, and he, the most noble, shone before all others.

Next come the Norman standards of Robert.

Both are supreme counts, both alone are royal offspring;

Hugh is more illustrious in lineage, Robert greater in everything else.

They did not undeservedly earn the foremost places in the battle.

Third, Godefrid draws out many in his column,

namely the Lotharingians together with the Alemanni.

Fourth falls to Tancred the order of the combatants,

[Col. 0547B] outstanding in arms, but not so numerous.

Lofty in strength and numbers, in the fifth position

shines the precious standard of the son of Guiscard,

partly distinguished by its material, partly by the image of the cross.

Raimund follows sixth, with a great roar,

to oppose the Turks, not to mingle with them in battle:

let him stand in support of the fighters and watch everywhere;

let him supply arms, from the youth who will destroy them, for those destined to perish,

be the strength of the battle, a wall, and a place of refuge.

The vigilance of the Flemish count presides over the city.

He himself governs the gates; he himself crowns the wall with arms.

He fills the towers with every kind of cloud of missiles:

arrows, stakes, weapons, stones, and fire-hardened pointed poles,

often turning freshly curbed horses toward the construction.

[Col. 0547C] Hence threats arise, hence fear lest, once breached, it admit the enemy.

Now he thunders from the commander’s mouth, now he cuts down with the soldier’s sword.

That sole barrier against the Turks’ descents,

that great protector, needed the support of a great guardian.

LXXVI.—Terror Seizes the Persians.

Rumor has it that the satrap of the Persians was engaged in playing chess

when the first standard-bearer raised the Gallic arms.

At once the report comes that the Franks are going out to battle.

The prince, unmoved, continued the game as before;

but when they shouted that the standards of the great count Robert

were also rising—oh, what arrogance!—he rose.

When the third standards moved forward, there was an enormous uproar.

At last, after calling prisoners from our own people—

for he held certain captives of our nation—

he asked whose standards they were and what they signified,

and immediately heard what they represented and whose they were.

“This one is Robert’s, this one Godefrid’s, and that one Hugh’s.”

“This is nobility, but greater power is in the city.

You will either fight now, or deny that you know how to fight.”

As Tancredus spoke, Boamundus also appeared,

and with the standard-bearers of Raimund the strength of the army.

When Corboran saw the Christians girded for battle and now about to charge,

he was afraid. He suddenly summoned the interpreter

and offered them again the terms that the Christians had previously

offered him, but which he had just rejected.

Again they were offered to them, and again they were spurned.

Then there was no delay: the Assyrians, Persians, Parthians, Libyans, and Elamites,

[Col. 0548A] Phoenicians, Arabs, Indians, Tyrians, and Medes

quickly fitted bows and quivers to themselves,

together with the many peoples whom, because of the tediousness involved,

we are forbidden to list by each of their own names.

LXXXVII.

The greatest fury of the Turks, nearly a hundred thousand strong,

had passed between the mountain and the Christian troops,

intending, of course, to hurl their missiles from behind, just as

a hunter tries to enclose deer in a hunting net.

Boamundus, opposing himself to them as a bronze wall,

turns his back toward his companions and his face toward the enemy.

Thus the battle is two-fronted for God, comparable to a two-faced figure:

or to a dragon whose painted image doubles its head;

on both sides each pours out blood for Christ’s blood,

and in turn expiates blood shed by the enemy with slaughter.

Courage, heroic steadfastness!

Athletes of Christ, glory of the whole world,

use your right hands: you are few, the enemy a hundredfold.

Use your swords: this plain needs them,

this field, this harvest, will feed you in the years to come.

On the other front of the battle, Boamundus alone,

without human aid, hoping in the power of heaven,

attacks the peoples who trust in their numbers, himself trusting in Christ as protector. The cross, leading the way, a noble sign,

shines forth as the sign of signs: terror to the enemy,

hope, wall, glory, and splendor to Christ’s soldiers.

Among outstanding soldiers he was by no means the least fierce.

Brave and high-spirited Boamundus was a fosterling and grandson of Mars.

[Col. 0548C] The renowned Robert, son of Girard, famous throughout the world,

bore that aforesaid device.

With right hand and tongue—indeed, with mind and body—

he was wholly devoted to Christ’s service,

most devoted, as a brother to a brother, to Boamundus,

and to every reciprocal duty toward him.

He passes through the Turkish ranks again and again,

encouraging his companions and assailing the charging enemy.

Robert presses the Turks; Boamundus supports Robert.

The former never ceases to press them, nor the latter to assist him.

LXXXVIII.—The Terrified Turks Are Put to Flight.

At the sight of the cross the Persian people lose their sight;

they become trembling, groaning—though they had come fierce and terrible.

There is no arrow, no one to draw the bow.

“Hurrah! Ha! Ha! He!” becomes “Ah! Ah!” and “Alas! Alas!”

Thus, confessing themselves beasts before the fierce leonine race of Franks, they prefer flight to death and life to glory.

Unable to return to the mountain, they flee beside the river.

The victors press on and never cease to strike them down,

until the allied troops received both lines:

the defeated, the victorious; the holy conquerors conquering those who were to be conquered.

Now the battle is no longer two-fronted, now it is more secure than before;

hope has increased for some, fear has been added to the weapons of others.

The still numerous host, whose number exceeds the sands, counsels some to fight and others to leave the battle.

And because few Latins ride the backs of spirited horses,

this hampers the Christians and gives comfort to the Turks.

Yet cunning comes to their aid; but no stratagem,

no deceit, can avail against Christ, without whom nothing is anything and nothing is accomplished.

LXXXIX.—The Battle Hangs in the Balance.

Eurus had swiftly come to the war from the Nabataean kingdoms

and had joined the Persians, his neighbors.

He himself guided the horses, the bows, and the quivers;

and, no less against his adversaries, with his whirlwind turned toward them,

he hurled back their missiles with the very weapons that had launched them.

The Frankish sword could scarcely stand against Eurus’s arrows.

The languid Zephyrus lay sluggish in the Aeolian cave,

the betrayer of the Franks in battle, though from Gades onward,

through the Pyrenean snows, through trackless regions and the Alps,

through straits, shoals, Scylla, and Charybdis,

he had brought them faithfully as a companion everywhere;

but now, treacherous, he withdraws his aid while France fights Eurus.

Observing this, the Persian people attempt by means other than arms

what they cannot achieve with weapons: with flames, smoke, and dreadful darkness

they try to envelop the Christians’ eyes as though in night.

They set fires beneath reeds, beneath marsh grass,

beneath wickerwork, and stir up Eurus as much as they can.

He blows his own mists, his smoke from the thorn bushes,

from the remaining shrubs, whether brambles or thickets,

against the opposing ranks with furious intent.

Thus daylight, shining, is turned into pitch-black shadows;

it weakens the strong and strengthens the feeble crowd.

In darkness swords fight; in light, arrows.

As though moles were entering combat against lynxes,

so the course of the battle wavers amid Eurus’s rages.

[Col. 0549C] Oh, how often, while Zephyrus delays at that moment,

it was shouted: “Come to our aid, Zephyrus; rise, you sluggish ones!

Eurus rages for the Turks—rise for us!”

XC.—The Christians Prevail.

While this was being shouted, God took pity on the afflicted

and opened his treasuries, bringing forth from them

a favorable Corus, who by blowing would drive Eurus back

and force the defeated wind to fly back into its own caves,

free from the western prison, Corus, who had disturbed the Turks’ eyes

with their own smoke.

Nor was there delay: he obeyed the commands, shaking everything,

tearing away everything that stood in the way of his flight.

Already he came into the battle; as he came, he struck not only

weapons and men, but also terrified the horses and tore away the tents.

[Col. 0549D] The mountain, valley, plain, and tree all bristled and trembled.

You flee, Eurus, and are yourself wrapped in your own smoke;

upon your own Persians your deception, by a just law, rebounds.

Then the Turk, his eyes closed, fights, while the Frank’s are open,

and suddenly, with the situation reversed, the one who had nearly been defeated prevails;

the one who had been defeating is overcome.

One flees, the other pursues; Baal falls and overwhelms Alpha.

The Persian horse is swift, fat, and fierce;

the Frankish horse, by contrast, is slow, lean, anxious, and sick.

The Persian flees easily; the Frank cannot vigorously press on in pursuit.

The former seems innumerable; the latter scarcely six hundred.

After the dangers had been turned into flight, the Persians, watchful,

whoever was swift or was carried by a swift horse as though by fire,

fled, bursting forth, stumbling off the road and bewildered.

But the man whose horse was sluggish and whose feet were not swift—

he either died by the sword or was dragged along to be taken into servitude.

Here, they say, a young man found a foot amid the slaughter,

with which he could repel the sun or rain in place of a roof.

Then the setting sun carried away what the rising sun had sent.

So too the remaining riches—dishes, cups, tables,

jars, tripods, litters, basins, cauldrons,

pots, flasks, tents, cloaks, garments—

everything of pure gold or work more precious than gold,

the victor possesses.

The people, previously poor, now become wealthy.

Now they sit and devour Turkish cakes with greedy mouths.

Now many feast on the game obtained from the Persian satraps.

Now they contend among themselves for the purple taken from the captives.

XCI.—Tancred Pursues the Defeated and Makes a Remarkable Slaughter of Them.

[Col. 0550B]

But Tancred’s proven courage, hungry and thirsty for praise,

greedy for nothing except praise,

poor in wealth, fasting from food, disdainful of rest in the sweat of labor,

takes the road between the two arms of the divided Farfar,

where there is nowhere more suitable for him.

He pursues many, accompanied by only a few armed men.

Thus, amid Parthians, Persians, and Indians,

amid all the diverse forces of the worshipers of Muhammad,

like a leopard among sheep, the son of Guiscard creates slaughter.

He drives the horses with his heels; he drives them on with reins pulling backward;

he drives them with terrifying shouts and goads,

and by every possible art presses upon the shoulders of the fleeing line.

He thrusts his spurs into their necks and mutilates whatever part

[Col. 0550C] bears the burden, whether before the manes or behind with useless tails.

To escape death, they do not delay in loosening their saddles;

even after casting away swords and quivers, they are still driven onward.

Tancred sprinkles the green earth with blood.

Tancred packs the ditches with heaps of the dying.

Many perish from wounds, and many perish without wounds,

while the crowd, fearing wounds, avoids wounds.

Some plunge down of their own accord, abandoning bridle and saddle,

and enter the thickets, hoping to hide beneath the rain.

The hoof of a swift-footed horse tears out the entrails of some;

as another rushes forward, death delays him with an outstretched foot.

One was not held back by his foot: for one, the heart burst; for another, the liver.

Many thought they could be saved by the river,

but, entering its helpful channels, they perished in the water.

[Col. 0550D] Horse and rider alive enter the open burial mounds;

as they reach the banks, the river openly swallows one and another.

Thus the quiver-bearing, cuirassed, and ornamented men,

as they approach the Styx in this way, make the others tremble.

Pluto himself fears being revisited, and his wife is terrified and flees.

But those to whom fortune offered firm fords

partly emerge from the waters and partly are submerged in them.

Nor do those who seek to escape in this way escape.

Tancred follows, fording the river as the Lyncus is forded.

[Note: [Col. 0549D] The Lyncus is a river in Macedonia that flows into the Erigon; Ovid mentions it in Book XV of the *Metamorphoses*, in this verse:

“This Lyncestian river flows with a different effect.” [Col. 0550D]]

While everything is still fresh and fierce, and every newly won and vigorous resource

brings the approaching Hareng into his presence,

the Turk, secure by nature and by art,

did not fear arrows amid so great a disaster.

Surrounded on every side by towers and supported by a strong garrison,

he now opens the gates that had long been closed.

The suitable young men come out to meet their arriving lord.

He calls out: “Bring replacements! Bring fresh horses!”

At once he finds arms, men, and horses—all prepared.

XCII.

The grassy plain above Arthasium, beneath the walls of Emma,

is surrounded by the divided river’s course.

Previously it excluded travelers and was an inconvenient cause

of a long detour for those hurrying onward.

A twin bridge, cut from the mountain,

removed this inconvenience, admitting the traveler by an arch on the other side.

Between these bridges the Persian people, now almost safe,

now almost having found, after the long weariness of flight, rest,

[Col. 0551B] rested exhausted and thought they had escaped the war.

Then Tancred arrived, and with him horse, arms, and men.

A fresh battle! On seeing each other, the one who had been pursuing cries:

“Hurrah!” The fleeing Turk mutters: “Ah! Ah!”

Great was the slaughter beneath the walls of Antioch,

where a numerous and fresh executioner had joined battle.

On this side and on that, mutual wounds produced tears;

on this side and on that, laughter—but not on this occasion.

One side laughed only, the other wept only:

the fleeing Turk wept; the warlike Norman laughed.

The Norman strikes down; the Turk falls.

The sudden attack of the spears and the narrowness of the twin bridge

hold back escape; the terror of joining battle prevents it,

as do the difficulty of flight, their weakened strength,

[Col. 0551C] and the great quantity of blood poured from many wounds.

Thus the Persians carry almost as many wounds as they have limbs.

Therefore, woe to the wretched, whatever they attempt.

For neither battle consoles flight, nor flight battle.

Whichever the Turk attempts, he is glad that neither succeeds.

Thus the flock perishes when a lion, to which a leopard clings, attacks it.

XCIII.—The Fortress of Arthasium Is Surrendered.

From so great a multitude, flight and the arm save only a few.

Some having been struck down and others put to flight by slaughter,

a fortress still remains for the Turks, filled with soldiers and prepared for war.

It remains, I say, but is as impregnable as though it were

not the work of men but the construction of gods.

Pergamum of Neptune and Phoebus’s Ilium, both together,

compared with this, must yield in every other respect.

Yet that garrison, terrified by the slaughter of its allies,

trusting in nothing of its own resources and equally poor and helpless,

considers delay on both sides.

When the scales of delay had been removed,

the decision to depart outweighed all else and was approved.

They say they have nothing to do with the Franks and nothing with heavenly arms,

after the Turks had been defeated by the power of the heavenly ones.

The same enclosure that held the Turks also held certain men of Raimund’s people—

whether compelled by dreadful hunger or ensnared by false desire—

who, setting Christ aside, observed the law of Muhammad and had become Turks.

They consulted among themselves which of the Christians was greater,

which more trustworthy in faith, to whom they should return the fortress,

to whom they should entrust themselves and their own safety.

They advised trusting Raimund.

“He is more trustworthy in faith, a count, and greater in strength,” they said.

[Col. 0552A] “There is no reason to fear if you entrust yourselves to him.”

Why linger over words? The matter is concluded in a few:

trust is given, the offer is accepted, it is reported, they depart, and the agreement is entered into.

XCIV.—The Words of the Dying Bishop of Le Puy to the Army.

Meanwhile the bishop of Le Puy dies, and is buried within

the basilica of blessed Peter.

But as he dies, he summons the leaders to him,

and, after summoning them, delivers words,

a memorial of himself and instruction in salvation:

“While God granted me the opportunity, and while health remained in me,

neither zeal nor diligence on my part was lacking in your service.

I cared for you anxiously, as a mother cares for her child;

I taught, admonished, and spurred you on.

I tore away deadly things and scattered seeds of life.

With sleepless care I discharged the obligations entrusted to me.

[Col. 0552B] Now I am being cut down; now the end of life is near.

Thus Pope Urban entrusted me to you as a minister of teaching;

thus I entrust this man to you.”

He entrusted Arnulf to no one inferior to himself in this struggle:

“This is my beloved son,” he said; “in him I am well pleased.

Turn your ears to him.

But you, my son, remember your father’s admonition.

Scatter generously the seeds of divine instruction.

Return freely what was freely given to you.

Call sinners back; crown those who do well with praise.

Press on with your purpose; show yourself a minister of Christ.

Prove it by your diligence; carry out the duties entrusted to you.

Let no one, burdened with gifts, bend you toward injustice.

And, to speak briefly in brief: live chastely.

[Col. 0552C] Be temperate, prudent, humble, devout, and tranquil.”

XCV.—His Epitaph.

Thus he counsels, and, pausing briefly, passes over to him

whom his mind, his strength, and his voice had honored—Jesus.

A man of great merit, a man worthy of every honor,

a man worthy of this title, if not of a better one.

Here lies this most renowned imitator of Moses

in teaching, zeal, character, and office.

Moses was leader of the people, and this man was also leader of the people.

Both were leaders of Christ, both nourished from heaven,

both devoted to righteousness, both devoted to teaching.

Both were the mediating voice of God and of the people.

The reason for Moses’ journey is said to have been the land of Canaan.

For this man too, the land of Canaan was the reason for his journey.

Moses was granted the sight of it, not its use;

to this man too it was almost granted to see it, not to use it.

Long fasts reconciled Moses to God;

long hunger likewise consecrated this man to God.

God himself sent Moses; Pope Urban sent this man, and he himself, the herald of God, followed him: God sent them both.

XCVI.—Tancred, with the Counts of Normandy and Provence, Besieges Marra.

After the city had been captured—when the victors were rewarded with riches,

the defeated with slaughter, when some were lifted from humiliation to the stars

and others were plunged from luxury and drunkenness beneath Tartarus—

Boamundus, having obtained the principality of Antioch, remained to defend it.

Tancred renewed the interrupted labor of the journey.

He preferred cold, heat, hunger, thirst, mountains, valleys,

fields, and towns to rest.

Before their loveliness, the Thessalian Tempe

grew ashamed, Emma lamented that its own Helicon was despised,

the meadows of Harenc, the vines of Barisan,

and the crops of Hersen likewise lamented.

Beyond these, the great number of other towns each grieved

that foreign resources were preferred to their own.

But the other Julius, Marchisides, thinking that nothing had been accomplished

while anything remained to be done, recalled that the purpose of the journey

was Jerusalem, and that they had to make pilgrimage through Antioch,

not merely to have made a pilgrimage through Antioch.

Therefore, seeking battle, he joins the Norman and Provençal counts to himself

and attacks with them the populous and fertile town of Marra.

The people of Marra had prepared themselves,

whether terrified after the capture of Antioch,

or because they had resisted the Franks vigorously during the siege,

or because the flying report brought by their fellow sufferers from Antioch had forewarned them.

Warned by one of these causes, perhaps by all of them,

[Col. 0553B] they had stripped the entire surrounding region bare,

filling their city and leaving nothing for the besieging army.

They had also blocked the suburban wells,

thinking that the newcomers could be driven back by scarcity.

But the Christians, who, after raising the cross, had denied themselves,

who for God’s sake had handed their bodies over to suffering,

nevertheless rejoiced when the city was surrounded,

as though they had been invited to a feast.

Some built siege engines; others assisted those who were building.

Some shook the towers with Balearic slings;

others carried on their shoulders the stones and tools for battering them.

You could see some agile men hurrying in hope of grain,

and others returning groaning beneath their burden.

Some restored wells to their ancient use;

others were occupied with constructing new ones.

[Col. 0553C] Some, awaiting aid from the cataracts of heaven,

prepared a prison for the heavenly water.

Seeing their prayers, he who alone weighs labor and pain,

who does not abandon those who presume upon him,

sent rain from heaven and supplied them all.

For such heavy and abundant rain followed

that those who had previously begged for rain afterward begged it to stop,

and the builders of reservoirs regretted their useless labor.

XCVII.—Horrible Famine in the Camp of the Faithful.

This excessive abundance produced famine:

the grain brought into the camp rotted,

nothing was brought in from outside,

and victory was prolonged.

Bread had failed; hunger grew stronger.

I am ashamed to report what I heard,

and what I learned from the very authors of the shame.

For I heard men say that, compelled by scarcity,

they had turned to eating human flesh;

that they had plunged adults of the gentiles into a cauldron,

impaled children on spits, and devoured them roasted.

By eating they imitated wild beasts—by roasting humans, dogs.

They threatened the same fate for their own limbs

when those of others failed,

unless either the capture of the city or the arrival of grain

had intervened to soften their hunger.

XCVIII.—Dissension between Tancred and Raimund.

While these things were happening,

dissension agitated Tancred’s and Raimund’s servants,

and soon rose from the servants to their masters.

Tancred scarcely—ah, scarcely—restrained his anger

from easing itself by slaughtering the Provençals.

But reason came to the man and forbade Christian blood to be shed.

It advised him rather to return to the arts of Guiscard,

through which he had become famous throughout the world.

Therefore, without delay, he came to Antioch,

whose guardians still knew nothing of this quarrel.

On the way he instructed his soldiers how to hold their swords concealed

and how to lower them.

Then, wearing cloaks, he and his companions approached the fortress.

They called the gatekeeper; the gates were opened.

Those who pretended peace were admitted peacefully.

Once inside, one after another, when their number was sufficient for battle,

they all together, all at once, bared their arms, minds, and swords.

They drove Raimund’s soldiers out and sent them back to Raimund himself,

not without blows.

Thus, having avenged himself upon Raimund as far as he could,

Tancred, more cunning than the more powerful man,

restored the severed head to the body by returning the Ilium of his Troy to Boamundus.

For while Boamundus, still excluded from it, gazed upon the town,

he seemed so mutilated to himself that he called himself a half-prince,

not a prince, and named Raimund his colleague in the principality of Antioch.

This trouble tormented the prince both waking and in dreams.

But when hatred and affection, colliding on either side,

restored a horn, as has been said, to the mutilated principality,

Boamundus’s throne was raised.

Now more fully awakened, he joined Tancred with a large force

as Tancred returned to Marra.

Both hostile to the Provençal count,

they splendidly fortified their own position against the enemy’s arms.

XCIX.—The Origin of the Dissension.

It is pleasing to return to the source of this hatred,

so that we may be less surprised when we divert the surging force of the stream.

While Antioch still resisted, closed against the leaders of Gaul,

[Col. 0554C] dissension arose between the servants of Boamundus and Raimund.

Men sent out by both sides to procure grain found both food and battle.

Grain was divided by iron.

The two terrified parties wounded one another,

and both groups of wounded men returned home.

When the leaders saw the blood of their servants, they were disturbed.

Whenever a similar incident occurred,

they inflamed the spirits of the wounded toward retaliation.

They ordered the fire to be concealed within the camp

and outside it to have its flames stirred up by a swift storm.

Open ears willingly received this order,

and it was difficult to call them back once they had been forbidden.

Therefore, whenever a larger crowd of one side met a smaller crowd of the other, burdened with provisions,

the men immediately put down their loads of provisions,

and their necks were loaded instead with storms of slaps.

The stronger side rejoiced in its strength and spoils.

The weaker side, grieving that it had labored for nothing,

was stripped of its possessions.

Anyone who spoke the other side’s language was beaten along with it;

sometimes an innocent man was beaten on its behalf.

The Narbonnese, Auvergnats, Gascons, and all of that kind

supported the Provençals.

The Apulians, however, were supported by the rest of Gaul,

especially the Normans.

The Britons, Suebi, Huns, Rũthenians, and those of similar speech

defended whatever they heard in the barbarism of their own language.

This occurred outside the walls.

C.—A Commentary on the Lord’s Spear.

Within the city too the sedition did not ebb but surged.

For when the besieged people were thrown into turmoil by the famine described above,

there arose from Raimund’s people a crafty inventor of lies, Peter,

who proclaimed that the people’s salvation had been revealed to him in this manner:

“I was half asleep,” he said, “when blessed Andrew the apostle appeared to me

and imposed this command upon my ears:

‘Rise, and announce to the suffering people the consolation sent down from heaven,

which will be brought by the spear that pierced the Lord’s side,

once it has been found.

It lies hidden beneath the ground within the basilica of blessed Peter.

You—at such and such a place”—and he indicated the place—

“loosen the pavement.

There, by digging, you will find the iron that has been announced.

When the terror of arms descends upon you,

hold it up against the enemy; by it you will conquer.’

When I awoke, I thought that sleep had deceived me,

and I kept silent, intending never to reveal it,

unless I were admonished a second and third time.

A second night’s rest again held me,

when the same apostle returned,

repeating precisely what he had said before,

but resembling one who was rebuking me and was angry:

‘Why,’ he said, ‘do you remain silent after despising me?

Why do you delay the salvation of so many?

The people cried to the Lord, and they were heard,

yet your negligence still makes him seem neglected.

Hurry, therefore, and correct this as quickly as possible,

so that you may live.’

Terrified by these words, when I escaped from sleep

I was at once more certain and more anxious.

Yet I still hesitated whether to reveal it secretly or publicly.

I spent the whole day in this concern,

and devoted the second part of the night to prayer and fasting,

asking God for a third visitation, if the two had truly come from him.

The cock had twice announced the dawn

when at last, during the third crowing,

sleep bound my weary limbs.

Nor was there delay:

the one who had come first and the one who had come second

immediately came for a third time,

always more terrifying, always more commanding:

‘Rise, come,’ he said, ‘you sluggish beast,

silent dog, delay of salvation, hesitation of triumph,

loss to your fellow citizens, comfort to the enemy!

There you trembled from fear where there was no fear;

where fear is present, there you do not fear.’

More threats and reproaches still remained,

when my spirit, terrified by fear,

withdrew from the threats into sleep.

Sweat and trembling alternately shook my body,

as though fire scorched one side

while the other grew stiff with ice.

By these stages I have come to teach what I learned.

You, however, fathers and brothers,

do not delay in testing the truth of the matter.

It remains for me to point out the place;

it remains for you to dig.’”

When this rumor reached Raimund’s ears,

he immediately held an assembly.

Peter was summoned to the basilica of Peter,

and, when asked for the place,

he indicated the altar just as he had previously devised,

and advised them to dig.

To give weight to his words,

he also feigned an expression on his face.

They therefore dug, but made no progress.

The excavated earth could not yield what had neither been entrusted to it

nor placed there.

But he himself secretly kept with him an iron spearhead of Arab make.

From its accidental discovery he had obtained the material for his deception.

For when he saw it rough, worn away, and ancient,

unlike anything used by us in shape and size,

he immediately guessed that faith in his new inventions would cling to it.

When he found the time ripe for deception,

he seized a mattock, leapt into the pit,

and, turning toward the corner, said:

“Here it must be dug; here lies what we are seeking;

from here it will emerge.”

Then, multiplying the blow again and again,

he struck the digging tool against the spear

that he had fraudulently lowered there himself.

The darkness assisted his tricks,

the numerous crowd assisted the darkness,

and the narrowness of the place assisted the crowd.

CI.

But when the iron struck against iron and rang,

the same inventor of deceit raised the spear

and filled the ears of the simple with these words:

“Look, look! This is what heaven promised,

what the earth preserved,

what the apostle revealed,

what the prayer of the contrite people obtained.”

Hardly had these words brought the object into the open

when they accompanied the spear with hymns and songs,

honored it with gifts,

and wrapped it in gold and cloaks.

Raimund and those who supported him arranged these things.

But the simple-minded people of the other factions also devoted themselves to offerings,

before the victory eagerly,

but after it much more eagerly,

as though the glory of the trophy brought into battle

were to be credited, at the Provençals’ insistence, to the spear.

Thus Raimund’s treasury expanded,

his spirit was exalted,

and his army grew insolent.

Some of the leaders favored him,

men whom he had attracted to himself

sometimes by flattery and sometimes by services.

CII.—Boamundus Suspects Deceit in the Spear.

[Col. 0556B]

But Boamundus, being no fool,

examined the whole sequence of events:

who that dreamer was,

by what evasions he had entangled the people,

what place he had indicated to the diggers,

how he himself had leapt in,

dug, and found the object.

At once he detected the deceit.

He showed by clever arguments that the discovery was invalid

and that the discoverer was a fraud.

“Fine indeed,” he said,

“that blessed Andrew should have appeared to a man

whom I hear frequents taverns,

rushes through marketplaces,

is a friend to trifles,

and was born in the crossroads.

The holy apostle chose an honorable person

to whom he might open heaven’s secret.

As for the place—what place does not admit fabrication?

If a Christian hid it, why did he avoid the hiding place

of the nearest altar?

Or if a gentile or a Jew hid it,

why was it within the church walls?

Why beside the altar?

But if it belongs to neither of them and is attributed to chance,

in what historian is Pilate found to have come to Antioch?

We know, of course, that the spear belonged to a soldier,

and that the soldier belonged to Pilate.

But consider what follows:

I hear that when the diggers labored in vain,

this discoverer leapt in,

and that one man was permitted in darkness

to do what many were openly denied.

O rustic folly!

O credulous rusticity!

O credulity easily convicted!

Let the man be honorable;

let the nearby Crucifixion lend strength to the place.

Even this latest fraud of that man is not sufficiently exposed.

If he had walked purely and simply in the way of God,

if he had trusted in the apostle whom he had summoned to himself,

he would not himself bear witness to his discovery;

he would have earned the testimony of another.

For what greater insult could I return to him

than that the Provençals attribute to their iron

our victory, which descends from above,

from the Father of lights?

Let the ambitious count and the foolish crowd

attribute their own victory to themselves.

But we have conquered, and will conquer,

in the name of the Lord our God, Jesus Christ.”

These things were said by Boamundus,

and with him by the counts Norman and Flemish,

who discerned the leaders’ affairs more subtly,

and by Arnulf, the vice-bishop, and Tancred.

CIII.—In Which Raimund Also Takes Offense.

Therefore Raimund, wounded by Boamundus’s sharp darts of argument,

searches out revenge by a thousand devices and a thousand paths.

Thus, without pause, he says to himself:

“Either I shall die first, or I shall take revenge.”

If an open confrontation is unavailable,

let a hidden one be available.

Where the spear cannot prevail,

let the dagger prevail.

> “Who would ask whether an enemy has fraud or valor?”

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book II.)

“When,” he says, “the city’s protection is mine,

when the mountain stronghold, the royal palace,

the marketplace, the bridge, and the gate obey me,

the spear too, and the number of the people,

are subject to my control.

What remains except that, once Boamundus has been destroyed,

I should obtain the principality?

As he turned these and many more thoughts over,

above all he anticipated that sedition would be stirred among the common people,

so that it would overflow from foot to head;

that quarrels would first be rehearsed on the marketplace from both sides;

that a clamor would arise and throw the people into confusion;

that the leaders on both sides would bring aid to their own men;

and that every bow and every javelin would be aimed at Boamundus.

While Raimund, like a lion in its cave,

was plotting these ambushes,

God did not allow iniquity to remain concealed.

It was disclosed to Arnulf,

and immediately through him it was disclosed to Boamundus.

Thus the plot was foiled,

and the life of a man was saved from death—

a man whose life had already benefited those seeking Jerusalem greatly,

and would benefit them greatly still.

This, then, was the origin of their anger;

from this began the kindling of hatred.

CIV.—Marra Is Captured.

But the siege recalls me, like a crop interrupted to the reaper while he turns back to gather the fallen ears. Accordingly, they undermine Marra, which is entirely encircled by war; arrows fly over Marra, slings shake it, threats make it tremble: everywhere clamor, everywhere assault, everywhere a blow. The townsmen, for their part, return like for like: they hurl back sling-engines with similar weapons, missiles and javelins from a distance, and close at hand they let down stone blocks like ploughshares. They wound many, and many are wounded; these die so that they may live, are weakened so that they may prevail, and bleed so that they may endure. Their intention is to complete what they have begun, the work already half-finished, to seek an end to so great a labor, to attain glory by conquering, and to overcome fortune by suffering.

But while the walls are struck again and again, like an anvil by hammers or a threshing-floor by flails, they begin to gape: the tower splits, the wall comes apart, the battlements collapse. In its collapse, the ruin simultaneously opens the barriers and constructs steps. Therefore, woe, woe to the worshipers of Muhammad, but joy to the worshipers of Christ: all things prosper for these, while everything—even their own hopes—works against those others.
