Nor is there delay. Once an entrance has been opened, an entrant is not lacking. The city, however, tries to resist and opposes the entry with whatever strength it possesses. The struggle is waged with the utmost intensity: while this fighting grows stronger, while it rages on one side and the defense grows weaker on the other, the shields now resound less and less—those which shortly before had almost been shattered by the hail of stones. Then ladders are set against the wall; the climber overtops the towers and insults the captured city. But when the defenders hear the uproar and see the movement, their courage falls: the foot soldiers flee to hiding places, and, throwing down their weapons, hope to preserve their lives.

Once the city is captured, some of our men persist in slaughter, others in plundering its treasures. One part seeks food, another carries out the pillage. Those who have won the victory find it all the more pleasant to remember their heavier labors. Thus I once saw a band of hunters—and the hunter himself—celebrating, though fasting: they had been wearied from the eleventh hour of the preceding night until the middle of the third hour of the following day. [Col. 0558A]

**CV. — The Siege of Arcas**

The worshipers of Christ, therefore, who had often become accustomed to rising from the valley of tears to the lofty mountain of joy, continued to press their successes and did not cease to persist in the favor of God’s will. They attacked the town of Arcas, with an effort no less than that expended against Marra, but with a different outcome.

On the edge of the plain rises a hill, whose descending slopes reach from the south as far as Lebanon; it looks toward the sea, almost twenty stadia distant, toward the west. A river washes its foot. Flowing from the east toward the shore, it yields its left side to the dominion of Jerusalem and its right to Antioch; it is a well-known boundary between Tortosa and Tripoli. A stronghold fortified by both art and nature, it threatened a difficult approach to an enemy attempting an advance. [Col. 0558B]

The worshipers of Christ, however, having already learned through many struggles that everything yields to valor, surrounded Arcas. Some crossed the river to block the exits from the gates; others remained on this side, where they could more easily be supplied with provisions from the resources of the towns of Crac and Raphania and of the rest of the nearer surrounding region.

Tancred stood out among the first to cross, rejoicing exceedingly that he had been deemed worthy to enter the shore of the kingdom he desired. A stone bridge of ancient construction, however, carried the army onward, so that they could easily pass from one side to the other. Thus, when the barriers had been closed by arms, the princes, as was customary, constructed engines of war against the walls: each built one—one, the Norman count; another, Raymond; a third, Tancred. Bohemond had returned to Antioch after the overthrow of Marra, where Duke Godfrey and the Count of Flanders were still wintering. A war had recalled Hugh the Great to Cilicia; he is said to have carried an injured thigh to Tarsus for treatment—or rather for burial. The labor of the siege therefore rested upon the three princes named above. They attacked without ceasing, and were themselves fiercely attacked in return.

While the struggle continued in this way, something occurred which it would be negligent to pass over and useful and honorable to remember.

**CVI. — The Remarkable Vision of Anselm, Foretelling His Near Death**

There was in our army a noble hero, to whom a great name had been conferred by his integrity on one side, his lineage on another, his honor as a third distinction, and, as a fourth, his hereditary possession of Mount Ribot, renowned for its excellent military stock. The name of this man, Anselm, was celebrated at the court of the king of France, indeed throughout the courts of the three Gauls.

At midday, as is customary, when sleep had lowered his weary eyes, he saw a dream. On awakening, he reported it to Arnulf, my wise adviser and informant:

“I seemed in my dream to be standing upon a heap of mud, from which I was looking up at a lofty palace. Everything about it surpassed ordinary use to the greatest degree: its breadth, height, material, form, solidity, and adornment. Its foot was formed of marble, ivory, and silver; the rest of its body was entirely gold and precious stones.

“Countless persons walked through the lofty porticoes, each of whom was worthy of the dignity of so great a building. Princes stood out, so beautiful, so tall, so adorned, and so graceful in every respect. As I gazed at them more intently and marveled, I recognized in some of them remnants of familiar forms, by which I understood that these had been companions of our present military expedition.

“Then, as my heart and mind eagerly longed for them, and as I panted to climb up if any entrance should be open, one of our men appeared—the one whom we then lost in such a manner. He recalled the man’s name, manner, place, and day of death. ‘Do you recognize this crowd of the blessed, Anselm?’ he said to me.

“‘Hardly,’ I replied, ‘for no other signs remained by which they could be recognized—just as we recognize some fifty-year-old man who has returned, although he left us as a seven-year-old boy.’

“Then he said: ‘These are the pilgrims to Jerusalem who undertook from the beginning the way of God in which you too are still laboring, departed from human affairs, and deserved to possess everlasting crowns. You too will soon climb up to us, lest you perhaps envy us; for you have fought the good fight and completed your course.’

“At this the sleep and the vision left me, astonished. May your wisdom, Lord, provide for me.”

Then Arnulf, driving fear from the man’s breast with consoling words, nevertheless warned him that he must confess his sins, receive penance, and afterward receive the Eucharist. This was done immediately, and he additionally returned the due payments to his servants and fellow soldiers.

Now, fearless, he sat upon his horse and rode around the walls, accompanied by a band of soldiers, as noblemen customarily do. Suddenly an unexpected stone slipped down from the towers and shattered Anselm’s skull and brain. The army immediately caught him as he fell. [Col. 0559C] They carried his body back in tears to the place from which they had just gone out rejoicing; his spirit ascended to the promised blessedness.

**CVII. — The People of Arcas Resist Fiercely**

After the illustrious man had been buried as befitted him, and since our army was making no progress in the siege, they gave Arnulf the following order: he was to return to Antioch, so that he might rouse Godfrey and Robert of Flanders from their delay and announce that the Damascene war was at hand.

Arnulf, ever most ready to serve the common good, willingly and of his own accord boarded a vessel. He sailed past the naval stations of the enemy at Tortosa, Heraclea, Valonia, and Gibel. At last he reached Laodicea, and from there, amid many dangers and accompanied by only a few men, hurried on to Antioch. There he found the princes and, seizing the opportunity, urged them to awaken. He explained that war threatened and that, unless they hastened, their absence would determine its outcome.

When the report of the war became known, the French military leadership was spurred on, and it in turn spurred on the army. With one accord they made their weapons resound, and spent little time preparing and setting out. Thus, when rumor spread among the neighboring peoples that the army had assembled, the war ceased: the enemy hastened to defend himself rather than to attack others.

Our men, however, pressed their purpose with unceasing but ineffective force. They fired arrows, javelins, stones, and whatever else could be hurled against the towers; they sent them without hesitation, but nature fought on behalf of the place, and they accomplished nothing.

Many had learned and experienced that sometimes one conquers by remaining still, when labor has been expended in vain. Therefore they gradually inclined toward this counsel: to torment the townsmen with hunger by delaying. The abundance outside, threatening that it would produce want within, served as the teacher of this plan.

**CVIII. — By the Test of Fire, the Fraud Concerning the Lance Is Exposed**

While the weapons were therefore idle, and leisure excluded the cares of Mars, a question arose concerning the discovery of the spear mentioned above, and was to be put to the test. For the schism was disturbing the people: some praised the deed, others condemned it, and neither side regarded it as fully established.

Accordingly, the leading nobles decided that the man who had been the beginning of the error should himself end the dispute, making the doubtful matter credible by a fiery proof. Peter was therefore summoned to the council. Nine paces of flaming thorns were assigned on either side of the middle passage, so that by this trial the discovery might either be proved true if he emerged unharmed, or false if he were burned.

Three days were granted for fasting, with a lawful interval for prayer and watching. Thus they departed, but met again on the following day. The thorns blazed in two ordered rows. Peter, covered by a tunic and breeches but otherwise naked, walked through the middle. At the exit he fell, burned; on the following day he died.

When the people saw what had happened, they confessed that they had been led astray by verbal cleverness. They repented of their error and declared that Peter had been a disciple of Simon Magus.

**CIX.**

Raymond and his fellow Provençals, however, obstinately defended the accused. They proclaimed him holy and threatened Arnulf, who had revealed the fraud and was its foremost investigator. Finally, they sent an armed band against him to overpower him unawares in his home—unless, having been warned beforehand, he had hastened to the Norman count whom he served.

The count was dining with the Count of Flanders; the two were seated together at table. When Arnulf’s reason for his hurried arrival was heard, he was summoned to sit among them. The counts withdrew to either side, and weapons were sent to meet the armed men.

The attackers, however, hearing the uproar of the Normans, were frightened. They concealed their purpose, pretending that they were seeking something else and heading elsewhere. By this device they protected themselves; otherwise they would have regretted taking up arms not merely fruitlessly but disastrously, if those whom flight had saved had been captured.

**CX. — It Is Proposed to Make a Golden Image of the Savior**

After Peter, the inventor of the fraud, had paid the punishment he deserved, another assembly was held so that, once the joy of the rejected discovery had passed, a new consolation might take its place.

It was proposed that an image of the Savior be fashioned from the purest gold, following the construction of the tabernacle of the people of Israel. The expenses incurred in each case were recalled; the devotion of that age was remembered, and the reward that had never failed—frequent victories over the enemy—was not omitted. They were urged both to give thanks to God for dangers already removed and to pray for those still to be removed.

By this exhortation Arnulf, himself the preacher, inclined his hearers wherever he wished. The bishop of Marthran, a man somewhat more learned than the uneducated and almost a literate man without letters, stood nearby so that, when the speech was finished, he might extend his right hand over the people as the emblem of blessing. Authority over the work rested with these two; all the others devoted themselves to the offerings.

Thus, in a short time, a great work was completed. Had diligent urgency not hastened it, an unformed mass would have been carried to Jerusalem. For the labor of the third month had already extended into the fourth, and the princes regretted the delays; they were also ashamed to have kept watch so long beside a little town, with their journey interrupted.

**CXI. — The Army Proceeds to Jerusalem**

Therefore, abandoning their fruitless work before the gates of Tripoli, Gibleth, Beirut, Sidon, Tyre, Acre, Caiphas, and Caesarea, they passed on successfully. From all these places they boldly demanded large quantities of money and provisions; these were supplied without hesitation and distributed generously. For all these towns, lying along the shore that runs from north to south, fortified it with high towers in the order already described and stood in the way of the pilgrims. [Col. 0561B]

But when they left the shore behind and came to Ramla, Tancred, having kept vigil through the night, moved the camp and, before dawn, went ahead of his companions. He reached Jerusalem and surrounded the walls.

[Note: The material enclosed in parentheses had been added in the margin, and consequently the sentence is not particularly well connected.]

(Nevertheless, on arriving, he freed Bethlehem from the enemy. The besieged town had cried out to him through an envoy the day before.)

From a distance, at the first sight of Jerusalem, he greeted the city, fixing his knees to the earth, his eyes upon the city and his heart upon heaven. The image of that salvation is plainly present in the following poem:

Hail, Jerusalem, glory of the world,

In which our salvation, Christ’s passion,

Mocked by Jewish insults,

benign, with heaven and the sun alone as witnesses,

After the enemy of the human race had been slain,

Drew the guiltless forth from the underworld;

In you, having suffered the cross and been enclosed in the tomb,

The Light from Light, the bright divine offspring of God,

Penetrating hell, brought back from it

Those whom deceived Adam had plunged beneath the Styx.

But soon the third day taught

That she had risen again, restored to life.

After this he ascended to the heavenly dwellings,

For a radiant cloud received him,

And while the people of Galilee looked upward,

They heard: “Thus he will come when he seeks the stars.”

You know these things, sacred mountain spoken of by the Olives.

Hail also, royal Zion,

In which, when the disciples cried, “Kyrie eleison,”

With mighty sound,

As though a whirlwind from heaven had been sent down,

You suddenly filled them, holy Spirit,

Coming in tongues of terror and fire.

Hail, star of the sea, gate of heaven,

Psalm-born child, daughter of your own offspring,

Ever remaining a virgin after, in, and before

Childbirth, ignorant of even the smallest stain.

O rivers, banks, fountain, grove, city, cottage, mountain, valley,

hail all around!

**CXII. — Tancred Alone Observes the City from the Mount of Olives**

When he had fixed his standards near the Tower of David and issued the order for measuring out the camp, he himself climbed the mountain alone and at a distance, without companion or armor-bearer. From there, he had learned, Christ, the God-born one, had ascended to the Father.

Behold the audacity; behold a new kind of siege. Tancred’s soldier besieges the west, Tancred the east: one part is held by a few, another by one man; one part by an army without its commander, another by a commander without an army. Neither relied on the help of the other—or rather, he relied on the help of no one. He was especially isolated because the nearer he was to the rising sun, the farther he was from the support of the French: his own men were laying out their camp far away in the west, and the following army was still farther away in the west beyond them.

Thus Tancred himself was both horseman and foot soldier, himself standard-bearer. From the Mount of Olives he fixed his gaze upon the city, separated from him only by the valley of Jehoshaphat. He watched the people rushing about, the towers armed, the army roaring; men turning to weapons, daughters-in-law to tears, priests to prayers; the streets thundered with wailing, uproar, trumpeting, and neighing.

He marveled at the airy roundness of the Lord’s temples, the unusual length of Solomon’s temple, and the circuit of the spacious portico, as though there were another city within the city. More often he directed his eyes toward Calvary and the temple of the tomb—indeed a more distant sight, but open to view because of its height, while he himself stood higher in place.

At these sights he sighed and grew still. He would gladly have exchanged an age for a single day if ever he might be permitted to kiss the traces of Calvary whose heights he was observing.

**CXIII. — An Anchorite Meets Him**

Chance had provided him with a suitable and learned guide for discerning these places: Turricola, an anchorite who had been consulted. He instructed him where the praetorium of Caiaphas was, where Judas was hanged, which gates were the Golden and the Beautiful, from where James had been thrown headlong, where Stephen had been cast out to the stones, and precisely which places were this or that of the kind.

The anchorite also asked him in return what his sect, homeland, lineage, and name were. He answered that he was Tancred, a Christian of Norman stock, a Wiscardid.

When the man heard that he was descended from Wiscard, he marveled, looked more intently at him, and said:

“Then you are the blood of that commander whose thunderbolt made Greece tremble so often; whose warfare drove Alexius to flight; whose siege opened Dyrrachium; under whose command all Bulgaria as far as Bardal obeyed. You do not speak to one ignorant of these things: for so great a ravager of my homeland did not escape me.

“That former enemy of mine has now, through your arrival, at last wiped away the injuries inflicted upon me. He still lives in you; that man feared by nations still lives in you—the vigor of your uncle’s audacity. You bring me new signs of his former glory.

“At first I marveled that an unknown foreign enemy, rejecting a companion, should ride about alone, relying only upon his arms and horse. I expected him either to follow or precede allied troops. My ignorance was the cause of my astonishment, and with it you have driven that astonishment away from me.

“Now you have been created for me at once: known instead of unknown, vigorous instead of reckless, and a new brother instead of an old enemy. Henceforth I shall not be amazed if you do astonishing things; indeed, I shall be amazed if you do not. It is not fitting that one born of that family should tread the common path of men.

“Nevertheless, beware, beware, my son: behold the enemy.”

**CXIV. — He Alone Routs the Soldiers Rushing from the City**

Behold, a gate pours out soldiers—the gate which at that time sent five men down into the valley of Jehoshaphat to climb up against him. They approached with all the greater confidence because a commander with five men has the advantage over a companion with one, the number five over unity.

Each hurried ahead of the others to seize the spoils. But Tancred, having said farewell and ended the conversation, turned his face, courage, horse, and ash spear toward the attack. The first man he found to have rushed up the mountain he forced to surrender his breath beneath the Styx, while his body fell into the valley.

The second met the same fate. But the horse, condemned to destruction, saved its rider: I mean that fortunate horseman whose forehead found the ground, while his chest was not found by the waiting spear. An unexpected fall cut short the fall that had been expected, though [the text is materially uncertain here; the surviving reading is incomplete] it makes the man more likely to fall than to be thrown down, if [the following text is also lacunose] becomes hateful.

Although the outcome benefited both—saving one from labor and the other from death—the benefit must nevertheless be condemned when the damaging will of both is thwarted.

A third was advancing rapidly. I would call him fortunate too, if, while lying there, he himself mourned the man lying beneath him as equally unfortunate. But, having obtained what he desired, he made himself powerless: while he postponed his fall until the encounter, in the encounter he fell more harshly and miserably.

Two remained unharmed, though the Fates, breaking their threads, held them back. Their threads had begun to break as they went out, but were soon restored for those who fled. Tancred’s roar, more than leonine, sent the stunned men fleeing rapidly back to the gate. So once young animals return to the fold when the barriers keep away the wild beast whom harsher hunger had driven against the guardians themselves.

The victor, driven back from the walls, was not moved by the spoils offered to him: by the free movement of the horses, their ornamented trappings, and the rich weapons scattered here and there in golden brilliance. He returned to his men to console them by his return, for, already desolate, they had been doubly oppressed by the delay caused by his absence.

Meanwhile, numerous forces arrived willingly as reinforcements, with ardent youth. Even the tender and the more hardened age groups were present, as was the gentler sex. Thus, in the clash, the equal—or rather united—devotion of those who fought together made the weak equal to the strong.

**CXV. — Description of the City**

It is time to take some pleasure in explaining the situation of the holy city, so that those whose eyes cannot be nourished by its nearness may at least have their minds helped by what is transmitted to the hand and poured through the ear.

The circuit of this holy city is quadrangular in shape and broad in extent. Its eastern face [lacuna] is directed northward; the other, and the second [lacuna], are winding. For the intervening bends in the middle run southward toward Galilee in the west, [lacuna]. The other face [lacuna] reaches the Tower of David; its sides [lacuna] form a straight line. But from the point where, toward the east, the valley of Jehoshaphat separates the Mount of Olives, [lacuna], the site is low, though it surpasses in dignity by reason of the things it contains.

There are Gethsemane, the brook Kidron, the palace of God’s palace, the tomb of the Queen of Heaven, and the stoning of the protomartyr Stephen. There also, with bloody sweat, the prayer of the Lord is displayed. [Col. 0564A]

To proceed in order, there are two pyramids: the upper, the round one of King Jehoshaphat, and the lower, square, said to be that of blessed James. Below them lie Siloam and Jacob’s well. All around, on both sides of the valley, are very many hermits’ retreats.

Likewise, on the south, a valley separates Mount Zion from Haceldama. Beginning beside the well mentioned above, emerging from the valley of Jehoshaphat and extending its circuit as far as beneath the Tower of David, a hill presents a continuous flank to this front. It descends from the city’s corner toward the west; on the right side it is somewhat steeper, while on the left it is nearly level with the neighboring ground. This neighboring ground joins the fourth side as far as Jehoshaphat and is suitable for establishing a camp.

**CXVI. — The Disposition of the Army**

The Norman and Flemish counts therefore besiege the city on this side, opposite the gate that is still called Saint Stephen’s. Tancred is on their right, if one measures the position of the land according to the rising of the sun; in that respect he is lower. If, however, one considers the depression and elevation of the ground, he is somewhat higher.

His assigned task is to storm the aforementioned corner, where the tower that was captured is still called Tancred’s Tower. The valley obscures the duke’s camp; its aforementioned front reached the elevated territory of Tancred.

Mount Zion rejoices in Count Raymond as its surveyor. It is separated from Jerusalem only by the barrier of a low wall. Now it is a suburb; in ancient times it was part of the city, indeed a city, with the present Jerusalem as its suburb.

Three gates therefore received a threefold siege: two directly opposite them, and the third—the western gate—obliquely. The valley beneath leaves the latter free from attack, while the nearby plain makes the former suitable for assaults.

The valley of Jehoshaphat, however, remained free both because of the configuration of the place and because of the condition of its inhabitants. For that part of the city, knowing no fear, is defended by the recessed valley, an embankment, and a steep, impregnable wall.

**CXVII. — Bohemond and the Other Leaders Are Absent**

The newly arrived army, worn down partly by wars and partly by illnesses, diminished especially by the absence of the French counts Stephen and Hugh and by the absence of Bohemond, its prince, was not sufficient even to attack the lower wall, much less to attempt to encircle the naturally fortified towers at east and west.

Yet, armed on what might be called the middle length of both sides, the Christian people awakened all the more fiercely: a smaller number had attacked a larger enemy; it was certain that the enemy’s multitude would increase while their own force would diminish; and the month of June was scorching the soldiers with ever drier thirst.

It drove those within toward food, shade, rest, leisure, and sleep, and wore down those outside with hunger, sun, labor, war, and watchfulness.

**CXVIII. — The Engines Are Prepared**

Eager for rest, they therefore applied themselves to the labor. They anxiously sought ladders and designated the dawn of the coming Friday for scaling the walls. For the monk who lived by the tower, whom I mentioned earlier, had foretold this to me; Tancred was his informant, and he announced to our people that the assault would take place on that day.

After the surrounding area had been searched in every direction, there was no grove, palace, or tower that could supply wood for making ladders. Egypt had driven from Jerusalem its old expeller, Damascus, by means of a new carrier; therefore that recent year of the Egyptian expedition had left nothing dry or green unattempted. Nevertheless, hidden recesses concealed some beams, which Tancred’s diligent concern could not fail to discover.

They were therefore dragged out and brought in, and filled only one ladder. At that moment this was judged sufficient to remove every shortage, for the day appointed for taking up arms was at hand. Difficulties pressed heavily on both sides: on this side, because the search for material for ladders had allowed only a narrow interval, a brief two days; on the other, because if they did not attack the walls on that appointed day—or did not attack them at all—the monk’s prophecy would be annulled.

For these reasons the ladder had no companion, and without a companion they celebrated the one. It was set against the wall that joins Tancred’s left-hand towers, the second to the third. Now it stood lofty, as though boasting:

“Since, although I waited for companions, I have none, henceforth I shall not wait to have them.”

**CXIX. — The Wall Is Scaled**

The neighboring ground, the discovery, and the workmanship gave Tancred, as the one nearest their discoverer, the means of climbing the walls. Yet if fortune had turned against someone else, an equally bold spirit might have claimed for himself so great a glory.

Knowing nothing of delay, he was already leaning upon the first steps; already, with drawn sword, his right hand flashed like lightning. But the majesty of his lineage, the dignity of his name, the favor earned by his achievements, and the hope of earning more stood against his undertaking: on one side the common people protested, on the other the nobles resisted. They had already disarmed the right hand of the man whose left was clinging to the wall, seizing it as he climbed.

A young man took the place of the man recalled by duty, himself worthy of rejoicing if fortune helped him, and worthier of mourning if it opposed him. Fortunate through every step from the bottom to the top, he was unfortunate at the completion of the work. He had already grasped the summit of the walls with his left hand when an enemy sword descended upon him. Thus the man who had just climbed, two-handed and flashing like lightning, could scarcely descend deprived of his sword and almost of that hand.

He was therefore carried back to the camp for treatment, the driver of Tancred’s chariot, whom Simon had held back, though he had fallen from great enterprises. And lest favor, by leaving the soldier’s name unspoken, fail to reward his courage, the young man’s name was Raibaldus; his land was France, his surname Cremius, his noble origin Chartres, and his strength and integrity were great. Greater still was that deed, for he was brought back wounded.

No one thought it useful to take his place: they feared the swords of those descending, a thousand against the one climber. For the entire interior battle had concentrated in that corner, while the whole circuit of the rest of the city was empty, as though asleep.

When diligent effort saw that fortune favored the defenders but opposed the attackers, it carried the ladder back—not merely useless but harmful, though the singularity of the attempt may provide an excuse.

**CXX. — Timbers Suitable for the Siege Are Found, Apparently by Divine Providence**

The leaders met in council and decided to search the hiding places, traverse roads and pathless regions, and gnaw out timbers from every quarter, so that this investigation would spare no prince. What was decided was immediately carried out.

While the others labored in vain, Tancred was not deprived of what he desired. What I shall relate has the appearance of a miracle, and you, whoever carefully considers the matter, will not deny that it happened through heavenly agency.

Tancred was tormented by severe dysentery, although he did not spare himself even while riding. Hardly had he mounted his horse when that disease repeatedly forced him to dismount, go far away, and seek hiding places. Often troubled by this distress, when his companions, weary from the journey, and he himself were planning to yield to the labor and return without glory, the usual affliction increased. He began to grow worse, moved farther away, and dismounted. As he descended, he thought he had escaped the eyes of his companions, but, looking back, he discovered that he had not.

Seeking a more distant hiding place, he again saw others wandering here and there. Thus he changed his location a third time, then a fourth. At last, in a distant retreat beneath a hollowed rock, enclosed on every side by trees and thickets, he found rest.

Ah! Who is like God? He who brings water from rock, speech from an ass, and all things from nothing—he himself healed an army through the wound of a stricken soldier, strengthened it through weakness, and fashioned from a trivial injury an antidote more precious than any metal.

For while the expulsive power was at work there, with his face turned toward the hollow of the opposite rock, he saw four timbers projecting inside. Nothing more suitable for the work intended could have been desired. These, it is said, were the very timbers by whose aid the king of Egypt had conquered Jerusalem.

When he saw them, he was filled with such joy that he believed neither himself nor his eyes. He rose, approached, touched them, and examined the matter. Then he shouted:

“Ho! Ho! Companions! Come here, come running here!”

“Here, here!” he repeated. “God has given us more than we ask. We sought rough wood and have found wood already fashioned.”

His companions came immediately when called. They rejoiced where they had groaned. He hurried to console the army, which was still groaning, by sending a messenger.

When the joy was proclaimed among the people, a cry of happiness and exultation rose through the tents of the French, and they went out singing to meet him as in a litany.

**CXXI. — Robert of Flanders Is Appointed Protector of the Craftsmen**

Robert of Flanders was then chosen as protector of the craftsmen for the work, while the smiths searched for the remaining timbers, cut what they found, and brought back what they had cut.

There was a grove in the mountains, and the mountains were nearer to the place now called Neapolis, formerly Sebaste, and earlier Sychar, than to Jerusalem. The road was still unknown to our people, though now it is famous and almost the only route used by pilgrims.

The aforementioned count was sent there with his usual companions, nearly two hundred men, and was exposed to countless thousands of the enemy, who surrounded him in front and behind, on the right and on the left. He feared their troops and trumpets no more than he feared his homeland and the shepherd’s pipe. By day, through [a lacunose description of a] construction, he shot wild beasts; by night, he feasted with the craftsmen in the wilderness.

Thus that labor was both a pleasure to the lord, with profit, and a fearless refreshment to the servants who labored. When enough of the grove had been successfully cut down, the count returned, wisely securing the road beforehand with arms. He himself followed boldly with the rear guard and carefully protected the crowd in the middle. He crossed unharmed through the bows of Damascus, the reeds of Arabia, and the javelins of Ethiopia.

The count’s prosperity never deserted him: it accompanied his departure and return with hymns and ceremony, winning favor from many and earning praise from all.

**CXXII.**

Between the camp and the valley of Jehoshaphat there stood an orchard. No place was more suitable—or equally suitable—for assaults against the enemy, and none threatened the citizens with greater fear. For on that side the wall was somewhat lower, the towers were few, and the open ground, as I have said, extended farther outward.

Yet this area was empty of the enemy, a source of astonishment to the inhabitants. The foresight of the commanders, however, had reserved it for the final battle, while the wooden tower was being built, from whose summit the wings of the French would fly onto the walls.

Fir, cypress, and pine were brought there. They disguised genuine threats and imitated artificial ones: the raw material was awaiting its form, so that, once formed, it might fight toward the east.

**CXXIII. — The Dreadful Hunger of the Besiegers; the Engines Prepared and Brought to the Walls**

Meanwhile, both grain and water were scarce. Wars also raged fiercely: one threatened, another pressed close—the Egyptian in fury, the Palestinian, Arabian, and Damascene. The hills, already covered all around with armed men, bristled with the very harvest they had grown: spears and steel.

Thus scarcely any grain, or indeed none at all, now came from outside to relieve the soldiers’ hunger. They could eat whatever they found, but they were wholly forbidden to go outside the camp to seek food. The people who had earlier besieged others could now, much more truly than those they besieged, be called besieged themselves.

A single and universal lament wandered through the army: the wars of Romania had been endured in vain, the hunger of Antioch in vain, and all the remaining labors in vain. For, after traversing the whole sea, they had now become shipwrecked men caught by the sand of the shore.

You might therefore have seen a mournful yet devout consolation, pitiable even to the enemy. Wearied of life, a company willingly called for death. There were men who, in a sworn rush, fell upon the walls as though upon their wives, embracing them. It was as if this were the single thought and purpose of each one:

“I shall kiss my desired Jerusalem before I die.”

Wretched men! Into whose embraces the walls poured sometimes iron, sometimes stones, and at other times fire-hardened stakes—each suddenly kissing death.

Nor could devotion, once begun, be frightened even by this. Again and again, some repeated the same embraces in the death of others.

The labor had already extended into July, five seven-day periods having revolved from the beginning of the long struggle. The work was completed, the engines fashioned, the machines constructed, and everything required by the urgency of the present necessity was ready. Yet the posts, planks, wickerwork, and unconnected joints still needed to be joined and raised—but first transported.

The night was therefore chosen for the transport. The following day raised what had been lying on the ground and restored the scattered limbs here and there to their proper body.

The transport of the engines was immediately followed by the relocation of the camp, so that it became clear to the besieged no less than to the besiegers that this wall had been designated for attack.

The evil grew heavier for the citizens. Everyone’s mind was thrown into confusion, deprived of counsel, because the approach to the battle had been cut off. The lofty structures had expelled fear.

Moreover, anxious labor had fortified that side with a great deal of timber, specifically for attacks by sling-engines against the enemy. But these measures were useless: once the fear had been removed from this side and transferred elsewhere, as has been said, the interior engine—the consolation that remained in their extremity—was moved, so that it might strike the transported exterior engine opposite it.

**CXXIV. — The Battering Ram Pushes Against the Towers**
The two sides were therefore ready for battle: some shook the walls, others defended them. The battering ram, boring from its base, battered the towers; marble stones came crashing down upon the ram’s neck. One tower, itself made of wood, advanced against the city; yet it did so unwillingly, as though willing against its will. It swayed against what stood firm; the other tower confronted the immovable one and stood ready to meet it. But if it were permitted, let it yield! At the sight of this spectacle, the elephant described in fables would rightly come running back—the elephant said to tremble at the sight of a wall.

Meanwhile there was no end to shouting, crashing, or wounds. Stones, darts, and arrows flew from both sides; shields, helmets, wicker screens, and walls echoed under the blows. Because of the din and the missiles, eyes and ears were no more able to perform their own functions than to follow the alternating movements. Yet the wooden mass did not delay its advance; leaping forward, it made its way so that, once the barbican had been buried beneath it, the passage opened more freely.

But when it had approached so closely that the iron of one pointed weapon already rang against the opposing point, the same ram which had earlier removed the obstacles—crying out like a Greek herald, “mylanys, lord!” [The printed Greek transliteration is uncertain; perhaps “do not forget, lord.”]—now stood alone in the way of the little tower that had followed it. The obstruction of the wall prevented the tower from moving forward; the machine following behind prevented it from retreating. The nature of the passage denied it a turn either to right or left: it allowed only what it itself demanded—now to go out, now to go back, never to turn aside. Thus the Norman tower paid the penalty, its sides scorched, because the sluggishness of its hoof had degenerated from the vigor of its horn. [Col. 0568C] The inner flame had attempted the same thing earlier, but an external wave, surging forward against the fire, met the conflagration; the tower remained unharmed.

Again the Muslims, taking up lightning, rained it down upon the Christians, so that the jar which had dripped its harmful contents might drink them up—the jar that had earlier been made useful by pitch, sulphur, and firebrands, and had been burned. Thus the same object, inflamed twice and drenched twice, experienced Muhammad twice defeated and Christ twice victorious. Here too the elements recognized their own author, exchanging the turns of victory at his command. With the way opened, the machine advanced, fortunate in leaping once and again, but lamentable on the third occasion: the fresh timber gave way beneath its burden, not yet mature enough for the service demanded of it.

### CXXV.—The besieged evade the effect of the machines by stratagems.

The beam commonly called *soliva*, as though because it travels along the ground, [Col. 0569A] splits and weakens one side, since it has been placed beneath the left-hand wall as a foundation. The machine, therefore, with one foot damaged, stands motionless, incapable of advancing and unwilling to retreat, content merely to remain where it is.

Behold again grief, both old from long use and new from the accident; desolation has been renewed, and an old scar reopened. “Well,” they say, “hope too was slow; indeed, unwillingly did we trust the one by whom, after we had trusted him, we were to be injured. Behold the outcome which our foreseeing minds predicted from the beginning.”

Amid these groans, however, a pole is armed with a curved blade, a piece of steel effective for cutting the ropes by which the beams hanging from the walls were held fast. As soon as these were cut, the release of the beams followed, and then their collapse. The support of the towers on the right and left was removed; Tancredus and the Norman count, with the whirl of their sling-projectiles, demolished the one farther away and the one nearer at hand. [Col. 0569B] The neighboring district, already alarmed on its own account, did not hear the men shouting. The Norman tower, especially, being more dangerous the nearer it came and therefore more hated, would easily have succumbed by now to the assaults; but straw placed before the weapon delayed its fall. The walls were concealed behind sacks, so that they no longer trembled at the marble stones flying toward them.

There was therefore much labor, very little result, abundant lamentation, and no laughter. Yet who would not be moved to tearful laughter at the sight of the military priesthood? As the army’s strength failed, that delicate order, carrying a ladder in white robes and stoles, wept as they carried it, groaned as they wept, and sang psalms as they groaned. This carrying was indeed both work and speech, but more speech than work. Then military courage, dulled by toil, was awakened by the unfamiliar sight. [Col. 0569C]

They returned to the walls, accompanied by that devout “Kyrie eleison”—that cry, I say, which came forth from the depths of the heart and effectively reached the ears of the supreme Judge. For the Lord heard the cry of the brokenhearted and could no longer endure the blasphemies of the faithless. He who divided the Red Sea into separate channels and led Israel through its midst now comforted his desolate people; when hope of life had already failed, he opened a way to victory. For after many devices had been tried, though all the others had failed, it pleased him also to imitate the rivers, so that in this way they might strip the fortress of its purple covering. [Col. 0569D]

The reed, accustomed to thirst for blood, now vomited flames—not, I say, thirsting to be extinguished or to extinguish, but raging to kindle. Its bow sent forth darts; one might think that, in a reversal of roles, the earth were hurling thunderbolts into heaven. Thus the glowing iron cut the air from below upward, while, assisted by the oar-like motion of the following feathers, the fire-spitting point pierced and ignited the straw at once. Its own protective device could not withstand the force of the fire. Those who had not yielded to arrows or crossbows now yielded to the flames.

The walls, emptied of their citizens, were soon filled with the enemies’ ladders. A palm tree, laid across like a bridge, connected the citizens with the enemy, wood with stone, and wall with machine. By this means too the eager young men crept into the city, swimming with hands and feet from the storms into harbor.

### CXXVI.—Bernard of Saint-Valéry, Lettholdus, and Engelbert mount the walls.

First among them a young man flashes with drawn sword,

[Col. 0570A] the glory of warfare and also the glory of a distinguished family.

Bernard, calling upon you as his holy patron, Valéry,

from whom he drew both his surname and his byname—

yet upon the walls he found you, and grieved to find you there,

the noble pair of brothers, Lettholdus,

and Engelbertus, second to his brother in birth and in the climb.

Flanders sent them up the ladder and onto the walls:

they spread through the fortifications, he toward the east wind,

the brothers toward the west wind; they tear and thrust apart what has been torn:

bodies fall everywhere, and crashing follows this man, crashing follows that.

Yet the first neck, leaving its shoulders severed,

felt the right hand that deals death; the third neck, which crawled forward,

still stood as a headless trunk, when the helmeted head

had already fallen to the depths. Soon the other followed him,

[Col. 0570B] and, both cut down, one experienced the heel, the other the sword.

But now the battle grows savage, and the people pour

more thickly into the fortress. The walls, indignant that their ancient citizen

should be overcome by a newcomer, are astonished at the weight

of victorious feet—at what the hard, relentless advance

presses heavily, what it attacks swiftly, what it strikes fiercely.

### CXXVII.—The city is captured.

The terrified inhabitants, therefore, having sufficiently rejected flight,

shake their trembling feet across the transverse ridge

and assail the victor. The admitted victor raises up those crushed

beneath the inert crowd. Assaults, prizes, walls, and the ascent—

the scarcity of steps delayed the eager people’s hopes.

The neighboring threshold is reached and broken, and, when the doors

had been struck, only the shoulders’ force was needed;

[Col. 0570C] soon the strength of the gates of Jehoshaphat was opened.

Once the barriers lie open, everything hastens forward and nothing resists:

here and there, to right and left, upward and downward,

across fields, thickets, roofs, farmland, and gardens,

they leap forth, kill, seize, and plunder.

One takes livestock, another a house; one gold, another brass,

deceived by its false appearance and its yellow gleam;

most take silver, some jewels, others purple cloth;

some take slaves—everything in haste, everything in a rush.

Yet, as the common saying goes, according to the serious itch

that each person has for his own possessions, each first flies

toward whatever his hands desire.

Thus, setting aside costly ornaments,

[Col. 0570D] each stops wherever his need drives him:

the hungry man does not hunger for arms when he finds a bakery;

the thirsty man does not thirst for bronze, livestock, or whatever else he finds.

The injured man enters houses; the naked rushes toward coverings;

the drinker hastens to cups, the miser to wealth.

The nobles labor to strike down; the common people to strip.

The soldier reddens with slaughter; the commander exhorts and presses them on.

From one side the two powerful counts, both companions, both named Robert—

one count of the Normans, the other of the Flemings—

and Duke Godfrey, a man renowned above all in war;

from the other, the magnanimous count of Saint-Gilles,

rushing directly against them, had climbed the neighboring towers

and surrounded with arms the one which the inhabitants call David’s Tower,

not without the death of many fleeing headlong,

whom flight had drawn from the walls to that tower as a place of refuge.

### CXXVIII.—Tancredus.

[Col. 0571A]

But Tancredus—a man who was not a man, but a lion,

yet not a lion in mouth or eyes, but, more than that,

a lion in his very heart—rushes toward greater things.

Neither Ajax, of whatever Ajax might dream,

nor Hector, nor Achilles, conqueror of Hector,

would dare what this leader of the Guiscardian line

easily and readily undertakes.

The court of the temples—now of one Lord, formerly of two,

now the Lord’s alone, formerly both the Lord’s and Solomon’s—

still girded this side, while the south held the other.

This spacious, capacious quarter, enclosed by lofty walls,

secured by two iron gates against flight and fear,

against terror and war, had received the whole city within it.

This part Tancredus strikes—diamond-hard iron, hard indeed,

but he harder still—breaks, crushes, and enters.

[Col. 0571B] At his entrance the unyielding crowd flees,

and they burst into the side of Solomon’s fifteen-forum hall.

The sluggish falls by the sword; the swift escapes the sword.

The one who succeeds in escaping bars the gate and strengthens it with a barrier,

or hopes to preserve his life; or, delaying death for however short a time,

turns toward the Lord’s temple.

And behold, the thresholds open to the standard-bearer,

and the roofs open to the standard.

### CXXIX.—He plunders the temple.

A cast statue stood upon a lofty throne,

plainly of massive silver, so heavy that scarcely six strong

right hands could support it, and scarcely ten could lift it.

When Tancredus looked upon it, he said:

“Shame! What does this present image mean, standing so high?

What does this effigy mean? What do the jewels mean? What the gold?

[Col. 0571C] What does the purple mean? For Muhammad was wholly crowned

with jewels and purple, and shone with gold.

Perhaps this is an image of Mars or Apollo.

Can it be Christ? It bears none of Christ’s insignia:

no cross, no crown, no nails, no pierced side.

Therefore this is not Christ, but rather the former Antichrist,

the wicked Muhammad, the destructive Muhammad.

O, if his companion were now present—the one who is to come—

may that future one suppress both Antichrists beneath his feet.

Shame! A guest from the abyss possesses God’s citadel,

and Pluto’s servant is god over Solomon’s work.

Let this image therefore fall quickly; let it have fallen long ago.

Does it still stand proudly, as though it too had swallowed us?”

Hardly had the order been given when you could see it already accomplished,

no soldier carrying out any command more willingly than this one.

It is torn away, dragged off, broken apart, and beheaded.

The material is costly, but the form is vile metal;

thus what was cast from a base substance becomes precious.

### CXXX.—He distributes the spoils among the soldiery.

The inner wall shone all around,

with a broad sheet of silver nearly a cubit wide,

running lengthwise in a dense strip almost a finger’s breadth thick,

and tracing long, winding circuits through the halls.

The weight of the sheet was nearly seven thousand marks.

A wise man drew this out of its useless repose and put it to use:

from it he armed servants who had been unarmed,

[Col. 0572A] clothed the naked, and fed the needy;

from it too he increased the number of the army,

which pleasure alone had enlarged, and caused his standards

to shine among foreign battalions.

Beneath jewels a wall lay hidden; beneath jewels, many a column;

much lay concealed beneath silver, much beneath gold.

The glory of a distinguished structure, an art worthy of celebration throughout the world,

a material that delighted the eyes of the luxurious—

as though fleeing sight and hating the light,

it lay hidden beneath such coverings and under bronze.

Tancredus’s favor therefore restored daylight to those

who had long been shut in prison and to the standards that had suffered darkness;

and, opening up the now-uncovered gold for the hungry needy,

stripping the marble bare, he restored the members of Christ.

### CXXXI.—He lays the enemy low.

After arranging what needed to be arranged,

[Col. 0572B] and admiring the jewels, bronze, and marble of the sacred temple,

Tancredus, after devoted prayer, takes up his arms.

He encounters resistance; but as he penetrates the ranks,

the enemy either falls or flees—he finds no middle course.

The outer field is now empty and feels no battles.

They run, and advance inward through the slaughter.

Once the entrances are open, what can compare with Tancredus, what with his sword?

What courage could accomplish, the pools of blood made clear:

who has leisure to recount one by one the mourning and rejoicing of the crowd, whether slain or slaying,

and the great benefits arising from such great losses,

in a thousand forms, through a thousand ways, amid a thousand ruins?

Mars roars; rage rages; the sword devours; the enemy falls.

Forward, holy fury; sacred sword; sacred abyss!

[Col. 0572C] Scatter and be scattered, wicked people, criminal men,

you who shed innocent blood—guilty men, pour out your blood—

you who so often tore Christ apart in his members.

Now receive the members of Christ in return for what you inflicted upon them.

### CXXXII.—The city is plundered; the enemy rally their courage.

Meanwhile, as the roar of war resounded through the city,

some gathered there in hope of slaughter, others in hope of profit.

Soon each person’s desire carried him off to seize different things.

Thus steel, iron, cedar, bronze, cypress, and electrum,

the strength and ornament of the gates and of Solomon’s buildings,

all broken, came crashing down; hiding places were revealed

and opened to the assault.

[Col. 0572D] What benefit was it to you, criminal denier of Christ,

to have hidden? What did it profit you to have closed the gates

of the divine palace?

Even if you close a thousand entrances and hide in a thousand places

beneath them, still you are dragged through a thousand entrances

despite the thousand that have been closed.

Behold, courage has found flight, and boldness has found fear.

As wolves plunder a flock when they have broken open its fold,

so the Gallic sword cut down the exposed people with equal slaughter.

A small number cut down an innumerable crowd:

some made it their task to butcher the old,

others to tear away the little ones;

many took care to strip the jewel-studded ears.

Yet when the slaughter was seen, the avenger rushed upon the slayers,

soon to be slain himself. The army, without number or order,

was like a swarm driven from a hidden cavern,

which either a shepherd forced out with water or with smoke.

It leaped forth and burst through every opening it found:

forehead, ears, or nostrils—it cut whatever gaped before it.

[Col. 0573A] Thus, when ruin had opened the hiding places of their kinsmen,

a thousand darts flew, like a thousand showers of spring hail.

Rage was the weapon; number did not gather the swords.

### CXXXIII.—The battle hangs in the balance; the faithful are driven back. Ebrardus of Puiset rallies the fugitives.

Gallic courage, great and small, a little band

but a strong one, could not for long withstand so many bodies.

They yield, and those who had just been yielding press upon them.

As much as breaking through the shattered thresholds

had earlier helped the victor, so much now helps them

to hasten their headlong retreat and fly back through the windows

opened by their own blows.

[Col. 0573B] Again these drive those away, and those again drive these away,

and soon they are driven from there to here and from here to there.

Thus now some yielded to others, now turned and pressed forward,

in varied alternation, fleeing from and driving

the Christians and the Muslims—the Muslim troops

driving the Christians. The outcome of the battle was uncertain.

As though playing with them, Mars favored now one side, now the other,

and through repeated flight had already toyed with both armies,

when at last the martial force of Puiset came rushing up,

Ebrardus, as the story relates, alone bearing a shield,

after chance had stripped his companions of their shields.

One shield alone stood against countless spears.

“And with a great thunderous voice he cried:

‘Shame, France! Shame on this disgraceful flight!

Shame! Have we come to fight, or to dance?

Certainly boys are accustomed to invent battles in this way,

and girls are accustomed to celebrate them with applause.

Behold the threats so often uttered at banquets.

Are you Frenchmen? No—you are not even worthy to be called French.

I would not deem you worthy even to be called Frankish daughters-in-law, since you have long been afraid

to break open folds and slaughter the enclosed flock.

Cast off your fear, therefore, and take up again the strength of your fathers.

Behold, I shall bear the leading standards; let the remaining standards follow me.’”

Thus, growling, he spurred them on; but he inflamed them even more

by his deeds than by his words. Immediately protected by his shield

as by a barrier, and with his right hand and sword extended,

the martial hero alone attacked a thousand men.

His voice was sufficient, but the slaughter he caused moved the young men more.

Whether all were stirred by the same roar, the same anger, and one heart,

[Col. 0573D] whether they shared the same mind, all alike pressed on in an unbroken charge,

approved the man who exhorted them, and followed the one who ran ahead.

### CXXXIV.—A dreadful slaughter of the unbelievers.

Although a few defeat countless thousands,

their smaller number neither harms them nor benefits the larger number of the others.

Number becomes a disadvantage: the larger the heap,

the denser it is, and therefore the weaker the crowd.

They stab and kill one another in close-packed ranks;

in varying turns, now the unwounded [strike] wounded bodies,

now those laid low without a wound, when they have fallen by chance.

[The syntax of the last two lines is defective in the supplied text.]

The slain, laid low by wounds, killed the living.

The greater the mass of the people, the greater the slaughter;

for the falling suffocates the standing, and the standing the falling.

Thus the sword passes by none even when he lies asleep:

it searches the ribs and is driven through necks and loins,

through backs and bellies, smearing the building—

the glory of every structure in the world—with abundant gore.

The vast temple became a dreadful lake, at the sight of which its maker might recoil. Its thresholds, walls, seats, ceilings, and columns were all blood; nothing was visible but blood.

The pavement lay completely hidden beneath the heaps of slaughter, so that no knee could touch the marble without being submerged. For so great was the blood, so vast the flood that stained the sanctuary, as neither Emathia under Caesar, nor the Phrygians under Achaean Mars, nor the Latins under Marius or Sulla had known.

### CXXXV.—Tancredus incurs the jealousy of Arnulfus. The latter’s speech against Tancredus before the nobles.

[Col. 0574B]

Yet this festival day must not be without a name. It is the day on which July illumines the year, the Ides of July; it is also the sixth day in the sequence of the festivals, and, counted in forties from the beginning of the siege, the penultimate day.

O blessed Ides, and more glorious than all others! For on these Ides those men were divided who were commanded to scatter the first seeds of faith throughout the world. From them began the origin of the Church’s seed; in them the renewed harvest fills the granary. Behold, on these Ides the master of the household sent out workers in the morning; behold, on these Ides the vineyard fills its storehouse at evening.

Therefore, rightly did this Ides of the Ides deserve to be proclaimed by its own glory! O Tancredus, here too, after victory came a contest over the fruits of victory, and after the contest you found peace, the fruit of the contest!

For jealousy arose among the leaders against Tancredus, because God had bestowed upon one man more abundantly than upon all the others. Armed with the darts of Arnulfus’ eloquence, like another Ulysses, he challenges the man, summons him inside, and calls the nobles together.

The leaders sit down, and the second Ulysses rises. After lowering his face toward the ground for a while, he begins as follows:

“Many things urge me, Fathers, to submit my obedience to your will, among them this very injury recently inflicted upon me. It teaches me how far one man differs from another, a benefactor from a plunderer, a defender from an invader.

You raised me from obscurity; you made me famous from unknown; you appointed me as one of yourselves and a participant in your revenues. This favor was new, but descended from the ancient generosity of your forefathers.

You, O leaders, are of royal blood. How well the source from which you flowed into me was revealed, when you were generous and wealthy toward me, though you were sparing and poor toward yourselves.

But Tancredus persecutes me, exercises savage tyranny, and rages against me. What your common consent had decreed for me, he himself withdraws; he takes from me the office of pontiff which you gave me; he strips me of what you invested me with.

Defend, therefore, O strongest nobles, your own right; avenge your own injury; punish the injury. Let no one think this insult is mine. It is yours; it belongs to all of us. My possessions have indeed been diminished, but your injury has increased: the loss falls upon me, the disgrace upon you.

For whoever tramples upon the dispensation condemns the dispenser altogether. It is written: ‘He who despises the law despises the king.’ But why would he not despise you, since he despises God? Why would he obey you, since he spares not the altars? Why would he tolerate you in your cloaks, since he has stripped the temple of the Lord of its outer adornment?

The temple, I say, of the Lord—not built yesterday or the day before, not established by some arbitrary dispenser, not founded anywhere, at any time, in any manner, or by just anyone. This is the house of the Lord, firmly built; the Lord himself founded it.

This is the place in which the patriarch Jacob truly declared that the Lord was present, and called it the gate of heaven, where he saw a ladder touching the heavens and angels ascending and descending.

Christ the Lord glorified this place both by his presentation as an infant and, as a young man zealous for reverence, by driving out the merchants. It is written: ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer.’

It would be long to enumerate the praises with which the pages of the Old and New Testaments heap majesty upon this holy house. If you had paid sufficient attention to this, O son of the Marquis, you would at least have spared it, as though it were heaven on earth—this one place on earth, I say, most like heaven, if anything on earth resembles the heavens.

Yet the Guiscardian must be excused: he has followed in the footsteps of his fathers. Who, amid embraces and kisses, hurled his godfather from the walls by means of a wheel? Guiscardus, surely. Who carried a living man in place of a dead one, a living man in place of one destined for burial, to Monte Cassino? Guiscardus, certainly. Who poured hot liquid over his nephew summoned to reconciliation, and then cold liquid? The same Guiscardus.

Yet he is said to have been a founder of churches, not their destroyer; not to have stripped them bare, but to have adorned many.

Alas, son of Guiscardus! Did you not know that I was a minister of the house of God? Or did you knowingly and deliberately, despising and trampling upon me, profane the sanctuary by bringing forward this crime? If it was a sin committed in ignorance, why, once informed, did you not turn to pardon? But if you sinned deliberately, why does the plunder now cease?

There are still churches; there are still jewels on the altars. Come, rush in, seize them, expel the ministers, take the place of those expelled. Let Arnulfus be silent; let Tancredus give counsel.

But you, O nobles: if I have deserved well of you, I have labored with you and never abandoned you. From the very beginning of the wars, Nicaea experienced my vigilance. When I rebuked laziness, vigor burned; when I exhorted the young, old age was made young; when I awakened the sleeping slings, the walls trembled.

Soon, surrounded by enemies in the valley of Dorylaeum, and seeing death before our eyes, we despaired of life. Yet fear did not confuse our minds; fraud did not intrude upon our counsel; nor was our labor without result.

I remember that a message had to be sent to our allies, that those who did not know had to be informed, and that the scattered had to be gathered. I gave the counsel; I carried it out.

I did not fraudulently burden the shoulders of others with a load which they themselves refused. Accompanied by one Achaeus—and he as unfit for battle as he was unarmed—I fled through thousands of enemies, escaped despite countless pursuers, reported the outcome, brought victory, and conquered.

What I was at Antioch, the enemy is witness. This day cannot unfold that long struggle. Let us say nothing of Marra, which was nearly redeemed; let at least Archas return to our memory, [Col. 0576A] where I experienced a manner of escape different from that earlier one, but the same fear. In a small boat near the walls, outside the harbor and within the shores of Marachea, Tortuosa, Valonia, and Gibellum, I was at last carried to Laodicea. Scarcely had I landed when, through a thousand dangers, I reached Antioch and rebuked the delays of the leaders.

O nobles whom I brought here! I call you as witnesses; I brought you here.

From that time until the present, Phoebus has not seen me at leisure, nor Phoebe in sleep; neither table nor mind has known rest, while I serve the commonwealth, keep watch, grow old, and die.

I was about to add much more to what I have already said, O Fathers, but, for the sake of brevity, I shall leave the rest aside and grant the day to my adversary.”

### CXXXVI.—Tancredus replies.

Tancredus rises from their midst, initially uncertain whether to take the ardor of his spirit as his guide or to seek the judge’s favor. He begins as follows [the name “Tancredus” is missing here in the source]:

“You know, nobles, my devotion. Military service, not persuasion or loquacity, advanced me; the sword and the lance did so. I therefore ask that I be indulged if, dragged into litigation, I exceed the rules of an art unknown to me; if, like an inexperienced novice, I press the reins either short of the mark or beyond it.

My adversary, I think, took this into account. Hence he found the audacity to challenge me. Like a scorpion whose whole strength lies in its tail, he has all his military power in his tongue. Woe, I say, woe to the tongue—it is the scorpion’s tail.

You yourselves have heard; no external witness is needed, by what force of persuasion he attacked my family. He disparaged Guiscardus, whose boldness was second only to Alexander’s—so great a prince—though no one had ever seen a prince among his detractor’s offspring.

Guiscardus’s deeds are known throughout the world. No one can diminish them except one who has always made a practice of coloring white black and black white. What of the fact that he used wealth to help, postponed pleasures to necessity, redeemed life with gold, and trampled enemies beneath jewels? Does this man, by twisting and corrupting the matter, call it ‘stripping churches’ because soldiers were created from silver?

Is this not the same man who is accustomed to speak throughout the parishes, crying: ‘Tell me, bishops, what use is gold in a holy place?’ Surely it is for the defense of the commonwealth and the defeat of unbelief. Compelled by pressing danger, with war at hand and necessity demanding it, I awakened idle bronze, as though sleeping, so that what had served while shining might serve better while fighting.

I did not have bracelets minted from it to please my nieces; I merely transferred the resources; I did not consume them. I advanced them so that they might multiply their fruit, as though they had felt no movement and would not rise in increase. I sowed them so that, after the harvest, I might pay my creditor tenfold.

Nor will Arnulfus—or any keeper of the temple keys able to ransom so many *neptes* [a corrupt or uncertain reading]—be lacking when I replenish its treasures with hoards. Meanwhile I shall also try to keep the claws at bay. While Tancredus is fighting at Jerusalem, Arnulfus shall not strip the temple of the Lord.

Consider, O nobles, what this is, if not an injury. While we were still strangers from abroad, I myself chose this judge and consulted him on this matter, asking whether each person should possess whatever he occupied, whether it were a house or a curia. I received this answer from the one I questioned:

‘It has been decreed and universally sanctioned that whatever any person first occupies after entering the city, whatever it may be, is to remain in that person’s possession.’

Perhaps he himself thinks he has passed over this. I have it present; it has not slipped from my memory; it stands fixed.

Let the judge be ashamed to change his decisions from day to day—let alone deny today what he sanctioned yesterday—and to resemble the slippery serpent and Proteus. For how shall I hold Proteus when he changes his forms?

But if he claims the first entrances for himself, in this matter too he is defeated and must yield. One soldier perhaps testifies for him, but an army for me—one who heard, but a thousand who saw.

I rushed in first; I broke the gates first. Where no one else dared to follow, I went ahead; those whom no one dared even to look upon from behind, I defeated from the front.

But he boasts to us of his flights, of having taken precautions in danger, of having advised that a message be sent, and finally of having delivered it. What noble, O nobles, would be so foolish as not to recognize his fear from these things? To send someone away from danger means to be absent from danger and to be saved.

And what of the fact that he gave advice, thrust himself forward, and then voluntarily withdrew? From these facts it is clear that he fled. For this should not be called a withdrawal, but, by its true name, a flight.

Rightly has this word been cut away from his boasting, since his whole purpose, his sole passion, his only thirst, was flight. Yet he departs excused on account of those whom he lists, the men whom fear overtook. Let him consider what these words signify: in a thousand forms that death which made the timid begin to die was a terror to them.

I am ashamed, Fathers, of this dispute. Yet my adversary did not compel me to it, lest he attribute it to himself; let him ascribe it to your reverence, for that moved me.

Now, therefore, I shall check the reins of my wearied horse. You must judge what is owed for the course already run.”

### CXXXVII.—The judgment of the nobles.

When this discord of words had sounded in the ears of the leaders, they themselves, now made even-minded toward the fairness of the speaker, examine justice after their jealousy has been put to sleep.

They find a middle course by which Arnulfus will not have spoken in vain, nor Tancredus be deprived of the wealth he obtained at the cost of his own blood. They judge that the breasts which have poured forth so much milk ought not to be left dry, especially since Tancredus’s generosity is not lacking toward other churches. This church in particular, which enriched an unworthy man, ought in turn to be supported by him in its need.

What more is there to say? On the advice of the leaders, the son of the Marquis restores seven hundred marks to the temple, not unwillingly. By this settlement the men who had been separated are brought together—both distinguished, both powerful though once obscure, both the object of everyone’s jealousy, although perhaps neither envied anyone except the other.

Of them I too may confidently repeat what the Mantuan poet wrote of Hector and Aeneas:

> If the Gallic land had sent two more such men,  
> Memphis and Babylon would long ago have had Gallic kings.

So greatly did excellence shine in the eloquence of one, in the boldness of the other, and in both alike in generosity, discernment, vigilance, justice, and wisdom.

### CXXXVIII.—The Franks victorious near Ascalon.

After the events just described, two [units unspecified in the surviving text] had passed, and that same fourth *parasceve* shone forth; it too doubled the joy, for beneath the walls of Ascalon it saw the Franks victorious. [Col. 0578A]

The capture of Jerusalem had disturbed the king of Memphis. Therefore all Egypt, roaring with rage, had assembled three hundred and sixty thousand horsemen and had sent an infantry force to battle as numerous as the sand of the sea.

But when the Franks were informed of the army’s arrival, they rushed upon it as though from hunger to a banquet. Our men routed, as has been said, the many by the few. The manner in which this happened Tancredus, because of the urgency of the matter, commands us to pass over.

After the victory, however, he permitted the people of Ascalon to submit themselves and their towers to the standard of Count Raymond, who had raised his banner. For under that commander the Davidic Tower had admitted its defenders unharmed, and from that time the faith of this man had been held in high esteem by that people.

But a dispute arose in the magistracy concerning the magistracy itself, because Raymond refused to support Godfrey, who had been chosen for the kingdom. The newly converted city returned to idolatry, rejecting both the count and the yoke of the king and the reins of those who had subdued it. This wickedness has no expiation, even though many good deeds already glorify the same man and still greater deeds may remain for him.

The proud and empty contempt of the indignant man now defiles the entire count—past, present, and future.

Alas, wretched man! You do not know what bonds and what slaughter of innocence you are constructing, while by releasing Ascalon, the instrument of bonds and slaughter, you free the guilty man rather than restrain him and remove the yoke.

This most sorrowful day of your indignation transmits immeasurable destruction to posterity.

### CXXXIX.—Tancredus fortifies the town of Bezan.

But Tancredus was always surpassing himself, always better through goodness, always humbler as God exalted him. [Col. 0578C] Although he possessed more than others in the acquisition of temple wealth, he served under the new king without resenting the yoke or fearing solitude.

For, when he departed, he had reduced the whole military force to such a small number that, once everyone had been gathered, barely two hundred cuirasses defended Jerusalem. Of these, the son of Guiscard took about eighty for himself and continually gathered rich spoils from every direction. He vigilantly kept raiders away from the city, enriching its citizens and impoverishing its enemies.

This concern drove the man to fortify the town which we now read was called Bezan, formerly Bezamis. That place, far from Jerusalem, was defended neither by stone, nor stake, nor embankment; its own squalor frightened the inhabitants and offered nothing pleasant to newcomers. Moreover, besides its other disadvantages, the crowd of people surrounding it already oppressed the innocent, and would soon besiege the guilty in much greater numbers.

But the man’s courage had foreseen this very matter. Just as a hunter knows the forest and a fowler the thickets, he knew where the greatest abundance of prey could be seized.

Accordingly, having enclosed Bezan with a makeshift rampart, he stripped the surrounding towns, separated the cultivated fields, transferred the yoke from the ox to the peasant, closed the roads to merchants and the gates to cities. Afflicted by these blows, Caiphas, although the city was enclosed by the sea and by towers, nevertheless weakened: first buried beneath sling-projectiles, then assaulted by swords sent in over ropes, bridges, and ladders.

### CXL.—Boamundus and Baldwin go to Jerusalem.

In those days Boamundus and Baldwin, the brother of King Godfrey, [Col. 0579A] of whom mention has been made above, wishing to fulfill their vow of going to Jerusalem, set out with a considerable band of soldiers.

As they traveled through the valley of Camela and the vicinity of Damascus, and also by way of Caesarea Philippi, they passed freely through the midst of enemies who were running about in every direction to reconnoiter—a marvelous thing to relate. It was the season of Lent.

When they hastened to Jerusalem, they celebrated the Paschal joys there with King Godfrey.

At that time Daybertus, bishop of Pisa, a man most powerful and eloquent in letters, who had attacked Joppa with many ships with Boamundus’s assistance, was elevated to the patriarchate of Jerusalem.

Arnulfus, a man of great natural ability, although he had been honored by election to this dignity, [Col. 0579B] nevertheless gave his consent most willingly, hoping that the Christian cause would benefit more through Daybertus than through himself.

Four bishops were appointed there: Roggerius of Tarsus, Bartholomeus of Mamista, Bernardus of Artas, and Benedictus of Edessa. They had come with Boamundus and Baldwin after being placed in the priestly office.

When the Paschal solemnity had been completed, Boamundus returned with his three bishops, restoring to each city its own prelate. Baldwin likewise returned to Edessa with his archbishop Benedictus, whose county he held.

### XLI.—Boamundus frees the city of Meletania from the siege; captured by the Turks after battle, he is carried away.

[Col. 0579C] Bohemond himself, as soon as he heard from informants that the city of Melitene was surrounded by Turkish forces—it lay ten days’ journey or more from Antioch—assembled the army and tried to go to its liberation. But when the Turks learned that he was already near, they deliberately abandoned the siege, as is their custom, and withdrew. They are more successful in turning their backs for a time or an hour than in advancing. Indeed, even while fleeing they shoot their arrows and wound those pursuing them.

As Bohemond approached the city and found no Turkish army, his men advised him to enter and rest there for a while, and then, after his exhausted strength had been restored by repose, to go out against the Turks to defeat them. He did not heed their advice. In foolish audacity, presuming beyond measure, he said: “Far be it that Bohemond should now do what he remembers never having done; for foxes do this: as soon as they hear barking dogs, they seek hiding places and conceal themselves.”

He therefore went after the Turks, found them, and immediately began a battle with them—a battle he would that he had never begun. While both sides were fighting, Bohemond was seized and bound, bringing great joy to the followers of Muhammad and grievous woe to the Christians. He was then taken to Romania, to be consigned in chains to King Anismas; after his capture, Antioch was left in such misery that there was no one to help or console it.

### CXLII.—The death of King Godfrey.

[Col. 0580A]

Immediately there followed the most wretched calamity, by which Jerusalem was afflicted with no less grief. For Godfrey, an excellent king who feared God, departed this life soon after Bohemond was captured. Only one year had passed since he had begun to reign when he reached his death.

Before he was deprived of the light of the present life, however, while he was confined by bodily illness, he ordered Patriarch Daybert and Arnulf, together with the others, to be summoned. He said to them:

“Behold, I am entering upon the way of all the earth. Therefore, while I am still alive, let counsel be taken among you, and let it be determined who should reign in Jerusalem in my place.”

They replied:
