“We place this more in your foresight, and whoever you choose for this purpose, to him we shall undoubtedly submit.”

He said:

“If the matter is left to my disposition, I judge my brother Baldwin fit to assume this high office.”

When they heard the name of Baldwin, they immediately and unanimously agreed, praised him, and submitted to him after confirming their loyalty by oath. They had known him as a man generous with money, devoted to military service, humble in speech, and exalted in courage. Nature herself, so to speak, had carved all these qualities into him with her own hand.

For he had been appointed leader in Rages, which is also called Edessa, as has been stated above, and was then residing there.

### CXLIII.—Baldwin succeeds Godfrey in the kingdom of Jerusalem; Tancred is installed at Antioch and subjects Mamista, Adana, and Tarsus.

[Col. 0580C]

Meanwhile, after the aforesaid king had been buried before Golgotha, a messenger was sent to Edessa, at whose summons Baldwin was to come to Jerusalem and be appointed successor to his brother’s scepter. This would have provoked great dissension and kindled war; but the departure of Tancred, who was summoned to govern Antioch by the same necessity that had called Baldwin, cut short the dispute.

Thus the heirs having been installed—Baldwin at Jerusalem and Tancred at Antioch—they hastened eagerly toward renown, both so that the younger might not degenerate from the virtue of the elders and because each was inflamed by jealousy of the other. Moreover, the dignity of Marchisides pressed upon him with suspicion, since he seemed to himself more a guest than a prince. He therefore ought to have been all the more alert, since the brevity of his rule was suspect and awaited its end upon Bohemond’s return.

These anxieties first drove Baldwin away from Tancred, for Baldwin, being more powerful among the Antiochenes, resented the new yoke. He had held the chief command of the army under Bohemond; but by then his courage had been raised partly—as commonly happens—by the new prince and partly by the authority entrusted to him for governing Edessa.

When this had been accomplished, Tancred immediately turned his attention to enlarging the frontiers that the Greeks had contracted shortly before, while Bohemond was reigning. In a brief but fierce campaign he therefore defeated Mamista, Adana, and Tarsus, and subjected them to his own laws, after they had first escaped from the negligence of his predecessor.

### CXLIV.—He captures Laodicea.

[Col. 0581A]

Returning from there, he attacked Laodicea with all his strength. But fortified by the defenses of nature, it resisted the man against whom neither iron, steel, marble, nor any human labor at all knew how to prevail.

That city, as can be discerned today from its own ruins, was once noble. It possessed, among other things, churches, a population, wealth, towers, palaces, theaters, and all the other features found in cities. Except for Antioch, no city in the surrounding region preserves such tokens of ancient nobility. Its many rows of columns, water conduits carried over precipices, towers raised to the stars, and statues keeping watch at the crossroads—all its precious works—bear witness through their art and materials to a past that has become present, to what was whole now being ruined, and to what was populous now being deserted. Even after so many suns and so many hailstorms, it remains a remarkable work.

A hill marks its length to the east, the sea to the west; plains define its breadth on either side; around it there is either a wall or a ruin. Its countless population feared nothing, while the city itself was a terror to other peoples. In its own time it disdained being enclosed by a massive earthwork and was content with a modest fortification.

But I return to the hill, which was now the only defense remaining against the enemy. It was steep and broader at the summit, and had received citizens who, abandoning the plain, had fled there, struck by terror at the din of war. Its steepness alone would have repelled besiegers even without a wall; crowned with a wall, however, it presented the enemy with a double strength, partly artificial and partly natural.

Trusting in these barriers, the Greeks awaited Tancred’s arrival. The prince, who both understood and thirsted for war, sent forward several scouts, who were either to capture those who had been lured out or to lure out those destined to be captured. But the Greeks, as vigilant as ever, took precautions against this: they would neither be caught wandering about nor go out when provoked.

They considered it madness to leave the gates. When they saw men shut out from the towers, they trembled within. From this the prince drew an indication of fear and cried:

“Ho, comrades! Let us attack this sheepfold. You see that it is steep; know that it is empty. It is full of wealth but without strength. There is no courage at all in a soldier who is not ashamed to be shut behind gates. Let us climb the earthwork. Let the wall, I say, yield either to axes or to ladders.”

The prince gives the order; the soldiers hasten; they run to the walls. Hammers, mattocks, axes, and every such implement roar against the gates. Although the gates are double and made of iron, they cannot withstand the assault; they tremble as though they were single and made of wicker.

Seeing iron cutting marble with blows, the city—distrusting its barriers and recognizing the enemy’s vigor—also turned to arms. A mass of stones rained down from the towers; no kind of weapon was absent from the attack, and no one within the walls was idle. Fear of the enemy’s slaughter had driven out fear; and as the effect approached, its efficient cause was repelled more forcefully.

The very convenience of the defense also encouraged the people, since dropping stones from the towers was easy for every age and sex. Arrows, meanwhile, flew toward the towers, often gouging out an eye or piercing a hand. They fought in this manner by turns until both their strength and their quivers were exhausted and demanded renewal. In particular, while the steel [calybs] was breaking the gates, the gates themselves now split apart and now shattered.

### CXLV.—Count Raymond besieges Tripoli; he asks aid from the emperor; he is captured and taken to Antioch with his wealth.

While the fighting continued in this way, a year passed. During it Count Raymond at one point wished to aid the Greeks but was repulsed; at another, the Turkish princes were scattered. Finally, he came most vigorously to the aid of suffering Jerusalem.

Tancred alone accomplished all these things, though in such a way that he did not lift the siege, and the city always remained safe. He himself defeated the Persians, the Egyptians, and, as we have said, the Provençal count.

That count, a man of extraordinary boldness, was besieging Tripoli with approximately four hundred Christians, partly foot-soldiers and partly mounted soldiers. Trusting in this number, he began to fortify a hill near the city with a wall and towers. With a certain urban courtesy, he called it the “Pilgrim Mountain,” since he did not arrogate to himself what was common to all.

Stationed there, he harassed the nearby city with frequent assaults, while the townspeople in turn nearly demolished that new settlement. A day was exceedingly rare that did not see the intervening plain stained with blood from one side, the other, or both. The strength of the multitude urged some to battle, while the helpless smallness of the few urged others; for where warriors are scarce, their very scarcity inflames courage, while where they are numerous, the loss of blood is easily endured and the horror of war becomes a pleasure.

Thus, as the fortress and the city resisted, the diminution of his people terrified Raymond. The same circumstance compelled him to cross the sea and seek aid from the Greek emperor. He carried with him that apocryphal spear mentioned above, whose discoverer it had conveyed through temporal flames to eternal ones. He brought it, I say, to Alexius as a gift.

He too was rewarded most generously: Alexius was grateful that Raymond had offered his possessions, but far more grateful that he had offered himself. On his journey to Jerusalem, Raymond had not known how to beg; on his return, he begged. The more deaf Alexius had been when he was asked before, the more readily he became persuaded when Raymond asked afterward.

A harmonious favor increased the hatred of Antioch, which was hostile to both of them. Raymond was therefore sent back with the great gifts I have mentioned, to attack the enemy of both, Marchisides.

Men deliberate below; God, who sits above the cherubim in heaven, judges.

You send, Alexius, treasures to Tancred, while Raymond’s biremes, laden with your gifts, are almost submerged. Nevertheless, after passing many places of misfortune under favorable auspices, the ships, driven by raging adverse winds and unable to avoid the enemy’s hands, were carried with their cargo into the enemy’s treasury at a harbor near Tarsus.

When the report flew to the prince’s ears, orders were given that the count and the Greek wealth be taken to Antioch—the count to be preserved, the wealth to be dispersed. Yet nothing that is ordered is maintained for long: he forswears and swears an oath. Thus the barriers were opened for the man placed under oath; otherwise they would have had to be closed in order to preserve the count’s life.

The rest is rolled about at Fortune’s nod: now someone becomes rich from poverty, and then poor from wealth.

### CXLVI.—After a year and a half, Laodicea is conquered and captured.

[Col. 0583A]

Tancred nevertheless remained constantly in the same struggle and never abandoned what he had once begun. He besieged Laodicea and would not leave it until it had been captured.

By now, however, he had begun to weary of the delay, which had lasted a year and almost half another, when God inspired him with a method by which the city could be taken. Those shut inside had grown accustomed to ambushing those who enclosed them. Whenever the besiegers slept outside at midday, the inhabitants would sometimes burst out suddenly, breaking their sleep with slaughter and plunder.

At the cry, the Franks would be roused and arm themselves; meanwhile, after completing their work, the Laodiceans would return unharmed. By deceiving the army once, twice, and even a third time, they showed Tancred the way to deceive them: whenever the same thing is repeated too often and in the same manner, Tancred repays ambush with ambush in order to outwit their strategy by his own.

He ordered a tent to be constructed, the capacity of which had never before been seen or heard of as having an equal. A very tall pine was also sought to serve as a pillar capable of supporting so great a burden. He spoke, and it was done. The tree’s broad folds were spread around; ropes and nooses both crowned and stretched the fabric.

Those who saw it thought that, as is customary, it had been built ostentatiously, as townspeople raise lofty palaces in their cities out of vanity. But at dawn Tancred summoned the army and packed it beneath the shelter, with horses lying in ambush, ready to act without delay whenever necessary; they lacked neither spurs nor eagerness for battle.

When the sun rose, he sent a considerable part of the army in full view of the enemy to gather grain. The rest, after taking food, pretended to give themselves over to sleep, promising the spectators hope and opportunity for plunder.

Seeing that profound silence held everything in the camp, the townspeople hoped to disturb the army as usual and, by a swift return, escape the delayed vengeance of an unexpected attack. They therefore rushed out together toward the spoils, each begrudging the others the lead.

With only a few remaining, almost everyone went out. So greatly did the feigned opportunity deceive them. They ran to the plunder, and were allowed to do so. When they were laden and returning to the gates, the counterattack began.

Those who had been concealed and prepared, as soon as the way had been opened, hastened forward, took up positions opposite the gates, and blocked the return. Tancred fell upon those who had been shut out; without delay, they were either captured or killed.

The remaining guards were terrified and reduced to very few. They trusted neither the walls nor themselves. They voluntarily sought peace, offered to open the barriers, and invited the besiegers to enter, secure in an agreement that guaranteed their departure.

The prince approved, and after his long labors he returned to Antioch, the house of rest.

### CXLVII.—The archbishop of Milan and the count of Poitiers are defeated by Danisman; Bohemond is ransomed.

At that time Anselm, archbishop of Milan, and William, count of Poitiers, fought against Danisman in Romania. The archbishop was killed, while the count barely escaped the hands of the Turks by fleeing. At last, poor, destitute, and naked, he took refuge in Cilicia, where he reached Tancred and found Tancred.

He was received and heaped with an abundance of every good thing, though he had been destitute of everything. Then, strengthened, he crossed to Pilgrim Mountain; there the count assigned him an escort of those who were going to Jerusalem.

At that time the ransom of Bohemond concerned the people, especially Count Baldwin, who was Tancred’s chief enemy. By admonishing, promising, and reproaching them, he pressed the Antiochenes to open Bohemond’s prison.

Bernard, the new patriarch, also exerted himself to the utmost, as though repaying Bohemond for having raised him from that very prison. Tancred, however, did not oppose this effort, although Bohemond’s return seemed likely to work against his own prosperity.

With some on one side and some on the other expressing their disapproval, Bohemond returned, barely ransomed for ten myriad Michelati.

[Note: [Col. 0583] A type of gold coin then famous in public commerce, named after an emperor of Constantinople called Michael.]

Tancred returned to him what he had received and what he had not received: the former willingly, the latter under compulsion. He was forced to surrender Laodicea, Mamista, Adana, and Tarsus, which he had won by his own sweat; otherwise he would have been consigned to chains and iron.

Thus stripped of all his possessions and of his allied army as well, he was at last scarcely compensated with two small towns.

### CXLVIII.—The Assyrians make war, surround Edessa, and engage in battle.

Meanwhile the Assyrians made war and surrounded nearby Edessa with an immense multitude. The report flew to Antioch. Bohemond, asked to bring aid, did not delay. He crossed the Euphrates, accompanied by the patriarch and Tancred. Goscelin also crossed, at that time governing Maresium, bringing with him all the forces he possessed.

When the Turks heard of Bohemond’s arrival, they abandoned Edessa and withdrew a short distance, eager for battle but concealing their purpose. By this stratagem they pretended to flee so as to deceive the newcomers who would thoughtlessly pursue them: the Turks would reach safety by familiar roads, while the newcomers would come to danger by unfamiliar ones; the Turks to bread, the newcomers to hunger; the Turks to reinforcements of arms, the newcomers to losses.

Thus, gradually luring them for three days beyond the city of Carrhae, they deceived some and were deceived by others, until they reached and crossed the Chobar River. The delay of battle at the city was now sufficient for the Turks. Abandoning the pretense of flight, they provoked war and waged it both in word and by hand.

They thought that the Christians were finished, as though, once they had crossed the river, freedom of flight had been taken from them and their strength exhausted by the journey. Nor should this be considered far from the truth: so it happened.

The Christians advanced in three columns. Bohemond was on the right; on the left, both by position and by lot, was Count Baldwin. Both were unarmed, unprepared, and unwary. Tancred was in the center, prepared, watchful, and armed.

The Turks advanced not far ahead, as though serving as a vanguard, while they kept near them scouts who would report every movement of the Franks. Only a quarter of the daylight remained, while three-quarters had passed, when the Franks began to make camp in the order prescribed.

As soon as the Turkish scouts learned who was prepared and who was not, the Turks suddenly turned. Avoiding the armed Tancred, they threw the army of Bohemond into confusion on one side and Baldwin’s on the other. Neither side had time to put on armor; they fought with bare heads and unprotected chests.

The Antiochenes tried to resist but, unarmored, could not, and were forced to leave the camp. There, while the enemy was occupied with the baggage and the ostentatious equipment, our men drew breath. Belatedly, as far as circumstances allowed, they prepared themselves for battle and saved their lives at the cost of their possessions, calling it gain to lose those things.

### CXLIX.—Baldwin and the archbishop Benedict are taken captive; Benedict is freed by Tancred.

The Edessans, however, suddenly perished; they were unable to defend either themselves or their possessions. Baldwin was captured and led away in chains. The unfortunate archbishop Benedict was also captured and dragged along, with a double load of clubs placed upon his shoulders.

As he was being led before Tancred’s line, he cried out:

“Tancred! Tancred! Bring help! Let Benedict’s suffering move you.”

His cry was heard. When Marchisides recognized whose cry it was, he immediately charged, freed him, and brought him back. After freeing him, he restored him with great honor, saying that he himself stood by Benedict’s side. He comforted the trembling man and told him that, while he was present, there was nothing to fear.

Then he ardently attacked the enemy, but evening and the soldiers’ warning held him back, pointing out that night was near. The same consideration restrained Bohemond, and it was decided to postpone the battle until the following day.

Meanwhile darkness covered the world. The princes, having stationed sentries, gave their bodies to sleep; but the common people and those whom the court did not support kept watch for flight.

[Note: [Col. 0585] William of Tyre also reports this flight of the Christian soldiers, in Book XI, section 30, but without all these circumstances.]

They feared that they would see the fate they had witnessed repeated on the following day.

### CL.—The Christians take flight.

[Col. 0585C]

A river obstructed their return. It had only one ford; elsewhere, the projecting banks of the channels made passage impossible. Watchmen guarded that ford as though it were the only gate, so that no refuge might be open through it to the terrified people.

Thus, while those attempting to flee were few, they were kept from the ford; when they became numerous, they could no longer be held back. The prince’s order was disregarded when fear of death threw the people into confusion. The forbidden barriers were broken, as the swelling crowd multiplied.

Others had also carried pieces of wood from bank to bank and used them as a bridge. The guards therefore yielded under compulsion, awakened Bohemond, complained of the force applied to the guard, and announced the flight. The rumor had already roused Tancred as well. Both prepared to return when they saw that they had been abandoned by the people.

Some wished to hurry and go ahead; Tancred preferred to follow and delay. He himself stood like a wall against the weapons of the enemy for those following; the others hastened their flight. He used the reins, while the others used their spurs.

God nevertheless pitied his people. The Turks were unaware that they were fleeing, for deep sleep held them. Meanwhile, flight kept watch, adorning the roads with precious equipment. The fugitives threw away clothing, tents, silver and golden vessels, everything heavy and everything that delayed flight—even the weapons that were the very protection of life.

Rain had damaged the roads and changed the dust into mud. Horses and foot-soldiers were slowed by the slippery ground, as were the loads tied to the animals’ tails. Patriarch Bernard was present; he too fled with the fugitives, and his muddy mule was slowed along with those who were slow.

No one was pursuing them, yet they seemed to see countless pursuers with drawn swords and bows at the ready. His eye, troubled by fear, was no less disturbed inwardly than outwardly.

He therefore begged his companions in flight:

“Listen, sons; listen to your father. Cut off this oar that hangs from the stern, which not only fails to govern your course but actually restrains it. Cut it off, I say. I am not ashamed in this storm to press the back of a shortened beast, provided it is lightened. Cut it off, and may God likewise cut away your sins; as for me, I absolve everything belonging to the one who cuts it off.”

Many passed by with stopped ears. Blind fear had closed their ears, so that their own misery left them no pity for another. He had already grown hoarse from shouting when at last a fugitive soldier offered a remedy, though in exchange for the remission he had been promised.

Thus two things were absolved in a single act: the soldier from guilt and the animal from its tail. As the soldier cut off the tail, he sowed among blessings and also reaped from blessings, while the patriarch blessed him with mouth, heart, and right hand.

When the reaper had harvested both the tail and the blessing, he thereafter accompanied the patriarch all the way to Edessa and ran with him whose ability to run he had restored by removing what had taken it away.

### CLI.—Edessa is entrusted to Tancred; after capturing the neighboring towns, the enemies enter Arthasium.

The rest of the people also gathered there, including those who had held the highest rank, though they arrived last. There they considered whom they should appoint as Baldwin’s successor, someone capable of bearing the weight of so great a burden.

Tancred was chosen as worthy. He remained and governed; Bohemond, however, returned to Antioch.

When the loss of the Franks was announced throughout the neighboring cities, the Cilicians, Syrians, and Phoenicians rejoiced, both those already subjected and those still to be subjected. Some shook fear from their hearts; others cast off the yoke from their necks.

Tarsus, Adana, and Mamista returned to their own jurisdiction. They welcomed the Greeks and expelled our countrymen. The Turks entered Arthasium and ravaged the entire region as far as the Farfar bridge.

Finally, a very large number of Greek ships filled the harbor of Laodicea. They too were full of arms, both instruments of manufacture and weapons of war, waging war and carrying on construction at the same time.

After bringing cement and masons, they began to build. The ruins supplied abundant stone for those who requested it; the harbor was fortified, and the construction rose.

Bohemond had scarcely received the report when, driven by hope of the unfinished work, he arrived and found everything still incomplete. Above the harbor stood an ancient tower called by the name of Saint Elijah, separated from the new construction only by the intervening space of the harbor.

The Greeks fortified this tower as well and joined it to their fortress, building an arch over the harbor to provide access from one to the other and a strong defensive structure against hostile oarsmen.

### CLII.—Bohemond recalls Tancred.

Seeing that everything was turning against him, Bohemond returned to Antioch and soon decided to deliberate publicly about the condition of his principality. He recalled Tancred, whose sharing of the burdens was especially necessary. When summoned, Tancred came without delay; he had never accomplished anything by delaying.

After an assembly had been held inside the basilica of Saint Peter, Bohemond began as follows:

“Great prudence, nobles, is necessary in this crisis; if we neglect it, we perish. The pagans have grown strong against us. The Greeks and Turks have blocked our roads on every side. We have provoked the two richest powers in the whole world: Constantinople and Persia.

“The East terrifies us by land, while the West does so by both land and sea. To omit other matters, Arthasium has until now been Antioch’s shield; now it bends its bow and sharpens its arrows against us.

“We are few, and yet we are always becoming fewer from few. Our number has been greatly diminished by the loss of the count of Edessa.

“Therefore keep watch and consider attentively what must be done at this critical turning point. I shall briefly set out what I think. We must seek forces from across the sea [or: from beyond the Alps], and stir up the peoples of Gaul. That boldness will either free us or nothing will.

“Use me—me, I say—as your agent in this matter. For your safety I do not refuse the labor; that labor of mine is most pleasing to me, through which rest may be prepared for you.”

He ended there and sat down. Tancred rose and began:

“Nobles, you have heard a prudent and clear exposition of both the strength of the enemy and our weakness, as well as of the beginning and end, the causes and the remedy. Our lord Prince Bohemond has spoken beautifully, well, and rightly on these matters, and has not disdained to offer himself as the minister who seeks medicine for the disease.

“But, nobles, what is the purpose of this? Is there no one among us who can be sent? Unless the one is sent away who ought rather to be acclaimed as one who had been far away. When a pack of wolves surrounds the folds, what is needed is the presence, not the absence, of the shepherd. Present, he confronts the danger, rouses the dogs, keeps off the robbers, and frees the flock. If he is absent, the barking ceases, plunder grows savage; he himself rests, and the flock is scattered.

“My hearer will rightly and severely reproach my sluggishness when it is said that Bohemond has gone away while Tancred has remained at home. But perhaps I have been tested by that word, so that I might reveal what spirit I possess when I heard it.

“My will is plain; I do not restrain what is boiling within me. I demand this danger for the common safety, I undertake it secure in purpose, and I embrace it as my duty. So that my request may obtain consent, I promise before God diligence in service and speed in returning. And lest my judgment perhaps be clouded by gluttony, I shall be content with water and shall know no wine until Antioch receives me back.

“Afterward, let it also be permitted me to take two days’ rest beneath the same roof; before then, let it not be permitted. If you order it, I shall gladly place these burdens upon my shoulders; if you impose heavier ones, I shall willingly be burdened with heavier burdens.

“Bohemond objected: ‘The matter under discussion is great; it must be treated at length and is scarcely penetrable to anyone of ordinary standing. Our purpose is to stir up powerful rulers. This is not granted to every man; no one can move weighty powers unless he himself is weighty. A great blast is needed to uproot a tall oak from its roots.

“They will not listen to Tancred; scarcely—ah, scarcely, would that they listen to Bohemond—those who must be summoned to the labor of exile, though now they rule in settled and peaceful security.

“Therefore, from this point onward, so that no one’s rashness may obstruct my decision, I have resolved to go. It cannot be changed; it stands fixed. The vow must be fulfilled, which my devotion, bound with iron, has made.

“The intercession of blessed Leonard has absolved me. I shall either visit him or die before doing so; either way, I shall fulfill my vow.’”

### CLIII.—Leaving Antioch wholly destitute to Tancred, Bohemond crosses the sea.

After this no one opposed the prince’s will, for the proverb known among the people is: “The law follows the king, wherever the king wishes to lead the law.”

A fleet was therefore prepared. Ten biremes had their oarsmen ready, joined by three vessels with a single bank of oars, commonly called sandalia. Content with this number, Bohemond crossed the sea in sight of the Pelasgian fleet, leaving Antioch to Marchisides.

Gold, silver, gems, and robes were carried away. The city was left to Tancred without protection, without funds, and without paid troops.

I remember having heard truthful informants who said that, in this poverty, Tancred abstained from wine and was content with drinking plain water. When he was gently urged to take even a little of the wine of Lyaeus for the sake of his stomach, he said:

“Let me abstain with those who abstain. I have firmly resolved not to take anything from the fruit of the vine until I can give enough to everyone. Far be it from me to be swollen with drunkenness while my fellow soldiers waste away from hunger!”

### CLIV.

[Col. 0588C]

Nearly forty days had now been spent in want when abundance arrived with full horn, and no small amount of gold seemed to rain from heaven.

One of the citizens, having heard of the poverty of the court, was moved by pity. He approached Tancred and, asking for a reward, immediately obtained permission to relieve the shortage and provide assistance.

“This city,” he said, “has a hundred citizens, and it would be easy for each of their purses to pour out a thousand gold pieces. If asked, they will not withhold them. You, lord, ask; I shall reveal the names of those whom you should ask.”

His advice was followed. Those to be written down were named, those to be summoned were recorded, those to be asked were summoned, and those summoned were asked within.

The pressing necessity was explained. The immediate request was thereby excused; the promise of repayment supported and justified the excuse, so that the money seemed to be requested not so much as a gift as a loan. Nor was the neighboring hostility concealed: it could not be repelled unless armed men came to meet it, and they would not come unless provoked by the intervention of gold.

When so many arguments had been brought together, the prescribed number of gold pieces was finally obtained. Once they had been received, Marchisides was strengthened, and he strengthened the army: he raised what was lying prostrate, armed the unarmed, replenished the number that had fallen away, and did not cease increasing the military force as long as the gold lasted.

From then on Antioch began to rise after its collapse and, from having been terrified, to become terrifying. He immediately attacked Arthasium, which, together with the others, had harassed Antioch and was the most bitter and nearest of all the Syrian enemies.

Tancred therefore surrounded it. At his assault the towers, shaken by stones, scarcely stood. Hearing this, King Raduan of Aleppo came running with thirty thousand men, trusting in his multitude against the few.

The people of Arthasium also joined him, and all advanced against Antioch.

[Note: [Col. 0589C] William of Tyre calls him Roduanus.]

### CLV.—He drives Raduan out of Arthasium.

Between them lay a rocky plain. Horses could somehow pass across it, but running was entirely impossible. If anyone was ever forced to run, neither hoof nor shoe could protect the foot, for the rough rocks ground down the horse’s heel and caused horse and rider to fall.

When Tancred learned this, he withdrew a little and allowed the enemy to approach to the point where the difficulty of the terrain would hinder flight. Raduan, whether negligent or ignorant of this, attacked the Christian army there. It remained in place as though numbed and held out until the lance had its moment.

Once the Turks had passed beyond the rough ground, Tancred, as though awakened from sleep, thundered into their midst. They readily turned their backs, hoping—as is their custom—to wheel while fleeing and shoot while wheeling.

Their hopes and their skills were both deceived by the lance and the road: the one pressed them, the other did not permit them to run. The former pierced their backs; the latter halted their steps.

Their horses, quivers, and bows therefore became useless. They abandoned them and trusted their own feet where they distrusted those of their animals, using their human powers as best they could, though they would have preferred to possess the speed of deer.

Raduan did not accomplish nothing, however: he shot a few of the Christian forces; the rest of his effort went into flight. Some of his archers escaped wounded, while others were struck down dead.

### CLVI.—He returns victorious to Antioch and surrounds Apamea.

Tancred therefore took Arthasium in victory. After fortifying it, he returned to Antioch. The Christian faith, strengthened by the spoils of the unbelievers—or rather, awakening as though rising from the dead—rejoiced that the renewal of its prince had renewed its fortune.

Tancred himself was like a hawk whose freedom to fly had long been denied and whose spirit had been wasted by prolonged confinement. Once freedom was finally restored, if fortune aided its first flights when it was sent out to plunder, it desired a second opportunity; and when it saw a flock of cranes, it tormented its master by flying over it at every convenient and inconvenient moment.

Tancred was inflamed with equal ardor. Having gained victory, he grew rich from the spoils of Aleppo.

As he was preparing to attack New Laodicea, he was advised to support the old city with a greater number of warriors. He himself surrounded Apamea with the rest of the army, and this was done.

Tancred repaid the Greeks in kind. They had set fortress against fortress; now he himself fortified the Christians against the fortified places. He surrounded Apamea with not a large but a vigorous force, as though devoted to death and himself devoted along with it.

Near Sysara, near Hama, near Raphania, and near many other towns and cities, everything was full of threats and bristling with enemies. The Christians therefore besieged one city, while many cities besieged the Christians. Those who needed provisions could obtain them only by dividing the army in two: one part remained while the other went out. Thus, divided, they avoided the danger that they could scarcely withstand when assembled.

These things must be attributed to God, not to human strength. Christ was openly fighting on behalf of the Christians.

### CLVII.—The extreme crisis of the people of Laodicea.

He was informed of the poverty of his people in Laodicea: the provisions supplied for feeding them threatened to run out. Soon either grain would enter the city or a fighting force would come out.

Entry was prevented by the great number of the enemy, who kept sleepless watch in the streets. Troubled by the report—for he knew that hunger alone secures cities, and that a starving populace does not know how to fear—the prince divided his thoughts among various alternatives: whether he should postpone what was already possessed in favor of what was to be possessed, or what was to be possessed in favor of what was already possessed.

It was difficult to abandon Laodicea, won through great labor; it was grievous to abandon Apamea, which could easily be obtained. For it seemed almost impossible both to do the one and not neglect the other.

But courage, which alone turns impossible things into possible ones, strengthened the man. He urged the soldiers who remained to govern the camp to hasten to the aid of those requesting it, and encouraged them as follows:

“Come, martyrs of Christ! Prepare to pour out your blood for him and to be poured out for him. Stand firm. You began well; bring it to a good conclusion. Let your small number not terrify you. Victory lies not in numbers but in the power of God.”

[Note: [Col. 0589C] Thus the History of Radulf ends. What the outcome of so great a danger was, however, Fulcher of Chartres briefly reports in Book II of his History of Jerusalem, under the year 1105:

“Tancred, placing the anchor of his hope not in a great multitude but in the Lord, arranged his battle lines properly and rode without hesitation against those enemies. Why delay with anything more? Boldly he charged them before Arthasium, and, with God’s support, they were immediately surrounded by fear and turned their backs to flight. They fled and were put to flight; whoever could not flee did not escape death. There was no counting the slain. Tancred obtained many of their horses. He also kept the standard of the fleeing king, and so forth.”]

[Col. 0591]

# History of the Franks Who Captured Jerusalem, by Raimundus of Agiles, Canon of Le Puy

*(In Bongars, **The Deeds of God through the Franks**, or the history of the eastern expeditions and of the Frankish kingdom of Jerusalem, committed to writing by various authors of that age—Hanover, 1611, folio, p. 139.)*

## Notice

Raimundus de Agiles, or Agilaeus, canon of Le Puy and chaplain of his bishop—who was also count of Toulouse—went with him to the Holy Land in 1095 and, as an eyewitness, described the events that took place there over five years. In his preface he declares that he will write especially about the count of Saint-Gilles, that is, the count of Toulouse, and the bishop of Le Puy. He was present when the lance was excavated, and carried it in battle. He was promoted to the priesthood during this journey.

He wrote at the request of Pontius de Baladuno and dedicates his work to all the Orthodox and Transalpine people, specifically to the bishop of Viviers. This Pontius was a soldier, a nobleman, and a familiar associate of the count of Toulouse; besides the present author, William of Tyre, book VII, chapter 17, and others record this fact. French manuscript parchments call him Poinces de Baladon and Baladun. He was killed by a stone from a stone-throwing engine during the siege of Archados, rashly begun by the count; worthy of posterity’s remembrance, he himself remembered posterity amid such dangers. Robert below calls him Pontius of Balon, column 744, lines 32–33.

In Gesner’s *Bibliotheca* we read that a history of this war written by him survives in London; it also recognizes Raimundus of Le Puy as the author of a work written on the same subject. Unless I am mistaken, both are the same as our present work. Petavius’s *Principal Book of the Wars of the Lord* cites Raimundus of Arguilliers, as Petavius himself informed us by letter.

We possess this work from one manuscript of Vulcobius, belonging to Guillelmus Ancelius, and from another of our own, given to us by Joannes Russatus, recently prefect of the judicial district of Langres and deeply devoted to the commonwealth. The final portions of the book are by another author, as the style indicates and the Vulcobian manuscript confirms; we have enclosed them in brackets. The work begins with the count of Toulouse’s entry into Slavonia and follows the narrative of that same five-year period, namely up to the victory over Babylon, which he calls the victory over Ammiratus.

## Author’s Preface

### [Col. 0591A]

Pontius de Baladuno and Raimundus, canon of Le Puy, send greetings and a share in our labor to my lord the bishop of Viviers and to all the Orthodox.

We have considered it necessary to make known to you and to all the Transalpine people the great things that God, in accordance with his customary goodness, has done with us and never ceases continually to do—especially because the unarmed and fearful, departing from us, strive to assert falsehood in place of truth. But whoever has witnessed their apostasy should flee their words and company.

For although the army of God endured the scourge of its Lord because of its sins, through that same Lord’s mercy it proved victorious over all pagan peoples. But because some came through Slavonia, others through Hungary, others through Lombardy, and others through [lacuna], it was tedious for us to write about each group separately. Therefore, setting the others aside, we have undertaken to write about the count of Saint-Gilles, the bishop of Le Puy, and their army.

## Chapter One

Those men, then, having entered Slavonia, suffered many hardships on the journey, chiefly because of the winter that was then prevailing. Slavonia is indeed a deserted land, trackless and mountainous, where for three weeks we saw neither wild animals nor birds. The inhabitants of the region are so savage and uncivilized that they were unwilling to provide us either with trade or with guides. Instead, fleeing from their villages and castles, they slaughtered the weak, old women, poor people, and sick persons who, because of their infirmity, followed the army from a distance—as though these people had done them great harm, and as though they were cattle.

It was not easy for our soldiers to pursue unarmed bandits familiar with the terrain through mountain precipices and dense forests; rather, they endured them continually. They could neither fight effectively nor remain free from fighting.

Let us not pass over one remarkable deed of the count. Once, when the count had been surrounded by Slavs together with some of his soldiers, he attacked the Slavs and captured as many as six of them. When the Slavs therefore pressed him more fiercely and the count was compelled to follow the army, he ordered the eyes of some to be torn out, the feet of others to be cut off, and the noses and hands of still others to be severed, so that, with the others thus terrified and overcome by awareness of the pain, the count could escape safely with his companions.

Thus, by God’s grace, he was delivered from the peril of death and from the difficulty of the place. It would not be easy to recount how greatly the count displayed courage and judgment there.

For we spent nearly forty days in Slavonia, during which we endured such a dense thickness of fog that we could, to some extent, touch it and push it away from us by moving our hands. Throughout this time the count was continually fighting at the rear and always defending the people; he was never the first to take lodging, but always the last. While some arrived at their lodging at midday and others in the evening, the count frequently reached his lodging in the middle of the night, or at cockcrow.

At last, through God’s mercy, the count’s labor, and the bishop’s counsel, the army crossed the region in such a way that we lost no one to hunger and no one in open combat there. I think God wished his army to cross Slavonia for this reason: so that the savage people who did not know God, having learned the courage and endurance of his soldiers, might either at some time recover from their ferocity or be brought before God’s judgment as without excuse.

At last, after many dangers and hardships on the journey, we reached the king of the Slavs at Scodra. The count frequently confirmed a bond of brotherhood with him and gave him many gifts, so that the army might safely purchase and obtain what it needed. But this was only an appearance; we regretted the peace we had sought, since on its account the Slavs, raging in their customary manner, killed our men and seized whatever they could from the unarmed. We sought a place for flight, not for vengeance.

So much for Slavonia. We came to Dyrrachium and thought that we were in our own homeland, supposing that the emperor Alexius and his retainers would be our brothers and helpers. But they, growing savage in the manner of lions, attacked peaceful people who were thinking of anything but arms; they slaughtered them by stealth, in the woods and in villages far from the camps, and stole whatever they could throughout the night.

Although they behaved so madly, their leader nevertheless promised peace. During the truce, they killed Pontius Rainardus, mortally wounded Peter, his brother, and these men were among the noblest of the princes. When an opportunity for vengeance was offered us, we preferred the journey rather than revenge for injuries, and we began our march.

We had letters from the emperor promising peace, brotherhood, and, so to speak, filial relationship; but these were words only. For before and behind us, on the right and on the left, Turks, Cumans, Huns, and Tenaces, Pechenegs and Bulgarians lay in wait for us through the emperor’s intrigues.

One day, when we were in the valley of Pelagonia, the bishop of Le Puy had withdrawn a short distance from the camp in order to find suitable lodging. He was captured by Pechenegs, who threw him from his mule, stripped him, and struck him heavily on the head. But because so great a bishop was still necessary to the people of God, by God’s mercy he was preserved alive. For while one of the Pechenegs was asking him for gold, he defended him from the others. Meanwhile an alarm arose in the camp, and in the interval between the enemies’ delay and the attack of his companions, the bishop was rescued.

In this way, proceeding through ambushes, we came to a certain castle called Bucinat. The count learned that the Pechenegs intended to attack our army in a mountain pass. Remaining concealed with some soldiers, he encountered the Pechenegs, killed many of them, and put the rest to flight.

Meanwhile the emperor’s peaceful letters surrounded us, while enemies, through imperial treachery, surrounded us on every side. When we came to Thessalonica, the bishop fell ill and remained with a few men inside the city.

After this we came to a certain city called Rossam. When its citizens were openly plotting many evils against us, our customary patience displeased us for a while. We therefore seized our arms, destroyed the outworks, captured immense booty, and compelled the city to surrender. After carrying our standards into the city and shouting “Toulouse”—the count’s battle cry—we departed.

We came to another city called Rodestol. When the emperor’s troops there wished to act against us in revenge, many of them were killed and a small amount of booty was captured.

There our envoys arrived, whom we had sent ahead to the emperor. Having received money from him, they promised us every advantage with the emperor. What more can I say? The words of the emperor’s envoys and of our own reached the point that the count, leaving the army, should hasten alone and unarmed, with only a few companions, to the emperor.

They said that Bohemond, the duke of Lorraine, the count of Flanders, and the other princes were asking that the count hurry to meet the emperor concerning the journey to Jerusalem, so that, having taken the cross, the duke and the emperor might become leaders in the army of God. They added that the emperor had said he would arrange everything with the count, both concerning himself and concerning the other matters useful for the journey.

They further announced that a war was imminent and that, if the authority of so great a man were absent, it might perhaps cause harm. Thus the count was to come with a few men so that, when his army arrived, everything having been settled with the emperor, no one would be delayed.

At last the count was persuaded that, leaving a small garrison in the camp, he should go ahead of the army. In this way he came unarmed to Constantinople.

## Chapter Two

Up to this point the events that I, the writer, have narrated were easily accompanied by certain steps of joy and prosperity. Now, however, they are weighed down by such a burden of bitterness and sorrow that I regret having begun, although my vow is to complete the work.

What should I undertake to say first and above all? Should I describe the emperor’s most fraudulent and detestable deceitfulness in his counsel? Or the shameful flight and unbelievable despair of our army? Or, by enumerating the deaths of so many princes, leave behind a memorial of perpetual sorrow?

But whoever desires to know these things should seek them from others rather than from us. We excuse ourselves for mentioning only one matter of great significance, worthy of remembrance: while all our people were contemplating abandoning the camp, taking flight, deserting their companions, and leaving behind everything they had carried away from such distant regions, through the saving help of repentance and fasting they were restored to such strength of steadfastness that shame alone over their former despair and flight afflicted them most severely.

Let this suffice concerning these matters.

## Chapter Three

### [Col. 0595A]

The count having thus been received with the greatest honor by the emperor and his princes, the emperor demanded from him the homage and oaths that the other princes had rendered to him.

The count replied that he had not come in order to make another man his lord or to serve anyone except the one for whom he had abandoned his homeland and the goods of his homeland. Nevertheless, he said that if the emperor went to Jerusalem with the army, he would entrust himself, his men, and all that he possessed to him.

But the emperor excused the journey, saying that he feared the Alemanni, the Hungarians, the Cumans, and other savage peoples, who would devastate his empire if he himself crossed through it with the pilgrims.

Meanwhile, hearing of the death and flight of his men, the count believed that he had been betrayed. Through certain princes from our army, he reminded the emperor Alexius of the treachery that had been committed.

Alexius, however, said that he had not known that our men had devastated his realm and that his own people had suffered many injuries. There was nothing about which the count could complain, except that, while the count’s army was ravaging villages and castles in its customary manner, the inhabitants had seen his army and taken flight. Nevertheless, he promised to satisfy the count and gave Bohemond as a hostage for the satisfaction.

They came to judgment, and the count was compelled, contrary to justice, to release the hostage.

Meanwhile our army came to Constantinople. Afterward the bishop joined us with his brother, whom he had left sick at Dyrrachium. Alexius sent messages back and forth and promised that he would give the count many things if he rendered the homage he demanded, as the other princes had done for him.

The count was constantly considering how he might avenge the injury done to his men and drive away from himself and his people the disgrace of so great an infamy. But the duke of Lorraine, the count of Flanders, and the other princes detested such a course, saying that it was extremely foolish to fight against Christians while the Turks were threatening them.

Bohemond, however, promised that he would help the emperor if the count attempted anything against him or continued for long to refuse homage and oaths.

After taking counsel with his men, the count swore to Alexius that he would preserve his life and honor and would not take them away either himself or through another. When the matter of homage was raised, he replied that he would not perform it at the risk of his life. Therefore Alexius gave him only a few gifts.

## Chapter Four

### [Col. 0595D]

We then crossed the sea and reached Nicaea. The duke, Bohemond, and the other princes had gone ahead of the count and were engaged in the siege.

Nicaea is an exceedingly well-fortified city, both by nature and by human ingenuity. To the west it has a great lake flowing up to its walls; on the other three sides it has a ditch filled by the stagnation of certain streams. Moreover, it is surrounded by walls so lofty that it fears neither the assault of men nor the attack of any engine. The ballista emplacements of the neighboring towers face one another in such a way that no one can approach without danger. If anyone tries to come closer, since he cannot do harm, he is easily overwhelmed from the height of the towers.

Bohemond therefore besieged this city, as we have described it, from the north; the duke and the Alemanni from the east; and the count and the bishop of Le Puy from the south, for the count of Normandy was not yet with us.

But we must not keep silent about this one matter. When the count wished to lodge there with his men, Turks descending from the mountains attacked our army in two squadrons. Their plan was that, while one group attacked the duke and the Alemanni on the eastern side, another group of Turks would enter through the southern side of the city and leave through another gate, easily driving our men from the camp while they were expecting nothing of the kind.

But God, who customarily overturns the plans of the wicked, so emptied their preparations that, as the Turkish squadron was already almost entering the city in ordered formation, he sent it against the count and his men, who wished to take lodging there. At the first attack the count put them to flight, killed many, and pursued the rest to the summit of the mountain.

The other group of Turks, which had intended to attack the Alemanni, was similarly routed and struck down.

After this, engines were constructed and the wall was attacked, but in vain. The wall opposite us was extremely strong and was defended bravely with arrows and engines. Thus we fought for five weeks to no purpose.

At last, by God’s will, certain members of the count’s and bishop’s households approached the corner tower facing south, at considerable danger. After constructing a protective tortoise, they began to hollow out one of the towers, and by hollowing it out brought it down to the ground.

The city would therefore have been captured had not the darkness of night intervened. The inhabitants repaired the wall during the night and rendered our earlier labor useless.

Nevertheless, the terrified city was compelled by that fear to surrender itself. It was further influenced by the fact that the emperor’s ships, dragged overland, had descended into the lake.

For these reasons, when the inhabitants no longer hoped for any further relief and saw the Frankish army increasing daily, they lost confidence in their strength and surrendered to Alexius.

The count of Normandy had arrived. Alexius had promised the princes and the Frankish people that he would return to them all the gold and silver, horses, and every kind of property that was inside the city; that he would establish there a Latin monastery and a hospice for the poor Franks; and, in addition, that he would give so much from his own resources to each person in the army that they would always wish to serve him.

The Franks therefore praised the surrender, trusting these words as entirely reliable. Alexius, having received the city, gave the army such a reward of gratitude that, for as long as he lives, the people will always curse him and proclaim him a traitor.

## Chapter Five

We then learned that the emperor had betrayed Peter the Hermit, who had come to Constantinople long before our armies with a great multitude. For the emperor compelled him—although he was ignorant of the region and inexperienced in every aspect of military affairs—and his people to cross over and exposed them to the Turks.

When the Turks from Nicaea saw that unarmed multitude, they beheaded as many as sixty thousand of them without labor or delay. The rest, fleeing to a certain fortified place, escaped the Turks’ swords.

The Turks, consequently, having become bold and proud, sent the weapons they had captured there and the prisoners to the nobles of their own people and of the Saracens far away. They wrote to peoples and distant cities that the Franks were worthless in war.

Having therefore departed from the city of Nicaea toward Romania, on the second day Bohemond rashly separated from the count, the bishop, and the duke.

On the third day after his departure, while he was arranging his tents to pitch them, they saw 150,000 Turks advancing to battle. While he organized his ranks as circumstances required and arranged the battle, he lost many who were following from his army.

Meanwhile he sent word to the count and the duke to come to his aid, for they were two miles away. As soon as Bohemond’s messenger reached the camp, everyone seized horses and arms and hurried to meet him.

When Soliman and those who were with him realized that our army—that is, the army of the bishop, the duke, and the count—was advancing against theirs for battle, he despaired of victory and was forced to flee. Through God’s power he abandoned the prisoners and many tents he had taken from Bohemond’s camp.

A notable miracle is reported, although we did not see it ourselves: two mounted men in gleaming armor and with wondrous faces went ahead of our army and pressed upon the enemy so severely that they allowed them no opportunity to fight. When the Turks tried to strike them with lances, they appeared invulnerable.

We learned these things from those who, scorning the companionship of the others, joined us. The evidence we offer in testimony is this: throughout the first and second days, along the entire road, we found the dead horses of the enemy together with their dead masters.

Thus, after the Turks had been defeated and routed, we came peacefully and cheerfully through Romania as far as Antioch. But the count delayed the army somewhat because of his illness.

Although we know very well that this will be unwelcome to unbelievers, we must not conceal what divine mercy accomplished. There was a certain count from Saxony in our army who came to Count Raimundus and claimed to be a messenger of Saint-Gilles. He said that he had been instructed once and again to tell the count:

“Be confident; you will not die from this illness. I have obtained for you a respite from God; I shall always be with you.”

Although the count believed these words to a considerable degree, he was nevertheless so afflicted by the illness that, when removed from his bed and placed on the ground, he scarcely had a living pulse. Accordingly, the bishop of the city of Orange performed the rites for him as though he were dead. But divine mercy, which had made him leader of its army, immediately raised him from death and restored him to health.

When we approached Antioch, many of the princes did not advise besieging it, especially since winter was approaching and the army, which had been dispersed among the castles, had been reduced during the summer. They said that the emperor’s forces ought also to be awaited, as well as the army from France that was reported to be coming; they therefore ordered that we remain there until spring.

But other princes, among whom was the count, said that we had come through God’s inspiration; that by his mercy we had gained possession of the extremely well-fortified city of Nicaea; and that through his clemency we had obtained victory and security against the Turks. There had been peace and concord in our army, and therefore the decision should be entrusted to us.

They said that there was no need to fear kings or the leaders of kings, nor to dread places and seasons, since the Lord had rescued us from so many dangers.

We therefore came to Antioch and pitched our camp nearby, so close that the enemy frequently wounded our men and horses in their tents from the towers.

Since Antioch has now offered us an occasion, it seems necessary to describe the situation of the place, so that those who did not see it may more easily understand the battles and assaults that took place there.

There is a certain plain between the mountains of Lebanon. In width it occupies one day’s journey for a traveler, and in length a day and a half. On the west this plain has a marsh; on the east, a river. The river surrounds part of the plain, running at the foot of the mountains that lie along its southern side, so that there is no passage between the mountains and the river; thus it flows into the Mediterranean Sea, which is close to Antioch.

Antioch is situated in those narrow places formed by the river as it clings to the mountains just mentioned. On the western side, the river flows up against the lower wall and leaves between itself and the city a section of land shaped somewhat like an arrow.

In this manner the city, situated on the eastern side, rises toward the east and encompasses within its circuit the ridges of three mountains. The mountain it has to the north is separated from the others by an enormous precipice, so that access from it to the others is either impossible or extremely difficult.

On the northern hill there is a castle; in the middle of the hill there is another castle, called in Greek *Colax*. On the third hill there are only towers.

The city extends for two miles in length and is so fortified with walls, towers, and outworks that it fears neither the assault of any engine nor the attack of men, even if every kind of person were to assemble against it.

The Frankish army therefore besieged this city, so strongly fortified as we have described it, from the north. Yet, although there were 300—or perhaps 300,000—armed men in the army, they made no assault there, but merely established their camp beside the city.

Inside the city there were 2,000 excellent soldiers, 4,000 or 5,000 ordinary soldiers, and 10,000 infantry, or more. The walls were so lofty and were protected by a ditch and marshes that the gates could be guarded while everything else remained secure.

When we first arrived, we pitched our camp so rashly that, had the enemy known in advance, some part of it could have been seized by them, since no watch was ever maintained in our army and no regular method of lodging was observed.

It also happened that all the castles of that region and the neighboring cities surrendered to our men, partly from fear of our army and partly from their desire to escape Turkish servitude. This greatly dispersed our army, for everyone wanted to enlarge his private possessions and no one thought about the common good.

Meanwhile those who remained in the camp had such an abundance of provisions that, from the cattle, they were unwilling to take anything except thighs and shoulders, and only very rarely the breast. As for grain and wine, it is unnecessary to say how cheaply they were acquired.

While these things were happening in the camp, the enemy at first concealed themselves so completely inside the walls that no one except the guards could be seen on the ramparts.

When they had learned that our men were openly and unarmed ravaging villages and fields, I do not know whether enemies sent out from Antioch or coming from another city two days away, called Caleph, began to kill those of our men whom they found traveling openly and unarmed.

This reduced the numbers in our camp somewhat. The enemy, however, taking advantage of the opportunity for slaughter and plunder, blockaded the roads with much greater boldness.

When this became plainly known in the camp, Bohemond was chosen to go out against them. The counts of Flanders and Normandy went with him.

They could take no more than 150 soldiers with them; and, had shame at turning back not prevented it, they would have returned because of the small number of their men.

Thus, compelled by God, they set out, found the enemy, pursued them, and forced them to be killed in the river. Having won the victory and secured the spoils, they returned to the camp amid immense rejoicing.

## Chapter Six

### [Col. 0599C]

Meanwhile ships from Genoa reached the shore, which was ten miles from the camp. That place is called the port of Saint Simeon.

By now the enemy were gradually leaving the city and killing the squires or peasants who were grazing horses or oxen beyond the river, then carrying the booty inside the city.

We had pitched our tents beside the river and had built a bridge there from ships that had been found at the site. The city also had a bridge, as it were at the lower western corner, and a certain hill opposite us, where there were two *bafumariae*—structures of uncertain type—and some clusters of burial houses.

We have mentioned these details so that the events we shall relate may be readily understood.

As we have said, when the enemy’s boldness had gradually increased to some degree, our men, going out boldly from the camp, did not fear attacking them, although they were often fewer in number than the enemy.

Although the Turks were frequently routed and put to flight, they immediately returned to the battle. This was partly because they possessed extremely swift horses and were lightly equipped, burdened by no weapons heavier than bows; partly because they had the hope of retreating to the bridge we have mentioned; and partly because from the hill they had the opportunity to shoot from a distance.

Their bridge was approximately one mile from our bridge. On the plain between the two bridges there were continual assaults and daily fighting.

## Chapter Seven

At the beginning of the siege it happened that the count and the bishop of Le Puy pitched their camp beside the river. For this reason they were very frequently attacked by the enemy, being closer to them.

Through assaults of this kind it came about that they lost all their horses, since the Turks, being prepared to fight not with lances or swords but with arrows, were formidable at a distance both when they fled and when they pursued.

When, in the third month of the siege, provisions began to be purchased at a higher price, Bohemond and the count of Flanders were chosen to lead the army into Spain for supplies, while the count and the bishop of Le Puy were left as a garrison in the camp. At that time the count of Normandy was absent, and the duke was suffering from a serious illness.

When the enemy learned this, they began their customary assaults. The count was compelled, as usual, to attack them. Having drawn up the infantry in formation, he himself pursued the attackers with a number of soldiers, captured and killed two of them as they descended the hill, and forced all the enemy to enter across the bridge.

When our infantry saw this, they abandoned their positions and left their standards, rushing in a confused mass as far as the enemy’s bridge.

When they had become almost confident there and were throwing stones and missiles at those defending the bridge, the Turks formed their ranks and began to charge against our men across the bridge and through the ford below it.

Meanwhile our soldiers were pursuing toward our bridge a certain horse whose rider they had thrown down. When our people saw this, they supposed that the soldiers were fleeing from the enemy’s attacks and, without delay, turned their backs to the enemy.

The Turks, however, continually killed those who were fleeing. When the Frankish soldiers wished to resist and fight on behalf of their men, they were seized by the multitude of fleeing infantry and, caught by their weapons, the manes and tails of the horses, were either thrown from their horses or carried along in flight for the sake of their companions’ mercy and safety.

The enemy, without delay or mercy, pursued the slaughter and began stripping the corpses of the dead.

It was not enough for our men to abandon their weapons, take flight, and disregard shame; they also plunged into the river, where they were overwhelmed by the stones or arrows of the enemy or remained beneath the water. If skill and strength in swimming carried anyone across the river, he reached the camp of his companions.

Our flight extended from their bridge to our bridge. As many as fifteen of our soldiers fell there, together with approximately twenty infantrymen. The bishop’s standard-bearer was killed there, and his standard was captured.

A certain most noble young man, Barnard Raimundus, a native of Béziers, also died there.

Let the servants of God neither blame nor become angry with us for committing the shame of our army so openly to memory. For God, who wished in this way to shake the minds of men guilty of disgrace, adultery, and plunder toward repentance, gladdened our army in Spain at that same time.

A report leaving our camp announced every kind of success and informed Bohemond and his companions that the count had won a most noble victory. This report raised their spirits considerably.

For when Bohemond was attacking a certain village, he suddenly heard some of his own peasants fleeing and shouting. When he had sent soldiers to meet them, they saw an army of Turks and Arabs at close quarters.

Among those who had gone out to investigate the causes of the flight and shouting was the count of Flanders, accompanied by certain men from Provence. All those from Burgundy, Auvergne, and Gascony were called Provençals; the others, in this army, were called Frenchmen. Among the enemy, however, the Franks were called “French.”

The count of Flanders, as we have said, considering it shameful to report the enemy before attacking them, charged irresistibly into the Turkish ranks. The Turks, unaccustomed to wage war with swords, took flight as their refuge.

The count did not sheath his sword until he had deprived a hundred of the enemy of life.

When he was returning victorious to Bohemond, he saw 12,000 Turks coming after him, and from the hill nearest on the left he saw an innumerable multitude of infantry rising.

After conferring with the rest of the army, he again took up a position with a larger force and attacked the enemy bravely. Bohemond followed at a distance with the rest and guarded the rear ranks.

For this is the Turks’ customary method of fighting: although they may be fewer in number, they always strive to surround their opponents. They also attempted to do this in the present battle, but Bohemond’s prudence forestalled the enemy’s ambush.

When the Turks and Arabs who were advancing against the count of Flanders saw that the matter would no longer be conducted with arrows at a distance but with swords at close quarters, they turned to flight.

The count pursued them for two miles, and, just as one might see sheaves of harvested grain lying on their backs in a field, so in that broad field one could see the bodies of the slain lying face upward.

The enemy ambush that Bohemond had endured was likewise routed and put to flight. The innumerable multitude of infantry mentioned above escaped by fleeing through places inaccessible to horses.

I would dare, were I not judged arrogant, to prefer this battle to the battles of the Maccabees. For if the Maccabee, with 3,000 men, struck down 48,000 of the enemy, here more than 60,000 enemies were put to flight by the aid of 400 soldiers.

But we neither despise the Maccabee nor proclaim the courage of our soldiers. We proclaim that God, then wondrous in the Maccabee, was more wondrous in our men.

### [Col. 0601D]

It is worth noting that, after the enemies had been routed, our men’s boldness diminished, so that they did not dare pursue those whom they saw being driven headlong.

## Chapter Eight
Therefore, when the victorious but depleted army returned, such great famine prevailed in the camp that barely two solidi sufficed to provide a man with bread for one day, and the other necessities were no less expensive. The poor began to leave, and many rich men, fearing poverty, did likewise. If any remained in the camp out of love for valor, they were forced to watch their horses waste away from prolonged hunger. Indeed, there was not even enough straw, and grain was so costly that seven or eight solidi were insufficient for a horse for one night.

Another calamity also befell the army: Bohemond, who had become highly distinguished in Spain, [Col. 0602A] declared that he would depart, because he had come for honor and now saw his men and horses perishing; he also said that he was not wealthy enough for the resources of his household to suffice for so long a siege. We later learned that he said this because, out of ambition, he was coveting the city of Antioch.

Meanwhile, a great earthquake occurred on the Kalends of January, and we saw a remarkably portentous sign in the sky. For during the first watch of the night, the sky in the north was so red that it seemed as though dawn had arisen and was bringing the day. Although God was scourging His army in this way so that we might attend to the light arising in the darkness, nevertheless the minds of certain men were so blind and headlong that they were not recalled from lust or plunder.

At that time the bishop proclaimed a three-day fast [Col. 0602B] to the people, together with a procession, prayers, and almsgiving; to the priests he sent instructions that they should devote themselves to Masses and prayers, and the clerics to psalms. Thus the merciful Lord, remembering His own compassion, delayed vengeance upon His children, lest the arrogance of their adversaries grow.

Moreover, there was in our army a certain man from the emperor’s household, whom Alexius had handed over to us as his representative. His name was Tatic; he was mutilated in the nose and utterly lacking in every virtue. I had almost forgotten him, since he was destined to be consigned to perpetual oblivion. Yet every day he whispered into the ears of the princes that they should depart to the neighboring camps and from there, by frequent attacks and ambushes, drive the people of Antioch away.

When all this became clearly known to the count [Col. 0602C]—for he had been ill from the day on which he had been forced to flee at the bridge—he summoned his princes and the bishop of Puy to a single meeting. After taking counsel, he gave them five hundred marks of silver, expressly on the condition that, if any of his soldiers lost his horse, it should be replaced for him from those five hundred marks, as well as from the other resources granted to the brotherhood.

This arrangement concerning the brotherhood was very beneficial at that time. The poor men of our army who wished to cross beyond the river to gather herbs feared the frequent attacks of the enemy; and, since scarcely anyone wished to go out against the enemy when the horses were hungry and weak, and since there were very few horses—so that scarcely a hundred could be found in the entire army of the count and the bishop. [Col. 0602D]

The same thing had happened to Bohemond and the others. For this reason our soldiers were not afraid to encounter the enemy, especially those who had worthless or weak horses, since they knew that, if their own were lost, they would receive better ones.

Another circumstance was added to this: all the princes except the count had made an agreement with Bohemond concerning the city while it was being captured. By this pact Bohemond and the other princes swore that they would not withdraw from the siege of Antioch for seven years unless the city were captured.

## CHAPTER IX

While these things were taking place in the camp, a report also announced that the emperor’s army was coming. It was said to have been gathered from many peoples, such as Slavs, Pechenegs, Cumans, and Turcopoles. Turcopoles [Col. 0603A] are those who have either been raised among the Turks or have been born of a Christian mother and a Turkish father.

These peoples, because they had harmed us on the journey, admitted that they feared an association with us in advance. But all this had been contrived by that mutilated Tatic, who was devising such stories so that he could depart. He slipped away by flight, not only through fabrications but also through enormous expenditures, compounded by the betrayal of his companions and perjury. For he granted Bohemond two or, I do not know, three cities: Tursol, Mamista, and Addeva. Thus, having purchased for himself and his people everlasting disgrace, he set out under God’s curse, pretending to be traveling to the emperor’s army, while abandoning his tents and his household.

At that time we were informed that the duke of Aleppo, having recruited [Col. 0603B] a large army from Chorasan, was coming to relieve the city of Antioch. Therefore, after a council had been held in the bishop’s house, it was decided that the infantry should guard the camp, while the soldiers should go outside the camp to meet the enemy. They said that many of our army, being unwarlike and timid, would display examples of fear rather than courage if they saw the multitude of the Turks.

Accordingly, they set out toward evening so that those who were in the city would not perceive them and inform those who had come to their aid. They hid themselves among the thickets, two leagues from our camp. When morning came, the enemy appeared with the sun.

Let those who have at any time attempted to harm the army hear—yes, let them hear, I beg—that when they recognize God magnifying His mercy toward us, they may strive to make satisfaction through the lamentations of repentance. The soldiers were arranged in six divisions, and God multiplied them so greatly that although scarcely seven hundred had appeared before the formation, after the division had been made it was asserted that more than two thousand were present in each unit. What should I say about their courage, when the soldiers performed even their military songs so joyfully that they seemed to regard the impending battle as a game?

The battle took place in a place where a marsh and a river lay close to one another, about a mile apart. This prevented the enemy from moving freely and from forming up in their customary manner. For God, who had granted us everything else, provided six continuous valleys for those advancing to battle. They emerged in a single hour and occupied the field; and, with the sun still shining, battle was joined with arms and shields. [Col. 0603D]

At first our men began to advance little by little. The Turks, however, darted about and shot arrows, yet withdrew. Our men endured this for a while, until the foremost Turks were packed together with those behind them. For, as we learned from their fugitives, no fewer than twenty-eight thousand Turks are said to have been present in this battle.

When the first Turkish line had been sufficiently hemmed in by those behind it, the Franks invoked God and charged forward. Without delay the Lord was present, “strong and mighty in battle” (Ps. 23:8): He protected His children and struck down their enemies. The Franks pursued them as far as their very strongly fortified castle, which was ten miles from the place of battle. When the castellans saw their people fleeing, they set fire to the castle and took flight. [Col. 0604A] This was entirely a source of joy and exultation for us, so that we acknowledged a second victory in the burning of the castle.

## CHAPTER X

On that same day such a great battle took place in the camp that, on the side facing the city, there was no place where fighting was not occurring. The enemy had arranged that, while those under siege attacked us with the utmost ferocity, their unexpected auxiliaries would crush us from behind. But God, who was granting victory to our soldiers, was fighting in our infantry.

That day our soldiers carried off no less a triumph over those under siege than they had won glory over their supporters. After gaining victory and booty, the heads of the slain were carried to the camp. To display fear to the enemy and to provide testimony [Col. 0604B] of the defeat of their relief force, the heads were carried out and hung upon stakes. We later believed that this had happened by God’s design. For, having recently captured the banner of the Blessed Ever-Virgin Mary, they had planted its spear in the ground as though to insult us. Thus it came about that, when they saw the heads of their own men set upright, they were recalled from insulting us.
