At that time there were envoys in our camp from the king of Babylon. When they saw the wonders that God was accomplishing through His servants, they glorified Jesus, the son of the Virgin Mary, who through His poor men was trampling down the most powerful. These envoys promised us the king’s favor and goodwill; moreover, they reported several benefits bestowed by the king upon the Christians of Egypt and upon our pilgrims. Accordingly, our envoys were sent back with them, so that they might enter into a treaty of friendship and alliance with the king.

At the same time our princes decided that a castle should be fortified on the hill above Bohemond’s tents, so that, if the enemy came against us again, they would in no way be able to assault our tents. When this had been done, our camp was made so strongly fortified that, enclosed like a city, we were protected on every side by both construction and nature. This castle lay to our east; to the south were the city walls and the marsh, which strengthened the walls and also protected our camp, while granting those in the city no opportunity to fight unless they came out through the gates. To the west was the river; to the north was an old rampart which, descending from the mountain, extended as far as the river. [Col. 0604D]

The people also urged that another castle be fortified on the hillock above their bridge. Engines were constructed in the camp to batter the city walls, but this proved useless.

When we had reached the fifth month of our siege and ships carrying provisions began arriving at our harbor from every direction, the Turks in the city began to blockade the sea routes and kill the carriers of food. At first our princes merely endured this. But the Turks, emboldened by impunity in their crime and by hope of plunder, pressed us day and night.

At last it was decided that we should fortify a castle at their bridge. But, because many of our men had gone to the harbor, the count and Bohemond were chosen to bring them back, carrying mattocks and other tools with which the rampart of the new castle could be built. When it became known in the city that the count and Bohemond were absent, the enemy began their usual attacks.

Our men, advancing too rashly and without order, were shamefully routed and put to flight. On the fourth day, when the count and Bohemond were returning from the harbor with a very large force, the Turks reconnoitered them; our men, however, thought themselves secure merely because of the commotion they themselves were making.

But why delay over details? Battle was joined, and our men turned their backs. We lost as many as three hundred men; how much booty and how many weapons were lost is not for us to say. While we were slaughtered and dashed to pieces like cattle throughout the mountains and over every precipice, the men from the camp began to advance to meet the enemy. Thus it happened that they were recalled from killing the fugitives. [Col. 0605B]

What then, Lord God? They have been defeated in the camp, and these two greatest princes in Your army have been defeated outside the camp! Shall we flee to the camp, or shall those from the camp come to us? “Rise up and help us, Lord, for the sake of Your name” (Ps. 43).

For if it became known in the camp that the princes had been defeated, or if it happened that we learned of the flight of those in the camp, a common flight of everyone would follow. Therefore the Lord, “who rises as a helper in times of trouble” (Ps. 9), arose and inspired those whom He had previously driven back to be the first to enter the battle.

When Cassianus, who was governor of the city, saw the spoils of our men, the victory of his own people, and the continuing courage of some of our men, he sent out all his soldiers and infantry. Then, moved by hope of victory, he ordered the city gates to be closed behind his men, announcing to his soldiers [Col. 0605C] that they must conquer or die.

Meanwhile our men advanced little by little and in accordance with command. The Turks darted about, shot arrows, and charged with excessive boldness. Our men endured this for a time, until they could attack in close formation; they were not held back from their assault.

Such was the mourning and clamoring in the camp before God that one might have thought that the abundance of tears was bringing down God’s mercy. When the matter had to be settled at close quarters, a certain soldier, Isuardus of Gagia, a most noble man of Provence, with one hundred and fifty infantrymen, invoked God, knelt down, and exhorted his comrades, saying: “Come, soldiers of Christ!” Then he charged the enemy; and our other lines charged in the same way.

The arrogance of the enemy was thrown into confusion; the gate was closed, the bridge was narrow, and the river truly immense. What then? The enemy, thrown into confusion, were struck down and slaughtered, and buried beneath stones in the river, while no avenue of escape lay open to them. Had Cassianus not opened the gate of the bridge, we would have had peace from Antioch on that day. I heard from many who were there that they had overwhelmed more than thirty Turks in the river with the bridge’s wooden planks.

The duke of Lorraine distinguished himself greatly there. He reached the bridge before the enemy and, having climbed the steps, divided those who were coming by cutting through their midst. After celebrating the victory with immense exultation, much booty, and many horses, our men returned to the camp.

A memorable thing happened there—would that those who pursue us with their prayers could have seen it! One of the enemy’s horsemen, in fear of death, was entering the river’s precipitous depths when many of his own people seized him and pulled him from his horse; he was overwhelmed in midstream together with the multitude that had apprehended him. [Col. 0606A]

It was well worth seeing certain poor men returning from the victory. Some rode about among the tents on various horses, displaying to their comrades the relief of their poverty. Others, dressed in two or three silken garments, magnified God, the giver of victory and bounty. Still others, protected by three or four shields, eagerly displayed the triumph of their victory.

Although by these and other displays they had persuaded us of the reality of the magnificent victory, they could not persuade us concerning the number of those killed. Since the victory had been won at nightfall, the heads of the slain were not brought to the camp.

When, on the following day, the castle before their bridge was being built, some Turks were found in the rampart. That mountain had been a burial place for the Saracens. The poor men, provoked by these discoveries, broke all their tombs. When the Turks had been dug up, no one could doubt what sort of victory had been won. For approximately fifteen hundred were counted. I say nothing for the moment of those buried in the city or dragged into the river.

When the corpses, whose intolerable stench afflicted those in the castle, became an obstruction, they were thrown into the river. The sailors who had been scattered and wounded during the flight of the count and Bohemond still doubted the victory out of fear. But when they saw so great a multitude, they began, as though recovering from a certain illness, to magnify God, [Col. 0606C] who is accustomed both to correct and to gladden His children.

Thus, by God’s design, it came about that those who had given the carriers of provisions, killed on the shore and along the riverbanks, to wild beasts and birds became, in those same places, provisions for wild beasts and birds themselves. After the victory had been celebrated and recognized, and the castle had been built, the city of Antioch was besieged from the north and the south.

## CHAPTER XI

At that time it was considered which of the princes might move over to guard the castle, since a common responsibility is frequently neglected by many when each supposes that it is being guarded by the others. While some of the princes were seeking, almost as payment, the assistance of guards from others, the count, against the wishes of his own men, took upon himself the guardianship of the castle, both to excuse their indolence and greed and to show those who were sluggish the path of courage and prudence.

For he had been exhausted by a severe and prolonged illness during the previous summer and had been so debilitated throughout the entire winter that he was said to be ready neither to fight nor to give generously. Although he was capable of much, because he was believed capable of more, he was regarded as being of no account. When he encountered this difficulty—namely, an opportunity for virtue—he suffered such great envy from everyone that he was almost separated from his own personal retainers.

Meanwhile, while the count was neglecting these matters, hoping that the enemy in the city, largely overwhelmed, would immediately flee, he was surrounded by the enemy at dawn one day. There the great miracle of divine protection became evident: sixty of our men withstood a battle against seven thousand Saracens. What makes it even more remarkable is that, in the preceding days, an excessive rain had moistened the fresh earth and filled the rampart of the new castle. Thus it was not any impassable terrain but solely God’s power that held back the enemy. [Col. 0607A]

I do not think that I should now pass over the outstanding courage of certain of our soldiers. Caught by the enemy while guarding their bridge, they were unable to retreat to the castle, for the castle was about one arrow-shot away from their bridge. These soldiers therefore made a circuit through the midst of the enemy and reached the corner of a nearby house. There they bravely and fearlessly withstood the enemy’s assault, the fury of their arrows, and the cloud of stones hurled from every direction.

Meanwhile the sound of the battle, heard in the camp, roused our men. Thus the castle was freed from the enemy. Although the enemy had abandoned the attack when they saw reinforcements approaching from afar, and although their bridge was nearby, their rear ranks were nevertheless killed.

The rampart and walls of the castle were then rebuilt, and the carriers of provisions were able to go safely to and from the harbor. The envy that the count had endured was so greatly softened that everyone called him the father and protector of the army. From that time the count’s renown increased, because he alone had withstood the attacks of the enemy.

After the bridge and the city gate had been blockaded, the Turks began to come out through another gate, which faced south beside the river, and to send their horses to a certain secluded place between the mountains and the river that provided excellent pasture. Our men reconnoitered the place, chose a day, and, circling the city by a difficult route over the mountain, arrived at those pastures. Some crossed by the ford and brought back two thousand horses, besides the mules and she-mules that were recovered.

For during the preceding winter, on the sea route, they had taken many mules from us. These were now captured and recognized by their owners, and returned to their former masters. [Col. 0607C]

After this, Tancred fortified a certain monastery beyond the river. For this purpose the count gave him one hundred marks of silver, and the other princes contributed as they were able. This placed the enemy under considerable pressure.

It is pleasing to observe that the fewer we are in number, the stronger God’s grace has made us. Meanwhile messengers began to arrive with great frequency, reporting that reinforcements were coming to the enemy. This report reached us not only from Armenians and Greeks, but was also announced to us by those who were in the city. For the Turks had held Antioch for fourteen years, and, because of the scarcity of members of their own households, had made Armenians and Greek youths Turkish in custom, as it were, and had given them wives.

When such men had the opportunity to escape, they came over to us with horses and weapons. As this report of the enemy’s reinforcements grew more widespread, many of our people, overcome by fear, began to flee, as did the Armenian merchants.

## CHAPTER XII

Meanwhile the good soldiers who had been dispersed among the castles began to come and to buy, fit, and repair weapons. When the swelling pride of our army had sufficiently wasted away and the courage that was always ready to face dangers with and for the brothers had returned, a certain Turk who was in the city sent word through Bohemond to our princes that he would surrender the city to us.

After taking counsel together, the princes sent Bohemond, the duke of Lorraine, and the count of Flanders to test the matter. When they arrived in the middle of the night at the city hill, the intermediary, sent back by the man who was surrendering the city, said: “Wait until the lamp passes.” For three or four men carrying lamps went along the city walls throughout the night, rousing and warning the guards.

After this, as our men approached the wall and raised a ladder, they began to climb. The first was a certain Frank named Fulcher, the brother of Budellus [Col. 0608B] of Chartres; he climbed the wall fearlessly. The count of Flanders followed him and ordered Bohemond and the duke to climb. When everyone hurried so that one might get ahead of another, the ladder broke.

Those who had climbed nevertheless descended into the city and opened a small postern gate. Our men all entered, but they did not seize any of those whom they found. When dawn appeared, they raised a shout. At this cry the whole city was thrown into confusion, and their women and children began to weep.

Those who were in the count’s castle, all roused by this cry—for they were nearer—began saying to one another: “Their reinforcements have arrived.” Others, on the contrary, said: “That does not sound like the voice of rejoicing.”

As daylight increased, our standards appeared on the city’s southern hill. The citizens were thrown into confusion when they saw our men above them on the mountain. Some began to flee through the gates; others threw themselves down. No one stood firm, for the Lord had thrown them into confusion.

At last, after so much time, a delightful spectacle was presented to us: those who had held Antioch against us for so long were now unable to flee from it. If some of them dared to attempt escape, they nevertheless could not evade death.

Something happened there that was especially joyful and pleasing to us. As certain Turks tried to slip away through the precipices that divide the hill from the north, they encountered some of our men. When the Turks were forced to turn back, they threw themselves into flight with such force that, driven backward, they were all hurled down together. [Col. 0608D]

We rejoiced at the enemy who had been thrown down, but we grieved over more than three hundred horses that were beheaded there. How many Saracens and Turks perished then we do not know; to explain the various deaths by which they fell would be cruel. As for the amount of booty captured within Antioch, it is not for us to say—believe and estimate as much as you wish, and then add more.

Those enemy troops who guarded the castle in the middle of the hill, seeing the death of their people and our men abandoning the attack upon them, retained their castle.

Cassianus, however, went out through a small postern gate, was captured by Armenian peasants, and beheaded; his head was then presented to us. I believe this happened by the ineffable providence of God [Col. 0609A], so that he who had caused many men of the same people to be beheaded … [the sentence is incomplete in the source].

The city of Antioch was therefore captured on the third day before the Nones of June, while the siege had begun approximately on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November.

Meanwhile, while our men abandoned the attack on the upper castle in order to count and identify the booty, and while they feasted splendidly and arrogantly, listening to the dancing women of the pagans, utterly unmindful of God, who had bestowed such a great benefit upon them, they were besieged by the pagans on the third day afterward, on the Nones of that same month of June.

Thus it came about that those who, through God’s mercy, had besieged the Turks of Antioch for so long were, by His disposition, themselves besieged by the Turks. And, to make us even more afraid, the aforesaid upper castle—which is almost the guardian of the city—was in the hands of the enemy. [Col. 0609B] Compelled by fear, our men therefore undertook the siege of the castle.

At the beginning of his arrival, Corbaras, lord of the Turks, expecting battle to begin immediately, pitched his tents far from the city, about two miles away, and, after forming his ranks, advanced as far as the city bridge. On the first day our men fortified the count’s castle, fearing that, if they went out to battle, the city might be seized by the enemy who were in the castle; or, if they abandoned the castle before the bridge and the enemy occupied it, they would close off our opportunity for battle and our means of departure.

## CHAPTER XIII

There was in the army a very distinguished soldier, beloved by everyone, named Rotger of Barnevilla. [Col. 0609C] While he was pursuing the army of all the returning enemies, he was captured and beheaded.

Grief and fear therefore invaded our people, to such an extent that many were driven almost to despair of escape. After the Turks had once and then twice been repulsed when attempting to fight, on the third day they attacked the castle. The battle there was waged with such force that it seemed that only God’s power could defend the castle and resist the adversaries.

For when they were already preparing to cross the rampart and tear down the wall, they suddenly conceived fear—from I do not know where—and rushed headlong into flight. After they had covered a short distance, seeing no reason for their flight, they blamed their own hesitation and returned to the attack. As though they wished to make amends for the shame of having fled, they pressed forward more violently and again fought for a long time with greater ferocity. Thus the enemy returned to their camp that day. [Col. 0609D]

On the following day, they began to return to the castle with the greatest preparation. Our men, however, set fire to the castle and withdrew within the city walls.

The fear of the Franks increased, and the courage of the enemy grew, since we had nothing outside the city and our enemies retained the castle, which was the city’s chief stronghold. The Turks therefore, emboldened, decided to enter against us through the castle.

Our men, relying on the advantageous position and elevation of the place, hastened to meet the enemy and struck them down at the first assault. But while they forgot the impending battle and gazed greedily at the booty, they were shamefully turned to flight. More than a hundred men were suffocated at the city gate, and very many horses as well. [Col. 0610A]

After entering the castle, the Turks wished to descend into the city. There was a valley between their castle and our mountain, not very large, with a cistern and a modest level area in the middle. There was no descent into the city except through the middle of our mountain.

Therefore they strove with all their concentration and strength to defeat us and remove us from the route by which they intended to enter the city. There the fighting was so fierce from morning until evening that nothing like it is ever heard of. Something happened there that was especially horrifying and, until then, unheard-of among our men: amid a hailstorm of arrows and the continuous blows of stones and missiles, and amid the deaths of so many, our men fell asleep.

If you ask how this battle ended, the answer is: night. At night, although our men ought to have hoped in God’s mercy, many began to despair and were thrown headlong from the height of the walls by ropes. Others, withdrawing from the battle into the city, announced to everyone that a general beheading had arrived. And, even while some urged others to resist bravely, they themselves turned to flight.

## CHAPTER XIV
Therefore, as we have said, while our men were thrown into confusion and rushing toward despair, divine clemency came to their aid; and, having corrected its wanton sons, it consoled them in this way when they had become excessively sorrowful. Thus, after the city of Antioch had been captured, the Lord, using his power and goodness, chose a certain poor peasant, a Provençal by birth, through whom he comforted us all, and sent these words to the count and the bishop of Le Puy:

“Andrew, the apostle of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, formerly warned me four times and ordered me to come to you and, once the city had been captured, return to you the lance that opened the Savior’s side. Today, however, when I had gone out of the city with the others to battle and, on the way back, had been seized by two horsemen and nearly suffocated, I withdrew there sorrowfully, as though lifeless, onto a certain stone. As I stumbled about sadly from grief and fear, blessed Andrew came before me with a companion and threatened me severely unless I quickly returned the lance to you.

“When the count and the bishop asked him to explain the circumstances of the apostolic revelation and vision, he replied:

“‘At the beginning of the earthquake that occurred at Antioch, when the Frankish army was besieging it, such fear seized me that I could say nothing except, “God, help!” It was night, and I was lying down; nor was there anyone in my hut whose company might comfort me. When, as I have said, the shaking continued for a long time and my fear kept increasing, two men appeared before me in exceedingly bright clothing. One was older, with reddish-gray hair, black eyes suited to his face, and a gray, broad, and long beard; he was of medium height. The other was younger and taller, handsome beyond the sons of men.

“‘The older man said to me, “What are you doing?” I was extremely frightened, because I knew that no one was there. I replied, “Who are you?” He said:

“‘“Rise, and do not be afraid; listen to what I shall say to you. I am the apostle Andrew. Gather the bishop of Le Puy, the count of Saint-Gilles, and Peter Raymond of Hautpoul, and say this to them: Why does the bishop neglect to preach, to admonish, and to sign the people with the cross that he carries before them? For this would greatly benefit them.”

“‘He added: “Come, and I shall show you the lance of our Father Jesus Christ, which you shall give to the count; for God granted it to him from the time he was born.”

“‘I rose, therefore, and followed him into the city, clothed in nothing but a shirt. He led me into the church of blessed Peter through the northern gate, which the Saracens had formerly made into a gate called the Baphumaria. In the church there were two lamps, which gave so much light there that it seemed as though midday had dawned. He said to me, “Wait here,” and ordered me to stand beside a column that was near the steps by which one ascended to the altar from the south. His companion stood at a distance, before the altar steps.

“‘Then blessed Andrew entered beneath the earth, brought out the lance, and placed it in my hands. He said to me: “Behold the lance that opened the side from which the salvation of the whole world flowed.” While I held it in my hands, weeping for joy, I said to him: “Lord, if you wish, I shall carry it and return it to the count.” He said to me: “Leave it for now, for the city is destined to be captured. Then you shall come with twelve men and seek it here, from where I have taken it and where I shall put it back.” And he put it back.

“‘When this had been done, he led me back over the city wall to my house, and then they departed from me. Reflecting afterward on my poverty and your greatness, I was afraid to approach you.

“‘After that, when I had gone to a certain fortress near Rûj, in search of food, on the first day of Lent, at cockcrow, blessed Andrew appeared to me in the same clothing, with the companion with whom he had previously come; and a great brightness filled the house. Blessed Andrew said: “Are you awake?” Thus roused, I replied: “No, my lord, I am not sleeping.” He said to me: “Have you said what I formerly commanded you to tell them?” I replied: “My lord, did I not ask you to send someone else to them? For, fearing my poverty, I hesitated to approach them.” He said to me:

“‘“Do you not know why God brought you here, how much he loves you, and how especially he chose you? He made you come here to avenge contempt for himself and his people. He loves you so much that the saints already placed in rest, foreseeing the grace of the divine arrangement, would wish to be in the flesh and strive alongside you. God chose you from all nations, as ears of wheat are gathered from among oats. For in merit and grace you surpass all who came before and will come after you, just as gold surpasses silver in value.”

“‘After this they departed, and such illness overwhelmed me that I lost the sight of my eyes and began to dispose of my extremely meager possessions. Then I began to think that these things had justly happened to me because I had neglected the apostolic vision. Thus strengthened, I returned to the siege.

“‘Again reflecting on the weakness of my poverty, I began to fear that, if I came to you, I would be hungry and that you would accuse me of reporting such things for the sake of food. So on that occasion too I kept silent.

“‘As time passed, when I was at the port of Saint Symeon and was lying beneath a tent with my lord William Peter, blessed Andrew appeared with his companion, in the same clothing in which he had come before, and spoke to me as follows: “Why have you not told the count and the bishop and the others what I commanded you?” I replied: “Did I not ask you, lord, to send someone else in my place, someone wiser and whom they would wish to hear? Moreover, there are Turks on the road who kill those coming and going.” Saint Andrew said: “Do not be afraid, for they will harm you in no way.

“‘“You shall also say this to the count: when he comes to the Jordan River, he must not enter it but cross by boat. After he has crossed, clothed in a shirt and linen breeches, he shall be sprinkled from the river. When his clothing has dried, he shall put it away and preserve it with the Lord’s lance.”

“‘My lord William Peter heard this as well, although he did not see the apostle. Thus strengthened, I returned to the army.

“‘When I wished to tell you these things all together, I could not assemble you. Therefore I went to the port of Mamista. There, when I wished to sail to the island of Cyprus for provisions, blessed Andrew threatened me severely unless I returned quickly and reported to you what had been entrusted to me. As I considered how I might return to the camps—for that port was about three days’ journey from the army—I began to weep most bitterly because I could find no way to return.

“‘At last, after my companions and my lord had urged me on, I boarded a ship, and we began to row toward Cyprus. After we had been driven along all day by oars and favorable winds, until sunset, a storm suddenly arose, and within the space of one or two hours we returned to the port we had left.

“‘There I fell into a very serious illness. Once the city had been captured, I came to you. And now, if it pleases you, test what I say.’”

The bishop thought that there was nothing in it except words. The count, however, immediately believed him and entrusted the man who had said these things to his chaplain Raymond to be kept under guard.

## CHAPTER XV

On that very night that followed, our Lord Jesus Christ appeared to a certain priest named Stephen, who was weeping over the death of himself and his companions, which he expected to occur at once. Certain men who had come down from the citadel had terrified him, saying that the Turks were already descending from the mountain into the city and that our men were fleeing and had been defeated.

Therefore, wishing to have God as a witness to his death, the priest entered the church of blessed Mary, ever-virgin. After making his confession and receiving absolution, he began to sing psalms with certain companions. The others fell asleep, while he kept watch alone; and when he had said, “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest upon your holy mountain?” (Psalm 14:1), a certain man stood before him, possessing beauty beyond all human appearance, and said to him:

“Man, what sort of people are these who have entered the city?”

The priest replied: “Christians.”

He said: “What kind of Christians?”

The priest answered: “Those who believe that Christ was born of the Virgin, suffered on the cross, died, and was buried; that he rose on the third day and ascended into heaven.”

The man said: “And if they are Christians, why do they fear a multitude of pagans?”

He added: “Do you recognize me?”

The priest replied: “I do not recognize you, lord, except that I see you to be the most beautiful of all.”

The man said: “Look at me most carefully.”

When the priest gazed intently at him, he saw a figure in the shape of a cross proceeding from the man’s head, brighter than the sun. The priest said to the man who had asked about his identity:

“Lord, we say that these are images of our Lord Jesus Christ that bear an appearance like yours.”

The Lord said to him: “You have answered well, because I am he. Is it not written of me, ‘The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle’?” (Psalm 23:8.) “And who is the Lord in the army?”

The priest replied: “Lord, there has never been only one lord there; rather, they trust the bishop more.”

The Lord said: “You shall say this to the bishop: ‘This people has distanced me from itself by doing evil.’ Therefore say to them: ‘Thus says the Lord: Turn back to me, and I shall turn back to you.’ And when they enter battle, let them say: ‘Our enemies have gathered, and they glory in their strength. Crush their power, Lord, and scatter them, for there is no other who fights for us except you, our God.’

“You shall also say this to them: ‘If you do what I command you for five days, I shall have mercy on you.’”

As he was saying this, a certain woman whose face was exceedingly inflamed approached. Looking at the Lord, she said to him:

“Lord, what are you saying to this man?”

The Lord answered her: “Lady, ask him about these people who have entered the city, and what sort of people they are.”

She said: “O my Lord, these are the people for whom I so greatly entreat you.”

When the priest struck his companion, who was sleeping nearby, wishing to have him as a witness to so great a vision, they were taken from his sight.

When morning came, the priest climbed the mountain where our princes were staying, opposite the Turkish citadel; the duke was absent, for he was guarding the citadel situated on the northern hill. The priest summoned an assembly and spoke these words to our princes, swearing upon the cross to show that they were true.

Wishing to satisfy those who did not believe, he was even willing either to pass through fire or to throw himself from the height of a tower. Then the princes swore that they would not flee from Antioch or leave it except by the common counsel of all. At that time the people believed that the princes wished to flee to the port.

Many were therefore encouraged. Indeed, on the preceding night only a few had remained steadfast in the faith and had refused to flee. Had the bishop and Bohemond not opened the city gates, scarcely anyone would have remained. William of Grandmesnil nevertheless fled, together with his brother, as did many others, laymen and clerics. It happened to many that, after escaping from the city at the greatest danger, they incurred an even greater danger of death in the hands of the Turks.

At that time many revelations came to us through our brothers, and we saw a wondrous sign in the sky. A very large star stood over the city throughout the night; shortly afterward it divided into three parts and fell on the Turkish side.

Our men, somewhat encouraged, awaited the fifth day that the priest had foretold. On another day, after the necessary preparations had been made, we began to dig with the man who had spoken of the lance, after all the others had been expelled from the church of Saint Peter. Among the twelve men were the bishop of Orange, Raymond the count’s chaplain, who wrote these things, the count himself, Pontius of Baladun, and Farald of Thouars.

They dug from morning until evening. In the evening some began to despair of finding the lance. The count had left because of the guarding of the citadel; in place of him and the others who were exhausted from digging, we brought in fresh men who would apply themselves bravely to the work.

Seeing that we were fatigued, the young man who had spoken of the lance unbelted himself and, barefoot and wearing only his shirt, descended into the pit. He urged us to pray to God that he might return his lance to us, for the strengthening and victory of his people.

At last, moved by the grace of his mercy, the Lord showed us his lance. I, who wrote these things, kissed it while only its point was still visible above the earth. I cannot say how much joy and exultation then filled the city. The lance was found on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July.

## CHAPTER XVI

On the second night blessed Andrew appeared to the young man through whom he had returned the lance to us, and said to him:

“Behold, God has granted the count what he never wished to grant to anyone else, and has appointed him standard-bearer of this army, provided that he perseveres in his love.”

When the young man asked him for mercy for the people, Saint Andrew replied that the Lord truly would have mercy on his people.

Again, when the young man asked him who his companion was, whom he had seen so many times, blessed Andrew said to him:

“Come and kiss his foot.”

Hurrying forward and wishing to approach, he saw upon the man’s foot a wound so fresh and bloody that it seemed to have just been made. When he hesitated to approach because of the wound and blood, Saint Andrew said:

“Behold the Father who was wounded for us on the cross, and this is the wound from it.”

“The Lord also commands you to celebrate the day on which he returned his lance to you. Since it was found in the evening and that day could not be celebrated solemnly, you shall celebrate the solemnity on the following week, during the octave; and thereafter every year on the day of the finding of the lance itself.

“You shall also say this to them: let them practice restraint, as the Epistle of my brother Peter teaches, which is read today.”

The Epistle was this:

“Be humbled under the powerful hand of God” (1 Peter 5:6).

“And every day let the clerics sing this hymn before the lance:

‘Six lustrums now completed …’

“And when they say, ‘The Lamb is raised upon the wood of the cross to be sacrificed,’ let them finish the hymn on bended knees.”

When the bishop of Orange and I asked whether he knew his letters, he replied: “I do not know.” He thought that if he said he did know them, we would not believe him. He knew them to some extent, but at that very moment he was so ignorant that he could not recognize even the letters, nor remember anything he had learned through letters, except the “Our Father,” the “I Believe in God,” the “Magnificat,” the “Glory to God in the highest,” and the “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel.” He had lost all the rest as though he had never heard them, and afterward he was able to recover only a few of them, and that with the greatest difficulty.

Meanwhile, such famine prevailed in the city that, apart from the tongue, a horse’s head was sold for two or three solidi; a goat’s entrails for five solidi; and a hen for eight or nine solidi. What shall I say about bread, when five solidi were not enough to drive hunger from one person?

Nor could this seem strange or burdensome to those who bought such things at so high a price, since they had an abundance of gold, silver, and cloaks. These things were expensive because the soldiers lacked the boldness of conscience to take them freely. They plucked unripe figs from the trees and sold them cooked at an exorbitant price. The hides of oxen and horses, as well as other neglected things that had likewise been boiled for a long time, were sold at an exorbitant price, so that anyone could eat two solidi’s worth.

Many soldiers lived on the blood of their own horses and, awaiting God’s mercy, were unwilling to kill them yet. These and many other evils threatened the besieged, and it is difficult to enumerate them.

There was also another sufficiently serious matter: some of our men fled to the Turks and informed them of the misery that existed in the city. Through these and other circumstances the Turks became emboldened and pressed upon us with the greatest force.

One day, around midday, about thirty Turks climbed onto one of our towers, and they greatly terrified our men. Nevertheless, our men, fighting for their lives with God’s help, killed some and forced others to throw themselves down.

For this reason everyone promised obedience to Bohemond until fifteen days after the battle, so that he might direct the guarding of the city and the war himself. The count and the bishop were growing very weak. Count Stephen, whom the other princes had chosen as commander before the city was captured, heard the report of the battle and had fled.

As we have said, when our men had been defeated, crushed, and distressed, heavenly assistance came to them. Blessed Andrew taught us, through the young man who had spoken of the lance, how we ought to act before and during the battle:

“You have all gravely offended,” he said, “and therefore you have been humbled; and you cried out to the Lord, and the Lord heard us. Now let each person, for his offenses, entrust himself to the Lord and make five almsgivings, because of the Lord’s five wounds. If he cannot do this, let him say the ‘Our Father’ five times, and so forth.

“When these things have been done, begin in the name of the Lord, in whatever decision the princes may agree concerning the battle, whether by day or by night, because the Lord’s hand will be with you.

“If anyone doubts the victory, let the gates be opened to him and let him go to the Turks; he will see how their god will save him.

“But if anyone refuses to fight, let him be with Judas, the Lord’s betrayer, who deserted the apostles and sold his Lord to the Jews.

“Let them fight in the faith of blessed Peter, holding to what Christ promised him: that after the third day he would rise again and appear to him; and also because this land belongs by right to blessed Peter and not to the pagans.

“Let the sign of your battle cry be ‘God, help!’ and truly God will help you. All your brothers who have died since the beginning of the journey will be present with you in this battle. You must defeat a tenth part of the enemy, for they, by God’s power, will defeat nine parts.

“Do not delay concerning the battle. For if you do not do what I say, the Lord will bring from the other side as many enemies as you have on one side, and he will keep you shut in here until some consume others.

“But know for certain that those days have arrived which the Lord promised to blessed Mary, ever-virgin, and to his apostles: that he would raise up the kingdom of the Christians, after the kingdom of the pagans had been cast down and trampled underfoot.

“Do not turn aside to their tents for gold and silver.”

## CHAPTER XVII

Then God’s power decreed that he who had ordered the things recounted above to be preached to us through his apostle so greatly strengthened everyone’s hearts that each person seemed already to have triumphed over his enemies through faith and hope.

They encouraged one another, and by encouraging one another regained their strength for battle. The common people, who in the preceding days had seemed to be consumed by want and fear, now even reviled the princes because of the delay in battle.

When the day for battle had been fixed, our men sent Peter the Hermit to Corbaran, the Turkish commander, to cease attacking the city, since it belonged by right to blessed Peter and to the Christians.

That proud man replied that, by right or by wrong, he wanted to possess the Franks and the city. He forced Peter the Hermit, who was unwilling to yield, to bow down and plead with him.

At that time it was asked who would guard the city against those who were in the citadel while the others went forth to battle. On the hill of our mountain, opposite the enemy, they built a wall of lime and fortifications. They equipped these with many stone-throwers and left there Count Raymond, who was weakening toward death, together with as many as two hundred men.

The day of battle had arrived. In the morning everyone received Communion and gave himself over to God, whether to death, if that was his will, or to the honor of the Roman Church and the Frankish people.

They arranged the battle in this way: from the count’s and the bishop’s forces there would be two double formations, so that the foot soldiers would go before the knights, march and stand at the command of the princes, and the knights would follow them and guard them from behind.

The same arrangement was made for Bohemond’s and Tancred’s forces; likewise for the forces of the Norman count and the Franks; and likewise for the duke’s forces and the Burgundians.

Heralds went through the city shouting that every man should join the princes of his own people. It was also ordered that Hugh the Great, the count of Flanders, and the Norman count should proceed first to battle, then the duke; after the duke, the bishop; and Bohemond should follow them.

Thus each man gathered according to his standard and kin-group inside the city, before the bridge gate.

O blessed people, whose God is the Lord! (Psalms 32, 143.) O blessed people whom God has chosen! (Psalm 32.) How changed was the appearance of this army, from sadness to joy!

In the preceding days, princes and nobles, together with those from the common people, had gone barefoot through the streets of the city, calling upon God’s help at the churches, weeping and beating their breasts, so sad that a father would neither return the greeting of a son who met him nor look at him, and a brother would do neither for his brother.

Now, however, you would have seen them joyfully sending out their horses, shaking their weapons, and brandishing their spears, unable to remain still without doing or saying something joyful, whether in word or deed.

But why delay over many details? Permission was granted them to leave, and the plans agreed upon by the princes were carried out in order.

Meanwhile, the Turkish commander Corbaras was playing chess inside his tent. When he received the news that the Franks were advancing to battle, he was disturbed in spirit, since he heard this contrary to expectation. He summoned a certain Turk named Miredalin, who had fled from Antioch, a nobleman known to us for his military skill, and said to him:

“What is this? Did you not tell me that the Franks were few and would never fight me?”

Miredalin replied: “I did not say that they would not fight. Come and look at them, and I shall tell you whether you will be able easily to overcome them.”

A third formation was also advancing. When he had seen the arrangement of the formations, Miredalin said to Corbaras:

“These men can indeed be killed, but they cannot be put to flight.”

Corbaras then said to him: “Can none of them be driven back at all?”

Miredalin replied: “They will not yield even as much as the sole of a foot, if every kind of pagan should attack them.”

Then Corbaras, although disturbed, arranged many and varied formations against us. Although they could initially have prevented our exit, they allowed us to leave peacefully.

Our men, however, directed their lines toward the mountains, taking care that the enemy not surround us from behind. The mountains were far from the bridge, nearly two large miles away.

We advanced with measured breadth, as clerics usually proceed in processions; and indeed it was a procession for us. Priests and many monks, dressed in white stoles, went before our lines of soldiers, singing and invoking God’s help and the protection of the saints.

The enemy, by contrast, wanted to attack us and shot arrows. Corbaras also sent word to our princes:

“He was ready now to do what he had recently refused: that five or ten Turks should fight the same number of Franks, and that whichever side’s soldiers were defeated should peacefully yield to the others.”

Our men replied:

“You refused when we wanted this; now, since we have prepared ourselves for battle, let each side fight for its own right.”

When, as we have said, we had occupied the entire plain, part of the Turks remained behind us and attacked our foot soldiers. The foot soldiers, however, forming a circle, bravely withstood the enemy’s assault.

When the Turks could in no way drive them back, they set fire around them, so that those who did not fear swords might at least be seized by fire. Thus they forced them to yield, for that place had much dry grass.

After the formations had gone out, priests stood barefoot upon the walls of the city, dressed in priestly garments, invoking God to defend his people and to attest in this battle, through the victory of the Franks, the testament that he had ratified with his blood.

During the distance we advanced from the bridge to the mountains, we suffered greatly because the enemy wanted to surround us. Meanwhile, although the enemy’s larger formations pressed upon us who were in the bishop’s contingent, through the protection of the Lord’s lance, which was there, they wounded no one among us, nor did they shoot a single arrow at us.

I saw what I am describing, and I was carrying the Lord’s lance there. If anyone says that Heraclius, the viscount and the bishop’s standard-bearer, was wounded in this battle, let him know that he had handed his standard to another and had left our formation far behind.

When all the fighting men had left the city, five other lines appeared among us. As has already been said, our princes had established only eight lines, and thirteen formations had gone out of the city.

Let us not pass over one very memorable event. At the beginning of our departure for battle, the Lord sent a divine rain over his entire army, slight but so welcome that whoever was touched by it was filled with every grace and strength, despised the enemy, and leapt about as though he had always been raised amid royal delights.

The same marvel no less occurred with our horses. Whose horse failed him before the battle was over, even if it had tasted nothing but tree bark and leaves for seven days?

Moreover, the Lord multiplied our army so greatly that although before the battle we were fewer than the enemy, during the battle we became more numerous than they.

Thus, when our men had advanced and taken their positions, we had no opportunity to engage in battle, because the enemy turned to flight. Our men pursued them until sunset.

The Lord worked marvelously there both in our men and in our horses. The men were not held back from battle by greed, while those famished horses, whom their masters had scarcely been able to lead into battle by feeding them, easily overtook the Turks’ horses, which were fat and extremely swift.

Nor did the Lord wish us to have only this joy. The Turks who had fortified the citadel of the city, seeing the headlong flight of their own men and despairing, surrendered themselves to us: some after securing only an agreement for their lives, while others fled headlong.

Although this battle was so terrible and fearful, only a few of the enemy’s knights fell there, but scarcely any of their foot soldiers escaped. All their tents were captured, together with much gold and silver and a great quantity of spoils; and provisions, livestock, and camels without measure or number.

That saying of Samaria was renewed for us, concerning the measure of fine flour and barley that was bought for a shekel.

These things happened on the vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul. Through their intercession, Jesus Christ our Lord granted this victory to the pilgrim Church of the Franks. He lives and remains with his servants, a merciful God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER XVIII
After the victory, it happened that our princes—Bohemond, the count, the duke, and the count of Flanders—jointly took possession of the city’s fortress. But Bohemond took the higher towers, already then conceiving the grief that brought forth iniquity. For shortly afterward he violently expelled from the fortress the men of the duke, the count of Flanders, and the count of Saint-Gilles, saying that he had sworn to the Turk who had surrendered the city that he alone would possess it.

For this reason also, since he had committed that act with impunity, he began to demand the city’s fortresses and the gates [Col. 0619B] which the count, the bishop, and the duke had guarded from the time when we had been besieged. All conceded them to him except the count. Although he was ill, he nevertheless refused to surrender the bridge gate, either by entreaties, promises, or threats.

Nor was it only discord that at that time shook our princes; it also so dissolved the people’s goodwill that there were few who did not quarrel with their companions or household members over matters of theft or robbery. There was no judge in the city who could or would settle disputes; rather, each person inflicted injury to the extent of his ability. The count and the bishop, meanwhile, were growing very weak and could not protect them from injury.

But why do we delay over these matters? Our people, relaxed through idleness and wealth, postponed the journey for which they had come until the Kalends of November [Col. 0619C], contrary to God’s command. At that time the cities, terrified and exhausted by fear of the Saracens, were in flight before the Turks to such an extent that, if our Franks had ridden out then, there would not have been a city all the way to Jerusalem that, as we believe, would have thrown a stone at them.

Meanwhile, the lord Adhemar, bishop of Le Puy, beloved by God and human beings, a man dear to everyone in every respect, departed in peace to the Lord on the Kalends of August. The mourning of all the Christians living there at his death was so great that we who saw it could not, despite wishing to write about it in proportion to the magnitude of the event, adequately comprehend it.

How useful he had been to God’s army and to the princes became evident after [Col. 0619D] his death, when the princes divided among themselves: Bohemond returned to Romania, and the duke of Lorraine departed toward Roais.

After the bishop had been buried in the church of Saint Peter at Antioch, on the second night the Lord Jesus appeared, together with blessed Andrew and that same bishop, to Peter Bartholomew, who had spoken about the lance, in the count’s chapel, where the Lord’s lance was. The bishop spoke to him, saying:

“Give thanks to God, to all my brothers, and to Bohemond, who have freed me from hell. For I sinned gravely after the Lord’s lance was discovered. Therefore I was led into hell and flogged there most harshly; my head and face were burned, as you can see. My soul remained there from the hour when it departed from my body until my little body was handed over [Col. 0620A] to the dust.

“Amid the very fires of the flames, the Lord restored to me the garment you see, because when I received the episcopal office, I gave it to a poor man for God’s sake. Although hell was boiling and the ministers of Tartarus raged against me, they could not injure anything beneath it.

“Yet nothing of all that I brought from my homeland benefited me so greatly as this candle, which my friends offered here for me, and those three denarii which I offered to the lance. These restored me when I came out of hell, starving almost to death.

“My lord Bohemond said that he would carry my body to Jerusalem. May he receive this grace: let him not move me, because some of the Lord’s blood is still there, to which he joined me. But if he doubts what I tell you, let him open my tomb, and he will see that my head and face have been burned through.

“I entrusted my household to my lord the count. Let him do good to it, so that God may show mercy to him and fulfill what He promised him.

“And let my brothers not grieve if I have ended my life, for I have never benefited them as much as I shall benefit them if they are willing to keep God’s commandments. For I shall dwell with them, and with all my brothers who have ended their lives as I have; I shall appear to them and console them much better than I have until now.

“And you, my brothers, remember the punishments of hell, which are so grave and dreadful. Serve, therefore, the Lord, who can free you from these and from other evils. Oh, how blessed is the one who is born and will not know the punishments of hell! The Savior can grant this to those who keep His commandments.

“Preserve whatever remains of this candle in the morning. And let the count, with whomever he wishes, choose a bishop in my place, since it is not right that, if I have died, the blessed ever-virgin Mary should be without a bishop. Give one of my cloaks to the church of Saint Andrew.”

And blessed Andrew appealed to him. After this blessed Andrew, coming nearer, spoke as follows:

“Let everyone hear what God speaks through me, saying: Remember, count, the gift that the Lord gave you. Whatever you do, do it in His name, so that the Lord may direct your deeds and words and hear your prayers.

“The first gift that the Lord bestowed upon you—namely, Nicaea—has turned away from Him. The Lord gave you this city and took it from your enemies, and afterward He was not acknowledged there. If anyone invoked the Lord’s name there, he was flogged, and the Lord’s works were not performed there.

“But because of His goodness the Lord did not wish to abandon you. He granted you what you asked for, and even more than you dared to seek. For He gave you the lance that pierced His body, from which the blood of our redemption flowed.

“And He did not grant you permission to treat this city as you treated the other; you can see that the Lord did not give it to you because of your merits. The Lord commands you, count, to discern the man who wishes to make himself lord of this city above the others, and ask him what sort of lordship he wishes to bear for the Lord’s sake.

“If you and your other brothers, to whom God gave this city, discover that he is faithful and willing to uphold or administer justice, let him have it. But if he is unwilling to uphold or administer judgment and justice, and wishes to hold the city by his own power, then ask God for counsel, you and your brothers together, and God will give it to you.

“Those men who keep the right path or love God will not fail you. But those who do not wish to keep the right path should return to the one who refused to uphold justice, and they will see how God will save them. Yet they will have the curse from God and His mother—the curse Lucifer had when he fell from heaven.

“And you, if you are united in mind, ask for counsel in prayer, and God will give it to you. If there is concord among you, take counsel concerning the patriarch, so that he may be of your law.

“Do not release those men who came to you from captivity in order to keep your law. Nor receive those who went into Corrozan to worship the god of the Turks; treat them as Turks, and put two or three of them in prison. They themselves will point out the others.

“After these things have been done by you, ask the Lord for counsel concerning the journey for which you came, and He will counsel you well. Jerusalem is ten days’ journey from you; and if you are unwilling to observe the things mentioned above, you will not go to Jerusalem for ten years. After ten years I shall bring the unbelievers back in honor, and one hundred of them will prevail against one thousand of you.

“And you, men of Christ, ask the Lord for the petition which the apostles asked; just as He granted it to them, so now He will grant it to you.

“Count and Bohemond, go to the church of Saint Andrew, and he will give you excellent counsel before God. Whatever God places in your hearts, do it. And after blessed Andrew has visited you, visit him; and see to it that your brothers visit him.

“Among you, count and Bohemond, let there be concord and love of God and neighbor. If you agree well with one another, nothing will be able to scatter you.

“The first justice you ought to administer should be demonstrated in this way: let the men from each bishopric declare their wealth, and let them help the poor of their homeland as they are able and as necessity requires. In other matters, act as you agree. But if they are unwilling to uphold this and the other forms of justice, constrain them.

“If anyone wishes to hold another city among those God will give you, act according to what is written above, so that he may conduct himself accordingly. But if he is unwilling to do so, let the count, together with the sons of God, flog him.”

These things were first believed and then forgotten. Some said, “Let us return the city to the emperor”; others disagreed. Thus, through such dissensions and revolts, the affairs of the poor were annulled. As for the counsel which the princes ought to have received at Saint Andrew’s, nothing came of it.

## CHAPTER XIX

Meanwhile the Turks besieged a certain fortress of Aleppo. The Turks inside, being afflicted, sent word to the duke, who was in those regions, asking him to receive their fortress, since from then on they wished to have no lord except one of Frankish lineage.

For this reason the duke returned to Antioch and earnestly asked the count—who had now recovered from his illness and had summoned all his knights and foot soldiers together for the cause of the poor, intending to lead them to Spain for plunder—to come to the aid of the Turks who were calling upon God, for God’s sake, for the glory of the Frankish people, and for his own sake. He added that the besieged Turks held up a cross against the siege engines of the besieging Turks.

Moved by these and similar requests, the count departed with the duke. When the Turks learned of this, they withdrew from the siege. When our army reached Asa, the duke received hostages from the fortress as a pledge of future loyalty, and the count, at great cost to his army, returned to Antioch.

Again the count assembled his knights so that they might lead the people of the poor into Spain, for they were wasting away from hunger and weariness at Antioch [Col. 0622B].

At that time Saint Andrew appeared to Peter Bartholomew at Rhodian—inside the tent where the bishop of Atus, the count’s chaplain Raymond, and another chaplain named Simon were staying. Simon heard them conversing with him, namely Saint Andrew and Peter Bartholomew. He covered his head and, as he himself reported, heard many things, but retained only this:

“Lord, I shall speak,” said the bishop of Atus. “I do not know whether it was in a dream or not. An old man stood before me, dressed in a white stole and holding the Lord’s lance in his hands. He said to me, ‘Do you believe that this is the lance of Jesus Christ?’ And I replied, ‘I believe, Lord.’

“When he had asked me the same thing a second and a third time, I said, ‘I truly believe, lord, that this is the lance which brought forth blood from the side of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which we have all been redeemed.’

“After this he abruptly awakened me, Raymond, who was sleeping nearby. When I awoke, I saw an unusual radiance and, as though conceiving some grace in my mind, began asking those present whether they sensed something like a disturbance among the people.

“They all began to say, ‘Not at all.’ But Peter, to whom this revelation had been made, replied, when we asked one another about the things mentioned above: ‘And rightly you see a gracious radiance here, since that Father has stood here for a long time, from whom all grace proceeds.’

“When we asked him to reveal to us what had been said to him, he told the count and us:

“‘This night the Lord and blessed Andrew came here in the form in which they had previously been accustomed to come, together with a third man of short stature, dressed in linen and with a very long beard.

“‘Blessed Andrew threatened me severely because they had left the relics of his body, discovered at Antioch, in his church there, in an unworthy place. He said: “When I was thrown down from a certain mountain by unbelievers, I broke two of my fingers. After my death this man received them and carried them to Antioch. When you found them, you treated them negligently: you allowed one to be stolen from you, and you left the other there unworthily.”’

“And he showed me his hand, without two fingers.

“Then he complained at length about you, count. For although you have received a venerable gift, granted by the Lord to no one else, you do not fear committing grave and wicked sins in the sight of the Lord. Therefore the Lord showed you this sign.

“Five days ago, when you offered a large candle at the feast of blessed Faith, intending that it should last for three days and as many nights, it gave no light at all; but immediately melting, it fell to the ground.

“Yet this night, when you offered a small candle which could scarcely have lasted until cockcrow, it is now daylight and it still burns, and not even a third of it has been consumed.

“Therefore the Lord commands you this: Begin nothing unless you have first done penance. Otherwise you and whatever you do will fall to the ground like the melted candle.

“But if you do penance, whatever you begin in the Lord’s name, God will perfect and complete. Just as you see the small candle lasting, so the Lord will make great whatever you begin, even if it is small.’”

When the count excused himself, saying that he had sinned so gravely, Peter then told him his sin, and the count confessed in this way and performed penance.

Peter again said to the count:

“Blessed Andrew complains, count, about your counselors, because many evils are knowingly counseled to you. Therefore you are commanded not to admit them to your council unless they first swear to you that they will not knowingly counsel you to do evil.

“Hear further, count: the Lord commands you not to delay any longer, because unless Jerusalem is first captured, you will receive no assistance. When you are near Jerusalem, let no one ride within two leagues of it. If you do this, the Lord will give you His city.”

After this Saint Andrew gave me many thanks because I had arranged for the church built in his name at Antioch to be consecrated. Saint Andrew spoke these and other things to me, which there is no opportunity to relate now; then he and his companions were taken away.

## CHAPTER XX

The count therefore departed into Syria with the people of the poor and a few knights. He vigorously captured the first Saracen city, called Barra, and killed many thousands of Saracens there; many thousands were brought back to Antioch and sold. Those who, while the city was being attacked, surrendered themselves to him through fear of death, he allowed to depart free.

At last, after taking counsel with his chaplains and princes, he chose there, in a sufficiently praiseworthy and honorable manner, a certain priest as bishop. After summoning everyone who was there with him, one of the count’s chaplains climbed a certain wall and disclosed the count’s desire to the whole assembly.

When the people pressed earnestly for an election to be held, the same chaplain again began to ask whether there was anyone among the clergy who would receive the votes of the faithful and, resisting the pagans as far as he could, serve God and the brothers there.

When everyone was silent, we summoned a certain Peter, a native of Narbonne. In the presence of the entire council we explained to him the burden of the episcopate, asking him not to hesitate to undertake it for God and for the brothers if he had this intention: that he would prefer to die rather than abandon that city.

When he professed this, the people unanimously praised him and gave great thanks to God, who had wished to have a Roman bishop in the Eastern Church for its administration.

The count granted the bishop half the city and the whole territory. Barra, however, was two days’ journey beyond Antioch. The Kalends of November were already approaching, on which all the princes had promised to assemble at Antioch and begin the journey for which they had come.

Therefore the count, leaving his army at Barra with his chosen bishop, together with many captives and great spoils, returned to Antioch in great rejoicing. All the princes had gathered there except Baldwin, the duke’s brother.

This Baldwin, before the capture of Antioch, had departed toward the Euphrates and had taken Roais, an exceedingly wealthy and famous city; he had also successfully fought many battles with the Turks.

Before we come to the remaining events, one thing concerning the duke of Lorraine should not be omitted. When he was coming to Antioch at that time with twelve knights, he encountered one hundred and fifty Turks. Taking up arms and encouraging his knights, he bravely attacked the enemy.

When the Turks saw that the Franks preferred death in battle to flight with their lives preserved, a portion of the Turks dismounted so that the other portion might fight more securely, knowing that their companions would not withdraw from the battle after abandoning their horses.

Thus, when the battle had begun and continued for a long time with great severity, the duke’s knights encouraged one another, since they numbered twelve, corresponding to the number of the apostles, and regarded their lord as Christ’s vicar. Undaunted, they attacked the Turkish ranks.

There God granted the duke such a victory that he killed as many as thirty of them and captured an equal number. He pursued the rest into the nearby marshes and river, forcing some to be killed and others to drown.

Thus he came to Antioch in great victory. For he had the heads of the slain carried by other living Turks, which was sufficiently pleasing to our men.

## CHAPTER XXI

When all the princes had assembled in the church of Blessed Peter, they began to discuss our journey. Then certain men who possessed fortresses and revenues in the region of Antioch said:

“What will become of Antioch? Who will guard it? The emperor will not come. For when he received the news that the Turks were besieging us, not trusting in his own strength or in the multitude of men he had with him, he fled.

“Shall we still wait for him? Certainly he will not come to our aid—the man who forced our brothers, who had come to aid God, to turn back. If we abandon this city and the Turks occupy it, the last things will be worse than the first.

“But let everyone grant it to Bohemond, since he is wise and will guard it exceedingly well; moreover, his name is great among the pagans.”

Count Raymond and the others, on the contrary, said:

“We swore to the emperor, upon the Lord’s cross, the crown of thorns, and many other holy things, that we would retain neither the city nor any fortress belonging to his empire without his consent.”

Thus, while some opposed them in this way and others in another, our princes fell into such discord that they nearly came to arms. The duke and the count of Flanders cared little about the city of Antioch. Therefore, although they wanted Bohemond to have it, they did not dare openly approve this, fearing the disgrace of perjury.

In this way discussion of the journey and of other matters that might be useful to the journey and to the poor was postponed.

When the people saw this, each began to say to his companion, and then openly to everyone:

“Since the princes, either because of fear or because of the oaths they made to the emperor, do not wish to lead us to Jerusalem, let us choose from among the knights some strong man whom we can faithfully serve and under whom we can be safe; and, if it is God’s will, let us reach Jerusalem under the leadership of that knight.

“Ho! Is it not enough for our princes that we have been here for a year, and that two hundred thousand armed men have been consumed here? Let those who wish have the emperor’s gold, and those who wish have the revenues of Antioch. We, with Christ for whose sake we came as our leader, shall undertake our journey.

“May those who wish to dwell at Antioch perish miserably, just as its inhabitants recently perished. If this great dispute over Antioch continues any longer, let us destroy its walls; then the peace that held the princes together before the city was captured will hold them together once the city has been destroyed.

“Otherwise, before we completely waste away here from hunger and weariness, we ought to return to our own lands.”

For these and other reasons, the count and Bohemond made a discordant peace between themselves. When the day had ended, therefore, the people were ordered to prepare for the devout journey.

## CHAPTER XXII

After the necessary preparations had been made, on the appointed day the count of Saint-Gilles and the count of Flanders departed into Syria. There they besieged Marra, a very wealthy and populous city.

Marra was eight miles distant from Barra. The citizens of Marra were extremely proud because at some time, in a certain battle, they had killed many of our men. They cursed and insulted our army, and, in order especially to provoke us, placed crosses upon their walls and subjected them to many indignities.

For this reason, on the second day after our arrival [Col. 0625D], we attacked them so fiercely that, if we had possessed four more ladders, the city would have been captured. But since we had only two, and those same ladders were short and fragile—so much so that we were afraid even to climb them cautiously—it was decided that engines, hurdles, and embankments should be made, by means of which the wall could be battered, excavated, and leveled.

Meanwhile Bohemond arrived with his army and besieged it from the other side. Since the equipment mentioned above had still not been assembled, and apparently at Bohemond’s urging, since he had not been present at the earlier assault, we wished to attack the wall by filling in the ditch.

But this was futile; for the fighting was then much worse than before.

After this such a great famine arose in the army that it is pitiable even to say: you could see more than ten thousand men [Col. 0626A] going through the fields like animals, digging and searching to see whether they might find some grains of wheat, barley, beans, or any kind of legume.

Meanwhile, although the engines mentioned above were being prepared for the assault, some of our men, seeing the misery of our people and the boldness of the Saracens, despaired of God’s mercy and fled.

But God, who cares for His servants, did not delay any longer in showing mercy to His people, whom He saw placed in the extremity of tribulation. Therefore, through the blessed apostles Peter and Andrew, He sent us a message by which we might know His will and appease His grave anger toward us.

They came, therefore, to the count’s chapel in the middle of the night and awakened Peter, to whom they had shown the lance.

Suddenly seeing them dressed in a deformed and extremely filthy garment and standing beside the chests where the relics were kept, Peter thought that they were some poor men who wished to steal something from the tent.

Saint Andrew was wearing an old tunic, torn at the shoulders. A piece of cloth had been sewn into the hole in his left shoulder, while on the right there was nothing; his footwear was poor. Blessed Peter, however, was dressed in a coarse shirt reaching to his ankles.

Then Peter Bartholomew said to them:

“Who are you, lords, and what are you seeking?”

Blessed Peter replied:

“We are God’s messengers. I am Peter, and this is Andrew. But we wished to appear to you in this clothing so that you might understand how much the one who devoutly serves God advances. In this age and clothing, as you see us, we came to God, and such are we.”

After he had said this, they became such that nothing was brighter and nothing more beautiful.

Peter, who saw these things, was terrified by the sudden brightness and fell to the ground as if dead. In his excessive anguish he was sweating and soaked the mat upon which he had fallen.

Then blessed Peter lifted him up and said:

“You have fallen lightly.”

He replied:

“That is so, lord.”

And blessed Peter again said:

“So shall all those fall who are in unbelief or transgression of God’s commandments. But if they repent of their evil deeds and cry out to God, the Lord raises them up, just as I raised you when you had fallen.

“And just as your sweat fell there upon the mat and remained, so God removes and takes away the sins of those who cry out to Him.

“Tell me, how is the army?”

He replied:

“Certainly, lord, they are in great fear of hunger and every misery.”

Blessed Peter said:

“And indeed they may be in great fear, since they have abandoned almighty God and do not remember the dangers from which He rescued them, so as to give Him some thanks.

“For when you were all there, conquered and humbled beneath Antioch, you cried out to the Lord so loudly that all of us who were in heaven heard you. The Lord heard you and gave you His lance as a pledge of victory. Then He caused you to triumph marvelously and gloriously over your enemies who had besieged you.

“And now how do you believe yourselves safe, when you have gravely offended God? Will lofty mountains or caves be able to protect you? Even if you were in some lofty and very strong place and had an abundance of all the necessities of life, you still could not be secure when one hundred thousand adversaries threatened each one of you.

“Among you there are killings and robberies, thefts and no justice, and very many adulteries, although it is pleasing to God that all of you take wives.

“Concerning justice, the Lord commands this: whoever inflicts violence upon a poor man, let everything in the oppressor’s house be confiscated.

“Concerning tithes, I say that if you pay them, He is ready to give you whatever you need.

“As for this city, in His mercy and not because of your merits, He will give it to you.”

When Peter had reported these things to the count in the morning, the bishop of Orange and Barra summoned the people, and we explained the matters written above to them.

The faithful, therefore, having been led to great hope of capturing the city, offered very generous alms and prayers to almighty God, asking Him to free His people of the poor for the sake of His name alone.

After this, ladders were quickly made, a wooden tower was constructed, hurdles were joined together, and, when the day had ended, the battle began.

Those inside the city threw at our men, who were excavating the wall, stones from engines, missiles, fire, wood, beehives with bees, and lime, all mixed together. But through God’s power and mercy these things injured none or only a few of our men.

Our men, meanwhile, attacked the wall fearlessly with stone-throwing engines and ladders. The battle lasted from sunrise to sunset, so extraordinarily that no one was ever allowed rest; and the outcome was still uncertain.

At last everyone cried out together to the Lord, asking Him to be merciful to His people and fulfill the promises of His apostles.

The Lord immediately came to our aid and, according to the apostles’ words, gave us the city. Golfer of Turris climbed up before everyone else; many followed him and attacked the wall and some of the city’s towers.

Night came and ended the battle. The Saracens still held certain towers and part of the city. Therefore the knights, hoping that the Saracens would not surrender before morning, kept watch outside the city walls so that no one might escape secretly.

But those whose lives were not very dear to them, whom prolonged fasting had reduced to contempt for themselves, did not fear attacking the Saracens in the darkness of night.

Thus the poor men obtained the city’s spoils and houses.

When morning came, the knights entered the city and found little that they could take. The Saracens had shut themselves in underground caves, and few or none appeared.

After our men had taken everything they found above ground, supposing that everything was with the Saracens, they searched the caves with fire and sulfurous smoke. Since they found little spoil there, they tortured to death as many Saracens as they could find, for the sake of plunder.

It happened to some of our men that, when they were leading Saracens through the city in search of spoils, the Saracens led our men as far as wells. Then they suddenly threw themselves inside, choosing the short path of death rather than reveal either their own property or anything else they wished to conceal.

Therefore they all died, and were thrown into the city’s marshes and [Col. 0628A] outside the walls. Thus not much spoil was captured in the city.

Meanwhile contention arose between Bohemond’s men and the count’s men because, although Bohemond’s knights had not labored much in the assault, they held most of the towers, houses, and captives.

The Lord had performed a remarkable deed there. For when, before the capture of Marra, we explained to the people the commands of the holy apostles Peter and Andrew, as written above, Bohemond and his companions mocked us. Therefore neither he nor those who were with him helped in the battle; rather, they hindered it.

When they now possessed very much spoil, certain members of the count’s household bore this indignantly.

Yet the lords themselves were also badly at odds, because the count wanted to give the city to the bishop of Albara, while Bohemond was unwilling to surrender certain towers which had given themselves to him. He said:

“Unless the count relinquishes to me the towers of Antioch, I shall agree with him in nothing.”

## CHAPTER XXIII
Meanwhile the soldiers and the people began asking when it would please the princes for the march to begin. For although the journey had been undertaken long before, every day it seemed to us that we were beginning it anew as we traveled, because it had not yet been completed. Bohemond said that it should be postponed until Easter. It was then the season of the Nativity of the Lord. Many were also despairing because there were few horses in the army, the duke was absent, and many of the soldiers had gone to Baldwin of Rohais. Thus many were turning back.

At last the bishop of Albara and certain nobles, together with the poor people, assembled and summoned the count. When the bishop had finished his sermon, the soldiers and all the people prostrated themselves before the count, and with many tears begged him—he to whom the Lord had given His lance—to become the leader and lord of that army.
