They added that he had deserved the Lord’s Lance for this purpose: if the other princes failed, he, bound by so great a benefit from the Lord, would not fear to proceed safely with the people. Otherwise, he should hand the lance over to the people, and the people would go to Jerusalem with the Lord Himself as their leader.

The count hesitated because of the absence of the other princes, fearing that, if he alone fixed the day of the march, the others would not go out of jealousy toward him. Why say more? The count was overcome by the tears of the poor [Col. 0628D] and appointed the fifteenth day for the march. For this reason Bohemond, angered, ordered the fifth or sixth day to be proclaimed throughout the city as the day of departure, and afterward returned to Antioch.

The count and the bishop were considering how they might retain the city and which men, and how many of them, they could leave there for its defense. Meanwhile the count sent word to the duke of Lorraine and to the others who had not been at Marra that they should gather in one place and deliberate about those matters that would be useful for the march and for the people of God. Thus they assembled at Roais, which lies almost midway between Antioch and Marra. There all the princes held a council, but matters turned for the worse. For the princes excused themselves from the march, and many others did so on their account [Col. 0629A].

At that time the count wished to give the duke ten thousand solidi, and the same amount to Robert, count of Normandy, and six thousand to the count of Flanders, and five thousand to Tancred, and to the other princes according to their rank. Meanwhile, when they had reached the poor who had remained at Marra, and it became known that the count intended to leave many soldiers and infantry from the army in the city of Marra for its defense, they said to one another:

“Ho! There are disputes on account of Antioch, and disputes on account of Marra; and in every place that God gives us, will there be quarrels among the princes and a diminution of the army of God? Certainly, there will be no further disputes on account of this city. Come, let us destroy its walls; then there will be peace among the princes, and the count will be secure, lest he lose it.”

And so the weak and sick rose from their beds [Col. 0629B], leaning on staffs, and reached the walls. Some famished man would easily roll far from the wall stones that barely three or four pairs of oxen could drag. The bishop of Albara, however, went around the city, protesting and forbidding this from being done in any way, accompanied by the count’s household. But as soon as these guardians had passed, those who had hidden themselves or withdrawn at the arrival of the bishop and his companions immediately returned to the work they had begun. Those who did not dare to destroy the walls by day, or could not do so because they were occupied with other matters, continued the work at night. Scarcely any weak or sick person among the people failed to take part in breaking down the wall.

Meanwhile such a great famine afflicted the army that the people eagerly ate many corpses of Saracens already stinking, which had lain for two weeks and more in the marshes of that city [Col. 0629C]. This terrified many, both men of our own people and foreigners. Because of it, very many of our men turned back, despairing of the march and lacking aid from the Frankish people.

The Saracens and Turks, on the other hand, said: “Who will be able to withstand this people, so obstinate and cruel that for a whole year they could not be recalled from the siege of Antioch by hunger, sword, or any dangers, and now they feed on human flesh?” The pagans said that these and other acts of the utmost cruelty were found among us. Indeed, God had instilled the fear of us in all nations, but we did not know it.

Meanwhile the count returned to Marra from the council of the princes [Col. 0629D] and was gravely angry with the people over the destruction of the wall. When it was explained to him that neither the bishop nor any of his other princes could drive the people away from destroying the wall by threats or beatings, he immediately understood that the matter was divine and ordered them to demolish the wall completely.

In the meantime the famine grew worse each day. When the appointed day for the march was now approaching, we preached that alms and prayers should be offered by the people to God for the journey. But when the count saw that none of the greater princes was coming to him and perceived that the entire people were wasting away, he ordered the people to go into the interior of Spain for provisions, and he himself went ahead with the soldiers.

This was not pleasing, however, to certain members of his household. They said: “There are scarcely three hundred soldiers in the army, and the number of the other armed men is not great. Shall some go on an expedition while others remain here inside this destroyed city, which has no defenses?” They considered the count excessively rash.

At last, nevertheless, the count set out for the sake of the poor, and captured many castles and prisoners, and took enormous booty. When he returned with great rejoicing and victory, after many Saracens had been killed, six or seven of our poor men were captured and killed by the pagans. All of these dead men had crosses on their right shoulders.

## CHAPTER XXIV

When the count and those who were with him saw this, they gave as much thanks as they could to almighty God, who had remembered His poor; and for this reason they were especially comforted. Therefore, in order to satisfy all those who had remained at the baggage train at Marra, they brought back one of the slain men who was still breathing. In that man we certainly saw something astonishing: although he scarcely had enough of his body intact to contain his soul, he remained for seven or eight days without food, bearing witness that Jesus—before whose judgment he would undoubtedly appear—was the author of that cross.

Thus, strengthened by the outcome of events and by the cross, they left their booty in a certain castle called Capharca, which lay on the road four leagues from Marra, and those who had companions at Marra returned there with the count. When the day had been fixed and the city had been burned, they set out. But the count, with his clerics [Col. 0630C] and the bishop of Albara, proceeded barefoot, invoking God’s mercy and the aid of the saints.

Tancred caught up with us, accompanied by forty soldiers and many infantrymen. When the kings and nobles of that Arab land heard this, they sent messengers to the counts with petitions and many gifts, saying that they would now and thereafter be their tributaries and would bring provisions, both freely and for trade. Thus, after receiving from them guarantees by oath and hostages as security for our passage, we continued onward.

We had guides from the king of Caesarea, who, on the first day, as it seemed to us, led us badly. For we were in that lodging in want of everything good except water. On the second day those same guides imprudently led us into a certain valley where the king’s herds and those of the entire region had taken refuge because of fear of us [Col. 0630D]. The king had known long beforehand that we would arrive there, and had ordered all the Saracens to flee before us. If, however, he had ordered everyone from that region to come out to meet us, things would not have turned out in this way.

Raimund of the Island and his companions captured a Saracen that day who was carrying letters from the king to everyone in that region, ordering them to flee before us. When the king learned of this, he said: “I had indeed ordered my men to flee before the face of the Franks as far as they could; but they came to them. I see that God has chosen this people. Therefore, whatever they may do, I shall not harm them.”

Then the king himself blessed God, who sufficiently provides what is necessary for those who fear Him.

When our soldiers and many strong men from the common people saw such a sudden and abundant supply [Col. 0631A], they took all their money and went to Caesarea and Camela to buy horses there, saying: “Since God takes care of our food, let us take care of the poor and of His soldiery.” And so it came about that we had as many as a thousand excellent warhorses.

The poor grew stronger each day; the soldiers were strengthened each day; and thus the army increased daily. The farther we advanced, the greater were the benefits God provided for us.

Although everything came to us sufficiently, certain men nevertheless persuaded the count that, almost for the sake of Zibellum—which is a city on the coast—he should turn aside a little. But Tancred and many other strong and worthy men prevented this from happening in any way, saying:

“God has visited the people of the poor, and should we turn aside from the journey? Let the labors we endured at Antioch suffice: war, cold, hunger, and finally every misery. Shall we alone conquer the world? Shall we kill all the inhabitants of the world? Behold, of one hundred thousand horsemen we scarcely have a thousand soldiers; and of two hundred thousand armed infantry and more, there are now not five thousand armed men in our army. Shall we wait until we are all destroyed? Will others therefore come from our land because they hear that Antioch, Zibellum, and the other Saracen cities have been captured and are ours? Let us go to Jerusalem, for which we came, and truly God will give it to us.

“And then, through the mere fear of those who will come from our land and [Col. 0631C] from other lands, the other cities on our route—namely, Zimel, Tripoli, Tyre, and Accaron—will be abandoned by their inhabitants.”

As we advanced, certain Turks and Arabs followed the army. The poor who, because of their weakness, remained far behind the army were killed and plundered. After they had done this once and again, the count remained hidden on another day until the entire army had passed. The enemy, encouraged by the impunity of their slaughter and the hope of plunder, followed our army in their usual manner. But when they had passed the ambush, our men came out from hiding with the count, attacked the enemy ranks, threw them into disorder and confusion, and killed them. They brought their finest horses back to the army with great rejoicing [Col. 0631D].

After this no enemy could overtake the army, because the count went behind all the weak with an armed multitude of soldiers. Other armed soldiers, with the count of Normandy, Tancred, and the bishop of Albara, frequently went ahead of the army, lest enemies should unexpectedly disturb us from behind or in front.

When the count was departing from Marra, because he had few soldiers with him, he asked the bishop to come with him after placing a garrison in Barra. When the bishop heard this, he left there a certain soldier of his named William, son of Peter, of Cimiliac, with seven soldiers and thirty infantrymen—a faithful man devoted to God. With God’s help, within a short time he increased the bishop’s resources tenfold. Instead of thirty infantrymen, he had seventy, and sixty horsemen, and more [Col. 0632A].

At that time a decision was made concerning our route: we would abandon the road leading to Damascus and turn toward the coast, since, if our ships—which we had left in the port of Antioch—came to us, we would have trade with the people of the island of Cyprus and of the other islands. As we traveled according to this plan, the inhabitants of the land abandoned cities, castles, and villages filled with every good thing.

## CHAPTER XXIV bis

Thus, after we had crossed great mountain ranges and reached a very wealthy valley, certain peasants, proud of their numbers and of the fortification of their castle, were unwilling either to send to us for peace or to abandon their castle. Instead, they attacked our armed men and infantry, who were unarmed and were moving through the villages in search of provisions. After killing some of them, they carried the plunder inside their castle [Col. 0632B].

Our men, angered, reached the castle. The peasants did not hesitate to come out to meet us as far as the foot of the mountain on which the castle stood. Our men then took counsel and arranged the formations of the infantry and soldiers. Thus, ascending the mountain’s height from three sides, they forced the ranks of the peasants to flee.

There were about thirty thousand Saracens, and their castle stood on the slope of a great mountain. For this reason, whenever they wished, they could take refuge in the castle, while others remained on the upper part of the mountain; and in this way they resisted us for a little while.

At last we shouted the customary signal in our times of need: “GOD, HELP! GOD, HELP!” Our enemies were so thrown into confusion that as many as a hundred of them, solely through fear and the force of their companions, remained dead without wounds at the entrance of the castle.

There was an enormous quantity of cattle, horses, and sheep outside the castle, where our people were occupied. While the count was engaged in battle with certain soldiers, our poor men, having taken the booty, began returning one after another. Then the infantry held the road, followed by the common soldiers. Our tents, however, were far from the castle, nearly ten miles away.

Meanwhile the count ordered the soldiers and people to find lodging. But when the Saracens who had climbed to the upper mountain, and those who were in the castle, saw that the greater part of our men had departed, they began discussing among themselves how they might join together [Col. 0632D]. While the count was disregarding this, he found himself almost abandoned by his soldiers.

The hill on which the castle stood was extremely steep and rocky, with a difficult path along which scarcely one horse after another could proceed. Caught in this difficulty, the count began advancing with his companions as though he intended to fight those who had descended from the upper mountain. At first they did not hesitate to face the count’s approach for a little while.

Then our men changed direction and proceeded down into the valley as though secure. When the Saracens saw that they had been deceived and that our men were descending safely, both those from the castle and those from the mountains attacked our men together.

Thus compelled, some of our men dismounted from their horses, while others threw themselves headlong down the precipices; and so, amid the greatest danger, they escaped death. Some, however, died fighting bravely [Col. 0633A].

This much we know for certain: the count was never in greater danger of his life. Angered with himself and his men, he therefore returned to the army, summoned a council, and complained bitterly about the soldiers because they had returned without permission and had left him in danger of death.

Then all promised that they would never withdraw from the assault on the castle until, by God’s grace, it had been completely overthrown. But God, who was leading them, so terrified the people of the castle during the night that, while they were fleeing headlong, they did not even bury their dead.

When morning came [Col. 0633B] and we arrived there, we found only the booty and the castle empty of people.

At that time envoys were with us from Ammirat of Camela, king of Babylon, and from the king of Tripoli. When they saw our boldness and strength, they begged the count for permission to depart, saying that they would certainly return. They were therefore sent away with our men, and within a short time they returned with great gifts and many horses.

The assault on the castle had terrified the entire region, because it had never before been conquered by anyone. Therefore the inhabitants of that region sent to the count, with many entreaties and gifts, asking that, while he arranged for their cities and castles to be received, he meanwhile send them his standards and seals.

It was the custom in the army that, if the standard of any Frank were found in a city or castle [Col. 0633C], no one afterward attacked it. For this reason the king of Tripoli placed the count’s standards in his castles. At that time the count’s name carried such weight that no one’s name among those who had preceded him seemed ever to have been equal to it.

When our soldiers who had been sent to Tripoli saw the royal wealth, the exceedingly rich kingdoms, and the populous city, they persuaded the count to besiege the extremely well-fortified castle of Archados, impregnable by human strength. They said that within four or five days the king of Tripoli would give him as much gold and silver as he desired.

Thus, according to their wishes, we besieged the castle, where our strong men endured such great labors as they had never endured elsewhere. Moreover, we lost there so many and such excellent soldiers that it is grievous to recount [Col. 0633D].

There the lord Pontius of Baladun was killed by a stone from a mangonel. On account of him I appeal to all orthodox Christians, and especially to those beyond the Alps, and to you, reverend bishop of Viviers, for whom I have undertaken to write this work.

Now, with God inspiring me—He who accomplished all these things—I shall endeavor to complete what remains with the same joy with which I began. I therefore beg and implore all who will hear these things to believe that they happened in this way.

But if I strive to report anything beyond what I have believed and seen, or have added anything out of hatred for someone, may God bring upon me all the punishments of hell and erase me from the book of life. For although I am ignorant of many other things, I know this one thing: since I have been advanced to the priesthood on the journey of God, I ought to obey God more by testifying to the truth [Col. 0634A] than, by weaving lies, to seek the profit of any reward.

My dearest Pontius of Baladun died in the Lord, as has already been said, at the castle of Archados. But because, according to the Apostle, “love never fails” (1 Cor. 13:8), I wish to carry out this work in that same love. May God assist me.

## CHAPTER XXV

After we had spent some time in this siege, our ships came to us from Antioch and Laodicea, along with many other Venetian and Greek ships carrying grain, wine, barley, pork, and other goods for sale.

But because this castle was a mile from the sea, and the ships could not remain in the harbor, the sailors returned to the port of Laodicea [Col. 0634B] and to the port of Tortosa. The citizens of Tortosa—a very strongly fortified city, built with walls and outer defenses and filled with every good thing—had abandoned it, being terrified solely by our army.

For God had instilled such fear of us in the Saracens and Arabs of that region that they believed us capable of everything and willing to destroy whatever we could. But this was before the siege of Archados.

As for that siege, because we had undertaken it more for others and against justice than for God, God did not wish to advance it, but brought every adversity upon us. It was remarkable that, although everyone was ready and prepared for all other battles and assaults, for this one they were found sluggish and ineffective. If anyone, fervent in spirit, wished to accomplish something, either he himself was wounded or what he had begun came to nothing [Col. 0634C].

Anselm of Ripamondo departed gloriously. For when he had risen in the morning, he called the priests to him, confessed his negligences and sins, and begged mercy from God and from them, announcing that the end of his life was near.

When they marveled at this, since they saw him healthy and unharmed, he said to them: “Do not marvel, but listen to me instead. Last night I saw the lord Egelrannus of Saint-Paul, who was killed at Marra—not in a dream, but while awake. I said to him: ‘What is this? You were dead, and behold, now you are alive.’ He replied: ‘Those who end their lives in the service of Christ do not die.’

“When I asked him again about his beauty, which was exceedingly great, and from where it had come to him, he answered me: ‘You should not marvel at my beauty when I dwell in so beautiful a house.’ Immediately he showed me a certain house in heaven, so beautiful that I believed nothing could be more beautiful. As I stood amazed at the splendor of that house, he said to me: ‘A much more beautiful one is being prepared for you, by tomorrow.’ And after saying this, he was taken away.”

On that day, after the same Anselm had recounted these things to many people, it happened that he went out to fight against the Saracens. They used to leave the castle secretly and come as far as our tents, in order to steal something from there or harm someone.

But when the battle had intensified on both sides, and Anselm was resisting bravely, he was struck in the head by a stone from a siege engine. Thus he departed from this world for the place God had prepared for him [Col. 0635A].

An envoy from the king of Babylon came to us. He sent back with him our envoys, whom he had held captive for a year. For he had hesitated whether to make friendship with us or with the Turks.

We wished to reach this agreement with him: if he gave us aid concerning Jerusalem, or if he returned Jerusalem to us with its dependencies, we would return to him all the cities of his that the Turks had taken from him when we captured them. As for the other Turkish cities that had not belonged to his kingdom, if they were captured with his assistance, we would divide them.

The Turks, as we were informed, wanted to offer him this agreement: if he came against us in battle, and if they worshiped Alim, whom he worships, who is of the lineage of Bahumeth, and accepted his coinage [Col. 0635B], and remitted certain tributes, and did many other things that I do not know well, they would do these things for him.

He knew that we were few and that the emperor Alexius was hostile to us even unto death. Accordingly, we found letters of the emperor Alexius concerning us, written after the war that we had fought with that same king of Babylon at Ascalon, in the tent of that king.

For these and other reasons, the Ammiratus held our envoys captive in Babylon for a year. But now, when he heard that we had entered his land and were devastating villages and fields, he sent word to us that two or three hundred of us should go unarmed to Jerusalem, worship our Lord, and return.

We mocked this, trusting in God’s mercy and threatening that, unless he freely returned Jerusalem to us, we would bring a charge against him concerning Babylon [Col. 0635C]. At that time the Ammiratus held Jerusalem.

For when he heard that the Turks had been defeated by us at Antioch, he came to attack Jerusalem, knowing that the Turks, so often routed and put to flight by us, would not face him in battle. At last, after giving enormous gifts to those who defended it, he recovered the city of Jerusalem and offered candles and incense at the Lord’s Sepulcher and on Mount Calvary.

But now let us return to the siege.

## CHAPTER XXVI

While, as we have said, our army was laboring greatly in the assault on Archados, word was brought to us [Col. 0635D] that the pope of the Turks was coming against us for battle and that, because he was of the lineage of Bahumeth, innumerable peoples were following him. We were therefore ordered to prepare ourselves for battle.

They sent the bishop of Albara to the duke and to the count of Flanders, who were besieging Zibellum—a castle above the sea, almost midway between Antioch and the castle of Archados, two days’ journey from each. When they received the news of the war, they abandoned the siege and came quickly to us.

Meanwhile it was discovered that the report was false and had been fabricated by the Saracens so that, after terrifying us in this way, the besieged might obtain some respite.

When the armies had joined, the men on the count’s side began displaying horses and riches that God had given them in the regions of the Saracens, because they had exposed themselves to death for God. Others, however, displayed their poverty.

At that time it was preached that the people should give tithes of everything they had captured, since there were many poor and many sick in the army. They were also ordered to return one quarter to their priests, whose Masses they attended, and one quarter to the bishops; the remaining two parts were to go to Peter the Hermit, whom they had placed over the poor of the clergy and the people. Thus he received two portions: one for those who belonged to the clergy, and the other for those who belonged to the people.

God therefore multiplied our army so greatly in horses, mules, camels, and other necessities of life that it became a matter of wonder and astonishment even to us ourselves [Col. 0636B].

From this abundance of possessions there arose contention and pride among the princes, to such a degree that those who loved God most intimately preferred that we suffer want and that terrifying wars threaten us.

The king of Tripoli wished to give us fifteen thousand gold pieces in Saracen coinage, as well as horses and mules, many garments, and annual tribute thereafter—much greater than these gifts—if we did not conquer him. One gold piece was worth eight or nine solidi in the coinage of our army.

Our coinage was as follows: Poitevins, Chartres, Mans, Lucca, Valence, Mergores, and two Pogesi for one of these.

The lord of Zibellum, fearing that he would again be attacked, sent our princes five thousand gold pieces, horses, mules, and much wine [Col. 0636C]. We had a sufficient supply of grain.

Some Saracens were also baptized through fear and zeal for our law, anathematizing Bahumeth and all his offspring. For this reason each of our princes sent envoys to the Saracen cities with letters, saying that he was the lord of the entire army.

This was how our princes acted at that time. Tancred especially caused trouble. After receiving from Count Raimund five thousand solidi and two excellent horses, so that he might remain in his service until Jerusalem, he now wished to depart and join the duke of Lorraine. For this reason there were many disputes. At last he left the count on bad terms.

## CHAPTER XXVII

[Col. 0636D]

Many revelations were announced to us at that time, revelations sent to us by God. One of them is the following, written under the name of the man who saw it:

In the year 1099 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the seventh indiction, with the twenty-sixth epact and the fifth concurrent, on the Nones of April, during the night, when I, Peter, was lying in the chapel of the Count of Saint-Gilles at the siege of Arqah, I began to think about that priest to whom the Lord had appeared with the cross while we were being held under siege by the Turks at Antioch. I was greatly surprised that He had never appeared to me with the cross. Suddenly I saw the Lord entering, with His apostles Peter and Andrew, and another large and stout man, dark-complexioned and somewhat bald, with large eyes.

The Lord said to me: “What are you doing?”

I replied: “Lord, I am standing.”

Again the Lord said: “You were almost submerged with the others. But what were you thinking about just now?”

I replied: “Lord and Father, I was thinking about that priest to whom You appeared with the cross.”

And the Lord said: “I know this.” Then He continued: “Believe that I am the Lord for whom you have all come here, and that I suffered on the cross for sinners in Jerusalem, as you will now see.”

At that very moment I saw a certain cross made of two black, rounded pieces of wood, neither polished nor fitted together, except that in the middle the cut beams clasped one another. The Lord said to me: “Behold the cross you were seeking.”

On that cross the Lord was stretched out and crucified, just as He had been at the time of His Passion. Peter supported it at the head on the right; Andrew supported it on the left, at the neck; and the third man supported it from behind with his hands.

The Lord said to me: “You shall tell my people that this is how you saw me. Do you see these five wounds of mine? In the same way, you are divided into five orders.

“The first order consists of those who do not fear arrows, swords, or any kind of torment. This order is like me, for when I came to Jerusalem I did not hesitate before swords, lances, clubs, staffs, and finally the cross. They die for me, and I too have died for them. I am in them, and they are in me. When such men die, they are placed at God’s right hand, where I sat after my resurrection, when I ascended into heaven.

“The second order consists of those who support the first and guard them from behind, to whom the first may also flee. These are like the apostles who followed me and ate with me.

“The third order consists of those who supply the first with stones and missiles. They are like those who, when they saw me on the cross, grieved over my Passion, struck their breasts, and proclaimed that I was being wronged.

“The fourth order consists of those who, seeing battle arise, withdraw into their houses and turn to their own affairs, believing that victory does not depend upon my power but upon human prowess. Such men are like those who said: ‘He is guilty of death; let him be crucified, because he made himself king and called himself the Son of God’ (Matthew 26).

“The fifth order consists of those who, when they hear the battle cry, watch from afar and ask the causes of the shouting. They offer others examples of cowardice rather than courage; they are unwilling to undergo dangers not only for me but also for their brothers. Under the pretext of caution, they invite those who wish to fight, or those supplying weapons to the fighters, to watch with them. These are like Judas the traitor and Pilate the judge.”

The Lord was naked on the cross, but girded with a linen cloth from the knees to the loins. The cloth was of a medium shade, between black and red. Around it were bands of white, red, and green.

After the cross had been removed, the Lord remained in the clothing in which He had first come. I said to Him: “Lord God, if I say this, they will not believe me.”

The Lord replied: “Do you wish to know those who will not believe these things?” [Col. 0638A]

I said: “Yes, Lord.”

And the Lord said: “Let the count gather the princes and the people, and, when the time comes, let him make some arrangement for battle or for assaulting the fortress. Let the most renowned herald proclaim three times: ‘God, help!’ Let him then proceed to carry out what has been arranged. At that time you will see the orders as I have told you, and you and the others who believe these things will distinguish the unbelievers.”

I said: “Lord, what shall we do with the unbelievers?”

The Lord replied: “Do not spare them, but kill them, because they are my traitors, brothers of Judas Iscariot. Give their possessions to those of the first order, as necessity requires. If you act in this way, you will find the right road around which you have hitherto gone in circles. Just as the other things you told them came to pass unchanged, so these too will come to pass.

“You know which nation I loved especially.”

I replied: “Lord, the nation of the Jews.”

And the Lord said: “Because they were unbelieving, I hated them and established them beneath all other nations. Therefore see to it that you do not become unbelieving. Otherwise, while you remain with the Jews, I will take other peoples and through them fulfill what I promised you.

“You shall also say to them: Why are they afraid to do justice? And what is better than justice? I want them to uphold this justice: let them appoint judges by families and kinships. Whenever anyone injures another, let the injured man say: ‘Brother, would you want this done to you?’ Afterwards, if the wrongdoer does not desist, let him be confronted in the name of his authority. Then let the judge lawfully take all the wrongdoer’s goods from him; half shall belong to the man who suffered the injury, and the rest to the authority.

“If the judge delays doing this for any reason, go to him, rebuke him, and tell him that unless he corrects himself, he will not be released until the last day of the age—unless you forgive him.

“Do you not know how serious a prohibition is? I forbade Adam to touch the tree of knowledge. He transgressed my prohibition, and he and his descendants remained in miserable captivity until I came in the flesh and redeemed them by dying the death of the cross.

“As for tithes: some have done well, giving them as I commanded. I will therefore multiply them and make them known among others.”

When the Lord had said these things, I began to ask Him, for the sake of His charity, to restore to me the knowledge of letters which He had recently taken away from me.

The Lord said: “Are not the things you know sufficient for recounting them, and yet you wish to know more?” [Col. 0638D]

Immediately I seemed so wise that I asked to know nothing further. The Lord said: “Is what you know still sufficient for you?”

I replied: “It is sufficient.”

The Lord again said: “What did I tell you? Answer.”

I knew nothing. When He pressed me to answer something of what He had said, I replied: “Lord, I know nothing new.”

The Lord said: “Go and announce what you know, and let what you know be sufficient for you.”

When we had shown these things to the brothers, some began to say that they would never believe that God would speak to such a man, pass over bishops and princes, and reveal Himself to a rustic. They consequently also doubted the Lord’s lance.

Therefore we summoned those brothers to whom the lance had once been revealed, and then Arnulf, chaplain of the Count of Normandy, who was the leader of all the unbelievers. Because he was learned, they placed great trust in him. We asked him why he doubted.

When he said that the Bishop of Le Puy had doubted the matter, a certain priest named Peter Desiderius replied: “After his death I saw the Bishop of Le Puy, with blessed Nicholas beside him. After many other things, the bishop said to me: ‘I am in one choir with blessed Nicholas, but because I doubted the Lord’s lance—though I above all ought to have believed—I was led into hell. There the hair on the right side of my head and half of my beard were burned. Although I am not undergoing punishment, I shall not be able to see God clearly until my hair and beard have grown back as they were before.’” [Col. 0639B]

## CHAPTER XXVIII

This priest foretold these and many other things on God’s behalf, and they later happened to us; but these matters can be related in their proper place.

Another priest, named Ebrardus, came forward and said:

“At the time when the Turks were besieging our army within Antioch, I was in Tripoli. I had gone there before Antioch was captured, to obtain the necessities of life. When I heard that Antioch had been captured and that our men were being held inside under such a siege that none of them dared enter or leave, and when I heard of the many other evils threatening the besieged, as well as the numerous falsehoods which the Saracens and Turks added to the real evils, I feared for my life and took refuge in a certain church. [Col. 0639C]

“There I prostrated myself before an image of the majesty of the Lord’s mother and began, with tears and prayers, to appeal through her to God’s mercy. I continued this for several days without eating, saying to her:

“‘O queen and lady, these are pilgrims who, leaving behind their children, wives, and all that is dear to them for the sake of your Son’s name and for your sake, have come here from far away and are fighting for your Son. Have mercy on them. O Lady, what will be said of you and your Son in their lands if you hand them over to the Turks?’

“When I had repeatedly uttered these and similar words in sorrow and lamentation, a certain Syrian who was a Christian came to me and said: ‘Be of good courage, and see that you do not weep any longer.’

“He said: ‘Just now I was before the doors of the church of blessed Mary, the Lord’s mother, and a certain cleric dressed in white garments came to me. When I asked him who he was and where he came from, he replied: “I am Mark the Evangelist, and I come from Alexandria. I have turned aside here because of the church of blessed Mary, ever-virgin.”’

“When I again asked where he was going, he said: ‘Our Lord Jesus Christ is near Antioch. He has ordered all His disciples to come there, because the Franks are to fight the Turks, and we shall be their protection.’ Having said this, he went away.

“Although I scarcely believed these things and did not cease from grief or tears, that same Syrian said to me: ‘Understand this: It is written in the Gospel of blessed Peter, which we possess, that the Christian people who will capture Jerusalem will be shut up inside Antioch and will not be able to leave until they first find the Lord’s lance.’” [Col. 0640A]

The priest said: “If any of you doubt these things, let a fire be made, and in God’s name and with these things as witnesses, I will pass through its midst.”

Another priest, named Stephen, surnamed Valentinus, a man of great reputation and good life, came forward and said:

“The Lord Jesus Himself spoke to me during the very intensity of the tribulation that occurred at Antioch, and promised me in the presence of His mother, the most blessed virgin Mary, that on the fifth day that was to come He would show mercy to His people and bring their many hardships to completion, if they returned to Him with all their heart. On that day the Lord’s lance was found. I believe that the Lord’s promise was fulfilled there.

“If you doubt anything concerning this, as soon as I saw these things I offered myself as testimony to the Bishop of Le Puy, before the whole multitude: if he wished, I would pass through fire or throw myself from the highest tower. I still offer you this same proof.” [Col. 0640B]

The Bishop of Athens also came forward and said:

“Whether I saw these things in sleep or while awake, I do not know for certain; God knows. A man came dressed in white, stood before me, held this Lord’s lance in his hands, and said to me: ‘Do you believe that this is the Lord’s lance?’

“I replied: ‘I believe, Lord.’ I too had once doubted it.

“When he had pressed the matter upon me gravely a second and third time, I said to him: ‘I believe, Lord, that this is the lance of our Lord Jesus Christ.’ After this he dismissed me.”

And I, Raymond, who wrote these things in the presence of the brothers and bishops, said there:

“I was present when the Lord’s lance was excavated, and before it had appeared entirely above the ground, I kissed its point. There are many in the army who saw these things with me.”

I added:

“There is also another priest, named Bertramus, of Le Puy, who during the bishop’s lifetime was close to the Bishop of Le Puy. This priest became ill to the point of death. When he had already despaired of his life, the Bishop of Le Puy appeared to him with his standard-bearer Heraclius. In the great battle fought at Antioch, Heraclius had been struck in the face by an arrow while fearlessly overthrowing the Turkish ranks, and had thereafter ended his life.

“The bishop said to the priest: ‘Bertramus, what are you doing?’

“Heraclius said: ‘Lord, he is ill.’

“The bishop replied: ‘He is ill because of unbelief.’

“The priest then said: ‘Lord, do I not believe in the Lord’s lance just as I believe in the Lord’s Passion?’

“The bishop said to him: ‘You must also believe many other things.’” [Col. 0640D]

Although this does not pertain to the present matter, because it is an admirable story I shall add something for the sake of good men.

When the priest, who was ill and unable to stand, had sat in the presence of the bishop and his lord Heraclius, he saw that his lord’s facial wound had not been healed.

The priest said: “What is this?”

Heraclius replied: “When I came before my Lord, I begged Him never to close this wound, since I had ended my life for His sake. The Lord granted me this.”

After hearing these and many other things, Arnulf believed, confessed, and promised the Bishop of Albaria that before the whole multitude of the people he would ask forgiveness for his unbelief.

On the appointed day, when Arnulf had been summoned to the council, he began to say that he believed rightly, but that he wished to speak with his lord before asking forgiveness for the matter.

When Peter Bartholomew heard this, he became extremely angry and said, as a simple man who knew the truth well:

“I wish and beg that a great fire be made, and that I pass through its midst with the Lord’s lance. If it is the Lord’s lance, let me pass through unharmed; but if it is false, let me be burned in the fire. I see that neither signs nor witnesses are believed.”

We all approved these words. We imposed a fast upon him and said that the fire should be made on the day when our Lord, wounded for our salvation, was on the cross. The following day was Good Friday.

At dawn on the appointed day, the fire was prepared for the afternoon. The princes and the people gathered, as many as forty thousand men. Priests were present barefoot and dressed in priestly vestments.

The fire was made from dry olive wood. It was fourteen feet long, with two heaps of fuel. Between the two heaps was a space of about one foot, and the heaps were four feet high. When the fire had been lit and was burning fiercely, I, Raymond, said before the whole multitude:

“If almighty God spoke face to face with this man, and blessed Andrew showed him the Lord’s lance while he was awake, let him pass unharmed through the fire. But if the matter is otherwise and it is a lie, let him be burned with the lance that he will carry in his hands.”

All, kneeling, answered: “Amen.” [Col. 0641C]

The blaze boiled up so fiercely that it occupied the air to a height of thirty cubits; no one could come near it.

Then Peter Bartholomew, wearing only a tunic and kneeling before the Bishop of Albaria, called God as his witness that he had seen the Lord face to face on the cross; that he had heard from Him the things written above and from the blessed apostles Peter and Andrew; and that he had composed nothing of what he had said in the name of Saint Andrew, Saint Peter, or the Lord Himself. If he had lied in anything, he would never pass through the fire then present.

As for the other things he had committed against God and his neighbor, he asked that God forgive him, and that the bishop, all the other priests, and the people who had gathered for this spectacle pray for him.

After this, when the bishop had placed the lance in his hands while he was kneeling and had made the sign of the cross, he entered the fire courageously and without fear, carrying the lance. He remained for some time in the middle of the fire and thus, by God’s grace, passed through it. [Col. 0641D]

There are still some who saw this sign there: before he entered the fire, a certain bird flew overhead, circled the fire, and then plunged into it. Ebrardus, the priest mentioned above, saw this. He later remained in Jerusalem for God’s sake. William, son of Boni, an excellent soldier of good reputation from Arles, also testifies that he saw the same thing.

There was another excellent soldier, of Nîmes descent, named William Malus Puer. Before Peter entered the flames, he saw a man dressed in priestly clothing—except that he had a chasuble folded over his head—enter the fire. When he saw that the man did not emerge, believing him to be Peter Bartholomew, he began to weep, thinking that Peter had been consumed in the fire.

There was a multitude of people there, and not everyone could see everything. Many other things were reported and done, but because we feared that writing them would weary our readers, we did not wish to record them; three suitable witnesses are sufficient for every matter.

Let us not pass over one thing. After Peter had passed through the fire, although the blaze was still raging fiercely, the people gathered the logs, coals, and ashes so greedily that shortly nothing of them could be seen. In the faith of those people the Lord afterward worked many miracles through these things.

When Peter Bartholomew came out of the fire, neither his tunic nor even the very fine cloth in which the Lord’s lance had been wrapped showed any sign of damage. After he had signed the people with the Lord’s lance and cried aloud, “God, help!”, the people seized him and dragged him along the ground. The entire multitude trampled him, each person wanting to touch him or take something from his clothing, and each believing that someone else had received him.

Thus they inflicted three or four wounds on his legs, cutting pieces from his flesh, breaking his backbone, and crushing him. Peter would have died there, as we believe, unless Raymond Pilet, a most noble and courageous knight, had broken into the ranks of the disordered crowd with a band of his companions and, fighting to the death, rescued him. [Col. 0642C]

But we are now placed in such anxiety and distress that we cannot write more about these matters.

When Raymond Pilet had carried Peter to our house, we bound his wounds and began to ask him why he had lingered in the fire.

He replied:

“The Lord met me in the middle of the fire. Taking me by the hand, He said: ‘Because you doubted the finding of the lance, although blessed Andrew had shown it to you, you will not pass through unharmed in this way; but you shall not see hell.’ Having said this, He released me.

“See, if you wish, the burns I have suffered.”

There was some burning on his legs, but not much; the wounds, however, were large.

After this we summoned all who had doubted the Lord’s lance, so that they might come and see his face, head, and remaining limbs and understand that everything he had said about the lance and the other matters was true, since he had not feared to enter such a fire as testimony to them.

Many came and, seeing his face and entire body, glorified God, saying:

“The Lord can surely protect us among the swords of our enemies, since He rescued this man from so great a fire of flames. Certainly we did not believe that any arrow could pass unharmed through fire as this man did.”

After this Peter summoned the count’s chaplain, named Raymond, and said to him:

“Why did you want me to pass through the fire as testimony to the Lord’s lance and to the other things I had spoken on God’s behalf? I know well that you thought this and that.”

And he told him what he had been thinking.

When the chaplain denied having thought such things, Peter Bartholomew replied:

“You cannot deny it to me, because I know it for certain. For on that night the most blessed virgin Mary and the Bishop of Le Puy were here, and through them I learned what you deny. I am greatly surprised that, although you did not doubt the words of the Lord and His apostles, you wished to test these few matters at the risk of my life.”

When Raymond saw that his thoughts had been exposed and that he was guilty before God, he burst into bitter tears.

Peter said to him:

“Do not despair, because the most merciful virgin Mary and Saint Andrew will obtain forgiveness for you from God. But you must earnestly beseech them.”

## CHAPTER XXIX

Meanwhile such serious and bitter disputes arose among the princes of our army that almost the entire army was divided. But God, who was its leader, and our Lord prevented such things by His benefactions.

There was a city named Tripoli, mentioned above, not far from our camp. When the lord of this city learned of the discord among our princes, he replied to our men, who were demanding that he pay tribute:

“Who are the Franks? What sort of soldiers are they? How great is their power? Look: the third month has now begun since the Frankish army besieged the fortress of Arqah, and I have neither suffered an assault from them nor seen any armed man among them, although they are only four leagues from me. Let them come here, and let us see them and test their soldiership. Why should I become tributary to men whose faces I have not seen and whose strength I do not know?” [Col. 0643C]

When this was reported to our army, everyone said to one another:

“See what we have gained from our contentions and dissensions: God is blasphemed, and we are despised.”

Our princes therefore assembled and decided that the Bishop of Albaria should guard the camp with part of the army, while the princes, with the ranks of foot soldiers and knights, should assault the city walls in the customary manner of battle.

On the appointed day, when our men were setting out in this fashion, the people of Tripoli came out to meet them, trusting in their numbers and tumult and preparing to fight our men.

There is a very strong and high wall belonging to an aqueduct leading into the city. Between it and the sea there is a road that is not very wide, since the sea surrounds Tripoli on three sides. The Saracens fortified the aqueduct wall we have mentioned so that, if anything adverse happened, they could go out and return as though from one fortress into another.

When our men saw this multitude trusting in its position and weapons, they invoked God and, with their lances raised, foot soldiers and knights advancing in close formation like a procession, came up to them. If you had seen our men before they met, you would have said that they were friends rather than enemies; once they had mingled, you would have believed them enemies rather than friends.

The ground was defiled with the blood of the Moors, and the aqueduct was filled with their corpses. The Lord struck such fear into the enemies that after the first blows scarcely any of them could flee. It was indeed pleasant enough to watch, as the stream of the aqueduct swiftly carried the dismembered bodies of nobles and commoners into the city.

One or two of our men fell there; of the enemy, we heard that as many as seven hundred fell.

Returning with a great victory and much booty, our princes said to the people:

“Today the king of Tripoli saw us, and we saw the roads of the city and examined its approaches. Now, if you approve, we judge it right that tomorrow the king should learn what sort of soldiers we are.”

Returning the next day, they found no one outside the city.

After this the king of Tripoli sent word to our princes that, if they would desist from besieging Arqah, he would give them fifteen thousand gold pieces, many horses and mules, clothing and provisions, and would establish a market for all goods for the entire people. Moreover, he would return all the captives he held from our people. [Col. 0644B]

At that time envoys came from the Emperor Alexius with very serious complaints against Bohemond, because he was retaining the city of Antioch contrary to the oaths he had sworn to the emperor. Bohemond possessed Antioch at that time.

For when he had heard that the count had departed from Ma'arrat into the interior of Syria, he violently expelled the count’s men from the towers of Antioch, which they were guarding.

Therefore Alexius sent word to our princes that he would give them much gold and silver and would come with them to Jerusalem if they would wait until the feast of Saint John. The Lord’s Easter was then approaching.

Many, including the count, said on this account:

“Let us wait for the emperor, and we shall have his gifts and the emperor himself. He will arrange a market for us by sea and land, and under his authority we shall reach agreement. All the cities will give themselves to him; he will clothe those he wishes and destroy those he wishes.

“Our people, shaken by long and continual hardships, may perhaps wish, after arriving in Jerusalem, to turn back once they have seen it from outside. You can judge what and how many dangers await those who wish to complete the journey.

“Moreover, we are still besieging the fortress of Arqah; within a month they will either surrender or be captured by force. Since this siege is widely known, if we abandon it as impossible to resolve, our army will be greatly despised—the army which until now has begun nothing that it has left unfinished.” [Col. 0644D]

But others said in opposition:

“The emperor has always harmed us, has always lied, and has always plotted against us. Now, because he sees that he can do nothing and that we are strong through God’s grace, he is deliberately acting to turn us back from our planned journey, so that those who hear of it will not decide to come after our example.

“But those whom he has so often injured in word and deed should beware of placing their trust in his faith. Let us therefore, with Christ as our leader, enter the road by which we came. He has delivered us unexpectedly from so many dangers and protected us against all the emperor’s efforts and deceptions. Through God’s promise we shall easily obtain what we desire.

“When the emperor hears that Jerusalem has been captured, he will fulfill in deed the free passage which he now pretends to offer in words. His gifts will likewise be praised.”

The people strongly favored this opinion. But many of the count’s close associates were present; indeed, the count had exposed himself to death for his people without the other princes and had granted many substantial private benefits. For this reason the counsels of the princes and the wishes of the people were obstructed.

## CHAPTER XXX

At that time we proclaimed fasting, prayers, and almsgiving among the people, so that almighty God, who had brought them there from so many regions, might deign to inspire them concerning what was pleasing to Him regarding this journey.

Thus the wishes of the faithful obtained easily from God what they sought.

The Bishop of Le Puy appeared to Stephen Valentinus, whom we mentioned above as having seen the Lord with the cross. The bishop struck him with a rod as he was returning to his house at night and said to him:

“Stephen.”

He replied: “Lord.”

Looking back, he recognized him.

The bishop said:

“Why have you neglected once or twice what I told you about the cross of our Lady and mother, the ever-virgin Mary? I mean the cross which I had ordered to be carried before me and brought to the army. And what sign is better than the cross? Was that cross not sufficiently stoned for us? Did that cross not lead you well, all the way to the Lord’s lance?

“Now our Lady, the most blessed ever-virgin Mary, says that unless you possess that cross, you cannot have counsel.” [Col. 0645C]

Immediately the priest said:

“O most reverend lord, where is the most blessed virgin Mary?”

At once the bishop showed her to him. The most blessed virgin Mary was about nine or ten cubits away from him, exceedingly marvelous in appearance and adornment. Blessed Agatha and another virgin stood beside her, with two candles.

Then the priest said to the bishop who stood beside her:

“Lord, many things are said about you in the army: that your beard and hair were burned in hell, and many other things which are not believed. Now I ask you to give me one of these candles as testimony to the things you say, so that I may take it to the count.”

The bishop said:

“Look carefully; look at my face. Is it burned?”

After this the bishop approached the most blessed Virgin. Having learned her will, he returned to the priest and said:

“You cannot obtain what you seek. But this ring which you have on your finger is of no use to you, nor should you carry it. Go and give it to the count, saying: ‘The most holy virgin mother sends you this ring. Whenever you fail in any matter, remember that Lady who sends you this ring, and call upon her; then the Lord will help you.’”

Again, when the priest asked him what he wished his brother to do, the bishop replied:

“Let him ask the worthy bishop to celebrate three Masses before the Lord for the souls of our parents.”

He said again:

“Our mother has commanded that henceforth the lance should be shown only by a priest clothed in sacred vestments, and that the cross should be carried before it, as follows.”

The bishop held a cross mounted on a staff, and a man dressed in priestly vestments followed him, holding the lance between his hands.

The bishop began this responsory: “Rejoice, Virgin Mary; you alone have destroyed all heresies.”

Immediately countless hundreds of thousands of men began it, and thus that holy company departed. [Col. 0646A]

When morning came, the priest arrived and first asked whether we had the lance. When he saw it, he began, with many tears, to recount the things we have related above.

The count therefore sent William Hugh of Montlhéry, brother of the Bishop of Le Puy, to Laodicea, where the cross had been left, together with the bishop’s chapel.

## CHAPTER XXXI

Meanwhile Peter Bartholomew, exhausted by illness resulting from his injuries and wounds, summoned the count and his princes and said to them:

“The end of my life is near, and I know well that before God I shall be judged for everything I have done, said, or even thought wrongly. In His presence today I testify before you that I have composed nothing of all that I announced to you on behalf of God and His apostles, nor of what I shall yet tell you.

“Just as you have seen the things I announced to you, so without doubt you will see the things I shall tell you, provided that you serve God faithfully.

“But you, count, when you come to Jerusalem, see that the army entreats God to prolong and continue your life, and God will prolong it by as much time as you have lived.

“When you have returned to within about five leagues, you shall place the Lord’s lance in the church of Saint Trophimus, have a church built there, and establish a mint there, which you shall swear will not produce counterfeit money. Nor shall you permit anything else false to be made there.

“That place shall be called the Mount of Joy. These things shall take place within the province. For the blessed apostle Peter promised his disciple Trophimus that he would send him the Lord’s lance.”

After this Peter Bartholomew, secure and at peace, departed to the Lord at the hour appointed for him by God. He was buried in that place where he had passed through the fire with the Lord’s lance.

## CHAPTER XXXII
Meanwhile the count and the other princes were inquiring of the inhabitants of the region which route to Jerusalem would be better and easier. Then certain Syrians came to us. For there are mountains of Lebanon where about sixty thousand Christians lived [Col. 0646D]; and Christians had possessed that land and those mountains for a long time. They are called Syrians because of the city of Tyre, which is now commonly called Sur.

But when, by God’s judgment, the Saracens and Turks rose against them, these Syrians were subjected to such oppression and servitude for four hundred years and more that many of them were compelled to abandon their homeland and the Christian faith. If any, by God’s grace, had scorned to do so, they were forced to surrender their beautiful little children to be circumcised or made Turks; or the children were snatched from their mothers’ arms, after the father had been killed and the mother violated.

Indeed, those peoples had burned with such wickedness that they overturned God’s churches, destroyed images of Him and of His saints, and, where they could not destroy them by taking the necessary time, gouged out their eyes or shot them with arrows. As for all the altars, they dug them up. In the large churches they made *bafumaria*—bathhouses. If one of those afflicted Christians wished to keep an image of God or of some saint in his house, he either had to redeem it month by month or year by year, or else it was trampled in dung and crushed before his eyes. And what is still too grievous to relate: they placed young men in brothels and exchanged their sisters for wine, so that they might commit even worse deeds. Yet neither the mothers nor anyone else dared openly to weep over these or other sorrows.

Why say much more about these things? Certainly that nation had conspired against the Holy of Holies and against His inheritance. Unless, by God’s command and inspiration, the peoples of the Franks had come to meet these evils [Col. 0647B], God would surely have armed brute animals against them—as He once did in our presence. Let this, for now, suffice.

Those Syrians, I say, of whom we spoke above, who had come to the count, answered when questioned about the better route:

“There is a road through Damascus, quite level and full of provisions, but you will find no water for two days. There is another through the mountains of Lebanon, quite safe and well supplied, but very difficult for pack animals and camels. There is also another beside the sea, where there are so many and such formidable narrow passes that, if fifty or a hundred Saracens wished to hold them, they could prevent the entire human race from passing.

“Nevertheless, in the Gospel of blessed Peter which is with us, it is written that, if you are the people who are destined to capture Jerusalem, you must cross by the coastal route, although its difficulty makes this seem impossible to us. Moreover, not only this concerning your journey, but many other things also—how you have acted and how you ought to act—are written in his Gospel, which is with us.”

While some were persuading them in these and other ways, and others were objecting, William Hugh of Montilio returned with the cross about which we spoke above. When the count’s household also saw this cross, they were so stirred to undertake the journey that, without the advice of the count and the other princes, they burned their tents and abandoned the siege of Archados; the count’s household did so first.

The count was therefore disturbed even to tears and to hatred of himself and his own people. Nevertheless, because of this, God did not lessen the willingness of his people. The duke of Lorraine, however, especially desired this journey and urged the people to undertake it.

Thus, departing from that hated and detested siege of Archados, we came before Tripoli. At that time Count Raymond was also striving, through prayers and gifts offered to all the nobles, to persuade them to besiege the city of Tripoli, but they all opposed him.

At that time the holy apostle Andrew appeared to Peter Desiderius, who was mentioned above, and said to him:

“Go and say to the count: Do not trouble yourself or others, because unless Jerusalem has first been captured, you will receive no aid. Do not be troubled by the unfinished siege of Archados, and do not be burdened because this city or the others along the route are not presently captured, for a battle is shortly impending in which these and many other cities will be conquered [Col. 0648A]. Therefore do not trouble yourself or your people, but whatever God grants you, distribute willingly in His name, and be a companion and faithful friend to your men.

“If you act in this way, the Lord will give you Jerusalem, Alexandria, and Babylon. But if you neglect these things, you will neither obtain what God has promised you nor have His messenger, until you are placed in such distress that you do not know where you can turn.”

The count therefore accepted these words of the priest—accepted them, I say, in words, but denied them in deeds. For although he had received a large sum of money from the king of Tripoli, he never wished to give any of it away. Instead, he daily abused his own men with beatings and insults.

The priest said not only these things, but also many others [Col. 0648B] that had occurred earlier, some of which we add to this work. Once, when we were intending to depart from Antioch, this priest came to me, Raymond, and told me that someone had appeared to him in a vision and said:

“Go to the church of Saint Leontius, and there you will find relics of four saints. Take them with you and carry them to Jerusalem.”

In the vision he showed him the relics and their reliquaries and taught him the saints’ names. When the priest awoke and did not quite trust his own vision, he began to plead and beseech God that, if this revelation came from Him, it might at least be made known to him a second time.

After several days the same saint appeared to him in a vision and threatened him severely because he had neglected the command of the Lord [Col. 0648C]. Unless he removed those relics by Thursday, he and his lord, Count Ysoardus, would suffer serious loss. For Ysoardus was count of Die, a man, as far as he knew, faithful to God and useful to all of us through his wisdom and goodness.

When the priest had told me, Raymond, this story, I related it to the bishop of Orange, the count of Saint-Gilles, and certain others. Taking candles, we went to the church of Saint Leontius. We offered candles and vows to God and to the saints of that church, asking that almighty God, who had sanctified them, grant them to us as companions and helpers; and that those saints would not disdain, for God’s sake, the company of pilgrims and exiles, but would rather join themselves to us and unite us to God [Col. 0648D].

When morning came, we went with the priest to the reliquaries of the saints and found them, just as had been foretold to us. These are the names of those saints: Cyprian, Omezios, Leontius, and John Chrysostom.

Among the reliquaries we also found a certain small box containing relics. When we asked the priest which saint’s relics they were, he replied that he did not know. When we asked the inhabitants whether they knew whose relics they were, they said that they did not know: some said Saint Mercury, others some other saints. The priest wished to lift them and gather them with the other relics.

To him I, Raymond, said forcefully before everyone who was present: “If this saint wishes to come to Jerusalem, let him reveal his name and his will; otherwise let him remain here [Col. 0649A]. Shall we be honored by unknown bones?”

Thus those relics were left behind that day. But when the priest had gathered the other relics and wrapped them in cloths and a pallium, a very handsome young man, apparently about fifteen years old, appeared to him while he was awake during the following night and said:

“Why did you not take my relics today with the others?”

The priest answered: “And who are you, lord?”

He said: “Do you not know who is the standard-bearer of this army?”

The priest replied: “I do not know, lord.”

When the priest gave him the same answer a second time as he asked him again, the young man threatened him terribly, saying: “You will indeed tell me.”

Then the priest said: “Lord, it is said of Saint George that he is the standard-bearer of this army.”

The young man replied: “You have spoken correctly. I am he. Therefore take my relics [Col. 0649B] and place them separately with the others.”

When the priest delayed doing this for several days, the same Saint George came and sternly commanded the presbyter:

“By no means fail to take my relics in the morning. Beside them you will find, in a little flask, some of the blood of the holy virgin and martyr Thecla; take that also, and afterward sing Mass.”

The priest found all these things just as he had been told and carried them out.

Before we come to the remaining events, we must not pass over those who, for love of the most holy expedition, did not hesitate to sail across the unknown and very long waters of the Mediterranean and the Ocean. For the English, having heard of the name of the vengeance of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0649C] against those who had unlawfully occupied the land of the Lord’s birth and of His apostles, entered the English Sea, circumnavigated Spain, crossed the Ocean, and then plowed through the Mediterranean. With great labor they secured the harbor of Antioch and the city of Laodicea before our army arrived there by land.

At that time their ships benefited us, as did those of the Genoese. Through these ships and their protection we had supplies for the siege from Cyprus and the other islands. These ships were constantly moving about the sea, and Greek ships had followed them, because the Saracens feared attacking them.

When those Englishmen saw our army setting out for Jerusalem and realized that the strength of their fleet had diminished through the long passage of time—for at the beginning they had possessed as many as thirty ships, whereas now they could scarcely muster ten or nine—some left their ships and disembarked, while others burned theirs and hastened on the journey with us.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

While our princes were delaying before Tripoli, the Lord placed such a love of going to Jerusalem in the people that no one could restrain himself or anyone else there. Instead, we set out in the evening, contrary to the princes’ decisions and contrary to the wishes of our army; traveling throughout that entire night, we reached Beirut on the following day. After that, unexpectedly seizing the narrow passes called Buccatorta, we came to Accaron within a few days and without hindrance.

The king of Accaron, fearing that we might besiege his city, swore to the count, in order that we might depart, that if we captured Jerusalem, or if we had been in the region of Judaea for twenty days and the king of the Babylonians did not meet us in battle, or if we were able to defeat that king, he would surrender himself and his city to us; meanwhile, he would be our friend.

Accordingly, having departed from Accaron one evening, we pitched our camp beside the marshes near Caesarea. While, as was customary, some were moving about the camp for necessary purposes, and others were asking acquaintances where their companions had lodged, a hawk struck down a dove flying above the army, mortally wounding it amid those moving about.

When the bishop of Atina picked it up [Col. 0650B], he found letters which it was carrying. The substance of the letters was something like this:

“The king of Accaron to the duke of Caesarea:

‘A canine generation has passed through my land: a foolish and contentious people, without leadership. Through you and others, harm them as much as you love your law. If you wish, you can easily do so. Send the same command to the other cities and camps.’”

In the morning, when we ordered the army to rest, the letters were read to the princes and to the whole people. We also explained how gracious God was toward them, so that not even birds could cross the air to harm us, and so that He disclosed to us even the secrets of our enemies. Therefore we offered praise and thanks to almighty God.

From there we departed secure, joyful, and numerous, advancing with the first part of the army and ahead of the last. When the Saracens living at Ramla heard that we had crossed the nearby river, they abandoned their fortification and weapons, along with much grain in the threshing floors and the crops they had gathered.

When we arrived there the next day, we recognized that God truly was fighting for us. Accordingly, we made vows to Saint George. Since he had declared himself our leader, the elders and the whole people decided that we should appoint a bishop there, because we had found it to be the first church in the land of Israel, and also so that blessed George might intercede with God for us and faithfully lead us through the land of his dwelling.

Ramla is near Jerusalem, about sixteen miles away [Col. 0650D]. There we held a council. Some said:

“Let us not go to Jerusalem for the present, but toward Egypt and Babylon. If, by God’s grace, we can defeat the king of Egypt, we shall gain not only Jerusalem but also Alexandria, Babylon, and very many kingdoms. But if we now go to Jerusalem and, finding insufficient water, abandon the siege, we shall accomplish neither this nor that afterward.”

Others, on the contrary, said:

“There are scarcely fifteen hundred knights in the army, and there is no great number of armed foot soldiers. Is it now being proposed that we go to unknown and very distant regions, where we can receive no aid from our own people, capture neither the holy city, establish no garrison, and not even be able to return from there when necessity requires? But this is nothing: let us follow our road, and let God provide for His servants concerning the siege, thirst, hunger, and everything else.”

We therefore left a garrison with the new bishop in the fortress of Ramla, loaded our oxen and camels, and indeed all our beasts of burden and horses, and turned our journey toward Jerusalem.

We forgot and regarded as worthless the command that Peter Bartholomew had given us: that we should draw near to Jerusalem for two miles only with bare feet. Each man wished to outstrip the others, driven by ambition to seize castles and villages.

For this was our custom: if someone reached a castle or village first and placed a marker there with a guard, no one else afterward could take possession of it. Thus, rising in the middle of the night and not waiting for their companions, all those ambitious men seized the mountains [Col. 0651B] and the villages in the Jordan plain.

A few, to whom this command of God was dearer, walked barefoot and sighed deeply because of their contempt for the divine word. Nevertheless, no one recalled a companion or friend from that ambitious race.

When, proceeding so proudly, we had come near Jerusalem, the Saracens came out of the city to meet the foremost of our men. They severely wounded men and horses; three or four of our men fell that day, and many were wounded.

The duke, the count of Flanders, and the count of Normandy besieged the city from the north. They besieged it from the church of Saint Stephen, which is approximately at the center of the city, northward to the corner tower nearest the Tower of David.

The count [Col. 0651C] and his army sat to the west and besieged it from the duke’s siege-line to the descent of Mount Zion. But because his men could not approach the city wall directly for an assault, since a certain valley lay between them, he wished to move his towers and change their position.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

One day, when the count had gone around the city and had come to Mount Zion, seen the church, and heard of the wonders God had performed there, he said to the princes and to those who were present:

“If we abandon these sacred places which God has presented to us here, and afterward the Saracens occupy them, what will become of us? What if, because of their hatred of us, they defile and break them [Col. 0651D]? Who knows whether God has given us these things as a trial, to test how much we love Him? I know this with certainty: unless we carefully preserve these sacred places, God will not deliver to us those within the city.”

Therefore Count Raymond, contrary to the wishes of his princes, ordered his tents to be moved there. As a result, he suffered such envy from his own men that they were unwilling either to lodge there or to keep watch there by night. Each remained in the place where he had previously lodged, except for a few who moved there with the count.

Nevertheless, every day the count hired knights and foot soldiers, at great expense, to guard his camp.

These sacred places are in that church: the tombs of King David, Solomon, and blessed Stephen, the first martyr; the most blessed Virgin Mary departed from this world there; the Lord ate there, and, after rising from the dead, appeared there to His disciples and to Thomas; and there the apostles were inflamed by the coming of the Holy Spirit.

After the siege had been established, one day the princes came to the recluse who is on the Mount of Olives. He said to them:

“If tomorrow you assault the city until the ninth hour, the Lord will deliver it to you.”

When they replied, “We do not have the equipment with which the wall can be attacked,” he answered:

“Almighty God is able, if He wishes, to attack the wall with a ladder of rushes. The Lord is present with those who labor for the truth.”

Accordingly, after obtaining whatever equipment could be procured that night, they assaulted the city so vigorously from morning until the third hour that the Saracens were forced to abandon the inner wall, after our men had broken through the outer wall and some of our men had climbed to the height of the inner wall [Col. 0652B].

But when the city was already being captured, indolence and fear crept in, the assault was halted, and we then lost many of our men. On the following day no assault was begun.

After this, everyone went throughout that region to gather provisions. There was no longer any talk of obtaining what was necessary to capture the city. Each person served his belly and his appetite; and what was much worse, they did not call upon the Lord to deliver them from the many and great evils under which they were being oppressed even unto death.

For when we arrived, the Saracens had closed the mouths of the wells, destroyed the cisterns, and blocked the channels of the springs [Col. 0652C]. The Lord Himself had turned rivers into wilderness and watercourses into thirsty ground, because of the wickedness of those who inhabited those lands (Ps. 106:33). Therefore water was obtained there only with great labor.

There is a certain spring on the descent of Mount Zion called the pool of Siloam. It is a large spring, but it flowed only on the third day. The inhabitants said of that spring that it was accustomed to flow only on Friday; on the other days it was like a marsh. What this may have signified, apart from God’s will, we do not know.

When, as has been said, water began to flow for us on the third day, it was drawn with such force and pressure that people threw themselves into it against one another, and many beasts of burden and cattle perished. Thus, when the spring had been filled with bodies and the carcasses of animals, the stronger men crushed one another to death at the outlet of the water, which emerged through a cleft in the rock; nevertheless, the weaker men took that filthy water for themselves.

Many sick people lay beside the spring, unable to utter a sound because their tongues were parched. They merely held out their hands with open mouths toward those whom they saw possessing water. Across the fields stood horses, mules, oxen, and many other animals unable to move a step. Once, exhausted and dried up by the aridity of thirst, they had stood there for a long time, they collapsed; hence there was an exceedingly foul stench in our camp.

Thus, in our affliction, we repeatedly sent people to springs two or three miles away so that water might be brought back from there and the animals watered [Col. 0653A]. But when the Saracens learned that our men were moving unarmed toward the springs through the most rugged mountains, they lay in ambush for them, killed as many as they wished, and took others captive. They also drove away their beasts of burden and cattle.

If anyone had brought water for sale in the streets, he could receive as much as he wished for it. Indeed, five or six coins were scarcely enough for a thirsty person for one day if he wished to buy clear water.

There was no talk of wine, or very little. Besides this, heat, dust, and wind aggravated the thirst, which was already more than sufficient by itself.
