But why say much about these things? Even among us there were few who remembered God or cared about the things needed either to assault the city or to arouse God’s mercy [Col. 0653B]. Thus we neither recognized God amid the blows, nor did He show favor to the ungrateful.

## CHAPTER XXXV

During these events messengers arrived announcing that nine of our ships had put in at Joppa. The sailors requested that a garrison be sent there, both to guard the tower of Joppa and to keep them safe in the harbor.

Joppa is a destroyed city, except for its castle; and that too is largely ruined, apart from one tower. But there is a harbor there, and Jerusalem is nearby, a day’s journey away. There the sea lies closer to Jerusalem.

When our people heard about the ships, they all rejoiced. The count sent Galdemar, called Carpinellus, with twenty knights and approximately fifty foot soldiers. After him came Raymond Peleth [Col. 0653C] with fifty knights, and William of Sabrano with his companions.

When Galdemar reached the plains beyond Ramla, four hundred Arabs and about two hundred Turks met him. He arranged his knights according to their small number, placing the archers in the front line, and advanced toward the enemy without hesitation, trusting in God’s aid.

The enemy, believing that they could overwhelm him and his men, charged, shot arrows, and surrounded them. Three or four knights from Galdemar’s side fell there, as did Achard of Mount Merulo, a most noble young man and renowned knight; others were wounded. All the archers fell. On the enemy’s side, however, many were killed.

Nevertheless, this did not lessen the battle that threatened from the enemy; nor did the courage of our knights despair of God’s mercy. Instead, growing hot from their wounds and from death itself, they pressed upon the enemy all the more fiercely because they felt that they had suffered heavier things at their hands [Col. 0653D].

But when our leaders, now more exhausted by weariness than overcome by fear, wished to withdraw from the battle line, Raymond Peleth, seeing dust rising in the distance, rushed headlong and swiftly into the fight. He raised such a cloud of dust that the enemy believed a very large number of knights were with him.

Thus, by God’s grace, our men were rescued, the enemy was routed and put to flight, about two hundred of them were killed, and very much booty was captured. For it is the custom among those peoples that, if they flee and sense their enemies pressing upon them, they first throw away their weapons, then their clothing, and afterward their saddles [Col. 0654A]. It therefore happened in this battle that our few knights continued killing men from that multitude of enemies until they were exhausted, while retaining the spoils of the rest.

After the spoils had been gathered and divided, our knights came to Joppa. The sailors received them with such joy and confidence that they even forgot about their own ships and failed to keep watch over the sea. They shared with the soldiers the bread, wine, and fish that they had brought with them.

Thus, made careless by their joy and security, the sailors failed to keep watch during the night, and the enemy suddenly surrounded them by sea. When they saw at daybreak that they could not fight against such a multitude, they put their ships ashore, carried off only the spoils, and so both victors and vanquished returned together to Jerusalem [Col. 0654B].

But one of the ships was not intercepted, because it had gone out on a raiding expedition. When this ship returned with very great booty and saw the other ships enclosed by the enemy fleet, it rowed and sailed back to Laodicea. There it reported to our companions and friends what had happened to us who were in Jerusalem, exactly as it had occurred.

We later recognized that all these events had happened justly, since we had rejected the faith in the messages God sent to us, and, despairing of God’s mercy, had gone down to the plains of the Jordan. There we gathered palm branches and baptized ourselves in the river, chiefly so that we might transfer ourselves to Joppa, having seen Jerusalem and abandoned the siege, and might return by whatever means we could. But the Lord provided for His unbelieving servants through the ships.

At that time we held councils because the princes were badly divided among themselves. The matter of Tancred was also discussed, because he had occupied Bethlehem and had placed his standard over the church of the Lord’s Nativity as though over a common house.

It was proposed that one of the princes should be chosen as king, to guard the city, lest, if God delivered it to us as a common possession, it should be destroyed through being left without a common guardian.

The bishops and clergy replied that no king ought to be chosen there, where God had suffered and been crowned. If someone should say in his heart, “I sit upon the throne of David and possess his kingdom,” then, degenerate from David’s faith and virtue, he might cause God to destroy him and become angry with both the place and the people.

Moreover, the prophet cries out, saying: “When the Holy of Holies comes, anointing will cease”—a thing which it was evident to all nations had now come to pass.

Instead, there should be an advocate who would guard the city and distribute the region’s taxes and revenues among the city’s guardians.

For these and many other reasons the election was delayed and obstructed until the eighth day after the capture of Jerusalem. Nor was this the only matter that did not turn out as we wished; each day labor and tribulation doubled among the people.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

At last, for the sake of His name, the merciful and gracious Lord [Col. 0655A]—and also so that our adversaries might not insult His law by saying, “Where is their God?”—sent us word through the bishop of Puy, Lord Ademar, how we might appease His anger and obtain mercy.

We too, while concealing the Lord’s command, proclaimed that this had to be done, lest, if the people disregarded the command, they should be more culpable and suffer more severely. For the Lord was so kind toward us that He sent His messengers to us; but because they were brothers, the people did not believe them.

Therefore the bishop spoke to Peter Desiderius, saying:

“Speak to the princes and to all the people, and say: You who have come from such distant regions to worship God and the Lord of hosts here, cleanse yourselves from your impurities, and let each man turn back from his wicked deeds [Col. 0655B]. After this, go around Jerusalem barefoot, calling upon God, and fast. If you do this and assault Jerusalem manfully for nine days, it will be captured. Otherwise, all the evils you have suffered will be multiplied for you by the Lord.”

When the priest had told these things to the bishop’s brother, William Hugh, to his lord Count Ysoardus, and to certain members of the clergy, they assembled a council of the princes and the entire people and said:

“Brothers, you know the reason for our journey and for such great weariness. Yet we are acting negligently, so that we neither obtain what is necessary for assaulting the city nor take care how to reconcile to ourselves God, whom we have offended in so many ways, whom we have driven away from us, and whom through our wicked deeds we have caused to flee far from us [Col. 0655C].

“Now, if it seems right to you, let each man be reconciled to the brother whom he has offended, and let each brother kindly forgive his brother. After this, let us humble ourselves before God, go around Jerusalem barefoot, and appeal for God’s mercy through the intercession of the saints.

“May that almighty God, who for our sake assumed flesh from us His servants, emptying Himself of the form of His lordship, and who, humbly seated upon a donkey and about to suffer the punishment of death on the cross for us, entered this city while the crowds came out to meet Him with great processional honor—may He, for the honor and glory of His name, open the city to us and grant us all the power to execute judgment upon His and our enemies, who unworthily occupy and defile the place of His passion and burial and who strive to exclude us from so great a benefit of divine humility and our redemption.”

These words pleased the princes and the whole people. Therefore it was publicly ordered that on the following Friday the clergy should prepare themselves with crosses and the relics of the saints for a procession, and that the knights and all the strong men should follow them with trumpets and standards, walking barefoot and armed.

We joyfully fulfilled all these commands, according to the order of God and the princes. When we had come to the Mount of Olives and were at the place from which the Lord ascended into heaven after His resurrection, we preached to the people, saying [Col. 0656A]:

“Since we have followed the Lord as far as the place of His ascension and can go no farther, let each man forgive his brother who has been injured, so that almighty God may become gracious to us.”

Why say more? Everyone forgave, and with very generous almsgiving they appealed for God’s mercy, asking that God not abandon His people at the end, since He had led them gloriously and wonderfully all the way to the end.

Thus God’s mercy was appeased, because all the things that had previously opposed us now turned out favorably for us.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

Although we pass over many things, we do not wish to pass over this one. When we went around the outside of the city amid the tumult of the procession, the Saracens and Turks moved about inside the city, mocking us in many ways. They placed many crosses upon the walls, on gibbets, and treated them with beatings and insults [Col. 0656B].

Seeing these signs from nearby, we hoped in God’s mercy and worked day and night with great effort to attack the city.

The duke and the count of Normandy and Flanders therefore placed Gaston of Béarn in charge of the workers who were constructing the siege engines and preparing the hurdles and embankments for attacking the wall.

This Gaston, a most noble prince, was honored by everyone on account of the usefulness and goodness he had demonstrated. Therefore, skillfully dividing among the workers the task entrusted to him by the princes, he wisely hastened the work.

The princes took responsibility only for transporting the timber, while Gaston supervised the construction of what was needed [Col. 0656C]. Similarly, Count Raymond placed William Richau in charge of his workers on Mount Zion, and placed the bishop of Albano over the Saracens and the others who were bringing wood.

The count’s men had captured many castles and villages of the Saracens and imposed work upon the Saracens as though they were their slaves. Fifty or sixty of them carried on their shoulders an enormous beam which four pairs of oxen could scarcely have transported, for the construction of the siege engines at Jerusalem.

Why say more? Everyone worked and labored with one mind and equal agreement: they built and helped, no one was idle, and no one withheld his hand. Everyone worked voluntarily, except the craftsmen. The craftsmen were paid from the collections that had been made among the people [Col. 0656D]. But the count paid his own workers what was owed to them from his revenues.

Certainly the hand of the Lord was at work and helped those who worked.

When, after a short interval, all our undertakings and siege engines had been prepared, our princes held a council and said:

“Let every man prepare himself for battle on Thursday. Meanwhile, let us devote ourselves to prayers, vigils, and almsgiving. Lend your beasts of burden, together with the boys who work for us and the woodcutters, so that they may carry beams, poles, stakes, and rods for making the hurdles. Let two knights together make one curved hurdle or one ladder. Do not hesitate to labor for God, because He will soon bring your labors to an end.”

All these instructions were willingly accepted. After this, orders were issued concerning which prince, with his people, would assault each part of the city and at which places the siege engines should be brought up [Col. 0657A].

## CHAPTER XXXVIII
Seeing this, the Saracens who were inside the city fortified the weaker places of the walls against us so thoroughly, because of the multitude of engines being constructed, that to some it seemed hopeless that the city could be captured. As the appointed day of the assault approached, the duke, the count of Flanders, and the count of Normandy, when they saw that the Saracens had prepared such and so many defensive works against all our engines, transported their engines, mantelets, and earthworks throughout the entire night to that part of the city which extends from the church of Saint Stephen [Col. 0657B] to the Valley of Jehoshaphat.

But you who read this must not suppose that the labor and ingenuity expended there were slight. For it is nearly a mile from the place where the dismantled engines were carried piece by piece to the place where they were assembled. When morning came and the Saracens saw all the instruments and tents that had been brought there during the night, they were astonished. This caused wonder not only among the Saracens but also among us. For every faithful person could plainly recognize that the hand of the Lord was with us.

This transfer was made because the ground was level and suitable for bringing the engines up to the wall, since they could be transported only across level ground; and also because that part of the city seemed weaker. Since it lay far from the camp, that section had remained unfortified. This part of the city was on the north. Nevertheless, the count and his men labored on Mount Zion, which lies south of the city; but he then had many helpers, namely William of Ebraic, and with him all the Genoese sailors who, as we related above, had lost their ships at Joppa. They had, however, taken from their ships ropes, iron hammers, nails, axes, adzes, and hatchets, which proved extremely necessary to us.

But why delay? The appointed day of battle had now arrived, and the assault began. First, however, we wish to say this: according to the opinion of many, as well as our own, there were inside the city as many as sixty thousand fighting men [Col. 0657D], apart from children and women, whose number could not be determined. Of our own men fit for arms, as far as we can estimate, there were no more than twelve thousand; and many of these were weak and poor. In our army there were, as I reckon, twelve or thirteen hundred knights, no more.

We have said this so that you may understand that, whether what is begun in the name of the Lord is great or small, nothing happens in vain, as the following page shows. When our men began to undermine the towers and walls, stones hurled from siege engines and stone-throwers flew from every side, and arrows fell like innumerable hailstones. But the servants of God endured these things patiently, holding firmly to their purpose in faith: either they would fall, or they would soon avenge themselves upon their enemies [Col. 0658A].

The battle continued with no sign of victory. When our men were already approaching the walls with their engines, not only stones and arrows but also wood and straw were thrown at them. In addition, fire, and wooden hammers wrapped in pitch, wax, sulfur, tow, and little pieces of cloth set alight were cast against the engines. I mean hammers studded with nails on every side, so that wherever they struck they would stick fast, and, sticking fast, set the engines on fire.

They threw the wood and straw so that fires kindled from them might at least delay those whom neither sword nor lofty walls could stop, and whom even the deep moat could not hold back. Thus the battle lasted from sunrise to sunset on that day, so extraordinarily that nothing more remarkable is thought ever to have taken place. Even then we continued to call almighty God our leader and commander, trusting in his mercy.

When night came, it doubled the fear felt by both sides. The Saracens feared that the city might be captured by our men during the night, or that on the following day, once the outer defenses had been broken and the moat completed, the wall might be penetrated very quickly. Our men, on the other hand, feared only that the Saracens might somehow set fire to the engines that had been brought up and thus gain strength. Therefore there were watches on both sides, labor on both sides, and sleepless vigilance on both sides. On one side was the surest hope; on the other, uncertain fear.

These men labored for God voluntarily, with works directed toward capturing the city; those men labored unwillingly for the laws of Mahomet, with works directed toward resistance. Believe me, it is astonishing to consider what works and what devices both sides prepared during the night [Col. 0658C].

When morning came, such ardor seized our men that they advanced as far as the walls and brought the engines there. But the Saracens had made so many engines that they could set nine or ten against each one of ours, and thus greatly impeded our efforts. Yet this was the ninth day, concerning which the priest had said that the city would be captured by that day.

But why prolong the account? Our engines were already being battered by the frequent blows of stones, and our men were failing, exhausted in many ways. Yet the mercy of God still remained—never to be conquered, nowhere overcome, always present in tribulation. Nor should this be passed over: while two women wished to bewitch one of our stone-throwers [Col. 0658D], a stone hurled with force struck the women who were chanting, together with three children; and, striking their souls from them, it turned aside their incantations.

When about midday all our men were becoming confused, both from weariness and from despair—for several adversaries were resisting each one of ours—there was also the strongest and highest wall, together with abundant resources and every advantage, which served the enemy for defense but worked against us. In the midst of our exhaustion and the enemy’s exultation, the mediating mercy of God intervened and turned our mourning into joy—a joy which may no day take away from us.

Indeed, a plan was already being discussed to withdraw our engines, one part of which had been burned and the other shattered. Then suddenly a certain soldier began waving his shield from the Mount of Olives toward those who were on the count’s side and toward the others, urging them to enter. We could not discover who this soldier was.

Encouraged by this sign, our men who had already been weakening began to rush at the walls; others threw ladders and ropes upward. Moreover, some young men had set arrows on fire and shot them at the mattresses with which the Saracens had protected the defensive work they had constructed against the duke’s wooden tower and those of the two counts. The mattresses were made of quilted padding.

A fire was kindled there and drove away those defending the fortification. Then the duke and those with him quickly loosened from above the mantelet protecting the front of the siege tower, from its top down to the middle. Once this had been done as a bridge, they began bravely and fearlessly to enter Jerusalem [Col. 0659B].

Among the first to enter were Tancred and the duke of Lorraine. It is scarcely credible how much blood they shed that day. After them everyone else climbed up, and the Saracens were already suffering.

But hear the astonishing thing I shall now relate. Although the city had almost been seized by the Franks, the Saracens still resisted those who were on the count’s side, as though they could never be captured. When our men had gained possession of the city’s walls and towers, astonishing things could then be seen.

Some of the Saracens, in the easier manner of death, were beheaded; others, struck by arrows, were forced to leap from the towers; still others were tortured for a very long time, burned by fire, and consumed in flames. Throughout the lanes and streets of the city there seemed to be heaps of heads, hands, and feet [Col. 0659C]. Amid the corpses there was a public rushing about of men and horses.

But these things we have mentioned are small and few. Let us come to the Temple of Solomon, where they had been accustomed to sing their rites and ceremonies. But what happened there? If we tell the truth, we exceed belief. Let it suffice to say that in the Temple and in Solomon’s portico, people rode in blood up to their knees and up to the horses’ bridles—a just and wondrous judgment of God, so that the same place might receive the blood of those whose blasphemies against God it had endured for so long.

When the city had been filled with corpses and blood, some fled to the Tower of David and requested the count Raymond’s pledge of safety; and they surrendered the citadel to him [Col. 0659D].

## CHAPTER XXXIX

After the city had been captured, it was well worth seeing the pilgrims’ devotion at the Lord’s tomb: how they clapped their hands, rejoicing and singing a new song to the Lord. Their minds offered vows of praise to God, victorious and triumphant, which they could not adequately express. A new day, new joy and exultation, new and perpetual gladness, the completion of labor and devotion—all demanded new words and new songs from everyone.

This day, I say, celebrated throughout every age to come, transformed all our sorrows and labors into joy and exultation. This day, I say, was the confirmation of all Christendom, the emptying of paganism, and the renewal of our faith. “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Psalm 117:23), because on this day the Lord shone forth and blessed his people.

On this day the lord Adhemar, bishop of Puy, was seen by many in the city. Many also testify concerning him that he was the first to climb the wall and that he urged his companions and the people to climb after him.

On this day the apostles, expelled from Jerusalem, were scattered throughout the whole world. On this same day, the apostles’ sons reclaimed the city and homeland for God and for their fathers.

This day is celebrated on the Ides of July, to the praise and glory of the name of Christ, who gave his Church the city and homeland that he had sworn to the fathers, and restored it in faith and blessing to their children.

On this day we sang the office of the Resurrection, because on this day he who rose from the dead by his own power raised us up by his grace. Let this suffice concerning these matters.

## CHAPTER XL

When six or seven days had passed, on the eighth day the princes began solemnly to arrange for someone to be chosen as king. He would take charge of everything, collect the region’s taxes, serve as the person to whom the peoples of the land would return, and ensure that the land was not again laid waste.

While they were engaged in this, certain members of the clergy assembled and said to the princes: “We approve your election, provided that you proceed correctly and in due order. Just as eternal things precede temporal things, so first choose a spiritual vicar; afterward choose someone to preside over secular affairs. Otherwise we judge your election invalid.”

When the princes heard this [Col. 0660C], they were extremely angry, but nevertheless continued to hasten the election. The clergy, however, had been diminished by the death of Lord Adhemar, bishop of Puy, who in his lifetime, a second Moses, sustained and restrained our army by his counsel and divine exhortations.

After him, William of Orange, a bishop and a man of good memory, wished to help us with all his strength, but within a short time he rested in peace at Ma‘arra. Thus, deprived of good men, the clergy conducted itself humbly, except for the bishop of Albara and certain others.

The bishop of Mâṭrûna, having proceeded by a path other than the straight one and fraudulently obtained the Church of Bethlehem, was captured by the Saracens on the third or fourth day and never again appeared among our people.

The princes therefore disregarded the clergy’s admonition and opposition and urged the count of Saint-Gilles to accept the kingship. But he declared that he shrank from the royal title in that city; he would, however, give them his consent if someone else accepted it.

For this reason they unanimously chose the duke and presented him at the Lord’s tomb. Afterward the duke demanded the Tower of David from the count. The count excused himself, saying that he wished to remain in that region until Easter and, in the meantime, wished himself and his men to be treated honorably.

The duke, however, said that he would rather abandon everything else than the tower. From this disputes multiplied. The counts of Flanders and Normandy favored the duke, as did nearly all the count’s men from his own land, believing that, once the tower had been returned, they too would return with him.

Nor did only the provincials oppose their lord, the count, in this matter. They also fabricated many disgraceful things about him so that he would not be chosen king [Col. 0661A].

The count, deprived of the counsel of his companions and friends, handed the tower over to the bishop of Albara in order to submit to judgment. The bishop, however, without waiting for judgment, handed the tower over to the duke.

When the bishop was accused concerning this act, he said in his defense that he had been compelled and subjected to violence. But I discovered the truth of the matter: a great many weapons had been brought into the patriarchal residence where the bishop lived near the Church of the Lord’s Sepulchre. He himself claimed that violence had been done to him and frequently accused the count’s retainers of this matter in secret.

Once the tower had been surrendered, the count burned with great hatred against his own people, saying that he had been dishonored and could not remain in that country. Thus we departed from Jerusalem for Jericho, took palm branches, and came to the Jordan. As Peter Bartholomew had instructed, we made a raft of reeds, placed the count upon it, and ferried him across; since we had no boat, this seemed best to us.

Afterward, having summoned the multitude, we required them to pray to God for the life of the count and the other princes. Then, dressed in a shirt and new breeches, we carried out what had been commanded us; but why the man of God had given such an order, we still do not know.

## CHAPTER XLI

[Note: [Col. 0661D] What follows is not by Raymond.]

After these things had been completed, we returned to Jerusalem. At that time Arnulf, chaplain of the count of Normandy, was chosen patriarch by certain people, while the good men opposed the choice—both because he was not a subdeacon and especially because he was of priestly lineage. During our journey he had also been accused of unchastity, to such an extent that the common people had composed disgraceful songs about him.

But he neither respected the decrees of the canons nor, seized by such ambition, paid heed to his lineage or the disgrace upon his conscience. He stirred up the people against the good men and had himself raised to the patriarchal seat with hymns and songs, amid the great applause of the people.

The divine punishment inflicted upon the bishop of Mâṭrûna, who had been the instigator and organizer of this affair, did not frighten Arnulf. On the contrary, he did not cease depriving the clerics who held altars in the Church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, or who had been assigned payments for its custody, of their benefices [Col. 0661D].

Having obtained this power, Arnulf began asking the inhabitants of the city where the cross was—the cross that the pilgrims had been accustomed to venerate before the capture of Jerusalem. When they denied knowing it and tried to prove this by oath and by other signs, they were finally compelled and said:

“It is evident that God has chosen you, delivered you from all your tribulations, and granted you this city and many others—not through the strength of your own valor, but by blinding the impious in his fury and opening the most strongly fortified cities to you. Your leader and Lord himself advances before you in terrible wars.

“With what obstinacy, then, since we see that the Lord is with you, should we conceal his benefits from you?” [Col. 0662A]

Afterward they led them to a certain courtyard of a church, and, digging there, they handed it over. All our men rejoiced and rendered praise and thanks to almighty God, who had restored to us not only the city in which he had suffered, but also the emblems of his Passion and victory, so that we might embrace him more closely with the hands of faith in proportion as we beheld more certain signs of our salvation.

## CHAPTER XLII

As we said above, it had been arranged that the duke of Lorraine should retain the city. The count, however, was distressed by grief and injury because he had lightly lost the Tower of David, the head, that is, of the entire kingdom of Judah, and because he was planning to return with the greater part of our people.

Then we were informed [Col. 0662B] that the king of the Babylonians had come to Ascalon with an innumerable multitude of pagans. We were told that he had come to attack Jerusalem, kill all the Franks aged twenty years and above, and take the rest captive together with the women. He would give the men to women from his own people and women to the young men, so that thereafter the lords of Babylon might possess warlike families of Frankish stock.

Not content with this, he said that he would do the same to Antioch and Bohemond; he also declared that he would place the crowns of Damascus and the other cities upon his head. Considering the number of his infantry and soldiers, he said that neither the Turks nor the Franks, conquerors of the Turks, were anything.

Nor was he content even with this [Col. 0662C]. He hurled blasphemies against God, saying that he would so destroy the place of the Lord’s Nativity, the manger where the Lord had lain, the place of the Passion and Golgotha—where, it is said, the Lord’s blood flowed while he hung upon the cross—and the place of the Lord’s burial, together with all the other holy places revered by the Christian people in or near the city, that he would tear them from the earth root and branch, crush them, and afterward throw the dust into the sea. Thus, he said, there would no longer be any memorial of the Lord for the Frankish people to seek in those regions.

When these and many other things were reported to us, as well as the multitude accompanying that tyrant, and when we learned that they had all assembled at Ascalon, which was a day and a half from Jerusalem [Col. 0662D], our princes and clergy assembled. Walking barefoot before the Lord’s tomb with many prayers and tears, they implored mercy from the Lord, asking him now to deliver his people, whom he had until then made victorious over all things, and not to allow the place of his sanctification, which he had cleansed, to be defiled any further for the sake of his name.

Afterward, likewise walking barefoot with psalms and hymns and calling upon God’s mercy through the protection of the saints, we came to the Temple of the Lord. There we poured ourselves out in mind and body, so that he might remember the blessing poured out there:

“If your people sin against you and repent, and come and pray in this place, then hear from heaven, O Lord, and deliver them from the hands of their enemies” (3 Kings 8).

After receiving the blessing from the bishops, the princes made arrangements for the conduct of the war and for the city’s defense. The duke and his soldiers therefore departed to verify with certainty whether matters concerning Admiravis were indeed as rumor reported.

When he reached the plain of Ramla, he sent the bishop of Mâṭrûna to the counts at Jerusalem with a report of the situation. Once they had been informed about the war, they presented the common cause of battle to all the strong men who had remained in the city.

Thus, after praying to God and taking up our arms and the Lord’s lance, we departed from Jerusalem and came to the plain [Col. 0663B] that same day. On the following day, after joining the army and arranging firm defenses on every side, we advanced.

In the evening, when we had come near the river lying on the route from Jerusalem to Ascalon, Arabs were grazing flocks of sheep, herds of cattle beyond number, and camels without number. When our men saw this multitude of people and animals, they thought it was the enemy army. Taking up their arms, they sent ahead as many as two hundred soldiers to investigate. The rest, armed as we have said, advanced in nine divisions.

Three were at the rear, three at the front, and three in the middle, arranged so that wherever battle might arise, it could be met by those three ranks, while the middle division remained in support of all.

When the Arab shepherds saw the soldiers sent ahead [Col. 0663C], they abandoned the animals, as though they ought to engage all of us in battle if God looked upon them as favorably as upon us. About three thousand of the shepherds were armed. We hesitate to claim that our army numbered more than twelve hundred, and we do not dare to put the number of our infantry at more than nine thousand.

After the shepherds had been driven away, we seized booty such as we had never seen before that day. Some of the shepherds were killed and a few were captured. We then remained in the same place because it was evening.

We compelled the captives to reveal the enemy’s intentions, condition, and numbers. They confessed that their intention was to besiege Jerusalem, attack all the Franks, kill and capture them. They added that Admiravis was encamped nearby, about five leagues away, and would depart against us on the following day.

Hardly anyone knew the number of the enemy with certainty, because their forces increased daily. When asked about themselves and their companions, they said that they were shepherds of the animals that were to be distributed as provisions throughout the Babylonian army.

Once our men were certain that battle was at hand and were eager for it, they forgave their companions the causes of injuries and disputes. Afterward, having confessed their sins and negligences, they were so encouraged in spirit that it scarcely seemed credible to them that the enemy was prepared for battle.

Such confidence arose in the hearts of each one that they believed their enemies more timid than deer and more innocent than sheep. This confidence existed because we believed that the Lord was with us, as in our other undertakings, and because, on account of the blasphemies directed against him, we believed that he would act for his own sake even if our cause were weak. Therefore we wished him to be a defender on our side and them to be helpers on theirs.

Then it was proclaimed throughout the army that everyone should be ready for battle in the morning, that each man should join his own prince’s contingent, and that no one should touch the booty. All who touched it before the battle was completed were excommunicated.

We spent that night in extreme poverty. We had no tents, little bread, no wine, and very little grain or salt. There was an abundance of meat, almost like sand, and we lived on meat: instead of bread, there was mutton.

Dawn was already rising on the following day, and the sleepless multitude was encouraged to battle by trumpets and horns [Col. 0664B]. At first light, therefore, we departed. With defenses arranged on every side as we have said, we led the army of God toward Mahomet’s camp.

The enemy, however, remained inside its camp, never imagining that we had barely been able to contain ourselves within the walls at their arrival. When they heard about the shepherds’ death and flight, they said: “The Franks came for plunder and are returning with it.” They were informed daily by those who had fled from Jerusalem about our small numbers and the weakness of our common people and horses.

Moreover, trusting in their own numbers and strength, they believed that they could drown us and our camp in nothing more than spit. Their chanters and soothsayers, it is said, had also told them not to move their fortified camps until Saturday, nor to fight against us. If they attempted to do anything earlier, it would turn against them.

We, however, as we have said, advanced in nine divisions. God multiplied his army so greatly that we did not appear inferior in number to the enemy. The animals we had abandoned had joined us. Forming herds, they accompanied us without anyone driving them: they stood when those who stood did, ran when those who ran did, and advanced when those who advanced did.

This was an immeasurable multitude of valuable animals. Who could count the total number of weapons and tents?

When our enemies saw both the multitude of their own men cut down and our men proceeding confidently and eagerly through their camp as victors and plunderers [Col. 0664D], they came to their senses and said: “Flight is our only refuge. Why do we delay? If, exhausted from the journey, almost half-dead from hunger and thirst, they have overthrown all our multitude in a single charge, what will they do when rested and refreshed, victorious against men half-dead, diminished, and frightened?”

Thus the enemies, their spirits thrown into confusion, returned to Ascalon, which lay a mile from our camp—but not all of them.

Then Count Raymond decided to send a certain Bohemond, a man of Turkish origin, to Admiravis under the pretext of entering into friendship. He was to accuse Admiravis of refusing to restore Jerusalem, since he had brought arms against us, and at the same time determine whether he was preparing flight or battle and how he would conduct himself if defeated.

## CHAPTER XLIII

[Col. 0665A]

Meanwhile a messenger came to Tancred and Count Eustace, telling them to prepare themselves and proceed to receive the city of Nablus (Neapolis). They went out, taking many knights and foot soldiers with them, and reached the city. Its inhabitants immediately surrendered.

Afterward Duke Godfrey, who was also king of Jerusalem, ordered them to come quickly to the battle that the admiral of Babylon had prepared for them at Ascalon. They hastened through the mountains, seeking battle with the Saracens, and came to Caesarea.

Proceeding beside the sea to the city of Ramla, they found many Arabs there who were scouts for the army. Our men pursued them and captured several. These men reported all the news of the war [Col. 0665B], where it was taking place, how many there were, and where they intended to fight against the Christians.

When Tancred heard this, he immediately sent a messenger to Duke Godfrey in Jerusalem, to the patriarch, and to all the princes, saying: “Know that battle has been prepared for us at Ascalon by the admiral. Therefore come quickly with all the strength you can muster.”

The duke then ordered everyone to be summoned, so that they might go faithfully prepared to Ascalon to meet our enemies. He himself, together with the patriarch and Robert, count of Flanders, left the city on Tuesday, and the bishop of Mâṭrûna went with them.

Then the count of Saint-Gilles and Robert of Normandy said that they would not leave unless they knew for certain that there was a battle. They therefore ordered their soldiers to go and see whether there truly was a battle and to return as quickly as possible, since they themselves would soon be ready to come [Col. 0665C].

Those men went, saw that the battle was ready, and quickly reported that they had seen it with their own eyes. Immediately the duke seized the bishop of Mâṭrûna and ordered him to Jerusalem, so that the soldiers there might prepare themselves and come to the battle.

The bishop of Mâṭrûna, however, turned back, carrying the message sent to the patriarch and the duke. The Saracens came out to meet him, captured him, and led him away with them.

Peter the Hermit remained in Jerusalem, arranging and instructing Greeks and Latins, as well as clerics, to celebrate a procession faithfully before God and to give alms and offer prayers, so that God might grant victory to his people. Clerics and priests, dressed in sacred vestments, led the procession to the Temple of the Lord [Col. 0665D], and celebrated Masses and prayers so that God might defend his people.

Finally, the patriarch, the bishops, and the other elders assembled at the river on this side of Ascalon. There they plundered many animals—cattle, camels, sheep, and every kind of property.

About three hundred Arabs came upon them, and our men rushed at them. They captured two and pursued the others as far as their army.

When evening came, the patriarch ordered a proclamation to be made throughout the army that, early the next morning, everyone was to be ready for battle. He excommunicated anyone who directed his attention to any booty until the battle had been fought; once it was over, they were to return in joyful triumph and take whatever had been predestined for them by the Lord [Col. 0666A].

At first light, they entered a very beautiful valley beside the seashore and arranged their battle lines there. The duke arranged his, the count of Normandy his, the count of Saint-Gilles his, the count of Flanders his, Count Eustace his, and Tancred and Gaston theirs.

They also arranged infantry and archers to go before the knights and set everything in order. Immediately they began to fight in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

On the left was Duke Godfrey with his division; the count of Saint-Gilles was near the sea; on the right were the count of Normandy and the count of Flanders; Tancred and all the others rode in the middle.

Then our men began to advance slowly. The pagans stood ready for battle. Each of them had a small vessel hanging around his neck, from which they intended to drink while pursuing us; but by the grace of God they were not permitted to do so.

When the count of Normandy saw the admiral’s standard-bearer carrying a certain golden apple at the top of a spear covered with silver, he charged him fiercely and wounded him mortally. On the other side, the count of Flanders attacked them with great violence. Tancred then charged through the middle of their tent.

When the pagans saw this, they immediately took flight. The multitude of pagans was innumerable, and no one knows their number except God alone. Their battle forces were immense, but divine power accompanied us—so great and strong that we immediately overcame them [Col. 0666C].

The enemies of God stood blinded and bewildered. Seeing Christ’s soldiers with open eyes, they saw nothing; and, shaken by God’s power, they did not dare to rise against the Christians.

In their extreme fear they climbed trees, thinking that they might escape or hide there. But our men knocked them to the ground with arrows, lances, and swords. Others threw themselves upon the ground, not daring to rise against us. Our men then cut them down as one cuts animals for the butcher’s shop.

The count of Saint-Gilles killed countless numbers of them beside the sea. Others threw themselves into the sea, while others fled in every direction.

When the admiral of Babylon came before the city of Ascalon, grieving and mourning, he wept and said: “O spirits of the gods! Who has ever seen or heard of such things? Such power, such strength, such an army—never overcome by any people—has now been defeated by so tiny a band of Christians.

“Alas for me, sorrowful and distressed! What more shall I say? I have been overcome by a beggarly, unarmed, and utterly impoverished people who possess nothing but a sack and a pouch. They now pursue and kill the Egyptian people, who formerly gave them many of their alms when they begged throughout our whole country.

“I brought here two hundred thousand soldiers to share in the campaign, and I see them fleeing along the Babylonian road with loose reins. They do not dare to turn back against the Frankish people.

“I swear by Mahomet and by all the divine powers of the gods that I shall no longer retain soldiers under any agreement, because I have been expelled by a foreign and immigrant people. [Col. 0667A]

“I brought every kind of weapon and every kind of engine so that I might besiege them in Jerusalem, and they forestalled me on the road to battle by two days. Alas for me! What more shall I say? I shall forever be dishonored in the land of Babylon.”

Our men took the *stantarum*—a standard—which the count of Normandy had purchased for twenty marks of silver, and he gave it to the patriarch in honor of God and the Holy Sepulchre. A certain man bought the sword for sixty bezants.

Thus our enemies were overcome by us, with God’s favor. All the ships of the pagans were there. When the men inside them saw the admiral fleeing with his [Col. 0668A] army, they immediately hoisted sail and drove out into the open sea.

Our men returned to the enemy’s tents and took innumerable spoils: much gold and silver, every kind of animal, and every kind of weapon and equipment. Whatever they wished to carry away, they carried away; they consumed the rest by fire.

Our men therefore returned joyfully to Jerusalem, bringing with them all the goods necessary for them. This battle was fought on the day before the Ides of August, by the generosity of our Lord Jesus Christ, who granted victory to his faithful and lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0667]

# THE JERUSALEM HISTORY OF ROBERT THE MONK OF SAINT-REMI OF THE DIOCESE OF RHEIMS

(In Bongars, *Gesta Dei per Francos*, p. 30.)

## NOTICE.

Robert the monk himself testifies, in an apologetic preface, that he composed this History, which he entitled *The History of Jerusalem*, in the cloister of a certain cell of Saint Remigius situated in the diocese of Rheims, at the command of an abbot named Bernard. We recently read the following statement in full in an old manuscript: the abbot disliked a narrative of this subject written by someone else—I do not know whom—because it was both headless and composed in a rather careless style.

Robert himself attended the Council of Clermont, from which this movement of the West toward the East began. Blondus cites him more than once, and cites him as a companion of the expedition:

> “We were pleased,” he says in decade II, book IV, “to see the monk Robert describing the engines in this manner,” etc.

And shortly afterward:

> “The monk Robert, who was then at Jerusalem,” and: “The monk Robert frankly admits, and from this writer more reliable accounts are derived.”

Of the same man Trithemius writes:

> “Rupert, a monk of the monastery of Saint Remigius in the diocese of Rheims, of the order of the holy Father Benedict, a Frenchman by nationality, a man trained by constant study in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular disciplines, distinguished in intellect and clear in speech. He wrote several little works of his own ingenuity, through which his name became known to posterity. Among them I myself saw only the notable ten-book *History of the Deeds of the Christians in the Holy Land, in the Time of Urban II, against the Infidels*. Among all historians. Of the others I have seen nothing. He flourished under Henry V, in the year of our Lord 1120.”

This is what Trithemius says. He either possessed a fuller copy than our book, or one divided into two books; this is how, in the earlier editions, the seventh and eighth books were combined into one. It appears, however, that Trithemius lacked the apologetic preface, which Reuber published and which is also found in our manuscripts.

Orderic Vitalis praises both his elegance of style and his truthfulness, and frequently transcribed him. The author of the *Book of the Principal Wars of the Lord in the Time of the New Law*, which is preserved in manuscript in the library of Father Petau, cites Robert, abbot of Saint Remigius. Possevinus confuses him with the continuator of Sigebert in the *Apparatus*, under “Robert the Monk,” although earlier, following Arnold Wion, he had distinguished him under “Robert the Englishman.”

We used the manuscript codices of Nicolas Fabri, Laurentius Bochellus, and our own; among the printed copies, our oldest and best, without any indication of place, printer, or date; another, the extremely corrupt Basel edition of Heinrich Petri, 1533; and the more carefully corrected edition of Justus Reuber, printed by Wechel.

Know, reader, that the copy of our edition formerly published—now column 757, line 26—contains many insertions from Fulcher, namely fifteen chapters, from the twentieth through the thirty-fifth, beginning thus:

> “On the day before the Ides of August. When these things had been accomplished, some wished to return to the homeland of their nation,” etc.,

which are read at the end of Fulcher’s nineteenth chapter, with only a very few words differing; and finally it returns to the passage with which Robert concludes his work:

> “But since this historical discourse,” etc.

These passages are found in exactly the same form in an old manuscript book, which, perhaps after this edition had been completed, we discovered lying among our own books. Andreas Schottus also sent various readings from his copies; these will be used in the third volume, if God preserves this life and mind. We placed the verses of that age on the final page, as they appeared in the manuscripts, so that we might omit nothing.

He begins his composition with the Council of Clermont, in the year 1095, and ends it with the victory over Admiraviso.

# THE APOLOGETIC PREFACE OF THE MONK ROBERT TO THE HISTORY OF JERUSALEM BEGINS

[Col. 0669]

I entreat all who will read this history, or hear it read and understand what they have heard, that whenever they find anything inelegantly composed in it, they grant pardon, because I was compelled to write it in obedience.

There was an abbot, named N., endowed with knowledge of letters and uprightness of character, who showed me a certain history on this subject, but he was greatly displeased with it: partly because it did not contain its own beginning, which had been established at the Council of Clermont; partly because the sequence of so beautiful a subject lay uncultivated, and the arrangement of its written expressions wavered in disorder.

He therefore ordered me, since I had attended the Council of Clermont, to place a head at the beginning of this headless material and to compose it in a more careful style for those who would read it. But I had no other secretary than myself: I both dictated and wrote. Thus the hand followed the mind continuously, the pen followed the hand, and the page followed the pen. The truth of this can sufficiently be attested both by the simplicity of the verse and by the entirely unornamented arrangement of the language.

Therefore, if this edition of ours displeases anyone nourished on academic studies, perhaps because, proceeding in plain speech, we have behaved too rustically in it, we wish to make it known to him that, in our judgment, it is more plausible to clarify hidden things by rustic expression than to obscure open things by philosophizing. For speech that is always too exact is always unpleasant, because what is grasped with difficulty by the understanding is received by a duller ear.

We wish our speech to proceed with a common, ordinary gait, so that anyone who hears it may hope to do the same; yet if he should perhaps attempt to be the same, he will be far removed from being so.

If anyone wishes to know the place where this history was composed, let him know that it was the cloister of a certain cell of Saint Remigius situated in the diocese of Rheims. If the name of the author who composed it is required, he is called ROBERT.

# THE PROLOGUE BEGINS

[Col. 0669]

Among all the historians of the New and Old Testament, holy Moses holds the chief place. Through the divine spirit of prophecy, and in Hebrew letters—of which he himself was the author—he described the beginning of the world, the more wondrous deeds of the first and second ages, and also brought before us the deeds of the patriarchs.

Following his example were Jesus son of Nave, Samuel, and David. The first of these wrote the Book of Joshua; the second and the third wrote the histories of the Kings. From this it can clearly be gathered that it is truly pleasing to God when some wondrous work that he has ordained to be accomplished at appointed times on earth is committed to the knowledge of his faithful in writing.

But after the creation of the world, what has been accomplished more wondrously—apart from the mystery of the saving cross—than what has occurred in these present times on this journey of our people to Jerusalem? The more attentively anyone considers it, the more abundantly he will marvel within the expanded recesses of his mind.

For this was not a human work, but a divine one. Therefore its account ought to be commended in written form to the knowledge both of the present and of future generations, so that through it Christian hope in God may be made more solid, and praise of him kindled more vividly in their minds.

For what king or prince could subdue so many cities and fortresses, fortified by nature, art, or human ingenuity, except the blessed nation of the Franks, whose Lord is God—the people whom he chose as his inheritance? (Psalm 32:12.)

May the wisdom of God therefore supply us with what we may bring forth to the praise of his name. And let those who read or hear these things know that we shall relate nothing frivolous, nothing false, nothing foolish—only what is true.

# THE PROLOGUE ENDS

# THE FIRST BOOK BEGINS

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0669C]

In the year 1095 of the Incarnation of the Lord, a great council was held within the boundaries of Gaul, namely in Auvergne, in the city called Clermont. Pope Urban II presided over it with the bishops and cardinals.

That council was exceedingly famous, with an assembly of Gauls and Germans, both bishops and princes. After ecclesiastical matters had been arranged there, the lord pope went out into a broad and spacious open place, because the enclosure of any building could not contain them.

There, by persuasive words of rhetorical sweetness, he addressed everyone generally in these terms:

[Note: “You who read these words, let your mind not be falsely disposed:

Receive the sweet words of Pope Urban.”]

> “People of the Franks, people from beyond the mountains, a people beloved and chosen by God, as is manifest in many of your deeds; distinguished from all nations both by the position of your lands, by the Catholic faith, and by your honor toward the Holy Church—to you our speech is directed, and to you our exhortation is extended.
>
> “We wish you to know what sorrowful cause has brought us to your lands, what necessity has drawn you and all the faithful. A grievous report has arisen from the regions of Jerusalem and the city of Constantinople, and it has now very frequently reached our ears: namely, that the people of the kingdom of the Persians, a cursed people, a foreign people wholly alienated from God, a generation that did not direct its heart and whose spirit was not faithful to God (Psalm 77:8), has invaded the lands of those Christians; has devastated them with sword, plunder, and fire; has carried some of the inhabitants captive into its own land; has struck down others with pitiable slaughter; and has either utterly destroyed the churches of God or subjected them to the practice of its own rites.
>
> “They overturn altars polluted by their filth. They circumcise Christians, and either pour the blood of circumcision upon the altars or immerse it in the vessels of the baptisteries. Those whom they choose to punish with a shameful death they pierce through the navel, tear out their vital organs, bind them to a stake, and then drag them about while flogging them until, their entrails pulled out, they fall prostrate upon the ground. Some, bound to stakes, they shoot with arrows; others they attack with necks extended and swords bared, testing whether they can sever them with a single blow.
>
> “What shall I say about the unspeakable violation of women? It is worse to speak of it than to remain silent. The kingdom of the Greeks has already been mutilated by them and appropriated for their own uses—a kingdom that cannot be traversed in less than two months.
>
> “Who, then, ought to undertake the labor of avenging and rescuing it, if not you, to whom the Lord has granted, above all other nations, the distinguished glory of arms, greatness of spirit, agility of body, and the strength to humble the head of those who resist you?
>
> “Let the deeds of your ancestors move and incite your spirits to manliness: the courage and greatness of King Charlemagne, of his son Louis, and of your other kings, who destroyed the kingdoms of the Turks and extended within them the boundaries of the Holy Church.
>
> “Above all, let the holy sepulcher of our Lord and Savior move you. It is possessed by unclean peoples, and the holy places are now dishonorably treated and irreverently befouled by their impurities.
>
> “O strongest soldiers, offspring of invincible ancestors, do not degenerate, but remember the virtues of your forefathers. And if affection for your children, parents, and wives holds you back, recall what the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me’ (Matthew 10:37). ‘Everyone who has left house, father, mother, wife, children, or fields for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life’ (Matthew 19:29).
>
> “Let no possession, no concern for household property, delay you, since this land which you inhabit, enclosed on every side by the sea and surrounded by mountain ranges, is constricted by your numbers. Nor does it overflow with an abundance of riches; it scarcely supplies its inhabitants with mere food. This is why you bite and consume one another, wage wars, and often kill one another with mutual wounds.
>
> “Let hatred therefore cease among you, let quarrels fall silent, let wars come to rest, and let the disagreements of every dispute be lulled to sleep. Begin the road to the holy sepulcher; take that land away from the wicked people and subject it to yourselves. That land was given by God into the power of the children of Israel, as Scripture says, ‘a land flowing with milk and honey’ (Numbers 13:28).
>
> “Jerusalem is the navel of the earth, a land more fruitful than all others, almost another paradise of delights.”

[Note: “Jerusalem, rejoice; praise without deceit belongs to you.”]

> “The Redeemer of the human race illumined this city by his coming, adorned it by his conduct, sanctified it by his passion, redeemed it by his death, and honored it by his burial.
>
> “This royal city, situated in the middle of the world, is now held captive by its enemies and, by those who do not know God, is enslaved to the rite of the nations. It seeks and desires liberation, and does not cease to implore you to come to its aid.
>
> “It demands assistance especially from you, since, as we have said, God has granted you above all nations the distinguished glory of arms. Seize this road, for the remission of your sins, secure in the unfading glory of the kingdom of heaven.”

## CHAPTER TWO

When Pope Urban had concluded these and many similar words in an urbane speech, he so united the feelings of all who were present that everyone shouted, “God wills it! God wills it!”

When the venerable Roman pontiff heard this, he lifted his eyes, gave thanks to God in heaven, and, signaling with his hand for silence, said:

> “Dearest brothers, today it has been shown in you what the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst’ (Matthew 18:20).
>
> “For unless the Lord God had been in your minds, one voice would not have come from all of you. Although your voice came forth from a multitude, the origin of the voice was one. Therefore I tell you that God drew this voice from you, he who implanted it in your breasts.
>
> “Let this voice be for you a military signal in matters of war, because this word has been uttered by God. When a warlike attack is made against the enemy, there shall be this one cry from all, on God’s side: ‘GOD WILLS IT! GOD WILLS IT!’
>
> “We neither command nor advise the elderly, the weak, or those wholly unfit for military service to undertake this journey. Nor should women set out without their husbands, brothers, or legitimate protectors. Such people are more a hindrance than a help, more a burden than a benefit.
>
> “Let the wealthy provide assistance from their resources and take with them, at their own expense, those equipped for war. Priests and clerics of whatever order may not go without the permission of their bishops, because this journey would be useless to them if they went without that permission. Indeed, it is not advantageous even for laymen to make the pilgrimage without the blessing of their priest.
>
> “Whoever therefore forms the intention of making this holy pilgrimage, makes a pledge concerning it to God, and vows to offer himself to him as a living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice, should carry the sign of the Lord’s cross upon his forehead or breast. Whoever wishes to undertake the journey after fulfilling his vow should place it upon his back, between the shoulders. Such people will fulfill in two ways the Lord’s command, which he gives through the Gospel: ‘Whoever does not carry his cross and come after me is not worthy of me’ (Luke 14:27).”

When these things had been completed, one of the cardinals, named Gregory, made confession on behalf of all who had prostrated themselves upon the ground. Then, beating their breasts, they all obtained absolution for the things they had done wrongly; and once absolution had been granted, they received a blessing, and after receiving the blessing, permission to return to their homes.

To make clear to all the faithful that this journey had been established by God, not by man—as we later learned from many sources—on that very day when these things were done and said, the fame proclaiming so great an undertaking stirred the entire world. It was even spread among the islands of the Ocean that the journey to Jerusalem had thus been established at the council.

From this came glory and rejoicing to Christians, but grief and trembling to the pagan Persians and the inhabitants of Arabia. Courage was added to the former, while fear and dullness of mind were inflicted upon the latter. The heavenly trumpet sounded so loudly that everywhere every people hostile to the Christian name trembled.

It is therefore clear that this was not the work of a human voice, but of the Spirit of the Lord, who fills the world (Wisdom 1:7).

Each of the laymen then returned home. On the following day Pope Urban caused an assembly of bishops to sit. When they were seated, he sought their counsel as to whom he should place over so great a multitude desiring to make the pilgrimage, since none of the named princes was yet among them.

They all chose the bishop of Le Puy, declaring him highly suitable for human and divine affairs, most learned in both kinds of knowledge, and exceptionally capable in his actions. Although unwilling, he therefore accepted, like another Moses, the leadership and governance of the people of the Lord, with the blessing of the lord pope and the entire council.

Oh, how many men of different ages, powers, and household means received crosses at that council and pledged themselves to the road of the holy sepulcher! From this the venerable council was proclaimed throughout the world, and its honorable decree reached the ears of kings and princes.

It pleased everyone, and more than three hundred thousand conceived the journey in their minds and strove to fulfill it, as the Lord granted each one the ability. Soon the unanimity of the Frankish people began to rejoice in companies, and their brave fierceness was already fighting the Turks in desire.

## CHAPTER THREE

In those days there was a certain man who had been a hermit, named Peter. He was highly esteemed by those who set their minds on earthly things and was raised above bishops and abbots in the height of religious reputation because he ate neither bread nor meat, although he enjoyed wine and all other foods, and “sought the highest abstinence amid luxuries.”

[Note: “The first duke advanced, and afterward advanced no farther.”]

At that time he gathered for himself a considerable multitude of horsemen and foot soldiers and directed his journey through Hungary.

He was joined by a certain German duke named Godfrey, who was the son of Eustace, count of Boulogne, but by virtue of his dignity was duke of the Germans. He was handsome in appearance, tall in stature, gentle in speech, excellent in character, and so mild that he seemed more like a monk than a soldier. Yet whenever he sensed that the enemy was near and battle was imminent, he conceived courage in a bold mind and, like a growling lion, feared no one who confronted him. What breastplate or shield could withstand the thrust of his sword?

He set out through Hungary with his brothers Eustace and Baldwin and a large force of soldiers and footmen, along the road which Charlemagne, the incomparable king of the Franks, had once ordered to be made for his army all the way to Constantinople.

Peter the Hermit was therefore the first to arrive at Constantinople with his followers and a large number of Alemanni. There he found a numerous people of Lombards and many others gathered from various distant places.

The emperor never allowed them permission to enter the city, because he had always regarded the military strength of Christians, and especially of the Franks, with suspicion. Nevertheless, he allowed them to have a market, which was also within the city, and he forbade them to cross the stretch of neighboring sea called the Arm of Saint George until the formidable army of the Franks should arrive.

For there was an infinite number of Turks, who thirsted for their arrival with bestial minds. If these people had fallen into their hands in the absence of the Frankish princes, as the later outcome proved, they would all alike have been subjected to death.

> “But every gathering of men that is not governed by a good leader, if a feeble head rules it, falls into worse things, grows weaker day by day, and is distanced from safety.”

For this reason, since they had no prudent leader to rule them, they committed reprehensible acts. They destroyed churches and the palaces of the cities, stripped away what was inside them, removed the lead with which they were roofed, and sold it to the Greeks.

Therefore the emperor, whose name was Alexius, was exceedingly angry and ordered them to cross the Arm of Saint George. When they had advanced beyond it, they chose a leader for themselves and placed a certain Rainald over them. Although they had a prince, they nevertheless did not cease their former acts of plunder. They burned with fire the houses they found and stripped the churches of their goods and possessions.

Thus they came as far as Nicomedia, and from there entered the land of Romania.

## CHAPTER FOUR

After spending three days traveling on foot, they proceeded beyond the city of Nicaea and found a certain castle, named Exerogorgo, empty of inhabitants. Upon entering it, they discovered an abundant supply of grain, meat, wine, and every kind of good that sustains human life.

The Turks, terrified by fear of the Franks, had withdrawn far from that land, but they had nevertheless left scouts behind to report the arrival of our people and their condition. When they learned through messengers that the newcomers had come to plunder, not to possess; to destroy, not to retain, they immediately rushed against them and surrounded the castle in which they were with a siege.

Their number and multitude were indeed immense. Before the castle gate there was a well, and nearby, on the other side, a spring of running water. Rainald, the prince of the Christians, had gone out beside it and, having laid an ambush, was awaiting their arrival.

The Turks attacked him without hesitation and killed many who were with him; the others fled into the castle. They then completely cut off the Christians’ water and subjected them to great torment through the lack of it.

It was the feast of Saint Michael, which every faithful soul ought to honor. Those under siege were reduced to such distress from thirst that they cut the veins of horses and drew out and drank the blood of oxen, asses, and other animals. Others dug up moister earth, placed it in their mouths, and so tempered the burning of their thirst. Some urinated into a vessel or into their hands and—remarkable [or pitiable?] to relate—swallowed it.

What more can be said? There was no comfort of life; for those who were perishing, death alone was their relief.

At last their prince Rainald secretly entered into a pact with the Turks.

[Note: “Lightly touched, Rainald became an apostate;

By renouncing God, he proves himself guilty.”]

He preferred to preserve temporal life rather than undergo death for Christ amid such martyrdom. Having arranged his troops, he pretended to engage the enemy, but as soon as he had gone out, he withdrew to them with many others.

Alas, alas, timid soldier! Advancing not from the south but from the north, how weakly and effeminately did he fight for the heavenly King and kingdom! Though not yet touched even by a light straw, he dreaded suffering martyrdom and, sound, mounted, and armed, renounced the profession of the Christian faith.

Rightly therefore he deserved before God the loss of his fading glory and came to share the lot of him who chose his seat in the north. Those who remained and refused to change the title of the Christian faith endured the destruction of death.

## CHAPTER FIVE

From that entire multitude the Turks killed whomever they wished and took captive whomever they pleased. They set some up as targets and shot them with arrows; they subjected the servants of God to every insult, as it pleased them. Those servants preferred to fall gloriously in this way rather than deny the faith of God and live unhappily with them.

God, as we believe, received them into the enclosures of his everlasting paradise, because they refused to wander away from their faith.

By now the devil’s victorious army was exulting and fighting against Peter the Hermit, who was in a certain castle named Civito. That castle stood above the city of Nicaea.

As the Turks directed their course against it, they encountered Walter, who was the chief officer and standard-bearer of the Hermit’s army. Although he had distinguished himself as an excellent soldier by so many military titles, he was nevertheless unable to resist them entirely. Yet he ennobled his precious death with much Turkish blood.

He rushed upon them like a hungry bear upon animals, struck down those whom he found confronting him, and deprived them of life. Likewise, the armed men who were with him, though still alive, were already bravely avenging the death they were about to suffer. As long as their weapons were effective, the enemy never celebrated victory.

But there the multitude prevailed over courage, not courage over the multitude—except insofar as their courage reduced the numerical advantage sixfold.

At last, their weapons broken but not their courage, they ended their lives in battle with a praiseworthy death, as they had fought for God, and angelic spirits transferred them to the company of the heavenly beings.

[Note: “This death of Walter ought to be considered precious.”]

Then for the first time the Turks, turning over the corpses of their own men, recognized that those with whom they had fought were Franks.

After these events, part of the Turkish force ran to the Christian camp. There they found a priest celebrating Mass and beheaded him before the altar.

[Note: “Thus also this priest’s death ought to be honored.”]

O blessed martyrdom of a blessed priest, to whom the viaticum of the Lord’s body provided leadership on the way!

Likewise, all whom they found they either killed or carried away. Peter the Hermit, however, had departed and returned to Constantinople.

In the castle mentioned above, whose name was Civito, a very large multitude of Christians had remained. Those who had escaped alive from the camps or the battle had gathered back at that castle. The Turks pursued them and surrounded them with piles of wood in order to burn our people.

But those who were besieged, concerned for the preservation of their lives, set fire to the piles. By God’s will, the wind blew and burned many of the enemy. At last the Turks captured the Christians by force and, after subjecting them to various kinds of punishment according to their own mockery, killed some and sold others into captivity.

Those who escaped by some chance or ingenuity returned to the Arm of Saint George and, at the command of the most wicked emperor, went back to Constantinople.

The emperor, with his Greeks, rejoiced over the Turks’ victory and craftily purchased all our people’s weapons in order to leave them unarmed.

With these events completed, let us bring this narrative to an end. Turning our style back, let us explain how our Frankish people gathered there and with which princes.

# THE FIRST BOOK ENDS

# THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0677A]

[Note:

“Companies gather, and countless thousands are formed.

If you could see their nobles joining together,

you would rightly praise the beautiful company

for which they had thus rejected their own homeland.”]

Meanwhile, while these things were taking place, from the distant western regions, from the northern side, the Lord stirred up two counts—the Count of Normandy and the Count of Flanders—who shared one name, one kinship, equal power, and equality in arms, spirit, and even the glory of their comital rank.

With them came Hugh the Great, brother of Philip, king of the Franks, who at that time was subjecting France to his authority. By the dignity of his character, the elegance of his body, and the virtue of his spirit, he honored the royal lineage from which he had sprung.

With him also came Stephen, count of Chartres, who, after a good beginning, eventually met with evil outcomes. O how many other nobles and counts of lesser fame were associated with these men, from France itself and from greater and lesser Brittany alike!

From the southern region the camps of the bishop of Le Puy and of the count of Saint-Gilles, named Raymond, set out. This man, although exceedingly rich and abundantly supplied with temporal goods, sold everything he possessed and undertook the road of deliberation toward the holy sepulcher.

Behold, we now see in reality what the Lord once promised through the mouth of the prophet Isaiah. For he says:

> “Do not fear, because I am with you. I will bring your seed from the north, and I will gather you from the west. I will say to the North: ‘Give!’ and to the South: ‘Do not withhold!’ Bring my sons from afar and my daughters from the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 43:5–6; Psalm 67:5).

Now, as we see, the sons and daughters of God are journeying to Jerusalem from the ends of the earth; the South and the North do not dare to withhold those whom they have nourished.

Truly now the Lord ascends above the setting sun, because he rests in the souls of the western peoples. Now the West prepares to illumine the East and, having stirred up its new stars, to drive away the darkness under which it had been oppressed.

And although amid such great companies the dreadful brilliance of weapons shone forth, the splendor of their spirits, if it could have been observed, would have outshone it.

They advance unanimously to war, not in order to flee, but either to die or to conquer. They consider dying no loss of life; conquering, however, they regard as a proclamation of divine assistance.

These princes whom we have mentioned therefore left their homes at a sufficiently suitable time. But, crossing their native land, they passed over the Alps at different times and by different routes. They made their way through Italy and, under divine protection, reached Rome on a favorable journey.

And O glorious army of Christ! The dwellings and homes of so spacious a city could not contain it within the areas of its habitation; therefore many of the princes pitched their tents outside the city.

They remained there for several days, visiting the holy places according to the custom of pilgrims and commending themselves to the merits and prayers of the holy apostles and others. Then, having received the apostolic blessing, they departed from the city and directed their forces through Apulia.

## CHAPTER TWO

As they proceeded in this way, news of so great an army reached the ears of a certain prince of that region, named Bohemond, who at that time was besieging Malphi, situated on the shore of the Sea of Scafardi.

[Note: “The rumor circling the world came to Bohemond.”]

When he heard this, he had inquiries made concerning which princes governed so great an army, with what weapons it was equipped, in what order they advanced, and whether they had come to plunder or to obtain what they needed.

The investigators reported to him concerning the princes that Hugh the Great, brother of Philip, king of the Franks, was standard-bearer and leader of so great an army; that Robert, count of Normandy; Robert, count of Flanders; Stephen, count of Chartres; Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles; and the bishop of Le Puy were its leaders and commanders.

The army advanced with such devotion and order that there was no one whom it harmed. The cavalry’s weapons were so suitable, as befitted such a great military expedition of God. For who could endure looking upon the breastplates, helmets, shields, and lances when the sun shone upon them?

The foot soldiers were so fortified with every kind of missile that, if they came against anyone, they would inspire terror in all the East. And although they were girded with missiles and weapons, they nevertheless purchased what they needed like unarmed pilgrims.

When the prudent and exceedingly wealthy man heard these things, he spoke such words before everyone:

> “We must all give thanks to God, who holds the hearts of all in his power and inclines them wherever he wills. For who would have gathered so many princes and so great a people into one body, unless he himself presided over their minds?”

When he inquired what sign they carried as a mark of pilgrimage, he learned that they bore the sign of the holy cross either on the forehead or upon the right shoulder-blades.

When they ran across the fields practicing for military service and, in play, hurled lances at one another, they all shouted with one voice:

> “God wills it! God wills it!”

[Note: “But this vow is shouted with the whole heart.”]

This was the sign of their war cry. When the prudent and intelligent man heard this again, he rejoiced more and more in God, because he understood that all these things were not merely human.
