Immediately inflamed with the same devotion, he ordered two precious cloaks to be brought. He commanded that crosses be cut from them in strips. Then he said to all, both foot soldiers and knights:

> “If anyone belongs to the Lord, let him join me. O soldiers, now mine, be God’s; begin the road of the holy sepulcher with me, and take what belongs to me as your own.
>
> “Are we not Franks too? Did not our ancestors come from France and subject this land to themselves by military arms? What shame! Our kinsmen and brothers will go without us to martyrdom—or rather, to paradise!
>
> “In all future times, the backward poverty of our spirit must be attributed both to us and to our children if, in our absence, this divine army sets out.”

[Note: “Bohemond does not reject the burden of the military expedition.”]

When the brave soldier had finished these and similar words, all who were present shouted:

> “We will go with you, and without hesitation we promise the road of the holy sepulcher.”

Then the wise and clever man ordered the crosses he had commanded to be made to be brought forward. When they had been brought, he said:

> “If you wish to unite deeds with your words, let each of you take one of these crosses; and let the taking of the cross be your pledge of the journey.”

So many flocked forward to take them that the crosses ran out while many still desired to receive one.

When the nobles of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily heard that Bohemond had taken the cross for the road to the holy sepulcher, they all flocked to him. Both the poor and the powerful, the old and the young, servants and masters, promised the road of the holy sepulcher.

When the duke of Apulia saw and heard this, he was deeply distressed, because he feared being left alone in his duchy with the children and women.

[Note: “The Calabrian peoples and the Apulians join themselves to him.”]

[Note: [Col. 0679D] (The note begins here but is cut off in the supplied text.)]

[Yet the duke of Apulia disdained to become their leader; the damaged reading is uncertain.] That duke was Bohemond’s brother; both were sons, that is, of Robert Guiscard. While Bohemond was preparing what was necessary for the journey, the Franks reached the maritime ports: some, namely, Brindisi; others, Bari; others entered the sea at Otranto. Hugh the Great and William, the son of the Marquis, entered the sea at the port of Bari and sailed as far as Dyrrachium. When the governor of that place learned that they had arrived, seized by an evil thought, he immediately ordered them to be arrested and, once arrested, carried to Constantinople. For the deceitful emperor had ordered that all the Jerusalem-bound pilgrims be captured and brought to him at Constantinople. He wanted them all to swear allegiance to him, so that whatever they acquired by arms would belong to him.

But when they were brought to the city, they found great consolation, for they discovered Duke Godfrey there with a large army. Anyone who saw Hugh the Great and Duke Godfrey embracing and kissing one another could have wept for joy. Hugh the Great rejoiced that he had been arrested, because through this circumstance he had deserved to be brought to Duke Godfrey. The duke rejoiced because he embraced his intimate friend and kinsman, a nobleman distinguished by every mark of high birth. Each rejoiced in the other that the bond of friendship and ancient familiarity had been renewed, and that in both there was the conspicuous excellence of uprightness.

In these two men the emperor’s frauds were first exposed, as the following events will soon make clear. Duke Godfrey arrived at Constantinople before all the Frankish princes [Note: [Col. 0680D]

The duke also was the first of royal rank to reach the city.], because he had set out directly through Hungary. He arrived two days before Christmas and wished to lodge outside the city; but the deceitful emperor received him among the suburbs. Meanwhile the duke hoped that he could remain there safely until the armies of the Frankish people arrived.

When he began, over several days, to send his retainers to obtain provisions, the treacherous emperor ordered his Turcopoles and Pincenates to lie in ambush, attack them, and kill them. But Baldwin, the duke’s brother, having learned of their wickedness, concealed himself and forestalled their ambush. For while they were following his men in order to kill them, he attacked them with courageous spirit and manly force and, with God’s help, defeated them, killed many of them, and presented the captives to his brother the duke.

When the emperor heard this, he was enraged, because he realized that his deceit and ambushes had been exposed to the Franks. When the duke learned that the emperor was angry with him and his men, he left the emperor’s suburbs and pitched his tents outside the city.

At sunset, when night had covered the face of the earth, the emperor’s agents dared to attack the duke. But, with divine grace assisting them, they could scarcely escape his hands, and only at great cost to themselves. The one side rushed upon the other, but one was stronger than the other: the duke, roaring with his men like a lion, quickly scattered them, killed seven, and pursued the rest as far as the city gate [Note: [Col. 0680D]

As the Frankish forces arrive together at the city,

They display the terror of death to their countrymen.].

The duke then returned to his tents and remained there peacefully thereafter. The emperor sought peace from him through intermediaries, finally obtained it, and permitted him and his people to maintain a market, as it existed in the city [Col. 0680D].

Meanwhile the Gallic people began to approach the imperial city: the bishop of Le Puy, the count of Saint-Gilles, and also the Norman, Flemish, and Chartres counts. While these events were taking place, as we have said, Bohemond of Apulia, having prepared provisions suitable for so great a journey, entered the sea and sailed across to the region of Bulgaria [Col. 0681A]. With him were the most noble princes: namely, his nephew Tancred, the prince Richard, son of the Marquis, and all the leading men of that land. In Bulgaria they found such abundance that everyone was supplied with grain, wine, and oil.

Then, descending into the valley of Andrinople, they rested there until everyone had crossed the strait. There the prudent Bohemond threatened his army that no one should violently take anything from anyone else, but that each person should purchase whatever he needed. At last, when everyone had crossed, they entered a region exceedingly rich in all good things. Advancing from village to village, from castle to castle, and from city to city, they reached Castoria. There they celebrated the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity and remained for many days.

When they sought a market for purchasable goods from the natives, they could not obtain one, because everyone fled from their presence, believing that our men had come to plunder and lay waste the entire land. Therefore our men, compelled by lack of food, seized and plundered sheep, oxen, rams, goats, pigs, and whatever else was useful as food.

Leaving Castoria, they came to Pelagonia, where there was a certain fortress of heretics. They attacked it on every side and, with the trumpets blaring and weapons and arrows flying, captured it immediately. After stripping it of all its goods, they burned it with its inhabitants. Nor did this happen to them unjustly, because the heretics’ detestable teaching was spreading like cancer and had already defiled the surrounding regions with its perverse doctrine, just as their shameful purpose had removed the heretics themselves from the true faith.

Finally, on the following day, they came to the Bardarius River. Many crossed that same day, but others who could not cross while the sun still stood remained behind. On the next day, the emperor’s army attacked those who had remained [Note: [Col. 0681D]

The emperor’s army attacks our men.], at the earliest dawn, when the dawn was already brightening, intending either to kill them all or to lead them away bound as captives.

While our men were bravely resisting them, the report reached Bohemond and Tancred. Tancred could not long endure seeing his men suffer such injuries. Flying on horseback, he returned to the river, plunged into it with horse and arms, and two thousand horsemen followed him. When they arrived, they found the Turcopoles and Pincenates fighting there. Our men suddenly rushed upon them like unbridled horses, killed many of them, threw more into chains, and brought them to Bohemond bound with straps.

When Bohemond saw them, he gave thanks to God and, smiling with cheerful face, said to them through an interpreter:

“Mad and misguided people, why do you seek to kill our people and God’s people? We share the Christian faith; we are members of the same household and pilgrim soldiers of the Holy Sepulchre. We seek to harm none of you, nor do we intend to take anything from your emperor.”

They answered him:

“Lord, we are the emperor’s hired soldiers, and we desire to earn from him the gifts he has promised us. Wherever he wishes, we go; whatever he commands, we do, and we obey him more than God. Yet we recognize clearly that one ought to obey God rather than human beings (Acts 5:29). Our emperor fears your armies more than the thunderbolts of heaven, because he understands that you wish to deprive him of his kingdom more than you wish merely to make a pilgrimage. Therefore he never ceases to devise evil against you. But for the sake of God, whose pilgrims and soldiers you are, deign to have mercy on us.”

Moved by these words and by the spirit of mercy, the distinguished man spared their lives and allowed them to depart unharmed.

While he was thus proceeding with good fortune, the Frankish army had assembled at Constantinople and was awaiting his arrival, having heard that he would soon be there. But when the emperor saw the camps of God pouring in from every side and his army, which he had sent against Bohemond, so thoroughly scattered, he began, boiling with anger, to grow extremely anxious, and fraudulent thoughts revolved in his heart [Note: [Col. 0681D]

When Bohemond is joined to our men,

[Col. 0682D] The Constantinopolitan king became mad.].

At last he pretended to be well disposed and, as though rejoicing in Bohemond’s arrival, sent men to meet him, instructing them to receive him graciously throughout his cities and castles and escort him to the emperor with honor. Our men, however, knew that he was not doing this out of any service arising from friendship, but through a secret simulation of the heart.

The natives of that land, after receiving the emperor’s command, brought provisions in great quantities and sold them at a sufficiently reasonable price. Thus they came to a city called Susa. Bohemond left his army there and proceeded to Constantinople with a few men to confer with the emperor. Tancred remained as commander and guardian of the army. He did not wish to stay there longer, because the food was foreign and had to be purchased. He led the army away to a valley abundantly rich in all good things and exceedingly fertile in bodily provisions.

## CHAPTER III

Meanwhile, as Bohemond approached the city, the greater part of the Frankish army came out to meet him, and they received him unanimously as a mother receives her only son. When Bohemond saw so many counts, so many dukes, and so many nobles coming to meet him, he raised his hands to heaven, and tears breaking forth from joy, wept profusely. After kissing many of them, and only with difficulty suppressing his sobs, he was at last able to speak. His face wet with tears, he began to say [Note: [Col. 0682D]

Bohemond’s words do not praise the world’s prosperity.]:

“O warriors of God and unwearied pilgrims of the Holy Sepulchre, who brought you to these foreign lands except the one who led the children of Israel across the Red Sea from Egypt on dry ground? Who else implanted in you the resolve to leave your possessions and your native soil? You have renounced kinsmen and relatives, wives and children—indeed, every bodily pleasure.

“Now you have been born again a second time, through the confession and repentance that you display daily in hard labors. O happy are those who die in such a work; they will see paradise before they see their homeland [Note: [Col. 0683D]

He almost praises the warfare of Christ’s worshipers.].

“O order of soldiers, now thrice and four times blessed: until now you were stained by the blood of homicide, but now, made equal to the martyrs by the sweat of the saints, you are crowned with the heavenly diadem. Until now you existed as an incitement to God’s anger; now you are the reconciliation of his grace and the bulwark of his faith.

“Therefore, unconquered soldiers, since we have only now begun to serve God as soldiers, let us not glory in our strength or in our arms, but in God, most powerful over all, because this war of ours belongs to him, and he will rule the nations.”

When Bohemond had set forth these and many other words of this kind, he won the hearts of his hearers and found great favor in the sight of all. Then everyone came with him to the city and led him to his lodging, which the emperor had ordered to be prepared for him outside the city.

The treacherous emperor, seeing the camps of God grow and increase day by day, being weak in spirit, lacking judgment, and poor in counsel, began to burn with vehement anger. He did not know what to do, where to turn, or where he might flee if necessity pressed him. For he feared that so great an army, belonging to so many men, might rise against him.

“For a mind full of deceit is always anxious and troubled, and it always fears that what it plots against another is being plotted against itself.”

But our men had no such intention at all, because they did not wish to fight against Christians.

At last the emperor ordered Bohemond to be summoned and held the following counsel with him and with his Greeks. He requested that the princes of the army swear homage to him—that is, a guarantee of peace—and promised that he would provide them with a market for every kind of purchasable good throughout the deserted regions they were about to enter, as well as his presence in all military affairs and the assistance of his people. He also swore generally to all of them that he would supply everything they needed in arms and clothing, and that he would no longer harm any pilgrim of the Holy Sepulchre or permit one to be harmed.

When this plan was disclosed, it pleased almost everyone, since many were troubled by the lack of material necessities. Accordingly, they rendered him homage with an oath, on the condition that it should last only so long as he himself remained faithful to his oath and promise.

When the count of Saint-Gilles was asked about the homage, however, he absolutely refused to perform it. If he were believed, he said, the entire city, with its inhabitants and the emperor himself, would be destroyed. But it was unreasonable that so royal a city, and so many churches consecrated to God, should be destroyed, and that the bodies of so many saints should either be burned by fire or driven from their resting places.

At last the count of Saint-Gilles was overcome by the persuasion of the others, gave his assent, and promised fidelity to the emperor in these words:

“I swear to the emperor Alexius that neither by me nor by my men will he ever lose his life or honor, or anything that he now possesses, whether justly or unjustly.”

He swore this assurance to him, and the emperor accepted it. Then the emperor himself swore, saying [Note: [Col. 0683D]

What the king swears does not last long;

[Col. 0684D] He swears and forswears, who does not take proper care of himself.]:

“I, Emperor Alexius, swear to Hugh the Great and to Duke Godfrey, and to the other Frankish princes who stand here, that never in my lifetime will I injure any pilgrim of the Holy Sepulchre, nor permit one to be injured; and that I will go with them in military matters and, to the best of my ability, provide them with an adequate market.”

Let no one wonder that so many and such noble Franks made homage as if compelled, for if the matter is carefully weighed, it will be found that they truly were compelled. They were about to enter a deserted and trackless land, entirely deprived of all good things, and they knew that “he who lacks daily sustenance is not strong enough to endure daily labor.”

For such hardship this agreement of homage was made; but in the emperor’s mind there always remained a fraudulent intention. The agreement of homage would indeed have been fittingly established if the emperor had possessed an affirmation of sound faith. But whatever he stipulated, he nullified entirely by his word; he preferred to incur the guilt of perjury rather than fail to drive the Frankish people far from his borders.

## CHAPTER IV

But lest we seem altogether to have passed over the royal city in silence, let us say something about it, since this does not appear foreign to history.

We read in a certain history that the Roman emperor Constantine, having fallen asleep one night in the city called Byzantium, saw a vision [Note: [Col. 0684D]

This was Constantine’s plain vision.], which appeared to him in the following manner. A certain old woman, wearing a disordered garment and seemingly wrapped in a half-belted covering, came to him and begged his help. She requested clothing with which to dress herself, a covering with which to protect herself, and food with which to nourish herself. The emperor immediately promised that he would assist her and grant her requests without hesitation. Then the vision disappeared.

When the most powerful man awoke from sleep, he pondered in his heart what the vision might mean and, by divine prompting, understood that the city itself in which he stood was seeking assistance and greatly desired to be restored to a better condition. Thus Constantine rebuilt it from its foundations and called it Constantinople after his own name. He made it equal to Rome in the height of its walls and the nobility of its buildings, and raised it to equal earthly glory and honor:

“Just as Rome is the head of the West, so that city ought to be the head of the East.”

It is situated between the Adriatic Sea and that which is now called the Arm of Saint George, above which the city’s walls are placed. Before all other cities it is fertile in rich soil and in every kind of commerce involving the wealth of the sea.

Let no one doubt, therefore, that this city was founded by divine prompting, since God foresaw what would happen and what we now see fulfilled. For if such a city had not been founded, where would Eastern Christianity have found refuge? There are now preserved there the most holy relics of the holy prophets and apostles and of countless holy martyrs, which were transferred there from the presence of the pagans.

Asia and Africa were once Christian lands, but now they are subjected to the impure rites of the gentiles. Therefore Constantinople was made such a royal city, so that it might be the safest royal dwelling for the holy relics mentioned above. For this reason it ought rightly to be made equal to Rome in the dignity of its sanctuary and the excellence of its royal dignity—except that Rome has been exalted by the papal summit and is the head and summit of all Christianity.

Let this suffice concerning these matters, and let this second book here reach its end.

## THE SECOND BOOK ENDS

## THE THIRD BOOK BEGINS

## CHAPTER I

After the Frankish princes had entered into an alliance with the emperor, the emperor ordered ships to be brought to the port, so that the entire army could cross without great delay [Note: [Col. 0685D]

Now the sea is crossed, but now they come to trackless regions.].

Duke Godfrey and Tancred crossed first, proceeded as far as Nicomedia, and rested there for three days. Seeing that there was no road by which he could lead such a large army across, the duke sent ahead four thousand men with axes, ploughshares, and other tools suitable for preparing a road.

That land was trackless, obstructed everywhere by mountain ridges, hollow valleys, and excavated ground. Accordingly, with great labor, they constructed a road all the way to the city of Nicaea, suitable for infantry, horses [Col. 0685C], and every traveler. They also set up wooden crosses at the bends of the roads as testimony, so that everyone might know that the road belonged to pilgrims.

Thus the entire multitude passed along it, except that Bohemond remained with the emperor to arrange with him the promised supply of provisions. But that promise seemed to be delayed beyond measure, because before it arrived, the poorer members of the army were suffering the greatest torment of hunger.

The strength of the army assembled at the city of Nicaea on the day before the Nones of May [Note: [Col. 0685D]

You too, Nicaea, will give these men great trophies.]. Before the market was supplied, one loaf of bread was being sold for twenty or thirty denarii. But after Bohemond arrived with provisions, scarcity vanished and abundance of every good thing appeared.

On the day of the Lord’s Ascension they surrounded the city with a siege and brought up ballistae, battering rams, and other instruments of that kind by which the inhabitants could be overcome [Note: [Col. 0686D]

When they ravage you, they will prevail over you once ravaged.].

On the eastern side, because the city seemed more difficult to capture and more strongly fortified there, these leaders stationed the strength of their armies: the bishop of Le Puy, Count Raymond, Hugh the Great, the Norman count, the Flemish count, and Count Stephen of Chartres; Duke Godfrey on the north; Bohemond at sunset, that is, in the west; while there was no force on the south, because a large lake served there as a defense.

The citizens entered the lake with ships and brought in timber, herbs, and other necessities. When the princes learned this, an embassy immediately hastened to the emperor, asking him to have ships transported as far as Civito, where there was a port, together with oxen to drag them to the lake. He promptly obeyed their words, and it was done according to the princes’ wishes.

What more is there to say? Once the armies had been arranged around the city, the worshipers of Christ pressed on bravely, while the Turks, since their lives were at stake, resisted with strength. The Turks shot poisoned arrows so that those whom they wounded even by a light touch might be killed by a grievous death. Our men, however, not fearing to die for life, raised tall machines around the walls, from which they looked down upon those who were on the walls. Wooden towers were brought against stone towers, and now the enemy was attacked at close quarters with lances and swords.

Now stakes, torches, and stones are hurled into the city.

The enemy is terrified, because fear of death is already upon them.

From this arose the crash of the crowd and the shouting that rang through the city [Note: [Col. 0686D]

Instead of “crowd,” the tumult of the crowd is stirred throughout the city.]. Mothers fled everywhere with their sons and daughters, their hair unbound, seeking hiding places because they had no hope of life anywhere.

When the enemy was already preparing to surrender, he saw sixty thousand Turks approaching from a distance. For the people in the city had sent word to them, telling them to come to them through the southern gate and assist them. Meanwhile our men had besieged that gate with a large force, and the bishop of Le Puy and the count of Saint-Gilles guarded it.

When the Turks descended from the mountains and saw the ranks of our men from afar, they were struck with fear. Had they not trusted in their own multitude, they would have turned their bridles backward and sought the protection of flight. They formed three divisions: one was to break through the gate mentioned above, while the other two, engaging in battle if necessary, were to follow the third more freely.

Thus the Turks arranged themselves, but by God’s plan our more experienced men altered this disposition. For as soon as the bishop of Le Puy and Count Raymond’s army caught sight of them, they left the city and rushed upon them at the swiftest pace, fearing their multitude no more than dogs fear a fleeing hare.

O how many thousands of chosen soldiers pursued them, more ready to draw souls from Turkish bodies than any hungry man is ready to go to a wedding. But when the Turks saw such excessive brilliance of weapons—for the sun supplied a gleam with its flaming rays—so many swift encounters of neighing horses, and so many spears brandished against them, they turned their backs [Note: [Col. 0687D]

Now the Turks flee and become fearful in every way.]. They wished, too slowly and sluggishly, to return to the mountains, but none of those who had descended from them could climb back up.

Badly punished, they were tortured by dreadful death.

With God’s help, our army thus rejoices in such a trophy

And returns joyfully to the city.

They again climbed the siege engines and, to inspire greater fear in the enemy, hurled the heads of the slain Turks inside the city with ballistae and slings.

Nor was there any delay: at that very hour

The ships from Constantinople were brought.

But they did not put them into the lake that day; they did so at night, filling them with Turcopoles, the emperor’s people, well trained and accustomed to ships.

At dawn on the following day, when those who were in the city saw the ships, they were terrified by overwhelming fear. Having no breath left, they fell to the ground as though already dead [Note: [Col. 0687D]

The enclosed enemies, overcome by great fear,

Are no longer sure where they can turn.].

All the daughters howled with their mothers, the young men with the maidens, and the old with the young. There was mourning everywhere, misery everywhere, because there was no hope of escape. Within was grief and dullness of mind; outside, joy and exultation.

At last they found a plan for escape. Through the Turcopoles they informed the emperor that they would surrender the city to him if he allowed them to depart unharmed and safe, with their possessions. When this was reported to the emperor, he rejoiced greatly; but in his mind he also conceived a fraud from which he would later give birth to iniquity [Col. 0687C].

He ordered the city to be handed over to his men, complete confidence to be granted to the Turks, and the Turks to be escorted to Constantinople. He did this—as the event itself later revealed—so that when the time came he might find them prepared to the detriment of the Franks.

Thus the city was surrendered, and the Turks were led to Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0688D]

The captive enemy, spared death and preserved alive,

Is surrendered by the Franks to the people of Constantinople.].

Nevertheless, the emperor did not forget such a great benefit, for he ordered generous alms to be distributed to the poor who were in the army.

The assault on the city of Nicaea therefore extended over seven weeks and three days. It would not have been overcome by any human force had it not been for God’s help. It was fortified with very dense walls and high towers, so that it was the chief city and unequalled throughout Romania.

In this city, in the time of the emperor Constantine, three hundred and eighteen bishops once assembled. Because of the cunning of the heretics who existed at that time, they deliberated concerning our faith and unanimously established everything as the Catholic Church now holds it.

For this reason it was worthy that the city should be taken from the enemies of the holy faith, reconciled to God, and restored to our holy mother the Church as one of her members. God had foreseen and arranged this new restoration, for the city was consecrated by the martyrdom of many who were killed there.

Thus, as we have said, the city of Nicaea was liberated, and every demonic captivity was expelled from it.

## CHAPTER II

When these things had been accomplished, our men immediately

Pitch their tents and prepare to depart, leaving the city

After sending envoys to Constantinople.

After they withdrew from the city, the joined armies advanced together for two days and reached a certain bridge. They rested there for two days and refreshed their horses and beasts on the green grass.

Since they were about to enter a deserted and waterless land, they took counsel to divide themselves and split into two armies. One land and one region could not suffice for so many men, so many horses, and so many animals.

The first and larger battle line was therefore entrusted to Hugh the Great. The other was joined to Bohemond. In the first division, with Hugh the Great, were the bishop of Le Puy, Count Raymond, Duke Godfrey, and Count Robert the Fleming. In the second, with Bohemond, were Tancred, Count Robert the Norman, and many other princes whose names we do not know.

Thus, with favorable success, they rode through Romania as though already secure. But after three days had passed, on the fourth day, at the third hour, those who were with Bohemond saw three hundred thousand Turks coming against them and shouting loudly, uttering some barbarous cry that I do not know.

Because of their immense multitude, some of our men began to hesitate, wondering whether they should resist or seek paths of flight. Then Bohemond, a man of great foresight, and the Norman count, as a courageous soldier, when they saw the courage of some wavering, ordered all the soldiers to dismount and drive in the tent stakes.

There was a flowing stream passing nearby. Along it they set up their tents in a long line. Promptly and wisely, Bohemond sent a swift messenger,

Who would fly on a swift horse and summon our men,

So that they might hurry to the battle already prepared.

Before the tents had been fully pitched, one hundred and fifty Turks, carried on swift horses, approached our men and, with their bows drawn, shot their poisoned arrows at them. But our men let their horses loose against them, captured them, and killed them.

It is indeed the custom of the Turks to flee backward while drawing their arrows and, as they flee, to inflict a wound upon those pursuing them. But there was no place for flight, because the mass of the enemy occupied the very summits of the mountains [Note: [Col. 0688D]

Behold here a battle that was not the same for all.].

Therefore our men slaughtered them insistently on the right and left, and bows and arrows had no useful place there. At last, when the Franks’ lances had been broken upon the bodies of the impious, the struggle was carried on with swords.

O how many bodies fell there, their heads cut off or some of their limbs mutilated! There you might have seen the rear part of the enemy driving the front part onto the swords of the slayers.

While battle was thus being fought, while the first division was thus being killed,

That part of the Turks which had crossed the stream immediately attacked the Christians’ tents. They tore them down and slaughtered mothers with their children, as well as those whom they found unprepared for battle and without arms.

The cry of the dying reached Bohemond’s ears, and he immediately understood what had happened. He entrusted the battle to the Norman count and hurried back to the tents with a few men.

When the Turks saw them, they immediately turned their backs. Bohemond, seeing many corpses lying there, began to lament and beseech the Lord to be a refuge for the living and the dead. He hurried back to the battle, but left soldiers in the tents as a rampart and defense.

Before he returned to the battle, our men had already been so exhausted by thirst, labor, and the heat of the burning sun [Note: [Col. 0689D]

On one side labor, on the other heat, thirst, the relentless enemy, and weapons

Assail our men, and for this reason they were already preparing to turn their backs.],

that unless the women had brought them drink from the passing stream, many would have succumbed to the battle that day.

By now our men had once given way before the attacking Turks, and unless the Norman count, brandishing a golden banner in his right hand, had turned his horse around and cried out the military signal with repeated shouts—“God wills it! God wills it!”—

that day would have been exceedingly ruinous for our men.

But when they saw Bohemond and the Norman count returning, they recovered their courageous spirit and chose to die rather than flee any farther. For the Turks’ pressure was so great, and one pushed another forward so forcefully, that nowhere was there an avenue of escape for anyone. They had surrounded our men so completely that no open space could be found except around the tents.

Many of our men then died, killed by Turkish arrows. None of our men was without a duty; no one lacked an assigned task. The soldiers, equipped for battle, fought; the priests and clerics wept and prayed; and the women, lamenting, dragged the bodies of the dead into the tents.

While our men were thus hemmed in and overshadowed by a cloud of flying arrows, Duke Godfrey and Hugh arrived [Note: [Col. 0689D]

Duke Godfrey and Hugh are present as aid.]. When they reached the mountains with forty thousand chosen soldiers, they saw the tents of their companions surrounded on every side by Turkish ranks [Col. 0689D]. They saw their comrades fighting as best they could and the women crying out with great wailing in the tents. Their spirits caught fire, and like an eagle rushing upon prey,

Whom the hungry cries of its young spur on,

So, inflamed with anger, they pierced the dense ranks.

O what a crash of weapons there was, what a clatter of splintering spears, what a cry from the dying, and how joyful the voice of the fighting Franks, loudly proclaiming their military signal [Col. 0690A]! Those voices were repeated as the valleys, mountain peaks, and clefts of the rocks caught them and sent them back.

Wretched were those whom the Franks first encountered, for they were now men and now mere corpses—those whom neither coat of mail nor shield protected, and whom neither arrow nor bent bow could help. They howled and groaned, struck the earth with their heels as they died, or, falling down, tore the grass with their teeth.

When those stationed far away heard these sudden sounds, some rejoiced and others became sorrowful. The Franks recognized the military signal of their fighting comrades; the Turks recognized the lamentable groans of their dying companions. The hands of the wicked, numbed with astonishment, grew weak; the already weary hands of the Christians grew strong.

## CHAPTER III

Meanwhile, when the Turks who were attacking our men looked toward the mountains, they saw the bishop of Le Puy and Count Raymond descending from the mountains with the rest of the army, both cavalry and infantry, and attacking their own people. They froze with great fear at the multitude of warriors [Note: [Col. 0690D]

Never before had there been a battle involving so great an army.

Hence fear entered them, by which they withdrew to the far side.],

thinking either that warriors had been poured down from heavenly dwellings or that they had emerged from the mountains themselves. The battles began anew, and many thousands of Turks were freshly laid low.

What could the Turk do, and the people filthy in every way,

Unless he turned his back and returned where he had come from?

But he who had previously been the tail begins to be the head.

And so the head follows the tail, fleeing with those who flee.

Our men, who had nearly been shut up within their own tents, recovered their spirit, took courage again, and avenged their wounds and grievous injuries upon the enemy.

Those who had previously pressed upon them now flee [Note: [Col. 0690D]

Now the Saracens flee—the Arabs, Hagarenes,

With the Publicani, Medes, Persians, and Agulani.], through every pathless place.

They do not care where—to the front or backward—

But the soldier of Christ lays them low by a grievous death.

The earth is wet with blood; the mountainside is red everywhere,

And the stream is filled throughout with flowing blood.

So many bodies of the slain lay prostrate across the field

That scarcely any horse could run.

Thus, from the third hour of the day until the twilight of night, that battle continued without interruption. It might well have seemed astonishing where so great a people had gathered. But, as those who believed themselves better informed asserted, Persians, Publicani, Medes, Syrians, Chaldaeans, Saracens, Agulani, Arabs, and Turks had assembled there and covered the surface of the earth like locusts and grasshoppers, whose number is without counting (Psalm 104:34).

Night, indeed, brought the conflict to an end and gave them great protection; for unless darkness had concealed them, few would have survived from so great a multitude.

[Col. 0691A] Great glory to God for such a great and mighty trophy.

He who destroys the harmful and glorifies his own. Thus, compelled by the darkness, our men returned to their tents, while the priests and clerics sang this hymn to God:

> “You are glorious, Lord, among your holy ones, wonderful in your holiness, awesome and praiseworthy, and you perform wonders. Your right hand, Lord, struck down the enemy, and by the greatness of your glory you cast down your adversaries. The enemy had said: ‘I shall pursue and overtake them; I shall divide the spoils; my soul shall be satisfied; I shall draw my sword; my hand shall destroy them’ (Exodus 15:9). But you, Lord, were with us like a mighty warrior, and in your mercy you were the leader and protector of your people whom you redeemed. Now, Lord, we understand that in your strength you carry us to your holy dwelling, namely, to your holy sepulchre.”

After these words they lowered their voices, and, now safe from the enemy, rested that night. On the following day, when the sun had beautified the world with its blazing light, they all hurried to the battlefield. There they found many of their own dead, and, had it not been for the crosses, they could scarcely have distinguished them from the others. Those who had sounder judgment honored them as martyrs of Christ and buried them with the greatest honor they could.

> **Note [Col. 0691D]:**  
> The bodies of our men are buried with praise of God.  
> The bodies of the Turks are stripped of their possessions across the field.

The priests and clerics poured out the chants proper to burial; mothers uttered mournful laments for their sons, and friends for their friends. When this had been completed, they hastened to strip the enemy corpses. Who could recount the abundance of clothing they found there, or the quantity of gold and silver? O, how great a multitude of horses, mules, female mules, camels, and asses our men then acquired! Those who had previously been poor became rich with God’s help. Those who had previously been half-naked were clothed in silken garments. Weapons and arrows were collected, and emptied quivers were filled. Care was provided for the wounded, and they were entrusted to the physicians’ care.

Thus our people remained there throughout the entire day. If anyone wishes to direct the eye of his mind toward this deed worthy of exceptional praise, he will be able to perceive God as wondrous in his works. For he filled his hungry people with good things, while he sent the rich who were not his own away empty; he brought down the powerful and exalted the humble (Luke 1:52–53), making the powerful abject and the humble glorious.

This is what he promised through the prophet Isaiah to his beloved Jerusalem:

> “I shall make you the pride of the ages, the joy of generation after generation; you shall suck the milk of nations and be nursed at the breast of kings, and you shall know that I am the Lord, your savior, and that your redeemer is the Mighty One of Jacob” (Isaiah 60:15–16).

“The pride of the ages” means the nobility of illustrious men; “the breast of kings” means the riches of those who dig their treasures into the earth. That nobility is nourished at the breast of kings when worldly power is subjected to it. From this it obtains joy and gladness not only in the present generation but also in the future generation of the ages.

## CHAPTER IV

On the following day, the third of July, they struck their tents at first light and hurried to follow the tracks of the fleeing Turks. But they fled before them like frightened doves before the face of a hawk. After they had fled here and there for four days, it happened that their leader Soliman encountered ten thousand Arabs coming to his aid.

Soliman was the son of the elder Soliman, who had taken all Romania away from the emperor. After fleeing from the city of Nicaea, he had gathered this people together and had brought them against the Christians, as though to avenge his injury. When he saw them—and they saw him—he fell from his horse to the ground from excessive grief, began to wail loudly, and proclaimed himself miserable and unfortunate.

The Arabs, unaware of the cause of his misfortune, said to him:

> “O most shameless of all men, why are you fleeing like this? You are greatly degenerating, since your father never fled from battle. Recover your courage and return to the fight, for we have come to your aid.”

With his voice broken by sighs, he replied:

> **Note [Col. 0692D]:** Great was the terror by which Soliman was terrified.
>
> “A great madness afflicts you. You have not yet recognized the valor of the Franks, nor have you experienced their courage. Their strength is not human but heavenly—or diabolical. Nor do they rely solely on their own aid, but also on divine assistance. Had we not defeated them so thoroughly that we were already preparing elm and hemp ropes to place around their necks? Then suddenly an innumerable people, who neither feared death nor dreaded the enemy, burst out of the mountains and fearlessly thrust themselves into our ranks.
>
> “Whose eyes could endure the brilliance of their terrible weapons? Their lances flashed like sparkling stars; their helmets and cuirasses shone like the trembling lights of the spring dawn. The crash of their weapons was more terrible than the sound of thunder. When they prepare for battle, holding their lances upright toward heaven, they advance in rivalry; and, as though they were without a voice, they fall silent. But when they draw near their adversaries, then, loosening their reins, they charge with such force as lions driven by the spur of empty stomachs and thirsting for the blood of animals.
>
> “Then they shout, gnash their teeth, and fill the air with their cries. These strangers show mercy to no one whom they seize; they kill everyone. What can I say about such a savage people? No people can resist them or find a place to flee, because they are supported either by divine or by diabolical aid.
>
> “All other peoples dread our bows and fear our arrows. But these men, once they have put on their armor, fear an arrow no more than a straw; they dread a missile as little as a wooden club. Alas, alas! We numbered three hundred and sixty thousand, and all of us were either killed by them or scattered in flight. This is now the fourth day since we began fleeing before them, and we still tremble no less fearfully than on the first day.
>
> “Therefore, if you are willing to follow sound advice, withdraw from all Romania as quickly as you can, and take the greatest care that their eyes do not see you.”

When the Arabs heard this, they immediately took flight with Soliman himself. The Christians, however, followed the tracks of the fugitives with greater diligence. Yet the fugitives never remained in one place; and although their minds were utterly confused, whenever they came in flight to any Christian city or fort, they put on a cheerful expression, as though they had won a victory.

> **Note [Col. 0693D]:** The Arabs fabricated deceptions while fleeing in this way.

They said:

> “Open your gates to us joyfully and with gladness, for we have killed all the Franks who had come to plunder you and your lands. Not one of them remains who is not either dead or held in our chains. Our leader Soliman is proceeding by another road and has taken the captives with him.”

Those who were credulous enough to believe their words opened the gates, but, deceived, they paid a heavy penalty. For the Arabs plundered their possessions, burned their houses, and either slaughtered the inhabitants or bound them with ropes and took them away. They did not want the Franks who were pursuing them to find anything, so that, compelled by want, they might at least abandon the pursuit.

In this the Arabs acted with prudent judgment, for it greatly benefited them but harmed our entire army. Our men found that land deserted, without water, and empty of every good thing.

> **Note [Col. 0693D]:** Our men found famine after fertility.

They pulled up the ears of grain that were nearing ripeness, rubbed them clean between their hands, and by such food alleviated their hunger as best they could. Most of the horses died there, and many who had previously been cavalrymen became foot soldiers. They rode cows and oxen, as well as the rams and dogs of that land, which were of great strength and size.

They therefore crossed that territory as quickly as they could and entered Lycaonia, a province extremely rich in every good thing. They came to Iconium.

> **Note [Col. 0693D]:** This city received our men and took them in completely.

Iconium is an exceedingly wealthy city in temporal goods; the apostle Paul mentions it in his Epistles. Those who had wandered in the desert, in that waterless land, found a city suitable for lodging and, through the Lord’s provision, were filled with earthly goods.

When they decided to depart from the city, the inhabitants advised them to carry water with them in vessels and skins, because nowhere did they find water on the following day. On the second day, toward evening, they reached a certain river, where they stayed for two days.

On the next day, the scouts who went ahead of the army first came to a city called Heraclea, in which a very large multitude of Turks was gathering. When the Turks recognized from a distance the fluttering banners of the Franks, they immediately fled like a fawn torn from a snare or a wounded hind.

Our men, praising the Lord, entered the city without opposition and stayed there for four days. On the fifth day they all left the city. Then Count Baldwin, brother of Duke Godfrey, and Tancred separated from the others with their soldiers and turned aside toward the city of Tarsus.

> **Note [Col. 0693D]:** Here the scattered army makes for a city called Tarsus.

There were many Turks in it, who went out to battle against them, but they could not hold out for long. Unable to withstand the swift charges, winding attacks, and terrible blows of our men, they withdrew into the city’s fortifications after many of their number had been struck down. Our men pitched their camp before the city and stationed sentries.

The Christians who were in the city came to the camp at midnight, shouting with great joy:

> “Rise, invincible soldiers of the Franks, for all the Turks are fleeing from the city and no longer dare to fight you.”

Our men nevertheless did not wish to pursue them, because it was night, a time entirely unsuitable for pursuit. At daybreak our men entered the city, and the citizens received them most gladly.

A dispute then arose between Count Baldwin and Tancred over which of them should rule the city, or whether it should be placed under the authority of both. Tancred resisted, because he wanted to possess it for himself; but finally he yielded to Baldwin, because Baldwin’s army was the stronger.

Within a short time two cities were handed over to them—one called Athena and the other Manustra—as well as many forts. They were now advancing through favorable successes, since the Turks no longer rode out but were concealed in very strongly fortified positions.

Most of the Franks entered the land of the Armenians.

> **Note [Col. 0694D]:** The fierce nation of the Franks enters the land of the Armenians.

For they eagerly desired to drench the land with the blood of the Turks. The whole land fell silent in their presence, while the Armenians came out to meet them and received them into their cities and forts.

They came to a certain fort that was so strongly defended by its natural position that it feared neither weapons nor any kind of siege engine. Nevertheless, they did not wish to remain there long, since the entire surrounding land was subject to them and inclined toward them willingly.

## CHAPTER V

There was in the army a brave and energetic soldier, a native of that region, who requested that land from all the princes, so that he might guard it in fidelity to God, the holy sepulchre, and them, and protect his life and honor.

> **Note [Col. 0694D]:** The soldier obtains what he requests and takes possession of his homeland.

The princes unanimously granted his request, because they knew him to be a faithful man, capable and courageous in military matters.

Afterward, advancing successfully, they came to Caesarea of Cappadocia. Cappadocia is a region situated at the head of Syria and extending toward the north. Its inhabitants voluntarily surrendered the city and received them kindly.

After leaving Cappadocia, they prosperously reached a certain beautiful and very fertile city, which the Turks had besieged not long before and attacked for three weeks, but had been unable to capture. As they approached it, the citizens immediately came out to meet them with the greatest joy and received them favorably.

Another soldier, named Peter of the Alps, then requested this city and obtained it very quickly from all the princes.

> **Note [Col. 0695D]:** Caesarea and the homeland are handed over to him as well.

That very night a tale-bearing informer came to Bohemond and told him that as many as twenty thousand Turks were nearby, unaware that the Frankish army had arrived there. Believing the informer’s lying words, Bohemond selected chosen soldiers, took them with him, and traversed the places where the Turks were said to be lurking. But just as the informer had been worthless, so the outcome of the search was frustrated.

Afterward they rose and came to a certain city called Cosor, which was full of every good thing useful to human bodies. When they approached it, the Christians who were there received them with the greatest courtesy. They rested there for three days. Each person attended to his own need: the weary found rest, the hungry food, the thirsty drink, and the naked clothing.

> **Note [Col. 0695D]:** Here joyful abundance followed the famine that had been destroyed.

God therefore provided them with such a lodging that they might more easily endure the severe torment of the famine that was to come.

Meanwhile it was reported to Count Raymond that the Turks, terrified by fear, had fled from Antioch and left the city insufficiently defended. He consequently decided to send five hundred soldiers there to seize the city’s citadel before anyone else learned of it.

When they reached a valley near Antioch, they heard for the first time that it was untrue that the Turks had departed from the city; rather, they were exerting every effort to defend it. They therefore proceeded to the fort of the Publicans and, after subduing it, turned aside by another route. They reached the valley of Rugia and found many Turks and Saracens there, whom they defeated in battle and killed by the sword.

When the Armenians, the inhabitants of that land, saw this, they rejoiced, because the Turks and Publicans had been killed so manfully by the Christians, and immediately they surrendered themselves and their land to them. The Christians obtained the city of Rusa and subjected many forts to their rule.

The entire army that had remained set out on its journey, but with a wretched and unfortunate outcome.

> **Note [Col. 0695D]:**
>
> The fortune of the world is changeable like the moon:  
> If good goes before, evil follows; prosperity gives way.
>
> This is evident in many things, as in these battles.

They traveled through a mountainous region accessible to no one except wild beasts and reptiles. There was a path there no more than a foot wide, constricted on both sides by cliffs and dense thickets of thorns and brambles. The bottoms of the valleys seemed to plunge into an abyss, while the summits of the mountains rose to the stars.

Along this uneven path, the soldiers and armor-bearers carried the weapons hanging from their necks. All were equally on foot, since none of them rode. Many would gladly have sold their cuirasses, helmets, and shields if they had found a buyer. Many, overcome by extreme weariness, threw them away so that, at least thus lightened, they might be able to continue.

The pack animals could in no way proceed with their burdens; in many places human beings carried the animals’ loads. No one could stand still or sit down, because each person pushed against the next. No one could help his companion except the last could help the one before him, since the man in front could scarcely turn around toward the one following.

At last, when that wretched and impassable road had ended, they came to a city called Marasim, where the inhabitants received them with honor and joy. There they found an abundance of temporal goods; there they received consolation for their misery and deprivation.

There the front waited for the rear, but an entire day passed before the tail could join the head. After gathering together and resting for one day, on the second day they came to the valley in which Antioch is situated. It is a royal city founded by King Antiochus and named after him.

It is the metropolis and head of the entire region of Syria, formerly distinguished by the worship of the Catholic faith through blessed Peter, chief of the apostles. He established an episcopal see there and ordained the apostles Barnabas and Paul.

Now, to show mortal eyes that there is no strength or power except from him, the Lord first wished to acquire this city through the humility of speech preached by the mouths of preachers; now he wished to recover it through the exalted power of those who fight with weapons.

Thus our men, hastening toward the city in the strength of God, came to the Iron Bridge. There they found a large number of Turks attempting to cross the bridge in order to bring aid to those in the city. But it does not belong to human beings to direct their own steps; that belongs to the one to whose rule all things are subject.

Our men immediately attacked them as one body and spared no one. They killed a great multitude of them by the sword; others, overcome with terror, fled and thus took care of their present lives.

Having won the victory, the Christians found much booty there: pack animals, asses, and camels loaded with wine, grain, oil, and other necessities essential to those under siege.

They then pitched camp on the bank of a river not far from the city walls. On the following day, loaded with every kind of good, they planned to go to the city. Under God’s guidance they reached it and encircled it with camps on three sides. On one side, mountains prevented access and kept every military operation at a distance.

On Wednesday, the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, the siege of Antioch was established, to the future praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is always wondrous in his works.

[Col. 0695] **THE THIRD BOOK ENDS.**

**THE FOURTH BOOK BEGINS.**

[Col. 0697]

## CHAPTER I

Because the city of Antioch was defended not only by its natural position but also by lofty walls, towers extending high into the air, and very dense defensive works on the summits of its walls, the princes formed the plan of fighting against it not by strength but by ingenuity; by skill, not by Mars; by siege machinery, not by armed conflict.

First, therefore, they built a bridge over the river, so that they might cross it more easily whenever it was necessary to cross. At that time they found near the city an abundance of excellent fruits, plentiful vineyards, pits full of grain and barley and other foodstuffs, and trees laden with many kinds of fruit.

The Armenians who were in the city also informed them of this. These men came over to the Christians with the consent of the Turks, but their wives and children remained in the city. Although they were Christians, they acted deceitfully in all this, because they reported the words and deeds of our men to the Turks inside.

The Christians constructed suitable engines of war for attacking the city: wooden towers, ballistae, hooks, rams, sappers, missiles, stakes, slings, and whatever else could be devised by any art. But what could these accomplish against an impregnable city, especially when it contained so many defenders, who could even have fought our men in open battle?

After the morning star had preceded the dawn’s ruddy rising,

and dawn itself was already shimmering with dewy brightness,

and the sun was beautifying the world with its blazing light,

the nobles and the nobles’ throngs rose quickly,

seized their weapons, and ran to the city walls.

A battle was fought with strong hands, both inside and outside.

The defenders held their ground while our men hurled spears,

missiles together with clubs, and also stones and stakes.

Immense toil ensued, but the result was fruitless.

Thus they withdrew, because they could not overthrow

the towers and walls, which no force could make collapse.

When our men saw that they could accomplish nothing, they abandoned that attack but maintained the siege.

The Turks, trusting in their unconquerable city, went out at night with the gates open and shot arrows into the camp. It happened that by shooting in this way they killed a woman in front of the tent of Prince Bohemond. For this reason they stationed more vigilant guards throughout the camp, and they also guarded the gate through which the Turks customarily went out.

The military princes and nobles therefore decided to build a fort for themselves, so that they would be safer if the enemies of God should somehow prevail—enemies who were swarming everywhere like bees to their hives. This was done.

Meanwhile, as the daily supply of food began to diminish, they formed a plan to seek provisions and sent armor-bearers and many soldiers to obtain them as guards. But those who wished to plunder were:

Partly successful in plundering, and partly killed.

For there was a certain fort in the mountains not far from the city, called Arech, full of rebellious Turks. They laid an ambush for our men, wounded many, killed even more, and took many captives away. They forced the rest, after shamefully mistreating them, to return to the camp.

When the army of God learned of the misfortune of this wretched event, it grieved deeply; but afterward it found a salutary plan. They sent ahead one thousand armor-bearers, followed by Bohemond and the count of Flanders with chosen soldiers, toward the aforementioned valley, where the advance party could take refuge if the Turks pursued them.

This happened without delay. When the Turks recognized them from a distance, they loosened their reins, urged on their horses with spurs, pursued them, and put them to flight.

Our men fled to their own forces as to a most secure refuge and found the protection of divine assistance. When the Turks came very close and discovered that our soldiers were ready, they would gladly have withdrawn at first, hesitating in place, if they had been able to retreat. But when they recognized that the Christians were fewer than they were, they joined battle, though with trembling, trusting in their numerous multitude.

But what can a battle accomplish against which divine aid fights? For God is strong and powerful; the Lord is powerful in battle (Psalm 23:8).

Only two of our men were killed there. But of the Turks, whose number was beyond counting and who were driven back by the hand of God, an uncountable number were killed. They brought many captives among them back to the camp and beheaded them before those who were upon the walls of the famous city.

To cause the defenders still greater grief and terror, they hurled the severed heads into the city with ballistae.

Afterward our men were able to go more freely to the villages and settlements of the Armenians in search of food, while the Armenians themselves and the natives of that land brought provisions to our men for sale.

Meanwhile the most sacred day of the Lord’s Nativity arrived, a day God has granted to all his faithful as supremely celebrated, because the one who granted birth to all creatures chose to be born for human beings alone. The Christians therefore celebrated that feast as well as those in the tents were able.

There was, indeed, greater joy in the camp than within the walls of the famous city. I call it famous not because of the disgraceful habitation of paganism, but because of the position of the human condition, and especially because of the reconciliation with God of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles.

## CHAPTER II

After this celebration had been completed, they took counsel about what they should do, because provisions were running out in the camp and the icy winter did not allow those bringing goods for sale to come to them.

The more those who were in the city knew that our men were hungry, the more fiercely they began to rage against them. On one side the harshness of the weather oppressed them; on another, the poverty of wretched deprivation; and on another, the violence of their adversaries.

As commonly happens among a gathered multitude, the voices of those who murmured did not cease. Nor was it surprising that human weakness, pressed by so many torments, should give way. Hail, snow, ice, and storm winds violently oppressed those whom no shelter covered. Why should it be surprising that those outside the tents were in a desperate state, when the tents themselves were floating in water?

Therefore, as we have said above, they took counsel about what they should do and reached the following agreement. Bohemond and the count of Flanders offered themselves to provide assistance, and everyone approved and most willingly consented.

They selected thirty thousand cavalrymen and infantrymen and entered the land of the Saracens.

O God, mediator of all things, how timely is your help in dangers and for those laboring in need, so that what Solomon wrote in Proverbs might be fulfilled: “The substance of the sinner is kept for the righteous” (Proverbs 13:22).

Persians, Arabs, and Medes had gathered from Jerusalem, Damascus, Aleppo, and the other regions—a very great multitude that had planned to come to Antioch and defend it against the Christians. But a different plan had been established in heaven, and that plan bent their arrangement downward.

When they heard that part of the Christians had entered their land, they rejoiced greatly, believing that the Christians were already caught as though in chains. Then they divided themselves into two battle lines, so that, once our men were surrounded by them, they would find nowhere the means of escape.

This division was foolish, because “folly always rests in the hearts of unbelievers.” When the two battle lines saw one another, one immediately rushed upon the other: the one trusting in its multitude, the other in God’s omnipotence. Therefore the outcome of the battle was unequal.

They struck down all the armed soldiers who came against them, as a reaper strikes down a harvest. When they wished to turn back in a circle by means of their reins, they found no one to strike again except those who were fleeing. Those who fell into the hands of our infantry plunged into utter ruin. Those who know battles understand that “infantrymen kill with more severe attrition than cavalrymen.”

The other battle line, which had separated from the first in order to surround our men, heard the voices of the combatants and the crashing of breaking weapons and rushed to the aid of its own people with loosened reins. But when it recognized their wretched fate and looked around at those fleeing, the most violent terror fell upon them, and it brought them into the company of the fugitives.

What else could our men do but pursue them? As the common proverb says: “If there is someone who flees, there will be someone who pursues.” All our men were now pursuing them, because those who had come on foot were being made into riders of horses.

What more is there to say? Whoever was able to escape was joyful and glad; whoever was intercepted died a most wretched death. How many asses and camels, and how many pack animals loaded with grain, wine, and other provisions, were captured there—provisions welcome to the hungry army of God!

How great were the joy and triumphant exultation in the camp on that day, when they saw such gifts from the supreme provider! It was a thing to wonder at and rejoice over: the Lord was restoring his faithful through the merchandise brought from afar by their enemies. He filled the hungry with good things (Luke 1:53), while stripping their adversaries of them.

So too he had once acted for the children of Israel, when they wished to pass through the land of foreign kings and those kings denied them passage along the public royal road. All who took up the sword against them perished by the sword, and their land and possessions were given to the Israelites as a possession.

Now the same Lord, by the same recompense, takes from the adversaries of his own people, so that they may truly believe that what was written of them has been accomplished:

> “May God, who must be blessed, be blessed in all things; without him we can do nothing.”

## CHAPTER III

Meanwhile, while these glorious princes were absent, those who were in the city suddenly came out and attacked our men between the camps, killing many of them. On that very day the bishop of Le Puy lost his dapifer, who customarily carried the banner of his battle line.

Had the river not flowed between the camp and the city, they would have inflicted greater and more frequent injuries. Afflicted by these outcomes of war, and especially by the lack of food, many of our men were trying to leave, because it was exceedingly difficult for unwilling men to endure the fast. They therefore plotted to escape from the siege.

Bohemond, a man eloquent and pleasing in speech, addressed them as follows:

> “Men who have until now been exceptional warriors, whom God has already made victorious through many dangers of war, and whom the strength born of experience has adorned with distinction, why do you murmur against the Lord because the hardship of poverty weighs upon you?
>
> “When he extends his hand to you, you rejoice; when he withdraws it, you despair. In this you seem not to love the giver but his gifts; not the benefactor but the offering of the benefactor. When the Lord gives generously, he is your friend; when he ceases, he appears to you an enemy and a stranger.
>
> “To what people has God ever granted, in so short a time, the opportunity to fight so many battles, overcome so many fierce enemies, grow rich on so much of the spoils of nations, and be marked by so many palms of triumph? Behold, we have now subdued countless enemies; behold, we have now brought their spoils to you. Why do we lose confidence when we win every day in this way?
>
> “He who fights for you in this way is not far from you. Often he tests his faithful so that it may become known whether they love him. Now he is testing you through the troubles of poverty and through the constant pressure of those who oppose you.
>
> “What if they had inflicted upon us as many injuries as we have inflicted upon them? What if they had killed as many of us as we have struck down of them? If any one of us had survived, he could justly have complained. But certainly there would have been no one to complain, because no survivor would have remained.
>
> “Therefore do not lose confidence, but be men of courage. For if you live in him or die for him, you are blessed.”

By these and similar words he restored their weakened spirits to strength and brought manliness into their effeminate minds.

After a few days had passed, harsh winter broke upon them, and the abundance of food in the camp disappeared. Those who were accustomed to sell food could not come, because snow and ice blocked the way. The army’s scouts, who ranged as far as the land of the Saracens, found absolutely nothing, because everyone from the whole border of that land had either fled far away or hidden themselves in caves and hollows in the rocks.

When the Armenians and Syrians saw that our men were placed in such great danger from famine, they traveled through familiar places, carefully searching for anything they might find and bring to our men. But among so many people there was little, and it did not suffice for such a multitude. Consequently, an ass-load of grain weighing seven pounds was sold for a high price, an egg for twelve denarii, and a single nut for one coin.

> **Note [Col. 0701D]:**
>
> A nut was valued when it was sold for a single coin.  
> Here something excessively and extraordinarily costly is meant: an egg was sold for twelve coins.

Why should I recount everything, when whatever had previously been regarded as cheap was now sold at an exorbitant price? Because of this, many perished there from hunger, having nothing with which to buy anything.

A great instability of spirit, failure of mind, and distrust of every good hope therefore began to arise among them. And why should it be surprising if the spirits of the poor and weak wavered, when those who seemed to be pillars were failing altogether?

Peter the Hermit and William the Carpenter slipped away by night, took to flight, and separated themselves from the holy company of God’s faithful.

Let us say who William was, since we have mentioned Peter above. William was born of royal lineage and had once been viscount of a certain royal castle called Milidunum. He began to be called “the Carpenter” because no one in battle wished to confront him. No cuirass, helmet, or shield could withstand the blows of his lance or sword.

It is therefore astonishing—and grievous to contemplate with astonishment—that such dullness of mind should have entered so great and distinguished a man that he withdrew so shamefully from the camp of illustrious men. But, as we hope, he had not done this through fear of battle; rather, he had never learned to endure so great an injury from famine.

When Tancred, a brave soldier of steadfast courage, learned of this breach caused by their flight, he was deeply grieved, pursued them, caught them, compelled them to return in disgrace, and brought them to Bohemond’s house.

There is no need to ask whether he felt shame, since he had begun to flee without anyone pursuing him. Many who knew him grieved; all who did not know what sort of man he had been hurled insults at him.

At last, after being assailed by many insults, he obtained peace out of regard for Hugh the Great, whose kinsman he was, and because he had fought honorably with them in earlier battles. But he swore publicly that he would never again depart in this way.

Nevertheless, he did not keep his oath for long, for as soon as he could, he secretly departed.

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0702A]

God therefore allowed this severity of famine to occur, both to test his own people and to make their terror known among all nations. For he was pressing his own people with fasting, while with the sword he was cutting off the neighboring nations around them. A thousand fell at the side of one man, and ten thousand at the right hand of another. Therefore one must never despair of the Lord in such circumstances, because whatever he does works together for good for those who love him (Rom. 8:28). Lest they grow arrogant because of so many victories in war, he oppressed them with the severe hunger of fasting. For throughout the entire army scarcely a thousand horses could be found fit for battle, so that it might become clear that they did not place their trust in the strength of horses, but in him through whom, and by whatever means, and whenever he wished, they overcame.

[Col. 0702B] There was a certain soldier in that same army named Tetigus, wealthy among his own people and very famous, well known in the regions of Romania, but concealed beneath a cloak of foolishness. He came to the princes and said to them:

“Why are we lying idle here like this? Why do we not seek what will benefit us? If it seems good to you, I shall go into the region of Romania and bring back from there, under the protection of the emperor, an abundant supply of provisions. I shall have ships laden with every necessity—grain, wine, oil, barley, meat, flour, and cheeses—brought by sea, and horses, mules, and female mules by land. And so that you may have no distrustful doubts about me, I shall leave behind my tents and all my possessions, except only what I shall carry with me. And if you still distrust me, I shall swear that I will return to you as quickly as possible.”

The princes believed his lying words and also accepted his oath. But he neither kept his oath nor fulfilled his promise. I report this concerning these two soldiers so that everyone may understand how great the want was in the camp, since it compelled even the wealthy to flee and to commit perjury.

When they were already so severely constrained, and every human hope had completely failed, a very large part of the army asked the princes for permission to return, and they unanimously granted it to them with tears. Why should they retain those whom they could not console? While desolation was thus growing ever more severe throughout the camp, and no one had any counsel, divine mercy supplied them with its customary aid. A messenger arrived and reported that countless thousands of Turks were nearby, and asserted that on that very night they would assemble in the fortress nearest to them, called Arech, which we mentioned above. They were coming secretly and in profound silence so that they might find the men in the camp unprepared.

This report became known to everyone, and it roused those whom it found sluggish and benumbed in the sleep of indolence. The man who previously could scarcely walk now leapt and danced. The spirit of those whom lack of food had lulled to sleep revived. Raising their hands to heaven, they praised God and, as though they had already conquered, clapped their hands. For they preferred to die honorably in battle rather than be tortured by the lack of food.

[Col. 0703A] Then the leaders of the army resolved that one part of everyone should remain in the camp to guard it, while the other should go to meet the approaching enemy in battle. Those who left the camp by night took up positions in ambush, lying in wait for the enemy’s arrival between the river and the lake. At the first light of dawn, when the morning was bringing brightness to the earth, they sent scouts to observe the enemy’s columns and report how numerous they were.

The scouts reported that they had never seen so many thousands of them gathered together at once. From the side of the river, two separate battle lines were seen rushing forward from the multitude on swifter horses. Then our men, stationed on a certain slope, fortified themselves with the sign of the cross and their weapons, stretched their hands toward heaven, commended themselves to God, and begged his help.

[Col. 0703B] Soon our men came upon them, received their attack, and, striking with stabbing blows, threw down all whom they encountered. Others, scattered across the plain, wheeled around and sent showers of poisoned arrows. They gnashed their teeth and barked like dogs, thinking that in this way they would terrify their opponents. But our men mocked them, and, protected by shields, coats of mail, and helmets, despised the missiles they hurled.

When their innumerable multitude drew near, they attacked our men with such force that our men were briefly turned to flight. When Bohemond saw this—he had been observing the guard at the rear—he burst into the midst of the battle with his own line, rallied his companions, and brought the enemy to destruction.

For when they saw our banners hanging above their heads and our men, like roaring lions, moving among the enemy, while everyone around them was being torn apart, they became afraid and confused. Turning their horses’ reins backward, they retreated as quickly as possible toward the Iron Bridge.

But what could the Franks do then except strike them at close quarters with the sword? The road was strewn with the bodies of the dying, and the air was filled with the cries of those lamenting. The earth, moistened with the blood of the dying, was pierced by the feet of the trampling horses. When they reached the bridge, the road narrowed, and the bridge could not receive them all. Many therefore plunged into the river, while those whom the current caught it swallowed as it carried them around in its swift whirl.

Why should I linger over the details? More perished than escaped. More were killed than remained alive. Those who escaped fled for refuge to the fortress we mentioned above, but they did not remain there long. After it had been plundered, they left it empty and departed in flight.

Our men, however, seized it, appointed guards to protect it, and established a bridge. The Armenians and Syrians also pursued the fugitives; by seizing the narrow places in advance, they killed many and detained even more as captives. Thus the sons of the devil, according to their deserts, passed from one ruin into another and met destruction.

Our men returned to the camp with great joy, bringing with them horses, mules, female mules, abundant spoils, and many other things that were greatly needed by their impoverished companions. They also brought many heads of the dead, which they placed before the city gate, where the men of Admiraldus of Babylonia had their lodging. Their companions who were in the camp received them with the greatest joy, as did those who had fought all day with the citizens who had come out of the city and had carried away the palm of victory.

[Col. 0704A]

CHAPTER V

Then the doubled joy of a twofold victory made the time festive and restored those who had nearly been consumed by grief over their poverty. By now the Armenians and Syrians were bringing provisions to the camp and rejoicing together over our men’s successful outcome.

The citizens used to leave the city, hide among the mountain rocks, and lie in wait for those bringing provisions; whenever they could seize anyone, they killed him. This greatly saddened the leaders, who took counsel over the matter and found a remedy for the calamity. They built a fortress before the city gate, over the bridge beside Machumaria, [Col. 0704B] and this brought them thoroughly under control, since from then on none of them dared to leave by way of the bridge.

At that time, because the men in the camp were insufficient to complete this work, Bohemond and the count of Saint-Gilles went to the Port of Saint Symeon and endeavored to bring workers from there at a price.
