While they were bringing them back, they found Turks who had left the city that night and were lying in ambush. In a sudden attack, the Turks assaulted our men so fiercely that they drove those who were mounted into the mountains without any effective resistance.

The foot soldiers who could not flee suffered a terrible death; but the more bitter it was, the more glorious it became. Nearly a thousand of those who died there were killed, [Col. 0704C] but those who killed them did not long rejoice. For news of the slaughter reached the camp and stirred so many princes and leaders. Mounting their horses, they flew forth in ordered ranks to avenge the death of their men, and found the enemy still in the field, cutting off the heads of the slain.

The Turks were not at all frightened. Trusting in their multitude, they joined battle. But our men, trusting with all their hearts and all their strength, soon overcame them once our foot soldiers had joined the cavalry. For when the Turks saw those whom they had forced to flee into the mountains rushing back, and saw our lines growing powerfully and pressing forward with even greater strength as they grew, they turned their backs and took the road of flight toward the bridge.

But the difficulty of the narrow path greatly impeded them, because they could neither flee farther nor turn around. They could not go back, since the enemy was pressing them; the narrowness of the road made it impossible to turn to the right or left; and the dense crowd of fugitives prevented them from advancing. Thus, by divine design, it happened that they were permitted neither to flee nor to fight.

There the Turk’s poisoned arrow was of no use, nor did the speed of his horse help him. There the foot soldiers caused a greater slaughter than those mounted on horses, for they cut them down in rivalry with one another, as a reaper cuts down meadows or a harvest. There swords and weapons might have been satisfied with the blood of the other nations of the Turks; but because they belonged to the Franks, they could neither be blunted nor filled with blood.

Our men alone were fighting; they were suffering. Our men were striking; they were dying. The tireless hand could not tear apart as much as it found there to tear apart. Between the living stood the dead, unable to fall because they were supported by the density of the living. So great was the disaster that one man crushed another into death. Such fear had seized them that each one pressed forward against the man in front of him so that he might escape.

The duke Godfrey, an outstanding ornament of knighthood, saw that no one could strike them except from behind. Flying swiftly on his horse, he reached the entrance to the bridge before them. What tongue could explain how great a slaughter that duke alone inflicted there upon the bodies of that wicked people? They had begun to flee and had thrown their weapons onto the ground. They dreaded the duke’s sword as death itself, yet they could not avoid it.

With his arms extended and his sword drawn, he cut off their necks. They offered their unprotected bodies unwillingly, making scarcely any resistance. There anger, place, sword, and mighty strength were fighting, and all of it rebounded upon the limbs of those wretched men.

When one of them, bolder than the rest, superior in bodily size, and stronger in his powers like another Goliath, saw the duke raging so mercilessly against his people, he drove his horse against him with bloodied spurs. Raising his sword high, he struck downward with all his strength and pierced the duke’s shield over his head. Had the duke not presented the boss of his shield against the blow and leaned to the other side, he would have paid the debt of death.

But God guarded his soldier and armed him with the shield of his protection. The duke, inflamed with fierce anger, prepared to repay the blow and cut off the man’s neck in the same manner. He raised his sword and, from the left side of the shoulders, drove it through him with such force [Col. 0705C] that it split the middle of his chest and severed his spine and vital organs. Thus the slippery sword came out whole above his right thigh.

[Note: [Col. 0705D] The duke strikes; the man perishes, and burst apart in the middle.]

In this way he plunged the entire head, together with the right side of the body, into the whirlpool, while he sent the part that had been seated on the horse back toward the city.

At this dreadful spectacle, everyone who was in the city came together. Seeing it, they were amazed, disturbed, and shaken; trembling seized them. There were pains like those of a woman in labor (Ps. 47), and the cries of mourners, because that man had been one of their Admiralds.

Then they unsheathed their swords, drew their bows, and prepared their arrows in the quiver (Ps. 10:3), so that they might shoot at the duke, desiring, if it were permitted them, to extinguish so great a light of Christian knighthood.

[Col. 0705D] But God did not consent to their wicked desire, because the duke withdrew; he could not long endure the hailstorm of their weapons and arrows.

O praiseworthy, unconquered right hand of the duke, and extraordinary strength of his courageous breast! The sword, too, deserves praise, because, remaining intact, it faithfully offered its service to the flashing right hand of its master.

Whose heart could pour forth, whose tongue recount, whose hand write, and what page could contain the deeds of the other princes who were his equals in all the victories of war? The duke’s victory shone above the rest, because the part of the divided body that remained became a testimony to his praise; while the wave that swallowed the bodies of the slain concealed the astonishing blows of the others.

But just as a whirlwind wind grips the branches of an ancient tree, so the severed limbs of the dying fell. In this battle, one pursued a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight (Lev. 16:8). Those who were plunged into the river’s swift current emerged and embraced the wooden pillars of the bridge, but our men pierced and killed them with spears from above.

The spilled blood gave the river a bloody color and struck great horror into all who looked on. Indeed, the mass of bodies obstructed the river’s course and forced it to move backward against the current. And why is this surprising? Five thousand lay prostrate upon the bridge, and all of them were hurled down into the water. And who could count how many the raging sword forced into the river with a sudden leap?

In that conflict the son of Cassian, the great king of Antioch, was killed, along with twelve Admiralds of the king of Babylonia, whom he had sent with their armies to bring aid to the king of Antioch. Those whom they call Admiralds are kings who govern the provinces of various regions. A province is said to be one that has a single metropolitan, twelve consuls, and one king. Thus as many provinces had come together as Admiralds were killed there.

Those who were captured there were reckoned at seven thousand. No one could retain in memory the quantity of clothing, weapons, and other equipment. Thus the Turks were magnanimously defeated by the Franks, and thereafter their chattering voices, the gnashing of their teeth, and the daily clamor of their insults fell silent.

Now they went with downcast faces, and many, utterly despairing, slipped secretly out of the city and fled. Night came and ended the conflict, and our victorious men returned to the camp; but the others, having barred the gates, withdrew within the city.

On the following day, as soon as the morning light appeared, the Turks came out of the city and gathered the bodies of the dead, as many as they could find, and committed them to burial. When the young men of the Christian army heard this, many gathered together, ran to the cemetery, and cast outside with great disgrace what the Turks had buried with great honor.

They had buried the bodies beyond the bridge, at Machumaria, which stood before the city gate, [Col. 0706D] and had wrapped many of them in cloaks. They had also placed Byzantine gold coins, bows, arrows, and many other things with them. Such, indeed, is their custom in burial; our men, however, are very willing to take such things away.

After all the bodies had been exhumed, they cut off the heads, wishing to learn the number of those who had been killed on the riverbank. They brought the severed heads back to the camp and left the unburied corpses to wild beasts and birds.

Those who watched this from the high walls and lofty towers grieved exceedingly. Tearing their cheeks and pulling their hair, they began to call upon their teacher Machomet for help. But Machomet could not restore those whom Christ had willed to destroy through his soldiers.

[Col. 0707] HERE ENDS BOOK FOUR.

HERE BEGINS BOOK FIVE.

CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0707A]

While these events were repeatedly being carried on through the impulses of changing circumstances, a certain herald arrived, announcing that messengers of the prince of Babylonia would come on the following day, and asking the princes of the camp for assurance that they might come safely. They willingly agreed and solemnly prepared themselves to receive them.

The tents were beautified with various kinds of ornament. Shields were set against stakes driven into the ground, for the game of the Quintana—that is, the mounted game—was to be practiced on the following day. Games of dice and chess were not lacking, nor swift races of horses with the reins turned in a circle; military charges and the brandishing of spears against one another were also displayed there. These activities showed that those who performed them were not trembling with fear. The young men cultivated such exercises, while the older men, advanced in age and understanding, sat together and discussed matters of counsel and prudence.

Meanwhile, as the Babylonian messengers approached and saw so many men celebrating with such great joy, they were astonished, because the report had traveled all the way to Babylon that the Franks were being tortured by hunger and shaken by fear.

They were therefore brought before the princes and delivered the message entrusted to them in these words:

“Our lord Admiravissus of Babylonia sends greetings and friendship to you, princes of the Franks, if you are willing to obey his will. In the court of the king of the Persians and of our lord, a great assembly has been gathered on your account, and the council was prolonged for seven days concerning what should be done with regard to you.

“For they wonder why, armed in this way, you seek the tomb of your Lord while exterminating his people from lands they have possessed for a long time—or rather, which is an abomination in foreigners, slaughtering them at the point of the sword.

“But if from now on you wish to travel with purse and staff, they will cause you to pass through to that place with the greatest honor and abundance of possessions. They will make horsemen of your foot soldiers; those who are poor will hunger no more throughout the entire journey or on the return. And if you wish to remain for a month at the tomb, you will not lack an abundance of goods. You will be granted permission to go throughout Jerusalem, so that everyone may honor both the temple and the tomb with whatever honor he pleases.

“But if you despise these concessions and trust in the greatness of your spirits and in your weapons, you must consider again and again to what danger you are exposing yourselves. Among us, at any rate, we consider it rash for any human power, however great, to assemble against the Babylonians and the king of the Persians.

“Now tell us openly what pleases you about these matters and what displeases you.”

To this the common judgment of the princes replied in these words:

“No wise man should wonder that we have come armed to the tomb of our Lord and are driving your people from these lands, since all of our people who have formerly been accustomed to come here with staff and purse have been treated with shameful mockery. Enduring the disgrace of insults, they were finally put to death.

“The land of that people is not theirs, although they have possessed it for a long time, because from ancient times it belonged to our people. Your nation, on account of its wickedness and injustice, took it away from them by force. Yet it ought not to be yours merely because you have held it for a long time. For by heavenly judgment it has now been decreed that what was unjustly taken from the fathers should mercifully be restored to their sons.

“Let your people not boast that it overcame the effeminate people of the Greeks, for, with divine power supporting us, the deserts of your people will be repaid upon your necks by the sword of the Franks. And it may be made known to those who are ignorant that it is not the work of men to overthrow kingdoms, but of him through whom kings reign.

“They say that they wish to indulge us if from now on we are willing to travel with purse and staff. Let their mercy return upon themselves, for whether they wish it or not, our poverty will be enriched—or relieved—by their treasures.

“Since Jerusalem has been granted to us by God, who can prevail to take it away? No human power can in any way inspire us with fear, because when we die, we are born; when we lose temporal life, we recover eternal life.

“Therefore report to those who sent you that we shall not lay down the weapons we took up in our homeland, even when Jerusalem has been captured.”

[Note: [Col. 0707D] The words of the Franks resound with proud piety.]

“For we trust in him who teaches our hands for battle and makes our arms like a bronze bow. He will open the way for our swords, every obstacle will be uprooted, and Jerusalem will be captured. Then it will be ours, not through the indulgence of a man, but through the equity of heavenly judgment. For this judgment has proceeded from the face of the Lord, because Jerusalem will be ours.”

The envoys found nothing further to say. But when they heard this declaration, they were scandalized, and, with the consent of our men, entered Antioch.

CHAPTER II

When these events had taken place, on the third day after the battle had been completed, they began to build the fortress of which we spoke above. It was constructed at the entrance to the bridge, specifically at Machumaria, on the site of the cemetery before the city gate. They destroyed all the stone tombs of the dead and fortified the fortress with their stones.

When it had been completed, it was entrusted to Raimund, the illustrious count of Saint-Gilles. This greatly constrained those who were in the city, since thereafter they could no longer leave from that side. Our men, however, now traveled securely wherever they decided to go.

Then the leaders selected excellent men and swifter horses. They crossed the river not far from the city and found immense booty: horses and mares, mules and female mules, asses and camels—five thousand animals. The distinguished company brought all these things to the camp, and great joy was celebrated among the Christians.

This misfortune severely weakened the citizens, because the abundance of goods that strengthened our men, once lost, weakened them.

In the place where the booty was captured there was an ancient fortress, ruined through neglect and age, but a certain monastery still flourished there. To constrain their enemies still further, the leaders decided to rebuild it and surround it with strong fortifications.

When this had quickly been completed, an inquiry was made into who would guard it. While the question of the guard was being discussed and many words were being thrown to the wind, Tancred, an illustrious prince and distinguished young man, as lively in speech as in action, sprang into the midst and said:

“I shall guard the fortress, if a reward worthy of my service is granted.”

They all therefore assessed the price together and gave him four hundred marks of silver. Tancred entered the fortress and strengthened it with companies of foot soldiers and strong troops, making it more secure than any other fortification.

He undertook this successfully, with God’s help, because on that very day a great multitude of Armenians and Syrians was coming to the city and bringing abundant provisions to the townspeople. Tancred, lying in ambush, seized them all. Yet because they were Christians, he did not wish to kill them; instead, he led them with their loads to his fortress.

Finally, he allowed them to depart unharmed on this condition: they promised him, on their Christian faith, that they would bring the Christians the necessities they required at a suitable price until Antioch was captured. They diligently fulfilled this promise, just as they had pledged.

Tancred had blocked the roads and paths for those who were in the city, so that no one dared to leave. For this reason they sought a truce, saying that during that interval they would deliberate among themselves under what law and on what terms they might surrender themselves and the city to the Christians.

The princes believed them. After arranging the agreements and establishing the time, they exchanged oaths to maintain the peace. The gates of the city were opened, and each side was given permission to go to the other. Then the Franks moved freely around the walls, stood with the citizens at the defenses, and the citizens came joyfully to the camp.

CHAPTER III

As time passed, when the final day of the truce had arrived, a certain Christian soldier named Walo—distinguished in arms and very famous among the foremost men—was far too trusting of the treacherous people. One day he was walking among their shrubs, delighting his eyes with the pleasantness of the place.

Armed curs attacked him while he was unarmed and, tearing him limb from limb, ripped him apart in pitiable torture.

Alas, alas! With Walo’s death the peace is broken.

[Note: [Col. 0709D] Walo is mutilated; by his death the peace is violated.]

The oaths given in pledge are violated, the city gates are closed again, and the treacherous pagans shut themselves within the recesses of their walls and towers.

There was immense mourning in the camp, since men and women alike lamented Walo’s death with repeated sobs.

[Note: [Col. 0710D] Great grief began over Walo’s death.]

His wife stirred everyone to tears. She tore herself lamentably beyond the custom of other women and, because of her frequent sighs and sobs, which moved others to mourning, could neither speak nor cry out. She had been born of the noble blood of the leaders and, according to the weakness of this flesh, was exceptionally beautiful.

For the most part she was motionless like a marble column, so that she was often thought dead, unless the vital warmth pulsing in the upper part of her chest could be felt. A hidden vein still throbbed beneath her scarcely hairy skin, at the down that separated the eyelashes [the transmitted anatomical wording is uncertain].

When she breathed, forgetting feminine modesty, she rolled upon the ground, tore her cheeks with her fingernails, and ripped apart her golden hair. Other married women ran to her, prevented her from doing such things to herself, and watched over her with compassionate care.

When she was able to speak, she burst forth in these words:

“King, threefold in persons, have mercy on Walo,

and grant him the gift of life, since you are the one God.

What did Walo deserve, that he died without battle?

Born of a virgin mother, wipe away Walo’s guilt,

whom you rescued from so many dangers of war,

and whom at last you permitted to be martyred.”

[Col. 0710C] “Alas, how greatly he desired to see your tomb, for which he despised everything he possessed, and himself as well! By what unhappy misfortune was his sword kept away, though it so well suited his side? O that I at least might have been happy, if I had been permitted to close his eyes in his final breath, wash his wounds with my tears, wipe them with my hands and clothing, and commit his sweet limbs to the tomb!”

At these lamentations, her brother Euvrard intervened and, as far as the force of grief permitted, restrained her.

CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0710D]

It must certainly not be passed over that, before the death of this man, something occurred while the truce remained intact and faithfully observed. There was indeed in that royal city an admiral of Turkish descent, with whom Bohemond held many private conversations during the time of peace. One day, among other things, he asked him where that innumerable army of the white-clad soldiers had encamped, whose aid they relied upon in all their battles. For he said that they could never withstand their arrival: as soon as they saw them, they began to fear that these men would crush them like a whirlwind, while the others wounded them; those would overwhelm them, and these would kill them.

To him Bohemond said: “Do you suppose there is another army besides this one you see here, ours?”

To which the other replied: “By my teacher Muhammad I swear that, if they were here, this entire plain could not contain them. They all have white horses of astonishing speed, and garments, shields, and banners of the same color. But perhaps they are hidden for this reason: so that your strength may not be revealed to us. But, by the faith you place in Jesus, where are their camps situated?”

Bohemond, therefore, enlightened by the Spirit of God, immediately perceived that the vision he had seen was a vision from God, and that the man’s question proceeded not from temptation but from good will. He replied:

“Although you are outside our law, because I see that you are well disposed toward us and animated by a good spirit, I shall disclose to you a mystery of our faith. If you possessed such depth of understanding, you ought to give thanks to the Creator of all things, who has shown you the white-clad army; and you should know that they do not dwell upon earth, but in the heavenly abodes of the kingdom of heaven. These are those who endured martyrdom for the faith of Christ and fought against unbelievers throughout the whole world. Their principal standard-bearers are George, Demetrius, and Maurice, who bore military arms in this temporal life and were beheaded for the Christian faith. Whenever it is useful to us, at the command of the Lord Jesus Christ, they come to our aid, and through them our enemies are hurled down.

“And so that you may know that I speak the truth, inquire today, tomorrow, and the following day whether their camp can be found anywhere in this entire region. If it is found, then, exposed before you as liars, we shall be ashamed. But when you are unable to find them anywhere in the region, you will see them present tomorrow, if we have need of them. From where, then, do they come so quickly, unless from the heavenly dwellings in which they reside?”

To him Pyrrhus replied—for that was his name: “And if they come from heaven, where are so many white horses, so many shields, and so many banners found?”

Bohemond answered: “You ask about great matters, beyond my understanding. Therefore, if you wish, let my chaplain come, and he will answer you concerning these things.”

The chaplain then said:

“When the omnipotent Creator determines to send his angels, or the spirits of the righteous, upon earth, they assume aerial bodies so that through them they may make themselves known to us, since they cannot be seen in their spiritual essence. That is why they now appear armed: to indicate that they have come to assist those who are laboring in battle. For if they appeared as pilgrims or as priests clothed in white stoles, they would announce not war but peace. Once the task for which they come has been completed, they return to the heavenly places from which they came, and the bodies which they assumed so that they might appear visible they restore to the same material from which they took them. Do not be surprised that the omnipotent Maker of all things transforms matter made by him into whatever form he wishes, since he brought all things from nothing into existence.”

At this Pyrrhus said: “By the very Creator whom you affirm, you speak of marvelous and reasonable things, and things unheard of by us until now.”

Bohemond added:

“O Pyrrhus, does it not seem to you a great miracle that the Lord Jesus Christ, in whom we believe, works through us? For the fewer we are, the stronger we become; whereas the more numerous you are, the weaker you are. To what do you attribute this power—to humanity or to divinity? Man does not exist from himself, but from his Creator; from the one from whom he has being, he also has power. From this, therefore, you can infer that, although one Creator created both us and you, he nevertheless grants us a more abundant outpouring of his power than he grants you. We are confident in his power that we shall possess not only Antioch but also all Romania, Syria, and Jerusalem itself, because the omnipotent Son of God, Jesus, has promised this.”

Pyrrhus wisely understood these and similar words of Bohemond, and Bohemond drew him strongly toward his friendship. When, through the persuasion of the enemy of the human race, the event concerning Walon mentioned above had occurred, Pyrrhus was no longer able to speak with his Bohemond. Nevertheless, through an intermediary, he secretly conveyed these words to him:

“I know you to be a noble man and a faithful Christian. I commend myself and my household to your faith. I shall do what you urged me to do: I shall hand over to you the three towers which I guard in Antioch, and one of the gates, to you and your Christian people. And so that you may not think this a frivolous matter or distrust my faith, I am sending you my son, whom I love uniquely and dearly; I entrust him to your faith as I would entrust myself.”

When Bohemond saw and heard these things, he was inflamed with great joy, and his devotion to God grew greatly within him. Abundant tears burst from his eyes, and, giving thanks to God, he stretched his hands toward heaven. Without delay he summoned the princes together and reported these matters to them, saying:

“Excellent princes and warrior men, you know how many injuries we have suffered in this siege, how many we are suffering, and how long God may wish us to suffer them. If God wished to give this city to someone by some stratagem, tell me: would your authority grant it to him?”

At this many shouted together:

“We shall possess it together, since together we have endured the hardships of necessity.”

Then Bohemond, smiling slightly, said:

“Woe to the city that will be subject to so many masters! Do not speak thus, brothers. Let it be subjected to the rule of the one who will be able to acquire it.”

When he saw that he was accomplishing nothing, he returned to his camp, but he detained the messengers of Pyrrhus who had come to him.

The princes, however, after Bohemond had withdrawn, took counsel, saying:

“We do not have good judgment, since we oppose the words of Bohemond, a most wise man. If this could have been done from the first day we came here, great advantage would have come to us from it. None of our men left his own land out of ambition for the city of Antioch; let the one to whom God wishes to give it have it. Let us all have one common purpose: namely, the liberation of the holy sepulchre.”

All approved this. Bohemond was summoned, and Antioch was willingly granted to him by everyone, if he could acquire it.

Bohemond, therefore, losing no time, sent men faithful to him at twilight to his friend, instructing them to report both the manner and the time of the undertaking. Pyrrhus sent back word that the Frankish army should set out on the following day, as though intending to go plundering in the land of the Saracens. When night began to fall, they were to return to the camp on the side of the city—“where,” he said, “I myself shall stand listening intently in my towers. Let them come prepared close to the wall and fear absolutely nothing.”

Bohemond entrusted this plan to some of his intimates: Hugh the Great, Duke Godfrey, the bishop of Le Puy, and Count Raymond. He said to them:

“On the coming night, with divine grace assisting us, Antioch will be handed over to us.”

He explained the message to them. When they had heard everything, they rejoiced and blessed the Lord.

On the following day they assembled the commanders of the armies, immense companies of soldiers, and as many troops of footmen as possible. They went out and crossed the mountainous country as though to plunder the land of the Saracens. When night came, they returned in profound silence and prepared themselves with good hope.

Bohemond went with only his own soldiers to the place designated by his friend. He remained at some distance from the walls with a few men, while he sent the others with a single ladder to the walls themselves, which, when raised, could reach the battlements. Once it had been raised, no one among so great a multitude dared to climb first.

While everyone hesitated in this way, a soldier named Fulcher, a native of Chartres, bolder than the others, said:

“In the name of Jesus Christ, I shall be the first to climb, to undertake whatever God calls me to endure—whether martyrdom or the prize of victory.”

When he had climbed, the others followed, and soon they reached the very summits of the walls.

Pyrrhus was standing there, awaiting their arrival and displeased by their excessive delay. When he did not see Bohemond, he asked where he was. He was told that Bohemond was close at hand, but Pyrrhus was deeply saddened by his absence and said:

> What is that sluggish man doing? Why does he delay and linger?  
> Send someone to tell him to come more quickly.  
> Send someone to tell him that today’s daylight is drawing near,  
> And that the frequent singing foretells the coming of clear weather.

A messenger was chosen to announce these words to Bohemond. When he heard them, he hurried up; but when he reached the ladder, he found it broken.

Meanwhile Fulcher, who had climbed with sixty armed young men, had seized three other towers by military valor, apart from Pyrrhus’s towers, and had killed two of Pyrrhus’s brothers in them. Although Pyrrhus was not unaware of this, he nevertheless did not withdraw from his pledged agreement of faith. When he heard that the ladder had broken, he opened the gates to Bohemond and the entire Frankish multitude as they approached.

Although he drew heavy groans from the depths of his breast and long sighs, no injury inflicted upon him could turn him back from the faith he had promised. Bohemond greeted him at the very entrance of the gate with bowed head and thanked him for the favor he had conferred. But when he learned the cause of Pyrrhus’s lamentation, he was deeply grieved and left a faithful guard of his own soldiers to protect him and safeguard his property.

Nor should it be left unmentioned that on that night a comet, which foretells a change of kingdoms, shone among the other stars of heaven and sent forth rays of light. Between the north and the east, a fiery redness flashed in the sky. With these evident signs shining in heaven, and with the dawn bringing light back to the earth, the army of God entered through the gates of Antioch, by the power of him who shattered the bronze gates of hell and broke the iron bars (Psalm 106:16), whose power endures for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0713] HERE ENDS THE FIFTH BOOK.

HERE BEGINS THE SIXTH BOOK.

CHAPTER ONE.

[Col. 0713C]

All you faithful followers of this Pyrrhus, attend to his faith; and, having attended to it, if you promise anything through faith, fulfill it without any contradiction. No remembrance of fraternal death, no force of grief, and no incitement of sorrow could turn him away from the steadfastness of his pledged faith. The pact of faith prevailed more powerfully in him than the cruel anguish of the killing of his two brothers.

And if we wish to bring forward that ancient riddle of Samson, we can propose one equivalent to it. Samson said: “Out of the eater came food, and out of the strong came sweetness” (Judges 14:14). But now, out of an unbeliever came faith, and out of a stranger came intimate and wholehearted affection.

But lest we seem to make our digression tedious, let us return to the subject of the history with which we began. On the fourth day before the Nones of June, the Christians entered the city of Antioch and avenged themselves upon its invaders at the edge of the sword.

Fulcher and his companions, who had climbed the walls with him, attacked the towers on every side. They pierced the unsuspecting guards, released from sleep, with spears and swords, and threw them from the summits of the towers to the ground. Those who were sleeping in their houses were awakened by the sound of shouting; when they came outside, eager to learn what was happening, they did not return, because they found swords ready to receive them.

The Christians resounded with “Kyrie eleison” and other praises of God, so that by this they might make it known to our men that they were Christians, not Turks. The streets of the city were everywhere strewn with the bodies of the dying, for none of the inhabitants resisted at that time; instead, all sought hiding places and the protection of flight. No distinction of honor was observed: boys were killed with girls, young men with old men, and mothers with their daughters.

Those who could flee went out through the gates, but they did not escape death, for they fell into the hands of those coming from the camps. It happened that Cassianus, the king and lord of the city, escaped dressed in cheap rags and reached the land of Tancred by flight. But, to his misfortune, the Armenians recognized him and immediately cut off his neck. They brought his head and belt to the princes, and they valued the belt at sixty bezants.

A large part of the population fled into the fortress overlooking the city. Its position and natural defenses were such that it feared no device of any siege engine. There is a mountain adjoining the city, whose summit rises to the stars, so high that the eyes of those looking upon it can scarcely reach it. From there the whole region can be surveyed.

A great multitude of Turks took refuge in it, and it became their sole place of shelter. Near this fortress stood a tower which Bohemond and his followers already held, and through it he was preparing to attack the fortress. But the Turks, having recovered their strength, sent down from above showers of arrows and spears like hail, since they stood considerably higher than the tower. Our men could not fight against them; they were forced to cover themselves with their shields and defend themselves with their arms.

The narrowness of the place hemmed them in, while the enemy pressed down upon them from above, for the combatants had no other avenue than the breadth of the walls. Consequently, when the Turks charged against the tower, one pushed another forward. There was no possibility of retreat, nor was there any way to turn aside either to the left or to the right. Whenever the force of the attackers’ charge struck our men, they received it with lances, spears, and sword-points, and threw the wounded to the ground. They also struck down those who were laboring beneath them to undermine the tower. Thus the dead brought death upon the living, and in the body of the man whose life had departed, death became visible.

In this encounter Bohemond was severely wounded by an arrow in the thigh, and could no longer walk except by limping. Blood began to drip abundantly from the wound, and the heart of the most noble prince began to fail in its former strength. Against his will and unwillingly, he withdrew to another tower and abandoned the battle.

With his illness the courage of the others collapsed, since each man was deeply grieved by the lamentable misfortune of his commander. They abandoned the fight, leaving the Turks and the tower. One man, however, remained on the upper summit of the tower, and the whole of our army unanimously mourned his noble death.

When he saw that he had been left alone, he nevertheless maintained an unconquered spirit and began to defend himself on both sides like a bear among mastiffs. He tore stones and mortar from the walls and threw them upon those attacking him. At last, laden with a thousand arrows, when he saw that he could not escape death, he hastened his own death. With shield and weapons, he leapt into the midst of the enemy wherever he saw the crowd densest, and became a torment to his killers.

No tongue of flesh is capable of adequately recounting what the hands of the Franks managed to destroy there. If the fortress had not been so strongly defended, the Lord would have granted great relief from the future calamities of its inhabitants on that very day. But God willed that the city of Antioch should be acquired with difficulty, so that, once acquired, it would be held more dearly. Things acquired quickly become cheap; what we have long desired, we embrace more dearly.

Night intervened and ended the conflict, bringing moderation to the labor of the day. It removed the need for fighting, but did not grant the exhausted men the opportunity to sleep. For where an enemy is present within the walls, there can be no possibility of rest.

On the following day, that is, Friday, some dragged the stripped corpses of the dead outside the walls, while others fought with the defenders of the fortress from the towers, using javelins and arrows.

CHAPTER TWO.

While matters were proceeding in this way, behold: those standing in the towers and on the walls saw from a distance an immense cloud of swirling dust. Having different opinions about it, some said that it was the emperor of Constantinople, coming to their aid; others said—and this was true—that it was the host of the Persians.

But those who came first, when they saw the city of Antioch, sat down together and waited for the strength of their army that was following behind. Corbanan was the commander of the army of the Persian king; for a long time he had been gathering that host of various peoples.

There were Persians and Medes, Arabs and Turkish Azimites, Saracens, Kurds, and Publicans, as well as many others of different nations. Three thousand Agulans were there, carrying no weapons except swords. They were all covered with iron and feared no opposing arms. Their horses disdained to bear banners and lances, and they were inflamed with excessive rage against those who carried them.

When all these men had gathered together, they sent their runners before the city to challenge our men to battle and urge them to come out of the city. But our men, exhausted from the previous day’s conflict, judged that it was safer to remain within the walls than to undertake a battle outside.

The others, however, ran through the fields and open ground, summoning our men to battle and hurling terrible insults at them. They tossed lances and swords high into the air and caught them in their hands, playing and exulting. But when they could draw none of our men out, they decided to return to their camp.

As they were returning, one of our men, Roger of Bardavilla, followed them with three other armed men, hoping that they might lure some of them out. But the others did not wish to enter into combat with equals, since they had already heard much recounted about the battles of the Franks. They set an ambush behind them beneath a hollowed-out rock and left some of their men there to provoke our men into battle as though challenging them.

When our men passed the place of ambush, the “thieves” came out of their caves and attacked them from behind. Those who had gone ahead turned back to meet them and directed a swift charge against them. When our men realized that they had been trapped, they turned their bridles and hoped to find safety in flight, but no escape could be found.

Roger sent his companions ahead of him and, with his shield thrown behind his back, endured the repeated blows of the enemy. He had almost escaped and was already reaching places near safety when his horse collapsed upon the ground. Roger fell with it and clung to the fallen animal; he could not rise in any way, because he was crushed beneath the horse’s weight.

Alas, what grief and gnashing of teeth there was then upon the walls of Antioch, when the noble youth of the Franks saw their illustrious soldier being so savagely killed by rabid dogs and torn apart in this way. They turned their eyes away and could not watch as he was mangled limb by limb. Finally, they cut off his head, fixed it upon a stake like a trophy-banner, and carried it to their camp.

Their camp was beside the Iron Bridge. Sensadolus, the son of the recently deceased king of Antioch, had gone to Corbanan and, falling humbly at his feet, begged him to take pity on him and assist him against the Franks, who had killed his father and disinherited him from the illustrious city. He had no refuge except in the city’s fortress, since the whole city was already subject to the rule of the Franks.

“My father,” he said, “while he was still alive, sent an embassy to you asking you to help him, promising either to enrich you with great gifts or to receive Antioch and the entire kingdom from you. I make you the same promise: if you can recover Antioch, I shall receive it from you and render you every form of loyalty. But if you cannot, you and all the people of our nation must flee. Romania, Syria, and Corozaim will not suffice for them, since they say that Jerusalem is theirs, as well as the kingdom of Damascus.”

The kings of these provinces were present and heard these words. After he had spoken, Corbanan replied:

“If you wish me to assist you in every way and restore you to your kingdom, place the fortress that you still possess in my hands, for through it Antioch will be restored to you.”

Sensadolus replied:

“If you prevail in expelling the Franks from the city and deliver their severed heads to me, I shall hand the fortress over to you and perform homage to you for it.”

Both agreed, and Sensadolus handed over the fortress. Corbanan entrusted it to one of his faithful men to guard. He accepted custody on the following condition: if the Franks were defeated, he would guard it; but if they were victorious, he too, like the others, would abandon the fortress and flee.

The man replied: “And if we are defeated, what would we do with the fortress? It is fitting that the victors should have it, since victory will be a greater prize than the fortress.”

After these matters had been settled, Corbanan said nothing further about them and turned his attention to making other arrangements. As he sat upon his throne, they brought before him a Frankish sword, very contemptible and blunt, covered with foul rust. They also brought a lance of similar deformity; indeed, by its wretchedness it made the sword seem comparatively excellent.

When Corbanan saw them, he said:

“Who will tell us where these weapons were found? Or for what reason have they been presented before us?”

Those who had brought them replied:

“Glorious prince and glory of the Persian kingdom, we took these weapons from a certain Frank and brought them to you, so that you might see and recognize with what weapons that ragged people attempts to plunder us and our lands—indeed, to lay waste to all Asia.”

Then Corbanan, smiling, said:

“It is clear that this people is sufficiently foolish and makes little use of reason, since it thinks that with such weapons it can subjugate the Persian kingdom. It is an arrogant people, excessively covetous of another’s jurisdiction. A people that trusts in its own boldness—but, by Muhammad, it has entered the lands of Syria and the walls of the royal city of Antioch to its misfortune.”

He said this and ordered his notary to be summoned. When the notary had arrived, he said:

“Take several sheets and write to our religious pope, the Caliph, and to the sultan, the king of the Persians, glorious above all, and to the leading nobles of the Persian kingdom. Wish them long life, continual peace, and lasting bodily health. Fortune, prosperous and joyful, is favorably advancing for us and smiling upon us with successful outcomes, since I hold the Frankish army enclosed within the walls of Antioch, and already possess in our hands the fortress that dominates the city.

“Therefore let it be certain to you that the reports you had heard about them do not describe the kind of men you were told they were, since a wolf does not become as great as the howling that follows it. But because you ordered me utterly to erase them from the land and deprive them of life by the sword, do not be angry with me if I send you some of the better men among them in chains. You will then decide whether you wish them to die or to live. For it seems fitting to us that those who came to make us captives should become captives themselves and perform harsh service among us.

“It will indeed bring honor to the Persian kingdom if the brother of the Frankish king lives there in exile. As for you, live in peace and the greatest tranquility, devote yourselves to every bodily pleasure, and beget sons without ceasing—sons who, if necessity requires, may resist other Franks and, when our own strength fails, may prove capable.

“I shall not see your face again until I have subjected all Syria, Romania, and Bulgaria to your rule.”

Corbanan spoke these words in arrogance and abuse, but they were turned against him as disgrace and shame.

After this, his mother came to him grieving and sorrowful, bearing a mournful expression. When the two of them had met in a private chamber, his mother said to her son:

“My son, consolation of my old age and the only pledge of all my love, I have hastened to you, wearied by the long journey. I was in the great city of Aleph when a grave report concerning you struck my ears and, through its force, inflicted the greatest pain upon my heart. For it was said that you were arranging your armies and intended to fight against the Christians. Therefore I came quickly, wishing to learn from you yourself whether the matter is truly so or not.”

Her son said to his mother:

“Mother, you have never heard anything truer.”

His mother replied:

“Who, my son, gave you such an evil counsel? You have not yet experienced the power of the Christians, and especially of the Frankish people. If you had read the writings of all the prophets and the ancient sages, you would certainly not be ignorant that he is the omnipotent one and the God of all gods.

“If you fight against the Christians, you will fight against him and his angels. But it is utter madness to fight against the omnipotent one, since that is simply to wish to destroy oneself. Concerning that unconquerable God, the prophet says:

> I kill, and I make alive;  
> I strike, and I heal;  
> and there is no one who can rescue from my hand.  
> If I sharpen my sword like lightning,  
> and my hand takes hold of judgment,  
> I shall repay vengeance to my enemies  
> and render recompense to those who hate me.  
> I shall intoxicate my arrows with blood,  
> and my sword shall devour flesh.  
> (Deuteronomy 32:39–42)

“It is fearful to enter into conflict with one who knows how to sharpen his sword in this way, to intoxicate it once sharpened, and, once intoxicated, to make it steep in flesh.

“My son, who drowned Pharaoh, king of Egypt, in the Red Sea with his entire army? Who drove out Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan, and gave them to his own people as an inheritance? (Psalm 135:11–12).

“That same God has shown how greatly he loves his people and with what protection he surrounds them when he says:

> Behold, I shall send my angel before you,  
> to guard you always.  
> Observe and listen to my voice,  
> and I shall be an enemy to your enemies,  
> and I shall afflict those who hate you;  
> my angel shall go before you.  
> (Exodus 23:20–22)

“God has become angry with our people, because we neither listen to his voice nor do his will. Therefore, from the distant regions of the West he has stirred up against us his own people and given it this entire land as a possession. There is no one who can turn it aside, nor anyone who can destroy it any longer.”

After this the son said to his mother:

“I believe, mother, that you are either insane or driven by infernal furies. Who told you that this people cannot be destroyed? I have more nobles and admirals with me than all the Christians gathered together. Tell me, mother: are Hugh, their standard-bearer, Bohemond of Apulia, and the swordsman Godfrey their gods? Are they not nourished by temporal food just as we are? Can their flesh not be cut by iron just like ours?”

His mother replied:

“They are not gods, those whom you name, but men and soldiers of the Most High God, who gives them courage, increases their strength, and makes them great-hearted, just as he himself says through the prophet:

> One of you shall pursue a thousand,  
> and two shall put ten thousand to flight.  
> (Leviticus 16:8)

“This has already been demonstrated in those who drove our people from all Romania. Therefore, my son, I adjure you by the names of all our gods to turn away from the presence of these men and not enter into battle against them. For, as I said above, it is foolish to rage against the Omnipotent and to act savagely against his people.”

Her son replied:

“Dearest mother, do not weep, and do not distress yourself with repeated sighs, for by no device or stratagem will you turn me back, even if I knew that I would perish in battle.”

Then his mother, becoming still sadder, said again to her son:

“I know that you will fight, and that you will not die now; but before the year has passed, you will depart from this life. At present you possess a reputation of distinction throughout the entire eastern region, and in the court of the Persian king you are second to no one. But when you have now been defeated, you will be without glory in proportion to the glory you presently possess. For the more someone surpasses others, the more shamefully he falls if he collapses dishonorably.

“Now, surrounded by all the splendor of the eastern kings and wealthy men, and encircled by a countless host of such attendants, if you are defeated, with whom will you thereafter contend, whether in equal or unequal numbers? You who once used to put many to flight with a few men will now also learn to flee with a mighty force of troops, and to be outstripped by a few despite your many men, as hares outstrip a dog.””

Then the son, unable to endure his anger, could no longer tolerate his mother’s words. Interrupting her, he said:

[Note: [Col. 0719D]

> Subjected wickedly to the dark Furies,  
> Corbanan scorns his mother’s words  
> and harbors an unsound mind. [Col. 0720D]
]

“What is the point, mother, of stirring up the air with empty words and wearying us with your unlearned speeches? No power of war can resist us, nor can any other army prevail against ours. But tell me, my mother, how do you know that we must be defeated in this battle, that I shall die not here but before the year has passed by a sudden death, and that the Christian people will possess our lands?”

His mother said:

“For a hundred years and less, our fathers have found in the sacred responses of the gods, in their lots and divinations, and in the entrails of animals, that the Christian people would come against us and conquer us. Our haruspices, magicians, soothsayers, and the responses of our gods agree on this, as do the words of our prophets, in which it is said:

> From the rising and the setting of the sun,  
> from the north and from the sea,  
> your boundaries shall extend,  
> and no one shall stand against you.

“We believe that all this will come to pass, but we do not know whether it is to happen now or in the near future. To some of our people it seems near, because the continual ruin of worldly affairs foretells it, and the observation of the stars has announced it beforehand.

“Concerning the battle you are about to undertake, I shall tell you the truth, and what knowledge I possess concerning your death from it. From the time you began gathering soldiers to wage this war, I have carefully investigated all those who might be able to predict the future, and they agree that no one at all will be able to overcome the Christians.

“With the astrologers I wisely contemplated the courses of the stars, namely the seven planets and the twelve signs. Whatever can be determined through natural divination I examined with the haruspices, using the entrails and weapons of animals; with diviners by lot I combined lots. Everything agrees as one and foretells titles of victory for the Frankish people, while, as I said above, threatening you with death.”

Then he said:

“Mother, cease from these things hereafter, for I shall fight the Franks as soon as I can.”

When she saw that she was accomplishing nothing, she did not linger long but returned from where she had come, carrying back with her whatever spoils she had been able to obtain.

CHAPTER THREE.

Now let us relate something of what meanwhile took place in the city. The Turks had unrestricted freedom to enter the fortress and leave it, and by hurling and shooting at our men day and night they drove them to battle; and whenever the strength of the combatants failed, new and fresh men took their place. Thus, as fresh troops continually arrived, their strength increased, while that of our men declined through daily exhaustion. For there was no rest at all, nor did they lay down their arms [Col. 0721A]; they were always prepared for military action. The streets of the city were obstructed by darts and arrows, and the roofs of the houses were weighed down by them.

Every day a new engagement took place before the fortress, and very often our men and theirs became mingled together in a single mêlée. Yet, by God’s protection, few of our men died, whereas the Turks were slaughtered in great numbers. As time slipped by in this way, hunger—more cruel than any enemy—attacked our men and weakened their strength day by day. Their faces withered, their arms failed, and their trembling hands could scarcely pluck from the ground the grasses, tree leaves, and roots of wild plants. All these things were cooked and eaten. A donkey’s leg was bought for sixty solidi, and the man who bought it was not considered a squanderer of his wealth; a small loaf of bread was valued at one [Col. 0721B] bezant. The flesh of donkeys, horses, camels, oxen, and buffaloes was consumed; moreover, their hides were boiled and eaten.

Mothers hung their sons, dying of hunger, at their breasts, but the children found nothing at their mothers’ breasts and, because of the lack of milk, trembled with closed eyes. One day Corbanan urged our men to battle, outside the city, on the side where the fortress stood. But the soldiers and horses, tormented by hunger, could not long withstand their swift assaults. Therefore, gathering together, our men realized that it would be safer to return to the city; but, pressed by the Turks, they found the gate far too narrow, so that some were crushed there to death. Thus fighting took place both inside and [Col. 0721C] outside, and no rest was granted to our men, who were dying of hunger.

Because of this and similar circumstances, some of our soldiers were excessively terrified and slipped away during the very night. They tied ropes to the fortifications, by which they so completely stripped the skin from their hands that they made their way on foot to the sea. When they reached it, they told the sailors to flee, since all the Christians were either dead or captive. The sailors, however, in grief, put out to sea and withdrew themselves from the power of the Turks.

Count Stephen of Chartres, who among the other princes appeared to be a great man, prudent in counsel and distinguished for the nobility of his character, was seized by a serious illness before Antioch was captured. He withdrew to a certain fortress belonging to him, called Alexandretta. There he heard from the fugitives [Col. 0721D] this report concerning our men. He climbed the mountains overlooking the city to see what was happening and whether the report would prove true. But he saw from afar countless troops of Turks and discovered that our men were shut up inside the city. Struck with fear, he fled [Note: [Col. 0721D]

*The consul of Chartres, a renowned city dear to those who know it,*

*Terrified, fled, and abandoned the war and his comrades.*],

and, returning to his fortress, stripped it completely. Then he began riding toward Constantinople.

Those who were besieged in the city were eagerly awaiting his arrival, thinking that he would bring the emperor with him and provide them, together with the emperor, with the necessities of life. But he turned in another direction and, when he reached Philomelium, found the emperor there. In a private conversation he said to him: “Lord emperor, our men truly hold Antioch; but the fortress that remains above it is still held by the Turks. Countless Turkish troops besiege them from outside, while those in the fortress attack them from within. But what remains to be said about this, except that they are either already dead or will all die very soon? You, however, reverend emperor, if you trust our counsel, should go no farther, but return to your own city. No human power can rescue them; and if you go there with your army, you may perish.”

When the emperor heard these words, he became very sad and openly disclosed to his princes and magistrates what had been told him in secret. Everyone was overcome with grief, and they wept for the funerals of our men. There was present a certain soldier named Wido, who had acquired a famous name for himself through his military service and had been very close to Bohemond. When he heard this, he was so distressed that he collapsed to the ground as though he were dead.

When, having recovered his breath, he returned from that derangement of mind, he began to weep uncontrollably. Furrowing his cheeks with his fingernails and tearing out his hair with his hands, he compelled everyone to mourn and said [Note: [Col. 0722D]

*Guido weeps greatly and entreats the Lord with tears.*]:

“O almighty God, where is your power? If you are almighty, why have you allowed these things to happen? Were they not your soldiers and pilgrims? What king, emperor, or mighty lord has ever permitted his household to be killed in this way, if he was in any manner able to help? Who will ever again be your soldier or pilgrim?

“O Bohemond, honor of other leaders, crown of the wise, glory of soldiers, consolation of the desolate, strength of the army, and distinguished ornament of the whole world, why has such misfortune befallen you, that you should lie subject to the mockery of the Turks? Alas, alas! Why has it been granted me to live after you? What light will henceforth be pleasing to me, what appearance beautiful, what glory delightful, what life joyful, if you are not alive?

“O God, if what this most foolish and fugitive count has reported is true, what more can be said of the road to your tomb? For what reason were they killed in such a way, as though your servants had no master? O Bohemond, where is that faith of yours, which you always held in your Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ?

“O emperor and noble soldiers, who mourn with me the deaths of so many great men, who can fully believe that so great an army has perished in this way? Certainly, if they had been surrounded in an open field by all the peoples of the East, they would not have been killed before taking vengeance. But they had a city in which they could defend themselves, and yet they were slaughtered?

“O emperor, know with absolute certainty that if the Turks have killed our men, few of them themselves remain. Therefore do not fear going there, because you will be able to recover Antioch.”

The emperor refused to accept his counsel. Too credulous of the foolish words of the fugitive count, he ordered a retreat and commanded that the regions of Bulgaria be devastated, so that if the Turks reached those parts, they would find absolutely nothing. [Col. 0723A] Wido himself returned together with him, as did those who had gone with the emperor, because they did not dare to proceed farther. Thus our men were deprived of every human consolation [Col. 0724A] and for nearly twenty days fought without interruption against the enemy and hunger, against the sword and deprivation.

EXPLICIT LIBER SEXTUS.

THE SIXTH BOOK ENDS.

INCIPIT LIBER SEPTIMUS.

THE SEVENTH BOOK BEGINS.

CHAPTER ONE.

[Col. 0723A]

If heavenly mercy had not foreseen the plight of those deprived of human assistance, not one of the Franks—now citizens of Antioch—would have survived. But when they had already lost hope of life and everything threatened them with death, it pleased God our Savior, King of kings, Jesus Christ, to appear to one of his priests [Note: [Col. 0723D] *God appears to him because he thus obeys without fault.*], while the priest was sleeping one night in the church of his holy and chaste Mother. With him were that Mother herself, the Virgin Mary, and blessed Peter the apostle, to whom the Lord himself had entrusted the shepherding of his sheep.

The Lord said to him: “Do you recognize me?”

The priest replied: “No. Who are you, Lord?”

Then a cross began to appear on the Savior’s head. The Lord said to him again: “Do you not recognize me now?”

Again the priest replied: “I recognize you only because I see a cross on your head, as I am accustomed to see in the images that are made in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

And the Lord said to him: “Behold, I am he.”

When the priest heard that he was the Lord, he immediately prostrated himself at his feet, humbly begging him to help his Christians, who were suffering from hunger and the oppression of their enemies.

The Lord said to him: “Does it not seem to you that I have helped them well enough up to this point? For I gave them the city of Nicaea and caused them to conquer all the wars that subsequently came upon them. During the siege of Antioch I pitied their misery; now, at the very end, I have granted them entry into the city. I allowed all the tribulations and obstacles that they suffered to occur because they committed many shameful acts with Christian and pagan women, acts that are exceedingly displeasing in my sight.”

At this, the most compassionate Virgin, mother of mercy, and blessed Peter fell at his feet, asking him to have mercy on his people. Blessed Peter added to his prayer and said:

“Lord, I give you thanks because you have placed my church in the power of your servants. Because of the wickedness of those who inhabited it, you allowed it to be defiled for so many years by the filth of pagans. Therefore your holy angels in heaven rejoice, as do my fellow apostles.” [Col. 0723D]

Then the Lord said to his priest: “Go and tell my people to return to me, and I will return to them. Within five days I will send them sufficient aid. Meanwhile, each day let them sing this responsory: ‘Our enemies have gathered together and exult in their strength,’ with the verse in full.”

When this vision had ended, the venerable priest awoke from sleep and rose. With his hands extended, he prayed as the Holy Spirit gave him utterance. Then, on that same day at the third hour, he went directly to the leaders of the army. He found them above, before the fortress, fighting against their enemies and engaging one another in battle. After summoning them, he said with a joyful and cheerful face:

“O warriors of the eternal King, I announce to you, on behalf of our Savior, joy and exultation, together with the blessing that he sends you; and if you obey him, you will obtain his favor as well.”

When everyone was listening attentively and gathering from every side, he explained the entire vision in order. Having explained it, he added:

“If you distrust this vision [Col. 0724B] and suspect it to be false, I will submit myself to whatever test you wish, since it is true; and if I am found to be a liar, inflict every injury upon my body.”

Then the bishop of Le Puy ordered that a cross and the holy Gospel be brought, so that the priest might swear before everyone that this was true. And this was done.

And so that divine goodness might heap good things upon the good and make its sorrowing servants increasingly joyful, there was present a certain pilgrim named Peter, who related this vision before them all:

“Hear me, people of the Lord and servants of the Most High God, and incline your ears to my words. While we were besieging this city, the holy apostle Andrew appeared to me one night in a vision and said: ‘Good man, listen to me and understand me.’

“And I said to him: ‘Who are you, lord?’

“And he replied: ‘I am Andrew the apostle.’

“Then he added: ‘Son, when you have entered this city and have it in your power, go quickly to the church of blessed Peter. In the place that I will show you, you will find the lance with which the side of our Savior was pierced.’

“That was all the apostle said to me at that time. I did not dare disclose it to anyone, thinking that I had seen a vain vision. But this very night he appeared to me again and said: ‘Come, and I will show you the place where the lance is hidden, as I promised you. Hurry, then, to draw it out, for victory will follow those who carry it.’ And the holy apostle showed me the place. Come, see it, and draw it out with me.”

When everyone wanted to run to the church of blessed Peter, he added further and said:

“Saint Andrew the apostle commands you: Do not be afraid, but confess and repent of your evil deeds, for within five days you will again triumph over your enemies.”

Then everyone unanimously glorified God, who deigned to console their sorrows. At once they ran to the church of blessed Peter, eager to see the place where the lance was to be found. Thirteen men dug there from morning until evening, and thus, by the Lord’s providence, they found it. There was great joy among all the [Col. 0725A] people, and they resounded with loud voices: “We praise you, O God. Glory in the highest to God.”

Then they all swore together that none of them, because of any tribulation or death, would flee or withdraw from the journey they had begun toward the holy sepulcher. The entire common people rejoiced when the leaders swore this oath, and each encouraged the other to show manly strength. Everyone applauded the divine assistance that each confidently awaited.

On the following night, a fire coming from heaven appeared in the west and fell into the Turkish army. This sign greatly astonished everyone’s hearts, especially those of the Turks, upon whose tents it fell. They began to prophesy among themselves what later came to pass: “The fire descending from heaven is the wrath of God.” Since it had come from the west, it signified the armies of the Franks, through whom he was exercising the punishment of his wrath.

Now the older men began to soften somewhat from their ferocity and to grow numb with respect to the hostility they had previously displayed. But because the number of fools was infinite, and they were urging our men to battle without rest by day or night, the elders decided to build a wall between themselves and them, so that they might at least breathe for a little while.

For on one day they attacked our men so fiercely that they shut three of them inside a tower standing before the fortress. Two of these men, wounded, were forced to leave the tower and were beheaded; but one remained, resisting bravely until evening. He killed two of the enemy and eventually ended his life by the sword. While they were still alive, Bohemond wished to come to their aid, but he could scarcely extract anyone, because they were oppressed not so much by the enemy as by severe hunger. Therefore, angered, he ordered fire to be set to the houses on the side where the palace of Cassian was located, so that those who were unwilling to leave voluntarily might at least be compelled to leave against their will.

Then such a violent wind arose together with the fire, and the flames grew so powerful that they burned as many as two thousand houses and churches. When Bohemond saw the fire rising so fiercely, he was overcome with repentance and grieved bitterly, fearing for the church of blessed Peter, for the holy Mother of God Mary, and for many other places. The fire lasted from the third hour of the day until midnight [Col. 0725D], and then, as the wind blew from the right, the flame turned back upon itself.

CHAPTER TWO.

When the lance had been found, as we said above, by God’s will, the elders and military leaders took counsel to send an embassy to Corbanan and convey to him their message and counsel through an interpreter of his language. Many inquiries were made, but no one dared to carry these messages. At last two men were found: Helvinus and Peter the Hermit. With an interpreter, they set out toward the Turkish camp and then reached Corbanan’s tents.

Turks gathered from every side, eager to hear what the Christian envoys had to say. Corbanan was seated on a throne, dressed in royal attire and pompous garments. When they came before him, they did not bow at all, but stood upright with their heads held high. When the Turks saw this, they took it badly; had the men not been envoys, they would have punished such arrogant self-restraint.

Then the envoys, without hesitation, although everyone around them was stirred with anger and growling, said to the proud prince [Note: [Col. 0725D]

*The Frankish peoples, naturally raging with Mars,*

*Command the Parthians to be prepared for war.*]:

“Corbanan, the nobles of the Franks command you: How has such drunken audacity come upon you, that you have come against them with armed force, when you, your king, and your people are guilty in their sight because you invaded the lands of the Christians with immoderate greed and killed all those whom you had injured? Your infernal gods could not have dishonored you more shamefully than by sending you to fight against them.

“If justice were on your side, and you wished to reason with us according to the standard of equity, we would reason with you while preserving the honor due to law, and by incontrovertible argument we would demonstrate what belongs to the Christians. But if law and reason have equal weight with you and with your pleasure-seeking will, let a decisive battle between your men and ours decide the matter, and let the whole country be granted to the victors without the loss of anyone else’s blood. If neither this nor that pleases you, either take flight at once or prepare your necks for the swords of our men.”

When he had spoken these words, the mediator of the speech fell silent. Corbanan, however, inflamed with great anger, could scarcely speak. At last he burst into these words [Note: [Col. 0726D]

*Corbanan speaks and reviles our men.*]:

“Truly, the Frankish people are a proud people; but their pride will be curbed by our sword. They demand the proposed battle so that whoever wins the victory may also possess the rule, since without the loss of anyone else’s blood they wish either to enrich themselves with this country or to free themselves from our hands. Yet they did not find sound counsel when they took up arms for an effeminate people.

“Nevertheless, go now and report to them that if they wish to deny their God and renounce their Christianity, we will receive them all into favor, give them this land and a much better one, and make them all knights. But if they refuse to do this, they will all soon die or be taken captive and bound in our land.”

After this Helvinus, who knew their language, added [Note: [Col. 0726D]

*This servant of God also reviles him*]:

“O prince not of any army but of every wickedness, if you knew how utterly insane it is among Christians to say, ‘Deny the Lord,’ such a word would never leave your polluted mouth. We know with certainty, by the revelation of the very God whom you urge us to deny, that our salvation and your destruction, our joy and your ruin, are near.

“But who sent you the fire recently, which so terrified you and so disturbed you from the place where you had pitched your tents? This sign will become a portent for you, but salvation for us, because from it we have received a sure message from our God.”

Corbanan could not long endure Helvinus’s insults and ordered him removed from his presence. Those standing there told him to withdraw quickly, otherwise his embassy would never succeed and he would immediately perish. He departed in this manner with his companion and returned to the city.

Nor should we pass over what Corbanan said to his men after they had left:

“You have now heard what those ragged men, contemptible in appearance and insignificant little nobodies, said, and how boldly they spoke. They were not frightened by our anger or our flashing weapons. There is one explanation: they are desperate, wish to die, and prefer death to captivity. Therefore, O bravest soldiers, when they come to battle, surround them on every side, so that none of them has a place to turn aside or room to live for long. For if they are allowed to live for any length of time before they are all killed, they will inflict great slaughter upon our men.”

From this it is clear that Corbanan was foolish, because by speaking in this way he was instilling terror into the minds of his own men. Nor is it surprising when a fool speaks madness, since “the spirit of wisdom does not enter a malevolent soul” (Wis. 1:4).

CHAPTER THREE.

Peter the Hermit and Helvinus returned to the leaders of the army and reported what Corbanan had answered. Then, with the approval and consent of everyone, the bishop of Le Puy proclaimed a three-day fast for all. Each person confessed with a pure heart, and whoever had anything to eat distributed it to one who had nothing.

They spent those three days with complete humility and purity of heart, making processions around the churches and imploring the Lord’s mercy. At dawn on the third day, Masses were celebrated in the churches, and everyone received Holy Communion of the Lord’s body.

Then, by common counsel, six divisions were organized inside the city, and the order in which they would go out, first and later, was arranged. The first division was Hugh the Great’s, together with the count of Flanders; the second belonged to Duke Godfrey; in the third was Count Robert the Norman with his men; the fourth belonged to the bishop of Le Puy, who carried with him the lance of our Savior, and with him was a large part of the army of the Count of Saint-Gilles, which remained behind to guard the city; the fifth was Tancred’s; and the sixth was Bohemond’s, with whom were the foot soldiers most fit for battle and the soldiers who, compelled by necessity, had sold their horses.

The bishops, priests, clerics, and monks, dressed in sacred vestments, went out of the city gate with the soldiers, carrying crosses in their hands, with which they signed the people of God. With loud voices and their hands extended toward heaven, they cried:

“Save your people, O Lord, and bless your inheritance; shepherd them and lift them up now and forever. Be for them, O Lord, a tower of strength against the face of their enemies.”

They sang this and other psalms, especially those suited to their tribulation. Likewise, those who were in the towers and upon the wall did the same and sang the same songs.

Thus the soldiers of Christ went out against the servants of Antichrist through the gate that lies before Machumaria. Corbanan, standing on a certain hill, watched them as they came out and said:

“Stand quietly, my soldiers, and allow everyone to come out, so that we may be better able to capture them.”

Beside him stood a certain Aquitanian, whom we call a Provençal, who had renounced our faith. Compelled by the craving of his appetite, he had left the city and gone over to the camp of the enemy. He had said many shameful things about our men: that they were dying of hunger and were all seeking means of escape; that they had eaten their horses and were wasting away from lack of food; and that nothing remained for them except either to flee or to submit to Corbanan’s authority.

As the divisions went out from the city in their appointed order, Corbanan asked whose each one was, and the Aquitanian reported this to him in sequence. The sun, casting its rays upon the gilded breastplates [Col. 0728B] and lances, struck back against the eyes of those who looked upon them and instilled terror in the enemy, as Holy Scripture testifies: “Terrible as an army set in battle array” (Song 6:3).

When Corbanan saw them all together, he groaned inwardly and said to those standing nearby:

“That people is great and honorably armed. It does not seem to me that they intend to flee, but to attack; nor that they intend to submit, but to pursue.”

Then he turned to his apostate and said:

“Scoundrel and most wicked of all men, what foolish things did you tell us about these men—that they had eaten their horses and, tormented by hunger, were preparing to flee? By Machomus, this lie will be turned back upon your head, and the loss of your head will be your punishment.””

Then a swordsman was summoned. He obeyed the tyrant’s command, drew his sword, and cut off the apostate’s head. Thus he suffered a death worthy of his loquacity and apostasy.

At that moment Corbanan instructed his admiral, who guarded his treasure, that if he saw a fire kindled at the head of his army, he should immediately take flight, carry away with him everything that belonged to him, and compel the others to flee as well. For Corbanan knew that the battle belonged to the Frankish people and that victory had turned against him.

When our soldiers first came to a certain plain, they stopped at the signal of the bishop of Le Puy and listened in profound silence to his speech. He was wearing a coat of mail, and in his right hand he held high the lance of the Savior. He opened his mouth and spoke these words:

“All of us who have been baptized in Christ are sons of God and brothers to one another. Therefore, let those whom one spiritual bond has united be joined also by a single love. Let us fight as brothers, with one mind, for our souls and bodies, as men placed in the most desperate circumstances.

“Remember how many tribulations you have suffered because of your sins, just as the Lord our God has now deigned to make known to you in visions. But now you have been purified and reconciled to God in every respect. What, then, should you fear? No misfortune at all can befall you.

“Whoever dies here will be happier than one who lives, because in place of temporal life he will obtain eternal joys. Whoever survives will triumph over his enemies in victory, will be enriched by their wealth, and will suffer no want.

“You know what you have endured and what you now see before you. Your Lord has brought the riches of the East before your faces—or rather, into your hands. Take courage and be men of brave hearts, for the Lord will now send the legions of his saints, who will avenge you upon your enemies. Today you will see them with your own eyes.
