And when they come, do not fear the terrible tumult they make. Their appearance should not be unfamiliar to you, for they have come to your aid once before.

“Yet human sight trembles at the arrival of the citizens of heaven. Consider how your enemies, with their necks stretched out like frightened stags and does, gaze at your approach, more ready for flight than for battle. And you know their methods of fighting well, for once the arrow has been drawn, they trust more in flight than in combat.

“Go, then, against them in battle in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and may the Lord our almighty God be with you [Note: [Col. 0729D] *The speech ends, and the divisions are also arranged.*].”

When everyone had answered “Amen,” the legions extended in a long line. Hugh the Great, who was rightly called Great because he demonstrated this distinction by his actions and character, went first with the standard held upright. The others followed him, as they have been named above. Their line extended over a great distance, from the river to the mountains—two miles lay between them.

Then Corbanan began to retreat and approached the mountains. Our men followed him little by little, since they all advanced at a measured pace. The Turks then divided into two groups: one proceeded from the direction of the sea, while the larger remained in the field [Col. 0729C]. They therefore planned to enclose our men between them and shoot at them from behind.

A seventh division was accordingly organized to fight against the separated group. It was formed from the soldiers of Duke Godfrey and of the Norman count, and was commanded by a certain leader named Rainald. They sent him against the enemy, and the two sides fought; many fell on both sides.

When the other six divisions came within bowshot, the Turks refused to advance closer. They drew their bows and pulled them taut, but in vain, because the wind blowing across their path deflected their shots and rendered them useless. When the Turks saw this, they turned their bridles and fled backward. Thus the first division sought battle in the battle, but did not find it; it sought someone to strike or someone by whom it might be struck, but found no one.

Meanwhile a messenger was sent from Bohemond to Hugh the Great to bring him assistance, because Bohemond was being hard pressed by the oppression of the Turks. Hugh immediately turned and said to his men:

“O warrior men, battle is fleeing from us. Let us seek battle and go to the distinguished leader Bohemond. There is the battle you seek; there the iron enemy presses, whom you desire.”

Then every warrior flew there more swiftly than words can say, and the distinguished counts joined together [Note: [Col. 0729D]

*The warrior Hugh runs to Bohemond’s aid.*]

[Col. 0730D] The young Godefrid follows him, renowned in arms. [Col. 0730A] When Godefrid, the commander of commanders, saw that his great friend was rushing about so swiftly with all his men, he followed him, since he too was without a battle. For there the strength and greater force of the Persian army was concentrated; and it was fitting that Godefrid and Hugh should run there. Indeed, one was, as it were, the other’s very counterpart, for they shared a single friendship.

When Hugh the Great arrived first at the battle, he caught sight of one of the adversaries who was bolder than the rest and was urging the others to fight by shouting to them. Hugh directed his foaming horse against him, pierced his throat with his lance, and thus stopped his mouth. What could the wretch do? He immediately fell to the ground and commended his soul to the infernal gods.

After this, a great misfortune befell our men: Odo of Belgentier, who carried the banner, was wounded by a poisoned arrow; and as the pain of the wound grew worse, he fell to the ground with the banner. But William of Blesme, drawing his unsheathed sword, opened a path through the midst of the enemy and lifted the standard from the earth.

What the commander of commanders Godefrid, what Bohemond, what the renowned young men did there, neither tongue can tell, nor hand write, nor page contain. None of our men was idle there, none timid, because there was no room for timidity, and the overwhelming enemy pressed upon each one. For the more they were killed, the more they seemed to increase. Just as flies commonly swarm upon decay, so they gathered from every side.

While the fighting continued in this way, and the length of so protracted a struggle might have become wearisome, and the number of our enemies did not seem to diminish, an army of white-clad soldiers was seen descending from the mountains [Col. 0730C]. Their standard-bearers and leaders were said to be George, Maurice, and Demetrius [Note: [Col. 0730D] Names of the saints who bore the heavenly standards.]

As soon as the bishop of Le Puy saw them, he cried out in a loud voice: “O soldiers, behold, the aid that God promised you has come!” And certainly our men would have been greatly terrified had they not possessed the hope they had in the Lord. Then a very great trembling seized the enemy; turning their faces, they covered their backs with their shields and seized flight wherever the ground allowed each man to do so.

That division which had been fighting on the seaward side, when it saw its comrades fleeing, scattered fire over the field’s grass, which quickly burned because the heat of summer had dried it. They did this so that, at the sight of the signal, those who were in the tents would immediately flee and carry away with them the more valuable spoils.

[Col. 0730D] Those who were in the mountain strongholds, recognizing the signal, fled at once with all the spoils they were able to carry. But what good did this do them, when they were not permitted to carry them for long? For when the Armenians and Syrians saw that they had been defeated and that our men were pursuing them, they came to meet them and killed them.

Hugh the Great, Duke Godefrid, and the count of Flanders, together with their forces, rode beside the water, where the enemy’s army was stronger and denser. They began to press upon them with such force [Col. 0731A] that the fugitives could not return to their tents, toward which they had been making their way.

And so that they might pursue them more swiftly, they mounted the horses of those who were dying, while they removed the bridles from their own horses, which were leaner and weakened by hunger, and abandoned them in the field.

O wondrous virtue of almighty God, and boundless power! Your soldier, worn down by a long fast, pursued men swollen with fat and flesh, so that they did not even dare look back at the possessions they had left behind. Your good Spirit was in their minds: it supplied strength to their bodies and granted courage to their hearts. No desire for spoils delayed him, no greed for any object, because victory stirred his mind more keenly.

As it is customary to tear apart the bodies of beasts in a slaughterhouse, so our men were permitted to rend the bodies of the Turks. Blood flew from the wounded bodies; dust flew up, stirred by the feet of the horses racing about. The sky grew clouded and darkened as though twilight had fallen.

It happened that the fugitives came to a certain hill and hoped there to regroup against our men. Then Gerard the Elder of Melun, who had lain sick for a long time during the siege, was carried swiftly on horseback and rashly fell among them. He was pierced by their spears and thus killed by a fitting death.

When those who followed him more closely saw this—namely Everard of Puteolo, Pagan of Beauvais, Drogo, Thomas, and Clarenbald, together with the other young men of Hugh the Great [Col. 0731C]—they rushed upon the enemy without hesitation. They indeed found a formidable battle, but, with God’s help, as their own company increased, they scattered the enemy courageously.

Much blood was shed there, and many heads were severed—men who, if they had continued to flee as they had begun, might have escaped. Our men pursued them as far as the Iron Bridge and Tancred’s castle, but they could pursue them no farther, because the dark night put an end to the affair.

That day one hundred thousand horsemen died; but, because of the tediousness of the task, no one counted the whole multitude of infantry. The exhausted soldier, being far from the city, returned to the tents that had belonged to his enemies and found much that was sufficient for his food.

Before the fear of God had entered their hearts, they had prepared meat for a feast in frying pans [Col. 0731D], cauldrons, kettles, and pots. But the wretches were not permitted to cook or take away what they had prepared.

There one could see the venerable priest, the bishop of Le Puy, clad in a coat of mail and helmet, with the holy lance in his hands; from excessive joy, his face was wet with abundant tears. He urged them to give thanks to God, through whom they had proved victorious, and said to them:

“Since you began to be soldiers, no others have been your equals, because no others, in so short a time, have fought as many and such great battles as you have completed since crossing the Constantinopolitan Sea. Surely he is far removed from Christian faith who sees what you have seen today and does not remain constant in the love of God.”

The venerable bishop spoke these and similar words, instructing the people entrusted to him by such speeches and moderating their jokes and laughter. The sight of his face and presence so restrained everyone that no one dared utter idle words in his presence.

## CHAPTER IV

When that night had passed, fifteen thousand camels were found the next day. Who could count the horses, mules, and asses, the sheep and cattle, and livestock of every kind? Many gold and silver vessels were found, very many cloaks, and great spoils of high value and varied kinds.

With all these things they came triumphantly to the city, where the clerics, priests, and monks who had remained received them in solemn procession.

Admiraldus, who was in the castle, saw his prince and those who had been with him turning away from the battlefield in flight. Then he saw countless thousands of white-clad horsemen racing across the plains with white banners, and he was greatly terrified. He asked that one of our banners be given to him for his protection.

The count of Saint-Gilles, who had remained there to guard the city, handed him his own banner. Admiraldus gladly accepted it and fastened it to the castle wall. But when he learned from certain Lombards who were standing there that it was not Bohemond’s banner—Bohemond being the one to whom the whole city had been granted—he returned the standard to the count and asked for Bohemond’s banner. Bohemond sent it to him.

When he received it, he sent word to Bohemond to come to him. Bohemond promptly went on foot to the envoy and listened to what he wished to say. The pagan sought an agreement in good faith [Col. 0732C]: those who were with him and wished to depart were not to suffer any injury or harm, but were to be escorted as far as the land of the Saracens; whoever wished to become a Christian with him was to have permission to do so.

Filled with immense joy, Bohemond said: “Friend, we gladly grant you what you ask; but wait a little, because I shall report this to our princes and quickly return to you.”

He immediately hurried away, gathered the princes together, and recounted the pagan’s words. They all approved, giving thanks to almighty God. Bohemond returned to the now-domesticated pagan and confirmed the promise of the agreement he had requested.

The man then surrendered himself to the bishop of Le Puy and to the holy Christian faith [Col. 0732D], together with three hundred of his own soldiers, very handsome and young. At that time there was greater joy among the Christians over their conversion to Christianity than over the surrender of the castle.

Bohemond took possession of the castle and escorted those who did not wish to become Christians into the land of the Saracens. After a three-day fast had been completed, the pagans were baptized with great rejoicing, and the praise of God and Christian glory increased there.

They themselves were later accustomed to report that, when they watched the battle from the castle’s citadel, they had suddenly seen countless thousands of white-clad soldiers, whose appearance greatly terrified them. Nor was this surprising, for the entire castle shook to its foundations. When they saw these men join the ranks of the Christians and their own people turn to destruction and flight, they immediately understood that they were heavenly powers and that the God of the Christians could not be overcome [Col. 0733A]. Their hearts were thereby pierced with remorse, and they promised to become Christians.

This battle was fought on the fourth day before the Kalends of July—that is, on the vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul. Thus, through the merciful regard of God, the storm of Antiochene tribulation, which had swelled for almost ten months, was calmed; and the royal city, which for a long succession of years had been subjected to the yoke of diabolical captivity, recovered the grace of its former freedom.

The enemies who had enslaved it themselves became captives, and were scattered in the hiding places of forests, the caves of rocks, and the ravines of the mountains. The Armenians and Syrians who inhabited that land searched for them for many days. They found some half-dead, others wounded, some missing part of the head [Col. 0733B], and others pressing their hands against their bellies so that their vital organs would not completely spill out; after stripping them of their spoils, they killed them.

Thus the enemies of God were laid waste, while the Christians, servants of the Most High God, gathered with joy and gladness in the glorious city.

One day they assembled and decided to send envoys to the emperor of Constantinople, announcing that he should come to reclaim his city. And, alas, they all judged that since they were sending to a king, a royal messenger ought to go. Hugh the Great was chosen, truly royal both by birth and by character. They would never have chosen him if they had known that he would not return.

After he had completed his embassy to the emperor, death cut him off and he died; he could not in the end return to the place where he had intended to go back.

But the fox-like emperor of Constantinople did not dare come to receive so great a city, because he recognized that he had violated his faith, the obligations of his oath, and the pledges he had given to the Franks, and had in no way kept them. Thus all the agreements that had been made between them were annulled.

Meanwhile, those residing in the city began to discuss the journey to the Lord’s Sepulchre: what they should do, whether they should begin at once, or when they should bring the delay to an end. A common decision was reached that the resumption of the journey should be postponed until the Kalends of October.

The heat of summer had grown excessively intense, and the land of the Saracens into which they were about to enter was waterless and extremely dry. Therefore they waited for the season that then becomes moist, when the earth bursts forth with hidden streams [Col. 0733D].

It was likewise necessary to decide what such a large population should do meanwhile, and where and how it should live. After taking counsel on this matter, they sought a herald to announce what had been decided. The herald was sought and found; he mounted a platform and proclaimed that anyone who was entirely destitute should remain in the city and make an agreement with those who were wealthier, serving them.

The princes, however, dispersed among their castles and cities.

## CHAPTER V

There was a certain soldier from the army of the count of Saint-Gilles, named Raimundus and surnamed Piletus, a man courageous in spirit and impressive in body. He hated the Turks with a perfect hatred and could no longer endure their remaining idle for so long.

He gathered a very large multitude of soldiers and footmen around himself and led them into the land of the Saracens. He crossed the boundaries of two cities, and they came to a certain castle called Talamania, ruled by a Syrian people.

The Syrians received our men and most willingly surrendered themselves to their authority. After spending eight days there, they proceeded to another castle in which a great multitude of Saracens was hiding.

When they reached it, they attacked with military force. Fighting all day with less strenuous effort, they captured it as evening fell. Once it had been taken, they killed everyone except those who accepted Christianity.

After this devastation had been accomplished, they returned to the castle we have called Talamania. They remained there for two full days [Col. 0734B]; on the third day they all departed and proceeded to the city called Marra.

A considerable multitude of Turks and Saracens had gathered there from Aleppo and from the other cities and castles surrounding it, awaiting their arrival. When our men began to approach, those barbarians came out against them. But they did not wish to maintain the encounter with our men for long, and, turning to flight, withdrew inside the city.

Our men could not remain there long, because the summer heat pressed upon them severely, and nothing could be found to drink. As the shadow of day was already declining, they returned to their castle at Talamania.

Many Christians who were natives of that land had gone with our men, but they refused to return with them. The Turks, hiding in ambush, captured and killed them [Col. 0734C]. They perished through their own folly, for if they had returned with our men, none of them would then have died. But, as the common saying goes: “A foolish people fears nothing until unhappy fortune overwhelms it.”

Raimundus did not return to that city afterward, because he had no army with which to besiege it. Instead, he remained in his castle until the appointed time of the Kalends of October, continually taking possession of the land of the Saracens in the meantime.

Those who had remained in Antioch lived in great peace and joy until they lost their lord, the bishop of Le Puy. While supreme peace prevailed in the army of God, he began to fall ill in the month of July. But he was not sick for long, because the Lord did not allow him to be tormented by a prolonged illness.

On the Kalends of August, his holy soul, released from the bonds of the flesh, was carried into the paradise of God, on the glorious feast of Saint Peter called *Ad Vincula* (“At the Chains”). And so that it might be clear that this had occurred by the judgment of God, on the day when the chains of the prince of the apostles were brought from Jerusalem to Rome, the bishop’s soul was released from its bodily bonds.

Never, on account of any tribulation, was there such grief or such sorrow in that army of God as at his death. Everyone bewailed him as was right, because he was the counsel of the wealthy, the comforter of the sorrowful, the support of the weak, the treasure of the needy, and the reconciler of those at odds.

He was accustomed to say to the soldiers: “If you wish to be victors and friends of God, preserve purity of body and show mercy to the poor. No thing will free you from death so completely as almsgiving, for it protects better than a shield and is sharper against the enemy than a lance. Whoever is not able to pray for himself should give alms, and it will pray for him.”

Because of these deeds and such speeches he was dear to God and to all the people. If someone wished to enumerate all the graces of his virtues, he would seem already to be departing from history.

After he had been fittingly buried in the church of Saint Peter, the count of Saint-Gilles crossed into the land of the Saracens and approached the city called Albarria. He surrounded and attacked it with strong soldiers on every side, and for a long time fought with missiles and arrows against those on the walls.

But when he saw that he was making little progress in this way, armored soldiers raised ladders against the wall, climbed up, and forced the enemy to flee.

When the soldier climbs the wall, he becomes taller than they;

And the enemy is inferior to him in strength.

From the wall they descend upon the hidden roofs of the houses;

[Col. 0736A] From the houses they leap out across the open streets.

Here and there old men flee, and boys and young men,

But absolutely no flight benefited anyone.

For the count ordered that everyone be captured and that those unwilling to believe in Christ be beheaded. There many were seen punished by decapitation, and the lives of very many boys and girls were cut short before their time.

This was the judgment of the Lord, because that city had belonged to the Christians and had been taken from them in a similar mockery of death. No one from so great a multitude was spared except one who freely trusted in Christ and was baptized.

Thus that city was cleansed and restored to the worship of our faith. Then the count and his leading men took counsel that a bishop should be appointed there, by whose counsel and assistance the city might be governed and the faith [Col. 0736B] of Jesus Christ strengthened in the hearts of the newly baptized.

Accordingly, a wise and dignified man was chosen, distinguished by learning in letters and endowed with both branches of knowledge, and he was sent to Antioch to be ordained.

[Col. 0735] HERE ENDS THE SEVENTH BOOK.

HERE BEGINS THE EIGHTH BOOK.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0735B]

As summer, its solar heat restrained, was already passing away, and night was surpassing day in the number of its hours, the soldiers of Christ, who had spent the summer in every direction, returned to Antioch. On the Kalends of November, the feast day of the solemnity of All Saints, they gathered there.

Blessed be the glory of the eternal King, for the crowd of those returning was then larger than it had been when they had separated from one another. From every part of the world many distinguished soldiers and footmen had followed in the footsteps of the earlier ones, and the Christian army increased daily.

When they were thus assembled and were planning where to direct their journey to the Holy Sepulchre, Bohemond demanded the agreement concerning the city that they had promised him. The count of Saint-Gilles said that this could not be done because of the oaths that, through Bohemond, they had sworn to the emperor of Constantinople.

For many days thereafter an assembly was held in the church of Saint Peter, and there was a great dispute in words between the two sides [Col. 0735D]. When no decision suitable to peace could be reached in the public assembly, the bishops and abbots, together with the leaders and counts of sounder counsel, entered the place where the chair of Saint Peter is located. There among themselves they determined how they might keep their promises to Bohemond while also observing the oaths made to the emperor.

When they left the place of counsel, however, they did not wish to disclose their decision to everyone. The decision was therefore revealed privately to the count of Saint-Gilles, and he approved the arrangement, provided that Bohemond would continue with them on the journey they had begun.

Bohemond was consulted; he too approved it. Each of them then promised, in the hands of the bishops and by a pledge of faith, that neither would ever abandon the journey to the Holy Sepulchre, nor would either be disturbed by any dispute that might arise between them [Col. 0736B].

Then Bohemond fortified the castle that overlooked the city, while the count fortified Cassian’s palace and the tower above the city gate on the side of the harbor of Saint Simeon.

Since Antioch detained us through the long course of this narrative and wearied our pilgrim soldiers with its eight-month siege, and since it could not be overcome by any human force, skill, or ingenuity, let us say something about its position and size and reveal something of it to those who have never seen it.

## CHAPTER II

According to its history, this city was founded by sixty-five kings, all of whom rendered the service of subjection to its rule. It is surrounded by two walls. The first is made of large stones cut square and polished with refined craftsmanship; within it four hundred and sixty towers are arranged and distinguished in their proper places.

To those who look upon it, this wall delights them with the beauty of its construction, and it is extremely spacious in breadth. Within the enclosure of the walls are four great mountains rising high above the ground. On the highest of them a castle has been built, so strongly fortified by its natural position that it fears neither a military assault nor the ingenuity of any siege engine.

Within its territory it contains three hundred and sixty churches, and the patriarch has one hundred and fifty-three bishops under his authority. On the east it is fortified by four great mountains, while on the west it is washed by a river called the Farfar.

As we said above, King Antiochus founded this city together with his sixty-five kings, and gave it a name derived from his own. Our pilgrim soldiers besieged this royal and most famous city for eight months and one day; they were enclosed within it by the people of the Parthians for three weeks; after overcoming them with divine assistance, they then rested in it for four months and eight days.

When this period had ended, Count Raimundus of Saint-Gilles was the first to leave Antioch with his people. He reached the city called Rugia. On the following day he came to another city called Albarria. With his small force he had subjected these two cities to his rule and consigned them to the service of Christ.

On the fourth day, as November was ending, he came to the city called Marra. Raimundus Piletus, his soldier, had first attacked it but withdrew after being vigorously repelled.

That city was populous and extremely crowded with people from every surrounding region. When this hostile population saw our men from a distance, they despised them because they seemed few in comparison with themselves, and attempted to resist them outside the city.

But they immediately learned that a small and courageous force is superior to a drunken multitude, especially a people whose hope and trust are in the name of the Lord. When our men saw them prepared to resist, with shields held before their chests and the points of their lances advanced, they burst upon them with military force and, penetrating their midst, broke them apart.

There the Lord broke the power of bows, shield, sword, and battle, for once fighting is carried on with swords, bow and arrow are useless. Whoever was nearer the city gate considered himself happier; whoever was farther away longed with all his heart either to draw nearer to the gate or for the gate to come to him.

This encounter greatly benefited them because it took place near the city gate. Nevertheless, not all those who had gone out unharmed returned from the retreat in safety. Those whom our men encountered in the first assault suffered the worst retreat.

They shot many of our horses with arrows, but when their riders had fallen to the ground, they left behind far more of their own men. After the enemy had withdrawn into the city, our men pitched their tents within one arrow-shot of it.

After keeping watch throughout the night, when the sun’s radiance mingled with the light of day on the following morning, our men, armed for battle, surrounded the city on every side and attacked it in a fierce assault.

Missiles, stakes, and stones fly, as do fires and torches,

[Col. 0737D] By which the roofs of the houses within might be burned.

But because the enemy’s immense multitude resisted, our men accomplished nothing that day; exhausted, they returned to their tents.

That same day Bohemond arrived there with his people and many others, following the count. They pitched their camps and surrounded the city on every side. When those inside saw this, they were struck with overwhelming terror and blocked all the city gates with heaps of stones.

The counts therefore took counsel together, since the battle was not being fought on equal terms. They ordered rams to be made—iron-shod beams which, hung from ropes and drawn by the soldiers’ hands, would be driven against the wall, so that the walls might be destroyed by their repeated blows.

A wooden tower was also constructed, sufficiently higher than the stone towers and taller than all the siege engines within [Col. 0738A]. It had three platforms, well protected by shields and pulleys. On the two upper platforms were armored men with missiles, stakes, arrows, stones, javelins, and torches. Below were men similarly armed who pushed the wheels on which the tower itself had been built.

Others brought a wooden covered structure up against the wall and leveled the enormous ditch, so that they could join the tower to the wall and, protected by its shelter, pierce the wall. This was done.

But the wretched citizens prepared an instrument with which they hurled great stones against the tower, and they also cast Greek fire to burn it. Yet, with God’s grace protecting it, all their efforts and all their engines [Col. 0738B] were frustrated and brought to nothing. For when the wooden tower came close to the wall, it looked down upon and struck down all who were on that section of the wall beneath it.

William of Montpellier [also called Pessulano] was on the upper platform with many others. With him was a certain hunter named Ewardus, who was gifted with the spirit of trumpeting. By the sound of his tumultuous voice he terrified the adversaries and stirred his own men to battle.

While William and his men were destroying everything around them—for by hurling millstones they were smashing the roofs of the houses—the men beneath him were digging through the wall, and others were raising a ladder to the wall’s battlements.

When the ladder had been raised and no one dared climb first, a certain honorable soldier, Gulferius of La Tour [Col. 0738C], could not bear it; he climbed the wall without hesitation, and many brave men followed him.

When the pagans saw them climbing onto the wall, they were stirred by violent anger and rose against them from every side. They hemmed them in with so many javelins and arrows that some of our men who had climbed the wall threw themselves down to the ground; they met, dashed against the earth, the death they had thought to escape.

When the renowned young men of our army saw this—Gulferius fighting with a few companions on the wall’s battlements—they forgot themselves but remembered their comrades. They immediately climbed up and covered part of the wall with their multitude.

Priests and Levites, the ministers of the Lord, stood beside the wooden tower, invoking Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the defender of the Christian people, and they said:

“Lord, have mercy on us. Be our arm in the morning and our salvation in the time of tribulation. Pour out your anger upon the nations that have not known you, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon your name (Psalm 78:6). Scatter them by your power and bring them down, O Lord, our protector (Psalm 58:12).”

While this was taking place—some fighting, others weeping and singing psalms, and others undermining the walls—Gulferius labored in the more difficult battle. All the adversaries fought against him and his companions, while he and his men fought against them all.

His shield was a strong protection for all his companions, namely those who were on the wall. The wall’s narrow and confined breadth allowed no companion to join him and permitted no adversary to approach except one at a time. Yet none of the enemy triumphed over Gulferius, although he himself triumphed over many of them.

Therefore no one now dared confront him, because each feared for himself the misfortune that had befallen others at his sword. They hurled missiles, arrows, stakes, and stones at him, and so loaded his shield with them that it could not be lifted by one man.

By now the strongest warrior was exhausted; by now sweat was pouring from his entire body onto the ground; by now the urgent need for another to take his place was pressing upon him, when those who had undermined the wall burst in with great force, cutting down all whom they first encountered.

Struck with amazement at this unexpected event, all who were on the walls were stunned, and

The vital heat of life quickly departed their bones,

[Col. 0739B] And chill fear seized the hearts of the guilty.

What could a people given over to death and deprived of reason do, pressed on every side by its enemies, both within the city and upon the wall?

Gulferius, who shortly before had been exhausted and failing, had meanwhile recovered new strength. Now, protected neither by shield nor helmet, but holding a red sword in his right hand, he swiftly pursued the fleeing enemy. He killed more by terror than by his sword, for they threw themselves from the wall.

Above the gate there was a tower that seemed the finest and stronger than the others. Through an interpreter, Bohemond ordered its wealthier citizens to flee, promising that he would free them from death if they redeemed themselves from him. They did so and entrusted themselves to his faith.

The pursuit then ceased, because the darkness of evening refused to allow it to continue farther [Col. 0739C]. Since it was Saturday, however, there could be no rest for either victors or vanquished. The count placed watchmen around the city, inside and outside, so that no one might flee and carry away the city’s spoils.

When day began to dawn on the following day, our men rushed to arms and raced savagely through the streets and squares and over the roofs of the houses, like a lioness deprived of her cubs:

They tear apart and hand over to death boys and young men,

And those whom old age weighs down and bends.

They spared no one; indeed, they hanged many with nooses so that they might finish them more quickly.

A marvelous thing and a marvelous spectacle: so great a multitude of armed people was being killed with such impunity that none of them resisted.

Since whatever each man found belonged to our men, they tore open the entrails of the dead and drew out Byzantine coins and gold pieces [Col. 0739D]. O detestable greed for gold!

All the city’s streets were stained with streams of blood and strewn with the corpses of the fallen. And, O blind people, wholly destined for death! Not one among so great a multitude was willing to confess the name of Jesus Christ.

Finally, Bohemond ordered those whom he had commanded to be confined in the tower-palace to come before him. He ordered the women of advanced age, decrepit old men, and the weak and infirm to be killed; but he ordered pubescent youths, adults of more mature age, and strong-bodied men to be spared and all to be sold and taken to Antioch.

This slaughter of the Turks took place on the twelfth day of December, on Sunday, although it could not all be completed that day [Col. 0740A]. On the following day, whoever was found in whatever place was subjected to the same punishment of death. There was no place in the whole city, nor any pit, that was not polluted by their corpses or blood.

## CHAPTER III

After the city had thus been acquired and freed from the rebellious Turks, Bohemond sought peace with the count—that is, that he should surrender Antioch to him outright and permit him to possess it in peace.

The count, however, objected that this could in no way be done without perjury, because of the oath that had been made to the emperor Alexius with his own participation.

Bohemond therefore returned to Antioch and left his company there. The Frankish army wintered in that city for one month and four days [Col. 0740B]. During this delay, the bishop of Orange died a precious death.

They wintered there for a long and excessively prolonged period, because nothing to eat or seize could be found. Thus, compelled by the injustice of famine, something occurred that is even horrifying to relate: they cut the bodies of pagans into pieces and ate them.

Moved by this hardship, the count of Saint-Gilles sent word to all the princes who were in Antioch to assemble at the city of Rugia and there decide among themselves about the journey to the Holy Sepulchre.

They assembled there, but did not speak at all about the matter for which and on account of which they had come. Instead, they held discussions about peace and concord between the count and Bohemond.

Since they could not reconcile the two, all the princes [Col. 0740C] returned to Antioch and abandoned both the count and the journey. Many young men remained with the count besides his own people, for they were filled with eagerness to complete the journey.

He therefore placed more confidence in the Lord than in the princes and returned to Marra, where the pilgrims were awaiting him. There was great sorrow throughout the Christian army because of the princes’ disagreement.

Everyone knew that pure justice was with Raimundus, and that no love or ambition could make him turn aside toward what was unjust. Nevertheless, when he saw that the journey to the Holy Sepulchre was being obstructed on his account, he was deeply grieved and traveled barefoot from Marra as far as Capharda.

There they lingered for four days. When the princes [Col. 0740D] assembled again and there was renewed verbal dispute about the same matter, Count Raymond said:

“Men, brothers and lords, who have renounced all your possessions and yourselves for the love of God, show me whether I can make peace with Bohemond, if he requires it, without perjury; or, if this cannot otherwise be done, whether for love of him I ought to commit perjury.”

Since no one dared to presume himself judge of this speech, and everyone praised concord without saying how it ought to be achieved, they separated from one another and returned to Antioch. But the Norman count remained with Raymond together with all his men, knowing and understanding that justice was on Raymond’s side.

Therefore the two counts arranged their forces and made for Caesarea. The king of Caesarea had repeatedly informed the count of Marra and Capharda [Col. 0741A] that he wished to have peace with him and would gladly serve him from his own resources. Trusting in this, they proceeded there and pitched their camp near the city.

When the king saw the Frankish forces encamped beside him, he was greatly astonished and distressed, and forbade any market to be supplied to them. On the following day he sent two of his own counts to show them the river fords and lead them to places where they could seize booty. The river was called the Farfar. They led them into a valley sufficiently suitable and richly supplied with every good thing. A very strongly fortified castle stood over it; beneath it they found twenty thousand animals grazing in the fertile valley, and our men seized them all.

When they wished to besiege the castle, the castellans immediately surrendered and made with the counts an agreement to maintain the following pact forever [Col. 0741B]. They promised on their faith and swore by their law that they would never again harm Christian pilgrims, but would provide them with market and lodging just as they did for their own people.

They remained there for five days. On the sixth day, after loading their camels and beasts of burden with grain, flour, oil, cheeses, and other things suitable for eating, they departed joyfully and came to a certain castle belonging to the Arabs. The lord of the castle, acting with prudent counsel, came to meet Count Raymond and made peace with him.

From there they came to a certain city situated in a beautiful and spacious valley, well fortified with walls and towers and abundantly [Col. 0741C] filled with every kind of fruit. The inhabitants called it Caphalia. When the people of this city heard the report of the Franks, they were terrified, abandoned their own homes, and fled to those of others. For the misfortune that had occurred at Antioch and Marra had terrified everyone and made them fugitives from their homes.

When our men wished to pitch their tents around it and besiege it on every side, they were astonished that no one from so great a city came out to meet them, nor appeared on the lofty towers or the battlements of the walls. A deep silence prevailed within, and no sound of any voice could be heard.

Then they sent scouts to investigate the matter carefully and report what they discovered. When these men had set out and approached the gates, they found the door open [Col. 0741D], but saw that no one was inside. Then, holding their shields before their faces, they entered the gates with some hesitation; but they found inside neither men nor women nor any animal.

They did, however, find beautiful stores there: granaries full of grain, winepresses overflowing with wine, and chests filled with nuts, cheeses, and flour. Then they quickly returned to the counts and reported what they had found. There was no need to pitch tents there, since God was causing them to enter into their labors without iron or battle.

There was fulfilled there what is said in the proverbs of Solomon: “The wealth of the sinner is stored up for the just” (Prov. 13:22). There they found gardens full of vegetables, beans, and other [Col. 0742A] legumes already ripening early. They rested there for three days; then, appointing guards to watch over the city, they climbed some steep mountains and descended into a valley.

That valley was delightful and exceedingly full of every kind of grain and fruit. They remained there for fifteen days. Near the valley was a castle filled with a multitude of Saracens. When our men attacked it one day, the Saracens threw many sheep and a great number of animals over the wall, thinking that our men sought nothing but food. Our men gladly accepted them and led them to their tents.

On the following day they gathered up their pavilions and tents and moved their camp there. But when they arrived, they found the place deserted by every people [Col. 0742B]. For everyone had fled during the night, leaving behind a great abundance of grain and fruit, milk and honey. There our men celebrated the Purification of holy Mary, Mother of God, glorifying God, who supplied them with such great blessings.

## CHAPTER IV

While they were there, the king of the city of Camela sent his messengers to the counts [Note: [Col. 0741D] “The king of Camela sends shining weapons.”], asking for the things that make for peace and sending beforehand desirable gifts, horses, and gold. He sent a golden bow, precious garments, and gleaming weapons. Our men accepted all these things, but at that time gave him no definite reply.

The king of Tripoli, moved by the same fear, sent ten horses and four mules, likewise asking for the things that make for peace. They accepted the gifts, but sent him word that they would never have peace with him unless he became a Christian [Col. 0742C].

For the Count of Saint-Gilles greatly desired his land, because it was excellent, and his kingdom, because it was more honorable than the others. Accordingly, after fourteen days had passed, on the fifteenth day they left the excellent valley and went to a very ancient castle called Archas. Although it bore the name of a castle, it could be compared with distinguished cities both in the position of the site, the enclosure of its walls, and the height of its towers.

Because of its strength, a great population had gathered there, since it feared neither weapons, an enemy, nor any engine of war. Nevertheless, our men quickly surrounded it with a siege and attacked it with haste; but the castellans bravely withstood their assault. They attacked them repeatedly with every kind of weapon and artillery, but did not prevail; rather, they lost more than they gained.

Then fourteen of our knights, who did not know how to remain idle, proceeded toward Tripoli. They encountered sixty Turks who had carried off many captives and more than one thousand and fifty animals and were driving them before them. When our men saw them, although they were very few, they stretched their hands toward heaven, invoked the King of Sabaoth, and attacked them in knightly fashion. With the Lord of hosts assisting them, they overcame them, killed six of them, retained their horses, and returned rejoicing to the camp with immense booty.

There was great joy throughout the army at the great victory and abundant plunder achieved by so few [Col. 0743A]. When the others saw this, more men came out from Raymond’s army, inflamed by zeal for valor. Raymond Piletus and Raymond, Viscount of Tentoria, led them; with their banners raised high, they rode against the city called Tortosa.

When they reached it, they attacked it with a powerful assault, but accomplished nothing that day. When night came, they withdrew to a certain corner and made enormous bonfires throughout the night, as though the entire Christian army had remained behind them. The people in the city were terrified by these globes of flame. Thinking that all our men were present, they suddenly fled and abandoned the city, which was full of valuable possessions.

That city was entirely free from every necessity [Col. 0743B], for it stood in the finest harbor of the sea. On the following day, when our men came to conquer it, they found it completely empty. Giving the highest praises to God, they entered it and remained there for as long as the siege of Archas lasted.

## CHAPTER V

There is also another city not far from it called Maraclea. Its ruler made peace with them and received them and their banners into the city.

O marvelous power of God, and wondrous might! While the princes who seemed to govern and sustain the people were far away, the Lord began, through men who were fewer and lesser, to overcome even kings themselves, lest human presumption should say: “We subdued Antioch and the other cities; [Col. 0743C] we conquered so many and such great wars.” For assuredly they would never have prevailed had he not been with them through whom kings reign.

When Godefridus, the leader of leaders and soldier of soldiers, heard of the fortunate events and notable triumphs of the fighters, he was moved by zeal for victory. Then, for the first time, both he himself and the Count of Flanders [Note: [Col. 0743D]

“Duke Godefrid, whose sword is truly faithful.”

[Col. 0744D] “The Flemish count, whose sword does not deceive.”] and Bohemond moved their camps from Antioch and came to the city of Lycia.

There Bohemond separated himself from them and from the whole army of God. From his father, who had been a Frank, he possessed excellent beginnings; but from his mother, who had been Apulian, he retained her traces.

Then the duke and the count directed their forces toward the city called Gibellum and surrounded it with a siege. At that very moment a messenger came to the Count of Saint-Gilles, reporting that the Turks had prepared themselves for battle against him and that a very grave and exceedingly great war was imminent.

At once the count sent a messenger to the duke and the Count of Flanders, asking them to come as quickly as possible to that battle and bring him aid. When the duke heard this, he sent word to the city’s ruler concerning the peace he had already sought many times. Once peace had been made and the gifts promised in the agreement had been received, they hastened to the hoped-for battle, joined the siege that was at the aforementioned castle, and pitched their camp on the opposite bank of the river.

But when the duke saw that he was accomplishing nothing, he directed his forces against Tripoli and found all the enemies there prepared [Col. 0744A]. For the enemy stretched their bows and opposed themselves to our men, but our men, thrusting their shields before them, despised their bows and arrows like straw.

Battle was therefore joined, but it was not an equal contest. When they had shot their arrows, the enemy, as was their custom, wished to flee, but our men placed themselves between them and the city. And why should I use more words? So much human blood was shed there that the water flowing into the city became red and filled their cisterns. The nobler men of that city were killed there, and those who survived lamented greatly the contamination of the cisterns.

After this slaughter, our men were not satisfied, since they had gained nothing there except weapons and the spoils of clothing. They rushed into the aforementioned valley of Desen and plundered sheep, oxen, asses, and livestock of various kinds without number [Col. 0744B]; they also seized three thousand camels at once. Our men were greatly astonished at where such a multitude of animals had gathered, since they had lodged in that same valley for fifteen days.

With so great a quantity of booty, they returned to the camp. There was never any shortage during that siege, because ships came to a certain harbor bringing everything necessary. They celebrated the Lord’s Pasch there; it then fell on the fourth day before the Ides of April.

That siege lasted three months, less one day. There Ansellus of Ribodimonte died, a man worthy of much praise and outstanding in his military rank. While he lived in this world, he accomplished many deeds worthy of report, but this deserves first mention: he was an indefatigable helper of the monastery of Aquiscinge in all things.

Pontius of Balon [or of Baladino] likewise died there; a blow from a stone hurled by an engine pierced his temples. Willermus Picardus and Guarinus of Petra Mora also died there: the first from a spear, the other from an arrow. When these men had died, our men abandoned that siege, because the impregnable castle feared no violence from its attackers.

After striking their tents, they proceeded to Tripoli and established the peace that they had long sought from the king and the citizens. Having exchanged right hands, the nobles entrusted themselves so completely to their good faith that they entered the city as far as the king’s palace.

To make it more certain that he for his part could be trusted to keep the peace, the king released three hundred of our pilgrims from their chains [Col. 0744D] and gave them to the nobles. He also gave fifteen thousand bezants and fifteen horses of great quality, and sent the entire army a fine supply of provisions, completely freeing them from every necessity.

He also agreed and swore to them that, if they could acquire Jerusalem and overcome the war that the admiral of Babylonia threatened to wage against them, he would become a Christian and submit to the rule of the king of Jerusalem.

They remained at Tripoli for three days. When the nobles and fighting men saw that the time of the new crops was already approaching, they agreed [Col. 0745A] to undertake the journey to Jerusalem in full and, abandoning everything else, to take the more direct route.

It was the fourth day of May when they left Tripoli. Ascending some steep mountains, they reached a castle called Betelon. On the following day they came to the city called Zabaris. In its territory no water could be found with which to quench their excessive thirst. It was hot, and the horses and the whole multitude of men were thirsty.

On the next day they came to a river called Braim. They spent the night there and relieved their thirst. The following night was the eve of the Lord’s Ascension. They ascended a mountain on which there was an extremely narrow road. They thought they would encounter enemies there, but God, because he alone was their leader and no foreign god was with them, enabled them to cross without harm.

Then they came to the city of Baruth, situated beside the sea; afterward to another called Sagitta; after that to another called Sur; then to Acre; from Acre to a castle called Caiphas; and from there to Caesarea.

Caesarea is a distinguished city of Palestine. It is said that the apostle Philip had a house there, which is still shown today, as well as the chamber of his prophesying daughters. It is situated on the seashore and was formerly called Pirgos, that is, “the Tower of Strato.”

But King Herod rebuilt it more nobly and beautifully and made it more useful against the violence of the sea; in honor of Caesar Augustus it was called Caesarea. In it he also built a temple of white marble for Caesar. There his grandson Herod was struck by an angel, Cornelius was baptized, and the prophet Agabus was bound with Paul’s belt.

Our men pitched their tents beside it and celebrated the holy Pentecost of the Lord. Then they came to the city of Ramola, which the Saracens had abandoned empty out of fear of them. Near it was the illustrious church of Saint George the martyr, in which his most holy body rests; at that place he suffered martyrdom for Christ’s name.

There the Christian soldiers, out of veneration for Christ’s soldier, elected a bishop, established the man they had elected, and enriched him, once installed, with tithes of all their wealth [Col. 0746B]. It was fitting that George, the unconquered soldier and standard-bearer of their army, should receive this honor from them.

Thus the bishop remained there with his people, rich in gold and silver, horses, and animals. The Christian army immediately directed its march toward the city of Jerusalem, in the power of the name of him who lay dead there and rose again on the third day, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, belong equal power and unending glory. Amen.

[Col. 0745] HERE ENDS BOOK EIGHT.

HERE BEGINS BOOK NINE.

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0745C]

O good Jesus, when your camps saw the walls of this earthly Jerusalem, how many streams of tears their eyes poured forth! And at once, falling prostrate upon the earth, they greeted your holy sepulchre with the sound of their mouths and the inclination of their bodies; and they worshiped you, who had lain in it, as the one seated at the right hand of the Father and as the judge of all who would come.

Truly, at that time you removed the heart of stone from them all and gave them a heart of flesh, and placed your Holy Spirit in their midst. Thus they fought against your enemies who were within it, though they were already far away, because they summoned you so earnestly to their aid. They fought better with tears than by hurling javelins, for although their tears flowed abundantly down to the earth, they nevertheless rose before you in heaven as before their champion.

Rising from prayer, they hastened toward the royal city. They found the enemies of the eternal King within and arranged their camps around them in the following order. Two counts, the Norman and the Flemish, camped to the north beside the church of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, where he was stoned by the Jews. Duke Godefrid and Tancred camped to the west. To the south was the Count of Saint-Gilles, on Mount Zion, near the church of Saint Mary, the Mother of the Lord, where the Lord supped with his disciples.

While they rested, fatigued by the hardship of the journey, with their tents arranged around Jerusalem and their engines prepared for attacking the city, [Col. 0746C] Raymond Piletus, Raymond of Taurina, and many others went out from the camp to patrol the neighboring region, lest the enemy should unexpectedly come upon them and find them unprepared.

They encountered three hundred Arabs, fought them, defeated them, killed many, and took thirty horses from them. On the second Monday of the week, the fourth day before the Ides of June, the Christians attacked Jerusalem. They did not prevail that day, but their labor was not fruitless. They leveled the outer wall so completely that they raised a ladder to the greater wall; if they had then possessed a sufficient number of ladders, that first labor would have been the last.

Those who climbed by the ladder fought for a long time at close quarters with the enemy, using javelins and swords. Many of our men died in that conflict, but far more of the enemy [Col. 0746D]. The unsuitable hour of evening brought the battle to an end, and the coming night gave both sides rest.

This repulse inflicted a severe and very long hardship on our men, because for a period of ten days they could not find bread to eat, until their heavily laden ships reached the harbor of Japhia. Excessive thirst also wore them down, because the spring of Siloam, which rises at the foot of Mount Zion, could scarcely provide water even for the men alone.

The horses and other animals had to be led six miles to drink, and then under a strong guard of soldiers. Consequently water was precious among them [Col. 0747A] and was sold at a high price.

After taking counsel, they chose soldiers to go to the ships and guard them against foreign peoples. At first light, one hundred soldiers therefore went out from the army of the Count of Saint-Gilles: namely, Raymond Piletus, who had always been accustomed to every military hardship and wholly a stranger to idleness; with him went the other Raymond of Taurina, Achard of Monte Merulo, and also Guillermus of Sabrata. They proceeded toward the seaport as men prepared for battle.

As they went, thirty of them separated from the others to learn the paths and discover whether enemies were approaching. When they had advanced a short distance, they saw seven hundred Turks and Arabs from afar. Although they were very few, they attacked them without hesitation. But the enemy’s numbers [Col. 0747B] were so great that our small force could not resist.

Nevertheless, those whom our men encountered in the first assault they consigned to certain death. But after that engagement they thought they might be able to turn back; surrounded by the multitude, however, they could not accomplish what they wished.

There Achard, a brave and distinguished fighting man, was killed, together with some of the foot soldiers [Note: [Col. 0747] “Had he been slower, Achard would not have died thus.”]

Before the battle began, a messenger had hurried on a swift horse to Piletus to report that the Arabs and Turks had attacked our men. When Piletus heard this, he immediately spurred his horse, but arrived there too late. Achard was already dead. Yet before he died, he exchanged his life for much blood and his death for the deaths of many others [Col. 0747C].

When the enemy saw our men from afar, they fled just as doves customarily flee the hawk with trembling wings, turning their backs to our men. Our men pursued them, killed many, and captured one of them alive to report the Turks’ stratagems and reveal beforehand what evil they were planning. They also took one hundred and three horses from them and sent them to the camp, while they themselves carried out the task assigned to them at the ships.

The ships, laden with food, relieved their hunger, but they could not relieve their intense thirst. So great was the thirst during the siege that they dug into the earth, placed moister clods against their mouths, and licked stones wet with dew.

They sewed together the fresh hides of oxen, buffaloes, and other animals. When they prepared to go to water the horses, as many as six thousand armed soldiers went with them. They filled the containers with water, carried them back to the camp, and drank that foul-smelling water. Many fasted as far as they could endure, because fasting moderated their thirst.

And who would believe that hunger could be beneficial, or that pain could drive out pain? While they suffered these things, the nobles had wooden beams brought from a great distance across the land, so that towers and engines could be made to attack the city.

When the beams had been brought, Godefrid, the leader of leaders, constructed his tower and ordered it to be brought from the eastern side [Col. 0748A]. The venerable Count of Saint-Gilles, in turn, built a similar fortress and brought it up from the southern side.

On Thursday our men observed a fast and distributed alms to the poor. On Friday, the twelfth day of July, as dawn flashed with clear light, the distinguished warriors climbed the towers and set ladders against the walls.

The adulterous citizens of the splendid city were astonished and trembled when they saw themselves surrounded by such a multitude. But because they saw that their final day was approaching and death hanging over their heads, they began to resist fiercely and, as men no longer uncertain of death, to defend themselves.

Duke Godefrid stood prominently in his tower—not then as a soldier, but as an archer. The Lord directed his hand to battle and his fingers to war, for when he shot his arrows he pierced the breasts and both sides of the enemy [Col. 0748B].

Beside him his brothers Eustachius and Baldwin, like two lions beside a lion, received the hard blows of javelins and stones and repaid them fourfold. And who could recount the valor of them all, when the eloquence of all the philosophers now living would scarcely suffice for such praises?

While the battle was being fought above on the walls, a procession was conducted around those same walls, carrying crosses, relics, and sacred altars.

All day they fought with alternating blows. But when the hour approached at which the Savior of all suffered death, a certain soldier named Detoldus, from the duke’s castle, was the first to leap in. After him came Guicherus [Col. 0748C], who by his own strength struck down and killed a lion.

Immediately the duke followed his soldiers, and all the other soldiers followed their duke. Then bows and arrows were abandoned, and lightning-like swords were seized. When the enemy saw this, they immediately abandoned the wall and slipped down to the ground, while the soldiers of Christ pursued them at a swift pace with loud cries.

When Count Raymond heard these cries—for he was eager to bring his fortress nearer to the wall—he immediately understood that the Franks were in the city and said to his soldiers:

“Why do we stand here and labor in vain? The Franks possess the city, and it resounds with great cries and blows.”

Then he quickly went with his company to the gate beside the Tower of David and called to those who were in the citadel to open it [Col. 0748D]. As soon as the admiral who guarded the tower recognized who he was, he opened the door to him and entrusted himself, his people, and his possessions to Raymond’s protection, so that he might keep them from destruction.

But the count said that he would never do this unless the man surrendered the tower to him. The admiral gladly agreed, and the count gave him, as he requested, his full assurance of protection.

Duke Godefrid sought neither the citadel, nor a palace, nor gold, nor silver, nor spoils. With his Franks, he sought to avenge upon the enemy the blood of his servants that had been shed around Jerusalem, and desired to punish the mockeries and insults they had inflicted upon the pilgrims [Col. 0749A].

Never in any battle had he possessed such an opportunity for killing—not even on the plain of Antioch, when he split a gigantic pagan in two. But now, without any resistance, he himself and Guicherus, who had cut the lion in half, together with many thousands of chosen soldiers, were cutting human bodies from head to waist and through both sides, right and left.

None of our men was idle there, and none was fearful where no one resisted. Everyone fled as best he could, but no one could escape, because the multitude, entangled within itself, became an obstacle to itself.

Those who were able to escape the torment of so great a disaster entered the Temple of Solomon and defended themselves there for a long time. But when the day already seemed to be declining [Col. 0749B], our men, fearing sunset, gathered their courage, burst into the hidden parts of the temple, and struck them down with a wretched death [Note: [Col. 0749D]

“In the year one thousand one hundred, minus one,

[Col. 0750D] the Franks captured Jerusalem by mighty valor.”]

So much human blood was shed there that the bodies of the slain were rolled across the pavement by the force of the blood’s current. Arms, or severed hands, floated upon the gore and became attached to foreign bodies, so that no one could discern to whose body belonged the arm joined to a mutilated corpse.

Even the soldiers who carried out this slaughter could scarcely endure the clouds of hot vapor exhaled by the burning heat. When this indescribable massacre had been completed, they yielded somewhat to nature and spared many of the young, both men and women, preserving them for life and enslaving them to their service.

Then they ran through the streets and squares [Col. 0749C], seized whatever they found, and whatever each man seized became his own.

At that time Jerusalem was filled with worldly goods and lacked nothing except spiritual delights. It enriched its sons, who had come to it from far away, so greatly that no poor man remained in it.

Thus enriched with such vast wealth, they went with joyful steps to the holy sepulchre of the Lord. Giving thanks to him who had been buried in it, they offered him their headgear.

On that very day, as had been foretold through the Prophet, the Lord’s sepulchre was glorious (Isa. 11:10), when everyone proceeded not upright on his feet but prone upon knees and elbows, flooding the pavements with a rain of tears.

When this solemn offering had been completed in devotion [Col. 0749D], they returned to their houses, which God had assigned to them. Indulging in the necessities of nature, they gave food and sleep’s rest to their weary bodies.

On the following day, when dawn showed its head above the earth, they ran armed to the Temple of Solomon, so that no place in the city would remain for ambushes and so that they might destroy those who had climbed above the temple roofs [Col. 0750A].

A very great multitude of Turks had climbed there. They would gladly have fled if they could have taken wings and flown. But to those whom nature denied wings, miserable life granted an unhappy end.

When they saw our men approaching them from the opposite side above the temple, they came against them with naked swords, preferring to die with the utmost speed rather than perish over a long period under the yoke of wretched servitude. For they threw themselves headlong to the ground and found death upon the earth, which provides nourishment for life to all mortals.

Yet they did not kill everyone; they reserved very many for their own servitude. Then it was decreed that the city should be cleansed. The surviving Saracens were ordered to drag out the dead and cleanse the city entirely of all the filth of so great a slaughter.

They immediately obeyed the commands, both mourning and dragging out the bodies. Outside the gate they built enormous pyres, like small fortified and defensive houses. They gathered the severed limbs in baskets and carried them outside, and washed the pavements of the temples and houses with water to remove the blood [Col. 0750B].

## CHAPTER II

After all the enemies had been expelled from the city of peaceful name, the question of appointing a king had to be debated, so that one of them might be chosen to govern so great a city and so great a people.

By the common decree of all, with equal vote and general consent, Duke Godefrid was chosen, on the eighth day after the city had been conquered. The agreement of all was rightly reached in his case, because in that rule he displayed himself in such a way that he commended royal dignity more than royal dignity commended him.

Honor did not make him illustrious; rather, glory was multiplied for honor because of him. He governed and benefited royal dignity so greatly that, if it were possible for all the kings of the earth to stand beside him, he would be judged to rule them all by the standard of equity, by the merit of knightly excellence, by the beauty of his bodily appearance, and by the distinction of noble character.

It was also fitting thereafter that those who had decently and worthily chosen a governor of their bodies should in like manner set over themselves a ruler of their souls. They therefore chose a certain cleric named Arnulf, well educated in divine and human law.

He was a learned scribe in the kingdom of heaven—that is, in the holy Church—who could rightly bring forth from his treasure new things and old (Matt. 13:52). His election took place on the feast of Saint Peter in Chains. That feast was especially appropriate for a city that had been bound for so long by demonic chains, because on the very day when it received a worthy priest, it became free and released.

Thanks therefore be given to God, the Savior and liberator of his own people, who so often permitted it to be destroyed and enslaved, so often rebuilt it after its destruction, and freed it from slavery by his wondrous power.

Through these conflicts of war, as has been said, the Gallic people penetrated the regions of the East and, by divine assistance, cleansed Jerusalem from the impurities of the pagans by which it had been defiled for approximately forty years.

When a priest had been canonically consecrated there and a king elevated, the celebrated name of the Franks became known throughout the whole East, and the omnipotence of Jesus Christ, crucified there, shone even in the minds of unbelievers [Col. 0751A].

When the organization of priest and king had been displayed with solemn rejoicing in the radiance of this resplendent grace, messengers came from the city of Neapolis to King Godefrid, bearing the commands of their fellow citizens: he was to send some of his men to them and receive both their citizens and their city under his rule and authority.

For they wished to extend their own dominion of their own accord, preferring their own rule to that of another. Neapolis is a city of Caria, which is a province of Asia.

After taking counsel, the king sent them his brother Eustachius and Tancred, with a large force of knights and foot soldiers. They received them with great ceremony and honor and surrendered themselves and their city to his authority.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0751B]

When these things began to happen, that crooked and slippery serpent, who always envies the happiness of the faithful, was exceedingly distressed that the title of the Christian name should thus be enlarged and the kingdom of Jerusalem, newly restored, thus extended. He stirred up against them Clement—or rather the demented—admiral of Babylonia, and with him aroused the whole East. For the author of every wickedness hoped to destroy them all and the city, and utterly abolish the memory of the Lord’s Sepulchre. But just as human plans are vain, so human powers also vanish.

He therefore gathered whatever men he could and reached Ascalon with an imposing display. When he had arrived there, a messenger hurried to the king and informed him of the situation as it was. [Col. 0751C] There was no long delay: the king sent to those whom he had dispatched, ordering them to hasten to the battle that the admiral of Babylonia had prepared. He himself was already at Ascalon with an innumerable host and was preparing to besiege Jerusalem.

When Eustachius, Tancred, and the other warriors heard this, they pointed out to the citizens of Neapolis the impending business of war; then, bidding them farewell with joy and friendship, they departed. For our men, eager to encounter the Turks, climbed into the mountains and, sleepless and restless throughout the day and night, reached Caesarea. On the following day they traveled beside the sea and came to a certain city called Ramola, where they found many Arabs who were the advance guard of the army. Our men bravely pursued them, [Col. 0751D] and captured several, who truthfully disclosed to them all the preparations for war. Having learned this, they quickly sent messengers mounted on swift horses to the king, urging him to summon everyone without delay and march to battle against Ascalon.

Ascalon is a distinguished city of Palestine, twenty-five miles distant from Jerusalem. It was once founded by the Philistines, who named it Ascalon after Celon, a grandson of Ham and son of Mesraim. It had always been an adversary of Jerusalem; although nearby, it never wished to be joined to it by any bond of friendship. The admiral of Babylonia was therefore at Ascalon when the messengers came to the king and reported what we have described above. [Col. 0752A]

When the king heard this, he ordered the patriarch to be summoned and sought his advice. The patriarch advised that a proclamation should be made throughout the city, so that everyone would assemble at the church early the next morning, receive the Eucharist of the Lord’s body after the solemn celebration of Mass, and then ride toward Ascalon to battle.

This report did not disturb the spirits of those who heard it at all. Rather, the following night seemed longer than the others because it passed so slowly:

> As soon as dawn raised its morning head,
>
> The ringing bell summoned all to Mass.
>
> Mass was concluded; the people joined themselves to the Lord.
>
> While the blessed gifts were received,
>
> The populace left the church and ran to arms,
>
> Fasting, it marched against the enemy.
>
> After the king left the city, war-trumpets, sistra, and trumpets
>
> [Col. 0752B] Sounded together; their blasts made all
>
> The surrounding mountains, with their valleys, resound,
>
> And struck terror into their enemies.

Thus the Christian ranks advance to battle, carrying God, the victor in war, in body and mind. For this reason they are not terrified by any multitude of men: they trust not in their own strength but in his.

The patriarch, for his part, entrusted his duties to Peter the Hermit, so that he might arrange the Masses, establish the prayers, and organize processions to the Sepulchre, so that the God-man who had lain there might become a defense for his people.

When the king came with his army to the river near Ascalon, he found there many thousands of oxen, camels, asses, mules, and mares. These animals belonged not only to the city but had also come with the army of the admiral. [Col. 0752C] One hundred Arabs were guarding them. But as soon as they saw our men, they abandoned the booty and sought safety in flight. Our men pursued them but could capture only two. They seized all the booty and richly endowed Jerusalem with it.

As evening was already falling, the king ordered a proclamation to be made throughout the entire army that everyone should rest, rise at first light, and prepare for battle. The patriarch, however, anathematized all who should seize anything in that conflict before victory had been won.

When the night had passed, a dawn brighter than usual shone forth and roused our men from sleep. It was Friday, [Col. 0752D] on which the Savior of the human race cast down the devil, the king of Babylonia, by the trophy of the cross; and now once again the Lord overcame the admiral of his Babylonia through his servants. The king, as we said above, crossed the river, but the patriarch remained on the nearer side with the bishops and other religious men, both Greeks and Latins.

The king therefore descended with all his men into a beautiful and spacious valley. He entered beside the seashore and there arranged his battle lines. He established his own as the first; the count of Normandy, the second; the count of Saint-Gilles, the third; the count of Flanders, the fourth; Count Eustachius, Tancred, and Gaston de Béarn, the fifth. All the infantry, with bows, spears, and other weapons, were placed before the cavalry. Thus arranged, they began to advance against the Babylonians. On the right, beside the sea, was the count of Saint-Gilles; on the left rode the king, where the enemy’s greater strength was concentrated. All the others were between them. [Col. 0753A]

Nor must we pass over what Clement the admiral said when he was informed that our men were riding against him to battle. No one had told him about the booty our men had captured the previous evening, since no one dared tell him anything except what was joyful and favorable: he always wished to remain in a state of gladness. Whoever reported bad news to him thereafter found no favor in his sight. Yet the loss of any possession did not trouble him, because the wealth that remained was so great. [Col. 0753B]

And lest anyone think what we are about to say frivolous, we learned it from a certain Turk who later reported these events in Jerusalem. He voluntarily became a Christian and was called Bohemond at baptism. Early in the morning it was reported to Clement that the Franks were truly prepared for battle and were already close, coming against him. Then, it is said, the demented man said to the messenger:

“What you tell me I scarcely dare believe, since I do not think they are even within the walls of Jerusalem.”

The messenger replied:

“Let Your Greatness know with complete certainty that they are coming prepared for battle and are already near.”

Then Clement ordered everyone to take up arms and hurry to the battle. When all stood prepared opposite the enemy, and he himself had seen our men, he said:

> “O kingdom of Babylonia, surpassing all kingdoms, [Col. 0753C] what disgrace you suffer today, since such a tiny people dares to come against you! I never imagined that they could be found even within the enclosures of any city; and now they have dared to come against me after a journey of one day? Either they have lost their senses, or they love to die as much as they love to live.
>
> “Therefore I command you, O Babylonian warriors, to remove all these men from the earth. Let your eyes spare no one, and show mercy to none.”

Thus the battle began.

The fearless count of Normandy was the first to begin the engagement with his line, in the region where he saw the admiral’s standard—the object they call a *standardum*. Breaking a path through the battle lines with his sword, he inflicted great slaughter. At last he reached the man who held the standard, struck him down at the admiral’s feet, and seized the banner. [Col. 0753D] The admiral barely escaped and, fleeing to Ascalon, halted before the city gate. From there the wretched man gazed upon the most wretched slaughter of his people.

With equal boldness the king and the other counts rushed upon their opponents and, with savage slaughter, killed on the right and left all who met them. The Turkish bow was of no use to any of them there, because the attack of our men was so swift and so densely pressed that none had an opportunity to draw his bow; they could only flee. Many thousands died there who would not have died had they been able to escape. But the crowd was so great that those behind pushed those in front into the deadly swords of our men. [Col. 0754A]

Tancred and Count Eustachius of Boulogne rushed into their tents and performed many glorious deeds there, which, if written down, would deserve remembrance. None of our men was found sluggish, none afraid. All animated by one spirit, they pursued the enemies of Christ’s cross with one accord.

It was indeed astonishing that the small number of our men did not fear so great a multitude of armed men. Rather, with divine grace assisting them, they grew stronger and stronger and bent the stubborn necks of their enemies.
