Thus the battle continued throughout the day until the sun climbed to the center of the heavens, at the hour when our Lord Jesus ascended the cross. At that same hour all the strength of the opposing people withered. Their minds were so changed that they could neither flee nor defend themselves. [Col. 0754B]

They climbed trees, thinking that by doing so they would protect themselves from being seen by our men. But our men shot them down like fowlers shooting birds and slaughtered them when they had fallen to the ground, like executioners killing animals in a slaughterhouse. Others, holding swords in their hands, fell at our men’s feet and bowed themselves to the earth, not daring to raise themselves against the Christians.

By now the first division of the Babylonian army was fleeing entirely, while the rear division still wondered to whom the victory belonged. It had expected nothing less than the flight of its own people and the Christians’ victory. When they saw their own men running across the open fields in flight, they thought that the Christians were pursuing them and wished to kill them. But when they discovered [Col. 0754C] that the victory belonged to the Christians, the joy they had felt was overcome by sorrow.

Then they too fled in terror and gave their followers the example of flight. As the north wind scatters clouds and a storm driven upon it scatters heaps of straw, so our men scattered the wings and wedges of the fugitives.

## CHAPTER IV

While these things were happening, while the soldiers of Christ were destroying the devil’s servants, and while the count of Saint-Gilles, fighting beside the sea, was killing innumerable men and forcing many more to plunge into the sea, let us hear what Clement—now truly the demented admiral—said as he stood before the gate of Ascalon. We shall report it as the proselyte mentioned above later related it in Jerusalem. [Col. 0754D] He had been beside Clement as his follower, household servant, and domestic attendant.

Clement, therefore, speaking like a madman, said, while the Christian people were cutting down his own people:

[Note: [Col. 0753] These are Clement’s sorrowful words, befitting a demented man.]

> “O Muhammad, our teacher and patron, where is your power? Where is the power of the heavenly gods with whom you boast? Where is the effective power of the Creator, in whose presence you are always said to stand? Why have you thus abandoned your people, whom the poorest and most ragged people, the refuse of other nations, the dregs, rust, and slag of all humanity, are pitilessly scattering, destroying, and killing?
>
> “I mean the people who used to come to ours seeking bread, who possessed absolutely nothing except a staff and a pouch. [Col. 0755A] So many times we gave them alms; so many times we pitied them. Alas, alas! Why did we spare them? Why did we indulge their misery? Why did we not kill them all?
>
> “Now we can know that they came here not as true worshipers but as deceitful spies. They saw the glory of our prosperity, coveted our riches, carried their desire back to their own land, and reported it to these men. Now these men thirst for our gold and silver, and for that reason they pour out our blood so cruelly.
>
> “Are these men truly human, possessing such power—or rather, are they infernal gods? Perhaps hell has burst open and this people has escaped from it. The abyss cracked, and from it this people boiled forth. They have no human feelings, no signs of compassion. If they were human, [Col. 0755B] they would fear death; but, since they have emerged from wherever it was, they do not fear returning to hell.
>
> “O glory of the kingdom of Babylonia! How shamefully you are dishonored today, losing your warriors, once strong, now weakened! What nation will henceforth be able to resist this wicked people, when your own people cannot withstand them even for an hour?
>
> “Alas, alas! Now those who never learned to flee are fleeing, and those accustomed to overthrowing others are shamefully cast down. Alas for our grief! Everything turns against us. We used to conquer, and now we are conquered. We were constantly immersed in joy of heart; now we are afflicted with sorrow.
>
> “Who can restrain his eyes from tears and hold back the sobs bursting from his inmost heart? For a long time I devoted myself with great anxiety to gathering this army, and I wasted much time in vain. At immeasurable cost I hired [Col. 0755C] the strongest soldiers of the entire East and brought them to this war, and now at the end I have lost both them and the price I paid.
>
> “At great expense in silver I had prepared timber for constructing wooden towers and every kind of engine around Jerusalem, so that I might besiege them; but they have come far from the city to meet me.
>
> “What honor shall I have henceforth in my land, when an immigrant people, a foreign nation, has thus dishonored me?
>
> “O Muhammad! Muhammad! Who has ever been worshiped with more splendid devotion than you—in shrines adorned with gold and silver, decorated with beautiful images of you, and with ceremonies, solemnities, and every rite of worship?
>
> “[Col. 0755D] Yet this is what the Christians are accustomed to reproach us with: the power of the Crucified is greater than yours, because he is powerful in heaven and on earth. It is now evident that those who trust in him conquer, while those who venerate you are defeated.
>
> “But this is not due to our negligence, for your tomb is more richly adorned with gold, gems, and every precious wealth than Christ’s. The city honored by your body has never been deprived of honor, but has always grown in every kind of splendor and shone with all the service owed to proper veneration.
>
> “But this city in which he was crucified and buried has never afterward possessed honor. It has often been destroyed, trampled underfoot, and reduced to nothing.
>
> “[Col. 0756A] By whose fault, then, are we made so degenerate, when we show you every honor and you return no favor to us?
>
> “O Jerusalem, deceitful and adulterous city, if it should ever happen that you fell into our hands, I would level you entirely with the ground and utterly destroy the tomb of your buried one.”

While Clement the admiral rolled out these and similar words in a plaintive voice, our men, mindful of their accustomed valor, attacked the Babylonians before the city gate with such force that they left none of them outside the gate except dead or exhausted by wounds. Thus divine power conquered the battle and crowned our men with victory.

Who could fully recount how many were killed in the narrow entrance of the gate? Then Clement had good reason to weep when he saw so many corpses of his people lying dead before him. Some, already at the point of death, still writhed and cursed Clement, who had brought them there. Clement is said then to have wept and howled and to have cursed our men.

[Col. 0756B] There were sailors and ships in the sea beside the city, belonging to the surrounding regions. At the admiral’s command they had brought supplies of every kind of wealth necessary for the siege of Jerusalem. When they saw their people and their lord so shamefully defeated, they were terrified by fear, raised their sails, and drove themselves into the open sea.

Our men, however, raised their hands toward heaven, gave thanks to God in their hearts, and returned to the enemy’s tents. There they found gold and silver, countless spoils of clothing, an abundance of food, every kind of animal, and weapons and equipment. [Col. 0756C] They also found horses and beasts of burden, mules and mares, little asses and she-asses, and one dromedary.

What shall I say of the sheep and rams and other livestock that had been prepared for food? Cauldrons and kettles, cooking pots, beds and their coverings, baskets full of gold and silver, golden garments, and all their equipment were found there. They were enriched by the richest booty, for they had taken the admiral’s tents, filled with royal treasures.

The standard, whose summit had a golden knob on a silver spear, was presented by the count of Normandy to the Lord’s Sepulchre and was valued at twenty marks. Another sword he purchased for sixty bezants.

[Note: The count brings a beautiful gift before the Sepulchre.]

As our men were returning in triumph, they encountered [Col. 0756D] groups of peasants carrying wine vessels and water containers, which they thought necessary for the siege and intended for the use of their lords. Like beasts, these men stood stupidly without turning anywhere and, with bowed heads, awaited our men’s swords. Many rolled about in the blood of the dead and hid like corpses among the dead bodies.

When our men reached the river where they had left the patriarch, they rested and, exhausted, slept. When dawn returned daylight to the earth, they rose and hastened the journey they had begun. As they began to approach within about two miles of the city, like conquerors they sounded trumpets, rattles, horns, and musical instruments of every kind, so that the mountains and hills answered with harmonious and measured reverberations and, in a sense, joined them in singing to the Lord. [Col. 0757A]

Then was literally fulfilled what Isaiah spiritually says of the Church of the faithful:

> “The mountains and hills will sing praise before you” (Isaiah 55:12).

The harmony was exceedingly pleasing and delightful in its many-voiced sweetness, as the echoes of the mountains, the hollows of the rocks, and the depths of the valleys resounded to the voices of the soldiers and the sound of the trumpets.

When they came before the gates of the city, those who had remained behind proclaimed their arrival with divine praises—not now by earthly mountains but by heavenly heralds. And rightly God was praised for this, because now his pilgrims were received through open gates with praises, whereas formerly they had been received with great difficulty and great insults, even after gifts had been given.

Isaiah speaks of these pilgrims and gates:

> “Your gates will continually be open to them; day and night they will not be closed” (Isaiah 60:11).

[Col. 0757B] This prophecy is fulfilled in our times, because now the gates of Jerusalem are opened to the sons of pilgrims, whereas formerly they were closed to them day and night.

This battle took place to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, on the day before the Ides of August.

## CHAPTER V

Since this historical account took the beginning of its name from Jerusalem, and retains its ending there just as it does its middle, no one should find it incongruous if, at the end [Col. 0757C] of this work, it is recorded who first founded the city and who gave it this name.

Melchizedek is said to have founded it after the Flood, and the Jews assert that he was the son of Noah.

[Note: He indicates who first founded Jerusalem.]

He founded it in Syria and called it Salem, and afterward ruled there for a very long time. Later the Jebusites held it and added to it the part of their own name, Jebus. Combining the names, they called it Jerusalem, with the *b* changed into *r*.

Later, when Solomon had made it more splendid by the temple of the Lord, his royal palace, and many other buildings, gardens, and pools, it was called Hierosolyma; and from its name it was understood almost as “Hierosolomonia.” The poets corruptly [Col. 0758A] call it Solyma, while the prophets call it Sion, which in our language is interpreted as “watchtower,” because, being established on a mountain, it surveys from afar those who come.

Jerusalem, in our language, is translated as “peaceful.”

We find written in the books of Kings about the glorious wealth of this ancient city, that Solomon made silver as abundant in Jerusalem as stones. But it shone with far greater riches when the Son of God endured the cross there for the universal redemption of all, darkened the heavens with their stars, and the earth trembled; the rocks were split, the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had slept rose again.

In what city has such a wondrous mystery ever occurred, from which the salvation of all the faithful flowed? [Col. 0758B] From this it may be inferred that the Son of God so illuminated this city by his glorious death that, if it had pleased our authorities, it ought to have been called not Jerusalem but Jebussalem, with the *r* changed into *b*, so that in our language its name might be interpreted as “peaceful salvation.”

For these and similar figurative actions, it is an image of the mystical sacrament of that heavenly Jerusalem of which it is said:

> “The city of our strength is Sion the Savior; he will place a wall and a rampart in it. Open the gates, and the righteous nation, keeping the truth, will enter” (Isaiah 26:1–2).

We cannot report everything said about its praise by the prophets and teachers of the Law.

In our age, however, this earthly city was abandoned by God and hated because of the wickedness of those who inhabited it (Psalm 106:34). But when it pleased the Lord himself, he brought the French people from the ends [Col. 0758C] of the earth and determined through them to free the city from the unclean Gentiles.

Long before, God had foretold this through the prophet Isaiah, when he said:

> “I will bring your sons from afar, with their silver and gold with them, for the name of the Lord your God and for the Holy One of Israel, because he has glorified you. The sons of foreigners will build your walls, and their kings will serve you” (Isaiah 60:9–10).

We find in the prophetic books many other passages that correspond to this liberation accomplished in our times.

Blessed in all things and above all things is God, who by just judgment strikes and wounds, and by free goodness, whenever and however he wishes, has mercy and heals.

Amen.

Here ends.

[HISTORY OF THE JOURNEY TO JERUSALEM.]

[Col. 0757]

## PREFACE OF JOANNES BESLY, OF POITIERS, TO THE HISTORY OF PETER TUDEBODUS, PRIEST OF SIURACUM, ON THE JOURNEY TO JERUSALEM

Jacobus Bongarsius, a man who rendered distinguished service to letters, arranged for a great volume of authors on Eastern history to be published at Hanau in 1611. The first of these authors, who leads the procession without a name, he judged from his style and his affection for Bohemond [Col. 0759] to have been an Italian. Whether this is true or not, I would not press the question too sharply or contentiously.

This one assertion I would make boldly: that this Anonymous took almost everything from the History of Peter Tudebodus of Poitiers, which he entitled *On the Journey to Jerusalem*. In order that he might secretly claim for himself the labors he had exhausted and whatever reputation they had won, the plagiarist removed Tudebodus’s name and tore throughout the work the frequent and unmistakable marks by which the genuine author could be recognized—an offense deserving legal punishment.

He did occasionally insert a few things taken from elsewhere, which I do not find unwelcome. But he rashly truncated and rejected without judgment many things that it would be useful to know and harmful to ignore. Finally, he changed very many passages either into a worse form or into no better one. And if his ability to speak had been as great as the confidence he assumed for himself, that stinking schoolmaster might have taught Tudebodus to speak Latin.

Whoever he was, he owes his fate to Fortune’s mockery: while trying to steal another man’s name, he lost his own—not the other man.

Robert the monk, Baldric, archbishop of Dol, and Guibert the abbot, all contemporaries, more honestly declared themselves interpreters of another man’s history. For the most part, in a fuller style and with loose reins, sometimes word for word and always as carefully as they could, they reproduce that Anonymous. They also mingled into their own books other material valuable to students of history, which they had learned from those who took part in the expedition to Jerusalem, and handed it down to posterity.

Our author wished to inform us, according to the solemn custom of the ancients, about himself: his name, family, homeland, profession, books, the titles of his books, and the age in which he lived and wrote.

When the Christian army was suffering under the siege of Jerusalem in the month of July, in the year 1099, “from thirst, the most burning season of the year, the scorching sky, and the parched ground” (these are the words of Aemilius), prayers were held and the sacred places in the suburbs were visited with the utmost reverence, barefoot and in the dress of supplicants. Tudebodus adds the following, which I shall quote from Book V:

> “At that place, wishing to enter the church, a certain cleric, coming ahead in the procession, came. At the door of that monastery he was wounded in the middle of the forehead by an arrow and died. He who wrote this first should be believed, because he was in the procession and saw it with his bodily eyes—namely, PETER, priest of SIURACUM, TUDEBODUS.”

He indicates his name and homeland through an anxious joining of words. For if “priest of Siuracum” were connected as one phrase, the wording would be ambiguous, would leave us uncertain, and might perhaps lead us into error.

Siuracum is a town of no obscure standing situated in the territory of the Pictones. Today it is the seat of a royal jurisdiction, one of the four great seneschalties by which that extensive and flourishing region is distinguished. At that time it was under the rule of Hugh of Lusignan, surnamed “the Devil” because of his unconquered courage.

The author mentions Rainaldus, the military commander of this same Hugh, whom he calls the steward. When our men attacked Jerusalem on the fourth day before the Ides of June, on the fifth day after their arrival, in the year 1099, and, after breaking through the outer defenses, brought up ladders to seize the interior, Rainaldus himself, among the boldest men who had climbed the walls, was struck down by those inside and died there—not without avenging death.

For although William VIII, count of Poitiers and duke of Aquitaine, had not yet personally served in the holy war, he, a most powerful prince, had nevertheless sent troops under arms, neither few nor insignificant.

On the fourth day before the Kalends of July in the preceding year, battle was fought at Antioch against Corbona, with two hundred thousand cavalry and an innumerable number of infantry. The entire Christian army was divided into six lines. On that day the Pictones obeyed Gaston, viscount of Béarn, a client of the duke, who commanded the fifth line with Tancred.

Tudebodus himself, a Pict of the Pictones, who had supplied the courage, strength, and blood of his own people so that they might carry away the immortal victory won by pouring out, routing, and slaughtering the barbarians, recorded this alone in writing, in favor of glory and burning with love of his homeland. Anonymous and all the others, who were not involved in the matter, passed it over in silence.

He nowhere shows when he entered upon the journey to Jerusalem, and in history it is unlawful to guess. I nevertheless conjecture that from the beginning he attached himself as a companion to Hugh the Great. But after the Great Hugh, having rashly crossed to Dyrrachium with William, the marquis’s son, born of Bohemond’s sister, was captured by ambush and sent in chains to the emperor Alexius, I suppose that our author then joined Bohemond, who had not yet led his forces out of Apulia, and went with him to Constantinople, reaching it on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April in the year 1097—or, in the words of Albert of Aachen, “when Easter had already passed after three weeks had elapsed.”

For in that year Easter had fallen on the day before the Nones of April. The bishop of Tyre writes that Bohemond “met Alexius on the fifth day before the solemnity of Easter,” somewhat later, namely on the fourth day before the Nones of the same month.

In his History Tudebodus indicates that he was with the expedition at least from the fifth day before the Kalends of March of that year. At that time Tancred and the count of Roussillon attacked troops belonging to Alexius which had unexpectedly fallen upon them while they were unprepared and secure from their enemies, thinking themselves to be in a peaceful situation. They defeated these troops in a bloody slaughter at the river Bardarus in Illyria.

“This battle,” he says, “took place on the fourth day of the week, which is the beginning of Lent. When these things had happened, the most wicked emperor ordered one of his most faithful men, named Corpolatius, to escort us safely through his land until we came to Constantinople.”

And so forth.

He had two brothers, Arveus and Arnaldus, devoted to military affairs. As his own men, he praises them piously as “most excellent and best soldiers”—that is, outstanding in military valor and character—in a noble commendation. If their origin were not otherwise known, their names would themselves show that they were Franks.

When our men, formerly besiegers, had become, through a reversal of fortune, the besieged at Antioch, and had made a bold sortie against the Saracens, Arveus fell while fighting splendidly. His brother Peter performed the funeral rites for him and gave him burial at Saint Peter’s, before the gate that faces west.

Arnaldus, fighting under unfavorable conditions, was pierced by the enemy’s wounds and killed near Marrha.

Robert the monk complains, though to no purpose, that the Anonymous’s History “did not have as its beginning the matter established at the council of Clermont, and therefore placed the head of an acephalous work at its front.” He boasts somewhat too grandly.

For Tudebodus, from whom the Anonymous draws, begins his History at that same council, but carries out in three words the speech that Robert himself and the others, vying with one another and employing great and ambitious display, attribute to Pope Urban; and Anonymous, following him, does the same, each according to his own judgment and capacity of mind and talent.

He closes his narrative with a distinguished crown: namely, the most celebrated victory that the Christian princes miraculously won at Ascalon against Ammaravisus of Babylon on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September in the year of Christ’s birth 1099.

Neither Anonymous, nor Robert, nor Baldric went any farther. Guibert alone is longer by an addition of two years. He wrote and finished writing while Duke Godfrey was still alive, that is, before the fifteenth day before the Kalends of Sextilis in the year 1100, when that great prince died.

For in Book I he offers a good wish for “him and his brother Baldwin, most wise athletes of Christ”:

> “May the Lord fortify and protect them with the glory of the world.”

No sane person would ever say this of a dead man.

He comprised his History in five books; Anonymous contracted them into four. Baldric interprets Anonymous in the same number, Robert in nine, and Guibert in seven, though Guibert carried the last down to the second year of King Baldwin I.

He entitled the work *On the Journey to Jerusalem*. Baldric retained this title, borrowing it from Anonymous, and I judge that it ought to be restored to both works, on the evidence of Baldric’s own letter to Peter the abbot:

> “I have sent you the little book which I composed in some fashion under the title *On the Journey to Jerusalem*, so that you may correct it. I wish you to restrain it by regular criticism, polish it, and return this letter together with the book, not without recompense.”

The letter was returned, and it is precisely the one that is read prefixed to Baldric’s books. The same abbot seems to allude to it in his own letter of recompense at the inscription of those books:

> “We also return the Jerusalem book, sent to me by a Jerusalemite, together with the letter placed at its front and filled with extraordinary sweetness.”

The manuscript codex of Camden, which Bongarsius used in publishing Anonymous, bore these words at the end:

> “Here ends the good way.”

There, “the good way” means nothing other than *On the Journey to Jerusalem*, in the sense of *On the Jerusalem War* or *On the Jerusalem Expedition*.

Torquato Tasso, the phoenix of the Italian poets of his age, later preferred, after changing his mind, to entitle that divine work of his not *The Conquest of Jerusalem* but *The Liberation of Jerusalem*. And our author, somewhere under the title *On the Journey to Jerusalem*, adds “and the liberation of the cities.”

“The Way of God,” used absolutely in the manner of that age, means the same thing. Guibert writes in Book II:

> “When the council held at Clermont, which had convened around the octave of Saint Martin in the month of November, had ended, a great excitement spread through all the regions of France and stirred up even those who were neighbors and close associates concerning the undertaking of the WAY OF GOD—for so it was antonomastically called.”

Furthermore, the Peter about whom Baldric writes was abbot of Malleacum, not Malleocum, which would be erroneous. Gaufredus, his uncle, whom he succeeded, formerly a monk of Cluny, was appointed abbot of Malleacum in 1083, while Baldric ruled Burgulium from the year 1089.

[Col. 0761] A long-established relationship and great familiarity existed between the abbots of the two monasteries. Both monasteries acknowledge as their founders Emma Campana and her son William IV, dukes of Aquitaine.

This is enough to untie the knot that had troubled certain wavering minds. Meanwhile, let us turn our pen to TUDEBODUS.

How much faith and authority he deserves in what he committed to memory, let contemporaries and interpreters judge at their own risk. Robert says: “Let those who read or hear these things know that we shall relate nothing frivolous, nothing false, nothing momentous unless it is true.” Baldricus says: “Some compiler, whose name has been suppressed, had published a very crude little book on this subject, but had woven it together with truth.” Abbot Guibert says: “Indeed, I repeatedly compared what was reported in the book with the testimony of those who had witnessed the events, and I undoubtedly found that neither differed from the other.”

All this is said about the Anonymous author; but Tudebodus too is understood to be included under the same judgment, since, as I have already said, the Anonymous drew everything from him as from a fountain. From the Anonymous, however, all those streams flowed. Therefore, when he wishes to be believed the first writer of this sacred expedition, he easily wins me to his side, since no one older than he has yet been found who took such a burden upon his shoulders.

Nevertheless, there survives a near-contemporary of his, Raimundus de Agiles, chaplain to Raymond, count of Toulouse, who seems to have recorded whatever our men did each day during that war. He and our author, comrades in military service, perhaps shared their commentaries with one another. Certainly, when compared, they agree remarkably and differ very little; even today one can read in both of them a page or two composed in almost exactly the same terms. The records of both likewise come to an end at the battle of Ascalon.

Nor should the excellent Bongarsius have doubted that the first fragment, as he calls and considers it, belonged to someone other than Raimundus; but it is mutilated and incomplete. The other is a severed part taken from his Anonymous, at the end of the final book. It is therefore not without cause that one may wonder why he did not notice this when he was reviewing the books. But that great man, occupied with so many public and private affairs, refrained from making the observation.

Tudebodus and Raimundus, being such writers, are, in my judgment, worthy of receiving greater credence than others concerning these matters. I shall not dwell on Fulcherius of Chartres. For the military forces of Robert, duke of the Normans, and of Stephen, count of Chartres—among which was Fulcherius—joined the others only at the very end, when Duke Godfrey, Hugh the Great, and other nobles had surrounded Nicaea on the day before the Ides of May, and finally joined the rest in the first week of June, as Fulcherius himself admits, in the year 1097. Nicaea was surrendered on the third day before the Nones of July; Antioch was reached on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November.

Several days earlier Fulcherius had already withdrawn from the camp and, attached to Baldwin of Boulogne, the count, had gone with him toward the Euphrates and from there to Edessa. Having become an inhabitant of that region, he remained there until, when Duke Godfrey had died, Baldwin his brother was substituted in the deceased man’s place.

Meanwhile, Fulcherius went once to Jerusalem to fulfill his vow, on the Ides of December—or, in his scholastic language, “on that day when the sun, having completed its winter descent, resumed its ascending return”; or, as William of Malmesbury presents it, “on the day of the winter solstice,” in the year 1099. “But on the second day of the following year, 1100, he began the return journey.” Accordingly, what our men accomplished during the interval of his absence he reports only from hearsay and rather thinly.

Our author, however, once he had girded himself for the journey of the sacred pilgrimage, held firmly to his purpose and turned aside to nothing else. He was, for the most part, an eyewitness of so many battles and so many glorious deeds. I have read no ancient or modern writer, apart from the Anonymous of Bongarsius, who knew or had read Tudebodus, who cites him or makes his own meal richer and better furnished from Tudebodus’s table.

Otto, bishop of Freising, and Chunradus, abbot of Ursperg, may nevertheless raise a doubt, from what they relate about this war at the beginning of the reign of the Emperor Henry IV. For Chunradus says that he “read at Jerusalem a little book, beginning from the present point”—when Duke Godfrey and the other nobles had reached the fortresses of Constantinople—“which pursued the whole sequence of this history most diligently and concluded the many labors of the people of God with the most joyful victory at the capture of Jerusalem. Therefore, I shall here relate a few things from the many.”

Our author likewise ends his History with these words: “Let these things, said about the journey to Jerusalem over three years and the liberation of the cities, suffice.” Certainly, to complete the liberation of Jerusalem, the victory at Ascalon was of the greatest importance. Once it had been won, the holy city, having completely shaken off the yoke of the impious, could finally and truly be considered delivered and confirmed under Christian rule. Chunradus also speaks of this from the same little book.

Baldricus likewise gives the books of the Anonymous and his own four books no other designation than “little books.” Furthermore, although Tudebodus begins with the Council of Clermont, he nevertheless reckons the years of his History only from the time when the Christian princes reached Constantinople and, after crossing the Bosporus, entered Asia—that is, from the year 1097, which had already begun. He does not count the time spent preparing and equipping the army.

Freisingensis says nothing at all about the little book, but nevertheless draws from the same source as Chunradus; and he openly admits that everything he includes in his Chronicles up to the year 1106 he took from the books of earlier writers, borrowing from one another.

A passage of that same Chunradus presses in the opposite direction: “When the armies had been receiving newcomers at Byzantium day after day for almost two months, they were finally counted, apart from the incredible multitude of common people, children, and women, as three hundred thousand fighting men.” Otto expressed this in Book VII, and Paulus Aemilius in Book IV repeated it.

They seem to disagree about the place. Chunradus assigns it to Byzantium; Aemilius to Chalcedon. Whichever one may be preferred, I shall accept neither. Indeed, one finds nothing similar in Tudebodus or the Anonymous, nor can one suspect that it was omitted through the carelessness of hurried copyists, since Robert, the interpreters of the Anonymous, Raimundus, Fulcherius, and the archbishop of Tyre—in short, all the ancient writers—are silent about it.

The event itself is consistent with military discipline and must be thought to have occurred; but not all of them were assembled there at one time, which the History does not permit. Fulcherius says: “The armies were not all gathered together in one place until we reached Nicaea.” It is preferable, then, to suppose that Chunradus and Otto had other authors before their eyes whom they followed.

They themselves also report more from a letter of Duke Godfrey, brought to Pope Paschal by Count Robert—whom I think to have been the count of Flanders—than from elsewhere. Sigebertus, a contemporary author, copied from it under the years 1097, 1098, and 1099, and Dodechinus, abbot, could reproduce it in full under the year 1100. It may be that they took as certain a number which they found uncertain in the same letter.

The letter says: “When the whole army had departed from Nicaea after its capture, more than three hundred thousand armed men were there.” Pope Urban II likewise says in a letter to Alexius, emperor of Constantinople: “So great a multitude of men was signed with the cross that nearly three hundred thousand men were counted.”

Whatever the truth may be, the author of that little book misled Otto and Chunradus on this point. The incomparable Nicolaus Vignerius had seen the Anonymous before Bongarsius released him from his fetters and restored him to freedom. For Vignerius cites him three times, including that most celebrated emblem of the warlike valor of the Franks, which he adduces from a manuscript in Book III of his *Bibliotheca*, under the year 1097. Today it is found in the printed Bongarsian edition, Book III, taken from Tudebodus, Book II; it was carelessly neglected by Robert, celebrated by Guibertus in Book III and Baldricus in Book II, and from Baldricus taken up by Ordericus in Book IX.

Tudebodus and his four interpreters were unknown to the archbishop of Tyre, who had placed two men, Raymond of Agiles and Albert of Aachen, ahead of them as guides on this journey. Aemilius imitates the archbishop of Tyre and Baldwin. No one will deny this who has the inclination and leisure to compare all of them with one another.

Tudebodus’s speech is everywhere thick with solecisms, and it is entirely the rustic language which, five hundred and fifty years ago, was commonly used by those who thought they were speaking Roman. It is Latin only insofar as the endings and inflections of its words strike and beat upon our ears with some kind of Latin sound, however harsh and uncouth. We may readily allow that sound to pass by and disappear, provided that the events themselves—which will bring no small benefit and delight for all time—remain fixed in the mind through their weight and solidity, and attract and flood it with the marvelous variety and truth of their deeds and outcomes.

Even in our little children, when they first learn to speak, we seek and love truth stammering on their lips.

The parchment codex from which I transcribed this is extremely old and, as I believe, unique in our Europe. The blessed [Greek: ho makaritēs, “the late”] Pilingenius, Baron Cressonerius, gave it to me as a gift. He was a man of the highest nobility among the people of Poitou, most distinguished in his achievements, and, while the fates permitted it, my very dear friend.

In turn, I entrusted the copy to André Duchesne, royal geographer, very dear to me for many reasons, to make it public. The commonwealth already owes him much, and will one day owe him more, when he has brought into the daylight what he is preparing and what longs to emerge into the open air of light.

The remaining matters will be explained to you in the *Collectanea ad Tudebodum*.

[Col. 0763]

# THE HISTORY OF PETER TUDEBODUS, PRIEST OF SIURACUM, CONCERNING THE JOURNEY TO JERUSALEM

(Duchesne, *Rerum Francicarum Scriptores*, IV, 777, from the parchment codex of the distinguished Joannes Besly of Poitou, councillor in the county court of Fontenay and royal advocate.)

## HERE BEGINS BOOK ONE

[Col. 0763A] When that appointed time had already drawn near which the Lord daily demonstrates to his faithful, especially saying in the Gospel, “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9:23), a movement arose among all the nations of the Gauls: if anyone earnestly and with a pure heart desired the Lord, and wished faithfully to carry the cross after him, he should not hesitate to take the road to the Holy Sepulchre as quickly as possible.

For the apostolic representative of the Roman See set out as quickly as possible into the mountain regions with his archbishops, bishops, and priests, and began to speak and preach earnestly, saying that if anyone wished to save his soul, he should not hesitate to take the Lord’s road; and if he lacked an abundance of money, divine mercy would provide him with enough.

The lord apostolic Urban said: “Brothers, we must suffer many things for the name of Christ: namely, the hardships of poverty, persecution, want, sickness, nakedness, hunger, and thirst, and other things of this kind, just as the same Lord says to his own: ‘You must suffer for my name’; and again: ‘Do not be ashamed to speak before the faces of men; I shall give you a mouth and wisdom’ (Luke 21:15).” Thereafter, abundant reward would follow them.

[Col. 0763B–0764A] When this speech had gradually begun to spread throughout all the regions and provinces of the Gauls, the Franks, hearing such words, immediately made crosses on their right shoulders, saying unanimously that they would follow the footsteps of Christ, by whose hand they had been redeemed from the infernal realm.

Now the Gauls had already departed from their homes. The Gauls divided themselves into three groups.

One group entered the region of Hungary: namely, Peter the Hermit, Duke Godfrey, and his brother Baldwin, the wise athlete of Christ—may the glory of the world’s Lord strengthen and protect them. These most prudent soldiers, and many others whom I do not know and whose leader I lack, came by the road which long ago the marvelous Charles, king of France, had caused to be made as far as Constantinople.

Peter the Hermit reached Constantinople first, on the third day before the Kalends of August, and with him came a very great multitude of Germans. There he found Italians, Lombards, and many others gathered together. The emperor had ordered that a market be supplied for them, as had been done in the city, and he said to them: “Do not cross the strait until the great strength of the Christians arrives, because you are not numerous enough to be able to fight the Turks.”

Those Christians, however, behaved wickedly in everything. They destroyed and burned the city’s palaces, took the lead with which the churches had been covered, and sold it to the Greeks. Therefore Emperor Alexius, greatly angered, ordered them to cross the strait.

After they had crossed, they did not cease committing every evil. They burned and ravaged houses and churches. At last they reached Nicomedia. There the Lombards and the Longobards, and the Germans, separated from the Franks, because the Franks were full of envy and swollen pride.

They chose an elder named Rainaldus, entered Romania, and traveled for four days beyond the city of Nicaea. They found a certain fortress called Xerigordon, which was empty of inhabitants. They seized it and found there an abundant supply of grain and wine, meat, and every good thing.

When the Turks heard that Christians were in the fortress, they immediately came to besiege it. Before the fortress gate there was a well, and at the foot of the fortress there was a living spring. Rainaldus went out to keep watch beside it because of the Turks.

When the Turks came on the feast of Saint Michael’s dedication, they found Rainaldus and all the others who were with him and killed many of them. The others who remained fled into the fortress, which the Turks immediately besieged and deprived of water.

Our men were therefore in such distress from thirst that they had their horses and asses bled and drank their blood. They committed many other terrible acts because of the shortage of water. Some put girdles into the cistern and then put them into their mouths. Others urinated into one another’s fists and drank it. Still others dug up damp earth, lay on their backs, and placed it on their chests or bodies because of the extreme dryness caused by thirst.

The bishops and priests who were there encouraged them, saying: “Be strong, beloved ones, in the faith of Christ, and do not fear those who persecute you. For the Lord said: ‘Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul’” (Matthew 10:28).

This persecution lasted eight days. Meanwhile, the lord of the Germans conferred with the Turks about how he might betray all the others. Pretending to go out to battle, he fled to them with many men.

Those who refused to deny the Lord received the sentence of death. The Turks seized the others and divided them among themselves like animals. Some they sent to the target and shot with arrows; others they sold or gave away as they pleased. Each man led his captives to the places where he lived: some to Chorasan, others to Antioch, others to Aleppo.

These first men happily received martyrdom.

After this, when the Turks heard that Peter the Hermit and Walter had been at Civetot, which lies above the city of Nicaea, they hurried there with great joy, desiring to slaughter them. When they found Walter with his soldiers, they immediately killed them all.

Peter the Hermit, however, had shortly before returned to Constantinople because he could not restrain the madness of the untamed people, who were unwilling to obey even slightly his most salutary warnings.

Accordingly, when the Turks fell upon them, they killed many—some while sleeping, others while lying down, others naked. They also martyred priests who were celebrating Mass upon the altars.

Those who were able to escape fled to Civetot. Others threw themselves into the sea, others into the forests, others into the mountains. The Turks pursued them to the fortress, gathered wood, and prepared to burn them together with the fortress.

The Christians who were in the castle set fire to the gathered wood, and by God’s will the fire turned back upon the Turks; for that reason they left them.

The Turks then divided those whom they had captured alive. They dragged some to Chorasan, others to Persia, and still others through various provinces. All this happened in the month of October.

When the emperor heard that the Turks had scattered our people in this way, he was joyful and glad, and he caused them to return across the strait. Afterward he bought all their weapons. These things all happened in this way.

The second group entered the regions of Slavonia: namely, Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles, and with him the honorable bishop of Le Puy.

The third group came through ancient Rome. In this group were the count of Flanders, Robert the Norman, Hugh the Great, and many others. They all arrived at the ports of Brindisi, Bari, and Taranto.

Soon Hugh the Great and William, the son of the marquis, put out to sea from the port of Bari and crossed to Dyrrachium. When the city’s duke heard that they had arrived, immediately inflamed by an evil thought, he ordered them to be seized and brought before the emperor at Constantinople, so that they might swear fidelity to him.

Duke Godfrey arrived at Constantinople with his army on the day before Christmas. He was lodged beside the city and remained there until the emperor ordered that he be received into the suburb.

When he had been received, he freely chose men from his own forces whom he sent outside each day to carry away straw and other necessities. But the treacherous emperor secretly ordered his Turcopoles and Pincernates to attack and kill them.

When Baldwin, the duke’s brother, noticed this, he immediately began carefully investigating whether he might somehow find them. At last, finding the emperor’s men devastating them, he attacked them with courage and, with God’s help, defeated them. He captured sixty of them, killed some, and led the others before the duke.

When the emperor heard this, he became extremely sad. The duke, perceiving the emperor’s anger, ordered his fellow soldiers to leave the suburb and, as before, pitch their camp outside the city.

When evening came, the emperor sent an army to attack the duke and the holy people. The invincible duke pursued them with his Christian soldiers, killed seven of them, and chased the rest as far as the city gate. He then returned to the tents and remained there for five days.

After this, the duke crossed the strait of Saint George with his entire army, having first made an agreement with the emperor, namely, that everything necessary for them would be sold to the army at a much lower price than it had previously been bought for in the city. Moreover, the emperor promised to distribute provisions to all the poor who arrived, so that they could live abundantly.

## HOW BOAMUND RECEIVED THE CROSS

Meanwhile Boamundus, who was besieging Malphi, namely the bridge of Capharda, heard that an innumerable multitude of Franks had arrived in order to wrest the road to the Holy Sepulchre from the hands of the worst pagans, so that it might thereafter be liberated and stand open everywhere to all Christians.

He immediately and most wisely began carefully to inquire what weapons this people carried for battle, what display of Christ they bore upon the road, and what signal sounded in combat. Everything was reported to him in due order.

“They continually carry weapons suitable for war; on their right hands or between their shoulders they bear the cross of Christ. As a cry, they proclaim together with one voice: ‘God wills it! God wills it! God wills it!’”

At once, moved by the Holy Spirit, he ordered a most precious cloak which he possessed to be brought out. He commanded that it be cut up, and all of it was expended in making crosses.

A very large part of the soldiers who were in that siege began to flock to him, so that Count Roger remained almost alone and, having returned to Sicily, regretted that he had lost his people.

Boamundus [the supplied text reads *Romandus*] therefore returned once more to his own land. He carefully adorned himself in every way for beginning the journey to the Holy Sepulchre.

At last he crossed the sea with his army. With him was the very prudent Tancred, son of the marquis, and many others. They all crossed and arrived in the regions of Bulgaria. There they found an abundance of grain, wine, and bodily provisions.

Then, descending into the valley of Andrinople and arriving there, they waited for their people until all had crossed equally. Then they set out from that place and proceeded amid great abundance, from village to village and from fortress to fortress, until they reached Castoria, where they solemnly celebrated the Nativity of the Lord.

After leaving Castoria, they entered Pallagonia, where there was a certain fortress of heretics. They attacked it from every side, together with its inhabitants, and drove them into the lake beside which it had been built. They immediately subjected it to our rule.

They then set fire to the fortress and burned it together with its inhabitants, namely, the assembly of heretics.

Afterward they reached the river Vardar. Boamundus went forward with one part of his people. Another part remained with the count of Russinolo and with his brother, the bishop.

The army of the accursed emperor arrived and attacked the count, his brother, and all the others. When the very prudent soldier Tancred heard this, he threw himself into the river and reached them by swimming.

Two thousand soldiers entered the river, following Tancred. At last they encountered the Turcopoles and Pincernates fighting together with our men. They suddenly attacked them with force and wisely defeated them.

They captured many of them and led them bound before Boamundus. Addressing them, Boamundus said: “Why, wretches, are you killing the people of Christ who are subject to me? I have no quarrel with your emperor.”

They replied: “Obeying the commands of our emperor, we hasten to carry out whatever he orders us.”

Boamundus allowed them to depart without any punishment.

This battle took place on Wednesday, which is the beginning of Lent. Blessed be God in all things. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0767D] In the edition, Book I ends here.]

After these events, the most wicked emperor ordered one of his most trusted bodyguards to escort us safely through his land until we reached Constantinople.

When we came before their cities, he ordered the citizens to bring us provisions safely; and they did so. Nevertheless, they feared Boamundus’s people so greatly that they would not allow them, for any reason, to enter the city.

Thus they reached the city of Rusium and lodged there. Then Boamundus dismissed his people and went to speak with the emperor, instructing his retinue to follow him as he approached the city. He took only a few soldiers with him.

When the emperor learned that Boamundus was coming to him, he ordered that he be received and honorably lodged in the city. After he had been received in this manner, he sent word to the emperor that they should confer together.

Then the two of them reached an agreement. For the emperor granted Boamundus fifteen days’ journey of land in length through Romania and eight in breadth.

## HERE BEGINS BOOK TWO

[Col. 0767]

[Col. 0767D] Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles, together with the bishop of Le Puy, left Slavonia. In that region he had suffered many things for the name of Christ and for the road to the Holy Sepulchre—things he should not have had to endure—and had also lost many most honorable soldiers.

From there he reached Dyrrachium, which is the emperor’s city, thinking that he was already in his own land because he had escaped from the hand of his worst enemies.

The people of the Greeks, lying in wait for these most prudent soldiers of Christ, did not cease, day and night, secretly and covertly, from harming or offending them wherever they could.

There was a duke of that city who immediately and gladly promised them protection wherever they might be in his land. Under this protection, which he had granted them as a gift, his men treacherously killed one of our outstanding soldiers, whose name was Pontius Rainaldus. They also severely wounded his brother.

Soon afterward, as they set out on their journey, they encountered messengers of the emperor carrying letters concerning peace and a firm alliance to be maintained with them as with his own sons.

Meanwhile, the Turks, Pincernates, Comati, Slavs, Usi, and Athenasi lay in wait for the Christians, hoping to harm them somewhere.

One day, while the bishop of Le Puy was lodging at a certain place, it happened that he was captured by the Pincernates. They threw him from his mule, stripped him, and severely wounded him on the crown of his head.

But because so great a pontiff of God was still necessary to the people of God, he was preserved alive through God’s mercy. Meanwhile a noise was heard in the tents. Everyone ran to him and without delay rescued him from their hands.

Thus they came to a certain fortress called Buinath. The count was told that the Pincernates were lying in wait for him in a narrow road through a mountain. He remained behind with several soldiers, found the Pincernates, killed one part of them, and put the rest to flight.

Meanwhile the emperor sent his letters to them peacefully; but on the other side his enemies were lying in wait for them everywhere.

At last they reached a certain city named Reusa. The citizens of that city openly did whatever they could against them. When the count saw this, he became extremely angry, ordered the weapons to be taken up, and with a great assault attacked the city, whose name was Rodosto.

On that day the emperor’s soldiers attacked them from behind, at the rear. The count fought them, killed thirty of them, and captured sixty horses.

Meanwhile envoys sent by the emperor arrived and said that the emperor promised carefully to restore everything that had been lost, provided that the count would hasten to Constantinople with only a few men and without weapons.

Duke Godfrey, Boamundus, the count of Flanders, and all the other princes also urged him to do this. They further said that the emperor, having taken up the cross, had promised to come to Jerusalem as the leader and head of the Christians.

When the count heard this, he immediately left his army and hastened to Constantinople to speak with the emperor. The emperor told him to become his man and swear fealty to him, as Boamundus and the other princes had done.

The count replied: “Far be it from me, on this journey, to establish any lord over me except the one whom I have, for whose love I have come this far. But if you wish faithfully to carry the Lord’s cross and come with us to Jerusalem, I and all my subjects shall obey your authority.”

While the count was in Constantinople, the emperor’s army laid an ambush for the count’s army, attacked it unexpectedly, and wounded very many of its men.

When the count heard of the injury done to his army, he groaned and became deeply saddened. He immediately summoned Boamundus and the other princes, sending word to the emperor and asking why, as an act of treachery, he had caused him to come to Constantinople and had consented to harm his army.

The emperor denied this entirely under oath, saying: “In truth, this was not done by my counsel, although I know for certain that your army has caused me very great damage by ravaging my own fortresses and cities. Nevertheless, I faithfully grant you satisfaction.”

After this, before they came to judgment, the count renounced the agreement. Once the agreement had been dissolved, his army came to Constantinople.

Then the emperor sent word to the count, as we said above, that he should perform homage to him, as the other thieves had done. The count, however, considered how he might avenge himself upon the emperor’s army.

But Duke Godfrey, the count of Flanders, and the other princes restrained him, saying that it was unjust to fight against Christians. Boamundus also said that if he did anything unjust against the emperor and refused to give him an assurance, Boamundus himself would take the emperor’s side.

Accordingly, after taking counsel with his men, the count swore to Alexius, upon his life and honor, that neither by himself nor through another would he take land from him. When he was pressed concerning homage, he replied that he would not do it even at the risk of his life.

The emperor then told Boamundus, whom he greatly feared—for Boamundus had often defeated him with his army—that if Boamundus would willingly swear the oath, he would grant him fifteen days’ journey of land in length from Antioch and eight in breadth.

Boamundus swore to him under this agreement: if the emperor faithfully kept that oath, Boamundus would never violate his own. Then Boamundus’s people approached Constantinople.

All the Christians of the religion, gathered together in one body, reached the port. They crossed the strait together and arrived at Nicomedia, where they remained for three days.

Duke Godfrey and the count of Flanders besieged the city of Nicaea with their armies. Nicaea is the capital of all Romania. Boamundus came to them and besieged it from the north on the sixth day of May; there they pitched camp.

On the day of the Lord’s Ascension they began to attack the city on every side and to construct wooden engines outside the wooden towers, with which they could bring down the city’s stone towers.

They attacked the city together so forcefully and fiercely for two days that they even had the city wall undermined.

The Turks, although a barbarian people, sent messengers to the others who had come to give aid to the city, saying: “Come boldly and safely, and enter by the southern gate, because no one will meet you from that side or trouble you.” On that very day, the count of Saint-Gilles and the bishop of Le Puy successfully occupied that gate.

The count, arriving from that side, protected by divine power and shining with earthly weapons, came with his very brave army. When he found Turks coming from every direction, armed with the sign of the cross, he rushed upon them fiercely. They were defeated and fled, and the greater part of them were killed.

Then, coming again at the message of the others, joyful and exultant and prepared for a decisive battle, they carried with them ropes with which to bind us and lead us captive to Chorasan.

When they came rejoicing to the summit of the mountain, they began gradually to descend. All who descended into that valley were captured by the hands of the Franks and remained in the custody of the city.

After their heads had been cut off, the heads were thrown into the bottom of a certain engine directed against the city, so that the enemy might suffer greater grief.

The count of Saint-Gilles and the bishop of Le Puy conferred together about how they might have a tower undermined, with crossbowmen and archers to defend them.

They dug beneath it as far as the foundations of the wall, placed posts and timbers beneath it, and then set fire to them. When evening came, the tower collapsed during the night; and because it was night, they were unable to fight the enemy.

That same night the Turks arose and rebuilt the wall so strongly that no one could have harmed them from that side.

When the Turks saw that they could obtain aid in no way, they sent word through an embassy to the emperor that they would willingly surrender the city to him, provided only that he allowed them to depart alive with their wives and children and all their possessions.

Then the emperor, filled with an evil purpose, ordered them to be brought safely and without fear to Constantinople. The Christians consented to this for the emperor’s sake.

They had been in that siege for seven weeks, and many of our men received blessed martyrdom for the name of Christ.

## THE CHRISTIANS FIGHT WITH SOLIMAN</numerusform
[Note: In the edition, Book III begins here.]

Meanwhile, after the city had been surrendered and the Turks had been led away to Constantinople, the emperor rejoiced more and more because the city had been brought under his authority, and ordered abundant food to be distributed to the poor.

After we had withdrawn from the city, we came on the first day to a certain bridge, and remained there for two days. At dawn on the third day, our men arose; and, not seeing how to keep to the road, they separated from one another. One part of the army—namely Bohemond, Robert the Northman, Tancred, and many others—went in different directions. The other part, namely Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles, Duke Godfrey, the bishop of Le Puy, the count of Flanders, and many others, proceeded by another road.

On the third day the Turks attacked Bohemond violently, together with those who were with him, shouting, shrieking, and uttering something—I do not know what—diabolical in their barbarous language. At once Bohemond, a most wise man, seeing innumerable Turks shouting and shrieking in the distance, ordered all the soldiers to dismount quickly and pitch the tents. But before the tents had been raised, he said to the soldiers:

“Most valiant soldiers of Christ, behold, the battle has been forced upon us, and now the enemy is above us on every side. Therefore let all the mounted soldiers go bravely to meet them, while the foot soldiers wisely and quickly pitch the tents.”

While this was being done, the Turks, already pressing upon us from every side, surrounded us, fighting, hurling javelins and darts, and shooting arrows far and wide. When we could neither resist nor endure the weight of so many enemies, we stood immovably in a single formation.

Our women also were a refuge for us on that day. They brought us water, encouraging us, fighting bravely, and protecting the men. Therefore the most wise Bohemond immediately sent word to the count of Saint-Gilles, the illustrious Duke Godfrey, Hugh the Great, the honorable bishop of Le Puy, and all the other soldiers that they should hasten to the battle. When they heard this, they first thought that it was a complete falsehood. For they did not believe that those who had once been defeated would again dare to rise and fight.

As soon as Duke Godfrey and Hugh the Great heard the message, they came with their armies. The bishop of Le Puy followed them, as did Count Raymond with a large force. When they saw the innumerable multitude of Turks, Arabs, Saracens, and others whom it would take too long to enumerate, they were astonished, since all the mountains, hills, valleys, and every level place, above and below, were everywhere covered with that excommunicated people or race.

A secret discussion then took place among us, as we praised and advised one another, saying:

“Be wholly united in the faith of Christ and in the victory of the banner of the holy cross, for today, if it pleases God, you will all become rich.”

Immediately the battle lines were arranged. On the left were Bohemond, Robert the Northman, the prudent Tancred, Robert of Ansa, and Richard of the Principality. The bishop of Le Puy came by another mountain route and surrounded the unbelieving Turks on every side. On the right were the most prudent soldier, Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles, the venerable Duke Godfrey, the fierce soldier, the count of Flanders, Hugh the Great, and many others whose names I do not know.

As soon as our soldiers arrived, the Turks, Arabs, Saracens, Agulans, and all the barbarian nations rapidly fled by the mountain passes and across the open ground. The number of Turks, Saracens, Publicans, Persians, Agulans, and other pagans was three hundred and sixty thousand, apart from the Arabs, whose number no one knows except God.

When they had fled with great speed as far as their tents, they were unable to remain there long. They took flight again, and we pursued them, killing them throughout the day. We seized much booty: gold and silver, horses and donkeys, camels, sheep and cattle, and many other things that we do not know how to name.

Yet if the Lord had not been present in the battle and had not quickly sent another army, not one of our men would have escaped. But almighty and merciful God, who did not allow his soldiers to perish or fall into the hands of their enemies, promptly sent them assistance.

Who could ever be so wise or learned as to dare to describe or foresee their wisdom, military skill, and courage? They had thought that they could terrify the Frankish people with the threat of those arrows, just as they had terrified the Arabs, Saracens, Armenians, Syrians, and Greeks. But, if God wills, it will never be seen, done, said, or even imagined that they possess such power.

Nevertheless, they say that they are of Frankish stock, and they say that no man is naturally meant to be a soldier except the Franks and themselves. I shall tell the truth in every respect, which no one will dare to forbid. Certainly, if they had been firm in the faith of Christ and in holy Christianity, and had believed with a right mind and faith in the one who remains in the Trinity, was born of the Virgin Mother, suffered and rose again, and thereafter sent perfectly the consolation of the Holy Spirit, reigning equally in heaven and on earth, no one could have been found more prudent, stronger, or more ingenious in warfare.

There two honorable men were killed: Geoffrey of Mont-Scabioso and William, the son of the marquis and brother of Tancred, as well as other mounted and foot soldiers whose names I do not know.

What more should I say about the Turks’ prudence and courage? They are exceedingly fierce, carrying on their shoulders bows, arrows, and quivers filled with poison; by nature they are most warlike, boasting, as we have said, of Frankish descent. But almighty God subdued their previously untamable pride through the humility of the Christians.

The battle lasted from the third hour until the ninth hour. This battle took place on the first day of the month of July. Therefore blessed be God in all things, who delivered the impious. Amen.

## Here Soliman Is Defeated by the Franks

[Note: The beginning of Book IV in the edition.]

After the enemies of God and of holy Christianity had been utterly defeated and had fled here and there for four days and nights, it happened that, while Soliman, their commander and the son of the elder Soliman, was fleeing from the city of Nicaea, he encountered one day ten thousand Arabs. They said to him:

“O unhappy and most wretched of all the gentiles, why are you still fleeing in terror?”

Soliman answered them tearfully:

“Once, indeed, when I had defeated all the Franks and thought that I already had them bound in captivity, as I was gradually intending to bind them together, I looked behind me and saw such an innumerable multitude of them that, if you or anyone else had been there, he would have thought that all the mountains, hills, valleys, and level places were filled with their multitude. When we saw them, we immediately began to take a sudden course of flight, fearing them so greatly that we scarcely escaped from their hands. Hence we are still in great terror. And if you are willing to believe me and my words, get away from here; for if they merely learn of you, scarcely one of you will remain alive.”

When they heard this, they began to turn their backs and scattered throughout Romania, but … [lacuna] our army pursued the most wicked Turks, who were fleeing daily before them.

Those Turks came to every camp or city, deceived and mocked its inhabitants, and said:

“We have defeated all the Christians and overcome them, so completely that none of them will ever again dare to stand before us. Only allow us to enter inside.”

Once they entered, they plundered the churches, houses, and everything else; they took away with them horses and donkeys, gold and silver, mules, and whatever else they could find. They also took Christian children with them, and burned and devastated everything suitable or useful, fleeing and greatly fearing our presence.

Our men pursued them through deserts, waterless regions, and uninhabitable country, from which we scarcely escaped alive. Hunger and thirst pressed us on every side, and we had absolutely nothing to eat, unless perhaps we pulled and rubbed ears of grain with our hands; on such food we lived in the greatest misery.

There the greater part of our horses died. Consequently many of our soldiers remained on foot; because of the scarcity of horses, oxen served us in place of mounts, and in our extreme necessity, does, rams, and dogs sufficed to carry our belongings.

Meanwhile we began to enter an excellent land, full of worldly goods and other delights—in short, full of every good thing—and thereafter approached Iconium. The inhabitants of that place advised and urged us, bringing along with them skins filled with water, because for a day’s journey there was an extreme scarcity of water. We followed their advice until we reached a certain river, where we remained for two days.

Our couriers went ahead until they reached Heraclea, where a great multitude of Turks had gathered, waiting and lying in ambush to discover how they might harm the soldiers of Christ. When the soldiers of almighty God found these Turks, they boldly attacked them. With God’s consent our enemies were defeated that day and turned their backs in flight.

Our men immediately entered the city and remained there for four days. Tancred, an honorable and very fierce soldier, the son of the marquis, and Baldwin, an illustrious count and brother of Duke Godfrey, separated from the others and together entered the valley of Borentot.

Tancred separated from them and came to Tarsus alone with his soldiers. The Turks came out of the city to meet them; they gathered together and prepared for battle against the Christians. Our men approached and fought them, and all our enemies fled, returning quickly to the city.

The prudent and honorable soldier of Christ Tancred reached the camps before the city gate with loosened reins. From the other side came the most wise Count Baldwin with his army, asking and begging the fierce soldier Tancred to graciously receive him into the city as a partner. Tancred said to him:

“I utterly deny you entry into this city.”

When night came, all the terrified Turks suddenly took flight together. The inhabitants came out in the darkness of night, shouting and saying in a loud voice:

“Run, unconquered Franks, run, for the Turks, awakened by fear of you, are all departing together.”

As night withdrew and light gradually began to rise, the city’s leaders came and voluntarily surrendered the city. They said to those who were quarrelling among themselves:

“Stop now, lords, stop for the moment, for we demand and ask that the man who fought so bravely with the Turks yesterday should rule and reign over us.”

The remarkable Count Baldwin, quarrelling and disputing with the most prudent Tancred, said:

“Let us enter together and strip the city; let whoever can get more have more, and let whoever can seize something seize it.”

Tancred opposed him, saying:

“Far be this from me! I do not wish to strip Christians. The inhabitants of this city have chosen me to be their lord, and they desire to have me.”

At last Tancred could not continue struggling with the learned Count Baldwin, because Baldwin had a very large army. Nevertheless, willingly or unwillingly, he let him have his way and withdrew bravely with his army.

Two excellent cities were thus surrendered, namely Athena and Mamistra, together with many fortresses.

The larger army—Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles, Bohemond, Duke Godfrey, and many other princes—entered the land of the Armenians, thirsting and burning for the blood of the Turks. At last they reached a certain fortress so strong that they could do nothing against it.

There was a certain man named Simeon who had been born in that region. He asked them for this land so that he might defend it from the hands of the Turks. They willingly gave him the land, and he remained there with his people.

We departed from there and happily reached Caesarea of Cappadocia. Leaving Cappadocia, we came to a very beautiful and exceedingly fertile city, which the Turks had besieged shortly before our arrival for three weeks, but had been completely unable to conquer. As soon as we arrived there, it immediately surrendered into our hands with great joy.

A certain soldier named Peter of Alup requested this city from all the lords, so that he might defend it in fidelity to God, the Holy Sepulchre, the lords, and the emperor. The lords freely granted it to him with great affection.

As day withdrew and night approached, Bohemond heard that the Turks who had been besieging the city were frequently moving ahead of us. He immediately prepared himself with soldiers alone, intending to fight them everywhere, but he could not find them.

Afterward we came to a city named Coxan, which was exceedingly fertile and well supplied with every good thing necessary for us. The Christians—namely, the inhabitants of that city—immediately surrendered themselves, and we remained there quite comfortably for three days. Our men were greatly restored there.

When Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles heard that the Turks who had been guarding Antioch had departed, he resolved in council with his men to send people there to guard it carefully. At last he chose those whom he wished to send: Peter of Castellion, viscount; William of Montpellier; Aral, viscount; Peter of Roias; and Peter Raymond of Alphul [Note: “Of Altopullo,” R. of Agiles, p. 150, line XLVIII.], with five hundred soldiers.

They came into a valley near Antioch, to a certain fortress of the Publicans, and there they learned that Turks were in the city and were preparing to defend it vigorously. Peter of Roias separated from the others and, on the following night, passed near Antioch. He entered safely the valley of Rugia, found Turks and Saracens, fought them, killed many of them, and pursued the others vigorously. He sent Count Raymond a spear filled with the lips and noses of Turks.

When the Armenians—namely, the inhabitants of that land—saw that he had decisively defeated the pagans, they immediately surrendered themselves to him. He at once seized the city of Rursia and many fortresses.

We who had remained behind departed from there and crossed a diabolical mountain region, which was so exceedingly high and narrow that none of our men dared go ahead of another along its track or on the path that opened across the mountain. Horses plunged over the precipices there, and one pack animal caused another to fall.

The soldiers therefore stood sadly on every side, clapping their hands in extreme sadness and grief, uncertain what they should do with themselves and their weapons. They sold their shields, excellent coats of mail, and helmets for only three or five denarii, or for whatever more they could obtain. Those who could not sell them threw them away for nothing, “in numere” [reading uncertain], and continued on.

Leaving that accursed mountain region, we came to a city called Marusim [Note: Marasin. Bal. Book II, p. 101; Marasin. Guib. [Book IV, p. 499.]].

[Col. 0776D] The inhabitants of that city came out joyfully to meet us, bringing a very large market. There we had an ample supply of everything while awaiting the arrival of Bohemond.

Our soldiers then came and approached the valley in which the royal city of Antioch is situated, the capital of all Syria. The Lord Jesus Christ handed it over to blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, so that he might call it to the worship of the holy faith—he who lives and reigns, the triune and one God, throughout all ages. Amen.

## How the City of Antioch Was Besieged by the Christians

When we began to approach the Iron Bridge, our couriers, who customarily went ahead of us, found innumerable Turks gathered to meet them. They were hastening to bring assistance to Antioch. Our men rushed upon them with one heart and mind and wisely attacked them. The Turks were decisively defeated; all the barbarians were thrown into confusion and fled as quickly as possible, and many of them were killed in that engagement.

Our men, with God’s help, overcame them and took much booty: horses, mules, camels, and donkeys loaded with grain and wine.

Our men then arrived and made camp on the bank of the river. Immediately Bohemond rode out with four thousand soldiers and came before the city gate to watch whether anyone might secretly leave or enter the city by night.

On the following day, a Wednesday—12 Kalends of November—we reached the city of Antioch at midday. We wonderfully besieged three of the city’s gates, since we lacked a place for a siege on the other side, where an exceedingly high mountain confined us.

Our Turkish enemies, who were inside the city, towered over us on every side to such an extent that none of them dared attack any of our men for nearly fifteen days.

As soon as we lodged around Antioch, we found there an abundance of the dew of heaven: vineyards everywhere full, pits filled with grain, trees laden with pleasant fruit to eat, and many other good things useful as bodily nourishment.

The Armenians and Syrians who were inside the city came out and showed themselves as they fled. They were with us every day, although they had their wives inside the city. They cleverly investigated our being, condition, and character, and reported to those inside everything they saw being done outside.

After the Turks had learned about our strength and our actions, they gradually began to come out of the city and hem in our pilgrims on every side. They were not lying in wait for us in only one place, but everywhere, from the sea to the mountain.

Not far from the enemy there was a certain fortress called Aregh. A considerable number of very strong Turks had gathered there, and they frequently harassed our men.

When our soldiers, who were carefully searching for them, discovered the place where they were hiding, they went to meet them. As our men gradually retreated to the place where they knew Bohemond was hidden with his army, many of our soldiers were immediately killed there.

When Bohemond heard this, he rose at once like a most valiant athlete of Christ. The barbarians attacked there because our men were few; nevertheless, the two sides joined battle.

Many of our enemies were killed and captured. They were brought before the city gate and beheaded there, so that those inside the city would become even more sorrowful.

Others came out of the city, so that when they shot arrows they fell into Bohemond’s street. One day a woman was killed by an arrow.

All our leaders then gathered and held a council, saying:

“Let us build a fortress on the summit of Mount Maregart, the mountain above Bohemond’s enemy, so that we may remain there secure and safe from the strength of the Turks.”

After the fortress had been built and fortified, all the leaders diligently guarded it in turn.

By then grain and all bodily provisions had begun to become exceedingly expensive, before the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ. We dared go nowhere outside and could find absolutely nothing to eat in Christian territory. No one dared enter Saracen territory except with a very large force.

At last our lords adopted a plan, arranging how they might properly govern these peoples. They decided that one part of our force should diligently go out to obtain supplies and there guard the army, while another part should remain confidently to guard the enemy.

Bohemond therefore said:

“Lords and most prudent soldiers, if you wish it and it seems good and honorable to you, I shall go with the most prudent count of Flanders.”

After the solemn celebrations of the Nativity had been held most gloriously, they departed on Monday, that is, the second day of the week, together with more than twenty thousand mounted and foot soldiers, all healthy and unharmed, and entered Saracen territory.

Many Turks, Arabs, and Saracens had gathered from Jerusalem, Damascus, Aleppo, and that region … [lacuna] who were coming to strengthen Antioch.

When these men heard that a Christian force had entered their land, they immediately prepared for battle against the Christians. At first light they came to the place where our people were gathered together.

The barbarians divided themselves from one another and formed two battle lines, one in front and the other behind, wishing to surround us on every side.

The distinguished count of Flanders, armed on every side with the guidance of faith and with the sign of the cross—which he faithfully carried—went to meet them together with the most prudent Bohemond.
