Our men attacked them unanimously. They immediately took flight, rapidly turned their backs, and many of them were killed; the others remained alive and fled swiftly. From then on they went into the anger of perdition.

We returned with great rejoicing, praising and magnifying the triune and one God, who lives and reigns now and forever, unto the ages. Amen.

The Turks, enemies of God and of holy Christianity, who were guarding the city of Antioch, heard that Bohemond and the count of Flanders were not in the siege. They came out of the city and boldly attacked us, lying in wait everywhere, wherever they knew the siege to be weaker, since they knew that those most prudent soldiers were outside.

They discovered that on one Tuesday they could harm and resist us. The most wicked men came cautiously and attacked us violently, while we were unaware and ignorant of this battle. They killed many of our mounted and foot soldiers.

On that bitter day the bishop of Le Puy lost his seneschal, who carried and directed his banner. If there had not been a river between us and them, they would have attacked us more often and inflicted the greatest harm on our people. They even rode with loose reins into our tents.

The prudent Bohemond was returning with his army from Saracen territory. He came to Tancred’s mountain region, considering whether he might find there something that could be defended, and sent men to search the entire land [Note: “By spying and searching on every side,” which the interpolator did not understand. It is French.]. Some found something; others returned empty-handed.

Those who could not find anything hastened to return immediately. Then Bohemond rebuked them severely, saying:

“O unhappy and most wretched people! O most worthless and most sorrowful of all Christians! Why do you wish to leave so quickly? Stay now, stay. How long shall we all remain gathered together? Do not wander like sheep without a shepherd. If our enemies find you wandering, they will kill you, for they keep watch and guard day and night so that they may find us separated or alone, without any leader; they labor daily to kill us and lead us into captivity. What will you do, wretches?”

When he had finished speaking, he looked before and behind him and found himself alone on every side. Nevertheless, with those whom he was able to find, he returned to his army, more empty-handed than laden.

When the Armenians, Saracens, and Greeks saw that our men had returned utterly empty-handed and had brought nothing with them, they deliberated together and departed through the mountains and known paths. They carefully sought out and bought grain and bodily provisions, which they brought to the army, where hunger was immense. They sold one donkey-load for eight purple coins, which were valued at one hundred and twenty silver solidi.

Many of our soldiers died there because they did not have the means to buy such expensive provisions.

William the Carpenter and Peter the Hermit, knowing the immense unhappiness and misery that afflicted them, took counsel together and secretly departed. Tancred pursued them, captured them, and led them back with great disgrace. William gave him his word that he would willingly return to the army and make satisfaction to the lords.

All night he lay in Bohemond’s tent—an ill business indeed. At dawn the next day he came shamefacedly into Bohemond’s presence.

Bohemond addressed him, saying:

“O unhappy disgrace of all France! O dishonor and crime of the province of Gaul! O most wicked of all whom the earth supports! Why did you flee so shamefully? Perhaps you wished, through this wicked act, to betray these soldiers and the army of Christ, as you betrayed others in Spain?”

He remained completely silent, and no word came from his mouth.

All the Franks then gathered together and humbly asked Bohemond not to do anything worse to him. He said:

“I shall willingly do this for your love, provided that he swears with all his heart and mind that he will never turn back from the journey to the Holy Sepulchre, whether circumstances are good or bad, and that he will not consent to any harm being done to Tancred, either by himself or through any of his friends.”

When he heard these words, William immediately agreed willingly.

Afterward William the Carpenter, overcome by shame, did not remain long but secretly departed.

God granted us this poverty and misery because of our sins. In the entire army no one could find a thousand soldiers who possessed good horses.

Therefore [Note: Tetigus. Tyre, Book II, final chapter, p. 664, where he is called Tatinus; concerning this passage, Book IV, chapter 21, p. 694. Taticus, Raymond of Agiles, p. 145. Tatingus, Baldwin, Book II, p. 103.] a certain wealthy and noble soldier from the emperor’s army, whom the emperor had entrusted to the Franks so that he might lead them properly and receive the land, once liberated from the hands of the Turks, in the emperor’s allegiance—this unhappy man heard that the Turkish army had come against us. He groaned, supposing that everyone had perished and fallen into the hands of our enemies.

He fabricated and devised every deceitful scheme that he could continually contrive, and said to them:

“Lords and most prudent men, see that we are compelled to remain here in this extreme necessity, and that no help reaches us from anywhere. Now allow me to return to my homeland in Romania; without any doubt I shall return to you. I shall arrange for many ships to come here by sea, loaded with grain, wine, barley, meat, flour, cheese, and every good food that is necessary. I shall also arrange for horses to be brought for sale, and I shall quickly arrange for a market from the emperor’s territory to come here. Behold, I shall faithfully swear to you that I will keep all these promises. Moreover, my household servants and my tent will continually remain in the field. Do not be incredulous in any way; believe firmly that I shall return to you as quickly as possible.”

That enemy departed and left everything of his in the field, with the result that then, now, and forever he will be perjured.

Thus great necessity came upon us. The Turks pressed us on every side, and none of our men now dared go outside the tents; such was the fear of the Turks. They confined us on one side, while cruel hunger hemmed us in on another. We were extremely wretched and sorrowful. Our leaders too were in great fear. We lacked all relief and assistance.

The common and poorest people fled, some to Cyprus, some to Romania, and others into the mountains. We did not dare go to the sea because of fear of the worst Turks; no route was open to us at all.

# BOOK THREE BEGINS

[Col. 0781]

## The Christians Again Fought with the Turks

Meanwhile our princes heard that an innumerable multitude of Turks had come against us, and they took counsel, saying:

“Behold, an innumerable Turkish army has come against us. What shall we do? We are not strong enough to fight them on two fronts. Let us therefore divide ourselves into two parts. One part of the soldiers shall remain continually to guard our tents and resist those who are in the city. The other part of the soldiers shall ride together to meet our enemies who are camped near us in a castle called Areg, beyond the Iron Bridge.”

When evening came, they went out from the tents and held a council, saying:

“Let us all go against our enemies, who, as we are told, number twenty-five thousand. But let the bishop of Le Puy, Robert the Northman, and Count Eustace remain to guard against those who are in the city.”

At first light they sent some of their soldiers to observe the Turkish army, where it was and what it was actually doing. These men went out and began carefully searching for the places where the Turkish battle lines were concealed.

Immediately they saw them coming separately from the direction of the river, divided into two battle lines; their main strength was coming behind.

Our men therefore returned quickly, saying:

“Behold, behold, they are already coming. Let everyone be ready on every side, for they are already near us, as you can see.”

Our men decided that each of the leaders should arrange his own battle line independently. They immediately formed six battle lines. Five of them went together to attack the Turks. The count of Flanders was at the head of the first. Bohemond gradually moved backward with his line.

When our men joined battle successfully with the Turks, each man struck down another. Their shouting echoed to heaven, and showers of missiles darkened the air.

When the main strength of the Turks, which was behind, arrived, it attacked our men fiercely, so that our men began to withdraw slightly. When Bohemond saw this, he groaned. He then ordered his constable, Robert son of Gerard, saying:

“Remember the prudent men of old and our brave ancestors—what they were like and what wars they fought.”

That man armed himself with the sign of the cross like a most valiant athlete, and, as a wise and prudent man, attacked them while carrying Bohemond’s banner.

When the other battle lines saw that Bohemond’s banner was being carried so wisely before the others, they turned back and attacked the Turks unanimously.

Our men numbered seven hundred, while the Turks numbered twenty-five thousand. But by God’s grace all the Turks were astonished, took flight, and immediately turned their backs.

Our men pursued them, overcoming and cutting them down. The Turks returned quickly to their own camp. Those who remained alive seized everything they could find there, stripped the entire camp, set it on fire, and fled.

The Armenians, Syrians, and Greeks, knowing that the Turks had unquestionably lost the battle, came out and kept watch in the narrow places. They killed and captured many of them.

Thus, with God’s consent, our enemies were defeated that day. A sufficient number of horses and many other things that were extremely necessary to them were recovered.

After taking much booty, they led many of those enemies away alive and brought many heads of the dead before the city gate, where the envoys of the Emir of Babylon had pitched their camp; these were sent to Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles and the other lords.

Those who had remained in the tents fought all day with those who were in the city, before the city’s three gates.

This battle took place on the Tuesday before the beginning of Lent, on the fifth day before the Ides of February, with the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

Therefore our men returned, with God bringing this about, rejoicing in the triumph that they had achieved that day over their enemies. These were everywhere completely defeated, fleeing, wandering here and there, and straying: some entered Khorasan, while others entered the land of the Saracens.

When our leaders and elders saw that our enemies in the city were treating us harshly and constraining us—for day and night they kept constant watch and lay in ambush, seeking whatever place might enable them to harm and distress us—[Col. 0782C] they assembled in council and said:

“Before we lose God’s people and our own, let us build a fortress at Macomaria, which lies before the gate where the bridge is; perhaps there we shall be able to constrain our enemies.”

All agreed to this counsel and approved it as a good thing to undertake. The Count of Saint-Gilles spoke first:

“Assist me in building the fortress, and I shall fortify and guard it.”

Bohemond replied:

“If you wish it, and the other lords approve, I will go with you to the port of Saint-Simeon and carefully bring from there the men who can faithfully carry out this work. Let those who remain fortify themselves on every side for defense, in case our enemies—and God’s enemies—should come out of the city; and let them all assemble in that place, namely where we shall indicate.”

And so it was done. The count and Bohemond therefore went to the port of Saint-Simeon.

We who remained assembled together at the place where we were to begin the fortress were then seen by the Turks. They prepared themselves and immediately came out of the city to meet us in battle. They fell upon us, put us to flight, and killed many of our knights. For this we were sad and grieving.

On the following day, when the Turks saw that our leaders were not at the siege, but had fought the previous day at the port, all the principal men of the Turkish army prepared themselves and marched out to meet those who were coming from the port. When they saw the count and Bohemond approaching with the people from the port, they immediately began to shriek, chatter, and shout with the loudest cries. They surrounded our men on every side, shooting arrows, wounding them, and cruelly cutting them down with swords.

They attacked our men so fiercely that they fled through the nearest mountain passes and wherever the road lay open. Whoever could escape by swift steps got away alive; but whoever could not flee received martyrdom for Christ’s name.

On that day more than a thousand of our knights and foot soldiers were martyred. Rejoicing, they ascended to heaven, bearing the white robe of their received martyrdom, glorifying and praising the triune and one God, in whom they triumphantly rejoiced. In harmonious voices they said:

“Why do you not defend our blood, O our God, which today has been shed for your name?”

Bohemond did not take the road that the others had followed. Instead, he came more swiftly with a few knights, their reins loosened, until he hurried to us, who were assembled together beyond the Pharphar River. Then, inflamed with anger at the slaughter of our men, invoking Christ’s name and trusting in the path of Christ’s holy sepulchre, we joined together and advanced against them for battle, attacking with one heart and one spirit.

Our enemies and God’s enemies stood everywhere astonished and greatly terrified. They had thought that they would defeat and kill us as they had the people of Count Raymond and Bohemond. But almighty God by no means wished to permit this.

Then Duke Godfrey, the most powerful soldier of Christ, rushed upon them with drawn sword and struck a certain exceedingly fierce pagan so manfully that he divided him into two parts, from the crown of his head down to the horse’s saddle [Note: [Col. 0783D] See Tyre, Book V, chapter 6, p. 701; and Albert of Aachen, Book III, chapter 65, p. 238; Robert the Monk, [Col. 0784D] Book IV, p. 50, and Book IX, p. 75.]. By God’s providence, although the man had been split in two, he did not fall completely from the horse.

Afterward Godfrey attacked another from the side and cut him through the middle. From that moment the greatest terror and horror struck all the enemies of Christianity—not only those who were present, but also all who could in any way hear of it.

Then the duke, worthy of all remembrance, pursued them as they fled. Rushing upon now these, now those like a mighty lion, he cut them down and hurled them into the river. In the same way Hugh the Great, the Count of Saint-Gilles, Bohemond, the Count of Flanders, and the other nobles slaughtered them and cast them into the river.

There was no place for flight except across the bridge, which was then extremely narrow for them; and as they obstructed one another, they were drowned in the river. The true soldiers of God, protected everywhere by the sign of the cross, rushed upon them with great ferocity [Col. 0784A] and attacked them bravely.

The Turks seized a rapid flight across the middle of the narrow bridge, to their own destruction. Those who could not cross alive because of the overwhelming multitude of people and horses there met eternal death and surrendered their wretched souls to the devil and the ministers of Satan.

We, overcoming them, drove them into the river with our deadly spears. Everywhere the wave of the swift river seemed to flow red with Turkish blood. If any of them tried to crawl across the bridge’s pillars, or, wounded while swimming, attempted to reach the shore, we drove him back from every point along the riverbank, killing him in the force of the rushing stream.

The uproar and shouting of our men and theirs resounded to heaven [Col. 0784B]. A shower of missiles and arrows covered the sky and the daylight; loud voices were heard inside and outside the city.

The women of the city came to the windows in the Christian wall, watching the Turks’ miserable fate, and secretly clapped their hands, as is their custom. The Armenians, Syrians, and Greeks, by order of the principal Turkish tyrants, shot swift arrows every day, willingly or unwillingly.

In that battle twelve Amiralios of the Turkish host were killed in soul and body, together with 1,500 other wise and valiant soldiers who had defended the city most effectively by fighting. Those who remained alive no longer dared to shout or chatter, by day or by night, as they had formerly done.

Thus no one separated us from them [Col. 0784C] except the night. Night therefore divided the two sides as they fought, cast weapons, and shot arrows. By the power of God and of the holy sepulchre, our enemies were defeated, to such an extent that afterward they could no longer show such strength either in voice or in action as before.

That day we were greatly refreshed by their horses and by many other things that were quite necessary for us.

On the following day, at first light, some other Turks came out of the city and gathered all the stinking corpses of the dead Turks that they could find along the riverbank, except those hidden in the riverbed. They had them buried at Macomaria, which lies beyond the city bridge before the gate.

With them they buried cloaks, gold bezants, bows and arrows, and many other implements that we cannot name. When our men heard that the Turks had buried their dead, they immediately all prepared themselves, hurried to the devil’s court, ordered the bodies to be disinterred, broke open their tombs, and dragged them out of their graves.

They threw all their corpses into a certain pit and carried the severed heads to our tents, so that their number might be accurately known, except that four horses laden with their heads were taken to the sea to the messengers of the Amir of Babylon [Col. 0785A].

When the Turks saw this, they were exceedingly sad and grieved almost to death. Weeping every day, they could do nothing but weep and howl.

On the third day, when it arrived, our men, assembled together in joy and exultation, began on that same day to build the fortress already mentioned, using the same stones that we had removed from above the buried bodies of the Turks.

When the fortress was completed, we immediately began prudently to constrict our enemies on every side; their swollen necks had now been reduced to nothing. Each of our leaders built part of this fortress with a massive embankment and wall, and they constructed two towers in Macomaria.

We then moved safely here and there, to the port and to the mountain, praising and glorifying [Col. 0785B] our Lord God with joyful, happy, harmonious voices. To him be honor and glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## Raymond Erected His Fortress against the City

All our leaders and princes entrusted this fortress to Raymond of Saint-Gilles for its defense, because he had more knights in his household than the others and could provide more. He guarded the fortress with his army. With him were Gaston of Béarn with his men; Peter, Viscount of Castellon; Raymond, Viscount of Turenne; William of Montpellier; Geoffrey; Peter Raymond d’Alpoz; and William of Sabran. All these, and many others with their men, were with him.

Raymond of Saint-Gilles also retained by agreement, to guard the fortress, as many knights—that is, retainers—as he could procure for pay.

One day the Turks came out of the city and approached the fortress. They surrounded it on every side, shouting and shooting arrows, wounding and killing our men, so that even our tents were covered with embedded arrows. Had assistance not come from another army, they would have inflicted immense damage upon us.

Seeing this, our men immediately arranged to make a great *talpa*—a siege engine—with which they could pierce the bridge; and they made it. One day the battle turned upon the bridge, and they brought up the *talpa*. Many Turks were killed, and the bridge was pierced.

But at night, while we slept, the Turks came out of the city, burned the *talpa*, and repaired the bridge. For this Christ’s army was exceedingly angry.

On another day the Turks brought upon the city wall one of our noble knights, named Rainald Porchet. They had long held him in a harsh prison. They told him to speak with Christ’s pilgrims, so that they might redeem him for a great ransom before he lost his head.

When he was upon the wall, he spoke to the leaders and said to our men:

“Lords, my worth is now no greater than if I were already dead. Therefore I beg you, as my brothers, not to offer any ransom on my account. But remain secure in the faith of Christ and of the holy sepulchre, because God is with you and always will be. You have killed all the leading and bravest men of this city—namely, twelve Amiralios and 1,500 nobles—and no one remains who dares to fight you or defend the city” [Col. 0786A].

The Turks asked their interpreter what Rainald was saying. He told them:

“He is saying nothing good about us.”

Then Cassianus, the Amiralius, immediately ordered Rainald to come down from the wall and said to him through the interpreter:

“Rainald, do you wish to live honorably with us and rejoice?”

Rainald replied:

“How shall I be able to live honorably with you without sin?”

The Amiralius said:

“Deny your God, whom you believe in and worship, and believe in Malphium and our other gods. If you do this, we shall give you everything you ask for—gold and silver, horses and mules, and many other ornaments that you may desire—and we shall enrich you with wives and inheritances and the greatest honor” [Col. 0786B].

Rainald replied:

“Give me time in which I may come to an agreement with myself.”

The Amiralius agreed willingly and granted it.

Then Rainald threw himself upon the ground, his hands joined in prayer, facing east, humbly asking God to help him and graciously to receive his soul into Abraham’s bosom.

When the Amiralius saw this, he called the interpreter and asked him:

“What is Rainald saying?”

The interpreter replied:

“He has in no way denied his Lord God.”

When the Amiralius heard this, he became exceedingly angry. He immediately ordered Rainald to be beheaded, and the Turks beheaded him with great joy.

The angels promptly received his soul and joyfully carried it before the sight of the Lord, for whose love he had accepted martyrdom.

Then the Amiralius was vehemently angry because he had been unable to convert Rainald to his gods. He immediately ordered all the pilgrims who were in the city to be brought before him, their hands tied behind their backs.

When they had come before him, he ordered them all to be stripped naked. Once they had been stripped, he had them tightly gathered together and bound in a circle with a rope. He ordered wood, straw, and hay to be arranged around them, and then, as an enemy of God, had fire put to it.

The Christians—that is, Christ’s soldiers—shrieked and cried out greatly. Their voices resounded to heaven, to God, for whose love their flesh and bones were burned in the fire. Thus all these men were martyred on a single day, carrying white robes into heaven before God, for whose love they had faithfully suffered these things. Our Lord God was reigning, to whom be honor and glory unto ages of ages. Amen.

Since all the roads had now been closed to the Turks, except on that side of the river where there was a fortress in a certain monastery—and if it were fully strengthened, no one would dare to leave the city gate—the leaders among us took counsel together and unanimously said:

“Let us choose one of our number who will hold that fortress firmly and bravely block our enemies from the mountains, the plain, and the entrance to and exit from the city.”

Many of them refused to undertake its defense unless perhaps a large number were together. Tancred therefore came forward first before the others and said:

“Nevertheless, if I knew what benefit would come to me, I alone, with my men, would carefully strengthen the fortress and completely block the road along which our enemies are accustomed frequently to rage.”

They immediately promised him 400 silver marks. Tancred did not hold back, although he was alone; nevertheless, he went with the most honorable knights and servants. At once he seized and blocked the road on every side from the Turks, and he did not withdraw on account of grass, wood, or any other necessities.

Tancred remained there with his men and began vigorously to constrict the city everywhere. On that very day a large part of the Armenians and Syrians came safely from the mountains, carrying provisions to the Turks in aid of the city. Tancred met them, immediately seized them and everything they were carrying—grain, wine, oil, and other things of this kind.

Thus Tancred proceeded successfully and firmly. He had all the roads and paths blocked and cut off from the Turks until Antioch was captured.

I cannot recount everything that we did before Antioch was captured. I wish to explain a little about what was done, or how matters came about afterward. I say “a little” because no one in these regions, whether cleric or layman, can entirely tell or narrate how the event actually took place.

Meanwhile there was an Amiralius of Turkish origin named Pyrrus, who had formed a very close friendship with Bohemond. Bohemond often approached him through messengers sent between them, asking him to receive him most amicably within the city. He freely promised him Christianity and ordered that he be made rich and greatly honored.

Pyrrus agreed to these promises and said:

“Nevertheless, I guard three towers, and I willingly promise them to him. At whatever hour he wishes, I shall voluntarily gather him into them.”

Bohemond was therefore already confident of entering the city.

One day, rejoicing and with a tranquil face and serene mind, he came to all the other leaders and addressed them with cheerful words in this manner:

“Most prudent warrior-men, see how we have all been cast into extreme poverty and misery, both great and small, and how we are utterly ignorant from which side success may come to us. Therefore, if it seems good and honorable to you, let us unanimously permit whichever one of us you choose to attempt, by whatever means or device, to acquire or outwit the city, either personally or through others.”

They all firmly rejected and denied this, saying:

“This city will never be granted to anyone; all of us shall possess it equally. Just as we have endured equal labor, so shall we receive equal honor from it.”

When Bohemond heard these words, he withdrew at once with an almost imperceptible smile.

Not long afterward all our leaders heard news of the army of our enemies—the Turks, Publicans, Angulans, Azimites [Col. 0788A], and many other pagan nations whose number and names I cannot recount.

Immediately all the leaders assembled together and held council, saying:

“Since Bohemond may be able to acquire the city, either personally or through others, we willingly and voluntarily grant it to him, provided that, if the emperor comes to our aid and wishes to fulfill the entire agreement as he promised and swore to us, we shall lawfully return it to him. Otherwise, let Bohemond possess it under his own authority.”

Bohemond then began every day humbly to entreat his friends, preceding his request with the greatest humility and speaking in a gentle voice as follows:

“Behold, we now truly have a suitable time in which we can accomplish whatever good we wish. Therefore let my friend Pyrrus help me.”

Pyrrus, greatly pleased by the message, said that he would help him as he ought.

When the following night came, Pyrrus cautiously sent his son as a pledge to Bohemond. To make him still more secure about entering the city, he sent him this message:

“Let him have the whole Frankish people publicly proclaimed tomorrow, so that they may go to plunder the land of the Saracens and then quickly return by the left-hand mountain. I shall be on the alert, awaiting those troops, and I shall receive them into the towers that I guard.”

Bohemond immediately ordered one of his servants, named Malacrown, to be summoned. He instructed him to proclaim to the great mass of the Franks that they should faithfully prepare to go into the land of the Saracens [Col. 0788C].

And so it was done.

Bohemond therefore entrusted this plan to Duke Godfrey, the Count of Flanders, the Count of Saint-Gilles, and the Bishop of Le Puy:

“If it pleases God, Antioch will be delivered to us this very night.”

All these arrangements were made. The knights held the plains, and the foot soldiers the mountains. They fought throughout the night and until near dawn. Then they began to approach the towers that Pyrrus was guarding.

Bohemond immediately came down and addressed them all:

“Go with confident hearts and happy unity, and climb by the ladders into Antioch, which, if God wills, we shall soon have in our keeping.”

They came to the ladder, which had already been raised and firmly fastened to the city walls. Nearly sixty of our men climbed it and divided themselves among the three towers that Pyrrus guarded.

When Pyrrus saw that so few of our men had climbed up, he immediately began to panic. Fearing for himself and for our men, lest they fall into the hands of the Turks, he said:

“Micro Francos echomai”—that is, “I have few Franks. Where is Bohemond? Where is the invincible knight?”

Meanwhile a Lombard servant came down and ran as quickly as possible to Bohemond, saying:

“Why are you standing here, prudent man? Why have you come here? Behold, we already possess the three towers.”

The man was moved, and with all the others—who were rejoicing and exulting—he reached the ladder.

When those who were below in the towers saw them, they began to shout in joyful voices:

“God wills it.”

We likewise said the same.

They immediately began to climb up marvelously. They climbed into one tower and hastened to the others. Whoever they found there they instantly condemned to death; they also killed Pyrrus’s brother.

Meanwhile, the ladder by which our men had climbed happened to break. Immense distress and sadness arose among us, and we were all immediately stunned and grieving.

Although the ladder had broken, there was a certain gate beside us on the left, closed and unknown to some of us—for it was night. Nevertheless, by searching, feeling our way, and carefully investigating where it lay hidden, we all ran to it. After breaking it open, we entered through it.

An innumerable uproar was already resounding marvelously throughout the entire city. Bohemond did not remain there. He ordered an honorable banner to be carried up before the castle on a certain mountain.

All together, the people in the city shrieked terribly.

At first light, those who were outside at the tents heard an exceedingly great uproar echoing through the city. They hurried out and saw Bohemond apart on the mountain. They all ran swiftly and came together, each to his own gate. They entered the city and killed the Turks and Saracens whom they found there outside the castle. Some of the Turkish soldiers, however, went out through the gates and escaped alive by fleeing.

## The Death of Cassianus: How He Was Killed by the Syrians

Cassianus, their lord, greatly terrified of the Frankish people, fled completely with many others who were with him. In his flight he reached Tancred’s territory, not far from the city.

Their horses were exhausted, so they entered a certain rural settlement and went into a house. The inhabitants of that mountainous region—namely, the Syrians and Armenians—recognized him. They immediately seized him, cut off his head, and offered it before Bohemond, so that they might fully receive their freedom.

His belt and *gaina*, that is, his scabbard, were valued at sixty bezants.

All the streets of the city were now filled everywhere with the corpses of the dead, so that scarcely anyone could pass through the city’s paths except by treading on the corpses of the Turks.

All this happened on the third day after the beginning of June, on a Thursday. Blessed therefore be God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# BOOK FOUR BEGINS

[Col. 0789]

[Col. 0789C] While Cassianus, mentioned above, was still in Khorasan, Curbalan, the commander of the army of the Sultan of Persia, had sent him an embassy to Antioch, asking him to come to his aid at the proper time, because the most powerful and vigorous Frankish people were besieging him severely in Antioch. If Curbalan faithfully supplied assistance, Cassianus would immediately surrender the city of Antioch into his hands or enrich him with a very great gift.

When Curbalan had already gathered a very large Turkish army over a long period and had received permission from their apostolic Caliph to kill Christians, he immediately began the long journey to Antioch.

The Amiralius of Jerusalem was with him and with his army. The king of Damascus also arrived there with a very large force. He gathered countless pagan peoples from every side: Turks, Arabs, Saracens, Publicans, Azimites, Kurds, Persians, Agulans, and many other peoples whom no one could name or number.

The Agulans numbered 3,000. They feared neither spears nor any weapons, because they were entirely covered with iron, as were their horses. They would carry no weapons into battle except swords.

All these people came to the siege of Antioch to disperse the Frankish host. When they approached the city, Sanzedona, son of Cassianus, the Amiralius of Antioch, came out to meet them. He immediately ran to Curbalan, tearfully begged him, and said:

“O most invincible prince, I humbly beseech you; with humble devotion I entreat your wisdom to come to my aid, because the Franks are besieging me on every side in the city of Antioch and hold the city under their authority. They also demand that we be removed from the region of Romania, or Syria; and the people of Khorasan demand this as well.

“They have carried out everything they desire. They have also killed my father, and nothing remains except for them to kill me and you and all those of our lineage by the sword. I have long awaited your arrival faithfully, to see whether you would come to my aid in this danger.”

Curbalan replied:

“If you wish me to be entirely beneficial to you and faithfully to aid you in this danger, first place that city in my hands. Then you shall see how beneficial I shall be to you, and I shall have my men guard it.”

Sancedola also said:

“If you can kill and cut down all the Franks and carefully deliver their heads to me, I shall faithfully give you the city mentioned above. Thereafter I shall become your man, your vassal, and shall guard this city in your fealty.”

Curbalan replied:

“It will not be as you think and imagine. Commit that fortress into my hands.”

Whether he wished it or not, Sancedola immediately committed the fortress to him.

On the third day after we entered the city, their scouts ran ahead before the city. Their army encamped at the Iron Bridge, assaulted a Turkish tower, and killed everyone whom they found there. No one escaped alive except their lord, whom we later found bound in iron chains, after the greater battle had taken place on the eve of the blessed apostle.

On the following day, when the pagan army had moved, they approached the city and encamped between two rivers. They remained there for two days.

After receiving the fortress, Curbalan immediately summoned one of his Amiralios, whom he knew by reputation to be truthful, gentle, and peaceable. He said to him:

“I want you to enter this fortress under my authority and guard it. For a very long time I have known you to be exceedingly faithful, and therefore I ask you to hold this city with the greatest care. I also know that you are most prudent in action, and I can find no one here more truthful or courageous.”

The Amiralius replied:

“I would always wish to obey you in such a duty, but before you spur me to it, I shall do this on the condition that, if the Franks drive you from the deadly battle, I shall immediately return this fortress to them.”

Curbalan said:

“I know you to be so honorable and prudent that I shall certainly consent to whatever good you wish to do.”

Curbalan then hurried back to his army in the valley where it was encamped.

Immediately the Turks, mocking the Frankish host, brought before Curbalan a very worthless sword covered with rust, a very wretched wooden bow, and a highly useless spear, which they had recently taken from poor pilgrims. They said:

“Behold the weapons that the Franks have brought against us for battle.”

When Curbalan saw these weapons, he began to laugh openly and said to everyone in that host:

“These are the warlike and polished weapons that the Christians, born in the western land—namely, in [Col. 0791C] Europe, which is the third part of the world—have brought against us in Asia. With these weapons they think and trust that they can drive us out and repel us beyond the borders of Khorasan, and erase all our names beyond the rivers of the Amazons. Those are the men who drove all our ancestors from Romania and from the royal city of Antioch, which is the honorable capital of all Syria.”

He immediately summoned his faithful notary and said:

Here Curbalan sent letters to the Sultan of Persia and to the apostolic Caliph.

[Note: [Col. 0791D] Robert the monk, Book VI, p. 57 and following.] “Write, therefore, quickly, several letters to be read in Corosan, in this manner:

‘To our apostolic Caliph, and to our lord king, the sultan, the most valiant warrior, and to all the most prudent warriors of Corosan: greeting and boundless honor. Let them be sufficiently cheerful and rejoice in pleasant concord; let them satisfy their bellies, exercise their will, and converse throughout that entire region; and let them wholly give themselves over to wanton luxury, rejoicing whether they may beget many sons who can prevail mightily in war against the Christians. Let them gladly accept these three weapons, which we once took from the Frankish troop, and now learn what weapons the Frankish people brought against us, and how excellent and perfect they are. Alas! They wished to fight against our weapons, which have been purified twice, thrice, or even four times, like silver or the purest gold.

Let everyone also know that I have all the Franks shut up inside Antioch, and [Col. 0792A] that I hold the fortress entirely at my own discretion. They are down below in the city. I now have them all in my power: either I shall make them undergo capital punishment, or I shall lead them captive to Corosan in the greatest captivity, because they threaten to drive us away and expel us beyond the borders of Corosan with their weapons, or to erase all our names beyond the rivers of the Amazons, or to drive us beyond Upper Judaea—although they have driven all our ancestors out of the whole of Romania and Syria.

Therefore I swear to you now by Muhammad and by all the names of the gods that I shall not return into your presence until, with my strong right hand, I have acquired royal Antioch, all Syria, Romania, and Bulgaria as far as Apulia, for the honor of the gods, and of you, and of all our Turks.’”

Thus he brought his speech to an end. But the mother of that same Curbalan, who was in the city of Aleph, immediately approached him tearfully and said: “Son, are the things I hear true?” He replied: “What things?” And she said: “I have now heard that you intend to wage war against the Frankish people.” He replied: “Nevertheless, you must know that this is entirely true.”

She said: “I appeal to you, son, by the names of the gods and by your great courage and immense goodness: do not be willing to wage war together with the Franks. For you are an unconquered warrior, and I have never heard of any folly arising from you or your army; nor has anyone ever found you fleeing from the field before a victor. Your military renown has been spread from east to west, and all prudent warriors tremble when they hear your name. We know well, son, that you are powerful in war, strong, and ingenious in battle, and that no Christian or pagan people has ever been able to possess any strength in your presence. They fled merely on hearing your name, just as sheep flee before a lion’s fury.

Therefore I beg you, dearest and most beloved son, to heed my counsels, and never let it remain in your mind or be found in your deliberation that you wish to begin a war together with the Christian host.”

Then Curbalan, hearing his mother’s admonitions, answered at last in harsh speech: “What is this, mother, that you tell me? I think that you are insane, or filled with madness. In truth, I have with me alone more Amiralios than there are Christians, great or small.”

His mother replied: “O sweetest son, the Christians cannot fight against you. I know this well: they themselves are not capable of engaging you in battle, but their God fights daily on their behalf, defends them day and night by his protection, and watches over them like a shepherd who watches over his flock. He does not allow them to be harmed or disturbed by any people; and whoever wishes to oppose them, their God immediately confounds, as he himself says through the mouth of the prophet David: ‘Scatter the nations that have not called upon your name, O Lord’ (Ps. LXXVIII, 6).

Before they are prepared to begin the battle, their most excellent and warlike God, together with his saints, already has all their enemies defeated. How much more will he now act against you, since you are his enemies and are preparing with all your strength to oppose them?

Know this truly: these Christians are called the sons of Christ; through the mouths of the prophets they are the sons of adoption and promise, and through the Apostle they are ‘heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ’ (Rom. VIII, 17). Christ has already given them the inheritances promised to them, saying: ‘From the rising of the sun to its setting, or toward the west, your borders shall extend, so that no bold man shall stand against you.’ And who can contradict or resist these words?

Certainly, if you begin this war against [Col. 0793B] them, it will bring you the greatest loss and disgrace. You will lose many of your warriors, surrender all the spoils you possess, and be driven into a very great flight. Yet you will not die now in this war, but you will lose everything you possess in this battle. For that reason I tell you that you will not die now, because their God does not immediately judge one who offends him by displaying his anger; but when he wills, he punishes with open vengeance. I fear that he will judge you with punitive sorrow, and I tell you now that you will die this year.”

Curbalan, deeply grieved in his inmost being, replied after hearing his mother’s words: “Dearest mother, I beg you: who told you these things about the Christian people—that their God loves them so greatly, that he retains in himself the greatest power for fighting, that those Christians will defeat us in the battle at Antioch, that they will seize our spoils in this battle, that they will pursue us with immense victory, and that I shall die this year by a sudden death?”

Then his mother replied, speaking in sorrow: “Son, it is more than a hundred years since it was found written in your books and in the volumes of all the gentiles that the Christian people would come against us, defeat us everywhere, reign over the pagans, and that our people would everywhere be subject to them. But I do not know whether it will now come again.

Thus, in my grief, I did not cease to follow you into the most beautiful city of Aleph. There, by observing and searching cleverly, I looked upon the stars of heaven; by astutely applying my intelligence and diligently examining the planets of heaven, the twelve signs of the zodiac, and countless lots, I discovered in them that the Christian people would defeat us everywhere. Therefore I fear greatly and mourn exceedingly, lest I remain deprived and unhappy because of you.”

Curbalan said to her: “Sweetest mother, tell me everything that is doubtful in my heart.”

She replied: “I shall gladly do this, dearest, if I truly learn what is unknown to you.”

He said to her: “Then Boamundus and Tancredus are not gods of the Franks, and did they not rescue them from the persecution of all their enemies?”

His mother replied: “Dearest son, Boamundus and Tancredus are mortal, like other men; but their God loves them above all others and supplies them daily with greater power for battle than he gives to others. For their God—the Almighty is his name—is the one who made heaven and earth, founded the seas, and all that is in them; his throne is in heaven, prepared forever, and his power is to be feared everywhere.”

Her son said to her: “If that is the case, I shall not cease to fight them.”

When his mother heard that he would in no way heed her counsels, she withdrew in intense grief to the city of Aleph, taking with her all the spoils she was able to carry away.

On the third day Curbalan armed himself, and a very large part of the Turks with him, and they came to the city on the side where the fortress stood. Our men, intending to resist, entered the city whether they wished to or not. Its gate was so extraordinarily narrow and confined that many there were crushed to death by the press of others. Meanwhile, some fought outside the city and others inside, on Thursday, throughout the entire day until evening.

On Friday they likewise fought throughout the whole day, and killed many of our men. On that day a certain most distinguished warrior was wounded, namely Arveus Tudebodus. His companions carried him down into the city; there he remained alive until Saturday, and between the ninth and sixth hours he departed from this world, living in Christ.

A certain priest, Peter, his brother, buried his body before the western gate of the church of blessed Peter the apostle, while he and all the others who were in the city were in the greatest fear, as though they might lose their heads. We beg all who read or hear this to give alms and prayers, and to say them for his soul and for the souls of all the dead who died on the road to Jerusalem.

The next day Guillelmus of Grentamasnil, his brother Albericus, Ivo of Grentamasnil, Guillelmus of Bernonvilla, Guido Trosselus, Guillelmus son of Richardus, and Lambertus Pauper—all of them terrified by fear of the previous day’s battle, which had continued until evening—secretly let themselves down over the wall during the night and fled on foot toward the sea, so that nothing remained on their hands or feet except their bones. Many others fled with them, whom I do not know how to name.

When they reached the ships that were at the port of Saint Simeon, they said to the sailors: “Why do you wretches remain here? They are all dead, and we have scarcely escaped death, because the Turkish army has surrounded us on every side in the city.”

When the sailors heard this, they stood astonished and terrified with fear, rushed into the ships, and put out to sea. Then the Turks arrived; they killed those whom they found, burned with fire the ships that remained in the riverbed, and seized their spoils.

Finally, we who remained were unable to bear the burden, nor could we carry the weapons of those who were in the fortress. We therefore built a wall between ourselves and those who kept watch day and night. At times we were so severely oppressed that we ate horses and donkeys. On the other side we were in the greatest terror of the Turks, so much so that many of our leaders wished to flee by night, as others had done.

One day, while our leaders were standing sadly and sorrowfully on the mountain above, in front of the fortress, not knowing what they ought to do, a certain priest named Stephanus came to them and said:

“Lords, if it pleases you, hear something that I saw. While I was lying last night in the church of Saint Mary, the mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior of the world appeared to me with his mother Mary and blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. The Lord stood before me and said: ‘Stephanus, do you recognize me?’

“I replied: ‘I recognize you in no other way than that I see a cross on your head, as on our Savior.’

“The Lord said to me: ‘I am he.’

“Then I immediately fell at his feet, weeping and humbly begging him to help us in the oppression of that accursed people who held us shut up in the city.

“The Lord replied to me: ‘I have helped you well, and I shall help you well. I allowed you to possess the city of Nicaea; after conquering all the wars, I brought you here; I have felt compassion for the misery you suffered during the siege of Antioch. And now, at the proper time, I have sent you healthy and unharmed into the city as a great aid.

“‘But many Christians are doing a very wicked thing, because they lie with pagan women, from which an immense stench rises into heaven.’

“Then the blessed Virgin Mary and blessed Peter the apostle fell at his feet, asking and entreating him to help his people who remained in this distress, saying:

“‘Lord, for a long time the pagan people held our churches, in which they committed many unspeakable evils. But now that the Christians have expelled the enemies, your angels rejoice in heaven.’

“Then the Lord said to me again:

“‘Stephanus, go and tell my people to return to me, and I shall return to them. Within five days I shall send them great assistance. Every day let them sing “Congregati sunt,” etc., with the verse. Let them undertake penances, make processions through the churches barefoot, give alms to the poor, have Masses celebrated by priests, and receive communion in the body and blood of Christ. Thus let them begin the battle, and I shall send them blessed George, Theodore, and Demetrius as aid, together with the pilgrims who died on this road to Jerusalem.’

“This is what the Lord told me. And all you leaders, if you do not believe that this is true, let me now climb the highest tower and throw myself down. If I remain safe and unharmed, believe that this is true. But if I suffer any injury, behead me and throw me into the fire.”

Then the bishop of Le Puy ordered the Gospels and a cross to be brought, and made him swear that it was true. Afterward, at that hour, all our leaders took counsel and swore that none of them would flee from the city as long as they remained alive, neither in death nor in life. Boamundus is said to have sworn first, then the count of Saint-Gilles, Robert the Norman, Duke Godefridus, Robert count of Flanders, and the other leaders.

Tancredus swore in this manner and promised that as long as he had forty warriors with him, he would not return—not only from that city, but even from the road to Jerusalem. Therefore the whole Christian army rejoiced exceedingly.

There was also a certain pilgrim from our army named Petrus Bartholomaeus. Before we entered the city, the apostle Saint Andrew appeared to him and said: “What are you doing, good man?”

He replied: “Who are you?”

The apostle said to him: “I am Andrew the apostle. Know, son, that when you have entered the town, go to the church of blessed Peter the apostle. There you will find the lance of our Savior Jesus Christ, by which he was wounded while hanging upon the cross.”

After saying all this, the apostle immediately departed. But Petrus, fearing to reveal the apostle’s command, did not wish to tell our men, namely the pilgrims. They thought that he had seen a dream.

On another occasion Saint Andrew appeared to him again and said: “Why did you not tell the pilgrims what I commanded you?”

He said to him: “Lord, who would believe this?”

At that hour Saint Andrew took him and carried him within the city to the place where the lance was hidden in the ground. While he watched, Saint Andrew the apostle drew the lance from the earth and placed it in his hands, saying: “This is the lance of our Lord Jesus Christ, which my brother the apostle Peter and I placed here.”

While he watched, he put it back in the same place and afterward said to Peter: “Return to the army.”

He replied: “Lord, how can I go? The Turks are already upon the walls of the city, and when they hear of me they will immediately kill me.”

The apostle answered him: “Go; do not be afraid.”

Then Petrus began to leave the city in the sight of all the Turks, and they said nothing to him.

The Turks who were in the fortress separately were pressing our men so severely that one day they shut three of our warriors in a tower situated in front of their fortress. The gentiles came out and attacked them so fiercely that the three could not withstand their strength. Two of them came out of the tower wounded, while the third defended himself manfully throughout the whole day against the Turkish assault. He fought so skillfully that on that day he felled the Turks at the entrance to the wall with a broken spear. That day he broke three spears in his hands. His name was Hugo lo Forsennet, from the army of Goffredus of Monte-scabioso.

Boamundus ordered the city to be set on fire.

When Boamundus and Tancredus saw that they were entirely unable to lead the people up the mountain before the fortress for battle, since some were shut up in their houses by fear of hunger and others by fear of the Turks, they became exceedingly angry. Boamundus therefore immediately ordered fire to be set to the city, on the side where the palace of Cassianus the Amiralius stood.

When those who were in the city saw the fire burning and rising so high, they abandoned their houses and fled with their spoils toward the mountain—some before the fortress, others before the gate of the count of Saint-Gilles, others before [Col. 0797A] the gate of Duke Godefridus, and each to his own people.

Then Boamundus was very sorrowful, fearing that the church of Saint Peter and the church of Saint Mary would burn, because the fire continued from the third hour until midnight. Nevertheless, two thousand churches and houses were burned. When midnight came, the wind ceased and the fire fell.

Thus the Turks living in the fortress fought with us inside the city day and night, and nothing separated us except weapons. At times the other four Amiralios came out with them; all of them were covered with gold, and their horses likewise, up to the joints of their knees. Those Amiralios led them.

Our men saw this and could not endure it for long, for the one who had bread was not allowed to eat, and the one who had water was not allowed to drink. Then our men built a wall between ourselves and the mountain and constructed something like a fortress, together with engines, so that they might be secure.

Another part of the Turks had encamped around the city in a valley on the opposite side. When night came, fire descended from heaven. It appeared in the west and fell within the Turkish army. The Turks and our men were greatly astonished by this.

When morning came, the Turks were shaken with fear and fled here and there because of the terror of the fire. Nevertheless, they besieged us so closely around the city that none of our men dared leave or enter the city except secretly by night.

We were so oppressed and so besieged by those pagans, the enemies of holy Christianity, that they numbered [Col. 0797C] three hundred and sixty-five thousand, apart from the Amiralius of Jerusalem, who was with them with his people. The king likewise came from the city of Aleph.

These profane enemies of God held us shut up in the city of Antioch so tightly that many died of hunger, for a small loaf of bread was sold for one gold bezant. I shall say nothing of wine, except that what I drank was *grassem*, that is, not wine. One hen cost fifteen solidi, one egg two solidi, one nut one denarius, three or four beans one denarius, a small she-goat sixty solidi and nine denarii, and a camel’s tongue, which is small, four solidi.

They ate and sold the meat of horses and donkeys. They boiled fig leaves, vine leaves, and tree leaves in water and ate them. Others put the hides of horses, donkeys, camels, oxen, or buffaloes—dried for six or five years—into water for two nights and one day to soften them; afterward they boiled and ate them.

We suffered these anxieties and many other hardships that I cannot name for the sake of Christ’s name and to liberate the road to the holy sepulchre. Thus the servants of God endured such tribulations, hunger, and fears for twenty-six days.

Count Stephanus departed with his army.

Thus the imprudent Stephanus, count of Chartres, who was our leader and whom all our chiefs had chosen to be the commander of our men, pretending that he was overcome by a very serious illness, disgracefully withdrew to another fortress called Alexandreta before Antioch was captured.

Every day we awaited his arrival, hoping that he would come to our aid, for we were shut up in the city and deprived of saving assistance. But after he heard that the Turkish people had surrounded and besieged us in the city, he climbed the nearest mountain, which overlooked all the mountains around it and stood near Antioch.

When he saw the countless tents, he was greatly terrified and withdrew. Seized by this excessive fear, he suddenly and disgracefully fled with his army in great haste. When he reached his fortress, he stripped it bare and then imprudently retraced his path at a swift pace.

[Col. 0798B] The emperor Alexius withdrew through fear of the Turks, and Guido lamented Boamundus his brother with great mourning.

After he came to meet the emperor at Philemia, Guido approached him secretly and called him aside, saying: “Know for certain that Antioch has been captured, while the fortress has not yet been captured at all, and our men are besieged in grievous oppression. As I believe, they have already been killed by the hands of the Turks. Therefore turn back as quickly as you can, so that they may not find you and the people whom you lead.”

Then the emperor, terrified by fear, secretly called Guido, Boamundus’s brother, and all the others, and said to them: “Lords, what shall we do? Behold, all our men are held fast by a close siege, and perhaps at this hour they have all been killed by the hands of the Turks or [Col. 0798C] led into captivity, as this wretched count, fleeing imprudently, reports. If you wish, let us turn back at a swift pace, so that we too may not die a sudden death, as they have died.”

When Guido, a most honorable warrior, heard these deceitful words, he immediately began to weep and howl with the others in the most vehement lamentation. With one voice they said:

“O true God, triune and one, why have you permitted this to happen? Why have you allowed the people who followed you to fall into the hands of their enemies? Why have you allowed those liberating the road of your journey and your holy sepulchre to die so quickly? Indeed, if what we have heard from these wicked men is true, we and the other Christians shall abandon you, nor shall we remember you any longer, and none of us will dare to invoke your name again.”

This speech was exceedingly sorrowful throughout the whole army, so that for many days none of our men—not archbishop, bishop, abbot, priest, cleric, or any layman—dared invoke the name of Christ.

No one could console Guido as he wept, struck his hands together, broke his fingers, and said:

“Alas for me! Boamundus, honor and glory of the whole world, whom the entire world feared and loved. Alas for me in my sorrow! I did not deserve, grieving, to see your most honorable face, although there was nothing I desired more to see. Who will grant me that I might die for you, sweetest friend and lord? Why, when I came forth from my mother’s womb, did I not die immediately? Why did I reach this mournful day? Why was I not drowned in the sea? Why did I not fall from my horse, break my neck, and suffer sudden death? Would that I had received a blessed martyrdom with you and seen you receive the most glorious end!”

When everyone came to him and comforted him, urging him to end his lamentation, he came to himself and said:

“Perhaps you believe this foolish half-grown soldier? I have never truly heard him speak about any military action that he had carried out. He withdraws disgracefully and dishonorably, like a most wicked and wretched man, and whatever the miserable fellow reports, know that it is entirely false.”

Meanwhile the emperor ordered his men: “Go, lead all the people of this land into Bulgaria, explore the whole region, and lay waste to every place, lest when the Turks come they be able to find anything here.”

Whether willingly or unwillingly, our men turned back, grieving and mourning bitterly unto death. Many of the pilgrims who were suffering from extreme illness died. Those who were too weak to continue with the army remained behind, dying on the road, and all the others returned to Constantinople.

How the lance of the Lord Jesus Christ was first found

While we were therefore confined within the city, Petrus Bartholomaeus came to the count of Saint-Gilles and told him to go to the church of Saint Peter, where the lance was hidden. When he heard this, the count went to the church with great joy.

Petrus showed him the place before the doors of the choir, on the right-hand side. Thirteen men dug there from morning until evening. When the pit had been made very deep, Petrus himself found the lance of Jesus Christ, just as blessed Andrew had indicated to him, on the fourteenth day after the beginning of June.

They took it up with great joy, singing the *Te Deum laudamus*, and carried it in praise to the altar. Thus there was immense joy throughout the whole city.

When the Frankish army heard this, they came with great joy to the church of Saint Peter to see the lance. The Greeks, Armenians, and Syrians likewise came, singing *Kyrie eleison* and saying: “Kalo Franci . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Christo”—that is, “The Franks are good, for they have the lance of Christ.”

The Christians sent messengers to Corbalan.

[Col. 0799D] Afterward they all held a council about how they should begin the war against the Turks. But first they all approved sending someone to Curbalan and the other Turkish enemies of God to ask them: “Why have you entered the land of the Christians?”

They sent Petrus the Hermit and Arluinus the dragoman, instructing them to ask: “Why have you entered the land of the Christians so boldly and arrogantly?”

When they arrived, they said to them:

“Know that our people are greatly astonished at why you have come here. But perhaps you have come here because you wish to become Christians and to believe in the one true God born from the Virgin Mary, in whom we believe.

“If you have not come here for this reason, all our leaders, both elder and younger, humbly ask you to withdraw quickly from the land of God and of the Christians. Blessed Peter the apostle preached this land long ago, recalled it to the worship of Christ, and was first chosen bishop there.

“If you do this, they permit you to take away with you all your possessions: horses, mules, donkeys, camels, sheep, oxen, and all your other goods.”

Then Curbalan, commander of the army of the sultan of Persia, together with all the Amirali, filled with swelling pride, answered in harsh speech:

“Since we neither desire nor wish for your God and your Christianity, and utterly reject you together with them, we have come this far because we are greatly astonished that your leaders and elders, or your lesser men, call that land yours—the land that we took by great force from effeminate peoples—and say that it belongs to them.

“Do you wish, then, to know what we shall say to you? Return as quickly as possible and tell your leaders that if they all become Turks and wish to deny your God, whom you worship by bowing down, we shall give them this land and much more besides: cities, fortresses, wives, and the greatest inheritances. Moreover, none of your men shall remain on foot; they shall all be warriors, as we are, and we shall always hold them in great friendship.

“Otherwise, let them know that they shall undergo capital punishment in every respect, or be led in chains to Corosan into perpetual captivity, and shall serve us and our children forever.”

The war begins

[Col. 0800C] Our messengers therefore frequently returned to the Christian Franks, reporting all these things and how this most cruel people had answered them.

Meanwhile our army, shaken on both sides, did not know what it ought to do. On one side, torturing hunger was constricting them; on the other, fear of the Turks was binding them.

Nevertheless, they did as the Lord Jesus Christ had commanded them through the priest Stephanus: they fasted for three days, confessed their sins, made processions from one church to another, received absolution, faithfully received communion in the body and blood of Christ, gave alms to the poor, and had Masses sung.

Then they formed six battle lines within the city. In the first was Hugh the Great with the Franks and the Flemish count Robert; in the second, Duke Godefridus with his army; in the third, Robert the Norman with his men; in the fourth, Adhemar, bishop of Le Puy, carrying with him the lance of our Savior Jesus Christ, with his people and with the army of Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles, who remained above at the fortress to guard the mountain, for fear that the Turks might descend into the city; in the fifth, Tancredus, son of the marquis, and Gaston of Béarn with their people and with the people of the count of Poitou; in the sixth, Boamundus with his army.

Our bishops, priests, clerics, and monks, clothed in sacred vestments, also went out with those from the city, carrying crosses in their hands, praying and entreating the Lord to save them, guard them, and rescue them from every danger and every evil.

Others stood upon the wall of the city gate, holding holy crosses in their hands, signing and blessing them. Thus arranged and protected by the sign of the cross, they began to leave the city through the gate situated before Machomaria.

When Curbalan saw the Frankish battle lines emerge so beautifully ordered, one after another, he said: “Let them all come out now, so that we may take their heads more easily.”

First the foot soldiers of Hugh the Great and of the Flemish count Robert came out, and afterward each division in its proper order. When they had come outside the city, Curbalan saw the distinguished Frankish people and was greatly afraid.

Immediately he ordered his Amiralius, who had everything under his charge at the tents, that if he saw a fire kindled at the head of the enemy, he should at once have his army proclaimed and return it backward, knowing that the Turks had lost the field.

Curbalan immediately began gradually to withdraw toward the mountain, while our men gradually pursued them. Finally the Turks divided: one part went toward the sea, while others remained there, thinking to enclose our men between them.

When our men saw this, they formed a seventh battle line from the division of Duke Godefridus and the count of Normandy, and its leader was Count Rainaldus. They sent it to meet the Turks who were coming from the sea.

The Turks fought with them and killed many of our men by shooting and arrow fire. Our other troops formed themselves from the river to the mountain, a distance of two miles.

Saint George, Saint Theodore, and Saint Demetrius came to aid the Christians.

The Turkish troops began to emerge from both sides and surrounded our men everywhere, hurling javelins, shooting arrows, and wounding them. Countless armies also came out from the mountains, leading white horses, whose banners were all white.

When our men saw this army, they did not know who they were until they recognized them as the aid of Christ, just as he had commanded them through the priest Stephanus. Their leaders were Saint George, blessed Theodore, and Saint Demetrius.

These things should be believed, because many of our men saw them.

Those Turks who stood on the side of the sea, seeing that they could endure no more, set fire to the grass so that those at the tents, seeing it, would begin to flee. When the men at the tents recognized this signal, they seized all their honorable goods and spoils and fled.

Our men, meanwhile, gradually fought their way toward the place where the enemy’s greatest strength lay, namely, toward their tents. Duke Godefridus, the Flemish count Robert, and Hugh the Great rode beside the water, where the enemy’s greatest strength was.

These, first fortified by the sign of the cross, attacked them with one accord. The Turks and the other pagans cried out diabolical sounds in a foreign language and began to flee.

Our men, invoking the one living God, rode against them; thus, in the name of Jesus Christ [Col. 0802A] and of the holy sepulchre, they began the battle, and with God’s help defeated them.

The Turks, terrified, took flight, and our men pursued them to their tents. The soldiers of Christ preferred to pursue them rather than acquire any spoils. They pursued them as far as the Iron Bridge, and from there as far as Tancredus’s fortress.

The Turks left there their tents, gold and silver, many ornaments, sheep and oxen, horses and mules, donkeys and camels, grain, wine and flour, and many other things that were necessary for us.

The Armenians and Syrians who lived in those regions, hearing that the Turks had been defeated, ran toward the mountain to meet them and killed as many of them as they found.

Our men returned with great joy, praising [Col. 0802B] and blessing God, who had given victory to his people.

The Amiralius who was guarding the fortress, seeing Curbalan and all the other pagans fleeing from the field, became extremely angry and felt the greatest fear in his heart. Immediately, with great haste, he began asking for the Franks’ banners.

The count of Saint-Gilles, who was standing on the mountain before the fortress, ordered a banner to be carried to him. He received it with joy and carefully placed it in the highest tower.

The Amiralius surrendered himself to Boamundus, who was guarding the fortress, and received baptism.

Afterward he requested Bohemond’s standard, and after the battle Bohemond gave it to him. The emir (Ammiralius) also received it with the greatest joy and gladness, and reached an agreement with Bohemond that those pagans who wished to become Christians would remain with him, while those who wished to go to Khorasan would be allowed by him to depart unharmed and without injury. Bohemond agreed to everything Ammiralius requested and immediately sent his men into the castle. Not many days later Ammiralius was baptized together with those who wished to acknowledge Christ. Those who did not wish to abandon their own laws Bohemond had escorted as far as the land of the Saracens.

This battle was fought on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, on the vigil of the Apostles Peter and Paul, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigned—to him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

And when all the enemies of God had been defeated—and to God and the most high and holy Sepulchre we render worthy praises—fleeing here and there, some half-alive and others wounded, they fell dead in valleys and woods, in fields and on roads. For the Greeks, Armenians, and Syrians, knowing that they had been defeated in battle, lay in ambush for them in narrow places, wounding and killing them. Our pilgrims, however, returned to the city, rejoicing and exulting in the greatest and most blessed triumph over the enemies of God and of holy Christianity.

Then all our leaders assembled and held a council in the church of Saint Peter concerning how they might successfully govern and lead this people until they could begin the journey to the Holy Sepulchre, for whose sake they had faithfully endured many necessities. It was therefore determined in the council that at that time they could not enter the land of the Saracens, because in the summer season it was extremely dry and without water. They did not dare to travel by that route, or to lead, govern, and conduct the people of Christ along it. Nevertheless, they set a deadline at the Kalends of November, namely the feast of All Saints, so that on that day everyone would be assembled from all directions at Antioch and would then begin the road to the Holy Sepulchre with the greatest joy. For everyone alike approved this plan, which was also honorable to carry out.

Afterward each of our leaders departed for his own territory, namely to the cities and castles, until that deadline approached. All the leaders had proclamations made throughout the entire city that if anyone there was in need and lacked some gold or silver, and wished to enter into an agreement with them, he should not hesitate to remain faithfully, because they would willingly provide whatever had been agreed upon.

There was a certain knight from the army of Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles, whose name was Raymond Piletus. This knight also retained many knights and retainers with him. He therefore went out of the city with them and entered the land of the Saracens, passing beyond two pagan cities. He reached a certain castle called Talamanite. The inhabitants of that castle, namely Syrians, surrendered it to him.

### Here Raymond Piletus is defeated.

After they had stayed there for eight days, messengers came to him, saying that nearby there was a Saracen castle filled with pagan people. The soldiers of Christ immediately marched to this castle and attacked it from every side. With God’s and the Holy Sepulchre’s help, it was promptly captured by them. They seized all those pagans. Those who wished to accept Christianity and desired holy baptism they kept alive; those who in no way wished to accept Christianity they immediately condemned to death.

Our men therefore returned with great joy to the first castle. On the third day they went out and came to a certain city called Marra, which was nearby. Many Turks, Arabs, Saracens, and other pagans from the city of Aleppo, Damascus, and the other castles around it had gathered there. The barbarians therefore came out against them for battle. Our men expected to fight them, but the barbarians immediately began to flee; then, turning back, they fought with our men throughout the entire day until evening.

When our men, because of the excessive heat, could no longer endure such thirst—for no spring could be found there to refresh them—they wished to return safely to their castle, but they could not. Because of their sins or offenses, the Syrians and the common people, terrified on the one hand by extreme thirst and on the other by excessive fear, immediately began fleeing back to their castle. But when the Turks saw them withdrawing, they at once attacked them with the greatest uproar. Nor is this surprising: victory was supplying them with strength.

There, along with many others who happily surrendered their souls to God—for whose love they had gathered there—a certain excellent knight, Arnaldus Tudebodus, was killed. When the battle was over, our men who had survived returned to their castle, where they stayed for several days. The others who had remained in the city of Antioch were experiencing the greatest joy and gladness, because they did not know that this had happened to their companions.

### Here died Adhemar, bishop of Le Puy, of blessed memory.

[Col. 0804B] Meanwhile Adhemar, bishop of Le Puy, a Father wholly worthy of veneration and worthy of God, was overcome by a serious illness. By God’s will he departed from this world and, resting in peace, fell asleep in the Lord, in the bosom of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, on the feast of Saint Peter in Chains. His most holy soul rejoices with the angels.

Therefore there was the greatest anguish and tribulation, and immeasurable sorrow, throughout the whole army, because he was the supporter of the poor and the counsel of the rich. He himself ordained clerics, preached to the knights, and admonished them, saying:

> “None of you can be saved unless you honor the poor clerics; and you cannot be saved without them, nor can they live without you. Therefore they must beseech God in daily prayer on behalf of your sins, since you offend him in many ways, which ought never to happen. You must govern and nourish them, because they do not know how to seek or obtain things as you do. I ask you, for the love of God, to love them and to support them insofar as you are able.”

### How the city of Albara was captured.

Not long afterward the venerable Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles entered the land of the Saracens and reached a certain city called Albara. He attacked it with his army and, by God’s will, captured it. He killed all the Saracens whom he could find there, both men and women, old and young. After immediately bringing it under his authority, he recalled it to the faith of Christ. He began to seek the advice of his wisest men so that he might devoutly choose a bishop for this city, one who would faithfully convert it to the worship of God and consecrate the devil’s house as a temple to the living and true God and as a pure-hearted sanctuary of the saints.

Afterward he chose a certain cleric and brought him to the city of Antioch to be consecrated. This man later held counsel in the place of Adhemar, bishop of Le Puy.

# BOOK FIVE BEGINS

[Col. 0805]

### Concerning the journey to Jerusalem.

In the year 1098, as the appointed time approached, namely the feast of All Saints, our leaders returned to the city of Antioch, except Bohemond, who had been stricken by a serious illness in the regions of Romania. For that reason he was unable to come by the same appointed time. When the time arrived at which he was able to travel, he quickly came to the city of Antioch, where the others had assembled.

Then all the leaders assembled together and began to consider how they might undertake the journey to the Holy Sepulchre, saying:

> “For the time is good and most favorable. Why do you delay any longer?”

But Bohemond was seeking each day the agreement which all the other leaders had made, namely concerning the surrender of the city. He was especially pressing Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles, because Raymond did not wish to bind himself by any agreement with Bohemond, fearing that he would commit perjury against the emperor.

Nevertheless, they often assembled in the church of Saint Peter to render a just judgment between them: Bohemond, Raymond of Saint-Gilles, Duke Godfrey, Robert the Norman, and other leaders both great and small, so that they might reconcile them. Bohemond recited his agreement before all who were listening, and the Count of Saint-Gilles recited his. He recounted the words and the oath he had sworn to the emperor on Bohemond’s advice.

The bishops, Duke Godfrey, Count Robert of Flanders, Count Robert of Normandy, Count Eustace, and the other leaders separated from the others and entered the cathedra of Saint Peter. The cathedra was there so that in that church they might distinguish between the two sides.
