But, fearing that the journey to the Holy Sepulchre might be abandoned, they did not wish to pronounce judgment openly.

When Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles saw this, he said:

> “Before the journey to the Holy Sepulchre is abandoned, if Bohemond wishes to come with you, whatever the bishops, Godfrey, Robert the Norman, Count Robert of Flanders, and the other leaders approve, I shall willingly carry out, preserving my loyalty to the emperor.”

Bohemond approved this and agreed, and so both men made this promise into the hands of the bishops, in the presence of the pilgrims of the Holy Sepulchre.

Then Bohemond took counsel with his men about how to fortify the castle on the high mountain with good weapons and provisions that would not run out for a long time. Raymond of Saint-Gilles likewise fortified the palace of Cassian the emir and the tower above the bridge gate, on the side facing the port of Saint Simeon.

### Concerning the situation of Antioch.

Only a little need be said about the city. This city is very large, beautiful, and distinguished, because within its walls are four enormous and exceedingly high mountains. On the highest of them a castle has been built, extremely strong and very lofty.

Below lies a distinguished and well-appointed city, adorned with every honor, since it contains the most beautiful waters that flow down from the mountains. Twelve hundred churches have been built in it, and it contained three hundred and sixty monasteries of monks. Under his authority the patriarch holds one hundred and fifty bishops.

The city is enclosed by two walls. The larger wall is exceedingly high and wonderfully broad, constructed of great stones, and has four hundred and fifty towers arranged along it. In every respect the city is beautiful.

On the east it is enclosed by four great mountains. On the west, beside the city walls, flows a great river called the Pharphar. Because it is so good and so beautiful, they did not foolishly wish to abandon the royal city of Antioch, which possessed such authority that previously seventy-five kings had established it. Their names are these:

Murgulandus, Elirandons, Lamulafres, Rademons, Elias, Brumandus, Margorias, Pharaoh, Brumandus, Brelion, Laidus, Rudandus, Judas Maccabaeus, Nubles, Samson, David the heretic, Solomon, Pilate, Herod, Elidius, Gaferius, Rudandus, Gaclerius, Morplurius, Fortis Castrius, Maraon, Argolas, Ordocius, Fortis-Lamusteo, Alapres Ammiralius, Morabilis, Orgilandus, Morabilis, Morlianus, Organdus the impious of Saramania, Brajerandus, Morus the King, Fulcher, Darandus, Ariandon, King Thanas, Esconius, Duras, Dormandus, King Vision, Sicharius, Tobias, Lintion, Malardus, Deiramordus, Mordandus, Oralionus, Brumornel, Apparandus, Effrenion, Noirandus, Fortis-Bruas, Gorgandus, Udonus the impious, Tomandus, Tolandus, Delufres, Troandus, King Candelos, Rambulandus, Gazami, Mirmion, Oringes, Brulion, Maxdolienes, Bariandus, Barilion, Gazianus, Bronurius, and Antiochus, who was the leader of the others; from him Antioch is said to have received its name.

The pilgrims of the Holy Sepulchre held this city under siege, as you heard above, for eight months and one day. Afterward they were shut inside it for twenty-six days by the Turks and other pagans. Nevertheless, with God’s and the Holy Sepulchre’s help, after those enemies had been defeated, the pilgrims rested in Antioch with great joy and gladness for five and a half months.

[Col. 0806D] The city of Marra is besieged by the Christians.

On the eighth day of the month of November, Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles departed from Antioch with his army. He came through one city called Lica and another called Albara. On the fourth day thereafter he reached the city called Marra, where a very large multitude of Saracens, Turks, Arabs, and many other pagans had gathered.

The next day Count Raymond attacked it with his people, but he could not capture it, because it was not God’s will. Not long afterward Bohemond followed Raymond with his army and encamped near the city on Sunday. On Monday they attacked the city so fiercely from every side that, if ladders had been raised to the city wall, the city would have been in our power. There they fought at close quarters with lances and swords.

But the strength of the pagans was so great that our men could do them no harm, and they suffered many hardships there. Food was running out, since they did not dare to go anywhere in search of it; such a multitude of pagans surrounded them on every side.

### Saint Andrew appeared to Peter Bartholomew.

When blessed Andrew, who does not sleep but always watches over the afflicted Christians, saw this, he announced to Peter Bartholomew that if the Christians repented of their evil deeds, maintained good faith toward one another—as the Lord commanded, saying, “Love your brothers as yourselves”—and restored the portion which he himself had retained as his own when he created the world and all the creatures in it, namely a tenth of all possessions, he would give them the city within a short time and fulfill all his will.

He commanded that this aforementioned portion, namely the tenth, be divided into four parts: one to be given to the bishop, another to the priests, another to the churches, and another to the poor. After this had been recited in the council, everyone consented.

Not long afterward Raymond of Saint-Gilles had a strong and very high wooden siege tower made. This tower was designed and built on four wheels, and many knights stood upon it, with Euvard the huntsman sounding trumpets loudly. Before it, honorable standards were displayed. It was very beautiful to behold.

Under the tower were more than one hundred armed knights, who brought it close to the city wall beside a certain tower. When the pagan people saw this, they immediately made many engines with which they hurled enormous stones at the tower, so that they nearly killed our knights. They pierced the standards above with arrows; others struck them with stones; still others cast Greek fire upon the tower, thinking that it would burn. But the merciful and compassionate God did not permit it to burn.

The next day it loomed over all the walls and towers of the city. Our knights who were above on the upper platform—namely William of Montpellier and many others—hurled immense stones at the Saracens standing on the city walls. They struck them so hard upon their shields that both shield and pagan fell dead down into the city.

They also placed standards upon spears, and in this way, with lances and iron hooks, the pilgrims thought they could drag the defenders toward them. Knights and retainers fought with such courage, while priests and clerics, clothed in sacred vestments, prayed and implored the Lord Jesus Christ to defend his people, grant victory to the Christian soldiers, exalt his holy Christianity, and destroy paganism.

Then a certain most honorable knight, Golferius of the Towers, was the first to climb by a ladder onto the wall; the ladder was immediately broken by the multitude of the defenders. Once Golferius was on the wall, he began to fight them with his lance, killing them.

Others found another ladder, quickly raised it to the wall, and climbed up. So many knights and foot soldiers ascended that the wall could scarcely contain them. The Saracens therefore attacked them so vigorously along the city wall and from within the city, shooting arrows and thrusting at close quarters with their lances, that many of our men, terrified by fear, threw themselves down from the wall.

Those most prudent men who remained on the wall endured their assault. Others who were beneath the tower were digging below the city walls. When the Saracens standing on the wall saw that our men had dug into the city wall, they were immediately terrified and fled into the city.

All this happened on Saturday, at evening, when the sun was setting, on the eleventh day from the beginning of the month of December.

Bohemond therefore had the leading Saracens addressed through an interpreter, telling them to place themselves, with their wives, children, and other possessions, in a palace above the gate; he would protect them from the death sentence.

All our men entered the city, and whatever good things they could find in houses and pits, each man kept as his own. On the following day, wherever they found any of the inhabitants, whether male or female, they immediately put them to death.

There was scarcely a corner of the city in which a Saracen corpse did not lie, and scarcely anyone could walk through the streets of the city except by trampling on Saracen corpses.

Bohemond seized those whom he had ordered to enter the palace and took from them everything they possessed, namely gold, silver, and the other ornaments they had. He had some killed and others led away to be sold at Antioch.

Thus many of our men who entered the city came upon everything they needed to take, while many others found nothing to seize. Afterward the delay in the city became so long that many were oppressed by hunger there, because they did not dare to go far outside into the land of the Saracens, while nearby they could find nothing to seize.

Our poor pilgrims therefore began cutting open the bodies of the pagans, because they found bysantios hidden in their bellies. Others, constrained by hunger, cut their flesh into pieces and cooked it for food.

### Here the Christians ate the flesh of the Turks.

After our leaders saw this, they had the pagans taken outside the city to the gates. There they made what looked like mountains out of them, and afterward they set them on fire.

Bohemond, however, unable to reach an agreement with Raymond of Saint-Gilles, returned to Antioch. Not many days later Raymond of Saint-Gilles sent his envoys from Antioch to Duke Godfrey, the Count of Flanders, Robert of Normandy, and Bohemond, asking them to come to the city of Rusia to speak with him.

All those leaders came there and held a council concerning how they might begin the road to the Holy Sepulchre, for whose sake they had set out and come so far. But they could not reconcile Bohemond with Count Raymond unless Raymond returned Antioch to him. Raymond refused to do so because of the pledge he had made to the Emperor Alexius. Therefore the duke and the other counts returned to Antioch.

Raymond, the athlete of Christ, also returned to the city of Marra, where the pilgrims of the Holy Sepulchre were. He sent his men to Antioch to fortify and guard the palace of Cassian the emir, which he held under his authority, and the tower above the bridge gate opposite Machomaria.

In this city the wise bishop of Oriens also died, and the pilgrims remained there for one month and four days.

Bohemond, wishing to possess the city of Antioch by his own power, expelled all Raymond of Saint-Gilles’s men by force. When the athlete of Christ, Raymond, heard this, he paid little attention to it and, like a servant of our Lord Jesus Christ, began the journey to the Holy Sepulchre. He left the city barefoot on the thirteenth day from the beginning of January and reached the castle of Capharda, eight miles away. There he stayed for three days.

There Robert of Normandy joined him. The king of Caesarea had often sent his knights and messengers to Raymond of Saint-Gilles at Marra and Capharda, saying that he wished to reach an agreement with him and become his friend. He wished to give him from his revenues as much as he desired, greatly desired to love the Christians, and wished to give him his assurance that, throughout the extent of his kingdom, they would be safe without any fear. He also promised to provide a market of horses and bodily provisions.

The pilgrims went out and came to encamp above the river called the Pharphar, beside Caesarea. When the king saw the Frankish army encamped so near the city, he was deeply grieved in his heart and ordered that the market be forbidden unless they departed from the city.

The next day he sent Turks with them to show them the ford of the river and conduct them until they could find something to seize. Then they came to a certain valley below a castle, where they found more than a thousand animals, abundant grain, and other goods. Thus the entire army of Christ was greatly refreshed.

Nevertheless, the lord of that castle reached an agreement with Raymond, gave him horses and many other things, and swore by his law that he would no longer harm the pilgrims. Raymond remained there with his army for five days.

Departing from there, the pilgrims of Christ reached another castle of the Arabs, whose lord likewise reached an agreement with Raymond. Going out from there, they came into a valley and reached a city called Caphalia, very beautiful and adorned with every good thing.

When the inhabitants of that city heard that the Christian pilgrims were coming, they abandoned the city, leaving gardens full of vegetables and houses full of abundant bodily provisions.

On the third day, departing from that city, they crossed a high and immense mountain and entered the valley of Issem, where there was an immense abundance of grain and livestock. They remained there for fifteen days.

There they found another empty castle, which the Saracens had set on fire before fleeing. Beside it was another castle in which a very large multitude of pagans had gathered. Our pilgrims attacked it so fiercely that they would have had it in their power, unless the Saracens had driven out innumerable herds of animals.

Our men returned, leading the animals with them to their tents. At first light they gathered their tents and came to the same castle mentioned above to besiege it, wishing to pitch their tents there. But the pagan people entirely took flight around midnight and abandoned the empty castle to the pilgrims of the Holy Sepulchre.

When the pilgrims entered the castle, they found there an abundance of the dew of heaven, namely grain, wine, flour, oil, chickens, and everything that was needed. There they devoutly celebrated the feast of the Purification of Saint Mary, which is on the second day of February.

Messengers also came from the city of Camela, bringing horses and gold, which the king of that city was sending to Raymond of Saint-Gilles. He wished to reach an agreement with him, promising to love the Christians and honor them diligently everywhere.

The king of Tripoli likewise sent his messengers to Raymond of Saint-Gilles, wishing to have peace with him if Raymond was willing. He sent him ten horses, four mules, and many bysantios. But the count said that he would have peace in no way unless the king became a Christian. The king promised and agreed.

Our men departed from that excellent valley and reached a certain castle called Archas on Monday, namely the second day of the week, in the middle of February, and pitched their tents around it.

That castle was full of an innumerable pagan population, namely Turks, Saracens, Arabs, Publicans, and other pagans. They had fortified the castle wonderfully and defended themselves bravely. The castle was also extremely strong and high on a certain mountain and was enclosed by two walls.

One day fourteen of our knights went out and rode to the city of Tripoli, which was eight miles from the castle. These knights were Raymond of Torena, the viscount; Peter, viscount of Castellon; Amanevus of Lobreto; Sicardus; Bego of Riberie; William Botius; and others whose names I do not know.

These fourteen knights found sixty men—Turks, Arabs, Saracens, and Kurds—driving before them our people and more than fifteen hundred animals. Our men attacked them under the protection of the sign of the cross. They killed six of them and kept six horses.

On another day Raymond Piletus and Raymond, viscount of the city of Torena, went out from the army of Christ and came before the city of Tortosa with their knights. They fought it fiercely; it was fortified by a very large multitude of pagans.

When evening had come, our men withdrew to a certain place beside a forest. There they encamped and had innumerable fires lit, as though the entire Christian army were present. When the pagans saw this, they were terrified by the greatest fear, secretly fled during the night, and abandoned the city, which was filled with many good things and situated above an excellent seaport.

The next day our knights came, intending to attack it from every side, but found it empty of inhabitants. They entered it and lived there for as long as the siege continued before the castle of Archas.

Near this city is another town called Maraclea. The emir who ruled it made an agreement with our men and admitted our men and our standards into the city.

### Here they besieged the city of Gibellum.

The other leaders who were at Antioch—namely Duke Godfrey, Count Robert of Flanders, and Bohemond—came as far as the city of Lichia, following Raymond of Saint-Gilles. Bohemond separated from the others and returned to Antioch.

Duke Godfrey and the Count of Flanders, however, following Raymond of Saint-Gilles, reached a certain city called Gibellum, which they strongly besieged and attacked.

Raymond was also at the siege of Archas. Messengers came to him saying that the pagans were coming to fight him. He therefore sent the bishop of Albara to Duke Godfrey and Count Robert of Flanders, asking them to come to the castle of Archas, since the pagans were gathering from every direction to fight him and his people.

When Duke Godfrey and the Count of Flanders heard this, they made an agreement with the Ammiralius, who gave them horses and bysantios and promised them that he would no longer cause harm to the pilgrims of the Holy Sepulchre.

Duke Godfrey and Count Robert of Flanders hastened to Raymond of Saint-Gilles’s aid and encamped beside the castle near the river. Thus they besieged the castle. But the aforementioned pagans did not come to battle at all.

Not many days later our men rode toward Tripoli and found Turks, Arabs, and Saracens outside the city. They immediately attacked them, put them to flight, and killed most of the city’s nobles.

The slaughter of the pagans and the shedding of their blood were so great that even the water flowing through the city seemed to pour red into their cisterns with their blood. Consequently, the others who survived inside the city were extremely sad and sorrowful. They were already so terrified that scarcely any of them dared to go outside the city gate.

The next day our men rode beyond the valley of Desem. They found oxen, asses, sheep, and many animals beyond counting. Sixty of them separated from the others and found three thousand camels. They led all these animals to the army of Christ, and the entire army of Christ was sufficiently joyful.

Our ships also came near us in a certain port while we remained in that siege, bringing a great market—namely grain, wine, meat, cheese, oil, and barley—so that there was great abundance throughout the entire host.

During that siege many of our men happily received martyrdom, namely Poncius of Baulan, Anselm of Risbemund, William the Picard, and others whose names I do not know.

Thus they held the aforementioned castle for three months less one day. There judgment was made concerning the Lance of the Lord on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, and there they celebrated the Lord’s Pasch on the fourth day before the Ides of April.

### Here judgment was made concerning the Lance of the Lord.

The king of Tripoli also frequently sent messengers to Raymond of Saint-Gilles, asking him to surrender the fortress. When our leaders heard this—namely Raymond of Saint-Gilles, Duke Godfrey, Robert, Count of Flanders, Robert the Norman, and the other pilgrims—and when, on the other hand, they saw that the new crops had arrived, since in March they were eating fresh beans and in the middle of April new grain, the great and the small took counsel and said that it would be good to begin the journey to Jerusalem with the new crops. Thus they all approved making an agreement with the king.

They therefore departed from the fortress and reached Tripoli [Col. 0812C] on Friday, the thirteenth day of May, and stayed there for three days. The king of Tripoli reached an agreement with Raymond of Saint-Gilles and the other leaders, and immediately released to them more than three hundred pilgrims who had been captured there in the earlier war. He gave Raymond fifteen thousand bezants and fifteen very valuable horses, and arranged for a great market to be held for them, with horses, asses, bread, cheeses, cloth, and every kind of good. Thus the entire army of Christ was greatly enriched.

It was agreed with them that, if they were able to win the battle which the admiral was preparing against them, and could capture Jerusalem, he would become a Christian and receive the land from them. Such an agreement was discussed and concluded. Afterwards they departed from the city on the Monday in the middle of May, and traveled the whole day and night along a narrow and steep road. They reached a fortress called Bethelon. Then they approached a city called Gibelon beside the sea, where they suffered great thirst; exhausted, they reached a river called Braym.

Next, on the day and night of the Lord’s Ascension, they crossed a certain mountain on which the road is exceedingly narrow and constricted, and there they expected to find our enemies. But, with God’s favor, none of them prepared to face our men. Thus they reached a city called Baruth, and from there another called Sagitta; from Sagitta they went to another called Sur, and from Sur they reached the city of Acre. From Acre they passed [Col. 0813A] beside a fortress called Cayphas; from there they reached the city of Caesarea, where they celebrated Pentecost as the month of May was drawing to a close.

From there they came to the city called Ramma, which the Saracens had abandoned empty out of fear of the Franks. Near it stood a noble church in which the most precious body of Saint George rested, because there he had gloriously received martyrdom for the name of Christ at the hands of faithless pagans. At once our leaders took counsel to appoint there, with the greatest devotion, a bishop who would guard and govern this church. They gave him their tithes—of gold and silver, animals, and horses—so that he could live honorably together with those who remained with him. He too remained there joyfully.

The others, rejoicing—namely Raymond of Saint-Gilles and Duke Godfrey, with the other pilgrims—reached the city of Jerusalem on Tuesday, the seventh day of June, and laid siege to it with great strength near the city walls. Robert the Norman besieged it from the north, beside the church of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, where he gladly received stones for the name of Christ; beside him was Robert, Count of Flanders. Duke Godfrey besieged it from the west, with Tancred beside him. From the south, Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles also besieged it, on Mount Zion, beside the church of Saint Mary, the Mother of the Lord, where she departed from this world, and where the Lord dined with his disciples, and where the Holy Spirit descended into the hearts of the disciples.

On the third [Col. 0813C] day, some of our soldiers went out from the army of the Holy Sepulchre to plunder: Raymond Piletus, Raymond of Torena, and others with them. They found two hundred Arabs. The soldiers of Christ fought those pagans and, with God and the Holy Sepulchre assisting them, defeated them, killed many of them, and kept their horses.

On the following day they attacked the city so fiercely that, if ladders had been ready, the city would have been in their power. Nevertheless, they overthrew the lower wall and raised a ladder against the higher one. Our soldiers climbed it and struck the city’s pagans at close quarters with their swords and spears. Rainaldus, the steward of Hugh of Lusignan, and many others died there, but still more of the enemy were killed.

For ten days they remained there in the siege, finding nothing to eat, until a messenger arrived from our ships, which had put in at the port of Jaffa. After the ship’s messengers arrived, our leaders took counsel among themselves and decided to send soldiers and attendants to guard faithfully the men and ships that had come to the port of Jaffa.

At first light one hundred soldiers went out from the army of Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles: Raymond Piletus, Gaudemar Carpinellus, Achard of Mommerlo, William of Sabra, and others whose names I do not know. While they were traveling toward the port, thirty of our soldiers separated from the others—namely Gaudemar and Achard—and found seven hundred Arabs, Turks, and Saracens. The soldiers of Christ attacked them boldly.

But the pagans’ strength against our men was so great that they surrounded them on every side and killed Achard of Mommerlo and many poor men who were on foot. While they held our men enclosed in this way, and all expected to die, one of them came as a messenger and said to Raymond Piletus:

“Why are you standing here with these soldiers? Look, all our men are in the greatest distress among the Arabs, Turks, and Saracens, and perhaps they have all been killed at this very moment. Therefore, come to their aid.”

When our men heard the messenger’s words, they immediately ran swiftly and reached those whom they found still fighting. When the pagans saw the Jerusalemite soldiers, they at once divided themselves and formed two battle lines. Our men, invoking the name of Christ and the Holy Sepulchre, attacked the unbelievers so forcefully that each man struck down his opponent.

When the enemy saw that they could no longer withstand the strength of the Christians, terrified by overwhelming fear, they turned their backs and fled. Our men pursued them for nearly four miles, killed many of them, and kept one alive, so that he could tell them the latest news in detail. They also kept three [one hundred and three in the edition] horses.

During the siege of Jerusalem they suffered such great thirst that they sewed together the hides of oxen, buffaloes, and goats, in which they carried water for six miles. From these vessels they used foul and malodorous water; indeed, in extreme hardship and affliction they subsisted daily on nothing but foul water and barley bread.

The spring of Siloam, which is at the foot of Mount Zion, sustained us for a short while. Yet water was sold at a high price among the Christians of God and of the Holy Sepulchre, so that one man could not quench his thirst for a single coin. The Saracens also hid beside all the springs and wells that existed, leaping upon our men, killing those whom they could find, and leading away the animals with them into their caves, caverns, and mountain fastnesses. Elsewhere they killed those who went into the vineyards for grapes.

When our leaders saw this, they became extremely angry and held a council. There the bishops and priests approved the holding of a procession around the city. Thus the bishops and priests, barefoot but clothed in sacred vestments and carrying crosses in their hands, came from the church of Saint Mary on Mount Zion to the church of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, singing psalms and praying that the Lord Jesus Christ might free his holy city and the Holy Sepulchre from the pagan people and grant them into the hands of Christians, so that they might perform his holy service.

The clerics were clothed in this manner, while the soldiers and attendants went beside them armed. When the Saracens saw this, they likewise proceeded along the city walls, carrying Muhammad covered with a cloth on a certain spear. When the Christians reached [Col. 0815A] the church of Saint Stephen and halted there, as is customary in our processions, the Saracens, standing above on the walls, shouted and howled with trumpets and performed every kind of mockery they could devise.

Moreover, they made a wooden cross in the likeness of the one by which merciful Christ, shedding his blood, redeemed the human race. In full view of all the Christians, to inflict pain upon them, they beat it with a piece of wood; then, to cause still greater pain, they smashed it against the city wall, saying in a loud voice: “Frangi, ogit salio,” which in our language means, “Franks, it is a good cross.”

When the Christians saw this, they were stirred by great grief. Without ceasing their prayers, they continued with their procession [Col. 0815B] up to the church on the Mount of Olives, from which place Christ ascended into heaven. There a most worthy cleric named Arnulf delivered a sermon, displaying the mercy that God had shown to the Christians who had followed him from the time when he ascended into heaven.

Then the Saracens, seeing the Christians standing there—for they could see them very clearly—stood between the Temple of the Lord and Solomon’s Temple, running back and forth with swords and clubs, and threatening the Christians.

From there the Christians again came with the same procession to the monastery of Saint Mary in the Valley of Jehoshaphat, from which monastery her most holy body was taken up into heaven. From there they returned once more to Mount Zion. As they wished to enter the church, a cleric who was coming first in the procession was wounded in the middle of the forehead by an arrow at the door of that monastery, and died there. His soul, I believe, will reign with Christ through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

We should believe the man who first wrote this, because he was first in the procession and saw it with his bodily eyes: Peter, priest of Tudebode of Sivrac.

At once our leaders arranged how they might besiege this city and, by prayer, enter the tomb of our Savior. They made two wooden siege towers and many other engines. Duke Godfrey made his tower with engines, and Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles likewise.

They brought timber from distant lands. Fifty or sixty Saracens who were in Christian hands carried each piece of wood on their shoulders, and the Christians treated the Saracens as . . . [lacuna]. Seeing our men constructing these engines, the Saracens therefore fortified the city wonderfully, and the towers grew higher day and night.

One day the Saracens sent a Saracen to see what sort of engines the Christians were making. When the Syrians and Greeks saw that Saracen, they pointed him out to the Christians, saying: “Mate Christo caco Sarrazin.” This means in our language, “By Christ, this is a cowardly Saracen.”

The Christians seized him and questioned him through a drogomannus—that is, through an interpreter—about why he had come. He answered:

“The Saracens sent me here because they wished to know what sort of engines you were making.”

The Christians replied that they were good, and, after tying his hands and feet, placed him in the sling of an engine called a Perrea. They all thought of throwing him into the city, but they could not do so. For when he was hurled with such force, his bonds broke and he was torn apart before he reached the city wall.

When our leaders saw on which side the city was weak, on a certain Saturday night they brought our engines and wooden siege towers there. At first light they raised, fitted, and decorated them, working day and night on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday. On Thursday, until the first hour, and then on Friday, they attacked [Col. 0816B] the city wonderfully from every side, up to the mountain.

On Friday early in the morning they attacked the city from all sides, but could do it no harm, and everyone was astonished and filled with great fear.

## Jerusalem Was Captured on Friday

As the hour approached—namely, the hour at which our Lord Jesus Christ deigned to suffer his Passion for us—our soldiers were fighting bravely in the fortress, specifically Duke Godfrey and his brother, Count Eustace. Then one of our soldiers named Lethold climbed onto the city wall.

Immediately after the soldier of Christ had climbed onto the city wall, Count Eustace and Duke Godfrey followed him. All the city’s defenders therefore fled along the walls and through the city, while our men pursued them, killing and cutting them to pieces.

Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles, meanwhile, brought his siege tower from the south close to the wall, but there was a ditch between the tower and the wall, and it was exceedingly deep. Raymond therefore decided at that moment to have the ditch filled. He had it proclaimed that anyone who carried three stones to the ditch would receive one denarius for the three stones. The ditch was filled in three days and two nights.

Those who were in the city tower fought our men fiercely with fire and stones, so much so that they broke the upper part of Raymond of Saint-Gilles’s tower and set it on fire. Thus Raymond was angry and troubled, as were his soldiers, because the pagans had already broken and set fire to the upper part of his tower.

Suddenly Raymond of Saint-Gilles saw three soldiers from Duke Godfrey’s army coming over the Mount of Olives and shouting that Duke Godfrey and his men were already in the city. When Raymond of Saint-Gilles heard that the Franks were already in the city, he said to his men:

“What are you waiting for? Look, all the Franks are already in the holy city of Jerusalem.”

Hearing this, they took ladders, raised them against the wall, and entered the city while fighting.

The admiral who was in the Tower of David also surrendered to Raymond of Saint-Gilles and opened for him the gate through which the pilgrims customarily used to pay their tribute, on the condition that he would escort him and the others who were with him in the tower safely and unharmed as far as the city of Ascalon. He did this willingly.

Our pilgrims entered the holy city of Jerusalem, pursuing and killing the Saracens as far as Solomon’s Temple and the Temple of the Lord. There the pagans gathered and gave our men a great battle until evening. Our men killed so many of them that blood flowed throughout Solomon’s Temple and along the street around the Temple of the Lord.

At last, after overcoming the pagans, our men seized males and females in the Temple, killed those whom they wished, and kept alive those whom they did not wish to kill. Above Solomon’s Temple there was a great gathering of pagans of both sexes, to whom Tancred and Gaston of Béarn gave their banners.

Afterwards they ran throughout the entire city, taking gold and silver, horses and mules, and houses full of every kind of good. Then they all came joyfully, and weeping from excessive joy, to the tomb of our Savior.

When morning came, Tancred had it proclaimed that everyone should go to Solomon’s Temple and kill the Saracens. When they reached the Temple, each man began to shoot with his bow and kill many of them. Others climbed onto the roof of the Temple from the other side and attacked the Saracens, both males and females, decapitating them with bare swords. Some of them threw themselves headlong from the Temple; others died above.

## Here They Elected Godfrey King

On the following day they held a council before the Temple of the Lord, saying that everyone should offer prayers and alms, and that God should choose for himself someone whom he wished to reign over the others, govern the holy city of Jerusalem, and fight against the pagans.

But the bishops and priests approved first expelling all the dead Saracens, lest the great stench that was there harm them. The entire city was full of their corpses. Thus they had the dead Saracens dragged through the streets to the exits of the gates. They piled them up in heaps as though they were houses, and afterwards burned them all in the fire.

Who has ever seen or heard of such slaughter of the pagan people? No one knew the number, except God alone.

On the eighth day after the city had been captured, they celebrated a festival throughout the city of Jerusalem. On that same day they held a council, at which they elected Duke Godfrey as ruler of the city, so that he might fight the pagans and protect the Christians.

Likewise, in place of the patriarch, they elected a most wise and honorable cleric named Arnulf, on the feast of Saint Peter in Chains.

This city was captured by the Christians of God on 15 July, on a Friday, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1099, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory through ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0818A] After Jerusalem was captured, the Christians fought against the admiral of Babylon near Ascalon.

Meanwhile a messenger came to Tancred and Count Eustace, telling them to prepare themselves and proceed to the city of Naples. They therefore set out, taking soldiers and infantry, and reached the city, whose inhabitants immediately surrendered themselves to them.

Again, through a messenger, Duke Godfrey instructed Tancred and his brother Eustace to come to him quickly. He had heard that the admiral of Babylon was at the city of Ascalon, where he was preparing to attack Jerusalem. He was bringing chains and other iron implements with which he intended to bind the Christian youths, so that they and their descendants might remain in servitude to him, and he had ordered all the old people of both sexes to be killed.

When Count Eustace and Tancred heard this, they came with great joy through the mountains, seeking battle with the Saracens and fully equipped for war. Reaching the city of Caesarea, they then came along the sea as far as the city called Ramma.

There they found many Arabs who were forerunners of the admiral’s army. Pursuing them, he captured several. Whether they wished to or not, they told them all the news of the war in detail: where the forces were, how many there were, and where they intended to fight against the Christians.

When Tancred and Count Eustace heard this, they immediately sent word to Duke Godfrey in Jerusalem, to Patriarch Arnulf, and to all the leaders, saying:

“Know that battle is prepared at the city of Ascalon. Therefore come quickly, with all the strength that you can muster.”

Then the duke ordered it proclaimed throughout the city of Jerusalem that they should faithfully proceed, prepared for war, to meet the enemies of God at Ascalon.

He therefore left the city of Jerusalem with Patriarch Arnulf, Robert Count of Flanders, and the bishop of Marthoron on Tuesday. Raymond of Saint-Gilles and Robert the Norman said that they would not go at all unless they knew that a battle was certain. They therefore sent their soldiers to see whether the battle was real.

They told them: “If this is true, return as quickly as possible, and we shall be ready to go at once.”

They went, saw the battle, [Col. 0818D] and quickly returned to Jerusalem, saying: “It is certainly true, just as we saw with our own eyes.”

Afterwards Duke Godfrey sent the bishop of Marthoron from Jerusalem to Raymond of Saint-Gilles, Robert the Norman, and the other leaders, telling them to come quickly to him if they wished to fight the pagans.

When the bishop of Marthoron returned, carrying the words of the patriarch and the duke, he encountered Saracens, who captured him and took him away with them; we do not know where.

Raymond of Saint-Gilles and the other leaders also departed from the city on Wednesday, and, protected by the sign of the cross, traveled to Duke Godfrey.

Peter the Hermit remained in Jerusalem, organizing and preaching to the Greeks and Latins that they should faithfully make processions and prayers to God and distribute alms to the poor, so that God might grant victory to his people.

Thus the clerics made a barefoot procession, clothed in sacred vestments and carrying crosses in their hands, with the litany and other prayers, from the Holy Sepulchre to the Temple of the Lord.

Duke Godfrey, Raymond of Saint-Gilles, the patriarch, Robert the Norman, Robert Count of Flanders, the bishops, and all the other leaders came to the river on the side of Ascalon, and there they gathered together.

There they found innumerable animals—oxen, camels, sheep, asses, and other livestock—which the Saracens had sent as a treacherous device. But God still did not wish to abandon them because of the Holy Sepulchre. The soldiers of Christ and the attendants of the Holy Sepulchre seized all the animals.

When evening came, Patriarch Arnulf, carrying with him a piece of the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, which the pilgrims of the Holy Sepulchre had found in Jerusalem, and likewise the chaplain of Raymond of Saint-Gilles, carrying with him the lance of our Lord Jesus Christ, began to excommunicate, in the name of God, the Holy Sepulchre, the most precious lance, and the most holy cross:

“No one is to pay attention to any booty until the battle has been fought and the enemies of God have been defeated. Afterwards they shall return in joyful happiness and with the greatest victory, and take whatever the Lord has predestined for them.”

When the pilgrims of the Holy Sepulchre and the soldiers of Christ heard this, at first light on Friday they entered [Col. 0819C] a very beautiful valley beside the seashore and arranged their battle lines there.

Duke Godfrey, who had already been elected king in Jerusalem, arranged his line; Raymond of Saint-Gilles likewise arranged his; Robert the Norman likewise his; Robert Count of Flanders his; Count Eustace his; and Tancred and Gaston of Béarn theirs.

Thus six battle lines began to advance. Archers went ahead of them, while beside them, on the right and left, all the animals mentioned above proceeded without a driver. This was a great miracle of God.

They immediately began to advance in the name of Jesus Christ and the Holy Sepulchre, carrying the lance of our Savior and one part of the Savior’s cross, which the patriarch carried.

On the left was Duke Godfrey with his line. Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles rode beside the sea on the right. The count of Normandy, the count of Flanders, Eustace, Tancred, Gaston of Béarn, and all the others rode in the middle.

Then our men gradually began to advance to battle. The pagans stood ready for war. Each man had a vessel hanging from his neck, from which he could drink while fighting the Christians.

## Here Begins the Battle against the Turks and the Other Peoples

Robert of Flanders attacked them with great ferocity, and Tancred and all the others did likewise. At once, when the pagans saw this, they fled.

Those battles were immense, for the multitude of pagans was innumerable. Six hundred and sixty thousand, as it is said, were there, yet no one knew their number except God.

But divine power accompanied our men. It was so great and so strong that our men regarded their multitude as nothing. The enemies of God stood blinded and stupefied. When they saw the Jerusalemite soldiers of Christ, they could see nothing with their open eyes and did not dare rise against the Christians, shaken by the power of God.

Out of excessive fear they climbed into trees, where they hid themselves. But our men shot arrows at them and killed them with spears. Afterwards our men cut them to pieces with swords and other blades.

Other pagans threw themselves to the ground, not daring to rise against the Christians. Our men therefore cut them to pieces, as someone cuts up animals for the butcher’s shop.

Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles killed countless numbers of them beside the sea. Those who could not flee drowned themselves in the sea or fled into the city.

When the admiral reached the area before the city of Ascalon, grieving, mourning, and weeping, he said:

“O Muhammad, and our gods, who has ever heard or seen such things? What power, what strength, what might, what army—such as no people had ever overcome—has now been defeated by such a tiny people, a people who could be enclosed in one’s fist?

“Alas for me, sorrowful and grieving! What more shall I say? Why have I been defeated by a beggarly, unarmed, and utterly poor people who possess nothing but a sack and a bag, and who now pursue our Egyptian people, which has often bestowed its alms upon them?

“Once they begged throughout our whole country, and now they pursue the innumerable multitude that I brought here, both soldiers and infantry: Turks, Saracens, Arabs, Angulans, Kurds, Parthians, Azimites, and other pagans. I see all of them disgracefully fleeing with loose reins along the Babylonian road, not daring to turn back against such a fragile people.

“Now I swear by Muhammad and by the divine powers of the gods that I shall never again retain soldiers for any agreement, since I have been cast down by this most feeble people.

“I brought here every kind of weapon, every instrument and engine, and all the iron chains with which I thought I would lead them bound to Babylon or besiege them in Jerusalem. Yet they came against me for battle after a journey of two days. What would have happened to me if I had led my people to Jerusalem? Surely neither I nor any one of my men, I believe, could have escaped from there.

“What more shall I say? I shall always be dishonored throughout the entire land of Babylon.”

Thus he ended his speech.

One of our men took the admiral’s standard, above which was a golden apple; the whole spear was covered with silver. Among us this standard is called a banner. Count Robert of Normandy bought it, giving twenty marks of silver, and presented it to the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre.

A pilgrim likewise took the admiral’s sword, giving sixty bezants.

Thus, with God’s help, all our enemies were defeated, so that they no longer had the strength to resist us. Ships from every land of the pagans were present there. But when their sailors saw the admiral fleeing with his army, they immediately hoisted their sails, took the admiral aboard their ships, and put out into the open sea.

Our men then returned to their tents and took immeasurable booty of gold, silver, garments, mules, and heaps of many goods—horses, mules, camels, sheep, oxen, asses, and many other animals. All the mountains, hills, and plains stood covered with a multitude [Col. 0821B] of animals. They found heaps of weapons, and kept whatever they wished to take from them. [Col. 0822A] The rest, which they did not want, they gathered together and burned there.

Our men returned rejoicing and glad to the holy city of Jerusalem, after defeating all the pagans. They brought with them many good things: camels and asses loaded with hard-baked bread, flour, grain, cheese, bread, oil, and everything necessary for them.

As a result, such abundance arose among the Christians that an ox could be obtained for eight or ten coins; a measure of grain for twelve coins; and a measure of barley for eight.

And so that this may not remain unknown to all Christians, let them know that this battle was fought on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September, on the vigil of the most holy Mother of God, Mary, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1099, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigned, to whom are honor and glory through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0821] Let this account of the journey to Jerusalem over three years and the liberation of the cities suffice. Blessed throughout all things is God, who delivered the impious. Amen.

# [HISTORY OF JERUSALEM]

[Col. 0821]

## NOTICE CONCERNING FULCHER

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini, vol. II, p. 214.)*

[Col. 0821C] Fulcher of Chartres, who followed Robert, Duke of Normandy, to Palestine in the year 1095 and was thereafter chaplain to Kings Baldwin I and II, wrote around the year 1127 the *Deeds of the Frankish Pilgrims Who Went Armed to Jerusalem*, or *History of Jerusalem*, together with an account of the events in which he himself had taken part. Jacobus Bongarsius first published this work, covering the years 1095 to 1124, in volume I of *The Deeds of God through the Franks*, pp. 381–440, dividing it into fifty-six chapters.

Gaspar Barth, using the Basel manuscript—though it was not more complete—divided it into ninety-nine chapters and supplied notes, which Johannes Petrus Ludewig published from the manuscript of the Ittig Library in volume III of *Remains of Manuscripts*, etc., pp. 291–360.

In André Duchesne, volume IV of *Writers on Frankish Affairs*, p. 816, there is likewise the same [Col. 0821D] *History of Jerusalem* by Fulcher, divided into three books from a manuscript of the monastery of Saint-Quentin of Monte near Péronne, and expanded in its final part for the year 1124 [Col. 0822C] and for the years 1125, 1126, and 1127, from pp. 879 to 889.

The first book begins in the year 1095; the second at the beginning of the reign of Baldwin I, that is, in the year 1100 (chapter 22 of Bongarsius’s edition); the third at the beginning of Baldwin II, in the year 1118 (the middle of chapter 44 of Bongarsius’s edition).

Finally, Edmund Martene published the Preface from the manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in volume I of the *Anecdota*, p. 364 and following. In it Fulcher says that, moved several times by the insistent prayers of certain of his companions, he carefully arranged in a rustic but truthful style those things which he himself had seen with his own eyes.

As Vossius noted, Fulcher is criticized by Abbot Guibert in *The Wars of Antioch*, chapters 29, 30, 31, and 38. But Orderic Vitalis commends him for his good faith in book IX of the *Ecclesiastical History*; likewise William of Malmesbury, book IV, who adds that he used a style not indeed uncultivated, but, as the saying goes, without polish and without rhetorical training, and one that could encourage others [Col. 0823A] to write more accurately.

This same Fulcher, who acted cautiously and bravely in the siege of Antioch in the year 1098, is mentioned by Gilo of Paris in book VII, in Edmund Martene, vol. III of the *Anecdota*, p. 241:

[lacuna]

“Fulcher approaches before them,

Through the darkness he reads the roads with faltering step,

While a comet, shedding its rays in those times,

Foretells a happy change of kingdom,” etc.

[Col. 0824A] And on page 241:

[lacuna]

“That Fulcher,

Born at Chartres, does not fear to precede a thousand nobles,

Hastening toward the walls of the unconquered city.

The burden of his shield does not delay him; leaning forward toward the heights,

He flies forth bearing arms and clings manfully to the ladder.

A Venetian follows him; the wicked enemy is astonished.

When Fulcher stood upon the walls, the guards were slain by his lightning sword [Note: [Col. 0823A] I believe this should be read in this way, not *ecce*, as Martene’s edition has it, since in Duchesne the entire word is lacking.], and hurled down below.

The victor rejoices,” etc.

[Col. 0823]

# FULCHER OF CHARTRES, *HISTORY OF JERUSALEM*, FROM THE YEAR 1095 TO THE YEAR 1127

*(Duchesne, *Hist. Franc. Script.*, IV, 816, from an ancient manuscript of the monastery of Saint-Quentin of Monte near Péronne. The beginning of this history, through chapter 19 of book I, is taken from Bongarsius’s edition because it was missing from the manuscript; the remainder is fuller than the printed editions, and the chapter headings from the manuscript have also been added.)*

# PREFACE OF FULCHER OF CHARTRES TO THE *HISTORY OF JERUSALEM*

*(Edited by D. Martene, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum* I, 364.)*

Here begins the Prologue to the *Deeds of the Franks Who Pilgrimed to Jerusalem*.

[Col. 0823B] It is pleasing to the living and profitable even to the dead when the deeds of courageous men, especially of those who serve God, are either read in writing or retained by memory in the mind’s treasury and soberly recounted among the faithful. For those who live in the world, when they hear of the pious resolve of faithful predecessors—how, spurning the flower of the world, they adhered to God, and, leaving behind parents, wives, and possessions of every kind, followed God in accordance with the evangelical command—are moved and inspired by him to love God more ardently.

It is exceedingly profitable to those who have died in the Lord when, having heard of their good and devout works, the faithful accordingly bless their souls and charitably offer alms and prayers for them, whether known or unknown. Therefore, [Col. 0823C] at the urging of certain of my companions, I was moved several times to set down in writing, as far as I was able and with my own eyes observed during the journey itself, the deeds of the Franks, most renowned in the Lord, who by God’s ordinance made pilgrimage to Jerusalem under arms. I considered it worthy of being entrusted to memory in a rustic but truthful style, and carefully arranged it.

Although I do not dare to compare this work, as outlined above, with the privileges of the Israelite people, or of the Maccabees, or of the many others whom God glorified with such frequent and magnificent miracles, nevertheless I have taken care to commend it to writing, since it should not be judged far inferior to those deeds, for God’s miracles are known to have been accomplished in it in many ways.

[Col. 0824B] Indeed, in what respect do these latter men differ from those former ones—the Israelites or the Maccabees—whom we saw, often in their own regions, or heard of, though far removed from us, being mutilated, crucified, flayed, shot with arrows, cut to pieces, and brought to completion by various kinds of martyrdom for the love of Christ, unable to be overcome by either threats or any enticements? Indeed, if the executioner’s sword had not been lacking, many of us would not have refused to be killed for the love of Christ.

O how many thousands of martyrs ended this expedition with a blessed death! But who is so stone-hearted that, hearing of these deeds of God, would not, moved by sighs of devotion, burst forth into God’s praises? Who can fail to wonder how we, a small people, were able not merely to resist amid so many kingdoms of our enemies, but even to live? Who has ever heard of such things?

On this side were Egypt and Ethiopia; on that side Arabia and Chaldaea, and Syria; on another side Assyria and Media; on another Parthia and Mesopotamia; on another Persia and Scythia. The great sea also shut us off from Christendom and enclosed us among the hands of those who would tear us apart, if God had permitted it. Yet he himself piously protected us with his strong arm. Blessed indeed is the nation whose Lord is its God (Ps. 22:12).

The course and beginning of this work, and how the whole western people was shaken into undertaking so great a journey, and voluntarily extended both minds and hands toward it, will be made clear by the historical account that follows.

# FULCHER OF CHARTRES’S HISTORY OF JERUSALEM

[Col. 0825]

## HERE BEGINS BOOK ONE

### CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0825A]

In the year 1095 from the Lord’s Incarnation, when the emperor called Henry was reigning in Alemannia and King Philip in France, while manifold evils were growing throughout all the regions of Europe and faith was wavering, Pope Urban II, an excellent man in life and character, presided over the city of Rome. He always strove carefully and energetically above all things to guide the condition of the holy Church toward greater elevation.

Seeing, however, that the faith of Christianity was being disgracefully undermined by everyone, clergy and people alike; that the rulers of the lands, engaged in continual armed conflict, now quarrelling among themselves on one side and now on the other, entirely set peace aside; that the goods of the earth were alternately plundered; that many people were unjustly bound and taken captive; and that they were cruelly thrown into the most dreadful prisons, excessively ransomed, or within them tortured in three ways—namely by hunger, thirst, and cold—and extinguished by a secret death; that holy places were violated; monasteries and villages burned with fire; that no mortal was spared; and that divine and human things were treated as objects of mockery; hearing also that the inner provinces of Romania had been occupied by the Turks and disastrously subjected to their savage attack against the Christians, he compassionately shared their suffering and, moved by God’s will and love, crossed the Alps and descended into Gaul.

There, in Auvergne, he caused a council to be assembled at Clermont, the city so called, having suitably sent advance notice in every direction by messengers. Three hundred and ten bishops and abbots attended, bearing their pastoral staffs. When these men had been summoned to him on the day appointed for this purpose, he carefully explained the reason for the assembly in a sweet and persuasive address.

For, speaking as the lamenting Church, he expressed a considerable lament and delivered a lengthy discourse to them concerning the storms of the troubled world, in so many ways, as was stated above, laid low with faith undermined. Thereafter he earnestly exhorted them all, with humble entreaty, to take up again the strength of faith and, with great zeal, courageously prepare themselves to overthrow the devil’s schemes; and to strive fittingly to restore the condition of the holy Church, most cruelly weakened by the wicked, to its former honor.

[Col. 0825C] “Dearest brothers,” he said, “by God’s permission I have been placed above the world as its chief, at the summit of the apostolate. Since an urgent occasion has arisen, I, Urban, have come down into these parts to you servants of God as an envoy of divine admonition. I wished to find those whom I had judged to be stewards of God’s ministries faithful as well, once the flood of hypocrisy had been swept away.

“If anything, whether humped or crooked, stands opposed to the law of God, with the modesty of reason and justice removed, I shall diligently strive to set it right, with divine assistance present. For the Lord has appointed you stewards over his household, so that you may provide it at the proper time with food seasoned with a moderate flavor. You will be blessed if the examiner of your stewardship finally finds you faithful.

“You are also called shepherds; take care, however, not to act like hirelings. Be true shepherds, therefore, always holding your staffs in your hands, and guard on every side the flock entrusted to you without falling asleep. For if through your carelessness or negligence a wolf carries off even one sheep, you will surely lose the reward prepared for you with our Lord; and, first being beaten most harshly with the scourges of your sins, you will afterward be brutally thrust into the custody of a deadly way of life.

[Col. 0826B] “You, moreover, according to the evangelical saying, are the salt of the earth (Matt. 5:13). But if you fail, it is uncertain how the earth will be salted. O what a great salting is required! Truly it is necessary for you to salt the foolish people, who hunger excessively after the wantonness of the world, by correcting them with the salt of wisdom, lest, when the Lord wishes at some time to address them, they should stink, having become unsavory through their sins and putrefaction.

“For if he finds worms—that is, sins—in them because of your negligent administration, he will immediately command that they, despised, be driven into the abyss of filth. And because you will have been unable to restore what has been so greatly lost to him, he will condemn you in judgment and utterly expel you from the fellowship of his love.

“But such a salter must be prudent, watchful, moderate, instructed, peaceful, discerning, devout, just, fair, and pure. For how will the uninstructed be able to make the instructed so, the immoderate the moderate, or the impure the pure? If he hates peace, how will he make peace? Or if someone has dirty hands, how will he be able to wipe away another’s filth and contamination?

“It is also written that if the blind lead the blind, a pit will be open for both of them (Matt. 15:14). First correct yourselves, therefore, so that you may amend your subjects without reproach. If you wish to be friends of God, willingly practice what you know pleases him.

“See especially to it that ecclesiastical property remains under its proper right, and beware lest the Simoniac heresy take root among you. Let those who sell or buy be scourged alike with the Lord’s scourges and miserably driven through the alleys toward the destruction of shame. [Col. 0827A] Support the Church, wholly free in its proper orders from every secular authority, and see to it that the tithes belonging to God are faithfully given from all the produce of the earth; let them neither be sold nor withheld.

“Whoever captures a bishop shall be regarded as entirely outside the law. Whoever captures or despoils monks, clerics, nuns, or their servants, or pilgrims or merchants, let him be anathema. Let raiders, arsonists, and those who consent to them be expelled from the Church and struck with anathema.

“Above all, therefore, it must be considered with what punishment he should be chastised who seizes what belongs to another, if the man who does not give away what is his own is struck with condemnation to hell. So it happened to the rich man mentioned in the Gospel: he was not punished because he had taken away another’s possessions, but because, after receiving his own goods, he abandoned himself to evil (Luke XV).

[Col. 0827B] “By these and the other iniquities I have mentioned, dearest ones, you have seen the world long and grievously confused, so that, as has been made clear to us by those who report it, perhaps because of the weakness of your justification, no one in some of your provinces dares to walk along the road by day without being carried off by plunderers, or by night by robbers, whether by force or by malicious cunning, inside or outside his house.

“Therefore the truce, so called in the vernacular, which was long ago determined by our holy Fathers, must be restored. I earnestly urge each of you to ensure that it is most firmly observed throughout his bishopric. If anyone, whether led by greed or pride, willingly violates it, let him be anathematized by the authority of God and by the sanction of the decrees of this council.”

When these and many other matters had been suitably arranged, all who were present, clergy and people alike, gave thanks to God, willingly assented to the words of the lord Urban, supreme pontiff, and confirmed by faithful promise that those decrees should be carefully observed.

But immediately he added another matter, no less grievous than the tribulation mentioned above, and perhaps even greater or worse, arising from another region of the world. He said:

[Col. 0827C] “Since, O sons of God, you have promised God more courageously than usual that peace should be maintained among you and the rights of the Church faithfully preserved, it is worthwhile that, newly strengthened by the Lord’s correction, you should turn the strength of your virtue to another undertaking of God and of your own.

[Col. 0827D] “For it is necessary that you hasten to aid your brothers living in the eastern region, who have so often called for your assistance. The Turks and Arabs have invaded them—as has already been told to many of you—as far as the Mediterranean Sea, to the place they call the Arm of Saint George, near the borders of Romania. By occupying the lands of those Christians more and more, they have now defeated them in war seven times over, killing or capturing many, overthrowing churches, and laying waste the kingdom.

“If you allow them to remain in peace like this for any length of time, they will overrun many more of God’s faithful over a wider area. For this reason I exhort you with humble prayer—not I, but the Lord—that by repeated proclamation you, heralds of Christ, persuade all, of whatever order, foot soldiers and horsemen, poor and rich, [Col. 0828A] to strive in good time to aid the Christians in exterminating that wicked race from our regions.

“I say this to those present; I command it to those absent. Christ, however, commands it. To all who go there, if they should end their lives while walking, crossing the sea, or fighting against the pagans, immediate remission of sins will be granted. I grant this to those who are going, endowed by God with so great a gift.

“O what disgrace it would be if a people so despised and degenerate, enslaved to demons, should so overcome a people endowed with faith in almighty God and radiant with the name of Christ! O what reproaches the Lord himself will lay upon us if you do not help those who are reckoned Christian by profession, as we are!

[Col. 0828B] “Let those who once habitually prolong private quarrels abusively against the faithful now advance against the unbelievers to a battle worthy of beginning and destined to be completed with a trophy. Let those who were formerly robbers now become soldiers. Let those who once fought against brothers and kinsmen now rightly fight against barbarians. Let those who formerly worked as mercenaries for a few coins now obtain eternal rewards. Let those who wearied themselves to the detriment of body and soul labor for a double honor.

“Indeed, here they will be sorrowful and poor; there, wealthy. Here they will be enemies of the Lord; there, his friends. Let delay not postpone the journey of those who are going; once their property has been placed in order and their expenses gathered, when winter has ended and spring has followed, let them joyfully enter upon the road with the Lord going before them.”

After these words had been spoken, and the hearers had been gladly encouraged toward this undertaking, judging nothing more worthy of such action, many of those present immediately promised that they would go and that they would diligently summon the others who were absent. Among them was a certain bishop of Le Puy, named Adhemar, who afterward served as papal legate, prudently and carefully directing the entire army of God and vigorously encouraging it in the tasks to be accomplished.

When what we have related had thus been established in the council and confirmed by all, and the blessing of absolution had been given, they departed. Those who had been unaware of this later returned to their homes and clearly spread the news of what had taken place.

When the proclamation had been published throughout the provinces, they established among themselves, with the solemnity of an oath, that the peace which they call the truce should be observed. Thereafter many people engaged in every kind of occupation, having obtained remission of their sins, vowed with purified intention that they would set out for the place to which they had been ordered to go.

O how worthy and delightful it was for all of us who saw those crosses—whether of silk, woven with gold, or adorned with any kind of cloth—which the pilgrims, at the command of the aforesaid pope, sewed upon their shoulders, on their cloaks, mantles, or tunics, after taking the vow to go!

The soldiers of God deserved to be marked and fortified with the sign of victory, since they were preparing themselves to fight for his honor. And those who painted this sign upon themselves as an indication of their recognition of the faith finally obtained the more genuine meaning derived from it. They marked the outward appearance so that they might attain the reality signified by that appearance.

This is clear enough, because good meditation devises a good work to be performed; and a good work wins salvation for the soul. If it is good to meditate well, it is better, after deliberation, to perform a just deed. The best course, therefore, is the saving profit that is gained for the soul’s sustenance through worthy action. Let each person accordingly think of some good which he may complete by improving it through a worthy deed, so that at last, as a veteran soldier, he may receive what is best and does not fail for eternity.

Thus Urban, a prudent and venerable man, conceived an undertaking from which the world afterward flourished. He renewed peace and restored the rights of the Church to their former order. He also strove with vigorous zeal to drive the pagans from the lands of the Christians. And because he strove in every way to exalt all that belonged to God, almost everyone willingly submitted themselves in obedience to his fatherly authority.

[Col. 0829B] But the devil, who always strives for harm and, like a lion, seeks by circling about whom he may devour (1 Pet. 5:8), stirred up against him a certain adversary named Guibert, provoked by the goad of pride and inciting confusion among the people.

Supported formerly by the arrogance of the emperor of the Bavarians, while his predecessor Gregory, also called Hildebrand, was rightfully regarded as occupying the papal seat, Guibert began to usurp the office of the apostolate, after Gregory himself had been excluded from the doors of the basilica of Saint Peter. Because he acted perversely in this way, the better part of the people refused to recognize him.

After Urban had been rightly elected and consecrated by the cardinal bishops, the greater and holier part of the people, after Hildebrand’s death, gave its support through obedience. Guibert, however, encouraged by the support of the aforesaid emperor and by the agitation of many Roman citizens, kept Urban away from Saint Peter’s monastery for as long as he could.

But while Urban was thus expelled from that Church, he went through the regions and reconciled to God some of the people who had gone astray. Guibert, puffed up over the primacy of the Church, presented himself to the erring as a complaisant pope and, though unjustly, exercised the office of the apostolate among his supporters, treating Urban’s acts as though they were invalid.

Urban nevertheless acquired full apostolic power in the year when the Franks first passed through Rome on their way to Jerusalem, with the aid of a certain most noble matron named Matilda, who at that time wielded great power in the Roman territory. Guibert was then in Alemannia.

Thus two popes presided over Rome, but very many people did not know which of them should be obeyed, from which one advice should be sought, or which one could heal the sick. Some favored one, others the other. As was evident to human eyes, Urban was more prosperous and more just. He should rightly be considered the stronger, because he subjected his desires as though they were enemies.

Guibert, bishop of the city of Ravenna, was exceedingly resplendent in honor and wealth. It is remarkable that such riches were not enough for him. He ought to have been regarded by everyone as an example of just action and humility; why, then, did he rashly, being a lover of pomp, presume to seize the scepter of God’s dominion, which was his charge to govern? It should not be seized by force, but received with reason and devotion. The one who receives it should not swell with pride over the honor, but faithfully administer what has been entrusted to him; and, if the things belonging to so great an honorable dignity have been scattered, he should gather them together at the proper time.

It is no wonder that the whole world was then troubled and thrown into confusion. For if the Roman Church, in which the chief authority for correcting all Christendom is held, is thrown into disorder by any storm, its subordinate members immediately become weakened, suffering sympathetically as pain spreads from the governing fibers to them.

That Church—our mother, whose milk nourished us, whose instruction enabled us to be taught, and whose counsel fortified us—had been struck violently by that proud Guibert. When the head was thus battered, the members were immediately injured. If the head is sick, the other members suffer.

But since the head had been so wounded, and the members also withered as pain spread to them, and since peace, goodness, and faith throughout all the regions of Europe, in the Churches and outside them, were being forcibly suppressed by great and small alike, it was necessary that, with such evils laid aside, they should, at the prompting begun by Pope Urban, turn against the pagans the conflicts that they had long been accustomed to wage among themselves and against one another.

Now, therefore, it is fitting to return to the undertaking. For concerning those traveling to Jerusalem—what happened to those who went, and how the undertaking and the labor themselves gradually became successful with God’s help—it is proper to explain more fully to those who do not know. I, Fulcher of Chartres, who went with the other pilgrims, afterward carefully and diligently gathered these matters for the memory of posterity, as I saw them with my own eyes.

### CHAPTER TWO

[Col. 0830C]

In the year 1096 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the month of March, after the Auvergne council mentioned above, which the lord Urban held in November, some, better equipped than others, began the holy journey. Others followed in April, May, June, or July, and likewise in August, September, and October, according as the opportunity to obtain expenses arose.

In that year, by God’s arrangement, peace and a great abundance of grain and wine flourished throughout all the regions of the earth, lest bread should fail on the road for those who had chosen to follow him with their crosses in accordance with his commands.

Since it is appropriate that the names of the leaders of such pilgrims be preserved in memory, I name Hugh the Great, brother of Philip, king of the Franks. He was the first of the nobles to cross the sea and land with his men at the city of Durazzo in Bulgaria. But, traveling imprudently with a small troop, he was captured there by the citizens themselves and brought before the emperor of Constantinople, where for some time he remained not entirely free.

After him Bohemond of Apulia, son of Robert Guiscard but by origin a Northman, traveled by the same route with his army. Godfrey, duke of the kingdom of Lotharingia, went through the land of the Hungarians with a large force. Raymond, count of Provence, with the Goths and Gascons, and the bishop of Le Puy crossed through Slavonia.

A certain Peter the Hermit went first through Hungary with many foot soldiers who had joined him but few knights. A certain Walter, called “Without-Money,” afterward became the leader of this people. He was an excellent knight, but later, between the cities of Nicomedia and Nicaea, he was killed by the Turks along with many of his companions.

In September Robert, count of Normandy, son of William, king of the English, undertook the journey after gathering a large army of Normans, English, and Bretons. Count Stephen of Blois, son of Theobald, and Robert, count of Flanders, also went with him, together with many other nobles.

Thus, as so great a company proceeded from the western regions, an army of armies gradually grew along the road, day by day, from the innumerable people converging from every direction, so that one might see an infinite multitude speaking many languages and coming from many regions.

[Col. 0831B] Nevertheless, the armies were not all gathered into one until we reached the city of Nicaea. What, then, shall I say? The islands of the seas and the kingdoms of all the lands were shaken by God, so that we should believe David’s prophecy was being fulfilled, in which he said in the psalm: “All the nations that you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord” (Ps. 85:9); and so that those who reached that place might at last rightly say: “We shall worship in the place where his feet have stood” (Ps. 132:7).

We also read much about this journey in the prophecies. O what grief there was! What sighs, what weeping, what lamentation among friends, when a husband left his beloved wife, his children, possessions of every kind, or his father, mother, brothers, or relatives!

Although so many tears were shed for the friends who were going, flowing from the eyes of those who remained behind, nevertheless the travelers were not thereby softened so as to refrain from leaving everything they possessed for the love of God, firmly believing that they would receive the hundredfold which the Lord promised to those who followed him (Matt. 19:29).

Then one spouse set a time for the other’s return, saying that, if he lived, he would return home to her within three years. He commended her to the Lord, gave her a kiss, and promised that he would return.

But she, fearing that she would never see him again, was unable to support herself in her grief, but fell senseless to the ground, mourning for her beloved, whom she had lost alive as though he were already dead.

He, however, as though he had no compassion—and yet possessing it—neither shared the tears of his wife, his children, or any of his friends, and yet secretly did share them; but, remaining firm with a hardened heart, he departed.

There was sadness for those who remained, but joy for those who went. What can we say about this? “This is the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes” (Ps. 118:23).

Accordingly, we western Franks, traveling through Italy after passing across Gaul, reached Lucca. Near that city we found Urban the pope, with whom Count Robert the Norman, Count Stephen, and the rest of us who wished spoke. After receiving his blessing, we went joyfully to Rome.

When we entered the basilica of Saint Peter, we found before the altar foolish men belonging to Pope Guibert. Holding their swords in their hands, they were wickedly seizing the offerings placed upon the altar. Others were running about on the beams of the same monastery and throwing stones down from there upon the place where we lay prostrate in prayer.

For whenever they saw anyone faithful to Urban, they immediately wanted to slaughter him. In one stronghold of the monastery were Urban’s men, who carefully guarded it in loyalty to Urban and resisted their opponents as best they could.

We grieved greatly when we saw such wickedness being committed there. But we could do nothing else except hope that the Lord would take vengeance for it.

After no delay there, many who had traveled with us as far as that place returned cowardly to their homes. We, however, traveling through Campania and Apulia, reached Bari, an excellent city situated on the seashore. There, after pouring out our prayers to God in the church of Saint Nicholas, we went to the harbor, thinking to cross the sea without delay.

But because the sailors were absent and fortune was unfavorable, and because it was then winter, which hindered us, it became necessary for Robert, count of Normandy, to turn aside into Calabria and spend the entire winter there.

At that time Count Robert of Flanders crossed the sea with his company. Then many of the poor or cowardly, fearing the poverty that lay ahead, sold their bows, took up their pilgrim staffs again, and returned to their homes. Thus they became contemptible both to God and to human beings, and the matter was turned into a reproach against them.

### CHAPTER THREE

[Col. 0832C]

In the year of the Lord 1097, when spring returned in the month of March, the Norman count and Count Stephen of Blois, who had likewise waited nearby for a suitable time, immediately returned to the sea.

With the fleet prepared, on the Nones of April—on which day Easter then fell—they boarded ships with their men at the port of Brindisi. O how unknown and unsearchable are the judgments of God!

For we saw one ship among the others suddenly split apart near the seashore, without any preceding circumstance causing it. Nearly four hundred people of both sexes were drowned and perished. Yet joyful praise to God immediately sounded concerning them.
