When those standing around had gathered their already dead bodies as best they could, they found on the flesh of certain people, namely upon their shoulders, marks stamped in the form of a cross. What they had carried while alive upon their clothing remained, by the Lord’s will, upon those who had been thus taken beforehand into his service: the same victorious sign remained upon them as a pledge of faith.

It was also rightly worthy of being revealed to observers through such a miracle that these dead, under God’s mercy, had already obtained the rest of eternal life, so that it might most truly be evident that what is written had been fulfilled: “The righteous man, whatever death overtakes him, shall be at rest” (Wis. 4:7).

Of the others, who were still struggling with death, a few men survived. The horses and mules perished beneath the waves, and much money was also lost.

When we saw this misfortune, we were overwhelmed with great fear, so much so that many who were fainthearted, though they had not yet boarded the ships, returned to their homes and abandoned the pilgrimage, saying that they would never again commit themselves to such a deception.

We, however, placing our hope entirely in almighty God, raised the sails, proclaimed God with a loud trumpet blast, and, with him as our pilot, put out into the open sea while the wind blew somewhat.

After we had been held among the high waves for three days because the wind failed, on the fourth day we safely reached a harbor near the city of Durazzo, about ten miles away. Two harbors received our fleet.

Then we gladly resumed our journey by land and afterward proceeded onward before the aforesaid city. Thus we crossed the regions of the Bulgarians through steep mountain passes and fairly deserted places.

We all came to a swift river called by the inhabitants of that land the Demon’s River—and rightly so. For in that demonic river we saw many people, while they hoped to wade across on foot, perish by sudden drowning in the torrent’s dreadful force, and none of those watching could help them.

For this reason we shed many tears there out of compassion. If horsemen with trained horses had not come to the aid of the foot soldiers after entering the river, many would have lost their lives there in the same way.

Then we pitched our camp beside the bank and rested there for one night. Vast mountains surrounded us on every side, and no inhabitant appeared in them.

In the morning, as dawn brightened and the trumpets sounded, we began our journey by climbing the mountain called Bagulatus.

Afterward, leaving the mountains behind, we finally reached the river called the Baldarius. Although previously it could usually be crossed only by boat, with God’s help—he who is always present everywhere to aid his own—we joyfully crossed it by wading.

After crossing it, on the following day we pitched our tents before the city of Thessalonica, rich in every good thing.

### CHAPTER FOUR
After remaining there for four days, we then crossed Macedonia through the valley of Philippi, and afterward through Lucretia, Chrysopolis, and Christopolis, as well as the other cities that are in Greece, and arrived at Constantinople. There, after pitching our tents outside the city, we alleviated our weariness for fourteen days. Since we were unable to enter the city—because this did not please the emperor, who feared that we might perhaps be plotting some harm against him—we had to purchase the daily provisions brought to us outside the walls, which the citizens delivered to us at the emperor’s command. Nor did the emperor permit many to enter the city together; rather, he allowed five or six of the more prominent men to enter the churches ceremonially for an hour.

O how noble and beautiful a city! How many monasteries and palaces there are in it, marvelously constructed! How many works, too, in its squares and streets, wonderful to behold! It would be tedious to recount how great is the abundance there of every good thing—gold and silver, garments of many kinds, and holy relics. At every season, moreover, everything necessary for human beings is brought there by the frequent traffic of ships. There are also, as I believe, nearly twenty thousand eunuchs residing there continually.

When we had sufficiently refreshed ourselves from our fatigue by resting, our nobles, after taking counsel, became the emperor’s men and swore an alliance with him, just as he had already requested of them. Those who had preceded us on the journey—Bohemond, namely, and Duke Godfrey—had likewise already done this under oath. Count Raymond, however, at that time refused to do so. The Count of Flanders, like the others, did swear the oath. For it was necessary for them to establish friendship with the emperor in this way, so that they might more safely seek and receive from him counsel and assistance, both present and future, for themselves and for all who would follow us along the same route.

For this reason the emperor himself supplied them, from his own coinage, with as much as he wished: horses, garments, and money, of which they were greatly in need to complete so long a journey. When this had been accomplished, we crossed the sea called the Arm of Saint George. Then we hastened to the city of Nicaea, which Bohemond, Duke Godfrey, Count Raymond, and the Count of Flanders had already been besieging since the middle of May.

The city was held by the eastern Turks, pagans fierce in spirit and skilled archers. They had come from Persia and, after crossing the Euphrates about fifty years earlier, had subjected the whole land of Romania as far as the city of Nicomedia. O how many severed heads and bones of the slain, lying in the fields beyond Nicomedia, we found there! The Turks had killed them that very year—people ignorant of warfare and unaccustomed to archery. Moved by compassion, we shed many tears over them.

When those who were already besieging Nicaea heard that our princely counts—Robert the Norman and Stephen of Blois—were coming, they joyfully came out to meet them and us, and escorted us as far as the place where we pitched our tents, south of the city. The Turks had already once assembled and prepared themselves, wishing either, if they could, to drive the siege away from the city or to strengthen the city’s defenses with their soldiers. But they were bravely and fiercely repulsed by our men, and nearly two hundred of them were killed.

When they saw that the Franks were so spirited and powerful in valor, they withdrew in flight into inner Romania, until they judged that a more suitable time had come to attack us.

We were the last to come to the siege, in the first week of June. Then a single army was formed there from many armies. One hundred thousand of them were protected by coats of mail and helmets; those who understood numbers estimated that there were six hundred thousand capable of fighting, not counting the unarmed—namely, clerics, monks, women, and children.

What more can be said? If all those who had left their homes and begun the journey under vow had been present there together, there would unquestionably have been six million warriors. But some from Rome, some from Apulia, and others from Hungary or Sclavonia, refusing the hardships, had returned home; or, in many places, after many thousands had been killed, and many of our own companions had fallen ill while traveling with us, they had ended their lives in death. You would have seen many cemeteries along the roads, in the fields, and in the groves, where our pilgrims had been buried in this manner.

It should be known that, as long as we surrounded Nicaea, food was brought there for us to purchase by sea, with the emperor’s consent. Then our leaders had machines constructed: battering rams, “sows,” wooden towers, and stone-throwers. Arrows were shot from bows, stones were hurled, and each side returned the contest to the best of its ability. Often, armed with those machines, we attacked the city, but the strong wall opposing us rendered the assault ineffective. Frequently men from both the Turks and the Franks were killed, struck by arrows or stones.

Indeed, you would have grieved and sighed with compassion when they had slaughtered one of our men near the wall by some means, and then, lowering iron hooks on ropes, dragged the slain man up to themselves—sometimes still wearing his coat of mail. None of us dared or was able to wrest him from them. After stripping the body, they hurled the corpse outside.

But when we had besieged the city for five weeks and had often made the Turks fearful through our assaults, an agreement was made through embassies with the emperor. The Turks craftily surrendered the city to him, when it had already been severely constrained by force and siege engines. Then they admitted into it the Turcopoles sent by the emperor, who preserved the city, together with its internal treasury, for their lord the emperor, just as he had ordered them.

Therefore, retaining that money, the emperor ordered gold, silver, and costly garments from his own stores to be given to our nobles; and he had his bronze coins distributed among the foot soldiers. These coins they call tartarones.

On the day when Nicaea was thus captured, or surrendered, [the event] was reflected by the solstice of one month [the wording is uncertain], and on the third day before the Kalends of July, when our barons had received permission from the emperor to depart, we left Nicaea to enter the inner regions of Romania.

But after we had traveled for two days, we were informed that the Turks, having laid ambushes ahead of us, were waiting in the plains through which they thought we would pass, intending to fight us. When we heard this, we lost none of our courage on that account. But when, late that day, several of our scouts saw some of them in the distance, they immediately warned us. For this reason we had our tents guarded all around that night by watchmen.

## CHAPTER V

When morning came—which fell on the Kalends of July—we took up our arms. At the sound of the trumpet, we followed against them by wings; with tribunes and centurions leading cohorts and centuries, and with standards raised, we began to advance in orderly fashion.

At the second hour of the day, behold, their advance troops approached our scouts. When we heard this, we immediately had our tents pitched beside a certain reed bed, so that, after putting down our packs—that is, our baggage—we might be readier and more nimble for battle.

When this had been done, behold the Turks, whose prince and emir was Soliman, who held the city of Nicaea and Romania in his power. He had gathered Turks from the eastern regions, who had been summoned to his aid after a journey of thirty days or more. Many other emirs were with him: namely, Amudaradigium, Miriatos, Comardigus, Amirchai, Lachin, Boldagis, Caradigus, and many others. Altogether they numbered three hundred and sixty thousand fighters, namely, archers. Their custom is to use such weapons. They were all cavalry, whereas we had both infantry and cavalry.

At that time, however, Duke Godfrey, Count Raymond, and Hugh the Great were absent from us. For two days they had foolishly separated themselves from us with a very large force, taking a forked route. This caused us irreparable harm, both through the number of our men killed and through the Turks whom we neither captured nor killed. But because our messengers reached them late, they came to our aid late.

The Turks, boldly shouting their war cries, began to rain arrows upon us with great force. Stunned by such frequent blows, dead and wounded in great numbers, we soon became afraid and turned to flight. Nor was this surprising, since such warfare was unknown to all of us.

Already, from the other side of the reed bed, dense Turkish ranks had violently rushed as far as our tents. They seized our possessions inside and killed members of our force. Then, by God’s providence, the advance troops of Hugh the Great, Count Raymond, and Duke Godfrey came running up from behind in the midst of this misfortune.

When we had already been driven back as far as our tents, those who had entered among the tents immediately withdrew, thinking that we were retreating so quickly because of them. But what they took for courage or valor might instead have been expected to produce extreme fear.

What shall I say? We had gathered together into one mass, like sheep shut into a fold, trembling and terrified, and were surrounded on every side by the enemy, so that we could not advance anywhere at all. We thought that this had happened to us because of our sins. For some were polluted by lust, while others were corrupted by greed or pride.

There was an enormous cry striking the heavens—from men, women, and children, and also from the pagans who were rushing upon us. Now there was no hope of life. We all acknowledged that we were guilty and sinful, devoutly asking God for mercy.

There was present the bishop of Puy, our patron, and four others. Very many priests were also there, dressed in white garments, humbly beseeching the Lord to overthrow the strength of the enemy and pour out upon us the gifts of his mercy. They sang while weeping, and prayed while singing. Many then ran to them, confessing their sins because they were afraid that they would soon die.

Our nobles—Robert, count of Normandy; Stephen of Blois; the Count of Flanders; and Bohemond—tried as best they could to resist the Turks and often attempted to attack them. The Turks, for their part, assailed them vigorously.

But perhaps the Lord was appeased by our supplication—for he does not favor triumph through the splendor of rank or through shining weapons, but mercifully assists the pious mind fortified by divine virtues in its hour of need. He gradually restored our strength and weakened the Turks more and more.

When we saw our companions, who were hastening behind to help us, we recovered our courage, praising God, and attempted to resist them through the crowds and cohorts. Alas! How many of our men, who were slowly coming behind us along the road that day, were killed!

From the first hour of the day until the sixth, as I have said, they held us tightly confined. But then, as we gradually regained courage and our companions gathered to us, divine grace wonderfully came to our aid. In what seemed a sudden moment, all the Turks turned their backs and fled from our sight.

We, shouting loudly behind them, pursued them through the mountains and valleys. We did not cease driving them away until our foremost pursuers reached their tents. There some of our men loaded their horses and camels with their possessions and with several animals that they had abandoned there out of fear; others pursued the fleeing Turks until nightfall. But because our horses were hungry and exhausted, we captured only a few of them.

It was a great miracle of God that on the following day and the day after that they did not cease fleeing, although no one except God alone was driving them farther away.

Made exceedingly joyful by so great a victory, we all gave thanks to God, because he had not allowed our journey to be utterly destroyed, but had caused it to prosper more honorably than usual, for his own honor and that of Christianity. Therefore its fame will resound perpetually from east to west.

Then we proceeded steadily behind them. The Turks, fleeing before us in bands, sought quarters for themselves throughout Romania. We then went to Antioch, which they call Little Antioch, in the province of Pisidia, and afterward to Iconium. In those regions we very often lacked bread and sufficient food.

For we found Romania—a land excellent and most fertile in every good thing—utterly devastated and desolated by the Turks. Nevertheless, you would often have seen so great a multitude of people well refreshed by the scanty cultivated fields that we occasionally found in various places, through the provision of that God who fed five thousand people with five loaves and two fish (Matthew 14:19–21). We rejoiced greatly at this and, sharing one another’s joy, declared that these were gifts of God’s mercy.

At that time you would truly have laughed, or perhaps wept with compassion, when many of our men, lacking pack animals because they had already lost many of their own, loaded sheep, goats, pigs, and dogs with their belongings—namely, clothes, bread, or any baggage necessary for the pilgrims’ use. We saw the backs of these little animals deformed by the weight of their heavy loads. Sometimes mounted soldiers even climbed upon oxen with their weapons.

But who has ever heard of so many tribes of different languages in one army, when there were Franks, Flemings, Frisians, Gauls, Bretons, Allobroges, Lotharingians, Germans, Bavarians, Normans, Scots, English, Aquitanians, Italians, Apulians, Iberians, Dacians, Greeks, and Armenians? If a Breton or a German wished to speak to me, I would have known how to answer neither.

Yet although we were divided by so many languages, we appeared to be united like brothers under love of God and neighbor. For if anyone lost something from his belongings, whoever found it would carefully carry it with him for many days, until, by inquiry, he found the person who had lost it, and would gladly return what he had found. This is fitting for those who undertake a pilgrimage justly.

## CHAPTER VI

When we had reached the city of Heraclea, we saw a certain sign in the sky. It appeared then, shining with a whitish radiance, shaped like a sword, with its point extended toward the east. But we did not know what it promised for the future; we entrusted both present and future to the Lord.

Then we went to a certain excellent town called Mariscum, where we rested for three days. But after we had traveled a day’s journey from there and were not far from Antioch in Syria—about three days away—I left the army and turned into the left-hand part of the province with Lord Baldwin, count and brother of the aforementioned Duke Godfrey.

He was an excellent soldier, very renowned for valor and courage. Earlier, after leaving the army with those whom he had taken with him, he had captured with great boldness the city called Tarsus of Cilicia. Tancred, however, violently took it away from him, having already brought his own men into it with the consent of the Turks. Baldwin therefore left guards there and returned to the army.

Trusting in the Lord and in his own strength, he gathered a few soldiers around him and set out toward the Euphrates River. There he captured many fortified camps, by force and by stratagem. Among them he seized one of the finest, called Turbessel. The Armenians who lived there peacefully surrendered it to him, along with many other places subject to it.

When news of him had spread far and wide, the ruler of the city of Roais—that is, Edessa—sent an embassy to him. The city was quite famous and exceedingly rich in the produce of the land. It lies in Mesopotamia of Syria, nearly twenty miles beyond the aforementioned Euphrates, and is about one hundred miles, or somewhat more, from Antioch.

Baldwin was therefore summoned to go there, and they were to become friends with each other for as long as both lived, like father and son. If that ruler of Edessa should happen to die, Baldwin would immediately possess, as though he were his son, the city and all his land, whatever amount he possessed, as an inheritance. For he had neither son nor daughter.

And because he could not defend himself against the Turks, that Greek wished Baldwin to defend both himself and his land. He had heard that Baldwin and his fighting men were exceptionally valiant.

When Baldwin heard this, and after the envoys had made him believe it by oath, he crossed the Euphrates with his very small army—only eighty soldiers. After crossing it, we hurried throughout the entire night, passing very close to the Saracens’ camps and leaving them on either side, in great fear.

When the Turks who were in the strong town of Samosata heard this, they laid an ambush for us on the road by which they thought we would travel. But on another night, when an Armenian had carefully hosted us in his castle, we were informed that we needed to guard against those enemies lying in ambush.

For this reason we concealed ourselves there for two days. But when the others grew impatient at such a delay, on the third day they suddenly sprang out from their place of ambush and, with their standards raised, rushed up before the castle where we were. In our sight they seized the booty they found grazing in the pastures there.

We went out against them, but because we were few we could not fight them. When they began to shoot arrows at us, however, they wounded none of our men, God assisting us. They themselves left one of their companions, killed by a lance, lying in the field; they retained his horse, which had thrown him. Then they departed, while we remained there.

On the following day we resumed our journey. You would have marveled when, as we passed before the camps of the Armenians, they came humbly to meet us with crosses and banners out of love for Christ, and kissed our feet and our garments, because they had heard that we would defend them from the Turks, under whose yoke they had long been oppressed.

At last we reached Roais. There the aforementioned ruler of the city and his wife, together with their citizens, joyfully welcomed us and promptly fulfilled what they had promised Baldwin.

After we had remained there for fifteen days, the citizens of the city plotted wickedly to kill that ruler and elevate Baldwin to rule in the palace. They hated him. It was proposed, and it was done.

Nevertheless, Baldwin and his men were greatly saddened, because they could not obtain pardon for him. When Baldwin had accepted the rule as a gift from the citizens, he immediately began a war against the Turks who were in the country, and often defeated or killed them.

It happened, however, that several of our men were killed by the Turks. I, Fulcher of Chartres, was Baldwin’s chaplain. I now wish to resume my account of the army of God, which I left.

## CHAPTER VII

In the month of October the Franks reached Antioch in Syria, after crossing the river called the Fernus, or the Orontes. They were ordered to stretch their tents within the first mile from the city, where afterward the worst fighting repeatedly took place on both sides.

For whenever the Turks sallied out of the city, they killed many of our men; but when the turn was returned, they likewise mourned their own defeat.

Antioch is a great city in circuit, strong in situation, and powerful in its walls. No external enemy could ever capture it if its inhabitants, supplied with sufficient bread, wished to defend it.

There is in it a highly venerable basilica dedicated in honor of Saint Peter the Apostle. There he sat in the cathedra, elevated as bishop, after he had received from the Lord the leadership of the Church, having received the keys of the heavenly kingdom. There is also another church built in honor of blessed Mary. There are many other churches, handsomely constructed.

Although these churches had long existed under the power of the Turks, God, who foreknows all things, preserved them intact for us, so that one day he might be honored in them by us.

The sea is about thirteen miles from Antioch. Since the river Fernus flows into the sea there, ships laden with every kind of good are brought from distant regions along the river’s channel to a point near Antioch. Thus, supplied with goods both by sea and by land, the city abounds in riches of many kinds.

When our leaders saw that it would be so difficult to capture, they confirmed by oath among themselves that they would hold it under siege until, with God’s assistance, they could take it either by force or by stratagem.

As they were walking beside the aforementioned river, they found ships in it. After seizing them, they joined them together into a bridge, by which they later crossed to conduct their affairs, since previously they had not been able to wade across the river safely.

When the Turks saw that such a great Christian multitude was surrounding them in siege, and feared that they could in no way drive us away, they took counsel together. Gracianus, the emir of Antioch, sent his son, named Sansadole, to the sultan—that is, to the emperor of Persia—begging him to come to their aid as quickly as possible, since they had no hope of assistance from anyone else except Mahomet, their advocate.

Sent there for this purpose, he carried out the embassy with great speed. Those who remained guarded the city while awaiting the promised assistance, and frequently plotted many kinds of harm against the Franks. The Franks resisted their cunning as best they could.

It happened one day that they killed seven hundred Turks. Since the Turks had laid an ambush for the Franks, they were likewise defeated by those lying in ambush. The power of God was present there. For all our men returned unharmed, except for one who was wounded by them.

Alas! The Turks, driven by rage, killed many Christians living in the city—Greeks, Syrians, and Armenians—and, while the Franks watched, hurled the heads of those they had killed outside the walls with their stone-throwers and slings. Our people were deeply saddened by this. They hated those Christians because they feared that they might somehow strengthen the Franks.

When the Franks had besieged the city for some time and had ravaged the neighboring province everywhere while plundering it for the provisions they needed, and could find no bread anywhere to purchase, they were forced to endure a great famine.

As a result, they were all extremely despondent, and many secretly considered fleeing from the siege, either by land or by sea. They had no pay with which they could live. They were also compelled to seek their food far away, at enormous risk, withdrawing forty or sixty miles from the siege; there, especially in the mountainous regions, they were often killed by Turks lying in ambush.

We thought that these misfortunes had befallen the Franks because of their sins, by which many were bound, and because they could not capture the city for so long. For very many were weakened by both excessive pride and immoderate lust and plunder.

Therefore, after taking counsel, they expelled the women from the army, both wives and unmarried women, lest, stained by the filth of lust, they should offend the Lord. The women then found lodging for themselves in the neighboring camps.

All were desolate, both because of hunger and because of daily slaughter, the rich as well as the poor. And unless God, like a good shepherd gathering his sheep into a flock, had held them together, they would unquestionably have fled from there altogether, although they had sworn to maintain the siege.

Many, however, because of their need for bread, searched for several days through the nearby castles for the necessities of life, and afterward did not return to the army but abandoned the siege completely.

At that time we saw a remarkable redness in the sky. We also felt a great earthquake, which made us all afraid. Many further saw a certain sign shaped like a cross, whitish in color, moving in a straight path toward the east.

## CHAPTER VIII

In the year of the Lord 1098, after the entire region around Antioch had been utterly devastated everywhere by the multitude of our people, both great and small were increasingly tormented by extreme hunger.

The hungry ate bean stalks still growing in the fields, and many kinds of herbs without salt. They also ate thistles, which, because of the lack of firewood, were not properly cooked and tore the tongues of those who ate them; they ate horses, donkeys, and camels, as well as dogs and mice. The poorer people even ate the hides of animals and—shameful to say—mice and grains found in dung.

They endured cold, blows, heat, and heavy rains for God’s sake. Their tents had already grown old, rotted and torn apart by the flooding rains. Consequently many of them had no covering except the sky.

Thus, like gold tested three times in fire and purified seven times, they had long before been chosen by the Lord, as I believe, and were tested amid such great calamity and cleansed of their sins. After struggling for so long, many would willingly have completed the course of martyrdom, even if the sword of the executioner had not been lacking.

Perhaps they received the grace of so great an example from righteous Job, who, purifying his soul amid the torments of his body, always kept God in his mind.

They fight with pagans and labor for God’s sake. Although God, who creates all things, governs what he has created, sustains what he governs, and directs it by his power, can destroy whatever he wishes in a single moment, I understand that he ordains the pagans to be overthrown in this way by the scourge of the Christians. For many years, with his permission, they had vilely ruined everything belonging to God.

He permits Christians to be killed by those same Turks for the increase of their salvation, but the Turks for the destruction of their souls. Nevertheless, God was pleased that some of them, already predestined for salvation, should then be baptized by our priests. “Those whom he predestined, these he also called, and whom he called, these he also glorified” (Romans 8:30).

What more can be said? As you heard above, some of our men withdrew from that exceedingly arduous siege. Some because of poverty, some because of cowardice, and others because of fear of death—first the poor, then the rich.

Then Count Stephen of Blois left the army and returned by sea to France. We all grieved over this, because he was a most excellent and very noble man. On the day after his departure, the city of Antioch was surrendered. If he had persevered, he would have rejoiced greatly with the others.

For this reason what happened to him was turned into disgrace. A good beginning benefits no one if he does not finish well. In the affairs of the Lord, since I do not wish to lie, caution is necessary; lest I go astray in some details, I shall abbreviate much.

The siege of the city continued from that October, through the following winter, and then through the spring until the month of June began. Meanwhile the Franks and Turks repeatedly carried out attacks, battles, and ambushes against one another. They conquered and were conquered. Nevertheless, our men triumphed more often than they did.

Once, it happened that many of the Turks fell into the river Fernus while fleeing and, submerged in it, perished miserably. On either side of the Fernus, the two peoples often fought one another.

Our nobles constructed castles before the city. From them they repeatedly restrained the Turks, who frequently sallied out to attack. Thus they often took away the grazing lands of the Turks’ beasts. Nor was anything brought from the Armenians of the outer province. Yet those Armenians often came out to harm our men.

When it pleased the Lord to bring the labor of his people to completion—perhaps appeased by the prayers of those who daily poured out humble supplications to him there—he granted in his mercy that, through the treachery of those same Turks, the city should be secretly surrendered to the Christians.

Hear, then, of a deception—and not a deception.

## CHAPTER IX

For our Lord appeared to a certain Turk, chosen beforehand by his grace, and said to him: “Awake, you who sleep. I command you to surrender Antioch to the Christians.”

The man was astonished, but concealed the vision in silence. Again the Lord appeared to him: “Give the city to the Franks,” he said; “for I am Christ, who command you to do this.”

Reflecting on what he should do about it, he went to his lord, namely, the ruler of Antioch, and disclosed the vision to him. The ruler replied: “Do you wish to obey a phantasm, you brute?”

The man returned and afterward remained silent. Again the Lord appeared to him and said: “Why have you not fulfilled what I commanded? You must not hesitate, for I am the Lord of all, who command this.”

No longer doubting, the man prudently negotiated with our men so that, under cover of his scheme, they might take the city. After this agreement had been stated, and after he had given his son as a hostage to the Franks—namely, to Lord Bohemond—one night he brought twenty of our retainers inside by means of rope ladders over the top of the wall.

Without delay, the gate was opened. All the Franks entered the city, fully prepared. Forty soldiers had already entered by ropes, and those forty immediately found Turks there guarding three towers; they killed them.

Then all the Franks cried out together in a loud voice: “GOD WILLS IT, GOD WILLS IT!” This was the signal of our cry whenever we wished to undertake some action concerning our enterprise.

When the Turks heard it, they were utterly terrified. As dawn began to whiten, the Franks started attacking the city everywhere. When the Turks first saw Bohemond’s red banner unfurled high above, and heard the Franks making such a tumult with so many horns at the top of the wall, and saw them running widely through the streets and along the walls with drawn swords and ferociously killing their people, they were utterly stunned and began fleeing in every direction.

Many of them were soon killed; more fled into the castle situated on a high rock and entered it. Our common people, meanwhile, seized without restraint everything they found in the streets or houses. The soldiers, however, maintained the discipline of their military valor, pursuing and killing the Turks.

Then the emir of Antioch, namely Gratianus, was beheaded while fleeing from a certain Armenian peasant. The peasant immediately brought his severed head to the Franks.

## CHAPTER X

After the city had been captured, a certain man found a lance. He asserted that it had been discovered buried in the ground in the church of blessed Peter the Apostle and that it was the lance with which Longinus pierced the Lord’s side. He said that this had been revealed to him by Saint Andrew the Apostle.

After the apostle had appeared to him three times in a vision and admonition, he dug beneath the pavement where the vision had shown him, and found the lance—perhaps fraudulently concealed there.

He first disclosed this vision to the bishop of Puy and to Count Raymond. The bishop, however, thought it false, while Count Raymond hoped that it was genuine.

But when it had been found in this manner, and the entire people had glorified God in exultation, and it had been held in great veneration by everyone for nearly a hundred days, and Count Raymond had treated it gloriously—he often distributed to the needy the offerings devotedly made by the people to the lance, since he was its custodian—then it happened that Bishop Barae and many others, both clerics and laypeople, began to doubt whether it was the Lord’s lance that had been hoped for, or whether it was another one fraudulently discovered by that foolish man.

Therefore, after taking counsel and following a three-day fast and supplication, they kindled a pile of wood in the middle of a field beside the castle of Archa, which they were then holding under siege. After the bishops had bestowed a judicial blessing over the fire, the discoverer of the lance voluntarily and quickly passed through the middle of the blazing pyre.

When he had crossed it, they saw that the man had been burned by the flames almost to the skin like a criminal, and they understood that he had died injured internally. The outcome of the matter demonstrated this, since he died in that agony on the twelfth day.

Because everyone had venerated the lance for the honor of God and out of love, once this judgment had taken place they became doubtful and were greatly saddened. Count Raymond nevertheless kept it for so long that, through some event of which I know not the circumstances, he lost it.

Now I shall return to the other matters left aside.

## CHAPTER XI

After the city of Antioch had been captured, as has been said, an innumerable multitude of Turks surrounded that same city and laid siege to it on the following day.

For when the sultan—the king of the Persians, of whom I have already said a little—received the report that the Franks were besieging Antioch, he immediately gathered a large force and sent his army against the Franks. Its commander and emir was Corbagath.

They had remained for three weeks before the city of Edessa, where Baldwin then was, but, accomplishing nothing there, they hastened to Antioch to bring aid to Gratianus.

When the Franks saw them, they were again no less desolate than before. Because of their sins, their punishment had been doubled. For after they had entered the city, many of them immediately lay with outlawed women.

Then nearly sixty thousand Turks entered the city through the elevated fortress on the side of the high rock. They pressed our men very severely with repeated attacks. But there was no delay: struck by great fear, they went out of the city, abandoning it, to the siege outside.

The enclosed Franks, however, remained in anguish beyond what can be believed. Nevertheless, God, who had not forgotten them, often appeared to many of them—as they affirmed in their accounts—and by encouraging them promised that the people would soon rejoice in victory.

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 0844C]

Then a certain cleric, fleeing through fear of death, was visited by the Lord, who said: “Where, brother, are you directing your journey?” He replied: “I am fleeing, lest I, unfortunate man, perish. Thus many flee, lest they perish by an evil death.” The Lord said to him: “Do not flee, but go back and tell the others that I shall be with them in the battle. For, appeased by the prayers of my mother, I shall show them mercy. But because they have sinned, they have almost perished. Let their hope in me be firm, and I shall make them triumph over the Turks. Let them repent, and they shall be saved. I am the Lord who speaks with you.” At once he returned and reported what he had learned.

## CHAPTER XIII

Meanwhile, while several men wished to descend from the wall at night by ropes and flee—for this had happened to many who feared perishing either from hunger or by the sword—the already dead brother of one of those descending again appeared beside him and said: “Where are you fleeing, brother? Stay; do not be afraid, for the Lord will be with you in your battle, and your companions who have already preceded you in death on this journey will fight against the Turks together with you.” Astonished at the words of the dead man, he ceased going on and recounted to the others what he had heard.

## CHAPTER XIV

But when it pleased the Lord to bring an end to the labor of his servants, who could no longer endure such great anguish and had nothing left to eat—so that both they themselves and their horses were exceedingly weak—they mutually resolved to undertake a three-day fast with prayers and almsgiving, so that, when they had repented and devoutly supplicated the Lord, he might be reconciled to them. Meanwhile, after taking counsel, they sent word to the Turks through a certain Peter the Hermit that, unless they left undisturbed for the Christians the land that had belonged to them from ancient times, they would without fail begin battle against them on the following day. Alternatively, if they preferred, the battle could be fought by five, ten, twenty, or one hundred soldiers chosen from each side, so that the movement of the multitude of peoples would not be provoked by all fighting at once; and whichever side overcame the other would rightly receive the city and the kingdom.

This message was delivered, but the Turks did not accept it. Because they were numerous and well supplied with horses, they therefore thought they would win; they were estimated to number six hundred and sixty thousand, both cavalry and infantry. [Col. 0845B] They knew that our soldiers had become foot soldiers, weak and poor. When the envoy Peter returned, the answer was delivered. Hearing it, the Franks prepared themselves for battle with weapons, hesitating at nothing but placing their entire hope in the Lord.

There were many Turkish princes, whom they called emirs. They were: Corbagath, Meleducac, Amirsoliman, Amirsolendas, Amirhegibbe, Amirmazoane, Amirmahummet, Caraiath, Coteloseniar, Mergascotelon, Baldus, Boelquenari, Boldagis, Amirrilias, Gersaslan, Gigremis, Amirgogus, Artubech, Amirdalis, Amirmoxe, Amircharaor, and many others.

The Frankish nobles present were these: Hugh the Great; Robert, count of Normandy; Robert, count of Flanders; Duke Godfrey; Count Raymond; Bohemond; and many other nobles. [Col. 0845C] May God bless the soul of Adhemar, bishop of Le Puy, who, as an apostolic man, always charitably encouraged the people and strengthened them in the Lord.

O pious undertaking! The previous evening he himself had ordered the entire army of God’s soldiery, under public proclamation, that each person should, to the best of his ability, strive to provide his horse with a ration of grain, lest on the following day, while riding below, they should collapse from hunger during the hour of battle. The order was given, and it was carried out.

Thus, when everything had been prepared for battle, they went out of the city very early in the morning; this occurred on the fourth day before the Kalends of July. The standards of the squadrons and battle-lines went before them, and the forces were suitably divided separately into companies and battalions. Among them were priests clad in white garments, who, weeping, sang psalms to the Lord for the entire people and poured forth many prayers [Col. 0845D] with devout hearts.

Then a certain Turk named Amirdalis, a man of outstanding military distinction, saw our people advancing against them with their standards raised and was greatly astonished. When he saw the standards of our leaders, which he recognized individually because he had usually lived in Antioch, he thought that battle would soon take place. He immediately informed Corbagath, the chief emir.

“What are you playing at? Look, the Franks are coming.”

Corbagath replied: “Are they coming to fight?”

Amirdalis answered: “I do not yet know; but wait a little.”

When he again saw the standards of our princes being carried in orderly formation on either side, with the divided battle-lines properly following, Corbagath said again: “There are the Franks. [Col. 0846A] What do you think?”

“I think it is battle,” he replied, “but wait a little longer. I know whose standards these are that I see.”

Looking more attentively once again, he recognized the standard of the bishop of Le Puy advancing with the third company.

They are no longer far away, and Corbagath then said:

> “Look, the Franks are coming; flee now, or fight well.  
> For I see the standard of the great pope going before them.  
> Those whom you thought already utterly crushed—  
> today beware lest they overcome you.”

Corbagath said: “I shall send to the Franks and grant today what they demanded of me yesterday.”

Amirdalis said: “You have spoken too late.”

Nevertheless, Corbagath sent the message; but he did not obtain what he sought. Amirdalis, however, immediately left him and spurred his horse with his heels.

> He considers fleeing, yet he himself warns his companions  
> to fight bravely, all of them, and to shoot their arrows.

Look: Hugh the Great, Robert the Norman, and the count of Flanders were positioned in the first battle-line as attackers. In the second, Duke Godfrey followed with the Germans and Lotharingians. After them came the bishop of Le Puy and the forces of Count Raymond, the Gascons and the Provençals. The count himself remained in the city to guard it. Bohemond skilfully led the final company.

When the Turks saw themselves being attacked by the entire Frankish army with the fiercest assault, they began to rush out in scattered groups and shoot arrows. But the fear of the Lord was cast upon them, as though the whole world had suddenly fallen upon them. They all took to an uncontrolled flight, and, fleeing as best they could, were driven away by the Franks.

Because the Franks had few horses and were weakened by hunger, they did not hold back as many of the pagans as they should have; but all their tents remained behind. In those tents they also found many different possessions: gold, silver, cloaks, clothing, utensils, and many other things. The Turks, overcome with fear, had scattered them across the fields as they fled, abandoning or throwing away horses, mules, camels, and asses, as well as excellent helmets, bows, arrows, and quivers.

Corbagath fled faster than a stag—the man who, by threats and such savage words, had so often already killed the Franks. But why did he flee, when he had such a great people and was well supplied with horses? Because he had attempted to fight against God. The Lord, seeing his pomp and will, utterly brought them to nothing. Yet he did not allow him to fall into the hands of the Franks, nor his soldiers either, since he does not avenge himself on his enemies every day. And because they had swift horses, they escaped; the slower ones, however, remained for our Franks.

Many of them, including Saracen infantrymen, were cut down by swords. Of our men, only a few were wounded. The women found in their tents they killed with the sword.

Then all blessed and glorified God with shouts of rejoicing, because he had delivered from such savage enemies those who, placed in such great need and anguish, had hoped in him and in the right hand of his mercy. After their defeat, they became triumphant there and rejoiced. Enriched by their possessions, they returned happily to the city.

> When the noble Antiochene city was captured,  
> eleven hundred, if from that number you subtract twice one,  
> such was the number of years of the Lord born from the Virgin.  
> Under the Gemini, Phoebus had risen with them nine times.

At that time Bishop Adhemar died, namely on the Kalends of August. May his soul enjoy eternal rest. Then Hugh the Great, with the consent of the leaders, departed for Constantinople and afterward for France.

## CHAPTER XV

After all these events, the illustrious company of the leaders of the entire army sent this letter to the Roman pontiff: [Col. 0847B]

> “To the holy and venerable lord Pope Urban: Bohemond; Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles; Godfrey, duke of Lorraine; Robert, count of Normandy; Robert, count of Flanders; and Eustace, count of Boulogne, send greetings, faithful service, and true submission in Christ as sons to their spiritual father.
>
> We all wish and desire it to be known to you how great was God’s mercy, and by how evident an assistance of his, Antioch was captured by us, and the Turks who had inflicted many insults upon our Lord Jesus were captured and killed; and how we, the Jerusalemites of Jesus Christ, avenged the injury done to the Most High God; and how we, who had previously besieged the Turks, were afterward besieged by Turks coming from Chorasan, Jerusalem, Damascus, and many other lands [Col. 0847C]; and how we were delivered by the mercy of Jesus Christ.
>
> After we had captured Nicaea and, as you have heard, defeated a very great multitude of Turks in the flowering field on the Kalends of July, driven that great Solyman into flight, and stripped him of all his land and possessions, we acquired and pacified the whole of Romania and came to besiege Antioch. During that siege we suffered many evils, both from the battles with neighboring Turks and from pagans who attacked us so frequently and in such numbers that we might more truly be said to have been besieged by those whom we had besieged in Antioch.
>
> At last, when all the battles had been overcome, the Christian faith was exalted through their favorable outcome in this manner. [Col. 0847D] I, Bohemond, having made an agreement with a certain Turk who handed the city over to me, placed ladders against the wall shortly before dawn. Thus, on the Nones of July, we captured the city that had previously resisted Christ, and we killed Gratianus, the tyrant of that city, together with many of his soldiers. We retained their wives, children, and households, along with their gold and silver and all their possessions.
>
> But we could not take possession of the citadel of Antioch, which the Turks had strongly fortified. When we wished to attack that citadel on the following day, we saw across all the fields an infinite multitude of Turks whom we had awaited for many days, expecting them to come out of the city to fight us. On the third day they besieged us, and more than one hundred of their soldiers entered the aforesaid citadel. Through its gate they tried to break into the city situated beneath the citadel, which was common to us and to them.
>
> We, however, being on another mountain opposite the citadel, guarded the road descending between the two armies toward the city, so that they could not break in upon us in much greater numbers. Fighting inside and outside, we forced them to enter the gates of the citadel descending toward the city and to return to their camp. When they saw that they could harm us nothing from that side, they surrounded us on every side so completely that none of our men could go out or come to us.
>
> For this reason we were all so desolate and afflicted that, dying of hunger and many hardships, we killed our hungry horses and asses, and many of us ate them. [Col. 0848B] Meanwhile, when the most merciful compassion of almighty God came to our aid and watched over us, the Lord’s lance, by which the side of our Savior had been pierced by the hands of Longinus, was revealed three times by the holy apostle Andrew to a certain servant of God, who also pointed out the place where the lance lay. We found it in the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.
>
> By this discovery and by many other divine revelations we were so comforted and strengthened that, although previously afflicted and fearful, we then encouraged one another to fight with the greatest boldness and readiness.
>
> After being besieged for three weeks and four days, on the vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul, trusting in God and confessing all our iniquities, we went out through the city gates with all our military equipment. [Col. 0848C] We were so few that they claimed we were not going out to fight them but to flee.
>
> Once we were all prepared, with both infantry and soldiers arranged in their appointed ranks, we boldly attacked the place where their power and strength were greatest. With the Lord’s lance and in the first engagement of the battle, we forced them to flee.
>
> As is their custom, they began to scatter in every direction, occupying hills and roads and attempting to surround us wherever they could. For they thought in this way to kill us all. But, having been instructed by many battles in their cunning and stratagems, we were so aided by God’s grace and mercy that, although we were very few in comparison with them, we forced them all together into one body. Once gathered, with God’s right hand fighting alongside us, we compelled them to flee and to abandon their camp with everything that was in it.
>
> After defeating them, driving them in flight throughout the entire day, and killing many thousands of them, we returned to the city joyful and glad. The aforesaid citadel was surrendered to Bohemond by a certain emir who was in it with one thousand men, and through Bohemond’s hand they unanimously submitted themselves to the Christian faith.
>
> Thus our Lord Jesus Christ subjected the whole of Antioch to Roman religion and faith.
>
> But because something sorrowful usually intervenes in joyful affairs, that bishop of Le Puy whom you had entrusted to us as your vicar, after the battle in which he had acted honorably and after the city had been pacified, died on the Kalends of August. [Col. 0849A]
>
> Therefore, now that your sons have been deprived of their father, we command you, our spiritual father, that you who began this road, who by your words made us all abandon our lands and whatever was in them, who ordered us to follow Christ carrying crosses, and who urged us to exalt the Christian name—fulfill what you exhorted us to do. Come, and summon all whom you can to come with you.
>
> For here the Christian name first took its beginning. After blessed Peter had been enthroned in the chair that we see daily, those who had previously been called Galileans were first and principally called Christians here.
>
> What, then, appears more fitting in the world than that you, who are the father and head of the Christian religion, should come to the principal and chief city of the Christian name and complete on your part the war that is yours? We have conquered the Turks and pagans, but we have not been able to conquer the heretics, Greeks, Armenians, Syrians, and Jacobites.
>
> Therefore we command and again command you, our dearest Father, that you, as Father and head, come to the place of your fatherhood; that, since you are the vicar of blessed Peter, you sit in his chair; that you keep us, your sons, obedient in all right actions; and that by your authority and our strength you eradicate and destroy every heresy, of whatever kind.
>
> In this way, together with us, may you open to us the gates of both Jerusalems along the road of Jesus Christ that we began and that you preached; may you make the Lord’s sepulcher free; and may you exalt the Christian name above every name. [Col. 0849C]
>
> For if you come to us and complete with us the road begun through you, the whole world will obey you. May he cause you to do this, the God who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.”

## CHAPTER XVI

When our men at Antioch had rested for four months with their horses, refreshed by rest and food, and had recovered their former strength—for they had been worn out by labor over so many days—one part of the army, after taking counsel, entered inner Syria, desiring to delay the Jerusalem journey still further. Bohemond and Count Raymond were the principal leaders of this army. The other princes still remained in the Antiochene regions.

These two, with their people, captured two cities by a very bold assault, namely Baram and Marra. The first of these they captured with the utmost speed, utterly laying waste its citizens and carrying off everything they found in it; then they hastened to the second. There, after conducting a siege for twenty days, our people suffered extreme hunger.

I shudder to say that many of our men, maddened by the fury of hunger, cut from the buttocks of a dead Saracen one piece or two. Having lightly roasted it, they ate it with grim mouths. Thus the besiegers suffered more anguish than the besieged.

Meanwhile, after constructing siege engines and at last bringing them up to the wall, the Franks, in a daring assault and with God’s aid, entered over the top of the wall. On that day and the next they killed all the Saracens, from the greatest to the least, and seized all their possessions.

After the city had been crushed, Bohemond returned to Antioch, from which he expelled the men of Count Raymond whom he had placed there as custodians of his portion. Later he possessed that city together with the entire province. For he claimed, through his own advocacy and contrivance, that it had been handed over to him.

Count Raymond, however, joined by Tancred, continued along the road he had begun. Robert the Norman, who had departed on the second day from Marra, the city they had captured, also joined that same army.

## CHAPTER XVII

In the year 1099 from the Lord’s Incarnation, they set out for a castle called Archas, situated at the foot of Lebanon. Because of the strength of its location, it was extremely difficult for external enemies to capture. They remained encamped before it for nearly five weeks.

Araceus, son of Canaan, founded that very ancient town, as we read. Duke Godfrey and Robert, count of Flanders, followed that army not long afterward. Before they reached it, they had surrounded with a siege a certain very famous castle called Gibellum. But after receiving a message from the army urging them to hasten to their aid against the Turks whom they were awaiting for battle, they immediately abandoned Gibellum and set out to carry out the assigned task.

When they reached the army, they sat down with them, but they did not have the battle they had perhaps expected. During that siege, however, Ansellus of Ribotimonte, a vigorous knight, died from a blow by a stone.

Then, after taking counsel together, they decided that if they remained there for some time and could not capture the castle, irrecoverable loss would result for everyone. They said it would be worthwhile to abandon the siege and travel by a road known to them to be free of trade, while the season of harvest still awaited them on their journey to Jerusalem; and that, once they had gone, they could live on the harvest prepared for them everywhere by the Lord and, supported by such provisions, reach the most desired place under the Lord’s guidance.

This advice was approved, and it was carried out. Gathering their tents, they proceeded on their journey and passed through the city of Tripoli. After passing it, they traveled near the castle of Gibellum.

It was the month of April, and they were already living from the harvests. Proceeding farther, and passing not far from the city of Beirut, they found beyond that city another city which we read was called Sidon, in the land of Phoenicia. Sidon, son of Canaan, founded it; from him came the name Sidonians. From there they went to Sarepta of Sidon.

After that they found the excellent city of Tyre, from which Apollonius came, as is recorded in 1 Maccabees 3:10. The evangelist also speaks of these two cities: “Into the regions of Tyre and Sidon” (Matthew 15:21).

Now the inhabitants of the region call the former Sagitta and the latter Sur. For in Hebrew it is called Soor, and it lies within the allotment of Naphtali.

After these places they passed Ptolemais, formerly called Achon. Certain mistaken readers used to read Accaron, and so did we when we first entered the land of the Palestinians. But Accaron is a city of the Philistines [Col. 0851A] between Azotus and Jamnia, near Ascalon.

Acon, that is, Ptolemais, has Mount Carmel to the south. Passing beside it, they left on their right a town called Cayphas, and from there proceeded beside Dora, or Pirgul. After this they traveled beside Caesarea of Palestine, which was also called by another name, the Tower of Strato. There Herod called Agrippa, the grandson of that Herod during whose reign Christ was born, was struck by an angel, consumed by worms, and miserably breathed his last.

Then they left the coastal region on their right and continued through a city called Ramla. Its Saracen inhabitants had already fled the day before the Franks arrived there. They found a great quantity of grain there, with which they loaded all their beasts of burden, and afterward carried it as far as Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER XVIII

After remaining there for four days, they appointed a bishop over the basilica of Saint George and stationed men in the fortifications to guard the city. Then they set out on their journey toward Jerusalem.

That same day they traveled as far as the castle called Emmaus. During that night one hundred of our soldiers, moved by cunning and ready for action, mounted their horses. At dawn, passing near Jerusalem, they hastened as far as Bethlehem. One of them was Tancred, and another was Baldwin of Bourcq.

When the Christians living there learned that the Franks had arrived—Greeks and Syrians, that is—they rejoiced with very great joy. At first, however, not knowing what people they were, they thought them either Turks or Arabs. But when they looked at them more closely and realized without doubt that they were Franks, they immediately took up crosses and banners, went out to meet them weeping, and sang devoutly.

They wept because they feared that such a small number of men would easily be killed by the great multitude of pagans whom they knew to be in the country; they sang because they rejoiced over those whose coming they had long desired and whom they perceived would restore Christianity, so long cast down by the wicked, to its recovered honor.

After they had immediately made a devout supplication to God in the basilica of blessed Mary and visited the place where Christ had been born, they exchanged a joyful kiss of peace with the Syrians and quickly returned to the holy city.

Behold, our following army then approached the city, leaving Gabaon on its left; Gabaon is fifty stadia distant from Jerusalem. When the vanguard displayed its raised standards to the citizens, the internal enemies immediately came out against them. But those who had come out so hastily were driven back into the city even more hastily and withdrew:

> The yearly custom gave the seventh Ides of June;  
> June was already warm with the fire of seven lights,  
> when the Franks surrounded Jerusalem with a siege.

The city itself is situated in a mountainous place, lacking streams, woods, and springs, except for the spring of Siloam, where water is sometimes available in sufficient quantity, but at other times is drawn only rarely. This little spring lies at the bottom of a valley, below Mount Zion, beneath the course of the torrent of Kidron, which usually flows through the Valley of Jehoshaphat in winter.

There are many cisterns in the city, sufficiently abundant in water. If properly maintained, they provide an unfailing supply at all times for all the inhabitants, both people and beasts, since they preserve the winter rains.

The city is of becoming size and well arranged around its circuit, so that no one finds it displeasing either through smallness or through excessive extent. On the western side it has the Davidic Tower, which completes the city wall on both sides. Up to half its height from below, it is solidly built of squared stones cemented together and sealed with molten lead. If it is supplied with provisions, and if only twenty or fifteen men remain inside as defenders, it could never be captured by force by any army.

Within the same city is the Lord’s Temple, round in form, built on the very site where Solomon formerly established another marvelous temple. Although it cannot at all be compared with that earlier structure, it was nevertheless made with marvelous workmanship and an exceptionally beautiful form.

In its center is a huge outcrop of natural rock, which greatly disfigures and obstructs the temple itself. I do not know why it has been permitted from eternity to occupy the place instead of being entirely cut away. But they say that this is the place where the angel stood while striking, and where David, greatly afraid, said to him: “I am the one who sinned; but these, who are sheep, what have they done?” (2 Samuel 24:17).

They also say that within the same rock is the ark of the Lord’s covenant, together with the rod and the tablets of the testimony, securely sealed there because King Josiah ordered it to be placed in the sanctuary of the temple, saying: “You shall by no means carry it from this place” (2 Chronicles 35:3). For he foresaw the captivity that was to come.

But this is contradicted by what we read in the writings of Jeremiah, namely, that Jeremiah had hidden it in Arabia and said that it would not be found until many nations had gathered together (Jeremiah 3:17). He was a contemporary of King Josiah, yet he ended his life before Jeremiah died. We therefore do not believe that the ark is in the temple.

I am neither able nor willing to recount the things of such great holiness that are said to be found there, lest I deceive my listeners in any respect. But, according to the statements of certain people, I have gathered these few details out of honor and love for God.

This is certainly the house of God of which it is written: “It was founded securely upon a firm rock” (Matthew 7:25). When Solomon devoutly poured out his prayer to God in it, asking that his eyes might be open over it day and night and that whoever prayed toward that sanctuary with a true heart might be heard by him, the Lord granted his request and answered him according to what he had asked.

All the Saracens had held this house—that is, the Lord’s temple—in great reverence until we took it from them. There they used to deliver their sermons more willingly than elsewhere, although they profaned it with an idol made in the name of Muhammad; they permitted no Christian to enter it.

The other temple, called Solomon’s, is large and marvelous, but it is not the same one that Solomon himself built. It is now a matter of considerable grief that, oppressed by poverty, we were unable to restore its roofing after it came into the hands of King Baldwin and us. He himself even sold the lead to merchants when it sometimes fell from the roof or when he ordered it to be torn down.

There is also a handsome basilica built in a circular form over the Lord’s sepulcher. Its circular summit is so artfully left without a covering that, being open through that aperture to the sunlight, it is always bright.

The city also has water channels throughout all its streets, through which all impurities are washed away during the rainy season.

The emperor Aelius Hadrian also adorned this city magnificently and suitably paved its streets and squares. From his name Jerusalem was called Aelia.

For these and many other reasons, the city itself is venerable and glorious. When the Franks saw it and realized that it would be difficult to capture, our leaders ordered wooden ladders to be made. Afterward, once these had been raised against the wall, they might perhaps enter the city with a strong assault by climbing them to the top of the wall, with God’s help.

After they had done this, on the following seventh day, at the command of the nobles, with trumpets sounding, they attacked the city on all sides at first light with a remarkable assault. They attacked until the sixth hour of the day, but because the ladders they had fixed were few, they could not enter by them; so they sadly abandoned the assault.

Then, after taking counsel, the craftsmen were ordered to construct siege engines, with which, once brought up to the wall, they might achieve the fulfillment of their hope with God’s aid. And so it was done.

Meanwhile, they suffered no shortage of bread or meat. But because, as has been said above, the place is without water and without rivers, our men and their beasts greatly needed water to drink. Therefore, as necessity required, they sought water far away and laboriously carried it in their skins from four or five miles away to the siege.

When the engines had been completed—rams, namely, and stone-throwers—they prepared themselves again for the assault. Among the other works, they assembled one tower from small pieces of wood, since large timber was lacking. Then, after an order had been issued for this purpose, they carried it at night in sections to the most suitable corner of the city.

At dawn they prepared stone-throwers and other equipment and very quickly raised the assembled tower not far from the wall. Once it had been erected and well covered on the outside with interwoven hides, they gradually pushed it closer to the wall.

Then a few soldiers, yet courageous ones, climbed into it at the sound of the horn. From there they immediately began throwing stones and arrows. The Saracens likewise defended themselves against them, and hurled fire mixed with oil and fat, attached to torches, from their slings against the said tower and the soldiers who were in it.

Thus, while many on both sides fought against one another in this way, death was often present. On the side where Count Raymond and his men were stationed, namely at Mount Zion, they launched a great assault with their engines. On the other side, where Duke Godfrey, Robert count of Normandy, and Robert of Flanders were, the assault against the wall was greater.

This they did on that day. On the following day, amid the sound of trumpets, they undertook the same labor more vigorously, so that by striking the wall with rams they pierced it at one place.

Two beams hung before the wall’s battlements, fastened there with ropes. The Saracens had prepared them to serve as a barrier against those attacking and throwing stones at them. But what they had made for their own advantage, through the Lord’s providence they received to their own detriment.

For when the aforesaid tower had been brought up to the wall and the bundles binding the ropes from which the beams hung had been cut, the Franks then joined one of those beams to the others to make a bridge. They cleverly extended it from the tower and cast it over the wall.

By then one of the stone towers on the wall was burning; our engineers had thrown fire-bearing projectiles onto it. As the fire gradually took hold within the wooden material, smoke and flame began to emerge so fiercely that none of the citizens’ guards could remain there any longer.

Then, at midday, on the day that was Friday, the Franks entered the city. Trumpets sounded, everyone was in uproar, and they attacked bravely, crying out, “Help, God!” One standard had already been raised upon the top of the wall. The pagans, utterly ashamed, changed their courage into swift flight through the city’s alleys and narrow streets. As they fled swiftly, they were pursued and driven away even more swiftly.

Count Raymond, who was attacking from the other side, did not yet know this, nor did his men, until they saw the Saracens leaping before them over the top of the wall. When they saw this, they hastened to the city with the greatest joy and, together with the others, began to drive away and kill the wicked enemies.

Then other Saracens—Arabs as well as Ethiopians—fled into the citadel of David; others shut themselves inside the Lord’s Temple and Solomon’s Temple. In the courtyards of the temples the attack upon them was immense; nowhere was there a place where they could escape our swordsmen.

Many of them were shot to death on top of Solomon’s Temple, which they had climbed while fleeing, and were hurled irreparably down from the roof. In that same temple nearly ten thousand were beheaded. If you had been there, our feet would have been stained up to their bases with the blood of the slain.

What shall I say? None of them was spared alive. Nor did they spare the women or the children.

You would have seen something remarkable: when our shield-bearers and poorer infantry discovered the cunning of the Saracens, they split open the bellies of those already killed in order to extract from their intestines the bezants that the living had swallowed.

Therefore, after several days, they made a great heap of the corpses and burned them, so that they might more easily find that aforementioned copper in the ashes.

Tancred, however, entered the Lord’s Temple at a swift pace and seized much gold and silver—which it was unlawful to plunder—as well as precious stones. But he later made amends for this and returned all of it, or its value, to the holy place.

[Col. 0855A]

> With drawn swords our people run through the city,  
> and they spare no one, not even those who plead for mercy.  
> The people lay strewn as when, after being stirred, rotten …

Fruits fall from the branches, and acorns from the shaken holm oak.

After such a slaughter they entered the houses and seized whatever they found in them, in such a way that whoever first entered a house—whether poor or rich—could suffer no injury from anyone else, but might take and possess the house itself or palace, and whatever he found in it, as though it were entirely his own. They had mutually established this as a law to be observed. Thus many who had been poor became wealthy.

Then, going to the Lord’s Sepulchre and his glorious temple, clergy and laity together, singing a new song to the Lord with voices raised in exultation, all joyfully visited the long-desired holy places, with offerings and most humble supplications.

O time so greatly desired! O time worthy of remembrance among all other times! O deed to be preferred above all deeds! Truly it was desired, because all worshipers of the Catholic faith had always desired inwardly in their hearts that the place where the Creator of all creatures—God made man—had bestowed upon the human race, through his manifold mercy, the gift of saving restoration by being born, dying, and rising again, should at last be cleansed from the contagion of its pagan inhabitants, after having so long been defiled by their superstition, and should be restored by those who believed and trusted in him to the dignity of its former state.

And truly it is a memorial, and rightly worthy of remembrance, because everything that our Lord Jesus Christ did and taught on earth, living as man among human beings, was recalled and restored to most renowned memory. And what that same Lord willed to be accomplished through this people of his—so greatly beloved, as I believe, and his fostered household, chosen beforehand for this undertaking—will resound in the tongues of all the tribes until the end of the age as a memorial.

July, boiling hot, was warmed by thrice five days of light.

If from the number eleven hundred you subtract one,

they said that the years of the Lord had then been completed,

when we, the Gallic people, captured Jerusalem.

Thrice five days of July shone with gleaming light,

when the Franks captured the city by mighty valor,

in the year one thousand one hundred, less one,

[Col. 0855D] from the birth of the Virgin who gave birth to him who rules all things.

It was the Ides of July, in the two hundred and eighty-fifth year after the death of Charles the Great, and in the twelfth year after the death of William, first king of England. For when Godfrey had immediately been made prince of the homeland, the entire people of the Lord’s army chose him as prince of the kingdom in the holy city, to preserve and govern it, on account of the excellence of his nobility, his military virtue, his modest endurance, and the refinement of his character.

At that time canons were also established in the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, to serve in that same temple. They decided that a patriarch should not yet be appointed there, until they had asked the Roman pope whom he would approve for that office.

Meanwhile the Turks and Arabs, together with nearly five hundred black Ethiopians who had entered the citadel of David, asked Count Raymond, who was lodging near that tower, to allow them to depart alive, provided that their money was left in the citadel itself. He granted this, and they then went to Ascalon.

It pleased God at that time that a fragment of the Lord’s Cross was discovered in a hidden place, where it had been concealed by religious men since ancient times; now, by God’s will, it was revealed by a certain Syrian. He had carefully hidden and preserved it there with the knowledge of his father.

This fragment, fashioned in the form of a cross and partly covered with gold and silver workmanship, they all carried openly to the Lord’s Sepulchre and then to the temple, singing psalms joyfully and giving thanks to God, who for so many days had preserved this treasure of his—and of ours—for himself and for us.

## CHAPTER XIX

[Note: The material that follows has been emended and corrected on the authority of a manuscript codex.]

When the king of Babylon and the commander of his army, named Lavendalius, heard that the Franks had already drawn near to the Babylonian kingdom in order to subdue it, they gathered a multitude under orders from the Turks, Arabs, and Ethiopians, and hastened to march against them in battle.

When the commander mentioned above, the Babylonian, heard again through messengers that Jerusalem had already been captured with such ferocity, he was enraged and hastened either to engage them in battle or to besiege them shut up in that same city. When this was announced to the Franks, they adopted a plan of great boldness and directed their forces toward Ascalon against those tyrants, carrying with them the wood of the life-giving Cross mentioned above.

One day, while the Franks were wandering about not far from Ascalon and awaiting battle, they found there a considerable quantity of booty consisting of oxen and camels, sheep and goats. When, as the sun was declining, they had gathered this herd near their tents, our princes strictly ordered that it should not be driven along with them on the following day, when they expected battle, so that they might be free of every burden and ready to fight.

When morning came, they learned from scouts sent ahead that the pagans were approaching. Having learned this, the tribunes and centurions most prudently arranged the battle, stationing their people in wings and wedges, and boldly advanced against the enemy with their standards raised.

You would have seen the booty mentioned above proceeding straight ahead, as though directed by the command of its leaders, on the right and left of the battle lines, although no one drove it forward. Thus many pagans, watching it from a distance moving along with our soldiers, thought that the whole was the Frankish army.

When that countless people had drawn near our wedges, like a stag displaying the branches of its antlers, they made their forward wedge forked and, spreading out the advancing Arab forces, attempted to surround our rear, where Duke Godfrey, following behind with a dense column of armed soldiers, was pressing forward and guarding the rear. The other nobles proceeded, some in the first line and others in the second.

But when the enemies on both sides had drawn within a stone’s throw, or a little more, of one another, our infantry immediately stretched their bows and shot arrows at them. Lances followed the arrows most appropriately, while our horsemen, as though they had all confirmed one another by oath, charged them with tremendous force. Those whose mounts were not then swift enough in their running were immediately overwhelmed by death beneath their riders, and within a brief hour many bodies lay pale and lifeless.

Then many of them, fearing death, climbed to the tops of trees. Yet, wounded by arrows and struck with death there, they fell miserably to the ground, while the Saracens everywhere feared the penetrating attack against them.

After the tents had been passed, those who escaped were driven as far as the walls of Ascalon. This city is seven hundred and twenty stadia distant from Jerusalem.

In the first line their commander Lavendalius, although he had previously despised the Franks, turned his back and fled—not slowly. He unwillingly abandoned his tent, together with the other tents that had been pitched and fortified with money.

The Franks then returned, regrouped, and rejoiced in victory, giving thanks to the Lord. They entered the enemy’s tents and found in them many treasures: gold, silver, cloaks, garments, and precious stones, which are named in this order: jasper, sapphire, chalcedony, emerald, sardonyx, sardius, chrysolite, beryl, topaz, chrysoprase, hyacinth, and amethyst.
