They also found vessels and utensils of many kinds, gilded helmets, excellent rings, marvelous swords, grain, flour, and many other things. That night they lodged there and kept careful watch. For on the following day they thought that the Saracens would renew the battle; nevertheless, overcome by great fear, they all fled during that very night.

When the scouts reported this in the morning, they blessed and glorified God with voices full of praise, because he had permitted so many thousands of unbelievers to be scattered by a small Christian army.

“Blessed be God, who did not give us as prey to their teeth” (Ps. 123:6). “Blessed is the nation whose Lord is its God” (Ps. 32:12).

Had not those Babylonians themselves threatened, saying: “Let us go and seize Jerusalem with the Franks shut up inside it. When all of them have been killed, let us eradicate that sepulchre so precious to them, cast its building stones outside the city, and let no mention of it ever be made again”?

But by God’s mercy, when this had come to nothing, the Franks also loaded their horses and camels with the Babylonians’ money. Since they could not carry the tents, the many javelins lying in the fields, the bows, and the arrows to the holy city, they committed all these things to the flames; then they joyfully returned to Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER XX  
### On the Return of the Princes to Their Homeland

After these events, some decided to return to the homeland of their people. Once they had promptly washed in the river Jordan and had gathered palm branches at Jericho in the garden called Abraham’s, Count Robert of the Normans and Count Robert of Flanders sailed toward Constantinople and then returned to France, to their own lands.

Raymond, however, returned as far as Laodicea in Syria, leaving his wife in Constantinople and intending to return to Laodicea. Duke Godfrey, retaining Tancred and several others with him, governed the principality of Jerusalem, which he had undertaken to hold with everyone’s consent.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### On Bohemond and Baldwin, and Their Pilgrimage

When Lord Bohemond, who at that time ruled Antioch, a prudent and energetic man, heard that Jerusalem had been captured by his fellow leaders who had gone ahead, and when Lord Baldwin, the aforementioned Godfrey’s brother, who likewise ruled Edessa and the neighboring region beyond the Euphrates, heard it, they were filled with the greatest joy and offered humble praises to God.

If those who had preceded them because of the haste of their journey had acted well and usefully, there can be no doubt that these two, although they would follow later with their own men, would nevertheless share in the same reward.

For it was necessary that the land and cities already taken from the Turks with such great labor should be carefully guarded, lest, if the land were imprudently abandoned and everyone went to Jerusalem at that time, it should be retaken in a sudden return by the Turks who had already been driven back as far as Persia. This would have brought no small loss upon the Franks, both those going and those returning.

Perhaps divine providence delayed them, judging that they would be more useful in affairs still to be carried out than in those already completed.

O how often in the meantime Baldwin himself was exhausted by battles fought against the Turks in the regions of Mesopotamia! The number of their heads cut off there cannot be recounted. It often happened that he and his small force fought against their great multitude and, with God’s help, rejoiced in triumph.

But when Bohemond had warned him through messengers that the two of them, with their own men, should complete the journey they had not yet finished and go to Jerusalem, Baldwin immediately arranged his affairs suitably and prepared to depart.

Then, however, when he heard that the Turks were invading one border of his homeland, he abandoned what he had begun. Before he had even gathered his little army, he went with a few men to meet the enemy.

When they thought that he had already begun his journey, one day, while they were secure in their tents, they saw the white standard carried by Baldwin and, terrified, fled as quickly as possible. After pursuing them for a short distance with his few men, he returned to what he had begun earlier.

He then set out and, with Antioch on his right, came to Laodicea. There, after purchasing provisions for the journey and repairing the pack saddles, we departed. It was the month of November.

When we had passed Gibellum, we caught up with Bohemond, who was lodged in his tents before a town called Valenium. With him was a certain Pisan archbishop named Daibert, who had arrived by ship at the port of Laodicea with some Tuscans and Italians; they were waiting there to travel with us.

There was also a certain bishop from Apulia. He was the third with Lord Baldwin. When these men had been assembled so amicably, we were estimated to number twenty-five thousand of both sexes, infantry and cavalry alike.

When we entered the interior regions of the Saracens, we could obtain neither bread nor any other food from the inhabitants, who were strongly hostile to us, because there was no one either to give or to sell anything. As our provisions were increasingly exhausted, many became tormented by hunger.

The horses and other animals, too, suffered greatly, their distress doubled by the failure of grain: they went on, but did not eat.

At that time, in the cultivated fields through which we were passing, there were certain crops that the common people call “cannamelles,” almost resembling reeds, their name being compounded from *canna* and *mel*, “reed” and “honey.” Hence, I think, wild honey is also so called, because it is skillfully made from these plants.

Hungry, we chewed them with our teeth all day because of their honeyed taste, though with little benefit. Indeed, for the love of God we endured this and many other things—hunger, cold, and excessive rains.

Many even ate horses, asses, and camels for want of bread. Moreover, we were very often tormented by extreme cold and an abundance of rain. There was not enough sunshine to dry our soaked garments when the unbroken rain afflicted us for four or five days at a time.

I then saw many people without tents perish from the cold of the rain. I, Fulcher of Chartres, who was present during these events, saw one day many people of both sexes, as well as very many animals, die in this bitterly cold rain.

It would take too long to recount, and perhaps it would weary the listener, since no anxiety and no pain was absent from the people of God.

Often several were killed by Saracens lying in ambush along the road near narrow passages, or while they went out to obtain provisions. You would have seen noble knights become infantrymen after losing their horses in one way or another. You would have seen, when the pack animals failed, goats taken from the Saracens and loaded with baggage, and rams burdened with packs and greatly fatigued, their backs damaged by the weight of that load.

Twice, and no more, along this road we obtained bread and grain through very costly trade, from the people of Tripoli and Caesarea. It is therefore clear that hardly anyone can acquire anything great without great labor.

It was indeed a great thing when we reached Jerusalem. After visiting it, our long labor was completed. When we looked upon the most desired Holy of Holies, we were filled with immense joy.

O how often we recalled that Davidic prophecy in which he says: “We shall worship in the place where his feet have stood” (Ps. 131:7)! We then saw this fulfilled in us, although it likewise applies to many others: “We went up there, the tribes of the Lord, to confess his holy name” (Ps. 121:4).

On the day when we entered Jerusalem, the sun, having completed its winter descent, resumed its upward course.

After we had visited the Lord’s Sepulchre, his glorious temple, and the other holy places, on the fourth day we went to Bethlehem, intending to celebrate that very night the annual commemoration of the Lord’s Nativity and to keep vigil in prayer in the presence of the manger where Jesus was laid by Mary, his venerable mother.

When this had been completed during the night with fitting observance, and when the third hour of the day had come and the third Mass had been celebrated, we returned to Jerusalem.

O what a stench there then was around the city walls, inside and outside, from the corpses of the Saracens still lying there, whom our companions had slaughtered wherever they had caught them after the capture of the city!

When we and our animals had been somewhat refreshed by the rest we needed, and when the duke and the other nobles had appointed a patriarch in the church of the Holy Sepulchre—namely, the aforementioned Lord Daibert—we renewed our provisions, loaded our animals, and descended on our return journey to the river Jordan.

Then some of the later army decided to remain in Jerusalem, while some of the earlier army returned with us. The duke, as before, governed the land of Jerusalem energetically:

On the third Ides of August, when he was then sufficiently ill,

Urban, the venerable bishop of Rome, fell.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### On the Return of Bohemond and Count Baldwin to Their Own Lands

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1100, on the first day of the year, after palm branches had been cut at Jericho, we all took them up to carry them, as is customary, and on the second day began our return journey.

Our princes decided to pass through the city of Tiberias, beside the sea. This sea, formed from fresh water, is eighteen thousand paces in length and five paces in breadth; or, according to Josephus, forty stadia in breadth and one hundred in length.

Then, passing through Caesarea Philippi, which in the Syrian language is called Paneas, situated at the foot of Mount Lebanon, where two springs emerge from which the river Jordan rises, we proceeded onward. The Jordan then cuts through the Sea of Galilee and pours itself into the Dead Sea.

This lake is called Gennesar; according to Josephus, it is forty stadia in length and one hundred in breadth. The river then runs through a single channel and pours itself into the sea called the Dead, because it produces nothing living.

This lake, called Asphaltites, is believed to be bottomless and to descend into the abyss, the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah having been overturned there.

I, however, made a more learned conjecture about these springs, following blessed Jerome, whom I read in his exposition of the prophet Amos: that Dan lies at the borders of the land of Judah, where Paneas now is, and that the tribe of Dan built a city there, which they called Dan after their father.

For this reason I think that the one spring is called Dan, and the other Jor, which joins it.

We came to a very strong city called Balac, founded by Solomon and surrounded by lofty walls, which he called Thadomor. It was two days’ journey from Syria and six stations distant from greater Babylon, while from the Euphrates it was one day’s journey. The Greeks call it Palmyra.

In that place springs and wells abound exceedingly, for nowhere in the lower land is water found.

There about four hundred Damascene Turkish soldiers came out to meet us. Because they had learned that we were unarmed and very weary from our labor, they thought that they could weaken us in some way.

If Lord Baldwin had not carefully and cautiously protected the rear that day, they would have killed many of our men. For, because of the downpour of rain, their bows and arrows had failed them, since in those regions they are fastened with glue.

Bohemond was leading in the first wedge. Thus, with God’s help, they gained nothing from us.

We then pitched our camp before the town mentioned above. On the following day, drawing nearer to the sea, we passed before the cities of Tortosa and Laodicea. There too we found Count Raymond, whom we had left there.

Because provisions were expensive, we found nothing there to buy with which we could live. Therefore we did not cease hastening as far as Edessa.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### On the Capture of Bohemond

Bohemond first arrived at Antioch, where he was joyfully received by his people. Thereafter he held his kingdom as before for six months.

But in the following month of July, when he approached a city called Melitene with a small force—intending to hand it over to Gabriel, who was lord of that city, after an agreement of mutual friendship had already been made through messengers—a certain emir named Danishmend, with a large Turkish force, came out against him, intending to capture Bohemond as he traveled so imprudently.

Not far from the city just mentioned, that wicked people, who had been lying in ambush, sprang upon him from every side. Since our men did not dare to fight, being few in number, they immediately fled and were scattered. The Turks killed many of them and took all their money.

They captured Bohemond and carried him away with them into captivity.

When this misfortune was spread abroad by those who had escaped, great desolation arose among our people. Nevertheless Baldwin, lord of Edessa, gathered as many Franks as he could—namely, the Edessenes and Antiochenes—and did not delay in seeking the aforementioned enemies wherever he heard that they were.

Bohemond too, having cut off a lock of his hair, sent this token to the aforementioned Baldwin, asking him to come to his aid as quickly as possible for the love of God.

When Danishmend heard this, fearing their boldness, he did not dare remain any longer before the city of Melitene, which he had surrounded with a siege. Instead, he gradually withdrew before us, fleeing toward his own lands.

We were therefore deeply grieved, since we pursued them beyond the city for three days and would gladly have fought against them.

When we were returning in this manner, the aforementioned Gabriel handed the city of Melitene over to Baldwin. After they had become friends and Baldwin had brought in his guards, he returned to the city of Edessa, while the Antiochenes, mourning their lord, went back to their own country.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### On the Death of King Godfrey

While Baldwin himself was enjoying his prosperity, behold, a messenger arrived from Jerusalem and announced to him that Duke Godfrey, his brother, had died at Jerusalem on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August.

[Col. 0862C]

At the beginning of this year, after the city had been captured, it happened.

To increase your merit, Lord Godfrey,

the Lord granted you this kingdom.

But after you had held it for no long time,

you fell, nature having given you over to death.

When the sun had risen once beneath the burning Lion,

you ascended joyfully to heaven, with Michael raising you up.

# THE SECOND BOOK OF THE DEEDS OF BALDWIN I BEGINS

## CHAPTER I  
### How Baldwin Set Out to Govern Jerusalem

When it had been announced to Lord Baldwin that the entire people of Jerusalem were awaiting him as heir to be appointed prince of the kingdom, he grieved somewhat over his brother’s death but rejoiced more over the inheritance. Having taken counsel, he leased out the land he possessed and entrusted it to a certain Count Baldwin, his kinsman.

Gathering a small army of about two hundred knights and seven hundred infantrymen, he began the journey to Jerusalem on the sixth day before the Nones of October.

Some wondered that he had dared to travel with so small a force through so many hostile regions. Indeed, many of our companions, frightened and fearful for this reason, secretly withdrew without our knowledge.

When the Turks and Saracens learned that we were traveling in this manner, they gathered all their forces, as many as they could, and came armed to meet us wherever they thought they could most obstruct us.

We traveled first through Antioch, then proceeded before Laodicea, Gibellum, Maraclea, Tortosa, Archa, and Tripoli.

Then the king of Tripoli sent Lord Baldwin, to his tent, bread, wine, wild honey—that is, *chuerum*—and rams for food. Through his message he informed him that King Duchat of Damascus and King Ginahadoles of Egypt, together with many Turks, Saracens, and Arabs, had gathered and were waiting along the road by which they knew we would travel.

Although we did not believe this to be entirely certain, we later perceived that it was true.

## CHAPTER II  
### On the Turks’ Ambushes Laid in the Road, and the Astonishing Valor of Count Baldwin

Not far from the city of Beirut, about five miles away beside the sea, there was a very narrow passage on the public road, utterly unavoidable for us and for everyone traveling that way. If the enemy, having prepared themselves, wished to block travelers there, not even one hundred thousand soldiers could have passed without one hundred or sixty armed men waiting there and forcibly holding the entrance against them.

For this reason our enemies thought that they could intercept and kill us there from every side.

We reached that place. When our advance guard approached the aforementioned passage, they saw several of those Turks separated from the others, coming forward without scouting. When our scouts saw them, they supposed that a larger force was lying in ambush behind them.

As they had seen, they immediately reported this to Lord Baldwin through one of their number. On hearing it, he suitably arranged his army, divided into battle lines, for combat. With the standards raised, we gradually advanced against them.

When we thought that battle was about to begin, our hearts were pierced with compunction, and as we approached them we prayed for aid from heaven.

Those men immediately engaged our first wedge, and some of them were promptly killed; four of our soldiers, however, lost their lives.

When both sides had broken off that engagement, it was decided, after deliberation, that our camp should be taken down and pitched again where we had first approached, lest the enemy see us as cowards if we abandoned the place as though retreating.

But we displayed one thing while thinking another. We feigned courage, but feared death. It was difficult to turn back, but more difficult to go forward. We were surrounded by our enemies on every side.

On one side they pressed us continually in boats upon the sea; on the other, from the high mountains. That day we had nothing good and nothing peaceful, and our animals, though thirsty, were not watered.

For my part, I would rather have been at Chartres or Orléans—and so would others.

Throughout that very night we languished in watchfulness outside our tents. At first light, when dawn had begun to remove the shadows from the earth, we took counsel together, whether we should live or die. We gathered the tents and chose to return by the road we had come, with our animals going ahead loaded with baggage and our servants driving them forward.

The soldiers following defended the baggage against the attacking Saracens. For when those wicked men saw us returning so early in the morning, they immediately descended to pursue us as fugitives.

Some came by sea in boats, others behind us along the road by which we traveled, and still others over the mountains and hills, both horsemen and infantry, driving us before them through the narrow pass like sheep to a sheepfold. They intended to cut us off from a certain plain that lay at the narrowest exit between the sea and the mountain, so that they might easily intercept and kill us.

But it did not happen as they thought.

Our men said among themselves: “If we can intercept those who are pursuing us in that broad plain, perhaps, with God’s help, by turning back against them and fighting bravely, we shall be rescued from them.”

Already they were leaping from their ships; already they were beheading those whom they had taken by force as they traveled near the sea; already they had descended behind us into the aforementioned plain and were shooting many arrows.

Shouting against us from every side, howling like dogs or wolves, and brandishing their swords, they hurled insults at us.

But what shall I say? There was nowhere a place of escape, nor any hope of safety for those who remained. Solomon would not have been wise enough, nor Samson strong enough, to overcome them.

But God, great in power and mercy, looking from heaven upon the earth and seeing our humility, our distress, and the danger into which we had fallen for love of him and in his service, was moved by the compassion with which he is always rightly present to help his own. He granted our soldiers such boldness and valor that, turning back suddenly, they put the pursuers to flight, so that they no longer had the courage to defend themselves.

Some threw themselves headlong from the lofty precipitous rocks; others fled without delay to a place of safety; still others, overtaken, were killed by the sword.

Then you would have seen their ships fleeing across the sea with great speed from fear, as though we could seize them with our hands. Over the mountains and hills they fled on foot as quickly as they could.

Thus, rejoicing in so great a trophy, we returned happily to the servants who meanwhile were guarding the burdened animals on the road.

We then offered the most grateful praises to God, who proved himself a magnificent helper in such great and immeasurable danger.

O how wondrous are the works of God! O what a great miracle, worthy to be entrusted to memory!

We were defeated, and yet, though defeated, we conquered; but we did not conquer. How, then, did we not conquer? He conquered, for he alone is the almighty Creator of all things, mercifully helping his creature.

“If God is for us, who can be against us?” Truly he was for us and with us, fulfilling in us what he said through the prophet to the Israelites: “If you keep my commandments, I will enrich you with this gift, so that five of you shall pursue a hundred foreigners, and a hundred of you ten thousand” (Lev. 26:8).

And because we endured manifold labor day and night in God’s service and trusted in no one else, he magnificently brought their pride to nothing. And because we devotedly served the Lord with troubled hearts, he looked upon our humility.

Then our tents were ordered to be pitched again. There, before Lord Baldwin, several wealthy Turks were captured alive and carried away, together with the spoils of the slain and the weapons that had likewise been brought in.

We obtained horses with saddles and gilded bridles.

After that night had passed, we withdrew in the morning, following wiser counsel, a journey of four miles backward. There, after our prince had distributed the aforementioned plunder, night came upon us, and we rested in a depopulated castle beneath olive trees and in the thickets.

At first light Baldwin once again embraced his customary valor. Taking some of his soldiers, he rode as far as the narrow passage already mentioned to investigate whether any Saracens were still there who had previously barred our way.

When he found no one, because all had fled after hearing of the rout, he gave praise to God. Immediately he climbed to the summit of the same mountain and made a fire as a signal, so that those of us who had remained in the camp, seeing that smoke, might more readily follow those who had gone ahead in that manner.

When we saw it, we praised God and quickly followed them. We found our road free and crossed the desired passage.

That day we lodged near the city of Beirut. When the emir of that city learned this, he sent Lord Baldwin a daily supply of provisions by boat, more from fear than from affection.

The same was done by the other cities before which we passed: Sidon, Tyre, and Accho, that is, Ptolemais. They pretended friendship but had evil hearts.

Tancred already possessed the town called Haifa, which the men of Jerusalem had captured that same year. Because Tancred was then hostile to Baldwin, we did not enter it.

He himself was not there at the time, but his citizens sold us bread and wine outside. They treated us like brothers and desired to see us.

After passing Caesarea and the fortress of Arsuf, which we then mistakenly thought was Azotus—but it is not, since Azotus was one of the five cities of the Philistines and has been reduced to a village between Joppa and Ascalon—and after passing Antipatris, we finally came to the maritime city of Joppa, which lies in the tribe of Dan.

There our Franks joyfully received Lord Baldwin as their king.

Without delaying there, we hastened to Jerusalem. When we drew near the city, all the clergy and laity came out to meet him, as did the Greeks and Syrians, with crosses and candles.

With immense joy and honor, they escorted him as far as the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, giving praise in voices raised on high.

The patriarch Daibert did not attend this celebration, because accusations had been made against him before Baldwin concerning certain matters, and they were at odds with one another. Most of the clergy also hated him at that time.

For this reason he remained deprived of his see on Mount Zion, and stayed there until the offense arising from their hostility toward him had been removed.

After we had been relieved from our labor by six days of suitable rest in Jerusalem, and after the king had settled some of his affairs, we resumed our journey in order to undertake the campaign.

For everyone who has enemies—which I say in human terms—must frequently restrain them vigorously, so that, wearied by combat, they may either overcome them by force or compel them to agreements of peace.

## CHAPTER III  
### On Baldwin’s Expedition into Arabia

[Col. 0865D]

Therefore Lord Baldwin, having regrouped his people, set out for Ascalon, passing through Azotus, a city situated between Joppa and Ascalon and one of the five cities of the Philistines. We had Accaron on our right, near Pamnia, which lies beside the sea. When we had come before Ascalon, those who had come out against us were driven back violently as far as the walls. Since it was not advantageous for us to begin anything more extensive, we returned to our already-pitched tents to spend the night. On the following day we entered the inland region, where we might find provisions for ourselves and our beasts in fertile places, [Col. 0866A] and might also lay waste the land of our enemies.

As we proceeded, we found villages where the Saracen inhabitants of that region had hidden themselves from us in caves with their animals and possessions. Since we could extract none of them, we lit a fire at the mouth of a cave; soon, because of the intolerable smoke and heat, they came out to us one after another. Some of them were brigands who customarily lay in ambush between Ramla and Jerusalem and used to kill our Christians. When certain Christian Syrians, who had been hiding with them in the secret places, informed us that these men were such criminals, as soon as they emerged from the cave they were beheaded. We spared the Syrians and their wives. Of the Saracens, we killed nearly one hundred.

When we had consumed all the animals there, both by eating their grain and by slaughtering their beasts, and could find nothing else useful for ourselves, we took counsel with certain natives of the country—formerly Saracens but recently Christians—who knew the cultivated and uncultivated places far and wide. It was decided to withdraw into Arabia. Crossing the mountains, we came near the tombs of the patriarchs, namely Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and also Sarah and Rebecca, where their bodies are gloriously buried, about fourteen miles from the city of Jerusalem. We came to a valley where the wicked cities of Sodom and Gomorrah had been overthrown by God’s judgment.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the Dead Sea

There is now a great lake there, which they call the Dead Sea, because it produces nothing. Its length extends southward for five hundred and eighty stadia, while its breadth is 150 stadia. It is so salty that no animal or bird can drink from it. I, Fulcher, learned this by experience: when I dismounted from my mule beside it, drew water with my hand, and put it to my mouth, I tasted it and found it more bitter than hellebore. From the north it receives the Jordan River; from the south it has no outlet, nor does any river flow out of it.

Beside this lake there stands a single enormous and lofty mountain, likewise salty; the salt is like naturally formed stone, though not everywhere, but in places it resembles ice. It is not easy for anyone to sink deliberately into its depths. I conjecture that the place is so extremely salty for two reasons: either because it swallows the salt of the mountain, which the waves along the shore continually wash, and because rainwater flowing from the mountain into the lake carries salt with it; or because the abyss is so hollow that the great sea, which is salty, flows invisibly underground back into the same abyss.

After circling the lake on its southern side, we found a particularly pleasant village, very rich in the fruits of palm trees, which they call dates. We ate these as agreeable food throughout the day. We rarely found anything else there. For the Saracen inhabitants had fled from the place, already informed about us by rumor-mongers, except for a few who were blacker than soot; we left them there as though they had been taken from the seaweed of the sea. [Col. 0867A]

There, among the other trees, I saw some bearing fruit. After gathering some of it, wishing to learn what sort of fruit it was, I found, when the rind was broken, something like black powder inside, from which empty smoke emerged. Then we entered the mountains of Arabia, and spent the following night resting in their caves.

In the morning, when we had climbed the mountains, we immediately found villages, but empty of every good thing. For when our arrival had been discovered on the hill, the inhabitants had hidden themselves with their possessions in underground caves. Consequently, we accomplished little there. We therefore promptly extended our journey elsewhere, with our guides always going ahead.

Then we found a valley exceedingly fertile in every kind of produce of the earth. In it Saint Moses, at the Lord’s prompting, struck a flint twice with his staff, [Col. 0867B] and a living spring flowed forth. It still flows no less abundantly than then, so that mills are made to turn and grind grain by the current of its stream. I watered my horses in that spring.

Moreover, on the summit of the mountain we found the monastery of Saint Aaron, where Moses himself was accustomed to speak with God. We rejoiced greatly as we looked upon such holy places, previously unknown to us. Since beyond that valley the land was impassable, deserted, and uncultivated, we did not wish to proceed farther. After spending three days at leisure in that valley, rich in every good thing, while our animals were refreshed with food and our pack animals were loaded with the provisions necessary for the journey, on the fourth day, at about the second hour, when the royal trumpet gave the signal, we were ordered to resume the road by which we had come.

We therefore returned beside the Asphaltite Lake, as we had traveled before, and by the tombs of the aforementioned patriarchs; then through Bethlehem and by Rachel’s tomb. Thus, on the day of the winter solstice, we reached Jerusalem safely. After the ornaments appropriate for the king’s coronation had been prepared, and after Daibert had been reconciled with Lord Baldwin and with certain canons of the Holy Sepulchre—for prudent men had negotiated this matter—their dispute came to an end.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning the succession of King Baldwin and the king’s limited resources

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1101, on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, in the basilica of Blessed Mary at Bethlehem, with the aforementioned patriarch, the bishops, the clergy, and the people in attendance, King Baldwin was solemnly raised to the kingship under holy anointing and crowned. What they had not done for his predecessor, his brother, because he had refused it—and what some had not approved at the time—they now decided should be done for this man, after more prudent consideration.

“For what harm is there,” they said, “if Christ our Lord was dishonored in Jerusalem as though he were some criminal, degraded by insults and crowned with thorns, since in the end he willingly endured death for us? That crown, in their understanding, was not a mark of honor or royal dignity, but rather of disgrace and dishonor. Yet what those savage men did to him as an insult was, by God’s grace, turned to our salvation and glory.

“Nor is a king appointed contrary to the commands of God. For one chosen lawfully and according to God is sanctified and consecrated by an authoritative blessing. When he accepted that rule with a golden crown, he also accepted the honorable burden of maintaining justice. To him, as to a bishop concerning his bishopric, this saying may properly be applied: ‘He who desires the office desires a good work’ (1 Tim. III, 1). If he does not rule lawfully, he is not a king.

“Although at the beginning of his reign he possessed only a few cities and a small people, throughout that winter he vigorously protected his kingdom from enemies on every side. Since they had learned that he was an exceptionally brave warrior, although he had few people, they did not dare attack him. If he had a larger army, he would gladly confront his enemies.

“Even then the road was sufficiently obstructed for our pilgrims. At times Franks, English, Italians, and Venetians, traveling by sea in only one, three, or four ships, sailed among hostile pirates and past the cities of the Saracens, and reached Joppa under the Lord’s guidance, though in great fear. For at first we had no other port.

“When we saw them arriving from our western lands, we went out joyfully from Tripoli to meet them as though they were saints. Each of us carefully asked them about his own nation and family. They told us about these matters according to their knowledge. When we heard of prosperity, we rejoiced; when we heard of hardship, we grieved. They went to Jerusalem and visited the holy of holies for which they had come. Thereafter some remained in the Holy Land, while others returned to their own country.

“As a result, the land of Jerusalem remained empty of people, and there was no one to defend it against the Saracens if they had dared to attack us. But why did they not dare? With so many peoples and so many kingdoms, why did they fear invading our little kingdom and our tiny people? Why did they not assemble from Egypt, Persia, Mesopotamia, or Syria at least one hundred times one hundred thousand warriors, so that they might bravely attack us, their enemies, and, like locusts consuming an innumerable harvest in a small field, utterly destroy us, so that no further mention of us would be made in the land that had long been theirs?

“For at that time we had no more than three hundred soldiers, together with as many foot soldiers, who guarded Jerusalem, Joppa, Ramla, and also the fortress of Caypha. We scarcely dared assemble our soldiers when we wished to devise an ambush against our enemies, fearing that in the meantime, if the fortifications were left empty, they would cause us harm.

“Thus it is clear to everyone that it is a very astonishing miracle that we lived among so many thousands upon thousands, and even dominated them—making some of them tributaries, while we brought ruin upon others by plundering or capturing them. But from where came this courage? From where this power? Truly, from him whose name is Almighty. He was not forgetful of his people, who labored on behalf of his name; in their necessities he mercifully gave them aid, because they trusted in no one else but him alone. At times God himself gladdened them with a small temporal reward, while promising to repay them in the future with eternal glory.” [Col. 0869A]

O times most worthy of remembrance! Often we were saddened because we could obtain no help from our friends overseas. We feared that, once our enemies discovered the smallness of our people, they might someday attack us from every side in a sudden assault, when no one but God himself would bring us aid. Nothing useful would have been lacking to us, if only people and horses had not been lacking; but those who came to Jerusalem across the sea could not bring horses with them. No one came to our aid by land. Neither could the people of Antioch help us, nor we them.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning Tancred’s replacement at Antioch

At that time, in the month of March, it happened that Tancred left his town of Caypha, which he possessed, and also Tiberias, to King Baldwin, and traveled by land with his men to Antioch. For the Antiochenes had sent their envoys to him, saying:

“Do not delay, but come to us and, ruling over all of us, possess Antioch and the land subject to it until our lord and yours, Lord Bohemond, emerges from captivity. You are his kinsman, an exceptionally brave and prudent soldier, and more powerful than we are. You will be able to govern our land better than we can. If, God willing, Lord Bohemond returns, then he will show what right belongs to him.”

Thus the message was given, and thus it was done.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the siege and capture of the fortress of Arsuth

During that same winter a fleet of beaked ships belonging to the Genoese and other Italians had wintered at the port of Laodicea. When they saw that spring was suitable and calm for sailing, they sailed with a favorable wind as far as Joppa. When they reached the harbor, the king received them joyfully. Since Easter was near, a solemnity which, according to custom, all who can celebrate, they dragged their ships onto land and went with the king to Jerusalem.

After the Easter solemnity had been completed—when everyone had been troubled because on Holy Saturday we had not received the fire at the Lord’s sepulchre—the king departed for Joppa. He made an agreement with the consuls of the aforementioned fleet: for as long as they wished to remain in the Holy Land for the love of God, if, with God granting and aiding them, they were able during that time to capture some Saracen city together with the king, they would commonly possess one-third of the money taken from the internal enemies, without any injury being done to the Genoese. The king, however, would possess the first and second parts, and would additionally hold one district in that city, once captured, by perpetual and hereditary right.

After this agreement had been confirmed by an oath of faith given by both sides, they immediately besieged by sea and land the town called Arsuth. When the Saracen inhabitants realized that they could in no way defend themselves against the Christians, they cunningly negotiated with the king and, on the third day, surrendered the walls to him. As they departed, they carried away their money. The king made them leave for Ascalon in deep sorrow.

We then joyfully gave thanks to God because, without the loss of any of our men, we had captured this fortification, which had been so hostile to us. The fortress had been founded by Solomon and was a great annoyance to the Franks. Duke Godfrey had besieged it in the previous year but had not captured it. Its inhabitants had often killed or saddened many of our men. By then the Franks had seized the wall’s battlements at close quarters when, by chance, a wooden tower attached externally to the wall collapsed into pieces under the weight of the multitude climbing it. Nearly one hundred Franks fell from it and were grievously wounded. The Saracens then detained some Franks there, whom they hung on a cross in full view of everyone and shot with arrows. They killed some and kept others alive in a vile captivity.

## CHAPTER VIII. How the city of Caesarea was captured

After the king had garrisoned Arsuth with as many of his people as was necessary, he went to the city of Caesarea in Palestine and surrounded it with a siege. But because it was very strongly defended by walls, it could not be captured quickly.

He therefore ordered three stone-throwing engines and one very tall wooden machine to be made, constructed from the masts and oars of ships. Our craftsmen, as I believe, erected it twenty cubits higher than the wall, so that when it was brought up to the wall our soldiers could stone and shoot the internal enemies from it. Thus, after they had emptied the wall of Saracens, our men would have free entry and could capture the city.

But after they had resisted the siege for fifteen days, and the stone-throwers had damaged the upper parts of the walls somewhat, while the wooden tower had not yet been completely assembled, the Franks’ courage refused to prolong the delay. On a certain Friday, without the aforementioned machine or any other supplementary equipment, they boldly attacked the city with shields and lances.

The Saracens defended themselves as strongly as they could, encouraging one another. But the Franks, whose God was the Lord, raised the ladders they had already prepared for this purpose and climbed by them to the top of the wall without delay. Those whom they found confronting them there they immediately killed with swords.

When the Saracens saw our people so fierce and the city already captured by them, wherever they could continue living they fled there in great haste. But they could hide neither here nor there without being slaughtered in deserved death. Only a few males were spared alive. They spared many women so that they might always serve in turning hand-mills. After capturing them, some sold and bought them among themselves, some beautiful and some ugly; they also bought and sold males.

The ruler of the city itself, and the bishop whom they call Arcadius, the king kept alive; he spared them more for money than for friendship. It is impossible to describe how many utensils of various kinds were found there. As a result, many who had been poor became wealthy.

I saw many Saracens who had been killed there burned in a heap made from their bodies. The excessive stench of their corpses greatly troubled us. This was done in order to find bezants, which the wicked men had swallowed there, unwilling that the Franks should possess anything of theirs. Some of them hid bezants in their mouths beside their gums. Thus it sometimes happened that, when one of our men struck a Saracen on the neck with his fist, ten or sixteen bezants were shaken out of his mouth. Women also shamelessly concealed bezants inside themselves. It was both a wicked thing to hide them in this way and, for me, much more shameful to recount.

> It was the year one thousand one hundred and one  
> when with ladders we captured the city of Caesarea.  
> With the tower called Straton’s Tower we captured the city.

## CHAPTER IX. That a bishop was ordained in Caesarea

After we had done as we pleased with Caesarea and with all the things we found in it, together with the Genoese, and had jointly elected and installed an archbishop there, we left a few men to guard the city and hurried to the city of Ramla, which lies near Lydda.

There we waited twenty-four days for a battle to be launched against us by the people of Ascalon and Babylon, who had gathered there for that purpose. But because we were few and feared to go against them, we did not do so, lest, if we appeared before Ascalon, they might repeatedly rush out from behind their walls and embankments, intercept us, and kill us.

They did not wish to come against us because they thought this would happen. Once we learned of their cunning, we cunningly countered their cunning by remaining inactive until their spirits withered from fear; then they entirely ceased coming against us. Consequently, many who had grown weary of the delay and were oppressed by poverty departed from their army.

When we heard this, we returned to Joppa and gave praise to God because we had thus been freed from an encounter with them.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the sufficiently bloody battle between the Christians and the Turks, in which the Christians were victorious

For seventy days afterward we remained at peace, though always keeping our ears attentively turned toward them. Then it was reported to the king that our adversaries were again becoming aggressive and preparing to attack us.

When he heard this, the king promptly ordered his people to assemble from Jerusalem, Tiberias, Caesarea, and Caypha. Since necessity pressed us, and we were short of soldiers, the king advised that whoever could do so should turn one of his armed retainers into a soldier. Thus all our soldiers together numbered only 240, while the foot soldiers numbered 900.

Those who were against us numbered 11,000 soldiers and 21,000 foot soldiers. We knew this, but because we had God with us, we were not afraid to attack them. We placed our hope entirely in the Lord God, not in weapons or in a large people. It was great boldness, but it was not merely boldness; rather, it was faith and charity. For we hoped willingly to die for love of him who, in mercy, had consented to die for us. [Col. 0872A]

We went to battle, or perhaps to the death prepared for us. The king had the sign of the Lord’s cross carried there, and it gave us salutary comfort. On one day we went out from Joppa; on the following day we fought against them.

When we had approached them, and they likewise had approached us, though we did not know this, we observed their scouts from our watchtower and immediately understood that the rest were following. As the king proceeded farther with some of his men, he looked into the distance and saw their tents spread out and shining white across the plains. At once he spurred his horse and ran back to us, reporting to everyone what he had seen.

We therefore began to rejoice when we learned that battle was imminent, for we desired this to happen. If they had not come to us, we would certainly have gone to them. It was better for us to fight on the broad plains, so that, once they had been defeated with the Lord’s assistance, their flight would be longer. Thus they would suffer greater loss in flight than if we engaged them near their walls.

The king then ordered the weapons to be taken up. Once everyone was armed, our battle lines were properly arranged. Entrusting ourselves confidently to the hands of God, we rode against them. An abbot, whom the king had commanded to do so, carried the Lord’s cross openly before everyone.

Then the king piously addressed his soldiers in these words:

> “Come, soldiers of Christ, take courage and fear nothing. Act manfully, be strong in this battle, and, I beg you, fight for our souls and exalt the name of Christ utterly. These degenerates continually reproach and insult him virulently. They do not believe in his birth or resurrection. If you die here, you will certainly be blessed. The gate of the heavenly kingdom is already opened to you. If you remain alive as victors, you will shine gloriously among all Christians; but if you wish to flee, France is indeed far from you.”

When he had said this, everyone agreed with him. They hastened to battle, for the long delay wearied them all. Each was already considering whom he should strike or bring down.

And behold, the detestable people confronted us and rushed upon us violently from right and left. Our people, although very few, divided into six battle lines, inserted themselves among their great companies, crying, “ADJUVA DEUS” (“Help, O God”), just as bird-catchers spread themselves among a multitude of birds. [Col. 0872D]

Their multitude immediately covered us so completely that one man could neither see nor recognize another. They had already driven back and shaken our first two lines when the king, seeing what was happening, hastened to their aid from the rear. When he saw and recognized that the enemy’s strength was greater, he accelerated with his squadron and bravely placed himself against the assault of the wicked men. Before their more powerful leaders, he brandished a lance from which a white standard hung and struck an Arab who confronted him. When he hurled him from his warhorse to the ground, the same standard remained attached to him. I myself, standing nearby, saw this clearly. He pulled the lance free and promptly carried it forward to wound others.

Here one side fought bravely, and there the other. You would certainly have seen, after a considerable space of an hour, many horses without riders. We saw the ground heavily covered with Saracen and Ethiopian shields and breastplates, daggers and quivers, bows and arrows, belonging both to the dead and to those mortally wounded. There were also Franks, but not so many.

The Lord’s cross was present there, utterly opposed to the enemies of Christ; against it, by God’s grace, their pomp could not prevail. As though ashamed by its presence, they not only ceased attacking us, but all, struck with heavenly fear, turned their purpose swiftly toward flight. Those who then had a swift horse escaped death by fleeing.

It was a wearisome task to gather all the shields, missiles, bows, and arrows which the fugitives had thrown across the fields. If anyone wished to count all the bodies lying there dead, he would certainly fail in the calculation. Nevertheless, it is said that five thousand of those soldiers and foot soldiers were killed there. The Babylonian commander who had led the army into battle also died with the others. Of our soldiers we lost eighty, and of our foot soldiers more.

The king conducted himself most bravely that day. He proved an excellent comforter and a stern striker. His soldiers, though few, were also exceptionally brave. The contest did not remain uncertain for long. They fled promptly, while these men swiftly drove them away.

## CHAPTER XI. How many of the Christians fell there

O war hateful to the innocent and terrifying to those who watched it! “War”—for it was called war by antiphrasis. I saw the battle and trembled inwardly; I feared the blows. Everyone rushed into the iron as though he had never feared death. A dreadful calamity, where there was no charity. There was an immense crash from the blows exchanged on both sides. One struck; another fell. One knew no mercy, nor did the other seek it. One lost a fist, another an eye. The human mind recoils when such misery is seen.

A wondrous thing to relate: at the head we conquered, but at the tail we were defeated. At the rear the Christians fell, while at the front they conquered the Saracens. We drove these latter as far as Ascalon, while they, after killing our men, rode immediately as far as Joppa. Thus on that day no one knew the outcome of the affair.

When the king and his men had emptied the fields of them by killing and driving them away, it was ordered that we rest that night in the tents they had abandoned in flight. It was ordered, and it was done.

> On the seventh of the Ides of September, when it was read,  
> we fought this battle, worthy enough to be recounted,  
> and divine grace was the Franks’ ally.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the varying fortune of this battle

On the following day, after we had heard Mass in the king’s pavilion for the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary—for that day was a solemnity—we loaded our animals with the possessions of our enemies, namely bread, grain, flour, and also their tents. On the advice of the trumpeter, we were ordered to return to Joppa.

As we were returning, we passed through Azotus, the fifth city of the Philistines, now deserted, which they currently call Iben. We saw about five hundred Arabs coming toward us, returning from Joppa. They had run there on the day of the battle and seized the plunder they had found outside the city.

For when they had inflicted a great slaughter upon our foot soldiers in the rear, and had completely destroyed one line on the right wing, and believed that the front lines had been defeated like the rear ones, they had taken the shields, lances, and shining helmets of the slain. After adorning themselves pompously with these, they hastened at once to Joppa and showed our weapons to the people of Joppa, saying that the king and all his men had been killed in battle.

When the guards who had remained in Joppa heard this—for it seemed credible—they were greatly astonished and terrified, and believed their words. But when the Arabs thought that the city would immediately be surrendered to them by its frightened inhabitants, their plans were frustrated. Having accomplished nothing there, they began to return to Ascalon.

When they saw us returning to Joppa, they suspected that we belonged to their own people and intended, after all of us had been killed in battle, to attack the remaining Christians as they traveled toward Joppa. We were therefore greatly astonished when they came so close to us without realizing that we were Franks, until they saw our soldiers attack them in a swift assault.

Then you would have seen them fleeing rapidly in every direction, so that no one wished to wait for another. Whoever did not then have a swift horse soon lost his head to the sword. But because the Franks were very tired and many had been wounded in the battle, they could not pursue them. Thus they departed, while we reached Joppa joyfully.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the embassy sent by the people of Joppa to Tancred, prince of Antioch

What do you think was the rejoicing and thanksgiving when those whom we had left in Joppa saw us returning with raised standards from the top of the wall? Certainly it cannot be described as slight. For two foolish messengers had come there, one after the other, and had deceived the people of Joppa by saying that the king had died with all his men.

Consequently, they were saddened beyond belief, thinking this true, and sent a written embassy to Tancred, who was then ruling Antioch. A certain sailor carried it as he boarded his ship, the king’s wife having arranged this. The letter contained the following salutary words:

> “Tancred, eminent man and excellent soldier, receive this little letter, which the inhabitants of Joppa—namely the queen and a few citizens of the city—are sending to you through me, their swift messenger. And so that you may perhaps believe this writing more than me, have it read aloud. For, alas, the king of Jerusalem, who engaged in battle against the Babylonians and the people of Ascalon, was defeated in their encounter, or perhaps was killed together with all those whom he led with him to battle.
>
> “For the man who barely escaped the misery of this calamity, fleeing to Joppa, reported this to us. Therefore I come to you, a prudent man, as an envoy seeking help, so that, setting aside every hindrance, you may hasten without delay to aid the people of God, who are greatly distressed and, as I believe, already near the threshold of death.”

He said this. Tancred listened and remained silent for a short time. But when he believed what he had heard to be true, both he and all the others present, overcome by great sadness and grief, began piously to weep. After a response had been given to the envoy, preparations were ordered throughout his entire land to aid the people of Jerusalem.

When they were already prepared to undertake that journey, suddenly another messenger arrived, carrying a second letter different from the first, and presented it to Tancred. Whereas the first had written of disaster, the second reported prosperity. For it stated that the king had returned safely from the battle to Joppa and had undoubtedly won a magnificent victory over the Saracens.

Then those who had grieved over the disaster rejoiced at the favorable outcome. O wondrous mercy of God! We did not conquer through the multitude of our people, but, relying on divine power, we scattered them. Thus, having been delivered from our enemies, we went to Jerusalem and rendered praises to God. Thereafter we remained free from war for eight months, until the turning of the year brought back the summer season.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the Babylonian army assembled against the Christians

In the following year, in the middle of May 1102, the Babylonians assembled at Ascalon. Their king had sent them there so that they might strive to destroy us Christians utterly. There were 20,000 horsemen and 18,000 foot soldiers, besides the baggage carriers, who drove camels and asses laden with provisions and carried in their hands clubs and missiles for fighting.

One day they approached the city of Ramla and spread their tents before it. In one fortified tower of the city there were fifteen soldiers whom the king had stationed there as guards. Before it, certain Syrian peasants lived as though in a suburb. The Saracens repeatedly tried to destroy these Christians, harming and harassing them, and to demolish the fortress, because, on account of those inhabitants, they could not move freely across the plains.

Moreover, they attempted to capture the bishop of the same city, who lived in the church of Saint George with his household. One day, after they had surrounded the monastery with a hostile assault, they considered the strength of the place and returned to Ramatha. [Col. 0875D]

When that bishop saw the smoke and flames, their fires already burning among the reeds, he feared that they would besiege him when they returned. Taking precautions for the future, he immediately sent word to the king, who was in Joppa, asking him to come swiftly to his aid, because the Babylonians had encamped before Ramla, and one of their companies had already rushed around his monastery.

When the king heard this, he took up his weapons, mounted his horse, and hurried out. At his command, and at the signal of the royal trumpet, his army followed him very swiftly.

At that time there were many soldiers in Joppa who were waiting for a favorable opportunity to cross the sea and return to France. They had no horses, because in the previous year, when they had traveled through Romania on pilgrimage to Jerusalem, they had lost their horses and everything they possessed. For this reason, it is not inappropriate to insert an account of the matter here.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the second disastrous pilgrimage of the Franks and the death of Hugh the Great

When the great Frankish army, as has been said, was heading toward Jerusalem, the multitude included William, count of Poitiers, and Stephen, count of Blois, who had left the army at Antioch but was now striving to restore what he had then abandoned.

Hugh the Great was with them; after the capture of Antioch he had returned to Gaul. Raymond, count of the Provençals, was also with them; he had remained at Constantinople after returning from Jerusalem as far as that place. Stephen, the noble count of Burgundy, was likewise present, together with an innumerable people, in an army divided between cavalry and infantry.

On the borders of Romania, Soliman the Turk opposed them. The Franks had long before taken the city of Nicaea from him. But mindful of his loss, he disastrously scattered, routed, and brought almost the entire Frankish army to destruction with a great multitude of Turks.

Yet, because by the Lord’s providence they were traveling in groups along several roads, he could neither fight all of them nor kill them all. But when he learned that they were exhausted, distressed by hunger and thirst, and untrained in archery combat, he killed more than one hundred thousand horsemen and foot soldiers with the sword.

Of the women, he killed some and took others away with him. Many who fled by remote roads and through the mountains perished from the anguish of thirst. The Turks took their horses, mules, other animals, and possessions of many kinds.

There the count of Poitiers lost everything he possessed, his household and his wealth. Barely escaping death, he reached Antioch on foot, miserable, grieving, and confounded. Tancred sympathized with his distress, received him kindly, and supported him from his own resources. The Lord chastised him with punishment, yet did not deliver him to death (Ps. CXVII, 18).

This, as it seemed to us, happened to him and to the others because of their sins and pride. Those who escaped did not delay in coming to Jerusalem, except for Hugh the Great, whom they buried after he died at Tarsus in Cilicia. When they had reached Antioch, some proceeded to Jerusalem by sea and others by land. Those who were able to obtain horses preferred to travel by land.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the capture of the city of Tortosa
When they had reached Tortosa, which the Saracens then possessed, they did not delay but attacked it by sea and land. Why prolong the account? They captured the city, killed the Saracens, took possession of their money, and afterward did not cease their journey. But everyone was distressed when they saw Count Raymond remaining there. They had all hoped that he would go with them to Jerusalem. But because he was unwilling, he remained there and obtained the city, for which they brought blasphemous accusations against him. [Col. 0877A]

Proceeding farther, they passed Archas, the city of Tripoli, and Gibellum. From there they came to a narrow passage through a hill near the city of Beirut. King Baldwin had waited for them there for twenty-eight days, meanwhile guarding that road lest the Saracens occupy it and prevent the pilgrims from passing. For the king himself had received a petition from that advancing army. When they found the king meeting them there, they greatly rejoiced; and after exchanging kisses, they proceeded to Joppa, where those who had travelled by sea had already arrived.

## Chapter XVII. On the wretched battle between the Christians and the Turks, in which the Christians were killed and the Turks were victorious [Cols. 0877B–0878A]

Easter was near, and they then went to Jerusalem because they desired this. After celebrating the solemnity there, as is customary, they returned to Joppa. At that time, because the Count of Poitou was destitute and utterly ruined by poverty, he boarded a ship with a few companions and returned to France. Stephen of Blois then wished to cross the sea with several others; but when the wind opposed him in the open sea, he could do nothing other than turn back.

The one who had then returned from the sea to Joppa was there when the king mounted his horse, as was said above, intending to go against the enemies who were encamped before Ramla. There were still present Geoffrey, a certain count of the Vendômois, Stephen, Count of Burgundy, and Hugh of Lusignan, brother of Count Raymond. Having borrowed horses from their friends and relatives, they immediately mounted them and followed the king.

This was indeed a great failing in the king’s judgment: he neglected to wait for his people and did not proceed to war in an orderly manner, as wisdom requires. Instead, without waiting for his infantry and soldiers, he hastened to attack the enemy, until, unknowingly, he thrust himself into the midst of the Arab multitude. Because he trusted more than he ought in his own prowess and did not expect them to number more than a thousand or seven hundred, he hurried forward, hoping to meet them before they could flee.

But when he suddenly caught sight of their army, he was terrified by fear and trembled inwardly. Nevertheless, taking courage, he looked back at his men and addressed them kindly:

> “O soldiers of Christ and my friends, do not reject this battle; but, armed with God’s strength, fight manfully for your own sake. For whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s (Rom. 14:8). And if anyone should attempt to flee, there is now no hope of escape. You will conquer by fighting; by fleeing you will fall.”

Then, since this was the place and time to display their courage, they suddenly threw themselves upon the Arabs with a vigorous attack. Because our men numbered no more than two hundred soldiers, they were surrounded by twenty thousand. When they were being grievously hemmed in by the pressure of the pagans, and most of our men had been killed within a very short time, they could not bear such a burden, and the survivors were forced to take flight. Yet, although matters went so badly for them, they had first taken a most courageous revenge upon the enemy. They killed many of them and drove them from the fields, depriving them of their tents.

Finally, by God’s permission, the defeated were defeated by those whom they had overcome. The king escaped by God’s grace, together with several of the nobler soldiers of his army; they quickly forced their way into the city of Ramla. They could not flee any farther.

## Chapter XVIII. On the flight of King Baldwin [Cols. 0878A–C]

Since the king did not wish to be shut up there, preferring to die elsewhere rather than be captured there to no purpose, he immediately took counsel, entrusting himself alike to death and to life, and attempted to get out. Taking with him only five companions—whom, however, he did not retain for long, since the adversaries detained them—he fled on a swift horse toward the mountains.

Thus the Lord rescued him from the hands of his stronger enemies. He would gladly have gone then to Arsuf, if he could, but because the enemy blocked his way, he was unable to go there. Those who had remained in the city of Ramla likewise could not later get out through the gate. Besieged on every side by that impious people, they were finally—alas!—seized by them. Some of them they killed, while others they led away alive with them.

When the bishop, in the church of Saint George, heard that this misfortune had occurred, he secretly fled to Joppa. Alas, how many noble and excellent soldiers we lost at that time, both earlier in the battle and later in the tower just mentioned! Stephen, Count of Blois, a prudent and noble man, was killed, as was another Stephen, Count of Burgundy.

Three soldiers escaped from there. Severely afflicted by wounds and blows, they rode to Jerusalem by night on the following day in desperate flight. Entering the city, they announced to its inhabitants the misfortune that had occurred. As for the king, whether he was alive or dead, they said that they knew nothing certain about him. Hence great mourning immediately arose.

## Chapter XIX. That the king entered Arsuf [Cols. 0878C–D]

The following night, out of fear of the Arabs, the king hid in the mountains. On the third day he emerged from the mountains with only one soldier and his squire, entering his town of Arsuf like any unknown wanderer, hungry and thirsty, by the deserted byways.

One circumstance in particular brought him safety: five hundred enemy soldiers had withdrawn from there shortly beforehand. For some time they had circled the town’s wall like scouts. He would certainly not have escaped them had they seen him.

When the king entered Arsuf, his men received him joyfully. He ate and drank, and then slept securely. Humanity required this.

## Chapter XX. That Hugh of Tiberias and the patriarch of Jerusalem hastened to the king’s aid; and on the battle fought, in which the Christians prevailed through the strength and assistance of the holy cross [Cols. 0878D–0880D]

On that very day, behold, Hugh of Tiberias arrived from the city. He was one of the king’s nobles and, having heard of the king’s humiliation, already wished to bring some comfort to the remnant of his people. When the king saw him, he rejoiced greatly, for Hugh had with him eighty soldiers, whom the impending situation required.

Having received a message from Jerusalem, Hugh was hastening to assist the people of Joppa. But the king did not dare lead them by land, because enemies lay in ambush for travellers. Instead, he entered a small boat and sailed to Joppa. When he reached the harbor, he was received with great joy, since, in the words of the Gospel, “he had been dead and came to life; he had been lost and was found” (Luke 15:32). The man whom they had already mourned as dead they now saw alive and well.

On the following day the aforesaid Hugh left Arsuf and hurried anxiously to Joppa. The king hastened to assist him, lest the enemy attack him on the road. When he reached Joppa, the king, without prolonging the council, was warned by necessity to send word and summon those who had gone to Jerusalem and to Saint Abraham, so that they might come to Joppa and engage in battle with the Arabs, who were encamped nearby and plotting to seize Joppa.

While he was considering whom to send as messenger, he saw there a certain Syrian, a humble man of mean appearance. He earnestly begged him, for the love of God, to undertake this embassy, since he could find no one capable of fulfilling it. No one dared travel along the road because of the enemy ambushes.

The man, however, taking courage from God, did not delay setting out beneath the cover of night. So that the enemy would not see him, he travelled through pathless and very rough places, and on the third day reached Jerusalem, utterly exhausted. When he made the citizens aware of the welcome news concerning the king and declared that he was alive, they all rendered due praise to the Lord.

There was no long delay. After the written message he had brought was read, all the soldiers who could be found there immediately prepared themselves. Ninety men, as I believe, both soldiers and those who were able to obtain horses or pack animals, set out without delay, though they mounted willingly enough with considerable fear.

As far as possible they avoided the ambushes of the enemy who remained in the area. Taking byways and turning aside from the road toward Arsuf, they made their way onward. As they hurried along near the seashore, a wicked people encountered them, hoping to intercept and kill them there.

Some of them had to leave their pack animals behind and throw themselves into the waves to swim, so that one sorrow might serve as a remedy for another. By swimming they escaped the wicked, but they lost their animals. The soldiers who had swift horses carried themselves to Joppa, though they barely escaped.

The king was heartened and greatly invigorated by their arrival. He did not wish to delay his undertaking any longer but went out the following morning to fight his enemies, having arranged his soldiers together with the infantry.

The enemy were not far from Joppa—about three miles away—where they were already preparing their siege engines so that they might immediately besiege Joppa and capture it once it had been hemmed in. But when they saw our people advancing against them for battle, they promptly took up their weapons and boldly met them.

Because they were a great multitude, they surrounded our people on every side. Once our men had been enclosed, nothing could help them further except divine assistance. But placing complete confidence in the omnipotence of the Lord, when they saw where the enemy formation was densest and strongest, they did not delay striking it with astonishing force.

When they had penetrated the enemy lines by fighting bravely in one sector, they immediately had to run back elsewhere, because, whenever they saw our infantry without the protection of soldiers, they hurried there and killed those at the extremities.

Our infantry, however, were not sluggish. They shot such a rain of arrows at those attacking them that they saw many arrows fixed in their faces and shields. Thus, when the enemy had been violently driven back by our infantry archers, many wounded by the soldiers’ lances and already deprived of their tents, with God’s help they turned their backs and fled before the Franks.

They were not pursued for long, however, because their pursuers were few. The enemy left all their tents in the field for the Franks, together with all their supplies. They took away nearly all their horses, except for a few that were wounded or died from thirst during the flight. We acquired many of their camels and donkeys. Many of them, whether wounded or tormented by thirst, died on the road as they fled.

It was truly fitting and just that those fortified by the wood of the Lord’s cross should prove victorious over the enemies of that same holy cross. If the same gracious cross had been carried with the king in the earlier battle, there should be no doubt that the Lord would have shown mercy to his people.

But there are some who place greater confidence in their own strength than in the Lord, who rely excessively on their own judgment, and who despise the counsel of the wise. They rashly and thoughtlessly presume to carry out their plans. Hence great loss often befalls not only them but also many others who have no part in their deeds. Such people therefore tend to blame the Lord more than to acknowledge their own folly.

When a fool begins something, he does not consider how it will end. “The horse is prepared for battle, but the Lord grants salvation.” If the prayer of the righteous is not always heard by the Lord, how much less that of the wicked? Or why does a man blame God when he does not immediately fulfill his desire? Why should he be heard when he has deserved no good? Does he not himself know what must be done in every matter?

Boethius says concerning such matters:

> “Whatever you see happening contrary to hope has a proper order in reality, but in your opinion a confused perversity.”

The fool considers not the merits of things but the outcome attributed to fortune. Often a man thinks at the time that something is harmful to him which afterward turns to his advantage; and the opposite also happens, when something succeeds well for someone, only for what greatly harms him to befall him shortly afterward.

When the battle had been completed, as stated above, and the king had emerged victorious, he gathered the enemy’s tents and returned to Joppa. Afterward the land rested, free from warfare, during the following season, namely autumn and winter.

## Chapter XXI. That the king besieged the city of Acre [Col. 0881A]

In the spring of the year 1103, after we had celebrated Easter in Jerusalem according to custom, the king attacked and besieged the city of Acre, called Ptolemais. But because it was very strongly defended by its wall and outer fortification, he was then unable to capture it, especially since the Saracens inside defended themselves with remarkable courage. After he had devastated both their crops and their shrubs and gardens, he returned to Joppa.

## Chapter XXII. On Prince Bohemond, released from captivity [Cols. 0881A–B]

At that time welcome news concerning Lord Bohemond was spread abroad: by God’s grace he had been freed from the custody of the Turks. He made known through his messenger how he had been ransomed and released from captivity. He who had formerly ruled at Antioch was afterward joyfully received by his citizens and ennobled and possessed that land.

Bohemond also received the city of Laodicea, which Tancred had later captured and taken from the men of the emperor of Constantinople. In return, he suitably granted Tancred a portion of his own territory and gladly made peace with him.

## Chapter XXIII. On the king, wounded almost to death [Cols. 0881B–C]

At that time, while King Baldwin was fighting the Saracens in the customary manner, it happened one day that he charged a few of them. While he was already rejoicing in the hope of their destruction, confident of victory, an Ethiopian hiding behind a rock lay craftily in wait for him in order to kill him.

Having powerfully hurled a projectile, the man deeply wounded the king from behind near the heart. That blow injured him almost to the point of death. But afterward, when he had diligently sought treatment, he eventually recovered after the troublesome scar had been cut open.

## Chapter XXIV. On the capture of the city of Acre, commonly called Achra [Cols. 0881C–D]

In the year 1104, after winter had passed and the solemnities of Easter had been celebrated in Jerusalem amid the flowering of spring, King Baldwin assembled his people, set out for Acre, and again besieged it.

The Genoese came to the siege with a fleet of seventy ships equipped with beaks. After they had hemmed in the city on every side for twenty days with siege engines and repeated assaults, the Saracens, greatly terrified, surrendered it to the king, whether they wished to or not.

It was very necessary to us, for it possesses a harbor so useful that it can safely accommodate a great many ships within its walls.

> Now Phoebus had risen nine times beneath the sign of the Twins,  
> The city of Acre, called Ptolemais, was captured,  
> In the year one thousand one hundred and four.
>
> It is not the city Acharon that everyone calls Acre.  
> That one is Philistine; this one is called Ptolemais.

After the city had thus been captured, they killed very many of the Saracens, allowed some to live, and took possession of all their property.

## Chapter XXV. That Bohemond resolved to cross over to Apulia [Col. 0882A]

After the summer had passed, Bohemond, distressed by extreme necessity, crossed over to Apulia in a small vessel, entrusting all his land to Tancred. Daibert, formerly patriarch of Jerusalem, a prudent man powerful in counsel, crossed with him at that time.

Bohemond went in order to bring back with him a people from the regions across the sea. Daibert went to make known to the Roman pope his own case and the injury inflicted upon him by the king. He went and obtained what he sought, but he did not return, because he died on the journey.

## Chapter XXVI. How the men of Antioch, fighting against the Parthians, were captured and some were killed [Cols. 0882A–0883C]

In that year the Parthians, Medes, and Chaldaeans, together with our neighboring peoples who lived in Mesopotamia, were stirred up to attack us Christians and utterly destroy us.

When this report had spread as far as us, all the nobles nevertheless prepared themselves to meet them. Lord Bohemond and Tancred made ready with all haste, as did Baldwin, Count of Edessa, and Goscelin, along with that Daibert of Jerusalem and Benedict, archbishop of Edessa, accompanied by a military and popular multitude.

After crossing the Euphrates and then passing the city of Carrhae near the river called the Chaboras, they encountered the enemy’s battle lines. When battle was joined, the Christians were immediately, because our sins demanded it, thrown into disarray and confusion near Raqa.

The outcome of events showed that this battle had been more dreadful than all the earlier wars. There Lord Baldwin, Count of Edessa—who was destined to become king of Jerusalem and was second after the first king—was captured, and with him Lord Goscelin, his kinsman; the aforementioned archbishop was captured with them.

Very many were submerged and killed in the river just mentioned. Horses and mules, together with an immeasurable quantity of wealth, were lost. Lord Bohemond and Lord Tancred, fleeing here and there through byways and turnings, choosing neither the proper road nor the more useful path, finally escaped, wandering and confused. Many others, pierced by arrows and daggers, fell dead.

They could have captured Carrhae without great difficulty if they had besieged it at the outset; afterward, however, they were unable to obtain it either at the beginning or on the return journey.
