Since security sometimes deceitfully produces loss, fear and vigilance prepare advantage for the prudent and cautious. As it is written, it often harms those who are ready to delay. Two enemies—discord and envy—certainly harmed our people in this undertaking, or misfortune. They also commonly reduce men from acquired possessions to extreme poverty. We have often seen this; experience has taught us this.

I am not mistaken, nor am I composing trivialities by being lured into deceptive ambiguity. Truly, on this journey, so dangerous and terrifying, they aggravated one another with bitter words and, before this downfall, nearly wished to withdraw from one another and break their mutual alliance.

Whoever does evil and hopes for good is indeed out of his mind. For without peace or mutual love, nothing is acceptable to God. It is cowardly, then—indeed, utterly wicked—to abandon the company of one whom I ought to assist unto death.

But God helped the archbishop of Edessa even after he had been placed in chains. When the Turks had loaded him down with his belongings and utensils like a pack animal, a powerful soldier, who charitably offered his own life for him, with God’s assistance rescued him from their hands by a remarkable act of daring. For he did not make his own life more precious than the archbishop’s.

Thus many in this pilgrimage of ours, burning with zeal for God and wishing to shorten their lives, strove to die a blessed death and enjoy rest with Christ. This happened, for example, in the presence and hearing of some of our men while I was at Antioch. When a treacherous man blasphemed the Lord’s name with great insult, one of our men, animated by the life-giving Spirit, contradicted him by word and deed.

Immediately spurring his horse, he entered the arena and declared most vigorously, asking those standing by:

> “If any of you desires to dine in paradise, let him come with me now and dine with me. For I am about to depart at once.”

Then, brandishing his lance, he thrust himself into the midst of thousands of enemies. Overthrowing and killing the first man who met him, he was himself immediately killed as he killed the other. Thus supported by faith and hope and fortified by charity, he fell happily.

Who has ever heard of such a thing? While still on earth, he was already rejoicing in heaven. Therefore, “Rejoice, heavens, and you who dwell in them.” We too ought certainly to rejoice and be glad, because the angels rejoice at being increased by so great a companion. The one who heard him was near at hand, weighing out his reward for him and preparing an everlasting seat.

## Chapter XXVII. On the liberation of Count Baldwin and the battle between him and Tancred [Cols. 0883C–0884A]

After Lord Baldwin had been held in chains for nearly five years, he gave selected hostages and pledged his faith with an oath, under threat of punishment, that he would pay the ransom. Later, however, after the hostages had most cunningly killed the prison guards, he escaped from prison.

He therefore had the most faithful Goscelin as his helper. But when he later returned to his city of Edessa, he could not enter it, because Tancred and his men barred his entrance.

Finally, since reason permitted this to be done, and because of the oath which Lord Bohemond had previously caused to be sworn—that whenever Baldwin escaped from captivity in any manner, his land would be returned to him without dispute—there was no further delay. Baldwin and Goscelin, two against Tancred alone, engaged him in battle.

They would not yield to him when he begged and sought peace. Instead, Baldwin and Goscelin, having gathered seven thousand Turks, persistently challenged Tancred to battle; with the aid of the Turks, five hundred of Tancred’s retainers fell.

Although Tancred was at first almost defeated, in the end, with God’s help—whose face always sees the victorious riding—he remained the victor in the field and in honor. But when the nobles of the land saw that loss was arising on both sides, they took useful counsel together and restored the two men to concord.

## Chapter XXVIII. That Bohemond crossed over to Gaul [Col. 0884A]

Then Bohemond, desolated in many respects, crossed over to Gaul, as has already been stated above. There, among his other affairs, he married Constance, daughter of King Philip, and brought her back to Apulia. By her he had two sons. The elder of them died, while the younger, who was called by his father’s name, remained as heir.

## Chapter XXIX. That Tancred, fighting against the Turks, gained the victory [Cols. 0884B–C]

In the year of the Lord 1105, Count Raymond, a veteran soldier, died in his own town before the city of Tripoli on the day before the Kalends of March. His nephew William Jordan succeeded him.

At that time the customary insolence of the Saracens and Turks was not lacking. Then, in the month of April, the king of Aleppo—that is, of Calipti—named Raduan, gathered a considerable army from the region adjoining his own and raised his wing, fiercely eager for battle, against Tancred, prince of Antioch.

Tancred, however, placing the anchor of his hope not in a large army but in the Lord, set his lines in good order and rode without hesitation against those enemies. Why delay any longer? He boldly charged them before Artah, and, with God’s support, they were immediately enveloped in fear and turned their backs in flight.

They fled, and they were pursued. Whoever could not flee did not escape death. There was no counting the slain. Tancred acquired many of their horses. He also retained the standard of the fugitive king. Its horn having been shattered, the king departed mutilated.

Therefore God was glorified, for he always comes to the aid of his faithful. This much have we said concerning Antioch. Now I shall not be silent concerning Jerusalem.

## Chapter XXX. That the king of Babylon again sent his entire army against King Baldwin, and how Baldwin prepared himself against them [Cols. 0884C–0886A]

It must be related how, in that same year, the king of Babylon assembled a large people and sent it against Christianity by the commander of his army at Ascalon, believing and striving to expel us all from the Holy Land. For he had learned that we were very few and without the customary reinforcements of pilgrims.

Thus, near Ascalon, there gathered both Arab cavalry and Ethiopian infantry. With them were also approximately one thousand Damascene Turks, who were exceptionally skilled archers.

When this was announced to King Baldwin, he assembled all his people and awaited them at Joppa. Since necessity demanded it, everyone living in the cities who was capable of bearing arms went to war, except only those who were to guard the walls at night.

Then fear and trembling came upon us. We feared that they might either seize one of our cities emptied of its people or kill the king and his people in battle.

It was the month of August. Both sides were eager to fight but delayed; neither we nor they attacked the other. At a divinely appointed moment, as I believe, the wicked people advanced from Ascalon and began to draw near us.

When the king learned this, he returned to Joppa and rode as far as the city of Ramla. Since it was in every way good for our people to cling to the Lord and place firm hope in God (Ps. 72:28), the king, inspired by counsel from the Lord God, sent a swift messenger to Jerusalem—to the patriarch, the clergy, and the common people—begging them earnestly to implore the mercy of almighty God, so that he might deign to give aid from on high to his Christians placed in distress.

The messenger did not wish to accept any payment despite repeated requests, fearing that he might be unable to complete the embassy or live to receive any payment. But hoping that he would at some time receive from God a recompense for this devout labor, and commending his soul and body into the hands of his Creator, he did not delay hurrying to Jerusalem.

With the Lord guiding him, he arrived there, entered the city, and concealed nothing of what he sought. When this was made known, the patriarch ordered the great bell to be rung and the entire people to assemble before him.

> “O brothers,” he said, “friends and servants of God, behold the battle you heard was to come; for, according to this messenger’s report, it has undoubtedly been prepared against us. Since we cannot possibly withstand so great a multitude without divine assistance, all of you implore God’s clemency, that he may deign to be a merciful helper to our king Baldwin and all his men in this approaching battle.
>
> “The king has postponed the battle today, as this swift messenger has just made known to us, so that tomorrow, which will be Sunday—the day on which Christ rose from the dead—he may fight more securely and, strengthened before God by your prayers and almsgiving, battle with greater confidence.
>
> “Therefore, during this night, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying, ‘Be watchful, stand firm in the faith; let all that you do be done in charity’ (1 Cor. 16:13–14). Tomorrow you will go through the places of this holy city, afflicting and humbling yourselves with bare feet, and piously beseeching the Lord our God to free us from the hands of our enemies.
>
> “I myself am going there now; I am departing from you at this very moment. I urge you: if any of you remaining here is able to bear arms, let him promptly come with me. The king needs everyone.”

Why delay any longer? One hundred and fifty men, both cavalry and infantry, mounted their horses together, and as night approached they hastened onward, reaching the city of Ramla at dawn.

Those who remained in Jerusalem devoted themselves most earnestly to prayers, almsgiving, and acts of penitence. They did not cease visiting the churches until noon. They wept while singing and sang while weeping, for the clergy did this in procession.

I too prayed barefoot with them. The elders did not eat until the ninth hour that day, nor did infants suck their mothers’ breasts, until, tormented by hunger, they began to cry. Abundant alms were distributed to the poor. These are the works by which God is appeased, by which he is stirred to grant salvation, and by which, being turned toward us, he does not leave a blessing behind him.

## Chapter XXXI. The battle of the people of Jerusalem with the Turks, and the victory gained through the power of the holy cross [Cols. 0886A–0887D]

When the patriarch had reached Ramla, as stated above, and the following dawn began to drive away the glittering stars, everyone rejoiced at his arrival. All were stirred to run to the priests, so that they might confess their sins to God and to them. The nobles likewise approached the patriarch, desiring to hear from him some saving word and to be absolved from their sins.

When this had been done, the patriarch put on his pontifical vestments, took in his hands the glorious Lord’s cross that was customarily carried on such occasions, and, having arranged the companies of soldiers and infantry as was proper, they advanced against the hostile army.

Our soldiers numbered five hundred, apart from those who were not counted under the military designation but nevertheless rode horses. Our infantry were estimated at no more than two thousand. The pagans, both infantry and soldiers, numbered fifteen thousand. That night they had encamped not far from Ramla, about four miles away.

When they saw the king advancing against them with his men in the morning, they immediately prepared for battle. Yet their strategy was somewhat disrupted. They had planned to send one part of their army, the smaller, before Ramla in order to deceive our army, while they intended to send the larger part toward Joppa so that they might attack it and capture it without our knowledge.

But when they saw the king riding against them in this manner, they all gathered together, their plan thrown into confusion. There was no long delay: they attacked one another. Then shields resounded and the sharp edge of iron shrieked.

When the charge had been made, all our men shouted against them:

> “Christ conquers, Christ reigns, Christ commands!”

They had been ordered to do this.

The enemy surrounded us and thought they could completely crush and confuse us. The Turks, as was their custom, being archers, circled around us from behind and struck us with a rain of arrows. Then, abandoning the work of their bows, they drew swords from their scabbards and struck us at close quarters.

When the king learned this, fortified by courage he snatched his white standard from the hand of one of his soldiers. Racing there at full speed with a few men, he strove to aid those who were being overwhelmed. With God’s help he immediately attacked and scattered the Turks, killing them, and then rushed against the larger multitude of Saracens, Arabs, and Ethiopians.

I shall not dwell further on the attacks and blows exchanged by either side, because I wish to compress the account within a shorter compass. Almighty God, never forgetful of his servants and unwilling that his Christians—who had come to Jerusalem from distant regions for love of him and the enlargement of his name—should be destroyed by those treacherous men, caused the impious people to take sudden flight. They fled as far as Ascalon.

If only Semelumuch, the commander of that army, could have been captured! He would have paid many coins to King Baldwin for his ransom. But Gemelmulch, the admiral of Ascalon, did not escape; he was extremely wealthy. When he was killed, no small lamentation arose among all the others.

They kept alive another admiral, formerly of Acre, whom our king had ransomed for twenty thousand coins, in addition to horses and other property. The Ethiopians, because they could not flee, were slaughtered in the fields. Four thousand of them, both cavalry and infantry, are reported to have been killed.

Of our enemies’ possessions, sixty tents remained for us, along with many pack animals, camels, donkeys, and dromedaries. Then God was praised and glorified, in whom we had performed a great deed of valor, and who had also reduced our enemies to nothing.

O wondrous ordering of divine judgment! Behold, they had said:

> “Let us go and kill all those Christians, and we shall possess their sanctuary.”

But “not so are the wicked, not so” (Ps. 1:4), for God made you like a wheel and, like straw before the face of the wind, confused you in his anger (Ps. 72:14).

They had even sworn by their law that they would never flee because of the Franks. In the end, however, flight was their safety. They preferred to incur perjury rather than foolishly perish by death.

The king returned joyfully to Joppa, where he distributed among his soldiers and infantry, with due accounting, the spoils captured in the battle.

A Babylonian fleet was still before Joppa. For some time its men had been waiting there, wishing to discover how and when they might utterly destroy us all, both by sea and by land, together with the maritime cities.

But when the king had his sailors throw into one of their ships the head of Gemelmulch, the admiral who had been beheaded in battle, they were greatly disturbed and terrified when they learned this and did not wish to remain there any longer. When the confusion of their people became known, and the south wind began to blow gently, they withdrew to the ports of Tyre and Sidon.

Later, when that fleet was returning to Babylon, a storm wind, by God’s grace sufficiently favorable to us, drove the ships in various places to our ports in miserable shipwreck. We obtained twenty-five ships filled with Saracens; the rest barely escaped under sail.

Thus the Lord, in his goodness, being our helper in tribulations, made his omnipotence manifest in this way.

Therefore I wish to make the day of the battle known to all:

> Now Phoebus had risen ten times beneath the Virgin’s star,  
> While the moon, in her full form, looked upon the earth;  
> When the sixth day before the Kalends of September was being read,  
> The Almighty granted the Franks joy in triumph:
>
> When Arabs, Turks, and Ethiopians flee together,  
> One part seeks the mountains; another remains dead upon the fields.

## Chapter XXXII. On the earthquake [Cols. 0887D–0888A]

So that neither the negligence or ignorance of writers, nor perhaps their scarcity, nor the fact that they were occupied and laboring under their own concerns, might consign these deeds to oblivion by leaving them unwritten, I, Fulcher, preferred to be marked by the blemish of rashness—unskilled in knowledge and weak in intellect—rather than allow these events to remain unknown. I have reported them as I saw them with my own eyes or learned them carefully through diligent inquiry from truthful narrators.

I ask the reader to indulgently forgive my lack of knowledge and, if he wishes, to correct this composition playfully, since it has not yet been revised by any orator. Nevertheless, let him not alter the sequence of the history for the sake of the pompous beauty of its parts, lest he deceitfully confuse the truth of what was done.

After these events had taken place, as related above, and as that year was drawing to its close, we all who were in Jerusalem felt a great earthquake. It greatly terrified us on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On Signs Appearing in the Sky

Then, in the year 1106, a comet appearing in the sky frightened us as we gazed at it. In that part where the sun usually sets during winter, it wonderfully extended a ray of whitish brightness lengthwise, like a linen thread. This portent, beginning to glow in the month of February on the day when we declared the moon to be new, announced a presage of things to come. But since we did not dare to prophesy anything about it, we entrusted everything it signified to the Lord.

For fifty days and more that comet was seen every evening throughout the whole world. It should be noted that from the beginning of its rising, both the comet itself and its snowy radiance gradually diminished from day to day, until in its final days, having already lost the force of its light, it ceased entirely to appear.

In the same month, on the day when we declared the moon to be twenty days old, we saw in the sky from the third hour until midday, on the right and left sides of the sun, as though two other suns—yet not shining as brightly as the greater one, but glowing moderately, with a rarer form and light. Around them there also appeared a single circle, white with brightness and so large in extent as to resemble some city. Within it another circle shone halfway, bearing the likeness of a rainbow and distinguished by four colors; in its upper part it embraced the sun in an arc and reached as far as the two suns already mentioned.

Then, in the following month, at midnight, the stars of heaven were seen to rain down.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Battle of the Christians against the Damascenes

Afterward Hugh, who at that time possessed the city of Tiberias, fought against the Damascene army during the summer. Although in that very battle he had already been driven back by them twice, on the third renewal of the fighting, with the Lord’s help, he overcame them as victor over the vanquished. He killed two hundred of them and likewise captured an equal number of their horses; the rest turned their backs in flight.

Strange to relate! They scattered six times twenty and forty times a hundred—that is, four thousand one hundred and twenty.

Afterward, when he himself was on campaign with King Baldwin, Hugh died in that same land from an arrow wound.

## CHAPTER XXXV. How the Patriarch Went to Rome, and on the Battles of the Men of Joppa and Ascalon

In the year 1107 the patriarch, named Ebremarus, crossed the sea, making for Rome. For he was going to ask the apostolic authority whether he should remain patriarch. Daibertus, mentioned above, had recovered the patriarchate, but afterward had died on his return.

Finally, in November of that same year, when the men of Ascalon were raging with extraordinary savagery, they laid an ambush at the foot of our mountains, between Ramla and Jerusalem, intending to attack by sudden assault a band of our people whom they had learned was then traveling from Joppa to Jerusalem.

But when this was reported to the men of Joppa, they hurriedly mounted their horses. When, guided by the messenger who had brought the news, they reached the place of the ambush, they were still doubtful whether he had spoken truly; but when they saw the enemy, they were greatly terrified. There were nearly five hundred horsemen and almost a thousand infantry. Our own soldiers, however, numbered no more than seventy-five.

Since they were not even permitted time to consider what they should do, and since there was no safety for them if they fled, while death was unavoidable if they engaged in battle, they more gladly chose to die honorably, if that should happen, than afterward to be branded with the disgrace of flight.

Accordingly, they immediately attacked them with a sudden charge and, in a remarkable fashion, penetrated the enemy line, throwing them down and killing them. When, in this struggle, the Saracens saw themselves being crushed ever more fiercely, they lost their boldness, as the Lord willed, and ceased fighting. When our soldiers saw this, they pressed upon them more powerfully, and those whom the enemy had thought to put to flight were compelled by our men to flee.

They killed many of them and seized very many of their horses. Of our soldiers we lost no more than three. Their retainers, however, carried off some of our pack animals; our men doubled the retaliation with animals taken from them.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. How Bohemond, Having Gathered an Army, Laid Waste the Emperor’s Land

In that same year, after Bohemond had returned from Gaul, he gathered as many people as he could and prepared his fleet in the port of Brindisi, which is in Apulia. After waiting for a suitable time to cross the sea, they boarded the ships on the seventh day before the Ides of October, sailed to Bulgaria, and put in at the port of Aulon. Having captured Aulon very quickly, they proceeded to the city of Durazzo and besieged it on the third day before the Ides of October.

But because that city was well supplied with both men and provisions, it wearied the besiegers for a long time. Lord Bohemond had five thousand cavalry and sixty thousand infantry. At that time he allowed no woman to cross with him, lest they should hinder and burden the armies.

The emperor of Constantinople was then named Alexius. He was strongly hostile to our people and, whether by secret fraud or open violence, was a disturber and tyrant toward those journeying as pilgrims to Jerusalem, both by land and by sea. Therefore Bohemond, having gathered the army as described, entered his territory, striving to seize its cities and fortified places.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the Agreement Confirmed by Oath between the Emperor and Bohemond

In the year 1108 from the Lord’s Incarnation, after he had already spent a year before Durazzo without accomplishing anything—except that he plotted certain ambushes against the emperor, while the emperor did the same against him—an agreement was finally negotiated through intermediaries. When the emperor had also approached him with his army, they became friends with one another after incorporating various terms into their agreement.

The emperor swore to Bohemond upon the most precious relics that he would, from that day forward, protect and preserve the pilgrims—of whom mention has already often been made—both on land and at sea, throughout the whole extent of his empire, so that none of them would be robbed or mistreated. Bohemond likewise swore to the emperor that he would maintain peace and complete fidelity.

Afterward, when the opportunity arose, Bohemond returned to Apulia, taking back with him the smaller part of his army. The larger part set out by sea for Jerusalem, as they had vowed.

In that same year King Philip of France ended his life.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the Siege of the City of Tripoli

In the year 1109, the eleventh after the capture of Jerusalem, Bertrand, son of Count Raymond, came to Tripoli, bringing the Genoese with him and nearly seventy ships of war. They all put in there. He wished to attack the city of Tripoli and possess it as his own by hereditary right under the authority of his father.

When they had surrounded it with a siege, a dispute immediately arose between Bertrand and his kinsman William Jordan, who had always attacked it after Count Raymond died. William was staying there in the fortress called Mont-Pèlerin, near Tripoli.

Bertrand said:

> “The city ought to be mine by hereditary right, because my father, who first began to attack it, built this fortress—Mont-Pèlerin—with great valor while he was reducing the city, and, before his death, left it to me to obtain.”

William, however, said:

> “It ought to be mine, and rightly so, because after the count’s death I have always bravely restrained the enemies who inhabit this land with my arms, and I have striven and labored to enlarge the territory adjoining the city.”

Since people commonly fall from their position amid great discord and increase it through even the smallest concord, William withdrew from the affair out of hostility, while Bertrand and his men held the city bravely. The one did not want the other to be able to prosper; the other did not even want this one to live.

They contend for uncertain things and are uncertain about uncertain things. They strive for momentary matters and do not labor for eternal ones. They run, though perhaps they do not grasp the prize. Thus the reward remained at the crossroads.

“Therefore it is not a matter of the one who runs, nor of the one who wills, but of God who shows mercy” (Romans 9:16).

They had not yet captured the city, and already they were disputing over its capture. At God’s command, moments fly past, and human thoughts are overturned as vanity.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. How the City of Tripoli Was Captured

There was no delay. After King Baldwin came to the siege, he asked the Genoese to help him in that same year capture Ascalon, Beirut, and also Sidon.

While an agreement was beginning to be made between the two counts mentioned above, through some misfortune, as William Jordan was riding at night, he suddenly died secretly from the blow of a small arrow. Everyone asked who had done this, but they were unable to discover it.

Some mourned; others rejoiced. Some grieved for a friend; others celebrated the destruction of an enemy.

Bertrand remained, having become King Baldwin’s man. Then the city was hemmed in on every side. Those outside labored; those inside were harassed. But when the Saracens were being pressed very hard and had no hope of escape, they were allowed, under a sworn agreement confirmed by the king, not to be killed but to leave without opposition wherever they wished. On that condition, the king and his men were permitted to enter one part of the city.

While this was happening, through some unforeseen occurrence a great and sudden tumult arose among the lesser men of the Genoese. They climbed the wall by ropes and ladders and entered the city. Every Saracen found there was immediately beheaded. Those who were in the king’s district, however, were protected by him according to the agreement that had been made.

Phoebus had already given his light to Cancer thirteen times,

if, after removing three from the number,

the warlike people capture the city of Tripoli by force.

## CHAPTER XL. How the City of Beirut Was Captured

In the year 1110, while the month of February still confined the earth under winter rains, King Baldwin set out for the city of Beirut and besieged it. Count Bertrand of Tripoli came to his aid, and the army settled at the first stone from the city.

After they had hemmed in the city on every side for seventy-five days, as I believe, and after our ships had shut inside the harbor the ships that had come there to aid the enemy, the Franks, with great daring, leapt upon the wall from the wooden towers that had been brought up against it, carrying swords and exposed above the wall. Descending into the city, while many others also entered through the gates, they vigorously pursued the fleeing enemy and finally overcame them by killing them; they also plundered all their wealth.

In the year one thousand one hundred and ten,

the valor of armed men captured the city of Beirut.

Phoebus had risen ten times beneath the sign of Taurus,

and three times four, when this deed took place.

## CHAPTER XLI. How King Baldwin and Prince Tancred Set Out against the Turks Besieging Edessa

After these events, the king returned to Jerusalem to render due praises to God, through whom he had triumphed. Then he prepared to go against the Turks who were besieging Edessa, a city of Mesopotamia.

At that time we saw a comet for several nights, extending its rays toward the south. Tancred also gathered at Antioch as many of his people as he could, having already awaited the king for several days. Together they assembled before the Euphrates River.

After crossing it, they immediately found the Turks whom they sought. These were moving about the region in bands and awaiting the king’s arrival. But because they knew that our soldiers were excellent warriors and remarkable attackers with lances, they did not dare engage them in battle. Instead, by a flight full of cunning, they turned away from them: they neither dared to fight nor wished to withdraw into their own land.

After trying for many days, through wearisome stratagems, to fatigue our men, who did not wish to fight, the king, taking counsel for necessity and advantage, supplied the city of Edessa with provisions, of which its inhabitants were greatly in need because the Turks had devastated the surrounding region. After seizing the castles and villages on which the city depended for food, they did not linger longer but returned to the river mentioned above.

When they had gradually crossed it with a few small rafts, the deceitful and rapacious Turks immediately came after them. They seized many of our infantry there and carried them off into Persia—Armenians, that is, impoverished people whom the Turks had already wickedly ravaged.

Because it was difficult for them to cross the river at that time, and because they were deeply grieved by this, they continued along the route they had begun: Tancred going to Antioch, while the king returned to Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER XLII. How Sidon, Called Sagitta, Was Besieged and Captured by the King and the Norsemen

Meanwhile, a certain people from Norway had arrived at Joppa. God had stirred them from the western sea so that they might make pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Their fleet consisted of fifty-five ships. Their leader was a young man of very handsome appearance, the brother of the king of that land.

When the king had returned to Jerusalem, he rejoiced at their arrival and spoke with them amicably. He urged and entreated them, for the love of God, to remain for a while in his land and to help advance and enlarge Christendom, so that, once the work of Christ had been accomplished in some fashion, they might afterward return to their own country and render great thanks to God.

They kindly accepted this request and replied that they had come to Jerusalem for no other reason, but that wherever the king wished to proceed with his army, they themselves would willingly go by sea with him, provided only that he took care to supply them with the food they needed.

The request was granted on one side and fulfilled on the other. Although at first they had decided to go to Ascalon, they finally adopted the better plan and approached the city of Sidon, which they besieged.

The king moved his army from Ptolemais, more commonly called Acre. The Norsemen proceeded by ship from Joppa. At that time the fleet of the admiral of Babylon was hiding in the port of Tyre. Following the practice of pirates, it frequently harassed our Christian pilgrims and strengthened the coastal cities that the king of Babylon still possessed.

When they heard the Norsemen being discussed, they did not dare leave the port of Tyre or engage them. When Sidon was reached, the king besieged it from land, while the Norsemen blockaded it from the sea.

After siege engines had been constructed, the enemy was so greatly terrified that the stipendiaries asked the king to allow them to leave safely, and, if it pleased him, that farmers remain in the city to cultivate the land for his benefit.

They asked this and obtained it. Thus the stipendiaries departed without a gift; the peasants, however, remained peacefully under the agreement described above.

The sun had already looked upon the Bear-Bearer nineteen times,

when, in the month of December, they surrendered the city of Sidon.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the Turks’ Most Evil Disturbance and King Baldwin’s and Tancred’s March against Them

In the year 1111, a very great people of Turks boiled up from Persia. Passing through Mesopotamia, they crossed the Euphrates River and besieged the castle called Turbessel, remaining there for a month.

When they were unable to capture it immediately, since its position was perhaps too strong, they were wearied by the effort and abandoned the siege, withdrawing toward the regions of the city of Aleppo. For by cunning stratagems they were trying to provoke Tancred to come out against them and fight, so that, once he had been drawn away from Antioch, they might intercept and completely destroy him with his large force.

But Tancred opposed cunning with cunning. He did not wish to compromise his valor through foolish boldness. Instead, he sent envoys to King Baldwin, humbly asking through them that he hasten to assist Christendom.

When he heard this, the king promised to provide the requested aid. Entrusting his own land to guards, he hurried to the war, taking with him Count Bertrand of Tripoli.

When they reached the fortress called Rugia, near Rusa, Tancred was there. He had already been awaiting the king’s arrival for five days. The king was received with great joy. The tents were pitched and spread out beside the Fernus River, where the people of Jerusalem and Antioch extended hospitality to one another.

They did not remain there but went on as far as the city of Apamea, which was then governed by Tancred and which he had captured some time earlier with great valor. Then they advanced against the Turks, who had pitched their camp before the city called Sisara. I do not know how to give the city its name in literary form, but the inhabitants of the region commonly call it Caesar. It lies six miles from Apamea.

The Turks, having already heard that the Franks were marching against them, had hidden themselves in the thickets and enclosures of the city mentioned above, so that they might defend themselves more securely if the Franks should attack them.

Nevertheless, when they saw our soldiers approaching, they came out of the fortifications just mentioned and showed themselves to our people. Yet, being cautious, they neither dared to fight nor wished to flee.

Our soldiers, arranged in bands, saw them scattering through the fields without preparing for battle. Avoiding danger, they did not attack them. Thus, constrained on both sides by fear and cunning, the Turks remained there. Our men, too, returned by the route they had come.

Since provisions for both themselves and their animals were running short, they could not remain there longer. The king returned to Jerusalem, and I was there with him. Tancred returned to Antioch.

## CHAPTER XLIV. How the King Besieged Tyre, Called Sur, but Accomplished Nothing

There was no delay. Having hastened his preparations, the king attacked the city of Tyre, which is called Soor in Hebrew, and besieged it.

After harassing it severely for four months and more, he himself and his men, worn out by weariness and labor, withdrew from there in sadness.

When he had brought close to the wall two towers of wood, which he had ordered to be skillfully constructed higher than the city wall, he thought that from them he would capture the city. The Saracens, realizing that they were near death unless they defeated skill with skill, opposed ingenuity with ingenuity and valor with valor.

When they saw that they could not surpass the height of our towers, they immediately raised two wall-towers high above them by nighttime labor, taking every measure necessary. From the upper battlements of these towers they defended themselves most effectively, while they set fire to our lower towers and burned them.

Overcome by this misfortune and surrounded by grief, our soldiers saw the cord of their hope snapped, and the king returned to Acre.

Truly true is this rustic proverb:

> Sometimes the open mouth is frustrated by the spoon.

Our people had already distributed the booty from the capture. Some were already envying others according to uncertain proportions. They were already imagining the day of the capture as though it were certain for them.

“ A horse is prepared for battle,” says Solomon, “but the Lord grants victory” (Proverbs 21:31).

Sometimes people trust in their own strength, not considering what merit they have acquired before God. They often invoke him with their lips but deny him by their deeds; and they praise their own valor in what they have acquired more than they glorify the gift of God’s mercy.

## CHAPTER XLV. On the Death of Prince Tancred

In the year 1112, Tancred, who ruled the principality of Antioch, paid his debt to death.

The sun had looked upon the Bear-Bearer twice thirteen times,

when he underwent what had to be undergone, so that he himself might become what he had been.

His kinsman Roger succeeded him. That year we were entirely free from wars.

## CHAPTER XLVI. On Signs That Appeared

In the year 1113 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in March, when we had the moon at twenty-eight days, we saw the sun diminished on one side by a certain eclipse from morning until the first hour and beyond.

The part that first began to waste away from the top eventually descended toward the bottom, as though into a rounded form. Nevertheless, the sun did not lose its brightness. It was diminished only, as I estimate, by about a quarter of its form, becoming somewhat horned.

This was an eclipse, by which the sun was thus obscured.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On the Battle Fought against the Turks, in Which the King and the Christians Were Defeated, and through Which Many Evils Came

Then, in the summer, the Turks gathered and crossed the Euphrates, intending to enter the regions of Jerusalem and, as they thought, destroy us Christians.

Leaving the Antiochene region on their right, they crossed Syria not far from Apamea, leaving Damascus on their left. Passing through the Phoenician regions between Tyre and Caesarea Philippi, which is called Paneas, they skillfully sought to attack King Baldwin.

When he heard of their arrival, he had already moved his army from Ptolemais, that is, Acre, and gone out against them. But perceiving what they judged more useful to themselves, while our men did not know what they were planning, they went around the Sea of Galilee by way of the land of Naphtali and the land of Zebulun, until they reached the southern end of that sea, where the two rivers, the Jor and the Dan, flow together.

This island between the two bridges is so strongly defended that, because of the narrow entrances of the bridges, those who are there cannot be attacked.

When the Turks had stretched out their tents there, they immediately sent two thousand of their men across the bridge to prepare an ambush for ours, whom they did not doubt would hasten there without delay.

As the king was moving toward the place in order to set up his camp near the aforementioned bridge, from which one travels to Tiberias, he saw nearly five hundred Turks bursting from their ambush to attack our men. At once some of our men imprudently ran against them and did not fear to pursue them while striking them, until two thousand came out from the ambush. These drove our men back with a violent assault, and, after inflicting threefold slaughter, scattered them in flight.

Alas! On that day our great sins brought about great disgrace. The king also fled, having lost his banner there, along with his finest tent, many possessions, and silver vessels. The patriarch who was present likewise fled. We lost about thirty of our best soldiers and two hundred infantrymen.

The sun had risen three times four beneath the sign of Cancer,

when the treacherous people savagely scattered the unsuspecting Franks.

Not yet had the king’s entire army arrived there. Nor was Roger, prince of Antioch and son of Richard, present—the man who, summoned for the love of God and out of devotion to the king, had hurried there from Antioch. Part of the people of Tripoli had also already joined the royal army.

Therefore all these men were greatly saddened and condemned the king’s rashness, because without their counsel or assistance he had advanced in disorder and without forethought against those enemies.

Since they had been unable to harm the Turks in any way at that time, they camped not far from them, so that throughout the day each side could see the other.

Their army was commanded by a leader called Maledoctus, who had joined to himself the king of Damascus, named Tughtakin. The former had brought a large people; the latter had gathered an innumerable host from the Syria subject to him.

The Turks were in the valley; the Franks were stationed on the mountain. The Turks did not dare leave their island, and the Franks could not attack them. The former were cunning; the latter cautious. These were crafty; those were wary. The heat of summer held both sides back, yet it could not bring an end to so great a distress.

Those who were absent then wondered what the people present were waiting for. The Saracens who were subject to us withdrew from us, hemming us in on every side as though they were strangers. The Turks, too, coming out from their army in bands, ravaged our land and sent booty and provisions through our Saracens to their army.

They both occupied and plundered Sichen, the city we call Neapolis, and added to themselves the Saracens whom we held in the mountains.

The men of Ascalon—Arabs and Saracens, though a small force—approached Jerusalem. One day they advanced as far as the outer wall of the city, burned the gathered harvest there with fire, and wounded some of our men on the wall’s battlements with their arrows. More of them, however, were wounded unto death. The city lacked soldiers because they had gone out against the enemy.

The following night these men of Ascalon departed. Our people were greatly rejoiced, because they had feared that they would be besieged by them.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On the Great Fear That Restrained Everyone

At that time it was scarcely ever possible for a messenger sent by any of our people to reach the king, nor for one to pass from him to our cities, because of the ambushes. No one knew what the former were doing, nor what the latter were doing.

In many rural districts the mature harvest was withering. You would not see anyone going out into the fields to gather it. They did not dare. That year the harvest had indeed been abundant.

But when the sea is troubled, people are frightened to fish. Everything hung in uncertainty for everyone, and all awaited with one accord which side God would grant victory.

Our Christians ceased from their businesses and labors, except that they repaired the breaches in the cities and fortifications.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On an Earthquake and on the King’s Marriage to the Countess of Sicily

Meanwhile, we experienced an earthquake twice: on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August and on the fifth day before the Ides of the same month—first at midnight, and second at the third hour of the day.

The deceitful Turks, after waiting for two months for an opportunity either to scatter or to overcome our men and having been unable to do so—because at that time, as is customary, our army was growing daily with pilgrims arriving from overseas, while the people of Antioch had not departed—withdrew toward the regions of Damascus.

King Baldwin returned with his men to Ptolemais, where he found the countess of Sicily. She had been the wife of Count Roger, the brother of Robert Guiscard, but was now to become King Baldwin’s wife.

Soon afterward, at Damascus, Maledoctus was killed by a certain Saracen [in the edition: Maudulfus, and Maulidulfus]. The Saracen concealed a sword beneath his garment and struck him three times in the belly, thereby completing a double murder. For after Maledoctus had been killed, the assassin himself was immediately killed by those standing nearby.

A dreadful victory, in which the victor is defeated. Thus it happened according to that saying of the philosopher:

> “Fortune is glass: when it shines, it breaks” (Publilius Syrus, in the *Sentences*).

Maledoctus was very rich and powerful, highly renowned among the Turks, and exceedingly clever in his actions. But he could not resist the will of God. The Lord allowed him for a while to chastise us; afterward he willed that he should perish by a shameful death at the hand of a weak man.

## CHAPTER L. On an Earthquake Occurring in Many Places

In the year 1114, an infinite multitude of locusts arose, flying from the region of Arabia into the land of Jerusalem. For several days in April and May they greatly devastated the crops.

Then, on the feast of Saint Lawrence, an earthquake occurred. Later, on the Ides of November, at the city of Mamistria, an earthquake destroyed part of a fortress.

Another, greater and unheard-of earthquake shook the Antiochene region so severely in various places that it brought many fortresses—some entirely, others halfway—crashing to the ground, both houses and walls. In that ruin, part of the common people also perished by suffocation.

They say that Mariscum is a city sixty miles, as I estimate, from Antioch, toward the north. That upheaval overturned it so completely that its houses and walls collapsed entirely and, alas, extinguished all its inhabitants.

Another fortress, called Traleth, near the Euphrates River, likewise collapsed.

## CHAPTER LI. On the Arrival of the Turks and the Siege of the Men of Joppa by the Ascalonites and Babylonians

In the year 1115, renewing their customary valor and boldness, the Turks secretly crossed the Euphrates in June and entered Syria. They pitched their camp between Antioch and Damascus, before the city called Caesar.

They had likewise established their station there four years earlier, as has already been written above.

Tughtakin, king of the Damascenes, learned and understood that he was no less hated by them than we Christians were, because of Maudulfus, whom, as is related above, he had deceitfully agreed to have killed in the preceding year and who had been the chief commander of their army.

Therefore he made peace with King Baldwin and Roger, prince of Antioch, so that, joined to them as a third, he might form something like a threefold cord, which the Turks would not afterward easily break. For he feared that, if he remained alone, he and his kingdom would be utterly ruined.

But necessity pressed, and the command of the Antiochenes urged him, so the king went to the battle that was expected. When the Turks heard that he was already approaching them—the Antiochenes and Damascenes having waited for him for nearly three months—they feared the danger of their own death if they fought against so great a people, although they were much more numerous.

They therefore withdrew backward in near silence and hid themselves in certain hollows, though not far from our men. When they had done this, the king and the others thought that they had entirely departed from our regions. Therefore the king returned as far as Tripoli.

While these events were taking place, the men of Ascalon, knowing that the land of Jerusalem was empty of soldiers, hurried as far as our city of Joppa and laid siege to it by both sea and land.

The Babylonian fleet was present there, consisting of nearly seventy ships. Some were triremes, others ships of war, and others merchant vessels laden with provisions. Those who came from the sea disembarked, while the others prepared to attack the city from land.

They attempted to climb the wall by means of ladders they had brought with them, but the citizens, though few and weakened by illness, bravely drove them back.

When they saw that they could accomplish nothing, as they thought, except to burn the city gates with fire, they feared that the people of Jerusalem might bring help to the men of Joppa, to whom this had already been reported. Those who had come by land returned to Ascalon; those who had come by sea sailed to Tyre.

After ten days the Ascalonites returned to Joppa, thinking that, through a sudden attack, they would outwit those who were prepared by confronting those who were unprepared. But almighty God protected and preserved them a second time just as he had the first.

While defending themselves, the citizens killed some of the attackers and captured some of their horses. The enemy began to harass the city with slings and, as before, attempted to enter with ladders, which they had brought with them in small boats. But after exhausting themselves for six hours of the day, they departed in deep sorrow with their dead.

## CHAPTER LII. On the Battle between the Turks and the Antiochenes, in Which the Antiochenes Won the Victory

When the Turks mentioned above learned that our people had returned, they went back to their former station and moved through the regions of Syria, capturing as many castles as they could, plundering villages, laying waste the country, and carrying away male and female captives.

When this was reported to the Antiochenes, who had already withdrawn by the route they had come, they returned to the Turks without delay. When they approached them and saw their tents nearer than they had expected, they immediately drew up their battle lines and descended onto the plain, riding against them with their banners unfurled.

This battle took place near the fortress of Sarmit. When the Turks saw them, one part of their archers immediately offered strong resistance. But our Franks, stirred by great courage and choosing either to overcome them, if God granted it, or to be overcome, if he permitted it, rather than be humiliated by them year after year, attacked them magnificently wherever they saw the denser mass.

The Turks at first resisted somewhat, but then, without delay, turned their backs and fled from both those striking and those killing them. They were estimated to have lost three thousand dead, and many were captured. Those who avoided death saved themselves by flight.

They lost their tents, in which much money and equipment were found. The value of this money was estimated at three hundred thousand bezants. They left there our captives, both Franks and Syrians; their own women and servant girls; and very many camels. Thousands of mules and horses were counted.

Truly, God is wonderful in all his wonders. When the people of Jerusalem, together with the Antiochenes and Damascenes, had been prepared to fight, they had accomplished absolutely nothing. Does victory in war depend on the multitude of the people? Remember the Maccabees, Gideon, and many others who, trusting not in their own strength but in the Lord’s, struck down many thousands with a few men.

With these events thus recorded, the deed will be known to those yet to come.

Three nights remained before the star of Virgo would depart,

when deceitful Fortune treacherously deceived the Turks.

From this it is sufficiently clear to everyone that one must beware:

before the end of an affair, never consider anything certain.

In that same year the city of Mamistria was again overturned by an earthquake. Other such events also occurred in the Antiochene region.

In the same year a certain bishop of Aurasius, sent by the apostolic authority, came to Jerusalem and deposed Patriarch Arnulf from his see. Therefore Arnulf went to Rome and recovered the patriarchate.

## CHAPTER LIII. On the Castle Built in Arabia

In that year King Baldwin set out for Arabia and built there a castle on a certain hill in a strong location, not far from the Red Sea, but about a three-day journey away; from Jerusalem it was four days.

He placed guards in it who were to rule that land for the benefit of Christendom. He ordered the castle to be called Royal Mount on account of its distinction, because he had built it in a short time with few people but with the greatest valor.

## CHAPTER LIV. On the King’s Expedition into Arabia and on What He Saw There
In the year 1116, when King Baldwin was setting out from Jerusalem to revisit his castle and was traveling into Arabia with nearly two hundred soldiers, he journeyed as far as the Red Sea, wishing both to see what he had not yet seen and, by chance, to find on the way some good thing he desired. Then they discovered the city of Elim beside the shore of that same sea, where we read that the people of Israel encamped after crossing the sea (Exod. 15:27). When those who were there heard of the king’s arrival, they came out; then, entering their little boats, they hurried fearfully into the sea. After the king and his men had inspected that place for as long as they wished, they returned to their castle on the Royal Mount and afterward to Jerusalem. When they related to us what they had seen, we took pleasure both in their account and in the sea shells and certain very delicate little stones which they had brought back and showed us. I myself eagerly investigated from them what sort of sea it was, since up to that time I had wondered whether it was salt or fresh; whether it was a pool or lake, or whether, like the Sea of Galilee, it received and discharged water; or whether it was enclosed by a final boundary, like the Dead Sea, which receives the Jordan but afterward sends nothing out. For on the south it ends at the city of Segor, Lot’s city.

## CHAPTER LV. On the Red Sea.

This sea is called the Red Sea because there are red ballast stones and pebbles on its bottom. Hence it appears red to those looking at it; yet when water is drawn from it into any vessel, it is clear and white, like that of any other sea. They say that it is derived from the Ocean Sea on the southern side, breaking forth like a tongue, and extending northward as far as the Elim already mentioned, where it ends not far from Mount Sinai, at a distance no greater than a man on horseback can travel in a single day. From the Red Sea—or from the Elim mentioned above—to the Great Sea, by which one travels from Joppa, Ascalon, or Gaza toward Damietta, the journey is estimated at four or five days on horseback. Within the gulf formed between these two seas lie all Egypt, as well as Numidia and Ethiopia, which the river Gihon of Paradise—that is, the Nile—encircles, as we read (Gen. 2:13).

## CHAPTER LVI. On the River Gihon.

I can marvel, but never investigate fully, how or in what manner this river Gihon, which is said to flow forth from Paradise together with three others, seems to recover its source again, since on its eastern side it has the Red Sea and on its western side, into which it flows, our own sea. Between it and the east lies the Red Sea, and in the east we understand Paradise to be situated. Yet how it takes up its source again around that Red Sea, and how it crosses that sea—or does not cross it—I greatly wonder.

## CHAPTER LVII. On the Euphrates.

We likewise add concerning the Euphrates that it has its source in Armenia and afterward passes through Mesopotamia, as I believe, twenty-four miles from the city of Edessa. Let whoever wishes inquire; let whoever is able learn. For I often endeavored to learn this by questioning many people, but I could never find anyone who could explain it to me. I leave it to him to elucidate who established that even above the heavens there are wondrously situated waters, who makes them rise in mountains, hills, and valleys, who provided them with many-forked channels through hidden passages and lively currents, and who finally brings them into the sea and draws them back in a wondrous manner.

As the end of the year approached, and bodily illness came upon him, because the king then feared that he might die, he dismissed his wife, mentioned above, the countess of Sicily, named Adelaide, because he had married her unlawfully, since his former wife was still alive—the woman whom he had previously and lawfully married at the city of Edessa.

## CHAPTER LVIII. On the Greatest Plague of Locusts.

[Col. 0900D] In the year 1117 from the Lord’s Incarnation, the aforementioned queen departed from the port of Ptolemais and crossed over to Sicily with seven ships in her retinue, on the day when the Greater Litany is sung according to ecclesiastical custom. Then, in the month of May, an immeasurable multitude of locusts flew into the land of Jerusalem, devouring more than usual both vineyards and crops, as well as trees of every kind. You could see them advancing carefully in ordered ranks along the roads, like an army of men proceeding according to deliberate strategy. When their daily expedition was over, some traveling on foot and others flying, they commonly chose a lodging for themselves. Thus, after the greener grasses had been consumed and the bark of the trees gnawed away, both the caterpillars and the locusts departed in swarms.

O the wickedness of men who perversely and continually do evil! Our Creator touches and forewarns us with so many and such great rebukes; He terrifies us with signs, urges us on with threats, teaches us through examples, and restrains us with scourges. Yet, persisting always in our iniquities, we hold His warnings in contempt and proudly oppose His commandments!

What wonder is it if the Saracens, or unjust lords, take away our lands, when we greedily stretch out our hands over the fields of our neighbors—fields which we either fraudulently cut short by plowing their furrows or deprive them of by stealthy acts of covetousness—and then maliciously enlarge our own holdings from them? What wonder is it if, with God permitting it, either mice destroy our crops after they have already taken root from the seed in the ground, or locusts devour them once they have matured in the ears, or they are damaged in the granaries by various worms or by the stench of lime, when we either fraudulently render the tithes owed to God or sacrilegiously retain them altogether?

## CHAPTER LIX. On the Sign of the Moon.

In the following month, which was June, the moon appeared to us as we looked up into the sky after the cockcrow. At first it was entirely red; finally, when its redness had changed into blackness, it became so dark that it lost the power of its light for nearly two hours. This happened on the day when we reckoned it to be the thirteenth. If it had been the fourteenth day, we would certainly have understood this to be its eclipse. Since we accepted it as a sign, some inferred from the redness that blood would be shed in battle; others interpreted the blackness as signifying an approaching famine. We, however, committed the matter to God’s disposition and providence, for He foretold to His disciples that signs would come in the sun and moon (Luke 21:25). He also, whenever He wills, makes the earth tremble (Ps. 103:32), and afterward become still. This subsequently happened in the same month, in the deep silence of the night, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July.

## CHAPTER LX. On the Castle Built near Tyre.

At that time the king built a certain castle near the city of Tyre, within five miles of the city. He called it Scandalion, interpreted as “the Field of the Lion,” repaired its ruined portions, and placed guards in it to restrain the aforesaid city.

## CHAPTER LXI. On the Miraculous Sign Appearing in the Sun.

In the same year, in the month of December, on the fifth night after the eclipse of the moon—which had occurred when we reckoned it to be the thirteenth—we all saw, once night had begun, the sky in the northern part sprinkled with a radiance of either fiery or blood-red color. Looking up at this sign, full of wondrous signs, we marveled greatly. For through the midst of that redness, which at first gradually began to increase, we saw many rays of whitish color rise from below upward in a remarkable manner—now forward, now backward, now in the middle. In the lower part, the sky appeared white, as though it were the dawn of day, which ordinarily grows bright near daybreak when the sun is already about to rise. At the front of this sign, in that part where the moon seemed likely to rise, we also saw a whiteness. Hence the earth on every side, and the other places around us, shone brightly. If this had happened in the morning, we would all have said that it was a clear day.

We therefore conjectured that either much blood would be shed in battle or that some other event no less ominously portentous would occur. But what we held to be uncertain we humbly committed to the Lord God’s disposition. Some interpreted this portent as signifying the deaths of the persons who died in that same year. For afterward Pope Paschal died in January, King Baldwin of Jerusalem in April, and his wife in Sicily, whom he had abandoned. In Jerusalem the patriarch Arnulfus also died, as did Alexios, emperor of Constantinople, and many other nobles in the world.

## CHAPTER LXII. On the Death of the First King Baldwin.

In the year 1118 from the Virgin’s birth, when King Baldwin had attacked and ravaged the city called Pharamia toward the end of March, one day, while he was walking beside the river which the Greeks call the Nile and the Hebrews Gihon, near the aforementioned town, he happily approached it with some of his men. They carefully caught some of the fish there with their cavalry lances, carried them to their lodgings in the aforesaid city, and ate some of them. Then the king felt himself weakened inwardly by the severe renewal of the anguish caused by his old illness.

When this was immediately reported to his men, all of them, hearing of his sickness, were consequently saddened and disturbed, sympathizing with him. Once the return journey had been decided, and since the king could not ride, they prepared a litter for him from tent poles and placed him in it. When the herald gave the signal on the horn, the order was issued to return to Jerusalem. When they had reached the village called Laris, the illness intensified and completely consumed him, and he died.

After they had removed his intestines, salted them, and placed them in a small coffin, they hastened to Jerusalem. On the day when palm branches are customarily carried, by God’s arrangement and through an unforeseen event, a mournful crowd bearing the body for burial arrived at the procession that was then descending from the Mount of Olives into the Valley of Jehoshaphat. When they saw and recognized what had happened, all who were present turned song into mourning and joy into groaning. The Franks wept, the Syrians mourned, and the Saracens who witnessed it did likewise. For who could have restrained himself from pious weeping there?

Then, returning to the city, both clergy and people did what grief and custom required. They buried him at Golgotha beside Duke Godfrey, his brother.

When this king fell, the pious people of the Franks wept;

He had been their shield, their strength, and their aid.

For he was a weapon to his own, a terror to his enemies, and an enemy to them:

A mighty leader of his country, like Joshua.

Acre, Caesarea, Beirut, and also Sidon

He took from the impious native enemies.

After the lands of the Arabs and those touching the Red Sea,

He added them to his empire and subjected them to his authority.

He captured Tripoli, and no less pressed Arsuf,

And accomplished many other deeds worthy of honor.

The king possessed the kingdom for eighteen years,

With three additional months added to them.

Sixteen times the Sun had visited the sign of Aries

When the outstanding King Baldwin died.

Eighteen times twelve months having been completed,

You have the years in which the king ruled his country most nobly.

# HERE BEGINS THE THIRD BOOK, ON THE DEEDS OF BALDWIN II.

## CHAPTER I. That Baldwin II Was Consecrated King on Easter Day.

[Col. 0903A–B] Therefore, after King Baldwin’s death, the people of Jerusalem immediately took counsel, lest, being thought to lack a king, they should be considered weaker. They created as their king Baldwin, count of Edessa and a kinsman of the deceased king. He had happened by chance to come to Jerusalem after crossing the Euphrates River, intending to speak with his predecessor. Chosen by common agreement, he was consecrated on Easter Day.

## CHAPTER II. On the Babylonian Army Gathered.

In that same year, when summer had arrived, the Babylonians gathered a very large army, estimated at fifteen thousand cavalry and twenty thousand infantry, intending to destroy the Christianity of Jerusalem. When they had reached Ascalon, the king of the Damascenes, Tuldequinus, advanced with his people to assist them, having crossed the Jordan. Moreover, a considerable fleet came by sea as far as that place, likewise intending to cause harm. From there, both warships and ships laden with merchandise approached Tyre.

Those who had come by land remained before Ascalon, awaiting battle. Then King Baldwin, intending to fight the hostile army, hastened forward with the Antiochenes and Tripolitans, whom he had ordered by messengers to come to this contest. After passing through the former Philistine city of Azotus, he arranged for the tents to be unloaded from the pack animals and pitched not far from the Babylonians, so that each army could see the other every day.

But because each side greatly feared attacking the other, and preferred to live rather than die, they cunningly prolonged the delay for nearly three months under this pretext. At last, wearied by it, the Saracens refused to fight, and the Antiochenes returned to their own country, leaving three hundred of their soldiers with the king. These were to strengthen him for battle if necessary, should the Egyptians attempt to renew the conflict.

## CHAPTER III. On the Battle and Slaughter of the Antiochenes Who Fought against the Turks.

In the year 1119 from the Lord’s Incarnation, Pope Gelasius, Paschal’s successor, died on the fourth day before the Kalends of February and was buried at Cluny. After him Calixtus was appointed, he having been archbishop of the city of Vienne.

We would find the history tedious if we wished to recount everything that happened miserably in the Antiochene region that year: how Roger, prince of Antioch, went out with his nobles and people to fight the Turks and fell slain near the town of Artah, where seven thousand Antiochenes were killed, while not even twenty Turks were killed.

Nor is it surprising that God permitted them to be confounded, since, although they abounded exceedingly in riches of many kinds, they neither feared God nor respected man in sinning. For the prince himself, besides his wife, shamelessly committed adultery with several others. He disinherited his lord, the son of Bohemond, who was staying in Apulia with his mother, and both he and his nobles, by their proud and luxurious way of life, committed many other offenses. To them this Davidic verse is appropriate: “Their iniquity came forth as from fatness” (Ps. 72:7). For scarcely any restraint was maintained amid their overflowing pleasures.

## CHAPTER IV. That King Baldwin, Taking the Lord’s Cross, Hastened to Give Aid.

[Col. 0904C] After this slaughter of the Antiochenes there followed a second and considerable victory, which, by God’s favor, turned out wonderfully for the people of Jerusalem. When the aforementioned Roger had informed the king of Jerusalem by messengers that he should hasten to help him, because the Turks were attacking him with a large force, the king abandoned the undertaking for which he had gone with his men not far from the Jordan to fight the Damascenes. Taking the patriarch with him and the Lord’s cross, and having violently driven them from their positions in the fields, he immediately turned back to assist the Antiochenes. He brought with him the bishop of Caesarea, who afterward carried the Lord’s cross excellently in battle against the enemies.

The king also took the count of Tripoli with him, and together they had two hundred and fifty soldiers. When they reached Antioch, the king sent an embassy to the Edessenes, ordering them to hasten by a rapid journey to the battle they were striving to wage against the Turks. When these men had been joined to the king and the Antiochenes who had fled from the first battle or escaped death by some chance, battle was joined near a town called Sardanium, twenty-four miles from Antioch. Our soldiers numbered seven hundred, while the Turks numbered twenty thousand. Their chief was called Gazi.

I do not think the following should be omitted. A certain Turk, noticing that one of our soldiers knew the Persian language, addressed him, saying:

“I speak to you, Frank: Why do you despise us? Why do you labor in vain? You will certainly not prevail against us in any way; for you are few, while we are many. Indeed, your God has abandoned you, seeing that you no longer keep your law as you used to, nor preserve faith or truth among yourselves. We know this, we have learned this, we have observed this. Tomorrow, without doubt, we shall defeat and overcome you.”

O what disgrace for Christians, when faithless men reproached us concerning faith! Therefore we ought to blush exceedingly, repent by weeping over our sins, and amend our ways.

## CHAPTER V. On the Battle and Victory Obtained through the Most Holy Cross, and on Its Reception in Antioch.

Battle was therefore joined on the following day, as stated, and it was exceedingly severe. For a long time victory hung in the balance on both sides, until the Almighty compelled the Turks to flee and magnificently strengthened the Christians against them. Yet they scattered the attacking Turks in such swarms that, although the pursuit continued as far as Antioch, the Turks could not afterward regroup with their companions for battle.

Nevertheless, God dispersed the Turks: some fled homeward into Persia, while others entered the city of Aleppo in order to save themselves. The king of Jerusalem and the count of Tripoli, since they had been companions of the glorious cross and had brought it to battle as servants bringing their lady, fought honorably around it at all times without abandoning it, and stood bravely in the field of battle. The Almighty God, through the power of that same most holy and precious cross, powerfully rescued them from the hand of the wicked people and preserved them for another undertaking of His, to come at some future time.

When the king had guarded that field for two days and no Turk had returned there to fight, he took the Lord’s cross and proceeded to Antioch. The patriarch of Antioch came out to meet the most holy cross, as well as the king and the archbishop who carried it. They all gave thanks to God and offered the sweetest praises to Almighty God, who through the power of His glorious cross had granted victory to the Christians and had brought the cross itself safely back to Christendom. They wept from devotion and sang for joy; repeatedly they bowed before the venerable cross in adoration, and, rising again, gave thanks to the soldiers standing upright.

For two days the sun had offered its light to the Virgin’s star,

When the battle was fought in which the Parthians were thus overcome,

And then the moon’s tenth horns were shining brightly.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Reception of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem.

After the Franks had refreshed themselves with a brief rest in Antioch, they decided, as was fitting, to return to Jerusalem with the blessed cross of the Lord. Taking as many soldiers as were necessary, the king sent it back to Jerusalem. On the day when they celebrate the feast of its Exaltation, just as the emperor Heraclius brought it back victorious from Persia, they entered the holy city with it in rejoicing, and all who were present received it with unspeakable joy.

## CHAPTER VII. That the King Obtained the Principality of Antioch.

The king remained in Antioch because necessity demanded it: he was to distribute the lands of the dead nobles among the living under proper accounting, to unite the many widows he found there to husbands in a spirit of compassion, and to restore many other things requiring renewal.

For just as he had until then been solely king of Jerusalem, so, after the death of the Antiochene prince Roger, he became king of the Antiochenes as well, with a second kingdom added to his own. I therefore admonish the king, and beg him, to love God with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his strength; to submit himself wholly to Him as a faithful servant with thanksgiving; and to acknowledge himself the humble servant of Him who has found such a Lord to be his friend.

Which of his predecessors did He exalt as much as this man? He made the former possessor of one kingdom the possessor of two, which he acquired without fraud, without bloodshed, and without the troubles of lawsuits, but by peaceful divine arrangement. For God gave him a land stretching far and wide from Egypt to Mesopotamia. He has been generous toward him. Let him beware of being ungenerous toward Him who gives abundantly and does not reproach.

If he desires to be king, let him strive to rule rightly. After the king had completed many undertakings and returned from Antioch to Jerusalem, he was crowned at Bethlehem with his wife, wearing the royal diadem, on the day of the Lord’s Nativity.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Remission of Exactions.

In the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation, King Baldwin II released from every exaction all who wished to bring wheat, barley, or legumes through the gates of Jerusalem, so that Christians and Saracens alike might freely enter and leave without disturbance, and sell wherever and to whomever they wished. He also remitted the customary fee on the measure.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Turks Gathered Together and the King’s Expedition against Them.

When six months of that year had passed for us in Jerusalem, messengers came from Antioch, telling the king and all of us who were present that the Turks had crossed the Euphrates and entered Syria to harm Christendom, as they had formerly been accustomed to do.

Accordingly, after taking counsel as necessity required, the king humbly asked the patriarch and clergy to hand over to him the victorious cross of the Lord. He said that he and his men ought to be armed for battle by it, because he believed that the aforementioned Turks could not be expelled from the country they were already devastating without a serious battle; and because he did not trust in his own strength or in the numerous people he possessed, he would, with the cross, God strengthening and favoring him, prevail against many thousands. Otherwise, without it, neither he nor the others dared proceed to battle.

Thus a sufficiently fitting debate arose there between those going to war and those remaining in Jerusalem: whether the cross should be carried to Antioch for so great a necessity of Christendom, or whether the Church of Jerusalem should then be deprived of so great a treasure. We said:

“Alas, miserable ones! What shall we do if, with God permitting it, we lose the cross in battle, as the Israelites once lost the ark of the covenant?”

What more need I report? Necessity counseled, reason instructed; we did what we did not wish, and wished what we had not wished. After many pious tears had been shed for it and songs sung in its praise, the king, the patriarch, and the entire people escorted it barefoot outside the city. The king departed with it in tears, and the people returned to the holy city.

It was the month of June. They therefore went to Antioch, which the Turks were already hemming in so tightly that those living outside the circuit of the walls scarcely dared advance even one mile. But when they heard of the king’s arrival, they immediately withdrew and departed toward the city of Aleppo, where they could be safer. Three thousand Damascene soldiers then joined them.

When the king approached them boldly for battle, and many on both sides had been wounded or killed by the arrows shot back and forth, the Turks nevertheless refused to fight. After three days of this conflict, with no definite conclusion reached, our men returned to Antioch, while the greater part of the Turks went back home to Persia. The king then honorably sent the holy cross back to Jerusalem, while he himself remained in the Antiochene region to protect the land. On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November, we received the glorious cross of the Lord in Jerusalem with great joy.

## CHAPTER X. On the King’s Expedition against the Damascenes.

[Col. 0907C] In the year 1121 from the Lord’s Incarnation, the king gathered his people from Sidon to Joppa. On the third day before the Nones of July, he crossed the Jordan and approached the king of the Damascenes, who, together with his allied and assembled Arabs, was devastating the lands near Tiberias without anyone resisting him. When he perceived our king approaching him with his army, he immediately gathered his tents, avoided battle, and retreated like a fugitive into his own territory.

The king pursued him for two days, but since that people did not dare to fight him, he returned to a certain castle which Tuldequinus, king of Damascus, had caused to be built the previous year to our detriment. We estimate it to have been sixteen miles from the Jordan. The king besieged it, constrained it with siege engines, stormed it by force, and received its surrender.

He allowed its guards and defenders—forty Turks—to depart alive under an agreed condition, and afterward razed the town to the ground. The inhabitants of the region call this castle Jarras. It had been founded in ancient times beside a certain city, in a remarkably and gloriously strong position, and had been built there of great square stones.

When the king discovered that it could not be held without great difficulty, nor adequately supplied with people and provisions without hardship, he ordered it destroyed and everyone to return to his own place. This had once been a notable city in Arabia, called Gesara, joined to Mount Gilead and established in the tribe of Manasseh.

This year too ends, second in all respects,

Prosperous in peace and abundant in every crop.

## CHAPTER XI. On Another Expedition of the King against the Count of Tripoli, and Then Again against the Turks.

In the year 1122 of the Lord’s Incarnation, Odo by name, the first archbishop from the Latin people, was appointed to the Church of Tyre at Jerusalem. Then the king went to Ptolemais. After gathering his people, both infantry and cavalry, he set his army in motion and departed for Tripoli, carrying the Lord’s cross with him.
