He intended to avenge the injury and contempt inflicted by Pontius, the count of that region, who refused to obey him, as his father Bertrand had done.

But by God’s will, and through the commendation of the nobles present on both sides, they became friends with one another, the count agreeing to reason. When they had thus been reconciled, a certain archbishop arrived, sent there by the Antiochenes, urging the king to hasten to Antioch as quickly as possible in order to bring aid against the Turks. For they were already devastating that land, with no prince resisting them.

On hearing this, the king immediately hastened there, taking with him three hundred select soldiers and four hundred excellent hired men. The others returned either to Jerusalem or to their own lands. When the king reached the place where he had heard that the Turks had gathered—near a certain castle called Sardanaium, which they were already holding under siege—they withdrew from there, wishing to await the king. When he learned this, the king withdrew to Antioch.

But the Turks returned again to their undertaking. When the king learned this by report, he promptly rode toward them. Yet because that Parthian people, in battle array or military preparation, never customarily remain in the same formation—for now they show their faces, now turn their backs more quickly than one would expect, and unexpectedly flee in feigned retreat, then attack with a sudden return—they did not quickly prepare themselves for battle, but entirely avoided an engagement and departed as though defeated.

Blessed, therefore, be the banner of the most holy cross of the Lord, everywhere a present aid to all the orthodox, under whose protection and consolation the faithful, strengthened, allowed our Christians to return to their own without any loss! They were estimated at ten thousand soldiers, while ours numbered twelve hundred, not counting the mass of infantry.

When the king had returned to Tripoli together with the Lord’s cross, an affair arose, and he returned to Antioch with some of his men. Thus the Lord’s cross was carried to Jerusalem and, with great joy, was honorably restored to its place on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October.

It was the time when Libra destroys equal hours,

Equal in number and alike in duration.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Capture of the Count of Edessa.

Meanwhile Goscelin, count of Edessa, was captured, together with Galerannus, his kinsman, while no fewer than one hundred of their men were killed. A certain admiral named Balac contrived to seize them by both cunning and ambush.

This year too ends, as prosperous as the one before it,

In every kind of crop harvested from the fields.

A bushel of wheat is sold for one coin,

Or for forty [units], for whoever wishes to weigh a coin (numisma).

At that time neither Persia nor Babylonia was stirring up war.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Peace between the Pope and the Emperor.

In the year 1123 from the Lord’s birth, in the first indiction, Henry, king of Germany, was reconciled with Pope Calixtus. Thanks be to God, because kingdom and priesthood were joined together in affection.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Venetians Preparing to Set Out for Jerusalem.

In that same year the Venetians, moved to sail to Syria with a great fleet, intended, with God’s help, to enlarge and exalt Jerusalem and the region adjoining it for the benefit and advancement of Christendom.

The previous year they had departed from their own land and spent the winter on the island called Curpho, awaiting a suitable time for sailing. Their fleet consisted of 120 ships, not counting the smaller craft or boats. Some were beaked ships, some cargo ships, and others triremes. They were constructed in three different forms. In them there was no lack of timber of great height, so that, once engines had been skillfully constructed by craftsmen, they could ascend to and seize the high walls of cities.

## CHAPTER XV. At What Time They Set Out.

Therefore, when the routes became open to ships in spring, they did not delay in carrying out what they had long vowed to God. Having abundantly prepared their naval provisions, they collectively set fire to the huts in which they had spent the winter. With many trumpets sounding, they joyfully unfurled and raised their sails after invoking God’s help.

The ships, painted in various colors, were a great delight to behold in their excessive splendor. In them were fifteen thousand armed men, both Venetians and pilgrims who had joined them. They also brought three hundred horses.

Since the north wind was then blowing gently, they plowed the sea in excellent fashion and directed their course toward Modon and Rhodes. Because it was necessary for them to travel together rather than scattered, and because the winds sometimes alternated, they feared that, if they altered their course imprudently, some would quickly become separated from the others. Therefore, during the short days they sailed by day rather than by night, and, finding harbors frequently, they put in each day as necessity required, lest, suffering from a shortage of fresh water, both they and their horses be burdened by thirst.

## CHAPTER XVI. That King Baldwin Was Captured and a Certain Eustace Was Appointed in His Place.

At that time it happened that Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, was captured. For Balac, who had previously captured Goscelin and Galerannus, also seized him, unprepared and ill-provided. Nothing could be more pleasing to the pagans or more horrifying to Christians.

After this report had spread as far as us in Jerusalem, everyone came together in an assembly in the city of Ptolemais to take counsel concerning what ought to be done. They elected and appointed a certain Eustace, a good and honorable man, guardian and governor of the land. At that time he possessed Caesarea and Sidon.

The patriarch of Jerusalem, together with the nobles of that land, proposed and decreed that this arrangement should be maintained until they heard a definite outcome concerning the captured king. Thus, in the middle of May, when we had already heard that the Babylonians had reached Ascalon with a divided army—by land and by sea—and after an especially swift light galley had been prepared, they decided to send an embassy to the Venetian fleet, entreating and exhorting them to hasten their voyage and come to our aid in the undertaking they had begun.

## CHAPTER XVII. That the People of Joppa Were Again Besieged by the Babylonians and Greatly Afflicted.

The Babylonians attacked Joppa with their fleet and, leaping pompously from the ships amid the immense sound of bronze trumpets, surrounded the city with a siege. They immediately erected their engines and instruments, which they had brought on the larger ships, attacked the city from every side, and, by hurling stones, restrained its defenders, who were unable to withstand the force of the assault.

Their engines were indeed extremely powerful, and they hurled stones farther than an arrow’s flight. The Arab or Ethiopian foot soldiers whom they had brought with them launched a great assault against the citizens together with the body of soldiers. Some on both sides threw weapons, others stones or arrows.

Meanwhile, by repeated blows they very often struck down the enemy; for they fought bravely on their own behalf. The Ethiopians, holding shields in their hands, covered and protected themselves with them. The women, however, were always freely present to help the hard-pressed citizens. Some supplied stones, while others provided water for drinking.

When the Saracens had already damaged the wall somewhat over five days and had thrown down many of its battlements by demolishing them from above, they heard of the arrival of our men, who were approaching them. At the sound of the trumpet they abandoned the contest and carried their engines back piecemeal to the ships. If they had dared remain there longer, they would undoubtedly have captured the city. The men defending it were few. They had already dug around the wall in places, intending to penetrate it more quickly. Their fleet consisted of eighty ships.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Battle and the Victory through the Aid of the Holy Cross.

When our people learned through rumor-bearers that disaster was imminent, they gathered from every direction into a single body before a certain fortress which the inhabitants of the region call Chacho. From Tiberias, that is, and Ptolemais, Caesarea, and Jerusalem, with the Lord’s cross already brought to that assembly, they hastened as far as the city of Ramatha, which lies beside Duspolis, intending to fight the enemy.

We, however, who had remained in Jerusalem, did not cease meanwhile to pray for our brothers thus placed in tribulation [Col. 0911A], to distribute alms to the needy, and, both Latins and Greeks and Syrians, to conduct pious processions barefoot through all the churches of the holy city.

Our leaders, rising at first light from Ramatha, arranged our people in companies as was fitting. After the patriarch had given the people his blessing and absolution, battle was joined near the city of Azotus, formerly one of the five cities of the Philistines, but now called Ibenium. It has been reduced to a small village.

This battle did not last for a long time. For when they saw our men attacking them in excellent armor, those soldiers immediately, as though bewitched by some burden, were put to flight and took flight as their counsel. The infantry were cut down [Col. 0911B]. All their tents, together with articles of many kinds, remained in the field. They seized from them three exceedingly precious standards, which we call *Standarz*. They also took utensils of many kinds, mattresses, and cushions. Our men likewise brought back much booty in carts, together with its loads: namely, four hundred camels and five hundred asses.

Sixteen thousand of them came to battle, of whom six thousand were killed. Of our men, only a few were lost. Our people were estimated at eight thousand, but they were exceedingly brave and excellent, greatly eager for battle, relying on the love of God and wholly strengthened by confidence in him.

> Beneath the Twins, when Phoebus had by then risen twelve times,
>
> The accursed people rushed forth, subdued by the Lord’s power;
>
> Their bodies now across the Philistines’ fields
>
> [Col. 0911C] Become food for wolves and likewise nourishment for hyenas.

## CHAPTER XIX. The reception of the holy cross

When the battle had thus been overcome through God’s power, and had been accomplished, as was said, for his glory and for the exaltation of Christianity, the patriarch returned to Jerusalem with the Lord’s cross. It was received outside the David Gate with a glorious procession and honorably escorted as far as the basilica of the Lord’s sepulchre. Singing *Te Deum laudamus*, we all rendered praise to the Almighty for his benefits.

## CHAPTER XX. The arrival of the Venetians and their naval battle against the Saracens

[Col. 0911D] After three days, following this successful outcome, further favorable news arrived. When we heard that the Venetian fleet had put in at many ports in Palestine, we rejoiced. Rumor had indeed promised this for a long time.

When the Venetian duke who commanded this fleet had arrived at Ptolemais, he was immediately informed of what had taken place at Joppa, both on land and at sea, and of how the Babylonians, having completed their business as best they could, had already departed from there. If he wished to pursue them at speed, he could undoubtedly overtake them with God’s help.

He immediately sought the advice of the sailors and adopted a twofold course of navigation. He sent one part of his fleet, in which he himself was sailing, toward Joppa [Col. 0912A]. He sent the other part farther out to sea with the greatest prudence, so that the unsuspecting Saracens would think them pilgrims traveling to Jerusalem from the direction of Cyprus.

When the Saracens saw eighteen ships of the Venetian fleet approaching them, they began to celebrate as though profit had already been secured, and prepared to sail against the Venetians and boldly engage them in battle. Our men, however, pretending to be reluctant to undertake a real military engagement and cunningly awaiting the other, stronger and rearmost division of the fleet, in which the aforesaid duke was sailing, gradually held back. They neither intended to flee nor dared to fight them, so that the Saracens could see the rearmost fleet rising toward them under sail and oar.

Then the Venetians’ courage increased, and they rushed upon them indescribably [Col. 0912B]. They surrounded them on every side so that they could find nowhere to flee. The Saracens were then restrained in a marvelous manner, and neither ships nor sailors could escape anywhere. The Venetians boarded their ships and cut down everyone.

It scarcely deserves belief that, beyond what human hearing can accept, the benches of the ships were stained with the flowing blood of the slain. Thus ships laden with many riches were captured. When the bodies had been thrown from the ships, one could have seen the sea reddened all around for as much as four thousand paces.

Afterward, as they sailed beyond Ascalon to investigate whether anything useful could be found, they encountered ten other ships filled with various provisions. They contained great, straight timbers suitable for constructing siege engines. These ships too they plundered, together with very many supplies, gold and silver, and numerous coins; also pepper, cumin, and various kinds of spices. They burned several ships that had fled to land on the very shore, but brought even more of them intact to Ptolemais. Thus the Lord gladdened his servants and enriched them in many ways with numerous gifts.

## CHAPTER XXI. That the people of Jerusalem were not at all despised, although their king was captive

Oh, how good and glorious it is always for human beings to have God as their helper! Oh, how blessed is the people whose Lord is their God!

They were saying: “Let us go and utterly confound the Christian people, [Col. 0912D] and erase their memory from the earth. They have no king now; the members are without a head.”

They spoke truly, because they did not believe that we had God. We had lost Baldwin, but we had taken as our king the God of all. We called upon him in our need, and through him we triumphed wondrously.

Perhaps he was not a king whom we had lost by mere chance. But this one who recently conquered is not only king in Jerusalem, but also in every land. We ought truly to confess that we had a king in battle, since in all our affairs we placed him before everything else. For he is always at hand and present to all who call upon him in truth (Psalm 144:18).

He had seen us greatly afflicted in our humiliation [Col. 0913A], and, looking mercifully upon our lowliness, he delivered us. He fought for us; he brought our enemies to nothing. He has always been accustomed to conquer, and is never conquered. He overcomes and is not overcome. He does not deceive, nor is he deceived.

He is indeed a king, for he has acted rightly. How, then, can one be a king who is always conquered by vices? Surely one who is always regarded as a lawbreaker does not deserve to be called a king, because he neither keeps nor protects God’s law. And because he does not fear God, he will indeed fear his human enemy.

He is an adulterer, or perjurer, or sacrilegious; such a man loses the name of king, being deceitful and fraudulent. Who trusts in him? He is favorable to the wicked. How will God hear him? If he is a destroyer of churches, if an oppressor of the poor, then he does not rule but brings ruin.

Let us cling to the heavenly King [Col. 0913B], and place our hope in him, and we shall not be confounded forever.

## CHAPTER XXII. The death of Eustace and the succession of William

At this time Eustace, who had been chosen guardian of our land, died after such an illness, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July. They decided that William of Bures should succeed him; he then possessed Tiberias.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How King Baldwin escaped from his bonds

Then, in the middle of August, through the providence of heavenly mercy, King Baldwin escaped from prison and from the bonds of Balak, by which he had been held captive in a certain town of exceptionally strong position, excessively steep elevation, and difficult access. Goscelin, count of Edessa, was imprisoned there with him, together with several other captives.

The account of this event is quite long, but it is endowed with heavenly grace and richly adorned with miracles. For when they had long been confined and distressed in that fortress, relying on no assistance, they began to consider among themselves, by various plans and devices, whether they might in some way escape from it.

Accordingly, through faithful messengers, they did not cease to seek assistance wherever they had friends, and they diligently contrived every means with the Armenians living around them, so that, if they could at any time obtain help from their friends outside, the latter would not fail to assist them.

After this bond of trust had been confirmed on both sides through certain gifts and many promises, nearly fifty of our servants were sent there very cunningly [Col. 0913D] from the city of Edessa for this purpose. Carrying and selling goods as though they were extremely poor, they gradually made their way through the gates of the inner fortress when an opportunity arose.

While the master of the gatekeepers was carelessly playing chess beside the gate with one of our faithful men, our servants approached him most craftily and attentively, intending to complain to him of an injury done to them. Then, casting off all sluggishness and fear, they drew their knives from their sheaths and killed him as quickly as possible. Seizing the spears found there, they did not hesitate to strike and kill with courage.

A great outcry was immediately raised, and everyone inside and outside was thrown into confusion. But those who hurried to the disturbance were killed even more quickly. There were nearly a hundred Turks [Col. 0914A]. At once the king and the others were brought out of prison.

Some were still in shackles when they were already climbing the steps to the top of the wall. When the banner of the Christians was raised on the summit of the citadel, the truth of what had happened became evident.

Balak’s wife was in the same fortress; she was dearer to him than all the others he had. But when the fortress was immediately surrounded on every side by Turks, entry and exit were forbidden to those inside and outside. The gates too were closed and secured with bars.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How the count of Edessa also escaped from prison

I do not think that this should be left unmentioned: a certain misfortune was revealed to Balak in a vision. He saw—for he later recounted it himself—that Goscelin was tearing out his eyes [Col. 0914B]. When he immediately disclosed this to the priests, he asked them for an interpretation of the dream.

“Truly,” they said, “this will happen to you, or something equivalent to it, if you fall into his hands.”

When he heard this, he sent a very swift message ordering Goscelin to be killed, lest Goscelin be able to kill him, just as they had foretold. But before the executioners reached him, thanks be to God, Goscelin had already escaped from such captivity in the manner described.

The king and all his companions therefore, using wise and common counsel so that they might be saved by whatever means possible, considered the time most suitable for this. The lord Goscelin entrusted his life to the Creator of all and, with three servants, both fearful and bold, escaped from the fortress through the midst of the enemy beneath the shining moon, placing himself in peril of death.

[Col. 0914C] Immediately he sent one of them back to the king, carrying his ring, to indicate in this way that he had extricated himself from the besieging enemy. For they had decided that this was how they would communicate with one another.

Afterward, fleeing and hiding, traveling more by night than by day, with his shoes torn and almost barefoot, he reached the river Euphrates. Since there was no boat, he did not delay doing what fear urged him to do. What more is there to say? He inflated with wind two skins that he had brought with him, placed himself upon them, and thus launched himself into the river.

His companions, who knew that he could not swim, supported him as best they could, and, with the Lord guiding them, brought him safely to the shore. Having been greatly exhausted by this unusual journey, hungry and thirsty, he breathed anxiously, and there was no one to extend a merciful hand to him.

At last, touched by sleep beneath a certain walnut tree found there [Col. 0914D], he surrendered his limbs, wearied by the journey, to rest. He shaded himself with brambles and thickets so that he would not be recognized if seen.

Meanwhile he ordered one of his servants to look for and entreat some native who might either give him bread or sell it to him at any price. For he was severely tormented by hunger.

That servant found a certain Armenian peasant nearby in the fields, addressed him prudently, and brought him to his master. The peasant had figs and grapes with him, which was precisely what hunger desired.

When he approached and recognized Count Goscelin, he fell at his feet, saying, “Greetings, Goscelin!”

Hearing what he did not wish to hear, Goscelin replied in fear: “I am not the man you name, but may God help him wherever he is” [Col. 0915A].

The peasant said: “Please do not conceal your identity, for I recognize you very well beyond any doubt. But reveal to me what has happened to you in these parts and how it happened. I tell you, do not be afraid.”

The count replied again: “Have mercy on me, whoever you are, and I beg you not to make my misery known to my enemies. Instead, lead me to a place of safety, so that you may earn one coin as your reward.

“For, with God’s favor, I have escaped from Balak’s captivity and am fleeing from the fortress called Cartapeta, which lies in Mesopotamia on this side of the Euphrates. You will do a good deed if you help me in this necessity, so that I do not again fall into Balak’s hands and perish miserably.

“If you are willing to come with me as far as my fortress of Turbessel, you will fare well all the days of your life. Tell me, therefore, what and how great your property is in these parts, so that, if you wish, I may carefully repay you with something greater in return” [Col. 0915B].

The peasant answered: “I seek nothing from you, but I will lead you safely wherever you wish to go. Long ago, as I remember, you kindly made me eat bread before you. Therefore I am ready to repay you in kind.

“I have a wife, one little daughter, one she-ass, two brothers, and two oxen. I entrust myself to you, because you are a very wise and prudent man. Now I will go with you, together with all that is mine. I also have one pig. I will cook it and bring it here for you.”

“No, brother,” he said, “for you are not accustomed to eating one pig at a single meal, and it is not advisable for you to arouse suspicion among your neighbors.”

Then the peasant went away and [Col. 0915C] returned with all his possessions, just as he had decided.

The count therefore mounted the peasant’s she-ass. He who had once been accustomed to ride an excellent mule now carried before him a child—a female child, not a male. She whom he had not been permitted to beget, he was permitted to carry as though he were her parent. Not so that he might have her close to him as offspring, but so that she might show to those who did not know a sure appearance of parentage.

But when the infant began to trouble the count continually by crying and shouting, and he could not calm her in any way, and there was no nurse to suckle her or soothe her with lullabies, he fearfully considered abandoning the company lest it perhaps harm him, and traveling separately in greater safety.

But when he noticed that this displeased the peasant, he did not wish to upset him and persevered in the undertaking he had begun.

When he reached Turbessel, the reception accorded such guests was exceedingly joyful [Col. 0915D]. His wife rejoiced, and the household exulted. Our conscience does not doubt how greatly everyone celebrated with joy, how many tears were shed from gladness, and how many sighs poured forth.

The peasant was immediately rewarded in a manner worthy of his humility. For one yoke of oxen he at once received two.

But because it was not fitting to linger there long, the count immediately went to Antioch and then to Jerusalem. There, after rendering the due thanks to God, he offered the two shackles he had brought with him. He devoutly presented them on Mount Calvary, as a memorial of his captivity and as a sign of the glory of his deliverance. One pair was iron, the other silver.

After three days he left Jerusalem, following the Lord’s cross [Col. 0916A], which had already been brought as far as Tripoli. For the Jerusalem army intended to go with it as far as the fortress of Cartapeta, Balak’s stronghold, where the king and many others were being held—not in prison, but within the fortress’s defenses.

Blessed, then, be the universal Lord, who so regulates his will and power that, whenever he wishes, he casts down the powerful from on high and raises the poor from the dust!

In the morning King Baldwin commanded; in the evening the servant served. Goscelin likewise experienced the same reversal.

It is plainly evident that in this world nothing is certain, nothing stable, and nothing long pleasing. Therefore it is not good to cling to earthly things, but to keep the heart always directed toward God; let us not trust in things that pass away, nor become estranged from eternal things.

[Col. 0916B]

> Now completing, as I estimate, my thirteenth five-year span,
>
> I have not seen a king punished in prison as this one was.
>
> If this signifies anything that I do not know, God knows it.

## CHAPTER XXV. The expedition of the people of Jerusalem, and the second capture of King Baldwin

As the people of Jerusalem proceeded toward the place they had determined to reach, the people of Tripoli and Antioch gathered to them at Antioch. But when they reached Turbessel, they were informed that the king had again been captured and that the town in which he was imprisoned was called Carras.

When they heard this, their plan was changed, and an immediate return was ordered. Wishing to accomplish something useful for themselves, at the signal of the trumpeter they turned aside toward the city of Calipht. They devastated and scattered everything [Col. 0916C] they found inside, after first driving back fiercely within the walls all who had come out against them.

But after remaining there for four days and accomplishing nothing more, they decided to return to their own lands, already troubled by a shortage of provisions. Count Goscelin, however, remained at that time in the territory of Antioch.

When they had returned as far as Ptolemais, they crossed the Jordan by a sudden march before the neighboring Saracens noticed it. After traversing that region adjoining Mount Gilead and Arabia, and carrying off flocks belonging to Saracens of both sexes, as well as many beasts, they returned to nearby Tiberias with an immense booty of camels and sheep, children and adolescents.

Then, distributing the spoils among themselves according to custom, they gathered from every direction in Jerusalem [Col. 0916D] and restored the Lord’s cross to its proper place.

But now it is fitting to return to what I had passed over briefly.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How Balak besieged the king and sent him into captivity again

When Balak heard what had happened at Cartapeta and how Count Goscelin had escaped from captivity, he did not delay going there as quickly as he could.

He then addressed the king graciously and demanded that he surrender his fortress to him on the condition that, after chosen hostages had been given, Balak would permit him to depart in peace and would have him faithfully escorted as far as Edessa or Antioch. Otherwise, he said, fortune would turn disastrously against either one or both of them [Col. 0917A].

But when the king refused to agree to this, Balak, enraged with a savage spirit, threatened to seize both the king and the fortress by force and undoubtedly take vengeance upon his enemies.

He immediately ordered the rock on which the fortress stood to be undermined. The works were suspended over a pile of stakes, and wood was brought in and set on fire. When the supports had been burned, the chamber suddenly collapsed, and a certain tower near the blaze fell with a great crash.

At first, together with the dust, smoke rose as the collapse enclosed the fire. But afterward the material that had been compressed began to appear more brightly through the flames. The king, who had suffered this assault with difficulty, was seized by astonishment at what had suddenly occurred, and the hope that had grown cold in him became empty; such a disaster terrified him.

Thus, with all his strength and understanding lost [Col. 0917B], the king and his companions were delivered as suppliants to Balak’s mercy, expecting nothing except punishment according to their deserts.

Nevertheless, he spared the king’s life, as well as that of one of his nephews and of Gualeranus. But the Armenians who had assisted the king against Balak he treated variously: some he hanged, others he flayed, and some he cut in half with a sword.

He expelled the king and three of his companions from the fortress and had them brought to the city of Carras.

Because these events took place far from us, we could scarcely learn the truth of what had happened. Nevertheless, I committed to writing what was reported to me, as accurately as I could.

[Col. 0917C]

> Thus the year, its limbs thirsty for rains, comes to an end.
>
> Therefore the people of Jerusalem have often complained with murmuring.
>
> The deeds now run through four times ten years,
>
> Since the journey began, known everywhere to pilgrims.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The preparations made for the siege of Tyre

In the year 1124 from the birth of the Lord Jesus, after we had celebrated the Nativity of the Savior both in Bethlehem and in Jerusalem, as was fitting—and the Venetian duke with his men had devoutly taken part in that celebration—it was confirmed by common and willing agreement, under oath, that after Epiphany we would undertake the siege of Tyre or Ascalon.

But because poverty then held all of us back, much money was collected from each person to distribute for military service and hired retainers. For such a great undertaking could not be carried out by gifts alone. Therefore it was necessary for us to gather even the more precious ornaments of the Church of Jerusalem [Col. 0917D] and pledge them to creditors in exchange for coin.

Thus, as had been sworn and at the place designated, everyone gathered from every direction.

> When the water-pourer’s vessel is repaired three times by the strong fire,
>
> The people of Jerusalem commonly go forth against the enemy.
>
> This occurs also on the first day of the week, when the moon is likewise new.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How Tyre was besieged by the patriarch and the Venetians

Accordingly, having departed from Acre, they decided to go together with the Venetians to Tyre and besiege it. The patriarch with his subjects, and the duke with his sailors and ships, surrounded the city of Tyre and began the siege on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, when the sun was entering the twin Fishes.

When the Ascalonites heard this, they—who through their customary insolence could never be tamed—did not delay doing us as much harm as they could [Col. 0918A].

One day, dividing their army into three parts, they brought the larger part of their companies to Jerusalem. Following their example, they brutally killed eight men outside the city who were pruning vines.

When their arrival was discovered, a trumpet immediately sounded above David’s citadel, signaling this to us. Our Franks and Syrians advanced against them and courageously resisted them.

After they had wearied one another for three hours of the day, facing each other, and after very many had been wounded, they departed in sorrow. Our men gradually pursued them. But because we lacked soldiers and feared an ambush, we did not dare to follow them for long.

At last, however, seventeen of their heads were cut off [Col. 0918B] and retained, together with an equal number of horses. Three horsemen were taken alive; the others were killed.

If we had had soldiers, few of them would have escaped. Our cavalry was away with the army.

Then God was praised, to whom praise is always due.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Tyre and its nobility

Meanwhile the Tyrians were confined ever more tightly within their city, neither seeking peace nor yielding to capture. Rich in wealth and protected by the sea, they had always been accustomed to be ungrateful.

This city is richer and nobler than all the cities in the land of promise, except Hazor, which Jabin, king of the Canaanites, possessed in ancient times and which Joshua later destroyed together with many others. As we read, it boasted fortification with nine hundred towers [Col. 0918C] (Judges 4:2–3).

Josephus, however, says that it had three thousand scythed chariots. It possessed three hundred thousand armed men and ten thousand horsemen; Sisera was commander of this force.

These cities, Tyre and Hazor, were established in the land of the Phoenicians. The former was strongly fortified with merchants and commerce; the latter was populous with an innumerable multitude. The former was situated on the seashore; the latter was placed in the plains.

When Gideon was avenging Israel, Tyre had been founded by the Phoenicians shortly before the time of Hercules. It is a city in the land of the Phoenicians.

This is the city to which Isaiah speaks, threatening it because of its pride (Isaiah 23), and in which the finest purple is dyed. Hence the expression “noble Tyrian purple.”

[Col. 0918D] Tyre is interpreted as “distress,” which in Hebrew is called *Seor*. King Shalmaneser of the Assyrians, waging war against Syria and Phoenicia, conquered it when Eliseus was ruling there. For the Tyrians did not wish to be subject to the Assyrian king.

This continued for five years. Menander writes about it, and Josephus at greater length.

At that time the Tyrians crossed the sea under the leadership of Dido, daughter of Belus, and founded Carthage in Africa. Orosius the historian describes its site as enclosed by thirty thousand paces of wall and almost entirely surrounded by sea, except for the entrance, which extended for three thousand paces.

That place had a wall thirty feet wide, built of squared stone to a height of forty cubits. The citadel, called Bisse [in the edition, [Col. 0919A] Birse], occupied a little more than two thousand paces. Seven hundred years after its foundation, when every stone had been removed, it was destroyed.

It is found to have been founded by Helyssa seventy-two years before the foundation of the city of Rome. Publius Scipio, consul in the preceding year, undertook its destruction by the final allotment; it burned miserably for seventeen continuous days.

## CHAPTER XXX. The ancient capture of Tyre and those by whom it was formerly conquered

The Tyre mentioned above languished in desolation for seventy years, according to Isaiah. When the Cetheans departed from it, King Eliseus restored them. King Shalmaneser of the Assyrians then rose against them again.

[Col. 0919B] At that time the city of Sidon, Arce, ancient Tyre, and many other cities withdrew from Tyre. They surrendered themselves to the king of the Assyrians.

Because the Tyrians did not submit, he again set out against them. The Phoenicians supplied him with seventy ships and eight hundred rowers. The Tyrians sailed against them in twelve ships, scattered the enemy vessels, and captured five hundred men.

As a result, the honor of the Tyrians increased greatly. When the Assyrian king returned, he placed guards along the river and surrounded the city by diverting the water, so that they might prevent the Tyrians from drawing drinking water.

When this had continued for five years, they endured it by drinking water from wells they had dug.

These events concerning Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, were therefore written in the archives of Tyre. He was the one who besieged Samaria and captured it in the sixth year of King Hezekiah, and transferred Israel to Assyria [Col. 0919C].

Before him came Pul, king of the Assyrians; after him came Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, who captured Kedesh and Hazor in Naphtali, as well as the region near Paneas, Janoah, Gilead, and all Galilee, and transferred them to Assyria.

Sargon, king of the Assyrians, also came. He sent Tartan to fight against Azotus and captured it.

Thus, because of the sins of the people, the land of promise was devastated and led into captivity, first to the Assyrians and afterward to the Chaldeans.

For Nebuchadnezzar, both Chaldean and Babylonian king, besieged and captured Jerusalem. Therefore King Zedekiah, while fleeing, was captured near Jericho and brought to the king of Babylon in the region called Riblah, in the land of Hamath.

Jerome says that Hamath is Antioch the Great, while the lesser one is [Col. 0919D] Epiphania. There Nebuchadnezzar had Zedekiah’s eyes torn out and his sons slaughtered before him.

Then Nebuzaradan, commander of his army, came and burned the house of the Lord and the king’s house, and destroyed the entire surrounding wall.

After an interval of time Alexander came, besieged Tyre, and captured it, after first subduing Damascus and then Sidon. Gaza too was captured by him over a period of two months. After spending seven months near Tyre, he hurried to the city of Jerusalem.

Received with honor, he treated the high priest named Jaddus with many honors. Jaddus wore a *thydar* upon his head, a golden hyacinth-colored stole, and above it a golden plate on which the name of God was written. Alexander approached him alone and reverently adored him.

Having arranged matters in Jerusalem, he turned his army toward the remaining cities [Col. 0920A].

After many years, because the sins of the Jews demanded it, Antiochus Epiphanes attacked their law and severely oppressed the Maccabees.

After him came Pompey, who disastrously laid Jerusalem waste. Finally Vespasian came with his son Titus, and they utterly destroyed it.

Thus, through varying turns of events down to our own time, both the holy city and the land subject to it have been violently afflicted.

Palestine was devastated most of the time, and at other times Phoenicia, which received its name from Phoenix, the brother of Cadmus. Then Samaria and Galilee were devastated, although Galilee is distinguished by a twofold division. One is called Upper Galilee, the other Lower Galilee; Phoenicia and Syria surround them on both sides [Col. 0920B].

The region beyond the Jordan extends in length from Macherus to Pella, and in width from Philadelphia to the Jordan. Pella is its northern boundary, the Jordan its western; to the south it is bounded by the region of Moab, and to the east by Arabia and Philadelphia, together with Gerasa.

The Samaritan region lies between Judea and Galilee.

The width of Judea extends from the Jordan to Joppa. Its central city is Jerusalem, as though it were the navel of that land.

Lower Galilee, extending from Tiberias to Zebulon and as far as Ptolemais, and including Mount Carmel of the Tyrians, contains Nazareth, the very strong city of Sepphoris [Col. 0920C], Mount Tabor, Cana, and many other places.

It is enclosed by Lebanon and by the sources of the Jordan, where Paneas is now situated—also called Dan, or Caesarea Philippi. Around it lie the region of Trachonitis [in the edition, *Traconitïdis*] and Nabatea.

To the south are Samaria and Scythopolis, that is, Bethshan.

The city of Beersheba marks the boundary of Judea. Within it are Timnah and Lydda, Joppa and Jamnia, Tekoa and Hebron, Eshtaol and Zorah, and many other places.

Now I return to the path along which I have long wandered through various tracks.

## CHAPTER XXXI. The battle and victory of the Antiochenes, and the death of Balak

While we were laboring around Tyre to prepare siege engines, Balak nevertheless did not cease to raise his horn against us with his associates [Col. 0920D].

Having gone out from the city of Calipht, commonly called Halab, at the beginning of May, he proceeded to Hierapolis with five thousand horsemen and seven thousand infantry. The populace calls that city Membij.

When its possessor refused to surrender it to him, Balak summoned him outside the city and then wickedly beheaded him.

Balak immediately besieged the city. Goscelin, who was then staying at Antioch, learned of this, and, after sending a message there, hastened to go with the Antiochenes.

Although the Christian people were very few, Goscelin was not afraid to attack the multitude of unbelievers. Without much delay, a fierce battle was joined.

With God’s support, after the Turks had been thrown into confusion three times and had three times boldly regrouped for battle, Balak was mortally wounded in the crush. As best he could, he turned aside from the fighting, already dying [Col. 0921A].

When his men immediately discovered this, those who could flee did not delay. Many were indeed able to flee, but by no means did they escape. It is reported that three thousand of them, who were horsemen, were killed. The number of infantry is unknown.

Of our men, thirty soldiers fell there, and about sixty of the foot retainers.

Wishing to know the truth—whether Balak was dead or still alive to some extent—Goscelin carefully investigated the matter with those who were searching for him among the slain. He was recognized by those who knew him through the identifying marks of his armor.

The man who had cut off Balak’s head brought it joyfully to Goscelin and received from him the coins Goscelin had promised to give him [Col. 0921B].

Goscelin immediately had the head carried to Antioch to proclaim what had happened. The man who carried it in his pack as far as Tyre and then Jerusalem himself recounted and explained all this to us. He had also been present in the aforementioned battle among the combatants and had been Goscelin’s armiger.

Because he brought the most desired news to our army stationed before Tyre, he was advanced from armiger to knight after receiving arms from his master. The count of Tripoli raised him to this rank.

We all praised and blessed the Lord, because that most savage dragon, who had long afflicted and overwhelmed Christianity, had been suffocated.

[Col. 0921C]

> The sun had nineteen times passed through Taurus with its light,
>
> When Balak fell, or fortune deceived him.

Behold, the interpretation of the dream mentioned above has thus been revealed—the dream which Balak himself had spoken of, as though prophesying, at the time when Goscelin miraculously escaped from captivity. For he had seen in a vision that Goscelin was tearing out his eyes.

He truly tore them out completely, since he entirely removed from him both head and limbs.

> He neither sees nor hears, neither speaks, nor sits nor walks;
>
> He has no place in heaven, nor on earth, nor in water.

## CHAPTER XXXII. The events that took place during the siege of Tyre
On a certain day, while those who were conducting the siege were resting securely, the opportunity having been carefully observed, the Tyrians—both Turks [Col. 0921D] and Saracens—came out of the city after opening the gates. Rushing toward our engine, which was stronger than the others, they charged together with drawn swords. Before our men could take up their arms, they drove out by wounding those whom they found guarding the engine. They set it on fire—the engine by which the towers had previously been battered and violently pierced with stones hurled against them. In this assault we lost thirty men.

They, however, encountered a double loss. For the citizens repeatedly inflicted severe injury and wounds upon our men from the threats of the wall, with arrows, stones, and darts. Meanwhile our Venetians, taking advantage of a sufficiently favorable opportunity, entered their *carabus*—there were only five of them—and plundered a small house which they found beside [Col. 0922A] the city wall, cutting off two heads there. Then, without delay, they returned outside rejoicing with their little booty. This happened on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July [21 June]. But it amounted to less, since shortly beforehand the Tyrians had stolen a *liburna* by night and dragged it into the city through the harbor. In such struggles, indeed, such things often happen.

Here one falls, here another rises; one weeps, while the other rejoices.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Very Troublesome Disturbances Caused by the People of Ascalon

The people of Ascalon, knowing the smallness of our forces, did not hesitate to harass us wherever they thought they could weaken us most or inflict the greatest damage. For near Jerusalem they ravaged and burned a certain village called Birr, and, carrying away all the little goods found there, departed with some people dead and many more wounded. The women and children, however, had taken refuge in a certain tower built there in our time, and so were saved.

Thus, ranging throughout the land, they plundered, killed, and captured; they did whatever evil they could, and there was no one to resist them. We were all intent upon the siege, awaiting heavenly mercy, so that with God as our maker and helper we might be able to complete our labor. For it was intolerable both to keep vigil by night and to labor by day.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Surrender of the City of Tyre

When the king of Damascus saw that his Turks and Saracens, [Col. 0922C] who were enclosed within the city, could in no way escape from our hands, he preferred to ransom them alive, though with some disgrace, rather than mourn them dead. Therefore, through negotiators and with shrewd deliberation, he sought a way to receive his men outside with all their possessions and leave the city emptied to us.

After we had long struggled over this matter on both sides, hostages having been given mutually, they came out of the city, and the Christians entered peacefully. Any Saracens who wished to remain in the city stayed in peace under an agreed arrangement.

Phoebus had risen sixteen times beneath Cancer,

when Tyre was captured, surrendered, and overcome;

for this happened on the Nones of July [7 July]. [Col. 0922D]

We must neither cease nor delay in seeking our Lord as our helper in tribulations, and in imploring him, pious and kind, so that when we knock he may grant us a gracious hearing. We had certainly done this at Jerusalem, visiting the churches very frequently, pouring out tears, distributing alms, and afflicting our bodies with fasts. God, I believe, looking down from above, did not leave this without a blessing, but heard our supplication.

While we were waiting with attentive ears to learn some little report, behold, three envoys came to us with the greatest haste, bringing letters from our patriarch and announcing that the city had been captured. When this was heard, a most joyful cry [Col. 0923A] arose, and *Te Deum laudamus* was immediately sung in ringing voices. Bells were rung, a procession was led to God, banners were raised on the walls and towers, many-colored decorations were extended through every street, thanksgivings were proclaimed, the messengers were suitably rewarded according to their merits, small and great alike rejoiced, and the girls delighted in songs and dances.

Rightly does the mother Jerusalem rejoice over Tyre, her daughter, who henceforth sits crowned at her right hand. Babylon also mourns, deprived of her consolation—that city whose support had until recently sustained her and whose fleet she received every year as hostile to us.

Although her pomp is diminished, divine grace is increased. For the city which among the pagans had a chief priest, or high priest, according to the institution of the Fathers shall have a primate or patriarch under Christian law. Where there were high priests, archbishops have been instituted under the law of the Christians, presiding over individual provinces. Where there was a metropolis, which is interpreted as “mother city,” there were metropolitans, who presided over three or four cities within a province on behalf of the mother and greater city. Where smaller cities had only priests or counts, bishops were appointed.

Moreover, the tribunes of the people may reasonably be understood as presbyters, or the remaining clergy of the lower order. Thus every worldly authority differs from the others by these ranks of dignity: first comes the Augustus, or emperor; then the Caesars; then kings, dukes, and counts. So says Pope Clement, Anacletus, Anicius, and many others. Let us therefore give praise to the most high God, because not by human strength but by his own gracious will he restored Tyre to us without bloodshed—a renowned city, a most powerful city, and one exceedingly difficult to capture unless God should extend his right hand.

In this matter the Antiochenes indeed failed, since they gave us no assistance and were unwilling to share in this labor. But blessed be Pontius of Tripoli, because he was our most faithful helper. May God reconcile the Church of Antioch with the Church of Jerusalem, which disagree over Tyre, the third. The former says that Tyre was subject to it in the time of the Greeks. The latter says that it has been fortified by privileges from the Roman [Col. 0923D] pontiff.

For at the Council of Auvergne, so authoritative and renowned, it was established by unanimous agreement that any city which could be wrested from the yoke of the pagans after crossing the great sea should be held permanently without contradiction. This was also repeated and granted by all at the Council of Antioch, under the presidency of Bishop Podiensis. At Jerusalem likewise Duke Godfrey and Lord Bohemond received their territory from Patriarch Daibertus for the love of God. Pope Paschal repeatedly confirmed this with his privileges and transmitted them to the Church of Jerusalem, by which authority of the Roman Church it shall be fortified with perpetual right. These privileges contain the following inscription:

## CHAPTER XXXV. Pope Paschal’s Privilege

“Paschal, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend brother Gibelin, patriarch of Jerusalem, and to his successors to be canonically promoted.

“According to the changes of times, the kingdoms of the earth are also transferred. Therefore it is expedient that the boundaries of ecclesiastical parishes likewise be changed and transferred in many provinces. The boundaries of the Churches of Asia had been distributed according to ancient definitions. The incursion of peoples of different and diverse faiths confused these distributions. But thanks be to God, because in our times the cities of Antioch and Jerusalem, together with their suburbs and the neighboring provinces, have been brought under the authority of Christian princes.

“Therefore it is necessary for us to apply our hand to this divine change and transfer, and to arrange according to the time what must be arranged, so that we may grant to the Church of Jerusalem those cities and provinces which through the prudence of the glorious King Baldwin and through the blood of the armies following him have been acquired by the grace of God.

“By the page of this present decree, dearest brother and fellow bishop Gibelin, we decree that you and your successors, and through you the patriarchal metropolitan Church of holy Jerusalem, shall govern and administer by right all the cities and provinces which divine grace has already restored, or will in the future deign to restore, under the rule of the aforesaid king.

“For it is fitting that the Church of the Lord’s Sepulchre should receive an honor proportionate to the desires of the faithful soldiers and, freed from the yoke of the Turks and Saracens, should be exalted more abundantly in Christian hands.”

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the Portions Established Around Tyre

When the necessary business at Tyre had been completed, and everything had been arranged by a threefold division, with an appropriate equalization of the two portions assigned to the royal dignity and the third portion, by hereditary right, separately granted to the Venetians both in the city and in the harbor, everyone returned to his own place.

When the patriarch of Jerusalem returned to Jerusalem with the people of Jerusalem, clergy and people received the most holy cross of the Lord with fitting veneration.

[Col. 0923] Up to this point is the first edition of Bongars. What follows has been added from a manuscript codex.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the Sign That Then Appeared

[Col. 0923D]

Then the sun appeared to us for nearly an hour with a many-colored brilliance, changed into a new or perhaps flashing form, and transformed into the appearance of the moon, as though by a certain twofold eclipse. This occurred on the third day before the Ides of August [11 August], when the ninth hour of the day was already passing.

Therefore do not marvel when you see signs in the heavens, because God works no less upon the earth. For just as in heavenly things, so also in earthly things, he transforms and orders whatever he wishes, and in whatever manner he wishes. If the things he has done are marvelous, he is more marvelous still because he did them.

Consider and reflect in your mind how in our time God has turned the West into the East. For we who were westerners have now become easterners. One who was Roman or Frank has become, in this land, a Galilean or Palestinian. One who was from Rheims or Chartres is now made Tyrian or Antiochene. We have already forgotten the places of our birth; for many of us they are now either unknown or even unheard of.

One man now possesses his own houses and families, as though by hereditary and paternal right. Another has taken a wife—not a countrywoman, but a Syrian or Armenian, and sometimes a Saracen woman who has received the grace of baptism. Someone has with him both a father-in-law and a daughter-in-law, or a son-in-law, or a stepchild, or even a stepfather. Nor is there lacking a grandson or great-grandson. One man enjoys vineyards, another cultivated fields.

People of different languages make use alternately of one another’s speech and service. A different language has now become common and familiar to both nations, and faith joins together those whose ancestry is unknown to one another. For it is written: “The lion and the ox eat straw” (Isaiah 11:7). One who was a foreigner is now like a native; one who was a resident alien has become, as it were, an inhabitant.

Our relatives and parents follow us day by day, abandoning everything they had possessed, and not even willingly. Those who were poor there, God makes wealthy here. Those who had possessed only a few coins now possess countless bezants; and those who had not owned a village now, by God’s gift, [Col. 0925C] possess a city.

Why, then, should one return to the West who has found such an East here? God does not wish those who vowed to follow him with their crosses—and finally to reach him—to be afflicted by poverty. You therefore perceive that this is an immense miracle, greatly astonishing throughout the whole world. Who has ever heard of such a thing?

God therefore wishes us all to gain others for him and to draw them to himself as dearest friends. Since he wishes this, let us also willingly desire it, and let us do what pleases him with generous and humble hearts, so that we may reign happily with him.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the King’s Liberation from His Bonds and the Siege of the City of Aleppo

[Col. 0925D]

With almighty God favoring him, the king of Jerusalem emerged from Turkish custody on the fourth day before the Kalends of September [29 August], after having been held under their bonds for twelve months and somewhat more. But because it was first necessary to hand over selected hostages to them for his ransom, he did not emerge entirely free, since he had anxiously bound both himself and them by an uncertain and precarious hope.

Accordingly, after counsel had later been applied to the necessity, he hastened to besiege the city of Caliptum, so that, once it had been restrained, he might either wrest his hostages from its citizens or perhaps capture it after it had been weakened by hunger. For he had learned that it was suffering severe distress from a shortage of bread.

This city lies forty miles from great Antioch. In this place Abraham, when he was traveling as a stranger from Carrhae into the land of Canaan, used to have his shepherds pasture his flocks there, both smelly and fertile; he also had their milk drawn into pails, then curdled, and the curdled milk pressed in baskets and made into cheese. For he was exceedingly rich in the possession of every kind of thing.

Pope Calixtus died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January [21 December].

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the Turkish Army Gathered to Break the Siege

In the year 1125 from the birth of the Savior of the world, in the third indiction, after five months had passed, the king of Jerusalem, together with his men, had confined the city of Aleppo but had accomplished nothing. The Turks, however, as is their custom, being not sluggish, crossed the paradisiacal river, the great Euphrates, and hastened by an extremely rapid march to the aforesaid city, to break the siege which our people had maintained around it for a long time. For they feared that, unless they came to its aid immediately, it would soon be captured.

There were seven thousand horsemen, and nearly four thousand camels loaded with grain and provisions. But because our men could not prevail against them, they necessarily withdrew and on the following day turned aside to the nearest town, called Careph. It was ours. One division of the Turks pursued our men for a while, but there lost two of their better horses, whose riders were thrown down and killed. We, for our part, lost one retainer and six tents.

Their arrival occurred on the third day before the Kalends of February [30 January]. But because they arrived suddenly at night, they found us unprepared and more easily threw us into confusion. Therefore: most disgraceful to tell, dishonorable to know, wearisome to relate, shameful to hear. Yet in telling this I do not depart from the truth.

What then? Who resists the will of God? The proverb is true which a certain Wise Man uttered: “Things that are destined do not fight, nor do they allow themselves to be overcome.” This was a future event, but known beforehand by no one. For if it had been foreknown, it could never have remained a future event, since it would have come to nothing through reflection without the will of God. The one who foreknew it would have annulled it, preventing the matter from reaching completion.

The king then withdrew to Antioch, and Goscelin with him. The hostages whom the king had given for himself when he left his bonds were neither returned nor redeemed. Thus both the people of Jerusalem and those of Tripoli returned to their own places.

But divine providence opposes the one whom human virtue makes too prosperous, lest it allow anyone whom it is fitting to enlarge to become enlarged. For who else is the giver of good things and the remover of evils except God, the ruler and healer of minds, who sees and distinguishes all things from the highest watchtower of heaven?

A short time before, he had graciously handed over to us Christians, his own people, the city of Tyre, so powerful and glorious, and had taken it away from its possessors. Now it pleased him to withdraw his hand from it. Perhaps he reserved his vineyard for freer cultivators, who would wish or be able to return its fruit to him abundantly at the proper time.

Some, indeed, when they have more, are capable of less, and do not show the giver of good things as much gratitude as they ought. Rather, in those promises which they make to God according to their desires, they deceive themselves—and again and again deceive him by lying.

## CHAPTER XL. That the King Was Received at Jerusalem with Joy

[Col. 0927A]

After the king had been held and fettered by the pagans for nearly two years with the utmost cruelty, he returned to his Jerusalem. On the third day before the Nones of April [3 April], we all received him with a solemn procession. After staying only a short time among us, he hastened back to Antioch, since the Turks were already ravaging that land, and their more powerful leader was named Borsequinus, with six thousand soldiers joined to him.

## CHAPTER XLI. On the Venetians Who, Returning Home, Ravaged the Emperor’s Islands

At that time it was reported to us that, after the capture of Tyre, the Venetians, on their return journey, had violently seized the emperor’s islands through which they passed—namely Rhodes and Mothone, as well as Samos and Chios—and had likewise destroyed their walls, miserably taken adult men and girls captive, and carried away with them money of many kinds.

But since we could not approve this, we grieved in our inmost hearts when we heard it. For these two sides were raging most cruelly against one another: the emperor against the Venetians, and the Venetians against the emperor. They were enemies of one another.

But woe to the world because of scandals! Woe also to those through whom scandals come! (Matthew 18:7.) If the fault is the emperor’s, then he rules badly. But if it is the Venetians’, they acquire condemnation for themselves. For all sins proceed from pride. Does a man not act proudly when he does what God forbids?

The Venetians have an occasion for taking revenge; the emperor also has, as he says, a more just occasion for defending himself. But the innocent, placed in the middle, suffer the consequences although they are not responsible for their injuries, and are unjustly ruined.

What more can be said to those who, through piratical robbery, do not cease to inflict whatever harm they can upon pilgrims of God and of Jerusalem, traveling across the sea with toil and anguish for love of their Creator? If, according to the Lord’s word, the merciful deserve to be blessed (Matthew 5:7), what do these merciless people, contrary to mercy, receive in return for their impiety?

They are cursed, excommunicated, and die unrepentant and faithless. Such men descend alive of their own accord into hell (Psalm 54:16). They do not obey the apostolic authority; they despise the patriarch; they scorn the sayings of the holy Fathers.

I know—I know what I am not afraid to say to them. For what they will hear from the very severe Judge will come to pass: “I do not know where you are from” (Luke 13:27), you who cry out that the door should be opened to you. You come late and bring nothing good with you. Indeed, the door is already closed (Matthew 25:10). For you were unwilling to listen to me, and I no longer deem you worthy of being heard. I once cried, “Come” (Matthew 11:28); now I say altogether, “Depart” (Matthew 27:41). I say it, I say it, truly I say it: I do not alter the sentence once given.

What remains is dreadful and intolerable, yet an everlasting woe according to your merits. To continue the order of events, and so that the history may not hang interrupted, I shall endeavor to indicate each matter briefly.

## CHAPTER XLII. On the Many Deeds Perpetrated by Borsequinus and the Battle Fought Against Him

[Col. 0928A]

Borsequinus, whose courage and wickedness we have already begun to recount, as his army gradually grew larger day by day, blockaded and captured a certain town called Capharda. Its guardians surrendered it to him when they could no longer hold it and had no hope of receiving help from elsewhere.

Our king had not yet arrived there, nor had the count of Tripoli, whom he was leading there with him. He had only a few men from Jerusalem, since they had been greatly exhausted in the present and preceding year. For how could they continually endure so many hardships, when they were scarcely allowed to rest in their homes for a single month?

Certainly he is cruel of heart who does not compassionately pity those who dwell around Jerusalem. Day and night they are sorely troubled in the service of the Lord, and even when they leave their lodging they anxiously fear and wonder whether they will later be able to return. If they travel far, they must necessarily go burdened with their provisions and equipment. If they are poor men, farmers, or woodcutters, they are either captured or killed in the forests and groves by the ambushes of the Ethiopians.

From one side the Babylonians come rushing by land and sea; from the north the Turks frequently make sudden attacks. Ears are always ready and attentive to hear the trumpeter, should the tumult of war suddenly break out. If we did not sometimes go astray by sinning, we would truly be altogether friends of God.

Borsequinus, trampling upon humble Syria and carefully seeking what would be most advantageous to him, laid siege to the fortress of Sardanaium. But, accomplishing nothing there, he turned his army toward the town called Hasar. He immediately surrounded it and confined it most violently with siege engines and artillery.

When the king of the Damascenes hastened to bring help at the appointed time, Borsequinus, having heard of the king’s arrival, had already cunningly collected and sent away his tents and baggage in fear. As the fortress was now being pressed toward capture and the time chosen for battle was constraining our men, behold, the king came with thirteen divisions arranged in perfect order.

The Antiochenes were stationed on his right wing. On the left were two counts, the count of Tripoli and the count of Edessa. [Col. 0928D] The king was in the third division, with the denser rear formation, while the Turks had been divided into twenty-one phalanxes. Their multitude was indeed considerable.

Just then they were laying aside their taut bows from their hands and arms, and fighting at close quarters with drawn and bared swords. When the king saw this, he delayed no longer. Armed with the protection of prayers and the sign of the cross, he cried, “Help, O God!” and, while the trumpets sounded loudly, he himself attacked them and ordered the attack to be made.

They did not dare begin the battle until the king had commanded it, although the Turks at first resisted with the greatest strength. Finally, with the Creator of all assisting, they melted away in despair; thrown into confusion amid great slaughter, they turned to flight and desperation, as far as each was able.

Five times wrested from five times five Twins,

this battle shone forth, the Lord granting triumph;

on the third Ides, when June grows hot in the breezes,

this battle was fought, the Lord’s glory to be remembered.

## CHAPTER XLIII. How Many Were Killed in the Battle

The truth concerning the number of those killed or wounded can be grasped neither in this nor in any other war, since no one determines such a total except by estimation. Moreover, the variation among writers is often plainly deceptive; the cause of this deception is certainly flattery, since they strive to heap praise upon the victors and exalt the valor of their own people, whether for those living at the time or for posterity.

Thus it is perfectly clear that, with such shamelessness in lying, they add to the number of enemies killed and diminish, or entirely conceal, the losses of their friends. Those who took part in the battle reported to us that two thousand Turkish soldiers had been killed, as the Turks themselves who escaped testified.

But an infinite number of horses on both sides perished from thirst, distress, and exhaustion.

It was hot, and great heat had doubled the heat;

a grievous battle was fought; one rages here, another kills there.

One puts him to flight, another flees; after falling, no one retreats.

The fields and roads redden with the blood of the slain;

the cuirasses gleam, and helmets and spears shine,

scattered everywhere across the fields in brilliant display.

One throws away his shield; another casts aside his quiver or bow.

Borsequinus would not then have wished to be without his whip, and Tuldequinus would have preferred to enter the city of Damascus barefoot and carefully preserve his own district. The Turks lost fifteen satraps in that encounter.

Our men, however, lost no more than twenty people, of whom five were soldiers. Our forces numbered one thousand one hundred soldiers when the battle was joined. The Turks had fifteen thousand soldiers, while our infantry numbered two thousand.

## CHAPTER XLIV. Borsequinus Returns to His Own Land; the King Gives Thanks to God for the Recovery of His Daughter, Formerly Given as a Hostage, and for the Victory

After Borsequinus had remained among us only a few days, he crossed the Euphrates and returned to his own country, carrying back to his friends there no honor but grief and lamentation. He who had come here threatening and horned returned, by God’s grace, mutilated and bereft of consolation.

Then, after our king had recovered his five-year-old daughter, who had been held as a hostage, together with several of his household who had likewise been kept in chains, by the payment of money as had been agreed by both sides, he hastened to Jerusalem to give thanks to God and to praise him earnestly for the splendid victory achieved against Borsequinus.

And rightly did he praise and thank him, because, after having long been brought low, placed beneath the wheel, and almost delivered over in the basest and most miserable condition, he had now, with God’s help, been restored to his former honor and strengthened.

Six decades and two three-year periods have passed

since I was born, up to the year to which we have now come.

May God justly order and govern what remains of my life.

## CHAPTER XLV. On the Castle Built by the King

In October of this year the king built a castle in the mountains of Beirut, in land sufficiently fertile and good. They call this mountain Glavianus, from *digladiari*, “to fight a duel,” because there those accused of crimes at Beirut were judged by combat. It lies six miles from the city itself.

Because the Saracen peasants had previously been unwilling to pay the taxes owed for their lands, they were afterward compelled by force and became compliant in payment.

## CHAPTER XLVI. On the King’s Expedition and His Battle with the Turks

[Col. 0930B]

The king then prepared to set out toward Syria, in the direction of Damascus. After breaking the peace between the king and Tuldequinus, he captured three excellent villages, routed and drove off their inhabitants, and, having seized as much booty as he could, returned to his own territory.

After dividing or distributing this plunder equally among his horsemen and companions according to customary right, he turned his expedition the following day toward the land of the Philistines.

At that time new and recent troops had gathered at Ascalon, sent there from Babylonia. The military division, eager to display its valor in our land, already imagined that it would be victorious. When they saw them approaching the aforesaid city with their standards raised, they came out against them with great shouting and boldness.

Although the king had not yet reached the front line [Col. 0930C] of his first ranks—for he cautiously held back in the rear so that, if necessity demanded, he might assist his men should they cunningly flee—the foremost of our cavalry, not lacking courage, rushed against them with indescribable force, crying, “Help, O God!”

They pressed so forcefully and boldly upon the enemy that they drove them within the gates of the city by striking, throwing down, and killing them. As far as one may estimate, if we had had somewhat more of our prepared forces there, they could undoubtedly have entered together with those who pursued them.

The people of Ascalon therefore remained behind, mourning and lamenting more than forty of their best men who had been killed, and greatly astonished at this unexpected misfortune.

The king, with trumpets signaling both beyond and near the city, rested beneath the tents that night. If, by God’s favor, our men enjoyed rest, our enemies spent the night sleepless and sorrowful. For, as Josephus says, one who trusts too greatly is heedless, whereas fear teaches prudence.

It should be known that on that day our cavalry found no booty around the city. For, forewarned of the king’s arrival, the inhabitants had prudently hidden all their animals.

## CHAPTER XLVII. That the Saracens Send Letters by Their Pigeons

It is customary among the Saracens living in Palestine to send letters cleverly from city to city by pigeons trained for this service. These birds carry writings to a dwelling already long known to them. The messages, written on little sheets and sewn onto the pigeons’ rumps, reveal when read what ought afterward to be done.

This was then clearly discovered to have happened.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On the Variety of Customs

Accordingly, according to the divisions of the earth, there arise variations in things and customs. France has one set of practices, England another, Egypt another, and India yet another. They also differ in birds, fish, and trees.

I have never seen a whale or a lamprey in Palestine, nor among birds a magpie or a jackdaw. There, however, are wild asses, *cirogrilli*, and also the hyena, which digs up the graves of the dead. Among the trees there I saw neither poplar, nor yew, nor hazel, nor elder, nor butcher’s broom, nor any maple.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On Various Kinds of Beasts and Serpents in the Land of the Saracens

Recently we all saw near Naples a certain beast whose name no human being knows or has heard. It had the face of a goat, a neck shaggy like that of a little ass, cloven hooves, a calf’s tail, and was larger than a ram.

In Babylonia there is another beast called the Chimera. It is high not at the rear but at the front; on it, during the greater festivals, they spread an excellent cloak, to serve their prince together with many other furnishings.

The crocodile is a four-footed animal. It is equally powerful on land and in the river. It has no tongue; it moves its upper jaw, and its bites close with terrifying tenacity. It often grows to a length of twenty cubits. It lays eggs like geese and broods its young nowhere except where the rising waters of the Nile cannot reach. It is armed with enormous claws. At night it lives in the water; during the day it rests on land. It is surrounded by an exceedingly tough hide.

In a certain river of Caesarean Palestine there are likewise such four-footed animals. They say, however, that they were brought there not long ago from the Nile itself by malicious cunning; there they now frequently cause immense damage in the territory, devouring animals.

The *appotamus* [hippopotamus] is born in that same river and land of the Nile, and in India. It closely resembles a horse in its back, mane, and neighing, but has an upturned snout, cloven hooves, boar-like teeth, and a twisted tail. At night it grazes on crops, approaching them backward with crafty cunning, so that no ambushes may be prepared for it when it returns by following its own tracks. They are larger in body than elephants.

God creates all these and other things, small and great. Since it pleases him to create them, they ought also to please us, and therefore we ought to give him praise.

True dragons have small mouths, which do not open wide for biting. They also have narrow passages through which they draw breath and extend their tongues. They have venom not in their teeth but in their tails, and they harm by striking rather than by opening their jaws. A stone called *dracontias* is cut from their brains.

The dragon is the largest of all serpents, or of all living creatures upon the earth. It is often said to be drawn from caves into the air, and the air is stirred because of it. It is crested. If it coils around anyone, it kills him; an elephant is now safe from it because of the elephant’s bodily size.

It is born in India and in Ethiopia, amid the very blaze of perpetual heat. It hides beside the paths along which elephants walk, ties their legs with its customary knots, and kills them by suffocation. It has no feet.

In Scythian Asia there are *frigriphes* (winged griffins), exceedingly savage and raging beyond all madness. There is also a people of Hyrcania, rough from its forests, abounding in enormous wild beasts and teeming with tigers. This species of beast shines with a tawny brilliance, marked by conspicuous spots. I do not know whether the speed or the tenacity of their foot movement helps them more. Nothing is so long that they cannot traverse it quickly; nothing gets so far ahead that they cannot catch it immediately.

There are also panthers in Hyrcania, covered above with small circular markings. They say that herds are wonderfully affected by their scent and sight, and that they sense everywhere that the panthers are approaching with deliberate speed; they are frightened only by the grimness of their faces. They kill them more often with poison than with iron; they possess a sluggish vitality.

There is the *alce*, comparable to mules. Its upper lip projects so far that it cannot graze unless it moves backward along its own tracks.

The chameleon is extremely abundant in Asia. It is a four-footed animal with the face of a lizard, except that its short legs are joined farther down to its belly. It has a long tail twisted into a spiral, finely hooked claws with a delicate curve, a sluggish gait, a rough body, and skin like that found on crocodiles. Its mouth is perpetually open and serves no useful purpose.

It is invulnerable to the crow. Whoever kills it is himself killed by the dead creature. For if the bird eats even a small amount of it, it dies immediately. But the crow has a remedy: after taking a laurel leaf, it recovers its health.

Its body is without flesh, its vital organs without a spleen; and whatever it attaches itself to, it becomes the same color as that creature.

In Greek it is called *salamandra*; in Latin, *stellio*,

> The flame-enduring *stellio*; the salamander; the dreadful chameleon,
The name is threefold, but the body is single and one. The pegasus is a bird that has nothing equine about it except its ears. Certain peoples are so tall that they leap over elephants as easily as over horses. There is also a race that is gray-haired in youth and grows black in old age.

The leucrocota is a beast that surpasses all animals in speed: the size of a wild ass, with the haunches of a stag, the chest and legs of a lion, [Col. 0932D] the head of a camel, cloven hooves, a mouth gaping all the way to the ears, and a continuous bone in place of teeth. Such is its form; in voice, however, it imitates the sounds of speaking human beings.
