Among these is born the manticore, with three rows of teeth meeting in alternating succession, a human face, gray-green eyes, a blood-red color, a leonine body, and a tail like that of a scorpion, armed with a barbed sting. Its voice is only a hiss, but it imitates the melodies of pipes. It craves human flesh most avidly. Its feet are so strong and its leaping so powerful that neither the greatest distances nor the broadest obstacles can delay it.

But who could either know or investigate all the many and great marvels of God in this great and spacious sea, in which so many animals and reptiles move, whose number cannot be counted? [Col. 0933A] What I have just said, so little in comparison, I extracted—as I preferred—from Solinus, a most diligent and learned investigator. But what Alexander the Great found and saw on his journey in India I shall indicate, if not all of it, at least something of it, in what follows.

Now this year departs; may God, the ruler, be another,

As time requires, while year leaps into year.

## CHAPTER L. On the expedition of the king of Jerusalem against the king of Damascus

In the year from the Nativity of the Lord 1126, in the third indiction, after the festal days of Christmas had been celebrated in Jerusalem, the king assembled his army to march against Damascus. When his proclamation had been made according to his command, the whole region of Jerusalem was stirred to this undertaking, on foot and on horseback. The men of Joppa and Ramla, and those who were in Lydda, traveling by way of Nablus, made their journey through Scythopolis. This is Beth-shean. In the northern district were the men of Acre and Tyre. Those, however, over whose company the king presided, leaving the city of Sepphoris and Mount Tabor on their right, came to Tiberias. The men of Jerusalem joined them there, and, after crossing the Jordan, all rested happily beneath their tents.

The weather was bright, for it was cloudless and clear,

And the horns of the moon’s seventeenth day shone forth.

Before daylight, when they were to leave the camp, the trumpet gave the signal. Then they gathered the tents and prepared everything for departure. They loaded the mules, beasts of burden, and camels with baggage, causing [Col. 0933C] much tumult. The asses brayed, the camels bellowed, and the horses neighed. When the guides of the travelers began to lead the way, with the horns sounding together, they carefully cut out the route they knew to be most useful. Once they had entered more deeply into hostile territory, they wisely took care to march with their standards raised and fortified themselves with their weapons, lest they be thrown into confusion by unforeseen danger.

Then they passed the cave of Roob and entered the land of the Damascenes, and rested for two nights beyond Meddem. There a river rises which descends outside the Sea of Galilee toward Scythopolis and joins the Jordan. At that point they threw down a tower they found before them. Thus they came to a castle called Solone. From there the Christian Syrians who lived in it came out to meet the king in procession.

Afterward they came to the valley called Marchisophar—that is, “of the emperor Sophar”—to the place where the apostle Paul received a blow from the Lord and lost his sight for three days; there they stayed for two days. There they saw the tents of the Damascenes, who were awaiting our army. When Tuldequin’s son had carefully gathered together approximately three thousand horsemen, as best he could, he returned to his father intent on battle and joined his people that day before the engagement.

Without further delay, twelve battle lines of both horsemen and foot soldiers were arranged on our side, so that one company might strengthen the other if necessity arose. When everyone had received communion from the consecrated bread [Col. 0934A] after hearing Mass, the two sides engaged, and, beginning the battle, cried out, “Help, God!” The Turks also shouted and fought with the greatest ferocity. They marveled at the extraordinary courage of those whom they had previously despised as though already defeated. When their strength began to fail, terrified by fear and panic, they thought of flight.

Tuldequin fled, and his son fled. Although they pressed our men beyond all measure, as their own spirit increased more and more, our men remained steadfast and in command of themselves. Yet such a cloud of arrows poured down from the Turks that no part of the Christians’ bodies was safe from blow or wound. No battle was more tumultuous or more terrible for our men. The running to and fro of those rushing about, the uproar, and the attack were excessive. Trumpets and horns blared loudly.

Our men, therefore, encircled by the Turks, were by then wounded in many places. After they had grown hardened by endurance while fleeing for four miles, willing or unwilling, they turned their faces toward the enemy and, filled with martial courage, began to fight. The sacred day of the battle was the Conversion of Paul, whom God chose. The fighting began at the third hour of the day; evening brought it to an end with victory.

A serious battle is a disgraceful flight. Yet it is more tolerable to live in weakness than to mourn forever as the dead. Thus the Turks chose flight in order to preserve their lives. Two thousand and somewhat more of the Turks remained on the field. Of the foot soldiers there was no count. Of our men, fourteen horsemen and eighty foot soldiers were lost.

Our king conducted himself excellently on that day, with all his cavalry and his retainers, with whom almighty God was present. The king of Syria fled with as many as he could take. The king of Jerusalem returned joyfully in triumph. When it had been decided to return, they invested one tower and captured it with ninety-six men. After these had been killed, the king seized another tower, in which twenty Turks who had fled were present. When they saw our men digging a trench all around it and hurling enormous stones, terrified, they surrendered themselves and the fortress to the king. He allowed them to depart on those terms, but ordered the tower to be destroyed.

It seemed very necessary to cut this tower down, lest it invite many of its people to revolt under its protection. For it could give the inhabitants a sure hope of safety, and those attacking it hesitation and fear. Perhaps the hearers of this history will grow weary if everything done in battle or because of battle, whether by force or cunning, is recounted. For the Damascenes took agile young men and had them sit behind the cavalry with their weapons. When they came near the enemy, these men leapt from the horses and, now fighting on foot from another side while the cavalry who had brought them fought, threw the enemy into confusion.

## CHAPTER LI. On the siege of the city of Raphania and the Sabbatic River

For it is written: “Nothing is blessed in every respect.” We could not be blessed in this respect, since [Col. 0935A] we lost there fourteen exceptionally brave soldiers, besides several foot soldiers equally valiant. But in comparison with the slaughter inflicted on them, this is little.

Damascus is interpreted as “the kiss of blood,” or “drinking blood.” We read that the blood of Abel was shed in Damascus. From the blood of the slain, the Damascenes could lick; they could even drink from the blood itself, bending down over it.

When at last the king returned with his army to Jerusalem, we observed a festal and thanksgiving day together. Shortly afterward, moved by the plea of the count of Tripoli, the king set out to help him and besiege the town we call Raphania, situated beyond Mount Lebanon.

In that region, as Josephus relates, between the cities of Arca and Raphania a river flows midway. It possesses a remarkable peculiarity. Although at times it flows in great volume and with a sluggish course, after six days it fails at its sources and leaves the place dry to behold. Then, as though no change had occurred, on the seventh day it rises again in the same form; and it has certainly been discovered that it always observes this order. Hence it was also called the Sabbatic River, taking its name from the sacred seventh day of the Jews.

Prince Titus, having stayed for some time at Berytus and then returned, celebrated magnificent spectacles in all the Syrian cities through which he passed. When he saw this river, so worthy of knowledge because of its nature, he greatly marveled.

## CHAPTER LII. On another river

The same historian also reports another marvel, saying that near the city of Ptolemais there is a little stream, scarcely two stadia in length, which they call the Belus, extremely small. Near it is the tomb of Memnon, worthy of great admiration.

It had the appearance of a rounded valley, producing glass-making sand. When many ships have taken up this sand and departed together, the place is again filled. For the winds, as though carrying out an appointed work, convey this common sand from the surrounding heights. That place immediately changes the metals it receives into glass. Even more marvelous to me is this: whenever any part of the sand already changed into glass is thrown over the edges of that place, it turns back again into common sand.

## CHAPTER LIII. On the capture of the city of Raphania

[Col. 0935D]

As for the city of Raphania, about which I have already begun to tell a little story, this was its outcome. After the king and the count had confined the Saracens inside with the utmost severity for eighteen days, hurling stones with their siege engines, they surrendered the city and departed unharmed. This happened on the last day of March. Accordingly, the aforesaid count took possession of the city and fortified it. The king returned to Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER LIV. On the death of the Roman emperor

While we were celebrating the Easter days in Jerusalem, a little rumor reached us from newly arrived pilgrims, who announced that the Roman emperor had died, [Col. 0936A] adding also that the duke of the Saxons, named Lothair, had been elevated as king and emperor.

When Henry fell, the rise of the Twins shone forth.

After him, King Lothair rules, born from a duke.

## CHAPTER LV. On the king’s expedition against the Babylonians

Not much time passed before the king, leaving Tyre, descended into lower Syria, leaving part of his cavalry behind and taking another part with him, although he had heard from rumor-bearers that the Babylonians were prepared for battle and were coming against him. It was necessary for him to hurry there first, where he heard that the enemies were pressing forward.

As a boar surrounded by dogs and harassed by their repeated bites must defend itself vigorously by striking with its right and left feet, so he had to act. We customarily express this proverbially: “Where there is pain, there is the hand.”

Before the king arrived there, the Turks had already besieged and taken by force a certain false castle. It was harmful to them but necessary for us. The soldiers escaped by night through a very clever stratagem, leaving their wives with their children behind, preferring that part be saved rather than that the whole be utterly lost.

At that time, in the summer season, midway through the month of July, a comet began to appear between the east and the north. Rising before dawn and sending out its ray toward the ninth hour, it showed itself with moderate brightness. We endeavored to observe it for eighteen days, entrusting its significance to the Creator of all things. [Col. 0936C]

The Turks, whose strongest man was Borsequinus, besieged a town called Cerepum. But when they heard of the king’s arrival, for he was already pursuing them, disappointed in their hope they withdrew to safer defenses. They were not more than six thousand soldiers. The king therefore returned to Antioch.

## CHAPTER LVI. On the Babylonian fleet

Then the Babylonians, having repaired and assembled their fleet, sailed with a south wind into the land of the Philistines. Passing Phara, Mialaris also of Gaza, as well as Ascalon and Joppa, Caesarea and Ptolemais, Tyre and Sidon, they explored and lay in ambush along the seacoast as far as the city of Berytus, watching and searching from harbor to harbor to see whether they could find anything useful to themselves and harmful to the Christians.

But because they were then greatly distressed by a lack of fresh water and were very thirsty, they had to go ashore in order to fill their buckets from streams and springs and relieve their thirst. The citizens of the aforesaid city, however, were angered by this and immediately advanced against them with the greatest boldness, joined by travelers who had perhaps hurried there. In the engagement, 130 of those pirates, including both the slain and those wounded to the point of death, were struck down.

Five thousand had gone out to battle, apart from those who meanwhile guarded the ships. Of these, twenty-two were triremes, or what they call *cauti*; the remaining fifty-three were of other kinds. Thus they paraded their cruelty against our people, pitiless and merciless toward all whom they could overtake.

But thanks be to God, they gained nothing here, for our horsemen with their lances and our archers with their arrows, charging unexpectedly into the open sea, put them to flight. They immediately raised their sails and directed themselves across the swift sea toward Tripoli, and from there toward Cyprus.

## CHAPTER LVII. On the voyage of the young Bohemond

How often this year did envoys or pilgrims announce and affirm to us the arrival of the young Bohemond? Yet, as the rumors multiplied, they deceived us. He was fearful because of the Babylonian or piratical fleet which he heard was spread widely over the sea. Moreover, he was very concerned about his land, which, unless he entrusted it to good and faithful men, he would deceitfully lose, surrounded by his malicious plotters.

It is written in rustic proverbs: “Whoever has a bad neighbor has a bad morning.”

At last, after he had repeatedly prepared his journey at Hydruntum, a city of Apulia, having gathered as many ships as he could—twenty-two, ten of them long ships equipped with oars—he began to make ready for the sea voyage.

After entrusting his territory to the duke of Apulia, whom he appointed as heir to his land and substituted for himself should he die first, he repeatedly confirmed this arrangement to the duke, who willingly accepted it, provided that he himself should die first; the leading men of both sides bore witness as they stood present.

Thus Bohemond, plowing the sea in the middle of September, crossed the scattered Cyclades and came to Methone. Afterward he passed Rhodes, Pamphylia, and Lycia, and often troubled those sailing across the gulf of Italy. From there, passing Little Antioch, he came to Great Antioch, crossing Isauria and the city of Seleucia. Leaving Cyprus on his right, he left Tarsus on his left, as well as the famous city of Mopsuestia, long since devastated.

At that time several double-dealers and gluttons, newly come from the sea, spread the report among us in Jerusalem that he had certainly landed at Antioch—and they were lying. Nevertheless, they thought they were telling the truth because they had come together with some part of his soldiers as far as Patara, along with the hawks, goats, fowlers, and dogs which he had sent on ahead—

## CHAPTER LVIII. On dangers occurring at sea

[Col. 0937D]

Many turbulent events often occur to those sailing at sea, whether by God’s will or by his permission. Sometimes the anchor is loosed; sometimes the mast is broken, or the stern ornament, or the ropes snap. When the winds change, attention is paid to the *cheruca*, so that, if they are making favorable progress, the situation may be assessed carefully and skillfully. One must beware lest everything be lost in a single night.

When the stars are obscured, if the keel of the raft is struck, death or shipwreck, an approaching disaster, immediately threatens. There are dangers on land just as at sea. Why should we wonder at what happens to us when we recall the shipwreck of the apostle Paul? To test the depth of the abyss, the sailors lowered the sounding line. [Col. 0938A] Unless he had seen an angelic vision bringing consolation at the extremity of life, he would already have entered into despair of life.

## CHAPTER LIX. On the great sea

Around the gulf of Italy ships often become accustomed to running into danger, and winds are stirred from every direction. Descending precipitously from the mountains through valleys, they customarily twist properly through underground winding passages and whirl wonderfully into the vortex of the abyss.

If sailors should at times encounter *paroni* [the term is uncertain], they are plundered and wickedly thrown into confusion. But those who suffer this for the love of God—will they perhaps be wickedly deprived of their rewards?

This much we have to say about our sea. Of the Mediterranean, however, it must not be omitted where its head rises. Some think that these gulfs arise from the strait of Cádiz, and that they have no other origin than the outflow of the bursting Ocean. Those who hold the opposite view say that all the water flows in from the mouths of the Black Sea. They support this with a substantial argument: the tide flowing from the Black Sea never turns back.

Therefore praise and honor belong to the Creator of all, who set boundaries for the sea, adding barriers and gates. For he said to it: “Thus far shall you come, and here your waves shall be broken” (Job 38:11). When it has dashed its force against the shore, it dissolves into foam and is beaten back by certain barriers of low sand.

Moreover, unless the force of the heavenly decree restrained it, what would prevent the Red Sea from mingling with the Egyptian sea across the plains of Egypt, which lie in especially low valleys? Those who wished to join these two seas together and pour them into one another teach this very thing: Sesostris of Egypt, who lived earlier, and Darius the Mede, who, in view of his greater power, wished to bring into effect what had previously been attempted by a native.

This matter indicates that the sea above is the Indian Sea, into which the Red Sea flows, since the Egyptian sea washes the lower region. Perhaps, lest the sea spread more widely by rushing from the higher to the lower regions, both kings recalled their efforts.

This is found in Ambrose’s *Hexameron*. Something else is found in Solinus. The works of God are therefore marvelous, but much more marvelous is he who makes and orders them. If some things appear misshapen to our eyes, they are nevertheless to be praised, because the Creator of all makes them; indeed, they are no less useful.

God even places a remedy in the bedbug, and puts cunning in the octopus or the sea urchin. He gives prudence to serpents as well. Sometimes they provide a remedy; sometimes they bring disease or even death. At times they furnish a service, and at other times harm.

For it is said that the antidote called *theriac* is made from the body of a serpent. The serpent’s poison and body, when taken alone, cause harm; but when mixed with other substances, they bring health and safety.

## CHAPTER LX. On the kinds of serpents

The basilisk is about half a foot long, white like a little mitre, with a striped head. It is given not only for the destruction of human beings and other animals, but also of the earth, which it pollutes and scorches. Wherever it is found, it takes possession of a deadly dwelling. In the end it destroys the grasses and kills the trees. It also corrupts the very air, so that no bird can fly through it safely, its breath having been infected with pestilence.

When it moves, it crawls with the middle part of its body, while the rest is upright and raised high. Even serpents dread its hissing. When it takes flight, all creatures hurry away wherever they can. Whatever is crushed by its bite is neither eaten by a wild beast nor touched by a bird.

It is defeated, however, by weasels, which people introduce into the caves where it hides. Finally, the Pergamenes bought the remains of a basilisk for a large sum of money so that, by the hand of Apollo, neither spiders would cover the temple nor birds fly into it.

The amphisbaena rises with two heads, the second being at the end where its tail is. The horned serpent displays four little horns; by displaying them as bait, it lures and seizes unsuspecting birds, while deliberately covering the rest of its body with sand.

The hemorrois draws blood with its bite and, by dissolving the veins, calls out whatever life remains through the blood. Whoever is struck by the prester swells up and dies from monstrous bodily enlargement; putrefaction often follows the swollen parts.

There are also the himodites, the chencheris, the elephantine chelsidra, and the medracontes. Finally, there are as many kinds of deaths as there are of human beings. There are also scorpions, skinks, and lizards, which are assigned to worms rather than to serpents.

These monsters, if they hiss, strike more gently; they have affections and do not wander without cause except toward their mates. There are also dart-snakes, which pierce whatever animal chance brings before them.

The scytale shines with such great variety on its back that, because of its markings, it delays those who see it. The *dipsas* kills by thirst. The *sippiale* [reading uncertain], which kills by sleep according to the witness (*teste*), is itself also consumed unto death. Its venom admits fewer remedies than that of other serpents, and it dies of hunger.

These things are exceedingly marvelous and nevertheless worthy of wonder—things which Alexander the Great saw in India. Therefore, in a letter to his teacher Aristotle and his mother Olympias, he said: “I would not have believed that there could be so many marvels in any place, unless I myself had weighed them with my own eyes.”

Truly, this king was altogether a magnificent man, shrewd and watchful in his affairs; he was mighty in strength and powerful in ability—not flying about like a feather nor drifting like a straw.

## CHAPTER LXI. On the arrival of the young Bohemond and his reception at Antioch

[Col. 0939D]

Since Bohemond had come late this year, contrary to expectation, we supposed that he would not come at all, as had been declared and as rumor had promised. But, in accordance with the prophet’s saying, “A man’s way is not in his own hand, nor are a man’s steps directed by man but by the Lord” (Prov. 20:24), expectation was largely disappointed.

For what human eagerness establishes does not come to pass; rather, what God, the judge, determines to be appropriate to human merits comes to pass. When the king informed us by letter in Jerusalem that Bohemond had already landed at Antioch, everyone was greatly pleased. We all praised God, who had brought him safely.

The sun had already set when he entered the harbor by night. When he approached Antioch, he was joyfully received by everyone. The king came out to meet him with a great procession and the loud praises of the people, and welcomed him gladly. After they had held a hurried conversation with one another, the king immediately handed over his entire territory to him and gave him one of his daughters in marriage.

Here are father-in-law and son-in-law; here one is father and the other son.

Let each love the other; thus both will become greater.

Then, when the wedding arrangements had been made, they were lawfully completed. When Bohemond, having been made prince, sat upon his couch and was dressed in a most splendid double robe, all his leading men were summoned. In the presence and with the approval of the king, they swore him the faithful allegiance owed by subjects, promising to preserve it from that day and thereafter.

When these things had been done, the king returned to Jerusalem.

When heavenly Scorpio shone forth among the stars,

Bohemond is received into the Antiochene kingdom;

Now the orbit of the renewed year turns backward.

## CHAPTER LXII. On the plague of mice

In the year 1127 from the Lord’s birth, in the fifth indiction, an immense multitude of mice boiled forth throughout the region of Palestine, so great that they attacked an ox from behind, ate it, and, suffocating it, devoured it together with seven rams.

After they had repeatedly laid waste the territory of the people of Acre, they sought water and climbed into the mountains of Tyre. Then, when a pestilential wind and savage storm suddenly arose, they were driven back in countless thousands toward the neighboring valleys. Because of the stench of their corpses, that region remained extremely unhealthy.

[Col. 0939] Here ends the *History of Jerusalem* by Lord Fulcher of Chartres.

# Genealogy of the King Called Charlemagne

From whose lineage arose Godfrey and Baldwin, kings of Jerusalem.

From an old manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint-Quentin at the end of Fulcher of Chartres’s *History of Jerusalem*.

[Col. 0939D] King Charles was anointed emperor in the Church of Saint Peter on Christmas Day. This Charles begot Louis Augustus. Louis begot Lothair, Pepin, and Louis by Ermengard, [Col. 0941A] and Charles the Bald by Judith.

Charles the Bald begot Louis, who accomplished nothing because he lived only four years [read: ruled for two years]. Louis, son of Louis [Charles], begot Charles the Simple and Carloman.

Charles the Simple was captured by Heribert. This Charles begot Louis by Ogiva. Louis begot King Lothair and Duke Charles by Gerberga.

King Lothair begot the young Louis. Charles, Duke and brother of King Lothair, begot Ermengard and Gerberga.

Ermengard begot Albert, count of Namur. Albert begot Albert and his brother Henry, count of Durbuy.

Gerberga, Ermengard’s sister, begot Henry the Elder, count of Brussels. Henry the Elder begot Count Lambert, his brother Henry, and their sister Matilda.

Count Eustace of Boulogne took this Matilda as his wife, and she bore him two sons, Eustace and Lambert.

Eustace took as wife Ida, daughter of Duke Godfrey, noble in lineage and character. She bore him three sons: Eustace, count of Boulogne, and Godfrey and Baldwin, kings of Jerusalem.

# History of the Deeds of the Jerusalem Journey of Our Time, by Gilo of Paris

(Martene, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum* III, 211, from a manuscript of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.)

## Preliminary Observation

Among the various events of war by which ecclesiastical history is especially illuminated, the holy expedition to Jerusalem claims the first place for itself. It was distinguished by so many glorious deeds, adorned by the blood of so many noble men, and confirmed by so many marvels and portents.

Therefore, all who at any time undertook to write ecclesiastical annals took care to review each of its circumstances with the greatest precision; many also committed separate studies of it to posterity. Yet among all those authors, the ancient writers easily win the palm in the judgment of the learned, especially those who took part in the events themselves or transmitted to posterity what they had received from eyewitnesses. They are always read not only with greater pleasure but also with greater profit, since they offer more reliable indications of the truth.

Although the distinguished James Bongars, who deserved very well of literary scholarship, gathered as many writers of the holy war as he could find into two volumes and published them in 1611, so great an effort nevertheless did not entirely satisfy the desire of learned men. After him, scholars who enlightened the republic of letters through their writings did not neglect, while searching the shelves of distinguished libraries and turning over ancient manuscript codices, to make public whatever of this kind they could discover, as precious monuments of antiquity.

Certainly, two of our own men, Lucas d’Achery and Jean Mabillon, contributed their efforts in this field. The former reprinted Guibert, abbot of Nogent, together with other works by the same writer, in his edition of the *Deeds of God through the Franks*. The latter inserted into his *Museum Italicum* a history of the holy war found in a manuscript codex at Monte Cassino.

Before them, the light of the Gallican academy, François Du Chesne, published Peter Tudebode and Fulcher of Chartres in a fuller and more correct form in volume IV of his *French History*. To these he added Gilo of Paris’s history of the expedition to Jerusalem, which he had received from Jacques Sirmond, although it was disfigured by so many lacunae that one almost has to seek Gilo himself within Gilo. Nevertheless, that learned man valued the work so highly that he did not hesitate to make that precious monument of antiquity public.

When I was turning over the manuscript codices of our Parisian library of Saint-Germain, the same work of Gilo of Paris came into my hands, bearing this inscription written by our Acherius:

“The following history was indeed published at the end of volume IV of the *History of the Franks* of André Du Chesne, but for the most part it differs. Moreover, the published version is full of lacunae; for that reason this manuscript deserves to be submitted to the press.”

When I had read it, I was immediately seized by the desire to compare the printed version with the manuscript. From the comparison I discovered that not only could approximately two hundred lacunae be filled and many corrupt passages corrected, but that part of the fourth book, together with the whole of the fifth and sixth, was missing from the printed editions.

I therefore judged it appropriate to append Gilo’s history to the *Deeds of Tancred*, nor could a more suitable place be assigned to it. Furthermore, the title of the work itself demonstrates that its author was a contemporary.

# BOOK I. TEXT OF THE DEEDS WORTHY OF REMEMBRANCE OF THE CHRISTIANS

[Col. 0943]

[Col. 0943A]

By divine aid the ruin of the Turks was brought about;

This I set down in an easy poem for God’s praise,

Although the subject exceeds my powers; I invent no idle fictions.

Christ, be present to my mind, which wishes to recount your wars;

You are the praise whose sequence forms this poem,

So that the verses may succeed well and be made under your guidance.

## The Christian army approaches Nicaea

The Christian peoples, relying on sword and faith,

To cleanse the holy places of pollution and overcome

The mad Turks, who defile shrines and profane them,

Conspired together and sought Jerusalem.

But when that blessed host, already weary and having suffered many dangers,

Touched the seashore,

It crossed the raging sea and sought Nicaea,

[Col. 0943B] In which the assembly of three hundred, three times five, and three Fathers [Note: [Col. 0943D] Edition: “of powerful men.”]

Established customs and taught their inferiors.

But, having been shamefully changed and emptied of Christ’s faith,

It despised Christ and worshiped pagan monsters.

And since it is believed that this place had formerly worshiped Christ,

It is rightly recalled to Christ after its corruption.

## The Christians besiege Nicaea

Therefore they arrange their battle lines and set up their tents.

They gather from every direction and prepare what is suitable for war.

Bohemond occupies the part that the world calls the west

And sets up his camp opposite the walls.

That place, joined to the wagon [Note: [Col. 0943D] Edition: “is below”] and opposite the south,

Was assigned to your brave company, Godfrey.

Others move into positions that they consider suitable,

The harbor of them all, turning toward the rising sun.

[Col. 0943C] Dense with soldiers were Raymond and the man of Le Puy,

The great count Hugh, a lion to the savage and a lamb to the gentle [Note: [Col. 0943D] Manuscript: “to the soldiers”],

And Robert, sufficiently experienced in savage battles [Note: [Col. 0944D] Edition: “savage battles”],

And the Flemish duke, whose sword never fails,

And Stephen; they were assaulting walls destined to fall.

But one part of the city remained safe from the crowds,

The part upon which the high sun looks down feared no assault.

At last they had sought those walls in vain, thinking them secure.

For an immense lake, thick with much marshland,

Defended them and prevented our men from crossing.

Nevertheless, by skill our men reached this part,

For they threw boats and many coverings over it,

[Note: [Col. 0944D] These two lines are absent from the manuscript.]

Which the man called Caesar had caused to be brought by yoked oxen,

As a vow made at that time to provide assistance,

[Col. 0943D] Thus, as though across bridges, they were able to touch the waters.

Our men press forward fiercely, and the Turks resist.

They drive them back fiercely, and the Turks repel them.

The savage people send poisoned arrows from the city.

The arrow killed anyone to whom it gave even a slight wound.

And when he gained ground, he insulted them with shameful words,

Calling the worshipers of Christ, “Beware, you worse men.”

After our men had been sufficiently provoked by these hateful words,

A higher siege engine was brought against the hard walls.

At last the wretched pagans began to be afraid.

Our men, not sluggish, hurled stones and fire.

They battered the towers and tore away the missiles fastened to the shields,

Striking the enemies with their own missiles.

And as dense rain mixed with hail falls,

So arrows that could not be avoided were sent everywhere.

Weapons fell, and the wretched groaned and died on both sides;

Some fought with swords, others with clubs and stakes.

Great was the cry of the trembling crowd within the city.

[Note: [Col. 0944D] The words enclosed in parentheses are absent from the manuscript.]

Therefore, weeping and also signaling with their hands,

[Col. 0944B] They begged for peace and cried out for surrender.

They extended their right hands and went to open the gates.

Our men rejoiced and praised the great deeds of Christ.

First they judged that the city should be cleansed of its impurities

And consecrated by water sanctified through prayer.

Then they entered the reconciled city with hymns and crosses.

Sacred ministers bearing the holy vessels were sent in.

They purified the secure walls with blessed sprinkling,

Singing melodies suited to the divine rites.

While the citizens observed and heard such things,

They immediately rushed back to their pagan monsters in anger,

Saying that everything was being profaned by magical frenzy,

And, driving them out, thrust the sacred companies outside.

Thus the legions of Christians were provoked,

And they grieved that the mysteries of the heavenly beings had been mocked.

[Col. 0944C] They rise up more fiercely, hurry back to arms,

And demand punishment, with blood, for the profaned things.

They press forward more fiercely and fit the crossbows to the sling.

They bore through the gates and enclosed the wretched as though in a prison.

They establish watches, guarding by night and by day,

Lest any outsider assist those within through conversation.

While the vigilant men, taking one another’s places hour by hour, kept watch,

They discovered someone walking through the black darkness,

Seeking [lacuna] or to enter by the gates,

Or, through [lacuna], to converse with those shut inside.

They seized him, bound him heavily with fetters,

And forced him either to reveal immediately everything he knew

Or to gain the dreadful experience of a harsh death.

Overcome by excessive fear and delaying no longer,

[Col. 0944D] He vowed to tell everything, so long as his life was spared.

Then, once he had been made faithful by suitable assurances,

He explained that he had been sent to enter secretly among the citizens,

So that they would not despair but hold their position by courage.

For on the following day they would have complete consolation,

[Col. 0945A] when [lacuna] the besieged were able to kill

and enjoy their resources in freedom.

For more than three hundred thousand men, compelled by the Sultan and by the commanders, including Solyman, had come nearer. They rejoiced so greatly in their own strength that, as though already victorious, they celebrated, supposing that the Christian forces had by then been destroyed, and preparing among themselves only battles over the spoils.

At first light they had also decided to move the camp and establish it before the city, in the deserted position that had formerly been left for you, commander Raymond, and your men. When the commanders who had still been two thousand away began to pitch their camps there, they sent for them without delay and ordered them to come; in that very plain they arranged their tents.

[Col. 0945B] Moreover, the envoy, now voluntarily made faithful, desired to be cleansed in the water of baptism. While this was quickly being done amid a gathering of priests, an outstanding man shone forth among the Christian order.

At first light, therefore, our men turn to arms, to punish the city’s treachery with the ultimate penalty. A great shout arises; the faces [lacuna] of those fighting on this side and of those groaning in extremity on the other are changed. Battles are fought with engines, javelins, and swords; they are very nearly entering at once.

Sixty thousand Turks who had come to bring aid are defeated. Nicaea is captured.

While our men were thus pressing forward and the wretched inhabitants were trembling, already constrained and wishing, once defeated, to surrender their own [Note: [Col. 0945D] In the printed editions, the following four verses are read in place of these two:

“Behold, when Nicaea resounded with a sudden howling shout,

the mountains seem covered, once the thousands have been heard.

[Col. 0946D] As they pour out from here down the mountain slopes,

others hasten through the hollows of the neighboring valley.”],

behold, sixty thousand Turks, equipped

[Col. 0945C] with swords and shields, came to Nicaea’s aid.

Your people, O Christ, fearing greatly, sigh from the depths of their hearts; renowned in war, they began to pray to God with suppliant voice, that he himself might grant them the trophy.

When the Turks saw our men, they roared. Soon, having formed three divisions, they arranged them so that one part might enter the walls and help the needy [Note: [Col. 0946D] Edition: “and their customs”] with strength and weapons, and furnish aid to those gasping for breath; they themselves would guard the gates and strike our men.

As soon as our side discovered the stratagem on both fronts, our army rushed upon the enemy with a mighty attack. The fighting is fierce, but the action is not equal on both sides: our men kill, while the others perish in enormous numbers.

[Col. 0945D] The rigid spears are broken by powerful thrusts; savage breasts resound, and streams of blood pour forth. Severed heads fly like apples from a trembling tree. No one who descended the mountain afterward returned to it; and what the enemy had foolishly predicted concerning our men, he himself suffers when defeated and cannot withstand the harsh blows. The swift bring matters to an end, while the slow become corpses.

One abandons his shield and flees while he takes up his weapons; another, thrown down, falls because he delayed in taking them up. Why should I describe each event? No one comes to a friend’s aid.

When the Nicaeans had been conquered by God’s mercy, they were afraid and, shaken by the movement of events, were finally compelled to yield. For two months, the reins of the besieged people were handed over to you, commander of Constantinople.

Thousands full of heads are also sent by ship; this is the first service rendered by the brave soldier.

Three hundred thousand Turks attack the Christians.

After these men had thus been defeated, the defeated were left under their king. Our men, joyful at their success and determined not to yield, move the camp and vow fasts to the Lord, by whose gracious aid they had overcome the crime of this people.

But since they would have to travel through difficult country, lest the people should collapse and perish from weariness and thirst, they divided into two companies: one is entrusted to you, Duke Bohemond, and one to you, Count Hugh.

[Col. 0946B] Thus, although our men were strong against hardship but weak in the face of these grievous hills, they crossed them in three days, not without labor. On the fourth day, after the road had been made through the [lacuna], those men, secure and ignorant of what was to come, whom Bohemond had led away from the host entrusted to him, rejoicing and thinking that no serious danger remained, while boasting badly of themselves and recalling their good deeds, insult the Turks and look upon three hundred thousand of them.

The gloomy Turks, however, doubting that they could resist so great a plague, dared not do so and at first avoided battle.

But fearing no death, Bohemond, you draw up a cohort so that the lowly soldier may drive them off with his spear, and you place the camp in orderly fashion beside the streams,

[Col. 0946C] which the local people, greatly hating them, call muddy.

Our men were not yet ready for battle when five hundred thousand Turks, armed and stained with rust,

were carried forward at a gallop of horses. They did not come gradually or in measured ranks, but quickly, advancing like a profane pack of dogs; they mingle with our men and join battle.

Our soldier strikes those mingled with them from a distance, protected by the shield of faith and fearing no weapons. The Turks surrounded our men and flew about at a gallop. Now they pressed forward, now they fled from the Christians. While the Turk flees, the curved bow is loosened. For they fight more with the bow, and not without wounds.

While Bohemond was waging a serious battle with the Turks, and the Turk in turn drove our men back by fleeing, in flight he inflicts a wound and flees at the same time. For the Turks of today are those who in former times were called Parthians, accustomed to trust in arrows shot while fleeing backward.

A large cohort, unaware of this great danger, about eight thousand men distant from the unknown people, was circling the hills and did not think the battle so near. But through an envoy it learned that battle was prepared, an envoy whom Bohemond sent to it, brilliant in counsel.

While the fighting continued and the summoned group delayed, that portion of the Turks whom the farther bank had held crossed over

[Col. 0947A] to carry out the slaughter of our men for which it thirsted. Reaching the Christian tents through places scarcely known, the enemy makes a massacre and seizes the dwellings; it puts to death the weary and those who have suffered many wounds, men guarding the settlements and unable to bear the battle [Note: [Col. 0947D] The edition reads, “now the battle.”].

If they could have died in battle, death would have been an honor. There you would have seen them cut down while clinging to their mothers.

When Bohemond learned this, he sought the camp, leaving the battle under the command of Count Northmannus to the army’s loss, and prepared to help those whom the wicked people had nearly killed.

At once he chose a few men and subdued this foul people with the few; he recovered the tents and the booty, and placed armed men around the tents. He fortified the camp with terrifying soldiers in place of a rampart.

While the two armies fought there, Bohemond on one side,

[Col. 0947B] and Count Northmannus, dangerous in arms, on the other, the Franks, overcome and compelled by excessive fear, fled with Count Northmannus, not without loss,

cruelly tormented by battle [Note: [Col. 0947D] The edition reads, “by death.”], heat, and thirst. And unless, while they fled and the Turks were almost holding the victory, their leader Northmannus had turned them against the enemy by shouting the signal of his own men, that day, full of evils, would have been fatal to our men.

Then the Franks, led by hope of a pleasant refuge, despising [Note: [Col. 0947D] Edition: “looking back.”] death as a good thing in exchange for a better life, turned back to their own men and, scattered around the tents, formed a fortress and again mingled in battle.

While the Turks pressed too hard and our men resisted,

[Col. 0947C] the boys gathered weapons, the clergy sang in order, the brave fought, and the women wept together.

One woman carried her fallen son to the settlements; [Note: [Col. 0947D] This verse is absent from the printed editions.] another drew cups from the streams for the living.

Everyone does something: one covers his companion. Here one flees, there one follows, and another seizes an enemy who has been carried off.

Although our men were almost triumphing and calling upon you, Christ, the Turks overthrow them and mock their fighting.

And just as a wolf, surrounding the villages, seeks little sheep, and when it sees them deceived and not brought back into the folds, slaughters the wretched ones and stores them in its mouth, so the Turks, surrounding our trembling men, killed the one whom they saw outside the fortifications.

What could our men do, except weep over such dangers? [Note: [Col. 0947D] The edition reads, “except bear such dangers.”]

[Col. 0947D] They could neither turn their backs nor fight separately. It is not enough for a people that does not doubt victory that our men had been shut in and dared not fight.

But that prudent group advised a thousand Turks to seek the mountains through which our men had passed. For these were doubtful and suspect matters [Note: [Col. 0947D] The edition reads, “doubtful and fearful”]; the thought that the mountains concealed some men moved the wicked ones.

[Col. 0948A] But an armed horseman, paying no attention to orders, searched the mountains and cruelly killed with the sword nearly a thousand men, women, and unarmed common people, leaving them lifeless and stupefied by excessive fear [Note: [Col. 0947D] The edition reads, “left lifeless and stunned by excessive fear”], delayed at length and burdened with their possessions.

Those who were hiding badly beneath the cliffs [Note: [Col. 0948D] The edition reads, “rocks”] were not concealed from the scouts but perished shamefully.

The Turks are defeated.

Behold, Count Hugh and Duke Godfrey, fearing nothing, urged the brave cohort with entreaties and threats. They hastened in a race and prepared to help their companions. When they saw their weeping companions already failing, they abandoned their horses, although they were unequal in strength; they did not hesitate and did not avoid the flying weapons.

Therefore Duke Godfrey, the star of the commanders, with a few men flies into the midst of the dense people with drawn sword,

[Col. 0948B] and, like a fierce boar that, once its rage is roused, when wounded by a dog's tooth or beaten with a stick or reed, torments the dogs with its teeth [Note: [Col. 0948D] Edition: “pierces”], rushes forward, and breaks the hunting spears.

Thus Godfrey tramples these men and cleaves their ranks. But the count’s companions send many terrible men to the underworld.

Across the bank of the stream they fought at the foot of the slope. After these men had been overthrown and hurled down the slope, the count climbed the hill and filled the stream with blood.

For he himself gave fifteen thousand to death.

But let us recount what, if anything, the count's joined force accomplished [Note: [Col. 0948D] Alternative reading: “if anything”], when all were inflamed [Note: [Col. 0948D] The edition reads, “stretched out”] for battle: the Puy count and the brave Count Raymond, commander of the cohort, together with bold men, as one usually goes to war, came gradually, and new battles were begun by them.

[Col. 0948C] These cut down the right wing, others the left, those who earlier had been scattered by fear and enclosed. A great din arose, and on both sides there was a mighty uproar.

Nor was the bow, tightened with horsehair, loosened with the slightest sound; without it their shots are light enough. Their hope lies only in the running of their horses, so that with one throw the Turk may inflict a double wound when they hurl weapons tipped with serpent poison.

While the fighting continued in this way, our men were driven back three times by the enemy.

[Note: [Col. 0948D] This verse is absent from our manuscript.]

Three times the gentiles were given flight, but they were recalled; they made their customary runs and again inflicted wounds.

But I think they would have yielded [Note: [Col. 0948D] The edition reads, “pressed forward”], and could not have endured the battles, if certain Turks hiding around the mountains had not pressed our men fiercely and killed many.

[Col. 0948D] When our companions perceived them, they decided that the more daring and skillful should undertake the battle and go to the hiding places, where they might first strike in battle [Note: [Col. 0948D] The edition reads, “unexpectedly”] those who were fighting with forks and killing many.

Immediately a thousand men, mighty in spirit and arms [Note: [Col. 0948D] Alternatively, “in years”], eager for glory and under cover of deception, leaving the battle as if fleeing from it,

[Col. 0949A] silently climbed the mountains. But once they had gained the mountain [Note: [Col. 0949D] Edition: “having delayed”], the Christian soldier did not remain silent; the enemy fled, but these men attacked them with swords and broke their bows and arrows.

The horsehair bow stretched under the Lord’s command, the quiver made from raw hide, and the horse, the running, and the cups smeared with gall are of no avail. They are thrown into confusion, killed, and hurled down.

With these men thus scattered and many plunged into the underworld, stunned and seized by fear of the sudden battle, the rest flee after them, compelled to turn their backs.

Therefore our men, recovering their courage, harass the fugitives; the Turks are scattered, flee, and die. Those who had come out later, or were exhausted by the turmoil of battle, rise up more fiercely and press their horses with the spurs.

The Franks lower their poles [Note: [Col. 0949D] Alternatively, “cones”] toward the chests of the prostrate men.

[Col. 0949B] The hoofed horses foam and, sprinkled with blood, smoke; they champ their bits and carry their masters with no little force.

As they rush forward, they strike the fallen; for many Turks lay on the field, killed by swords or the sword. They strive to surpass their equals; their nostrils become no small spectacle.

Stained white with gore, not overcome by dust, each man presses the enemy. But the dark night interrupted our men’s joys and the wretched men’s sad flight.

What the light and slack bow could not do, nor the swift horse suited to long runs, that one untimely and shameful night could do.

For through the hated night, dreadful and dark, the people hostile to the God of Christ, destined to be subjected to the trophy, found hiding places. Therefore, following the darkness, it fled; and through that night the people of Christ lost the enemy.

[Col. 0950A] At last, having followed the savage gentiles safely beneath that same night, the soldier returned to the tents, rich in garments and weapons [Note: [Col. 0949D] The edition reads, “citizens”], and in many camels. Soon the nobles gladly gave their limbs to rest.

When the rising of the sun brought the dawn, they arose. They uncovered their kinsmen, once their relatives but now corpses, poured out groans, and beat their breasts. Each gathered the bones of his kinsman in a small grave.

Some often gave the head of the hostile enemy to the tomb, hoping thereby to remove a recognizable head.

They touched the wounds and looked at the arrows fixed in the injuries; they wept and struggled with compassion.

They also looked upon good horsemen lying face down in the dust, who while alive had lain upon golden coverings.

And throughout the whole day the tents were not moved.

[Col. 0950B] Meanwhile those exhausted and wounded recovered; they were entrusted to the care of physicians, the weapons were collected, the quivers filled, and the reins repaired.

Everything whose use was needed was restored.

When the second light rose and drove away the stars of night, the soldier moved the camp, and the gentile camp followed. But while that soldier of God crossed a certain plain and traveled safely from the enemy, many in the column died from pestilence, heat, and thirst.

Departing from there, secure and fearing nothing, they ravaged the enemy’s lands under a favorable omen. The enemy granted them a safe road and paid tribute in weapons.

Thus, with fear shaken, all Romania lay open, and no one felt punishment until they reached Antioch, a beautiful city spacious in walls, wealth, and extent.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0949]

The Christians surround Antioch with a siege.

[Col. 0949C]

When they reached the walls of the immense city in the month of October, the greater part of the city was surrounded by the crowds. Yet the bridge was first made passable by iron—an obscure or corrupt reading in the text: *pons ... in ferro ... ferro*.

Although they had plundered much and were laden with many things, they drew up their lines and placed their tents between the inexhaustible river and the raised wall.

And because, if they had contended with a fortified and war-experienced people, they would have accomplished nothing by force, they seek by ingenuity what they could not achieve by strength [Note: [Col. 0950D] The edition reads, “whatever they see that might cause harm”]. They hasten to do what each man knows will be useful.

Therefore the army of Christ builds a bridge over the river, by which it might cross if the wicked host should prevail.

Many things are made; axes are made from bronze,

[Col. 0949D] ballistae, leaden missiles, fire-poles, tunnels,

sickles, weapons, torches, a battering ram, and threatening slings. Through craftsmen, many structures are raised to the height of the lofty towers.

The Turks are driven away by Bohemond and the Count of Flanders.

And whatever they prepared, whatever had to be prepared, they attack the walls in vain, while the Turks resist.

[Col. 0950C] Whatever they see our men preparing, they mock as useless. For who could have hoped that one people would overcome Antioch, a city full of so many soldiers, which no wise cleric—or Homer himself, had he lived—could have described?

The weary Christians returned to their own camps and thought that they would be safe inside them at night. But the enemies were also active by night, and, though not tranquil [Note: [Col. 0950D] The edition reads, “secure”], they harmed many of our men.

The very cunning people did not harm them by this trick only once. At night they harassed our men and attacked them at night, not at the closed gates of the hostile company’s camp.

Meanwhile fortune conducted the war lightly, and our people in turn oppressed the wretched nation.

[Col. 0950D] Often the strength of the Turks prevailed over our men [Note: [Col. 0950D] The edition reads, “over our walls”]. When our men were already exhausted and their resources diminished, the Christian foot soldiers were sent into the enemy's territory for booty.

While they wished to plunder the places of the greedy enemy, some plundered and some were killed.

[Col. 0951A] Yet the death of those men, recounted sadly by a few of their companions, makes their companions sad as well.

Then Bohemond, very sorrowful amid these events, humbly asks the aid of divine healing and prepares an ambush for the people who had killed by deceit those seeking food, if they had not been afraid among the mountains.

Accordingly, as before, they go out to seek food.

Bohemond joins the Count of Flanders. The undertaking was announced to the armed men [Note: [Col. 0951D] The edition reads, “was spoken of”], and a thousand were sent ahead. That prudent leader follows.

When the ambushers saw these men plundering, they leapt out immediately from numerous hiding places, shouted insults, and battered the chests of the horses [Note: [Col. 0951D] The edition reads, “turn the horses”]. They strike the armed men. While such battles [Note: [Col. 0951D] The edition reads, “such plunder”] were taking place, Bohemond suddenly disrupted the battle with a small force,

[Col. 0951B] killed many, and did not allow his companions to remain unavenged; there he ended their groans.

Here too the dreadful sword of the Count of Flanders killed many.

Thus the Turks yielded to the weapons of the faithful people. The victors return to the settlements and order the former sorrows to be laid aside [Note: [Col. 0951D] The edition reads, “they hasten to lay them aside”]; they lay them aside, and solemn rites are performed.

That victory provided peaceful times.

Provisions from the villages [Note: [Col. 0951D] Edition: “and from the villages,” less satisfactorily], with no one lying in ambush, were carried to the camps by people fearing nothing.

Winter’s severity afflicts the Christians.

But when a freezing winter full of evils arrived, a storm came and scarcity afflicted our men.

They feared the mountains because of rains and heavy snows [Note: [Col. 0951D] The edition reads, “the mountains swelled”],

[Col. 0951C] and the Armenians, who were accustomed to assist the camp with food, could not, amid the excessive floods, extinguish their excessive grief.

The people whom the hail weighed down wept [Note: [Col. 0952D] The edition reads, “burdened”]. Not only did scanty ice oppress them, but weapons as well.

Some did not reach the harbor of Saint Simeon, which provided a handsome maritime market for every kind of merchandise.

But the champions of faith considered bodily punishments too cheap to matter. They did not exchange their joys for punishments or their good things for torments; their steadfastness of mind did not waver, although their bodies endured harsh pressures.

But all who were able to endure, ready for weapons, scarcely formed a small and weak cohort, and with a small force seized booty across the fields.

Many perish in battles and fasts.

Bohemond plunders Syria and defeats three kings. With provisions, hope returns to the Christians.

[Col. 0951D]

It is possible to enumerate the events endured by the famous youth of the Gauls; but who could recount so many fierce battles, hardships, fasts, cold, and cares?

I say only a few things, sorrowful and not with dry eyes. Of three hundred thousand, as I estimate, scarcely a hundred could then be counted as distinguished in war.

Often indeed they had gladly given their limbs to rest and, free from anxiety, rejoiced in mild weather. But when a wind rose suddenly through the air, they were thrown down by the disturbance of the unpleasant weather.

Hardly, in their sorrow, could they resist the sudden plague. The rains searched out everything, and the camps floated.

Whoever had placed his horse beside him at night wept for it in the morning and dragged its empty body.

Of a thousand soldiers, the one who had earlier been enclosed, because of the excessive plague, did not even possess the honorable name of soldier; reduced to a foot-soldier, he went weeping into the dwellings.

It is shameful to say, but the destitute soldier, himself weeping from hunger, drove away the armed man who was also weeping and perishing from hunger, because he was not sufficient even for himself.

Alas! A father himself denied his son, and a brother his brother, to whom he had been saving provisions, when death came.

[Col. 0952B] While the commanders stood astonished [Note: [Col. 0952D] The edition reads, “stunned”], whom the whole world had sent from every direction, Bohemond, with the Count of Flanders, comforted them and ordered the better warriors to be armed.

That leader chose thirty thousand foot soldiers, and nearly a thousand armed men were equipped with helmets.

These turned their swords against the Syrians. Our men recovered themselves [Note: [Col. 0952D] Edition: “were silent”] by plundering the settlements of Syria,

[Col. 0952D] while rejoicing in the fertility of the gracious land. That blessed people, by stripping Syria’s crops, plundered three admiral commanders—thus kings are called—of Jerusalem, Aleppo, and Damascus.

They attack those rulers, and they in turn surrender their possessions to our men. For they withdrew defeated, and many perished.

[Col. 0952C] Relying on this victory, they return joyfully to the tents. Wealth is given, and the needy rejoice; they think the future will be better and believe that the wall cannot resist.

The best things are believed to be those good things that follow the first evils.

The Christians, despairing of capturing the city, demand that they withdraw from the siege.

After these events, a mountain rising with high walls is leveled above them and adorned with a small fortress. From it a watchman could observe whether the armed city was preparing any stratagem, from the summit of the accessible mass.

Here they expended much strength but could not tear away the naturally fortified castle with numerous forces, for the sons [Note: [Col. 0952D] The edition reads, “faithful ones”] of Christ, sufficiently harassed, were driving the inhabitants from the mountain’s summit with spears.

[Col. 0952D] Meanwhile, their strength broken, they seek aid from the city of Lycea, but did not obtain it.

The victorious English, having taken the city, had given it to Count Northmannus, better than their fathers. Nor did the English people wage the battles of others; rather, by naval warfare [Note: [Col. 0952D] The edition reads, “by equal warfare”], that people possessed the trophy.

This good company, which had acted in the siege, did not share in this kind of requested aid [Note: [Col. 0952D] The edition reads, “twice”].

For the Turkish host, observing the familiar divisions of the terrain,

[Col. 0953A] held the nearby fortresses from which it prevented the Christians from giving aid to our men [Note: [Col. 0953D] The edition reads, “to our man”].

After there was no longer any hope of assistance, fear and shame seized them; their bold spirits froze, and the leaders of the host trembled.

The authors of such great undertakings regretted having entered upon so many labors. They regretted the enterprise and soon withdrew to their own camp.

As they examined what they should do, their minds weakened further, thinking that whatever evils could occur would occur [Note: [Col. 0953D] The edition reads, “fearing”]. These things could happen, but the mind is ignorant of the truth.

The mind understands what is human; at last the nobles give the crowd an empty counsel: that each person should withdraw from the city and protect himself, lest he be killed by a shameful death.

The defeated Turks attempt to renew the battle.

[Col. 0953B] While so many peoples were stunned, rumor suddenly announced the unwelcome matter: a battle was being prepared near the camps.

For the three men mentioned above, defeated in the first engagement, did not doubt that they could break up the assembled troops and the camp tents, and they were still coming silently.

When the stupefied men heard this, as though returning from sleep, one warned another.

Faces grew pale; tumult was heard everywhere. And just as a suddenly violent wind disturbs the small murmurs of a sea not wholly calm, while the swollen sea resounds and opens its mouth, so harsh rumor, reporting sudden events, raises the minds of those lying there and stirs raging spirits driven by anger [Note: [Col. 0953D] The edition reads, “the spirits themselves raging”].

At once a cavalry line advanced from the camps, armed with four hundred and three hundred at once [Note: [Col. 0953D] The edition reads, “four hundred and three hundred”],

[Col. 0953C] not shrinking from approaching the dreadful host [Note: [Col. 0953D] Manuscript: “I may complete it”; perhaps “treachery”].

Then a stiff infantry troop, ready on foot with its right hands, was deployed in the field, resisting in small number; five hundred infantrymen went in it, counted out.

They did not advance all together, but withdrew in five companies [Note: [Col. 0954D] The edition reads, “in one company”]. After covering three leagues, and then two more, they saw from a distance the desired enemies prepared for battle beside the iron bridge. The Turkish forces could not be counted; the power of the eyes could not contain them.

The Turks attack the Christians, by whom they are put to flight.

The enemies, without delay and at that very hour, saw our men and rushed upon them.

[Col. 0953D] Javelins were thrown, and shouts followed the weapons. The pagans pressed forward but were frustrated by an empty throw.

The Turk, rejoicing in his horse but not daring to await close combat, thundered with words and surrounded our men.

Our men stood clustered together in the middle, enclosed on every side. They opposed the Turks, and shields and helmets rang beneath immense blows; sword struck back sword.

Now exhausted and killed in great numbers, the Turks no longer strive in hope of victory but of flight.

Soon, turning their shields, they seek flight, the cause of safety [Note: [Col. 0954D] The edition reads, “they suffer flight”].

[Col. 0954A] The Turk, giving his horse free rein, urges it with the reins. He flees headlong; the earth, driven by his feet, roars.

In the field a sluggish, dust-covered bow lies. One throws away his painted quivers; another takes those left behind. A third frees himself by running in a circular course.

Why should I describe each detail? They overcome the hostile people.

Some scarcely escaped; more perished. While they struggle to cross the ford, they are overcome.

In the battle only a few Christians were cut down and killed by the sword.

The Christians capture the unbelievers’ fortress.

Some gentiles watched this slaughter. They held a certain castle not far from there, but immediately fled and abandoned it.

Our nobles placed guards in it to protect the bridge; afterward they returned,

[Col. 0954B] strengthened by divine aid and having taken a strong revenge.

Their companions welcomed them and rejoiced because of the twofold battle in which the enemies had fallen.

For while the aforementioned men fought, those left behind at the camps won a notable victory over the inhabitants, and many, through God’s power, feared only a few.

The Turks burst out of the city and kill many Christians.

Yet confidence did not leave the bold people, nor did adverse fortune restrain their companions.

Therefore, suddenly emerging from the hollows of the towers, the Turks harassed those carrying provisions to the camps. Lest they should often suffer ruin through such a stratagem, our commanders found a remedy for this.

They decide to build a fortress on the mountain beside the river, near the bridge,

[Col. 0954C] and to guard the bridge.

But the matter was difficult to accomplish for men shaken by war and weakened in strength.

Soon Bohemond quickly mounted his horse and, like a herald, summoned some men from the camps as the stars declined.

The Count of Saint-Gilles joined him as he went.

Trusting, therefore, in good swords [Note: [Col. 0954D] The edition reads, “sons”], they hurry to the gate of Saint Simeon to seek assistance from those who were selling their goods there and favoring our men.

These are the Genoese, the English, and the Pisans who honor Venice, all skilled in naval warfare.

While the commanders were away, the rest hoped to grow sluggish, provided the inhabitants did not attack and harm the city.

At once, with their spirits inflated by the wind of lightheartedness, our men rashly approached the city bridge.

[Col. 0954D] Thus, with a band of foolish people acting without counsel, the soldier foolishly challenges the hostile Turks near the walls.

Suddenly shouts arise from the gates; the unprotected foot soldiers, whose javelins can scarcely be avoided, rush out, and the swift young men, crowned with ribbons, leap forth.

From a distance they hurl weapons with arms extended on both sides.

One throws stakes, another stones, another weapons; but one groans while being dragged, and another is struck by a thousand arrows.

Clouds of missiles dim the eyes of our men,

[Col. 0955A] and those constrained to yield to cruel death, who had so often conquered so many, first learned this here [Note: [Col. 0955D] The edition reads, “after this”].

They flee with loosened reins and lose much blood.

[Note: [Col. 0955D] These two verses are absent from the printed editions.]

The Parthian crushes the broken bows.

Here one groans from a wound in the foot, here another from a wound in the face; there a man, looking upon veins emptied of blood, slips between the reins and bites the sand filled with the dead.

No one turns his horse’s head until flight finds the bridge, which, as I said, they themselves had earlier built for the ships. But there remain men of better courage, troops that had not yet forgotten their honor.

They defend themselves with shields and hold back the enemies [Note: [Col. 0955D] The edition reads, “and the enemy”].

While many, trembling, delay in climbing onto the bridge, they are shamefully overwhelmed and die, drowned in the river.

The Turks rejoice; our men weep; they seek the camps.

[Col. 0955B] Nor was the savage enemy thus exhausted; it lies in ambush.

While an excessively cunning force comes up against the line that, at the commander’s urging, was coming with a strong and numerous escort, the enemies also overcome it and kill three thousand infantrymen of the cavalry host. One escaped by hiding among the hills and avoiding the battle.

Without delay, the Persians, rejoicing as they watched these things from the towers, laughed at our men who held the camps and announced the matter by signals, noise, shouts, and hymns.

The battle is renewed. The Turks are cut down.

Therefore the fearless man of Flanders, Duke Godfrey, Robert, Stephen, Tancred, Hugh, and Statinus, who while he lived lacked neither a nose nor praise,

together with the other brave men, arm themselves. Behold, the companies advance

[Col. 0955C] and weep, because they often labor in vain.

Each man desires to die, unless the battle should yield honor.

Death, unwelcome and grievous, would be welcome and gentle to him.

Their comforter restores their minds [Note: [Col. 0955D] The edition reads, “having restored”], and the bishop of Puy asks with earnest prayers that they not despair, because believers would overcome; he marks the necks of the highest flock with the cross of the king.

Encouraged by many words and ready either to face death or to overcome, the good nobles and champions of the faith hasten there.

They hasten to the place where they hope to meet the enemy. Hugh, leader of the Franks, advances first, silently and without conflict, and seizes one who is unsuspecting [the object is unstated in the source], while the Christian scouts have been moved a little away.

They see the commanders’ lofty standards standing like a grove.

[Col. 0955D] Without delay, Godfrey separates the wings along the ladders.

Behold, the leader, defeated and left over from the slaughter, suddenly emerged from the mountains. With the recovered soldiers bearing lowered standards and seeking flight, he recognized the standards he had seen and drove away fear.

He orders his standards to halt and the trumpets to sound.

Each rejoices to see the standards of the companions [Note: [Col. 0955D] The edition reads, “shields”],

[Col. 0956A] and the spirits of the men return to each other.

Victory recently won sharpens the Persians. The warhorse rears and impatiently carries its master.

The bowstrings curve like moons; now the arrogant Turks bend their weapons, now the horses leap like deer, now the harsh trumpet sounds and the air resounds.

Now the hollow rocks return the voices they have received, doubled.

Everywhere they fight; the fortune of war wanders.

For now the enemies turned their backs [Note: [Col. 0955D] The edition reads, “the Persians”], now our forces are put to flight; Bellona turns her whip through the war [Note: [Col. 0955D] The edition reads, “fortune”].

A missile is hurled in different directions, not with the same purpose. One aims a javelin at those nearby, another at those far away.

The long-haired youth, skilled not in repelling but in yielding, is poured onto the plain and wears away the air with an empty cast.

[Col. 0956B] And lest the people conspicuous for their hair win the victory, freedom of flight is closed to them.

Therefore the nobles of God, joining their shields in an ordered [Note: [Col. 0956D] The edition reads, “on every side”] line, so enclosed the men as a forest encloses mountain summits [the syntax is corrupt; the edition reads “had advanced”].

Crowds stand everywhere. Godfrey threatens the rear from the city; Bohemond stands face to face. Therefore the battle is savage, and all the less suited to arrows.

The Parthian turns his horse; nowhere does the place allow his limbs freedom.

The blood of the Persians stains the swords of the Franks.

The Turks, inexperienced with the sword [Note: [Col. 0956D] The edition reads, “inexperienced men”], strive with sluggish effort to make their way through the smallest opening in the field, so that an entrance might appear and the shore might touch the crack.

They exert themselves sufficiently, but the packed ranks restrain them; the enclosed defeated man cannot get past them.

[Col. 0956C] His senseless fury stands still; there is no road to safety. He is not allowed to use javelins or his customary winding maneuvers.

The bold and the timid [Note: [Col. 0956D] The edition reads, “fearful”] perish together. To this one, fighting in the battle is forbidden; to that one, faithful flight is denied.

An enormous crowd is confined within a small circle.

While the Turk repeatedly raises a blow against the opposing side, his companions having been pierced through the ribs, the enemy helps one part.

Breasts rub against breasts, limbs against limbs.

Our men alone wage the battle; the Turks suffer it.

Parthian and Arab, bent forward [Note: [Col. 0956D] The edition adds “Indian,” omitting “bent forward”], willingly succumb to the sword.

Our men cannot cast down as many as the dense ranks die. The earth, wet with blood,

[Col. 0956D] closes the road, because kindred blood had already filled the deepest cracks, and the gaps have no room to open.

When the dust yielded, suppressed by the flood of blood [Note: [Col. 0956D] Manuscript: “at its withdrawal”],

our men saw through the open field the sure sign of victory: streams made of blood, and living men supporting the bodies they had raised [Note: [Col. 0956D] The edition reads, “upright”].

[Col. 0957A] And since they had been allowed so much in the slaughter of the guilty, the foolish peoples considered themselves guilty.

When the soldier saw the eastern fields swimming in blood, he yielded and wished [Note: [Col. 0957D] The edition reads, “feared”] to renew his exhausted strength.

When that gathered cloud of men broke its formation, it rushed back upon itself with turned reins, spurring its weary horses, and there was no new slaughter.

Here one crushes a brother, there another a father; they wage civil wars, and the master presses down upon an overturned saddle.

And just as, in pools, when a snake is repeatedly released [Note: [Col. 0957D] The edition reads, “a stream”; the transmitted syntax is uncertain], the waters held back by the broken-open source suddenly burst forth—the first flee and the rest follow,

they impede one another, while others seem to be trying to fight.

So the unsound crowd prepares itself badly for the plain,

[Col. 0957B] and Duke Bullicus [perhaps the duke of Boulogne] flees to the bridge, trampling the enemy [Note: [Col. 0957D] The edition reads, “public”].

It occupies the bridge’s entrance and prevents retreat.

With bloodied sword and the people heavily overcome, anger, place, and sword fight; each gave strength to the commander [Note: [Col. 0957D] The edition reads, “whatever gave strength to the commander”].

This strengthens their courage, that obstructs, the other slaughters.

Duke Godfrey—the Turk in the midst [incomplete source fragment].
cuts.

The leader, the hope of our people, confusion and grief to the Turks,

Cuts down horses and horsemen, and the waves receive the corpses.

What neither Tydeus nor Capaneus is read to have done [Note: [Col. 0957D] Another reading: “Canapeus.”],

What neither Aeacides [Note: [Col. 0957D] The edition reads “Acaci.”], nor Hector, nor Diomedes

Could do, nor did we conceal a deed worthy of report.

The dread Arab, terrifying the nobles by his very bulk

And with much equipment, whirling his sword in a radiant circle,

Carried by a swift horse with headlong speed,

Stopped before the leader. He thinks to extinguish this light,

And raises his blow higher against the unconquered head.

The angry leader takes precautions and stands protected behind his shield.

Soon he raises his flashing sword [Note: [Col. 0958D] The edition reads: “He cuts with the sword.”] and strikes the enemy;

He smashes his face and head, and all his vital parts fall.

He scatters and bursts the fat, and breaks the spine together with the chest.

Thus the truncated man falls, divided into two halves,

And his parts, shattered into a thousand pieces, lie upon the shield.

One part falls, the other clings to the horse and is dragged on its back.

The rider is the master of his horse, though this is no rightful booty.

Jesus, by one man thus a great ruin—and not a single ruin—was made.

[Col. 0957D] If I wished to recount briefly the deaths of the defeated

People, and what deaths a thousand cohorts suffered,

What the count Northmannus accomplished, or mighty Hugh,

Or the Flemish force, I would, in my own judgment, be vain.

Neither Maro nor Macer [Note: [Col. 0958D] Macer was a poet who wrote about the powers of herbs]

Could express what the fierce Tancred accomplished there;

and their deeds would lack words.

The son of King Cassianus fell.

[Col. 0958A]

Here their glory fell, and no trophy

Afflicted the citizens more deeply. Here [Note: [Col. 0958D] The edition reads “thus.”] the right hand of our men,

Dead but sated with the blood of their warriors, revived;

Here the astonished nobles were slaughtered;

Here the great pillars of the city fell, broken;

Here too the son, chosen in vain as king,

Fell—the son of the great King Cassianus.

The Antiochene river stood full of bodies,

And the water, changing its pallor, imitated redness.

Five thousand were killed upon the bridge’s pavement,

And a pavement was made from the bodies of the dying.

Now, wearied and burdened with much spoil,

At night the joyful leaders return and give their limbs to rest.

But their senses keep watch, and they seem to drive away the enemy,

And each man moves his hands as though his sword-hilt were absent.

[Col. 0958B] After the bright day shone forth, our men shone in their garments;

They distributed the bronze among themselves as victors.

Then the captured horses were counted, and there were seven

Thousand; then the nobles set up an equal number of horsemen.

When these things had been accomplished, they gave Raymond

A castle established with tall towers and a solid foundation.

While success continued, while the dice of fate
