More and more engulfed the heathen, the bolder and better-prepared men

Were summoned outside the camp by the leaders.

Each man, rejoicing to encounter the enemy’s loss [Note: [Col. 0958D] The edition reads “and now.”],

Was led to the plunder, though with no great urging.

They hurried on and, wading across the river beneath the city,

Captured mules and male mules, and many camels,

And suddenly seized five thousand animals,

[Col. 0958C] With as many more on the other side, although the townsmen were hurling missiles.

Here too, where the young men had seized the booty, a certain castle

Was marked out, and an old rampart was repaired.

It was entrusted to Tancred under a happy omen;

For the guarding of the smallest wall

Foretold the future: it was a sign of the city’s guardian.

Now the besieged citizen fears, and the suppressed uproar

Of the attacking people, who are plotting against him,

Afflicts him deeply; but scarcity of provisions

Pressed more sharply, because he could scarcely get out.

Peace is secured for a time. Gualo is treacherously killed. The Christians swear to continue the siege for fourteen years.

After this the Persians decided among themselves

That peace should be maintained with the worshipers of Christ for a time.

[Col. 0958D] Meanwhile, the manner in which they should surrender themselves was debated.

Thus, in the presence of all, peace was confirmed for a time.

Meanwhile the concealed gates were unbarred;

The soldier, his fear laid aside, circles the hostile walls,

And at last, with their bows safely unstrung,

The Parthians mocked our men and went toward the camp.

But Gualo, a brave man, while he was enjoying the daylight in the gardens,

Too forgetful of the treacherous people who were pretending all this,

Was taking pleasure in the scene when their ill-founded faith was betrayed.

He fell, indeed, while he looked upon places resembling Tempe.

The laws and pledged faith that had been given were violated by the man’s death;

As soon as the citizen had deceived him, he withdrew into the city.

When the graceful Umberga heard the news of the funeral,

The daughter once married to Count Hugh, now married to Gualo,

She grew pale. She tore her cheeks with bold fingernails,

And was supported, surrounded by bands of matrons.

With her right hand she tears her hair; but what she tears is tearing her;

And her delicate hand is cut by the delicate hair.

Her suppressed voice, overcome by grief, left her lifeless for a long time [Note: [Col. 0959D] The edition reads “leaves her.”]

But at last a path is scarcely opened for her voice, and she says:

Has God endured so great a calamity to fall upon his people,

More hostile to me than to anyone?

Has the glory of the Franks fallen, that greatest enemy

[Col. 0959B] Of the enemies, he who was my hope and salvation for his own?

His right hand, never weary in war, languishes in grievous death [Note: [Col. 0959D] The edition reads: “Alas, who will give me, wretched woman, leave to depart this life?”]

He languishes, and Gualo, my life, has fallen.

Wretched woman that I am, I did not perform the wretched duty;

When you fell, I fell with you as your equal.

Alas for me! I did not warm, close, or wash

Your mouth, eyes, face—with clothing, hand, or tears.

You—you certainly, I remember, used to swear to me

That you would avoid ambushes more carefully.

But what the treacherous people could not take from you in war,

They took from you by deceit: your blessed life.

[Col. 0960A] [Note: [Col. 0960D] These two verses are absent from the printed editions.] What shall I do, living far from my homeland and far from my father?

What can a fragile woman do, following the camp?

Pierce me, you who possess compassion; turn the Parthians’ weapons

Against me, wretched woman; death is a light punishment for me.

Death, death is a light punishment, if I am joined to Gualo in death,

If I am not to become prey to the savage Turk.

Evrardus, a brother, consoles us in our mourning,

And restrains the heavy groans with gentle speech.

Thus, amid varying events, our countrymen

Conducted a long siege beside the hostile city.

Between the worshipers of Christ and the enemies of Christ’s name,

A harsh battle was prolonged near ten mountains.

The former pressed on, trusting in heavenly strength;

The latter resisted, relying on open deceit.

[Col. 0960B] They hoped either that our men, exhausted,

Would abandon their often-frustrated labors in the midst of them,

Or that myriads of the Persian people would be present for them,

Like locusts that devour everything in their way.

When this report became known, the blessed company

Brought the sacred pledges into view before the city.

There the siege was sworn for seven years,

And again for as many more, unless heavenly power

Should open the walls before them—the power that cut off

The citizens’ empty hope and inflicted excessive fear.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0959]

The people of Edessa send an embassy to the Christians.

[Col. 0959C]

While such varied events were taking place in Syria,

And evils or blessings were distributed now on one side, now on the other,

A suppliant embassy came to our heroes,

Seeking ministers of counsel and assistance,

And especially addressed the noble name of the leader,

A name spread throughout the whole earth by flying report.

But why and from where this embassy had come

The supplied narrative remains to explain.

Between two rivers lies a very rich land,

Famous among all peoples for the Tigris and Euphrates.

Retaining in Greek the name “Mesopotamia,”

It preserves, in its [lacuna], the significance of its name.

It seems to lie only [lacuna] from one river

[Col. 0959D] As much as [lacuna] can be traversed on foot in seven days.

Among the many cities that it contains in its bosom,

An ancient, powerful, splendid city, rich in resources,

Stands out, plainly as old as ancient Babylon.

For at the time when Semiramis built the quivered citadel of Chaldaea,

This city too was founded and shone forth;

Now called Rahasia through corruption of its name,

It once bore the ancient name Edessa.

It lies beside Assyrian Harran, six thousand [units] away,

Hated by Roman commanders because of the death of Crassus,

In which the ancient patriarch Abraham lived.

When he had escaped, rescued by divine power,

From the Chaldaean flame in which his brother was burned,

He was soon ordered by God’s voice to depart from there.

But let the text concerning Edessa, already begun, now be resumed.

In it that blessed Abgarus once held the kingdom,

Made illustrious by the letter of the Lord Christ [Note: [Col. 0960D] A note concerning Christ’s letter to Abgarus.],

And relieved from the torments of his ancient disease.

That letter remained there for many years,

And protected the walls from every hostile force.

For if barbarian fury reached that place,

A baptized boy would read it aloud from the lofty citadel;

Then either the fierce people would return to peace,

Or, touched by divine terror, would flee.

[Col. 0960D] Here also Thaddeus, approved among the Seventy,

Gave the rule of faith and came to rest.

Here too, it is believed, the body of Thomas,

Who felt Christ’s wounds and by doubting removed

The guilt of doubt from us,

Was brought from the regions of the Indians,

And here was heaped with great honors.

Once this land had [lacuna] love of Christ,

It never allowed its religion to grow cold,

Nor did it for a moment tolerate yielding to schismatics;

[Col. 0961A] It maintained the integrity of Catholic discipline,

And therefore endured many evils arising from the pagan condition,

And the savage impiety of heresy.

But this was the greatest and first cause of its hatred:

That a host of Christ’s people, coming into the region of Syria,

Was battering the city of Antioch with various conflicts.

Nor could they defeat them in a great battle,

Nor even drive them from the walls of the besieged city.

Hence arose heavy anger against the entire people of the devout,

And the desire to destroy their name.

For this reason, around lofty Edessa, where people were gathering,

They devastated all the fertility of the region.

Neighbors gathered there from every side,

And people from far away were summoned there by the spur of rumor.

[Col. 0961B] They shook towns, countryside, cottages, and castles;

They carried off mothers, fields, men, and animals.

Sometimes fighting also took place at those gates;

Mutual [lacuna] wounds burned from the weapons.

The exhausted citizens thought it not useless

To seek assistance from the worshipers of Christ.

For this reason the embassy already mentioned,

Sent for this purpose, entered the Frankish camp.

They displayed their fellowship in the religion of Christ,

And, since they had always preserved the integrity of their faith,

They maintained that these grave troubles had come upon them [lacuna],

And that aid ought rightly to be given them through the Christians.

They especially urged the person of the leader,

For they knew him to be [lacuna] more formidable.

An alliance is made with Edessa, whose guardianship is entrusted to Baldwin.

[Col. 0961C]

These things moved the compassionate hearts of the nobles.

After much investigation they considered what ought to be done.

They believed it would thereafter be useful to them

If support were provided to the affairs of the Edessans by their own people.

Thus they would join many to themselves in social treaties,

Would gain great praise from this,

And would spread their fear far and wide,

If, while maintaining the present siege,

They granted auxiliary help to distant peoples.

When this reasoning, and reasoning of other kinds, had been approved,

Ardor seized everyone, and they prayed to act more vigorously at once.

But because the leader’s greater concern was to crush

The thunderbolts of the present people, it drew him away from allied warfare.

[Col. 0961D] He decided that the dearest pledge he could give on his own behalf

Was to send his own brother to those who were asking.

With him he sent as much of the army as he thought appropriate,

To bring assistance to those being ravaged.

This was finally his younger brother,

Who later ruled the scepter of Jerusalem honorably after him.

Then, setting out along roads of great length,

Divided, in fact, into ten days’ journeys,

They at last reached the city so often mentioned.

They inflicted a fierce slaughter upon its devastators.

The Arsacids, defeated and unwilling to fight at close quarters,

Fled, casting aside their bows as useless,

Unable to extend the untried [lacuna],

And placed their whole hope of safety in their swift feet.

[Col. 0962A] None escaped except the man who hid from the Frankish wounds.

Nor did the man who leapt from his saddle ever recover it.

Nor did a wound coming [lacuna] the outer parts of the skin,

But, by slashing and thrusting, [lacuna] the soul.

Nor was it surprising that they feared the Gauls’ weapons,

And, after their chests had been struck too often, protected their backs.

Since everything had yielded to the valor of those men,

And the glory of the heathen had been held only in battle,

They were accustomed to wage wars with the Gauls

For the sake of mere survival, often considering flight their victory.

Those whom they remembered had defeated Crassus at his death,

And had, after taking the standards, sent them beneath their yokes:

While the Euphrates overwhelmed the Roman people under many names,

And the Tigris carried many corpses away to their lands and gave them back. Therefore, when the enemies had been driven back,

[Col. 0962B] And were hiding their faces in blind caverns,

The entire region was pacified and firmly established,

With no malignant appearance mingling with the joy;

The ruler of the city adopted the leader’s brother,

And, as a father strives to bind a son wholly to himself,

He assigned him the land and subjected the whole region,

Making the people themselves join their hands to his agreements.

The city’s joyful face was crowned, and the city sang.

Its rejoicing harmonized with the stars in various melodies.

Every day a crowd hastened to the lofty palace.

United, they vied to learn our law,

And peace and harmony were poured out upon all the citizens.

They settle disputes [lacuna] everywhere;

The recruit exercises military service under a fixed judge.

Here the horseman, there the foot soldier, moves the columns in a straight circuit.

[Col. 0962C] Black hunger is driven away; abundance reigns among all,

And common goodness allows no one to remain needy.

The people burn with excessive love for our leader,

Nor can their eyes and ears be sufficiently filled by seeing and hearing him.

They consider themselves destined to be fortunate under such a judge.

In him nothing but peace and goodness could be seen;

In him the honor of military service and of virtuous courage

Could commonly serve as an example to everyone.

For just as Paul became all things to all people,

So he was accommodating to everyone with measured gentleness:

Brave toward the brave, almost a companion to the weak,

Rejoicing with the joyful and grieving with the sorrowful.

He was generous to the generous, almost sparing toward the few.

Gentle toward the gentle, harsh toward those swollen with savagery,

[Col. 0962D] Adapting himself to all with wondrous restraint,

So that, as in a mirror, each person saw himself in him.

The king of Edessa plots Baldwin’s death.

To this enemy of the divine creation, who was watching these things,

Love could not exist, since he was the father of envy.

Therefore, when he had stirred up the fuel of inborn hatred

And gathered the poison of his impiety into weapons,

It moved the ruler of the city, who had previously rejoiced in this,

Toward envy and excessive grief of mind.

Whatever he saw growing in the people’s love for Baldwin,

He hoped, under the command of fear, would diminish his own standing.

Thus, falling into the perverse doctrine of an unrighteous heir

And fearing that he would be driven from the summit of the kingdom by him,

He sought by what kind, appearance, method, or device

He might roll him toward destruction and a pit—

This man whom, with lowered prayers and gifts,

He had previously begged to come to his aid,

And who, as guardian, had restored to him a homeland utterly lacking a protector,

Almost collapsing before the evil enemy’s sword and fire,

Groaning from every side beneath slaughter and plunder,

And had made it fearless through supreme effort.

If he succeeded, he thought the result would be the retention of his scepter;

If not, he despaired of gaining even a moment of life.

And so perverse was his mind and envy

That, although he wished to be called and to be a Christian,

He considered it beneath him to have approached the Christians,

And grieved that his safety had been achieved through them,

Preferring to be subject without honor to idolaters

Rather than to have entered into an allied pact with Christ’s servants.

He makes a pact with unbelievers.

[Col. 0963B]

But because the people’s love favored Baldwin

With excessive fervor—the man for whom this evil one was preparing a deadly plan—

He feared to reveal openly what he carried in his mind.

Therefore, having found envoys as wicked as himself,

He invited neighboring enemies, driven away by Christ’s soldiers,

To return to their own fields.

He told them that they should regret having taken foreign allies,

That he would send those allies to them under the pretext of war,

And would order his own men, at the first threshold of battle,

To abandon them by fleeing and retreating to the rear.

If the Christians remained, prevented by shame from fleeing,

Then all could perish together in a single death.

The Parthians exulted, receiving what they desired,

And hastened to be present so as to carry out his evil wishes.

He sharpened our men, who were wholly unaware of such a thing,

And gave them companions who were his partners in treachery.

Yet he did not attach even one of the citizens to them,

So that the wicked undertaking might not be exposed by any agreement.

Companies recruited from outside entered the camp,

Ordered to yield in everything to the native leaders.

Our men advanced eagerly to their customary exercises;

The others came against them with their legions drawn up.

At the first encounter the Gauls pierced the middle of the ranks;

They struck down and overthrew them, and a way was opened by spurs and force.

But after they had obscured the opposing ranks with hostile weapons,

And the battle was renewed with turned reins,

Behold, they saw their allies plainly committing treachery:

They were scattering and turning their backs, with no one pursuing them.

Then, when the deceit had been understood through the obvious signs,

They encouraged one another and placed their lives in their hands.

Embracing their shields, they draw their swords more fiercely,

And deliver powerful blows at close quarters and while seated.

They know that life depends upon their hands and weapons,

But on their feet there is only the pay of unarmed death.

They prefer to fall nobly in battle beneath wounds

Rather than give their necks to the savage chains of pagans.

They spare neither their right hands nor their weapons;

There is no place here for light javelins and arrows.

They see the Parthians wandering around and hurling missiles,

While our men are now properly fighting for the defense of their lives.

They consider what the situation was, since no praise would be sung for them

If they too died together with these dying men.

Unable to conquer, they abandon the field and flee,

Leaving the men fierce though death had been decreed for them.

[Col. 0964A] Thus, when safety had been despaired of, it was recovered through fighting,

So that the hope of wickedness was reduced to nothing and to dung.

Baldwin considers withdrawing.

The excellent leader addresses his brave companions,

Who by their own valor had returned from the pit of death.

It is never safe to leave behind a company

That has been nourished by the trophies of faith

Mixed among barbarian bands,

A people that offers cups of death beneath a smiling appearance.

Nevertheless, he orders these treaties to be displayed before the assembled troops,

So that all may know them and approve them, if they seem good to everyone.

At his word the whole assembly is quickly summoned,

And this complaint is soon made known to them.

They declare in conclusion that they have fulfilled the reason for which they were sent,

And that the time had come for them to revisit the Antiochene camp.

[Col. 0964B] If afterward they should ask for assistance and not deserve it,

They should not deny that this was being done to them according to their merits.

Because of the aid, they had been treated with death and had almost perished.

They owed the fact that they still lived no gratitude to these men;

They remained alive through Christ and their own right hands.

Therefore they would withdraw and seek better agreements.

But the people, after killing the treacherous king, retain him.

After these words they load themselves with what had to be carried,

And with whatever they themselves had acquired through heavy warfare.

Arranged in companies, they turn the war bands back,

And hasten to depart from the badly purchased kingdom.

At once lamentation arises throughout the entire people.

For, since the people had not known of this man’s guilt,

They cry that they are wretched, helpless, lacking judgment,

And cruelly left without a defender.

[Col. 0964C] After enough had been said—whatever grief and fear,

Their companions, had required to be said—

A question immediately arises concerning the conduct of the war.

Fervent complaint asks what had been the reason for the flight.

At first they threaten sword and death in silence,

Unless truthful answers are soon given them.

No one willingly and silently pays another’s sins.

Thus our men report that the king had commanded this by force.

Then they explain all the schemes of that evil man,

And for what reason he had instructed them to act together.

There is no delay: the people’s crowd gathers at the lofty palace,

And they conduct a judicial inquiry with the king.

Because he did not adequately clear himself and the charge of deceit was exposed,

His head was soon severed from his purple-clad neck.

[Col. 0964D] Then they immediately send ambassadors to the tents,

And, weeping, beg that he return to counsel them.

Although unwilling, the leader, overcome by much pleading,

Was brought back to the lofty walls for the sake of consultation.

As soon as he had been received through the gates and walls,

The entire company of the senate quickly surrounded him.

All clear themselves of the crime of treachery;

All lament the evils of their wicked suspicion,

Which had removed from the leader’s mind his kindness toward them,

Although nothing had been done by them to cause him to depart.

All beg him, with prayers and abundant tears,

Not to disgrace them afterward with shameful infamy,

Not to abandon them from the protection of his compassion,

Nor to wish to expose them to deadly dangers,

But to love their nobles above all things,

[Col. 0965A] And not to be indignant at remaining among them as their ruler.

He denies that he can be ruler over the man

At whose invitation he had come to the city,

Saying that he was grateful that they had cleared themselves before him,

But that he did not wish to retain their companionship.

They immediately show him what had been done,

And what requital they had received for the crime of treachery.

They display the head and offer it as a pledge of their love,

Since faithful vengeance had taken it for violated faith.

Then they join vows to vows and prayers to prayers,

And prepare to use force if his fixed decision is not bent.

The leader was astonished that so great an alliance should seek him,

And that the people, so stern on behalf of their lord, should show such ferocity.

He consults the company of his allies concerning what ought to be done;

They all praise the offered opportunity to ascend the throne.

[Col. 0965B] He enters the lofty citadel amid the joy of all,

And receives everywhere the terms of their oath.

Thus he establishes the entire people in his treaties,

And rules the defended city by his own virtues.

The king of Babylon sends a treacherous embassy to the Christians besieging Antioch.

When these matters had been settled, and rumor had made them known,

While the siege kept our men at the pleasant city,

Another embassy came to the heroes from the citadels

Of Babylon, and it was not free from treachery.

This Babylon, which is now inhabited,

Lies far from the climate of Chaldaean Babylon.

For the former extends toward the north, while the latter,

Facing the southeast wind, crosses the lands of Memphis.

The Euphrates washes the former with rushing waters;

The Nile makes the latter fertile with black sands.

After Nimrod had laid its foundations

And passionately desired to raise a tower to the heavens,

Semiramis built the former, equal in its square sides,

With each side measuring sixteen thousand [units],

Thus having a circuit of sixty thousand [units],

Its four sides together completing the whole circuit.

Surrounded on every side by walls of baked brick,

It rose to a height of two hundred gigantic feet.

It was thickened with twenty and thirty [courses],

And, in addition, resounded with so many bronze gates.

In its midst it enclosed a proud tower,

Which Scripture reports that the insolent people built,

When, coming from the eastern quarter after the Flood,

They found this open plain in the middle of the earth.

Immediately delighted by its spacious level,

They resolved to build this tower up to the summits of heaven.

And when it had already risen to four thousand [units]

And was equally broad and spacious on every side,

Divine piety cut down this folly,

Weakened the single language into many,

And thus the empty presumption of their work was interrupted,

Since their speech ran on without being understood by one another.

Constructed in this way, it flourished for many ages,

Commanding many kings and peoples.

It practiced many evils and repeatedly committed every cruelty,

Blinding kings and chaining nobles and peoples.

It violated God’s temples, defiling sacred vessels through idols,

And gave the bodies of the saints to fire and wild beasts,

[Col. 0966A] Until, under Cyrus, who ruled the Medes and Persians,

With the supreme God subjecting many kingdoms to him,

It suffered the fate of what it had done: it was captured and destroyed.

Plundering, it was plundered; taking captives, it was exiled.

And, in accordance with the prophecies of the sacred prophets,

It became a dwelling-place of many kinds of monsters.

But after Cyrus had been killed by a Scythian sword,

His son Cambyses imitated his father.

He founded the Babylon that is now inhabited,

And subjected Jews, Arabs, and Ethiopians to himself.

Thus from then until now Egyptian Babylon has ruled,

And has confined the kingdoms serving around it.

The treacherous ruler of this place sent distinguished ambassadors

To our men at Antioch.

The first of them was then second only to the king,

[Col. 0966B] A good and prudent man, not wicked in understanding.

Therefore, unaware of deceit and not conscious of the ambush,

He simply announced what he had been ordered to say.

He explained to our men that his king, who had been reading of their achievements,

Sent them many greetings.

Jerusalem, he said, had now been brought under his rule,

And for its sake these men had undertaken so much labor.

He wished some of our men to come to him quickly,

To share his sight, conversation, and food,

If either reason or the propriety of religion

Should persuade him that his association ought to favor our people.

It might now be possible for him to reject the monstrous pagan rites

And be the first to worship Christ after laying aside his diadem.

Then Jerusalem would be entirely open to them,

[Col. 0966C] And the holy tomb, and all honor, would yield to them.

Then the palm trees would offer innocent branches to his men,

And the fields would grant ears of grain suitable for the praises of God.

The Christians send an embassy to the king. The king orders the ambassadors to be beheaded, but, when their leader resists, they are spared.

Our men exulted, suspecting nothing hostile here,

And expecting that the Lord’s name would henceforth be celebrated.

That prince too, kind-minded toward the others,

Stood firm and encouraged them, promising that all would prosper.

For he was determined to escort them safely,

And had resolved in his heart to return them honorably and unharmed.

Therefore, among the foremost men powerful in the glory of war,

And among the distinguished men bearing clear insignia,

They summoned leaders, honorably adorned many,

[Col. 0966D] Armed them with every useful instrument of war,

And ordered ambassadors to travel with the ambassadors.

They declared that they would say or do whatever was appropriate.

What need is there of many words? Joined by a treaty of friendship,

Our men and the king’s men all entered the ships.

Carried across many divisions of the great sea,

They were at last brought near the Babylonian walls.

The leader of the embassy arranged for some men to go ahead,

And to report in due order to his king what had been done.

He, devising treachery, sent back such an order:

They were not to lead the Franks to the walls in the light of day,

Nor allow an alien hand to observe the city’s position,

Lest this warlike people raise its courage against him.

Fearing deceit, the ambassador obeyed, but with a sorrowful heart

He led the men inside the walls in the silent night.

[Col. 0967A] The evil prince, unwilling to allow us to stand before him,

Ordered all of them to be led into a certain hall.

There he kept them enclosed, advancing nowhere,

For no small time, sighing and giving vent to their distress.

Yet he ordered abundant food to be provided for them,

Wishing in this way to conceal the agitation of his wicked heart.

At last the guide, pressed by their complaints

And deeply disturbed by the suspicion of wrongdoing,

Approached the ruler and asked what the reason was

For ordering him, as ambassador of the Franks, to approach the camp

And to lead away distinguished men whom he wished removed

From his own sight.

If he was perhaps planning to inflict some evil upon them,

He could not endure being a partner in treachery;

But he would strive with the utmost risk to his life

[Col. 0967B] To ensure that his embassy proceeded entirely in the proper manner.

Either let him allow the magnificent knights to stand before him,

And grant them honors worthy of their homeland,

Or let him cause them, furnished from his own resources, to return to the camp of their allies.

When he had displayed such things through powerful companions,

The ruler was astonished, fearing to offend so many.

He ordered the men to be summoned, and, admitting them to conversation

Through an interpreter,

Asked who their companions were, what names they bore,

And what authority they possessed in their own country.

They gave fitting and truthful answers,

And impressed further increase of fear upon his frightened mind.

He concealed his fear beneath a feigned and smiling face,

And, examining the men’s gestures and appearance,

[Col. 0967C] Advised them to take possession of the open fields while armed,

And to demonstrate what Gaul could accomplish in war.

They obeyed; swiftly and eagerly they took up their insignia,

Mounted their horses, and formed two companies.

Their faces were visible beneath helmets, their bodies covered with cuirasses;

They took up flashing shields and shining spears.

They seized rough weapons, imitating Mars in battle,

And displayed their homeland’s skill through varied movements.

They engaged one another, skilled at withdrawing and at returning,

Now far apart, now close together,

Now giving their backs in flight, now pursuing those who had turned,

Impeding their movements with charges and circles within circles.

Now, as if with hostile weapons, they advanced toward mutual wounds;

But in reality everything was safe for those who possessed mastery.

The inhabitants of the Nile watched; the wicked king himself watched,

[Col. 0967D] And their senses were dulled by icy fear,

Because, if such a people of Frankish origin

Should overrun their lands after capturing Jerusalem,

Nothing seemed capable of resisting their valor,

[Col. 0968A] Since violent war was almost a game to them.

Then he summoned one unlike himself, who held the highest place after him,

And eagerly sought to make him rage through his reasoning.

He begged him to have these Franks, whom he had been ordered to bring to him,

Whom he judged to have understood all his plans,

Secretly beheaded, lest, once returned,

They arrange for all their companions to come there.

The other, as though pierced through the chest by a sword’s point,

Immediately replied to the man issuing such wicked orders:

What cause of madness drives you to compel

The ambassadors of the sacred name, whom you have summoned

To your presence in the name of peace before all peoples for all ages,

So that you may slaughter them beneath concealed treachery?

Never afterward will faith be safe, nor anything equitable among peoples,

If this damnable order is carried out.

He had indeed proceeded as a minister of peace,

And would never, while alive, be a partner in wickedness.

If it pleased the king that the Franks should be beheaded,

His own neck ought first to be cut by the advancing sword.

But he should consider wherever this report might travel:

Such great infamy would mark him incurably.

It would indeed be a loss to his honor and military reputation

If these few men should happen to perish.

Yet, among so many thousands, the Gauls would not feel

Very much weakened by the loss of a few.

Nevertheless, they would grieve their loss with immense sorrow,

And burn with greater fury for revenge.

No embassy thereafter sent to the pagans would help him,

While the example of this deed proved that such conduct should be imitated.

Rather, he should heap such men with great honor,

[Col. 0968C] Enrich them with possessions, and send them back to their own land.

Moved by such arguments, the tyrant

Changes his plan and follows what his friend advises.

Thus, noble soldier, after your immense fear,

You return to your companions, trusting in that same renowned leader.

And, returning by the Jordan and Jerusalem,

You receive palm branches and visit the holy places and homes.

You survey everything, feeding your eyes with the sight,

And learn things worthy to report to those who do not know them.

Nor did that good companion fail you,

Until he had given you back safely and unharmed to your allies.

Thus, returning swiftly to the camp,

You made your companions rejoice by your return.

But since the text of the city’s capture is now being woven,

The structure of the following book will report this better.

[Col. 0968D] Come now, Christ the King, reveal your accustomed power,

Which neither the strength of men nor the many weapons give to you.

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0967]

[Col. 0967D] Come now, Christ, often grant your people

The divine gift once granted to the Maccabees,

So that one man may conquer many thousands.

Favor, O Christ, the citizens of the famous city,

A people of a populous nation;

Restrain the force of the wicked people.

The Turks plan to surrender the city.

[Col. 0968D]

Thus the mercy of God, seeing through so great a weight of evils

That the spirits of his people had not failed,

Inspires a certain Turk, pitying their labors [Note: [Col. 0967D] The edition reads “of his people.”],

[Col. 0969A] To surrender the city and its splendid wall,

With its towers, and to receive the summit of honors as his reward.

After long turning these matters over within himself, the man judges it right

First to disclose them to Bohemond. Without delay he sends word,

Telling him how much he is preparing and ordering him to have no doubt.

He commands him to receive the messenger when this deed is to be carried out,

And not to prolong delay in preparing, designating the time and hour.

Here the leader shared the plan with the nobles;

The greater part of the counts thought the messenger genuine,

While the other part, doubting, hesitated.

On the appointed night, however, Bohemond gathers a company,

Better armed and tested by the sweat of war.

The leader burns with zeal and travels along familiar routes.

Everyone sighs with an equal desire in his whole heart.

Through the darkness the leader takes the road,

And, laying aside his shining helmet, keeps silent

And walks beneath the silent night.

The route is difficult for timid soldiers: remote ridges and valleys,

And whatever path shone through the dark ravines.

Although the leader himself feared that the affair might turn out badly,

His cheerful face concealed what troubled his mind [Note: [Col. 0969D] The edition reads “mind and deceit.”].

He gives hope to the lagging, and with his face brightens the sorrowful man who rejoices;

He spurs their courage, and now hints to the people

That the salvation they have so long desired is ready.

When they see the place sought by their prayers and much labor,

And see the enemy keeping expert watch,

They stand at a distance, concealed by hiding places and the darkness of night,

And watch the torches glow, the threatening bows,

And the Turks moving through the battlements,

Waving flashing swords beneath purple crests.

[Col. 0969C] Changing places and taking turns,

They relieve the night watches,

Calling out to the soldiers, “Who is there?”

And they did not know that the others were approaching.

Without delay the magnanimous leader gives words worthy of a leader,

Urging the men and their fierce hearts:

“Long desired by our prayers, sufficiently awaited,

The time has come, nobles, prepared by the Lord’s mercy.

For nine months this late victory has been delayed;

For nine months the Lord’s severe vengeance

Has chastised us. But true joys are near.

Therefore, brave men, persist with a brave mind.

And you, swift young men, suddenly climb the walls.

Conquer swiftly; be ashamed to conquer slowly.

Let that place”—and he points out the place—

Be attacked first. The palm of victory calls you there in confidence;

Let that point first be sought.

Gifts await everyone, but I shall not call them my gifts:

Whatever each man wins, I shall deny to no victor.

But I am delaying. Go, men; I shall stand here with a few.

Hasten, good nobles; I shall go more slowly.

If need requires it, I myself shall be the first on foot to enter the fight.”

He had finished. The uncertain leader falls silent,

And all the things thought likely to happen wander through his mind.

The young men hurry forward. Fulcherius presses on ahead.

He made his way through the darkness with faltering steps.

At that time, when a comet was leading forth its rays,

[Col. 0970A] a joyful change of kingdom was being foretold.

The stars and the heavens were darkened with a strange redness,

and human hearts were struck by overwhelming fear.

## The City Is Handed Over

It was midnight when a soldier, prepared for that undertaking,

took his stand at the tower which that blessed traitor

was guarding; and he was greatly astonished when a voice called from the tower.

“Come on!” the Turk shouted. “Climb the walls!

Let valor seek the summit; press upon the enemies who are now about to fall,

and bring here the ropes of the ladders, coiled as they are.”

At last, after being repeatedly urged, he stirred those who were hiding.

Finally, trampling down their fear, with their courage revived,

they were scarcely drawn out from the brambles; compelled to prevail,

they strengthen themselves, carry the ladders to the walls,

and then take steps backward again in shameful retreat.

[Col. 0970B] [Uncertain reading:] “Fructetis mersi” return to safety after being plunged [into danger]. [Note: [Col. 0969D] Edition: redeunt, “they return.”]

Although the Turk pressed them and daylight was approaching,

they nevertheless dared nothing, but stood stunned, their hearts frozen.

From the walls a man rebukes the troops with harsh words,

while night was already withdrawing and Matuta [Note: [Col. 0969D] Edition: matutina, “morning,” less well: Matuta is the dawn.] was reddening.

Then, as one younger man stood in the midst of the others,

he spoke thus: “Young men, do not despise the gift that has been offered.

Rise; I shall be first.” They obeyed. Fulcherius,

born at Chartres, does not fear to lead a thousand nobles,

hurrying toward the walls of the town [Note: [Col. 0970D] Edition: properare, “to hurry.”] that cannot be conquered.

The weight of his shield does not delay him; bent toward the heights,

he flies upward bearing his weapons, and clings manfully to the ladder.

A Venetian follows him. The wicked enemy is astonished.

When Fulcherius stood upon the walls, behold, the guards are killed

by a thunderbolt and hurled down to the lowest depths.

[Col. 0970C] The victor exults and tramples down their mangled faces.

Truncated bodies fall; beautiful limbs are torn apart.

Fortune favors the man, and throws the disorganized populace into confusion,

which had been enjoying secure rest amid its cups.

He tears out the doorposts, enters the towers,

crushes the unsuspecting enemies, and seizes the high vantage points.

Boellus captures three towers by his own valor.

The land calls him by this name according to his nature.

Here, good traitor of the city, he happens upon your Germans;

he fells them, blanching at adding them to the crowds of the dying,

and drives twin brothers backward from the citadel.

Now brave men were hanging from ladders everywhere.

No one hesitates to climb over the bodies of his comrades.

They surmount the walls as they ascend, grasp the battlements with their right hands,

and with their left hold out shields and weapons.

[Col. 0970D] The Turks recover their courage. They struggle in vain

to thrust back the first men, and with trembling hands they hurl their missiles.

The Turk grieves over the deaths of his brothers, but, unwilling

to exact vengeance for their killing and dissolve the feigned peace,

he restrains his anger and hurries to open the gates.

Drawing heavy sighs from his breast, he handed the keys

of the gate to Bohemond; and the duke, bowing,

humbly bent his body and stern face before the man.

The wretched citizens flee when they see that everything is held by death;

the entire wall is laid low by weapons.

[Col. 0971A] And the Parthians’ red standards are removed from the walls [Note: [Col. 0971D] Edition: partim, “partly.”]

and white standards are set there in place of the red ones.

Thus loyal troops are summoned to the common good,

and the wind carried the trumpet’s blare to the tents.

[Note: [Col. 0971D] This verse is missing in the printed editions.]

The horses are checked by their bridles; the young warriors’ weapons roar.

Without delay, dense troops leap forth from the camps.

The commanders leave their crowded tents in the fields,

while, without order, they rush upon the men fleeing from the city,

intercepting them and pressing them into the earth as they fall of their own accord.

They fall of their own accord—those whose minds had fallen away with their bodies. [Note: [Col. 0971D] Edition: “These do not fall of their own accord, whose minds also fell away with their bodies.”]

Soon the troops burst through the open gates

and pressed upon the backs of the men who followed the foremost.

Immediately they invade the city and inflict many wounds.

[Col. 0971B] Everywhere the crowd perishes, buried in wine and sleep.

Standards sound; mothers groan; mourning is everywhere,

and through all the streets the blood of the wicked people flows.

A child vomits brain through the skull’s shattered structure,

and mute kisses defile its nurse’s mouth. [Note: [Col. 0972D] Edition: “filthy spittle.”]

Captive daughters direct their eyes toward their mothers,

their eyes—for their hands are bound with a rigid cord.

Old men weep and cling to one another; after the temples have been stripped of gold,

they beat the hard places with their aged foreheads.

## Casianus Is Put to Death

Godefridus darts ahead, flying forward; he disregards the bodies

and fells all whom he sees bending their bows.

With his shining sword he cuts through corselets and shields alike.

He terrifies those pressing forward and turns this weapon against the fleeing man.

[Col. 0971C] The duke himself can scarcely restrain his sword from killing;

many whom he did not wish to die perish by the sword.

For if he attempts to graze someone with a small wound,

his hand, though unaware, kills him with a swift blade.

While the joyous victory directs everything among his men,

the light-minded multitude carries it out, mingling the dishonorable with the permitted.

The king, covered with years, concealed himself beneath rags,

and thus Casianus escaped the hands of the victors.

Yet he was not rescued from fate. Recognized by a certain Armenian

while fleeing and already far from the city,

he lost his head, encircled on every side with aged locks,

and it was carried back suspended by the hair.

They follow the head through the city streets, applauding,

while the Armenians [Note: [Col. 0972D] Edition: “the Armenians”] and Turks lament their king.

[Col. 0971D] A mountain adjoins the city, and its summit

is not easily taken in by human sight.

Upon it stands a fortress from which the beautiful Antiochene region

lies fully open whenever the light is clear.

The Persians escape there and from that position harass our men with arrows;

the victory does not come wholly without suffering.

Bohemond, with his legion, receives their blows;

the defeated enemy seeks him along the walls.

When the brave duke held a tower upon the wall,

a tower insufficiently fortified and clinging closer to the fortress,

a savage crowd, having recovered its strength, pressed upon him.

[Col. 0972A] The Arabs hurl missiles from the mountain’s summit,

while others try to drive him away with poles.

They thicken their wedges through the mass and seize the heights.

They join battle; scarcely have the foremost launched their missiles,

like snow, when the living tread upon corpses.

The duke and his horsemen stand firm and roll the dying

from the towers, killing the citizens who climb up.

Now they rush through the weapons with a stake, now with a stone;

they flee some and cast down others. The duke, holding the highest position,

cuts off hands with his sword, withstands the raging attackers

with his resounding shield, encourages the nobles, and is burdened with missiles.

While the lines were fighting, a javelin stuck in the duke’s thigh,

and the wound, though slight, seriously injured his manly thigh.

The duke, therefore, restraining the stream of his fleeing blood,

left the first tower and sought the second.

[Col. 0972B] When his men saw their duke’s spirit sink,

the Apulian and the Calabrian fled the people they had just defeated.

Yet one man alone remained in the citadel after the loss;

Bohemond mourned his sufficiently honorable death.

When he saw himself abandoned amid the enemy,

shaking the shield painted around his temples,

he terrifies the pressing crowds wandering beneath the tower.

He crushes them with stones slipping from the summit,

wearies a thousand hands; one hand shakes men with a stake [Note: [Col. 0972D] Edition: “and one hand shakes men with a stake.”]

and, scraping away pieces of masonry with a trembling fingernail,

strikes those standing below and pierces hollow temples with iron.

The citizens call this man under a promise of safety; but the thought comes to his aid

that it is beautiful to die in battle for the name of Christ.

By now the enemy had thickly covered the surface of his shield

with missiles. The inert round shield lies there, a heavy weight upon his ribs.

[Col. 0972C] Immediately, without fear, he threw himself upon the mass of troops.

He made a new weapon from his own body,

and, shattered, shattered many others. This was done by the Apulian.

But who could explain it in words? What tongue could record

so many deaths or count so many captives?

Nor could exaggeration itself disturb the truth.

Let it be enough for me to follow the chief traces of events.

## The Christian Army Enters the City

The ancient, powerful city, adorned with Peter’s cathedral,

rightly called the seat of the Church after Rome,

a city that had continually ruled countless cities,

fortunate in its walls and shrines, pleasant and healthful,

[Col. 0972D] had been submerged in the darkness of an ignorant people.

But from there it burst forth, transformed and more celebrated.

Our army possessed jeweled garments and houses hung with gold;

it possessed the city’s foreign purple,

and its abundance filled a single people,

while the powerful could take nothing from the poor.

In this city the slave possesses slaves, and the client possesses clients.

Your servant, Christ, enters it in the light of Jupiter’s day,

but he cannot overcome the rebellious men of the citadel.

Therefore he fights all day and continues the labor into the night,

taking no sleep during the night.

## Corbana, Commander of the Military, Advances against Antioch with the Persian Army

[Col. 0973A]

But when morning was given and Venus’s day was opened,

a mounted man stood upon the walls, supported by his spear.

Having taken his position, he surveyed the vast places in the light

and saw a dark cloud of dust in the air.

Soon he summoned the rest of the young men to a grim spectacle.

They stood along the battlements with anxious minds;

different men thought they saw different things.

One group foretold that the Turks were approaching [Note: [Col. 0973D] Edition: “the walls.”]

another believed that those they were watching would be Byzantines.

The sun struck their gleaming shields,

and the numerous army gradually approached.

Yet Corbana, commander of the military, and the other powerful men

settled at a distance, awaiting those who followed.

[Col. 0973B] But some Persians, already hoping to take the walls,

entered the open fields within sight of the city.

There, in various ways, they delight in behaving outrageously

and do not cease insulting those watching [Note: [Col. 0973D] Edition: spectantibus, “those looking on.”]

They strive to release their foaming horses across the grass,

throw out unsheathed swords and catch them again.

They howl, fly about everywhere, threaten those shut inside,

and recklessly hurl their weapons through the empty air.

Our men think it safer to hold their established positions

than to follow uncertain chance and begin a battle.

But when the Turks were already returning with shouts,

Roger of Barnavilla follows, exulting, with three armed men.

When the enemy, after being delayed, looked back [Note: [Col. 0973D] Edition: memorata, “remembered”; the printed reading is uncertain],

he set an ambush beneath a hollowed rock.

[Col. 0973C] While some of our men pursued those who were provoking them,

thieves leapt out from hiding, and our men were captured [Note: [Col. 0973D] Edition: “and the young men were captured.”]

and enclosed. Turning back, they are stunned; then, recovering their courage,

they break through the encircling force, with their shields thrown behind them.

Just as, when the deer’s legs have been released to the dogs,

the dogs pursue the prey on foot while the deer seeks a place of refuge,

hope gives him wings, and fear makes him swift;

soon, having attained his wish, the deer escapes the dog’s mouth.

Thus the Parthian drives us headlong, hanging over us in pursuit.

So this troop flees, making for the rewards of life.

Roger urges his companions on and receives the blows.

Now courage and conscious valor make him slow.

His rough shield scarcely withstands the forest of weapons.

[Col. 0973D] He supports his collapsing horse; blood stains his weapons.

Fortune harms the oppressed. Your men, Roger, were pressing hard,

and had already reached safety, when your badly stumbling horse threw you down,

and you are not relieved, weighed down by the mass of the overturned horse.

You, who did not spare the enemy, are disfigured by a deep wound.

Did the Turk, once you were captured, refuse to spare you?

The young men on the walls seethe with confused shame,

while the brave man, held by the enemy, is pressed by arrows.

The nobles who were watching turn their eyes away

when dogs drag his distinguished limbs over the stones.

[Col. 0974A] Then suddenly the sword cuts off the man’s head as he is dragged.

At that moment the dense troops resound with shouting.

The Parthian exults and grasps the bloody head with his fingers,

fixing its blood-soaked chin upon a stake [Note: [Col. 0974D] This verse is missing in the printed editions.]

and carrying the face back to the camp, dripping with black gore.

Now I shall return my account to the events of the city.

## The Turks Attack Antioch

Each day the Turks bring their camps close to the city.

By warfare and threats of blockade, they urge us to abandon what we have gained.

Many of them also enter the fortress,

and attack our men within and without.

Thus no hand was free from weapons,

nor did anyone remove the helmet from his burdened head.

At night they lie under cover with shields upon the worthless dust,

[Col. 0974B] and their limbs fail, tormented even in their beds.

The movement of missiles disturbed the city’s spaces.

The towers bristle there, as do the shaggy roofs of the houses.

The enemy themselves cast themselves into open danger

and fight nearby with swords, while their bows are laid aside.

Our men faced only a modest danger.

Each day they all gathered near the fortress.

Now, with the resources of many diminished almost to nothing,

scarcely any food remained for the blessed inhabitants of the city.

## The City Is Tormented by Famine

Therefore cruel famine is present, crueler than every plague.

The men keep watch; fasting drives sleep away.

Emaciation deforms their faces; bones shine blacker than those buried,

and the entrails appear in many.

The sluggish populace tears up doubtful herbs that threaten death

[Col. 0974C] and struggles with its teeth upon the hard turf.

Some rejoice to strip the trees of their leaves;

others, like wild beasts, devour roots and meadows.

They eat many things unknown to human tables.

The dried-up hand scarcely supports the weight of a sword.

O power worthy to be referred to God! Surrounded by plague,

our fasting troop is feared by the well-fed enemy.

A new thing! A donkey’s leg is valued at three pounds,

and the one who paid the price is not considered wasteful for doing so.

Children move their mouths and call for their dying mothers,

wearing away the air and the open sky instead of their customary feasts [Note: [Col. 0974D] Edition: tenentes, “holding.”]

The swift horse, which scarcely recently was restrained by its stall,

now sought the empty manger with eager bites.

[Col. 0974D] At last, its wildness laid aside and its fury removed,

the wretched creature collapsed, sobbing throughout its body.

The young men, distinguished in valor, devour it too,

and this food pleases the people, though the flesh was purchased.

While they perish—while he who could remain strong

lives, if anyone lives beneath the appearance of death—

a certain man, on a given night, reports sacred consolations to the community.

So great is the confidence of faith.

He reports that victory has been prepared for our men within five days

and cheers the men and the summoned people.

Moreover, the spear that pierced the Lord’s innocent side

made the minds of our men joyful.

## Peter the Hermit Meets the Commander Corbana

After this, our men refused a meeting with the men of the citadel,

but set themselves against the pagans at the wall.

After many examples in which hope of life was restored,

all fast for the third time, like the Ninevites.

Then Peter the Hermit approached Corbana, the Turkish commander.

The lofty commander Corbana was riding boldly toward the gate on his horse,

while a wanton crowd roared on both sides.

Suddenly Peter entered the obstructing crowd.

He did not fear a certain Turk who ordered him

to bend his head and worship the face of the powerful man [Note: [Col. 0975D] Alternative reading: patentis, “open/visible.”]

and thus, with a calm breast and lowered voice, plead his case.

While the man refused to render divine worship to a human being,

the pagan’s right hand bent his face down.

His honorable goodness was mocked by foolish men,

but he was nevertheless granted the ability to speak.

## Peter’s Speech to Corbana

“Great commander,” said the little man [Note: [Col. 0975D] Edition: “I am little.”], “we seek nothing belonging to another.

The city of Antioch belongs to our people.

Why, then, does your power drive us from our own seat?

If legal judgment moves you, withdraw from the city.

Or, if you wish to trust us, setting aside the law of error,

let all Romania be transferred to your kingdom.

You will become king of Syria, king of this region,

and, greatly powerful, you will be burdened with many gifts.

But if such a great desire to fight sits in your mind,

if you prefer to see hands joined in battle,

order the lot of the remaining men to be placed on equal terms.

Let those who yield in equal battle yield the region.

Let thirty or twenty fight against the same number;

let the defeated withdraw, if they are able to withdraw by the lot.”

He spoke. In reply, Commander Corbana shook a drawn sword:

“Do you think you can give me such a game with impunity?

You will lose your head by this sword; by it the people

that seeks to render obedience to some unknown Christ will be mutilated.”

Peter withdrew, stirred by the harsh words.

The nobles prepared their weapons in due order after hearing the speech.

That night the fathers kept vigil and confessed their errors;

the groaning crowd held the altars and filled the churches.

When daylight came, nine battle lines were appointed from the whole people,

and each followed its own commander.

They arranged at the front those whom they wished to have at the front,

those whom they wanted in the middle, and those whom they desired at the ends.

## The Christians Prepare to Fight the Turks. The Exhortation of the Bishop of Le Puy to the Army

Hugh the Prior was stationed; seven brave men held the center’s strength.

They assigned the final positions to Bohemond

and appointed guards along the walls [Note: [Col. 0975D] Edition: constituere, “to appoint/establish.”]

Here the bishop of Le Puy held the office of commander

and properly governed the people of the ailing Raymond.

The holy spear of God, carried before them, encouraged the men,

and the bishop’s shining corselet weighed upon his limbs.

Here he restrained the people’s voices with voice and hand.

[Col. 0976A] When he fell silent, the prostrate people alone grew silent [Note: [Col. 0976D] Edition: silebat, “was silent.”]

“Pour out all your strength in this extremity.

O nobles, renew your hands, well known to the Turks.

Go through the cowardly; break apart the peoples with your swords,

whom the first blows disarm as they grow weak.

God will send an angelic legion to our aid;

he will crush this people as he crushed Pharaoh [Note: [Col. 0976D] Edition: opprimat, “may he crush.”].

Oh, how this senseless people is swept along by madness!

In its deranged blood it purchases hell.

In the end it gains punishment; the flesh is tortured twice,

and through this death earns endless punishment.

But for us, whether it is necessary to suffer the final death,

or whether God conquers the pagans—which I pray may happen—

the outcome is blessed: a crown will arise from death.

[Col. 0976B] Victory will give different gifts to the soldiers.

You will conquer; it will be a monument to your valor.

I already see the slaughter of the dying Parthians.

Do not doubt: God will not allow his champions

to suffer more than they can endure, so that he may be glorified.

I feel the people stirred by the goads of joy.

Support me, men; your joys will carry me along.

May our most welcome prayers be fulfilled, Christ, I ask,

so that we may conquer.”

“Amen,” replied the people, roused again.

Meanwhile the Persian commander sends word to Bohemond

to count his horsemen first and ours second.

He orders him to erase his name from the rest of the people,

lest the glory of the world suddenly be sent into battle;

let them take precautions and let equal numbers fight on both sides.

[Col. 0976C] Then the commander rebukes the envoy: “Leave this aside.

Stop speaking foolishly; we are called to greater things.

Let us conquer together, comrades, or let us die together.”

He looked back at his companions. Whether good or evil

comes forth for the holy, they feared nothing meanwhile.

Our men entered through the gates and distributed the warriors

in their appointed places, while the messenger safely withdrew from the city.

Thus, O God, your providence brought matters to pass.

The priests encircled the towers with a sparse crown [Note: [Col. 0976D] Edition: “a small crown around the walls.”]

and most of them lay prostrate upon the walls.

Clad in the stoles they wear at the time of Mass,

some sang psalms more loudly, while others wept and prayed quietly.

## The Turks Are Driven Away

[Col. 0976D] When the trumpets sounded, Hugh the Prior first attacked

the savage peoples, who everywhere uttered their customary cries.

The Frankish troop, stretched out in a long formation,

joined in an equal line and advanced against the enemy with measured steps.

They stood within bowshot. With all their strength

the Turks bent their bows, tightened with the better string;

the arrows flew hissing through the empty air.

The Gallic people, forgetful of their brief life, pressed upon them.

Little by little the Parthians gave ground backward,

fearing to commit their right hands to nearby battle.

The wind turned the Turks’ missiles away from the army.

## Bohemond Is Surrounded. A Fierce Battle. Victory Goes to the Christians

[Col. 0977A]

Evrard of Puisac and the fiery young men,

seeking battle in battle, raised their swords,

but found no one whom they could strike.

Behold, a swift messenger came from Bohemond.

While he reported a few words, an arrow grazed his own

temples. “But this,” he said, “is what is happening: Bohemond

is pressed by enemies on both sides.

Hugh, leave the fugitives.”

Hugh immediately turned his men around

and saw Arabs armed with spears surrounding Bohemond.

Then he spoke thus: “What you young men desired is here.

The field bristles with iron spears. Let us turn

and fall upon these men with our great strength.”

Therefore Hugh and Bohemond join hands.

[Col. 0977B] Here too stood that duke of dukes, Godefridus.

Opposite them advanced the Arabs and powerful kings,

and Lucas, king of Damascus; there, raging,

two stood on behalf of a friend—for thus the crowd called the two.

Duke Bohemond still called out, “Godefridus!” [Note: [Col. 0977D] Edition: vacabat, “was unoccupied.”]

The great man begins the battle first and loosens the bridle

of his raging horse. With his spear he burst the throat

of a man who was moving others to battle,

took the life from the speaking man,

and the spearhead broke as he slowly uttered his cries.

Groaning, he sought the ground with his dying mouth.

Arabs and Franks rush together violently.

A grave battle arises; the sky is covered with missiles.

Here Odo of Balgentiacus rushed first everywhere,

holding the standard, unable to restrain himself.

[Col. 0977C] When an unseen arrow tasted his side,

the shrill spear deprived the standard-bearer of life.

As he fell, he moistened the standard with his blood

and drew the shaft from the wound in the place where he had fallen.

Soon William of Boemensis [Note: [Col. 0977D] Edition: Beniensis] succeeded him

and raised the standard; his sword made a path for the young man.

Not far away moved a small troop of our men,

whom the insolent crowd of Turks was pressing too hard.

The hostile crowd scattered them across the grass by deceit.

The wind fanned the fire, and thus the dry field burned.

That heat produced smoke and created darkness,

and the enemy draws it through the hollow air across the level field,

and destroys three hundred infantrymen by an unseen wound.

Then Rainald of Beauvais with Paganus,

and Thomas with Drogo, and the warlike Clarebaldus,

together with the others, escaped sudden deaths

and with rapid course sought the strength of the battle [Note: [Col. 0978D] Up to this point in the printed editions.]

When this brave troop joined the great Hugh,

just as herds yield to a huge lion,

so the Arabs turned away, their shields thrown aside.

“You have conquered, almighty God!” Godefridus cries.

He presses on in pursuit; Bohemond flies first,

driving the enemy’s horse by its reins; the air whistles.

Dust, foul with the blood of the dying, flies to the stars.

The fleeing peoples had reached a certain hill.

Then the Parthians, turning their side to the left,

wished to stand firm after their long flight,

and with their bows turned back attacked our men again.

[Col. 0978B] Therefore the tireless old man Gerald of Melione,

who had long been ill during the siege,

as he was unarmed, burst into the midst of the enemy

and earned a beautiful death by confessing. Against the enemy,

some of our men attacked for three days.

But my page will not suffice for such great events.

They capture fifteen thousand camels.

They find tents filled with many spoils.

Ten thousand Turkish horsemen were killed,

along with as many wretched infantrymen, who were not counted.

Moreover, those who held the civic fortress

surrendered the fortress to our men because they saw marvelous things.

Among them was a royal youth born in Persia,

along with three hundred who had been raised from the sacred font.

I erase from our little book, whatever it may be,

those who were not ashamed to withdraw from the battle.

This pitiable troop, as though recalled to its vomit,

preferred exile to its homeland and joined itself to the world.

I pass over why our men feared to give aid

through the counsel of Stephen of Constantinople.

The first troop and the foremost commanders guard the foremost positions.

The unarmed populace holds the center, and the walls are filled.

Then the royal Hugh, who is rightly called “the Great,”

whose name was filled out by his endowment, was asked by common voice

to go to the city called Constantinople.

It was his concern to return the conquered region to the Emperor:

law, rights, faith, pledges, and a pact.

The people’s voice and mingled prayers compelled him.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0977]

Raymond Piletus captures two camps. When he attacks the city of Marram, the Turks resist fiercely.

[Col. 0977D]

But the other nobles, already close to their desire in mind,

wisely decide to suspend the wars for a time.

For the heat and the dried-out earth oppressed the people;

the heat burned them, and the earth refused to provide water.

Therefore rest was restored to the limbs of the weary,

to be abandoned shortly at the first light of November.

[Col. 0978D] The troop divided, and different places were sought.

Whoever was rejoicing in profit remained in the city.

He was diligent in services and earned money.

Raymond supported many of them as soldiers,

and our people called him Piletus by surname.

Having spent his leisure with many men, not idly,

he made provision that the pagan might not live in safety.

Therefore he passed through two cities and unexpectedly appeared

at Talamana.

[Col. 0979A] This fortress was guarded by a Syrian people,

which willingly and in good health received the men.

They proceeded to a certain fortress, but a profane crowd

blocked the way, hurling useless missiles at our men.

Yet the hand of the Lord crushed it there, and the pagan foreigners

were summoned to baptism.

Those who rejected it perished, killed.

A boy was captured there, and whoever grew old

was killed; that kingdom knew not how to spare the unknown for long.

After the enemies were overthrown, those who had already been granted gifts

returned to the fortress laden with gold and spoils.

Nor was the courageous valor content with rest for long;

it remained continually intent upon the destruction of the enemy.

The courageous force, following the pagans’ tracks scattered over the land,

attacks Marram, a city full of pagans.

[Col. 0979B] Roboam, king of Aleph, had led a distant crowd into Marram,

guided by rumor, together with the entire surrounding population.

That people, not restrained by lowly fear,

properly arranged the battle and rushed violently upon our men.

An iron forest falls everywhere and roughens the bloodied field;

the crash reaches the stars, and the groans of the dying rise.

Spears meet throughout the morning; some hurl missiles,

others thrust out spears and draw them back again.

Our men attack more forcefully and fasten corpses

to the very gates. A soldier already stood firm upon the rampart;

the ditches were flooding, when suddenly, with horses turned back,

the army wheeled around.

The Christ-worshipers shamefully turn their backs,

disturbed by fear of death; the hostile troop, driven by fury, confuses them.

The ringing of the shield and the resounding helmets answer one another.

Falling from the cone’s bark, [the missiles] darken the eyes.

The young men hate the corselets as they bend forward beneath the blows.

Thirst splits their lips; the shield is not enough against the arrows.

[Col. 0979C] When Raymond saw them thinning out, he was first to cry:

“Take breath, men! Where, shamefully, are we going?”

Thus the worthy people, recalled from their frightened flight,

drive the pagans toward the walls, gathered together as one.

But the weakened Syrians do not turn back,

nor, unable to endure thirst, do they allow their comrades to live.

That people, softened by the warmth of its own air,

was not overcome in battle but by the heat of battle.

## The Christians Are Driven Away

When the Turks saw that our camps, which they had followed,

were turning their backs, they attacked the Christ-worshipers,

now fortified in large part.

The fleeing people gives them strength and courage to pursue;

fortune teaches the timid the harm they can do.

Without maintaining order, the army of the Christ-worshipers flees,

and no trumpet’s voice is awaited to recall them.

The horsemen and the crowd of infantry flee no more slowly

than the frightened deer once it has heard barking dogs.

Alas, the fortunate people are struck down through the shadowy roads,

exposed to Jupiter; they become martyrs and food for wild beasts.

Many breathe out their souls, and my verse will not tell it.

I scarcely remember what I am weary of recounting.

Raymond returned to the fortress and rightly enjoyed peaceful rest,

remaining there for some time with a people filled with grief,

ready for every useful undertaking, a brave man tested through many dangers.

Meanwhile excessive grief befell the people of Antioch.

[Col. 0980A] For the city’s ruler, moderate in all things and gentle,

the bishop died, and the city grieved that its father had died.

I do not believe that it grieved more when it was captured.

## The Bishop of Le Puy Dies. The Count of Saint-Gilles Captures Albarium

While the month called August was hot,

the bishop of Le Puy died—not for himself, but for the people.

While the city sings to you, Christ, about Peter brought out of prison,

this man was drawn out of the prison of the body.

On the day when they recall Peter loosening bonds,

the men lamented the bishop’s bier.

After excessive mourning and many misfortunes,

the Count of Saint-Gilles, standing firm through difficult times,

went to Albarium. Surrounding it with many soldiers,

he captured it, and its great wall did not help the city.

[Col. 0980B] Here the bent necks of old men were cut off with swords,

and the lovely temples of infants were broken no less.

Neither old women, worthy of reverence, nor wrinkled Persians found help,

nor did faces deserving not to be harmed protect the girls.

Death was not simple there, for thousands were killed.

They were torn apart in a thousand ways, according to the deserts of men.

At Albarium, thus recalled to the worship of the Lord,

a bishop of proven character was placed in authority.

Now winter was calling the nobles; it was time to begin new wars,

and it began, giving hope that they would be completed.

While a general feast was being held for all the saints,

the spiritual edict gathered the absent.

Then varied peoples flowed together into the walls of Antioch,

as different fish into full nets.

[Col. 0980C] A similar judgment pleases the dissimilar people.

They saw the holy places of Jerusalem with longing minds.

A secure force urges the men to be ready,

and they erase wives and children from their minds.

They are already carried in thought toward unknown regions of the world

and follow the feet of the Parthians in love of war.

## The Christians Besiege Marram

Meanwhile Bohemond, assembling his companions,

seeks the city promised by agreement; Raymond refuses this.

He orders them to await the arrival of the Constantinopolitan king

and fortifies Casianus’s house.

Thus, with the commander troubled, the impatient count crosses Rugia

and seeks Albarium and populous Marram.

[Col. 0980D] Lest the angry commander’s grief perhaps overflow

into common losses, the great prudence of the nobles

consults with him. The man’s lofty mind, moved by much prayer,

placed public prayers above private desire.

Immediately he led forth the troops of the formerly grieving people

and hastened toward Marram, mindful of honorable provisions.

The special law of the Lord was in effect when they filled the standards,

encircled the city, and the commanders placed their camps.

When the astonished people saw men from abroad,

who could tell how great the fear by which it was touched?

Everywhere in the city, as savage tumult hastened,

mothers ran about, and frightened daughters-in-law without adornment.

Public rumor declared that the enemies were more numerous than was right,

and fear overwhelmed many; no mind trusted its own eyes.

Whoever obtains sleep is tortured by sleep.

[Col. 0981A] The vain thing troubles him, keeps him sleepless, and threatens the day.

The commanders stand at servile work with the lesser people;

there is no shame in serving—extreme circumstances lack shame.

As Phoebus strips the earth of its black darkness,

our troop rises sluggishly in the slow hour,

and the good young men, roused by the blare of trumpets,

forgetful of their bodies but not forgetful of their souls,

hasten to Mars.

Now the surrounding [force] fits the stones to the sling;

now, rejoicing, it hurls them toward the heights.

They hurl rocks and torches carrying flames through the empty air,

wishing them to cling to the summits at which they look upward.

Others sweat to fill the open ditches.

The horsemen rush over steep places and cross the mountains.

There is no terror in the horses returning backward into the bridles.

Now, hiding beneath a hollow tortoise formation, the chosen troop

was undermining the strong walls; now the crowd was raising ladders,

[Col. 0981B] when suddenly the Arabs gathered and, with heavy arms,

rolled stones and inflicted wounds with well-aimed blows.

And just as, when hateful winter twists the storm clouds,

hail cuts through the air and the watery south wind rages,

the rattling roofs of houses are battered by rain,

and the following wave strikes the fleeing backs of men,

so these wretched men, for whom the only safety was to repel

what was hostile to safety, hurl spears.

Protected by their shields, they make them rattle,

while the horsemen flee beneath them, poorly covered.

When Raymond directed the battle from horseback,

he ordered a high wooden fortress to be built.

It resembled a mountain and was made of maple beams.

Its commanders were concealed in the lowest chambers.

[Col. 0981C] At the summit was a hunter, and Ebrardus sounded his horn;

the chosen troop roared in front.

Therefore the men, relying on their own feet and on the wheels,

although the narrow places of the roads hindered them,

brought a fortress still higher up against the tall tower

and prepared to make a sudden leap upon the astonished enemy.

Then a machine belonging to the townspeople was also brought out;

it hurled immense stones and shook the fortress.

That engine also cast pitchy Greek fires above it,

and foul black ash flew before the men.

Divine power preserved its servants in the fire

and made the harmful flames unable to harm.

The brave Christ-worshipers hurl [missiles] through the battlements of the walls,

and deaths fall from the summit of the fortress.

William of Mount Pislerium fights fiercely there;

[Col. 0981D] he too throws beams, stones, and spears in rivalry.

Opposed to the torches, he glows and is illuminated by fire.

I cannot worthily recount his valor.

The machine suitable for breaking walls does not hold them back;

rather, endurance rejoices—rejoices in hardships.

He is not softened backward by the sweetness of life;

nor, although it would have been proper to flee there, does he retreat.

He kills some, shakes others, turns around, repels weapons;

now he strikes walls, now shields, now tears away missiles.

Now far from the fortress, now at a distance from the citadel,

the crowd of priests shouted: “Merciful King, spare us!

Spare us, O God, and let the pagan fear your fold,

the one who strives to make the name of Christ contemptible.

If anyone prepares to loosen the structure of the wall,

his shaken right hand is condemned to the axe.”

[Col. 0982A] Angered by this, a man called Gulferius de la Turre,

who had long been planning a beautiful deed,

turbulently seized the timbers of an upright ladder,

which sweating shoulders had scarcely been able to support,

and dragged it upward by the steps, pulling his own limbs with his own arms.

Now he follows the one whom the hand of the Almighty leads to this deed;

such things transcend the measure of our minds.

But while the dense crowd strengthens its steps through the empty air,

the weight breaks the ladder, and the profane crowd is thrown back.

Yet the man mentioned above, destined to be lifted to the stars by favor,

through which he had already raised himself by valor and heavy labor,

stood out among those whom he had scarcely been able to lead upward.

Just as dogs feed upon a bear with their bites,

[Col. 0982B] while the people pressing upon it blocks its path of escape,

so the unjust hand presses upon this man, and the people press upon him.

He is carried forward by the approaching attackers;

he sets his shield against them, a protection for the comrade following.

Now he is first, now last, like one fleeing.

Now he harms the astonished people with his own weapons;

now he flees swords, javelins, and a thousand millstones.

Already his limbs smoke; already his nostrils foam with blood.

Against so many plagues, one man remains with life unharmed,

assailed by missiles, darts, stakes, clubs, and sword,

while the crowd resists as much as the trapped people can,

and the faithful troop once more sets ladders against the walls.

Soon, forgetful of himself but not of his companions,

he climbs the walls, hastening to aid his comrades.

[Col. 0982C] Without delay, when a signal has sounded, they rush together through the towers;

here the bow, its cord stretched tight, does not stand idle.

The matter is conducted with swords; from the walls, in ordered ranks,

they drag up stones, and death itself is shattered against their own walls.

Our men first turned their backs and yielded to the number of the maddened enemy,

and the groans of the dying oppressed the sound of battle.

Most of those hurled to the ground were fleeing death—

which, once thrown to the ground and broken, they nevertheless found.

Meanwhile the wall gives way; our young men enter the fortress through it,

nor is the knight held back by solid rock.

Entering through the narrow opening, the people crawl in;

the trumpet gave the most mournful signals to the defeated.

When those who stood above saw the enemies within their own walls,

and that they could no longer resist them,

[Col. 0982D] they fled headlong over the walls, casting away their shields,

and the ranks suddenly plunge into different houses.

Some perish from terror alone, and death, cowardly and uncalled by a red sword,

comes upon the falling populace.

The greatest crowd perishes, driven by the rushing tumult;

the wretched bodies, fixed upon the walls, glow red where they have been torn away.

While the rush is thus made toward the city’s lofty towers,

one death ravages these men in different ways.

Evening was less welcome to our men at that time,
