but, arriving too quickly, it gave the pagans hiding places.

The night, which was to pay the penalty in exchange for daylight,

had ashes for its possession, and the wall already reddened with much blood.

And while the joyful troop ravages the city without an avenger,

a pale pagan stands beside the wretched towers.

Then Bohemond warned them through an interpreter,

[Col. 0983A] that they should lessen their misfortunes by better counsel,

and enter the tower that commands the lofty gate:

His [Bohemund’s] right hand will surely protect them in their wretched peril of death.

Night makes both victor and vanquished restless.

The victor snatches up his conquests; the vanquished sees death rushing upon him.

Now dawn was calling the day and new mourning,

and the citizen in the city was preparing himself for approaching death.

The worshipers of Christ draw their swords and fill the houses

with bloodied bodies and with the blood of the falling people.

Here too they began a work of valor with swords—

men who possessed only slender bodies and modest strength.

The old men inflict a harsher punishment upon those being beheaded

than the young men do, for insufficient strength prolongs the pain.

And, as though they could have done the least harm,

they entangled the temples of some in nooses;

[Col. 0983B] as a stick tightens the noose and the stiff cord pierces

the bones within, while blood fills the interior,

then their eyes protruded from their sockets,

and corruption befouled the beards of the wretched.

A thirst for gold to be dug out devised such things.

For what does an immoderate love of possessing not persuade one to do?

The bloody right hand tears open entrails already chilled by grievous death

and, from the very entrails, the greedy hand draws out talents.

But while the duke’s concern wished to preserve others,

the relentless crowd dragged them toward impious fates.

The old men return to the depths of Erebus; the young men are sold.

A delay of a month held our men within these borders.

Meanwhile the bishop of Oria died there.

Our troop consumed much in a few days:

for victory knows no mercy toward the possessions of the defeated.

[Col. 0983C] There, therefore, the people endured immoderate hunger,

and most accepted the summoned death.

And because the people did not possess what they were permitted to possess,

they reached for what was forbidden and did what justice prohibited.

Alas for the grief! Alas for the deed!

They placed fresh Turkish flesh upon spits;

their teeth tore at the corpses.

### Discord between Bohemond and the Count of Saint-Gilles. Everything prospers for the Christians.

Then Bohemond’s case was examined a second time,

but the duke could not be reconciled with Raymond:

the count asserted that it was impious not to receive the emperor of Constantinople

and not to give him the sworn pledge.

Therefore the duke’s anger rejected responsibility for the holy journey;

anger made the duke, and the duke made the army, postpone the expedition.

He indeed returned with the princes to the beloved walls,

[Col. 0983D] while the people grieved, deprived of such fathers.

But the Count of Saint-Gilles remained restless,

anxious about many things and filled with a burden of cares.

Provided only that faith be preserved, he was willing that anything should descend to the depths,

and that the matter of the nobles should be taken up and examined.

He ordered his absent men to go to Rugia,

out of love for justice, and discuss the hateful dispute.

They assembled and discussed the matter, but there the dire fraud

of the demon took its seat, and the anger found no end.

Then the count proceeded toward Marrah, as the crowd expected,

while Bohemond gathered his companions in the city.

When the count saw that he had been abandoned by everyone,

[Col. 0984A] and that Marrah was now yielding very little food to the people,

trusting more in faith than in strength, he committed everything to Christ

and, with this leader, feared no changes of fortune.

Then, barefoot, with his customary preparations set aside,

he left Marrah with a commoner’s retinue.

He swore that every danger would yield to this people.

Nor did his confident faith concern itself with the companionship of kings.

That faithful man thought it strong to yield to the poor,

and he himself dared to entrust his vessel to torn sails.

The people, slowed by fasting, took up the road,

and the count’s companions first came to Capharda.

The consul Northmannus and the companies of the Northmen,

whom their own land makes sluggish but the unknown makes brave,

join themselves here to our men in spirit and body.

[Col. 0984B] They hesitate to undergo every hardship out of zeal for the faith.

The king of Caesarea also offered our men affection,

and under the appearance of peace he badly concealed his fear.

Finally, after a chain of misfortunes had fortified Caesarea,

the crowd approached it, since their long rest would be labor for them.

They encamped beside the river Farfar,

for that is the name of the river adjoining this city.

When the king of the city saw the tents brought too close to the walls,

he forbade commerce and broke the agreements.

But after the night had passed and the people were already advancing,

two Turks, at the king’s command, came to meet them.

Although enemies, they offered obedience to the enemy

and showed them the fords which they themselves did not wish to pass.

Our people also came, under the guidance of two men, to a certain valley

and captured oxen [Note: [Col. 0983D] One word is missing here.] and horses,

[Col. 0984C] booty—for oxen and horses were roaming widely across the grass,

rejoicing in the fertility of the grassy land.

And, according to those who attempted that raid,

five thousand of the plundered people were found.

A fortress stood there, fortified by a strong rampart and a rounded wall,

but it was surrendered to Raymond.

It was useful to live among the enemy for five days

and to load the animals with the spoils that had been given.

Then that people confirmed by oath that it had a perpetual alliance

with the worshipers of Christ and would harm no one.

Yet no trust ought to have been placed in this faith,

nor should their light promise have been accepted.

Afterward they approached the fortress of the Arabs, which was soon opened.

The next labor brought them to a pleasant valley,

full of countless fruits in the winter season.

[Col. 0984D] There a beautiful city remains splendid in its elevated position and lofty wall,

shining like a gem surrounded by pure gold.

The inhabitant who was then fleeing called it Caphalia;

when he saw more certainly those whom he had already seen by report,

the victors entered after the citizens had gone out,

remained three days in the city, and enjoyed its resources.

The hostile people, having stayed there for a long time, crossed the mountains

and placed their camp in the valley of Desem.

Here too God’s abundant mercy gave this army

fruit, grain, and sufficient nourishment.

But what comes according to one’s wish is despised.

Forbidden things are pleasing; they pursue what is more forbidden still,

[Col. 0985A] and they approach the neighboring fortress.

Then the enemy, with mouth agape, threw booty before the people,

and this matter proved so important that the victors,

overcome by deceit, abandoned the fortress—

compelled by a failing of the mind, not by the sword.

Nevertheless, when they attacked the castle on the following day,

it lay open to the attacker, empty of its defender.

The annual feasts of the Mother of God are celebrated there,

those which are especially illuminated with candles.

At that time gifts were sent from the city of Camela to the commanders:

a golden bow, horses, garments, and shining weapons.

Envoys, bearing the commands of their king,

begged for peace; the worshipers of Christ,

by making no definite arrangement, left them uncertain of everything.

The king of Tripoli too, touched by fear like these men,

sent the enemy seven horses and four mules.

[Col. 0985B] The commanders accepted the gifts, but these uncertain offerings were suspect.

And since they did not make the alliance sought with the men,

they abandoned the castle on the fifteenth day.

On the fifteenth day the nobles also set out on the road.

From there they approached Arqa, an ancient fortress comparable to cities,

a place to which the people traveled only with difficulty.

Arabs, Turks, and Publicans crowned this place with towers,

and supplied weapons, positions, and the fortifications of the walls.

Nevertheless, our men enclosed it in a siege,

believing that they could overcome it by force or treachery.

Our men rushed toward the walls at full speed,

struck those shut inside, and were struck back more heavily.

They do not wound more severely than they are hurled down from above.

With bow, crossbow, and engine, that people rages.

[Col. 0985C] A stone hurled by an engine and aided by the great strength of men

grinds down the bows of those opposing it;

flying through the shields, it opens a deadly path for itself

and sows death, killing whatever it strikes.

Here Anselm of Monte Riballo, the glory of the nobles,

was surveying the broad walls on his panting horse

when he received a mortal wound—

a man with the strength of Hector,

the counsel of Cato, and the foremost command in the army.

Again and again they attacked the walls, and again and again they were repulsed.

After this fourteen men set out toward Tripoli,

[Col. 0986A] to seize booty, and suddenly found sixty Turks.

With Christ coming to their aid, they attacked them,

killed six, and, as they joyfully returned,

captured several herds across the enemy’s countryside.

Not far away lay a city near the shore of the sea,

promising much plunder through its fertility,

famous by the very name with which it is called: Tortosa.

Raymond Piletus attacked it, and the proconsul of Tentoria joined him,

a man equal to him in sameness of name

and not inferior in integrity of character.

These two attacked Tortosa with few men,

but for a long time they were frustrated and did not enjoy success.

Nevertheless, when night came on not far away,

they pitched camp, while the people made an excessive din,

and the men, not slow to advance their own interests,

kindled many fires over the hills and fields for those keeping watch.

When the citizens observed these fires shining from afar,

they hoped what they feared and interpreted what they hoped:

that the worshipers of Christ had abandoned the siege of the fortress

and had already pitched their tents for the city’s destruction.

Therefore, overcome by fear alone, they abandoned

the walls and gave their backs to flight, with no one compelling them.

But when the sun returned and, with a greater light,

covered the nocturnal lights and revealed to our men

joys unknown to them, a sudden kingdom summoned them—

a kingdom long awaited, to which the city was preparing to submit.

Fugitive Parthian, where will you seek greater marvels?

Your late-arriving foreign enemy now suddenly becomes your heir.

This force suffices for many achievements with no great losses.

[Col. 0986C] From Arqa too, three times, death was sent like frost.

The brave men unexpectedly took possession of the city

and entered through its hostile gates as though they were citizens.

God was secretly stirring wars for His people,

and the leader who went before the soldiers was clearing their way.

He gave His own the gold hidden deep in the earth,

which the Parthian had not heaped up for the use of our men.

While the siege held the fortress, our men held

this city and kept ships in its harbor.

The king of Miraclea also could not withstand our men;

lowering his neck, he submitted and entered into the desired alliance.

## BOOK SIX

[Col. 0985]

### Gibellum is surrounded by siege.

[Col. 0985D]

Now, with the material of the poem as my guide, most of which has been completed,

we look more closely at the harbor and the end of our labor.

I confess that this childish page obscures a great history

and that weak powers weigh down the burden itself.

Nevertheless, I shall undertake what I began,

though not by the path on which I began it.

I shall follow the sense, not sonorous words,

nor shall I make the endings answer one another,

while the melody of the poem shall itch for no one’s ears.

What humble style and rough meter had confined

a long account of events will pour forth for the weary.

Thus the first runner, leaving the starting gate,

willingly draws in the neck and bridle of the struggling horse.

[Col. 0986D] But when he is near the goal, he soon slackens the reins.

Now I too have slackened mine, for the goal is near.

While God, casting down the leaders and pillars of the people,

gives kingdoms to His poor and triumphs through the few,

lest human nature, applauding itself,

claim for itself what ought to be ascribed to the powerful Lord,

the Count of Flanders and the dukes came to Lycaea,

but Bohemond there abandoned his joyful companions.

Having retraced the road he had traveled,

he returned sadly to his own lands.

But that great leader, Godfrey, free for arms,

flew forth and greeted his fatherland with his sword in motion.

Now earthly things seem base to the duke;

now he embraces heaven itself and, secure in his reward,

does not fear fate.

The Fleming clings to him and, with equal zeal, yearns for him,

admires the duke, and honors his excellence—

in the duke whom he rightly surpasses in the greatness of his honor.

Although these men rejoice in Raymond’s success,

they did not attach themselves to another man’s labor.

But disdaining to resist cities with their strength,

they surrounded the city of Gibellum with a siege,

whose walls were encircled by steep ditches.

### A great slaughter of the unbelievers.

Meanwhile rumor brought Raymond sinister reports:

that the Parthians were coming to meet his men in battle.

Then the consul sent both envoys and pleading words

to the nobles whom the besieged city held.

They called a common council for the common danger;

they neither feared battle nor refused to bear assistance,

and joyful hope of triumph struck their hearts.

[Col. 0987B] Without delay, they made a treaty with those shut inside,

and peace was purchased from a citizen;

then they went to seek their companions.

The troop, deceived in its hope of battle,

turned in hope toward Arqa,

and covered the sands of the Castrensis River with its camps.

And so that your sword, Godfrey, should not grow cold for long,

the nobles led the army toward Tripoli,

so that from there more certain booty might come to you,

as from a full sheepfold.

Enemy met enemy, and the foolish crowd dared

to provoke mighty spirits with light arrows.

Just as the insolence of flies can hurt only

what is bare, and is usually driven away by the crack of a whip,

yet clings on and fixes its bites into the thing opposed,

so the arrow, committed to the winds,

harassing them and giving wounds short of death,

strikes them.

[Col. 0987C] The sword cuts them down,

and the shield held before the body becomes its wall.

But why do I linger here, where victory has not lingered?

The Parthian, already having cast away the aid of arms behind him,

seeks help in his feet and, despairing of safety,

the pressing soldier urges his horses with spurs,

presses the enemy with swords, and moves amid a bloody slaughter.

The severed limbs blunt the edges of the swords;

the trembling blade cannot cut some, but crushes their bones.

When the citizens had been extinguished, the army entered the city in horror,

and the river, bearing witness to the slaughter, drew redness from it.

The crowd also drained blood from the river after the event.

### Peace is established with the king of Tripoli.

The commanders, not sufficiently satisfied with slaughter

and too little satisfied with booty,

approached Desem, now ravaged again,

and restlessly searched out the remnants of their plunder.

They marveled at this valley, as though it were untouched on every side:

it produced oxen and asses,

and after so many raids offered the raider something to carry away.

Soon the tireless enemy dragged into the booty whatever he saw,

and the valley’s abundance filled hostile hands,

because it provided them with three thousand camels.

The camp was filled, the plunder refreshed the crowd,

but it also gave the enemy’s delay and courage

against the Christian besiegers,

and the possessions of the enemy nourished the enemy.

Yet neither battle could overcome those shut inside,

nor could engines break the walls.

The next lines have defective syntax in the supplied text: “and the forces of the Persians … Corbana the victor …

[Col. 0988A] which the city of Antioch feared, the avenging people presses.”

The Christians lose their companions and favorable time.

Here Ponce of Balon fell;

a stone hurled with tremendous force passed through his temple.

There William the Picard died, and with him Guarinus of Petramora:

the former by an arrow, these by a javelin;

one death came to them in two ways.

Amid so many sorrows, the light of Easter was celebrated during the siege,

and the feast was a guest in the camps.

The clear solemn day lacked its customary observance,

lest the nature of the place and the valor of the men

should contend there for too long,

and lest labor should be spent in vain

on the attempt to storm an impregnable fortress.

After besieging Arqa for three months,

they abandoned it and approached Tripoli.

There, joining hands with the city’s leading men,

they dared entrust themselves to uncertain walls

and carried themselves to the king’s lofty palaces.

The commanders confirmed the peace, repeatedly sought from the king,

so that the chains of their brethren might be released.

Then the king released three hundred Christian captives,

heavy with fetters and chains, from both forms of bondage.

Man to men he gave gifts, and gave men more precious than gold;

he added horses and gold and sent provisions to the people.

The king even declared voluntarily that he would become a Christian

if the Christians could accomplish his wishes.

Now the tree, the harvest, the field, fruits, grain, and beans

were giving back what had been ripened by the warmth.

Therefore the fertility of things and the freshness of the new season

drew the joyful troops toward their customary labors.

[Col. 0988C] It was the month of May when the brave men,

having left the city, came to the fortress of Betholon.

The day extending beyond Clieta was scarcely overcome

by the heavy night.

From there the youth, harassed by heat, skirted the seashore

and, arriving at Zebarim, suffered the hardships of immoderate thirst;

nor did he see in the city any waters from which he could drink.

But the labor of another day’s light led the thirsty men

to the broad fords of Braym,

and the people rushed toward the streams.

Leaning over them, the crowd, scarcely able to breathe and placing little trust in its vessel, greedily seized the water with thirsty mouths.

That was the day on which Christ, victorious,

ascending to heaven, offered Himself as an example to His stars.

But our troop measured out a difficult journey on that day

and pitched its camp before Barulh, beside the sea.

[Col. 0988D] After passing the two cities of Sagitta and Sur,

the fortunate raider came to Acra.

From there they approached the fortress of Caiphas;

leaving the fortress, the companies pitched their camps beside Caesarea.

There, if the feast of joy had encountered them at a joyful time,

the faithful would have observed it [Note: [Col. 0987D] This verse limps by one foot.],

the feast in which the Lord gave His disciples power over all things,

using His right, while the world marveled at the new gifts.

At last Ramula received the pilgrims as citizens—

the city emptied of its own citizen,

who had fled from the new enemies.

And to you, holy George, and to the church consecrated to you,

which rises spaciously above the neighboring city,

the holy people left its bishop and its tithes.

### Jerusalem is besieged.

[Col. 0989A]

Thus far the troop, repressed by the severity and heat of war,

tormented by poverty, thirst, the night, and battle,

came to the desired city,

which Solomon enriched with wealth and Christ with honor.

June was burning, and the sun was burning upon the arms,

when the commanders chose suitable places for their camps.

One part, toward the north, received the camp of the count of the Northmen,

and the Fleming clung to him.

From the setting of the sun Tancred terrified the city;

from the setting of the sun Godfrey advanced against the enemy.

From the middle of the day, Raymond, your trumpets sounded,

after Jerusalem had been surrounded by the crown of our men.

Raymond Piletus led out men matched in swiftness,

while the nearby ground was surveyed on horseback and the distant ground by the eye.

[Col. 0989B] Chance offered the raiders two hundred Arabs,

whom neither the lavish courage of their defender

nor their more numerous force rescued, but only shameful flight.

Flight saved some of them, but more were hurled down;

neither flight nor sword saved those whom our troop deprived of life,

and it brought their horses back to camp.

After arranging many things suitable for the coming destruction,

the men hastened toward their objective

and attacked the first wall, summoning the enemy with loud cries.

Soon the pagan, Jew, Turk, and Arab were present;

they were resisted with missiles, darts, fire, and poison.

But our men opposed bare breasts to the darts

and, for the sake of the One who was scourged,

endured harsh scourges.

Without delay, the great-hearted men rushed through stones and weapons,

and brought down the defenses of the outer wall.

[Col. 0989C] The scattered companies fled toward the safe walls,

and while each terrified man strove to be first,

the pursuing enemy crowd crushed its own people at the gate’s threshold.

Here each Pilades threw down his own Orestes.

The greater part, shut outside, groaned,

and parents did not receive their children, though they begged,

while compassion stood amazed.

Immediately a ladder, raised with immense effort,

provided a way to the heights.

The brave soldier clinging to it,

Rambaud, fosterling of the castle of Ciminum in the district of Dunois,

fought with swords and attacked the enemy at close quarters.

If a supply of ladders had been prepared,

that enormous labor would have been the final labor of the disaster.

Only this opposed our men,

and the fortune of war aided those driven to the last extremity,

revisiting them with alternating turns.

[Col. 0989D] At last the troop returned to camp and breathed again from arms.

The man who once used to disdain new dishes

and to summon hunger by tempting his throat

with the sweetness of delicacies

is now filled with dry bread

and deceives his palate with water flavored as though with spices,

which the thirsty soldier values as highly as precious gold.

For the spring of Mount Zion, summoned from its root,

the spring of Siloam, reached only with a small drink

and after a long journey,

refreshes countless peoples,

and its water is sold,

although powerful nature granted it freely.

While our people were oppressed by varied labor,

ships following the worshipers of Christ arrived.

Japhia, now a city and then an image of a city,

received them in its desired harbor.

Therefore one hundred men were sent from the siege

to guard the ships and repel the Turks.

[Col. 0990A] Acardus of Mount Merulo commanded the company,

together with William of Sabrata and Raymond.

But the upright Acardus ran ahead with a few men,

driven by his rashness more than by reason.

Here, finding seven hundred Arabs in a deep valley,

he burst upon them and, throwing away his spear,

split with a lightning sword the enemy he faced.

At last he fell—not as an example of sluggishness,

but of honorable death,

through which he himself warns his companions.

One man who escaped from them

announced to the cruel company its destruction,

shouting savagely:

“Behold, nobles, give funeral rites to your companions,

whom you cannot give life,

but whose death you may avenge by the enemy’s death.”

### A great thirst torments the Christians.

Thus encouraged, Piletus and Piletus’ companions—

whom the valor, vengeance for their companions,

true faith, love of the other, and relief from their labors

encouraged still more—

adorned their minds within with heavenly weapons

and clothed and armed their bodies without with strength.

Then they were thrown into confusion by a sudden sight:

the enemy, having withdrawn, saw their own men

plundering the dead.

Although those who could soon be counted

appeared innumerable, they nevertheless came to meet them.

Each chose and struck down his man in the first encounter.

At once a horrible battle was mingled in the ranks.

Helmets lost their crests, shields their devices.

Swords changed men’s faces,

and, with their noses cut away,

the young recruit was terrified by the recognition,

already doubting whether these were men;

he thought them monsters rather than men.

[Col. 0990C] Our troop attacked some with spears,

drove others back with swords,

and while running killed these by a bitter fall.

Sudden fear struck those men down helpless.

Afflicted by various misfortunes,

the pagan and the Arab gave their backs to easy flight.

After many had been killed,

the victorious man, celebrating, spared one by postponing his death.

Through him the hidden treacheries of the Persians would be revealed.

The soldier also led away from the enemy three horses and a hundred [the noun is absent in the source].

While the people were at leisure in the camp,

immoderate thirst tormented them.

The soldier dug into the earth with swords

and thrust his head into caves, leaving the daylight behind.

The text is uncertain here; one man received in his upturned mouth what fell from a wineskin, as though to relieve parched lips with the moisture of the rich earth;

another licked the marble sweating with dew.

[Col. 0990D] You might have seen the plague of the languishing

already drawn through all their bones,

their weakened strength making their gait falter,

and their tongues losing the use of speech.

When a balanced axe sometimes slaughters an ox,

after the flesh has been cast aside,

the crowd drinks up the blood.

It is pleasant to endure hunger;

that pain lessens this pain.

Who would ever have believed hunger useful?

The savage people had closed the hidden channels of water

and, watching the immense reservoirs,

lay in wait for the Christians

and dealt death to those seeking water.

When the people, dried out by deadly heat,

lose their vital warmth,

and their intestines, watered by no liquid,

are deprived of nature’s gifts,

a machine is built through Godfrey’s diligence,

[Col. 0991A] retaining the shape of a castle.

Timber discovered with much labor supplies material to the craftsmen and terror to the city.

Raymond’s prudent care likewise raises

a corresponding castle,

and towers are prepared against the towers.

The wretched pagans were astonished

to see new masses rising.

They themselves labored through the night

to enlarge their own towers,

with zeal making the labor less burdensome.

No less did the builders of the enormous castle—

whom the duke’s presence pressed—

stay awake, anxious for the night’s rest,

and by various arts carry on untimely labor under cover of night.

The night that had passed left rest for the Jews;

a dark veil covered the shining stars.

When the duke’s craftsmen brought the timbers

of the castle up to the walls,

threatening the sun’s rising,

[Col. 0991B] for they could more easily break in at the rising of the sun,

the Christians carried around Jerusalem

the emblems of Christ:

banners, crosses, and holy altars,

multiplying prayers, tears, fasts, and vows.

It would be a long delay for me, looking toward the end,

to say how many things, and in what ways,

the enemy gained in the short time

whose death-dealing Fate was already preparing to cut the threads.

That day had come on which the Master was to be put to death.

The Jewish people, desiring to put Jesus to death,

put itself to death.

On this day the commanders led their troops to the walls.

Count Eustace stood in the castle with Godfrey

and returned the blows he received with harsh interest.

The arrow sent by the duke pierces the Turkish flank,

not content merely to pass through the side.

[Col. 0991C] The duke performs the duty of a duke

and, strong in labor, encourages the fighters;

he also fights himself.

He fights for a double kingdom,

because he seeks both Jerusalems:

he fights in this one so that he may live in the other.

Stones falling upon the wicker screens

break the timbers;

the shields refuse the men from the summit of the castle.

### Jerusalem is captured.

The enemy’s valor did not fail at the point of death,

until the hour came when the cross that sanctified Christ

had received Him.

The hour arrived, diminishing the day and the city’s strength.

At that hour a certain man from the castle,

named Letaldus, pressing forward bravely,

leaped first upon the city wall.

Guicherius followed him,

the man who had cut down the lion with excessive valor.

Now the duke flashes above the lofty walls;

now the sword ranges widely through wicked breasts;

now the wall glows with lightning from the swords.

Raymond, unaware of these events,

was still bringing up the movable castle.

But he caught unfamiliar voices with his ears

and hastened himself toward David’s tower.

Without delay the Turkish prince,

to whom the guardianship of the tower had been entrusted,

with lowered voice, a supplicating face, and downcast eyes,

begged the consul for his life,

asking that he remove the rewards due to a defeated sluggard.

Behold, the frightened Turk opens the gate without a murmur

to the enemy,

a gate bought so many times at greater cost by our men.

The agitated victor bursts into the desired city,

and his assault presses the men headlong and heavily.

The final day comes upon the pagans.

They flee from war into war;

everywhere they slip and fall.

[Col. 0992A] No one holds back the sword.

Turk, Arab, and Jew fall;

the battle takes pleasure in their slaughter.

With a bloody hand it is sweet to go on,

and one is ashamed to carry a shining sword

that has not sweated with drinking blood.

The unwary people rush to Solomon’s Temple,

driven by fear of death,

as though the only salvation to be given were there,

and as though they could be sheltered in such an asylum.

Most had filled the house we mentioned.

There the hands of the victors began their work,

rushing across the slippery marble in slaughter.

Who could know the number of those falling—

could it even be numbered in thousands?

Everywhere, vainly scattered across all the steps,

heads lay severed far from their necks,

their white heads swimming amid the bloody carnage.

You might see severed hands joined to strange bodies,

and even trunks carried without knees,

[Col. 0992B] and every limb either cut away from its former place

or remaining wounded where it was.

So much blood flowed through the chambers

that you might think a river was running across the plain,

as when immense hail falls from the highest mountains

and the sky thunders together with mingled rains.

Then the waters, gathered together, seek the valleys lying low beneath the stream; they sweep away crops, carry off forests, and range over the whole level expanse of the fields. The peasant gives a groan from his breast. No differently are the limbs of the slain borne away, swept along in their own blood, and just as many are said to have been in the city.

Nevertheless, a few of them climbed the steps of the Temple

and set up their standards there:

Tancred and Gaston,

moved by pious feeling.

From there they hurry greedily toward wealth

and enter the houses.

[Col. 0992C] They find garments, riches,

and whatever would be enough for a miser,

if a miser could be satisfied by riches.

No one loses what each man seizes,

nor does another, however nobler,

claim what the poor man counts as his own.

When these things had been completed

and the city had been cleansed in this fashion,

the joyful crowds returned to their own rejoicing.

The commanders prostrated themselves,

their faces sprinkled with tears,

and duly venerated the Lord’s tomb for the sake of the Lord.

Here each faithful man gives his capital to God.

When morning came, the avenger was not yet filled

with so many disasters.

The soldier drew the blood that he knew still remained in a few persons,

and, silently climbing the lofty Temple,

suddenly disturbed the inert men.

They hurled themselves headlong from above,

[Col. 0992D] and the earth, striking them back—

the earth that gives life to the other living creatures—

sent them dying to the shades.

Others came against them with swords and manly courage.

They complained of delay in death,

offering their necks beneath the blows.

Some cut one another down

and snatched their own deaths from their enemies;

others were cut to pieces while fighting.

While each makes a shipwreck of himself,

each is killed.

The bodies of the slain are tied to the tails of horses

and piled outside beside the walls,

burned.

Many, indeed, lay divided into pieces in different places

and had lost the recognizable form of the human body.

The pagans, not yet condemned, gathered them while weeping

and carried the collected remains together to the foot of the hill.

### Godfrey is established as king of Jerusalem.

[Col. 0993A]

Meanwhile it was asked to whom the government of the kingdom

ought to be entrusted,

and who knew how to give Christ’s worthy rewards

to soldiers able by war to overcome tyrants,

following the example of Melchizedek,

who is said to have offered the just gifts

to the faithful and victorious old man.

At last, by divine will and the wholesome counsel of the nobles,

the duke Godfrey receives the government.

[Col. 0994A] On the eighth day after the city was captured

he assumed the kingdom,

a man worthy of a kingdom together with the blessed King.

May he live in the octave.

In the year one thousand, less one from the hundred,

Jerusalem was captured when the Ides of July were proclaimed.

I, Gilo, a Parisian by name,

an inhabitant of Tucciacum and undeniably its fosterling,

composed these things.

## THE ANTIOCHENE WARS OF GALTERIUS THE CHANCELLOR

*(Edited by Bongars in the collection entitled* Gesta Dei per Francos, *p. 441.)*

### NOTICE

Galterius wrote the *Antiochene Wars*. He himself says that he was a chancellor and a participant in both fortunes, column 1009, line 12; he mentions the chancellor again at column 1013, line 19. His language reveals a Frenchman: “Four times twenty thousand fighters”—something no one but a Frenchman, or someone steeped in the French language, would have said. Nor was he forgetful of his mother tongue: “Disconfectura,” and so forth.

Galterius the chancellor is cited in the *Book of the Lord’s Wars*; the author himself, the lord Petavius, is our authority for this. The entire work is worthy of cancellation, except that it is history, which, however written, must be preserved. He himself complains that his intellect was dulled by the force of imprisonment, column 1001, line 29.

Moreover, the single manuscript that we used, our copy from Jean Russat, was written most corruptly; nevertheless, we have not wished to alter anything. It narrates what was successfully accomplished at Antioch in the year 1115 and what ended unsuccessfully in 1119.

### INFORMATION

Several writers make Gaultier the chancellor and Gaultier, canon and archdeacon of Thérouanne, one and the same man; they likewise make the historian of the wars of Antioch and the author of the *Life of Charles the Good*, count of Flanders, one and the same writer (Val. And., p. 21, etc.).

Others are uncertain on this subject and maintain that there is neither proof nor reason capable of deciding the matter. Nevertheless, it is certain that Gaultier the chancellor and Gaultier, archdeacon of Thérouanne, are two different men and two different writers.

If Casimir Oudin (*Scriptores*, vol. II, p. 1062) had taken the trouble to read and compare together the history of the wars of Antioch and the *Life of Charles the Good*, he would have found sufficient grounds to decide and convince himself that these two works cannot be the product of the same pen.

The difference in style between the two works is so clear and palpable that it is impossible not to recognize two authors. The man who wrote the wars of Antioch had made the journey to the Holy Land; but the author of the *Life of Charles the Good* had not been present on any of those famous expeditions, as is sufficiently demonstrated by the silence he maintains about them on several natural occasions when he would have had reason to speak of them.

Indeed, when he reports the journey to the East of Robert the Younger, son of Robert the Frisian, and that of the prince whose life he is writing, would he have failed to make known, at least by a few indications, that he himself had made that journey?

It is unnecessary to go further in order to show that Gaultier the chancellor and Gaultier of Thérouanne are two different men and two different writers. We shall find further proofs of this in what we have to say about their persons and their writings.

Gaultier the chancellor was French, as Bongars proves in the preface to his collection (above). We know neither his origin nor his homeland. The author of the Supplement to Moréri’s Dictionary says that he accompanied Godfrey of Bouillon on his expedition to the Holy Land. This may be so, but there is nothing in his work on which one can establish that he accompanied Godfrey. In any event, he took part in the devotion characteristic of that century and went to Palestine, where he was chancellor to Roger, prince of Antioch. He himself gives himself the title of chancellor in the prologue to the second part of his work: *Ego ipse Gauterius cancellarius* (“I myself, Gaultier the chancellor”), where he says that he experienced good and bad fortune, which is the subject of his work; and that his experience taught him that prosperity is more harmful to the soul than adversity is to the body [Note: [Col. 0993] “I myself, Gaultier the chancellor, having shared in both fortunes and having experienced that the prosperity of the flesh harms the soul more than adversity harms the body.”].

Since he assumes the title of chancellor, it seems impossible to doubt that he is speaking of himself when he says that Prince Roger, after sending the barons to rest, secretly summoned his chancellor to consult him about the present state of his affairs. But the situation was beyond remedy: the prince lost both the battle and his life, while the chancellor lost his freedom, having been taken prisoner by the infidels. He suffered greatly during his captivity, so that his mind was seriously weakened by it. The tortures of every kind that the barbarians inflicted on their prisoners, and which he describes, were quite capable of producing such an effect.

The Supplement to Moréri’s Dictionary says that, after returning from this journey, Gaultier wrote the history of the siege of Antioch and of what he had seen and learned up to 1119. This is not exact. First, his work contains no account of the siege of Antioch; second, neither the prologues placed at the head of each part nor the body of the work gives the impression that he composed it upon returning from his journey. On the contrary, there is considerable evidence that he published it in the very places where the events he recounts had taken place: everything tends to suggest this. The author declares that what moved him to write was the desire to instruct sensible people and the princes who were to succeed Roger, by setting before their eyes the virtues and defects of that prince. The exhortations he makes in various places to the Christians of the country, urging them to repent and reform their morals—which he depicts in terrible terms—sufficiently show that he was writing for them and in the very places concerned.

The work, which is divided into two parts, is a history of the war that the Christians had to wage in the principality of Antioch in 1115 and 1119. At the head of the first part are these two verses, which express its subject and make known the author’s name:

> Here was victorious Roger, lord and duke  
> Of the Antiochenes, as the author Gaultier declares.

Gaultier, without giving the history of the siege of Antioch, which was then in Christian hands, confines himself to recounting later events. He begins with the earthquake that occurred on the eve of Saint Andrew, that is, on 29 November 1119. He then reports the great victory won by Roger, prince of Antioch, over the infidels. This constitutes the first part of his history, which portrays the flourishing condition of the city of Antioch under Roger.

The second part concerns the misfortunes of this prince and his principality. Its subject, like that of the first part, is contained in two verses:

> How the Antiochene prince Roger,  
> A man of great goodness, perished, Gaultier here recounts.

Gaultier gives an account of the disastrous battle that Roger rashly fought against the infidels in 1119. The successful outcome he had achieved against them in the preceding war had inflated his heart; he remained in a fatal security and neglected to take the measures and precautions that prudence always requires against the enemy, and he became its victim: he lost both the battle and his life. Most of the army perished there with its commander; the remainder fell into the hands of the barbarians, who exercised the most unheard-of cruelties upon their prisoners. The author of this history was among them.

The harsh and prolonged captivity he endured among these infidels somewhat disordered his mind, as we have already said. He himself acknowledges this in the form of an apology, to justify himself for the defects that might be found in a work he composed as well as he could, since his mind had been weakened by the severity of his imprisonment: *Pro capacitate ingenii nostri vi carceris hebetati* (“according to the capacity of our intellect, weakened by the force of imprisonment”). The excuse is certainly entirely legitimate, and what our author says deserves indulgence.

Bongars published this history in his *Collection of Historians of the Crusade*, where it occupies the seventh place under the title *Gualterii cancellarii Bella Antiochena* (“The Antiochene Wars of Gaultier the Chancellor”). The editor would not have considered it worthy of publication, except that everything historical must be preserved, whatever its style [Note: [Col. 0995] “Except that it is history, which, however it may have been written, must be preserved.”].

This history is indeed poorly written, but it is no less interesting for that. It is an eyewitness who gives an exact and faithful account of what he saw. He is a historian who reports important events in great detail, with such candor, good faith, and simplicity that one cannot doubt the truth of what he recounts, and one even reads him with pleasure despite the defects of his style. Finally, he is a deeply religious Christian who writes piously, sees the hand of God in every event, regards successes as effects of divine goodness, and failures as punishment for the sins of people who glory in the blessings they have received. Such a work deserved to see the light. The author composed it after several years of captivity, that is, after 1119, when he was taken prisoner. This is all that can be said about it. For the rest, we know neither the time nor the place of his death. It is highly uncertain, to say no more, that he ever returned to France.

# THE ANTIOCHENE WARS BEGIN

[Col. 0995]

## PART ONE

> Here was victorious Roger, lord and duke  
> Of the Antiochenes, as the author Gaultier declares.

## THE PROLOGUE BEGINS

[Col. 0995A]

It is worthwhile to hear, and it accords with the public good, how, by what miracles, and through what favor God, the Judge, unexpectedly waged war against the Parthians by the hand of Roger, prince of Antioch [Col. 0996A]. For when the power of miracles and the deeds of good men have been heard, the wicked will more readily be struck down, while the good will be encouraged toward better things.

Therefore I beg the help of Him at whose prompting all good deeds are accomplished, who supplied that same prince with the strength of the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, by which he was able to shatter the pride of the nations and overcome their savagery. May He also deign to pour down from heaven upon me the power to write and the abundance of speech, since I desire to commit the sequence of these events to writing and to the memory of posterity, so that those capable of reason and defenders of the true faith, having heard the truth, may cling manfully to the command and service of their Creator. May their adversaries, struck with divine terror, both present and future, instead of trusting in the Lord, place their confidence in their own strength, turn their backs upon the Lord’s arrows, and not presume to return to a similar undertaking.

Nevertheless, after examining the necessary divisions of the battle and taking up a subject proportionate to my strength, it seems to me very useful, before narrating the battle, first to indicate the evils that preceded it [Col. 0997B], so that, from the causes already mentioned, the effects that follow may more easily be understood.

First, then, swarms of locusts, driven far and wide under the metaphor of enemies, took away entirely from the inhabitants of Syria everything necessary for food. Then, partly crawling upon the ground and partly dispersing through the air, they brought nearly all the eastern Christians into the same calamity. Although they knew that they deserved to be afflicted with fitting punishment, they did not seek their Lord and Creator, hoping that He might be reconciled to them; instead, clinging to their former vices, they even exceeded the bounds of shame and added crimes to crimes.

Some, haters of fasts and devoted to feasts, addicted to the allurements of the appetite, strove to imitate not the morals and life of those who lived well, but of those who feasted well [Col. 0997C]. Others, driven by incestuous desire, pursued the company of the shameless; they even endeavored to defile with indecency the dignity of the city’s public women, making it uncertain whether they themselves should be considered more foul or more criminal.

Some among those who possessed unjustly acquired wealth, having abused even what belonged to them, eagerly sought vessels suitable for luxurious excesses, engraved by the art of Solomonic workmanship. According to reports concerning the craftsman, they carefully endeavored to have coverings for their foul parts fashioned for their wives from Arabian gold and a great variety of precious stones. They did not do this to cover their shame or restrain the flame of lust, but so that what was forbidden might burn more fiercely those to whom what was permitted was distasteful [Col. 0997D].

Since in this way they wished to stimulate their lust and believed that they were beautifying and gratifying the women, they increased, as we have said, crimes by crimes. The women, for their part, had nothing sacred and considered nothing seriously when pursuing shameful pleasures. Enjoying themselves, they despised their husbands’ beds and served incest in brothels and houses of prostitution. At crossroads, in streets, and at chosen drinking places, they kept vigil day and night over extravagant drinking. Moving through the squares and the neighborhoods, with the dress and gait of wantonness, they confronted the eyes of passersby. They were purchasable for any price by those who wished to possess them. Even those whom they could not provoke to their own indecency, whether unwilling or not, they scarcely allowed to withdraw, even when offered money.

Thus, while they did not mourn the evils they had committed and voluntarily and publicly committed those over which they ought to have mourned, the author of supreme justice allowed them to be afflicted—not by destroying them, but by sparing them—with signs, portents, plagues, and even the tribulation of hostile nations, imposed over many successive years [Col. 0998A]. They are shown to have served under the authority of the Greeks while the Greeks ruled. Once the Greeks had been driven out of Asia, they yielded to the dominion of the ruling Parthians; finally, by the will of the Lord, they submitted to the still more intolerable descendants of the Franks.

Since the Syrians mentioned above and their rulers were corrected neither by this nor by that, they suffered from the earthquake that followed such calamity and destruction as no history had ever recorded before.

## CHAPTER ONE

In the year 1115 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, on the vigil of the feast of blessed Andrew the Apostle, during the silence of the night, when human frailty ordinarily rests more easily and pleasantly, an immense and dreadful earthquake struck Antioch and all its surrounding regions [Col. 0998B].

Suddenly and unexpectedly shaken with terror, people felt, saw, and heard the collapse of walls, towers, and various buildings threatening them from every side. Some, thinking they could escape by fleeing, got away from the walls; others threw themselves from high houses into the abyss. Many, caught asleep in the destruction, were carried away limb by limb, so that although part of a body remained intact, they disappeared without a trace.

Others, overcome by terror, abandoned their homes, rejected their possessions, and left everything behind. They wandered through the city’s squares and streets like madmen, yet with hands extended toward heaven, and, according to the varying forms of their fear and helplessness and in their different languages, they did not cease crying out in tearful voices: “Spare us, Lord; spare your people” [Col. 0998C].

When morning came and the miserable destruction of human beings and other creatures lay exposed beneath the ruins, all alike—Latins, Greeks, Syrians, Armenians, residents, and foreigners—declared that this had happened because their sins demanded it. Without delay, following sound counsel, they fled to the church of the blessed apostle Peter itself, seeking the protection of perpetual guardianship.

The One whom they had not acknowledged in prosperity, but whom His supreme goodness, working together with justice, revealed as powerful and merciful in adversity, they all recognized. They confessed that they had grievously sinned against Him and renounced their former and present pleasures. They most devoutly promised amendment to Lord Bernard, the first Latin patriarch, who, together with his clergy and the other faithful, humbly implored the Lord in the faith and prayers of their hearts. As we truly believe, the Lord took pity on the remnant of His people of Antioch [Col. 0998D].

After the divine office had been celebrated, a sermon delivered, and instructions given concerning how they should conduct themselves and what they ought to do, they supposed that nothing more serious had occurred. Suddenly, however, they were terrified by a dreadful report. Some people who, by divine providence, had escaped the danger of the ruin of the town of Miragium declared that the town itself, together with its lord and bishop, its clergy, and its entire population, had been utterly destroyed.

Not long afterward, the memory of the town of Mamistra, together with its inhabitants and most of the city, likewise overwhelmed them. Its earlier destruction on the feast of Saint Brictius multiplied their fear. What of the other territories of Antioch? What of Cyprus? One part, they say, is subjected to torments unlike those of the other. Thus fear mingled with terror was multiplied among the wretched people, so that they utterly did not know where they should remain or where they should flee.

For day after day, at the most desperate hours, earthquakes continued. Therefore they said to one another: “O wretched necessity of being born, miserable necessity of dying, harsh necessity of our living.”

Although they knew that it was nowhere and never possible to flee from God’s power, they nevertheless chose more readily to live outside with beasts than continually to fear buildings collapsing inside. Accordingly, they occupied the lanes, squares, gardens, and thickets, abandoning their homes; others used tents in place of their houses [Col. 0999B].

Many also, having left the cities, stayed from place to place in field huts. The patriarch of the place, the most learned man of the time, proceeding through the necessary branches of philosophical instruction, soothed the hearts of the desolate and of those who had nearly despaired of life, warming them with the sweetness of holy preaching.

Then, at last, he imposed upon the whole people a three-day fast in grief and a spirit of contrition, adding that they should avoid evil deeds and devote themselves diligently to every good work.

What, then, was the result? The people were brought back into the service of the Lord in the following manner. They fled feasting, detested drunkenness, avoided bathhouses [*baldea*, as printed], and abhorred fornication. Setting aside every bodily adornment, they changed their clothing to ashes and sackcloth. From square to square and from church to church, men separately and women separately, barefoot, with loosened hair, beating their breasts and drenching their faces with abundant tears, they attended litanies to the Lord day after day from the depths of their hearts [Col. 0999C].

At night, both in the churches and in their chambers, they devoted themselves earnestly to prayer. They recalled the scattered, corrected those who had gone astray, sought to bring comfort to orphans and widows, and to supply their needs. They also endeavored, with sufficient hospitality and cheerful expressions, to revive the bodies of the poor, needy, and destitute, and, once revived, to gladden them with gifts.

What more? Corrected by the fruit of repentance and adorned with good works, they were freed from the danger of earthquakes, which continued to threaten for five months and more—not by their own merits but by God’s grace—and joyfully offered thanksgiving to the Almighty [Col. 0999D] in His Church.

## CHAPTER II

The aforementioned prince, visiting his ruined buildings in the camps and elsewhere, quickly sought out what was necessary and hastened to repair and fortify those places that he knew were most useful for the defense of his land and closest to the enemy, if not completely, at least for immediate protection.

When summer returned, as was customary in that region, he hurried to the borders, where he could most quickly hear of the Parthians’ arrival and from which he could most swiftly meet the enemy’s troops. He therefore reached the Fountain of Faris, where he had previously ordered his army to meet him.

While he was there discussing the common good with his men, he decided to send scouts of various nations to those Parthian territories whose rulers, never disappointed by reports from their own messengers, were accustomed to bring support to the Christian army [Col. 1000A].

He left the army there and returned to Antioch with a few men. After summoning the Antiochene duke Ralph of Acre, a man of experienced counsel, he first deliberated with him about what should be done concerning reform and the condition of the entire city. He also consulted him about what ought to be done with the lord and the soldiers in preparation for war.

The duke therefore ordered that the viscount be summoned to him, the viscount the praetor, the praetor the herald, and the herald the judge. Once these men had been called, the matter described above was taken up. By command of the lord prince, the great were summoned, and the lesser were summoned as well. They assembled without delay.

The duke addressed them handsomely and explained the reason for the present business and his lord’s decree, saying that it should be carried out if it did not displease them in their judgment [Col. 1000B]. Having heard the matter and accepted the prince’s decree, they were all of one opinion.

The destructions of the walls and towers were therefore measured, and those who possessed lands and honors were assigned the necessary repairs according to the greater or lesser extent of their holdings. Meanwhile, the prince carefully requested guards and guardsmen whom he had recognized as especially loyal, both in the town and in the city, since he was about to go to war.

Then, after weapons and the other necessities of war and food had been prepared, and after hearing the divine office in the churches of the blessed intercessors—the holy Virgin Mary, Peter and Paul, George, and many others—he prayed, received permission and the patriarchal blessing, commended himself, the city, and all that belonged to him to God, the lord, and the patriarch, bade farewell to everyone, and set out on campaign [Col. 1000C].

From one side the lord arrived at the army; from the other, scouts arrived. Asked whether Persia rejoiced at the ruin and destruction of Syria, they publicly replied that it did. They reported that Sultan Corocos, having received omens from the sun and moon, had ordered the army of all Persia to march, and confidently asserted that Syria, abandoned by God and marked by the sign of the earthquake, with only a small remnant of inhabitants, could easily be subjected to his rule.

They hurried to reveal newer and more secret information to the prince alone, with an interpreter, after being admitted behind the chancel screens. Those who were to be dismissed were dismissed from behind the curtains so that they would not interrupt; those who were to be admitted were admitted by prudent counsel [Col. 1000D].

The prince therefore reflected to himself that “arrows which are anticipated strike less effectively, and the wise do not repent after taking counsel.” He explained the embassies and the reason for the embassies to his men one by one and consulted them about what would be most useful to do.

After the necessary matter had been discussed, they thought it appropriate to hasten to Cereptum. They had heard, as rumor reported, that Boldechin, king of Damascus, accompanied by Amirgazi, emir of the Turcomans, with ten thousand soldiers, had reached Aleppo with Rodoam, the son of Calep.

Their purpose, however, was to arrange, once an agreement had been made, to hand the place over to the sultan in exchange for the death of Maledoctus, if they could accomplish this. Therefore our men hurried forward, fervently accelerating their warlike preparations, in order to change their minds [Col. 1001A].

When they learned that our men had reached their territory, they concealed their state of mind by the expression of their voices, overcome by fear. For, having sent messengers to the prince, they said that they had come to fight against the Parthian enemy and to strengthen a treaty of friendship with him.

Dodechinus, however, although he feared the formidable power of Christian and Parthian soldiers, nevertheless preferred to enter into a false peace with the Christians in order to lead them to destruction rather than submit to the Parthians, whom he had discovered to be much more cruel to him in peace than in war.

They therefore met at the appointed place. There they established agreements and became, as it were, friends. They accordingly arranged where it would be most useful to march against the enemy, but they did so in different ways. The Damascene advised marching toward places that would be more advantageous to him and his men in either fortune; the Antiochene toward those from which they could attack the enemy more quickly in a direct assault [Col. 1001B].

Why recount every detail? The prince’s judgment prevailed. He had already been informed that the army of the barbarians would come through Salobria to Sisara, which had previously been tributary and subject to our people but had now turned against them, trusting in the support of those who later, through the actions of both sides, suffered losses.

At last our men, sending scouts against the enemy, set out for Apamia. There they seemed to meet as sons and fathers in a bond of fellowship and hospitality, and also in a tie of complete affection, although they differed in number and valor. The prince’s contingent could not be found to exceed two thousand fighters; the other allied force was considered by many to equal ten thousand.

Yet, although the latter was greater in number, it was inferior in valor. They camped before Apamia and remained there for two months before reliable news was brought of the Parthians’ approach.

In August, it was reported that Burno, the Parthian commander, surrounded by very powerful troops of fighters, had already crossed the Euphrates and had violently invaded the regions of Syria [Col. 1001C].

When the prince learned that this was true, he informed the king of Jerusalem and the count of Tripoli through messengers well known to him, sending sealed letters that named the enemy’s arrival and the location, which was not far from our men, at the Saltworks. There they were awaiting the omen of the waxing moon amid drinking and other pleasures. He urged them, to the best of their ability and with all speed, to come to the aid of the Christian army.

The king, always intent upon valor and acting without delay, sent messengers to the count that he should not linger and himself followed as quickly as possible on the same day [Col. 1001D]. Nevertheless, he gave the prince an advance message, under oath of Christian faith and brotherly friendship, that wherever they might be or wherever they might halt, they should not presume to engage the enemy without their assistance.

## CHAPTER III

Meanwhile, as rumor had foretold, the enemy marched through Salobria, obtained the supplies they needed there, and reached Hammam. When they found that the sultan’s forces had given the place to them—since they could obtain it neither by threats nor by entreaties—they attacked it most vigorously, accompanied by a very powerful force of armed men.

After attacking it on every side and cutting down many people, the stronger enemy entered by force [Col. 1002A]. Once inside, they exposed the lady of the town; after putting some of the stronger men of the village to death and exposing others, they distributed their possessions among themselves and stationed their own guards there.

When this had been done, they approached Sisara, relying on the friendship of the emir of Fisar, wishing to lodge with him. He, however, mindful of the misfortune of the people of Hammam, judged it more useful to provide them with the necessary supplies outside than to endure the trouble of admitting them within. He feared that the savagery of the enemy might overflow into his own affairs, but even more he feared that he himself might become their victim and be put to death.

He therefore sent his brother ahead, as rumor reported, accompanied by horses bearing gifts, so that he might offer richer gifts to Burso [Col. 1002B], and by presenting other gifts make the remaining nobles favorably disposed toward him. Through his mediation, he wished a treaty of friendship to be established among them, on the condition, however, that while the lord of Sisara remained to defend the town, his brother—an indigenous man who knew the approaches and retreats of the region and what was necessary for devastation and war—would march with them as their guide and provider of what was useful.

But, as I shall say in what follows, through the working of the Lord, the matter turned out contrary to their expectations. The brother, obeying his brother’s command, gladly carried out the task entrusted to him.

The army camped before the caves of Sisara. Once again, after arranging drinking parties, they attempted day after day to harass our men in battle with watchmen stationed at a distance. The prince, therefore, bound by the oath of Christian faith and by the king’s brotherly affection, universally renounced both the preliminary engagement and the opening of battle, even at the cost of having his eyes gouged out [Col. 1002C].

When this became known, the arrogant enemy unexpectedly reached the fortress of Cafarda, three leagues from our men. Although it was attacked repeatedly and the interior defenders were oppressed by frequent blows of arrows and stones and by dreadful wounds, it could not be captured on that occasion.

After one of their emirs had been killed and many wounded, they returned to the army, asserting that their grief could be lessened by revenge. While they were devising how they might attack our men more fiercely, news of the king’s imminent arrival struck their ears.

Trusting not in the power of the Holy Spirit but in the multitude of their army, they formed their troops before the king arrived and sent more suitable forces toward our tents as a preliminary engagement [Col. 1002D]. They decided that their battle lines, arranged according to their custom, should follow in scattered formation, with the place assigned to Burso as their commander and with a very large garrison remaining in the fortress they had attacked.

What more? Brandishing spears and shooting arrows, they ran almost up to our camp. When the aforementioned prince saw this, he mounted a swift horse, drew his sword, and rode around the camp of his men, declaring: “By the faith of God, by which we live, if anyone now presumes to leave, he shall perish by my sword.”

Indeed, he ordered everyone to remain by his fortress with armed hand and vigilant spirit, and in no way to presume even to display a signal for engaging them.

The Parthians therefore marveled that a people most ready for war and always impatient of insult, provoked so many times by arrows and so many times assailed with insults, could endure this so patiently, showing no signal for battle, as though already defeated and overcome by fear of them [Col. 1003A].

Some of our own men also attributed this conduct to cowardice. Others, of more penetrating judgment, inferred that the princes were acting in this way deliberately, so that, having determined the appropriate moment, they might attack them not at the enemy’s prompting or through confidence in their own strength, but according to the disposition of themselves and of the king, who was soon to arrive, and with a strategy suited to the circumstances.

For, as has often been observed, in war a small number of fighters, when combined with boldness and intelligence, frequently prevails over a large multitude of armed men that is foolish and wavering.

## CHAPTER IV

Meanwhile, as rumor reported with increasing speed, it became known that King Baldwin and Count Pontius were hastening forward manfully and rapidly [Col. 1003B].

Burso, the commander of deceitful cunning, therefore retreated, pretending to flee. As though wishing to return home, he divided his forces through the territories of Sisara and for a time concealed his wicked design, so that, once our men had withdrawn and separated, they might more safely destroy the border towns.

Meanwhile the king entered our camp, as was customary, with cymbals resounding and trumpets sounding everywhere. As soon as the king learned that the enemy had withdrawn, he complained that he had come much too late.

After a brief consultation, since they did not know where to pursue the enemy or where they might find them, they decided to go and attack a fortress then subject to the Parthians, called Gistrum, judging that by this action they might recall them to battle [Col. 1003C].

Our men reached the place without delay. Suddenly, having arranged their troops all around it, they vigorously attacked both the town and its suburb. At last, the suburb, seized by sword blows, was partly destroyed and partly burned by fire.

Although the Persians understood, from the report of the smoke-filled clouds and from what their own eyes saw, that our men had burned the town to their disgrace, they nevertheless feared to attack those whom they had previously invaded. By this judgment, they concluded among themselves that whatever they had earlier interpreted before our camp as inertia and cowardice was in fact the result of intelligence, boldness, and valor.

Since the enemy neither appeared nor was any rumor heard about where they had remained, the question arose what should be done about the matter. One party, which hoped to gain more through warfare than to retain at home what it already possessed [Col. 1003D], suddenly declared that it was best to pursue them.

The party whose minds were recalled by the sweetness of their possessions judged that, since the enemy was numerous and very strong, it would be more useful for everyone to return to his own territory in order to protect the towns.

Accordingly, the king of Jerusalem returned with his men to Tripoli; the Damascene to Damascus; and the Antiochene prince to Antioch. We understand that this was not accomplished by the power of those men, but without doubt by the power of Him who wished to separate the fellowship of Belial from our people.

Not long afterward, the enemy, exercising tyranny in the region of Sisara, attacked one day with extreme violence the fortress of Cafarda, where they had already suffered a loss. From one side they attacked; from the other they struck it with stone-throwers and other engines [Col. 1004A], so that, after breaches had been made in the wall, a wide entrance was opened.

Once inside, they killed some of the defenders who were present, avenging those who had previously been killed. Others they reserved because of their higher status, so that they could present them to the sultan as the prize of victory.

But afterward, by God’s grace, their prosperity turned against them. Having utterly destroyed that fortress and devastated the surrounding territory, cutting down everyone they found, they reached Marra, which they had devastated previously. There, remaining as though in their own territory, they carefully prepared engines by which Sardona might be captured.

These events and others like them were quickly revealed to Lord Roger, the prince, who was in Antioch. When he heard this, moved by manly courage, he withdrew to Rubea accompanied only by his household. He ordered all his men to hasten there without any delay or excuse [Col. 1004B].

He also asked the lord patriarch with the greatest devotion to come there, so that, having received the benefit of his office and blessing, they might carry out God’s service more freely and securely.

In the month of September, on Sunday, the day before the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, the Antiochene patriarch Philacabas arrived quickly at the appointed place.

He spoke distinctly and openly of what was more pleasing to God than to men. Whatever he knew in them to be reprehensible or contrary to God, he did not keep silent about there. Rather, as a father should, he taught them by reproving, pleading, and rebuking what they ought to avoid and what they ought to pursue.

They did not blush to confess their sins to God and to the lord patriarch. The lord patriarch imposed upon each of them, in place of true repentance, according to each person’s ability and with God’s help, the observance of complete justice.

He imposed it in such a way, he said, that those who died in that great war might be saved through his absolution and through the Lord’s favor. Those who returned were to assemble at the next feast of All Saints, at a council that had been appointed, and at the council of the Church of Antioch were to render full justice among themselves, both concerning possessions and in other matters.

The following supplement was added: if they were unable to fulfill everything completely through ignorance or inability, they should not refuse to submit to the counsel and judgment of those who were more capable of knowing the truth according to justice [Col. 1004C].

This arrangement having been explained and imposed, it was accepted by all. One by one, with joined hands, they placed their hands in the hands of the patriarch and promised it faithfully to God and to him during the truce and through the reconciliation of the Church: if anyone should happen to go astray, he could be saved through amendment and satisfaction rendered to the Church [Col. 1004D].

When these things had been completed, the venerable patriarch celebrated the solemn rites of the Mass. After first granting the people entrusted to him absolution from their sins, he strengthened them all with the patriarchal blessing. He humbly commended them to the spiritual care of the bishop of Gibellum, who was going with them to the war, and, after greeting everyone, returned to Antioch, continually supplicating and beseeching the Lord that He who humbles the proud and from the beginning crushes wars might crush the adversaries by the assault of His people.

On the following day, having stationed guards all around, the prince confidently ordered his columns to advance and to hasten toward the place where he had heard from the report of neighboring inhabitants that the Parthians were about to arrive at any moment. When they had approached the assigned place, prepared to rush upon the enemy, they did not find there those whom they were already seeking to destroy; they encamped before Hapa.

When the morning had passed, and the office of the Mass of the Life-Giving Cross had been celebrated—for that day was the feast of its Exaltation—Wiliermus, bishop of Gibellum, a man in every respect praiseworthy, instructed, admonished, and armed the people entrusted to him by God with words and examples appropriate to that feast. What more need be said? With the greatest devotion, before undertaking their march, they all hastened to adore the most sacred wood of the same Lord’s Cross. Strengthened by its permission and blessing, and sending ahead the scouts of the explorers lest a sudden enemy attack them, they took up the road in ordered formation. The count of Edessa, by the gift of the princes, held the place of precedence in the battle as the first to strike; the remaining columns were arranged according to the order required by warfare.

Suddenly Theodericus Barneville, one of the scouts, arrived in haste and spoke with a cheerful countenance:

“Behold what we were seeking; behold what we desired, through the working of divine grace: in the valley of Sarmit, near the springs, where we had planned to pitch our tents, there the enemy is unfolding its tents—some already erected, others still to be erected.”

At this the prince said: “In God’s name, to arms, soldiers!”

Having spoken thus, and relying on manly courage, he rode swiftly from one battle line to another, urging everyone to rejoice now that the contest was prepared in which it was fitting for a soldier’s duty to be exercised. He therefore ordered the weapons to be carried and commanded those who were ready not to delay any longer.

Immediately the aforementioned prelate, carrying the Cross of the Lord’s wood in his venerable hands, went around the entire army. As he displayed it to all, he declared that they would soon obtain victory through its power if they rushed upon the enemy with resolute hearts and fought as believers in the Lord Jesus. At once, all proclaiming together in heart and voice, “Holy God, holy mighty one, holy and immortal, have mercy on us,” they fell prostrate three times on bended knees before the Lord’s wood and, after reverently kissing it, commended themselves to it. Strengthened by this consolation and marked with this sign, they saluted the Cross again and again and swiftly mounted their horses.

The prince, however, maintaining an undaunted spirit, silenced the others with a gesture and spoke:

“Come, my brothers and fellow soldiers, and you infantry as well: let us now draw nearer. Remember with what praise, what veneration, and what commemoration in the writings the deeds of good men are recorded throughout the world. Behold, the time has come when our strength and courage may flourish, when our victorious name may shine more brightly than the barbarians throughout the regions of the world. Consider also that the Lord already promises a crown to those who fight lawfully. Let us therefore hasten to enter among them; when our lances are broken, let us approach more closely with bared swords, so that by our repeated blows their pride may be overthrown and, with God exacting vengeance, their destruction may not be delayed.”

As they proceeded in ordered formations, the prince gave a general command that no one, moved by desire for riches, should turn aside to plunder. Rather, as befits those engaged in battle, while protecting their own safety, they should strive to destroy the ferocity of the enemy. The aforementioned prelate therefore proclaimed that those who resisted this salutary judgment deserved to be punished by bodily vengeance and—what was more intolerable—confirmed that they were to be struck with perpetual anathema. Thus he girded each man more courageously for the contest.

## CHAPTER V

Meanwhile, against the weapons of our men, as the sunlight flashed, the Parthians’ eyes were dazzled. They supposed and said that the prince was not there, but that a wandering rabble was defending the march. Burso therefore ordered those men to be brought to him from behind, their hands twisted back and bound with ropes.

There was no delay: the prince’s standards appeared. Under God’s direction, they seemed so spread out to the Parthians that, seeing the soldiers and standards whitened, they believed the entire surrounding land to be covered with them. Burso and his men, however, all steeped in the filth of error, did not delay in climbing the mountain called Daniz with his brother and a very great force of fighters, so that our men might resist them there. At its summit they invoked to be present with them the aid of the lofty *mathesis* (astrological art) of false gods. At last they seemed to have burdened the mountain not only with themselves but also with a vast quantity of wealth, while Tumbaret lay hidden beyond the mountain with his formation as a reserve.

The others, captivated by wealth in their tents and outside them, confidently awaiting the strength of their own men and especially of their princes, arrogantly waited. Their situation was helped neither by repentance, because it was too late, nor relieved by the protection of their own people, because that protection had been lost.

For behold, Rotgerius, the most distinguished prince of the Christian army, arrived with his formation, exceedingly fierce against the enemy. With trumpets sounding through the middle of the camp, he freed his captives, cut down the enemy, and regarded wealth as dung. He directed his march toward the mountain where their standards and strength had been massed.
