The count of Edessa and Guido Capreolus, arranged for the first blows, advancing on the left, declared that one of them would attack the enemy directly across the mountain and the other obliquely. Burso, however, wounded by the dart of divine terror, descended with his brother and his companions as though to fight, ordered them to resist manfully and defend the mountain, but himself sought flight with as many as he could take.

Meanwhile, here the count and there Guido, at the first charge, broke their lances, drew their swords, and struck the enemy. The resulting cries, lamentation, and clash of arms from both sides of the combatants so deafened their ears that neither friend could understand friend nor brother brother. Our men, however, neither terrified by the shouting nor overcome by exhaustion, recovering their strength with equal courage, drove out, disemboweled, and cut down the enemy.

When he saw this, Tumbaret sprang obliquely to the left, accompanied by a shining formation of three hundred soldiers. He rode behind the prince’s line; although they dared neither attack it nor force it from its advance by their repeated volleys of arrows, they caused the Turcopoles, who were shooting against them, to plunge more rapidly into our ranks. In the very momentum of the charge, they encountered head-on the cohort of Robert Fulcoius, which was moving backward.

When they saw it, Rotbertus Surdevallis and Bocardus, excellent soldiers, did not fear to confront the ferocity of that desperate people. They suddenly threw themselves into the midst of the enemy, cutting down the treacherous men; at last they too were cut down and became martyrs of Christ. Rotbertus, without delaying to avenge the blood of his men, continued fighting valiantly. His horse’s girths having been cut, he was wounded by an arrow and died, while his cohort was completely scattered.

Alanus, a young man, and Guido Frenellus, advancing together, proclaimed in a living voice:

“Our most proven fellow soldiers, now our men must be given assistance.”

They were immediately admitted. Having completed the work of their lances, with blows of their swords they recovered our dead and protected the living men of that formation. Yet on both sides immense blood was poured out in turn.

Meanwhile, the formations of our men, looking to both the right and the left and seeing the multitude of Parthians roaring on every side, rushed into the midst of the enemy with one accord, proclaiming: “Christ Jesus!” At the first assault, when the divine sword struck, the enemy’s cry—which had previously been terrifying and immense—was transformed into something wholly different: the repeated gasps of the dying.

Why recount each detail? Some became the occasion of death through punishments of various kinds; the rest, struck by the dart of divine vengeance, turned their backs and fled. Thus the prince, devoted to God, obtained victory that very day through the power of the holy Cross. By the Lord’s generosity, the fortunate field of battle was opened to him.

Remaining in the field with his household, as was fitting, and praising his men, he immediately sent them to pursue the others. In this undertaking, the formation of blessed Peter earned the name of the foremost in praise. There the plain was partly covered with dead bodies and partly filled with a multitude of camels and other animals loaded with wealth. This was an impediment to our men in killing, but it became a means of escape for those who were fleeing. Nevertheless, our men pursued the enemy, striking, wounding, and cutting them down, for two miles beyond Sarmit.

At last, having returned as victors, carrying, sending, and leading away various spoils, burdened with wealth and giving thanks to God the Creator, they arrived rejoicing before the lord Rotgerius, the prince who held the field.

Why should I recount the sequence of the captured riches, when neither their quantity nor their variety can be assessed by anyone? Why the number of the slain enemy, when they were countless, while among us they were reckoned few? The prince held the field for three days. When the riches had been brought before him, he ordered that whatever was fitting for so great a prince be reserved for himself and that the rest be divided, as the rule and custom of his court required.

After this had been done, the prince, with an abundance of various treasures before him and a multitude of captives led ahead, supplicated God, gave thanks to all his men, and, out of pious paternal affection, dismissed them all, since they had performed God’s service manfully and wisely. When the principal nobles returned to their own estates and had visited their wives and children, he ordered them to return to Antioch at the appointed time to deliberate, in the council of the Church of Antioch, on the welfare of Christianity.

He himself, returning with the manifest palm of victory, was joyfully received by all the people through fields and fortified villages, with hymns and songs. When he had approached the venerable city of Antioch, the sound of his arrival resounded throughout the whole city. The venerable patriarch, preceded by an orderly procession of the holy relics and accompanied by his clergy, adorned with ecclesiastical vestments, went out to meet him, followed by a multitude of men and women. They received, praised, and venerated him while singing in angelic voices: “Fear God and observe his commandments” (Eccles. 12:13).

“To the honor of the highest King, and for the fulfillment of his kingdom, free man, slave, and maidservant rejoice on that day.”

Meanwhile, the people of the various nations strove to crown the city with flowers. Whoever possessed an expensive or rare ornament did not conceal it then but brought it forth, so that it might please the victor. They spread silk ornaments over the lanes and streets and adorned them with gold and jewels for the prince’s arrival. So great was the fragrance of the various spices that the place could be called entirely an earthly paradise.

The prince entered; the populace resounded with hymnic praises. They praised God and greeted him with high-pitched voices. Thus they came together to the church of Saint Peter, where they joyfully offered praises to God the Father.

The prince then carried the triumphal standard to the altar. He offered that special standard and afterward the lesser one. Having adored the true God, he gave thanks to all the clergy, through whose prayer he had been adorned and had emerged a blessed victor.

As he was leaving through the doors, everyone cried out with the voice of their hearts:

“Hail, king! Champion of the true God, may God’s enemies fear you, and may continuous peace, health, and victory be yours forever and ever. Amen.”

## PART TWO

The Most Valiant Prince Rotgerius of Antioch

Gauterius here relates how he perished. [Col. 1007]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1007D]

Among the various outcomes of the wars of ancient times, it is certainly true that some of them, recorded by historians, brought either sorrow or joy into the minds of their hearers. But that account of the greatest grief and of complete misfortune, by which sudden calamity entered upon the warlike host of Rotgerius, prince of Antioch, and upon the prince himself—because the weight of his crimes demanded it—so utterly removed joy and exceeded every limit and measure of misery that it cannot be expressed in words or conceived in the mind: how many punishments, and what unheard-of deaths, it inflicted upon our people, bringing upon them the horror of destruction.

Thus we are compelled to confess that neither can a historian fully describe the sequence of events, nor may anyone presume to say that it was anything other than divine vengeance. Nevertheless, lest what is worthy of recounting and capable of benefiting the salvation of its hearers seem to slip entirely from memory, I, Gauterius the chancellor, a participant in both fortunes and having learned that the prosperity of the flesh harms the soul more than adversity harms the body, have undertaken to describe the second part, which turned to the contrary. I do so with the help of him who, without any preceding good merits, inspires both faith in himself and love for himself, so that we may be able to fulfill what pleases him.

First, therefore, wishing to obey the divine law, I admonish us not to glory in wickedness or to be powerful in iniquity (Ps. 51:3), and never to grow proud of our good deeds. By this vice souls were cast down from the very summit of perfection; and by the same vice we, ungrateful to God and forgetful of his beneficence, attributed the victory of the earlier war to our own strength. In the second war, some of us suddenly became the material of death; others fell after being reserved for dreadful and prolonged torment. As our subsequent account will show, weakened by the force of imprisonment and according to the capacity of my intellect, I shall record these events for the memory of posterity.

## CHAPTER I

It happened, perhaps by chance, that Algazi, prince of the error and indolence of the Turcomans, reached the coastal region of Antioch with a military force. When he heard this, the prince, gathering his men from every direction and setting out from Artesium, begged the lord Bernard, the first Latin patriarch, to follow him as far as that place. If he would faithfully consent to the patriarch’s sacred teaching and counsel, he could wait there for Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, whom God was calling, and thereby provide for himself and his men.

At that time the location was abundant and healthy in food and drink, offered our side accessible and safe approaches, but the opposite to the enemy. For the density of the valleys, interspersed with mountains, and the cliffs obstructing each individual approach, in both its position and its accessibility, plainly offered our side an indication of the enemy’s great ruin.

After observing these matters on both sides with vigorous and effective attention, the patriarch—a man venerable in life and most honorable in conduct—made use of the aid of prophecy during the celebration of the divine office and delivered a discourse to the prince and to the entire people concerning what had been done and what was to be done.

Regarding what had been done, he earnestly entreated everyone, with paternal affection, to look upon those events and correct their conduct. Regarding what was to be done, he foretold the future and exhorted them not to attribute success to their own strength, but to preserve and restore the rights of the Churches—or agree to restore them—at the appropriate time, accompanied by the justice of the clergy and of the entire Christian people.

By these means and by other good works, resisting harmful vices and pleasures, they would begin to become warriors of God, so that, fortified by the arms of faith in the conflict against the treacherous, they might rightly be called soldiers of Christ.

But the prince, on that occasion—alas!—daring what ought not to be dared and presuming to do what ought not to be done, disregarding the safety of himself and his men, placed the teaching of so great a father beneath his own recklessness. Setting aside the effects of every lawful consideration, he delayed to correct, both in himself and in his other subjects, the harmful things that had been offered to them and that would harm them.

Though many entreated him out of pious affection and warned him to remain, he openly declared that he would wait there no longer for anyone. Moved by the counsel of certain barons, whose lands the enemy was accustomed to ravage every year and was ravaging at that very time, he summoned the members of his household and the leading men of his people and, acting with an unwise mind, resolved to leave a productive place with its tents and move to places of no use.

The patriarch, however, perceiving by the light of truth what would serve the common good, observed that the prince and many others were uncorrected and were proceeding against justice. With the clearest arguments he demonstrated that they were unafraid where fear existed and afraid where it did not. What he had previously foretold in figurative speech, he openly pointed out to the prince with his finger—the “woe, woe”—just as happened to him and to the greater part of his men not long afterward.

The prince, terrified in some measure by the voice of the blessed man, did not blush, in the presence of the following persons—the aforementioned father, the archdeacon, the dean, and the chaplains of the court—to confess in a single voice, more privately in a tent, the sins in which he had lived amid the world’s mockery. Would that it had been for his salvation! He also ordered, before those same witnesses, that his possessions, listed in writing, should be divided and distributed according to his will if he should happen to die in battle. And would that this too had been for his salvation!

The aforementioned father, therefore, pitying the weakness of him and of the entire people and acting in the place of blessed Peter, imposed upon the prince and upon all his men generally the manner of true repentance: to mourn the evils committed and, I say, not to commit again the things that ought to be mourned. More privately, for what would benefit his life, he imposed the same injunction upon him in the Lord.

Thus, after marking them with the patriarchal blessing, he bade everyone farewell amid flowing tears and frequent sobs torn from the depths of his heart, and returned to the church to pray for the people of God.

## CHAPTER II

We, however, seized by an evil omen and carried headlong, failing to consider that the proud are rightly cast down and the humble exalted, set out as though stronger than lions and fiercer than tigers, intending to encamp at the Field of Blood.

The Field of Blood, I say, was so called by the common people both in fact and by name. After remaining there for some time, compelled from day to day by the natural lack of food and drink—not by force inflicted upon us by the enemy, but by the scarcity of both necessities demanded by those places—we sent supplies elsewhere, to a place and from which those of us inside and outside the camp might be able to drive away our want.

At that time some of our men were also sent to fortify the outer camps. This did not remain hidden from the enemy’s troops for long. For after sending scouts, as though they were sellers of birds, and after those scouts had returned and reported what our situation was in whatever condition it might be, the lord and the leading men clearly observed it, as though they had seen it with their own eyes.

Those men, crafty in deceit, came openly in ordered formations, having already sent ahead their more capable troops as a preliminary maneuver, pretending that they intended to besiege Cereptus, in order to conceal what they were planning—namely, to attack us unexpectedly. They came to observe and to be observed.

They observed, I say, the outer parts of the routes and the approaches to the inner valleys, by which they could attack the prince more safely for themselves and more harmfully for us. They were observed so that they might be regarded as glorious because of the multitude of their army, while we, driven from our accustomed courage, might seem to have failed through fear of their numbers.

This was soon fulfilled in us—not by the force of that multitude, but because our offenses and crimes demanded it, by the just judgment of God. Shortly afterward, with God’s will and aid directing me, I shall try to explain it—not from myself.

But first, lest I seem, through prolixity of words, to have passed over the order of events, what follows. The leading men, leading soldiers of Cerebitus and the infantry of that fortress around themselves toward Cereptus, suddenly caught sight of some of our men who had gone there by night, standing near them in the manner of defenders and seemingly challenging them to battle.

When the enemy saw this, although they appeared to be surrounded by sixty thousand soldiers or more, they nevertheless held back their reins, took up bows from the sloping side, and drew their shields from their shoulders to their arms and from their arms back to their chests. As though wavering in spirit and seemingly afraid to strike, they turned their backs and roared.

But the matter was concealed by fraud and contrivance, so that by these signs they might draw our men farther away from the camp. This action is often judged improper by many cautious observers of warfare, although it is frequently shown to arise from the ingenuity of strategy.

Our men, however, relying on manly courage and setting aside both the enemy’s boldness and skill, fastened their shields to their sides, grasped their lances, pressed their spurs, and, as befits soldiers, threw themselves together into the midst of the enemy. Fighting as soldiers with harsh blows, they struck some to the ground and, with blood poured out in turn, compelled others to be carried down to Tartarus by a deadly wound.

## CHAPTER III

Amid these preliminary engagements, Rotbertus of the Old Bridge, acting without sluggishness and adhering, as usual, to courage, attacked and struck many of them riding together in a group, with the charge of a resolute spirit and the speed of his exceedingly fierce horse. Immediately, with a broken lance and drawn sword, he struck back at others.

At last, struck in turn by many, his horse pierced by numerous weapons, he was killed as unavoidable force closed in. Yet, although he was pressed to the ground by repeated blows of lances and arrows, he did not “forget his mother’s son.” Recovering his strength through the lightness of his courage, he rose and, striking back with his sword, attempted to resist. When he saw his men hastening to help him, he shouted more courageously:

“Come, comrades, come, supported by the strength of a steadfast soldier!”

There was no delay: they gathered and supplied him with another horse. As he mounted it, he brandished his sword and said to his companions: “The pain inflicted can be lessened by vengeance.”

Then, joining them, they again rushed together upon the enemy. But when his strength was impaired by an injury like the one previously inflicted, he fell to the ground; protected by his shield and aided by God, he escaped death.

What of his comrades? Each of the proven men of the army delivered valiant blows in his appointed place among the dense masses of the enemy. From another direction Alanus, lord of the same fortress, was also seen to act manfully, accompanied by his household. In resisting the enemy, he served in place of a wall; in pursuit, he was reputed a lion.

What of the others? Those coming later sought to surpass and to be seen surpassing those who had preceded them, each in the thousands of deeds to be performed. But, to speak more truly, they were not auxiliary but natural soldiers: in delivering blows and throwing down the enemy, each strove to become, in fact, a soldier of Christ.

Many who had been summoned to that conflict nevertheless recovered—not by fighting valiantly, but by resisting through God’s will. Our men, however, by that same will, unable to endure the enemy’s ferocity, as the sun inclined toward sunset each sought, both in the fortress and elsewhere, a way to rest, and not without reason. There the lesser loss became the greater loss for the greater number. For the poor are thought to be harmed more by the smallest loss than the rich by the greatest.

Of these men, some lodged in the fortress, while others returned late to the army. They reported to the members of the court that the day’s military actions had shone brilliantly, and, as became customary among soldiers, each complained that he had not been there.

When he heard this, the prince ordered the nobles to be summoned to him at once, so that, on the basis of the report of those who had been present in the conflict, he might decide with them what should be done that same night or in the morning concerning the impending matter. They were summoned and appeared; the aforementioned issue was discussed.

After hearing the reporters, the lord, as befitted a soldier of the most vigorous spirit, said:

“Let us approach Cereptus in the morning; let us draw nearer. If they come there, let the courage and love of God for the military cause—which have moved us to come and avenge the blood of his servants—not fear the multitude of the treacherous, but strive by valiant combat to destroy the ferocity of tyrants. If they do not come, let us take counsel and set out the following day toward their tents.”

## CHAPTER IV

Some of the nobles adhered to these words and resisted any contrary proposal; others advised moving the tents backward from that place, near the rock. A portion, however, approved the lord’s salutary counsel and advised that it be followed.

Thus, turning over and over what could be done most quickly for the present matter—what was fitting or unfitting, honorable or dishonorable, useful or useless—they judged it most useful to send both soldiers and infantry to the aforementioned fortress that same night.

They determined that Malgerius of Altavilla should go beyond the passes at first light with forty soldiers and that ten scout-soldiers should be sent to the tower located on the mountain’s summit, so that, if the enemy came again to Cereptus, the prince might be informed by a swift horse and a shrewd soldier.

On the advice of P., archbishop of Apamea, it was arranged that everyone should gather together before dawn at the chapel, after an edict had been issued throughout the army, so that there, corrected in life and conduct and refreshed by heavenly food and drink, they might be able to live or die in God’s service and in his name, as befits soldiers.

The edict was immediately issued.

While these things were being done, a lunatic woman appeared outside and used these words:

“Act, act—and not for long either. For tomorrow, when the enemy’s hand prevails, after cutting off the heads, you will leave to me the dominions that you have taken away until now.”

We judged from the outcome of the following day that these words accorded with the spirit of prophecy. When they heard them, some laughed, though shaken in spirit; others considered it more useful seriously to mourn within themselves the evils they had committed.

Why recount every detail? After dismissing the barons to be refreshed by the night’s rest, the prince summoned his household and ordered that what they had decided be carried out promptly from the appointed place. He showed them what was to be done, where, and how.

He also summoned the chancellor privately and discussed with him what ought to be done concerning the impending matter and the things that seemed burdensome to the soldiers. After the necessary issue had been debated on both sides, the chamberlain was summoned, along with the members of the household, and it was arranged that the precious vessels and all the cumbersome furnishings should be carried by night to the tower of Artesium and entrusted to the bishop.

Then the Turcopoles were summoned, as were the servants. The lord ordered them to carry this out immediately; prepared at a distance, they obeyed the command.

## CHAPTER V

The army, however, not forgetting the edict, gathered before dawn at the church. There they devoted themselves to prayer to the most high God in heart and voice and kept vigil with the morning praises.

When these were finished, the archbishop, a most distinguished man in both kinds of warfare, speaking of the heavenly and the earthly, “taught Christians to cleave to the earthly in such a way that, in the heavenly realm, by God’s gratuitous mercy, they might deserve to be crowned as his soldiers.”

## CHAPTER VI

When morning came and the divine office had been celebrated, all unanimously professed aloud, through public confession and public lamentation, that they had sinned against God’s law. Each, renouncing and confessing all the offenses with which he had been infected, promised most devoutly to God and to the pontiff that, with God’s grace cooperating and protecting them, he would never again fall into that offense or into anything similar.

When he heard this, the aforementioned prelate, observing their disposition toward good will, imposed upon each of them, in the name and under the authority of true repentance, that if they should enter into battle against the treacherous, they should not presume to act well through their own strength, but should commit wholly to God whether they lived or died.

Thus strengthened and marked with the pontifical blessing, refreshed by the body and blood of the Lord, and fortified with these weapons of faith, they returned to their tents, still unaware that battle was imminent.

The prince, however, supported by the divine Spirit, shed tears before the altar for all the ways in which he had sinned against God through sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. He surrendered himself as guilty to the divine majesty and confessed aloud to the pontiff each of his sins according to its quality and quantity.

Having accepted penance and been strengthened by the aforementioned viaticum of the Lord, he departed. Before the entrance to his tent, he charitably distributed with his own hand to the poor of Christ who were asking him for alms a principal gift consisting of weighed gold.

Prepared, as usual, to go out riding in the morning, he mounted his horse. Birds were brought to him, small dogs were brought, other animals were led up, and hunting spears were taken. Boys and huntsmen were sent ahead, and, as befits a prince, he followed them. Here he traversed fields and valleys; there he went around mountains and hills. Here he caught birds with birds; there he brought down wild animals with dogs.

Suddenly, however, moved in spirit and anticipating what was to come, he dismissed the games and directed his route toward the tower for the purpose of scouting. As he departed, a messenger arrived at a swift gallop. The lord asked him:

“What is the serious news?”

The messenger replied:

“With these eyes I have seen the enemy’s troops. I report as a true messenger that they are advancing against us from three directions in a threefold battle, through the precipitous places of the mountains and the ravines—places never open even to the footsteps of wild beasts. I firmly assert that countless formations, adorned with standards and with the other worldly-flourishing pageantry of the Zifeans, are following the first troops.”

At this the prince said:

“It has been granted to us for Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him (Phil. 1:29) and now to render to him the debt that we owe: namely, that all our rational will remain subject to his will. We who have violated his honor in ourselves must, according to the distress of the exhortation made to us, restore ourselves to our Savior, with his help, as those who will not sin.”

When he had finished, the lord summoned the agoson and the heralds and ordered the whole army to prepare its weapons at a distance. He wished the heralds to proclaim in a clear voice that, when all heard the first sound of the slender trumpet, they should hasten to put on their military equipment; at the second, prepared and arranged in their preassigned formations, both soldiers and infantry should gather together; and at the third, each formation, advancing under the leadership of its standard-bearers, should present itself before the sign of the Lord’s Cross.

There was no delay. The heralds proclaimed the order of the lord in a clear voice, and he himself, riding a swift horse, ordered the military weapons to be brought before him in front of the tents.

When this had been done, while the first messenger was present, another also arrived, asserting the same indications of war in different words. He said:

“They are here, on this side of the mountains and the passes; we have won.”

The prince therefore ordered everyone to be warned by the sound of the slender trumpet. There was no delay: at the first signal they moved forward, at the second they prepared themselves, and at the third they gathered. Before the chapel, where the Cross was, they assembled, presenting themselves before the Lord.

The prelate, carrying the Lord’s Cross in his venerable hands, said:

“What more is there to say? Fortified with the weapons of faith, with this saving sign of the Cross going before us, and not fearing to alter the judgment of the treacherous, let us advance into the midst.”

After saying this, the prince publicly renounced the pleasures of his body—past, present, and future—and, for the sake of the law of the Lord, surrendered himself to God and to the bishop as one who would die, as befits a Christian, by the cords of his helmet.

The archbishop, receiving him in the place of blessed Peter, ordered him, in the name of the Lord and in the name of true repentance, to undertake the present battle and to do or receive whatever might please the divine majesty—to die or to live—and prepared to absolve him from all his sins.

Joyful and exhilarated, he asked that the sign of the Lord’s Cross be carried before him by the hands of the priest, so that it might intercede for him. This was immediately done according to his desire.

## CHAPTER VII
Meanwhile Alberic, acting as steward, not in the manner of a fleeing man but of an attacking soldier, struck in the face by a lance and pierced by an arrow almost to the eyes, appeared as the third messenger, so as to warn our men. When first questioned, he replied that, of the forty soldiers with whom he had gone, some had been decapitated—namely Jordan Jordanides, [Col. 1015B] and Odo of the monastery of Foresti—and many others had already served God, freed from the mockery of this world; and that Malger had been compelled by force to be present. At once Malger appeared.

An adverse wind arose. Their horses, pierced by arrows and overwhelmed by leaden projectiles, fell dead. Immediately taking others, they said before the barons to the prince: “Concerning what threatens us, deliberate counsel is needed, so that we may act swiftly according to counsel [sic]. They are coming prepared; act bravely. Divided into three parts, they seek to destroy us by a threefold attack.”

Accordingly, certain of the nobles and of the others, assenting to what seemed a salutary plan, praised the proposal that all our men, as they stood, should be stationed together in ordered battle-lines around the tents, with infantry placed in front on every side. In this way, they declared, by enduring the enemy’s ferocity they could await them more safely and with less difficulty. In such matters, indeed, it belonged to human beings to plan and deliberate; but judgment belonged to God, “to whom every heart is open and every will speaks.”

What, then, happened? Suddenly the banners and standards of the faithless emerged from the sides of the mountains among the olive groves. When he saw them, the prince spoke as follows: “Come, soldiers of Christ! Let us not be frightened by the many-sided battle of the combatants. Rather, let it now put into practice the duty of a soldier in which we ought to be strong, so that we who have hitherto served the world as soldiers may today, by contending in our devotion, serve God, whether alive or dead.”

After saying this, he ordered Rainaldus Masuerus to be protected with three cohorts as quickly as possible, so that he might strike with full force those entering through the passes of Samartani. He declared that, with God’s help, wherever he went or stood—on mountain or plain—he would strike most manifestly at the force of the ungodly princes. Why recount each detail? Just as he had often previously arranged for the separate battle-lines to advance in their respective ranks, so then also he gave the order, but far better. For he said:

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, as befits soldiers defending the law of God, take up the march. When the place for striking has arrived, remember, without forgetting the blood poured out by God’s servants, to overthrow the pride of the wicked by pressing on with repeated blows and to pour out their blood.”

After these words, they adored the sign of the holy cross and reverently kissed it. Each group then set out under its appointed banner and in its assigned order. The thin pipes and trumpets sounded, and in God’s name they took up the march.

Meanwhile, missiles and arrows flew from one battle-line to another, as the custom of warfare requires. The battle-line of blessed Peter, advancing on the right—for it was its duty both to advance and to strike the enemy first—loosed the reins, lowered its lances, and hastened impetuously and bravely to strike the cohort approaching it. Overthrowing many of the faithless, it nearly routed the whole formation.

When Gaufridus the monk saw this, accompanied by a distinguished battle-line and relying on manly courage, he attacked and struck a cohort of the faithless numbering at least ten thousand soldiers. He so shattered it that he drove almost the entire cohort, as well as the others nearby, into flight and rout.

No less vigorously, for his part, the battle-line of Guidonus Frenelli attacked and shook the enemy with all the strength at its disposal. But [Col. 1016B] because our men ceased to persist as urgently as the situation required, both these and many others suffered destruction. The faithless, having recovered their strength at the Lord’s command, did not fear to attack our men; rather, they returned to the assault and struck them fiercely with missiles, lances, arrows, leaden and iron projectiles, and repeated blows of their swords. The blood poured out by both sides bore witness to this.

Meanwhile the cohort of Rotbert of Saint-Laud, advancing on the left with the Turcopoles, ought to have struck the enemy. But, under an evil omen, when the Turcopoles first fled and could not resist, the cohort was driven by their assault and by the shouts of the faithless against the prince’s battle-line, which was riding toward the force of the ungodly. It could not be recalled from its flight—not by straps, reins, or ropes, nor by any confidence of spirit. Worse still, it carried part of the prince’s cohort with it into the rout.

Then, as though something worse were to follow this evil sign, a whirlwind came forth from the north. In the middle of the battlefield, before the eyes of all, it clung to the ground and, crawling along the earth, snatched up dust. It filled the eyes of the combatants so that they could no longer fight, and, driving itself around in a circle, it rose toward the stars like a vessel being consumed by sulphurous flames.

When this was seen, an immense and horrible cry arose from all the ranks of the criminals. Yet the prince, steadfast in spirit, continued in the contest. Although his men were being overthrown and killed on every side, he never retreated or looked back. Obeying the command of the Lord and of the bishop, and accompanied by only a few, he fought bravely against the force of the entire battle. Struck by a soldier’s sword through the middle of the nose to the brain, he paid to death the debt owed to it in the name of the Lord; before the sign of the holy cross, he gave his body to the earth and his soul to heaven. [Col. 1016D]

After this event, the priest who carried that same cross in his hands was killed. Several of the faithless, seized by greed for gold and precious stones and ignorant of the power of God hidden in the cross, became there the instruments of death to one another by striking repeated blows among themselves; they slipped away to hell, to be consumed by the fires of the underworld, never to return.

Immediately all of them together, numbering one hundred thousand warriors as they stood, assigned from the four quarters of the world, fell with the utmost ferocity upon our men. Our men, however, overcome by the judgment of the supreme Judge and by divine vengeance—seven hundred soldiers and three thousand infantry fighters, as they were reckoned—together with many others who had gone to the battle either for pay or from desire for hostile plunder, were driven to destruction on that same field. The shouts of the faithless grew stronger again and again, and the enemy sword prevailed: some were wounded, some cut down, and some slaughtered by various attacks. Others, by the just judgment of God, fell into the snares of a most wretched captivity. [Col. 1017A]

Meanwhile Rainaldus Mansuerus, while these events were taking place among us, fought bravely on his own side against the enemy entering through the passes of Samartani. He overthrew and defeated no small number of them, so that, by the estimation of both armies, our men were considered the victors and the enemy the defeated.

But it pleased the divine majesty—whose pleasure is directed only toward what is fitting and expedient—that the defeated, having recovered their strength, should be regarded as victors, and that the earlier triumph of our men should have its end, not through the enemy’s hand but through the power exercised by God. For among those overthrown and defeated, some there put off their human life, while others fled; all met the same destruction as the rest.

It happened that Rainaldus Masuerus, afflicted by a serious wound, entered a tower at Samartani with a few of his men, intending to secure it as a refuge for himself and for the other fugitives and, if possible, to await there Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, who was hastening to the aid of Christianity. But the weakness of the tower and the lack of provisions, and above all Algazi’s arrival there, made it impossible for him to remain [Col. 1017C] and compelled him to surrender himself captive to the triumphant victor.

Protected by cunning, and as though he could defend himself in the tower, he spoke cautiously. He said to the triumphant man: “I shall not surrender myself to you unless you first assure me, by the faith and oath of your law, that you will grant me the protection of present security and assistance in escaping.”

The more cunning man replied to the cunning one: “Why not? While you were in battle, it was necessary to deal with you and the others as with enemies. Now, however, feeling humanely, I remember that you are human beings. And so that you may not suspect me, receive my ring under the guarantee of my faith and the oath of our blessed law, so that by this sign, when the period of one month has ended, you may receive freedom from me.”

The man who did not expect to be able to live even for a single day, hearing the promise of a month and grieving inwardly, nevertheless accepted the ring and, appearing outwardly joyful, surrendered himself captive.

Some of the nobles, however, who seemed distinguished by courage, skill, and nobility of birth, could not endure even the first blows. Leaving their living prince behind on the field, and abandoning relatives and friends, they departed without delay, before the battlefield and the entrance to the mountains were closed by the enemy’s ferocity, and entered Antioch as though it were the harbor they desired.

Others had entered before them, according to the customary saying: “First at the gates, last in wars.” But, lest I seem to indulge in excessive digression by speaking of those who escaped, I shall first explain what happened on the field. Then, proceeding step by step, I shall descend to a portion of the evils that occurred between the two battles, and shall relate how the Author of supreme justice, by the hand of Baldwin, the second Latin king of Jerusalem, [Col. 1018A] freed the people of Antioch, almost annihilated by hostile devastation, from the mouths of lions; and how the triumphal name lost in the principal battle was restored to that same people through the power of the most holy cross in a royal battle.

I shall therefore return to the order of the narrative. What follows.

## CHAPTER VIII

After the prince had been killed on the field, and a very large number of men from the four quarters of the world had been slain outside, apart from those who were raging against our men with swords within, the approaches through the mountains and valleys were so closed off by the battlefield and obscured by skirmishing [reading uncertain: *escaramis*?] that not one uninjured fugitive could pass through.

Our men, therefore, whoever remained alive on the field, stunned by the prospect either of fighting or of cautiously escaping, made their way toward the tents. But they did not find them: they had already been carried away by the hands of the impious, except for the tents of the prince and of the chapel. In these, the most wicked men, seized by desire for the prince’s gold, silver, and ornaments, were contending with their swords.

When Euterpius saw this, a most proven soldier in the battle of body and soul, he appeared in the contest and said to those who were fighting before the chapel and contending with blows: “What fellowship has Christ with Belial? (2 Cor. 6:15) You are dividing yourselves, but the portion is not equal.”

With these words he pierced with his lance, through the heart, the amiraldus clad in gold-woven fabric before the door of the chapel. Attacking the others as well, he passed happily into the blessedness of rest through martyrdom, stripping off his human life at the appointed limit of God, which he could not pass.

Amid these dangers, our assembly’s armor, together with the equipment of the entire army, took up position on a certain nearby mountain, believing that there it might await either the assistance of arriving soldiers or some means of snatching a refuge for escape.

What happened, then? Not long afterward, those escaping from the field saw our men stationed on the mountain, where death seemed nearer, and they thought and sought there the consolation of life. Deceived by a vain hope, they came together from every side and clung to the mountain, pressing one another. In a moment, however, it was so surrounded by the impious that the besieged preferred to die a brief death rather than endure their missiles—and rightly so. For the onslaught of missiles and arrows was so great on every side that, as the blows rebounded from their mutual collision, even the faithless outside were struck most fiercely; our men were struck much more savagely.

As a brief hour’s rain overcomes the wind, and as dried grass is damaged by hail, so our people, swiftly wounded, yielded to repeated blows. Nevertheless, some escaped under the guidance of the supreme Judge; others were captured by an evil lot and delivered over to punishment, being led to the camp of the wicked prince.

The punishment of the sinners follows.

There, near the battlefield, five hundred captives or more were held. Their hands were twisted behind their backs, their feet bound with iron fetters, and they were subjected to every other punishment with the utmost severity. In the manner of dogs, they were coupled two by two at the neck with ropes and kept lying in a circle on the ground, awaiting the capital sentence before the master of the crime.

The impious man, driven by deadly madness, ordered the ministers of slaughter to inflict lethal wounds upon the captives, and to drag those afflicted with severe wounds outside for beheading, striking them upon the hair with a rod; the rest, after being tormented through the night, were to be reserved for the following day’s slaughter. The impious men therefore obeyed their wicked master’s command with joyful hearts.

The effect of the wicked command was still more wicked. Led away for beheading, the captives fell one after another, not only with their heads cut off by the hands of the impious, but also with the skin stripped from their living heads and their bodies mutilated halfway down; thus they underwent the separation of a dreadful death.

The survivors, subjected to the torture that had been promised them, passed that dark night amid insults and terrors. In their minds they resisted death and reproached it in words, complaining that, though often called and recalled, it did not come to them in their sorrow. Yet in turn they reflected among themselves [Col. 1019B] that this had happened to them because the merits of their present life demanded it. They confessed that worse things justly and deservedly threatened them, and that such things and their like belonged not to the pure but to the corrupted nature of humanity. One nature tends toward misery; the other toward blessedness.

Pressed and bound throughout the night, at sunrise on the following day—under the same sun, I say, which was darker for them than that dark night—they were ordered to stand in the tents until the prince of crime should decide what could sufficiently be done with them according to his will.

And this pleased the wicked prince.

At the third hour of the day, two or three hundred naked captives, bound together by the necks, were led with swords and clubs, whips and ropes, across fields planted with thistles and brambles for the distance of a mile, to a vineyard newly cultivated beside Samartinum. There human pity, deprived of its natural right, had been transformed into sacrilegious fury, while the tyrant Algazi exercised tyranny over the worshippers of Christ in the following manner.

The heat was intolerable not only to the wounded and sick captives but also to the healthy and free enemies, so that each captive would gladly have given even one of his limbs, or life itself, in exchange for a cup of cold water offered by someone.

There, when the captives saw the clusters of grapes clinging to the ground, they threw themselves upon them in competition, lying face down. They greedily tore away even the plastered [or dust-covered] grapes with their mouths. After crushing them under their feet, whatever juice escaped from the mouth of one who pressed them was received by the mouth of another. Often, thinking that they had retained the juice that had escaped, driven by the heat they gnawed their tongues with their own teeth. Clinging to one another’s beards, they raged most miserably at the sight of a drop of liquid; and many, after drinking urine, became thirsty for the first time.

The minister of slaughter, observing this—and himself in need of a cold drink—ordered water to be brought from distant places on pack animals. When it arrived, he ordered the first portion to be reserved for himself and his men, while the dregs of mud were to be given to the captives. He decreed that they should be led two by two to the water-skins, and ordered that anyone who approached without being assigned to do so should immediately be beheaded.

When the water was brought into the midst of them, they desired to exchange life for a single taste and paid no attention to the order; many rushed with many others through the swords toward the water. Some were overwhelmed by stones, some pierced by missiles, and many were mutilated in various ways.

When the impious man saw this, he was delighted by their torments. As though refreshed by dishes served to him, he smiled at his own cruelty. Yet even this did not satisfy him, for he conceived still more cruel acts.

He ordered all who remained to be assembled in the middle of the field, so that the blood poured out drop by drop, which he had regarded as worthless for the complete destruction of the captives, might at least be replaced by a universal sacrifice in some manner, to increase his joy.

Thus they were assembled in the middle. At his command, a thousand soldiers or more were prepared, carrying naked swords in their hands, so that by striking all at once they might tear the captives apart and gladden the profane man.

When the soldiers were ready to rush upon them, one of the most powerful amiralds appeared and addressed the master of the slaughter in these words:

“Come, star of the law, why do you bring your joys to an end so quickly by disposing of these men? Once they are killed, what triumph will you present to foreign kings and princes of our law? Do not in this way hand them over to death. Do not refuse to trust my advice, offered for your honor. I shall advise nothing except what supports our law and accords with your honor.

“I therefore commend and advise your greatness to order that the richer, more distinguished, and nobler among these dogs be selected and separated. They may either escape by redeeming their lives, or be kept for you to be destroyed indoors at astrological or magical ceremonies, through the infliction of various torments. They can then be sent to the sultan and to the other lords and nobles to proclaim aloud the illustrious renown of your name and the triumph in which you exult. Once these have been separated, let the rest be cut limb from limb by your swords in the field, so that they may learn what and how much they and their parents and fellow countrymen have sinned against our most holy law.”

This criminal counsel pleased the criminal, and he ordered it to be done. The chosen were therefore separated for torture; the remainder were left in the field for immediate destruction.

The most wicked man said: “Come, soldiers, guardians and champions of the excellent law! A sacrifice of dogs has been prepared for your swords.”

And he shouted: “Ehoe! Ehoe! Rush upon them promptly and bravely.”

The impious men therefore struck those assigned to the instrument of death with their swords in a single assault. They did not stop cutting them until they could find no intact parts remaining among the bodies of the captives.

There, prostrate in the spilled blood like a pig in a muddy wallow, and not yet satisfied by the slaughter of the men, they fell to their knees before the power of the Judge and begged, asking that by his command they might be permitted to destroy the chosen with a similar slaughter.

The divine majesty did not, however, allow the full extent of his savagery to prevail. It therefore ordered the chosen captives to be handed over to his son, who, inflicting torments upon them, would lead them into captivity at Aleppo.

Nor was the wicked father’s command without effect. His son received the chosen captives and, on the first night, handed them over to their hosts among stones, thorns, and thistles mixed together. In place of food, he gave them harsh blows; in place of a bed, he fastened nooses around their feet and necks.

Alas, that night was reckoned worse than those among the infernal regions. On the following day they were led to Aleppo for execution. There some suffered destruction through repeated blows and various kinds of torture; others, through God’s mercy, were ransomed, as I shall explain at the end of the account of the royal war. There is a reason for this: several of the king’s men had by a most wretched fate been mixed among them, and I shall discuss rare matters concerning them from observation and report.

But lest I pass over the order of the narrative already begun, I shall now turn to what Algazi did more recently after the battle and descend to an account of his tyranny.

## CHAPTER IX

Having seen that Cerepi [reading uncertain] was there, he departed with the army of Artensians. There he peacefully subjected the episcopal tower to himself in the following manner: he promised that he would permit the bishop, together with all his people, both clergy and others, to go freely, released, and undisturbed to Antioch.

He fulfilled this promise in part, but in part acted contrary to it. For whatever gold, silver, and ornaments he discovered that the clergy were carrying, he took away entirely by sending raiders in the place of escorts. As for the priestly garments, so that he might conceal his wickedness beneath them, he openly returned them and, after they had departed, sent back what had been taken. He then pitched his tents before Artesium and decided to remain there overnight, intending first to capture Artesium and then to depart from there to conquer Antioch.

But it pleased the divine dispensation that he should be detained there by the words of a certain man named Joseph, a most prudent man. When Algazi himself demanded that the fortress be surrendered to him, Joseph, protected by cunning, replied—not by resisting but by seeming to agree—in the following manner:

“We know that everything in this principality outside Antioch lies beneath your swords and your dominion. If, therefore, you acquire Antioch itself, then this fortress and all the others will in an instant be subject to you as well. And do not think that my words are deceiving you.

“In the meantime, assign one of your men, Sahenas, to me, so that in your place he may guard your possessions with me and occupy the position of so great a lord. For if I admit you inside, my son, who is in Antioch, will unquestionably kill me with the most disgraceful death when he hears of it. And I, an old man full of days, if I did this, would be considered—God forbid!—a most wicked traitor. It is more proper that he should regard me as innocent rather than guilty.”

Deceived by these words, Algazi left the fortress untouched and placed there a certain Sahenas. He himself, intent upon drinking and, by God’s will, forgetful of Antioch, repeatedly sent thousands of soldiers through the surrounding and neighboring regions. From day to day, replenished by plunder both of human beings and of other things, they returned to him heavily laden.

Meanwhile, in the face of the evils and misfortunes that had recently occurred and of the imminent loss of the city of Antioch, every care, labor, fear, anxiety, and danger that could befall Christianity was necessarily transferred to the clergy, since military service had been abandoned and almost all the assistance of the Frankish citizens had already been lost.

Thus, I say, they feared much more that they might be deceived by the treachery of internal enemies than that they could in any way be overwhelmed within by the force of external enemies. Nor was this surprising. For the people of Antioch, deprived of their possessions and subjected to a wicked custom through the violence and evil disposition of our people, had often been shaken by sorrow. If they had wished, as justice’s reciprocity requires, to return evil for evil, they could at that time have burdened our men very seriously by treachery or in some other manner.

The patriarch, acting prudently in these and other matters, summoned the Franks to him and was strengthened by God’s power. Fortified by the protection of his clergy, he decided with them that, if the people wished to act treacherously, they should be unable to do so, and that he himself, together with the clergy and the Franks alone, should assume responsibility for guarding the whole city.

He decreed that wherever they might be and from whatever nation they might come, all the peoples in the city, except the Franks, should remain unarmed, and that they should never dare to leave their houses at night without a light. This was done so that they would not appear infected by any design of treachery and so that they could in no way be regarded as suspect.

He decreed that, wherever the weakness of the lower part of the entire city was exposed, tents necessary for the protection of Christianity should be placed there; and that each tower, wherever one existed, should, as far as possible and according to the number of Christ’s worshippers, be fortified from a distance with monks and clerics mixed together with laymen.

All together, diligently, obeyed the command of this most prudent father and teacher. Once the towers had been fortified, guards were assigned within and without, guard beside guard.

The patriarch himself, intending to fight more by prayers than by arms, supplicated God incessantly and from the depths of his being for the safety and defense of the Christian people. Nevertheless, at suitable hours, day and night, with his armed clergy and soldiers, in the manner of combatants, he did not cease to visit in turn the gates, battlements, towers, and walls all around, as well as their guards; he consoled them and urged them to undertake the care of Christian protection with watchful spirit and not to abandon the good work because of any enemy disturbance.

Why recount every detail? The clergy, together with the other faithful, prudently and bravely performed the duty of soldiers inside and outside. With God’s power, they preserved the city untouched by the enemy, to be protected for the long-desired arrival of King Baldwin.

## CHAPTER X

Amid these dangers, as we learned from reliable messengers, word reached Algazi that King Baldwin and Count Pontius of Tripoli were hastening toward Antioch with swift steps. He therefore immediately decided to send ten thousand soldiers against them, and ordered an equal or greater number to follow after them, more slowly.

Having selected whom he would send and whom he would retain with himself, he instructed those departing to lie carefully in ambush for the king’s arrival and, by whatever means they could, to work for the destruction of Christianity.

The impious men therefore set out at night, as was their custom, in ordered battle-lines, at the command of their lord, toward Laodicea and the mountain regions of Mount Paleri, so that they might both plunder and lie in wait for the king’s cavalry.

When they reached those regions, they divided into three groups: some were to go out to meet the king, some to devote themselves to capturing booty, and the rest to direct their course toward the port of Saint Simeon on the sea.

As those who had gone against the king were advancing, the king himself unexpectedly met them at Mount Hingronis. Attacking them bravely, he overthrew them and scattered them through the mountain ravines so completely that no companion could help a companion, nor an equal his fellow.

When this was done, the king ordered his men to make camp before Latorum [place-name uncertain], and arranged to set out from there in the morning, going ahead himself so as to be the first to encounter the enemy. He ordered the count, with the Provençals, to follow behind and guard the rear, so that, if he happened to see the enemy, he could quickly report it to the king and not hesitate to strike them.

As they proceeded in this order, it happened that the Provençals saw a portion of the enemy ahead of them driving away a very large amount of booty. They did not delay in attacking them swiftly and bravely, and so wrested the booty from them.

By a most wretched turn of fortune, the faithless, having recovered their strength, attacked the Provençals and brought matters to such a point that they could not return to the king that day. Some were killed, others scattered through the mountains, and the rest, wandering about, eventually found the king lodged for the night at Casa Bella.

They reported to him what had happened. There the king found reliable evidence of the enemy. For a camp belonging to four thousand soldiers was visible, still polluted by the dead bodies of men and animals, whose flesh had been shamefully eaten.

When the king heard this, he thought that he might catch up with them. As one who felt compassion for those formerly killed in battle, and whose duty it was to defend his country, he grieved deeply. Yet, since he did not know by what route he could follow them with certainty, he nevertheless judged it more useful to go to Antioch, for two reasons: to console the people of Antioch in their desolation and, after hearing the reports there, to follow the enemy with the patriarch’s counsel.

Meanwhile, three thousand or more men set out at night toward the port of Saint Simeon. At dawn they suddenly attacked those who were sleeping with the sword; the rest escaped by ship.

The impious men, gathering the booty of people and other things, escaped through the mountain ravines. After the sun had already moved on for two hours, they appeared not far from Antioch with their banners raised.

When the enemy was seen, an immense cry arose all around, as human custom requires. Therefore the clergy and soldiers who had come to Antioch from the battle, together with the citizens and all who were present, took up arms and went out as though to fight. Immediately they sent some of their number toward the enemy to investigate how large and powerful that enemy force was.

It happened that two of those sent were killed in the fields, while the rest, driven back by the enemy’s attack, returned swiftly.

When our men saw this, waiting not far from the city and seeing the unarmed populace fleeing—the people who had gone out with them—they began to move and to be stirred up. There was no delay: the enemy who were following the first fugitives, without restraining their reins but pressing their horses with the spurs, fell upon our men all at once. They forced some even of those wearing mail to drown in the river, and, striking the rest indiscriminately, did not stop pursuing them as far as the bridge.

Thirty-seven of our men were killed in this assault. Our men, however, resisting on the bridge, abandoned their horses and drew their swords; gradually recovering their strength, they drove the enemy away.

The enemy, thus expelled and proceeding together under the burden of the remaining booty, halted for a short time beyond Corbana, between two waters.

## CHAPTER XI

Not long afterward the aforementioned King Baldwin appeared, great in the expectation of all the Christian people—greater in his arrival, and greatest in his protection.

When he understood that the tyranny of the faithless against our people had burned beneath their skin and flesh, even to the marrow, and that the enemy were held back by no military force other than the separating waves of the sea, he was overcome by immense grief and hastened to enter the city. He did not go there to rest, but first to seek the kingdom of God, and, intending to fight for his country, to pray most devoutly to God in the church of blessed Peter, as befitted a king, asking that from there, strengthened by the ecclesiastical council, once its decision had been freely given, he might more safely undertake the march against the faithless.

He did not delay. After praying and being strengthened by the patriarch’s counsel, moved also by a twofold ardor—within, by the breath of a spirit longing for vengeance, and without, by the military duty urging him to war—he sent scouts ahead and took up the march in pursuit with swift steps and ordered battle-lines.

When, from the reports of messengers, he perceived that the enemy were far away and nowhere resting in a fixed place but riding more quickly than usual, as though driven by fear, and when he saw that his own men were exhausted by the march, he returned to Antioch, with the approval of all the clergy and the entire order of nobles, after considering the circumstances.

There, by God’s call and promoted through His gift, he assumed the dignity of the principate, rightly. For through his hand, by divine providence, he saw to it that the citizens were restored to the walls and the city to its citizens, from which both had been deprived by a most wretched fate.

After the matter requiring attention had been fully discussed, and since the enemies were numerous and strong and powerful in wickedness, the patriarch and the clerical order—whose duty it is to advise, perform, and teach what is good—supported by the strength of the inner person, declared that the faithless and unbelieving could easily be bent and overthrown, even by the hands of a few Christians, if they fought lawfully with true justice accompanying them.

To make this happen, the king and the others, following their counsel, strove to correct their conduct and to attend to other good works.

After the council had been established, it was decreed in the court of blessed Peter, for a matter of the greatest necessity, that the king—to whom the just and supreme Arbiter had subjected almost the entire kingdom of the eastern Christians—should, out of love of justice and for the common good, give the principate of Antioch to the son of Bohemond, to whom it belonged, together with his daughter, if he was also to marry her, and should come to protect the land and principate with his counsel and assistance. [Col. 1024D]

With this equitable principle of justice also taken into consideration, it was decreed that those who, in a foreign land, by the gift of their lords, and amid many insults and terrors, even through the shedding of their own blood and that of their parents, had acquired lands and honors in defense of Christianity should not lose, through any change in Christian rule, what they had acquired and possessed; rather, they should hold it by hereditary right.

This was sanctioned and confirmed by word and by the royal hand.

## CHAPTER XII
Having accomplished these things, the king, then in Antioch and able to summon people from distant regions, nearby places, and wherever else he could, very quickly assembled an army in the name of war. He diligently sought to equip himself and his men with weapons and every other kind of military apparatus, as befitted a king.

[Col. 1025A] When Algazi heard this, he abandoned the castles of Arthesium and Emine untouched and set out to besiege Cerep. For he had heard, as many reports related, that Alanus, lord of that castle, together with his soldiers, as well as the Edessan soldiers and almost all the men from the other castles, had come to Antioch by royal command, so that, once they had departed from there, they might strike him in war, whether he was there or elsewhere. Nor was this without result, either in this matter or in others that the King of heaven and earth willed to take place.

Since Algazi was unable to capture the castle by an assault of his men, he sent men to dig beneath it, making an underground passage from various directions. He also prepared incendiary carts packed with dry wood, so that, when they reached the towers, they might be driven beneath the thresholds of the platforms and, once fire had been set to them, cause the towers to collapse. Besides this, [Col. 1025B] day after day, three or four times, with stone-throwers and instruments of various kinds, and with armed men attacking in three ranks, they assailed the towers, shooting arrows amid a terrible storm of missiles; they deprived the towers of their defenses and struck down the exhausted defenders with savage blows.

At last the townsmen, terrified in part by these attacks and compelled in part by the subterranean fire brought against the towers, preferred still to live in the world rather than to be reduced in the castle to prolonged fear or crowned with martyrdom. By an unhappy and shameful agreement, therefore, they trusted the faithless men and surrendered the castle on the condition that they might escape alive and unharmed. Thereupon they were forced to make their way tearfully and shamefacedly to the king.

The faithless men, however, left guards and others necessary for the castle’s defense and departed to besiege Sardonas.

Meanwhile the king, believing that the wicked men might be found near Cerep, prepared everything that he could obtain on that occasion in the way of men and other necessities of war. [Col. 1025C] In a spirit of humility and with a contrite heart, clothed in a woolen garment and walking barefoot among the churches of the blessed intercessors, he hastened to beseech the Almighty and to plead with him from the depths of his heart. He prayed that, by whose will he had undertaken the governance of the kingdom, and with that same God beginning and completing the work, he might, for the honor and praise of his name, bring down and overthrow the tyrants and persecutors of Christendom by the power of the holy cross. They were puffed up with presumptuous pride and trusted in their own strength, by which they thought they would triumph; yet he prayed that, claiming no triumph or empty praise for himself, but entrusting everything to God, he might overcome them.

At last, when the entire clergy and people of the city had assembled in the church of blessed Peter, the patriarch celebrated the divine office. As befitted a father [Col. 1025D] instructing his sons who were going to war, and those who were remaining at home in the service of God, he instructed, admonished, and armed them with the Lord’s commandments, and marked them with a heavenly blessing.

When the sacred objects of the procession had been taken up, all bowed their heads together before the altar. With the biers of the sacred relics and the standards, the Lord’s cross going before them, the clergy proceeding in an ecclesiastically ordered array, and the whole people following, they prayed to God with humanity and gentleness through litanies and other prayers. Those who were going to war, and those who were remaining at home, all dressed in wool and walking barefoot, devoutly proceeded outside the city and reached the boundary assigned for their division.

There the patriarch again took up the sacred cross with consecrated hands, again signed them all with its power, and commended them wholeheartedly to the Lord in these words:

> “[Col. 1026A] May he who redeemed us with his precious blood himself be the merciful and gracious guide of our journey and the provider of our welfare, so that both those who go and those who remain, absolved from sins, may be able to serve him freely and without hindrance. Thus, having obtained through his gift the consolation and triumph of victory, may you rejoice in him and through him.”

When these words had been spoken, tears being shed on every side, the king, preceded by the sign of the holy cross, returned to war; the clergy returned to the church; and the people returned to their homes. They prayed and entreated that the Author of supreme justice, who from the beginning crushes wars, might, granting praise to his name through the assault of his people, crush their adversaries.

## CHAPTER XIII

On that same day and the following night, as the king was riding toward Cerep, [Col. 1026B] those who, compelled by a most wretched fate, had surrendered the castle to the enemy came to meet him. When he saw and heard them, the king was shaken by inward grief, amazed, and saddened. For, as he himself testified, he perceived that the surrender of the castle threatened Christ’s people, present and future, with two contrary losses: one temporary and recoverable with God’s consent; the other never recoverable—the loss of the castle recoverable, the disgrace of the surrender irrecoverable.

Inflamed by this, and having quickly taken counsel, he directed his journey toward Rubea, so that from there, riding through Hap, he might encamp at a mountain called Daniz. For there he hoped to obtain certain indications of the enemy, either by hearing or by sight. Nor did what his state of mind anticipated lack its outcome. On the very day when he lay down after fixing his camp on the mountain, he learned from reliable indications that the enemy was not far away.

[Col. 1026C] From the report of those who had heard and seen it, he clearly understood that the faithless men had besieged Sardonas. He also learned from a trustworthy messenger that on that same day, or in the morning, he would see some of them. On the following day, at first light, therefore, lighter and more agile troops were sent out in scattered groups to make preliminary attacks, and they assaulted our men with arrows from every side. Thus, as they passed the day two by two—few with few, more with more—they tried from here and there, from rear and front, to disturb or somehow drive back part of our army.

The king, however, relying on the strength of manly prudence, observed that they were not behaving like warriors and were not advancing in ordered battle lines. He urged his men and ordered everyone prudently to remain before his camp, to endure with steadfast courage, and to watch until he could seize them gathered in one place or advancing together.

[Col. 1026D] But they, full of deceitful cunning, even toward evening avoided lodging together. Instead, they lodged scattered around the army at twilight, holding their horses by hand, one at each position. That night, the servant and the master were alike.

## CHAPTER XIV

Meanwhile, Algazi demanded that the castle of Sardonas be surrendered to him by threats, blandishments, terrors, and promises. When he could not obtain this, he did not cease attacking the castle impetuously, two or three times a day and also by night, with an assault and stratagem like the former.

[Col. 1027A] When the grass and crops, as well as the water necessary for the sustenance of men and horses, began to fail, the faithless men, under the pretext of obtaining supplies and pay, gathered the Turcomans and Arabs into bands numbering in the thousands. They moved through the various regions in their usual manner, like rapacious wolves, clinging to the faithless men, devouring and carrying away with them whatever they could seize, and striving to return to their own country.

The Arab king Debeis himself, and Bocardus, the most renowned prince of his people, together with several other princes who had been involved in the conflict with Algazi, departed in the same manner after the first groups had withdrawn.

When Algazi saw this, he pressed his own strength toward capturing the castle before the king arrived; but he tried even more to deceive the townsmen by fraudulent cunning. He promised them, on the faith and oath of his law, that if they submitted the stronghold to his rule, he would lead them safe and unharmed, under his protection, to a place of secure escape, with all their possessions preserved and untouched.

[Col. 1027B] When they heard this, some, compelled by wounds and deprived of their strength through bodily exhaustion, placed a kind of trust in the prince and consented to his most wicked demand on these terms. Abandoning the town, and at the command of the profane prince, they ignorantly delivered themselves, as guides for their escort, into the hands of their executioners.

He therefore received the town joyfully and with a joyful heart. With far greater joy, however, he ordered his men to hand the departing Christians over to the most savage death. Why recount each detail? Almost all of them became the prey of death in a single moment.

## CHAPTER XV

The matter had not yet reached the king’s ears. On the night when he had encamped at Daniz, however, he learned from the report [Col. 1027C] of a certain priest, Rotbert Fulchoius, that this had happened.

It was then no wonder if the king—who, after the Lord alone, had been the lord and defender of Christendom—once again grieved over the loss and disgrace of Christ’s people. Nevertheless, strengthened by the power of the holy cross, he prepared himself manfully to fight the enemy in the morning.

Algazi, having learned that the king was staying at Daniz from those who had been making preliminary attacks around our army, joined those men in the evening, together with Dodechinus and his entire army, after fortifying Sardonas. The soldiers whom he had sent ahead were leaping about and setting ambushes near our men, so that they might suddenly attack them while they slept in the morning; this tactic had often benefited many people.

The king, slow to sleep [Col. 1027D] but attentive to the interests of his men, and strengthened by the venerable sign by which kings reign and enemies are conquered, prudently arranged—on the very day on which the enemy had first arrived, and together with the archbishop of Caesarea and other worshipers of the true faith—that his tents should be gathered during the night, the soldiers prepared, and everything necessary for the warriors arranged in such a way that, if the enemy suddenly rushed upon them, they would find nothing sluggish or disordered. Instead, amid blows delivered and enemies struck down, they would discover the Christians strengthened by God’s power and by his sign.

If, however, it proved possible to capture them in a mass, he arranged to ride with his entire army in ordered battle lines toward Hap as day was breaking over the land. For he judged—and so it proved—that war was unavoidable in this manner.

[Col. 1028A] At dawn, therefore, after the saving sign had been brought forward, nine battle lines were arranged by royal command. The Christians, commended to God and to the power of the holy cross, set out on their way in the customary manner, advancing in this order: three battle lines were placed in front; the infantry was stationed behind them, so that it might protect them and be protected by them. The royal force, prepared under the protection of these and the other formations, advanced in the order required for all things. The line of the count of Tripoli, a most vigorous soldier, was placed on the right; the barons’ lines were placed on the left and behind, each in its own position by the king’s command.

At twilight the enemy, stationed on every side, sent forth the clamor of drums and trumpets; with the clamor came shouting, with the shouting barking, and with the barking boldness. Believing that by this means they could drive the Christians from their initial advance and force them into disarray, they redoubled their shouts and pressed more fiercely, repeatedly sending savage volleys of arrows and other missiles from here and there.

[Col. 1028B] When they could not accomplish what they intended in this way, and perceived that our men advanced boldly and resisted manfully, they took courage from the arrogance of their great number of warriors. Ambitiously attempting to overthrow the infantry, by which they were more seriously restrained, and seeing that it was protected by the lines preceding it and that the lines themselves were protected by it, they were inflamed with the greatest force. After delivering their blows, they struck our men more vigorously with lances and arrows, shooting from their bows and wielding drawn swords.

After several formations had been scattered, they caused even the splendid line of the count to be submerged in the royal line. There it indeed became clear that the nature of military courage had not withered in the count. Even after his men had been scattered and completely put to flight, and after the three lines had been dispersed, he alone, or with a few companions, continued to resist the enemy in soldierly fashion, alternately delivering and receiving blows, and with steadfast courage joined himself to the cross of the Lord and to the king, prepared either to live or to die.

[Col. 1028C] Meanwhile, after the aforementioned lines had fled, the greater part of our infantry, shaken by the Lord’s permission, fell beneath the enemy’s sword. Immediately the enemy struck our men with a heavy assault from the right and left, from rear and front.

In this conflict the archbishop of Caesarea, a man venerable for his life, named Euzomerus, was not wearing a coat of mail but a priestly surplice. He carried the Lord’s cross in his venerable hands. Protected by it, he himself was struck by an arrow but, as many testified, remained unharmed; only a drop of blood appeared as evidence.

[Col. 1028D] There the king’s horse was wounded in the neck. When the archbishop learned this and perceived that the faithless men were gaining strength against our people, he turned the Lord’s cross toward them and said openly:
