> “By the most sacred power of this cross, may you be accursed, most wicked men, and, scattered and put to flight by divine vengeance, may you perish immediately.”

The king, relying on manly courage, perceived the point at which the enemy’s troops were most strongly prevailing against our men. Shouting for the protection and aid of the holy cross, he rushed upon them with the utmost speed, struck down the faithless men, and drove them into flight. Indeed, by striking first those in front and then those behind, he put them to flight in turn.

[Col. 1029A] Thus it happened that in that war, through the action of divine providence, both the defeated and the victors were found on either side, but in different ways. Our defeated men escaped by flight toward Hap, Antioch, and even farther, toward Tripoli, and reported that our people had been led to destruction. From another direction, the Turks, fleeing with some of our men toward Aleppo, declared that Algazi and Dodechinus, together with the entire Turcoman army, had been led to ruin.

The Author and Judge of supreme justice, however, granted King Baldwin—by the power of the holy cross and as the king’s life required—that he should put the enemy to flight and, with the triumph of divine victory, freely and without hindrance possess the field of battle, even with only a few men.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 1029B] It happened that a party of the enemy separately encountered a group of our men returning weary from the assault, their horses failing, together with a groom carrying some of the king’s standards.

When the faithless men saw that they were exhausted and afflicted by adverse fortune, they easily brought down their horses by shooting arrows. Some of the soldiers, compelled by the force of the missiles, they delivered to death; others, bound in the snares of captivity, they led to Aleppo without the king’s knowledge.

[Col. 1029C] The king, having secured the field, heard that some men had fled to Hap and remained there. He hastened to send them repeated announcements of the victory, twice and three times.

Although they perceived by a certain sign and reliable indications that the king had secured the field with the triumph of victory, some were held back by fear and others oppressed by shame, and they were afraid to approach him. Nevertheless, they did not cease returning, lest they be judged to have failed completely.

The king, compelled by a shortage of food and drink, set out late for Hap. In the morning he returned to the field and ordered the wounded and the dead from the field to be brought in, as was proper. He also sent brave men riding around to inspect whether anything of the war remained anywhere. He himself stayed in the field long enough to learn clearly, from reliable messengers and certain indications, that the faithless men had been defeated.

In that conflict, as was believed, five or seven hundred of our infantry and one hundred soldiers were killed. Of the Turks, however, according to the admission of those who escaped, two or three thousand fell by the sword of the Christians. The power of the holy cross obtained this victory on the eve of the feast of the Assumption of the blessed Virgin Mary.

[Col. 1029D] The king, therefore, rejoicing, entrusted his finger-ring—well known to the patriarch and to his sister, the princess—to a faithful messenger to carry to Antioch. By this sign he was to announce the victory of the holy cross and proclaim that the king had secured the field of battle.

The messenger set out without delay. He found all the people of Antioch sunk in grief, announced these things to them, and presented the patriarch, on behalf of the king, with the ring as a sign of Christian victory.

What more need be said? All together, recovering their strength and correcting their conduct and lives, joyfully rendered thanks to the Most High God in his church.

Afterward, through the divine power of the life-giving cross, and with the triumph of Christendom recovered, the king returned to Antioch. Outside the city, farther away than usual, he was victoriously received by the entire people and clergy with hymns and spiritual songs. Under the direction of a saving procession, [Col. 1030A] he was led back joyful and rejoicing to the church of blessed Peter, from which he had undertaken his journey and from which the beginning of the good expedition had proceeded, to the praise and glory of the highest King and supreme Lord,

> “to whom no one can please in any other way except through what he himself has given,”

the God who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER XVII

Now I shall relate in sequence, for the sake of sight and hearing, certain matters concerning the destruction of the captive Christians that I briefly introduced above for discussion.

On the day when King Dodechinus of Damascus and Algazi, prince of the Turcomans, were defeated by the power of the holy cross and the royal hand and driven into flight and dispersion, word was brought to Algazi’s son, who at that time was a resident of Aleppo, that the leaders themselves, together with the greater part of their army, had fallen by the sword of the Christians.

[Col. 1030B] When they heard this, certain of the more powerful men of Aleppo—some previously ransomed by the hand and command of the wicked prince, others deprived of their houses and other honors and assigned to those same Turcomans—pretended to participate in the public mourning and outcry, but inwardly rejoiced. They plotted to place various obstacles in the way of the fugitives who had escaped.

Cunningly, they sent other soldiers, plunderers, after the defeated men, ordering them to kill the fugitives while stripping them and, in revenge for the losses inflicted on the people of Aleppo, to destroy them in anger.

Thus it happened that those fleeing outside the city through various regions were punished by various exactions. Within the city, amid immense cries and with some genuine and some feigned tears, mournful lamentations were made for the slain. The result was that the city itself, on the surface and down to the foundations of its walls, towers, and various buildings, resounded as though it were about to be overthrown entirely by flashes of lightning and peals of thunder.

[Col. 1030C] This was done because their custom required it. Whenever they were defeated, they issued a proclamation that they had won. With feigned triumphal rejoicing, while female drummers, flutes, and trumpets sounded, they roused the minds of the desolate people to joy through these instruments, so that they would not despair.

[Col. 1030D] On that occasion they persisted in these things with greater than usual delight and boldness, so that the captive Christians, who were then being held in Aleppo under various forms of torture, on hearing it and being tormented more and more in spirit, might somehow make their resolve.

They, however, fortified by the weapons of faith, though suffering anguish of heart and many injuries, and having heard from the report of the faithless men that the king and his people had fallen in battle, nevertheless never abandoned the worship of the true faith. Instead, they prayed to God from the depths of their hearts, with greater fervor than usual, for the safety of the Christian army and for themselves, keeping vigils and offering prayers.

It happened that they heard, through the secret report of certain faithful and even unfaithful people, that the joys and various celebrations taking place publicly had in reality been filled with the greatest grief and mourning. They learned that these celebrations were for the destruction of the wicked men and the victory of the Christians, which had been made manifest and marked by the power of the holy cross and by the presence of King Baldwin, who had secured the field of battle.

They also heard that Dodechinus and Algazi had been brought to destruction.

What then? Whatever bitterness and sorrow they had previously suffered, on hearing this they considered it all changed into sweetness. They did not cease to supplicate him from whom all good things proceed, with devotion and pure affection of heart.

[Col. 1031A] Refreshed by this joy, they passed the day and remained cheerful until the third or middle hour of the night, rejoicing with the certain hope of victory. Unexpectedly, however, they heard from various directions shouts unlike those before, greater rejoicing than the rest, and instruments—female drums—sending forth sounds and tumult more fiercely than before.

The captives were amazed and wondered what this change signified and what unusual thing the people of the entire city were proclaiming with loud cries and with lights kindled everywhere.

Dodechinus and Algazi had in fact been driven from the battle toward the region of Berria and had returned to Aleppo unarmed and exhausted, with only a few men. From there the aforementioned praises and acclamations grew within and outside the city among the people of Aleppo, who marveled at them.

[Col. 1031B] Then what had been pleasing and sweet to the captives, once they understood it, was changed by their most wretched fate into the opposite. For at first light, while they were occupied with prayers, messengers of the wicked princes arrived, accompanied by a considerable crowd of the people already mentioned. They brought the heads of seven soldiers. With drawn swords, they struck and battered the iron-bound prison door, following the customary practice by which they regularly dragged out captives day after day to be beheaded.

They entered the prison and said:

> “On behalf of the victorious Algazi we bring you this message: your king and the rest of the Christian people have fallen in battle by his sword.”

After displaying the heads, they said to the captives:

> “[Col. 1031C] The star of our law now sends these dishes to you as food. Not long afterward, when you see the head and standard of your own king, you will learn what and how great is the power of our excellent law, which from now on you will not be able to oppose.”

Concealing the true sequence of events, the messengers returned as though joyful to their masters, who were lying in their tents outside the gate. They revealed their disgrace and loss by drinking wine.

The captives, however, watching through a crack in the wall where they had often observed the actions of the wicked princes through the reports of faithful people, then understood clearly that immense losses had come upon both sides. The profane men outside were pretending to rejoice, but inwardly they were tormented by the loss of their triumph. The Christians, having recovered their triumph, rejoiced in Christ with a certain and perfect victory.

[Col. 1031D] On the fifth day, Rotbert Fulcoius, dragged away and mutilated by the hands of the wicked, was presented to Algazi in Aleppo.

At this, all together clapped their hands amid doubled joy and unheard-of acclamations of praise. They flocked to him as to a monster—not to redeem him from punishments, but so that, by mocking him, mocking might become torture, and by torturing him they might tear him limb from limb. Through this savage form of vengeance, they rejoiced that they could lessen the pain which he had inflicted upon them for so long.

But, because the Lord prevented it, they did not dare touch him.

[Col. 1032A] What more is there to say? Since the people could not accomplish this against him, they did not cease pulling out their own hair and beards. The wicked prince, however, decided to send him to Dodechinus, the investigator and deviser of various tortures, for punishment.

He was therefore sent, bound most tightly at the neck and hands with iron chains.

When Dodechinus saw him, he displayed a grin of joy, his mouth stretched open like a wild beast’s. With a grim gaze he examined the soldier whose hand and ingenuity, together with those of the other faithful men, had so often brought losses upon him and many misfortunes upon his scattered body.

What more? He received the man who had been presented, looked at him, despised him, and, having despised him, decided that he should meet the death he deserved. He spoke as follows:

> “[Col. 1032B] Ah, Rotbert, ah! Look at what advantage our law confers and to what your error and unbelief have driven you. Why have you been brought to this point, that you try to overturn our law by means of your law and to make it better than ours and all other laws? Why does your hand—your hand, I say, so very small—rise into power and dominion over us, as a worm crawls upon the ground and then lifts itself up? Look: until now, as our fate required, we have advanced by falling and rising again. But now, with the situation changed, we believe that your right has been delivered into our hands as a gift from God. Yet I remember that you previously gave something of yours to me; therefore, on this occasion I find no reason within me to kill you.”

He sent him back to Algazi, saying through the messenger:

> “I prefer that he perish by your sword rather than by mine.”

He delayed inflicting death for no other reason than that, having been mocked in turn by both men, Rotbert might learn what terror and power each of them could exercise over him.

[Col. 1032C] Thus Rotbert, having been mocked in Algazi’s presence, was presented to him again. Dodechinus seized a sword and said to him:

> “Renounce your law, or die.”

Rotbert replied:

> “I renounce all the works of Satan and his pomp; but I do not renounce Christ.”

At these words the profane man, seized by fury, separated the Christian’s head from his body with a blow of the sword.

He handed the head over to the public herald for public display, while he gave the body to the populace, proclaiming that it was to be torn apart.

What then? The bearer of the head carried it through the streets and alleys of the city, displaying it and presenting it to the wealthy. Rewarded with five hundred bezants and various gifts, he returned to the profane man. Giving thanks on his knees from the depths of his heart for the benefit bestowed upon him, he returned the head.

[Col. 1032D] Thereupon that impious man immediately ordered the craftsman of the impious art to make for him a vessel for drinking, constructed of the purest gold and adorned with precious gems and marvelous workmanship. At his drinking during his festive celebrations, it was to be displayed to him and to his descendants as a sign of boldness and victory.

Immediately Dodechinus, having selected the leading men of his people as messengers, asked Algazi to promise him, as a reward for true friendship, that, once he had received from him sixty thousand Saracen bezants, he would enter the prison of the Franks. There he would be able to be refreshed in the blood poured out by his own hand, after beheading all who were in that prison, as in a desired bath, and be renewed like a living eagle.

Algazi, however, having taken counsel, replied to the leading men as follows:

> “I admit that the petition of so great a man is right and most just. [Col. 1033A] Yet I perceive that there is something else which must first be done, something beneficial to our law and our interests. Once it has been accomplished, I shall wholly comply with this great friend’s will and authority, both in this matter and in others.  
>   
> “But so that neither you nor he may be unaware of my intention, let your prudence understand what must be considered and report it to him. We still cannot possess the castle of Hasa, which is regarded as the gate of entry into and exit from Aleppo. The fact that the Franks, having recovered their strength, have grown strong against us greatly hinders both the recovery of that castle and the preservation, untouched by their ingenuity and power, of the castles already recovered.  
>   
> “[Col. 1033B] If we allow the noble and ignoble captives whom we hold from their people to be destroyed in this manner, we shall certainly suffer losses more serious than usual both in recovering the castles and in other matters. Our counsel is to contrive, by means of some simulated exchange of captives, whether at the surrender of the castle or in some other matter, to deceive their king by a crafty and prudent plan. While he lives, we may be sure that we shall possess neither that castle nor anything else subject to his rule except by force or cunning.  
>   
> “It is therefore necessary to tolerate the continued life of the captives, so that, after their princes and rulers have first been burdened by an avenging hand, Dodechinus himself may later turn whatever he desires against them and satisfy his thirsting heart.”

When they heard this, the messengers returned and reported what they had heard to their master. They praised the proposal, saying that it was fitting and useful that the star of their law had advised it.

When Dodechinus heard this, although unwilling, he nevertheless approved and endured it.

[Col. 1033C] Both men, terrified by the flight and destruction that had befallen them, set aside equity and every other matter beneficial to the commonwealth and devoted themselves solely to drinking.

During these drinking bouts, at desperate hours by night and day, they sent executioners, ordering them to lead away the captives in groups like sheep and bring them before them.

Some, suspended by ropes from a post, with their heads bent separately and their feet turned upward, were offered to the repeated blows of arrows as material for a cruel slaughter. Others were buried up to the pubes, others up to the navel, and others up to the earth’s surface (terrae specumentotenus; reading uncertain); and, as the wicked men hurled spears, they underwent the lamentable severing of life for Christ.

Some, after their limbs had been cut off one by one, were thrown into the streets and alleys as a spectacle of astonishing cruelty for passersby. The more fiercely the drunkenness of the faithless men burned, the more their perversity in torture increased.

[Col. 1033D] This became known to many through what was observed in the lordly palace during their drinking. On the day when, after the battle, Algazi lay drunk in the palace in a frenzy of wine, all the Christian captives then named who were in Aleppo were brought before him together at his command.

There, with nearly the entire population of the city gathered before the entrance to the palace, and with the people shouting and sighing in their desire for the captives’ destruction, twenty-seven soldiers and foot soldiers were handed over to a most wretched slaughter, all subjected to equal torment.

In an instant their bodies were beheaded, and the whole pavement of the portico and royal hall was spattered with a flowing stream of blood.

[Col. 1034A] After these men, during the revelry of that horrifying drunkenness, soldiers from both wars, nobles as well as others, were bound most tightly before the faithless man on the pavement. Mocked by those standing around, subjected to insults and terrors, struck by many slaps and goaded by the instruments of misery, disfigured by the plucking of beard and hair, and oppressed by shameful nakedness, they gnashed their teeth, trembled in their entrails, and longed for heaven.

On that occasion nothing in the world seemed more certain to them than the sword blows that threatened them; in mind and body they were tortured. Each in turn was summoned before the impious man, who through the messenger asked:

> “Which would he prefer: to renounce the law of the Christians, or in an instant to be cruelly beheaded by a blow of his sword?”

But he could extort from them nothing contrary to the true faith, either in word or in deed.

[Col. 1034B] When he heard the nobles’ response, full of faith, hope, and charity, and saw that they did not fear either his threats or death for Christ, he rose. Taking a sword, he went into their midst and walked around the circle, looking at each one with grim eyes. Thinking each of those whom he surveyed with grim eyes to be a priest, he ordered a certain soldier to be seized and himself cut off that man’s head with his own hand and sword.

Returning to the circle in the midst of the captives, he drew his sword before the face of each one and demanded that bezants be handed over to him immediately—not because he wished them to be ransomed on that occasion, but because, driven by drunkenness, he wanted to destroy them. At once he ordered another man to be seized, named Arnulf, a Marisian steward, a man of great religious devotion.

[Col. 1034C] He gave the sword to the patriarch of Damascus and said:

> “Strike, strike; this is certainly fitting.”

When he received it, Archadius, moved in his heart, said to a certain Amirald:

> “Perform this act of honor for our law in my place, so that so great a man may now be deprived of his head by the hand of so great a soldier.”

After Arnulf had been beheaded, Algazi again took up the sword and came into the midst of the captives, with no other intention than to destroy them all together in a similar slaughter.

But the Agent of supreme mercy granted the captives this: what that man’s perversity intended was changed by God’s will through a gift sent to him.

For it happened that at that moment, on behalf of King Debeis of the Arabs, a horse of extraordinary beauty arrived there. Its bridle, saddle, and hanging straps were adorned with workmanship of rare and precious art; from its ears to the trimming of its hooves it was decorated with Arabian gold and precious gems.

[Col. 1034D] When Algazi saw it, he threw down his sword, exchanged his fury for joy, and entered a chamber with the leading men. He clothed himself in ornaments exceptionally distinguished for their value and marvelous workmanship. He then ordered the leading men to compel the captives quickly to state how much each of them could give for the redemption of his life.

Having done this, he mounted the horse and proceeded toward Dodechinus, the servant of Antichrist. The leading men, acting in place of their master, asked each captive how much he could pay for his ransom.

After hearing the price of each according to the greater or lesser amount, they wrote everything down on tablets. When this had been completed, the captives were sent back to the prisons.

## CHAPTER XVIII
Of the various kinds of torments by which the captives were crushed in the prisons of the Saracens, I would indeed have many wondrous and astonishing things to describe and explain in words. But since kings, princes, and other powerful people of the world—even the powerless—who are of the same condition and faith as themselves, sometimes justly and sometimes unjustly capture men of the same condition and faith, punish those captured with various penalties in order to extort money from them, and since the whole human race, at the devil’s prompting, is accustomed to take examples from evil rather than from good, I judge it more useful to keep silent about the form and severity of the torments than to express them, lest Christian believers inflict similar things upon Christian believers and turn them into a custom.

But the miracle that occurred to the captives in prison I disclose in written memory, out of compassion for them, for those present and those yet to come. One night, when the captives had surrendered their limbs to sleep—sleep, I mean, such as could be had in misery—a certain soldier, Samson by name and surnamed of Bruera, learned through a vision that he had seen heaven opened, and from it our Lord Jesus Christ, in the beauty and splendor of his virtues, seated from the summit of heaven down above the prison. He had commanded Samson three times to come to him with his companions. When they arrived, he extended his right arm from the top of the prison to its end, and, dipping his right thumb in oil and chrism, impressed the sign of the holy cross upon the forehead of each one.

Among them, besides those designated by name, others were also present in the vision. When the Lord had not marked these in the same way, Samson asked why he had left them out. He is said to have answered him: “I do not want to do more; on another occasion, wherever it pleases me, I shall mark the others.”

Awakened by this vision, Samson roused his captive brothers at midnight, as was customary, to pray. When they had finished the morning praises, he disclosed the vision to them. Why relate every detail? On that same day, all those who had been marked, together with the others, were led outside the gate to the gallows, while the prince of crime, with the leading men of every rank in Aleppo, was occupied in festive drinking.

When he saw them, the master of crime rejoiced and said to the leading men: “Look with what ransom and what gift I wish these free soldiers to return to their own lord the king, and let each one come forward, brought one after another as is fitting, so that each may receive his gift from my own hand.”

Thus Samson was brought forward first, beheaded by the hand of Algazi himself, adorned with the gift of martyrdom, and presented to the Lord to reign with the saints. The same is proved to have truly occurred to the other twenty-four who had been marked.

Nor do I think it should be left unmentioned that among these there was a certain young man, the son of the viscount of Acre, who was beheaded. His body, through the Lord’s power and miracle, transported itself from the place where it lay to another place before all those present there. When this had happened, the profane man, deprived of his strength, foaming and crushed in the blood that had been shed, died; he was hideously disfigured by the most savage form of agony, so that, as I say, mouth with ears and ears with nostrils seemed to have formed a horrible chaos.

The remaining men who had not been marked were driven away, scourged, and dragged back to the prison with the utmost cruelty by the hands of the impious. Algazi himself was carried into a tent by his men. As usual, overcome by wine, he lay for fifteen days in the stench of his own excrement, as though dead; by this most shameful kind of suffering he was very often worn down amid great drinking bouts.

## CHAPTER XIX

After this, since on that occasion he was unable by force or ingenuity to deceive the king and the Christian believers, he took counsel with Dodechinus and the leading men. Having cast down the castle of Sardonas and fortified his own towns, he ordered that the noblemen and certain others captured on land be redeemed, and that the price of their ransom be assigned to the soldiers and servants who were to guard the land, until he himself had gone to Merdin, the special castle of his honor, and had gathered there, for the destruction of the Christian believers, a greater number than usual of the Turcoman people, and returned.

Why relate every detail? After setting out, he gathered a very great host of both Turcomans and Arabs. Once they had been assembled, and seeing so great a multitude, seized by an elation of immeasurable pride, he decided to ride out on campaign against King David with one of the Chorocenian sultans, so that, once he had killed or dispossessed him, he might freely and absolutely make Jerusalem and Antioch subject to his dominion after killing the Christians.

But their proud undertaking became the occasion of God’s anger. On the day when the sultan and Algazi himself entered the land of the Law to wage war, with six hundred thousand men, King David, fortified beforehand by the sign of the holy cross and having eighty thousand warriors among Medes and Christians, formed his ranks between two mountains thickly covered with woods and resisted in the valley through which, as rumor had reported, the enemies were daring to approach him.

He resisted and spoke as follows:

“Come, soldiers of Christ! If we fight lawfully for the defense of God’s law, we shall easily overcome not only the countless minions of demons but even the demons themselves. I have a plan which I see will benefit our honor and our advantage, if you approve it: namely, that with our hands raised to heaven we promise almighty God that, for love of him, we shall sooner die on this battlefield than flee; and, so that we may be unable to flee even if we wish to, let us block the open entrances of this valley through which we entered by piling up the densest barricades of wood. Then, with steadfast courage, let us strike most fiercely at the enemies who dare to fight us at close quarters.”

Why relate every detail? The judgment of that true and most perfect Christian king was praised, approved, and adopted. Without delay, when the individual battle lines had been arranged, the king placed before them the two hundred Frankish soldiers whom he had, to deliver the first blows. At once, on the other side, or front, of the valley, the fiercest standards of the wicked appeared, amid an enormous human outcry and a tumultuous din of horses and weapons. As they advanced, the mountains and valleys everywhere thundered with the sound of various instruments.

King David awaited the ferocity of so great a host with the deepest humility. He encouraged his men to act with manly courage and consoled them, asserting that, with the cooperation of the power of the holy cross, the exultant multitude of unbelievers could be crushed by a small and modest force.

Not long afterward, when they saw the Christian believers, the endless multitude, driven on by the spirit of pride, rushed upon them with immense shouting. But, first blinded by the blows delivered through the Lord’s power, they fell into confusion and were put to flight by the hands of the Franks.

Why relate every detail? By God’s decree, the perfidious men were offered together to the Christians and Medes as material for slaughter. As we learned from those who were present in the conflict, after the flight had lasted three days, four hundred thousand fell beneath the royal sword. Algazi himself, wounded in the head, and with nearly all his men killed by the Lord’s permission, was driven away with a few companions. Unarmed and famished, he returned half-dead to his homeland under the escort of the king of the Arabs.

The following year, having recovered, he returned in July to besiege Sardonas, which had been refortified by the king’s hand, accompanied by as many soldiers and footmen as he could gather in massed ranks. When Count Joscelin of Edessa heard this, he took counsel with the patriarch of Antioch and set out with his own men and the warriors of Antioch for Samartan, in order to disperse the siege of Sardonas by battle.

When the king of Jerusalem heard this, he came with the men of Jerusalem and reached the place with swift steps. Before his tents, soldiers from the side of the perfidious came forward to make a preliminary display and observe the army of the Christian believers.

What more is there to say? When the Christians appeared, the ferocity of the enemy was overcome by fear. At night they folded their tents, sent them ahead, and ceased attacking the castle. Algazi himself returned with his men to Aleppo, having been seized by a paralytic illness.

Because he did not wish this to become known, he pretended that he would once again bring together, in a short time, the greatest possible host of Arabs and Parthians. If this had been within his power, he would have devoted himself with burning zeal to the extermination of the Christian believers.

But it happened that, while he was being carried in a litter as a mark of honor and because of his incapacity, his filthy soul departed after a year, together with the discharge of the filth of his bowels, and, torn away by the claws of infernal scorpions, fell into the pots of the lowest hell, full of dreadful fires—burning without end, consuming without cessation, and unquenchable. From this may the grace and mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ deliver us, at whose command all things celestial, terrestrial, and infernal obey, for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1037] Here end the Antiochene wars, conducted by Rotger, prince of Antioch, the war which Fulcher described above at the beginning of this volume.

[Col. 1037]

# THE BOOK OF HOLY PLACES OF THE LAND OF JERUSALEM BY FRETELLUS, ARCHDEACON

*(Baluz, Miscellanea, edited by Mansi, I, 434.)*

## JOHN DOMINIC MANSI TO THE READER

[Col. 1037] The little book of Fretellus, which I now publish, immediately presents to scholars the author’s name and its title, neither of them unknown. Both were known from the *Latin Library of the Middle and Lower Ages* of Johann Albert Fabricius. But I believe that they knew nothing further either about the book itself or about the time when its author wrote. Concerning the date, I have nothing to offer except conjectures.

Fretellus dedicated this little work of his to Raymond, count of Toledo [Toulouse]. Could this perhaps be the same Count Raymond who was deemed worthy of a royal marriage with Urraca, daughter of Alfonso VI, king of Castile? In the century in which he lived, sacred pilgrimages to the holy places were being undertaken. Moreover, Raymond’s wife Urraca bore him a son, Alfonso, who, at the beginning of the twelfth century—that is, in the year 1109—was raised to the throne of Toledo and reigned under the name Alfonso VII.

From this it is possible to form a conjecture about the time when Fretellus was writing. This Fretellus calls himself an archdeacon, but he neither says of which church nor gives me any means of investigating the matter. It is clear that he discusses the holy places in such a way that he seems to have been present there; hence Raymond questioned him as an eyewitness on this subject.

I now publish this little book of Fretellus, which Adrichomius also declares that he consulted in his *Theatre of the Holy Land*. I have taken it from the *Collectanea* of Nicholas Rosselli of Aragon, who, under Pope Innocent VI, was transferred from being a monk of the illustrious Order of Saint Dominic into the college of cardinals in 1356, and became known under the name Cardinal Nicholas of Aragon.

He gave his miscellany the title: *Compilation of Brother Nicholas of Aragon, compiled from various registers and books of the Apostolic Chamber, and from various other books and Chronicles*. These words belong to Jacob the Tuscan, who in 1503 was copying a manuscript preserved in the cathedral church of Lucca, as he himself adds, from an ancient and perhaps original codex.

Since no one up to the present has carefully investigated this rich collection, I have been able to extract from it a great many things, almost all of them never before brought to light.

# THE BOOK OF HOLY PLACES OF THE LAND OF JERUSALEM

[Col. 1039]

## PROLOGUE OF THE BOOK

[Col. 1039A] To his venerable lord and brother Raymond, by the grace of God count of Toledo [Toulouse], Fretellus, by that same grace archdeacon, offers service to God under the spirit of counsel and fortitude.

When, because of your sins, you fled to the Eastern Church and made pilgrimage in the land of promise—that is, the homeland of our Savior Jesus Christ—from which you contemplate the second Jerusalem, even Sion itself, which allegorically signifies paradise, and in which the stronger members of the new Israel, the Maccabees, keep watch over the bed of the true Solomon and thence overcome the Philistines and Amalek; afterward, do not be reluctant carefully to set down what and where the sacred places of David’s kingdom are, and what they signify, lest on returning you fall into the lands of the Egypt of Babylon, and, for as long as you remain here, heed the judgment of that holy Jerome who says:

“It is not praiseworthy to have been in Jerusalem, but to live well, and not to offer at the holy places except what has been lawfully acquired.”

Therefore, since you have crossed the sea devotedly—as it seemed to us, indeed, in a Catholic spirit—and have come from the distant and remote regions of Spain, you who are generous and kind toward good men and toward all who serve God in the holy Church, and also a fellow soldier of the Maccabees [lacuna]—having lodged at Bethel, in the court of King Solomon, beside the resting place of merciful Jesus—do not grow sluggish in your labor. Rather, render to God what is God’s: namely, the image that he represents in you, so that through this pilgrimage of yours, ascending Lebanon, tasting fruit from the flower of Nazareth, and inhaling fragrances in the heavenly places, clothed in the robe of immortality in Sion, you may deserve to keep Sabbath with the true Solomon, to whom all things live, for infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## DESCRIPTION OF THE PLACES OF THE HOLY LAND

[Col. 1039]

[Col. 1039B] Now, my reverend lord, since you have deigned to seek from my smallness knowledge of the sacred places of the land of promise—that is, of the Israelite region—I shall not disdain carefully to elucidate them for your sublimity as soundly as I can. I shall therefore turn my pen and begin with Cheron, that is, Hebron.

Formerly it was the metropolitan city of the Philistines and of the giants, in the tribe of Judah; it was a priestly city and a city of fugitives. Hebron is situated in that field in which the supreme Disposer formed our father Adam and breathed into him the breath of life.

Hebron is called Anatarbe, which in Saracen speech means “cities.” The four revered fathers—Adam, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—and their four wives—Eve, our mother, Sarah, Rebecca, and Leah—were buried there in the double cave. Hebron is situated beside the Valley of Tears.

The Valley of Tears was so called because Adam mourned his son Abel there for one hundred years. Later, having been warned by an angel, he knew his wife Eve there and begot by her his son Seth, from whose tribe Christ was descended.

Two miles from Hebron is the tomb of Lot, Abraham’s nephew. At Hebron there is a certain field whose red soil is dug up and eaten by the inhabitants and carried to Egypt for sale, where it is purchased at a very high price as though it were a spice. The aforesaid field, however deeply and extensively it is dug, is opened again by God’s providence when the year has ended, with its soil restored.

Near Hebron is Mount Mambre, at the foot of which stands the terebinth called *dirps*, that is, holm oak or oak. Abraham remained beside it for a very long time. Beneath it he saw three angels, worshiped one of them, and, having received them as guests, treated and fed them as honorably as he could. Hence the aforesaid oak was called the first way of believing.

From that time until the reign of the emperor Theodosius, as Jerome testifies, it extended its own [growth?]. A piece is said to have been cut from it, which is kept by its possessors as a *cahra* [reading uncertain]. Although it is dry, it is said to be medicinal in this respect: as long as someone carries it with him while riding, his animal will not be harmed.

At Hebron, Caleb and Joshua and their ten companions first arrived to explore the land of promise. David reigned in Hebron for seven years and six months.

Ten miles from Hebron, toward the east, is the Asphaltite Lake, which is called the Dead Sea—truly dead, because nothing living exists in it; it neither gives nor receives—and it is called the Sea of the Devil because, at his instigation, those four most wretched cities—Sodom, Gomorrah, Seboim, and Adama—persisting in their shamefulness, were burned with sulfurous fire and overthrown in that place.

[Col. 1041A] Above the lake, in the lying-place of Judea, is Segor, also called Belzora. It is one of those five cities that was preserved from burning and destruction by Lot’s prayers, and it is still shown today. At the exit from Segor, Lot’s wife was changed into the likeness of a statue, and her traces are still visible.

Along the bank of the aforesaid sea the inhabitants find and collect much alum and much *Katrani* [a resinous substance; reading uncertain]. Bitumen is extracted from the sea, and in Judea it is considered necessary for many uses. Segor is called by its countrymen the town of the Palm.

Above the Asphaltite Lake, on the descent toward Arabia, is the cave of Carviaym on the mountain of the Moabites. To this place Dahac, son of Ebor, brought Balaam by divine command to curse the children of Israel. Because of its steep precipice it is called “the Cut-Off.” The Asphaltite Lake divides Judea and Arabia.

In the time of the children of Israel, Arabia was a solitude and a desert, an impassable and waterless land. There the Lord detained them for forty years, raining down manna for them to eat.

In Arabia was Elmon, where the children of Israel camped in the desert and found twelve springs and seventy palm trees after emerging from the Red Sea. In Arabia is the Valley of Moses, where he struck the rock twice with his staff and restored two streams of water to the people of God; the whole country is now watered by them.

In Arabia is Mount Sinai, where Moses remained for forty days and as many nights entirely without food, and where the Lord gave Moses the Law, written with his own finger on stone tablets.

In Arabia, a pillar of fire went before the children of Israel by night, and a cloud enclosed them each day. In Arabia are the forty stations of the children of Israel. In Arabia is Mount Hor, where Aaron lies buried. In Arabia is Abarim, where the Lord buried Moses, although his tomb has never appeared.

In Arabia is the Royal Mountain, which Baldwin, the first Frankish king in Jerusalem, made into a strong castle in order to subjugate that land to the Christian believers and defend the kingdom of David. Arabia joins Idumaea at the borders of Botoron.

Idumaea is the land of Damascus. Idumaea lies under Syria, whose chief city is Damascus. Lebanon divides Idumaea and Phoenicia. In Phoenicia is Sor, that is, Tyre, the most distinguished metropolis of the Phoenicians. As the Syrians assert, it refused to receive Christ when he was walking along the seacoast; yet, as the divine page testifies, it gave so many martyrs to God that only God himself knows their number.

Tyre conceals Origen, who was buried there. Near Tyre is that small marble stone upon which Jesus sat and remained unharmed. From the time of Christ until the expulsion of the Gentiles from the city, it remained there; but afterward it was carried off by the Franks and also the Venetians. Above the remaining part of that stone, a church was founded in honor of the Savior.

Eight miles east of Tyre, above the sea, is Sarphen, also called Sarepta of the Sidonians. The prophet Elijah once lived there. There he raised to life the son of the widow who had lodged him and had cared for and fed him out of charity.

Six miles from Sarphen is Sidon, an excellent city, from which came Dido, who built Carthage in Africa.

Sixteen miles from Sidon is Berytus, a very wealthy city. In Beirut there is an image of our Savior which, not long after his Passion, certain Jews mockingly crucified in disgrace. It produced blood and water, and many therefore came to believe in the true Crucified One and were baptized. Whoever was suffering from any illness and was anointed with what came from that image was restored to health.

Arphax is a city of Damascus, concerning which history says: “Damascus in Syria.” Damascus is the revered metropolitan capital of Syria, which Eleazar, Abraham’s servant, built.

In that field Cain killed his brother Abel. Esau lived at Damascus; he is also called Seir and Edom: Seir means “hairy,” and Edom “red” or “ruddy.” From Edom the whole land is called Idumaea, concerning which the psalm says: “Upon Idumaea I shall cast my sandal” (Psalm 59:10).

Hence the prophet says: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah?” (Isaiah 63:1.) Bozrah is a part of that land called Hus, from which blessed Job came; it is also called Sueta, from which came Bildad the Shuhite.

Teman is the metropolis of Idumaea; Eliphaz the Temanite came from Teman. Naaman is a town from which Zophar the Naamathite came. These three were Job’s comforters.

At the borders of Idumaea, two miles from the Jordan, is the river Jabbok. When Jacob crossed it while coming from Mesopotamia, he wrestled with an angel, who changed his name from Jacob to Israel.

In Idumaea, beneath Damascus, is Mount Seir. Two miles from Damascus is the place where Christ appeared to Saul, saying: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4.) There, too, no small charity shone around Saul from heaven.

In Damascus Ananias baptized Saul, giving him the name Paul. From the walls of Damascus Paul was lowered in a basket because he feared the savage fury of his persecutors.

Lebanon is interpreted as “whitening,” concerning which the Song of Songs says: “Come from Lebanon, my bride, my dove” (Song of Songs 4:8).

At the foot of Lebanon rise the Pharphar and Abana, the rivers of Damascus. Abana flows through the mountains of Lebanon and the plain of Arcados, joining the Great Sea in the region where Saint Eustace, deprived of his wife and children and left desolate, withdrew.

Pharphar flows through populous Syria—that is, Antioch—and, passing around its walls, gives itself to the Mediterranean Sea at the port of Solymi, namely the port of Saint Simeon, ten miles from Antioch.

Blessed Peter sat in Antioch for seven years, adorned with the dignity of the pontificate.

At the foot of Lebanon lies the city of Paneas, that is, Bilmas, also called Caesarea Philippi. In that place God gave Peter the power of binding and loosing.

At the foot of Lebanon rise those two springs, Jor and Dan, from which the river Jordan is formed beneath the mountains of Gibelli. In this river Christ wished to be baptized by John his precursor, at the distance of a stone’s throw three times. At that place the Father’s voice thundered, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew 3:17). There the Holy Spirit descended upon Jesus in the form of a dove.

From the mountains to the Asphaltite Lake, the valley through which the Jordan flows is called Corcus Aulon, which is a Hebrew name. It is also called the Valley, a very great and level plain. It is enclosed on both sides by continuous mountains, from Lebanon to the desert of Faran. The Jordan divides Galilee, Idumaea, and the land of Botoron, which is also the second metropolis of Idumaea.

“Jordan” is interpreted as “descent.” Dan, from its source, carries its subterranean current as far as the plain of Meldam, where it displays its channel quite clearly. That plain is called Meldam because it is better there. In Saracen speech it means “open square,” and in Latin “forum.”

It is called Meldam because, when summer begins, an innumerable population, bringing with it every kind of merchandise, gathers there, and a great military force of Parthians and Arabs remains throughout the summer to protect the people and feed its own flocks in those exceedingly rich pastures.

Meldam is composed of *Med*, *Dan*, and the Saracen word for water. The river Dan, leaving the aforesaid plain, proceeds into the river Suetan, in which the pyramid of blessed Job still survives and is held in honor by Greeks and Gentiles.

Dan, bending toward Galilee of the Gentiles, flows from the city of Cedar beside medicinal baths full of foam and joins the Jor.

Jor, far from the bell-shaped [or “campanile”] springs, gave forth milk; afterward the Sea of Galilee takes its beginning from it between Bethsaida and Capernaum.

From Bethsaida came Peter and Andrew, John, and James son of Alphaeus.

Four miles from Bethsaida is Chorazin, where the Antichrist, the deceiver of the world, will be nourished. Concerning Chorazin and Bethsaida John says: “Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida” (Matthew 11:21; Luke 10:10).

Five miles from Chorazin is that very wealthy city of Cedar, concerning which the psalm says: “With those who dwell in Cedar my soul was long an exile” (Psalm 119:5). Cedar is interpreted as “darkness.”

Capernaum is situated on the right side of the sea. It is the city of the centurion whose son Jesus healed there, concerning whom it is said: “I have not found such great faith in Israel” (Matthew 8:10). Jesus performed many other signs in Capernaum, teaching in the synagogue (John 6:60).

Capernaum is interpreted as “most beautiful daughter,” or “daughter of beauty.” It signifies for us the holy Church, to which they descend with Lebanon—that is, from the whiteness of virtues—and from which and in which they are more radiant.

Two miles from Capernaum is the descent of that mountain on which Jesus spoke to the crowds and instructed his people, teaching them; there, too, he healed a leper.

One mile from that descent is the place where he fed five thousand men with five loaves and two fish. Hence the place is called the Table, as though it were the place of restoration. Beneath it lies the place where Christ appeared to his disciples after his resurrection, eating with them a portion of roasted fish and a honeycomb.

Above the sea in that place the Lord walked with dry feet. Around the fourth watch of the night, he appeared to Peter and Andrew while they were fishing. There, when Peter wished to come to him across the sea and began to sink, Jesus said to him: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matthew 14:31). On another occasion, when his disciples feared that they were in danger at sea, he made the sea calm.

On the left side of the sea, in a hollow of the mountain, is the town of Gennesaret, Magdalum, from which came Mary Magdalene. This region is Galilee of the Gentiles, in the tribe of Zebulun and Naphtali (Matthew 4:15).

In the upper parts of this Galilee were those twenty cities which King Solomon gave as a gift to his friend King Hiram.

Two miles from Magdala is Chinnereth, also called Tiberias after the emperor Tiberius. Jesus used to visit it frequently in his youth.

Four miles from Tiberias is the city of Bethulia, from which Judith, in order to save her people, cunningly killed Holofernes during the siege of the city.

Four miles south of Tiberias is Bothan. There Joseph found his brothers grazing their flocks. Because they hated him, they sold him to the Ishmaelites.

Ten miles from Tiberias is the city of Nazareth, the proper home of the Savior in Galilee, because he was brought up there. Nazareth is interpreted as “flower” or “shoot.” Not without reason: in it appeared the flower from whose fruit the world has been filled—the flower, I say, concerning which the archangel Gabriel announced in that same Nazareth to the Virgin Mary that the Son of the Most High would be born from her, saying: “Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women” (Matthew 1:28), “and blessed is the fruit of your womb.”

Concerning Nazareth it was said: “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” (John 1:46.)

Two miles from Nazareth is the city of Sepphoris, on the road leading to Acre. Anna, the mother of blessed Mary, the mother of Jesus, was born at Sepphoris.

Four miles east of Nazareth is Cana of Galilee. Philip and Nathanael came from there. There, while the boy Jesus was reclining with his mother at a wedding, he changed water into wine.

In Nazareth a small spring flows, from which the boy Jesus used to draw water in his childhood and carry it both to his mother and to himself.

One mile south of Nazareth is a place called “the Beginning.” From there Jesus’ countrymen wished to hurl the young Jesus down, envying his wisdom, but he disappeared from them in an instant.

Four miles east of Nazareth is Mount Tabor, on which Jesus was transfigured before his apostles Peter, John, and James, in the presence of Moses and Elijah. There, too, the Father’s voice was heard: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 17:5). He told John and James not to reveal to anyone what they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead (ibid., 9).

There Peter said: “Lord, it is good for us to be here; let us make three tabernacles here, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah” (ibid., 4).

Two miles east of Tabor is Mount Hermon. On the descent of Mount Tabor, the lord Melchizedek met Abraham returning from the slaughter of Amalek. He was both king and priest, and he is called Salem. He presented Abraham with bread and wine, which signifies the offering of Christ’s altar under grace.

Two miles from Tabor is the city of Naim, at whose gate Christ restored a widow’s son to life.

Above Naim is Mount Endor. At its foot, above the stream Kadmium, which is the stream Kishon, Barak son of Abinoam, together with the son of the prophetess Deborah, defeated the Idumaeans. He pursued across the Jordan and killed with the sword Sisera, Agebel the wife of Abereneus, and Zeeb, Zebah, and Zalmunna; his arm was at Endor and his army beneath Endor and Kishon. Hence the psalm says: “Tabor and Hermon shall rejoice in your name, and your arm with power” (Psalm 88:13).

At a distance of five miles is Anain, the city of Jezreel, also called Zaraim. From there came Jezebel, the most impious queen, who seized Naboth’s vineyard. Because of her importunity, she was thrown down from the top of her palace and died; her pyramid is still said to be visible.

Near Jezebel is the plain of Megiddo, where King Josiah, overcome and defeated by the king of Samaria, fell. He was then transferred to Sion and buried.

One mile from Jezreel are the mountains of Gilboa, where Saul and Jonathan were defeated and fell silent while fighting. Hence David says: “Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain come upon you” (2 Samuel 1:21), and so forth.

Two miles east of Gilboa is the city of Scythopolis, the metropolis of Galilee, also called Bethsan—that is, “house of the sun,” or “city.” They hung Saul’s head upon its walls.

Five miles from Jezreel is the town from which Samaria begins, also called Sebaste and Augusta, after the emperor Augustus. There was buried that forerunner of the Lord, John the Baptist, the bridegroom’s attendant, who had been beheaded by Herod beyond the Jordan, below the Asphaltite Lake, in the castle of Machaerus. His disciples transferred him to Sebaste, where he was buried between Elisha and Obadiah.

Later, the emperor Julian the Apostate is said to have removed his body from there and, by his command, burned it, scattering the ashes to the winds. But the head was absent, for it had previously been transferred to Alexandria, afterward to Constantinople, and finally to Gaul, in the district of Poitiers. The index finger was also absent—the finger that had indicated Jesus coming to baptism, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

The blessed virgin Thecla carried that finger from there across the Alps; it is preserved with the greatest veneration in the church of Maurienne.

Samaria is the name both of the city and of the region.

[Col. 1045D] Four miles from Sebaste is Neapolis, also called Sichen, formerly named Sichem before Veteomor, situated between Dan and Bethel. From Sichem that land was called Sichen; from Sichem came Emor, who violated Dinah, the daughter of Jacob, while she was walking about those territories. In Sichem the bones of Joseph were brought from Egypt. At Sichem, beside the spring, Jeroboam made two calves, which he caused the ten tribes whom he had brought and led astray to worship; he placed one of them between Dan and the other at Bethel. The sons of Israel destroyed that city of Sichem and Emor, grieving over the violation of their sister Dinah.

In these days Sichem is called Neapolis, that is, “new city.” Near Sichem, beside the estate which Jacob gave to his son Joseph, is Sichar, where the Spring of Joseph is located, also called the Well. Beside it, as the Gospel tells, Jesus, weary from the journey, sat and spoke with the Samaritan woman; a church is now being built there. Near Sichem is the terebinth beneath which Jacob hid the idols.

One mile from Sichem is the city of Luza, in which Abraham lived for a very long time. There Jacob, while sleeping, saw a ladder reaching to heaven, with angels ascending and descending upon it. Immediately upon awakening he said: “Truly this place is holy, and it is the gate of heaven” (Gen. XXVIII, 17). Raising up a stone as a monument and pouring oil over it, he called that place Bethel, which had previously been called Luza. At Bethel Abraham wished, at the command of the angel, to sacrifice his son Isaac to the Lord.

Bethel is a neighboring mountain of Garizim, facing Mount Gebal to the east, and [Col. 1046B] Stada above Sichem. Twenty miles from Sichem, four from Jerusalem, on the road leading to Diospolis, are Mount Syla and the city also called Arama, where the ark of the covenant and the tabernacle of the Lord remained from the arrival of the children of Israel until the time of Samuel the prophet and David the king.

Twenty miles from Sichem, sixteen from Diospolis, sixteen from Hebron, thirteen from Jericho, four from Bethel, seventeen from Beersheba, twenty-four from Ascalon, and the same distance from Joppa, six from Ramah, is Jerusalem, the most holy metropolis of Judaea, also called Sion, of which it is said: “Glorious things are spoken of you, O city of God” (Ps. LXXXVI, 3). It is also called Aelia, after Aelius Hadrian, who rebuilt it.

Bethlehem is a city of Judah, also called Ephrata. Bethlehem is interpreted as “house of bread,” [Col. 1046C] and not without reason, because from the Nazarene flower there proceeded in it the fruit of life from the Virgin Mary, namely Christ Jesus, the Son of God, who is the bread of angels and the life of the whole world.

In Bethlehem, near the place of the Nativity, is the manger in which the infant Jesus himself lay hidden. Hence the prophet says: “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger” (Isa. I, 3). From that manger the hay where the infant had lain was brought to Rome, to the church of Saint Mary Major.

One mile from Bethlehem the star appeared to the shepherds when the Lord had been born, while the angel said: “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke II, 14), etc. In Bethlehem, guided by the new star, three kings came from the East to worship the newborn Jesus; they adored him as King of the angels and presented mystical gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.

In Bethlehem and its surrounding territory Herod ordered the Innocents to be beheaded. Part of them lies buried and rests four miles south of Bethlehem and two miles from Thecua. Four miles south of Bethlehem is the church of blessed Caritot. When he himself was passing from this world, the monks over whom he had presided as shepherd desired devoutly to die together with him, since he had previously been their father and, burning with love for him, they did not wish to live in the world after his departure. Their individual bodies can still be seen in the church in the condition in which they were when, in the desolation following their father’s death, they lay dying. They were later transferred to Jerusalem.

In Bethlehem, beneath the basilica and not far from the manger, rests the body of blessed Jerome, together with Paula and Eustochium, to whom Jerome likewise writes.

[Col. 1047A] On the road from Bethlehem to Jerusalem is Kabrata, the place where Rachel died after giving birth to Benjamin. There she rests, buried by her husband Jacob. On her tomb Jacob placed twelve substantial stones as a testimony of the children of Israel; her pyramid can still be seen by travelers.

Jerusalem, the glorious metropolis of Judaea, is situated, according to the philosophers, at the center of the world. David reigned there for thirty-three and a half years.

In Jerusalem there is Mount Moriah. Upon it David saw an angel striking with a drawn sword, who had grievously killed the people of God. Fearing that he would take vengeance upon him and the city for the sin he had committed in numbering the people, David fell prostrate upon the ground, truly repentant and severely afflicting himself. He was heard by the Lord and obtained pardon (II Reg. XXIV, 16–17). Concerning him the Lord says: “I have found a man after my own heart.”

On Mount Moriah, while David was king, the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite flourished. When David wished to purchase it in order to build the house of the Lord there, he obtained it because the angel of the Lord, sparing him and the city, had stood there. He did purchase it, but the Lord forbade him to undertake the work, because he was a man of blood. Therefore he handed over to his son Solomon the expenses he had prepared for this purpose, so that Solomon might build the house of the Lord with them.

King Solomon therefore built a temple and altar for the Lord at Bethel, at incomparable expense, asking that whoever consulted the Lord there, concerning anything whatsoever, might deserve to be heard. This was granted to him by the Lord; therefore the house of the Lord is a house of counsel.

Later, because of the prince’s and the people’s lack of restraint, Nabuchodonosor plundered it through Nabusardam, the chief of his cooks, in the time of King Sedecias. He deprived the city of its king, took everything precious that was in the temple and the city, ordered it to be brought to Babylon, and carried away the people. Shortly afterward Pharaoh necessarily destroyed the temple and the city as well.

So that it may not seem tedious to the reader and hearer to recount under which rulers, and by whom, the restorations and destructions of the first, second, and third temples took place, I omit that account here for the present.

It is unknown under which ruler, and by which ruler, Bethel was restored. Some say that under the emperor Constantine it was rebuilt by his mother Helena, out of reverence for the holy cross discovered by her. Others say that it was rebuilt by the emperor Heraclius, out of reverence for the wood of the Lord which he had brought back after triumphing over the faithless Persians. Others attribute it to Augustus Augustinianus; still others to a certain admirer, Mymphis of Egypt, out of reverence for Alachiber, the supreme God, whom every tongue venerates and honors here as worthy of worship.

At this present place the fourth temple is said to stand. On its penultimate eighth day the child Jesus was circumcised after his birth. His foreskin was presented from heaven in the temple at Jerusalem by an angel to King Charlemagne, and by him brought to Gaul, to Aachen. Later Charles the Bald transferred it to Aquitaine, in the district of Poitiers, near Chartres, to the church which he built there in honor of the Holy Savior and endowed richly with royal possessions under monastic observance. It is still solemnly venerated there.

In the temple, at his Hypapante (Presentation), Jesus was presented by his mother and received by blessed Simeon, who said: “O Lord, light of the nations and glory of Israel, now dismiss your servant, O Lord, according to your word in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke II, 29).

From the temple God drove out the buyers and sellers. In the temple he freed the adulterous woman from those accusing her, saying: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her” (John VIII, 7). To that woman he said: “Woman, go in peace, and from now on sin no more” (ibid., 10).

In the temple he praised the offering of the poor woman which she placed in the treasury, because she had given everything she possessed. While he remained in Jerusalem, he taught the Jews in the temple, although they were hostile to him.

The devil set Jesus upon the pinnacle of the temple while tempting him and saying: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down” (Matt. IV, 6). Blessed James, the first high priest in Jerusalem under grace, was thrown down from the temple.

In the temple Zechariah was told of the future birth of his son John the Baptist. Between the temple and the altar Zechariah, son of Barachiah, suffered martyrdom.

Above the temple, in the Old Testament, they used to sacrifice turtledoves and pigeons; this was later changed by the Saracens into a clock, and it can still be seen.

Passing through the Beautiful Gate of the temple, Peter, with John, replied to the man asking them for alms: “What I have, I give you” (Acts III, 6).

In Jerusalem there is the Sheep Pool. In the time of Jesus, the angel of the Lord used to stir it at appointed times; whatever sick person entered first after the stirring of the water was immediately healed of whatever illness afflicted him. It is therefore called a *probatica* (“sheep-pool”), because the extremities of the animals used in sacrifices were customarily washed there. It was red because of the victims cleansed there.

Before the Sheep Pool Jesus healed an infirm man, saying to him: “Take up your bed and walk” (Mark II, 9). In the middle of Jerusalem Jesus raised a girl from the dead.

Beneath Solomon’s palace, in the valley of Jehoshaphat and at the pool of Siloam, Jesus sent the blind man whom he had enlightened to wash his eyes. He went, washed, and saw. Siloam therefore means “sent.” According to the tradition of the Tyrians, Siloam is said to flow from Silo. Siloam carries its pool in silence because it is subterranean.

Near Siloam stands an oak beneath which blessed Isaiah rests. In the valley of Jehoshaphat blessed James was buried and was later transferred to Constantinople. In the valley of Jehoshaphat, beneath a sharp pyramid, the same King Jehoshaphat lies buried.

Two miles from Jerusalem, on the road leading to Sichem, is Mount Gabaath, in the tribe of Benjamin. One mile from Jerusalem, on the slope of the Mount of Olives, is the Mount of Offense, continuing toward the Asphaltite Sea.

Bethany lies beside the Mount of Olives, and the Mount of Offense continues beside it. A road divides them, leading from Jehoshaphat through Bethphage. [Col. 1049A] It is called the Mount of Offense because King Solomon worshiped the idol Moloch there.

Bethany is the village in which Simon the leper often received Jesus as a guest, and where Mary and Martha devotedly ministered to him. At Bethany Mary, watering his feet with her tears, wiping them with her hair, and anointing them with perfume, obtained forgiveness for her sins. At Bethany he praised Martha and Mary: Martha for her anxious service, and Mary for her attentiveness to his words. Moved by their prayers and tears, he restored their brother Lazarus to life after he had lain four days in the tomb.

Bethany is interpreted as “house of obedience.” Bethphage, also called the village of the priests, means “house of the mouth” or “of the jaws.” The Mount of Olives means “mountain of chrism” or “of sanctification.” The valley of Jehoshaphat means “valley of judgment.” Jerusalem means “vision of peace.” Sion means “mirror” or “contemplation of God.”

By this route Jesus ascended to Jerusalem, seated upon a donkey, on the day celebrated with palm branches. Thus every Catholic, under the obedience of the supreme counsel of the Angel, ought to approach and proceed to the presence of the priest, who chews over the word of God, so that he may be corrected and instructed by him, and by their teaching and counsel enter the valley of judgment—that is, the construction of sound compunction—in which he should afflict himself, so that he may worthily enter through the gate of immortality into holy, heavenly Jerusalem, Sion, adorned with a robe of joy.

On Mount Sion Jesus washed the feet of his disciples, saying to them: “Do this in remembrance of me” (John XIII, 15). On Mount Sion he supped with his disciples, giving them his body in bread to eat and his blood in wine to drink; this is the provision of our redemption.

On Mount Sion, also at the supper, blessed John reclined upon the breast of the Lord, drinking from the fountain of wisdom. On Mount Sion, at the supper, he gave a morsel of bread to Judas his betrayer. On Mount Sion Jesus said: “The one who dips his hand with me in the dish is at table with me; he is the one who will betray me.” Judas said to him: “Surely it is I, Rabbi?” Jesus answered: “You have said so” (Matt. XXVI, 23, 25).

To the left of Mount Sion is the field of strangers, called Acheldemach, that is, “field of blood.”

Beside the road leading to Ephrata is Mount Geon, on which King Solomon was anointed and received the royal diadem.

In Jerusalem Judas sold Jesus on the slope of the Mount of Olives, eastward across the Kidron, a stone’s throw from Gethsemane. There Christ prayed to his Father, saying: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI, 39). There, from fear of the cross, he shed a bloody sweat. There he said to Peter: “Could you not watch with me one hour?” (ibid., 40).

From there he returned to Gethsemane. Judas the betrayer, having already received the price for what he had returned concerning Jesus, had given the cohort a sign: they were to seize whoever he kissed. Recognizing him by this fraudulent kiss, they led him bound to Sion, to the governor’s praetorium, called in Greek Lithostratos and in Hebrew Gabatha. There Peter denied him three times. When he heard the cock crow, he piously remembered Jesus’ words, truly repented, and wept bitterly.

Fleeing into the enclosure now called the Cockcrow, in common speech Galilee, on the road leading to Jehoshaphat beneath the gate of Mount Sion, they led Jesus—covered with insults, grievously afflicted, beaten with blows, mocked with laughter, and carrying his cross—by order of Pilate and at the urging of the Jews to Golgotha, which is the place of Calvary. They stripped him of his tunic, gave him gall and vinegar to drink, and delivered him to death by hanging him on the gibbet of his cross.

The place was called Calvary because criminals were customarily “calvaried” there—that is, condemned. While Jesus suffered on his cross at Calvary, he commended his mother to his beloved friend, saying to the Virgin Mother: “Behold, your son” (John XIX, 26), and then: “Behold, your mother” (ibid., 27).

At Calvary, while he suffered upon the cross as the victim of the world, he promised the thief hanging at his right hand, who asked him for pardon, the robe of immortality. Pierced by a lance while hanging upon the cross, he poured forth blood and water. From a drop of these, the eyes of Longinus, who had struck him, were opened.

Below the place of Calvary, to the right as one enters the church, is the place where Joseph obtained from Pilate the body of Jesus, taken down from the cross. He reverently washed it with the most precious liquids, embalmed it with spices, and placed it in a garden, in a tomb which he had newly hewn for himself from the rock.

From there he descended to the underworld to redeem humanity. From there he rose again as the true Lion of the tribe of Judah, having conquered death. There the angel of the Lord appeared to the holy women after the stone had been rolled away from the entrance of the tomb, and announced that Jesus had truly risen from the dead: “Go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you into Galilee” (Mark XVI, 7).

Beneath the place of Calvary, at the head of the church, the cross of the Lord was discovered by Helena.

Two miles from Jerusalem grew that most worthy tree upon which the true Lion hung, who by his death destroyed death and restored the life of the world. Hence the prophet says: “O death, I will be your death” (Hos. XIII, 14).

As for the prison and the center of the world, this is proclaimed by storytelling, although the dignity of both places deserves reverence. The place now called the Prison was an open field during Christ’s Passion; he remained there only as long as they were contriving to hang him upon the cross. At that place Jesus appeared a second time to Mary Magdalene when he was returning from the underworld.

On the same day, as evening was already approaching, he appeared in the guise of a hidden pilgrim to two disciples who were traveling from Enteropolis—that is, the village of Emmaus, six miles from Jerusalem—lamenting his death. They recognized him there in the breaking of the bread, but he immediately disappeared from them.

On Mount Sion, on the eighth day, Thomas touched the wounds of Jesus together with all the others. Thereupon Thomas said to him: “My Lord and my God” (John XX, 28).

In Galilee, beside the sea and upon the sea, he manifested himself three times to his disciples. On the fortieth day, on the Mount of Olives, he was taken up by a cloud and ascended into heaven with his hands raised. On the fiftieth day, on Mount Sion—which signifies for us the jubilee, that is, eternal freedom—he sent the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, who inflamed the hearts of his apostles.

On Mount Sion the Virgin Mary, mother of Jesus, departed from the world and was buried by the apostles in Jehoshaphat. From there she was exalted by her Son above the choirs of angels.

On Mount Sion King David, Solomon, and the other kings of Jerusalem lie buried.

Before the gate of Jerusalem facing west, where the city was delivered under the second Israel, blessed Stephen was stoned to death between Nicodemus, Abilon, and Gamaliel. He was later transferred to Constantinople and finally buried with blessed Laurence at Rome. Hence the inscription on his tomb:

> “Whom Sion slew for us, Byzantium sent.”

Before the gate of Jerusalem, beside the lake facing south, is that enclosure in which, by order of Almighty God, a certain lion brought nearly twelve thousand martyrs killed under Chosroes in a single night. Hence it is called the “lion’s flesh.”

[Col. 1051B] Six miles from Jerusalem, on the road leading to Ramah, is Mount Modin. From there came Mattathias, father of the Maccabees, who are buried and rest there; their tombs can still be seen.

Eight miles from Modin, on the road leading to Joppa, is Lidda, also called Diospolis, where the body of blessed Gregory is reported to have been buried.

One mile from Ramah and four miles from Bethlehem is the village of Thecua, from which came Amos, who also lies buried there.

Four miles south of Jerusalem is the village where Zechariah lived at that time. Mary, the mother of Jesus, hastening there while already carrying the Son of God in her womb, came to greet her kinswoman Elizabeth, who was already pregnant with her son John. They say that John was also born there.

[Col. 1051C] Thirteen miles north of Jerusalem is Jericho. From there Rahab the prostitute lodged the four scouts of the children of Israel, supped with them, sheltered them, and fed them. From there also came Zacchaeus, who was small in stature. Hearing that Jesus was walking through that region, he climbed a sycamore tree in order to see God and speak with him, judging himself and asking for pardon. From there also came the boys who mocked blessed Elisha as he was ascending to Jerusalem, crying: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead” (IV Reg. II, 23).

At the second milestone from Jericho, on the left, is the desert called Carentena, where Jesus completed a fast of forty days and an equal number of nights. When the devil tempted him there in his hunger, he said: “Command that these stones become loaves of bread” [Col. 1051D] (Matt. IV, 3).

Two miles from Carentena toward Galilee is a high mountain on which that same devil again tempted Jesus, showing him all the kingdoms of the world and saying: “If you will fall down and worship me, I will give you all these things” (ibid., 9).

Below Carentena is the stream of that spring which blessed Elisha, after curing its barrenness, changed from bitter into drinkable water.

Before Jericho, beside the road, a blind beggar stood. Hearing that Jesus was passing by, he cried: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me” (Luke XVIII, 38). He deserved to be enlightened by him both outwardly and inwardly.

At the third milestone from Jericho, two miles from the Jordan, is Bethagla, interpreted as “place of the circle,” because there Jacob’s sons and his people, mourning, went around his funeral procession as they brought him from Egypt to Hebron.

Engaddi is in the tribe of Judah, where David hid himself in the wilderness, which lies in the Plain of Jericho—that is, in the level region of which we spoke above. It is called the very large village of the Jews. Engaddi lies beside the Dead Sea; from there balsam used to be brought and to grow, and hence the wines are also called Engaddi wines.

Eight miles from Nazareth toward Carmel is a mountain. At its foot, beside a spring, Lamech, the father of Noah, killed Cain with his arrow and, with his bow, his guide. Filled with fury, he said: “I have killed a man to my wound, and a young man to my bruise” (Gen. IV, 23). Concerning Cain the Lord had foretold: “Whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold” (ibid., 15).

Three miles from Mount Caim is Mount Carmel, of which it is said in the Song of Songs: “Your neck is like Carmel” (Cant. VII, 5). Blessed Elijah also wished to dwell there for a long time, and blessed Elisha, his disciple, with him.

Six miles from Nazareth toward the knee [perhaps an uncertain place-name or corrupt reading] is the place where Jehu, king of Israel, struck Ahaziah, king of Judah.

Sixteen miles east of Nazareth, above the Sea of Galilee, is the village of Gergessa, where the Savior restored to health those who were tormented by demons; from there the swine also plunged into the sea.

Sixteen miles south of Mount Carmel is Caesarea, the metropolis of Palestine. Cornelius the centurion came from there; blessed Peter baptized him there and appointed him bishop. There is also the Tower of Straton. There Herod built, in anticipation of the arrival of Augustus Caesar, a harbor of white marble. The same Herod, as Josephus testifies, built the tower which rises above Jerusalem, also called the Tower of David, and named it Antonia.

[Col. 1051] Immediately after this little work, Cardinal Aragonius—or perhaps Fretellus himself, the author of the same writing—added the names of the bishops who presided over the sacred offices in Jerusalem. They end with Arnulphus, the Latin patriarch of Jerusalem, who still held that office before the thirteenth century had come to an end. I therefore append these names, as a kind of supplement, to the preceding little book.

[Col. 1051D] The names of the bishops who were in Jerusalem before it became a patriarchate follow; there were forty-three.

The Jerusalemite bishops were: James, brother of the Lord; Simon the Just; Zacharias; Tobias; Benjamin; John; Matthias; Philip; Seneca; Justus; Levi; Effren; Jesse; Judas. These fifteen were circumcised.

Cassianus; Publius; Maximus; Julianus; Gamus. This last first celebrated Lent and Easter according to Christian custom.

Symmachus; Caius; Germanus; Julianus; Capito; Maximus; Antonius; Valens; Laycianus; Narcissus the Pious; Tordius Narcissus; Alexander; Maxalemus Nihirmentus; Taldis; Hermon; Macharius. In the time of the latter the cross of the Lord was discovered by Queen Helena.

Quiriacus; Maximus; Cyril. The latter built the place of the Lord’s Sepulchre, Calvary, the Mount of Olives, the Valley of Jehoshaphat, and Bethlehem.

[Col. 1053A] The names of the patriarchs of Jerusalem after it became a patriarchate follow; there were twenty-seven.

The Jerusalemite patriarchs were: Cyril the First; John; Parachilius; Juvenal; John; Zacharias. In the time of Zacharias, Chosroes, king of the Persians, came to Jerusalem, destroyed the churches of Judaea, and killed thirty-six thousand Christians.
