Modestus, appointed patriarch by the emperor Heraclius when he returned from Persia, bringing the wood of the Lord.

Sophronius, in whose time the Saracens expelled all the Christians from Jerusalem except the patriarch.

Theodore; Ilia; Gregory; Thomas; Basil; Sergius; Leonicius; Athanasius; Christodolus; Thomas; John; Mestus. In the time of Mestus, Archisidorus, nephew of Orestes, patriarch of Jerusalem, sent his army to Jerusalem to destroy all the churches of the patriarchate. After destroying four thousand of them, he had his uncle the patriarch led to Babylon and killed him there.

Theophilus, who rebuilt this church with the support of Archisidorus.

Sophronius, in whose time the Turks, attacking Jerusalem, killed the Saracens and took possession of the city; the Christians, however, remained in it.

Guitinus; Simeon the Elder. In the time of the Franks, they came, exalting the kingdom of David, restoring the churches to God, and restoring the city.

The Latin patriarchs of Jerusalem follow.

The Latin patriarchs were: Daybertus, archbishop of the Pisans; Ibelinus, archbishop of Arles; Arnulphus, archdeacon of Jerusalem.

[Col. 1053]

# DESCRIPTION OF THE HOLY LAND BY JOHN, PRIEST OF WÜRZBURG

(Recovered from the manuscript codex of the distinguished monastery of Tegernsee in Bavaria by the most reverend and illustrious Father Roman Krinner, a Benedictine monk of that place. Published by R. P. Bernardus Pezius, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. I, part III, p. 486.)

## NOTICE

[Col. 1053] Whatever can be stated with certainty about the author of this Description of the Holy Land is contained in the first verse of the preface, in which he says that he is John, by the grace of God what he is in the Church of Würzburg. From these words we conclude that he was at least endowed with the dignity of the priesthood in the Church of Würzburg.

He nowhere clearly indicates his own age. Nevertheless, even from the manuscript codex of Tegernsee, from which, at our request, the most reverend and illustrious Roman Krinner extracted this by no means inelegant little work, it becomes highly probable that this John, around the thirteenth century—the period in which the codex itself was written—applied his mind to recording what he had seen with his own eyes.

John’s chief concern was to mark, as clearly and carefully as he could, the venerable places which our Lord, the Savior of the world, together with his glorious Mother Mary, ever-virgin, and with the venerable company of his disciples, sanctified by his bodily presence—especially in the holy city of Jerusalem—and to collect by the work of his pen the events and epigrams found there, whether in prose or verse, as he himself writes after the beginning of the Prologue.

An outstanding and highly honorable passage for our nation is chapter 9, where John proves at length that the recovery of the Holy Land is wrongly attributed to the Franks alone, to the injury of the Germans. This province of Christendom, he says, would long ago have extended its boundaries beyond the Nile toward the south and beyond Damascus toward the east, if as great a multitude of Alemannians as of the Franks had been present. When the German soldiers departed from there—as though the whole strength of the Christian army had withdrawn—the other nations accomplished little or nothing more, and so forth.

We have also encountered several such Descriptions of the Holy Land and pilgrim journeys in the libraries of Austria and Bavaria. Since we cannot publish all of them, they deserve at least to be listed here by name.

In the library of Tegernsee there is a work of John Hess, priest of the diocese of Utrecht, concerning Jerusalem. John Hess, priest of the diocese of Utrecht, was in Jerusalem, etc. Paper codex in quarto.

In the same place there is a book by a certain Philip concerning pilgrimages to Jerusalem and throughout the Holy Land, which the author says he himself traversed, in a paper folio manuscript written by a fifteenth-century hand. It begins: “These are the pilgrimages to Jerusalem,” etc.

In the library of Heiligenkreuz is preserved an anonymous Itinerary of the Holy Land, beginning: “I went from Acre,” etc. The parchment codex is five hundred years old.

The monastery of Mariazell in Austria possesses a paper folio codex three hundred years old, containing an anonymous description of the Holy Land, beginning: “When we read in ancient histories, as blessed Jerome says,” etc. At the end: “Here ends the book of the Description of the Holy Land, whose author is unknown.”

The same work is held by the library of Melk in a parchment quarto codex, marked with the letter d. 12, approximately four hundred years old.

Nor should we pass over the Description of the Places of the Holy Land by Brother Nicholas of Farnad, of the Order of Friars Minor, from Hungary, of whom Lucas Wadding makes no mention even in his work *On the Writers of the Order of Friars Minor*. We have seen a copy printed before the year 1500, in quarto, at Vienna, in the Dorothean library. It begins with the preface: “Since every created thing,” etc. The work begins: “Jerusalem, the holy city,” etc.

In the same library we examined the *Treatise on the Holy Land* by Ludolf, parish rector of Saint Mary in Suche, in a fourteenth-century paper codex. It begins: “To the most reverend Father in Christ and his lord, the gracious lord Balderom of Scenordia, bishop of the Church of Paderborn,” etc. Simler says that it was written in the year 1336, but he does not mention any edition made by anyone.

There we also found the *Jerusalem Itinerary* of John of Mandeville, which begins: “Since the land of Jerusalem,” etc. Simler likewise mentions it, but does not indicate whether or where it was printed.

We are more certain about the editions of Bernard of Breydenbach, Friar Gabriel of Pech Waradino, a Hungarian by nation and of the Order of Saint Francis, and Haython of the Order of Prémontré.

For, in the frequently mentioned Dorothean library, we saw the first work, *Pilgrimages Overseas to the Holy Land*, printed by Peter Drach at Speyer in folio in 1502; the second, a *Compendium of the Places of the Holy Land*, published at an uncertain place and date, though before 1500, in quarto; and the third, the *Book of Histories of the Regions of the East*, or *Passage to the Holy Land*, written in 1300 and printed at Haguenau by Johann Sec in 1529, in quarto.

In the library of Klosterneuburg there is a paper quarto codex containing the *Itinerary of the Holy Land and Other Pilgrim Regions* by a certain Brother Ulrich, who is said to have dictated it in Latin at Padua to Brother William of Balonea. In the cited codex, however, there is only a German version, which the lay brother Chuenrat Der Techel of Tegernsee prepared at Vienna in 1359. It begins: “When I set out from home, determined that I wished to travel across the sea,” etc. That Brother Ulrich lived in the year 1330.

The work of Burchard of Mount Sion is also outstanding; he called it the *Description of the Holy Land*. It is found in a paper folio codex, marked H. 17, in the library of Melk, with this beginning: “To the most beloved Father in Christ, the lector of the brothers of the Order of Preachers, Brother Burchard of Mount Sion sends, with all devotion, prayers in the Lord Jesus Christ. What shall I write to you, dearest Father?” etc. The hand of our codex is from the fifteenth century.

Concerning the *Journals of the Pilgrimage to the Holy Land* by George, prior of the Carthusian monastery of Gaming, see what we stated in the third part of the second volume of our *Thesaurus*, where we published the work.

Finally, we note that the *Description of the Holy Land* by Anselm, a brother of the Order of Friars Minor, edited by Henricus Canisius in volume IV of his *Antiquae Lectiones*, beginning on page 1289, was committed to print nearly one hundred years earlier than the learned man supposed, together with certain geographical works of Aeneas Sylvius. A copy of that quarto edition, prepared at Kraków by Florian Ungler in the year of the Lord 1512, is in the library of Melk.

It will be enough to have noted these matters briefly.

# DESCRIPTION OF THE HOLY LAND

[Col. 1055]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1055A]

John, by the grace of God what he is in the Church of Würzburg, sends greetings to his beloved companion and household friend Dietrich, together with contemplation of the Jerusalem above, whose fellowship is one and the same.

The disposition of your character, known to me as being in every respect harmonious with all good men, and that devotion of yours so diligent in the worship and service of God, have, in addition to the bond of our household companionship, so bound the affection of my spirit to your will—which I always presume will be equitable and kind in the mutual exchange of our obligations—that none of your wishes, in the fulfillment of which the labor of my diligence is required, should be allowed to fail of their desired end, insofar as my strength permits.

For this reason also, while remaining on pilgrimage in Jerusalem for the love of our Lord Jesus Christ, I have not forgotten you in your absence. For the sake of your affection I have labored, as clearly and carefully as I could, to mark and gather through the work of my pen the venerable places which our Lord, the Savior of the world, together with his glorious Mother Mary, ever-virgin, and with the venerable company of his disciples, sanctified by his bodily presence—especially in the holy city of Jerusalem—along with the events and epigrams found there, whether in prose or in verse.

I believe that this description will be pleasing to you, because everything marked in it will at some time, by divine inspiration and protection, present itself spontaneously to your eyes as familiar when you come here, without the delay and difficulty of searching. Or, if you should not come there and therefore cannot see these things with bodily sight, nevertheless, through such knowledge and contemplation you will have a greater devotion toward their sanctification.

[Col. 1055C] I know, indeed, that long before modern times these same places, not only in the city mentioned above but also far beyond it, had been committed to writing by a certain reverend man. But because afterward, over so long a period, that city was often captured and destroyed by enemies, and the same most holy places within the walls or nearby outside them—those, namely, which alone we intend to describe—were overthrown and perhaps later wholly transformed, our devotion, following their arrangement as we observed and recorded it with our own eyes, should not therefore be judged excessive or superfluous.

As for those places which lie far outside in the neighboring province, we have not proposed to speak of them, since we know that others have already spoken sufficiently about them. Nevertheless, because the beginning of our redemption was celebrated in the city of Nazareth through the angelic announcement of the Lord’s Incarnation, we wish to begin this description from that city, which is about sixty miles from Jerusalem, and to touch briefly and summarily upon the places lying between it and the holy city, although we know that others have already treated these matters more fully and at greater length.

## CHAPTER ONE

Nazareth, Acco, Cana of Galilee, the Lord’s Leap, Mount Tabor and Hermon, Naim, Mount Endor, the torrent of Kishon, Jezreel, the plain of Megiddo, Mounts Gilboa, Scythopolis, Genunium, Dothaim, Samaria, Sichem, Sychar, Luza, Mounts Garizim and Gebal, Diospolis, and Jerusalem are briefly described.

This same city, lying ten miles from Tiberias, is the head of Galilee and is properly called the city of the Savior, because he was conceived and brought up there; hence he is also called the Nazarene. Nazareth is interpreted as “flower” or “shoot.” Nor is this without reason, since in it the flower arose through whose grace the world has been filled. That flower was the Virgin Mary, from whom the archangel Gabriel announced in the same Nazareth that the Son of the Most High would be born, saying: “Hail, Mary,” etc. And she replied: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord,” etc. Concerning Nazareth, formerly also the city of David’s birth, the following was commonly said at that time: “Can anything good come from Nazareth?”—as though great and holy souls were born only in great cities.

Two miles from Nazareth, on the road leading to Acco, lies the city of Sephoris. Anna, the mother of Mary, the Mother of our Lord, came from Sephoris. It is also said that the blessed Virgin Mary was born at Sephoris. But according to Jerome, as he says in the prologue to the sermon he composed for Heliodorus, *On the Nativity of Holy Mary*, she is said to have been born in the city of Nazareth itself—and indeed in the very chamber where she later conceived, through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, in response to the angelic salutation. This is still shown there in a distinct place, as I myself saw and recorded while present.

Four miles from Nazareth, and two from Sephoris, lies Cana of Galilee to the east. From there came Philip and Nathanael; there, while the boy Jesus reclined at a wedding with his mother, he changed water into wine. At Nazareth there flows a small but remarkable spring from which Jesus, in his childhood, was accustomed to draw water and bring it to his mother.

One mile from Nazareth, toward the south, is the place called the Precipice, from which the Jews wanted to throw Jesus, but he disappeared from them in an instant. Hence the place is still commonly called the Lord’s Leap.

[Col. 1057C]

Four miles from Nazareth, toward the east, is Mount Tabor, on which Christ was transfigured before his apostles Peter, John, and James, in the presence of Moses and Elijah. This feast is solemnly celebrated at Jerusalem, where the voice of the Father was heard: “This is my Son,” etc. The Savior then commanded Peter, John, and James not to reveal to anyone what they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. There also Peter said: “Lord, it is good for us to be here.”

Two miles east of Tabor is Mount Hermon. On the descent of Mount Tabor, the priest and king of Salem, Melchizedek, met Abraham returning from the slaughter of Amalek. He was descended from Noah and presented Abraham with bread and wine, by which the altar of Christ under grace was prefigured.

Likewise, two miles from Tabor, by another road, lies the city of Naim. At the gate of this city Jesus restored a widow’s son to life; the inhabitants say that he was Bartholomew, who later became an apostle. Above Naim is Mount Endor. At its foot, beside the torrent Cadumin, also called the torrent Kishon, Baruch son of Amon, following the counsel of Deborah the prophetess, defeated the Idumeans and killed Sisera. Pursuing Zeb, Zebee, and Salmana beyond the Jordan, he slew them with the sword. Baruch, however, did this at Endor and beneath Endor after destroying the army; hence the psalm says: “Tabor and Hermon shall rejoice in your name,” etc.

Five miles from Naim is the city of Jezreel, also called Zaraim, but now commonly called Lesser Hen. From it came Jezebel, the most impious queen, who seized Naboth’s vineyard and, because of her arrogance, was thrown down from the top of her palace and died. Her pyramid was still recently visible. Near Jezreel lies the plain of Megiddo, where King Uzziah was defeated and killed by the king of Samaria; he was afterward transferred and buried in Zion.

One mile from Jezreel are the mountains of Gilboa, where Saul and his son Jonathan fell after being defeated in battle. Hence David said: “Mountains of Gilboa, let there be neither dew nor rain,” etc.

Two miles from Gilboa, toward the east, lies Scythopolis, the metropolitan city of Galilee, also called Beth-shean, that is, “house of the sun.” Above the walls of this city they hung Saul’s head. Five miles from Jezreel is the town of Genunium, now commonly called Crassa, or Greater Hen. Between it and Sebaste a plain is shown called Dothaim, where, near the road, the old cistern into which Joseph was cast by his brothers is still visible. Samaria begins at the aforementioned town of Genunium.

Ten miles from Genunium [or Genuinum] lies Samaria, also called Sebaste and Augusta, the city named after Augustus. There was buried the Lord’s forerunner, John the Baptist, who had been beheaded by Herod beyond the Jordan near the Asphaltite Lake, in the fortress of Masconta, and was then transferred by his disciples to Sebaste and buried there between Elisha and Obadiah. It is said that afterward, under Julian the Apostate, the sacred body was seized and burned, its ashes scattered to the winds—except for the head, which had previously been transferred first to Alexandria and afterward to Constantinople, and finally to Gaul, to the region of Poitiers—and except for the index finger of the right hand, with which he pointed to Christ coming to baptism, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God,” etc. The blessed virgin Thecla carried this very finger with her across the Alps before Julian the Apostate’s savage flames consumed the sacred body; it is preserved there with the greatest veneration in the church of Moriac. Samaria, moreover, is the name both of the city and of the country.

Four miles from Samaria is Sebaste, Neapo[lacuna], also called Sichem. It was named after Sichem, father of Hamor, and lies between Dan and Bethel. The land itself is called Sichem after Sichem, that is, the father of Hamor, who seized Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, while she was walking about in those regions. Joseph’s bones were brought back to Sichem from Egypt. Moreover, at Sichem, beside the spring, Jeroboam fashioned two calves, which he caused the ten tribes he had brought away and led astray from Jerusalem to worship in imitation of Aaron. He placed one of them at Dan and the other at Bethel. The sons of Jacob destroyed that city of Sichem and killed Hamor as well, grieving over the violation of their sister Dinah. In these days Sichem is called Neapolis, that is, “New City.”

Sychar lies before Sichem, beside the estate that Jacob gave to his son. There is Jacob’s spring, also called the well, above which the Gospel says that Jesus, wearied from his journey, sat and spoke with the Samaritan woman; a church now stands there. Near Sichem is the terebinth beneath which Jacob hid the idols at Bethel.

One mile from Sichem lies the city of Luza, where Abraham lived for a long period. There Jacob, while sleeping, saw a ladder whose top touched heaven, with angels ascending and descending upon it. Immediately upon waking he said: “Truly this place is holy, and it is the gate of heaven.” He raised up a stone as a monument, poured oil over it, and called the name of that place Bethel, although it had previously been called Luza. Bethel is a neighboring mountain of Garizim, facing Mount Gebal to the east, near Dan above Sichem. It is said that Abraham wanted to sacrifice his son on this mountain of Bethel.

Twenty miles from Sichem, four from Jerusalem, lies the road leading to Diospolis, where Mount Shiloh and the city also called Ramah are found. There the ark of the covenant and the tabernacle of the Lord remained from the arrival of the children of Israel until the time of Samuel the prophet and David the king.

Twenty-four miles from Sichem, sixteen from Diospolis, sixteen from Hebron, ten from Jericho, four from Bethlehem, sixteen from Beersheba, twenty-four from Ascalon, likewise twenty-four from Joppa, sixteen from Ramah, etc., lies Jerusalem, the most holy metropolis of Judea. It is also called Zion, concerning which it was said: “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God.” It is also called Aelia, after Aelius Hadrian, who built it—or rather transformed it into the form of a city.

## CHAPTER II. Bethlehem; the Church of Saint Chariton the Martyr; Solomon’s Temple and its restorations at different times

[Col. 1059C]

Bethlehem is interpreted as “house of bread.” Bethlehem, the city of Judea, also called Ephrata, is so named not without reason, because in it, from the flower of Nazareth, there came forth from the Virgin Mary the fruit of life, namely the Son of the living God, Christ Jesus, who is the bread of angels and the life of the whole world. In Bethlehem, near the place of the Nativity, is the manger in which the infant Jesus himself lay hidden. Hence the prophet says: “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger.” The hay from this manger, in which the child Jesus had lain hidden, was brought to Rome by Queen Helena and honorably placed in the Church of Saint Mary Major.

At the place of the Lord’s Nativity, two verses are inscribed in gilded mosaic work:

> Light and keen brilliance of angelic power,  
> Here truly was God born of a Virgin Mother.

One mile from Bethlehem, when the Lord was born, the star shone for the shepherds, and an angel appeared to them, saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.” In Bethlehem, guided by a new star, three kings came from the East to worship the newborn Jesus. Adoring the King of angels, they presented him with mystical gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. In Bethlehem and its surrounding territory Herod ordered the innocents to be killed. Most of them lie buried and at rest four miles south of Bethlehem, two miles from Thecoa.

Four miles from Bethlehem, toward the south, is the church of blessed Chariton. When he crossed from this world and died, his monks, over whom he had presided as a pious shepherd, likewise struggled alongside him, having foreknown from God that they would share the grace of death. Their father had been pious, and they did not wish to live after him, burning with love for him. The bodies of each of them can be seen in the aforementioned church, transferred afterward to Jerusalem in the very condition in which they had been when, during their father’s desolation, they struggled in agony.

In Bethlehem, beneath the basilica and not far from the Lord’s manger, the body of blessed Jerome rests in a certain cave. Paula and Eustochium, to whom Jerome himself wrote, likewise lie buried and at rest in Bethlehem. One mile from Bethlehem, on the road leading to Jerusalem, is a crypt, the place where Rachel died after giving birth to her son Benjamin. There she lies buried by her husband Jacob. At her tomb Jacob placed twelve sizeable stones, as a testimony to his twelve sons. Her pyramid can still be seen by passersby.

Jerusalem, the glorious metropolis of Judea, is said by the philosophers to lie at the center of the world. David reigned in this city for thirty-four and a half years. In Jerusalem is Mount Moriah, on which David saw an angel with a drawn sword, grievously striking the people of God. Fearing that the angel might avenge upon him and the city the offense he had committed in numbering the people, David fell prostrate upon the ground, truly repentant and severely afflicting himself; he was heard by the Lord and obtained pardon. The Lord says of David: “I have found a man after my heart.”

Moreover, on Mount Moriah, while David was reigning, there was the threshing floor, or place, of Araunah the Jebusite. David himself wanted to buy that threshing floor in order to build the house of the Lord there, because in that place he had received mercy from the Lord, when the angel of the Lord, sparing him, had halted there. David did buy the place, but the Lord had forbidden him to undertake the work, because he was a man of blood. Therefore he handed over to his son Solomon the expenses he had prepared for this purpose, since the Lord granted Solomon permission to build the house for him.

Accordingly, King Solomon built a temple to the Lord on the aforementioned threshing floor—that is, Bethel—and an altar. He dedicated it at incomparable expense, asking the Lord that whoever, from whatever place, prayed to God in that temple might be worthy to be heard. The Lord granted him this request.

Later, because of the lack of self-restraint of the prince and the people, and as God’s punishment, King Nebuchadnezzar, through Nabuzardan, commander of his army, stripped the temple during the reign of King Zedekiah. He carried away from the city the king himself as a captive, together with everything beautiful and precious in the temple and the city, and ordered the people to be brought before him in Babylon. A little later Pharaoh Necho destroyed the temple and the city.

But now, lest it seem absurd to the narrator and wearisome to the listener to enumerate under which rulers, and by whom, the destructions and restorations of the first, second, and third temples took place, I shall try, beloved, to explain to you as truthfully as I can the present Bethel.

Concerning Bethel, it is truly unknown under which ruler, and by which ruler, it was restored; I have been unable to arrive at certain knowledge of the matter. Some claim that it was rebuilt under the emperor Constantine by his mother Helena, out of reverence for the holy cross that she had recovered. Others say it was rebuilt by the emperor Heraclius out of reverence for the wood of the Lord, which he had brought back in triumph from Persia; others by Augustus Justinian; others by a certain emperor of Memphis in Egypt, out of reverence for Allachiber—that is, the Most High Lord God.

The present temple, I say, is the one of which it is proclaimed that the child Jesus was circumcised there on the eighth day of his birth. His foreskin was presented from heaven in Jerusalem, in the temple, by the angel to King Charlemagne, and was carried by him to Aachen in Gaul. It was later transferred by Charles the Bald to Aquitaine, to the region of Poitiers, at Carusium, in the church that King Charles built in honor of our Savior and enriched with royal endowments of the greatest extent under monastic observance. From that time until now it has been solemnly preserved and venerated there.

## CHAPTER III. The events performed in the Jerusalem temple by the Savior of the world and his apostles, etc., with the places in which each occurred explained

[Col. 1061C]

First, as we said, the sacrament was celebrated in the city of Nazareth through the Lord’s Incarnation. The second was accomplished through his Nativity in Bethlehem of Judea. The third, called the Lord’s Hypapante—that is, the Presentation of Christ—was manifested in the temple of Jerusalem on the fortieth day after his Nativity.

Nevertheless, these three are included among the seals, which are said to number seven, by which that book in the Apocalypse was sealed and which no one could open except the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world. Hence the words: “You are worthy, Lord, to receive,” etc.

Some reckon these seven apocalyptic seals in the following way:

1. The Lord’s Nativity, or Incarnation;  
2. Baptism;  
3. Passion;  
4. Descent into hell;  
5. Resurrection;  
6. Ascension;  
7. The manifestation of the future judgment.

Of these seven, six have already been loosed or fulfilled by our Lord Jesus Christ in the regions of Jerusalem; the seventh is to be completed by that same Lord of ours. Neither a definite hour nor a definite place has been assigned to its completion, although the prophet Joel spoke in the person of the Lord: “I will gather all nations in the valley of Jehoshaphat, and I will contend with them.” But these matters belong elsewhere.

Now let us return to the Presentation of the Lord, adding this concerning his circumcision, which took place in the Lord’s temple on the eighth day. Although the cutting away of the flesh in it signifies the removal of vices from the minds of others, nevertheless, because it belongs to the Old Testament and receives its fulfillment in it, it ought now to cease, so that circumcision is not counted among the sacraments of the New Testament. For this reason it does not belong to any of the seven aforementioned seals.

As we have already said, our Lord Jesus Christ was presented in the temple by his mother and received into the arms of blessed Simeon, who, moved by the prophetic Spirit, said: “Now dismiss your servant, Lord,” etc. In the temple, when our Lord Jesus Christ had grown older and was staying in Jerusalem, at twelve years of age he disputed with the Jews. Although they hated him, he nevertheless often taught them. In the temple he praised the offering of the poor woman who had placed it in the treasury, etc.

Above the pinnacle of the temple—understood to be above the side of the circuit, with windows beneath it resembling pinnacles or battlements—the devil set Jesus and, tempting him a third time because of his baptism and fasting, said: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down,” etc.

In this same temple, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December, the blessed Virgin Mary, already a little girl of three years, is said to have been offered to God, as these verses inscribed there teach:

> Accompanied by seven maidens, the Virgin,  
> Three years old, was offered here to serve God.

There, without doubt, she often received divine and angelic consolation, as this further verse indicates:

> The Virgin is nourished by angelic ministry.

Our Lord Jesus Christ drove the sellers and buyers from the temple. As evidence of this event, a stone is still shown on the right side of the temple, with great veneration and lamps, as though it had been trodden and sanctified by the Lord’s foot. It is elegantly adorned. There Christ alone, by divine power, withstood so many people, driving them out by force.

This stone is joined to another stone upon which, as upon an altar, our Lord is depicted as having been offered. This is shown by the painting and inscription, which reads:

> Here was offered the King of kings, born of a Virgin;  
> Therefore this place is rightly called holy.

A little farther on, the following verses are also read there:

> Here Jacob saw a ladder, built an altar,  
> Hence this place is adorned and rightly called holy.

That Jacob is depicted on this very stone as having laid down his head when, while sleeping, he saw the ladder reaching to heaven, by which angels ascended and descended, is not true, saving the temple’s reverence. Another verse has been added there:

> Let this land be yours, Jacob, with your future offspring.

But, as we said above, the event occurred in a quite different place, namely on the road toward Greater Machumeria and Mesopotamia.

In the temple our Lord delivered the adulterous woman from her accusers, saying: “Let the one who is without sin,” etc. Then, when the accusers had fallen silent and departed, he said to the woman: “Woman, go in peace, and do not sin any more.” The place is represented in a small crypt of the same temple. Its entrance is on the left side of the temple, and it is called the Confession.

It is said that Zacharias entered this same place when he was informed by the angel of John’s conception. The whole event is indicated by the painting and inscriptions, which read as follows. The angel to Zacharias: “Do not fear, Zacharias; your prayer has been heard,” etc.

On the lintel is seen an image of Christ with this inscription:

> I absolve the nations that confess their sins from the heart.

In the temple, at the altar that stood outside beneath the slope, more than twenty paces distant from the temple, Zacharias son of Barachiah died a martyr’s death. Above it, in the Old Testament, the Jews were accustomed to sacrifice turtledoves and pigeons. Later the Saracens changed that altar into a clock, which can still be seen and noted. Many Saracens even today come to it to pray, since it is arranged toward the south, the direction in which they are accustomed to pray.

The same temple of the Lord, whoever may ultimately have built it, has an elegant form, with marvelous marble paneling inside and out. It is round—or rather octagonal in a circular arrangement, having eight angles around its circuit. Its exterior wall is adorned with excellent mosaic work up to its middle; the remaining part is made of marble stones. The lower wall is continuous except where it is interrupted by four doors. On the east it has one door, beside which is a chapel consecrated in honor of Saint James. From that side of the temple he was thrown down and killed with a fuller’s club; he was the first high priest under the grace of the new law in Jerusalem. Hence the following verses have been placed on the side wall of the same chapel:

> James of Alphaeus, like the Lord in appearance,  
> Dies for Christ, cast down from this temple.  
> Thus the wicked crowd punished James the Just,  
> Who publicly preached Christ, and felled him with a fuller’s club.

These verses are inscribed inside and outside, running around the chapel in a circuit, together with the following:

> James of Alphaeus, brother of the Lord of Nazareth,  
> A fisherman, truly an Israelite in life;  
> Driven from the temple’s pinnacle by wicked deceit,  
> He joyfully went to Christ, killed by a staff.

On the north there is one entrance toward the cloister of the Lords. Several Saracen letters have been placed on its lintel. Beside the same door is the place of that life-giving water of which the prophet says: “I saw water flowing out from the side,” etc.

At the entrance to the temple, toward the west, above the vestibule, there is an image of Christ, around which this epigram is inscribed:

> This house shall be called my house, a house of prayer.

It also has a door on the south, toward Solomon’s building. On the west it has a door toward the Lord’s tomb, where there is also the Beautiful Gate. Passing through it with John, Peter said to the poor man who was lame and begging alms from them: “Silver and gold I do not have,” etc.

Each of these two doors—the northern and the western—has six doorways, now joined as folding leaves. The one toward the south has four, while the one toward the east has only two. This concerns the lower wall.

In the upper part of the same wall, where the excellent mosaic work has been applied, windows are inserted so that each of the eight sides has five windows, except where the temple doors are located, where there are only four. The total number of windows is thirty-two.

Between this exterior wall, running around the building, and the great interior marble columns, which number twelve and support the inner, narrower, wider, and completely circular wall—which has twelve windows and rests upon four square bases—between this wall, I say, and the exterior wall, there are sixteen columns and eight bases with square marble stones. With a space of eight paces on either side, they support the middle roof between the inner and outer walls, as well as the inner, narrower wall, with its most beautiful coffered ceilings. Above them, beside the roof, they provide a walkway running all around and have lead gutters that discharge rainwater.

Above this narrower wall rises a high, rounded dome, painted inside and covered with lead outside. At its highest point the Christians have placed the sign of the holy cross. This sign is greatly offensive to the Saracens, and many would like to have it removed at the cost of much of their gold. For although they do not hold the faith of Christ’s Passion, they nevertheless venerate this temple and do it no harm. Indeed, although they are permitted to worship their Creator in this very temple, they must still be regarded as idolaters, according to Augustine, who expressly asserts that whatever is done apart from the faith of Christ is idolatry.

Around the temple, apparently beneath the roof on the outside, the following inscription is set out as one ascends toward the west:

> May eternal peace from the eternal Father be upon this house.  
> Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his holy place.

Toward the south:

> Well founded is the house of the Lord upon a firm rock.  
> Blessed are those who dwell in your house;  
> For ever and ever they shall praise you.

Toward the east:

> Truly the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it.  
> In your house, Lord, all shall speak of glory.

Toward the north:

> The temple of the Lord is holy;  
> It is the worship of God;  
> It is the building of God.

Inside the temple, on the upper line running around it, the responsory “Hear, Lord, the hymn,” etc., is written in large letters, together with its verse: “Look upon us, Lord,” etc.

Then, in the lower circuit, certain verses from that hymn, “Blessed city Jerusalem,” etc., are inscribed in golden letters.

The same temple, so elegantly arranged and adorned, has all around it a broad and level courtyard, paved and spread with joined stones and square in its circuit. It is approached from three sides by many steps. The courtyard is raised quite skillfully above the level of the ground, and on its eastern side has a broad entrance through five arches joined by four large columns. This wall opens toward the Golden Gate, through which the Lord solemnly entered on the fifth day before his Passion, sitting on an ass and welcomed by the Hebrew children with palm branches, praising him and saying: “Hosanna to the Son of David,” etc.

By divine providence, although Jerusalem was afterward often captured and destroyed by enemies, this gate always remained intact. Out of reverence for the Lord’s divine and mystical entry, as he went from Bethany through the Mount of Olives to Jerusalem, it is closed on the inside and blocked on the outside with stones. It is never open except on Palm Sunday, when each year, in memory of the event, it is solemnly opened for the procession and for the whole body of pilgrims and citizens.

After the patriarch has preached to the people at the foot of the Mount of Olives and the service of that day has ended, it is closed again for the entire year as before, except on the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, when it is opened once more. Around this same gate, below the walls, there is a famous burial place for the dead.

The courtyard of this gate has an open approach on the south through three great arches or vaults joined by two marble columns. On the same side it has another approach, wider than the first. On the west, toward the city, the beautiful courtyard has an open approach through four arches joined by three marble columns. On the north, the courtyard is narrowed in part because of the adjoining cloister of the Lords. In the remainder of that side it has a quite beautiful width and approach. A beautiful and sufficiently spacious level stretches outside the courtyard on the south and west, and somewhat toward the north as well.

Let this description of the aforementioned temple and its adjoining place suffice; we shall see the more important matters in the course of the rest of this account.

## CHAPTER IV. The River Jordan; the desert of Quarentena; Bethagla; Engaddi; the mountains of Charan and Carmel; Gerlicus; Gergessa; Caesarea of Palestine; Hebron; the Valley of Tears; the field of Gebal; the oak of Mamre; Segor; the cave of Karnaim; Mount Sinai; the mountains of Horeb and Abarim; Idumea; Tyre; Sarepta

[Col. 1065D]

When our Lord was twenty-nine years and thirteen days old, as Luke says, and was beginning what was almost his thirtieth year, he wished to bring circumcision to an end and renew the old man through sanctified water. He came into the desert to John his forerunner and was baptized by him in the Jordan, at the place three miles from Jericho. There the voice of his Father thundered over him, saying: “This is my beloved Son,” etc.

The Jordan is a river formed from two springs, namely Jor and Dan, which rise at the foot of Lebanon. After flowing separately for a long distance, they join beneath the mountains of Gilboa. At the same time the Holy Spirit came upon Christ when he was baptized, showing that Christ, not John, possessed the power to sanctify the waters.

Nearby, namely two miles from Jericho on the left, is the desert called Quarentena. On a certain rock in this desert, after receiving baptism, Christ completed a fast of forty days and forty nights. When he was hungry there, the devil tempted him, saying: “Command that these stones become loaves of bread,” etc.

Two miles from Quarentena, toward Galilee, is that high mountain on which the evil spirit again tempted Christ, showing him all the kingdoms of the world and saying: “All these I will give you,” etc.

Beneath Quarentena is the stream of that spring which blessed Elisha, after healing its barrenness, made drinkable from bitter water.

Before Jericho, beside the road, a blind man was begging. When he heard that Christ was passing by, he cried out: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me,” etc. He was deemed worthy to be enlightened by him both inwardly and outwardly.

Three miles from Jericho, two miles from the Jordan, is Bethagla, interpreted as “place of the circuit,” because there, in the manner of mourners, Jacob’s sons and their people went around his funeral procession while bringing their father from Egypt to Hebron.

Engaddi lies in the tribe of Judah, where David hid himself in the wilderness, which is in the Aulon of Jericho—that is, in the level region mentioned above. The Jewish village called Great Engaddi lies beside the Dead Sea. From there balsam used to grow and be brought forth; hence the vineyards were also called the vineyards of Engaddi.

Eight miles from Nazareth, toward Carmel, is Mount Karan. At its foot, beside a spring, Lamech, the father of Noah, killed Cain with his arrow and his guide with his bow. Filled with fury and anger, he said: “I have killed a man for my wound, and a young man for my bruise,” etc. Concerning Cain the Lord had foretold: “Whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold.”

Seven miles from Mount Karan is Mount Carmel, concerning which the Song of Songs says: “Your neck is like Carmel.” Elijah lived on this mountain for a long time, together with his disciple Elisha.

Six miles from Nazareth, toward Genunium, lies Gerlicus, where Jehu, king of Israel, struck Uzziah, king of Judea.

Sixteen miles from Nazareth, toward the east, on the Sea of Galilee, is Gergessa, the village where the Savior restored to health those who were tormented by demons, from which place he drove the swine into the sea’s precipice.

Sixteen miles from Mount Carmel, toward the south, lies Caesarea of Palestine. From there came Cornelius the centurion, whom blessed Peter baptized there and appointed bishop.

In this city of Caesarea stood Strato’s Tower. Herod, in anticipation of Augustus—whose arrival he feared for himself and for the tyranny of his kingdom—built a harbor and tower of white marble. This tower greatly surpasses the Jerusalem tower otherwise called the Tower of David. Josephus bears witness to this, saying: “He built a tower and called it Antonia.”

On the other side of Jerusalem, somewhat toward the south, lies the city of Hebron. It was once the metropolis of the Philistines and the dwelling place of giants, one day’s journey from the holy city. It belonged to the tribe of Judah and later became a priestly city and a city of refuge. It was situated in that field where God, the creator of all things, fashioned our father Adam and breathed into him the breath of life.

Hebron is called Kiriath-arba, which in the Saracen language means “fourth city”: *Kiriath* means city and *Arba* means fourth, because four revered fathers were buried there in the double cave—namely Adam, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—and their four wives: Eve, our mother, Sarah, Rebecca, and Leah.

Hebron lies beside the Valley of Tears. The Valley of Tears received this name because Adam mourned his son Abel there for one hundred years. Later, warned by an angel, he knew his wife there, and from her afterward begot his son Seth, from whose descendants and tribe Christ was born.

Two miles from Hebron is the burial place of Lot, Abraham’s nephew.

At Hebron there is a certain field called Gebal, whose soil is red. The inhabitants dig it up, eat it, and transport it for sale throughout Egypt, since it is sold as a highly prized substance for the healing of many. As deeply and widely as the aforementioned field is excavated, so extensively, by God’s providence, is it found restored after a year has passed.

Near Hebron is Mount Mamre. At its foot stands the terebinth called *dirps*, that is, a holm oak or oak, beside which Abraham remained for a long time. Beneath it he saw three angels, worshiped one of them, and received and cared for them with all the hospitality he could offer. From this place the first path of belief was opened.

The aforementioned holm oak continued to spread from that time until the reign of the emperor Theodosius, as Jerome testifies. It is said to be the same tree that is presently seen there by those who are present and held dear by them. Although it is now dry, it is nevertheless proved to possess healing power; especially in this respect: if someone carries away a piece of it while riding, his animal does not easily lose its way.

At Hebron Joshua, Caleb, and their ten companions first arrived in order to explore the promised land. David reigned in Hebron for seven and a half years.

Finally, ten miles east of Hebron is the Asphaltite Lake, also called the Dead Sea. It is truly dead because it receives nothing dead. It is also sometimes called the Sea of the Devil, since, at his instigation, the celebrated cities of Sodom, Gomorrah, Sephon, and Adama, persisting in their depravity, were most miserably overturned into that lake by burning sulfur.

Above the lake, in the region bordering Judea, is Segor, also called Bala or Zara. It is the fifth of those cities, preserved from destruction through Lot’s prayers, and is still shown today. It is now called by the glorious name Palmaria.

As Lot’s wife was leaving Segor—since nothing joyful exists without a mixture of sorrow—she was changed into the likeness of salt; traces of that prodigy are still visible. Along the shore of the aforementioned sea the inhabitants find and gather much alum. Bitumen is also extracted from the sea; it is called Judaic bitumen and is necessary for many purposes.

Segor, as we have said, is now called by the local people the town of Palma or Palmaria.

Above the Asphaltite Lake, on the descent toward Arabia, is Karnaim, a cave in the mountain of the Moabites, to which Balach, son of Beor, brought Balaam to curse the people of Israel. This mountain is called “cut off” because of its exceedingly steep precipice. [Col. 1068B] Moreover, the Asphaltite Lake separates Judaea from Arabia. In the time of the children of Israel, Arabia was a solitude, or that desert—an impassable and waterless land—in which the Lord detained his people for forty years, raining down manna upon them for food and bringing water forth from the hardest rock.

In this Arabia is Mount Sinai, where Moses remained for forty days and as many nights without any food. In that place the Lord afterward gave Moses the law, written with his own finger on stone tablets. In the valley of Arabia Moses struck the rock twice; when struck, it gave back two streams of water to the people of God, by which that entire land, formerly without water, is still irrigated today.

[Col. 1068C] In Arabia a pillar of fire preceded the children of Israel by night, while a cloud surrounded them each day. In Arabia is Elim, where the children of Israel encamped—that place in the desert where, when the said children of Israel came out of the Red Sea, they found twelve springs and seventy palms. In Arabia are the forty stations of the children of Israel. In Arabia is Mount Horeb, where Aaron lies buried and rests. In Arabia is Mount Abarim, where the Lord buried Moses through the angels, although no trace of his burial mound appears anywhere. In Arabia is that royal mountain which Lord Baldwin the First [Note: [Col. 1067] That is, the first of this name among the kings of Jerusalem, the second among the kings.]—king of the Franks in Jerusalem—subdued for the Christians and made secure for the defense of the kingdom of David.

[Col. 1068D] Arabia, moreover, joins Idumaea at the borders of Bostra. Idumaea, however, lies under Syria, and Damascus is the head of Syria. Lebanon divides Idumaea from Phoenicia. In Phoenicia is Sor, or, as the Syrians say, Tyre, the most noble metropolitan city of the Phoenicians, which refused to receive Christ as he walked along the seashore. Yet, as the divine page testifies, it gave very many martyrs to God, whose number God alone has recorded. Moreover, Tyre conceals the buried Origen [Origenem?]. Before Tyre there is a fairly large marble stone on which Jesus sat. From the time of Christ until the expulsion of the Gentiles from the city it remained unharmed, but afterward it was broken by the Franks and Venetians. [Col. 1069A] Above the remaining part of that stone a church was built in honor of the Savior.

At the eighth mile from Tyre, toward the east and above the sea, is Sarphen, otherwise called Sarepta of Sidon; the prophet of the Lord Elijah once lived there. Here he raised the widow’s son, namely Joanas, because the widow had kindly sheltered and fed the prophet of the Lord.

## CHAPTER V. Sidon, Berytus, Damascus, Arphat, Huss, Suita, Thema, Naamon, Mount Seir and the mountains of Lebanon, the rivers Farfar and Abbana, the town of Paneas, the spring of Dan, Medan, Jor, Bethsaida, Chorazin, Kedar.

At the sixth mile from Sarphen lies the distinguished city of Sidon, from which Dido, who founded Carthage in Africa, originated. At the sixteenth mile from Sidon is the exceedingly wealthy city of Berytus. In Berytus an image of our Savior, placed shortly after his Passion by certain Jews beneath the figure of the Crucified in an insulting and ridiculous manner, sweat blood and water. This became the reason that many of the Sidonians, believing in the true crucified Jesus, received the sacred bath of baptism. Whoever was anointed with a drop from the said image was made well of whatever illness afflicted him. Finally, Arphat too is a city of Damascus. Let us now speak more fully of Damascus.

Damascus is the head of Syria and its venerable metropolis. Eliezer, Abraham’s servant, built it in the field where Cain killed his brother Abel. Esau lived in Damascus; hence it is also called Seir and Edom. [Col. 1069C] For *Seir* means “hairy,” and *Edom* means “red” or “ruddy.” From Edom that entire land is called Idumaea; concerning it the Psalm says: “Into Idumaea I shall extend my sandal.” And again another prophet says: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bosra?”

There is a certain part of that land, Huss, in Edom, from which blessed Job came; it is also called Suita. Hence the man of that region is called Baldat the Suite. In it is also Thema, the metropolis of Idumaea; from Thema came Eliphaz the Temanite. In it too is the town of Naamon, in which lived Sophar the Naamathite. These three were Job’s comforters.

At the borders of Idumaea, two miles from the Jordan, is the river of Jacob. After Jacob had crossed it on his return from Mesopotamia, he wrestled with an angel, who afterward changed his name from Jacob to Israel and, by touching his thigh, made him limp. [Col. 1069D] In Idumaea is Mount Seir, beneath which lies Damascus. Two miles from Damascus is this venerable place where Christ appeared to Saul, afterward called Paul, saying: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” In that place a considerable light from heaven shone around Saul. In Damascus Ananias baptized Saul, giving him the name Paul. Paul was let down from the walls of Damascus because he feared the fury of his persecutors.

Lebanon is interpreted as “whiteness”; hence in the Song of Songs: “Come from Lebanon, my dove.” At the foot of Mount Lebanon the rivers Farfar and Abbana of Damascus rise. Abbana, moreover, flows through the mountains of Lebanon and the plain of Archados, joining the great sea at the boundaries [Col. 1070A] where blessed Eustace, deprived of his wife and bereft of his children, withdrew. Farfar runs through Syria toward Antioch, flowing beside its walls; ten miles farther, at the port of Solim—that is, the port of Saint Simeon—it gives itself to the Mediterranean Sea. Saint Peter the apostle first held the episcopal seat at Antioch, for seven years, adorned with the episcopal mitre. At the foot of Lebanon lies the city of Paneas, otherwise called Caesarea Philippi.

Likewise, at the foot of Lebanon rise Jor and Dan, those two springs from which, as we mentioned above, the Jordan is formed beneath the mountains of Gilboa. From the mountains of Gilboa to the Asphaltite Lake there is the valley through which the Jordan flows. As we said, this valley is called exceedingly great or level, [Col. 1070B] and on both sides it is enclosed by continuous mountains, from Lebanon to the desert of Pharan. The Jordan divides Galilee from Idumaea and from the land of Bostra, which is also the second metropolis of Idumaea. Moreover, *Jordan* is interpreted as “descent.”

From its source the little spring of Dan carries its stream underground as far as Medan, that plain where, when its waters have increased, it sends its channel out quite visibly. That plain is called Medan because Dan lies in its middle. In the language of the Saracens that place is called *Medan*, while in Latin it means “street” or “open place.” The market, however, is called Medan because, when summer begins, an innumerable crowd gathers there, bringing with them everything for sale; in addition, a great multitude of Parthians [Parthorum?] and Arabs remains there throughout the summer to protect the people [Col. 1070C] and feed their flocks in those pastures. *Medan* is composed of *med* and *dan*. *Med*, in the Saracen language, means “water”; *dan*, “river.” From the aforesaid plain, Dan turns into the river Sueta or Suita and is traveled along; there the pyramid of blessed Job, still surviving, is held in solemn honor by kings and peoples.

Finally, Dan bends toward Galilee of the Gentiles and, beneath the city of Kedar and beside medicinal baths, flows across the plain of Spineta, where it joins Jor. Not far from Paneas, Jor forms a lake in that region and makes it from itself; afterward the Sea of Galilee begins from it between Bethsaida and Capernaum. From Bethsaida came Peter and John, Andrew and James son of Alphaeus.

[Col. 1070D] At the sixth mile from Bethsaida is Chorazin, in which the Antichrist, the deceiver of the world, will be nourished. Concerning Chorazin and Bethsaida Jesus says: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!” At the sixth mile from Chorazin is the most excellent city of Kedar, concerning which the Psalm says: “I dwelt with those who dwell in Kedar.” Elsewhere *Kedar* is interpreted as “in darkness.”

## CHAPTER VI. Capernaum, the place of the Table, Magdala, Tiberias, Bethulia, Dothaim, the Lion’s Charnel House, Mount Modin, Diospolis, Tekoa, Jericho, Shechem, the Mount of Offense, the pool of Siloam, the oak of Rogel, the Valley of Jehoshaphat.

Capernaum is that city on the right side of the sea in which Jesus healed the centurion’s son, concerning whom he himself also said: “I have not found such great faith in Israel.” In this city of Capernaum Jesus performed many signs, teaching in the synagogue. Finally, Capernaum is interpreted as “most beautiful village,” or rather “daughter of beauty.” This signifies for us the holy Church, to which all who come from Lebanon—that is, from the whiteness of virtues—are made more radiant by it and in it.

Two miles from Capernaum is the descent of that mountain on which the Lord spoke to the crowds and instructed his apostles, teaching them; there the Lord also healed a leper. One mile farther from there—that is, from the descent of that mountain—is the place where Jesus fed five thousand men with five loaves and two fish. Hence that place is called the Table, which is the same as the place of refreshment. Below this place lies the one where Christ appeared to his disciples, [Col. 1071B] eating with them a portion of a roasted fish, above the sea that the same Lord walked across on dry feet when, around the fourth watch of the night, he appeared to Peter and Andrew while they were fishing. There, when Peter wished to come to him across the sea and began to sink, Christ said to him: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” There too, on another occasion, when his disciples were in danger, he made the sea calm.

Two miles from Gennesaret is the town of Magdala, from which came Mary Magdalene. This region is otherwise called Galilee of the Gentiles and lies in the tribe of Zebulun and Naphtali. In the upper part of this Galilee there were once twenty cities, which King Solomon gave as a gift to Hiram, king of Tyre, his friend.

Two miles from Magdala is the city of Chyneret, also called Tiberias, named after Tiberius Caesar; Jesus used to frequent it in his youth. [Col. 1071C] Four miles from Tiberias is the city of Bethulia, from which came Judith, who, to save her people, cleverly killed Holofernes during the siege of the city. Likewise, four miles from Tiberias toward the south is Dothaim, where Joseph found his brothers tending their flocks; there, out of hatred, they sold him to the Ishmaelites for Egypt.

Before the gate of Jerusalem that faces west, blessed Stephen, the protomartyr, died beneath a shower of stones. After being buried, he was transferred from the place of his martyrdom to Zion, between Nicodemus, Gamaliel, and Abibon; afterward to Constantinople, and finally buried at Rome beside blessed Lawrence. Hence these verses are written on his tomb:

[Col. 1071D]

He whom Zion killed, Byzantium sent to us.

Before the gate of Jerusalem, beside the lake that faces south, a cave can be seen into which a certain lion, by the command of almighty God, carried during the night nearly twelve thousand martyrs killed under Khosrow. Hence it is called the Lion’s Charnel House.

Six miles from Jerusalem, toward the south, is the road that leads to Ramah, and Mount Modin, from which place Mattathias, father of the Maccabees, originated. The Maccabees are buried there, and their burial mounds are still visible. Eight miles from Modin, on the road leading to Joppa, is Lydda, also called Diospolis, where the body of blessed George is shown to have been buried. It is one mile from Ramah.

[Col. 1072A] Three miles from Bethlehem is the town of Tekoa, from which Amos came and where he was also buried.

Four miles from Jerusalem, toward the south, is the town where Zechariah lived at the time when Mary, the mother of Jesus, hastening while already carrying the Son of God in her womb, came to greet her kinswoman Elizabeth, who was pregnant with her son John. They also claim that John was born there.

Thirteen miles from Jerusalem, toward the north, is Jericho, from which came Rahab, the prostitute who rescued, concealed, and fed the four spies of the children of Israel after receiving them as guests. From there also came Zacchaeus, who, being short in stature, heard that Jesus was walking through that region and climbed a sycamore tree to see Jesus and speak with him, judging himself and asking [Col. 1072B] forgiveness. From there too came those boys who mocked blessed Elisha as he was ascending toward Jerusalem, saying: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead,” and so forth.

Two miles from Jerusalem is the road that leads to Shechem, and Mount Gabaoth in the tribe of Benjamin.

One mile from Jerusalem, on the slope of Mount Olivet, are the Mount of Offense and the Continuous Mountain. The road that leads from Jehoshaphat through Bethphage to Bethany divides them. The Mount of Offense is so called because King Solomon placed an idol named Moloch there and worshiped it.

Not far from Jerusalem, beneath Solomon’s royal residence, on the slope in the Valley of Jehoshaphat, is the pool of Siloam, to which Jesus sent the blind man whom he had enlightened, so that he might wash his eyes in it. He went away, washed, and saw. [Col. 1072C] Therefore *Siloam* is interpreted as “sent.” Naaman, commander of Syria, was not sent to this same water, but to the Jordan by the prophet Elisha, so that after bathing in it three times he might be cleansed of leprosy. Looking at that water, Naaman said, almost indignantly: “Are not Farfar and Abbania, the rivers of our province, much better than this?” In the end, however, agreeing with the advice of his servant, he fulfilled the prophet’s command and was healed.

According to the tradition of the Syrians, Siloam is said to flow from Shiloh. Siloam carries its stream silently, because it is underground. Near Siloam there once stood the oak of Rogel, beneath which blessed Josiah lies buried and rests.

[Col. 1072D] Blessed James son of Alphaeus was buried in the Valley of Jehoshaphat. As we said above, he had been thrown down from the Temple. A beautiful chapel still stands in the same valley, in which evidence of his burial remains, with these verses inscribed:

The Jews, without law, press upon Alphaeus’ son;

They make death his lot, because of the love and name of God.

Alphaeus’ son, hurled down from the Temple,

Was brought here and devoutly buried.

But afterward he was transferred to Constantinople as an apostle of God.

In the Valley of Jehoshaphat, beneath a pointed pyramid, King Jehoshaphat himself was buried; the entire valley took its name from him. It is interpreted as “valley of judgment,” according to the passage: “I will gather all the nations,” and so forth. Moreover—

[Col. 1073A] The same valley has many caves on every side, in which religious persons lead an eremitical life. The entire valley belongs to the monastery situated at its summit above the bed of the torrent Kidron, beside the garden in which our Lord often used to meet with his disciples. In the crypt of this monastery the burial place of the most blessed Virgin Mary is still shown today; we shall speak of it later.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning Bethany, Bethphage, the village of Gethsemane, the Lord’s upper room on Mount Zion, and the things worthy of remembrance at each place.

It has already been said that our Lord, sent forth like a lion from the tribe of Judah, loosed two seals in the sealed book of John—namely, those of the Nativity and [Col. 1073B] Baptism. Now let us speak of the other seals.

As the time of the Lord’s Passion approached, Jesus Christ our Lord came to Bethany in the evening, on the day before Palm Sunday. Then, on the following day, namely Sunday morning, he entered the holy city with the solemnity that we have already described above. Bethany lies two miles from Jerusalem. It is the town in which Simon—or, as is more truly believed, Lazarus—often received Christ as a guest; Martha and Mary ministered to him devotedly.

In Bethany Mary Magdalene broke an alabaster vessel and poured out precious ointment over the head of the Savior, who was reclining at table, as an act of devotion. The fragrance of the ointment filled the entire house. It is also said that Mary Magdalene came in this same place, or rather in another place, namely [Col. 1073C] in the house of Simon the leper, when she was still a sinner, having been led by repentance to the feet of the Lord, who was likewise reclining at table. She bathed the feet of Jesus Christ with her tears, wiped them with her hair, anointed them with another ointment, namely one of compunction, and thus obtained from the Lord forgiveness for her sins.

Accordingly, since sacred Scripture is found in some places to mention another Mary approaching his feet and another anointing the Lord’s head, and so forth, the teachers of the holy Church explain the meaning in this way: it was another—that is, a different or transformed—Mary, because there she approached while still a sinner, in the bitterness of repentance, whereas here she approached already justified, with the exultation of devotion.

[Col. 1073D] There is nevertheless a certain church within the walls of the holy city, near Saint Anne and toward the north, close to the city walls, consecrated in honor of Saint Mary Magdalene. Jacobite monks live there. They claim that the house of Simon the leper was there, the man who invited our Lord to a banquet, at which Mary Magdalene arrived, falling at Jesus’ feet, bathing them with tears, kissing them, wiping them with her hair, and anointing them with ointment. This, I say, is what the monks of that place claim; they confirm it by pointing out the place on the pavement marked in the form of a cross where Mary came to Jesus’ feet, and by showing that the same event was represented in the painted panels. They also show a strand of that Mary’s hair, which was found there and is still kept in a vessel of clear glass.

[Col. 1074A] They further say that there was another Mary, who was the sister of Lazarus and Martha, and who, in Bethany—the town belonging to those three—broke an alabaster vessel and poured precious ointment over the head of the same our Lord. They say that her tomb can still be seen today in the *tabaria*, with her body buried there. They admit, however, that the body of Mary Magdalene rests in our regions at Vizeliacum [Vizeliacum]. But only those people assert this, as I myself heard when present. Nevertheless, as we have said, they say that the woman who anointed the feet and head of Jesus was one and the same Mary, and that she was also the sister of Lazarus and, at one time, a sinner.

[Col. 1074B] Meanwhile, the reading of the holy Gospel concerning this same event is highly intricate and even leaves a careful listener uncertain as to whether Simon the leper had a house in Bethany and invited the Lord there. This nevertheless does not seem suitable, since it is said and written that the entire town of Bethany belonged to Lazarus and his sisters. If the same Simon had a house elsewhere, perhaps in the place mentioned above, it is necessary to say that on that first occasion Mary is said to have anointed not only the feet but also the head of Jesus, as may be understood from the words of the Lord himself in the Gospel: “Simon, I entered your house,” and so forth. On another occasion in Bethany, as in her own house, the same Mary anointed only his head, breaking the alabaster over him. Hence the Gospel says: “When Jesus was in Bethany,” and so forth.

If anyone wishes to become more certain about these matters, [Col. 1074C] let him come in person and inquire from the wiser inhabitants of this land about the sequence and truth of what happened. For I have found no writing that says so much about these matters. Between Bethany itself and the summit of Mount Olivet, almost midway, was Bethphage, a certain village of priests. As evidence of it, two stone towers still remain, one of which is a church.

At the foot of Mount Olivet, toward the city, where the tomb of blessed Mary the Virgin is now shown, there was a little village called Gethsemane.

As we have said, when the Lord’s Passion was approaching, after the raising of Lazarus, Jesus came to Jerusalem on Palm Sunday. Having completed the solemnity already mentioned, he returned that same day to the mountains of Olivet, where he was to remain until Thursday. On that day he was to eat [Col. 1074D] the Lord’s Supper with his disciples, by which he would establish the end of the Old Testament and the beginning of the New Testament.

When his disciples asked where he wished the Passover to be prepared for him, he sent some of them into the city to come and prepare a dwelling or a place suitable for completing the sacraments of such a sacred supper. The Gospel gives a fuller account: “Go into the city, and you will find a man carrying a jar of water; follow him,” and so forth.

This upper room was found on Mount Zion, in the place where Solomon is said once to have constructed a magnificent building, concerning which the Song of Songs says: “King Solomon made himself a litter,” and so forth. That upper room was large and spacious in its upper part. For the sake of the mystery, our Lord is said to have eaten supper there with his disciples, [Col. 1075A] where he carefully revealed his betrayer, strengthened the others concerning the Passion that awaited him, and gave them his body to eat under the appearance of bread and his blood to drink under the appearance of wine, saying: “As often as you shall do this,” and so forth.

After the supper had taken place in the upper part of the dwelling, it is plausible, in keeping with the same mystery, that our Lord demonstrated an example of humility in the lower part of the house by washing the disciples’ feet. Or, if you prefer, this may have been done before or after the supper, as a certain exposition suggests concerning John’s words in the Gospel: “And when supper had been made, he rose,” and so forth.

Whether this was done before or after supper makes little difference. [Col. 1075B] It is nevertheless useful to know that the arrangement of the place, or even today the representation of what happened, suggests a distinction between the locations in the church on Mount Zion. For on the left side of the same church, in the upper area, the supper appears depicted, while below, namely in the crypt, the washing of the disciples’ feet is shown.

Having completed these mysteries, he returned with his disciples to Mount Olivet for the sake of prayer. At the foot and on the slope of that mountain he left his disciples and withdrew from them alone about a stone’s throw. There he prayed to his Father, saying: “Father, if it is possible,” and so forth. There he also poured out a sweat like blood from the trembling of his flesh. Returning to his disciples and finding them asleep, he rebuked Peter in particular, saying: “Could you not watch with me for one hour?” and so forth. And again: “Sleep now and rest,” and so forth. [Col. 1075C]

Thus he withdrew from them to the same place three times and offered the same prayers to God his Father. Finally, according to his humanity, he was strengthened by an angel; and, according to his divinity, returning to his disciples a third time, he said: “Watch and pray.”

The distinction between these places—namely, where the disciples remained and where the Lord prayed—is clearly visible in the Valley of Jehoshaphat. For beside the larger church, in which the burial place of blessed Mary the Virgin still stands, as we shall discuss later, there is on the right a chapel with a cave in which the sorrowful and sleeping disciples remained while the Lord came to them after his Passion and withdrew from them three times. A painting still present there indicates this.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the Church of the Savior, Pilate’s praetorium, the Tower of David, and Mount Calvary.

[Col. 1075D]

The place where the Lord prayed is surrounded by a new church called the Church of the Savior. Three unworked stones, like a kind of rock, project from the floor of this church. The Lord is said to have prayed on these stones and bent his knee three times. Therefore these stones are held in the greatest devotion and veneration by the faithful of Christ even to this day.

Near the cave mentioned shortly before, our Lord, knowing that Judas was approaching with the crowds—for Judas, while the other disciples remained with the Lord after supper, went alone to the Jews, negotiating with them concerning the price of [Col. 1076A] betraying and handing over his Master, agreeing to and receiving thirty pieces of silver, and undertaking that unspeakable crime—Jesus, I say, knowing this, said to his disciples in that same cave: “Rise, let us go; behold, he has drawn near,” and so forth.

Thus he went out from Gethsemane, was handed over through Judas’s kiss, recognized by the cohort sent there, seized, bound, and led away by them. Nevertheless, in the aforesaid cave five holes are shown in a single stone, as though impressed by the five fingers of the Lord’s hand. I say “of the Lord,” but of the Lord already captured and violently dragged by his persecutors, as though he had wished to hold himself back on the stone at that place.

Whatever the truth of this may be, we undoubtedly know that he could have done greater things through greater power and strength. [Col. 1076B] Thus handed over by his disciple, captured and bound by a Roman soldier, our Lord was led back to Mount Zion, where Pilate’s praetorium then stood, called the Lithostrotos and, in Hebrew, Gabbatha.

At that time the finest and strongest part of the whole city was situated on the height of that mountain. The Tower of David, which served as a lookout and defense for the rest of the city, also stood elevated there. Hence, by reason of maternal generation and of governance—or rather protection—the lower part of the same city is called its daughter, according to the passage: “Say to the daughter of Zion,” and so forth.

After the city there had been destroyed and transferred to another place, where it now stands, and rebuilt under the emperor Aelius, that same mountain was greatly lowered and leveled from its height, [Col. 1076C] its tower and other buildings and fortifications having been thrown down, lest in time the enemy should harm the new city from that same place.

Nevertheless, the place where the praetorium and the Tower of David stood is still shown today. At that time, toward the south on Mount Zion, there was also that large building where the Lord ate his final supper with his disciples.

Near the aforesaid praetorium, toward the east, was a courtyard, or rather a prison, in which Jesus was held in chains and guarded throughout that entire night by the soldiers and leaders of the Jews amid a thousand insults, reproaches, and mockeries, until they should bring him before the judgment seat at the proper time in the morning.

In that same praetorium Peter denied the Lord three times before the cockcrow. When he then heard the cock crow and the Lord looked at him, he piously remembered the most gracious word of his Master, truly repented, wept bitterly, and fled into the cave which is now called the Cockcrow, but in the common tongue Galilee.

Moreover, to complete the other things that either existed or occurred in Zion at that time, it is worth remembering that after his resurrection the Lord Jesus appeared to his disciples in Zion. As testimony to this, these verses are read, placed on the right side of the church there:

Christ appeared here to his Galilean disciples,

Rising; therefore the place was called Galilee.

On the road by which one descends from Zion into the Valley of Jehoshaphat, beneath the gate of Mount Zion and above the often-mentioned cave, a church has been built, which is now inhabited by Greek monks.

Let us return once more to Jesus in chains. When morning came, innocent Christ, condemned to death by an unjust judgment, was scourged before the praetorium in a certain place, struck with blows, spat upon, dressed in a red garment in mockery of the royal title that he had claimed among the Jews, pierced with a crown of thorns, and—incredible to say—treated most foully in every respect.

A verse later placed at the same spot indicates this, saying:

Here he is crowned, by whose right the world is ruled.

The same place is marked by a chapel before the larger Church of Zion, situated toward the north. [Col. 1077B] It contains a painted history of the event with this inscription:

The Holy of Holies is condemned by the voice of the guilty.

For servants God suffers war and the scourge.

This good cross of Christ comes to the aid of this Simon;

He does not carry it for nothing, for it grants all good things to the blessed.

From that place, after the sentence of the cross and the condemnation of Jesus had been pronounced, they placed upon the Lord’s shoulder the cross prepared for this purpose, so that, carrying his own cross, he might bear it to the place of execution. Then Isaiah’s prophecy was fulfilled: “And the government was upon his shoulder,” and so forth.

When Jesus, exhausted by the great weight of the cross he had to drag, was delayed on the way and was almost unable to bear the burden, a certain Cyrenian came along. They compelled him to carry the same cross as far as [Col. 1077C] the place of Calvary.

At that time, beside the site of the ancient city, the place of Calvary lay outside the city and was designated for those condemned by a capital sentence. This place was called Calvary because those condemned to death were shaved there: their hair was cut off, their heads were consumed by the slow air, and their flesh was exposed, though they were not buried in the earth. It was certainly therefore a place of Calvary; or finally, it received this name because the guilty were made bald there—that is, were customarily condemned.

The same place, called Golgotha in Hebrew, was on an elevated rock. Even today, outside cities, elevated, conspicuous, and prominent places are commonly assigned for the punishment of the condemned. Meanwhile, while everything necessary for the crucifixion was being prepared on that same rock, [Col. 1077D] our Lord was held bound as if in a prison in a place somewhat removed from Calvary. At that time this place, being outside the mountain, was level; now it represents a chapel and is still called the Lord’s Prison. It lies directly opposite Calvary, in the left apse of the church. Others, however, hold a different view concerning the same place, as I myself heard when present.

Afterward, at the place of Calvary, by Pilate’s order and at the instigation of the Jews, the Roman soldiers stripped our Lord of his tunic, gave him gall and vinegar to drink, and fastened him to the crossbeam of the cross.

While Jesus was suffering there, John received Jesus’ mother, entrusted to him, into his own care, so that a virgin might guard the Virgin. Jesus said to his mother: “Woman, behold your son,” making the reference, as some claim, either to John [Col. 1078A] or rather to himself; as if he were saying: “Woman, behold your son: what I now suffer comes from the sonship that I received from your motherhood; but I do not possess from it the power to perform miracles.” Hence, elsewhere, at the wedding in Cana of Galilee, he said to his mother: “What is there between me and you, woman?”

Then to John he said: “Behold your mother,” entrusting her, whom he commended to the disciple he loved above the others, to his filial devotion and care.

At Calvary, while the victim of the world suffered on the cross, he promised the thief hanging on his right, who asked him for forgiveness, the robe of immortality. Then, while Jesus hung on the cross, his side was pierced on the right by a lance, and he gave forth blood and water. From a drop of that blood and water, through the movement of piety and confession, the eyes of Longinus, who had struck him, were opened, so that he too believed in Christ. [Col. 1078B]

When our Lord had died on the wood of the cross and voluntarily surrendered his soul, the veil of the Temple was torn from top to bottom. The same rock in which the cross had been fixed was split down the middle on the side touched by the Savior’s blood; through that fissure the blood of Christ consequently flowed into the interior of the rock.

Some say that Adam was buried in this same place and was thus baptized in the blood of Christ. To signify this, they claim, the head of a dead man is customarily attached at the feet of the Crucified. But this is more easily asserted than proved true. For sacred Scripture itself clearly testifies that Adam was buried in Hebron.
