[Col. 1078C] The distorted face of a dead man, which is placed beneath the Crucified, signifies rather death and its destruction. Hence the Lord says: “O death, I shall be your death,” that is, “your destruction.”

On the right side of the larger church, at the entrance, is a certain part of Calvary. In its upper section the fissure in the same rock is shown and recalled with the greatest veneration; even today it is displayed there with great devotion to those who come. In that same upper section the Passion of Christ and his burial are beautifully depicted in a splendid mosaic, together with the testimony of the prophets, harmoniously presented on every side.

[Col. 1078D] Note that at the place of Calvary the sacred cross, with Christ’s body, was fixed and secured in a round opening in the rock. The opening is still exposed and visible, so much so that many offerings of the faithful are cast into it—especially at the place where the sacred cross stood and where the most holy blood flowed from the right side toward the fissure of the said rock.

It seems consistent with the opinion of the more authoritative view that, by necessity of interpretation, the face of the Lord hanging on the cross looked and was turned toward the east. Beside the same place, often mentioned above, an altar now stands in the upper part on the right, consecrated in honor of the Lord’s Passion; the entire place is named after that Passion.

The lower part of Calvary beneath it contains an altar and is called “At the Holy Blood,” because the Lord’s blood is said to have flowed through the fissure of the rock as far as that point. [Col. 1079A] Today that place is marked behind the same altar by a hollow in the rock, where a lamp hangs and burns continually.

Thus, at the place of Calvary, as we have said, the third sacrament was fulfilled, and the third seal of the sealed book of the Apocalypse was loosed. Let us now pass to the remaining matters and to the seals still left of this sealed book.

## CHAPTER IX. The place at the center of the world, Emmaus, the Lord’s tomb, and certain matters concerning the distinguished merits of the Germans in Palestine against the Franks.

In the middle of the choir of the canons, not far from the place of Calvary, there is a certain site marked out in the form of an altar by marble slabs raised above the ground and by an interlacing of iron grilles joined together [Col. 1079B]. Beneath these slabs, on the pavement, certain circles have been made, and they say that this is the center of the earth, in accordance with the verse: “He has worked salvation in the midst of the earth.” At this same place, they also assert, Christ appeared to Mary Magdalene after his resurrection. For this reason the site is held in great veneration, with a lamp burning continually within it.

Moreover, some affirm that at this same place Joseph obtained Jesus’ body from Pilate; then, on that same day—that is, Friday—Joseph took the body down from the cross, washed it, reverently seasoned it with precious ointments, liquids, and spices, wrapped it in a clean shroud, and buried it not far from there in a garden, in the tomb that he had carved for himself from the rock. Meanwhile Jesus, having died on the cross for us, descended to hell [Col. 1079C] in order to free the fathers. And through this descent into hell we say that the fourth sacrament, or seal of the apocalyptic book, was opened and loosed by Christ.

As for the fifth seal, or the mystery and sacrament of the sealed Apocalypse, Christ opened it when he rose gloriously from death, which he had conquered. Thus, at the very place of his burial, the Lord truly rose from the dead, the lion from the tribe of Judah, death having been subdued. There also the angel of the Lord appeared to the holy women and announced that Jesus had truly risen from the dead on the third day, saying: “Go, announce it to his brothers,” etc. And again: “Go, tell his disciples, and Peter.”

On that same day of the holy resurrection, as evening was already approaching [Col. 1079D], Christ, concealed under the appearance of a pilgrim, appeared to two disciples who were discussing and debating the Lord’s death on the road and were making their way to Eleutheropolis, that is, the town of Emmaus, which lies six miles west of Jerusalem. They recognized him, whom they had received as a guest under the guise of a pilgrim, in the breaking of bread. Yet, once their eyes had been opened and doubt removed from their minds, he immediately disappeared again.

After this he appeared to all the apostles, Thomas alone being absent on that occasion, on Mount Zion, with the doors closed, saying: “Peace be with you.” Then, eight days later, he appeared again on the same mountain and in the same place to his disciples, who were assembled together with Thomas. In particular, to remove Thomas’s mind from doubt, he offered him his wounds to touch. When this had been done [Col. 1080A], Thomas exclaimed: “My Lord and my God!”

These appearances of the risen Christ are represented in a painting at the place on Mount Zion, namely in the crypt of the principal church. There our Lord is also depicted washing the feet of his disciples, with an explicit description of both events. After the resurrection Jesus also manifested himself to his disciples beside the Sea of Tiberias and in the sea three times; besides these appearances, he showed himself many times elsewhere, to provide full and indisputable proof both of his resurrection, which had already taken place, and of our resurrection in the flesh, which is still to come.

The arrangement of the monument containing the Lord’s tomb may be depicted as follows. The site of this monument is almost round in shape and is decorated within with mosaic work. At its entrance on the eastern side [Col. 1080B] there is a small doorway, before which stands a protected square portico, or vestibule, with two doors. Through one of these those entering to visit the tomb are admitted; through the other they are allowed to leave. The guardians of the tomb also sit in this vestibule. Finally, there is a third door facing toward the choir.

On the western side of the monument, that is, outside at the head of the tomb, an altar has been placed with a certain square superstructure. Three of its walls consist of beautifully arranged iron grilles. This altar is called the altar at the Lord’s tomb. The monument itself is sufficiently spacious and has above it something like a round ciborium, covered above with silver and raised high, facing that large opening which is open above in the principal building. This building [Col. 1080C], circular and round in form and sufficiently spacious around the monument, has at its outer edge a continuous wall illuminated by various images and many lamps. Within the narrower circuit of the same principal building, eight round marble columns, with an equal number of square bases and an equal number of square marble slabs ornamented externally, stand all around and support the upper structure beneath the roof, which, as we have said, is open toward the center.

We said that the columns were arranged in a circle in the number specified above; but their arrangement and number have now been altered toward the east because of the construction added for the new church, to which there is a passage from that point. This new and newly added building contains a very broad and spacious choir of the canons and a sufficiently long and ample sanctuary, in which the principal altar has been consecrated in honor of the Anastasis—that is, the holy resurrection. A painting set above it in mosaic work appropriately makes this clear. It contains an image of Christ rising after breaking the bars of hell and drawing out from there our ancient father Adam.

Outside this altar-sanctuary and within the rather broad enclosure there is sufficient space, suitable for processions, extending all around through both the new building and the old building of the aforementioned monument. This procession takes place every Sunday night, from Easter until the Advent of the Lord, at Vespers, at the holy sepulchre, with the antiphon “Christ rising,” etc. The text of this antiphon [Col. 1081A] is also displayed outside, at the outermost edge of the monument, in raised silver letters. When the antiphon is finished, the cantor immediately begins: “But toward evening,” etc., with the psalm *Magnificat* and the collect for the resurrection: “Almighty, eternal,” etc., preceded by the verse: “The Lord has risen, NB, from this tomb.” Likewise, throughout this entire period, namely from Easter until Advent, every Sunday the Mass “I have risen,” that is, the Mass of the Resurrection, is celebrated.

At the head of the same new church, toward the east beside the canons’ cloister, there is a deep place in the form of a crypt, of considerable brightness, where Queen Helena is said to have found the Lord’s cross. For this reason an altar consecrated in honor of the same holy Helena [Col. 1081B] is maintained there. This queen carried the greater part of the sacred wood with her to Constantinople; the remaining part was left in Jerusalem and is carefully and reverently preserved in a certain place in the other part of the church, opposite the place of Calvary.

Although this same place had already been consecrated and sanctified from that time onward by the abundant shedding of Christ’s blood there, nevertheless in modern times—although this was more than sufficient—a consecration was performed by venerable men on the fifteenth day of July. The following verses, written there in gilded work, provide testimony to it:

This place is sacred, consecrated by Christ’s blood;

By our consecration nothing sacred is added to it,

But the house built above and around this holy place

Was consecrated on the fifteenth day of July.

On that very same day, namely 15 July, although at a much earlier time and in far earlier years, when the same holy city had long been held captive under the dominion and power of various kinds of Saracens, it was freed by the army of the Christians. In commemoration of this liberation, after the renewal of the consecration, they make the same day celebrated by a spiritual office in the Mass “Rejoice, Jerusalem,” etc. They celebrate the principal Mass, or the more solemn office, for the Dedication, beginning: “Terrible is this place.”

Moreover, on the day of the dedication of this church, four altars placed there were also consecrated [Col. 1081D]: namely, the principal altar, the one above in Calvary, and two on opposite sides of the church, one in honor of Saint Peter and the other in honor of Saint Stephen the protomartyr. On the day following the annual feast of the Dedication, they solemnly commemorate all the faithful departed, both in almsgiving and in prayers, especially those killed on the occasion of the capture of this city; their burial is regarded as especially notable near the Golden Gate.

Then, on the third day, the whole city solemnly observes the anniversary of the distinguished duke Gotefridus, of blessed memory, the leader and master of that holy expedition, descended from the Alemannic stock, with a generous distribution of alms in the principal church, according to an arrangement made while he was still alive [Col. 1082A].

Nevertheless, although our Gotefridus is honored there in this way, the capture of the holy city of Jerusalem is attributed not to him and to the distinguished laborers and experienced soldiers who worked alongside him, the Alemanni or Germans, but almost exclusively to the Franks—which is entirely false. For this reason, the detractors of our German people erased the distinguished epitaph of that famous Wigger, proven by many courageous deeds, because they could not deny that he was an Alemannian, and substituted the name of another soldier from France, as can still be seen and noted by those present.

For his sarcophagus, still standing outside in a certain corner between the principal church and the chapel of Saint John the Baptist, is visible even today, with his name erased and another name attached. As proof [Col. 1082B] and indication of the contempt shown toward our men, and as praise of the Franks, the following poem is inscribed outside on the side of this monument:

In the year one thousand one hundred, less one,

From the Virgin’s birth, when the Lord’s birth shone forth,

When the sun’s light had already touched the fifteenth of July,

The Franks captured Jerusalem by mighty force.

But against them the order of these words is rightly turned.

Not Franks, but *Francones*, superior by the sword,

Freed holy Jerusalem, captured for so long,

From the yoke of various pagans:

Franco, not Francus; Wigger, Gundram, Gotefridus—

These prove that the truth of this matter is known.

[Col. 1082C] Although Duke Gotefridus and his brother Baldwin, who was crowned king in Jerusalem after him—for the duke had refused, out of humility, to have this done while he was alive—were from our German regions, nevertheless, because only a few of our countrymen remained with them while very many others returned to their native land with great eagerness and haste, the entire city was occupied in this way by other nations: Franks, Lotharingians, Northmen, Provençals, Auvergnats, Italians, Spaniards, Burgundians, and Germans who had come on that expedition.

Thus the whole holy city was inhabited by these auxiliary forces of Christendom, so that not even one part of the city, or even the smallest street, was distributed [Col. 1082D] and assigned to the Alemanni. Consequently, since the Germans had no desire to remain there or to seek residence in the city, partisan historians, suppressing the German name, attribute the liberation of the holy city solely to the Franks. Together with the other peoples named above, they still rule the Province adjoining the city to this day.

Indeed, this province of Christendom would long ago have extended its boundaries beyond the Nile toward the south and beyond Damascus toward the east, if as great a number of Alemanni as of those peoples had been present. For when the German soldiers departed, it was as though the entire strength of the Christian army had departed; all the other nations accomplished little more, or nothing. But let us set these matters aside for the present and return to the subject proposed.

## CHAPTER X. The place of the Lord’s Ascension on the Mount of Olives; the tomb of Saint Mary, Mother of God, in the Valley of Jehoshaphat; and related matters

[Col. 1083A]

We have reached the fulfillment of the sixth sacrament and the opening of the sixth seal, which, we say, was completed through the Ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ on the Mount of Olives. At the place of the Ascension, namely on the Mount of Olives, there now stands a great church. In its center, through a large open aperture, the place of the Lord’s Ascension is indicated. From this place he was lifted up into heaven, borne by a cloud, while his disciples and other Galileans were present and marvelling, together with his mother. Beforehand he had commanded the disciples not to depart from Jerusalem until they had received from the Father the Paraclete Spirit promised for their complete strengthening [Col. 1083B].

This took place on the tenth day after the Ascension and the fiftieth after the Lord’s Resurrection, namely on the day of Pentecost, while the disciples remained in a certain upper room on Mount Zion, where Christ our Lord had also eaten his final supper, and were awaiting together the fulfillment of the promise that had been given. A mosaic painting in the sanctuary, in the apse of the same church, clearly demonstrates this very event. For there the number twelve of the apostles, together with their images, is represented, with the Holy Spirit descending upon each of their heads in the form of fiery tongues, accompanied by this inscription: “Suddenly there came a sound from heaven,” etc.

In this church, at the entrance on the right, an altar is marked out in a place furnished with polished marble slabs in the form of a ciborium. Here the most blessed Virgin Mary is said to have departed from this world after giving up her spirit. There her Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, is depicted taking her most holy soul up into heaven, on the adjacent wall, in the presence of the apostles.

Around the building erected above this place there is the following inscription:

The holy Mother of God has been exalted above the choirs of angels.

Moreover, on the very day of her departure, the body of the most blessed Virgin Mary, with all twelve apostles present by divine disposition at that time [Col. 1083D], was carried from Mount Zion to the Valley of Jehoshaphat. There, in the middle of a crypt, it was buried with the greatest honor, in a remarkable manner, amid wonderful marble paneling and distinguished painting.

At this place of burial, although the body of the most blessed Virgin is not present, a distinguished structure has been erected above it in the manner of a ciborium, both in the marble paneling mentioned above and also in silver and gold. There the following poem is read:

Here is the Valley of Jehoshaphat; from here the road rises to the stars.

Here Mary was buried, supported in the Lord.

From here she was exalted, untouched, and sought the heavens,

The hope, way, light, and mother of captives.

Here, according to Hebrew custom, when the tomb was visited and examined before the eighth day after the most blessed Virgin’s passing [Col. 1084A], her body was no longer found. Hence it is devoutly believed that not only her soul but also her body was taken up by her beloved Son Jesus in glorification.

Jerome, however, seems to intimate this in that letter—“You compel me, O Paula and Eustochium,” etc.—more by hesitation than by assertion. Whatever the truth may be in this matter, we believe that the blessed Virgin Mary, simply because she was worthy to bear her Creator, must be worthy of every honor and beatification not only in soul but also in body; and that her Son, supremely benevolent toward Mary and supremely powerful, both wills and is able to accomplish this.

Furthermore, this most holy burial place is honored and venerated in imitation of the honor shown to the tomb of her beloved Son. At the entrance to the same [Col. 1084B] crypt the following painting and inscription are seen:

Come, heirs of life, to praise the Lord,

Through whom life is given and the salvation of the world restored.

Her tomb is shown, as we ourselves saw, still to the present day in the Valley of Jehoshaphat, in the middle of the church erected there in her honor, in which everyone affirms that she was buried.

On the right side of the same entrance there is an image of blessed Basil the bishop, containing the following:

By the dignity

And exalted power

Of Christ’s mother,

Julian was found

A savage and profane enemy,

A deserter and traitor.

But now the wretch pays the penalty,

[Col. 1084C]

Cast down into Gehenna;

For, as the devout mother commanded,

The martyr of Christ, Mercury,

Struck him with a lance.

To the saving Queen

Be praise and honor without end,

Who chose to be buried here.

What better thing could be given to us

By this treasure?

These and many other things in praise of the Virgin have been placed at the entrance of the crypt in paintings. But on the inner walls, standing here and there around the tomb, and on the ceiling, the following inscriptions have been set. On the right-hand wall: “The Virgin Mary has been taken up into the heavenly bridal chamber,” etc.; then, around the circuit: “I saw a beautiful woman like a dove,” etc., ending with “and the lily of the valleys”; and then the following is added: “The daughters of Zion saw her” [Col. 1084D]. From here, certainly, the glorious Virgin ascended into heaven: “I pray you, rejoice, for, ineffably exalted, she reigns with Christ forever.”

On the front: “Mary has been taken up into heaven.”

On the opposite side: “The holy Mother of God has been exalted,” etc.

And in the middle there is a multitude of angels standing around the blessed Mary, who is seated upon a throne; through her, the way to the heavenly kingdom is declared.

## CHAPTER XI. The author returns to a description of the holy places enclosed within the walls of Jerusalem: the hospital of Saint John the Baptist, the Greater Parthenon of Mary, the monastery of Saint Mary the Latin, and of Saint Sabas, the church of Saint James, and the hospital of the Alemanni

Now that we have briefly examined the matters pertaining to the opening [Col. 1085A] of the sixth seal, let us finally proceed to the still-unfulfilled opening of the seventh; and this, as we have said, is the day of judgment.

Having examined these matters and briefly indicated the places in which they occurred, together with a description of the other neighboring sites, let us return to describe the holy city of Jerusalem itself, including the new and venerable holy places newly constructed and devoted to divine worship within its walls.

For this purpose, let it be added that Judas received thirty pieces of silver in the same city for betraying our Lord. After Judas, in despair, threw them at the feet of the Jews and Pharisees, the field called Haceldama—that is, the Field of Blood—was purchased with them and designated for the burial of pilgrims, as it remains to the present day. This field [Col. 1085B] lies to the left of Mount Zion, beside the road leading to Ephrata. Above this field is Mount Geon, joined to it; there King Solomon received the royal diadem, and other kings were accustomed to be anointed on the same mountain.

Then, in the middle of Jerusalem, our Lord raised a girl from the dead and performed many miracles there.

Beside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, which we described above, there is a beautiful church opposite it toward the south, built in honor of Saint John the Baptist. Attached to it is a hospital in which a very large number of sick people, both women and men, are gathered and cared for in various wards, and are daily restored with the greatest expense. Their number, at the time when I was present, I learned from the servants who reported it to be two thousand invalids. Of these, sometimes more than fifty are carried out dead within a single night and day, while again and again many others arrive anew.

What more need be said? This house supports its inmates with its own provisions, both inside and outside, besides the immeasurable almsgiving that is distributed daily to the poor who seek bread from door to door and remain outside. Thus the total of the expenses can scarcely be determined, even by the procurators and administrators of the house.

In addition to all these expenses incurred for the sick and for outside paupers, the same house maintains throughout its castles many persons equipped with abundant military resources for the defense of the Christians’ land [Col. 1085D] against incursions by the Saracens.

Beside the same church of blessed John and its hospital is a monastery of nuns constructed in honor of Saint Mary. It is almost contiguous at its head with the buildings of the aforementioned church, and is called Saint Mary the Greater. Not far from there, in the same alignment of the same street, is a monastery of monks likewise founded in honor of Saint Mary, called Saint Mary the Latin. There the skull of Saint Philip the Apostle is held in great veneration; it is also shown devoutly to visitors who come and ask to see it.

Beside that street, which descends from David’s Gate toward the Temple, on the right-hand side near David’s Tower, is a monastery of monks [Col. 1086A] of Armenians, in honor of the most reverend abbot Saint Sabas, for whom the blessed Virgin Mary also performed many miracles while he was still alive.

In the same area, not far away down the slope beyond another church, stands that great church erected in honor of Saint James the Greater. Armenian monks also live there, and they possess a large hospital for gathering only the poor of their own language.

In this very place, the skull of the same holy apostle is venerated with the greatest reverence. He was beheaded by Herod, and his disciples placed his body on a ship at Joppa and carried it to Galilee, while his head remained at the place of his martyrdom, namely in Palestine. This same casing is still shown to pilgrims who come to this church.

On the descent of the same street [Col. 1086B], toward the gate by which one goes to the Temple, on the right-hand side there is a certain side passage along a long portico. On this route there is a hospital with a church, newly being built in honor of Saint Mary. It is called the House of the Alemanni, to which few or none of those who speak another language contribute anything charitable.

## CHAPTER XII. The prison of Saint Peter the Apostle; the church erected there; the Iron Gate; Solomon’s palace; the Temple of the Templars; the house of Simeon the Just; the church of Saint Anne and its Parthenon; the Probatica Pool; the church of Saint Mary Magdalene; and that of Saint Chariton

On the same road toward the gate by which one goes to Mount Zion, there is a chapel built in honor of Saint Peter [Col. 1086C]. In the crypt of this chapel, situated at a considerable depth, there is said to have been a prison in which blessed Peter, bound with iron chains and guarded by soldiers both outside and inside, was carefully confined at Herod’s command.

But human diligence was foiled by divine power. For that same night, through the ministry of an angel, while the guards stood around him, his iron bonds were broken of their own accord, and the doors both of the prison and of the city opened of themselves. Blessed Peter departed unharmed under the angel’s guidance, saying: “Now I know truly that the Lord has sent his angel,” etc.

At the entrance of the same little church, verses concerning the miracle performed there are displayed:

Peter, put on your clothes, rise, and depart, freed;

For the bonds of your chains have been broken.

Now I know with certain knowledge, since the gate has been opened for me.

[Col. 1086D]

O mercy of Christ, because you have saved me.

In the enclosure of the same Church of Saint Peter *ad Vincula*, on its celebrated feast, I celebrated Mass with the collect appropriately pronounced there:

O God, who caused blessed Peter the Apostle, NB, to be released from his chains in this place and to depart unharmed, etc.

This little church is modest, and neither so richly endowed with revenues nor so splendidly adorned as such a great divine miracle and so great a prince of the apostles would deserve.

That gate which leads toward Mount Zion is called the Iron Gate, because it was opened of its own accord for the angel and Peter. Then, descending along the earlier and larger street from which the road just mentioned branches off, there is a great gate through which access is open to the broad courtyard of the Temple.

On the right-hand side, toward the south, stands the palace which Solomon is once said to have built [Col. 1087A]. In this palace or building there is a stable of such astonishing and immense capacity that it could hold more than two thousand horses or one thousand five hundred camels.

Beside the same palace the Templar knights have many adjoining buildings, large and spacious, together with the construction of a new and magnificent church, which, when I was there, had not yet been completed. This very extensive house of the Templars also possesses many properties and revenues, both in that land and in other regions. In addition, it gives quite substantial alms to Christ’s faithful and to the poor, though not a tenth as much as the larger hospital gives.

The same house of the Templars also maintains and supports a great many knights for the defense of the Christians’ land. But these men, I do not know through what misfortune, whether falsely or truly as reported by rumor, have been stained with the charge of treacherous deceit. This, however, was plainly demonstrated by that event at Damascus involving King Conrad.

Beside the buildings of these same Templars, toward the east, on the city wall, stood the hospice of Simeon the Just. In his dwelling he is said often to have received, cared for, and supplied food to the blessed Virgin Mary, the mother of the Lord, out of hospitality and friendship. He did so also on that night when, on the following day—namely, the fortieth day after the Nativity of the Lord—he was to present the child himself, together with his mother, in the Temple. Holding and offering the child in his arms at the altar, and recognizing through prophetic inspiration that he was the one whom the ancient fathers had awaited for so many ages with indescribable longing, he proclaimed prophetically: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord,” etc.

In that same house, now converted into a church, blessed Simeon lies buried.

In the crypt below the same church, Christ’s wooden cradle is still preserved and displayed. Opposite this same courtyard of the Temple, toward the north, on the road leading to the Valley of Jehoshaphat, there is a large church built in honor of Saint Anne. In it, by means of a painting, the manner is shown in which, through divine providence and admonition, the blessed Virgin was conceived by her and Joachim, as is more fully read in the *Life of Saint Anne*.

The feast of this holy mother is celebrated there with great solemnity on the day of Saint James the Greater [Col. 1087D]. I myself was also present at it. In the same church a community of nuns serves God—if only they also served him in holiness!

At the exit of the same church, on the right and not far away by a side passage, is that Probatica Pool which, in the time of Jesus, the angel of the Lord was accustomed to stir at certain times. Any sick person who entered the water first after it had been stirred was healed, whatever illness afflicted him.

In Greek, *probaton* means “sheep,” because the entrails of sheep used to be washed there for sacrifices. For this reason the water was especially red, because the victims were cleansed there.

Before this Probatica Pool Jesus restored a wretched and sick man to health after thirty-eight years, saying to him: “Take up your bed and walk,” [Col. 1088A] etc.

From that same street, which rises from the Gate of Jehoshaphat, along the nearest road branching off from this street, on the right, up toward the city wall, is the church built in honor of Saint Mary Magdalene. Jacobite monks are present in this place; we have already said what we know ought to be said about this place and church.

On the aforementioned street, from the Gate of the Valley of Jehoshaphat, one goes straight toward the street leading to Saint Stephen’s Gate. From there, northward, one proceeds toward those threefold—or rather manifold—streets displaying goods of various kinds for sale, and then toward the front of the principal Church of the Holy Sepulchre.

In the middle of that street, I say, there is an ancient stone arch bent over the same street. At this place the blessed Virgin Mary is said to have rested with her happy and blessed offspring, while he was still small and an infant, and to have given him milk there. This event is represented in a painting; consequently, the place has been set apart from public use by a little surrounding structure. Even without a church having been built there, it is venerated and held in honor.

Likewise, on the street rising directly from Saint Stephen’s Gate toward the side of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, not very far from it toward the north, there is a small street. Beside it, in a certain church of the Syrians, rests the sacred body of the holy martyr Chariton [Col. 1088B]. It is devoutly honored there by Syrian monks and, being almost entirely intact, is kept in a certain wooden chest and shown to visiting pilgrims when its lid is raised.

The same holy Father was killed by unbelievers in his monastery situated beside the Jordan River, together with his monks, for confessing the name of Christ, as we reported above.

And so, in describing the venerable places in the holy city of Jerusalem, beginning at the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and making our circuit from David’s Gate until we returned to it again, we have omitted the many chapels and less celebrated churches maintained there by various nations.

For it should be known that there are Greeks, Latins, Alemanni, Hungarians, Scots, Navarrese, Bretons, English, Ruthenians, Bohemians, Georgians, Armenians, Syrians, Jacobites, Syrians, Nestorians, Indians, Egyptians, Copts, Capheturici, etc., and whatever else may be found among peoples of different languages and nations, which it would take too long to enumerate [Col. 1088D].

For the present we bring this description of the earthly Jerusalem to an end. We have set down in the description what we saw there for inspection, and we desire only that God may also deign to admit us to see the heavenly Jerusalem. Amen.

## CHAPTER XIII. The Mass customarily said in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre on the anniversary of the Dedication, concerning the recovery of the city of Jerusalem by the Christians; another Mass for the Transfiguration of the Lord; a prayer in the Mass of the feast of the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary in the Temple; various inscriptions existing in the holy places; conclusion of the work

There follow further matters concerning the Holy Land that are more worthy of knowledge, which we communicate to the devout reader, as it were in addition to what is necessary. They are as follows:

On the Ides of July, the dedication of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. [Col. 1089A] On the same day, the celebrated commemoration of the recovery of the holy city of Jerusalem by the Christians and its rescue from pagan power. In memory of this event, Mass is celebrated on the same day as follows.

**Introit:** “Rejoice, Jerusalem.”

**Kyrie:** “Lord, have mercy.” “Almighty begetting God.”

**Prayer:** Almighty and eternal God, who by your wondrous power rescued your city Jerusalem from the hand of the pagans and handed it over to the Christians, be graciously present to us, we beseech you, so that we who recall the holy solemnity each year with devotion may deserve to attain the joys of the Jerusalem above. Through the Lord, etc.

**Epistle:** “Arise, shine, Jerusalem,” etc.

**Alleluia:** “The day has been sanctified,” with the Gradual: “All from Sheba,” etc.

**Gospel:** “When Jesus entered Jerusalem,” etc.

**Creed:** “I believe in one God.”

**Offertory:** [Col. 1089B] “The right hand of the Lord,” etc.

**Secret:** Graciously receive, we beseech you, holy Lord, almighty Father, this offering which we suppliantly present to you, and make us worthy through its mystery, so that we who celebrate this day because the city of Jerusalem has been rescued from the hand of the pagans may at last deserve to become fellow citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem. Through the Lord, etc.

**Communion:** “Jerusalem, arise,” etc.

May the sacrifice which we have received, Lord, profit us for the salvation of body and soul, so that we who rejoice in the freedom of your city Jerusalem may deserve to become heirs in the heavenly Jerusalem. Through the Lord, etc.

On the eighth day before the Ides of August, the Transfiguration of the Lord is celebrated on Mount Tabor. The Introit and the entire Mass are: “Blessed be the holy,” etc.

**Prayer:** O God, who on this day revealed from heaven your only-begotten Son, wondrously transformed, to the fathers of both Testaments, grant us, we beseech you, through deeds pleasing to you, always to attain the contemplation of his glory, in whom you testified that you were well pleased as his Father. Through the Lord, etc.

**Secret:** Receive, we beseech you, holy Lord, almighty Father, the gifts which we present for the glorious Transfiguration of your Son; and mercifully grant that we may be freed from temporal troubles and joined to eternal joys. Through the Lord, etc.

**Communion:** O God, who consecrated this day through the Transfiguration of your incarnate Word and through the paternal voice sent to him by you, grant, we beseech you [Col. 1090A], that by these divine nourishments we may deserve to be transformed into members of him who commanded these things to be done in his memory, Jesus Christ, your Son, our Lord, who with you, etc.

On the eleventh day before the Kalends of December, the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary in the Temple is celebrated. Hence the following prayer is said in the same temple:

**Prayer:** O God, who willed that the holy Mother of God, the temple of the Holy Spirit, should be presented after three years in this Temple of the Lord, look upon the people devoted to you and grant that we who venerate the feast of her presentation may ourselves be made a temple in which you may deign to dwell. Through the Lord, etc.

There follow certain verses that are read in various places of the holy city. In particular:

**I. On the lintel of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre:**

[Col. 1090B]

Why do you weep, woman? Behold, now you adore the one whom you seek.

You have been deemed worthy to honor me; do not touch me now, living.

**II. Outside, at the entrance to Calvary:**

This distinguished place, Calvary, is held to be holy,

For the leader, the price, the cross, and the cleansing.

That is, the blood of Jesus, the inscription, the sacred water of his body,

Save us, redeem us, protect us, and wash us.

**III. Inside, at the deposition of the Lord:**

From the cross the beloved flesh of God,

Lamented by dear ones, is lifted down;

For the wretched the merciful King suffers this.

**IV. Inside, near the Lord’s burial:**

Christ, wrapped in spices, is laid in the tomb;

The just one is lifted to the heights by the governance of merit;

Humanity rejoices, the spirits tremble, and the whole abyss groans.

The transgression of Adam is remitted when Christ comes.

[Col. 1090C]

**V. Also there, across the middle, as follows:**

While Christ is thus buried beneath the stone of the tomb,

Heaven is opened to humanity for his funeral rites.

**VI. At the place of the Lord’s Nativity:**

Here the light and keenness of angelic power—

Here God was truly born of a Virgin Mother.

**VII. On the lintel of the inner entrance to the Lord’s tomb.**
Christ rising, the place, and the guardian of the tomb,

The angel and the garment were, and remain, witnesses of redemption.

We have set out several other verses in the course of the *History*.

[Col. 1089]

# ANONYMOUS BRIEF ACCOUNT OF THE SACRED WAR

*(Martene, Amplissima Collectio, V, 536, from a manuscript of Florence.)*

## TITLE OF THE FOLLOWING WORK

[Col. 1089D]

That little book contains the history in brief verses:

How Nicaea was captured by the Frankish people,

For which one hundred thousand Franks fell,

Whom Jerusalem struck down, when the prince departed defeated.

[Col. 1090D]

And how more fell through toil, hunger, and war,

Those who conquered illustrious Antioch,

And those who came to Jerusalem, the city of peace,

And drove the Turks from the holy sepulchre of the Lord,

[Col. 1091A]

With the Lord’s help—and established their seat;

Thus the kingdom became renowned,

Suppressing kings and rebellious peoples.

Whoever was slain in this battle of war,

And whoever, as a pilgrim, died from the hardships of the journey,

May be joined to the heavenly citadel of Christ’s army.

This kingdom alone Duke Godfrey held for one year.

For eighteen years Baldwin ruled that city.

These two brothers, worthy of the royal diadem,

Renowned in warfare, strong and feared in battle,

With their small following fought many battles,

Laying low in slaughter the hostile throngs,

And, through God, they were brave against the enemies of Babylon.

They enlarged the kingdom which they then possessed,

[Col. 1092A]

In Christ’s kingdom; now may they be blessed without end.

One of their kinsmen assumed their rule:

Another Baldwin, distinguished for uprightness of conduct,

Who ruled it successfully for fifteen years,

Except for the single year in which he was captive.

Count Fulk of Anjou reigns in place of his father-in-law;

He dies in the thirteenth year of his reign.

After his father, Baldwin the Third, for three years

Was placed over the kingdom, already renowned by his ancestral name.

He compiled this work and also had it written;

May an eternal recompense be granted him.

Here begins the history of Nicaea, or Antioch,

And likewise of illustrious Jerusalem.

# BRIEF ACCOUNT OF THE SACRED WAR

[Col. 1091]

[Col. 1091B]

1. In the year 1907 of the incarnate Word, the peoples of the West, grieving that the holy places at Jerusalem were being profaned by the Gentiles, and that the Turks had already invaded a large part of the boundaries of the Christians, were moved together by one impulse and by many signs shown to them. Encouraged by one another, leaders, counts, the powerful and the humble, rich and poor, free men and slaves, bishops, clerics, monks, old men and young men, even boys and girls—all of one mind, compelled by no one—assemble from every direction: from Spain, Provence, Aquitaine, Brittany, Scotland, England, Normandy, France, Lorraine, Burgundy, Germany, Lombardy, Apulia, and other kingdoms. Marked and armed with the power and sign of the holy cross, they prepare to avenge the injuries done to God upon the enemies of the Christian name. And the more eagerly someone had previously been inclined to practise the warfare of the world, the more readily he now becomes willing to practise the warfare of God. Meanwhile, firm peace is established everywhere; and first they attack the Jews in the cities where they lived, compelling them to believe in Christ. Those unwilling to believe they deprive of their possessions, slaughter, or expel from the cities. Some afterwards return to Judaism.

2. In this army of God the following stood out: Godfrey, duke of Lorraine, and his brothers Eustace and Baldwin; Baldwin, count of Mons; Robert, count of Flanders; Stephen, count of Blois; Hugh, brother of the king of the Franks; Robert, count of Normandy; [Col. 1091D] Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles; and Bohemond, duke of Apulia.

3. The army of God courageously advances against the boundaries of the pagans. Its first battle with them was at the bridge of the river Pharphar, on the ninth day before the Kalends of March, where many Turks were killed.

4. Their second battle was near Nicaea, on the third day before the Nones of March; in it also the pagans were defeated. After Nicaea had been captured, and Laodicea likewise, when there were more than three hundred thousand armed men in the Christian army, such abundance of every kind of thing was available to them that a ram was sold for one coin and an ox scarcely for twelve coins.

[Col. 1092B]

5. When Antioch had been besieged, the Christians were so weakened by the scarcity of everything that scarcely one hundred good horses could be found in the entire army. Nevertheless, although many withdrew because of that desperate shortage and many others returned home, Antioch was captured in the ninth month of the siege. The Christians, in turn besieged by the pagans, were afflicted by such great hunger that scarcely any refrained from human flesh. But they were strengthened by God through the discovery of His lance, unseen since the time of the apostles; with that lance preceding them, the besieged engaged the besiegers on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, and won the victory in this, their third battle.

6. Their fourth battle was in Romania on the Kalends of July, and there the Turks were defeated.

7. Antioch having been entrusted to Duke Bohemond, the Christians, to avoid weariness and hunger, and especially because of disagreements among the princes, set out toward Syria. After conquering the Saracen cities of Marra and Barra, and many castles of the region, they were again afflicted there by such great hunger that they were compelled to eat the already-rotting bodies of Saracens.

8. At God’s command, the army of God proceeded into the interior of Spain [Note: [Col. 1091D] A part of Syria. *Editor.*], and was refreshed by God’s generous hand. For the citizens and castellans of that region sent envoys ahead to them with many gifts, prepared even to surrender their towns or cities to them. The Christians accepted security from them and imposed tribute upon the cities. Meanwhile, many of those who had withdrawn returned to them at Tyre. At length they reached [Col. 1092D] Jerusalem. While they laboured in the siege because of the shortage of provisions and especially of water, all, by common decree, went around the city every day barefoot, praying.

9. On the eighth day of such humiliation, therefore, and on the thirty-ninth day of the siege, Jerusalem was captured on the Ides of July, on a Friday. In Solomon’s Temple and its portico, the Christians engaged the pagans in their sixth battle and raged with such slaughter among them that they rode through the blood of the slain up to the horses’ knees.

10. When it had been arranged who should retain Jerusalem, and the princes were already discussing their return home, behold, the king of the Saracens came to Ascalon to fight them, with one hundred thousand cavalry and four hundred thousand infantry. The army of the Lord met them; it had no more than five thousand cavalry and fifteen thousand infantry. God fought for His servants as they cried out to Him, and a cloud protected them from the heat of the sun. The Saracens, terrified solely by the Christians’ assault, all threw down their arms and fled. In this sixth battle, fought on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, one hundred thousand pagans were slain. At the gate of Ascalon two thousand were suffocated; and the number of those who perished in the sea and those consumed among the thickets of the forests is unknown.

11. With Duke Godfrey elected to rule by those remaining in Jerusalem, the other princes returned home. Jerusalem had been captured approximately [Col. 1093B] four hundred and sixty years after it had been captured and occupied by the Saracens for the second time under the emperor Heraclius. Five years after this, the people of Jerusalem captured the city of Accaron; and in the following year they crushed an innumerable multitude of pagans in a glorious victory.

12. After all these events, in the eighteenth year Baldwin [Note: [Col. 1093] The codex notes in the margin: “This Baldwin was king, the son of Hugh, count of Rethel.”], king of Jerusalem, was captured by the Saracens. At this, losing their senses with grief, they were summoned from every direction and gathered to the number of sixty thousand, intending to exterminate the Christians from their borders. At Ascalon they placed their baggage—namely, their wives, children, and provisions—in safety.

The Christians, placed in desperate straits and having no hope except in God, following the example of the Ninevites, proclaimed a fast for both sexes, even for nursing infants; food was also denied to all the livestock. The day of battle was appointed. Christ’s followers went forth with soldiers and infantry, scarcely numbering three thousand. The princes marched at the front: the patriarch, offering the cross of Christ as a standard, [Col. 1094A] and Pontius, formerly abbot of Cluny, carrying the lance that had pierced Christ’s side. The bishop of Bethlehem carried in a reliquary the milk of Saint Mary, perpetual virgin.

The Saracens, poured out on every side, surrounded the Christians in a circle from all directions, so that no one could escape [variant: *evade*]. While the Christians stood thus in battle order, they saw, with God as their auspice, a brightness suddenly fall from the riven sky upon the pagans. It was not favourable to them but highly destructive, although the Saracens themselves did not see it. Immediately, deprived of all their strength, they were cut down as they fled in every direction—not only by men, but also by boys and women. Seven thousand perished in the battle, and five thousand were drowned in the waters.

13. In the second year after these events, Tyre—called *Sur* in the Hebrew language—the maritime and ancient city of Phoenicia, situated in the heart of the sea, a colony of the Sidonians, the commerce of the sea and the marketplace of the whole world, celebrated in the prophecies of the prophets and renowned in the songs of poets—once indeed an island, but made continuous with the mainland by Nabuchodonosor or Alexander, who brought together many embankments in the narrow strait for its conquest; previously conquered by Nabuchodonosor, partly taken captive, and afterwards utterly destroyed and levelled to the ground by Alexander; but, according to the prophets, rebuilt after seventy years and restored to its former condition—was in our own times, at the end of the world, besieged by Christians by land and sea, captured, and subjected to the rule of Christ.

In the third year after this, Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, was released by the Saracens after a ransom had been paid. In the fourth year after this, the nephew of the aforesaid king was captured by the Saracens and cut in half like a piece of wood.

# VERSES ON THE ILLUSTRIOUS MEN OF THE DIOCESE OF THEROUANNE WHO TOOK PART IN THE HOLY EXPEDITION

*(Marten[e], in the same work, from the manuscript of the most illustrious lord Chauvelin, keeper of the royal seals.)*

[Col. 1093]

[Col. 1093D]

Something remarkable happened in our days at Therouanne,

For which you ought to render immense praises to God,

Who, in His condescension, chose your parishioners,

Whom He made kings and patriarchs of Jerusalem.

First Godfrey; Baldwin was the second,

His brother. After him both ruled in turn,

The sons of Count Eustace, whom noble Ida

Happily gave birth to for all your people’s hope.

Evermarus was the first to sit as patriarch of the Sepulchre;

After him Arnulfus, both natives of Cickes,

Held authority; and before him your archdeacon,

The good, wise, and religious man Achardus.

[Col. 1094D]

Afterwards others held lesser offices of power.

Falkemberg gave you his lord Hugh, who

Obtained the whole region of Tiberias.

Harbel of Ramla became prince of Caesarea.

Eustace, a renowned knight surnamed Gernirs,

And Fulk of Gisnes held the city of Beirut,

In which Baldwin of Boulogne sat as bishop;

And a certain castle called Saint Abraham

Was held by the noble knight Hugh of Rebecq.

These were kings, these pontiffs, these were lords

In Jerusalem and likewise in its territories,

Which your episcopate, Therouanne, sent forth.

# A WEEPING LAMENT FOR THOSE WHO DIED IN THE JERUSALEM EXPEDITION BY VARIOUS DEATHS, INDEED ACCORDING TO GOD’S JUST BUT HIDDEN AND UNSEARCHABLE JUDGMENT

*(Marten[e], in the same work, from the manuscript of Anchin.)*

[Col. 1095]

[Col. 1095A]

Jerusalem, mourn: in the midst of the world’s grief,

Change your soft garments for sackcloth and ashes.

Pour out tears, O Zion, and you, frontiers of the earth;

Illustrious land, sprinkle your cheeks with dust and grieve.

You once knew how to overthrow kingdoms, tribes, and nations.

Alas! Now your savage people rejoices that its necks are being crushed.

How many places, camps, and foreign leaders you subdued—

Behold, you see your own people subdued and oppressed by the enemy.

The voice of the cross thundered and filled land and sea;

The voice of the cross drew countless men to arms.

Leaders fell; the assembled multitude perished,

Many beyond number, like the sand of the sea.

A sluggish and insignificant people before, but now armed with triumphs,

The nation bends the holy places beneath its commands.

Gaul, mother, honour, primacy, glory, splendour

[Col. 1095B]

Of empire, kingdom, warfare, and people—

Tell me where are your ready hand, strength, power, and courage?

Behold, your noble condition has collapsed.

Fame is silent, your glory falls, blasphemy rises.

Your honour, once spread abroad, now everywhere becomes grief.

The heralds of the cross are silent; the enemy’s trumpet resounds.

Night has overcome day, and perfidy faith.

Severe hunger, enduring thirst, and a more violent enemy

Were the cause of death for you, Franks.

And you, lawless Constantinople, guilty through deceit,

Promising obedience, gifts, strength, and resources,

You close the waters and deny the people the goods of the land;

They perish from pestilence, toil, and hunger.

[Col. 1095C]

By artifice and deceit you subject them; subjected by the sword, you will perish.

A monstrous blow and grievous ruin await you.

You Saracens, wicked people and savage enemy;

You Arabs, Turks, enemy people of the cross;

Faithless, full of deceit, polluted by profane custom,

Sunk in a pool of crimes, foul with dregs and filth—

What hope, what confidence sharpened your strength,

So that you did not hesitate to destroy those marked with the cross?

Your custom is to submit, to succumb, to yield to the Franks,

To hasten flight and fear the standards of the cross.

Now rich in spoils, savage with slaughter, proud in triumphs,

You bring back a sure laurel, raging as enemy against enemy.

You compel these men to endure torments, chains, and hardships;

You are drenched in ugly blood by the cruel slaughter of these men.

[Col. 1095D]

Fury sharpens you, anger moves you, pride lifts you up.

You crush submissive necks and trample brave deeds.

You insult your enemies and gladly stamp the earth with your foot.

Alas for the grief! O crime! O shame! Indeed, abomination!

[Col. 1096A]

You wrinkle your nose and stir up a chattering laugh.

You feed on enemy blood like dogs.

“Behold,” you say, “a joyful, serene, health-giving day,”

But for the Frankish kingdom it is sad, bitter, and grievous.

What madness is this? Whence comes it, blind people, that you have grown strong?

Your power is established in nothing here, but in God’s anger.

France, the cross of the Arabs, conqueror of foreigners—

Where now is your former fame, name, and empire?

You were an iron tower, a people invincible to the enemy;

Behold, you lie as prey and plunder for the swift dog.

Unconquered might, enduring strength, unshaken power—

Why and whence do you fall, you who were the glory of the world?

It remains for you to breathe again through faith itself

And to rise again through hope.

To breathe again is pious; to refuse to rise is wicked.

I was mighty Gaul, powerful in sword and hand,

[Col. 1096B]

Now exhausted, I am oppressed and forced down to the depths.

Once secure, powerful, and unconquerable by the enemy,

Now weak and collapsing, I am conquered by the savage enemy.

Beautiful, pleasing, wealthy, vigorous, renowned for triumphs—

My people lie foul, despised, and subdued by calamities.

Fields, regions, towns, and villages are abandoned;

From them my native inhabitants have perished.

The house bereft of its husband weeps; the nursing child without its father;

The people, pressed beneath the yoke, mourn in exile.

Alas for me! Fertile land, beauty, wealth, strength—

You wither, darken, decay, and are overwhelmed.

Once a rejoicing mother, I conceived a burden of grief;

With my womb stretched by its weight, I gave birth in travail.

My offspring are lamentation, complaint, and suffering;

[Col. 1096C]

Behold, my face has swollen with tears.

Alas for those whom I bore: the robber seizes them, the stranger carries them away.

O grievous oppression, a cross for me, punishment for my people.

Light departs, shadow enters; piety grieves, anger exults.

Sweetness is given to gall, and sacred justice to crime.

Right collapses and wickedness rises—a new and wondrous plague;

Harshness confronts the gentle, anger the devout.

Foxes burst forth; mice grow new horns,

While the devouring lion roars and the lamb and sheep tremble.

Parthian, Mede, and Arab insult, provoke, and press hard;

They hiss with the mouth, snarl with the teeth, and shake the head.

Hissing expresses reproach, snarling reveals still more anger,

Head-shaking mockery. What should I pursue, or what should I do?

The honour of the king, the strength of the people, the reverence of the clergy,

[Col. 1096D]

The pontifical crown are forced to endure close constraint.

The sacred order, the lower rank, the mass of the people—

Countless thousands fall in a thousand ways.

The enemy denies them passage, and the road is winding and rugged;

[Col. 1097A]

winter, heat, and a harmful wind grievously torment them.

Hostile deceit oppresses, fury afflicts, anger exhausts.

Bitter pestilence strikes; lamentation resounds everywhere.

Hunger compels them to eat horseflesh;

Thirst, parched, compels them to lick the earth of a ditch.

Man devours man, and flesh devours flesh; enemy feeds enemy—

Alas for the unlawful gluttony!

Whatever the fleeing, feeble generation possesses, it abandons;

The poor man leaves his possessions; the stronger man takes up arms.

Overcome by the labour of flight, grave, anxious, and slow old age

Offers itself to the swords and joins both hands.

One part, consumed by hunger; another, by air,

Disease, and thirst, breathes out its life.

The strong and healthy are dragged along; the wanderer, exile, and outlaw are dragged along;

[Col. 1097B]

The sick man and the old man collapse beneath the sword.

Slaughtered bodies lie unburied in waterless places,

Left scattered as food for winged wild beasts.

Few are covered with earth; blood flows through land and sea;

The fields are drenched, the waters are stained.

The tongue is silent; evils are joined to evils, and no number of ears can contain them.

To know each thing is grief; to recount them all is toil.

Mother Gaul, I grieve over these things; the world grieves with me.

I lament so many losses inflicted upon me—and that God permits them.

Christ, be mountain, wall, right hand, and tower to the holy places;

give hope, bring help, and look upon the disgrace of the cross.

May that savage enemy not long exult over the enemy,

[Col. 1098A]

But, with his horn broken, may he feel the weapons of the cross.

The glory of the Franks once conceived honour,

But, heavy in labour, gave birth—and gave birth to grief.

It was a wondrous thing when glory, while giving birth to the summit of honour,

Collapsed in labour and became the cause of grief.

The mountains are in labour, and pride has given birth to mice.

The mountain falls, the heights collapse, and many perish in blood.

This hungry army is reduced to nothing.

Wash away our sins, O God, and cleanse them, O Christ.

The Greek destroys us by his hunger as he hungers;

He seizes and ravages us, striking us with his harsh hand.

By cunning and hunger the Greek destroys us who are hungry,

and the Parthians devastate the weakened with the sword.

While we suffer hunger, we experience hostile enemies.

As food fails, we find few friends.

The illustrious people are wholly deceived once bread is taken away.

[Col. 1098B]

The glory of the Franks, the fear of the enemy, and the arms of your people—

Pious nation, celebrated people, once famous for triumphs—

Now, through the treacheries of the Greeks, you suffer evil,

And sword and hunger undeservedly; while enemies feast upon enemies.

Who will rejoice now? Not I, while Gaul mourns.

All Gaul grieves, while I do also; the wicked people rejoice,

And exult while it presses upon such great forces.

The evil people of the Parthians, the savage multitude of the Medes—

The Elamites sell and buy the empire of life.

Glory may weep; glory does not benefit us.

Glory is worn down by mourning, like a flower without fruit.

# ON THE ORIGINS AND DISCOVERY OF THE SACRED RELIGION OF JERUSALEM

*(Monasticon Anglicanum, vol. II, p. 489, from an old manuscript belonging to Gilbert North, esquire, in the year 1652.)*

[Col. 1097C]

Until now there has been great uncertainty among most people concerning where, and from whom, the Hospital of Jerusalem took its origin. Some, introducing empty dreams, seem to have fabricated ravings rather than truth; for they joined together ancient histories widely separated from one another with a kind of contrived glue. I have no desire to relate their vain tales here. Rather, I shall bring forward the truth of the matter: what I have been able to extract from the sacred annals, and what I have been able to attain by conjecture and reason, without placing before the reader a prearranged account.

I consider that the sacred religion of Jerusalem began in this way. After Alexander Philip, king of the Macedonians, had died, and after the people had proclaimed, through the efforts of the Maccabees, the city of Jerusalem freed from profane nations [the text is corrupt: “to a. p. and liberty”], [Col. 1098C] great wars were waged by neighbouring kings against Jerusalem. At length, when the Lord willed it, and the Maccabee had reclaimed the city, the citadel, and the Temple from the profaned hands of the nations, it became necessary to go out again to wage war. After first putting affairs in the city of Jerusalem in order, the Maccabee set out against the enemy with a large force.

When many of God’s people had fallen by the sword and many had been weakened by wounds, the Maccabee is said to have established in the city of Jerusalem a *xenodocheion*, that is, a pious place for the weak; and he sent to that place great quantities of silver and gold drachmas, to expiate the souls of the dead. He decreed that it should thereafter be a refuge for the wretched and an expiation for the dead.

[Col. 1099A]

As the years passed, and the religious institution of the renowned Maccabee was being enlarged, the time of our salvation was reached. Jesus Christ Himself did not disdain a humble lodging and displayed great works of piety. Since He certainly possessed nothing, saying, “The birds of the sky have nests, and the foxes have dens, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head,” we may reasonably suppose that He Himself inhabited this place. For if He instructed His disciples to hold everything in common and not to be anxious about the following day; if He wished His disciples to be without sandals and without a purse, who would doubt that the Master, teaching such things, possessed everything in common and inhabited a humble place?

[Col. 1099B]

Strengthened by these considerations, we may confidently say that this common and humble place was the dwelling of the heavenly Emperor. Here the Master washed the feet of His disciples and made them priests, and here He left the memory of His most precious body. Here He gave Peter authority over the Church and the keys. Here was the end of the Old Testament and the beginning of the New. From this place [*acenti*, sic; the reading is unclear] Christ departed toward His glorious Passion, so that the redemption of our flesh might be accomplished. Here, after His Passion, the disciples, taking refuge with His mother Mary, were permitted to receive the revelation of the wondrous Resurrection; and after forty days they received the promised Holy Spirit. Here, after the glorious Ascension, the first holy council was held [Col. 1099C] and the symbol of the faith was composed by the Twelve.

When the glorious princes of the Christian faith had divided the provinces among themselves for preaching, they chose seven men to care for the poor and the Hospital, and appointed Stephen, the first martyr, over them. Because the glorious precursor of the New Law, John the Baptist, had recently been beheaded by Herod while preaching Christ’s baptism, and because everyone admired the testimony of his life; and because he had been born in these places and raised there until his infancy, they named him patron of the Hospital in honour of his venerable memory.

Later, when opinion of the faith had become widespread among men, many people contributed to the society of the Lord’s poor disciples. In order to become participants in their prayers, they sold their possessions and laid the proceeds at the apostles’ feet, living a common life with them.

But as devotion to the Christian faith increased, the resources of this sacred house multiplied greatly. Soldiers were therefore hired and appointed to protect them, so that, under Brother Raymond, by whom the Rule was later established, they might guard the resources of the Hospital and repel the pagans. The priests themselves, occupied with the sacred mysteries and preaching, could not perform the tasks which the soldiers carried out.

But when the soldiers, driven by greed, had become so madly arrogant that they claimed to be the custodians of the Hospital’s resources and neglected the priests, [Col. 1099D] [Col. 1100A] it was accordingly decreed that the soldiers themselves should become members of the Hospital and defend the Christian religion. Hence they also began, as fighters for the name of Christ, to wear a cross upon their breast.

Later, as perfidy increased in the East and faith declined, it happened that, after the Hospital had been occupied by the Saracens, Christ’s soldiers were scattered everywhere. When they no longer had any place of refuge at Acre and in Syria, they were forced to put out to sea. Their first voyage was to Cyprus, the island near Jerusalem. There, received by Christian princes, they did not cease fighting against profane nations for Christ’s name.

After many years, the island of Rhodes rebelled against the people of Constantinople. Since the latter were unable to bring the island under their authority because of the immense forces of the Rhodians, [Col. 1100B] they permitted the Jerusalemite soldiers to occupy it. The soldiers, with prepared hands and assembled forces, sailed to Rhodes and brought it under their power within a short space of time. Fortified by a double defence, from Cyprus and Rhodes they waged—and continue to wage—wars against the enemies of our faith.

## How the House of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem Was First Established by the Will of Our Lord Jesus Christ

We make known to all present and future that the house of the Hospital of Saint John the Baptist and of the poor of Jerusalem was begun at the beginning, in the time of the first Julius Caesar, Roman emperor, and in the time of Antiochus, prince of Antioch. May He who made all things, and His blessed Son, send us the Holy Spirit, who are all three one, to our assistance, so that we may be able to speak and render this from Latin into grammatical Latin, in such a way and manner that praise may be given to the aforesaid Saint John the Baptist.

[Col. 1100C]

At the aforesaid time there was a certain priest, lord over the other priests in Jerusalem, named Melchiar. He broke open David’s tomb and extracted from it a great treasure, namely gold and precious garments that had been placed there by other kings after King David. Because of this deed, the said Melchiar was accused before the prince of Antioch, who at that time was lord and duke in Jerusalem by order of Julius [Col. 1100D] Caesar.

Antiochus was greatly disturbed by this and considered within himself how he might administer justice more honourably for the theft described above. On the following second night, while lying in bed, he thought deeply about what he should do concerning the matter. After he had thought sufficiently, sleep overcame him; then an angel took his spirit and carried him over Mount Calvary.

There the King of kings appeared to him and said: “Antiochus, do not lay hands upon this holy priest, and do not shed his blood, for in this place which I shall show you, you and he must build a house of piety and mercy, common to all the poor who come there. And I command you, Melchiar, that the entire treasure which was taken from David’s tomb [Col. 1101A] be placed in the building of the dwelling for the poor, for the Holy Spirit breathes where He wills.”

That same night He revealed Himself to the holy priest Melchiar and said to him: “Go before Mount Calvary, and wherever you find a foundation already built, build me there a strong and solid house, for many dwellings of nations will be received in it, because whoever receives the poor receives me.”

When the priest descended from Mount Calvary at dawn, he met the prince, and they began to speak with one another about how our Lord Jesus Christ had shown each of them the good path. What our Lord had shown them pleased them greatly and pleased their entire council. That holy priest offered himself and [Col. 1101B] all that he had found of the treasure in David’s tomb for the construction of the said sacred house, in order to serve the poor for all time, as is found written in the Book of the Maccabees.

When Judas Maccabee saw and understood clearly that it was a good thing to pray for the dead, he sent twelve silver drachmas to Jerusalem, to be offered to the Hospital of the poor, so that they might pray for the dead; and Melchiar was pleased to establish brothers to serve the poor of the dwelling.

In that sacred house of which we have spoken, many poor and sick people came from every part of the world. They were received and treated kindly for the sake of the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ. When the aforesaid prince of Antioch died, he donated a large part of his possessions to the sacred house of Jerusalem mentioned above.

[Col. 1101C]

We make known to you a great miracle, which all who believe in God ought to hear. Our Lord Jesus Christ appeared one day to the prophet Zachariah, when he was offering sacrifice to God. At that hour the Son of God appeared to him and said: “Melchiar, your brother has departed from this world, and his soul is in paradise. Therefore I command you, your son, and your wife to come to Jerusalem and serve me and my poor until Julian of Rome comes to Jerusalem.”

When Zachariah had completed the sacrifice that he was offering to God, he was partly very joyful and partly greatly astonished. When he came to his house, he told his wife and son, weeping, [Col. 1101D] what the Lord had commanded them. All three gave thanks to God, and as soon as they could, they went to Jerusalem. They surrendered themselves and their possessions to God and to the Hospital of the poor, and served the aforesaid Hospital very kindly and for a long time.

Another great miracle also occurred. The Roman emperor Accamanus, with certain other honourable men, was seeking to receive homage from the Jews. When they were at sea near an island of Crete called Rhochas, the stern of their ship broke apart, and everyone who was aboard was lost except Julian the Roman, who was carried safely to land [Col. 1102A] by the Son of God. When Julian saw the misfortune that had occurred, he asked the Lord: “Who are you who have drawn me out of this danger?” Our Lord answered him and said: “I am the Son of God, who has appointed you Hospitaller of the house of the poor of Jerusalem, and in the future I shall come bodily to that house.” And He blessed him.

Julian gladly received the blessing of our Lord and came to Jerusalem to Saint Zachariah, where Zachariah himself and the other brothers received him as a father.

Afterwards, when our Lord came into the world for the salvation of the human race and wished to reveal His glory to the people, He called His apostles and disciples. He came to Jerusalem, as He had foretold through the Holy [Col. 1102B] Spirit to the overseers of the Hospital’s dwelling. Being then physically present as a man, He performed a miracle before His disciples, and He brought salvation to souls through the apostles.

God, who had done great good for this house and had Himself wished to reveal Himself to them, extended His hands over His apostles and the poor of the aforesaid dwelling. Then He said: “Whoever honours you honours me, and whoever receives you receives me. Cursed be the man who despises one of them.”

We make known that this is the dwelling in which our Lord said to that wise man: “You shall love God with all your heart and with all your thought,” and many other things, according to what is found in the Gospel.

This is also the house in which the apostles hid themselves and shut the doors [Col. 1102C] for fear of the Jews, when our Lord Jesus Christ was crucified. In this holy house the Virgin Mary and Saint John the Evangelist came to our Lord when He was on the cross for us sinners, and He said to Saint John: “Behold your mother.” Afterwards He said to His mother: “Behold your son.”

This is also the Hospital house in which Jesus came on the eighth day after His resurrection. With the doors closed, He entered among His disciples and said to them: “Peace be with you.” He showed them His hands and His breast; but Thomas was not with them when Jesus came.

The disciples came to Saint Thomas and said to him: “We have seen our Lord.” [Col. 1102D] Thomas answered and said: “I do not believe. I do not touch and see the holes of the nails in His hands and feet, and I will put my hand into His breast.”

About eight days later, as Saint John the Evangelist testifies, when the disciples were in this holy house and Saint Thomas was with them, Jesus came with the doors shut and said: “Peace be with you.” He said to Thomas: “Put your finger here into the holes in my hands and my side, and do not be unbelieving but faithful.”

And in that holy house Saint Thomas recognized his Creator. Our Lord said to him: “Because you have seen me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.”

At the same time Ananias and Sapphira renounced [Col. 1103A] the world and gave themselves to the fellowship of Christ and His disciples. Because they did not return to God, to the sacred house of the Hospital, and to the poor what they possessed, and did not bring it to the disciples’ feet, they died a sudden death. Saint Peter did not permit their bodies to be placed in the cemetery; rather, he had them buried outside, as excommunicated persons.

At the time when God sent us His apostles and disciples to preach, they were elders, including Saint Stephen, who was the first martyr, and Philip the protomartyr, Nichauome, Thymocenn Permanan, and Nicholas of Antioch. These men guarded the houses of the Hospital and served the poor by the command of our Lord Jesus Christ.

At that time many different peoples were in the same place: [Col. 1103B] sometimes Greeks, sometimes Caryseni, who held the city of Jerusalem and the Promised Land. Nevertheless, although the said house was in great poverty, they received the poor and the sick.

And when at last the Saracens took possession of the house of Jerusalem and the Greeks lost it, a servant of Jesus Christ named Conrad guarded the sacred house of the Hospital. The alms that were given to him by the Saracens he himself gave to the poor, and he served them kindly.

At that time, when it pleased God that the Christians should possess the Promised Land, Godfrey of Bouillon and a great multitude of barons and pilgrims, who had been equipped through divine grace [Col. 1103C] and preaching, came through long stretches of land, across mountains and valleys, and through the land of Romania, to Antioch. They besieged it and, by the power of God, captured it. There they slew a great multitude of the perfidious Saracens. From there they went on to the city of Tripoli and captured it. Afterward they captured Acre, and from there they went to the land of Jerusalem. In their army they suffered such great hunger that they scarcely had bread to eat.

Then Conrad, who served the poor of the Hospital of Jerusalem, three or four times each day placed bread in the fold of his garment and threw bread over the walls of the city toward the Christians in place of stones. This Conrad, who guarded the poor of the Hospital, was accused before the sultan [Col. 1104A] by the Saracens who guarded the walls. The sultan ordered the Saracens who had accused him to seize him and bring him to the sultan with all the bread whenever he threw bread to the Christians; otherwise he would not believe them.

Then one day Conrad—or Gerard—did as he was accustomed, throwing bread to the Christians. The Saracens seized him with the bread that he had in his garment and brought him before the sultan. When the Saracens showed the bread to the sultan, that bread, by the power of God, became a stone. When the sultan saw the malice of the Saracens, he allowed Conrad to remain free and ordered him to continue, without fear, to provide for the Christians as he had been accustomed to do. When Conrad, or Gerard, heard this, every day he threw bread to God’s Christians.

[Col. 1104B] Godfrey of Bouillon remained with his army before Jerusalem for so long that he captured the city and slew many Saracens. He rejoiced greatly over the victory that God had granted them, and they came to the Holy Sepulchre of Our Lord, singing and giving thanks to God. Afterward they went to all the other places.

Then the barons divided the possessions of Jerusalem and gave the aforesaid Conrad, or Gerard, master of the Hospital of Jerusalem, a large share of the possessions, in honor of Saint John the Baptist, patron of that Hospital. Thereafter, during the time of the aforesaid master Conrad, or Gerard, God greatly increased the said establishment of the Hospital with revenues, possessions, and lordships throughout the kingdom of Jerusalem. [Col. 1104C] When Conrad died, his soul went to paradise. Brother Raymond du Puy was appointed in his place, and, for the praise of God, he built villages, residences, and castles; he greatly improved the establishment with substantial possessions.

That brother Raymond established the statutes of the Hospital, which are still observed in that same house, and its Rule; and he had it confirmed by Pope Innocent II, etc.

May God, Creator of all things, deliver the brothers of the Hospital from every evil and from their sins, and grant them the grace of coming to heavenly glory with all their benefactors. Amen.

[Col. 1105]

# Cartulary of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre of Jerusalem

Published from the Vatican manuscripts by M. Eugène de Rozière, professor at the École des Chartes, author of the *Formulae Andegavenses*, published from the Weingarten manuscript, currently at Fulda, and of the *Numismatics of the Latin Kings of Cyprus*. Printed by authorization of the government at the Imprimerie nationale. — 1849.

## Introduction

### I

The Church of the Holy Sepulchre, also called the Church of the Resurrection of Our Lord, has always been one of the most celebrated and most venerated churches in the Christian world. Built by Saint Helena and Constantine, it became the seat of the patriarch of Jerusalem and the metropolitan church of all the churches subject to that pontiff’s jurisdiction.

The conquests of the Crusaders, armed to liberate the tomb of Jesus Christ, made it more than ever the object of a particular devotion. Kings, princes, lords, and bishops of the new states founded in the East eagerly vied with one another to adorn and enrich it; the sovereigns and prelates of Europe who had been unable to visit it wished at least to demonstrate their respect through their gifts; and the popes watched with jealous care over the preservation of its goods and the maintenance of its privileges.

It is the evidence of this universal veneration, and the succession of these pious benefactions during the period of Latin rule in Syria, that the cartulary of the Holy Sepulchre contains.
