The number of acts of which it is composed, the famous names encountered on every page, and the information that may be drawn from it concerning political geography, the condition of persons and lands, and the religious organization of the kingdom of Jerusalem make it one of the most curious and complete monuments of the history of the Crusades.

### II

The accusations directed against cartularies by Father Hardouin [Note: [Col. 1105] The manuscript work of Father Hardouin is preserved in the Bibliothèque nationale.] and by the writers who, in the previous century, had systematically constituted themselves the enemies of religious communities [Note: [Col. 1105] Simon, *History of the Origin of Ecclesiastical Revenues*, vol. I. — *Memoirs of the Clergy*, vol. VI.] are well known. The authors of the *New Treatise on Diplomatics* answered them victoriously, and their conclusions are accepted by all sound minds.

Today, above all, now that there is no longer any question of attributing an authentic character to cartularies and admitting them as means of proof in court, no one hesitates to recognize that the historian finds in these collections a multitude of pieces of information that he would seek in vain [Col. 1107] elsewhere. Several scholars have consulted them with great benefit [Note: [Col. 1107] See especially the use that Brussel and Chantereau-Lefebvre made of the cartulary of Champagne.]; and the new impetus received by historical studies naturally gave rise to the idea of collecting and publishing those bequeathed to us by our old abbeys [Note: [Col. 1107] The care of this collection has been entrusted to M. Guérard; the first seven volumes have already appeared.].

Accordingly, I do not intend to revive an extinguished war or undertake a now-useless refutation. I wish only to show that the particular circumstances in which the cartulary of the Holy Sepulchre was compiled ought to cause it to be accorded complete credibility, and would place it beyond suspicion even if the criticisms directed against cartularies in general still retained some force.

I acknowledge that, in the absence of any positive evidence, it is impossible to determine precisely the date of its compilation. The age of the manuscripts, which I shall try to establish below, cannot guide us, because these manuscripts are probably only copies of earlier transcriptions. One may nevertheless affirm that the collection of the documents contained in the cartulary of the Holy Sepulchre was not completed before the second half of the thirteenth century, since it contains the oath of fidelity sworn around 1240 by the abbot of Saint Mary Latin to Patriarch Robert.

Now Jerusalem and all the inland cities had already fallen into the power of the Saracens, and the Christians possessed only the coastal cities. Is it probable that the canons of the Holy Sepulchre fabricated false acts in order to create titles of ownership for themselves in countries occupied by the enemy? Yet this is what one would have to suppose if one attacked the authority of their cartulary, in which we see that the greater part of their estates was situated in or around the city of Jerusalem.

### III

It was a manuscript brought from the East by Philip of Maizières, chancellor of the king of Cyprus, that made the cartulary of the Holy Sepulchre known in Europe. This manuscript, which became the property of Paul Petau, passed into the library of Queen Christina and from there into that of the Vatican [Note: [Col. 1107] The celebrated library of the queen of Sweden had been composed, for the most part, of manuscripts belonging to the Petau family. After the queen’s death, this library was purchased by Pope Alexander VIII, who gave several hundred manuscripts to his nephew, Cardinal Ottoboni, and united the rest with the Vatican Library, where they still form a distinct collection. (Arckenholtz, *Memoirs Concerning Christina, Queen of Sweden*, vols. I and II, passim. — Blume, *Iter Italicum*, vol. III. — Paulin Paris, *Catalogue of French Manuscripts*, vol. IV.)].

While it was still in France, André Duchesne made several excerpts from it for his own works. These excerpts, preserved in the Bibliothèque nationale [Note: [Col. 1107] Cartulary Collection, no. 195. — Duchesne Collection, vol. 56.], successively served Du Cange for his still-unpublished *History of the Families of Outremer*, Father Helyot for his *History of the Monastic Orders*, and M. Count Beugnot for his edition of the *Assizes of Jerusalem*.

### IV

These four scholars are, so far, the only ones who have made use of the cartulary of the Holy Sepulchre. If it has not been consulted more often, this is chiefly because its contents, and even its existence, were generally unknown.

M. Count Beugnot, led by the nature of his work to study it in detail, soon recognized all the historical interest it presents. He published most of the excerpts copied by André Duchesne [Note: [Col. 1107] *Assizes of Jerusalem*, vol. II, in the Appendix.], adding the following reflections, which I am pleased to reproduce:

> “If Father Paoli rendered a genuine service to scholarship by printing the diplomatic code of the Hospitallers of Saint John of Jerusalem, it is certain that the publication of the Cartulary of the Holy Sepulchre would be no less welcomed by scholars concerned with the history or jurisprudence of the Middle Ages . . . . . We did not think of inserting in our Appendix a historical monument whose publication would require much labor, time, and space . . . . . But from Duchesne’s excerpt we have drawn fifty-two unpublished charters, all of which provide information about the condition of persons and the transmission of property among the Latins—information that one would seek in vain in the law books. It is to be hoped that this partial publication will induce some scholar to produce a complete one [Note: [Col. 1107] *Assizes of Jerusalem*, vol. II, Preface.].”

### V

This opinion, expressed by so competent a judge, first gave me the idea for the work I offer to the public. I first had to search for the manuscript of Philip of Maizières; I found it in the Vatican Library, Vatican Collection, no. 7241 [Note: [Col. 1107] It is known that the Vatican Library is divided into five distinct collections: 1. the old collection, or properly speaking the Vatican Collection; 2. the Queen of Sweden Collection; 3. the Ottobonian Collection; 4. the Palatine Collection; 5. the Urbino Collection. The manuscript of the cartulary of the Holy Sepulchre, originating in Christina’s library, ought naturally to be found in the Queen’s Collection; indeed, it certainly originally formed part of it, since Montfaucon saw it there and recorded it under no. 1340 (*Bibliotheca Bibliothecarum*, p. 44). But there are several examples of manuscripts which, in the internal rearrangements of the Vatican Library, were removed from the Queen’s Collection and incorporated into the Vatican Collection proper.].

Its identity cannot be doubted, for these words are written on the flyleaf: “This book belongs to Lord Philip of Maizières, chancellor of the kingdom of Cyprus.” It is a small quarto, bound in white parchment, consisting of 158 parchment folios, written in a fourteenth-century hand. It contains 184 documents, a number that must be reduced to 181 because three of them were repeated by the copyist.

In the same library and collection, under no. 4947, I found another manuscript of the cartulary, a small folio of 129 parchment folios, written in a very regular and careful fourteenth-century hand [Note: [Col. 1109] The history of this manuscript is connected with the vicissitudes undergone, before its entry into the Vatican, by one of the most celebrated libraries in Italy, of which it originally formed part. I hope to be excused for entering into some details on this subject, which may interest bibliography and are generally unknown in France. Marcel Cervino, who became pope in 1555 under the name Marcel II, founded this library. At his death he left it to his secretary Sirleto, who, after being raised to the cardinalate, considerably increased the collection that had been bequeathed to him. Sirleto’s library, generously opened to the public and consulted with benefit by Baronius, Panvinius, and other writers, who called it the Sirletiana, was purchased after the death of its learned owner by Cardinal Ascanio Colonna. It then took the name Colonnese; and it was in the palace of that illustrious family that Father Sirmond and Antonio Possevino saw it. Difficulties arising after the cardinal’s death over the settlement of his estate forced his heirs to sell his library. It became the property of Duke Altaëmps, who had the finest apartments of his palace prepared to receive it; there it bore the name Altaempsiana and was visited by Holsten, Suárez, the Bollandists, and the Roman editors of the Greek-Latin Councils. During the vicissitudes it had undergone, this rich collection had several times nearly been transported away from Rome. Philip II, king of Spain, and Cardinal Federico Borromeo had in turn made efforts to acquire it. Pope Paul V, therefore, fearing that it might one day pass into the hands of a foreigner, forced Duke Altaëmps to surrender one hundred of the principal manuscripts, which he united with the pontifical library established several years earlier by Sixtus V in the Vatican rooms. The cartulary of the Holy Sepulchre was one of the hundred manuscripts chosen by Paul V. Thus, under the reign of that pontiff, it left the library successively owned by Marcel Cervino, Sirleto, Colonna, and Altaëmps, to be incorporated into the Vatican Library. The Altaempsiana Library was later sold to Cardinal Ottoboni, who became pope under the name Alexander VIII; it remained in the Ottoboni family, whose name it definitively retained, until the reign of Benedict XIV, who purchased it in order to unite it with the other collections of the Vatican. While it was still the property of the Ottoboni family, it was enriched, as I stated in one of the preceding notes, by some of Queen Christina’s manuscripts and received, among other illustrious visitors, Dom Montfaucon. Mabillon had consulted it a few years earlier, during the brief interval between the death of Duke Altaëmps and its acquisition by Cardinal Ottoboni. (Mabillon, *Iter Italicum*. — Montfaucon, *Bibliotheca bibliothecarum*. — Arckenholtz, *Memoirs Concerning Christina, Queen of Sweden*, vol. II, p. 322. — Ruggieri, *Historical Memoirs of the Ottobonian Library*.)].

This manuscript is far from being as complete as the preceding one. It contains scarcely anything except the diplomas issued by kings, bishops, and the principal lords; the compiler generally neglected the charters of ordinary individuals. The number of documents it contains is 97, of which only 4 are not duplicates of pieces contained in no. 7241. By joining these 4 documents to the 181 in the first manuscript, I obtained the number 185, which in my edition constitutes the cartulary as a whole.

I shall mention only in passing a third manuscript, also found in the Vatican Library, Ottobonian Collection, no. 985. It is not, strictly speaking, a manuscript, but merely a modern copy of no. 4947 [Note: [Col. 1109] This is the copy that Duke Altaëmps had made when he was compelled to surrender his manuscript to Paul V. The following note, placed at the head of this copy, leaves no doubt on the matter: “One of the codices of the Altaempsiana Library, taken by the royal hand of Paul V, but now most faithfully transcribed from the originals at his own expense by Giovanni Angelo, Duke of Altaëmps, so that the aforesaid library might not lack a possession already so honorably acquired.”].

### VI

I have little to say about the plan I followed. Manuscript 7241, which naturally had to provide my principal text, was copied with the greatest fidelity; I have designated it by the letter A. Manuscript 4947 supplied me with numerous but unimportant variants; I have designated it by the letter B. As for manuscript 985 and André Duchesne’s excerpts, they could obviously be of no use to me.

I long hesitated to print the documents in the order in which manuscript 7241 presents them. It seemed more rational to restore them to chronological order. What made me abandon this plan was that the compiler of the cartulary appears to have wished to follow a certain method of classification.

In the first part of his work, he generally arranged the charters according to the dignity of the persons, beginning with the diplomas of popes, patriarchs, and kings, ending with those of ordinary individuals, and placing together those concerning the same locality. I admit that he did not always remain faithful to this system, and that in the second part of the cartulary pieces of every kind are accumulated somewhat at random. But I recognized the original intention that directed him, and I wished to respect it.

### VII

I have one duty of gratitude remaining, toward Monsignor Lauriani and Monsignor Molza, custodians of the Vatican Library [Col. 1111]. Their extreme kindness enabled me to complete in a short time the various tasks that had brought me to Rome; one would have thought that by their eagerness they wished to protest against the reproaches so often directed at Italian librarians. I earnestly desire that the expression of my gratitude may reach them in the refuge to which the revolutions may perhaps have forced them to flee.

June 1849.

# Privileges of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre of Jerusalem

## I

[Note: [Col. 1111] This charter is found in manuscript A, on the verso of the flyleaf; it is missing from manuscript B.]  
[Without rubric.]

[Col. 1111A]

I, Peregrinus, abbot of Saint Mary of the Latins, from this hour henceforth shall be faithful to the holy Church of Jerusalem, and to Lord Robert, patriarch of that same church, and to his canonically appointed successors.

I shall not participate in counsel or action by which they might lose life or limb, or be taken in an evil captivity. I shall disclose to no one, to their detriment, any counsel that they reveal to me either personally, through a messenger, or by letter.

I shall be an assistant in defending and retaining the patriarchate of the Church of Jerusalem and the rules of the holy fathers against all persons, saving my own order. I shall not alienate the property of my church, nor newly enfeoff anyone with it. When summoned to a synod, I shall come, [Col. 1111B] unless prevented by a canonical impediment.

I shall treat honorably, both on their going and return, the messengers [Note: [Col. 1111] Correct to *nuncios*.] of the Church of Jerusalem and of the lord patriarch whom I recognize as trustworthy, and I shall assist them in their needs. Each year I shall visit the threshold of the Church of Jerusalem, either personally or through a reliable messenger, unless I am released by their permission.

And this I promise before you, Lord Arnold, bishop of Lydda, vicar of the aforesaid lord patriarch, in his name and in that of the holy Church of Jerusalem. So may God and these holy Gospels of God help me.

## II

[Note: [Col. 1111] A, folio 1 recto; missing from B.]  
[Without rubric.]

To the archbishops, bishops, and other prelates, and to all the faithful of Christ established in the kingdom of Thessalonica [Col. 1111C] to whom this letter may come, William, by the mercy of God humble prior of the Church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, together with the chapter of that same church, sends sincere prayers in Christ.

We wish your entire community to know that, recognizing the prudence and honesty of the bearer [Note: [Col. 1111] Correct to *latoris*.] of this letter, our beloved canon N., we have appointed him prior and administrator of all our houses and possessions that we hold in the kingdom of Thessalonica and of the others in Romania that are not subject to our house at Constantinople.

We add this provision, however: neither he nor the other administrators of our houses shall have power to sell, pledge, or uselessly alienate slaves, female slaves, or other possessions of the church. Therefore, if any such act has been performed by one of us without the consent of the chapter, it shall have no validity. We ask, therefore, that none of you grant your writings [Col. 1112B] or seal in such matters.

We have also given him authority to make brothers and sisters whom he sees to be useful and expedient for the church. Finally, we beseech your piety that, for love of the Crucified, you may be willing to offer the aforesaid prior N. your counsel and assistance in whatever he may need, bearing in mind that we continually entreat the Lord on behalf of all the faithful, and especially on behalf of our benefactors.

## III

[Note: [Col. 1111] A, folio 1 recto; missing from B.]  
### Letter of William, Prior, and the Chapter of the Holy Sepulchre

William, by the mercy of God humble prior of the Lord’s Sepulchre, together with the same chapter, sends fraternal love in the Lord to all the brothers established in the obediences of the Lord’s Sepulchre at N.

Recognizing the fidelity and discretion of the bearer of this letter, our beloved canon N., we appoint him prior of the houses, possessions, and everything that we hold at N., [Col. 1113A] charging him that, if anything has been destroyed, he should recover it as far as he can, and direct everything entrusted to him for the benefit of our church and the honor of the Lord.

We inform you, however, that neither he nor the other administrators of our houses shall have power to sell, pledge, or uselessly alienate slaves, female slaves, or other possessions of the church. Therefore, if anything [Note: [Col. 1113] Correct to *quid*.] of this sort has been done by one of us without the mandate of the chapter, know that it is void and lacks all force. None of you, moreover, should presume to lend consent or testimony to such excesses.

We have given the same N., the prior [Note: [Col. 1113] Correct to *priori*, “to the prior.”], authority to make brothers and sisters whom he sees to be useful and expedient for the church. We command you, by virtue of obedience, that when you have seen this letter, you render manual obedience to the aforesaid [Col. 1113B] prior, showing him the reverence due to him.

Finally, we admonish you to keep the Lord before your eyes through good works, so that you may pass from the miseries of this life to the joys of eternal happiness.

## IV

[Note: [Col. 1113] A, folio 1 verso; missing from B.]  
### On the Obedience That Maurus, Abbot of the Temple of the Lord, Rendered to the Church of the [Holy] Sepulchre

I, Maurus, abbot to be blessed of the Church of the Temple of the Lord, from this hour henceforth shall be faithful and obedient to the holy Church of Jerusalem, to my lord patriarch R[obert], and to his canonically appointed successors.

I shall not participate in counsel or action by which he might lose life or limb, or be taken captive, [Col. 1113C] nor by which the Church of the Temple of the Lord might be separated from its jurisdiction and obedience to the Church of Jerusalem.

I shall disclose to no one [Note: [Col. 1113] Correct to *nulli*.], to their detriment, any counsel that he reveals to me personally [or through a] messenger. I shall assist in defending and retaining the patriarchate of the Church of Jerusalem and the things belonging to it, saving my own order, against all persons.

When summoned to a synod, I shall come, unless prevented by a canonical impediment. I shall treat his messenger, whom I recognize as a trustworthy messenger, honorably on his going and return. So may God and these holy Gospels help me.

## IX

[Note: [Col. 1113] A, folio 3 verso; missing from B.]  
[Without rubric.]

[Col. 1114A]

After Antioch had been captured, the bishop of Le Puy, legate of the Apostolic See, using the prudent counsel of the leading men, established a boundary between the kingdom of Jerusalem and the principality of Antioch, namely the river that flows between Tripoli and Tortosa. He decreed that Jerusalem should possess by perpetual right all the land on the southern side as far as that river, while Antioch should likewise possess everything on the other side of the river.

When Pope Paschal was celebrating a council at Benevento, messengers were sent by the patriarch and prince of Antioch. At that council they requested that the Church of Antioch be restored to them by right. He gave them the following response:

“We do not usually respond quickly concerning the affairs of churches; but because you have come from far away and a long journey awaits you on your return [Note: [Col. 1113] Correct to *redituros*, “returning.”], we must not delay giving the answer that we have prepared.

“It is remembered and known that Pope Urban, of holy memory, when he celebrated a council at Clermont before a most numerous assembly and aroused the expedition to Jerusalem, decreed that whenever princes conquered provinces or cities from the pagans, once the rites of the pagan peoples had been removed [Note: [Col. 1113] Correct to *eliminatis*.], those territories would belong to the churches restored to them.”

## XXV

[Note: [Col. 1115] A, folio 23 recto; B, folio 22 recto.]  
### Privilege of Patriarch Arnulf

The transformation of the secular canons into regular canons, carried out by Patriarch Arnulf with the assent of King Baldwin I, and the provisions he established for their food and clothing: namely, half of the offerings of the Holy Sepulchre; all the offerings of the Holy Cross, except on Good Friday; all the tithes belonging to Jerusalem, except the tithes of Funda (*funde*); the Church of Saint Peter at Joppa with all its honor and dignity; and the Church of Blessed Lazarus with all its appurtenances. Let them possess all these things freely and arrange them according to their will [Note: [Col. 1115] This summary is missing from B, where the rubric reads: “On the transformation of the secular canons into regular canons.”].

[Col. 1115C] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

I, Arnulf, by the grace of God patriarch of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “Iherosolimitanus”], the least servant of the servants of that same divinity [Note: B reads “eiusdem divinitatis”], notify Balduin, by God’s will the most glorious king of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “Iherosolimorum”], who reigns and wholeheartedly agrees with us in every good thing, and all who worship Christ throughout the world, of the privilege which, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1114, the third of my patriarchate, the fourteenth of the reign of the aforesaid king, in the seventh indiction, with epact 12, was established and confirmed for the renewal of the church of the Holy Sepulchre with the counsel of that king.

Since our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, loved his Church so greatly that, having become man for her sake, he deigned to redeem her with his most precious blood [Col. 1115D], and since in his ineffable mercy he deigned to love so deeply the place of his passion and most glorious resurrection that it pleased him, by his own divine power, to snatch it from the hands of the Turks and Saracens and to hand it over to his Christian faithful, countless of whom had suffered for the liberation of that place, nothing would the strength of men, nothing wisdom, nothing the multitude of our armies accomplish, unless divine power fought invincibly for us [Note: B reads “unless divine power fought for us”], unless he mercifully [Col. 1116A] placed us in the pasture of his own choosing, unless also, after the pagans had been destroyed, he mercifully made us, though unworthy, heirs of his inheritance.

But the wickedness of the ancient enemy [Note: B reads “nequitia”], grieving that he had lost the vessels of wrath, began to contrive how he might destroy the vessels of mercy—the enemy who, like a roaring lion, strives by a thousand devices to break into the Lord’s sheepfold. For he corrupted the new inhabitants, who had forgotten the Lord’s commandment, more and more from day to day [the manuscript reading is corrupt: “de d e in diem”]. And he, who considered the lesser members worthless, extended even to the clergy, agitating them with his illusions and making them his slaves. Those whom it befitted to exist as more devoted to God and to provide a good example of themselves to their lesser brethren, alas, served the pleasure of the flesh rather [Note: B reads “inservivit”], and did not hesitate to pollute their own honor in incredible ways.

And the pious Lord, who looks kindly with the eye of mercy [Col. 1116B] upon the place of his burial, corrected their wickedness in our times through his severity. For when our predecessor, Lord Gibilin, had died, I, Arnulf, the most humble of all the people of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “of all the people of Iherusalem”], was elected pastor by the king, clergy, and people and raised to patriarchal dignity. Fearing for my soul’s peril and desiring to heal their souls, I refused any longer to consent to their crimes; I had often admonished them with paternal correction to amend their way of life.

For I urged them to live together and follow the apostolic life, and that their life should be governed canonically according to the rule of blessed Augustine [Note: “pro” is supplied from B], so that their service might please the Lord Jesus Christ more devotedly and that we might receive the reward with them in eternal glory. But when some of them, by God’s inspiration, embraced the salutary admonitions [Col. 1116C], while others rejected them through diabolical instigation, I properly ordered the former, as servants of Christ, in the church of the Holy Sepulchre; but I completely expelled the latter from that church as disobedient and resisting the precepts of the Rule.

Therefore, consulting the holy way of life of those now living and providing for the good purpose of those to come, with the counsel of the renowned King Balduin and the assent of the clergy and people of our patriarchate, I assigned them a portion and, with zeal for God, arranged that they should have sufficient food and clothing.

From all the offerings that come to the Lord’s Sepulchre, they shall receive one half in every respect. Of the wax, however, the church shall have two parts for the lights, while the patriarch shall have the third. As for the Cross of the Lord, which the canons guard, they shall receive its offerings at all times, except only on the holy day of Good Friday [Note: B reads “parasceve”], or if the patriarch should carry it with him on account of some necessity.

I also gave them the tithes of the entire holy city of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “Iherusalem”] and of the places adjoining it, except the tithes of Funde, which belong to the patriarch; likewise, one half of that benefice which the king granted to the Sepulchre in exchange for the bishopric of Bethlehem.

I also granted them in the city of Joppa the church of Saint Peter, with its honor and with all the dignity [Col. 1117A] that belongs to the mother church. I also granted them the church of Saint Lazarus with all its appurtenances, and everything that the church had previously possessed. Whatever property they have, possess, or God will grant them, they shall hold freely and order according to their will.

But if anyone should presume to violate this privilege of ours, let him suffer the penalty which the Lord promised to all the accursed, unless he repent. May grace, however, and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ be with whoever preserves this privilege and defends the rights of the holy church. Amen.

### XXVI. PRIVILEGE OF PATRIARCH WILLIAM CONFIRMING ALL POSSESSIONS

[Note: A, folio 25 recto; B, folio 25 recto. B reads “Item privilegium.”]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father and Son and Holy Spirit. Amen.

William, by the grace of God patriarch of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “Iherusalem”], sends greetings to his dearest sons in Christ, Peter, prior of the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, and the other brothers professing canonical life in that same church, both present and future.

The authority of our office compels us to labor for the gain and advancement of the souls entrusted to us and, with paternal care and solicitude, to provide for the support of your common life. For if, by the duty of the governance entrusted to us, we ought to protect and love the churches established within the bounds of our patriarchate and their children, we judge it more just that you, who as special sons [Note: B reads “specialiores”] cling more closely to us and whose care has been entrusted to us in every respect, should be cherished in the embrace of our protection [Col. 1117C], so that you may more freely offer the service of most devoted devotion to the same Redeemer [Note: Correct “devotissimo” to “devotissimi”; B reads “devoti”] in the church which our Redeemer illumined through the humility of his passion and the glory of his resurrection, insofar as you see that our assistance is not lacking to your filial community in the administration of temporal matters.

Therefore, following with pious eagerness the institutions of our predecessor of blessed memory, Lord Arnulf the patriarch—which have been sanctioned both by the privilege of apostolic authority and by confirmation [Note: B reads “sanccita”]—we too grant to you, son Peter, and to your brothers, present and future, to possess freely and perpetually whatever he ordained, with zeal for God and for the sake of good order, for the food and clothing of the regular canons established or to be established in their time in the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, over which, by God’s authority, we are now known to preside [Note: In A this sentence is written unintelligibly as: “quecumque preesse disnocimur in ecclesia Sepulcri Domini cui auctore Deo nunc”]. He also secured these provisions in perpetuity by the inscription of his privilege [Col. 1117D].

And, so that you may have more ample necessities, we add further provisions. For it is fitting that we, who wish our institutions to be observed, should strive not only not to violate the pious acts and arrangements of our predecessors but also, insofar as we can, to imitate them in every way.

Accordingly, we grant you one half of all offerings that belong or will be brought to the Lord’s Sepulchre, provided that, of the wax, the church receives only two parts for making the lights, while the third goes to our uses and those of our successors. We decree [Note: B reads “sanccimus”] that you shall receive and retain at all times the offerings of the holy Cross, which is entrusted to your custody, except on the day of Good Friday [Note: B reads “parascheve”], or when some necessity compels me or my successors to carry it elsewhere.

We also grant you the tithes of the entire holy city of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “Iherusalem”] and of the places adjoining it, except the tithes of Funde, which are known to belong to our jurisdiction. Likewise, we decree that you shall possess one half of all that Balduin, king of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “Iherusalem”], the first of the Latins, of blessed memory, granted to the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre in exchange for the bishopric of Bethlehem [Col. 1118B].

In the city of Joppa, we grant you the church of Saint Peter, with its dignity and the full extent of its honor, which is known to belong to that mother church. Moreover, we grant you the church of Saint Lazarus with all [its] appurtenances [Note: “its” is supplied from B], together with four villages—Benahatie, Benehabeth, Ragabam, and Roma—which are shown by the privilege of that same King Balduin to have been given by him to the Sepulchre of the Lord. We likewise grant you the villeins with their families who, by the gift of that king, are transferred to you through the page of his written instrument [Note: In A there is “ut”].

From our own property, we further add to you the church of Quarentene [Note: B reads “Quarantene”] to possess henceforth. We also assign to your jurisdiction all the ovens of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “Iherusalem”] that you hold by the gift of the venerable Duke Godfrey [Col. 1118C] [Note: B reads “Godefridi”], except three, of which two serve and are subject to the needs of the poor of the Hospital, while the third is assigned to the uses of the church of Saint Mary of the Latins.

We also decree that all the villages which the same venerable Duke Godfrey [Note: B reads “Godefridus”] granted to the church of the Lord’s Resurrection [Note: A reads “Resurrextionis”; B reads “Resurrectionis”] shall be freely possessed by you in perpetuity, as is contained in the privilege of the aforesaid King Balduin.

To this gift of our grant we deem it right to add four villages—Gath [Note: B reads “Gith”], Capharruth, Crefesilta, and Porphiria—with their appurtenances, which you are at present known justly to possess by the gift and grant of our brother and fellow bishop Roger, bishop of Ramatha [Note: B reads “dinoscimini”].

And, to conclude briefly, not only the things which divine grace has granted you within the bounds of our patriarchate, but also whatever you possess across or beyond the sea, or may hereafter justly acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the gift of kings and princes, or the offerings of the faithful, subject to the respect due to diocesan bishops, we perpetually subject to your jurisdiction, so that in all things the right and reverence of patriarchal dignity may also be preserved.

But so that all these things may be preserved for you whole and inviolate [Note: This sentence is absent from B] [Col. 1119A], we sanction this present document by the application of our seal and strengthen it by the attestations of those whose names are written below. For the following were present at this grant of ours:

Gaudentius, archbishop of Caesarea [Note: B reads “Gaudencius”]. Roger, bishop of Ramatha. Anselm, bishop of Bethlehem. Robert, archdeacon of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “Iherusalem”]. Gaufridus, abbot of the church of the Temple of the Lord. Arnold, prior of Mount Zion [Note: B reads “Arnaldus”]. Henry, prior of the Mount of Olives. Robert, abbot of the church of Saint Mary of the Valley of Jehoshaphat. Solbrand, abbot of Saint Mary of the Latins, and many others.

[Col. 1119B] Therefore, if anyone should attempt to diminish or take away the aforesaid possessions, or retain what has been taken away, and, knowingly disregarding this document of our determination, should presume to rise against it or weaken it, then, after a second and third admonition, if he does not come to suitable satisfaction, let him incur excommunication; and, excluded from reception of the sacred body and blood of the Lord Christ, let him undergo the vengeance of strict judgment. But let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ and participation in our benefactions be granted in the present age to all who observe the provisions of this privilege, so that through these they may deserve to be brought to the joys of eternal blessedness. Amen.

This present document [Note: B reads “presentis pagine”] was written in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1137, in the first indiction, with epact 7, while the same our lord Jesus Christ reigned [Note: B reads “eodem domno”], and while Fulco, the third king of the Latins, presided over the kingdom of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “Iherusalem”], in the seventh year of our patriarchate.

### XXVII. ANOTHER PRIVILEGE OF PATRIARCH WILLIAM CONCERNING THE GIFT OF QUARENTENE

[Note: A, folio 26 verso; B, folio 24 recto. B reads “Quarantene.”]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father and Son and Holy Spirit. Amen.

Let it be known to all, present and future, that Lord William [Note: B reads “Guillelmus”], by the grace of God patriarch of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “Iherusalem”], gave the place of Saint Quarentene, with everything belonging to it, to the canons of the Most Holy Sepulchre to possess perpetually.

The canons, for the dignity and reverence of that place and also for their own salvation, with the counsel and assent of that lord patriarch and Lord Peter the prior, made one of their confraternity, namely Rainald, prior in that place. And, so that the priory might continue there forever, they established the following arrangement: the prior himself should exist as one of those canons and should always obey the prior of the Holy Sepulchre and the canons thereof; his successors, however, should perpetually be appointed from among the aforesaid canons by their common counsel. [Col. 1120A] They likewise granted to him and his successors free power to enlarge the place and to associate and receive brothers.

This institution was made in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1134, in the twelfth indiction. The authors and witnesses of this institution [Note: B reads “Huius”] are:

Lord William [Note: B reads “Guillelmus”], patriarch, and Lord Peter, prior. Peter, subprior. Gilbert. Anselm, precentor. Peter Bernardi. Goffridus, treasurer. Fulcherius. Master Robert. William [Note: B reads “Guillelmus”]. Oshertus [Note: B reads “Osbertus”]. Haimericus [Note: B reads “Aimericus”]. Balduin.

Among the deacons: Walter [Note: B reads “Galterius”]. Moses. Roger. Peter. Gerald, who composed this charter.

Among the subdeacons: Gerald. Peter Clementis. Evrard. Gervasius.

For the confirmation of these provisions, Lord William [Note: B reads “Guillelmus”] the patriarch affixed his seal, and the canons affixed theirs [Note: B reads “placed theirs”].

### XXVIII. ANOTHER PRIVILEGE OF PATRIARCH WILLIAM CONCERNING THE TITHES OF JERICHO

[Note: A, folio 27 verso; B, folio 24 verso. B lacks “another.” B reads “Iherico.”]

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

To give good counsel [Note: B reads “consultum”] for a good matter is considered a support for the present life, and to await the reward of eternal recompense is recognized as a benefit. Let the charity of all, both clerics and laymen, therefore know that I, William, by the grace of God patriarch of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “Iherosolimitanus”], although any bishop may enrich a church in his parish that has been deprived by poverty with the resources of the church over which he presides, provided that equity and moderation are maintained, at the pious request of my sons and canons—namely, at the request and counsel of the entire convent [Note: B reads “tocius”] of the Most Holy Sepulchre—give and grant in perpetuity the tithes of Jericho [Note: B reads “Iherico”] to the aforesaid Most Holy Quarentene, so that this may be reckoned before God in our account.

Since I had already given Quarentene—that is, this most glorious place, in which our Redeemer fasted for forty days and forty nights and afterward grew hungry—to those same sons and canons as a possession, and had granted them perpetual, free, and unrestricted power to appoint and canonically remove any prior in that place, and since the aforesaid convent lacked the means by which it could relieve the poverty of that place, I give and [Note: “et” is absent from B] grant this gift at its request and with its approval; and [Note: supplied from B], so that it may be firmer and more binding, So that it may be firmer and more binding, consecrating the altar of that place, I offer it by placing it upon the consecrated altar.

This gift was made and granted to Rainald, prior of Quarentene, and to his successors canonically enthroned by the convent of the Holy Sepulchre, with the confirmation of our present seals and the subscription of the entire convent [Note: B reads “tociusque”] of the Most Holy Sepulchre and of the other credible witnesses, in the year from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1136, with epact 15, in the fourteenth indiction. The witnesses to this matter are:

Roger, bishop of Lydda. Anselm, bishop of Bethlehem. Peter, prior of the Lord’s Sepulchre. Achard, prior of the Temple of the Lord. Arnard, prior of Mount Zion [Note: B reads “Arnaldus”]. Henry, prior of the Mount of Olives. Robert, abbot of the Valley of Jehoshaphat. Soibrand, abbot of Saint Mary of the Latins.

From the convent of the Holy Sepulchre:

Lord Richard [Note: B reads “Ricardus”]. Peter of Barcelona. Robert of Artois. Gaufridus of Constantinople. Anselm, precentor. Ralph of Paris. [Col. 1121B] Peter Bernardi. Garnerius. Gebertus [Note: B reads “Gerbertus”]. Robert. William. Wlgrinus. Lambert. Another Lambert. Godfrey. Moses. Roger. Bartholomew. Gervasius. Gerald. Evrard. Dionysius.

### XXIX.

[Note: A, folio 28 recto and folio 158 recto; B, folio 35 recto.]

Confirmation by King Balduin I of everything that Duke Godfrey bestowed upon the church of the [Holy] Sepulchre: namely, twenty-one villages, whose names are written below; the ovens of Jerusalem; the villeins at Saint Lazarus with their families; four villages above Saint Lazarus; one thousand modii of wheat in the territory of Naples; and one half of the exchange-property of the bishopric of Bethlehem [Note: This summary of the charter is absent from B].

### PRIVILEGE OF THE VILLAGES AND TITHES GRANTED BY KING BALDUIN TO THE PRIOR[S]

[Note: The printed heading reads “priori[s]”; B reads: “Privilege of King Balduin I concerning the grant of Duke Godfrey’s gift.”]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

It is fitting that all whom divine grace has chosen to raise to the height of royal power should not turn away the ear of their clemency from holy and just petitions, but should diligently assent to pious vows and desires pleasing to God, so that they may be well advanced.

Therefore, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1114, likewise in the fourteenth year of my reign, in the seventh indiction, with epact 12, I, Balduin, by God’s disposition holding the kingdom of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “Iherosolimitanum”], having been asked by Arnulf, the venerable patriarch of that holy city of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “Iherusalem”], and by the entire convent of the canons of the church of the Holy Sepulchre, will and grant by the decree of this writing that whatever I have learned was given by Duke Godfrey, my predecessor and brother, to that same church shall remain inviolate [Note: Correct “inviolata permaneant” to “inviolatum permaneat”]:

namely, twenty-one villages [Note: A reads “casella”; B reads “casalia”], called as follows: Ainquine, Armotie, Kefreachab, Kefredil Bubil, Hubin, Aram, Kalendie, Betligge [Note: B reads “Beitligge”], Byrra [Note: B reads “Birra”], Subahiet, Ataraberet, Urniet, Zenu, Helmule, Beitelamus, Aineseins, Barimeta, Beitiumen, Beitfuteir [Note: B reads “Beitfuteier”], and Betsuri [Note: B reads “Bethsuri”]; and all the ovens of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “Iherusalem”], except two belonging to the Hospital and one belonging to the Latins; and at Saint Lazarus the villeins with their families, whom I gave to the Holy Sepulchre; and four villages above Saint Lazarus, whose names are these: Benehatie, Benehabeth, Ragabam, and Roma; and one thousand modii of wheat every year in the territory of Naples; and one half of the possession which I gave to the Holy Sepulchre in exchange for the bishopric of Bethlehem.

And so that my royal command may possess firmness in our times and in those to come, I strengthen this privilege by my authority, confirm it below with my own hand, and seal it with my seal, so that it may be firmly and inviolably lawful for the holy congregation of that church to possess all these things by perpetual right.

But if any of my successors, whether living in clerical or lay order [Note: A reads “ordinavi”; B reads “ordine”], should—God forbid!—presume to go against this royal institution and decree of mine and attempt to violate it, and should diminish anything from the prebend established for the canons, let him suffer forever the penalty owed to sacrilegious persons. But may grace and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ be granted to all who defend the rights of the holy church, and also to the canons serving that church. Amen.

### XXX. PRIVILEGE OF KING BALDUIN II CONCERNING A VILLAGE SITUATED NEAR TYRE

[Note: A, folio 29 recto; B, folio 37 recto. B calls it “Another privilege.”]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father and Son and Holy Spirit.

I, Balduin, by the grace of God second king of the Latins of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “Iherusalem”], for the salvation of the soul of my predecessor, King Balduin, of worthy memory [Col. 1122C], and also for the remission of my sins, give and grant within the boundaries of Tyre to the church of the Most Holy Sepulchre of the Lord and to the canons serving God there in regular life, present and future, a certain village named Derina, above the great spring from which the water-channel flows, with all its territory and appurtenance, except another village if it should at any time have been subject to it, so that the aforesaid church may have and possess it by perpetual hereditary right, without any claim from me, my heirs, or my successors.

Moreover, in the same manner, I grant the garden [Note: B reads “ortum”] which [is—supplied from B] between the wall and the outer wall of that city, on the seaward side; and, in the boundaries of the aforesaid village, around the mountainous area, as much land as four pairs of oxen can cultivate from year to year.

For the security and confirmation of this gift of mine, I ordered this privilege to be made and strengthened with my leaden seal in the presence of the witnesses whose names are written below:

Seal of Gedduin [Note: B reads “Gelduin”], abbot of Saint Mary of the Valley of Jehoshaphat. Seal of Pagan, the king’s chancellor. Seal of Walter Brisebarre. Seal of Pagan of Mineriis. [Seal of] William of Saint-Bertin. Seal of Sadon, marshal.

Given in the royal palace at Tyre [Note: B reads “aput”], in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1125, in the third indiction.

### XXXI. PRIVILEGE OF KING FULCO III CONCERNING TWO CARRUCATES OF LAND IN THE TERRITORY OF ACRE

[Note: A, folio 29 verso; B, folio 39 verso. B reads “Achonensi.”]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father and Son and Holy Spirit. Amen [Note: Absent from B].

I, Fulco, by the grace of God third king of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “Iherosolimorum”], with the consent of Queen Milesendis [Note: B reads “Milissendis”] and of my son Balduin, have granted and confirmed by this privilege to the church of the Holy Sepulchre, to Peter the prior, and to the brothers serving God there two complete and fully constituted carrucates of arable land at the village of Mimas. Lambert Alsus of Naples had given them to that church and to those brothers in the presence of Lord William the patriarch, myself, and Queen Milesendis, and had placed this gift in the hand of the aforesaid prior as alms for the soul of his wife Agnes, for his own soul, and for the souls of his parents.

This grant was made at Acre [Note: B reads “Achon”] on the second day before the Nones of December, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1138, in the presence and hearing of the following:

The aforesaid William, patriarch of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “Iherosolimitano”]. John, bishop of that Acre [Note: B reads “Achon”]. Robert, archdeacon. Balduin, chancellor. Peter, the queen’s chaplain. Hodierna, countess of Tripoli. Haluisa [Note: B reads “Alois”]. Anselm [Note: B reads “Anselmus”] of Bria. Sada [Note: B reads “Sado”], marshal [Note: B reads “marescalcus”]. John, chamberlain. Gervasius Burgundian. [Col. 1123C] Gunfrid of Freisnel. Adelard of Retest. Goscelin, chamberlain, Simon [Note: B reads “Symon”] of Capella.

I, Elias, the king’s chancellor, dictated this privilege.

### XXXII. ANOTHER PRIVILEGE OF KING FULCO III CONCERNING HOUSES IN JERUSALEM

[Note: A, folio 30 recto; B, folio 40 recto. B lacks “another privilege.” B reads “Iherusalem.”]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father and Son and Holy Spirit. Amen.

To remove forever every claim, contradiction, or any disturbance by wicked persons, I, Fulco, by the grace of God third king of the Latins of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “Iherusalem”], together with the assent of Milesendis, my wife and queen, and of my son Balduin, have decreed that it be made known and ratified, both to those now living and to those to come, that for the souls of our predecessor kings, as well as for our own souls [Note: B reads “pro”] and those of our parents, and also for all the faithful departed—especially those who gave their blood or sweat for the acquisition of the Holy Land—I freely and willingly, solely out of piety, grant to the church of the Holy Sepulchre, to Peter the prior, and to the whole convent of brothers serving God there under the regular devotion of canonical life, present and future, the houses listed below, which are within the walls of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “Iherusalem”]:

the house of Peter Bernardi, the canon; the house of Evrard, the canon; likewise the house of another Evrard, the canon; the house of Meinard [Note: B reads “Mainard”]; the house of Garsion; the house of Walter Lentornior [Note: B reads “Lo Tornaor”]; the house of Bernard Bursarius; the house of Herluin; the house of Mabilia; the house of Roger, brother of the same canons; and the shop of William [Note: B reads “Willelmus”] Bastard, together with the share that the same William held in the money-changers’ market [Note: B reads “money-changers”].

I, King Fulco, grant and confirm these houses free and undisturbed, to be held and possessed [Note: “possesiones” is absent from B] in perpetuity by the aforesaid church and its canons, exempt from every customary levy, without prejudice to the royal right which the king ought to have in the alms that he himself gives to the holy church [Note: B reads “alms”]. And so that this grant may remain firm and unshaken forever, I have chosen to fortify this charter with my royal seal and to strengthen it by the truthful testimony of the witnesses written below [Note: Correct “supscriptorum” to “subscriptorum”]. Their names are these:

William, patriarch of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “Iherusalem”]. Robert, elected bishop of Nazareth. Gaufridus, abbot of the Temple. William of Buris. Rainer of Bruns. Barisan. Balduin of Ramla. Roard, viscount of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “Iherusalem”]. Anselm of Bria. Gervasius of Burgundy. Ulric, viscount of Naples. Bernard Vacers. John, chamberlain. [Col. 1124C] Meinard [Note: B reads “Mainardus”] of Port. Nicholas.

This grant was made at Naples, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1138 and in the thirty-ninth year after the liberation of the holy city of Jerusalem [Note: B reads “Iherusalem”], in the first indiction.

And this privilege was issued through the hand of Elias, the king’s chancellor.

### XXXIII. ANOTHER PRIVILEGE OF KING FULCO III CONCERNING THE EXCHANGE OF THECUA

[Note: A, folio 31 recto; B, folio 41 recto. B reads “concambio” and “Thecue.”]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father and Son and Holy Spirit. Amen.

Regal anointing and the equity and propriety of royal majesty demand that he who is divinely deemed worthy to be exalted upon the royal throne should strive to bring about the overthrow of the churches [Note: B reads “to erect”] and, insofar as he can rightly do so, enlarge the worship of sacred religion. With this enlargement of religion in view, I, Fulcho [Note: B, Fulco], by the grace of God king of Jerusalem [Note: B, Iherusalem], third of the Latins, with my wife, Queen Milesendis, encouraging me to this, for the remedy of the soul of her father, King Baldwin, my predecessor, and of pious memory Baldwin, the first Latin king in Jerusalem [Note: B, Iherusalem], and of his brother Duke Godfrey [Note: B, Godefridus], and for the salvation of our souls and of the souls of our heirs, ancestors, and parents, have obtained from Lord William, patriarch of the Jerusalemite see [Note: B, Iherosolimitane], and from Peter, prior of the Lord’s Sepulchre, and from all the brothers of that same chapter—namely Robert the archdeacon, Anselm the precentor, Godfrey the treasurer [Note: B, thesaurarius], Wulgrin the provost, Peter Bernard, Girbert, Goisbert, Obert, Robert, Peter the almoner [Note: B, elemosinarius], Peter the chamberlain, Lambert, Aymeric [Note: B, Aimericus], Peter, Gerald, Anscheric, Everard [Note: B, Eurard], Burchard, William of Poitiers, William of Beirut—together with the rest of the convent, the church of Blessed Lazarus situated in Bethany, which both I and the aforementioned wife of mine, Queen Milesendis [Note: omitted in B], obtained after many prayers, so that, as has been said, through us that church might serve a religious community of monks or nuns more devoutly than before, and might remain perpetually in fidelity and obedience to the church of the Lord’s Resurrection [Note: B, Resurrectionis] and to the Jerusalemite patriarch [Note: B, Iherosolimitani], with the liberty and obedience exercised by the freer church of the same order in the Jerusalemite diocese [Note: B, Iherosolimitana].

And so that in that church of Saint Lazarus all those who are to be regularly introduced as religious devotees might not lack bodily sustenance, with the approval and gift of Lord William the patriarch, Peter the prior and the aforesaid canons and brothers of the Lord’s Sepulchre grant them, for the necessities of life, both buildings and benefices—namely, houses belonging to that same church, situated both outside and within Jerusalem [Note: B, Iherusalem], together with the villeins and Bedouins, or the farmsteads of the same dependency: Benehatie, Benehabeth, Ragabam, and Romha [Note: B, Roma], all of these with their appurtenances [Note: B, with their appurtenances], free and quit, just as they were previously held freely by them; and, releasing them from every payment of tithes [Note: B, “releasing”], they promise by canonical undertaking that they will defend themselves against the injury of every claimant [Note: B, calumniator].

In exchange for all these things, by equal vote and common consent, I, Fulco, king of Jerusalem [Note: B, Iherusalem], and I, Queen Milesendis, with the assent of our son Baldwin, and also with the agreement of the aforementioned Lord William the patriarch, and with the agreement and approval of the ecclesiastics who were present [Note: B, “who were present”], with the approval and confirmation of the barons, grant to the church of the glorious Passion and Resurrection of the Lord and to the canons professing or intending to profess canonical life therein, both present and future, a certain farmstead named Thecue, with all its appurtenances, both lands and villeins and Bedouins and their heirs—namely, all those who from the siege of Antioch until today are known, or shall be known, to have paid any revenues to the lords of that farmstead for its appurtenances and adjoining pastures—free and quit in perpetual right, with the liberty in which we are known to have held it; and from now on we promise to defend ourselves against every impediment of claim.

Furthermore, to the free gift of this exchange we add, with royal generosity, that the inhabitants of Thecue may, as they have been accustomed to do in our times, freely collect from the Dead Sea that bitumen commonly called *catran*, and may likewise take salt from the surrounding places.

But so that the gift and agreement of this holy exchange and settlement may remain valid and unshaken, we decree that this present document, written concerning the truth of the aforesaid matters and their common arrangement, fortified by the affixing of our patriarchal and royal seals, shall remain valid forever. Having been strengthened by the truthful testimony of the legitimate men whose names are subscribed here, we leave it to posterity to preserve it forever inviolate. The following were present at all these matters, giving their assent and prepared to offer testimony:

Gaudentius [Note: B, Gaudencius], archbishop of Caesarea. Roger, bishop of Ramla. Anselm, bishop of holy Bethlehem. Reinerius [Note: B, Rainerius], bishop of Sebaste. Bernard, bishop of Sidon. Robert, elect of Nazareth. Geoffrey, abbot of the Temple of the Lord. Arnaud [Note: B, Arnaldus], prior of Mount Zion. William, abbot of Mount Tabor. Helias [Note: B, Helias], abbot of Palmaria. Herbert, archdeacon of Tiberias [Note: B, Tyberiadis]. Gerald, prior of the Valley of Jehoshaphat. Philip, dean of Caesarea. Bernard and Arnulf [Note: B, Arnulfus], canons of Bethlehem. Peter, chaplain. Bartholomew, priest. Amelius and Henry, deacons of the patriarch. Baldwin, chancellor of the patriarch. Ralph, canon of Mount Zion. Peter, canon of Sebaste [Note: The signatures of this witness and of the following two are missing in B]. Baldwin, canon of Saint George. Adam, canon of Acre. Saginus [Note: B, Siginus], canon of Tyre [Note: B, Tyrensis]. William of Bures, lord of Tiberias. Walter, lord of Caesarea; Guy, lord of Beirut. Baldwin, lord of Ramla. Rohardus, viscount of Jerusalem [Note: B, Iherusalem]. Reinerius [Note: B, Rainerius] Brusch. Barisanus. Vivian, lord of Cayphas. Rainerus [Note: B, Rainerius] Parvus. Anselm of Bria. Robert of Franc Loet [Note: B, Loeth]. Philip, son of Guy of Milly. Ulric, viscount of Naples. Peter of Podio Laurentii. Roland Gunter. Oliver, his brother. John Dunda. Godfrey of Bures. Walter Maldunz [Note: B, Malduiz]. Arnulf of Hames. Bernard [Note: B, Bernardus] Vacers. Theobald [Note: B, Tibaldus] of Nazareth. William, nephew of the patriarch. Theobald [Note: B, Tibaldus] of Herlebecke. Sado, marshal [Note: B, marescaicus]. Gerald Passerels. Eustace of Roitest.

From Jerusalem [Note: B, Iherusalem]:

Alard, knight. Hildred. Siger. Humbert with the beard. Milo, chamberlain. Bachelor [Note: B, Bachelarius].

From Acre [Note: B, Achon]:

Mainard [Note: B, Mainardus] of Port. Nicholas [Note: B, Nicholaus] Dorez. Albric. Aurentius. Rotland [Note: B, Roland] of Lucca.

From among the pilgrims:

Ivo of Nigella. Arnulf, advocate of Thérouanne. Ingelram of Bova. Richard of Herecurch. Anscherius [Note: B, Anscherius] of Encre, and many others.

Therefore, if anyone, knowing the inscription of this matter to be so firm, should dare rashly to oppose it or presume in any way to weaken it, let him, as a transgressor of our ordinance and common decree, be struck by the sentence of our curse and punishment; and, having been smitten with eternal anathema, if he does not repent, let him, by judgment of the persons named above, be handed over to the unquenchable fires of Gehenna, there to be punished perpetually without reprieve. Amen.

Given at Jerusalem, on the Nones of February, by the hand of Helias, the king’s chancellor, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1138, indiction 1 [Note: This final sentence is absent from B].

### XXXIV. Privilege of Baldwin, fourth Latin king, to the canons, concerning the grant of the farmstead called Thecue

[Note: A, fol. 33r; B, fol. 46v.]

[Column 1127C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen.

Those things which have been done for the good of peace or established with pious intention ought to be observed by all, and especially by royal magnificence, with every care, lest either the passage of time erase them from the memory of succeeding posterity or the malicious disturbance of wicked men later corrupt them through various scruples of dissension. Therefore I, Baldwin, by the grace of God fourth Latin king of holy Jerusalem [Note: B, Iherusalem], providing for the future peace of ourselves and of the churches, approve the exchange which my father Fulcho [Note: B, Fulco], of pious memory, illustrious third Latin king of Jerusalem [Note: B, Iherusalem], and my mother Queen Milesendis [Note: B, Milissendis], made with the canons of the Lord’s Sepulchre [Note: B, Sepulchri Domini] for their own salvation and that of their predecessors, concerning the temporal benefices belonging to the church of Saint Lazarus situated in Bethany; and, confirming it by this present document, I decree that it be preserved forever unaltered.

That church, namely, Pope Celestine of blessed memory, at the request and with the assent of William [Note: B, Willelmus], patriarch of Jerusalem [Note: B, Iherosolimitanus], and with the grant of all the canons of the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, raised to the status of an abbey; and he also decreed that the aforesaid exchange should remain valid and inviolate—namely, that the canons of the Lord’s Sepulchre should possess, in perpetual right, a certain farmstead called Thecue, with all its appurtenances, both lands and villages [Note: B’s reading, “villeins,” seems better], and Bedouins and their heirs, namely all those who from the siege of Antioch until today are known, or shall be known, to have paid any revenues to the lords of that farmstead for its appurtenances and adjoining pastures, free and quit, by my gift and grant, with the liberty by which my father is known to have held it.

I further promise that I shall defend it for them from every impediment of claim, from now on and thereafter, granting that the inhabitants of Thecue may freely collect from the Dead Sea that bitumen commonly called *catran*, and may likewise take salt from the surrounding places.

In exchange for all these things, with the approval and gift of Lord William [Note: B, Willelmus], patriarch of Jerusalem [Note: B, Iherusalem], Peter the prior and the aforesaid canons and brothers of the Lord’s Sepulchre grant to Matilda the abbess and to the nuns regularly established or to be established in the aforesaid church, for the support of temporal life, both buildings and benefices and houses belonging to that church, situated both outside and within Jerusalem [Note: B, Iherusalem], together with villeins and Bedouins, or the farmsteads of the same dependency—Benehatie, Benehabeth, Ragabam, and Romah—all these with their appurtenances, free and quit, just as they were previously held freely by them; and, releasing them from every payment of tithes, they promise by canonical undertaking that they will defend themselves from the injury of every claimant [Note: B, calumniator].

But so that my grant of this holy exchange and settlement may remain valid and unshaken, I decree that this present document, written concerning the arrangement of the aforesaid matters and fortified by the affixing of my seal, shall remain valid forever; and, strengthened by the truthful testimony of the legitimate men whose names are subscribed here, I leave it to posterity to preserve. The witnesses of this matter are therefore [Note: B, “The witnesses of this matter are”]:

[Column 1128D]

William, patriarch of Jerusalem [Note: B, Iherusalem], and those who follow [Note: B, “follow”]:

Baldwin, archbishop of Caesarea. Robert, archbishop of Nazareth [Note: B, Nazareth]. Helias, bishop of Tiberias. Roger, bishop of Ramla. Reinerius [Note: B, Rainerius], bishop of Sebaste. Geoffrey, abbot of the Temple of the Lord. Sehebrand, abbot of Saint Mary of the Latins. Peter, prior of the Lord’s Sepulchre. Henry, prior of the Mount of Olives. Raymond, master of the Hospital. Peter William. Stephen of the Chapel. William Fauco. Geoffrey and Fulcher, both brothers of the Temple of Solomon [Note: omitted in B]. Godfrey, treasurer of the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre. William, provost. Peter Bernard. Peter of Barcelona. Nicholas. Lambert the Great. Bertrand of Podio. Master Beda. Obert Gamaliel. Gerald the Bastard. Moses [Note: B, Moyses]. Bonefatius [Note: B, Bonefacius]. Eurard. Robert of Acre [Note: B, Achonensis]. William of Beirut. William the Englishman.

Of the barons:

Balian. Reinerius of Ramla. Joscelin of Courtenay. Walter of Beirut. Roardus [Note: B, Rochardus], viscount. Sado, marshal. Bernard Vacherius. Geoffrey Acus. Tosetus. Imbert of Bar.

This charter was made in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1144, indiction 7.

### XXXV. Privilege of Pope Alexander concerning the confirmation of possessions and the wealth of the church of the Holy Sepulchre

(See under Alexander III, for the year 1181.)

### XXXVI. Concerning the arrangement of prebends of the church of Jerusalem

[Note: A, fol. 35r; B, fol. 21r.]

[Note: In B the heading reads: “Concerning the prebends which Ebremar the patriarch established for the secular canons.”]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

In the year from the incarnation of Jesus Christ, Son of God, 1103, indiction 11, while Ebremar, by the grace of God, held the patriarchal see at Jerusalem, and the renowned and most Christian King Baldwin governed the kingdom of Babylon and Asia, it pleased the aforesaid patriarch to arrange the prebends of the canons of Saint Sepulchre in the following manner and to reform them according to the earlier custom: that every year he should provide each one with 150 bezants [Note: B, bisantios] in perpetual right, until at some time he should complete those prebends for them from the possessions of the church, according to their free will [Note: supplied from B].

Moreover, it pleased his fatherly benevolence to give those same brothers perpetually two altars in the church of the Holy Sepulchre: namely, the principal altar which the canons themselves serve in the choir, with the patriarchal chair added behind that altar; and the other, the parish altar, which is at the head of the Sepulchre [Note: B, capud], except for the ecclesiastical ornaments, if they have been placed upon those altars, which shall remain the property of the church.

Likewise, all those things which are offered at its hand or foot, wherever he celebrates Mass, or whenever the patriarch himself or any bishop sings at the principal altar, he grants that offering to the canons. But if the patriarch sings Mass at the principal churches outside the church of the Holy Sepulchre, that offering shall not belong to them.

He also gave them the greater church of Saint Peter, which is near Joppa [Note: B, aput], together with the cemetery belonging to the church [Note: B, cimetterium], and with all the customs appropriate to a metropolitan church.

Moreover, he granted them this dignity, which sufficiently belongs as a prerogative to the church of the Holy Sepulchre: if a person in the churches of the Jerusalemite kingdom is to be changed, the matter shall be completed by their counsel and election wherever necessity demands it.

He established these things as stated above, and, marking this privilege with the royal seal, confirmed it with the approval and grant of the aforesaid king, without prejudice to his pontifical dignity and reverence.

Grace and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ to all the canons who hold [Note: B, “protect”] these rights of this holy church and serve it. Amen!

But if anyone, whether placed in the ecclesiastical or secular order, should presume to do anything against these statutes of the pious father, or should diminish anything from their established prebend, let him rightly fear on the dreadful day of judgment the punishment owed to sacrilegious persons [Note: B, “sacrileges”].

It also pleased the patriarch’s benevolence, as was fitting, to appoint officers in the same church: namely, a cantor, a primicerius—that is, a schoolmaster—as well as a treasurer and a sacristan. To the cantor, in addition to the customary prebend, he provided an equal amount, namely 150 bezants; likewise to the schoolmaster and also to the treasurer; but to the sacristan only 100.

It also pleased King Baldwin to give the succentor 150 bezants perpetually from his own revenues. The patriarch established that he would give the subdean 150 bezants, but only after the death of Lord Arnulf [Note: B, Arnulfus], the archdeacon; Arnulf himself, however, would provide that subdean with 100 bezants for as long as he lived.

### XLI. Concerning the tithes of the farmstead of Saint Giles

[Note: A, fol. 38r; B, fol. 27v.]

William, by the grace of God patriarch of holy Jerusalem, to his beloved sons in the Lord, Pontius [Note: B, Poncius], abbot of the church of Saint Saviour situated on Mount Tabor, and to the monks who profess and shall profess common life therein, forever.

The office of dignity entrusted to us requires that we provide for the churches committed to us with fatherly concern, and that, if any controversy should arise among them, we strive by every means to remove it and restore unity of spirit among them. Therefore, attending to these matters with particular care [Note: B, “with greater care”], we have settled, with the common counsel of our brothers and fellow bishops and with the assent of our beloved son Peter, prior of the Lord’s Sepulchre, and of our entire chapter, the long-standing dispute concerning the tithes of the farmstead of Saint Giles between the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre and your church.

Thus, so that perpetual peace may be preserved between these churches, we freely and absolutely grant to you the church of the aforesaid farmstead of Saint Giles, with its offerings and those of its two farmsteads—namely Turbasaim and Dere—together with half the tithes. We further add that the tithe of your three vineyards, which you now possess, shall likewise remain your right, all disturbance having been put to rest. We reserve the other part of the tithes for the canons of the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre.

From those things which you possess by our grant, you must provide for the church and for the clerics serving God therein. If later you are able to acquire anything from which a tithe ought to be paid, you shall pay half the tithe to the church of the Holy Sepulchre [Note: absent from B].

And so that these things may not be erased from the memory of future posterity, every year, on the feast of Jerusalem, you shall give to the aforesaid church of the Lord’s Sepulchre a candle of one *rotulus* in recognition [the exact unit is uncertain].

So that these things may be preserved for you, dearest sons in Christ, firm and unaltered forever, we decree that they be confirmed by this present document, fortified by the affixing of our seal. The following men were also present at this grant of ours and unanimously gave it their approval with counsel:

Baldwin, archbishop of Caesarea. Robert, archbishop of Nazareth. Roger, bishop of Ramla. Anselm, bishop of Bethlehem. Reinerius, bishop of Sebaste. Helias [Note: B, Helias], bishop of Tiberias [Note: B, Tyberiadensis]. Geoffrey, abbot of the Temple of the Lord. Henry, prior of Mount Olivet. Letard, prior of Nazareth. William, provost of the Lord’s Sepulchre.

The other canons of ours whose names are subscribed also gave their assent to this matter:

Godfrey, treasurer. Bertrand of Podio. Nicholas. Gamaliel. Robert, cellarer, and all the others.

This document was made in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1145, indiction 8 [Note: B reads “was made, however”].

Given at Jerusalem, by the hand of Ernesius the chancellor, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September.

### XLII. Constitution that the canons should eat together

[Note: A, fol. 39r; B, fol. 28v.]

[Column 1132A]

Gibelinus [Note: Both manuscripts read Willelmus; this is evidently an error, which can be corrected from the historical indications supplied by the document itself], servant of the Jerusalemite church [Note: B, “of the Jerusalemite church …”], to his lord and dearest brother Baldwin, glorious king of Jerusalem: greetings in the Lord Jesus and the affection of the entire brotherhood.

By the providence of God’s clemency, and at the request of the goodwill of your nobility [Note: B, benivolentia], which you have continually shown me, I remained in these foreign regions. As the moment of death approached, I greatly desired to speak with you as with my greatest friend, and with my son Arnulf the archdeacon. Since I could not do so, I offer you many thanks for such generosity as you showed me [Note: restored from B], and I commend your body and soul into the hands of the Most High Creator.

Since God’s mercy has appointed you defender and protector of His church, sprinkled with the outpouring of His blood and marked by His glorious Sepulchre, I earnestly beseech your kindness to protect it and defend it manfully.

As I lay at the point of death, I fully disclosed all my wishes to the canons of that same Lord’s Sepulchre, my sons and your brothers, so that I firmly commanded them under obedience to eat together according to the custom of good churches, especially that of Lyon or Reims [Note: B, “more particularly”]. I also charged them, declaring this as my testament, and for this reason I humbly ask you to confirm the same and, so that it may be more fully accomplished, to strive as a good fellow worker to assist them.

Therefore, concerning all these matters and others which I ordered and confirmed in my testament to be done for the remedy of my soul, I ask and command you to confirm them in the same manner and to act as their helper.

### XLIII. Privilege concerning a certain farmstead called Cafermelech, situated in the territory of Naples

[Note: A, fol. 39v; B, fol. 38v.]

[Note: In B the heading reads: “Another privilege of Baldwin, second king, concerning the same.”]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen.

I, Baldwin, by the grace of God second Latin king of Jerusalem, rightly judging that the stains of faithful souls can be wiped away through devotion in prayer and generosity in almsgiving, had granted, for the soul of my predecessor, King Baldwin of blessed memory, and for the souls of my wife the queen and my parents, to the holy church of the Lord’s Sepulchre [Note: B, “of Saint”] and to William the prior and the other canons serving God there according to the rule, both present and future, a certain farmstead in the territory of Naples called Cafermelech, with all its lands and appurtenances, except for the villeins of that farmstead whom Romanus of Podio had transferred to the farmstead of Betheflori.

I had granted it in such a way as is written in another privilege of mine, marked with my royal seal, so that the church of the Most Holy Sepulchre and the aforesaid canons might have and possess that farmstead in perpetuity, without any claim by my heirs and successors or by any other persons [Note: B, “and possess it in perpetual right”]. In return for the gift of this farmstead, those canons quitclaimed to me the 200 bezants which they had as revenue from Naples.

Later, however, at the friendship and request of those same canons, I gave and granted to the Most Holy Sepulchre, and to Peter its prior and the other canons, together with the aforesaid farmstead and all its appurtenances, the peasants whom I had previously excepted, with all their offspring and heirs, in the presence of the count of Anjou and of my daughter Milesendis, these persons approving and consenting.

But if anyone, driven by the goad of wickedness, should rashly attempt in any way to oppose or annul this lawful gift of mine, let him, unless he repents, be struck by God’s sentence of anathema and be held answerable to our royal power; nevertheless, let this gift of mine always remain firm and stable.

I therefore ordered Amelinus, my chancellor, to write this confirmation of my gift and the addition of the aforesaid peasants, and confirmed it with the royal leaden seal, in the presence of the venerable Lord William, patriarch of Jerusalem, and before the other witnesses whose names are written below:

Peter, my chaplain. Ralph, my chamberlain. Martin of Nazareth. Anscatinus, viscount of Jerusalem. Ulric, viscount of Naples, and many others.

### XLIV. Likewise, of King Baldwin II, concerning the gift of the farmstead of Cafermelich

[Note: A, fol. 40r; B, fol. 38r. This first heading is absent from A.]

[Column 1133C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen [Note: absent from B].

I, Baldwin, by the grace of God second Latin king of Jerusalem, rightly judging that the stains of faithful souls can be wiped away through devotion in prayer and generosity in almsgiving, for the soul of my predecessor, King Baldwin of blessed memory, and for the souls of my wife the queen [Note: B, uxoris] and my parents, give to the holy church of the Lord’s Sepulchre and to William the prior and the other canons serving God there according to the rule, both present and future, a certain farmstead in the territory of Naples called Cafermelich [Note: B, Cafermelic], with all its lands, villeins, and appurtenances, except for the villeins of that farmstead whom Romanus of Podio had transferred to the farmstead of Betheflori [Note: B, Beteflori].

I give it in such a way that the church of the Most Holy Lord’s Sepulchre and the aforesaid canons may have and possess that farmstead in perpetual right, without any claim by my heirs and successors or by any other persons. In return for the gift of this farmstead, those canons quitclaimed to me the 200 bezants which they had as revenue from Naples.

But if anyone, driven by the goad of wickedness, should rashly attempt in any way to oppose or annul this lawful gift of mine, let him, unless he repents, be struck by God’s sentence of anathema and be held answerable to our royal power; nevertheless, let this gift of mine always remain firm and stable.

To confirm this gift of mine, I ordered it to be written by Pagano, my chancellor, and confirmed with the royal leaden seal, in the presence of Lord Stephen, venerable patriarch of Jerusalem, and before the other witnesses whose names are written below:

Milisenda [Note: B, Milissenda], the king’s daughter, approves and consents to this. William, archbishop of Nazareth. Baldwin, bishop of Sebaste. Anselm [Note: B, Anselmus], bishop of Bethlehem. Gelduin, abbot of the Valley of Jehoshaphat. Arnald, prior of Mount Zion. John, chamberlain. Bernard Vaccarius. Hugo, lord of Joppa. Anselm of Bria. Henfred of Toron. Walter, lord of Caesarea. Guitterius, the king’s nephew [Note: this restoration is authorized by B]. Roardus. Sado, marshal. Paganus, cupbearer. Romanus of Podio. Geoffrey Tortus. Baldwin of Saint Abraham. Ulric, viscount of Naples [Note: B, Neapolis], and many others.

This was done and given in the king’s palace at Acre [Note: B, at Accon], in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1128, indiction 4, in the month of March.

### XLV. Privilege of King Baldwin II concerning the remission of the custom at the gate of Jerusalem

[Note: A, fol. 41r; B, fol. 35v.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

I, Baldwin, second king of Jerusalem by the grace of God, yielding to the prayers of our father, Lord Guarmund the patriarch, and also of the clergy and chapter [Note: B, people] of the holy city of Jerusalem, with the assent of my nobles, remit from now on and thereafter the custom which until now was exacted and paid at the gate by those bringing in grain, barley, and legumes [Note: B, legumina], both for the remedy of the soul of my predecessor, the glorious King Baldwin [Note: supplied from B], and for the safety and welfare of myself and my successors.

For that custom seemed exceedingly harsh and burdensome both to pilgrims visiting the Lord’s Sepulchre and to the inhabitants of that holy city.
