But when that privilege, at my insistence, had been brought forward and, in the presence of the surrounding court, read through openly and distinctly to the end, its worthy refutation became so evident to all who heard it that, although certain other points by which it contradicted itself were set aside, it was supported by not even the slightest assertion of a single witness, as the truth of deeds properly accomplished requires.

Thus, once the authority of the privilege had been entirely nullified, it was subsequently determined by the common judgment of the court that, since the monks of the monastery of Saint Paul had absolutely no grounds for obtaining a hearing from the church, both they and the canons of the Holy Sepulchre, without any evasion, were to bring the arguments of their respective cases before my public court. There their controversies were to be resolved by a proper judgment and concluded as justice dictated.

Since I did not wish to detain the aforesaid canons any longer, with the solemn feast of Easter approaching, I fixed a definite period of fifteen days for both parties. The monks, however, firmly resisting me, declared that they would accept no other date for pleading than one that the common court, after deliberation according to justice, should assign and announce to them.

When I had kindly assented to their request, the unanimous consideration of the entire court assigned to both parties an extension of forty days. The final day of this period is known to have fallen on the third day before the Kalends of April, the seventh feria, which at that time preceded the vigil of the Lord’s Day of Palm Branches.

On the appointed day, the monks of the church of Saint Paul and the canons of the Holy Sepulchre came to a place outside Antioch called the Iron Bridge, where I was then staying in camp, to conduct their case in my presence [Note: Col. 1187, B reads “in the presence of me”]. It seemed more convenient to me, however, since I needed sufficient time to obtain fuller counsel, to postpone the matter until I had entered Antioch. I therefore prudently extended the deadline until the third day.

On that day, when the monks and canons were intent upon arguing their case before me in the palace of Antioch, I likewise prolonged the same case until the Saturday of Easter week. I had not been able to summon the sufficient counsel of my nobles in so short a period.

When, after the Lord’s Easter, the appointed day arrived and I had gathered with me the entire order of the court for that hearing, the canons of the Holy Sepulchre came together at the first hour of the day for their case. The monks of the church of Saint Paul, however, did not appear before us either then or at any later time throughout the day.

When I had learned of their delay, I earnestly consulted the barons who were present about what I ought thereafter to do in this matter. After deliberation, they replied that, since the church of Saint Paul stood under the protection of my defense, I ought, out of grace, to invite the monks by the living voice of my messengers to the appointed hearing of the case. I should also instruct my messengers to inform the monks on my behalf that, unless they came to plead at the ninth hour of that very day, their absence would harm them just as much as if a judgment had been pronounced that completely refuted them.

Without delay, taking from among the other barons Guiterius of Mozo and Richard of Belmont, I summoned the abbot and the monks carefully, just as I had been advised. All of them replied with one voice, without offering any lawful excuse for exemption [Note: Col. 1187, B reads “excuses”], that they would neither come before me nor submit to the judgment of my court.

When I had received so obstinate a reply from them, I asked the canons patiently to wait until the third day, lest something perhaps be done precipitately and therefore with less justice. They too agreed quite peacefully.

After the third day of waiting had passed, only the canons, demanding justice, appeared. I kindly assented to their just petition [Note: Col. 1187, B reads “petition”] and placed upon my court the entire burden of discussing [Note: Col. 1187, B reads “deferring”] the justice of the matter, particularly through consideration of the circumstances that had to be brought forward.

Therefore, by the unanimous and common consultation of all the barons, it was approved that the canons, who had never evaded either the day or the case, ought by a just judgment to be invested with full possession of their right. This was to be done, however, in the following manner: after receiving the investiture [Note: supplied from B], they were to execute against both the monks of the church of Saint Paul and anyone else making a claim whatever my court should adjudicate.

Accordingly, in that manner and on that condition, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May I freely and peacefully invested the aforesaid canons of the Lord’s Sepulchre with the aforesaid garden and the remaining adjoining land, in accordance with their right.

Immediately after receiving the investiture, Lord the prior and the other canons freely offered to carry out the justice due to the church of Saint Paul [Note: Col. 1187, B reads “the fellow canons”]; but no one appeared to bring any charge against them.

We also do not wish to allow it to pass in silence as though neglected that the aforesaid canons produced Greek witnesses, mature in character and age. All of them affirmed that they would establish the justice of the Holy Sepulchre of which we speak, in accordance with the court’s decree, not by ordinary conjectural opinion but by the certain testimony of their own observation.

Since their testimony could properly be heard only at its appropriate place, especially while the opposing party was absent, the witnesses nevertheless, fearing that through their perhaps speedy death the justice of the glorious Sepulchre might be weakened, left written down in full what they were prepared to confirm with truthful speech and faithful memory, so that, if necessity should later require it, written authority would not be lacking in place of their living voice.

The names of the witnesses are:

Gregory, cantor of the church of Saint Mary; Thomas, subcantor; Michael, son of Molkem [Note: Col. 1189, B reads “Molkim”]; Abraham, son of Sucar.

When, finally, all matters had been brought to completion by God’s help, not without the burdensome prolixity of discussing [Note: Col. 1189, B reads “deferring”], I, Raimund, by God’s will prince of Antioch, and the most illustrious lady Constance, princess and my wife, by common assent and grant give and concede to the Most Holy Lord’s Sepulchre, to be possessed peacefully forever, the lawful gift of the investiture that had been made. We secure it with perpetual stability, adorned with the princely confirmation of this privilege and of our seal.

This privilege was made in the year of the incarnate Word of God 1140, in the month of April, indiction 3, in the fourth year of the principate of Lord Raimund, most invincible prince of Antioch. The witnesses are:

Lord Gaudin, archbishop of Mamistra; Lord Hugh, bishop of Gabala [Note: Col. 1189, B reads “Gabulanus”]; Aimericus, dean of Antioch; William Brachet, Aimericus, and William of Poitiers, chaplains of the palace; William, cleric of Peter; Peter, canon of the Temple; Godfrey [Note: Col. 1189, B reads “Godefridus”], canon of Saint Abraham; Drogo and Goisbert, knights of the Temple; Roger of Montibus, constable; Walter of Surdavalle; Garento of Saône; Fulk of Boino; William Fraisnelli; Leo Maiopolus, duke of Antioch; Geoffrey of Guirchia; Peter Armoini, castellan; Guiterius of Mozo; Richard of Belmont [Note: Col. 1189, B reads “Belmunt”]; Robert, son of Geoffrey; Pagan of Fai; Garnerius of Burgo; Hugh of Boleira; Abo of Molins; Chalo of Masiaco [Note: Col. 1189, B reads “Masiago”]; Basil, chamberlain, and Oliver, his brother [Note: Col. 1189, B reads “his brother Oliver”]; Garinus Malmus [Note: Col. 1189, B reads “Malmuz”], marshal; Raimund, marshal [Note: Col. 1189, this witness’s name is absent from A]; Gotefridus [Note: Col. 1189, B reads “Godefridus”], viscount; Theodore, notary; George, master of the secretariat.

Given at Antioch, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, by the hands of Odo, chancellor.

## XC. Charter of Prior Peter concerning the two mills belonging to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Antioch

[Note: A, folio 82 recto; B, folio 96 recto.]

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, amen.

I, Peter, by the grace of God prior of the Lord’s Sepulchre, make known to all the faithful, present and future, that when I came with certain of our fellow canons from Jerusalem to Antioch, in order that we might investigate the rights of the Lord’s Sepulchre—rights which in the time of the ancient Greeks and thereafter under the Turks had served that same Sepulchre—among other things I found, at the head of the bridge of the gate called “of the Count,” on the bank of the river Orontes, two sites for mills, one built and the other ruined, which for a long time the predecessors of the canons of the Lord’s Sepulchre had possessed freely and peacefully by hereditary right, as we have said.

Therefore, after careful investigation with Lord Raymond, prince of that city, and with the ancient Syrians [Note: Absent from B.], who faithfully took part with us in this concern, we jointly resolved to assign two mill-wheels in those mills, called Funeidec, which had already been partly rebuilt, on the river side, to three Syrians—namely Nichefor, Michael, and Nicholas—for them and their legitimate heirs to maintain in villeinage tenure. They were to provide all expenses necessary for the operation of the wheels, whether in iron and wood or in stone and all implements, both in the water and outside the water, both within the mill building and outside it. But they were to build the weir on the river side, as best they could, for the common benefit of all the wheels that were in the building.

They were also to have half of all the income they obtained from the two aforesaid wheels, whether from grain, flour, fish, or anything else; from their half they were to hire a guardian of the wheels, namely a miller, and they were to render the other part to our fellow canon or brother who would govern the place on our behalf [Note: Restored from B.], on the condition that the portions kept together were in no way to be divided without our servant who held the key.

If, however, by any misfortune that mill should be destroyed, the aforesaid Syrians were to rebuild, at their own expense, those wheels together with the mill and all its equipment, and preserve them as they had done before. But if they were unwilling to rebuild it, after being warned under triple testimony, they were to be permanently disinherited. Again, if their miller were convicted of theft [Note: B, “convicted.”], whatever number of *marcibans* he stole [Note: This word seems related to the Arabic *markeb*, meaning “boat”; it may perhaps refer to boats loaded with grain, from which the miller might divert the milling charges.], he was to pay twice that number of bezants as compensation. If he did not possess enough of his own, our canon or servant was to exact from the Syrians’ share the bezants assessed for the damage.

Moreover, if those Syrians dared to sell or pledge the aforesaid villeinage to outsiders, they were not permitted to do so except by the common decision of the chapter [Col. 1190D], because we had granted them the villeinage charitably and without payment. These provisions, therefore, shall remain firmly in force under the authority of our canon who will have dominion over all.

This charter was made in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1111, in the third indiction, in the fourth year of the principate of Lord Raymond, the revered prince, and of his wife Constance. The witnesses are:

Wlgrin, provost of the Holy Sepulchre. Also Aimeric, canon of the same church [Note: Absent from B.]. Nicholas, Gamaliel, Garnerius [Note: Restored from B: “of Maimundus the constable”; “of William.”], and Robert, fellow canons. Also Angerius [Note: B, Ansgerius.], abbot of Saint George. Benedict, cantor. Guido and Sylvester, fellow canons of the same church. Joscerand, chaplain. Theodore, notary.

## XCI. Charter of Raymond, Count of Tripoli, concerning the gift of the house at Mount Pilgrim

[Note: A, folio 83 recto and 87 verso; B, folio 97 recto.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, amen [Note: Absent from B.].

It is plainly evident from the numerous and authentic, invincible testimonies of divine and secular writings that it is fitting for the clemency of faithful princes to assent to the equitable petitions of the servants of God and, with devoted mind, to approve just desires pleasing to God so that they may be brought to fulfillment.

Accordingly, when John of pious memory, son and canon of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, earnestly and reasonably requested this, Raymond, count and most excellent prince of the Christian militia in the regions of Syria, wisely knowing that the price of the redemption of a man’s soul is a possession acquired justly, for the redemption of his own soul and those of his parents, with the common favor and counsel of his men, gave to God and to the glorious Church of the Most Holy Sepulchre of Our Lord Jesus Christ, which is in Jerusalem, a certain house on Mount Pilgrim. In ancient times that house had been devoted to the impure superstitions of the pagans, so that, every wicked gentile rite having been driven from it, it might now become a perpetual dwelling worthy of God.

After that house had been beneficially transferred by Christian religion into the Church of Christ for Christian worshippers, at the request of the same John Count Raymond also granted the Church of Saint George, which is in the mountains, with its appurtenances [Note: B, “appendages”; that is, appurtenances], in the presence and hearing of the dean of Poscheries and of his chaplain Pontius [Note: B, Poncius] of Grilione, and of Rostagnus of Port and Bernard, prior of Bethlehem.

Furthermore, since, because of the outbreak of wars, he could not at that time give as much as he wished, he did what he could: he firmly granted that, when the divine will, satisfying Christian desires, should deliver the city of Tripoli into their power [Note: B, “to their posterity”] for possession, the aforesaid Church of the Holy Sepulchre should have and possess in perpetuity whatever church in the whole aforesaid city would be the most excellent and worthy after the principal church. To that church he promised—indeed, insofar as he could establish it for the future—so much honor or revenue as could honestly suffice for the needs of thirteen clerics serving God there.

When, meanwhile, he paid the debt of death according to human necessity, his illustrious nephew William Jordan, leader of the Christian militia, succeeded him by hereditary right. Since he endeavored not only to preserve undefiled but also diligently to bring to the proper perfection the good works begun or established by his uncle Raymond, by this decree he lawfully confirmed the gifts and promises made by his uncle Raymond to the Holy Sepulchre.

Moreover, taking thought for the souls of himself and his parents, and striving to increase the aforesaid church through his own largesse, at the request of the same John he gave it a certain village called Buiora, with everything belonging to it, both trees and all other things.

Furthermore, overflowing with pious affection, he granted to the same church the free power to acquire and possess in perpetuity anything which any of the holders of his *terrarium* might wish to give permanently in these regions from their honors [Note: B, “from their holdings.”].

Therefore, so that the authentic disposition of this donation [Note: Supplied from B.] may remain perpetually unchanged, undefiled and unshaken against every wicked will and unlawful presumption, I, William Jordan, servant of Christ and leader of the Christian militia [Note: Supplied from B.], by placing the sign of my own hand [Note: B, “by affixing”] upon it, took the greatest care to corroborate it with a devout disposition of mind.

The sign of Count William.

For the soul of the illustrious and faithful servant of God Raymond, the originator and author also of this donation, all you who read or hear this, pray humbly to God.

The lawful confirmation of this donation was made in the year from the incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ 1106, in the month of August, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September, in the presence of all the people assembled for the dedication of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, which is on Mount Pilgrim; specifically, in the presence and hearing [Note: Absent from B.] of the following men who are written here:

Aicard of Arles and dean of Poscheries; Stephen of Brino; Geoffrey [Note: B, Gaufred] of Pennes; William son of Peter, constable; William son of Raymond, constable; William Berall; Raymond of Balcis.

I, Raymond, son of Pontius [Note: B, Poncius], count of Tripoli by the grace of God, grant and confirm forever, by the impression of my seal, everything whatsoever that my predecessors—whether the venerable Count Raymond [of Saint-Gilles] or William Jordan—gave to the aforesaid Church of the Holy Sepulchre for the salvation of their souls, as well as whatever other persons belonging to my dignity and honor have given or shall give as alms [Note: Supplied from B: “more frequently”] to the aforementioned church from their rightful possessions.

## XCII. Charter of Cecilia, Countess of Tripoli, granting permission for anyone who wishes to bake in the oven that we have at Mount Pilgrim

[Note: A, folio 84 recto; B, folio 99 recto.]

[Col. 1193A]

Oppressed by the misery of the human condition and, as though by a second law of nature, always inclined to sin under the burden of habit, placed amid such great waves of disturbance, we have considered it very necessary and useful to flee to the aid of the benefits and prayers of the servants of God, who are joined to him more intimately by constant and blessed union, so that what we do not dare hope to obtain through our own merits, we may at least deserve to obtain from God through theirs [Note: Absent from B]. This is properly accomplished when, from our abundance, we supply their poverty; while by the reciprocal gift of charity we bestow our material goods upon them, although small, we receive from them the better things, namely spiritual goods.

Therefore I, Cecilia, countess, for the salvation of the soul of my lord Pontius, count, and for the salvation of my own soul and of the soul of my son, Count Raymond, with the consent of that same son of mine, and also at the request of Fulk, king of Jerusalem, and Melisende, queen, have granted as a perpetual alms [Note: B, “alms”], into the hands of Wlgrin, prior of Mount Pilgrim and canon of the Holy Sepulchre, that whoever wishes may bake freely and without any complaint in the oven which the aforesaid canons of the Holy Sepulchre possess at Mount Pilgrim.

I and my son Count Raymond [Note: B, “Raymond count”] made this grant in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1139, with the following witnesses:

Gerald, bishop of Tripoli; Peter of Podium Laurentius; Peter Raymond of La Balma; Jocelin of Calmont [Note: B, Calmunt]; Silvio Robert; Peter of Podium, prior of the Hospital; Master Alberic, prior of Bethlehem; William Apieres, *placearius* of Mount Pilgrim; and Homudeus [Note: B, Homodeus].

## XCIII. Charter of Raymond, Count of Tripoli, concerning the freedom that we have in the port of Tripoli

[Note: A, folio 84 verso; B, folio 100 recto.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, amen [Note: Absent from B.].

I, Raymond, count of Tripoli by the grace of God, and my wife Hodierna, countess of Tripoli by the same grace and daughter of the king of Jerusalem, wish it to be known to the sons of Holy Mother Church, present and future, and to be retained in memory in this charter, that, moved by the petitions [Note: B, “petitions”] of Lord William, patriarch of Jerusalem by divine grace, returning from Antioch, and of his suffragans—Fulcher, archbishop of Tyre; Robert, archbishop of Nazareth; Bernard, bishop of Sidon—and of many others, we give and grant to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre of the Lord [Note: Absent from B.] and to the brothers serving and destined to serve the Lord in it freedom in our port of Tripoli to bring in, remove, and carry away from there whatever things may be necessary for their needs, quietly and without any exaction [Note: Supplied from B.].

For the remedy of our souls and those of our parents, we likewise confirm to them in perpetuity all those gifts, whether in villages, lands, vineyards, olive groves, villeins, or other possessions, which Lord Raymond, Count of Saint-Gilles, his nephew William Jordan, and Count Bernard [Note: B, Bertrand], and Count Pontius [Note: B, Poncius], my father, as well as other barons or holders of land, faithfully gave to the Church of the Lord’s Sepulchre and its canons. We grant, approve, and confirm all these by our seal, and also Saint George [Note: B, “except Saint George”].

The witnesses to this gift are:

Gerald, bishop of Tripoli; John, canon; Master Gilbert [Note: B, Gislebert]; Rainerius, constable; Peter of Podium Laurentius; William Rainoard; Gauscelin [Note: B, Goscelin] of Cavomonte; William Porcellet; Saxo; Pontius [Note: B, Poncius] of Sura; Gerald [Note: B, Giraldus] Isnelli; Brunellus, steward; Raymond [Note: B, Raimondus] Lamberti; Pontius [Note: B, Poncius] Giraldi; Stephen, monk; Otrannus, count’s chancellor, who dictated this charter.

This charter was made in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1140, in the month of January, in the third indiction.

## XCIV. Another [charter] of the same [person] and concerning the same matter, but more universal [Note: B, “more universal.”]

[Note: A, folio 85 recto; B, folio 100 verso.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

I, Raymond, count of Tripoli by the grace of God, and Hodierna, countess of Tripoli by the same grace and daughter of the king of Jerusalem, wish it to be known and retained in memory in this charter that, for the sake of our souls and those of our parents, we give, approve, and grant to William, patriarch of Jerusalem by the grace of God, and to the canons of the Most Holy Sepulchre, our freedom in our port of Tripoli: that they may freely carry away from our port, without any charge, their oil and all other revenues which they have from all our land, and likewise freely carry away from our port whatever they wish to purchase for the use [Note: B’s reading, *ad usus*, is much preferable to *ad versus*] of the church and canons of the Most Holy Sepulchre.

Moreover [Note: B, “Then”], we grant, approve, and confirm by our seal all those gifts which Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles, Count Bertrand, and Count Pontius [Note: B, Poncius] gave to the Church of the Most Holy Sepulchre and to the canons of that place, and also Saint George [Note: B, “except Saint George”].

The witnesses to this gift are our barons:

R[ainerius], constable; P[eter] of Podium Laurentius; W[illiam] Porcellet; William Rainoard; Saxo; Bertrand [Note: B, Bertrandus] son of Humbert; Gauscelin of Cavomonte; P[ontius] of Suira [Note: B, Sura]; Brunellus; G[eraldus] Isnel; O[trannus], chancellor, who dictated this charter.

This charter was made in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1140, in the month of December. The following are additionally witnesses to this gift:

Robert, archbishop of Nazareth; Fulcher, archbishop of Tyre; Bernard, bishop of Sidon; Guido of Beirut; Elias, king’s chancellor; Baldwin, chancellor of the patriarch of Jerusalem; John, canon of Tripoli; Rainald, chaplain of Nazareth.

## XCV. Charter of Raymond, Count of Tripoli, confirming certain houses

[Note: A, folio 85 verso; B, folio 101 recto. In B the heading reads: “Another [charter] of the same [person] concerning the houses which Lord Wlgrin bought at Tripoli from William of Sira.”]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, amen.

Since the memory of this age is fleeting, and its condition cannot always endure [Note: Absent from B.], it is proper and useful to commend to written memory those things done before us, so that present and future inhabitants of the land of Tripoli may have true and complete knowledge of them. Thus, if perhaps after the passage of time any disagreement should arise concerning something, it may be clarified by the record of the writing.

Therefore I, Raymond, count of Tripoli by the grace of God, and Hodierna, countess of Tripoli, and Raymond, our son, wish it to be known and retained in memory in this charter by all people, present and future, that Lord Wlgrin, canon of the Most Holy Sepulchre, bought certain houses in our city from William of Sira for eighty-one bezants, with our assent and goodwill and that of our barons [Note: The word “bought” is repeated here in both manuscripts]. For the remedy of our souls and those of our parents, we approve and grant these houses in good faith and without evil intent [Note: “evil intent” supplied].

Furthermore, out of love for Lord Wlgrin, we likewise give and grant to the Church of the Most Holy Sepulchre and to the canons serving God in that place, for the remedy of our souls, a certain yield [Note: B, “piece”] of land from our *tambulum* [Note: B, “stable”] and the vault of the church tower. And so that this charter may remain firm, let it be confirmed by the impression of our seal.

The witnesses to this charter are:

Rainerius, constable, with his mother; Radulphus Caslan, brother of the Temple of Solomon; Peter of Podium Laurentius; William Rainoald; his son Saxo; his brother Raymond; Goscelin of Calvo Monte; Robert Silvius; Pontius of Sira; Brunellus, steward; Gerald Isnelli; Stephen, monk; Pontius Giraldi; Hermengard; Pellicius; Albert, chamberlain; William, countess’s chaplain; Otrannus, chancellor, who dictated this charter.

This charter was made in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1143, in the sixth indiction [Note: B, “This charter was made”].

In addition, we approve and grant in perpetuity to the Lord’s Sepulchre and to the canons serving God in that place that vault which Lord Wlgrin bought from Guido, to be held and possessed in perpetuity in good faith and without evil intent.

## XCVI. Charter of Lady Adelaide, wife of Hugh the Hebrew, concerning the twelve bezants which she granted us annually

[Note: A, folio 86 recto; B, folio 102 recto.]

In the year of the Lord 1135, I, Adelaide, formerly the wife of Hugh the Hebrew [Note: B, “Ebriacus”], first for the honor of God and of the Holy Sepulchre, and for the soul of my lord and husband Hugh the Hebrew [Note: B, “Ebriacus”], and for my salvation and that of my sons and for the souls of us all, and because the canons of the Holy Sepulchre received me, the soul of my husband, and all my sons into their fellowship, prayers, and fraternity, give and confirm, together with my son William Hebrew, that these canons [Note: B, “the aforesaid”] shall receive from our property twelve bezants each year, or 120 *rotulae* of oil; and that they shall celebrate each year the anniversary of Hugh the Hebrew, which is on the sixth day of October, the vigil of the holy martyrs Sergius and Bacchus; and that on that same day they shall commemorate the souls of our sons and daughters. The witnesses are:

Guidofressus; Guiniguisus; Stephen; Bertrand [Note: B, Bertrandus]; Segnoretus; Pagan, blacksmith.

Peregrinus was present at all these proceedings, and at the command of the lady and her son William Hebrew he placed this seal and wrote this.

## XCVII. Charter of Count Raymond concerning all the possessions that we have in the County of Tripoli

[Note: A, folio 86 verso; absent from B.]

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, amen.

Let it be known to all, present and future, that I, Raymond, count of Tripoli by the grace of God, for the love of God and the salvation of my soul and the repose of my parents, and also at the request of Lord William, patriarch of Jerusalem by the grace of God, Peter, prior of the Lord’s Sepulchre, and the entire chapter of that church, grant, confirm forever without disturbance, and corroborate by the impression of my seal, all the possessions which our predecessors gave to the glorious Sepulchre throughout our entire County of Tripoli, namely Lord Raymond, Count of Saint-Gilles; Count William Jordan; Count Bertrand; Count Pontius; and also the barons and other faithful men:

First, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, which is on Mount Pilgrim, with its houses and its entire court; also the oven with the houses belonging to it, so that, without contradiction from us or our heirs, all who wish may bake there for the benefit and profit of the aforesaid church’s house, according to what my mother, Countess Cecilia, gave and granted in our presence, with us confirming the same.

Also the houses which they possess on Mount Pilgrim and in Tripoli, from the slope of the mountain, on both sides of the old road, just as they now possess them, from the wall as far as the aqueduct; also the garden.

We likewise give and grant them freedom in our port of Tripoli to bring in and carry away from it whatever things are necessary for their needs, quietly and without any customary payment or exaction; and we confirm with the same freedom and quiet the right of passage through the city gates and throughout our entire land.

The Church of Saint George in the mountains, with its villages and all its other appurtenances, in the manner in which it is known and proven that Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles gave it to the aforesaid church; the village of Buiola with its villeins and appurtenances and its entire olive grove, which Count William Jordan gave at the dedication of the Church of the Sepulchre on Mount Pilgrim; three other villages in the mountains, with their villeins and appurtenances, namely Abdin, Bebula, and Benehara, which Count Bertrand gave to the same church; and on the other side of the mountain the village of Medera with its villeins and appurtenances, which William Ermengard gave.

Also the *gaustina* called Loisan, which Raymond of Raisac gave; the village of Helmedel with its villeins and appurtenances near Guibelacard, which Ribod gave; the village of Cafarsequel in the territory of Gibelet, which is called the village of the Bridge of Sici, which Stephen of Brolo gave; in the village of Bocumbe, one villein with one *carrucata* of land, whom Raymond of Narbonne gave; in the village called Aer, one villein with one *carrucata* of land, whom Bernard Derat gave; also in the village of Derie, one villein with one *carrucata* of land and ten jars of oil, which the lord whoever he may be of the village must pay annually, which Peter of Podium Laurentius gave with the consent of his wife; also one villein with one *carrucata* of land, whom Peter, nephew of Roger the constable, gave in the village of Ardin; and in the village of Buissera, one villein with one *carrucata* of land, whom Adalard gave; in the village [Note: Correct to “in the village”] of Sorbe, one villein with one *carrucata* of land, whom Geoffrey of Pennes gave.

In the territory of Nophis, also twelve bezants or 120 *litrae* of oil, which Adalaxia gave to the aforesaid church for the soul of her husband Hugh Hebrew, together with her son William Hebrew, to be paid annually forever; also one villein with all that belongs to him, and the lands of another villein, whom William of Boschet gave.

We grant the aforesaid villeins and their heirs, with their lands, to the church to have perpetually.

We fortify all the foregoing and all other things which the canons may thereafter justly acquire, whether by the donation of any persons, by purchase, by any exchange, or which they presently possess, for the aforesaid Church of the Holy Sepulchre by this charter; and, as stated above, we mark them with our seal, so that they may possess them freely and quietly, without any exaction or service, forever. The witnesses written below also confirm the same, so that our decree may remain an inviolable memorial and may never at any time be violated by us or our successors.

Rainerius, constable; Peter of Podium Laurentius; Gocelin of Cavomonte; Saxo; Gerald Isnel; Brunellus, steward; Raymond Lamberti; Pontius Giraldi; Stephen, monk; Otrannus, chancellor.

This charter was made in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1143, in the sixth indiction.

## XCVIII. Charter of Bertrand, Count of Tripoli, concerning the three villages Abdin, Habela, and Beniharan

[Note: A, folio 89 recto; B, folio 104 verso. B, “Count of Tripoli.”]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1112, on the Kalends of December [Note: The reading of the manuscripts is very doubtful; perhaps one should read: “in the year 1110, on the second day before the Kalends.”], I, Bertrand, illustrious count, [son of] Raymond of Saint-Gilles, restore and release to the Lord God and to the Church of the Sepulchre of Our Lord Jesus Christ, which is situated in the fortress of Mount Pilgrim, three villages, namely Addin [Note: B, Abdin], Habela [Note: B, Babela], and Beniaran [Note: B, Beniharen], with all their appurtenances. I formerly gave them to the aforesaid church for the remedy of the soul of William Jordan, my kinsman, in the presence of Lord Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, and of the archbishop of Albano and Archdeacon Arnulf, and of other good men, and into the hands of Lord John, who at that time was prior of the same church, as is manifest to all people, just as the charter declares.

It is manifest that I, Bertrand, the aforesaid count, through my sins having entangled me, unjustly placed the aforesaid holding under my dominion and power. By God’s will it came about that the chapter of Jerusalem chose one of its brothers for the priorate of the Church of Mount Pilgrim, namely Arnaldus [Note: B, Arnaldum], who was sent by us so that he might preserve the holding acquired for the aforesaid church and acquire what had been lost.

When he came and proclaimed to me the loss of the holding, divine fear suggesting it, I took counsel from the Lord; and with all my nobles, moved by piety and concern for the remedy of my soul and the souls of my father, mother, and all my parents, I, Count Bertrand, and my son Pontius restore and release it under this condition and with this stability: that neither I nor my son Pontius, nor any of my heirs, nor any power, should dare to break up or alienate this aforesaid holding, but that it should belong freely and absolutely, now and always, to the Lord God and to the aforementioned Church of the Holy Sepulchre, without deceit or evil intent.

Moreover, I, Count Bertrand, approve and confirm all donations already made and confirmed by my father, namely Raymond, Count of Saint-Gilles, and by William Jordan, my cousin, together with the entire assembly that was present at the dedication [Note: Restored from B.] of the aforesaid church; and my son Pontius likewise approves them, as is written in the charters of the aforesaid church. Henceforth this release and the aforesaid approval shall remain firm and stable for all time.

For this release and relinquishment of the aforesaid holding, for the blessing and reverence of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Prior Arnald gave Lord Count Bertrand a good horse and an excellent mule.

This charter of release was made, confirmed by Count Bertrand, approved by his son Pontius, attested by the bishops, and corroborated by the laymen. If anyone should come against this donation, release [Note: B, “release”], or approval in order to violate it—whoever he may be, whether I, the aforesaid count, or my son Pontius [Note: B, “my son Pontius”], or any of my heirs or relatives, or any power, or any sacrilegious person who wishes to take away or diminish this aforesaid holding from the Church of the Holy Sepulchre—let him first incur the wrath of almighty God; be cast outside the thresholds of the church as a plunderer [Note: B, “as an outsider”]; become a participant with Judas the traitor in hell; suffer eternal punishment with Dathan and Abiron [Note: B, Abyron]; be subject to the excommunication [Note: Supplied from B.] of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, of all the bishops, of the patriarch of Jerusalem, of the bishop of Tripoli, of the archbishop of Femia, and of the bishop of Béziers; and, moreover, let the anathema *maranatha* [Note: B, *maranatha*] remain upon him without end.

The sign of Bertrand, count. The sign of Pontius, his son. The sign of Bishop A[lbert] of Tripoli [Note: B, “A[lbert], bishop of Tripoli”]. The sign of P[eter], archbishop of Femia [Note: B, “P[eter] of Femia”]. The sign of A[rnulf], bishop of Béziers [Note: B, “A[rnulf] of Béziers”]. The sign of Roger, constable. The sign of Udalard of Pontiano. The sign of Pontius [Note: B, Poncius] of Grilione.

## XCIX. Charter of Baldwin IV, king, concerning the grant of John Gothman’s land

[Note: A, folio 90 recto; B, folio 106 recto.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, amen.

Let it be known to all, present and future [Note: B, “future and present”], that I, Baldwin, by the grace of God the fourth Latin king in holy Jerusalem, have approved, granted, and confirmed to the canons of the Lord’s Sepulchre all the villages called by the following names: Bethahatap [Note: B, Bethaatap], Derhassen, Derxerip, Culi, and the Lion’s *vastina*, with their entire integrity—that is, their *gastinae* and appurtenances, wherever they extend in length or breadth—which John Gothman sold for 1,400 bezants to the canons of the Lord’s Sepulchre, with his wife Amandala and his son Ancherius and that son’s wife Stephania, and with the daughter of the aforesaid John, Elizabeth, wife namely of Hugh, lord of Caesarea, and with that same Hugh and all others to whom the grant of this present sale appears to belong, or to whom hereditary possession of the aforesaid sold property may belong in the future.

Persuaded to a very great degree by the plea of that John Gothman and his son Ancherius, and moved by the brotherly affection with which I have long been bound to the aforesaid canons, I approve, grant, and confirm these things to those same canons who now serve God there in the Church of the Lord’s Resurrection and who will serve him there in the future.

I do not wish to pass over in silence what the aforesaid John and his son Ancherius stipulated in their agreement with the canons in question: namely, that if any complaint should arise now or in the future, from any quarter whatsoever, concerning the aforesaid villages, their *gastinae*, or their appurtenances [Note: B, “appurtenances”], the aforesaid John, his son Ancherius, and the successors of their inheritance must forever settle, quiet, and completely remove it from the aforesaid canons by virtue of the agreement made.

Therefore, so that the Church of the Lord’s Sepulchre and its community, present and future, may have all these things, expressed and recorded one by one, freely, peacefully, and without complaint from anyone, and without any service [Note: B, “service”], exaction, or lordship, now and in the future, and may possess them forever by perpetual right, I confirm them by this present page, marked by the witnesses written below and by the impression of my seal [Note: B, “the pressing of my seal”].

This was done in the year from the incarnation [Note: B, “of the incarnation”] of the Lord 1161, in the ninth indiction. The witnesses to this matter are:

Amalric, count of Ascalon. Humphrey of Toron, constable. Philip the Neapolitan. Hugh of Ibelin [Note: [Col. 1199] B, Ybelino.]. Hugh of Caesarea. Baldwin of the Island. Walter of Saint-Omer, castellan and lord of Tiberias [Note: [Col. 1199] B, Tyberiadis.]. Gormund of Tiberias [Note: [Col. 1199] B, Guormundus.]. Clarembald, viscount of Acre. William of Hursa. Guy de Maneriis.

Given at Acre, by the hand of Stephen, acting as deputy in this office for Lord Ralph, [Col. 1200D] bishop of Bethlehem [Note: [Col. 1199] B, Bethleemite.] and royal chancellor, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December.

### C [Note: [Col. 1199] A, fol. 90 verso; B, fol. 107 recto.] PRIVILEGE OF JOHN GOTHMANNUS CONCERNING THE SALE OF LAND

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen.

Since, on account of the instability of human life—for it is transitory [Col. 1201A] and daily tends toward decline—the memory of accomplished deeds quickly slips from the mind, the authority sanctioned by the example of the Fathers has established that memory should be entrusted to writing. Therefore, wishing to imitate their praiseworthy enactments according to the measure of my strength, I, John Gothmannus, wish it to be made known to all, present and future, by the memorial of this writing, that I, the aforesaid John Gothmannus, with the praise and consent of my wife Amandala and my son Ancherius together with his wife Stephania, and also my daughter Elizabeth, namely the wife of Hugh, lord of Caesarea, as well as the aforesaid Hugh himself and all others to whom consent for this sale appears to belong, or to whom hereditary possession of the property sold below may hereafter belong, [Col. 1201B] have sold to my lords and brothers, the canons of the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre—namely, lord Nicholas the prior and all the others now serving God there and those who will serve him there in the future—the estates called by the following names: Bethaap [Note: [Col. 1201] B, Bethaatap.], Derassen [Note: [Col. 1201] B, Derhassen.], Derxerip, Culi, and Vastina of Leo, with their entire extent, namely their wastelands and appurtenances, wherever they extend in length or breadth, for 1,400 bezants, so that they may hold and possess them by perpetual right, entirely free, released, and peaceful from every claim of men, service, exaction, and lordship [Note: [Col. 1201] B, “of all men”], and so that no service whatsoever may be rendered to any person on account of the aforesaid estates.

Indeed, driven by great necessity—namely, liberation and redemption from pagan captivity—and with the counsel and consent of my lord King Baldwin, in whose fief the possession sold here belonged, and who also confirmed it by the authority of his privilege and fortified this present page with my seal [Note: [Col. 1201] B, “his seal”], I sold the estates in question, with all their aforesaid appurtenances [Note: [Col. 1201] B, pertinenciis.], to the aforementioned canons, my son Ancherius cooperating with me in every way and in all things.

Therefore, if any claim should arise now or in the future concerning the aforesaid estates or their appurtenances, we and our successors shall bring it [Note: [Col. 1201] B, “shall remove it”] and make complete peace concerning it; thus, then, for as long as we live. But when we have departed this life in the human manner, those to whom our inheritance passes after us shall remain perpetually bound to the convent of the Holy Sepulchre [Col. 1201D], so that, if any loss should befall that convent on account of a claim that has been brought, it may be restored in full to the aforesaid convent by them, and the aforesaid sale may remain valid forever.

Therefore, unwilling that anything should be lacking from the authority of this privilege of mine, I asked my lord King Baldwin to strengthen this present page with the impression of his seal; this I finally obtained through the persistent petitions of both myself and my son Ancherius and my friends. Accordingly, my lord, as I said above, fortified this present page with his seal [Note: [Col. 1201] B, “with his seal”]; he also confirmed by another privilege, written in his own name, this sale of mine to the aforesaid canons.

But I, taking care for my soul and prudently providing for the future for the canons so often mentioned, ordered this present page to be written by means of a chirograph [Note: [Col. 1201] B, cyrographum.], as the upper part indicates, so that it could not later be shaken or challenged by any of my successors. The witnesses to this matter are:

Odo of Saint-Amand, castellan of David’s Tower [Note: [Col. 1201] B, “castellan of David’s Tower.”]. Marmio. Ralph Bornio. Adam the Black and Fulk, his brother. Thomas Patricius. Peter Hermenius. Baharam. Geoffrey of Tours, seneschal of Lord Amalric the patriarch. Briccius [Note: [Col. 1201] B, Brictius.]. Rainald Sicherius. Gerald Aldenarius. Albert the Lombard. [Col. 1202B] William Beraldus. Arbertus Tortus. William the Norman.

This was done in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1161, in the ninth indiction, on the third day before the Nones of December.

### CI [Note: [Col. 1201] A, fol. 92 recto; absent from B.] PRIVILEGE OF BERNARD OF BOURGES CONCERNING A HOUSE THAT HE GAVE TO THE CHURCH OF THE HOLY SEPULCHRE

Let it be known to all people, future and present, that I, Bernard of Bourges, and my wife Ahoys, have become brothers of the church of the Holy Sepulchre and of its canons by the grace of God. For the salvation of ourselves and our parents, we give to them our house and whatever we possess, as well as the land that we acquired near the gate of the Holy Sepulchre for a rent of two bezants, to be possessed by hereditary right under the following condition:

In our house, for as long as we live, we shall remain possessing our other property and protected by the defense of the aforesaid canons. When either of us has died, the canons shall have a third part of everything. The survivor, if he or she wishes, shall go to the church with his or her other third part and receive food and clothing from it. Otherwise, the survivor shall remain in his or her house and live from his or her own property, and after his or her death the church shall have that third part together with the preceding portion, without any impediment.

A third part shall belong to one of our daughters, likewise joined as a participant to their brotherhood, when she reaches marriageable age, or even if she marries; alternatively, the canons shall give her 100 bezants. [Col. 1202D] If she dies without heirs, everything shall remain entirely with the church without any claim. If we beget other children, excluding all others, we establish that they shall share with the aforesaid daughter only in the third part. Moreover, if, after our deaths, any debt remains, we order it to be repaid jointly from our portions and from the daughter’s portion.

For this arrangement, therefore, Lord Peter, prior of the Holy Sepulchre, and all the canons who are brothers with him have granted that we shall forever be their brothers and participants in all their spiritual goods. Three times a year—namely, at Christmas, Easter, and the feast of Jerusalem—they have also permitted us to receive, in memory of our brotherhood, one proper measure of wine with two loaves of bread.

The witnesses are:

Lord William the patriarch. Fulk, his chaplain. Amelius, deacon. Aschetinus, viscount. Humbert, goldsmith. Herbert with the beard. Gerald, deacon of the Holy Sepulchre, who composed this charter. William of Babylon.

### CII [Note: [Col. 1203] A, fol. 92 verso; absent from B.] PRIVILEGE OF PETER, PRIOR OF THE HOLY SEPULCHRE, AND THE CANONS CONCERNING THE SALE OF THE SAME HOUSE

In the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1135, in the thirteenth indiction, Peter, prior of the Holy Sepulchre, and the entire group of canons who were his brothers of that place sold the house that had belonged to Bernard of Bourges, and another house that had belonged to William the dragoman and was contiguous to the aforesaid house, to Petronilla, a Hungarian woman, for 440 bezants, to be used as a hospital house for her people, so that she might possess them eternally as houses bought with her own rent and, as stated, sold to her and her people.

If she or her Hungarian successors should later wish to sell or mortgage the aforesaid houses because of any necessity that might arise, they shall offer them for sale or mortgage to the prior and canons of the Holy Sepulchre. If the prior and canons should not wish to buy or mortgage the same houses on the same terms as others, they may sell or mortgage them without objection to whomever they wish.

The aforementioned woman received daily from the refectory of the Holy Sepulchre the prebend of four persons. But, for the salvation of her soul, caring as a sister of the church for the needs of the brothers, she remitted part of the prebends, so that henceforth she would remain content with two prebends, one for a canon and the other for a servant.

This charter was drawn up while Lord William presided over the patriarchate of the holy church of Jerusalem and the most noble King Fulk was reigning. The witnesses are:

Roger, bishop of Ramla. Anselm, bishop of Bethlehem. Acard, prior of the Temple of the Lord. Arnold, prior of Mount Zion. Henry, prior of the Mount of Olives. Robert, abbot of Jehoshaphat Valley. Cosmas the Hungarian, hermit. [Col. 1203D] Boniface, his companion. Simeon the Hungarian, archdeacon. Roard, viscount. Raymond, master of the Hospital. Rainald of Pons, and many others.

Whoever attempts to invalidate or violate this agreement, let him be anathema before God and men.

### CIII [Note: [Col. 1203] A, fol. 93 recto; absent from B.] CONCERNING THE PURCHASE OF A CERTAIN HOUSE, WHICH BERNARD OF CASTELLO-RADULPHI BOUGHT FROM GEORGE RAICO

Bernard of Castello-Radulphi and Havidis, his wife, bought a house from George Raico and Bursardus, which George had bought from Peter the Breton and Geoffrey, his associate, for 80 bezants including all customary charges.

This Bernard bought the house in the time of Patriarch Gormund and the second King Baldwin, when the latter went to fight at Bursechinum, before Aschetinus, viscount of Jerusalem, who received the legal dues concerning it. The witnesses were:

Odo, father-in-law of Pisellus; Bertran the Auvergnat; Robert without a beard; Andrew, his son-in-law; Fulk Berruer; Stephen of Auvergne; Pagan the Fool; William the Fat, the placer; Albert, son of A[schetinus], the viscount; Eudebert the Red; Baldri of the Temple; Roger of Bayeux; Soibert; [Col. 1204B] Ralph of Baugency; Cudener; Berenger; Ralph Fabri; Theobald; Brunet, the money-changer; Robert, gatekeeper of David’s Gate; and Peter Fabri.

Cleric Ogerus made this charter in David’s Tower. Bernard bought this house from George and Bursardus without any claim, to sell or give it as he wished.

Marages, son of Bursardus, who was present at the drinking associated with this transaction, is a witness to it.

### CIV [Note: [Col. 1203] A, fol. 93 verso; absent from B.] PRIVILEGE THAT PETER, PRIOR OF THE HOLY SEPULCHRE, MADE FOR BERNARD AND HIS WIFE

Let it be known to all, future and present, that I, Peter, prior of the Lord’s Sepulchre, and the entire convent thereof grant to Bernard and his wife, received into our brotherhood, a certain house with one shop for possession under the following condition:

For as long as they live, they shall have the whole house and shop, except for two chambers of the same house and also the stables, which we retain under our authority for the lodging of Lambert of Ptolemais and for the safekeeping of his belongings. If they wish to leave their own property and come to us with all that is theirs, we shall thereafter provide them with the necessities of food and clothing.

But when one of them dies, we shall have half of all the money, and the survivor shall come to us with his or her other half, if he or she wishes, to receive necessities from us as well. Otherwise, the survivor shall remain in the house for the whole of his or her life; and when he or she dies, the house and shop, free and released, together with all his or her possessions, shall be left to us.

Moreover, if they have a child when they die, they shall leave us two parts of their money and give the third to the child; the child shall neither make nor possess any claim in the house or shop.

Furthermore, if the man, after his wife’s death, takes another wife, or the woman, after her husband’s death, marries another man, they shall likewise possess the house and shop for as long as they live. But when both have died, the foreign husband or foreign wife shall not have the house or shop; rather, the house [Col. 1205A] and shop shall return to us, free and released, together with the money of the deceased.

The money shall be distributed in this manner: they shall leave half to the foreign wife or foreign husband; and if they have a child from such a foreign union, she shall give one part of her money to us, another to the child, and a third to the husband.

This charter was made in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1133, in the eleventh indiction.

Concerning the retention of the chambers and stables that we retained for Lambert’s lodging, we make a release upon Lambert’s death. Lambert’s wife, however, for as long as she remains without a husband, shall likewise lodge in them.

The witnesses are:

Humbert, goldsmith; Holdreus; Turstanus Angelus; John Galiga; Milo Curvesarius; Peter of Périgord; [Col. 1205B] Elias, his brother; Robert the Cook; Peter of Ramla; Bernard, goldsmith; and Gerald, deacon and canon of the Holy Sepulchre, who composed this charter.

### CV [Note: [Col. 1205] A, fol. 94 recto; absent from B.] PRIVILEGE OF RICHARD IAFERINUS CONCERNING A CERTAIN HOUSE

Let it be known to all cultivators of the Lord’s vineyard that I, Nicholas, prior of the Holy Sepulchre, with the consent of our entire chapter, grant the house held by Bernard Bursarius to Richard Iaferinus and his heirs, to possess and improve freely and peacefully forever, on the condition that every year, on the Kalends of March, the aforesaid Richard or his successor shall pay us and our successors fourteen bezants as rent.

We add that, if they wish to sell that house, they shall first offer it for sale to us. If we wish to retain it, we shall have it for one mark of silver less; otherwise, they shall have permission to give or sell it to whomever they wish, entirely excepting all knights and churches, while the aforesaid rent remains secured.

This was enacted on the fourth day before the Nones of March, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1160. The witnesses are:

Nicholas, prior. Arnulf, subprior. Bernard, cantor. Godfrey, treasurer. Ebrard. Ilbert. Peter of the Sepulchre. Peter Clement. Achilles. Hugh of Nigella. Peter of Latina. Peter the Lombard. [Col. 1205D] Rainald of Ochis. Robert of Antioch.

Among the laymen:

Pisellus, goldsmith. Baldwin Borne. Peter Salomonis. Robert the Cook. Uldretus, goldsmith. Gerald Salomonis. Peter Petragorc.

### CVI [Note: [Col. 1205] A, fol. 94 verso; absent from B.] CONCERNING A CERTAIN GARDEN THAT MABILIA GAVE TO THE CHURCH OF THE HOLY SEPULCHRE

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen.

It should be known and committed to worthy memory that I, Mabilia, for the redemption of the soul of my husband and my son, and for relieving the poverty of my own soul and body, gave and granted to the canons of the Holy Sepulchre, my fellow brothers and lords, my garden during my lifetime and, after my death, my house, both to be possessed by perpetual right.

It was not entirely without payment. For this they repaid me 170 bezants; they spent 40 bezants on enclosing the garden with a wall and repairing the cistern that was there; and, for as long as I lived, they granted me food determined by common agreement, namely, every day, one canon’s loaf, half a measure of tempered wine, and a bowl of cooked food; on Sundays and great solemnities, a fresh piece of meat or some portion of the food that the lords would eat.

[Col. 1206B] This was done in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1132, on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, while Fulk, king of Jerusalem, was reigning and Lord William was presiding as patriarch. The witnesses to this matter are:

Lord William the patriarch.

And the canons of the Holy Sepulchre:

Peter, prior. Peter of Barcelona. Hugh, provost. Geoffrey of Constantinople. Ralph of Paris. Peter Bernard. Garnerius of Le Mans. Guy. Gerald. Peter Clement. Evrard, and the other canons. Aschetinus, viscount. Rainald of Pons. Geoffrey Acus. Tosetus. Hildredus.

### CVII [Note: [Col. 1205] A, fol. 94 bis recto; absent from B.] PRIVILEGE OF ANDREW AND HOSANNA

[Col. 1206C]

Let it be known to all, future and present, that I, Peter Bernard, canon of the Holy Sepulchre, with the consent of Peter the prior and my fellow canons, have granted Andrew and Hosanna, his wife, permission to build a house at their own expense on the land of the Holy Sepulchre that is in Jerusalem, in the king’s quarter. On one side it is enclosed by the house of the Holy Sepulchre, on another by the house of the Hospital that belonged to Garcia, and on the other side by the house that belonged to Robert Galatine.

The condition is that they shall have and possess it for as long as they live and shall pay two bezants each year as rent to the Holy Sepulchre. If Andrew dies, his aforesaid wife may remain in the house for as long as she lives, paying two bezants each year as stated; Andrew may likewise do so if he outlives his wife. After the death of both, the entire house shall remain free and peaceful with the church.

Moreover, we have granted him the right to take sufficient water every day from our cistern, which is at the foot of the stairway.

The witnesses to this agreement are:

Holdredus, judge. Albert of Verdun. Richard. Roger, master of the servants of the Holy Sepulchre. Arnold Fellarius. Peter Porcellus. Habert of Falkenberg. Bernard Riquitie.

[Col. 1207A] Done in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1136, in the thirteenth indiction, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December.

Written by the hand of John of Pisa, who at that time taught the little clerks at the Sepulchre.

### CVIII [Note: [Col. 1207] A, fol. 94 bis verso; absent from B.] CONCERNING THE SALE OF TWO SHOPS OF THE CHURCH OF THE HOLY SEPULCHRE

In the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen.

I, Alois, together with my husband Girard and my children Roger, Alboim, Mark, and Amelina, sell to the convent of the Most Holy Sepulchre two shops with their upper floor, for 170 bezants, to be possessed by perpetual right, bounded by the following established limits: on the east is a public road; on the west, the courtyard [Col. 1207B] of the Holy Sepulchre; on the south, Michael’s house; and on the north, the house of Guisla of Saint Abraham.

This was done in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1155, in the third indiction, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, while the venerable brother Fulcher was presiding in Jerusalem as venerable patriarch and Baldwin IV was king.

The witnesses to this matter are:

Peter Salomonis, Gibert Papais, sworn to the royal majesty. Albert Lombardi. Gerald Aldenarius. Robert the Cook. William, nephew of Aimeric, prior of Mount Olivet.

### CIX [Note: [Col. 1207] A, fol. 94 bis verso; absent from B.] RECORD OF THE AGREEMENT AND DONATION MADE BETWEEN MARIA OF SAINT LAZARUS AND ROGER

A brief record of the agreement and donation once made between Maria of Saint Lazarus, wife of a certain Roger, a servant of the Holy Sepulchre, and Bernard, a servant of the patriarch and brother of Peter, prior of the Holy Sepulchre.

The aforesaid Maria gave her daughter in marriage to the aforesaid Bernard in the presence of the chapter of the Holy Sepulchre and of lawful men. She had had this daughter by her former husband, named Peter. She endowed her with a dowry of 100 bezants, clothed her, so to speak, on her back and in her bed, and also gave her the usufruct of a certain vineyard that the girl’s father had planted.

Moreover, in the same betrothal, before witnesses and guarantors, she granted Bernard a quarter of a certain house situated in the Temple quarter of Jerusalem beside Bentulinus’s house, after her death. She reserved another part for a son whom she had; after the death of that son, the aforesaid Bernard and his heirs were to have and possess another quarter by perpetual right, without dispute or contention.

After a number of years had passed, the aforesaid Maria denied that she had made this donation of the house. Thus a considerable dispute arose between her and her son-in-law. It was later settled in the chapter of the Holy Sepulchre before Lord Patriarch William, Peter the subprior, Anselm the cantor, [Col. 1208A] Geoffrey the treasurer, and Master Robert, canons of the Holy Sepulchre, and before Aschetinus, formerly viscount of Jerusalem, Rainald of Pons, and Geoffrey Acus.

The condition was that the aforementioned Bernard should possess freely and without any claim, after Maria’s death, the quarter of the house that Maria had acquired with Roger, her second husband; and that after the death of her son he should likewise have the other quarter without contention.

This charter was made at the command of William the patriarch, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1135, in the twelfth indiction, while Fulk, third king of the Franks, was reigning in Jerusalem.

The witnesses to this agreement are:

Peter, prior. Peter of Barcelona. William the Norman. Godfrey. Wlgrinus. Evrard. Gervasius.

Among the burgesses:

Holdreus. Milo. Bentulinus. Bernard of Limoges. Peter Petragorici. Arnulf of Gorranti. Bernard of Bourges.

### CX [Note: [Col. 1207] A, fol. 95 verso; absent from B.] CONCERNING THE GRANT OF A CERTAIN HOUSE MADE TO BENSCELINUS AND HIS WIFE

In the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen.

Let it be known to all dwelling in the holy city of Jerusalem that I, Amalric, prior, together with the full chapter of the church of the Most Holy Sepulchre, grant to Benscelinus, his wife Gode, and their heirs the house of Roger and Maria of Saint Lazarus, which they hold from the Holy Sepulchre. It is situated between the house of Leodegarius the miller and that of the aforementioned Gode, on the right side of the street by which one goes to the Temple.

We grant it to them on the condition that all disputes previously existing between us and them be settled—namely, concerning the land, vineyard, and entire fief that Gode herself and her predecessors held at Saint Lazarus. In return, we grant to Benscelinus, his wife Gode, and their heirs one half of the house to possess freely and peacefully, and we grant them the power to sell or give it to whomever they wish, according to their pleasure and will.

For the other half they or their heirs shall pay four bezants annually at Easter to the chapter of the Holy Sepulchre. If they do not pay the aforesaid four bezants annually at Easter to the convent, the named chapter shall have the free power, fifteen days after Easter, to take possession of half of the aforesaid house.

We make this grant of half of that house to Benscelinus, Gode his wife, and their heirs on the condition that, if they should ever wish, compelled by some necessity, to sell that half, they may sell or give it to whomever they wish, provided that the aforesaid rent owed to the church is paid each year, except to the Templars, Hospitallers, and any other monasteries. If they wish to sell it, they shall first offer it to the aforesaid chapter. If the chapter wishes to buy it, they shall sell it one mark of silver cheaper than to anyone else.

This grant was made between the canons of the Holy Sepulchre and Benscelinus and his wife Gode in the presence of Lord Patriarch Fulcher, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1154, and in the presence of the canons whose names are subscribed:

Namely, Lord Amalric, prior; Arnold, subprior; Gerald, precentor; Godfrey, treasurer; Nicholas, almoner; Beltold; Peter of the Sepulchre; Stephen, provost; Constantine; Peter of Golgotha; Peter of Nazareth; [Col. 1209B] Bernard; Baldwin of Beirut; Hugh of Nigella; John of Poitiers; William of Spain; Rainald; Peter of Bologna.

Among the laymen:

Odo of Verdun. Rainald Secher. Peter of Périgord. William Patronus. Benedict. Albert Lombard.

### CXI [Note: [Col. 1209] A, fol. 96 recto; absent from B.] CONCERNING THE RESTORATION OF A CERTAIN FIEF TO ROGER OF SAINT LAZARUS

In the year from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1135, in the thirteenth indiction, on the third day before the Kalends of July, while Fulk, third king of the Franks, was reigning in Jerusalem, William the patriarch and Peter, prior of the Holy Sepulchre, with the common counsel and consent of the canons thereof, restored to Roger of Saint Lazarus and his wife Maria the fief that they had lost, under the following condition:

From that day until two years had passed, they were to sell the house they had in Jerusalem and, with the counsel of the canons, bring all their possessions, wherever and whatever they had, back to the land of the Holy Sepulchre, to Saint Lazarus, or to Jerusalem. If they happened to die within the period, all their property would remain in the possession of the church. But if within two years they did not sell that house as stated, or return it into the hands of the canons, and did not bring their possessions, wherever they had them, back to the land of the Holy Sepulchre, they would irrecoverably lose the fief, the brotherhood, and the friendship of the house.

### CXII [Note: [Col. 1209] A, fol. 96 verso; absent from B.] CONCERNING THE DONATION MADE TO MARTIN AND HIS WIFE

Let present and future people know that I, Anfredus, castellan of Saint Abraham by the grace of God, and my wife give and grant to Martin, his wife, and their heirs a small plot, in return for the payment of two bezants each year, under the agreement that he shall have the power to sell it and to pledge it.

All this was done in the present royal court, with the following witnesses:

Lord Boart Benscelinus, viscount. Brictius. Rainald Sicherius of Périgord. Peter Salomonis. [Col. 1210A] Humbert of Baro. Simon. Hugh of Toulouse. Arbert of Arcu. Judas, and many others.

While Fulcher was patriarch and Baldwin was king, the witnesses were:

Lord Philip. John of Valentina. Gervasius. Peter Burdillus.

All this was done on a certain Thursday in the month of July, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1149.

### CXIII [Note: [Col. 1209] A, fol. 96 verso; absent from B.] ANOTHER DONATION [TO MARTIN]

I, Hugh, by the grace of God of the castle of Saint Abraham, give one small plot to Martin and his heir for two bezants. In this first year he gave me four bezants for two years; thereafter, for each year, he shall give me two bezants for the aforesaid plot. He and his heir shall have the power to give, sell, and mortgage it, while the aforesaid rent remains secured.

William of Alesnes, son of Ralph of Alesnes, a Norman of Saint Abraham. William of Babylon. Titger and his father Augerius. William Bornicus and his son Bartholomew. And I, William, wrote this.

All these witnesses written above heard and saw it.

### CXIV [Note: [Col. 1209] A, fol. 97 recto; absent from B.] CONCERNING THE INHERITANCE THAT MARTIN CAROANA GAVE TO THE CHURCH OF THE HOLY SEPULCHRE

Let it be known to all, future and present, [Col. 1210C] that I, Martin Caroana, give, transfer, and grant all my inheritance to the canons of the Lord’s Sepulchre, with the praise and consent of my son Bonnetus, in the same manner in which I made this donation while my first wife, named Teiza, was alive and consenting: namely, after my death, all my inheritance shall pass into the right and power of the church of the Sepulchre, so that the canons of the Sepulchre shall have the power to do with it whatever they wish, without anyone’s opposition.

For as long as I live, however, I shall possess my inheritance, but I shall not be permitted to sell or mortgage it. If I have offspring by this wife whom I am taking, neither my wife nor my offspring shall claim a share in the inheritance.

The witnesses to this matter are:

Peter of Périgord. Peter Bernard. Brictius. Rainald. Sicherius. William the Norman. Peter Salomon and Constantine, his brother. Ralph, burgess.

This was done in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1152, in the fifteenth indiction, while Fulcher held the patriarchate and Baldwin IV held the kingdom, successfully.

### CXV [Note: [Col. 1209] A, fol. 97 recto; absent from B.] PRIVILEGE OF THE CANONS OF THE HOLY SEPULCHRE AND BONETUS

Let it be open and clear to all the sons of holy mother church that the dispute which had long been argued between the canons of the glorious Sepulchre and Bonetus, [Col. 1211A] son of Martin Caroana, concerning the houses that his father donated to the Holy Sepulchre, has been brought to an end by the good men of Jerusalem named below, for the purpose of establishing concord.

For the preservation of this concord, I, N[icholas], prior of the Holy Sepulchre, with the common consent of the entire chapter, grant to the aforesaid Bonetus and his heirs one vaulted chamber of those houses, wholly above and below, to be held by perpetual hereditary right. He thereby entirely relinquishes to us whatever he claimed or could claim by paternal or maternal right, or in any other manner.

We add that Bonetus and his heirs shall pay us and our successors two bezants each year as rent on Palm Sunday. If it should happen that the aforesaid Bonetus departs this life without leaving any heir, that vaulted chamber, in its entirety, shall return to our power and lordship.

This was enacted on the sixth day before the Ides of June, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1160. The witnesses to this matter are:

Arnulf, subprior. Godfrey, treasurer. Evrard. Peter Clement. Peter of the Sepulchre. Achilles. Bernard, cantor. Rainerius. Hugh of Nigella. Peter of Latina. Rainald of Loches. Peter the Lombard. Robert of Antioch.

Among the laymen:

Albert Lombard. Albert Tortus. Robert the Cook. Robert of Pinqueniac. William the Norman.

### CXVI [Note: [Col. 1211] A, fol. 98 recto; absent from B.] CONCERNING THE SALE OF A CERTAIN HOUSE THAT MORAGE SOLD TO THE CANONS OF THE SEPULCHRE

[Col. 1211C]

Let it be known to all, present and future, that I, Morage Raiz, compelled by the necessity of a debt owed to the king, and with the consent of the king himself and of my heirs and relatives, sold to the canons of the Holy Sepulchre a certain part of my house, in which I had had a mill, from the foundation upward as high as it can be built, to be possessed freely and peacefully by perpetual right, for 120 bezants and twelve measures of grain.

The canons made this purchase in order to enlarge the shops that they had established in exchange for land that they had received from the Hospital beside my house.

The agreement between me and the canons was that, throughout all the parts of their land adjoining my house, they would have full power to place their pillars beneath my walls and to set the ends of their vaults into those same walls. All openings in my walls facing their side—namely, doors, windows, conduits, and any others—shall be closed, both below and above [Note: [Col. 1211] Correct to “above.”]. Whenever the aforesaid canons, or anyone acting through them, wishes to work on their land beside my house, they shall notify me or my people, and my wall shall be supported by me and my people. If my house [Col. 1212A] or wall should happen to fall, however, they shall owe nothing on that account either to me or to my people.

### CXVII [Note: [Col. 1211] A, fol. 98 verso; absent from B.] PRIVILEGE OF THE AGREEMENT CONCERNING THE TITHES OF THE ESTATES OF EMAUS MADE BETWEEN THE CANONS OF THE HOLY SEPULCHRE AND THE HOSPITAL

In the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen.

Because the stain of sins hinders them, the hearts of mortals quickly slip into oblivion. Therefore I, William, by divine appointment sixth Latin patriarch of Jerusalem, and Peter, prior of the Glorious Sepulchre, together with the entire chapter of the same, have taken care that a written record be preserved: the brothers of the Hospital of the Church of Saint John the Baptist, with the common assent of King Fulk and his princes, entered into a settled lease agreement with Robert of the casale of Saint Giles for the land of Emmaus, together with its casalia and all their appurtenances, on the following terms: that they should faithfully and without deceit render to the canons of the Lord’s Sepulchre half the tithe of all crops—namely, of wheat and oil, beans and chickpeas, lentils and peas, and all other legumes—and of vineyards and olive groves; while the brothers of the Hospital should retain all the other revenues that might arise from them, for the administration of their chaplains and churches, in which they should have the offerings, marriages, purifications, confessions, and visitations of the sick, as well as baptisteries and cemeteries.

Moreover, from the land and the other casalia lying adjacent in those same mountains—namely, from the casale of Huldre, and from Porcel, Gaufridus Agulle, Anschetino, Bacheler, and Girardus Bocher—which they possess, or from others which they may justly acquire in those same mountains, they shall likewise peacefully render half the tithe to the same canons. If, however, the brothers of the Hospital lease any casale or land belonging to them to Christians or Saracens, for grain, bezants, or any payment whatsoever, the aforesaid canons shall likewise have half the tithe, as we have already stated.

We make this agreement or concession to Raymond, master of the aforesaid Hospital, and to his successors and to the brothers serving God there: namely, Stephen of Antioch, Peter William, Raymond [Col. 1212D] of the Palace, Stephen Lauret, Arnold Gascon, Stephen the deacon, Stephen of the Chapel, Peter the treasurer, Gerard the cupbearer, Bernard Gascon, and all others present and future. But if any of those brothers of the Hospital should defraud this agreement by scheming to evade all or part of it, then, after being warned twice or three times, we decree that, unless they make amends, they shall be struck by the sword of anathema.

I, William the patriarch, was present at these agreements and concords, and granted them, without prejudice to the dignity of my patriarchate.

This was done in the year of the Lord’s incarnation [Col. 1213A] 1141, in the sixth indiction, while the venerable William presided in the patriarchal see and the illustrious King Fulk ruled from the royal throne. These are the witnesses:

Geoffrey, abbot of the Temple; Peter, prior of the Lord’s Sepulchre; Godefrey, treasurer; Americ, canon of the same church; William, provost; Garnerius; Lambert; and other canons; and Lord Roard, in whose fief the land itself lies.

## CXVIII [Note: [Col. 1213] A, fol. 99 verso; lacking in B]. ON THE RESTORED PEACE BETWEEN THE CANONS OF THE HOLY SEPULCHRE AND THE MONKS OF SAINT MARY MAGDALENE

Since the human mind, intent upon so many worldly matters, is drawn in different directions, the ancient fathers established that events and their witnesses should be written in a charter. Therefore, let it be known to all the sons of holy mother Church, present and future, that the long-contested dispute over the land of Ramatha and Hadesse between the Latin canons of the most glorious Sepulchre and the Jacobite monks of Saint Mary Magdalene was brought to an end in concord, by the common counsel of the good men dwelling in Jerusalem, with divine grace cooperating. And so that this complaint of the dispute between them might be silenced forever, both parties agreed that this concord should be entrusted to written memory. Those whose counsel brought about this peace and concord subscribe:

Arnulf, viscount; Brother Leo of the Temple; Adam Niger; Fulk, his brother; Robert of Retest; Peter Harmenius; John Raimundi; Robert Banchelini; Salem; Albert Lombard; [Col. 1213C] Albert the Crooked; Peter of Périgueux; Rainaldus Siccarius.

## CXIX [Note: [Col. 1213] A, fol. 99 verso; lacking in B]. THE PRIVILEGE OF EUSTACHIUS GRANERIUS CONCERNING A CERTAIN MILL

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

In the year 1116 from his incarnation, I, Constantius, servant of Saint Quarantena, and William earnestly petitioned Lord Eustachius Granerius and his wife to return to us the land formerly possessed by the inhabitants of Saint Quarantena. Inspired by God, they did not refuse to do so. They returned to us the aforesaid land, and one mill standing on that [Col. 1213D] land, through the hand of Lord Arnulf the patriarch, so that every fourteenth day, together with its night, we should have water without delay. The witnesses of this gift are:

Lord Arnulf, patriarch; Anselm of the Tower; Hugh of Nellis; Ardonetus; Azo of Drouino; Aimeric of Fraisna; Aaluns of Belram; Arnulf, viscount of Jericho.

The first grant of this privilege was made on the third day before the Nones of May, while Lord Arnulf, patriarch of Jerusalem, presided in the see.

After the death of Lord Eustachius, I, Constantius, and the other brothers, seeing the scarcity of water, deemed it necessary to petition Lady Emma, wife of the aforesaid Eustachius, to remember her husband’s soul and, for the love of God, to increase the water granted to us each week. When she heard of our shortage, moved by compassion, and with the consent of her sons Eustachius and Walter, she assented to our petition through the hand of her husband Lord Hugh, prince of Joppa, so that every seventh day—namely, Saturday—with the preceding night, without delay, we should have water in perpetuity by right. The witnesses of this matter are:

Lord Guarmund, patriarch; Barisanus; Paganus of Osca; Isaac, brother of Rainaldus of Bruges; Godefrey Fleming; John of Belram.

[Col. 1214B] And I, Arnulf, viscount of Jericho, was present at these grants, and caused this charter to be dictated and written by the hand of Lord Eustachius and Lord Walter [and Lady Emma] [Note: [Col. 1213] The words “her husband,” which follow, clearly indicate that the copyist omitted the words restored here in brackets] and her husband, Lord Hugh, prince of Joppa.

If anyone wishes to violate this charter, may he be blotted out of the book of the living.

The second grant of this privilege was made on the sixth day before the Ides of April, while the venerable Lord Guarmund presided in the see of Jerusalem, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1124.

## CXX [Note: [Col. 1213] A, fol. 100 verso; lacking in B]. ON THE EXCHANGE OF THE TWO CASALIA, MEGINA AND MEZERA

[Col. 1214C] In the name of God the Most High, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, amen.

I, John Patricius, wish it to be known, present and future, that I exchange my two casalia, namely Megina and Mezera, with all their appurtenances, for the two casalia of the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, namely Caphermelic and Anquina, likewise with their appurtenances, through the hand of Lord Peter, venerable prior of the Lord’s Sepulchre, and of the entire chapter.
