I was charged with the embassy concerning which the abbot of Adrianople and the prior of the Hospital of Constantinople visited your presence together with the envoys of Lord R., count of Saint-Gilles; I was charged with it alongside them, as the most faithful servant of the empire, by my lord E., the illustrious and holy emperor. Since they have now begun to return to my lord the emperor by sea, with my equipment and provision, I confidently advise and beseech you, and in beseeching advise you, out of the fidelity which I desire to show you as my lord, to send your envoys and letters without hesitation or delay to my lord E., the holy emperor.

For I know that he loves your person, the honor of your kingdom, and your glory with brotherly love and kindred affection, and desires to be joined and united with you by an indissoluble bond and fraternal partnership. May your sublimity live and prosper for many years, and may you deem me worthy to be counted among the faithful of your kingdom.

## VIII. Of A[malric], king of Jerusalem

To Louis, by the grace of God most illustrious king of the Franks, long beloved by him from ancient times. A., by the same grace king of Jerusalem, sends greetings and a sign of true love.

Since we know that for a long time past you have held the Holy Land of Jerusalem and the exaltation of the kingdom of Jerusalem at heart, we humbly beseech your pious serenity to take care to accomplish in action what you have long carried in your heart, and with watchful concern to strive to provide assistance for the aforesaid land. Remember also the matter for which the venerable archbishop of Mamistria was sent to the regions of Gaul, since what is now urgently necessary must be done—more than the tongue can express.

Moreover, since the archbishop of Mamistria departed from us, it is said that the emperor is arriving every day. As soon as he comes, all the Easterners, together with us, fear—without any doubt—that he will possess Antioch, since it lies prostrate in such weakness and defeat that no help has come to it from elsewhere. Antioch must certainly be surrendered either to the Turks or to the Greeks.

Therefore, with devoted mind, anxious heart, and swift course, strive to forestall that emperor whom we fear most, because you will come not into a foreign land, but into one that in every respect and entirely will be placed at your disposal. Both we and all the others will obey your commands.

## IX. B. de Blancesfort, master of the Templar militia

To Louis, by divine grace most illustrious king of the Franks, B. de Blancesfort, by the same grace called master of the poor militia of the Temple, together with the entire convent of that same militia, offers every kind of service with due reverence in the Lord.

We have thought it worthwhile to make known to you in writing the disturbance of the Eastern kingdom and the grave events woven into its misfortunes, since we are almost universally denied the opportunity to report anything prosperous. Yet, lest we seem to embitter your majesty with a lengthy account of our reproaches, we are unwillingly compelled to write these matters to you point by point.

Behold: the persecutors of truth and faith, seeing the multitude of our hardships, arm themselves against us with the audacity of an unprecedented fury. They are exalted by the captivity of R., prince of Antioch, and by the slaughter of his men and of the nobles of the principality carried out when the prince was captured. Here, the devastation of the land delights them. Here, by divine will, because of the burden of our sins, the fortifications were shattered by an earthquake, very many castles were overthrown, and countless people were crushed beneath the collapse of the ruined walls; all this has kindled their fury against us far more fiercely than usual.

Behold again: upon these grave events, many still graver and more lamentable have most recently followed. For King Baldwin, who throughout his life stood as an unconquerable wall for the house of Israel, paying the debt of nature, has entered upon the way of all flesh—a loss incomparable in our days. Seeing these things and others like them, the persecutors of the Church gather from their farthest regions as one man against the sanctuary of God, striving to erase our memory from the earth and, God forbid, to corrupt the Church of the faithful by the oppression of their innumerable multitude.

Concerning this we ask, with groaning, for the help, counsel, and support of God and of you. For although the kingdom of Jerusalem is greatly deprived of its own strength, it must nevertheless extend a hand of consolation to the principality of Antioch, utterly desolate, and bravely bestow the strength which, so to speak, it does not possess. But what can one afflicted by poverty and distressed within himself provide for the needy?

Let your own conscience, therefore, carefully examine the oppression of the Eastern kingdom and of the Church; let it be inflamed to assist the place of the Passion and Resurrection. We ask and implore whatever we can: may the place of the Lord’s Resurrection itself obtain for us what we seek. The multitude of our reproaches, our weakening, the exaltation of our enemies, and the Passion and Resurrection of Christ prevent us from writing to you the number of each of our evils. We have faithfully entrusted these matters to the account of the bearers of the present letters—that is, our brothers—and have judged that they should be disclosed under their testimony.

## X. Of the same

[Col. 1270C]

To Louis, by the grace of God most illustrious king of the Franks, B., called master—although unworthy—of the house of the Temple, together with the convent of that same house, sends loving service.

We wish it to be known to your nobility that Lord William de Donner, after crossing overseas to the Eastern regions to visit the Lord’s tomb and go around the other places of prayer, had his land cruelly invaded by certain of his neighbors, who devastated it most grievously with fire. Therefore we earnestly beseech your serenity in every way, insofar as the matter concerns you, not to permit this to happen, but to exact vengeance upon those who presume to do it, so that the others, hearing of your justice, may not dare to commit so great a crime again.

The Eastern Church could indeed suffer great harm from this, because many, fearing to lose their own possessions in this way, will hesitate to cross overseas. We continually render thanks to your majesty for the benefit bestowed upon us and our brothers.

## Gilbert, custodian of the Hospital of Jerusalem

To the most illustrious and excellent lord Louis, by the grace of God most gracious king of the Franks, Gilbert, by the same grace, custodian—although unworthy—of the holy Hospital of Jerusalem, together with the entire convent of the brothers, sends greetings and the eternal participation of Jerusalem’s sacred prayers.

Among the works of charity by which one ascends to the heavenly kingdoms, almsgiving holds the highest place, as every page of both the Old and the New Testament bears true witness. With this devotion in view, your royal majesty, divinely enlightened by the Holy Spirit, has always been accustomed lovingly to cherish the most holy house of the poor of the Hospital of Jerusalem, pleasing and wholly acceptable to God; to maintain it; and to enrich and refresh it with the benefits of your alms, bestowed by a generous hand.

There is no doubt that this is because of the sincere affection of your kindness, which you show especially toward God and toward all that belongs to him, throughout your entire kingdom, with the desire to attain the heavenly kingdom. So many barbarous peoples and such great nations of different populations are daily being brought under your rule.

For we judge it right and just that one who loves God and strives to obey his commands with a pure heart should rejoice in, hold, and victoriously possess the good things of the Lord and those that belong to him. For if Adam, the first-created man, because he disobeyed the Lord’s voice, deserved to have the world, with all the creatures in it, as his adversary and opponent, then, whenever a faithful person is found to obey the Lord’s will well—which happens rarely—he ought to have both the world and all worldly things subject to his good pleasure and find them ready for him without any obstacle.

Therefore, most illustrious king, so that the clemency of divine goodness, without whose assent no good can be done, may grant these things according to the desire of your heart, always keep God before your eyes; preserve safe and secure in your kingdom the things that belong to God; and especially and particularly cherish and maintain the aforesaid house of the holy poor of the Hospital of Jerusalem. In it Christ is truly received in his members, as you have seen with your own eyes, and is served in various ways.

According to the custom of your accustomed piety, love and maintain this house, and, like a good patron, protect and defend it from every hostile hand, so that through the prayers and intercession of the blessed poor, to whom Christ has entrusted the heavenly kingdom, you may merit to obtain happily, in the present life, prosperity of mind and body, peace and tranquility in your kingdom, triumph over your enemies, and, after the passage from this life, the robe of immortality with those same poor in the kingdom of heaven. Amen.

## XII. Of A[malric], king of Jerusalem

[Col. 1271D]

To Louis, by the grace of God most glorious king of the Franks and incomparable man, his beloved, A., by the same grace king of Jerusalem, sends greetings and affection.

Alas, alas! Through this present letter we make known to you the tearful and mournful report concerning our illustrious lord and brother, King B., announcing to you that on the day of the virgin Scholastica he departed to the heavenly realms by divine summons. Nevertheless, we now possess his kingdom, which had come to us by hereditary right, and without any impediment, with the good will of all our people, we have been firmly established upon the throne of our kingdom.

But because all Christendom in the East, grievously worn down and oppressed more heavily than usual, suffers greatly—both because of the misfortune of R., the once-illustrious prince of Antioch, who, as we suppose you have already long since heard, was captured while returning from an expedition, almost all those in his company having been killed or captured, and because of the earthquake which last August utterly overthrew and leveled to the ground almost all the castles, towers, and towns of the entire principality of Antioch—we ask your serenity and highness to be concerned for that land which the Lord deigned to visit, illuminate, and consecrate by his bodily presence, and which, as is clearly established, your kingdom also powerfully rescued from the filth of unbelievers and vindicated for divine worship.

While it is possible and time remains, make known to everyone with what mind, what affection of heart, and what inward sincerity you have until now loved the Lord’s tomb. Know that from the beginning, as you will be able to hear more certainly from the bearers of this letter, such a great undertaking would not have occurred without your counsel and your prompt assistance. And if it should come into your mind to visit the Lord’s tomb, you would come not into a foreign land, but into one that is wholly yours and will be placed entirely at your disposal in our time, without doubt.

For we, in order to honor and love you, so great and exalted a lord, in every way, and to do everything that is or has been within your right …

Given at the fountain of Sephoria, 8 April.

## XIII. B. de Blancesfort, master of the Templar militia

[Col. 1272C]

To Louis, by the grace of God most glorious king of the Franks and his excellent lord, B. de Blanc., by the same grace humble minister of the poor militia of the Temple, together with the entire convent of his brothers, sends the gift of prayers with greetings.

We believe that it has often been reported in the presence of your venerable highness how, for how long, and with what purpose we served beneath the standard of the saving cross and with the lord king in Egypt. For if that most wicked man Noredinus, through the audacity of Syracon, had gained possession of the kingdom of Babylon as he desired, he would have attacked the kingdom of Christ with such multiplied forces that, with the sea closed by piracy, he would not even have left the timid and cowardly a safe place for flight.

Such was the sum of his intentions, and for this reason he had sent Syracon into Babylon: to enlist the countless multitude of the Babylonians either by force of domination or by the stratagem of feigned peace, and to unite the two most powerful kingdoms, Babylon and Damascus, against the destruction of the Christian name.

But divine clemency looked down upon us from above, and our Christ granted his worshipers a victory over unbelief, though not without bloodshed. For the aforementioned Turk, whom we indicated as having been sent to obtain the kingdom, was finally compelled by the power of the triumphant wood—the cross—to surrender Berbesium, a very strong city of Egypt which he had fortified and supplied with thirty thousand warriors; and he was driven from the homeland which, had relief been delayed for more than three days, he would have possessed as his dominion without opposition, though not without great loss to his men.

After all this, when we returned, we found the Holy Land, because of our sins, utterly desolated; the city of Paneas, which had no more strongly fortified place in the whole kingdom, seized by stealth and handed over to the Turks through the hands of traitors; and Antioch, wretched and pitiable, lamenting with inconsolable tears the destruction already near and the indescribable slaughter of its people. There is no doubt that it will soon fall either into the hands of the Greeks or of the Turks, unless divine mercy and your surpassing greatness provide it with speedy aid.

For our king A., although great and magnificent, thanks be to God, cannot bring a fourfold army to the defense of Antioch, Tripoli, Jerusalem, and Babylon, which is in bondage together with her children and which above all must be feared. Norad[inus], if he wishes, can attack all of them at the same time with the abundant forces of his dogs.

Therefore let your greatness know that our beloved brother, and your servant and friend as well, Brother Heustan, compelled by bodily illness to seek discharge and relief, has pleaded so many times that we could no longer refuse him without violating charity. We are therefore sending in his place the bearer of this letter, Brother Walter, a prudent and discerning man, conspicuous for a twofold nobility—that of ancestry and of character. In this present letter we entrust and submit him to you and to your command as though he were physically present, and hand him over, so to speak, from hand to hand.

We ask you to support him, for the love of God and of us, in carrying out our affairs—which are also yours—with your assistance, and to sustain him in every respect through your gracious favor as your own servant. For, as you will learn from his long association with you, he is also by his own merits fully worthy of honor.

## XIV. G. Fulcher, procurator of the houses of the Templar militia

To Louis, by the grace of God most holy king of the Franks, his greatest lord and friend, Brother G. Fulcher, unworthy procurator of the houses of the poor militia of the Temple, sends greetings and offers the matter itself, if one who lacks it is able to send it.

We are compelled to make known to you the desolation of the land of Antioch, the disturbed kingdom of Jerusalem, grave events, untimely disasters, and the continual wounds of Christendom, since the opportunity to report favorable news is lacking. Yet the multitude of our evils prevents us from writing to you each detail of our vexation and reproach, while prosperity scarcely ever comes to us. Passing over, therefore, the multitude of so great a misfortune, we strive to reveal to you our graver events, since tears of desolation impede the tongue of the speaker.

In the month of July of this year, it happened that our king A., our master, and the other nobles of the Holy Land entered the territories of Babylon; and that they besieged Syracon, Noradinus’s constable, who had turned toward those regions to claim them for himself, in Berbesium. As that month came to an end and the following month began, they fixed their tents there.

When Noradinus heard this, he was angered in spirit and confused in mind. At that same time, through letters and envoys, he gathered from every region that had heard and trembled at his name, and, in his long-standing arrogance and pride, besieged the castle called Harenc, situated on the borders of Antioch and Aleppo. Having brought up his siege engines and stone-throwers, they attacked the besieged with so many and such great assaults that, almost deprived of food and water, they could no longer endure.

While these things were happening, Prince Bohemund, who governed Antioch, courageously attending to the care of his new principality, summoned the count of Tripoli, Lord Toros, the duke of Mamistria, and as many of our brothers as possible, and resolved to bring aid to his brothers and men, like a good son of Mattathias. He gathered so many knights, Turcopoles, and infantry that in our time no such splendid gathering of the faithful, armed against the unbelievers, had ever proceeded from those regions.

It happened that, as they marched armed against the enemies of the cross on the twelfth day, as August was drawing to a close, they put the enemy to flight in the first engagement. But, trusting in the multitude of their nations and offering very strong resistance, the enemy stood firm against our men and defeated them; they captured the prince and the count, although many of them fell by the sword.

What more is there to say? They won a victory, but a bloody one. Moreover, running here and there through the land, they captured Harenc and besieged Antioch. For there is no one to resist their savagery. Of six hundred knights and twelve thousand infantry, scarcely a few escaped to report what had happened.

The horn of our enemies has therefore been raised, and our strength has been humbled amid its labors. Therefore, suppliant, falling on the knees of our hearts at the feet of your charity, we ask and await aid from your generosity. Let your own conscience appeal to you; let the affection of sincere charity move you, as well as the place of our redemption, the Holy Land, the city of strength, and the primitive Church.

Once and repeatedly we have entrusted such matters to you; now we do so more earnestly and emphatically. To us divine grace has granted prayers and entreaties; to you it has granted actions and the accomplishment of what is requested.

## XV. Of A[malric], king of Jerusalem

To Louis, by God’s grace most excellent king of the Franks, his most beloved father in Christ. A., by the same grace king of Jerusalem, sends greetings and greeting from him who is King of all kings to a king.

Since we know that your royal majesty is able, and do not doubt that your pious devotion desires, for the aid of all who suffer need, to make your intervention beneficial, we have judged it worthwhile through this letter to set before your highness—even though perhaps you have already heard it—the lamentable depression of all the Christians who are in the Holy Land of Jerusalem, brought about by the raised horns of the Turks.

While we were fighting against Syracon in Egypt and, by the power of the Lord’s cross, driving him from there—especially since, had he remained there, he would have harmed the whole of Christendom—it happened that the count of Tripoli and the prince of Antioch went with a large army to free the castle near Antioch called Haring, which Noradinus had besieged with an innumerable multitude; and, by divine assistance, when the enemies withdrew before their arrival, they liberated it.

But it happened that, while the aforesaid prince and count, not content with so great a benefit from God, proudly pursued the enemies into places naturally most strongly fortified, they were captured by the enemy, and almost their entire army was partly captured and partly killed.

To this sorrow another sorrow was added. For the hands of traitors handed over to the aforesaid Noradinus, while we were still in Egypt, Paneas, which is commonly called Belinas. Thus, as though hanging in the balance of distress, the Holy Land in its suffering implores, together with us, your aid and that of your people, which we hope will be most effective.

Farewell.

Given at Antioch, 12 January.

## XVI. H., formerly prior of Mount Tabor

To the most excellent king of the Franks, H., formerly, though not now, prior of Mount Tabor, although unworthy, sends greetings and the expression of intimate affection in Christ.

Since it belongs to each person to declare to his lord in writing the state and course of his condition, my letter has preferred, despite the great distance between our places, to reach your hands; and there is nothing about which I could be happier than that it should come into your presence, God permitting.

Even the least cleric of your court may observe and know that I hold first place at the court of the lord emperor of Constantinople, above all his familiars. Yet there, since I cannot personally serve even the least of your people, I am greatly in need of an abundance of every good thing. For this reason, with bowed head, I implore your benevolence to deign to send your letters to the emperor of Constantinople, so that he may allow me to come to you, my dearest lord, without any obstacle; and, if I have ever performed some service pleasing to you, let it now become especially evident.

G. and R. de Merlo, my relatives, also on bended knees, appeal to the integrity of your benevolence, asking you not to disdain to do what is made known to you by my letter. Moreover, I earnestly request the excellence of your name to arrange that this bearer, who will return to me as soon as he can, receive some assistance from your somewhat generous hand—not on account of my merit, but on account of your clemency.

Farewell.

## XVII. Peter, prior of the Hospital of Constantinople

To Louis, most illustrious king of the Franks by the grace of God, P., brother of the Jerusalem Hospital and prior of the church of blessed John in Constantinople, and messenger of the most holy emperor E. N., wishes happiness in both lives.

Let your highness know, most reverend lord, that we have been sent specifically to you on behalf of our lord the emperor, and by imperial command we are required to visit your presence sooner than that of the lord pope. Therefore we earnestly beseech your kindness to be willing and to command that, according to the emperor’s arrangement, we may fulfill this without causing scandal to the apostolic lord, since his messenger is with us and compels us to go first to his court. We would in no way do so before seeing your majesty.

May your highness prosper for a long time.

## XVIII. A., patriarch of the Church of the Lord’s Resurrection

[Col. 1276B]

To the invincible Louis, by the grace of God most pious king of the Franks, A., by the same grace patriarch of the Church of the Holy Resurrection of the Lord, together with N., the prior, and the entire convent of canons serving God there, sends greetings and due prayers in Christ.

The goodness and gentleness of your pious highness, proclaimed by report, has truly become known to us, as we have learned by experience: in the cause of the servants of God you diligently take part and provide the consolations of your sincerity to religious men.

First, therefore, we render immense thanks to your generosity, because, as we have learned from the report of many, you do not cease, out of love for God, to increase everywhere, as far as you can, the affairs of the Lord’s tomb, whose servants we are, although unworthy. In these matters that concern God, as we continually remain before the sacred places of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection praying for you, and establish you as a sharer in our brotherhood and benefits, we commend to your kindness with particular insistence our beloved brother and canon S., the bearer of this letter.

We humbly ask that, out of reverence for the most glorious tomb, you deign to bestow your assistance upon him wherever he may need it, and that your highness deign to maintain both him and the affairs entrusted to him through your favor.

Moreover, we earnestly beseech the excellence of your goodness to deign, for the salvation of your soul and of all your noble parents, to grant the aforesaid canon S. some hospital or any suitable place under the protection of your wings, where we may have a refuge in honor of the Lord’s Resurrection.

May so great and most powerful a king prosper.

## XIX. Hugh, abbot of Saint Mary of Adrianople and prior of Saint John of Constantinople

To the most excellent and magnificent king of France, Louis, Hugh, by the grace of God abbot of Saint Mary of Adrianople and prior of Saint John of Constantinople, his most faithful servant, sends greetings and wishes to please the supreme Ruler in the government entrusted to him.

Let it not be unknown to your greatness, most reverend Father, that if the urgency of the present time did not constrain us in this way, we would have departed from the regions of Provence. But know, in truth, that the galleys are ready at Narbonne; and because of the rumor, we do not want them to come to Saint-Gilles, since we do not want our route to be evident to everyone.

Now let your majesty’s greatness know, most reverend Father, that we have been greatly saddened because we saw your envoys go to the king of Sicily without letters. For you know well that we shall go and return through him with money, and that we can neither go nor return by another route. This is the business of the king of Sicily, just as it is that of the emperor and of you, and we know well that you love him.

Therefore we ask your greatness to send him, through your envoys, letters of such a kind that they will be honorable both to your kingdom and to him, and that he may trust your envoys as though you yourself were speaking with him. And, if it pleases your greatness, send us letters as soon as you can, so that they may be carried with us by the bearer of this letter, and let him not spend even a single day with you.

May your most holy highness prosper.

## XX. Of Amalric, king of Jerusalem

To Louis, by the grace of God most serene king of the Franks, his most beloved father and friend, Amalric, by the same grace king of Jerusalem, sends greetings.

The whole of the Eastern Church, afflicted by grievous misery for all Christendom, hopes especially in the clemency of your fatherhood and in your kingdom for help and counsel. Hence, trusting greatly in your innate kindness, while we beseech your fatherhood on behalf of all the devotees of the Holy Land, we especially entreat your majesty on behalf of the brothers of the Temple to keep them continually commended to you in the customary manner. They die each day for the Lord and his service, and through them we are able to do whatever we can.

For in them, after God, rests the entire substance of all that is carried out by sound counsel in the regions of the East. Therefore, whatever your royal majesty and the munificent hand of your piety do for them, consider that you have bestowed it chiefly upon our own person.

Farewell.

## XXI. Bertrand de Blancafort, master of the Templar militia

[Col. 1277D]

To Louis, by the grace of God illustrious and venerable king of the Franks, his most beloved lord, Bertrand de Blancafort, by the same grace called master of the militia of the Temple, wishes to be happily transferred from kingdom to kingdom.

How many and how great are the benefits bestowed upon us and our predecessors through the abundance of your munificence—if we attempted to pursue them one by one, neither writing nor speech would suffice. For from the beginning of your life your generosity has diligently labored, with devoted zeal, for the advancement of our house; and still, thanks be to God, it persists in the same course, destined, with God’s favor and life permitting, to continue hereafter. And when we review the times that have passed, it will rarely, or never, be found that your holy devotion has failed: rather, it has always either more generously bestowed its own resources upon us, or applied those of others to our needs through the assurance of its benevolent favor.

For all these things, since we cannot render worthy thanks for the reverence and honor you have shown to Brother G. Fulcher, we entrust the rendering of thanks to him alone who will recompense him in eternal glory with that which “eye has not seen nor ear heard.” For that same Brother G. Fulcher, prostrating himself on his knees in the presence of our whole community, extolled your diligence toward him with such praises that to everyone it seemed almost beyond belief and surpassing wonder. Therefore, here and everywhere, we submit and commend ourselves and all that is ours to your will.

What more shall we say about the oppression of the Holy Land, and especially of Antioch? To whom shall we go? Whom shall we implore? You have been told so often that it is easier to elicit a refusal from weariness than tears from compassion. Yet the affairs of Antioch have been so shattered and reduced to such poverty that the emperor is willing and preparing to come with forces gathered from every side to receive it as his own. For through so many stages of misfortune it has been brought to this depth of servitude that at the first encounter it lies exposed to the savagery of the Greeks or Turks. Nevertheless, the wretched mother and the apostolic see of Antioch still look to you, exhausted by bitterness and grief. Farewell.

## XXII. AMALRIC, KING OF JERUSALEM

[Col. 1278C]

To Louis, by the grace of God most glorious king of the Franks and his most serene friend, Amalric, by the same grace king of Jerusalem, greetings.

Because we love your person and your kingdom, are ready to serve you, and place particular hope in you and your kingdom, we have thought it appropriate to notify your majesty of our fortunes. Let your excellence therefore know that we entered Egypt with whatever troops we were able to obtain. We left our land fortified as far as we could against Nureddin, who had summoned everyone he could from Baghdad and the Euphrates, and from all their territories. Before the most noble Egyptian city called Bilbeis, we engaged with the Egyptian forces, both sides arrayed and positioned face to face. But God, to whom victory does not belong to the multitude, turned the multitude of his enemies to flight; after countless men had been put to death and many of the better and greater men of the land had been captured, we spent the night on that field.

On the following day we assaulted the aforementioned city with great force. Had we not been hindered by the interposition of the River of Paradise, which unexpectedly came upon us—as it is accustomed to do each year—the city, as we hope, would either have been captured or surrendered. If, therefore, your magnificent power should, as usual, wish to assist us, then, with God’s help, Egypt could easily be marked with the sign of the holy cross. Farewell.

## XXIII. GAUFRID OF FULCHER, COMMANDER OF THE JERUSALEM HOUSE

[Col. 1279A]

To Louis, by the grace of God most glorious king of the Franks, his dearest lord, Brother Gaufrid of Fulcher, commander of the Jerusalem house, greetings.

Just as fires that have been extinguished too inadequately eventually revive in a greater flame, so Nureddin, recently routed by our forces, himself crossed the Euphrates and is rousing the Persians, Turcomans, the people of Nineveh, E~., and whatever nations extend to the farthest boundaries, to avenge his disgrace. Having gathered a multitude beyond reckoning, he began to besiege the town of Harem in the territory of Antioch.

Seeing this, our young man of noble character, Bohemond, now prince, recalling his great father, did not fear to confront such a multitude. While engaging them with his father’s courage, however, he was defeated and captured by the hidden judgment of God. What we cannot say without tears is that he himself and the count of Tripoli, together with the duke of Mamistra and Lord Vg~. of Lusignan, along with very many others, were led to Aleppo and imprisoned. The rest of the army, although large and formidable, was almost entirely killed or captured.

Sixty of our brothers, very brave knights, also fell by the sword, besides the serving brothers and Turcopoles; only seven escaped the danger. Antioch, having lost its warriors from first to last, lies wholly exposed. Indeed, nothing at all remains throughout its territories except the body of the wretched city itself. Even for that city there is fear, since it is being constricted by a shortage of arms, men, and provisions; for it does not possess enough food for two months.

That it has not yet been delivered into the power of the enemy was accomplished and is being accomplished, after God, by the patriarch alone. For a time he has set aside his patriarchal dignity: he fortifies towns, distributes food, gives gifts, and does not hesitate even to risk his life for his country. But what does that avail? He will indeed withstand the Turks; but, deprived of all human aid, he will not be able to resist the emperor of Constantinople who is coming.

Our king—may the Almighty preserve him by his grace—set out under the banner of the holy cross for Egypt with his own men and with the other part of our brothers. Since the first day of August he has kept shut up in the city of Herbesium the constable of Nureddin, Syracon, who has usurped for himself the kingdom of Babylon. We, meanwhile, very few in number in Jerusalem—for the multitude of Turks, or, more truly, filthy men, is immense—are not secure from attack and assault.

You therefore see our necessity. You see that, if you dissemble, or believe us only after delay, as is your custom, and do not provide aid before what remains of Christianity is consumed, it must be feared that, when you wish to do so, you will no longer be able. Let those who belong to God, and who are counted by the Christian name, therefore gird themselves and come to liberate their father’s kingdom and the homeland of our freedom, lest what was bravely acquired through the blood of our fathers should shamefully and irreparably fall into the hands of their sons. Do not expect other messengers from here; for, with the king and master absent, we do not dare to release good men in this crisis.

## XXIV. B., SON OF RAYMOND, PRINCE OF ANTIOCH

To Louis, by the grace of God most noble king of the Franks, his lord: B., son of Raymond, formerly prince of Antioch, his man and servant, from him who gives salvation to kings.

Because, most serene of kings and lord, we place no small confidence in the clemency of your greatness, prostrate at the knees of your compassion, we are wholly wrapped in the inmost feelings of our mind, so that the frequent and tearful misery and devastation of the eastern regions, and especially of Antioch, may move the depths of your heart. For our hope and refuge in every respect look to and rest uniquely upon your aid and counsel; and daily we await it with sighing hearts, saying: “When will he come? Do you suppose I shall endure?”

Our land has now been brought into dire straits, while we have been snatched from the jaws of the enemies of Christ’s cross. Let us render praises to God, and may you in the heavens be crowned by God himself. For unless we are soon raised up by God’s help and yours, we, together with our homeland and people, are already sinking into misery and tearful death. The axe has indeed been laid at the root of the tree.

Alas! What disgrace it will be for all the people and for you if you permit this land—land acquired through such a great outpouring of the blood of your parents, and through such thirst and hunger—to be violated and destroyed by a wicked people?

You know, my lord, as I believe, and have heard sufficiently, what kinds and how great were the losses suffered in the territories of Antioch in the past year: namely, the capture of the prince and of the other men who were with him; the plundering and destruction of so great a part of the Christian people; the destruction and eradication of so many fortifications by fire and sword; and also such a great and unprecedented earthquake, which overturned almost all the fortifications of the principality of Antioch and all its castles to the ground. But I pass over these matters for the present.

As for the rest, whatever the bearer of this letter—a man of great religion and good life—may tell you on our behalf, believe it faithfully.

## XXV. G. FULCHER, HUMBLE SERVANT OF THE TEMPLE KNIGHTS

[Col. 1280D]

To Louis, by the grace of God most beloved king of the Franks, his lord, Brother G. Fulcher, by the same grace humble servant of the Knights Templar, greetings.

Who could extol in worthy praises, or equal with recompense, the benefits and honors you have bestowed upon my smallness? Only God, may he deign by his grace to repay you in eternal blessedness.

I, thanks be to God, arrived safely and unharmed at Acre. After first conveying greetings from you to the master and brothers, I explained how much honor you had shown me for the love of God and out of respect for them. They, giving you thanks for this, and commending themselves and what is theirs to your highness, offer you and for you the earnestness of their prayers.

Do not believe that I, your servant, have forgotten what I rejoice to have received from your mouth when I departed from you. For you told me to greet the holy places on your behalf and, when visiting them, to make remembrance of you at each one. Not forgetting this charge, I carried this ring, which I send you, around the sacred places and, applying it to each one, placed it upon each in remembrance of you. For the sake of this reverence, I ask you to keep the ring and to hold it dear. Farewell. Farewell again, with remembrance of me.

## XXVI. B., MASTER OF THE TEMPLE KNIGHTS

To Louis, by the grace of God most excellent king of the Franks, Berctinus, humble minister of the Knights Templar, greetings, and may you reign in Christ.

[Col. 1281B]

We do not doubt that it has reached the ears of your highness with what fear our lord King Amalric, by common counsel of Christendom, set out against Sairan, whom Nureddin had sent with a large army to bring the kingdom of Babylon under his power, bearing the precious sign of the holy cross, and how he returned.

For had not the land of Antioch been thrown into such disturbance and desolation because of the deserving faults of our own people, our lord the king, with the protection of the Lord’s cross, would have accomplished his will against the enemy. But when he heard of Antioch’s troubles, he withdrew from there, as prudence counseled. For the aforementioned adversary thought that the kingdom of Babylon was subject to his lord and that he could block the way to Jerusalem, by land and sea, for those who worship Christ. But God, who knows how to guard his own everywhere, arranged his wicked plan quite otherwise.

Yet, most serene king, the troubles of both lands—namely Antioch and Jerusalem—are so great that, because of their enormity, we do not wish to communicate them to you in writing. Finally, we are sending to your distinguished dignity the bearer of this letter, Brother Walter, an honorable man zealous in God’s affairs. He remained involved in those affairs and saw their beginning and end; he himself will disclose to your holiness what is fitting concerning them.

Attend confidently to whatever he tells your highness, as though it had been spoken from our own mouth. And let your excellence know that the eyes of all the Christianity of the East, after the Lord, look to you, so that, while the opportunity is at hand, it may be rescued through you from such great evils.

[Col. 1281]

## B. LETTER OF LOUIS, KING OF THE FRANKS, TO HIS SUBJECTS ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF FRANCE, CONCERNING HIS CAPTURE AND RELEASE. Written at Acre in the year of the Lord 1250

*(Bongars, Gesta, etc., p. 1196.)*

[Col. 1281C]

Louis, by the grace of God king of the Franks, to his beloved and faithful prelates, barons, knights, citizens, burghers, and all others established in the kingdom of France to whom this letter may come, greetings.

Desiring to pursue the business of the cross, to the honor and glory of the divine name, we have thought it necessary to make known to all of you that, after taking common counsel, we withdrew from Damietta following the capture of Damietta—which the Lord Jesus Christ, through his ineffable mercy, had delivered almost miraculously and beyond human strength into Christian power, as we believe is not unknown to you—we withdrew from Damietta on the twentieth day of the month of November just past. Having assembled both a naval and a land army, we advanced against the army of the Saracens, which had gathered and encamped at a place commonly called al-Mansurah.

On that very journey we endured several attacks by the Saracens, in which they continually suffered no small loss of their men. On one day, some of those from the Egyptian army who had encountered ours were killed. During the journey we learned that the Sultan of Babylon had recently ended his wretched life. As he had publicly declared, and had sent word to his son residing in the eastern regions so that he might come to Egypt, he had caused all the chief men of his army to swear allegiance to that son, while leaving the guardianship of his entire land to one of his emirs, named Fakhr al-Din. As we approached the aforementioned place, we found these reports to be true.

When we therefore approached that place on Tuesday, before the feast of the Lord’s Nativity, we were initially unable to gain access to the Saracens because of a certain river flowing between the two armies. This river is called the Thaneos and, at that place, branches off from the great river. We placed our camp between the two rivers, extending from the greater river to the lesser. After a clash with the Saracens had taken place there, many of them fell, killed by our swords, and an even greater multitude was drowned in the powerful and deep waters.

Since the aforementioned River Thaneos could not be forded because of the depth of its waters and the height of its banks, we began to build a causeway across it, so that it might provide passage for the Christian army. We labored at this for many days with immense exertion, danger, and expense. The Saracens, however, resisting with all their strength, set up several engines opposite the engines we had erected there. With these they battered with stones and then completely burned with Greek fire the wooden towers we had constructed and placed over the crossing.

When this had been done, and nearly all hope and expectation of crossing by that causeway had been frustrated, a Saracen who came from the Egyptian army finally made it known to us that, somewhat farther downstream, the river could be forded and that the Christian army could cross there.

Accordingly, after counsel had been shared with the barons and other leading men of the army, it was unanimously arranged on the Monday before Ash Wednesday that on the following day—Shrove Tuesday—we would assemble at the aforementioned place at first light to cross the river, while part of the army was assigned to guard the camp.

On the following day, therefore, after the battle lines had been arranged, we came to the place and crossed the river, though not without grave danger. The place was deeper and more perilous than had been reported to us, so that our horses had to swim there. Because of the high, muddy banks, the exit from the aforementioned river was also dangerous.

After crossing the river, we came to the place where the Saracen engines stood beside the aforementioned causeway. When we attacked the Saracens, our men who were in front slaughtered many of them with their swords, sparing neither sex nor age. Among them they killed their commander and several other emirs.

Then, when our battle lines had become dispersed, some of our men ran through the enemy camp and reached the village called al-Mansurah, killing with their swords all of the enemy whom they encountered. But at length the Saracens, recognizing their rash advance, regained their strength, fell upon them, and surrounded them on every side. They overwhelmed them, and there a considerable slaughter of our barons and knights took place, both religious and secular—a loss for which we rightly grieved greatly and still grieve.

There too we lost in this earthly life our dearest and outstanding brother, of blessed memory, and the count of Artois. We recall this with bitterness of heart and grief, although we ought to rejoice over him rather than mourn, since we firmly believe and hope that he flew, crowned with martyrdom, to the heavenly homeland and there rejoices eternally with the holy martyrs.

Thus, on that day, while the Saracens attacked us from every side and sent down a shower of arrows, we endured their severe assaults until approximately the ninth hour. We had been entirely deprived of the support of our crossbowmen, and many of our men had been wounded there; most of our horses had been injured by various wounds or killed. Nevertheless, with the Lord’s help, after our strength had been gathered again, we held the field. There, beside the Saracen engines that we had captured, we set up our camp that same day.

We remained there that day with only a few men, having first built a wooden bridge by which those who were beyond the river could cross to us. On the following day, more of our men crossed the river at our command and pitched their camp beside ours. Then, after destroying the Saracen engines, we made cables for the boat-bridges, by which our men could pass freely and safely from one army to the other.

On the following Friday, the sons of perdition, having gathered their forces from every side and intending to destroy the Christian army completely, assembled against our plankways in the greatest strength and with an infinite multitude. From every side of the army they made attacks so numerous and terrible that, as many people said, they had never seen the Saracens make such attacks in those maritime regions.

Nevertheless, through the prevailing power of God, we resisted them with the forces of our men arranged on every side and repelled their assaults; a very great multitude of them fell beneath our swords.

After several days had passed, the Sultan’s son arrived at al-Mansurah, coming from the eastern regions. At his arrival the Egyptians, beating their drums and rejoicing, received him as their lord; and by this their strength was greatly increased.

Thereafter, by some judgment of God, everything turned against our desires. The plague of various illnesses began to rage, together with a general mortality among both men and horses, so that scarcely anyone in the army remained who was not mourning his dead or those sick unto death. Thus the Christian army was greatly diminished and consumed.

The shortage of provisions was so great that many collapsed from starvation and hunger. The naval vessels could not pass from Damietta to the army, because Saracen galleys and pirate vessels obstructed them; these they had placed in the aforementioned river by transporting them overland. After first capturing several of our vessels in the river, they eventually seized two successive caravans carrying provisions and many other valuable goods to the army, killing a multitude of sailors and others, to the detriment of the entire army.

Thus, when the supply of provisions and fodder for the horses had completely failed, almost everyone in the army began to grow weak and to fall into no small desolation and terror. Constrained by these difficulties—both by the lack of food and horse fodder and by the disasters noted above—inevitable necessity compelled us to withdraw from the aforementioned place and return to the region of Damietta, if the Lord should so provide.

But since the ways of man are not in himself, but rather in him who directs everyone’s steps and orders them according to the good pleasure of his will (Jeremiah 10:23), while we were on our journey of return—namely, on the fifth day of April—the Saracens, having gathered all their forces together with an infinite multitude, attacked the Christian army. And, as happened by divine permission, our sins demanding it, we fell into the hands of our enemies.

We were captured and committed to prison, together with our dearest brothers, the counts A. of Poitiers and C. of Anjou, and all the others who were returning with us by land; no one escaped. This occurred amid a very great slaughter of our men and a considerable shedding of Christian blood. Most of those who were returning by river were likewise captured or killed by the sword. The naval vessels were for the most part destroyed by fire, and in their flames a grievous multitude of sick people were burned.

After our capture, the aforementioned Sultan had us summoned for several days to negotiate a truce. He urgently demanded, not without threats and harsh words, that without wasting time we should have Damietta restored to him, together with everything found there, and should repair all the damage and expenses he had incurred up to that time, from the day on which the Christians had taken Damietta.

Finally, after many negotiations, we entered into a truce for ten years, in the following form:

The same Sultan would release from prison us and all the Christians who had been captured by the Saracens after we came to Egypt, as well as all others from whatever regions who had been captured since the time when Sultan Kyemel, the grandfather of that Sultan Caym, had entered into a truce with the emperor; he would permit them to depart freely wherever they wished. He would also keep in peace, with all their appurtenances, the lands that the Christians held in the kingdom of Jerusalem at the time of our arrival.

We, however, were bound to return Damietta to him, and to pay eight hundred thousand bezants of Saracen currency for the release of the captives and for the aforesaid damages and expenses. Of this sum we had already paid four hundred thousand. We were also to release all Saracens captured by the Christians in Egypt after our arrival there, as well as those captured in the kingdom of Jerusalem since the time of the former truce made between the emperor and the aforementioned Sultan.

It was further agreed that all our movable goods, and those of everyone else remaining at Damietta after our departure, would be safe and under the custody and protection of that same Sultan, to be transported to Christian territory whenever an opportunity arose. All sick Christians, and all others who remained at Damietta in order to sell the goods they had there, would likewise be safe and could depart by land or sea whenever they wished, without any impediment or opposition. To all who wished to leave by land, the same Sultan was bound to provide a safe-conduct as far as Christian territory.

When this truce between us and the aforementioned Sultan had thus been confirmed by oaths on both sides, and the same Sultan was already on his way with his army to come near Damietta in order to fulfill all the agreements stated above, it happened, by divine judgment, that certain Saracen soldiers—apparently with the connivance of the greater part of the army—attacked the aforementioned Sultan as he rose from the table in the morning after dinner. They grievously wounded him and, as he left his tent in order to escape by flight, they cut him to pieces with their swords in the sight of nearly all the emirs and a multitude of other Saracens.

After this deed had been carried out, many armed Saracens immediately came to our tent in the heat of their fury, as though they intended—as many feared—to rage against us and the other Christians. But divine clemency calming their madness, they urgently demanded that we confirm the previous truce with the Sultan and that the city of Damietta be quickly released.

After they had first thundered threats and denunciations, we finally—according to the will of the Lord, who, as the Father of mercies and the compassionate comforter in tribulations, hears the groans of prisoners—confirmed with oaths the truce we had previously made with the Sultan. From each and every one of them we received oaths, according to their law, that they would observe our truce, with definite periods established within which the captives on both sides would be released and the city of Damietta restored.

We agreed to its restoration with those emirs at that time, and previously with the Sultan for the same reason, only with difficulty. For there was no hope of retaining the city, as we learned with complete certainty from those who had come to us from Damietta and knew the truth without question.

For this reason, on the advice of the barons of France and of very many others, we judged it more advantageous for Christendom that we and the other captives should be released under such a truce than that the city, together with the remaining Christian population in it, should be surrendered, while we and the others remained imprisoned amid such dangers.

On the appointed day, therefore, the aforementioned emirs received the city. Once they had received it, they released us and our brothers, as well as the counts of Brittany, Flanders, and Soissons, and many other barons and knights from the kingdoms of France, Jerusalem, and Cyprus.

At that point we firmly hoped that, since they had released us and the others mentioned above, they would faithfully observe their oaths concerning the return and release of all the other Christians, according to the terms of the truce.

After these matters had been completed, we withdrew from Egypt, leaving trustworthy messengers there to receive the captives from the Saracens and to guard the goods we had left behind, since we did not possess enough ships to transport them.

Later, while we were in the process of recovering the captives and were anxiously considering this matter, which weighs heavily upon our heart, we sent other solemn messengers and ships to Egypt to bring back the captives and the other goods we had left there—namely, our engines, weapons, tents, a certain number of horses, and many other valuable things.

But the aforementioned emirs detained our messengers in Babylon for a long time. Although our messengers urgently demanded that the captives be returned to them according to the terms of the truce, and that the other things mentioned above likewise be restored, the emirs kept them there under the hope of returning everything that had been demanded.

Finally, after a long wait, concerning all the captives whom they were bound to release—said with certainty to number more than twelve thousand, both old and newly captured—they released to our messengers only four hundred. Some of these had left prison after money was paid. Of all the remaining goods, they refused to return anything at all.

Indeed, what is more detestable, after the truce had been made and sworn, as we learned through our messengers and through certain trustworthy captives returning from those regions, they led selected young men from among the Christian captives to slaughter like sheep. As far as they were able, they compelled them to apostatize from the Catholic faith, placing swords upon their necks and ordering them to proclaim the law of the most wicked Muhammad. Many of the weak and fragile among them strayed from the faith by professing that detestable law.

The others, however, like the strongest athletes, rooted in the faith and remaining steadfast in their firm resolve, could not be overcome by the threats or scourges of the enemy. Fighting lawfully, they received martyrdom’s crowns, reddened with blood. Their blood, as we firmly hold, cried out to the Lord on behalf of the Christian people, and they will be our advocates before the supreme Judge in the heavenly court in the case we are pursuing against the enemies of the faith. In that homeland they will be more useful to us than if they were living among us on earth.

They also slaughtered with their swords many sick Christians who had remained at Damietta. We had no certainty whatever concerning the release of the Christian captives or the restoration of our property, although we had fully observed the conditions and agreements we had made with them and had been ready to continue observing them.

Furthermore, after the truce had been made and we had been released, we had firmly trusted that, once the captives were freed, the overseas land held by the Christians would remain in a peaceful condition until the time defined in the truce. We therefore intended and planned to return to the kingdom of France, and I had already arranged for a ship and for the other things that seemed necessary for our passage.

But when we clearly saw, from the matters expressed above, that the aforementioned emirs were openly acting against the truce and did not hesitate to mock us and Christendom in violation of their own oaths, we sought the advice of the barons of France, the prelates, the houses of the Temple and of the Hospital of Saint John and Saint Mary of the Germans, the barons of the kingdom of Jerusalem, and others. We consulted together about what we ought to do in these circumstances.

The greater part of them unanimously asserted that, if we happened to depart in those days, we would abandon the aforementioned land at the very point of its surrender, and that our departure would amount to exposing it entirely to the Saracens—especially since, alas, it had been brought in those days into so weak and miserable a condition.

The Christian captives held by the infidels could also, after our departure, be regarded as lost, all hope of their release having been removed. If, however, we remained, it was hoped that some good might result from our delay. Through it, with the Lord as author, the release of the captives, the retention of the castles and villages of the kingdom of Jerusalem, and certain other benefits useful to all Christendom might come about, especially since a serious conflict had arisen between the Sultan of Aleppo and the Babylonians.

That Sultan, having gathered his armies, has already taken Damascus and certain castles under Babylonian rule. As many assert, he intends to proceed into Egypt to avenge the death of the murdered Sultan and to occupy as much of that land as he can.

Having carefully considered these matters, and grieving over the miseries and afflictions of the aforementioned Holy Land—for we had come to its aid—and sympathizing with the captivity and sufferings of our own captives, although many advised us against remaining overseas, we nevertheless preferred to postpone our passage and remain for some time in the kingdom of Syria rather than abandon Christ’s cause in utter despair and leave our captives exposed to such dangers.

We have therefore decided to send our dearest brothers, the counts A. of Poitiers and G. of Anjou, to France, for the consolation of our dearest lady and mother and of the entire kingdom.

When, therefore, all who are reckoned among Christians ought to show zeal for the undertaking mentioned above—and you especially, clerics, who are descended from those whom the Lord chose as a special people to acquire the Holy Land, which, by virtue of that acquisition, you ought to regard as your own—we invite your whole community to the service of him who served us upon the cross and, by pouring out his own blood for your redemption, stood forth, so that your hearts [might be] new in Christ Jesus.

For that most wicked people, in insult to the Creator, besides the blasphemies they uttered in the presence of the Christian people, beat the cross with whips, spat upon it, and then shamefully trampled it underfoot, to the disgrace of the Christian faith. Come, therefore, soldiers of Christ! Gird yourselves, [as] the special [ones] of the pope of the living God (*peculiaris papae*, textually uncertain), and be mighty men to avenge the injuries and insults described above. Bring your actions back to the example of your predecessors, who, more than all other nations, were especially devoted to the exaltation of the faith and, with sincere affection, served their temporal lords; by their distinguished deeds they filled the whole world.

We have gone before you in the service of God. Come, you also; follow us for God’s sake. At last, although you may arrive with us later, you will receive, by the Lord’s generosity, the reward which the evangelical householder gave both to the first laborers in his vineyard and to the last (Matt. 20:8).

Moreover, in addition to the general indulgence granted to those signed with the cross, those who come—or send a suitable subsidy to our aid, or rather to the aid of the Holy Land—while we are present there will acquire great favor and honor for themselves with God and with men.

Set about the undertaking promptly, so that those whom the power of the Most High inspires to come or send the aforesaid aid may prepare to come or send it in the crossing of the coming month of May or April. Those who cannot be ready to send aid on that passage should at least arrange to cross over for the aforesaid assistance on the second following passage, that of Saint John. For haste is necessary, and delay appears damaging in view of the nature of the undertaking.

You, prelates and other faithful of Christ, should earnestly entreat the Most High in your prayers for us and for the aforesaid undertaking of the Holy Land; and in the places subject to you, have special prayers offered, so that, with the clemency of his divine propitiation consenting, what our sins impede may be accomplished through the support of your prayers and those of other good people.

Done at Acre, in the year of the Lord 1200, in the month of August; the printed dating phrase *quinquagesimo* (“fiftieth”) is corrupt or unexplained.

[Col. 1289]

# Poems

## Notice concerning the following poems

(Edelestand Du Méril, *Ancient Poems of the Twelfth Century*, p. 408.)

The enthusiasm produced by the Crusades successively inspired a large number of popular poems. We have thought it appropriate to add several of them which, although later than the formation of the new languages, seemed to us to possess genuine interest. This one is found in the *Annals* of Roger of Hoveden, in Saville, *Rerum Anglicarum Scriptores*, p. 639. It was composed around 1188; its author was called Bertier or Bertère, whom Symphorien Guyon, without offering any reason in support of his opinion, makes a counselor of the king of England, *Histoire d’Orléans*, p. 409.

## I. Song of the Crusaders

[Col. 1289B]

### In the manner of the Laments of Jeremiah

Truly the roads of Zion mourn,

because on the solemn day

there is no one who visits

the tomb,

or raises up from its fall

this prophecy.

Against this the prophet writes:

that from Zion the law shall go forth;

never there shall the law perish,

nor shall it lack a defender,

where Christ drank

the cup of his Passion.

The wood of the cross,

the standard of the leader,

the army follows;

it did not yield,

but went before,

in the power of the Holy Spirit.

To bear the burden of Tyre,

should strong men

not test their strength,

who strive daily

to be honored freely

with the praises of military service?

But for those about to join battle,

the athletes must be hard,

not softened Epicureans.

For those who care for their skin

at great expense

do not purchase God through cares

[Note: Saville has *precibus* (“prayers”); but throughout the rest of the poem the final verse of the stanza rhymes with the preceding three. *Pressuris* (“pressures”), proposed by the *Histoire littéraire*, vol. XV, p. 338, gives the verse one syllable more than it should have.]

The wood of the cross,

the standard of the leader,

the army follows;

it did not yield,

but went before,

in the power of the Holy Spirit.

The new Philistines,

having captured the cross,

the enemies of the cross

have taken back the ark of God,

the ark of the new covenant,

the reality of the ancient figure

after the figure of the reality.

But since it is clear that these are

the forerunners of Antichrist,

against whom Christ wishes resistance:

what will the one who has not resisted

be able to answer

at Christ’s coming?

The wood of the cross,

the standard of the leader,

the army follows;

it did not yield,

but went before,

in the power of the Holy Spirit.

The despiser of the cross presses the cross,

from which the oppressed faith groans:

who does not rage for vengeance?

As much as someone values the faith,

so much let him redeem the cross,

if the cross has redeemed him.

[Col. 1291A]

Those who have less silver,

if they are found faithful,

should be content with pure faith.

For one defending the cross,

the Lord’s body

is sufficient as provisions for the journey.

The wood of the cross,

the standard of the leader,

the army follows;

it did not yield,

but went before,

in the power of the Holy Spirit.

Christ, handing himself over to the torturer,

lent himself to the sinner.

If you, sinner, do not wish to die

because of the one who died

for you,

you repay your debt badly

to your Creator.

Surely the one to whom you refuse

to bow may be indignant,

while, in the winepress of the cross,

made a victim for you,

he stretches out his arms to you

and you refuse to embrace him.

The wood of the cross,

the standard of the leader,

the army follows;

it did not yield,

but went before,

in the power of the Holy Spirit.

When you consider what I am aiming at,

lift up the cross, and, by making a vow,

say: “I commend myself to him

who expended his body and soul

as a sacrifice

by dying for me.”

The wood of the cross,

the standard of the leader,

the army follows;

it did not yield,

but went before,

in the power of the Holy Spirit.

[Textual readings: in the preceding crusaders’ song, *qui* [read *quis*], “the one who” [“who”], occurs in “*In vindictam qui non fremit*”; the refrain after “*Crucem defendenti*” prints *cessi* (“I yielded”) rather than *cessit* (“it yielded”). In the following meal prayer: *De* (“of”) [read *ad*, “to”]; *ille* (“he”) [read *ut*, “that”]; *Haec sonat* (“this sounds”) [read *hic sonent*, “let these sound here”]; *melli fluat* (“may it flow like honey”) [read *melli fluant*, “may they flow like honey”]; *hiero sonet* [read *hic resonet*, “let it resound here”]; *cum* (“with”) [read *ut*, “that”]; *laetabitur* (“he will rejoice”) [read *perpetuum laetatur*, “he rejoices perpetually”]; *illi* (“to him”) [read *illud*, “that”]; *hoc* (“this”) [read *in*, “in”]; *perpetuam* (“perpetual”) [read *aeternam*, “eternal”). In the pilgrims’ hymn: *cunctis* (“to/with all”) [read *cunctos*, “all”]; *in regno tuo* (“in your kingdom”) [read *regni tui lumine*, “in the light of your kingdom”]; *gloriam* (“glory,” accusative) [read *gloria*, “glory,” nominative]; and *in saeculorum saecula* (“unto ages of ages”) [read *tempore*, “in time”).]

## II. Song of the Pilgrims

[Note: Ms. B. of Clermont, no. 189 (eleventh century). These songs of the pilgrims must have been quite numerous. For in the *Life of Blessed Altmann, Bishop of Padua*, who died in 1091, we read: “Among them two canons were especially prominent, namely Ezzo the schoolmaster, a man endowed with every wisdom and knowledge, who nobly composed on that same journey a song about the miracles of Christ in his native language”; in Pezius, *Scriptores rerum Austriacarum*, vol. I, p. 117. The account of Jost Artus’s journey to the Holy Land in 1483, printed in *Curiositaten*, vol. II, pp. 405, 422, proves that so natural a custom still existed at the end of the fifteenth century. It tells us that, as the pilgrims approached Venice, they sang:

> In Gotes Nansen varen wir  
> Und sind in disem Schiffehier.

> We travel in God’s name  
> and are in this ship here.

And on arriving in Palestine:

> Sed uns gegrüsst  
> Du heilges Lant  
> Wo unser Christ  
> Lein Leiden vant!

> Be greeted by us,  
> O holy land,  
> where our Christ  
> found suffering!

See also two songs inserted by M. O. Wolf in his *Collection of Historical Folk Songs and Poems of the Germans*, pp. 2 and 5. We owe this piece, as well as the following one, to the inexhaustible kindness of M. Champollion-Figeac, curator of the manuscripts of the Royal Library. The language is so evidently corrupt that we have not attempted to restore it everywhere. Our corrections concern only the errors that seemed to us to have originated with the copyist. This is a prayer sung before the meal, doubtless in a monastery:]

Let us first say a little verse

about God the Father and the Son,

that he may grant us assistance

at this our meal,

so that no danger may arise.

[Col. 1292B]

Let no quarrel arise here,

nor any evil slander;

let us go joyfully to dinner,

with pure heart and mind;

may the angels rejoice over us.

Let these words sound peaceful;

let sweet and good things flow like honey.

If you wish to say something,

let Sacred Scripture resound here

[reading: “let it resound here”],

so that every person may be edified!

Lord God Almighty,

preserve our pontiff,

so that he may always do what is right;

may he gladden the priests

and preach to his people;

may he care for the poor,

assist all widows,

and be a father to orphans;

may he be the redemption of captives

and acquire an everlasting kingdom.

[Col. 1292D]

Let us beseech the Lord . . . . . . .

to grant life to the pontiff

through the span of this world,

so that he may be renewed like the eagle

and rejoice forever

[reading: “rejoice perpetually”].

Lord Jesus Christ, sweetest Lord,

may what has been said to him

in these seven verses

reach him,

and may he be the redemption of captives

and acquire this kingdom

[reading: “in the age”].

Glory to the Father and to the Son,

together with the Holy Spirit.

May he who lives and reigns

[reading: “may he”]

lead us to everlasting life

[reading: “eternal life”]. Amen.

[Col. 1292B]

Hear us, King Christ;

hear us, Lord,

and direct our way!

God, have mercy;

God, have mercy,

and direct our way!

[Note: This stanza was repeated after all the others, since it was evidently sung by the chorus.]

O Three and One,

protect us all

on this holy journey.

Provide us with a guide;

send an angel

who may lead us before you!

[Col. 1293A]

Rule our journey;

defend us from the enemy

and bring us back to our homeland.

Stretch out your right hand;

remove the left-hand path

[reading: “remove the left”];

defend us from adversities!

[Col. 1294A]

You, good Creator,

command us to live

in the light of your kingdom

[reading: “of your kingdom’s light”].

May the glory

[reading: “glory”]

May eternal glory remain with the Father

through ages of ages

[reading: “through time”]. Amen.

# In the year of the Lord 1100, Radulphus Ardens

[Col. 1293]

## Notice

(*Literary History of France*, vol. VIII, p. 254)

Raoul, to whom the liveliness of his mind and the ardor of his zeal seem to have given the surname Ardent, was born in the diocese of Poitiers a few years before the middle of the eleventh century. The editor of his writings identifies the precise place of his birth as the village of Beaulieu, near Bressuire, now in the diocese of La Rochelle. We do not know what his family was, although it is nevertheless said to have been illustrious and noble. Nor are we told at what school he was educated, though probability favors the cathedral school of Poitiers. It was then flourishing, and its reputation attracted students from far away (*Literary History of France*, vol. VII, p. 50).

In whatever place Raoul may have studied, he succeeded beyond what was ordinarily accomplished in his time. His writings announce as much. They show that he was versed in the poets, the philosophers, sacred and profane history, canon law, and that Sacred Scripture was familiar to him. They also reveal that he had some knowledge of Greek and Hebrew. As for Latin, he spoke and wrote it with as much purity as delicacy. His style is clear, easy, and flowing, while at the same time compact, vigorous, and energetic. It is also claimed that he combined all these advantages with the title of doctor of theology, which he is said to have received before the age of thirty. But academic degrees, particularly that of doctor, were not established until long after him, as we have shown elsewhere.

Raoul was ordained a priest and counted himself among those who possessed the power to bind and loose (see col. 000), though he exercised it only with the prudent caution that he prescribes to others. In speaking of those entrusted with the instruction of the faithful, he clearly implies that he had been entrusted with the care of a portion of the flock of Jesus Christ (col. 000), apparently as parish priest of some parish, as is indicated in the brief summary of his life placed at the head of his work. We must believe that he did not write otherwise than he thought; consequently, we shall be persuaded that he was not one of those mercenary and timid pastors against whom he rises with great force and fiery zeal (see col. 000). He could scarcely have shown his indignation against this class of spiritual guides—whom he says were very common in his time—or demonstrated more clearly how far he was from imitating them.

On the contrary, anyone reading his fine account of the qualities of the good shepherd will easily perceive that he succeeded in portraying himself in this moving picture. In any event, that he really was such a shepherd requires no other proof than the collection of homilies we possess from him. While waiting to present them as they are, we shall say that they reveal the assiduous care he devoted to breaking for his people the bread of the word, not only every Sunday but also on all the feasts of the year, and his attention to instructing them in every point of the Christian religion. They further show that their author united in his person the three principal talents he required in a preacher: the gift of speech, a sufficient fund of knowledge to sustain the holy ministry, and adequate strength of mind to rebuke the vices of the great. His vigorous attacks on bad pastors and false scholars, who used their knowledge only for purposes of ostentation and vanity, and finally on the bishops themselves, whose pomp and other vices he does not conceal, all clearly show that Raoul spared no one when the interests of God and the salvation of his neighbor were at stake.

His concern was not limited to instruction; it also extended to establishing good order and decorum in the church when the faithful assembled there for divine worship. This detail should give us an idea of his other, more important concerns. Raoul wanted them to be placed in such a way that the clergy alone would occupy the choir and sanctuary; the laymen would then take their places, with the lord of the parish at their head; and the women would take their places after the men.

A pastor of such merit could not fail to become famous. The brilliance of his reputation having reached William IX [Note: The brief summary of the life of our preacher placed at the head of his homilies reads William IV, and this has been followed by those who copied it. But the reference here is to William IX, as is shown by the detail concerning the crusade in which he took part, as will be seen in his history. William IV had died as early as 990, a century before Raoul Ardent became known at the court of the counts of Poitiers.], count of Poitiers and duke of Aquitaine, that prince summoned him to his court.

This was apparently not because he wished to benefit from Raoul’s instruction and reform his own morals. It is only too well known [Col. 1295] that this count always led a scandalous life and behaved outrageously toward certain holy bishops. It is nevertheless supposed that William made Raoul his ordinary preacher—a claim that is highly doubtful, if not entirely implausible, for the reasons just given. What is certain is that, if our preacher ever preached at William’s court, the works he delivered there have not been preserved for us, and nothing in his printed homilies suggests that any of them was delivered before a prince or his courtiers. William may nevertheless have used Raoul in his councils, as the author of the brief account of his history claims, although, all things considered, it must seem surprising that a priest of Raoul’s character consented to live at a court such as that of the count of Poitiers then was. It may be presumed either that he was not free to refuse or that he hoped to remedy the disorders prevailing there.

Whatever the case, when Count William departed for the crusade in 1101, Raoul made the journey with him, still in that prince’s service (William of Tyre, book X, chap. 12). Those who relate these historical details add that it was in the army’s wake and amid the din of arms that he wrote his homilies. But they are certainly mistaken if they take the word “write” strictly to mean “compose.” It is evident that the homilies had been delivered orally before a people who were not engaged in the military profession, as the crusaders were. All Raoul could have done on this occasion was to write them out fairly, assuming that he had enough peace and leisure for such an operation. But it is more likely that he did not even have time for that, and that he was among those crusaders who, while making their way to Palestine in 1101, perished in the barren mountains and defiles into which they had imprudently ventured. This conclusion is suggested by the fact that nothing more is said of him after that time, and that all bibliographers who mention him bring his life to an end in that same year (Cave, p. 558; Oudin, *Scriptores*, vol. II, p. 883; Supplement, p. 354).

It is unfortunate that those who knew this writer personally, and who were in a position to acquaint us with him, neglected to preserve the events of his life. A critic of the last century (Barth., *Adversaria*, book IV, chap. 7, etc.) could not admire enough the beauty of his genius, the breadth of his learning, the solidity of his doctrine, and the power of his eloquence, and admitted that he was little inferior to the ancients. We must acknowledge that it is a highly favorable testimony to the eleventh century that it produced and formed so accomplished an orator.

The impression just formed of Raoul’s learning and manner of writing, in what has been said about the history of his life, can only predispose us favorably toward his writings. It is a great misfortune that all the works he left were not printed; and it would be an even greater loss if those preserved in manuscript could no longer be found anywhere.

### 1
