He left two collections of homilies on the epistles and gospels for all the Sundays and feasts throughout the year—not only the obligatory feasts, but also those that are not obligatory and that the Church celebrates with some solemnity. There are also homilies on the epistles and gospels of the common of saints. All these homilies exceed two hundred in number, which, together with the variety found in them, although the same subject is treated more than once, demonstrates the fertility of their author.

Raoul follows the same method consistently throughout. Whether the subject is an epistle or a gospel, he divides the sacred text into as many principal parts as it contains—ordinarily three or four, sometimes five or six, and even more—and brings the remainder of the text under the part to which it relates, then explaining each part in order. In doing so, he confines himself precisely to his text, never losing sight of it, and never enters into the history of the mystery or saint for whose feast the epistles and gospels have been chosen, unless the sacred text itself contains clearly marked details concerning it. Thus Raoul’s homilies are at once continuous explanations of the New Testament and familiar instructions in religion, because he took care to include in them almost every point of doctrine, morality, and even discipline relating to it.

First he explains each part literally and draws from it moral lessons as natural as they are instructive. What he says about the literal and moral senses, he is careful to support with other texts of Scripture, ordinarily well chosen. Often he adds the authority of the ancient Fathers, reporting their words; at other times he introduces details drawn from ecclesiastical or civil history, the Acts of the saints, the canons of councils, and sometimes even profane poets and philosophers. But from these pagans he cites only points of doctrine on which they agreed with Christians. And if he cites others in which they were mistaken, he is careful to mark their error so that it may be avoided. The Fathers and other ecclesiastical authors whom Raoul used are Saint Jerome, Saint Augustine, Pope Saint Gregory, Sulpicius Severus, Saint Benedict, patriarch of the monks of the West, whose Rule he cites, and the Venerable Bede. Among these, he seems to have selected Saint Augustine as his favorite author on doctrine and Saint Gregory on morality. He sometimes copies long passages from the latter without naming him, for he knew Gregory’s *Dialogues* thoroughly.

It is easy to judge from this the learning of our orator. His style suits the purpose of his work. It is clear, simple, precise, moving, and concise. The divisions and subdivisions that have been fashionable among the preachers of our century occur constantly in it. His eloquence is natural, drawn from the subject itself, and at the same time lively, animated, and well sustained. His Latin is sufficiently pure for the century in which Raoul wrote. Nevertheless, he sometimes uses barbarous terms to make his meaning clearer; such is the word *mititudo*, used to express gentleness of character. Since these homilies were delivered before an unlettered audience by a pastor whose apparent aim was simply to instruct the flock entrusted to his care, we would not deny that the author may first have preached them in the vernacular, after which he put them into Latin, in the form in which they now stand, to preserve them for posterity. We have observed elsewhere that scholars of the highest rank claim that the same was true of the sermons of Saint Bernard preached before the lay brothers, or conversi, of Clairvaux.

The author included in one of his homilies a detail of great interest for the history of his century, which escaped all the writers of his own time and those who followed them. M. de Meaux nevertheless mentions it in his *Variations*. The detail concerns a kind of Manichaean heretics who were then troubling [Col. 1297] the diocese of Agen. Raoul’s portrayal shows that they were a branch of those who had already appeared at Toulouse around 1018, at Orléans in 1023, and at Cambrai and Liège two years later; from this branch there later emerged those who appeared at Soissons in 1114, at Toulouse in 1118, and in Périgord around 1147, eventually forming the sect of the Albigensians. Since the doctrine of these Manichaeans of Agen differed from that of the others in several points, although it was the same in substance, readers will not object to seeing here the account Raoul preserved for us:

“They boast, but falsely, that they lead the life of the apostles and never lie or swear. Under the pretext of abstinence and continence, they condemn the use of meat and marriage, claiming that using marriage is as great a crime as committing incest with one’s own mother or daughter. They also reject the Old Testament, together with part of the New, retaining only certain things from it. And what is even more criminal, they acknowledge two creators: God, who is the creator of invisible things, and the devil, who is the creator of visible things. On this principle they secretly worship the devil, whom they regard as the creator of their bodies. With regard to the sacrament of the altar, they claim that it is nothing but bread. They deny baptism and the resurrection of bodies, and maintain that no one can be saved outside their sect.”

Another remarkable detail found in another of Raoul’s homilies concerns the dominant character of certain nations, which he had occasion to describe there. He assigns pride as the characteristic vice of the French, avarice to the Romans, and gluttony and chatter to the people of Poitiers. Since he names this last nation in particular, it is evidence that he was speaking before them and that he himself belonged to them.

The large number of editions made of this collection of homilies shows the esteem in which it was held in past centuries. Perhaps it would be no less valued today if it were better known. It is divided into two parts, as has been said. The part containing the homilies on the epistles and gospels of Sundays and of the Lord’s mysteries throughout the year was first printed in Paris by Claude Fremy in 1564. The volume, in octavo, was dedicated to Jean Coquée, abbot of Maurimont, in the name of the bookseller. The privilege, however, dates from the preceding year. It appears to be an error in Possevin (*Appendix*, vol. III, p. 115), where we read that this first edition appeared at Antwerp, from the heirs of Stelsius, in 1563. The same is true of the second part of the collection, for which the same writer also records an edition at the same place in 1570, and of both parts a third edition produced at Louvain in 1565. We have found none of these editions in any other bibliographer or in any of the multitude of libraries that we have visited personally or through the assistance of our friends.

The second part, which includes the homilies on the epistles and gospels of the principal feasts and of the common of saints, appeared in Paris, again from Claude Fremy, in 1567, in the same format as the first part. This volume is dedicated to Antoine Trusson, abbot of Toussaint on the island of Châlons-sur-Marne. The editor, in his dedicatory epistle, in which he speaks for the bookseller, expressly says that this was the first time this second part of the homilies had seen the light, and clearly implies that the edition of the first part produced by the same bookseller had preceded all the others.

After the publication of this second part, both parts were always reprinted together in two octavo volumes. They were thus printed in Paris by Fremy as early as the following year, 1568; at Antwerp by Pierre Beller in 1571 and 1576; again in Paris by Nicolas Chesneau and Jean Poupy in 1573, 1574, and 1586; and at Cologne by Quentel in 1604. M. Dupin lists an edition as having been produced in Paris in 1583, which we do not find elsewhere; this makes us suspect that 1573 should be read instead of 1583. The same, and an even more significant, error must have been made in the catalogue of the books of the widow Edmond Martin, in which an edition is dated 1675. We have no doubt that 1575 should be read.

These homilies were once judged so useful for the instruction of all the faithful that a translation was made into our language. They were printed in that translated form, in two octavo volumes, in Paris by Poupy and Chesneau in 1575. The translator of the first part was Fr. Jean-Robert, who dedicated it to Jean Brolly, abbot of Notre-Dame de la Victoire near Senlis, in an epistle dated Paris, October of the same year. The other part was translated by F. Fremin Capitis, who dedicated it to Nicolas Pseaume, bishop of Verdun; his epistle is dated January 27, 1575. This translation does not appear to have been reprinted, which suggests that it was not received as favorably as the original text. There is also a very great difference between the two.

### 2

The person who composed the brief historical eulogy of Raoul, printed at the head of his homilies, asserts that, in addition to this work, he composed another, divided into fourteen books and entitled *Speculum Ardentis*, *The Mirror of Raoul Ardent*. But we are not told whether it was a historical or moral mirror—that is, whether the subject of the work was history, morality, or some other subject that the author undertook to treat. Various other writers later chose the same title for some of their works. This mirror of our orator was preserved in manuscript, at the time of the editor of his homilies, in the library of the Cordeliers of Bressuire; and it is said that the author declares there that he composed several other works as well. To make this claim as confidently as seems to have been done, one must have read the passage in which Raoul speaks of them. And if it had been read, why not specify these other works and even copy what the author says about them?

Besides the manuscript copy of the *Mirror* just mentioned, three others are known: one in the Vatican Library and two in that of the Abbey of Saint-Vincent at Besançon (Montfaucon, *Bibliotheca bibliothecarum*, pp. 101, 1190, 1194). In the Vatican copy and one of the other two, the work is entitled *Speculum universale*, *Universal Mirror*, which might suggest that the author treats a large number of different subjects in it. But the title borne by the third manuscript restricts this idea and indicates that it concerns only morality. The title is as follows: *Diversi tractatus theologici morales* (“Various theological and moral treatises”). A foreign hand, to show that this was the same work under another title, added: *Speculum universale magistri Adulphi Ardentis* (“Universal Mirror of Master Adulphus Ardens”), in accordance with the title of the other copy in the library. In that title the copyist mistakenly wrote *Adulphi* for *Radulphi*, or better, *Rodulfi*.

### 3

It is also said that Raoul wrote a history of his own time—that is, as it is immediately explained, of Godfrey of Bouillon’s war against the Saracens. But it is not stated that this work was one of those Raoul mentions in his *Mirror*; and what is added immediately afterward creates a difficulty requiring clarification. It is said that this crusade was the one in which William, count of Poitiers, took part. But, as we have seen, that prince did not depart for Palestine until 1101, and therefore after the death of Godfrey of Bouillon. Thus, if the history written by Raoul Ardent concerned the military exploits of the Christians against the Turks at the time when Count William was on that expedition, it contained only events that occurred in 1101 and could be no more than the beginning of a history, since the author is assumed not to have lived beyond that same year. If, on the other hand, it included what took place in the crusade under Godfrey of Bouillon, it must have been a work preferable, at least in style, to those of Tudebode, Raymond of Aguilers, Fulcher, and so many others; for it has been shown that its author possessed the talent of writing well, which those other historians did not possess.

### 4

Finally, Raoul is credited with a collection of letters divided into two books. The historical, literary, and other details they contained, together with their author’s manner of writing, should make us regret their loss. If they still existed, like the preceding work, and it were possible to discover them, they would unquestionably be a delightful gift to offer the public.

[Col. 1299]

## Of the very ancient theologian Raoul Ardent of Poitiers, the most distinguished preacher of William IV, illustrious duke [the printed text reads *aucis*, probably *ducis*] of Aquitaine

### Homilies on the Epistles and Gospels of the Saints

Most necessary for all ecclesiastics who care for souls, and written by the author nearly five hundred years ago; now published for the first time. To these we have taken care to append his homilies on the epistles and gospels customarily read in the common of saints.

(Paris, at the house of Claude Fremy, Jacob Street, at the sign of Saint Martin—1567.)

## Dedicatory Epistle

To the Reverend Father Antoine Trusson, abbot of the illustrious monastery of All Saints on the island of Châlons, Claude Fremy offers greetings and wishes for peace.

In previous years, at the command of a certain bishop, I undertook, reverend abbot, to rescue from bookworms and moths the Homilies of Radulphus Ardens, a very ancient author, on the Epistles and Gospels for Sundays, and I delivered them to the press after having carefully cleansed them, as far as this could be done. When I discovered that they had been approved by the judgment of many devout and learned men and that they brought great benefit to the Christian commonwealth, since, besides their singular instruction, they also breathe the piety and holiness of the ancient Fathers in matters of religion, I once again devoted every effort to transcribing the same author’s homilies, as they are called, on the saints.

To these I added the Lives of certain saints, whose examples, like so many goads, might urge and press us to imitate those virtues which we admire in the pattern of their lives. For when, by the light of faith, we contemplate that eternal glory which the saints attained through their contempt for this world, we cannot fail to be intensely inflamed—provided that, like genuine sons, we aspire to our blessed heavenly homeland and Father—to follow the footsteps of those who now triumph securely in that ineffable glory. We have been firmly persuaded by apostolic teaching that, if we become companions in suffering, we shall also be companions in consolation.

In order that we may more easily reach that eternal consolation, it will be worthwhile to read these homilies of our Ardens. In them, to use the words of Saint Jerome, “the infant has something to suckle, the child something to praise, the adolescent something to correct, the young man something to follow, and the old man something to pray for.” In them likewise, as our Ardens teaches, we shall learn the method of following Christ: namely, that, despising the world, we should distribute all that we possess to the poor; that, naked, we should follow the naked Christ; that we should crucify our flesh with its vices and desires; that we should shine forth in chastity, charity, and the other virtues; and that we should strive toward heavenly things with our whole desire.

Reflecting on all these matters in my mind, I gladly saw to their publication, both so that the Christian and Catholic people might remain steadfast in the simplicity of the faith received from their parents, and so that, through reading the work of so great an author, the vices that daily put forth ever more abundant growth might be torn out by the roots. I wished to entrust them to your faith, so that you might deign to protect this ancient theologian by your dignity and name. If you undertake this, you will do what belongs to your office and dignity.

Farewell. Paris, on the Ides of February, 1567.

## THEODORETUS, *On the Cure of Greek Affections*, Book Eight, which concerns the Martyrs

> “For Antiochus too was called a god, as was Caius, who succeeded the emperor Tiberius; Vespasian and Hadrian likewise erected immense temples to themselves. Yet they were deprived both of the breath of life and of impious honor. The temples of the martyrs, however, are seen to be conspicuous, with a grandeur distinguished by excellence and varied with every kind of ornament, spreading far and wide the splendor, as it were, of their beauty. Nor do we approach them once, twice, or five times a year, but we very often celebrate feast days in them, and frequently, on each day, we sing praises and hymns to the Lord of those martyrs.

> “Those who enjoy good health ask the martyrs to preserve it for them; those who suffer from some illness request health. Moreover, barren men and women ask that children be given to them; those who are parents ask that the gifts they have obtained be kept safe and secure for them. Likewise, those who depart on a journey abroad ask the martyrs to be their companions on the road—or rather, the guides of their journey. Those who have already returned safely give thanks, acknowledging the benefit they have received.

> “They do not imagine that they are approaching gods; rather, they pray to the martyrs of God, appeal to them as divine men and intercessors, and ask them to plead for them before God. That those who pray with piety and faith obtain especially what they desire is demonstrated by the gifts which those who have received what they vowed offer in payment—manifest signs, clearly, of the health they have obtained. Some hang up representations of eyes, others of feet, and others of hands, fashioned from silver or gold.

> “For their Lord gratefully accepts gifts of whatever kind they may be, and does not disdain gifts that are small or of little value, since he measures them according to the resources of the one who offers them. These objects, therefore, displayed for all to see, testify to the expulsion of diseases; they are brought by those who have regained health, and are the most certain signs of it. These, I say, show what power resides in the martyrs’ tombs. The power of the martyrs declares that the God whom they worshipped is the true God,” and so forth.

Then:

> “But philosophers and celebrated orators have already been consigned to oblivion; and of emperors and great commanders many today do not even know the names, whereas all mortals know the names of the martyrs better than those of their own relatives. Indeed, they take care to give those names to their newborn children, thereby securing for them the surest protection and guardianship,” and so forth.

Likewise:

> “While he rendered those men bereft of glory and vain, he gave honor to his own martyrs. In place of the Paudia, the Diasia, and the Dionysia—that is, the solemn festivals of Jupiter and Father Liber—popular feasts are celebrated for Peter, Paul, Thomas, Sergius, Marcellus, Leontius, Antoninus, Mauritius, and the other holy martyrs. In place of that ancient pomp, that shameful obscenity and shamelessness, festivals full of modesty, chastity, and self-restraint are held—not festivals drenched in unmixed wine, not marked by frivolous banqueting, not dissolved in laughter, but resounding with divine songs and intent upon hearing sacred discourses, in which prayers are offered to God, not without holy tears and sighs.

> “Since, then, you see that such and so great a benefit proceeds from the honor bestowed upon the martyrs, flee, I beg you, the error of demons; and, guided by the martyrs and using their torches, take the road that leads to God, so that in the immortal age you may enjoy their choirs and presence.”

## HOMILIES OF RADULPHUS ARDENS

# I. HOMILIES ON THE LITURGICAL YEAR

## I. On the Solemnity of Saint Andrew the Apostle

> “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10), and so forth.

This reading, my brothers, has three parts. First, the Apostle shows that salvation comes from faith and confession; second, he shows from where these arise in us; third, he shows that hearers are more lacking in relation to preaching than preaching is lacking in relation to hearers.

Showing, therefore, by what means we advance toward righteousness and salvation, the Apostle says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but confession is made with the mouth unto salvation.” Faith of the heart is not sufficient without confession of the mouth, especially where faith is endangered. Peter had faith in his heart, but because he denied it with his mouth, he sinned mortally.

For we must both preach the cross of Christ openly, display it in the most prominent part of ourselves, and bear it upon our forehead; we must not, like certain heretics, be ashamed of the reproaches of Christ. Hence the Lord says: “Whoever confesses me before men, I also will confess him before my Father” (Matthew 10). Conversely: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed before my Father” (Luke 9).

This openly condemns us, my brothers. Although we are not ashamed of the cross of Christ, which is now honored everywhere among Christians, we are nevertheless ashamed to confess humility, poverty, patience, and the other virtues of the Crucified One. For just as the Lord will confess as his own those who confess and bear these virtues, so conversely he will deny as his own those who are now ashamed to confess these virtues.

Again, confession of the mouth is not sufficient without faith of the heart. For it benefits false Christians and hypocrites nothing to confess with their mouths the God whom they do not possess in their hearts. Hence the Lord says: “This people honors me with its lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah 29; Matthew 15).

This too condemns us, my brothers. Although by praying to and invoking God we confess him, nevertheless through evil thoughts we withdraw ourselves from him.

Again, neither faith of the heart nor confession of the mouth is sufficient without the testimony of works—for one who has time to act, I mean. False Christians, and even demons, believe and confess God. Hence James says: “The demons believe and tremble” (James 2). And, as we read in the Gospel, when they came out of the bodies of those who were possessed, they acknowledged that Jesus was the Christ (Mark 1); yet this harmed them rather than benefited them.

To believe Christ with the heart or confess him with the mouth while denying him by one’s works—hence James says: “Faith without works is dead” (James 2). And Paul says: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1).

Therefore, after this Apostle had said, “With the heart one believes unto righteousness,” he added, “but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” For righteousness may be possessed in this life without salvation in the future. We, therefore, my brothers, if we wish to deserve to attain eternal life and salvation in the future, must here firmly believe with the heart, confess with a united voice, and bear witness to Christ by a life of purity.

That one comes from faith and confession to salvation the Apostle proves. First, concerning faith, he adds: “For Scripture says: Everyone who believes in him shall not be put to shame.” Whoever firmly believes in Christ with a faith working through love (Galatians 5), even if he may sometimes appear to be put to shame amid the tribulations and miseries of the world, will nevertheless not be put to shame at the end; rather, he will be honored as a son.

That the word “everyone” is universal he proves when he adds: “For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek.” The Jews were close to Christ according to the flesh, familiar with him in worship, and instructed through the Law. The Greeks, or Gentiles, on the contrary, were far from God and unknown to him, and had been instructed neither through the Law nor through the prophets.

But with God, who is not a respecter of persons (Acts 10), there is no distinction between Jew and Gentile, because he saves believing Jews and Gentiles equally; equally the layman and the cleric, the religious and the secular, the learned and the unlearned, the noble and the base-born. Indeed, the same fervor of faith appears to be of greater merit in a layman than in a cleric, in a secular person than in a religious, in an unlearned person than in a learned one.

For services seem more pleasing when they are offered by those who are less obligated to offer them. “For the same God is Lord of all, rich toward all”—understand, “in order to enrich”—who call upon him. It is as though he were saying: The kings of the earth, because of their poverty, sometimes either do not reward some of their attendants or do not reward them as much as they ought. But the almighty Lord, rich in all things, abundantly rewards all his soldiers.

Then he introduces Isaiah’s authority concerning confession, adding: “For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.” The person who calls upon the Lord is one who calls upon him from the innermost affection of the heart. That affection, without doubt, is sufficient for salvation if it cannot be followed by action.

The second part follows, in which it is shown from where faith and confession arise in us, when he adds: “How then shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe him whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach unless they are sent?”

Through this progression he shows that confession or faith cannot be possessed except through the grace of God, who sends preachers and teaches preaching within the human heart. Whenever God withdraws preaching from certain people, so that they neither hear nor submit to preaching, this proceeds from the hidden judgment of God. Hence he himself says: “I will make your tongue cling to the roof of your mouth, so that you may not be like a man who rebukes, because the Lord is provoking” (Ezekiel 3).

But whenever he sends and instills his preaching among people, this proceeds from the grace of divine mercy. Therefore, my brothers, we must pray with all our strength that the Lord send true preachers to his people, according to what he himself says: “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest” (Matthew 9), and that he prepare the hearts of hearers to believe and confess. For unless there is one within who teaches, the labor of the tongue that teaches works in vain.

How beneficial the arrival of preachers is to the people the Apostle shows by the authority of the prophet, when he adds, as it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!”

What arrival could be more beneficial to us, and what announcement could be more welcome to us, than that of those who bring and offer us reconciliation and peace with God and promise us eternal blessings?

This openly condemns certain perverse people who are unwilling not only to perform or accept the preaching offered to them, but even to hear it, although they are always ready to listen to every kind of vain rumor and idle talk. The great condemnation awaiting them the Lord shows when he says to his disciples: “Whoever does not receive you, truly I say to you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom or Gomorrah than for that city” (Matthew 10; Mark 6; Luke 9).

The third part follows, in which he shows that hearers are more lacking in relation to preaching than preaching is lacking in relation to hearers, when he adds: “But not all obey the Gospel.” It is as though he were saying plainly: Although the proclamation of the Gospel is beneficial, not everyone obeys it.

Some scarcely even hear the Gospel; others hear it but do not receive it; others hear and receive it by profession, but do not put it into practice; still others hear, receive, and practice it for a time, but do not persevere. All these, although they hear, do not obey the Gospel, which requires faith, action, and perseverance.

Today true preachers grieve and complain about their disobedience, just as Isaiah once complained, saying: “Lord, who has believed our report?”—that is, what we have heard inwardly from God and minister outwardly to our hearers. It is as though Isaiah were saying: “Therefore,” he says, “faith comes into the heart of the hearer from hearing,” namely, from preaching.

Hearing takes place through the word of God, sounding outwardly, and through the spiritual word, working invisibly within. But I ask: “Have they not heard?” Indeed they have heard, because from the time the Gospel was spread throughout the whole world by the preaching of the apostles, no one can excuse himself on the grounds that he did not hear.

Hence he also introduces the authority of the Psalmist, who says: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” For the fame of the apostles went forth through every part of the world, and their very words were proclaimed everywhere.

Peter and Paul evangelized the Romans; James, the Spaniards; Thomas, the peoples of Greater India; Bartholomew, the peoples of Lesser India; Matthew, the Ethiopians; John, the peoples of Asia; Simon and Jude, the Egyptians and Persians; and Andrew, whose feast we celebrate today, the Greeks.

Their preaching could not be despised; rather, it was admirable, swift, and effective. What they preached in words they confirmed by examples, by miracles, and by the pouring out of their blood.

We, therefore, my brothers, should hold their words firmly, follow the examples of their lives, believe their miracles, and imitate their martyrdom—not with blood, if that is beyond us, but at least by crucifying in ourselves our carnal desires; by hating the world; by despising the world’s riches and honors; by enduring persecutions courageously; by shining through good works; by showing charity to all our enemies; and by hastening toward heavenly things with our whole desire. Thus, through the merits and prayers of those apostles, may we deserve to attain their fellowship in heaven, by the generosity of our Lord Jesus Christ, and so forth.

## II. On the Solemnity of Saint Andrew the Apostle

> “As Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea” (Matthew 4), and so forth.

Three things are shown to us in this reading, my brothers. First, how solicitous the Lord is in showing mercy; second, how effective he is in calling; third, how swift Peter and Andrew were in obeying.

How solicitous the Lord is in showing mercy is demonstrated when it is said: “Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee.” For our Lord Jesus Christ not only showed mercy, but also sought someone upon whom he might show mercy; and he walked to the place where he knew those whom he would pity were to be found.

Thus the Lord walked beside the Sea of Galilee, where he was about to call Peter and John, Andrew and James, through mercy. Imitating him, my brothers, let us go rather to places where we know that we shall find an opportunity to show mercy.

Let us not resemble those who avoid places where they know that the poor are to be found, lest perhaps, because of their inconvenience, they be forced to show them mercy. Rather, brothers, let us go where we know that there are people wandering in error, so that we may call them back from error. Let us go where we know that there are poor people, so that we may help them. Let us go where we know that there are mourners, so that we may console them.

“He saw,” it says, “two brothers casting a net into the sea,” because God especially has mercy on those who love brotherhood, who help one another, and who live by their labor. But those who hunt down their brother unto death, who persecute one another, and who “are not in the labor of men” (Psalm 72), are not worthy of a calling.

The second part follows, in which it is shown how effectively the Lord called Peter and Andrew, when he said to them: “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of men.”

In this calling, my brothers, three things must be considered: the place, the order, and the effectiveness.

The place: God calls from the shore those who are laboring at sea, from the sea itself. What else is signified by this except that he invites them from the anxiety of this world to rest, from fear to security, and from instability to the stability of eternal life?

In this he also instructs us sinners that we must remain outside worldly desire if we wish to recall others from that desire. Otherwise, if a covetous person admonishes another covetous person, Paul’s saying may perhaps be applied: “You preach that one must not steal, and you steal; that one must not commit adultery, and you commit adultery” (Romans 2).

The order too must be noted: he saw, he called, he commanded them to follow him, and he promised a reward. He saw them through election; he called them through faith; he commanded them to follow him through obedience; and he promised a reward through the recompense of obedience.

Through election one comes to faith; through faith, to obedience; through obedience, to reward. For it is a great reward and a great dignity to be a fisher of one’s own soul and of the souls of others. Whoever draws the souls of others out of the world but allows his own soul to be submerged is not a good fisherman.

The effectiveness appeared in this, that as soon as the Lord called them, they immediately followed him. For he did not call them only outwardly; just as he called them outwardly by his voice, so he called them inwardly by inspiration.

He alone is the true caller and the true preacher, because he calls and preaches inwardly. We, however, are not true preachers, because we call and preach only outwardly.

The third part follows, in which it is shown how swiftly Peter and Andrew obeyed, when it is added: “But they, immediately leaving their nets and boat, followed him.”

Behold these men: they had as yet seen none of the Lord’s miracles; they had heard nothing concerning eternal recompense; they saw the Lord himself as a mortal and observed that he possessed nothing; yet at his first call they believed, left everything, and naked followed the naked one.

What shall we say, brothers, who see miracles every day; who read and hear daily about eternal blessedness; who know that the Lord himself reigns immortal in heaven; who know that he is rich in all things; and yet refuse to follow him at his frequent calls?

We do not follow him whether we abound or lack. We are corrected neither by threats, words, blows, nor promises.

“They left,” it says, “their boats and their father.” But you may say: “What did these men leave, since they possessed scarcely anything?”

They left much, brothers, because they left everything they possessed and from then on wished to possess nothing. They left everything they could have desired.

Let no one, therefore, say to himself: “I wish to imitate those who despised the world, but I have nothing to leave.” You leave much, brothers, if you renounce your desires.

Certainly, since the kingdom of heaven has no fixed price, it is worth as much as you possess. Peter and Andrew, leaving their nets and boat, bought the kingdom of heaven; Zacchaeus bought it with half his possessions (Luke 19); the widow with two small coins (Luke 21; Mark 12); another with a cup of cold water (Matthew 10); another with good will alone. Whoever has nothing should give himself, and he will possess it.

“They followed him,” it says—not only with their feet, but also with love, life, and death.

With their feet, because neither death nor life could separate them from the love of Christ; with their life, because they became holy as he is holy, devout as he is devout, righteous as he is righteous; with their death, because just as Christ suffered for them, so they suffered for Christ, and were even crucified as Christ was crucified.

But Christ, who was without stain, was placed and stretched out straight upon the cross. Peter, however, because he had denied Christ, was crucified upside down. Andrew was crucified diagonally, because, although he did not deny Christ, he nevertheless sinned in some way.

Because they followed in this manner through obedience, Christ likewise made them, as he had promised, “fishers of men” (Mark 1).

A fisherman guides and arranges a boat, catches fish, draws the fish he has caught to shore, and separates them. In the same way, these men ruled boats—that is, churches—and arranged the net of preaching; they caught fish—that is, people—by preaching and drew them to the shore of judgment: Peter to Antioch and Rome, Andrew to Achaea. At the judgment they will separate the good from the evil. For they will sit with the other apostles “upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 10).

We, therefore, brothers, should celebrate the feast days of such great Fathers, so that, assisted by their prayers and merits, we may deserve to hold fast to their life and teaching.

And if we cannot, like them, leave everything for Christ, let us at least leave what is superfluous. If we cannot, like them, naked follow the naked one, let us at least, content with what is necessary, follow him. If we cannot follow him through the suffering of the cross, let us at least follow him through abstinence and the mortification of the flesh.

Let us crucify our members, so that we may die to sin. Let us crucify our feet, so that they may not go along the way of sinners; our hands, so that they may not be extended toward wicked deeds; our eyes, so that they may not look upon vanity; our ears, so that they may not hear slander; our hearts, so that they may not conceive evil thoughts. Thus, in the resurrection, even if we do not judge with the apostles, may we nevertheless deserve to be assigned to eternal life by the apostles.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, and so forth.

## Life of the Blessed Apostle Andrew, by Dorotheus

[Note: [Col. 1307D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 1.]

Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter (Matthew 10), as our forefathers have handed down, preached the Gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ to the Scythians, the Sogdians, the Sacae, and in inner Sebastopolis, where the wild Ethiopians dwell. He was buried at Patras, a city of Achaea, after being crucified by Aegeas, king of the Edessans.

## The Same, by Saint Isidore

[Note: [Col. 1308D] *Book on the Fathers of the New Testament.*]

Andrew—whose name means “manly” or “beautiful”—was Peter’s brother, first according to John (John 1), and second from the beginning according to Matthew (Matthew 10). He received Scythia and Achaea as his allotted field of preaching, and in Achaea he died suspended upon the gibbet of the cross. See his fuller Life in Abdias and in Ado, bishop of Trier.

## III. On the Day of Saint Stephen

> “Stephen, full of grace and fortitude, performed wonders and great signs among the people” (Acts 6), and so forth.

Today, dearest brothers, we celebrate the feast of Saint Stephen, the first martyr, whose admirable life and precious death the reading just presented sets before us. It shows us seven things: how great he was in virtue, in action, in prudence and eloquence, in contemplation, in patience, in charity, and how blessed he was in death.

First, therefore, how great he was in virtue is shown when it says: “Stephen was full of grace.”

Here “grace” is used collectively for all the gifts of the Holy Spirit, such as faith, hope, charity, and wisdom, which are called, by eminence, “graces.” Blessed Stephen is said to have been full of these, like a wine-vat full of new wine or an alabaster vessel full of ointment.

For just as a vat full of new wine pours forth its contents and fills those standing nearby with its warmth and fragrance, and just as an alabaster vessel full of ointment exhales outwardly and delights those around it with its fragrance, so blessed Stephen, filled with divine grace, could not merely give off a fragrance but rather delighted those around him through the reputation of his virtues.

“Full,” it says, “of grace and fortitude.”

There are some who possess grace in their minds but do not exercise it in action, because of faintheartedness, fear, or weakness.

Because of faintheartedness: some have good intentions, yet through weakness shrink from undertaking the way of righteousness, saying, “Who could endure such hardships?” To them the Lord says through the prophet: “You who are fainthearted, take courage and do not fear” (Isaiah 35).

Because of fear: some, out of fear of wicked people, do not dare to defend righteousness. To them it is said: “The one who fears the frost will be overtaken by snow” (Job 6).

Because of weakness: some, when undertaking works of righteousness, collapse through infirmity. To them the Lord says through the prophet: “Strengthen the weary hands and make firm the failing knees” (Isaiah 35).

Blessed Stephen, therefore, after being called full of grace, is also said to have been full of fortitude, because neither faintheartedness, nor fear, nor weakness of mind could hold him back from works of righteousness and holiness.

Thus, while the Jews were raging around him, he rebuked them for their harshness and wickedness, saying: “You always resist the Holy Spirit with hardened faces and stubborn hearts.”

In this we unworthy preachers are confounded: fearing the malice of wicked people, or afraid of losing their favor, we do not rebuke their evils, but rather flatter them or remain silent.

Second, how great he was in action is demonstrated when it says: “He performed wonders and great signs among the people.”

Although “wonders” and “signs” may refer to the same things, wonders are so called because they produce astonishment, while signs are so called because they signify something. Wonders are said to be those things that occur contrary to the customary course of nature; they are therefore also pointed out with the finger by the one who sees them, because of the astonishment they produce.

Of these wonders or signs, some do not make the one who performs them holy, but merely signify the faith and holiness of the performer—or rather, the power of the one in whose name they are performed, such as the miracles that even the rejected are said to perform (Matthew 7).

Others, however, both signify and produce the holiness of the one who performs them, such as the works of the inner virtues: loving one’s enemy, living angelically in the world, and similar acts. Such works both make the one who performs them holy and demonstrate that holiness.

Blessed Stephen shone in both kinds of works. He was admirable in himself: despising all worldly things, loving God above all things, distributing everything to the poor, loving his enemies, living in the flesh but not according to the flesh, behaving angelically in the world, praying for his persecutors, and dwelling in heaven in mind.

He was also admirable in outward works: illuminating the blind, raising the lame, enabling the deaf to hear, cleansing lepers, casting out demons, healing every illness, and raising the dead.

But we, dearest brothers, should not aspire to perform outward miracles, which belong to the perfect and are often for the imperfect, such as we are, occasions of pride. Rather, we should strive to possess the inner virtues and their works, which both produce and demonstrate inner holiness. They produce it for our benefit and demonstrate it for the example of our neighbor.

Third, how great he was in wisdom and eloquence is demonstrated when the number of those whom he surpassed in debate is revealed by what follows:

“Certain men arose from the synagogue called that of the Libertines, and of the Cyrenians and Alexandrians, and of those who were from Sicily and Asia, disputing with Stephen.”

Although wise men chosen from the synagogues of so many nations had risen in the pride of their wisdom to dispute with Stephen, nevertheless, it says, “they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit who was speaking.”

It does not say, “They could not withstand him,” but “they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit who was speaking through him,” according to what the Lord had earlier promised his disciples: “When you stand before kings and governors, do not consider how or what you should speak. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10).

Blessed Stephen did not rise to dispute against the Jews in his own wisdom and eloquence, but rather in the wisdom of God and in the eloquence of the Holy Spirit, “who makes the tongues of infants eloquent” (Wisdom 10).

In this the wise men of this world are confounded. If they think or speak anything keenly, correctly, or eloquently, they attribute it to themselves, not to God, boasting, as the Prophet says, in the utterance of their mouths: “Our lips are our own. Who is our lord?” (Psalm 11).

We, therefore, my brothers, if we understand or speak anything well, should attribute everything not to ourselves but to God, who has given us understanding and speech, and the ability to use both.

“But when they heard these things, they were cut to the heart and gnashed their teeth at him.”

Because they could not contend against the holy man in wisdom and eloquence, they attacked him, like a rabid dog, with the madness of their hearts and the gnashing of their teeth, showing by the very gesture of their bodies that they had been emptied of wisdom and moderation.

Fourth, how great he was in contemplation is shown when what follows is added:

When Stephen was filled with the Holy Spirit, [Col. 1310C] and gazing intently into heaven, he saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. In speaking of Stephen’s contemplation, Luke first stated that he was filled with the Holy Spirit, showing that contemplation is given through the Holy Spirit, so that here the adverb *when* should be understood not temporally but causally: “gazing,” he says, “into heaven.” He gazed into heaven, for “where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matt. VI). He gazed into heaven, toward which he was hastening with all his desire; and “he saw,” he says, “the glory of God.” This vision was partly bodily and partly spiritual. For he could not, with bodily eyes, somehow see the opened heavens and Jesus glorified in the flesh. I say “somehow” because the glory of a glorified human being is so great that mortal sight cannot endure it. Thus, at the Transfiguration, where Christ’s glory was brief and imperfect, Peter and the other disciples could not endure it, but immediately fell on their faces (Matt. XVII). If mortal eyes could not endure the glory of a transfigured human being, how could they endure the perpetual and immeasurable glory of a truly glorified human being, and indeed the immeasurable and inaccessible glory of God the Father? And how the Son stands at God’s right hand—that is, in equality with him—only the spiritual eye could somehow see; and I say “somehow” because the glory is so great, the splendor so great, and the blessedness of the divine majesty so great that no intellect, not even an angelic one, as it presently exists, can contemplate it perfectly.

Certainly, the man was truly blessed to whom heaven and its secrets were thus [Col. 1311A] opened. For this reason, even while he was placed among the hands of his persecutors and about to suffer, heaven was opened to him, and the glory of the Father and the Son was shown. This was done to show that heaven is opened not only to him but to all who suffer for Christ, and that the glory of God is prepared for them; and that Jesus stands for them at the right hand of God—that is, Jesus, equal with us and with the Father, is prepared, together with the Father, to help them. To stand is the posture of one who fights and gives assistance.

Therefore, my brothers, let us be encouraged to endure insults, persecutions, and tribulations for the name of our Redeemer, because without doubt he will not fail us when we suffer for him and for righteousness. He will provide us with the help of steadfastness and victory, open for us the gate of the heavenly kingdom, and place us in the glory of divine blessedness.

But blessed Stephen, who could not be restrained by any terror of the persecutors surrounding him [Col. 1311B] when he publicly bore witness to the vision revealed to him, saying, “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God,” gives us an example that, out of fear of no one, we should keep silent about the testimony of truth—especially when it must be given. But the wicked, who shouted so as not to hear the testimony of truth, stopped their ears and rushed upon the holy man. They show how hostile the wicked are to witnesses of truth: they are not merely unable to hear them, but even repay them with evil for good.

Fifth, how great he was in patience is shown when it is said:

“And they rushed upon him with one accord. And having cast him out of the city, they stoned him. And the witnesses laid aside their garments [Col. 1311C] at the feet of a young man called Saul. And they stoned Stephen, calling upon and saying: ‘Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.’”

The Jews persecuted Stephen with a persecution worse than any other. To suffer persecution from someone whom we have at some time injured in some way is little; to suffer from someone whom we have never injured is great; but to suffer from someone to whom we have rendered much good is greatest of all.

Such was blessed Stephen. He had bestowed many benefits upon the Jews, while they, on the contrary, inflicted evils upon him. Stephen sought the Jews for their salvation, while they, on the contrary, attacked him for his death. Stephen desired to lead them into the heavenly Jerusalem, while they, on the contrary, cast Stephen outside the earthly Jerusalem. Stephen [Col. 1311D] bore witness to them with words of truth, while they, on the contrary, testified against Stephen with words of falsehood, saying: “For we heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and change the traditions that Moses handed down to us.”

Stephen sent them words of preaching and prayer, while they, on the contrary, sent against Stephen stones of cruelty. And although the Jews thus repaid Stephen with evil for good, he was nevertheless not changed. He did not murmur, but bore everything patiently, maintaining the same patience and charity, always calling upon God and praying both for himself and for them.

In this we are put to shame, my brothers, because whenever someone inflicts some punishment, injury, or insult upon us, we immediately become inflamed, lose patience and charity, and hasten to repay injury with injury and insult with insult. And while we wish in this way to overcome, we are inwardly overcome by anger and impatience, failing to heed the words of Solomon: “The patient man is better than the strong, and he who rules his spirit than he who captures a city” (Prov. XV).

Sixth, how great he was in charity is demonstrated when it is said:

“But kneeling down, he cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘Lord, do not hold this sin against them.’”

In himself, blessed Stephen displayed two things that seem almost contradictory but that pastors of the holy Church ought to imitate: while correcting them with the greatest severity, he loved them with the greatest fervor; and while loving them with the greatest fervor, he corrected them with such severity. This happened because he perfectly hated vice [Col. 1312B] and perfectly loved human nature.

Wonderful was Stephen’s charity, my brothers! Few are found who truly love themselves; very few, indeed, who truly love their enemies. But Stephen loved his enemies—even amid the deadly blows of the stones raining down upon him. Where someone might have forgotten even his friends, Stephen did not forget his enemies. He pleaded, cried out, and prayed for them.

He pleaded—not so much with his knees as with his mind; he cried out—not so much with his voice as with his devotion; he prayed—not so much under the compulsion of a command as from free charity. We must not think, my brothers, that blessed Stephen, in whom there was no duplicity, pleaded for his enemies bodily but not mentally, or prayed for them with his voice but not with devotion. Far be this from a martyr imitating Christ’s charity! Without doubt, he pleaded for his enemies without any bitterness of mind; he prayed for them without hypocrisy or coldness: “Lord,” he said, “do not hold this sin against them.”

He was the true imitator of Christ, who in his Passion prayed for his enemies: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII). Thus Stephen became the first imitator not only of the Lord’s Passion but also of his charity.

With the affection with which a father is moved toward a frenzied son who strikes his father, grieving more over the son’s madness than over his own misery, blessed Stephen was moved toward the Jews, whose destruction he mourned more than his own suffering. For all wicked people are mad and possessed by demons, since they are tormented by a demon and incited to evil, and do not know what they are doing or toward what end they will come.

Therefore, my brothers, when wicked people persecute us, let us consider who is riding them and inciting them against us. Just as a rider does not fight against the horse but against the rider, and strives to throw down the rider while struggling with the horse, so let us fight not against human beings but against the demon who sits upon wicked people; and let us strive to overthrow the demon and win the people for God through benefits, prayers, and admonitions.

Thus Stephen won his persecutor Saul, and many others as we believe, for God. For the prayer that proceeded from such fervent charity could not have been ineffective.

Seventh, how blessed he was in death is shown when it is added:

“And when he had said this, he fell asleep in the Lord.”

From the work and prayer of perfection, he passed to the perfection of rest. Beautifully, my brothers, it is said not that he died but that he fell asleep. For one who sleeps appears to be, as it were, dead, but is not; rather, he lives, rests, and will eventually awaken. So also, when the saints depart from this life, “they seemed, in the eyes of the foolish, to have died, but they are in peace and rest” (Wis. III). For, as we read in the Apocalypse: “From now on, says the Spirit, let them rest from their labors” (Apoc. XIV). And at last—that is, at the dawn of the day of judgment—their bodies will awaken together with their souls, so that they may forever enjoy blessed and eternal light.

Blessed Stephen also fell asleep. But he fell asleep in the Lord—that is, in the hand and protection of the Lord—according to the words: “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and the torment of wickedness shall not touch them” (Wis. III).

Therefore, brothers, if we wish to share in the rest and glory of blessed Stephen, let us, insofar as we can, share in his virtue. And if we cannot imitate him in suffering, let us at least imitate him in charity. Martyrdom and suffering are two immense goods. Yet martyrdom without charity profits nothing, as Paul says: “And if I deliver my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. XV).

Let us hold fast to charity, through which martyrs triumph, confessors are justified, virgins flourish, and sinners are reconciled. Charity without martyrdom profits greatly. Let us love God for his own sake; our friend in God; our enemy for God’s sake. Let us do good to those who hate us; let us pray for those who persecute and slander us, so that we may deserve to be sons of the heavenly Father, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matt. V), through his only-begotten Son, our Lord, who lives with him, etc.

## IV. SERMON ON THE SAME SOLEMNITY

Jesus said to the crowds of the Jews: “Behold, I send to you prophets, wise men, and scribes, and some of them you will kill, crucify, and scourge in your synagogues, and you will persecute from city to city” (Matt. XXIII), and so forth.

In this reading from the holy Gospel, dearest brothers [Col. 1313D], our Lord and Redeemer complains of the hardness and perversity of the Jews and those like them. He does three things: he shows how good he himself was toward the Jews, how perverse the Jews were against Christ, and how great a vengeance will come upon them.

First, he shows how good he himself was toward the Jews, and what benefits he had bestowed upon them and what affection he had held toward them. He first enumerates the benefits he had bestowed upon them when he says: “Behold, I send to you prophets, wise men, and scribes.”

Passing over temporal benefits—that is, those which he bestowed upon the Jews—as though they were small, he recounts only spiritual ones, showing that he continually sent teachers and pastors for their correction and spiritual instruction. For he sent them prophets to preach to them his first and second coming, the punishments of the reprobate, and the glory of the just. He sent them wise men to teach them how they ought to live, avoid the punishments of the reprobate, and attain the glory of the just. He sent them scribes to write all these things down, lest they should ever be forgotten, and to recall them to memory.

He shows what affection he held toward the Jews when he says: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling!”

“How often,” he says, “I wanted to, and how often I showed that I wanted to!” For I showed through many signs that I wanted to gather you: whether when I brought you back from Egyptian slavery, or from Babylonian captivity, or from the various errors of idolatry [Col. 1314B] to the worship of the one divinity. I wanted to gather your children, if you were willing; but you were unwilling, and therefore I did not gather you. And if I gathered any of your children against your will, I gathered them despite you.

Now, my brothers, gathering belongs to God and godly people, just as scattering belongs to the devil and devilish people. Hence the Lord says: “He who does not gather with me scatters” (Matt. XII). God gathers people into the virtue of faith, hope, and charity, and finally into union with the divine vision and peace. Conversely, the devil scatters people through the errors of idolatry, distrust, hatred, discord, and unrest.

“As a hen,” he says, “gathers her chicks under her wings.” The hen is a most affectionate and devoted bird toward her chicks, so much so that she becomes weak from the love she has for them. With a hoarse voice adapted to theirs, she calls them together to gather them under her wings and, by confronting the hawk, to defend them.

So, my brothers, our most affectionate and devoted Lord and Redeemer is not only toward the Jews but toward all human beings, whom he created in his image and likeness. Thus, “because of the great charity with which he loved us” (Eph. II), he took on our weakness. Adapting the voice of his preaching to our capacity, he called us—not with lofty but with simple words—and, speaking to us in a simple voice, drew and gathered us beneath the wings of his arms stretched out upon the cross, in accordance with what he himself said: “And when I have been lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John XII). By opposing himself to death for our sake, he powerfully rescued us from the jaws of the devil.

Behold, brother, how admirable and affectionate is God’s charity toward human beings, and why we ought to be affectionate in loving him. Why do such great love and such great benefits, bestowed upon us little ones by one so great, not move us to love him in return?

The Lord shows how perverse, on the contrary, the Jews and those like them were toward God and his saints when he says: “And some of them you will kill, crucify, and scourge in your synagogues.” To intensify their wickedness, he rejects them, addressing himself to Jerusalem, gathered from their evil deeds, and saying twice: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to you!”

It would have been a great sin, my brothers, if they had either refused to hear preachers sent to them or, after hearing them, had wished to despise them. But now their wickedness was complete, since they persecuted and killed the ministers of both their own salvation and his, repaying them with evil for good—a repayment worse than any other.

Those men called the Jews to the salvation of eternal life, and therefore the Jews killed them. They admonished the Jews to chastise and purify their bodies, and therefore the Jews crucified them. They corrected the Jews, and therefore the Jews scourged them. With fatherly affection they loved the Jews’ nature and persecuted their vices, and therefore the Jews persecuted them from city to city. They hurled words of life at the Jews, and therefore the Jews stoned them.

They killed John the Baptist, James the Greater, and James the Less; they crucified Peter and Andrew; they scourged the twelve apostles [Col. 1315B] when they “went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been deemed worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus” (Acts V). They also persecuted them from city to city, so that, once driven out, they might rightly move on to others. They likewise stoned Stephen, whose solemnity we celebrate today.

Many people today indeed condemn the wickedness of the Jews, yet imitate them. For all who persecute their preachers, teachers, or admonishers imitate the Jews. There are many such people today within the holy Church—which is even more grievous. Although they do not kill their preachers and pastors with a sword—for they do not dare—they nevertheless kill them with the sword of evil will, tongue, and insults: when they hate them, slander them, defame them, and inflict insults upon them; and when they cause them disturbances and losses. They do not consider that, whoever the one sent may be, the person who dishonors the one sent dishonors the one who sent him. For even if the one sent is not honorable in himself, nevertheless, because of God—or rather, God in him—is to be honored.

Therefore, my brothers, love, honor, and listen to your pastors, preachers, and admonishers. If they correct us worthily, they benefit us; if unworthily, let us consider that they wish to benefit us, and for this reason they should not be hated but rather loved.

The Lord shows what great vengeance will come upon the Jews and those who imitate them when he says: “So that”—understand, through imitation—“all the blood of the righteous may come upon you,” that is, the guilt and vengeance for all the blood of the righteous that has been shed upon the earth, “from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar.”

Just as it is written that “the father shall not bear the iniquity of the son, and the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezek. XVIII), so it is written: “I am a jealous God, visiting the sins of the parents upon the children” (Exod. XX). For just as it is true that a good father will not bear the sins of an evil son, and a good son will not bear the sins of an evil father, so it is also true that an evil father will bear the iniquity of a son corrupted by his example, and an evil son will bear the iniquity of a father whom he has imitated. For just as parents participate in their children’s sins because of their evil example, so children participate in their parents’ sins through imitation, so that those who participate in guilt may also participate in punishment.

The Jews, however, not only imitated criminals but surpassed them. Those men killed prophets; these killed even the Lord of the prophets.

It is not surprising that he said “from Abel,” since Abel was the first holy person to be killed. But why does he say “to Zechariah,” when many saints were killed after him? These two signify two classes of martyrs. Abel, who was killed in the field, signifies the martyrdom of laypeople. Zechariah, the priest, who was killed between the temple and the altar, signifies the martyrdom of ecclesiastical persons—as if he were saying: “So that all the blood, both of laypeople and of ecclesiastical persons, may come upon you.”

“Amen, I say to you, all these things will come upon this generation.” By these words he does not mean a generation composed solely of the perverse Jews who existed at that time, but generally the generation of all wicked people who have existed or will exist, from the beginning to the end. Upon it will come the vengeance for all the crimes that have taken place in this world.

Then he explains what punishments will come upon them when he adds: “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate. Amen, I say to you: You will not see me from now on until you say: ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’”

He foretold two punishments that would come upon them: abandonment and the withdrawal of visitation. He speaks of abandonment when he says: “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate.”

By their house he means either the temple or the city, Jerusalem, which were destroyed and laid waste by Titus and Vespasian in the forty-second year after the Passion of the Lord, because angelic powers were heard crying from the temple: “Let us depart from these dwelling places.”

Or he means the synagogue, which was abandoned by God because of its sins, so that thereafter it would lack God’s grace, prophecy, anointing, and sacrifice.

Or he also means their minds, which were abandoned by God and thereafter inhabited by evil spirits.

He speaks of the withdrawal of visitation when he says: “Amen, I say to you, you will not see me from now on.” Many captivities of the Jews had preceded this, through which the Lord had visited them and brought them back to his land through prophets and teachers. But through this final captivity he did not wish to visit them or bring them back to his land, as if he were saying plainly: “From now on I will not visit you, either through prophets or through my presence, which you are soon going to kill, until you say”—he says—“‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,’” that is, until the second coming.

Then everyone, both the good and the evil, will confess him coming to judgment with great majesty, and “every knee will bend before him, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II). But the Jews who will be converted through the preaching of Elijah and Noah will always confess the Lord willingly and gloriously together with the others. The unbelieving and reprobate will confess him unwillingly and uselessly, because it will profit them nothing then to confess the one whom they were unwilling to confess here.

Those who do not kindly receive the correctors, scourges, and chastisements sent by God for their correction, but rather persecute, reject, and resist them, worsening the very thing by which they ought to have been improved, know that these punishments will also come upon them. For God abandons such people to their own will and to the devil. Hence he speaks to such people through the prophet under the guise of a man abandoning his adulterous wife, who had not been corrected by any admonitions: “Now,” he says, “so that I may be angry with you, my jealousy has departed from you” (Ezek. XVI).

This, my brothers, is the punishment we ought most to fear: that perhaps God, offended by our crimes, may even withdraw the corrections themselves and hand us over, through our desire, to the sinner—that is, the devil—and may no longer wish to visit us through scourges and chastisements until he comes as a terrifying judge to condemn such people forever.

Let us therefore imitate, brothers, the first martyr Stephen, who loved both his enemies and his persecutors, paying no attention to their disposition toward him but rather to the crown and glory that he attained through them. Blessed Gregory also relates this of a certain saint of remarkable patience and charity: he especially loved all those who inflicted any insult or injury upon him, calling them his co-workers, since through their ministry he was either cleansed from his sins or advanced to a greater crown.

Imitating these men, dearest brothers, whenever we suffer persecution from someone, let us consider four things. First, that this happens because our sins demand it, and therefore we ought to be angry not with our persecutors but with ourselves. Second, that it is not a human being but the devil who is tempting us, and therefore we ought to fight not against the human being but against the devil who incites him. Third, that neither this nor anything else in the world happens without God’s just judgment, and therefore we ought patiently to bear it as God’s judgment. Fourth, that the injury inflicted upon us will benefit us if we endure it patiently, and therefore we ought to bear it calmly and joyfully.

Thinking in this way, we shall be able to maintain a peaceful disposition toward our persecutors and eventually to love them truly. May God grant us this charity through the intercession of blessed Stephen, who pleaded with our Lord Jesus Christ for his persecutors, etc.

## The Life of the Blessed Stephen by Bishop Dorotheus

[Col. 1317D] Stephen, the first martyr and one of the seven deacons, was stoned by the Jews in Jerusalem and died, as Luke testifies in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts VI, VII). Concerning him Peter Chrysologus also says the following (Sermon 154):

“As Peter,” he says, “received his name from *petra*, ‘rock,’ because he first deserved to establish the Church through the firmness of faith, so Stephen was called from *stephanos*, ‘crown,’ because he first deserved to enter the struggle for Christ’s name. He first deserved to dedicate the martyrdom of Christ’s soldiers with his own blood.”

Blessed Augustine (Sermon 4, *On the Season*):

“After that most festive final day on which the Nativity of Christ our Savior shone upon us, this present day is also illumined by the crown of the blessed martyr Stephen. No nation in the world is ignorant of the merits of that martyr. For he suffered at the very beginning of the Church, that is, in Jerusalem itself. There he served as a deacon, and in the very flower of his youth he marked the beauty of his age with purple. His suffering is remarkable and exceedingly wondrous. Just now, when it was read from the book of the Acts of the Apostles, we not only heard it but also saw it with our eyes.

“Christ, therefore, the head of the martyrs, suffered first for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow his footsteps. Blessed Stephen first followed the footsteps of his Passion. By confessing Christ and being stoned by the Jews, he deserved the crown, as though it had been assigned to him by his own name. For *Stephen* in Greek is called *corona* in Latin. He already bore the name ‘crown,’ and therefore carried before him the palm of martyrdom in his own name.

“When he was being stoned, he not only did not expect to exact vengeance from his persecutors, but rather asked God to forgive them. For he remembered that the Lord had said: ‘Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord’ (Rom. XII). And again: ‘Do not say, “I will avenge myself on my enemies,” but wait for the Lord, so that he may be your help.’”

Concerning the miracles of Saint Stephen, see Blessed Augustine, *The City of God*, book XXII, chapter 8; and Gregory of Tours, archbishop, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, book [Col. 1318B], chapter 32.

## V. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT JOHN THE EVANGELIST

“He who fears God will do good” (Eccli. XV), and so forth.

In this reading, dearest brothers, the subject is wisdom—not the wisdom of the world, for whoever loves it “is made an enemy of God” (James IV), but true and heavenly wisdom, and whoever possesses it possesses the Lord. It is so precious and glorious that the Son of God called himself by its name, saying: “I am Wisdom, who came forth from the mouth of the Most High, begotten before every creature.”

This reading is divided into two parts. First, it shows by what means true wisdom is obtained; second, once possessed, how great are the benefits it bestows. It therefore sets out three things necessary for acquiring wisdom: namely, the fear of God, justice, and grace.

Through fear and justice we prepare a dwelling for wisdom. Wisdom itself, however, dwells with us not because of our merits but solely because of its grace. Through fear and justice we prepare wisdom’s dwelling by purifying ourselves from vices through fear and adorning ourselves with virtues through justice.

Therefore you labor in vain, study in vain, and turn the books over and over in vain, because unless you first remove vices and sins from yourself and incline your heart toward justice, you cannot receive wisdom. For it is written: “Wisdom will not enter a malicious soul, nor will it dwell in a body enslaved to sin” (Wis. XI).

He first speaks of fear: “He who fears God will do good.” He does not say, “does good.” For one who fears servilely does not yet do good, since he avoids sin not because of love for God. Rather, he “will do good” when, gradually avoiding sins and ceasing to fear, he begins to love God.

But you say: “Does not a sinner who fears God because of the consciousness of his sins, and therefore gives many alms, do good?” Certainly he does—that is, he performs an act belonging to the category of good works. But he is not said to do good, because he does not do it well, since he does it out of fear alone. Therefore, by doing it he does not deserve the reward of eternal life, but merely some alleviation of punishment.

And what good will he do? Those by which one reaches wisdom: he will abstain from injustice and maintain justice. Hence, adding a word about justice, he says: “And he who holds fast to justice will apprehend it,” that is, wisdom.

Justice is rendering to each person what belongs to that person: religion to God, purity to oneself, honor to parents, reverence to those superior, discipline to subjects, mercy to the afflicted, admonition to the rich, friendship to the good, correction to the wicked, and equity to all.

Whoever exhibits this justice in his works in such a way—or at least does what he can, retaining it within himself—will indeed apprehend wisdom, not through his merits or intelligence but solely through the grace of Wisdom itself. Hence it is added: “And she will meet him freely, like an honored mother.”

This is an image of an honorable and loving mother who, when her thirsty son asks for milk, does not turn away from him but rather offers her breast to him. Behold, my brothers, God’s compassion toward us is like this—or rather, greater—if we wish to be his children. Hence James says: “If anyone,” he says, “lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously and does not reproach” (James I).

The second part follows, in which ten gifts are enumerated that wisdom, once acquired, bestows upon its disciples. It gives seven in this life and three in the life to come.

The first is food—not bodily food but food for the soul—of which he says: “He will feed him with the bread of life and understanding,” that is, with the body of Christ or with the teaching of the Word, without which the soul perishes from hunger in the desert of this world. It is called the bread of life and understanding because it makes one live rightly and understand rightly.

The second is drink for the soul, of which he says: “And he will give him to drink of the water of saving wisdom” [Col. 1319C]—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit, without which a person perishes from thirst in the heat of this world. Concerning this water the Lord says: “Whoever drinks the water that I will give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John IV).

The third is the strength to endure persecutions, scourges, and worldly miseries patiently. Concerning this it is added here: “And he will be strengthened in him”—that is, he will make him firm—and he will not be bent away from the rigor of truth and justice by any harassment, as certain false pastors of the holy Church do today. Concerning them the Lord says: “The hireling,” he says, “and he who is not the shepherd, sees the wolf coming, abandons the sheep, and flees” (John X).

The fourth is continence, concerning which it is added: “And he will contain him”—that is, he will make him continent—and he will not be confused or poured out through unlawful desires or temptations of the flesh. Thus he will be firm against outward persecutions and continent against inward temptations.

The fifth is authority, which is appropriately placed fifth. When a person possesses the preceding gifts—that is, teaching, grace, strength, and continence—he is worthy to be elevated to the office of preaching and teaching. Hence it is added here: “And he will exalt him among his neighbors.” It does not say “among his servants” or “slaves,” indicating that a pastor should not regard his subjects as inferiors but rather as neighbors and brothers. Hence it is written: “They have appointed you a ruler; do not exalt yourself, but be as one of them” (Eccli. XXXII).

The sixth is preaching, which is the pastor’s office, without which he presides culpably. Concerning this it is said here: “In the midst of the Church he opened his mouth,” as if he were saying plainly: Let the preacher not presume upon his own eloquence, because he cannot preach by himself unless the Lord opens his mouth. Hence the Psalmist also prays: “Lord, open my lips” (Ps. L).

The seventh is the fullness of the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, who alone supplies the preacher with what he is to say. Hence: “For it is not you,” he says, “who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X). Concerning these gifts it is added: “And the Lord will fill him with the Spirit of wisdom and understanding.”

Above he had said: “He will give him to drink of the water of wisdom.” Here, however, he says: “He will fill him with the Spirit of wisdom,” which is greater. By this he indicates that when someone is worthily elevated to the office of preaching, the grace of the Holy Spirit is increased in him more and more.

And these are the seven gifts that true wisdom confers in the present life. The three that follow it confers in the other life. [Cols. 1320C–1321B]

The eighth, therefore, is the garment of the glory of immortality, both of soul and of body. Concerning this it is added: “And he will clothe him with the garment of glory.” For then, thereafter, the souls of the saints will no longer be able to be corrupted by sins or disturbances, nor their bodies by death or illnesses. “For then God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints, and there will no longer be mourning or crying, because the former things have passed away.
