They will hunger no more, nor thirst any longer, and the sun will not fall upon them, nor any heat” (Rev. XXI).

The ninth is the ineffable joy with which God will fill the saints forever. Concerning this it is added: “He will store up gladness and exultation”—that is, he will ceaselessly heap them upon him. Gladness of mind, exultation of body—or gladness arising from the vision of God, and exultation arising from the common salvation. For then they will see him “whom the angels desire to behold” (1 Pet. I), and they will rejoice without envy in the goods of each person as goods held in common. Indeed, a single will and charity will make the goods of individuals common, and thus, though their brightness differs, their joy will be equal.

The tenth is eternal honor, concerning which it is added: “And he will inherit him by an eternal name.” What greater honor, my brothers—what greater honor—can there be than that, when God calls and establishes the saints as children of God, “heirs indeed of God, but fellow-heirs with Christ” (Rom. VIII)? What greater honor than that the adopted son should be there in name, honor, and inheritance where the natural and only-begotten Son of God is?

Now, dearest brothers, let us see how all these things were fulfilled in the blessed John the evangelist, whose solemn feast we celebrate today. He feared the Lord, avoiding evil and doing good. He was an observer of justice, offering God religious devotion; preserving purity both of body and soul; honoring his parents; showing charity toward his brother; and living from the labor of his hands together with his father and brother. To him the Wisdom of God, honored as a mother, came to meet him when it called him and his brother from the sea (Matt. IV).

It fed him with the bread of life and understanding and gave him to drink of the saving water of wisdom when, reclining upon its breast (John XXI), it more abundantly than the others intoxicated him with heavenly teaching and wisdom from the fountain of its breast. It strengthened him: neither the persecutions of Jews or Gentiles, nor a vat full of boiling oil, nor exile could weaken him from the truth. It made him continent, because he did not give himself over to any desires of the flesh. It exalted him among those near to him when it raised him to be an apostle. It opened his mouth in the midst of the Church when it appointed him preacher and evangelist. It filled him with the Spirit of wisdom and understanding—not only on the day of Pentecost with the others, but more abundantly than the others—so that he understood, wrote, and proclaimed beyond all understanding: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John I).

The Lord clothed him with the garment of glory when he transferred him to the heavenly realms without the pain of the flesh. He stored up gladness and exultation for him, making him rejoice with him forever. “By an eternal name he will inherit him,” because he made him an heir and participant in his own name and honor.

By the merits and prayers of this man, may our Lord Jesus Christ make us, however insignificant we are, fellow-participants in his glory. He lives and reigns with the Father, and so forth.

## VI. SERMON ON THE GOSPEL FOR THE SAME FEAST [Cols. 1321C–1324B]

“Jesus said to Peter: Follow me. Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following him” (John XXI), and the rest.

My brothers, this reading of the holy Gospel was written by John the apostle and evangelist, whose solemn feast we celebrate today. In this reading he does three things. First, he shows that the Lord indicated by what death Peter would glorify the Lord. Second, he shows how John himself would depart from this life. Third, he reveals his own person through certain expressions.

The Lord indicated by what death Peter would glorify him when, in the preceding reading, he said to him: “When you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish” (ibid.). Afterwards, he said to him what we have just heard: “Follow me.” As though he were saying openly: “Imitate me, and especially in this: just as I died for you, so you too should die for me.”

The prince of the apostles is told above all others to follow the Lord, because although everyone ought to follow him, this applies especially to the leaders of the holy Church, who hold his place in the Church. Everyone, indeed, is bound to follow him. Hence it is written: “Whoever wishes to remain with Christ ought also to walk as he walked” (1 John II). But for the lesser ones it is sufficient if they follow Christ’s way from a distance. For the prelates of the holy Church, however, it is not enough unless they follow Christ closely and explicitly and rely upon his footsteps. Hence it was said to them especially: “Whoever serves me must follow me” (John XII). As though he were saying: “Whoever carries out my ministry must follow my footsteps, so that whoever follows him may follow me,” and so that he may safely say with Paul: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. IV and XI).

This stands openly against us preachers, who carry out the ministry in Christ’s Church and yet do not follow his footsteps. For Christ displayed for us in this world the way of poverty, humility, labor, and patience. But we, on the contrary, desire here to become rich, to enjoy glory, to rest, and to delight ourselves. Hence—and I cannot say this without tears—it happens that we pastors stray from Christ’s footsteps, make those subject to us stray along with us, and thus bring ruin not only upon our own souls but also upon the souls of others. Hence it is written: “The prophet is a snare of ruin” (Hos. IX).

But we, dearest brothers, just as we see our own danger if we do not follow the footsteps of the supreme shepherd, should likewise fear danger for you if you disdain to follow us as we walk rightly. Therefore, let both you and we correct our ways and strive to follow the way of our Redeemer. Let us also imitate his imitator Peter, who followed Christ in life, teaching, and the cross. In these three things all of us preachers are especially bound to follow him: namely, that we live purely, teach rightly, and crucify our members together with their vices and desires.

Second, the Lord indicated how John the evangelist would depart from this life when, in response to Peter’s question about his death, he said: “Thus I will have him remain until I come.” As though he were saying: “I wish him to live in the flesh longer, even after the death of all the apostles, until I visit him and transfer him to the heavenly realms by a peaceful death.” For we read that John the evangelist lived for a long time after all the apostles. When he was ninety-nine years old, the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him and said: “Come, my beloved, to me, for it is time for you to feast with me at my banquet with my brothers. Therefore, on the Lord’s Day that will come in five days, you shall come to me.” When he had said this, he was received into heaven.

When the Lord’s Day arrived, blessed John went to the church. After celebrating the divine mysteries there from the first cockcrow until the third hour and exhorting the people, he alone descended into the place dug for his burial, returned his spirit to God, and was found to be as free from the pain of death as he was untouched by the corruption of the flesh.

The Lord did not therefore say to Peter alone, “Follow me,” as though this John would not follow him. For who would follow the Lamb more closely than the one who follows him wherever he goes (Rev. XIV)? Rather, he indicated that John would not follow him through the bitterness of passion. Yet John was not for that reason deprived of the crown of martyrdom, as the Lord himself testifies, since he had foretold to John and his brother James: “You will indeed drink my cup” (Matt. XX).

John himself, together with the other apostles, was scourged by the Jews. He himself was placed by Domitian in a vat of boiling oil because of the name of Christ. He himself was sent into exile on the island of Patmos. He himself endured many persecutions for Christ’s sake. Therefore, by both labor and willingness, he is a martyr.

For this reason, my brothers, let us patiently and joyfully endure labors, tribulations, persecutions, and afflictions of the flesh for God’s sake. For while we do these things, according to the Lord’s word, we drink his cup and earn the palm of martyrdom.

When the Lord rebuked Peter for inquiring too curiously about the death of his fellow disciple, saying, “What is that to you? You follow me,” he teaches us, my brothers, not to inquire curiously—as some do—into the lives of our neighbors, especially those subject to us, but rather always to be concerned about our own. Let us always judge not another’s life, but our own.

Third, we must consider how John commends his own person for the benefit of those who follow, and does so in three respects: through the privilege of grace, the privilege of intimacy, and his office. Yet in all these matters he speaks about himself as though about another. It is customary among the holy Fathers that, when they speak of good things about themselves, they speak of themselves as though of another, in order to avoid boasting. Thus Moses, speaking of himself as of another, says: “Now Moses was the meekest of all human beings” (Num. XII).

So John, speaking from the privilege of grace, commends himself when he calls himself “the disciple whom Jesus loved.” This was not because Jesus loved him alone, but because he showed him a greater sign of love. He loved them all, since he said to them all: “Remain in my love, just as I have loved you” (John XV). But he loved John especially because he was chosen by the Lord as a virgin and remained a virgin forever. Truly fortunate and most blessed is the one whom the Lord is said, by antonomasia, to love.

He commends himself through the privilege of intimacy when he says of himself: “He also reclined at supper upon his breast” and said: “Lord, who is it that will betray you?” To recline upon the breast of the master and to be a confidant of his secrets is the greatest sign of intimacy.

If someone asks why the Lord showed this disciple such love and such intimacy, we reply that the virginal and contemplative life is a heavenly and angelic life. God and his angels have great intimacy with virgins and contemplatives. Hence the Lord loved the virgin and contemplative disciple more tenderly and familiarly than the others, and entrusted the Virgin Mother to that virgin, because among virgins and contemplatives there is holy fellowship, pure intimacy, and a flourishing appearance.

Since the virginal and contemplative life is heavenly and angelic, I therefore think that the Lord wished the blessed Virgin and this disciple to pass easily and painlessly to the heavenly realms; for the passage from like things to like things is easy. Just as the farther someone is from heavenly life and conduct, the more difficult the passage to them is, so, conversely, the closer someone is to heavenly life and conduct, the lighter the passage he earns to them.

Saint John reveals himself through his office when he says: “This is the disciple who bears witness concerning these things and wrote them, and we know that his testimony is true.” We ought to embrace his writings, my brothers, all the more firmly and dearly because he himself was more familiarly and closely involved in the mysteries that he writes, and because he drew more abundantly and deeply than the others from the streams—that is, from the very fountain of the Lord’s breast.

Therefore, my brothers, let us entreat him with prayers and with groans, so that by his merits and prayers he may obtain for us from his beloved Lord that we may rightly understand his writings, observe chastity, contemplation, and his other virtues from afar, despise the world, love God above all things, hasten toward the heavenly realms with our whole desire, and reach them by a blessed course. May our Lord Jesus Christ grant this; he lives and reigns in perfect Trinity forever, and so forth.

## The Life of the Blessed John the Evangelist, by Dorotheus [Col. 1324C]

[Note: [Col. 1323] Eusebius, book III, chapter I, *Ecclesiastical History*, and chapter 18]

John, the brother of James, who also became the Lord’s evangelist and whom the Lord loved, preached the Gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ in Asia. He was condemned by Trajan to exile on the island of Patmos because of the word of the Lord. There he also composed his holy Gospel, which he later had written at Ephesus by his host Gaius, to whom the apostle Paul also bore witness when writing to the Romans, saying: “Gaius, my host and that of the whole Church, greets you” (Rom. XVI).

After Trajan’s death, he returned from the island of Patmos and remained at Ephesus, living for 120 years. When these years were completed, while he was still alive and the Lord so willed, he buried himself there. Some nevertheless say that he was not banished to the island of Patmos under Trajan but under Domitian, the son of Vespasian. Jerome, Eusebius in the *Chronicles* and in the *Ecclesiastical History*, and many others hold this latter opinion, although that same Eusebius, in book *On the Preparation of the Gospel*, and Tertullian write that he was banished to the island of Patmos by Nero.

## VII. ON THE FEAST OF THE HOLY INNOCENTS [Cols. 1324D–1328D]

“I saw upon Mount Zion a Lamb standing” (Rev. XIV), and so forth.

Dearest brothers, the apostle and evangelist John—who was chosen by Christ as a virgin and remained a virgin forever—relates that this vision was revealed to him by the Lord (John XII). He also reclined upon the Lord’s breast at supper; hence he learned the heavenly secrets more deeply than the others.

First, therefore, he speaks of the one whom he saw. Second, of those whom he saw with God.

Speaking, then, of the one whom he saw, he says: “I saw upon Mount Zion a Lamb standing.” In this he says three things: whom he saw, where he saw him, and how he saw him situated.

Whom did he see? “I saw,” he says, “a Lamb.” My brothers, Christ is called a Lamb for three reasons: because he was prefigured in the paschal lamb; because he is gentle and innocent like a lamb; and because, like a lamb, he feeds us with his flesh and blood and clothes us with the garment of his purity and immortality.

Where did he see him? “Upon Mount Zion,” that is, above the eminence and contemplation of the whole Church. He presides as head over all the members, not only by divinity but also by benefit, teaching, and example.

By benefit, because, since he is the fountain of all graces, we all receive participation from his fullness, as members receive it from the head. By teaching, because we are instructed by him in the teaching of life and conduct. By example, because, with him preceding us as light and guide, we reach eternal life.

For this reason, brothers, it is worthwhile for us, if we wish to reach eternal life rightly and without stumbling, always to stand upon his footsteps and always to keep the eye of our mind fixed upon him, according to what the Wise Man says: “The eyes of the wise are in his head” (Eccles. II).

How did he see him situated? “Standing,” that is, ready to help us and to fight on our behalf. For while we labor, my brothers, amid the tribulations and miseries of this world, the Lord stands for us if we hope in him with our whole heart. Hence blessed Stephen, placed among his persecutors, confessed that he saw him not sitting but standing, as though fighting on his behalf.

Let us therefore fight and suffer securely for Christ, because we shall undoubtedly feel him standing and bringing us aid.

But did you, O John, see the Lamb without companions? Certainly not. For this reason he came from the bosom of the Father into the world; for this reason he became a Lamb and was sacrificed, so that he might have participants and fellow-heirs with him in the paternal inheritance. Although all the good are with him, virgins nevertheless cling to him more familiarly and closely. Since he himself is always a virgin and the son of a virgin mother, he especially loves and seeks the companionship of virgins. Hence it follows: “And with him were a hundred and forty,” and so forth.

This is the second part, in which John describes those whom he saw with the Lamb, presenting ten details concerning them: how many they were; what profession they had; what kind of voice they possessed; what song they sang; where they sang it; how chaste they were; how closely joined to the Lamb; how chosen; how truthful; and how pure.

He shows how many they were when he says: “A hundred and forty-four thousand,” that is, twelve times twelve thousand. Here a finite number is used for an infinite one, more to express a mystery than a quantity. Each number—the twelve and the thousand—is perfect. One multiplied by the other shows that those who were with the Lamb possessed perfection.

The summit of all virtues is virginity. I do not mean every kind of virginity by this. There is a forced and useless virginity, such as that of those who are virgins because of fear or guardianship. There is also a natural and useful virginity, such as that of those who are virgins because of rank, age, or bodily frigidity. And there is a virtuous and highly meritorious virginity, such as that of those who are virgins because of the ardor of divine charity.

It is this virginity that I call the summit of all virtues, since it is crowned with every virtue, every merit, and martyrdom. For what greater virtue or greater merit is there than to live in the flesh but not according to the flesh; to be in fire and not burn; to remain in mud and not be defiled; and amid the wickedness of this world to lead an angelic life? What greater martyrdom is there than to crucify oneself becomingly, to struggle daily with oneself, and to renounce one’s pleasures and wills?

He shows what profession they had when he says: “Having his name—that is, the Lamb’s—and the name of his Father written upon their foreheads.” This means that they openly confessed the name of the Father and the Son, concealing it neither out of shame, fear, nor torments, and being more ready to die than to be silent about or conceal the name of Christ.

In this our pride is put to shame. Although we confess that we are Christians because the name of Christ is now honored, we are nevertheless ashamed to bear poverty, humility, patience, and the other insignia of Christ.

He shows what kind of voice they have when he adds: “And I heard a voice from heaven like the voice of many waters, and like the voice of a great thunder. And the voice that I heard was like that of harpists playing their harps.”

As though he were saying: “I heard a great and delightful voice”—great because of the multitude of those singing psalms, delightful because of the sweetness of their harmony. And if, according to James, “the constant prayer of a righteous person is very powerful” (James V), how pleasing and delightful do you think the praise or prayer of countless virgins must be to the Lord when it is offered with great devotion and harmonious sweetness?

Beautifully he compared the praise of those who “crucify their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. V) to the melody of harpists, because just as harpists twist and constrain a string so that, when struck, it may resound with a sweet sound, so virgins and the continent twist and press their flesh, so that the more it is struck by the hand of persecution, the more it may sing psalms to God. And just as the different sounds of strings on a harp come together in one harmonious melody, so the different virtues in the choir—or the distinct virtues in one person—come together in the harmony of a single charity.

Therefore, my brothers, let us discipline our carnal will through abstinence, compel it to sing psalms to God in adversity, and make it harmonize with the melody of right intention and charity.

He shows what song they sang: a new and singular song. He shows that it was new when he says: “And they will sing as if a new song.” The song of virgins is new because it was established by Christ, the new man, to renew human beings. The ancients did not strive for virginity but for posterity. To them it was said: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. I). But in the time of the new grace Christ urged the observance of virginity and said to them: “Increase in purity of mind and body, and fill heaven.”

He shows that the song was singular when he says: “And no one could sing the song except those hundred and forty-four thousand who were purchased from the earth.”

Even a very small bell, if it is broken or damaged, cannot produce the sweetness of melody that a whole and sound one can produce. Nor can sexually mature or corrupted persons sound and sing as sharply as small, sexually immature, and undefiled children. In the same way, married and widowed persons cannot in any way be before the Lord in spiritual melody, nor can they equal virgins.

Virgins sing a singular song, blessing and praising God from the singular incorruption of mind and body. Others can hear this song, but they cannot sing it in any way. They hear the song of virgins and delight in it—those who love the virtue of virginal melody in others and rejoice with them in it. Nor are those who, through charity, make it common to themselves entirely without it.

In a certain way, my brothers, we make the virtues of our neighbors our own when we rejoice in them and praise God. He shows where they sang it when he says: “Before the throne and before the four living creatures and the elders.”

By the throne we understand the holy Church of God, in which God rests. By the four living creatures, the four evangelists. By the twenty-four elders, the Fathers of the Old and New Testaments—that is, the twelve patriarchs and the twelve apostles.

Before the throne, therefore, and the four living creatures and the elders, the virgins sing a new song. By the novelty of their virtue and praise they delight God, his saints, and the officials and senators of the heavenly court.

O how blessed are the virgins who are appointed as new musicians in the heavenly court and, as it were, while the angelic song grows old, deserve to delight God and the whole court of God with a new melody! Human virginity is more wondrous than angelic virginity, since what an angel possesses by nature, a human being strives to obtain through virtue against nature.

He shows how chaste they are when he says: “These are they who were not defiled with women, for they are virgins.” Here the term “woman” is applied to whatever can provoke the pollution of the flesh. He properly describes lust, calling it defilement. Lust is a vile thing: vile in the service of shameful members, foul in its act and conclusion, and followed by shame and repentance.

Four things accompany lust: the brutalization of the mind, defilement, shame, and repentance. Virginal purity knows none of these. For virgins are virgins in body and in mind. Whoever is corrupted in mind is no longer a virgin. Hence the Lord says: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. X).

He shows how closely joined they are to the Lamb when he adds: “These follow the Lamb wherever he goes.” Above all others, virgins are more familiar and closely joined to Christ, for they alone follow him wherever he goes.

Married and widowed persons, although they follow him along the way of charity, humility, patience, and the other virtues, nevertheless do not follow him wherever he goes, because they cannot follow him by the way of virginity. Virgins alone follow him by this way and by all the other virtues.

He shows how chosen they are when he adds: “These were purchased from all as firstfruits for God and the Lamb.” “These were purchased,” he says—that is, implicitly, they were purchased from all the dangers, temptations, and tribulations of the world. Or, “purchased” means chosen from all the chosen, even the pre-eminent chosen, so that they might be firstfruits for God and the Lamb.

Firstfruits are called early fruits which, because of their newness and earliness, are usually more pleasing than other fruits. Thus the newness of virginal chastity delights the divine majesty more than the other fruits of virtue.

He shows how truthful they are when he adds: “And no lie was found in their mouth.” As though he were saying: “They are chaste not only in mind and body but also in tongue.” This is directed against certain people who, although they preserve chastity of mind and body, nevertheless commit adultery with their tongue by pouring forth lies, detraction, filthy speech, excessive speech, empty speech, and other abuses of the tongue. They do not consider that one who is truly chaste keeps not only the body but also the tongue, ears, eyes, and other senses chaste.

For it is written: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. V).

He shows how pure they are when he adds: “They are without blemish before the throne of God.” As though he were saying: “They are not pure only in the matters already mentioned, but pure universally.” Even if they once contracted certain blemishes from worldly life, which cannot be lived without sin, they were nevertheless completely cleansed and sanctified through baptism, penance, passion, and the other means of purification—not merely before human beings, who can be deceived, but also before the Lord, who cannot be deceived.

How pure are those who are pure according to divine judgment!

Therefore, my brothers, you who are virgins are blessed if you persevere in true virginity. Yet know that the flower of virginity, the more precious it is, the more dangerous it is to guard amid so many temptations of the flesh, the devil, and the world. Therefore devote yourselves to fasts, vigils, labors, humility, and prayer, which are the guardians of virginity.

You also who are continent are blessed in the second place if, the freer you are, the more you devote yourselves to God and his works; if, despising the things of the world, you think upon and do the things of God with your whole desire; knowing that prolonged chastity is an imitator of virginity.

You also who are married are blessed in the third place if you preserve marital chastity undefiled; if you govern your wives and households justly; if you raise your children in the fear of God; if you redeem the blemishes of marriage through almsgiving; if you devote yourselves to hospitality, care for the poor, and the other works of mercy; if you attend church; and if you heed the Lord’s commandments.

By doing this, you follow the Lamb—even if not wherever he goes—and through this you attain his eternal blessedness, with the help of him who lives and reigns, and so forth.

## VIII. ON THE SAME FEAST [Cols. 1329A–1330A]

“An angel appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying: Arise and take the child and his mother and flee into Egypt, and remain there until I tell you” (Matt. II), and so forth.

In this reading of the holy Gospel, dearest brothers, three things are shown to us according to the literal sense.

First, it is shown to us that Christ possessed true divinity and true humanity. He is shown to have true humanity when, like a human being, he flees and hides himself. In this he also gave his followers an example of yielding at times to persecution, so that it might not at some time be reproached to his members if they fled, since Christ the head had at some time fled.

Second, it is shown that human fury rages in vain against the divine purpose, in that Herod’s intention to plot Christ’s death is frustrated. For it is written: “There is no wisdom, no understanding, no counsel against the Lord” (Prov. XXI).

Herod is deceived in his wickedness in three ways: he does not harm Christ, whom he attempts to kill; he benefits those whom he kills because of Christ, by making them martyrs; and he harms himself by acquiring condemnation for himself. Thus it is rightly said of him and those like him: “He opened and dug a pit, and he fell into the hole that he made. His pain will return upon his own head, and his iniquity will descend upon his own crown” (Ps. VII).

Third, it is shown to us that earthly people grieve inconsolably over the death of their children, when it is said: “Then was fulfilled what had been spoken through Jeremiah the prophet, saying: A voice was heard in Rama, weeping and great wailing, Rachel weeping for her children; and she refused to be comforted, because they are not.”

In these words Jeremiah, recalling the ancient history, foretells that there would be such great mourning because of the slaughter to be carried out by the Chaldeans as there had been because of the Levite’s wife, who was killed and divided into twelve parts. Almost the entire tribe of Benjamin was destroyed, except for a few, and their mourning is said to have been heard as far as a distant place called Rama (Judg. XX).

It is therefore as though the evangelist were saying: The mourning of the mothers who grieved for their sons killed by Herod was so great that it resembled both the mourning over the slaughter of the sons of Benjamin, killed because of the Levite’s wife, and the mourning over the slaughter of the Jews carried out by the Chaldeans. Just as then either the tribe of Rachel, from whom Benjamin was born, or the tribe of Judah wept inconsolably for their slain, so then the mothers inconsolably wept for their sons killed by Herod.

But we Christians ought not to imitate either these women or those others, so as to grieve inconsolably over the death of our children or friends. If they were good, we ought not to mourn them but rather rejoice with them, since we are confident of their salvation. If they were sinners, we ought to come to their aid through almsgiving, prayers, and offerings, so that we may obtain forgiveness and salvation both for ourselves and for them and may rejoice with them in the resurrection.

It is the part of those who have no faith in the resurrection or hope of glorification to despair and grieve inconsolably over the death of their friends. Hence the Apostle says: “I do not want you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the others who have no hope. For we say this to you by the word of the Lord: We who are alive and remain until the coming of the Lord will not precede those who have fallen asleep” (1 Thess. IV), and so forth.

Then he adds: “We will be caught up with them to meet Christ in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord. Therefore comfort one another with these words” (ibid.).

Mystically, however, four things are signified for us here. The fact that Christ, as soon as he was born, suffered persecution from Herod and was transferred with his mother into Egypt by Joseph signifies that the primitive and newly beginning faith of the Church would suffer persecution from the Jews. It also signifies that the faith of Christ itself, together with the Church, would pass from the Jews to the Gentiles through the order of preachers, until Herod—that is, Jewish unbelief—had died, when the faith of Christ would return to the Jews at the end of the world.

Second, the slaughter of the children signifies the passion of all the martyrs. These children suffered at the hands of Herod’s members, while those martyrs were destined to suffer at the hands of the devil’s members. These were infants and children; those were destined to be humble and pure. Some of these were two years old, others younger; and among those, some were destined to be perfect in doctrine and conduct, others imperfect. These were killed so that Christ might be killed among them; those were to be killed so that Christ might be killed with them.

Third, the fact that the infants are killed for Christ, while Christ is not killed, signifies that the martyrs were indeed to be killed for Christ, yet Christ could in no way be killed in them or taken away from them, in accordance with what Paul says: “Neither death nor life will be able to separate us from the love that is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. VIII). And elsewhere: “Whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s” (Rom. XIV).

Fourth, in the statement that a voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and great lamentation, Rachel weeping for her children, it is signified that the voice of the martyrs’ blood, crying out from the earth, and also Rachel’s lamentation—that is, the Church’s lamentation over the unjust death of the martyrs—does not, as unbelievers think, vanish into nothing. Rather, in Ramah, that is, on high, it ascends to the ears of God the Judge, who will deservedly crown these and punish those eternally.

But concerning the death of the martyrs, the Church does not wish to be consoled, because they are no longer—understand, no longer of this world—and therefore she does not wish to weep over them in such a way as to call them back to the world, since she knows that they reign eternally with Christ. Although we grieve that the martyrs and saints of God have been taken from us, we must not wish them to return here; rather, we should rejoice with Christ and pray for ourselves.

Morally, too, in the fact that Jesus, immediately after being born, suffered persecution from Herod, it is shown to us that as soon as someone is converted to God and begins to live for God, he will suffer temptation and persecution from the devil. For when the devil sees a person dying to him and beginning to live for God, he rages against that person all the more fiercely, so that he may kill him in soul. Hence it is written: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in fear and prepare your soul for temptation” (Eccli. II).

But at the command of God’s messenger, such a person flees the secular life, in which Herod—that is, the devil—reigns, and takes refuge in Egypt, that is, in the monastic life, in which the devil has no power; and there he lives more securely. But many of the infants—that is, the inexperienced and weak—who remain in secular life are slain in soul by the devil. Rachel—that is, the Church—mourns their destruction and weeps almost inconsolably, because she loses through the devil’s snares the infants whom she had brought forth for Christ through baptism. She scarcely wishes to be consoled over the loss of such persons, because they have been removed from the number of the elect, among whom they had seemed to belong. For these it would indeed have been better never to exist at all than to be damned eternally.

You, therefore, sons, who are still infants and weak in Christ, and who rush toward every kind of damnation imposed by the devil, the flesh, or the world, flee secular life, lest you should at some time be utterly slain by the devil. Enter a monastery or solitude, so that you may live there more securely the farther you are removed from the temptations of the world.

But you who are strong in Christ and, with God’s help, are able to resist the devil, the world, and the flesh, do not withdraw yourselves from the gatherings of secular people. Rather, win sinners for God by your word and by the example of your good conduct. Hence the Lord says: “No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light” (Luke VIII).

Therefore, you who are more perfect in Christ, shine upon others by good words and example; enlighten those in darkness; advance those who have begun well; strengthen the weak; admonish those who live well to strive for better things, so that, with the gain of many souls, you may deserve to come to Christ, to be crowned with them and for them throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1331C] On the Holy Innocents, from the books of D. Haymo, *On the Memory of Christian Matters*.

When Christ had been born, and, according to the testimony of the evangelist Matthew, the three Magi were approaching him under the guidance of a star, Herod was disturbed, incredibly fearful for the security of his position and kingdom. After the Magi had investigated and, from the prophecies of Micah, revealed the place of the birth, he ordered all boys from two years old and younger to be killed, according to the time he had learned from the Magi, so that he might destroy the Lord along with them. But Joseph, warned by an angel, transferred the child to Egypt, and so forth.

Concerning these Chrysostom says as follows [Note: [Col. 1331D] 1 Serm. 3 in the work *Twenty-Two Sermons*, vol. II]:

“But O blessed glory of the suckling infants, to whom it was granted to dedicate martyrdoms for Christ! At one and the same time they conquer birth and death, entrance and departure, beginning and setting, so that in them, as I have said, at one and the same time Christ might both enter the world by being born and dedicate heaven through martyrdom.

Christ tests new armies; he appoints inexperienced soldiers; when victory has been achieved, he crowns legions of suckling infants. Those who were equal in age become victors for Christ; infants, I say, become strong without combat, victors without battle. Those who did not know how to fight know how to conquer; those who were weak in age become participants in victory. They merit the punishment of martyrs and obtain glory through blood; they exchange temporal death for eternal life.

That age neither feared death nor shuddered at it; for it could not fear what it did not know how to fear. The infant Christ sends infants to heaven, new gifts, presenting to the Father, their Begetter, the firstfruits of the harvest. He displays the future, most fruitful harvest, showing such abundance in the seed. The enemy’s savagery mocked itself and was mocked: it thought that it could disturb God’s plan, Christ’s glory, and the salvation necessary for the world. Yet it bestowed martyrdom upon many infants while seeking to kill the infant Christ.

The enemy confers a benefit while doing harm; he grants a gift when he kills. He would have begrudged them their glory had he loved them. But earthly battles are one thing, heavenly victories another. In Christ’s battle one lives by dying; by falling one rises; victory is won through destruction.”

## IX. On the Conversion of Blessed Paul the Apostle

“Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord” (Acts IX).

Today, dearest brothers, we celebrate the conversion of blessed Paul the apostle, and therefore the reading recounting the history of his conversion is appropriately read today. Three things are shown to us in this reading: how evil he was before his conversion, what his conversion was, and how good he was after his conversion.

First, how evil he was before his conversion is shown when it says: “Saul, still breathing threats.” Other wicked men persecute human beings; Saul, however, persecuted not only human beings but God himself in his disciples. He persecuted him in four ways: in mind, in word, in deed, and by habit—ways by which all wickedness is brought to completion.

In mind, by hating the Lord in his disciples; this is indicated when it says “breathing.” For when we breathe, we send outside the breath conceived within. Paul likewise emitted outward the hatred he had conceived within.

In word, by reviling and threatening the Lord in his own people; this is indicated when it says “threats.”

In deed, by killing; this is indicated when it says “murder.”

By habit, by persecuting with obstinate wickedness; this is suggested when it says: “He went to the high priest and asked him for letters to Damascus, to the synagogues, so that if he found any men or women belonging to this Way, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.”

It is as though he were saying: “Like a wolf accustomed to innocent blood, after killing those who were present, he thirsted for the blood of those who were absent and asked that greater power to rage be granted to him.”

And who, my brothers, would ever have thought that so cruel and bloodthirsty a man could attain such grace? But the Lord, whose mercy is without number, had mercy even on him, to show that he is the one of whom it is written: “He brought out those who were bound in strength, and likewise those who provoke him, and those who dwell in tombs” (Ps. LXVII).

The second part follows, in which it is shown when and how the Lord converted him.

When this happened is shown in the statement: “And as he was travelling, it came to pass that he drew near to Damascus.” It is as though it were said: When he was resolved and already on the way to rage more and more fiercely, the Lord called him and turned both his evil purpose and his path toward good. In this, the greater effect of divine grace becomes apparent.

How he converted him is shown in the statement: “And suddenly a light from heaven shone around him, and immediately, falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him.”

There are three kinds of conversion. The Lord converts some through inward inspiration, as Mary Magdalene; some through outward preaching, as Peter and Andrew; and some through scourging, as the children of Israel, of whom it is written: “When he slew them, they sought him and returned” (Ps. LXXVII).

In this way he converted Paul. First he scourges him; second, he teaches him the reason for the scourging; third, Saul seeks medicine; fourth, medicine is given to him.

When he scourges him, he blinds him and casts him down by causing a light from heaven to shine around him. He weakens him, showing that he possesses divine power, while Saul possesses human frailty.

He blinds him because he could not truly be enlightened unless he were first blinded to his evil knowledge. He casts him down because he could not rise rightly unless he were first cast down from his evil pride. He weakens him because he could not be strong in the right way unless he were first weakened in his evil strength.

For no one can receive divine strength unless he abandons and despises his own strength. Hence Paul himself says: “When I am weak, then I am stronger and powerful” (II Cor. XII).

The Lord teaches him the reason for the scourging when he says: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” It is as though he were saying: “You deserve not only to be scourged, but even to be condemned, because you persecute me, the Savior of the world.”

He does not say, “Why do you persecute my people?” but, “Why do you persecute me?” In this we are shown how great is the union of the head and the members. For just as the head speaks for a trampled foot and says, “Why do you trample me?” and for a beaten back, “Why do you beat me?” so the Lord says that what is inflicted upon his own is inflicted upon him.

At this Saul, trembling with fear, conscious that he had persecuted Jesus and amazed to perceive that the one he had thought a mere human being was God, as though compelled to obey, seeks medicine, saying: “Lord, what do you wish me to do?”

It is as though he were saying: “It is true, Lord, that I persecuted you, but I did not know that you were Christ. From now on, however, I obey you; command whatever you wish.”

The Lord begins to apply medicine to him by commanding him to enter the city and obey what would be told him. The men accompanying him stood astonished. They heard the voice, so that they might bear witness to him, but, since they had not been reborn, they were not worthy to see him. They led him by the hand, and so forth.

“This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. LXXVI).

He who had come to drag away sheep is himself dragged like a sheep; from a wolf he becomes a lamb, from Saul Paul, from a persecutor a preacher.

“And he was there for three days and three nights, neither seeing nor eating nor drinking.” In the manner of the Lord’s three-day burial, he died to sin in order to rise for God.

Although the Lord had already taught him the Gospel inwardly and personally—for he boasts that he received it “not from a man,” nor was he taught it, but “through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (Gal. I)—he nevertheless sends Ananias to enlighten, raise up, and strengthen him. By this he shows how much reverence is owed to ministers, that salvation should be revealed only through them and through the ministries of God.

For as soon as Ananias laid hands on Paul, something like scales fell from his eyes—the scales of serpentine wickedness—and he was enlightened. After he had taken food, both bodily and spiritual, he was strengthened.

In this way the Lord converts many of us to himself every day. For often, while we are resolved upon and engaged in sinning and doing evil, the Lord sends us the scourges of sickness, persecution, and misery in order to convert us to himself, so that those who are unwilling to be corrected through prosperity may at least be corrected through adversity. If we are truly humbled and promise amendment, we are inwardly enlightened by the Lord, raised up, and strengthened.

The third part follows, in which it is shown how good Paul was after his conversion, when it is added: “He was with the disciples who were at Damascus for several days.”

He who had previously been wholly opposed to Christ and his disciples was now wholly with Christ and his disciples. Above all, he loved Christ and his disciples as himself.

How greatly he loved Christ he shows when he says: “For I am certain that neither death nor life, nor things present nor things to come, nor height nor depth, nor any creature will be able to separate me from the love that is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. VIII).

How greatly he loved Christ’s disciples he shows when he says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not inflamed?” (II Cor. II.)

The one who had previously blasphemed and persecuted Christ’s name most fiercely now carried Christ’s name before kings, rulers, and the children of Israel. Hence it is also said here: “And immediately Paul entered the synagogues and preached Jesus to them, showing that he is the Son of God.”

The one who had previously assisted the Jews with all his strength in persecuting Christ now persecuted their unbelief with all his strength. Hence it is also said here: “Saul grew much stronger and confounded the Jews, showing”—that is, affirming—“that this is the Christ.”

The one who had previously stoned and killed those confessing Christ now did not escape being stoned and killed for Christ.

Behold, my brothers, from how perverse a man Paul became how holy a man. In Paul, in Mary Magdalene, and in others of this kind, the Lord wished to demonstrate the depths of his mercy, so that he might offer other sinners an example of repentance and hope of forgiveness. Thus no one should despair, however great the enormity of his crimes, but should rather hasten through repentance toward the hope of forgiveness.

Conversely, in the downfall of Judas and others like him, who fell from a high degree of holiness into the pit of perdition, he wished to demonstrate the depth of his severity, so that he might inspire fear in other righteous people. Thus no one should presume upon however great a height of virtue he may have attained; rather, he should humble himself, fear, and remain watchful, trusting not in himself but in God, through whom he can stand.

Hear this, sinner. Paul is not set before you as an example of sinning, but of repenting. If you followed the sinner, follow the penitent. Do not postpone from day to day. Do not add sin upon sin and say: “The mercy of God is great; he will have mercy on my sins.”

For neither life nor repentance is in the power of human beings, but in the hand of God. Just as he grants the humble and fearful a time for repentance through his mercy, so through his justice he takes it away from the presumptuous and contemptuous.

Therefore, my brothers, whoever among us is righteous should, while in this unstable life, always fear and remain watchful. Whoever is a sinner should not despair, but, while it is permitted, hasten to the remedy of repentance; let him be pierced with remorse, weep, confess, and redeem his sins by good works, so that both kinds of people may deserve to attain eternal life.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## The Life of the Blessed Apostle Paul, by Isidore

Paul, formerly Saul, apostle of the nations and advocate of the Jews, was called by Christ from heaven and cast down upon the earth. He fell with sight and rose up blind; from a persecutor he became a vessel of election, and from a wolf a lamb. Among the apostles he was last in calling, but first in preaching. He was a disciple in the law of Gamaliel and a servant in the Gospel of Christ. His homeland was Judaea, and his lineage was from the tribe of Benjamin.

He was baptized in the second year after the Lord’s ascension, merited the dignity of the apostleship, and, laboring more than all the others, sowed the grace of the word of God much more widely among them. Through his preaching he completed the evangelical teaching, beginning from Jerusalem and extending as far as Illyricum; he also proceeded into Italy and Spain, making the name of Christ known among the peoples of many nations to whom it had not previously been proclaimed.

His miracles are known to have been these: he was caught up and ascended to the third heaven; he condemned the deceiving spirit of Python by commanding it to depart; he restored the spirit of life to a dead young man; he closed the eyes of a magician with blindness; he restored the proper gait to a lame man; he neither felt the bite of a deadly serpent but instead threw it into the fire to be burned; and by prayer he also healed Publius’s father from fevers.

For the love of Christ he also endured many sufferings: above all, Jewish persecutions, the hardships inflicted by the nations, labor, hunger, thirst, cold, and nakedness, day and night; the dangers of the deep and shipwreck, a thousand perils, iron, blows, prison darkness, the tortures of chains, heat, and bonds.

Amid these things he was bound and handed over to the Jews; he was stoned to death by the nations; he was lowered in a basket through a wall; he was beaten with rods; he was confined in prison under punishment; and, after an earthquake had occurred, he was released while bound.

Finally, he was killed by the sword under Nero on the same day on which Peter was crucified. For it was fitting that those who had confessed together should be crowned on one day.

He was buried at Rome on the Ostian Way, thirty-six years after the Lord’s Passion, at the third milestone from the city, toward the eastern region.

## X. On the Same Feast

“Simon Peter said to Jesus: ‘Behold, we have left everything and followed you. What, then, will there be for us?’” (Matt. XIX.) And so forth.

This Gospel reading, dearest brothers, has three parts. First, Peter tells the Lord what he has done for the Lord. Second, he asks what good he will receive from it. Third, the Lord explains what he has asked.

First, Peter shows what he has done for the Lord when he says: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you.”

Although Peter had possessed no wealth in this world, but supported himself as best he could by the craft of fishing, he says that he left not only his boat and nets but everything, because he had abandoned every desire to possess. He indicates that he left as much as he could have desired.

Therefore, the person who leaves everything is the one who leaves even the little he possesses entirely and completely lays aside the desire to possess.

There are two things: leaving desire and leaving possessions. The first is a precept; the second is a counsel. We are bound by precept to leave desire. We are not bound to leave possessions, but are advised to do so. If we do not leave desire, we are condemned. If we do not leave possessions, we are not thereby condemned, but we are impeded in some way.

Some people leave both desire and possessions; some leave desire but not possessions; some leave possessions but not desire.

The apostles and their imitators left both desire and possessions. They completely cast away from themselves the desire to possess and also left behind all necessities. To them the Lord says: “Carry nothing on the road, neither bag, nor sack, nor sandals” (Luke X), and so forth. They ought to have such trust in God that, even if they carry none of these things, they should nevertheless be certain that, through God’s providence, nothing necessary will be lacking to them.

Hence the Lord says: “When I sent you without purse, sack, or sandals, did anything lack for you?” They said: “Nothing” (Luke XXII).

This is plainly directed against those in monasteries who, after leaving everything, return through desire to possessing bags and purses, becoming much worse than secular people, who possess such things lawfully.

The good secular person leaves desire but not possessions: he abandons every illicit desire but does not abandon the possessions necessary for him. For anyone, however, it is damnable to retain superfluous possessions.

Therefore, whoever possesses excess and superfluous goods should distribute them to orphans, widows, and the needy, lest he become guilty because of the poverty of so many souls who might have been sustained from the goods he needlessly keeps for himself.

Hence John the Baptist says: “Whoever has two tunics, let him give one to the person who has none; and whoever has food, let him do likewise” (Luke III).

For according to the evangelist John: “If anyone has the substance of this world and sees his brother suffering need, yet closes his heart to him, how does the love of God remain in him?” (I John III.)

The covetous leave possessions but not desire. Although they cease to possess riches either through extortion or through death, they are still unable at death to distribute them to the poor. Of such people it is written: “They will leave their riches to others, and their graves will be their houses forever” (Ps. XLVIII).

Thus Peter, who had left both desire and all necessities, truly said: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you”—naked, following the naked; unencumbered, following the unencumbered.

It is as though he were saying plainly: “We did not follow you, as some are accustomed to do, for the sake of profit from greater secular riches, since you do not possess them, but solely for your own sake.”

The second part follows, in which Peter asks what good he will obtain from this, when he adds: “What, then, will there be for us?”

It is as though he were saying plainly: “We have followed your command, counsel, and example. What is the reward you promised us when you said: ‘If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have, and come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven’” (Matt. I)?

The inference expressed by the conjunction “therefore” does not arise from an obligation of debt, but rather from a promise. The Lord will not give his chosen ones eternal life because they have earned it, but because he freely promised it to them. As the Apostle says: “Not from works that we have done, but according to his mercy, he saved us” (Tit. III).

Therefore Peter does not say here, “What will you repay us?” but, “What, then, will there be for us?”—as though to say, “What will come to us from your promise?”

He rightly says “what,” because the things we give or leave here for God are not comparable with the good we will receive from him. These things are small, fleeting, and transitory; that good will be—what?—great, enduring, and eternal.

The third part follows, in which the Lord responds to what Peter had asked, saying:

“Amen I say to you, that you who have left everything and followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

By this confirming adverb, “amen,” the Lord confirms that what he promises is true. It is almost an oath of God: “You,” he says, “who have left everything.”

But because many have left everything for empty glory or madness, such as Socrates and Diogenes, who also left necessities, he adds: “and followed me”—which is proper to the faithful.

“In the regeneration,” that is, in the resurrection. It is called regeneration because by our first birth we are regenerated to mortal life, while afterward, by rising again, we will be generated to eternal life.

“When the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also will sit.” It is as though he were saying plainly: “You who have followed not only my command but also my counsel and example will sit with me in a special way.”

The twelve thrones signify here the judicial authority of all the perfect, just as the twelve tribes signify the totality of those who are to be judged. Otherwise neither Paul, who says that he will judge angels, will judge, nor will those belonging to tribes other than the twelve be judged.

The Lord alone will judge by authority, as Lord and Judge. The apostles, however, will judge by agreement, like senators in a council.

Elsewhere the Lord also says that those who are moderately good will judge by comparison with a better deed, saying: “The men of Nineveh will rise in judgment with this generation and condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah” (Matt. XII; Luke II).

“And everyone,” he says, “who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life.”

It is as though he were saying: “Not only will you, who have left everything and followed me, attain eternal glory with me, but also the lesser ones who, together with their desire, will leave for my sake not everything but at least some temporal things. Although they will not be as great as you in the power of judging, they will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life.”

But what is this, my brothers? Here the Lord promises a reward to those who leave father, mother, or wife for his sake, while elsewhere the same Lord commands that father and mother be honored (Matt. XV; Mark VII), and that a wife not depart from her husband (Matt. XIX).

The Lord does not wish the nature or affection of father and mother to be abandoned for his sake, but rather carnal attachments, especially when they hinder us from the way of God.

This often happened in the early Church, when an unbelieving father, mother, or wife held a believer back from the way of God. If someone placed the carnal affection of father, mother, or wife before God, that person was unworthy of God, since he himself says: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. X).

He does not say “for my sake” or “according to me,” but “more than me,” or “against me.”

Therefore, my brothers, when parents hinder us from the way of God, and we cannot win them for God, but they seek to win us for the world, they must be left, lest we perish together with them.

Hence the Lord says: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword. For I have come to separate a son from his father and a daughter-in-law from her mother-in-law” (Matt. X), and so forth.

And Jerome says: “If your father obstructs you at the threshold as you make your way into the desert, go on by trampling over your father.” In this matter, being cruel is a kind of piety.

But if our parents do not hinder us altogether, but only delay us somewhat from the way of God, and we have hope of winning them for God, they should not be abandoned. Rather, through charity and good conduct, they should be drawn to God.

Hence Paul says: “If an unbelieving husband consents to dwell with a believing wife, let the believing wife not depart. For the unbelieving husband is sanctified through the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife through the believing husband” (I Cor. VII).

The person who descends from his perfection for the sake of winning a neighbor’s soul does not become weaker but rather makes progress. Hence Paul also says: “I became weak to the weak, so that I might win them” (I Cor. IX).

When he says that whoever leaves something for his sake will receive a hundredfold, this is not to be understood according to the interpretation of the Jews or heretics, who think that all the temporal things they have left in this life for God will be restored to them a hundredfold in the next life. They do not consider how shameful and inappropriate it would be if someone who had left one wife for Christ were to receive a hundred in return.

Rather, these words signify to us that the things received will be a hundred times more valuable than what was given or left for God.

What another evangelist says—“He will receive a hundredfold here, and in the future eternal life”—makes this clear. Whoever has truly left all temporal things for Christ will receive a hundredfold here in the grace of virtues.

He also receives a hundredfold in temporal things, because, with God adding everything, he has become “as having nothing and possessing everything” (II Cor. VI). For it is a hundred times better to have everything without anxiety and fear than with anxiety and fear.

Therefore, my brothers, since it is necessary either for us to leave all temporal things or for them eventually to leave us—for being abandoned by temporal things brings punishment, not reward—let us leave them before they leave us.

If we cannot leave what is unnecessary, let us at least leave what is superfluous, distributing it to orphans, widows, the sick, captives, and other good uses. Let us also restrain ourselves as far as we can even from necessities, restricting ourselves in food, drink, and other necessities, so that we may live here without desire and fear, “as having nothing and possessing everything,” following the commands, counsels, and examples of Christ.

Thus, even if we cannot judge with the apostles, we may nevertheless deserve to be assigned to eternal life by the apostles, through the generosity of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## XI. On the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary

[Col. 1339B] “Behold, I send my angel, who will prepare the way before my face” (Mal. III), and so forth.

Here, my brothers, the prophet Malachi—or rather, the Lord through him—speaks about the coming of Christ. He sets out five things.

First, God the Father says that he will send an angel before the coming of his Son. Second, he says that the Son himself will come immediately afterward. Third, he says that few will understand his coming. Fourth, he says what his office will be. Fifth, he says what he will do.

First, therefore, God the Father, speaking to his Son, says that he will send a messenger before his coming, saying: “Behold, I send my angel.”

Although God had sent many messengers of his Son’s coming at various times, such as patriarchs and prophets, here he singularly says that he will send one messenger, meaning John the Baptist. Because of the prerogative of his holiness and office, he also calls him his angel.

Just as an earthly king who is about to come to a city sends many heralds ahead as messengers of his arrival, but when he is already about to enter sends ahead a messenger more closely associated with him, so the Lord acted. First he sent patriarchs and prophets, but when he was about to come, he sent ahead a precursor especially dear to him. He also bore witness to him, saying that “among those born of women there has not risen one greater than John the Baptist” (John I).

Like an angel, he was also a messenger of divine mysteries to human beings. He preached the secrets of the Trinity and the Incarnation, indeed even demonstrated them; he sought not his own glory but the Lord’s.

What this angel was to do he shows when he adds: “Who will prepare the way before your face.”

The precursor prepared the way for Christ by preaching and baptizing. But also, by his wondrous birth he went before and foreshadowed Christ’s more wondrous birth; by his holy conduct, Christ’s holier conduct; and by his precious passion, Christ’s more precious passion.

If, however, the reading has “before my face,” the Son is called the Father’s face because through the Son God the Father is known on earth.

Second, he says that the Son will come immediately after the precursor, when he adds: “And immediately he will come,” and so forth.

The conception and birth of the precursor were followed, after half a year, by the conception and birth of Christ.

And who will come? “The Ruler whom you seek, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire.”

Because the Fathers of the Old Testament were oppressed by the harsh dominion of the devil and evil rulers, they sought Christ’s gentle yoke. They were unable to bear the burden of the Old Testament and the severity of its ministers; they desired the angel of the New Testament.

This is what the old man Simeon, who had received the promise that he would not die before seeing Christ (Luke II), said daily in his prayers: “When will he come? When will he be born? When will I see him?”

This same desire of the ancient Fathers is signified by the seven antiphons that begin with the desiderative adverb “O,” as follows: “O Wisdom,” “O Adonai,” and so forth.

And where will he come? “To his holy temple,” that is, to the womb of the blessed Virgin, which was, antonomastically, holy—that is, sanctified.

Or also to the material temple in Jerusalem, in which on this day he was presented by his parents with offerings.

Or certainly to the temple, that is, to the holy Church, which he came to signify and join to himself.

And lest you despair because of the delay, “behold, he comes,” says the Lord of hosts.

Third, he says that few will understand Christ’s coming, when he adds: “And who will be able to consider the day of his coming? And who will stand to see him?”

As though he were saying: Few.

For there were few—Simeon and Anna and a few spiritual men—who understood through the Spirit when he was going to come. And there were few of his disciples who understood through the Spirit that the Son of God had come in the flesh they saw.

He appropriately says “will stand,” because although many saw Christ with bodily eyes, they did not stand in order to see him. Through unbelief they fell away from the very thing by which they ought to have progressed.

Fourth, he says what his office would be when he adds: “Behold, he is like a refiner’s fire and like fullers’ herb.” As if he were saying: His office will be to cleanse and purify the Church. For at his first coming he came to justify the ungodly through mercy; at his second he will come to condemn the ungodly through justice. Yet he does not say, “Behold, he is like a refiner and like a fuller,” because Christ is not merely the minister of purification and cleansing, as other teachers are, but also their cause.

Moreover, fire does six things: it warms, melts, burns, illuminates, strengthens, and kindles. Christ likewise, coming into this world, warmed the coldness of human beings, melted the hardness of their hearts, burned away the rust of their sins, illuminated their foolishness, strengthened their weakness, and also kindled the torpor of their hearts. Fullers’ herb likewise does two things: it removes stains from cloth and makes it white. Christ similarly removes the stains of souls and makes them white. Hence the Prophet says to him: “You will sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you will wash me, and I shall become whiter than snow” (Psalm 50 [51]).

There are two kinds of people. Some are hard-hearted and cruel; these are signified by rusty metals. Others are gentle in spirit and yielding; these are signified by filthy garments. But Christ, looking upon both through his mercy, becomes for the former a refining fire and for the latter fullers’ herb.

We signify both, dearest brothers, in today’s solemnity: today we carry lighted candles, and we are made white in white garments.

Fifth, what he will do is shown when it is added: “And he will sit refining and cleansing silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi.” By silver, which is resonant and suitable for the vessels of the altar, preachers and ministers of the Church are signified. The same is also signified by the sons of Levi, who had been appointed to the Lord’s ministry. For their correction and purification Christ sat, as a teacher, and devoted himself to the task.

First he purified and illuminated his apostles and disciples with the fire of the Holy Spirit, so that through their ministry the others too might be purified and illuminated. “And he will refine them,” he says, “like gold and like silver”—that is, he will make them illustrious through wisdom and eloquence, by which preaching is administered. “And they will be offering sacrifices to the Lord in righteousness”: attributing every good thing to God and only evil things to themselves, sacrificing not what belongs to others but themselves to God for God’s sake. For this is to sacrifice a sacrifice of righteousness.

Would that that divine fire might purify, illuminate, and kindle us also, unworthy sinners and priests, so that we might deserve to sacrifice to him the sacrifice of righteousness worthily!

“And the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem,” he says, “will please God”—that is, the sacrifice of the primitive Church formed from the Jews—“as in the days of old,” that is, of the first days, understood; “and as in ancient years,” that is, like the sacrifice of Abel, Abraham, Melchizedek, and the other ancient Fathers, whose sacrifice certainly pleased God—indeed, it pleased him even more than theirs, because they offered a figure, whereas these have offered the true Lamb and the true bread.

In the moral sense, just as God the Father sent his angel beforehand, namely John the Baptist, to prepare the way for his Son coming in the flesh, so each day he sends his angels, who prepare a way for that same Son when he comes invisibly to human hearts. By “angels” I mean priests and preachers, who first preach the word of God to their hearers, so that afterward the Son himself may come to their hearts. For it is written: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 2).

And not only we, but any one of you, my brothers, who announces the word of salvation to his neighbor, can be called an angel of the Lord. Thus, when the preacher’s word sounds outwardly in the ear and God works invisibly within, the Word of the Father immediately comes through faith into the heart and sanctifies it as a temple for himself. “The temple of God,” says the Apostle, “is holy, and that is what you are” (1 Corinthians 3).

But who will be able to consider or understand the day or hour of his coming to the heart? As if he were saying: No one. For he alone knows how he changes human minds for the better, or how he comes to them, or sanctifies them. For it is written: “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes” (John 3).

Yet this we know: he is like a refining fire and like fullers’ herb. That is, he has the authority to soften minds through compunction and to cleanse them through baptism or penance. Hence Job says: “Who can make clean what has been conceived from unclean seed? Is it not you, who alone are?” (Job 14.)

“And he will sit,” he says, “refining and cleansing silver.” As if he were saying: He does not correct those in whom God dwells for an hour, but only those in whom he sits and remains; these he makes pure silver and vessels of election.

“And he will purify the sons of Levi”—that is, those who seemed to have been added to the number of the rejected: by purifying them, he will add them to the number of his chosen ministers, and make them offer sacrifices in righteousness, so that righteousness may be present in the offerer, in what is offered, and in the intention.

“And the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem will please God.” As if he were saying: Because they will sacrifice in true confession and peace, they will please God like the sacrifices of the ancient saints.

Let us cry out, therefore, my brothers, let us cry out with our whole heart to that holy purifier of souls, so that he himself may soften the hardness of our souls, boil away the rust of our sins, clothe us in the whiteness of his virtues, and kindle us to love and long for him. Thus, regarding all passing things as dung (Philippians 3), may we hasten toward him with our whole desire, offer ourselves to him as a sacrifice of sweetness, and deserve to be received by him—through the intercession of the Mother of God, who on this day deserved to offer her Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## XII. Likewise, on the Same Feast

“After the days of Mary’s purification were completed according to the law of Moses” [Col. 1342C] (Luke 2), etc.

Today, dearest brothers, we celebrate the purification of the blessed Virgin and Mother of the Lord. Therefore the Gospel, recounting her history, is read today in the holy Church and sets before us four apparent paradoxes: that she who is pure is purified; that God is offered; that the Redeemer is redeemed; and that an old man, now about to die, rejoices.

Why, my brothers, did the Lord will that his mother, though pure and not needing purification, should be purified; that he, though God, should be offered; and that he, though Redeemer, should be redeemed? For three reasons: that he might show that he did not abolish but fulfill the law (Matthew 5); that in every respect he might set before us an example of humility; and that, by paying for us what was not owed, he might redeem us debtors from our debts.

First, therefore, the Evangelist sets before us the purification of the most pure Virgin when he says: “After the days of Mary’s purification were completed according to the law of Moses”—understand, she did what she was required to do in undergoing purification. For the law commanded that a woman who, having received male seed, bore a male child should be regarded as unclean for seven days; that the child should be circumcised on the eighth day; and that thereafter, for another thirty-three days, she should be kept from entering the Temple. When these days had elapsed, on the fortieth day she was to offer the child at the Temple with victims, namely a lamb and a turtledove or pigeon. But if she bore a female child, she was unclean for fourteen days, and for another sixty-six days was kept from entering the Temple, until on the eightieth day she came to the Temple with victims (Deuteronomy 12).

Let us therefore examine the words of the law carefully, first according to the letter. It says that a woman who, having received seed, bore a male child was unclean for seven days. But it does not say that she who gave birth without seed was unclean or subject to the aforesaid purification. It is therefore clear that the blessed Virgin, who conceived without seed by the Holy Spirit, since she was not unclean, had no need of purification.

Therefore, my brothers, if the mother of purity did not refuse to undergo the purification of the law, what ought we impure and ungodly people to do, who need purification every day? The mother of cleanness and holiness did not shrink from cleansing; and do you, adulterer or adulteress, unclean man or unclean woman, flee from being cleansed through the purification of discipline and penance?

But in the moral sense, the faithful soul which, having received the seed of God’s Word, inwardly conceives through good will the fruit of a manly and holy life [Col. 1343B], and begins outwardly to give birth through good works, ought not immediately to consider itself clean, but rather unclean. For who, however righteous, will boast that he has a clean heart? It should therefore consider itself unclean in God’s sight, especially while its conversion is still new and unformed. On the eighth day—that is, in faith and for the faith of the resurrection—it ought to circumcise itself from its old and vain custom. Moreover, for forty days—that is, throughout the whole course of this present life—it ought to purify itself from past sins through penance and discipline, and wash itself with tears born partly from the remembrance of sins and partly from the desire for the heavenly homeland, until, this present life having ended, it deserves to enter the Temple of the heavenly homeland with its fruit, with the sacrament of the spotless Lamb, the chastity of the turtledove, and the innocence of the dove.

But the soul which conceives a female—that is, a soft will—and by its works gives birth to a soft life, needs purification twice as great as the other. It is not worthily purified even through forty days, that is, through this whole present life. Rather, after death it is purified in purgatorial places, until on the eightieth day—that is, at the resurrection—being fully purified, it is admitted to the Temple of eternal blessedness.

Second, he sets before us that God, though he is every offering, is offered, when he adds: “They took Jesus to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord: Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” [Col. 1343D]. Because the Lord had preserved the firstborn of the Hebrews in Egypt from the smiting angel, he willed that their firstborn thereafter should be consecrated and offered. In accordance with this institution, our Lord Jesus willed to offer himself to God the Father, namely that through the victim of his body he might reconcile us to God.

Otherwise, by what means could a human being be reconciled to God? If a human being offered himself to God the Father, being guilty, he would provoke him rather than appease him. If he offered what was his own, such as a lamb, goat, or something similar, the offering would be inferior and insufficient to satisfy for the beloved. If an angel offered himself for a human being, the offering would be alien to the human being. Therefore the Word was made flesh (John 1), so that, as a man pleasing to God in every respect, offered for humankind, he might reconcile humankind to God; as the Father himself testified when he declared to him: “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” [Col. 1344A] (Matthew 3; 17; Mark 1).

Therefore, brothers, whenever we sin or offend God, let us seek reconciliation not through ourselves but through Christ, through whom alone prayers, offerings, and sacrifices can be acceptable before God the Father. Hence every prayer is made and concluded through our Lord Jesus Christ.

Third, he sets before us that the Redeemer of the world is redeemed, when it is added: “And to give a sacrifice according to what is written in the law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.” This was the offering of the poor, who could not provide a lamb. For the Lord deigned to become poor for us; he deigned to be redeemed for us. The offering was indeed given which was given for those conceived and born in sin, for the Lord who was neither conceived nor born in sin.
