He was also redeemed according to the written provision that a firstborn not of the tribe of Levi was redeemed with five silver shekels (Leviticus 27).

For he willed to commend to us a life of humility both by example and by word. By example: although he was rich in all things, he was born poor and willed to become poor for us. Although he was the Redeemer of the world, he willed to be redeemed; although he was king of all, he willed that tribute should be paid for him; although he was Lord of all, he willed to be subject to human beings. Hence he himself says: “I came not to be served but to serve” [Col. 1344B] (Matthew 20). By word: to disciples still carnal and disputing about precedence, he said: “Let the greater among you become as the younger, and the leader as one who serves” (Luke 22), teaching them to contend only in humility.

In this our pride is rebuked: we prefer to rule rather than to be subject; we flee human lordship but do not flee the lordship of vices; we flee paying tribute to human beings as though it were a plague, but do not shudder at paying tribute to the devil; we flee monetary losses and exactions as though they were the gravest crime, yet do not fear the loss of innocence. If some layperson takes money from us, we exclude him from the Church, forbid divine things to the faithful, and withdraw from our God the service due to him. Because money is taken from us, we ourselves take away from God his divine ministries [Col. 1344D]. Why do this, except because we reject God’s way—poverty and humility—and set money above God and our soul? Against such people the Apostle speaks: “Indeed, it is altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another. Why do you not rather suffer wrong?” (1 Corinthians 6).

Fourth, the Evangelist also introduces the old prophet, now about to die, who, having seen what he desired, asks to be dismissed to death. He is described as one worthy to bear witness to God. For he was righteous, rendering to each his due; devout, not with servile but filial fear, because he feared God with love and loved him with fear; awaiting the Redeemer not doubtfully but with certainty. And the Holy Spirit, with his seven gifts, was in him. By praying and desiring, he had merited to receive from the Holy Spirit the answer that he would not see death until he saw Christ. And he came into the Temple not by chance but enlightened by the Spirit; and in that same Spirit he understood him to be Christ and received him into his arms [Col. 1345A].

Who can weigh, my brothers, how great was the joy of this old man when he saw with his eyes, lifted in his arms, and bore exultantly his Redeemer and the Redeemer of the world, whom he had so long desired, longed for, and awaited? Since he could neither express nor wholly conceal the greatness of his joy, bursting into thanksgiving, he blessed God for his immense benefits and said: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace.” As though he plainly said: Now, Lord, since what you promised has been fulfilled, I ask to be dismissed in peace, so that, after the greatness of this joy, I may not feel death.

And why do you rejoice so greatly? “Because my eyes have seen your salvation.” The outer eyes saw the outer flesh; the inner eyes, the inner divinity. Their union is your salvation and ours: yours, because you give it; ours, because we receive and experience the benefit. For this salvation is not private but common to all. Hence it follows: “Which you have prepared before the face of all peoples, a light for the revelation of the Gentiles,” hitherto blind, “and for the glory of your people Israel,” from whom Christ was born according to the flesh.

And because today that holy old man was so enlightened by the Holy Spirit that he recognized and bore in his arms the light of the whole world, the custom arose in the holy Church that today we all bear lighted candles in our hands as though Christ. For the fire signifies divinity; the wax, the work of the virgin bee, signifies the humanity taken from the Virgin [Col. 1345C].

Therefore, brothers, let us seek by every means the purification of our souls; let us redeem our sins by generous almsgiving; let us offer God in holocaust the chastity of the turtledove and the innocence of the dove. And as each bird gives a groan instead of song, while we are in this valley of tears let us always have groaning; and, after the manner of holy Simeon, let us hunger and thirst for righteousness. Let us desire peace and to see good days, so that, enlightened by God’s visitation and filled with the joy of the Holy Spirit, full of days and rejoicing, we may be dismissed in peace [Col. 1345D] to death, to live forever, through Christ our Lord, to whom be honor and glory throughout the endless ages of ages. Amen.

## Annotation

Observe the Church’s very ancient custom by which, on the day of the Purification of the blessed Virgin Mary, candles of blessed wax are carried in the hands of the faithful. Cyril, archbishop of Jerusalem, also asserts this in his sermon on the meeting of our Lord Jesus Christ and on Simeon, who received God. Therefore, he says:

“Come, then, all you who love Christ and God; let us joyfully and purely meet the Lord—not legally, but spiritually; not filling our bellies with delicacies, but exulting in spirit; not making ourselves drunk with wine, but burning with the Spirit. Joyfully let us adorn our lamps today. As children of light, let us offer wax to Christ, the true light. Since the light for the revelation of the nations has appeared to the world, let us therefore shine forth from the light, brighter than snow. Made whiter than milk, illuminated above sapphire, soaring heavenward like spotless columns, let us go forth in the clouds to meet God.

Today, beloved, let us complete the course of the feast forever; let us form choirs with the angels, be illuminated with the shepherds, adore with the orthodox, celebrate the feast with Bethlehem, and embrace Christ in our arms with Simeon, so that we may be within Christ’s eternal blessings through the grace, mercy, and clemency of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power throughout the ages of ages.”

## XIII. On the Chair of Saint Peter

“Peter, apostle of Jesus Christ, to the chosen resident aliens of the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in the sanctification of the Spirit, for obedience and sprinkling with the blood of Jesus Christ: may grace and peace be multiplied to you,” and so forth.

My brothers, the blessed apostle Peter writes this epistle to disciples who, coming from various nations, had been converted to faith in Jesus Christ and, during the persecution that arose in the Church of Jerusalem when Stephen was stoned, had been scattered through different regions. But the blessed Peter, leaving Jerusalem as one who was steadfast and did not know how to yield to persecution, and as a good shepherd who cared even for those who were absent, wrote them an epistle of consolation and encouragement.

First, he greets them; second, he blesses God for their progress; third, he exhorts them to endure passions and tribulations as beneficial things.

But what the blessed apostle Peter then said to them, I now say to you also, brothers, whatever kind of man I may be who hold the office and apostleship of Peter—for I have been sent to evangelize you. I too must be Peter, that is, steadfast. For amid persecutions and temptations a pastor must be steadfast and strong, so that by word and example he may strengthen those who are imperfect.

You too, my brothers, are chosen—provided that in your works you hold fast to what you are by vocation, provided that you are Christians in truth as well as in name. You are also resident aliens in this world, if, understanding that you have no enduring city here, you hasten with your whole desire toward your eternal homeland; if, groaning amid the miseries of this exile, you sigh for your homeland and say with the Prophet: “Alas for me, that my sojourning has been prolonged!” (Psalm 119 [120].) And also: “I am a resident alien with you and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were” (Psalm 38 [39].)

You are also placed in dispersion, because you are few among innumerable wicked people, just as a few grains are mixed among much chaff. One of the elect lies hidden in Pontus, another in Cappadocia, another in Galatia, another in Asia, another in Spain, another in Britain, another here, and another there. God, who alone knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2), will separate them from the wicked at the end of the ages and gather them together as one. For, as John testifies, Christ died in order to gather into one the children of God who were scattered (John 11).

You were chosen not according to your merits or those of your parents, but according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, who by his grace alone predestined you from eternity. For what purpose? “For the sanctification of the Spirit,” namely so that in baptism he might cleanse you through the Holy Spirit from all your sins; “and for obedience,” so that, cleansed from sins, you would not return to your vomit, but thereafter would obey God’s commandments; “and for the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ,” so that you might share in Christ’s passion, through which alone the kingdom of heaven is opened to you and heavenly things are joined to earthly things.

This, my brothers, is the order of our salvation. First, before we existed, we were freely predestined by God for life; once born, we are sanctified through baptism; then, through obedience, we lead a life pleasing to God; and finally, through Christ’s passion, we enter through the gate of the kingdom.

What Peter then wished for his people, I now wish for you, brothers: “May grace and peace be multiplied to you.” I do not wish you riches, honors, or the glories of this age, which are the cause of perdition for many. Rather, I wish you an increase of graces: faith, hope, charity, wisdom, justice, fortitude, temperance, and the other virtues that make people holy and friends of God and lead them to eternal life.

I also wish you peace: peace with God, by obeying him; peace with yourselves, by keeping yourselves pure; and peace with your neighbors, by loving them in God. For this peace makes people children of God. It is written: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matthew 5).

The second part follows, in which Peter blesses God for the benefits he had conferred upon his disciples, saying: “Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ”—let it be understood, “blessed be.” But how, my brothers, do we wish a blessing upon God, from whom all blessing comes and from whom comes everyone who is blessed? Or how can we bless God, when we cannot be blessed unless we are blessed by God?

But the Creator blesses creation in one way, creation blesses the Creator in another, and one creature blesses another creature in yet another way. The Creator blesses creation by sanctifying it. A creature is said to bless the Creator by giving him thanks. One creature also blesses another by wishing divine blessing upon it. We therefore bless God, my brothers, when we give him thanks for his benefits.

Hence he adds: “Who regenerated you unto a living hope”—that is, although you were generated from Adam for death, he regenerated you through baptism unto a living hope, that is, the hope of eternal life. Or certainly he calls it a living hope because it works well through charity. For hope, like faith, is dead without works (Galatians 5), and does not bring forth the fruit of eternity. This is contrary to those who, although they live wickedly, presume that they will be saved.

But did he regenerate us unto a living hope because of our merits or those of our parents? Certainly not, but “according to his great mercy.” And how? “Through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.” His resurrection is not only the cause of our regeneration and cleansing, but also the proof and cause of our future resurrection. For just as he died for us so that we would not fear dying for him, so he rose for us so that we might hope to rise through him.

And where is that hope? In you, who are guarded not by your own strength but by the power of God. And how do you possess that hope? Through faith. For you would not hope unless you believed. And toward what does that hope tend? Toward the inheritance of eternal blessedness, from which we had been disinherited through the sin of the first Adam and in which we are now made heirs through the new Adam.

I call it an inheritance that is incorruptible, subject neither to old age, sickness, nor any defect; undefiled, untouched by sin, vice, or any stain; and unfading, unaffected by change or deterioration. I call it an inheritance preserved in heaven for those who deserve to possess it. And where is it preserved? In heaven: “where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal” (Matthew 6).

Toward this inheritance he prepares those who advance toward the eternal salvation of soul and body, to be revealed at the last time, in which you will rejoice. As John says: “We are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. When he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

And what is sweeter, what is more glorious, my brothers, than to be co-heirs with the Son of God in eternal blessedness and glory, and to rejoice with him forever? For the sake of this inheritance, let us despise—indeed, let us sell—all temporal inheritances, my brothers, because those who love these cannot attain the eternal one.

The third part follows, in which Peter exhorts us to endure sufferings, adding: “If now for a little while it is necessary for you to be saddened by various trials.” He rightly says “it is necessary,” because grain is not stored in the granary unless it has first been threshed, and just as gold is not placed in the treasury unless it has first been tested, so the just person is not received into the kingdom of heaven unless first tested through tribulations.

He also rightly says “to be saddened,” because although, as the Apostle says, the just rejoice in tribulations in the hope of the glory of the children of God (Romans 5), the flesh amid the bitterness of tribulations cannot help being saddened. Hence the Lord says: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26; Luke 22).

He also rightly says “by various trials,” because just as the variety of bodily members requires a variety of medicines, so the variety of dispositions requires a variety of tribulations.

He rightly says “for a little while,” because, in comparison with eternal blessedness, whatever we suffer in this age appears little and momentary. Hence the Apostle says: “I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8).

He shows, moreover, what benefit tribulations confer upon us when he adds: “So that the testing of your faith”—that is, your tested faith—“may be found much more precious than gold, which is tested by fire.”

The first benefit of tribulations is that here they test and purify. They test because, just as a horse is tested in the racecourse—or a rider in battle—so faith is tested in tribulations. They purify because, just as fire makes gold completely pure, so tribulation purifies the just person.

The second benefit is the eternal reward. Hence he adds: “May it be found unto praise, glory, and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ our Lord.” What greater praise, my brothers, can come to us than to be praised by God when he says: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matthew 25), because you did this and that for my sake? What greater glory can there be than when God clothes us with the glory of immortality, makes us brighter than the sun, and introduces us into the company of the angels, saying: “Receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world”? What greater honor can there be than to be joined to angels, patriarchs, prophets, and apostles—to be there, indeed, where the only-begotten Son of God is—and not merely to be called, but also to be and to appear as children of God?

These things will take place “at the revelation of Jesus Christ,” that is, at the end of the world, when Jesus Christ, who is now hidden and is despised or ignored by many, will come to judgment with great power, splendor, and majesty. He will reveal his power, reveal the secrets of our hearts, and reveal how great a glory his lovers have deserved and how great a punishment those who despise him have deserved.

Therefore, so that our crimes, my brothers, may not then be revealed to our shame, let us now reveal them through confession, washing them away with tears and redeeming them with almsgiving, despising all passing things, and hastening with our whole desire toward heavenly things. May God and our Lord lead us to them, to whom be honor and glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1349C] **The Life of the Lord Peter, by Dorotheus.**

[Note: [Col. 1349D] Epiphanius, Book I, Tome II, *Against Heresies*.] Peter, chief of the apostles, as he seems to indicate in his epistles, preached the Gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Bithynia, and finally at Rome (1 Peter 1). There, afterward, under King Nero, he was crucified head downward on the third day before the Kalends of July—for he himself wished to suffer in this manner—and was buried there.

## XIV. On the Feast of Saint Matthias
“Peter stood up in the midst of the brothers and said” (now the gathering of persons was about one hundred and twenty) (Acts 1), and so forth.

Today, my brothers, we celebrate the feast of the apostle Saint Matthias, who by divine election was substituted in the place of Judas the betrayer, lest the sacrament of the number twelve should fall short of its perfection. Hence it is that the reading explaining his election is recited today in the holy Church. It has four parts. First, Peter rises among the brothers; second, he shows that Judas’s rejection and the substitution of another had been foretold by the Holy Spirit; third, he shows that one of the brothers ought to be substituted for him; fourth, it is shown how the substitute was chosen.

He therefore says: “Peter stood up in the midst of the brothers.” He says three things: “stood up,” “in the midst,” and “of the brothers.” These three things are indeed to be sought in a true shepherd.

He stood above the others, not only in rank but also in life and in the height of his virtues, in accordance with the saying: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion” (Isa. 40). Yet he did not therefore despise the others as though they were lesser and subject— as some do—but loved them as equals and brothers. Hence he himself says: “Not as domineering over the clergy, but becoming examples of the flock from the heart” (1 Pet. 5).

Again, he stood among the brothers in such a way that he was also in their midst through equity. For what is in the middle stands equally in relation to the things surrounding it. Peter likewise stood equally toward everyone. He did not, as some do, place one person above another because of blood relationship, temporal profit, or some temporal interest; rather, in exercising justice, in ordination, and in election, he observed equity and uprightness.

Therefore, whoever is a shepherd should, following Peter’s example, rise above others through the loftiness of his life; through charity, regard those who are lesser as brothers and his equals; and through the uprightness of equity hold the middle place.

“Now the gathering of persons was about one hundred and twenty.” This number is obtained by multiplying twelve by ten. It shows that the assembly of the disciples was complete for the undertaking. Yet the word “about” is added because the number, diminished by Judas’s fall, still had to be completed.

They are all said to have been together—not only in place, but also in faith, love, and fellowship. Hence it is said of them: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and everything was held in common among them” (Acts 2).

The second part follows, in which Peter shows that Judas’s rejection and the substitution of another had been foretold by the Holy Spirit, saying: “Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David concerning Judas.”

Although he ought then to have appended the Scripture, he inserts the cause of Judas’s rejection, saying: “He was the leader of those who seized Jesus”—that is, he was the leader of the betrayal—“and he was numbered among us and received a share in this ministry.” It is as though he were saying: He was with us in number, not in merit; in calling, not in election; in ministry, not in virtue.

“And he acquired”—that is, caused to be acquired—“the field of iniquity,” the price of Judas’s wicked betrayal having been handed over to the Jews. Or “he acquired” it because perhaps he was buried there. “And, hanging, he burst open in the middle, and all his entrails were poured out.”

Although he had sinned most grievously by betraying Christ, he sinned more grievously still by despairing. His throat, from which the voice of betrayal had emerged, was strangled by the noose. His belly and entrails, which had conceived the betrayal, were poured out.

He died neither on the earth nor in heaven, but in the air, because, unworthy of the fellowship of human beings and angels, he was to be added to the powers of the air. For it is written in the Book of Psalms: “Let his dwelling become desolate” (before the appointed time), because the wicked “shall not halve their days” (Ps. 54).

“And let another receive his episcopate.” The talent entrusted to him, which he used badly, will be taken away from him and given to another who will use it well (Matt. 25).

Many, my brothers, curse today the crime of Judas, who betrayed the Lord, yet they themselves fall into a similar crime. Whoever speaks the truth for a price or administers justice for a payment sells God, who is truth and justice. Whoever sells the laying on of hands, ecclesiastical administration, or any sacrament of Christ sells Christ himself, insofar as it lies within him.

Such people tighten a noose around their own necks. By taking from themselves, through the net of their iniquities, the voice and office of preaching, they hang and kill themselves. By living badly, they suspend themselves from the office that they administer unworthily, and they kill themselves spiritually.

Their bellies burst and their entrails are poured out because their counsel is scattered—that is, all their thoughts perish. Their days are few because they have been completed in evil and not in good. Their dwelling becomes desolate, and another receives their episcopate, because their manner of life perishes as it deserved to do, and another takes up the talent that they administered badly.

The wicked Jews who, when Judas said, “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood,” answered, “What is that to us? You see to it” (Matt. 27), have their counterparts in those who consider guilty of simony the persons who sold themselves to them through simony, but not themselves, who paid the money. But condemnation envelops both buyers and sellers of ecclesiastical things, except that those who were superior in rank and knowledge will precede the others in punishment.

As for what the Jews said—“Let us not put the thirty pieces of silver into the treasury, because it is the price of blood,” yet they bought with them a field for the burial of strangers (ibid.)—some today imitate them. They are afraid to offer to God money that has been acquired wickedly, yet they contribute it as alms or devote it to other uses, failing to understand that what was not lawful to offer was not lawful either to give away or to retain for themselves.

The third part follows, in which Peter shows from whom, that is, for what purpose, the substitution was to be made, when he adds:

“Therefore, from these men who have been gathered with us throughout the whole time in which the Lord Jesus entered and went out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us, one of these must become with us a witness of his resurrection.”

“From these,” he says, “who have been with us.” The election must be made from the brothers of the same congregation, if someone worthy can be found there. This stands clearly against those who, out of envy, despise their good brothers and choose outsiders.

He says “men,” because men should be chosen as pastors both in age and in character. Hence they are called presbyters—that is, elders. This stands clearly against those who choose as pastors people who are young either in age or in character, although our Lord Jesus Christ, the very Wisdom of the Father, did not wish to preach openly until he was thirty years old; the heavens were not opened to the prophet Ezekiel until he was thirty; and the canons prohibit ordaining anyone to the priesthood who is not thirty.

He also says, “from those who have been with you throughout the whole time in which the Lord Jesus entered and went out among you, beginning from the baptism of John,” and so forth. Only those should be chosen as pastors who have been trained for a long time in the school of the sacred Scriptures and in the ordering of morals.

This stands clearly against those who choose inexperienced and novice men as pastors, although the Apostle commands that a bishop who is to be ordained must not be a recent convert, lest, being puffed up, he fall into the devil’s ruin.

He also says, “to become with us a witness of the resurrection.” Here he shows for what purpose someone ought to be chosen as a priest or pastor: namely, so that he may always testify to Christ’s resurrection—not only by the testimony of preaching, but also by the testimony of a good life and good works. He should preach, live, and act in such a way as to show that he truly believes in Christ’s resurrection and truly hopes for his own.

This clearly condemns us unworthy priests who, although we preach Christ’s resurrection and our own with words, deny it in our conduct and deeds. When we love the present life so excessively that, for its sake, we desire beyond measure and do many things that are unlawful and contrary to the future life, we show that we neither believe nor hope for the resurrection or the life to come. Thus we also cause those of lesser rank to doubt the resurrection and say: “If our pastors, who are wise, hoped for the resurrection, they would never live in this way; they would never commit such deeds. Since they do not await the future life, they refer everything to the present.”

Their ruin—which I cannot mention without grieving—is attributed to us.

The fourth part follows, in which he shows how Matthias was substituted, when it is said:

“And they chose two: Joseph, who was called Barsabbas, who was surnamed Justus, and Matthias.”

It is as though he were saying: They were not outsiders; they themselves chose them. Nor did one or two make the choice, but the community did. It was not outsiders but the brothers themselves—those who, through daily association, knew their fellow brothers more familiarly—who ought to choose.

This stands clearly against rulers or bishops who presume to choose people whose lives they do not know. Nor should one or two choose for themselves someone beloved or useful, unless perhaps all together freely entrust a common election to some honorable person who is not suspect to them.

The apostles chose two whom, according to their own judgment, they preferred to the others. One of them is commended by the surname “Justus”; for the other, it is enough by way of commendation that he was chosen by the Lord. But because they did not know which of the two ought to be preferred to the other, they fled to prayer and consulted God, saying:

“You, Lord, who know the hearts of human beings, show which one you have chosen from these two, to receive a share in this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas transgressed so that he might go to his own place.”

In this they gave us an example: when we are about to conduct an election, we should pray to God together with all the brothers, so that he alone, who knows the hearts of human beings, may choose and reveal the person whom he knows to be more worthy of his ministry.

“And they gave them lots, and the lot fell upon Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.”

From this some people derive authority to cast lots for themselves. Yet they should know that the privileges of a few do not establish a general law. If they nevertheless wish to use lots, they should do what the apostles did, and do so only in necessary and doubtful cases. Otherwise they sin gravely and do not deserve to be given certainty by the Lord.

But the apostles, who gave lots in a matter so necessary and doubtful, and did so with prayer, were heard by the Lord. For Matthias was chosen by God, who directed the lot, and he was numbered with the other apostles in merit as well as in number, in election as well as by lot, in authority as well as in ministry, both in heaven and on earth.

Thus, on this day, having been taken from the earth, he was glorified in heaven with the other apostles, and with those same apostles he will judge the world. May his merit and intercession cause us to be adjudged to eternal life, through the generosity of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## Life of the Blessed Matthias, by Dorotheus

[Note: [Col. 1353D] Eusebius, Book 2, chapter 1, *Ecclesiastical History*.]

Matthias, having been one of the seventy disciples, was afterward numbered as the twelfth among the eleven apostles, in the place of Judas the betrayer (Acts 1). He preached the Gospel to all the barbarians and cannibals in the interior of Ethiopia, where Hyssus is a harbor of the sea and the river Phasis is located. He died at Sebastopolis and was buried there near the temple of the Sun.

## XV. On the Annunciation of Blessed Mary

“A shoot shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. 11), and so forth.

In these words, dearest brothers, the prophet Isaiah once foretold that Christ would come in the flesh. He showed three things: from where Christ would originate, with what gifts he would be illuminated by the Holy Spirit, and what he would be toward others.

First, he shows from where Christ would originate when he says: “A shoot shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root.”

Figuratively, my brothers, he calls the root the seed of Jesse, the father of David; the shoot, the Blessed Virgin; and the flower, Christ.

The root lies low and hidden in the earth, yet from it a great tree rises. So the stock of Jesse was lowly and hidden, because Jesse was a commoner—that is, a man of no renown—yet from him a royal line was born. And just as no one would know where the root was if it were not for the tree rising from it, so there would be no knowledge of Jesse except through the royal line proceeding from him.

A shoot, moreover, is smooth, green, straight, and round. So the Blessed Virgin was smooth, free from every knot of vice; green with every verdure of virtue; straight in the uprightness of her intention; and round in the roundness of perfection.

In a flower there are three things: beauty, fragrance, and the hope of fruit. In Christ also there was the beauty of every virtue. Hence it is written of him: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Ps. 44).

In him also was the fragrance of every good virtue. Hence it is written of him: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 27). And in the Gospel we read that “his reputation spread through the whole region” (Matt. 4).

In him also was and is the hope of eternal fruit. Hence he is called by the prophets “the Expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49) and “the Desired One of all the nations” (Hag. 2).

At that time he is called a flower; now he is called fruit. For he who is a flower for us on the way will be fruit in our homeland. Now, through the beauty of his virtues and the fragrance of his works and conduct, he delights and attracts us, and through the hope of the sweetness enjoyed by the saints in their homeland he draws us to himself. In the future, through the taste of his ineffable sweetness, he will satisfy us forever.

If we wish, my brothers, to be satisfied forever with that ineffable sweetness, let us admire him in his beauty, run after him in his fragrance, and be drawn by hope, praying with the bride and saying: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song 1).

Appropriately he says, “And a flower shall rise from his root,” because Christ was conceived not from a grafted shoot but from the Virgin’s flesh alone, without the work of a man.

He also appropriately says “shall rise,” because Christ, by the merit of humility, rose to the height of virtue. He rose not only to be the head of the whole Church, but also above the cherubim and seraphim and above the heavens of heavens, even to equality with the Father, leaving us an example so that we might deserve to ascend to the heights of heaven.

He shows with what gifts Christ would be illuminated by the Holy Spirit when he adds: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him.”

For not only the Holy Spirit but the whole Trinity rests in the man Jesus Christ—that is, rests in him with delight. In other human beings there is something that displeases God; in Christ, however, there neither is nor was anything that did not please God, as the Father testified when he said of him: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3).

Therefore, my brothers, let us remove from ourselves everything that displeases God. If we want God to rest in us, let us avoid the sins by which God is driven away from us.

The text continues: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.”

There is one Spirit, but his gifts are diverse. He gives his name to his gifts because he never abandons them in anyone. Whoever has the gifts of the Holy Spirit has the Holy Spirit; and whoever has the Holy Spirit has his gifts, especially since to have the Holy Spirit is nothing other than to have his gifts.

In our Lord there are seven gifts—that is, all the gifts of the Holy Spirit. He possesses them all in his power, since he can give them to whomever he wishes, but in actual use he has only those that it is fitting for him to have. Repentance and restraint of lust are gifts of the Holy Spirit, but Christ does not have them in himself, because it is not fitting that he should.

The first gift is wisdom concerning divine things: knowledge of the Trinity in unity and of unity in the Trinity; knowledge of divine mysteries; knowledge of creating, preserving, propagating, and governing all things.

Who possessed this gift more fully than he who is essentially the wisdom of God the Father, who with the Father disposed all things from eternity, and who in time creates, preserves, and rules all things? Yet he is said to receive this gift in time because what belonged to him according to his nature as God became his according to grace, insofar as he is human.

The second gift is understanding hidden things: understanding the secrets of hearts, the secrets of future events, the secrets of Scripture, and the secrets of absent and invisible things. This may properly be called the spirit of prophecy.

Who possessed this gift more fully than he who rebuked the hidden thoughts of the wicked Jews and narrated future and absent things as though they were past? Hence he is called a prophet—indeed, the Lord of the prophets.

Moses said of him: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers” (Deut. 18). And in the Gospel: “This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world” (John 6).

The third gift is counsel amid the snares and dangers of this world. Who possessed this gift more fully than he who gave counsel concerning salvation to the human race despairing of salvation, and who daily gives counsel to those who lack counsel? For this reason the prophet calls him, by a distinctive title, “Counselor and Angel of great counsel” (Isa. 9).

The fourth gift is fortitude for resisting the persecutions and temptations of this world. Who possessed this gift more fully than he who completely overcame the devil’s temptations and persecutions, conquered the powers of the air, bound the strong armed man, and distributed all his possessions?

For this reason the prophet calls him “the strong God and Lord of hosts” (Isa. 1).

The fifth gift is knowledge for distinguishing virtue from vice, truth from falsehood, good from evil, and justice from injustice. This gift is properly called discernment of spirits.

Who possessed this gift more fully than he who is “the Lord of knowledge” (1 Sam. 2), who “searches the kidneys and hearts” (Rom. 8), who distinguishes not only between good and evil but also between good and good, evil and evil, and who will render to each according to his merits?

Hence the Apostle says: “The word of God is living and more penetrating than any two-edged sword, reaching to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions; and no creature is invisible in his sight” (Heb. 4).

The sixth gift is piety for loving, showing compassion, and doing good. Who possessed this gift more fully than he who gave himself not only for his friends but also for his enemies, even praying for his persecutors?

For this reason he is called not only pious but piety itself and charity itself.

The seventh gift is filial fear of the Lord. Jesus Christ did indeed possess not the painful experience of fear but reverence and obedience, attributing everything to the Father and obeying him even unto death.

These gifts are enumerated here by descending order because Christ, of whom these things are said, humbled himself for us from the height of divine wisdom down to the final gift—that is, the fear of the Lord, which is the beginning of wisdom (Ps. 110).

But we, brothers, who are placed in the lowest regions, should advance upward from the lesser gift, the fear of the Lord. Let us pray to him who possesses the fullness of the gifts without measure, that he may distribute them to us according to the measure of his will.

Let us pray and say:

“Lord, pour into our hearts the fear of your name, so that for your sake we may avoid sins and every disgrace. But because this is not enough, also give us, Lord, the spirit of piety, so that we may be pious toward you and toward our neighbors, loving you above all things and our neighbors as ourselves.

“But since some possess zeal for God but not according to knowledge, give us also, Lord, the spirit of knowledge, so that we may know to whom we owe piety and to whom correction.

“But since some know what ought to be done yet, because of faintheartedness, do not dare to undertake it, give us likewise, Lord, the spirit of fortitude, so that we may act bravely and be able to withstand both harshness and flattery.

“But since some are also brave yet are troubled amid the straits of danger, give us also, Lord, the spirit of counsel, so that we may be able to give sound counsel both to ourselves and to others.

“But since sound counsel is supplied through the spirit of understanding, give us also, Lord, the spirit of understanding, so that, enlightened by it, we may understand what ought to be done in doubtful matters.

“But since understanding is bestowed through participation in true and eternal wisdom, give us, Lord, the wisdom that stands beside your thrones, so that we may know at all times what is acceptable before you.”

The third part follows, in which he shows what Christ would be toward others. He demonstrates that Christ would be a discerning Judge, an incorruptible defender of the good, a persecutor of the wicked, and one who would join the just and faithful to himself.

He demonstrates that Christ would be a discerning Judge when he says: “He shall not judge according to the sight of the eyes, nor reprove according to the hearing of the ears.”

It is as though he were saying: He will not judge according to outward appearance but according to the inner conscience, in accordance with what is written: “A human being looks upon the face, but God looks upon the heart” (1 Sam. 16).

Human sight is very often deceived because it sees not what is inward but only what is outward. Hence it frequently judges a person to be just who is unjust, and conversely; and it judges a work to be upright when it is perverse, or conversely.

Human hearing is likewise deceived because, unaware of the thoughts or intentions from which words arise, it attends only to the external voice and judges a word true when it is false, or good when it is evil.

Hence judging in this age is very dangerous. Although a judge may intend to deceive no one, he is nevertheless often deceived, acquitting someone who ought to be condemned or condemning someone who ought to be acquitted.

For this reason the Lord warns us, saying: “Do not judge, and you will not be judged” (Luke 6). And the Apostle says: “Do not judge before the appointed time, until the Lord comes, who will bring the hidden things of darkness to light and reveal the counsels of hearts” (1 Cor. 4).

He demonstrates that Christ will be an incorruptible Judge when he adds: “But he shall judge the poor in justice”—that is, the case of the poor, on account of which almost all worldly judges are corrupted.

Some are corrupted by contempt, so that they disdain to hear the case of the poor as though it were useless to them. Hence Isaiah says: “They do not judge the fatherless, and the widow’s case does not come before them” (Isa. 1).

Others, although they hear the case, are corrupted by a gift, or by favor, friendship, or fear of relatives, so that they do not judge it justly. Against such people the Psalmist says: “How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to sinners? Judge the needy and the fatherless; vindicate the humble and the poor” (Ps. 81).

Others, even if they are not corrupted by these things, are corrupted by an immoderate movement of mercy. Against the uprightness of justice, out of mercy they grant the poor what they take away from the rich out of envy.

But a judge who sits in judgment must not recognize faces in judgment. He must be free from greed, favor, fear, contempt, love, hatred, mercy, and envy.

Hence the Lord says to Moses: “You shall not consider the person of the poor in judgment, nor honor the face of the powerful” (Lev. 19). Do not consider the person of the poor by pitying him to the prejudice of the rich; do not honor the face of the powerful by favoring him to the prejudice of the poor.

The prophet foretold that Christ would be such a one: that in judgment he would recognize no person but would judge all equally, including the poor; he would not spare the poor who lived wickedly, nor condemn the rich who lived rightly.

Hence it is written: “God does not reject the powerful, since he himself is powerful” (Job 36).

He shows that Christ would be the defender of the good when he adds: “And he shall reprove in equity for the meek of the earth”—that is, he will reprove with equity the powerful who unjustly oppress the meek.

Hence it is also said to him: “To you the poor man is left; you will be the helper of the orphan” (Ps. 9). If he sometimes appears to delay bringing help to the meek, it is because he knows that tribulations are necessary for them; nevertheless, “the poor will not be forgotten forever, nor will the patience of the poor perish forever” (ibid.).

He shows that Christ would be the persecutor of the wicked when he adds: “And he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth.” That is, he will reprove earthly people through the uprightness of his preaching, turning them away from love of earthly things and directing them toward love of heavenly things.

“And by the spirit of his lips”—that is, by a spiritual word—“he shall kill the impious”: he will kill impiety in a person and generate piety in him. Or, if someone persists as incorrigible, he will condemn that impious and earthly person eternally by the uprightness of his judicial sentence.

Some think that this was said specifically about Antichrist.

He shows that Christ would join the just and faithful to himself and take delight in their fellowship when he adds: “And justice shall be the belt of his loins, and faith the girdle of his reins.”

By “loins” and “reins,” delight is understood; by “belt” and “girdle,” the fellowship surrounding him. Justice, therefore, shall be the belt of his loins, and faith the girdle of his reins, because he will delight in the fellowship of the just and faithful.

“For his delights are to be with the sons of men” (Prov. 8)—not, of course, with the old but with the new.

Therefore, my brothers, if we want Christ to delight in dwelling with us, indeed in us, let us cleanse ourselves through repentance from every impurity. Let us strive to have justice and faith within us.

Because Christ delights in those who resemble him, let us be such as he is: just as he is just, faithful as he is faithful, pure as he is pure, merciful as he is merciful. Then we shall delight in him and he in us; we shall dwell in him and he in us—through the gift of him who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## XVI. On the Same Feast

“The angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary” (Luke 1), and the rest.

This reading, my brothers, has five parts. First, an angel is sent by God to a virgin; second, after entering, he greets her; third, he strengthens her when she is troubled; fourth, he explains the manner to the woman who asks; fifth, she, professing her humility, desires the promise to be fulfilled.

First, therefore, the archangel is sent by God to the virgin, carrying the ministry of our redemption.

But since almighty God could redeem us by a mere nod, why did it please him to redeem us in so laborious and humble a manner—namely, to take flesh from a woman for our sake, to be born, to be nourished, to suffer human infirmities, and even to die?

For three reasons.

The first is that in this way he better demonstrated the excessive love that he had for us: he redeemed us not through another but through himself; by taking on our infirmities he condescended to us and made himself our equal; and he gave not something else but himself as the price for us.

It is as though he were saying plainly: “Love me, because I have loved you so greatly.”

The second is that in this way he more clearly demonstrated for us an example of humility to imitate. He emptied himself for us, chose a very poor mother, and willed to endure poverty, degradation, and persecution.

It is as though he were saying plainly: “Follow the way that I have shown you.”

The third is that in this way he applied a medicine more suited to our misery. He saved the human race, which had been condemned through a woman, through a woman; just as flesh had sinned, so flesh would be cleansed, in accordance with the hymn-writer’s words:

“Flesh incurs guilt, flesh cleanses; God reigns, the flesh of God.”

Therefore, just as the devil deceived the woman through the serpent and the man through the woman, so the Lord instructed the woman through an angel and through the woman saved the human race.

Although by sinning the human being had offended God and had therefore been justly expelled by him, nevertheless, because God does not forget to have mercy, he first sends an ambassador of peace and offers peace to the human being.

In this he instructs us that, if someone has ever earned God’s anger by offending us, we should not wait to be entreated by that person. Rather, we ourselves should first offer forgiveness and peace through ambassadors of peace, so that we may be sons of the heavenly Father, who always desires to convert those turned away from him and call back those who have fled.

Appropriately, the angel Gabriel—whose name is interpreted as “strength of God”—is sent to Mary: a virgin to a virgin, the strength of God to a strong woman.

Solomon desired and foresaw her when he said: “Who will find a strong woman? Her price is from far away and from the remotest ends” (Prov. 31).

The Blessed Virgin was the strongest of all women who have existed or will exist from the beginning to the end. She was the first, and without example, to overcome flesh, sex, and age; by the strength of her mind she preserved humility in nobility, dignity in poverty, and virginity in marriage.

For this reason it was also granted to her, without example, to have fruitfulness in virginity. Nobility ordinarily attacks humility, poverty attacks dignity, marriage attacks virginity, and virginity attacks fruitfulness.

The Blessed Virgin was therefore marvelous. Although she was born from royal stock, although she was greeted by an angel, although she was filled with grace and blessing, and although she was chosen as the Mother of God, she nevertheless did not know how to become exalted amid such sublimity, as some do. Rather, she confessed herself to be a handmaid and subject.

“Behold,” she says, “the handmaid of the Lord.”

Again, although she was very poor, although she was betrothed to a craftsman, and although she was a commoner and unknown, she did not despise herself, nor did she squander herself in dishonorable pursuits, as some poor people do—more expansively because they are more hidden. Rather, she preserved dignity and holiness in poverty.

Again, although she was married and although she was a tender young girl, she was not ensnared by the allurements of marriage; rather, she preserved virginity within marriage.

Thus she also deserved to have singular fruitfulness in virginity, and to bear not just any son but the very Son of God.

Let the noble, therefore, admire and imitate her, so that following her example they may learn to preserve humility in nobility.

Let married men and married women likewise admire and imitate her, so that following her example they may learn to preserve chastity in marriage.

Let virgins also admire and imitate her, so that following her example they may learn to possess fruitfulness in virginity—not the fruitfulness of the flesh, for they cannot have that while preserving virginity, but the fruitfulness of faith and good works. Thus they may conceive Christ in their hearts through faith and give birth to him through good confession and action.

She is rightly called the most blessed virgin Mary, a name interpreted as “star of the sea.” For she is like a certain light and like a guiding star for us as we sail upon the great and perilous sea of this world. By her example she leads us, by her virtues she illuminates us, and by her intercessions she helps us.

Therefore, my brothers, if the evil spirit harasses us, if the flesh tempts us, if the world attacks us, let us look to Mary, let us flee to Mary, let us cry aloud to Mary.

Second, the angel enters to Mary and greets her. Where did he enter? I think into her chamber, or into some private place where the holy Virgin, with the door closed, was praying to her Father. From this let our virgins learn to love the privacy of their chamber, not to frequent public places, not to run about inquisitively through the streets, and not to wish to be seen and to see, lest perhaps, like Dinah, they be desired and violated (Gen. XXXIV).

“Hail,” he says, “full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women.” This greeting, my brothers, which the Lord gives through the angel to the Virgin, and through the Virgin to the human race, is a sign of peace, a demonstration of love, and an announcement of salvation. Through this greeting from God to the Virgin, and through her to the human race, peace is offered, love is demonstrated, and salvation is announced.

Imitating this, therefore, my brothers, when we greet one another, let us greet one another from true peace, not from agreement in wickedness, as some do. Of such people John says: “Do not even say ‘Hail’ to him. For whoever says to him ‘Hail’ shares in his works” (II John I). Let us greet one another from true love, not merely because of an occasion of travel. Of such people the Lord says: “Salute no one along the way” (Luke X). Let us greet one another with a true wish for salvation, not with the duplicity of deceit and betrayal, as Judas did.

What salvation is announced to Mary is explained when it is added: [Col. 1360B] “Full of grace.” She is called, in an excellent and almost specially appropriated designation, “full of grace,” because there is no virtue, no merit, and no honor that does not abound in her, and because the graces that are distributed individually to each of the saints are conferred upon Mary universally. Moreover, something occurred to no one else ever: together with the glory of virginity, she rejoices in the honor of motherhood, carrying within herself not just anyone, but God and the Son of God, the source of all graces, through whom grace and truth have come, Jesus Christ.

Let us therefore ask, my brothers, the Mother of graces to obtain for us some little stream from the fountain of graces whom she bears. “The Lord is with you.” With you in essence, with you by grace, with you in love, with you through the Incarnation; the Lord is with you in heart, with you in mouth, with you in deed, with you in the womb. Reconcile us, therefore, most merciful Lady, to him who is so familiar to you and who is always with you, so that through you he may deign to be with us also.

“Blessed are you,” he says, “among women”—indeed, above all women—for you are the remedy, honor, and example of the other women. You are their remedy because you atone for the scourges of other women; their honor because you honor the dishonor of other women; their example because, by your example, you show other women the way of virginity and every virtue. Well, therefore, are you blessed among women, for above all women you are worthy to be blessed. Hence all women, indeed all generations, will call you blessed.

Third, the angel strengthens her when she is troubled. For when she heard the unusual greeting, “she was troubled at his saying.” Virgins—for those who are true virgins—are accustomed always to be fearful and to tremble at the sudden encounter with unfamiliar men. For they fear the dangers to the flower of virginity, which is quickly lost and, once lost, cannot be recovered.

Thus the blessed Virgin was troubled by the sudden sight of the angel and by the unusual greeting, but she was not thrown into confusion; rather, she prudently considered what sort of greeting this was. For she knew that sometimes Satan disguises himself as an angel of light (II Cor. II), and that beneath a greeting he conceals fraud, and beneath praise, deception. She was therefore considering whether this greeting and praise were false or true, whether they arose from flattery or from love.

This too we ought to consider, my brothers, when someone greets and praises us. If the greeting and praise are false, let us blush and contradict them, and let us strive to be what we are proclaimed to be. But if they are true, let us not be exalted in our own eyes, but attribute everything to God and nothing to ourselves. If the praise arises from flattery, let us not accept it, but reject it as falsehood. If, however, it arises from love, let us not entirely believe our friends, who are often deceived in judging the person they love.

The angel therefore strengthens the blessed Virgin, who was troubled and thinking—something proper to good angels—and, in the manner most accustomed to drive away fear, calls her by her own name, saying: “Do not be afraid, Mary.” And he added why she should not fear, but rather rejoice: “You have found grace with God.” As though he said plainly: Because you desired to please God, not human beings, you have found grace with God. Those who please human beings are confounded, because God has rejected them. Hence the Apostle says: “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. I).

Alas, how vain are those who expend their entire lives, body and soul, to earn the empty glory of mortal princes—a glory they can scarcely obtain and, once obtained, quickly lose! How much more easily they could find true and eternal glory with God!

“Behold,” he says, “you will conceive and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.” The prophet Jeremiah had foretold this conception, saying: “The Lord will create a new thing upon the earth: a woman will encompass a man” (Jer. XXXI). For a woman to conceive and bear a son is not new. [Col. 1361C] But in this birth God did something new and wondrous: either because the Virgin did not receive him outside the womb, but only in the womb and from the womb; or because flesh was not first separated from the flesh of his mother and then, after some days, a spirit infused, but she conceived at once a complete man, constituted of true flesh and a true soul, our God and Lord Jesus Christ.

Isaiah says the same concerning this: “Behold, a virgin will conceive in the womb and bear a son” (Isa. VII). Since here only the nominative “virgin” is placed, it must refer to both verbs. This clearly demonstrates that, just as she would remain a virgin in conception, so also she would remain a virgin in childbirth.

“And he will be called,” he says (ibid.), “Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us.” But here the angel says: “You shall call his name Jesus,” which is interpreted, “Savior.” For what else is it for God to be with us than to save us? And what is it to save us other than to be with us? Through the Virgin’s childbirth, therefore, God saves us and is with us. He is with us by assuming our flesh; he is with us in love; he is with us in protection.

“He will be,” he says, “great.” And truly great, since there is no end to his greatness. “And he will be called the Son of the Most High,” not adopted, but natural.

But since he was great and the Son of the Most High from eternity, why does he say, “He will be great” in the future, and “the Son of the Most High”? This must be referred to his humanity and to human knowledge, since he who was first regarded as small according to his humanity was afterward regarded as great, and afterward became known—his works bearing witness—as great and the Son of God. For he is that little stone which was cut from the mountain without hands, and afterward grew into a great mountain and occupied the whole world (Dan. II).

“And the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father,” so that in the people over whom David ruled bodily and temporally, Jesus might reign spiritually and eternally. “And he will reign in the house of Jacob forever,” that is, in the Church, which through the imitation of faith belongs to the lot of the patriarchs.

Let us follow, brothers, the faith of the patriarchs. Let us be Jacob—that is, supplanters of vices. Let sin not reign in our mortal body, and Jesus will reign in us. “For wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wis. I). “And of his kingdom,” he says, “there will be no end.” There will be no end to his power and glory; there will be no end to his rewards.

Fourth, the angel determines the manner for her who asks about it. For when the blessed Virgin believed the angelic promises, yet, wondering about the manner of their fulfillment, said: “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?”—that is, I have resolved not to know one. She ought not otherwise to have doubted about this, since she could have conceived from her husband.

The angel therefore determines the manner, saying: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you.” As though he said plainly: You will conceive not from male seed, but from the power of the Holy Spirit. But since above the blessed Virgin is described as full of grace, how is the Holy Spirit now said to be about to come upon her? Not in order to fill her with grace, since she was already filled, but in order to make her pregnant in a holy and wondrous manner.

“And the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” The power of the Most High may mean either the Holy Spirit, according to what Luke says: “But remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke XXIV); or the Son himself, according to what Paul calls him, “the power and wisdom of God” (I Cor. I).

He therefore says: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you,” that is, the Holy Spirit will exclude from you the heat of vices, so that a pure dwelling place might be prepared in you for the Son of God. Or certainly, the power of the Most High—that is, the Son of God—will overshadow you, that is, he will receive in you the shadowing-covering of flesh. Because the weakness of our eyes could not contemplate the immensity of the divine radiance, Jesus Christ, the Sun of righteousness, veiled himself in flesh, so that in this way we might somehow contemplate him more easily beneath a cloud.

Therefore, because you will conceive not from male seed but from the power of the Holy Spirit, “what will be born from you will be holy and will be called the Son of God”—that is, the one who will be born. For by this relative pronoun, “what,” it is not merely flesh but a person who is signified. Nevertheless, the neuter form is used for greater expression of the matter. If he had said “that holy man” or “that holy male,” he would seem to have said too little; but he says “that holy thing,” as though it were said plainly: He in whom there is nothing but holiness, nothing but goodness.

“And behold, Elizabeth your kinswoman has also conceived a son in her old age.” After the blessed Virgin’s own joy has been announced to her, the joy of her kinswoman and friend is also announced, so that joy might be heaped upon joy, and so that, at the mutual visitation and shared rejoicing of the mothers, the holy infants might also rejoice together in holy wombs.

“And this is the sixth month for her who is called barren.” As though it were said to her: Just as your kinswoman preceded you in conceiving, so her son will precede yours in preaching and baptizing.

“For no word will be impossible with God.” As though he said plainly: Not only is the childbirth of a virgin, or of an old woman, or of a barren woman possible for God; rather, whatever seems impossible to human beings is possible for God. For whatever he wishes to do is easier for him than it is for us to utter a word, and for this reason “every word” was said rather than “every deed.”

Therefore, let no barren soul despair. Even if throughout its whole life it has produced no good fruit, let it nevertheless hope in the Lord, who regards sinners barren of every good work even in old age and at the final moment of life, and makes them fruitful through repentance.

Fifth, the blessed Virgin professes her humility, saying: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord.” Behold, my brothers: although the blessed Virgin is full of grace, although she has been chosen as the Mother of God and of our Lord, she professes in herself only the humility of submission—and not merely with voice and pretense, as some do, but with heart and deed.

Thus, immediately after the angelic annunciation, she rises—as the following passage relates—and goes to greet and serve Elizabeth: the Mother of God serves the mother of a man; the mother of the King serves the mother of a servant.

This stands against many of us, my brothers. If at some time, through our pretenses, the Church is deceived and, by God’s permission, promotes us to some ecclesiastical office, we attribute this to our own merits. Forgetful of our frailty, we despise others, oblivious of the Lord’s example (Matt. XX). We wish not to minister but to be ministered to; we show ourselves not fathers but lords. We accumulate for ourselves a number of horses, a heap of riches, and changes of soft garments; we proceed with pomp and glory; and, raised up on high, we disdain to look upon mortal people. In doing this, we imitate not the humility that the Lord demonstrated to us, but diabolical pride.

Then, through a verb expressing desire and entreaty, the blessed Virgin desires with her whole mind and prays that the promise be fulfilled, when she adds: [Col. 1363D] “Let it be done to me according to your word.” This stands against the tepidity of some of us, my brothers, who grow sluggish with regard to God’s eternal and blessed promises, while we burn with desire for temporal promises.

Certainly, if some earthly king promised us honors and empty riches, we would wish and ask with all our desire that they not be delayed. And behold, God promises us an eternal and blessed kingdom; he promises us heavenly goods “which no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (I Cor. II)—and toward these we grow sluggish and negligent. Why is this, except that we love temporal things too ardently, while we either do not believe in heavenly goods or despise them?

“Let it be done to me,” she says, “according to your word.” Let the Word of the Father be made in me and for me, according to your word.

And behold, glorious Virgin, your desire has been fulfilled. According to the angelic word, the Word of the Father has been made in you and for you—indeed, for me also and for all who firmly believe and hope in him, who love him ardently, and who do his commandments.

But behold, most merciful Lady: while we wish to do this, our enemies, who lie in wait for our souls, hinder us and wish to draw us over to their side. But you, Lady, in your maternal compassion, be concerned for us, your little servants. If the devil tempts us, help us; if the flesh tempts us, help us; if the world tempts us, help us. Indeed, help us always, so that, aided by your most powerful intercessions and merits, we may deserve to reach eternal joys through your Son, our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## XVII. ON THE FEAST OF THE APOSTLES PHILIP AND JAMES

Jesus said to his disciples: “Let not your heart be troubled. You believe in God; believe also in me” (John XIV), and so forth.

The all-knowing Lord, my dearest brothers, foreseeing that the minds of the disciples would be disturbed by his Passion, deigned to fortify and console them beforehand. For arrows that are foreseen wound less than those that are not foreseen. Therefore, on the very night when he was about to go to his Passion, he fortified and instructed them beforehand, as you have just heard in the aforementioned Gospel reading.

In this reading he does four things. First, he consoles them. Second, in response to Thomas’s question, he shows that he is the way by which one goes to the Father. Third, in response to Philip’s request, he says that the Father is known through him. Fourth, he shows what true faith merits.

Thus, consoling them, he says: “Let not your heart be troubled,” as though he said: Because of my Passion, let your heart not be moved from the stability of faith and its tranquility.

He shows why they should not be troubled when he adds: “You believe in God; believe also in me.” That is: If you believe that the Father is almighty, it follows that you must also believe me, his consubstantial Son, to be almighty—one whom death cannot hold, but who is Lord of death and life.

Even if it should happen that you are so troubled by my Passion as to flee, doubt, or even deny me, do not nevertheless be troubled unto despair, because in the house of my heavenly Father there is room not only for those who have never fallen, but also for those who have fallen and rise again through repentance. Hence it is added: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places.”

What the Lord then said to his disciples, I also say to you now, my dearest brothers. If it should happen that you are troubled by falling into some grave sin, let not your heart be troubled unto despair, because no one can become so entangled in enormities and crimes that he cannot be restored through repentance and obtain a place in the kingdom of heaven, where there are different dwelling places—that is, differences of merits and rewards.

For even if one denarius of eternal blessedness is given to all the elect, nevertheless “star differs from star in glory” (I Cor. XV), and according to degrees of merit there are different degrees of reward. Yet greater glory is not lifted up there by pride, nor is lesser glory tormented by envy. Rather, in unequal glory there is equal sufficiency and equal joy. For love and one will make all the goods of each person common to all.

Let us hasten, therefore, my dearest brothers, with complete desire toward those true and eternal goods, despising the false and fleeting goods of this age, in which neither sufficiency nor true joy is found.

It follows: “If it were not so”—that is, if different dwelling places had not been prepared in my Father’s house—“I would have told you, because I go to prepare a place for you. And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself.”

Many dwelling places have indeed been prepared in the kingdom of heaven from the beginning of the world, but inhabitants had not yet been prepared for them. Therefore the Lord descended and returned, in order to prepare inhabitants for those dwelling places.

The Lord has ascended and prepares a place for us while he prepares us for the place. Do this, Lord Jesus Christ, as you promised. You have prepared dwelling places; prepare us for the dwelling places. Make us worthy of those dwelling places, who are unworthy in ourselves.

The dwelling places are holy and nuptial; clothe us also with holiness and a nuptial garment, so that we may recline there in safety.

“And if I go,” he says, “and prepare a place for you, I will come again to you and take you to myself.” The supreme and humble Lord performs the office of messenger and forerunner: he departs and prepares a place for us, and then returns to meet us, so that he may lead us to the prepared place.

For the powerful of this age customarily do this. When they go to some city, they send ahead a messenger who prepares lodging. When it has been prepared, he returns to meet them and leads them to the lodging.

So too our God and Lord, who came into this world not to be served but to serve (Matt. XX), departed as a forerunner before us and ascended into heaven to prepare a place for us. He returns to meet us either when we depart from this age, in order to receive our souls, or certainly at the final judgment, when, glorified in body and soul, “we shall be caught up to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (I Thess. IV).

This is what is said here: “And I will take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be.” He does not say, “where I will be,” but “where I am,” showing that by his divinity he is always present in glory with the Father, though according to his humanity he was not yet there.

And what, my brothers, is more blessed than to be in that blessedness in which God the Father and his Only-Begotten Son are? Why, then, do we not burn with desire for this promise? Why do we not regard all temporal things as dung for its sake? Why do we not grasp it through every bitterness and suffering?

“And where I am going,” he says, “you know, and you know the way.” As though he said plainly: You ought not to be troubled by my departure, because you know where I am going—to the Father, in order to prepare a place for you. And you know the way: namely, my example and teaching, by following which you can reach God the Father and the glory prepared for you.

Thomas knew this by hearing it. Yet because he did not know what it meant to go to the Father, he says that he does not know, replying: “Lord, we do not know where you are going, and how can we know the way?”

This is the second part, in which the Lord responds to Thomas and says that he is the way by which one goes to God the Father, when he adds: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.”

Christ is called the way for four reasons: because through knowledge of him, through his example, through his teaching, and through his help, one goes to God the Father.

He is also called the truth for three reasons: because he is true and unchangeable with God the Father; because in him the Law and the Prophets are fulfilled; and because he is truthful to his faithful in every promise.

He is likewise called the life for three reasons: because he lives essentially and unchangeably with God the Father; because through him one lives, whether bodily or spiritually, by causation; and because through him the dead, whether in soul or body, are brought to life by his power.

As far as the present passage is concerned, the meaning of “I am the way, the truth, and the life” is this: I am the guide by whom one goes to the true life, which the Father and I are.

Explaining this, he adds: “No one comes to the Father except through me.” As though he said plainly: No one comes to the blessed knowledge and vision of God the Father except through me as guide, through knowledge of me, through my example, teaching, and help.

O Lord Jesus Christ, so that we may reach the blessed and desirable vision of God the Father and of you, give us your guidance; give us knowledge of you; grant us to follow your example and teaching; give us the help of your hand.

Indeed, Lord, we are rather slow, since we are weighed down by the habitation and misery of the body. But you, “draw us after you, and we will run in the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song I).

“If you had known me,” he says, “you would certainly have known my Father also.” This sequence is understood as necessary for two reasons: because of the relation between them and because of their consubstantiality.

The Father and the Son are relatives, and therefore they are alike in nature and in knowledge. Again, God the Father and God the Son are not merely alike, but of one and the same substance; therefore, when one is known, the other is also known.

If the disciples had known the Son of God with perfect faith, they would certainly also have known God the Father.

“And from now on,” he says, “you will know him,” namely, when you have received the Holy Spirit and are strengthened in faith. “And you have seen him,” he says, already by imperfect faith, such as that by which you have seen me to be the Son.

How, then, do we now see you and your Father, Lord Jesus? Perfect within us what is lacking through the Holy Spirit, so that here we may believe with more perfect faith that you and the Father are one God, and in the future may see the blessedness of your face without the obscuring cloud.

It follows that this is the third part, in which Christ responds to Philip, who asks that the Father be shown to him, by saying that the Father is known in himself: “I have been with you for so long a time, and you have not known me? Philip, whoever sees me sees my Father also.”

By asking that the Father be shown to him, Philip admits that he does not know him. Therefore, because the Son is not known when the Father is not known, the Son himself rebukes Philip, criticizing him for not truly knowing him, although by living with him for so long he could have recognized through his divine miracles, powers, and preaching that he was the true Son of God.

“Whoever sees me,” he says, “sees the Father also.” This is said of two things that are very similar, on account of accidental similarity: whoever sees one sees the other. But it can be said most truly of God the Father and his Son, whose substance is not merely similar but one and the same, that whoever sees the Son of God with the eyes of faith also sees the Father, to whom he is consubstantial.

It is therefore as though he said: Whatever I am, my Father is precisely the same. Just as you see that I am wisdom, justice, mercy, and love, so believe that my Father, with whom I am one, is wisdom, justice, mercy, and love.

“Do you not believe,” he says, “that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” If it is said that a human father is in his son and the son in the father merely because of similarity, how much more truly can it be said that God the Son is in God the Father and God the Father in God the Son because of the same substance of both!

That God the Father is in God the Son, the Son himself proves by the fact that he neither speaks nor acts from himself, but from God the Father, who speaks and acts in him and through him. Hence he adds: “The words that I speak to you I do not speak from myself, but the Father who remains in me himself does the works.”

But if God the Son, although of the same power and authority as the Father, attributes nothing to himself but everything to God the Father, how great is the pride of human beings, who, although they can do absolutely no good from themselves, presumptuously dare to claim for themselves the good granted to them by God?

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us always consider our weakness. If we have any good, let us attribute it not to ourselves but to God; let us ascribe the evil we have to ourselves.

“Do you not believe,” he says, “that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? Otherwise, believe because of the works.” As though he said plainly: If you do not wish to believe me without experience, you have the evidence of the divine works that I perform, and because of them you ought to believe.

This is the fourth part, in which the Lord shows what true faith merits, when he adds: “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these, because I go to the Father. And whatever you ask the Father in my name, I will do.”

The Lord promises two things to those who believe in him: namely, that they will perform divine works, and that whatever they ask the Father in his name, they will obtain.

Believers in him have indeed performed the divine works that the Son of God performs, according to what the Lord also foretold elsewhere: “In my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues” (Mark XVI), and so forth.

“And they will do greater works,” he says. For it is greater to heal the sick merely by one’s shadow—as happened through Peter—than by the touch of a fringe, as happened through Christ. It is also greater to convert the whole world to faith—as happened through the disciples—than to convert a few Jews, as happened through Christ.

It is also greater and more wondrous that a dead person should be raised by a mortal human being, and even by one who is himself dead, than that he should be raised by almighty God.

He shows how Christ, and how his disciples, would perform these works when he adds: “The works that I do, he will also do. I will be the helper; he will be the minister.” As though he said: “Without me you can say or do nothing” (John XIV).
