That he can give his disciples the power to work in this way, he shows when he adds: “Because I go to the Father.” As though he said plainly: I can rightly give this power to believers in me because I have the power to ascend and sit in equality with the Father.

And I will grant this not only to you who believe, but also, “whatever you ask the Father in my name, I will do.” He does not say, “he will do,” but “I will do,” to show that his operation and the Father’s are the same.

A person asks in the name of Jesus—that is, of the Savior—when he asks for eternal salvation. Whoever undoubtedly asks for this with complete desire and perseverance will obtain it.

Therefore, my brothers, let us firmly believe in Jesus Christ our Savior, and let us cling to him with faith working through love (Gal. V), because he will grant us also to do the works that he himself does: namely, mercy, justice, wisdom, strength, and temperance.

He will also give us the power to give sight to the blind—not outwardly, perhaps, but inwardly, which is greater; to raise the spiritually lame along the way of God; to rescue through prayer and correction those captured by the devil’s jaws; and to raise through good counsel those dead in sins.

He will also undoubtedly grant eternal salvation to us when we ask for it with complete desire and perseverance, so that we may see him and bless him throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## Life of the Blessed James the Younger, by D. Isidore

James, son of Alphaeus, the first bishop of Jerusalem, surnamed the Just, son of the sister of the Lord’s mother—and therefore called the Lord’s brother—was a man of light and a worker of truth. He possessed such holiness that the people eagerly sought to touch the fringe of his garment.

He wrote an Epistle to the twelve tribes that are scattered among the nations. While preaching Christ the Son of God in Jerusalem, he was thrown down from the Temple by the Jews, crushed beneath stones, and buried there beside the Temple. Josephus declares him to have possessed such holiness that Jerusalem is believed to have been destroyed on account of his death.

## Life of the Apostle Saint Philip, by the same author

Philip, whose name is interpreted as “mouth of the lamp,” was from the city of Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter. He preached Christ to the Gauls. He led barbarian peoples and their neighbors, joined to darkness and to the swelling Ocean, into the light of knowledge and faith.

Then, in the city of Hierapolis in the province of Phrygia, he died after being crucified and stoned, and was buried after a tomb had been erected. His feast is on the Kalends of May.

## XVIII. ON THE FINDING OF THE HOLY CROSS

“I am confident in the Lord concerning you that you will think nothing otherwise” (Gal. V), and so forth.

My brothers, Paul says this to the Galatians, to whom false preachers had preached that the Law was to be maintained together with the Gospel. The Apostle writes to them against this false preaching.

In this reading he does six things. First, he says that he trusts in God concerning the stability of their faith. Second, he threatens the false preachers with judgment. Third, he demonstrates that he does not preach observance of the Law. Fourth, he wishes for the separation of the disturbers. Fifth, he shows how much they preach observance of the Law. Sixth, he says that he glories not in the Law but in the cross of Christ.

First, therefore, he says that he trusts in God—that is, concerning the stability of their faith—when he says: “I am confident in the Lord concerning you that you will think nothing otherwise.”

As though he said: Although false preachers proclaim to you things contrary to the faith, nevertheless I trust in the Lord concerning you that you will think nothing contrary to the power of faith.

It is the mark of a good teacher never to despair, while erring disciples are still in this life, of correcting them, and therefore never to cease praying. Even if, as far as the disciples themselves are concerned, he distrusts the correction of the incorrigible, he ought nevertheless to trust in the Lord concerning them, since the Lord can not only recall those who have gone astray, but even raise children of Abraham from stones (Matt. III).

This is why he says, “I am confident in the Lord concerning you,” not in you, because “cursed is the man who trusts in man” (Jer. XVII). No one can stand by himself, still less rise again.

What the Apostle then said to the Galatians, I now say to you, dearest brothers: Although you live among the wicked and heretics, some of whom corrupt you by bad example and others by false teaching, nevertheless I trust concerning you—not in you, but in the Lord—that you will think and act in accordance with nothing other than the unity of the faith.

For whoever is separated from the unity of ecclesiastical faith is devoured like a wandering sheep by wolves.

This is the second part, in which the Apostle threatens the false preachers with judgment, adding: “But whoever is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be.”

If God leaves no evil unpunished, with how great a punishment must he be punished who disturbs the faithful from the uprightness of life and faith? If it is such a great sin to kill a mortal human body, how great a sin is it to kill immortal souls?

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever scandalizes one of these little ones who believe in me, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depths of the sea” (Matt. XVIII; Mark IX).

For a preacher who causes little ones to fall in faith through the offense of a bad example or teaching would be better off if the heavy course of worldly life hurled him into eternal damnation, since, if he alone were guilty of his soul, a lesser punishment would torment him. But now he will endure as many punishments as the souls he has caused to fall.

“He will bear the judgment,” he says—either willingly here, or unwillingly in the future. Whoever here accuses and judges himself concerning the sin he has committed, through contrition, confession, and satisfaction, avoids eternal judgment.

Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (I Cor. II).

Therefore, my brothers, let us anticipate the divine judgment. Here let us accuse ourselves of our sins, so that we may not be accused in the future. Here let us judge ourselves, so that we may not be judged in the future.

For whoever he may be, and however great he may be, who causes the lesser to deviate from the way of God will bear his judgment according to his rank. For “a severer judgment will be passed upon those who rule, and the powerful will suffer powerful torments, and a harsher torture awaits the stronger” (Wis. VI).

The third part follows, in which the Apostle demonstrates that he does not preach observance of the Law together with the Gospel. For the legal sacrifices and observances prefigured the observance of the Gospel that was to come; therefore, when the Gospel shone forth, they ought to cease. The Lord demonstrated this consummation and cessation of the Law in his Passion when he said: “It is finished” (John XIX). Whoever, therefore, from that time onward observes the figures of the Law demonstrates that Christ has not yet come but is still to come. Thus, from that time onward, to observe the legal figures is not merely useless but even condemned, and for those who place their hope in them it is harmful. Hence the same Paul says elsewhere: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Galatians V).

Paul therefore demonstrates that he does not preach observance of the Law when he says: “And I, brothers, if I still preach circumcision, why am I still suffering persecution?” As though he were saying plainly: This is also clear, because I do not preach circumcision: I suffer persecution from the Jews who love circumcision. They persecute me for no other reason than that I abolish the circumcision which they love and preach the cross of Christ, in which they take offense. Therefore, he says, “the offense of the cross has been abolished” if I do not preach the cross but circumcision, in which the Jews take no offense but rather rejoice.

What Paul then suffered from the Jews, we too suffer today, although unworthy preachers, from certain perverse Christians. For when we say to them not what is pleasing but what is true, not what they like but what is severe, we suffer from them plots, insults, and injuries. When we rebuke this one for lust, that one for greed, this one for anger, that one for cruelty, another for softness and dissipation, wishing to win them for God, they hate us because of the very things for which they ought to love us.

[Col. 1370D] The fourth part follows, in which the Apostle desires the separation of those who disturb them, adding: “Would that those who are disturbing you would cut themselves off!” Just as a prudent shepherd separates a diseased sheep or pig from the sheepfold, lest the whole flock perish through its contagion, so the Teacher of the Gentiles desires that wicked people—those who teach or live badly—be separated from the flock of the faithful, lest they corrupt them by their contagion and kill them in soul.

We ought to retain in our flock those who become better through our companionship, or through whose companionship we become better. But the incorrigible person—one who does not become better through our good conduct, while we could become worse through his—we should exclude from ourselves. For it is written: “Remove the evil person from among you” (1 Corinthians V).

Hence the holy Church has been accustomed to excommunicate and expel adulterers, usurers, heretics, and others entangled in public crimes, thereby taking thought both for herself and for them: for herself, lest she be inwardly corrupted by their contagion; for them, so that, when they see themselves cast out on account of their crimes, they may feel shame and be salutarily confounded.

The fifth part follows, in which the Apostle explains why observance of the Law is preached by false preachers, and he gives two reasons. The first is that they may avoid persecution; the second, that they may acquire a reputation for themselves.

“For all who desire to please in the flesh”—that is, carnally and not spiritually—“and not God but human beings, compel us to be circumcised,” only, that is understood, in the flesh, or only for this reason: so that they may not suffer persecution for the cross of Christ.

For the Roman emperors Augustus, Tiberius, and Gaius had granted the Jews the freedom to serve their ancestral laws peacefully everywhere, for as long as they lived. Therefore, when the false preachers saw Christians suffering persecution, they maintained the legal observances and compelled their followers to maintain them, so that they would not displease people and might avoid persecution.

Even today there are certain people like them—pastors in name only—who say and do for people not what is true but what is pleasing, not what is severe but what is agreeable, expressly so that they may please them. But as the Psalmist says: “Those who please human beings are confounded, because God has rejected them” (Psalm LII). And the Apostle says: “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians I).

[Col. 1371C] He gives the second reason when he adds: “For those who are circumcised”—that is understood, only in the flesh—“do not keep the Law,” which commanded a spiritual circumcision rather than a carnal one. “But they desire you to be circumcised,” he says, “so that they may glory in your flesh,” that is, in your carnal circumcision, while they acquire a reputation for themselves by making more proselytes.

There are many such people today—and this is cause for grief—who preach and read not so that their hearers may profit, but so that they may glory in the multitude of their hearers and acquire a reputation for themselves. But all such people, whoever they are, have already received their reward.

The sixth part follows, in which the Apostle says that he glories not in the Law but only in the cross of Christ. It is as though he were saying: They glory in circumcision, but for me, may it be far from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ!

The Apostle could have said, “May it be far from me to glory except in the wisdom or power, or in some other virtue, of Jesus Christ,” but he did not wish to say this; instead he said, “except in the cross.” Why? Because the cross is the weapon by which Christ, redeeming us, conquered the devil and taught us to conquer him. Therefore, just as a soldier glories in the weapons by which he overcame his enemy, so Paul glories in the cross of Christ, through which he was victorious over all his adversaries.

He does not simply say “in the cross,” but “in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.” For there are many crosses—that is, causes of suffering. There is the cross of the thief on the left, who suffers unwillingly for his sins but is not amended; in that cross there is nothing for him to glory in, but something for which he is condemned.

There is also the cross of the thief on the right, who suffers for his sins but nevertheless repents and confesses; even in that cross there is nothing for him to glory in, but something for which he must be corrected.

There is also the cross of the Cyrenian, who bears it under compulsion but does not die—that is, of the hypocrite who afflicts his flesh while living for the world. In this cross there is nothing in which he can truly glory, but something for which he will be judged.

There is also the cross of the innocent Christ, who willingly dies for our sins; in it there is very much for him to glory in. Paul glories in this cross, since, following the example of Christ hanging on the cross, he had crucified his own flesh with its vices and desires (Galatians V), dead to the world but alive to God. Hence the same Apostle says: “I live, yet it is no longer I; rather, Christ lives in me” (Galatians II).

He also suffered daily for Christ insults, injuries, scourging, imprisonment, stones, and such things. Hence he says: “I bear the marks of Christ in my body” (Galatians VI). And again: “I make up,” he says, “what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ” (Colossians I).

[Col. 1372B] With these weapons, therefore, the Apostle had already overcome not only the world but also himself. Hence he adds: “Through whom”—that is, through whose love and through whose imitation—“the world has been crucified to me,” so that it may not draw me by its desires, “and I to the world,” so that I may not follow it; that is, through him I have conquered the world and also myself.

But if we, brothers, still live for the world and for the desires of the flesh, how can we glory in the cross of Jesus Christ? When we impress the sign of the cross upon our foreheads and yet do not mortify desires and vices within us, when we do not patiently bear poverty, humility, insults, injuries, infirmities, and other anxieties, have we not become like the Cyrenian, who indeed carries the cross but does not die?

Therefore, brothers, if we wish to glory with Christ, let us suffer with him. Let us walk by the way in which he himself walked. Let us despise the riches, honors, and glories of the world. Let us crucify our members with their vices and desires. Let us show compassion and mercy toward pitiable persons. Let us embrace every hardship in hope of the kingdom of heaven. Let us contend for Christ and his righteousness even unto death, so that we may deserve to share in his glory, by the gift of him who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## XIX. On the Same Feast

[Col. 1372D]

Jesus said to his disciples: “As lightning comes forth from the east and appears even to the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matthew XXIV), and the rest.

In this reading from the holy Gospel, dearest brothers, our Lord and Redeemer prepares us for his second coming, showing us six things: namely, how he will come; whom he will gather with himself for judgment; what changes he will make in the order of things; with what signs he will come; what evil he will bestow upon the wicked; and what good he will bestow upon the good.

First, therefore, he indicates by a comparison that his second coming will not be hidden and humble as was his first, but rather manifest and glorious, saying:

“As lightning comes forth from the east and appears even to the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.”

Lightning, moreover, has eight properties. It comes suddenly, openly, with storm, with fire, with brilliance, and with terror; it strikes and burns what is high, and spares what is lowly.

Our Redeemer likewise will come suddenly and unexpectedly for judgment. Hence he himself says: “As in the days of Noah they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, and suddenly the flood came and swept them all away, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Luke XVII). And elsewhere: “For the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians V; 2 Peter III).

He will also come openly, as is shown in this Gospel and in the Psalm: “Our God will come openly” (Psalm XLIX).

He will come with a storm that shakes the elements. He will come with fire that consumes the four elements. Hence it is said there: “Fire will blaze before him, and a mighty storm will rage around him” (ibid.).

He will come with brilliance, since, as he himself said, he will come with glory and majesty (Mark XIII).

He will come with terror, since he will be terrifying to the rejected, although gentle toward the just. This was well signified by the angel who appeared at his resurrection, whose “appearance was like lightning, and his clothing like snow” (Matthew XXVIII).

The Lord will also strike what is high, like lightning, eternally burning with the fire of Gehenna those who are exalted and proud, while sparing the humble, “for the Lord is exalted, and he regards the lowly, but he knows the lofty from afar” (Psalm XLVI).

Second, the Lord demonstrates whom he will gather with himself for judgment when he adds: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will also be gathered.” As though he were saying more plainly: Just as eagles sense corpses even across the sea and gather there, so the heavenly powers and the saints will gather wherever the flesh of the Son of Man will be, in order to judge the world with him, in accordance with the saying: “He will summon heaven above and earth, to distinguish his people” (Psalm XLIX).

Appropriately he used the word “body,” which is more significantly called a corpse, indicating that although Christ died on the cross, although he was placed as if in a tomb, nevertheless he who was judged will come to judge, and all the saints will gather to him as to the bread of life.

The saints are compared to eagles because of three of their properties: they are lifted higher toward heavenly things on the wings of virtues; with the eyes of contemplation they gaze more subtly upon the Sun of righteousness; and they are not corrupted by old age but are renewed like the youth of the eagle.

To deserve to be associated with them, my brothers, let us cast off the oldness of our sins through repentance; let us be renewed from day to day through the newness of virtues; and with the whole desire of our minds let us sigh to see the God of gods in Zion.

Third, the Lord demonstrates what things he will do at his second coming when he adds: “Immediately after the tribulation of those days, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven will be shaken.”

According to the literal sense, the sun, moon, and stars will for a time be deprived of their light, in order to signify the imminent coming of the Lord; but afterward, when the world has been renewed, they will receive a greater light.

There will also be such great brightness from the true Sun and from the saints who come for judgment that, by comparison with them, the sun and moon will be darkened, and the stars will fall from their brightness. And there will be such severity from the strict Judge against the rejected that the powers and authorities of heaven will be shaken—not because they themselves are afraid, but because they see such severity being exercised.

Hence Job says: “The pillars of heaven tremble and fear at his coming” (Job XXVI). And if the angels will tremble, my brothers, how much more human beings? And if, as the Apostle says, “the righteous will scarcely be saved” (1 Peter IV), where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?

In the mystical sense, many who here seemed, through the rays of good works, to illuminate the world like the sun and moon will be darkened when the Lord comes, “who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and disclose the counsels of hearts” (1 Corinthians IV). Many who seemed to shine like stars will fall, and those who here seemed firm like the powers of heaven will collapse.

Fourth, the Lord also shows with what signs he will come to judgment when he adds: “And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven.”

Just as, when an earthly king comes with his cavalry, his standards commonly go before him, so, my brothers, it will happen when the Lord comes to judgment. The standard of the holy cross will go before him.

This will happen for three reasons. The first is to show what the sign of his victory is—the sign that previously seemed to be one of disgrace and humiliation. The second is to inspire joy in those who love him and bear his cross. The third is to bring shame and fear upon those who crucified him and those who despise his cross.

Hence it is written: “Every eye will see him, even those who pierced him” (Revelation I).

They also relate that he will then display the marks of the wounds that he bore for us and reproach the rejected with them.

Therefore, my brothers, let us love him who was crucified for us, and, as far as we can, let us carry his cross. Let us crucify within ourselves the desires of the flesh and the love of the world. Let us endure poverty, humility, insults, injuries, infirmities, and pains with patience. Let us show compassion and mercy toward pitiable persons. Let us not fear to suffer every hardship in hope of the kingdom of heaven. Let us contend for Christ even unto death, so that we may deserve to behold Christ crucified at the judgment with confidence.

Fifth, the Lord demonstrates what evil the wicked will suffer at the judgment when he adds: “And then all the tribes of the earth will mourn”—that is, some from all the tribes who persecuted Christ or despised him in this world.

He then gives the reason why they will mourn: namely, because they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven, just as he ascended in the clouds of heaven. He will come, I say, with great power and majesty, to repay each person according to his works.

The rejected will indeed mourn and repent, with their own conscience accusing them inwardly, but too late, since that mourning and repentance will not be purgative but the beginning of eternal misery. In that misery there will be mourning without consolation, repentance without pardon, pain without remedy, torment without relief, burning without dew, punishment without hope, and death without end.

Sixth, the Lord demonstrates what good he will bestow upon his own when he adds: “And he will send angels with a trumpet and a loud voice”—a voice so immense and powerful that it can awaken all the dead, wherever they may be, and summon them to judgment.

“And they will gather,” he says, “his elect from the four winds”—that is, from all parts of the world—“from the heights of the heavens to their farthest bounds,” that is, from every place beneath heaven, from the interior regions to the furthest ends of the earth.

These are the reaping angels who, according to the Gospel parable, will gather the weeds and the wheat together. But they will gather the weeds into bundles to be burned, while they will gather the wheat into the heavenly granary (Matthew XIII).

Therefore, brothers, so that we may then deserve to be gathered not to fire but to life, let us keep the fear of the final judgment always before our eyes. Let us always consider how terrifying the supreme Judge will come. Let us wash away our sins with the tears of repentance. Let us despise all transitory things and hasten with our whole desire toward those eternal goods. Let us love God above all things, and our neighbor as ourselves.

And if we desire to find that Judge merciful toward us then, let us now be merciful. Let us have compassion on those who suffer. Let us feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, welcome the stranger, visit the sick, and redeem the imprisoned, so that then we may deserve to be fed, given drink, clothed, welcomed, and consoled eternally by the supreme Judge, by the gift of him who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## How the Lord’s Cross Was Found, from Eutropius the Historian, Book II of *Roman Affairs*, in the Account of Flavius Constantine

The mother of the emperor Constantine, named Helena, having been warned in a dream, hastened to Jerusalem and, although with the greatest difficulty, found Christ’s tomb covered with filth. A temple of Venus had been built above it, where virgins mocked with their songs. She ordered the most wicked structure to be destroyed, and the very dust, polluted by funeral sacrifices, to be removed and scattered far from the city.

Then, when she commanded the place to be cleansed, the Lord’s monument immediately appeared openly. Around it three crosses were also found, dug into the ground, together with the nails and the inscription written in Greek and Latin letters: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.”

It is said that a dead person also rose again when touched by the cross. Concerning this wood, the Sibyl said among the Rigani: “O thrice-blessed wood upon which God was stretched!”

Then they began to doubt which cross was the Lord’s and which belonged to the thieves. Accordingly, Macarius, bishop of the city, resolved the doubt by an act of this kind. Bringing one of the crosses, with fervent prayer, to a woman of distinguished birth who had been worn down by a long illness, he recognized the power of the Savior. As soon as the cross touched the woman, it drove away the torment of her most severe illness and restored the woman to health.

See Paulinus’s eleventh letter to Severus, where he treats the finding of the Lord’s cross at length.

## XX. On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist

[Col. 1376A]

“Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you, and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you, and I appointed you a prophet among the nations” (Jeremiah I), and the rest.

These, dearest brothers, are the words addressed to the prophet Jeremiah concerning his election as a prophet. But since they also apply no less to the blessed Forerunner of the Lord, they are appropriately recited at his nativity, which we celebrate today.

This reading has four parts. First, the Lord says that he predestined Jeremiah as a prophet. Second, Jeremiah excuses himself. Third, the Lord consoles him. Fourth, he entrusts him with the ministry of prophecy.

As the Lord was about to send Jeremiah to the office of prophecy, lest he, conscious of his own inexperience and weakness, refuse the office entrusted to him, he first demonstrates that he himself had been chosen for this purpose, saying:

“Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you”—that is, I approved and chose you—“and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you, and I appointed you a prophet among the nations.”

Behold, my brothers, how marvelous and astonishing is the effect of divine predestination: it chooses a person before he exists; it cleanses him before he emerges from uncleanness; before he speaks, it makes him a prophet, in accordance with what is written of God: “He makes the things that are to be.” And elsewhere: “He calls those things that are not as though they were” (Romans IV).

What is said here about Jeremiah applies similarly, indeed more excellently, to the most holy Forerunner of the Lord. The Lord likewise chose him before he formed him in the womb; indeed, he foretold through the prophets that he would come and announced through an angel that he would be born.

He also sanctified him before he came forth from the womb; indeed, according to the word of the archangel, he filled him with the Holy Spirit from his mother’s womb.

Likewise, before he came forth from the womb, he appointed him by predestination as a prophet among the nations; indeed, through prophetic joy and through the mouth of his mother, he caused him to prophesy the coming of Christ in the womb of the holy Virgin.

Behold how all these things apply more excellently to blessed John than to Jeremiah.

Let none of you, my brothers, take from the words spoken here—“Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you”—an occasion for error by supposing that the Lord chose either Jeremiah or John because he foresaw that they would become good. It was not their good life that was the cause of divine predestination; rather, divine predestination was the cause of their good life.

For he chose nothing else in them except what he was going to accomplish in them. It is therefore as though he were saying: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you”—that is, before I formed you in the womb, I chose in you what I was going to form in you.

Thus, my brothers, the fact that the Lord predestines his own from eternity, sanctifies them in time, and continually arouses them to do good is wholly a matter of divine grace, not human merit.

Conversely, the fact that in his foreknowledge he eternally rejected the ungodly, that he withdraws his grace from them in time, and that he abandons them to do evil belongs to divine judgment and human merit.

Therefore, my brothers, let us unceasingly beseech his immense mercy with all the depths of our hearts, so that he may deign to rescue us, his unworthy servants, from the mass of perdition and count us among his elect.

The second part follows, in which Jeremiah excuses himself from the office of prophecy, saying: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am a child.”

Behold, my brothers: although Jeremiah had heard from God that he had been chosen by him, sanctified, and appointed as a prophet, nevertheless he shows that he shrinks from and fears the grave and dangerous office of prophecy. By the expressive interjection he says: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God!” As though he were saying: Lord God, whom I am bound to serve and obey, I dread the office to which you wish to send me, because it exceeds my strength.

He shows why he fears it when he adds: “Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am a child.” I am a child in age; I am a child in eloquence; I am a child in inexperience; I am a child in timidity.

Each of these four conditions impedes the office of preaching. A child in age is not yet able to speak perfectly; a child in eloquence does not know how to speak fluently; a child in inexperience does not know how to speak prudently; a child in timidity does not dare to speak boldly.

John the Baptist, however, because he began to prophesy in his mother’s womb, is not recorded as having excused himself. He merely showed himself unworthy of the office of prophecy when, asked by the Pharisees who he was and whether he was a prophet, he denied that he was a prophet (John I).

He openly excuses himself from the office of baptizing our Redeemer when, overcome with awe, he says: “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” (Matthew III.)

Some therefore excuse themselves laudably, like Jeremiah and John the Baptist; others offer themselves laudably, like Isaiah, who, when the Lord said, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” replied: “Here am I; send me” (Isaiah VI).

It must nevertheless be considered that Isaiah, who offered himself, knew that he had already been cleansed either by a coal or by a small stone taken from the altar. Jeremiah and John the Baptist, although they excuse themselves, do not openly reject the office.

But who, my brothers, understands himself to be cleansed today? For this reason, today the office of preaching is declined more safely than it is sought. Yet the person who understands that he has been called by God ought not to decline it stubbornly.

Moses demonstrates both attitudes in himself. When the Lord sent him to Pharaoh, he excused himself, yet when the Lord persisted he humbly obeyed (Exodus IV), giving us an example: however approved we may be, we should always fear the pastoral office; but if we recognize that it is the divine will, we should not resist altogether.

By this, the presumption of certain people is refuted. Although they are conscious that they are not clean but rather polluted, they nevertheless do not fear the pastoral office; indeed, they seek it eagerly.

Those too are refuted who take from the fact that Jeremiah prophesied as a child an example of error for themselves, supposing that they too, while still beardless, ought to preach. They do not consider that what was lacking in Jeremiah because of age was supplied by grace, and that the privileges of the few do not establish a common law.

Those also are refuted who, although they do not possess eloquence of speech, attempt to preach. But how will they preach if they do not know how to speak?

Likewise those are refuted who, although they do not possess the teaching of wisdom, dare to preach. How will they teach others if they do not know how to teach themselves?

No less are those refuted who, although they do not possess strength of mind, presume to undertake the office of preaching. How will they preach to principalities and powers if they do not dare to rebuke them?

The Psalmist shows himself to be free from this timidity when he says: “I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not ashamed” (Psalm CXVIII).

The third part follows, in which the Lord consoles and strengthens the prophet’s fear, saying:

“Do not say, ‘I am a child,’ for you will go to all those to whom I send you, and you will speak everything that I command you. Do not be afraid of their presence, for I am with you, to rescue you.”

As though he were saying plainly: Although you are a child in age, I will give you the ability to do what I send you to do. Although you are a child in eloquence and understanding, I will give you eloquence and wisdom so that you can proclaim my commands. Although you are a child in timidity, I command you not to fear your adversaries, because I am always with you for steadfastness and defense.

Moreover, in saying, “You will go to all those to whom I send you,” he shows that a prophet or preacher must always go to those to whom he has been sent, but must never go to those to whom he has not been sent.

Hence Jonah experienced divine indignation: he was fleeing from going to preach to the Ninevites, to whom he had been sent (Jonah I). Balaam too was condemned: corrupted by payment, he went to curse the people blessed by God, although he had not been sent to them (Numbers XXIV).

There are certain false pastors like them even today. Corrupted by favor or hatred, by fear or payment, they go to absolve those who ought to be bound, or to bind those who ought to be absolved; and, according to the prophet, they “give life to souls that do not live, and put to death souls that do not die” (Ezekiel III).

“But I will curse,” says the Lord God, “your blessings, and I will bless your curses” (Malachi II).

By saying, “You will speak everything that I command you,” he shows that a prophet or preacher must always preach the words of God and no others.

Accordingly, those are equally refuted who remain silent about the word of the preaching entrusted to them—because of which they are called “mute dogs” by the Lord (Isaiah LVI), and the blood of those who perish is required from them on account of their silence—and those who presume to preach words other than the Lord’s, although the Lord says to Ezekiel: “You shall announce to them from me” (Ezekiel III).

By saying, “Do not be afraid of their presence, for I am with you,” the Lord also refutes those preachers who fear human beings; for by this they demonstrate that they do not have God with them. If they have God with them, why do they fear human beings?

Therefore, we preachers ought to imitate Jeremiah and John the Baptist. They did not fear the savagery of the Jews or the power of kings, but harshly rebuked their vices.

For John the Baptist cries out against the Jews: “Brood of vipers, who taught you to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matthew III; Luke III.)

And against Herod: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Mark VI).

But how did the Lord rescue them from their persecutors, when Jeremiah was stoned by the Jews in Egypt and John was beheaded by Herod?

He rescued them, my brothers, from their persecutors, not by preventing them from afflicting and killing them, but by ensuring that they did them no harm; indeed, they benefited them by giving them an occasion for a crown.

The fourth part follows, in which the Lord assigns Jeremiah the prophetic office. When he stretches out his hand and touches his mouth, he says: “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth; behold, I have appointed you today over nations and over kingdoms, to uproot, to destroy, to ruin, to overthrow, to build, and to plant.” Since Jeremiah had been sanctified from the womb, his lips are not cleansed as Isaiah’s were; rather, by the touch of his hand—that is, by the efficacy of his power—he bestows on him three things necessary to a prophet or preacher: namely, abundance of speech, the rank of authority, and the exercise of ministry.

He shows that he has given him abundance of speech when he says: “Behold, I have given my words into your mouth.” “I have given,” as though he had not sold them. Therefore, because you have received freely, give freely. In this he condemns those who sell the word of preaching. He also says, “my words,” as though they were not someone else’s. In this he condemns those who preach not the words of God, but the words of dialectic, rhetoric, or some secular discipline. Again, he says, “in your mouth,” as though to say: “I have placed my words in your mouth, so that you may preach with your own mouth, not with another’s.” In this he shames those who, disdaining to teach the flock entrusted to them, and from whose stipends they live, wish to teach them through the tongue of hirelings. Yet, as the Lord testifies, “the sheep do not listen to the voice of strangers” (John 10).

He shows that he has given him the rank of authority when he says: “Behold, I have appointed you today over nations and over kingdoms.” “I have appointed you,” he says, as though you had not thrust yourself forward through ambition, as many—lamentably—do today, but that I chose and appointed you. For no one ought to assume the honor for himself, but only he who has been called by God, as Aaron was (Heb. 5). He also says, “over nations,” because a prophet or preacher ought to stand above the nations in rank, life, and wisdom alike, so that he may govern those beneath him by example and teaching. For it is most shameful when a priest is like the people. This plainly applies against certain preachers of today, who in life and wisdom not only do not stand above the people but are even beneath them. Hence they neither dare nor know how to correct them.

But because they do not dare to correct rulers, he adds, “and over kingdoms,” that is, over kings, since the excellence of a prophet or shepherd ought to be so great that he should govern not only the peoples but even the kings themselves. Yet this should not be understood as dominion over human beings, but over vices. Hence the Gospel says: “Let the greater among you become as the younger, and the leader as one who serves” (Luke 22).

He shows that he has given the prophet the exercise of ministry when he adds: “To uproot and to destroy,” and so forth. It is as though he were plainly saying: “I have not appointed you over nations and kingdoms so that you may devote yourself to sleep and idleness, but rather so that you may labor diligently like a farmer who, intending to make a good planting in his field, first uproots from it thorns and thistles and whatever else is harmful.”

He names six things, four of which remove evils and two of which establish good things. Some harmful things in a field can be uprooted easily by the farmer, roots and all. Others are so deeply rooted that he cannot uproot them, but destroys them with much labor and a cutting blade. Others lie hidden, like roots; turning them over with the mattock and plow so that they cannot revive, he destroys them with fire. Still others are naturally produced by the earth, such as flints; because they cannot be entirely removed, he often breaks them apart with a sickle. There are also good plants that the field perhaps produced spontaneously, such as a vine, a wild apple tree, or something similar; these he does not destroy but rather builds up. Finally, there are excellent plants of which the field was entirely devoid; these the farmer diligently seeks out and plants.

So, my brothers, so must the preacher act, since he is like the spiritual cultivator of the Church. First he must remove evils, then sow good things; for it is written: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36). Let him uproot from the hearts of his people by easy correction those vices that cling less deeply. But those that have fixed their roots more deeply, let him destroy with great care and repeated threats of eternal damnation. Those also that lie hidden—such as thoughts and the causes of vices—let him seek out through careful investigation, overturn through each person’s own confession, and destroy by the fire of compunction and divine love. But those things that human nature naturally produces, which a human being cannot entirely cast off while in this life—such as greed for food, covetousness, and concern for temporal affairs—let him break apart and restrain with the sickle of moderation.

The good habits that nature naturally produces in certain people—such as natural piety, natural justice, and natural truthfulness—the good preacher should not destroy, but rather build up. Those virtues that were entirely absent, let him plant through frequent admonition and commendation.

Thus, my brothers, the Lord commanded; thus Jeremiah also acted, and so did John the Baptist. He uproots and destroys when he cries: “Behold, the axe is placed at the root of the tree. Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. 3). He builds and plants when he cries: “Bear fruits worthy of repentance. Whoever has two tunics, let him give one to the one who has none; and whoever has provisions, let him do likewise” (Luke 3).

Therefore, my brothers, at the exhortation of the Lord’s forerunner, let us uproot from our hearts, through true repentance and amendment, the thorns of vices—namely gluttony, drunkenness, lust, greed, anger, envy, sloth, vainglory, pride, and the other vices—and let holy virtues spring up in us: abstinence, sobriety, chastity, generosity, gentleness, charity, devotion, contempt for the world, humility, and the other virtues. Thus worthily adorned, may we deserve to take part joyfully and endlessly in the continual celebrations of the heavenly wedding feast, through him who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## XXI. On the Same Feast

“The time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son” (Luke 1), and what follows. Today, dearest brothers, throughout the entire world we celebrate the venerable birth of the holy forerunner and Baptist of the Lord, an honor that we bestow upon no other saint. The Church celebrates the departures of the saints, by which they are born into eternal life. But in the births by which human beings are born into misery and punishment, she customarily remains silent.

The birth of the forerunner, however, is solemnly celebrated because it is honored by the Lord with eight privileges. The first honor is that God the Father foretold his birth long beforehand, saying through the mouth of the prophet Malachi to his Son: “Behold, I send my angel, who will prepare the way before your face” (Mal. 3; Mark 1).

The second is that through the same archangel through whom he was going to announce his Only-Begotten Son to the Virgin, he announced to the father that this man would be born.

The third is that he not only sanctified him in his mother’s womb but also filled him with the Holy Spirit.

The fourth is that at the arrival of the most holy Virgin, carrying the Son of God in her womb, he caused him to leap in the womb and to prophesy through his mother’s mouth—something unheard of from the beginning of the world—as Luke clearly demonstrates in the preceding passages of his Gospel.

The fifth is that he was wondrously born contrary to nature from a barren mother and two aged parents. Hence we have just heard at the beginning of the Gospel reading: “The time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son.” It is as though it were said: “Elizabeth, whose time for bearing children had already passed, miraculously, through the Lord’s working, found the time for giving birth fulfilled in the days of her old age, and she bore a son.” And fittingly he was born from an old man and a barren woman, since he came to proclaim the one who would be born from a virgin, so that one born wondrously might reveal even more wondrously the one who was to be born.

The sixth honor is the joy at his birth. Hence it is added: “And his neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had magnified his mercy toward her, and they rejoiced with her.” For the archangel had foretold concerning the Lord’s forerunner that many would rejoice at his birth (Luke 1). This was fulfilled on the very day of his birth, when not only his parents rejoiced at the gift of so great a son, but his neighbors and relatives also rejoiced with them; and those farther away were moved by astonishment and wonder at the novelty of so great an event. The same thing is fulfilled each year, since the faithful everywhere on earth rejoice and exult at the glorious solemnity of his Nativity. Since other children of human beings are born in sins and sadness, it is no wonder if we rejoice at the birth of him who was born in sanctification and joy, and who came to announce joy to the whole world.

The seventh honor is that at the declaration of his name, speech is restored to his father. When they had gathered to circumcise the child, and his relatives called him Zachariah after his father, while his mother, instructed—as we believe—by the Spirit, called him John, his mute father, wishing to remove all doubt, indicated his name both in writing and by voice, as he had received it from the angel, saying: “John is his name.” Fittingly, the man who had lost his speech through disbelief concerning the son who was to be born recovers it when naming the son who had been born, and blesses and magnifies God’s mercy toward him.

Struck by wonder at this event, not only the neighbors but also those farther away considered and conjectured among themselves with how many virtues he would shine in his life who was already radiant with such great virtues at his birth. He is rightly called John, that is, “grace,” since he came to preach grace. “The law and the prophets were until John” (Luke 16), and from John the time of grace begins.

The eighth honor is that through the grace of the prophet-son, the father himself also becomes a prophet. Hence it is added: “And his father Zachariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying: Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and wrought redemption for his people.” In this hymn he does three things. First, he blesses the Lord for the fulfillment of the promise made to the fathers. Second, he shows that the infant prophet will prepare the Lord’s ways. Third, he declares that the true light has risen from on high to illuminate the darkness of the world. Hence the holy Church customarily sings this hymn at morning praises.

Since, therefore, the birth of the forerunner is distinguished by these eight gifts, it is celebrated throughout the world by the holy Church. Two of these gifts, namely the last two, are fulfilled on the eighth day at the circumcision; therefore the feast of the Nativity itself is solemnly extended to the eighth day.

Morally, my brothers, six things are set before us for imitation in this reading.

First, because the Lord gives a son to a barren and aged woman, an example is offered to us: no sinner, however barren of goodness and however long he has grown old in sin, should ever despair of the fruit of repentance, even at the very threshold of life. Rather, he should always hope in the ineffable mercy of God, which never rejects anyone, however wicked, who wishes to be converted. This mercy made Mary Magdalene holy from such foulness, and did not deny the mercy requested by the thief already expiring on the cross.

Second, because the neighbors and relatives rejoice with Elizabeth over her good fortune, an example is offered to us that we too should rejoice in the good conduct and conversion of others. If, as the Lord testifies, there is joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance (Luke 16), how much more ought human beings especially to rejoice at the conversion and amendment of human beings? This plainly stands against certain malicious people who customarily not only fail to rejoice in the good of others but even grieve over it through envy. But, my brothers, just as it belongs to godly people to rejoice at the good of others and grieve at their evils, so it belongs to devilish people to grieve at the good of others and rejoice at their evils.

Third, because the child is called not by his father’s name but by the name John, that is, “grace,” an example is offered to us that we should never attribute our good work to our own name, but rather to divine grace, which alone gives both the will and the power to accomplish it (Phil. 2). He himself testifies to this when he says to his disciples: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). This plainly stands against certain arrogant people who, if they have done anything wisely or bravely, attribute it to their own intelligence or strength, as though saying: “Our mighty hand, and not God, has done all these things” (Deut. 32).

Fourth, because at the declaration of the name of grace the mouth of the mute father is opened to bless God, it is shown to us that only those can worthily bless and praise God who attribute entirely to God’s grace—not to their own name—the good they do. Just as God is more provoked by the devilish presumption by which someone attributes to himself what belongs to God, so God is more pleased by the humility by which a person thinks humbly of himself and attributes to God everything good that he possesses.

Fifth, because, on account of the miracles that had been seen, fear came upon the neighbors, and all these words were spread throughout the hill country of Galilee, an example is offered to us that, when we see the virtues of God and of godly people, we should learn to fear God and always and everywhere proclaim works of virtue. This plainly stands against certain malicious people who either deny or silence the virtues and good works that God performs through his saints, while they immediately believe and spread abroad people’s sins and evil works.

Sixth, because the mute father was rightly granted not only speech but also prophecy on account of his son, an example is offered to us: often those who had previously been mute in praising and preaching God, if they begin to bear fruit and live well, are granted not only the ability to praise God worthily but also an increased grace of teaching and preaching. Conversely, it very often happens that certain people who were previously suited to teaching, either by natural talent or by diligence, are later blinded because of their sins and deprived of their former grace, according to what is written: “To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will abound; but from the one who has nothing, even what he seemed to have will be taken away” (Matt. 13; Mark 4).

Therefore, my brothers, let us cast off through repentance the barrenness and old age of our sins, and let us bear fruit in new life through good works. Let us attribute the good works we possess not to our own name but to divine grace. Let us always bless God’s mercy toward us. Let us strive to convert others to God by good example and word. Let us pursue mercy and charity above all. Let us despise the world and sigh for God with our whole desire, so that, through the intercession of blessed John the Baptist, whose feast we celebrate today, we may be able to reach the eternal festivals, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1383D] It is found in his book *On the Lives of the Prophets*.]

### The Life and Death of the Divine John the Baptist, written by Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus

John the Baptist, born of Zachariah and Elizabeth, arose from the tribe of Levi. He is the one who, as though with a finger, points out to us the Lamb, the Son of God the Father, who takes away the sins of the world. He constructed a road for mortals and opened the gates of the kingdom of God. Truly, no one among those born of women is greater than John the Baptist. He completed his life and was beheaded by the tyrant Herod because of Herodias, his sister-in-law—that is, the wife of his brother Philip.

### By the same author, St. Isidore, bishop of Seville

[Note: [Col. 1384D] In the book *On the Fathers of the Old Testament*.]

John the Baptist, son of Zachariah, born in Jerusalem from the tribe of Levi, conceived at the announcement of an angel, the forerunner of Christ, the herald of the Judge, the prophet of the Most High, the voice of the Word, the friend of the Bridegroom, the witness of the Lord, the lamp of the Light, the limit of the prophets, the beginning of baptism.

He who, when foretold, took away his parent’s voice, when born released the function of his tongue. Though not yet born, he prophesied Christ; he greeted him from the womb, recognized him in the dove, and pointed him out in the desert. His clothing was camel hair, his dwelling the wilderness, and his food honey and locusts. When he forbade Herod to violate his brother’s marriage, he was consigned to the darkness of prison. The king’s daughter, dancing, demanded his head as a reward from her father. But he, drunk amid the drinking, gave the severed head to his wickedly demanding daughter. He was buried in the Palestinian town of Sebaste, which was formerly called Samaria. Herod, king of Judea and son of Antipater, called it Augusta in the Latin language in honor of Caesar Augustus.

## XXII. On the Feast of the Blessed Apostle Peter

[Col. 1384C]

“King Herod stretched out his hands to afflict some of those belonging to the Church” (Acts 12), and what follows.

In this reading, dearest brothers, three matters must be considered according to the literal sense.

First, for what reason does the omnipotent and just Lord grant the wicked such great power to rage against his saints? I rightly say “grant,” since, as the Apostle says, “there is no authority except from God” (Rom. 13), and our Redeemer also testifies, saying to Pilate: “You would have no authority against me unless it had been given to you from above” (John 19). Hence the devil could do nothing against Job before he had asked the Lord for authority and received it (Job 1).

The Lord therefore gives the wicked power to rage for three reasons.

First, for the testing of the good. What a furnace does for gold, a file for iron, and water for cloth, tribulation does for the righteous. Through the testing imposed by the wicked, as though they were his smiths, God files the vessels of election, making them purer, brighter, stronger, and more precious.

Second, for the mockery and condemnation of the wicked, according to what is written: “This dragon, whom you formed to be played with” (Ps. 103). The devil and his members are mocked in this respect: while they desire to harm the saints, they benefit them and harm themselves even more.

Third, for the demonstration of divine wisdom and power, which are so great that God knows how and is able to use the evil works of the wicked for good. Whatever evil they plot against God and his members serves God, who through them and by means of them accomplishes his will and glory.

Second, it must be considered that the Lord does not wish some of his saints to remain longer in this world. Although, if they survived, they might seem likely to benefit both themselves and others greatly, he nevertheless brings them joyfully out of the tribulations of this world, as he did James the Greater, whom, while still young and before the other apostles, he removed from this world by Herod’s sword.

The all-knowing Lord does this for three reasons. First, he knows that they have completed the merits they were destined to possess, according to what is written: “Having been perfected in a short time, he fulfilled many years. For old age is venerable not because of length of time or number of years. The gray hairs of human beings are understanding, and an undefiled life is the measure of old age” (Wis. 4). Thus, although the saints die young, they complete their days, whereas of the wicked it is said: “Men of blood and deceit will not reach half their days” (Ps. 54).

Second, he does this so that they might not at some point stumble and perish on the slippery road of this world, according to what is written: “He was taken away lest wickedness change his understanding or deceit beguile his soul” (Wis. 4). Therefore he hastened to remove him from the midst of iniquity.

Third, the saints are quickly taken from this world because, as the Apostle says, “the world was not worthy” of them (Heb. 11). And therefore, on account of its sins, the world is deprived of the light of the saints. Hence it is written: “The righteous man is taken away, and no one considers it; the just man is removed from the face of iniquity” (Isa. 57).

But whatever the reason, my brothers, that the saints are taken so quickly from this wretched world, things have gone well and blessedly for them, since they have been granted to pass so quickly through the labor and misery of this world and enter everlasting glory.

Third, it must also be considered that the Lord, rescuing other saints powerfully from tribulations, causes them to lead a long life here, as in the case of Peter and John the Evangelist. He does this both for the greater reward of their greater labor, for the consolation and instruction of his Church, and for the confusion and plundering of the opposing party, whom they confound especially when they snatch away their vessels of captivity.

For these reasons, therefore, the Lord reserved Peter longer for his Church and powerfully freed him from Herod’s prison. In this liberation he plainly demonstrates both his mercy and his omnipotence to us. He shows his mercy in that he was moved and took pity on his Church, which was desolate because of the imprisonment of her teacher, in response to her prayers. He shows his power in that he powerfully rescued Peter, who was bound with two chains, surrounded by several guards, and shut in by an iron gate—not through human precaution but through his angel—and mercifully restored him to his Church. By this he shows us that he is always ready to be entreated by the devout prayers of his Church and always powerful to deliver her.

Moreover, the imprisonment and liberation that once took place in Peter occur daily in us. For Herod—that is, the devil, who is the king of all the wicked—daily, with God’s permission, stretches out his hands to afflict as many as he can from the Church. It is not enough for him that he devours pagans, Jews, and other unbelievers every day, unless he also kills in soul those Christians whom he can. Hence the Lord says of him to blessed Job: “He will swallow the river and not be astonished; he trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth” (Job 40). It is as though he were saying: “The devil does not consider it a great matter that he has swallowed almost the whole river—that is, the human race—from the beginning of the world nearly to Christ, unless he also gulps down the Jordan—that is, the baptized—into the belly of his wickedness.”

Nor is it enough for him to kill some of the lesser members of the Church each day; he hastens especially to kill the greater members and prelates of the holy Church. For, as Habakkuk says, “his food is chosen” (Hab. 1). Hence it is said here that he killed James, the brother of John, with the sword, because he kills great despisers and overthrowers of vices with the sword of his temptation.

Seeing that this pleased the Jews—that is, the supporters of his wickedness—he also adds the attempt to seize Peter, that is, the order of steadfast bishops, so that, when the head has been wounded, he may subject the lesser members to himself universally. He does this especially during the days of Unleavened Bread, because during solemnities and fasts, when the faithful discipline themselves toward greater purity, the devil exercises a greater assault against them.

Having seized the sinner through his attacks, he sends him into the depths and darkness of vices. To prevent him from leaving by the gate of repentance, he hands him over to four squads of soldiers for guarding. A *quaternion* is said to be one who has four tyrants under him, just as a centurion has one hundred.

The first quaternion to which the sinner is handed over by the devil for guarding is the spirit of foolish shame, which brings confusion upon the sinner about confessing his sin. Hence Solomon says: “There is a shame that brings sin” (Ecclus. 4). Under it are four things: shame at confessing, shame at humbling oneself before a priest, shame at seeking medicine, and shame at carrying out the penance imposed.

And lest this one prove insufficient to keep the sinner guarded in his sin, a second quaternion is added: the spirit of false security. It likewise has four under it: security concerning a light and remissible fault, security concerning a long life, security that there will be sufficient time to do penance, and security concerning divine mercy.

And lest these two prove insufficient, a third quaternion is added, namely the spirit of obstinacy. It has four things under it: obstinacy in sin, obstinacy in contempt, obstinacy in hardness of heart, and obstinacy in impenitence.

And lest these three prove insufficient, a fourth quaternion is added, namely the spirit of unbelief. It likewise has four things under it: unbelief in the gravity of sin, unbelief in the resurrection, unbelief in the final judgment, and unbelief in eternal punishment.

With these grievous guards, therefore, the devil confines and keeps the sinner in the prison of sins, intending after Easter—that is, after the passage of death—to bring him forth to be tortured by the people of demons.

Thus the sinner is kept in prison. But the Church ought to pray without ceasing to God for him. Hence it is clear that the person who does not pray unceasingly for the children of the Church when they are so greatly imprisoned is truly not of the Church. This plainly stands against certain Christians who, whenever they see their pastor or someone else bound by the chains of sins, not only fail to pray for him but rather rejoice, slander, and defame him. Without doubt they incur the curse of Ham, since, following his example, they do not cover their father’s nakedness but mock it (Gen. 9).

When the devil hopes that he will now bring the sinner who has been so captured forth to eternal punishment, the sinner meanwhile is sleeping between two soldiers in the night of his sins: between the spirit of presumption, which prevents him from escaping on the right, and the spirit of despair, which prevents him from escaping on the left. He is bound with two chains—that is, the love and delight of his sins—which prevent and restrain him from good work and the good way.

“And guards before the door were guarding the prison.” The door of the prison of sins is repentance. The aforementioned quaternions—foolish shame, false security, obstinacy, and unbelief—prevent it from opening to the sinner.

Although the sinner thus sleeps hopelessly in the depths of vices, bound and oppressed, already about to be led forth to eternal damnation, nevertheless, when divine clemency hears the unceasing prayers of its Church, an angel of divine power—or even some preacher—stands by him: one who stands by and makes others stand; and the light of compunction shines upon the one who dwelt in the darkness of sins.

Striking Peter’s side—that is, the sinner’s conscience—he awakens him, saying: “Rise quickly from the sleep of your sins, lest you now be dragged to eternal damnation.” And immediately the chains of the love and delight of sins fall from his hands, because the sins that he previously loved and in which he delighted begin to displease and torment him.

He is prompted to gird and restrain the softness of his wandering thoughts through continence, and to shoe the feet of his affections so that they do not cling to earthly desires. He is also prompted to wrap himself in the garment of charity and the other virtues, and to follow the admonition of salvation.

The sinner rises and follows the angel of saving admonition. Yet, conscious of his own frailty and weakness, he does not think it true that he can escape from the habit of his sins. He is held so firmly by habit that he thinks he cannot abstain.

But, through the Lord’s working, he passes the first guard—that is, the spirit of presumption and despair—and the second, namely foolish shame, false security, obstinacy, and unbelief. At last he comes to the Iron Gate, that is, to the obstacle of an evil and hardened habit, which, through the Lord’s working, is opened to him.

He goes out and proceeds along one street, because after escaping from the habit of sins he advances along the way of good action. Immediately the angel departs from him, since, having been rescued and instructed, he no longer seems to need a guide; indeed, he himself becomes a guide to others.

The sinner, now made righteous, looking back upon the depth of sins from which he has been rescued, comes to himself and says, affirming what he had previously dared not hope of himself: “Now I truly know that the Lord sent his angel and his mercy, and rescued me, unworthy as I am, from the hand of Herod”—that is, the devil—“and from all the expectation of the demons.”

Thus, my brothers, let the person who now knows that he has been rescued by God’s mercy from the former habit of his sins confess and bless the Lord. But whoever still sleeps in the prison of his sins should heed the angel of saving admonition and quickly rise from his sins. Let him gird his loins with the belt of chastity, keep the feet of his affections from clinging to earthly things, fortify himself with the garment of charity and the other virtues, and redeem his sins through works of mercy. Thus, escaping from the prison, the chains, the devil’s double guard, and the iron gate of habit, may he thereafter follow the way of righteousness and bless and confess the Lord’s mercy, now and forever, through the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## XXIII. On the Same Feast
Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi and was questioning his disciples (Matt. 16), and so forth.

In this reading from the holy Gospel, dearest brothers, our Lord and Redeemer does five things. First, he comes into the region of Caesarea Philippi. Second, there he asks and hears what people say about him. Third, he asks and hears whom the disciples believe him to be. Fourth, he commends Peter’s answer. Fifth, he rewards it.

Therefore, intending to obtain from his disciples a confession of their faith, the Lord first leads them into the region of [Col. 1388D] Caesarea Philippi—which is the city that Philip founded in honor of Tiberius Caesar—where, they say, tribute was customarily paid to the ancient kings. And the Lord rightly wished to carry this out especially in that region, so that in the very place where an earthly king once demanded tribute from his subjects, the heavenly King might now demand from his disciples the tribute of confession.

The name also corresponds to this, for “Philip” is interpreted as “the mouth of a lamp.” “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10). Here the Lord shows how he differs from an earthly king: whereas an earthly king demands from his people a tribute of metal, he demands from his own nothing but the tribute of pure confession. Hence he himself says: “Whoever confesses me before men, I also will confess [Col. 1389A] him before my Father” (Matt. 10; Luke 12). This confession is pure when, in the confession of God, there is harmony of heart, mouth, and deed. Otherwise there is neither purity nor integrity of confession, and it can be called merely an admission, not a confession.

Second, the Lord asks what opinion people hold of him when he says: “Whom do men say that the Son of Man is?” This is not because he was ignorant of it—he who knows all things—but so that he might leave an example for us who hold his place in the Church: that we likewise should ask our familiar associates what reputation we have among people. And why? Because, when we are excessively indulgent toward ourselves, we are accustomed to ignore our vices. It is innate in every mind to judge another’s matters more accurately than its own. For in judging our own affairs we are hindered by excessive affection [Col. 1389B].

A monkey likes its little monkey, even though it is ugly; a raven likes its own voice, even though it is hoarse. We too like our vices, even though they are foul and displeasing to others. Therefore, my brothers, let us submit the judgment of our life not to flatterers, who do not know how to speak what is true but only what is agreeable, but to familiar censors of our conduct. Let us charge them not to conceal from us what sort of people we are judged to be either by others or by themselves. If we hear that we have a good reputation, let us attribute the whole of it to God’s grace, not to ourselves, and let us strive to be what we are said to be.

But if we hear ourselves criticized in some respect, let us amend our life for the better and flee not only vices but even the shadows of vices, so that such holiness may shine forth in us as will wipe away every disgrace [Col. 1389C] and close the mouths of those who curse.

“Whom,” he says, “do men say that the Son of Man is?” Here, my brothers, we must ask why our Redeemer so often calls himself not Christ, not Jesus, but rather the Son of Man. He does this for three reasons: to recall to us how much he humbled himself for our sake; to declare frequently, against the Manichaeans, that he possesses true humanity; and to admonish us, by his example, both to think and to speak humbler things about ourselves.

Behold, the Son of God is silent about being the Son of God, but repeatedly calls himself the Son of Man. In this, my brothers, he confounds our pride: we are ashamed to acknowledge our lesser parents, always mention the richer ones, and, like the proverbial mule, when asked [Col. 1389D] who our father was, are ashamed to admit the donkey while boasting that our grandfather was a horse.

As for the answer that some said John the Baptist, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, and still others one of the prophets, it shows that the opinions of the crowd almost always differ and depart from the truth. Therefore, my brothers, we ought not readily to lend the ear of our credulity to popular rumors, lest, if we affirm a popular report and the matter should prove otherwise, we ourselves be found to be liars.

Third, the Lord asks his disciples whom they say he is. He does this for three reasons: to cause them to earn his favor by confessing him; to strengthen them in faith; and to praise and reward their confession.

“But you,” he says, “whom do you say that I am?” Here we should note that, after saying above, [Col. 1390A] “Whom do men say that the Son of Man is?” he now says, “But you, whom do you say that I am?”—as though the disciples were not men. By this, my brothers, he indicates that those who understood only humanly about Christ were “men.” But those who understood divinely about him were not merely men, but gods. They were men who confessed the humanity they saw. They were spiritual and divine who confessed the divinity they did not see.

We too, my brothers, whenever we understand only the things that belong to the flesh, are carnal and natural.

Peter, however, answers the Lord on behalf of all, since it is fitting that he, first among them, should speak first of all and for all: “You are,” he says, “Christ, the Son of the living God.”

In a brief statement Peter embraces everything. He confesses not only [Col. 1390B] the Son, but also the Father and the Holy Spirit, as well as the divine nature and the name. He confesses the Father when he names the Son. In the name “Christ,” that is, “anointed,” he signifies both the Father who anoints and the Spirit who is the anointing. He asserts Christ’s divine nature when he calls him the Son of God. He also indicates his human nature when he calls him Christ, that is, “anointed,” for he could be anointed according to his humanity. He does not omit the name when he calls him Christ, that is, the Messiah promised in the Law.

He also adds “living,” to distinguish him from those whom the pagans considered gods from among the dead or constructed out of lifeless matter. God is called such in three ways: by nature, as Christ; by adoption, as the saints; and by estimation, as Jupiter.

Therefore, my brothers, taught by Peter, let us firmly confess Christ, the Son of the living God, so that through this confession we may, with Peter, be found worthy of adoption into divinity, and let us flee with the utmost care the attribution of divine authority to a creature.

Fourth, the Lord commends Peter’s answer when he says: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona,” that is, “son of John”—understand, blessed in the truth of this confession—“yet you do not have this confession from yourself.” Hence he adds: “For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you,” that is, the nature of flesh and blood, or any merely carnal person, has not revealed it to you. It is as though he said: “You have not received this from yourself or from another human being; rather,” he says, “my Father who is in heaven has revealed it to you.”

Here, my brothers, the presumption of certain people is rebuked: those who rely on their own intelligence and attempt to investigate heavenly things by human reasoning. Such people, as Solomon says, “are crushed by glory” (Prov. 25). Therefore, when they go astray, they do not come together in one confession like the apostles, inspired by the supreme Father; instead, according to their own will, they form various little opinions, like those people who held different views about Christ—some saying that he was John the Baptist, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.

Fifth, the Lord rewards Peter’s answer in four ways: by conferring his own name, by granting primacy, by the power of perseverance, and by office.

He honors Peter by conferring his own name when he calls him Peter from the word “rock.” For just as a rock is firm, suitable for a building, emits sparks, and sends forth water, so Peter was firm in confession [Col. 1391A], most suitable for the building of the Church, sent forth sparks of miracles, and poured out water of wisdom.

He rewards him with primacy when he adds: “And upon this rock I will build my Church.” For just as, although Christ alone is substantially the shepherd, Peter is nevertheless called shepherd from him by denomination; and although Christ alone is substantially the foundation of the Church, Peter and the other apostles are nevertheless called foundations of the Church; so, although Christ alone is the rock, Peter is nevertheless called rock by denomination from him.

Moreover, the Church was founded upon Peter because he supports it by his office, merit, preaching, example, care, and intercession.

He rewards him with the power of perseverance when he adds: “And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” The gates of hell are understood [Col. 1391B] as sins, temptations, torments, or deaths. These do not prevail not only against Christ, but even against Peter armed with Christ’s power, because he dissolves sins, repels temptations, overcomes torments, and conquers death of both soul and body through the resurrection of each.

And he draws not only himself but also many sinners away from those gates and jaws of hell. Nor is it only he, my brothers; anyone faithful who, by correcting, warning, or teaching a sinner, rescues him from the jaws of the devil—what else does he do but break the gates of hell and bring back the vessels of captivity?

He rewards him with office when he adds: “And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose [Col. 1391C] on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.”

Two keys, moreover, are given equally to all the apostles. Hence, after his resurrection, the Lord breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven” (John 20), and so forth. Here, however, the speech is directed to Peter alone, so that it may be shown that whoever does not follow the unity of the Church is deprived of the keys of binding and loosing.

There are two keys: discernment and power. By discernment it is determined who are to be bound and who are to be loosed; by power those who are to be bound are bound, and those who are to be loosed are loosed.

But what shall I say today, my brothers, when many priests lack discernment, and many who possess discernment misuse the power of binding and loosing? The former—for this is to be lamented—do not know who should be bound [Col. 1391D] or who should be loosed. The latter, even when they know, bind someone who should be loosed out of hatred or love, or loose someone who should be bound. But whoever unjustly looses or binds deprives himself of the power of binding or loosing.

For there is one invisible priest, who alone baptizes, alone absolves, and alone binds. His ministers loose or bind solely by ministry, not by any authority of their own; that is, they show that people have been loosed or bound.
