Hence, in Leviticus, lepers are commanded to show themselves to the priests (Lev. 14). The priests do not make them lepers or clean; they discern that they are lepers or clean.

The Lord alone raised Lazarus in the tomb and commanded his disciples to loose the one who had been raised (John 12), not so that they might raise him, but so that they might show that he had been raised.

[Col. 1392A] But when a priest either lacks discernment or looses or binds unjustly, the one whom God binds is not loosed, nor is the one whom God looses bound. Nevertheless, the shepherd’s sentence, whether just or unjust, must be feared, lest, if you despise it, you become bound through that very contempt.

Let us therefore pray, my brothers, to Peter, shepherd of our souls, that by his merits and prayers he may obtain for us absolution from our sins, grant it to us through his office, protect us from the devil by his care, govern us by his rule, and lead us to the pastures of eternal green growth; through the gift of God himself, our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1392B] The Life of Saint Peter, Prince of the Apostles, by Saint Jerome, in the book *On Illustrious Men*.

Simon Peter, son of John, from the province of Galilee, from the village of Bethsaida, brother of the apostle Andrew and prince of the apostles, after his episcopate of the Church of Antioch and his preaching to the dispersion of those who had believed from the circumcision, proceeded to Rome in the second year of Claudius to defeat Simon Magus. There he held the priestly chair for twenty-five years, until the final year of Nero, that is, the fourteenth. By Nero he was fastened to a cross and crowned with martyrdom, with his head turned toward the earth and his feet raised upward, declaring himself unworthy to be crucified in the same manner as his Lord.

Concerning him Haymo also speaks as follows in the book *On the Memory of Christian Matters*: “Nero condemns Peter and Paul, leaders and standard-bearers of the apostles of Judea and of the people of God, in that very city of Rome: one by the sword, the other by the punishment of the cross. Peter is crucified with his head lowered [Col. 1392C] because he requested that he not appear equal to his Lord.”

See Eusebius, book II, chapter 25; and Epiphanius, book I, volume II, *Against Heresies*; and Dorotheus, bishop, in the *Synopsis*.

XXIV. ON THE FEAST OF BLESSED PAUL.

“I make known to you the Gospel that was preached by me, because it is not according to man” (Gal. 1), and so forth.

Many, my brothers—not only pagans and Jews, but also, which is more grievous, certain false Christians—when they hear the simplicity of the Gospel narrative, think that it is nothing other than a human invention, or the teaching of Plato, Cicero, and others. Against them the Apostle speaks in the reading we have just heard.

[Col. 1392D] He does three things. First, he says that the Gospel is not according to man. Second, he says that it was delivered to him not by man but by God. Third, he demonstrates this by a certain argument.

He says, then: “I make known to you the Gospel that was preached by me, because it is not according to man.”

From this, my brothers, it is clear that the Gospel is not according to man, because it is above man. The height of the Gospel surpasses every height of human reason. No human reasoning can reach the height of the Trinity or of the other mysteries that the Gospel commands us to believe, nor the height of the rewards that it commands us to hope for.

The humility of the Gospel likewise surpasses all human humility. No human being can sufficiently marvel at, much less [Col. 1393A] follow, the humility of the Son of God, who humbled himself from the height of divine majesty to such an extent that he took from a woman the form of his servant; that God subjected himself to man and ministered to him; and that, for the sake of his servant and from his servant, he endured insults, injuries, and death.

The righteousness of the Gospel also far surpasses every human righteousness, even that handed down in the Law. For it condemns not only murder but also insult and anger. It condemns not only evil action but also evil will. It not only forbids perjury but also oaths. It commands that enemies be not merely free from hatred but also loved.

The mercy of the Gospel likewise exceeds all human mercy. It commands us to show mercy not only to the miserable but also to enemies; to have compassion [Col. 1393B] not only on the need of the afflicted but also on the madness of the wicked; to pray for persecutors and to do good to enemies.

That the Gospel is above man is therefore evident from these things. That it is from God appears from this: it was ordained from eternity by God the Father, prefigured by the Holy Spirit through the patriarchs, foretold through the prophets, announced through the angels, fulfilled and proclaimed by the Son, and preached everywhere by the Holy Spirit through the apostles.

To confirm this, there are also works of virtue. For the sake of this faith, the saints despised the whole world, distributed everything they possessed to the poor, followed the naked Christ naked, crucified their flesh with its vices and desires, shone in chastity, charity, [Col. 1393C] and the other virtues, stretched toward heavenly things with their whole desire, bravely endured insults, injuries, tortures, and inhuman and unbearable deaths, and through these things gloriously reached the heavenly realm.

There are also works of miracles. Through this faith the blind were given sight, the demon-possessed were freed, many thousands of people were fed from a few loaves, the sick were healed, the dead were raised, people walked upon the waters, fire was extinguished so that it would not harm the saints, poison was drunk without injury. Through this faith serpents did not harm, wild beasts obeyed, birds ministered, the elements submitted, and the lower regions were opened.

Whoever therefore does not believe that the Gospel is from God is without God.

The second part follows, in which the Apostle says [Col. 1393D] that the Gospel was delivered to him not by man but by God, when he adds: “For I neither received it from man, nor learned it, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ.”

The Apostle says that he received neither the ministry of preaching the Gospel nor the Gospel itself from man or learned it from man, but received it through the revelation of Jesus Christ. He was sent to the office of preaching together with Barnabas when the Holy Spirit said, as it is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles: “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have appointed them” (Acts 13)—that is, for preaching to the Gentiles.

Hence Paul and Barnabas were called apostles of the Gentiles, as the Apostle himself testifies: “He who worked through Peter for the apostleship among the circumcised also worked through me among the Gentiles, and they recognized the grace that was given to me by Christ” (Gal. [Col. 1394A] 2).

He learned the Gospel itself through the revelation of Jesus Christ, either when he remained blinded on the road to Damascus, or when for three days in Damascus he neither ate nor drank while praying. Hence, immediately entering the synagogues, he confounded the Jews, affirming that this man is the Christ.

Or he learned it when he was caught up to the third heaven, or when he was caught up into paradise and heard words that it is not permitted for a human being to speak.

Truly blessed is Paul, who was deemed worthy to receive the truth of the Gospel not from an interpreter or through any intermediary, but from the very author of the Gospel, and who was suddenly made perfect in it, without delay, practice, or labor.

But we, brothers, who have gradually learned the truth of the Gospel from a human being, shall be blessed in this respect if we hold it [Col. 1394B] firmly in our hearts and confess it steadfastly even amid torments. But if—which God forbid!—we confess the Gospel in words and deny it in our deeds, what else do we do but condemn ourselves by our voice, becoming like Judas the traitor, who betrayed in deed the Christ whom he confessed and greeted as his teacher?

The third part follows, in which the Apostle demonstrates that he did not learn the Gospel from man. He demonstrates this in two ways: first, through times and deeds; second, through an oath.

He demonstrates it through times and deeds when he says: “For you have heard of my manner of life formerly in Judaism, how beyond measure I persecuted the Church of God and ravaged it, and advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries [Col. 1394C] among my people, being more exceedingly zealous for the traditions of my fathers,” and so forth.

It is as though he plainly said: “From this it is evident that I did not learn the Gospel from man, either before or after my conversion.”

That I did not learn it before my conversion is clear from my deeds. Before my conversion I did not follow the Gospel; rather, I persecuted it. I did not learn the Gospel; rather, I attacked it.

That I did not learn the Gospel from man after my conversion likewise appears from my deeds. For after my conversion I did not go to Christ’s apostles in order to learn the Gospel from them. Rather, I immediately went to Arabia to preach the Gospel; and after preaching it there, I returned to Damascus and preached it there.

He says this in these words: “When it pleased him who set me apart”—that is [Col. 1394D], who drew me out from my mother’s womb, or separated me from the pit of my native unbelief—“and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me, so that I might preach him among the Gentiles, immediately I did not submit to flesh and blood,” that is, to the counsel of my kindred, carnal people.

In Greek it is expressed more clearly, namely: “I did not confer with flesh and blood,” that is, with a human being, about the Gospel.

This is stated still more clearly when he adds: “Nor did I go to the apostles who were my predecessors, but I went to Arabia, and from there returned to Damascus.”

In these words the Apostle gives three reasons for his calling.

He gives the first when he says, “When it pleased him,” and when he adds, “and called me through his grace.” He says openly: “He called me not because of my merits, which were nothing but evil, but solely because of his good pleasure [Col. 1395A] and his grace.” In this, my brothers, he gives us an example, so that we may think the same about ourselves.

He gives the second reason when he says: “To reveal his Son in me,” that is, the mercy of his Son. For this reason the Lord called Paul, Mary Magdalene, and persons of this kind who had committed crimes: so that in them he might demonstrate the surpassing mercy of his Son, who came into this world to seek sinners whom he would save.

It is as though he said: “God called me, a great sinner, for this reason: to demonstrate in me that no sinner, however great, ought to despair of God’s mercy.” In this, my brothers, he gives us sinners an example of always accusing our faults and always proclaiming God’s mercy.

He gives the third reason when he adds: [Col. 1395B] “So that I might preach him among the Gentiles.” For this reason God called him, as he himself said to Ananias: so that he might carry his name before the Gentiles, kings, and the children of Israel.

Indeed, for these three reasons God calls not only Paul but also every one of us sinners each day. God calls us, dearest brothers, solely because of his good pleasure; he calls us so that he may reveal his great mercy in us; he calls us so that we may always and everywhere proclaim his immeasurable goodness.

When the Apostle says, “Immediately I did not submit to flesh and blood,” he shows the swift effectiveness of the divine calling in his own case: it made him so quickly good from evil, spiritual from carnal, and wise from foolish. God does not know delay; [Col. 1395C] he suddenly changes the mind, suddenly teaches, suddenly heals.

Here those people are refuted who, when they see someone guilty of crimes, despair of his amendment and say: “How can this man become good, since he is so evil?” They do not consider how quickly God changed Paul, how quickly he changed Magdalene, how quickly he changed the thief, and made such good people from such evil ones.

In the fact that Paul, converted at that moment, immediately hastens so energetically, going and returning for the sake of preaching, he demonstrates the fervor of his conversion. Just as he had previously been fervent in persecuting the Gospel and destroying souls, so afterward—or rather, even more—he became fervent in preaching the Gospel and gaining souls.

In this, brothers, the tepidity of myself and those like me is confounded. Just as I was never very fervent [Col. 1395D] in great wickedness, so I am not fervent in great goodness, failing to consider what the Lord says in the Apocalypse to people of this kind: “I wish that you were cold or hot; but because you are neither cold nor hot, I am beginning to vomit you out of my mouth” (Apoc. 3).

Human nature is that of a fervent mind: whatever people do, whether good or evil, they do it fervently. Conversely, people of a tepid mind do whatever they do, whether good or evil, tepidly. And although a cold mind is worse than a tepid one, nevertheless a cold mind more often and more quickly comes to fervor than a tepid one.

Therefore, my brothers, let us shake off our tepidity, lest it become nauseating to God, and let us burn with love of God and neighbor. Whatever good we do, let us do it with the fervor of great love. For according to the prophet: “Cursed is the one who does the work of God negligently” (Jer. 48).

[Col. 1396A] “Then,” he says, “after three years I went up to Jerusalem to see Peter, and I remained with him for fifteen days”—not, of course, chiefly in order to learn, but to confer with him about the Gospel.

Paul gives an example of visiting our fathers and brothers, especially those who are spiritual: not so that we may observe their faces, stature, and personal qualities, but so that we may consider one another’s conduct, life, virtues, works, and studies; so that we may confer about the religion and teaching of Christ; so that we may build one another up and make progress; and so that we may rejoice together in spiritual joy.

“But I saw none of the other apostles,” he says, “except James, the brother [Col. 1396B] of the Lord.”

It is as though he said: “If I did not learn the Gospel from the apostles whom I saw, much less did I learn it from those whom I did not see.”

James was called the brother of the Lord either because he imitated his holiness more expressly than the others—and therefore succeeded him in the episcopate of Jerusalem—or because he was his kinsman, both on his mother’s side and through Joseph, his putative father.

The Apostle demonstrates by an oath that he did not learn the Gospel from man when he adds: “In the presence of God, I assure you, I am not lying in what I write to you.” This is a form of oath. It is as though he said: “Behold, I speak before God”—that is, with God as witness—“because I am not lying in what I write to you.”

But since the Lord entirely forbids swearing—not by heaven, nor by earth, nor by any creature—but says, “Let your speech be: Yes, yes; No, [Col. 1396C] no. Whatever is more than these is from evil” (Matt. 5), why does the Apostle swear?

The Lord, my brothers, gave counsel concerning what is more perfect, forbidding anyone to seek an oath as though it were good, lest through the habit of swearing he fall into perjury. The Apostle, however, swears as though compelled by human unbelief. The Church also permits her members to swear for the sake of a covenant of peace and faith.

An oath is not good—that is, it is not to be sought as though it were good—yet it is not evil when it is necessary. Nevertheless, it is always “from evil,” that is, from the unbelief of those who compel people to swear.

An oath, whenever it is made, ought to have three companions: truth, judgment, and justice.

Truth: so that one may feel in one’s heart what one swears. Judgment: so that one swears with discernment and [Col. 1396D] only concerning matters for which it is necessary to swear. Justice: so that one swears for the sake of God and justice.

If there is no truth in an oath, it is perjury—as when someone swears with his mouth what he does not feel in his heart, or when he swears by verbal trickery. For God accepts an oath according to the understanding of the person to whom it is sworn.

If judgment, that is, discernment, is absent from an oath, it is a foolish oath. And if what one has sworn to do is a criminal sin, it must not be done; rather, the foolish oath must be corrected through repentance. Hence it is written: “In evil promises, withdraw your pledge; but in a shameful matter, change your decision.”

If justice, that is, a good end, is absent from an oath, it may be called a false or wicked oath (*dejeramentum*) [Col. 1397A], as when someone swears for the sake of profit, favor, hatred, or some other temporal cause.

Therefore, my brothers, a false oath is a grave sin because it lacks a proper end. A foolish oath is more serious because one swears to things that one ought not to swear. Perjury is most serious because one swears falsely in place of truth and brings God forward as a witness to falsehood.

More serious than all these, however, is the habit of swearing. Whoever swears daily frequently commits perjury. And if it is such a great sin to commit perjury even once, what a crime it is to commit perjury frequently!

Therefore, brothers, let us flee the habit of swearing as we would death. Let us never swear except in great necessity, and then with fear and reverence. Let us not compel others to swear [Col. 1397B], especially those whom we know to possess a false oath, lest we kill them in soul.

And so that we ourselves may never be compelled to swear, let us show ourselves so truthful to everyone that our simple word may be believed as though it were an oath. Let there be truth in the mouth, simplicity in the heart, innocence in deed, justice in intention, and Christ as the reward.

May he grant this to us, he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

XXV. ON THE FEAST OF BLESSED MARY MAGDALENE.

“A certain Pharisee asked Jesus to eat with him” (Luke 7), and so forth.

This reading from the holy Gospel is divided into five parts. First, Jesus, invited by the Pharisee, reclines at table. Second, the penitent sinner approaches [Col. 1397C] him. Third, the Pharisee murmurs. Fourth, Jesus answers him. Fifth, the Pharisee’s further murmuring and the sinner’s dismissal are presented.

First, then, when invited by the Pharisee, the Lord enters his house and reclines at table. Elsewhere, however, the Lord instructed his disciples that, when they came into a city, they should ask who in it was worthy and remain there (Luke 10).

Since this Pharisee is said to have murmured against the Lord, how was he worthy for the Lord to recline with him?

He was not worthy, brothers; rather, the Lord reclined with him in order to make him worthy. Thus, brothers, the Lord reclines with the Pharisee only when invited, and for this reason: he had foreseen that he would benefit several people there—both the sinner [Col. 1397D] through forgiveness and the Pharisees through rebuke. He gives us an example that we should not eat with anyone unless invited and unless we intend to do good.

For those who come uninvited are blameworthy, as are those who seek only food. When someone therefore asks us to eat with him, if he is a person whom we are able to benefit, or from whom we may benefit, let us go. Otherwise, let us not go.

The imperfect and inexperienced person should therefore avoid entirely the banquets and companionship of the wicked, because he would not convert them but would rather be corrupted by them. But the person who is strong in virtue should, when invited by persecutors, go to them, so that while they nourish him bodily, he may nourish them spiritually.

If anyone should murmur, let him answer with the Lord’s saying: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. 9).

[Col. 1398A] Secondly, the penitent sinful woman is introduced, when it is added: “And behold, a woman who was a sinner in the city,” etc. Four things are to be considered here: the greatness of the sinner, the hidden summons, the hastened conversion, and the fervent repentance.

This woman was indeed a great sinner, since she is called “sinner” by antonomasia. Hence it is also said here: “A woman who was a sinner in the city”—not because there was no other sinful woman, but because, in comparison with her, any other sinner would have been holy. Thus Mark also testifies that seven demons had been driven out of her by the Lord (Mark XVI; Luke VIII). Mary had seven demons, for she had been full of every vice. Whoever is possessed by lust is possessed by the spirit of fornication; whoever is possessed by avarice is possessed by Mammon, the spirit of avarice. [Col. 1398B] And so it is with the others. Therefore, as many crimes as a person serves, so many demons does he serve.

But the greater this sinful woman’s iniquity had been, the more wondrous was her sanctification, so that what is said may seem to have been spoken especially of her: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. V). She is set before sinners as an example, so that they may not despair because of any enormity of their crimes, but may rise again through repentance after her example.

Hear this, sinner: Magdalene is not set before you as an opportunity for excusing your sins. She did not excuse hers, but accused them. If, therefore, you followed the sinner, follow the one who corrected herself.

Her calling was also hidden, and for that reason more worthy. She was not called by the voice of preaching, as Peter and Andrew were, nor by necessity, as Paul was, but solely [Col. 1398C] by inward inspiration. He who was bodily present at Simon’s house invisibly called and drew Mary, who was absent, to come to him. It is therefore no wonder that he received her outwardly who had summoned her inwardly.

Her conversion was also hastened, because she did not procrastinate, delay, or wait until she could find the Lord in a secluded place and at a free hour. Instead, she immediately hurried into another man’s house, among the guests, burst in upon the Lord while he was occupied at the meal, and sought healing.

This, my brothers, condemns our negligence. Though we are burdened with great crimes, we postpone the time of repentance; we wait for Lent, for a secluded place, for a familiar priest, as though the whole time of our life were not suitable for repentance. We promise ourselves a span of life, although we are not secure even about the present hour. Hence death, coming like a thief in the night, alas, snatches away many unrepentant and intestate. [Col. 1398D]

Let us therefore imitate this sinful woman’s hastened conversion. And because we fall daily, let us daily hasten to the physician of our souls. Let us never sleep in sin, but always fear the impending death.

Her repentance was also fervent, as she showed by standing behind Jesus beside his feet, beginning to wet his feet with her tears, wiping them with the hair of her head, kissing his feet, and anointing them with ointment. While she stands behind the Lord beside his feet, she signifies that henceforth she will follow his footsteps. While she wets the feet of Jesus [Col. 1399A] with tears, she shows that she can no longer conceal her inward contrition and fervor.

For consider, my brothers, with what ardor she was burning within: she did not blush to weep amid the courses of a meal, but among those who were eating and rejoicing she was pierced with compunction and wept. And since, as Solomon testifies, “it is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” (Eccles. VII), how fervently did she mourn within, since she made a house of feasting into a house of mourning!

She remembered how immoderately she had sinned, and therefore did not care how immoderately she repented. Why, then, my brothers, do this sinful woman’s tears not shame the hardness of our minds? We come not weeping but laughing; we find tears for mourning over earthly losses, but for mourning over sins and spiritual [Col. 1399B] losses we cannot find tears.

Because this woman had desired earthly things through her eyes, she now wet Jesus’ feet with their tears. She had nourished her hair for bodily adornment, and therefore now spent it in the service of wiping the Lord’s feet. She had spoken vain and false words with her mouth and had given unlawful kisses, and therefore now gave kisses with her mouth to the Lord’s feet. She used to anoint herself with ointment so that she might smell pleasant to people; now she anointed the Lord’s feet with ointment. As many pleasures as she had enjoyed in sin, so many sacrifices of repentance did she now offer.

Third, the Pharisee is introduced, murmuring and saying within himself: “If this man were a prophet, he would surely know who and what sort of woman this is who touches him, that she is a sinner.” As if he were saying: “This man is not a prophet, since he allows himself to be touched by a sinful woman.” [Col. 1399C]

This Pharisee, my brothers, arrogated righteousness to himself, and yet he was not truly just. Since all the virtues are joined together, he did not possess true righteousness because he lacked humility and charity, its companions. If he had humility, he would have judged not the sins of others but his own, since it is written: “The just man is the first to accuse himself” (Prov. XVIII).

But this man prides himself on a false righteousness, despises the sinful woman, and judges the Lord for receiving her. He is perverse in both respects, especially since he saw that the Lord had received none but a humbled and weeping woman. Again, if he had charity, he would have pitied the sinful woman through mercy and imitated the Lord in his compassion. But he is indignant both against the one who permits it and against the one who shows compassion. [Col. 1399D]

There are such people today—and what is more grievous, even among our own order—who, whenever they do something good outwardly, immediately despise their inferiors and, in the manner of the Pharisee, shrink from being touched by a sinful woman. If she had sat down at the Pharisee’s feet, she would have withdrawn, driven away by his kicks. Those who are filled not with true righteousness but with their own righteousness think that they are defiled by the sins of others.

But we, my brothers, avoiding these things, what should we do except mourn over ourselves in the sins of others? For we have either fallen into similar sins or may fall into them. If we have fallen, let us not judge those who have fallen, but rather mourn with them. If we have not fallen into such things, nevertheless, because we can fall, let us fear for ourselves.

[Col. 1400A] Fourth, the Lord responds to the Pharisee’s thought, introducing a comparison between one who owed less and one who owed more. After a creditor had forgiven both of them, the Lord asks which of them ought to love him more. He replied: “I suppose the one to whom he forgave more.” The Lord said to him: “You have judged rightly.”

Behold, the Pharisee is bound by his own sentence and, like a madman, tied with the rope he himself carries. Through this parable the Lord shows that the sinful woman’s sins had been forgiven, and that she burned with greater love because she had obtained forgiveness for more numerous and greater sins.

We often see this, my brothers. We see some who, the more fervent they had been in sinning, become just as fervent in repenting. And sometimes we see others who, the less they have sinned, are correspondingly less fervent in doing good. But I mourn for certain people—and I myself am one of them—who, although they have committed many great crimes, are nevertheless lukewarm in repentance and secure as though they had committed no sin, or only a little.

But whoever we are who are like this, what else ought we to do except daily repeat in our hearts the multitude and greatness of our crimes, and always keep before our eyes the torments deserved and prepared for their punishment? Thus, ashamed on one side and fearful on the other, we may be pierced with compunction in tears; and, as long as we live, may we never promise ourselves holiness. For it is written: “Do not be without fear concerning a sin that has been forgiven” (Ecclus. V).

Adapting the parable he has introduced, the Lord adds: “You see this woman?” [Col. 1400B] The Lord proves to the Pharisee that the sinful woman, to whom many sins had been forgiven, loves more than he to whom fewer had been forgiven. He proves this through outward works, which are evidence of love, speaking by antithesis, now of one and now of the other, in this way:

“I entered your house, and you gave me no water for my feet”—which is the lesser thing. “But she”—which is the greater—“has not ceased wetting my feet with her tears. You gave me no kiss, but she”—which is the greater—“has not ceased kissing my feet.”

He could also have added: “You did not feed me spiritually, but she fed me spiritually.” “Therefore,” he says, “her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much.” As if he were saying plainly: “Through the fervor of her love she burned away the former rust of her sins.” [Col. 1400C]

But beware, my brothers, lest you understand this to mean that the sinful woman’s sins were forgiven because she performed those works for Christ, or because she loved him. The sinful woman’s love or service was not the cause for which Christ forgave her sins; the opposite is true. Christ did not forgive her because the woman loved him and performed those works for him. Rather, because Christ had forgiven her, she loved Christ and performed those works for him.

For God, by grace alone, anticipates the sinner, freely bestowing upon him both contrition and the forgiveness of sins. Therefore, when he says “therefore” and “because,” these words are not to be understood as causes, but rather as signs to be understood and recognized. The meaning is thus: “From the works mentioned above you can understand both that she loved much and that her sins were forgiven.”

Fifth, the Pharisees’ counter-murmuring follows. Although they saw that their thoughts had been detected and refuted by divine power, they were not ashamed; nor did they give honor to God. They continued to think evil, saying: “Who is this who even forgives sins?”

But the Lord, passing them over as unworthy of a response, adds the reason for the sinful woman’s absolution, saying to her: “Your faith has saved you.” But if her faith saved her, how can this be by grace alone? Because faith itself is also grace. She would not have believed unless divine grace had inspired her.

What she ought to do after her absolution is shown when she is told: “Go in peace”—that is, what is said to the other sinful woman: “Go, and sin no more” (John VIII). She is commanded to go in peace so that she may follow not the way of scandal but the way of righteousness. For lamentation is of no benefit if sins are repeated.

[Col. 1401A] Let us therefore, dearest brothers, follow the example of this sinful woman. Let us not postpone repentance, but be converted quickly. If it is evening, let us not wait for morning; and if it is morning, let us not wait for evening. Let us run as soon as possible, with tears of compunction and the ointment of devotion, to the physician of our souls. Let us sit beside his feet in humility, and behind him—not before him—in the shame of conscience. Among those who feast and rejoice, let us learn to weep.

While we mourn our sins, let us wet the final members of Christ—that is, the poor—with the gift of compassion. Let us serve them with the abundance of our temporal goods; let us offer them the kiss of brotherly love, so that we may love with fraternal affection those to whom we give alms. Let us sprinkle them—and indeed the whole Church—with the fragrance and reputation of our devotion, and rejoice in them, so that we may deserve to obtain complete forgiveness of our sins and henceforth follow the way of peace. May God grant this, our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

## On Saint Mary Magdalene. From Sedulius

Then the Lord, seeking the Pharisee’s banquet at dinner,

shared the fare of his friend who had invited him.

[Col. 1401D] Then the woman whom a guilty reputation and the many

sins of her life tormented, humbly pleading,

fell down, embracing the feet;

leaning over them, she drenched them with abundant tears,

and, with her hair loosened,

did not cease to wipe and lick the sacred feet.

She cherished them with fragrant ointment,

until the gracious judgment of God—who is never unwilling to extend his hand

when we repent of having sought our former ruin—

said: “Go; faith, woman, has saved you

from whatever evil you are seen to have done.

Use my peace. It is a great medicine to confess

what it is harmful to conceal. For the one who hides

nourishes the wound and fears to uncover the injury

to the physician who can heal it.”

She who had long been polluted withdrew, cleansed in a little while

through her groaning, washing herself in the flood

of her own tears. She returns clean through her tears,

and dried with her hair.

## On Saint Mary Magdalene

Magdalene, leaving her sister and the others behind, climbed a steep hill scarcely two thousand paces from the town of Aix, never afterward to depart from it. There, in a cave terrible in its darkness but itself venerable in its awe, she spent thirty years praying and continually turning heavenly things over in her mind, without any food supplied by mortals. [Col. 1402A]

She was nourished, however, by angelic ministry, and sustained by heaven, which abundantly supplied what she had renounced so as not to be indebted to the world. For afterward no mortal saw her except Bishop Maximinus, who, having been warned by an oracle, went to her once to administer the Lord’s body, when she was already near death.

Concerning Magdalene, Francis Petrarch says:

“Mary did the same after her sin. She did not choose to remain long in public view among the crowds or to dwell in palaces. Fleeing her homeland, she was carried into these lands as though into another world, and here she remained hidden until the end. She made her home in that bare and hollow rock, which I think you have seen—for it is not far from here—a place venerable with a certain sacred awe and not unworthy even of being visited from afar. I remember that I myself was often there and once spent three nights and as many days, not without a pleasure different from that usually found in cities.

[Col. 1402B] There the sweet and blessed guest of Christ lived and died, served not by the attentions of maidens who adorned her, but by the ministry of obedient angels. Yet Martha, her sister, did nothing of this kind, someone may say, and nevertheless she is holy. I do not deny that; but certainly Mary, who did these things, is much holier.”

This is what Petrarch wrote. He was also exceedingly devoted to this most holy woman, and had certain verses hung in honor of her on her tomb, which we have thought not unworthy to transcribe. They begin in this way:

Sweet friend of God, bend to our tears

and heed my prayers; take care of our salvation,

for you can. It was not permitted you in vain

to touch the sacred feet and drench them with groaning,

[Col. 1402C] and thus dry them with shining locks,

and carry kisses to his feet,

and scatter precious perfumes upon the Lord’s head.

Nor did Christ the heavenly King, rising from death,

deny you the first approach,

or the privilege of hearing his voice,

or of seeing his limbs,

you who were destined to possess immortal glory

and light throughout the ages.

He had seen you clinging to the cross,

not fearing the dreadful torments

of the Jewish hand and of the raging crowd,

whose tongues matched their blows in quarrels

and insults; sorrowful and fearless alike,

handling the bloodied nails with your fingers,

filling the wounds with tears,

beating your fair breast with violent fists,

and tearing your golden hair with your hands without restraint.

He had seen these things, I say, while the faithful hearts

of his own people fled, driven away by fear.

Remembering this, he revisited you first before all others;

to you alone he first offered himself.

After departing from the earth and returning to the stars,

he nourished you for twice three lustrums,

never needing mortal food,

beneath this rock, content for so long

with divine banquets and health-giving dew.

[Col. 1402D] This house, this cave, damp with dripping rocks,

dark in its dreadful wildness,

surpassed the golden roofs of kings,

all their pleasures, and their wealthy fields.

Here, enclosed and willingly clothed in long hair,

lacking any other garment,

you are said to have endured thirty Decembers.

Here you were neither broken by frost nor overcome by fear,

for love and hope fixed deeply in your heart

made hunger, cold, and even the hard rocky bed sweet.

Here, unseen by human eyes,

surrounded by angelic throngs

and carried upward for seven hours each day,

you were worthy to hear the heavenly choirs

singing antiphonal songs,

as befitted one released from bodily prison.

# XXVI. ON THE FEAST OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE JAMES

“The mother of the sons of Zebedee approached Jesus, worshiping him and asking something of him” (Matt. XX).

This reading, dearest brothers, is divided into three parts. First, the mother of the sons of Zebedee makes a request of the Lord; second, the Lord responds to her by rebuking; third, by instructing.

The sons of Zebedee, James and John, had heard that the Lord would come in his kingdom and sit in his majesty. Therefore, still carnal and captivated by the sweetness of reigning, they wanted, through the intercession of their mother—whom they knew to be the Lord’s maternal aunt and close associate—to claim for themselves seats beside Christ, one at his right hand and the other at his left. [Col. 1403A]

They thought they would obtain this before the others because they were more familiar with Christ and because, in certain matters, they had been privileged together with Peter, as at the Transfiguration and in certain other secrets.

Although their request was indiscreet, they nevertheless gave us this example: whenever we ask something of the Lord, we should ask through the intercession of those whom we know to be pleasing to God. When a displeasing and unwelcome person asks for something, he does not bend the one he petitions; rather, he provokes him further. And if a guilty person begs us to intercede for him with the king, we are accustomed to say: “I cannot intercede for you with the king, because I do not have his familiarity.” [Col. 1403B]

Let us therefore, brothers, ask for the forgiveness of our sins through the intercession of those pleasing to God, both living and dead, so that although we displease him by our own merits, we may be helped by theirs. Let us therefore honor, venerate, and invoke those whom we know to be closer to God through the holiness of their merits.

The mother herself acted prudently when she was about to ask on behalf of her sons. First she approached; then she worshiped; [Col. 1403C] afterward she asked for something. By her example she instructs us that, when we wish to ask something of God, we should first approach God by faith and conduct, like the woman with the hemorrhage. Second, we should worship, humbling ourselves as unworthy and relying upon God’s grace alone, like the humble publican. Third, we should ask for something.

Let us not ask for temporal things, the death of our enemies, or empty vanities. When the apostles had asked for these, they heard: “Until now you have asked nothing in my name” (John XVI). Rather, let us ask in the name of Jesus—that is, the Savior—for salvation. To ask for this is to ask for something. Let us therefore ask first for “the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to us” (Matt. VI). [Col. 1403D]

The Lord asks the mother what she wants, not because he does not know, but so that she may answer him accordingly. “Say,” she says, “that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and the other at your left, in your kingdom.”

This woman, my brothers, possessed great faith and prudent piety. She had great faith when she believed him to be the eternal King whom she saw possessing nothing in the world. She had great faith when she said to him not “Do this,” but only “Say this,” knowing without doubt that for God to say is to do, “for he spoke, and they were made” (Ps. XXXII).

She also possessed prudent piety, since she asked for her sons not riches or earthly possessions but an eternal kingdom. Let our married women imitate this mother, so that with perfect faith and prudent piety they may ask for their sons not wealth, honors, or empty glories—which have been the cause of perdition for many—but an eternal kingdom. [Col. 1404A]

Let them not disinherit others, as many do today, in order to enrich their own sons. Let them not condemn their own souls in order to enrich their sons in this world. Rather, through prayers, offerings, and almsgiving, let them deserve to obtain a divine inheritance for their sons, imitating that outstanding matron Paula, who, when she had stripped her sons of everything by distributing it to the poor, said: “I cannot acquire a greater inheritance for my sons than the mercy of God.”

Second, the Lord responds to them by rebuking them, when he adds: “You do not know what you are asking.” Here the Lord does not respond only to the mother, but to the sons at whose prompting she made the request.

They were asking for a good thing, but indiscreetly. They displayed indiscretion in five respects. First, in the person from whom they asked, since they thought that the Lord was a respecter of persons. He would be a respecter of persons if he exalted his relatives out of love for their blood and despised those who were distant; if he loved the Jews solely because of their kinship and rejected foreign peoples.

But, as Peter says: “God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears God and does righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts X). [Col. 1404B]

Second, they showed indiscretion in the order of their request, asking for the reward before the merit, the harvest before the sowing, rest before labor, the kingdom before warfare, and triumph before battle.

[Col. 1404C] Third, they showed indiscretion in the thing requested, asking that one should sit at the Lord’s right hand and the other at his left, when all the elect are to be placed at the right hand.

Fourth, they showed indiscretion in the excess of what they asked, striving to surpass in honor the other apostles, whom they did not surpass in virtue. The following events show this, when the ten heard of it and became indignant at the two brothers.

Fifth, they showed indiscretion in the manner of asking, since they sought the heavenly kingdom not through humility but through ambition. Hence they also hear what follows: “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them. But you are not to be so. Rather, let the greater among you become like the younger, and the leader like the one who serves.”

[Col. 1404D] Let us therefore, my brothers, ask the Lord for anything with discretion. Let us ask confidently, not on the basis that we are ministers of God or that we seem to be something in this world, but solely on the basis of God’s mercy. “For God is not a respecter of persons.”

Let us ask in the proper order: first, that he grant us the ability to do his commandments, and afterward that we may obtain his rewards. Let us also ask for what it is fitting for us to ask and what we know from the Scriptures that God will give his saints.

Let us ask moderately, requesting that God make us not the greatest in his kingdom but even the least. Let us ask not with ambition but with humility. For the kingdom of heaven is reached not through ambition but through humility.

Third, the Lord instructs us to whom the kingdom of God should be given, when he adds: “Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?” Through the cup by which a sick person ordinarily drinks bitterness, the Lord signifies his Passion. As if he were saying plainly: “Do you wish to come to the honor of the kingdom? First drink the Passion after my example. For through a bitter drink one reaches the joy of salvation. If you wish to come to the summit of honor, first let the way of labor train you.” [Col. 1405A]

When they confidently replied, “We can,” he said to them: “You will indeed drink my cup”—understand: “and by drinking it you will attain the kingdom.”

But since John ended his life in peace, it is clear that martyrdom is obtained not only by blood but also by abstinence, continence, labor, and compassion. Therefore, my brothers, let us learn to crucify our flesh with its vices and desires. Whoever crucifies carnal desires within himself will not lack the crown of martyrdom.

“But to sit at my right hand or at my left,” he says, “is not mine to give you”—understand: “now, before labor.” Or: “It is not mine to give you”—understand: “to people such as you, ambitious and vain.” Or: “It is not mine to give you,” for this reason: “because you are my relatives and of my blood,” since I am not a respecter of persons.

In this, my brothers, he condemns the prelates of the holy Church who, when conferring ecclesiastical dignities and offices, consider not merit but blood relationship. They do not seek God’s honor or the benefit of souls, but the honor of their own flesh.

Because Eli did this, he is rebuked and condemned by the Lord, who says: “You honored your sons more than me” (1 Kings II), etc. [Col. 1405B]

Behold, today our prelates, who indeed hold Christ’s place but not his example: if a mother or maternal aunt comes with her two little sons asking that ecclesiastical honors be given them, they do not hesitate to confer the deanery upon one and the archdeaconry upon the other, setting aside the older, religious, and discerning men. They do not consider that the Lord, although James and John were holy and prudent, did not wish to establish them as princes over the apostles, lest he seem to prefer the younger to the older or a relative to a stranger.

To the one who said, “Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking to speak with you” (Matt. XII), he himself replied: “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers? Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (ibid.).

He gives an example [Col. 1405D] that no one should acknowledge the face of a friend or relative in the affairs of the Lord, but only the will of God and the benefit of the Church.

Behold, here the Lord says to two of his relatives and closest friends: “To sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine”—that is, “since I am not a respecter of persons”—“to give to you, my relatives and friends, especially while you are still arrogant and ambitious, but to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.”

For the Lord the Father prepared his kingdom so that it might be given not to unworthy intimates or relatives, but to all who are worthy, whatever their language or nation.

Let us therefore, my brothers, seek the kingdom of heaven not through ambition and arrogance, but through humility, patience, [Col. 1406A] labor, abstinence, continence, charity, and works of charity and mercy. The kingdom of heaven is not given to the lazy and sleepy, but to those who labor.

“Not everyone who says, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. VII; Luke III).

Therefore, brothers, let us always seek the will of God and always do it as far as we are able, asking first that God grant us the ability to do his will, and afterward that he establish us even as the least in his kingdom. May he himself graciously grant this, he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

## Life of Saint James the Apostle, brother of John the Evangelist, written by Eusebius of Caesarea

[Note: [Col. 1405D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 9.]

[Col. 1406B] In the time of the emperor Claudius, when there was a famine, Herod the king “sent forth his hands to afflict some of those belonging to the Church, and killed James the brother of John with the sword,” as Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XII).

Concerning this James, Clement of Alexandria also writes a memorable story in the seventh book of his *Outlines*, which had come down to him through the tradition of his predecessors:

“Since, indeed,” he says, “the man who had handed him over to the judge for martyrdom—James, that is—was himself moved and confessed that he was a Christian, both of them, he says, were led together to punishment. As they were being led along, he asked James to grant him forgiveness. After considering for a little while, James said to him: ‘Peace be with you,’ and kissed him. Thus both were beheaded together.”

## Life of the same saint, by Isidore

James, whose name means “supplanter,” son of Zebedee and brother of John, was fourth in order; [the text then appears defective: “to the twelve tribes that are dispersed among the nations”]. He preached the Gospel in Spain and the western regions, and at the setting of the world shone forth with the light of his preaching. He was struck down by the sword of Herod the tetrarch in maritime Achaea and was buried there.

# XXVII. ON THE TRANSFIGURATION OF THE LORD. SERMON ON THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED PETER, WHICH IS READ ON THE SAME FEAST

“I will take care, and frequently, that after my death you may have these things so that you may remember them” (2 Pet. I), etc.

This reading, dearest brothers, is divided into four parts. First, Peter shows how great his concern is for the progress of his children. Second, he shows that his teaching is such and so great that they ought to remember it. Third, he establishes its truth by apostolic and prophetic testimony. Fourth, he commends the writing of the prophets.

First, then, he shows how great is his solicitude for the progress of the souls entrusted to him, when he says that he will take care, and frequently, to impress evangelical teaching upon them in such a way that they will retain it in memory after his death. [Col. 1406D]

He instructed them by the living voice; he instructed them through the transmission of his letters; he instructed them by the good example of his life. And they, like good sheep, remembered what they had heard.

We too, my brothers, who hold Peter’s place in the Church, ought, as far as we can, to follow his footsteps: we should be solicitous in instructing the souls entrusted to us and impress evangelical teaching upon them, if not through blood and martyrdom, as Peter did, nevertheless through example and word. [Col. 1407A]

Every shepherd must possess these two things; whoever lacks them is not a true shepherd. An example without words is not sufficient. Hence Eli, although, as far as he himself was concerned, he lived rightly, is nevertheless rejected because he did not correct his sons well (1 Kings II). Thus the Lord says through the prophet: “If a man commits iniquity, and you do not announce to him that he should turn from his evil way, he himself will die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. III).

Again, words without example are not sufficient. Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “You yourselves drank the clearest water, but you trampled the rest with your feet, and your sheep drank the water muddied by your feet” (Ezek. XXXIV). [Col. 1407B]

Shepherds drink clear water when they both understand and preach sound doctrine. They trample the rest with their feet when, by living badly, they defile their preaching. The sheep drink muddied water when they draw not the preaching they have heard but the example of an evil life.

But, my brothers, when I consider both our life and the life of our subjects, I find few true preachers—and this is grievous—and few true sheep. For today’s shepherds neither remember the Scriptures themselves nor make others remember them. Neglecting the care of souls, they devote themselves to temporal profits and show by both their purpose and their deeds that they are not shepherds but hirelings.

They are not shepherds in their purpose because they seek what is their own, not what is Jesus Christ’s. Are ecclesiastical offices today sought not so that they may benefit souls, but so that the officeholders themselves may be exalted, honored, and pleased? They do not ask in which Church they can benefit souls more, but in which they can collect more and which they can sell for more. [Col. 1407C]

They show by their deeds that they are not shepherds, since they do not care to feed the sheep either by example or by word, but fatten themselves on the sheep’s offerings.

Hence the prophet says: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves! Are not flocks fed by shepherds? You ate the milk and clothed yourselves with the wool. You killed what was fat; you did not strengthen what was weak; you did not heal what was sick; you did not bind up what was broken; you did not bring back what was cast away; you did not seek what had perished. Instead, you ruled them with severity and with power.

My sheep were scattered because there was no shepherd, and they became food for the beasts of the field. Therefore, shepherds, hear the word of the Lord: ‘Behold, I myself will require my flock from their hand’” (Ezek. XXXIV). [Col. 1407D]

Behold, brothers, as we read, so today we see. We destroy what is fat by bad example. We do not heal what is weak through sins by counsel. We do not strengthen what is broken by tribulations through admonition. We do not call back what has gone astray. We do not seek what has been lost through despair.

A donkey falls, and someone is there to lift it up; a soul perishes, and no one is there to care for it. How is he a shepherd who is more affected by the sickness of his pig or his she-ass than by that of a Christian soul?

If shepherds do these things, what do the sheep do? [Col. 1408A] Certainly, it is no wonder that when the head suffers, the limbs suffer also.

It is the sheep’s duty to hear and obey. But today evil sheep do not wish to hear their shepherds, and they say: “The priest preaches in order to extort money.” Even if they listen, they certainly do not remember what they have heard. Nor do they wish to obey their shepherd, but to judge him.

“Why,” they say, “do you yourself not do what you preach? ‘You who preach that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery; you who preach that one must not steal, do you steal?’” (Rom. II).

When two or three go to the marketplace or the village, they judge, slander, and condemn their shepherd, not considering what the Lord says: “A disciple is not above his teacher” (Luke VI), and: “Whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not act according to their works” (Matt. XXIII). [Col. 1408B]

These evil sons incur the curse of Ham. When Noah appeared drunk and his nakedness was exposed, Ham mocked him. Shem and Japheth, however, turned their eyes away and covered him. When Noah awoke, he cursed Ham’s offspring but blessed Shem and Japheth (Gen. IX).

No shepherd, my brothers, is so perfect that he never does something shameful. But the evil son mocks and defames him. The good subject, however, conceals, covers, and excuses his master’s sin. Therefore, the former receives a curse, while the latter obtains a blessing.

Thus, brothers, because both have sinned, let both mourn; let both return to repentance.

And let us, as good shepherds, henceforth take care, and frequently, to impress evangelical teaching upon you through word and example. You too, as good sheep, henceforth take care, and frequently, to ensure that by hearing and obeying you retain what you have heard.

The second part follows, in which he shows that his teaching is so great and of such a character that they ought to remember it, adding: “For we did not make known to you the power and wisdom of our Lord Jesus Christ by following inept fables.” As though he were saying: We have made known to you not fables, but truth and wisdom. Here he condemns those who, neglecting the Gospels, read poetic fables, bucolic poems, and comedies. Although such conduct may be excused in boys on the grounds of necessity, in others it is nevertheless a crime of the will. How, moreover, can the mouth that daily cries out “Almighty Jupiter,” invokes the goddess Venus, and so forth—things that are rather demons than gods—bless God, praise him purely, and pray?

“We made known,” he says, “to you the power and wisdom of our Lord Jesus Christ, Savior and King.” He does not say his humanity or weakness, which are known to everyone, but his power and wisdom—dubious to unbelievers, certain to the faithful. Brothers, although the Lord could have redeemed us by manifest power and wisdom, he did not wish to do so; instead, he concealed divine power in human weakness, and wisdom in what appeared to be foolishness. For it seemed foolish to human beings that God should become man, that the impassible should suffer, and that the immortal should die. Thus the power of God, through weakness, conquered diabolical power; the wisdom of God, through foolishness, overcame worldly cunning. “We preach,” he says, “Christ crucified: to the Jews, indeed, a stumbling block; but to the Gentiles, foolishness; yet to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. For what is weak in God is stronger than human beings, and what is foolish in God is wiser than human beings” (I Cor. I).

Let us therefore, brothers, learn by the example of our Redeemer to overcome the world’s wickedness not through pride, but through humility, patience, and gentleness. Let us learn to overcome the wisdom of the age not through cunning, but through the foolishness of God. To this wicked age, contempt for the world, rejection of the age, abandoning everything, loving poverty and lowliness, and desiring invisible things appear foolish. Yet this foolishness overcomes both diabolical and human wisdom.

The third part follows, in which he establishes the truth by apostolic and prophetic testimony. First, by apostolic testimony, when he adds: “Having become eyewitnesses of that greatness.” Peter himself, James, and John, who were with the Lord on the mountain when he was transfigured, were able to offer true testimony concerning what they had seen and heard, so that, according to the Law, “every word might stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deut. XIX). The Lord displayed his glory to the disciples on the mountain for three reasons: to strengthen them in faith in his divinity; to confirm them in the hope of the resurrection; and to make them reliable witnesses concerning both. Hence he says here: “Having become eyewitnesses of that greatness.”

And whose greatness does he mean? He adds: “For Christ received honor and glory from God the Father”—glory in that “his face shone like the sun, and his garments became white like snow” (Matt. XVII). This, however, was little in comparison with what was in the Son, since every saint in the heavenly homeland will shine more brightly than the sun. But only as much radiance was shown in him as the weak sight of mortal disciples could in some way endure.

Mystically, however, by the face is understood the knowledge of divinity, which will shine in the saints like the sun. The sun performs three things: it dries, illumines, and warms. So also the knowledge of the divine countenance will dry up and burn away every earthly quality in the saints. It will also illumine them, so that they know all hidden things. It will warm them as well, making them fervent in love, so that the more they see him, the more they desire to see him.

By the garments are understood either Christ’s flesh or the saints, concerning whom it is written: “You will clothe yourself with all these as with a garment” (Isa. XLIX). These garments “will be white like snow.” Snow is formed and whitened from heavenly rain by the intensity of cold. Snow therefore signifies chastity, which is possessed only through grace, by the cooling of the flesh; for it is given neither through grace without cooling, nor through cooling without grace. Those therefore are mistaken who, wishing to chastise their bodies, seek to obtain chastity through grace alone and without labor. The Lord grants virtues not to those who sleep, but to those who labor. Again, those are mistaken who strive to possess chastity through the chastisement of the flesh alone. Labor without grace is useless. Thus, even in emaciated and pale bodies, passions still burn unless they are restrained by God’s grace. Hence Jerome, speaking of himself, says: “My face grew pale through fasts, while my mind burned with desires.”

The Son received honor from God the Father in that he designated him Lord of the Law and of the prophets through Moses and Elijah, between whom he was seen in majesty. The Father also bore testimony to him in this. Hence it follows: “A voice having descended from such magnificent glory”—that is, from the glorious Father magnifying the Son. “Which?” [The text reads *Qua?*] This one, namely: “This is my beloved Son”—that is, this one, not another, is my Son; not adopted, as the others are, but of the same substance. “In him I am well pleased,” whereas in Adam and in the other saints, however holy, something displeased me.

“And this voice,” he says, “we ourselves heard brought from heaven, when we were with him on the holy mountain.” Above he had said, “Having become eyewitnesses”; here he says, “We heard.” As though he were saying: You ought rightly to believe us when we testify to what we saw and heard. “And we have,” he says, “the prophetic word made more firm.” He calls it “more firm,” that is, exceedingly firm; or “more firm” in the sense of more authoritative for the Jews, who were more inclined to accept the testimony of the prophets than that of the apostles.

The fourth part follows, in which he commends prophecy and those who attend to it, saying: “To which you do well to attend.” By contrast, he condemns those who do not wish to attend to the words of Scripture. Many such people are found today even among teachers of the holy Church: scorning the Scriptures, they devote themselves to bird-catching, hunting, dice, games, and vanities; and, likewise scorning the holy Scriptures, they devote themselves to secular laws, lawsuits, and empty inventions. The common people too are reproved, since they more willingly listen to songs, lyres, and vanities than to sacred Scripture.

“Attending to it,” he says, “as to a lamp shining in a dark place.” The world is darkened by three kinds of darkness: the darkness of sins, the darkness of ignorance, and the darkness of misery. Sacred Scripture, however, is light for us in this world. By following it, we avoid sins, ignorance, and, finally, misery. This lamp is necessary for us while we remain in this age, until the day dawns—the great day of judgment, which will have no evening—in the resurrection, which will be like the morning of eternity, and until the morning star, that is, divine brightness, rises in our hearts, entirely banishing from us the darkness of sins, the darkness of ignorance, and the darkness of misery; then, with unveiled face, we shall see God as he is (I Cor. XIII).

By his gift, he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## XXVIII. ON THE TRANSFIGURATION OF THE LORD

“Jesus took Peter, and James and John his brother, and led them up onto a high mountain apart, and was transfigured before them” (Matt. XVII).

In the preceding passages of this Gospel, my brothers, the Lord Jesus had said these words to his disciples: “There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man in his kingdom” (Mark VIII). He showed who those disciples would be when he immediately added: “And after six days he took Peter, and James and John his brother,” and so forth.

The Lord wished to show his disciples his glory before his death, his power before his passion, and his honor before his humiliation—and this for three reasons. First, so that he might strengthen them in faith in his divinity and power, so that, when they saw him suffer, they would know that he suffered not from necessity but willingly. Second, so that he might kindle their hearts with longing for the glory he had revealed. Third, so that, having seen his glory, he might make them both firm and true witnesses. Hence he showed it to three, since, according to the Law, “every word stands on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deut. XIX). He showed it to those who were more intimate and more perfect, in order to demonstrate that the mysteries of divinity are to be revealed only to the intimate and the perfect.

This reading is divided into four parts. First, the Lord is described as leading three disciples onto the mountain; second, as revealing to them the promised vision; third, as raising them after they had fallen prostrate; fourth, as forbidding them to reveal what they had seen until after his resurrection.

First, then, the Lord is described as leading three disciples, when it is said: “After six days Jesus took Peter, and James and John his brother,” and so forth. In this, my brothers, he indicates to us six things: when, how many, who, how, through whom, and where people will attain the contemplation of divine glory.

When? “After six days,” that is, after the six ages of worldly life. In the seventh age, which belongs to the dead, the saints will begin to enjoy the glory of God in the soul. They will enjoy it in both soul and body in the eighth age, that is, in the resurrection. Hence another evangelist, describing this same event, says: “After eight” (John XX), including the first and the final day.

How many? Only three: the three orders of the holy Church, namely, the married, the continent, and virgins, who live rightly according to their order. For fornicators, adulterers, sexual sinners, Sodomites, and the rest of the polluted will in no way attain the vision of divine glory (I Cor. VI; I Tim. I).

Who? Simon Peter, James, and John—that is, the obedient, those who overthrow vices, and those endowed with grace. Those who do not obey God and their superiors, those who do not conquer vices by struggling against them, and those who are empty of God’s grace cannot attain the vision of divine glory.

How? By ascending, laboring, and advancing from virtue to virtue. Those who remain at the lowest level of pleasures and vices cannot attain the contemplation of God; rather, they are overthrown and condemned. Hence the angel advised Lot, who was fleeing the overthrow of Sodomite pleasure and lust, saying: “Do not remain here, nor in all the surrounding region; save yourself on the mountain” (Gen. XIX).

Through whom? Through Christ. No one can ascend by his own strength or merits unless he has been taken up by the grace of election and led by cooperating grace by him who alone gives both the will and the accomplishment (Phil. II). Perceiving this, the bride cries out to the bridegroom in the Song of Songs: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song I). Hence also the Psalmist says: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you” (Ps. LXXXIII). Why? Because, with you inspiring him with a good will, “he has arranged ascents in his heart” (ibid.), so that, while he still remains bodily “in the valley of tears, in the place which he has established” (ibid.), he may advance. And through whom will he be able to do what he has resolved? “For the lawgiver will give blessings; they will go from virtue to virtue; the God of gods will be seen in Zion” (ibid.).

Where? “On a mountain apart.” Those who will deserve to enjoy the divine vision will be exalted above all the reprobate, according to the saying: “The righteous will rule over them in the morning” (Ps. XLVIII), and they will be separated from them forever. Hence it is also written: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. XXVI).

Second, the Lord is described as revealing the promised vision to the apostles, when it is said: “And he was transfigured before them,” and so forth. Three things, my brothers, are revealed to the apostles in this vision: the glory, authority, and divine nature of Jesus Christ.

His glory—the glory that he was to possess or give to his own in the resurrection—is demonstrated when it is said: “He was transfigured before them, and his face shone.” Someone is properly said to be transfigured when, while the substance remains the same, only the quality and condition surrounding him are changed. Wishing therefore to demonstrate the glory of the resurrection, the Lord does not change his substance but merely transfigures himself, indicating to us that in the resurrection the substance of human beings will not be taken away, but only their condition will be changed: that of the wicked for the worse, and that of the good for the better.

This is shown more explicitly when it is added: “And his face shone like the sun, while his garments became white like snow,” as the Lord elsewhere testifies: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIII). The glory of Christ, and also that of many saints, is therefore much greater, as we believe, than that of the sun. But if he had found a clearer example, he would have used it. Even the Lord Jesus, however, displayed neither his own glory nor that of the saints except to the extent that the weak sight of the disciples could somehow behold it here.

Hence he showed his garments white as snow, although, clothed in the robe of blessed immortality, they will have no need to be clothed in garments, since thereafter they will suffer neither cold nor shame. By the face he signified the soul; by the garment, the body. For it is fitting that the soul, which was created in the image and likeness of God, should be called the Lord’s face, since through it the Lord is known by us and in us. Hence the Psalmist says: “My heart has said to you: My face has sought you; your face, Lord, I shall seek” (Ps. XXVI). Since like things rejoice in like things, the face of our soul ought always to desire the face of God, in whose image it was created.

The face, therefore, of Jesus Christ, and also that of the saints, will shine in the resurrection like the sun—that is, like God, not as much as God. For in the resurrection the soul of each person, according to its measure, will be clean as God is clean, upright as God is upright, holy as God is holy, and ardent as God is ardent.

The garments, that is, the bodies, will be white like snow. Snow is formed and whitened from heavenly rain through the intensity of cold. Snow therefore signifies chastity, which is obtained only from heavenly grace through the cooling and chastisement of the flesh. Accordingly, those are equally mistaken who think that they can attain chastity either without God’s grace or without chastisement of the flesh.

The bodies of the saints in the resurrection will therefore be white like snow—that is, shining with chastity—for thereafter they will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but will be virgins and chaste like the angels of God in heaven (Matt. XXII).

The authority of Jesus Christ is demonstrated when it is said: “And Moses and Elijah appeared to them, speaking with him.” In this our Redeemer demonstrated that he is Lord of the Law and of the prophets, Lord of the living and of the dead, Lord of heaven and earth.

He showed himself to be Lord of the Law and of the prophets when he displayed the great lawgiver and the chief of the prophets standing beside him whenever and wherever he wished. He showed himself to be Lord of the living and of the dead when he presented dead Moses and Elijah, living in paradise, standing beside him and conversing with him whenever and wherever he wished. He demonstrated himself to be Lord of heaven and earth when he commanded them with such authority that earth immediately presented Moses and heaven presented Elijah there.

Luke explains what they looked like and what they spoke about, saying: “They appeared in majesty, speaking of the departure that he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem” (Luke IX). Clearly, by displaying the lawgiver and the chief of the prophets with himself in the glory of majesty, the Lord demonstrated that he would glorify with himself in glory the spiritual fulfillers of the Law and of the prophets. In the fact that they spoke of the departure he was about to accomplish, it is plainly demonstrated that the Law and the prophets foretold these things in agreement and were truly fulfilled in him.

Peter, delighted by the contemplation of the divine splendor and glory, said to Jesus: “It is good for us to be here.” But if Peter, when he had enjoyed and delighted in the vision of a shadowy and brief glory for a short time, wished to remain there forever, how great, my brothers, do you think the joy and love will be in that true, eternal, and blessed glory of the divine vision, “into which the angels always desire to look” (I Pet. I)?

“If you wish,” he said, “let us make three tabernacles here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” While still in the flesh, Peter recognized Moses and Elijah, whom he had never before seen, during the manifestation of a shadowy and brief glory. How clear, then, do you think the knowledge of all things will be in that true and eternal blessedness?

Yet Peter also errs in his request to build the tabernacles, because, overcome by sudden and excessive joy, he did not know what he was asking, as another evangelist testifies (Luke IX). He did not know what he was asking when, in the eternal blessedness where there is no inclement weather, he requested tabernacles. He did not know what he was asking when, before the redemption of the human race through the blood of Jesus Christ and before the preaching of the Gospel, he requested glory. He did not know what he was asking when, in constructing the tabernacles, he made the servants equal to the Lord.

Nevertheless, he judged rightly in desiring always to be with the Lord and in placing the divine will before his own when he said: “If you wish, let us make them.” As though he were saying: “Not my will, but yours be done.” Imitating him, my brothers, let us always desire to remain with the Lord, and in our petitions let us always place the divine will before our own.

The divine nature is revealed when it is added: “While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them; and behold, a voice from the cloud said,” and so forth. Whether the pronoun “them” refers to Moses and Elijah or to Peter, James, and John, the meaning is the same, since both groups were overshadowed: Moses and Elijah, so that they would not be seen by the others; and the disciples, so that they would not see Moses and Elijah. Why? So that it would be certain to the disciples that the voice of the Father bore witness from the cloud to Jesus alone, who alone appeared.

Behold the mystery of the Trinity: the Son is transfigured; the Holy Spirit, through the cloud, separates him from the others; the Father, through the voice, identifies him. Just as, when the Lord was baptized, the Father bore witness in the voice and the Holy Spirit in the dove, so, when he was transfigured, the Father likewise bore witness in the voice and the Holy Spirit in the bright cloud.

It was fitting that the Holy Spirit should appear as a dove above the baptized Lord, when he was demonstrating Christ’s innocence and simplicity, through which and toward which Christ summoned human beings by baptism. It was likewise fitting that he should appear as a cloud above the transfigured Lord, since this demonstrated that in the other life he alone would be the covering and light of the saints, when the tabernacles requested by Peter and the use of the sun would alike cease, as John testifies in the Apocalypse: “And I did not see a temple in it, for the Lord God Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb. And that city has no need of the sun or the moon, for the glory of God illuminates it, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Rev. XXI).

“Behold,” he says, “a voice from the cloud saying: This one, and no other, is my beloved natural Son”—that is, this one in whom there is nothing except what is worthy of love; “in whom,” that is, in whose generation, “I was well pleased.” Formerly, in the formation of the human being, I was in a certain way displeased with myself when, because of the multiplication of human crimes, I said: “It repents me that I made man” (Gen. VI). “Listen to him,” he says.

As though he were saying: This is the one of whom Moses said: “God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers; you shall listen to him as to me in all the things he speaks to you. And the soul that does not listen to him, whether in himself or in his preachers, will perish from his people” (Deut. XVIII).

The third part follows, in which the Lord raises the disciples who had fallen prostrate: “For when the disciples heard the voice of the Father, they fell upon their faces and were very much afraid.” The sequence is reversed. They were afraid as a result of hearing the voice, and they fell as a result of fear. For wherever divine greatness is revealed, human weakness is shaken and cast down.

But Jesus, the constant lifter-up of human frailty, approaches, touches, raises, and consoles them. “And lifting up their eyes, they saw no one except Jesus alone.” From this they were certain that the voice from the cloud had indicated Jesus alone and borne witness to him alone.

Moreover, what then happened to the apostles happens daily in us, my brothers. When, in contemplation, through inspiration or reading, we hear with the mouth of the heart the power and greatness of God, the awareness of our weakness is afraid and agitated, and is humbled upon its face—that is, into the knowledge of its own weakness. But, lest it be cast down into despair, Jesus is present with his customary clemency. He approaches us by having compassion on us; he touches us by granting us his grace; he raises us by directing our desire toward heavenly things; and he consoles us by giving us confidence in his love. Thus, when we lift up our eyes, we see no one except Jesus alone—that is, when we raise the gaze of our contemplation toward God, we see in him nothing except the salvation by which he desires all human beings to be saved (I Tim. II). Therefore we ought to love him more than fear him.
