The fourth part follows, in which the Lord forbids the disciples to reveal what they had seen to anyone until after his resurrection, saying: “Tell no one about the vision until the Son of Man has risen from the dead.”

Why did he do this? For three reasons. First, lest, if Christ’s divine power and glory were openly manifested to everyone, his passion and our redemption should be prevented; for, as the Apostle testifies, if the rulers had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (I Cor. II).

Second, lest, if the Lord’s transfiguration were manifested to everyone, he should be thought to possess not a true body but a phantom body. Once the truth of that body had been proved through the passion, nothing thereafter prevented the preaching of his transfiguration.

Third, so that he might give his faithful an example: if they possessed any virtue or glory, they should never wish anything to be revealed during their lifetime. If something should happen to become known to one of their intimates, they should require that person not to reveal it to others while they were alive. We read that blessed Nicholas did this. For just as the north wind burns flowers, so rumor and popular favor burn the little flowers of virtue.

Although we may be ashamed to be praised and call ourselves unworthy, the soul, which naturally loves itself, nevertheless rejoices inwardly at praise and begins to take pleasure in itself. The more we please ourselves, the more we displease God. Therefore, my brothers, let us always flee human glory and praise; let us transfer our treasure, glory, and desire entirely to heaven; let us love being despised, cast down, and oppressed here for Christ’s sake, so that in the other life we may deserve to be honored, exalted, and glorified by him—by his gift, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## XXIX. ON THE PASSION OF BLESSED LAWRENCE

“He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly; and he who sows in blessings will also reap from blessings” (II Cor. IX), and so forth.

In this reading, my brothers, the Apostle urges the Corinthians to give alms to the saints who were in Jerusalem. Since they had placed all their possessions at the apostles’ feet (Acts IV), they were in need. In urging them, he also urges us, my brothers, to give alms, especially to those who are good and in need. Hence he says elsewhere: “Do good to all, especially to those who are of the household of faith” (Gal. VI).

This reading has four parts. First, he shows for what reason we ought to give alms generously; second, how; third, for what purpose; fourth, with what confidence we ought to give them.

First, he shows for what reason we ought to give alms generously when he says: “He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and he who sows in blessings will also reap from blessings.” As though he were saying plainly: Sow generously, because each person will reap according to what he sows. He who sows nothing will reap nothing; he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly; and he who sows in blessings—that is, in generosity—will reap generously from his generosity.

He calls generosity “blessings” because it is the cause of blessing. He also metaphorically calls the giver of alms a sower. For just as a sower scatters a small amount of seed on the ground in winter and gathers an abundant harvest in summer, so the giver of alms gives a small amount in this life and will receive eternal blessedness in the future.

But it must be observed, my brothers, that sparseness or generosity in giving alms does not refer to one’s possessions. Otherwise the poor, who are able to give little or nothing in alms, would be most miserable, since in the other life they would receive little or nothing; and the rich, who give very much to the poor here, would be most blessed, since in the other life they would have an exceedingly great reward.

It does not therefore refer to possessions, but rather to charity and ability. The Lord does not consider how much is given, but from how much charity and ability it is given. Hence the Lord says that the widow who offered two small coins in the treasury gave more than everyone else, because the others gave from some abundance, whereas she offered whatever she had (Mark XII; Luke XXI). From this it is also clear that she did so out of greater charity.

Therefore, my brothers, he sows much who gives all that little which he has for God. He sows much who, when he cannot give more, offers a word of correction and salvation. He sows much who, when he cannot give a material gift to one who is suffering, gives at least the compassion of charity.

Conversely, a certain rich person, although he may appear to give much for Christ, nevertheless gives little because he gives from no charity or from lukewarm charity. This is evident because, in comparison with what he possesses, he gives little.

It must also be known that eternal rewards will not be commensurate with our merits, since our merits are nothing or very small, whereas the rewards will be immeasurable. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Good and faithful servant, because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things” (Matt. XXV).

No one, therefore, will reap sparingly in the future age, since even the least saint will have sufficient abundance in the future. But the expression “will reap sparingly” is spoken in comparison with greater rewards, since, as the Apostle testifies, “star differs from star in glory” (I Cor. XV).

Second, the Apostle demonstrates how alms are to be given when he adds: “Each one”—understand, “should give alms”—“as he has determined,” that is, proposed in his heart, freely. And because sadness and necessity usually cloud and hinder the devotion of the heart, he adds: “Not from sadness or necessity,” that is, from the sadness that arises from necessity.

Someone gives from sadness when, placed in doubt whether to give or not to give, he almost refuses, but, compelled by a certain necessity, gives. The Apostle calls necessity a kind of coercion produced in certain lukewarm or cold people by a command, importunity, shame, a promise, kinship, or something of this sort.

Some give to the needy not out of compassion but as though compelled by the force of a command; in this they merit nothing or little. Others, compelled by the importunity of those in need, give in order to escape annoyance; these undoubtedly lose both the gift and the merit. Others, seeing many people beside them giving many alms, give under the compulsion of shame rather than from any compassion; these certainly merit nothing or little.

Others give not from any piety but because they are compelled by a promise they have made; these likewise merit little or nothing, but merely redeem their word. Others, compelled by the closeness of the flesh, give to their parents and relatives not from charity; from this they merit nothing, but merely follow the use of the flesh.

[Col. 1417C] Let us avoid these necessities, dearly beloved brothers, if we truly love God and our neighbor. Then no command of God, no importunity of the poor, and no other reason for giving will be burdensome to us, but rather lovable. For the person who wills what is compelled overcomes necessity.

Through true love, therefore, by embracing the very necessities of giving, let us drive sadness away from us. Let us give freely and devoutly, and let us make those gifts that we offer to our parents, relatives, intimates, and friends—and to which we seem bound—free and richly meritorious.

“For God loves,” he says, “a cheerful giver.” Just as it belongs to an unwilling and constrained spirit to give sadly, slowly, and reproachfully, and thus to sell its gift, so it belongs to a benevolent and devoted spirit to give joyfully, promptly, and with blessing, and thus to make its gift pleasing to God and to human beings.

Moreover, it is not the empty cheerfulness of just any giver that pleases God, but only that which proceeds from true love. Even that cheerfulness must be restrained, lest the spirit become excessively joyful and take too much pleasure in the alms it has performed, and thus begin to displease God. For the more we please ourselves, the more we displease God.

Therefore, my brothers, when we give alms or do some other good deed, let us consider that we distribute not our own possessions but another’s, and that we are not givers but rather ministers. Hence let us say what the Lord commands: “When you have done all that was commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have not done what we ought to do” (Luke XVII).

Third, the Apostle demonstrates for what reason alms should be given when he adds: “God is powerful enough to make every grace abound in you, so that, having sufficiency in all things, you may always abound in every good work.” As though he were saying plainly: You ought always to give alms, not for the favor or praise of human beings, who are either ungrateful, incapable, or deceitful in repaying, but for God alone, who alone is powerful both always to give us the means of giving alms and to reward what has been given.

He is himself both the final cause and the efficient cause of almsgiving. For it is only on his account that we can give alms, and for his sake alone that we ought to give them. He gives us the will and the power, the material and the affection for every good work, as well as the eternal reward for all these things.

For this reason he says “every grace,” that is, cooperating grace, working grace, perfecting grace, and rewarding grace. He proves this by the authority of the Psalmist, adding: “As it is written: He dispersed”—that is, by dispersing he gave—“he gave to the poor” (Ps. CXI).

Not everything should be given to one person, but it should be distributed among many, according to what we can give and according to what they need, so that we may deserve to have many advocates and intercessors before God. Nor should such things be distributed to those who are not poor, lest generosity perish through generosity. For it is a part of sacrilege to give the possessions of the poor to those who are not poor.

And what did the righteous man gain by distributing to the poor? “His righteousness”—that is, the reward he earned through righteousness—“remains forever and ever,” that is, eternally.

But it must be carefully considered, my brothers, that when the Psalmist had said, “He dispersed; he gave to the poor,” and ought consequently to have added, “the mercy of his alms remains forever and ever,” he instead says: “His righteousness remains forever and ever.” Similarly, when the Lord was urging almsgiving in the Gospel and could have said more plainly, “Beware lest you perform your alms before human beings in order to be seen by them,” he did not say this, but said: “Beware lest you perform your righteousness before human beings” (Matt. VI).

Why is this, except because almsgiving is righteousness? For just as we owe God religion, parents honor, superiors reverence, subjects discipline, and sinners correction, so we owe mercy to the wretched.

Moreover, the possessions themselves were created in common for everyone. God, however, entrusts them more abundantly to the rich, commanding them to understand that they are not their owners but their distributors to the poor. It is therefore clear that, when we give alms to the poor, we do not give them our own possessions but return what is theirs. This is indeed an act of justice.

Those who therefore retain for themselves an abundance of common goods while the poor perish from want—what else do they do than take away the poor’s own possessions and kill them? They have become murderers of as many poor people as they retain the means of supporting the poor.

Fourth, the Apostle demonstrates with what confidence we ought to [Col. 1419A] give alms when he adds: “He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for eating will also supply you; and he will multiply your seed and increase the fruits of your righteousness.” It is as though he said plainly: Do not be timid or fainthearted about giving alms, like those who make excuses to the poor asking for alms, saying that they have little money in the chest and little grain in the granary. For the Lord, who gives seed to the sower—that is, material to the giver of alms—will undoubtedly supply you, when you give alms, with bread for eating as well; and he will multiply your seed—that is, on account of the alms you have given, he will multiply your resources, so that you can give greater alms—and thus he will increase the fruits, that is, the rewards, of your righteousness; and by multiplying them, he will increase both merits and rewards. [Col. 1419B]

He possesses the smallest degree of faith who refuses to give alms because he fears that what he needs will be lacking. For if God supplies what is necessary to those who are not his own, how much more will he supply it to his faithful? And if he supplies what is necessary to those who seize the property of others, how much more to those who distribute their own?

The confidence of the farmer who sows—for the Apostle takes his metaphor from him—ought also to encourage us. Although the hope of harvest has sometimes deceived him, he nevertheless does not fear to sow again as much as he can, retaining only a very small amount for what is necessary. Indeed, at times he sows even what he himself needed; at times, when he has none of what is necessary, he borrows what belongs to others in order to sow it. And if, my brothers, the farmer sows present seed with such confidence in hope of a future harvest, perhaps an empty one, with what confidence ought we here to give alms in hope of the certain reward of eternity? [Col. 1419C]

Blessed Nicholas, blessed John the patriarch, and the other saints, retaining scarcely what was necessary for themselves, sowed into the hands of the poor whatever they could, and God abundantly supplied them with what they could give. They seemed almost to compete with one another: God by supplying them, and they by distributing for God.

He also supplied what was necessary to the widow of Zarephath. Although the famine was so severe that whoever had more bread would live longer, she nevertheless, trusting in God, fed the prophet first from the small amount of flour that alone she possessed, while she herself was hungry. Thus she deserved both the multiplication of her temporal flour and an eternal reward.

The guest of Elisha, though he had nothing of his own, also borrowed what belonged to others in order to offer hospitality to the prophets; and by this he deserved, after his death, both the multiplication of oil to pay off his debt and support his wife and children, and an everlasting recompense. [Col. 1419D]

Every day, too, my brothers, we see that some are always seizing things and are always in need, while others are always giving and always abound, because God, for whose sake they give, supplies them with everything.

Therefore let us learn to feed Christ in the hungry, give him drink in the thirsty, clothe him in the naked, receive him in strangers, visit him in the sick, and ransom him in captives, so that we may deserve to hear from him that sweetest voice: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. [Col. 1420A] For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink” (Matthew 25), and so forth—the one who grants this, God who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## The Life of Saint Laurence the Martyr, Written by the Divine Ambrose, Bishop of Milan

[Note: [Col. 1419D] Book I of *The Offices*, chapter 41.]

Let us not pass over Saint Laurence. When he saw his bishop Sixtus being led to martyrdom, he began to weep—not over Sixtus’s suffering, but over his own being left behind. Thus he began to address him in these words:

“Where are you going without your son, Father? Where are you hastening, holy priest, without your deacon? You were never accustomed to offer sacrifice without a minister. What, then, has displeased you in me, Father? Have you perhaps judged me degenerate? At least test whether you have chosen a suitable minister, to whom you entrusted the consecration of the Lord’s blood, to whom you entrusted participation in the completion of the sacraments—and to this man you deny participation in your blood? See that your judgment does not endanger you while your courage is praised. The rejection of a disciple is the loss of a teacher. What of the fact that illustrious and distinguished men conquer more through the contests of their disciples than through their own? Abraham finally offered his son; Peter sent Stephen ahead. And you, Father, display your strength in your son: offer the one whom you instructed, so that, secure in the noble distinction of your judgment, you may reach the crown.” [Col. 1420B]

Then Sixtus said:

“I am not leaving or abandoning you, my son, but greater contests are owed to you. We, like old men, are undertaking the course of a lighter battle; you, like a young man, are awaited by a more glorious triumph over the tyrant. You will come soon; cease weeping. After three days you will follow me. Here, the number between priest and Levite is fitting. It was not yours to conquer before your teacher, as though you were seeking an assistant. Why do you desire participation in my suffering? I leave you its entire inheritance. Why do you seek my presence? Let the weak disciples precede their teacher; let the strong follow, so that those who no longer need instruction may conquer without their teacher. [Col. 1420C] Thus Elijah also left Elisha. To you, therefore, I entrust the succession of our virtue.”

Such was the contest—truly worthy of a priest and a minister—over which of them would suffer first for Christ’s name. In tragic fables they say that great applause was aroused in the theater when Pylades claimed to be Orestes and Orestes, as he truly was, insisted that he was Orestes: Pylades wanted to be killed in Orestes’ place, while Orestes did not want Pylades to be killed on his behalf. Yet those men were not permitted to live, since both were guilty of parricide: one because he had committed it, the other because he had assisted.

No one compelled the holy Laurence to this except the love of devotion. Nevertheless, after three days, when he was placed upon a gridiron and burned, having deceived the tyrant, he said: “This side is cooked; turn it over and eat.” Thus, by the courage of his spirit, he overcame the nature of fire.

### Thus Peter Chrysologus Speaks of Saint Laurence

[Note: [Col. 1420D] Sermon 235, in his collection of homilies.]

Accordingly, the most blessed martyr, showing how calmly he lay upon that burning iron, said to those standing around him: “Turn me over now, and if one side is cooked, devour it.” We marvel at his endurance; let us marvel at the gift of God. There faith not only did not burn, but even consoled the one who was burning.

Why did faith console the one who was burning? Because it held fast to the one who promised, so that faith might not fail, hope might not turn away, and charity might burn more intensely amid bodily fiery torments. These were gifts of God, my brothers; let no one claim for his own power what God alone gives. The Apostle rightly addressed the martyrs, as you heard today when his Epistle was read: “To you,” he says, “it has been granted for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Philippians 1). [Col. 1420D]

Therefore let us praise and love martyrdom as a gift of God, and let us add our will to it; for the will follows, it does not go before. Yet charity is not absent if the will is not absent, for that burning will itself is called charity. Who is there who fears while willing? Who is there who loves unwillingly? Let prayer burn fervently, and let the martyr’s feast be celebrated. [Col. 1421A] But so that the one who celebrates may not do so in vain, let him imitate the martyr.

## XXX. On the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary

“I sought rest everywhere, and I shall dwell in the inheritance of the Lord” (Ecclesiasticus 24), and so forth.

These words, dearest brothers, are words of wisdom—not worldly wisdom, which is hostile to God, but the wisdom that came forth from the mouth of the Most High, namely, our Lord Jesus Christ, in whom and through whom God made and remade all things. We ought to receive his words with complete eagerness, knowing that what he speaks, he speaks to us and for us.

He says four things. First, he says that he sought and chose rest, as he demonstrates when he says: “I sought rest everywhere, and I shall dwell in the inheritance of the Lord.” [Col. 1421B]

But what does this mean, my Lord Jesus Christ? You are rest itself, and whoever rests, rests through you. Hence you yourself cry out: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11)—that is, I will make you rest. How, then, did you yourself, since you are rest, seek rest?

But I know that we find rest in those things that agree with us and please us; in those things that oppose and displease us, however, we cannot find rest. You too, Lord, although you always possess rest and peace with yourself, nevertheless have no rest among those who through uncleanness and iniquity are unlike you and displeasing to you; nor do they similarly have rest with you. But among those who through purity and righteousness are like you and pleasing to you, you have rest, and they likewise have rest with you. Hence you also said: “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, if not upon the humble and gentle and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66).

Here too you show with whom you choose to rest when you add: “And I shall dwell in the inheritance of the Lord.” The inheritance of the Lord, moreover, means those whom God has chosen as heirs of his kingdom and coheirs of his Son. Having despised all transient things, they choose God alone as their inheritance, saying with the Prophet: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Psalm 15)—that is, my portion and my inheritance. [Col. 1421C]

This is why the blessed and venerable Virgin Mary, whose Assumption we celebrate today, because more than all who have been or will be from the beginning to the end she strove to imitate the Lord in purity, humility, gentleness, [Col. 1421D] simplicity, holiness, and the other virtues, and desired in every way to become the Lord’s inheritance, was singularly chosen by the Lord from the number of all who are, who were, or who will be. In her he would rest not only spiritually but also bodily, and according to the humanity he assumed he would dwell, be nourished, and grow.

In us too, dearest brothers, if we follow the ways of our Lord Jesus Christ according to our measure; if we are pure, humble, gentle, holy, and righteous, as he himself is righteous, without doubt he will dwell, rest, and take pleasure in us. Or certainly divine wisdom says that it sought rest everywhere and would dwell only in the inheritance of the Lord because it makes wise people test all worldly pursuits; and, when they do not find rest in them, it makes them pass over to the inheritance of the Lord and dwell there. [Col. 1422A]

The second part follows. In it the wisdom of God the Father shows that the Father himself commanded and consented to its dwelling in his inheritance, when it adds: “Then the Creator of all things commanded and said to me”—understand: that I should also dwell in his inheritance.

Although the Father and the Son are of the same substance, essence, authority, will, and power, nevertheless the Son, always looking both to the fact that he is from the Father, whereas the Father is from no one, and to the fact that according to the humanity he assumed he was humbled, says: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me” (John 6). And: “The Father is greater than I, and as the Father gave me a commandment, so I do” (John 14). [Col. 1422B]

He indicates consent when he adds: “And he who created me”—that is, begot me, or certainly created me according to the humanity assumed—“rested in my tabernacle.” For since God the Father and the wisdom begotten from him have always been of the same essence and will, wherever the wisdom of God rests, there too does God the Father. Hence the same wisdom says in the Gospel: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14).

Moreover, it calls its tabernacle either the humanity assumed by him, in which the fullness of divinity dwells bodily, or the most sacred womb of the blessed Virgin, in which the wisdom of God dwelt according to the flesh. God the Father and his Son alike rested in her, both in essence and in the fullness of grace.

We too, my brothers, if we eliminate every stain of uncleanness from ourselves, if we adorn ourselves with virtues and good works, and if through true charity we have God within us, are undoubtedly the tabernacle and temple of God the Father and of his wisdom, as the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Corinthians 6); and elsewhere: “Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit? For if anyone violates the temple of the Lord, God will destroy him” (1 Corinthians 3). [Col. 1422C]

He violates the temple of God who, through shameful and evil thoughts and through a reprobate life, drives [Col. 1422D] the wisdom of God far from himself. For it is written: “Wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wisdom 1).

The third part follows. In it it is explained in whom the wisdom of God rests, when it adds: “And he said to me: Dwell in Jacob, and inherit in Israel, and put down your roots among my elect.”

It is the will of God the Father that his wisdom dwell in Jacob—that is, in those who wrestle against vices; that it inherit in Israel—that is, in those who are strong against vices; and that it put down roots only among the elect. For often those who wrestle succumb to vices, and the strong fall, and they lose the wisdom of God that seemed to dwell or inherit in them. But the elect alone, in whom divine wisdom has put down roots, do not lose it.

“And thus,” it says, “I was established in Zion”—that is, among the contemplative, who chose for themselves the better part, which will not be taken away from them (Luke 10). [Col. 1423A] “And in the city”—that is, in the congregation of the saints—“I likewise rested, sanctified.” “For where two or three are gathered in my name, I am there in the midst of them” (Matthew 18).

“And in Jerusalem is my power”—that is, among the peacemakers. The power of divine wisdom appears especially among the peacemakers, who will be called sons of God (Matthew 5), because they calm all disordered movements not only in themselves but also in others. Divine wisdom is peaceful, like deep water. Worldly wisdom, however, is contentious, like shallow and chattering water.

“And I took root in an honored people,” to whom the Lord says: “You are my people, and I am your God.” Explaining this, he adds: “And in the portion of my God, [Col. 1423B] his inheritance”—that is, I took root in the people whom God chose as his portion and who chose God as their inheritance. “And in the fullness of the saints is my dwelling.” For where there is greater holiness, there the divine wisdom is more greatly invited and detained.

Although divine wisdom rests in all these, it rests especially and singularly in Mary. For she possesses all these things, and more than these. Who was Jacob—that is, a wrestler against vices—as Mary was? Who was so chosen, indeed pre-chosen, as Mary? Who was so much Zion—that is, contemplative—as Mary? What city was so sanctified as the city and cloister of God, Mary? Who was so much Jerusalem—that is, peaceful—as Mary, mediator between God and human beings? What people were so honored, as the portion or inheritance of God, as Mary, the unique Mother of God, Virgin, and Queen of Heaven? Who possessed such fullness of holiness as Mary? [Col. 1423C]

Therefore the wisdom of God rested in Mary in a singular and supremely excellent manner.

The fourth part follows. In it wisdom shows what it is like: it says that it is exalted, beautiful, and fragrant.

It shows that it is exalted when it adds: “Like a cedar I was exalted in Lebanon.” But since divine wisdom cannot be greater or higher than it has always been, how does it say that it is exalted? Not because it is exalted in itself, but because it is exalted in its own people when it exalts them. For divine wisdom causes the saints, rising from vices, to place themselves on the heights of virtue, and to heap virtue upon virtue and [Col. 1423D] good upon good.

This is what it says: “Like a cedar I was exalted in Lebanon, and like a cypress on Mount Zion. Like a palm I was exalted in Kadesh.”

Through Lebanon, which is interpreted as “whitening,” the brightness of an innocent life is signified. Through the cedar, whose fragrance drives away serpents—as the poet says:

> Learn to kindle fragrant cedarwood in the stalls.  
> *(Virgil, Georgics, Book III, line 414.)*

And because its resin preserves books from moths and age, faith is understood: its understanding drives away heretics and preserves the meaning of the Scriptures from corruption.

Through Zion, the height of contemplation is understood. Through the cypress, which is fragrant, loses its foliage under no assault, is solid, and cannot yield to a burden, is understood the strength of eternal hope, fragrant and incapable of being overcome. [Col. 1424A]

Through Kadesh, which is interpreted as “mandate” or “holy,” the commandment of God is understood. Through the palm, which is slender around its root and spreads out above with the grace of ever-green leaves and sweet fruit, charity is signified: it begins from narrowness, then expands even toward enemies, and always remains green and fruitful.

Divine wisdom, therefore, is exalted like a cedar in Lebanon, like a cypress on Mount Zion, and like a palm in Kadesh, when through it the saints are exalted as they observe faith in innocence, hope in contemplation, and charity in the commandment.

It shows that it is beautiful when it adds: “Like a plantation of roses in Jericho, like a beautiful olive tree in the fields, and like a plane tree I was exalted beside the water in the streets.”

Jericho, moreover, is interpreted as “fragrance” or “moon.” Through the plantation of roses in Jericho, the crown of martyrdom is designated. Through the olive tree, whose liquid rises above all other liquids, mercy is understood, which triumphs over judgment. Through the plane tree—so called from the breadth of its leaves, and because it is spreading and broad, growing beside water in the streets—magnanimity is signified. In accordance with the commandment of divine wisdom and through the breadth of charity, magnanimity receives everyone, protects everyone, and benefits everyone. [Col. 1424B]

Divine wisdom, therefore, is beautiful like a plantation of roses in Jericho, like a beautiful olive tree in the fields, and like an exalted plane tree beside water in the streets, because it crowns some with the fragrance of good works, even with martyrdom; it adorns others in the field of this life through the virtue of mercy and compassion; and it illuminates others more broadly through the breadth of charity and the greatness of doing good. [Col. 1424C]

It shows that it is fragrant when it says: “Like cinnamon and balsam giving fragrance, I gave forth an odor; like chosen myrrh, I gave the sweetness of fragrance.”

Cinnamon is a short shrub, darkish or ash-colored, which, when broken, emits a visible breath in the form of mist or dust. It signifies humility, which casts itself down as short and worthless; and when wounded, becomes still more humble, returning to those who wounded it a visible breath of a good word or deed.

Balsam rises two cubits high, has white leaves that remain ever-green, and, when wounded with a sharp stone, emits drops of exceptional fragrance. It signifies kindness, which, always white and green, knows how to return the grace of benefits even to those who injure it. [Col. 1424D]

Myrrh, moreover, is bitter and preserves bodies incorrupt. It signifies chastity and the mortification of carnal desires, which preserve body and soul incorrupt from vices. Divine wisdom, therefore, is fragrant like cinnamon, balsam, and myrrh, because it makes its saints fragrant through the virtues of humility, kindness, and chastity.

And if, my brothers, the wisdom of God the Father, our Lord Jesus Christ, thus exalts, adorns, and makes the other saints fragrant, how much more does he do so for his most beloved and unique mother? And the commandment that he gave us concerning the honoring of father and mother—how much more does he himself observe it.

He therefore exalted his most beloved mother like a cedar in Lebanon, like a cypress on Mount Zion, and like a palm in Kadesh. In this life he exalted her supremely above the height of faith, hope, charity, and all the other virtues; and in the homeland he singularly raised her above every height of angels and archangels. [Col. 1425A]

He also adorned her like a plantation of roses in Jericho, like a beautiful olive tree in the fields, and like an exalted plane tree beside water in the streets, because even in this life he adorned her through the works of martyrdom—for Simeon testified that a sword would pierce her soul (Luke 2)—and through mercy, magnanimity, and the other virtues. In the homeland he made her wondrous with every crown, every glory, every beauty, splendor, and honor, beyond what the human heart can contain.

[Col. 1425B] He also made her fragrant like cinnamon and balsam giving forth fragrance, and like chosen myrrh, because he made her fragrant with the excellent odor and reputation of humility, kindness, singular virginity, and all the other virtues. All the faithful—both those who are still on the way and those who are already in the homeland—and the entire heavenly host delight in and marvel at her incomparable fragrance, saying:

> “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness like a little branch of smoke from the spices of myrrh and incense, and every powder of the perfumer?”  
> (Song of Songs 4.)

Let us therefore, dearest brothers, marvel at the ineffable fragrance of the most sacred Virgin and Mother of God; by marveling, let us delight in it; by delighting, let us emulate it; and by emulating, let us [Col. 1425C] imitate it from afar according to our strength. Let us flee every stain and every disgrace; let us pursue the practices of virtue and good conduct; let us preserve purity of mind and body; let us devote ourselves to fasts and prayers; let us continually shine through works of compassion and mercy; let us invite others by the example of a good reputation; and let us beseech the glorious Mother of God with tears and sighs to help our slowness, saying:

“O glorious Mother of God, by your merits and prayers draw us after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments.”

Nor can he fail to hear her on our behalf who deigned to be born from her for our sake, our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## XXXI. On the Same Feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Mary

[Col. 1425D]

“At that time, Jesus entered a certain village, and a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house” (Luke 10). And the rest.

In this reading, according to the tropological sense, three examples of ways of life are proposed to us. For there are three lives alone that deserve the kingdom of heaven: the active, the contemplative, and the mixed. The active life belongs to those who labor; the contemplative to those who pray; the mixed to rulers or preachers.

The duty of the active life is to administer earthly things rightly: to return to each person what belongs to that person; to give God religion; oneself, purity; parents, honor; one’s household, care; children, instruction; superiors, obedience; one’s homeland, defense; inferiors, protection; everyone, equity; the erring, correction; the hungry, food; the naked, clothing; strangers, hospitality; and things of this kind. Since this life is laborious, it is frequently called “active” from its activity. [Col. 1426A]

The duty of the contemplative life is to contemplate the glory of God, meditate upon heavenly things alone, hasten with complete desire toward eternal blessedness, and disdain all things that pass away. Its practice is threefold: prayer, reading, and meditation. In prayer one speaks to God; in reading, God speaks to one; in meditation, what has been read is remembered. Through prayer one is cleansed; through reading one is instructed; through meditation one philosophizes. Since its concern is occupied with contemplation, it is called contemplative.

The duty of the mixed life is alternately to perform now the role of the contemplative life and now that of the active life: at one time, by contemplating, to worship, read, and meditate; at another, by laboring, to [Col. 1426B] instruct the uneducated, correct the erring, help the needy, and perform similar works.

The Lord carried out this duty, for at one time he prayed in the mountains and in deserted places, and at another he preached and healed in cities and populous places. Hence here too we read that Jesus entered a certain village.

Martha carried out the duty of the active life when she received the Lord in her own person or in his members, when she ministered to him and was constantly occupied with the ministry. Mary carried out the duty of the contemplative life, as though leaving aside care and administration: sitting beside the Lord’s feet, she gazed upon and listened to him with complete desire. She was sitting—that is, she was quiet in body and mind, intent upon contemplation alone and upon the word of God.

[Col. 1426C] This stands against certain false contemplatives who, although they sit bodily in a cloister or in solitude, wander mentally throughout the whole world. They are not attentive to prayer or reading, but to rumors and vanities. This commonly happens to them through listlessness, which especially tends to afflict contemplatives when they lack the comforts of companions or activities by which they might relieve their weariness. But you, contemplatives, drive all sluggishness from yourselves through the fervor of love: “Cursed is the one who performs the work of God negligently” (Jeremiah 48). Vary your studies too—now praying, now reading, now doing something—for sameness is the mother of satiety.

Moreover, according to the sequence of the Gospel, three things are to be considered by us: why these ways of life, though so different, are called sisters; why Martha complains; and what the Lord answers her. [Col. 1426D]

These two lives are rightly called sisters because they proceed from the same origin, tend toward the same end, and always assist and accompany one another. Both Martha’s labor and Mary’s contemplation and prayer arise from the same love of God and neighbor. They also tend toward the same end, because one labors for this purpose and the other philosophizes for this purpose: that she may please God and arrive at the vision of God. Otherwise neither is this a true Martha nor is this a true Mary.

They also always assist one another. Martha, by ministering what is necessary to Mary, sustains her so that she may devote herself to contemplation, and thus in a certain way shares in and makes her own Mary’s good. The Lord says: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward” (Matthew 10). [Col. 1427A] He does not say, “A reward from the prophet,” but “the prophet’s own reward”: the one who supports the prophet so that he can prophesy makes the prophet’s reward his own.

Mary likewise helps Martha by praying to the Lord for her, lest she should at some time collapse amid so many cares; and thus she makes Martha’s merit her own. In this way the contemplative and active lives assist and accompany one another, not only in different persons but also in one and the same person.

No active person lives rightly unless he also sometimes contemplates and prays; otherwise he cannot act rationally. Nor can any contemplative in this life devote himself so entirely to contemplation that it is not necessary for him to descend to active work. He is like an eagle which, after flying to the stars and contemplating the sun, descends again to the corpses on the earth. [Col. 1427B]

But why does Martha complain to the Lord about Mary, saying: “Lord, is it no concern to you that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her, then, to help me”?

She does not say this because she thinks Mary’s duty is idle and worthless, as some people today think, and therefore wants Mary to pass over to her good work. Rather, she knows that Mary’s duty is exceedingly excellent, and therefore wishes to be helped by her sister in her own inferior but necessary duty, so that, once it has been completed quickly, she may devote herself with her sister to the contemplation she has so long desired.

This is clearly directed against certain false active people who never desire to pass over to the repose of contemplation, but always love to handle secular cares and labors. Even when they happen at some time to be at rest bodily, they are nevertheless troubled and labor mentally; and in their cares and business they do not seek to have co-workers, but rather want to handle everything themselves, treating cares and labors as repose, and repose as labor. But when will they be able to have repose amid cares, if they cannot have repose even in repose itself? [Col. 1427C]

What the Lord answers on Mary’s behalf is shown when it is added:

“Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things. But one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the better part, which will not be taken away from her.”

In these words the Lord does not condemn Martha’s portion, but places Mary’s portion above it. He demonstrates that Martha’s duty pleases him when he accepts it and when, out of great affection, he repeats the name “Martha, Martha.” But he shows that it is inferior to Mary’s duty in three respects: Martha is anxious about many things; she is troubled; and her portion is taken away.

Because she is anxious about many things, she is less intent upon the one necessary thing. Because she is troubled, she is less able to contemplate the truth. Because her portion is taken away, it is less desirable. Conversely, Mary’s portion is commended through the opposite qualities: she is intent upon the one necessary thing alone; she is not troubled but remains undisturbed; and her portion is not taken away but will always remain. Therefore it is more desirable.

Nevertheless, Martha’s portion is more fruitful in works and benefits more people, nor is it of lesser merit. For if she contracts some dust from earthly business and daily cares, the charity and advancement of her neighbors wash it away. [Col. 1428A]

What that one thing is which is necessary for everyone, the Psalmist shows when he says: “But it is good for me to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God” (Psalm 72). To this one thing, as to an anchor—the one thing toward which contemplatives alone direct themselves—we active people too must always cling, while the whirlwinds and storms of temporal anxieties, labors, and tribulations toss us about.

It should be noted, however, that although the Lord was asked, he does not command Mary to pass over to Martha’s activity; and although he praises Mary’s portion, he does not command Martha to pass over to it. Why? Because he knows that the one is more suited to contemplation than to action, and the other more suited to action than to contemplation, [Col. 1428B] and therefore he wishes to save each in the kind of life more suited to her. For there are certain persons of slower and coarser understanding, more suited to temporal than to spiritual matters; and conversely, there are some of subtler understanding, more suited to spiritual than to worldly matters. Let each, therefore, exercise himself in what he is more suited for, lest, if he should pass over to what he is not suited for, he become useless.

This is well signified by the fact that Moses’ tabernacle was externally covered with skins and coarse goat-hair cloths, to ward off the harshness of the weather. Inside, however, it shone with scarlet, purple, and fine linen. Since some people of coarse mind are less suited to handle spiritual matters, they ought to do what they are suited for: namely, by taking upon themselves external cares and disturbances, to protect contemplatives from their injuries. [Col. 1428C] And since spiritual people are less suited to handle external affairs, they ought to handle the inner and spiritual matters for which they are better suited, lest, if purple and fine linen should be brought outside into the harsh weather, they lose their beauty; and conversely, if goat-hair cloths and skins are placed inside, they become unbecoming and useless.

For I have seen some who departed from the cloister of contemplation and did not return, but, like the raven sent out by Noah, clung to corpses. There are also other persons suited to both, who know how to handle external and internal matters appropriately. These ought to be appointed rulers of the churches: they should know how, with Moses, to consult the Lord through contemplation in the tabernacle, [Col. 1428D] and then go outside to instruct and govern the people. Having gone out like Noah’s dove, and finding no rest in external affairs, they hasten to return to the ark of contemplation with the olive branch—that is, with an outwardly acquired work of mercy. Like Jacob, they should love the beauty of Rachel—that is, contemplation—more, yet not refuse to endure Leah—that is, the active life—for the sake of the fruitfulness of its works.

In the mystical sense, the fortress into which the Lord entered is the womb of the blessed Virgin. This corresponds to it well both in name and in meaning. In name, because *castellum*, or *castrum*—“fortress”—is said to derive from *castrare*, “to castrate,” since, on account of vigilance and the labor of arms, every lust is driven out of a fortress. Likewise, every lust was excluded from the womb [Col. 1429A] of the blessed Virgin through labor and honorable exercises. In meaning, because a fortress is said to be something surrounded by walls and defensive works, fortified with guards, and filled with necessities.

The fortress of the blessed Virgin, too, was enclosed by defensive works: abstinence against gluttony, chastity against lust, generosity against avarice, patience against anger, and humility against pride. Hence, in the Song of Songs: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain” (Song IV). Likewise: “Your neck is like the tower of David, which was built with battlements; a thousand shields hang upon it, every kind of armor of the mighty” (ibid.). The blessed Virgin was indeed a neck, through which the Word of God came forth to us. She was also fortified with guards, since Gabriel and the other angels, as well as holy men such as Joseph [Col. 1429B] and John the Evangelist, guarded her most sacredly as the temple of God. She was also filled with necessities, since in her he made for himself a storeroom of the bread of life and the water of wisdom.

The blessed Virgin, therefore, was a fortress—and a singular one. Although other virgins can be pure and chaste, none can be like her, both Virgin and Mother. Even if we grant that such a thing could happen, no other woman could be the mother of the Son of God. Just as he is the only Son of the one Father, so he is the only Son of his one Mother.

Into this most chaste fortress, then, Jesus entered. The gate through which he entered is faith. Because she believed, everything that had been spoken to her by the Lord was fulfilled for her. [Col. 1429C] Nor, on entering this fortress, did Jesus violate it; for Jesus saves, he does not violate. As his name is, so is his work.

“And a certain woman named Martha received him into her house,” and so forth. No one fulfilled Martha’s office as did the blessed Virgin. Others receive some guest into their house; she is believed to have done this literally, and, what is greater, she received in her womb the very Son of God, who had nowhere to lay his head (Luke IX). Others cover someone naked with clothing; she is believed to have done this too, and, what is greater, she clothed the very Son of God with her own flesh. Others refresh someone who is hungry with food or drink; she is believed to have done this too, and even gave the very Son of God, hungry according to the flesh, drink from her inward milk. She also diligently provided him with the other services of human care, [Col. 1429D] so that it may rightly be said of her: “But Martha was busy with much serving.”

In these matters she was also anxious and troubled when she fled into Egypt from the face of Herod, who was persecuting her such a son (Matt. II). She was troubled when she recognized the Jews lying in wait for him and plotting his death. She was present when he was seized and crucified; indeed, the same sword of suffering pierced her soul also (Luke II). Thus what is said applies to her very fittingly: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things.”

[Col. 1430A] No one doubts that the blessed Mary wished her son to be freed from every tribulation, and that she herself, in her distress, wished to be helped by the divinity which she knew to dwell in that same son through the contemplation that is Mary’s portion. And this is what Martha complains of: that her sister leaves her alone to serve. If such is Martha’s portion in the blessed Virgin, what do you suppose is the character of that part in her which is proclaimed to be Mary’s best portion?

Oh, how great was the multitude of sweetness within her when the Holy Spirit came upon her, and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, and she conceived from that same Holy Spirit! What did she not behold concerning God, in whom the Wisdom of God was hidden? And what did she not taste concerning God, she who carried within herself the very treasure of wisdom and knowledge? No one ever tasted so deeply how sweet the Lord is.

She kept all the words of the angels, the shepherds, and the Magi, as well as those of her own son, pondering them in her heart (Luke II). She was occupied with many things, like Martha; she delighted in the one thing, like Mary. Thus she uniquely fulfilled Martha’s portion, and uniquely chose Mary’s better portion. [Col. 1430B] But Martha’s portion is taken away from her for her good, while Mary’s portion is perfected in her and will not be taken away from her. For she has been exalted above the choirs of angels, and her desire has been filled with good things. She rejoices and reigns with her son forever, always interceding with him for us—provided that, following her example, we are either Martha, receiving Christ in the poor, feeding and clothing him, and performing the other works of mercy; or Mary, cleaving to Christ alone after rejecting all transitory things, devoting ourselves to contemplation, reading, prayer, and the other virtues, and hastening toward God with our whole desire until we reach him.

[Col. 1430C] May he grant this to us through the glorious prayers of that most blessed Mother of his, he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## XXXII. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT BARTHOLOMEW

“There arose a dispute among the disciples as to which of them seemed to be the greater” (Luke IX), and so forth.

This reading, my brothers, is divided into five parts. First, the disciples dispute about precedence. Second, the Lord, rebuking them, shows what they should not dispute about and what they should dispute about. Third, by his own example he invites them. Fourth, he demonstrates what constitutes the highest measure of their merit. Fifth, he reveals what reward he will give them.

First, then, the disciples are said to have disputed about precedence, when it is said: “There arose a dispute among the disciples as to which of them seemed to be the greater.” [Col. 1430D] Just as it belongs to the good to attend in Scripture to what may advance them toward better things, so it belongs to the wicked to seize from Scripture what may either defend or excuse their wickedness. Therefore they attend far more eagerly to the statement that a dispute arose among Christ’s disciples as to which of them seemed to be the greater than to the statement that “the multitude of believers were of one heart and one soul” (Acts IV). They remember much more tenaciously that a dispute arose between Paul and Barnabas, so that they separated from one another, than that Paul himself says: “When there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal?” (I Cor. I.)

It is as though the weakness of the saints were set before us for imitation, rather than this: that “they recovered from weakness and became strong in battle” (Heb. XI). The contention or weakness of the saints is not set before us for imitation, but rather for avoidance.

[Col. 1431A] Nevertheless, it is uncertain what kind of precedence they were disputing about. If they were disputing about external precedence, it is clear that, being still carnal, they were in error. Hence the Lord rebukes them, saying: “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who have power over them are called benefactors. But you are not so.” As if he were saying: “Do not, in the manner of worldly people, dispute about precedence and praise.”

If, however—as I am more inclined to believe—they were disputing about precedence in virtue, according to what the Lord had commanded them, “Strive to enter through the narrow gate” (Matt. VII; Luke XIII), then they were not sinning in this, nor were they rebuked by the Lord for it; rather, they were instructed by him that they ought to strive for virtue and holiness, not through pride but through humility.

[Col. 1431B] Moreover, my brothers, it is naturally implanted in us to desire and seek advancement. Since every created soul has been made desiring, it naturally desires its own progress and honor. But worldly people are deceived in choosing what to desire: either ignorant of spiritual and eternal goods or neglecting them, they admire and covet only transitory things, and strive to seize them by any means. Spiritual men, however, already tasting spiritual goods and having some foreknowledge of eternal ones, seek and desire those alone, despising worldly riches and honors. But because they know that advancement in virtue without humility is a precipice, they strive to advance in virtue through humility.

Therefore, my brothers, since we cannot refrain from desiring, let us desire true and eternal goods. For the more we desire eternal things, the more earthly things become worthless to us.

[Col. 1431C] The second part follows, in which the Lord instructs the disciples about what they should not dispute over and what they should dispute over. He instructs them about what they should not dispute over when he adds: “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who have power over them are called benefactors.” As if he were plainly saying: “They seize kingship for themselves through ambition, or power over the nations. They exercise over them not governance but rather domination through pride, and they love to be praised and honored by them through vainglory. But you are not so”—that is, do not seek precedence. And if you are called to it, do not love to dominate and be honored, but rather to be humbled, to labor, and to serve.

[Col. 1431D] Hence Peter also says: “Not as domineering over the clergy, but becoming examples to the flock from the heart” (I Pet. V). Since all human beings were created equal, it is pride to wish to dominate equals. But because some people, deviating from reason, become animal-like through sin, it is necessary that rational and spiritual people be placed over them to correct and govern them; and in this they dominate not human beings but souls.

A prelate ought, therefore, to show himself toward the good as a companion and toward the perverse as a master, yet in such a way that, among the perverse themselves, he prudently knows how to pursue their fault and foster their nature, so that he neither falls away from love on account of correction nor from correction on account of love. Even the person whom he rebukes outwardly he should place above himself inwardly, considering that, although he is superior in rank and knowledge, he has committed or may commit similar or even graver faults.

[Col. 1432A] This is plainly directed against certain people who, through ambition, seize authority over those better and wiser than themselves, and exercise tyranny rather than kingship over them, “loving the first couches at feasts, and greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by men” (Luke XIV), nourishing vices both in themselves and in their subjects and extinguishing the spirit.

What Christ’s disciples ought to dispute over he himself shows when he says: “But the greater among you must become as the younger, and the leader as the servant.” As if he were plainly saying: “You shall not dispute over precedence and domination, but rather over humility and service.”

[Col. 1432B] “The greater among you,” he says—that is, greater in the merit of virtues—“must become as the younger,” that is, inferior, not merely in word and pretense, like hypocrites, but also in genuine self-estimation. This will happen if, truly knowing himself, he always considers his own weaknesses, vices, and sins, but the good qualities of others. Reflecting on this, he will not dare to place himself above merely lesser good people, nor even above the greatest sinners, thinking that he himself might fall while they might through repentance rise even to the highest virtues.

Who, considering the fall of the apostle Judas and the restoration of Mary Magdalene, would dare, however just he might be, to place himself above any sinner, however great?

[Col. 1432C] “And the leader,” he says, “must become as the servant”—not merely in resemblance but in truth. Since a bishop is called an overseer, and to oversee means to watch, guard, fear, and be concerned for one’s subjects, which is more the duty of a servant than of a ruler, it is clear that the bishop’s duty is more to serve than to be served, and that a bishop ought to be called a servant rather than a lord.

He proves this by comparison when he adds: “For who is greater, according to worldly judgment, the one who reclines at table or the one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines?” The servant’s duty is to be concerned both for himself and for others, to prepare what is necessary, and to set before each person what he needs. The duty of the one reclining is to be concerned only for himself, to sit, and to make use of what has been set before him.

[Col. 1432D] A bishop and priest, therefore, is in the Church like a servant: he is concerned not so much for himself as for others; he must prepare the sacraments and the words of preaching for others; and he must set before each person the word or sacrament that is necessary for him. The people, however, are in the Church like those reclining at table, since each person is concerned only for himself, and does not stand as though to perform some task, but always sits as though at table to listen, receiving the preaching that has been set forth and explained.

The third part follows, in which the Lord invites the disciples to humility and service by his own example, when he adds: “But I am among you as one who serves.”

[Col. 1433A] The Lord shows how he fulfills the office of a servant when he demonstrates through the prophet Ezekiel that he will perform the office of shepherd and physician, saying: “Behold, I myself will seek my sheep and visit them, as a shepherd visits his flock on the day when he is among his scattered sheep. I will seek what was lost, bring back what was cast away, bind up what was broken, strengthen what was weak, guard what was strong and fat, and feed them in judgment and righteousness” (Ezek. XXXIV).

And Isaiah says: “Like a shepherd, he will feed his flock; with his arm he will gather the lambs, and carry them in his bosom; he himself will carry the ewes” (Isa. XL).

[Col. 1433B] The Lord sought what was lost when he came to redeem the lost human being. He brought back what had been cast away when he called the nations, cast away through idolatry, to the faith. He bound up what was broken when he bound up Mary Magdalene, Saul, and others like them, who had been broken by despair. He strengthened what was weak when he strengthened the weakness of the disciples through the Holy Spirit. He guards what is strong and fat when he guards holy men so that they do not at some time fall in temptations. He feeds them in judgment and righteousness because he instructs them rightly and with a just intention.

“With his arm he will gather the lambs,” because he calls his elect from different parts of the world into the unity of the faith. “He lifts them in his bosom,” because he cherishes and preserves their tenderness in the bosom of his mercy. “He himself carries the ewes,” because he supports through the benefit of his graces those souls who give birth to other souls through preaching, so that they do not grow weary of this labor.

[Col. 1433C] We too, whatever sort of shepherds we may be, should imitate him according to our measure. What was lost through unbelief, whether Jew or Gentile, let us seek through preaching. What has been cast away through excommunication, let us restore through reconciliation. What has been broken by tribulations, let us bind up through consolations. What is weak, let us strengthen through encouragement. What is fat and strong, let us guard through pastoral concern.

Let us teach Christ’s sheep rightly and justly; let us gather the scattered and diverse into unity; let us cherish the weak and inexperienced in our bosom; and let us help souls that are giving birth to other souls, so that they do not fail in this work.

[Col. 1433D] The Lord not only undertook the office of a servant, but also that of a slave. For, my brothers, was it not more the office of a slave than of a lord—or even of a servant—to assume the form and humility of a slave, submit himself to human beings, pay tribute, wash feet, endure scourges, insults, injuries, and death, and offer himself to death for others?

We too, my brothers, whatever we may be, hold Christ’s place in the Church. Let us offer our brothers not only the office of ministers but also that of slaves. Let us not hesitate to submit ourselves to them, wash their feet, endure insults and injuries for their sake, and lay down for them not only what is ours but even our lives. Otherwise, we do not hold the office of the true shepherd.

The fourth part follows, in which the Lord shows what the highest measure of his disciples’ merit is, when he adds: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations.”

[Col. 1434A] No inward temptation assailed the Lord; rather, he calls external weaknesses and persecutions temptations, by a figure of speech. Weaknesses include hunger, thirst, weariness, and the like. Persecutions include the snares, insults, scourges, injuries, and deaths inflicted by the devil or by his members.

Amid these temptations, the disciples remained with Christ not only in faith and love, but also experienced them together with Christ. Great and wondrous was the faith and merit of the apostles. Was it not great and admirable that they believed the one whom they saw to be a human being to be God; that they believed the one whom they saw to be mortal to be immortal; and that they believed the one whom they saw to be weak to be omnipotent?

[Col. 1434B] But what shall we say to this, my brothers? They remained with Christ, still weak, poor, and mortal, in faith and love; and we cannot remain with that same Christ, now glorified, now immortal, commanding heaven and earth, in true faith and love? They suffered with Christ and for Christ while he was suffering, and we fear to suffer for him now that he glorifies his own?

The fifth part follows, in which the Lord reveals the apostles’ reward, when he adds: “And I appoint to you a kingdom, as my Father appointed one to me, so that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

[Col. 1434C] This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High: those who now humbly rejoice to serve their fellow servants with Christ will then reign in exaltation with Christ. Those who now rejoice to hunger with Christ will then be refreshed with Christ by eternal delights. Those who now labor and suffer with Christ will then sit with Christ. Those who are now unjustly judged will then, with Christ, judge their judges.

He establishes the apostles’ reward in four things: the honor of reigning, the pleasure of feasting, the rest of sitting, and the power of judging—although then every kind of precedence, every necessity of feasting, sitting, and judging will cease. Since those eternal goods are such “as eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (I Cor. II), it is clear that they cannot be expressed in human words.

[Col. 1434D] But since it was necessary for them to be signified to us in some way, they are therefore signified by words transferred from those things that are more greatly desired here. In this life, honor, pleasure, rest, and power are more greatly desired. These will indeed exist in that eternal life, but not as they do now: there will be true honor without end, true pleasure without disgust, and true rest without limit.

May the almighty Lord, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, grant this to us through the merits and prayers of blessed Bartholomew. Amen.

## Life of the Apostle Bartholomew

Eusebius, concerning Saint Bartholomew: Bartholomew received Further India as his allotted region. In Book III, chapter 1, and Book V, chapter 10, he writes as follows: “They say that when Pantaenus reached the Indians, he found that the apostle Bartholomew had first sown among them the seeds of the faith and had left them the Gospel of Matthew written in Hebrew letters,” and so forth.

Joachim Vadianus mentions Saint Bartholomew as follows: “Among the kinds of punishments, the Persians had flaying.”

Marcellinus, in Book XXIII, reports a punishment [Col. 1435A] undoubtedly known also among neighboring peoples, so that it is plausible that what has been handed down about Bartholomew, the flayed apostle of the East, is true.

Saint Jerome has the following concerning Saint Bartholomew [Note: [Col. 1435D] Book *On Illustrious Men*]: “The apostle Bartholomew preached the Gospel of Christ to the Indians who are called the Fortunate, and delivered to them the Gospel according to Matthew. He died at Albanopolis, a town of Greater Armenia.”

## Miracle of the Body of the Apostle Saint Bartholomew, Written by Blessed Gregory, Archbishop of Tours

History relates that the apostle Bartholomew suffered his martyrdom in India. Many years after his passion, when Christian persecution arose again and the pagans saw the whole people hastening to his tomb and bringing offerings of incense to him in continual prayer, they were stirred by envy. They removed his body, placed it in a lead sarcophagus, and threw it into the sea, saying: “You will no longer lead our people astray.”

[Col. 1435B] But with God’s providence cooperating, through the hidden working of his power, the lead sarcophagus was lifted from that place by the waters carrying it away and was borne to an island called Liparis. It was revealed to the Christians so that they might gather it; they gathered it and buried it. They also built a great church over it, where, when he is now invoked, he is shown to benefit many peoples through numerous miracles and favors.

## XXXIII. ON THE BEHEADING OF THE BLESSED JOHN THE BAPTIST

“Herod sent and seized John and bound him in prison because of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, whom he had married” (Mark VI), and so forth.

[Col. 1435C] In this reading of the holy Gospel, dearest brothers, four matters are set before us: how great is the kindness of the just toward the wicked; how great is the wickedness of the wicked toward the just; how the wicked fall from evil to worse; and how the good advance from good to better.

How great is the kindness of the just toward the wicked is first shown here through the most blessed John the Baptist. Like a good preacher, he displayed toward the wicked and adulterous Herod discerning charity, stern justice, and rightly ordered compassion.

He showed discerning charity toward him when he loved his nature so much that he hated his wickedness, and hated his wickedness so much that he truly loved his nature. Human beings should indeed be loved in such a way that their errors are not loved. This is contrary to certain people who either, because of their love for human beings, foster their vices, or, because of their hatred of vices, persecute human nature.

[Col. 1435D] He also exercised rigorous justice toward Herod. Although Herod was a king, and although he was cruel and a persecutor of the saints, John nevertheless opposed him for the sake of justice when everyone else was silent, and did not hesitate to correct him harshly for his adultery with his brother’s wife and for his other evils.

This is directed against us unworthy preachers, who either flatter the vices of the powerful or correct them mildly, while we correct the vices of the poor and inferior with cruelty and pride. Why is this? Unless it is because we truly love neither group and exercise true justice toward neither: toward the powerful we show indulgence because of their wealth, and toward the poor we show cruelty because we despise their poverty, becoming respecters of persons.

[Col. 1436A] John also showed rightly ordered compassion toward Herod. Although he endured injuries, chains, and imprisonment from him, he grieved more over Herod’s madness and destruction than over the injury inflicted upon himself. This too is directed against us, who, if we happen to be injured by one of our brothers, do not sympathize with his folly but grow inflamed with anger against him, seek revenge, and desire his ruin.

Second, how great is the wickedness of the wicked toward the just is shown through Herod. He repaid such a holy and diligent admonisher with evil for good, as a serpent does: hatred for love, injustice for justice, and savage cruelty for compassion, according to the Psalmist’s words: “They repaid me evil for good, and hatred for my love” (Ps. CVIII); and elsewhere: “With perfect hatred I hated them; they became enemies to me” (Ps. CXXXVIII).

[Col. 1436B] Perfect hatred—that is, the hatred of the perfect—is to hate the wickedness of human beings and not their nature. For this good hatred, the wicked repay them with unrighteous hatred, hating and persecuting their nature and holiness.

Because John wished to free Herod from the hand of the devil and from the chains of sin, Herod therefore seized and bound John. Because John wished to snatch Herod from the prison of death and hell, Herod therefore imprisoned him. Because John wished to give Herod life, Herod therefore killed him.

This is what the evangelist says: “Herod sent and seized John and bound him in prison because of Herodias, the wife of his brother, whom he had married.” For John was saying to Herod: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”

[Col. 1436C] Herodias, however, lay in wait for him because he wished to separate her from adultery and restore her to her lawful husband; and she wished to kill him, but could not. For Herod feared John, knowing him to be a holy and just man, and protected him from Herodias’ hand.

Behold, my brothers: although Herod held holy John in chains and in prison, he nevertheless feared him. And why? The reason follows: “Knowing him to be a holy and just man.” Thus, my brothers, thus the wicked person always fears the just, however powerful he may be; the bad person fears the good; the lustful person fears the chaste. For his conscience bears witness that he is guilty and the other innocent, that he deserves death and the other life. Therefore, whatever the innocent person may suffer here, his innocence is blessed; and however greatly wickedness may prosper here, its misery remains, because it condemns itself within itself and justifies the other.

[Col. 1436D] “And when he heard him,” it says, “he did many things”—namely, minor things, leaving greater matters undone, like one who strains out the gnat but swallows the camel (Matt. XXIII). “And he heard him gladly.” John had become for him, according to the prophet, like a musical instrument (Job XXX), whose sound it was more pleasant for him to hear than to obey.

All these details—that Herod knew John to be a holy and just man, that he heard him gladly, and that he did many of the things he heard—are repeated to heighten the wickedness of Herod, who knew such a great and holy man, and nevertheless killed him.

[Col. 1437A] Third, how the wicked fall from evil to worse is shown through Herod and Herodias, when it is added: “When a suitable day had come.” Suitable for whom, and suitable for what? Suitable for Herodias, so that she could kill John, which previously she had been unable to do; and suitable also for Herod, who then seemed to himself to have a just occasion for killing the saint, which he had not had before.

Herod made a banquet on his birthday. Because Herod celebrated the day of his birth festively, he deserved to have a mournful death. On the day of our birth, my brothers, we ought not to celebrate but rather to mourn, because when we enter this world, we fall into misery and guilt. Hence, when a human being is born, he can mourn but cannot laugh. We ought, however, to solemnize the death of the saints, since then they cast off misery and receive glorious and eternal life. Hence we call their death-days their “birthdays.”

[Col. 1437B] And for whom did Herod make the banquet? Not for the poor and strangers, but for rulers, military tribunes, and the leading men of Galilee, disregarding the Lord’s command: “When you make a dinner, do not invite your friends, or your brothers, or the rich, lest they perhaps invite you in return and repayment be made to you. But invite the poor and the weak, and you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you; you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just” (Luke XIV).

When the daughter of that Herodias entered, danced, and pleased Herod and those reclining with him, the king said to the girl: “Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you.” And he swore to her: “Whatever you ask, I will give you, even half my kingdom.”

[Col. 1437C] Behold how many evils arise from gluttony. Since Herod was devoted to excessive and frequent feasting, he fell in love with prostitutes. For just as the genitals depend upon the belly, so lust arises from gluttony. The order of the vices follows the order of the bodily members. Hence it is written that the abundance of bread was the cause of the Sodomites’ shameful fornication (Ezek. XVI).

Again, because he was devoted to excessive and frequent feasting, he fell in love with a dancing girl, with actors, and with buffoons. For it is written: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. XXXII).

[Col. 1437D] Again, from the same cause he fell into an inconsiderate promise and a rash oath. At feasts, excessive talk is accustomed to abound, from which inconsiderate speech and rash oaths arise. For crimes are punished through crimes. Hence John says in the Apocalypse: It is just that “the one who is filthy should become filthy still” (Rev. XXII).

It follows: “When she had gone out, she said to her mother, ‘What shall I ask for?’ But she said to her, ‘The head of John the Baptist.’” Behold what is more cruel than a prostitute. For it is written: “There is no head more wicked than the head of a serpent, and there is no malice above the malice of a woman” (Ecclus. 25). Forgetful of her sex, forgetful of modesty and reverence, at so solemn a banquet and before so many princes, she does not blush to request the throat of so holy a man, and for so shameful a reason.

“And the king was grieved,” it says, “because of the oath and because of those reclining at table with him; he did not wish to grieve her, but, sending an executioner, he ordered the head of John the Baptist to be brought on a platter” [Col. 1438A]. Behold, my brothers, to what blindness of mind Herod came through the intemperance of gluttony and lust: he preferred to kill so holy a man rather than alter a rash oath; he preferred to offend God and human beings rather than grieve an adulteress and a dancing girl; he preferred to appear impious rather than a man of empty words; he preferred to stain his birthday and such a solemn banquet, and the presence of so many princes, with the bloody head of a murdered man rather than deny the adulteress’s sacrilegious request.

Impious were those among whom no one was found who, with sounder counsel, might advise that the king’s rash promise and oath should be changed—especially when they saw that he was grieved because of the oath—unless perhaps they understood that the king’s grief was feigned [Col. 1438B], and that under such a pretext he had prepared the fulfillment of his own desire.

Behold Herod and Herodias: falling from gluttony into adultery, from adultery into blindness of mind, from blindness into the murder of a patriarch, and finally being hurled into eternal damnation.

Fourth, it is shown how the good advance from good to better through John the Baptist. As was demonstrated above, from the good of charity he advanced to the good of preaching; from the good of preaching to the triumph of martyrdom; from the triumph of martyrdom to eternal blessedness, according to what is read in the Apocalypse: “It is right that the one who is holy be sanctified still more” (Rev. 22). And the Psalmist says:

> Blessed is the man whose help is from you [Col. 1438C];  
> he has set ascents in his heart  
> in the valley of tears, in the place that he has established.  
> For the lawgiver will give a blessing;  
> “they will go from strength to strength;  
> the God of gods will be seen in Zion” (Ps. 83).

Therefore, my brothers, detesting the life and wickedness of the depraved, let us flee banquets and drunkenness; let us flee and avoid the plague of prostitutes, dancing girls, and buffoons; and, eating in silence and moderation, let us listen to sacred reading. Let us beware of excessive talk, foolish talk, and rash oaths. And if by chance we have rashly promised or sworn something, it is better to change it than to fall into something worse.
