David also swore that he would kill the fool Nabal, but at the first intercession of Abigail, a prudent woman, he returned his sword to its sheath [Col. 1438D], nor did he grieve that he had incurred any guilt through such perjury (1 Sam. 25). Let us also, emulating the holiness of John, learn truly to love our neighbor; to correct the vices of those who offend; to lay down not only our possessions but even our life for justice; to despise worldly things; and to hasten with our whole desire toward eternal blessedness.

May God and our Lord Jesus Christ grant this to us through the prayers of his forerunner and baptizer, he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## XXXIV. On the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary

“Behold, like a vine I have brought forth sweetness of fragrance, and my flowers are fruits of honor and uprightness” (Ecclus. 24), etc.

These words, my brothers, are the words not of worldly wisdom, which is rejected, but of that wisdom which came forth from the mouth of the Most High, and through which God the Father created and redeemed the world. Therefore, like a most loving mother, it invites us to the breasts of its sweetest teaching. It does so in this way. First, it shows itself to be fruitful. Second, it invites us to itself. Third, it says what it is like. Fourth, it shows how useful it is.

First, then, it shows itself to be fruitful when it says: “I have brought forth fruit like a vine,” etc. As if it plainly said: “I am not barren like worldly wisdom, which generates nothing but death; rather, I have borne fruit through the prophets, the apostles, and the other saints who cling to me like branches to a vine.”

Now a vine has three characteristics: it gives you no fruit unless you cultivate it diligently. Once cultivated, however, it gives you sweetly fragrant flowers and intoxicating fruits. Divine wisdom likewise benefits you nothing unless you cultivate it with the greatest diligence and labor. For it hates the lazy and the sleepy. Hence it cries out: “Blessed is the one who hears me, and who watches daily at my gates” (Prov. 8).

Once cultivated, it gives you fragrant flowers and intoxicating fruits. For when you begin to devote yourself attentively to divine wisdom, it will gradually delight and attract you more and more by its wondrous fragrance, and at last intoxicate you with its wondrous flavor and turn your mind from earthly things toward love of heavenly things, so that you may say with the Prophet: “And how splendid is your intoxicating cup!” (Ps. 22). With this new wine the apostles were drunk on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2). With this new wine spiritual men are drunk even today: desiring only invisible things, they despise all earthly things as dung [Col. 1440A], and therefore are regarded in this world as fools and madmen.

The cup of Babylon also intoxicates some—that is, the wisdom of worldly greed. But this cup is not splendid, because it does not illumine people’s minds as divine wisdom does; rather, it blinds them and hurls them into the pit of eternal damnation.

“And what have you brought forth?” “Sweetness of fragrance,” and sweetly fragrant flowers—namely, the virtues and their works, which make the saints so famous and esteemed that they delight even those who are absent and very far away.

“And my flowers are fruits of honor and uprightness.” As if it said: “My flowers are not empty and fruitless, like the flowers of worldly and carnal wisdom, of which it is said: ‘All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. The grass has withered, and the flower has fallen, but the word of the Lord remains forever’ (Isa. 40).”

But my flowers—that is, the virtues and good works with which I make my people flourish—produce fruits of honor and uprightness, that is, eternal and blessed life, where no one will be honored without uprightness, and no one will be made upright without honor, unlike in this wretched world, where many have honor without uprightness, and many have uprightness without honor.

Next, she explains more openly what those flowers and fruits are when she adds: “I am the mother of beautiful love, and of fear, and of knowledge, and of holy hope.”

She places love of God and neighbor before the other virtues, because it is itself the cause of all the virtues. She calls it beautiful in contrast to carnal love, which is often shameful and foul. She joins fear to it, because we must love with fear and fear with love. But since we can neither truly love nor truly fear unless we recognize what must be loved and what must be feared, she adds knowledge—that is, faith—which she calls knowledge because by it alone we recognize what we ought to fear and love. To these she also adds hope, because we love uselessly, fear uselessly, and believe in God uselessly unless we have holy—that is, firm—hope in him.

“In me,” she says, “is all grace of the way and of truth; in me is all hope of life and of virtue,” that is, of eternal life, which is always virtuous and flourishing.

The second part follows, in which the wisdom of God invites us to itself, adding: “Come over to me, all you who desire me, and be filled with my fruits” [Col. 1440D].

She says three things: who should approach it, how they should approach it, and with what benefit.

Who? Those who desire it. Thus divine secrets are revealed to Daniel through an angel, because, it says, he is “a man of desires” (Dan. 9). For the negligent and lukewarm cannot come to true wisdom.

How? By crossing over—from evil, of course, to good; from laziness to moral excellence; from sleepiness to vigilance; from vices to virtues; from temporal things to eternal things. Only the Hebrews—that is, those who cross over—are worthy to eat the flesh of the lamb. And our Redeemer promises that he will be seen by his disciples in Galilee, that is, in “transmigration.”

With what benefit? “Be filled with my fruits,” that is, with my fruitfulness [Col. 1441A]. True wisdom refreshes the mind, whereas worldly wisdom does not refresh it but inflates it. Hence it is well signified by the sounding, swelling husks with which the prodigal son wished to fill his belly but could not (Luke 15). For secular wisdom is talkative and inflationary, food more suited to pigs than to human beings.

The third part follows, in which divine wisdom shows what it is like. It shows that it is sweet, eternal, and desirable.

It shows that it is sweet when it says: “My spirit is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance is sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.” If it had found anything sweeter, it would have put it there. Indeed, the inspiration of divine wisdom in the saints, although partial and shadowy, is above every sweetness [Col. 1441B]. But how great, do you think, will be the sweetness in the open perception and inheritance of that wisdom which will take place in the vision of God?

It shows that it is eternal when it adds: “My memory is through the generations of ages.” As if it plainly said: “The wisdom of worldly people will perish, and there will be no memory of it, because on that day all their thoughts will perish. But I remain forever, and I cause those who remember me to remain forever. The knowledge they have of me in this life will not be taken away; rather, it will be perfected for them in eternal life.”

It shows that it is desirable when it adds: “Those who eat me will still hunger, and those who drink me will still thirst.” This is the difference between bodily and spiritual delights, and between earthly and eternal delights: bodily and earthly delights, when they are not possessed, are considered great and desired. But when they become habitual, they grow cheap and turn into disgust. Spiritual and eternal delights, by contrast, when they are not possessed, are considered nothing; but once possessed, they kindle desire—yet in such a way that there is satisfaction in the very desire, and desire in the very satisfaction.

The fourth part follows, in which divine wisdom shows how useful it is to us, adding: “Whoever hears me will not be put to shame; those who work in me will not sin; and those who make me shine forth will possess eternal life.”

“Whoever hears me,” it says—that is, hears me with the heart and with the intention of obeying—and even if he does not have time to act, will not be put to shame for condemnation on the day of judgment, because he heard this counsel of wisdom, so that he might be put to shame unto repentance [Col. 1441D]. This is what the Wisdom of the Father itself says in the Gospel: “Whoever is not ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of Man will not be ashamed of him when he comes in his majesty and that of the holy angels” (Luke 9).

“And those who work,” it says, “in me will not sin,” understood: unto death, for if they sin, they will no longer be working in me.

“And those who make me shine forth,” it says—that is, those who explain and expound me to others by word and example—“will possess eternal life.” This is what is read elsewhere: “Those who instruct many will shine like the stars of the firmament” (Dan. 12).

There is a progression among these three, both in merit and in reward. It is great to hear wisdom with the heart; greater to act according to it; greatest to make it shine forth to others by word and example [Col. 1442A]. Likewise, those who hear wisdom with the heart will receive a great reward; those who act according to it, a greater reward; and those who explain it by word and example, the greatest reward. Nevertheless, all will possess everlasting life.

Since, then, my brothers, these words are words of wisdom, they can also apply to the Blessed Virgin, whom the Wisdom of the Father itself chose, fashioned, and adorned as its singular resting place. For this is a figure called metonymy, when what is contained is attributed to the container.

The Blessed Virgin, therefore, inviting us to admiration and veneration—that is, to imitation of her—can say: “I have brought forth sweetness of fragrance like a vine,” not only by offering the whole world an example of holy life and good reputation, but also by giving birth to him through whose fragrance the dead rise again.

“For I am that branch of which Isaiah foretold: ‘A branch shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root’” (Isa. 11). “And my flowers are not empty, but are fruits of honor and uprightness: for my son is himself the flower, and himself the fruit—the flower of sweetness and the fruit of satisfaction.”

Of his sweetness Isaac, speaking in the person of God the Father, says: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 27). Of his satisfaction the Psalmist foretold, saying: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16).

He is the fruit of honor and uprightness, because he possesses in himself every honor and uprightness, and grants them to whom he wishes.

“I am the mother of beautiful love, and of fear, and of knowledge, and of holy hope”—of these virtues and of the others, not only by offering examples, but also by giving birth to him who is the love, faith, fear, and hope of all the faithful.

“In me is all grace of the way and of truth; in me is all hope of life and of virtue.” For I not only display these things in myself by example, but also carry in my womb him who is “full of grace and truth” (John 1), who is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14), who is the hope, virtue, and refreshment of all the faithful.

“Come over, therefore, to me by imitation, you who desire me”—that is, my life, holiness, and glory—“and be filled with my fruits,” that is, with the blessings of my Only-Begotten Son. For “my spirit”—that is, the Holy Spirit, who came upon me in a unique manner and rests in me—“is sweeter than honey.”

“And my inheritance,” which I possess with my Son, “above the choirs of angels, is sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.”

“My memory is through the generations of ages,” because “from now on all generations will call me blessed” (Luke 1).

“Those who eat me will still hunger, and those who drink me will still thirst.” For the more the faithful begin to perceive and imitate my customs and virtues, the more they will admire them and thirst for them.

“Whoever hears me,” through imitation, “will not be put to shame; and those who work in me,” that is, according to me, “will not sin.”

“And those who make me shine forth,” that is, those who explain and proclaim my customs, virtues, and holiness by words and deeds, “will possess eternal life.”

Behold, our lady and mother, we, your least servants, admire, praise, and proclaim your holiness and glory; yet we are unable to imitate you worthily. Therefore, help us by your most powerful prayers. Make us cross over to you through desire; make us flee our vices and sins and cross over to customs and virtues; make us despise earthly things and desire heavenly ones. Sustain us amid the temptations of the flesh, the snares of the devil, and the tribulations of this world, so that, with your help and under your guidance, we may attain those joys in which you rejoice forever with your Son, to whom be honor and glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## XXXV. On the Same Feast: A Sermon on the Gospel

“The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” [Col. 1443B] (Matt. 1), and the rest.

There are two generations of our Lord Jesus Christ, my brothers: one eternal, the other human. Through the former he was born before the ages, true God from God the Father. Through the latter he was born in time, true man from a human mother. Through the former he was born eternally from the Father without a mother. Through the latter he was born temporally from a virgin mother without a father.

The former generation is incomprehensible; the latter is wondrous. Of the former the prophet Isaiah said: “Who,” he says, “will declare his generation?” (Isa. 53). Of the latter the evangelist Matthew says here: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ,” understood: “This is it.” It is like a title explaining the subject matter of the book that follows.

There are, moreover, four temporal generations. The first was neither from a man nor from a woman, as when God formed the first human being from the earth. The second was from a man without a woman, as when God formed the woman from the side of the sleeping man. The third is from man and woman, and this is the ordinary generation. The fourth remains: from woman without man, and this is the singular generation of Jesus Christ.

The first, second, and third generations were for the propagation of the human race. This last, fourth generation was for its redemption. Those three fell through disobedience; this fourth restored their ruins. Therefore this generation is greater, more wondrous, and more useful to us than the others.

It is greater because the one born is greater, namely the Son of God. It is more wondrous because it is more wondrous that God deigned to be born from a woman in the form of a servant than that he fashioned a servant. It is more useful to us because rebirth to eternal life—which we possess through Christ’s nativity—is more useful to us than birth in this world to death through the birth of the flesh.

Since Matthew intends to discuss here only this one generation of Christ, why does he begin farther back by weaving together many generations? Clearly, so that he might show the Jews, for whom he wrote, that he was not writing the generation of just any Christ, but of the one who had been promised to the ancient fathers in the Law.

Hence he places two fathers first, namely David and Abraham, to whom the promise was specifically made concerning Christ, who was to be born from their seed. For it was said to Abraham: “In your seed all nations will be blessed” (Gen. 22). And to David: “I will establish his seed for age upon age, and his throne like the days of the age” (Ps. 88) [Col. 1444A]. Hence, long after David, when the kingdom of the Jews was already tending toward its end, Jeremiah said: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous Branch; and a king shall reign, and he shall be wise, and he shall execute judgment and justice in the land. And this is the name by which they will call him: ‘The Lord our righteousness’” (Jer. 23).

Beginning Christ’s genealogy, therefore, the evangelist says: “Abraham begot Isaac, and Isaac begot Jacob,” etc.

In this genealogy, dearly beloved brothers, you must consider four things: the character of the genealogy itself, the diversity of the persons, the number, and the order.

First, what kind of genealogy is this? It is wondrous, holy, and fruitful. It is wondrous both at its beginning and at its end. Abraham, though he was old, wondrously begot Isaac from a barren and aged mother. More wondrously still, the most holy Virgin Mary, without the companionship of a man, gave birth not to just anyone but to God’s own Son, her God and Creator.

The first generation is wondrous because it is contrary to nature; this one is more wondrous because it is above and contrary to nature. Hence it was rightly prefigured by the miraculous fruitfulness of Aaron’s rod. For just as Aaron’s rod, though dry and without the support of a root or moisture, wondrously blossomed and produced almonds, so—or rather, more wondrously—the Blessed Virgin Mary, when every desire in her had been dried up by the ardor of the Holy Spirit, conceived and gave birth without external assistance.

This generation is holy because its root is holy, its stock is holy, and its trunk is holy; holier is the Virgin Mary, and most holy is the flower and fruit. Abraham and the other patriarchs were holy, for they are the first path of faith. The prophets were also holy, for they were instruments of the Holy Spirit. The kings were also holy, for they possessed the wisdom to govern themselves and others.

Holier, however, was the Blessed Virgin Mary, who is the temple of God, the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, a chamber of spices, and a paradise of delights. Most holy is the Holy of Holies, our God and Lord Jesus Christ, in whom “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2), and the seven spirits sent throughout all the earth.

Foreseeing the holiness of this generation, Isaiah said: “A branch shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him—the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety—and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11).

The genealogy is also useful to us, provided that we imitate the holiness of the fathers set before us: if we live and teach rightly according to the example of the patriarchs; if, following the example of good kings, we correct and govern ourselves and others well; if, following the example of the Blessed Virgin, we strive to possess purity, humility, and every holiness; and if, loving Jesus Christ as our Redeemer, following him, and carrying out his commandments, we strive to become participants in his redemption.

Through this genealogy God sent his Word like a hook hidden in flesh into the waters of the human race, so that by it he might catch the devil and free us from his jaws. Hence he says to blessed Job: “Can you catch Leviathan with a hook?” (Job 40)—understood: “As I can, when I hide my Son like a hook in flesh, and catch the devil, who is greedy for flesh. While he desires to swallow the one over whom he had no right, he also loses the human race over which he seemed to have a right.”

Second, the diversity of the persons placed in this genealogy must be considered. Here are placed both men and women; Jews and Gentiles; kings and those of lower status; older and younger; good and evil. For all needed Christ’s redemption. Therefore he took flesh from the lineage of all, so that he might redeem all.

Just as the evil needed forgiveness of sins, so the good needed the opening of the kingdom of heaven, which could not be opened except through Christ’s blood. But some evil people are also inserted into this holy generation to show that wickedness does not harm holiness, since, according to the prophet: “The soul that sins, it shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, and the father shall not bear the iniquity of the son” (Ezek. 18).

“The justice of the just shall be upon him, and the impiety of the impious shall be upon him.” The wickedness of a son does not harm a good father, provided that he corrected him as far as he could. Nor does the wickedness of a father harm a good son, provided that the son did not imitate him.

At other times the wickedness of a son harms a negligent father, as is evident in Eli; and the wickedness of a father harms a son who imitates his father. Hence the Lord says: “I am a jealous God, visiting the sins of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation” (Exod. 20) [Col. 1445C].

Conversely, the goodness of a father does not benefit an evil son; indeed, it harms him, since he scorns following the example and course of conduct placed immediately before him. Nor does the goodness of a son benefit an evil father who instructed him neither by word nor by example.

Third, the number must be considered. Forty-two generations are enumerated here up to Christ. The sons of Israel likewise reached the Promised Land by forty-two encampments. Through the sacramental meaning of the same number—that is, through the Decalogue in the four Gospels, and the four Gospels in the Decalogue, fulfilled through the twofold love—we also reach the Promised Land and Christ.

For the Decalogue and the four Gospels, without the twofold love of God and neighbor, cannot lead us to the Promised Land and to Christ. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22). And the Psalmist says: “I have run the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118)—understood: through charity, which extends even to one’s enemy. Explaining this elsewhere, he says: “I have seen the end of all perfection; your commandment is exceedingly broad” (ibid.). For the more fervently we love God and neighbor, the more easily and quickly we traverse God’s commandments.

Therefore, just as the sons of Israel reached the River Jordan through forty-two encampments and, crossing it wondrously on dry feet, entered the Promised Land, so our Redeemer came through forty-two generations to the river of our mortality; crossing it most victoriously, he entered heaven.

We too, my brothers, through the fulfillment of the Decalogue in the four Gospels and of the four Gospels in the Decalogue, together with the twofold love, run happily through the course of this life to death. Crossing over safely, we enter the desired rest of the Promised Land.

Fourth, the order must also be considered. The aforesaid number is arranged in three sets of fourteen [Col. 1446B]. The first extends from Abraham to King David, that is, from the way of believing to governance; the second from David to the transmigration; the third from the transmigration to Christ.

In this order, my brothers, the order of our progress and of our salvation is shown to us. We begin the way to Christ from faith, which is the foundation of all virtues and without which nothing can please God (Heb. 11). Faith is not sufficient, because “faith without works is dead” (James 2); but, progressing from it and passing through fourteen—that is, through the teaching of the Decalogue and the four Gospels—we reach the kingdom, where we learn to govern ourselves and others well.

Nor should we stop here. Rather, with our whole desire we must strive toward the transmigration of divine contemplation, which we acquire through fourteen—that is, through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, doubled in the twofold love.

For the anointing of the Spirit teaches us inwardly where we ought to go (1 John 2), and inflames us through true love, so that with our whole desire we may cross over from earthly things to eternal things and from the world to God.

But this transmigration of contemplation is an enigma and a shadow. “For here we know in part, and we prophesy in part” (1 Cor. 13). Hence the Lord says to Moses: “No one shall see me and live” (Exod. 33).

Therefore, my brothers, from this shadowy transmigration of contemplation we must hasten toward the true vision of God, desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Phil. 1). We reach this through fourteen—that is, through a double seven, namely, through the twofold rest of body and soul, which is granted to the righteous when this mortality is laid aside.

Hence the Psalmist says: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord: sons, the reward, the fruit of the womb” (Ps. 126) [Col. 1446D]. As if he said: While the elect are in this world together with the reprobate, the sons of the free woman together with the sons of the slave woman, they are beaten, afflicted, and suffer the tribulations of this world together. But “when the Lord gives his beloved sleep,” the sleep of bodily death, “behold,” the “inheritance of the Lord” is now given to them: “sons, the reward, the fruit of the womb,” namely, the virginal womb.

For this reason the Son of God humbled himself and was born of a Virgin: to earn eternal inheritance for us. For this reason he became a participant in our lowliness: to make us coheirs of his blessedness, his splendor, and his glory.

Let riches, honors, pleasures, and worldly glories therefore become cheap to us, dearly beloved brothers. Let everything that we see in this world and everything that we possess here become cheap to us. Let us distribute these things through works of mercy in exchange for that eternal blessedness and inheritance. Let us hasten toward it with our whole mind and desire, and strive to reach it through a good life and good conduct.

May our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ grant this to us through the merits and prayers of the most blessed Virgin and his mother, he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## XXXVI. On the Exaltation of the Holy Cross

“Now is the judgment of the world; now the prince of this world will be cast out” (John 12), and the rest.

This reading from the holy Gospel, my brothers, has four parts. First, the Lord says that through judgment the prince of this world is to be cast out of the world [Col. 1447B]. Second, he shows by what means and how this will be accomplished. Third, the Jews, in their response, show that they are ignorant of the mystery of the cross. Fourth, the Lord urges them to faith.

First, then, the Lord shows that through judgment the prince of the world is to be cast out of the world when he says: “Now is the judgment of the world.”

There are, moreover, three judgments of God. One is the judgment of retribution, which will occur at the end, when God “will repay each one according to his works” (Matt. 16). Another is the judgment of discernment, which takes place daily in the holy Church, when God distinguishes the merits of individuals. “The Lord,” he says, “is the one who judges me. For I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified” (1 Cor. 4).

The third is the expulsion of the devil from human hearts. It is of this that the Lord, as his passion drew near, said what we have just heard: “Now is the judgment of the world.”

Now the case concerning the inhabitants of the world is being heard: who ought to possess them more rightly, God or the devil. For although it was certain that God ought by right to possess the world and its inhabitants as his creatures, the devil nevertheless seemed to possess them justly, because humanity had willingly subjected itself to him and because he had already possessed it by a long prescription.

Although the Lord could have brought his creature back to himself by authority, he did not wish to do so, lest the devil complain that he was being despoiled not by justice but by power. Therefore it pleased him to conquer the devil’s fraud and injury not by power but rather by wisdom and justice, and to overcome him not through another nature but through the very nature that he had overcome.

Accordingly, he concealed the hook of divinity beneath human flesh, which possessed not sin itself but the likeness of sin. When the wicked predator, according to his customary manner, desired to seize the hook, he himself was caught; and when he presumed against one over whom he had no right, he also lost the one over whom he seemed to have a right.

This, then, is what follows: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out.” He calls the devil the prince of the world not because he possesses dominion in the world, but because he is the author of worldly wickedness and rules in the hearts of the wicked, who, because they love the world, deserve to be called by the name of the world.

Nevertheless, he was cast out of a large part of their hearts through the Lord’s passion, when peoples throughout the earth believed at the preaching of the apostles and renounced the devil and his pomps. Although that devil had long ago been cast out of the hearts of the patriarchs and prophets, he is now said especially to have been cast out because what formerly occurred in a few has now occurred in many, and because, just as he is now cast out from these through faith in the Passion, so formerly he was cast out from those.

The second part follows, in which the Lord shows by whom and how the devil is to be cast out of the world, when he adds: “And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself.” As though he were plainly saying: “I, in whom the prince of this world has nothing, because he will unjustly lift me up on the cross, will justly cast him down; and what he unjustly possessed I will justly bring back to myself.”

[Col. 1448B] Hence, explaining this, the Evangelist adds: “Now he said this, signifying by what death he was going to die.” Moreover, although the whole Trinity cast the devil out of human hearts and brought human beings back to itself, the Son of God nevertheless says specifically that he will do this, because he himself was not only, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, the author of our liberation, but also its minister. For he himself was our advocate, champion, and patron in this cause.

Why, however, did the Lord prefer to conquer the devil by the cross, rather than in some other way, and bring his own people back to himself? The Lord shows this through the threefold symbolism of the cross, which he intimates in his words. For although the cross is the most ignominious kind of death, it nevertheless stands high above the earth, and the one who is crucified upon it must be lifted up from the earth. The Lord therefore willed to die a shameful death, yet to be lifted up on the cross, in order to signify that he would overcome the devil through humility and patience and be exalted above every power, in accordance with what the Apostle says of him: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even the death of the cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow” (Phil. II).

Again, the cross has arms extended outward, and the one fastened upon it, with outstretched arms, resembles a lover embracing and wishing to draw someone to himself. The Lord therefore willed to die on the cross with his arms extended for the sake of human beings, so that he might show the immense love he had for them and signify that he would draw them to himself in an embrace. This is what he says: “I will draw all things to myself.”

Again, the cross has four arms, by which it faces the four regions of the world. Christ too, placed upon the cross, faces the east with his head, the west with his feet, the south with his right hand, and the north with his left. By this the Lord signified that through the cross he would draw human beings to himself from every part of the world. This is what he means by saying “all things.”

In doing this for us, my brothers, the Lord also showed us what we ought to do for him. Hence Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps” (I Pet. II). He therefore gave us an example, so that, if we wish to be exalted with him, we may not fear to be humbled and to suffer for him and with him. For through humility and [Col. 1449A] patience one comes to the kingdom, just as through pride one comes to hell.

Again, he gave us an example, so that for his sake and in imitation of him we might embrace all human beings through love and draw them, by acts of kindness, to love God and ourselves—not only those known to us, but also anyone from any part of the world—and so that, following his example, we might strive to cast down the devil, take away from him the vessels of captivity, and bring them back to God.

The third part follows, in which the crowd of Jews, responding to the Lord, shows that it did not understand the mystery of the cross, when it adds: “We have heard from the Law that Christ remains forever. And how can you say, ‘The Son of Man must be lifted up’?”

Although the Lord had obscurely signified his death on the cross, the Jews quickly understood it, since they were already considering it in their minds. “Who is this Son of Man?” they say, as though they were saying: “He is not the Christ, because he is to be crucified.”

Furthermore, just as the perpetuity of Christ’s kingdom was signified in the Law, so too was his passion. For just as it was said concerning the perpetuity of his kingdom, “His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace” (Isa. IX), so also it was said concerning his passion: “He shall be led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a sheep before its shearer is silent, so he shall not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII).

But the Jews understood the perpetuity of the kingdom as something wholly fitting for Christ; the passion, however, which they thought in no way suited Christ, they could not understand. For this is, as the Apostle says, “the mystery hidden from the ages,” and one which “none of the rulers of this age knew” (Col. I). Who could understand that God would die in this way for human beings, the immortal for mortals?

Yet even today some do not wish to believe Christ’s passion, although it has already been accomplished and attested. Because they think in a devilish and proud manner, and despise the power of humility and patience, they do not believe that such things are fitting for God. On the contrary, just as God detests all pride, so he loves humility. And just as the human race had been brought low through pride, so God determined that it should be restored through humility.

Let us too, my brothers, following our Redeemer, love humility, patience, poverty, and charity. These are the weapons by which Christ conquered the devil and redeemed us, showing that by these same weapons we must conquer the devil and return to our homeland.

The fourth part follows, in which the Lord exhorts the Jews to faith, saying: “Yet a little while the light is among you.” This means: “You have just said that Christ remains forever, but this is not enough, because it is not enough for you to believe in Christ’s eternity unless you likewise believe in his passion.”

Or certainly: “Yet a little while the light is among you,” that is, “I, who am the light, am still among you”—that is, for a short time. “Walk”—understand, by believing and doing good—“while you have the light present and offering itself to you, so that the darkness of unbelief, blindness, and condemnation may not overtake you.” For one who walks in darkness does not know where he is going.

Whoever lacks true faith can wander, but cannot walk. Even if some unbelievers appear to advance in goodness, adding good works to good works, nevertheless they do not thereby attain salvation, because it is impossible for anything done without faith to please God. Faith is the way to salvation; good action through charity is the walking. Therefore, just as neither walking without a way nor a way without walking can bring us to the appointed goal, so neither good action without faith nor faith without action, when time and opportunity are available, can lead to salvation.

For just as it is written that whatever is done without faith is sin, so it is also written that “faith without works is dead” [Col. 1450B] (Jas. II). Hence he also adds: “While you have the light”—understand, the light that is present and offers itself to you—“believe in the light”; and not in just any manner, for the devil believes and trembles, but in such a way that you may be sons of light through imitation, adoption, and inheritance.

What the Lord then said to the Jews, I now say to you, my brothers: “Walk while you have the light, so that the darkness may not overtake you. Work while it is day, because night is coming, when no one can work” (John IX). Repent and turn to the Lord while you have time, because the time is already approaching when you will not be able to do so. Whoever does not wish to work now, when he can, will then be unable to work when he wishes.

Let us consider, my brothers, that the Lord, who now mercifully waits for us to repent and cries out, “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Zech. I), will then cry out more severely to those who despise him: “Amen, amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. XXV).

Therefore, my brothers, let us not waste the time given to us for repentance. Let us wash away the filth of our sins with tears; let us crucify our body with its vices and desires; let us change our life for the better; let us devote ourselves to prayers, fasts, and works of mercy; let us despise the world and its desire; and let us strive with our whole longing toward our heavenly homeland.

May our Lord Jesus Christ, who for our sake willed to be crucified, lead us to that homeland. He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## XXXVII. ON THE FEAST OF BLESSED MATTHEW

[Col. 1450D]

“Jesus saw a man sitting at the tax booth, named Matthew” (Matt. IX). And what follows. Since today, my brothers, we celebrate the solemn feast of blessed Matthew, apostle and evangelist, it is right that the Gospel reading containing the story of his conversion should be recited in the Church.

This reading has five parts. First, the Lord sees and calls Matthew; second, Matthew follows him; third, Jesus eats at his house with sinners; fourth, he is reproved for this by the Pharisees; fifth, the Lord exposes the Pharisees’ foolish response.

First, then, the Lord sees Matthew—not only with bodily eyes, but also with the eyes of mercy and the eyes of foreknowledge. Perhaps at that time he saw many people there with bodily eyes, but it is reported that he saw only this man there with the eyes of mercy, with which he saw Peter denying him, so that Peter might repent, and with which he says that he saw the children of Israel afflicted in Egypt: “Seeing, I have seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt” (Exod. III).

But he also saw him with the eyes of foreknowledge, since from eternity he had predestined him to become a vessel of election and an apostle in his Church.

What did he see? A man. And what kind of man? A tax collector, as another evangelist records. And where did he see him? Sitting at the tax booth. As though he were plainly saying: He saw a man, indeed, but a sinner, and one persisting in his resolve to sin.

A tax collector is so called either because he is defiled by public crimes or because he is entangled in public business, which can scarcely or never be carried out without sin, such as commerce and the tax office. For *telos* (τέλος) in Greek means “tax” or “tribute” in Latin. It is clear, however, that collecting tributes and making exactions is not without guilt.

The Lord therefore saw a man bearing within himself the image of God, but disfiguring it with sins and persisting in this course. Thus, my brothers, his misery is brought out, so that the mercy of the merciful God may appear all the greater: from such an evil man he made one so holy that he established him not only as his disciple but also as his apostle, and granted him authority not only to preach but also to write the Gospel, so that, sharing a name with the heavenly spirits, he might be called and become an evangelist.

The almighty and merciful Lord wished to do this for three reasons. First, to demonstrate to us the effect of his omnipotence, by which he can justify even the most wicked person as quickly as he wishes. Second, to disclose to us the immensity of his mercy, which no disgrace of sins can overcome. Third, to offer hope of forgiveness to all, no matter how criminal they may be.

Yet listen, sinner: Matthew the tax collector is not set before you as an example of sinning, but as an example of repentance. Take care not to sin. If, however, you do sin, do not despair, because, following Matthew’s example, you can rise again through repentance if you accuse your sin.

Matthew does not excuse himself, but rather accuses himself of his former sin when he says that he was sitting at the tax booth. And when he names himself by the name more commonly known—“Matthew by name”—he accuses himself still more. The other evangelists, however, call him by the name “Levi.” For he had two names. The other evangelists wished to name their fellow evangelist by the less familiar name, so that they would not appear to mark him with his former way of life. He himself, however, in accordance with what is written, “The just man is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. XVIII), calls himself by the more familiar name.

In the catalogue of the apostles also he calls himself a tax collector, saying: “Thomas and Matthew the tax collector.” In this, my brothers, an example is set before us, so that we may learn reverently to conceal the sins of our neighbors, but humbly to confess our own.

Hence Paul also says: “Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first” [Col. 1452A] (I Tim. I).

He continues: “And he said to him, ‘Follow me.’” As though he were saying: “Leave the world’s profit and its desire, and follow me. Follow me in body; follow me in heart; follow me in imitation. Follow my way of life in body; follow my will in heart; follow my life in imitation.”

Second, Matthew shows that he followed the Lord who called him, when it is added: “And rising, he followed him.” Luke says more fully: “Leaving everything, he followed him” (Luke V).

In this, my brothers, we must observe both the wondrous efficacy of the Lord’s call and the swift obedience of the one called. The wondrous efficacy of the Lord’s call appears in this: as soon as he speaks, he accomplishes. Thus it is shown that just as the Lord’s saying is his making, according to the words, “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. XXXII), so his calling is his drawing.

For he calls not so much outwardly as inwardly. The swift obedience of the one called is demonstrated by this: the one called did not hesitate, did not delay, did not render an account of his tax collections, but, disregarding the danger from the authorities, as soon as he received the one and only call, followed the Lord both outwardly and inwardly.

And what shall we be able to say to this, my brothers? Matthew followed the Lord, still mortal, at a single call; yet we disdain following him now that he is immortal, rich in all things, reigning in heaven and on earth, and after many calls, threats and terrors, scourges and promises.

Therefore, my brothers, we ought to fear greatly lest God, angered against us and moved by the demands of our deserts, no longer call us outwardly and inwardly, as he did Matthew, but outwardly only, in order to remove our excuse. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John XV). And elsewhere: “I called, and you refused; I, however, will laugh at your destruction” (Prov. I).

Moreover, in the words “rising” and “leaving everything, he followed him,” complete and total renunciation is demonstrated. There are three renunciations. The first is to renounce vices and desires. The second is to renounce possessions themselves. The third is to renounce one’s own will.

The apostle is understood to have made the first renunciation when he is said to have risen—understand, from his vices and desires. He is understood to have made the second when he is said to have left everything. The third is indicated when it is added, “he followed him,” that is, Christ’s will, not his own.

He therefore renounced everything perfectly who renounced his vices, his possessions, and even his own will. And we, my brothers, if we cannot renounce our possessions, let us at least renounce our vices and desires. If we cannot leave everything, let us at least leave what is superfluous. Having food and clothing, let us be content with these (I Tim. VI), so that we may possess as though not possessing, and use this world as though not using it (I Cor. VII).

[Col. 1453A]

Third, it is shown that the Lord ate at Matthew’s house, when it is added: “And it came to pass, as he was reclining at table in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and were reclining with him and his disciples.”

Matthew, for the sake of humility, speaks of himself indistinctly; Luke explains the matter more clearly, saying: “Levi made him a great feast in his house” (Luke V). From this let hearers learn to receive, feed, and honor their preachers and admonishers. Hence the Lord says: “Eating and drinking what they have” (Luke X). And the Apostle says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?” (I Cor. IX).

For just as these owe spiritual things to those, so those owe temporal things to these. Matthew, having been converted, therefore receives Christ not only bodily but also spiritually, as the Lord himself testifies: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV).

He also feeds him not only bodily but spiritually, as the same Lord attests when he says: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter in to him, and I will sup with him, and he with me” (Rev. III).

The Lord stands at the door and knocks when he seeks to put his will into our heart, either through the voice of a preacher or through his own inspiration. When we have heard his voice, we open the door to him when we gladly accept his will and devote ourselves to fulfilling it.

He sups with us, and we with him, when he is nourished and delighted by our devotion, and we by his love. From this let preachers and pastors of the holy Church learn that when they dine with their subjects, they should take greater delight in their devotion than in the food set before them—more in their progress than in their own eating.

For whoever seeks to be fed bodily by his subjects more than spiritually is not a shepherd but a hireling.

Matthew feeds not only the Lord and his disciples, but also many tax collectors and sinners. By a beautiful and true omen, he who was destined to be an apostle and teacher of the nations, at the beginning of his conversion, draws and feeds behind him a flock of sinners, and begins from the outset of his faith the ministry of evangelizing which he was to fulfill.

For not only the one who instructs his brother by word, but also the one who instructs him by example, performs the ministry of a teacher. Those tax collectors and sinners were already following Christ in imitation of Matthew, as Mark testifies, saying: “Many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus” (Mark II). For there were many who also followed him.

Since, therefore, not one but many had been converted, it was not a private but a solemn feast and joy that had to be celebrated. For if, according to the parable, it was necessary to feast and rejoice, the father saying, “Because my son was dead and has come to life again, he was lost and has been found” (Luke XV), it was much more necessary to feast and rejoice now, because many sons had been dead and had come to life again.

For if “there is joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance” (ibid.), how much more over many sinners doing penance!

Fourth, the Lord is reproved by the Pharisees when they say to his disciples: “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” As though they were plainly saying: “He is a partner in their guilt who is their partner at table.”

These men sin in three ways. First, because they arrogate to themselves a righteousness they do not possess. Second, because they judge the Lord concerning doubtful matters. Third, because they do not have compassion on sinners, but despise and disdain them. In these three things they show that they are not righteous.

First, if they were truly righteous, they would not arrogate to themselves a good they did not possess; rather, they would conceal the good they did possess and consider themselves small or nothing in their own eyes. For who will boast that he has a clean heart? Hence the Psalmist says to the Lord: “In your sight no living person shall be justified” (Ps. CXLII).

And if the stars are not clean in his sight, as Job says (Job XXV), how much less is a human being, whose life is nothing but temptation and who dwells in a house of clay, whose foundation is earthly?

We ought, my brothers, to say with the prophet: “All our righteousnesses are like a menstruous cloth before you, O Lord” (Isa. LXIV).

Second, if they were truly righteous, they would not judge the Lord for eating with sinners. Eating with sinners, since it can be done with either a good or a bad intention, is an indifferent action. Therefore we ought neither to judge someone in such a matter nor interpret it in a bad sense, but rather in a good one.

Third, if they were truly righteous, they would have compassion through charity for the misery of sinners. They would neither despise nor disdain them, but would rather accommodate themselves to them in order to win them for Christ.

Fourth, the Lord refutes the Pharisees’ unjust reproach when he answers them: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.” As though he were plainly saying: “The righteous, such as you consider yourselves to be, do not need a justifier; sinners, such as these know themselves to be, do.”

In this saying the Lord appropriately refutes the Pharisees’ reproach, showing, against the three things they had signified in their words, that he is not an accomplice of sinners but rather the physician of sinners; that they, according to their own opinion, do not need a justifier; and that these people are sinners and need a justifier.

It is therefore as though he were saying: “I am indeed the justifier of sinners. But you, puffed up by a false righteousness because you think you have no need of a justifier, will scarcely or never be justified. These humble sinners, however, because they know that they need a justifier, will be justified quickly.”

Nevertheless, the pious and merciful Lord gives them counsel when he adds: “Go, then”—understand, away from your rashness in reproving—“learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.’”

As though he were plainly saying: “Understand what is signified by that word of the Lord spoken through the prophet: ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice’” (Hos. VI).

As though he were saying: “Because of the legal sacrifices you perform, you consider yourselves righteous; but, as the prophet testifies, the merciful God requires mercy rather than sacrifice.”

External sacrifices and offerings, without inward mercy, cannot please God. Mercy, however, has pleased God and is acceptable to him even without those external rites. Nothing appeases God so much as mercy that comes to the aid of misery or has compassion on another’s distress.

For at the judgment the Lord will not say to the reprobate: “Go, you cursed, into everlasting fire,” because you did not sacrifice a victim to me, did not offer an offering to me, and did not build a church for me, although these are great gifts. Rather, he will say: “For I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger, and you did not receive me” (Matt. XXV), and so forth.

Then the Lord invites the Pharisees to follow mercy by his own example, when he adds: “For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” That is: “I have not come to call the righteous angel, who had no need, but the human being who had need.” For every human being was guilty either of another’s sin or of his own.

Or certainly: “I have not come by my call to gather proud righteous people, but humble sinners.” Although proud righteous people are sometimes called, they do not come to God unless, first humbled, they confess themselves to be sinners.

Therefore, brothers, if we wish to be called by God with an eternal calling, let us both believe and confess that we are sinners. Let us redeem our sins with tears of true repentance and works of mercy; let us always hold ourselves humble in our own eyes; let us always judge ourselves, but take care never to judge others; let us despise no sinners, but strive to win them for God through gentle corrections; let us despise the world after the example of blessed Matthew, and hasten toward God with our whole desire.

May God and our Lord Jesus Christ grant this to us through Matthew’s intercession, he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## Saint Matthew the Apostle (Matt. IX; Luke V)

[Note: [Col. 1455D] From Juvencus, a Spanish presbyter]

“Proceeding from there toward the tax office, he saw,

Sitting in the midst of the assembly, Matthew;

At once he orders him to cling to the disciples;

Refusing nothing, he obeys Christ’s command,

Rejoices, and follows him.”

[Note: [Col. 1456D] From Eusebius of Caesarea]

Our Eusebius has the following concerning Saint Matthew:

“But the other disciples also of our Lord and Savior—not only those of the twelve, but also any who, although outside that number, nevertheless, being of the school of our Lord and Savior and divinely inspired, left some account in memory—wished in every respect that this account should be brief and concise.

Accordingly, of the Lord’s disciples, only Matthew and John are reported to have applied themselves to writing, compelled to this task by a certain necessity. For Matthew first preached to the Hebrews. But when he was preparing to go to the nations, he composed the writing in his native language, gathering together what he had preached, and left it as a memorial for those from whom he was departing in order to preach to the nations. After him came the evangelical writing of Luke and Mark,” and so forth, book III, chapter 24.

The same author speaks of the Gospel of Matthew written in Hebrew in book III, chapter 39, and likewise in book V, chapter 10.

Saint Jerome, in *On Illustrious Men*, speaks of Saint Matthew as follows:

“Matthew, who is also Levi, an apostle from being a tax collector, first composed the Gospel of Christ in Judea, for those who had believed from the circumcision, in Hebrew letters and words.”

It is not sufficiently certain who later translated it into Greek. Moreover, the Hebrew text itself is still possessed today in the library at Caesarea, which the martyr Pamphilus assembled with the greatest devotion. I too had the opportunity to have it copied from the Nazarenes who use this volume in the city of Beroea in Syria.

In this connection, it should be noted that whenever the Evangelist, whether in his own person or in the person of the Lord and Savior, uses testimonies from the Old Scripture, he does not follow the authority of the translators of the Septuagint, but the Hebrew text. Two examples of this are: “Out of Egypt I called my Son” (Matt. II); and “For he shall be called a Nazarene” (ibid.).

## XXXVIII. ON THE FEAST OF THE ANGELS: A SERMON ON THE APOCALYPSE

“There was a great battle in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon, and the dragon fought, and his angels” (Rev. XII).

In this vision, dearest brothers, it was revealed by God to John, and through him to us, how solicitous and watchful the holy angels are in our protection and defense, and how greatly they rejoice in our progress and salvation.

This reading has three parts. First, it says that a great battle took place in heaven between Michael and the dragon. Second, it says that the dragon was defeated. Third, it says that, as a result, great rejoicing took place in heaven.

First, then, it says: “There was a great battle in heaven.” By this battle is understood a certain invisible struggle which good spirits have against evil spirits, and evil spirits against good spirits, for the acquisition of human beings.

The good spirits strive to draw human beings to their side and win them for God, moved solely by the goodness and love of God and of their Lord, and by love of their fellow citizens among humanity. For they rejoice, following the example and will of God their king, to fight for human beings, for whom they see him having fought in person.

They also rejoice to draw human beings to themselves, from whom they expect the diminution of their own number to be repaired. Conversely, the evil spirits strive to draw human beings to their side and make them companions in their damnation, moved solely by the malice and envy in which they have become so hardened that they can love no good thing, but always envy the success of others and, as far as they can, hinder it—especially the advancement of human beings to the glory from which they themselves fell through pride.

This battle is called great because those who fight are great, the result for which they fight is great, and the cause for which they fight is great. Those who fight are great because both good and evil angels are great in natural power and knowledge. And just as the good angels are great in goodness and virtues, so the evil angels are great in malice and deceit.

The result for which they fight is great because fervent love of their king and their fellow citizens arouses the good; the evil are aroused by the fervent hatred and envy they have toward human success.

The cause for which they fight is great because they do not fight for gold or silver or for any perishable reward, but for the human being made in the image and likeness of God, for the restoration of the angelic fall.

If, therefore, my brothers, we are so important in the sight of the heavenly beings that angels and archangels, the entire heavenly court, and indeed the Son of God himself fight for us, why do we not fight for ourselves? Why do we despise our condition? Why do we not labor to free ourselves from the power of demons? Why do we not assist the angels and archangels who fight for us?

If we now allow ourselves to be overcome by the devil, we can have no excuse, since we have so many helpers. But since this battle between good and evil still takes place daily, why is it said here that it has already taken place?

Because in the primitive Church, when the battle and the traces of Christ’s blood were still fresh, it took place especially at that time, when many thousands were being rescued every day, and then human beings and angels alike fought against the devil with equal fervor.

Now, however, because few resist the devil and almost everyone willingly hands himself over to him, our negligence makes the angels negligent, so that they assist lukewarmly those whom they see fighting lukewarmly.

Therefore, my brothers, let us fight ardently against the devil, so that we may deserve to have ardent angels as our helpers. They are watchful and ready to help us if they see us watchful and eager on our own behalf.

In the higher heaven there are only the good, just as in hell there are only the evil. But in this dark air that surrounds us, where both good and evil angels fly about and dwell near us, both groups fight over us.

Therefore, since they are always present to us, our deeds cannot be hidden from them. And out of reverence for the heavenly citizens who are always around us, we ought always to live honorably, my brothers, so that by our honorable conduct we may always make the good angels rejoice and put the evil angels to shame.

Or certainly, this heaven may be understood as the Church in which God sits, and in which and for which both groups of angels fight.

“Michael,” it says, “and his angels fought with the dragon, and the dragon and his angels fought.”

The good angels fight for us, my brothers, by suggesting good things to us. The evil, on the contrary, fight against us by suggesting evil things. The former fight by helping us; the latter fight by harming us. The former fight by protecting us; the latter fight by plotting against us. The former fight by excusing us before God; the latter fight by accusing us. The former fight by interceding for us and offering our good works to God; the latter fight by charging and defaming us. The former fight by revealing to us their frauds and plots; the latter fight by secretly and deceitfully deceiving us as far as they can.

The second part follows, in which it is shown that the evil angels were overcome by the good, when it is added: “And they did not prevail, nor was a place found for them any longer in heaven.”

Although the evil angels fight strongly, cunningly, watchfully, and without ceasing, they cannot resist the good, in whom God is and in whom God fights. Hence Michael is said here to have fought. He is said to be sent whenever some deed of extraordinary power is accomplished.

For Michael means “Who is like God?” As the Psalmist says: “Who is a great God like our God? You are the God who works wonders” (Ps. LXXVI).

“Nor was a place found for them any longer in heaven.” When the struggle between the good and evil angels is finished—which will not occur until the end of the world—from that time onward the angels will be so confined in hell that thereafter they will have no power to roam through the air or trouble anyone.

“And that great dragon,” it says, “was cast down, the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, who deceived the whole world.”

It gives four names, of which the first two demonstrate the devil’s malice, and the remaining two his misery. He is called “that great dragon” because of his great and openly exercised violence in doing harm. He is called “the ancient serpent” because of his ancient and secretly exercised cunning in doing harm.

He is called “the devil,” that is, “the one flowing downward,” because of the greatest misery into which he always falls by doing evil. He is called “Satan,” that is, “adversary,” because of his stubborn persistence in always opposing.

For what misery is greater than always to fall into worse things by continually exalting oneself, always to increase one’s own punishments by continually harming others, and to be unable to cease from one’s own destruction?

“He deceives,” it says, “the whole world”—understand, as far as lies within him. Although he does not deceive everyone, since he nevertheless tempts everyone and desires, as far as he can, to deceive everyone, he will be punished for the deception of all.

“And he was cast down,” it says, “to the earth”—namely, into the depths of the earth, that is, into hell—because his angels were sent there with him. For it is just that the one who through pride exalted himself up to the height of God should be cast down into the depths of hell.

Or certainly, if we understand the devil to have been previously cast out of heaven—that is, out of the Church of the faithful—we may here understand him to have been cast down to the earth, that is, to the lovers of earthly things whom he torments, although he grieves most grievously that he has been cast out from the faithful.

The third part follows, in which it is said that, because of the devil’s expulsion, great rejoicing took place in heaven, when it is added:

> “And I heard a loud voice in heaven saying: Now”—that is, from the devil’s expulsion onward—“salvation and the kingdom of our God and the power of his Christ have come” [Col. 1458D]; that is, now salvation, strength, the kingdom of our God, and the power of his Christ are shown to have come about. The salvation of God will appear in this: that he will powerfully save his own. His strength will appear in this: that he will powerfully cast down his adversaries. His kingdom will appear in this: that, once the just have been glorified, the reprobate condemned, and all have done his will, he will reign forever with his own in the blessed realm. The power of Christ, however, will appear most fully then, because he who appeared here as weak will then appear omnipotent. He who was judged here will then judge. He who was condemned here by the impious will condemn the impious and save his own.

Hence it is also added: “For the accuser of our brothers has been cast down by God”—that is, by the Father and by Christ, his Son—“the devil,” whose office it is to accuse human beings, that is [Col. 1459A], to make them liable to accusation and infamous through sins. “Who accused them,” it says, “before our God day and night.” What treachery and deceit the devil displays, my brothers: he accuses us of the very thing that he suggests to us! And not in the presence of just anyone, but in the presence of God. For he especially suggests to us those things that offend God more than human beings. He considers it of little importance merely to disgrace some people before human beings, unless he can also disgrace them before God. And he does this day and night, that is, always.

How greatly he is to be feared, my brothers, since he never sleeps but is always awake for our destruction! Therefore, brothers, let us keep watch against his snares; and because at times we must sleep, let us nevertheless do such things while awake that they may guard us while we sleep.

And the devil was not only cast out by God the author [Col. 1459B]; indeed, it says, “our brothers themselves conquered him,” with God fighting in them and through them. And on account of what did they conquer him? “On account of the blood of the Lamb,” that is, on account of faith in the Lamb’s Passion. And because faith alone is not sufficient for a person who has time to confess, it adds: “And by the word of testimony,” that is, by confession. “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10).

And because neither faith nor confession is sufficient for salvation for one who has time to act, it adds: “And they did not love their souls,” that is, their lives, “against God, but rather offered them for God even unto death.” As if he were saying: They gave not only what was theirs but also themselves for Christ.

We too, my brothers, if we wish to conquer the devil, must believe firmly, confess boldly, and bravely offer what is ours [Col. 1459C] for Christ—and our will and pleasure, and, if the occasion should arise, even our life.

After the angelic voice had praised the Lord and his saints over the devil’s expulsion, it displayed its own feeling in rejoicing and invited others to rejoice when it added: “Therefore rejoice, heavens,” that is, you who dwell in them as well.

Behold, my brothers, how they love us; how the holy angels are always fighting for us; how they rejoice in our victory and praise God. Why, then, are we not stirred to fight? Why are we so sluggish on our own behalf, when we hear that the angels are so concerned for us? Why do we not keep watch against the devil, whom we know to keep watch against us always?

Therefore, my brothers, let us arm ourselves with the weapons of faith and charity [Col. 1459D]; let us keep watch in prayer; let us fight courageously against the devil’s temptations; let us call upon our fellow citizens above for help; let us venerate and frequently commemorate them; let us make them favorable to us by purity of mind and holiness of works. Thus, aided by their assistance and prayers, may we deserve to overcome the devil and be crowned with the victors, by the gift of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, who in perfect Trinity lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## XXXIX. ON THE SAME FEAST. A SERMON ON THE GOSPEL

> “The disciples came to Jesus, saying: ‘Who, do you think, is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?’” (Matt. 18). And what follows.

This reading is divided into six sections, dearest brothers [Col. 1460A]. First, the disciples ask the Lord who is greatest in the kingdom of heaven. Second, the Lord answers them. Third, he shows how great a good it is to receive little ones in his name. Fourth, how great an evil it is to scandalize them. Fifth, he commands that those who cause scandal be avoided. Sixth, he shows why the little ones must not be despised.

First, then, the disciples ask the Lord: “Who, do you think, is greatest in the kingdom of heaven?” Another evangelist says: “A dispute arose among the disciples as to which of them seemed to be the greatest” (Luke 22).

Now, since every created soul is both concupiscible and irascible, it is innate in every soul naturally to desire its own advancement and honor. When, therefore, a soul desires what it ought to desire and in the manner in which it ought, such desire is good [Col. 1460B]. The desire of the apostate angel was evil, for through ambition he desired to rise to equality with God.

When, therefore, the disciples contend over greatness in the kingdom of heaven, they sin in two ways: because they desire what they ought not and in a manner they ought not. They desire what they ought not because they desire greatness in the kingdom of heaven, where it ought to be sufficient simply to be even the least. They desire in a manner they ought not because they wish to ascend to the kingdom of heaven through ambition, not through humility.

The second part follows, in which the Lord answers them. First, by rebuke, when he called a little child, placed him in their midst, and said:

> “Amen, I say to you, unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.”

As if he were saying more openly: You seek through ambition to be greater in the kingdom of heaven [Col. 1460C], but in the very manner in which you seek this, you cannot enter the kingdom of heaven at all, much less become greater in it. You seek to enter the kingdom of heaven through ambition, but one enters it only through humility. If, therefore, you wish to enter the kingdom of heaven, be in virtue and conduct what this little child is by reason of age.

You will be like this little child if you are innocent, do not know how to lie, do not persist in anger, remember injuries no longer, do not lust after a woman whom you have seen, and are similar in these respects.

“Whoever,” he says, “humbles himself like this little child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.” As if he were saying plainly: Whoever is smaller in his own eyes through humility, as this little child is smaller in age, will be greater in the sight of God. For just as ruin causes ruin, so humility causes exaltation [Col. 1460D]. And just as the more someone grows proud, the more grievously he is cast down, so the more someone humbles himself, the more he is exalted in the sight of God.

If, then, you desire to become greater in the kingdom of heaven, be humbler here. I say humbler not merely in speech or by pretense, but believe, confess, and show in the truth of your heart that you are less than the others.

Humility is the virtue by which a person, through the truest knowledge of himself, becomes contemptible in his own estimation. We become contemptible to ourselves and place all others before us if, considering our own good qualities small or nonexistent, we keep all our sins and weaknesses always before our eyes, while overlooking the sins of others and multiplying their good qualities before our eyes [Col. 1461A].

But if someone presently appears openly wicked, we nevertheless attend not to how wicked he is but to how good he may become; and because we who now stand may fall, we must not dare to prefer ourselves to him.

Although, my brothers, we are commanded to despise and humble ourselves, we must not therefore treat ourselves carelessly. For although we ought to despise ourselves with regard to what we have done, we ought not to despise ourselves with regard to what we have been made by God and what we are capable of becoming.

For this reason God calls us his children in Holy Scripture: so that we may not believe that we are neglected by him and consequently neglect ourselves badly—as certain people, and especially the poor, do. Because they think that they are neglected by God, they neglect themselves so completely that they pay no attention to what they do or how they live [Col. 1461B].

The third part follows, in which the Lord shows how great a good it is to receive faithful little ones in his name, when he adds:

> “And whoever receives one such little child in my name”—that is, one who is humble and innocent—“receives me.”

Although it is generally true that whoever feeds or receives someone in the name of Christ receives Christ, for whose sake he does this, he indicates that he has spoken especially of the poor in spirit by saying here “one such little child,” and by what he will say at the judgment:

> “As long as you did it for one of the least of these my brothers, you did it for me” (Matt. 25).

For although, as Paul says, “we must do good to all, especially [Col. 1461C] to those who belong to the household of faith” (Gal. 6), we receive little ones in Christ’s name in two ways: bodily, as when we provide them hospitality and necessities; or spiritually, as when, by the hand of spiritual counsel and assistance, we support their weakness and imperfection so that they do not fall.

Hence Paul also says: “Receive one another, as Christ has received you” (Rom. 15). And elsewhere: “Brothers, if a person is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should receive such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you too be tempted” (Gal. 6). And elsewhere: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (ibid.).

Both are works of great merit, but the latter is the greater.

The fourth part follows, in which the Lord shows how great an evil it is to scandalize his little ones [Col. 1461D], when he adds:

> “But whoever scandalizes one of these little ones who believe in me, it would be better for him if an ass’s millstone were hung around his neck and he were drowned in the depth of the sea.”

A person scandalizes a little one when, by an unsuitable word or deed, he gives that person an occasion of falling.

Just as a fleshly father takes greater care in guarding his little children than his grown children, so a spiritual father ought to take greater care in guarding and instructing the simple and the weak. The perfect are not easily scandalized; they are not quickly moved from their state. But the simple and weak are moved by any small occasion.

And just as little children eagerly imitate whatever their parents do or say, so in the Church the simple and weak always wish to imitate the conduct and actions of their superiors [Col. 1462A]. Therefore we who are greater, even if not for our own sake, must at least for their sake conduct ourselves more wisely and honorably in the Church of God, and seek not what is useful to us but what is useful to all.

So that none of them may be scandalized by our word or example, we must avoid not only all evils but also the appearances and likenesses of evils, and even certain good things—those without which salvation can be attained, such as fasting and the use of what is lawful.

Hence the Apostle says: “If food scandalizes my brother, I will never eat meat, lest I scandalize my brother” (1 Cor. 8).

But good things necessary for salvation must not be abandoned on account of anyone’s scandal, lest, while we wish to gain others for God, we lose ourselves [Col. 1462B].

> “Whoever, therefore, scandalizes one of these little ones who believe in me, it would be better for him if an ass’s millstone were hung around his neck and he were drowned in the depth of the sea.”

That is, it would be better for him to be put to death as an innocent man by the punishment of criminals than to be condemned eternally as guilty in this way.

Or certainly, by the ass’s millstone the circuit of secular life is signified; by the depth of the sea, final damnation. Whoever, therefore, while bearing the appearance of holiness, destroys others by word or example would be better off being condemned to a secular manner of life, because, if he alone fell, a more bearable punishment would torment him. But now he is guilty of as many souls as have perished because of his word or example.

Hence it is also added:

> “Woe to the world”—that is, to worldly people—“because of scandals,” that is, because of the scandals they cause. “For scandals must come,” that is, they are useful to the saints, who are to be tested through them. “Nevertheless, woe to that person through whom the scandal comes!” For he is not to be judged according to the benefit that results from it, but according to what he intended.

The fifth part follows, in which the Lord commands that the little ones avoid those who cause scandal, when he adds:

> “But if your hand, or your foot, or your eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter life maimed and lame, or having one eye, than, having two hands, or two feet, or two eyes, to be cast into eternal fire.”

The Lord is speaking metaphorically [Col. 1462D]. If a disease, a serpent, or some swiftly fatal affliction attacks your hand, foot, or eye, the advice is that, lest the disease suddenly seize and destroy your whole body, the affected member should quickly be cut off along with the disease. It is better to live one-handed, or lame, or one-eyed, than to die with two hands, two feet, and two eyes.

Similarly, if some criminal vice has invaded a friend of yours who was your hand by defending you and supporting you through you, and your eye by providing for you, it is better for you—since you are weak and unable to resist vices close at hand—to separate him from yourself and live without him rather than perish with him.

Hence it happens that, although marriage is indissoluble, if a man compels a woman, or a woman a man, to steal, rob, kill, worship idols, or pursue certain abominable arts with him or her, it is better for one spouse to leave the other and be saved without a spouse [Col. 1463A] than to sin with a spouse.

But if you are strong in your good purpose and can draw your vicious friend or spouse toward yourself more than you would be drawn away by him or her, do not abandon that person; rather, win that person for God.
