“For,” as Paul says, “the unbelieving husband is sanctified through the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife through the believing husband” (1 Cor. 7).

For, as the Wise Man says, you ought to retain with you the person whom you can make better, or who can make you better.

The sixth part follows, in which he shows why the little ones must not be despised, when he adds:

> “See that you do not despise one of these little ones who believe in me.”

That is, do not despise them because they are little. You despise them if you do not fear scandalizing them, if you do not receive them, if you do not take care in correcting and instructing them, and if you do not love them as brothers [Col. 1463B].

And he adds why they must not be despised:

> “For I tell you that their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.”

As if he were saying plainly: They must not be despised because they are children of the heavenly Father, who values them so highly that every day he sends his angels, appointed for their protection.

Although these angels continually move within the immensity of God, their commission does not hinder their contemplation of God.

From this passage, from that passage in the Acts of the Apostles where, when a girl asserted that Peter was standing at the door, the disciples replied, “It is his angel” (Acts 12), and from other passages as well, we learn, my brothers, that every soul, from the beginning of its birth, has an angel assigned to it for protection.

But if all people, both good and evil, have angels assigned to them, why are the little ones here described as if they were privileged? Because the good angels belong to them insofar as, through their consent, they make them their own; whereas they do not belong to the wicked [Col. 1463C], since the wicked, by consenting, make not good angels but rather evil ones their own.

We read in the *Lives of the Fathers* that Abba Paul had this grace: when he looked upon people entering the church, he perceived from each person’s face that person’s thoughts, whether good or evil.

It happened once that, as he watched people entering the church with bright faces and joyful spirits, and their angels entering with them and rejoicing, he saw one person who was black and clouded, with demons dragging him from either side, a cord having been placed in his nostrils, while his holy angel followed him from a distance in sorrow [Col. 1463D].

Blessed Paul therefore began to weep as he stood before the church.

A little later, when they had been dismissed and were departing, he again examined everyone’s faces to see whether they were leaving as they had entered. He saw the man whom he had previously seen as black now leaving bright and radiant, with the demons following him from a distance and his holy angel rejoicing close beside him.

Paul rose up and cried out, blessing the Lord: “Come and see the mercy of God.”

He then explained to everyone what he had seen and asked the man how God had granted him such a great transformation.

The man, weeping, replied: “I am a sinner, and for a long time I have been devoted to fornication. But when I entered the church just now, I heard the words of the prophet Isaiah—and, more truly, of God speaking through him [Col. 1464A]:

> ‘Be clean, and remove your wickedness from your souls before my eyes. Learn to do good; seek judgment. And if your sins are like scarlet, they will be made white like wool’” (Isa. 1).

“Therefore, pierced by this speech, I said within myself: ‘Lord, you are the one who came to save sinners. Fulfill in me, an unworthy sinner, what you promised through the prophet. For from now on I renounce all injustice, and henceforth I will serve you with a clean conscience. Receive me as I repent. For I have sworn and resolved within myself to keep all your ordinances.’

“Under this pledge, therefore, I left the church.”

When the elders heard this, they glorified God.

Therefore, dearest brothers, since the holy angels have such great charity toward us—since they are so concerned to defend us, suggest good things to us, pray for us, rejoice in our salvation, and praise the Lord—let us love the Lord, venerate and entreat the angels, and frequently commemorate them. Thus, by their prayers and assistance, may we deserve to recognize and evade the devil’s snares, conduct ourselves irreproachably, serve our God gratefully, and deserve to contemplate and praise him eternally together with them, by the gift of him who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## On Angels, by Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam

[Col. 1464C]

Angels too are to be loved by us for many reasons: either because they serve our common Lord familiarly, or because, by command of the supreme Prince, they sincerely will the good of the elect and have been added to us as guardians against impious spirits. Their presence ought to deter us from sinning.

For we grieve them and drive them away from us whenever, despising God’s commands, we obey Satan’s promptings. He, with his satellites, is always vigilant to destroy; they are always vigilant to protect.

Human life is exposed to so many dangers that few infants would reach adolescence, few adolescents adulthood, and few adults old age, unless the angels constantly cared for us.

It is right to love in return those who wish us well; it is right to venerate those who are of a higher nature and established firmly in the love of God. They carry our prayers to God and bring his generosity back to us; they bring comfort in afflictions. For they are also said to have strengthened Christ in his agony.

They inspire holy desires, assist us in temptation, rejoice in our good deeds, in a certain sense grieve over our evil deeds, and all await the consummation of Christ’s body.

There is no need to philosophize more deeply about the nature of angels than what has been handed down in the canonical books. It is certain that angels exist, and that through them God administers human affairs. The titles of certain orders have been revealed, and the proper names of some as well.

They are incorporeal minds which, whenever they appear, present an assumed form to the eyes. They are called “men” not because there is any sex among angels, but because they display themselves in that form.

Since the dullness of the human mind finds it difficult to believe that something exists which it does not see, it is useful to instill immediately in tender minds the teaching that there are invisible spirits who are witnesses of all our actions and even of our thoughts, and who take pleasure in sobriety, chastity, truth, simplicity, and whatever belongs to true piety. Even if you exclude all human observers, you still have an angel as a spectator.

One should act similarly so that people may absorb a religious belief concerning the saints who have departed this life.

## XL. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT LUKE

[Col. 1465A]

> “Jesus appointed seventy-two others and sent them into every city and place where he himself was about to come” (Luke 10). And what follows.

The Lord had already chosen the twelve apostles, dearest brothers; but because, as he himself says here, the harvest was great and the laborers few, it was necessary that assistants and laborers be added to them. This is what is said here: “Jesus appointed seventy-two others,” and so forth.

First, therefore, his choosing them is described; second, his sending them; third, his instructing them.

His choosing them is described when it says: “Jesus appointed.” For what else does *designavit*—“appointed”—mean than that he selected and displayed them as notable through a certain sign and privilege of grace? Those who are appointed shepherds and teachers of peoples ought to shine forth with signs of virtue [Col. 1465B].

For how great and what kind of person must an ecclesiastical teacher be, in comparison with whom the people are called a flock? It is fitting that he should excel in reason, conduct, and knowledge; that he should not bend down like cattle toward earthly things, but rather stand upright toward heavenly things; that he should set his mind on what is above, not on what is upon the earth; and that he should be capable of ruling and feeding both himself and his subjects.

But, alas! Today the priest is like the people, indeed worse. Those who ought to be the light of the world are rather smoking than aflame.

And how many did he appoint? Seventy-two. One of this number is thought to have been blessed Luke, who wrote this and whose solemnity we celebrate today.

Certainly, seventy-two were chosen so that they might preach Christ’s Gospel to peoples speaking the same number of languages [Col. 1465C]. Thus, just as the twelve apostles were first assigned on behalf of the twelve tribes of Israel, so the seventy-two disciples were appointed to instruct the peoples represented by the seventy-two languages.

And just as the apostles provide the model of bishops, so the seventy-two provide the model of lesser priests.

Second, his sending them is described when it adds: “And he sent them two by two ahead of him into every city and place where he himself was about to come.”

Behold, my brothers: here the disciples are chosen and sent not by themselves but by the Lord. “For no one,” as the Apostle says, “takes the honor upon himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was” (Heb. 5). And elsewhere: “How,” he says, “will they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. 10.)

This is plainly directed against certain people [Col. 1465D] who shamelessly choose themselves, who thrust themselves forward, and who seize ecclesiastical dignities by prayers, money, or force.

Of such people the Lord says: “They have made themselves kings, but not through me; they have appointed rulers, and I did not acknowledge them” (Hos. 8).

Those who reign from themselves and not by the will of the supreme Ruler are those who, supported by no virtues and called not by God, but inflamed by their own desire, seize authority rather than attain it. The internal Judge promotes them and does not acknowledge them, because those whom he tolerates by permitting them, he disregards through the judgment of rejection.

“And he sent them,” it says, “two by two.” No arrangement displays fraternal charity more than two brothers, and no fewer than two are sufficient for the testimony of truth, since the Lord says: “By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Matt. 18) [Col. 1466A].

They are therefore sent to preach two by two. As if it were said to them: You who undertake the office of preaching must show charity toward one another with harmonious hearts and testify to the truth with harmonious speech. For anyone whose heart is discordant with the unity of truth is entirely unworthy to undertake the office of preaching.

And where did he send them? “Ahead of him, into every city and place where he himself was about to come.” He sent them ahead as though they were to prepare a place for him. For order requires that the voice of preaching go before, so that the Lord may come to the dwelling place of the mind.

Hence the prophet says: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight” (Isa. 40). For when, my brothers, we preach to you, when we rebuke and instruct you, we prepare the way of the Lord to your hearts.

[Col. 1466B]

Third, the Lord’s instruction of them is described when it adds: “And he said to them,” and so forth.

There are ten matters in which he instructs them. He shows them how great a labor rests upon them; what they ought to ask of him; how readily he is disposed to hear them; what kind of people they ought to be; how unencumbered and how prompt they ought to be; what they ought rather to preach; with what benefit they should preach; where they should remain; and from whom they should receive necessities.

He shows how great a labor rests upon them when he says: “The harvest is indeed great, but the laborers are few.”

As if he were saying plainly: Since the harvest is great and you laborers are few, you must not be idle or sleep, but rather devote yourselves to the work with every exertion and concern, so that you few laborers may be able to gather the great harvest.

What the Lord said then we can say now [Col. 1466C]. For, though I cannot say it without a groan, if there are people who hear good things, there are not enough who speak them.

Behold, there are innumerable priests, and yet in God’s harvest a good laborer is rarely found, because we willingly undertake the priestly office but do not fulfill the work of the office. The abundance of the harvest perishes through the laziness of the laborers.

Second, he shows what they ought to ask when he adds: “Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest.”

The whole Church ought daily to ask the Lord to send into his harvest enough laborers of such quality that they are worthy and upright enough to guard it and gather it into the barns of eternal blessedness.

Let us therefore ask the Lord, we shepherds. And you also, my brothers, pray for us, so that he may make us good laborers and supply others for the honor of his name and for our benefit and yours [Col. 1466D].

For our benefit is your benefit, and your benefit is ours. If you are good sheep, you sustain us by your prayers and good works. Our loss is also yours, because, if—as may God forbid—we stray from the office and life of a good shepherd, we cause you to stray as well. Your loss is also ours, because, if—as may God forbid—one of you perishes, fear and grief increase for us as a result.

Certainly, because of the sins of the people, God allows a hypocrite to reign, as appears in Saul. And because of the sins of rulers or priests, persecution comes upon the people, as appears in the sons of Eli and in David.

Since, therefore, we shepherds and you subjects are so closely joined [Col. 1467A], let us love one another; let us bear one another’s burdens—you ours, and we yours; let us remember one another—you us, and we you—in prayers, offerings, and almsgiving. Thus, just as we live together here, so may we rejoice together in the life to come.

Third, the Lord shows how readily he hears those who ask him to grant good shepherds, when he adds: “Go. Behold, I send you.”

From this, my brothers, it is clear that if we ask for a good shepherd with devout and urgent prayer, we will unquestionably not be refused.

Therefore, when a pastoral see is vacant, priests ought to assemble with their congregations in the churches and ask the Lord for a good shepherd through vows and sighs, fasts and prayers, offerings and almsgiving.

But what is grievous is that today, in the elections of shepherds, each person seeks not God’s will but his own temporal advantage; not spiritual profit but temporal profit. And, disregarding suitable persons, he eagerly and shamelessly thrusts forward either himself or a friend.

For this reason the angry Lord now permits tyrants to become bishops, and poets—not instructors but destroyers—of souls [Col. 1467B].

Fourth, he shows what kind of people those who are sent to preach ought to be when he adds: “Like lambs among wolves.”

As if he were saying plainly: If you rejoice in the office of preaching, consider what kind of people you must be. You must be like lambs among wolves: innocent among the guilty, patient among persecutors, gentle among the savage, beneficent among those who inflict injury.

An ecclesiastical shepherd must not inflict injury but endure those who inflict it; he must soften the savage through his gentleness, overcome the injurious by his benefactions, and heal the wounds of sinners in others while himself wounded by afflictions [Col. 1467C].

Although at times zeal for righteousness may raise him up so that he rages against his subjects, that fury itself should arise from love, not cruelty.

But many today, when they undertake rule, burn to tear their subjects apart. Because they do not possess the inward compassion of charity, they desire to appear not fathers but lords, and they transform the place of humility into the exaltation of domination.

The prophet reproves them, saying: “You ruled over them with severity and with power” (Ezek. 34).

Let them hear that God sends his disciples like lambs among wolves: that is, to suffering, not pleasure; to patience, not glory; to humility, not domination.

Fifth, he shows how unencumbered they ought to be when he adds: “Do not carry a purse, or a bag, or sandals.”

What Luke says less fully, Matthew supplies:

> “Do not possess gold, or silver, or money in your belts, or a bag, or sandals for the journey” (Matt. 10).

A preacher ought to have such trust in God that, even if he does not provide for the expenses of the present life, he nevertheless knows with complete certainty that they will not be lacking to him, lest, while his mind is occupied with temporal matters, he provide less for eternal things for others.

He is also forbidden to have two tunics, lest, while he reproves excess in others, that same excess be reproved in him. Sandals too, although they appear necessary, are forbidden to him, so that he who cuts away superfluities in others may, as far as he can, restrain in himself even those things that appear necessary [Col. 1468A].

Mystically, however, money enclosed in a purse is hidden wisdom. But what benefit is there in hidden wisdom or a hidden treasure? The preacher is therefore forbidden to carry money in a purse because whoever hides the talent of the word is rejected. For it is written: “Whoever hides grain will be cursed among the peoples” (Prov. 11).

He is also forbidden to carry a bag, that is, the burden of secular affairs, lest, if it weighs down the neck of his mind, he fail to rise to proclaim heavenly things to others. Hence Paul says: “No one serving as a soldier for God involves himself in secular business” (2 Tim. 2).

He is forbidden to have two tunics, that is, duplicity [Col. 1468B]. For the person who must preach simplicity to others ought to be simple. Hence it is said: “Woe to the person who enters the earth by two ways” (Sir. 2).

He is also forbidden sandals, that is, to protect his feet with the hides of dead animals—meaning to defend his evil works by the examples of dead works—as certain people do when they defend their own wickedness by the wickedness of others.

But, according to Mark, he ought to use sandals or soles (Mark 6), so that the foot is neither covered nor bare upon the earth: thus his affections will not cling to earthly things, but he may receive heavenly things with an unencumbered heart.

Sixth, he shows how prompt they ought to be for preaching when he adds: “Greet no one along the way.”

Elisha says something similar in the Book of Kings when he sends Gehazi hastily with his staff [Col. 1468C] to raise the Shunammite’s son:

> “If you meet anyone,” he says, “do not greet him; and if anyone greets you, do not answer him” (2 Kings 4).

As if he were saying plainly: Do not allow the conversation of anyone you meet to detain you. And how many other vain occupations ought he to avoid, my brothers, who is even forbidden to offer a greeting on the way!

Mystically, everyone who greets someone along the way does so because of the occasion of the journey, not from a deliberate desire for that person’s salvation. The preacher is therefore forbidden to greet along the way, that is, to preach the word of salvation from an occasion arising from some temporal intention. What must be preached should proceed solely from charity toward God and neighbor.

Seventh, he shows what they ought to preach when he adds: “Into whatever house you enter, first say: ‘Peace to this house.’”

Peace, especially the peace of charity [Col. 1468D], is not only to be desired but also to be preached and offered. Peace is the whole subject matter of evangelical preaching.

For this reason God the Father sent his Son as mediator into the world: to reconcile human beings to God and God to human beings through his blood; to join Jew and Gentile in himself as the cornerstone; to preach mutual charity; and to show that the rebellion between flesh and spirit must be brought to rest.

Therefore, at Christ’s birth the angels announce peace, saying:

> “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will!” (Luke 2).

And Christ himself, after making heavenly and earthly things peaceful through his blood, stood in the midst of the disciples and said:

> “Peace be with you!” (John 20).

This peace, my brothers, is especially to be desired, preached, [Col. 1469A] and offered. For all of us preachers are ambassadors of this peace.

Hence Paul says:

> “We act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting you through us. We beg you: be reconciled to God” (2 Cor. 5).

By sinning, my brothers, we had provoked God; and yet he himself first sends messengers of peace to us and seeks your peace, giving us an example: whenever someone has offended us, we should not wait for that person, but should ourselves approach first and offer peace, so that through winning that person’s soul we may deserve a reward.

Eighth, he demonstrates the benefit of offering peace when he adds: “And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him. But if not, it will return to you.” Certainly, whether it is preaching, prayer, or any other good work, nothing can go without reward: for either it benefits both the one who does it and the one for whom it is done; or, if it does not benefit the latter, it cannot fail to benefit the one who does it. Hence the Psalmist says: “And my prayer, he says, shall return into my own bosom” (Ps. 34). Therefore, brothers, one must never cease from doing good, because whoever may receive it, if both the deed and the intention are good, it cannot be without fruit.

Ninth, he shows where they ought to remain when he adds: “But remain in the same house”—that is, in the house where your peace has been received. Nor, as is demonstrated in what follows, should they wander from house to house with fickle ease. Therefore, according to the other evangelist, those entering a city are commanded to inquire who in it is worthy (Matt. 10), lest afterward, compelled to change their lodging, they should be reproved either for being fickle or for having made a poor choice. For from the house in which the preacher lodges, the success of his preaching ought to begin, so that he may have a good testimony from those among whom he lives. For how can he convert strangers who cannot convert those with whom he lives every day? Or how will he be loved by outsiders who is not loved by his own household?

Tenth, and finally, he shows the preachers—whom he had forbidden to carry provisions—where they should obtain them, when he adds: “Eating and drinking what they have.” Preachers ought to be nourished bodily by those whom they nourish spiritually. Hence Paul says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?” (1 Cor. 9).

“Eating,” he says, “and drinking what they have.” As though he were plainly saying: “You may justly receive what is necessary from those to whom you preach, but you ought to be content with what they have.” This is plainly directed against those who either burden their hosts by asking for more luxurious things or distress them by demanding harsher and rougher ones. For just as it is a vice to demand greater riches than are possessed at home, so it is a vice to request harsher foods than those found at home, when one can satisfy his religious obligation by using what has been modestly served.

Why they ought to eat and drink what those people have, he shows when he adds: “For the laborer is worthy of his wages.” Yet he improperly calls a stipend a wage. A stipend is one thing, and a wage another. A stipend is an expense given to soldiers, by which or for the sake of which military service is performed. A wage, however, is an everlasting crown. One ought not to preach for the sake of temporary stipends, but for the sake of the eternal reward. Whoever preaches either for temporary stipends, or for glory, or for any other temporal reason, deprives himself of the eternal reward.

We must therefore not evangelize in order to eat, but rather eat in order to evangelize—and evangelize in order to attain eternal life. But what are we, wretched shepherds, able to say—what can we say, who receive stipends and yet do not wish to work? We take the preacher’s stipend and do not preach. We live from the offerings of the faithful and from the redemptions of sinners, yet against those same sins we do nothing, whether by preaching or by prayer, as we ought. Let us always consider, brothers, what is written: “They eat the sins of my people” (Hos. 4). For when we eat offerings made for sins and remain silent—or perhaps, which is worse, handle them indulgently and encourage them—we surely eat the sins of the people; that is, we make them our own.

Therefore, my brothers, let us awaken our laziness and strive to be what we are called: shepherds. Let us labor diligently to possess the holiness that we preach; let us cast away the burdens of worldly business; let us be content with little; let us devote ourselves to preaching by example and by word; let us ceaselessly pursue the gain of souls; and let us endeavor to draw the sheep entrusted to us with ourselves to God, so that for them and with them we may receive from the supreme Shepherd the pastures of eternal verdure, by the gift of him who lives and reigns for ever and ever.

### Life of Saint Luke the Evangelist, written by Saint Isidore

[Note: In the book *On the Fathers of the New Testament*.]

Luke the evangelist, and author of the apostolic history, was a Syrian by nationality, a physician by profession, and learned in the Greek language. Many report that he was a proselyte and did not know Hebrew letters. He was a disciple of Paul and his constant companion on his journeys. From early childhood he was exceedingly chaste, and after becoming a disciple of the apostles, he carried out the work of evangelical preaching. He died in the seventy-fourth year of his life and was buried in Bithynia. His bones, however, were transferred to Constantinople during the reign of Constantius.

## XLI. On the Feast of All Saints

“Behold, I, John, saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, having the seal of the living God” (Rev. 7), and so forth.

This vision, my brothers, which John the evangelist testifies that he saw, is understood to concern Christ. This reading has four parts. First, it designates Christ indirectly. Second, it demonstrates how great a power he has over the opposing powers. Third, it declares how powerfully he saves his own. Fourth, it reveals how great a praise follows from this.

First, therefore, it designates Christ indirectly when it says: “Behold, I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, having the seal of the living God.” It commends Christ in three respects: by his office, by his nature, and by his power.

By his office, insofar as it calls him an angel. For he is not just any angel, but “the angel of great counsel” (Isa. 9), who was sent by the Father and came, as the Apostle says, “preaching peace to those who were far away and to those who were near” (Eph. 2).

It commends him by his power when it says: “Ascending from the rising of the sun”—that is, by his own power, not another’s. Hence the Apostle says: “He who descended is the one who also ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things” (Eph. 4); and the Psalmist says: “Sing praises,” he says, “to the Lord who ascends above the heavens of heavens toward the east” (Ps. 67).

Christ, moreover, who humbled himself, is said to have ascended from the rising of the sun. The devil, on the other hand, who became proud, is said to have wished to ascend toward the north, because those who humble themselves ascend to the kingdom of light, while those who become proud are hurled down into the region of cold and darkness.

He commends him by his nature when he adds: “Having the seal of the living God”—that is, divine authority and power, by which, as though by a certain seal, he shows himself in all things coequal with God the Father. Some, however, understand the “seal” here as the cross by which God seals his own.

The second part follows, in which it is demonstrated how great a power Christ has over the opposing powers, when it says: “And he cried out with a loud voice to the four angels to whom it was given to harm the earth and the sea.” To cry out on God’s part is to act. Christ therefore cried out with a loud voice when by a great and effective command he restrained the demons.

The four angels who were especially appointed to harm those laboring on land and sea are the spirit of lust, the spirit of pride, the spirit of gluttony, and the spirit of greed. Hence Joel says: “What the caterpillar left, the locust ate; what the locust left, the grub ate; what the grub left, the rust consumed” (Joel 1).

The caterpillar, which is born from vegetables and leaves and consumes them, signifies lust, which is born from the flesh and consumes it. The locust, which leaps upward and is quickly cast down, signifies pride. The grub, which is the offspring of the locust before it has wings, always lying low and utterly gnawing the grass, signifies gluttony. Rust, which attacks metals, signifies greed.

Lust consumes many. Those whom lust does not consume, pride puffs up. Those whom these do not overcome, gluttony overcomes. Those whom none of these conquers, greed conquers. Against these four vices John warns us, saying: “Beloved, do not love the world or the things that are in the world. Everything that is in the world is either the desire of the eyes, or the desire of the flesh, or the pride of life, which is not from God the Father” (1 John 2). By the desire of the flesh he signifies gluttony and lust; by the desire of the eyes, greed.

The Lord therefore restrains these four kinds of vice, so that they may not harm his elect, saying: “Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees.” It is clear that some demons especially cause harm on land, some in the waters, and some in the forests. Or understand “earth” as those devoted to earthly things; “sea” as the unstable, flowing through various vices; and “trees” as those who rise above earthly concerns and bear fruit.

“Until,” he says, “we seal the servants of our God upon their foreheads.” From this it is understood that, because of the elect who dwell in this world among the reprobate, demons are sometimes forbidden to persecute the reprobate, lest, while uprooting the weeds, they should uproot the wheat at the same time (Matt. 13), until the elect are fortified and strengthened, or, like Lot, removed from their midst.

This is the third part, in which it is shown how powerful Christ is to guard and save his own among the wicked. “Let us seal,” he says—that is, let us distinguish, fortify, and strengthen: I inwardly, and my ministers outwardly. I inwardly, by faith in the cross; my ministers outwardly, by the sign of the cross. I inwardly, by invisible oil; my ministers outwardly, by visible oil.

By faith in the cross and by the oil of spiritual grace, Christ inwardly distinguishes his own from those who are not his, fortifies them against persecutions, confirms them in goodness, and makes them steadfast. The ministers of Christ, by sealing them outwardly with the visible cross and visible oil, demonstrate that they are inwardly distinguished, fortified, and strengthened.

“Upon their foreheads,” he says. When a child is catechized, he is marked with oil in the form of a cross upon the chest, so that he may have the faith of Christ in his heart; he is marked between the shoulders, so that he may bear the burden of Christ alone; he is marked on the crown of the head, so that he may preserve reason, which is the judge of a human being.

This is well signified by the fact that both doorposts and the lintel of the house in which the lamb was eaten were smeared with the lamb’s blood. In confirmation, however, anointing is performed in the form of a cross upon the forehead, which is the seat of modesty and the more prominent part of the body, so that one may not be ashamed of the faith of Christ in tribulation, but rather confess and proclaim it openly.

This is well signified by the fact that the Lord commanded in Ezekiel that the letter *tau* be marked upon the foreheads of those grieving and lamenting over the sins of others, so that they might thereby be distinguished and protected in advance and not be destroyed with sinners.

“And I heard,” he says, “the number of those who were sealed: one hundred and forty-four thousand sealed from the tribe of the children of Israel.” Literally, this number appears to signify the elect from the Jews, and the innumerable crowd that he adds afterward, the elect from the Gentiles. But because we are uncertain about this and almost the whole of this book is enigmatic, let us refer it to the mystical sense, so that we understand this number to indicate not how many, but what kind, are sealed from every tribe of the children of Israel—that is, from all the peoples who imitate the faith of Jacob.

By the one hundred and forty-four thousand, therefore, all the elect from the four regions of the world are signified. Forty signifies penitents, one hundred the perfect, thousands those more perfect, and four the four regions of the world.

“From the tribe of Judah,” he says, “twelve thousand sealed.” By Judah, whose name is interpreted as “confessing,” those who confess are signified. Twelve of them—that is, three times four—are sealed: namely, all from the four regions of the world who are perfected in the confession of the Holy Trinity are sealed and chosen by God. The same is to be understood of the others.

These twelve tribes signify twelve virtues. Those who follow them are saved.

By Judah, those who confess are understood, for whom confession alone is sufficient when they have no time for works, as with the thief confessing on the cross. And because confession alone is not sufficient for one who has time for works, Reuben follows. His name is interpreted as “seeing a son,” and he signifies those who are reserved for good works, who will see the fruit of their hands forever.

And because some who work well are less watchful regarding temptations, Gad follows. His name is interpreted as “armed,” and he signifies those who prepare and arm themselves against temptations, according to the saying: “My son, when you approach the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation” (Sir. 2).

And because some, even after a long struggle, succumb, Asher follows. His name is interpreted as “blessed,” and he signifies those who are granted to fight successfully against temptations and to have temptations result in their advancement, according to the saying: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life” (Jas. 1).

And because charity ought to accompany patience, Naphtali follows. His name is interpreted as “breadth,” and he signifies those who, from the breadth of their charity, give even to their persecutors.

And because some, although they give their external possessions to their persecutors, nevertheless retain injuries in their hearts, Manasseh follows. His name is interpreted as “forgetful,” and he signifies those who are forgetful of injuries.

And because some become excessively cheerful over attaining the virtues mentioned above, Simeon follows. His name is interpreted as “hearing of sadness,” and he signifies those who, lest they become too cheerful over their virtues, always turn their hearts toward consideration of past sins and the misery of this world, so that they may be saddened and humbled by them, according to the saying of Solomon’s Wisdom: “The heart of the wise is in sadness, but the heart of fools is in gladness” (Eccles. 7).

And because we are bound by precept to fulfill the seven preceding virtues, Levi follows. His name is interpreted as “entrance,” and he signifies those who do not merely fulfill the commandments but also the counsels and things not enjoined.

And because such people groan amid the labors of worldly misery, awaiting the redemption of their bodies, Issachar follows. His name is interpreted as “reward,” and he signifies those who are weary of living here, desiring to die and be with Christ.

And because the life of such people is necessary for those who are less advanced, Zebulun follows. His name is interpreted as “dwelling of strength,” and he signifies those who, not refusing labor for the needs of their brothers, descend from Mary to Martha.

And because from this comes the increase and advancement of the Church, Joseph follows. His name is interpreted as “increase,” and he signifies those who, through their teaching, increase the Church in the number of the faithful.

And because pride usually attacks so many and such great virtues at the end, Benjamin follows. His name is interpreted as “son of the right hand,” and he signifies those who remain humble amid their great virtues, considering that they possess nothing from themselves but have everything from the blessing of the divine right hand, and attributing whatever good they have to him.

These virtues advance by ascending step by step from below—from simple confession to the highest virtue, which is maintaining humility at the summit of the virtues. Let us strive to possess these virtues, dearest brothers, if we desire to belong to the number of those who are sealed.

Having enumerated in figurative form the virtues of those who are sealed, John now speaks about the sealed themselves, adding: “After this I saw a great crowd.” He calls them a crowd because of their multitude and incomprehensibility.

Concerning this crowd he says seven things: namely, how great it was, where it had come from, how and where it stood, whom it looked upon, what it was clothed in, what it held in its hands, and what it said.

He shows how great it was when he adds: “Which no one could number.” In accordance with this, the Lord had said to Abraham: “I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea” (Gen. 22 and 26). Only he can number the elect who can number the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea. This is directed against those who say: “Who can be saved?”

He shows where they had come from when he adds: “From every nation, and tribe, and people, and tongue.” This is directed against those who think that Catholics exist only in the Latin or Greek language. For, as Peter says: “In every nation, whoever fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts 10). And Paul says: “Where is male or female, Jew and Gentile, circumcision and uncircumcision, slave and free?” (Gal. 3.) “But Christ is all and in all” (Col. 3)—that is, no difference before God is prejudicial, whether of sex, nation, observance, language, or condition; Christ alone is all in all.

No one is harmed by the fierceness of his nation, the wickedness of his tribe, the vice of his people, or the barbarism of his language, provided that Christ is held in life, conduct, and faith.

He shows how they stood when he adds: “Standing before the throne”—that is, standing in attendance upon God as judge and king. Because in this world they had always stood with Christ in their minds, while he was judged and suffering, they are worthy to stand in heaven before him as judge and king.

He shows whom they looked upon when he adds: “In the sight of the Lamb,” upon whom the angels desire to gaze. To see him in his glory is to live blessedly. Only those deserve this who throughout this life have constantly directed the eyes of their intention toward him, according to the saying: “The eyes of the wise are in his head” (Eccles. 2).

He shows what they were clothed in when he adds: “Clothed in white robes”—that is, clothed in body and soul with the brightness of immortality. Those deserve this who have kept their robes, whitened in the baptism of Christ’s blood, undefiled, or have cleansed them when stained with the tears of repentance.

He shows what they carried in their hands when he adds: “And palms in their hands”—that is, victorious and unfading rewards in their works. Those deserve this who have not been idle in this life but have labored tirelessly for Christ.

He shows what they proclaimed when he adds: “And they will cry out with a loud voice.” This is the fourth part, in which it is shown how great a praise follows the Savior. Those who have been saved, just as in this life, and even more in that eternal life, always bless their Savior with praises of great devotion, according to the saying: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 83), saying:

“Salvation belongs to our God who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb.”

As though they were plainly saying: “Whatever salvation we have obtained, whether in the remission of sins, in good works, or in glorification, is to be attributed not to our merits but to the grace of God the Father and of his Son.”

Only those deserve to sing this song before the throne of God who have learned to attribute whatever good they possess not to themselves but to God. For this is the praise that most delights the divine majesty.

To invite us more strongly to this praise, he shows that all the angels approve and confirm it. So that we may yield more fully to their testimony, he first indicates that the angels themselves are our protectors and examples.

He shows them to be our protectors when he says: “And all the angels stood around the throne”—that is, around the Church in which God sits—according to the saying: “The angel of God will encamp around those who fear him and will deliver them” (Ps. 33).

And not only around the throne, but also around the elders and the four living creatures—that is, the preachers of the Old and New Testaments. The elders and the four living creatures are around the throne, but the angels are around the elders, the four living creatures, and the throne, because the preachers go around the Church in vigilance, while the angels go around and guard both the preachers themselves and the Church together.

He shows them to be our examples when he shows them prostrating themselves on their faces and worshiping the Lord. They do this in the presence of the throne—that is, the Church—so that, when the Church considers those angels who have never sinned yet humble themselves and acknowledge their own weakness, she may learn, having sinned, to humble herself much more, to recognize her weakness, and to attribute whatever good she has to God her creator.

“And they worshiped,” he says, “saying: Amen.” It is as though they were saying: “You do well, human beings, because you attribute your salvation not to yourselves but to God. For not only salvation, but also every blessing—that is, every gift worthy of blessing—and glory, whether outward or inward, and wisdom, by which we avoid evil and choose good, and thanksgiving for the good things bestowed, honor, whether temporal or eternal, inward virtue, and outward strength—all these belong to God and must therefore be referred to God. He holds them in his hand and grants them to whomever he wishes. To him belong honor and glory throughout all ages. Amen.”

## XLII. On the Feast of All Saints

“When Jesus saw the crowds, he went up onto the mountain” (Matt. 5), and so forth.

This reading from the holy Gospel, dearest brothers, we must hear and retain with all our heart, because in it the Lord sets before us the teaching without which salvation cannot be attained.

This reading has two parts. First, the Lord instructs us by his example; second, by the teaching of his word.

He instructs us by his example when, seeing the crowds, he goes up onto the mountain and, sitting there, teaches his disciples. He thereby warns us generally that, if we wish to follow him, we must not remain below with the crowds, but must flee the tumult and noise of the world and the depths of vice, ascend to the height of the virtues, and sit at that very height of the virtues—that is, conduct ourselves not proudly but humbly, and by lowering ourselves to those of lesser capacity make ourselves their equals, so that we may be able to teach them when they approach us and win them for God.

More particularly, he instructs us preachers that, before preaching to others, we must first climb to the height of life and doctrine, according to the saying of Isaiah: “Ascend onto a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion; lift up your voice with strength, you who evangelize Jerusalem” (Isa. 40).

We must also sit at that height of life and doctrine, both through our calling and through condescension. Through our calling, because it is the role of teachers not to run about but to sit, and not to entangle themselves in worldly affairs. Hence it is also read in the *Acts of the Pontiffs*: “That bishop sat for so many years,” or “that bishop sat for so many years.”

Certainly, the lower part of one who sits reclines and remains at rest, while the upper part is raised and remains upright. Likewise, the lower part of a spiritual teacher—that is, the senses—ought to rest from worldly wandering and entanglement, while the upper part—that is, reason—ought to rise up to proclaim heavenly things.

Through condescension, because it belongs to a spiritual teacher to condescend both to the weakness and to the capacity of his subjects, so that he does not first preach to them things too lofty or unbearable, but gradually communicates them according to their capacity, in accordance with what the Lord says to his disciples in the Gospel: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16). Thus he neither burdens nor frightens his hearers, as some do, but by condescending to them draws them to himself.

He must also open his mouth—that is, open and explain the closed and obscure word, and teach doctrinally. For one teaches, as it were, with a closed mouth when one does not teach intelligibly.

But the ecclesiastical teacher, as we read in Ezra, ought to speak distinctly and clearly for understanding, so that he speaks not only for himself but for others. This is directed against certain people who, in order to display themselves, speak in obscure and unusual words, like those who formerly desired more to speak in tongues than to interpret them. Paul rebukes them, saying: “Unless you give a clear statement, how will what is said be known?” (1 Cor. 14.) And shortly afterward: “In the Church I would rather speak five words with my understanding, so that I may instruct you, than ten thousand words in a tongue” (ibid.).

The second part follows, in which the Lord instructs us by the teaching of his word, exhorting us to the eight virtues that lead to eternal blessedness.

The first is voluntary poverty. He invites us to this when he says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

This teaching is certainly contrary to worldly wisdom. For the world thinks the poor miserable and the rich blessed, according to the saying:

“Their sons are like young plants in their youth, their daughters adorned and beautified like the likeness of a temple; their storehouses are full, overflowing from one thing into another; their sheep are prolific, abundant in their pastures. There is no breach in the wall, no passage, and no outcry in their streets. They called that people blessed which possesses these things” (Ps. 144).

But the Lord, judging otherwise, says here: “Blessed are the poor in spirit”—that is, in will. For voluntary poverty, if undertaken for God, is a virtue. The prophets called it frugality.

There are, moreover, four kinds of poverty. Some are poor in possessions but not in spirit; others in spirit but not in possessions; others both in spirit and in possessions; and others in spirit and with moderate possessions.

A person is poor in possessions but not in spirit when, although he does not possess worldly riches, he nevertheless burns with desire for them. Yet because he is poor, he considers himself miserable and hated by God. He thinks the rich fortunate. Therefore he steals, robs, deceives, lies, commits perjury, and kills. He becomes all the worse and more condemnable because he is not corrected by the scourge of poverty. Of such people the Lord says through the prophet: “We treated Babylon, but she was not healed” (Jer. 51). It is as though he were saying: “We did what could have been sufficient for her correction, yet she persists in her wickedness.”

A person is poor in spirit but not in possessions when, although he has riches, he despises them, and while living amid wealth considers himself a steward, not a master. He is generous toward the poor but frugal toward himself. He believes those alone to be true riches which do not abandon their possessor: faith, hope, and charity, and the other virtues that both sanctify and bless a person. He is all the greater and more remarkable because he is surrounded by greater wealth. He is not held, weakened, puffed up, or troubled by its vices. Wealth may smile upon him, but it does not mock him.

Abraham was such a poor man; David was such a poor man, who, placed amid secular riches, says: “I am poor and sorrowful” (Ps. 68). Job was such a poor man, who says that he did not rejoice in his riches (Job 31). This is the poverty of strong men who know how to restrain themselves firmly amid the softness of riches.

A person is poor both in spirit and in possessions when, following not only the commandments but also the counsels, he sells everything he has and gives it to the poor, and, naked, follows the naked Christ. The prophet Elijah was such a poor man, as was John the Baptist; such poor men were the apostles and hermits. This poverty belongs only to perfect men, who are strong in faith, self-controlled in life, and patient in hardships. They know with complete certainty that they ought to claim nothing for themselves, since God provides what they need.

A person is poor in spirit and moderate in possessions when, although he despises riches as vain, he nevertheless does not wish to abandon them altogether, fearing that he might become needy, deceitful, a thief, a robber, or a fraud. Again, he does not wish to possess great riches, fearing that riches might make him effeminate, puffed up, excessively anxious, or careless.

Therefore he wishes to possess necessities in moderation, praying to the Lord with Solomon: “Lord, do not give me riches or poverty, but grant me only what is necessary for my sustenance” (Prov. 30). This is the poverty of the imperfect, who do not possess enough virtue to say with Paul: “I know how to abound and how to suffer want” (Phil. 4). For one who is neither loosened by prosperity nor broken by adversity knows how to abound and how to suffer want.

Therefore, brothers, if you cannot abandon everything, nor live self-controlled amid riches, at least retain only what is necessary, distribute what is superfluous, and be poor and humble in mind. For the riches of the kingdom of heaven are promised only to those who despise earthly riches. A lover of earthly riches is not a lover of heavenly riches.

The second virtue is meekness, or gentleness. The Lord invites us to this when he adds: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.”

Meekness is a virtue of the mind that mitigates anger, rage, impatience, and every kind of harshness. It is opposed to anger: just as an angry person drives people away, so a meek person draws them to himself.

The boundaries of meekness are harshness and softness. We hold the virtue of meekness rightly, my brothers, when we neither drive away our people by harshness, as some do, nor corrupt them by softness, as Eli did. Since firmness and meekness are companion virtues, each must be exercised according to the cause, the time, and the person.

We ought to be firm toward the stubborn, but meek toward the simple and inexperienced. Yet firmness must always accompany meekness, and meekness firmness, so that we may always possess both firm meekness and gentle firmness. Otherwise, firmness will become cruel or meekness will become weak.

The Lord shows how great a virtue meekness is when he says that he himself is its teacher: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11).

Moses is praised for this virtue when it is said: “Moses was the meekest of all human beings” (Num. 12). David is also praised for it when it is said: “Remember, O Lord, David and all his meekness” (Ps. 131).

Let us therefore learn, my brothers, to be meek and gentle, because only such people will possess the earth. It is fitting that possession of the earth should be promised to the meek, because only those who are meek in conduct, such as Moses and David, can possess either the land of the living or the land of the dead. The unmeek can possess neither themselves nor others.

The third virtue is sadness or mourning. The Lord invites us to it when he adds: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” No Scripture commends laughter, brothers dear, but rather condemns it. For Solomon says: “I accounted laughter an error, and to joy I said: Why are you deceived in vain? (Eccl. II),” and elsewhere: “Laughter will be mingled with sorrow, and mourning takes possession of the end of joy (Prov. XIV).” And elsewhere: “In the mouth of a fool there is always laughter.” The Lord also says in the Gospel: “Woe to you who laugh, for you shall mourn (Luke VI).”

For every kind of laughter arises either from vanity, envy, or malice of mind. Whoever laughs at vain things is vain. Whoever laughs at another’s losses is envious and malicious. Whoever laughs at those who are mourning is cruel. Whoever laughs amid serious matters is foolish. Whoever bursts into laughter while the others are silent clearly has some foolish thought occurring to his memory. Much laughter also makes a person burdensome and hateful.

The Lord, however, commends mourning here. Indeed, he himself is read to have wept, though he is never read to have laughed. Yet not every kind of mourning is praiseworthy. Some mourn because they were unable to do things that ought to be mourned, and they are wicked. Some mourn over the loss of temporal possessions, and they are greedy. Some mourn over bodily affliction, and they are faint-hearted. Some mourn at the funerals of the dead, and they are merely human. Such mourning, if it is moderate, is not blameworthy. For it is written: “Son, shed tears for the dead as one who has suffered grievously; begin to weep (Ecclus. XXXVIII).”

Sacred Scripture especially commends two kinds of mourning. The first is when someone mourns for his own sins or those of others. The second is when a perfect person weeps because the heavenly homeland is delayed. The first kind of mourning arises from consideration of sins committed and from fear of the punishments of Gehenna owed to them. The second likewise arises from two things: consideration of the present misery and desire for eternal blessedness.

The first kind of mourning is good, provided it does not become excessive; the second is better. Of these it is said that those who mourn shall be comforted, through the remission of sins and the attainment of heavenly joy, when, namely, “God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints, and death shall be no more, nor mourning nor pain, because the former things have passed away (Rev. VII),” and so forth.

The fourth virtue is desire. The Lord invites us to it when he adds: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.”

Universally speaking, justice is rendering to each person what belongs to him. Human justice, however, is to render religion to God, purity to oneself, love to one’s neighbors, honor to one’s parents, care to one’s children, obedience to one’s superiors, discipline to one’s subjects, and fairness to all. The justice of God is to render to each person according to what he has deserved.

Neither kind of justice is perfected in this life, since neither can a human being in this life render perfectly to each person what belongs to him, nor will God here render fully to each person what he has deserved. Both kinds of justice, however, will be consummated in the life to come. Therefore he fittingly says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness,” as though righteousness were food and drink for the soul.

Let us too, brothers dear, hunger and thirst for righteousness with our whole desire—understanding that we desire both to do it and to have it done—namely, so that we may be able to render perfectly to each person what belongs to him, and so that God may render to every righteous person according to what he deserves; so that goodness may not suffer any longer to be oppressed by wickedness, justice by injustice, piety by impiety, and honor by dishonor. Those who hunger for this in the present life will undoubtedly be satisfied in the life to come, when God will perfect the saints in righteousness and render to each according to what he has deserved. Then “they shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more, and the sun shall not fall upon them, nor any heat (ibid.).”

The fifth virtue is mercy. The Lord invites us to it when he adds: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” Mercy is a virtue that suffers together with another’s misery. It has two effects: giving and forgiving. Hence the Lord says: “Give, and it shall be given to you. Forgive, and you shall be forgiven (Luke VI).”

This virtue extends even to enemies. Hence the Lord says: “Be merciful, as your heavenly Father is merciful (ibid.),”—“who makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked, and sends rain upon the righteous and the unrighteous (Matt. V).” And the Apostle says: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink. For by doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head (Rom. XII).”

The limits of this virtue are inhuman harshness and indiscriminate compassion. We rightly possess the virtue of mercy, brothers dear, when we are neither inhumanly harsh toward the nature of our needy neighbor nor indiscriminately compassionate toward the vices of the offender. Since mercy and justice are virtues, mercy is to be exercised toward nature, and justice against vice. Rather, let us have in all things both just mercy and merciful justice; otherwise neither is true mercy nor is the other true justice, but rather a vice.

Mercy is elegantly promised to the merciful, just as, conversely, “judgment without mercy will be shown to the one who has not practiced mercy (James II).”

The sixth virtue is purity of heart. The Lord invites us to it when he adds: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” Perfect purity of heart is not admitting any shameful thought into oneself. But who can do this in the present life? No one. Whether we wish it or not, we often think shamefully and take pleasure in such thoughts. But if we immediately restrain the shameful thought and pleasure arising in the heart by refusing consent, we are not for that reason said to lose purity here, since we rebuke and punish ourselves for having thought and delighted shamefully.

We can say with the Apostle: “If I do what I do not want, it is not I who sin, but sin dwelling in me (Rom. VII).” Purity of heart, according to the condition of the present life, is consenting to no shameful thing. Those who are pure in this way are not yet wholly pure; therefore it is said of them: They do not see God already, but they shall see him in eternal life, when they will no longer be able to think anything shamefully.

Therefore, brothers dear, if we wish to see him there, let us strive here to cleanse the eye of the mind.

The seventh virtue is peace. The Lord invites us to it when he adds: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God.” Perfect peace is the tranquil state of a perfect mind, with all things harmoniously agreeing within it. But since here the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh (Gal. V), this peace belongs not to the way but to the homeland.

According to the condition of the present life, peace is called a tranquil state of mind in which all things agree harmoniously, or at least yield to one another in proper order. When all our impulses agree in due order, or at least yield in due order to one another—so that evil impulses yield to good ones and bodily impulses to spiritual ones—then we have peace with ourselves, by subjecting the flesh to the spirit; peace with God, by obeying him; and peace with all human beings, insofar as it lies within us, by willing and seeking their good.

Those who are peaceful in this way are called children of God—not, he said, “are already called,” since some rebellion still remains in them, but “shall be called” in eternal life, when, with every rebellion quieted within them, they will be made like God.

Therefore, brothers, let us have within us here as much ordered peace as we can, so that we may deserve to attain that peace of God which surpasses all understanding (Phil. IV), and to be called and to be children of God.

The eighth virtue is patience. The Lord invites us to it when he adds: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Patience is the virtue that bears injuries inflicted upon it with an even temper for God’s sake. Therefore, when it is said, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake,” “with an even temper” must be understood.

Three things make a martyr: innocence, equanimity, and the cause. Innocence means that he does not deserve punishment on account of sins. Equanimity means that he bears punishment unjustly inflicted with a calm and gentle spirit. The cause means that he suffers for God. To suffer for righteousness is the same as to suffer for God, since God is righteousness.

If someone suffers innocently but not with equanimity, he does not possess the merit of a martyr. Again, if he suffers both innocently and with equanimity but not for God, he is not a martyr. But if he suffers innocently, with equanimity, and for God, he is undoubtedly a martyr.

When it is said that he suffers for the Lord, understand that the punishment is inflicted for God’s sake: punishment is both imposed for God and endured for God, so that hatred of Christ is the cause in the one who inflicts it, while love of Christ is the cause in the one who suffers. Those who suffer in this way are truly called martyrs.

Nevertheless, we sometimes use the term “martyrs” in a broader sense: either when someone suffers punishment for God’s sake, though not because of God, but punishment inflicted because of God—as in the case of Saint Leodegarius—or when someone suffers, without any intention directed toward God, punishment inflicted because of God—as in the case of the infants who suffered under Herod.

What the Lord had said about patience he explains more openly when he adds: “Blessed are you when they curse you,” or, as another translation has it, “when people hate you, and persecute you, and say every evil thing against you, lying, because of me.”

He encompasses persecution in three ways: in hatred, in deeds, and in words. In hatred, when he says “they curse you,” or “hate you,” as though they were invoking evil upon you in their hearts out of hatred; and “persecute you,” namely, through injuries, exile, and torments. In words, when he says “they say every evil thing,” namely, by slandering, insulting, and accusing.

He adds “lying,” so that no one may glory in being cursed when the curses are true. He also adds “because of me,” since it is not the punishment but the cause that makes a martyr.

“Rejoice,” he says—understand, in mind—“and exult”—in body—“because your reward is abundant in heaven.”

These virtues, dearly beloved brothers, are so connected with one another that we advance step by step, ascending toward the last. First, by considering the misery of the world, we begin to despise the world. Second, we moderate the inner passions within us. Third, seeing that we cannot completely cleanse them here, we mourn. Fourth, we hunger for the eternity of righteousness in which we shall be able to moderate them; and since that eternity is attained not through our merits but through mercy alone, fifth, we learn to have mercy on others, so that God may have mercy on us.

And since mercy without purity is insufficient, let us strive to drive every shameful thought from our hearts. So that we may do this more effectively, let us seek to bring the rebellion of flesh and spirit within us into peace, and to have peace with all human beings. Then we shall be able to endure equably the perfection of martyrdom for God.

Although one reward of blessedness is owed to these eight virtues, they are nevertheless named individually because of their appropriateness to one another. In that one reward all things will be found: there our poverty will find eternal riches; our meekness, an inheritance; our mourning, consolation; our hunger, nourishment; our mercy, mercy; our purity, the vision of God; our peace, likeness to God; and our patience, dominion over the kingdom. This is granted by God and our Lord Jesus Christ, who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God, throughout all ages of ages.

XLIII. SERMON ON THE COMMEMORATION OF THE DEAD, ON THE APOCALYPSE

“I heard a voice from heaven saying to me: Write: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord (Rev. XIV),” and so forth.

The apostle and evangelist John, who was chosen by the Lord as a virgin and remained a virgin forever, writes this, dearly beloved brothers. He reclined at supper upon the breast of Jesus, and to him, a virgin, he entrusted his Virgin Mother. His writings deserve all the greater faith because he himself received and recorded the heavenly secrets more deeply than the others from the fountain of the Lord’s own breast.

He therefore writes that this was commanded to him by an angel—or rather, through the angel by the Holy Spirit—so that, while writing in a book about the rest of the faithful departed, he might insert this teaching to strengthen our faith and hope. Thus we might be certain of the resurrection and rest of the faithful departed, and therefore not fear death, but rather await it more securely with good works; nor grieve over the death of our friends as do those who have no hope.

Thus blessed John writes what he had heard from the Holy Spirit, saying that those who die in the Lord are blessed. In what respect are they blessed, and why? Since they are blessed who die in the Lord, let us first examine what it means to die in the Lord.

To die in the Lord is to die in his faith, hope, and love. Whoever possesses the Catholic faith, hopes for salvation, and loves the author of salvation—if he dies in these three things—dies in the Lord. Whoever dies lacking one of them dies not in the Lord but in the devil.

First, those die in the Lord who die not only in the Lord but also for the Lord, as martyrs do. Second, those also die in the Lord who, although they do not die for the Lord as martyrs do, nevertheless die with the Lord and in the Lord—that is, with innocence and holiness of life—as confessors do.

Third, those also die in the Lord who, although they sinned greatly during their lives, die in confession and amendment of their sins, as true penitents. Fourth, likewise those die in the Lord who, although because of their age or the shortness of time they were unable to possess faith and the works of faith during their lives, nevertheless die departing with the sacrament of faith, that is, with baptism, as infants and neophytes do.

But what of those who persist in sins throughout their whole lives and repent at the end? Do they die in the Lord? I do not know. I do know, however, that if true faith and repentance are found in them, they undoubtedly die in the Lord. For it is written: “Repentance, however late, will not be fruitless.” The thief dying on the cross obtained mercy through repentance.

Yet such negligent people are rarely truly penitent at the end, brothers dear. Because their sins demand it, one is overtaken by death, another loses the power of speech, another his memory, another despairs, and another becomes so hardened that he regrets having abandoned temporal things more than having sinned.

Therefore, brothers dear, while we have the ability, while we can still sin, let us abandon our sins and be secure. Otherwise, when we can no longer sin, we do not abandon our sins; rather, our sins abandon us.

The second part follows, in which it is shown in what respect those who die in the Lord are blessed, when it is said: “From now on,” says the Spirit. There is no doubt that this is the Holy Spirit, whose speaking is doing.

“From now on,” says the Spirit, “let them rest from their labors.” “From now on” means from the resurrection of Christ, or from the death of any righteous person who died after Christ’s resurrection. For those who died before Christ’s passion and resurrection were held and labored in hell—if not in another respect, at least in this, that they lacked the vision of God.

“Let them rest,” he says, “from their labors.” The preposition “from” has both a removing and a causal force. It is removing because the faithful departed cease from every labor: from the labors of necessity, the labors of infirmity, the labors of error, the labors of repentance, and the labors of righteousness.

They cease from the labors of necessity because they no longer need to labor or be anxious for food, clothing, or other necessities. “They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more, and the sun shall not fall upon them, nor any heat (Rev. VII).”

They cease from the labors of infirmity because thereafter they will be afflicted neither by illness, old age, nor any other hardship. “For God,” as John says, “will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints, and death shall be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, nor any pain, because the former things have passed away (ibid.).”

They cease from the labors of error because thereafter there will be in them neither ignorance, deviation, nor any disorder. Eternal Wisdom will illuminate them, and “they shall all be taught by God (John VI).”

They cease from the labors of repentance because thereafter they will not be pierced with remorse, weep, fast, or afflict themselves on account of the consciousness of sins that were forgiven them in this life. If someone is cleansed for a time in purgatorial places, nevertheless he already rests in the certain hope of rest.

They cease from the labors of righteousness because thereafter there will be no need to struggle for the defense of the faith or the Church, or for the relief of the needy, since all enemies and necessities have been driven far away.

The preposition “from” is also causal, because on account of the labors of righteousness they have endured, the faithful departed will attain eternal rest. Understand, however, that the cause is not sufficient in itself but contributory. Salvation does not come from works of righteousness but from the grace of God alone.

Be careful, however, that when you hear that the faithful departed rest from their labors, you do not understand them to pause or sleep as though from weariness. In that blessedness there will be neither labor nor sleep. The saints are said to rest from their labors, that is, to cease from them. For in that eternal rest the saints will not be idle; rather, they will contemplate, praise, and bless the Lord forever. Such activity will produce neither fatigue nor weariness, but rather complete rest, delight, and joy.

When it is therefore said that the saints rest from their labors, this is litotes: saying less and signifying more. In that eternal blessedness there will be heaped up ineffably not merely rest, but every sweetness, every beauty, every delight, every pleasure, every brightness, every joy, and every glory.

The third part follows, in which the cause of their rest is added when it is said: “For their works follow them”—that is, the reward of their works; or, if they did not have time to work, the reward of faith and good will, which are counted as deeds.

He rightly says “their works,” not the works of others, since, as the Lord says through the prophet: “The soul that sins, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, and the father shall not bear the iniquity of the son. The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him (Ezek. XVIII).”

But do prayers, almsgiving, offerings, and the other good things that we perform for our departed friends not follow them? Do they not benefit them? For we read in the Book of Maccabees that “the very brave Judas sent twelve drachmas of silver to Jerusalem, to be offered there for the sins of the dead (II Macc. XII).” If this were useless, he would not have hoped that it would benefit them.

They do benefit them, therefore—but those who need such help and who merited during their lives that such things should be able to benefit them. There are three kinds of departed persons.

Some are very good: after death they pass immediately into rest, and they need neither our prayers nor our benefits; rather, they help us by their own. Others are moderately good: they descend in true confession and repentance, and because they are not yet perfectly purified, they are purified in purgatorial places. Without doubt, prayers, almsgiving, and sacrifices benefit these. Yet new merits are not acquired for them after they have died; rather, these subsequent works are rendered in consequence of their preceding merits.

Others are wholly damned, and they have not merited that such benefits should help them. Nevertheless, brothers, because we do not know who needs them, who does not, whom they benefit, or whom they do not benefit, we ought to offer prayers, almsgiving, and offerings for all and for those concerning whom we are uncertain.

For the very good, these are acts of thanksgiving; for the moderately good, acts of expiation; and for the reprobate, whatever consolation the living can provide. Whether such works benefit the dead or not, they can nevertheless benefit those for whom they are performed in devotion. It is written: “My prayer shall return into my own bosom (Ps. XXXIV).” Whoever prays for another labors for himself.

Likewise, the honor of burial and the construction of tombs, which benefit the dead nothing, are nevertheless not without fruit for the living who perform such acts. Hence Tobias and certain others are commended among the saints.

Therefore, brothers dear, let us be mindful and concerned for our departed—our parents, friends, benefactors, and others—and let us frequently offer prayers, almsgiving, and offerings for them.

Blessed Gregory relates in his Dialogue that Paschasius, a deacon of the Roman See, was a man devoted to almsgiving, a caretaker of the poor, and contemptuous of himself. Excellent books by him on the Holy Spirit are also extant. During the dispute that arose between Laurentius and Symmachus, he chose Laurentius. Yet although Laurentius had been defeated by the general election of all, Paschasius never abandoned him but supported him until death.

At last, when Paschasius died and was placed on a bier, a demon-possessed man touched his dalmatic and was delivered. When Germanus, bishop of Capua, was bathing in the baths at Angulanum in order to recover his strength, he found the aforementioned Paschasius serving among the hot baths. When he asked in astonishment what so great a man was doing there, he heard from him that he had been placed in that place of punishment because he had supported Laurentius against Symmachus.

“But I ask you,” he said, “pray for me. Then you will know that I have obtained rest if, when you return here, you do not find me.” And so it happened. For blessed Germanus entreated the Lord for him, and when he returned he did not find him.

From this we learn that the aforementioned Paschasius had merited while alive that the prayers of others might benefit him after death.

Therefore, brothers dear, while we can, let us amend our lives, wash away our stains with tears, devote ourselves to works of mercy, and assist the souls of the departed with prayers and almsgiving, so that we may deserve to be helped after death by the prayers and almsgiving of others. This is granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

XLIV. SERMON ON THE SAME SUBJECT, ON THE GOSPEL

Jesus said to the crowds of the Jews: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the living Son of God, and those who hear shall live (John V),” and so forth.

As we gather from this and other passages of Sacred Scripture, brothers dear, there are three lives and three corresponding deaths. The first life is spiritual life, by which the spirit—or the human being—lives while living justly and spiritually, namely, when through true grace he has within himself the life that is God.

Opposed to this life is spiritual death, by which the spirit, or the human being, dies when he sins, excludes God from himself, and receives the devil as an inhabitant. For just as God gives life to the soul by dwelling in it through his grace, so the devil kills it by dwelling in it through sin. This does not mean that the soul can cease to exist, but that it would be better for it not to exist at all than to exist without God.

The second life is bodily life, by which we live while our body is enlivened by the soul. Opposed to this is bodily death, by which we die when the soul is separated from our body.

The third life is eternal and blessed life, which is truly called life because, lacking every corruption, every defect, and every sadness, it will be filled with the happiness of every good and every joy. Opposed to this is eternal and miserable death. It is called death not because it annihilates or dissolves the reprobate, but because it would be better for them to die a thousand times than to live in eternal misery and punishment.

Just as the righteous pass from spiritual life through bodily death to eternal life, so the reprobate pass deservedly from spiritual death through bodily death to eternal death.

The three lives are from God as their author, but the three deaths are not. Spiritual death, that is, sin, is not from God but rather from the devil or from the human being. Hence it is written: “God did not make death (Wis. I),” but human beings summoned death to themselves with hands and feet. “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world (Wis. II).” Those who belong to his side imitate him.

Bodily and eternal death, however, have God as their author, since they are punishments justly inflicted on account of sin. Hence the Lord says: “I kill, and I make alive; I strike, and I heal (Deut. XXXII).”

Since there are therefore three deaths, a person can rise from the first and second, but not from the third. For just as eternal life cannot fall into death, so eternal death cannot rise into life.
