From spiritual death the Lord causes us sinners to rise through repentance in this life. From bodily death he will cause us to rise in the general resurrection. The Lord speaks of these two resurrections in the reading just mentioned: first of the first, and second of the second.

He speaks of the first when he says: “Amen, amen, I say to you,” and so forth. “Amen” is an adverb of affirmation, derived from the noun for faith, meaning “faithfully” or “truly”; it is, as it were, God’s oath. When it is doubled, a greater affirmation of the matter is shown. The Lord therefore did not wish us to doubt this; rather, he wished to confirm it as though by a double oath.

“For,” he says, “the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the living Son of God, and those who hear shall live. For just as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son to have life in himself,” and so forth.

He says four things about the first resurrection: when it occurs, in whom it occurs, through whom it occurs, and from what it occurs.

He shows when it occurs when he says: “The hour is coming, and now is.” Since the Lord had already raised some dead persons from their sins by preaching, and was going to raise many more through himself and through his own, he rightly says: “The hour is coming, and now is.”

Generally speaking, this hour is the present life. While we live here, while we can still sin and do good, we can repent of our sins and rise again.

In the other life there will be no time for sinning or doing good, but only for receiving. Those who here refused to rise from guilt will not be able there to rise from eternal death.

He shows in whom this resurrection occurred when he says: “The dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God.” But because some hear Christ’s words only with the bodily ear and not with the ear of the heart, he repeats the word “hear”: Who will hear? Only those are raised from sins in mind who hear Christ’s words with the ear of their whole heart—that is, who retain in their hearts what they carry out in their actions.

Hence the Lord says: “Whoever believes in me”—understand, with faith working through love—“even if he has died, shall live (John XI).”

Behold, brothers dear, you truly hear the voice of the Son of God, for the words that I speak to you are Christ’s words. If, therefore, you hear them with your whole heart, even if you are dead in sins, you will undoubtedly live.

But if, like the Jews, you hear Christ’s words only with the bodily ear, they will not merely fail to benefit you; rather, they will heap up greater condemnation for you, as they did for them. Hence the Lord says: “If I had not come,” he says, “and spoken to them, they would not have sin. But now they have no excuse for their sin (John XV).”

He shows through whom the resurrection from sins takes place: through the Son, not as through a minister but as through the author. He adds the reason: the Son has life abiding in himself, just as the Father does, substantially and causally.

Substantially, because he is life itself in essence; causally, because he is the efficient cause of all living beings—whether those living bodily life, spiritual life, or eternal life. He can rightly give life because he is the author of life.

He shows from whom he has this, namely, from the Father. For just as he is God from God, so he is life from life. This is what he says: “For just as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself.”

This does not mean that the Son, as though previously lacking it, received life at some point as a gift. Rather, “he gave life” means that he generated from his own substance one who lives substantially.

If, therefore, the Only-Begotten of God says that he has everything from the Father, how much more should we, brothers, if we possess anything good, or think, say, or do anything good, acknowledge and say that we do not have it from ourselves but from God the Father.

The second part follows, in which the Lord speaks about the bodily resurrection. He accordingly says that he has received from the same Father the power both to judge, to raise the dead, and to reward. He speaks of the power to judge when he says, “And he gave him power to exercise judgment,” and he supplies the reason when he adds, “Because he is the Son of Man.” Three reasons may here be understood: the reason for the giving, for the power, or for the judgment.

Because he is the Son, it is said that power was given him as to one who is greater. Again, because he is the Son of Man and deigned to appear among human beings as though powerless, it is fitting that at the resurrection he should appear to possess everything under his power. Again, because he is the Son of Man and allowed himself to be unjustly judged, it is fitting that in the judgment he should appear as judge of all. For not the person of the Father, but the person of the Son alone, will appear in the judgment, so that the Jews may plainly see the one whom they unjustly judged; the crucifiers, the one whom they pierced; all the reprobate, the one whom they despised; and all the elect, the one whom they loved.

He also says that he possesses the power to raise the dead when he adds, “Do not marvel”—that is, do not marvel that the Son of Man has the power to judge, and also, what appears still more marvelous, that he has the power to raise the dead in body and soul together. He says this because “the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God.” This is that cry of which he himself says elsewhere in the Gospel: “At midnight a cry was made: Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him” (Matt. XXV). This is the voice of the archangel, or the trumpet, of which the Apostle says: “For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first” (I Thess. IV), and so forth.

“They will hear,” he says, “the voice of God and will come forth”—that is, by the force of the voice they will hear and rise. Behold, my brothers, how great and marvelous is the omnipotence of the Son of God: at his voice all the dust of the departed, however thoroughly covered and however widely scattered, will immediately be joined together, given life, and come forth from the tombs. Although I distinguish these events verbally in this way, the Apostle shows how quickly they will occur, saying: “We shall all rise in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye” (I Cor. XV).

“In a moment”—that is, at an instant of time. He defines the brevity of this instant by the action that can take place within it when he adds, “in the twinkling of an eye”—that is, for as long as the movement of the eye lasts, namely, the emission of a ray. From the moment it is emitted, it reaches not the nearer object before the more distant one, but both the nearer and the more distant at once, passing simultaneously through all the intervening air, so that in what it sees it seems rather to have found its visual power than to have carried it there. By this we understand that it is just as easy for God to raise newly dead corpses as those that have fallen away over a long period of time.

The Apostle likewise shows what sort of persons will come forth from the tombs when he says: “For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible” (I Cor. XV)—that is, whole in their limbs and immortal, both the good and the wicked. Nevertheless, the wicked will always remain capable of suffering and will continually be renewed for the bitterness of punishments, without being able to die.

He also shows that he possesses the power to reward the good and the wicked when he adds that at his voice “those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment,” that is, of condemnation. All will rise, both good and wicked, so that they may receive in soul and body alike the good things they did in body and soul.

Those have done good who have accomplished good works with good intention and perseverance. Those have done evil who have performed evil works, or good works with evil intention, or good works without perseverance.

But since both the good and the wicked are to come to judgment, why does the Lord say that not the good but the wicked rise to judgment? Because he will heap glory upon his saints beyond their merits, whereas to the wicked he will assign punishment only according to their merits.

But you will say: How will the reprobate be judged according to their merits? What? Will they be punished without end for having sinned temporarily and for a moment? It is just that those who did not put an end to their sin should find no end in their torment. For one who does not cease sinning during the short span of this life would have ceased sinning still less if he had thought he would live here forever. Hence, deservedly, one who was always going to sin was always going to pay the penalty.

Therefore, my brothers, let us put an end to our evil wills and pleasures before our end [i.e. death]. While it is permitted, let us correct our ways. Let us keep our death always before our eyes and consider how terribly the supreme Judge will come. Let us wash away the stains of our sins with the tears of repentance. Let us devote ourselves to works of mercy, so that at that fearful judgment we may deserve to obtain mercy. Amen.

## II. HOMILIES ON THE SAINTS

### ON THE APOSTLES (FROM G. VICELIUS)

[Col. 1489]

Four of these men have only one name, namely Andrew, John, Philip, and Bartholomew. All the rest have either two or three names.

Those with two names are James the Greater, who is also called the son of Zebedee (Matt. X; Mark III); and James the Lesser, who is likewise called the son of Alphaeus (Matt. X; Mark III; Luke VI; Acts I). He was also called Justus and Oplia, that is, “armor.”

Matthew, who had been a tax collector, is likewise called Levi, the son of Alphaeus—without doubt of another Alphaeus, different from the former, the father of James the Lesser (Mark II). For James and Matthew were not brothers by birth.

Thomas is likewise called Didymus (John XX), although the same name might seem to be involved, merely pronounced in different languages. For what the Hebrews call *thom* or Thomas, the Greeks call δίδυμον (*didymon*), which in Latin we call “twin.”

Those with three names include Simon, who is also called the Cananaean (Matt. X) and the Zealot (Acts I). Yet “to be called Cananaean” is not altogether different from “to be called Zealot,” since what the Hebrews call *Canani* or “Cananaean,” the Greeks call ζηλώτην (*zēlōtēn*), and we call “zealot” or “emulator.” That Simon was called the Cananaean not because he belonged to the nation of Canaan, but from the Galilean village Cana (John II).

The other Simon—for the apostolic order contains two Simons—was surnamed Cephas and likewise Peter, indeed also Bar-Jonah, or “son of the dove.” Here too, however, the variation of names arises from the diversity of languages. For what the Chaldeans call Cephas, the Greeks call πέτραν (*petran*), and we call “rock.”

In the same way, that girl is called Tabitha and likewise Dorcas (Acts IX), namely, “from looking,” although according to the original it is more correctly read *Tabeia*.

The last is Judas, who is sometimes surnamed Lebbaeus and sometimes Thaddaeus (Matt. X). Saint Luke calls this man “Judas of James” (Luke VI), “the brother of James” (Acts I), explaining what he had previously said, “Judas of James.”

So much for the names of the apostles.

Moreover, some of the apostles were related by blood and kinship. Simon, namely Cephas or Peter, and Andrew were brothers, natives of Galilee. James the Greater and John were also brothers; their father was Zebedee and their mother Salome. These two are given the surname *Beneregesch* or *Beniaregesch* by Mark (Mark III), that is, “sons of thunder,” because of the firmness and greatness of their faith, as Jerome testifies.

James the Lesser, Simon, and Judas were also brothers. Their father was Clopas and their mother Mary, who was called the sister of Mary the God-bearer (John XIX). But either that Clopas was surnamed Alphaeus, or Alphaeus must have been a second husband of this Mary.

I wish to distinguish these two Simons by epithets, just as I have distinguished the two Jameses: let one be called the Greater, namely Simon Peter, and the other the Lesser, namely Simon the Zealot. The two Judases are likewise distinguished: one is called Lebbaeus, “from the heart,” and the other Iscariot, “from payment.”

In the place of the latter Matthias was substituted. Franciscus Picus calls him *Donatus* in a poem, interpreting in Latin what is called *Matthi* in Hebrew (Acts I). Matthew has the same name, except that Matthias and Matthew are distinguished by the final syllables.

## COMMON OF THE HOLY APOSTLES I

[Col. 1489C]

“You are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (Eph. II), and so forth.

The apostle Paul speaks these words to his disciples, the Ephesians; but he speaks the same words to us also, dearest brothers, provided that you live according to God’s commandments and apostolic teaching.

He says three things. First, he says that we are citizens of God’s city. Second, which is greater, that we are also stones of that same city through Christ’s building. Third, which is greatest, that we are also the temple of God.

First, then, he shows that we are citizens of God’s city when it is said: “You are no longer strangers and foreigners.” Strangers are those who remain for a short time; foreigners are those who come from elsewhere.

In God’s city, strangers are false Christians who belong to this Church militant in number but not in merit, in name but not in divine reality—like useless chaff, destined to be winnowed and burned. But you, my brothers, if you persevere in faith and love of God, are not strangers.

Again, you are not foreigners, because in that heavenly city in which you were created in the first man, you already dwell through desire and hope. Rather, you are citizens—that is, fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household.

Three things make someone a fellow citizen of the same city: dwelling together, observance of the same laws and customs, and love of the same fellowship and commonwealth.

Our city, my brothers, is that heavenly and blessed Jerusalem, whose citizens are all who are already blessed. By God’s generosity we too will become its citizens, and even now belong to it in part, if we dwell in that blessed city through hope and desire; if we observe the customs and laws of the saints; if with all our ardor we love, desire, and seek the fellowship and commonwealth of the saints; and if we labor and struggle for it even unto death.

But those who dwell in love of the world, who follow the laws and customs of worldly people, who tear apart the fellowship of brotherhood, and who quarrel and fight over temporal possessions will be utterly exiles from that blessed city.

Two things also make someone a member of a household: familiar service and knowledge of its secrets. We too, my brothers, if we strive to serve God familiarly and specially according to his will, and if through Sacred Scripture and the revelation of the Spirit we already know something of God’s secrets, are without doubt not only citizens but also members of his household.

The second part follows, in which the Apostle shows that, if we are true Christians, we are also stones of the heavenly city, when he adds: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone.”

There is one foundation of the apostles and prophets: Christ. He is called the foundation for three reasons.

Just as a foundation supports the whole building and is supported by no one, so Christ governs and carries the whole Church, and is carried or governed by no one. Again, just as a building cannot stand without a foundation, so no structure of virtues or good works can stand without faith in Jesus Christ. “For it is impossible to please God without faith” (Heb. XI).

Again, just as the foundation is not seen and yet the whole structure rises from it, so the faith of Jesus Christ concerns invisible things, and from it proceeds the whole building of virtues and good works.

Because the prophets and apostles first adhered to this foundation and taught others to adhere to it, they too are called, by derivation, foundations of the Church. Hence the Psalmist says: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI), that is, in the apostles. Like mountains, they first received the rays of faith; upon their foundation we have been built, in accordance with what Peter says: “Coming to him, a living stone rejected indeed by human beings but chosen by God, you also, like living stones, are being built upon him into spiritual houses” (I Pet. II).

Now a stone that is to be placed in a building is first separated from the quarry by hammers. Then every projection and distortion is cut away from it with tools. Next it is squared according to the rule, and finally it is placed in the building with mortar.

So each one of us, my brothers, if we are to be placed in the building of the heavenly city, is first separated from the mass of perdition by the hammers of threats, through the operation of God’s grace. It is like a hammer when it is said to us: “Repent, for the axe has been laid to the root of the trees” (Matt. III; Luke III).

Then, through the discipline of teachers, every distortion and projection of vices is cut away from us. Third, we are squared according to the rule of the divine commandments, so that we may be solid and firm: so that we may not be cast down by prosperity on the right or adversity on the left; by open temptation from before or hidden temptation from behind; nor be shaken upward by pride or downward by despair.

But the mortar of love is also necessary for us. Without it we cannot be joined either to God or to our neighbor, nor can we be placed in the heavenly building. Without this, all the rest are possessed in vain.

This heavenly building is founded and completed not by a human being but by Christ Jesus himself, the chief cornerstone.

Three things are said about Christ: that he is a stone, that he is chief, and that he is a cornerstone.

He is a stone because he is immovable and firm; because he pours forth living water, from which human beings and animals drink; and because he sparkles with virtues and miracles. To the reprobate, however, he is “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” (I Pet. II), “over which whoever falls will be broken, and upon whom whoever falls will be crushed” (Matt. XXI).

He is chief because, just as he is the founder and foundation of the holy Church, so he is its perfection and its perfecter. He himself is the beginning and the end—not the end of destruction, but the end of consummation.

He is a cornerstone because he is the mediator who reconciles humanity to God and God to humanity in himself; who makes peace between angels and human beings and between human beings and angels in himself; and who unites Jews with gentiles and gentiles with Jews in himself.

Whatever, therefore, my brothers, we build—however much rectitude we may seem to possess in our conduct and good works—we build upon sand and in vain unless we have Christ, both as foundation and as cornerstone, that is, as beginning and end.

In him alone every building constructed grows into a holy temple in the Lord, whether it is constructed from many persons into the unity of the same Church, or from many virtues, good habits, and good works into the sanctification of the same person.

The third part is that in which he shows that, if we are true Christians, we are the Lord’s holy temple and also God’s dwelling place, when he adds: “In him you too are being built together into a dwelling place of God in the Holy Spirit.”

Not only, dearest brothers, are all of us who are faithful together one temple and dwelling place of God, but each individual believer is also a temple and dwelling place of God, as Paul testifies when he says: “Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own?” (I Cor. VI).

It is a temple because, just as God is worshiped, sacrificed to, and entreated in a temple, so in the soul of each believer God is worshiped, sacrificed to, and entreated.

God is more truly worshiped in the soul. Hence the Lord says to the Samaritan woman: “The hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. But true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth” (John IV). “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and in truth.”

God is also more truly offered sacrifice in the soul, through compunction and contrition, as the Psalmist says: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. L).

God is more truly entreated in the soul, as the Lord says: “When you pray, do not be like the sorrowful hypocrites who love to stand praying in synagogues and at the corners of the streets, so that they may be seen by human beings. But when you pray, enter your room”—that is, the secrecy of your heart—“and, having shut the door, pray to your Father. And your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matt. VI).

The faithful soul is also God’s dwelling place, or house, because just as each master dwells, is nourished, and rests in his own house, so God is nourished, dwells, and rests in the faithful soul.

He dwells there through indwelling grace, as the Lord himself says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV).

He is nourished in the soul through the devotion of good will and desire, as he says: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone opens to me, I will enter in to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. III).

He rests in the soul through the peace and quiet produced by merits. Hence the same Lord says: “Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI).

Therefore, my brothers, because we are called and are God’s temple and dwelling place, let us cast out from ourselves every disgrace and impurity, lest we offend and exclude the one who dwells in us. For if God takes it grievously when his handmade temple is polluted and profaned by impurities, he bears and avenges far more grievously the violation and profanation of his spiritual temple by crimes.

Hence Paul says: “Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit who dwells in you?” (I Cor. VI). And: “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (I Cor. III).

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us avoid every stain, every vice, and every uncleanness. Let us adorn ourselves with the ornaments of virtues and good conduct, and with every effort prepare ourselves to be such as are worthy for God to dwell in us, and for us to dwell in him.

May he grant this through the intercession of the holy apostles, he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## II. SERMON ON THE SAME, ON JOHN

The Lord Jesus said to his disciples: “This is my commandment: that you love one another, as I have loved you” (John XV), and so forth.

This reading from the holy Gospel is divided into three sections. First, the Lord commands us to love one another according to his example. Second, he explains the reward of this commandment. Third, he shows that we can obtain neither the reward nor the merit through our own wisdom, but only through his grace.

First, then, he commands us to love one another when he says: “This is my commandment: that you love one another.”

There are many commandments of the Lord, my brothers, but he specifically and properly calls the commandment concerning love his own, because every commandment arises from and is perfected by love alone. Just as many branches of a tree grow from one root, so many virtues proceed from one love; and a branch of good works has no greenness in itself unless it remains in the root of love.

The Lord’s commandments are therefore many in the diversity of their works, but one in the root of love. Hence Paul says: “Love is the fullness of the law” (Rom. XIII). And: “I have seen an end of every perfection; your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. CXVIII).

It is therefore as though he were saying: “This is especially and particularly my commandment.” It is mine because I especially demonstrate it in myself, humbling myself through my excessive love for you and enduring death. It is mine because I command it to you above all others, repeating and urging it again and again. It is mine because through it I make you mine and myself yours.

Let us hold fast to this commandment, my brothers. Let us love God, and in God let us love one another.

True love is very strong, very sweet, and very useful. It is very strong because, according to Solomon, brothers who love one another are a bronze wall, and “love is strong as death” (Song VI)—indeed, stronger than death. For through true love we despise death, overcome it by dying, and are made immortal from mortal beings.

What is sweeter than to observe kindness, harmony, and love? Admiring its sweetness, the Prophet says: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. CXXXII).

It is exceedingly useful because true love makes us friends from enemies, eternal from temporal beings, and gods from human beings.

And because love is so necessary for us, the devil tries above all else to take it away from us. For he draws us, as far as he can, toward the delight in and love of earthly things, so that, while the same things are desired by us and by others, envy and hatred may be sown among us and charity extinguished.

If, therefore, my brothers, we wish to preserve the love of God and neighbor within us, let us despise all earthly things, so that we neither envy them in others nor grieve when they are taken from us. For whoever hates his brother on account of some temporal thing loses the love of God and neighbor by placing that temporal thing above them.

From this it is clear that no one can possess simultaneously the love of God and the love of the world.

The Lord then exhorts us to mutual love by his own example when he adds: “As I have loved you. Greater love has no one than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends.”

It is as though he were saying plainly: “Love one another as much as, and in the manner in which, I have loved you.”

And how has the Lord loved us? Freely, spiritually, and fervently.

He loved us freely, because not on account of our merit—for we deserved nothing but evil—nor on account of his own merit, since he needed no one, but for our advantage, since we were greatly in need.

He loved us spiritually, because he did not love us for earthly things but for heavenly things, so that he might make us spiritual from carnal beings, heavenly from earthly beings, and eternal from temporal beings.

He loved us fervently, because he did not love us lukewarmly or falsely, but most fervently, giving not only what was his but also himself for us.

Let us therefore love as he also loved us.

Let us love freely, not waiting for others to love us, but loving them ourselves first, and seeking not our own advantages but those of others.

But since some love carnally, and freely—as parents love their children—let us also love spiritually: let us love our brothers not for earthly and vain things, but for heavenly and eternal things.

But since some love freely and spiritually yet lukewarmly, let us love fervently, not in word and tongue but in deed and truth. For God is nauseated by and hates those who are lukewarm.

The Lord shows how greatly he loved us when he adds: “Greater love has no one than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends.”

But is it not greater to lay down one’s life for one’s enemies? It certainly is. And Christ laid down his life for his enemies. Yet he calls enemies friends, not because they already loved him, but because he loved them and was going to make friends from enemies. Thus he showed us plainly that, when by loving we can gain our enemies, those who persecute us are themselves friends.

But no one persecutes us unto death. How, then, can we prove whether we love our enemies? If we have no occasion to lay down our life, certainly we have an occasion every day to lay down our possessions.

Our neighbor is hungry: let us break our bread for him. He is cold: let us give him clothing. For whoever, in a time of peace, does not give his tunic to a needy neighbor for God’s sake, how will he give his life for him in a time of persecution? Therefore, for the virtue of peace to remain unconquered in persecution, let it be nourished by mercy in peace.

The second part follows, in which the Lord sets forth the reward of his commandment when he adds: “You are my friends.”

O how great is the mercy of our Creator! We are not worthy to be servants, yet we are called friends. O how great is the dignity of human beings, to be friends of God!

But you have heard the glory; hear also the labor: “If you do what I command you.”

It is as though he were saying plainly: “You rejoice at the summit; consider by what labors one reaches the summit.”

Hence, when the sons of Zebedee asked the Lord for seats in his kingdom, he said to them: “Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink?” (Matt. XX). It is as though he were saying: “The height of the position already delights you, but first let the way exercise you through labor.”

Since someone is sometimes called a friend who loves and is not loved, and sometimes one who does not love but is loved, here the word “friend” is used more properly and absolutely of one who both loves and is loved.

The holy men are friends of God because God loves them, laying down his life for them, as he said above. And they are friends of God because they love God by keeping his commandments, as is added here.

It is therefore as though the Lord were saying: “Do what belongs to you, because I am doing what belongs to me. I do what a friend does by laying down my life for you; you also do what friends do by loving me and keeping my commandments.”

“If you do this,” he says, “I will no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you.”

He assigns the difference between a servant and a friend in this: the servant is ignorant of his master’s secrets, whereas the friend is familiar with and conscious of them.

The servant is ignorant not only of the spiritual works that the Lord performs here in the saints and of the eternal things that he prepares for them in the future, but also of the visible works themselves. He does not understand their purpose and end; indeed, he is ignorant even of the things God does through that servant, because he does not understand God’s authority and purpose in them.

Hence the Apostle says: “The natural person does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God” (I Cor. II).

But to his friends the Lord has revealed everything that he heard—that is, everything he knew was to be revealed—from the Father. For he has made known to them not only the sweetness of his love, the purity of conscience, and the pleasantness of spiritual virtues, but also the festivals of supreme blessedness. He has inspired them with these things here not only through faith and hope but also through a certain foretaste of contemplation.

The Prophet exhorts us to this when he says: “Taste and see how sweet the Lord is; blessed is the person who hopes in him” (Ps. XXXIII). And elsewhere: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you” (Ps. XXX).

For when, my brothers, we love heavenly things, we already know them in a certain way, because love itself is a kind of knowledge.

Admiring such friends of God, the same Prophet says: “Your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored by me” (Ps. CXXXVIII). And why? “Their dominion has been exceedingly strengthened” (ibid.).

Behold, God’s elect discipline the flesh, strengthen the spirit, command demons, shine with virtues, despise present things, and proclaim the eternal homeland by voice and conduct. They can be killed on its account, but they cannot be bent; indeed, they reach it. In the very passion through which they fell into the death of the flesh, see how great was the height of their spirit.

Why was this so, unless because their dominion had been strengthened? But if they are great, perhaps they are few. Therefore he adds: “I will number them, and they will be multiplied beyond the sand” (ibid.). Although they are countable, they are innumerable to us.

Behold, my brothers, the whole world is full of martyrs and friends of God, so that we may have countless witnesses to the truth and may not despair of becoming part of their number.

The third part follows, in which the Lord shows that we can attain his merit and reward not through our own wisdom but only through his grace, when he adds: “You did not choose me, but I chose you.”

But when Moses says to Israel, “You have chosen the Lord today as your God” (Deut. XVII), and every righteous person chooses to serve God rather than the world, what does the Lord mean by saying, “You did not choose me”?

Our choosing to serve God does not come from our own wisdom but from divine election and grace. For he first chose and loved us, so that we might love and choose him.

“I chose you,” he says, “and appointed you, so that you might go and bear fruit, and that your fruit might remain.”

I chose you freely by predestining you from eternity. I appointed you on the way by freely inspiring faith, so that you might go through cooperating grace by willing what is good, bear fruit by doing what is good, and that your fruit might remain by persevering well.

Whatever, my brothers, we labor for on account of the present age flees and perishes. Hence the Prophet says: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” (Ps. CXXVI). For when temporal inheritance comes to an end, eternal inheritance begins.

Let worldly labors therefore become cheap in our eyes, and let us produce such fruits as remain. Let us devote ourselves to virtues and to works of virtue, which will always remain—not only in the reward, but some of them also in their own reality.

For love, wisdom, justice, fortitude, moderation, and things of this kind will not only remain in that blessed life; they will also be perfected and strengthened there.

“Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you”—that is, eternal blessedness, in which all desired things will come to pass, indeed more than were desired.

Since in that eternal blessedness there are good things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (I Cor. II), it is clear that God will give us there more, greater, and better things than we are able to ask or desire.

To attain these things, my brothers, let us keep God’s commandments, and especially love. Let us love God more than ourselves and our neighbors as ourselves. Let us lay down not only our possessions but also ourselves for our neighbors.

Since our temporal possessions and even temporal life itself pass away and perish, what is wiser or better than to purchase an everlasting inheritance with perishable things?

Behold, we admire and bless as happy the saints who, for love of God and neighbor, laid down not only their possessions but also themselves. Why, then, do we not imitate them?

Blessed Gregory relates that a certain priest named Sanctolus was a man of extraordinary charity. He asked the Lombards to spare the life of a certain deacon whom they were holding bound. When they refused, he asked them to hand the man over to him for safekeeping.

“To you,” they said, “we give him to guard, but on this condition: if he flees, you must die in his place.”

The man of God agreed and accepted him under his protection. At midnight, when he saw all the Lombards asleep, he awakened the deacon and said: “Rise and flee as quickly as possible; may the almighty Lord set you free.”

The deacon replied: “I cannot flee, Father, because if I flee, you yourself will die in my place.”

But the man of God compelled him to flee, saying: “I am in God’s hand. They can do only as much to me as God permits.”

In the morning the Lombards asked for the man entrusted to him. When he said that the deacon had fled, they replied: “You yourself know what is fitting.”

He said: “I know.”

“You are a good man,” they said. “We do not wish you to die through various tortures; choose your death.”

He replied: “I am in God’s hand. Kill me by whatever death he himself permits.”

They therefore chose a strong man who could behead him with a single blow. But the man of God, having requested time to pray, prostrated himself and prayed.

As he prayed for a long time, the executioner kicked him with his foot so that he would rise and stretch out his neck. He extended his neck, looked at the drawn sword, and said: “Holy John, receive her.”

Then the executioner raised his sword to strike, but his arm became stiff. When all who were present saw this, and marveled at and praised the man of God, they asked him to heal the arm of their executioner.

“I will not pray for him,” he said, “unless he first swears that with this hand he will no longer kill a Christian.”

When the executioner had sworn, he restored freedom to his arm.

When the Lombards offered him the things they had plundered, he rejected them; instead, he asked for and received the souls of the captives.

Thus it happened that, while one man offered himself to death for one person, he freed many from death.

Let us therefore hold fast, my brothers, to charity, which, according to the Apostle, “believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things, and never fails” (I Cor. XIII), nor permits those who observe it to fail, but leads them to eternal blessedness.

May the almighty and merciful Lord be willing to lead us to it through charity. Amen.

## III. ON THE APOSTLES
[Col. 1498D] “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called saints according to his purpose” (Rom. VIII), and so forth.

Here the Apostle says four things, my brothers. First, he says that all things work together for the good of the elect. Second, he shows in what order God fulfills the purpose of his election in them. Third, he says that no one can harm them. Fourth, he says that nothing can separate them from God.

First, then, he shows that all things work together for the good of the elect when he says, “We know,” and so forth. It is as though he said: We apostles of God, whose authority must be believed, know—not through knowledge alone but also through experience—that all things work together for the good of those who love God. But because some love God only for a time, he adds, “who are called according to the purpose of the divine [Col. 1499A] election,” so that they may be holy.

All things alike—prosperity and adversity, health and illness, favor and opposition, peace and conflict, love and hatred, life and death, and everything else. For just as prosperity, health, favor, peace, love, and life give the elect opportunity and material for doing good, so their opposites give them occasion and exercise for doing good. Through adversity the patience of the saints is exercised; through illness, humility; through opposition, wisdom; through conflict, fortitude; through hatred, benevolence; and through death, the entrance into rest is opened.

Nor do these things alone work together for the good of the elect, my brothers, but even transgression and falls do so, since they rise again more humble and more instructed. Conversely, all things work together for the evil of the reprobate [Col. 1499B]—not only evil things, but even good things, when they grow proud of them, when they are ungrateful to God, when they abuse them, when they uselessly conceal them, or when they fail to persevere.

Therefore, my brothers, let us always fear, and let us unceasingly implore the Lord with sighs, groans, and tears, so that he may rescue us from the number of the reprobate, enroll us by his mercy among the number of his elect, and cause all things to work together for our good.

The second part follows, in which the Apostle shows the order by which God brings the purpose of his election to completion in the saints, when he adds: “For those whom he foreknew to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined, he also called. And those whom he called, he also justified. And those whom he justified, he also glorified.”

But because foreknowledge applies both to good and to evil, he specifies to what glory he foreknew them, when he adds, “to be conformed to the image of his Son,” and so forth: namely, so that they may first become conformed to his Son through renewal of mind and afterward through immortality—his Son “who is the image of the Father” (Heb. I)—so that, just as they bore the image of the earthly, they may bear the image of the heavenly. Yet this is so that Christ himself may be the firstborn: that is, the first conceived and born without sin, and the first to rise again among many brothers, that is, among many brothers. He is not ashamed to call them brothers, not in respect of his being the only-begotten, but in respect of his being the firstborn.

“Those whom he predestined”—that is, before they existed, he prepared grace for them. [Col. 1499D] “Those whom he predestined,” when they already existed, he called to that grace through preaching or in some other way. Those whom he called in this manner, he justified by the bestowal of that grace, so that they might be like him in eternal blessedness.

Similarly, we can speak conversely about the reprobate. Those whom God foresees will become like the devil, he rejected; and those whom he rejected, although he called some of them to the faith, he cast away. Those whom he cast away, he handed over to a debased mind and to dishonorable passions; and those whom he handed over to this, he condemned.

Yet there is a difference: God rejected the reprobate by condemning them because he foresees that they will become evil. But he did not predestine the elect because he foresaw that they would become good; rather, they were going to become good because God predestined them. For God did not predestine the elect, my brothers, on account of their future merits; rather, he predestined them freely, called them freely, justified them freely, and glorified them freely. But he rejected, cast away, and condemned the condemned on account of their merits. Why? Because the elect are good not from themselves but from God, whereas the evil are evil not from God but from themselves.

Nevertheless, dearest brothers, God repels no one from his grace; he offers it to everyone. He repels only the one who repels himself. Therefore, if we will, we are predestined and saved. We will if we do good, insofar as we are able. If we do not do so, it is clear that we do not will perfectly.

The third part follows, in which it is shown that no one can harm the elect, when it is added: “What then shall we say to these things?”—understand, except that everything is from God for us, and no one will be able to harm us. If God, he says, is for us—predestining us when we did not yet exist, calling us when we were enemies, justifying us as sinners, and glorifying us as mortals—who, he asks, will be able to prevail against us, so that God does not make all things work together for our good? No one at all.

The wicked are indeed opposed to the saints in their will, but not in their effectiveness. Rather, while they strive to harm the saints, they benefit them and harm themselves, according to the saying: “That dragon whom you formed to mock them” (Ps. CIII). For, he says, he also bestowed upon us this singular and wondrous benefit: that he did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up as a sufficient offering even for all sinners. “How will he not also, with him, freely give us all things?”

The argument proceeds from the greater. For he who gave us the Lord himself also gave us the things belonging to the Lord. Thus the same Paul says: “All things are ours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas, whether the world or life or death, whether things present or things to come” (I Cor. III).

Good things—whether human beings or angels—are ours because they help us. Evil things—whether human beings or demons—are ours because they exercise us. The world is ours, so that we may use its service well. The present life is ours, so that through it we may gain merit. Death is ours, so that through it we may pass into rest. Present good things are ours, so that through them we may be strengthened in God’s service. Future things are ours, so that we may enjoy their happiness forever.

“Who,” he says, “will bring an accusation against God’s elect?”—that is, so that their accusation harms God’s elect? No one. “God is the one who justifies. Who is the one who condemns?”—that is, who can inflict punishment for sin? No one. God does not wish it; another cannot accomplish it.

“Christ,” he says, “Jesus,” who died to save them—or, more greatly, who also rose again, who is at the Father’s right hand and equal to him in honor, and who, standing between us and God, intercedes for us by presenting his humanity. His petition cannot be ineffective.

Behold, brothers: if we are faithful, Christ intercedes for us, God the Father is for us, all things are ours, and all things work together for our good. Who, then, can harm us? No one.

The fourth part follows, in which it is shown that no thing can separate the elect from the love of God, when it is added: [Col. 1501A] “Who will separate us from the love of God?”

It is as though he said openly: God loves us so greatly and bestows such great benefits upon us. Who, then, will separate us from the love of God? Will bodily tribulation separate us? Or mental anguish? Or hunger? Or nakedness—that is, lack of food and clothing? Or persecution from place to place? Or danger of death? Or the sword—that is, death itself? Certainly not.

And do these things happen so that some may be separated from the love of God? They do happen, indeed, as it is written: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep destined only for slaughter.” But “in all these things,” he says, “we conquer,” not on account of ourselves, but on account of him who loved us.

It is as though he said: Although the things I have listed are greatly feared in this world, nevertheless, for the sake of God, whom we fear and [Col. 1501B] love above all things, we overcome them.

“For I am certain”—that is, on the basis of God’s promise, when he says, “I will not desert you; I will not abandon you”—that neither death, which they threaten, nor life, which they promise; neither angel nor principality; neither powers—that is, promises of glory from a lower, intermediate, or higher order, or threats from lesser, greater, or greatest demons; neither things present—that is, the present time—nor things to come, whether good or evil; neither strength—that is, anyone’s violence; neither height—that is, human power or Satan’s exaltation; nor depth—that is, hell, the precipice displayed by the threatening devil (or he calls prosperity and adversity “height” and “depth”); nor, he says, any other creature, or anything made contrary to nature, such as a two-headed horse or things like those produced by Pharaoh’s magicians, will be able to separate us from the love of God—the love that God has for us and we have for him—which exists, that is, is manifested, in Christ Jesus.

The Apostle has listed both the things most feared and the things most loved in this world, in order to show that the elect do not fear even the things most feared in this world for the sake of God, whom they fear above all else, and that they despise the things most loved here for the sake of God, whom they love above all else.

Whoever, therefore, fears or loves anything more than God shows by this that he is not among the elect. Moreover, whoever prefers riches, honors, and pleasures to God loves them more than God, because he acts against God for their sake.

Of such a person the Lord himself says: “Whoever loves father or mother, or wife, or anything else, more than me, is not worthy of me” (Matt. X).

Therefore, brothers, let us think of ourselves as Paul thought of himself and of those like him. Let us burn with love for God; let us always recall the immense love that he has shown toward us; let us strive to follow his commandments; let us not be torn away from God by many bitterness and many pleasures, and let us always be most ready to lay down our lives for him, so that he himself may cause all things to work together for our good and enroll us among the number of his elect.

## IV. ON THE APOSTLES. SERMON ON JOHN

Jesus said to his disciples: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the cultivator” (John XV), and so forth.

This reading from the holy Gospel, dearest brothers, has three parts. First, Jesus metaphorically calls himself the vine, the Father the cultivator, and human beings the branches. Second, he shows that the branches must receive purification and bear fruit. Third, he makes clear what evil awaits the wicked branches and what good awaits the good.

First, then, he calls himself the vine when he says: “I am the true vine”—true in respect of likeness, not of kind. For the Lord Jesus is God and man. Inasmuch as he is God, he is one author and one cultivator with the Father—not one who merely performs the ministry, but one who also gives growth. For “neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God, who gives the growth” (I Cor. III).

But inasmuch as he is man, he calls himself the vine, because as man he is of one nature with us, just as the vine and the branch are of one nature. And just as a vine, although it appears to be a worthless little tree, nevertheless produces noble wine, so the Lord Jesus Christ, although he appeared contemptible in this world, according to the prophet’s saying, “We saw him without appearance or beauty, and therefore we did not esteem him” (Isa. LIII), nevertheless yields the noble fruit of teaching.

For just as wine by its nature is dry, hot, gladdening, and intoxicating, so the teaching of Christ’s Gospel dries up vices in us through warning, warms hearts through the fervor of charity, gladdens minds through the promise of heavenly rewards, and intoxicates and detaches us from love of the world toward love of heavenly things through contemplation.

The disciples of Christ were intoxicated with this new wine when, on the day of Pentecost, after setting aside all fear and earthly love, they “spoke in various tongues of the mighty works of God” (Acts II).

God the Father is called the cultivator by a certain likeness. For just as a cultivator chooses a vine, plants it in the earth, waters it, digs around it, and prunes it—cutting off unfruitful branches and cleansing fruitful ones—so God the Father chose his only Son beforehand, sent him into the earth through the incarnation, watered him with the dew of the Spirit, dug around him with the mattock of tribulations, and pruned him with the pruning knife of discernment: cutting off the unfruitful from him, such as Judas, but cleansing the fruitful so that they might bear more fruit, such as Peter and Andrew.

Hence the Son himself adds here: “Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he will take away. And the one that bears fruit, he will cleanse, so that it may bear more fruit.”

Human beings too are called branches when they ought, after the manner of branches, to cling to Christ through faith and bear the fruit of good works.

There are, however, three kinds of branches. One clings to Christ through faith and charity and bears fruit, like a good Christian, who must be cleansed more and more from every vice and excess so that he may bear more fruit.

Another clings to Christ through faith alone and participation in the sacraments but bears no fruit, like a false Christian. Like an unfruitful branch, lest he harm those who bear fruit, he must be separated from Christ by sentence—either here through excommunication or in the future through condemnation.

Another does not cling to Christ even through faith, but to a foreign vine, like the gentile, the Jew, and the other unbelievers. As the Lord says, they have already been judged (John III).

Moreover, the foreign vine is the devil. Hence the Lord says to the Jews: “My vineyard, how have you been changed into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” (Isa. V). And Moses says: “From the vine of Sodom is their vine, and from the outskirts of Gomorrah. Their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster is most bitter; the wine of dragons is their gall, and the venom of asps is incurable” (Deut. XXXII).

Second, the Lord shows from where the branches receive purification and fruitfulness when he adds: “Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you.”

It is as though he said: You are not clean because of yourselves, but because of my word. In this he shows that he is not only the vine but also the cultivator. To prune the vine is the work not of the vine but of the cultivator.

The disciples were therefore clean, but nevertheless still in need of cleansing. For who in this life can be so clean that he does not need to be cleansed more and more? If the disciples were not clean, they could not bear fruit; and if they did not still need cleansing, they would not say: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I).

They were therefore clean from mortal sins, but still needed to be cleansed from certain venial sins. Hence the Lord said to them: “The one who has bathed does not need except to wash his feet” (John XIII).

“Now you are clean,” he says, in large part, “because of the word that I have spoken to you,” not merely heard but also believed and carried out. An unbeliever hears, yet is not clean; the devil hears and believes, yet is not clean; the faithful person hears, believes, and carries out, and is clean.

But why did he not say, “You are clean because of baptism, repentance, and amendment”? Because the word of God draws us to all these things: it pierces us with remorse for repentance, makes us abandon vices and pursue virtues, and does so not only by sounding outwardly but also by inspiring inwardly and working invisibly.

For this is the one who alone baptizes, who alone absolves, who alone cleanses and illumines.

He shows from where the branches receive fruitfulness when he adds: “For just as a branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me.”

It is as though he said openly: You can bear fruit not from yourselves but from me.

The branch remains in the vine and the vine in the branch, but in different ways. The branch remains in the vine, contributing nothing to the vine but rather receiving vigor from the vine. The vine remains in the branch, receiving nothing from the branch but rather supplying it with strength.

Neither, therefore, contributes anything to the vine; the benefit is only for the branch. So too, when we remain in Christ, we contribute no benefit to him. When Christ remains in us through indwelling grace, no benefit accrues to him from this, but to us.

But since Christ’s remaining in us is the reason why we remain in Christ, why did he not put his own remaining first and say, “I remain in you; remain in me”? So that he might show us that we possess freedom of choice, and that his grace is ready to remain in us, never to abandon us unless we first abandon him.

It is therefore as though he said: Persevere in remaining in me, because I am always ready to remain perseveringly in you.

Behold, my brothers: he who ought to be asked asks us. He asks us to remain in him, whom we ought always to ask to remain in us.

Our Creator and Redeemer desires to have us as companions and intimates. Why, then, do we despise his friendship and familiarity? Why do we not embrace him with all our desires? Why do we not burn with love for him?

If some secular king or prince offered us his friendship, we would embrace it with great joy. Why, then, do we reject the King of heaven when he offers himself to us?

“The branch,” he says, “cannot bear fruit by itself.” Nor can a human being do good by himself. For just as vigor rises from the moisture of the vine, causing the branch to bud, leaf, and bear fruit, so grace proceeds from Christ into us, enabling us to will, speak, and do good.

“Neither can you,” he says—understand, do good works—“unless you remain in me.” Therefore Jews and gentiles, and all who do not remain in Christ through faith, cannot do good. “For without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI).

“I am the vine; you are the branches.” It is as though he said: I perform the nature of the vine; you too must perform the nature of the branch. I am the vine by supplying grace to you; you too must be branches by remaining in me and bearing fruit.

For if both you and I do what belongs to us, then much fruit will result. And this is what follows: “The one who remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit.”

It is more correct and more usual to say that the vine bears fruit than that the branch does. For the branch receives from the vine both what it possesses and what enables it to bear fruit.

Thus, since we receive everything from Christ—both what we are and whatever good we can do—it would be more accurate for him to say: “The one who remains in me, and I in him—I bear much fruit through him.”

But in his great mercy he attributes to us what is his own, saying that we do what he himself does through us. “For without me,” he says, “you can do nothing.”

I am everything for you; without me, you are nothing. For when unfruitful branches have been cut off, I can produce better ones from myself and bear fruit through them.

Therefore, my brothers, let us not hold the place and grace we have in Christ uselessly and idly, but let us diligently bear fruit, lest the supreme Cultivator cut us off as useless branches and produce others in our place.

Third, the Lord shows what evil awaits the wicked branches and what good awaits the good branches.

He shows what evil awaits the wicked when he adds: “If anyone does not remain in me”—understand, through faith, as the Jew, the pagan, and the other unbelievers, or through charity, as the false Christian—“he will be cast out like a branch.”

Here he is separated from the union of the faithful through rejection, and in the future from the kingdom of blessedness through condemnation. Then, according to another parable, when they say, “Lord, Lord, open to us” (Matt. XV), the reply will be made to them: “Amen I say to you, I do not know you” (ibid.).

And he will wither—not only from the power of doing good but also from the power of doing harm.

“And they will gather him,” he says. Who? The reaping angels, into bundles, according to the parable of the weeds (Matt. XIII): gluttons with gluttons, adulterers with adulterers, the greedy with the greedy, murderers with murderers, perjurers with perjurers, the proud with the proud, unbelievers with unbelievers—like with like—gathering them into similar punishments.

“And they will cast them into the fire,” he says. Of two things, one necessarily happens to a branch: either it clings to the vine or it is handed over to the fire. For it is useful neither for a building nor for any other purpose.

So there is no middle condition for a human being: either he will cling to Christ and bear fruit, or he will be cast into the fire, which does not require a supply of wood but burns continually of itself and eternally punishes souls together with bodies.

And he will burn like a useless branch, not so that he may perish entirely, but so that he may endure forever and burn forever. For there death will be immortal, the end without end, and failure without cessation. For according to the Apocalypse: “The wretched will desire to die, and death will flee from them” (Apoc. IX).

Ah, how much better it would be for them to die a thousand and a thousand times than to live forever in torments!

He shows what good awaits the good branches when he adds: “If you remain in me”—understand, through faith and charity—“and my words remain in you through good works, whatever you wish, you will ask, and it will be done for you,” in the other life, where all the elect’s desires will be fulfilled.

But even in this life, whatever we ask that pertains to our remaining in Christ and to the remaining of his words in us will undoubtedly be done for us.

Therefore, brothers, if we ask for something and it is not done for us, it is clear that it did not pertain to our remaining in Christ or to the remaining of his words in us. Let us therefore ask only for what pertains to the love of God and his commandments.

But behold: when we gather in church for prayer, one asks for food, another for clothing, another for a wife, another for other necessities. When these things are lacking, it is not a sin for us to ask the Lord for them with moderation.

But we must always heed Christ’s commandment: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Luke XII).

More seriously, however, one person calls down harm upon his neighbor and death upon his enemy, although God commands us to pray for our enemies and not to curse them (Matt. V).

Beware, brothers, lest you pray in this way against God’s commandment; and, according to the Psalmist, lest “our prayer become sin” (Ps. CVIII).

Matthew says: “When you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have in your hearts” (Matt. II). Those are especially able to obtain what they ask in prayer who not only retain no hatred in their hearts but can also pray purely for their enemies.

This is clear from the fact that when the Jews had provoked God, he forbade the prophet to pray for them, saying: “You shall not accept praise and offering for them” (Jer. XI). Again: “Even if Moses and Samuel were to stand before me, my soul would not be toward this people” (Jer. XV).

Why, passing over so many Fathers, does he mention these two alone, unless because these two alone in the whole sequence of the Old Testament are found to have prayed even for their enemies?

Moses is attacked by the people with stones, yet he prays for them (Exod. XVII). Samuel is excluded from leadership, yet he says: “Far be this sin from me, that I should cease to pray for you!” (I Reg. XII).

It is therefore as though he said: I do not even hear Moses and Samuel praying for them, although I know that by the merit of their charity they are especially powerful in prayer.

But often we force a reluctant mind to pray for enemies; we pray more from compulsion by the commandment than from charity, and yet we fear that our prayer may be heard. But what does duplicity of mind deserve before God except punishment?

Therefore, my brothers, when we consider how much our neighbor has sinned against us, let us also consider how much we have sinned against God. And just as we want God to forgive us, let us forgive our neighbor.

Let us be toward our debtors as we want God to be toward us. And if we cannot deliver our bodies to martyrdom, like those saints whose feast we celebrate, let us at least overcome our own spirit. This victory will not be without a crown before God.

May he himself grant us such victory and such a crown, to whom belong honor and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## V. ON THE APOSTLES. SERMON ON THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED PAUL

[Col. 1506C] “We have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing greatness may be the power of God and not from us” (II Cor. IV), and so forth.

There are three parts to this reading, my brothers. First, the Apostle says that he and the other disciples have a treasure in earthen vessels. Second, he gives the reason. Third, he explains what good the treasure confers upon earthen vessels.

First, then, he says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels.” He calls divine wisdom, preaching, and the virtues that the apostles carried within themselves a treasure. A treasure is a collection of precious things, such as gold, silver, and precious stones. The apostles likewise possessed within themselves things more precious than all these: a golden radiance, a silver resonance, and a variety of eloquence and precious things.

Concerning such a treasure it is written: “Its acquisition is better than trade in silver and gold; its first and purest fruits are better. It is more beautiful than all riches, and everything that is desired cannot compare with it” (Prov. III).

He calls himself and the other apostles earthen vessels. Earthen vessels are earthly and, among all kinds of vessels, the lowliest and most fragile. The apostles too, according to the world, were lowly and fragile: lowly because they were commoners, unknown, obscure, poor, uneducated; fragile because through prolonged mortification of the flesh they were emaciated, pale, and weak.

For this reason they were regarded by the world as rejected and contemptible. Hence the same Apostle says: “We have become as the refuse of this world, the scum of all things, even until now” (I Cor. IV).

[Col. 1507A] Because of their outward lowliness and fragility, the rich, wise, and noble of the world despised Christ’s disciples, failing to consider the spiritual treasure they carried within.

Some false Christians today are like them: they show partiality toward persons, despising the poor and obscure because of outward circumstances, while venerating the rich and noble because of outward circumstances. For often foul things lie hidden in a vessel gilded on the outside, and precious things in a vessel outwardly worthless.

Second, the Apostle gives the reason why God placed his treasure in earthen vessels when he adds: “so that the surpassing greatness may be the power of God and not from us.”

For this reason the Lord first willed the Gospel to be preached by unlearned and insignificant people, rather than by wise men and orators: to show that this was the work of God and not of human beings, and to demonstrate himself as wondrous both in the preaching and in the preachers.

The preaching is indeed wondrous: to preach that God became human, died, rose again, and was lifted to the right hand of God the Father. But it is more wondrous to have established so incredible a matter through a few insignificant and unlearned people.

Hence the Apostle says: “Look,” brothers, “at your calling”—that is, through whom you were called—“for not many are wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble. But God chose the foolish things of the world to confound”—that is, to put to shame—“the wise; and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong. God chose the things that are not”—that is, those not counted among the rest—“to destroy”—that is, to humble by conquering—“the things that are” (I Cor. I), that is, those that seemed to themselves to be something.

He would indeed at some time choose the learned, powerful, and noble. But he did not choose such people first, lest they seem to have been chosen on account of merit of that kind and, puffed up, fail to accept humility, without which no one can return to the life from which humanity fell through pride.

For this reason also Nathanael, learned in the Law, was not chosen as an apostle. And to show that this was done for the sake of humility, the same Apostle adds: “so that no flesh may glory in his presence on the basis of its merits” (ibid.).

Therefore, brothers, let us always think usefully about ourselves. Let us despise no one, however insignificant or contemptible, since often where we least expect it a greater treasure of divine grace is hidden, and those who are rejected among human beings are chosen by God.

And so that we may be worthy to possess so great a treasure, let us not shrink from being insignificant and despised by the world.

Third, the Apostle explains what the aforesaid treasure confers upon earthen vessels, whether here or in the future. He shows that the treasure of wisdom and the other graces bestows upon its possessors in this life strength for steadfastness and perseverance, and in the future eternal life.

He explains that it gives them strength for steadfastness and perseverance when he adds: “In all things we suffer tribulation, but are not distressed”—in mind, like certain fainthearted people who fail and despair in adversity—but rather we rejoice and are enlarged in the consciousness of the good treasure.

Then he lists certain forms of tribulation, saying: “We are reduced to poverty”—that is, deprived even of necessities, we become poor—“but are not abandoned,” even in inward steadfastness, like some who, because of poverty, become liars, perjurers, murderers, and thieves. Rather, from the abundance of the inner treasure we are sufficient for ourselves, knowing equally “how to abound and how to suffer need” (Phil. IV).

“We suffer persecution,” whether hidden persecution from the devil or open persecution from his members, “but are not abandoned”—that is, abandoned by the steadfastness of the inner treasure, like some who succumb in persecution—but rather we overcome our persecutors, either by resisting or by enduring them calmly.

“We are humbled,” he says, “but are not put to shame”: in our adversity we are considered insignificant, yet we are not ashamed, like those who are ashamed to bear humility, poverty, and the cross of Jesus Christ.

To such people he himself says: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his majesty” (Luke IX).

Rather, from the inner treasure of a good conscience, let us glory in our very insignificance and contempt, saying with the Apostle: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI).

“We are cast down,” he says, “but do not perish.” It is as though he said: We are cast down like a useless piece of pottery in the shattering of death, but since the immortal treasure remains in us, we do not perish through eternal death like the reprobate. Rather, we then begin to live eternally, when death becomes our birth.

Therefore, brothers, let us acquire, retain, and preserve this most precious treasure of wisdom and the other virtues with our whole desire, so that through it we may be worthy to have joy in tribulation, sufficiency in poverty, victory in persecution, glory in humility, and life in death.

“Always carrying,” he says, “the mortification of Jesus in our body.”

Then, my brothers, we carry the mortification of Jesus in our body when, for Jesus and in imitation of his crucifixion, we crucify and mortify our vices.

We must carry this mortification not in only one part of the body, like those who crucify their loins but not their tongue, eyes, or ears, but throughout our body: so that our heart may likewise be mortified, lest it meditate evil; our tongue, lest it speak evil; our hand, lest it act wrongly; our foot, lest it walk wrongly; our sense of taste, lest it desire delicacies; our sense of touch, lest it desire lustful things; our ears, lest they hear vanity and wickedness; and our eyes, lest they see vanity.

And for what benefit? “So that the life of Jesus,” he says, “may be manifested in your bodies.”

This is what John says: “Beloved, now we are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know, however, that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III).

There are two lives of Jesus Christ, brothers: the life of virtue, which he displayed in this world, and the life of glorification, which he will display and give in the future.

The life of the virtue of Jesus Christ is manifested in us even in this age, if we are clean as he is clean, just as he is just, and holy as he is holy.

But the life of glorification will be manifested in the future not only in our souls but also in our bodies: when we are immortal as he is immortal, beautiful as he is beautiful, glorious as he is glorious, and blessed as he is blessed.

May he himself grant this to us through the merits and intercession of his holy apostles, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## VI. ON THE APOSTLES. SERMON ON LUKE
“Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves” [Col. 1509B] (Matt. 10), and so forth.

In this reading of the holy Gospel, dearly beloved brothers, our Lord and Redeemer instructs his disciples beforehand—those whom he was about to send to preach throughout the whole world. In this he likewise instructs us preachers, who hold their place in the Church. He therefore does four things. First, he appoints them apostles. Second, he explains where he is sending them. Third, he shows what sort of people they must be. Fourth, he prepares them in advance for the persecutions that will come.

First, he appoints them apostles when he says: “Behold, I send you.” It is as though he were saying plainly: “I, your Lord and teacher, appoint you, sent out from being disciples, as my apostles.” For *apostle* means “one who is sent.” In this he shows them three things: who is sending them, from whom they are taken, and what he appoints them to be.

Who is sending them? “I, your Lord and teacher, send you”; you do not presume to undertake the apostolate by your own authority. Hence the Apostle says: “How will they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. 10). And again: “No one takes this honor upon himself, but only the one who is called by God, as Aaron was” (Heb. 5). This plainly condemns those who, without being called, seize the pastoral office rather than attain it. Of such people the Lord says through the prophet: “They themselves have reigned, and not through me; they have become princes, and I did not know them” (Hos. 8). For the inner judge both advances and does not know: those whom he tolerates by permitting them, he does not know through rejection.

From whom are they taken? “From disciples I appoint you apostles.” It is as though he were saying: “You alone, who have learned and keep my life and teaching, are worthy of the apostolate and of teaching.” In this he confounds those who presume to become teachers before they have learned to be disciples, who presume to teach a life which they neither possess nor have learned. To them the Lord says through the Psalmist: “Why do you recount my ordinances and take my covenant upon your lips? Yet you hate discipline and cast my words behind you” (Ps. 49).

What does he appoint them to be? “I appoint you as my apostles,” namely, so that you who have learned and keep my life and teaching may also hold my place in the Church. Hence elsewhere he says to them: “Whoever hears you hears me; whoever receives you receives me; whoever despises you despises me” (Matt. 10; Luke 10).

The disciples and their successors hold Christ’s place in three matters: in preaching, in the administration of the sacraments, and in the power of binding and loosing. But they must observe that in all these things they are not originators but vicars, not lords but those who have been sent. They preach outwardly, but Christ teaches inwardly. They wash only outwardly, but Christ baptizes inwardly. They raise their hands outwardly, but the Lord blesses and consecrates. They pronounce the sentence outwardly, but Christ inwardly absolves and binds. Hence the Apostle says: “Let a person regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of God’s mysteries” (1 Cor. 4).

Moreover, the one who has been faithfully sent and is Christ’s vicar is the person who conforms himself to Christ’s ways; who proclaims not his own words but Christ’s; who seeks not his own glory but Christ’s.

Second, he explains where he is sending the disciples when he says: “As sheep in the midst of wolves.” It is as though he were saying plainly: “I send you not to security but to danger, not to domination but to submission, not to glory but to suffering.” In this those people are refuted who seek the pastoral office in order to live in security, domination, and glory, paying no attention either to what is said here or to what the Lord says elsewhere: “As the Father sent me, so I send you” (John 20). That is: “As the Father sent me to humility, poverty, and suffering, so I send you to the same.”

Thus he shows that he has not been sent by God who seeks domination, riches, and glory in a place of humility. By the name “wolves” he designates demons and demonically minded people, who, like wolves, lie in wait for Christ’s sheep, inflict evil upon them, rage against them, and devour them. Against their malice, good Christians persevere in the manner of sheep—kind, gentle, and most patient.

But since persecutors attack not only Christ’s sheep outwardly, but also, like wolves attacking the throat and vital organs, seek to cut off the voice of preaching and confession and extinguish the spirit within them, they need not only knowledge but also wisdom and vigilance. Therefore, in the third place, he shows what they must be like against this danger when he adds: “So be wise as serpents.”

Certainly, the serpent’s wisdom consists in guarding above all else its head, in which its life resides. For the sake of its head it disregards its whole body and sets it like a shield against the blows of the attacker, in order to preserve its head. The wisdom of the serpent must indeed be imitated not only by pastors but also by all the faithful, so that we may guard above all else the faith of Jesus Christ, who is our head, without which there is no salvation for us. For the sake of confessing and preserving it, we must expose not only our possessions but also our bodies to death.

There is another form of the serpent’s cunning: while fasting and constricting itself through narrow spaces, it sheds its old skin. We too must imitate this wisdom, mortifying our flesh, constricting ourselves through the narrow gate of God’s commandments, stripping off the old person with his vices and desires, and putting on the new person, who is renewed day by day (Col. 3).

But because the serpent is a venomous beast and possesses cunning for doing harm, lest anyone wish also to imitate that cunning, after saying, “Be wise as serpents,” he immediately adds, “and innocent as doves.” It is as though he were saying plainly: “Be wise as serpents, so that you are not deceived by the idols of others; and innocent as doves, so that you yourselves do not deceive others.”

Neither wisdom without innocence nor innocence without wisdom is beneficial. Wisdom without innocence is wicked cunning, while innocence without wisdom is foolish dullness.
