Therefore, my brothers, let us possess both innocent wisdom and wise innocence, so that we may know how to avoid evil and not commit it, and may know and do what is good.

The innocence of the dove is free from the malice of gall—behold, gentleness. It harms no one with beak or claws—behold, innocence. It shelters the young of others as though they were its own—behold, charity. Let us therefore, my brothers, be innocent as doves, so that we become angry with no one and harm no one.

Fourth, he prepares his disciples in advance for the persecutions that will come when he adds: “But beware of people”—that is, of those who, by flattery, promises, or threats, will seek to deceive you or separate you from the faith. You must wisely beware of them, either by avoiding them or by resisting their deceptions firmly.

“For they will hand you over,” he says, “to councils”—that is, to the place where the decision is made as to which sentence should be accepted. There, by common agreement, they will forbid you to preach in my name, so that you may be overcome by a general council and decree. And if you act contrary to this, “in their synagogues,” where correction takes place, “they will scourge you,” so that you may be overwhelmed by shame.

If you still do not consent to them, then, since they cannot themselves inflict violence upon you, “you will be led before kings and governors,” as though before a higher court, “because of me,” so that at least fear of a greater authority may frighten you. But although you are few, neither a general council, nor public shame, nor fear of a greater authority will overcome your steadfastness. You will confess my name publicly.

“For a testimony,” he says, “to them and to the nations”—that is, your testimony will be a witness to all who hear it, either of salvation, if they believe, or of condemnation, if they do not believe.

Now also, my brothers, when we least preachers proclaim the words of God by bearing witness to you, we are a testimony to you—either of salvation, if you believe and obey, or, God forbid, of condemnation, if you do not wish to obey.

Against these aforementioned terrors the Lord adds consolation when he says: “When they hand you over, do not worry about how or what you are to speak”—that is, do not worry either about finding an answer or about embellishing it. Why? “For what you are to say will be given you at that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you,” as in instruments.

For he is the one “who opens the mouth of the mute and makes the tongues of infants eloquent” (Wis. 10). How, my brothers, do you suppose that blessed Catherine, certainly a simple girl, could argue so cleverly against a tyrant and against fifty accomplished sages and overcome them, unless the Holy Spirit spoke in her and through her? How could blessed Agnes, while she was still only twelve years old, speak so wonderfully against the wise men and judges of this world, unless the Holy Spirit spoke in her and through her? How could the child Quiricus, while he was still only three years old, argue so wonderfully for the faith of Christ against a tyrant?

Then the Lord prepares his disciples in advance for a greater persecution when he adds: “Brother will hand brother over to death,” and so forth. The evils inflicted by outsiders cause lesser pain; those we suffer from people whose affection we trusted cause greater pain. Hence it is written: “If my enemy had cursed me, I could surely have endured it. But you—a man of one mind with me, my guide and my acquaintance” (Ps. 54).

“Brother,” he says, “will hand brother over to death, and children will rise against their parents and put them to death.” All these things, my brothers, were happening in the primitive Church, when the devil, raging because of his expulsion, had so inflamed the fury of the persecutors that the fervor of idolatry overcame natural affection. They hated and persecuted even their children and friends—those whom human beings ordinarily love by the force of nature—and did so both against nature and against God.

Even today there are some like them. They have become so drunk on the cup of Babylon—that is, worldly greed—that they hate and persecute their brothers and parents for the sake of temporal inheritances. Parents too persecute their own children, not physically, perhaps, but in what is worse, spiritually, when, in the manner of ravens, they feed them on plunder and deceit and instruct them to do the same. Thus they are also held responsible if their children commit the evils they have seen their parents commit, and if the children rise against those very parents whom they have seen rising against their own parents.

“And you will be hated by all,” he says—understand, by unbelievers—“because of my name.”

Then he adds consolation against this when he says: “But whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.” It is as though he were saying: “Those who suffer these things for my sake will be saved, provided that they persevere.” For just as endurance and its cause are necessary, so perseverance is also necessary. It is not beginning to do good but completing it that is praiseworthy. Hence even in the Law Moses commands that the tail of the sacrificial victim be offered (Lev. 7).

Therefore, brothers, since we know that countless people, even infants, persevered in the faith through torments and sufferings, let us at least persevere in prosperity. Let us be ashamed that we bearded men cannot do in peace what those infants did even amid persecution. Torments did not overcome them; at least let blandishments not overcome us. Hunger did not overcome them; at least let gluttony not overcome us. Hardship did not overcome them; at least let pleasure not overcome us. Need did not overcome them; at least let abundance not overcome us.

And if there is no outsider to torture, crucify, and kill us, at least let us crucify and torture ourselves through abstinence and continence, putting ourselves to death together with our vices and desires, so that, with those martyrs interceding for us, we may deserve to be their companions in heaven, by the generosity of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever.

Amen.

## VII. On the Apostles. Sermon on the Apocalypse

“I, John, saw in the right hand of the one seated upon the throne a book written within and without, sealed with seven seals” (Rev. 5).

These words are spoken, my brothers, by John the apostle and evangelist, to whom we must all the more believe because he drank not from another source but from the fountain itself.

He tells us four things: in whose hand Holy Scripture rests; how greatly its understanding is to be desired; by whom it is opened; and what praise follows from this upon the one who opens it.

In whose hand Holy Scripture rests he first shows when he says: “I saw in the right hand of the one seated upon the throne a book.” Since God, my brothers, is without limits and is infinite spirit, he neither sits nor possesses bodily members. But we can be instructed concerning an invisible reality more effectively through the likenesses of visible things.

A throne is the seat of kings. To sit upon a throne, therefore, signifies the peaceful rule of one who reigns. And who reigns more perfectly than the one who created and governs all things? Who rules everything more peacefully than the one whose willing is doing, and whose “wisdom reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly”? (Wis. 8.)

Although he is essentially everywhere, he dwells especially in the hearts of the faithful. In whom does he dwell if not in those whom he himself loves, who love him, and who are like him? Thus the pure one dwells in the pure, the just one in the just, the holy one in the holy, and the friend in friends.

In the right hand of this supreme King—that is, in his power—the book of Holy Scripture is held, since it is produced, written, fulfilled, and revealed through his inspiration and authority.

This plainly stands against those who think that Holy Scripture is nothing other than a human invention and composition, paying no attention to what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke will pass from the Law until all things have happened” (Matt. 24; Mark 13). And Peter says in his canonical Epistle: “Prophecy was not brought forth by human will, but holy men of God spoke as they were inspired by the Holy Spirit” (2 Pet. 1).

Moreover, in the fact that the book of Holy Scripture is written within and without, an exterior reading of history and an interior reading of spiritual understanding are signified. In this, those who seek only the surface of the letter in Holy Scripture—like the reclining Jews—and those who refer nothing to the literal meaning but turn everything toward mystical meaning—like certain presumptuous people who are wiser than is proper—are alike confounded.

Some things in Holy Scripture are to be understood literally alone, such as: “You shall love the Lord your God” (Exod. 20), and “Honor your father and your mother” (ibid.), along with the other moral commandments. Some things, however, are to be referred only to the mystical meaning, such as what is read in Job: “Under him those who carry the world are bowed down” (Job 9). Some things must be understood both literally and mystically, such as the Lord’s command that a male be circumcised on the eighth day (Gen. 17), and that a lamb be sacrificed at Passover (Exod. 12), along with the other figurative commandments.

In the fact that the book is described as sealed with seven seals, it is signified that Holy Scripture is closed and, by seven—that is, by the totality of every kind of obscurity—generally enveloped. It also conceals within itself seven mysteries in particular, which the same John subsequently explains, while nevertheless leaving them sealed.

Hence it is also said to Daniel through the angel: “And you, Daniel, close up the words and seal the book until the appointed time” (Dan. 12). Hence Isaiah also says to the Jews: “The vision of all the prophets will be for you like the words of a sealed book, which, when they give it to one who knows letters, they will say, ‘Read this’; and he will answer, ‘I cannot, for it is sealed’” (Isa. 29).

This plainly stands against certain secular philosophers who think that Holy Scripture is plain and open because outwardly it has simple and straightforward words. They do not perceive that in Holy Scripture, beneath the simplicity of its words, a great and useful depth lies hidden. Conversely, in books of secular learning, beneath the multiplicity and obscurity of words, no usefulness lies hidden.

The Lord sealed his mysteries in Scripture for three reasons.

The first is that he wished them to be hidden from his enemies and disclosed only to his friends and intimates. Hence he appropriately says that the book is sealed with seven seals. We seal what we wish to reveal only to our friends. Hence the Gospel says: “Do not give what is holy to dogs” (Matt. 7).

The second is that he wished us to exercise ourselves and gain merit in the depth of Scripture. Thus, when the angel had said to Daniel, “Close up the word and seal the book,” he added: “Many will pass through, and knowledge will be multiplied” (Dan. 12). Hence Solomon says: “It is the glory of God to conceal a word, and the glory of a king to investigate a matter” (Prov. 25).

The third is that, just as he reserved the publication of Holy Scripture to his own name, so too he reserved its revelation to himself, lest anyone boast of human ingenuity in understanding it, but instead seek divine assistance for understanding it.

How greatly the understanding of Holy Scripture is to be desired is shown when it is added: “And I saw,” he says, “a strong angel proclaiming with a loud voice: Who is worthy to open the book and loose its seals?”

This angel, my brothers, represents any one of the ancient Fathers who, although strong in virtue and wisdom, nevertheless, because of his great desire for and delay in the opening of Holy Scripture, laments and asks who is so worthy, so wise, and so powerful that he can open it.

But we already know who that one is. Therefore, with all our desire and all our strength, let us implore him to deem it worthy to open for us the seals of his Holy Scripture.

“And no one,” he says, “could open the book, either in heaven, or on earth, or under the earth, or look upon it.” For no one was found among the angels, human beings, souls separated from bodies, or even demons who could perfectly understand the mysteries of Holy Scripture.

Hence it is clear that neither the prophets and writers of Holy Scripture nor the angels themselves fully understood the mysteries they proclaimed. In this certain foolish and presumptuous people are condemned: they boast that they have grasped the understanding of Holy Scripture, and by doing so they make those who understand fail to understand.

“And I,” he says, “wept greatly, because no one was found worthy to open the book or to look upon it.” Here John clearly indicates that he represents the ancient Fathers, who either did not understand the opening of Holy Scripture through Christ or grieved that it had been delayed.

Hence the Lord says:

“Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Luke 10).

Consider Daniel, who says that he wept, fasted, and prayed for a long time so that he might deserve to have the mysteries of the vision revealed to him. In this our negligence is confounded, brothers: we neither understand Holy Scripture as we ought nor ask the Lord for its understanding with weeping, fasting, and prayer, as the ancient Fathers are said to have done, because we devote ourselves to vain and perishable things.

By whom the book of Scripture is opened is explained when it is added: “And one of the elders said to me: Do not weep.” He represents any one of the ancient prophets who, by announcing Christ’s coming, consoles others.

“Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he may open the book and loose its seven seals.”

He calls Christ the Lion of the tribe of Judah in order to indicate that he is the one of whom Jacob foretold: “A lion’s cub is Judah” (Gen. 49). For he is like a lion, a strong king, with the tail of humanity concealing the traces of divinity, sleeping in death with the eyes of his divinity open.

He calls him the Root of David to show that he is the one who, according to Isaiah, “has the key of David; he closes and no one opens, he opens and no one closes” (Isa. 22). It is therefore as though he were saying: By conquering the difficulties of the devil and death, Christ opens the obscurities of Holy Scripture.

“And I saw,” he says, “and behold, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth.”

The throne signifies the Church, because God sits in it through charity. The four living creatures signify the preachers of all four quarters of the world, who ought to be rational and gentle like a human being, to strike adversities fearlessly like a lion, to mortify themselves like a calf, and to seek heavenly things like an eagle.

The twenty-four elders signify the more perfect Fathers of both the Old and the New Law. Like senators, they are mature in conduct, full of wisdom, and honored with the power of judgment.

Among all these Christ is in the midst: in benefit, like a fountain in the middle of paradise; in charity, as he himself says, “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. 18); and in assistance, as he likewise says, “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28).

Hence here too he says that he saw him standing: “a Lamb,” he says, “as though slain.” A Lamb because he is innocent and gentle, and because he was prefigured in the lamb; like a lamb sacrificed, like one slain in his humanity but always living in his divinity; like one slain in the eyes of the Jews but always living for us; like one slain in the daily sacrament but always living in heaven.

“Having,” he says, “seven horns and seven eyes.” By the seven horns and seven eyes the same totality of the gifts of the Holy Spirit is signified. The gifts of the Holy Spirit are horns—that is, virtues—by which the adversary is defeated. They are also eyes—that is, illuminations—by which the mind is enlightened.

Our Redeemer possesses these not in measure but universally, and throughout the whole world he gives them to whom he wills, when he wills, and as much as he wills.

“And he took,” he says, “the book from the right hand of the one seated.” Insofar as he is human, he received what, insofar as he is God, he has always possessed.

“And when he had opened the book.” My brothers, Christ is said to have opened the book of Holy Scripture in three ways: either by fulfilling in himself the figures of the Law—hence at his death “the veil of the temple was torn” (Matt. 27; Mark 15); or by explaining the Scriptures—hence, to the two going to Emmaus, “beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them the Scriptures” (Luke 24); or by giving his disciples the sense by which the Scriptures are to be understood.

He did this after the Resurrection, and he still does it for us every day, if we ask, if we seek, if we knock, if, with Daniel, we are men of desire, and if, following the example of John and Daniel, we persist with weeping, fasting, and prayer.

For those who are negligent and seek carnal rather than spiritual things, the book of Holy Scripture remains sealed. Even when they wish for it and read it, a veil still lies before their eyes, as it did before the Jews.

How great a praise follows Christ from the opening of the book is shown when choirs both of holy human beings and of angels are brought forward to praise him on this account. Hence it is added:

“The four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down”—that is, worshiped—“before the Lamb” through faith, “each having a harp” through confession, “and bowls full of fragrances” through prayer.

Then he explains: “which are the prayers of the saints.” Through faith we know God to be Christ; through confession, as through the harmony of a harp, we praise him; through the devotion of prayer, as through fragrances, we delight him.

Because people are especially delighted by harmonies and fragrances, the saints are here described as having harps and bowls full of fragrances, so that it may be shown how greatly God is revealed in their confession and devotion.

He rightly says that they “fell before the Lamb.” For whoever worships Christ through faith, understanding his majesty to be incomprehensible, regards himself as nothing but earth.

He also rightly says that they had harps. In a harp there are wood and strings. By the wood the cross or mortification is signified. By the strings the members of the saints are signified, twisted and stretched by the mortification of the cross. Whenever a persecutor strikes any one of them, he hears a harmonious confession.

But even when persecution ceases, the saints compel all their members and virtues to resound in the praise of God.

He also rightly says that they had “golden bowls full of fragrances.” The bowls, which are broad vessels, signify the hearts of the saints, enlarged through charity even toward their enemies. They are golden—that is, pure—and full of the fragrances of devotion.

For prayers that proceed from a charitable, pure, and devout heart rise to God like incense and fragrances. It is rightly followed that after worship comes confession, and after confession comes the prayer of charity and a pure heart, because neither faith without confession—especially where confession is necessary—nor both together without charity and purity of heart can please God.

“And they sang,” he says, “a new song,” because, renewed by the newness of the mystery, they praised together the new person.

“Worthy are you,” they say, “Lord, to open the book and to loose its seals.” Why? “Because you were slain and redeemed us for God by your blood.”

It is as though they were saying: By being slain and redeeming us, you opened Holy Scripture, gathering us from every tribe and language and people and nation.

“And you made us a kingdom and priests for our God.” All of us, my brothers, if we are true Christians, are spiritually kings and priests for our God.

We are kings for our God if we rule all the movements of our heart and body well for his service, restraining what is evil, nourishing what is good, and observing justice and peace.

We are priests for our God if each day on the altar of our heart we offer him the sacrifice of a contrite heart and the incense of devoted prayer; if through purity we are intimate with him; and if we are able to act as mediators between him and human beings.

“And we shall reign,” he says, “upon the earth.” It is as though he were saying: Only those will reign forever in the land of the living who here have subjected to themselves every earthly attachment and every vanity.

Therefore, let us be vigilant in governing our household; let us carefully examine the movements of our heart and body; let us immediately restrain evil impulses as they arise; let us compel the flesh and all our members to serve the spirit; and let us subject to ourselves the worldly enticements that rule worldly people, so that we may deserve to attain the kingdom of eternal blessedness, by the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever.

Amen.

## VIII. On the Apostles. Sermon on Matthew

“Jesus sent his disciples, commanding them and saying” (Matt. 10), and so forth.

This reading, my brothers, has five parts. First, the Lord sends the Twelve. Second, where they must go or not go. Third, what they must preach. Fourth, what they must do. Fifth, how this becomes known.

First, the passage shows that the Lord sent the Twelve when it says: “Jesus sent his twelve disciples.” In the reading preceding this one, the evangelist shows that the Lord chose twelve from the common company of the disciples, and he gives their names. Then he adds what we have now heard: “Jesus sent these twelve,” and so forth.

In this, my brothers, four things are signified for our understanding: that the apostles were chosen, from where they were chosen, how many were chosen, and for what they were chosen.

In the fact that the apostles were chosen by the Lord, an example is given to us: pastors ought to be chosen in the Church of God, with the Lord consulted through fasts and prayers. Those who are not chosen but thrust themselves forward are likewise condemned, as are those who are chosen not divinely but in a worldly manner.

In the fact that they were chosen from the common school of the elect, it is shown that neither neophytes nor inexperienced people, but those who have been more thoroughly trained than others in the school of holy virtues and conduct, ought to be chosen as pastors, so that they may be not only chosen but also pre-eminent among the chosen pastors.

This plainly condemns those who presume to become teachers before they have become disciples, teaching what they have not learned, and seeking to exercise authority over those who surpass them in both conduct and knowledge.

In the fact that twelve are chosen, the degree of perfection required of the pastors of Holy Church is shown to us. The number twelve is a perfect number, and hence is called *solidus*, “whole” or “solid.” Pastors of Holy Church ought to be so perfect and solid that they yield neither to prosperity nor adversity, neither to blandishments nor hardships, neither to favors nor threats; rather, they should be able to sustain the weak and those who are falling.

In this we unworthy pastors are confounded: adversity frightens us, blandishments caress us, threats from the powerful cast us down, favors lift us up; we are driven here and there like a reed; we do not rebuke the vices of the powerful but flatter them; we do not dare to exercise justice; and we are unable to sustain either the weak or even ourselves.

In the fact that they are sent, what they were chosen for is shown. For *apostle* means “one who is sent.” Let the pastors of Holy Church therefore understand that they are sent, not lords; sent for humility, not exaltation; sent not to be served but to serve (Luke 10); sent not to honor and glory but to labor and suffering.

Hence he says to them in what follows: “Behold, I send you as lambs among wolves.” Bishops will then understand that they have truly been sent by Christ when they display in themselves Christ’s humility, poverty, patience, and the other virtues of Christ; when they preach not their own words but Christ’s; when they seek not their own glory but Christ’s in all things; and when they offer not only what they possess but also themselves for their brothers.

Second, the Lord shows where they must or must not go when he says to them: “Do not go by the road of the nations, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans, but go rather to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel.”

Since it is clear that the Lord came for the salvation of the nations—for elsewhere he himself says, “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and there will be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10)—what does he mean here by saying, “Do not go by the road of the nations, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans,” unless we infer from the outcome of the deed that he first came especially to the Jews, to whom he had been promised, and, rejected by them through unbelief, passed over to outsiders?

For three reasons, then, the Lord wished to preach first to the Jews and not to the nations.

First, to show that he was the Messiah promised to the Jews in the Law.

Second, to remove from the Jews every excuse for not receiving the Gospel, if he had preached it first to the nations.

Third, because at that time there were among the Jews people who were to be saved, and among the nations people who were not to be saved. For at Peter’s preaching three thousand believed in one day (Acts 2), and another five thousand on another day (Acts 4); and when the apostles wished to preach in Asia, they were prevented by the Holy Spirit (Acts 16).

Yet afterward the Holy Spirit converted that same Asia through the apostles. For Asia has long since believed.

Thus, by a subtle and hidden judgment, preaching is withdrawn from certain people because they do not deserve to be raised up by grace.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, it is necessary for us to fear God’s hidden judgments in everything we do, lest, while our mind, poured out externally, does not withdraw from its own will, the Judge within may terribly decree against it. The Psalmist, observing this well, says: “Come and see the works of the Lord, how terrible he is in his counsels concerning the sons of men” (Ps. 65). For he saw that one person is mercifully called, while another is secretly rejected by justice; and because God arranges one thing by sparing and another by anger, he was terrified at what he could not penetrate. And because he saw that God’s judgment was not only unsearchable but also, in some cases, inflexible, he remembered that it was terrible.

[Col. 1519C] In a moral sense, he commanded the pastors of holy Church not to go along the way of the Gentiles—that is, not to follow the errors and affairs of worldly people—and not to enter the cities of the Samaritans, that is, not to enter into the turmoil of anxieties and cares, but rather to go to the sheep that had perished of the house of Israel, that is, to restore ruined souls. For the Lord wishes the preachers and pastors of holy Church to flee not only the errors and public affairs of secular life, but also every other anxiety and care, so that they may devote themselves continually to the restoration of souls alone. This openly rebukes us unworthy pastors, who, while attending to secular business and being occupied with various and empty cares, do not watch over the welfare either of ourselves or of those entrusted to us, as we ought.

[Col. 1519D] Third, the Lord shows what they should preach when he adds: “But as you go, preach.” It is as though he were plainly saying: “Be so active and attentive to preaching that you preach even as you go, and go while preaching, so that neither the journey hinders preaching nor preaching the journey”; that is, preach not only in villages but also on roads, not only to crowds but also to individuals, not only to citizens but also to foreigners, farmers, and travelers. In this we unworthy pastors are confuted: we are slow and lazy in preaching; we wait for the day, the place, and an assembly of people, and when we have only a few hearers, we disdain to preach. We do not consider that it is better to gain one soul for God than none, and that we lose all the time in which we are not occupied with the gain of souls.

[Col. 1520A] Nor do we regard the Lord’s example. He did not neglect to preach to the Samaritan woman alone on the road beside the well; rather, he showed that he did not neglect her salvation but was himself her salvation, when he said to his disciples: “I have food to eat of which you do not know” (John 4). “The kingdom of heaven has drawn near,” he says.

All the preaching of the Gospel, my brothers, concerns the end of the world and the blessedness of the eternal kingdom. The Lord preached this; the apostles preached it; the holy martyrs and confessors preached it. We preachers preach it—but would that we did so in our actions as well as with our voices! [Col. 1520B] By our actions we preach the end of the world and the coming of the kingdom of heaven if we despise the world and its enticements; if we reject its riches, honors, glories, and pleasures; if with our whole desire we hasten toward another life; if for its sake we do whatever we can [do]. But—and I cannot say this without tears—we act in the opposite way. While we embrace and pursue the world and its desires, and neglect to labor for the kingdom of heaven, we oppose our preaching by our actions.

In this we scandalize the weak, who, observing our actions, say: “If a priest or bishop were awaiting the kingdom of heaven, he would certainly not cling so closely to the world and worldly desires.” Thus, led astray by our bad example, they do not await the kingdom of heaven but cling to the world, which they suppose will last forever. [Col. 1520C] Yet surely the world’s own ruin accuses both us and them: though we are silent, it already cries out that it is about to fall and shows that another kingdom is coming. For the world has become so embittered by so many and such great miseries and tribulations that, through its bitterness, it even drives its own lovers away from itself.

Therefore, brothers, because we see the world falling, let us flee it, lest we fall together with what is falling. Let us withdraw as quickly as possible from the world’s ruin, draw out from it as many as we can, and send them ahead to purchase the kingdom of heaven.

[Col. 1520D] Fourth, he shows what they should do when he adds: “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons.” Since at that time the world was still flourishing, human beings lived long, the abundance of visible goods overflowed, and it drew people to itself so that they thought there were no other goods except those they saw, miracles were added to the holy preachers, so that displayed power might give credibility to their words. Those who preached new things were to do new things, so that, through the miracles they performed in visible matters, people might believe them concerning invisible things. For miracles flash forth for this purpose: to draw the hearts of those who see them to faith in invisible realities.

Hence, since faith has now been spread almost everywhere, there are many in the Church who possess the life of virtue but do not possess signs of virtue. For, as Paul testifies, tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers. Thus the same Paul who, through his preaching, raised Eutychus—who had fallen asleep, fallen from his window, and died—before unbelievers (Acts 20), and who healed Publius’s father, afflicted with dysentery, on the island of Malta, full of unbelievers (Acts 28), does not heal his sick disciple Timothy by a word, but prepares to treat him by medical means, saying: “Use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses” (1 Tim. 5).

[Col. 1521A] Why, then, does he not heal the believer by a word as he did the unbeliever? Only because the one was to be healed inwardly through an outward cure, while the other, who was living healthfully within, did not need to be instructed by an outward sign.

Therefore, my brothers, since the faithful now do not need outward signs, let us devote ourselves to the inward healing of souls. Let us heal and strengthen the sick in faith through instruction and admonition. Let us raise the dead in sins through correction and spiritual counsel. Let us cleanse lepers—those infected by the variety of heresies and errors—with faithful teaching. Let us free those tormented by the suggestions of the devil through priestly ministry.

[Col. 1521B] Fifth, he shows how these things should be done when he adds: “You received without payment; give without payment.” For the Lord foresaw that some would turn the gift of the Holy Spirit toward avarice. Thus Simon, desiring the miracles performed through the laying on of hands, wanted to buy this power with money, so that he might sell at a worse price what he had wrongly acquired (Acts 8). For this reason the Lord drove the crowds from the Temple with a whip made of cords and overturned the seats of those selling doves (Matt. 21). To sell doves, then, is to bestow the laying on of hands by which the Holy Spirit is received, not for the merit of life but for payment.

[Col. 1521C] There are also some who, even if they do not confer ordination or some other ecclesiastical ministry, nevertheless confer it for money, or for service, or for favor, or because of kinship, or familiarity, or persistent entreaty, or fear of powerful people, or some other earthly motive. All these, without doubt, give neither freely nor justly, because in giving they regard not God but an earthly cause. Concerning them the Psalmist says: “In whose hands are iniquities; their right hand is filled with gifts” (Ps. 25). And Isaiah, describing the blessed man, says: “Blessed is he who shakes his hands free from every gift” (Isa. 33).

[Col. 1521D] Therefore, only he gives freely and justly who gives for God alone and to one who is worthy. Let us accordingly, my brothers, examine and survey our entire life. Let us beware of doing evil in any way, and also of doing good with a vain intention. Let us direct the intention of all our desires and actions toward God. Let us cut away all vanity from ourselves. Let us despise the world with its desires. Let us live content with little. Whatever we can, let us transfer from the ruin of this world to our heavenly homeland through the hands of the poor. Let us sigh and strive toward that homeland with our whole desire and all our strength.

May the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit grant this to us.

## COMMON OF MARTYRS. IX. ONE MARTYR. SERMON

“Consider it all joy, my brothers, whenever you fall into various trials” [Col. 1522A] (James 1), etc.

This reading, my brothers, has four parts. First, the Apostle urges us to rejoice in our tribulations. Second, he urges us to ask wisdom from God. Third, he promises exaltation to the humble and humiliation to the rich. Fourth, he shows that blessed is the person who possesses patience.

First, then, because many of us, my brothers, grieve excessively in adversity, collapse, and despair, the Apostle exhorts us not to grieve in adversity but rather to rejoice, saying: “Consider it all joy, my brothers, whenever you fall into various trials.” He calls the adversities and tribulations of this world trials because through them we are tested to see whether we are strong or weak. He calls them various because, just as there is a variety of remedies corresponding to the variety of bodily members, so, corresponding to the variety of dispositions, the supreme Physician applies a variety of tribulations.

[Col. 1522B] Because some sin through excessive love and use of temporal things, they are therefore justly punished by the loss of those things. Because others sin through excessive love of spouses, children, and friends, they are therefore justly punished by losing them. Because still others sin through pleasure in their own flesh, they are therefore justly punished by affliction of that same flesh. The same applies to similar cases.

Appropriately, according to the judgment of the weak, he says “you fall,” as though from a height and unexpectedly. The weak regard temporal prosperity as a kind of height and happiness, and adversity as a kind of depth and misery. While they rest securely, as it were, at the height of prosperity and do not foresee tribulations, they fall as though unexpectedly.

[Col. 1522C] But the wise person understands that all temporal prosperity is not exaltation but rather ambushes, and knows that trials and adversities are highly beneficial to the just because he always foresees and expects them. When they come, he does not fall but rather receives them gladly.

Therefore he says, my brothers: “When you fall into various trials, consider that complete joy will come to you.” Now one kind of joy is “all joy,” another is “no joy,” and another is “a certain joy.”

“All joy” is general, true, and eternal joy: general, without any sorrow; true, without falsehood; eternal, without end. Hence the Lord says to his disciples: “Your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John 16).

[Col. 1522D] “No joy” is worldly joy, concerning which Solomon says: “I counted laughter as error, and to joy I said: Why are you deceived in vain?” (Eccl. 2).

“A certain joy” is rejoicing amid the adversities of this age in hope of future joy. Hence the Apostle says: “And not only that, but we glory in tribulations” (Rom. 5). This particular joy truly refreshed, consoled, and sustained the saints amid the miseries and tribulations of this world.

Let us therefore learn, my brothers, to rejoice amid the adversities of this world and to mourn amid its prosperity, so that we may neither be lifted up in prosperity nor cast down in adversity.

[Col. 1523A] The Apostle shows why we should rejoice amid adversities when he adds: “Knowing that the testing of your faith produces patience, and patience produces testing, so that you may be perfect in all things and deficient in nothing.” He calls tribulation the testing of faith because faith is tested through tribulation. This is what Paul says in these words: “Knowing that tribulation produces patience, patience produces testing, testing produces hope, and hope does not disappoint” (Rom. 5).

Tribulation therefore produces patience through practice. Just as an unbroken colt is impatient at its first blows but later, through daily training, becomes gentle and grows accustomed to the bridle and saddle, so the inexperienced human spirit recoils from its first tribulation and is impatient; but gradually, through frequent practice in tribulations, it becomes gentle and patient—especially when it understands both that it must not resist God’s ordering and that it is being purified through such things, and that its anger should be directed not against the file but against its own vice.

[Col. 1523B] Patience produces testing, or a perfect work—that is, perfection; the meaning is the same. When a righteous person endures all adversities with equanimity, not merely refusing to murmur in them but also blessing God, he is tested—that is, he is shown to be perfect—according to the saying: “The furnace tests gold, and persecution tests the righteous through tribulation” (Prov. 27).

[Col. 1523C] Testing produces hope. For one who understands that he has been purified and tested through tribulations awaits future glory not with a vain hope, as some do, but with certain hope. Although this hope is placed not in a human being, who is a liar, but in God, who cannot deceive, and although it may seem vain to the wise of this world because it cannot be established by human reasoning, it nevertheless does not disappoint; indeed, it leads to blessedness. In this you will be perfect and complete, deficient in nothing.

[Col. 1523D] Second, the Apostle urges us to ask wisdom from God so that we may understand how tribulations are useful to us, when he adds: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask from God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach, and it will be given to him. But let him ask in faith, doubting nothing,” etc.

In these words he makes four things known to us: who should ask, what he should ask, from whom, and how.

Who should ask? The one who lacks. For if someone does not lack and asks, he asks idly and wrongly. This plainly applies both to those who ask for temporal possessions, of which they have an abundance, to be multiplied still further, and to those who ask for things unnecessary and even useless to them—honors, offices, and the like. Hence the same James says later: “You ask and do not receive because you ask wrongly, so that you may spend it on your desires” (James 4).

Therefore, my brothers, let us ask God only for what is necessary and beneficial. If we are uncertain whether what we wish to ask will be useful to us, let us ask conditionally, saying: “Lord, give us this, if you know that it is expedient for us.”

What should he ask? Above all, wisdom. There can be no doubt that this request is just and expedient. For we all need either to be given wisdom or to have the wisdom already given to us increased. When the Lord gave Solomon, who was asking for a choice, the opportunity to ask, he asked, saying: “Lord God, I am a little child, not knowing my coming in or my going out. Give therefore to your servant a teachable heart, that I may be able to judge your people and discern between good and evil.”

[Col. 1524A] And it pleased the Lord, who said: “Because you did not ask, according to the manner of men, for many days, riches, or the lives of your enemies, I have done according to your words. I have given you a wise heart, so that no one before you has been like you. But the things you did not ask for I have also given you, provided that you walk in my ways, as your father did” (1 Kings 3).

Therefore, my brothers, let us ask the Lord not for long life, riches, honors, or other empty things of this kind, which have been the cause of ruin for many, but for true wisdom, praying with the Wise Man: “Send forth wisdom, Lord, from the seat of your greatness, that she may be with me and labor with me, so that I may know what is acceptable before you at all times” (Wis. 9).

[Col. 1524B] From whom should wisdom be requested? From God, because all wisdom is from the Lord God. In vain, therefore, do you rely on your intelligence or on a human teacher; in vain do you study and keep watch, because you cannot obtain wisdom except from the Father of lights.

“He gives,” he says, meaning to those who ask worthily. He gives generously, causing the devout to abound without diminishing his treasure. “And he does not reproach,” as some people reproach others for low birth, weakness, wrongdoing, or matters of this kind.

How should he ask? With faith, confidence, and simplicity. Whoever asks in this way will undoubtedly receive.

[Col. 1524C] That he must ask with faith he shows when he says: “Let him ask in faith,” that is, firmly believing that God, the Almighty, can give this and everything else. Hence the Lord says: “If you believe, all things are possible to the one who believes” (Mark 9). And elsewhere: “If you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you will say to the mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will happen” (Matt. 17; Luke 17).

He shows that he must ask with confidence when he adds: “Let him ask, doubting nothing.” A person doubts in prayer when an inwardly gnawing conscience causes him to distrust that his request will be granted. For, he says, “the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind.” The wave yields to the wind. So the person who, through unbelief or an evil conscience, distrusts God yields to every wind of temptation and withdraws from God.

[Col. 1524D] “Let not that person,” he says, “suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord.” He may indeed receive the hay of temporal wages along with the beasts, but not eternal stability.

He shows that he must ask with simplicity when he adds: “A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways,” meaning that therefore he cannot obtain anything. For this reason one must ask with simplicity.

We ask with simplicity when we ask God for what we ask for because of God himself. A person is double-minded when, although he appears to ask something from the Lord God and for God’s sake, he inwardly intends something earthly. He is also double-minded when, dividing his intention, he intends to act partly for God and partly for the world.

[Col. 1525A] He is likewise double-minded when he seeks both to rejoice here with the world and to reign in the future with God.

Therefore, brothers, if we wish to be heard by God, let us ask him for wisdom and for the other spiritual and heavenly gifts, asking with steadfast faith, with the confidence of a pure conscience, and with simplicity of intention.

Third, the Apostle promises exaltation to the humble and humiliation to the rich person when he adds: “Let the humble brother glory in his exaltation.” It is as though he were saying: Even if a faithful person is humble and despised amid tribulations, let him not grieve because of this but rather glory, because through the merit of his humility he will undoubtedly be exalted.

[Col. 1525B] Present abasement is small, momentary, and contemptible; future elevation will be immense, eternal, and glorious.

“But let the rich person,” he says, “glory in his humiliation.” This is irony. It is as though he were saying: Because he now glories in riches, he is rightly humbled. Present glory is small, brief, and contemptible; the humiliation of his condemnation will be immense, eternal, and terrifying.

He implies this when he adds: “For like the flower of grass he will pass away.” “The sun rose with its heat and dried the grass; its flower fell, and the beauty of its appearance perished. So also the rich person will wither in his ways.”

Grass gradually becomes green, grows, flowers, dries, and dies. So the rich person is green through prosperity, grows through temporal exaltation, flowers through worldly glory, dries through death, and dies through eternal condemnation. These are the ways of the vain and proud rich person.

[Col. 1525C] Although the flower of grass appears beautiful, it is a small and worthless thing. So worldly glory, when God’s anger burns, falls away; the flower of grass dies without any fruit, and worldly glory passes away without any benefit.

Hence the Psalmist says: “I saw the wicked exalted above measure and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; I passed by, and behold, he was not; I sought him, and his place was not found” (Ps. 36).

Therefore, my brothers, let us despise false riches, honors, pleasures, and the little glories of the world. Let us burn with our whole desire for the true riches of the kingdom of heaven. For their sake, let us gladly endure present tribulations, poverty, and abasement.

[Col. 1525D] Fourth, the Apostle demonstrates that blessed is the one who possesses patience when he adds: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life, which God promised to those who love him.”

He says four things: who will be blessed, in what respect, when, and through whom.

Who? The one who endures temptation. Here a distinction must be made, because neither everyone who endures temptation nor everyone who endures anything will be blessed.

There is an inward temptation, caused either by the devil or by one’s own flesh. Concerning this he says later: “Each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire.” We must not endure this temptation but rather conquer it and drive it away from us.

There is also an outward temptation, which God sends either directly, such as illnesses and weaknesses, or through the ministry of evil people, such as persecutions, injuries, and things of this kind. We must bear this patiently, as the blows of a loving father, inflicted upon us either for purification, testing, or preservation in humility.

[Col. 1526A] When will he be blessed? When he has been tested. Just as wheat is not stored in the granary until it has first been threshed, and wine is not placed in the cellar until it has first been pressed, and gold is not placed in the treasury until it has first been assayed, so the faithful person is not received into the kingdom of heaven until first purified and tested.

Stones and timbers are squared and polished outside; in the temple of eternal blessedness, however, no sound of hammer or axe will be heard.

In what will he be blessed? Because he will receive the crown of life. Since a crown is a royal insignia, it signifies a kingdom. Since it is round, it signifies perfection. Since it has neither beginning nor end, it signifies eternity.

[Col. 1526B] In this, then, my brothers, we shall be blessed: we shall receive the kingdom, perfection, and eternity of heavenly life—a kingdom without incapacity, perfection without insufficiency, and eternity without limit.

Through whom will he be blessed? Not because of his own merits, but through the grace of the divine promise. Hence he adds “which he promised,” that is, which God, who is almighty and truthful, promised again and again through the prophets and apostles.

He promised it “to those who love him.” Therefore, so that we may be able to obtain the crown promised to us by God, let us love God with our whole desire, obeying his commandments, despising all passing things for his sake, patiently enduring every adversity, and hastening with our whole desire toward what he promised.

[Col. 1526C] May he grant this, to whom belong honor and glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## X. ONE MARTYR. SERMON ON JOHN

Jesus said to his disciples: “Amen, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falling into the ground dies, it remains alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit,” etc. (John 12).

Before the coming of our Redeemer, dearly beloved brothers, the world was oppressed by the darkness of ignorance and unbelief. For people did not know about the resurrection; they did not know about the future life of the saints; they did not know about the future condemnation of the reprobate. They knew only temporal life and referred everything to it.

[Col. 1526D] To preserve that life, they practiced thefts, robberies, frauds, sacrilege, and killings. For its sake they sank into every lust, disgrace, crime, and abomination. Therefore our Redeemer, when he came, taught the resurrection; he taught the good life of the saints and the condemnation of the reprobate. He taught that the present life should be despised and that the just should not fear temporal death, but rather desire it as an entrance into rest.

The Lord speaks about this, then, in the reading just cited, in the following manner. First, he says that his death and the death of his followers are fruitful, like the death of a sown grain. Second, he says that whoever foolishly loves his soul destroys it, while whoever wisely loves it preserves it. Third, he exhorts us to follow him. Fourth, he promises a reward.

[Col. 1527A] First, then, he foretells that his own death and that of his followers will be fruitful when he says: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the ground dies, it remains alone,” etc.

A grain of wheat is white within and red on the outside; it is food for human beings, not for beasts. It is also more strengthening than other foods.

Our Redeemer likewise is white within, with the whiteness of his innocence, and red outside, with the blood of his Passion. Hence the Bride says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is white and ruddy” (Song 5). And Isaiah says: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah? Why is your clothing red, and your garments like those of one who treads the winepress?” (Isa. 63).

[Col. 1527B] He is not food for animals—that is, for those who understand in an animal-like manner—but for rational beings, according to the saying: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77). He is also more strengthening than other foods, because in the strength of this food we walk for forty days and forty nights to the mountain of God, Horeb (1 Kings 18).

For this reason holy Church has become accustomed to celebrating the sacrament of Christ’s body not with anything else but with bread made from wheat.

Therefore, just as a grain of wheat is not renewed and multiplied unless it is first cast into the ground, covered, and dies, so Christ would not be renewed through the resurrection or multiplied through the faith of many unless he had been sent by the Father into the earth and had died and been buried. For this reason he descended and died: to call many brothers and co-heirs to himself.

[Col. 1527C] Likewise, unless the holy apostles and martyrs were cast into the earth by the hands of persecutors and died, they would not be renewed through the glory of the resurrection or multiplied through the imitation of many.

We too, my brothers, unless we cast ourselves down into the earth through humility; unless we mortify our members with their vices and desires; unless we patiently endure the death of the body itself, will be unable either to be renewed through the glory of the resurrection or to expand through the good things of heavenly rewards.

Second, the Lord demonstrates that whoever foolishly loves his soul destroys it when he adds: “Whoever loves his soul will lose it.”

[Col. 1527D] We love our soul foolishly and wrongly, my brothers, if we satisfy its sensuality in gluttony, lust, pleasure, glory, and the other desires of the flesh.

For this reason, when a certain reprobate was dying, he is said to have spoken to his soul: “My soul, why are you abandoning me? Did we not feed you well? Did we not give you good drink? Did we not clothe you well? Did we not serve your other desires well?”

If we love our soul in this way, brothers, we undoubtedly destroy it and obtain for it the death of eternal condemnation.

Therefore the Lord next demonstrates that whoever hates his soul in this world loves it when he adds: “And whoever hates his soul in this world preserves it for eternal life.”

[Col. 1528A] We rightly hate our soul, brothers, and acquire eternal life for it when we hate and mortify its desires and vain longings. I mean vice, not nature; sins, not the creature. Otherwise, just as the person who nourishes even the vices of body and soul is condemned, so also is the person who kills nature itself.

Although, my brothers, we ought to despise the present life and hasten toward the eternal life with our whole desire, we must not cut short the present life, as certain indiscreet people have done by excessive mortification or by taking their own lives. Rather, we must patiently endure this present life and direct it in God’s service, not break it. We should receive death itself—whether inflicted upon us by a persecutor or by God—with thanksgiving.

But we—we have reason to grieve—do not merely fail to hate the present life; we love it beyond measure. Therefore we are anxious, wishing to live here for a long time, either not believing in the future life or neglecting it as though it were of no concern.

[Col. 1528B] Alas! How unlike the apostles and the holy martyrs and the other Fathers we are! They hated the present life intensely and ran toward eternal life with such desire and eagerness, even through torments, that they seized it rather than merely attaining it, according to the Lord’s word: “From the days of John the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11).

Third, the Lord exhorts us to follow him, when he adds: “Whoever serves me, let him follow me.” Although, in a general sense, all the faithful who serve and obey God may be called soldiers and ministers of Christ, nevertheless Christ specially calls us his ministers: we who minister to him at the altar, who are the messengers and preachers of his words [Col. 1528C], who hold his place in the Church. Therefore, my brothers, we above all are bound to follow him—not from a distance, as the other faithful among the people do, but to cling closely to his footsteps.

We ought especially to follow him in teaching and obedience, in purity, in charity, in contempt for the world, in humility, in patience, and in purity of life, so that in the sight of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is not only pure but purity itself, we may be pure ministers. Hence he himself says: “Be holy, because I am holy (Lev. XIX).” And also: “Purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the Lord (Isa. XLII).” For if earthly kings and lords wish to have pure ministers, as David says: “He who walks in a pure way [Col. 1528D] ministered to me (Ps. C),” how much more does the King of kings and Lord of lords wish this!

With what audacity, then, with what face, you fornicator, you polluted man, do you dare to minister in the sight of God, to approach the sacred altar, and to handle the Son of the Virgin with unclean hands?

In obedience, we must always obey him, just as he was obedient to the Father even unto death. We must always seek to do not our own will and glory, but his, just as he sought not his own will but that of the Father: “For I have not come to do my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me (John VI).” Nor should we seek what is our own, but what belongs to Jesus Christ, just as he sought not his own advantage but the benefit of all.

This is contrary to most of us, my brothers, who in ecclesiastical offices seek what is ours rather than what belongs to God and our neighbors, since there we seek the profit of temporal stipends rather than that of souls [Col. 1529A]. We seek a church not where we can benefit souls more, but where we can gather more; we are more concerned with the care of our animals than with the souls of the faithful, for whom Christ died. But however many of us are such, without doubt we are not shepherds but hirelings.

In charity, we must love God for his own sake and our neighbor for his sake, according to what he himself commanded, saying: “This is my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you (John XV).” We must love not only our friends but also our enemies, do good to those who hate us, and pray for those who persecute and slander us [Col. 1529B], just as he himself both did and commanded (Matt. V).

This too is contrary to most of us, my brothers, who bear resentment against those who have injured us in some way or spoken some insult against us. Even if at times we forgive them with our lips because of the commandment, we still retain bitterness in our hearts. Against such people the Lord said: “If you love those who love you, and if you do good to those who do good to you, what reward will you have? Do not the tax collectors and the pagans do the same?” (Matt. V; Luke VI.)

We must therefore forgive those who injure us for two reasons: to avoid harm and to gain benefit. To avoid harm, because if we do not forgive our neighbors [Col. 1529C], God will not forgive us either (Matt. VI). Indeed, he will demand back everything that seemed to have been forgiven. To gain benefit, because if we forgive, we shall be forgiven (ibid.). If we are merciful, we shall find mercy; and with the measure with which we measure, it will be measured back to us (Matt. VII).

In contempt of the world, we should imitate him who desired neither riches nor even a place where he might lay his head (Luke IX), who loved and preached poverty, and withdrew from those who wished to make him king (John VI). So should we either entirely flee the riches, honors, and little glories of the world, or at least despise them.

In this respect—for I cannot say it without a groan—we are put to shame: we neither flee nor despise these things, but pursue and embrace them more and more, piling wealth upon wealth [Col. 1529D], vineyard upon vineyard, house upon house. Having a church, we seek a deanery; having a deanery, we seek a bishopric. There is no end to our greed and ambition.

We do not heed what the Apostle says: “Those who wish to become rich in this world fall into a snare and into the temptations of the devil. Having food and clothing, let us be content with these. We brought nothing into this world; there is no doubt that we can take nothing away (1 Tim. VI).”

In humility: just as he, although God and Lord of all, humbled himself by taking the form of a servant, submitting himself to his servants Mary and Joseph, paying tribute to Caesar, washing the feet of his servants, and wishing not to be ministered to but to minister, crying out and saying, “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart [Col. 1530A] (Matt. XI),” so should we humble ourselves not only before our superiors but also before our inferiors.

We must not merely confess with our lips that we are lesser than others; we must also feel it in our minds. Let us contend only for humility, always conceding to others precedence in speaking, acting, sitting, and similar matters.

This is contrary to some of us, my brothers, who always seek to appear superior and are unwilling to yield to anyone in an argument. We consider it disgraceful to humble ourselves and ask forgiveness of our neighbor, while seeking the first couches at banquets, the chief seats in the synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by men (Matt. XXIII).

We do not consider that whenever we wish to be exalted above others, we imitate the devil; whenever we are humbled, we imitate Christ.

In patience [Col. 1530B]: just as he patiently endured insults, abuse, scourging, spitting, suffering, and death for us, so should we not fear suffering the same things for him, according to what Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps (1 Pet. II).”

But we—for I cannot say it without a groan—do not patiently endure the illnesses, chastisements, and adversities inflicted upon us for our sins. Rather, we murmur and become defiled by the very things through which we ought to be cleansed. If someone injures us, we return evil for evil and cursing for cursing; or, if we cannot do so openly, we curse him in our hearts. We do not consider that both those who inflict injury and those who return it [Col. 1530C] are alien to Christ, who exposed his back to the scourges and, when cursed, did not curse in return.

Fourth, he promises a reward when he adds: “Where I am, there also will my minister be”—that is, in that glory, that splendor, that honor, that blessedness where I am substantially and naturally with the Father, there my minister will be by grace, if he has followed me in imitation.

Explaining this, he adds: “If anyone ministers to me, my Father who is in heaven will honor him.” And what greater honor, my brothers, can there be than to be in that indescribable glory in which the Son of God is? What greater honor than to be a co-heir and sharer with the Son of God? What evil does he have, and what good does he lack, who remains forever in that eternal blessedness with the Son of God?

Therefore, my brothers [Col. 1530D], let riches, honors, glories, pleasures, and whatever else we see in this world become worthless to us. Let us restrain the lusts and unlawful desires of the flesh; let us possess purity of mind and body; let us love God above all things and our neighbor as ourselves; let us have compassionate and merciful hearts toward the afflicted. Let us seek God’s will, not our own; let us love poverty and humility; let us hasten with all desire toward the promised blessedness; let us rejoice to suffer adversities and persecutions for Christ; let us always meditate upon and long for those heavenly joys in our hearts. Let our dwelling in this world seem a delay to us, and let however much we labor here for Christ seem little.

If we do this, my brothers, without doubt we shall share in that supreme [Col. 1531A] blessedness. May our Lord Jesus Christ grant this to us through the merits of his holy martyrs, he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages.

## XI. SERMON FOR ONE MARTYR, FROM THE BOOK OF WISDOM

“If the righteous man is taken by death prematurely, his soul will be in refreshment” (Wis. IV), etc.

Since the righteous especially suffer tribulations, illnesses, and persecutions in this world, and are often removed from it by the sword or some other sudden death, without a will and without arranging their affairs, worldly people, observing this, suppose either that they have been rejected by God or that God does not care about worldly matters.

Against [Col. 1531B] this opinion of worldly people the Wise Man speaks in this reading, showing three things. First, that however prematurely the righteous man may appear to be taken, he nevertheless enters into rest. Second, that he dies in a good old age. Third, he demonstrates why the righteous man is removed from the world so quickly.

First, then, he demonstrates that however prematurely the righteous man may appear to be taken, he nevertheless enters into rest. I rightly say “appear to be taken prematurely,” because he is not taken prematurely but only appears to be. For one who always awaits death prepared cannot be taken prematurely. But one who is unprepared, even if he dies old and decrepit, dies prematurely. Hence the Psalmist says: “Wicked men will not complete half their days (Ps. LIV).”

But the righteous man, to whom the present life is burdensome and who longs for the life to come [Col. 1531C], prepares himself for it with all his strength, like people awaiting their master’s return from the wedding feast. Whether he comes in the first, second, third, or fourth watch, blessed is the servant whom his master finds watching, for he will set him over all his possessions (Matt. XXIV).

Therefore, since the Lord’s day will come like a thief in the night, let us always watch, my brothers; let us always be prepared; let us always think that death is close at hand. For this reason the Lord wished the time of our death to be uncertain, so that we might always fear death as present and prepare ourselves to receive it.

Second, it is shown that however prematurely the righteous man may be taken by death [Col. 1531D], nevertheless he dies in a good old age, when it is added: “For old age is honorable—not measured by length of time,” that is, not calculated by a number of days or years. “The gray hairs of a person are understanding,” that is, a person’s good gray hair is wisdom; “and an undefiled life is the maturity of old age,” that is, a good life is a good old age.

Two old ages are presented to us: one of years and the other of conduct. The first without the second is extremely bad. The first together with the second is good. The second without the first is best. For an old man in days but not in conduct is detestable. It is written: “A child of a hundred years shall be accursed (Isa. LXV).”

What is more detestable than to grow gray in body but not in heart, in chin but not in mind; to bear outwardly a wrinkled old man while inwardly carrying a wanton youth [Col. 1532A]?

Such were the two old men “grown old in the days of evil,” who wished to corrupt the tender girl Susanna but were overcome by her (Dan. XIII). Such old men are more condemnable than all other ages, because in them neither the coldness of age can overcome the heat of lust, nor the heaviness of the body the levity of the mind.

But an old man who is good both in days and in conduct is good and venerable. He appropriately responds to the maturity of his body with maturity of heart, to the whiteness of his hair with the whiteness of his mind, and to the gravity of his flesh with the gravity of his spirit.

Such were the two most holy elders Simeon and Anna. They were righteous and God-fearing before God, never departing from the temple, serving God with fasts and prayers night and day. Therefore they deserved to be enlightened by the Holy Spirit and to receive the answer [Col. 1532B] that they would see Christ before they died, to receive him into their arms, and to prophesy about him (Luke II).

But an old man in conduct and not in years is all the holier and more admirable because the virtue of his mind surpasses the nature of his age: he preserves maturity in youth, chastity in the heat of the flesh, and gravity amid the lightness of youth.

Such elders were Daniel and the boys cast into the furnace; such an elder was Joseph; such an elder was John the Baptist and John the Evangelist. Such elders were countless virgins, who overcame not only age but also sex, the world, and even death itself, and reached God through the enormity of their torments.

True, therefore, is the saying, my brothers: however prematurely the righteous man may die [Col. 1532C], he dies only gray-haired and mature. Let us strive, my brothers, to possess the gray hair of conduct and the maturity of life. Once we possess these, we may await death securely: death cannot overtake us prematurely; we shall pass from the world to heaven not halfway through our days but in the fullness of our days.

Third, it is shown why the righteous are quickly removed from the world. Five causes are given here.

The first is that he is quickly removed from the world because God loves him and wishes to have him quickly with himself in blessedness. This cause is indicated when it is added: “Having become pleasing to God, he was beloved.” As if he were saying: Because he had pleased God by an undefiled life, God therefore wished him to become beloved and familiar [Col. 1532D] with him in the blessed life.

The second is that the righteous man is quickly removed from the world because the world was not worthy of him. This cause is given when it is added: “While living among sinners, he was taken away.” As if he were plainly saying: Because he lived holily among sinners, and yet the sinners were not corrected by his example and teaching, he is rightly removed from the unworthy, for his glory and for their shame.

It was for his glory that he lived well among sinners. For it is not a great glory to have lived holily among the holy, but it is highly praiseworthy to have lived holily among sinners. Hence Job is praised when it is said: “There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job, simple and upright (Job I).” Hence also it is said in the Song of Songs: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters (Song II).”

It is for the shame [Col. 1533A] of those who were unwilling to be corrected either by his example or by his teaching while he was present, and who did not understand that the hasty removal of the holy man from among them was God’s anger against them. Hence it is written: “Behold how the righteous man dies, and no one understands in his heart; righteous men are taken away, and no one considers. The righteous man has been removed from the face of evil, and his memory will be in peace (Isa. LVII).”

We ought greatly to fear this anger of God, brothers, whenever we see a holy person removed from our midst, lest he be removed from us because, despising his teaching, we were unworthy of him.

The third cause is that sometimes the righteous man is quickly removed from the world so that he may not at some point stumble on the slippery road of this world. This cause is given when it is added: “He was snatched away [Col. 1533B] lest wickedness change his understanding or deceit deceive his soul”—that is, lest the wickedness of those with whom he lived, whether through bad example, bad teaching, or more severe persecution, change his understanding from good to evil; or lest deceit—that is, a hidden temptation, whether of the flesh or of the devil—deceive his soul, as has often happened to many.

The fourth cause is that the righteous man is quickly removed from the world because he was complete in merits. This cause is given when it is added: “Being perfected in a short time, he fulfilled many years.” As if he were plainly saying: Although he lived for a short time, he died full of days and complete in merits, because what others acquire as merit over long periods, he acquired in a short time.

And does not [Col. 1533C] the one who accomplished much in a short time seem more commendable and fortunate, my brothers, than the one who could accomplish it only over many years? Is it not more fortunate to reach the prize quickly rather than late? “His soul was pleasing to God,” it says. Therefore he granted him to accomplish in a short time what others accomplish only over a long period.

“For this reason”—that is, for this and the preceding reasons—“he hastened to remove him from the midst of iniquity.”

The fifth cause is that sometimes the Lord quickly takes the righteous man from the world in order to spare him his labors. This cause is indicated when it is added: “For there is grace and mercy with his elect, and he watches over them.”

Grace is given when he grants them the grace of virtues along the road of this world. Mercy [Col. 1533D] is given when, amid tribulations, he sustains them lest they fail. His watchfulness is shown when he quickly transfers them from labor to rest.

Let us therefore pray, brothers; let us pray to God and our Lord with groans and sighs, that he may grant us, his little servants, his grace to illuminate and guide us through the darkness of this world; that he may provide us with the support of his mercy amid the tribulations of this world; and that he may transfer us from the labors of this world to the refreshment of eternal blessedness. Amen.

## XII. ALSO, A SERMON ON MATTHEW, ON THE SAME SUBJECT

Jesus said to his disciples: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross [Col. 1534A], and follow me” (Matt. XVI), etc.

This reading is divided into four parts, my brothers. First, the Lord shows what we must do if we wish to follow him. Second, he demonstrates why we ought to surrender our souls and all temporal things for him. Third, he threatens that in the future he will be ashamed of those who are now ashamed to follow him. Fourth, he says that some of the disciples will see the promised kingdom of God before their death.

First, then, he shows what we must do if we wish to follow him, when he says: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me.”

He says three things: Let him deny himself; let him take up his cross; let him follow me. In these, both the number and the order are necessary. For neither the first [Col. 1534B] without the two that follow, nor the first two without the third, can suffice.

First, therefore, he commands us to deny ourselves. There are, my brothers, three kinds of renunciation: to deny oneself, to deny one’s possessions, and to deny one’s own will.

To deny oneself—that is, one’s own vices—is commanded here of every person, so that we deny not nature but vice: not what we were made by God to be, but what we have made ourselves by sinning. For it is written: “Turn the wicked, and they shall no longer exist (Prov. XII),” that is, convert them from wickedness to righteousness, and they will no longer be wicked but rather righteous.

If someone had lived as a fornicator, let him be converted and abandon fornication; he denies what he was. If someone had lived as a miser, let him cease to be a miser; he denies what he was [Col. 1534C]. Hence Paul, after abandoning unbelief and cruelty, says that he no longer lives as he lived before: “I live,” he says, “yet it is no longer I (Gal. II).” What, then, do you live? “Christ lives in me,” he says (ibid.). As if he were plainly saying: My former wickedness has been extinguished in me, and the grace of Christ lives in me. I do not live as a wicked man, but as a Christian.

To deny one’s possessions, however, belongs only to the perfect, who, fulfilling not only Christ’s commandments but also his counsels—“If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and come, follow me (Matt. X)”—leave everything and follow the naked Christ naked.

By commandment, my brothers, all of us, both perfect and imperfect, are bound to deny our greed and love of possessions. But we are not bound by commandment [Col. 1534D] to abandon the possessions themselves; rather, we are advised to do so by counsel, because one who is unburdened and naked is more unencumbered for running the course. A runner cannot run well under a load, nor can a swimmer swim well under one.

Hence Paul says: “Everyone who competes in the contest abstains from everything (1 Cor. IX).” And: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly business (2 Tim. II).”

While we are on the road of this world, we are engaged in combat with the devil, who possesses nothing in this world. Let us therefore wrestle naked with the naked; for if a clothed man wrestles with a naked man, he is easily thrown down, because the other has something by which he can be held.

Therefore, my brothers, let us cast away the impediments of temporal possessions, lest, being tempted by the devil through them, we be thrown headlong or delayed in our course.

To deny one’s own will belongs to the perfect, who deny not only their own vices and possessions but also their own wills, submitting themselves to the command of their spiritual father. From then on they do not do what they themselves wish, but what he commands.

All of us, my brothers, are indeed bound to deny evil desires. But these people also deny their good desires, so that thereafter they cannot even pray, fast, or perform any good act of their own choosing except according to the judgment and will of their abbot. Thus they become spiritual imitators of Jesus Christ, who said of himself: “I have not come to do my own will [Col. 1535A], but the will of him who sent me (John IV).”

And who, my brothers, could carry out his own will better than he whose will [Col. 1535B] is always perfect and who always wills the same thing as the Father? Yet he says that he does and seeks not his own will but that of the Father, in order to show us that much more should we, who frequently have evil thoughts, seek and do not our own will but rather the will of our spiritual father.

Second, the Lord commands that the one who has denied himself—because this is not enough—undertake the labor of the virtues, when he adds: “Let him take up his cross.”
