The cross, my brothers, is labor and torment. We are therefore commanded to take up our cross—that is, to undertake voluntarily the labor and torment of acquiring the virtues, or gratefully to endure what is imposed upon us by others [Col. 1535C].

We take up the cross in three ways: when we afflict our body through abstinence and chastisement; when our mind is moved by compassion for our neighbor; or when injuries inflicted by persecutors are patiently endured in body and spirit. Through the first we attain the virtue of abstinence and continence; through the second, the virtue of charity and mercy; through the third, the virtue of courage and patience.

The Teacher of the Gentiles shows that he bears the first cross when he says: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude (1 Cor. IX).” He shows that he bears the second when he says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. XI.) He shows that he bears the third when he says: “I rejoice now in my sufferings [Col. 1535D] for you, and I complete in my flesh what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ (Col. I).”

But these things do not suffice for anyone, my brothers, unless the third thing that the Lord adds is also supplied: “and follow me.”

Many indeed bear the cross of abstinence and chastisement, but through an intention of vainglory they render it useless to themselves. That Simon aptly signifies who, found on the road, carries the Lord’s cross under compulsion (Matt. XXVII), because when someone is not led to a good work by good will, the sinner carries the righteous man’s cross without profit.

Thus Simon carries the cross but does not die, because those who abstain for the sake of glory afflict their bodies through abstinence but live for the world through their desire for vainglory.

Many also carry the cross of compassion in their hearts [Col. 1536A], but through lack of discernment they render it useless to themselves, allowing themselves, through false piety, to yield even to vice. Compassion is owed to the person, but strictness to the vices, so that in one and the same person we may love the good that has been done and pursue the evil that has been committed. Otherwise, by carelessly forgiving faults, we may appear not to have compassion through charity but to have fallen through negligence.

Many indeed carry the cross of sufferings in body and spirit, such as pagans and philosophers, but they render it useless to themselves because they carry it not for charity and imitation of Christ but merely for the vanity of their philosophy.

If, therefore, my brothers, we wish to undertake these crosses, let us follow Christ through them: in the cross of chastisement [Col. 1536B], let us follow Christ in our intention; in the cross of compassion, let us follow him with the rectitude of discernment; and in the cross of persecutions, let us follow Christ in both cause and imitation.

The second part follows, in which the Lord demonstrates for what reason we ought to surrender our souls and all temporal things for him, when he adds: “For whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it. And whoever loses his soul for my sake will save it.”

Just as there are two powers of the soul—namely, sensuality, which the soul exercises through the workshops of the body, and reason—so there are two kinds of salvation and loss of the soul: one temporal and the other eternal.

Temporal salvation [Col. 1536C] of the soul occurs when someone carefully preserves its sensuality and bodily life, feeding it well, drinking well, clothing it well, and satisfying its desires, refusing to surrender it even for Christ. Whoever wishes to save his soul in this temporal way will undoubtedly lose it eternally.

Temporal loss of the soul occurs when a believer afflicts his sensuality and bodily life by laboring, fasting, chastising himself, restraining its cravings and desires, and, when necessary, even exposing it to death for Christ. Whoever in this way loses his soul temporally for Christ will undoubtedly save it eternally.

Thus the Lord speaks to us when he says: “Whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it. And whoever loses his soul [Col. 1536D] for my sake will save it.” It is as though one were saying to a farmer: If you preserve the grain, you lose it; if you sow it, you renew it. Unless it is lost in the dust, it is not renewed in the harvest.

Thus temporal life, when preserved against God, is of no benefit; rather, it does harm. Therefore, temporal profits acquired for its sake against God are much less beneficial; rather, they do great harm.

And this is what he adds: “For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but loses himself and suffers the loss of himself?”

In a time of persecution, the soul must be surrendered; in a time of peace, earthly greed must be broken. When persecution from adversaries is absent, then the heart must be guarded with the greatest vigilance. For in a time of peace, since it is permitted to live, it is also permitted to seek advancement.

We shall rightly restrain that ambition, my brothers [Col. 1537A], if we always meditate upon the brevity of life. The shortness of the road rebukes our long desires. For what is more foolish than, as the road grows shorter, to increase one’s provisions, and, as the days run out, to multiply one’s daily allowance?

The third part follows, in which the Lord threatens that in the future he will be ashamed of those who are now ashamed to follow him, when he adds: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in his majesty, and in the majesty of the Father and of the holy angels.”

By this sentence he rebukes us, my brothers. Although we are not ashamed to confess Christ and his words with our mouths, because others confess him, nevertheless we are ashamed to confess him truly in our conduct and life.

The insignia of Christ, which he displayed in himself and preached to others, are humility [Col. 1537B], poverty, lowliness, patience, suffering, and similar things. Therefore, brothers, when we are ashamed to be humbled, to become poor, to be rejected, despised, and to suffer for Christ, are we not ashamed of Christ and his words?

If we have quarreled with our neighbor, we are ashamed to be the first to make amends, and we wait for him to make amends to us first. What is this, except that we seek to be honored rather than humbled, and are ashamed to follow Christ’s example?

For when there was hostility between Christ and us, demanded by our sins, he did not wait for us to seek him first. He himself sought us first, offered us reconciliation, sent the apostles and their followers as ambassadors of peace, and still sends them every day.

Hence one of them, namely Paul [Col. 1537C], says: “We act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us; we beseech you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God (2 Cor. V).”

Let our pride, then, be ashamed. God, though offended, first begs us sinners through his ambassadors to come to peace, while we wretched sinners are ashamed to be the first to make amends to our sinful neighbors!

The fourth part follows, in which the Lord, to confirm the promised kingdom, promises that some of the disciples will see him even before their death, when he adds: “Truly I say to you: There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man in his kingdom.”

These disciples are Peter, James, and John, to whom, as is contained in what follows, after seven days the Lord displayed his glory on Mount [Col. 1537D] Tabor when he was transfigured (Matt. XVII).

Something had to be promised in the present life to the disciples, who were still inexperienced, so that they might be strengthened in faith and in hope of the future. Thus the land of promise was also promised to the Israelite people, and when they were to be called to heavenly things, they were persuaded by earthly promises (Exod. III).

Why was this done? Because while there was something close at hand for them to receive, they would believe more certainly what had been promised to them from afar. A carnal people, if they did not receive small things, would not believe great ones.

Hence it is said of them: “He gave them the lands of the nations, and they possessed the labor of peoples, so that they might keep his ordinances and seek his law (Ps. CIV).”

And even now there are some [Col. 1538A] who are Christians in name alone, who love only visible things, do not desire invisible things, and do not even believe that they exist. The holy martyrs whom we celebrate refute them.

For would they have given themselves so readily to death unless it had been certain to them that the future life exists? And behold, those who believed in this, who shone forth through wondrous works, show by miracles that they live even after death.

The sick who are alive come to their extinguished bodies and are healed; perjurers come and are tormented by demons; the possessed come and are freed. How gloriously, then, do they live where they live! If they live here in so many miracles, where they are dead, how much more gloriously do they live there?

Let us therefore believe firmly in eternal life, brothers; let us hope for it and desire it. For its sake let us despise all earthly things; let us deny our carnal pleasures and wills [Col. 1538B]; let us patiently bear Christ’s cross—in chastisement of the flesh and in compassion for our neighbor—and patiently endure persecutions with equanimity. Let us strive in every way to follow Christ’s life and teaching, so that we may deserve to share in his blessedness, by the gift of him who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## XIII. SERMON FOR ONE MARTYR, FROM THE BOOK OF WISDOM

“Blessed is the man who is found without blemish, who has not gone after gold and has not placed his hope in treasures of money (Ecclus. XXXI),” etc.

This reading is divided into four parts, my brothers. First, it shows who is blessed. Second, it commends him. Third, it says from what he has deserved [Col. 1538C] this. Fourth, it shows in what his reward consists.

First, then, it shows who is blessed, when it says: “Blessed is the man who is found without blemish,” etc.

Who is blessed? A man, namely, who is not soft or effeminate but rather manly and virtuous. For God delights in a hard-fighting soldier, not in one who gives himself over to idleness, luxuries, and pleasures, but in one who exercises himself in abstinence, hardships, and labors: “For no one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully (2 Tim. II).” Nor does one reach a great reward except through great labor.

Next he explains the virtues of the blessed man when he adds: “Who is found without blemish.” He does not say, “who had no blemish,” since no one is clean from defilement, not even an infant [Col. 1538D] whose life is a single day upon the earth; rather, he says, “who is found without blemish”—that is, one who, even if he once had a blemish, nevertheless washed and cleansed it with the tears of true repentance, according to the Psalmist: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered (Ps. XXXI).”

In general, every serious sin is called a blemish; specifically, lust may be called a blemish, because more than other serious sins it stains both body and soul. Hence the Apostle says: “Every sin whatever a man commits is outside the body; but whoever fornicates sins against his own body (1 Cor. VI).”

That is, no other sin so completely subjects and enslaves the whole person to the pleasure of the body as fornication, because in other sins—even those carried out through the body, such as drunkenness and robbery—it remains possible for the mind at the same time to perform something else and to wander elsewhere in thought. But the fornicator is wholly absorbed [Col. 1539A], so that the mind is not free, and the whole person becomes flesh.

And he says, “who has not gone after gold”—that is, one whom greed for riches and ambition has not caused to deviate from the rectitude of life.

These two things, namely lust and greed, are, according to Solomon (Prov. XXX), “the two daughters of the leech,” that is, of desire, which always say: “Bring, bring.” Both are insatiable. The more you pursue lust, the more you long for it, and after abundance you suffer want again. No abundance satisfies greed either; rather, like a dropsical person, the more it drinks [Col. 1539B], the more it thirsts.

And:

“Love of money grows as money itself grows.”

Nor did he, he says, hope in treasures of money—that is, he was not miserly with money, but rather a distributor, in accordance with the saying: “He scattered; he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures for ever and ever” (Ps. 111). For just as it is characteristic of the covetous to covet what ought not to be coveted, so it is characteristic of the miser to retain what ought not to be retained and to place his hope in such things. Hence avarice is called “the service of idols” by the Apostle (Col. 3). For the miser worships money in place of God.

Therefore, my brothers, whoever is not soft in mind, let him be virtuous. Whoever is undefiled in mind and body, despises temporal things, and, if he possesses them, distributes them to the poor for God’s sake—he is already said to be blessed. Let us therefore labor with our whole desire to attain these virtues, so that we too may deserve to be counted among the number of the blessed.

The second part follows, in which he praises the person previously described, when he adds: “Who is this”—that is, “How great is this man”—“and we shall praise him? For he has done marvelous things in his life.” He does not say “a marvelous thing,” but “marvelous things.” For those who observe virtues of this kind in the present life demonstrate three marvelous qualities in themselves.

Marvelous by its rarity: for it is wondrous that anyone should be found in this world virtuous, undefiled, a despiser of the world, and one who distributes to the poor, in a world where all are soft, defiled, lovers of the world, and regarded as despisers of the poor, in accordance with the poet’s saying:

> A rare bird upon the earth, and very like a black swan.  
> (Juv. *Sat.* 6.164)

[Col. 1539D] Marvelous by its virtue: for it is wondrous that what belongs not to human but to divine virtue should occur—that a person placed in the flesh should live not according to the flesh; in the world, but not according to the world; among human beings, but not according to human beings; rather, that he should live spiritually, heavenly, and angelically. Hence Job cries out to God: “Who, he says, can make clean what was conceived from unclean seed? Is it not you, who alone are?” (Job 14.)

Marvelous by its difficulty: for it is wondrous, and exceedingly difficult, to live among human beings day and night without being corrupted by their perverse association or stained by their filth. For what is more marvelous than to be dry and sober among drunkards and those vomiting, or to live in sound health among the diseased? Whoever, he says, is found perfect in that”—that is, in the practice of the virtues mentioned above—“will have eternal glory.” He will receive a great, marvelous, and glorious merit, and will obtain a greater, more marvelous, and more glorious reward.

The third part follows, in which it is shown from what the merit arises, when he continues: “Who was able to transgress,” by not doing what is commanded to be done—which is properly called a transgression—and yet did not transgress; and by doing the evils that are forbidden—which is properly called sin—and yet did not do them. For, my brothers, because we possess freedom of choice, whether toward good or toward evil, we are said to merit when, avoiding the evil that we are able to do, we choose and practice the good. For an act that we cannot perform merits neither punishment nor reward.

Therefore, the greater freedom someone possesses, the more he merits if, having avoided evil, he practices good. Great indeed was the merit of the saints who, possessing freedom of choice, freedom of grace, and bodily freedom, did not therefore—as some have done—sin all the more expansively the more freely they could do so, in accordance with Peter’s saying: “As free people, and not as though you had freedom as a veil for wickedness, but as servants of God” (1 Pet. 2).

According to this rule, therefore, the one who lives innocently in freedom merits more than the one who lives in servitude; the one who lives abstinently in abundance merits more than the one who lives in poverty; and the one who lives continently among the people merits more than the one who lives in a monastery. But because some feel themselves too weak for this, they choose not a greater crown but greater security, surrendering themselves to voluntary servitude, poverty, and discipline. In this too they merit greatly, if they steadfastly and willingly keep their promise.

Therefore, my brothers, let each person choose the way most suited to him. Whoever knows how to use temporal freedom and abundance well, let him use them and thereby merit eternal life. But whoever does not know how to use them well should choose voluntary submission and poverty, so that he who does not know how to govern himself may be governed by another’s will.

The fourth part follows, in which it is demonstrated in what the reward of the righteous consists, when it is added: “Therefore his goods have been established in the Lord.” The righteous person who has always clung to the Lord in firm hope, who has referred all his works to him, and who has transmitted his temporal possessions to him through the hands of the poor, has his goods—that is, his rewards—established in God: firm in the firm, eternal in the eternal, blessed in the blessed.

“And his almsgiving,” he says, “the whole Church of the saints will recount”—namely, both the Church militant and the Church triumphant. The Church militant recounts it for imitation; the Church triumphant, for praise. For when we, my brothers, recount or hear recounted how compassionate and merciful Nicholas was toward the afflicted, how devout and generous in almsgiving John, patriarch of Alexandria, was toward the needy, and how the other saints were toward the poor, we are instructed and stirred to similar deeds, so that through similar works we may strive to attain a similar crown. Thus our good works may be established not on earth, “where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal” (Matt. 6), but in the Lord, who bestows on his own immense rewards for small things, eternal rewards for things that pass away, and heavenly rewards for earthly things. To him be honor and glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## XIV. OF ONE MARTYR. SERMON ON LUKE

Jesus said to his disciples: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, wife and brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14), etc.

In this reading of the holy Gospel, dearest brothers, the Lord shows us what is necessary for us in order that we may be able to belong to the number of his elect. There are four things: to hate vices, to love virtues, to persevere in them, and to presume not upon our own merits but upon God’s mercy alone.

First, therefore, the Lord urges us to hatred of vices when he adds: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, wife and sons, brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.” The Lord does not command us in these words—although elsewhere he commanded us to honor father and mother and to love our neighbor (Exod. 20)—to hate these persons, but only their vices.

Therefore, in the same way that we ought to hate ourselves, we ought to hate our parents and our neighbors. We ought to hate ourselves as we have made ourselves by sinning, and we ought to love ourselves as God has made us. We ought to attack our vices, which come from us and not from God, and cherish our very nature, which comes from God and not from ourselves.

In the same way, toward our parents and neighbors we ought to hate their vices and cherish their nature, with such discernment that we neither attack their nature on account of their vices nor cherish their vices on account of our love for their nature. For this reason he expressly mentioned the names of those bound to us by carnal affection—father and mother, wife and sons, and one’s own life—in order to show that no one was to be supported in sin or loved against God on account of any carnal affection. Rather, for the love of God, if necessary, all carnal affections must be cast aside.

As long as the carnal affections either of our own souls or of our parents or of our children do not obstruct us on the way of God, let us retain them. But if they impede us, let us cast them aside. Certainly, when Paul was going to Jerusalem, the prophet Agabus seized his belt and bound his own feet with it, saying: “The man whose belt this is will be bound in Jerusalem” (Acts 21). But Paul, who perfectly hated his own life, said: “I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of Jesus Christ” (ibid.)—“Nor do I hold my life more precious than myself” (Acts 20).

Behold how he hated his own life—or rather, by hating it, loved it: he cast aside its carnal affection, willing that it should die temporally for the love of Christ, so that it might live eternally with him. Likewise, if the affection of parents or children impedes us from the love of God—as happened in the primitive Church when unbelieving parents, children, and friends were drawing the faithful away from the faith—let us regard them as strangers. Even if they place themselves in our way, let us trample them down and flee to God. For in this matter it is a kind of piety to be cruel.

Second, he urges us to virtues when he adds: “And whoever does not carry his cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.” Many were indeed disciples of Christ who nevertheless did not experience the gallows of the cross. Therefore, the Lord calls not only the gallows of the cross a cross, but also every labor or affliction of body or soul.

Moreover, without great labor and affliction we cannot ascend from the depths to the heights, from vices to virtues. For the way of vices is easy, but the way of virtues is exceedingly difficult. Hence the Lord says: “Broad and wide is the way that leads to life” (Matt. 7). Here, therefore, the Lord tells us that we cannot be his disciples unless we carry our cross—that is, unless we embrace the labor and difficulty of the virtues.

This cross is carried in three ways. Either the body is chastised through labor and abstinence; or the mind is afflicted through compassion for one’s neighbor; or injuries inflicted upon us are endured with equanimity. In the first we possess abstinence and continence; in the second, charity and mercy; in the third, fortitude and patience.

But because some bear the cross of bodily chastisement for the sake of empty glory, or the cross of compassion because of carnal and indiscriminate pity, or the cross of injuries for the sake of empty glory, and because all these people carry the cross but do not follow the Lord, the Lord adds: “and come after me.” Thus, my brothers, we are to embrace both the labor of the virtues in chastising the body, compassion in the mind, and patience in persecution, and we are to do all these things solely for the love and imitation of Christ.

Third, he shows that perseverance is necessary for us when he adds by means of a parable: “For which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the expenses that are necessary, whether he has enough to complete it? Otherwise, after he has laid the foundation and has not been able to finish, all who see it may begin to mock him, saying: ‘This man began to build and was not able to complete it.’”

When, laboring in God’s building, we arrange ascents in our heart (Ps. 83), adding good work to good work and virtue to virtue, what else are we doing than building a tower? For just as a tower does, so the structure of the virtues defends us from enemies and raises us to the heights. Faith lays its foundation; hope raises the walls; charity binds stone to stone; and the lowest virtue constructs its own bulwark. Humility elevates and completes the entire building.

If we wish to build this tower, we must first sit down—that is, resting from the world’s tumults—and calculate the expenses. We calculate the expenses when we discern that, for the heavenly building, every vice must be fled, virtue must be pursued, the soul must be prepared against adversity, the world must be despised, temporal substance must be expended for the love of our Lord, and we must persevere in all these things.

For, just as in constructing an earthly building, so in constructing a heavenly one it is not necessary for us to gather expenses; rather, we must expend them. Hence, when the rich man heard the Lord’s command to leave everything, he went away sorrowful (Matt. 19; Mark 10); and his mind was all the more constricted the more expansive his possessions had made him.

All these expenses, therefore, are necessary for us together with perseverance. If we do not persevere in a good beginning—which God forbid—we render all our labors useless to us, and our enemies, that is, demons and worldly people, will begin to mock us, saying: “This man began to build and was not able to complete it.” As Paul testifies: “We have become a spectacle to the world, to angels and to human beings” (1 Cor. 4).

Therefore, in everything we do we must always think of our hidden adversaries, who lie in wait for our resources; and unless we keep watch against them, we suffer as mockers those whom we had as persuaders toward evil. Hence the Psalmist asks the Lord, saying: “Let not my enemies mock me” (Ps. 24).

Fourth, the Lord demonstrates that, after we have done the things mentioned above, we must never presume upon our merits, but upon God’s mercy alone, when he adds by an analogy from the lesser to the greater: “Or what king, going to engage in war against another king, does not first sit down and consider whether he is able with ten thousand to meet the one who comes against him with twenty thousand? Otherwise, while he is still far away, he sends an embassy and asks for terms of peace.”

The King of kings comes against us, miserable sinners, for judgment. With what an embassy of tears, sighs, and devout works ought we therefore to implore mercy and pardon from him, with whom we are unable to contend in judgment! Foreseeing this and fearing the judgment, the Psalmist asks for mercy, saying: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, Lord, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142).

He comes to judgment against us with twenty thousand, because he sets against us the twofold fulfillment of the Decalogue, which we ought to have fulfilled both in mind and in deed. But if we make much progress, we scarcely meet him with ten thousand—that is, with the outward fulfillment of the Decalogue. For although lust may already have been cut away from the flesh, it has not nevertheless been completely cut away from the heart. He who comes against us examines inner and outer things alike.

What, then, my brothers, shall we do? We can scarcely render an account to the supreme King, who demands double, for half of what is owed, unless, while he is still far away—that is, while he patiently awaits us and delays coming to judgment—we send ahead an embassy of tears, penances, almsgiving, prayers, and every good endeavor, and ask for the pardon of his mercy. For when he is near to us as we are dying and coming to judgment, then there will be no time for sending an embassy and pleading, but rather for receiving according to our merits.

The Lord draws the conclusion from the analogies just given: “So therefore, whoever among you does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple.” It is as though he were saying openly: Just as no one can complete a building properly unless, after sitting down and putting aside other concerns, he calculates the expenses; and just as no one can safely meet a stronger opponent unless, distrusting his own strength, he sends an embassy and asks for peace; so no one can be my elect unless he renounces everything for my sake.

What things? Vices, affections, possessions, and merits. For if, my brothers, we wish to belong to the number of Christ’s elect, we must, for his sake, renounce vices by fleeing them completely; renounce our affections by subordinating them to the divine will; renounce temporal possessions by expending them for the heavenly building; and renounce our merits by distrusting them, however much good we may have done, and taking refuge in God’s mercy alone. Through him may he deign to save us, who lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## XV. OF MANY MARTYRS. SERMON ON THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS

“The saints through faith conquered kingdoms, practiced righteousness, obtained promises” (Heb. 11), etc.

In this reading, my brothers, the Apostle commends faith—not just any faith, but that faith alone which works through hope and charity. Some possess faith without hope, as do the demons. Some possess an apprehension of the truth of invisible things pertaining to religion, together with assent, but nevertheless do not possess hope of salvation, only fear of damnation. Hence James says: “The demons believe and tremble” (Jas. 2).

Others possess faith and also a certain hope of salvation, but do not possess charity, like certain false Christians. They indeed believe and hope, but without benefit, since they do not possess works of charity. Of such people James says: “Faith without works is dead” (ibid.).

Others possess faith and hope working through charity, like true Christians. Concerning this true faith the prophet Habakkuk says: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Hab. 2). The Apostle had described this true faith above, saying: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen” (Heb. 11)—that is, faith is what already causes the promised rewards to subsist through hope in the hearts of the faithful.

By this the faith of demons is excluded, for in them faith is not the substance of things hoped for but rather of things feared. “The proof,” he says, “of things not seen,” because the faith of the righteous, while it works through charity in hope of future rewards—fleeing vices, pursuing virtues, and enduring many dreadful things—is proof to us of the resurrection and future recompense. For unless they had been certain of it, they would never have endured so much to attain it.

By this the faith of false Christians is called into question: while they do not work well but badly, they do not show us proof that they themselves believe; rather, they show that they do not believe in the future resurrection and recompense.

The Apostle therefore commends here the true faith of the righteous, showing two things: namely, how much the righteous accomplished on account of faith, and how much they suffered on account of faith.

First, he shows how much they accomplished through faith when he adds: “The saints through faith conquered kingdoms,” as did Moses, Joshua, Gideon, Samson, and David in the Old Testament. In the New Testament, Constantine through faith in the cross of Christ conquers Maxentius and the army of the barbarians; Heraclius conquers Chosroes, king of the Persians; John and Paul conquer the king of the Scythians; and many other kings conquered many kingdoms.

“They practiced righteousness,” by obeying divine commands, chastising themselves, defending the good, and punishing the wicked. Thus Moses in the Old Testament killed idolaters; Phinehas pierced the Israelite who was fornicating with a Midianite. In the New Testament there was Peter, who in his zeal for righteousness killed Ananias and Sapphira; and Paul, who struck the magician Elymas with blindness.

“And others obtained promises,” as Abraham received the son promised to him in his old age; the children of Israel received the promised land; Aaron received the promise of the priesthood; and David received the promise of the kingdom. In the New Testament, the disciples received the Paraclete promised to them on the day of Pentecost, together with the power of miracles and signs over the sick; and all the faithful in the present life receive grace. After death they receive eternal life.

“They stopped the mouths of lions”: in the Old Testament, David and Samson by destroying the mouths of lions that rose against them, and Daniel by restraining the mouths of hungry lions so that they would not devour him. In the New Testament, hungry lions did not merely refrain from harming the saints exposed to them; they even obeyed them, guarded their flocks, and prepared pits with their claws for burying the bodies of the saints.

“They extinguished the force of fire”: in the Old Testament, the three youths sent by Nebuchadnezzar into the furnace; in the New Testament, the holy Polycarp, Saint Agnes, Saint Agatha, Saint Cecilia, and many other holy men and women extinguished by faith the fire so that it would not harm them.

“They escaped the edge of the sword”—that is, armies of armed men—as did Joshua, Samson, and David in the Old Testament; in the New Testament, Germanus of Auxerre, Bishop Lupus, and many others.

“They recovered from infirmity”: in the Old Testament, Job and Hezekiah; in the New Testament, Paul in Lycaonia, who was stoned and considered dead. Nevertheless, by God’s mercy he recovered for the benefit of many. Saint Sebastian too, shot with arrows by Diocletian and covered with arrows like a hedgehog, nevertheless recovered by God’s grace, as did many others.

“They became strong in war,” in which the few conquered the many under the leadership of Joshua, Samson, or Judas Maccabaeus. In the New Testament, Constantine, Theodosius, Heraclius, Charles, and many other emperors and princes were strong and victorious in war through faith.

“They routed the camps of foreigners”—that is, many in both the Old and New Testaments often put the camps of their enemies to flight.

“Women received their dead back by resurrection”—that is, through resurrection: those who were raised by Elijah and Elisha. In the New Testament, many were raised by Peter and Paul, by the other apostles, and by martyrs and confessors, such as Martin and Hilary, as well as by many others.

All these things, my brothers, although we do not perform them bodily, nevertheless perform them daily in a better way if we possess faith working through charity. For we conquer daily the kingdoms and powers of demons if we resist them and drive them away from ourselves and from others. We also conquer the kingdoms of tyrants if, fearing God more than them, we confront them on behalf of God’s justice.

We practice righteousness if, obeying God’s commands, we correct the wicked and defend the good; if we do not even obey our own sins; and if we chastise ourselves harshly. We also obtain promises when, progressing from good to better, we receive God’s grace working and cooperating with us, as he promised us; and thus, departing from this life, we receive the promise of eternity.

We stop the mouths of lions if, through prayers, we restrain the jaws of demons that hunger for our souls, so that they do not harm us or others. We also extinguish the force of fire if, through fasts and prayers, we quiet within ourselves and in others the fire of lust and covetousness. We escape the edge of the sword if, through prayers and good endeavors, we drive away from ourselves the army of demons seeking to slaughter our souls.

We also recover from infirmity if, after realizing that we have sinned, we immediately rise through repentance and amendment to our former and better state, more cautious than before. We are also strong in war if we struggle manfully against vices and temptations. We put the camps of our enemies to flight if, by the stronger force of prayers, fasts, and good works, we scatter the devil’s fortifications and ambushes. And we raise their dead through resurrection if, by prayer, correction, and instruction, we restore to spiritual life the children of the holy Churches who are dead in sins.

Second, he shows how much the saints suffered through faith when he adds: “Others were tortured”—understood, in torments—not accepting deliverance, that is, not caring about present release from torments, in order that they might obtain a better resurrection. Thus, in the Old Testament, Eleazar, who was afflicted and killed by Antiochus with his wife and seven sons under various torments; in the New Testament, countless martyrs did the same.

“Others experienced mockeries and scourges, and moreover bonds and prisons.” Scourges were endured by Noah and Elisha; bonds and prisons by Joseph, the prophet Micaiah, and many others. In the New Testament, the apostles and countless martyrs experienced the same.

“They were stoned”: in the Old Testament, Jeremiah in Egypt and Ezekiel in Babylon; in the New Testament, Stephen the protomartyr, the apostle Paul, and many others.

“They were sawn in two”: in the Old Testament, Isaiah; in the New Testament, the apostle Bartholomew and many others.

“They were tempted”—understood, by promises—as Joseph was tempted by Potiphar’s wife, and the Maccabees by Antiochus. In the New Testament, many saints were tempted by promises from the devil and from diabolical people, so that, abandoning Christ, they might worship idols: Saint Sebastian, Saint Hippolytus, John and Paul, Saint Agnes, Saint Agatha, Saint Catherine, and many others.

“They died by the slaughter of the sword”: in the Old Testament, Abimelech together with the seventy who wore the ephod, and Uriah; in the New Testament, John the Baptist, the apostle Paul, and many others.

“They wandered”—understood, through various regions of the world—“in *melotes*,” that is, clothed in cheap and rough tunics. Or what it says, “in *melotes*,” is explained by the words that follow, “in goatskins.” For some say that a *melote* is a kind of garment made from goatskins, which, because of its roughness, is worn by Elijah, John the Baptist, and certain other hermits.

“Always in need”—understood, of necessities—“distressed in mind, afflicted by various tribulations.” The world—that is, lovers of the world—was not worthy of their manner of life. “Wandering in deserts, in mountains, in caves, and in holes in the ground,” as did Elijah and the sons of the prophets, whom Obadiah fed by the fifties at that time. In the New Testament, many solitaries lived in this way.

All these things, my brothers, we too endure daily in our measure if we are truly faithful. If we are truly faithful, we are stretched; and even if not in torments, at least through fasts and labors we stretch ourselves toward what lies ahead, not accepting deliverance from bodily affliction, in order that we may find a better resurrection.

If we are truly faithful, we experience mockeries from worldly people who ridicule our good purpose and call us either insane, hypocrites, or impostors. We also frequently suffer scourges, either from human beings or from God, who instructs us with whips like a loving father, for our purification or testing.

If we are faithful, we experience prisons daily: namely, the bonds of divine law and charity, by which we are held lest we either wish or act contrary to God’s will, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4).

Our soul also suffers prisons daily—if not other prisons, at least the constrictions and troubles of the body—while, desiring to depart and be with Christ (Phil. 1), we cry out with the Prophet to the Lord: “Lead my soul out of prison, so that it may confess your name” (Ps. 141).

We are also frequently stoned, if we are faithful, by worldly people—at least with the stones of insults, injuries, slanders, and accusations. We are also divided by all those who hold various opinions about us, some saying: “He is a good man” (John 7), and others saying: “No, but he deceives the crowds” (ibid.).

We are also tempted by our own flesh, by the devil, or by diabolical people who wish to lead us astray. Against them we need divine assistance and daily struggle. We also die by the slaughter of the sword if, by the sword of God’s word penetrating even to our innermost parts, we mortify ourselves, so that we may die to the world but live to God.

We also journey through this world as exiles if, understanding that we do not have here “a permanent city,” we seek the one that is to come (Heb. 13). We do this in goatskins—in literal sackcloth and sacred penitential garments—or by continually considering the lowliness, roughness, and corruption with which we are surrounded.

We are also needy, my brothers, more in divine grace and spiritual virtues than in earthly wages, so that each of us may say daily with the Psalmist: “But I am needy and poor; God, help me” (Ps. 69).

We are also distressed daily when we see another law in our members resisting the law of our mind and taking us captive under the law of sin (Rom. 7), and each of us cries out with the Apostle: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body?” (ibid.).

We are also frequently afflicted for our sins, both in body and in mind, or even in mind for the sins of others, when, considering the countless transgressors of the divine law, each of us can say with the Prophet to the Lord: “My zeal has made me waste away, because my enemies have forgotten your words” (Ps. 118).

We also wander in deserts if, fleeing the frequented and broad paths of worldly destruction and leading a secluded life, we appear to worldly people to be wandering, each of us saying with the Prophet: “Behold, fleeing, I have gone far away and remained in solitude” (Ps. 54). We ascend daily to the mountains of virtues, and yet we hide ourselves in caves by humbling ourselves, and in holes by fleeing human glory.

“And these,” he says, “were approved by the testimony of faith”—understood, by the testimony of their works. It is as though he were saying: All such people, who did and suffered so much, were approved before God by the testimony of faithful works. May the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit deign to help us through both their merit and their reward. Amen.

## XVI. OF MANY MARTYRS. SERMON ON LUKE

“When you hear of wars and seditions, do not be terrified” (Luke 21), and so forth.

Because tribulations, especially those that come unexpectedly, commonly overthrow even the stronger, the Lord and our Redeemer foretold disturbances to his disciples long beforehand, so that they would trouble them less in proportion as they were more strongly armed with the shield of foreknowledge.

First, therefore, he foretold them of the tribulations that would precede and signify the end of the world, together with consolation against them. Second, he foretold that they would be seized and dragged before judges, together with consolation against them. Third, he said that they would be killed by their enemies, together with consolation against this.

First, then, he foretold the tribulations preceding and signifying the end of the world when he said: “When you hear of wars and seditions.” Wars concern enemies, my brothers, but seditions concern citizens. Thus, to indicate that we would be troubled both outwardly and inwardly, he foretold that we would suffer from enemies and from brothers.

For just as the human body in old age suffers more frequently from the preliminary afflictions of death—outwardly from external accidents and inwardly from the discord of the humors—so it will happen, as the end approaches, in the body of the world’s structure. “Nation,” he says, “will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom; and there will be great earthquakes in various places, pestilences and famines, and terrors from heaven,” and, as it is read in certain books, “storms, and there will be great signs.”

These signs are shown to be of various origins: some from heaven, some from earth, some from the elements, and some from human beings. He says: “Nation will rise against nation”—behold, human disturbance. “There will be earthquakes in various places”—behold, the wrath of God from above. “There will be pestilences”—behold, the imbalance of the air.

Because everything must be brought to an end, everything is disturbed before the consummation. And those who offend in all things are punished in all things, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “The world will fight on his behalf” (Wis. 5). Because we misuse everything we had received for the necessities of life, everything is therefore turned against us for vengeance.

We turn the good of peace to the use of security. We love the earthly pilgrimage as though it were the dwelling place of our homeland. We turn the health of our bodies to the abuse of vices. We use the abundance of fertility not for necessity but for pleasure. We turn the serenity of the air toward the vanity of worldly joy. It is just that we should be struck by all things, since we abused all things; and as many perverse pleasures as we derived from them, so many torments should we experience from them.

Why did he add storms among the signs, unless because storms do not preserve the customary order of the seasons? This we have recently experienced, when we saw the entire summer season transformed.

Against these future evils, the Lord consoles his disciples when he adds: “Do not be terrified.” And consequently: “For these things must happen first.” These signs will be for the righteous a source of consolation and instruction. Hence it is first said: “When these things begin to happen, raise your heads, for your redemption is drawing near.” For certain sinners they will be an incentive to hasten repentance. For the reprobate they will be the beginning of eternal punishment.

“But the end,” he says, “will not come immediately.” For the final tribulation is shown through many tribulations. And therefore many evils must precede it, so that they may be able to announce evil without end.

The second part follows, in which the Lord foretells that the disciples will be seized, dragged away, and judged, when he adds: “But before all these things, they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, handing you over to synagogues and prisons and dragging you before kings and governors on account of my name.” As though he were plainly saying: Signs and eternal condemnation are therefore to come upon the reprobate, because they will first deserve this by repaying evil for good. For when you wish to free them from the hand of the devil, they will lay hands upon you. When you likewise wish to free them from condemnation at the eternal judgment, they will drag you before the tribunals of kings and governors. “And they will do these things to you,” he says, “on account of my name.” It is as though he said: They will hate you because of me, although because of me they ought to have loved you. This same cause will be for you the cause of a crown, [Col. 1550A] and for them the cause of eternal condemnation. Hence he adds: “It will happen to you for a testimony.” For a testimony, namely, to your crown and a testimony to their condemnation: when you seek their salvation—which is for you the cause of a crown—they did not believe, but even persecuted you. It is a testimony on your behalf and a testimony against them. For from the very thing from which you receive a crown, they will receive condemnation. Hence the Psalmist says:

“God, do not be silent about my praise,
for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of deceit
have been opened against me.
They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue;
they surrounded me with words of hatred
and attacked me without cause.
In return for loving me, they slandered me,
but I prayed;
they repaid me with evil for good
and hatred for my love” (Ps. 108).

But what will be the outcome for such a man? “When he is judged, let him go forth condemned” (ibid.). Yet God consoles the disciples against the foregoing betrayals and accusations when he adds: “Therefore, take it into your hearts not to deliberate beforehand how you should answer. For I will give you a mouth”—that is, eloquence—“and wisdom, which all your adversaries will not be able to resist or contradict.” It is as though he said: Do not deliberate beforehand against such people, for even if you produce the words, I speak through you; and if you enter the contest, I fight through you.

The third part follows, in which the Lord foretells to his disciples that they will also be put to death by friends, when [Col. 1550C] he adds: “You will be handed over by brothers, parents, and relatives, and they will put some of you to death.” It is more bearable to suffer at the hands of strangers than at the hands of friends. Torments inflicted by friends cause us greater pain, because, along with bodily harm, the evil of lost affection tortures us. Hence the Lord says through the Psalmist concerning Judas the betrayer:

“Indeed, if my enemy had cursed me,
I would certainly have borne it.
But you, a man of one mind with me,
my leader and my acquaintance” (Ps. 54).

And again:

“The man of my peace, in whom I trusted,
who ate my bread,
has magnified his treachery against me” (Ps. 40).

All these things, my brothers, were happening in the primitive Church, when the devil, raging because of his expulsion, had stirred up such fury among the persecutors that the fervor of idolatry overcame natural [Col. 1550D] affection. They even hated and persecuted, both against nature and against God, their sons and friends, whom human beings ordinarily love by the force of nature. But because he had foretold that they would be put to death, he immediately consoles them, adding: “Not a hair from your head will perish.” A hair, my brothers, is the smallest part of our body, and even when it is cut off it is not felt. This is therefore an argument from the lesser. It is as though one were saying: If that which is least in you, and whose cutting causes no pain, cannot perish, much less can that which is greater in you, and whose cutting causes pain, perish.

Mystically, however, not only will our bones—that is, our mighty deeds or words—not perish, but they will be rewarded; even our hairs—that is, our good thoughts, which proceed from the brain as though from the heart—will not perish before God, but will be granted their just recompense.

“In your patience,” he says, “you will possess your souls.” Just as, my brothers, the impatient person does not possess his own soul, but is rather overcome by anger, sadness, indignation, and the other disturbances of the soul, so the patient person possesses his soul when he rules over the soul’s disturbances. Through patience, therefore, we possess the souls that possess the body, when we govern them by reason toward the evenness of patience. Solomon says of this:

“The patient man is better than the brave,
and he who rules his spirit is better than one who captures cities” (Prov. 16).

Little is overcome by strength, but everything is overcome by patience. Solomon says again concerning patience:

“The discipline of a man is known through patience” (Prov. 19).

Therefore, the more patient someone is, the more learned he is.

It should be noted, moreover, that we endure some things from God, some from the devil, and some from our neighbor. From God we endure scourges, from the devil temptations, and from our neighbor injuries. We ought to bear God’s scourges with such equanimity that we do not murmur, but rather, understanding that he acts justly in all things and chastises his own with paternal affection, bless him. We ought likewise to endure the temptations of the devil or of the flesh in such a way that, with God’s help, we do not despair of victory, but resist them manfully, lest we incline toward delight in them or consent to them.

We ought to endure our neighbor’s injuries in such a way that we are moved not to revenge but rather to compassion, understanding that before God it is not the one who suffers, but the one who inflicts the injury, who is miserable. We will be able to do this if we consider the matter in the following way: that we suffer nothing without the just judgment of God, whose ordering must not be resisted; that we suffer justly for our sins, and therefore must not be angry against *lunam* [“the moon”; perhaps an OCR corruption], but against our vices; and that it is not the human being, but the devil, acting through the human being upon whom he sits as upon an instrument, who persecutes us. Therefore, we must fight not against the human being, but against the devil, the persecutor of the wretched person, so that we may drive out the devil and, rescuing the human being from his power, win him for God through love and good deeds.

For all wicked people are harassed by the devil and, as though driven mad, pay no attention to what they are doing. Hence the protomartyr Stephen suffers at the hands of the Jews and, taking pity on their madness, prays for them, saying: “Lord, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Acts 6).

Blessed Gregory relates that Stephen, the father of a monastery situated near the city of Reate, was a very holy man and distinguished in penitence. For the love of heavenly things he had despised all earthly things and avoided possessing anything in this world. He avoided the tumult of human beings and devoted himself to frequent and lengthy prayers. He had such patience that he considered anyone who inflicted some annoyance upon him to be his helper. In return for insults he gave thanks, and he regarded harm done to his poverty as his own gain.

When the day of his death summoned him, many gathered to commend their souls to the holy man. Some saw angels entering with bodily eyes, while others saw nothing; but such great fear seized both groups that, as that holy soul departed, no one was able to remain there. Consider, my brothers, how greatly almighty God terrifies when he comes as the strict and visible judge, if, when he came as the gracious, rewarding, and invisible one, he so terrified those standing nearby. Behold how that patience, preserved in ecclesiastical peace, raised him to such a height of glory. He died without being struck by any sword, yet he received in reward the crown that he had held by the merit of the virtue of patience.

We too, my brothers, if we preserve the virtue of patience, will by no means be deprived of the crown of martyrdom. For John the Evangelist is said to have drunk from the cup of suffering at the Lord’s hand, yet he is recorded to have died in peace rather than by the sword. Therefore, my brothers, let us hold fast to the virtue of patience; let us learn to love our enemies and do good to our persecutors, so that by the prayers of the holy martyrs we may deserve to share in their fellowship, by the generosity of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## XVII. OF VERY MANY MARTYRS. SERMON ON THE BOOK OF WISDOM

“The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and the torment of wickedness will not touch them” (Wis. 3), and so forth.

When unbelievers and false Christians see the righteous brought low in this life, suffering insults, injuries, and tribulations, and departing this life amid distress and torments, they think either that God does not exist or that he does not care for mortals, and that human beings perish in soul and body. Since we believe that souls cannot die, but that the souls of the righteous always live blessedly and the souls of the wicked always suffer punishment, they say: “Where are the souls of the righteous?”

Therefore, dearest brothers, this sacred Scripture speaks against them, demonstrating three things: where the souls of the righteous are; that those righteous people are not dead; and to what great blessings they have attained through tribulations.

First, then, it shows where the souls of the righteous are when it says: “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God.” But are not all things in God’s hand? Certainly they are, but in different ways. The hand of God is called either God’s power, in which all things are without exception, “for all the ends of the earth are in his hand” (Ps. 94); or punishment inflicted by God: “The hand of the Lord,” Job says, “has touched me” (Job 19); or God’s protection, whence the prophet says: “The hand of the Lord was with me, strengthening me” (Ezek. 3).

Thus, my brothers, the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God because they are in God’s protection. Explaining this, he adds: “And the torment of eternal death”—or “the torment of wickedness,” namely, the torment owed to the wickedness of the reprobate, which is to be punished forever—“will not touch them.”

The souls of the righteous, therefore, are undoubtedly in the heavenly dwellings of eternal blessedness, which were prepared for them from the beginning, as the Lord says: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John 14). Where are they, then? In the hand of God, who bestows every good and pleasant thing upon them and removes every evil and sorrowful thing from them, according to the saying: “God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints, and death will be no more, nor mourning, nor crying” (Rev. 21).

The souls of the reprobate, however, are undoubtedly tormented forever in the punishments of Gehenna, which we believe to be beneath the earth, as the prophet says: “You have delivered my soul from the lowest hell” (Ps. 85). Many believe that this place is in the mountains of Sicily, which belch forth perpetual fire, because many souls of the reprobate are said either to have been seen or heard to be carried there by demons.

Gregory relates that a certain hermit who lived in Sicily saw the soul of the tyrant and heretic Theodoric—who had killed the religious men Symmachus and Boethius—being hurled into that cauldron of Vulcan. We read, however, that the souls of sinners who departed this life in confession, penance, and the intention of amendment are purged, by God’s disposition, not in hell but in places of punishment, until, having been completely purified, they enter the heavenly dwellings.

Hence we read in the Dialogues that blessed Germanus, bishop of Capua, found the soul of the Roman deacon Paschasius in the heat of the baths and, after he had prayed, obtained forgiveness for it. We read in the same work that a certain very religious priest, who went daily to the nearby baths to wash before celebrating Mass, found there someone in a miserable condition who removed his shoes and ministered to him. When on the following day he brought him bread, the man replied that he had died there and was doing penance there, and that he had no need of material bread but rather of sacrifices and prayers. “Please,” he said, “do these things for me. And if, when you return, you do not find me, know for certain that I have obtained pardon.” And so it happened.

The souls of the reprobate who are tormented in the punishments of Gehenna fear the day of judgment, because then, when they have taken up their bodies again, their punishments too will be doubled. The souls of the elect, however, long for that day, because then they will be glorified more perfectly in body as they already are in soul. Hence John says in the Apocalypse:

“I saw beneath the altar of God”—that is, in holy and hidden repose—“the souls of those slain because of the word of God, crying out in a loud voice: ‘How long, O holy and true Lord, will you not judge our blood and avenge us upon those who dwell on the earth?’ And individual white robes were given to them. And they were told to rest for a little while longer, until the number of their brothers should be completed” (Rev. 6).

Second, it is demonstrated that although the righteous seem to die, they nevertheless live eternally and blessedly, when it is added: “In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died, and their departure was regarded as affliction. But they are in peace.”

The foolish have only bodily eyes, such as irrational animals also possess. They do not have spiritual eyes, by which God and invisible things are seen, and therefore they think that nothing else exists except what they see with bodily eyes. Thus, like beasts, they eagerly pursue only visible things, while they do not care about invisible things because they do not even suspect that they exist.

“And their departure,” he says, “was regarded as affliction, and their journey from us as destruction.” It is as though he were saying more plainly: They think that the death of the righteous—which is a departure into rest and a journey from this age to the homeland—is merely affliction, that is, punishment, and destruction, that is, alienation from life.

Beautifully, then, he calls the death of the saints destruction, departure, and journey, because at that time they go out and travel from prison to freedom, from fear to security, from darkness to light, from sadness to joy, from exile to the homeland, and from misery to blessedness.

“But they,” he says, “are in peace,” possessing peace from all things and with all things: from demons, from human beings, and from their own flesh. From now on, demons can no longer trouble them, since they have not been banished farther away; nor can human beings trouble them, since there they can do nothing but remain at rest. Nor can the flesh rebel, since it will not be able to disagree with the spirit’s will. They have peace with all: with God, with their neighbors, and with themselves. For such harmony exists in that blessed life, my brothers, that the saints will in no way disagree either with the divine will or with one another.

Third, eight blessings are set forth that the righteous attain through the tribulations of this world.

The first is the immortality of soul and body, concerning which it is added: “Although they suffered torments in the sight of human beings, their hope is full of immortality.” The hope of hypocrites, who suffer for the sake of empty glory, is empty. Hence Job says: “The hope of the hypocrite will perish” (Job 8). But the hope of the righteous, who suffer for God’s sake, will attain the fullness of their desire, because “God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints,” and so forth (Rev. 21).

The second is the multiplication of divine rewards, concerning which it is added: “Afflicted in few things, they will be well provided for in many.” This is what the Apostle says: “I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8). Present sufferings are few, slight, and momentary; future rewards, however, will be many, immense, [Col. 1554D] and eternal.

The third is dignity, concerning which it is added: “For God tested”—that is, proved—“them, and found them worthy of himself.” Since they could not be separated from God through many temptations, they are worthy in their merits, so that they may be raised to such dignity of rewards that they may be called and be the friends and sons of God: “Indeed, heirs of God, and fellow heirs with Christ” (ibid.).

The fourth blessing that the saints attain through tribulations is complete purity, concerning which it is added: “As gold in the furnace, he tested them.” Gold examined in the furnace is rendered pure and clean; so the saints, through tribulations, are purified from every stain and become wholly clean and pure, so that they may be worthy of the divine presence.

The fifth is acceptability, concerning which it is added: “And he accepted them as a holocaust offering.” There was only one true holocaust—that is, wholly burned and consumed by the flame of charity—our Lord Jesus, whom God the Father smelled as an aroma of sweetness. In faith and imitation of him, the saints too offered themselves wholly to God as a sacrifice kindled by the ardor of charity. God also smelled them as an aroma of sweetness, and they were pleasing to him.

The sixth is radiance, concerning which it is added: “The righteous will shine.” This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of my Father” (Matt. 13). And if each of them will shine like the sun, how much more will they all shine together?

The seventh is the power of judging, concerning which it is added: “And like sparks they will run through the stubble; they will judge nations,” and so forth. This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “You who have followed me will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19).

The stubble signifies the assembly of the reprobate, who, like stubble, are light, empty, and destined for flame; the sparks signify judicial sentences, which, like sparks, are subtle, bright, and kindling. The saints, therefore, will run like sparks through the reprobate by the judicial sentence, distinguishing them subtly, judging them openly as material destined to be burned, and consuming them in greater or lesser eternal fires.

The eighth is dominion or kingship, concerning which it is added: “And they will rule over peoples.” This is what the Psalmist says: “And the righteous will rule over them in the morning” (Ps. 48)—without doubt, over the reprobate. “And their Lord,” he says, “will reign forever.” With him they too will reign, as the Lord says to them: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25).

May God cause us to be joined to them, and may our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, do so. Amen.

## XVIII. OF VERY MANY MARTYRS. SERMON ON LUKE

“Jesus said to his disciples: ‘Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy’” (Matt. 8; Luke 12), and so forth.

This reading from the holy Gospel has four parts. First, dearest brothers, the Lord commands us to beware of hypocrisy. Second, he commands us to fear not human beings but God alone. Third, he shows that God himself is also to be loved. Fourth, he shows what he will do to those who confess him and to those who deny him.

First, then, he commands us to beware of hypocrisy when he says: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.” “Beware,” that is, be watchful and guard yourselves. Other vices, because they are open, are immediately recognized. But because the vice of hypocrisy comes under the appearance of virtue, it deceives even many wise people. Therefore we must keep watch against it with greater caution and attention.

Hypocrisy is a vice concealed beneath the color of virtue; hence it received its name. For *hypocrisis* is interpreted as “gilded on the surface.” This vice is worse the more hidden it is. Simulated equity is not equity but doubled iniquity, because it possesses a double evil: iniquity and pretense.

The Lord warns us elsewhere to beware of it, saying: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matt. 7).

There are three kinds of hypocrisy. Some do not perform good works but pretend to perform them. Others publicly perform certain good works, but because they perform them for empty glory, they pretend to perform them for God. Still others perform certain good works as though secretly, appearing to avoid human glory, but in their very secret activity they desire to be discovered, so that they may thereby obtain greater human glory, because they seem to flee from it. Although they do not appear to be seen by human beings, nevertheless, because they do these things in order to be seen by human beings, they have received their reward.

The Lord appropriately calls hypocrisy “leaven.” For just as, according to the Apostle, a little leaven corrupts the whole batch (1 Cor. 5), so hypocrisy corrupts the whole life of a human being. Leaven makes bread swollen, sour, full of air-holes, and light. Hypocrisy likewise makes a person swollen through the inflammation of empty glory; sour through the bitterness of an alien life, which God does not wish to incorporate into himself; full of air-holes through the emptiness in which the devil can find a hiding place; and light through vanity, so that any favor or fear can move him here and there.

Thus the hypocrite is aptly signified by a reed, as the Lord says of John the Baptist: “What did you go out into the desert to see—a reed shaken by the wind?” (Matt. 9). A reed is externally beautiful, internally empty, mobile, and fragile. So the hypocrite appears beautiful outwardly, borrowing the color of virtues; inwardly he is empty of every good; he is driven here and there by every wind of praise or blame; and when adversity strikes, he is easily shaken.

Hence the Lord says to blessed Job concerning the devil: “He sleeps in the shade, in the secret place of the reed” (Job 40), because the devil inhabits dark and deceitful minds, which are light and fragile.

The Lord also appropriately says, “the leaven of the Pharisees.” For “Pharisees” is interpreted as “divided.” They were divided from the common fellowship of human beings in clothing and dwelling, in food, and in the pretense of certain observances. It is characteristic of the hypocrite, who seeks to appear singular and alone, to disdain the community and seek singularity, so that he may appear above others and be able to say: “I am not like the rest of humanity” (Luke 18).

He takes more pleasure in one fast performed alone than if he fasted seven days with others, and more pleasure in one private prayer uttered secretly than in a night of psalmody. In choir he begins first and ends last. The person who desires to be seen before others is always doing something before others. By contrast, it is characteristic of religious men to observe the whole of religion, restrain themselves beneath others, and not wish to appear above others.

The Lord demonstrates why hypocrisy must be avoided when he adds: “Nothing is covered that will not be revealed, and nothing hidden that will not be known.” It is as though he were plainly saying: You must therefore beware of hypocrisy, because certainly either here or on the day of judgment their hypocrisy and your goodness, which is now hidden, will be revealed and rewarded, when, according to Daniel, “the Ancient of Days will sit, the books will be opened, and everything will be made manifest to all” (Dan. 7).

No evil, therefore, is now so covered by the veil of pretense that it will not be revealed—either here to the priest through confession, for forgiveness, or in the future to everyone through the revelation of consciences, for everlasting shame. Nor is any good so hidden now through avoidance of empty glory that it will not be known, either here or in the future, for reward.

Works done in darkness or hiding places are secret. The intentions of hearts are even more secret, and the purposes and ends of intentions are most secret. Yet all these things will be revealed by the Lord, “who will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts” (1 Cor. 4).

Hence he adds: “For what you have said or done in darkness will be spoken in the light. And what you have spoken or done in the ear”—that is, in secret—“in bedrooms will be proclaimed on the rooftops”—that is, openly. He speaks according to the custom of Palestine, where heralds speak to the people from the rooftops, which are flat above.

These words can partly be referred to the present time, since what Christ’s disciples first spoke in darkness—that is, in the shadow of prisons and afflictions—and in secret is now proclaimed publicly throughout the world in the Church.

The second part follows, in which the Lord commands us to fear not human beings but God alone, when he adds: “I say to you, my friends: Do not be terrified by those who kill the body and after that have nothing more they can do. But I will show you whom you should fear. Fear him who, after he has killed, has power to cast into Gehenna.”

If we consider the matter carefully, brothers, God alone is to be feared. Neither human beings, nor demons, nor wild beasts, nor serpents, nor any other creature can harm us unless the Lord permits it. Thus the devil could not have touched even one of Job’s sheep unless he had first received power from the Lord (Job 1). Nor could he have entered the herd of swine unless the Lord had permitted it (Mark 5). “There is no authority except from God” (Rom. 13). Hence the Lord said to Pilate: “You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above” (John 19). “There is no evil in the city,” he says, “which God has not done” (Amos 3).

God, therefore, is the author of all punishments; demons and human beings are ministers. Thus the Lord calls the most wicked king of the Assyrians, through whom he scourged the idolatrous Israelites, his rod, saying: “Assyria is the rod of my anger” (Isa. 10).

The devil, therefore, neither human beings, nor wild beasts, nor serpents, nor any other creature is to be feared; rather, God alone is to be feared in all these things, for he scourges those whom he wishes through them as through instruments. Whoever can have God with him can fear nothing.

Hence the Apostle says: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Rom. 8). It is as though he were plainly saying: If God is for us, then even if someone appears to be against us, he is nevertheless for us, since the things he inflicts not only do us no harm but even benefit us. Hence it is written: “He who fears God will tremble at nothing” (Ecclus. 34).

And the philosopher says: “He who fears God fears nothing. And he who fears God is feared by all. But he who does not fear God fears everything.”

Therefore, my brothers, let us fear offending God above all things, because if we have God with us, we can fear nothing. Let us know that if God permits scourges and tribulations to befall those who fear him, he will nevertheless cause them to turn out for their good.

The third part follows, in which he demonstrates that God is also to be loved along with fear, when it is added: “Are not five sparrows sold for two asses, that is, for two small coins, and not one of them is forgotten before God? Therefore do not fear; you are worth more than many sparrows”—“in price” is understood.

It is as though he were saying: You must not only fear God but also love him, for he is so kind that he does not forget to provide for insignificant birds and, what is more, for those who despise him. How much more will he provide for us, his rational creatures who love him, and offer us his protection?

Mystically, the five sparrows are worldly people devoted to the five bodily senses. They fly upward through empty glory; they are brought down to the earth through love of earthly things; they live off what belongs to another through rapacity; they are caught by the devil through deception; and they are sold for two asses—that is, for the paltry price of earthly desire and pleasure—to the eternal condemnation of soul and body.

But if God remembers even such people, either by providing them with bodily necessities or by calling them many times to salvation through repentance, how much more will he remember his faithful, who always cling to him, love him with their whole heart, and obey him in all things?

“But even the hairs of your head,” he says, “are all numbered.” It is as though he were saying: You must fear and love not human beings but God alone, by whom not only your souls and bodies but also every smallest part of you, including those parts whose removal is not felt, are preserved according to their number.

You should not fear, therefore, that the greater things in you will perish, since even these smallest things cannot perish in you while the Lord preserves them.

Mystically, the hairs of your head—that is, the subtle thoughts of your heart—are numbered before God, because neither their subtlety nor their multitude can deceive the supreme Judge, who will render recompense for each one and for all of them. If, then, God reserves for judgment not only deeds and words but even the smallest thoughts, with what diligence ought we, my brothers, to guard our hearts, lest evil or empty thoughts arise in them, or, once they arise, grow; instead, the little ones of Babylon must immediately be seized and dashed against the rock, Christ.

The fourth part follows, in which the Lord shows what he will do to those who confess him and to those who deny him.

First, he shows what he will do to those who confess him when he adds: “Everyone who confesses me before human beings, the Son of Man will also confess him before the angels of God.”

Confession, my brothers, is not merely a matter of the mouth. Whoever proclaims Christ with the mouth alone does indeed acknowledge him, but does not confess him. Hence the Lord says: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matt. 15).

Confession is true, however, when heart, mouth, and deed are in harmony. For the faith of the heart alone is not sufficient unless there is also, especially where necessary, confession of the mouth. Thus Peter, believing in his heart but denying Christ with his mouth, would have incurred condemnation had he not washed away his sin with tears of repentance. As Paul says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10).

Neither faith of the heart nor confession of the mouth is sufficient, however, unless, when the time is present, testimony by deed follows. For James testifies: “Faith without works is dead. The demons also believe and tremble” (James 2). Hence in the Gospel they say: “Son of God, why have you come to torment us before the time?” (Matt. 8).

Whoever, therefore, wishes truly to confess Christ must confess him simultaneously with heart, mouth, and deed, and also before human beings: that is, he must neither fear nor be ashamed to confess or imitate Christ’s humility, passion, cross, and other reproaches publicly before human beings, where such confession can benefit many through example.

And what will Christ do for those who confess him in this way? “He will confess him before the angels of God.” It is as though he were saying: Those who confess publicly, he will confess publicly. He will confess them with heart, mouth, and deed: with the heart, by truly loving them as brothers and fellow heirs; with the mouth, by saying to them: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25); and by deed, by bringing them into the kingdom of eternal blessedness.

What he will do to those who deny him, he adds: “But whoever denies me before human beings will be denied before the angels of God.”

All who deny Christ—either with the heart, like Jews and pagans; or with the mouth, like imperfect Christians who fear dying for him; or by their deeds, like false Christians who confess God in words but deny him by their actions—all these, I say, will be denied by Christ likewise in heart, mouth, and deed: in the heart, by his hating and rejecting them; with the mouth, by saying to them: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity” (Matt. 7); and by deed, by casting them into eternal fire.
