Therefore, brothers, let us confess Christ: with the heart, truly believing in and loving him; with the mouth, continually blessing him; and by our deeds, imitating his life and conduct, striving after his poverty and humility, patience, charity, and other virtues, and obeying his commands. Thus may he confess us on the day of judgment and, with his saints, make us sharers in eternal joys. Amen.

## XIX. OF VERY MANY MARTYRS. SERMON ON THE BOOK OF WISDOM
The righteous will stand with great confidence against those who afflicted them and took away their labors [Col. 1560A] (Wis. 5), and so forth.

Since, brothers, in this world the righteous are stripped, oppressed, and harassed by the wicked, and consequently are often saddened and disturbed, while, conversely, the wicked glory in the plunder and oppression of the righteous, this reading offers consolation to the righteous and correction to sinners. First, it shows how great a power the righteous will have over the wicked at the resurrection; second, what the wicked will suffer; third, what they will say about their own misery and the glory of the righteous.

First, then, the power that the righteous will have over the wicked at the judgment is shown when it says: “The righteous will stand with great confidence against those who afflicted them,” and so forth. But since the Lord says in the Gospel that the righteous will sit upon twelve thrones at the judgment and judge the twelve tribes of Israel, what does it mean here when it says, “they will stand”? It means that sitting belongs to one who judges, while standing belongs to one who carries out vengeance. Thus, concerning Phinehas, who, out of zeal for justice, pierced the Israelite fornicating with the Midianite, it is written: “Phinehas stood, and made atonement, and the plague ceased” (Ps. 105).

One who exercises justice against the guilty must stand: stand in virtue, stand in uprightness, and stand in firmness. He must stand in virtue. For if he slips into vice, how will he condemn the vicious? How can an adulterer condemn an adulterer, a miser a miser, or a thief a thief? Hence Truth says: “Let him who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her” (John 8). He must stand in firmness, so that no mercy may turn him aside from the severity of the deserved sentence. For, as the philosopher says: “The judge is condemned when the guilty person is acquitted.” He must stand in uprightness, so that he condemns those who must be condemned according to the penalty they deserve and with the resolve required.

It is rightly said, therefore, of the righteous that they will stand with great confidence: confirmed in the confidence of virtue, in the confidence of firmness, in the confidence of uprightness, and in justice. Then, my brothers, there will be a time for exercising justice against the wicked, just as now is the time for exercising mercy and patience toward them. For the Lord came at his first advent to call sinners through patience and mercy; at the second he will come to judge sinners through justice. Thus, the righteous now exercise mercy and patience toward the wicked, but in the future they will exercise only justice [Col. 1560D] and punishment.

Then the elect will be so joined to the divine will that they will be able to desire nothing except what they know the Lord desires, and they will be able to love nothing except what they know the Lord loves. Therefore they will not be moved by the condemnation of their parents and friends; rather, they will consent to divine justice and rejoice in it, according to the Psalmist’s saying: “The righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance” (Ps. 58).

“Against,” he says, “those who afflicted them and took away their labors.” The wicked afflict the good in this world in two ways: either by inflicting evils upon them or by despising their goods. For even if they inflict no other evils, they nonetheless greatly afflict and torment the righteous inwardly by despising God, rejecting his commandments, and refusing even to hear words of salvation. Hence the Psalmist says: “My zeal consumed me, because my enemies forgot your words” (Ps. 118); and again: “The zeal of your house has consumed me” (Ps. 68).

The wicked likewise take away the labors of the righteous in two ways: either by plundering their temporal possessions or by rendering fruitless the labors that the righteous undertake in correcting and admonishing them for the sake of their conversion. Therefore the Lord commands them to shake the dust from their feet against those who refuse to receive their words, as a testimony against them (Matt. 10).

The righteous will therefore rightly stand with great confidence and pass sentence against them, so that just as the wicked took away the labors of the saints, their own labors may likewise be taken away, because “they will leave their riches to strangers, and their tombs will be their houses forever” (Ps. 48). But if they should happen to perform some good labor, it will be taken away from them so that it may not benefit them for salvation. And just as they afflicted the saints, so they themselves will be afflicted forever, both in soul and body, in the fires of Gehenna, according to what the Lord says in the Apocalypse to his saints, who were harassed by the synagogue of the reprobate: “Repay her,” he says, “as she herself has repaid you, and pay her back double according to her deeds. In the cup that she mixed, mix for her double. As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much give her torment and mourning” (Rev. 18).

Second, four punishments are shown that the reprobate will generally suffer in the life to come [Col. 1561C]. The first is terror, concerning which it follows: “Seeing, they will be shaken with terrible fear.” The preceding word “seeing” shows the source of such fear: they will see the majesty of the dreadful Judge and all the saints whom they will see pronouncing a sentence of condemnation against them; they will also see the terrifying demons to whom they will see themselves being handed over; and they will see the infernal torments prepared for them.

But they will see the majesty of the supreme Judge and of the saints only before the judgment or during the judgment itself. After the judgment they will in no way be able to see them. For it is written: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26). [Col. 1561D] The saints, however, will always be able to see the reprobate in their torments, so that, by seeing the punishments which the reprobate themselves incurred by sinning and which the saints escaped, they may always have causes for glorifying God and praising, on the one hand, God’s mercy and, on the other, God’s justice.

The second punishment is envy, concerning which it follows: “And they will marvel”—that is, they will be tortured by envy as they marvel at the suddenness of an unexpected salvation. For envy arises from astonishment and hatred. Since the reprobate will see those whom they hated suddenly and unexpectedly glorified with God, they will be inwardly tortured by envy and will waste away, experiencing as many and as great torments as they see glorifications among the saints.

How great a punishment envy is, Solomon shows when he says: “Envy is the rottenness of the bones” (Prov. 14). It is as though he said: it wastes away not only the flesh but even the bones. The poet also says:

> Nothing is more just than envy, which immediately  
> punishes and torments its own author.

And another says:

> The tyrants of Sicily never discovered  
> a greater torment than envy.  
> (Horace, *Epistles*, book 1, vv. 57–58.)

The third is repentance, concerning which it follows: “Repenting within themselves.” Indeed, the reprobate, who were unwilling to repent in this world, will then, whether they wish it or not, repent forever. Repentance will be forced from them by the public exposure of all their shameful deeds, which will be visible to everyone, and by the endless torment of their punishments.

The anguish of that repentance will therefore be greater inwardly in proportion as the shame of the deeds revealed to everyone is greater outwardly, and in proportion to the torment of the punishments inflicted. Moreover, that repentance will be utterly fruitless: it will not lessen punishment but double it. For in hell there will be no redemption, and therefore no remedies can avail there.

The fourth is sorrow, concerning which it follows: “And groaning in anguish of spirit.” Seeing that by a just judgment they are being handed over to eternal condemnation, where “the worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished” (Isa. 66), they will groan, lament, and howl with their spirit constricted by grief. They will wish to die, but death will flee from them.

Let us therefore, my brothers, anticipate these punishments while we may and turn them to our benefit. Let us fear that eternal condemnation, and, fearing it, let us cease from sin and strive to do good. Let us admire the virtue and blessedness of the saints, not through envy like the reprobate, but through emulation and imitation. Let us also repent of our transgressions and, while we may, redeem them through penitential tears and works of mercy. Let us likewise grieve that by sinning we have deserved eternal condemnation. Through continual sorrows of heart and compunction, let us anticipate eternal pains and turn them away from us. Let us repent here, so that we may not repent there forever. Let us mourn here, so that we may not mourn there forever.

Third, what the reprobate will say in the life to come is shown when it follows: “These are the ones whom we once held in derision and as a byword”—that is, as an object of reproach [Col. 1562D]. “We fools considered their life madness and their end without honor.”

Those whom, in this world, they thought foolish although they were wise and righteous, they will then understand, at the time of recompense, to have been wise; and they will recognize themselves, conversely, to have been foolish. Here it must be considered that the reprobate will retain the powers of the soul and the senses of the body intact in the life to come.

They will have a complete memory, so that, remembering how foolishly and wickedly they behaved toward the saints, they may be punished more severely for it. They will also have a complete rational faculty, so that, understanding that they are justly condemned while the righteous are justly saved, they may be punished more severely for it. They will likewise have complete foresight, so that, foreseeing their own condemnation and the blessedness of the righteous, they may be punished more severely for it [Col. 1563A].

They will similarly retain bodily sight intact, so that, seeing the horrors of the demons and of the punishments, they may be punished more severely for it. They will retain hearing intact, so that, hearing the shrieks of the torments and the roarings of the demons, they may be punished more severely for it. They will retain taste intact, so that, tasting every kind of bitterness, they may be punished more severely for it. Hence the rich man dressed in purple asks in hell for a drop of water from Lazarus’s finger to cool his tongue, but does not receive it, because he had received good things during his life, while Lazarus had likewise received bad things (Luke 16).

They will retain smell intact, so that, smelling every kind of stench, they may be punished more severely for it. They will retain touch intact, so that, feeling all the harshness of the punishments, they may be punished more severely for it. [Col. 1563B] Indeed, they will be punished in every respect because they offended in every respect.

By saying, “These are the ones whom we once held in derision,” they show that they despised the righteous in this life. For people deride those whom they despise. By saying that they held them as a byword of reproach, they show that they hated them. For people reproach by means of a byword those whom they hate, throwing their weaknesses and excesses in their faces, as in: “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matt. 27), and similar sayings.

By saying, “We fools considered their life madness,” they also show that they avoided the conduct and life of the saints as though they were madness, and loved a life opposed to theirs. “And their end,” he says, “without honor.” For when the reprobate saw the saints suffering many things here, departing from this life through tribulations and torments as though they were murderers, and their bodies either left unburied to wild beasts and birds or committed to a dishonorable burial, they considered their death wretched and without honor. Miserable people, they did not know “that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of heaven” (Acts 14), nor that, wherever and however the bodies of the saints may be laid, they are buried in peace, and their names live forever (Ecclus. 46).

But because the rich and powerful of this world die amid riches, services, and the mourning of their friends, and are buried with pomp and ceremony, they think that their death is honorable. They do not know that, just as Lazarus is carried from the dungheap by angels to blessed rest, so the rich man is thrown from his purple bed by demons into hell (Luke 16).

“How, then,” they say, “are they counted among the sons of God, and how is their lot among the saints?” And we”—understand: among the sons of God—“are counted, while our lot is among the condemned.

They marvel, wasting away with envy, at how those people could pass from such lowliness to such glory, from such affliction to such blessedness, and from so many tears to such joys; and, conversely, how they themselves could pass from such worldly glory to such misery, from such prosperity to such torment, and from such joy to so many tears.

Therefore, my brothers, let us imitate the life and conduct of the saints, so that through their intercessions we may deserve to be exalted, honored, and glorified with them in eternal blessedness. Amen.

## XX. OF MANY MARTYRS. SERMON ON LUKE

Jesus said to his disciples: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me; but whoever despises me despises him who sent me” (Luke 10), and the rest.

This reading, my brothers, has four parts. First, when the Lord sends the seventy-two to preach, he says that both he and the Father are either heard or despised in them, when he says: “Whoever hears you hears me,” and so forth.

In these words the Lord Jesus shows us three things: namely, that his disciples and their successors hold his place in the Church; that, for this reason, they must prepare themselves entirely worthy of this vicariate; and that their subjects must show them every kind of reverence [Col. 1564B].

The vicars of Christ hold his place in the Church in three things: in instruction, in the administration of the sacraments, and in the power of binding and loosing. In these matters they should understand that they are not authors but only ministers, according to Paul’s saying: “Let a person regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God” (1 Cor. 4).

The vicars of Christ must show themselves worthy of his vicariate in three things: in teaching, in life, and in intention. In teaching, so that they preach not another doctrine but Christ’s doctrine; in life, so that, as far as they are able, they maintain not another life and conduct but Christ’s life and conduct; in intention, so that they seek not their own glory but Christ’s glory and the salvation of souls. Hence the Lord says: “Whoever serves me,” he says, “must follow me” (John 12).

Likewise, subjects must show reverence to the vicars of Christ in three things: in obedience, in honor, and in the provision of temporal support, so that they honor Christ in Christ’s vicars, minister to Christ, and obey Christ.

But if the vicars of Christ do not hold to Christ’s doctrine, Christ no longer says to them, “Whoever hears you hears me.” If they do not follow Christ’s life and intention, Christ no longer says to them, “Whoever despises you despises me.” Subjects ought to despise and flee the corrupt doctrine and life of vicars, while nevertheless honoring the author in the ministers.

Second, the seventy-two disciples return with joy, saying: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name.” In three respects they act well and offer a good example to future preachers: namely, in returning through preaching to the school of Christ; in confessing Christ the Lord and author of what they have accomplished; and in attributing these things not to their own virtues or merits but to the power of Christ’s name [Col. 1564D].

So we preachers, after preaching has been done, must return to the master of the sacred Scriptures, so that we may review what we have preached. If we have exceeded ourselves in anything while preaching, we must correct it, and we must foresee what we are going to preach again. We must also confess our Lord Jesus Christ as the author and Lord of everything we have preached or done well, acknowledging that we are merely unworthy servants and ministers, and attributing everything that is done well through us not to our virtues or merits but solely to the power of Christ’s name [Col. 1565A].

But in this respect they err: being still inexperienced and weak, they glory and become elated more over the performance of signs than over the salvation of souls. For this they are reproved by the Lord in the third place, when he says to them: “I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning.”

It is as though he said openly: You have no reason to exalt yourselves because the demons have been so cast down and subjected to you, since they have been cast down and subjected not through your virtue or merit but rather through the vice of pride. You have reason instead to fear, because if the devil, heavenly by origin, could be so hurled down by exalting himself, much more can you, who are earthly and more fragile, be hurled down by exalting yourselves [Col. 1565B].

He rightly compares Satan to lightning because of five properties of lightning. Lightning is formed in the heights and immediately falls; it seeks not low places but high ones, and it burns; and although it first shines, it is first darkened and smokes. Satan likewise was heavenly by creation but soon fell through pride; he seeks not humble but lofty hearts, burns them with the flames of vices, and, although he first transforms himself into an angel of light, he first darkens and blinds them.

Again, the Lord shows that they must not be elated by the power of signs, because they do not have this power from themselves but from God. This is what follows: “Behold, I have given you power,” and so forth. This is what the Apostle says: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4).

“I have given you,” he says, “power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing will harm you.”

My brothers, the Lord also gave these things literally to his disciples, because serpents, scorpions, and poisons did not harm them, just as the viper did not harm Paul’s hand (Acts 28), and swallowed poison did not harm John.

Mystically, however, serpents are devils or devilish people who inject the poisons of evil suggestion into those who are beginning to live well. Scorpions are those who strive to corrupt the end of good works as they are being brought to completion.

But, with the Lord protecting them, these things do not harm the saints, who distinguish and avoid open and hidden temptations, whether those that come before or those that come after. Rather, such temptations benefit them, making them more practiced and acquiring for them a greater crown of victory.

Fourth, the Lord shows what the disciples should or should not rejoice over. First, he shows what they should not rejoice over, when he adds: “Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you.” This is a litotes.

We ought not to rejoice in anything that is common to the good and the evil. Casting out demons and performing miracles belong not only to the good but also to the evil. Thus, on the day of judgment the reprobate will indeed say: “Did we not cast out demons in your name and perform many mighty works?” (Luke 10) [Col. 1566A] Yet they will be told: “I do not know you” (ibid.).

Sometimes casting out demons and performing miracles is not a merit of the one who performs them, but results from invoking Christ’s name, to the condemnation of the one who invokes it and to the benefit of those who see and hear. Thus, although they may despise those who perform miracles, they nevertheless honor God, at whose invocation the miracles occur.

Above all, however, we are forbidden to rejoice over temporal power, honor, dignity, and prosperity, because rejoicing over such things is vain. We are commanded to rejoice in humility, poverty, and adversity, because rejoicing in such things does not proceed from vanity but from virtue.

Therefore, just as the soft and effeminate person is one who rejoices in prosperity and grieves in adversity, so, conversely, the magnanimous person is one who grieves in prosperity [Col. 1566B] and rejoices in adversity.

The Lord shows what we ought to rejoice over: the salvation of our souls. This is what follows: “But rejoice that your names are written in heaven,” either according to eternal predestination or according to present righteousness.

Those whose names are written according to predestination will not be erased. But who knows that he is predestined? The names of those who are said to be written in heaven according to present righteousness can be erased, because some begin well and end badly. Concerning such people the Psalmist says: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous” (Ps. 68).

Therefore, my brothers, even if our names appear to be written in heaven according to present righteousness, because the end of our contest is uncertain, we must always fear. For this reason we cannot have great joy here over the salvation and progress of our souls. Nor is there great joy where fear is accompanied by joy and joy by fear.

We must therefore rejoice in good fear. For joy without fear nourishes complacency; complacency, sleepiness; sleepiness, contempt; and contempt, danger and destruction. Therefore, brothers, in this land of fear let our joy be sober and restrained. Let us rejoice with fear and fear with joy, so that without fear we may always deserve to rejoice in heavenly joys. Amen.

## COMMON OF ONE CONFESSOR. XXI. OF ONE CONFESSOR. SERMON ON THE BOOK OF WISDOM

[Col. 1566D]

[Note: These passages are excerpted here and there from Ecclesiasticus, chapters 44 and 45, but not verbatim.]

“Behold a great priest, who in his days pleased God and was found righteous.” And the rest.

My brothers, literally these words are spoken about Aaron the priest. Mystically, however, they concern Christ; and they can also be applied to any holy priest. Morally, they show what the other priests ought to be like.

Aaron was a great priest because he was the first and highest pontiff of the Jews. Christ likewise was a great priest—indeed, the greatest—because just as he is King of kings, so he is Priest of priests and Bishop of bishops.

But that holy pontiff whom we celebrate today was also a great priest: great in rank, great in virtue, and great in reward. Priests and pontiffs ought to be such that, just as they are great in authority, so they may be great in holiness, and thus deserve to be great in the recompense of reward.

For it is a monstrous and most shameful thing when rank is high but life is base. This is true of some among us—something to be lamented, my brothers—who, although low in life and conduct, nevertheless, through ambition and simony, raise themselves above their superiors, so that they appear to have been lifted above the heads of giants, to the derision, mockery, and shaking of the head of the people.

This great priest is therefore commended in eighteen graces.

The first is election, concerning which it follows: “Who in his days pleased God,” understood as: through election [Col. 1567B]. For it is certain that those who are chosen by God please God.

It is clear that Aaron pleased God, since he was chosen and called by him, manifested by the sign of the dry staff that revived and bore fruit, and preferred above the others. The Father himself testifies that Christ pleased God the Father and was chosen above others, both at the baptism and at the Transfiguration, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3; 17). And through the prophet: “Behold my chosen servant, whom I have chosen, because my soul has been pleased with him” (Isa. 43).

This holy bishop also, my brothers, whom we celebrate today, was chosen, manifested, and preferred by God above others through a good life, instruction in the virtues, and the evident performance of signs. There is no doubt, therefore, that he was chosen by God and pleased God. This occurred “in his days,” that is, through his life, teaching, and marvelous works he made those days illustrious and his own.

Priests and bishops ought likewise to become such that they are shown to please God and to be chosen by him through good life, teaching, and holiness of works. Those who, supported by neither virtue nor learning, seize the pastoral office through ambition rather than attain it are condemned by this example.

The second grace is righteousness, concerning which it follows: “And was found righteous.”

Aaron was righteous: he did not turn either to the right or to the left from the commandments of God; he punished idolaters; he interceded for sinners; and he judged each person according to the causes of his merits.

Christ likewise is righteous—indeed, he is righteousness itself. From him comes the righteousness of everyone who is righteous, and he either saves or condemns each person according to his merit. Hence Isaiah foretold concerning him: “Righteousness will be the belt of his loins” (Isa. 11).

The holy bishop whom we celebrate today was also righteous, giving each person what was his: religion to God, purity to himself, discipline to his subjects, honor to those who acted well, correction to those who offended, and fairness to everyone. By doing these things he was found righteous, because no one or scarcely anyone was found righteous.

For a virtue is more precious when it is rarer. Priests and bishops ought to be such that, even if justice and virtue are found in no others, they are found in them; they ought to give each person what is his and, in judging their subjects, attend not to their own affections but to the causes of merit. Hence it is said of them: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. 131).

This condemns the priests and bishops of our own day, among whom virtue and justice are found more rarely than among others. They do not give each person what is his but refer everything to their own profit; they do not practice justice but sell it; and in judging cases they attend not to the merits of individuals but to their own affections.

The third grace is mediation, concerning which it follows: “And in the time of wrath he became reconciliation.”

Aaron was truly a mediator between God and human beings, reconciling God to human beings and human beings to God. For when God, in anger, was consuming the murmuring people with fire, Aaron hurried with a censer, “stood between the living and the dead, prayed to the Lord, and the plague ceased” (Num. 16).

When God was angry with humanity because of the sin of the first parent, Christ likewise assumed our humanity and became the mediator between God and humanity, reconciling God to humanity and humanity to God by his blood.

This holy bishop whom we celebrate today also frequently interposed himself for the sake of his sins, turning aside God’s imminent anger through prayers and offerings and obtaining pardon for sinners.

This is the office of priests and bishops: that they should always stand between God and human beings as mediators, joined on one side to God through the intimacy of charity and on the other side to human beings through the closeness of compassion, so that they may reconcile God to human beings and human beings to God.

But what shall I say about us, wretched priests, who possess neither intimacy of charity with God nor, as we ought, closeness of compassion with our neighbor? How shall we reconcile others, when we cannot reconcile ourselves? For when we ourselves displease God because of our offenses, and yet intercede with God for the offenses of others, do we not offend God more than we appease him?

The fourth grace is supereminent obedience, concerning which it follows: “No one was found like him who kept the law of the Most High.”

In his days and among his people Aaron excelled in obedience and observance of the law. Christ likewise excelled in obedience and fulfillment of the law, becoming obedient to the Father “even unto death” (Phil. 2).

Nor was anyone like this holy bishop whom we celebrate today, in his days and among his people, who kept the law of the Most High. A priest ought not to be like the people (Isa. 24), nor a shepherd like the flock. Rather, as we read concerning Saul: “He who is placed over the whole people ought to be greater than the whole people,” so that the one to whom others owe obedience may know obedience above all others, and the one who teaches the law to others may keep the law above all others (1 Sam. 12).

This confronts us unworthy priests, who are not only like the people but are often worse than the people.

The fifth grace is advancement, concerning which it follows: “Therefore, by an oath”—that is, immutably—“he made him increase over his people” [Col. 1569A].

Since Aaron excelled in observing the law, he was exalted and established by God as high priest over the Jewish people. Since Christ was obedient to the Father even unto death, the Lord exalted him and “swore to him, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109).

The blessed pontiff whom we celebrate today, because he excelled in observing the law, was rightly advanced by God not only spiritually and eternally but also temporally to the highest priesthood. This is what the Apostle says: “Those who have served well acquire a good standing for themselves” (1 Tim. 3). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will have abundance” (Matt. 25; Luke 19).

This condemns those who are promoted perniciously, not because of their merits but rather because their money provides support. Concerning them the Lord says through the prophet: “They have reigned, but not from me; they have appointed princes, and I did not know them” (Hos. 8).

The inner Judge both advances and does not know such people: those whom he tolerates by permitting them, he does not acknowledge through the judgment of rejection.

The sixth grace is a good reputation, concerning which it follows: “He gave him the blessing of all nations.”

The good reputation of the saints is indeed the reason why they are blessed and praised by all nations. Aaron was given such a pleasing reputation that all who read about him bless him. Christ likewise was given such sweetness of name that all nations not only bless him but are also blessed in him [Col. 1569C].

Whoever hears or reads of the glorious life and conduct of this blessed confessor likewise praises and blesses him. For just as a good conscience is necessary before God, so a good reputation is necessary before human beings, especially for a shepherd, who ought to teach the people not only by word but also by example. Hence the Lord says: “Let your works shine before human beings, so that they may glorify the Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5).

This is plainly directed against those who, even if they live well in secret, nevertheless allow others to form a bad opinion of them outwardly. They are as guilty for the souls of others as those who have perished because of the scandal caused by their bad reputation.

The seventh grace is confirmation, concerning which it follows: “And he confirmed his covenant over his head”—that is, he confirmed sacred Scripture, which is the covenant of the future inheritance, in his mind [Col. 1569D].

Aaron was firm in the law he had received. Christ was not only firm but also the confirmer of both Testaments. This glorious pontiff was likewise so confirmed by Christ that he contended for the law of his God unto death and did not fear the words of persecutors and heretics. Thus, although the sword did not take his life, he did not lose the palm of martyrdom.

It is fitting that a bishop should be learned and firm in the law, since he must teach others the law. Hence he wears a two-horned mitre on his head, so that he may be able to defend and confirm the faith of both horns of the Testament.

This condemns the most wretched bishops who, ignorant of the law of God, know neither how to govern themselves nor how to govern others [Col. 1570A]. In accordance with the prophetic saying: “Alas, today the law has perished from the priest, counsel from the wise, and speech from the prophet” (Ezek. 7).

From whom, then, will inferiors seek the law, when it is written: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth” (Mal. 2)?

The eighth grace is the approval of blessing, concerning which it is added: “He knew him,” that is, he approved him in his blessings. Aaron, indeed, had efficacious power to bless in Israel in his own time. Christ, however, not only blessed always and everywhere, but is himself blessing, without which no one can be blessed. God also so recognized this glorious confessor in his blessings that, at his blessing, God would bless: he would free those possessed by demons [Col. 1570B], heal the sick, drive away plagues, and absolve sinners.

A bishop ought to possess the grace and discernment to bless; hence he has his hand anointed with sacred oil. But what shall I say about certain wicked bishops who, following their own affections rather than the grounds of merit, bless those who are accursed and curse those who are blessed? These, according to the prophet, “give life to souls that are dying, and put to death souls that are not dying” (Ezek. XIII).

The ninth grace is mercy, concerning which it is added: “He preserved his mercy for him,” as though he were saying: The mercy that he sparingly gave to others, he multiplied for the just man. Nothing befits a priest more than mercy, since through compassion he ought to become all things to all people.

Aaron, indeed, possessed great mercy, for he prayed on behalf of transgressors and even of those who murmured against him. Christ, however, was not only merciful, but is and was mercy itself; even for those who crucified him he prayed upon the cross (Luke XXIII). This glorious confessor likewise overflowed with the full depths of mercy: sympathizing with the suffering, grieving with the sorrowful, bearing the burdens of others, distributing his possessions in works of mercy, mourning the sins of others, praying for his persecutors, and doing good even to his enemies.

In this we miserable priests are confounded: we are moved by no compassion toward the poor and afflicted; toward the weaknesses of others we are iron and hard; we are more troubled by the ruin of our own falling soul [Col. 1570C] than by the destruction of a Christian soul that is perishing.

The tenth grace is an abundance of grace, concerning which it is added: “And he found grace before the eyes of the Lord.” Certainly, a priest ought to be adorned not with one or two graces, but with an abundance of many graces.

Aaron, indeed, was steeped in an abundance of graces, as was signified by the oil poured over his head and flowing down to his beard and even to the hem of his garment (Ps. XXXII). Christ, however, possesses the fullness of every grace; God the Father anointed him with the oil of gladness above his companions (Ps. XLIV). From him this glorious confessor was so abundantly filled that, if you read his holy life, character, and deeds, you would say that he lacked no virtue and no grace.

But what shall we miserable priests do [Col. 1570D], who, although we ought to be a light to the nations, are rather smoking than burning?

The eleventh grace is exaltation in the sight of kings. A priest or bishop ought indeed to be such that, on account of his virtue and uprightness, he is held in honor and reverence in the sight of kings.

Aaron, indeed, was held in high regard not only by the leaders of his own people but also by the kings of foreign nations. Christ, however, on account of the majesty of his name, subjected to himself every principality and power, even those of heaven, earth, and the underworld.

This glorious confessor likewise, through the reputation of his virtues and wondrous works, was admired and revered by princes and great men themselves. In this we miserable priests are put to shame: because of the contempt and worthlessness of our lives, we are held in contempt and derision not only by our superiors but [Col. 1571A] even by our inferiors. And it is not they who fear us; on the contrary, we fear them.

The twelfth grace is the crown of glory, concerning which it is added: “And he gave him a crown of glory.” A crown, which signifies the perfection of life, befits a priest. Hence Peter says: “A royal priesthood” (1 Pet. II). A priest ought to be so perfect that he can govern not only himself but also others.

To signify this, Aaron wore a diadem on his head, in which precious stones shone when the work of God was completed. Christ, however, who came into the world not to prosper but to suffer, wore a crown of thorns inflicted upon him in mockery, showing that whoever here has bravely borne the crown of virtue and patience will glory in an eternal crown [Col. 1571B].

Following him, this glorious confessor strove here to be crowned with the crown of virtue and patience, through which he attained the glorious crown. We priests, therefore, possess a crown; and if we express in our conduct what that crown signifies, it is truly for us a crown of glory and honor; otherwise, it is a crown of reproach and disgrace.

The thirteenth grace is inheritance, concerning which it is added: “He established an everlasting covenant for him.” Levi and Aaron, moreover, did not receive a portion in the promised land with the other tribes; rather, their inheritance was the Lord—that is, the first fruits, tithes, offerings, and sacrifices presented to God—and they possessed these with perpetual stability for as long as the Jewish priesthood endured [Col. 1571C].

To Christ, however, God gave an eternal inheritance, saying: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession as the ends of the earth” (Ps. II). Hence he himself said: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII).

This glorious confessor likewise despised every earthly inheritance; God alone was his inheritance, and in him he possessed sufficiency and an eternal inheritance. In this we miserable priests are confounded: although we ought to have God as our inheritance, we contend for an eternal inheritance. But what will be sufficient for one to whom God is not sufficient? Therefore, brothers, I greatly tremble lest, because we desire an earthly inheritance, we should deservedly be deprived of the eternal one. For, according to the Wise Man, “An inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end” (Prov. XX) [Col. 1571D].

The fourteenth grace is the great priesthood, concerning which it is added: “And he gave him a great priesthood.” Aaron alone, indeed, among the entire Jewish people, first held the chief and highest priesthood. Christ, however, possesses a supreme and eternal priesthood over every power. Hence the Apostle says: “Many became priests according to the law because they were prevented by death from continuing; but Christ, because he remains forever, possesses an everlasting priesthood” (Heb. VII).

This glorious confessor also possessed a great priesthood—not so much great because of the size of his parish as because of the greatness of his pastoral vigilance, nor so much because of the magnitude of his revenues as because of the greatness of his virtues [Col. 1572A]. In this we unworthy priests are confounded, for we seek a great priesthood that is great in temporal revenues, not in spiritual progress. We seek a church in which we may gain not souls but an abundance of money. In this we show that we are not shepherds but hirelings.

The fifteenth grace is beatification, concerning which it is added: “And he made him blessed in glory.” That is, he made him blessed and glorious both in merit and in reward.

Aaron, indeed, as he faithfully served him, was happily led through the goodness of his merit to the blessedness of reward. Christ, his only-begotten Son, faithfully obeying him even unto death, he “exalted and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II) [Col. 1572B].

This confessor, too, faithfully serving him, God has happily brought today to the completion of his temporal course of service and has gloriously adorned him with the crown of eternal blessedness among the choirs of angels.

And we also, my brothers, if we faithfully serve him, if we love him above all things, and if, having rejected all temporal things, we direct our whole desire toward him, he will make us happily complete the course of life and gloriously attain eternal joys.

The sixteenth grace is the exercise of the priesthood, concerning which it is added: “To exercise the priesthood.” Aaron, indeed, worthily and vigorously exercised the priesthood until his final day. Christ also, who came to minister and not to be ministered to (Matt. XX), himself, in his own person, exercised the office of a humble preacher and minister until his passion [Col. 1572C].

This holy confessor likewise exercised his ministry with complete humility and solicitude until death. This condemns us lowly priests, who neglect to perform our ministry, appointing deputies and hirelings in our place while we ourselves devote ourselves to vain temporal matters and secular business. We find enough people to whom we may entrust the souls for whom Christ died; but we cannot find anyone to whom we may entrust our vain possessions.

The seventeenth grace is praise, concerning which it is added: “And to have praise in his name.” Aaron, indeed, because he benefited both himself and others, received praise from the exercise of his priesthood. Christ also, because he returned with the restoration of the human race, has in heaven ineffable and eternal praise from the exercise of his priesthood [Col. 1572D].

This confessor likewise, because he returned from the exercise of his sacrifice with the acquisition of many souls, undoubtedly has eternal praise in heaven, so that it may rightly be said of him: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much” (Matt. XXV).

But what praise will the shepherd have who returns empty, after all the sheep have been devoured and scattered by wolves? What praise will the shepherd have who does not even return having preserved himself?

The eighteenth grace is: “To offer God worthy incense as a sweet-smelling fragrance.” Aaron, indeed, praying on behalf of his people, offered incense to God as a sweet-smelling fragrance [Col. 1573A].

Christ, however, offered himself, spotless and consumed by the fire of charity, upon the altar of the cross for the redemption of the human race, to God the Father as a sweet-smelling fragrance. In this sacrifice God the Father found a fragrance surpassing all others.

This glorious confessor likewise, praying on behalf of his people, offered—and still offers daily—to God a contrite heart, kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit, together with the fragrance of sweet devotion, propitiating the divine majesty for us with the vessel of his perfumes [Col. 1573B].

Imitating him, my brothers, let us learn to offer sacrifice to God—not something belonging to another, like Cain, who, abandoning himself, offered what belonged to another, but a worthy sacrifice, namely, a contrite and humbled heart.

Nor let us offer it with alien fire, that is, with the fire of earthly desire, like Nadab and Abihu, who were struck down by God for this reason (Lev. X), but with divine fire, that is, with charity [Col. 1573C].

Nor let us offer it with lukewarmness, like the lukewarm, whom God vomits out (Rev. III), but with the fervor of the most devoted prayer, so that God may smell and delight in our devotion.

May God deign to grant this to us through the prayers of this most holy confessor. Amen.

## XXII. OF ONE CONFESSOR. SERMON ON MATTHEW

“Jesus said this parable to his disciples: ‘A certain man going abroad called his servants and entrusted his goods to them’” (Matt. XXV), etc. [Col. 1573D]

There are some who think that they possess the goods they have from themselves. Others think that they have them from God, but that these goods were given only for their own use; therefore, they do not consider themselves to sin if they do not share them with others. Others, although they know that these goods ought to be shared with others, are nevertheless slow to share them.

Against these the Lord sets forth the foregoing parable, showing that all the goods we have have been bestowed by God; that they have been entrusted to us not only for our own use but also for sharing with others; and that those who are slow to share them are rightly to be deprived of them and condemned.

There are four parts to this reading. First, the Lord shows that all the goods we have have been entrusted to us by God. Second, he shows that some use what has been entrusted to them well and others badly. Third, he shows that those who act well will be saved. Fourth, he shows that those who act badly will be condemned [Col. 1574A].

First, therefore, he shows that all the goods we have come from God, when it is said: “A certain man going abroad.” For who is this man, unless he is the one of whom the prophet says: “He is also a man, and who will know him?” (Isa. LIII). He certainly went abroad when he placed our nature, which he had taken from the earth, above the heavens.

The proper place of the flesh is the earth; it goes abroad when, through our Redeemer, it is raised above the ether. He is now a stranger to us, so long as we remain in this exile, because he is separated from us both by the absence of his flesh and by the concealment of his aid.

He called his servants when, either through himself or through his preachers, he called human beings from the four parts of the world [Col. 1574B]. He entrusted his goods to them, and still entrusts them daily, because he distributes his graces among individuals.

Hence the Apostle says: “Grace has been given to each of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. IV); for this reason the Psalmist says: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men” (Ps. LXVII; Eph. IV).

We must carefully consider that he says, “his servants,” and “he entrusted his goods to them.” If we are his servants, therefore we do not belong to ourselves. If he entrusted them, he did not give them away but rather committed them to our care. If they are his goods, therefore they are not ours.

What, then, is shown by this except that neither we ourselves nor the things we possess belong to us by right, but rather belong to the Lord? If, therefore, we misuse either ourselves or what belongs to us apart from the Lord’s service and will, what are we doing other than defrauding the Lord of what is his? [Col. 1574C]

“And to one,” he says, “he gave five talents; to another two; to another one.” We can understand this simply, since God gives one person many gifts, another a few, and another fewer still.

Or certainly, by the five talents is signified knowledge of external matters, acquired through the five senses. By the two are signified understanding and action. By the one, understanding alone is signified.

“To each,” he says, “according to his own ability.” As though he were saying: He entrusted them not with as much as he himself possessed, but with as much as each one could receive—a principle of discernment that the teachers of Holy Church ought always to observe.

The Lord shows why he entrusted the talents to them, saying, according to another Evangelist: “Trade with them until I come” (Luke XIX) [Col. 1574D]. “And he departed,” he says, “immediately”—not changing his location, but granting them free power to act; neither saving those who acted well at once nor condemning those who acted badly at once, but silently awaiting both for judgment.

The second part follows, in which it is shown that some act well and others badly, when it is added: “But the one who had received five talents went away, worked with them, and gained another five.”

There are some who, even if they cannot grasp inner mysteries, nevertheless do not grow sluggish after receiving knowledge of external matters. They go forth, insofar as they can, acting well with the knowledge they have received; through the active life they spend external goods in works of mercy and other good uses [Col. 1575A], and they make ever greater progress until their gain is doubled.

This happens either when knowledge itself is doubled within them through practice, or when, by advancing their neighbors through word or example, they acquire a twofold reward.

“Likewise,” he says, “the one who had received two gained another two.” There are some who understand subtle matters concerning inner realities and perform wondrous works outwardly. By teaching spiritual things and doing good, they benefit both themselves and others, and thus acquire what is, as it were, a doubled gain.

“But the one,” he says, “who had received one went away, dug in the earth, and hid his master’s money.”

A person hides the talent in the earth when he conceals the understanding given to him in an earthly and greedy heart and does not make it known to others. Against this Solomon says: “Hidden wisdom and hidden treasure—what benefit is there in either?” (Eccli. XX). And Jesus son of Sirach says: “He who hides grain will be cursed among the peoples” (Prov. XI) [Col. 1575B].

A person hides the talent when he devotes the intelligence he has received entirely to earthly concerns; when he delights in entangling in earthly cleverness the understanding by which he could grasp heavenly wisdom. Of such people the prophet says: “They are wise to do evil, but they have not known how to do good” (Jer. IV).

The third part follows, in which it is shown that those who act well will be well rewarded, when it is added: “After a long time, the lord of those servants came and settled accounts with them.”

The Lord comes to judgment only after a long time, because he waits for sinners for a long time and with great patience, so that he may save many [Col. 1575C]. “And he settled accounts with them,” he says.

The Lord alone knows how to settle accounts with his servants, because he alone repays each person reasonably according to his merits. He cannot be deceived, because he is truth itself; nor can he be corrupted, because he is justice itself. Nothing can be hidden from him, since he is all-knowing, nor can he be deflected in any matter, since he is all-powerful.

“And the one who had received five talents came forward,” etc. The faithful servant who is secure in his conscience comes first to meet the one who rewards him and offers another five talents, saying: “Lord, you entrusted five talents to me; behold, I have gained another five,” etc.

Each faithful person offers the profit acquired from the talent entrusted to him: Peter the people of the Jews; Paul the Gentiles; John Asia Minor; Andrew Achaea; James Spain; Thomas Greater India; Bartholomew Lesser India; Matthew Ethiopia; Simon and Jude Persia [Col. 1575D]. One offers a thousand souls, another a hundred, another ten, and another, though possessing less, offers his own soul.

The Lord applauds, praises, and rewards each of them when he adds: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord.”

He applauds him by rejoicing with him and inviting him to rejoice with the word “well done,” an interjection signifying joy. He praises him when he calls him good and faithful. Good, because he desired what was good and acted vigorously and bravely. Faithful, because in everything he sought not his own glory but that of his lord.

He rewards him when he says: “Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord.” For all the goods of the present life, however great they may seem, are considered small and few in comparison with those of the future [Col. 1576A].

The faithful servant is set over much when he receives those immense and eternal goods that “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart” (1 Cor. II). He is admitted into the joy of his lord when, having been taken up into that eternal homeland and joined to the choirs of angels, he rejoices inwardly in the gift, so that there is now nothing left for him to grieve over on account of corruption.

For what greater thing can be given to a faithful servant than to live and rejoice eternally with the Lord of blessedness?

The fourth part follows, in which it is shown that lazy and wicked servants are rejected, when it is added: “But the one who had received one talent also came forward” [Col. 1576B].

The one who is conscious of his own wrongdoing comes last and late. “Lord,” he says, “I know that you are a hard man, reaping where you did not sow and gathering where you did not scatter. And, being afraid, I went away and hid your talent in the earth; behold, you have what is yours.”

Truly, what is written—“to make excuses for sins” (Ps. CXL)—happens to this servant: to laziness and negligence is added the crime of pride. For although he ought simply to have confessed his inactivity and begged forgiveness, he instead slanders the Lord and says that he acted prudently, lest, while seeking to gain money, he should endanger his share.

He slanders the Lord when he calls him hard, reaping where he did not sow and gathering where he did not scatter, as though he were saying: You are hard because you command hard things and inflict harsh punishments. You reap where you did not sow because, with the sickle of judgment, you cut down even those as guilty to whom you did not entrust the law. You gather where you did not scatter because you gather into your kingdom even the good among the nations on account of the deeds of those who observe the natural law, while condemning those who neglect the written law as well [Col. 1576C].

He says that he acted prudently when he adds: “And, being afraid, I went away,” as though he were saying: I was afraid that, if I undertook to gain others, I myself might be endangered. For this reason I hid the talent of understanding in my heart.

There are many such people in Holy Church, saying to themselves: “It is enough for me to render an account of myself. Why should I undertake the office of preaching to others, so that I might be compelled to render an account of others?”

Or certainly, being afraid that, if I undertook a more holy way of life, I might at some point look back and thus be condemned all the more, I hid the talent of understanding that had been given to me in secular life, neither diminishing nor increasing it [Col. 1576D].

There are many such people who fear undertaking a better life, yet do not fear lying inert in their sloth. Peter, while still weak, displayed their likeness when, after seeing the miracle, he said: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke V).

No, Peter: if you recognize yourself as a sinner, you ought not drive the Lord away from you. Thus those who do not want a better life because they see themselves to be weak, as though confessing themselves sinners, drive away from themselves the Lord by whom they ought to have been sanctified.

Like people in confusion, they have no counsel while they die, and they fear life. For “he who fears the frost, snow will fall upon him” (Job VI).

Hence the servant is immediately answered: “Wicked and lazy servant, you knew that I reap where I do not sow and gather where I did not scatter; therefore you ought to have given my money to the money-changers, and when I came I would have received what was mine with interest” [Col. 1577A].

From his own words the lord constrains the servant, as though he were saying: If, according to your statement, I demand what I did not give, how much more do I demand from you what I gave you to distribute?

To give money to the money-changers is to devote the understanding of preaching, by example and word, to those who are able to exercise it. But just as you see our danger if we retain the Lord’s money, so understand, brothers, your danger if you do not return with interest the money expended upon us [Col. 1577B].

You return it with interest when you strive either to retain what you have heard or to gather from what you have heard things that you had not heard.

Let us hear the sentence by which the lord strikes the lazy servant: “Take the talent from him and give it to the one who has ten talents.”

The good talent of spiritual understanding is given to the person who, possessing only an understanding of external matters, has administered it well. We see this happening daily in the Church. Many, while properly administering the external things they have received, reach also, through the grace added to them, an understanding of mystical matters.

Conversely, many who are naturally sharp and intelligent become dull through their own laziness because they are idle. At the judgment, many who now possess knowledge will be reckoned among the unlearned. Conversely, many who are now simple will, on account of their devotion, be rewarded with spiritual understanding among the apostolic teachers [Col. 1577C].

“For to everyone who has, it will be given, and he will abound. But from the one who does not have, even what he seemed to have will be taken away from him.”

A person is rightly said to possess something when he uses it well. One who lacks the good use of a thing is as though he did not possess it. Therefore, to everyone who possesses and uses a thing well, it will be given, and he will abound. But to the one who does not possess it and does not use it well—as though he did not possess it—what he seemed to have will be taken away from him.

Or certainly, to everyone who possesses charity will be given charity and a diversity of other graces, and he will abound. But whoever does not have charity will lose even the gifts he seemed to have received.

Therefore, my brothers, we must always strive to possess charity in all things, since whoever has it possesses everything; whoever does not have it is punished even for the talent he possessed and, according to the Lord’s sentence, is cast into the outer darkness [Col. 1577D].

Through punishment he falls into the outer darkness who, through his fault, had fallen into the inner darkness. There will be there the weeping of eyes that here desired unlawful things, and the gnashing of teeth that here delighted in gluttony. The tongue that here loved talkativeness will burn. The nose that here delighted in luxurious perfumes will be afflicted with intolerable stench. The ears that here took pleasure in empty and evil speech will be tormented by the terrifying cries of demons. The whole body that here delighted in lustful touches will be tortured by various punishments. And according to the variety of sins there will be a variety of punishments.

Therefore, my brothers, let each one of us keep watch over the business of the talent entrusted to him, since there is no one who has not received a talent from God [Col. 1578A].

One has received spiritual understanding; another, earthly substance; another, temporal power; another, familiarity with the wealthy; another, an art by which he earns his living; another, at least reason itself or the senses of the body.

Therefore, the one who has spiritual understanding should devote himself to preaching. The one who has earthly substance should distribute it through works of mercy. The one who has earthly power should protect the weak. The one who has familiarity with the wealthy should speak on behalf of the poor. The one who has an art by which he earns his living should give from it whatever he can to those in need. The one who has reason or the five bodily senses should employ them well for himself and for others [Col. 1578B].

Thus, when the Lord returns, each person may be secure concerning the account of his talent. Let him weigh daily, with trembling, what he has received. He who went abroad is already about to return.

Let us therefore hasten to trade with the talent entrusted to us, so that, with the talent doubled, we may be able to meet the Lord when he comes—he who grants this and who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## XXIII. OF ONE CONFESSOR. SERMON ON THE BOOK OF WISDOM

“Behold, a great priest who was tested in his faith and known in his words as faithful” [Col. 1578C] [Note: These words are excerpted from verses 1–5 of Ecclesiasticus, chapter I, but not literally.] (Eccli. L), etc.

This reading, my brothers, although literally spoken in part about the prophet Samuel and in part about Simon, the high priest of the Jews, is nevertheless appropriately read today in Holy Church concerning this holy pontiff whom we are celebrating today.

He was indeed a glorious pontiff, a great priest—great in office, great in merit, and great in reward. Great outwardly, great inwardly, great above. Such, surely, must a priest be, so that a lofty life may correspond to a lofty rank, and so that a lofty reward may correspond to both.

This priest is commended in four respects: in faith, in brightness, in the variety of his virtues, and in the performance of his office.

He is commended in faith when it is added: “Who was tested in his faith and known in his words as faithful” [Col. 1578D]. “Tested and known,” he says, as though he had become known through testing. For when a matter is tested, it becomes known.

This holy man was tested and known in his faith, that is, in the works of his faith, and was shown to be faithful in his words. Since faith is invisible in itself and concerns invisible things, he could be tested and known as faithful only through his outward works, because for the faith of Christ he left behind beloved things, followed difficult paths, performed wondrous deeds, and endured hardships.

For the faith of Christ, following the example of Abraham, he left land and kinship, his father’s house, and the pleasant habits of richer food and clothing and of the other enticements of the flesh [Col. 1579A]. He followed the narrow and arduous way of God’s commandments, despising the world, crucifying himself, embracing poverty, lowliness, humility, and the other virtues, loving even his enemies and praying for his persecutors.

Through faith in Jesus Christ he also performed wondrous deeds: giving sight to the blind, raising the lame, healing those possessed by demons, curing the sick, and raising the dead. For, according to the Lord’s word, “all things are possible to the one who believes” (Mark IX).

For the faith of Jesus Christ he also endured hardships: insults, injuries, losses, persecutions, exiles, and various afflictions. He would even have gladly endured the sword of martyrdom, if there had been someone to inflict it. Therefore, because in his mind he was not absent from martyrdom, he will not lack the crown of martyrdom [Col. 1579B].

Through his words also he was tested and known to be faithful, because he demonstrated how great a faith he possessed by confessing the word of faith steadfastly in time of persecution, preaching earnestly, writing brilliantly, refuting unbelievers and heretics, instructing present peoples with the living voice, and teaching those absent and those yet to be born through his writings.

He taught while alive; he teaches also after death. And if the one who teaches deserves reward, this man also deserves it daily, when he teaches us through his writing.

But what do we miserable priests do today? We are proved faithful neither in deeds, words, nor conduct, as we ought to be. Indeed—what I cannot say without tears—while we prefer carnal things to spiritual things, and transitory things even to eternal things, we show that we neither believe nor even doubt in the faith. But if at times we preach the faith, we attack it with deeds contrary to it [Col. 1579C].

Second, this holy man is commended in brightness when it is added: “He shines like the morning star in the midst of a cloud, and like the full moon in its season. And like the shining sun” (Eccli. L). Thus this holy man shone in the temple of God.

The morning star, my brothers, announces the day and shines in the midst of a cloud, but it is not sufficient to overcome the cloud or to show the way to travelers.

The full moon, shining in its season, is sufficient for the most part both to overcome the night and to show the way to travelers; yet it does not entirely drive away the night, nor does it warm people with its heat.

The shining sun sparkles among the clouds, overcomes them, shows the way to travelers, completely excludes the night, and warms people with its heat [Col. 1579D].

The morning star, therefore, in the midst of a cloud is the beginning of a good life, which foretells the day of eternity; yet of itself it is not sufficient to overcome the darkness of unbelief and error or to show the right way.

The moon shining in its season is evangelical teaching, which shines amid the darkness of unbelief and error, overcomes it, and shows people the right way; yet it does not entirely exclude the darkness of unbelief and error, nor does it warm all people with its heat.

The shining sun is the evident display of wondrous virtues. It sparkles amid the darkness of unbelief and error, overcomes it, and shows the right way; it completely excludes the night of ignorance and doubt, and by the admiration it inspires kindles people to faith and charity [Col. 1580A].

For this reason, when the Lord sent his disciples to illuminate the whole world through faith, he added to the spiritual life and evangelical teaching—with which they already shone forth—the evident display of spiritual virtues and miracles. Illuminated wondrously by this threefold light, “they preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word by the signs that followed” (Mark XVI).

Adorned with this threefold light, therefore, this glorious pontiff shone through the brightness of his life among unbelievers, heretics, and people living in darkness, like the morning star in the midst of a cloud.

He also shone like the full moon in its season through spiritual teaching, overcoming the night of unbelief and ignorance and showing people the right way [Col. 1580B].

He also shone in the temple of God like the shining sun through the evident display of virtues and miracles, excluding all ignorance and doubt concerning the faith and drawing people, through their admiration for him, toward faith and the charity of God.

But what shall we say about this, we lowliest priests, who do not shine as we ought in life, teaching, or virtues? Indeed, although we ought to be the light of the world, we are darkness.

And if, as the Lord says, “the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness itself be?” (Matt. VI). We see this clearly, brothers: because the teachers who ought to be the eyes of Holy Church are becoming dark today, how dark are the other members of the Church, who do not lead but are led!

And when the blind presume to lead the blind, do they not—as I cannot say without groaning—both fall into the pit of eternal destruction? (Matt. XV.) [Col. 1580C]

Third, this saint is commended for the variety of his virtues when it is added: “Like a shining rainbow amid the clouds of glory.” The heavenly rainbow, also called the Iris, is many-colored, illumined by the reflection of the sun, set as a sign of the covenant between God and human beings (Gen. 9), and a minister of the rains. This glorious confessor likewise was God’s bow, piercing the enemies of the faith with arrows—that is, with the judgments of Sacred Scripture; many-colored, that is, flashing with a great variety of virtues; set as a sign of the covenant between God and human beings, because “in the time of wrath he became reconciliation” (Ecclus. 44). Indeed, this saint and the other saints placed between God and human beings: what else are they but a sign of God’s peace toward humanity? But when they are removed from among human beings, what else are they but a sign of God’s anger toward humanity? And we, brothers, who today grow dark because true saints have been removed from our midst: what else are we experiencing but God’s wrath, since God’s covenant has been withdrawn?

This saint was also a minister of the rains, for he watered human beings with the rain of his teaching; indeed, amid the clouds of glory, he shone among the other glorious preachers through the distinction of his teaching and virtues. How this saint shone like a many-colored rainbow is explained subsequently, when the eight virtues by which he radiated variously and wondrously are enumerated.

The first is martyrdom in the mortification of the flesh, concerning which it is added: “Like a rose blossom in the days of spring.” Indeed, a rose blossom in the days of youth is the virtue of martyrdom in the days of youth. The virtue of martyrdom is acquired not only through the shedding of blood, but also through the mortification of the flesh for Christ. For when this saint wore down his body through continual abstinence, labor, and vigils; when by many chastisements he subjected the rebellion of the flesh to the spirit; when he crucified his flesh with its vices and desires—what else did he endure but continual martyrdom?

The second is chastity, for which this saint is commended when it is added: “Like lilies that are beside flowing water.” Lilies beside flowing water signify the brightness of chastity amid the passage of transitory life. This saint shone wondrously through that virtue: while in the flesh, he lived not according to the flesh; while among human beings, he lived angelically. Indeed, in this respect he somehow surpassed the angels, since he merited to possess chastity amid the instability of his nature, whereas they possess it in the confirmation of their nature.

The third virtue is patience, for which this saint is commended when it is added: “And like fragrant incense in the days of summer.” Incense is an Arabian tree with a very smooth bark, emitting drops of the sweetest fragrance through cuts in its bark; it is also called *thura*. Thus, fragrant incense in the days of summer signifies patience sweetly fragrant in the days of persecution. This saint gave off a wondrous fragrance through that virtue, delighting those who injured him by the gentleness and mildness of his patience.

The fourth virtue is charity, for which this saint is commended when it is added: “Like a shining fire.” A shining fire is the brilliance of ardent charity. Hence the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke 12). This saint displayed that virtue wondrously, loving his enemies and persecutors as sons.

The fifth virtue is devotion, for which this saint is commended when it is added: “And incense burning in the fire.” Burning incense in the fire signifies the devotion of prayer in the fervor of charity. Hence the Psalmist says: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. 140). Through this virtue the holy pontiff shone wondrously: by the power of prayer, appeasing divine anger, he reconciled God to human beings and human beings to God.

The sixth virtue is wisdom, for which this saint is commended when it is added: “Like a solid vessel of gold, adorned with every precious stone.” A solid vessel of gold adorned with every precious stone signifies a minister of God properly adorned with wisdom and the other virtues. Hence Paul is also called a vessel of election. Through this virtue this saint shone wondrously, ministering wisely and graciously in the Church of God, before the eyes of God and human beings.

The seventh virtue is mercy, for which this saint is commended when it is added: “Like an olive tree putting forth shoots.” A flourishing olive tree signifies the virtue of mercy spreading itself through various branches of compassion. For *eleos* means “mercy” in Greek; and mercy, like oil, floats above all liquids. This precious saint and confessor shone abundantly through that virtue, readily opening his compassionate heart and generous hand to the afflicted and needy.

The eighth virtue is the strength of perseverance, for which this saint is commended when it is added: “And like a cypress lifting itself to the heights.” The cypress, fragrant and beautiful in its foliage, does not lay aside its beauty under any impulse; it is strong and solid and does not yield to burdens. A cypress therefore lifting itself to the heights signifies the height of enduring strength. Through that virtue this saint shone, steadily growing in the esteem attached to the virtues mentioned above and persevering courageously.

But what can we, wretched priests, say about these things? We are not adorned with the radiance of diverse virtues; rather, on the contrary, we are stained and made foul by the filth of diverse vices, and we corrupt others with our stench. We are guilty not only of the ruin of our own souls, but also of all those corrupted by our evil example.

Fourth, this holy confessor is commended for the execution of his office when it is added: “In receiving the very robe of glory and clothing him with the fullness of virtue.” In ascending to, or approaching, the holy altar, he gave glory.

Priestly garments and offices are not only judgments concerning one’s order; they are also symbols of the spiritual virtues with which priests ought inwardly to be adorned, and of the heavenly rewards toward which they ought to strive. The white or shining-white stole signifies two things: the brightness of priestly purity and its reward, the stole of immortality. The *infula*, which covers and surrounds the other vestments, signifies both the perfection of priestly virtue and its reward, the consummation of perfect blessedness.

The priest’s approach to the holy altar signifies the closer approach by which a priest ought to draw near to God: here through greater charity, and in the future through greater blessedness. Thus this glorious priest was adorned not only with priestly garments and offices, but also with what they signify. For “in receiving the very robe of glory”—that is, in receiving the priestly stole signifying future glory—“and clothing him with the fullness of virtue”—that is, in being clothed with the *infula*, signifying the consummation of the virtues—“and in approaching the holy altar”—that is, in approaching the holy altar—he gave glory to God.

He attributed and referred all these things not to himself, as some do, but to God alone, displaying through the vestments the garment of holiness, and through his approach to the altar the approach of holiness. Through these he now and forever enjoys the stole of eternal perfection and approach to divine glory.

In this respect we unworthy priests are condemned. Although outwardly, before the people, we shine sufficiently in our garments, inwardly, before God, we are darkened by the most shameful vices. Although we presume to approach more closely to the altar, inwardly we are distanced from God by our reprobate life.

What remedy, then, my brothers, remains for us except to wash away our shameful deeds with the tears of true repentance; to redeem our guilt through works of mercy; to change our life for the better; to devote ourselves to fasts, prayers, readings, and other good pursuits; and to feed by example and word the people entrusted to us? May we thereby deserve, through the merits and intercession of this most holy priest whose solemnity we celebrate today, to be joined in merit and reward to the company of holy priests. This may our Lord Jesus Christ grant, he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever.

## XXIV. OF ONE CONFESSOR. SERMON ON MATTHEW

Jesus said to his disciples: “Watch, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come” (Matt. 24), and so forth.

Our merciful Lord and Redeemer, dearest brothers, preferring to find in us something to crown rather than something to condemn, has sought in this reading of the holy Gospel to awaken our drowsiness. He does four things. First, he exhorts us to keep watch. Second, he shows why we must always keep watch. Third, he shows who in particular must keep watch and against whom. Fourth, he says that a pastor who keeps good watch is indeed rare, but blessed.

First, therefore, he exhorts us to keep watch when he says: “Watch.” Now, just as there is bodily watchfulness, so there is spiritual watchfulness. We keep bodily watch when our outward person, with the eyes of the body open, guards external things. Likewise, we keep spiritual watch when our inward person, with its eyes open, guards its inward realities through reason.

Therefore, just as the soul is more precious than the body, so we must watch over it more than over the body. Since many crafty enemies attack it from every side, we must always and everywhere keep watch over it. The enemies that persecute our soul are the devil, the flesh, and the world. The devil is always near us; the flesh is also within us; the world is everywhere and all around us.

These enemies attack us from before and behind, from the right and the left, from above and below: from before, through open persecution; from behind, through hidden persecution; from the right, by flattering; from the left, by terrifying; from above, by lifting us toward pride; from below, by dragging us toward despair.

They also attack through all the senses of the body, as though through all the gates of the soul. They tempt the sight through beautiful and desirable things; hearing through sweet melodies and pleasing words; taste through refined flavors and the provocations of gluttony; smell through the allurements of prostitute-like scents; touch through the delights of pleasant contact.

Recognizing that he was surrounded by so many and such great snares, the Psalmist cries: “My enemies have surrounded my soul” (Ps. 16). Therefore, my brothers, since we are always and everywhere assailed, let us always and everywhere keep watch. Let us exclude the cares of temporal affairs from our hearts, so that each day we may be more free to attend to our souls.
