We read in the Apocalypse that the holy “living creatures were full of eyes before and behind” (Rev. 4); indeed, as Ezekiel says: “Their whole body was full of eyes” (Ezek. 1). For the righteous do nothing without circumspection, but turn the eyes of their hearts in every direction to guard the parts of their life that lie before and behind them—indeed, every part of it.

The wicked, however, are all blind, for they do not notice the snares laid for them. As the Lord says: “They do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23), or where they are going, while, as though the eyes of reason were closed, they move toward destruction.

Second, the Lord demonstrates that we must keep watch in this way when he adds: “Because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come.” He gives a twofold reason why we must keep watch, and why we must do so always.

First, why must we keep watch? Because our Lord will come to condemn those who sleep and save those who keep watch. If, my brothers, our Lord were never to come for judgment, nor render to each person according to his merits, we would not need to keep watch. But now, because he will most certainly come to judge, we must necessarily keep watch.

And why must we always keep watch? Because “you do not know at what hour he will come.” If the hour of his coming were determined for us, we could sleep at some times and watch only when we knew that he was coming. For this reason the Lord wished us to be ignorant of the day of his coming: so that we would always await him as though he were about to come immediately, and thus always keep watch and always prepare ourselves for his coming.

He likewise proves that we ought to keep watch by an argument from the lesser when he adds: “But know this: if the householder had known at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly have kept watch and would not have allowed his house to be broken into.” It is as though he were openly saying: If a householder, fearing that a thief might come, watches over and guards his house and his temporal possessions, how much more ought you to watch over your souls and the souls entrusted to you?

This clearly reproves our negligence. We are careful and watchful in guarding our temporal possessions—things that are truly worthless and empty—but in guarding our own souls and those entrusted to us, for whom Christ died, we are negligent and drowsy. We surround our earthly houses with walls, establish strong and well-bolted doors, and urge a watchman to keep watch; but we neglect to close the house of our heart, bolt the doors of our senses, and rouse reason to vigilance. Why is this, except that we love temporal things more than spiritual and eternal goods?

This is the third part, in which it is mystically shown who in particular ought to keep watch and against whom. This householder is the ecclesiastical pastor who, like a householder, presides over the Church, correcting, governing, and feeding it.

The thief is the devil, who, like a thief—called *fur* from *furvus*, “dark”—loves darkness, breaks into the enclosure of the Church through evil suggestion, and snatches souls away from communion with the Church. Therefore, if the ecclesiastical pastor knew—that is, understood and recognized—at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly keep watch. He would always watch over the Church entrusted to him in such a way that the devil, when he came, would find it watchful, and thus he would not allow his house to be broken into.

In the moral sense, the householder is the mind, which, like a householder, ought to preside in the dwelling of the human body, avoiding what is harmful and providing what is useful. The thief is the death of the body, because it comes secretly, breaks through bodily life, and takes away the soul.

Therefore, brothers, if our mind understood, it would certainly keep watch, always avoiding evil and following good. When death came, it would not allow the house of bodily life to be broken into for condemnation.

“Therefore,” he says, “you also must be ready, because at an hour you do not expect, the Son of Man will come.” And although the Lord will come generally to all for the general judgment, nevertheless, since death comes daily to each one of us, the Lord comes to us. At the very point at which we are called by the Lord from this life, we shall be judged.

For Solomon says: “Wherever the tree falls, whether toward the south or toward the north, there it will remain” (Eccl. 11). Therefore, because death—and thus the Lord—comes secretly, we must always keep watch, just as death comes.

He aptly says: “At an hour you do not expect.” Although each of us certainly knows that we shall die, no one, however old, does not still hope to live longer. When the day of judgment approaches, those who are then alive in the flesh—even if they know that the Lord will come for judgment—will not expect him to come so soon. In this also people are deceived: at the hour when they do not expect it, both death and the Lord come.

But we, brothers, if we are always watchful in good works, cannot be deceived.

Fourth, it is shown that a pastor who keeps good watch is indeed rare, but blessed, when it is added: “Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent servant whom his master has set over his household, to give them food at the proper time? Blessed is that servant,” and so forth.

By these very words he shows that such a servant is rare, setting out five qualities that must be sought in every pastor: that he be faithful, prudent, appointed by God, placed over that household, and that he feed it at the proper time.

He must be faithful—not only in faith but also in fidelity—not merely believing in the Lord but also loving him; doing God’s will rather than his own; seeking God’s glory rather than his own. And because life is not sufficient without teaching, he adds: “Prudent.” Again, because no one ought to preach unless he has been sent, he adds: “Whom his master appointed.” And because it is not enough for a pastor to be like the people, he adds: “Over his household,” so that he may precede them not only in rank but also in life and knowledge.

And because it is not enough for him to possess all these qualities unless he is constant in the preaching for which he was appointed, he adds: “To give them food at the proper time”—that is, to feed them by example and word at the appropriate time—and, according to the other Evangelist, “to give them their measure of wheat” (Luke 12), that is, to measure the word of preaching according to the capacity of his hearers.

I cannot say this without groaning: how rare today, my brothers, is the pastor who serves the Lord for the Lord’s sake; who feeds Christ’s sheep not for profit but from love of Christ! How rare is the pastor who makes good provision for himself and his subjects with a view to the future! How rare is the one who has been called by God like Aaron and does not thrust himself forward! How rare is the one who feeds Christ’s sheep and does not instead feed himself!

Even if someone attains one or two of these qualities, how exceedingly rare is the person who possesses them all together. But the rarer he is, the more precious and blessed is that servant whom, when his master comes, he finds doing so.

He shows in what respect that servant is blessed when he says: “Amen, amen, I say to you, he will set him over all his goods.” This does not mean that only pastors will possess eternal rewards, but that, above others, they will possess greater glory, both on account of their own life and on account of their care of the flock.

For just as there is a difference in merits between good teachers and good hearers, so there is also a difference in rewards. He will set good stewards over all his goods, which is the greater reward. But good hearers, as another Evangelist says, he will make recline at table, and, passing by, will minister to them (ibid.), which is the lesser reward.

Yet, my brothers, whoever has less will have enough, because the same charity will make the particular possessions of each common to all.

Therefore, my brothers, since our Lord will come at an hour when we do not expect him, let us always and everywhere keep watch. Let us watchfully guard our souls and the souls entrusted to us. Let us exclude the cares of fleeting things from our hearts. Let us always keep the eyes of reason open against invisible enemies. Let us watchfully inspect the enclosures of our hearts and of our flock.

Let us devote ourselves to prayer, reading, sacred meditation, fasts, almsgiving, and other good pursuits. Let us persist watchfully in preaching and in the profit of souls, so that, both for the sake of our own custody and for that of those entrusted to us, we may attain a blessed recompense.

May the almighty and merciful Lord grant this through the prayers and merits of this glorious confessor, whose solemnity we celebrate today. Amen.

## XXV. OF ONE CONFESSOR. SERMON ON THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS

“Many have become priests according to the law, because they were prevented by death from continuing. But Jesus, because he remains forever, has an everlasting priesthood” (Heb. 7).

In this reading, dearest brothers, the Apostle assigns the difference between the priest of the law and the evangelical priest; between the priesthood of the law and the priesthood of the Gospel of Jesus Christ. He demonstrates the superiority of the privileges of the new priesthood of Jesus Christ over the legal priesthood.

The first privilege is the unity of the priesthood. For although priests were made according to the law not only at different times but also at the same time, there were many of them and they were particular. Jesus Christ, however, in the time of grace, is universal and one.

He is universal because, as John says, “He is the propitiation not only for our sins but also for those of the whole world” (1 John 2). He is one because, although there are many priests under him today, they possess not authority but only ministry. Jesus alone possesses both office and authority.

Hence it was said to John: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending, he is the one who baptizes” (Matt. 3). For we ministers of Christ immerse a child in the sacred font, yet Christ baptizes. We raise our hand, but Christ blesses. We pronounce the sacred words, but Christ consecrates.

And yet, “neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3). “Thus let a person regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Now what is required among stewards is that one be found faithful” (1 Cor. 4).

If we priests are found faithful among the other stewards, well and good; but if unfaithful—which God forbid—woe, woe to us!

The second privilege is the eternity of the priesthood. Whereas the legal priests passed away, and as some died others succeeded them, the evangelical priest Jesus Christ has an everlasting priesthood, since “the Lord swore and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109).

It is the priest’s function to hand on to God’s people the testament of his commandments and promises, to offer on account of their transgressions, and to intercede for them. Therefore Christ is said to be so much more excellent insofar as he handed on the testament to the people more excellently than the others, prayed for them, and offered himself as a sacrifice.

Although he died according to the flesh, he nevertheless performs the office of priest every day: invisibly teaching the hearts of his people each day; daily presenting the signs of his passion to the Father on our behalf; daily interceding for us with God; and daily baptizing, absolving, and binding people invisibly.

We, however, unworthy priests, are not always priests, because at death we lose the office of our stewardship. Even while alive, we are deprived of our priesthood through sinning, since we are not found fit to preach, sacrifice, or pray as we ought.

The third privilege is the power to save, for which Christ is commended when it is added: “He is able to save forever, always living to intercede for us.” Because he has coeternity with the Father, he also possesses with the Father the omnipotence to save.

He possesses not only the authority to save but also the ministry: giving himself as the price of the world’s redemption; rescuing his own from the jaws of hell; opening the kingdom of heaven to them; and always interceding for them with the Father. Hence, by antonomasia, he is called Jesus, that is, “Savior” and “Redeemer of the world.”

The legal priests, however, could save neither themselves nor others through their sacrifices and ceremonies. “For it is impossible,” as the Apostle says, “for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (Heb. 10).

We evangelical priests likewise ought to be ministers of eternal salvation, even if not its authors. Yet—something I cannot say without groaning—we are often, for some, ministers of condemnation rather than of salvation. We do not correct them but corrupt them by our evil example; and, what is worse, we flatter their vices and encourage them in their sins.

The fourth privilege is access to God through himself, for which Christ is commended when it is added: “Approaching God through himself,” without any mediator. For who can be more closely joined to God the Father than he who is consubstantial with him?

He is said to approach the one from whom he never departs because he intercedes for us before him by presenting his humanity. Yet neither the former legal priests nor the evangelical priests of the present can approach God without our high priest, the Lord Jesus Christ, mediator of God and human beings.

Indeed, because our iniquities demand it, we are now unable even to approach that mediator by ourselves. The most blessed Mother of God, ever-Virgin Mary, must certainly be entreated and implored with tears; the citizens of heaven must be entreated; the prophets, apostles, martyrs, and glorious confessors whose solemnities we celebrate today, together with the other saints, must be entreated, so that they may be our intercessors and mediators before God.

For the more numerous and greater the crimes by which we are distanced from God, the more numerous and greater the mediators we need. And because we ought to be mediators for others before God, we ourselves need mediators and reconcilers before God. We do not consider that, if someone sins, the priest will pray for him; but if the priest sins, who will pray for him? (1 Kings 2.) And if an enchanter is struck by a serpent, who will heal him? (Ecclus. 12.)

The fifth privilege is freedom from sin, for which Christ is commended when it is added: “For such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners.”

It is as though he were saying: It was fitting for us to have such a holy high priest, who could approach God through himself—that is, who would be holy. He explains in parts what it means for him to be holy: innocent with respect to his neighbor, undefiled in himself. And, stated generally, he was wholly separated from sinners through complete freedom from sin.

It is fitting that he be holy who sanctifies the guilty; innocent who judges the guilty; undefiled who washes sinners; separated from sinners who reconciles sinners to God.

In this respect all priests of both the New and the Old Testament are found imperfect, because no one is clean from defilement. “And, as John says, if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1).

But—something I cannot say without groaning—what are we priests of today like? Are we not, although we ought to sanctify the guilty, corrupting them instead by our evil reputation? Although we ought to absolve the guilty, do we not harm them by our evil example? Although we ought to wash the defiled, do we not defile others through the contagion of our own vices? Although we ought to reconcile sinners to God, do we not, through our sins, provoke God against sinners?

The sixth privilege is the height of dignity, for which Christ is commended when it is added: “Made higher than the heavens.” For he who sits equal to the Father sits higher than all the powers of heaven.

Although some legal or evangelical priests may appear greater in merit than other human beings, none of them is proclaimed greater than the angels. Hence, when the Lord had said, “Among those born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptist,” he immediately added: “But the one who is lesser in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he” (Matt. 11).

But what shall we say today, we unworthy priests, who are not greater but worse than other human beings? Although before human beings we appear higher than others by the eminence of the priestly order, in life and conduct we lie beneath the rest. And when through ambitious presumption we lift ourselves up like vain men above giants, what else are we but the reproach, contempt, and mockery of the people?

The seventh privilege of Christ is that he does not need to offer sacrifices for himself, as the other priests do. Hence it is added: “He does not have the necessity, daily like the other priests, first to offer sacrifices for his own sins, and then for those of the people.”

Because Christ is free from every stain, he does not need to offer sacrifices for himself. His humbling of himself, his assumption of the weakness of our flesh, and his endurance of insults, injuries, scourges, and the cross—all this was for us, who were in need, not for himself, who needed nothing.

Hence he himself says through the Psalmist: “What I did not steal, I then repaid” (Ps. 68).

But we priests of both the old and the new law, since none is free at least from venial sins, must first offer sacrifices for ourselves. We infirm priests, however, entangled in more serious sins and unable to offer worthy sacrifices for ourselves—how shall we be sufficient to offer for our own sins and those of others? And we who cannot carry our own burdens—how shall we appear able to carry both our own and those of others?

The eighth privilege is that Christ did not offer for the people the sacrifices of others, but himself. His offering was so fitting, so great, and so pleasing to God that, in itself, it is sufficient for the redemption of the entire human race.

The sacrifice of the legal priests, who sacrificed the blood of animals, was unfitting, small, displeasing to God, and therefore insufficient. It was unfitting because it was foreign to humanity; small because it was unequal to humanity; displeasing to God because the Lord took pleasure not in it itself, but only in its significance and in the devotion of those who offered it.

Hence the Psalmist says in the person of the Son to the Father: “You did not desire a burnt offering for sin; then I said: Behold, I come” (Ps. 39).

We evangelical priests, however, do not offer the sacrifices of others; rather, we daily repeat the sacrifice of Christ’s passion in the sacrament, according to what he himself commanded us: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22; 1 Cor. 11).

When we offer this sacrifice to God through the crucifixion of our bodily members, with true contrition of heart and fervent devotion of charity, we undoubtedly offer a sacrifice pleasing to God for our sins and those of others.

But if, remaining in the oldness of sin—which God forbid—we offer the new sacrifice of Christ with an unclean conscience and polluted lips and hands, what else do we do but aggravate divine anger against ourselves?

The ninth privilege of Christ is that, by offering himself for the people only once, he satisfied God the Father. Hence it is added: “For he did this once by offering himself.”

The legal sacrifices, because they were insufficient and only shadows of future things, were multiplied and repeated many times. But the sacrifice that is Christ, because he is the truth of the figures and is sufficient for the sins of all—the past, present, and future—is not repeated, since “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6).

Nevertheless, because we sin daily, if not mortally then venially, we repeat the sacrifice of Christ’s passion in the sacrament, so that his daily sacrament may be the cleansing of our daily transgressions. Let it be expiation for past sins and a provision and strength against future ones.

This indeed takes place if we are renewed more and more each day; if we advance daily toward what is better; if, forgetting what lies behind, we reach forward more and more toward what lies ahead.

But if we return to our vomit—which God forbid!—(2 Pet. 2); if we rot in our own filth; and if we approach the altar in such a condition, what else do we do but, like Judas the traitor, eat and drink judgment upon ourselves?

Therefore, my brothers, let us correct our ways; wash away our transgressions with the tears of repentance; devote ourselves to fasts, prayers, and works of mercy; despise all fleeting things; hasten toward God with our whole heart and desire; strive to feed the people of God by word and example; and then approach the most holy altar with a pure conscience and clean hands, until we may deserve to be worthy intercessors and mediators for the people before God.

May this be granted by that supreme mediator of God and human beings, Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## XXVI. OF ONE CONFESSOR. SERMON ON LUKE
Jesus said to his disciples: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke XII), and so forth.

This reading is divided into two parts, dearest brothers. First, the Lord shows how we ought to prepare ourselves for his coming. [Col. 1590D] Second, why we ought always to keep watch.

Now he shows how we ought to prepare ourselves for his coming when he adds, saying: “Let your loins be girded,” etc. By these words, my brothers, the Lord arms us against the evils of the present life, which are three. The way of this present temporal life is slippery, dark, and full of ambushes. It is slippery because, through frailty, it inclines toward sin; dark because, through ignorance, it is blind; and full of ambushes because it is surrounded by temptations devised through diabolical fraud. Hence the Psalmist says against the reprobate: “Let their way be darkness and slipperiness, and let the angel of the Lord pursue them” (Psalm XXXIV).

Accordingly, the Lord arms us against the slipperiness of this life when he says, “Let your loins be girded.” [Col. 1591A] Indeed, that the lust of a man is in his loins, but that of a woman is in her navel, the Lord testifies when he speaks of the devil to blessed Job, saying: “His strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly” (Job XL). We therefore gird our loins when, through continence, we restrain the lusts and pleasures of the flesh.

He arms us against ignorance when he adds: “And your lamps burning in your hands.” By burning lamps, the teaching and examples of the holy Fathers are signified. We therefore have burning lamps in our hands when, holding the light of teaching and the examples of the holy Fathers in our works, we show by our example the straight way to Christ. Concerning such works the Lord says: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew V).

[Col. 1591B] He also arms us against diabolical ambushes when he urges us to keep watch, adding: “And you yourselves like men waiting for their lord, when he shall return from the wedding.” To wait is to hope for the beloved object with watchfulness and desire. Therefore, if we love the Lord, we hope with watchfulness and desire that he will come, and we shall adorn ourselves worthily for his coming.

He takes his argument from the lesser. For if servants keep watch while their temporal lord is absent, both against thieves and for their lord’s arrival, so that when he comes he may find them watching, how much more ought we to keep watch both against invisible enemies, who are always watching us in ambush, and for the coming of our Redeemer?

[Col. 1591C] Mystically, the Lord went to the wedding when, rising from the dead and ascending into heaven, he joined to himself the heavenly multitude as the new man. He will return when he returns for judgment. Meanwhile, the faithful servants keep watch and wait, so that when he comes and knocks, they may immediately open to him.

The Lord comes to each one of us, my brothers, when through death he approaches to judge us. He knocks when, through the distress of illness, he already indicates that death is near. We open to him immediately if we receive his command with love. He does not wish to open to the Judge who comes and knocks if he is afraid to leave the body and fears seeing as Judge the one whom he remembers having despised. But whoever is secure in his conscience [Col. 1591D] opens immediately to the one who knocks, because when he recognizes that the time of near death has arrived, he rejoices in hope of recompense.

Therefore, my brothers, while it is permitted and while we are strong, let us prepare ourselves for the coming of the Judge. Let us live and act in such a way that, when he calls us through death, we may meet him secure and rejoicing.

The second part follows, in which the Lord gives a twofold reason: first, why we ought to keep watch; second, why we ought to do so always. He shows why we ought to keep watch when he explains what good those who watch obtain and what evil those who sleep obtain.

He shows what good those who watch obtain when he adds: “Blessed are those servants whom, when the Lord comes, he finds watching.” Just as three things are necessary for bodily [Col. 1592A] watchfulness, so also for spiritual watchfulness. First, we must awaken from the darkness of the body and of negligence. Second, we must always keep the eyes of reason open toward the true sun. Third, while avoiding harmful things and providing for good things, we must guard ourselves and all that belongs to us on every side.

Hence the Apostle says: “Awake, you righteous, and sin no more” (1 Corinthians XV). Again he says: “It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Romans XIII).

What reward, then, will the Lord bestow on those who watch? “Amen I say to you, he will gird himself and make them recline, and passing by he will minister to them.” These words signify honor and service. It is as though the Lord said in so many words: “Because you honored me, I also will honor you; because you ministered to me, I also will minister to you.” This is what the Lord says elsewhere: “Whoever confesses me before men, I also will confess him before my Father” (Matthew X). And again: “If anyone honors me, my Father who is in heaven will honor him” (John XII).

[Col. 1592B] Mystically, the Lord’s garments are called the saints. The Lord will gird himself with them, because he will surround himself with the saints and will bind them inseparably to himself with the belt of familiar love. He will make them recline, that is, rest at the eternal and blessed banquet. He will minister to them, that is, satisfy them with the sweetness of eternal delights, in accordance with the words: “The sound of rejoicing and confession, the voice of those feasting” (Psalm XLI).

And he will do this “passing by,” that is, distinguishing rewards according to the diversity of merits: “For star differs from star in glory” (1 Corinthians XV). [Col. 1592C] Or certainly, “passing by” means making them pass from judgment to the kingdom, from the vision of his humanity—in which the Lord will be seen by all at the judgment—to the vision of his divinity, in which he will be seen by the elect alone in the kingdom, according to the words: “Let the wicked be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of God” (Isaiah XXVI).

The Lord grants these good things, my brothers, to those who watch. But what will become of those who sleep in their sins throughout all their childhood, or even throughout all their youth? Let them not despair, but awaken quickly. For it follows: “And if he comes in the second watch or in the third watch, and finds them so, blessed are those servants.”

Therefore, my brothers, whoever was drowsy in the first watch, that is, in childhood, should at least keep watch in the second, that is, in youth, and then begin to act well. Whoever was also drowsy in youth should at least keep watch in the third watch, that is, in [Col. 1592D] old age, and then begin to work well.

Who is sufficient to weigh the greatness of divine patience? The Lord is offended, and yet he calls to forgiveness. He is despised, and yet he waits. He does not even reject those who have slept in their sins until extreme old age, if they repent. He did not reject the thief converted on the cross, but opened paradise to him (Luke XXIII).

Let no one, my brothers, take from this an occasion to abuse God’s patience. Let no one say: “I am young; I shall repent in old age.” Who knows whether he will reach old age, when he is not even certain of one hour? Perhaps this is your old age. Those who promise themselves a long life and postpone repentance [Col. 1593A] are either overtaken by death or hindered by desire.

Hear Solomon: “Do not delay,” he says, “to turn to God, and do not put it off from day to day. For his wrath will come suddenly, and at the time of vengeance he will destroy you” (Ecclesiasticus V). And again: “Do not add,” he says, “sin upon sin, and do not say, ‘The mercy of God is great; he will have mercy on the multitude of my sins.’ For mercy and wrath quickly draw near from him, and his wrath looks upon sinners” (ibid.).

For the more patiently God now waits for us, the more severely he will rage in the future. Hence Paul says: “Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? According to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s just judgment” (Romans II).

[Col. 1593B] Hence the Psalmist says: “God is a judge, just, strong, and patient” (Psalm VII). In saying “patient,” he first said “just,” because the one who now waits with the greatest patience will judge with the greatest severity in the future judgment.

Hence the Wise Man warns: “Do not say in your heart, ‘I have sinned, and what sorrowful thing has happened to me?’ For the Most High is a patient requiter” (Ecclesiasticus V). Although he now waits patiently, in the future he will repay each person according to his merits.

He shows what evil those who sleep obtain when he adds the parable, saying: “But know this: if the householder knew at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly watch and would not allow his house to be broken into.”

This too is an argument from the lesser. For if a householder watches to preserve his house, which is certainly lowly and perishable, how much more ought each one of you, my brothers, diligently to watch for the preservation of his soul, [Col. 1593C] which is certainly precious and eternal?

Mystically, this householder is our mind, which has authority in the dwelling of bodily habitation to govern and provide. When, through inertia, it sleeps in sins and withdraws from guarding itself, the thief—that is, sudden and unforeseen death—comes, breaks into the house of bodily habitation, and swiftly snatches away the spirit for condemnation.

But if our mind were wise, it would watch; and while watching, it would guard against the thief, that is, death. Then death would not harm it; rather, it would benefit it, since through death it would have entrance not into condemnation but into eternal life.

[Col. 1593D] After the Lord had shown why we ought to keep watch, he next shows why we ought always to keep watch, when he adds: “And you also be ready, because at an hour when you do not expect it, the Son of Man will come.”

If the hour were determined for us at which the Son of Man would come either to call us from the body or to judge us, it would not be necessary for us always to keep watch, but only at the hour when we knew beforehand that he would come. Therefore the Lord willed that we should be ignorant of the day of our death and of the day of judgment, so that we might always fear, always await death, and always be ready to receive it.

It should also be noted that he does not say, “At the hour you expect,” but, “At the hour you do not expect, he will come.” No one is so old, no one so infirm, that he [Col. 1594A] does not hope to live a little longer. And so every person dies at a time when he did not think he would die.

But if we always keep watch, if we are always ready, we cannot be overtaken by death. Therefore, my brothers, let us always keep watch in good works and always prepare ourselves for imminent death. Let us wash away our sins with tears of true repentance and redeem them through works of mercy. Let us devote ourselves to fasts, prayers, and other good works. Let us consider as gain whatever is spent for God and for our souls, and regard everything else as loss.

While it is now permitted, let us do whatever good we can, because the time will already be present when we shall be able to do no work. Therefore Solomon says: [Col. 1594B] “Whatever your hand is able to do, perform diligently, for there is neither work, nor reason, nor knowledge, nor wisdom in the underworld, where you are hastening” (Ecclesiastes IX).

Therefore, my brothers, let us not let a day or an hour pass idly. Let all our thought, speech, and action tend toward heavenly things. Let us hasten there, awake and asleep, with our whole desire, so that at last, through the intercession of the saints whose solemnity we celebrate today, we may deserve to reach that place. Amen.

## XXVII. OF ONE CONFESSOR, NOT A BISHOP. SERMON FROM THE BOOK OF WISDOM

“Beloved by God and by men. For blessed is he whose memory is in benediction” (Ecclesiasticus XLV), etc.

By these words, [Col. 1594C] dearest brothers, Jesus son of Sirach commends Moses, the lawgiver. Since these words also apply to this glorious confessor, whose solemnity we celebrate today, we appropriately recite them today in his praise.

Fifteen graces are enumerated here, by which blessed Moses formerly, and this present confessor now, surpasses others.

He therefore sets forth the first grace when he says: “Beloved by God and by men.” Some are beloved by men and not by God, and they are evil. Others are beloved by God and by men, and they are very good.

Some are pleasing not to God but to men, through flattery and adulation, and they are evil. Of them it is said: “Those who please men are confounded, because God has despised them” [Col. 1594D] (Psalm LII).

Others are pleasing to God through purity of mind, but displeasing to men because of the strictness and correction of their conduct. Paul belonged to their number when he said: “If I were still pleasing men, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians I).

Others are of such great gentleness and mildness that they please both God and men. They please God through a pure conscience, and even evil men through the mildness and kindness of their conduct, which they show even to their enemies.

Such was Moses, such was David, such was Saint Clement, and such was this glorious confessor whose festival we celebrate today. Through his gentleness and sweetness, he softened many who were hard and fierce, and won them for God.

Let us strive, my brothers, to be such people, so that through our gentleness and kindness [Col. 1595A] we may strive and be able to draw many to ourselves and win them for God.

He sets forth the second grace when he adds: “Whose memory is in benediction.” Whenever we recall to mind the good life and deeds either of blessed Moses or of this glorious holy confessor, we bless and praise him. And if the memory of the deceased is thus in benediction, how much more will his life, whether temporal or eternal, be in greater benediction?

He was blessed while alive, blessed when dead, blessed when glorified; blessed with himself, blessed among men, blessed with God. With himself, by the blessing of graces; among men, by the blessing of praises; with God, by the blessing of eternal rewards. [Col. 1595B]

In order that we too may deserve to be blessed by God and by men, let us always strive, my brothers, never to curse but to bless and to act well. For it is written: “He loved cursing, and it shall come to him; and he did not desire blessing, and it shall be far from him” (Psalm CVIII).

He sets forth the third grace when he adds: “He made him like the saints in glory.” Who made him? Without doubt, God, who gives both willing and accomplishing (Philippians II).

He therefore made him like them—not merely in resemblance, but in the reality itself. He made holy Moses like the earlier saints, namely Seth, Enoch, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; and he made this glorious confessor like the holy apostles, martyrs, and confessors.

And in what respect? In the glory of virtues, in the glory of good works, and in the glory of rewards. [Col. 1595C] The saints possess the glory of virtues, the glory of good works, and the glory of rewards, but not with themselves; rather, with God.

In order that we too may deserve to become like them, let us, my brothers, be their imitators, because through imitation one comes to likeness. God indeed grants the likeness of the saints, but only to those who imitate them. Let us therefore imitate them in labor, so that we may deserve to become like them in recompense.

He sets forth the fourth grace when he adds: “He magnified him in the fear of his enemies.” He magnified Moses among the Egyptians, Amalekites, Amorites, Midianites, and the other enemies whom he overcame, and made him great and terrifying.

He also magnified this blessed confessor in the fear of his enemies, and made him a triumphal victor over both visible and invisible enemies. [Col. 1595D] The Lord gave him power to overcome the devil’s ambushes, break his camps, and forcefully free the vessels of captivity from his jaws. Hence “the wicked one was brought to nothing in his sight” (Psalm XIV).

Supported equally by his prayers and example, my brothers, let us learn to rebel bravely against the devil, to frustrate his ambushes, overthrow his strongholds, and free captives from his fetters, so that from now on he may fear to attack us.

He sets forth the fifth grace when he adds: “And by his words he appeased monsters.” Moses indeed performed the monstrous signs that the Lord inflicted upon Pharaoh and all his servants, and by his prayers turned them away and appeased them, with Pharaoh permitting the release of the children of Israel—such things as dog-flies (Latin *cynomyiae*, OCR “cimonias”), blisters, locusts, and the like. [Col. 1596A]

But this distinguished confessor, which is greater, appeased the monstrous conduct and lives of perverse men through the teaching of his words and brought them back to uprightness: those who were wolves in their cruelty he recalled to gentleness; those who were dogs in their uncleanness, to purity; those who were swine in their sensuality, to continence; and those who were proud, to humility.

Following him, my brothers, let us also strive first to bring the monstrosity and crookedness of our vices and conduct within ourselves, and then within our neighbors, back to uprightness and virtue.

He sets forth the sixth grace when he adds: “He glorified him in the sight of kings.” God glorified Moses in the sight of kings when he appointed him, as it were, god of Pharaoh; [Col. 1596B] when he performed wonders and signs through his hand; and when he displayed him as glorious in the sight of Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, and of the other kings.

He likewise glorified this glorious confessor in the sight of kings, raising him up as a revered and wondrous lamp to those very kings in the governance of conduct and souls.

Imitating him, my brothers, let us strive first to correct and govern ourselves, so that thereafter we may be able to govern and correct others.

He sets forth the seventh grace when he adds: “And he joined to him the heart of his people.” The Lord joined the heart of his people to Moses, so that they would love him, [Col. 1596C] follow him, and listen to him as a good shepherd and leader.

The Lord also joined the heart of his people to this holy confessor, because he gave him such grace that his people loved him, imitated him, and obeyed him as a good father.

In order that we too, though unworthy, may deserve to have this grace, let us learn to join the heart of our people to ourselves through love and condescension, in accordance with the Lord’s command: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John XV).

Through condescension, in accordance with what is written: “They have appointed you leader; do not exalt yourself, but be as one of them” (Ecclesiasticus XXXII); through bearing with and accommodating others, as the Apostle urges: “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians VI).

[Col. 1596D] He sets forth the eighth grace when he adds: “And he showed him his grace.” He showed Moses his glory when he displayed his power to him through created things. For the Lord said: “Man shall not see my face and live” (Exodus XXXIII).

God also showed his glory to this glorious confessor when he enabled him to understand the Creator through creatures, and when, through grace, revelation, and contemplation, he enlightened his heart to understand him.

If we are wise, my brothers, may we too, enlightened by grace, be able to understand through the wondrous fullness of the elements how beautiful their author is; through the wise arrangement of the elements, how wise their author is; through the immensity of the elements, how immense their author is; through the power of the elements, how powerful their author is; and through the perpetuity of the elements, how perpetual their author is.

[Col. 1597A] He sets forth the ninth and tenth graces when he adds: “He made him holy in his faith and gentleness.” Although Moses possessed the other virtues, he is especially commended in these two, because in them he shone more excellently than the others.

He possessed faith excellently, since he firmly believed the Lord and obeyed him in everything; for his sake he regarded labors, dangers, threats, and the power of kings as nothing.

He possessed gentleness, since he patiently endured the contradictions, insults, injuries, complaints, and slanders of his own people, and prayed for his enemies and for those who wished to stone him.

This glorious confessor also shone in the virtue of obedience. For God’s sake he despised the world with its desires; he regarded it as riches to suffer every hardship and difficulty for him; he fought bravely against heretics and unbelievers; he faithfully ministered in all things with the talents entrusted to him; [Col. 1597B] and, if there had been someone to inflict it, he did not fear to suffer death.

Therefore, since in spirit he was not lacking in martyrdom, he will not lack the crown of martyrdom.

He shone exceedingly in the virtue of gentleness. He endured insults, injuries, and persecutions not only patiently but joyfully; he regarded sinners as his helpers; he did good to his enemies; and he prayed for his persecutors.

Imitating him, my brothers, let us learn to believe the Lord firmly, to endure adversity bravely for his sake, and through our gentleness to overcome those who injure and persecute us, winning them for God through benefits and prayers.

[Col. 1597C] He sets forth the eleventh grace when he adds: “And he chose him from all flesh.” The Lord chose Moses from among all men as judge of his people, minister of his signs and wonders, and lawgiver.

The Lord also chose this glorious confessor to be, through example and teaching, a leader of his people; a minister of wondrous works; and a preacher of divine commandments.

Would that the Lord had chosen us too, my brothers, as leaders of his people, ministers of his sacraments, and preachers of his commandments—not, as I fear, to our destruction, but rather for the benefit of our own souls and those entrusted to us!

[Col. 1597D] He sets forth the twelfth grace when he adds: “For he heard him and his voice.” Moses indeed heard the Lord speaking to him not through an intermediary but mouth to mouth, since, as Scripture testifies, he spoke with him as familiarly as a friend with a friend (Exodus XXXIII).

This blessed confessor also heard the Lord—not only through an interpreter and through Scripture, but also spiritually, with the Lord speaking inwardly to him. From him he received the ability both to hear and to obey.

Would that the Lord also make us hear his voice inwardly, giving us his grace so that we may both hear and obey.

He sets forth the thirteenth grace when he adds: “And he led him into the cloud.” The Lord led Moses into the cloud covering Mount Sinai (Exodus XIX), where he gave him the law, thereby showing that he was leading him into the secret of intimacy and into the obscurity of the law.

[Col. 1598A] In the same way he led this glorious confessor into the cloud, since he received him into the secret of his intimacy, disclosed to him the obscurity of his law, and filled him with the clouds of his teaching.

But what are we, unworthy shepherds, to say about these things, when, because our sins demand it, we are excluded from the secrets of God? In the obscurity of the law we are blind guides, and we wither away from the rain of heavenly teaching.

He sets forth the fourteenth grace when he adds: “And he gave him a heart for the commandments.” God gave both of them alike—Moses and our confessor—a heart for understanding, directing, and carrying out his commandments. If they are not understood, they are not loved; and unless they are loved, they are not carried out. In all this God is at work, who gives both willing and accomplishing (Philippians II).

Let us unceasingly implore him, my brothers, with all the depths of our souls, so that he may also give us a heart for doing his commandments: that we may understand them, love what we have understood, and accomplish what we have loved.

[Col. 1598B] He sets forth the fifteenth grace when he adds: “And he gave him the law of life and discipline,” that is, he gave him the law.

God gave Moses the law of life and discipline, that is, the law which leads to life through discipline, when it is understood spiritually.

God also inspired into the heart of this glorious confessor the law of life and discipline, that is, the law by which he himself lived spiritually and taught his disciples, leading them with him to eternal glory.

Through his glorious merits and intercessions, may the Lord also grant us [Col. 1598C] to understand his law spiritually, to live spiritually in it, and effectively to instruct by example and word those entrusted to us, so that together with them we may deserve to attain the blessedness of those whose memory we celebrate. Amen.

## XXVIII. THE SAME, ON THE SAME. SERMON FROM THE BOOK OF WISDOM

“The Lord led the just man through straight ways and showed him the kingdom of God” (Wisdom X), etc.

In this reading, my brothers, sixteen benefits are enumerated which divine Wisdom bestowed upon the patriarch Jacob. Since these benefits are also rightly found in this holy confessor, whose solemnity we celebrate today, the reading itself is recited today in his commemoration.

The first benefit, therefore, is that divine Wisdom led the just [Col. 1598D] Jacob through straight ways, namely when, after obtaining the blessing by supplanting his brother, he fled from his brother Esau on the advice of his mother and went to his uncle Laban in Mesopotamia.

The same Wisdom, the Son of God, also led this glorious confessor through the straight ways of God’s commandments, so that he would not turn aside to the left or to the right.

And how did he lead him? By inviting him through promises, showing him the way by his own example, and drawing him after himself by the hand of his aid.

In order that the Lord may also lead us through straight ways, let us call out to him with our whole desire, my brothers. Let us call out thus: “Draw us after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song of Songs I).

The second benefit is that the Lord showed Jacob the kingdom of God, namely when he showed him [Col. 1599A] in a dream both a ladder reaching from earth and angels ascending and descending upon it, and the Lord resting upon the ladder and saying to him: “I am the God of Abraham and Isaac” (Genesis XXVIII).

The Lord also showed this blessed confessor his kingdom even in this life through understanding of Sacred Scripture, through spiritual contemplation, and through a certain foretaste of future blessedness. Now, having been stripped of the flesh, he has shown it to him through the presence of its enjoyment in the kingdom.

Would that he also show his kingdom to us, my brothers, so that we may be drawn by its fragrance and desire, saying with the Psalmist: “How great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have shown to those who fear you!” (Psalm XXX).

The third benefit is that the Lord gave Jacob knowledge of the saints, [Col. 1599B] which he possessed both in temporal and in divine matters. He perceived the natures of things, prudently administered temporal affairs, understood visions, and possessed the spirit of prophecy at the end of his life.

This holy confessor also possessed knowledge of both earthly and heavenly things. Like a prudent merchant, weighing things according to their nature rather than according to opinion, when he found one precious pearl, he sold all that he had and bought it (Matthew XIII).

May the Lord grant us this knowledge also, my brothers, so that, regarding all earthly things as dung in comparison with heavenly things, we may hasten to give and exchange these for those.

The fourth benefit is that the Lord honored Jacob in his labors, [Col. 1599C] namely by directing his labors, making them turn out for good, and even multiplying Laban through his service.

The Lord also honored this glorious confessor in his labors, because in his labors and worthy studies he gave him diligent exercise, and in worthy exercise an honorable accomplishment. For just as the shamefulness of one’s labors disgraces the laborer, so the worthiness of one’s labors ennobles him.

Hence, my brothers, let us strive to flee dishonorable occupations and frequent honorable ones.

The fifth benefit is that God brought his labors to completion, because he completed Jacob in full happiness—of wives, children, household, years, possessions, and all things.

He also brought the labors of this holy confessor to completion, since, according to the purpose of his calling, working all things together for his good, he filled him with an abundance of virtues, conduct, and merits.

Through his glorious prayers, may the Lord also deign to bring our labors to completion for good, and bring the course of our life from good to better fulfillment.

The sixth benefit is that the Lord stood by Jacob against those who were deceitfully plotting against him. [Col. 1599D] For when Laban planned to deceive Jacob and reduce his wages by changing them, the Lord gave Jacob counsel, so that the fraud would not harm him, but rather Laban would deceive himself.

The Lord also stood by this glorious confessor amid the fraud of those who sought to deceive him. When the devil and diabolical men prepared to entrap him through temptations, by the Lord’s providence they harmed themselves instead and helped him, giving him an opportunity for victory and piling up greater condemnation for themselves.

Would that through his glorious prayers the Lord also stand by us in temptations, reveal Satan’s ambushes to us, and make them turn out for our victory.

The seventh benefit is that the Lord made Jacob honorable, [Col. 1600A] adorning him with good conduct, illuminating him with virtues, beautifying him with works, and deeming him worthy of his speech, so that he would be venerated and praised throughout all ages.

The Lord also made this glorious confessor honorable: honorable in the holiness of his way of life, honorable in his good reputation, honorable in virtues, and honorable in miracles.

Would that the Lord also make us honorable, my brothers, so that, fleeing every dishonor, we may deserve to minister to him honorably.

The eighth benefit is that the Lord protected Jacob from his enemies, namely, from his brother and from the Canaanites: he reconciled his brother to him and restrained the others so that they could not harm him. The Lord likewise protected this blessed confessor from his enemies—not in such a way that they did not inflict injuries, but so that, while injuring him, they did not harm him; indeed, they rather benefited him. Thus, in fact, the Lord has been accustomed to deliver his apostles and martyrs in the better way. Therefore, my brothers, when we pray, we ought to say to him: “Give us help in tribulation” (Psalm 59), not “from tribulation,” as though we were asking to be removed from it, but as if we said: Make the tribulation itself turn out for our advancement.

The ninth benefit is that the Lord guarded Jacob from seducers, namely, from the crime of Simeon and Levi, who deceitfully killed the king and people of Shechem [Col. 1600C], and whom he afterwards rebuked, saying: “Let my soul not enter into their counsel” (Genesis 49). The Lord likewise guarded this blessed confessor from seducers and other sinners, so that he would not become their accomplice by flattering them, consenting to them, or remaining silent. In this many of us sin: by keeping silent about the sins of others, we encourage them. Hence we are called by the Lord “mute dogs unable to bark” (Isaiah 56).

The tenth benefit is that the Lord gave Jacob a vigorous struggle in which to conquer, when he wrestled with the angel—that is, with the Lord under the appearance of an angel—and, although wounded, did not let him go until he blessed him (Genesis 32). The Lord likewise gave this glorious confessor the strength to struggle and persevere, so that, although weak, he would not cease asking and knocking until, as it were, he overcame the Lord’s severity and inclined him to bless him [Col. 1600D]. Following his example, my brothers, let us persevere in prayer and not desist until we are blessed by him.

The eleventh benefit is that the wisdom of God did not abandon the just Joseph, who had been sold, but delivered him from Potiphar, who had bought him in order to hand him over to vile uses, and also from Potiphar’s wife, who desired him. This holy confessor, likewise sold under the sin of the first parent, or certainly sold and dispersed through the slanders of false brothers, was not abandoned by the wisdom of God, but was delivered from sinners, so that they would not harm him either through their persecution or through the contagion of their vices. Would that the Lord also deliver us, my brothers, who have been sold into sins, so that sinners may not harm us, either by openly persecuting us or by secretly smearing us with their contagions! [Col. 1601A]

The twelfth benefit is that the wisdom of God was with Joseph when he was cast into the pit—that is, into Pharaoh’s prison—and did not abandon him in his chains. The wisdom of God likewise did not desert this glorious confessor when he was placed in the prison of tribulation, but freed him from the chains of snares—or certainly of sins—in which even the saints have sometimes been held. Would that the Lord, through his holy intercessions, deign powerfully to free us from the prison of evil habit and from the bonds of our iniquities!

The thirteenth benefit is that divine wisdom gave Joseph the scepter of the kingdom, when he was exalted in Egypt by Pharaoh as virtually a second king. To this holy [Col. 1601B] confessor also the wisdom of God gave royal power, by which he ruled himself and his own faithfully and prudently, with the rod of justice restraining the wickedness of vices and imitating the goodness of morals and virtues. Would that the Lord grant us this royal power, so that we may be able to rule and govern both ourselves and those subject to us!

The fourteenth benefit is that the wisdom of God gave Joseph power over those who had oppressed him, because it humbled beneath him the wickedness of his brothers who had sold him, and the wickedness of Potiphar and his wife, who had bought him and wished to dishonor him. To this blessed confessor also, on account of the merit of his humility and patience, God gave power over demons and over demoniac men [Col. 1601C] who had previously troubled him, so that he might make the proud humble and patient, and drive demons out of possessed people and torment them. Would that, through his glorious merits, the Lord grant us the ability to resist the temptations of demons and wicked men!

The fifteenth benefit is that the Lord showed those who had stained Joseph with a false accusation to be liars, such as Potiphar and his wife, demonstrating him to be innocent. God likewise demonstrated to be liars the envious and slanderers who had dared to fabricate evil things about this holy confessor, when he revealed his innocence and holiness through wondrous works and virtues. Following his example, my brothers, let us learn to endure our envious people and slanderers patiently, since God will reveal their falsehood and our truth. “For nothing is covered that will not be revealed” (Matthew 10).

The sixteenth benefit is that the Lord gave both Joseph and this holy confessor eternal glory: the glory of wondrous holiness, the glory of wondrous reputation, the glory of eternal blessedness, glory in the soul, glory among the people, and glory in heaven, where the saints shine like the sun (Matthew 13). May almighty and merciful Lord grant us this glory through the merits and intercessions of this holy confessor. Amen.

## XXIX. ALSO ON THE SAME SUBJECT. A SERMON ON LUKE

“No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place, nor under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light” (Luke 11), etc.

Here the Lord speaks metaphorically, dearest brothers. This metaphor can be interpreted in three ways. For there is a universal lamp, a particular lamp, and an individual lamp.

The universal lamp is the sun of justice, our Lord Jesus Christ, who, as John says, “is the true light which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). Insofar as he is God, he is one eternal light with the Father. Insofar as he is human, he is a lighted lamp, the flame of divinity in the earthen vessel of humanity.

A lamp does three things. It enlightens the eyes by dispelling darkness; it shows the way; and it refuses itself to no one except the person who withdraws from it, for “he is near to all who call upon him in truth” (Psalm 144). Christ [Col. 1602B] likewise enlightens the eyes of reason by dispelling the darkness of sins; he shows the way of life by his example and teaching; and he denies his grace to no one except the person who withdraws from it: “For he is near to all who call upon him in truth.” Hence Paul also admonishes us “that no one fail to obtain the grace of God” (Hebrews 12). It is as though he said: The grace of God, so far as it depends upon itself, is lacking to no one, except only to the person who, by withdrawing from it, is himself absent from it.

God therefore kindled the lamp in the man Jesus not in order to place it in a hidden place—that is, under the shadow of the Law—but rather in the open, in the evident light of the New Testament. For this reason God sent his Son through the Incarnation: so that the divinity hidden from human beings might appear in the lamp of humanity.

Nor did he kindle it in order to place it under a bushel—that is, under the measure of the Law—but rather on a lampstand, that is, on the eminence of the universal Church [Col. 1602C]. And for what purpose? So that those who enter—that is, the darkness of this world—may see the light, and, by following it, may be able to keep to the straight path and reach the heavenly homeland.

Christ is not only a lamp; what is more, he is the eye of the Church. Hence he adds: “The lamp of your body is your eye.” The eye is not only the light of the body, but also its watchman and guardian, and it belongs to the integrity of the body. Thus Christ is both the light and the watchman of the Church, according to the saying: “The watchman stands above” (2 Kings 9), for he observes us and our deeds every day. He is also the guardian of the Church, since “he who guards Israel will neither slumber nor sleep” [Col. 1602D] (Psalm 120). He also belongs to the integrity of the Church. Therefore, in guarding his body, which is the Church, he is exceedingly watchful and solicitous.

“If your eye,” he says, “is simple, your whole body will be full of light. But if it is evil, your body also will be dark.” Truly, Christ is the simple eye. An eye is called simple when it sees clearly and usefully. Christ indeed sees clearly, since no creature is invisible in his sight. He also sees usefully for us, since, if we wish it, he provides for us only what is beneficial. He sees rightly for us as well, since he provides for our advancement with a right and good intention.

If, therefore, the Church or any believer follows Christ, who is the simple eye, as guardian and provider, the whole body [Col. 1603A]—that is, the entire congregation of the faithful—or the whole life that follows such an eye will be full of light.

The evil eye, however, is the devil: “the eye, because he transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Corinthians 11). He is evil because he sees darkly, obliquely, and uselessly. He sees darkly because the obstinacy of his malice has so blinded him that he loves and seeks only what is dark. He sees obliquely because in all his promises he intends to deceive. He sees uselessly because, even if by a lively intelligence he perceives certain things sharply, he nevertheless sees them uselessly both for himself and for others. Even if, at times, he succeeds by lying in wait for someone contrary to expectation, this was not the intention he had.

If, therefore, someone follows the devil, who is certainly an evil eye, as counselor and provider, the whole body—that is, his work or his life, by following such a provider—will be dark [Col. 1603B]. “See,” he says, “that the light which is in you is not darkness”; that is, beware lest the one whom you follow as light, guide, and provider be dark.

This is plainly directed against those who do not hesitate to consult the devil concerning doubtful and future matters through magical arts. For the devil can conjecture future events and the hidden things of hearts; he cannot know them, except perhaps through revelation by angels. But whether he knows them or does not know them, what greater madness is there than to consult one’s enemy, who has never known how to counsel anyone, but only how to deceive?

“If, therefore,” he says, “your whole body”—that is, the whole Church, or the whole of someone’s life or work—“by following the simple eye,” namely, our Lord, “is full of light,” so that it contains no part of darkness, “it will be wholly luminous, and, like a lamp of brightness, it will illuminate you”—understand: the light of the eye and of the lamp [Col. 1603C].

The Church’s perfect purity, however, will be in the other life, where it will be without spot or wrinkle. For while it suffers defects in this life, there will always be a spot on the moon. Yet the life of a saint can also be so luminous in this life that it nevertheless has something dark at some time, if not in mortal sins, at least in venial sins.

Therefore, my brothers, let us follow the lamp—that is, our eye, Jesus Christ—and hasten with our whole desire toward that blessed life where we may attain perfect purity and radiance.

The particular lamp is every distinguished and spiritual teacher. Of such persons the Lord says: “You are the light of the world” [Col. 1603D] (Matthew 5). Like the sun or a lamp, such a teacher enlightens the eyes of reason in all things, if not as author, at least as minister; he shows the way of life by example and teaching; and he denies the light of his teaching to no one. Whoever denies it deprives himself of the office of a lamp.

The Lord kindles such a lamp in the saints, not so that it may be placed in the hidden place of a solitary and concealed life, nor under the bushel of a secluded life, but upon the eminence of the Church, so that those who enter the Church may see the light of good example and teaching.

The Lord would always do this, unless the merits and morals of human beings prevented it. For the merits of an evil people demand that there be raised up over them not a man luminous in life and teaching, but a dark one, to the greater detriment both of himself and of the people. Job testifies to this very thing, since, on account of the sins of the people, the Lord permits a hypocrite to reign (Job 34) [Col. 1604A].

The disposition of many people is also such that they advance more when placed below than when placed on high, in a hidden life than in an exalted one, and in the contemplative life than in the active one.

“For the lamp of your body is your eye.” An ecclesiastical teacher ought to be not only a lamp but also an eye—that is, a watchman, a guardian, and a principal member of the Church. He is a watchman so that, established on high, he may observe the conduct of each person. Hence the Lord says: “Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezekiel 3). He is a guardian so that he may keep watch through the night over his flock, lest the prowling lion tear away any of his own. He is a member so that, joined to the other members of Christ by the sinews of charity [Col. 1604B], he may suffer with them.

If this eye is simple—seeing clearly, usefully, and rightly—the whole body of the Church that follows it will be luminous. But if it is evil—seeing darkly, uselessly, and obliquely—the whole body of the Church that follows it as guide will be dark.

Just as clear sight in the eyes brightens and beautifies the whole face, and just as a darkened or blinded eye darkens and disfigures the entire human face, so a dark pastor blinds and defiles the whole face of the Church.

“See,” he says, “that the light which is in you is not darkness.” As though he said: Take every precaution lest your teacher, who ought to enlighten you, be dark. For, as he says elsewhere: “If the light which is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness itself be?” (Matthew 6) [Col. 1604C].

Let the children of the Church therefore beware lest they choose a dark eye as their guide. Even if such a person has been imposed upon them by force, or has later been corrupted from a former good condition—as was thought—they must not follow his leadership, lest, being blind, leading the blind and following them, they should plunge together with him into the pit of eternal damnation (Matthew 15). Rather, as quickly as they can, let them tear out the evil eye, according to the Lord’s command: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you” (Matthew 5).

This plainly condemns those who, neglecting men distinguished in life and teaching, exalt upon the lampstand of the Church smoking rather than burning coals, so that those who enter do not see the light [Col. 1604D].

The individual lamp is the rational faculty of the mind in each person. Like a light, it enlightens a person, shows what must be avoided or pursued, and, like a flame, naturally rises upward. Once kindled by divine grace, this flame must not be placed in a hidden place—that is, among bestial habits and bodily pleasures. It must not be suppressed or concealed, nor placed under a bushel, enclosed under the measure of bodily senses. Rather, it must be raised upon a lampstand—that is, upon the eminence of the whole person—so that all the person’s members and senses may be subjected to it, while it itself rules, provides, and exercises dominion.

This is not only a lamp but also an eye: that is, a watcher, preserver, and superior part of the human being. The eye of reason [Col. 1605A] is simple when it sees clearly, usefully, and rightly.

Some people see clearly with their eyes but not usefully. Others see clearly and usefully, but not rightly. A person sees clearly but uselessly when he sharply distinguishes good from evil but does not choose the good with discernment. A person sees clearly and usefully but not rightly when he prudently distinguishes and usefully chooses what has been discerned, but does not direct what he has chosen toward its proper end.

The simple eye, therefore, is the one that prudently distinguishes, usefully chooses what it has distinguished, and directs what it has chosen toward God by a good intention.

If the eye of reason is simple in this way, the whole body of the life or work governed by such an eye will be luminous. But if the eye of reason is evil—whether by distinguishing darkly, choosing badly, or directing itself obliquely toward an evil end [Col. 1605B]—the whole body of the life or work governed by such an eye will be dark.

“See, therefore,” he says, “that the light which is in you is not darkness”; that is, see that your reason, which ought to enlighten you, is not dark through seeing darkly, uselessly, or obliquely.

“But if your whole body”—that is, your life or work—“is luminous,” containing no darkness either through ignorance, bad choice, or an oblique intention, “it will be wholly luminous,” that is, the whole person will be luminous. For if your reason is wholly luminous and your life is wholly luminous, then you will be perfectly luminous in your entirety, and your eye will be entirely simple.

Then, “like a lamp of brightness, it will illuminate you,” so that you are luminous in yourself, before the people, and before God.

Therefore, my brothers, let us strive to purify the eye of our mind. Let us flee not only dark works but also dark thoughts. Let us do good works with a good intention. Let us make God the end of our works and hasten toward him with our whole desire. Let all the things we possess in this world become worthless to us; let us transfer everything we can to the heavenly treasures through works of mercy, so that we may deserve to be clothed in the robe of eternal radiance. This is granted by God and our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever. Amen.

## COMMON OF ONE VIRGIN. XXX. ONE VIRGIN. A SERMON ON THE LETTER TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 1605D]

“Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord” (2 Corinthians 10), etc.

This reading has three parts, my brothers. First, the Apostle urges the person who boasts to boast in the Lord. Second, he wishes his foolishness to be endured. Third, he says that he is jealous for us with the jealousy of God.

First, therefore, he urges that the one who boasts should boast in the Lord. For someone to boast in the Lord, three things must come together: that he attribute both his joy and the cause of his joy to God; that he give thanks to God for it; and that he make God the end of his joy.

There are some who attribute their joy and the cause of their joy to themselves rather than to God, and they are proud, like those who say: “Our hand is exalted, and the Lord did not make all these things” (Deuteronomy 32).

There are some who attribute their joy and the cause of their joy to God, but do not give him the thanks that are his due; they are ungrateful, like the nine lepers who did not return to give thanks to the one whom they knew to be the author of their healing [Col. 1606A].

There are some who attribute both their joy and the cause of their joy to God and give him thanks, but divert the end of their joy toward some empty intention; they are vain, like hypocrites and all lovers of vanity.

Whoever, therefore, attributes to God both what he rejoices in and the source of his joy, gives him thanks for it, and makes him its end, certainly boasts in God—and boasts well, if he boasts of what is good.

There are some who boast of an evil in something good, such as Paul and the other zealots of the Law, who boasted in the persecution of the apostles, thinking that they were “offering service to God” [Col. 1606B] (John 16); they did indeed have zeal “for God, but not according to knowledge” (Romans 10).

There are also those who boast of something good in something evil, such as hypocrites, and they are worse. For hypocrites boast vainly about the good, if they do anything good.

There are those who boast of something evil in something evil, and they are the worst, such as those “who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Proverbs 2).

There are also those who boast of something good in something good, and they are good: namely, those who boast in God concerning the good they possess.

Those, therefore, who boast of the good in the good act well and discerningly.

Why a person ought to boast not in himself but in God, he shows when he adds: “For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom God commends.” That is, a person is not approved and praiseworthy because he approves himself, but because God approves and commends him [Col. 1606C].

There are some who approve themselves in the sight of human beings through empty praises or feigned works, and are rejected, such as braggarts and hypocrites.

There are others who presume upon their faith and charity in the sight of God and approve themselves. For this reason they are not rejected, but rather disapproved and humbled, so that they may recognize their weakness. Thus Peter, presuming upon himself, said: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matthew 26). He was permitted to fall so that thereafter he might recognize his weakness and trust not in himself but in God alone.

David likewise, when he had said, as though presuming upon himself, “I said in my abundance: I shall never be moved” (Psalm 29), immediately shows that he was corrected for this presumption when he adds: “You turned your face away from me, and I became troubled” (ibid.) [Col. 1606D].

Similarly, when he had said, presuming upon himself, “I swore and resolved to keep the judgments of your justice” (Psalm 118), he immediately shows that he was corrected for this presumption when he adds: “I have been humbled exceedingly, Lord; give me life according to your word” (ibid.).

There are also others who, compelled by necessity, approve themselves humbly and for a proper end. Yet they are not rejected on this account; rather, God approves and commends them, as he did Paul, who, compelled by the pseudo-apostles, commended himself to the Corinthians (2 Corinthians 11), so that they might listen to him preaching the truth rather than to a pseudo-apostle preaching falsehood.

A person therefore praises himself with words alone, whereas God praises a person by deeds. A person praises himself by merely saying that he is praiseworthy; God praises a person by making him praiseworthy, namely, by granting him his graces, and especially the virtue of humility, by which he is instructed always to think humbly about himself, to presume nothing about himself but always about God, to attribute everything to God, and to refer everything to God.

These things make a person approved and praiseworthy. For the more someone flees glory, the more glory follows him.

Second, the Apostle wishes his foolishness to be endured, when he adds: “Would that you could bear with a little of my foolishness! But do bear with me” (2 Corinthians 11).

The Apostle calls it his foolishness that he was compelled to commend himself, although it is written: “Let another’s mouth praise you, and not your own” [Col. 1607B] (Proverbs 27). For no one’s virtues are so splendid that they do not become sordid when they come from his own mouth.

It would truly be foolishness for the Apostle to commend himself, unless he did so humbly and for a proper end, and unless he commended God more than himself.

Three reasons are found in sacred Scripture for which the saints are compelled humbly to recount their own good deeds. They do so either when they are oppressed by severe adversity, recounting their good deeds humbly for consolation and hope, as Job did when he said: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame” (Job 29); or when they wish to move God, the supreme Judge, to mercy, as Hezekiah did. When the Lord had said to him, “You shall die and not live,” he replied: “Remember, Lord, how I have walked before you in truth” (Isaiah [Col. 1607C] 38); or when they wish to persuade their hearers to listen to them rather than to false preachers, as Paul does here: “They are ministers of Christ, and I”—I speak as one less wise—“am more.”

The Apostle therefore wishes this foolishness of his to be endured, as though he said: I wish you not to rebuke me for commending my own person, but to endure me; and, what is more, do bear with me.

We endure things we do not approve. We bear with things to which we consent.

It is therefore as though he said: If you ought to endure and excuse the weaknesses and excesses of your spiritual father, and if the person who, like Ham, mocks his father’s nakedness is accursed, how much more ought you to bear with my foolishness, which I have undertaken for your sake?

He shows why they ought to bear with him in this when he adds: “For I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God.” More plainly, he says: You ought to bear with me in this because I do all this out of love for you and for your salvation.

This is the third part, in which the Apostle says that he is jealous for us with the jealousy of God. “I am jealous” is used here in the sense of “I am zealous.”

The person who is jealous for his bride does four things: he loves her ardently; he adorns her with ornaments; he removes all persons suspected from her; and he chastises her with warnings, threats, and blows.

Paul acted in this way. Every ecclesiastical pastor ought to do the same. He ought to love the Church entrusted to him ardently, adorn her with good morals and virtues, remove from her heretics, criminals, and all corrupters of souls, and summon her to chastity and holiness through promises, exhortations, threats, and blows [Col. 1608A].

The Apostle shows for whom the ecclesiastical pastor ought to be jealous for the Church when he adds: “For I betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.”

There are many bridal attendants, but there is only one bridegroom, Jesus Christ. There are many persons betrothed to Christ, but there is only one bride of Christ, namely, the Church.

Although she consists both of those who are incorrupt in body and of those who are corrupt in body, she is nevertheless called a chaste virgin because of the integrity of her faith, which she preserves inviolate.

Although this betrothal was celebrated in the virginal womb, Paul nevertheless says, “I betrothed you,” because, as far as the Corinthians were concerned, he was the messenger and mediator of the betrothal.
