In betrothal four things come together: consent, a marriage pact, a pledge from the virgin’s side, and a dowry from the man’s side [Col. 1608B].

These same things exist in the betrothal of Christ and the Church. The Church, or any faithful soul, consents freely to cling to Christ through faith. For although a person can do other things unwillingly, he cannot believe unless he wishes to.

She pledges herself to persevere in love of him and in observance of God’s commandments. Christ the bridegroom, however, grants her the dowry of an eternal inheritance.

Therefore, my brothers, because in baptism you promised to cling through faith to Christ the bridegroom; because you made a pact to persevere in his love and commandments; and because you received the Holy Spirit in the remission of sins, consider carefully whether you persevere in these things. Without doubt, you are blessed, and you will receive the dowry of an eternal inheritance [Col. 1608C].

But if you have broken the consent and pact of your betrothal, hasten as quickly as you can to restore it through the remedy of repentance, because the Lord is kind and merciful. After many fornications, he not only deigns to receive the soul, but urges it to return to him.

Hence he himself says through Jeremiah: “If a woman, having left her husband, takes another man, will she return to him again? Will that woman not be polluted? And you have fornicated with many lovers; nevertheless, return to me, and I will receive you, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 3).

Who could sufficiently weigh the depths of divine mercy? A sinful human being disdains to receive a woman returning to him after fornication, while God, who is purity itself, urges the soul to return to him after many fornications [Col. 1608D].

No room for excuse is now left to us. Therefore, my brothers, after our many shameful acts and transgressions, let us return to God. Let us wash away our crimes with the tears of true repentance and redeem them through works of mercy. Let us chastise our bodies with fasts and afflictions. Let us implore the grace of the heavenly Bridegroom through prayers and good works. Let us cry out to him with every sigh and groan, so that he may deign to bring us into his eternal wedding feast and grant us the promised dowry.

Our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## XXXI. ONE VIRGIN. A SERMON ON MATTHEW

[Col. 1609A]

“Jesus said to his disciples: The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins who, taking their lamps, went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride” (Matthew 25), etc.

In this reading of the holy Gospel, dearest brothers, the Lord urges us to prepare ourselves with every concern and vigilance, lest, when he suddenly comes, we be found unprepared.

There are some among us who prepare themselves in no way at all—something that must be mourned. Others prepare themselves in some respect, yet remain unprepared in another.

Some have neither the faith of Christ; these, as the Lord says, have already been judged (John 3). Others have faith but no works; such faith, as Saint James testifies, is dead (James 2).

Others have both faith and works, but seek human glory from them rather than the glory of God; these, as the Lord says, “have already received their reward” (Matthew 6).

There are others who seek both divine glory and human glory from their works, but behold, as James says, “a double-minded person is unstable in all his works” (James 1).

Others, although in the purpose underlying their work they principally seek divine glory, nevertheless allow human glory secretly to join itself to the work, and this removes a large part of the merit of the good work.

Against this the Lord warns us: “When you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing” [Col. 1609C] (Matthew 6).

There are others who, although they entirely reject the glory that secretly arises from their work, nevertheless cannot entirely disregard glory offered by human beings. Although they blush and say that they are unworthy, their inward spirit still rejoices in praises, grows, and is exalted. Unless it is restrained at the proper time, the entire reward of the work is emptied.

No one perceives how subtle the battle with vainglory is except the person who has engaged it. The others, whether seeking human glory or not rejecting it when it is offered, are found unprepared and without light at the Judge’s coming.

Hence the Lord compares the kingdom of heaven—that is, the Church hoping for the kingdom of heaven—to prudent and foolish virgins (Matthew 25).

This parable has seven parts. First, the virgins prepare themselves for the bridegroom’s coming. Second, they sleep. Third, when the bridegroom comes, they rise. Fourth, the foolish ask the prudent for oil but do not receive it. Fifth, after the prudent have entered the wedding feast with the bridegroom, the door is closed. Sixth, the foolish cry out and suffer rejection. Seventh, through all this we are admonished to keep watch.

First, all the virgins are shown to hope for the bridegroom’s coming and to prepare themselves in some way, when it is said: “The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins who, taking their lamps, went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride.”

It is clear from this that unbelievers and those who make no preparation for the coming of the supreme Judge are not included in this parable; their damnation is certain [Col. 1610A].

These virgins are represented by the number ten because the fall of the nine orders of angels is to be restored through them, and, as it were, a tenth order is to be reestablished.

They are rightly called virgins, as though abstaining from carnal allurements. Hence both these and those are appropriately called five, since they know how to restrain the five doors of the senses from what is unlawful.

Both groups also rightly take lamps, which are broad and bright vessels, because both strive to perform broad and distinguished works.

The foolish do not take oil with them because they seek glory for their works not from their conscience before God, but from the mouths of human beings in the world.

The prudent, however, take both lamps and oil in their vessels, because together with their good works they store the intention of divine glory in their consciences [Col. 1610B].

Hence the Apostle says that our glory is the testimony of our conscience (2 Corinthians 1); and elsewhere: “Let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself and not in another” (Galatians 6).

Therefore these are rightly called prudent, because they know how to purchase eternal glory with temporal and passing works. Conversely, those are called foolish because they have sold all their labor for the little breeze of vainglory.

It must nevertheless be noted that, according to the text of the Gospel, it appears that these foolish virgins did not perform their works with the intention of human praise, but because of the bridegroom’s coming. For it is written: “Taking their lamps, they went out to meet the bridegroom.” This seems to signify the final cause, as though it said: They took them for the purpose of going out to meet the bridegroom [Col. 1610C].

They are therefore not called foolish because they principally sought vainglory in their works, but because they did not despise glory arising incidentally or offered by human beings.

What, then, will those suffer who principally seek vainglory from their works, when even those who do not seek it but do not despise it when offered are rejected in this way?

Third, concerning their sleep, it follows: “But while the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy and slept.”

This delay extends from Christ’s first coming to his second. It is not to be measured according to Christ’s divinity, for all things are present to him. Hence it is said of him: “A thousand years in your sight are like yesterday, which has passed away” (Psalm 89) [Col. 1610D].

Nor is it to be measured according to the mind of the reprobate, who would never want Christ’s second coming to arrive, because then their punishments will be doubled. Rather, it is to be understood according to the mind and desire of the elect, who desire him to come in the completion of his glory. To their desire, every delay is reckoned as haste.

Hence to those crying out in the Apocalypse it is said: “Wait a little longer, until the number of your brothers is complete” (Revelation 6).

“They all became drowsy,” he says, “and slept.” To become drowsy is to be sick; to sleep is to die. All the virgins therefore became drowsy and slept, because through sickness they approached the sleep of death.

Third, their awakening is described when it says:

> “But at midnight a cry was made: ‘Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him.’” [Col. 1611A]

The tradition of the Jews is that the Lord will come to judgment at midnight, because at midnight he struck Egypt. But here we understand “night” as ignorance, since the Lord will hasten to judgment so unexpectedly and suddenly that no one will be able to comprehend or foresee it. For it is written: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (2 Peter 3).

“A cry,” he says, “was made.” This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God” (John 5). And the Apostle says: “The Lord himself will descend from heaven with the voice of an archangel and with the trumpet of God” (1 Thessalonians 4).

What cry? “Behold, the bridegroom is coming,” to join the Church, his bride, to himself forever. “Go out to meet him.” This is what the Apostle says: “And we shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air” (ibid.).

At this voice all the virgins rise, since at Christ’s command all, both good and evil, will come forth from the tombs. They adorn their lamps, because they are preparing to give an account of their deeds, but differently: the good prepare to display them in the purity in which they performed them, while the reprobate strive to conceal the impurity of their deeds beneath a covering of pretense.

Fourth, the foolish ask the prudent for oil, saying to them:

> “Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.”

The lamps of the foolish go out because their deeds, which had appeared outwardly bright to human beings, are inwardly darkened at the Judge’s coming and receive no recompense from God, since they have already received, on their account, the praises they loved.

What does it mean, then, that they ask the prudent for oil at that time? It means that, when they find themselves inwardly empty at the Judge’s coming, they seek, as usual, testimony from outside. As though, deceived in their confidence, they were saying to their neighbors: “Since you see us being rejected as though we had no good works, tell us what you have seen in our works.” Thus they wish to have before God—the inspector of hearts—the testimony of human beings, who do not see the heart.

But let us hear what the prudent virgins reply:

> “Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you.”

For on that day each person’s testimony will scarcely suffice for himself; how much less for himself and his neighbor! No one is helped before God by another’s testimony, since every heart lies open to him. Nor can the virtues of the good redeem the vices of the wicked, since each will receive according to his own merits.

“Go,” they say, “rather to the sellers and buy some for yourselves.”

They do not give advice, but rather rebuke them and call their crime to mind. The sellers of oil are flatterers, who give empty praise and receive some reward in return. Concerning this oil the Psalmist says: “But let the oil of the sinner not fatten my head” (Psalm 140). By “head” the principal part of the human being, namely the mind, is signified. The sinner’s oil therefore fattens the head when the flatterer’s praise caresses the mind.

It is as though they were saying: “Go, and in your customary manner hunt for human praises; then let us see what their praises can profit you.” [Col. 1612A]

Fifth, the bridegroom comes, and the prudent enter with him into the wedding feast. Thus it is added:

> “While they went to buy, the bridegroom came.”

For while the foolish seek outside a testimony to their life, the Judge comes, who attends not to works but to minds.

> “Those who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast, and the door was shut.”

Who could sufficiently consider, my brothers, the terror contained in the words, “The bridegroom came”? What sweetness there is in the words, “They went in with him to the wedding feast”? What bitterness in, “The door was shut”?

For what is more dreadful to us sinners than when the supreme Judge and avenger of sinners comes? At his coming he shakes the elements, sets earth and heaven aflame, and brings human beings and angels to judgment. Hence he himself says through the Prophet: “Yet once more, and I will shake not only the earth but also heaven” (Haggai 2). Even if the powers of heaven will be shaken before his sight, as is said in the Gospel (Luke 21), and the pillars of heaven will tremble, as Job testifies (Job 26), what will sinners do? “If the righteous person is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?” (1 Peter 4.)

How great will be the terror of seeing him angry whom the human mind cannot even grasp when he is tranquil? How great the shame when all hidden indecencies are exposed before all human beings and angels? How great the despair when they see the torments prepared for them and find no remedy?

Considering that day, the Prophet says:

> “That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and tempest, a day of trumpet and battle cry” (Zephaniah 1). [Col. 1612C]

With how many harshnesses did he see that day made bitter for the reprobate, when he could not express it with all those bitter descriptions?

What greater sweetness could come to the righteous than to rejoice in the sight of him at whose presence the others will tremble, to enter with him into the eternal wedding feast, and never to be separated from the embraces of divine love?

And what greater bitterness could come to the reprobate than to be separated forever from the company of the saints when the door is shut, and to be joined to the dreadful fellowship of demons in eternal torments?

Then the door of the kingdom will be closed to those who mourn—a door that is opened daily now to those who repent. There will indeed then be repentance, but fruitless repentance, because the one who now neglects the time suited for forgiveness will in no way obtain pardon. Hence the Apostle says:

> “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6). [Col. 1612D]

Sixth, the foolish suffer rejection. Thus it is added:

> “At last the other virgins came, saying, ‘Lord, lord, open to us.’ But he answered, ‘Amen, I say to you, I do not know you.’”

It is not said that they bought oil, because at that time there will be no joy in the praises of others; rather, in their distress they return to implore the mercy of God, who says to them, “I do not know you”—that is, I do not acknowledge you by the merit of your life.

Consider, my brothers, how great will be the shame and how great the grief: for momentary and worthless pleasures, to be excluded forever from the fellowship of God and the saints; to knock and suffer rejection; to repent and find no one who grants pardon; to mourn and find no consoler; to pray and find no one who hears.

For there no one can merit from God what he asks who here refused to hear what God commanded. Whoever wastes here the time of timely repentance comes fruitlessly with tears before the door. Hence the Lord says through Solomon:

> “I called, and you refused; I stretched out my hand, and there was no one who looked; you despised all my counsel and neglected my rebukes. I also will laugh at your destruction and mock you when what you feared comes upon you” (Proverbs 1). [Col. 1613A]

Seventh, a general admonition follows:

> “Therefore keep watch, because you know neither the day nor the hour.”

It is as though he were saying: “Keep watch in preparing yourselves, lest you be found unprepared when the supreme Judge comes.”

He shows why we must always keep watch when he adds:

> “Because you know neither the day nor the hour.” [Col. 1613B]

If we knew the hour of our summons, we could assign one period to repentance and another to pleasures. But the one who gave us the present day for repentance did not promise us tomorrow. Therefore we must always keep watch and always be ready.

Yet we not only fail to mourn the sins we have committed; we also increase the sins that ought to be mourned. Behold, even now, the very day of which we are speaking—the day we have received for the wedding feast of conversion—and still we refuse to weep over our guilt.

And if some illness seizes us, if the signs of illness indicate the approach of death, we beg with tears for delays that we now despise when they are granted to us.

Blessed Gregory relates that there was a certain nobleman in the province of Valeria, named Crisorius, as full of possessions as of vices: swollen with pride, subject to the pleasures of his flesh, and inflamed by the fires of greed. When he came to the end, at the hour when he was about to die, he saw with open eyes foul and exceedingly black spirits standing before him and threatening to drag him away with great force.

He began to tremble, grow pale, and sweat, and with loud cries he begged for a delay. Calling out, he summoned his son, Maximus:

> “Maximus, run, and receive me in your faith.”

Maximus, immediately disturbed, came; the grieving servant woman approached. But they could not see those wicked spirits. They saw their presence only in the confusion, pallor, trembling, and terror of the man being dragged away.

Overcome by their terror, he turned about on his bed. He lay on his left side, unable to endure their appearance, and turned toward the wall so as not to see them. When, already terribly contracted, he despaired, he began to cry out for a delay until morning. Amid these cries he was torn from the dwelling of his flesh.

It is plainly evident that he saw these things for our sake, not for his own, so that his vision might benefit us, whom God’s patience awaits. For what did it profit him, since he did not receive the delay he requested?

Therefore, my brothers, let us always consider the final day to be imminent; let us always strive to prepare ourselves more and more. Let us live and conduct ourselves as though we were already about to die, so that when the supreme Bridegroom comes we may be ready to meet him and enter with him into the eternal wedding feast.

This is granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God. Amen.

## XXXII. OF A CONTINENT WOMAN. A SERMON ON THE BOOK OF WISDOM

> “Who will find a strong woman? Her price is from afar and from the ends of the earth,” etc. (Proverbs 31.)

According to the literal sense, my brothers, Solomon saw that the female sex was so inclined toward vices that scarcely any respectable matron could be found. Hence he himself said: “Among a thousand men I found one, but among a thousand women I did not find one” (Ecclesiastes 7). Therefore, in wonder, he complains and asks:

> “Who will find a strong woman?”

There appears to be a contradiction between the noun and its adjective: if she is a woman, how is she strong? Or if she is strong, how is she a woman?

A woman has a threefold weakness: the weakness of the flesh, of sex, and of marital softness. Who, then, will find a woman strong in this threefold weakness? [Col. 1614B]

> “Her price is from afar and from the ends of the earth.”

It is as though he openly said: “She can rarely be found.” And if she can be found, she can certainly be compared with rare and precious riches sought from afar. She is indeed rare; but the rarer she is, the more precious. For it is written: “Grace upon grace is a holy and modest woman” (Sirach 26).

Next he explains the duties and rewards of the virtuous woman.

The first duty of a strong woman is that she be faithful, not only toward God but also toward her husband. He demonstrates this in what follows:

> “The heart of her husband trusts in her.”

From the woman’s faithfulness follows the fact that her husband trusts her—that she will preserve faith and affection toward him, both in heart and in deed, and will safeguard his possessions. Therefore, under his provision, he will not lack spoils; that is, he will abound in acquired wealth.

This is directed against the woman who violates marital fidelity, defiles the marriage bed, and despises her husband, and who therefore will be subjected to eternal poverty.

The second duty is that she be grateful to her husband for the goods entrusted to her. Hence it is said:

> “She will render him good and not evil all the days of her life.”

For just as it belongs to an ungrateful woman to render evil to her husband in return for good—or good, but not perseveringly, or with an evil intention—so it belongs to a grateful woman to render her husband good: reverence, submission, obedience, and dutiful service, and to do so with love and perseverance.

The third duty of a strong matron is always to perform some honorable and useful work, lest the devil, who is always lying in wait for the idle, find her idle. Hence it is added:

> “She sought wool and flax and worked with wise skill,”

that is, by the craft of her hands. Working wool is appropriate, so that she may have with which to clothe her family, cover a guest, and clothe the naked. This is directed against the woman who prefers to idle, lie about, and rot in her own filth rather than do any work.

The fourth duty is wisely and justly to provide and preserve food for herself, her household, and those in need, so that she may complete the course of this life. Hence it is added:

> “She became like a merchant’s ship, bringing her bread from afar.”

For this reason Joseph, who stored up grain for the future famine, is commended and called a savior.

The fifth duty is to assign work at dawn to each of her male and female servants, so that they do not remain idle, and to distribute provisions so that they do not fail. Hence it is added:

> “She rises while it is still night and gives food,”

that is, she procures for her household and her maidservants the task of acquiring provisions. For it is written: “Food and a rod, and a burden for the donkey; bread, discipline, and work for the servant. Idleness has taught much wickedness” (Sirach 33). Hence the Apostle says: “If anyone does not work, neither let him eat” (2 Thessalonians 3).

The sixth duty is to consider a more upright and honorable way of life and to live in that manner. The more upright and honorable way of life is agriculture. Hence it is added:

> “She considered a field,”

that is, agriculture,

> “and bought it. From the fruit,”

that is, from the labor of her hands,

> “she planted a vineyard.”

The Psalmist commends this way of life, saying:

> “You shall eat the labor of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you” (Psalm 127).

The seventh duty is to exercise herself vigorously in the virtue of chastity and in the works of the other virtues. Hence it is added:

> “She girded her loins with strength and strengthened her arm.”

These are the ornaments that chiefly adorn a good matron: the belt of chastity, the bracelets of good works, the veil of modesty, the necklace of good instruction, the earring of obedience, the torque of prudence, and the bracelet of submission.

This is directed against those women who gird themselves for no good purpose, but are strong only in lust.

The eighth duty is to taste and experience how good it is to provide for herself and for those in need from the work of agriculture and from other upright labors, and therefore to persist in just labors not only by day but also by night.

The labor of the hands confers four benefits: it destroys vices, nourishes virtues, procures necessities, and gives alms. Hence it is added:

> “She tasted and saw that her business was good; her lamp will not be extinguished at night.”

For this reason Paul, so as not to burden anyone with the support of himself and his own, says that he worked, and exhorts others to work, saying:

> “Let each one work harder with his hands, so that he may have something to give to the one in need” (Ephesians 4).

> “For it is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20).

The one who gives imitates God; the one who receives is a moneylender. [Col. 1615D]

The ninth duty is to apply her hand not only to strong and great works but also, when the situation requires it, to lowly and humble works. Hence it is added:

> “She put her hand to strong things, and her fingers grasped the spindle.”

For just as it belongs to a proud mind to shrink from humble works, so it belongs to a humble mind to avoid no lowliness of work, when the situation requires it.

The tenth duty is to devote herself to works of mercy and to extend her hands generously to the needy—not only to those who ask, but also in anticipation to those who are ashamed to ask. Hence it is added:

> “She opened her hand to the needy and extended her palms to the poor.”

Hence the Psalmist says:

> “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor” (Psalm 40).

One understands concerning the needy when, recognizing that someone is in need, one does not wait to be asked but anticipates the request and extends a gift. The one who anticipates the needy person’s embarrassment gives twice. [Col. 1616A]

The eleventh duty is to provide her household with protection against the cold and other necessities. Hence it is added:

> “She will not fear the cold for her household from the snow, for all her household are clothed in double garments.”

Hence the Apostle says:

> “If anyone does not care for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith” (1 Timothy 5).

And the poet says:

> “Need is burdensome not to itself but to the master whom it serves.”

The twelfth duty of a good matron is to adorn herself honorably and decently so that she may please her husband, lest, if she should displease him, she become an occasion of fornication for him. Hence it is added:

> “She made herself a variegated garment; linen and purple are her clothing.”

> “The married woman thinks about how she may please her husband” (1 Corinthians 7). [Col. 1616B]

For just as more elaborate adornment is blameworthy in a widow, so it is dishonorable in a married woman—provided, however, that through it she seeks to please not another man but her own husband. A woman who adorns herself in order to please others has already, by that very act, committed adultery.

The thirteenth duty of a strong woman is to honor and sanctify her husband by good example and speech, in accordance with what the Apostle says:

> “The unbelieving husband is sanctified through the believing wife” (1 Corinthians 7).

This, then, is what follows:

> “Her husband is noble at the gates,”

that is, in judgment,

> “when he sits with the elders of the land.”

For just as a dishonorable woman makes her husband ashamed and inclined to hide, so an honorable woman makes her husband noble and distinguished.

The fourteenth duty of a good and holy matron is to begin and complete a kind of fabric of an innocent and pure life, and, in order to sell it profitably, to gird a Canaanite—that is, any foreign merchant seeking good merchandise—with emulation. Hence it is added:

> “She made and sold a linen garment, and gave a belt to the Canaanite.”

This is directed against those women who weave a fabric of infamy and, by their evil example, gird other women for the same.

The fifteenth duty is to clothe herself in strong and honorable conduct as though in garments. Hence it is added:

> “Strength and beauty are her clothing, and she will laugh on the last day.”

He does not say, “She laughs,” because “Woe to you who laugh” (Luke 6). This too is directed against those who clothe themselves in dissolution and disgrace and give themselves over to laughter.

The sixteenth duty is to instruct her children and household in wisdom and in the law of the Lord by examples and words. Hence it is added:

> “She opened her mouth in wisdom, and the law of kindness is on her tongue.”

Although the law is both a law of kindness and of justice, it is here called the law of kindness so that the matron may remember to show the kindness commanded by the law toward her household, just as she wishes to find the Lord kind toward herself.

This is directed against those women who learn obscene speech and immodest songs and do not care about the law of God.

The seventeenth duty is to examine all the paths of her household, whether useless, useful, or harmful. Hence it is added:

> “She considered the paths of her household, and she did not eat the bread of idleness.”

Rather, by keeping watch and laboring, she opened the paths through which good could come to her household and closed those through which harm could come to it.

This is directed against luxurious widows, whom the Apostle rebukes, saying:

> “At the same time they learn to go around from house to house—not only idle, but also talkative and inquisitive” (1 Timothy 5). [Col. 1617A]

The rewards of the strong woman follow.

Her first reward is the praise of her children. Hence it is added:

> “Her children rose up,”

that is, toward good conduct, virtues, and works,

> “and they proclaimed her most blessed.”

They did so in the same way that a work proclaims its craftsman, a product its maker, and a manufactured object its creator; thus well-instructed children proclaim their mother, the one who instructed them.

The second praise is that of her husband. Hence it is added:

> “Her husband praised her,”

as though he were saying: “She is one to whom trust should rightly be given, as to one who carefully examines the secrets of her marriage.”

The words with which he praises her are shown when it is added:

> “Many daughters have gathered riches, but you have surpassed them all.”

For you have gathered for yourself not deceptive and empty riches like the others, but spiritual and eternal ones. Hence it is added:

> “Deceptive is grace,”

that is, the appearance of temporal riches,

> “and vain is beauty.”

The beauty of bodily goods is also vain, because such things not only do not benefit inward riches but even harm them. Hence Solomon says:

> “What profit is it for a fool to possess riches when he cannot buy wisdom?” (Proverbs 17),

and indeed they harm him. “Riches in the hand of a fool are a sword in the hand of a madman.”

Again:

> “A gold ring in a pig’s snout is a beautiful but foolish woman” (Proverbs 11).

Even if a pig has a gold ring in its snout, it is no less driven to turn over dung. Likewise, although a beautiful and foolish woman shines with golden beauty, she does not on that account hesitate to subject herself to the filth of lust.

He shows from where true riches proceed: from the fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom (Psalm 110). Hence it is added:

> “The woman who fears the Lord—she herself will be praised.”

For the woman who fears God, not with servile fear but with chaste fear, is truly praiseworthy, because she will be praised with eternal praise.

The third reward is present or future recompense. Hence it is added:

> “Give her from the fruit of her hands.”

For her husband, recognizing his wife’s fidelity and virtue, rewards her here with affection, benefits, and honor. And God, for whose sake she was faithful, will reward her at the end according to what she has merited, with eternal and blessed glorification.

The fourth reward is praise both in the present judgment and in the eternal judgment. Hence it is added:

> “And let her works praise her at the gates.”

For here the elders will praise the virtues of the wise woman in their council; and on the great day of judgment God, the Judge and Rewarder of all, will praise her, saying to her and to the other righteous:

> “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25). [Col. 1617D]

Mystically, however, Solomon sees the human race entangled in so many errors, and sees that human beings, placed in the weakness of the flesh, in the slipperiness of worldly life, and amid temptations, can scarcely resist sin. He complains and asks:

> “Who will find a strong woman?” [Col. 1618A]

It is as though he were saying more openly: “Who, finding the Church—or even the soul—soft and weak amid so many weaknesses, will be able to make her strong against those same weaknesses?”

> “From afar.”

As though he were saying: “She is not of our time, nor like us, but is distant by an interval of time—from Solomon to the Virgin’s childbirth.”

> “And from the ends of the earth is her price.”

For “his going forth is from the end of heaven” (Psalm 18). Christ gave no other price for us than himself.

Next he commends the Church, or the strong soul, first for her virtues and then for her rewards.

First, therefore, he commends her for her faithfulness when he adds:

> “The heart of her husband trusts in her.”

The husband is Christ. Hence Paul says:

> “I betrothed you to one husband, to present a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11).

Christ therefore trusts in the Church or in the strong soul when he makes her faithful and confident in him, so that no adversity, not even death itself, can separate her from him. Hence the Apostle says:

> “Who will separate us from the love of God? Tribulation, or famine, or the sword?” (Romans 8.) [Col. 1618B]

Second, he commends her for acquisition when he adds:

> “She will not need spoils.”

The Church, or any faithful soul, plunders the devil when she daily snatches the vessels of captivity from his jaws and gathers them into the flock of the faithful. To do this is to imitate Christ’s victory.

Third, he commends her for gratitude when he adds:

> “She renders him good and not evil all the days of her life.”

The Church or the soul renders Christ good when, by the gifts of a life ordered according to his commandments, she responds to him by living rightly.

But because some do good and corrupt it by an intention of vainglory, he adds:

> “And not evil.”

Because some do good with a good intention but not perseveringly, he adds:

> “All the days of her life.”

We are therefore truly grateful to Christ when we practice good simply and perseveringly.

Fourth, he commends her for her diligence in present activity when he adds:

> “She sought wool and flax and worked with the wise skill of her hands.”

The Church, or each faithful soul, seeks wool and flax when she strives in simplicity of life and in the chastening of the flesh, exercising herself wisely in these things so that she neither falls short nor goes beyond what is proper.

Fifth, he commends her for good purpose and perseverance when he adds:

> “She became like a merchant’s ship, bringing her bread from afar.” [Col. 1618D]

The Church, or the faithful soul, crosses the waves of the present age like a ship, driven by desire, and makes for the harbor of salvation, exchanging good merchandise for better and buying heavenly things with earthly ones. Meanwhile, so that she does not fail, she carries with her the bread of the divine word, by which she strengthens herself.

Sixth, he commends her for her solicitude in brotherly love when he adds:

> “She rises while it is still night, gives food to her household, and provisions to her maidservants.”

Thus every faithful soul rises, for the salvation of her neighbors, from the repose of contemplation, and gives food to her household when she joins to the faithful those whom the devil had seized. She gives provisions to her maidservants when she sustains and refreshes the weaker, lest they grow weary in carrying out God’s commandments.

Seventh, he commends her for spiritual commerce when he adds:

> “She considered a field and bought it. From the fruit of her hands she planted a vineyard.”

The primitive Church, and still every faithful soul each day, considered the world, rough with the thorns of vices, and bought it when she entrusted the talent of the word to her hearers. In that same field she planted a vineyard—that is, the Church—which she planted from the fruit of her hands, because she confirms it not only by words but also by deeds and virtues.

Eighth, he commends her for strength when he adds:

> “She girded her loins with strength,”

restraining within herself, by the virtue of continence, loose pleasures and desires.

> “And she strengthened her arm,”

preparing herself to accomplish works of virtue.

She rightly girded her loins first and afterward strengthened her arm, because a good work is not accepted by God unless lust has first been restrained. Hence it is written:

> “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12). [Col. 1619B]

Ninth, he commends her for watchfulness when he adds:

> “She tasted and saw that her business was good,”

namely, acquiring others and chastising and exercising herself.

> “Her lamp will not be extinguished at night.”

For just as she keeps watch by day for the instruction of her brothers, so she keeps watch by night for her own benefit, in psalmody, reading, and contemplation.

Tenth, he commends her for strong action when he adds:

> “She put her hand to strong things.”

Strong works are the works of perfect charity, such as doing good to those who hate us (Matthew 5), selling everything and giving to the poor (Matthew 19). Through such works “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11).

“And her fingers,” he says, “grasped the spindle.”

The distaff is properly in the left hand and the spindle in the right. The left hand signifies the present life, while the right hand signifies eternal life. We transfer wool from the distaff—that is, the spindle from the left to the right—when by works of mercy we transfer temporal goods to heavenly treasures.

Eleventh, he commends her for mercy when he adds:

> “She opened her hand to the needy and extended her palms to the poor.”

For the holy Church, or each faithful soul, opens the hand of spiritual counsel and instruction to the soul that is needy and asks. To the one who does not even know that she is in need, she freely gives, offers, and displays the alms of doctrine.

Twelfth, he commends her for charity when he adds:

> “She will not fear the cold for her household from the snow.”

The snow is the devil, who, having fallen from heaven through pride, still transforms himself into an angel of light. His cold consists in unbelief and iniquity, as it is said:

> “Because iniquity will abound, the charity of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24).

The Church will not fear such cold, because her household are clothed in double garments—that is, in the double charity of God and neighbor, which is the wedding garment in which, once clothed, they recline securely.

Thirteenth, he commends her for the variety of her virtues when he adds:

> “She made herself a variegated garment; linen and purple are her clothing.”

A *stragulatam vestem*—a variegated garment—is of diverse and strong workmanship. [Col. 1620A] It signifies the variety of different virtues with which the holy Church or faithful soul is adorned, in accordance with:

> “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, surrounded by variety” (Psalm 44).

Linen is brought to whiteness through many exercises. Purple is dyed from the blood of the sea-snail. The Church, or the faithful soul, is clothed in linen and purple when she is adorned with the whiteness of chastity and the blood of martyrdom.

Fourteenth, he commends her for the nobility of her bridegroom when he adds:

> “Her husband is noble at the gates when he sits with the elders of the land.”

He calls the judgment “the gates,” because in ancient times judgments were rendered at the gates, so that the judges might be available to those seeking them.

Thus Christ, who appeared ignoble before Pilate’s tribunal, will appear noble and glorious in judgment, at the gates of the eternal city, with the apostles and with those who followed him, in accordance with:

> “You who have followed me will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19). [Col. 1620B]

Fifteenth, he commends her for the doctrine of preaching when he adds:

> “She made and sold a linen garment, and gave a belt to the Canaanite.”

The weaving of the linen garment signifies the weaving of preaching. The Church made and sold it, because she composed and wrote the fabric of evangelical doctrine, sold it to the Gentiles, and received from them in return the currency of charity.

The Canaanite, whose name means “changed” or “exchanged,” is the Gentile people. The belt signifies either chastity, military service, or commerce. The holy Church therefore gave the belt to the Canaanite because she girded the Gentile people—to whom she had handed over the fabric of evangelical doctrine—for chastity, for military service, and for the commerce of divine talents.

Sixteenth, he commends her for strength and beauty when he adds:

> “Strength and beauty are her clothing.”

The Church, or the faithful soul, possesses the beauty of holiness and uprightness and the strength of patience, because she suffers persecution for the sake of righteousness. Therefore, although she now grieves in the struggle, she will laugh on the last day, in accordance with:

> “Blessed are you who now weep, for you will laugh” (Luke 6). [Col. 1620C]

Seventeenth, he commends her for the doctrine of wisdom and the law when he adds:

> “She opened her mouth in wisdom,”

implicitly, for teaching, in accordance with Paul:

> “Let no corrupt speech proceed from your mouth, but only such as is good for building up the faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephesians 4). [Col. 1620D]

Or she opened the mouth of her heart to receive wisdom, by which she might teach others.

> “And the law of kindness is on her tongue,”

that is, the Gospel, which teaches one always to forgive a sinning brother and to return good for evil.

Eighteenth, he commends her for guarding the paths of her household when he adds:

> “She considered the paths of her household,”

that is, she carefully watched over all the senses and gates of her body and soul, so that she might close them against invading evil and open them to receive good.

> “And she did not eat the bread of idleness.”

For even if she sometimes appeared idle, she was then less idle, because inwardly she was engaged in spiritual and heavenly affairs.

The rewards of the Church, or of the strong soul, follow. The first is the praise of her children, whence it is added: “Her children rose up [Col. 1621A] and proclaimed her most blessed.” In prophetic fashion, he puts the past for the future. For then the daughters of the Church will rise and praise her who regenerated them through water and the Holy Spirit, when, tasting her eternal joys, they will celebrate her with eternal praise.

The second reward is the praise of her husband, concerning which it is added: “Her husband praised her.” Christ then praises the Church, or each individual soul, his bride, when he makes and shows her praiseworthy. Or certainly he will praise her at the end, when he says: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV).

“Many daughters,” he says, “have gathered riches.” Many churches of heretics or false Christians, who, on account of their confession of Christ’s name and their participation in the sacraments [Col. 1621B], appeared to be daughters of Christ, gathered riches of good works—fasts, almsgiving, prayers, devotion to sacred reading, and things of this sort. These are indeed true riches when they are performed in faith and simplicity; otherwise they are of no or little benefit. But the Church surpasses these daughters: with pure faith and right intention, she gathers a treasury of virtues and good works in heaven.

And why is this so? He adds: “Deceptive is grace, or appearance, and vain is beauty.” Human praise is indeed a deceptive appearance or grace. The beauty of displayed chastity and holiness is vain. “But the woman who fears God, she shall be praised,” because that conscience is truly worthy of praise which fears God with love, loves him with fear, and in all things considers and preserves the fear and love of God.

The third reward is eternal recompense, concerning which it is added: “Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates.” These are the words of Christ to the angels, the reapers, saying: “Give her of the fruit of her hands, because the Spirit took care to produce fruit—namely, charity, joy, patience, and the remaining virtues and works of the virtues. And let them praise her in the gates,” that is, at the judgment or at the entrance into the heavenly homeland—not the vain praises of human beings, but the very works she performed, when God examines, approves, and rewards them. To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

### XXXIII. OF A VIRGIN. A SERMON ON MATTHEW

[Col. 1621D]

Jesus said to his disciples: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field. When a man finds it, he hides it, and for joy over it goes and sells everything he has and buys that field,” etc. (Matt. XIII).

In this reading from the holy Gospel, dearest brothers, the Lord sets before us four parables. In the first and second, he generally urges us to buy the kingdom of heaven; in the third, to fear and avoid the punishments of hell; in the fourth, he specially urges preachers to understand and proclaim this earnestly.

In the first, therefore, he urges us to buy the kingdom of heaven when he says: “The kingdom [Col. 1622A] of heaven is like a treasure.” It is compared with visible and desirable things so that our mind may learn the invisible through visible things, and through those things that are desirable in this world may learn to desire those that ought to be desired above all.

Behold, the kingdom of heaven is compared with a treasure because, like a treasure that has been found, it gives its finder an abundance of joy and confidence—but incomparably greater. An earthly treasure provides empty joy, namely, a failing abundance and an untrustworthy confidence. The heavenly treasure, however, provides true joy, unfailing abundance, and reliable confidence.

The field is the practice of a good life. Like a field, it is first cleared of the thorns and thistles of vices by the sickle of correction, cultivated by the plough of preaching, and sown with the seed [Col. 1622B] of the word of God; thus it produces the flowers of virtues and the fruits of good works. At the end of this field the heavenly treasure is hidden, just as a reward is hidden in labor and fruit in the flower.

We perceive this treasure through faith and Sacred Scripture; through devotion to good works we seek it; through contemplation we contemplate it and in a certain way already taste it; and through divine revelation we find it. Once found, we now hide the treasure so that it may be preserved for us, concealing in our hearts our resolve and intention to acquire the heavenly treasure from evil spirits and from human praise.

In the present life we are, as it were, on a road by which we hasten toward our homeland. Evil spirits lie in wait for us like bandits. Whoever openly carries a treasure desires to be robbed. I say this not so that our neighbors should not see our works, since it is written: “Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V), but so that, through what we do outwardly, we may not seek human praise.

Let the good therefore be public in such a way that the intention remains hidden: let us provide our neighbors with an example of goodness, while through our intention of pleasing God alone we always desire secrecy.

We purchase the field, having sold everything, when, for the practice of the good life—that is, for the acquisition of the heavenly treasure hidden at its end—we renounce all pleasures and desires of the flesh, regard all perishable things as dung, and do not shrink from suffering any hardship for its sake.

Just as a field that is sterile and worthless in itself is made desirable and worth buying by the treasure hidden in it, so the practice of the good life, although in itself it may seem worthless and useless to human beings, is made desirable and greatly worth acquiring by the treasure of eternal blessedness hidden at its end.

Carnal people despise the spiritual life, and, if it were for sale, I believe they would not buy it. But for us who are true Christians it is considered supremely precious in itself, even without a reward—how much more with a reward, and such a reward at that! Is it not in itself a great thing to live rightly, to have a pure heart, to be truthful and fair toward everyone, to trample demons and vices underfoot, to flourish in virtues and good [Col. 1623A] works, to despise all worldly things, to have God as witness, and not to fear death but rather to await it? Are these things not great in themselves? How incomparably greater, then, do they become with the treasure of eternal blessedness!

In the second parable also the Lord urges us toward the same goal when he adds: “Again, the kingdom of heaven”—that is, the business of acquiring the kingdom of heaven—“is like a merchant seeking good pearls.”

Certainly all people seek good pearls, that is, blessednesses, but most are deceived in their search and their evaluation. Some think blessedness lies in an abundance of riches, some in worldly honor, some in human power, some in temporal glory, and some in bodily pleasure. [Col. 1623B] But all these are deceived, because temporal wealth is needy; worldly honor is dishonorable; human power is powerless; temporal glory is false; and bodily pleasure is wearisome. Moreover, each of these things is vain and momentary.

Therefore, when the prudent merchant sees that he cannot find the pearl of true blessedness in any of these things, he seeks through Sacred Scripture and discovers through faith and good works that the pearl of eternal blessedness has been stored up in the other life, and he says: “In all things I sought rest, and in the inheritance of the Lord I shall dwell” (Ecclus. XXIV).

Thus he burns with desire to obtain it; for its sake he neglects and gives away all temporal things. For its sake he renounces all his possessions and himself; he desires it alone and hastens to possess it through every hardship.

Of this kind of desire and love Solomon rightly says: “Love is strong as death” (Song VIII), because, just as death destroys the body, so love of eternal blessedness kills love of the world. For whoever has been perfectly intoxicated by it becomes insensible to earthly desires.

Indeed, the blessed woman whose nativity we celebrate today could not have died bodily for the Lord unless she had first died in mind to earthly desires. Raised upright in steadfast virtue, she trampled equally upon flatteries and threats, promises and torments, for the hope of ineffable and eternal blessedness. Led before kings and governors, she was loftier than the judge and stronger than the enraged persecutor.

What can we bearded men say in response to this, when we see girls seize heaven through the sword, while anger disturbs us, pride inflates us, ambition blinds us, and lust defiles us? If we do not wish to attain the kingdom of heaven through blood, let it at least be a disgrace to us that we are reluctant to follow the Lord through peace. Behold, God says to none of us, “Die for me,” but only, “Kill your carnal desires within you.” If, then, we do not wish to sacrifice the vices of our flesh in peace, when will we offer the flesh itself to be sacrificed for the Lord in war?

In the third parable the Lord urges us to guard against the punishments of hell when he adds: “Again, the kingdom of heaven and the judgment of the kingdom of heaven are like a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind. When it was filled, they drew it out, sat down beside the shore, and chose the good fish into their vessels, but threw the bad outside.”

The preaching of the holy Church is compared with a net because it has been entrusted to fishermen, so that through it we may be drawn from the waves of the world to the shore of our eternal homeland—or plunged into the depths of eternal death. Hence the Lord says through Jeremiah: “Behold, I will send many fishermen to you” (Jer. XVI).

After Peter and Andrew, James and John heard, “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Mark I), they wove a net for themselves from the New and Old Testaments and cast it into the sea of the world; it gathers fish of every kind. For it calls to the forgiveness of sins the wise and foolish, free and enslaved, rich and poor, strong and weak. Hence it is said to God through the Psalmist: “All flesh shall come to you” (Ps. LXIV).

This net will finally be filled universally when, at the end, the totality of the human race is brought to completion. They draw it out and sit beside the shore when they drag it to the end of the world, and the judges themselves sit; the good fish are chosen into vessels, while the bad are thrown outside, because the elect are received into heavenly dwellings, whereas the rejected are cast far away into eternal darkness.

For now the Church’s net holds the good and the bad together; but the shore reveals what it has drawn in. Captured fish cannot be changed, but we can be changed through repentance from evil to good. Therefore, while it is permitted, my brothers, let us change our life for the better, lest at the end, separated from the company of the saints, we be cast into eternal condemnation.

Accordingly, in explaining this parable, the Lord adds: “So it will be at the consummation of the age. The angels will go out and separate the wicked from among the righteous, and they will cast them into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

My brothers, this is something to be feared rather than explained. The torments of the rejected are plainly announced so that no one could excuse himself through ignorance if eternal condemnation were indicated obscurely.

Hence it is also added: “Have you understood all these things?” They say to him: “Yes.” The address is directed to the disciples who were to become teachers of others, to whom it was given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, while to the rest they were given in parables.

Finally, in the fourth parable the Lord teaches us preachers so that, as his scribes and notaries, we may keep his words written on the tablets of our hearts and proclaim them earnestly to others. He adds: “Therefore every learned scribe in the kingdom of heaven,” that is, in the Church, “is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old.”

This can be understood in three ways.

First, the householder brings forth from his treasures new and old fruits, new and old wine, with which he strengthens and refreshes the hearts of his guests. So the learned preacher brings forth from the treasure of his teaching both the new and the old law, by which he confirms and nourishes the hearts of his hearers.

Second, the householder brings forth from his treasure both old riches left by his fathers and new riches acquired by himself. [Col. 1625A] So the learned preacher brings forth from the treasure of his teaching both old sayings and parables written by the ancient Fathers and new ones devised on the model of the ancient.

Third, the householder brings forth from the treasure of his prudence promises of new rewards or threats of old punishments, by which he either draws or frightens his household. So the learned preacher knows how to bring forth new things concerning the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom and old things concerning the terror of punishment in Gehenna. For the merit of the old Adam was to descend into hell, while the merit of the new man, Christ, is to enter heaven.

Thus, in his conclusion, he sets forth what he had previously introduced. First he produced the treasure and the good pearl under the likeness of the kingdom; afterward he added the burning of the wicked [Col. 1625B]. Concluding from this, he adds: “Therefore every learned scribe in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old.”

As if he were saying openly: The learned preacher in the Church is the one who knows how to bring forth new things concerning the promise of the kingdom of heaven and old things concerning the threat of the torments of Gehenna, so that punishments may frighten those whom rewards do not entice.

Let each person hear about the kingdom, so that he may love it; let him hear about punishment, so that he may fear it; so that a sluggish soul, clinging stubbornly to the earth, may be drawn to the kingdom by love—or, if love does not draw it, at least by terror. For behold, concerning the description of hell it is said: “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

Since following present glory leads to perpetual lamentation, let us flee, my brothers, from vain joy here, lest there we lament forever. No one can rejoice here with the world and reign there with God.

Hence Solomon says: “There is a time for weeping, and there is a time for laughing” (Eccles. III). Here, my brothers, is the time for weeping over our own or others’ sins; in the other life is the time for laughing—both because dangers have been escaped and because eternal joys have been attained.

Let us therefore change temporal joy into tears of repentance; let us renounce the pleasures of the flesh; let us exercise ourselves in the labors of justice; let us redeem our offenses through works of mercy; for the desire for the heavenly treasure let us distribute what we possess; let us regard all perishable things as dung for its sake; let us hasten there with sighs and desires, so that through the intercession of this holy woman, whose festival we celebrate today, we may at last arrive there rejoicing. Amen.

### In the Year of the Lord 1100: Thomas, Archbishop of York

[Col. 1625]

### Epitaph of King William

(See under William, *Patrologia*, vol. CXLIX, col. 1271.)

[Col. 1625]

### Letters to Lanfranc

(See under Lanfranc, *Patrologia*, vol. CL, col. 518 and following.)

[Col. 1625]

### Letter to the Archbishops and Bishops Established Throughout England, Concerning the Health Restored to Him from Heaven

(Roger of Hoveden, *Annals*, part I, p. 263, London edition, 1596.)

[Col. 1625C] Thomas, by the grace of God archbishop of York, to the bishops and abbots established throughout England, both those now living and those who will succeed them in the future, and to all the archbishops who will succeed him in York, perpetual greeting.

Although it is our duty to offer everyone the service of piety, we owe the service of our devotion especially to the saints of God, from whom it is evident that we have received the singular benefit of a gift.

We, chastised by God’s scourge and consumed for two years by the torments of fevers in an extraordinary manner, while all the physicians promised that only death awaited us and there was never anything by which they could relieve the continuing harm of our illness, were therefore admonished in a vision. Groaning and raging, I spent the night at the tomb of Saint Cuthbert. Worn out at once by the disease and by the burden of it, when sleep stole over me, blessed Cuthbert appeared to me in a vision. Passing over each of my limbs with his hand, he immediately restored me, once awake, sound from every illness. He also commanded that I should be devoted to him in all things and that whatever he himself or his people were to possess in my diocese should be secure and free from every burden.

Having been aided by the benefits of the blessed confessor, I became all the more devoted to him as I understood that I ought to repay greater benefits. Meanwhile, when William, bishop of Durham, brought letters from the Apostolic See, from Pope Gregory VII, to King William’s council at Westminster, he obtained, with everyone’s consent, permission to remove the canons from his church and substitute monks in their place.

I rejoiced greatly at this. In accordance with the command of the aforesaid pope and the order of the lord King William, and out of the devotion owed to blessed Cuthbert, with the consent and permission of the chapter of York [Col. 1627C] and the confirmation of the entire synod, I gave and granted the following letters to Saint Cuthbert, to his bishop, and to all the monks serving him; I confirmed them by this present charter and afterward offered it with my own hand upon the altar to Saint Cuthbert.

Let both those now living and those who come after know that I, Thomas, archbishop of York, by order of Pope Gregory VII and with the confirmation of the lord King William, under the testimony of the universal council of the English [Col. 1628A] and with the consent of the chapter of York, give and grant to God and Saint Cuthbert, to all his succeeding bishops, and to all monks who will be there in the future, that all the churches which they now possess in my diocesan parish, or which they may canonically acquire in the future through royal grants, the generosity of the faithful, or which they may build on their own land, shall be held by them forever, entirely free and undisturbed by me and all my successors from everything pertaining to me or to my successors.

Therefore I wish and command that they hold all their churches in their own hands, possess them peacefully, and freely appoint their vicars in them. These vicars shall attend to me and my successors only with respect to the care of souls. Concerning all other alms and benefices, I moreover grant, confirm, and command that both they and their vicars shall forever be free and undisturbed from every synodal payment and from all aids, burdens, rents, exactions, or lodging imposed either by me, by deans, by archdeacons, or by any of our vicars and ministers.

Under penalty of anathema I also prohibit anyone from troubling them or their clerics in any way or under any pretext, or compelling them to attend synods or chapters unless they freely wish to do so. If anyone has a complaint against them or their people, let him come to the court of Saint Cuthbert at Durham, so that there he may receive whatever justice he is owed.

For all the liberties and dignities that I or my followers have possessed in our own churches or lands, we grant freely and forever to them and to Saint Cuthbert in all their churches and lands; and without evasion or accusation we confirm them as free and undisturbed by me and my successors.

### In the Year of the Lord 1100: Richard of Dumellis, Abbot of Préaux

[Col. 1627]

### Historical Notice

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latinitatis*, vol. VI, p. 77)

Richard of Dumellis, abbot of Préaux—which is a monastery in Normandy, in the diocese of Lisieux, founded around the year 1057—lived in the year 1100 and wrote a very extensive Commentary on the first twenty-eight chapters of Genesis, which is preserved in the Lambeth Library. Henry Wharton cited from it certain passages relevant to his subject in the *Auctarium* to Jacob Ussher’s *Dogmatic History of Scripture and the Sacred Vernaculars*.

[Col. 1629]

### Fragments of Richard of Dumellis’s Commentary on Genesis

(Wharton, *Auctarium* to J. Ussher’s *Dogmatic History*, quarto, p. 395.)

[Col. 1629A] There is preserved in the Lambeth Library a very extensive manuscript Commentary on the first twenty-eight chapters of Genesis, whose prologue begins as follows: “To Anselm, archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, a certain servant of the Lord’s cross and minister of the monastery of Préaux,” etc.

In it the author habitually—and at times rather inappropriately—draws almost everything toward Scripture and accommodates to it allegorically the most ordinary things, such as heaven, the sun, waters, paradise, and so forth.

Thus, in Book I, commenting on “Let the earth produce green grass,” after having extensively proclaimed the usefulness of Scripture, he says:

“What else is green grass than the meaning of the simple letter? To the uneducated people, namely, the animals of the supreme King, it supplies saving nourishment. For it is written: ‘He gives food to their animals.’ Behold the green grass from which the understanding of little ones is nourished.—And the stars. What else are the stars set in the firmament than the souls of the elect, who keep watch over the sacred Scriptures?”

And in Book II, on “Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea”:

“And rightly are the waters said to produce creeping things, because Sacred Scripture fosters the little ones in understanding, as though with a living warmth, and forms their limbs, until their understanding, having advanced, can swiftly attain the higher meanings of mystical expressions.—For the rational creature grows in devotion to its Creator; it multiplies through the completion of good works; it fills the waters of the sea through the investigation of the mystical law.

“When few understand the depth of Sacred Scripture, it is as though the waters produce few creeping things. But when they have become capable of receiving solid food and have revealed to others the inner meanings of the mysteries insofar as they understand them, they seem to grow, multiply, and fill the waters of the sea.

“Thus the waters of the sea are filled when the threefold meaning of the sacred law is disclosed even to the simple. What are pastures except the Sacred Scriptures, which provide nourishment to clean animals? From them it supplies strength to the inner person,” etc.

Concerning paradise:

“What is that paradise which the Lord planted and in which he himself placed the human being, except the holy Church or Sacred Scripture, where every kind of delight is found and where the tree of life and also the tree of the knowledge of good and evil are planted?”

[Col. 1629D] Book III:

“To have the Lord walk in paradise is for him, through the various places of the Sacred Scriptures that are read daily in the Church, to seek the salvation of souls and, by manifold exhortation, to lead all who have gone astray back to the way of truth.—There. What, then, is more fittingly understood by the cherubim (Gen. III), which are interpreted as ‘the fullness of knowledge,’ than Sacred Scripture, through which the burden of our miseries and the road by which we return to our homeland are fully and abundantly disclosed?

“In it, certainly, the promises of heavenly glory are described; and again, in the same Scripture, the threats and terrors of the fire of Gehenna are contained. These, unless I am mistaken, are prefigured by the name of the flaming sword, etc.

“Do you wish to return to paradise? ‘I do,’ he says. ‘Approach the cherubim,’ I reply; that is, search out the profound mysteries of Sacred Scripture. Through its instruction you have the means of returning to paradise, which you lost through the alluring desire of your first parent. Otherwise the way of paradise is closed to you [Col. 1630B] unless you submit the ear of your heart to the counsel of Sacred Scripture.”

Book V. He praises the wondrous depth of the divine Scriptures, which contain all the mysteries of the Catholic religion.

Book IX:

“This fountain [of life] becomes a well according to the capacity of its readers. For the divine word makes itself capable of being received by the smallest and the greatest; it rises up, becoming all things to all people.

“Blessed is the Lord God, who offers Scripture to little ones lacking a vessel for drawing water, allowing it to flow, after the manner of a spring, on the surface of the earth for them to drink; but for others who already possess trained understanding and are able to draw drink from the depth of sacred discourse, he prepares by excavation the Well of the Living and Seeing Me (Gen. XVI, 14).”

Book X. He laments the diminished and gradually vanishing study of Sacred Scripture in the Church.

“As the end of the collapsing world now approaches, and the charity of very many grows cold, the rigor of the Christian religion becomes exceedingly cold; and the work of sacred reading, which is known to be the fuel of the soul striving toward heavenly joys, has almost been reduced to nothing.”

Book XI. Speaking of the translation of the Seventy, produced at the initiative of King Ptolemy, he begins:

“For the mysteries of those letters became genuinely clear to the wise and the foolish.”

And shortly afterward he adds:

“[The devout man], lest he ever fail, sees the strength of sacred reading set before him. The Lord’s word is a marvelous [Col. 1630D] mirror for everyone who has already climbed, or is striving to climb, the citadel of holiness.”

Finally, he urges all householders, even common people, to instruct their wives and children in knowledge of Sacred Scripture according to their ability.

[Col. 1631A] Book XV:

“Who are those who remain with the baggage, fettered by the bonds of marital union? They are certain members of the Christian common people, to whom the burden of guarding the law is entrusted—namely, the form of simple instruction by which a man governs his household.

“For it is no small praise for a man to have a wife obedient to his commands and children subject to spiritual discipline. Since, because of slowness of intellect, they cannot penetrate the profound mysteries of Sacred Scripture, they are commanded to remain with the simple understanding of the historical sense.”

[Col. 1632A] The Lambeth codex bears the name of no author. Nevertheless, it is clear from the beginning of the dedicatory letter itself that the work was written by a certain abbot of Préaux. A manuscript codex preserved in the monastery of Préaux shows that he was the abbot Richard; from it Gerberon published the dedicatory letter to Anselm in the recent edition of Anselm’s works, p. 451. Finally, the brothers Sammarthanus indicate that this Richard bore the surname “of Dumellis,” vol. IV, p. 756.

[Col. 1631]

### Richard of Dumellis’s Letter to Saint Anselm of Canterbury, the Dedicatory Letter of His Commentary on Genesis

(See among the Letters of Saint Anselm, Book IV, letter 102, *Patrologia*, vol. CLIX, col. 251.)

### In the Year of the Lord 1100: Alberic, Bishop of Ostia

[Col. 1631]

### Letter to the Monks of the Monastery of Saint Orientius of Auch, Concerning the Agreement Between the Archbishop of the Church of Auch and the Monastery of Saint Orientius

(De Brugelles, *History of the Church of Auch*, Proofs, part II, p. 49.)

[Col. 1631B] Alberic, by the grace of God bishop of Ostia and legate of the Apostolic See, sends greetings to the brothers of the monastery of Saint Orientius of Auch, and wishes them a grateful concord.

The most reverend lord archbishop of Auch has himself, in accordance with his grace and goodwill, granted you a most welcome concord, for the greater part, with your prior; and, in our presence at Senones before the bishops and abbots, he promised that henceforth he would love, honor, and support the monastery of Saint Orientius. For the restoration of your monastery he will also gather, for up to ten years, a meeting of the people in each year.

He has entirely remitted all exactions, both from priests and from the other clerics. If the count should demand any new custom from any of your people, the lord archbishop will have no part in it; and concerning the count himself, as concerning your other complaints, he will do what justice dictates.

We have done this while reserving in every respect the rights of your cemetery and your other complaints, until Abbot Hugh has agreed that this agreement should stand.

### Around the Year of the Lord 1100: Sulcard, Monk of Westminster

[Col. 1633]

### Notice

(*Literary History of France*, VIII, 138)

Pitseus (*English Writers*, p. 188), who gives a brief but favorable eulogy of Sulcard’s great qualities, supposes him to have been English by nationality. On this basis he claims that, having become a monk at Westminster, Sulcard applied himself so successfully to the study of letters and the practice of virtue that he acquired a great store of learning and piety. Consequently, Sulcard was loved and honored by all who knew him. It is even added that he had a considerable share in the honor of enjoying the confidence of King Saint Edward the Confessor. Such is the picture that Pitseus gives us of this pious and learned monk.

It may be true in all its parts except for what concerns the country in which he is supposed to have been born. It is in fact much more probable that he was born in Normandy and afterward went to England with so many other Normans, either during the reign of William the Conqueror or even in the time of King Saint Edward, who had already begun to attract many of them there.

Two principal reasons are sufficient to establish this. Everyone acquainted with history admits that, before the period just mentioned, it was extremely rare to see learned men in England during the eleventh century. They became more common after the reign of these princes, but that was because the princes had summoned them from our provinces, especially from Normandy. Moreover, it is certain that under William the Conqueror in particular, the period in which Sulcard flourished, the monks of Westminster, like those of certain other English monasteries, were almost all Normans.

Pitseus places the end of Sulcard’s life in the year 1070. But it must be moved considerably later. The proof is decisive, since it was only in 1070 that Vital succeeded Eadwin, or Edouin, in the dignity of abbot of Westminster, an office he held until 1082, and Sulcard lived under Vital, to whom he dedicated one of his works.

Let us add, to strengthen our preceding proofs, that this Vital was a Norman and that his successor was Gilbert Crispin, another Norman and a great man of letters for his age. Sulcard was buried in his monastery, where, in Pitseus’s time, one could still see, it is said, his tomb with this inscription:

**SULCARD, MONK AND CHRONOGRAPHER.**

Several writings are attributed to him. Except for one, of which something has been printed, the attribution of the others rests chiefly on the authority of Pitseus.

1. A chronicle about which no further information is given, of which the compilers of the *Monasticon Anglicanum* published a fairly lengthy extract. Judging by this specimen, the work, apparently preserved in manuscript in the libraries of England, must be very extensive and deals principally with the history of Westminster. Possevin seems to have known of it (*Appendix*, vol. III, p. 443). The printed extract contains a description of the place and the first arrangements for establishing the monastery under the invocation of Saint Peter. But what concerns this latter subject is based only on a rather singular vision, which the author describes in all its smallest details, showing that he was extremely credulous. The work is dedicated to Vital, abbot of Westminster.

2. A collection of sermons, about which no information is supplied except that one of Sulcard’s ordinary occupations was instructing the people by announcing the word of God. This collection is apparently the product of the author’s preaching.

3. Another collection of letters, without telling us to whom they were addressed, what they concerned, or even whether any of them still exist.

4. A third collection of various short works, without indicating or specifying any of the subjects that might form their content. In general, it is added that Sulcard had written other works as well, but that the misfortunes of the times are responsible for the titles themselves not having come down to us.

[Col. 1635]

### Sulcard the Monk’s Little Book on the Foundation of Westminster Abbey

(*Monasticon Anglicanum*, I, 57.)

[Col. 1635A] The Thames, flowing beneath it with all the vastness of its waters, adorns the city of London; now sending forth and again receiving waves in the ebb and flow of sea and river, it bathes the island called Thorney, two miles from the city. It was pleasing to God, as is believed, and to the blessed prince of the apostles, that a dwelling should be prepared for him on this island, where God would be worshiped in his apostle and, through his patronage and intercession, would have mercy on his suppliant people.

Thus the exceedingly wealthy worshiper of Christ, Sebert, applied himself to founding a church, and in a short time rendered it complete through his persistent labor and work. Meanwhile he admonished Mellitus, the bishop of his diocese, to consecrate the place founded for blessed Peter [the wording *beato Mellito cordis Petro* is textually uncertain]. When the work had been completed, the minister of God rejoiced in the honor of blessed Peter and appointed the day on which he wished the dedication to be completed.

In the meantime the things necessary for so great a dedication were prepared and announced to the worshipers of God dwelling all around, so that they might hasten to the solemn celebration of the heavenly wedding. The beloved pontiff Mellitus anticipated the appointed day, and at evening, half a mile from the newly built church, the tents gleamed in the distance on the holy day. For the swelling Thames had closed in the island of Thorney on every side and offered those wishing to enter no route except by boat.

The sky was shut by the darkness of night, and all things rested in sleep granted from heaven. The remains of the night completed the labors of the day, while heavenly favor, accepting every devotion, clearly attended to the glory of its chosen client, humble and peaceful in heart.

Hear, I beg you, and receive into every mind by what sublime privilege the prince of the apostles deigned to consecrate the island of Thorney to himself, and how confidently those serving God there ought to implore his aid. While all, as has been said, were overwhelmed by sleep, our own shepherd, blessed Peter, appeared beside the bank of the Thames. Seeing a fisherman on the opposite side of the river, he called him to come to him; if he had wished, he could perhaps have opened a way even on the island itself. But, I think, he wished to have as witness of the work to be done a man engaged in his own occupation. Therefore, after calling the fisherman two or three times, he had him come with his boat.

At last the fisherman ferried across the apostle who requested it, though he was astonished at what that unknown man could want across the river in the universal stillness of all things. Having been carried across, [Col. 1635D] the keeper of heaven’s keys told him to wait there for his companion and promised him the surest reward for his labor.

[Col. 1636A] He stepped from the boat onto dry land and, while the fisherman watched, planted his staff in the earth and created behind him a flowing spring.
