Advancing a little farther, he again planted the staff he carried and, by his power, drew out another spring. These two springs flowed for a long time, until they were swallowed in the riverbed, the watery current devouring the bank.

Having accomplished this in the sight of his guide, he went to the church assigned to him. Heavenly choirs accompanied him, producing a heavenly harmony, and angelic voices resounded up to the height of the air. The new bride of God, consecrated by him who closes and opens heaven, shone with heavenly lights. An army of the baptized illuminated the island with the entire circle of the sun shining, the heavens opened above, and the power of divine majesty favored in heaven what the apostle did on earth.

[Col. 1636B] The spectator stood amazed and stunned. He could not even depart; he lacked the strength to remain standing, held helpless by the trembling of his body alone, bound by the apostle’s command. If he had been free to act as he wished, he would certainly have departed; but he was held by apostolic bonds, to be released as a witness of the glorious vision.

When the apostle had completed the duty for which he had come, he returned to his trembling boatman and gently urged him in soothing words not to be afraid any longer:

“Do not be afraid,” he said, “of what you have heard and seen. These things have occurred by the Lord’s will. Do not hesitate to tell me what you have heard and seen, so that I may know whether, despite your fear, you were able to understand what you saw, and what you have perceived through yourself concerning the deed and its author.”

As the apostle spoke with increasing gentleness, fear was cast off and confidence to speak was introduced. At last, having recovered his strength, the fisherman gave this answer:

“Although the vision greatly exceeded my understanding, my lord, I shall say what I perceive at your command. I heard the voices of the singers with marvelous sweetness; I saw the brilliance of a great light; and at these things I was terrified beyond what I can comprehend. But who or what you are, my lord, I do not know with certainty. Nevertheless, believing you to be something good, I do not doubt it.”

Then the apostle received his confession in these words:

“Understand more clearly what you rightly perceive to be good, and explain it also to others. I am Peter, the apostle of Christ. That friend of mine, Sebert, built this church for me. Because of his love and devotion, and for the eternal sanctification of this place, I myself wished to consecrate it to God and to myself.

[Col. 1636D] “You have now seen and heard what has taken place. In what remains, obey me. When day has come, go to Bishop Mellitus and inform him how the matter occurred. When he arrives, he will be able to see the signs of consecration, with the walls anointed with chrism; in this we no longer need his labor. But let him complete the remaining matters, that is, the Masses and the episcopal ministry.

“To bear witness to your vision and to our conversation, therefore, you shall cast your nets into the river, and through our intervention the result will prosper for you. Of the fish caught, present one to him on my behalf, so that he may believe both what has been reported to you and what you tell him from me, and may carry it out—although I believe that something of our action has already been shown to him from heaven, so that your account may be more certainly confirmed.

“I also admonish you not to wish to fish any longer on the Lord’s night or day. The result will prosper for you and for your future prosperity, and you will advance greatly in the art of fishing.”

For it was the Lord’s night when this fisherman experienced the apostolic vision and conversation. [Note: According to some, the fisherman’s name was Edricus.]

After these words the apostle vanished from his sight and, having been received into heaven, aided the fisherman, as he had promised, with an exceedingly abundant catch. For when he spread his nets in the river, he drew onto the bank such a quantity of fish, called salmon, that the nets could scarcely contain the catch.

The credulous fisherman, when day had come, came before the appointed bishop, still a youth. In a novel manner he greeted him, reporting the commands of blessed Peter and at the same time presenting the gift that Peter had sent him. The bishop rose with the greatest devotion and, giving thanks to God and the apostle, rejoiced that he had been remembered and honored by so great a prince of heaven.

Entering the church, where he prayed diligently, he went around and examined the walls. He found them marked with sacred chrism, and visible on the wall were the signs of candles that had been fixed there. Accordingly, everyone was summoned; people came from the streets and lanes, and from every side they hastened from the city and the towns. With devout hearts they attended the celebration of the Mass by the bishop chosen by God.

After a sermon on what had occurred and on the other benefits to souls, many were roused to joyful sighs of holy compunction. Giving thanks to God and his apostle, they were sent back with festive joy, each to his own dwelling.

When the church had been consecrated, [Col. 1638B] as a new bride of God, it received a new name. It lost its old name, Thornege—that is, “island of thorns”—and, from its situation in relation to the city, took the name “Western Monastery.”

These events occurred in the time of King Ethelbert of Canterbury. After he had entered upon the way of all flesh, and after the same church had been subjected to much neglect—for it was not especially large—it remained so until the reign of King Offa, king of the East Saxons. He, therefore, honoring the memory of the apostle more diligently, enlarged the church by his work.

# In the Year of Our Lord 1101 Amatus, Archbishop of Bordeaux

[Col. 1637]

## Notice

*(Gallia Christiana nova, vol. II, p. 806)*

[Col. 1637C] Before he ascended this metropolitan see, Amatus had acquired great fame in the small though respectable see of Oloron. For Pope Gregory VII had judged him worthy to whom he could entrust his responsibilities in Gaul and Spain, and whom he could take as a participant in and assistant with regard to his very greatest counsels.

Just as the pontiff, whose minister he was, was undertaking great enterprises and had summoned great courage to carry them out, so his legate Amatus excelled in greatness of spirit and boldness, using the thunderbolts of the Church, whose arbiter he was, to exact the reverence he considered owed to himself. This was especially evident at the council of Exoldunum, where he cut off the canons of Saint Martin of Tours from communion because they had refused to receive him with solemn pomp. They relied on certain privileges by which they admitted no one to the reception procession, except the Apostolic representative, the king, and the archbishop of Tours, and even these only once in his lifetime.

Urban II recounts the event in Baronius, under the year 1096:

“And because our son Amatus, archbishop of Bordeaux, was one of the legates of the Roman Church sent into Gaul by Gregory VII, our predecessor, and was not received by this church with the solemnity of a procession, he was therefore gravely angered against those same clerics and had struck them with excommunication at the council of Exoldunum. We restored him to their concord and peace. We neither compelled them to make any satisfaction, since they had fortified themselves with powerful authority, nor judged them in need of any absolution for such an excess.”

Here we read that Amatus was “sent” into Gaul by Gregory VII, and indeed he was sent from the city of Rome. The very learned Stephanus Baluzius conjectures in the preface to the second volume of his *Miscellanea* that he was that Amatus, a monk of Monte Cassino, whom Peter the Deacon mentions in book 20 of *On the Illustrious Men of Monte Cassino*. Peter says that under Gregory VII he was a bishop, although he deliberately omits the name of his episcopal see. Elsewhere the same learned man proves that he was a monk.

Amatus was created archbishop at the council of Bordeaux over which he presided in the year 1088, on 4 November, as is recorded in the *Chronicle of Maillezais*. This council was called “of Bordeaux” because it belonged to the province of Bordeaux, but it seems to have been held at Saintes. This may perhaps be indicated by these words of Ademar, bishop of Angoulême, in a letter by which he made certain gifts to the monastery of Saint-Maixent, copied from the register of that place:

“I, Ademar, by the grace of God bishop of the see of Angoulême, was at Saintes for the synod at which Amatus was elected archbishop of the city of Bordeaux by all of us. There the abbot Adam of Saint-Jouin de Marnes served and honored us with due courtesy.”

Amatus, having become archbishop, proceeded to exercise the legation of the Apostolic See with greater authority and less envy. What he did as legate outside [Col. 1639C] his own province is not our present purpose to record; but what he did as archbishop must be briefly related.

In the year 1090 he confirmed to the monastery of La Sauve-Majeure all the churches that Goscelin, his predecessor, had given to that then highly renowned monastery. Peter, dean and archdeacon of Saint Andrew’s, was a witness to and participant in this confirmation. To the same holy place he gave the church of Saint Lupus of Entre-deux-Mers and the sanctuaries belonging to it.

In 1093 he held a council at Bordeaux, according to the *Chronicle of Maillezais*. The cartulary of Saint Peter of Réole supplies us with the names of the bishops who attended and tells us what was done at this assembly: namely, Otger of Landeron, prior of Réole, brought accusation and suit against Bernard, bishop of Aire, for the restoration of the cell of Saint Caprasius of Pontons in the district of Auch, on the Adour, which the bishop had claimed for himself. The council fathers judged that it ought to be restored. After Amatus, the following subscribed to this judgment: William Bernard, archbishop of Auch; Simon, bishop of Agen; Rainald, bishop of Périgueux; Ademar, bishop of Angoulême; Odo, bishop of Bigorre; Bertrand, bishop of Comminges; Peter, bishop of Adour; Stephen, bishop of Bazas; and Bernard himself, bishop of Aire.

In 1095 he sat at the council of Clermont under Urban II, at which a holy war was decreed for the recovery of the Holy Land. In the same year he was present at Limoges for the consecration of the churches of Saint Martial and Saint Stephen, and at Tours for the consecration of the Major Monastery. There, in 1096, he attended the council held by Pope Urban II and subscribed the decree concerning Saint Martin.

The council of Saintes that Amatus celebrated belongs to approximately the same period. The Sammarthani state that this council is recorded in the charters of Saint-Jean-d’Angély and Saint-Hilaire. Its date, however, is indicated by a charter of La Sauve-Majeure, in which we read:

“The land of Doeria, etc., which Elias, prince of Didonne, with his wife Avicia and their sons [lacuna], donated to the church of La Sauve-Majeure for the salvation of their souls, was afterward pledged by the abbot of Maillezais without our knowledge. But after we learned of it, and after a complaint had been made by our abbot Achelmus at the council of Saintes, we recovered [lacuna] by the judgment of the bishops [Col. 1640B] and abbots [lacuna], confirmed by the hand of Lord Amatus, legate of the Holy Roman Church and, by the grace of God, also archbishop of Bordeaux [lacuna]. This was done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1091.”

In the same year Pope Urban solemnly dedicated the church of Bordeaux on 1 May, although the anniversary solemnity of this dedication is celebrated not on that day but on 21 April, perhaps because of the concurrence of the feast of the holy apostles Philip and James.

We omit the dedication of Saint Saturninus at Toulouse and the consecration of the principal altar at Caroffe, at which he is recorded as having been present at approximately this period, as well as the revelation of the blood of the Lord in the same monastery of Saint-Sauveur at Caroffe and the foundation of the abbey of Saint Mary de Rota, whose charter bears his subscribed name.

[Col. 1640C] In 1097, while proceeding into Spain, he consecrated the great church at Huesca after the city had been surrendered by the Muslims to Peter, king of Navarre and Aragon; or else he purified and reconciled it after it had been polluted by the profane rites of the Muslims. This occurred on the sixth day before the Kalends of January, with Peter of Huesca, Fulk of Barcelona, Peter of Pamplona, and Sancho of Lascuarre assisting as bishops, as John Mariana records after the *Chronicle of Maillezais*, *On the Affairs of Spain*, book X, chapter 2.

It should not be left unmentioned that he gave his support at the council of Nîmes, held on 12 July. At that council Philip I, king of France, who had been suspended and excommunicated because of Bertrada of Montfort, the wife of Fulk, count of Anjou, whom he had abducted and married while Bertha, his lawful wife, was still living, was restored to the embrace of the Church after making the required satisfaction, according to the same *Chronicle of Maillezais*.

In 1098 he held a council at Bordeaux on 5 October, in the sixth indiction. Roland, archbishop of Dol, Peter, bishop of Agen, and others subscribed it. A charter published among the instruments, column 276, no. 14, tells us much more about him. He brought an end to the dispute between the dean and canons of Saint Andrew’s and Fulk, abbot, and the monks of Sainte-Croix, concerning the church of Saint Michael outside the city on the Garonne. He adjudicated it to the monks after the abbot had sworn an oath concerning possession. We give the charter drawn up concerning this matter; at its foot the year of Christ 1099 and the twelfth year of Pope Urban II are noted.

[Col. 1641A] The Sammarthani, Lopesius—who cites the *Chronicle of Maillezais*—and others state that Amatus died in 1101. I nevertheless read that in 1112 he gave the church of Saint Vincent of Barriac to the monastery of Uzerche. I think, however, that 1102 should be read instead of 1112. Certainly, in that year the church of Bordeaux was widowed by the death of Archbishop Amatus, according to a charter published by Besly in his *History of the Counts of Poitou*, p. 410.

In a charter of Saint Stephen of Vaux, a donation to this monastery is recorded as having been made through the hand of Amatus, archbishop of Bordeaux, in 1104; on this matter see Reginald, abbot of that place. Nevertheless, in the proofs to chapter 28 of his *History of the County of Poitou*, Besly presents a charter of the monastery of Saint-Jean-d’Angély in which we read:

“In the year 1102, Pope Paschal being pontiff, Philip king of the Franks, William duke of Aquitaine, Ramnulf bishop of Saintes, Bordeaux being widowed of its shepherd through the death of Amatus the archbishop.”

[Col. 1642A] In 1103 Arnaldus, the successor of Amatus, is named in the *Chronicle of Maillezais*. We therefore judge that Amatus either breathed his last in the year 1101, on 22 May, or in 1102, which seems to be indicated by the charter of Saint-Jean-d’Angély in these words:

“In the year 1102 [lacuna], Bordeaux being widowed of its shepherd through the death of Amatus the archbishop.”

Under this archbishop, William VIII, duke of all Aquitaine, gave many things—or rather confirmed things already given by others—to the church of Bordeaux, once enriched by Charlemagne, his son Louis the Pious, and others, but at that time miserably fallen into decay: namely, a third part of the treasury or coinage, or even of all tolls; the royal court [lacuna]; and a ship free from all tolls. The remaining details may be read in the charter published by Lopesius in the third part of his *History*, chapter 8, p. 365.

[Col. 1641]

# Letters of Amatus, Archbishop of Bordeaux

## I. To Radulfus, Archbishop of Tours  
### That he should attend the Council of Bordeaux, and concerning Gervasius, Abbot of Saint-Savin

*(J. Sirmond, note to letter 26 of book I of Geoffrey of Vendôme; and Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. V, p. 313.)*

[Col. 1641B]

Amatus, bishop of Oloron, by the grace of God legate of the holy Roman Church, sends greetings and every good thing in the Lord Jesus Christ to Radulfus, venerable archbishop of the people of Tours.

Let your charity know, dearest brother, that by the authority of almighty God and with the consent of all the bishops, abbots, and princes of our legation, we have decreed that a council shall be held at Bordeaux on the octave of Saint Michael. Therefore, with brotherly affection, we admonish you by entreaty and command you by apostolic authority that, setting aside delay, you come to the aforesaid council with all your suffragans and with the privileges of your church, so that by your counsel and assistance the cause of God may be strengthened and, with God’s favor, justice for your church—on account of which great and varied disputes have hitherto arisen—may be restored.

If God permits, on our return from Brittany we shall speak with you, so that, with almighty God granting it, we may prudently arrange what ought to be established concerning these and your other affairs.

Furthermore, we wish your fraternity to know that we recently visited the church of Saint-Savin, situated in the district of Poitou, and proved its abbot in the chapter of the monks to be a Simoniac. By apostolic authority we ordered him to go to Poitiers, so that in our presence his heresy might be made manifest to the bishop of Poitiers. Struck by fear of his guilt, he refused to go to Poitiers and, disregarding the reverence owed to his order and office, seized certain relics and ornaments of his church and fled like a thief.

Therefore we command you that, if you are able to find such a man in your diocese, you have him captured and return him to the bishop of Poitiers with the church’s aforesaid spoils. If you cannot return him with the spoils, at least return the spoils, if you can.

## II. To Goffridus, Abbot of Vendôme  
### He announces the restoration to his monastery of the church of Oleron

*(Mabillon, *Annals*, V, p. 657.)*

[Col. 1642C]

Amatus, by the grace of God archbishop of Bordeaux and legate of the Apostolic See, sends greetings to his beloved son Goffridus, abbot of Vendôme, and to the congregation entrusted to him.

Just as our dearest son William, duke of the Aquitanians, saddened us when he took from you the church of Saint George, which is on Oleron, together with its dependencies, and gave it to Eblo of the castle of Allion, so he gladdened us when, coming to his senses after his injustice, he restored what had been taken from you and confirmed the gift that the venerable count of Anjou, Goffridus, had made to your monastery of that church and of other properties in the districts of Poitiers and Saintes.

[Col. 1643A] Moreover, he humbly asked us to confirm, by the authority of the holy Roman Church and our own, this same restoration and concession of his, so that you and your successors might possess by perpetual right, freely and peacefully, everything that the venerable count Goffridus and his wife Agnes, countess of Poitou, had given you, just as they possessed it on the very day on which they transferred it to your monastery.

We therefore confirm this restoration and the liberty that he granted, as we have said, forbidding under anathema, by the authority of God and our own, that anyone henceforth presume to take these things from you or to violate the liberty granted to you in them.

We also testify truthfully that Eblo of the castle of Allion granted you this restoration of the church of Saint George and its dependencies, invoking the curse of God upon all those who might take them from the monks of Vendôme or disturb them in possession of them in any way.

[Col. 1643]

# Synod of Girona

Celebrated in the time of Pope Gregory, with Bishop Amatus, his legate, presiding, in the year 1078.

*(Recovered from the Girona manuscript by the most illustrious Lord Joseph de Taverner d’Ardenne, canon of Barcelona. Edited by D. Martène, *Anecdota*, vol. IV, p. 1187.)*

[Col. 1643B] In the year 1078 after the Incarnation of the Lord, a holy synod of bishops and abbots assembled in the church of Girona. Bishop Amatus, legate of the holy Roman Church, presided in the place of the Lord Pope Gregory. With the concurrence of the others, he enacted many decrees according to the canonical statutes, of which a few are reported so that they may not fall from our memory.

### I

First, he decreed concerning those who assist at the altar in ministering the body and blood of the Lord—namely priests, levites, and subdeacons—and those assigned to the clergy who have devoted themselves to a more excellent life: they are not to associate with women in any domestic partnership. If thereafter anyone openly marries or takes a concubine, he shall be subject to the loss of his rank and honor and shall leave the choir until he has made canonical satisfaction.

### II

Likewise, he decreed that no bishop should dare to raise or promote any cleric in his church by means of money, or to sell ecclesiastical honors. Whoever buys one shall not only be deprived of the dignity he acquired with money but shall also lose his own rank and suffer excommunication until he relinquishes what he wrongly obtained.

### III

Likewise, he promulgated that no son of a priest, deacon, or subdeacon should possess his father’s honors in the same church.

### IV

Likewise, that the sons of clerics should not be promoted to higher ranks; but they may remain in the ranks they have received, unless their way of life prevents it.

### V

The sons of clerics, whether laymen or clerics, shall in no way possess ecclesiastical honors that their fathers held or retained as a benefice of the Church. Whoever neglects this shall be excommunicated.

### VI

He also decreed that clerics who carry weapons, unless they lay down their arms, shall be excluded from the body and blood of the Lord, from entry into any church, from Christian burial, and from all ecclesiastical communion. If they remain rebellious, they shall never again be promoted in the Church of Christ to higher honors or ranks.

### VII

Likewise, he decreed that a cleric should not grow a beard or long hair, or conceal the crown of his head by failing to shave or by shaving only a little, as though ashamed that he had been chosen for the hereditary lot of Christ. Nor should he thereafter wear military garments variegated in different colors.

### VIII

Those joined by consanguinity, unless they are separated after worthy satisfaction has been made, shall remain separated from the Church and from the body of Christ.

### IX

Men living with concubines and usurers, unless they repent, shall be excommunicated.

### X

They also decreed that the tithe of all lands which the accursed cruelty of the unbelieving Jews had been cultivating should be rendered to the church in whose parish those lands were situated, just as if they were cultivated by Christians.

### XI

They further decreed that if any churches had been consecrated for money, or by a Simoniac, they should be consecrated canonically by a legitimate bishop. If any clerics had been ordained by giving money or by a Simoniac, they too should be ordained in the same manner by a Catholic bishop. For this is not a repetition, but the consecration itself, since nothing had previously occurred that could be regarded as valid.

### XII

Clerics from another region shall not be received without letters from their own bishop.

### XIII

We indeed know that churches do not belong to laymen; but where they cannot be taken away from them altogether, we at least entirely prohibit laymen from receiving the offerings of Masses, the altars, or the first fruits. We entirely prohibit the exaction of payments from cemeteries, burials, and baptisteries.

I, Amatus, bishop and legate of the holy Roman Church, have subscribed these synodal acts in the place of my lord the pope.

I, Berengarius, bishop of Girona, have subscribed.  
I, Berengarius, bishop of Vic, have subscribed.  
I, Raimundus, bishop of Elne, have subscribed.  
I, Raymundus, bishop of Roda, have subscribed.  
I, Humbertus, bishop of Barcelona, have subscribed.  
I, Guillelmus, bishop of Couserans, have subscribed.

I, Fulco, archdeacon, acting in the place of the bishop of Urgell, have subscribed.

[Col. 1645]

# Synod of Bordeaux

Held in the year 1080, with Amatus, legate of the Apostolic See, presiding.

[Col. 1645B] All things that arise perish, and what grows old declines; a human life is not extended very far, and its memory proves exceedingly brief. Therefore, lest oblivion entirely swallow up what has passed, it is necessary for writing to preserve knowledge of events, so that what is changeable may not be hidden from those to come.

Accordingly, the present Church does not ignore—and posterity should not remain uncertain about—what was done in our presence.

I, Geraldus, abbot by God’s gift, though unworthy, had long desired to be snatched from the worldly waves by which I was battered more fiercely than a fragile spirit could endure. Moreover, my subjects obeyed me inadequately, and their iron breasts could not be softened; worldly affairs had hardened them excessively.

Finally, when divine clemency showed the harbor of salvation, I resolved to seek the caves of solitude, where there would be no secular habitation of man. Entrusting the care of the flock committed to me to the bishop, I left the monastery accompanied by a few men, entirely ignorant of where our journey would lead.

At last, however, with the Lord guiding us—for he is never absent from those who hope in him—we reached Lord William, count of Poitou, a man of exceptional nobility and also duke of all Aquitaine. He assigned us a suitable place called Silva Major. He returned this allod to us so completely free that no right whatsoever was claimed there by him, as another charter also testifies.

When I wished to begin a monastery there, I went to Lord Goscelin, archbishop of Bordeaux, in whose bishopric the aforesaid allod lay, to ask his benefaction. With the intervention of the aforesaid duke, he granted the monastery already begun such complete liberty that neither he nor anyone after him—neither an archbishop, nor an archdeacon, nor an archpriest, nor a person of any order—could have any right or domination over it, so that the monks dwelling there might serve God freely and without any disturbance.

He also established, at the request of the aforesaid William, that if at some time, by Christ’s disposition, the settlement should grow, neither the archbishop nor any of his ministers would have any greater right there, whether over clerics or laymen; rather, everything would be referred to the disposition of the abbot or congregation.

He also provided for this, for himself and for us: that nevertheless we should receive the consecration of churches, sacred orders, and chrism from the archbishop whenever necessary.

This constitution was again confirmed by him at the next council, in the presence of the Roman legates Hugh and Amatus and a large college of other bishops. It was also decreed that if anyone attempted to violate this decree, he should know himself to be excommunicated until he had made satisfaction, both by the archbishop and by all who had been present at the council.

Moreover, at the advice of Lord Amatus, we established that this monastery should be subject solely to the Roman Church and should pay the Apostolic Lord five solidi each year for his protection.

But I, already declining into the weakness of extreme old age, wished to relinquish the care of the monks and yield my place, as less useful, to a better man. Yet Lord Amatus, at the request of our brothers, although I resisted with all my strength, nevertheless, on behalf of the Apostolic Lord, testified to me that obedience was required and commended their provision.

The aforesaid confirmation was enacted in the city of Bordeaux at the council in the year 1080 from the Incarnation of the Lord, indiction 3, epact 26, on 6 October, in the eighth year of Pope Gregory VII, while Philip was reigning in France.

The subscription of William, duke of Aquitaine. Confirm this, O God.  
I, Amatus, legate of the Apostolic See, confirm.  
I, Hugh, legate of the Apostolic See, confirm.  
I, Goscelin, archbishop of Bordeaux, grant and confirm in the presence of the council.  
The subscription of Radulfus, archbishop of Tours.  
The subscription of William, archbishop of Auxerre.  
The subscription of Boson, bishop of Saintes.  
The subscription of Ademar, bishop of Angoulême.  
The subscription of William, bishop of Périgueux.  
The subscription of Raimundus, bishop of Bazas.  
The subscription of Hugh, bishop of Bigorre.  
The subscription of Donald, bishop of Agen.  
The subscription of Peter, bishop of Aire.  
The subscription of Odo, abbot of Saint-Jean.  
The subscription of Drogo, abbot of Maillezais.  
The subscription of Raynald, abbot of Saint-Cyprien of Poitiers.  
The subscription of Bertrand, abbot of Saint-Julien of V. Nobiliacensis.  
The subscription of Hildebert, abbot of Nantilly.  
V. Nantol in the valley.

The subscription of Ancelin, archdeacon of the church of Bordeaux, and of Goscelin.

[Col. 1647]

# Charters of Amatus, Archbishop of Bordeaux

## I. Judgment of Amatus, Archbishop of Bordeaux and Legate of the Apostolic See, in Favor of the Monastery of Sainte-Croix

*(Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 276.)*

[Col. 1647B]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Amatus, legate of the holy Roman Church and also archbishop of Bordeaux.

Since human memory is very often so obstructed by worldly cares that it forgets not only events of long ago but even those that occurred very recently, it has pleased us briefly to set down in writing and to impress upon the minds of the faithful of the holy mother Church, both present and future, how we settled by an unbreakable judgment the controversy that arose between Lord Fulco, abbot of Sainte-Croix, and Lord Peter, dean, concerning the church of Saint Michael; so that the mind of those now living, awakened by writing, may readily recall what it has seen and heard, and the minds of those to come may be instructed by the same record concerning the past.

The abbot with his men and the dean with his men were standing in our presence. After carefully examining all the arguments of the entire case on both sides, we imposed the following judgment upon their dispute. If the abbot of Sainte-Croix should prove by an oath, together with two of his monks, the tenure of Saint Michael held by his predecessor A. and by himself, as he affirms with many assertions, he would possess the church peacefully thereafter. Otherwise, we decreed that his claim should be set aside.

When examined by the test of justice, this judgment appeared to all to deserve the highest praise. Accordingly, in the presence of everyone standing there, Lord Fulco, abbot of Sainte-Croix, rose with his men and swore over the four Gospels that his predecessor, A. of Trencard, together with his monks, had acquired the church of Saint Michael, situated outside the city on the Garonne, entirely and in full right from our most reverend predecessor, Lord Goscelin, and from the chapter of Saint Andrew’s, except for what is called the thirtieth and the confessions.

[Col. 1648B] And so that the aforesaid abbot and his successors might possess the aforesaid church firmly and peacefully, according to the decrees of the holy Fathers, by way of an exchange, they were to pay two solidi each year, on the feast of Saint Andrew, to the canons of the mother church.

The aforesaid abbot possessed this church, thus granted to Sainte-Croix, peacefully for as long as he lived. He also swore that, after he himself had been made abbot, he had held the same tenure.

Therefore, so that thereafter the church of Saint Michael might be administered inviolably and peacefully, though always through chaplains, according to the deliberation of Sainte-Croix, we have confirmed this privilege by our authority and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

It was enacted and granted in our presence, with P., the dean, and E., the archdeacon, assisting together with the other canons of Saint Andrew’s and very many other distinguished clerics and laymen, in the year 1099 from the Incarnation of the Lord, indiction 7, epact 26, with [lacuna] in the twelfth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban II.

## II. Amatus, Archbishop of Bordeaux, Gives the Church of Saint Lupus to La Sauve-Majeure

*(Gallia Christiana, II, 275, new instruments.)*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, Amatus, by the grace of God archbishop of Bordeaux.

[Col. 1648D] If we bestow some gift of our generosity upon places dedicated to God, for love of divine worship, we undoubtedly trust that the reward of eternal recompense will be repaid to us. Let it therefore be known to all the faithful, present and future, that, for the advancement of divine worship, we perpetually grant to the church of Saint Mary of Silva Major a certain little church built between the two seas, in honor of Saint Lupus the Confessor, together with the sanctuaries belonging to the aforesaid little church. And so that this grant may remain firm and unshaken through succeeding ages, [Col. 1649A] we have ordered this charter to be marked with the seal of our authority.

III. Certain acts relating to Amatus of Bordeaux.

Amatus, by the grace of God archbishop of Bordeaux and legate of the Holy Roman Church, at the request of the venerable Asculf, abbot of the angelic—or rather, Angeriac—congregation of Saint John the Baptist, granted a privilege concerning certain churches which Odo, abbot of blessed memory and Asculf’s predecessor, had acquired from Archbishop Goscelin during the latter’s archiepiscopate of Bordeaux, so that the aforesaid angelic congregation, together with those little churches, might increase through succeeding ages both in temporal possessions [Col. 1649B] and daily advance more fully in divine service.

These churches are: Saint Mary of Vairas, Saint Peter of Vals, Saint Sulpicius of Averniac, Saint Martin of Ison, Saint Martin of Boiseth, Saint Mary of Grisiliac, Saint Vincent of Molon, and Saint Laurence of Medulco; and these churches are between the two seas. Peter, dean and archdeacon; Eblo, archdeacon; Arnaldus Simonis, cantor; and the other canons in the chapter of Saint Andrew confirm this privilege.

Done and granted at Bordeaux in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1098, [Col. 1650A] indiction 6, concurrent 4, epact 15, while Lord Urban II was seated as pope of the Roman see.

Given by the hand of Peter, dean, to the same abbot A. in the chapter of Saint Andrew, on the fifth day before the Ides of March. From the cartulary of Angeriac, folio 97.

The same Amatus settled at the Council of Bordeaux the dispute that existed between Ansculf, abbot of Saint John of Angeriac, and Garnerius, abbot of Saint Maxentius, and the monks of both monasteries, concerning the church of Saint Peter of Mareistais, situated near the castle called Mastacius; the matter was decided in favor of the people of Angeriac.

Done and granted at the Council of Bordeaux [Col. 1650B] in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1098, indiction 6, epact 26, with the attendance and presidency of R., archbishop of Auch, and R., archbishop of Dol, together with their suffragan bishops and abbots, and also of S., bishop of Agen, and R., bishop of Périgueux, with their suffragan abbots. In the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban II, given on the third day before the Nones of October. From the cartulary of Angeriac, folio 95.

The deposition of Lord Amatus, archbishop, is recorded in the necrology of the New Monastery of Poitiers on the tenth day before the Kalends of June.

# In the Year of the Lord 1103: Poppo, Bishop of Metz

[Col. 1649]

## Notice

*(Gallia Christiana nova, vol. XIII, col. 734)*

[Col. 1649C] Poppo succeeded Burchard. He was an archdeacon of the church of Trier and brother of Henry, count palatine; he was as opposed to the faction of the schismatics as he was devoted to the Catholic party. For this reason he encountered a rival, Adelbero or Adelbert, whom the citizens of Metz excluded, although he was supported by the emperor’s authority. Thus Poppo remained in possession of the bishopric.

Yet an archbishop was needed to consecrate him, for Egilbert, the metropolitan of the province, followed the schism. Overcome by the entreaties of Jarento, abbot of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon, Hugh, archbishop of Lyon and legate of the apostolic see, undertook this responsibility. In the midst of dangers, accompanied by several prelates, he came to Metz and ordained Poppo bishop in the first week of Lent.

Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, a contemporary author, relates this in his Chronicle [Col. 1650C] under the year 1093. The writer of the manuscripts of Saint-Hubert, somewhat less ancient, reports the same concerning Burchard. Hence some have judged that Burchard and Poppo were the same person.

On the other hand, Berthold, continuator of the Chronicle of Hermann the Lame, maintains that Gebhard of Constance, apostolic legate, consecrated the man whom the people of Metz had chosen as bishop, on 27 March, in the middle of Lent.

However the matter stands, it seems likely that the historians of Metz concluded from the delay in the inauguration that the see of Metz had been deprived of pastors for several years, although Burchard had succeeded Hermann immediately. But while consecration was lacking, the see was considered vacant, even though several persons were contending for that episcopate: namely, Burchard, Poppo, Bruno Adelbero, and [Col. 1651A] perhaps Nicodemus, mentioned in the charter of Bosonville, or even another person designated by the letter O, to whom the pope sent letters.

Nevertheless, in 1094 Poppo confirmed to the monastery of Cluny the church of Thiecourt, which Gerard of Thiecourt and his son Arnulf had given to it. In 1094 he granted testimonial letters to Richer, bishop of Verdun, so that he might receive consecration from the archbishop of Lyon, and he accompanied him when he took possession. In the same year he visited the monastery of Saint-Pierre at Spinal, in order to restore the observance instituted there long before by Adalbero.

The fifth year of Bishop Poppo corresponds to the year of the Incarnation 1094 in a charter of Bruno, archbishop of Trier, confirming the church of Saint Peter in the Sands to the monastery of Saint Clement. It can therefore be inferred that Poppo’s episcopate began in 1090.

When he visited the monastery of Spinal, a nun named Cecilia was living there at that time, as is recorded. She reproached him for the decline of regular discipline and then foretold that one day what is now seen would come to pass: the sisters, having renounced the Rule of Saint Benedict, would turn wholly to secular customs.

Poppo attended the Council of Clermont in 1095, where he acted as mediator between Varnerus, abbot of Gorze, and Vezelo, advocate, concerning authority over Amel. He is also mentioned in 1097 with Hildebert, archbishop of Trier, and Wido, abbot of Saint Arnulf. In 1098 he arranged for Antony of Lay, prior, to be appointed in place of Bercher, the deceased abbot of Sens.

Since he was always hated by the emperor, the prince placed all the property of the church of Metz situated in Hasbania under his own control and granted it as a fief to Count Arnulf of Los. This bishop died in 1103.

[Col. 1651]

## The Charters of Poppo

### I. He grants the entire lordship of the abbey of Saint Julian to Saint Vincent and confirms all its possessions.  
*(1094, 1 October)*

*[History of Metz, vol. III, Documents, p. 98, from the archives of the abbey of Saint Vincent, bundle 1, no. 1.]*

[Note: [Col. 1651C] *Seigneurie*, lordship or jurisdiction.]

[Col. 1651B] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, and of the most blessed Virgin Mary, and of Saint Michael the archangel, and of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and of the most blessed apostle Paul, and of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, and of the glorious martyr Saint Vincent, and of Saint Lucy, most precious virgin and martyr, and of all the heavenly orders: Poppo, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of the Mediomatrici, to all the spiritual sons of holy mother Church.

[Col. 1651C] The venerable authority of the Fathers commends to us that we honor, with the highest devotion, the bodies of the saints whom we believe will be gracious intercessors with almighty God, so that the more devoted we are to the precious adornment of the saints, the more quickly we may enjoy their patronage in our necessities.

Attentively pursuing this venerable devotion, our beloved son Lanzo, the most reverend abbot of the monastery of Saint Vincent, conceived the intention of honorably transferring the most sacred body of Saint Lucy, which rests there, because it had for many years been placed less worthily within a certain receptacle. He therefore labored at great expense to construct a reliquary adorned with gold, silver, and gems, so that he might fulfill the most sacred desire he had conceived.

When the work had been completed and the day appointed for the blessed undertaking announced, we transferred and placed the precious body of the aforesaid virgin within the artistic receptacle, in the presence of several religious persons who had freely gathered from various regions for so great a joy.

We, contemplating more deeply the praiseworthy deed of the venerable abbot, resolved to enlarge this translation by contributing something distinguished from our possessions, with the support of our faithful, clerical and lay. Therefore I, Poppo, bishop of the holy Church of Metz, make known to all the faithful, present and future, that, for the salvation of myself, my predecessors, and my successors, I irrevocably grant to the most blessed Lucy the entire lordship of Saint Julian’s borough, with all its appurtenances, [Col. 1652C] so that the aforesaid abbot, and all his successors, may exercise that jurisdiction freely through their own officials, with every other authority excluded.

Whenever wine is sold by ban in the city or outside the city, we grant the abbot and all his successors permission to have wine for sale by ban in the court of Saint Vincent, with all persons—both sellers and buyers—exempt from accusation.

Furthermore, we approve and earnestly confirm whatever our predecessor bishops granted to the abbey of Saint Vincent, both whatever belonged to their own table and whatever had been acquired in villages, vineyards, lands, new holdings, people, churches, and all possessions, so that the abbot and those serving God there may possess everything perpetually, without any injury, as valid property.

[Col. 1653A] In addition, whatever the most serene popes—namely John, Benedict, Leo, and Urban—granted to the abbots of Saint Vincent through their privileges, and whatever regulations they established concerning property belonging to the abbey, we grant and order to be preserved inviolably, our dignity and authority and that of all the bishops of the Church of Metz being balanced in every respect, provided that they were Catholics.

Therefore, confirming everything noted above so that it may remain valid and unshaken for all time, by the authority of God almighty, Father and Son, and by the power of the Holy Spirit, we exclude from the thresholds of holy Church, with the sword of a strict anathema, all violators of these provisions, so that they may have no share in the lot of the elect unless they repent through amendment.

[Col. 1653B] Done at Metz, in the church of Saint Vincent, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1094, indiction 3, on Sunday, the Kalends of October, in the fifth year of the episcopate of Lord Poppo.

Present and approving were Lord Adalbero, primicerius and archdeacon; Lord Gerard, archdeacon; Arnulf, treasurer; Emicho, Accho, Folcuin, Leubrin, Thiefrid, Sigifrid, canons; Walo, abbot of Saint Arnulf; and Albert, abbot of Saint Martin.

Among the laymen there were present and cooperating Burchard the judge, Becelin and Albert, brothers, Ebroin, and innumerable others, whose names are written in the book of life.

### II. He regulates the rights of the advocates of Amel.  
*(1095)*

*[As above, p. 100, from the cartulary of the abbey of Gorze, title 138, pp. 188–190.]*

[Col. 1653C] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, and of Mary, blessed Mother of God, and of Saint Michael the archangel, and of Saints Peter and Paul, and of Saint Gorgonius, and of all the heavenly orders: Poppo, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of the Mediomatrici.

We make known to all the faithful, present and future, that the venerable abbot of the monastery of Gorze, named Warnerus, together with his provost, Brother Adelo, humbly came into our presence and complained about his advocate, Wezelo. In the jurisdiction of Amel, where he was advocate, Wezelo was claiming certain things extraordinarily, both personally and through his men, exceeding the equity that had been exercised by the others who are remembered as having been advocates there.

Thus, satisfying his request and complaint, we came to Amel with a multitude of our faithful. There the aforesaid advocate, having been convicted of illicit invasions, justified himself before us and our abbot according to the judgment of those present. Finally, he abandoned what he had unjustly usurped, approving to the abbot and his men whatever dignity and advantage had openly been declared to belong to Amel by ancient custom.

So that no ambiguity might arise about this among those now living or those to come, we set out, in the following order, what are the rights of the abbot and what are those of the advocate:

At Amel [Col. 1654A] no one has the ban—that is, jurisdiction—or authority except the abbot of Gorze, his provost, and their officials, together with all appurtenances.

In the three annual courts and in the other courts held throughout the year, the provost and the reeve shall act and conclude whatever pertains to the courts, without the advocate.

Every investiture shall be made under the ban of the abbot, provost, and reeve, without any mention of the advocate.

The abbot and the provost shall appoint the reeve and all the officials, without the advocate.

The reeve who exercises the ban shall seize any rebel, personally and through his men, and hand him over to the stocks, compelling him until he performs justice, without the advocate, unless perhaps necessity should require his intervention.

In the entire lordship of Amel’s jurisdiction, concerning both a thief and a robber and all other matters, the reeve shall decide everything without the advocate, according to the judgment of the assessors of Amel’s court.

If the thief or robber is a stranger and redeems himself, the advocate shall receive a third part. But if he flees while being held in custody, the advocate shall have no interest in demanding anything from the reeve, provided that the reeve can clear himself by his own agreement that he did not permit the man to escape.

The abbot shall have the right of selling wine by ban for two months, choosing whichever months he wishes except July and August.

Concerning the *leuda*—the fine for a slain man—only the reeve shall hold court, receiving the *leuda* for the abbot’s benefit. The advocate shall receive nothing from it unless he has been summoned.

Concerning the changing of coinage and the duel, whether begun or concluded, nothing belongs to the advocate’s jurisdiction.

For, so that everything else may remain in the abbot’s free authority, the advocate holds ten *mansi* in fief, apart from the ban retained by the abbot. He holds these *mansi* separately in order to defend the whole jurisdiction, without any other claim except what is written here.

The same advocate also has residents on those *mansi*, owing him a head-tax; he has there his own reeve, dean, and assessor, and all the revenues of those ten *mansi*, without the ban.

Furthermore, from each resident within this ban, over whom he is advocate and who pays him the head-tax, he receives on the feast of Saint Martin one *sonia*—a lodging-right, or rather a payment made in order to avoid lodging—measured by the quarter-measure of Amel’s court.

[Col. 1654D] If the *sonia* has not been paid on that day, the advocate shall nevertheless commit no violence; rather, the abbot’s reeve shall exact justice for him after the abbot’s annual court has ended.

On the following day the advocate shall hold his own court over his men who hold land from his ten *mansi* and over those who owe him the head-tax.

If any case in his court proceeds as far as a duel, it shall be concluded in the abbot’s court at Amel. The abbot’s reeve shall impose the penalty, give the abbot his due, and give the advocate his.

If any boundary has been removed from those ten *mansi* held in the advocate’s fief, the abbot’s reeve shall impose the entire penalty, giving the advocate his due, restoring the ban to the abbot, and restoring the boundary.

The advocate shall have no private house at Amel, [Col. 1655A] nor shall his servants have one, nor shall he lodge there, unless he comes on account of his court; and then he shall lodge only with his own men.

The provisions written above constitute the whole law of Amel’s jurisdiction. Earlier holders preserved this law inviolably down to our time. Although it had been violated by Advocate Wezelo, as we have stated above, he nevertheless approved and promised that he would preserve it henceforth.

So that it may remain valid and unshaken forever, we bind violators of this renewed decree with the indissoluble bond of anathema. And so that it may be supported by firmer strength, we set down below the inscription of our name and those of our faithful, as a testimony of the truth, by the power of almighty God, against any transgressors who may arise, so that they may have no share with the saints.

Poppo, bishop of the holy Church of Metz.

Abbots: [Col. 1656A] Warnerus, Walo, Lauzo, Petrus the provost, Adelo.

Clergy: Adalbero the archdeacon, Emicho the archdeacon, Rotcelinus the archdeacon, Arnulf the treasurer.

Laity: Duke Theoderic; Gerard, count; Gotbert of Asperomonte; Albert of Briaco and his two sons; Theoderic, Albert, and Wigeric of Spinal; Hugh of Asperomonte; Bertald of Turre; Theoderic of Confluentia; Wigeric of Donobrium; Burchard the judge; Anselm the steward; Girard the *scanzo*; Walter, advocate of Gorze; Wipald, first assessor of Metz.

Done publicly at Metz, while Henry Augustus was emperor and Folmar was count, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1095, indiction 3. I, Andreas the chancellor, dictated and sealed this at the command of my most serene lord Poppo, bishop of the Mediomatrici by the grace of God.

[Col. 1655]

## Letters of Poppo to Lambert, Bishop of Arras

*(See among the letters of Lambert, Patrologia, vol. CLXII.)*

# In the Year of the Lord 1100: Anselm, Archbishop of Milan

[Col. 1655]

## Notice

*(Ughelli, Italia sacra, vol. IV, col. 116)*

[Col. 1655B] Anselm, the fourth of this name, a Valvasorian, otherwise called de Buis, formerly provost of the Laurentian basilica, was made archbishop of Milan and confirmed by Pope Urban II in 1096.

Following the example of his excellent predecessor, he too undertook to preach what is called the Crusade. After enrolling and marking with the cross fifty thousand Lombards, he crossed over to Syria for the holy war.

Landulf of Saint Paul describes his election, expedition, and character in this manner in his Chronicle, chapter 1:

> “That monk Armanus—for he was practically a Roman cardinal—had been elected bishop in the church of Brescia with the support of the citizens of Brescia and through the favor of Countess Matilda. After the death of Arnulf, archbishop of Milan, he came to participate in the election of another archbishop. When he perceived that a distinguished multitude of Milanese was assembling to elect Landulf of Badagio, provost of the canonry of Saint Ambrose, as archbishop—a man most excellently adorned with good morals and a good life—he stopped and did not consent to the election.

> “Then the crowd of the populace, thinking him a religious man through favor toward the Roman and Brescian Churches and Countess Matilda, as soon as it perceived that Armanus was obstructing this election, began to rage against it and violently tear the clerics and priests with fists and clubs. He even presumed to kill, in the very church called Hiemalis, a man named Paganus, from the citizens of …, at the eastern gate …

> “Landulf avoided this madness. He descended from the sacristy of the church and reached his domestic church, which is called Saint John at the Four Faces. But that Armanus, amid such disturbance, said to his assembled people in the church of Saint Ambrose: ‘It shall happen to you as the proverb says: To a foolish people, a deaf bishop.’ Having said this, he immediately chose for himself and for them as archbishop Anselm de Buis, a simple man and provost of the canonry of Saint Lawrence.

> “When the latter learned that he had been elected by that Brescia-born Armanus and approved by the impetuous crowd, he immediately ascended and sat upon the archiepiscopal chair. Since his suffragan bishops were lacking, he received all the ecclesiastical orders up to the priesthood, as well as episcopal ordination, from foreign bishops. He also attached himself to the pastoral staff through the hands of Countess Matilda, while he put on the stole delivered to him by the legate of Lord Pope Urban.

> “Then this man, having become prudent, disregarded Obert, surnamed Baltricus, who opposed Armanus because he had received from his king Henry the investiture of the bishopric of Brescia; and he ordained as bishop Armanus, who had elected himself archbishop.

> “He attempted to go to Tuscany. When he had reached Florence, the king himself—a prudent and wise man, handsome in appearance, alas, a young man—after taking a potion from Avianus, the physician of Countess Matilda, ended his life.”

The same author continues in chapter 2:

> “When the king had died in his kingdom, the aforesaid Anselm de Buis, archbishop of Milan, as though instructed by apostolic authority, although the priest already mentioned was unwilling, undertook to gather an army from various peoples with which he might seize the kingdom of Babylon. In pursuit of this aim he urged the chosen youth of Milan to take up crosses and sing the song ‘Ultreja, Ultreja’ (“Onward, onward!”). At the voice of this prudent man, many men of every condition throughout the cities, villages, and castles of the Lombards took up crosses and sang the same song, ‘Ultreja, Ultreja’ (“Onward, onward!”).

> “While this simple man was still living in Milan and gathering his army, he decided to appoint himself a vicar, a man of many arts. Therefore certain very clever men, ordained priests by him, received the order to go to Savona, so that in that city they might, by his command and authority, urge and compel the election of a bishop.

> “As they were traveling, they came to Ferrara, in whose forest they embraced Grosulanus and his counsel. The activity of those priests was so effective that certain men from Savona, finding Grosulanus afflicted in his food and shabby in his clothing, chose him as their bishop. The electors, together with the elected man and the two priests sent by the archbishop—namely, the priest John Aculeus and the priest Nazarius Muricula—came to Milan.

> “There, by order of the archbishop, who had already set out on the expedition, Grosulanus was ordained bishop and vicar of the archbishop by Armanus of Brescia, Arialdus of Genoa, and Mainardus of Turin. But because the man who had been ordained had not yet ascended the see of Savona, he attempted to go to that city and reached it, in a manner of speaking. Yet if he had any rest there, it was exceedingly brief. Departing from there as quickly as possible, he returned to Milan.

> “He stirred up the people of that great city so that every week, on the second day, they would gather at the church of Saint Ambrose and celebrate litanies for that archbishop Anselm and his army. Grosulanus himself, not only on those days but on nearly every feast, addressed that great crowd splendidly, seeking to win it over to himself no more by his preaching than by the harshness of his clothing and food.”

Thus far the contemporary author.

In 1098, or at the beginning of the following year, Anselm returned from Syria to Milan, before Jerusalem had been captured by the faithful of Christ; for on the Ides of July 1099 it came into their hands under the leadership of Godfrey, to the immense joy of the entire Christian world.

On the fourth day before the Nones of February, Anselm pronounced at Milan a judgment in favor of the abbot of Saint Simplicianus. Since this judgment is very famous, we have decided to present it in order to investigate and establish the truth of the matter, from an authentic copy supplied to us by the learned and highly experienced Constantinus, abbot of Cajetanus.

[Col. 1658B] Beside the basilica of Saint Simplicianus there later arose a noble monastery of the Benedictine order. Simplicianus had led a solitary life there, and after him other men of the same institute lived there; Benedictine monks succeeded them around the year of the Lord 700. At that time they were staying with monks at Saint Protasius, having been endowed with rights and privileges by the archbishops of Milan; and to the present day the illustrious monastery has continued under the noble and devout congregation of Cassino.

Moreover, when Godfrey of Bouillon had taken possession of the holy city of Jerusalem after expelling the barbarians, Archbishop Anselm, as a testimony to the victory at Jerusalem, restored the church of Ronzone, which had formerly been erected in honor of the Holy Trinity, and brought it into a true likeness of the Holy Sepulchre of Jerusalem, or of that Jerusalem church. When the work was completed, he solemnly consecrated it to that same Sepulchre in the year 1100, on the Ides of July. Chalcus has a brief account of this consecration, while Puricellus gives a fuller one [Col. 1658C] and quotes Anselm’s letter, or public document, copied from an authentic original, which is given below.

Anselm, therefore, having returned from Syria to Milan, soon consecrated that church of the Holy Trinity, renewed in honor of the Lord’s Sepulchre, on the Ides of July in the year 1100.

Then, on the Kalends of August, he departed from Genoa with the Genoese fleet, concerning which Ubertus Folieta speaks in book 1 of his Genoese History. Having set out for Syria, he was driven away by the Saracens and died at Constantinople in that same year 1100, on the Kalends of October [Note: [Col. 1657D] According to the catalogue, Anselm occupied the see for 3 years, 10 months, and 28 days; he died on the second day before the Kalends of October and was buried at Constantinople as a pilgrim in the monastery of Saint Nicholas. According to this calculation, Anselm began to sit on the see on 3 November 1097, on the third weekday after a vacancy of 1 month and 8 days, and lived until 3 September 1101. Ughelli therefore erred when he wrote that this Anselm died in the same calendar year, since in that year he was still in Milan and had celebrated the dedication of the church of the Holy Sepulchre, whose notable monument Ughelli himself reports. PAPAEBROCHIUS.], and was buried in the church of Saint Nicholas, leaving to posterity the immortal renown of his name. Thus Chalcus, the Acts of the Church of Milan, and Landulf of Saint Paul, chapter 2, explicitly assert: driven away by the Turks and Saracens, he died in great sorrow at Constantinople.

[Col. 1657]

## The Privileges of Anselm

### I. Privilege for the church of Saint Simplicianus  
*(1099)*

*[Ughelli, Italia sacra, IV, 118.]*

[Col. 1657D] Since, having contemplated the grace of the Holy Spirit, we have climbed the lofty tower of Mount Zion for the house of Israel, let us watch carefully over all those entrusted to us, not giving sleep to our eyes. Rather, with all our heart, we keep watch all around, with eyes like burning coals.

We display faces of the fiery flame of lamps, in the manner of living creatures, with twice-living faces of differing forms flashing above wheels [the wording is textually corrupt], so that the whole city may rest in tranquility when it sees a vigilant staff above its flock. Therefore, if from that watchtower we see anyone secretly stealing, or openly rushing upon the houses of God in a public assault, let us not hesitate to oppose them and fight in battle as a wall for the house of Israel.

Now, because we see certain people contending in the house of God with superstitious religion, ignorant of God’s justice and seeking to establish their own, we must oversee them with pastoral care and bring the discordant and contentious—those who are in the Church—back to peace and unanimity by the weapons of justice and under ecclesiastical statutes.

We have recently heard that divisions have arisen in the Church of God under our rule, with the neighbors of Saint Protasius, under the pretext of religion, contending with the abbot of Saint Simplicianus over a certain church.

But let the reason why this scandal has arisen be pursued by our orderly writing, so that it may become clearer to all what, by the authority of the holy canons, ought first to be judged by us. The petition of the neighboring parties must be clearly presented.

They say that the church of Saint Protasius was formerly a monastery of an abbot and monks, whereas the basilica of Saint Simplicianus had long belonged to canons. But when the abbot and monks wished to avoid the crowds of the people in order to lead a solitary life, while the canons, as though established in the countryside, did not refuse to live among the people, an exchange was made between them: the abbot and monks, with all the possessions belonging to the monastery, moved to the church of Saint Simplicianus, while the canons, with all their possessions, came to the church of Saint Protasius, so that the former might live in solitude and the latter among the people.

Trusting in these arguments, and unwilling that any monks should remain there any longer, the neighbors chose Gualdo, provost of the brethren who were officials of Saint Protasius, while the abbot, because they had shamefully murmured against him, consented unwillingly to his election and proclaimed before everyone:

“Lest there perhaps be a tumult among the people, I consent in some manner to this election, while preserving the dignity of our monastery and our privilege.”

After hearing the neighbors’ argument, it follows that we must present the abbot’s objection. He says that a monastery of monks had long ago been established at Saint Protasius. But when the number of monks in all the monasteries grew abundantly, so that the multitude of monks, together with many others attached to their fellowship or service, created an intolerable inconvenience because of the narrowness of the place and the urban confusion, the abbey was transferred outside to the basilica of Saint Simplicianus, which the former abbot had acquired as property by decree of the archbishop who was then in office. Nevertheless, certain monks remained there with their monastic instruments in the monastery of Saint Protasius.

It is evident to all that from that day monks always remained in the aforesaid church of Saint Protasius, together with chaplains administering the ecclesiastical office to the people, subject in all things to the abbot and to the congregation subject to him.

Since the abbot and the neighbors disagreed so gravely over these matters that the Church of God was shaken by unrest and the entire city disturbed, they were finally softened by our repeated admonitions and decided to have the whole dispute settled by our judgment and that of our clergy.

Therefore, together with our clerics and abbots, we entered the sacristy so that, after the matter of the lawsuit had been examined canonically by their counsel, its reason might be clarified.

There, when the lamp of wisdom had been placed upon the lampstand to shine for those in the house, and when we were required to give an account of this matter with our fellow servants, no one was found who would hide his entrusted talent by burying it. Rather, with open treasures they brought forth the talents they had multiplied, when we asked them to do so.

When these had been displayed, ignorance was expelled and truth introduced through the lucid exposition of wisdom. We embraced one another in the arms of concord. After that embrace, in agreement with the chosen clerics, we established that justice, which had until then been trampled underfoot in the aforesaid disputes, should now be brought forth from its chamber through legal expertise and lawfully promised to the people by the sword of our mouth on the following day.

In the morning, [both objections are mentioned, but the text breaks off]; with our people requesting to hear the judgment, we ascended the pulpit with the same clerics and the abbots of Saint Mary.

After silence had first been made, [the damaged text reads: “hoc locum capitalium est Gre.”] [lacuna] … Having carefully considered several chapters by ourselves and our clergy in the sacristy, and having examined the ancient foundation of the monastery of Saint Simplicianus and of the church of Saint Protasius, [lacuna] [the damaged text appears to provide that] the cloistered monks were to remain at the church of Saint Protasius by the constitution of the abbot of Saint Simplicianus. We likewise approve and confirm that same church, and the monastery of that church, with all possessions belonging to both monasteries, [lacuna] shall henceforth remain under the authority and governance [Col. 1660C] of the same abbot.

Then the chapter of Pope Anacletus was read. After it had been explained, we said to the people:

Furthermore, we decree that what we did when we gave you our chaplain Gualdo, whom you had chosen to be provost of the priests and clerics of the church of Saint Protasius, shall be regarded entirely as void. For the abbot of Saint Simplicianus now says—and, if we wish, can affirm by oath—that he consented to Gualdo’s election not voluntarily but through fear. He also says that from ancient times the election of the chaplains of the church of Saint Protasius has always belonged to him and no one else.

Therefore, just as we must always defend our rights and dignities legally against their attackers, so we must not, together with our brothers, take away what belongs to another [lacuna]. We also decree that from this hour and henceforth the abbot of Saint Simplicianus shall elect the official chaplains of Saint Protasius. They shall be subject to his authority and obedience and shall have no other provost except the abbot himself, who shall govern and guard them. If they sin among themselves or against others, he shall correct them with the rod of righteousness.

He shall make them live at that same church, or regularly in the cloister with the aforesaid monks if the chaplains themselves prefer that life, or canonically in other houses.

These provisions, brothers, we have enacted canonically. Together with our clergy we have approved them, and we wish the same to be firmly approved by all of us, so that the neighbors and the abbot may inviolably observe what we have now decreed.

And all the people said: “Let it be done, let it be done.”

[Col. 1661A] I, Anselm, archbishop by the grace of God, have subscribed this document made by me. This was drawn up and dictated by Ariprando, chancellor, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1099, on the fourth day before the Nones of February, in the seventh indiction. I, Armannus, bishop of Brescia, was present, and have subscribed. I, Guillelmus, abbot of Saint Ambrose, was present, and have subscribed. I, Bonus Senior, bishop of Reggio, was present, and have subscribed. I, Arialdus, unworthy abbot of Saint Dionysius, was present and have subscribed. I, Bellottus, son of the late Ambrosius Gambarelli, notary of the sacred palace, saw and read the original of this copy: it contained what is written in this copy, except for letters more or fewer. I, Niger, son of the late Giramus of the Fragia family, of the district of the Cuman Gate, notary of the lord Emperor Henry, saw and read this copy from the original copy, and it contained in it what is written in this copy, apart from letters more or fewer. [Col. 1661B] I, Martinus, son of Nigro of the Vagia family, of the district of the Cuman Gate, notary and envoy of the Lord Emperor Otto, copied this copy from the sealed original: it contained what is written in this copy, except for letters more or fewer.

## II. He consecrates the church of Ronzone, which he had remodeled in the likeness of the Sepulchre of Jerusalem. (Year 1099.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, IV, 124.]

[Col. 1661C] In the name of the holy, everlasting, and undivided Trinity, and of the holy Sepulchre of our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 1661] Muratori doubts the authenticity of this document in *Anecdota*, vol. I, p. 244.]

I, ANSELMUS, archbishop of the holy Mother Church of Milan, by the great aid of God’s mercy. Although, as a good shepherd, I ought to lay down my life for my sheep, yet, hindered by worldly cares, I cannot do this; nor do I without reason grieve that I do not exercise the office of a good shepherd. Yet, lest I should altogether fail to see through being given over to ignorance, the supreme mercy of God—who did not permit the city set upon a mountain, namely the church of the Holy Sepulchre situated in the midst of this city, to remain hidden any longer, but caused it, as it were, to be exalted and to rejoice as a sign of the victory of the Jerusalem Sepulchre—to whose glory we proceeded with our brethren, dedicated the altar to the Lord together with the church within, and offered upon it to our God a sacrifice of praise.

[Col. 1661D] Therefore, when an assembly of clergy and people had gathered, it was decreed by us, with the common counsel of all and their repeated exhortation, and laudably confirmed, that each year this solemnity should be celebrated with glory and honor in commemoration of the Holy Sepulchre. The cardinals of Saint Mary are reverently to come there in procession; when they reach the entrance of the church, they are to intone *Te Deum laudamus* in a loud voice, holding one another’s hands as a sign of the victory gained at Jerusalem. Among them a subdeacon is also to approach with a lamp, lighting the lamps in the customary manner morning and evening.

[Col. 1662A] When the office is ended, the chief participants are reverently and honorably to receive three solidi from the offering of obedience; the custodians are to receive twelve denarii with the *veglioni*; he who has carried the golden cross is likewise to have two denarii; and the boys who have performed the office of the Mass are likewise to receive two denarii. Moreover, before the magistracy we decree that, for eight days before the aforesaid solemnity and eight days afterward, peace and truce shall be firmly maintained throughout our county, so that all who wish to come to this solemnity may assemble safely from every direction and without molestation.

Whoever, detained by any impediment, cannot come to that sepulchre in which Christ’s body slept, but comes with sound mind and good intention to this sepulchre made in its true likeness, shall have remission of a third part of his sins, and shall know that he has done this to the praise of the Jerusalem Sepulchre.

[Col. 1662B] And if anyone inflicts any molestation upon a person coming to this observance of ours, let him lie stricken by the sword of anathema until he resorts to that same church to make amends for it. It is also established and approved by our common ordinance that there shall be there an annual market, abundant and with every kind of thing for sale. No one may presume to seek a curatorship from it; no one may dare to hold more than one stand in it; nor may they give to anyone, or sell as private property, what is common to all, or in any way call it their own right. But as the solemnity is common for the benefit of all souls, so the market shall be common for the sale of all bodily goods.

[Col. 1662C] Furthermore, moved by the prayers of Ilderatus and Deibertus, devout priests of this church, who said that they had possessed the parish long before, and having taken counsel with the cardinals of our brethren of the Major Church and with other wise men of this city, we grant, give, and confirm that the aforesaid priests of the church of the Holy Sepulchre and their successors shall henceforth hold and possess the aforesaid parish: namely, the houses of Nigro Martha and of Lanfrancus Litta, and from there all the houses as far as the house of Anselmus Mugetus; on the other side of the street, the houses of Ambrosius de la Carzere, and from there all the houses as far as the house of Romedius the chancellor, including that house; and on the other side, the houses of Rozonus, Albericus, and Arnaldus Farolus, and from there all the houses as far as the houses of Benzo Amblator and his brother Vatfredus, the houses of Lanfrancus and Marchisius Amblatores, and from there all the houses as far as the houses of Otto de Samblatore and Gratianus Canton, including the houses of Dionysius Dodo, Petrus Butellus, Petrus Gualasecca, and Lanterius Patella; on the other side of the church, the houses of Homobonus de Calagana, Petrus Patricius and his brothers Rolandus and Albertus, Lanzo Cioglia, Petrus Vexa, Albertus Buntarus, Petrus Samaruga, Guiredus Bionoldus, Landulfus Clericus, and Joannes Spata in Zotta.

[Col. 1663A] This was enacted with the testimony and confirmation of all the Milanese, in the year one thousand one hundred from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the eighth indiction, on the Ides of July.

I, Anselmus the fourth, archbishop by the grace of God, confirmed and subscribed. I, Grosolanus, unworthy bishop, approved and subscribed. I, Andreas, priest and primicerius, approved and subscribed. I, Landulfus, by the grace of God, though unworthy provost of the Nazarene church, approved and subscribed. I, Landulfus, notary, also called provost, approved and subscribed. ## III. Privilege for the church of Saint Mary of Calvenzano with its appurtenances

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, ed. Mansi, III, 6.]

In the name of the Son of God, who is supreme truth, ANSELMUS, by the mercy of God alone archbishop of the Church of Milan.

It is fitting for our Christian governance, through devout religion and benevolent compassion, to grant with eager mind the assent requested by those who petition us. Therefore it belongs to our authority to love all the children of our Church with paternal affection and not to deny the assistance of the piety they desire. For by this we chiefly earn a reward of profit before God, the creator of all.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all our faithful, present and future, that we, while deliberating in our Milanese church with our cardinals concerning the salvation of our souls, at the petition of our faithful Arialdus and Lanfrancus, brothers, and Alonus, their kinsman, of Meregnano, have granted to the holy Church of Cluny the church of Saint Mary at Calvenzano, which they had held from our church for a long time, together with the land and the tithes of their own estates—namely, those of Arialdus and Lanfrancus—which they have now granted, and with all the property it now possesses or may acquire forever.

Moreover, we desire and decree that if any of their heirs, or any other person, should wish to grant to the aforesaid church, under the inspiration of him who breathes where he wills, either the churches built or to be built upon their estate, or their tithes, let him grant them with God’s blessing and by this our concession. The order shall be that from now on our aforesaid church of Calvenzano, freely and without payment or condition, shall serve the Cluniac monastery, and shall not in any way be subject to the authority of any other church throughout the endless ages.

But if any of our successors, or any person of high or low rank, should oppose this most salutary concession of ours, let him be anathema *maranatha*; let him have no part with him who was crucified for us on Golgotha, until, coming to his senses, he has made satisfaction and undertaken fitting penance, and has satisfied the abbot of the holy Cluniac church and the monks who shall be there at the time.

So that this may be believed more truly and firmly, and may be held perpetual, secure, and unshaken by our descendants, we have confirmed this present document as testimony with our own hand, and have ordered it to be marked with the seal of our chancellor Heriprandus, as is customary.

[Col. 1664D] + I, Anselm, archbishop by the grace of God, have subscribed in confirmation. Gothefridus, archpriest, have subscribed. Ato, archdeacon, have subscribed. Arnulfus, deacon, have subscribed. Bonifatius, priest, have subscribed. Tedaldus, deacon, have subscribed. Albertus, priest, have subscribed. Rozo, deacon, have subscribed. Landulphus, priest, have subscribed. Odelricus, priest, have subscribed. Landulphus, deacon, have subscribed. Gualbertus, deacon, have subscribed. Ariprandus, chancellor of the holy Milanese Church.

## ADDENDA

After the historical notice above, cols. 1299–1300.

The first volume of Radulphus’s *Homilies*, which, although sought everywhere, had hitherto escaped us, was about to be bound with the volume when, unexpectedly, this earlier work of Ardens came into our hands, destined to bring to completion the final quires where our volume had been lingering for two years.

[Col. 1665]

## HOMILIES ON THE SUNDAY EPISTLES AND GOSPELS

By Radulphus Ardens of Poitiers, an extremely ancient doctor of theology and most eloquent preacher of William, the fourth of that name, the illustrious duke of Aquitaine; exceedingly necessary for all ecclesiastical persons entrusted with the care of souls, written by the author nearly five hundred years ago and now published for the first time.

(Paris, at the shop of Claudius Fremy, Jacobaea Street, at the sign of Saint Martin.—1564, in twelves.)

## DEDICATORY EPISTLE

To the Reverend Father Joannes Coqueius, abbot of Morimond and doctor of theology in Paris, Claudius Fremy wishes health and peace through Christ.

You know well, most prudent abbot, how great in these corrupt times is the itch of those who must write, and how great is the luxury and affectation of writing.
