I therefore judge that those earn greater merit for our Christian religion who transcribe books of the ancient Fathers, inspired by the divine Spirit but consumed by decay and age, cleanse them, polish them, restore them to their original purity, and arrange for their publication, than those who, seized by the spirit of self-love, thrust upon us, not without great loss to our people, their frivolous, empty, and sometimes harmful trifles and questions—which generate disputes—while presenting nothing except what the ancients had already said, merely with a swollen freedom of language and without any weight of meaning.

Accordingly, since I had undertaken to cleanse many books of the ancients of bookworms and moths, and had especially learned that these homilies of the most learned Radulphus Ardens, delivered among his own people five hundred years ago, had been approved by the judgments of not a few learned and devout men, I applied all my labor and diligence to transcribing them and committing them to the press.

For they contain instruction on how one ought to accustom oneself to justice. Our Ardens teaches that each person must be given his due: religion to God; purity to ourselves; honor to parents; care to members of the household; obedience to superiors; governance to inferiors; companionship to equals; love to the good; correction to the wicked; mercy to the oppressed; and equity to all.

Finally, these homilies instruct us how love of neighbor is to be preserved. This love, to use the words of our Ardens, makes God favorable to us, makes our neighbors benevolent, reconciles enemies, overcomes the devil, knows no evil, bears adversity with equanimity, wisely moderates prosperity, shares everything, and never fails.

Reflecting on this with myself, I gladly arranged for them to be published, both so that the Christian and Catholic people might remain in that unity, charity, and love which they received from the ancient Fathers, and so that, through the writings of such an author, the plagues of sectarianism and division in our age, which daily grow and multiply, might be torn out by the roots.

I have resolved to entrust them to you, who love antiquity and piety above all, so that you may undertake their defense. If you do so, you will soon receive the remaining works of that Ardens. May almighty God preserve you, glory of abbots, safe and sound for a long time in the service of his holy Church. Farewell. Paris, the Nones of May, 1564.

## EXCERPTS FROM THE AUTHOR’S LIFE, TAKEN FROM HIS OWN BOOKS

[Col. 1667]

Radulphus Ardens, a native of Poitiers, from a village commonly called Beaulieu, in the territory of the Berchorati [reading uncertain], whom Pliny mentions in book IV, chapter 19, was born of distinguished and very noble parents. From childhood onward he devoted himself to books. In them, being of ardent intellect, he made such progress that before reaching his thirtieth year he attained the degree of doctor of theology.

He was ready in teaching in the schools and assiduous in addressing the people in churches, especially in the church over which he presided. Thus he became more famous and was carried off by William IV, duke of Aquitaine, to his court—as he writes of himself in the prologue—and composed these homilies amid warfare, while serving the prince as counselor and preacher. He wrote in a language both sweet and eloquent:

Two books of *Homilies on the Temporal and Saints’ Feasts*.

Also a large work entitled *The Mirror of Ardens*, divided into fourteen books [Note: [Col. 1667] See the literary notice on Radulphus above, col. 1299.] It is held at Bourges in the library of the Franciscans and has not yet been printed.

Also two books of letters.

Also a history of his own time, namely, the war of Godfrey of Bouillon against the Saracens, in which he took part as a follower of the duke of Aquitaine.

He wrote many other works, as he himself testifies concerning himself in his *Mirror*. He flourished around the time of Philip I, king of the Franks, from the year of the Lord 1040 until 1100.

# PART ONE

## FIRST HOMILY. FIRST SUNDAY OF ADVENT

[Col. 1667A]

“It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Romans 13), and so forth.

By these words, dearest brothers, the Apostle urges us to prepare for the second coming of the Son of God. For there are two visible comings of Christ: the first has passed, the second is to come. The first was in humility; the second will be in majesty. The first was hidden; the second will be manifest. The first was a coming of mercy; the second will be one of justice. In the first he came to be judged; in the second he will come to judge. In the first he came to call sinners through mercy; in the second he will come to repay each person according to what he has deserved, through justice.

The Apostle therefore urges us to await this coming watchfully in the following manner. First, he warns us to rise from sleep. Second, he adds the reason why we must rise quickly. Third, he shows how we are to rise from this sleep.

Warning us to rise, he says: “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep.” Here, brothers, we must consider what this sleep is and what the hour of rising may be.

There are three kinds of sleep: the first is natural sleep, the second is the sleep of death, and the third is the sleep of sin. Of the first the poet says:

> “That which lacks alternating rest does not endure.”  
> (Ovid, *Heroides*, epistle 4, verse 89.)

Of the second the Apostle says: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the others who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4), calling the dead “those who sleep,” because our bodies do not perish for God through dying but are changed for the better. For just as it is easy for someone to awaken a sleeping person, so it is easy—indeed easier—for God to awaken the dead.

Therefore the Lord himself says: “Lazarus our friend sleeps, but I am going to awaken him from sleep” (John 11).

Of the third it is written: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Ephesians 5). It calls those who persist in mortal sins both sleepers and dead, appropriately, because the one who does not perceive how badly he sleeps sleeps soundly. For just as a sleeping person, with closed eyes, does not guard against harm being done to him, so the person sleeping in sins, with the eyes of reason closed, does not guard himself against the Gehenna being prepared for him.

The Apostle therefore urges us to rise from this sleep of sin, saying: “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep.”

Moreover, there is an opportune hour, a late hour, and an unfruitful hour. The opportune hour is while we are alive, while we are well, while we are able to sin: then let us cease from sinning. Hence the Apostle says: “Let us do good, brothers, while we have the opportunity” (Galatians 6).

The late hour is the hour of death. Hence Augustine says: “Do penance while you are healthy and secure, because you did penance while you were able to sin; but if you wish to do penance when you can no longer sin, your sins have left you, not you them.”

Nevertheless, brothers, it is not denied here that at the end a person who has had true contrition may obtain mercy, since it is written: “Penance, however late, is not unfruitful,” and: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall live” (Ezekiel 18).

But because true contrition is scarcely or rarely granted at the end, one person is overtaken by death because of his sins, another loses his memory through the severity of illness, another loses his speech, and another is more grieved to leave the temporal things he loved excessively than for the sins he committed. Thus it happens that few truly repent at the end.

Even if someone does truly repent, he must nevertheless pass through the fire of purgatory, which exceeds every severity that can be felt here.

The unfruitful hour is repentance after death. The damned will repent in hell—indeed, they will repent greatly—but that repentance will not bring them the remedy of pardon; it will increase their punishment. For those who repent will weep and say:

> “When it was permitted, I lacked the will to work. Now the will is granted, but the ability is taken away.”

Therefore, brothers, while it is permitted, let us repent and do good while it is day, because night is coming, when no one can work (John 9). Then the time will be not for sowing but for harvesting.

The second part follows, in which the Apostle shows the reason why we ought to rise quickly from the sleep of sin, saying: “For now our salvation is nearer than when we believed,” that is, than when we were called to the faith.

It is as though he said: “Quickly, brothers, we must rise from the sleep of sin, because the time of our salvation is already at hand.”

The time of our salvation, brothers, is either the day of each person’s death, on which the soul is clothed in the robe of incorruption, or the day of judgment, on which the body, together with the soul, will rejoice in the robe of immortality. This day is already near. Even if the day of judgment seems more remote to some, nevertheless the day of each person’s death approaches more closely. At whatever moment someone departs from the world, at that moment he is judged by the Lord.

Hence Solomon says: “Wherever the wood falls, whether toward the south or toward the north, there it will remain” (Ecclesiastes 11).

Therefore let us rise, brothers; let us rise from the dregs of our sins while we can, because the time will soon be present when we will no longer be able.

Let no one put confidence in his youth, because according to the Gospel God calls some in the first watch, that is, in childhood; others in the second watch, that is, in youth; others in the third watch, that is, in mature manhood; and others in the fourth, that is, in old age.

Let no one say: “When I am old, I shall do penance.” For who has given you so much time to live? Children die every day; and if you cannot continue to live, this is your old age.

Alas, how many are overtaken by sudden death! Someone who was just now healthy is found cold in bed. For this reason, brothers, God wished us to be ignorant of the limit of our death, so that we might always fear, always expect death, and prepare ourselves to receive it.

Turn, therefore, brothers; turn while it is permitted. For those who delay these things meet one of two fates: they are overtaken by death, or they are hindered by desire. They are overtaken by death who die unexpectedly, without a will and without correction; they are hindered by desire who, impeded by the habit of their desires, are not corrected even in old age.

Let us therefore prepare, brothers, for death before it comes, and let us conquer desire before it hardens into habit. Let us keep watch, because we do not know the day or the hour (Matthew 25), because the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night (1 Thessalonians 5).

The Apostle adds another reason why we must rise, saying: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near.” Here, brothers, he calls the darkness that preceded the coming of Christ—the darkness of ignorance or sin—“night”; and he calls the time of grace, in which the marriage of Christ and the Church begins to be celebrated, “day.”

Therefore, brothers, so that we may be in harmony and of one color with the time of grace and of the wedding, let us rise from the darkness of sins. Hence he adds:

[Col. 1670B] “Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness.”

This is the third part, in which the Apostle shows how one is to rise from the sleep of sins. This is done through penance: namely, by turning away from evil and doing good, fleeing vices and following virtues.

Therefore, brothers, according to the Apostle’s command, let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the weapons of light.

Sins are called works of darkness for three reasons. First, because the person who acts wickedly naturally hates the light. Hence the first man, after sinning, hid himself under a fig tree. Second, because sins blind the mind inwardly. Thus the Lord says: “Whoever walks in darkness does not know where he is going” (John 12). Third, because they drag us toward outward darkness, that is, toward hell.

Conversely, good works are called weapons of light: weapons, because by them we repel and conquer the devil; and of light, because the person who acts well has no need to hide himself. Even if he sometimes hides himself out of humility, if he is found engaged in good work he has no reason to be ashamed; they are also of light because they illuminate the mind and lead us to everlasting light.

Let us therefore, brothers, put on these weapons of light, and let us walk honorably as in the day, so that at the wedding of Christ we may present ourselves in wedding garments.

The Apostle enumerates the works of darkness, saying: “Not in revelries and drunkenness, not in bedrooms and wantonness, not in strife and jealousy.”

A revelry is excessive, frequent, and luxurious feasting, observing no moderation in measure, time, or manner. This was the reason the Sodomites fell into the luxury of abomination. This made the Israelites despise manna and demand flesh to their own harm. Hence it is written: “While their food was still in their mouths, the anger of God descended upon them” (Psalm 77).

Drunkenness is an alienation of the mind arising from immoderate drinking. It stripped Noah of his manly covering (Genesis 9); it mingled Lot with his daughters (Genesis 19). It alienates a person from himself, deprives him of the use of his limbs, and plunges him into many crimes.

By “bedrooms” we understand here drowsiness and lethargy, which soften and enervate a person and plunge him into empty and wicked desires, according to the saying of the Wise Man: “Every idle person is in desires” (Proverbs 21). For where there is sloth, there are empty desires.

Certainly food, drink, and sleep should be taken with moderation, like medicines, in the proper place, time, manner, and measure; taken in this way they help, but otherwise they harm.

By wantonness we understand here every form of lust that occurs outside a lawful union, such as fornication, adultery, sexual immorality, incest, and Sodomitic lust. Even excessive sexual desire in the use of one’s own wife is blameworthy.

These four bodily vices we have mentioned harm in three ways: they condemn the soul, generate illnesses in the body, and squander inherited possessions.

Strife is an assault upon the truth through the confidence of shouting. But, as the Apostle says elsewhere: “The servant of God must not quarrel” (2 Timothy 2). If the matter does not concern you, yield to the one who is contending. If it does concern you, act reasonably and flee strife.

Jealousy is a perversity of mind that grieves at another’s good and rejoices at another’s harm. This, brothers, must be avoided by us all the more because it is opposed to charity, which knows how to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep (Romans 12).

There is, however, a certain good jealousy: namely, imitating another’s good through imitation. Hence the Apostle says: “Be zealous for the better spiritual gifts” (1 Corinthians 12).

After ordering that vices be removed from the body, the mouth, and the mind, the Apostle commands us to put on virtues opposed to the vices mentioned, saying: “But put on the Lord Jesus Christ”—that is, his newness, by imitating him.

Therefore, brothers, while it is permitted, let us cast off vices with all speed and put on the virtues opposed to them. Let us pursue abstinence, sobriety and watchfulness, chastity, peace, and charity, so that, adorned with these things, we may safely meet Christ as he comes to the wedding and may be able to reign with him forever, by the gift of him whose Advent we celebrate today, our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God. Amen.

## HOMILY II. FIRST SUNDAY OF ADVENT

“Beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet” (Mark 1), and the rest.

As you have heard, dearest brothers, the evangelist Mark begins his Gospel with the forecoming of John. And he immediately gives the reason for doing this at the beginning when he says: “Beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ,” and so forth.

He does three things. First, he says that the sending of John ahead is the beginning of the Gospel. Second, he proves the same by prophetic authority. Third, he shows how John prepared the way for Christ.

Beginning, therefore, he says: “Beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ,” with the implied meaning: this is the beginning, namely, that John was sent ahead before Christ.

Here, brothers, three things must be considered: what the Gospel is; why it is called the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God; and how it had its beginning from John.

The Gospel is therefore good news concerning faith and conduct leading to salvation. This definition shows where the word “Gospel” comes from, what it concerns, and toward what end it leads.

Its origin is shown through the etymology of the name. For *Evangelium* is interpreted as “good announcement,” from *eu* (εὖ), which means “good,” and *angelos* (ἄγγελος), which means “messenger” or “one who announces.”

What it concerns is shown when it is added: “concerning faith and conduct.” For the Gospel concerns faith in the triune and one God, the mystery of the Son’s Incarnation, and the other articles of faith contained in the Creed. It also concerns conduct, that is, the doctrine of living rightly.

The end toward which it leads us is declared when it is said: “to salvation.” For through true faith and a good life it leads us to eternal salvation.

For, brothers, faith without good conduct is not enough, nor is good conduct without faith. The devil has faith, but he does not have good conduct. A pagan or a Jew may have good conduct, but does not have faith; and thus each is rejected. But if someone has faith and good conduct, without doubt he is advancing toward salvation.

And what announcement, my brothers, can be better than announcing those things through which everlasting salvation is obtained?

Therefore, brothers, let us always receive the Gospel with our ears, hold it in our hearts, proclaim it with our mouths, and fulfill it in our works. For what is more insane than, after despising the word of life, opening one’s ears to fables, buffoonery, and slander? What is more insane than, after despising the Gospel, reading and teaching pastoral songs, comedies, and other vanities?

To such people Truth says: “Whoever is of God hears the words of God; therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John 8).

And why is it called the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God? Because, although there are several writers of the Gospel, the Gospel belongs to Christ alone, as its author, subject, and promulgator. From him, concerning him, and through him we have the Gospel.

Hence Paul boasts that he received the Gospel “not from a human being, nor through a human being, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (Galatians 1).

Here, brothers, the preeminence of the Gospel over all teachings is demonstrated. It is exalted not only by its own honesty and usefulness, but also commended by the dignity of its author, subject, and promulgator—namely, Jesus Christ, the Son of God.

John was the first to begin preaching the Gospel, because he openly preached the ministry of the Trinity and the Incarnation, which had previously been veiled. He both pointed out the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world (John 1) and understood the Father in the voice and the Spirit in the dove above the baptized Christ (Matthew 3).

He also preached repentance and the kingdom of heaven, things unheard of among the ancients. “Repent,” he said, “for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (ibid.).

The second part follows, in which the Evangelist proves by the testimony of the prophet that John’s forerunning is the beginning of the Gospel, in accordance with what the Lord says in the Gospel: “The Law and the Prophets were until John” (Matt. 11), as though he were saying: “The Gospel begins with John.” This, therefore, is what the prophet says, speaking in the person of the Father to the Son: “Behold, I send my angel before your face,” that is, before your presence or awareness.

An angel, that is, a messenger, does three things: he precedes the Lord’s coming; he bears not his own authority but the Lord’s; and he prepares lodging and seeks honor not for himself but for the Lord. Thus John preceded Christ’s coming as his forerunner, in accordance with what the angel had foretold about him: “He will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1). He proclaimed not his own authority but Christ’s. “I am not,” he says, “the Christ; I am not the bridegroom, but the friend of the bridegroom.” He prepared the way and lodging not for himself but for the Lord. Hence it follows: “Who prepared your way before you.”

For John prepared the way for Christ by preaching, baptizing, and pointing him out. Not only John, but also every preacher and every believer who announces the word of life to sinners may be called an angel of God, insofar as he prepares for God a way and lodging in human hearts. Hence Malachi says: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they will seek the law from his mouth; for he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2).

Therefore, brothers, let us who know the law of God not cease to announce it to others, and let us prepare for him a way to human hearts. Let us seek his honor in all things, not our own, so that we may deserve to be worthy of the office and name of angels. The Psalmist urges us to this, saying: “Make a way for him who ascends above the setting sun; the Lord is his name” (Ps. 67). The Lord ascended above the setting sun when, by rising again, he overcame death. We make a way for him when we announce his word to others. For when preaching resounds in the ear, the Lord comes into the mind.

Hence it also follows: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness.” A voice has three characteristics: it precedes the word, signifies the word, and quickly passes away, while the word remains in the heart. Thus, brothers, John was the voice of one crying. He went before the word of God and signified it by preaching and pointing it out. His preaching and reputation quickly passed away, while the word of God remains forever.

He cried out in the wilderness of Judea—that is, in a land already deserted of every good thing, in which not the seeds of virtues but the thorns of vices were growing, and where monsters of crime, not the image of God, dwelt. But not only John: we too, brothers, are the voice of one crying if we rebuke sinners in the wilderness of this world, if we terrify them with the threat of Gehenna, and if we sow the word of God in their hearts by word and example.

What did he cry? “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.” There is one great way along which many travel. There are many paths, narrow and direct. The way, therefore, is the Christian religion, by which many go to God and God comes to many. The paths are the direct and narrow ways of life, such as the eremitical, monastic, and enclosed life.

Both, brothers, must be prepared so that they possess four qualities: direction, evenness, straightness, and levelness.

Direction means that the end should lead to Christ, who is “the end unto righteousness for everyone who believes.” For unless it leads to Christ, it is not a way but a trackless place. Therefore the prophet says: “Make his paths straight.”

Evenness means that the way should not rise through the mountains of pride or plunge through the valleys of despair. For this reason the prophet adds: “Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low” (Isa. 40), so that an even course may be maintained between presumption and despair.

Straightness means that the paths should incline neither to the right nor to the left, but should keep to the middle. They should maintain the straightness of justice without turning to the right toward excessive laxity or to the left toward cruelty. They should maintain fortitude without turning toward rashness or cowardice. They should maintain wisdom without turning toward cunning or simplicity. They should maintain temperance without turning toward excess or deficiency. They should maintain generosity without turning toward prodigality or avarice. They should chastise the body without allowing it either to become wanton or to fail.

What more need be said? They should hold to the virtues in such a way as to avoid the vices that lie alongside them. Therefore Isaiah adds: “And the crooked places shall become straight” (ibid.), so that, once distortions have been removed, only straightness may be maintained.

Levelness means that the path should contain neither the swamps of pleasures and lusts nor the stumbling-blocks of worldly anxieties. For what, my brothers, are pleasures and lusts except certain swamps that stain and delay the soul? And what are the anxieties of this world except certain obstacles that cause the soul either to fall or to be delayed? Therefore the prophet says: “And the rough places shall become level ways” (ibid.).

The third part follows, in which the Evangelist shows how, according to the testimony of Isaiah mentioned above, John prepared the way for Christ, saying: “John was in the wilderness, preaching and baptizing with the baptism [Note: [Col. 1673D] The Vulgate has only ‘preaching baptism.’] of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.”

John, in the manner of a good preacher, prepared the way for Christ not only by word but also by example—and first in himself, then in others. In himself he prepared the way for Christ; hence the Evangelist describes his holiness: “John was,” he says, “in the wilderness.” In others he prepared the way for Christ; hence it is also reported that many flocked to him, when it is said: “And all the region of Judea was going out to him,” and so forth.

Thus the shining lamp went before Christ, preaching what Christ himself was going to preach. Christ was indeed going to preach repentance, baptism, the twofold nature of himself, moral teaching, his second coming, the glory of the righteous, and the punishment of the reprobate. The forerunner announced all these things beforehand.

He preached repentance not only by saying, “Produce fruits worthy of repentance,” but also demonstrated it by his own example in the austerity of his place, clothing, and food. His place: he lived alone in the wilderness, a place suitable for penitents, both lest association with worldly people cause them to fall back into their former sins—hence David says: “Behold, I have gone far away, fleeing, and I remained in solitude” (Ps. 54)—and because, by a bad example, they had corrupted [others] and made themselves unworthy of human society, just as Cain is reported to have been a fugitive after the murder of his brother (Gen. 4).

His clothing: he was clothed in a coarse garment of camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist. The hairs of camels and sackcloth are signs of repentance, both because of their roughness and prickliness, and because they signify the garments of skins with which our first parents were clothed after being expelled from paradise (Gen. 3). The leather belt is a sign of repentance, both because of its hardness and roughness, and because it signifies the restraint of lust.

His food: he ate wild honey and locusts. Coarse, raw, and unprepared food is fitting for penitents, who have often sinned through gluttony. If, therefore, brothers, John, sanctified from the womb, chastised himself with such austerity, what ought we miserable sinners to do?

He also preached baptism and administered it to many—not because he forgave sins, but because he urged people to repentance and accustomed them to baptism. He preached Christ’s twofold nature and also pointed him out: “Behold,” he says, “the Lamb of God,” and “he who comes after me was made before me” (John 1).

He also instructed them morally, saying: “Let the one who has two tunics give to the one who has none. And let the one who has food do likewise” (Luke 3).

He preached the second coming, saying: “The axe is already laid at the root of the trees” (ibid.).

He preached the glorification of the righteous and the condemnation of the reprobate, saying: “His winnowing fan is in his hand, and he has cleansed his threshing floor. He will gather the grain into his barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire” (ibid.).

By the grain, brothers, the good are signified, because by their union they form the body of Christ, that is, the Church; because God is nourished and delighted by them; and because they are worthy to be preserved. By the chaff the wicked are represented, because they are light in the wind of vanity and pride, because they are dry, without the dew of grace, and because they are fit only for flame.

Yet both, just as chaff and grain grow from the same seed, grow together, are gathered together, and are tossed together. Nevertheless, on the threshing floor—that is, in the judgment—they will be separated by the winnowing fan of the supreme Judge. The former will go into Gehenna, the latter into eternal life. May our Lord graciously unite us with them, both in merit and in reward. Amen.

# HOMILY III. SECOND SUNDAY OF ADVENT

“Whatever was written was written for our instruction” (Rom. 15), and so forth.

In this Lesson, dearest brothers, the Apostle exhorts us to three things: to have hope in adversity, unanimity in confessing the faith, and charitable acceptance of our neighbors. He therefore admonishes us by the authority of sacred Scripture to have hope in adversity, saying: “Whatever was written was written for our instruction.”

But you may say: How do David’s adultery, Saul’s pride, Solomon’s effeminacy, and the other evils that we read in Scripture pertain to our instruction? They do pertain, my brothers, if we consider the intention of the writer. Four kinds of things are written in sacred Scripture with different purposes: evils, goods, punishments, and rewards. Evils are written so that we may avoid them; goods, so that we may imitate them; punishments, so that we may be deterred; rewards, so that we may imitate them. Thus David’s adultery and the other sins are written so that we may avoid them. And if it should happen that we fall into such things, let us not despair, but, following David’s example, let us have recourse to the remedy of repentance.

How do the things that were written serve our instruction? “So that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures”—that is, of the things read in Scripture—“we might have hope.” He might similarly have said: so that through the threats of Scripture we might have fear. For just as sacred Scripture promises hope to those who grieve, so it offers fear to those who rejoice vainly.

If, therefore, you grieve in adversity, do not despair, but read how much patience Job had in adversity and how much consolation the Lord gave him; and you will have hope that, through similar patience, you may come to similar consolation. If you rejoice in prosperity, do not presume, but read how much prosperity Solomon had and into how great a disgrace he consequently fell; and you will have fear that, through similar prosperity, you may come to similar disgrace.

But because the Apostle was speaking to afflicted brothers, he mentions only patience and hope. Yet because hope alone is not sufficient for salvation, the second part follows, in which he prays that the God of consolation may grant them unanimity in confessing the faith, saying: “May the God of consolation grant you to have the same mind.”

But because some have a bad understanding, while others have a higher opinion than is fitting, he adds: “according to Jesus Christ.” But because certain heretics and schismatics, claiming to have the mind according to Jesus Christ, divide the faith of Christ, he adds: “the same thing,” that is, one and the same thing. But because some again have a good understanding yet refuse to instruct the inexperienced and those who are in error, he adds: “toward one another.”

For it is not enough for us to have a good understanding for ourselves unless we also understand good things rightly for the sake of others. Whoever hides the talent of wisdom is condemned according to the Gospel parable (Matt. 25). Hence it is also written: “Do not withhold the word in a time of salvation” (Ecclus. 4). And again: “Whoever hides grain will be cursed among the peoples” (Prov. 11).

Therefore, brothers, let the one who understands well understand well for others; let the one who knows how to correct correct the person in error; let the one who knows how to give good counsel give counsel to the uninstructed. For if you see people in error and remain silent, you are guilty of as many souls as you could have freed from error.

And what benefit is it for us to have the mind according to Jesus Christ, “the same thing toward one another”? “So that,” he says, “with one mind and one mouth you may honor God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Just as, brothers, it is not enough for us to confess God with one mouth unless we also confess him with one heart, so it is not enough to confess him with one heart unless we also confess him with one mouth—especially when the faith is endangered.

For if confession by the mouth alone were sufficient, the Lord would not say through the prophet: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29; Mark 7). If, on the other hand, confession of the heart alone were sufficient without confession by the mouth, the Lord would not say: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his majesty” (Luke 9). Thus confession both of mouth and of mind is necessary. As the Apostle says elsewhere: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10).

But because confession of heart and mouth is not sufficient for one who has the opportunity to act well without good works, it is said: “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2).

The third part follows, in which the Apostle adds the practice of charity, saying: “Therefore, so that you may honor God perfectly, receive one another, just as Christ also received you.”

To receive is to take hold of one who is failing so that he does not fall beneath. The Apostle therefore urges us, dearest brothers, that the strong should receive the weak through charity, the wise the beginner, the rich the needy, the healthy the sick, and the one who is standing the one who is falling.

Although God could have made everyone strong, wise, and rich, he did not wish to do so. Instead, he wished some to be strong and others weak, some wise and others foolish, some rich and others poor. For if everyone were strong, wise, and rich, no one would need anyone else. Conversely, if everyone were weak, foolish, and poor, no one would help anyone else.

He therefore wished some to be strong, wise, or rich so that they might save their souls by assisting others through charity. He wished others to be weak, foolish, or needy so that they might save their souls by enduring adversity with patience. Hence the Lord says: “You always have the poor with you, and whenever you wish, you can do good to them” (Mark 14).

Since, therefore, the needy remain beside the prosperous, they are for the latter either an occasion of good works or of condemnation. The Apostle shows that we ought to receive one another in this way by the example of Christ, who in his own person received not only our cause but also our nature.

Although he was wise—indeed, Wisdom itself—he received our foolishness. Although he was rich in all things, he received our poverty. He showed this way of charity in himself so that we might follow him along it. And he did this for the honor of God, so that, just as Christ sought the glory of the Father in all things and not his own, so we too might seek the glory of God in all things and not our own.

He received weakness not only in the form of circumcision—that is, of the Jews, to whom he was sent according to the promises of the prophets—but also in the form of the Gentiles, to whom he had not been promised. Therefore both groups ought to honor and glorify God: the Jews for the fulfillment of the promise, and the Gentiles for the bestowal of unexpected grace.

He proves this by the testimonies of the prophets, saying: “As it is written.” “For this reason,” the Son says to the Father, “I will confess you among the Gentiles, and I will sing to your name.” And again: “Rejoice, Gentiles, with his people,” that is, Gentiles together with Jews; and: “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles,” and so forth.

Just as Christ received not only the neighboring Jews but also the distant Gentiles, so we too, brothers, should receive not only those who are near to us by kinship or friendship, but also those who are distant and strangers. For God did not entrust his goods to us for our sake alone, but for the sake of the poor. Nor did he make us masters, but stewards, commanding us to provide, from his possessions, for his needy children.

Whoever retains the possessions of God and allows the children of God to perish in poverty—what, my brothers, what will he hear from the supreme Judge except that terrible voice: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25)? And why? “For I was hungry, and you did not give me food from my provisions; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink from my drink; I was a stranger, and you were unwilling to receive me into my lodging; I was naked, and you did not cover me with my clothing” (ibid.).

Let us therefore, brothers, think on these things, hold them in our hearts, and from the possessions entrusted to us by God let us feed him in the poor, clothe him, and receive him, so that we may deserve to receive eternal blessing from him. Amen.

# HOMILY IV. SECOND SUNDAY OF ADVENT

“There will be signs in the sun, the moon, and the stars, and on earth distress among nations because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves” (Luke 21), and so forth.

Our pious and merciful Lord and Redeemer, wishing his elect to be prepared in every way for his second coming, forewarns them in this Lesson. In what way? In three ways: so that their foreknowledge might give them certainty, vigilance, and consolation.

Certainty: so that they might await his coming more confidently than the permanence of heaven and earth. Hence he adds afterward: “Truly I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place; heaven and earth will pass away”—that is, they will be changed into another state—“but my words will not pass away,” without all these things being fulfilled in deed.

Vigilance: because things that are foreseen do less harm than things that are not foreseen. Hence he himself says: “Watch, because you do not know the day or the hour” (Matt. 25).

Consolation: so that, amid the miseries of this age, they might draw consolation from the certainty of his coming. Hence he adds afterward: “When you see these things happening, raise your heads, because your redemption is near.” For how sweet, my brothers, in a land of misery is the remembrance of one’s homeland!

First, therefore, the Lord sets forth the signs that announce his coming; second, he shows how he will come; third, what good will come to the good; fourth, he explains the sayings by means of a comparison.

He says, therefore: “There will be signs in the sun and moon.” Just as the Lord previously foretold the signs of his coming so that they might serve as consolation to his own, who mourn in this world, so they might serve as confusion to the reprobate, who are comforted here. Hence he adds afterward: “People will faint from fear and expectation of what will come upon the whole world.”

Because the wicked abused all the elements, they will be punished by all of them, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “The whole world will fight on behalf of him against the senseless” (Wis. 5).

Because they abused the brightness of the sun, moon, and stars, using them to see what they desired and what evil they might do, the sun will be turned into darkness for them, the moon into blood, and the stars will fall from heaven.

Because they abused temporal peace through foolish security, there will be distress among the nations. Because they abused the calm of the sea for plundering and robbery, there will be confusion of the sea and the waves.

For, as Jerome reports in his catalogue of fifteen signs, which he translated from Hebrew: “On the first day the sea will rise forty cubits above the highest mountains, like a wall; on the second it will sink so far that it can scarcely be seen.”

Again, because they abused the goods of the earth through excess, there will be for them, as the same Evangelist says above, earthquakes and famine. Because they abused the serenity of the air for empty pleasure, there will be terrors from heaven and storms. Because they abused the health of their bodies by living viciously, there will be pestilences for them—that is, disorders and sufferings of the body.

Some of these signs, brothers, we already see. Distress among the nations occurs daily; earthquakes in many places destroy cities; storms terrify us daily; pestilences empty cities of their inhabitants. The fulfillment of these signs assures us of the fulfillment of the others.

Behold, brothers: so many ruins of the world already announce that its end is near. Why, then, do we love it? Why do we fall with what is falling and perish with what is perishing? If our house threatens to collapse, we flee and save whatever we can of our possessions. Behold, the world is falling; why, then, do we not leave it with desire? Why do we not save whatever we can from its shipwreck?

Let us therefore save ourselves and our possessions, brothers, while it is permitted. Let us pass over in desire to heavenly things; let us transfer our possessions, through the hands of the poor and afflicted, to the heavenly treasures.

It follows: “People will faint from fear and expectation of what will come upon the whole world.” Some of the wicked will faint and fear when the judgment is already imminent, but in vain, since they will no longer be able to amend their lives. Let us therefore, brothers, while we can be corrected and cleansed, faint away from love of the world, fear the future, and, fearing, take care.

“For the powers of heaven will be shaken,” he says. Why? Not because they fear for themselves, but because they will shudder at the severity of the Judge. Brothers, if angels will fear, if, as Job says, the pillars of heaven will tremble (Job 26), what will sinners do? But if, as Peter says, the righteous will scarcely be saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear? (1 Pet. 4.)

The second part follows, in which the Lord shows how he will come to judgment, saying: “And then they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven, with great power and majesty.”

And who will see him? Everyone, both good and evil. Hence John says: “Behold, he comes with the clouds of heaven, and every eye will see him” (Rev. 1).

For he will not come hidden, humble, and meek, as at first, but rather open, exalted, and terrifying, as he himself testifies concerning himself: “As lightning comes out from the east and appears even to the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matt. 24).

Whom will they see? The Son of Man. For then only the Son will appear as judge—he who was first unjustly judged—in accordance with the saying: “They will see the one whom they pierced” (Rev. 1). The Jews and Gentiles will see him, and also false Christians—which I cannot say without a groan—will see the one whom they despised, whom they denied, against whom they swore and perjured themselves, and whom they dishonored.

But the glory of his divinity the reprobate will not see, because it is written: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God.”

They will see him coming in the clouds, just as he ascended with the clouds ministering to him and concealing his glory from the wicked.

He will come with great power, before whom all powers of heaven, earth, and the underworld will tremble. He will come with great power: at his coming he will shake all the elements; he will burn heaven and earth and make all things new; he will reveal human consciences; by a single nod he will glorify the elect and torment the reprobate forever.

He will also come with great majesty. At his glory the sun will be darkened, the things hidden in darkness will be brought to light, all the elect will shine, and they will be inflamed with love for him.

Let us think on this daily, brothers; let us weigh it carefully; let us here reveal the uncleanness of our consciences through confession, for pardon, so that there they may not be revealed by the Lord for confusion and punishment. Let us judge ourselves here, so that we may not be judged there. Let us accuse ourselves here, so that we may not be accused there.

The third part follows, in which the Lord shows what good will then come to the elect, saying: “When these things begin to happen, raise your heads and gladden your hearts” [Note: [Col. 1679D] The Vulgate does not have “gladden your hearts.”]

Why? “Because your redemption is near.” It is as though he were saying: When you see these things, rejoice, because, when the world—which is not your friend—is coming to an end, the eternal salvation that you desired is near.

Then, brothers, our Redeemer will redeem us from three miseries, both in soul and in body: from want, affliction, and death.

The Lord will redeem our soul from its lack of wisdom and virtue, giving it an abundance of every kind of wisdom and virtue. He will also redeem it from the affliction of passions—fear, sorrow, envy, and the others—giving it complete security, joy, and love. He will also redeem it from the death of evil thoughts and sins, giving it complete cleanliness and purity.

He will redeem the body from the lack of food, clothing, and other temporal necessities, giving it complete sufficiency. He will also redeem it from the affliction of illnesses, old age, and heaviness, giving it incorruption and agility in every respect. He will also redeem it from death, giving it true immortality.

O my brothers, consider how ineffably the elect will rejoice when their hope, their desire, their God and Lord comes—when he transfers them from the valley of tears to the heights of joy, from exile to the homeland, from misery to blessedness.

The fourth part follows, in which the Lord explains the sayings by means of a comparison. “Look,” he says, “at the fig tree and all the trees. When they produce fruit from themselves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near.”

He compares the preceding signs of Christ’s coming to the fruitfulness of trees, and eternity to summer. Hence it is clear that the fruit of the world is its ruin. It sprouts for the purpose of withering; it rises for the purpose of falling.

Summer is warm, bright, and fruitful. Eternal blessedness will likewise be warm through the heat of charity, bright through illumination by the true sun, and fruitful through the harvests of eternal recompense.

By contrast, the present life is like winter, because it is cold, dark, and barren: cold, without the warmth of charity; dark, through ignorance, tribulations, and sins; barren, because here things are not harvested but sown through the seed of good works.

The wicked, who here devote themselves to sleep and idleness, are like a lazy person who, unable to work because of the cold, begs in summer, but is not given anything. Thus in the future the wicked will reap nothing except the corruption they have sown in the flesh.

The good, however, who labor here in hope of eternal recompense, are like a good farmer who, in hope of the harvest, sows in winter through rain, hail, and snow. When he sees the fig tree and the other trees budding, he rejoices, knowing that winter has passed and the summer of harvest has come.

Let us too, brothers, in hope of heavenly joys, sow in the Spirit through tears for our sins and endurance of tribulations, so that at the resurrection we may reap eternal life from the Spirit and deserve to be united with those of whom it is said: “Those who sow in tears shall reap with rejoicing. Going forth, they went”—that is, they advanced from virtue to virtue—“and wept,” both from remembrance of their sins and from desire for heavenly joys, “casting”—that is, sending ahead—“their seeds; but coming, they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 125).

May he grant this, who lives and reigns, God, forever. Amen.

# HOMILY V. THIRD SUNDAY OF ADVENT

“Let a person regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God” (1 Cor. 4), and so forth.

The Apostle writes these words, dearest brothers, to the Corinthians, instructing not only them but also us. This Lesson has four parts.

In the first part he reproves the Corinthians for their mistaken opinion about the sacraments. They thought that sacraments administered by holier ministers were holier, and those administered by less holy ministers were less holy. Hence they said: “I belong to Paul, I to Cephas, I to Apollo, I was baptized with Christ’s baptism” (1 Cor. 1), thinking that one baptized by a better minister was better baptized. They therefore examined the lives of ministers with excessive curiosity.

Some in the Church today are like these people: they refuse to hear Mass from priests who keep concubines or are less respectable, or to receive other sacraments from them. But both groups sinned in three ways: first, because they attributed to human beings what belongs to God alone; second, because they judged people’s merits; and third, because they gloried in human beings, although it is written: “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10).

Speaking against them, the Apostle had said above: “Neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3). That is: just as the planter and the waterer are nothing with respect to the power of giving life and increasing the tree, so neither the one who preaches nor the one who baptizes is anything with respect to the efficacy of the sacraments, but God alone, who works invisibly within.

Hence the Holy Spirit said to John: “Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes” (John 1)—that is, he and no other possesses the authority to baptize.

Therefore, whatever the minister may be, the sacraments are the same. They are neither better when administered by better people nor worse when administered by less good people. Hence the Apostle says: “Let a person regard us as ministers of Christ’s sacraments,” not as their authors.

We merely immerse the child in the font, and God baptizes. We merely raise the hand, and God blesses. We merely pronounce the sacred words, and God consecrates. We impose the satisfaction, and God absolves.

We are also stewards of the mysteries of God, discerning who is to be bound and who loosed, who is to be baptized and who is not, who is to be ordained a priest and who a deacon.

Although the merits of ministers contribute nothing to the efficacy of the sacraments, nevertheless, because the faithful person benefits the people more by example than the unfaithful person, here—that is, in this life—it is required that someone be found faithful among stewards.

The second part follows, in which the Apostle shows, by his own example, that the judgment of people should be regarded as insignificant by a sound conscience.

Why? Because human judgment is both mistaken and misleading. It is mistaken because it often judges good to be evil and evil to be good. It is misleading because when someone unworthy is praised by the people, he often takes pride inwardly on that account. He is thereby led to believe more about himself from others than he believes about himself, although it is written: “Do not believe more about yourself from others than you believe about yourself.”

The Apostle therefore says: “It is a very small thing for me to be judged by you or by a human day”—though he does not say “nothing.” For although the reputation and judgment of the people regarding us ought to be despised for our own sake, they should not be entirely neglected for the benefit of our neighbors.

Just as a clean conscience before God is necessary, so a good reputation before one’s neighbor is necessary. For good preaching is of little or no value without a good example. If someone’s life is despised, what remains except that his preaching too should be disregarded? Hence the Lord says: “Let your good works shine before people, so that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5).

Hence it is also said: “He is cruel who neglects his reputation.” Therefore reputation should be neglected for our own sake, but sought for the benefit of the people.

“But neither,” he says, “do I judge myself, although I do not know better than you” [Note: [Col. 1681D] The Vulgate does not have “although I know better than you.”]—that is, I do not assert that I am good.

Behold, brothers: Paul himself, the vessel of election, does not dare to affirm that he is good. Who among us sinners, then, will dare presume that he is good or religious?

“But the one who judges me”—that is, who discerns my works and thoughts invisibly—“is the Lord.” “I am conscious of nothing against myself”—that is, my conscience does not reproach me—“but I am not thereby justified.” For “who understands his offenses?” (Ps. 18). And “let the one who glories glory in the Lord” that he has a clean heart (1 Cor. 1).

The third part follows, in which the Apostle forbids us to judge.

There are three things, my brothers, about which we neither ought nor are able to judge: an uncertain deed, an uncertain intention, and an uncertain end.

A deed is uncertain when we do not truly know whether someone did a particular act. An intention is uncertain when we know that the act occurred but do not know with what intention it was done—for example, when we see someone speaking with another man’s wife.

An end is uncertain when we know that an act occurred and that it was done with a bad intention, yet do not know whether the person will consequently be condemned or will obtain pardon through repentance.

In all these matters we must avoid rash judgment. Even if circumstances seem to incline more toward the worse interpretation, we ought to turn our judgment toward the better.

Hence the Apostle says: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls by his own master. And he will stand, for God is able to make him stand” (Rom. 14).

If you see a priest speaking with someone’s wife, say that he is blessing her with his hand raised.

There are, however, certain matters that are open and manifest, about which we are permitted to judge. Hence the Apostle says: “Is there then no one among you who can judge between brother and brother?”

Therefore, brothers, let us not judge the hearts or intentions of others, which we do not know, but our own. For it is written: “Do not judge, and you will not be judged” (Matt. 7). “Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned” (Luke 6). “If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged” (1 Cor. 11).

He therefore says: “Do not judge before the time.” The person who judges before the time is the one who judges before the matter is certain. While we are in this life, the thoughts of others, their works, and the end of their works are hidden from us; and therefore it is a sin to judge them.

The fourth part follows, in which the Apostle shows when we may safely judge concerning ourselves or others. “Do not judge,” he says, “until the Lord comes.” In this, dearly beloved brothers, he intimates that then we shall judge, when God reveals to us all hidden things—provided, of course, that we belong to the perfect. For there will be four classes at the judgment. Some will judge and will not be judged, namely, the perfect. Some will be judged and saved, namely, those who are moderately good. Some will be judged and condemned, namely, false Christians. Others will not be judged and will be condemned, namely, unbelievers. Hence John says: “He who does not believe is already judged.”

Then the Lord “will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of hearts” (John III), that is, he will expose hidden deeds and even hidden thoughts, both of the good and of the wicked. Then, brothers, hidden adulteries, hidden indecencies, and disgraces committed in darkness and in bedrooms will be laid open. Then, too, the hidden intentions of shameful desires will be revealed, even though they never came to fulfillment.

Consider, then, brothers—consider what shame, what disgrace, and what confusion will seize the rejected, when they see all their shame and abominations revealed before the sight of the dread Judge, the angels, and all the saints. Therefore, brothers, lest you blush with that great and eternal shame, blush now; repent; and be pierced with remorse for what you say in your hearts and in your bedrooms (Psalm IV).

Then, conversely, all the good works of the saints, which they secretly performed out of humility, and all their good intentions, will be revealed to their praise and glory. Hence it is also added: “And then there will be praise for each of the elect from God.” [Note: The Vulgate does not have “of the elect.”] For what greater praise, honor, and glory could there be than when servants are called and become sons; when earthly people become heavenly; when human beings become gods; when they are blessed, honored, and glorified by the divine majesty?

Meanwhile, brothers, let us wipe away our disgraces with tears, confessions, prayers, and almsgiving. For those who do this—even if they are not among the perfect who will judge—will nevertheless be blessed, because “blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Psalm XXXI). I say “covered” so that they may not be seen either for punishment or for shame. May God, our Lord, make us part of their number—he who, as perfect Trinity, lives and reigns as God. Amen.

## HOMILY VI. THIRD SUNDAY OF ADVENT

“When John had heard in prison about the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples to him and said” (Matthew II), and so forth.

You have heard, dearly beloved brothers, from the Gospel reading that Christ, after his forerunner had been imprisoned, began to demonstrate more clearly the power of his divinity. For, ordering all things properly, he did not wish to preach more openly before his forerunner had completed the office of his forerunning, so that, just as John had gone before him by birth, preaching, and baptism, so also he might go before him by dying.

As Lucifer—that is, John—moved toward setting, the true Sun of Justice, Christ, began gradually to display the rays of his splendor. This, therefore, is what is said here: “When John had heard,” and so forth.

This reading has three parts. The first contains John’s question; the second, Christ’s answer; the third, John’s commendation.

The Evangelist therefore shows when, from where, through whom, and what John asked the Lord.

When? “When he had heard about the works of Christ.” If you ask from whom he had heard, we must believe that he heard from the Spirit revealing them, and also from his disciples, whom he frequently sent to Jesus so that they might report to him both his deeds and his words.

From where? From the prison where he was held in chains. In this, brothers, he sets before us an example to imitate: if we should ever be detained in chains, in sickness, or by some other impediment, let us send our household or friends to the church on our behalf, so that they may make known to us the good things said or done there.

Through whom? Through his disciples, who also attended him in prison and did not abandon their teacher in adversity, but diligently ministered to him until his passion and burial. From this, brothers, let us also learn to show steadfast fidelity to our teachers and friends in every adversity. For just as the furnace tests gold and the course tests a horse, so adversity tests a friend. Hence the Wise Man says: “A friend is not recognized in prosperity, and an enemy is not hidden in adversity” (Ecclesiasticus XII). And Solomon says: “A rotten tooth and a failing friend on the road” (Proverbs XXV).

What did he ask? “Are you the one who is to come, or are we to expect another?”

John asks this not for his own sake—for by preaching, baptizing, and demonstrating he had testified that Jesus was the Redeemer of the world—but for the sake of his disciples, lest they think another was being preached by him, and so that they might receive certainty of faith both from the miracles and from Christ’s answer.

For this reason, he did not send his disciples to ask this before Christ had begun to perform miracles. The Evangelist himself indicates this when he says: “When John had heard in prison about the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples,” and so forth. It is as if he were saying: He sent his disciples to Jesus because he had heard that Jesus was openly performing miracles, so that the adverb “when” should be understood not so much temporally as causally.

The second part follows, containing Christ’s answer. “Go,” he says, “and report to John what you hear and see.” It is as if he were saying: Let words cease; let deeds speak. For he performed many miracles in the presence of John’s messengers. Hence he said, “what you see”—namely, through yourselves—and “what you hear”—namely, through others.

And what are these things? “The blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, the poor are evangelized,” that is, visited. “And blessed is the one who is not scandalized because of me.”

This answer is fitting, even though it does not seem to respond directly to the preceding question. The question was whether the redemption of the world was to be accomplished through him. He, however, answers by presenting the power of his divinity and the endurance of his humanity, through which redemption was accomplished. For unless he were human, he could not suffer for the world; and unless he were God, he could not overcome death.

It is therefore as if he were saying: “I have already begun to redeem the world. For while I work as God, I am an occasion of scandal and suffer as a human being.”

We believe, brothers, that the Lord performed the works listed here both bodily and spiritually. He gave the blind illumination both of heart and of body; to the lame, uprightness both of heart and of body; to lepers, cleansing both of heart and of body; to the dead, resurrection both of heart and of body; and to the poor, visitation both of heart and of body.

And although he bore witness to his divinity through so many signs, scarcely anyone was free from being scandalized by his humanity. Some slandered him; others laid snares for him; and almost everyone doubted his divinity.

And what wonder is it, brothers, if many were scandalized by Christ while he was still mortal, when many—even now, although he already reigns in heaven—are scandalized by him, which is a cause for sorrow? To say nothing of unbelievers, some who are Christians in name alone despise him, swear falsely by his holy name, attack him by their deeds, regard the words of the Gospel as vanity, and do not even believe that there will be a future resurrection.

The third part follows, in which the Lord commends John. Hence it is added: “When they had gone away, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John.”

The Lord did not wish to commend John in the presence of his disciples, lest his commendation appear to have the flavor of flattery. In this, brothers, he gives us an example: we should not praise our friend in his own presence or in the presence of his household, lest we appear to do so out of a desire to curry favor, and lest we give him an occasion for boasting.

Moreover, lest the crowds think John possessed no virtue because he performed no miracles, the one who had chosen him and knew him commends him. He commends him in four respects: in strength, severity, excellence in prophecy, and the grace of his forerunning.

He commends him for his strength when he says: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” It is as if he were saying: “No, but rather a strong man.”

A reed grows in a marsh. It is beautiful on the outside, empty within, and shaken by every wind. Such are the people of this world, who have nourished their souls on grossness and pleasure. Outwardly they are polished by hypocrisy and glory, but inwardly empty of virtue; they are lifted up by prosperity and cast down by adversity. They are exalted by praise and humbled by threats and insults; in such people the devil rests.

Hence Job says: “Under its shade it sleeps in the secrecy of the reed” (Job XL), because he loves minds that are dark, deceitful, and unstable.

John, however, was not a reed. He grew through the hardship of abstinence; outwardly he was rough and neglected, inwardly full of virtue. He was not lifted up by flattery nor cast down by adversity.

Let us also learn, brothers, to be strong and steadfast amid the changes of this world. Let us not love the riches of this world, and thus we shall neither grow proud of possessing them nor grieve over losing them. Let us not love the glory of this world, and thus neither human praise will inflate us nor disgrace make us sorrowful. Let us love not the present life but the life to come, and thus bodily pleasure will not entangle us, nor punishment or pain terrify us.

He commends him for his severity when he says: “A man dressed in soft clothing?” It is a litotes, since less is said and more signified. John pursued softness in nothing, but was hard in food, clothing, action, and speech.

His food was locusts and wild honey. His clothing was camel’s hair and a leather belt. His deeds were contempt for the world and desire for heaven. His words were not flattery but harsh correction of vices: “Brood of vipers,” he says, “who will teach you to flee from the coming wrath? Already the axe has been laid to the root of the trees” (Matthew III).

It follows: “Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in royal houses.” It is as if he were saying: Those who delight in softness are found not in the wilderness, as John was, but in royal houses—those who dress softly, feast delicately, work delicately, and speak delicately.

Therefore, brothers, let no one think that sin is absent from the flowing fashion and pursuit of clothing. If there were no sin in this, the Lord would not have praised the lowliness of clothing in his forerunner, nor reproved the rich man clothed in purple for the extravagance of his clothing, nor would Peter have recalled women from costly dress (1 Peter III).

We sin in clothing chiefly in five ways.

First, in excessive expense: when we buy a single garment for as much as would clothe many poor people.

Second, in vanity: when we take pleasure in beautiful and costly clothing.

Third, in contempt of our neighbors: when, considering the beauty of our own clothing and the poverty of our neighbors’ clothing, we admire ourselves and despise them.

Fourth, in excess: when we possess more changes of clothing than we need, lying unused—clothing that would better clothe the poor than feed moths—since it is written: “Let the one who has two tunics give to the one who has none” (Luke III), that is, let the one who has sufficient clothing give away the excess.

Fifth, in the manner of wearing it: when we make or wear our clothing in a way we ought not.

When we say these things, we do not condemn clothing but the vice of those who misuse it. I know that many have pleased God beneath purple garments, and, conversely, that many have displeased God beneath sackcloth. Some are not lifted up by purple, while others either grieve over or boast of being dressed in sackcloth. Great indeed is the person whom sackcloth does not cast down and whom purple does not exalt.

Such was David; such was John the Baptist. Neither the former beneath purple nor the latter beneath sackcloth was a reed shaken by the winds.

But you, brothers, who are imperfect, each of you should maintain moderation according to his rank. Dress yourselves in accordance with people of your order and station: not more splendidly than they, lest you despise them on that account; and not more poorly than they, lest you grieve that you are poorer than they. Let not the wind of glory or shame shake you in either direction.

Under a moderate garment, secretly wear sackcloth, especially on days of fasting, so that it may be all the more pleasing to God because it is more hidden. Give to the naked any clothing you do not need. And if you do not wish to give something new, give at least a reasonably good old garment, so that if you have sinned in the new one, you may make satisfaction in the old.

Brothers, also avoid softness in food, for the habit of luxurious food produces lust, softens the body, makes one disdain humbler foods, consumes one’s patrimony, and introduces anxiety. The less anxious person is the one content with less.

Just as Mars rejoices in a hardened soldier who can bravely endure heat, cold, and toil, so the Lord loves hardened soldiers and despises the effeminate and soft. For this reason, as we read in the *Lives of the Fathers*, the holy Fathers avoided baths, perfumes, and similar luxuries, lest they soften the hardness of their bodies.

Also flee, brothers, soft deeds—the deeds of those who serve the flesh and build wood, hay, and straw destined to be consumed by fire.

Likewise beware of soft words, that is, flatteries. The prophet shows how greatly they must be avoided: “Woe to those who place pillows under every elbow” (Ezekiel XIII). He places a pillow under the elbow who gently supports, through flattery, a soul falling from uprightness.

And the Psalmist says: “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the unjust man is blessed” (Psalm IX).

He commends John for excellence in prophecy when he adds: “But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.”

The office of a prophet, dearly beloved brothers, is to proclaim what is to come. John not only foretold Christ, saying, “After me comes one mightier than I” (Mark I), but also pointed him out: “Behold,” he said, “the Lamb of God” (John I).

We too, brothers, are like prophets if we proclaim Christ’s second coming to judgment by words and deeds; if we threaten the ungodly; and if we promise the elect everlasting glory.

He also commends him for the grace of his forerunning when he says: “This is the one of whom it is written through the prophet Malachi: ‘Behold, I, the Father, send to the Son my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’”

Truly, brothers, truly this John is great and wonderful: long before he was conceived, the Lord—or rather, the Lord through the prophet—promised him as a messenger and forerunner to his Only-Begotten Son.

Nor will John alone deserve to be called an angel and forerunner. We too, brothers, both you and I, may deserve to be called angels and forerunners of Christ if we announce him by word and example, and if, through correction and amendment, we prepare a way for him both to our own hearts and to the hearts of others. This he grants, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God. Amen.

## HOMILY VII. FOURTH SUNDAY OF ADVENT

“Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Philippians IV), and so forth.

In this reading, dearly beloved brothers, the Apostle does four things. First, he urges us to rejoice in the Lord; second, to be moderate; third, to pray without anxiety; fourth, he asks that we be kept in peace.

He says, therefore: “Rejoice in the Lord.”

If everyone rejoiced in the same thing, brothers, the Apostle would never have said with such emphasis, “Rejoice in the Lord.” For there are three kinds of joy: evil, empty, and good.

Some rejoice in evil, of whom it is said: “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Proverbs II). Evil pleases them so greatly that they rejoice in another’s suffering even when it brings them no benefit.

Others rejoice in what is empty, that is, in vain and worldly prosperity. Of these Solomon says: “I regarded laughter as error, and to joy I said: Why are you deceived in vain?” (Ecclesiastes II).

These two kinds of joy, my brothers, are evil. Concerning both, Solomon’s saying is understood: “Laughter will be mingled with sorrow, and mourning takes possession of the end of joy” (Proverbs XIV). So too the Gospel says: “Woe to you who laugh, for you will mourn” (Luke VI). And elsewhere: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation here” (ibid.).

Others rejoice in what is good—namely, those who rejoice in the Lord. Hence the Apostle says elsewhere: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians I). And here: “Rejoice,” he says, “in the Lord.”

But why does he repeat himself—“Again I say, rejoice”? Because joy is love in the hope of, or in the possession of, the beloved object.

Here, brothers, we rejoice only in hope of heavenly joys, not yet in their possession. Yet we rejoice in more than hope, because although we do not possess the reality here, we do possess the pledge, which the Apostle calls “the first fruits of the Spirit” (Romans VIII)—namely, the virtues and gifts of the Holy Spirit.

The Apostle therefore urges us to rejoice in the exercise of the virtues and in the hope of rewards; to rejoice in the practice of goodness and in the hope of blessedness; to rejoice in the possession of a pure conscience and in the hope of a blessed life.

The first joy is great, brothers, but the second is greatest. For what can be found here that is happier, more joyful, or more delightful than to live chastely among the pure and soberly among the drunken; to hold all worldly things beneath one’s feet; not to be broken by adversity or softened by prosperity; to fear God alone; to have a clean conscience; to live securely; not to fear death; and even to desire and await heavenly joys with certainty?

Through this, brothers, divine sweetness is not only awaited but also anticipated and tasted beforehand. The Prophet had tasted it beforehand, and in wonder and joy he said: “How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart!” (Psalm LXXII). He also urges us to taste it, saying: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm XXXIII).

This, brothers—this is joy in the Holy Spirit. This is true joy, the true sabbath of the mind. Of it Solomon also says: “A secure mind is a continual feast” (Proverbs XV).

This joy, brothers, will not be mingled with sorrow, but will lead us to supreme and everlasting joy: joy without grief, without end, without fear, and without decline; joy in the vision of God, into which the angels long to look (1 Peter I).

Because great joys ordinarily relax a person here and make him careless, the Apostle adds:

“Let your moderation be known to all.” This is the second part, brothers, in which he urges us to be moderate in all things. It is as if he were saying: Rejoice, brothers, but moderately; sing psalms to the Lord, but wisely.

Moderation is a virtue that maintains the mean between excess and deficiency. This virtue is the seasoning of all the others. Whatever is done without the bridle of restraint is impulse, not reason.

Moderation does three things. It gives a person mastery over himself; it makes him pleasing and well-regarded among people; and it brings the Lord near to him.

That it gives a person mastery over himself, he indicates when he adds “your”: as if he were saying, “Let your moderation make you your own.” In accordance with what the Philosopher says:

“Do you wish to possess great power? I will give you great power: rule yourself. Do you wish to govern many? Govern yourself. For you will govern many if reason governs you.”

Hence Solomon says: “The patient man is better than the strong man, and the one who rules his spirit than the conqueror of cities” (Proverbs XVI).

That moderation makes a person pleasing and famous among people, he shows when he says: “Let it be known to all,” as if he were saying: Let your moderation be so great that, through its admiration and example, it draws people to you.

That it brings the Lord near to a person, he shows when he adds: “The Lord is near.” The Lord is indeed near to the moderate: near by likeness, near by love, and near by reward, because he regards as like himself, loves, and rewards those whom he sees to be like him through moderation.

This virtue made Moses and David pleasing to God and to human beings. One of them is recorded as having prayed for his enemies; the other spared an enemy who sought his blood.

Let us also learn, brothers, to maintain moderation in all things: to restrain the movements of our hearts; to rule ourselves; to moderate the discord of others; and to become like God, who does all things without agitation, so that we may deserve to be loved and rewarded by him, in accordance with his promise: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matthew V, 4).

The third part follows, in which the Apostle urges us to pray without anxiety, saying: “Be anxious about nothing, but in every prayer,” and so forth.

Appropriately, brothers, while urging us to pray, he first said: “Be anxious about nothing.” For nothing impedes one who prays more than anxiety.

Indeed, brothers, no one is so free from worldly cares and so devoted to prayer that, while praying, he does not sometimes experience demonic assaults and phantoms of vain thoughts.

What, my brothers, what do you suppose happens to those whose entire mind and desire are occupied with anxiety about temporal things? If they ever begin to pray, their mind immediately flies back to its habitual concerns, because “where one’s treasure is, there also is one’s heart” (Matthew VI).

Therefore, brothers, the mind must first be cleansed of love and anxiety for temporal things and wholly fixed upon God, so that it may freely devote itself to prayer.

But even if, while we are engaged in prayer, the suggestions of demons and clouds of vain thoughts sometimes assail us, we must take the greatest care, brothers, lest they linger. Otherwise, in accordance with Solomon’s saying, “dead flies ruin the sweetness of the ointment” (Ecclesiastes X).

Instead, we should immediately become indignant with ourselves, drive vain thoughts away from us as quickly as possible, and return to him. For it is written: “The birds of heaven descended, and Abraham drove them away” (Genesis XV).

What are represented by the sacrifices, if not prayers? And what by the birds, if not vain thoughts? But when vain thoughts descend upon the prayer of a devoted worshiper, he immediately drives them away, following Abraham’s example.
