“But in every prayer,” he says, “and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known before God.”

Prayer, brothers, is offered for obtaining good things; supplication, for removing evil things. Let these requests “be made known before God,” that is, let such things be asked in such a manner and with such an intention that they are worthy for God to know and hear.

Let us therefore ask the Lord, brothers, not for wealth, not for honors, and not for a long life in this world. Those who ask for these things are not heard, as James says, because they ask wrongly (James IV). Rather, taught by the Lord, let us seek first the kingdom of God and his justice (Matthew VI).

Let us also ask in the manner we ought: with heart and deed, and with confidence. Hence James says: “If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach. But let him ask in faith, doubting nothing, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind” (James I).

Let us ask, brothers, also with the intention we ought to have: let us ask for everything on account of God, and let us seek and love God himself not for another reason but for his own sake.

He is said to have answered those who did not seek him with a simple intention: “Amen, I say to you, you seek me because you ate of the loaves. Work not for food that perishes, but for food that endures to eternal life” (John VI).

It is as if he were saying: You ought not to seek me for the sake of temporal bread, but for my own sake, because I am the true bread that satisfies forever.

The fourth part follows, in which the Apostle prays that we be kept in peace and by peace, saying: “And may the peace of God, which surpasses every understanding, guard your hearts and your minds.”

He says “the peace of God,” that is, God who is peace, and Christ who is our peace, who made both one (Ephesians II). Or the Holy Spirit, who is the concord of the Father and the Son.

This peace surpasses every understanding, not only in itself but also in creatures. If the peace of God in creatures surpasses every understanding, how much more does it surpass every understanding in itself?

For what understanding, dearly beloved brothers, can comprehend how the four elements, although opposed to one another, are joined into a single harmony? Who can comprehend how contrary humors in the human being are pacified into one healthy condition? Who can comprehend how contrary sounds on a lyre come together in one consonance?

And, to speak of heavenly creatures, what understanding can comprehend how the heavenly and holy spirits, although unequal in rank and merit, agree in glory in the unity of a single joy, will, and love?

And if, brothers, the peace of God in creatures surpasses every understanding, how much more does it surpass every understanding and intelligence in itself? For what intelligence could investigate the peace and concord of the Trinity—how, although there are three persons, they are united in one essence, will, and majesty?

Therefore, the Apostle says, may this peace of God, which surpasses every understanding, guard your hearts, so that they may will what is good, and your minds, so that they may understand rightly.

Let us also pray, brothers, that the peace of God, which surpasses every understanding, guard our hearts: that we may have peace toward him by obeying him; peace toward ourselves by avoiding what is harmful; and peace toward our neighbors by loving them.

May our peace, the God and Lord Jesus Christ, grant us this peace—he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God. Amen.

## HOMILY VIII. FOURTH SUNDAY OF ADVENT

“The Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to John to ask him: ‘Who are you?’” (John VI), and so forth.

This reading, dearly beloved brothers, contains, in alternating sequence, the questions of the Jews and the answers of John the forerunner.

The Jews knew from the book of Daniel that the coming of Christ was already near. They also saw John the Baptist, foretold by an angel, born miraculously, living most holy, preaching repentance, and baptizing. For this reason they suspected that he was the Christ.

Therefore the teachers of the Law sent people to question him, and asked him whether he was the Christ. In this the Jews’ curiosity and hardness are both evident: they were curious in questioning but hard in believing.

But why did they question one in whom they did not wish to believe? Or why did those who did not wish to believe question him? John removes them from himself and sends them to Christ, yet they do not heed him.

And I think that if John had said that he was the Christ, they would not have believed him. Instead, they would have said to him what they said to Christ: “You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true” (John VIII).

They similarly questioned Christ: “If you are the Christ, tell us openly” (John X). To them he said: “I speak to you, and you do not believe” (ibid.).

There are many such people today, which is a cause for sorrow. They inquire curiously into many things from the holy teachers of the Church, but are hard when it comes to obeying.

We too, brothers, teachers as we are—something I cannot say without groaning—seem like the scribes and Pharisees. We are curious in examining the Scriptures, but hard and slow in putting them into practice.

But what benefit does this bring us, brothers, except that the Lord threatens us with the warning that “the servant who knew his master’s will and did not do it will be beaten with many blows”? (Luke XII).

Conversely, dearly beloved brothers, John’s answer gives us a great lesson in faith and humility. It gives us a lesson in faith because he sets before us our Lord Jesus, in whom we must believe and hope, who alone truly baptizes; and he recalls that he himself is Christ’s voice and herald.

It gives us a lesson in humility because he thinks and answers humbly concerning himself in all things.

Here, brothers, we must carefully consider how the saints, although they shine with such excellence of virtues, glory only in humility. They know that the building of virtues without humility is ruin. For just as pride is the ruin of all virtues, so humility is their foundation.

Pride cast the first angel and the first human being from the heights into the depths. Humility recalls even the weak to heaven.

Indeed, humility is such a great good that any sinner with humility is better than any righteous person with arrogance. Humility corrects the sinner, whereas pride condemns the righteous.

For this reason our Redeemer, by example and word, set before us the way of humility, by which we might ascend to heaven, we who had fallen through pride: “Learn from me,” he says, “because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matthew XI).

The blessed Mother and Virgin, taught by him, conceals her virginity and the other virtues with which she incomparably shone, and confesses only this: “He has regarded the humility of his servant” (Luke I).

David too, a man according to the Lord’s heart, when he was despised by his wife because he had danced before the ark of the Lord, said: “I will play, and I will humble myself more than I have done, and I will be humble in my own eyes” (2 Kings VI).

And the teacher of the Gentiles, who had been caught up to the third heaven, says: “I am the least of the apostles, and I am not worthy to be called an apostle” (1 Corinthians XV).

Behold, brothers: as you pass through the Old and New Testaments, you will find that all the saints laid their foundation upon the virtue of humility.

This is why this John—of whom, according to the Lord’s testimony, no one greater has arisen among those born of women (Matthew XI)—confesses humility alone and completely in himself.

You will understand this better if you learn what humility is and what its parts are.

Humility is the virtue by which a person, through the truest knowledge of himself, becomes lowly in his own eyes.

Some wretched and despairing people regard themselves as lowly, but this does not arise from virtue, because it comes not from true self-knowledge but from adversity.

Every person, however, even in prosperity, if he knows himself properly, understands that he has nothing in himself except evil. If he possesses anything good, he possesses it from God.

Hence the Apostle says: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians IV).

Therefore, brothers, we have nothing from ourselves of which to be proud, but rather grounds for humbling ourselves.

There are four degrees of humility.

The first is that a person should not attribute to himself what he is not.

The second is that he should believe that what he has comes not from himself but from God.

The third is that, admiring the good qualities of others, he should regard his own as nothing or as little.

The fourth is that he should attribute the good he possesses not to his own merits but to the grace of God.

Thus, brothers, blessed John, becoming lowly in his own eyes through the truest knowledge of himself, shows that he possesses the first degree of humility when he denies that he is the Christ, as he was thought to be.

For he preferred to believe himself about himself rather than others. He preferred to stand firmly within himself rather than be carried above himself by human opinion.

He also denies that he is Elijah in the flesh, although, according to the Lord’s word, he was Elijah in a similar forerunning role. For just as Elijah will be the forerunner of the Judge, so John was the forerunner of the Redeemer.

He denies that he is a prophet because he did not preach someone who was to come, but showed that the one who had been promised had already come. Or certainly, just as no one is good in comparison with the goodness of God, so in the presence of God no one is a prophet, since he alone knows all things before they happen.

Therefore, brothers, with what face does anyone in this world dare to claim for himself any righteousness or goodness, when the Son of God himself says: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone” (Matthew XIX)?

And when John, who was more than a prophet, says, “I am not a prophet,” let no one, brothers, attribute to himself a good that he does not possess. Let no one wish to be called better or holier than he is.

For, according to the poet:

> False honor gives pleasure, and deceptive disgrace causes fear.

Whom does it benefit—or frighten—except one who is faulty and deceitful? If, therefore, you are proclaimed holy when you are not holy, do not rejoice in it, but blush and weep, because you are not what you are called; and work with all your determination so that you may become so.

After John had removed from himself what he was not [Col. 1694A], he cheerfully revealed what he was. For when asked who he was, he said: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness.” He did not say, “I am a man,” or “I am the son of Zechariah.” Nothing that he was by nature prevents him from being what he was by grace; but he said: “I am the voice of one crying.” A voice, of course, is not anything in itself, nor does it signify anything by itself, but only through the speaker. It is therefore as though he were saying: “I neither am nor speak anything from myself, but from God speaking in me. I am only the instrument of God speaking in me. Nevertheless, I am the herald of the word, uttering what is spoken through me, but not from myself.”

Behold, brothers, the second form of humility: that what one is is shown to come not from oneself but from God. In this he agrees well with the saying preached by the one who testifies about himself: “My teaching,” he says, “is not mine, but that of the Father who sent me” [Col. 1694B] (John 7). Hence he likewise says to his disciples: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10). And through the prophet: “They shall announce,” he says, “from me” (Ezekiel 3). And Peter: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God” (1 Peter 4).

How greatly, then, my brothers, do those rave who think that they are or can do anything from themselves—those who say: “Our lips are our own; who is our lord?” (Psalm 11). The Son of God says: “My teaching is not mine” (John 7). And you, proud ash, say that the teaching is yours?

Therefore, brothers, if we say or do anything good, let us give the glory not to ourselves but to the name of the Lord, who says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). Not only John, but anyone—whether cleric or layman—who announces the word of life in the wilderness of this [Col. 1694C] world may be called “the voice of one crying in the wilderness.” Therefore let us too, brothers, as far as we can, cry out with John in word and example: “Make straight the way of the Lord.”

“Why then,” they ask, “do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet?” The evangelist hints that they said this out of sheer envy when he says: “Those who had been sent were from the Pharisees”—people who do not know how to seek instruction, but only to envy.

Yet every holy person, even when questioned with a perverse intention, is neither moved nor changed from his goodness. Accordingly, John answers words of envy with words of life: “I baptize in water,” he says—that is, I wash bodies alone, not souls. But you say: Why, then, did he baptize? For three reasons. First, so that, just as by being born and preaching, so also by baptizing, he might go before Christ. Second, so that he might accustom the people to [Col. 1694D] baptism. Third, so that he might invite the people to repentance.

“I baptize in water,” he says; “but there stands among you one whom you do not know”—who, as is to be understood, baptizes in the Holy Spirit.

Behold the third form of humility: John humbles his own ministry and commends Christ’s authority. For this is how, my brothers, the saints have always been accustomed to admire not only Christ’s virtues but also those of other saints, and to consider their own imperfection, so that they might say that others were superior to them and humble themselves.

Hence Peter, the prince of the apostles, does not consider that great power by which his very shadow healed the sick, nor his own primacy, but admires Paul’s wisdom: “As our most beloved brother Paul,” he says, [Col. 1695A] “according to the wisdom given to him by God, also teaches” (2 Peter 3). What does this mean? It means that he places Paul’s excellence above his own and humbles himself, attending to his own imperfection.

By contrast, the proud always consider and exalt their own good qualities in their hearts, while constantly reproving the imperfections of others, so that they may always place themselves above others and despise others in comparison with themselves. Concerning such people the prophet says: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isaiah 5). And Paul says: “Do not be wise in your own estimation” (Romans 12).

For this reason the Lord says to the proud Saul: “When you were little in your own eyes, you became head among the tribes of Israel” (1 Samuel 15). It is as though he were saying: “When you considered yourself little, I made you great above the others. But now, because you consider yourself great, you are judged little [Col. 1695B] by me.”

Therefore, brothers, if we have any good qualities, let us in a certain sense diminish them in our minds and consider them small; but let us multiply our own faults in our eyes, so that we may always be humble toward ourselves. Conversely, let us either overlook or diminish the faults of our neighbors, especially those who have not been entrusted to us. While always admiring their good qualities, let us strive to imitate them, so that we may always set them before ourselves.

It follows: “He who comes after me has been placed before me.” It is as though he were saying: “He who came after me by being born in humanity was placed before me in majesty.” “Of whom I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal.”

Behold the fourth form of humility. For he attributes nothing to his own merits who says that he is unworthy [Col. 1695C] to loosen Christ’s sandal. But, my brothers, if John was not worthy to loosen his sandal, how was he worthy to undertake the office of preaching Christ or baptizing him? Surely, my brothers, are we to say either that Christ chose one who was unworthy, or that John lied out of humility?

Far be it from us to say that Christ, who cannot be deceived, chose one who was unworthy, or that John, the herald of truth, lied. How, then, was he both worthy and unworthy? John was worthy, brothers, by God’s gracious regard and choice; unworthy in himself. Worthy by grace, unworthy by his own power.

Let our presumption and pride, therefore, blush with shame. John, than whom no greater has arisen among those born of women, says that he is unworthy to loosen a sandal—and you say that you are worthy [Col. 1695D] of the priesthood, worthy of the episcopate? John, a burning and shining lamp, says that he is unworthy to loosen a sandal. And you, a smoking coal, say that you are worthy to handle Christ’s body, and to investigate or preach the mystery of the Incarnation, which is signified by the sandal?

What, then, shall we say, brothers, except that, however much good we may have done, we should always declare ourselves unworthy? And let us not say this with the mouth alone, as though lying through humility; let us believe it in our minds and confess it with our mouths. In accordance with this, Truth itself admonishes us, saying: “When you have done everything that has been commanded you, say: ‘We are useless servants; we have not done what we were obliged to do’” (Luke 17). [Note: [Col. 1695D] The Vulgate omits *non*—“we have not done.”]

May he grant us the grace to preserve this humility who for our sake became humble and poor, our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 1696A], who lives and reigns, etc. Amen.

## HOMILY IX. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

Reading from the prophet Isaiah at the nighttime Mass.

“The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light” (Isaiah 9), etc.

Today, beloved, we celebrate the temporal birth of our Savior. We ought to celebrate it with all the greater exultation of mind, the greater the cause of joy that we have received today. For today the calamity of the human race has been brought back from slavery to freedom, from misery to happiness, from death to life, from darkness to light.

Today, indeed, almighty and merciful God has fulfilled for the human race—already despairing of salvation—the promise long awaited and long desired, which he had preordained from eternity, promised to the patriarchs [Col. 1696B], foreshadowed in the Law, and foretold through the prophets. Today the One Desired by all nations has come. Today truth has sprung from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven.

Today, brothers, the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. As we have just read in the prophecy, today, when the heavens rain dew from above and the clouds pour forth righteousness, the earth has opened and brought forth the Savior (Isaiah 45).

This reading has five parts. First, the prophet shows that a light, namely Christ, has arisen for the people walking in darkness. Second, he shows Christ’s gracious condescension; third, his exaltation; fourth, he sets forth the mysteries of his names; fifth, the greatness and [Col. 1696C] perpetuity of his kingdom.

The prophet therefore says: “The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light.”

Certainly, beloved brothers, before Christ’s coming, because of the transgression of our first parent, all his descendants walked in darkness. In what darkness? In the darkness of ignorance, sins, and misery.

They walked in the darkness of ignorance when, by eating the forbidden fruit, the human being wished to know good and evil and fell into ignorance. Hence Moses says: “They sacrificed to demons and not to God, to gods whom they did not know” (Deuteronomy 32). And David: “They wandered in the wilderness and did not find the way to a city in which to dwell” (Psalm 106).

They walked in the darkness of sins because all who descended through desire from the transgressing mass of humanity were conceived in sins [Col. 1696D] and born with sin (Psalm 51). Hence the Apostle says: “Death reigned in the world from Adam to Moses” (Romans 5). But although through the Law the death of sin was recognized, it was not removed; rather, it was increased. And David says: “All have turned aside; together they have become useless” (Psalms 14; 53). Hence it is also written: “No one is clean from defilement, not even an infant whose life is one day upon the earth” (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint).

The people walked in the darkness of misery because, however just a person might be, he was wretched in this life, more wretched in death, and most wretched after death. Concerning this misery Hezekiah says: “In the middle of my days I shall go to the gates of the underworld” (Isaiah 38).

Alas, brothers, alas, in how great a darkness the human race [Col. 1697A] walked before Christ’s coming—or rather, wandered! For walking in darkness is not walking but wandering, since, as the Lord says, “Whoever walks in darkness does not know where he is going” (John 12).

But when Christ, the Sun of righteousness rising from on high, visited the world, it saw a great light. Observe, brothers, observe: it saw a great light. It did not kindle the light for itself; it did not purchase it at a price; it did not acquire it through its merits; it saw it offered freely.

But how could one who had been born blind see this? (John 8.) He could not have done so at all unless he had first been enlightened. Therefore, so that he might be able to see the light offered to him, Christ first enlightened him in mind with the salve made from spittle and earth—that is, from divinity and humanity. Thus, brothers, he saw a great light.

What light? The true light that enlightens every [Col. 1697B] human being coming into this world (John 1). Enlightened by the light, he saw the light itself; he saw the one who enlightens.

Nor, beloved, did only those who were then in the flesh see this light. For light also rose upon those dwelling or sitting in the region of the shadow of death—that is, upon the patriarchs and prophets and the other saints who, released from the flesh, awaited the coming of the Mediator like exiles, dwelling not indeed in death but in its shadow, that is, in the likeness of death, deprived of the vision of God.

Concerning them David says: “Light has risen in darkness for the upright in heart; the Lord is merciful and compassionate” (Psalm 112). And elsewhere: “Light has risen for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart” (Psalm 97).

Therefore, brothers, the true light, Christ, coming into this world, drove away the darkness of ignorance by preaching the truth [Col. 1697C]; he dissolved the darkness of sins by making atonement through his blood; and he brought the darkness of misery to an end by bestowing eternal blessedness.

Moreover, to show that the darkness of the world was to be enlightened by him, Christ was born at midnight and illumined that very night with splendors and the praises of the angels, as well as with the brightness of the new star. Therefore the reading that we are now explaining is read at the nighttime Mass.

The second part follows, in which Christ’s gracious condescension is shown, when it is said: “For a child is born to us, and a son is given to us.”

Unless, by looking upon us, he had become little, he would not have enlightened us. Unless he had veiled his inaccessible splendor beneath the cloud of flesh, the weakness of our sight could not have contemplated him.

He therefore became [Col. 1697D] little from immensity: little in body, little in humility, little in reputation.

First, little in body, because, newly born from a virgin, he was placed in a narrow manger. Little in humility, because he humbled himself and chose poor parents, chose poverty, and preached to all: “Learn from me,” he says, “because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11).

Little in reputation, because he was called the son of a craftsman (Matthew 13), in accordance with what he had said through the prophet: “I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Psalm 22).

In all things he displayed for us an example of humility, to show by what path we could ascend to heaven, we who had fallen through pride.

This little one, therefore, was born for us from a mother, and the Son of God was given [Col. 1698A] to us by the Father. He was not born for himself, since he needed nothing, but he was born and given for us, who needed very much.

He was born for us to commend his love for us, because, as the Apostle says, “he first loved us” (1 John 4). He was born and given for us to show us the way of life, so that we might follow his footsteps. He was born and given for us to redeem us from death, since he laid down his life for his sheep.

But what resulted from this love, this humility, this patience? What follows: “And the rule was placed upon his shoulder.”

This is the third part, in which, after Christ’s humiliation, Christ’s exaltation is proclaimed. Here, brothers, Christ’s rule is named by transferring the name of what follows to what precedes [Col. 1698B], because through the cross that he carried upon his shoulder, all power in heaven and on earth was given to him.

This is what the Apostle says: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death—even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2), etc.

This is also that small mustard seed which, though the smallest of all seeds, when thrown into the ground grew into a great tree. This is that small stone which, according to Daniel, was cut from the mountain without hands, grew, and occupied the whole world (Daniel 2).

The fourth part follows, in which six names of Christ are expressed when it is added: “And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the future age, Prince of Peace.”

Wonderful, because he performs new and unheard-of [Col. 1698C] miracles; Counselor, by preaching, suffering, and deliverance, counseling the wretched; God, because he raises his own body and the bodies of others from the dead; Mighty, because he binds the strong one, plunders his goods, and opens heaven to them; Father of the future age—that is, of Christians—nurturing and defending them and interceding with the Father on their behalf; Prince of Peace, because he crowns the righteous and condemns the wicked.

Then the saints will possess complete peace with everyone and from everyone: with everyone—with God, with the angels, with their neighbor, with body and soul; and from everyone—from the devil and his members [Col. 1698D], fearing nothing.

With God, by willing the same thing; with the angels, by agreeing with them in purity; with body and soul, by their concord in the good; with their neighbor, by loving him sincerely. From everyone: from the devil and his members, fearing nothing.

The fifth part follows, in which the multiplication and perpetuity of Christ’s kingdom are demonstrated when it is added: “His rule shall be multiplied.”

For although he now appears to rule only over the good and not over the wicked, in the future he will rule both without opposition, glorifying the former and punishing the latter eternally. Now he appears to reign only in heaven and not in hell; in the future it will be evident that he reigns everywhere.

And there will be no end to his kingdom—neither an end of time, nor of place, nor of rewards, nor of punishments.

Therefore, brothers, if we wish to be heirs of Christ’s kingdom, let us first be heirs of his love, humility, and patience; for through these virtues we shall come to that reward. Let us not fear anything lowly or harsh for the sake of him who, being so great and such as he is, suffered so many humiliations [Col. 1699A] and hardships for us. Let us love him more than ourselves, him who became so very little for our sake. Let us love and imitate his holy name, his holy words, and his examples with all our desire.

Let us celebrate his birthday with joy—not temporal but spiritual joy; not in drunkenness but in sobriety; not in revelries but in fellowship (Romans 13). If today we dress in new and splendid garments, let it not be for display but for the honor of him whose Nativity we celebrate. Let us do this, brothers, so that the naked person may receive, if not a new garment, at least an old one.

If today we also provide food more abundantly and splendidly, let it not be so that we ourselves may consume more abundantly, but so that we may distribute more abundantly to orphans, widows, guests, and the poor, so that those who are to be our fellow participants in heavenly goods may [Col. 1699B] share with us in all temporal goods.

This is granted by him who today wished to be born for us from a virgin, our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God. Amen.

## HOMILY X. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

“The grace of God our Savior has appeared to all human beings” (Titus 2), etc.

Today, beloved brothers, we celebrate the temporal birth of Christ, in which we ought all to rejoice both commonly and in many ways. It is common because, just as Christ assumed a common nature, so he accomplished a common redemption. It is manifold because his birth has brought us manifold [Col. 1699C] benefit.

The Apostle shows both points in the reading just recited, using a metonymic expression in this way: “The grace of God has appeared”—that is, God through grace—“teaching us,” etc.

Here he shows who and how great the one who appeared is, how and to whom he appeared, and for what benefits of ours.

Who and how great is he? God, the Son of God.

But how could the invisible one appear, when it is written: “No one has ever seen God” (John 4)? It is true, brothers, that the immeasurable glory of God cannot be seen as it is by either a bodily or a spiritual eye. Indeed, that splendor and that glory surpass all contemplation, not only of human beings but also of the archangels.

But when God’s immense mercy wished to illuminate the darkness of human blindness with its splendor, he veiled his radiance with the covering of flesh [Col. 1699D], so that the weakness of human contemplation might somehow be able to look upon him.

Certainly, the temporal sun instructs us concerning that eternal sun. If we try to gaze directly upon its splendor, we are blinded; but we can see it better when it is concealed beneath a cloud.

How did he appear? Freely. He did not appear to us because he himself needed anything, or because we were deserving, but solely because of his grace he appeared to us who were undeserving.

Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Not on account of works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy, he saved us” (Titus 3).

It is indeed a great grace when one who has brought us neither good nor evil takes pity on us; but it is a greater grace [Col. 1700A] when one who has inflicted evil upon us undeservedly takes pity on us. Greatest of all is when one who, though we deserved good from him, received evil from us, takes pity on us in return for good.

The Lord did this. Hence the Apostle says: “Not because [Note: [Col. 1699D] The Vulgate has *quasi*—‘as though.’] we loved him, but because he first loved us” (1 John 4). And elsewhere: “When we were enemies, we were reconciled by his blood” [Note: [Col. 1699D] The Vulgate has: “to God through the blood of his Son.”] (Romans 5).

Therefore, brothers, let us strive to imitate Christ. We imitate Christ if we reconcile our enemies to ourselves through acts of kindness.

To whom did he appear? “To all human beings,” with “offering himself” understood. Although God’s grace has not been acknowledged by everyone, God nevertheless offered it to us insofar as it depended on him. Just as the sun, insofar as it depends on it, shines upon everyone, and no one can withdraw himself so that it will not shine upon him.

Therefore, brothers, since God’s grace [Col. 1700B] offers itself to us all, let us not withdraw from it, but rather run toward it with all our desire. Let us not misuse time and the other gifts of God provided for us to do good; let us not pass them by idly, nor use them negligently, since, according to the Gospel, the person who hides his talent is justly deprived of it (Matthew 25), and the fig tree that occupies the ground is cut down (Matthew 21), and according to Jeremiah: “Cursed is the one who performs the work of God negligently” (Jeremiah 48).

For what benefits did Christ appear? For four.

The first, brothers, is that he might show us by word and example how we should live and toward what we should hasten. The Apostle sets this forth when he says: “Teaching us that, renouncing impiety”—that is, unbelief—“and worldly desires”—that is, all vices—“we should live soberly” [Col. 1700C] in relation to ourselves, justly in relation to our neighbor, and piously in relation to God, awaiting with confidence the blessed hope and the coming of the Lord.

The order is inverted: “the coming of God,” namely, the second coming for judgment; and “the blessed hope,” that is, the hope of blessedness.

The second benefit for which Christ appeared is that he might demonstrate the love he had for us by being born, suffering, and dying for us, in accordance with what he himself says: “No one has a greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15). The Apostle sets forth this reason when he says: “Who gave himself for us.”

The third benefit for which Christ appeared was to make satisfaction for the first transgression. That transgression was pride so great that the human mind raised itself [Col. 1700D] to equality with God. But since contrary things are cured by contrary things, it was necessary that, in satisfaction for that pride, some human being should be humbled from the height of divinity to the humility of humanity.

No one could do this unless he were God and man. Therefore God became man. The Apostle indicates this reason when he says: “an offering” [Note: [Col. 1700D] The Vulgate does not have *oblationem*—“an offering.”] to God, namely, to reconcile humanity.

The fourth reason, and our benefit, for which Christ appeared is the redemption, cleansing, and satisfaction of the human race: redemption from the power of the devil through Christ’s blood; cleansing from sins through baptism; satisfaction through the power and works of the virtues. [Col. 1701A]

The Apostle indicates this when he says: “a sacrifice” [Note: [Col. 1700D] The Vulgate does not have *hostiam*—“a sacrifice.”], namely, to overcome the enemy, so that he might cleanse for himself an acceptable people, a people devoted to good works.

In the first reason, therefore, brothers, Christ showed himself to be the true teacher, instructing us by word and example. In the second, he showed himself to be the true friend, giving himself over for us. In the third, he showed himself to be the supreme high priest, reconciling us to the Father by the offering of his own blood, in accordance with the saying: “And in the time of wrath he became reconciliation” (Ecclesiasticus 44). In the fourth, he showed himself to be our redeemer, purifier, and sanctifier, freeing us from the power of the devil, purifying us from vices, and sanctifying us through virtues.

Therefore, brothers, let us acknowledge that our Lord Jesus Christ is the true and supreme teacher [Col. 1701B], imitating and following his example and teaching. Let us acknowledge that he is our true and supreme friend, repaying him, as far as we can, and laying down our souls for him. Let us acknowledge that he is the true and supreme high priest, offering ourselves to him in purity. Let us acknowledge that he is our true redeemer, purifier, and sanctifier, presenting ourselves to him as those whom he has purchased, cleansed, and sanctified, so that we may deserve to behold him without fear when he comes as judge: our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God. Amen.

## HOMILY XI. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

[Col. 1701C]

“An edict went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be registered” (Luke 2), and the rest.

In this reading of the holy Gospel, beloved brothers, Luke clearly explains to us the reasons for today’s solemnity. Here he explains six things to us: namely, at what time Christ was born; in what place; from whom; how he was raised; by whom; and through what signs he was revealed.

The time at which Christ was born is shown when he says: “An edict went out,” etc.

When Caesar Augustus possessed almost the monarchy of the entire world in such great peace that he could include the whole world in a single registration, Christ wished to be born, beloved brothers, so that even literally that prophecy might then be seen to have been fulfilled: “They shall beat their swords into plowshares and their spears [Col. 1701D] into pruning hooks,” etc. “Nation shall not lift up sword against nation” (Isaiah 2), etc.

As far as the literal sense is concerned, Christ wished to be born at such a time in order to show that he was the Prince of Peace and the Monarch of heaven and earth, and that he would register his own in the book of life.

In the moral sense, however, brothers, the Lord wished to be born under the burden of tribute, so that in himself he might offer us an example of voluntary humility and mutual subjection. If he himself, although he is King of kings and Lord of lords, came into this world for our sake not to rule but to submit, not to be served but to serve, what ought we, wretched servants, to do for his sake?

For his sake, shall I say—or for our own? Better to say, both for his sake [Col. 1702A] and for our own. For we ought to humble ourselves both to gain Christ and to save ourselves.

If God, then, submitted himself to humanity for the sake of humanity, for what reason does a human being refuse to submit to another human being? Therefore, brothers, when we willingly humble ourselves, when we serve and minister to our neighbor, we imitate Christ. But when we desire to rule over people, to be served, and to be ministered to, in this we imitate not him but Satan’s pride.

How, then, brothers, do bishops, priests, and monks follow Christ’s humility and submission when they quarrel over domination, when they desire to subject not only persons but also churches to their authority?

Let us therefore, brothers, follow the safer and firmer way of Christ’s humility and submission, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “If you are a slave, do not be concerned; but if you can become free, make use of it rather” (1 Corinthians 7).

Mystically, while Caesar Augustus—that is, the proud devil—was already exercising tyranny over almost the whole world and enrolling it into his service, Christ was born.

“This registration,” he says, “was first made by the governor of Syria, Quirinius”—that is, by the first apostate, who through pride usurped domination over the angels under him. Quirinius (*Cyrinus*) is interpreted as “ruling” or “lord.”

“And they went, each one, to register in his own city.”

The city of the avaricious is avarice. The city of the lustful is lust. The city of the gluttonous is gluttony. The avaricious went and gathered together through their consent in the vice of avarice, so that, if not with the mouth, then at least by their works, they might profess themselves servants of the devil [Col. 1702C]. The lustful likewise went and gathered together through their consent in the city of lust, so that, if not with the mouth, then at least by their works, they might profess themselves servants of the devil—and similarly with the other vicious.

So greatly, brothers, had this service of the devil prevailed before Christ’s coming that even Christ’s mother and her husband—that is, the Synagogue and the priesthood—went to Bethlehem, that is, to the love of an earthly rather than a heavenly bread, thereby making their profession to the devil.

The winter and night in which Christ was born also signify the misery in which the world then was. When the whole world was therefore in such great slavery, Christ was born, “made a helper in times of trouble” (Psalm 9).

But even today, brothers—and I cannot say this without groaning—many false Christians, after being emancipated from the devil’s slavery through Christ, return by sinning to the devil’s service. For whoever does the devil’s works, what else does he do than make a profession to the devil? “Whoever commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8); and whoever does the works of the devil is a slave of the devil.

The place where Christ was born is shown when it is said: “In the city of David, which is called Bethlehem” [Note: [Col. 1702D] Something appears to be missing there.] “Ephrata, you are by no means least among the rulers of Judah, for from you shall come forth a ruler who will govern my people Israel” (Micah 5; Matthew 3).

It is fitting that he who is the true bread, destined to refresh his own with outward nourishment, should be born in Bethlehem, which is interpreted as “house of bread.” It is also fitting that he should be born not in his parents’ house but [Col. 1703A] on the way, to show by this that, in the humanity he had assumed, he was born as though in a foreign place.

I say “foreign,” not with regard to authority but with regard to nature. In this we too, brothers, are reminded that not only he but all of us human beings, when we are born into this world, come not into our homeland but onto the road, into pilgrimage and exile.

Hence David, although a wealthy king, says: “I am a sojourner and a pilgrim, like all my fathers” (Psalm 39).

For this reason, brothers, when an infant is born, he can weep but cannot laugh. Christ himself weeps. But other infants weep out of necessity; Christ weeps out of gracious condescension. Other infants weep because they suffer; Christ because he suffers with us.

If Christ, then, brothers [Col. 1703B], weeps for our sake, why do we not weep for our own sake? And if we infants weep because of the weakness of nature, why, as adults who understand our misery, do we not weep even more?

Let us therefore consider, brothers, how great human misery is, for the healing of which Christ had to weep; and let us not scorn the great remedy provided for us by so great a one, but let us venerate, love, and imitate it with such devotion.

From whom Christ was born is shown when it is added:

Because they were [Note: [Col. 1703D] Vulgate: “was”] of the house and family of David—namely, Joseph and Mary. For each man, according to the law, took a wife from his own tribe.

Christ, then, brothers, was born of a noble mother, but a poor one; a virgin, but betrothed. That he was born of a noble mother signifies mystery; that he was born of a poor one signifies humility; that he was born of a virgin signifies purity; that he was born of a betrothed woman signifies a sacrament.

He was born of a noble mother, who derived her origin not only from a royal lineage but also from a priestly one. Hence Elizabeth is mentioned as having been related to Mary (Luke 1). Christ therefore willed to be born from a royal and priestly tribe because he was to be King of kings and Priest according to the order of Melchizedek.

He was born of a poor mother, since she was unable to offer even a lamb at her purification, so that he might give us an example of voluntary humility and poverty. He was born of a mother who remained always a virgin, so that he might demonstrate that he loves purity and dwells in pure hearts. He willed to be born of a betrothed mother so that he might conceal from the devil the sacrament of his incarnation.

The mother of Christ, dearest brothers, who did not exalt herself in her nobility but loved poverty and humility, reproves those who take pride in nobility and hate humility and poverty. In this respect, too, she reproves those who think little of degenerating from their natural nobility through poverty.

Again, brothers, in that she adorned marriage with virginal chastity, she gives married women an example of preserving chastity within marriage. If they wholly abstain even from lawful intercourse, they plainly imitate the chastity of the blessed Virgin. But even if at times they render what is owed to their husband, they are not without the merit of chastity, provided that they keep the fidelity of the marriage bed [Col. 1704A] undefiled.

In this also—that the blessed Virgin concealed her virginity under marriage—she gives everyone an example of concealing chastity and the other virtues. For the flowers of virtue flourish and give off fragrance before God all the more abundantly the less popular approval scorches them.

Likewise Joseph, dearest brothers, who was chosen from among all men to be the Virgin’s husband, the confidant of heavenly secrets, familiar with angels, and the foster-father of Christ, is set before men as an example of justice and faith, humility and chastity. He too adorned marriage with chastity and concealed chastity beneath marriage.

What kind of upbringing Christ received is shown when it is said: “And she wrapped him in swaddling clothes and laid him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the lodging.” Christ’s clothing, therefore, was coarse cloth; his bed, a narrow manger; his food, virginal milk. For I do not believe that he ate milk drawn from corrupted flesh. Hence we also read: “The Virgin alone nursed at her breast, full of heaven, the King of angels.”

In this upbringing, dearest brothers, we find four things.

First, admiration: he who dwells in inaccessible light and clothed heaven with light is wrapped in coarse cloth; he who contains the whole world is contained in a narrow manger; he who gives food to all at the proper time is nourished on a little milk. Who could fail to marvel at these things?

Second, a ministry: the Lord willed to be clothed in swaddling clothes in order to show that he had put on our lowliness and corruptibility; he willed to be laid in a manger in order to signify that he himself is the nourishment of the godly; he willed to be fed with virginal milk in order to demonstrate that he delights in the pure teaching of Mother Church.

Third, a medicine: the Lord deigned to be wrapped in coarse cloth for us so that he might clothe us in the robe of incorruption; he willed to be laid in a narrow manger for us so that he might place us in the spacious palace of heaven; he willed to require nourishment of milk for us so that he might satisfy us with the bread of angels.

Fourth, an example: he was wrapped in coarse cloth for our sake so that we would not shrink from the lowliness of swaddling clothes for his sake but love it; he was placed for our sake in a cramped manger so that for his sake we would be content with a small and humble dwelling; he was fed with simple food so that we too might learn to be content with simplicity and the lowliness of our food.

And this, my brothers, is directed against those who delight in costly and soft garments, who glory in the construction of palaces and towers, and who are ensnared by their appetite for expensive foods.

To whom Christ willed to be revealed is shown when it is added:

“And there were shepherds in that region, keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night over their flock.”

In the literal sense, brothers, Christ, as the true shepherd, as the humble one and the poor one, first willed to be revealed to shepherds, humble people, and the poor. In the mystical sense, these shepherds of flocks signify all shepherds of faithful souls. If they are in the same region, if they keep watch over their flock and guard the watches of the night, the Lord will certainly deign especially to reveal to them the secrets of his mysteries.

These are shepherds in the same region in which the Lord was born: they strive, as far as they can, to govern themselves in the purity and chastity in which Christ was born and remained. They keep watch over their flock who are solicitous in governing the souls entrusted to them.

Here, too, dearest brothers, we must consider that it says “over their flock.” For it is not enough for shepherds to be like the people in knowledge and life. Hence, as a reproach, it is said to them: “And it shall be as with the people, so with the priest” (Ecclesiasticus 24). And just as the shepherd is superior in rank, so he ought to excel in wisdom and life. Hence it is also said: “Ascend a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion” (Isaiah 40). This is why the priest received a separated shoulder (Leviticus 10), because the shepherd’s action ought to be not only strong but also distinguished.

They guard the watches of the night over their flock who strive to instruct the people entrusted to them in youth, manhood, old age, and decrepitude. Those whom they could not correct in youth, they at least desire to correct in manhood, old age, or decrepitude.

But how, brothers, is it said here that they were guarding the watches of the night over their flock, when it is not in a man’s power to guard either himself or another—especially since it is written: “Unless the Lord guards the city, he watches in vain who guards it” (Psalm 126)?

A shepherd cannot lie down alone but only with a companion, nor can he go to the Lord alone but only with a companion. It is certainly true, my brothers, that it is not in the shepherd’s power to guard the flock; nevertheless, the obligation of his office requires him to keep watch over its protection as far as he can.

For if one of you entrusted a hundred sheep to his shepherd, and the shepherd, after all the sheep had been devoured and lost, returned alone to his master, what would his master say to him? Would he not imprison him or drive him away in disgrace?

What, then, brothers, what will God say to that lazy shepherd who brings none of the souls entrusted to him back to God? Will he not condemn him more severely than the others as the murderer of many souls? Certainly. For “a stricter judgment will be made of those who are in authority” (Wisdom 6).

By what signs Christ willed to be revealed is shown when it is said:

“And behold, an angel of the Lord stood beside them, and his radiance surrounded them.” [Note: [Col. 1705D] Vulgate: “the radiance of God.”]

It is fitting, brothers, that the angel announcing Christ’s birth is read to have stood. Standing is the posture of those who fight. He announced the birth of the one who came to battle the powers of the air. But the angel who announced his resurrection sat upon the rolled-away stone, because he was announcing one who already sat there as victor.

It is also fitting that the angel announcing the birth is remembered as having stood beside the shepherds, because he proclaimed that Christ would become near and propitious to human beings through the flesh and through mercy, according to the words: “His salvation is near those who fear him” (Psalm 84).

It is also fitting that the angel appeared with light at Christ’s birth—a phenomenon not read of throughout the whole Old Testament—because, according to the Prophet, then “light rose in the darkness for the upright in heart: the merciful and compassionate Lord” (Psalm 111).

“And they were afraid,” it says, “with great fear,” because human weakness is shaken when divine sublimity is revealed. But because they were worthy of consolation, the angel said to them: “Do not be afraid.” For just as it belongs to the devil and to devilish people to urge a person toward trembling and despair, so it belongs to good angels and good people to offer a person consolation and hope.

Why the shepherds ought not to fear but to rejoice, the angel shows when he adds: “Behold, I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people”—that is, the elect.

The angel announces great and common joy to the shepherds, brothers, because there is a kind of joy that is not great but small—or rather, no joy at all—such as the joy that is had over some transitory thing, concerning which it is said: “Woe to you who laugh!” (Luke 6). But this joy was great because it concerned our salvation. Again, it was common because it was to be shared with every believing person.

For this reason God became human: so that he might make human beings gods and share with many the joy that he possessed alone. This is directed, brothers, against those who wish to live only for themselves and refuse to communicate the good they possess to others. Therefore they are justly deprived of the common good of the saints.

What that joy is, the angel explains when he adds:

“For today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David.”

The angel calls the child by three names, brothers: Savior, Christ, and Lord. Christ, because he is anointed with the fullness of every grace, from whom we have all received; Savior, because he saves and glorifies the elect; Lord, because he condemns the reprobate.

But why does he say “today,” since Christ was born at night? Because Christ made that night bright and solemn through the sacrament of his birth, according to what is written: “And the night shall be illuminated as the day; and the night is my illumination in my delights” (Psalm 138).

He is said to have been born “in the city of David” in order to show that the one who was to be born in Bethlehem according to the prophets is truly the Christ.

But because the Jews ask for signs, the angel adds:

“And this will be a sign for you: you will find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger.”

It is as though he said: “You can prove what I say when you recognize as true both the things absent that I announce and the things future that I foretell. Once you have recognized me as truthful in these matters, you will not doubt that I am truthful in the others as well.”

The angel placed the sign in Christ’s humility and poverty, in order to show us by what means we would be saved and what we ought to imitate.

Moreover, lest the testimony of one angel seem insufficient, the testimony not merely of two or three but also of many is added, when it is said:

“And there was with the angel”—that is, joined with him in testimony—“a multitude of the heavenly host praising God and saying: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

It is as though he said: Through Christ’s birth, God is glorified and blessed by the heavenly powers, because the angelic ruin is repaired through the restoration of humanity, and peace and reconciliation with God are granted to people of good will.

He does not say “to people of good works,” because good works without good will are insufficient. Good will without good works, however, can suffice when ability is lacking.

Therefore, my brothers, if you cannot labor greatly, give generously, or fast extensively, at least have good will. If it is ready, it will unquestionably be reckoned as a deed. For God does not consider how much someone offers, but from how much.

Peter and Andrew, after all, left their boat and nets (Matthew 4), and are judged to have left everything (Matthew 19). The widow offered two small coins, and she is preferred to the rich who offered much (Luke 21).

Let us too offer, brothers, what we can. If we lack the means, let us at least offer good will, because Christ’s birth gives peace to people of good will.

May he himself grant it to us who on this day deigned to be born for us from the Virgin, Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XII. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

[Col. 1707C] “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1), and what follows.

With good reason, dearest brothers, the apostle and evangelist John is called Boanerges—that is, “son of thunder” (Mark 3): first, because on the mountain, with his brother James and Peter, he heard the Father’s voice thunder over the Son: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 17); and second, because he deserved to thunder so loftily about the coeternity of that same Word with the Father.

The son of thunder, therefore, is the one who speaks here, and what he speaks is thunder. For he speaks in the loftiest, darkest, heavenly—or rather super-heavenly—manner. What he says surpasses every understanding, not only human but angelic.

Hence, not without reason, in the figure of the four living creatures he is compared to a flying eagle—one that soars aloft and flies higher than the other winged creatures. The other evangelists, who adequately explain Christ’s temporal birth and the temporal deeds he performed as a human being, and who said little about his divinity, are like walking creatures that travel on earth with the Lord.

But John, while saying little about his temporal deeds and contemplating the power of his divinity more sublimely, flies with the Lord toward heaven.

Such qualities suited such a person, because he was lofty in life, lofty in understanding, and lofty in teaching. He was lofty in life because he was chosen by the Lord as a virgin; because he was loved by the Lord above the others; because, reclining upon the Lord’s breast (John 21), he drew more deeply from him; because the Lord entrusted his virgin mother to that virgin (John 19); and because he revealed his secrets to him more familiarly and profoundly than to the others.

Therefore, just as he flew most loftily on the wing of virtue, so he saw most loftily with the eye of contemplation, and so he thundered most loftily in the word of preaching.

He surpasses and outflies not only the other evangelists but even himself, according to what Ezekiel said: “The face of an eagle was above all four of them” (Ezekiel 1). For when he describes the eagle as being above not only three but four, he plainly signifies that John outflies not only the other evangelists but also himself.

Indeed, when speaking of the eternal birth of the Word, John’s understanding outflies the whole universe—and outflies his own understanding as well—because, illumined by the grace of the Holy Spirit, he both sees and sounds forth more than a human being.

The apostle Paul also bears witness to this: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him. But God has revealed it to us through his Spirit” (1 Corinthians 2).

It is as though he openly said that those illumined by the Holy Spirit contemplate realities beyond human understanding—indeed, more than they merely observe.

Hence the Lord himself, when he had asked his disciples, saying, “Who do people say the Son of Man is?” (Matthew 16), and they had reported human opinions, said: “But who do you say that I am?” (ibid.).

It is as though he said: “Those people speak only what is human, possessing merely human wisdom. But you, who through the grace of the Holy Spirit see more than human beings, who do you say that I am?”

Thus our spiritual eagle, flying beyond the whole created order, first thunders that Christ is consubstantial with God the Father before all ages; second, that all things were made through him; third, that through him humanity’s ruin was restored.

First, therefore, he thunders that Christ was consubstantial with God the Father before all ages, saying:

“In the beginning was the Word.”

In these words truth is intimated, heretical falsehood is slain, and the surpassing excellence of this evangelist is demonstrated.

Truth is indeed intimated to us in these words, provided that, with the Spirit revealing it, we attentively perceive the transference of the words themselves. In temporal matters, we come to knowledge of words through knowledge of things. In divine matters, however, it is necessary for us to arrive at whatever slight understanding of things we can attain through knowledge of the words.

For if we were addressed about unknown things by means of unknown names, no instruction would come to us. Therefore theologians had to borrow, from the known things of the created order and by some proportion of likeness, names with which to speak; and thus, through known words, to disclose to us some small knowledge of an unknown reality.

When such names as “Son,” “Word,” “Radiance,” “Mirror,” and the like are transferred to theology, no one should think that they retain there the meaning of their original invention. Rather, one should wisely investigate the reason for their transference. Nor should anyone suppose that the transference establishes an absolute likeness or proportion, since there is no comparison between creatures and the Creator. The theologian has spoken to us of the ineffable reality by whatever indications he was able to provide.

Logos (Greek: λόγος), therefore, for which we have the term “word,” has three meanings. It signifies reason; it also signifies a word conceived in the heart; and it signifies a word uttered.

Logos, or “word,” is transferred quite suitably from each of these meanings to signify the Son of God.

The Son is called the Logos of God, or the Father’s reason, in a proportionate sense: just as reason is coeternal with a human being, so, in his own manner, the Son of God is coeternal with God the Father. And just as a human being acts wisely through reason and wisdom, so God the Father wisely works all things through his Son. Hence it is said to him through the Wise One: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Psalm 103).

Again, the term is not incongruously transferred from a word conceived in the mind to signify the Son of God, because just as a word conceived in the mind arises from the mind and remains with the mind, so, in his own manner, the Son of God arises from God the Father and always remains with him. Hence it is said to him through the Psalmist: “Forever, O Lord, your word remains in heaven” (Psalm 118).

Again, the term is transferred proportionately from an uttered word to the Son of God, because just as a human being brings forth a word from his mouth, through it makes his will known to others, and through the command of his word accomplishes his work, so, in his own manner, God the Father begot from his substance God the Son. The Son himself testifies to this: “I, Wisdom, came forth from the mouth of the Father, the firstborn before every creature” (Ecclesiasticus 24). Through him the Father works, as the Psalmist testifies: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Psalm 32). And through the same Son the Father makes his will known to human beings, as the Son himself testifies: “I have manifested your name to the people” (John 17).

The substantive verb “I am” also signifies a simple and solitary substance. The divine essence likewise is a simple and solitary substance. It is a substance because it is a reality existing in itself, needing nothing else, whereas all other things need it for their existence. It is simple because it is without parts and without any combination of forms. It is solitary because it is without the addition of any forms.

Although God is called one, true, wise, just, and pious, none of these qualities in God is plural; all are one and the same reality.

For this reason the verb “I am” is more properly predicated of God than other verbs, and especially in the present tense. Hence God himself said to Moses: “I am who I am. Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exodus 3).

It is as though he openly said: “I alone truly am.” For all other things, in comparison with divine eternity, are not, because they are subject to generation and corruption, increase and decrease, alteration and movement from place to place; and according to the changes of time they come and go.

God alone truly is, because he is eternal, immutable, and always present. Eternal: without beginning and end. Immutable: without any variation of movements. Always present: without temporal accession or recession.

Therefore, if we look toward the presence of divine eternity, we find that he always specifically is, and that he never was or will be.

Nevertheless, when we wish to signify that God is absent from no time and transcends all times, since we are temporal and cannot speak without temporal verbs, we improperly employ the past and future tense in speaking of God. Hence John says: “Who was, and who is, and who is to come” (Revelation 11).

Similarly, here he says:

“In the beginning was the Word.”

With careful precision he does not say “was” in the sense of a completed past, nor “had been,” but says “was.” “Was” in the completed past indicates a fully completed past; “had been” indicates a pluperfect past, and therefore fits God less well. But “was,” because it indicates a past not yet completed, is more closely joined to the present tense and is used with greater significance.

This Word was “in the beginning,” whether of time or of creatures; for time and creation are coeval. It is therefore as though he said: “The Word did not begin to be at the beginning of time, because the Word was before the beginning of time.”

That the evangelist understood it in this way is proved by the fact that he confirms that all things were made through the same Word. For if both time and all creatures were made through the Word, it is plainly evident that the author preceded all the things he made.

Hence later he prays to the Father: “Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (John 17).

Therefore, what preceded all time is eternal. And what made every creature is the Creator.

It may also be said that “the Word was in the beginning,” that is, in the Father. The Word, therefore, was in the Father: the beginning in the Beginning.

The Son testifies that he is the Beginning when, asked by the Jews, “Who are you?” (John 8), he answered: “The Beginning, who also speaks to you.” But the Father is Beginning without beginning. The Son, just as he is God from God, is Beginning from Beginning. Yet there are not two beginnings but one Beginning.

Hence the Father himself says to the Son: “With you is the Beginning” (Psalm 109), that is, “it is with me.”

The Father, moreover, is called Beginning for three reasons. He is the Beginning of the Son through generation. He is the Beginning of the Holy Spirit through spiration. And he is the Beginning of creatures through creation.

The Son is called Beginning for two reasons. He is, with the Father, the Beginning of the Holy Spirit through spiration. And he is the Beginning of creatures through creation.

The Holy Spirit is called Beginning in only one respect: he is, with the Father and the Son, the one Beginning of creatures through creation.

But how was the Word in the Beginning—that is, in the Father—as one like another? For as the Father is, so is the Son. If it is said of two things that are very similar, by an explicit likeness, that one is in the other—so that whoever sees one sees the other—how much more may this be said of God the Father and his Son, whose essence is not merely similar but one and the same?

Hence, when Philip said to the Lord, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14), he heard from him: “Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father also. Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?”

“And the Word,” he says, “was with God.”

Certainly, the preposition “with” here indicates not a location but a personal distinction. Strictly speaking, nothing is said to be “with itself” or “with itself as companion,” unless perhaps this is said figuratively of someone who is with himself because, through mental alienation, he is not outside himself.

Thus, “in the beginning the Word was with God,” as one person with another.

“And God was the Word”: “God” must be understood as predicated. Here it is not who the Son of God was that is shown, but what he was.

“This was with God.” Since the evangelist had used the appellative noun “word” in three clauses, in order to exclude the charge of equivocation and confusion, he shows by means of the demonstrative pronoun that he is weaving his account concerning the same person of the Word.

Among the Greeks, however, it is not the neuter “this” but the masculine “this one” that is used, because *logos* is masculine in gender. Therefore the pronoun may be referred either to Logos or to Theos (Greek: θεός), but the sense remains the same.

Let us consider, brothers, that this evangelist says five things about the Word: when he was, where he was, what he was, with whom he was, and what he was doing.

When was he? “In the beginning was the Word.”

Where was he? “And the Word was with God.”

What was he? “And God was the Word.”

With whom was he? “For God was with God.”

What was he doing? “All things were made through him.”

In the first statement he demonstrates the Word’s coeternity with the Father; in the second, personal distinction; in the third, his divinity; in the fourth, his identity with the Father together with his distinction from him; and in the fifth, his authority to act.

The same wording also rebukes heretical falsehood.

There were heretics who said: “If the Son of God was born, then he did not always exist.” John refutes them at the beginning when he says: “In the beginning was the Word.”

Again, there were heretics who said: “The same God is sometimes the Father, sometimes the Son, and sometimes the Holy Spirit.” John also refutes this when he adds: “And the Word was with God.”

Again, there were heretics who, although they said that the Son of God had always been distinct from the Father, denied that he was God. John also rebukes them when it is added: “And God was the Word.”

There were heretics who, although they granted that Christ was God, nevertheless insisted that he was not God by nature but God by adoption and for a time. John likewise condemns them when he adds: “This was in the beginning with God.”

There were also heretics who maintained that all visible things had been made by the devil, while only invisible things had been made by the Word of God.

These same words also demonstrate the evangelist’s excellence. The other evangelists describe Christ as having been born in time; John testifies that he existed in the beginning, saying: “In the beginning was the Word.”

The others mention that he suddenly appeared among human beings; John declares that he had always been with God, saying: “And the Word was with God.”

The others present him as a true human being; John affirms that he is truly God, saying: “And God was the Word.”

The others describe him as having dwelt among human beings for a time; John shows him remaining eternally with God, saying: “This was in the beginning with God.”

The others report the mighty deeds he performed as a human being; John shows that every visible and invisible creature was made through him, saying:

“All things were made through him.”

This is the second part, in which the evangelist says three things about the Word of God: that every good thing was made through him, that no evil thing was made through him, and that what was made in time always existed in the Word.

He says that every good thing was made through him when he says: “All things were made through him.”

When he says “all things,” he excludes nothing but embraces every creature, both visible and invisible: things subject to forms as well as the forms of subjects; individual members of genera as well as the genera of individuals; the operations of genera as well as the genera of operations.

He worked all things from eternity in the present. Hence it is also written of him: “He who made the things that are to be, and immediately.”

He worked in the beginning by creating all bodies in matter. Hence it is written: “He who lives forever created all things together” (Ecclesiasticus 18).

He worked through six days by distinguishing and forming new kinds of things from the elements. Because of this newness, he is read to have rested on the Sabbath day (Genesis 2).

He still works by governing all things, propagating like from like, and creating new souls. Hence he himself says: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5).

He also works through the ministry of craftsmen. Hence it is written: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Psalm 126).

He worked our salvation in the fullness of time.

He worked—and still works every day—the works of miracles, the works of virtues, the works of mercy, and the works of justice.

Some of these things he works solely by himself; some through the ministry of subordinate nature; some through the ministry of rational creation. Yet he alone is the author of all things.

This plainly refutes those who think that, through their own strength, intelligence, or industry, they can be able, willing, or active in some good. Hence the Apostle says: “It is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish” (Philippians 2). And elsewhere: “Not I alone, but the grace of God with me” (1 Corinthians 15). Mark likewise says: “They went forth and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word through the accompanying signs” (Mark 16).

But when you hear “the grace of God with me” or “the Lord working with me,” take care not to understand the preposition “with,” or the prefix “co-,” as signifying number here—for propriety and impropriety do not fall within the category of number. Rather, understand them to designate ministry or instrumentality.

For it is not that we and the Lord work together as two agents; rather, he works with us as with ministers or as with certain instruments.

We have said all this because it is written “all things.” When it is then added, “through him,” take care not to understand the preposition “through” as indicating ministry; understand it rather as indicating authority.

For the Father does not work through the Son as through a minister, especially since the Son has the same authority and power as the Father. The Father is said to work through the Son, and not the Son through the Father, because the authority to act that the Son possesses he has from the Father, whereas the Father does not have it from the Son.

Having thus shown that all good things were made through the Word, the text consequently shows that no evil was made through him, when it adds:

And without him nothing was made—that is, sin or vice. This is what James says in his canonical Epistle: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow caused by turning” (James I). It is as though he were plainly saying: God confers good things in such a way that he does not cause evil; he changes people from evil to good in such a way that he does not change them from good to evil; he illumines people with the light of virtues [Col. 1713B] in such a way that he does not, in turn, overshadow them with the darkness of vices. For when God is read to blind or harden the wicked, he does this not by infusing the darkness of vices, but by withdrawing the light of his grace.

Nevertheless, it must be observed that the word “evil” has three meanings in Holy Scripture. Sometimes punishment, tribulation, anxiety, or scourging is called evil; and since these are imposed by the supreme Judge in just judgment, they are undoubtedly from God. Hence it is written: “There is no evil in the city which the Lord has not done” (Amos III), in accordance with what he himself says through Isaiah: “I am God and there is no other, forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evil” (Isaiah XLVIII).

At other times a thing that is bad is called evil, such as a bad person or a bad action. Insofar as such a thing is from God as its author, it is good. At still other times evil means malice or injustice, and every kind of sin. Since this is a privation of justice, it is nothing, and therefore it is not from God.

When, then, we read that sin, vice, or an idol is nothing, a distinction is necessary. If the statement concerns the thing designated by the name, it is false, since that which is called sin or an idol is not nothing. Homicide, for example, is a cruel and monstrous act, and an idol is a body. But if the statement concerns the quality signified by the name, it is certainly true. For that from which an idol received its name is nothing, since the corresponding divinity that false human opinion attributes to it is entirely nothing. Similarly, that from which homicide is so called is nothing, since it is not a privation of nature but rather of justice and what is due.

And when we investigate the matter more subtly, no act, however perverse, is deprived of its proper end. For although the agent’s evil intention, so far as it is able, perverts the act, nevertheless the supreme Author always directs his work toward its proper end, namely, the praise of his justice or mercy. Yet the wicked minister is justly condemned on that account, because he deprived the act, so far as he was able, of its proper end—just as the man who wished to betray the king is condemned, not because he betrayed him, but because he did what was in him to do so.

After the Evangelist had said that all things were made through the Word, lest anyone should think that, in accordance with the coming into being and mutability of things, God’s will and disposition also came into being and changed, so that he had suddenly willed something, he shows that the things made in time had always been and are present in the divine mind through its foreknowledge and disposition, when he adds: “What was made in him was life.” This is what is read elsewhere: “Who made the things that are to be.” Hence the Psalmist also says: “For the people that shall be born, whom the Lord has made” (Psalm XXI).

Whatever God was going to do in time, he foresaw from eternity: what, how much, of what kind, where, and when he would do it. For if a temporal architect, intending to make a chest, first possesses it in his mind through foreknowledge and afterward constructs and shapes it according to the pattern in his mind—and while the material chest perishes, the mental chest [Col. 1714B] remains, so that another and another thing can be made according to its pattern—how much more does the pattern of the divine mind remain immutable, although the things made according to it come and go in time?

The third part follows, in which the Evangelist begins to demonstrate that the ruin of humanity was repaired through the Word of God. He proceeds in this way. First, he demonstrates that the Word of God, which gave other things being or life, also gave human beings knowledge of their Creator. Second, that humanity lost this through its own fault. Third, how humanity recovered it through the Word of God.

First, therefore, he shows that the Word of God, which gave other things essence or life, also gave human beings knowledge of him, when he adds: “And the life was the light of human beings.” It is as though he were plainly saying: The Word, which by metonymy was essence for some things and life for others, was for human beings essence, life, and light.
