For God gave knowledge of himself not to insensible things or brute animals, but only to the rational creature.

Moreover, God illumines human beings in three ways: through the discernment of reason; through the illumination of faith and of the other graces; and through the revelation of himself. He accomplishes the first when he creates a person, the second when he recreates that person, and the third when he glorifies that person. The first belongs to human nature, the second to grace, and the third is the eternal reward.

Hence it is also written that he formed humanity according to his image and likeness (Genesis I): according to his image in reason, and according to his likeness in goodness. Thus, just as God is rational and good, so, in its own manner, humanity would be reasonable and good; and by reason it would know how to distinguish true from false, good from evil, and greater good from lesser good. In this way, above all things, it would discover and recognize the true and highest Good, while by goodness it would imitate and worship him.

Accordingly, when the Psalmist had posed the question of certain people who said, “Who will show us good things?” (Psalm IV), he immediately showed who had shown us good things when he added: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (ibid.). The countenance of God is the Son, through whom God is known; his light is called the grace of his virtues, whose ray marks and distinguishes us—and this “upon us,” that is, in the higher part of reason, in which alone the mark of God shines greatly, like a pattern in a mirror and the form of a seal impressed upon wax. For this part of us originally tastes, loves, and seeks the highest Good, and naturally always returns and tends toward its pattern and principle.

As the Psalmist testifies when he addresses him: “My heart has said to you, ‘My face has sought you’; your face, O Lord, I shall seek” (Psalm XXVI). And the more the divine image in us is purified from vices and made like God through virtues, the more it knows, burns for, and seeks him.

But while the mind is weighed down by its dwelling in the flesh, it cannot entirely avoid the filth of vices, nor imitate all the virtues of Christ, nor attain perfect possession of even those virtues it does possess. Therefore, in this life, it cannot contemplate the highest Good except, as the Apostle says, “through a mirror and in an enigma.” For here we know in part and prophesy in part. But when what is perfect has come, once mortality has been laid aside and every cloud removed, “we shall see him face to face” and “as he is” (1 Corinthians XIII; 1 John III).

Those, however, who neglect to purify the divine image within themselves, allowing it gradually to be obscured by vices, not only lose the divine likeness, but the image itself is diminished and clouded in them. Thus, forgetting God and heaven, for which they were created, they bend down to the earth with all their desires, like beasts, according to the Psalmist: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to foolish beasts and became like them” (Psalm XLVIII).

Nevertheless, even if the divine image in us is violated and darkened by the filth of vices, it is not entirely suffocated and destroyed. Rather, in every sinner, however great, the spark of reason always lives: it accuses the conscience, condemns evil, and commends good.

Hence, in the Gospel of Luke, the man who fell among robbers is said to have been stripped and wounded, but is by no means said to have been killed; rather, he was left half alive (Luke X). And this is what the Evangelist adds here: “And the light shines in the darkness.” It is as though he were plainly saying: Although human beings make themselves dark through their own fault and, so far as they are able, drive the divine light away from themselves, nevertheless the divine light is reflected in their minds as in its own mirror, accusing and condemning them.

Nor does the image of the Creator shine only in the mind; it also shines in the elements and in the other creatures, since the permanence, beauty, goodness, and wisdom of creation demonstrate the permanence, beauty, goodness, and wisdom of the Creator.

“And the darkness,” he says, “did not comprehend it”—that is, it did not understand it—not because it could not, but because it did not wish to. For they did not wish to understand so as to act well; or, certainly, however many vices darkened human beings and wrapped them round, they could not entirely comprehend—that is, extinguish—the divine image in their minds. This image will accuse them when they are placed in hell, and the worm of an evil conscience will torment them forever.

The following comes next: “There was a man sent by God.” Here the Evangelist begins to discuss the redemption, or restoration, of the human race, against those who said that human nature had been so corrupted in the first-created man that it would perish irreparably.

He proceeds in this way. First, he demonstrates that human redemption was foretold; second, through whom it was accomplished; third, that it was not received by everyone; fourth, what good it bestowed upon those who received it; fifth, how it was accomplished; sixth, by whose testimonies it was confirmed.

Although it had been prefigured from the beginning of the world, first by the patriarchs and then by the prophets, the Evangelist, for the sake of brevity, passes over those things that he would fittingly set forth in their appropriate places and begins with the nearer prediction of the Forerunner, who preceded the approaching sun like the morning star, and the approaching day like the dawn.

He therefore describes him as being such as it was fitting for the Forerunner of the Redeemer to be, and as one who deserved to be believed. He commends him by his nature, dignity, name, and office.

He commends him by his nature when he says, “There was a man sent by God.” This means: a rational being, illumined by the image and likeness of his Creator. The word “man” is sometimes used in the fullness of its meaning, as when it is said, “Man is a rational and mortal animal.” At other times it is used in only part of that fullness. Then it is used either for the higher aspect, as when it is said, “God created man according to his image and likeness” (Genesis I), or for the lower aspect, as when it is said, “Man, born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries” (Job XIV).

He commends him by his dignity when he says, “Sent by God.” In Greek, ἀπόστολος (*apostolos*), in Latin *missus*, means “sent.” He was therefore a great one: not merely an apostle, but one sent by God before the apostles, and thus made the Apostle of the apostles.

He commends him by his name when he adds: “Whose name was John.” Indeed, John is interpreted as “grace.” And fittingly he bore a name derived from grace, since he was filled with grace and came to preach grace. “The Law and the prophets were until John” (Luke XVI).

He commends him by his office when he adds: “He came for a testimony, to bear witness to the light.” He did not bear witness to the light by chance or incidentally, but was sent specially and principally for this purpose; he came for this, and was concerned with this. “That all,” he says, “might believe through him.” As though he were saying: So far as it depended on him, he made everyone believe. And if anyone did not believe, the failure did not remain in him.

Certainly, these four qualities commended here in John must be sought in every preacher: that he be not brutish but rational and intelligent; that he not thrust himself forward but be sent by God; that he be gracious and pleasing; and that he come not to seek wealth, glory, pleasure, or honor, but to bear witness to the light. How? By working, living, and teaching, so that all, so far as it depends on him, may believe through him, and so that no one among them may remain sunk in spiritual sleep.

John, however, although he shone with such rays of distinction, was not himself the light—understand, not light shining of itself—but rather a lamp illumined by the true Light for the purpose of bearing witness to the light. That is, he was not Christ, but Christ’s Forerunner and herald.

He demonstrates through whom human redemption was accomplished when he adds: “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world.”

Certainly Christ was and is the true light, since he shines not from another but from himself, and from himself illumines others. He is true light both in the truth of his shining and in the truth of his illuminating others from himself. In himself he shines with the light of supreme goodness and with the goodness of supreme light. He illumines others with the truth of light and the light of truth: with the true light of faith, hope, and charity, and with faith, hope, and charity belonging to the true light.

In himself he shines substantially, eternally, and immutably. He illumines others spiritually, universally, and powerfully.

Spiritually, because he illumines not brute animals but only the spiritual and rational creature with the light of his knowledge. Hence he says, “He enlightens the human being.”

Universally, because, like the sun, so far as it depends on him, he illumines everyone—unless someone withdraws himself from his rays. Hence he adds, “every.”

Powerfully, because he purifies and clarifies each and every person, however darkened by sins, so far as it lies in him. Hence it is added, “coming into this world”—that is, falling into the night of this world, equally blinded by the darkness of sins, ignorance, and misery.

He subsequently shows that the true light was not received by everyone when he adds: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him.”

In these words he embraces both Christ’s divine nature, through which he is infused into and present in all creatures, and his human nature, through which he came to us. “He was in the world, and he came into the world.” He was in the world through his divinity, and he came into the world through his humanity. Remaining belongs to divinity, whereas coming or departing belongs to humanity.

It is therefore as though he were saying: Although the Word of God was present in the world through the essence of his divinity and appeared in his creature through its making, governance, and preservation, nevertheless the world—that is, worldly people—did not know him. For this reason he came visibly through the humanity he assumed, so that at least in this way he might be known. And “his own”—that is, human beings, and especially the Jews, his particular people—not merely did not know him, but did not receive him.

He shows what good the Word of God bestowed upon those who received him when he adds: “But as many as received him”—understand, “through faith working by charity” (Galatians VIII)—which he later clarifies when he adds, “to those who believe in his name he gave power to become children of God.”

But do the wicked not have this power? Certainly not. Although they possess free will from themselves toward evil, only the good possess a will liberated by grace toward good, so that they may become children of God and possess by adoption what the Only-Begotten Son of God possesses by nature—namely, the fivefold property of sonship.

What are these? Birth, love, imitation, likeness, and inheritance.

Birth: so that we may be reborn as children from God through the Holy Spirit and water.

Love: so that God may love us as a father and we may love him as children.

Imitation: so that, according to our capacity, we may imitate him in conduct and virtues.

Likeness: so that in the future glorification we may be made like him.

Inheritance: so that we may receive the inheritance of eternal blessedness.

O wondrous condescension of the Son of God, wondrous charity, wondrous fellowship! Wondrous condescension, that one so great chose such little ones as brothers. Wondrous charity, that for our exaltation he humbled himself so greatly. Wondrous fellowship, that he established us, unworthy servants, as co-heirs of his kingdom.

How do human beings become children of God? “Not of bloods”—that is, not from the seeds of parents—“nor of the will of the flesh,” that is, of the woman, “nor of the will of man.” This means: not through the pleasure-seeking will of intercourse, from which the children of Adam are born, “but of God they are born,” through baptism, by which he regenerates them.

He shows how redemption was accomplished when he adds: “And the Word was made flesh.” By synecdoche, he used “flesh” for “human being.”

But could almighty God not have redeemed us in another way? Certainly he could. Yet this way was more fitting, more inflaming, more instructive, more revealing of God to us, and more directing us toward hope.

It was more fitting that, just as a human being had sinned through disobedience, so a human being should make satisfaction through obedience.

It was more inflaming us to love God that he himself loved us so greatly and suffered so much for us.

It was more instructive for us in humility, patience, and charity that he gave himself in this manner, first as an example and teacher.

It was more revealing of God to us that he appeared in human form, although he was incomprehensible in his divine nature.

It directed us more toward hope, since we should not doubt that we can become children of God when, for this very purpose, the Son of God became the son of a human being.

“And he dwelt in us”: through garb, concealment, and association.

Through garb, because in becoming human he wore the garb of our humanity. Hence the Apostle says: “Found in appearance as a man” (Philippians II).

Through concealment, because he veiled his divinity beneath the cloud of flesh in such a way that he appeared to believers but remained hidden from unbelievers. Hence the Apostle says: “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians II).

Through association, because, as the prophet had foretold, “After this he was seen on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch III).

He next shows by whose testimonies our redemption was attested, first introducing the authority of himself and the other apostles when he adds: “And we saw his glory.”

We saw it with the eyes of the flesh; we saw it with the eyes of the mind. With the eyes of the flesh we saw his humanity, glorious in its works and teaching. In that humanity he taught and worked miracles; in it he was transfigured; in it he rose from the dead and ascended into heaven. And thus, through his glorious humanity, we saw with spiritual eyes the inner majesty and glory of his divinity.

“We also saw the glory of the Only-Begotten [Note: [Col. 1717D] The Vulgate reads: ‘glory as of the Only-Begotten.’] from the Father”: glory not as of a minister but as of the Author; not as of some holy person but as of God himself; not as of an adopted son but as of the natural and Only-Begotten Son of God. For here the adverb “as” signifies not mere likeness, but rather an expression of truth.

“We also saw him full of grace and truth”: full of grace, full of truth; full of the truth of grace and the grace of truth.

He was full of grace because, whereas others possess it according to measure, he universally possessed the fullness of all spiritual virtues and gifts.

He was full of truth—that is, of divinity—because in him “all the fullness of divinity was pleased to dwell bodily” (Colossians II).

He was full of the truth of grace because the gracious promises once made to the patriarchs, together with the figures of the Law and the Prophets, were truly fulfilled in him.

He was full of the grace of truth because the divinity that was his true nature became, in a special way, grace to the human being he was.

Let us hold this faith firmly, dearest brothers, and practice it in our works, loving Christ, who loved us so greatly, with our whole heart, and imitating, as far as we can, his voluntary humility, poverty, subjection, obedience, patience, charity, and mercy, so that we may deserve to be children of God and co-heirs of Christ, through the favor of him who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God. Amen.

## HOMILY XIII. THE FIRST SUNDAY AFTER THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

“As long as the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a servant, although he is lord of all; but he is under guardians and stewards until the time predetermined by the father” (Galatians IV).

Because the Apostle, dearest brothers, was a debtor to all human beings, to the wise and the foolish, he uses human and familiar words when speaking about divine matters, so that through what is known we may better understand what is unknown. Hence he says elsewhere: “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh” (Romans VI).

In the preceding chapter, therefore, he compares the heir of the world with the heir of heaven, whether adopted or natural. Let us accordingly examine, in order, first the temporal heir, second the natural heir of heaven, and third the adopted heir of heaven.

You know, my brothers, that in the house of a temporal head of a family there are free persons and servants, but in different ways. For the father loves his son as an heir; nevertheless, while the son is a child, he raises him in poverty, subjection, and discipline.

In poverty, by leaving him control over nothing.

In subjection, by placing him under a tutor.

In discipline, by subjecting him to the teacher’s rod.

And in all these things the father has great affection and love for his son. For a father corrects the son whom he loves more; and the son also loves his father and obeys him out of love.

The head of the household, however, does not love a servant in order to establish him as an heir. Rather, he uses his service according to his own will and for the heir’s benefit. Yet he entrusts his property and the heir to the servant’s care, and even places the heir himself under the servant’s custody and correction.

Thus, brothers, while the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a servant; indeed, he is often subjected to the servant and corrected by him, although by hereditary right he is lord of all. But he is under guardians and stewards—that is, under tutors and teachers—until the time predetermined by the father.

When he has reached maturity, he is established as lord by his father and rules over the servants who had ruled over him.

The heavenly Father also, dearest brothers, had and has an heir, natural and co-omnipotent, co-eternal and consubstantial: his Son. In this respect he differs from a temporal heir: a temporal heir scarcely ever, or never, makes co-heirs for himself; rather, he is pleased to be the sole and only one who will possess the inheritance.

But the Son of God, whose goodness knows no envy, adopted angel and human being as his co-heirs. Yet because humanity, deceived by the devil, had been disinherited from the eternal inheritance, it pleased the Son of God to make his fellow heir—disinherited through fraud—an heir through mercy.

And because it was fitting that the one who had fallen through pride should be raised through humility, the Son of God humbled himself and became a little one in the form of a servant, so that he differed in nothing from a servant, although he was Lord of all; but he was under guardians and stewards until the time predetermined by the Father.

Why this? So that he might redeem us in this way, show us in this way his love for us, and demonstrate to us in this way the path of humility by which we might be made heirs.

He was therefore in this world in poverty, subjection, and patience.

In poverty, because he was born of a poor Virgin, wrapped in cheap swaddling clothes, placed in a manger, and possessed nothing in this world. Hence he himself says: “Foxes have dens and the birds of the air nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew VIII; Luke IX).

In subjection, because he was subject to Mary and Joseph, his servants, as Luke testifies (Luke II). He paid tribute to Caesar (Matthew XVII), washed the apostles’ feet (John XIII), and, as he himself testifies, came not to be served but to serve (Matthew XX). When they wished to make him king, he withdrew (John VI), although he willingly offered himself to his passion.

In patience, because he hungered and thirsted, and endured insults, bonds, scourges, spitting, and the cross—and, what is more grievous, endured these things from his servants, for whom he also prayed.

But when the time predetermined by the Father arrived—that is, the resurrection—all power in heaven and on earth was given to him (Matthew XXVIII), even power over his servants and enemies. Hence the Father says to him: “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool” (Psalm CIX). And elsewhere: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm II), and so forth.

We too, brothers, if we wish to be God’s adopted heirs, should follow the way of the natural heir, not that of wicked servants. For they are sons of the slave woman, who are not heirs with the sons of the free woman (Galatians IV). They are destined not for inheritance but for destruction; and just as Ishmael persecuted Isaac (Genesis XXI), so they persecute the sons of the free woman.

They abuse the possession of goods, the exercise of powers, and the correction of those inferior to them, which God has entrusted to them for the benefit of his chosen. Nevertheless, willingly or unwillingly, they serve God and his chosen, his heirs, since he knows how to bring good out of their evils.

But we, brothers, if we wish to be children of God, heirs of God, and co-heirs of Christ, let us follow his footsteps. Let us be like a child who is an heir in this age. Let us not fear—indeed, let us embrace—poverty, and, in accordance with the same Apostle, having food and clothing, let us be content with these things (1 Timothy VI). For, as the Apostle says, “Those who wish to become rich in this age fall into the snare and temptation of the devil” (ibid.).

Let us not fear but love subjection, and, according to the Apostle Peter, let us be subject to masters, not only to the good and gentle but also to the difficult (1 Peter II). “For this is grace.”

Let the sons of the slave woman obtain honors and positions of authority through simony, ambition, and right or wrong. They will be outside the inheritance of eternity, since, according to Solomon, “The inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end” (Proverbs XX).

But let us humble ourselves in the sight of the Lord, so that he may exalt us at the time of visitation. Let us not fear but love discipline, because, as the Wise Man says: “Blessed is the man who is corrected by the Lord” (Job V).

Let the sons of the slave woman take away our possessions, bring forward our faults, and inflict punishments upon us, for “they will fall when they have ruled over the poor” (Psalm X), and “the righteous will rule over them in the morning” (Psalm XLVIII).

Meanwhile, let us say to the Lord: “Burn here, cut here, lest you destroy us forever,” because blessed is the one who endures temptation; for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life that God promised to those who love him (James I).

In all these things, brothers, let us hold firmly to love of God and neighbor. Let us hate people’s vices in such a way that we love their nature; let us pray for our enemies and strive to conquer them by acts of service, so that, if in any way possible, we may rescue the vessels of captivity and win them for God.

Thus let us also acquire a double crown. For when we do these things, dearest brothers, and the time predetermined by the Father arrives, we shall receive the inheritance we have long desired in heaven, because, according to the Prophet: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” (Psalm CXXVI). In that inheritance, may Jesus our Lord make us rejoice with his co-heirs, he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever. Amen.

## HOMILY XIV. THE SUNDAY WITHIN THE OCTAVE OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

“Joseph, the father of Jesus, and his mother were marveling at what was said about him” (Luke II), and so forth.

This reading, dearest brothers, is divided into four parts. First, Joseph and the blessed Virgin are introduced as marveling at what was said about Jesus. Second, Simeon is introduced blessing them and prophesying about the child. Third, Anna the prophetess is introduced bearing witness to Christ. Fourth, their return and the child’s growth are added.

First, therefore, Joseph and Mary are introduced as marveling at what was said about him. But perhaps, brothers, you are troubled by why the Evangelist calls Joseph Christ’s father, when earlier he had established that Christ was conceived not from male seed but from the Holy Spirit.

We customarily call someone “father” in several ways. For, equivocally, one may be a carnal father, a spiritual father, an elder, a predecessor, or a benefactor. Since Joseph was Jesus’ craftsman, foster-father, and lover, and the husband of his mother, he wished him to be called his father, both for the sake of mystery and for the sake of example.

For the sake of mystery, because he was truly the son of a craftsman—namely, of the one who fashioned the dawn and the sun.

For the sake of example, so that no one, however lowly, might be ashamed to be called lowly.

This is plainly directed against those who are ashamed of their decrepit, weak, and low-born fathers. They are like the mule who, as the fable relates, when asked who his father was, concealed his low-born father and declared that his noble horse was his maternal uncle.

Be ashamed, then, proud worm! God was willing to be called the son of a craftsman, and you are ashamed of the lowliness of your father?

“They were marveling,” he says, “at what was said about him.” By whom was it said? By angels, shepherds, Magi, Simeon, and the other prophets—Zechariah, Elizabeth, and Anna.

And what was said about him? That this tiny little child was called “Savior” by the angel, glorified by the angelic choir, adored by shepherds, pointed out by the star, honored by the Magi with mystical gifts, and called by Simeon “the light of the nations and the glory of the people of Israel.”

They marveled not so much at the height of his divinity as at his condescension. They marveled at humility in exaltation, condescension in majesty, lowliness in glory, and poverty amid heavenly riches.

They marveled at, emulated, and imitated these virtues. Hear how the mother emulates the humility of her Son. Forgetting that she was a virgin, the Mother of God, and Queen of heaven, she says: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke I), and: “Because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (ibid.).

Let us therefore, brothers, not marvel at the false riches, honors, and glories of this wretched age, which deceive their lovers. For, according to the poet [Note: [Col. 1721D] Horace, *Epistles* I.6.1–2]:

> To admire nothing earthly is a thing which almost alone  
> Can make and preserve a person blessed.

Rejecting these things, let us marvel at, emulate, and imitate in Christ and in his mother humility, condescension, lowliness, voluntary poverty, and the other virtues through which human beings are made like God and become children of God.

[Col. 1722D] The second part follows, in which Simeon is introduced blessing them—namely, Mary and Joseph—and prophesying about the child, when it is said: “And Simeon blessed them.” I think, dearest ones, that in blessing the mother he said something like this:

“Blessed are you beyond comparison, who without precedent have believed, conceived, borne, carried, and nursed this—your son, your father, your creator, your God. You also, Joseph, are blessed, for among all the people of this world you have been chosen to raise, cherish, and carry Christ, the light of the nations and the glory of the peoples.”

Thus the blessing of a good son, my brothers, overflows upon his parents and fosterers, according to Solomon’s saying: “A wise son is the joy of his parents” (Prov. X). You therefore, fathers and mothers of households, be watchful in the good upbringing, education, and formation of your children, so that, on account of your children’s good disposition, you may yourselves deserve to be blessed. For just as an undisciplined son becomes a curse to his parents, so one who is well disciplined becomes a blessing (Ecclus. XXII).

Finally, while prophesying, Simeon said to Mary, his mother:

Behold, brothers, the blessed Virgin, although, herself a mother, she bore and nourished the source of all knowledge and grace, nevertheless knew certain things less fully and was to be instructed by the prophets. In this it is plainly evident that no one, however holy, can in this life attain the fullness of all graces. Therefore, to restrain the pride of mortals, the Lord did not wish anyone to possess every grace, so that each person might need another and admire in another what he did not possess in himself. Moreover, in this respect the Queen of Heaven, who did not refuse to be instructed by persons of lower station, rebukes the pride of those who are ashamed to be taught by their inferiors, although excellent wine is often contained in a worthless vessel, and bad wine in a golden one. Hence the Apostle says: “But we have this treasure in earthen vessels” (II Cor. IV). And elsewhere: “If anything is revealed to one who is sitting below, let the one who is greater keep silent” (I Cor. XIV) [Note: [Col. 1723D] The Vulgate reads “the one sitting.”] [Note: [Col. 1724D] The Vulgate reads “the one preceding.”] And the philosopher says: “Let the authority of the speaker not move you; attend not to who says it, but to what he says.”

“Behold,” he says, “this one is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel”: for the fall, that is, of unbelievers, and for the rising again of believers; for the fall of the proud and the rising again of the humble. Hence the Lord himself says: “For judgment I have come into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John IX). And the Apostle says: “We preach Christ crucified: to the Jews indeed a stumbling-block, but to the Gentiles foolishness; yet to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Cor. I).

Nor is Christ alone, brothers, but anyone who lives and teaches rightly among the people is set for the fall of the incorrigible and for the rising again of those who repent. Hence the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ: to some the fragrance of life unto life, and to others the fragrance of death unto death” (II Cor. II).

“And for a sign,” he says, “that will be opposed”—that is, for an example and teaching that will be opposed by unbelievers and perverse people, who will oppose Christ’s teaching and examples either in words or in deeds. Hence he also adds: “And your own soul,” he says, “a sword will pierce”—that is, the grief experienced at his passion will pierce through your inmost being.

Since intense compassion is martyrdom, it is clear that the blessed Virgin is not excluded from the crown of martyrdom. Indeed, she may be called more than a martyr, for she suffered in her soul, which is immortal. From this, brothers, let us also learn to share in the passions, afflictions, and needs of the saints, orphans, and widows, since those who share their sufferings for God’s sake will not be excluded from their crown, as the Lord testifies: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward” (Matt. X).

“So that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed”—that is, so that the prophecies that had been hidden, like thoughts in the heart, might be revealed as fulfilled in the child. Or certainly, so that the hearts of human beings might be opened through their outward works, showing whether or not they are devoted to Christ.

The third part follows, in which Anna is introduced bearing witness to Christ, so that “at the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may stand” (Deut. XIX). The evangelist commends her both for her holy lineage and for her marital sanctity, since she had lived seven years with her husband from her virginity, as well as for her widow’s chastity and her service to God. And because she was devoted to fasts and supplications, she is shown to be worthy of being illumined by the spirit of prophecy, of prophesying about Christ, indeed of recognizing him in the flesh and proclaiming him to others. Let fathers and mothers of households imitate her, so that they may live chastely with their spouses from the time of their virginity. Let widowers and widows likewise imitate her, forgetting the things of the world and devoting themselves to God alone, to fasts, supplications, and good works, so that they may deserve to be illumined by the Spirit and proclaim and contemplate Christ in word and example.

“And she,” he says, “arriving at that very hour,” because she was brought by the same Spirit as Simeon, “confessed to the Lord” through the confession of faith, the action of praise, and the word of preaching. Hence it is added: “And she spoke about him to all who were awaiting the redemption of Israel.” But she did not speak to the others, because pearls are not to be thrown before swine, nor is what is holy to be given to dogs (Matt. VII).

The fourth part follows, when it is said: “And after they had fulfilled everything according to the law of Moses, they returned to their own city, Nazareth.” In this, brothers, they offer us an example, so that we may not depart from the church until we have fulfilled our vows, offerings, and prayers according to what the law prescribes. This stands against those who, before paying their due vows and offerings to God, and before the divine services have been completed, return from church, considering it a waste of time to remain there.

“But the child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was in him.” My brothers, that Christ, the Son of God, grew and became strong belonged to his flesh. For he deigned to undergo the stages of our ages in order to give us the unchangeableness of his eternity. He was filled with wisdom, for he both is and was Wisdom itself. In Wisdom he first created us, and afterward came to recreate us. The grace of God was in him, not according to measure, but in all its fullness. For as God he possessed every grace in order to distribute it to each person, and as man he possessed every grace that he desired in its exercise.

Let us therefore entreat him with tears to enrich us from the fullness of his wisdom and grace, so that from him we may be able to believe in, love, and venerate him himself. He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever. Amen.

# HOMILY XV: ON THE CIRCUMCISION OF THE LORD

[Col. 1725A]

“When eight days had been completed, so that the child might be circumcised, his name was called Jesus” (Luke II).

This present day, dearest brothers, is adorned with a twofold dignity: both because it is the eighth after Christ’s Nativity and because it has been consecrated by his circumcision. For the radiance of the Lord’s Nativity was so great that all the seven days following it were made solemn by it. Moreover, his circumcision doubles the cause of our joys.

There are, dearest brothers, three circumcisions: the first is bodily, the second spiritual, and the third heavenly. The first belongs to the law, the second to grace, and the third to glory. The first is good in its own time, the second better and for every time, and the third best and everlasting. The first is the sacrament of a sacred reality, the second is both a sacred reality and a sacrament, and the third is the reality of the sacrament.

Let us speak of each in order.

There was therefore circumcision of the flesh: the circumcision of the excess skin, performed on the male member on the eighth day with a stone knife. Let us consider, brothers, first, for what reason it was instituted; second, why it was performed on the eighth day, on the male member, and with a stone knife; third, what benefit it conferred; fourth, why a new name was then imposed; and fifth, why Christ wished to be circumcised.

Circumcision was commanded, brothers, for three reasons: so that it might be a sign of Abraham’s great faith; so that through obedience a person might gain merit by being circumcised, just as the first man had incurred guilt through disobedience; and so that through the mark of circumcision the people of God might be distinguished from the others.

It was performed on the eighth day because it signified the circumcision of corruption that took place on the eighth day—that is, in the resurrection—in Christ personally; and it will take place on the eighth day, that is, in the resurrection, in everyone generally.

It was also performed on the male member through which the human race is propagated in concupiscence, because it was a remedy against original sin, which is transmitted through carnal concupiscence.

It was also performed with a stone knife, because every circumcision, whether of sin or of corruption, must be accomplished through Christ, signified by the stone. For “there is no other name given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts IV).

In its own time, circumcision conferred the same benefit that baptism now confers. Hence Bede says:

“Circumcision in its own time conferred the same remedy of saving healing that baptism has been accustomed to confer in the time of revealed grace, except that it did not open the gate of paradise, because the sacrifice of Christ’s blood had not yet been offered. A new name was given in circumcision because, when someone was circumcised, he was then first called faithful and numbered among the faithful, just as now takes place in baptism.”

Although Christ had no need of it, he wished to be circumcised for three reasons: to show that the sacraments of the law were sacred; to display in himself an example of humility and obedience for us; and to show that he did not abolish the law but fulfilled it.

At that time his name was also called Jesus, not imposed. For this name, by God’s providence, had been prefigured by the patriarchs, as in Joshua and Jesus the great high priest; foretold by the prophets; and announced beforehand by the angel. Although it has been given to others, it belongs substantively to Christ alone in its designation.

Moral or spiritual circumcision takes place when we circumcise from ourselves every vice and every excess. We circumcise vices from ourselves when we cut away gluttony, lust, greed, avarice, anger, envy, sadness, acedia, vainglory, pride, falsehood, and the other vices. We circumcise excesses from ourselves when we cut away the superfluity of cares, riches, pleasures, possessions, clothing, labors, and journeys, retaining only what is necessary.

This circumcision of vices and excesses is also signified by the cutting of the hair, beard, and nails, and by shortening long garments. For by the hair or beard, which grow from our flesh and yet are not felt when cut off, are signified the cares of necessities. These cannot be entirely cut away, but only their excess ought to be circumcised, lest they impede in us the sight of contemplation, the hearing of God’s word, or the fruit of prayer. Hence the Lord also commands the Levites to shave the hair of their flesh (Num. VIII).

The excess of the fingernails and toenails must likewise be circumcised—that is, the excess of works and journeys. The Lord also commanded that if an Israelite captured a virgin girl in war and wished to have her as his wife, he should shave her head, cut her nails, remove her hair, and then take her into his embrace (Deut. XXI).

The Israelite captures a virgin girl when a preacher, through the warfare of preaching, takes a soul barren of fruit from the power of the devil. If he wishes to make her fruitful for God, it is necessary not only to strip her of unbelief and the other vices, but also to circumcise her of the excess of worldly cares, works, and journeys.

The excess of a long garment must also be shortened and the belt tightened; that is, the excess of riches and worldly possessions must be circumcised and curtailed, lest they delay our course. Hence the Apostle says: “Everyone who competes in the contest abstains from all things” (I Cor. IX).

This circumcision also takes place on the eighth day, that is, in hope of the resurrection, both from the death of the soul and from the death of the body. It also takes place with a stone knife, that is, with Christ working, according to the saying: “Blessed is the one who will seize and dash his little ones against the rock” (Ps. CXXXVI)—that is, against Christ; in other words, who will destroy them through his love and help.

Then also a new name is given, because from that time a person is named among the saints both in number and in merit, according to the saying: “And I will write upon him my new name” (Isa. LXII).

Heavenly circumcision will take place on the eighth day, that is, in the general resurrection, both in soul and in body. From the soul are circumcised vices, defects, and disturbances. Vices are sins, namely, evil thoughts and evil works; defects include ignorance, forgetfulness, dullness, and the like; disturbances include fear, sadness, and the like.

From the body are circumcised vices, necessity, defects, and corruption. Vices include bodily deformities, for then excesses will be cut away and deficiencies supplied; necessity includes the need to eat, drink, dress, and sleep; defects include illness and old age; and corruption includes death.

All these things will then be removed by Christ, who is the true rock, when he glorifies his saints. Then a new name will be given to them, which the mouth of the Lord will name, so that they will be called not only the sons, friends, and heirs of God, but even gods, according to the saying: “I have said: You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. LXXXI).

Therefore, dearest brothers, the first of these circumcisions signifies the second and third, and is of no value without them. These two, however, are of great value without the first. The Jews now perform the first without the second and third, and therefore it not only does not benefit them but even harms them; according to the Apostle, “circumcision has become uncircumcision” (Rom. II).

True Christians now perform the second without the first, and await the third. Therefore, dearest brothers, we truly celebrate Christ’s circumcision when we cut away from ourselves vices, sins, and the excesses of necessities.

Let us therefore circumcise our hearts and senses: our hearts, so that they may not meditate upon what is harmful or empty; our senses, so that they may not be occupied with what is harmful or empty. Let us circumcise our eyes, so that they may not see vanity; our ears, so that they may not hear base or harmful words; our sense of smell, so that it may not desire lustful scents; our taste, so that it may not be captured by delicacies or enticements; and our tongue, so that it may not speak harmful or empty words.

Doing this, brothers—dearest brothers—we shall through this spiritual circumcision come to that true and eternal circumcision where there will be every good without evil, truth without falsehood, satiety without disgust, a kingdom without end, joy without sorrow, a festival without interruption, day without night, and life without death.

May God and our Lord Jesus Christ, who today wished to be circumcised for us, lead us to that circumcision. Amen.

# HOMILY XVI: ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

“Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, because your light has come” (Isa. LX, etc.).

The prophet—or rather, the Lord through the prophet—speaks this, dearest brothers, to the primitive Church from the Jews, or to each individual soul. For this utterance can be interpreted of both.

First, therefore, he urges Jerusalem to arise and be enlightened. Second, he adds the reason why it ought to arise and be enlightened. Third, he shows what evils follow the one who scorns arising. Fourth, he sets forth the good things that follow the one who rises.

Thus, exhorting Jerusalem, or any soul, the prophet says: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem.”

But how, brothers, does the Lord tell the soul to arise and be enlightened? It is in God’s hand, not ours, whether we arise or are enlightened. For the human being was created in such a way that he can stand and fall by himself, but cannot rise by himself. He fell by himself, indeed, but could not rise by himself, like an elephant, which is inflexible and of rigid nature and, once thrown down, cannot rise on its own.

A hunter lying in wait for it marks a tree against which it leans when resting, and secretly cuts almost all the way through it. The elephant then comes to the accustomed tree, leans against it, and, when the tree falls, falls with it. Unable to rise, it trumpets. At its cry the other elephants come; and when they cannot make it rise, they all trumpet together until a small elephant arrives and, with its trunk, lifts up the fallen elephant.

Mystically, dearest brothers, this elephant is the human being, who is of rigid nature, created more suited to standing than to rising. The wicked hunter cast him down through the deception of the forbidden tree. Unable to rise by himself, he clung to the earth for a long time, wept, and invoked help. The patriarchs and prophets approached him in compassion, but they could not lift him up; instead, they wept together and invoked help until the little one born from their lineage—Christ—came and raised him up by his preaching and grace.

Therefore, just as the human being fell by himself but could not rise by himself, so he was blinded by himself but could not enlighten himself. This is the man blind from birth in the Gospel, upon whose eyes the Lord placed mud made from earth and saliva, and whom he enlightened after he had washed (John IX). He showed that the one who had created the human being seeing from the clay had himself recreated his eyes from the same material.

For the saliva, which is salty and seasoned and flows down from the head, signifies the true Wisdom that descends from the Father. From himself and from the earth—that is, from divinity and humanity—he made a poultice and eye-salve, by which the blinded human being recovered the sight of the mind through baptism.

Thus the soul can neither rise nor be enlightened by itself. Let it therefore say to God: “Lord, what is this, that you command me to arise and be enlightened? Of myself I can do neither. You alone can do this and all else. Therefore, if you wish me to arise, give me your hand. If you wish me to be enlightened, give me light.”

The second part follows, in which the Lord shows why one ought to arise, saying: “Because your light has come.” As if he were saying: “Behold, I extend my hand to you so that you may arise. The light has come so that you may see. If you receive it, you make it your light; if you do not receive it, it will indeed always be light, but not yours—instead, it will be alien to you.”

It has come to you because you could not come to it by yourself. He shows what this light is by adding: “And the glory of the Lord has risen over you”—that is, the glorious Lord has arisen, not only bodily from the blessed Virgin, but also spiritually through faith in the mind.

And this glory has risen “over you,” because “his going forth is from the highest heaven” (Ps. XVIII), and in the higher part of you—that is, in reason—he has arisen through faith, according to the saying: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. IV).

Unless you therefore rise and are enlightened, you will have no excuse, since your light has already come and the glory of the Lord has already risen over you. This, brothers, stands against us, who live in the time of grace, for whom Christ, the light and glory of the Lord, has risen through faith, and the grace of God has been prepared, yet we withdraw ourselves.

The grace of God offered to us is despised by us while we do not take care to rise from the darkness of our sins. Hence what the Lord said to the Jews can now be said to us: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John XV).

From this the Apostle Paul warns us: “Take heed,” he says, “lest anyone be lacking the grace of God” (Heb. XII). He does not say, “lest some be lacking,” but “lest anyone be lacking the grace of God,” showing that, although God’s grace is present to all like the sun, it nevertheless withdraws from us through our negligence, while we either uselessly consume or abuse our senses, the time of our life, and temporal possessions, which God has granted us for acquiring merit.

The third part follows, in which it is shown what evils follow the one who scorns arising, when it is added: “For behold, darkness will cover the earth, and thick darkness the peoples.”

As if he were saying: “Arise quickly and be enlightened, for unless you rise quickly, you will be covered with darkness.” Whoever is covered with darkness, my brothers, neither sees nor is seen. Moreover, whoever lies in sin either through ignorance or through weakness, even if he does not see God with a clear eye, is nevertheless never without being seen by God in mercy.

But whoever, through contempt and obstinacy, scorns rising from his sin is so blinded by the demand of his own perversity that he neither sees God nor is seen by God in mercy.

These are the darknesses that cover the earth—that is, lovers of earthly things: the blindness of mind born from long habit in sin, because of which the guilty person will rightly be sent into the outer darkness.

Even if some spark of reason still remains among lovers of earthly things, the darkness of ignorance and unbelief will gradually blind it, so that they will not only despise God but even cease to believe that he exists.

Take note, brothers, take note of what I say. First, a person sins through ignorance or weakness. If he scorns arising and being corrected, then, accumulating sins upon sins, he finally falls into blindness of mind. Then the darkness of unbelief covers him, so that he already doubts that God exists and does not believe that the resurrection or the final judgment will come.

Continually ponder these things, my brothers, and hasten to rise from your sins, lest, through contempt, either the darkness of sins or the darkness of unbelief cover you.

[Col. 1729D] The fourth part follows, in which it is shown what good things follow the one who rises, when it is added: “But the Lord will rise over you,” and so forth.

Four good things are distinguished here.

The first is that the Lord will rise over you. God is said to rise in us when his love rises in us. Conversely, God then dies in us when his love dies in us. Therefore, brothers, let us love God more and more, so that he himself may rise in us more and more. Let us always love him, so that we may always have him alive in us.

The second is that “his glory will be seen in you.” The glory of God is seen in us when, in the things God works in us, he is shown to be glorious. God appears powerful, glorious, and wondrous in nothing more than in making the unjust just, the carnal spiritual, and the demoniac divine—for this is to strip hell.

And this glory of God, dearest brothers, is seen in us when the holiness of our outward works shows that we have been inwardly illumined by God.

The third is: “Nations will walk in your light, and kings in the splendor of your rising.” For the holy life of the righteous is like a light in the darkness of this world. When, therefore, we follow the examples of the saints, what else are we doing than walking in their light? And when, by governing ourselves well, we imitate the good conversion and conduct of others, what else are we doing than becoming kings who walk in the splendor of their rising?

Let every faithful person follow the way of life to which he is called. Hence the Lord says: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V). For just as the guiding star led the three kings today by the straight way all the way to Christ, so the life of the saints in this world, like a star, guides us and makes us kings of others, so that by following it we may reach Christ.

And what good will come from imitating your example? Many will gather to follow and imitate you. Hence it follows: “Lift up your eyes round about and see.” All these, gathered together in one faith and charity, have come to you: your sons, coming through imitation from far away—that is, from a very distant way of life.

“And your daughters,” that is, those who are less perfect, “will suck milk” [Note: [Col. 1729D] The Vulgate reads “will rise from the side”]—that is, their teaching.

The fourth is that then the whole Church will see fulfilled what I foretold to you: “You will overflow with subject sons, and your heart will marvel and expand with joy when the multitude of the sea has been converted to you through faith”—that is, the world—and “the strength of the nations”—that is, kings and princes—“will come to you.”

“The flood,” that is, the abundance, “of camels”—that is, the rich of this world, who are humped over and burdened with sins and riches—“will cover you,” bringing gifts: “the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah.”

“Dromedary” is interpreted as “swift”; “Midian” as “iniquity”; “Ephah” as “released.” By the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah, therefore, is signified the conversion of those swift in understanding who, released from iniquity, return to the Church.

And not only they, but “all”—that is, every kind of human being—“will come from Sheba”—that is, from captivity—“to the faith, bringing gold and frankincense”—that is, purity and prayer—and “proclaiming the praise of the Lord”—that is, the works of the Son in which the Father is praised—and preaching them to others.

These things, my brothers, have been fulfilled today not only spiritually but also historically. For the three kings, coming in the splendor of the Lord’s rising, offered gold and frankincense to the Lord, confessing him as king through the gold and as the true God through the frankincense, and signifying him as mortal through the myrrh added to these.

Let us also imitate them, brothers, and confess him as true king, true God, and true man. Let us offer him morally the purity of mind, the devotion of prayer, and the mortification of our flesh, so that we may deserve to be received by him and blessed with eternal blessing—by him who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

# HOMILY XVII: ON THE DAY OF THE EPIPHANY

“When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judah, in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying” (Matt. II, etc.).

The reading of the holy Gospel that you have just heard, dearest brothers, sets before us the history of today’s solemnity. This reading has five parts.

In the first it shows us the arrival of the Magi in Jerusalem, when it says: “When Jesus had been born,” and so forth. Here it is shown who they were, when they came, from where they came, and where they went.

Who were they? Magi. They were not called Magi as though they were sorcerers, but as wise men. For those whom we call philosophers, the Chaldaeans call magi.

When did they come? “When Jesus had been born in the days of King Herod.” In this, brothers, it is also suggested to us that when Herod—that is, the devil—was reigning in this world, Christ was born.

For the strong man, armed, possessed his courtyard in peace. But Christ, stronger than he, came upon him and gradually began to plunder his vessels (Luke XI), so that on the very night on which he was born he drew the shepherds to himself, and on the thirteenth day—that is, today—he brought those three kings to himself: the first fruits of the Jews, and these the first fruits of the nations. The former came from nearby, as those made near to God through worship; the latter from far away, as those made distant from God through idolatry.

He called the former, as rational beings, through a rational creature; these, as irrational beings, through an irrational creature—that is, through a star.

From where did they come? “From the East.” But how, brothers, could they have learned of Christ, newly born, in such distant regions? Those who were nearby did not know. How then did those who were so far away know? Who told them? A star. And who indicated to them what the star signified? Not flesh and blood, but the heavenly Father; not human reasoning, but the inspiration of the heavenly Spirit.

But how did they come so quickly from so far away? It is possible, brothers, that the star appeared to them for several days before Christ’s birth, and that they then began their journey. Or, if it appeared at the first moment of Christ’s birth, the Lord may have guided them so that they quickly covered the long journey on swift dromedaries.

Where did they go? To Jerusalem, so that in the royal city they might seek the royal heir. The Lord so ordained it that they might hear the law harmonizing with the star in testimony to Christ, so that “at the mouth of two or three witnesses every word might stand” (Deut. XIX).

The second part follows, containing the Magi’s inquiry: “Where is the one who has been born king of the Jews?”

What is this, brothers? They were Gentiles. Why, then, despising the kings of the Gentiles, did they seek the king of the Jews? Or, if they were seeking the king of the Jews, why did they disregard Herod and his sons?

This was not done, brothers—not through the judgment of human reasoning, but by the disposition of the Divinity. Archelaus, the king’s son, is despised, and the son of a poor woman is sought. Archelaus is despised in the palace, and Christ is sought in an inn. Archelaus is despised on a royal bed, and Christ is sought in a manger. Archelaus is despised wrapped in silks, and Christ is sought wrapped in humble cloths.

Those who seek the one who does not accept persons do not know how to show partiality. Let us also, dearest brothers, if we seek Christ, who does not accept persons, show no partiality. Let us not honor the powerful on account of their power, nor despise the poor on account of their poverty. For it is written: “You shall not shame the face of the poor, nor honor the face of the powerful” (Lev. XIX). And elsewhere: “How long will you judge iniquity and accept the faces of sinners?” (Ps. LXXXI)—as if he were saying: You judge iniquity in this, that by accepting the faces of sinners you honor them.

Therefore, when receiving people, let us consider not their status but their nature, not their power but their virtue, not how much they possess but how much they are worth.

How they know that the king of the Jews has been born, the Magi show when they add: “For we saw his star in the East, and we have come to adore him.”

“We,” they say, “being placed in the East, saw his star, which went before us and led us to him.” “His star,” they say—that is, his work, his minister, the sign of him.

Beware, brothers, beware of those who falsely claim that whenever someone is born, his star is born with him and determines his deeds, taking as an argument for their error what is said here about “his star.”

But since we read here not that the child ran to the star, but that the star ran to the child—if that expression may be used—the star was not the child’s fate; rather, the child was the fate of the star.

But far be it from the hearts of the faithful to say that fate is anything. For the one who creates alone governs human lives.

Beware, brothers, also of those who say that one hour is fortunate and another unfortunate, or that one day is good and another bad, supposing that people derive the cause of their destiny from the day or hour in which something happens.

That this is false is proved by the fact that Jacob and Esau were conceived and born in the same hour (Gen. XXV), and yet one was upright and the other rejected (Rom. IX). Many are also conceived in the same hour, yet some are rich and others poor, some clever and others dull, some good and others evil.

Many also begin a journey, a battle, or a lawsuit in the same hour, yet things go well for some and badly for others. Against such people the Apostle speaks: “You observe days, months, seasons, and years. I fear that perhaps I have labored among you in vain” (Gal. IV).

Beware also, brothers, of those who devote themselves to divinations, omens, and auguries, although this law forbids it, saying: “You shall not practice auspices, nor attend to auguries” (Lev. XIX; Deut. XVIII).

Beware also of those who say that some people, with burning eyes, bewitch others. For the evil eye is nothing. Rather, when one person looks upon another, the devil commonly uses the sight to cause harm, so that he harms both the one whom he makes infamous and the one whom he makes a slanderer.

The Psalmist rebukes all such people, saying: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. IV). And elsewhere: “Blessed is the one whose hope is the name of the Lord and who has not turned toward vanities and false insanities” (Ps. XXXIX).

[Col. 1733A] The third part follows, which shows Herod’s disturbance and fraudulent inquiry, when it is added: “But when King Herod heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.”

Herod was troubled, fearing a successor. His own people were troubled because of their favor toward him. Others were troubled because of the novelty of the report.

When Herod questioned them, the teachers of the law produce testimony concerning the place of Christ’s birth, so that it might become for them a testimony of condemnation and for us an aid to faith.

And whom do these people signify, brothers, except wicked teachers, who say but do not do, who benefit others but harm themselves? They are like “sounding brass and a clanging cymbal” (I Cor. XIII), which summons others and shakes itself apart. They are like a candle that gives light to others and destroys itself.

But Herod, who diligently inquires into the place and time of Christ’s birth while coloring the malice of his heart with the appearance of humility—what does he signify, my brothers, except hypocrites, who seek out and praise words of truth, yet do not cease to persecute Christ in his poor, in their hearts and, whenever they can, in their deeds?

The fourth part follows, in which the Magi’s being led to Christ by the star is demonstrated, when it is added: “When they had heard the king, they departed. And behold, the star,” etc. This star, brothers, which went before the Magi and led them to Christ, what else does it signify than the grace of God, which goes before us and leads us so that we may reach Christ? For just as these men would neither have begun nor completed the journey unless they had been led by God through the star, so we are able neither to will what is good nor to bring a good will to completion unless God’s grace goes before us and follows after us. Hence the Apostle says: “It is not of him who wills to will, nor of him who runs to run, but of God who has mercy” (Rom. IX).

Moreover, just as the star abandoned the Magi when they turned aside to Herod, and relit their way when they departed from him, so, brothers, when we turn aside toward evil, the grace of God does not abandon us; rather, we abandon it. But when we turn away from evil through repentance, God’s grace relights our way. The star went before the Magi until it came and stood above the place where the child was; and God’s grace goes before us until we come to Christ, “who is the end unto righteousness for everyone who believes” (Rom. X), beyond whom we must not proceed, because “there is no other name under heaven, nor on earth, in which it is necessary for us to be saved” (Acts IV).

When the Magi saw the star, “they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy.” We too, brothers, when we see that God’s grace has led us as far as beholding the God of gods in Zion, shall rejoice with great and ineffable joy, and “no one shall take that joy from us” (John XVI). And entering the house of eternal blessedness, we shall find the child with Mary his mother—that is, contemplating, adoring, and blessing the human being together with the divinity, forever.

The fifth part follows, in which the Magi’s adoration and offering are shown, when it is added: “And falling down, they adored him; and opening their treasures, they offered him gifts,” etc. They do four things: they fall down, adore, open their treasures, and offer. In this they show what we must do and in what order. Therefore, brothers, let us fall down before the majesty of God—that is, humbling our pride, let us confess ourselves to be sinful, weak, and unworthy. Let us adore—that is, let us acknowledge God as our Creator and Lord. Let us open the treasures of our hearts through confession, attributing our evils to ourselves; and if we possess any good or worth, let us attribute and offer it to God.

Moreover, by a threefold gift they make a threefold confession: they offer gold to the king, frankincense to God, and myrrh, with which dead bodies are embalmed, to the mortal man. We too, my brothers, should offer him the same offering, believing in our hearts and confessing with our mouths that he is the true king, true God, and true man, and proving this by our works.

Morally also, brothers, we offer him gold if we sanctify our heart for him, clean and pure. We offer him frankincense if we delight him with the fragrance of pure prayer. Hence the Psalmist says: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL). We offer him myrrh when we guard this mortal body from the putrefaction of lust by the seasoning of continence. For what else is it for the body to flow away through the stench of lust than for it to putrefy? Hence the prophet says of certain people: “They have rotted like beasts in dung” (Joel I). Therefore, lest the body putrefy through lust, let us season it with the myrrh of abstinence.

The sixth part follows, in which it is shown that the Magi, having been warned in a dream, returned to their own country by another way. We too, brothers, following their example, after having come to know Jesus, should return to our heavenly homeland not by the road on which we descended, but by another. For we departed from our country by becoming proud, pursuing visible things, tasting the forbidden food, and excusing our sins. It is necessary that we return to it by humbling ourselves, obeying, despising visible things, restraining the appetite of the flesh, and accusing our sins.

We departed from the joys of paradise through pleasures; by lamentations we must be recalled to them. For it is written: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V). “Woe to you who laugh, for you shall mourn!” (Luke VI.) Hence Solomon says: “Laughter shall be mingled with sorrow, and mourning takes possession of the end of joy” (Prov. XIV). Let us therefore wash away the stains of our faults with sighs and tears, for, as the Psalmist says: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit” (Ps. L), so that by another way we may return to our own country, under the guidance of him who today brought the Magi to himself from afar, our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

## HOMILY XVIII. THE FIRST SUNDAY AFTER THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

“I beseech you, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (Rom. XII), etc.

In this reading, dearly beloved brothers, the Apostle instructs us how we ought to live, teaching what we owe to ourselves, what to God, and what to our neighbors. We owe ourselves discipline, God obedience, and our neighbors compassion. In these three consists the perfection of Christianity.

Therefore, first exhorting us to discipline ourselves, the Apostle beseeches us by the mercy of God—that is, by the merciful God—and adjures us that, if we wish to obtain his mercy, we should present our bodies as a living, holy sacrifice, pleasing to God. A sacrifice, my brothers, was offered to the priest under the old law; afterward it was slaughtered, stripped of its skin, washed with water, cut into pieces, and burned with fire as a sweet fragrance. What was therefore done bodily under the law, the Apostle commands us to do spiritually. For he commands us to sacrifice not our body but the vices of our body, so that our body may die to sin and live to God, according to what the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth, which are fornication, greed, impurity” (Col. III, etc.), so that, according to that same Apostle, “the body of sin may be destroyed” (Rom. VI).

We conquer the members of the sacrifice when, through a resolve to repent, we bind our members so that they may sin no more. We offer the bound sacrifice to the priest when, with the intention of ceasing from sin, we present ourselves to the priest through confession. The sacrifice is slaughtered when sin is put to death by the knife of compunction. It is flayed when, once the veil of excuse has been removed, sin is laid bare through confession. It is washed with water when the filth of sins is cleansed with tears. It is cut into pieces when the several aspects of sins are separated through discernment. The sacrifice is burned with fire as a sweet fragrance when every sin is consumed by the fire of the Holy Spirit, so that God and one’s neighbor may thereby be pleased, according to the saying: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. L); and according to the other saying: “There is joy before the angels of God over one sinner doing penance” (Luke XV).

Yet it is not enough, brothers, to present our bodies as a sacrifice in this way through the mortification of sins, unless we present it as living—namely, so that we die to sin in such a way that we live to God—according to the Apostle’s saying: “As you presented your members to serve impurity and iniquity unto iniquity, so present them to serve righteousness unto sanctification” (Rom. VI); and according to the Psalmist: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI).

Because some present a living sacrifice but do not persevere, he adds “holy,” that is, persevering and firm. Hence, under the law, the head was offered together with the tail. Because others again persevere but nevertheless become displeasing through the admixture of empty glory or tepidity, he adds “pleasing to God,” through right intention. Hence it is written: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing” (Matt. VI).

Because still others, without discernment, either weaken their body excessively or nourish it too little, he says: “Your reasonable service.” For what is praiseworthy in itself becomes blameworthy through excess. Because, again, some, while they see the wicked flourishing here, and that “their sons are like young plants in their youth, their daughters adorned and embellished like the likeness of a temple, their storehouses full, bursting forth from one thing to another; their sheep fruitful, abounding in their pastures; their oxen fat; no breach in the wall, no passage through it, no outcry in their streets,” and because “they have called that people blessed which possesses these things” (Ps. CXLIII), see on the contrary the good afflicted here, and their feet almost moved from the right way, according to the saying: “But my feet were almost moved, my steps nearly slipped, because I was zealous over the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. LXXII), he adds: “And do not be conformed to this age,” that is, imitate it through rivalry. Hence David says: “Do not be jealous of the one who prospers in his way” (Ps. XXXVI). Rather, from the disfigurement produced by the oldness of sin, “be transformed in the newness of your mind,” so that your minds may emulate and imitate not the old but the new man.

The second part follows, in which what we owe to God is shown, when it is added: “That you may prove what is the will of God.” It is as though he said: Present your bodies as a living sacrifice, and be transformed in the newness of your mind, so that you may prove—that is, know by doing—what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.

Although God’s will in itself is always one, it has many signs in its works: promises, prohibitions, commands, and counsels. For he permits lesser evils, prohibits greater ones, commands good things, and counsels what is perfect. Considering these signs of the divine will, the Psalmist says: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” (Ps. CX). To turn away from evil is God’s good will; to do good is God’s pleasing will; to despise everything for God’s sake and give to the poor is God’s perfect will—that is, the perfection which God counsels us to pursue.

Therefore, brothers, in everything we must seek God’s will, and desire more eagerly whatever we recognize as pleasing to him. For if worldly people, in order to deserve the favor of a mortal king, hasten to do even his evil will, ought we not, my brothers, much more to do the will of God, which is always good and useful to us, so that we may deserve his unfailing favor?

The third part follows, in which the Apostle shows what we owe to our neighbors, when he says: “I say,” that is, I command, “through the grace that has been given to me,” that is, through the authority freely given to me: “Not to be wiser than it is necessary to be wise.” He is wiser than is necessary who is wise arrogantly: for example, one who places a stumbling block before the weak in food, drink, or similar ordinary matters; one who refuses to seek the usefulness of his neighbors, saying that not other people’s souls but only his own soul has been entrusted to him; or one who, presuming upon his conscience, allows others to think badly of him. In these matters some sin greatly.

Therefore the Apostle commands us to be wise unto sobriety, so that each person may seek not his own usefulness alone but also that of his neighbors. And just as God has distributed his grace to each person, so let each person administer it not to himself but to his neighbors. For God did not wish to give all graces to everyone, but separate graces to separate people, so that no one might become proud or despise another, and so that, seeing himself in need of the graces of others, each person might minister to others the grace he possessed.

For just as one foot has one function, one hand another, and one eye another, yet the foot carries not only itself but also the other members, the hand labors not for itself alone but also for the other members, and the eye sees not for itself alone but also for the other members, so God ordained in the Church that one should be a foot, carrying others by his labor, such as farmers; another should be a hand, defending others, such as rulers; another should be an eye, providing and advising others through wisdom, such as the wise.

Thus, dearly beloved brothers, let each person strive to communicate to others the grace he receives from God, lest, by hiding the talent entrusted to him, he be justly deprived of it and condemned. Let the one who has riches use them to assist the poor. Let the one who has power use it to defend the weak. Let the one who has wisdom correct and instruct others. Let the one who has eloquence make himself a patron of widows and orphans. Let the one who has the art of living use it for the benefit of others, so that each person may acquire gain for God and a reward for himself from the grace entrusted to him. May he deign to grant this, God, who lives and reigns forever. Amen.

## HOMILY XIX. THE FIRST SUNDAY AFTER THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

“When Jesus was twelve years old, and they went up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast, and when the days were completed and they returned, the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem” (Luke II), and the rest.

Dearly beloved brothers, this Gospel reading has five parts. First, it shows that Jesus went up to Jerusalem with his parents according to the custom of the feast. For the Lord had commanded in the law that everyone should appear before him three times a year, and not empty-handed. Thus people came even from distant regions for three principal solemnities—namely Passover, Pentecost, and the Feast of Booths—which lasted eight days—and, having washed their bodies and whitened their garments, they celebrated the solemnities with joy, sacrifices, and gifts.

In accordance with this custom, therefore, the blessed Virgin and Joseph went up to Jerusalem with the child, giving us an example of celebrating solemnities with devotion. For if our Lord Jesus Christ, although he had no need, celebrated the solemnities, what ought we miserable sinners, who have the greatest need, to do? Therefore, my brothers, whenever the solemnities of the Lord and of his saints arrive, let us celebrate them with the greatest devotion, washed more in our minds than in our bodies, adorned more with virtues than with garments, lest we be empty before the Lord.

Certainly, one is empty before God not who has no money in his hand, but who has no devotion in his heart. A hand is not empty of a gift if the treasury of the heart is filled with good will. Moreover, in this also—that the blessed Virgin and Joseph led the child Jesus every year to the solemnities in Jerusalem—they provide you, fathers and mothers of households, an example: once your children have begun to understand, lead them to church and teach them to fear God, to beseech him, and to pray. For we hold that life more firmly which we have been accustomed to follow from childhood.

The second part follows, in which it is shown that the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem and was sought by his mother and Joseph, when it is added: “The boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it.” And how, my brothers, could the Son of God, who was nourished by his parents with such care, be forgotten? It was the custom among the Jews that, when going to or returning from a feast, the men walked separately and the women separately. Even in the Temple itself, the women’s court was entirely separated from the men’s court. Younger children, however, went indifferently with either parent.

The blessed Virgin therefore thought that the child was with Joseph, while Joseph thought that he was with his mother; and thus, as it pleased him, he was left behind. Moreover, brothers, this custom of the Jews was excellent and should be imitated by us, so that when we are in church we remain separated from the women. For nothing removes our minds from prayer more than looking at women. If, brothers, even when we pray alone, vain thought assails us, what happens when a man looks at his wife—a fool at a foolish woman, a lecher at a lewd woman? Does this not increase guilt rather than obtain forgiveness?

Let there therefore be three distinct places in the church.
