In the first part, that is, in the choir, let the bishop or priest pray with the clerics; in the second, the king or lord of the village with his subjects; in the third, the lady with her women. For we read in ecclesiastical history that when the emperor Theodosius wished to enter the clerical choir at Milan, blessed Ambrose forbade him, saying: “There ought to be a distinction between clerics and laypeople. I must sing the psalms with my clerics in the choir, while you must pray outside with your laypeople.” When the emperor came to Constantinople, he remained outside the choir. When the bishop asked him why he did not enter the choir as usual, he replied: “I found only one bishop in the world who taught me what difference there is between laypeople and clerics.”

The third part follows, in which it is shown that after three days Jesus was found in the Temple, sitting in the midst of the teachers, listening to them and questioning them. The fact that Jesus is sought and found after three days signifies that he was sought both before the law and under the law, but was found only in the time of grace.

That he sits in the Temple in the midst of the teachers, listens, and asks questions gives an example to boys and adolescents: they should frequent the church, listen to teachers, and question them about the teaching of the soul. This also should be noted, my brothers: our Redeemer is read to have listened and asked questions when he was only twelve [years old], and not to have taught publicly until his thirtieth year. To Ezekiel also, in his thirtieth year, the heavens were opened, and he saw visions of God. The canons likewise prohibit anyone from presuming to approach the priesthood unless he is thirty years old.

Here, then, those are put to shame who, before the prescribed age, dare to aspire either to the priesthood or to the office of preaching. The Wisdom of God the Father did not wish to preach publicly before the age of thirty. And you, foolish and proud man, before you know how to be a disciple, do you desire to be a teacher? That all marveled at his wisdom and answers was a sign of the divine wisdom, which in a certain manner taught them while he prudently questioned them.

The fourth part follows, in which the Lord shows what we owe to our heavenly Father and what to our earthly mother. For when the blessed Virgin complained, “Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I, sorrowing, were seeking you,” he replied: “And why were you seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?”

He does not blame them for seeking him as though he were their son; rather, he indicates who his true Father is. In this, brothers, he teaches us to place the commandment of God the Father and the commandment of Mother Church before the commandment of an earthly father and mother. As he says elsewhere: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. X). Nevertheless, when the commandment of an earthly father or mother does not oppose the commandment of God, we ought to obey it humbly.

Hence the Lord Jesus, although he had first answered his mother and Joseph as though rebuking them, nevertheless immediately obeyed them in humility. For it follows that “he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them.” Be ashamed, proud dust; be ashamed. God subjects himself to a human being, and you disdain to be subject to a human being. O man, God subjected himself to you for the sake of your salvation, not his own; and you disdain to be subject to God or to a human being for the sake of your salvation, not theirs.

Here, brothers, here let us learn to be subject to God, subject to our parents, and also subject to every person for God’s sake. Whenever we disdain to be subject to others, we act against the example and commandment of Christ and imitate the pride of the devil. Let us learn especially to be subject to our parents and to repay them for the care with which they raised us. For whoever honors father or mother for God’s sake will not be dishonored before God.

The fifth part follows, in which the diligence and prudence of the blessed Virgin are shown, when it is added: “But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart.” She was no less worthy of imitation in purity of speech than in purity of body. Everything that she learned had been done or said concerning the Lord or by the Lord, whether or not she understood it, she silently stored in the memory, so that when the time came she might explain everything to those who asked and to those who wrote, just as it had been done or said.

Let us follow her example, dearly beloved brothers, according to our limited ability, keeping our lips restrained and our silence modest, and preserving all good things in the little treasury of our hearts.

The sixth part follows, in which the growth of the boy Jesus is shown, when it is added: “The boy grew in wisdom, age, and grace before God and men.” That he grew in age according to the nature of his humanity is evident. But how, my brothers, did he who was full of wisdom from eternity—indeed, who was Wisdom itself—grow in wisdom and grace?

He grew in wisdom and grace not for himself but for others, as he gradually revealed them to human beings. Thus God the Father was glorified, and human beings marveled. May he also grow in us, my brothers, so that he may graciously grant us his wisdom and grace, enabling us to deserve to abound in virtues and good works and to bless him forever for his good gifts, he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

## HOMILY XX. THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

“Having gifts that differ according to the grace that has been given to us” (Rom. XII), etc.

The all-knowing and foreseeing Lord God did not wish to give all graces to one person, lest he become proud like the angel, who grew proud because of the abundance of his graces; nor did he wish to give no grace to anyone, lest someone, despised in this way, despair, as Judas did, who, seeing himself stripped of every grace because of his sin, despaired.

Rather, he wished to give one grace to one person and another to another, so that each might be able to merit through what he possessed, be humbled by what he did not possess, and prefer the person who possessed it to himself; and so that each might minister his own grace to others, just as he wished another to minister to him from that other’s graces, so that, like the members of the human body, they might serve one another and labor together for their common salvation.

This, then, is what the Apostle says: “Having gifts that differ according to the grace that has been given to us”—that is, having diverse gifts according to what the Lord has freely given to each of us. And he subdivides the graces: “Whether we have prophecy, let us have it according to the rule of faith.”

By prophecy he means knowledge of hidden things and the interpretation of the Scriptures. Whoever possesses this grace should exercise it according to the intention of faith, so that he does not distort the Scriptures away from the truth of faith, as Arians, Sabellians, and the other heretics do. This is directed against those who do not expound the Scriptures but add to them; who do not draw out what is there but bring in what is not; who do not explain their own will according to Scripture but apply Scripture to their own will.

But what does “according to the rule of faith” mean, brothers, since faith in many matters is contrary to reason or above reason? And faith would have no merit if human reason supplied proof of it. For when it is said that the immortal one died, and that a virgin conceived and gave birth, this seems contrary to reason. Yet it is also according to reason, dearly beloved brothers, that the one who created reason and human nature should be above them and cannot be grasped by them.

“Or ministry, in ministering”—that is, whoever has the grace of ministry, whether of priesthood, diaconate, or another ministry, should exercise it in ministering, so that he is not lazy or negligent in his ministry but ministers carefully, devoutly, and energetically, because, as Jeremiah says: “Cursed is the one who does the work of God deceitfully” (Jer. XLVIII).

This is directed against those who prefer to rule rather than to benefit; who are diligent in gathering silver while disregarding the loss of souls, and who are more troubled by the loss of a donkey than by the loss of a soul.

“Or whoever teaches, in teaching”—that is, whoever has the office of teaching should teach in such a way as to instruct his hearers. This is directed against those who teach for glory or profit.

“Whoever exhorts, in exhortation”—that is, whoever has the grace of exhortation should be diligent in exhorting, lest he be condemned for the talent he has hidden.

This, brothers, is directed against those who, although they possess the grace of speaking to the people, remain silent through negligence.

“Whoever gives, let him give in simplicity”—that is, simply for God’s sake, not for glory or temporal reward, so that the left hand does not know what the right hand is doing (Matt. VI). This means that a temporal intention should not mix itself into a deed done for God’s sake, neither at the beginning, nor in the middle, nor at the end.

“Whoever presides, let him preside in diligence” [Note: [Col. 1741D] The Vulgate does not have *praesit* (“let him preside”).] For cursed is the negligent prelate, like Eli, whose negligence caused the ruin both of himself and of his sons. Cursed is the drowsing shepherd who allows the sheep entrusted to him to be devoured by wolves and returns empty-handed.

“Whoever shows mercy, let him do so with cheerfulness” [Note: [Col. 1741D] The Vulgate does not have *misereatur* (“let him show mercy”).] “For God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX). God does not measure how large the almsgiving is but from how much devotion it proceeds. A small alms, if given cheerfully, promptly, and devoutly, surpasses a large alms given secretly, slowly, and tepidly.

“Love without pretense.” For pretended love is not love but deception. Whoever pretends to love someone pretends in order that he may deceive that person more effectively. This is directed against those who, through flattering greetings and invitations, false promises, and services, pretend to be friends of those whom they see flourishing in this world. Against them John says: “Children, let us not love in word or with the tongue, but in deed and truth” (I John III).

“Hating evil, cleaving to good”—that is, naturally hating every evil and naturally loving every good. This virtue is called kindness. Its opposite, brothers, is malice, which rejoices in evil and grieves over good.

“Loving one another with brotherly charity.” This is directed against those who live with their brothers as though with strangers, showing them no sign of love or familiarity. The Apostle calls such people “without affection, without covenant.”

“Outdoing one another in honor”—that is, granting others the first place, the first honor, and the first order in speaking, sitting, drinking, and similar matters, according to the saying: “When you are invited to a wedding, recline in the last place” (Luke XIV). For just as the proud always desire precedence for themselves, so the humble always desire to yield precedence to others.

“Not slothful in diligence,” namely, in spiritual pursuits; for diligence is forbidden in temporal affairs. Hence the Lord says: “Do not be anxious, saying: What shall you eat, or what shall you drink?” [Note: [Col. 1741D] The Vulgate has: “What shall we eat or what shall we drink?”] (Matt. VI.)

“Fervent in spirit,” because God becomes nauseated and vomits. Hence he says: “You are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were cold or hot! But because you are neither cold nor hot, I am beginning to vomit you out of my mouth” (Rev. III).

“Serving the Lord,” not the world, not the flesh, and not the devil.

“Rejoicing in hope,” even amid the adversities and sorrows of this world. To rejoice in hope amid adversity belongs to spiritual people, whereas worldly people are disturbed and despair.

“Patient in tribulations”—that is, enduring tribulations with equanimity and sympathizing with those who inflict them. This is directed against those who, when provoked, immediately return evil for evil and curse for curse.

“Devoting yourselves to prayer,” and, even if not always praying, nevertheless always doing good works and living well. For the person who always, throughout life, makes his prayer worthy of being heard is truly devoted to prayer.

“Sharing in the needs of the saints”—that is, sharing your possessions, or, if you do not have them, your compassion. This is directed against those who, as though they were not human beings, do not know how to have compassion on human beings.

“Pursuing hospitality”—that is, do not have others seek you out in order to give hospitality; rather, be yourselves those who seek and offer it, as Abraham and Lot are read to have done.

“Bless those who persecute you” with your mouth. Bless them also in your heart, and do not curse them. This is directed against those who, although they bless their persecutors with their mouths, nevertheless curse them in their hearts.

Let us also strive to rejoice with those who rejoice, understanding “in God”; for we must not rejoice with those who rejoice in the world.

Let us weep with those who weep, showing them compassion. We do this when, through charity, we regard the goods and losses of our neighbors as our own.

“Being of the same mind,” that is, thinking one and the same thing with one another [Note: [Col. 1742D] The Vulgate has *sentientes* (“thinking, judging”) rather than *sapientes* (“being wise”).]—not dividing yourselves through schisms and heresies, but being of one mind through the same faith, hope, and charity.

“Not thinking highly of yourselves”—that is, not arrogantly, so that you do not raise yourselves above yourselves through proud estimation, but thinking humbly of yourselves, restraining yourselves below your own imperfection, and consenting to the humble. He says this because the proud cannot consent to the proud, nor live peacefully with them. The humble, however, always consent to the humble and live peacefully with them.

May God, the giver of graces, and our Lord, who in perfect Trinity lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages, grant us to obtain these and the other virtues. Amen.

## HOMILY XXI. THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

“There was a wedding at Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there” (John II), and the rest.

Dearly beloved brothers, the season of weddings now returns, and the Gospel speaks about the honorableness of marriage. Weddings are not damnable, as certain heretics have preached; rather, as the Apostle says: “Marriage is honorable in all, and the marriage bed undefiled” (Heb. XIII).

How honorable marriage is, its institutor, its time, its place, its definition, its goods, the merit of the persons, and the presence of the Lord himself demonstrate.

Who established marriage? The Lord God, who instituted nothing except what is good. And when? Before sin. Therefore that which existed before sin is good and was good. Where? In paradise. There the Lord took a rib from the side of the sleeping man, fashioned it into a woman, and joined her to the man. Hence he also said: “This now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh. Therefore a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II; Matt. XIX).

The Lord did not form the woman from the man’s head, lest she become proud over the man; nor from his feet, lest the man despise her; but from his side, so that he might love her as a companion.

What is marriage? The lawful union of male and female, maintaining an indivisible partnership of life. If marriage is lawful, then it is certainly good.

What are the goods of marriage? Three: faithfulness, sacrament, and offspring. Married couples ought to be faithful not only to God and their neighbor but also to each other, so that, just as they promise themselves to one another, there may be unity of souls, bodies, and possessions.

It is a sacrament because it is a sign of a sacred reality. For just as the woman was formed from the man’s side and joined to him, so Christ, through the blood and water flowing from his side, joined the Church, formed from it, to himself as his bride; and she gives birth to spiritual children for him through baptism.

Offspring is also a fruit of marriage, on account of which married couples ought to be joined. The merit of the persons also commends marriage, since, unless it were good, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the other saints would not have taken wives. Hence we read that the marriage of Abraham in his time was no less meritorious than the celibacy of John in his time.

The presence of Christ also commends the wedding. As the present Gospel testifies, by his presence he honored the wedding and adorned it with a miracle.

Thus, dearly beloved brothers, five things are shown in this reading: with what intention weddings should be celebrated; who should be invited; what should be absent; what should be present; and what should be changed.

The intention with which they should be celebrated is shown when it is added: “There was a wedding at Cana of Galilee.” *Cana* means “zeal,” while *Galilee* is interpreted as “transmigration.” We ought to marry with this zeal—not to remain with our wife in lust, but to avoid lust with her and transmigrate to chastity; to flee vices and transmigrate to virtues; to despise earthly things and transmigrate to heavenly things.

Hence the Apostle says: “Because of fornication”—understand, in order to avoid it—“let each man have his own wife” (I Cor. VII). For marriage has its own chastity. Therefore, my brothers, those who marry not with a right intention but for lust, beauty, or money are committing sin.

Who should be invited is shown when it is added: “Jesus was also invited, and his disciples, to the wedding.” The devil, therefore, should not be invited to the wedding through the flesh and magical arts; nor should mimes, male or female, enemies of honesty and chastity; nor shameful and infamous persons. Rather, Christ should be invited together with his mother and disciples.

Christ is invited to the wedding in three ways: through prayer, through purity, and through receiving the poor. Through prayer we ought to invite Christ with his mother and saints not only to weddings but also to all our works, so that he may go before our actions by inspiring them and accompany them by assisting us. Hence the Wise Man says: “In all your ways think upon God, and he will direct your steps” (Prov. III). For whatever is done without God is badly done.

The Lord should therefore be asked to guard our going in and our going out, from this time forth and forever (Ps. CXX).

God is invited through purity, because he flees impurity and rests in a pure heart. If, therefore, you celebrate weddings in holiness and purity, God will undoubtedly be present, as he himself testifies: “Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, I am there in the midst of them” (Matt. XVIII).

Therefore, as bridegroom and bride approach the sacrament of marriage, they ought to repent of their past excesses and confess their sins. For no one can begin a new life who does not put off the old person. Nor can anyone receive a blessing who keeps iniquity reserved in his heart.

After receiving the nuptial blessing, they ought not immediately to have intercourse, but to honor the sacrament, and on the first night to keep vigil in the church with lights and devote themselves to prayer. For we read that Sarah, the daughter of Raguel, married seven husbands, who, wishing to approach her immoderately on the first night, were at once strangled by the devil (Tobit 6). Fearing this, Tobias was unwilling to marry her, but the angel Raphael said to him:

“Do not be afraid: demons have power over the wanton and those who do not fear God. But when you have received her, you shall abstain from her for three days, and you shall devote the nights to prayer. On the first night, when the fish’s liver has been burned as incense, the demon will be driven away by your prayers. On the second night you shall pray that you may be admitted into the company of the patriarchs. On the third, you shall obtain a blessing, so that children may be begotten from you in safety. On the fourth, you shall take her in the fear of God, led more by love of children than by lust, so that through your children you may obtain a blessing.”

[Note: [Col. 1743D] The Vulgate does not have precisely these same words.] (Ibid.)

Christ must also be invited to the wedding through the welcoming of the poor, because Christ is welcomed in the poor, as he himself testifies: “Whoever receives one of these little ones in my name receives me” (Mark 9:37). Hence at the judgment he will also say: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25:40).

Therefore, when you celebrate a wedding, do what the Truth says: “When you give a banquet, do not invite the rich, but invite the poor, who have nothing with which to repay you; and your heavenly Father will repay you” (Luke 14:13–14).

What ought to be absent from a wedding? Wine—that is, drunkenness, lust, quarrels, tumult, and every kind of intemperance. Hence Solomon says: “Wine is a wanton thing, and drunkenness is tumultuous” (Proverbs 20:1). And the Apostle says: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is lust” (Ephesians 5:18). And elsewhere: “Wine and women make the wise apostatize” (Ecclesiasticus 19:2).

What ought to be present at a wedding? Six water jars—that is, six acts of mercy, which the Lord enumerates in the Gospel. The first is to give food to the hungry; the second, to give drink to the thirsty; the third, to clothe the naked; the fourth, to welcome the stranger; the fifth, to visit the sick; the sixth, to redeem or console the captive.

These jars are made of stone because they are strong against adversity, and they are placed there according to the purification of the Jews. For just as the Jews washed themselves daily on account of various kinds of excess, so married people, who frequently commit excesses either in their love of spouses or children or in their care of household affairs, ought daily to wash themselves through works of mercy, according to the saying: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41).

The Lord commands that the six jars be filled at the wedding because he commands married people to complete the six works of mercy and by them to wash away their daily excesses. At his command they are filled to the brim, because, with him commanding and assisting, pious spouses abundantly fulfill the six works of mercy, and fulfill them to the end.

What ought to be changed at the wedding? Water into wine. The water of the jars, my brothers, is changed into wine when, by the working of God’s grace, spouses have been so purified and perfected in virtues that the water of mercy no longer has the fear of a fault that must be washed away, but the fervor of divine charity. Concerning this the Prophet says: “And how excellent is my intoxicating cup!” (Psalm 22:5).

My brothers, water is rightly changed into wine when those who were previously cold become warm, those who were carnal become spiritual, and those who were worldly become religious. Truly blessed are those who live in marriage in this way, who, because of their love for their spouses and children and because of their care for household affairs, are not held back from the love of God.

Such married people are indeed blessed, but virgins or widows are more blessed, since, rejecting temporal marriage, they cling to the heavenly Bridegroom. More blessed, in truth, are those who are freer and more devoted, because the less they delight in earthly things, the more they seek heavenly things.

For, as the Apostle says:

“The time is short, and the form of this world is passing away. It remains that those who are married should be as though they were not married, and those who use the world as though they did not use it, and those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice” (1 Corinthians 7:29–31).

Therefore, all of us—whether married, widowed, or virgins—should think about and seek not the things that are on earth, but the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God, with whom he lives and reigns forever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXII. THIRD SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY

“Do not be wise in your own eyes” (Romans 12:16), and so forth.

This reading, my brothers, is divided into three parts. First, the Apostle warns us not to be wise in our own eyes, but before God. Second, he exhorts us to preserve peace. Third, he warns us not to repay evil with evil, but rather good for evil.

Warning us first not to be wise in our own eyes, he says: “Do not be wise in your own eyes.” As we gather from the sacred Scriptures, dearest brothers, some are wise before God, and they are good; some are wise according to the world, and they are evil; and some are wise in their own eyes, and they are proud.

Those who are wise before God are the ones who despise all vain things for his sake. Of them it is said: “The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls. When he had found one precious pearl, he gave away all that he had and bought it” (Matthew 13:45–46).

Those who are wise according to the world are the ones who, not knowing or scorning heavenly things, love only the world. Of them it is said: “The carnal person does not understand the things that are of God” (Romans 8:7). And again: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness before God” (1 Corinthians 3:19).

Those who are wise in their own eyes are the ones who despise others as though they were foolish and think themselves alone to be wise. Of them the Prophet says: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isaiah 5:21). Of them it is also said here: “Do not be wise in your own eyes.”

And because the proud are impatient and cannot endure the injuries of others, he adds: “Repaying no one evil for evil.” Rather, “Be wise before God, providing what is good, not only before God but also before human beings.”

A person provides what is good before God and human beings when he seeks to love God in such a way that he does not disdain to love his neighbor; when he seeks to please God in such a way that he also seeks to benefit his neighbor; and when he takes care to have a good conscience before God in such a way that he also takes care, through the reputation of good works, to provide an example for his neighbor.

Hence the Lord says: “Let your good works shine before human beings, so that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). And elsewhere: “He is cruel who neglects his reputation.”

But whoever disdains to benefit his neighbors, whoever scorns providing them with a good example, and, although he has a good conscience before God, nevertheless does not take care to appear good before human beings—concerning him Gregory says: “Whoever is now sufficiently able to trample upon human praise sins punishably if he hides the good that he does.”

Therefore, my brothers, much more grievously sins the person who, although living rightly inwardly, nevertheless allows the people to form a bad opinion of him, than the person who places a scandal before his brothers. For in order to avoid scandal, even certain lesser good deeds ought to be omitted.

Concerning such a person the Lord says: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be sunk into the depth of the sea” (Matthew 18:6). For whoever is such a person is guilty of as many souls as perish because of his bad example.

The second part follows, in which the Apostle warns us concerning peace, saying: “If it is possible, so far as it depends on you, live in peace with all human beings.”

Here, my brothers, three things must be considered: what peace is; between whom it can exist; and with whom and how it ought to be maintained.

Peace, then, is a tranquil state of affairs, with all things concordant with one another in an ordered way, or at least with some yielding in an ordered way to others.

True peace is of two kinds: perfect and imperfect. Perfect peace will exist in the other, eternal homeland, where there will be complete harmony, and where the elect will be so united to God that they cannot differ from his will. This is the peace of God “which surpasses all understanding” (Philippians 4:7).

With reference to that peace it has been said that “peace is a tranquil state of affairs, with all things concordant with one another in an ordered way.”

Present peace, however, is imperfect, because there is such variety in the world that scarcely anyone, even if perfect, can always be wholly harmonious with himself, much less can many people be entirely harmonious with one another.

But we say that peace exists here between certain people when, although they do not entirely agree, nevertheless some acquiesce to and yield to others, and do so in an ordered manner—namely, so that those who are less well-disposed yield to those who are better-disposed. With reference to this peace, the phrase means: “or at least with some yielding in an ordered way.”

True peace cannot exist among the wicked, because the wicked are divided within themselves and one from another, since vices are opposed to vices: this person is avaricious, that one prodigal; this one cruel, that one lax; this one fearful, that one reckless. Hence it is said: “There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isaiah 57:21). And in the Gospel: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be desolated” (Luke 11:17).

Although the wicked thus disagree among themselves, they unite in persecuting the good—Herod and Pilate in putting Jesus to death, and the Pharisees and Sadducees in persecuting Paul. This, however, is an evil peace and hostile to the righteous.

Among the good there is true peace, and the better they are, the greater is the harmony among them. For virtues cannot disagree with one another. Hence, in the eternal homeland, where there will be complete harmony among the virtues, peace will be entirely tranquil.

Now, however, because the virtues here are not wholly perfected, there is no perfect peace here.

Nor can peace exist between the good and the wicked, because the former are just and the latter unjust; the former devout and the latter cruel; the former chaste and the latter unchaste; the former patient and the latter impatient. True concord cannot exist among those who are so divided.

Recognizing this, the Apostle says: “If it is possible, live in peace with all human beings,” as though he were saying: “This cannot be achieved here, because even if you had peace with the wicked, they would not have peace with you.” For this reason he adds: “So far as it depends on you.”

Then, dearest brothers, we live in peace with all human beings as far as it depends on us when we do nothing to anyone by which he ought to become our enemy; when we desire and seek the good of everyone; and when, in order to win them for Christ, we do not relax from our perfection.

With whom ought we to have peace? With God, with our own soul, and with our neighbors, both friends and enemies.

Let us therefore have peace with God by obeying him and, as far as we can, conforming ourselves to his will. Let us have peace with ourselves by subjecting our animal impulses and senses to the spirit. Let us have peace with our friends by making them friends of God. Let us have peace with our enemies by reconciling them to God.

For this reason we ought to seek familiarity with the wicked and love for our enemies, so that by good words, example, and conduct we may win them for God.

Hence Paul instructed a faithful person to live with an unbeliever who consented to live with him. If the unbeliever did not consent, he was to depart. For it is better for each person to save his own soul alone than to perish with another.

Thus the Lord says: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword. For I have come to separate a son from his father” (Matthew 10:34–35), and so forth.

With the devil, however, and with vices, let us always have not peace but war: resisting the devil and uprooting vices from ourselves and from others.

Nor ought we to indulge our vices and sins; rather, we should persecute them more severely in ourselves than in others and subdue our hostile flesh, so that, even if it does not agree with the spirit, it may at least yield to it.

How greatly true peace ought to be desired the Lord shows: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9). And the Prophet says: “His dwelling has become in peace” (Psalm 75:3)—that is, with a tranquil mind and a tranquil congregation; for he alone makes those who are of one mind dwell in a house (Psalm 67:7).

The third part follows, in which the Apostle warns us not to repay evil with evil, but rather good for evil, when he adds: “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved”—that is, do not take revenge. For it is permissible to repel an injury without harming another person.

There are four kinds of repayment, my brothers:

- To repay evil for evil, which belongs to those who are moderately evil.
- To repay evil for good, which belongs to the most malicious.
- To repay good for good, which belongs to those who are moderately good.
- To repay good for evil, which belongs to the highest goodness.

When God the Judge inflicts punishment for sin, he does not repay evil for evil, but rather justice for injustice.

The Apostle therefore warns us not to repay evil for evil. “Give place,” he says, “to wrath”—that is, to divine vengeance. For whoever does not leave room for God’s vengeance sins in three ways: first, because he presumes to take what does not belong to him; second, because he anticipates the time of judgment; and third, because, regarding the blow by which he ought to have become better, he becomes worse.

For it is written: “Vengeance is mine”—understand, “reserve it for me”—“and I will repay.”

And not only should you refrain from repaying evil for evil; you should also repay good for evil. This is what he says: “But if your enemy is hungry”—whether bodily or spiritually—“feed him. If he is thirsty, give him drink.” For by doing this “you will heap burning coals upon his head”—that is, the ardor of charity in his mind—“so that he may be converted and reconciled to you.”

Or, if he refuses, you will heap the coals of eternal punishment upon his head. For because he was unwilling to be softened even by benefits, he will be tormented more severely in hell.

“Do not be overcome by evil.” A person is overcome by evil when he attempts to repay evil for evil; he is overcome by evil when he becomes worse because of an injury inflicted upon him; he is overcome by evil when he envies the prosperity of the wicked.

“But overcome evil with good,” he says. You overcome evil with good when through patience you conquer the injury inflicted upon you; when through benefits you reconcile your enemy to yourself; and when through a good example you invite the wicked to better things.

May our Lord Jesus Christ, who prayed for his enemies and laid down his life for them, grant us and you, my brothers, to fulfill this. Amen.

## HOMILY XXIII. THIRD SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY

“When Jesus had descended from the mountain, great crowds followed him” (Matthew 8:1), and so forth.

This reading, dearest brothers, is divided into two chapters. In the first, four things are shown: first, that Jesus descended from the mountain and was followed by great crowds; second, the leper’s approach to Jesus; third, his healing; and fourth, the command that he tell no one but show himself to the priests.

He says, therefore: “When Jesus had descended from the mountain, great crowds followed him.”

What does it mean, my brothers, that great crowds followed Jesus as he descended from the mountain, except that many peoples and many nations followed Jesus as he descended from heaven? For if he had remained forever in heaven, no one would have followed him, no one would have known him, and no one would have loved him.

How could the slow follow one who is incomprehensible? How could the dull recognize one who is invisible? How could the cold love one who is unknowable?

Since, therefore, human beings could not ascend to God, the good and merciful God descended to humanity. He descended by emptying himself in the form of a human being; he descended by having compassion on our misery; he descended by taking our infirmities upon himself.

Hence the Prophet says: “Truly he himself bore our infirmities” (Isaiah 53:4). And the Apostle says: “We do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our infirmities, but one who was tested in every respect according to our likeness, without sin” (Hebrews 4:15).

For whoever, dearest brothers, is accustomed to suffering knows better how to sympathize. Hence Dido says in the poet:

> “Not ignorant of suffering, I learn to succor the afflicted.”  
> (*Virgil, Aeneid* 1.630)

Because, therefore, the good and merciful Lord descended and accommodated himself to the infirmities of all, great crowds followed him. Who were they? The uneducated, the needy, sinners, and the sick. Why? Because he instructed the uneducated, fed the needy, absolved sinners, and healed the sick.

He did not rebuke or ridicule the uneducated, nor did he thunder over them with higher mysteries, as certain proud teachers are accustomed to do. Rather, having compassion on their simplicity, he instructed them with simple words, while on the mountains he taught the more perfect disciples with more perfect doctrine.

Following him, dearest brothers, let us learn to dispense the Lord’s teaching according to each person’s capacity. Hence the Apostle says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Corinthians 2:6). And again: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Corinthians 3:2).

For, according to the philosopher, the first part of wisdom is to assess the person to whom one is speaking.

Again, he did not shrink from or mock the needy, as certain proud rich people are accustomed to do. Rather, accommodating himself to them, he evangelized and cherished them. Concerning such people he himself says: “Do not prevent the little ones from coming to me, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Matthew 19:14).

Let us also, brothers, learn from his example to accommodate ourselves to and sympathize with the poor, according to the saying of the Wise Man: “My son, do not turn your eyes away from the poor” (Ecclesiasticus 4:1). And elsewhere: “Make yourself approachable to the assembly of the poor” (ibid.).

Again, he did not shrink from or scorn sinners, as certain proud righteous people are accustomed to do. Concerning them Solomon says: “There is a righteous person who perishes in his righteousness” (Ecclesiastes 7:16). And the proud Pharisee said of Christ, who welcomed Mary Magdalene: “If this man were a prophet, he would surely know what sort of woman this is who touches him, that she is a sinner” (Luke 7:39).

Rather, having compassion on them, he granted forgiveness through mercy, as to the woman caught in adultery, to whom he said: “Go, and do not sin again” (John 8:11).

Let us also, brothers, neither pass sinners by nor drive them to despair. Like the Samaritan, let us mix wine with oil (Luke 10:34), adding gentleness to reproach, and drawing them toward salvation in fear and hope alike, according to the Apostle’s saying: “If anyone is overtaken in some transgression, you who are spiritual should instruct such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Galatians 6:1).

Again, he did not shrink from the sick, as certain cruel people are accustomed to do, who recoil from the breath, bed, and touch of the sick. Rather, having compassion on them, he touched and healed them, as is demonstrated in this reading.

From this let us also learn, my brothers, to sympathize with the sick and to minister to them constantly, so that we may deserve to hear from him: “I was sick, and you visited me” (Matthew 25:36).

Although this compassion is necessary for everyone, it is especially necessary for bishops, abbots, priors, and heads of households. For unless they accommodate themselves to their subjects, those subjects neither love nor follow them.

I have seen certain abbots and priors who, although sufficiently religious in themselves, nevertheless, because they did not know how to accommodate themselves to each person’s infirmity but imposed their frugality and austerity upon them indiscriminately, had scattered and driven away their flock.

This must not be done, dearest brothers. For not all of us can do all things, and we have gifts from God: one person has this gift, another that one (1 Corinthians 7:7). Therefore, let the superior accommodate himself to everyone’s infirmity; let him become weak to the weak, rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep, and become all things to all people, as the Apostle says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not inflamed?” (2 Corinthians 11:29).

The second part follows, in which the leper’s approach to Jesus is shown, when it says: “And behold, a leper came and worshiped him, saying…”

Because he knew that Jesus accommodated himself to the infirmities of all, he dared to approach him. He approached him with his feet, and likewise with humility and faith.

He approached him with humility when he believed that Jesus could do all things by his mere will, and confessed, saying: “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.” As though he were saying: “Lord, I am indeed vile and unworthy for you to touch and heal, but you can cleanse me not because of my merits, but solely by your will and grace.”

Following this leper’s example, let us also, my brothers, who are covered with the foul leprosy of sins, humble ourselves before God and say: “We are indeed unworthy, but you alone, by your will and grace, can heal us.”

The third part follows, in which the leper is healed when the Lord says to him: “I will; be cleansed.”

Here, my brothers, the ineffable depths of divine mercy must be considered: the Lord awaits the leper whom people shunned, tolerates him when he comes to worship, listens to him when he speaks, and does what he asks—indeed, more than he asks.

When the leper had said, “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean,” the Lord not only willed and cleansed him, but also touched him.

Why? Because of compassion for his humility, because of the understanding of the law, and because of the significance of the mystery.

Because of compassion for his humility: to teach us not to shun the sick but to have compassion on them.

Because of the understanding of the law: to show that, through the touching of a leper and a dead person, which the law prohibited, it was not the leper and the dead person themselves that were signified as objects of avoidance, but consent to mortal sin.

Because of the significance of the mystery: to signify that the leprosy of grave sins requires the work of satisfaction. Venial faults, however, are often forgiven without the work of satisfaction. But the leprosy of a more serious crime requires the hand of satisfaction.

The fourth part follows, when it says: “See that you tell no one. But go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift that Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.”

In this, dearest brothers, when the Lord commands the healed leper to keep the miracle silent, he instructs us to seek not human praise but the praise of God alone in the good things we do.

In the fact that the man proclaims the miracle, it is shown that the Lord does not wish the virtues of the saints to remain hidden, but manifests them, even against their will, for the benefit of others, according to what he himself says: “No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place, but on a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house” (Luke 11:33).

He commands him to show himself to the priest so that no one may rely upon his own penance, but may make satisfaction according to the judgment of the priest, and may fear that the leprosy of his crime will return because of disobedience and contempt unless he shows himself to the priest through confession.

He also commands him to offer a gift: to show that he has not abolished the law; to teach the one cleansed from sin to give thanks to God; to demonstrate that offerings are to be made to priests; and to make it a testimony to them, either of faith if they believe, or of condemnation if they do not believe.

“When he had entered Capernaum,” and so forth.

In this second chapter, dearest brothers, the virtues of this centurion must first be considered, and then Christ’s works concerning him.

This centurion was distinguished by four great virtues and is worthy of our imitation. He possessed mercy, faith, humility, and wisdom.

He possessed mercy, by which he sympathized with the infirmity of his servant. As another Evangelist testifies, he asked the Lord through the elders of the Jews and, in order to move the Lord more deeply to mercy, pitifully emphasized the servant’s suffering.

He shows him to be pitiable in three respects: that he is lying there, that he is paralyzed, and that he is suffering terribly. For just as lying down is rest for a healthy person, so it is torment for a sick person. He was paralyzed—that is, deprived of the use of his limbs—for “paralysis” means dissolution or loosening. And because his limbs could have been withered without causing him pain, he adds: “And he is suffering terribly.”

Following this example, dearest brothers, let us learn to show kindness to our servants: not to despise them, not to treat them harshly, and not to drive away the sick at once, as certain proud people are accustomed to do. Rather, let us love them as human beings and brothers, provide them with what they need, give them their due, and accommodate ourselves to the sick.

Let it be enough for us if we are honored and loved by them, since this is enough for God. Let us also consider that they and we have one Lord, God. And if we think of them as servants of human beings, let us consider whether perhaps we ourselves—something more serious—are servants of sins.

Let us not despise what Job did not despise: to enter into judgment with his male servant and female servant.

The centurion had faith, brothers, because he believed that Christ could give health by a mere word. He also believed that, just as he himself commanded his soldiers and fulfilled his will through them, so the Lord could command angels and accomplish through them whatever he wished: he could tell the sickness to depart, and it would depart; he could tell health to come, and it would come.

Because he believed in this way, he deserved to be praised by the Lord and to obtain what he had requested. Let us also learn, dearest brothers, to possess the fervor of faith, since the Lord himself says: “All things are possible for the one who believes” (Mark 9:23).

He possessed great humility, because he considered himself unworthy that the Lord should approach him, that he should ask him personally, or that the Lord should enter his house. Since he was a Gentile, he had asked the Lord not personally but through the elders.

Following this example, let us also, brothers, think humbly of ourselves, judge ourselves unworthy in all things, and recognize that we are not worthy to ask him with our polluted mouth. Rather, let us incline him to mercy toward us through the intercession of the saints.

Let us be afraid to receive his body and blood into the foul lodging of our body—not because we wish to remain in foulness, but so that we may strive all the more to become clean and worthy.

Behold, brothers, both this centurion and Zacchaeus honored the Lord, but in different ways: Zacchaeus by gladly receiving him, the centurion by considering himself unworthy.

The person who frequently and joyfully receives the Eucharist imitates Zacchaeus; those who, considering themselves unworthy, fear receiving the Eucharist and withdraw, imitate the centurion.

Hence Augustine says: “I neither praise nor blame the celebration of daily Mass”—that is, “I neither praise it in the unworthy nor blame it in the worthy.”

He possessed great wisdom because he understood that the one whom he saw, according to his humanity, to be present in one place was, according to his divinity, absent from no place.

Following his example, dearest brothers, let us believe that Christ is in heaven according to his humanity, while according to his divinity he is present in every place.

Conversely, dearest brothers in Christ, let us consider four things: Christ’s condescension, the commendation of the centurion’s faith, the prophecy concerning the election of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews, and the granting of the petition.

Christ showed great condescension when he answered: “I will come and heal him.”

He promises to go, my brothers, to a servant, although he was not invited; but when asked to go to the son of a royal official, he refused to go. Why was this, except to correct our perversity, by which we honor the rich and despise the poor, regarding wealth rather than nature and power rather than the image of God in the honor we give to people?

Let us therefore avoid partiality, brothers, and learn to honor in people nature, not fortune; virtue, not power.

The Lord praises the centurion’s faith when, marveling, he says to those following him: “I have not found such faith in Israel.”

He does not marvel at the faith in himself who had given him that faith; rather, he shows him to be admirable in faith and worthy of imitation, because he believes without the law and the prophets, while Israel, instructed through the law and the prophets, is unwilling to believe.

“I have not found such faith in Israel”—that is, among those to whom he was then preaching. For he had previously found it among the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles.

He prophesied concerning the election of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews when he added: “I tell you that many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. But the children of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness.”

Behold, dearest brothers, this prophecy has been fulfilled today. For the elect from the Gentiles, from the whole world, ascend to heaven and are glorified with the patriarchs, whose conduct and faith they followed when they die.

But the Jews, among whom God first reigned and to whom the promise of the kingdom had been made, are sent into the outer darkness when they die, having here voluntarily entered the inner darkness.

“There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” By the weeping of the eyes and the gnashing of the teeth, the true future resurrection of bodies is indicated. The teeth gnash that here rejoiced in gluttony; the eyes weep that desired unlawful things; the tongue burns that slandered; and likewise the remaining members, according to the variety of vices, will undergo a variety of punishments.

Christ fulfills the centurion’s request when he says: “Go; let it be done for you as you have believed.”

My brothers, great is the merit of faith. Because the centurion believed that God could do all things, the Lord indicates that he deserved to receive what he sought and grants it according to the measure of his faith.

Hence it is added: “And the servant was healed in that hour.” The Lord’s faithfulness is proved when the servant’s healing follows.

Here, brothers, we should consider how much a person’s own faith avails, since another person’s faith avails so much.

Let us therefore imitate this centurion’s virtues—mercy, faith, and humility—through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXIV. FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY

“Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (Romans 13:8), and so forth.

In this reading, dearest brothers, the Apostle does three things: first, he exhorts us to justice; second, to love; and third, he proves that love is the fulfillment of the law.

Exhorting us to hold fast to justice, he says: “Owe no one anything.” For it is characteristic of justice, my brothers, to owe no one anything, but to return to each person what belongs to him, so that we may repay, as the Apostle himself said above: “To whom honor is due, honor; to whom tribute, tribute; to whom tax, tax” (Romans 13:7).

This justice is the preserver of peace and human society. Conversely, the injustice of failing to return to someone what belongs to him is the destroyer of peace and concord.

From what else, my brothers, do lawsuits and discord arise, or seditions and killings, except from the fact that one person does not do for another what he ought?

For this reason the Lord willed judges and authorities to be established in this world, so that each person, if unwilling, might be compelled to return to another what he owed.

But whoever is just in himself and willingly returns to each person what belongs to him has no need of a judge and does not fear authority.

Hence the Apostle says: “Do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will receive praise from it. But if you do evil, be afraid; for it does not bear the sword without reason” (Romans 13:3–4).

Therefore, brothers, that you may deserve praise from the eternal and supreme Judge, practice voluntary justice: “Return to each person what belongs to him.”

Give God the religious devotion you owe him; the Church, reverence; yourselves, purity; superiors, respect; inferiors, gracious consideration; equals, fellowship; parents, honor; children, discipline; members of your household, care; the needy, compassion; friends, love; enemies, patience; and everyone, fairness.

For in this way you will live justly before God and human beings, owing no one anything.

The second part follows, in which he exhorts us to love, as he adds: “Except to love one another.”

As though he were saying: “Return to each person what belongs to him, so that you owe no one anything except love alone.”

The Apostle says this, my brothers, because, although other debts cease to be owed once they have been paid, love is always paid and always owed.

It is such a necessary good that it is necessary to possess it at all times and toward everyone in every circumstance.

At all times: for just as an animal cannot live, whether asleep or awake, without breathing, and dies when breath is taken away, so the soul cannot live without love of God and neighbor, and dies when that love is lost.

Therefore, brothers, we ought always to love. And even if we are not always able to perform works of love, we ought always to have love toward everyone: toward God, toward ourselves, and toward our neighbors, both friends and enemies.

If we do not preserve love toward someone, we preserve it toward others in vain.

We ought also to have love in all our works, because just as a work cannot please God without right intention, neither can it please him without love.

It is indeed a good work, dearest brothers, to give alms, honor parents, love children, frequent the church, believe in God, and preach the Gospel. Yet none of these has value without love of God and neighbor.

Hence the Apostle says:

“If I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become like a sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. And if I have all faith and all knowledge, and if I distribute my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:1–3).

[Note: [Col. 1753D] The Vulgate adds: “but do not have charity.”]

Conversely, brothers, true love, even with a small work—or even without a work when someone lacks the means—is sufficient for eternal life.

For God does not weigh how much is given, but from how much love it is given. Hence the widow who offered a few small coins to God is preferred to the rich who contributed great gifts (Luke 21:1–4).

The third part follows, in which the Apostle proves that true love is the fulfillment of the law, when he adds: “For he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.” To understand this better, dearly beloved brothers, let us see what love is, how love of God and of neighbor are connected, and how the law is fulfilled through love of God.

Charity, then, is love by which we love God for his own sake and our neighbor for God’s sake [Col. 1755A]. There is therefore one love, but two commandments. For there is one God, whom we love either in himself or in our neighbor. Whoever loves his neighbor for something other than God, or for any reason other than God’s sake, does not truly love him. Let us therefore love our neighbor because he is or can be good, because he is God’s work, and because God commands that he be loved.

Love of God and of neighbor are joined together in such a way that God cannot truly be loved without one’s neighbor, nor one’s neighbor without God. Hence John says: “He who does not love his neighbor whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” Whoever does not love God, moreover, does not truly love either himself or anyone else. Therefore, when the Apostle speaks of love of neighbor, understand at the same time love of God, since one cannot be true without the other.

Through love of God and neighbor, then, the law is fulfilled—that is, the ten commandments of the law, of which the first four pertain to God and the remaining six to one’s neighbor.

The first is: “Hear, O Israel: your God is one” (Deut. VI). If he is one, brothers, then the fool who said in his heart, “There is no God” (Ps. XIII), is lying. If he is one, the pagan who says that there are many gods is lying. If he is one, the heretic who asserts that he is changeable is always lying; for he is one alone, undivided, and unchanging.

The second is: “You shall not make for yourself a graven image” (Exod. XX; Deut. V), that is, you shall prefer nothing to God, either in opinion or in love.

The third is: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain” (ibid.), that is, with contempt. He does this who invokes God’s name in testimony to vanity, falsehood, or [Col. 1755C] fraud.

The fourth is: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day” (ibid.). The Jew observed this according to the letter; now we observe it spiritually, when throughout the entire Sabbath of this life we abstain from servile work—that is, from sin—so that in the future we may keep Sabbath from every labor.

The fifth is: “Honor your father and your mother” (ibid.). This is to be understood both of showing them due respect and of doing them good.

The sixth is: “You shall not kill” (ibid.): neither by will, as one who hates his brother; nor by deed, as a man of blood; nor by evil teaching, as a heretic; nor by bad example, as a preacher who lives badly; nor by withholding temporal goods, as a miser; nor by withholding preaching, as a preacher who hides his talent [Col. 1755D].

The seventh is: “You shall not commit adultery” (ibid.): neither in spirit through idolatry, nor in the body through fornication, adultery, sexual misconduct, incest, sodomitical lust, or impurity.

The eighth is: “You shall not steal” (ibid.), by which robbery, plunder, usury, and deceit are condemned.

The ninth is: “You shall not bear false witness” (ibid.). By this every lie, perjury, detraction, whispering, and flattery is prohibited.

The tenth is: “You shall not covet” (ibid.), that is, you shall restrain covetous desire; and if it arises, you shall neither consent to it nor fulfill it.

These, dearly beloved brothers, are the ten commandments, which are fulfilled through love, because whoever truly loves God obeys all his commandments. Whoever loves his neighbor does not kill him, does not commit adultery with his wife, does not steal his possessions, does not lie to him, and does not transgress the other commandments that concern one’s neighbor [Col. 1756A]. Without true love, however, these cannot be fulfilled. For whether you honor your father, or do not kill, or do not commit adultery, or fulfill any other commandment, if you do it without charity, you deserve no reward.

Charity is the Lord’s broad commandment, in which the whole law is brought to completion. Concerning this the Prophet says: “I have seen the end of every perfection; your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. CXVIII). Charity is a broad commandment because it extends from friends even to enemies, and because it also enlarges us so that we may run and fulfill God’s law.

Although the way of God is difficult and arduous for fools, nevertheless, because nothing is difficult for one who loves, it becomes easy and broad for him, according to the saying: “I have run the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (ibid.).

Therefore, brothers, if you cannot know the whole law or the whole Gospel, at least hold fast to charity. For the person who holds charity in his conduct holds both what is manifest and what is hidden in the divine words. Love will teach you to render what you owe to God, to your neighbor, to your friend, and to your enemy. And if you are lacking in wisdom in some respect, love will excuse it; whatever you do, it will make pleasing to God, through the generosity of him who lives and reigns forever and ever.

# HOMILY XXV. THE FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

“When Jesus had entered the boat, his disciples followed him” (Matt. VIII), and the rest. This reading, dearly beloved brothers, instructs us according to the literal sense concerning faith in the Mediator between God and human beings, Jesus Christ. For it shows that true divinity and humanity exist in him. That he is carried in a boat with other human beings, and that he sleeps, belongs to his humanity. But that he stills the storm and commands the sea belongs to his divinity.

According to the mystical sense, however, the sea is the present age, since, like the sea, it stinks and swells, is salty and unstable. It stinks through lust, swells through pride, is salty through bitterness, and is unstable through vanity. And just as larger fish swallow smaller ones in the sea, so in this age the stronger devour the weaker.

The boat is the Church, in which we cross the storms of this age and make our way toward the harbor of our heavenly homeland. Whoever is not in this boat will not reach the harbor of salvation but will be submerged in the abyss. Those who follow Christ sail and cross over in it, and Christ is with them, for he himself says: “Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, I am in the midst of them” (Matt. XVIII). And elsewhere: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

The great disturbance of the sea is the tribulation and persecution of this world. The contrary wind is the evil spirit. For just as the Holy Spirit guides the Church’s boat to the harbor of salvation, so the evil spirit tries to drive it headlong into the shipwreck of perdition. The boat is covered by the waves when the Church is almost imperiled amid persecutions and storms.

Five things are therefore shown to us here: first, that even those who are with Christ are almost imperiled; second, why this happens; third, how the Lord is to be awakened; fourth, how God rebukes and delivers his own; fifth, how thanks are to be given to the Deliverer.

It is therefore shown that the Church, in which Christ is with his faithful, is almost imperiled, when it is said that the boat was covered by the waves. For Christ wishes, my brothers, that his own pass through tribulations, through which he himself passed. Hence he says: “He who serves me, let him follow me” (John XII). And the Apostle says: “All who desire to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution” (II Tim. III).

This is directed against those who wish to make their way to the reward of the kingdom through softness and the prosperity of this age, whereas it is the hard and laboring soldiers, not the soft and effeminate, who are crowned [Col. 1757B].

Second, the reason why tribulations come upon the saints is added, when it is said: “But he was sleeping.” The Church suffers because Christ sleeps. But how does he sleep, brothers, when it is written of him: “He neither slumbers nor sleeps who guards Israel”? (Ps. CXX.) Brothers, Christ’s sleep is the concealment of his help. Christ is awake in the Church when he delivers it; he is said to sleep when he delays delivering it. Hence the Prophet, placed in tribulation, cries out to him: “Rise up; why do you sleep, O Lord? Rise up, and do not reject us forever” (Ps. XLIII).

And why, brothers, does Christ delay delivering his Church? Because he knows that tribulation is useful to it. For tribulation makes a person more corrected, more humble, more radiant, more cautious, stronger, more contemptuous of earthly things, and more desirous of heavenly things.

It makes him more corrected because it washes away the stains of sins. Hence the Lord says through the Prophet: “I will smelt away your dross completely” (Isa. I). This is apparent in Mary, the sister of Moses: because she had sinned by murmuring against her brother, she was punished and cleansed through the affliction of leprosy.

It makes him more humble because it does not allow him to become proud through prosperity. For just as prosperity is accustomed to cause exaltation, so adversity causes humility. Hence Paul says: “Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me” (II Cor. XII).

It makes him more radiant, since the more a righteous person is attacked, the more radiant he becomes. This is apparent in Job and in the holy martyrs.

It makes him more cautious, since the more he is harassed, the more watchful he becomes. For just as prosperity produces security and security contempt, so adversity generates fear and fear watchfulness. Hence Peter says: “Be watchful in prayers, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour” (I Pet. IV).

It makes him stronger, because the more he is attacked, the more practiced and hardened he becomes in resisting. An athlete cannot bring great courage to the contest if he has never been taunted or struck. And the tree that is shaken by winds on a mountain is stronger than the one that grows in a sunny valley. Thus the person nourished in adversity is stronger than the one nourished in prosperity. “The furnace proves the potter’s vessels, and tribulation the righteous” (Eccli. XXVII).

It makes him a despiser of earthly things and a seeker of heavenly things, because one who has nothing on earth in which to delight is more easily inflamed with love of heavenly things. Hence the Prophet, knowing that tribulation is so useful to the righteous, cries out: “Lord, do not abandon me utterly” (Ps. CXVIII). He seemed to regard being abandoned to some extent as useful to him, since he asked not to be abandoned utterly.

The same Prophet says: “Give me help from tribulation” (Ps. LIX). He does not say “from tribulation” in the sense of removal of tribulation, but asks that help come to him out of tribulation. Foreseeing this, the Lord appears to sleep while he prolongs delivering them.

Third, it is shown how the Lord is to be awakened, when it is added: “And they came and awakened him, saying: ‘Lord, save us; we are perishing.’” We too, brothers, when we are tempted and afflicted, should approach Christ and, with faith working through love (Gal. V), awaken him by the cry of our prayers.

Let us not trust in our wisdom, strength, or riches, nor in human help, for it is written: “He who trusts in his riches will fall” (Prov. XI); and: “Cursed is the one who trusts in man” (Jer. XVII). Let us hope in God alone, who does not abandon those who hope in him, for “those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion” (Ps. CXXIV).

Let us therefore cry out to him with sighs, groans, tears, and prayers, and awaken him to mercy. Let us say: “[Uncertain: Petimus in nobis, literally ‘we ask in ourselves’]; but you, who alone can, save us” [Col. 1758C]. For if we possess these four things—true faith, pure prayer, distrust of ourselves, and confidence of salvation in him alone—he who said, “You will cry out, and I will hear you” (Jer. XXIX), will hear us. For, as the Apostle says: “God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure” (Ps. IX); and he will be a helper in times of need, in tribulation.

Hence it is added: “Why are you fearful, O you of little faith?” This is the fourth part, in which it is shown how God rebukes his children for their little faith and fear, and delivers them.

Perhaps, my brothers, God would often test us with greater and longer tribulations so that we might merit more; but because we fear through our littleness of faith, we compel him, as it were, to rise before the time and deliver us [Col. 1758D]. This is well shown, brothers, by Peter walking upon the waters. He would certainly have gone to Jesus if he had not feared and doubted; but because he feared the strong wind that was coming, he began to sink (Matt. XIV). In this way he somehow compelled the Lord to extend his hand to him before the time.

We walk upon the waters toward Jesus when, despising and trampling upon the tribulations and temptations of this world, we hasten to him. If we persevered, we would come to him with a greater crown. But if we doubt and fear in the face of strong tribulation, we begin to sink and urge Jesus to extend to us the hand of his help before the time.

For this reason, my brothers, God rebukes us for our little faith and for the fear that proceeds from it [Col. 1759A]. The person who fears while the Lord is present, who fears that God will abandon those who hope in him, and who forgets that God does not forget to show mercy, has too little faith and an excess of disordered fear.

Yet even if we are less faithful to God, God will always remain faithful to us. He rises who pretends to sleep, commands the winds and the sea—that is, the evil spirits and tribulation—and great calm comes to be in the mind, in life, and in conduct.

Therefore, my brothers, since the devil, every tribulation, and all peace are in God’s hand, we ought not to fear the devil or the world, but God alone, because, according to the Wise Man: “All things fear the one who fears God” [Note: [Col. 1759D] The Vulgate expresses the same idea in other words.] (Eccli. XXXIV). And he who does not fear God fears everything.

Fifth, it is shown how thanks are to be given to Christ the Deliverer, when it is added: “But the men were amazed, saying: ‘What sort of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?’” Whoever, after being delivered, does not give thanks to his deliverer deserves not to be delivered again.

Hence the Hebrews, after deliverance, sang a song to God: Moses after Pharaoh’s drowning (Exod. XV), Deborah after the killing of Sisera (Judg. V), and Judith after the slaughter of Holofernes (Judith XIII). Hence they say that Hezekiah fell ill (Isa. XXXVIII) because he had not given thanks to God for an incredible victory. The nine lepers healed by the Lord are likewise reproved because they did not return to give thanks (Luke XVII).

Let us therefore not be ungrateful to Christ our Deliverer. Rather, admiring, praising, and blessing his power and goodness, let us say: “Who and how great, how glorious and admirable is he, that the evil spirits and tribulations obey him?” And thus, singing a song of psalmody after the shipwreck, let us give thanks to Christ our Deliverer, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God. Amen.

# HOMILY XXVI. SUNDAY IN SEPTUAGESIMA

“Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run, but only one receives the prize?” (I Cor. IX), and the rest.

The stadium is the span of the present life; the prize is the reward of eternal blessedness. The way is faith; Christ is the guide. Hence he himself says: “He who follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John VIII). For he left you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps (I Pet. II). Whoever wishes to remain with him ought himself to walk as he walked (I John VI).

The incentives for traveling this way are hope and love of the heavenly prize. Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, we all run through the stadium of the present life, because without interruption we all hasten toward death. Yet not all strive toward the prize of heavenly life: some even think that there is no other life.

All who lack faith—the Jew, the pagan, and the Christian in name only, who doubt that life—are therefore outside the way. If at some time they perform good works out of natural goodness, this benefits them no more than the swiftest running outside the way. They are not proceeding; they are wandering.

Among those who are on the way of faith, some run quickly, some slowly, and some backward.

Those run quickly who, casting aside every impediment, hasten toward heavenly things with their whole desire. Hence Paul says: “Everyone who contends in the contest abstains from everything” (I Cor. IX). And elsewhere: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business” (II Tim. II).

For what are riches, honors, glory, pleasures, and other worldly affairs except certain impediments to the soul? Our Redeemer urged us to cast aside these impediments when he said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. XIX).

The holy apostles and evangelists, martyrs, and hermits did this. Leaving everything and distributing it to the poor, they followed Christ naked, the naked one [Col. 1760B]. They are well signified by Joseph, who, when the shameless woman held his cloak through lust and tried to compel him to act disgracefully, left the cloak and fled. They are also well represented by the disciple who, when seized during Christ’s passion, escaped naked after abandoning his linen cloth.

Whoever leaves everything to avoid lust and the world’s wickedness flees naked, as though he had cast aside a cloak or linen cloth.

These people, my brothers, because they run more quickly, when they reach the end of the stadium—that is, death—immediately receive not only the prize but also authority to judge the others. For the Lord promised them this, saying: “You who have left everything and followed me will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life. And you will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX).

Those run slowly whom concern for wives, children, household members, and worldly affairs delays from desiring the heavenly homeland, though it does not delay them altogether. In mind, prayer, and deed they strive toward the heavenly prize, but because of cares and carnal affections they are somewhat slow.

For they seek the things of God in such a way that they must also seek the things of the world; and, as the Apostle says, they are divided when they place love of heavenly things above temporal things.

These are well signified, my brothers, by those cows that carried the Lord’s ark from the land of the Philistines to the land of Israel. They are said to have been nursing cows, which is why they shut up their calves at home. For it is written: “The cows went straight along the road that leads to Beth-shemesh. They proceeded along one path, going and lowing, and did not turn aside to the right or to the left” (I Kings VI).

What do these cows signify, my brothers, except the faithful who always carry the ark of God’s commandments? Although carnal affections call them back and delay them, they nevertheless do not turn aside from the straight road to Beth-shemesh—that is, the house of the sun.

Therefore, you heads of households, if you are striving toward the dwelling of the true sun, do not turn aside from the straight road because of carnal affections. But just as the cows proceed and groan, so should you sympathize with your neighbors in such a way that you do not on that account deviate from the straight way [Col. 1761A].

Those who are delayed somewhat from God’s way by cares and carnal affections, when they come to the goal of the stadium—that is, death—often do not immediately receive the prize. Rather, they are cleansed in purgatorial fire from the stains they contracted through cares and carnal affections, and only then attain the prize.

Those run backward who, although they are on God’s way through faith, return to worldly desires through covetousness. These are the people who prefer the affections of wives, children, riches, honors, and pleasures to God. They seek with their whole desire not the things of God but the things of the world, and, according to the Apostle, “they profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus I).

They are well signified by the children of Israel. After the Lord had led them out of Pharaoh’s slavery by crossing the Red Sea and was leading them through the desert to the promised land, sustaining them with manna, they grew weary of the manna and forgot the promised land. In their hearts they were returning to Egypt, saying: “Let us return to Egypt, to the pots of meat, to the melons, and to the garlic” (Exod. XIV, XVI; Num. I, XIV).

Do not those false Christians do the same today who, after being freed by Christ from slavery to the devil and from love of the world, renounced him through baptism, and, nourished by the bread of heaven, began to hasten through the desert of religious life toward the heavenly homeland—yet again return in desire to the love and slavery of the devil?

For what is signified by the pots of meat except a powerful habit of gluttony? What by the melons except worldly sweetness? And what by the garlic, which is pungent and foul-smelling, except lust?

What is it, dearly beloved brothers, that smoke is produced from the pot of meat, and, I believe, tears from the melons and garlic, except that worldly gluttony, sweetness, and lust drag their lovers toward the weeping of hell and even here produce blindness of mind and sadness?

Then, as the Lord says, lovers of such things will be sent into the outer darkness, “where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. VIII); and according to Solomon: “Laughter will be mingled with sorrow, and mourning will take possession of the end of joy” (Prov. XIV).

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, after the renunciation made in baptism, do not return again to the slavery of the devil and to love of the world, because “no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke VI). But, “forgetting what lies behind, reach forward to what lies ahead” (Phil. III).

“The life of man upon earth is a warfare” (Job VII); and: “He will not be crowned unless he has contended lawfully” (II Tim. II).
