Behold, all indeed run, but only one—the one who runs well—will receive the prize. Run, then, so that you may obtain it.

And if those who seek a temporal prize so discipline themselves that they receive a corruptible crown, what ought we to do, brothers, who are hastening toward an incorruptible one?

Therefore, brothers, if you do not run with such freedom as contemplatives and those who have abandoned everything for God, at least run with those who possess as though they did not possess, who marry as though they did not marry, who rejoice as though they did not rejoice (I Cor. VII), and who know how to purchase heavenly things through temporal ones.

If you are somewhat slow, pray to the Lord who “rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (Ps. XVIII), and say to him: “Draw me after you; we will run in the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song I).

May he himself deign to accomplish this, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever. Amen.

# HOMILY XXVII. SUNDAY IN SEPTUAGESIMA

“The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard” (Matt. XX), and the rest.

In this parable, dearly beloved brothers, the Lord shows how great a care—how great, so to speak, a solicitude—he himself has for the human race. Here those who say that God does not care for human affairs are refuted.

For here the Lord shows that just as some householder carefully provides for his vineyard so that it may not become too hard, be overgrown with weeds, or lose the proper season for its pruning and restoration, so from the beginning he has been, so to speak, watchful over his Church, lest it become too hard, be occupied by vices, or lose the care of preaching and admonition.

The householder is therefore understood as God; the vineyard as the Church; the laborers as preachers or any of the faithful who cultivate their own hearts or those of others so that they may bear fruit for God; the hours as different ages. The morning is like childhood; the third hour, youth; the sixth, mature age; the ninth, old age; the eleventh hour, extreme old age; and the denarius, the reward of blessedness.

An agreement for a daily denarius is made when the reward of blessedness is promised to those who labor well.

This reading has five parts, my brothers. First, the laborers are sent into the vineyard; second, payment is made in the evening; third, the first laborers murmur; fourth, the householder answers them; fifth, the conclusion is given.

The sending of the laborers takes place first, when it is said: “After agreeing for a daily denarius, he sent them into his vineyard.” Here, my brothers, it must be considered that those who are sent in the morning are promised a daily denarius. Those who are sent at the third, sixth, or ninth hour are not promised a denarius; they are merely told: “Whatever is just I will give you.” But those who are sent at the eleventh hour are promised nothing. Rather, they are rebuked and sent into the vineyard when they are told: “Why do you stand here idle all day? Go, you also, into my vineyard.”

And why is this, my brothers? Because those who labor throughout their whole life in God’s work seem, according to human judgment, to have deserved the denarius of complete blessedness. Those who spend part of their life in idleness and vice and part in God’s service do not seem to have deserved the denarius of blessedness in its entirety. Those who begin to work well only at the end seem to have deserved nothing or little.

And truly, brothers, if someone spends his whole life in goodness, he is more worthy than one who begins to work well in the middle or at the end of life, provided that both are equal in degree of charity and labor.

But often, brothers, it happens that those who went out later overtake the earlier ones with faster running, because, as Jerome says: “Sudden fervor conquers long tepidity.” The earlier ones often grow weary from long labor, grow lukewarm through the security of hope, and place themselves above those who came later because of the greatness of their merits. By contrast, the later ones frequently become faster because of their late conversion, more fervent because of fear, humble themselves because of their brief labor, and place everyone above themselves. Therefore, like the tax collector, they go down justified rather than the others [i.e. the earlier laborers] (Luke XVIII).

The second part follows, in which payment is made, when it is added: “When evening had come, the lord of the vineyard said to his steward: ‘Call the laborers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last up to the first,’” and so forth.

By evening, dearly beloved brothers, the end of the world is signified. When the labors have ended, God the Father commands the steward and redeemer of the vineyard—namely, our Lord Jesus Christ—to summon the laborers to judgment and pay them their wages.

What does “beginning with the last up to the first” mean, especially since judgment and recompense will be completed not one after another but, as the Apostle says, “in the twinkling of an eye”? (I Cor. XV.) This priority and posteriority, brothers, refer not to time but to reward.

For all the elect will be rewarded at the same time, but not with the same measure of reward. Hence the Lord says: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John XIV); and the Apostle: “Star differs from star in glory. One is the glory of the sun, another the glory of the moon” (I Cor. XV), and so forth.

Although the elect therefore each receive a denarius, one will receive a bright one, another a brighter, another the brightest. The giving of the denarius, on which the king’s image and name were engraved, means nothing other than the restoration in us of the image and likeness of God, which had been disfigured in us by sins.

Just as one denarius bears a more distinct image and inscription than another, so the holier person will bear in himself a more distinct image and likeness of God than the less holy. Payment therefore begins with the last and proceeds to the first when the last, being more fervent, are placed by God ahead of the first, who are less fervent, in the measure of recompense.

The third part follows, in which the first, supposing that they would receive more, murmur against the householder, saying: “These last worked one hour, and you have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden of the day and the heat.”

This murmuring, my brothers, is to be referred to the state of the present life. No one will enter the heavenly homeland while murmuring, nor will anyone entering be able to murmur there.

But in the present life there are many who seem to themselves to have labored for a long time in God’s work. If they knew that those who began later were placed before them or made equal to them, they would murmur and say: “These last worked one hour, and you have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden of the day and the heat,” as though saying: We have endured the length of time and the heat of the flesh in God’s work.

They incur sins in four ways: because they criticize God’s judgment; because, despising their brothers, they call the last “last”; because they boast of their works; and because they grieve with envy that their brothers are made equal to them.

The fourth part follows, in which the Lord answers the one who speaks or thinks in such a perverse way through the Spirit or through Scripture, saying: “Friend, I do you no wrong.”

First, he shows that his judgment is right, when he adds: “Did you not agree with me for a daily denarius?” Let no one, brothers, infer from these words that God is bound, as though by a contract, to repay what he promised. For just as God is free in promising, so he is free in repaying—especially since both merits and rewards are his grace.

God crowns nothing other than his own grace in us. If he wished to deal with us strictly, “no living person would be justified in his sight” (Ps. CXLII). Hence the Apostle, who labored more than all the others, says: “I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII).

This agreement, therefore, is nothing other than God’s voluntary promise.

Then the Lord rebukes them for despising their brothers and boasting of their works, when he makes the last equal to them, saying: “I wish to give this last one, according to your opinion, as much as to you, who appear great in your own eyes. Is it not lawful for me, the Lord, to show mercy to whomever I wish?”

Afterward he rebukes them because they grieve with envy that their brothers are made equal to them, when he says: “Is your eye evil because I am good?”

Behold, brothers, how subtly he describes the evil of envy [Col. 1764C]: it grieves as much over receiving little itself as over another’s receiving something. It does not so much desire to receive more itself as to have others receive nothing, and it wastes away at another’s good.

Avoid this envy with every effort, brothers; no one can ascend to heaven with it. For the envious person, who weeps with those who rejoice and rejoices with those who weep, is far removed from the charity that says: “Weep with those who weep, and rejoice with those who rejoice” (Rom. XII).

The fifth part follows, in which the Lord concludes and applies the comparison, saying: “So the last will be first, and the first last.”

This is not a universal proposition, brothers, but an indefinite one, since not all the last will be first, nor all the first last. Rather, some who seem to themselves or to other people to be last will be first before God. And some who seem to themselves or to other people to be first will be last among the righteous before God, or even rejected.

Why? Because “many are called, but few are chosen.”

Behold, brothers, we have all been called to life; we fill the walls of the church, yet God alone knows who are his (II Tim. II). Some appear to us to be chosen because of their outward conduct, but are rejected by God, who sees the interior, as happened with the Pharisee (Luke XVIII). Others are thought by us to be rejected because of outward evils, but through inward humility and repentance they are acceptable to God, as happened with the tax collector (ibid.).

Some begin well, but their end grows lukewarm and they fall away, as Judas did [Col. 1765A] (Matt. XXVII). Others begin badly, but, converted at the end, are received by God, as the thief, who almost in the same hour both repented and breathed his last (Luke XXIII).

Therefore, brothers, let no one presume on his good works. Let no one judge or condemn another because of outward evils. Let no one trust in the long duration of a good life. Let no one despise one who repents late.

Whoever has lived well should fear lest he fall (I Cor. X), lest he grow lukewarm, lest he collapse through presumption, or lest he displease God through contempt for a slower brother.

Whoever has lived badly until now should hear what is said here: “Why do you stand here idle all day?” Let such a person fear lest death overtake him, but let him not despair. Trusting in God’s immense mercy, let him hasten, weep, and strive, so that what he lost through tepidity he may recover through fervor.

Let no one say, “At the eleventh hour”—that is, in old age—“I will begin to labor, and I will receive as much reward as the first.” Let no one say this, brothers, because no one is certain even of the evening, much less of the present hour; for neither life nor conversion lies in human hands.

The hour in which a person dies is his old age.

Let us all therefore hasten to labor in God’s vineyard. Let us stir up the hardness of our hearts with fear born from remembrance of our sins and consideration of hell, as with a mattock. Let us remove from ourselves and from others the branches of vices with the pruning hook of correction.

Let us beware lest the north wind wither the flowers of virtues in us, and lest the heat of persecution burn the fruits already ripening in us. Rather, always solicitous for our souls, let us never consider ourselves worthy or secure until we receive the rewards that have been promised [Col. 1765C].

May the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit grant this to us. Amen.

# HOMILY XXVIII. SUNDAY IN SEXAGESIMA
You gladly tolerate fools, since you yourselves are wise (2 Cor. 11), etc.

This reading is divided into two parts, most beloved brothers. First, he reproves the Corinthians to whom he is writing for receiving false preachers. Second, he compares himself with those preachers and places himself above them.

Reproving the Corinthians for receiving false preachers, he says: “You gladly tolerate fools, since you yourselves are wise.” A fool is a fool precisely because he thinks himself wise, and therefore always wishes to make his own counsel, not another’s, prevail. The first approach to wisdom is to understand that one is a fool and to submit to sounder counsel.

The wise, however, ought to tolerate and receive fools for this purpose: that they may correct and teach them, not agree with their errors—as the Corinthians did. They received false preachers who proclaimed that the law must be observed along with the Gospel, as well as other errors, and they accepted their falsehoods. There are similar people in the Church even today—which is grievous—who receive certain wandering and false preachers more readily than their own proper preachers, preferring to hear flatterers rather than those who rebuke them, and those who speak pleasing things rather than those who speak the truth. As Solomon says: “Stolen waters are sweeter to them” (Prov. 9). But, according to the Gospel, “true sheep recognize and follow the voice of their own shepherd; they do not follow a stranger, because they do not recognize the voice of strangers” (John 10).

There are, my brothers, four kinds of preachers. Some preach evil and live evil lives; these are heretics, who are neither to be heard nor imitated, but resisted. Others preach evil through ignorance, while living well in other respects; these are fools. Although they may be imitated in their conduct, they are nevertheless not to be heard. Others preach what is good and live good lives; these are true preachers, who are both to be heard and imitated. Others preach what is good but live evil lives; these are to be heard but not imitated, concerning whom it is said: “Whatever they tell you, observe and do, but do not act according to their works” (Matt. 23).

So great is the authority of true doctrine that, whoever the corrupt person may be and whatever his purpose in preaching it, it ought to be heard. Hence the Apostle says: “Whether Christ is preached in truth or under a pretext, I rejoice” (Phil. 1). Conversely, whenever corrupt doctrine is preached by an honorable person, whatever his purpose, it ought not to be heard. Hence the Apostle says: “Even if an angel from heaven should preach to you something else, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1).

The Apostle explains which fools the Corinthians tolerate when he adds: “For you tolerate it if someone brings you into slavery.” There are people like this even today who lead the simple-minded from the freedom of virtue into slavery to pleasures and carnal allurements, saying that everything was created for human use. My brothers, do not agree with them, for those who immoderately pursue what is permitted fall into what is forbidden. The only person who does not fall into what is forbidden is the one who cautiously restrains himself from what is permitted.

He says: “You tolerate it if someone takes what belongs to you, if someone devours your food, if someone exalts himself because of holiness or nobility, if someone strikes you in the face”—which, I say, is according to ignobility. Since a person is rightly recognized by his face, so also by his nobility, to be struck in the face means to be despised on account of ignobility. There are also many today, my brothers, who, although false preachers proclaim not what is true but what is agreeable and pleasing, tolerate them devouring what belongs to them, boasting of their holiness, and neglecting everyone else.

The second part follows, in which the Apostle compares himself with and places himself above the false preachers, adding: “In what does anyone dare?”—that is, dare to commend himself—“I also.” But how, my brothers, does the Apostle commend himself here, when elsewhere he says: “It is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom God commends” (2 Cor. 10)? And Solomon says: “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth” (Prov. 27).

Indeed, brothers, if someone praises himself out of a desire for boasting, he does not sin lightly. For the one who praises himself is not praiseworthy. But when the saints enumerate their good works, they do not do so out of a desire for boasting, but from necessity. We find three reasons why the saints are compelled to recount their good works.

When they are oppressed by severe adversity, they are compelled to enumerate their good works for the increase of hope and consolation, as Job says: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. If I ate my morsel alone, and the orphan did not eat from it” (Job 29).

When they wish to incline God, their judge, toward mercy, they customarily recount their good works, as Hezekiah says: “Remember how I walked before you in truth” (Isa. 38).

And when holy preachers wish to persuade people to heed them more than false preachers, they customarily commend themselves and place themselves above them, as the Apostle does here.

The Apostle commends himself in four respects: in his lineage, in his ministry, in his revelations, and in his humility. In the first he makes himself equal to the others; in the second and third he places himself above them; in the fourth he humbles himself both before others and before himself.

He commends himself in lineage and makes himself equal to the others when he says: “Are they Hebrews? So am I,” and so forth. The nobility and uprightness of one’s parents, my brothers, are of no use to their descendants except as an incentive to imitate them. Hence the ancients used to have the images and good qualities of their ancestors painted as an encouragement to their children and grandchildren, to incite them to live as their fathers had lived.

But if you degenerate, why do you boast of the nobility of your parents? It does not help you; it condemns you. For it is not praiseworthy to be born of upright parents, but to imitate upright parents. Hence the Lord says to the unbelieving Jews who gloried in their father Abraham: “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham. You are from your father the devil, and you wish to do your father’s desires” (John 8).

He places himself above the others in ministry when he says: “Are they ministers of Christ?—to speak as one less wise—I am more.” It is as though he were saying: “In placing myself above others, I speak as one less wise,” since the less wise person of the wise is the one who places himself above others. Hence he later says: “I have become a fool; you compelled me.”

Yet he was not foolish in placing himself above the others, because he did this truly and wisely, not for his own boasting but for the benefit of those subject to him. He proves himself to be more than the others a minister of Christ in two respects: because he follows and imitates Christ more, both in outward suffering—in labors, afflictions, and dangers—and in inward compassion, through his concern for all the churches. For he is weak with the weak and burns with the one who is scandalized.

Let the prelates of the Church who exalt themselves and glory in the ministry of Christ consider this—those who are priests, bishops, and teachers of peoples. If they are truly ministers of Christ, let them imitate him, not in wealth and luxury, not in worldly pomp and ambition, which Christ always detested, but in those things in which Paul imitates him: outward suffering, labors, afflictions, fasts, and persecutions suffered for the Church. Let them be concerned for the churches, not that they may strip them, but that they may instruct and support them. Let them mourn with those who mourn, rejoice with those who rejoice, become weak with the weak, and become all things to all people.

The Apostle commends himself in revelations when he says that he was caught up to the third heaven. From this, let the pastors of the Church learn to be carried away by desire toward heavenly things and to meditate upon them through reading and contemplation, so that they may deserve to be called “men of desires,” with Daniel, and so that the Lord may disclose to them the secrets of his wisdom for their own benefit and that of others.

The Apostle, however, admits that he does not know whether he was caught up in body and soul together or outside the body, with the soul alone taken up. My brothers, this stands against those misguided people who claim that in a single night they travel bodily through many regions, eat and drink, and then return. When the Apostle, filled with the Holy Spirit, says that he does not know how he was caught up into heaven, he likewise commends himself in humility when he says: “And lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to buffet me,” and so forth.

Behold, my brothers: although the Apostle had been exalted by so many and such great virtues, for the preservation of his humility God gave him a thorn in the flesh and an angel of Satan to trouble and humble him. When he asked that it be removed from him, the Lord said to him: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness.”

The greatness of virtue is accustomed to become proud unless it is tempered by humility. Such was the humility in Paul that, contrary to the custom of worldly people, he scarcely and only under compulsion recounted his good works, while he gladly disclosed his weaknesses. “I will gladly glory,” he says, “in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me.”

Therefore, my brothers, let none of us flee weaknesses, labors, and afflictions, or ask that they be removed from us, because what the furnace does for gold, the file for iron, and frost for seed, tribulation does for the righteous. What does it do? It purifies him, files him smooth, and makes him shine. Hence David says: “Give me help from tribulation” (Ps. 59), that is, cause tribulation to become help for me.

Let us therefore pray to the faithful purifier of souls that he may purify and cleanse us here, lest in the future he accuse us in his fury or rebuke us in his anger, but that, when we immediately depart from bodily misery, God and our Lord may receive us into his treasury—he who, in perfect Trinity, lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXIX. SUNDAY IN SEXAGESIMA

“When a very great crowd was gathering, and people were hurrying to him from the cities, he said by way of a parable: ‘The sower went out to sow his seed’” (Luke 8), and so forth.

Our Lord and Redeemer, most beloved brothers, instructing us in all things and showing that he very often spoke figuratively, explained this parable so that, in those parables which he did not explain himself, he might signify that a spiritual understanding was likewise to be sought.

Thus, as he himself says, the seed is the word of God, the field is the world, and the sower is Christ, who went forth from the bosom of the Father to sow the seed—that is, the word of God—in this world. The sower is also every preacher who, according to his measure, ought to go forth from the secret place of contemplation to instruct people.

But there are many kinds of people to whom the seed, the word of God, is offered. Some do not even wish to hear it, like those to whom the Lord says: “Whoever is from God hears the words of God. The reason you do not hear is that you are not from God” (John 8). And the Prophet says: “Their fury is like that of a serpent, like a deaf asp that stops its ears, which will not hear the voice of charmers” (Ps. 57).

The asp is a serpent with incurable venom. It is said that, so as not to hear incantations, it presses one ear against the earth and stops the other with its tail. Such are certain people of incurable wickedness, who stop the ears of their understanding—on one side through love of earthly things, and on the other through love of their lower part, that is, the flesh—so that they do not wish to hear the word of God.

Among those who do hear, there are four kinds. Some hear the word of God to such an extent that they take no delight in its savor or its work. They are well represented by the ground beside the road, enclosed by no hedge, where the seed is trampled and carried away by birds. The hearts of such people are not closed, but lie open to every assault of the spirits of temptation. The spirit of lust comes: it is not forbidden, but enters. The spirit of greed comes: it is not forbidden, but enters. The spirit of vainglory comes: it is not forbidden, but enters. The others likewise come, and are not forbidden.

Because the hearts of such people have been worn down and trampled by the continual presence of evil thoughts, the word of God cannot adhere to them after they have heard it. Rather, it is removed from their memory by evil spirits, which are like birds, airy and swift.

Others hear the word of God and receive it with desire, and even begin to do something good, but, occupied by the cares and pleasures of riches, they desist. They are well represented, my brothers, by ground overgrown with thorns. For the Lord says that riches are signified by thorns: although they appear to delight the body, they prick the soul with the barbs of anxieties, wound it with sins, burden it with pleasures, and extinguish it. Since riches are acquired with labor, guarded with fear, increased with greed, and lost with grief, what are labor, fear, greed, and grief except truly tormenting pricks of the soul? Hence it is also written of those who take pleasure among such thorns: “They will count riches as being among thorns” (Job 30).

Others hear the word of God and receive it with joy, and begin to do something good, but, oppressed by tribulations and persecutions, they desist. They are well represented by the rock, because they lack the depth of earth and moisture—that is, deep faith and charity—and therefore, when the sun of persecution grows hot, they wither and bear no fruit. Such were those to whom the Lord says through the Prophet: “I will take the heart of stone from you and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. 36).

None of those mentioned above bears fruit, because they do not cultivate the field of their heart properly. Of them Solomon says: “I passed by the field of a lazy man, and behold, it was entirely overgrown with nettles; thorns covered its surface, and its stone wall was destroyed” (Prov. 24).

Others, hearing the word of God, retain it in a good heart and bear fruit with patience. They are rightly represented by good soil, because just as good earth returns the seed entrusted to it multiplied, so a good person, by thinking, doing, and teaching the word he has heard, does not cease to multiply it, making progress for himself and for others.

He bears fruit with patience because, unless good soil endures uprooting, plowing, cold, and heat, it cannot bear fruit. Likewise, unless a person patiently uproots from himself the thorns and thistles of vices; unless he plows the hardness of his heart with the plowshare of repentance and compunction; unless he patiently bears the walls of the flesh—that is, afflictions and persecutions—the word of God cannot bear fruit in him.

Once the field has been sown, care must not be withdrawn. Unless what has been sown is enclosed by a hedge, unless it is weeded, unless the birds are driven away, and unless the proper season is requested from God, it will not reach the required abundance of maturity.

Likewise, once the word of God has been received in the heart, unless the heart is guarded from temptations by vigilant care; unless newly arising vices are diligently uprooted; unless demons are driven away by psalmody and prayers; and unless the growth and multiplication of the good begun are requested from God through constant prayers, it will not reach the perfection of fruitfulness.

According to another Evangelist, the seed in good soil bears fruit: one thirtyfold, another sixtyfold, and another a hundredfold (Mark 4). There are three orders in the Church: married people, widows and widowers, and virgins. Married people will receive a thirtyfold fruit, widows and widowers a sixtyfold fruit, and virgins a hundredfold fruit, if they persevere well in the purity of their own order. The rank of their rewards will correspond to the degree of their merits.

You, therefore, married people, if you preserve the order of your state well; if you place love of God above your wives, children, and everyone else; if you love your spouses with the restraint of modesty; if you teach your children and household according to God; if you redeem your faults through almsgiving; and if you persevere in God’s commandments, you are great before God.

But you, widowers and widows, if you guard the religious character of your state; if you are more devoted to God because you are freer; if you possess holiness in mind and body; and if you devote yourselves to fasts, prayers, and almsgiving, you are greater.

You also, virgins, men and women, if you are virgins by choice, not by necessity or fear; if with your whole desire you wish to please the heavenly Bridegroom; if you adorn yourselves more with virtues than with garments; and if, like wise rather than foolish virgins, you seek the glory of God and not that of the world, you are greatest.

Nevertheless, my brothers, just as some silver is worth more than some gold, so a married person may surpass some widow or virgin in merit. A married person fervent in God is better than a widow or virgin who is lukewarm.

Therefore, my brothers, let us all live honorably, each in his own order. Let us love God with our whole desire, despise the world, chastise the flesh, uproot vices from ourselves, receive the words of God with devoted hearts, and multiply them by doing and teaching them, so that we may deserve to receive the fruit of eternity.

May he deign to grant this to us, God who lives and reigns in perfect Trinity forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXX. SUNDAY IN QUINQUAGESIMA

“I show you a more excellent way. If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal” (1 Cor. 12–13), etc.

Among all the gifts that almighty and merciful God grants us, my brothers, so that we may earn the reward of eternal blessedness, true charity—that is, love of God and neighbor—holds the chief place.

The Apostle commends it in five ways: first, because it is the more excellent way; second, because without it all other things are of no value; third, because it excludes every vice; fourth, because whoever possesses it possesses everything; and fifth, because it never fails.

He shows here that charity is the more excellent way when he says: “I show you a more excellent way.” Charity is the more excellent way because it raises us higher, is more direct, and is more proper.

It raises us higher because nothing exalts more than charity, which makes slaves into sons, enemies into friends, and human beings into gods. Hence the Lord says: “I will no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15). And elsewhere: “He gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John 1). The Prophet says: “I said: You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81).

For just as charity is the way by which God comes to humanity, so it is the way by which humanity goes to God. Since majesty and love do not easily accord with one another, God, by loving humanity, made himself equal to it so that he might raise it up with himself.

Charity is oil, which cannot be pressed down to the bottom but floats above. Charity is also the more direct way, because through it we ascend to God more briefly and more easily. If you cannot possess great wisdom or great eloquence, give many alms, or endure martyrdom, it is enough for you if you truly love God and your neighbor. Love is sufficient in itself for meriting God. It does not merely await God; it already possesses him while it truly loves him.

Charity is also more proper to God and his elect, since although the rejected may possess the other goods, only the elect possess charity. Hence it is the proper spring to which a stranger has no access. Strangers are all those who will hear the words: “I do not know you” (Matt. 7). Charity is the wedding garment in which those who are clothed recline securely.

The Lord says of it: “This is my commandment, that you love one another” (John 15). It is as though he were saying: “This is my excellent and distinctive commandment, by which those who are mine are separated from those who are not mine.” Therefore, my brothers, let us always preserve charity, so that we may deserve to be sons and friends of God.

The second part follows, in which the Apostle shows that no matter how good something may be, without charity it is of no benefit, when he adds: “If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels.” Fruitful and eloquent preaching is certainly a great good, but without charity it benefits the preacher nothing, though it does benefit the hearers. A preacher who preaches not from charity but for money or glory is like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal: he calls others to God, but shakes and condemns himself by his own voice.

Prophecy concerning future things is a great good, but without charity it is of no benefit. It did Balaam no good; it did the Sibyl no good; it did Caiaphas no good that they foretold the future mysteries of God.

It is a great good to know the mysteries and sacraments of the Old and New Testaments, and every kind of divine and human knowledge, but without charity it is of no benefit. The sacraments that Judas shared with the other Apostles did him no good. It does the devil no good that, as Ezekiel says, he knows heavenly mysteries. It did the scribes, Pharisees, and false teachers no good to possess knowledge of the sacred writings.

It is a great good to possess faith so perfect that through it mountains are literally moved, or demons are expelled from those afflicted by them. But without charity it is of no benefit. It will profit nothing certain people who performed these and other good works without charity. Indeed, at the judgment they will confess that they did these things: “Did we not prophesy in your name? Did we not cast out demons in your name?” (Matt. 7). They will not be told, “You did not have these gifts,” but: “I do not know you” (ibid.), because without charity they possessed nothing. Such things benefit hypocrites nothing when they do them for vainglory.

Hence James says: “Whoever offends in one point has become guilty of all” (Jas. 2). Therefore, most beloved, let us strive above all to possess charity, without which the other goods can be of no value.

The third part follows, in which the Apostle shows that charity excludes every vice when he adds: “Charity is not jealous”—through envy; rather, it rejoices with those who rejoice and weeps with those who weep (Rom. 12). It does not act improperly, that is, perversely; rather, it does everything with a good purpose. It is not ambitious; it does not contend for honor, but for humility. It does not seek what is its own, but what is Christ’s; for it seeks Christ’s will and glory, not its own.

It is not irritated through anger; it does not think evil. It is strong not only in refusing to repay injuries, but also in refusing to dwell upon them. It does not rejoice over iniquity; rather, it grieves over it. In this way charity also excludes the other vices.

Hence it is also said: “Whoever has charity does not sin”—not because he does not sin, but because he does not sin unto death. Sin amid the fervor of charity is like a drop of water in a fire: it does not extinguish the fire but inflames it. Let us therefore have fervent charity, brothers, so that the filth of our sins may be burned away in its fervor.

The fourth part follows, in which the Apostle shows that whoever has charity possesses all the virtues, when he says: “Charity is patient” amid adversities; that is, it is kind toward enemies and loves even those from whom it suffers. It rejoices with the truth, that is, with the good of justice. Hence it is also said: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice” (Matt. 5).

Charity believes all things—that is, all the things concerning the future life that are read in the sacred Scriptures. It hopes all things—that is, all the things promised by God. Even when these are delayed, it endures all things.

Whoever possesses true charity possesses the other virtues as well. Although he may not possess some of them in practice, he possesses them in disposition. Even if he does not possess a virtue in himself, he possesses it in others, about whom he rejoices as though it were in himself.

Let us therefore hold fast to charity, brothers, through which all good things are possessed and through which the law is fulfilled. Hence the Prophet says: “I have seen the end of all perfection; your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 118). And the Lord says: “On these two commandments the whole law and the Prophets depend” (Matt. 22).

The fifth part follows, in which the Apostle shows that charity never fails. Therefore the one who clings to charity will never fall. The future life will not take charity away; rather, it will perfect it. What is given now for the earning of merit will then be given as a reward.

The other goods that now have their place will then cease. Prophecies will cease, because then nothing that is seen concerning God will be absent or hidden. Tongues will cease, because when reality and thought are open, they will not need to be revealed by signs. Knowledge will cease, because then knowledge will no longer be reflected and shadowy, but will be the open vision of God.

Faith will cease, because what we now believe to be invisible we shall then see present before us. Hope will cease when we obtain what we hoped for. Once the other things have ceased, charity will then increase and be perfected. For then we shall love God in such a way that we will be entirely unable to be separated from his love or to grow lukewarm.

Let us consider, therefore, my brothers—let us consider with our whole heart—how great and how wondrous that blessedness will be, where the saints will contemplate, embrace, and enjoy without fear, defect, or envy what they had always desired, hoped for, and sought during this pilgrimage.

There, although the glory of the saints will not be equal, their joy will be equal. For one love and one will will make everything common.

Therefore, my brothers, let us hold fast on the way, with our whole heart, to the love of God and neighbor, which will be our reward in our homeland. Above all, let us love God, who is above us. Let us love our soul, which is within us, in what is good. Let us love our neighbor, who is beside us, as ourselves. Let us nourish our flesh, which is beneath us, with discretion, so that together we may deserve to arrive at the vision of the God of gods in Zion, where there is a kingdom without end, fullness without weariness, health without disease, youth without old age, celebration without sorrow, and joy without end.

This is granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXI. SUNDAY IN QUINQUAGESIMA

## [Col. 1773D]

“Jesus took his twelve disciples and said to them: ‘Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that has been written through the Prophets concerning the Son of Man will be fulfilled’” (Luke 18), etc.

This reading, most beloved brothers, is divided into two sections. In the first, we must consider according to the literal sense why the Lord wished to foretell his passion and resurrection, why he told this only to the twelve disciples, and why he told it secretly.

Why did he foretell that he would suffer and rise again? For three reasons: to show that he was the omniscient God; to prove that he would suffer willingly; and to fortify his disciples against despair over his death.

Why did he tell this only to the twelve? To show that only the followers of apostolic teaching are worthy to recognize and share in the mystery of human redemption.

Why did he tell it secretly? To show that what is holy should not be given to dogs, nor pearls cast before swine (Matt. 7). Hence he also says: “To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, but to the others in parables” (Mark 4; Luke 8).

In the moral sense, my brothers, the Lord instructs us by his example how we ought to approach the Jerusalem above. Just as he ascended to Jerusalem, suffered, died, and rose again, and then ascended into heaven to the Father, so we, most beloved brothers, must avoid the depths of vices, suffer tribulations, die to the world, rise again in soul and body, and ascend to the heavenly homeland.

It is as though the Lord were saying: “Whoever serves me, let him follow me. And where I am, there also will my minister be” (John 12).

Therefore, brothers, we must strive with all our strength. If we climb the summits of mountains with such great exertion, how much labor is needed for our heavy nature, striving toward heaven? For, as the Lord testifies, broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction, and many run along it; but narrow and difficult is the way that leads to life, and few ascend by it (Matt. 7).

[Note: [Col. 1773D] Virgil, Aeneid, book 6, verse 126.] “Easy is the descent to Avernus.”

It is easy to descend from gluttony to lust, from lust to desire, from desire to greed, and so from vice to vice all the way to eternal damnation. But it is very laborious, my brothers, to ascend to abstinence, from abstinence to continence, from continence to contempt of the world, and so from virtue to virtue all the way to the heavenly homeland.

A human being cannot make this ascent by himself unless aided by God. Hence the Lord says: “No one can come to me unless my heavenly Father draws him” (John 6). Let us therefore cry out to him, brothers; let us cry out and say to him: “Draw me after you; we will run in the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song 1).

For, according to the Prophet: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you; he has arranged ascents in his heart, existing in the valley of tears, in the place he has established” (Ps. 83). Without doubt, to the faithful who presume nothing from themselves but everything from God, the Lawgiver will give the blessings of grace. Thus they will go from virtue to virtue, and at last “the God of gods will be seen in Zion” (ibid.).

We must also suffer tribulations, most beloved brothers, while we ascend to our homeland, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of heaven” (Acts 14). And elsewhere: “All who wish to live devoutly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3). For if this happened in the green wood—that is, in Christ—what will happen in the dry wood? (Luke 23.)

The righteous must suffer these tribulations. He must be handed over, mocked, scourged, and spat upon.

The righteous must be handed over, and this multitude of examples teaches you. At the beginning, righteous Abel was handed over into the hands of Cain (Gen. 4). Righteous Joseph was handed over and sold to the Ishmaelites (Gen. 37). Righteous Job was handed over into the hand of the devil—and, more astonishingly, by God himself. “Behold,” he says, “his flesh is in your hand; nevertheless, preserve his life” (Job 1).

The righteous Lord was handed over to the Gentiles through the hands of Judas and the Jews; and they could not have done this unless the Father—and he himself as well—had handed him over. The Apostle says of him: “He handed himself over for us” (Eph. 5).

Therefore, my brothers, since the disciple is not above the teacher, if we are true disciples of Christ, if we are truly righteous, then we too must be handed over into the hands of the wicked—that is, of the devil and evil people. But let us look toward Christ who was handed over, and find consolation in him.

The righteous must also be mocked. Righteous Noah was mocked by his son (Gen. 9). Joseph was mocked by his brothers, who said: “Behold, that dreamer is coming” (Gen. 37). Elisha was mocked by the boys, who said: “Go up, baldhead!” (2 Kings 2). Christ was mocked by the soldiers, who clothed him in a scarlet garment, crowned him with thorns, and gave him a reed for a scepter; derisively they said to him: “Hail, King of the Jews!” (John 19).

If we wish to ascend to heaven, brothers, we too must be mocked, either by the devil through phantasmal illusions or by false brothers who ridicule our simplicity and call us hypocrites. But let us look toward Christ who was mocked, and find consolation in him.

The righteous must also be scourged. Job was scourged; Tobias was scourged; the Lord was scourged and bound to the column, on which traces of blood are visible to this day. The Apostles too were scourged.

Likewise, brothers, we must be scourged, whether by illnesses, persecutions, injuries, or losses. But let us always look toward Christ who was scourged, brothers, and find consolation in him.

The righteous must also be spat upon and rejected. Joseph was despised and held in contempt among his brothers. David too was despised by his own people, who said: “What have we to do with the son of Jesse?” Job was despised by his own people amid his adversities. The Lord was despised, called the son of a craftsman, spat upon, and cast among the wicked. The Apostles likewise were despised and made like the refuse and offscouring of all things (1 Cor. 4).

We too, brothers, if we are righteous, must be spat upon and rejected by worldly people. But let us despise being despised, brothers, and, looking toward Christ who was spat upon, find consolation in him.

The righteous who strives toward heaven must also be crucified and die. Righteous Abel was killed by his wicked brother. Isaiah was sawn apart; Jeremiah was stoned; Christ was crucified; and the Apostles and holy martyrs suffered various torments.

We too, brothers, if we wish to ascend to heaven, must be crucified to the world—not necessarily by material punishment, but by our will, so that we may mortify our members that are upon the earth, according to the Apostle’s saying: “You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3).

But bodily death too must be awaited and received by us with goodwill.

The righteous must also rise from vices to virtue, from death to life, and from darkness to light, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead, we too may walk in newness of life (Rom. 6).

Let us therefore pray, most beloved brothers, that the Lord himself may draw us after him, make us rise from the depths to the heights, and grant us the blessings of his graces, so that, as far as we are able, we may imitate his passion, resurrection, and ascension.

It follows: “But they understood none of these things. For the saying was hidden from them.” The same thing happens today, dearly beloved brothers. For when we preach to carnal people that the righteous must in this world be handed over, mocked, scourged, spat upon, die, and rise again, they either do not understand or they despise it. For divine judgment is hidden from them. And when they see a righteous person suffering here, they think that he is either not cared for [Col. 1776B] or rejected.

“When he was approaching Jericho, a certain blind man was sitting beside the road, begging.” This is the second section, in which the Lord, after predicting his passion and death to his disciples, gives sight to a blind man. In this, dearly beloved brothers, he shows that he dies willingly, since he was able to give sight to the blind.

“Approaching Jericho, he gives sight to the blind.” Jericho is interpreted as “moon,” by which the decline of our mortality is understood. Therefore, when God approaches the decline of our mortality, he blinds the human race on account of the first transgression, or restores it to understanding the light of God.

This blind man was not without considerable merit, my brothers. For he possessed patience, faith, perseverance in prayer, discernment in petition, attainment of his request, obedience, and thanksgiving.

He possessed patience because, although he was afflicted by a twofold misery—namely, poverty and blindness—he did not despair. Preserving his innocence, he preferred to beg rather than steal, rob, or practice usury. This stands against certain people who abuse the Lord’s scourges and, although they ought to have been made better by them, become worse. When, as their merits demand, they are afflicted or struck blind outwardly, they are not corrected; rather, they become blind and afflicted inwardly, and become usurers, perjurers, rapacious people, and thieves.

Of such people it is said: “We treated Babylon, but she was not healed” (Jer. LI). And elsewhere: “All these are bronze and tin in the midst of the furnace” (Ezek. XXII). For the Lord, so far as it depends on him, heals them through scourges; but they are not healed. Rather, they are like bronze and tin, with their rust, in the midst of tribulation.

Just as a rich person who consumes alms is said to consume the sins of the people, so a poor person who lives on alms lives by grace.

The blind man also possessed faith, as the Lord bears witness, because he did not doubt that the one whom he so insistently begged to have mercy on him and give him sight was able to do so. This stands against those who ask hesitantly and with doubt. Hence James says: “If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask it of the Lord, without hesitation. For the one who hesitates is like a wave of the sea, moved and carried about by the wind” (Jas. I). Such a person must not suppose that he will receive anything from God.

The Lord shows how powerful true faith is for obtaining a request when he says: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain: ‘Move from here and throw yourself into the sea,’ and it will happen” (Matt. XVII; Luke XVII). Therefore, brothers, when we ask, let us ask with great confidence in faith for what ought to be requested.

He also possessed perseverance in prayer. The more the crowds going ahead of him rebuked him and told him to be silent, the more he cried out: “Son of David, have mercy on me,” until he overcame both the tumult of the crowds and moved Jesus, who was passing by, to stop and have mercy.

Imitating him, dearly beloved brothers, let us cry out to him with all the depths of our hearts: “Son of David, have mercy on us.” And if crowds and the tumult of vain thoughts or of evil spirits—as often happens—disturb and hinder us while we pray, so that we cease from prayer, Jesus passes by us because of the tepidity of our minds [Col. 1777B]. But let us, brothers, repel from us with all our strength the crowds and phantoms of our thoughts. The more they harass us, the more let us cry out: “Son of David, have mercy on us.” Then surely Christ will stand in our hearts and illuminate us by his grace.

He possessed discernment in petition. When the Lord asked him, “What do you want me to do for you?” he did not ask the Lord, as he ordinarily would have asked mere human beings, for temporal bread, money, or anything of that sort, but for light. And I think that he asked for both, just as he received both.

Imitating him, brothers, let us ask the God and Father of lights not for anything transitory, but for light—not for a light confined to a place and limited by time, but for the light of divine vision.

He possessed attainment of his request because, just as he had asked, he was enlightened both outwardly and inwardly when it was said to him: “Look up; your faith has saved you,” and immediately he saw. Imitating him, let us trust that we shall obtain eternal illumination if we persevere in fervent petition.

He possessed obedience because, after he saw, he followed him. For the one who does the good that he understands both sees and follows. This rebukes us, unworthy preachers, who see through knowledge and yet do not follow Christ through our actions. We show the way to others, yet do not take care to travel it ourselves.

Let us therefore admonish ourselves, dearly beloved brothers, to do what we know and what we preach, since “the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten with many blows” (Luke XII).

The blind man also gave thanks to the one who had given him sight and caused others to give thanks by his example, for it follows: “And he followed him, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.”

We too, my brothers, must not be ungrateful for his immeasurable benefits, but let us give thanks with our whole heart, in word and deed. Let us devote ourselves to his praises, as far as we can, in this age, so that we may deserve to see and praise him forever.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY XXXII. WEDNESDAY AT THE BEGINNING OF THE FAST

[Col. 1778A]

“Return to me with all your heart, with fasting and weeping and mourning; and rend your hearts and not your garments” (Joel II), etc.

By these words, dearly beloved brothers, the Lord formerly exhorted through the prophet his people, who had withdrawn from him by sinning, to return to him. What he formerly said to the Jews, he now also says to us.

This reading has four parts. First, he urges his sinful people to return to him; second, he gives the reason why they ought to return; third, he shows who ought to return; fourth, what benefit follows.

First, therefore, brothers, the Lord urges us to return to him when he says: “Return to me.”

Behold, my brothers, how great are the depths of divine compassion! He who ought to have been entreated entreats us. The offended Lord entreats the fugitive servant. The offended bridegroom entreats the adulterous bride to return.

Hence, through the prophet Jeremiah, he cries out to Judah, who had committed adultery with demons: “If a wife, having left her husband, takes another man, will she return to him again? Will that woman not be polluted and defiled? But you have prostituted yourself with many lovers; nevertheless, return to me, says the Lord” (Jer. III).

For as often as the soul transgresses criminally, so often it abandons its lawful bridegroom and commits adultery with the devil. Yet the Lord of infinite mercy urges this soul to return and, according to the prophet, entreats it to hear the voice of the one admonishing from behind: “Return to me.”

And as though we were to ask, “How shall we return to you?” he adds the manner: “With all your heart.”

Some people do turn to God, but not with their whole heart. For one does not turn to God with one’s whole heart who abandons one vice for God’s sake but remains in another. Let us beware of this completely, my brothers. For it is impious to hope for partial forgiveness from God, who is supreme justice. God either forgives everything or nothing.

Therefore, my brothers, what good is it to heal all the wounds of a wounded man if one deadly wound remains? What good is it to bar all the entrances of a fortress if one remains open through which the enemy may rush in? Let us therefore turn all sins away from us, so that we may turn to God with our whole heart.

But this too is not enough unless we also punish within ourselves the sins we have committed. Hence he adds: “With fasting and weeping and mourning.”

True repentance consists in two things: avoiding sin and making satisfaction for what has been committed. For repentance is to mourn the evils one has committed and not to commit what must be mourned.

Here he urges us to do both: not to commit what must be mourned when he says, “Return with all your heart”; and to mourn what has been committed when he says, “With fasting and weeping and mourning; and rend your hearts and not your garments.”

Through this he demonstrates that satisfaction for committed sins consists in three things: satisfaction in deed, contrition of mind, and confession of the mouth.

He urges us to satisfaction in deed when he says, “with fasting.” And because fasting is not sufficient without sorrow and contrition of heart, he subsequently urges us to contrition of mind when he says, “with weeping and mourning.” Through weeping and mourning, inward contrition is disclosed to the priest.

But because neither satisfaction in deed nor contrition of mind is sufficient without confession of the mouth when a person has the time and opportunity, he urges confession when he adds, “and rend your hearts.”

Some people keep their sins hidden in their hearts, like decay in a wound. But you know, my brothers, that a wound is not healed unless the decay is first expelled. Therefore, so that the wounds of our hearts may be healed, let the decay of our sins be disclosed through confession.

For this reason another prophet also urges us to fast by his own example when he says: “My knees have grown weak from fasting” (Ps. CVIII); and elsewhere: “For I ate ashes like bread” (Ps. CI); and, urging us to contrition, he adds: “And I mingled my drink with weeping” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “Because of the sound of my groaning, my bones have clung to my flesh” (ibid.).

As though he were saying: “So great was the pain of my groaning that my bones clung to my flesh.” And which of us, wretched sinners, does today what that great and holy man says he did?

Again, by his own example he urges us to confession when he says: “I made my sin known to you, and I did not hide my iniquity. I said, ‘I will confess my iniquity to the Lord,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (Ps. XXXI).

Moreover, in saying, “Rend your hearts,” and adding, “and not your garments,” he rebukes the custom of the Jews, who in afflictions tore their garments more than their hearts. Their likenesses today are those who wish to display repentance more in outward things than to possess it inwardly.

The second part follows, in which he gives the reason why we ought to return: “For he is kind and merciful, patient and very merciful, ready to relent over evil.”

As though he were saying: “Return to God, because he is easy to receive us, because he is naturally kind and loves every good. He is also merciful toward sinners; even when they do not immediately turn back, he is patient, waiting for them to repent.”

If they abuse God’s patience by adding crimes to crimes, he is nevertheless very merciful toward their many sins, to the extent that he is even “ready to relent over evil”—that is, his mercy surpasses and prevails over every evil, since no matter how great the evil, it can overcome divine mercy.

Behold, my brothers, how much we ought to contemplate the depths of divine mercy. Therefore, brothers, let no one, however shameful or criminal, despair. Let him run to the fountain of David, which, according to the prophet, is open for the washing of the menstruous woman (Zech. XIII), because when anyone turns to God, God turns toward that person. Forgiveness is denied only to the one who disdains to turn to God.

“Who knows,” he says, “whether he will turn and God will forgive, and leave behind him a blessing—a sacrifice and a libation for the Lord our God?” (Joel II). The conjunction “if” is used here in place of “not,” as also there: “To whom I swore in my wrath: ‘If they shall enter into my rest’” (Ps. XCIV). It is as though it were said: No one knows that God will not turn toward us; indeed, we ought always to hope that he will turn toward us, because God is slow to punish, swift to reward, and quick to show mercy. “He will neither forget to have mercy nor restrain his mercies in his anger” (Ps. LXXVI).

“And he will leave behind them”—that is, for those who have turned—“a blessing, a sacrifice, and a libation.”

A blessing is called a gift, or grace, in reality, because by it the giver is blessed. A sacrifice formerly consisted of flesh; a libation, of liquids.

But, my brothers, while a sinner persists in sin, he can neither bless God, sacrifice to him, nor pour out a libation, because “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Sir. XV). And according to the wise man, “the sacrifices of the wicked are abominable” (Prov. XV).

But when God turns toward the sinner, he gives him grace, opening his lips, first in this life, so that he may now be able to bless God. He also gives him a sacrifice—that is, devotion of mind kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit, by which he may sacrifice and be pleasing to God. He also gives him a libation—that is, tearful contemplation, by which he may desire heavenly things here and, in a certain way, taste them beforehand.

Let us therefore entreat him, my brothers, that according to his infinite mercy God may turn toward us and forgive us, and leave behind him for us who have turned a blessing of his grace, by which we may bless him; a sacrifice of a devoted and contrite heart, kindled by love of him, by which we may please him; and a libation of tears in contemplation, by which we may taste beforehand, sigh beforehand for, and desire beforehand the glory of his goodness in this valley of tears.

The third part follows, in which he shows who ought to turn: “Blow the trumpet in Zion,” etc.

My brothers, a general wound requires a general remedy. If one person had sinned, he could have been healed by an individual remedy. But just as formerly in the time of the Jews, so now in the time of Christians: “All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. XIII).

And as Isaiah says: “Every head is sick, and every heart is sorrowful; from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, there is no soundness in it” (Isa. I). Almost no member of the whole body of the Church is healthy.

For we priests and teachers of the Church, who ought to be the light of the world—something I cannot say without a groan—are rather smoking than burning. And if the light that is in the Church is darkness, as he says, “how great will the darkness itself be?” (Matt. VI).

What are the rulers and judges of the lands like? They are robbers. As the prophet says, with impious evening assaults, taxes, and exactions they devour the people like a morsel of bread (Ps. XIII).

And what is the people like? “All lie in wait for blood, and each man hunts his brother to death” (Mic. VII). “There is no truth, no mercy, no knowledge of God in the land. Cursing, lying, murder, and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood” (Hos. IV).

Therefore, because all have turned aside, the prophet urges all to repentance, so that by a general proclamation all may be summoned to the Church, when he says: “Blow the trumpet in Zion.” This is what we have done today, my brothers, when we were summoned to the church by the ringing of the bells.

“Sanctify the fast,” he says. Fasting, brothers, is considered meritorious in itself by no one unless it is sanctified by good works. He therefore urges us to sanctify our fast by avoiding evil and doing good. Then, above all, let us devote ourselves to prayer, almsgiving, vigils, and other good pursuits.

Next, he commands every rank, every age, and both sexes to be summoned: the greater, when he says, “Call an assembly,” by which those who are rational are summoned; the lesser, when he says, “Gather the people,” by which those who are irrational and brutish are to be gathered and compelled; age, when he says, “Gather together the elders and those sucking at the breast,” since no one is free from the lot of birth, not even an infant whose life is one day old upon the earth (Job XIV.4, according to the Septuagint), who, even if not actually, is nevertheless stained originally; sex, when he says, “Let the bridegroom go forth from his chamber, and the bride from her bridal room.”

He separates them for this reason: during times of fasting, sexual embraces must be abstained from.

He also introduces the sanctification of the Church. The Church is sanctified when every evil is removed from it. Often the sin of one person affects the whole Church. It is not only the sin of a ruler, such as David, or of a priest, such as the sin of Eli’s sons, but also that of a private person, such as the sin of Achor [Note: [Col. 1781D] Vulg. Achan; elsewhere Achar], who stole a golden plate from the devoted things of Jericho, on account of whose sin many of the people fell (Josh. VII).

Fearing these things, therefore, my brothers, let us drive sacrilegious people from the midst of the Church, especially the excommunicated and the obstinate, lest through the contagion of one wicked person many perish.

This stands against those who do not fear associating with excommunicated persons, not considering that “the one who touches an unclean thing is unclean” (Lev. XXII), and that the one who associates with an excommunicated person is excommunicated.

When the prophet urges everyone to repentance and amendment, he especially urges the priests, because just as the ruin of priests is the ruin of the people, so their progress is the progress of the people. They are bound to weep and pray not only for their own sins but also for the sins of others. Hence he adds: “Between the vestibule and the altar the priests, the ministers of the Lord, wept” [Note: [Col. 1781D] Vulg. “will weep”], “and said” [Note: [Col. 1782D] Vulg. “will say”]: “Spare, O Lord, spare your people,” etc.

He commands them to do three things: to stand between the vestibule and the altar, to weep, and to pray for the people.

The priests ought to stand between the vestibule and the altar—that is, between God and the people—as intermediaries by rank, intimacy, and meditation.

They must be intermediaries by rank, so that, just as they are greater with respect to God, they may also be greater with respect to the people. For a priest must not be like the people.

They must be intermediaries by intimacy, so that they may be intimate with God and with human beings through love.

They must be intermediaries by meditation, so that through their intercession they may be able to reconcile both the people to God and God to the people.

He also commands them to weep not only for their own sins but also for the sins of others. For just as priests live from the offerings and alms of the faithful, so by weeping, fasting, and doing other good works they ought to bear their sins, so that just as the people bear the priest’s burden in temporal matters, the priest may bear the people’s burden in spiritual matters.

Thus Samuel wept for Saul when he heard from the Lord: “How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him?” (1 Sam. XVI).

He also commands them to pray not only for their own sins but also for the sins of others. Their prayer must therefore be so pure and undefiled that it can appease an angry God and reconcile him to the people.

The fourth part follows, in which the benefit resulting from repentance is shown, when he adds: “And the Lord was zealous for his people, and spared his people.”

As though he were saying: The one against whom he had threatened, when converted, he regards with zeal and receives.

“Behold,” he says, “I will send you grain, wine, and oil, and you will rejoice in them.”

Formerly the carnal Jews, who served on account of carnal things, would rejoice in carnal promises. But if we are spiritual, brothers, he does not promise us who have turned to him temporal grain, wine, or oil—things he also bestows on unbelievers—but rather he promises us spiritual grain, wine, and oil.

Grain, which first adorns the table and strengthens the human heart, signifies the first of the virtues, faith, which confirms the human mind.

Wine, which gladdens and intoxicates the human mind, signifies hope in heavenly things, which cheers our mind and intoxicates it with desire for heavenly life.

Oil, which rises above all liquids, signifies charity, which rises above all virtues.

The Lord therefore promises these gifts of great virtues to us who have turned, so that in them we may rejoice both here amid the adversities of this age and in the future, in eternal blessedness, contemplating and blessing God forever. Amen.

# HOMILY XXXIII. WEDNESDAY AT THE BEGINNING OF THE FAST

“When you fast, do not become like the gloomy hypocrites” (Matt. V).

How we ought to fast, dearly beloved brothers, the Lord shows us in this reading. For he commands us to do four things: to have a right intention in fasting; compassion through mercy in the mind; purity in the conscience; and the storing up of treasures in heaven.

First, therefore, he commands us to have a right intention in fasting, not hypocrisy, when he says: “When you fast, do not become like the gloomy hypocrites”—that is, do not imitate the sadness of hypocrites in an excessive manner.

“For they disfigure their faces so that they may appear to people to be fasting.”

The Lord does not prohibit those who fast, dearly beloved brothers, from having sadness, a pale face, white clothing, or other such things that are signs of repentance and are rightly possessed before God by many religious people. He does not prohibit them from being present, but from being desired.

Hence he does not say, “Do not become sad,” but, “Do not become like the gloomy hypocrites.”

One who is saddened by remembering his own sins, or by another’s evil, or by the delay of the heavenly homeland, is rightly saddened. Hence the prophet says: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. L). And elsewhere: “Alas for me” [Note: [Col. 1783D] Vulg. “for me”], “because my dwelling has been prolonged!”

But one who is saddened by the loss of temporal possessions, or by some vain or evil thing, is wrongly saddened.

Hypocrites, however, either are not sad but pretend sadness, or, if they are sad, they pretend the motive: they pretend that they are saddened from a good intention, when in fact they are saddened by the delay of the vain glory they desire.

To make this pretense more convincingly, they disfigure their faces, removing their natural color and artificially making them pale. But what benefit do they gain? “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward”—namely, human praise, for the sake of which they did the whole thing.

Therefore, my brothers, when you fast, when you give alms, or when you do anything else good, do not do it for the praise of human beings, but to earn the love of God. For what life is more wretched than that of the hypocrite, who, because of empty human murmurs, will lose both the present life and the future one?

Moreover, my brothers, it is not necessary for the perfect, who do not desire human glory and despise it when it is offered, to avoid pallor of face and squalor of clothing or to hide their good works. Indeed, they would sin if they hid them, since it has been said to such people: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

But for the imperfect, who have not yet entirely despised human glory and do not know how to reject praise when it is offered, pallor, sadness, and squalor of clothing must be avoided, and their good works must be done secretly.

Hence, according to the literal sense, the Lord adds the following for such an imperfect person: “But you, when you fast, anoint your head with oil”—something the Palestinians did at festivals—“and wash your face, so that you may not appear to human beings to be fasting, but to your Father who sees in secret” [Note: [Col. 1783D] Vulg. “who is”] “and your Father who sees in secret”—that is, in the conscience—“will repay you.”

Spiritually, however, through these words the Lord commands the person who fasts to have mercy in mind.

By oil, which floats above all liquids, mercy is signified, for mercy exalts itself above judgment. Hence the word “mercy” in Greek is *eleos* [Note: [Col. 1784D] In Greek, however, it is ελεος (*eleos*, “mercy”), not ολεος (*oleos*).].

By the head, however, the mind is signified, since it rules over the whole human person. The Lord therefore commands the person who fasts to anoint the head with oil—that is, to enrich the mind with the grace of mercy.

The mind is dry when it has not been enriched with oil. Such are many today—for this is a matter for grief—who are no more moved by the pain, misery, and anxiety of the wretched than if they were stones rather than human beings. For, as the Apostle says, they are “without affection, without mercy, without covenant” (Rom. I).

Just as they are without mercy, so they will find the supreme Judge without mercy toward themselves. For it is written: “Judgment without mercy will be for the one who has not done mercy” (Jas. II). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Unless you forgive your brothers from your heart, your heavenly Father will not forgive you” (Matt. XVIII).

Conversely, the Lord says of the devout and merciful: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V).

Therefore, my brothers, let us exclude every hardness and inhumanity from ourselves and put on the depths of mercy. Although at all times we ought to grow rich in the oil of mercy, according to the saying, “Let oil not fail from your head” (Eccl. IX), nevertheless, especially during the days of fasting, we ought to overflow with mercy, when we await mercy for our own sins.

For it is written: “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” (Hos. VI). Mercy without fasting has value; fasting without mercy cannot have value.

When we fast, therefore, my brothers, let us first have mercy on ourselves, according to the saying: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Eccl. XXX). We have mercy on our soul when through repentance we recall it from the servitude of vices.

Let us also have mercy on our neighbors who sin against us by forgiving them. Let us have mercy on evil people by praying for them. Let us have mercy on the afflicted and poor by helping them, according to what Isaiah says: “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house. When you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh” (Isa. LVIII).

The Lord also commands the person who fasts to have purity in conscience, if we understand spiritually what he says: “Wash your face.” For the face by which God knows us is the conscience. He therefore commands that it be washed through repentance, according to the saying: “Wash yourselves, be clean; remove the evil of your thoughts” (Isa. I), etc.

And that of the psalmist: “Wash me more from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin” (Ps. L).

Without a clean conscience, neither fasting nor any other good work has value. Hence the Lord says through Isaiah: “Is this the fast that I desire, says the Lord—to bow one’s head like a reed and to spread sackcloth and ashes? Is this not rather the fast that I have chosen? Break the bonds of wickedness; remove the burdens that oppress” (Isa. LVIII).

Let us therefore wash the stains of our conscience, my brothers, with sobs, sighs, and tears of true repentance, for tears wash away the sin that shame prevents us from confessing with the mouth. Not that tears are sufficient without confession, but because shame arising from the crime increases the tears of the one confessing.

Let us do what the psalmist urges us to do by his own example: “I have labored in my groaning; every night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with my tears” (Ps. VI).

The Lord also commands the person who fasts to store up his treasures in heaven when he adds: “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth” [Col. 1785A].

One stores up treasure on earth either literally, by hiding one’s wealth on earth with an earthly intention, or by placing one’s hope in earthly things.

One stores up treasure in heaven either literally, by transferring one’s wealth to heaven through works of mercy and justice, or mystically, by placing all one’s hope in heavenly things.

He shows why treasure must not be stored up on earth when he adds: “Where rust and moth destroy, and thieves dig through and steal.”

Rust corrodes metals, moths clothing; whatever these do not touch, thieves steal. Through these three things, therefore, every treasure of the avaricious is signified as destined for destruction. For either they will leave their riches, or their riches will leave them.

Hence it is written: “The one who gathered wealth put it into a pierced sack” (Hag. I). And elsewhere: “He stores up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it, for when he dies he will not take everything, nor will his glory descend with him” (Ps. XXXVIII).

Mystically, however, rust—that is, pride—moth—that is, envy—and thieves—that is, demons—scatter and destroy the treasures of those who hope in earthly things. But neither pride, nor envy, nor demons can corrupt the hope of those who store up treasure in heaven.

He gives another reason why treasure must be stored up not on earth but in heaven when he adds: “For where your treasure is, there your heart is also.”

As though he were saying: Since we ought to fix our heart in heavenly things, not in earthly things, we ought therefore always to place the treasure of our hope in heaven, so that before we die we may send many things to heaven through almsgiving.

For if we gather up how much we spend every day on the needs of the body, how much on vain things, and how much on evil things, almost nothing will appear to have been done for the salvation of our soul, when we ought to do everything for its salvation.

Let us therefore weep, brothers, that we have stored up little or nothing in heaven, and let us hasten to do what we have done insufficiently. Let us consider how much we spend every day on the body, and let us strive to spend more for the salvation of the soul.

Let us regard as lost what we spend on the body. Let us rejoice that what we spend on the soul has been well invested, so that both our treasure and our heart may be in heaven. And when we have ascended there in the resurrection, may we find an unfailing treasure, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father [Col. 1785D] and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever. Amen.

# HOMILY XXXIV. THE FIRST SUNDAY OF LENT
We urge you not to receive the grace of God in vain (2 Cor. 6). This reading is divided into two sections, dearly beloved brethren. In the first, the Apostle does two things: first, he urges us not to have God’s grace empty within us; second, he shows which grace above all we must not have in vain.

Urging us, then, first of all not to let God’s grace be empty within us, he says: “We urge you not to receive the grace of God in vain.” Grace, dearly beloved brethren, is called whatever is given freely.
