We, however, possess nothing good that we have not freely received from God. Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: [Col. 1786A] “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 7.) Therefore, brethren, whatever we are, whatever we can do, whatever we possess, is God’s gift and God’s grace.

The Apostle therefore urges us not to have any grace received from God in vain. There are four ways in which God’s grace is had in vain.

The first is when someone proves ungrateful to God for the grace he has received. Concerning such a person the Lord reproves the nine lepers, saying: “Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine? None was found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner” (Luke 17). Moreover, whoever is ungrateful to God for grace received deserves not only not to receive the grace that remains to be received, but also to lose what he has already received.

[Col. 1786B] For this reason we often see certain people who, when they have received from God a good intellect or great learning, nevertheless become proud and show themselves ungrateful to God their author. The grace received in them is therefore not increased but rather diminished. Some, indeed, give thanks in prosperity, according to the saying, “They will confess to you when you have done good to them” (Ps. 48), yet in adversity they are silent, or murmur, or even—what is worse—curse the scourges, the timing, and the ordering of God, and thus blaspheme God’s grace.

The scourges by which God chastises us are great grace and signs of his great mercy. “For the father scourges the son whom he loves” (Heb. 12). Conversely, not scourging the delinquent is a sign of divine wrath, as he himself testifies through the Prophet: “I will no longer be angry with you; my jealousy has withdrawn from you” (Ezek. 16). [Col. 1786C] Understanding this, the Wise Man blesses God for the scourges inflicted and gives him thanks.

Hence holy Job, when his wife urged him to bless God and die, says: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not also endure evil?” (Job 2.) “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has been done. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1).

Let us therefore, dearly beloved brethren, following this example, give thanks to God both in prosperity and in adversity. To rejoice and bless God in adversity belongs only to the good, whereas blessing him in prosperity may also belong to the wicked. The voice of confession pleases God little when it is produced by the exultation of prosperity. Yet “by day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night his song” (Ps. 41), so that in prosperity we may give alms, and in adversity sing psalms to God.

[Col. 1786D] The second way is when someone uselessly hides the grace he has received. According to the evangelical parable, that lazy servant is condemned who hid the talent he had received in the earth (Matt. 25). What is called a talent there is called grace here. Whoever, then, has received from God grace—whether wisdom, wealth, power, a ministry, or anything else—and does not use and distribute it for the advancement of souls is condemned.

Here we must consider that the talent taken away from the lazy servant is given to another who had used well what he had received. This, dearly beloved brethren, we see happening every day: grace is taken away from the lazy and given to one who had previously been upright in other respects.

[Col. 1787A] Therefore, brethren, let us not uselessly hide the grace received from God, but communicate it to others, so that through it we may benefit both ourselves and others. For it is written: “Whoever hides grain will be cursed among the peoples” (Prov. 2). And elsewhere: “Do not withhold the word in the time of salvation” (Ecclus. 4); and elsewhere: “A hidden treasure and hidden wisdom—what profit is there in either?” (Ecclus. 20).

Wisdom is a noble possession: when distributed, it receives increase; but, scorning an avaricious possessor, unless it is made public, it slips away.

The third way is when someone misuses the grace he has received: for example, when he uses learning, wealth, power, or any other possession badly, persecuting God and his neighbor by means of what he ought to have used in the service of God and his neighbor.

[Col. 1787B] Hence the Lord, through Hosea, reproves the Israelites because they offered to Baal, their god, the gold, silver, grain, wine, wool, and linen granted to them by God (Hos. 2). The same is done today by those who spend the wisdom, eloquence, abundance, and other goods bestowed upon them by God against God, in the practice of crimes and in the service of the devil.

Let us therefore, brethren, serve God with his gifts and refer everything to him, from whom alone we have received it. He alone is the Alpha and the Omega, α and ω (Rev. 1; 22), that is, the beginning and the end of all good things.

The fourth way is when someone does not preserve the grace he has received with perseverance. No good that lacks perseverance can please God. Hence the law commands that the head of an animal be offered in sacrifices together with its tail (Lev. 3; 9), because he sacrifices well who begins well and completes well.

[Col. 1787C] For this reason the Lord also says through John: “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Rev. 2). It is as if he said: “Otherwise I will not give it.” Hence it is said through Ezekiel: “If the righteous man turns away and commits iniquity, he will die in his iniquity, and none of all the righteous deeds he has done will be remembered” (Ezek. 3).

You, therefore, my brethren, who have turned away from God through sins, turn back quickly through repentance. But you who are in a good purpose, persevere, advancing from good to better and persevering all the way to the end.

[Col. 1787D] Second, the Apostle shows what grace he urges us not to have in vain when he adds. For the Lord says, through the prophet Isaiah, concerning the time of grace: “In an acceptable time I have heard you, and on the day of salvation I have helped you,” namely, by granting cooperating grace. Explaining this, the Apostle adds: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation,” that is, of earning salvation (2 Cor. 6).

Therefore, my brethren, the grace which the Apostle urges us not to receive in vain is operative grace, by which God first works in us without us, giving contrition of heart and forgiving sins. It is cooperating grace, by which God afterward works in us and with us, giving us the ability to do good.

The very time of grace, in which God gave not only graces but also his own blood for the redemption of the human race, may likewise be called grace. In it God is more propitious to the sinner than in other times, freely justifying the ungodly and granting assisting graces.

[Col. 1788A] Therefore, my brethren, whoever has already received the first grace—that is, the forgiveness of sins—must beware lest, by being ungrateful or useless, he have received it in vain. Whoever, still persisting in sin, has not yet received either grace, must fear that he will pass idly through the acceptable time and the day of salvation. Rather, in the acceptable time let him cry out, so that God may hear him and draw him from the pit of misery and from the mire of filth (Ps. 39).

Let him cry out, I say, while it is permitted, and repent while he has time. For repentance can avail only in this life, and salvation can be earned only here. In the other life there will be no time for sowing but for reaping, not for earning but for receiving.

[Col. 1788B] Therefore, dearly beloved brethren, let us watch with all vigilance lest we spend in vain the time granted to us for earning salvation. But alas, brethren—for I cannot say this without a groan—we neglect the period of time given for repentance, and when we ought to be weeping over sins, we increase them. We pass a great part of our time sleeping, a great part in idleness, and a great part in wrongdoing.

Behold, brethren, yesterday has passed and will not return; and the present hour will already be no more. All time passes irreversibly like a river. Therefore, brethren, let us not pass uselessly through that brief time given to us by God. We lose all the time in which we do not think about God and about our soul.

Let us therefore see to it that we do not lose a day or an hour. Rather, as the ancient Fathers used to do, in the evening let us recall all the day’s work, and in the morning the thoughts or pleasures of the night. [Col. 1788C] If we have contracted any evil, let us cleanse it through repentance; if we have done any good, let us increase it; and let us mourn that we have lost the time in which we did no good. In the time that remains to us, let us strive to make good the loss of the time we have wasted.

Since we must observe the whole of our time, we must observe the Lenten season above all. It is, as it were, the tithe of the entire year, to be consecrated to God, so that during it we may correct what we have transgressed at other times.

Celebrate, therefore, my brethren, the fast you have begun—not in just any manner, but as the prophet Joel says: “Sanctify the fast” (Joel 2). The fast is sanctified through repentance, almsgiving, and prayer. Thus let the body be disciplined through abstinence from food; let the soul be humbled and purified through repentance; let God’s mercy be entreated through almsgiving; and let evils be driven away and good things obtained through prayer.

[Col. 1788D] Consecrate your fast, because our Lord Jesus Christ fasted for you. He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXV. THE FIRST SUNDAY OF LENT

“Giving no offense to anyone, so that our ministry may not be blamed, but in everything let us present ourselves as ministers of God” (2 Cor. 6), and so forth.

In this second section, dearly beloved brethren, the Apostle urges us to present ourselves blamelessly as ministers of God. Although all who rightly administer the grace given to them by God may universally be called ministers of God, the expression refers especially to the ministers of the holy Church.

[Col. 1789A] We, therefore, my brethren, who are ministers of the altar and dispensers of the word of God, are admonished by the Apostle to present ourselves in everything as ministers of God. For just as, according to Solomon, a wicked prince has wicked ministers (Prov. 29), so, conversely, it is fitting that a holy Lord should have holy ministers. Hence he himself says: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Lev. 19–20).

An unclean minister greatly provokes God. To the sinner he says: “Why do you recount my justice and take up my covenant in your mouth?” (Ps. 49).

[Col. 1789B] The Apostle therefore enumerates six areas in which above all we must present ourselves as ministers of God: avoiding offense, enduring affliction, good works, virtues, the word of right preaching, and the proper use of prosperity and adversity.

First, he admonishes us to present ourselves as ministers of God by avoiding offense, when he says: “Giving no offense to anyone, so that our ministry may not be blamed”—that is, we must offend neither God through disobedience or negligence, nor our neighbor through injury, evil speech, or bad example.

Although everyone ought to beware of offending God through obedience, we ministers of Christ must do so especially, since we must also intercede for the offenses of others. For if someone from the people commits an offense, the priest will pray for him. But if the priest commits an offense, who will pray for him? And if an enchanter is bitten by a serpent, who will heal him? (Eccles. 12.)

[Col. 1789C] Let us also beware, brethren, of offending God through negligence, for, according to Jeremiah, “Cursed is the one who does the work of God negligently” (Jer. 48). Eli rebuked his sons, but because he did so lukewarmly and negligently (1 Sam. 2), he thereby incurred destruction together with them (1 Sam. 4).

This applies to some of us, brethren, who are lukewarm and negligent in the divine office, in preaching and correction, in prayer and reading, and in other duties, although, according to John, Christ vomits out the lukewarm (Rev. 3). And according to the Wise Man: “A slack man in his works is brother to one who dissipates his own works” (Prov. 18).  
[Note: [Col. 1789D] Vulgate: “A brother to one who dissipates his works.”]

[Col. 1789D] We ministers of Christ must not offend our neighbor through injury either; rather, we ought to prevent and restrain those who inflict injury. For the Apostle forbids a bishop to be a striker (Titus 1), and he condemns the man who exposed his back to blows and, when cursed, did not curse in return (Acts 23).

We ministers of Christ must also beware of offending our neighbor by speech: we must not be slanderers, swearers, detractors, buffoons, or foul-mouthed. Rather, our speech should be seasoned with the salt of wisdom, so that it may give grace to those who hear.

[Col. 1790A] Let us also beware lest we cause others to go astray by a bad example. Whoever acts either badly or indiscreetly places a stumbling block for others by his example. Therefore, the minister of Christ must beware not only of doing evil outright, but also of doing good indiscreetly. He does this who causes scandal either through food or through some other moderate good.

Hence the Apostle says: “If you offend your brother because of food, you are no longer walking according to charity” (Rom. 14).  
[Note: [Col. 1789] Vulgate: “If your brother is grieved because of food.”]

Because of the offense of our brethren, therefore, not only evils but also all good things without which salvation can be attained must be avoided.

Second, he commands us to present ourselves as ministers of God in patience. He then specifies where patience is necessary:

“In tribulations,” namely, those of persecutions, according to the saying: “My son, when you come to the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2). This is directed against those who wish to be bishops, priests, and ministers of Christ in order to enjoy peace and tranquility here, although the Lord, sending his disciples to preach, said to them: “Behold, I send you as lambs among wolves” (Luke 10).

[Col. 1790B] “In necessities,” meaning hunger, cold, and poverty. This is directed against those who wish to become bishops, priests, and ministers of Christ in order to abound here in riches and luxuries. By contrast, our Master, who was poor here and had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9), says: “Whoever ministers to me, let him follow me” (John 12). But how, brethren, can a disciple weighed down with riches follow a naked and unencumbered master?

“In distresses,” namely, dangers. This is directed against those who wish to become prelates and ministers of churches in order to be secure. For whoever is the greatest guardian has more cause for fear. A private person fears only for himself. But a shepherd, even if he is secure concerning himself, must always fear concerning his sheep; he is in danger as often as any one of his sheep is in danger.

[Col. 1790C] “In blows,” namely, beatings.

“In prisons,” namely, chains.

“In seditions of peoples,” namely, disturbances raised against them. This is directed against those who wish to become leaders and teachers of churches in order to live without injury, insult, or disturbance.

But if they are true disciples of Christ, they will endure injuries and insults, since the Master himself says: “A disciple is not above his master” (Luke 6); “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John 15); and elsewhere: “Amen, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice” (John 16). Whoever in this age does not know how to suffer or weep proves that he is not a disciple of Christ.

[Col. 1790D] Third, he commands us to present ourselves as ministers of God in good works. In what works? “In labors.” This is directed against those who wish to be teachers of churches in order to become idle and sluggish, although the Apostle who says this worked with his own hands, made others work, and said: “Whoever does not work should not eat” (2 Thess. 3).

[Col. 1791A] The Psalmist likewise says: “You shall eat the labors of your hands. You are blessed, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. 127). And Jerome says: “Always be engaged in some work, so that the devil may find you occupied.”  
[Note: [Col. 1791] Jerome, Letter 125 to Rusticus the monk, Patrologia, vol. 31, col. 1078.]

Idleness is the enemy of the soul. This is directed against those teachers of churches who, abandoning necessary labors, devote themselves to hunting, dice, games, and other vanities.

Ministers of Christ ought to be watchful—always vigilant—not only in prayers but also in governing their subjects. This is directed against those who scarcely wish to rise for church even when the sun has barely risen, and who keep greater watch over the care of salted meats and pleasures than over the guardianship of souls.

“In fasts.” The minister of Christ ought to fast, both to mortify the desires of the flesh in himself and to teach others to fast by his example. For with what face will a very corpulent and ruddy priest dare to preach abstinence and mortification of the flesh to others?

[Col. 1791B] Fourth, he commanded us to present ourselves as ministers of God in virtues. In what virtues? “In chastity.” Although chastity befits every person, it especially befits a priest. Hence, in the law, when priests ministered in the temple, they were commanded to separate themselves both from their wives and from wine.

Even the pagans appointed only chaste men as priests. If any one of them, man or woman, were convicted of fornication, he or she was put to death while still alive. What, then, ought the evangelical priest to be like, who is continually bound to sacrifice not an animal or incense, but the Son of God?

Alas! With what spirit and what boldness does a priest who keeps a concubine, polluted in heart and body, dare to touch the Son of virginity, the purifier of souls?

“In knowledge,” namely, of divine and worldly matters. When possessed together with charity, knowledge is certainly a virtue. This is directed against those who say that a little knowledge is sufficient for a priest. For who needs to be wiser than the judge of souls?

[Col. 1791C] He ought therefore to know both Testaments, so that with both horns he may scatter the enemies of the cross of Christ (Ps. 43). He should always be ready to give an account of the faith and hope that are in us (1 Pet. 3), and should resemble the householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old (Matt. 13).

“In long-suffering,” namely, in patience and hope, so that he may not grow weary in the virtue of patience and hope through any burden or prolonged adversity. This is directed against those who are disturbed by any temporal loss and weep in a womanly fashion, although a minister of Christ ought to possess such courage that he can lose all temporal things with a smile.

[Col. 1791D] “In gentleness,” namely, so that the minister of Christ does not curse or mock sinners, but rather nourishes and attracts them through the gentleness of his word, example, and forgiveness. This is directed against those who arrogantly thunder and curse at the people entrusted to them, breaking the crushed reed and extinguishing the smoking wick (Matt. 12).

“In the Holy Spirit.” It is as if he said: Let the minister of Christ possess not merely this or that virtue, but also the very source of graces, the Holy Spirit.

“In sincere charity,” so that we may not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth (1 John 3). Charity is false when someone loves in prosperity but fails in adversity. This is directed against those who venerate the rich with flattering words, lavish promises, and feigned services, outwardly pretending to possess a love they do not have inwardly.

[Col. 1792A] Fifth, he commands us to present ourselves as ministers of God in the word of truth, according to the saying of Isaiah: “Cry out, do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet, and announce to my people their crimes and to the house of Jacob their sins” (Isa. 58, 38); and elsewhere: “Woe is me, because I have been silent” (Isa. 6). The Apostle likewise says: “Preach the word of God; be urgent in season and out of season” (2 Tim. 4).

The preacher ought to preach not his own word but the word of truth, because it is written: “You shall announce to them from me” (Ezek. 3). And Peter says: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God” (1 Pet. 4).

“In the power of God”—understand: with the word of truth making progress. For unless there is one within who teaches, the teacher’s tongue labors in vain, since “neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase” (1 Cor. 3).

[Col. 1792B] This is directed against those who are foolish and proud, who boast in their own words, their own power, and their own wisdom—not so that they may make progress, but so that they may appear glorious.

Sixth, he commands us to present ourselves as ministers of God in the right use of prosperity and adversity. This will happen if we are furnished with the weapons of justice on the right and on the left: that is, if we arm ourselves with justice against prosperity and against adversity, so that we may govern the former justly and endure the latter with equanimity.

[Col. 1792C] Explaining the right and left sides, he adds: “Through glory and dishonor,” meaning that we should present ourselves as ministers of God so that we are not exalted by the empty glory of nobility or virtue, nor cast down by the dishonor of this or that kind. This is directed against those who boast of the nobility of their parents or are ashamed of their lack of nobility.

“Through infamy and good reputation,” so that we may overcome infamy by the splendor of good works. Or, if the mouths of detractors cannot be silenced even by good works, let us endure this equably, knowing that Christ was called a deceiver, a glutton, a wine-drinker, and a lover of prostitutes, such as Mary Magdalene, and of publicans, such as Matthew (Matt. 2).

Let us prove our good reputation by our works, and through it seek not our own glory but God’s glory and the advancement of our neighbors, according to the saying: “Let your good works shine before people, so that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5).

[Col. 1792D] Explaining what he had said, “through infamy and good reputation,” he adds: “As deceivers and truthful.” By some we are regarded as deceivers, yet by others we are regarded—and are—truthful. Thus we are regarded by some as unknown and rejected, yet we are known to God.

“As dying”—that is, by some we are called worthy of death—and behold, we live: here in the life of virtues, and in the future in eternal life.

“As chastised,” since by some we are said to be punished on account of our sins, yet we are not put to death.

[Col. 1793A] It should be noted, my brethren, that the Apostle says “as deceivers,” “as those who are unknown,” and “as dying,” whereas, conversely, he says without “as,” without “like,” and without “as though”: “truthful,” “known,” and “we live.” This is because there ought to be such holiness in a preacher that no one can say anything evil about him except by lying.

“As sorrowful”—understand: we are sorrowful amid the miseries of this age—and yet we rejoice in the hope of heavenly life.

“As poor,” namely, in temporal possessions, yet enriching many with heavenly riches.

“As having nothing, yet possessing all things.”

We should also consider here, brethren, that the Apostle says “as sorrowful,” “as poor,” and “as possessing nothing,” whereas he says absolutely “rejoicing,” “enriching,” and “possessing all things.” By this he shows that all temporal things are not truly real, but appear as though in a dream. For just as someone speaks of what he saw in sleep—“I was as if riding,” “I was as if running,” and the like—so it is with temporal things.

[Col. 1793B] Spiritual and heavenly goods, however, truly exist, because they are everlasting. The riches, glory, and honors of this world, brethren, vanish so quickly that after death they seem not even to have existed. Hence the Psalmist says: “They have slept their sleep, and the men of riches have found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 75).

Conversely, the sorrow, poverty, and dishonor suffered by the saints in this age will pass so quickly that afterward they will seem to have existed only like a dream. In the future, by contrast, the rich will be given true and eternal poverty in place of their vain riches; true and eternal sorrow in place of vain joy; and true and eternal disgrace in place of vain honors.

[Col. 1793C] But to the saints will be given, in place of the vain sorrow of this age, true and eternal joy; in place of vain poverty, true and eternal riches; and in place of vain dishonor, true and eternal honor.

May God, our Lord, join us to them—he who lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXVI. THE FIRST SUNDAY OF LENT

“Jesus was led into the desert by the Spirit, to be tempted by the devil. And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry” (Matt. 4).

Because today, dearly beloved brethren, we begin Christ’s Lenten fast, the Gospel reading containing the history of this fast is appropriately recited today. In this reading, it first seems necessary for us to ask why Christ, our God and Lord, [Col. 1793D] who in his most holy flesh experienced no rebellion whatsoever, wished to fast and to be tempted.

He wished to fast and be tempted for three reasons: for ministry, for triumph, and for example.

For ministry, because he wished to show that he and his fast had been prefigured by the Law and the Prophets. The lawgiver Moses fasted for forty days; Elijah, the outstanding prophet, also fasted for the same number of days. Christ too, the Lord of the Law and the Prophets, fasted for the same number of days.

In these events, brethren, let us also consider the rewards of those who fast. Moses fasted for forty days, spoke with God, and received the Law. Elijah fasted, spoke with God, and was carried away in a fiery chariot. Christ also fasted, and angels approached and ministered to him.

[Col. 1794A] But although Moses and Elijah, who were certainly pure human beings, are not said to have been hungry after a forty-day fast, why did Christ, true God, wish to become hungry? For three reasons: to show himself to be a true human being; to redeem by his voluntary hunger our necessary hunger; and, by becoming hungry, to provide the devil with an opportunity to tempt him.

The Lord also wished to fast and be tempted for triumph, so that he might triumph for us over the flesh, the devil, and the world. The devil had conquered our first parent, Adam, by tempting him in three matters: gluttony, greed, and empty glory.

He tempted and conquered him through gluttony when he persuaded him to seek knowledge of good and evil. [Col. 1794B] He tempted and conquered him through empty glory, or pride, when he persuaded him to seek to be like God. In these three things, dearly beloved brethren, all the wickedness of the world is contained. John warns us against them, saying: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world, because everything that is in the world is either the desire of the flesh, or the desire of the eyes, or the pride of life, which is not from God the Father” (1 John 2).

Conquered through these three things, humanity became subject to every evil of the flesh, the world, and the devil. Christ therefore wished to fast and be tempted so that he might triumph for us over the devil, the flesh, and the world.

The devil had tempted and conquered Adam in these same three matters. He tempted Christ as well, but was conquered by him.

[Col. 1794C] He tempted him through gluttony when he said: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread.” But Christ overcame him in his temptation when he said: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.” It is as if he said: “In tempting me, you mention only bodily bread, although spiritual bread is more necessary to a human being.”

He tempted Christ through greed when he said to him: “I will give you all these things if you fall down and worship me.” But in that temptation Christ overcame him when it was said to him: “It is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.” It is as if he said: “No creature is to be worshiped with the worship due to God.”

He tempted him through empty glory, or pride, when he said to him: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down. For it is written: God has commanded his angels concerning you, that they guard you in all your ways. They will carry you in their hands, lest you ever strike your foot against a stone.”

[Col. 1794D] But Christ overcame him in that temptation when it was said to him: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God.” It is as if he said: “God is not to be tempted when we have reason to know what we ought to do.”

Since the devil was tempting Christ above all with the intention of investigating through temptation whether he was the Son of God—something he greatly desired to know—the Lord overcame his temptations by answering in such a way that he always left him uncertain. He did not say, “You shall worship me,” or, “You shall not tempt me,” but introduced only the testimonies of the Law in the third person.

Thus the devil, defeated and confounded, fled. And behold, angels approached Christ and ministered to him.  
[Note: [Col. 1793D] Vulgate: “The angels approached and ministered to him.”]

[Col. 1795A] This was both a sign of victory and a sign of his divinity.

Christ also wished to fast and be tempted for our example, so that by his example he might show beforehand how we ought to fast and how we ought to resist temptations. He instructed us not only in what we should do, but also in the order in which we should do it.

First he is baptized in the Spirit; immediately afterward he is led by the Spirit into the desert. He fasts, becomes hungry, is tempted, conquers, and is ministered to.

We too, dearly beloved brethren, following the example of our Savior, if we wish to fast purely, must first be baptized in the spirit. But because, after baptism, we have fallen and cannot be baptized again, let us at least be cleansed through repentance, which is the Church’s laver, according to the saying of Isaiah: “Wash yourselves, be clean; remove the evil of your thoughts from my eyes; cease to act perversely, and learn to do good” (Isa. 1).

[Col. 1795B] Repentance must precede fasting. Without it, neither fasting nor any good deed can please God. Therefore, so that our fast may be pleasing to God, let us hasten at the beginning of Lent to the laver of repentance.

Cleansed through the spirit of repentance, let us be led—not by ourselves, but in him, with the Spirit as our guide—into the desert, that is, into the religious life. This is rightly called a desert, both because it is deserted by many and cultivated by few, and because it contains none of the luxury and pleasures of sensuality. Instead, it follows the harshness of the virtues, striving upward along a difficult and narrow way.

In this desert, therefore, dearly beloved brethren, let us fast for forty days—that is, throughout this present life, which is extended through four seasons.

[Col. 1795C] Fasting is both spiritual and bodily. Spiritual fasting is fasting from sin; bodily fasting is abstaining from food. Spiritual fasting without bodily fasting is always beneficial; bodily fasting without spiritual fasting is never beneficial.

Hence the Lord says through Isaiah: “What is the fast that I have chosen? Is it perhaps to twist the head like a ring and to spread out sackcloth and ashes? Is this the fast that I have chosen, says the Lord? Undo the bonds of wickedness; remove the burdens that oppress” (Isa. 58).

[Col. 1795D] Let us therefore fast in two ways: from sin in the mind and from food in the body. But, brethren, for us who have offended through many illicit acts, it is not enough unless we also abstain from certain licit things.

Therefore, in order that by abstinence from what is lawful we may atone for all the unlawful things we have committed, let us also fast from certain lawful things: although we are permitted to eat fish, drink wine, dress softly, and lie comfortably, let us abstain from them. And that we ought to do so the Lord demonstrates, for through Isaiah he reproves the fasting Israelites not only for unlawful things but also for certain lawful ones, saying: “In your days of fasting your own desires are found. Behold, you fast for quarrels and contentions, and you strike impiously with the fist, and you exact all your debts” (ibid.). Behold, he rebukes them because they exacted their debts—not because this is unlawful, but because one who wishes to fast well ought also to abstain from what is lawful and from certain other things. [Col. 1796A]

We must also, my brothers, according to Joel, sanctify the fast (Joel I, II); and this is certainly done through works of piety and mercy. Almsgiving is effective without fasting, but fasting without almsgiving is not effective. Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “When you fast, do you fast for me? And when you have eaten and drunk, do you not eat and drink for yourselves?” (Zech. VII). He fasts for himself and not for God, and eats and drinks for himself and not for God, who does not distribute to the poor what he takes from himself by fasting, but reserves it for his own consumption.

Therefore, my brothers, when we fast, let us fast for God, not for ourselves. Let us give to the poor what we take away from ourselves; let us receive Christ at our table in the poor; let us clothe the naked, visit the sick, and ransom captives, as the Lord exhorts through Isaiah: “Release,” he says, “those who are broken free, and break every burden.” Share your bread with the hungry, and bring the poor and homeless into your house. When you see a naked man, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh” (Isa. LVIII).

We must also hunger, dearest brothers, following the Lord’s example, both bodily and spiritually. We must hunger bodily so that we do not anticipate hunger, turn it into disgust, or prolong it beyond measure. My brothers, we must not anticipate hunger, as do those who eat before they are hungry and do not wait for the canonical hour of eating. Esau is condemned for this vice: unable to endure a little hunger, he sold his birthright for a small amount of lentils. [Col. 1796C]

But let us, brothers, bear hunger manfully, and eat bread only at the ninth hour or after the ninth. Again, we must not turn hunger into disgust, as do those who reject humble foods and satisfy their appetite more than their nature with rich and elaborate dishes—or, if they cannot find such foods, with humbler foods carefully and delicately prepared. The Israelites are condemned for the first vice: disgusted with manna, they demanded meat to their own harm. For the second vice, the sons of Eli are condemned: disgusted with the ordinary meat of the sacrifice, they carefully procured meat for themselves from below.

But let us, brothers, always hunger in such a way that we do not despise humble foods, but eat humble foods, prepared manfully, as though they were delicacies. Again, let us not prolong our hunger beyond measure, as do those who remain without food for two or three days and then, being excessively hungry, seize an excessive meal, sinning equally through both extremes. Avoiding this, dearest brothers, let us eat a little every day, because it is better to eat a little every day than too much rarely. Let us eat in such a way that we always hunger, and let us always hunger in such a way that we eat a little every day. Such fasting is holier in proportion as it contains more moderation and less vainglory.

We must also hunger spiritually, with that hunger which the Lord promised he would send upon the earth: hunger not for bread or wine, but hunger for the word of God. Concerning this the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. V). Therefore, [Col. 1797A] my brothers, let us hunger for the word of God, eagerly devoting ourselves to reading, prayer, and meditation on Holy Scripture. Let us hunger and thirst for righteousness, eagerly pursuing it here, and hastening with all our desire toward its perfection in the life to come.

We must also be tempted, dearest brothers, following Christ’s example, by the devil, who envies and opposes those who have begun well. Against him the Wise Man exhorts us: “My son,” he says, “when you approach the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. II). For as long as you do not resist the devil, he does not trouble to oppose you; but when you begin to resist, he immediately opposes you. For as long as the children of Israel were in Egypt under Pharaoh, they are not recorded as having been tempted. But once they began their journey through the Red Sea, they were tempted concerning gluttony when they sought meat in the desert, in the land [Col. 1797B] of promise; concerning lust when they fornicated with the Midianites; concerning idolatry when they fashioned the calf; and concerning glory when they sought the priesthood and leadership.

All these things, my brothers, happened to them figuratively. We too, my brothers, while we serve the devil, are not tempted by him; but when we begin to depart from him and, through the baptism of repentance and the fast of the desert, to journey toward our eternal homeland, he immediately tempts us. But let us follow Christ, who conquered him not by power but by a humble reply, and let us resist him through humility.

If he urges us to eat either before the proper time, or luxuriously, or immoderately, let us answer him: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. IV). If he urges us to serve him, or money, or lust, let us answer: “It is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’” (ibid.). If he tempts us concerning glory, so that he casts us into open danger when we know by reason what ought to be done, let us answer: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (ibid.). If he tempts us concerning lust, let us answer: “It is written: ‘God will judge adulterers and fornicators’” (Heb. XIII). If concerning lying, let us answer: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. V). If concerning hatred, let us answer: “It is written: ‘Whoever hates his brother is a murderer’” (1 John III). And against similar temptations let us bring forward similar testimonies from Scripture.

If we do this, brothers—if we do this—then, with God’s help, we shall conquer and drive away the devil; and angels, ministering spirits, our fellow citizens and helpers, will be present to us as victors. Their joy is in heaven before the Lord over one sinner who repents. May he grant us to repent sincerely: Jesus Christ our Lord, who fasted for us and who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXVII. THE SECOND SUNDAY OF LENT

“Brothers, we ask and exhort you in the Lord Jesus that, just as you received from us how you ought to walk and please God, so also you should walk, that you may abound more” (1 Thess. IV), and so forth.

In the first part of this reading, dearest brothers, the Apostle asks and entreats us in the Lord Jesus—that is, he adjures us by the Lord Jesus. For what? Not, as worldly men do, for his own salvation, but for ours. In this he shows himself to be a true teacher and true father, concerned for our salvation with paternal affection. We too, dearest brothers, ought to hear and imitate him with filial affection.

Yet it is not enough for a true father to admonish his son once; rather, with fatherly concern, he often repeats the same instruction to him. As he himself says elsewhere: “To write the same things to you, brothers, is not burdensome to me, but is necessary for you” (Phil. III). Thus he repeats the admonition he had previously given when he adds: “That, just as you received from us how you ought to walk and please”—that is, please God by walking—“so also you should walk, that you may abound more.”

Here the Apostle compares life to walking. For one who walks correctly does three things: he sets before himself a goal toward which he hastens; he enters upon the road; and he moves forward, adding step to step, league to league, day’s journey to day’s journey, until he reaches his proper destination. So, my brothers, so must anyone who wishes to live correctly set God before himself as his goal, enter the road—that is, hold to the faith—and, progressing, add good work to good work, good zeal to good zeal, and one good day’s journey to another, so that he may be able to reach God.

Faith without works is not sufficient for one who has opportunity and time, just as a road without progress is not sufficient, because, as James says, “faith without works is dead” (James II). And again: “You say that you believe; even the demons believe and tremble.” But neither are works without faith sufficient, just as the swiftest running is useless outside the road. Therefore, my brothers, if you wish to go correctly, set God before yourselves as your end in everything. [Col. 1798C]

For one who goes without knowing where he is going does not walk but wanders. Hold to the road of faith, because without faith it is impossible to please God (Heb. II). Make progress also in works, without which there is not advancement but remaining where one is.

What constitutes correct walking and what pleases God he explains when he adds: “This is the will of God, your sanctification.” In what sanctification consists he shows when he continues: “That you abstain from fornication, that each of you know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honor,” and so forth.

Sanctification consists in two things: avoiding the passions of desire through purity, and avoiding offense against one’s neighbor through innocence. He shows that spiritual fornication must be avoided when he says, “that you abstain from fornication.” Idolatry is rightly called fornication, because just as through temporal fornication a bride is separated from her bridegroom, so through idolatry the soul is separated from God, its spiritual bridegroom.

Therefore, brothers, let us always cleave firmly to God in faith, believing him to be the author not of any evil but of all good. Let us believe that we receive from him every good thing we possess, while evil comes from us alone. Let us believe that he rewards all good and avenges evil. Let us believe also the other things handed down by the Catholic faith.

He warns that the passions of desire must be excluded through purity when he adds: “That each one know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passions of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God.” He calls our heart and body a vessel because it was created for God’s service. Concerning this the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Does the potter not have power over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. IX).

Indeed, my brothers, God made all our hearts and bodies, insofar as it depended on him, for honor. But the person who, through the disgrace and foulness of vices, makes himself foul and unclean makes his body and heart a vessel of dishonor. The Apostle therefore warns us that each one should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification—that is, cleansing—so that every foul thought may be removed from the mind and every foul deed from the body.

He should also know how to possess his vessel in honor, so that our heart and body may be adorned with virtues and thus honored by the indwelling Holy Spirit. “Not in the passions,” he says, “of desire.” He calls all foul wishes the passions of desire: these entangle the Gentiles, who do not know God and are ignorant of God and eternal life; like beasts, they run without restraint toward every pleasure of the flesh as though toward great goods.

But if they are passions, how are they desires? Or if they are desires, how are they passions? They are passions, my brothers, with respect to the spirit, which suffers through them, is blinded, and is separated from God. They are desires with respect to the flesh, which takes temporal delight in them.

Against this the Psalmist prays: “Do not hand me over,” he says, “to the desire of the sinner” (Ps. CXXXIX). A sinner is handed over to his own desire when, through the fulfillment of the desired sin, he is enslaved to the devil. Hence also the Lord says through the same prophet: “I let them go according to the desires of their heart; they shall walk in their own inventions” (Ps. LXXX). This, my brothers, is a sign of God’s great anger: when he does not hinder a sinner’s desire but permits him to fall into the sins he desires.

Therefore, brothers, let us flee these evil desires and guard the purity of mind—which alone will see God—with all vigilance, so that we may possess the vessel of our heart and body and not be possessed by them. Let us blunt their wicked impulses, so that we may be worthy to be honored by God, who dwells within us.

The Apostle also warns us to avoid offending our neighbor when he adds: “Let no one overstep or defraud his brother in business”—that is, let no one harm him through violence or fraud, openly or secretly. Here he especially refutes traders and merchants, and all who make a profit for themselves at the expense of their neighbor, since the natural law says: “Do not do to another what you do not wish to be done to you.”

He also refutes those who keep one weight and another, one measure and another, one cubit and another, as Solomon says: “A weight and a weight, a balance and a balance, both are an abomination before God” (Prov. XX). He refutes those who swear in order to deceive, as the same Solomon says: “Bad, bad,” says every buyer; but when he has gone away, then he boasts (ibid.).

He likewise refutes those who oppress the poor in court by influence or money, overturning rights so that they may join house to house, vineyard to vineyard, and field to field. Guard against this in every way, my brothers, because, as the Apostle adds, “God is the avenger of such things” (1 Thess. IV). He will punish those who do these things, either temporally for purification or eternally for condemnation. [Col. 1800A]

Therefore, brothers, while we have the opportunity, let us wipe away our sins with tears; let us cling to God through faith and obedience; let us sanctify our vessel through purity; and let us show innocence toward our neighbors. For, as the Apostle adds: “God has not called us to uncleanness but to sanctification and honor,” so that we may be holy as he is holy, merciful as he is merciful, just as he is just, and glorified in the future as he is glorified—gods as he is God.

May he grant us this sanctification and honor, our Lord Jesus Christ, who for our sake willed to be dishonored, and who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXVIII. THE SECOND SUNDAY OF LENT

[Col. 1800B]

“Jesus went away and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon; and behold, a Canaanite woman, coming out from those districts, cried out to him, saying” (Matt. XV), and so forth.

In this reading from the holy Gospel, dearest brothers, let us consider first what pertains to the literal sense, second what pertains to allegory, and third what pertains to moral interpretation.

First, according to the literal sense, the great virtues of this woman are commended to us. Her devotion is all the more admirable because, although she was a Gentile and unfamiliar with the Law and the Prophets, she was not without the holy virtues contained in them. She possessed faith, fervor, and humility. She had faith when she worshiped Christ as God and believed that, although he was absent, he could heal her daughter by his will alone. [Col. 1800C]

She had fervor of mind: with such devotion she cried out no less in her heart than with her voice, moving the apostles to intercede for her. She had perseverance: although at first and second she seemed to be rejected, she nevertheless did not desist from her requests until she obtained what she sought. She had humility: she compared herself not only to dogs but even to little dogs, and, declaring herself unworthy of the children’s bread, asked for the crumbs that fell.

And because she was such a woman and possessed such virtues, she deserved to be praised by the Lord for her faith and to be heard in what she requested.

Mystically, this woman signifies the Church gathered from the Gentiles. Having come out from the error of idolatry and the filth of vices, she begs the Lord on behalf of any member of her congregation who has been driven mad by the devil. Whoever labors under gluttony, lust, avarice, anger, envy, [Col. 1800D] or any other vices is tormented by the devil—and all the more grievously when he knowingly and willingly serves him.

If the holy Church begs the Lord for such a person with firm faith, great devotion, perseverance, and humility, the Lord will hear her through the intercession of the apostles and the other saints, and will free from the devil’s power the person for whom she has prayed.

Therefore, dearest brothers, whenever we see in the Church someone enslaved to the devil’s service, let us not cease from prayer. Let us cry out with the heart, cry out with the voice, cry out together, cry out individually, and cry out perseveringly. But if, as James testifies, “the continual prayer of a righteous person has great power” (James V), how much more powerful will be the continual prayer of many righteous people.

Let us not, brothers, be numbered among those who not only do not pity wicked Christians and false brothers but even curse them; who not only do not pray for their conversion but fear it, and, as though they themselves had never been sinners, refuse to let sinners find forgiveness. Why is this? Because they do not possess the inward parts of charity, failing to consider that “judgment without mercy will be for the one who has not shown mercy” (James II).

Therefore, brothers, let us always have inward compassion and mercy. Let us strive especially to recall sinners to correction through prayers and admonitions. For if, my brothers, greater compassion must be shown to the unfortunate, greater compassion must be shown to the unrighteous than to the poor. And if God did not come to call the righteous but sinners (Matt. IX), then, following his example, let us call sinners to conversion, knowing that “whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (James V)—not only the sins of others but also his own.

Morally, this woman also teaches us what each person ought to do for his daughter—that is, for his soul, grievously tormented by the devil—when he prays to the Lord: what he should ask, how he should ask, and through whom he may obtain it.

When this woman was about to pray for her daughter, tormented by a demon, she went out from her own territory and approached God. Let us first go out from our old and evil way of life through repentance, and approach the Lord in mind. Let us abandon our vices and sins in our minds, and follow the Lord in faith, hope, and love.

Hence he himself said to Abraham: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house,” and so forth (Gen. XII)—that is, go out from love of earthly things, from kinship with carnal vices, and from the power of the devil, and I will enrich you with spiritual goods.

And the Psalmist says: “Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. XLIV). Whoever still dwells in sin in his mind labors in vain. Hence it is said: “When you stretch out your hands to me, I will not hear you, for your hands are full of blood” (Isa. I).

The woman asked not for gold, silver, or honors, but only for the salvation of her daughter. Let us too, brothers, ask the Lord not for passing things but for eternal things—not earthly substance, but only the salvation of our soul.

Thus the Lord commands in the Gospel: “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. VI). Whoever asks for vain things, and asks vainly, is himself vain. I say “vainly” because when the Church asks for the fruits of the earth and for other temporal goods, she does not ask vainly, but asks in God and toward God; therefore she is not vain.

But whoever asks for vain things with a vain intention is certainly vain. Whoever asks for the death, loss, or punishment of his enemy is wicked. Concerning such people James says: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (James IV).

This woman also shows how one ought to ask: she made her request with faith, desire, perseverance, and humility. Let us too, brothers, ask with firm faith, believing that God is able to give the eternal good we seek, and awaiting with certain hope that we shall obtain it. Whoever doubts in any of these matters either despairs of himself or does not believe or hope properly, and therefore will not obtain what he asks.

Hence James says: “If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach anyone. But let him ask in faith, doubting nothing; for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind” (James I). Such a person must not suppose that he will receive anything from God.

Let us also ask with desire, my brothers, crying out more with the heart than with the voice, as Moses and Susanna cried out in silence. Let us not pray with the lips alone, like those whom the Lord accuses, saying: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matt. XV).

Let us not pray lukewarmly, for vain thoughts assail the lukewarm; and, according to Solomon, “dying flies spoil the sweetness of the ointment” (Eccles. X). If the phantoms of vain thoughts assail us, let us drive them away from us with great fervor, as it is written: “The birds descended upon the sacrifices, and Abraham drove them away” (Gen. XV).

Let us not pray with many words, like hypocrites, but as the Lord says: “When you pray, enter your room, and after closing the door, pray to your Father” (Matt. VI). Literally, brothers, we ought to choose a private and sacred place for prayer. But mystically, we must enclose ourselves within the secret place of our heart, both in intention and in thought, lest we wander toward outward things. We must bar the door of our senses, lest vain thoughts and diabolical temptations—which especially tend to assail those who pray—disturb us from the contemplation of prayer.

Let us ask with perseverance. For even if God delays what is requested, he does not take it away. God does not despise the prayers of the poor; rather, he delays so that we may ask more, and by asking more, deserve more. Hence he himself commands us in the Gospel to ask perseveringly: “Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find.” Seek by working; knock by persevering. “Everyone who asks perseveringly receives; whoever seeks finds; and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Luke XI).

Let us also ask with humility, dearest brothers, considering ourselves unclean dogs who have often returned to the filth of our own vomit, unworthy of the children’s bread—that is, of the grace of the apostles, martyrs, and other saints. Yet let us beg that a few crumbs of his generosity may be bestowed upon us, though we are unworthy.

Through whose intercessions we may deserve to be heard by the Lord is shown to us in this woman, who obtained from the Lord what she requested through the apostles’ intercession, for they said: “Send her away, because she is crying out after us.”

Let us too, my brothers, cry out after the Lord, and after the apostles and the other saints. Let us cry out with sighs; let us cry out with tears, so that by the devotion of our hearts we may move their inward compassion, and so that the saints may intercede for us with God. [Col. 1803A]

This will indeed happen if we honor God in his saints; if we illuminate their altars with gifts and lamps; if we devoutly celebrate their solemnities; and if we frequently commemorate them in litanies and prayers. Then, moved at last by our devotion, they too will cry out for us: “Lord, send them away, because they are crying out after us.” “Send them away” by hearing them, because they knock upon us with their prayers.

Then, without doubt, through their intervention the Lord will be appeased, freeing our soul from the devil—here, so that we may overcome his temptations, and in the future, so that we may no longer be able to be tempted by him. May he grant this, who in perfect Trinity lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXIX. THE THIRD SUNDAY OF LENT

[Col. 1803B]

“Be imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love, as Christ also loved us and gave himself for us, an offering and sacrifice to God for a sweet fragrance,” and so forth (Eph. V).

This reading, dearest brothers, is divided into two parts. First, the Apostle commands us to imitate the Lord. Second, he shows in what ways we ought to imitate him.

Commanding us first to imitate the Lord, he says: “Be imitators of God.” But because some perversely wished to imitate God by attributing to themselves divinity, authority, and those things that belong to God alone—like Jupiter, Simon, and Chosroes—and because there are still some who think that they can do or possess any good thing from themselves, the Apostle therefore adds: “as beloved children.”

A beloved son imitates a good father, not to usurp his dominion and authority, but to resemble him in conduct: to love his father as he is loved by him, and to be prudent, honorable, just, and adorned with good character as his father is.

Who, dearest brothers, could better imitate God the Father in equality, power, and authority than his only-begotten and consubstantial Son, our Lord Jesus Christ? Yet he, as the Apostle says, “did not consider it robbery to be equal with God” (Phil. II). He did not say that he was from himself, but from the Father. He did not say that he had come from himself, but from the Father. He did not say that he sought his own glory, but the Father’s glory. He did not say that his teaching was his own, but the Father’s, because, he says, “the Father is greater than I” (John XIV).

Therefore you, proud dust, how dare you claim for yourself either power, dominion, or authority? How can you think that you possess any good from yourself? How do you presume to seek not God’s glory or will, but your own?

Let us therefore, dearest brothers, flee this perverse imitation and idolatry, and imitate God with a good imitation. Let us imitate him in virtues and conduct. For through virtues, not through authority, he created man like himself; but by sinning, man made himself unlike God in an evil way, and made himself like him in an evil way. Let us too, brothers, avoid perverse imitation and return to good imitation.

[Col. 1804A]

The second part follows, in which the Apostle shows in what ways we ought to imitate God when he adds: “And walk in love, as Christ also loved us,” and so forth.

In three respects he commands us to imitate God: namely, to do for him what he did for us; to hate what he hates; and to love what he loves.

First, the Apostle exhorts us to do for Christ what he did for us when he said: “Walk in love, as Christ also loved us.” One walks in love who loves and performs works of love. He therefore exhorts us that, just as Christ loved us and, proving this by his deed, gave himself for us, so we too should love him and give ourselves for him.

“He gave himself,” he says, “for us, as an offering and sacrifice to God.” He was an offering when he offered himself to obey the Father for our sake. He was a sacrifice when he gave himself to suffering—and this “for a sweet fragrance,” because in this sacrifice the Father delighted more than in others. Hence he also said of him: “With him I am well pleased” (Matt. XVII).

Let us too, brothers, offer ourselves to the Father for his sake, to obey and suffer for him. And if there is no persecutor who will slaughter us for his sake, let us nevertheless slaughter within ourselves carnal desires and crucify our members with vices and desires (Gal. V), so that our hands may be crucified and no longer be extended to do evil; our feet may be crucified and no longer walk in evil ways; and our body may be crucified and no longer take delight in evil, together with our other members. [Col. 1804C]

Second, the Apostle warns us to hate what God hates when he adds: “Fornication and all uncleanness or avarice must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints.”

Fornication, brothers, means every sexual union of male and female outside legitimate marriage, including simple fornication, adultery, and illicit intercourse. By uncleanness the Apostle means every incestuous, Sodomitic, and bestial intercourse. By avarice he means every disordered desire to acquire or retain beyond measure. As he adds later, this is “the service of idols,” because whatever someone loves and worships more than anything else is his god.

Therefore whoever loves money more than God makes money his god. Whoever worships his belly more than God makes his belly his god. Whoever worships a prostitute more than God makes the prostitute his mistress.

You must avoid these things, my brothers, so that they may not even be named among you, much less be found in you, as is fitting for saints. You must live so holily, chastely, and justly that no one would dare to invent any disgrace concerning you.

And not only must these greater crimes be avoided by us, but also these lesser ones: obscenity, foolish talk, and coarse joking, which have no proper purpose. Let us also beware, brothers, of obscene speech, because we cannot love obscene talk and at the same time hate obscenity itself. For through obscene speech modesty is gradually shaken off; and conversely, speech passes into action if we speak honorably.

[Col. 1805A]

Foolish talk means whatever is said at neither the appropriate time nor the appropriate place nor for a just reason. Coarse joking means whatever is said with a certain urbanity or wit for the purpose of provoking laughter.

We must avoid these and similar things, brothers, because if—as the Lord testifies—we shall have to give an account for every idle word (Matt. XII), what then will be the account for coarse joking? What for slander? What for flattery? What for lying? What for perjury?

“You will destroy,” says the Prophet, “all who speak lies” (Ps. V). And “the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. I).

What kind of speech, then, ought there to be among us? “Thanksgiving,” he says, “blessing, prayer,” and other good words.

Are the things mentioned above to be avoided? Certainly. For—to say nothing of the other lesser matters—know this: no fornicator, unclean person, or avaricious person, who is an idol-worshiper, has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.

Let no one deceive you with empty words, saying either that these things are pardonable or that the impious ought not to be judged. For because of these things anger comes upon the children of distrust—that is, of unbelief—an anger of blindness and rejection.

But you, brothers, do not become partners in their deeds, whether through imitation or consent. For you were once darkness—that is, darkened by vices, as I have said—but now you are light in the Lord, that is, now you have been enlightened in the Lord.

Third, the Apostle warns us to love and do what God loves when he adds: “Walk as children of light.” Since you are children of God, who is light, perform works of light.

Evil works are called works of darkness, both because they lead to eternal darkness and because they blind the mind, and also because the person who does them wishes to remain hidden, according to the saying: “Whoever does evil hates the light” (John III).

Conversely, good works are called works of light, both because they lead to eternal light and because they enlighten a person inwardly, and also because those who do them love the light.

In what works of light consist he shows when he adds: “The fruit of light is in all goodness, justice, and truth.” Goodness is in the mind, justice in action, and truth in speech. In these three, therefore, the whole perfection of holiness is contained.

This is what the Psalmist says: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest upon your holy mountain? The one who walks without blemish and does justice, who speaks truth in his heart,” and so forth.

Therefore, my brothers, let us strive with all desire to imitate the true God and our Father, Jesus Christ. Let us love him as he loved us. Let us hate the obscenities and vices that he hates. Let us love the goodness, justice, and truth that he loves. Let us strive to follow his ways and examples, so that under his guidance and with his help we may deserve to reach him, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever. Amen.

## HOMILY XL. THE THIRD SUNDAY IN LENT
A demon was being cast out by Jesus, and it was mute, etc. (Luke XI). This reading, dearest brothers, ought to be heard by us with all the greater eagerness, the more necessary a remedy it contains for our souls. [Col. 1806A] Let us therefore, brothers, inquire first into what pertains to the historical sense, second into what pertains to the moral sense, and third into what pertains to the allegorical sense.

According to the historical sense, four things must be considered. First, the Lord heals a demoniac; second, he refutes his detractors; third, he shows what happens to the contemptuous; fourth, he corrects a woman who was praising him.

First, then, moved with compassion for the demoniac, the Lord drives out from him the demon who was called mute from its effect, because it made the man mute. Moreover, this demoniac was not only mute but also deaf, as another evangelist testifies [Mark VII]. Thus three miracles were performed by the Lord in one man: the deaf hears, the mute speaks, and the one possessed by a demon is freed; and the crowds marvel at the divine power in Christ.

Second, [Col. 1806B] he refutes and instructs his detractors. Some were speaking against him, namely those who said, “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons,” because they were attributing to the devil what belonged to God; and others who, testing him, were seeking a sign from heaven, because they considered the things the Lord did to be small or nothing and called him powerless to give a sign from heaven.

Here, my brothers, we must consider how great is the wickedness of detractors. Although they are always suspicious and ready to believe every evil, they are always unbelieving toward the good of others, always denying it. Or, if they cannot deny it, they say that it is small or nothing, or they distort the outcome or manner of what was done. But whoever attributes to the devil what belongs solely to the Holy Spirit, as another evangelist testifies, sins against the Holy Spirit and will obtain forgiveness from that sin only with difficulty, or never [Col. 1806C] (Matthew XII). Therefore, brothers, let us strive with every care to avoid the vice of envy and detraction.

But when the Lord, the examiner of hearts, had perceived the evil thoughts of the detractors, he nevertheless did not disdain to refute and instruct them according to his mercy. He refutes them by proving both that what they said was false and that they had said it out of envy.

He proves what they said to be false when he says: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be desolated, and house will fall upon house. And if Satan is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons.” Here the Lord calls Satan’s [Col. 1806D] kingdom that wickedness by which all evil spirits have become so hardened and bound together in conspiracy that they neither wish nor are able to do anything except evil. But if Satan casts out Satan, he does something good, since casting Satan out of a possessed person is certainly good. And if one Satan does evil while another does good, the concord and conspiracy they possessed in evil will not stand—which is plainly false.

He proves that they had said this out of envy when he adds: “And if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out?” As if he were saying: If you attribute the casting out of demons performed by your sons to God and not to the devil, why do you attribute the same deed, when performed by me, to the devil and not to God? You do not speak about me simply, but out of envy. [Col. 1807A] “Therefore,” he says, “they themselves will be your judges.” For they know that neither I nor they cast out demons by Beelzebub, but by the Holy Spirit; therefore they will be judges of your falsehood.

After the Lord had refuted the calumny of the envious, the kindly Lord immediately instructed them, adding: “But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God”—which is certainly true—“then the kingdom of God has surely come upon you,” namely that kingdom of which Isaiah says: “His dominion will be multiplied, and there will be no end of his kingdom” (Isaiah IX). As if the Lord were saying: Since I have now begun to cast demons out of human beings, I have already begun to reign in those human beings, taking away from the devil the kingdom he had usurped and restoring it to myself. You too could share in it if you believed.

He explains how he would take away from the devil [Col. 1807B] the kingdom he had long possessed when he adds: “When a strong armed man guards his courtyard, all that he possesses is at peace. But if one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, he takes away all his armor in which he trusted”—that is, he renders ineffective all his schemes in which he placed his confidence—“and distributes his spoils,” that is, freeing captives, making some apostles, others evangelists, others pastors and teachers (Ephesians IV), etc.

“Whoever is not with me,” he says, “is against me”—that is, whoever does not agree with me in faith and love does not belong to my kingdom but to the kingdom of the adversary. “And whoever does not gather with me scatters”—that is, whoever does not love concord with me loves discord and dispersion with the devil.

Third, the Lord shows what happens to the negligent when he adds: “When the unclean spirit [Col. 1807C] has gone out from a person, it wanders through dry and waterless places, seeking rest, and does not find it.” The devil cannot rest, my brothers, in dry and waterless hearts, because he loves only hearts that are soft, sensual, and flowing. Let us therefore pursue the rigor of justice, the austerity of religion, and the steepness of the virtues, so that the devil may not be able to find rest in us.

“I will return,” he says, “to my house from which I came.” And when it comes, it finds the house empty—namely, empty of good—swept with brooms and adorned. He speaks metaphorically: it finds for itself a house clean and prepared, and it takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself. They enter and dwell there, and the last condition of that person becomes worse than the first. “So,” he says, “will it be for this wicked generation.”

Indeed, because of the law given by the Lord, the devil was first expelled [Col. 1807D] from the Jews and passed to the Gentiles. But afterward, when the Gentiles believed in Christ and he could no longer find a place of rest among them, he returned to the Jews and found in them a house empty of every good, swept clean—that is, apparently cleansed by legal purifications—and adorned, as it were, with simulated virtues. He takes seven other spirits more wicked than himself; they enter and dwell there, and the last condition of that people becomes worse than the first. For the Jews blaspheming in their synagogues are worse than they were when, before the law, they were ignorant of God.

Fourth, the Lord corrects the woman who was praising him—not because she had spoken falsely or with false intention. Blessed—indeed, most blessed—is the womb that bore the Lord, and the breasts that nursed him. But he corrects her reason for saying this [Col. 1808A] with the corrective adverb, “rather.” His mother is not blessed because she bore and nursed him bodily, but, as Elizabeth says: “Blessed is she who believed, because the things said to her by the Lord will be fulfilled.” And as the Lord adds, blessed are Mary and all the others who hear the word of God and keep it.

Morally, brothers, the Lord instructs us in four ways.

First, by showing compassion and casting out demons, he teaches us by his example to do likewise. We ought, brothers, to have great compassion for people ensnared by the devil’s deceit and to free them, insofar as we can, from diabolical servitude by exhortations, threats, promises, and prayers, and win them for the Lord, so that the ear of their heart, previously deaf, may be opened to understand the word of God, and the mouth previously mute may be opened to bless God.

For what greater excellence can there be in a Christian than to imitate Christ’s triumph? Christ, by his own power, bound the armed strong man, shattered hell, and led out and brought back the vessels of captivity. [Col. 1808B] Let us also, brothers, with his help, shatter hell as far as we are able, break the chains of the devil, rescue our brothers as captives from his jaws, and return victoriously to Christ, destined to receive as many crowns as there are people freed from the devil through us.

Next, by showing that Satan always wishes to return to those who have been offered to him, the Lord instills fear in them and teaches the great necessity of vigilance. He is deeply grieved to lose those whom the devil has conquered by tempting them and held as victor for a long time. Hence he arms himself with every deceit and temptation in order to attack them.

Therefore, [Col. 1808C] brothers, you who were long held captive by the devil’s deceits but have now, through God’s mercy, been snatched from the devil’s jaws, keep watch and arm yourselves manfully against his temptations, in accordance with the warning of the Wise Man: “My son, when you approach the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclesiasticus II). For if—God forbid—he should succeed in taking possession of anyone again, he will rage against him with a greater tyranny than before, so that the last condition of that wretched person will be worse than the first.

By answering his detractors, who falsely claimed that he cast out demons by Beelzebub, [Col. 1808D] the Lord also instructs us by his example how we ought to behave toward our detractors and what we ought to say to them. The Lord patiently endured their detraction and did not wish to reproach them with the many vices they possessed; he merely showed that what they had said about him was false. And, more wonderfully still, he preached the word of salvation to them.

Let us likewise, brothers, not be disturbed by the detractions of the envious, nor repay evil for evil or insult for insult (1 Peter III). Rather, with all patience, while showing that the false abuse directed against us is false, let us also strive to instruct them and win them for God.

By answering the woman who praised him, the Lord also demonstrated how we ought to behave toward our praisers and flatterers and what we ought to say to them. He did not praise the woman who praised him, as some customarily do; he was not inwardly delighted [Col. 1809A] by the woman’s praise, as some customarily are; nor did he approve it by remaining silent, as some customarily do. Instead, he corrected her words, as though they were not true.

Some are so vainglorious that they immediately praise those who praise them, returning flattery for flattery. Others, although they say that they are unworthy of praise, nevertheless rejoice inwardly at praise. Others, even if they answer nothing at all, nevertheless consent to the praise by their silence.

Therefore, brothers, following Christ’s example, let us flee human praise. Let us beware of returning praise to our praisers, of rejoicing further in praise, or of consenting to it by silence. If the words of the one praising us are untrue, let us reject them entirely. If they are true, let us correct them, saying such things as, “Do not praise a person during his lifetime,” and in this way let us urge the praiser to praise God, from whom all goodness comes.

Let us avoid with the greatest care [Col. 1809B] the seductive poison of flatterers, which is all the worse the sweeter it is. For while the detractor searches out our vices more carefully, he benefits us in a certain way by bringing our vices back to our memory. But the flatterer, under the appearance of affection, deceives us, so that we believe him about ourselves more than we believe ourselves. Hence Isaiah says: “My people, those who call you blessed are themselves deceiving you” (Isaiah III).

In the mystical sense, the Lord does in many people every day what he is then read to have done literally in one demoniac.

Let us therefore see in whom this occurs, through whom it occurs, and what cleansing, remedy, vigilance, and fortitude they require. There are many today who are possessed by a demon because of [Col. 1809C] the shamefulness of their crimes: one by the spirit of lust, another by the spirit of avarice, another by the spirit of pride. Indeed, insofar as each person is ensnared by vices, he is possessed, as it were, by that many demons.

Since they knowingly serve demons, they are worse than madmen, who do what they do without knowing what they are doing. Thus the strong armed man—that is, the devil—exercises the weapons of his wickedness over them, possessing them in peace, that is, without opposition; making them deaf, so that they do not hear the word of God; and making them mute, so that they do not bless God.

When they are held captive by the devil in this way, they cannot by their own power shake off his yoke. This rightly applies to those who do not wish to repent in their youth but promise that they will repent in old age. Wretched people, who do not consider that neither a person’s life nor his repentance [Col. 1809D] is in his own hand but in God’s hand; and that God sometimes, by a just judgment, takes away from proud sinners the time for repentance.

Let no one therefore suppose that he can shake off the devil’s yoke by himself.
