Let him rely solely on God’s mercy, for God comes upon the devil, conquers him, and removes all his weapons—that is, renders all his schemes ineffective—distributing his vessels, that is, freeing their souls and bodies, senses and limbs, for right thinking, speaking, and acting.

And by what remedy does he do this? By repentance. And what is it to repent? To mourn past evils and not commit again the things that must be mourned.

“For,” as Gregory says, “the one who mourns sins in such a way that he commits others either does not know how to repent or pretends not to. For lamentations are of no benefit if sins are repeated.” And Isidore says: “He is a mocker [Col. 1810A] and not a penitent who does what he regrets; he does not appear humbly to ask God, but proudly to mock him.”

There are therefore two elements in repentance: to mourn what has been done and not to do what must be mourned. These are the action of repentance and perseverance; one without the other is of no benefit. For it is of no benefit to weep if one continues to sin, and it is of little benefit not to sin if one does not weep.

The action of repentance is performed in heart, mouth, and deed: in the heart through contrition, in the mouth through confession, and in deed through satisfaction. Contrition ripens the corruption within; confession opens the wound; satisfaction draws out the poison.

Contrition is sorrow of heart arising from remembrance of sin and fear of judgment. Of it Scripture says: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Psalm L). Three things form contrition: shame, fear, and sorrow. Shame arises when one considers that one has acted shamefully; fear, when one considers that punishment has been prepared for oneself; sorrow, when one sees oneself guilty and deserving of punishment.

Confession, then, is the tearful [Col. 1810B] recounting of sins. Of it Scripture says: “Declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified” (Isaiah XLIII); and again: “I said, ‘I will confess my injustice to the Lord,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (Psalm XXXI).

It must be made with tears. For unless the sinner groans, weeps, and sighs when he confesses that he has sinned, he proclaims his sin rather than confesses it.

Confession must be true and open, complete and undiminished, undivided. It must be true, so that one says what one has done and remains silent about what one has not done. For whoever, out of humility, says that he committed a sin he did not [Col. 1810C] commit, even if he was not previously guilty, then begins to be guilty.

It must be open, so that just as one acted shamefully, one reports the matter shamefully, without covering one’s shame with ornamented words; to do otherwise is to lessen one’s sin.

It must be complete, so that one explains all the circumstances of one’s sins: the place, the time, the person, the manner of sinning, the number of times, the temptation, and the contempt. The same kind of sin is more serious in a sacred place or time than in another, in the case of a wise person than an ignorant one, of a married person than an unmarried one, of an ordained person than a layperson. Likewise, it is more serious if one committed it repeatedly than if once; if one resisted a lesser temptation than if a great one; and if one showed greater contempt than lesser contempt.

It must not be diminished, so that, while confessing one sin, you do not remain silent about another. For it is unjust to hope for half-forgiveness [Col. 1810D] from God, who is supreme justice. What does it profit you to have only one of several deadly wounds healed?

It must not be divided, so that you do not reveal some sins to one priest and others to another. For this tends toward hypocrisy and not toward curing sins but toward increasing them.

Satisfaction is the worthy performance of the work imposed. Of this John the Baptist says: “Produce worthy fruits of repentance” (Matthew III), so that the amount of punishment corresponds to the amount of guilt. Satisfaction must have these three features: one must do what has been imposed, as much as has been imposed, and in the manner in which it has been imposed.

This, brothers, is the remedy by which Christ, who is stronger, drives the strong armed man from our hearts and makes vessels of the Holy Spirit out of the devil’s vessels. But then vigilance and fortitude are necessary.

When the devil sees that he has been expelled, [Col. 1811A] he rages more fiercely, lies in wait for us more intensely, and contrives to return to his place with greater violence. At first, when we have begun to mourn our sins, fast, and do good, he mocks us through the mouths of evil people and calls us hypocrites.

To whom, my brothers, are such people similar except to the Pharisees who said of the Lord, “He casts out demons by the prince of demons”? They attributed what belonged to the Holy Spirit to the devil. Likewise, when these people mock those whom the Holy Spirit cleanses through repentance and call them hypocrites and lovers of empty praise, what else do they do than attribute what belongs to the Holy Spirit to the spirit of hypocrisy and empty glory?

Since both these people and those attribute what belongs to the Holy Spirit to the evil spirit, without doubt they sin against the Holy Spirit. And if we ought to interpret for the good even those things that tend more toward evil, [Col. 1811B] what will become of those who interpret for evil even the things that tend toward good?

Beware, brothers—beware of this sin, for it is exceedingly great. But when you see a sinner turning to God, pray for him, that God may grant him good perseverance.

You also, penitents, do not be ashamed because of mockers or abandon your resolve, for, as Solomon says: “There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings honor and glory” (Ecclesiasticus IV). Be ashamed, then, of what is evil, not of what is good.

When the devil cannot overcome the penitent in this way, he tempts him through flatterers, saying: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts [Col. 1811C] that you sucked.” As if he were saying: You are a holy man, victorious over the devil, and a friend of God—thereby inviting him to pride and empty glory.

But we, brothers, must firmly despise flatterers just as we despise detractors; we must believe more about ourselves than others do about us, and always fear because of our sins: “Who understands his offenses?” (Psalm XVIII). But if we do not understand certain sins of ours, how do we know that they have been forgiven us? Therefore the Wise Man says: “Do not be without fear concerning a forgiven sin” (Ecclesiasticus V).

For where, brothers, there is no fear, there is foolish security. Where there is foolish security, there is contempt. Where there is contempt, there is danger and ruin. For if the devil finds you negligent and empty of good, the devil reenters you with seven other spirits more wicked than himself. Your sins return sevenfold, [Col. 1811D] and you become seven times worse than before.

Sins are said to return in three ways: when we return to our vomit; when, despising the penance imposed, we become sluggish; or when we take pleasure in remembering a past sin.

Let us therefore, brothers, always keep our sins before our eyes, always fear, groan, and weep over them, and redeem them through works of mercy. May God grant this to us, he who lives and reigns in perfect Trinity. Amen.

## HOMILY XLI. THE FOURTH SUNDAY OF LENT

It is written: “Abraham had two sons, one, namely Ishmael, from the slave woman Hagar, and one, namely Isaac, from the free woman, namely Sarah. But the one who was from the slave woman was born according to the flesh”—that is, according to the custom of the flesh, by which a young woman can conceive from an old man and give birth. “But the one who was [Col. 1812A] from the free woman was born through God’s promise” (Galatians IV), not according to the custom of the flesh, since an old and barren woman does not ordinarily conceive and give birth from an aged man.

When both had grown and were playing, Ishmael, the elder by birth, was as though persecuting Isaac. Understanding this, Sarah said to Abraham: “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman will not be heir with the son of the free woman.” Abraham therefore cast out the slave woman with her son, giving her a jar of water upon her shoulder; but he established the son of the free woman as heir (Genesis XXI).

The Apostle explains the mystery of this history to us, dearest brothers, and thereby suggests that the other histories of the Old Testament [Col. 1812B] are also to be understood mystically. We, however, brothers, accommodating ourselves to the understanding of the simple, will explain to you, with God’s generosity, what the Apostle presents more briefly and obscurely, more fully and clearly.

Abraham, then, brothers, signifies God, who is the Father of many nations, indeed of all nations. Thus he had two sons, because he created two peoples from the same mass: one, through hidden justice, he created for dishonor; the other, through his mercy alone, for honor; one for rejection, the other for election.

Four things must be considered here, brothers. First, who the slave woman and who the free woman are, from whom these two peoples were born. Second, how the slave woman is said to have been fertile and to have given birth first, while the free woman was initially barren and gave birth afterward. [Col. 1812C] Third, how the son of the slave woman persecutes the son of the free woman. Fourth, how the slave woman with her son and the jar of water is cast out, while the son of the free woman is established as heir.

The slave woman, then, brothers, [Col. 1812D] from whom the rejected people was born, is the flesh. She is called a slave because she is enslaved to sin, the devil, and eternal misery. “Whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John VIII). From this slave woman, that is, from the flesh, the rejected people is born according to the flesh, that is, according to carnal desire.

As it was born, so it remains: it perceives only the flesh, lives according to the flesh, and sows in the flesh, from which it will also reap corruption. “The works of the flesh,” the Apostle says, “are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, wantonness, the worship of idols” (Galatians V), etc.

The free woman, from whom the chosen people was born, is heavenly grace. She is called free because she frees a person from slavery to sin, the devil, and eternal condemnation. “If the Son,” he says, “sets you free, you will truly be free” (John VIII).

From this free woman, that is, from grace, a person is born not according to the flesh but according to the promise, that is, according to God’s election. This birth takes place in baptism, in which the one who was born from the flesh as a son of wrath is reborn from grace through the Spirit as a son of mercy.

For the Lord gave them, according to the Gospel, power to become sons of God—to those who believe in his name—who were born not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of a man, but from God (John I), that is, who were reborn. [Col. 1813A]

That people, therefore, was born from the flesh according to the flesh; this people was born from grace according to election. The former is the son of the slave woman, that is, of carnal servitude; the latter is the son of the free woman, that is, of spiritual freedom. The former is the son of the devil; the latter, the Son of God. The former is the son of the Old Testament, where people serve out of fear and for temporal things; the latter is the son of the New Testament, where people serve out of love and for eternal things. Yet to serve God is to reign.

We, therefore, brothers, are sons of the free woman, sons of election, and sons of God, provided that we persevere in the grace of baptism; provided that we utterly detest the devil and his works, which we renounced; and provided that we love and follow God and his commandments with complete devotion.

But if we have broken the covenant of baptism and returned to the devil’s service, what will become of us wretched people except that we should seek, while it is permitted, to be reconciled as quickly as possible through repentance and tears?

Second, brothers, we must consider how the slave woman is said to have been fertile and to have given birth first, while the free woman was initially barren and gave birth afterward.

Carnal generation first multiplied abundantly in the world, when people who were ignorant of God and of spiritual life devoted themselves only to the propagation and succession of the flesh. Spiritual regeneration remained long unknown and barren. It bore abundant fruit only in the time of grace.

For, as the Apostle says, “the spiritual is not first, but the natural, and afterward the spiritual” (1 Corinthians XV). Hence Isaiah: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not give birth”—that is, who at first gave birth to none or few—“break forth and cry out, you who do not labor in childbirth, because the children of the free woman are more numerous”—understand, more numerous because chosen by God—“than the children of her who has a husband” [Note: [Col. 1813D] The Vulgate has the same passage, but not precisely in the same words] (Isaiah LIV), that is, of the devil, the corruptor.

We, therefore, brothers, should seek spiritual rather than carnal succession. It is better to leave behind one good son than many bad ones, and it is better to die without children than to leave behind a bad son.

Those who have children should be vigilant in correcting and instructing them, because just as a wise son is the joy of his parents, so a foolish son is the shame and curse of his parents (Proverbs X, XV).

Those who lack children should not grieve, but should establish Christ as their heir, adopt the poor and orphans as children, and beget spiritual children by example and [Col. 1813D] word, so that it may rightly be said of them: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not give birth; break forth and cry out, you who do not labor in childbirth, because the children of the free woman are many, more than those of her who has a husband” (Galatians IV).

For the wickedness of carnal children has grown so greatly today, brothers, that one is a fornicator, another a gambler, another a thief, another a robber, and another seeks and desires the death of his parents. Thus it may truly be said today: “Blessed are the barren women who did not give birth, and the breasts that did not nurse” (Luke XXIII).

Third, brothers, we must consider how, as the Apostle says, the sons of the slave woman persecute the sons of the free woman. The sons of the flesh persecute the sons of the spirit, the sons of the world the sons of heaven.

How? In three ways: by evil example, by crafty suggestion, and by open persecution.

By evil example, when they flourish and prosper in their evil way, [Col. 1814A] for their sons are “like new plantings in their youth.” Their daughters are adorned and beautified like the likeness of a temple. Their storehouses are full, overflowing from one thing to another. Their sheep are fertile and abundant in their offspring; their oxen are fat. There is no breach in the wall, no passage through it, and no cry in their streets (Psalm CXLIII).

But David arms us against these things, saying: “Do not be envious of the wicked, nor jealous of those who do iniquity, for they will quickly wither like grass” (Psalm XXXVI).

They persecute by crafty suggestion when they say: “The world has always existed; people have always been born and died. Who has returned from the underworld [Col. 1814B] to announce that there is another life? It is foolish to lose present joys because of things that perhaps will never exist.”

Thus, brothers, the son of the slave woman wishes to deceive the son of the free woman. He lies in wait in order to seize the poor person; he seizes the poor person when he draws him in by crafty suggestion (Psalm X).

Against these things the Apostle arms us: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Corinthians XV). Therefore, “do not believe every spirit” (1 John IV).

Our faith is founded upon the testimonies of the patriarchs and prophets; it is completed in Christ’s birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension; it is supported by the testimonies of the apostles and strengthened by the blood of the martyrs, who prove by miracles that they live better after death.

They persecute by open persecution when they strip [Col. 1814C] the sons of the free woman, assail them with insults, and afflict them with injuries, exile, tortures, and death, according to the saying: “The saints experienced mockeries and scourging, and moreover chains and prisons. They were stoned, they were sawn apart, they were tempted; they died by the killing of the sword” (Hebrews XI).

Against this the Lord arms us, saying: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matthew X). And elsewhere: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of justice, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew V).

Fourth, brothers, we must consider how the slave woman and her son are cast out with the jar of water, while the son of the free woman is established as heir.

The sons of the slave woman, because they desire and embrace only an earthly inheritance [Col. 1814D], are separated from the heavenly inheritance by divine judgment. Nothing is granted to them except a jar of water upon the shoulder.

Water, my brothers, is worldly happiness. Water is flowing, drinkable, and navigable. Worldly happiness is likewise flowing, because it quickly passes and does not return; it is drinkable, that is, suitable for use, if taken in moderation, but if taken excessively it inflates a person and kills him; it is navigable, because with sound governance one can pass through it to the harbor of salvation, whereas in its abundance one is submerged and perishes.

The son of the slave woman receives this worldly happiness upon himself because he serves it, rather than it serving him. In the other life he will be entirely separated [Col. 1815A] from the heavenly inheritance, receiving nothing except eternal condemnation, because in this life he received his good things.

But the chosen people, who is the son of the free woman, is established as heir of the Father—now through election, and in the future through confirmation: now of spiritual goods, and in the future of heavenly rewards.

Therefore we, brothers, set free by Christ’s blood, are no longer sons of the slave woman but of the free woman, provided that we live not according to the flesh but according to the spirit; provided that we love God and not the world; provided that we desire heavenly things and not earthly things; and provided that, fleeing the slavery of vices, we pursue the freedom of virtues.

In the future we shall receive an eternal inheritance, incorruptible and undefiled, kept in heaven, so that we may indeed be heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans [Col. 1815B] VIII). For to us who are placed at his right hand it will be said: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV).

May Jesus Christ our Lord grant us both to merit and to obtain this inheritance, he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God. Amen.

## HOMILY XLII. THE FOURTH SUNDAY OF LENT
Jesus crossed to the other side of the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias; and a great multitude followed him, because they saw the signs that he performed (John VI), and so forth.

In this reading from the holy Gospel, dearest brothers, which we have just heard, let us consider first what pertains to the literal sense, second what pertains to the tropological sense, and third what pertains to the mystical sense.

As regards the literal sense, then, my brothers, our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ shows in this reading that he possesses true humanity and true divinity. He shows that he possesses true humanity and compassion when he has pity on the sick and hungry and accommodates himself to them. He demonstrates that he possesses true divinity when he heals the sick by a mere sign and when, from five loaves and two fish, he satisfies five thousand people, with even twelve baskets of fragments being gathered up. My brothers, would it not have been a great and divine miracle if he had satisfied five thousand people with five loaves, leaving nothing over? Yet how much more wondrous and worthy of God does the miracle appear when five thousand people are satisfied from five loaves [Col. 1815D] and, in addition, ten times more is gathered up than had been set out. It is as though the Lord did not perform the same miracle every day when he multiplies a few grains of seed cast into the earth a hundredfold. But no one marvels at what he sees every day; the rarity of an event, however, produces greater wonder.

Moreover, the fact that the Lord is here said to have tested Philip is not contrary to what James says: “God tests no one” (James I). For testing occurs in three ways. God tests in one way, the devil in another, and a human being in another. God tests in order to prove, as when he tested Abraham in order to prove his faith (Genesis XXII), and here Philip in order to demonstrate his weakness. The devil tests in order to deceive; God tests no one with this kind of testing. A human being tests in order to learn what he does not know.

According to the tropological sense, when Christ does this, he shows what Christians ought to do. Eight things are therefore set before us here for imitation: crossing the sea; ascending the mountain; compassion; the rejection of human testing; to whom and what alms we should give; how and for what purpose we should give them; how alms are multiplied; and how great a glory comes to God from them.

Thus, my brothers, when the Lord crossed the Sea of Galilee, he admonishes us to cross, through desire, the stormy sea of this world and to sigh for our heavenly homeland. For this world is, for the righteous who long for the life to come, an exile, a stormy sea, and a valley of tears. Hence they long to cross over quickly and for another life to arrive. Therefore the Psalmist says: “Woe is me, Lord, for my sojourning has been prolonged” (Psalm CXIX). For just as the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God (Psalm XLI). The same writer says elsewhere:

> Those who sow in tears shall reap in exultation.  
> Going forth they went and wept, casting their seeds;  
> but coming they shall come with exultation,  
> carrying their sheaves (Psalm CXXV).

Worldly people, however, who regard this world as their homeland and spend their days here in prosperity, would never wish to pass from the present life. Yet whether they wish it or not, they pass away and are snatched toward death. Even so, they cling in mind to things that are passing, like someone swept away by a torrent who clings to thorns and rough branches.

Therefore, brothers, let us pass over by desire to the heavenly life, and let us send there, through whatever works of mercy we can perform, whatever we are able to send. Let our treasure and our heart be there. Let us draw our neighbors there with us by good example and exhortation, by promises and love, so that, just as a great multitude followed the Lord, so a great multitude may follow us. This will happen everywhere if they see us perform signs upon those who are infirm.

We perform signs upon the infirm if we visit the physically sick with acts of kindness; if we strengthen those who are sick in mind; if we rebuke those who are sick through sin; if we patiently endure those who are frenzied with hatred or injuries against us; or if we cure all the sick of this world before God through our prayers.

When the Lord ascends the mountain and sits there with his disciples, he admonishes us to ascend from virtue to virtue, even to the height of virtue [Col. 1816D] and contemplation. There, amid the misery of this world, we possess, as far as we can, sitting and rest with the Lord and his saints. For such people the feast day of the Jews, Passover, is near. Those who rest with the Lord and his saints through contemplation are already near, in love, hope, and merit, to the true feast day of the confessing angels.

When the Lord, sitting on the mountain, accommodates himself to the lower crowds who are hungry and has compassion on them, he teaches us that we should rest through contemplation in heavenly things in such a way that we accommodate ourselves through compassion to the lower crowds, in accordance with what the Lord himself says: “Be merciful, just as your heavenly Father is merciful” (Luke VI).

Let us put on, brothers, the entrails of mercy and compassion [Col. 1817A], and whenever we see someone suffering, let us suffer with him. When we see someone grieving, let us grieve with him. When we see someone in need, let us help him as far as we can. For “blessed are the merciful, because they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew XXV). Conversely: “Judgment without mercy will be shown to the one who has not shown mercy” (James II).

When the Lord rebukes his disciples, still inexperienced, by testing them concerning human need, he teaches us to overcome human testing as far as we can. The disciples endured this human testing when, doubting whether there would be enough bread, one said: “Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for them, so that each might receive even a little.” Another said: “There is one boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are these among so many?” (John VI.)

Brothers, we too suffer this testing when, seeing a multitude of poor people, we complain that we have only a little grain in the granary and a little bread in the chest, and say: “Go your way. What I have would not be enough for me and for you.” We also suffer human testing when, seeing that provisions are expensive and crops are failing, we say: “What shall we eat, what shall we drink, or with what shall we clothe ourselves?” (Matthew VI.) This is undoubtedly human testing, my brothers, and it arises from imperfection of faith.

Therefore the Lord can say to us: “Why are you timid, you of little faith?” (Matthew VIII.) For if we had firm faith and charity in God, we would certainly believe that nothing would be lacking to us, since the Lord provides for his own [Col. 1817C], and he does not cease to provide even for unbelievers. We read that the Lord sustained his servants without food for many days. We also read that Saint Nicholas fed sixty people with three loaves. We read the same about many others.

I have seen, brothers, many charitable people give abundantly every day, and God supply them abundantly, so that they seemed almost to be competing with one another: the righteous person by distributing, and the Lord by providing.

The Lord shows chiefly to whom gifts should be given when he feeds the multitude that followed him. For by God’s command he shows that what is given should be given to those who follow him. Yet elsewhere the Lord says: “Give to everyone who asks you” (Luke VI). This appears contrary to the saying of the Wise Man: “Do good to the just, and do not give to the ungodly” [Col. 1817D] (Ecclesiasticus XII). And also: “Look to whom you give.”

It is not contrary, brothers. We ought, if we can, to do good to everyone in need—not sustaining his ungodliness, but sustaining his nature. If, however, we cannot give to everyone, we ought to give to the faithful, to the poor, and to the more righteous, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “While we have opportunity, let us do good to all, but especially to those who are of the household of faith” (Galatians VI).

The Lord shows what should be given and to whom by giving health to the sick, bread to the hungry, instruction to the ignorant, and freedom to captives. When the Lord says, “Give to everyone who asks you,” he does not say, “Give what he asks for,” but “Give what you can and what you see that he lacks.” Give the poor bodily sustenance; give the rich the word of God, the sustenance of the soul. Give advice to the uninstructed. To the laboring person, if you can do nothing else, give the assistance of prayer [Col. 1818A]. For a word of counsel, a word of correction, and a word of prayer are great gifts.

Since the soul is more precious than the body, the benefit done to the soul is more precious than that done to the body. The Lord shows how and for what purpose alms should be given: he first gave thanks and then distributed. Therefore, when we give, let us always give thanks to God, from whom every good thing comes, and let us distribute for his sake, according to what the Apostle says: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians IV). And elsewhere: “He who gives, with simplicity” (Romans XII).

For if we consider the matter carefully, our alms are not our merit but God’s grace. We have the very thing we give not from ourselves but from God; nor can we possess the good will or extend our hand to give from ourselves, but from God. “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Romans IX).

What, then, comes from us? Just as we have received the whole of our alms from God, so let us direct the whole of them toward him. Let us not give in order to escape the annoyance of one who lacks, for whoever does this loses both the merit and the thing itself. Let us not give for empty glory, since whoever does this receives his reward here. Let not the left hand give—that is, let not a temporal intention give. Let not the right and left hand give together—that is, let empty glory not mingle with alms given for God’s sake, but let the right hand alone give, with the left hand unaware.

How alms are multiplied is shown by the fact that five thousand people are satisfied from five loaves and twelve baskets are gathered up. Alms are multiplied in us in two ways: spiritually and eternally.

They are multiplied spiritually when, for example, we preach the word of life to others. The word is not diminished but rather increased both in us and in them, like several lamps lit from one lamp. Even if we give a passing material possession, although it passes to the recipient, it is nevertheless multiplied in us when faith, hope, charity, and the other virtues are increased in us by God through it.

Alms are multiplied eternally when a heavenly reward is received for an earthly one, an eternal reward for a passing one, and an incorruptible reward for a corruptible one, so that the saying may be fulfilled: “You who have followed me shall receive a hundredfold in this life, and in the future eternal life” (Matthew XIX).

Almsgiving is therefore valuable both according to the person for whom it is done and according to the person to whom it is done. Even if it does not benefit them, the one who does it well cannot fail to benefit. What greater multiplication could there be, brothers, than when one person, for the sake of two small coins (Luke XXI), another for a cup of cold water (Matthew X), and another for nothing but good will, will receive the kingdom of heaven?

How great a glory follows from almsgiving is shown when the text continues:

> When the crowds saw the sign that he had performed, they said: “This is truly the Prophet who is to come into the world.”

God, the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation (2 Corinthians XIII), who opens his hand and fills every living creature with blessing (Psalm CXLIV), must always be blessed for almsgiving.

But we, brothers, who are not the authors of almsgiving but merely its ministers, should neither wish nor permit thanks to be given to us along with it. Rather, let us say: “We are useless servants; we have done what we were obliged to do” (Luke XVII). We distribute not what is ours but what belongs to another. Nevertheless, when we do this, we will not be without glory before God, who counts the deeds of his own people as deeds done to himself. He will say:

> Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; and so forth (Matthew XXV).

According to the mystical sense, Jesus crossed the Sea of Galilee when, by suffering and rising again, he passed through the tribulations of this world. A great multitude followed him in faith and love, seeing the signs that he performed, either personally or through his disciples, upon those who were sick in mind or body [Col. 1819B].

Jesus ascended the mountain—that is, to the height of eternal glorification. There he sat, rested, and reigned, and the disciples were with him in mind, though not yet in body.

The Passover, the feast day of the Jews, was near. “Passover” is interpreted as “passing over.” The Passover was therefore near, the feast day of the Jews, because, with the Gospel already shining forth, the passing over and cessation of the old ceremonies was imminent.

When Jesus therefore raised the eyes of his mercy and saw that a very great multitude had come to him in belief, he said, inspiring him, to Philip—that is, to any preacher, for “Philip” is interpreted as “mouth of a lamp”—“Where shall we buy bread, so that these people may eat?” That is: From where shall we acquire wisdom and the teaching of the Word, by which the people of God may be refreshed?

He said this to test him. For he himself knew what he was going to do. This testing, brothers, frequently tests us by God’s permission when, seeing a multitude of believers gathered into the church, we doubt within ourselves and ask: “From which book shall I prepare today’s sermon? From where shall I refresh the people of God?” We forget what the Lord promised his own and what he would do through us.

For he says: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm VIII). And in the Gospel: “When you stand before kings and governors, do not consider how or what you will speak; for what you are to say will be given to you in that hour” (Matthew X; Mark XIII).

Therefore, brothers, always mindful of this promise of the Lord and placing our confidence in God’s grace, not in our own ingenuity [Col. 1819D], let us speak the word of God boldly to the people, because “the Lord will give the word to those who preach the Gospel with great power” (Psalm LXVII).

I certainly remember that at times I spoke better to the people when I spoke without preparation than when I spoke after preparation, the Lord bringing this about.

Let us suppose that we are capable of thinking something from ourselves, as though from ourselves. “Two hundred denarii worth of bread,” he says, “would not be enough for them”—that is, the teaching of two hundred preachers would not be enough to instruct the faithful people who follow God, so that each might receive even a little.

“There is one boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish.” This boy is Moses, the servant of God, who possesses the five books of the Law. These are aptly signified by barley loaves. Barley is covered by extremely tenacious chaff and is food for beasts of burden. The Law, too, is concealed beneath extremely tenacious coverings of figures and words, and, understood literally, is food for simple and animal-like people.

If it is understood more subtly, it contains two fish with it—that is, the moral and mystical senses, by whose sweetness the aridity of the Law is enriched.

Jesus therefore took the five loaves, blessed them, and broke them. Because he showed that the five books of Moses were fulfilled in him and were holy, he broke them and gave them, together with the two fish, to the disciples to set before the crowds. He opened the meaning of the Law to them so that they might preach it to the crowds together with its moral and mystical senses.

In the fact that the disciples set no other bread before the crowds except what had been handed down by Christ [Col. 1820B], and that they themselves do not break that bread but Christ breaks it for them, those are confounded who preach another Scripture than the divine one, or who do not wait for the Scripture itself to be broken and opened to them by God, but presume to break it open for themselves. They set things before others rather than explaining them, although the Lord commands the prophet: “You shall announce to them from me” (Ezekiel III).

They are satisfied from the five loaves together with the two fish—that is, from the five books of Moses with their mystical and moral meaning. The five thousand people signify the simple, who at first know only those things subject to the five bodily senses.

The baskets are filled with the fragments and crusts left over by those who have eaten, because the subtler and more profound teachings, which simple people cannot grasp, are reserved for apostolic and more perfect men to chew over [Col. 1820C]. As the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Corinthians III). “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Corinthians II).

This is also directed against those who speak higher things to simple people, not educating them but rather confusing them.

People, seeing that divine teaching overflows in all things and that the more widely it is received, the more abundantly it increases, praise and bless the Lord, who refreshes his people daily with spiritual bread and sustains them with that prophecy until they reach the promised land. May the almighty and merciful God lead us there, he who lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity. Amen.

# HOMILY XLIII. THE FIFTH SUNDAY OF LENT

> Christ, appearing as high priest of the good things to come, through a greater and more perfect tabernacle not made with hands, that is, not of this creation, and so forth (Hebrews IX).

In this reading, my brothers, the Apostle shows that Christ’s priesthood was prefigured in the priesthood of the Law, that the former was imperfect as a figure and shadow, while the latter is perfect as the reality and truth; that the former passes away, while the latter remains.

Four things, therefore, must be considered, my brothers, concerning the high priest of the Law: what he ought to be like; where he ought to stand; whose minister he ought to be; and what he ought to do according to the Law.

The legal high priest was required to be without blemish, sound, and whole. Without blemish, so that he would not have a small, large, or crooked nose; so that he would not be hunchbacked, bleary-eyed, or have a white film over his eye, a skin disease on his body, or a persistent scab. Whole, so that he would not be blind, maimed, or without genitals, or have anything of that kind. Sound, so that he would not be lame, have a broken foot or hand, be leprous, or be burdened by excessive weight.

These qualities existed figuratively in the legal high priest; in Christ they exist in truth. Christ was an unblemished lamb, for, as Peter says, “he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Peter II). He was also “beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Psalm XLIV).

He was whole, possessing in himself the perfection of every virtue; for, as John says, he was “full of grace and truth” (John I). He was also sound and perfect in all wisdom and knowledge, because in Christ “all the treasures of God’s wisdom and knowledge are hidden” (Colossians II).

Where did the legal high priest stand? In the middle—that is, between humanity and God. He stood before human beings; hence he was called “antistes,” one who stands before. He stood before God; hence he was called “bishop,” that is, overseer. Therefore the Apostle says: “Every high priest taken from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings in matters pertaining to God” (Hebrews V).

He was required to stand in the middle of the extremes by participation, affection, and order. By participation in the extremes, since by nature he was human with human beings and, by grace, divine with God. In the middle by affection, so that he would be near sinners through compassion and near God through familiarity. In the middle by order, so that through him human beings might have access to God, and God to human beings.

Christ, too, was the middle and true high priest, standing before God and before human beings. He was in the middle between God and humanity by nature, because he was truly human with human beings and truly God with God. He was in the middle by affection, because through compassion he suffered with human beings. Hence the Apostle says: “We do not have a high priest who cannot have compassion on our weaknesses” (Hebrews IV). Through love he was also one with God the Father.

He was in the middle by order, because through him we have access to God the Father, and through him God the Father is reconciled to us, and we to him. Hence Paul calls him the mediator of the New Testament (Hebrews IX).

Whose minister was the legal high priest? He was the minister of temporal and carnal sacraments, and only their minister, not their helper. Christ, however, is the high priest of the good things to come—that is, of the spiritual and heavenly goods signified beforehand by the legal figures. Christ is not merely their minister; rather, he is their author and giver. He baptizes; he washes away sins; he grants virtues; he bestows rewards.

What did the legal high priest do? Once a year, in the seventh month, namely on the feast of Atonement, he sacrificed. Clothed in priestly garments and carrying blood, he entered the Holy of Holies, and the interior was sprinkled with sacrificial blood so that God might be reconciled to his people.

So also the High Priest of high priests, the Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 1822A], sacrificed himself once in time for the salvation of the world. Rising again and clothed in the robe of immortality, he entered not only heaven but also the heaven of heavens—the tabernacle, greater in capacity and more perfect in perpetuity. There, seated at the right hand of the Father, he sprinkles the interior and exterior with his blood: that is, through his passion he reconciles heavenly things to earthly things and earthly things to heavenly things, God to humanity and humanity to God.

The Apostle therefore assigns the difference between the legal high priest and the evangelical high priest, Christ, in five matters, and in all of them demonstrates Christ’s superiority. The former entered a tabernacle made with hands; the latter entered one not made with hands. The former entered once a year; the latter once in time. The former died and another succeeded him; the latter remains a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek (Psalm CIX) [Col. 1822B].

Hence the same Apostle says: “Many were made priests according to the Law, because they were prevented by death from continuing. But Jesus, because he remains forever, holds an everlasting priesthood” (Hebrews VII).

The former entered with another’s blood; the latter with his own. The former interceded for his own sins and those of others; the latter, since he is free from sin, intercedes only for the sins of others. Hence the same Apostle says: “Such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens. He has no need, like the other priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people” (ibid.).

For, the Apostle says, “if the blood of goats and calves, or the ashes of a heifer, sanctifies those defiled by contact with the dead [Note: [Col. 1821D] The Vulgate omits ‘by contact with the dead’], according to the legal observance [Note: [Col. 1821D] The Vulgate omits ‘also according to the legal observance’], for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ cleanse our consciences from dead works to serve the living God?”

Truly, brothers, the blood of animals did not literally cleanse, because it did not prefigure the flesh, blood, or soul of Christ, through whom all cleansing is accomplished. Therefore the blood of Christ, dearest brothers, will cleanse us from all sins, provided that we truly believe in him, truly hope in him, and follow his footsteps. For, as Peter says, “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps” (1 Peter II).

He humbled himself for us, so that we would not fear being humbled for his sake. He became poor for us, so that we would not fear becoming poor for his sake. He died for us, so that we would not fear dying for his sake. He rose for us, so that through him we might rise. He ascended into heaven so that through him we might ascend into heaven.

Therefore, brothers, if we wish to be exalted with him, let us humble ourselves with him. If we wish to become rich with him, let us be poor with him and for him. If we wish to rise with him, let us die with him and for him—if not in the flesh, at least in the mind.

Let carnal desires, vices, and sins be crucified and die within us. Let spiritual virtues, good morals, and good works rise and grow within us, so that we may be able both to celebrate and to imitate purely the passion and resurrection of Christ, by the gift of him who suffered for us, our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY XLIV. THE FIFTH SUNDAY OF LENT

> Jesus said to the crowds of Jews and to the chief priests: “Which of you will convict me of sin?” and so forth (John VIII).

Our Lord and Redeemer, dearest brothers, just as he did not come for himself but for us, so what he fought and what he conquered, he fought and conquered not for himself but for us.

For just as the devil had been accustomed to attack and conquer human beings, so Christ wished to be attacked by him and to conquer him. The devil had been accustomed to attack human beings in two ways: first, by subtle temptation, and second, by open persecution. If he did not overcome a person in the first way, he attacked him in the second manner of combat.

When, therefore, the devil first attacked the Lord by subtle suggestion, attempting to deceive him through gluttony, empty glory, or pride, and was overcome by him, he afterward attacked him through open persecution, so that the one whom flattering words had not conquered might be conquered by harsh treatment.

Since persecution inflicted by relatives and intimates usually disturbs a person more, the devil persecuted Christ through the Jews, his fellow tribesmen and relatives, and also through a disciple who was his companion and intimate. Hence Christ says through the Prophet:

> My friends and neighbors approached and stood against me (Psalm XXXVII).

And elsewhere:

> If my enemy had cursed me, I would surely have endured it.  
> And if the one who hated me had spoken great things against me,  
> I might perhaps have hidden myself from him.  
> But you, a man of one mind with me,  
> my leader and my acquaintance,  
> who together with me used to take sweet food (Psalm LIV).

And elsewhere:

> The man of my peace, in whom I trusted,  
> who ate my bread,  
> has magnified his treachery against me (Psalm XL).

Those people, therefore, instigated by the devil, persecuted Christ with a retaliation worse than any other. Christ, however, answered them with a retaliation better than any other.

There are four kinds of retaliation: returning good for evil; returning good for good; returning evil for evil; and returning evil for good. The first belongs entirely to the good. The two middle ones belong in moderate measure to the good and in moderate measure to the wicked. The fourth belongs entirely to the wicked. The first belongs to Christ and his members; the last belongs to the devil and his members.

Since Christ loved the Jews and offered them true teaching and eternal life, they, on the contrary, returned hatred for love, a curse for a blessing, and death for life. Hence he says through the Prophet: “They repaid me evil for good, and hatred for my love” (Psalm CVIII). And elsewhere: “Those who repay evil for good slandered me” (Psalm XXXVII). And why? “Because I pursued goodness” (ibid.).

Thus, when the Jews persecuted Christ in this way, he showed them mercy and gentleness in all things, so that they would have no excuse for their unbelief, and so that by his example we might be instructed in how we ought to endure our enemies.

There are therefore four things to consider, my brothers, in this reading. First, how the Lord offers reconciliation and peace to his enemies. Second, how he responds to the insults of those who revile him. Third, how the envious corrupt words of truth. Fourth, how Christ yields to the injuries of his persecutors.

First, the Lord offers reconciliation and peace to his enemies when he says: “Which of you will convict me of sin?” It is as though he were saying: “My people, what have I done to you? Or in what have I troubled you? Answer me, and if you have anything against me, speak.”

The one who asks in what he has caused harm, my brothers, is seeking satisfaction and reconciliation. “If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me?” It is as though he were saying: “If I do nothing evil but very much good for you, why do you not love me? If I say nothing false but always speak the truth to you and on your behalf, why do you not believe me?”

In this he instructs us to maintain peace and reconciliation with those who envy us, hate us, and persecute us, asking them in what we have harmed them. If we have harmed them in some respect, let us make satisfaction to them with humility. If we have harmed them in nothing, let us offer them love and service, and show that we both desire and seek their good.

If they listen to us, we will have won our brothers. This is undoubtedly a matter of great merit before God.

Let us not be, brothers, among those who consider it shameful to humble themselves before their enemies and seek their peace, magnifying the injuries inflicted upon them and minimizing those they have inflicted—especially when the King of kings and Lord of lords sought peace with wicked servants and humbled himself before them.

When they despised the good of peace, he said to them: “Whoever is of God hears the words of God; therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God.”

We too, brothers, may say to our enemies who reject and spit upon our peace and satisfaction: “Whoever is of God hears the words of peace; but whoever does not wish to hear the word of peace is not of God.” For where there is peace, there is God. He himself testifies: “Blessed are the peacemakers, because they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew V).

Since the one who is of God hears the words of God, let each one of us, my brothers, question himself whether he hears the words of God with the mouth of his heart—that is, whether he retains them, acts upon them, and perseveres in them—and thereby know with certainty whether he is of God.

[Col. 1824D] The second part follows, in which Christ responds graciously to the insults of the Jews. For the Jews, having been made worse by the peace and correction that had been offered, replied with an insult. “Are we not right,” they said, “in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” Alas, how perversely they spoke! Thus, my brothers, thus the wicked always treat the good: they return a curse for a blessing, an insult for correction. But let us hear how gently the Lord answers them: “I do not have a demon,” he says. Two charges had been brought against him: he denies the one, that he has a demon; the other, by keeping silent, he concedes—namely, that he is a Samaritan, for *Samaritan* is interpreted as “guardian.” The Lord, moreover, is the guardian of his elect, who “will neither slumber nor sleep” (Ps. 120).

[Col. 1825A] Although he could truthfully have answered them, “It is not I, but you who have a demon,” he did not wish to do so, lest he seem to return insult for insult. In this, my brothers, he taught us by his example not to reproach someone with his vice when provoked by an insulting person. For whoever, out of anger and revenge, charges another with his crime—even if the charge is true—does not state it truthfully, that is, with a straightforward intention, and therefore cannot be called truthful but rather false. Whoever wishes to correct another concerning his vice ought to rebuke him privately and with good zeal.

The Lord proves that he does not have a demon by what he adds: “But I honor my Father,” attributing everything he does to him and seeking his glory in all things. It belongs to the devil and his members always to seek their own glory, not God’s, [Col. 1825B] and to arrogate divine authority to themselves. Therefore, whoever seeks God’s glory in all things shows that he does not have a demon and is not its member. “And you,” he says, “have dishonored me,” thereby showing that it is rather you who have a demon. “But I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks and judges,” that is, assigns it. For God’s judgment is just: whoever seeks not his own glory but God’s will be glorified by God. Conversely, whoever seeks his own glory rather than God’s may ever be without glory before God.

Here, my brothers, let us learn always to seek God’s glory, not our own, in all things; then God will seek and assign to us his everlasting glory.

The Lord not only does not return insult to those who insult him, but even offers them teaching, instructing us that we should not be disturbed from the tranquillity of our mind by any insult; rather, preserving charity and meekness unshaken, we should offer correction and instruction even to those who inflict insults upon us. He therefore says: “Amen, amen, I say to you: if anyone keeps my word, he shall never see death.”

But just as good people become better when they receive an insult, so, conversely, evil people become worse when they receive teaching. Hence it is added: The Jews answered him, “Now we know that you have a demon.” This is the third part, in which the malicious Jews perversely distort the Lord’s good words when they add: “Abraham and the prophets died, and you say: ‘If anyone keeps my word, he shall never see death.’”

Thus, my brothers, malicious people are accustomed to distort the sayings of the righteous and to interpret for the worse what has been well said with a good intention, either by expounding it badly or by altering certain words. For when the Lord said, “If anyone keeps my word, he shall never see death,” he meant spiritual or eternal death. There are three kinds of death: bodily death, which occurs through the separation of soul and body; spiritual death, which occurs through sin, which separates the soul from God; and eternal death, namely eternal punishment, which will torment soul and body together. It is called death because it would be better to die every day than to endure that eternal punishment. Therefore, although the Lord was speaking of spiritual or eternal death, they distorted his words by interpreting them of bodily death.

“Are you,” they say, “whose word, that is, makes people immortal, greater than our father Abraham, who died, and the prophets who died?”—with the implied qualification that their word makes neither them nor others immortal. As though they said: “No.” Envy, my brothers, blinded the Jews, as it always blinds people, so that they cannot form a right judgment of the person whom they envy. Although they had heard and seen the Lord perform miracles which neither Abraham nor any prophet had performed—giving eyes to one born blind, raising one dead four days, commanding winds and sea, and walking upon the waves—they nevertheless preferred Abraham and the prophets to him, for no other reason than that they envied him, because they had seen him small, born of a poor mother, and growing through the ages.

People today resemble them who despise their contemporaries and coevals, however good they may be, and maintain that they cannot equal those of earlier times, although the supreme Author can work equal goods in every age. “Whom do you make yourself?” He makes himself great who falsely attributes to himself a power which he does not possess, as hypocrites do.

Therefore the Lord shows both that he does not glorify himself and that he has true glorification from the Father when he answers: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me,” etc. Whoever glorifies himself, my brothers, seeks his own glory, not God’s; assuredly such a person’s glory is nothing. Christ, however, did not glorify himself, because in all things he sought not his own glory but the Father’s; and therefore he deserved to be glorified by him. Hence he adds: “It is my Father who glorifies me.” Let us also learn, brothers, in every good thing that we think, say, or do, to seek not our own glory but God’s, so that we may deserve to be glorified by him.

“Whom you,” he says, “claim to be your God, but you have not known him.” They did not know God the Father because they did not believe that he had a Son. For whoever is ignorant of the Son is also ignorant of God the Father, and by his wicked works demonstrates that he does not know him. Sadly, many false Christians today are like them: they say of God that he is their God, and yet they have not known him, since by their wicked works they show that they are ignorant of God’s will.

Because the Jews had opposed the Lord’s statement that whoever kept his word would never see death, by saying that Abraham was dead, the Lord shows that Abraham was not dead, but rather lived and rejoiced in faith in his coming, when he says: “Abraham your father rejoiced”—that is, “he eagerly awaited seeing my day,” that is, my coming. “He saw it”—that is, he recognized that the one whom he believed would come had come—“and rejoiced.”

But the carnal Jews, understanding the statement as referring to physical sight, reply: “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” Jesus answered them: “Amen, amen, I say to you: before Abraham came to be, I am.”

The Jews understood Christ as a mere human being, and by these words [Col. 1827A] he revealed his divinity to them. Thus, speaking of Abraham, he said “came to be,” but of himself he said “I am.” Abraham came to be as a creature; Christ, however, was begotten eternally from the Father, not made. His unchangeable essence is appropriately expressed by the substantive verb in the present tense. Hence he himself said to Moses: “I am who I am.”

But the Jews, according to their custom returning evil for good, took up stones to throw at him.

The fourth part follows when it is added: “But Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.” This shows how the Lord yielded to the injuries of his persecutors. Yet since he could have destroyed them with a mere gesture, why did he choose to flee and hide? For three reasons.

First, to demonstrate through his fear of death that he truly possessed human nature, although his fear in this case arose from his will, not from necessity. Second, to show by his example what he had taught the disciples in words: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another.” It was necessary for preachers sometimes to flee and hide, lest, once the preachers had been removed, the Gospel be silenced. Third, to give us an example: if at some time we could prevail over our persecutors in an argument, we should nevertheless yield and hide out of humility when they provoke us, so that we might care both for the salvation of those who provoke us and for our own.

Among Christians, the strong person is not the one who strikes forcefully, but the one who yields forcefully. For, as Solomon testifies, “one who conquers anger is stronger than one who conquers a city.”

But Christ himself, who now fled and hid, when he wished, offered himself to his persecutors to be crucified. He not only endured them courageously, but also mercifully prayed for them, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

Let us therefore imitate Christ our Redeemer: offering peace to our enemies in place of hatred; returning good for evil and blessing for cursing; yielding even to the injuries of the weak; courageously enduring death when necessary; and interceding for our persecutors, so that, by his favor, we may deserve to become participants in Christ’s resurrection and glory—he who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

# HOMILY XLV. PALM SUNDAY

[Col. 1827D] “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, although he was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God” (Phil. 2), etc.

In this reading, dearly beloved brothers, the Apostle exhorts us to follow the path that Christ followed. Christ followed humility, obedience, and patience; and for this reason he was exalted and was given the name that is above every name. Just as the first man followed pride, disobedience, and impatience, so for this reason he was cast down.

Since the ruin of the human race was brought about through these three vices, it was necessary that it be restored through three virtues opposed to those vices. In the first man, pride had four forms.

First, he wished to make himself equal to his superior when, through robbery, he considered himself equal to God; this is properly arrogance. Second, he wished to exalt himself above his equal, namely the angel; this is properly pride. Third, he wished to live according to his own law, not God’s; this is properly presumption. Fourth, he attempted to defend his sin; this is properly obstinacy.

In these things, my brothers, we too imitate the old Adam: when we strive to make ourselves equal to our superiors; when we continually exalt ourselves above our equals; when we wish to do our own will rather than God’s; or when we defend or excuse our sins.

To destroy this fourfold pride, Christ, by descending, displayed in himself a fourfold humility.

First, as this reading shows, he did not consider himself equal to God by robbery. What he possessed by nature, he did not presume to seize by robbery. Second, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and was made lower not only than those equal to him—namely, the Father and the Holy Spirit—but also than those beneath him, namely the angels, becoming lower than they (Heb. 1). Accordingly, the Prophet says to the Father concerning him: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8). He was also subject to human beings, such as Mary and Joseph (Luke 2); he even paid tribute to Caesar (Matt. 17) and washed the feet of his servants (John 13).

Third, in all things he sought to do the Father’s will, not his own. Hence he says: “I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6). [Col. 1828C] Fourth, although he had no sins of his own, he bore the sins of others. Hence Peter says: “He himself bore our sins upon the tree” (1 Pet. 2). The same writer says: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? The words of my offenses are far from my salvation” (Ps. 21; Mark 15), calling our offenses his own.

Therefore, my brothers, let us imitate not the old man Adam but Christ, the new man. Let us humble ourselves not only before our elders but also before our equals and inferiors. Let us seek to do not our own will but God’s. Let us take care to bear not only the burden of our own sins but also the burdens of others, by making satisfaction and praying for them.

There was also disobedience in Adam, because he refused to obey his Creator for his own good, while he obeyed the devil, his enemy, to his own harm. By contrast, Christ, as it says here, became obedient to the Father unto death, and this for the redemption of the human race, not for his own sake; he did not obey the devil to his own downfall.

Adam refused to obey God in the lightest matters, while Christ obeyed the Father in the most difficult. Adam refused to obey God either because of threats or because of rewards; Christ obeyed the Father, led by a spontaneous will. Adam refused to obey God so that he might live by abstaining from the tree; Christ obeyed the Father so that he might die, suspended upon the tree. Because Adam was disobedient, he lost the dominion he had over every earthly creature; because Christ was obedient, all power in heaven and on earth was given to him.

Let us therefore flee, brothers, the disobedience of the old man, lest we be excluded [Col. 1829A] from the inheritance of our heavenly homeland; let us imitate the obedience of the new man, Christ, so that with him we may deserve to be glorified.

Obedience is so necessary that no good can benefit without it, and no evil can harm when accompanied by obedience. Although eating an apple is a good thing, it became evil through disobedience—so great an evil that it expelled not only its author Adam but also all his descendants from paradise (Gen. 3).

Although sacrificing to God and mercifully sparing the defeated are also good things, Saul sinned gravely by doing these things against obedience. Hence Samuel said to him: “Obedience is better than sacrifices” (1 Sam. 15).

Conversely, although stealing or taking the property of one’s neighbors is evil, the Israelites did not sin when they stripped the Egyptians of their goods, because they did this in obedience; rather, they earned merit. Again, although taking a prostitute as a wife and begetting children of fornication is a grave offense, the prophet who did this at God’s command did not sin but rather earned favor.

How great a good obedience is is also shown by many miracles of the saints. For when Maurus ran at the command of his father Benedict to rescue the boy Placidius from the water, he is said to have walked upon the waters. Another man, leaping into a burning furnace at the command of his abbot, is said to have emerged unburned.

Let us therefore love obedience in all things, brothers: obeying God in everything, and obeying our superiors in all matters that are not contrary to God. Let us know that what appears in itself useless and idle becomes useful and meritorious if it is done in obedience.

There was also impatience in Adam, because he refused to endure God’s very gentle yoke so that, while living, he might avoid death. In Christ, by contrast, there was supreme patience, because he bore the Father’s harsh command so that, by dying, he might restore the dead to life.

Adam could not endure what was very easy for his own sake; Christ endured what was very difficult for the sake of others. Adam could not endure abstaining from the tree; Christ endured dying upon the tree.

What death could be more cruel, shameful, and prolonged? His patience was therefore greater, more abject, and more enduring. A cruel death is to be killed not quickly but slowly. A shameful death is to be counted among the wicked. A prolonged death is to be dissolved through extended torment.

The wicked suffered with him, but in different ways. The thief on the left suffered for his sin but was not corrected; rather, he reviled him and became still worse. The thief on the right also suffered for his sin, but he was corrected, prayed for himself, and was saved. Christ, however, suffered not for his own sins but for those of others; he prayed for his enemies, and his power was glorified more and more.

These three signify three kinds of sufferers. The thief on the left signifies those who, though scourged for their sins, are not corrected but murmur and are condemned still more. The thief on the right signifies those who, though scourged for their sins, are corrected, give thanks, and are saved. Christ signifies the innocent, who patiently endure undeserved scourging, give thanks, and pray for their enemies, and thereby shine ever more brightly.

Since Christ was thus humble, obedient, and patient, he was exalted to the right hand of the Father and was given the name that is above every name, so that he might be one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit. He is said to have been given this because what he possessed by nature insofar as he was God became his by grace insofar as he was human.

“So that at the name of Jesus every knee may bend”—that is, every power, heavenly, earthly, and infernal—“and every tongue”—that is, every kind of speech—“may confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.”

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, if we desire to attain God’s glory, let us follow his way. Let us humble ourselves, obey, and suffer. Whoever is proud, disobedient, and impatient does not walk the way of Christ but the way of the devil, and therefore will be cast down and condemned with him.

Whenever we seek to be exalted in this world rather than humbled, to command rather than obey, and to prosper in worldly pleasures rather than endure correction, we do not understand the things of God but the things of the devil.

Let us therefore humble ourselves not only before our elders but also before our equals and inferiors. Let us obey God and our superiors, not out of fear or for hire, but out of love. Let us endure scourges and tribulations with an even spirit. And if we are not as innocent as Christ, let us nevertheless say that, like the thief on the right, we suffer these things for our sins, giving thanks and praying for our persecutors, so that these very sufferings may be purifying and beneficial to us, and that with the thief we may deserve to enter paradise.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

# HOMILY XLVI. PALM SUNDAY

“When Jesus drew near Jerusalem and came to Bethphage at the Mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples,” etc. (Matt. 21.)

In this reading of the holy Gospel, dearly beloved brothers, we must consider first what pertains to the historical sense and second what pertains to the mystical sense. According to the historical sense, five points must be noted.

First, why did the Lord, who had previously hidden himself, wish, as his passion approached, to draw openly near the very place where he was to suffer? He did this to demonstrate that, when the time came, he would willingly undergo his passion. When he hid, he gave the imperfect an example of hiding; when he went to meet death, he gave the perfect an example of going to meet death. When he hid, he did what belonged to the flesh; when he went to meet death, he did what belonged to the spirit. Accordingly, he himself says: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26).

Likewise, when he said, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (ibid.), he spoke according to his humanity. But when he said, “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down myself” (John 10), he spoke according to his divinity. Thus, my brothers, Christ expressed in himself the true nature of flesh and spirit, of man and God. Nevertheless, he preferred the will of the spirit to the will of the flesh, and the divine will to the human.

Therefore, when according to his humanity he had said, “Let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26), he immediately showed that the divine will must be preferred to it when he added: “Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will” (ibid.).

We too, brothers, whenever out of the weakness of the flesh we desire something, should immediately correct ourselves by Christ’s example and subject our will to the divine will, saying: “Nevertheless, Lord, let not our will but yours be done.”

Second, we must consider why the Lord was accustomed to send two disciples to preach, to seek lodging, to bring the donkey, or to undertake anything else. There were two reasons: in two persons are displayed the testimony of truth and the example of charity.

The testimony of truth, because “upon the testimony of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Deut. 19). The example of charity, because the love of charity is demonstrated no less between two people. Hence he says: “I command you this, that you love one another.”

Two, therefore, are sent so that, with harmonious word and example, they may preach truth and charity. When we, brothers, agree with one another in truth and charity, we show that we are Christ’s disciples. But when—God forbid—we disagree in truth and charity, we show that we are disciples not of Christ but rather of the devil.

Third, we must consider how God shows that he possesses true divinity in that he narrates future events as though they were present and demonstrates that he foreknows human hearts. To know future things as though they were present and to foreknow human hearts belong to divinity alone.

He shows that he knows future things as though they were present when he says: “You will find a donkey tied and a colt with it.” He demonstrates that he foreknows human hearts when he adds: “And if anyone says anything to you, say, ‘The Lord has need of them,’ and immediately he will let them go.” For he not only knows human hearts but also inclines them wherever he wills. For it is written of him: “He changes the hearts of kings” (Prov. 21).

Let us therefore pray to him, brothers, that he himself may change our hearts for the better and incline them to follow his will.

Fourth, since the Lord was always accustomed to travel on foot, we must consider why on this occasion he sought a vehicle. He did this because the time had approached when he himself was to be exalted. Hence, as his passion drew near, he said: “Father, glorify your name. The hour has come for your Son to be glorified” (John 17). And the Father said: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again” (ibid.).

As his passion approached, he began to perform greater works, to preach more openly and more profoundly, to rebuke the Jews more sharply, and to lead more people with him. As his passion drew near, he raised a man who had been dead four days (John 12), openly proclaimed his divinity, came to Jerusalem seated upon a donkey, and was received with honor by the people (Matt. 21). The praises of the people, whom previously he had commanded to be silent, he now did not reject but rather said: “If these are silent, the stones will cry out” (Luke 19).

But, my brothers, Christ’s exaltation, because it was founded upon humility, will stand forever. He sought not his own glory but the Father’s. He ascended not upon the horse of pride but upon the donkey of humility. He was received with praise not by flatterers but by simple people who do not know how to flatter.

Those who wish to be exalted before they know how to humble themselves are confounded by this, since it is written: “Humility precedes glory” (Prov. 15). Those who seek their own glory rather than God’s are also confounded—those who ride ostentatiously upon ornamented horses and desire praise from flatterers.

Fifth, my brothers, we must consider the harmony and simultaneous fulfillment of the Old and New Law. The taking of the paschal lamb on the tenth day of the month and its sacrifice on the fourteenth, according to what is written—“On the tenth day of this month each man shall take a lamb, and it shall be kept until the fourteenth day; then it shall be sacrificed in the evening” (Exod. 12)—was fulfilled in him.

For Christ came to Jerusalem on the tenth day, that is, today, and on the fourteenth day, in the evening, he was arrested and led to sacrifice. The prophecy of Zechariah, namely, “Do not fear, daughter of Zion, because your king comes to you, gentle, seated upon a donkey’s colt” (Zech. 9), was fulfilled in him. The praise of the children, according to what is written, “You have perfected praise from the mouth of infants and nursing children” (Ps. 8), was fulfilled in Christ.

That very praise was taken from the Psalm. Where we say, “O Lord, save me” (*salvum me fac*), Hebrew has *Hosanna*, “prosper well,” [Col. 1832C] “blessed is he who is to come in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 117). The dense growth of palms and branches, concerning which the Psalm says, “Establish the feast day amid dense foliage” (ibid.), was fulfilled in Christ today.

Mystically, my brothers, the Lord came to the Mount of Olives—that is, to the height of mercy—when, through the flesh, he drew near to redeem Jerusalem. From there he sent two orders of preachers: one to bring the Jewish people through faith, the other to bring the people of the Gentiles.

The donkey is a tame, irrational, laborious animal devoted to usefulness. God seeks people who are tame, foolish in the world’s eyes, laborious, and devoted to the usefulness of their neighbors.

The she-donkey, therefore, which was under the yoke and was a mother, signifies the Jewish people, which was under the yoke of the Law and was the mother of the peoples of the Gentiles through faith. The free and wanton colt signifies the people of the Gentiles, which was without the Law and unrestrained in sinning.

The apostles place their garments upon both when they burden and honor them with evangelical teachings, so that the Lord may sit upon them and, governing them, lead them to the heavenly Jerusalem.

Those who practice the active life spread their garments along the road when, stripping themselves of temporal possessions, they spend them in the service of Christ and his members. Preachers cut branches from trees and spread them along the road when they select blossoms from books of moral teachings and display them along the way before the members of Christ.

The contemplatives cry, “Hosanna in the highest,” when they devote themselves to divine praises and prayers. And not only the contemplatives individually, but also the crowds generally—those who went before and those who followed—cried “Hosanna,” because all who preceded Christ’s coming and all who follow it are saved through faith in and confession of the Lord’s Incarnation.

Moreover, not only contemplatives but also active workers and teachers ought frequently to devote themselves to divine praises and prayers.

These three kinds of people are signified by Noah, Daniel, and Job, whom the prophet says alone will be delivered. Noah signifies rulers; Daniel, contemplatives and the chaste; Job, active people and the married. Therefore, brothers, only those who have followed the life of these men will be saved.

Whoever is a ruler should govern himself and others well, instruct them by word and example, and set before them the flowers of moral teachings so that they may be nourished by them. Whoever is contemplative should devote himself to divine praise and prayer, and should not lead a life of idleness and laziness; the freer he is from the world, the more intent he should be upon divine things. Let him smell and taste in the way the sweetness and pleasantness that are in the homeland.

Whoever is active and married should so conduct his external affairs that he does not forget the inner life; he should pass through the world without forgetting God. Let him spend his clothing and temporal goods for the use of the poor and the members of Christ. Let him offer hospitality to travelers, clothe the naked, redeem captives, visit the sick, support the poor, defend widows and orphans, keep his wife and children well disciplined and his household unstained, and know how, in the use of worldly things, to seek and gain Christ.

Thus, brothers, living with Christ, we shall be able to enter the heavenly Jerusalem and live with him forever, by the favor of him who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God forever. Amen.

# HOMILY XLVII. THE LORD’S SUPPER
