“When you come together in one place, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s Supper” (1 Cor. 11), etc.

This reading, dearly beloved brothers, we ought to hear with all the greater attention because it contains the sacrament of our salvation, which is so necessary. This reading has four parts. In the first, the Apostle reproves the Corinthians for their abuse of the sacrament of the altar. In the second, he transmits the form of that sacrament. In the third, [Col. 1833D] he shows how we ought to approach it. In the fourth, he shows what those who approach unworthily deserve.

The Apostle therefore first shows the Corinthians’ abuse of this sacrament when he says: “When you come together in one place, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s Supper.”

The Corinthians were sinning either because they approached this sacrament after having eaten, or because in this sacrament they sought bodily rather than spiritual satiety, or because, when offering their offerings, they did not share them with those who offered nothing.

The Corinthians sinned in approaching the Eucharist after having eaten. We ought not to approach any sacrament, and still less the sacrament of the Eucharist, which is greater and more worthy than the others, after having eaten, but rather fasting and sober, unless the necessity of illness compels us. The Lord transmitted this sacrament while dining in order to pass from the figurative Passover to the true Passover and to show that the former signified the latter.

They also sinned by seeking bodily rather than spiritual satiety in this sacrament. Although the taste of bread and wine remains in this sacrament, it is spiritual food, not bodily food. The person who seeks bodily satiety in this sacrament is not spiritual but carnal.

They also sinned by not sharing their offerings with those who offered nothing. For whoever offered less to God thereby lost his own right, and the sacraments of the Church belong not only to the rich but rather are common to everyone. This also stands against those who, because they have given something to the Church, wish to possess a privilege above others.

Hence this sacrament is specifically called the sacrament of communion. All the faithful ought to share in this sacrament—in the communion of the sacrament, of faith, and of charity. It profits false Christians nothing to share in the sacrament with the faithful when they do not share their faith. Again, it profits evil Christians nothing to share the sacrament and faith with the good when they do not share charity with them.

This communion is signified by the sacrament. Just as many grains are joined together in the making of one bread, so many Christians are gathered into the unity of the Church through faith and charity. Hence the Apostle says: “For we are many, one bread in Christ” [Note: [Col. 1833D] The Vulgate does not have *in Christ*.] (1 Cor. 10).

To share in the body and blood of Christ is nothing other than to belong to the unity of Christ and the Church. Hence the Lord says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me and I in him” (John 6).

But, as the Apostle says, when you come together in one place in body alone, not in charity, it is not to eat the Lord’s Supper. For each person takes his own supper—that is, his own offering, which ought to have been shared with everyone—and presumes to consume it, that is, takes it beforehand to eat by himself alone: “One is hungry, another is drunk.”

Some religious today are like these, my brothers: although they have offered themselves and their possessions to God as a holocaust, they nevertheless appropriate common goods again, and each presumes to possess his own supper and his own clothing. “One is hungry, another is drunk”: one is covered with two garments, another is cold.

But plainly, when you come together in this way, it is not to eat the Lord’s Supper.

We too, brothers—something I cannot say without groaning—seem like these people. Although we come together with the poor in one Church, in one faith, and participate in the same sacraments, each of us who possesses temporal goods more abundantly presumes to eat his own luxurious supper and to wear his own change of clothing, while the poor perish from hunger and cold.

But plainly, when you come together in this way, it is not to eat the Lord’s Supper.

Therefore, my brothers, in order that we may be able to eat the Lord’s Supper worthily, let us share our food with those who share the same sacraments with us. Let us share our clothing with those who will share eternal things with us.

“Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink?” He says this not because those who feast luxuriously in their homes are thereby excusable if they become hard-hearted and unwilling to share with the poor, but because luxuries do not torment poor people who are absent as much as they torment poor people who are present.

For delicacies seen by the needy torment them greatly, arousing envy, desire, and shame. This is why Lazarus, in his poverty, was greatly tempted—and therefore proved—by seeing the delicacies of the rich man dressed in purple. Yet the rich man himself is even less excusable because, seeing the poor man’s need every day, he was moved by no kindness.

“Or do you despise the Church?” Whoever presumes to scandalize God’s poor—who are certainly members of God’s Church—through his delicacies despises the Church of God. Whoever, although he has a house in which to eat, eats bodily food in the Church also despises the Church of God. For the Church is a place not of bodily but of spiritual nourishment.

“And do you shame those who have nothing?” As though he were saying: If you are so inhuman that you are unwilling to share your food with those who have none, then at least eat it away from the sight of the poor, so that you do not inflict shame and temptation upon those who are present. For if you eat in the sight of the poor without giving them anything, you sin in two ways.

The second part follows, in which the Apostle hands down the form of this sacrament, saying: “For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you.” As if he were saying: You ought to observe the form of the sacrament that was handed down all the more reverently because it was delivered not by a human being, but by God himself.

“For our Lord Jesus Christ, on the night in which he was betrayed,” etc. The Lord delivered this sacrament last, with his Passion impending, to show that it was to be recalled more dearly and memorably in remembrance of his death. He delivered it at night to show that, amid the miseries and ignorances of worldly life, it would be a support for the faithful. [Col. 1835D]

“He took bread and, giving thanks, blessed it, broke it, and said: ‘This is my body, which will be handed over for you; do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: ‘This cup is the New Testament,’ that is, the ratifier of the New Testament, ‘in my blood. Do this whenever you drink it in remembrance of me.’”

According to the literal sense, my brothers, this is the form of words which, when the priest pronounces it, the invisible Priest changes the visible bread into his body. Moreover, when the Lord commanded that these things be done in his memory, he spoke according to the custom of a friend speaking to his friend, who leaves him some memorial of their mutual love. Thus, “having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (John XIII), giving them, in remembrance of his love, something that would be for them not only a memorial but also comfort and consolation. [Col. 1836A]

It is a consolation for them because, while the saints in this valley of tears sigh toward God, they are in some manner consoled when they receive him in the sacrament as though visibly. It is also for their strengthening, since they are strengthened by it as by viaticum amid the labors of this age, and are spiritually refreshed lest they fail. Hence the Lord says: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John VI).

It is also a memorial for them, since this sacrament not only recalls Christ to our memory but also represents his Passion to us expressively. [Col. 1836B] Hence the Apostle adds: “For whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you will proclaim the death of the Lord,” that is, you will represent it. For when the priest raises the host and impresses upon it the sign of the cross, he represents Christ’s elevation upon the cross. The placing of the wine or bread in the chalice represents Christ’s burial. The wrapping of the altar linens around the chalice represents the wrapping of the shroud around the body.

Mystically, the Lord took bread when, in his own person, he assumed human nature. He gave thanks when, by obeying God the Father in the humanity he had assumed, he gave thanks. He blessed it when he filled his body with every grace and blessing. He broke it when, exposing it to the Passion, he separated his soul from his body. [Col. 1836C] He gave his body to his disciples not only as viaticum in the sacrament, but also as the price of redemption on the way, intending to give it as the reward of recompense in the homeland.

“Do this in remembrance of me”: just as I give and lay down myself for you, so also give yourselves for me and for your brothers.

Morally, when the Lord did this, he demonstrated what we ought to do. “He took bread and gave thanks,” showing that whenever we receive bread or any other food, we should give thanks to God the giver, receiving both great things and small things gladly and with thanksgiving, so that with the Apostle we may know both how to abound and how to suffer want (Philippians VI).

He also blessed the bread, instructing us that whenever we take bread, wine, or other foods, we should bless them beforehand. This is the office of the priest, if he is present; otherwise, of the deacon or subdeacon. If they are not present, the head of the household—or, in his absence, the mother of the household—ought to bless the meal. [Col. 1836D]

The Lord also broke the bread and gave it to his disciples, teaching us to break our bread for the hungry—not only bodily bread but also spiritual bread—according to what is written: “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house” (Isaiah LVIII). Let us not be among those of whom it is said: “The children asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lamentations IV).

“This is my body, which will be handed over for you; do this in remembrance of me.” By this he instructs us that, remembering his example, we too should hand over not only what is ours but also our own bodies to our neighbors. [Col. 1837A]

The third part follows, in which it is shown how one ought to approach the sacrament of the altar, when it is added: “Therefore, whoever eats this bread and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord,” that is, he will receive it not for merit but for guilt.

“But let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of the cup.” Let him examine himself—that is, let him judge, scrutinize, and amend his entire life, all his thoughts, all his offenses and deeds, summoning them to judgment, so that whatever he sees to be defective in himself he may cast away. Whatever he sees to be lacking in himself, let him acquire; whatever is uncultivated, let him cultivate; whatever is pure, let him purify more fully.

Let him avoid, as far as he can, not only mortal sins but also all venial sins. [Col. 1837B] Let him also abstain from certain intermediate and imperfect goods: even from the embrace of a lawful wife, even from the business of just legal cases, even from the just recovery of debts. Let him extend himself, as far as he can, toward perfect and very great goods: toward loving an enemy, forgiving injuries inflicted upon him, and doing good to persecutors.

Thus cleansed and purified, he will be able to approach the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood worthily.

The fourth part follows, in which it is shown what one who approaches the sacrament of the altar unworthily deserves, when it is added: “For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.” He eats and drinks unworthily who approaches either unbelieving, unclean, under an interdict, or without contrition. Such a person eats and drinks judgment upon himself—that is, by eating and drinking in this manner, he acquires punishment for himself. What is best in itself becomes evil for one who approaches unworthily. [Col. 1837C]

“Not discerning the body of the Lord,” that is, not distinguishing it from ordinary foods. He therefore receives judgment upon himself because, just as he approaches bodily food, so he approaches the Lord’s body without devotion and reverence.

And because many who approach unworthily acquire judgment—that is, punishment—for themselves, “there are among you many who are weak,” with some brief illness, namely those who sin less in this matter; “and many who are sick,” with prolonged suffering, namely those who sin more in this matter; “and many sleep,” with bodily death, namely those who sin greatly in this matter. Of these it should be understood that, if they repent worthily of having received the Lord’s body unworthily, that very death becomes for them a purifying punishment for their sin. [Col. 1837D]

“But if we judged ourselves,” he says, “we would certainly not be judged.” My brothers, we judge ourselves when we accuse, condemn, and punish ourselves for our sins. Therefore, let our conscience accuse our sins inwardly; let our memory bear witness against us; let our reason declare us guilty and deserving of punishment. Let a vehement fear of Gehenna, like a severe torturer, punish us within, and let it draw tears from the soul’s contrition as though they were blood.

For if, my brothers, we judged ourselves in this manner, we would certainly not be judged—that is, punished—by God, either by eternal punishment or even by temporal punishment, which is often inflicted upon us for contempt of repentance. [Col. 1838A] When we excuse ourselves, God accuses us; when we judge ourselves, God absolves and justifies us; and when we justify ourselves, God judges us.

It is better for us to be judged by God in this age than in the future. Hence he also adds: “But when we are judged”—that is, when we are scourged here—“we are chastened by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned eternally with this perverse world.”

Therefore, my brothers, let us kindly endure God’s scourges here as those of a loving father, and let us give him thanks for our scourges. For he punishes briefly in this life so that he may not punish us eternally in the life to come. To him be praise throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLVIII. ON THE LORD’S SUPPER

[Col. 1838B]

“Before the feast day of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them to the end” (John XIII).

My dearest brothers, this Gospel reading has three parts. In the first, it is shown that, with his Passion impending, the Lord displayed a greater sign of his love. In the second, it is shown in what way. In the third, the reason why he did this is demonstrated.

The evangelist therefore says: “Before the feast day of Passover,” namely, the Passover on which he was to be crucified, “Jesus, knowing that his hour had come”—an hour not of necessity but of his own will—“to pass from this world to the Father.” In these words it is shown why the feast is called Passover. Passover is a Hebrew name and is derived from “passing over.” For at this feast the children of Israel, through the sacrifice of the lamb, passed from Egypt to the promised land. [Col. 1838C] Christ too, through his blood, passed from this world to heaven.

We too, my brothers, if we truly wish to celebrate Passover, must desire to pass from Egypt to the promised land, from the world to heaven, and from vices to virtues. And, as the Law says, we must eat the flesh of the lamb in haste, so that, as pilgrims, we may hasten to pass from the exile of this world to the heavenly homeland.

“Having loved,” he says, “his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.” At the end he displayed to them a greater sign of love. For, about to depart from them, he showed them a greater tenderness of love so that he might impress the memory of himself more firmly upon their minds: he gave them the mysteries of his body and blood, commanded them to do this in remembrance of him, washed their feet, and consoled them, saying: “I will not leave you orphans; I will go and come to you” (John XIV). [Col. 1838D] He also promised to send them the Holy Spirit, and so forth.

We too, brothers, following the example of our Lord and Teacher, when we are about to depart from those with whom we have had a long association, ought at the end to show them greater love, so that we may leave them an example of true love and impress our love and memory more firmly upon their minds.

The second part follows, in which it is shown in what way the Lord displayed greater love to his own, when it is added: “And when supper had been served, the devil having already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him,” etc.

The Lord, my dearest brothers, left us an example of marvelous patience in this: he endured his betrayer so patiently, excluding him neither from his company, nor from the table, nor from the kiss. [Col. 1839A] We too, brothers, following our Master, should show patience toward our enemies, sharing with them our love, temporal goods, and piety, so that we may thus be able to incline their souls toward love.

This concerns those who cannot endure human nature, much less human malice. For, to say nothing of enemies, if a wife, friend, companion, or member of the household is somewhat angry, dull, or slow, they immediately scold, ridicule, or insult them. But whoever behaves in this way bears witness by his own impatience that he himself is blameworthy.

It must not be done so, brothers. If Christ, pure and holy, patiently endured his betrayer, will you, a sinner, not endure a sinner? If Christ endured an enemy, will you not endure a friend? Therefore, let us patiently endure the faults of our family members and neighbors. Let us conceal them openly and correct them privately. [Col. 1839B]

But when he says, “When the devil had put it into his heart,” this should not be understood, my dearest brothers, as though the devil were thought to insert or create thoughts in human hearts. The devil is not the author of thoughts but their suggester. He can persuade, but he cannot forcibly implant them. It lies within a person’s power to consent or not to consent. Hence the Lord says to Cain: “Your desire will be in your power, and you will rule over it” (Genesis IV).

This concerns those who, whenever they have committed some crime, say that the devil made them do it and attribute the fault to the devil while wishing to excuse themselves. In this they accuse themselves even more and increase their sin. For they consented willingly to the devil and are justly to be punished with him. [Col. 1839C]

“Knowing,” he says, “that the Father had given all things into his hands”—heavenly, earthly, and infernal things; the good and the wicked: the former for salvation, the latter for judgment; the former for election, the latter for rejection. And because he was powerful and Lord of all, he humbled himself to the feet of servants, according to the saying: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” (Ecclesiasticus III). And also: “Let the greater become as the lesser, and the leader as the one who serves” (Luke XII). [Col. 1839D]

“And because,” he says, “he had come from God and was going to God,” he therefore wished to leave his own a good example of going to God. “He rises from supper, lays aside his garments, and, having taken a linen cloth, girds himself.” After distributing the food of life, as Lord he gives an example of humility, becoming like a servant.

So also should every spiritual teacher act. After sitting as a teacher, instructing and correcting, let him rise and gird himself to serve as a humble minister. This is directed against certain prelates of the holy Church who always wish to sit and rule but refuse to rise to serve and humble themselves.

He therefore lays aside his garments, girds himself with a linen cloth, and pours water into a basin. The Lord performs the office of an alert and devoted servant, giving the example that one who serves should serve alertly and devotedly. [Col. 1840A] For the more prompt and devout someone is in service, the greater is his merit. “Cursed is he who performs the work of God negligently” (Jeremiah XLVIII).

Mystically, by the fact that the Lord himself supplies the water, washes the disciples’ feet, and wipes them, he demonstrates that he alone is able to provide human beings with the washing of contrition and tears; he alone is able to cleanse and wipe away the filth of our affections. No one is clean who has not been washed by him. Hence he later answers Peter: “If I do not wash you, you have no part with me.”

He therefore comes first to Simon Peter, showing that the first portions should be given to the first, and that no one in this age is so perfect that he has nothing requiring washing. [Col. 1840B]

When Peter sees the divine Majesty bending down to wash his feet, it is no wonder that he is astonished and recoils. But when he hears that, unless he is washed by him, he will be alienated from him, he consents.

We too, brothers, should decline out of humility if a person of higher rank humbles himself to serve us. But if he persists out of charity, let us consent, lest by refusing we be found guilty of hindering the fulfillment of a divine command.

Moreover, when Peter hears that through the washing of his feet he will have a share with the Lord, and wishes to have an even greater share with him, he desires to be washed entirely by him, saying: “Lord, not only my feet, but also my hands and my head”—that is, my mind and my activity.

But the Lord, who knows a person better than the person knows himself, says that he has no need except to have his feet washed: [Col. 1840C] “The one who has been washed needs only to wash his feet.” That is, whoever has been cleansed of mortal sins needs only to be washed of venial sins, without which the present life is not lived.

By the feet are signified the affections with which we go to perform a deed. Since our affections cannot touch earthly things while we are in this world, they nevertheless gather from them some dust—that is, the filth of venial sin—which must daily be cleansed through confession, prayer, almsgiving, and other good works.

For this reason the Lord commanded the apostles to shake the dust from their feet as a testimony against those who refused to believe them (Matthew X). Whatever stain of venial sin they had contracted in the care and preaching they had undertaken to convert those people would be shaken off against those for whose sake it had been contracted. [Col. 1840D]

“And you are clean,” he says, “but not all.” He refers to the one who was unclean without naming him, so that the person who was marked might blush and be converted. In this he gave an example to the teachers of the holy Church: when someone’s crime is hidden, they should not accuse him publicly, but should refer to it generally and without naming him, so that, recognizing himself as indicated, he may fear and be converted.

The third part follows, in which the reason for the deed is demonstrated, when it is added: “After he had washed their feet, he took his garments, and when he had reclined again, he said to them,” etc.

After the supreme Teacher had bent down from the dignity of the chair for the sake of displaying humility, he returned again to the office of the chair. [Col. 1841A] Imitating him, the teachers of the holy Church, when they have bent down toward their subjects for the sake of humility and example, should return again to the height and office of the chair, so that from humility they may gain the love and imitation of their subjects, and from the dignity of the chair, reverence and fear.

For if they are always bent down, they are loved by their subjects but not feared. If they are always raised up, they are feared but not loved, whereas a prelate ought to be both feared and loved.

“Do you know what I have done for you?”—that is, for what reason I have done this for you. “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am.” He alone is truly Teacher who teaches not externally but inwardly. Unless he teaches within, the tongue of the teacher labors outside in vain. Hence he says: “Do not be called teachers, because your one Teacher is Christ” [Col. 1841B] (Matthew XXIII).

He alone is also universally and always Lord. Hence it is said: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians IV). The others are not lords but should be called, in a diminutive form, *domni*.

“Therefore, if I, Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.” This is an argument from the greater. If the lord has washed the feet of the servant, how much more ought a servant to wash the feet of a fellow servant? If the teacher has washed the feet of the disciple, how much more ought a disciple to wash the feet of a fellow disciple? If God, who has no need, wished to humble himself for the sake of humanity, how much more ought a human being, who does have need, to humble himself for his own sake?

“He gave you an example, so that just as I have done for you, you also may do.” He gave an example of humility, an example of love, and an example of cleansing. [Col. 1841C]

First, he gave an example of love, so that in the example of the Teacher the disciples might learn to love one another. Hence he says: “I give you a new commandment: that you love one another, just as I have loved you.”

He gave an example of humility, so that in the example of the Teacher the disciples might learn to humble themselves toward one another.

He gave an example of cleansing, so that in the example of the Teacher the disciples might learn to cleanse one another from sins through confession, prayer, and acts of compassion, and to bear one another’s burdens.

Therefore, my brothers, following the footsteps of the true and supreme Teacher, let us humble ourselves toward one another, washing the feet of the poor and of our subjects. But even this is insufficient unless we also love them. [Col. 1841D] For there are some who humble themselves and wash the feet of the poor not out of love but even under a kind of compulsion; such people do not sincerely imitate Christ’s example, for he washed the feet of the poor out of true love.

Therefore, brothers, let us wash the feet of the poor as of our brothers, out of true love. Nor is this sufficient unless we also seek their cleansing and salvation in soul. Thus, after we have washed the poor, shod them, and satisfied them bodily, let us satisfy them spiritually, breaking for them the bread of the divine word—the bread of correction, instruction, and exhortation—and praying that they too may wash us through their prayers before God, so that we may deserve to celebrate Passover purely, by the generosity of him who was sacrificed as our Passover, Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever. Amen.

## HOMILY XLIX. ON GOOD FRIDAY

[Col. 1842A]

“The Lord said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt: ‘This month shall be for you the beginning of months’” (Exodus XII), etc.

In this reading, my dearest brothers, the Lord once taught the Jews historically how they ought to celebrate the Passover that had been prefigured. But for us, if we understand spiritually, he delivered in the same reading how we ought to celebrate the spiritual Passover.

We too, brothers, leaving the Passover of animal blood to the animal-like Jews, should inquire into these things to learn how we may celebrate Passover spiritually.

This reading, therefore, understood mystically, teaches us six things: where Passover ought to be celebrated, by whom and when it ought to be celebrated, what the paschal lamb ought to be like, what its sacrifice accomplishes, and how it was to be eaten. [Col. 1842B]

Where ought Passover to be celebrated? In the land of Egypt. For in Egypt the first command concerning the celebration of Passover was given by the Lord, as we read here, and the first Passover was celebrated there.

In Egypt, therefore—that is, amid the darkness and sorrow of this world—we received from God the command to celebrate Passover, that is, the passage from this world, so that, following the example of the Israelites, we may pass in desire from Egypt to the promised land, from vices to virtues, and from exile to the heavenly homeland.

By whom ought Passover to be celebrated? By Israelites—that is, by men who desire to see God; by Hebrews—that is, by those passing from vices to virtues and from the exile of this world to the heavenly homeland.

For these alone, my brothers, truly celebrate Passover: those who hate the world, who complain and say with the Prophet: “Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged” (Psalm CXIX), and who leap across in desire so that they may see the God of gods in Zion. [Col. 1842C]

Hence the Lord Jesus promises that he will be seen by Galileans in Galilee—that is, by those who are migrating into migration. But those who embrace the world with love, who would always wish to live here, and who contend over earthly inheritance, can by no means worthily celebrate the spiritual Passover.

When ought Passover to be celebrated? On the fourteenth lunar day of the first month. For in the first month—that is, in the lunar month of April, which according to our reckoning sometimes begins in March—God created the world, and in that same month he recreated it.

At the same time, indeed in the same month and on the same day, and perhaps at the same hour in which God created humanity, he recreated it. It is probable that humanity was created on the fourteenth day of the moon. For since the moon was created on the fourth day at the full moon, on the sixth day it could have been as it usually is on the fourteenth day.

For this reason also the paschal lamb was taken from the flock on the tenth day and sacrificed toward evening on the fourteenth day. Christ too came to Jerusalem on the tenth day for his Passion; on the fourteenth day, while eating the lamb, he was betrayed that same night and led to his Passion. [Col. 1842D]

Mystically, the lamb was sacrificed toward evening on the fourteenth day of the moon because it signified Christ, who, fulfilling the Decalogue and the four Gospels in himself, was sacrificed in the evening of the world.

It was also fitting that the legal lamb and the true Lamb, Christ, should be sacrificed at the time when all things grow green again and are renewed, because through Christ’s Passion the world is stripped of its oldness and grows green and is renewed in virtues. [Col. 1843A]

We too, brothers, ought to celebrate Passover in the springtime and on the fourteenth day of the moon, because unless we lay aside our oldness and begin to be renewed and to flourish in virtues, and unless we hold to the teaching of the Decalogue and the four Gospels, we cannot celebrate the spiritual Passover.

What ought the paschal lamb to be like? Without blemish, male, and a year old—that is, perfect in purity, in strength, and in age.

Who is this lamb except the Lamb of God, who took away the sins of the world? (John I.) He was without blemish because he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth (1 Peter II). He was also male—that is, manly and virtuous, perfect in virtue and wisdom—for he overthrew the aerial powers, bound the strong armed man, and distributed his spoils (Luke XII). [Col. 1843B]

He was also a year-old lamb—that is, perfect in age and body—because he suffered at the perfect age at which we too, according to the Apostle, will rise again, “until,” he says, “we attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the fullness of the age of Christ” (Ephesians IV).

What did the sacrifice of the paschal lamb accomplish? Liberation from the destroying angel, the drowning of carnal enemies, and strengthening on the way.

So also, my brothers, Christ’s sacrifice frees us from the devil, extinguishes carnal vices in us, and is our viaticum and strengthening on the road of this exile.

Just as the Hebrews, through the blood of the lamb smeared upon both doorposts and upon the lintel, were freed from the destroying angel, so we too, fortified on the right and on the left and on the forehead by Christ’s cross smeared with Christ’s blood, are freed from the devil lying in wait. [Col. 1843C]

And just as, after the sacrifice and through the sacrifice of the lamb, the Hebrews were saved when their carnal enemies had been drowned, so we too are saved through the Passion and eating of Christ’s body when our vices have been extinguished within us.

For just as the Hebrews, refreshed and strengthened by the flesh of the lamb, left Egypt and took the road to the promised land, so we too, refreshed and strengthened by the body of Christ as viaticum, leave the world in mind and take the road of virtues toward the land of eternal inheritance.

How was the paschal lamb to be eaten? Not raw, nor cooked in water, but only roasted by fire. [Col. 1843D] Raw flesh is merely a carcass without heat; cooked in water, it dissolves; but when roasted, it is compacted, so that the bones adhere to the flesh and the flesh to the bones.

Therefore, he eats the Lamb raw who believes Christ to be merely human. He eats him cooked and dissolved in water who divides him into two persons. But he eats him roasted and cohesive who believes that divinity and humanity cohere in the one person of Christ.

He must also be eaten whole—that is, with the head, feet, and entrails—because whoever receives Christ’s body ought to believe that he receives not only a human being but also God. The entrails signify certain hidden things that are proclaimed about Christ and humanity. Even if we do not understand them, we must nevertheless receive them by believing. [Col. 1844A]

“Nothing of it,” he says, “shall remain until morning.” That is, whatever it is necessary for you to believe about Christ on the way, you shall believe. Nothing that ought to be believed will remain for you to say that you do not believe, until morning—that is, until the resurrection—for then it will not be the time for believing but for seeing.

If anything remains—that is, if there is something concerning Christ whose truth you do not understand—you shall burn it with fire, that is, ascribe it to divine power.

“You shall not break any of its bones,” that is, you shall not believe that the power of his divinity was broken or diminished because of the suffering of his flesh.

You shall also eat the lamb with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. Unleavened bread lacks leaven, while bitter herbs have bitterness. Therefore, you shall eat the lamb with unleavened bread—that is, with the sincerity of innocence and truth—and with bitter herbs—that is, with bitterness and contrition of heart, so that we may presume to approach the Lamb’s flesh only with repentance and contrition expressed in tears. [Col. 1844B]

You shall eat it in this way: “You shall gird your loins,” that is, you shall restrain lust—not only illicit lust but also licit desire. For, my dearest brothers, we ought to approach the Lamb’s flesh with such purity that we abstain not only from everything illicit but also from certain things that are licit.

“You shall have shoes on your feet,” that is, your affections shall not cling to earthly things but shall desire heavenly things. For whoever, brothers, clings to earthly things through avarice and greed is not worthy to approach the Lamb’s flesh.

“You shall hold staffs in your hands,” that is, rectitude in your works, so that you direct your whole life and all your works toward a right end. [Col. 1844C]

“And you shall eat it in haste,” hastening from vices to virtues and from the world to the eternal homeland, after the likeness of the Israelites, who ate the lamb in haste to leave Egypt and go to the promised land.

Therefore, my brothers, let us approach so great a sacrament not sluggishly, negligently, or tepidly, but with fear and devotion. For “whoever receives it unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Corinthians XI).

Let us therefore approach the Lamb’s flesh with firm faith, believing that in one person he is true God and true man, and also believing that anyone who receives him receives not a part but Christ whole and entire. If there is anything in this that we cannot understand or investigate, let us leave it to God. [Col. 1844D]

Let us also approach the Lamb’s flesh without the leaven of hatred and ill will. Let us approach with purity of mind and the devotion of contrition, with the virtue of chastity, contempt for the world, rectitude of action, and haste toward the promised land, knowing that here we are inhabitants and pilgrims, as all our fathers were, and that here we have no lasting city but seek the one to come.

May Christ be our guide, our viaticum, and our way to that city, he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever. Amen.

## HOMILY L. ON THE VIGIL OF EASTER

“If you have risen with Christ, set your minds on the things that are above” (Colossians III), etc.

This reading, my brothers, has three parts. First, the Apostle shows what we ought to savor and what we ought not to savor. Showing first, therefore, what we ought and ought not to savor, he says: “If you have risen with Christ, set your minds on the things that are above.”

It is not the same thing, my brothers, to know and to have taste. To know is to grasp a thing intellectually. To have taste, however, is to know a thing not only intellectually but also through its savor and experience.

We ought to know both evil and good; otherwise we would not know how to distinguish between them. But we ought to savor only good things. The Apostle therefore commands us to savor only good things, not evil ones; heavenly things, not earthly things.

He savors heavenly things who, despising earthly things, smells out and desires only heavenly things. He savors earthly things who, ignorant of heavenly sweetness, loves and seeks only earthly things. [Col. 1815A]

Moreover, my brothers, humanity was created in such a way that it would naturally desire and seek heavenly things. For God gave human beings reason, which naturally desires heavenly things. Since our soul was formed according to the image and likeness of God, it naturally tends toward the image according to which it was created. [Col. 1815B]

Hence the prophet says: “My heart has spoken to you; my face has sought you; your face, O Lord, I shall seek” (Psalm XXVI).

God also created the human body in such a way that by the body’s very position he might show human beings toward what they ought to tend. For he created man upright and facing heaven, according to the following:

“While the other animals look downward upon the earth,

he gave man an uplifted countenance

and commanded him to look upon [contemplate] the heavens.”

(Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book I, verses 84–86.) [Col. 1815C]

But although humanity had been created in this way, on account of its transgression it was blinded and made brutish, so that, bent down in the manner of beasts, it would savor and seek only earth and, by dying, dissolve into it, according to the saying: “When a human being was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Psalm XLVIII)—in vices, and likewise in death.

Hence poets describe human beings as being changed into beasts. A human being who, forgetful of his divine origin, is devoted solely to the belly—what else has he become than a pig? Whoever is wholly devoted to satisfying lust—what else is he than one transformed into a foul-smelling he-goat? Likewise, human beings are said to be transformed into other beasts according to the likeness of their behavior. Whoever is devoted to cruelty and blood—what else has he become than a wolf? [Col. 1815D]

Therefore, my brothers, because of the first transgression we incurred a double death: one of the soul, blinded by sins, and the other of the body, returning to its own earth.

Yet God, who had not forgotten to have mercy, became human for us, died, rose again, and, ascending into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father. He died only the death of the body so that he might destroy within us both our deaths, that of the soul and that of the body. He rose with the resurrection of the body alone so that he might make us rise both in soul and in body. He ascended into heaven so that he might also make us ascend into heaven. [Col. 1846A]

Therefore, my brothers, if you have risen in soul and from sins with Christ—that is, through Christ rising bodily from the dead—do not return again to sins, and do not savor earthly things any longer. Rather, savor the things that are above, where Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God.

As if he were saying: You who are Christ’s members, direct your desire upward, where your head has gone before you. And from the fact that you have already risen in part, trust that you will ascend after Christ.

The second part follows, in which it is shown for whom we ought to die and for whom we ought to live, when he adds: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” As though he were saying: From now on you ought not to set your minds on the things that are on earth, but on the things that are above, since you have died to the world and live to God. Hence elsewhere he himself says: “If we have died to sin, how shall we live in it again?” (Rom. VI) [Note: [Col. 1815D] The Vulgate does not speak quite this way in the passage cited.]

Therefore, my brothers, we ought to be dead to the world, dead to the flesh, and also dead to our own will. Dead to the world, so that we seek not its riches, honors, powers, glories, or desires, but those of heaven. The Apostle showed that he was dead to the world when he said: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI). The world, my brothers, has been crucified to me if it does not draw me by its allurements. I, however, have been crucified to the world if I do not embrace it with my desires.

We ought to be dead to the flesh, [Col. 1846C] so that we do not seek gluttony, drunkenness, debauchery, pleasure, or the desires of the flesh, but the spirit. Hence the Apostle says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, debauchery, avarice, feasting, drunkenness” (Col. III), and so forth. And elsewhere he says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. V).

We ought also to be dead to our own will, so that we seek to do not our will but God’s. The Lord invites us to this by his own example, saying: “For I have not come to do my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me” (John VI). For who ought better to have done his own will than the Son of God, who always has one will with the Father? Nevertheless, he says that he seeks not his own will but God’s, in order to instruct us always both to seek and to do not our own will but God’s. Therefore, my brothers, let us always seek, and insofar as we can do, perform, not our own will but God’s, and let us say to him: “Not my will, Lord, but yours be done.”

If, then, we have died in the manner described above, undoubtedly our life will be hidden with Christ in God, so that with the Apostle we may say: “I live, yet now it is no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II)—a life both spiritual and eternal.

We live by spiritual life, my brothers, when, having eliminated the death of sins from ourselves, we live in faith, hope, and charity, and flourish and bear fruit in justice, mercy, chastity, and the other virtues. This life is now hidden with Christ in God, because although we appear to worldly people to be rejected and worthless, “the reproach of men and the outcast of the people,” and although we seem daily to hunger, lack, and suffer, regarded as sheep for slaughter, nevertheless we live in faith and hope, secretly before God, so that we may say with the Apostle: “As chastened, yet not put to death; as dying, and behold, we live” (II Cor. VI).

We shall live by spiritual life when this mortal body puts on immortality and blessedness. This life is now hidden with Christ in God. For although our body now seems to die, decay, and turn to ashes, and worldly people despair that it will rise again, nevertheless, secretly before God, to whom all things live, our bodies do not perish; rather, they are kept with Christ to be renewed for the better.

The third part follows, in which it is shown that, by doing good, we shall receive a reward, when he adds: “But when Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.” As though he were saying: Just as your life is now hidden with Christ, so it will be revealed with Christ when he comes to judgment.

Christ is called our life by metonymy, because he is the cause, giver, and author of our life—bodily, spiritual, and eternal. This now appears false to some, doubtful to others, and hidden to still others; but at the judgment, when Christ appears, it will be manifest to all, both good and evil. For the wicked, as Scripture testifies, will then say: “These are the ones whom we once held in derision and made into a reproachful image. We fools regarded their life as madness; and behold how they are now counted among the children of God, and their lot is among the saints” (Wis. V).

Then Christ, who first came hidden, will come openly. Hence he himself said: “As lightning comes forth from the east and appears even to the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Luke XVII). He who first appeared humble will then appear exalted above every height. He who previously appeared despised will then appear glorious above every glory. He who first appeared as the poor man of the poor will then appear as King of kings and Lord of lords. He who was first judged and suffered will then judge, condemning the unjust and glorifying the just.

We too, my brothers, if we humble ourselves with Christ on the way, shall be exalted with him in our homeland. If we are despised with Christ on the way, we shall be glorified with him in our homeland. If we are poor and subject with Christ on the way, we shall be enriched, and we shall rule as lords with him in our homeland. If we are judged and suffer with Christ on the way, we shall be judged and rejoice with him in our homeland.

Therefore, my brothers, let us not set our minds on earthly things, nor bend ourselves toward love of them like animals, which, without a bridle and with their whole force, are driven to fulfill the will of the body. Rather, let us be upright toward heaven in mind as in body; with our whole desire let us love [Col. 1848A] and seek heavenly things, dead to the world and alive to God, so that when Christ, our life, appears, we too may appear with him in glory.

By his gift, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LI. ON THE HOLY DAY OF EASTER

“Purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new dough, just as you are unleavened” (I Cor. V), and so forth.

Today, dearest brothers, we celebrate the resurrection of the Lord. Therefore we ought to correspond to the solemnity that we honor. Solemnities benefit only those who strive to conform themselves to them in mind and works. The celebration of the Lord’s cross and resurrection will therefore benefit us if we crucify vices within ourselves, and if we rise from vices to virtues and from oldness to newness.

For this reason the Apostle exhorts us, my brothers, in the reading just mentioned, as follows. First, he commands us to put off oldness; second, to put on newness; third, he gives the reason why we ought to do this; fourth, he urges us to feast; fifth, he shows how we ought to approach this feast.

First, then, he urges us, my brothers, to put off oldness—that is, the likeness of the old Adam, namely, sin. Sin is called oldness for three reasons. Oldness makes a person bent and weak; so sin makes the soul bent toward earthly things and weak for doing good. Oldness dulls a person’s senses; so sin dulls the virtues of the mind. Oldness draws a person to death; so sin draws the soul to death.

The Apostle therefore says: “Purge out the old leaven,” alluding to the custom of the Jews, who cast out leaven at Passover and ate unleavened bread. They did this both in remembrance of the fact that, after the sacrifice of the lamb, their fathers departed from Egypt—who left with such haste that they were not allowed to prepare loaves, but, carrying flour, made unleavened loaves from it upon the hearth—and also as a mystery signifying that those who wish to celebrate Passover purely must avoid the leaven of sin.

Moreover, leaven, especially old leaven, makes bread sour, light, less nourishing, and more full of cavities. So, my brothers, sin makes a person’s soul sour, so that God does not wish to unite it to himself and incorporate it into himself. It makes the soul light, so that the devil can carry it about. It makes it less solid and strong for resisting the devil; it makes it full of cavities, so that the devil can find a hiding place in it.

Therefore, my brothers, purge out the old leaven of sin—that is, remove sin through penance, correction, and amendment—not only from the mind, but also from the household and from communion with the Church. For the one who casts out the old leaven perfectly is not merely the person who, insofar as he can, rejects it from himself, but also rejects it from his household and from communion.

Perhaps Eli rejected the leaven from himself, but he did not reject it from his household, and therefore perished with it. Perhaps the Corinthians, to whom the Apostle is speaking here, rejected the leaven from themselves, but they did not reject it from their communion, since they did not avoid the corrupter of his stepmother, whom the Apostle had excommunicated, although John says of such a person: “Do not even say ‘Hail’ to him. For whoever says ‘Hail’ to him shares in his works” (II John I, 11). And the Apostle says in the same Epistle: “If anyone is named a fornicator or a miser, with such a one you must neither eat nor associate” (I Cor. 8).

This is directed against certain people, my brothers, who do not hesitate to participate, eat, and converse with the excommunicated, although it is written: “He who touches pitch will be defiled by it” (Ecclus. XIII), and: “He who touches a dead person will be unclean” (Num. XIX). By the same reasoning, whoever associates with an excommunicated person is himself excommunicated.

Second, the Apostle urges us to possess newness when he adds: “So that you may be a new dough”—that is, new paste, pure from old leaven and from every impurity. He speaks metaphorically here, comparing the purity of the Church with the purity of dough.

For whoever wishes to make pure dough first cleanses and purifies the grains of wheat, then grinds them and reduces them to flour, and afterward joins and binds them together by sprinkling water. In the same way, if the communion of the Church is to be pure and acceptable to God, each individual person must first be pure and clean within himself.

But certain persons, although they seem pure in themselves, are nevertheless, like grains, coarse and hard, because they join themselves to no one through fellowship or compassion. Subject and attached to themselves, they live for themselves alone and refer everything to themselves, unlike those whom we noted above. For those others join themselves in fellowship even with the excommunicated. These people do not wish to associate or form bonds even with the good. Both are vices: to form bonds with everyone, and to form bonds with no one. The former are fervent in evil; the latter are lukewarm even in good. The Apostle calls such people “without affection, without friendship, without covenant” (Rom. I).

Such persons, therefore, like grains, must be ground through remembrance of sins and completion of punishments, and reduced to humility. And lest dry humility go away like dust that the wind drives from the face of the earth (Ps. I), they must be joined by the dew of charity and united into a new dough, so that neither hatred, nor envy, nor earthly desire may be able to separate them from mutual charity or from the charity of Christ.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let each of us cleanse and purify himself; let us be transformed by the millstone of humility and contrition, and let us be united to one another by the bond of charity and compassion, so that through the purity of our charity and unity God may be nourished and delighted, and that, conversely, we may be nourished and delighted by divine charity and unity. For just as God is nourished and delighted by our charity, so we are nourished and delighted by divine charity.

Third, the Apostle adds the reason why we ought to be new, when he says: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed.” As though he were saying: Be new, because you have been invited to a new meal, lest the one who invited you to his wedding come and say to any one of you: “How did you enter here without a wedding garment?” (Matt. XXII). And, angered, send you into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (ibid.).

Therefore, my brothers, let us be new, so that as new people we may approach the new feast of the new Lamb, because today we are not going to feast, like the Jews, on the flesh and blood of brute animals, but on our very God and Lord Jesus Christ, who has been sacrificed as our Passover—a new, sufficient, and rich feast.

It is new because it is pure in itself from the oldness of sin, and because, if we receive it worthily, it makes us new through its newness. It is sufficient because, in place of the many figurative, insufficient, and repeated legal sacrifices, Christ has been sacrificed as the one true victim, offered once for all. Although he is offered, sacrificed, and broken sacramentally each day upon many altars, nevertheless Christ, the one and true victim, was sacrificed only once, because “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more” (Rom. VI).

Although the Jews had many insufficient sacrifices—such as the sacrifice for sin, the peace offering, the votive offering, and the victim—Christ is a sufficient sacrifice for all and on behalf of all: for the expiation of sins, for restoring peace between God and humanity, for fulfilling human vows, and for conquering enemies.

It is rich because our Lord Jesus Christ is filled with every grace, charity, and mercy. For he is that fatted calf which the father orders to be sacrificed when his son returns from the land of unlikeness.

Therefore, dearest brothers, since we are invited to this new, abundant, and fattened feast, let us carefully consider doing what the Wise Man says: “You have sat at a great table; pay attention, for you must prepare similar things” (Ecclus. XXXI). Invited, then, to Christ’s table, dearest brothers, let us prepare things like those found in him; let us love him as he loved us. Let us humble ourselves for his sake as he humbled himself for us. Let us be ready to die for his sake as he died for us.

Fourth, the Apostle urges us to feast when he adds: “Therefore let us feast.” We too, dearest brothers, urge you all to feast together on a feast necessary for our souls. For it is written: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John [Col. 1850D] VI).

Hence it was ordained that, immediately after baptism, children should be given the sacrament, at least under the appearance of wine, lest they depart without the necessary sacrament. And what if they depart? Will they be condemned? No, my brothers, because they will be saved in faith, although not their own, yet that of their sponsors.

There are two ways of eating the body of Christ: one sacramental and the other spiritual. Even an evil person receives Christ’s body sacramentally, but because he receives it unworthily, “he eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (I Cor. II). A good person, however, receives Christ’s body spiritually: even if he does not at some time receive it sacramentally, he is nevertheless in Christ’s body through faith and charity. Hence, explaining what it means to eat him spiritually, the Lord says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John VI).

And Augustine says: “Why do you prepare your tooth and your stomach? Believe, and you have eaten” [Note: [Col. 1851] St. Augustine, Tractate 35 on John VI, 12, vol. XXXV of Patrologia.]

Nevertheless, my brothers, all Christians who have the place and time to do so ought also to communicate sacramentally. Hence, in the primitive Church, all Christians were accustomed to communicate on every Sunday. But because some approached negligently, it was later established that blessed bread should be given in place of the Eucharist, and that people should communicate at least three times a year: at Christmas, at Easter, and at Pentecost.

But now, brothers, iniquity has grown so greatly that some can scarcely communicate worthily even once a year. There are also some who rejoice in communicating every day, and others who shrink from it. Both act well, provided that they avoid contempt and labor to communicate worthily. For both Zacchaeus and the Centurion honored Christ: Zacchaeus by receiving him joyfully, and the Centurion by considering himself unworthy.

Of those who celebrate Mass daily, Augustine says: “I neither praise nor blame the celebration of daily Mass”—that is, I neither praise it in the negligent nor blame it in the diligent.

Fifth, the Apostle teaches how we ought to approach the altar’s table. Today, dearest brothers, we are about to receive a great guest—indeed, our God and Lord Jesus Christ. Let us prepare a pure and honorable lodging for him.

Certainly, if we were about to receive a prince or some secular person in our lodging, we would cleanse the lodging itself of every stain and adorn it with decorations, so that no disgrace would offend the person entering, but rather the cleanliness and propriety of the house would gladden him. If, then, we do this for an earthly prince, what ought we to do for the King of kings and Lord of lords?

The Apostle commands us to receive our God not in old leaven, nor in the leaven of malice and wickedness. As though he were saying: Remove every stain from yourselves. From the confession of your sins remove the old leaven of excuse-making; do not, after the manner of the old Adam, excuse your sins, nor “incline your heart to words of malice, to make excuses in sins” (Ps. CXL). Rather, accuse yourselves, proclaim yourselves unworthy, weep, and make satisfaction.

Also remove from the mind the leaven of malice—that is, hatred, envy, and ill will. Likewise remove from your works the leaven of wickedness, that is, injustice, so that you do not do to others what you do not wish to be done to you.

He next commands us to feast on the flesh of the Lamb in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. As though he were saying: It is not enough for you to purge stains from yourselves unless you also adorn with virtues the lodging in which you are to receive the Lord. With what virtues? With the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, so that sincerity may be found in life and truth in speech.

Sincerity, my brothers, will be present in our life if we think sincerely, love sincerely, and live sincerely. Truth will be present in speech if we truly confess our sins, if we speak truth with our neighbor, and if we praise the Lord with a harmonious voice.

If we live in this way, my brothers, we shall be able to approach the flesh of the true Lamb in purity, so that through charity we may be united to God and to our neighbors, with our Lord Jesus Christ at work, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever. Amen.

## HOMILY LII. ON THE HOLY DAY OF EASTER

“Mary Magdalene, and Mary of James, and Salome bought spices, so that they might come and anoint Jesus” (Mark XVI), and so forth.

Since today’s solemn celebration summons us, my brothers, to the paschal wedding feast, we ought to occupy this day with spiritual joys and evangelical instruction. And because each person listens more willingly to what he loves more, if you love God and our Redeemer above all else, you will listen more willingly to the Gospel history of his resurrection.

Therefore, dearest brothers, we shall review the Gospel reading for you, explaining first what pertains to the historical account and second what pertains to its tropological meaning. With respect to the historical account, four matters must be considered. First, how devoted these holy women were to Christ; second, how they were heard when they made their request; third, how they were consoled by the angel and instructed about Christ’s resurrection; fourth, how they were sent first to proclaim the Lord’s resurrection.

Their devotion, then, was extraordinary, dearest brothers. They were fervent, courageous, and most dutiful toward Christ. They were fervent because the one whom they had ardently loved while he was alive they followed with tears even unto death, nor could they forget him after his death. They were courageous because, while the apostles and pillars of the Church fled, denied him, and hid themselves, neither loss, nor the terror of death, nor the sword could deter these women from standing by the cross and hastening to the tomb. They were most dutiful because they had ministered to him while alive, joyfully from their own resources; they stood beside him in death with groans and lamentations; and they ran to the tomb with sighs and spices.

But what can we, men who are effeminate, say about this? We are lukewarm, timid, and negligent toward Christ our Redeemer. Those women ardently loved Christ living, dying, and buried in mortal flesh. And we scarcely or lukewarmly love him who now reigns eternally and glorifies his own!

Those women could be prevented neither by the terror of death nor by the sword from standing beside him who was dead and buried. And we wretched men are separated by fear or desire from Christ, who lives and reigns eternally!

Those women ministered from their resources to Christ living in mortal flesh, and to him who was dead they ministered with their tears and spices. We disdain to minister to him who now reigns eternally and to feed him with his own food in the poor!

Let us therefore shake off, my brothers, our lukewarmness, timidity, and negligence. Following the example of these women, let us burn with love of God and learn to be courageous and dutiful in God’s service.

In the statement that, “very early on the first day of the week,” the women came to the tomb “after the sun had risen,” the fervor, courage, and dutifulness of the women are likewise demonstrated, since they began to come to the tomb with spices even during the night. But they reached the tomb when the sun—that is, the dawn arising from the sun’s nearness—had already appeared.

This also signifies that, when the sun of the day rose, Christ, the sun of righteousness, rose again. In his memory the Church also celebrates the morning praises. We believe that the general resurrection will likewise be celebrated in the morning, in accordance with David’s saying: “And the just shall rule over them in the morning” (Ps. XLVIII).

When, therefore, according to Matthew, a great earthquake occurred before the angel rolled the stone away from the entrance of the tomb, we should believe that Christ had risen and had raised with himself many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep.

It is not surprising if Christ, who had come forth to die from the closed womb of a virgin, came forth immortal from the closed tomb, since, generally, all the bodies of the just who rise again will be endowed with such subtlety that no wall or solid substance will be able to restrain or confine them in their agility.

The second part follows, in which it is shown how the women’s requests are heard. The women make their request, as it were, by suggestion when they say: “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?”

There are two kinds of requests. Some are in themselves worthy to be asked of God directly and openly, such as virtues and the kingdom of heaven. There are others concerning which we do not know whether they are beneficial for us. These should therefore be requested not directly, but conditionally or by suggestion.

The Lord requests conditionally that the cup of suffering pass from him when he says: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not my will but yours be done” (Matt. XXVI). The blessed Virgin requests by suggestion that wine be provided at the wedding when she says: “They have no wine” (John II). Similarly, Lazarus’s sisters request by suggestion that he be healed when they say: “Lord, behold, the one whom you love is ill” (John XI).

They do not ask openly for him to be healed, since they do not know whether that would be beneficial; they merely display their grief and desire. For whoever displays his need asks sufficiently. It is therefore as though they were saying: You see our need, but you, Lord, who know all things, do what you know is beneficial for us.

These women also make their request in this way when they say: “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?” The Evangelist adds that it was “very large,” and that the weakness of the women could not move it. Since their devotion was great, their pious request deserved to be heard.

Hence it is added: “And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away.” Their request is therefore granted, though not for the purpose they had in mind. They had asked that the stone be removed so that they might anoint the dead man. The stone, however, was removed so that, seeing the tomb empty, they might understand that Christ had risen.

Matthew explains by whom this stone was removed: “For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, and coming near, rolled away the stone” (Matt. XXVIII). The angel descended for two reasons: to roll away the stone and to be the messenger and witness of the Lord’s resurrection.

John therefore describes two angels appearing to Mary Magdalene, one seated at the head and the other at the feet (John XX), so that “every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deut. XIX).

Behold what fervor and devotion of mind deserve. Because these holy women were so fervent and devoted to Christ, they deserved to see an angel, to be helped, consoled, and instructed by him. From this let us also learn, my brothers, to be fervent and devoted in Christ, so that we too may deserve to be consoled, helped, and instructed by God through the angels.

For God hates and loathes the lukewarm and the sluggish, and does not take care to reveal to them the hidden mysteries of his sweetness and delight. But those who, like Daniel, are “a man of desires” (Dan. IX) deserve to be enlightened by God.

The third part follows, in which the holy women see the angel and are at once consoled and instructed by him, when it is added: “And entering into the tomb”—that is, into the little chamber in which the tomb was—“they saw a young man sitting at the right, clothed in a white robe, and they were amazed,” and so forth.

The angel who appeared in this way demonstrated in himself both what the one whom he had come to announce was like and what the faithful would be like in the resurrection. He appeared neither as a child nor as an old man, but as a young man, because the resurrection had already been celebrated in Christ at the perfect age, and was to be celebrated in us. Hence the Apostle says: “Until we meet him as a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. IV).

He also appeared seated, because he was announcing the repose of the resurrection, through which Christ was already reigning and through which we too shall reign. According to Matthew, he was seated upon the stone of the tomb (Matt. XXVIII), because he was proclaiming the one who had already overcome in himself the burden of death and would overcome it in us at the resurrection. Hence he likewise foretold through Hosea: “O death, I shall be your death” (Hos. XIII).

He appeared also at the right, because he was announcing the one who already sat at the right hand of eternal blessedness and who would place us at his right hand in the judgment. He also appeared clothed in a white robe because he was proclaiming the one who was already clothed in the robe of immortality and who would clothe his own at the end.

He appeared in a white robe—not because the citizens of the eternal homeland need to be clothed, but to display in its whiteness the splendor of his own festival and ours. For Christ’s resurrection both restored us to eternity and repaired the angelic fall, and it has increased the solemn joys of both together forever.

For, as Matthew says, “his appearance was like lightning, and his clothing like snow” (Matt. XXVIII). In the lightning of his face he terrified the guards; in the whiteness he consoled the women. This also demonstrates that the one whom he announced would be terrifying to the reprobate in the judgment and gracious to the just.

The angel consoles the women when he says to them: “Do not be afraid.” As though he were saying: Let those who do not love heavenly things be afraid; but you, who see your fellow citizens, what do you fear?

They are also instructed when he says to them: “You seek Jesus the Nazarene, the crucified; he has risen, he is not here.” Since many have been called Jesus in name, he is distinguished by the place when “the Nazarene” is added, and by the cause when “the crucified” is added: “He has risen; he is not here.”

The bitter root of the cross has vanished; the flower has burst forth with its fruits, because he who lay in death has risen in glory. “Behold the place where they laid him.” The place of death is shown empty to mortals, so that from it we may have hope within ourselves and give thanks to God.

## Part IV

The fourth part follows, in which the women are sent to proclaim the resurrection of Christ, when it is added:

> “But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he will go before you into Galilee” [Col. 1855B].

Just as death was brought near to the man through a woman, so now these holy women, through that same sex, have wiped away the reproach of the first mother. These women are privileged above the others because they were sent before the evangelists themselves to proclaim the resurrection of Christ. Yet when the Apostle says, “I do not permit a woman to teach in the Church” (1 Tim. II), these women nevertheless taught even the teachers themselves; hence they can be called “apostles of the apostles.”

“Tell,” he says, “his disciples and Peter.” Peter is called by name so that he may not despair because of his denial. For unless the angel had expressly mentioned him, he would not have dared to come among the disciples. But by a great dispensation the Lord permitted the chief of the apostles to deny him, so that he himself might learn through his own fault how he ought to show mercy and compassion toward others, and so that the holier might fear all the more in the fall of the chief of the apostles, while sinners, however great, might hope in his restoration [Col. 1855C].

“He will go before you,” he says, “into Galilee.” Although the Lord appeared to his disciples first in several other places, why, speaking only of Galilee, did he say both through himself and through the angels that he would go before his disciples into Galilee? First, because there he appeared more generally and more manifestly to all his disciples; second, because Galilee is interpreted as “a transmigration that has taken place.” Christ had already passed over from passion to resurrection, from death to life, and from punishment to glory. The apostles and the other faithful, however, following him, will see him glorified—those who now pass over from vices to virtues and from earthly things to heavenly things [Col. 1855D].

Let us therefore, brothers, now pass over from vices to virtues and from earthly things to heavenly things, so that we may deserve, ourselves glorified, to behold him glorified in his glory.

In the moral sense, however, through these three holy women, dearest brothers, we are instructed about when, with whom, and in what manner we ought to approach the chalice of the Lord’s body and blood. By the chalice, the tomb is signified; by the upper stone, the paten; and by the corporals, the shroud and the napkin in which Christ was wrapped.

These women, who came three to the tomb, show who ought to approach the tomb of the Lord’s chalice. Only those who profess the Trinity in faith and conduct are worthy to approach the chalice of the Lord’s body and blood: they must believe that the one whom they receive was one God before the ages with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and that in time he became man for us and suffered [Col. 1856A].

These women also show us when we ought to approach the Lord’s chalice, for they came to the Lord’s tomb after the sun had risen. We too, brothers, ought to approach the Lord’s chalice only after the darkness of our vices has been driven from our hearts through repentance and the sun of virtues shines within us through righteousness. For whoever, while still remaining in the darkness of vices—that is, of hatred or envy—approaches the Lord’s chalice, approaches it to his own judgment.

These women show us with whom we ought to approach the Lord’s chalice, for they approached the Lord’s tomb only with ointments and spices [Col. 1856B]. We too, my brothers, should approach the chalice of the Lord’s body and blood only with the sweetness of good works and the fragrance of virtues, by which we may delight God and our neighbor. Whoever approaches so great a sacrament lukewarmly and without compunction, without sighs, without the fragrance of prayer and devotion, approaches unworthily.

These women also show us how we ought to approach the Lord’s chalice, for they came to the tomb with humility, presuming nothing about themselves but conscious of their own weakness, invoking divine aid and saying:

> “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?”

We too, my brothers, should approach the Lord’s chalice with humility, presuming nothing on the basis of our own righteousness [Col. 1856C], but conscious of our weakness, invoking divine aid and saying:

> “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?”

That is: Who will give us the ability to approach the body of Christ purely? It is as though he were saying: Not our own strength, but divine assistance.

If we act in this way, brothers—if we act in this way—the stone, that is, the difficulty, is removed, and we are given the ability to approach that body purely.

Or certainly, “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?” means: Who will open for us the understanding of so great a sacrament? And if we persist in devout prayers, the Lord will send a messenger—namely, the Holy Spirit, or perhaps an angel, or some saint, as we read in the *Lives of the Fathers*—who will open for us the understanding [Col. 1856D] of so great a sacrament.

And he will say to us:

> “Why do you seek the young man among the dead? He has risen; he is not here.”

That is: Why do you seek that heavenly bread among mortal foods? It is not bodily food, nor does it descend to the place where bodily foods descend; rather, it nourishes the soul of each believer on earth while remaining whole in heaven.

Therefore, my brothers, although Christ is sacrificed, broken, and crushed every day, he nevertheless remains impassible in himself. Hence the Apostle says:

> “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death will no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI).

Therefore, as long as you see and handle the sacrament of the body and blood of Jesus Christ, sense it with your lips, and crush it with your teeth, know that Christ is bodily with you. Then seek him only in heaven, and do not believe that he is bodily with you, but only spiritually. Hence Augustine says:

> “Why do you prepare your tooth and your belly? Believe, and you have eaten” [Note: [Col. 1857D] See the note above, no. 41.]

Since, however, while we are in this life no one is perfectly able to see how Christ, although wholly received by each person, nevertheless remains indivisible and impassible at the right hand of the Father, we are rightly warned by the angel to admonish both ourselves and others, so that in heart, conduct, prayer, and life we may press forward toward Galilee—that is, toward our eternal homeland. There we shall see more fully the mysteries of Christ and shall behold him face to face, through the favor of him who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God. Amen.

## HOMILY LIII. EASTER MONDAY

> “Two of Jesus’ disciples were going out and were traveling that same day [Col. 1857B] to a village that was sixty stadia from Jerusalem, named Emmaus” (Luke XXIV). [Note: [Col. 1858D] The Vulgate has: “And behold, two of them.”]

And so forth.

This reading, dearest brothers, is divided into six sections. First, it is shown that on the very day of Christ’s resurrection two of his disciples went out and traveled to Emmaus. These two went out from the company of the apostles, not through apostasy, like those of whom John says, “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John II), nor through curiosity, like Dinah, who went out to see the women of that region and was seized (Gen. XXXIV). Rather, they went out in service, like bees that leave the common community of the hive in order to return laden with the chosen flower for the common benefit of honey.

That they went out for a proper and honorable reason is evident from the fact that they went out not singly but in pairs [Col. 1857C]; that they discussed among themselves no words alien to the teaching of their community; that they carried in their minds the common sorrow of their community; that they deserved to have the Lord appear to them; that they gladly listened to him explaining the Law and the Prophets; that they compelled him to enter their lodging; that they recognized him in the breaking of bread; and that they returned without delay to report to their community that he had appeared to them.

Imitate these men, you who live in monasteries, so that you do not leave your community through apostasy or curiosity, but only for a necessary reason. And then go out not singly but at least in pairs, knowing that, according to the prophet:

> “Woe to the one who is alone, because if he falls, who will lift him up?” (Eccles. IV).
