Speak not vain words, but only those appropriate to your profession [Col. 1857D]. Walk with useful sorrow and seriousness. Rejoice always to hear the reading of sacred Scripture. Love hospitality and charity. Bring back to your monasteries not empty rumors but useful examples, like a bee.

“To a village,” he says, “that was sixty stadia from Jerusalem, named Emmaus.” A stadium is an eighth of a mile. Sixty stadia, therefore, amount to seven thousand five hundred paces. This journey appropriately corresponds to those who, certain about Jesus’ death and burial but uncertain about his resurrection, were walking. They completed the sixth and seventh miles, since they knew that Jesus had suffered death on the sixth day, Friday, and had rested in the tomb on the Sabbath [Col. 1858A]. They traveled only halfway through the eighth, since they did not yet fully believe that Jesus had risen on the eighth day.

The second section follows, in which the Lord, while the disciples are speaking about him, showed himself to them in the form of a traveler, when it is said:

> “And they were speaking with one another about all these things that had happened.”

It is characteristic, my brothers, of those who love to speak frequently about the one whom they love. For:

> “Where your treasure is, there also is your heart” (Matt. VI).

And whatever abounds within hastens to come out outwardly. Thus the disciples always had upon their lips the Lord whom they had loved with their whole heart while he was alive and whom they could not forget when he was dead. The Lord, who cannot be absent from those who love him, and who said:

> “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. XVIII),

shows his presence to those who love him and speak about him. For it follows:

> “And it came to pass, while they were conversing on the way and questioning one another, that Jesus himself, drawing near, went with them.”

Let us therefore love the Lord Jesus, my brothers, and let us always rejoice to meditate upon him and speak about him. For he will not deprive those who love him and rejoice to meditate upon and speak about him of his presence; without doubt he will be their inseparable companion on the road of this world, just as he promised, saying:

> “Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

Although the disciples loved him, they nevertheless doubted his resurrection and divinity. Therefore, even though he appeared to them, he did not show them a form by which they could recognize him [Col. 1858C]. Rather, he displayed outwardly what they possessed inwardly. And because they doubted about him, he showed himself to them as doubtful. For it follows:

> “But their eyes were held, so that they would not recognize him.”

Therefore, my brothers, let us remove every doubt from our hearts, and let us believe with certain faith in Christ’s divinity and humanity, his passion and his resurrection, so that we may deserve to see him face to face, not in the appearance of a traveler, but as he truly is.

The third section follows, in which the Lord questions the disciples, rebukes them for their doubt, and instructs them, when it is added:

> “And he said to them: What are these words that you are discussing with one another as you walk, and why are you sad?”

Knowing this, dearest brothers, the Lord questions his disciples in such a way that, from their doubtful answer, he may rebuke, question, and correct them [Col. 1858D].

“As you walk,” he says, “and are sad.” This is what the Psalmist says:

> “Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds” (Ps. CXXV).

Thus, brothers, this is what we must do in the pilgrimage of this world: walk, weep, and cast seeds.

Where should we walk? Toward our eternal homeland.

Why should we weep? Because of the remembrance of our sins and because of the delay of the heavenly homeland.

What seeds should we cast? We must proclaim among ourselves the seeds of divine words, my brothers, and send ahead the seeds of good works, so that we may be able to reap sheaves multiplied a hundredfold with rejoicing.

“And one of them, whose name was Cleopas, answering, said to him: Are you alone a stranger in Jerusalem, and have you not known the things that have happened there in these days?” [Col. 1859A]

It is as though he were saying: The matter about which we are speaking is known and manifest to everyone in Jerusalem, both citizens and strangers. How then are you the only stranger in Jerusalem who is ignorant of these things?

> “Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, who was a prophet, a man powerful in deed and word before God and all the people.”

He commends him in four respects—not as God or the Son of God, but as the mere man Jesus before God and the people: he was manly in mind, spiritual in understanding, powerful in deed, and effective in speech. These four qualities are to be sought in an ecclesiastical shepherd. First, strength of mind is required, but it is not sufficient unless spiritual understanding is also present. Nor are these two sufficient unless he shines in conduct and wins others through preaching [Col. 1859B].

> “How the chief priests and our rulers handed him over for condemnation to death and crucified him! But we were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel.”

Behold: through the imperfect past tense, he reveals that his former hope was past and incomplete. He shows that he had almost entirely fallen away from faith and hope: from faith when he says, “a prophet”; from hope when he adds, “we were hoping.”

> “And some women from our group frightened us. They were at the tomb before dawn. And when they did not find his body, they returned saying that they had also seen a vision of angels who say that he is alive.”

This is foolish speech, since he shows himself more frightened by the removal of the body [Col. 1859C] than joyful at the proclamation of the resurrection.

He says to them in rebuke:

> “O foolish men and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken!”

“Foolish,” that is, dull in spiritual understanding; “slow” to believe what they had understood.

Then he instructs them, both by reason and by the authority of the Law and the Prophets. He does so by reason when he adds:

> “Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and so enter into his glory?”

It was necessary, dearest brothers, that just as condemnation had entered through one man, redemption should likewise come through one man. It was also necessary that just as man had fallen through pride, he should be restored through humility. It was likewise necessary that just as the human race had fallen into misery through the disobedience of the first man in eating from the tree [Col. 1859D], so through the obedience of the new man, in the death upon the tree, it should be revealed in glory.

He instructs them by the authority of the Law and the Prophets when he adds:

> “And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.”

For Moses foretold him:

> “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; you shall hear him as me” (Deut. XVIII).

The prophets, however, wrote many clearer things about Christ.

In this, my brothers, our sluggishness is put to shame: we know that the Law and the Prophets have been fulfilled in Christ, yet we do not take care to devote ourselves either to understanding sacred Scripture spiritually or to fulfilling it in our works.

[Col. 1860A] The fourth section follows, in which the disciples invite the Lord, who pretended that he was going farther, to lodge with them.

Do not be surprised, my brothers, that the Lord pretended to be going farther, for not every pretense contains the malice of duplicity. There is a bad pretense, and there is a good pretense. There is a pretense intended to deceive, by which an enemy pretends to be a friend in order to deceive more effectively. There is also a pretense intended to instruct or test, by which a teacher pretends to be angry with his disciples in order to make them fear and advance more greatly. Hence the Wise Man says:

> “If you have daughters, do not show them a cheerful face” (Ecclus. VII).

Let us therefore, my brothers, shun deceptive pretense as a crime and seek the kind that brings improvement. For the Lord pretends to be going farther [Col. 1860B] in order to test the disciples’ charity. But since those with whom charity itself was walking could not be strangers to charity, they invite—or rather compel—the Lord to lodge with them.

From this it should be understood that guests must not only be invited to lodge but also urged to do so. For the ancient fathers themselves went out to meet guests, searched for them through the lanes and streets, and received them with joy.

The disciples therefore present the Lord with their reason for why he should lodge with them, when it is added:

> “Stay with us,” they say, “because it is toward evening, and the day is now declining.”

This reproves those who tell guests that a later hour of the day still remains, so that they may thereby invite them not to stay but rather to continue farther on.

But let us, my brothers [Col. 1860C], imitate the welcoming of a guest who has arrived, without pretense. Let us ask him, urge him, and not put forward the convenience of time or place. Let us receive him joyfully and serve him even more joyfully.

The great merit of hospitality is evident from the fact that Abraham and Lot, because they were accustomed to receive human beings, deserved to receive angels, and indeed God himself (Gen. XVIII).

A certain head of a household, devoted to hospitality, was one day receiving a stranger and wished to offer him water with his own hands for washing them. Suddenly the stranger disappeared, but in a vision during the night he said to him:

> “On other days you received me in my members; today you received me in my own person.”

Thus also the Lord will say to the elect at the judgment:

> “I was a stranger, and you gathered me in” (Matt. XXV).

Therefore, my brothers [Col. 1860D], practice hospitality—and, as the Apostle says, do so without murmuring.

Thus the Lord, invited and compelled by the charity of his own, consented:

> “And he entered with them.”

For it is exceedingly sweet for a friend to dine with friends, while dining with the envious and hateful is bitter. Let us therefore rejoice to dine with our good and friendly companions; but let us avoid dining with the wicked and our enemies, unless perhaps it is in order to win them for God.

The fifth section follows, in which the disciples recognize the Lord in the breaking of the bread, when it is added:

> “And it came to pass, while he was reclining with them, that he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and offered it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him.”

While the Lord, according to his customary manner, blesses and breaks the bread, he is recognized—much more happily by their eyes opened to recognize the glorification of his nature in Christ than the first parents were by theirs to recognize the shame of their concupiscence [Col. 1861A].

Why is the Lord recognized not while explaining sacred Scripture but in the breaking of bread? Because a good shepherd is recognized more through his actions than through his preaching, more in charity than in speech, and more by giving himself and what belongs to him for his brothers than by preaching to them in words alone. Examples have greater effectiveness among those who are instructed than words.

Therefore, my brothers, let us strive even more to act well than to speak well.

> “And he,” it says, “vanished from their sight.”

But why, dearest brothers, did the Lord grant his disciples only a brief joy, so that immediately after being recognized he immediately vanished? [Col. 1861B] He did so to show that, because of their joy and their slowness, they were not yet worthy of a prolonged vision of him; to make them accuse their own slowness; to demonstrate to them the agility and freedom of glorified nature; and to kindle in them a greater desire for him.

Hence it is also added that they said:

> “Was not our heart burning within us concerning Jesus” [Note: [Col. 1861D] The Vulgate does not have “concerning Jesus.”] “while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?”

Their heart was indeed burning concerning Jesus while they heard him explaining the Scriptures, but it burned more ardently when, after being recognized, he vanished from their sight.

We too, my brothers, are often burning when we hear Christ speaking in the Scriptures. But if, through contemplation or some revelation, we taste his sweetness more openly, how much more ardent do we become? [Col. 1861C] When he gives himself to us to be seen face to face forever, with the cloud removed, how much more ardently, brothers, will we then burn with love for him?

The sixth section follows, in which they return to announce to the disciples that they had seen the Lord.

O true charity and true brotherhood, which neither the meal prepared nor the approaching night could delay from hastening to communicate their joy to their fellow disciples! Thus, my brothers, true charity ought to act: it should hasten to announce the joy of its prosperity to a friend, so that those who love one another equally may rejoice together.

Therefore, rising at that same hour, they returned to Jerusalem and found the Eleven gathered together, and those who were with them, saying:

> “The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon.”

And they themselves recounted what had happened on the way and how they had recognized him in the breaking of bread.

From both sides the manifest resurrection of Christ heaps up new material for joy, and those who possess a common cause for rejoicing rejoice together.

So it will be, my brothers, in that universal resurrection of the blessed. A common cause will produce common joys. By a common cause I mean one charity in all, which will make the individual goods of each person common to everyone through charity, since each person will love glory in his neighbor as much as in himself.

Let us hasten, therefore, dearest brothers, toward those joys where there will be glory without envy, joy without sorrow, abundance without want, security without fear, life without death, and blessedness without end. May the almighty and merciful Lord lead us to it. Amen.

## HOMILY LIV. FIRST SUNDAY AFTER EASTER

> “Everything that is born of God conquers the world” (John V), and so forth.

Since, my brothers, it seems difficult to some people to conquer the wickedness of the world, the Apostle shows in this reading, first, who is the victor over the world; second, by what means he conquers it; and third, he proves by testimonies that only one who is such and so great can conquer the world.

Showing first who the victor over the world is, he says:

> “Everything that is born of God conquers the world” [Col. 1862B].

There are, my brothers, three births: the first divine, the second carnal, and the third spiritual.

According to the first, the Son of God was ineffably begotten from eternity by God the Father. According to the second, man is born carnally from man every day. According to the third, through water and the Holy Spirit, the human being who is a servant of sin is reborn every day so as to become God’s adopted son.

Concerning the first, the Father says to the Son:

> “Before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. CIX).

Concerning the second, David says:

> “In sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. L).

Concerning the third, it is said:

> “But as many as received him”—that is, Christ—“he gave them power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name, who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God” (John III).

Therefore, my brothers [Col. 1862C], carnal generation, because it takes place through carnal concupiscence, does not conquer the concupiscence of the world but enters into alliance with it. Only divine birth and spiritual birth, because they are stronger than the world, conquer the world.

Hence the Lord says:

> “In the world you will have tribulation, but be confident, because I have conquered the world” (John XVI).

The natural Son of God conquers the world by himself and through his own power; the adopted son of God, however, does not conquer it by himself but through the natural Son. Hence the natural Son of God said to his adopted sons:

> “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV).

How could Vincent and Laurence, my brothers, and the other martyrs—who were indeed fragile flesh—have conquered so many temptations and torments of the world, unless God had armed them and conquered through them? In no way.

Therefore, let no strong person rely on his own powers; for if he does so, he is conquered. Peter himself, the first shepherd, fell through denial when he presumed upon himself.

Showing, therefore, that Christ alone conquers the world, the Apostle adds:

> “And this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith”—

that is, Christ whom we believe in.

And not only does he himself conquer, but so does the one who clings to him with true faith. Hence he also adds:

> “Who is the one who conquers the world except the one who believes, with faith working through charity” (Gal. V), “that Jesus Christ is the Son of God?”

Second, the Apostle shows by what means Christ conquers the world, adding:

> “This is the one who came”—understand, to conquer the world—“through water and blood” [Col. 1863A] of his passion.

Christ conquers the world in three ways, dearest brothers: by suffering, converting, and condemning.

In his first coming he conquers the world by enduring with equanimity the persecutions, insults, and scourges of the wicked. He also conquers the wickedness of certain people by converting and sanctifying them through charity. He displayed both—patience and charity—in his passion.

At his second coming, however, he will conquer the world through justice, condemning the wicked and crowning the elect.

If we wish to be sons of God, my brothers, we must therefore follow the footsteps of his only-begotten Son. Let us conquer the world by Christ’s example—that is, the wickedness of worldly people—by enduring them with equanimity. For whoever fails in tribulations and persecutions [Col. 1863B], whoever murmurs or seeks vengeance, no longer conquers but has been conquered, according to the saying:

> “Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good” (Rom. XII).

Let us also conquer the wickedness of worldly people by converting them to the Lord through a good word and example, returning good for evil and blessing for cursing, and praying for them, according to the Apostle’s saying:

> “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink. For by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head” (ibid.).

If, my brothers, we conquer the world in this way in the present age, then without doubt in the future we shall conquer by ruling over and judging the wicked who refused here to be converted from their wickedness.

For it is written:

> “And the righteous will rule over them in the morning” (Ps. XLVIII),

that is, in the resurrection.

Hence the Lord also promised his disciples:

> “When the Son of Man sits in the majesty of his glory, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX) [Col. 1863C].

Third, the Apostle proves that Christ is such and so great that he can conquer the world by himself, adding:

> “For the Spirit is the one who testifies that Christ is the truth”—

that is, true God and true man.

The Holy Spirit, who came upon him in the form of a dove and who was sent by him upon the apostles, testifies that Christ is the truth—that is, true God. The human spirit, which he gave up in his passion, testifies that Christ is the truth—that is, true man. For unless he were true man, he would not have a true spirit and true flesh.

And not only does the Spirit [Col. 1863D] testify to this; indeed, three give the same testimony:

> “For there are three who give testimony in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit.”

These three testified at the Jordan and on Mount Tabor that Christ is true God. And these three are one, not only in testimony but also in essence.

And there are three who give testimony on earth that Christ is true man: spirit, water, and blood—namely, the human spirit, and the water and blood that flowed from Christ’s side. These three are one, understand, in testimony; therefore their testimony must be believed.

> “If we receive the testimony of men,”

as it is written in the Law,

> “that every word may stand on the testimony of two or three” (Deut. XIX),

then we ought to receive the testimony of God, which is greater [Col. 1864A].

It is as though he were saying: If we receive the testimony of human beings, who can in fact lie, then much more ought we to receive the testimony of God, who cannot lie.

Because Christ is true God, he is so great that he could rightly conquer the world. And because he is true man, he is such that he could suffer in order to redeem it.

We too, brothers, if we are sons of God through grace, and if we keep our humanity pure and clean, can conquer the world in Christ.

> “The one who believes,” he says, “in the Son of God has the testimony of God within him”—

that is, the thing testified to: Christ and faith in him.

He also has the testimony of God within him in this sense: the testimony by which the Father testified concerning the Son—that the Son is his Son by nature—testifies concerning each believer that [Col. 1864B] he is God’s son by grace.

Therefore, my brothers, if we possess true faith, we shall be able to conquer the wickedness of the world through it: conquering some of the wicked by word and example and drawing them to Christ; patiently and equably enduring others and turning their wickedness to our own advancement; and judging and separating still others—here, from the fellowship of the Church, and in the future, condemning them and separating them from the fellowship of the saints.

And thus, as true victors over the world, we shall receive the triumph of victory with Christ and his martyrs, through the favor of him who lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LV. FIRST SUNDAY AFTER EASTER

> “[Col. 1864C] When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were closed where the disciples were gathered because of fear of the Jews, Jesus stood in their midst and said to them: Peace be with you” (John XX).

As we have gathered from the readings of the holy Gospels, dearest brothers, the Lord appeared six times on the very day of his resurrection.

First, to Mary Magdalene, as John reports.

Second, to her and the other two women returning from the tomb, concerning whom it is written:

> “They approached, took hold of his feet, and worshiped him” (Matt. XXVIII).

Third, to James, as the Apostle reports. The Gospel of the Nazarenes also relates concerning him that he had vowed not to eat until he saw him risen.

Fourth, to the two on the road to Emmaus.

Fifth, to Peter.

Sixth, to all who were gathered at home except Thomas, as John reports here [Col. 1864D].

Let us therefore, brothers, consider first what pertains to the historical sense and second what pertains to the moral sense.

According to the historical sense, the Lord here brings the joy of his resurrection to his disciples and proves by many arguments that he truly rose again.

This reading has four parts. First, it is shown that the Lord appeared to his disciples while the doors were closed. Second, what he bestowed upon the disciples. Third, how he confirmed the doubting disciple in faith. Fourth, after the disciple became confident because he had seen, the Lord declares blessed those who did not see and believed.

First, therefore, the Evangelist says that the Lord appeared to the disciples while the doors were closed. From this arises a many-sided question [Col. 1865A]: first, how the body that entered through closed doors was a true body. Or, if the body that entered through closed doors was subtle for this reason, how could it be seen with bodily eyes or handled with the hands? How could it speak, since speaking belongs to denser and more humid members? How could human eyes endure a glorified body, since it is brighter than the sun? How did it eat? And how could it be a true body that could now appear and now vanish?

To resolve these questions, my brothers, we must understand that in the resurrection the body will be adorned with seven gifts.

The first will be subtlety. The body will then be so subtle that it will be able to penetrate bodies that obstruct it and will not be prevented by bonds or barriers [Col. 1865B]. Thus the glorified body of Christ was able to leave the closed tomb and enter through closed doors.

The second will be swiftness. The glorified body will then possess such speed that it will be able in an instant to go from heaven to earth, from earth to heaven, from east to west, or in the opposite direction. Thus, after appearing to the two men at Emmaus (Luke XXIV), the Lord immediately appeared to Peter in Jerusalem, although the places are sixty stadia apart.

The third will be incorruptibility. Bodies will then be unable to be corrupted by death, old age, sickness, sword, hunger, thirst, or any other adversity. Hence John says:

> “God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints” (Rev. XXI), and so forth.

And Christ, it says,

> “rising from the dead, dies no more” (Rom. VI).

The fourth will be strength [Col. 1865C]. The glorified body will then possess such strength that it will even be able to overturn mountains, as we believe angels can do now. Thus one angel overturned the stone at the entrance of the tomb, which was exceedingly large, as though it were a feather.

The fifth will be beauty. The body will then possess such beauty and glory that it will shine like the sun (Wis. III). Hence the Lord says:

> “The righteous will shine like the sun in the house of my Father” (Matt. XIII).

If mortal eyes could not endure the glory that the Lord displayed for a short time on the mountain, how could glorified eyes endure his glory?

The sixth will be pleasure. All bodily senses will then delight in true and eternal pleasures. Sight will delight in the splendor of eternal brightness; hearing, in the sweet melody of heavenly hymns [Col. 1865D]; taste, in the sweetness of heavenly and eternal goods; smell, in the fragrance of every spice and perfume; and touch, in ineffable sweetness and softness.

The seventh will be freedom. The glorified body will be so free that it will be able to display itself in forms that now appear contrary to it. Although subtle in its own nature, it will be able to show itself substantial and palpable; when it wishes, it will be able to vanish. Although glorious and shining in its own nature, it will be able to show itself obscure and visible. Although it will need neither food nor clothing, it will be able to eat and to be clothed. We read the same concerning angels.

Since, therefore, the Lord wished to prove to mortal beings that his flesh had truly risen from the dead, he displayed himself in a form in which he could be seen, touched, heard, speak, and eat by them [Col. 1866A]. Thus he was truly seen by them, truly touched, truly speaking, truly heard, and truly eating. That food, however, did not descend to the place to which our food descends, but was consumed in the very act of chewing.

The second part follows, in which it is shown what the Lord bestowed upon his disciples in this apparition. First, since they were sad, he bestowed consolation upon them by announcing peace to them when he said: “Peace be with you.” It is as though he were saying: “Do not grieve, but rather rejoice, because through my Passion peace has been restored between God and humanity.”

Then, since he was about to send the disciples to preach this peace and was going to give them the power of binding and loosing [Col. 1866B], he strengthens them: first, in faith in the Resurrection; second, according to Luke, he opens their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24); third, he commands them to have peace and charity with God and with their neighbor; fourth, he sends them to preach; fifth, he bestows the Holy Spirit upon them; and finally he gives them the power of binding and loosing.

First, appropriately, he strengthens in faith those whom he was about to send to the ministry of preaching and the priesthood, since the one who is to strengthen others must first be firm himself. He confirms them in faith when he shows them his hands and side. And when, according to Luke, he eats with them (ibid.), he demonstrates that the very same flesh which had been nailed to the cross has risen again, flesh that, having been restored to life, can both be handled and eat food.

Second [Col. 1866C], appropriately, he opened the disciples’ understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures, since one who is going to teach others must not only possess faith but must also confirm that faith for others by the testimonies of Scripture, so that, as Peter says, he may be ready to give an account of the faith and hope that are in us (1 Peter 3). And this, my brothers, is directed against those who approach the ministry of preaching and the priesthood while ignorant of the Scriptures.

Third, also appropriately, he commands the disciples to maintain peace with God and their neighbor through charity, since one who is appointed mediator between God and sinners must first be peaceful and familiar, through charity, both with God and with human beings. For how can one reconcile two people who are at odds if he himself is separated from both by [Col. 1866D] hatred or ignorance? This is directed against those who, though unknown to God because of their reprobate life, presume to undertake the embassy of reconciliation on behalf of sinners.

Fifth, appropriately, the disciples are sent to preach, since those who are firm in faith, learned in the Scriptures, and at peace through charity both with God and with humanity can suitably be sent to preach. They do not assume the ministry of preaching on their own, but are rather sent by the Lord, since no one ought to thrust himself forward. And no one, as Paul testifies, ought to take the honor upon himself, but only the one who is called by the Lord, as Aaron was (Hebrews 5). This is directed against those who, through ambition and simony, presume to usurp the ministry of preaching [Col. 1867A] for themselves.

Fifth, appropriately, the Holy Spirit is given to those sent to preach, so that he may remind them of everything they are to say and grant them both abundance of speech and effectiveness in persuasion. Preachers speak in vain unless, through the word of God and the Spirit of his mouth, the net of preaching is cast out. This is directed against those who try to preach from themselves rather than from the Spirit of God, seeking not the progress of their hearers but rather to display their own knowledge.

Sixth, also appropriately, they are given the power of binding and loosing, so that they may absolve those whom they recognize as inwardly illuminated by the Spirit, and bind those blinded by God. Behold, my brothers, to what great dignity the Lord raised his disciples and their successors in this world: he made them fathers and shepherds [Col. 1867B], indeed even gods of human beings, and in his place granted them the power to release or impute sins. Divine mercy did this so that sinners would not despair when they could find counsel and healing for their sins close at hand; so that, by humbling themselves before other human beings and confessing their sins, they might appease through humility the God whom they had offended through pride; and so that human beings might have compassion on human beings, sinners on sinners, by praying for one another and bearing one another’s burdens. Nevertheless, priests should pay the greatest attention to whom they ought to absolve or bind, in what manner, with what intention, and under what authority.

**Whom ought they to absolve or bind?** Those who have been absolved and enlightened from their sins by the Holy Spirit [Col. 1867C]. For how can one who is himself bound worthily absolve or bind those who are bound, or how can an unclean person cleanse or condemn the unclean? Hence the Lord said to the accusers of the adulterous woman: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her” (John 8). Hence it is also written: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4).

**Whom ought they to absolve or bind?** Their own subjects, not strangers. Hence it was forbidden in the Law that anyone should put his sickle into another’s harvest; and they should deal with brothers, not unbelievers. Thus the Apostle says: “What business is it of mine to judge those who are outside?” (1 Corinthians 5). And if someone should be found—that is, a private person—for we ought not to excommunicate a prince and the multitude that accompanies him, but rather to bear with them [Col. 1867D], lest, while uprooting the weeds, we uproot the wheat together with them (Matthew 13).

**How ought they to absolve or bind?** Not precipitately, but slowly, discerningly, and justly. The sentence of excommunication must be pronounced slowly, both by the priest himself and through others. The sinner must first be admonished three times, and every remedy must first be tried before proceeding to a sentence of excommunication. This is directed against those who hastily excommunicate sinners at once, not observing that what is done too quickly is done badly.

The sentence, whether of absolution or of excommunication, must be pronounced with discernment. A priest ought not to excommunicate anyone on account of a venial sin, nor on account of an unknown fault—for example, if someone is insulting or talkative—nor on account of a hidden offense [Col. 1868A], but on account of a manifest crime. He may admonish people concerning other faults, but he should not excommunicate them for them. Thus Paul says: “If anyone among you is named as a fornicator or a greedy person, with such a one do not even eat” (Ephesians 5). A person is “named” when the matter has become public.

Again, he ought not to absolve one who has been bound unless the sinner renounces the sin, makes satisfaction, and demonstrates inward contrition of heart through groans, sighs, and the countenance of one who is penitent.

The sentence of absolution or excommunication must also be pronounced justly, that is, not on account of hatred or favor, but solely according to the justice of the person’s merits. This is directed against those who, in absolving or binding, weigh their own personal feeling rather than the merit of the person subject to them—binding those whom they ought to absolve out of hatred [Col. 1868B], or absolving those whom they ought to bind out of favor, judging a friend by one standard and an enemy by another. Their sentence will certainly be rejected before the supreme Judge, for, as Solomon says: “A weight and a weight, a measure and a measure—both are abominable before God” (Proverbs 26). Nevertheless, subjects ought to fear the shepherd’s sentence, whether just or unjust, lest through contempt they make themselves guilty of a fault that did not previously exist.

**With what disposition should an ecclesiastical shepherd absolve or bind?** He should absolve with a joyful mind and bind with a sorrowful one. Therefore he should excommunicate only with difficulty, in great necessity, and with a grieving spirit—just as we ordinarily amputate a member from the wholeness of our body only when it has become withered and harmful to the other members, and even then only with difficulty and great pain [Col. 1868C]. This is directed against those who easily, eagerly, and quickly excommunicate their sinful brothers.

Moreover, when they cut off a member from ecclesiastical fellowship without sorrow of heart, they show that they themselves are not joined to the members of the Church by the bond of charity.

**By what authority ought priests to absolve?** By divine authority, not their own. The power of releasing sins belongs to God alone. But he has granted the ministry—which is improperly also called “power”—to his vicars, who bind or absolve in their own manner; that is, they show that people have been bound or absolved. For God first absolves the sinner inwardly through contrition, while the priest, by pronouncing the sentence outwardly, shows that the person has been absolved. This is well signified [Col. 1868D] by Lazarus, who is first raised by the Lord in the tomb and afterward, through the ministry of the disciples, released from the vices by which he had been bound.

The third part follows, in which the Lord confirms the doubting disciple in faith when he adds: “Thomas, one of the twelve,” and so forth. If you ask, my dearest brothers, why the Lord willed his chosen disciple to doubt in the faith, it was certainly by a great dispensation. Mary Magdalene was of less benefit to us than Thomas, who doubted for a long time. For Thomas touched the scars of the wounds and cut away from our breast the wound of doubt. He doubted so that we would not doubt. He was confirmed by touching, so that we might be confirmed through him.

The Lord confirms him in faith in his Resurrection when he continues: “Put your finger [Col. 1869A] here,” and so forth. The Lord retained the marks of the scars in his glorified body for four reasons: to show that the crucified flesh had truly risen; to present them to the Father and continually intercede for us; so that the wicked might see at the judgment the one whom they had pierced or despised; and so that the righteous, seeing that they had been inflicted upon their Lord for their sake, might always burn more fervently with love for him.

For this reason too an image of the crucified is now painted in the Church: so that, seeing our Redeemer willingly endure poverty, weakness, insults, spitting, scourging, and death for our salvation, we may be inflamed more and more in our hearts to love him. For what ought we not to do for one who, so worthy himself, endured such unworthy things for us, so unworthy?

[Col. 1869B] The fourth part follows, in which it is said to the confessing disciple: “Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.”

“Because you have seen me,” he says, “you have believed.” What did he see? What did he believe? Since faith concerns things that are not seen, he saw one thing and believed another. He saw scars in the flesh and believed that, by the power of his divinity, he had truly risen. He saw visible humanity and believed in the divinity hidden within it.

“Blessed,” he says, “are those who have not seen me and have believed.” What does this opposition of words mean, my brothers? Are only we blessed, who have not seen and yet believe? And are the Apostles, who saw and believed, not blessed? Or are they blessed, while we are more blessed than they? No. Rather, these words show that the faith which believes without the experience of the senses [Col. 1869C] is more meritorious than faith that believes through experience. Indeed, our faith would be more meritorious than that of the Apostles if it were equally great, equally fervent, and equally effective. But the more certain their faith was, the more fervent it was.

The Apostles were therefore most blessed, to whom it was said: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see” (Matthew 13). But we too, my brothers, who have not seen the Lord in the flesh, are blessed if we truly believe in him, truly love him, and fulfill his commandments.

According to the tropological sense, we are shown first what we ought to do by the example of the Apostles, and then what benefit we shall gain from it. All the disciples gathered together at home in the evening, with the doors shut for fear of the Jews [Col. 1869D]; they spoke about the Lord and longed for him.

We too, my brothers, after going out through prolonged activity to external affairs, should return in the evening through contemplation to ourselves and gather ourselves within ourselves, so that we may inquire what in us needs correction, what needs nourishment, what must be uprooted, and what must be planted. Let us not be like certain people who seek only external things while remaining ignorant of and neglecting themselves.

Let us also be together through the unity of charity, loving God more than ourselves and our neighbors as ourselves, just as it is said of the Apostles themselves: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4). They were not divided by the possessiveness of greed, since no one called anything his own of what they possessed; rather, everything was held in common among them.

[Col. 1870A] The doors of our hearts must also be closed because of the snares of demons, so that they may not penetrate our interior through an evil suggestion (ibid.). Therefore, according to Solomon’s command, we must guard our hearts with every vigilance (Proverbs 4). And according to Peter’s command: “Be sober and watchful,” especially in prayers, “because your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5).

If, my brothers, if we are gathered within ourselves through both contemplation and charity, with the doors closed through vigilance, frequently speaking about Jesus and longing for him, he will undoubtedly enter into us and be with us, just as he himself promised when he said: “Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matthew 18).

[Col. 1870B] And what will he bestow upon us? The peace of his consolation. Excluding all doubt from us, he will confirm us in faith, open our understanding to the Scriptures, give us the peace of twofold charity, and send us to win the souls of our brothers. By inspiring us with his Holy Spirit to suggest all good things to us, he will also make us like gods, whether here we bind or absolve sinners in his place, or in the future judge the obstinate.

But if anyone is harder and slower in faith, let him not despair. Rather, let him ask with a devout mind to be strengthened, and the Lord will confirm him in his faith through clearer signs and proofs. Gathering his chosen from every direction and bringing them into his kingdom, he will feast with them in everlasting joy. Hence he himself says [Col. 1870C]:

“And I appoint for you a kingdom, just as my Father appointed one for me, so that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22).

May he deign to grant this, the God who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LVI. SECOND SUNDAY AFTER EASTER

“Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps” (1 Peter 2), and so forth.

In this reading, dearest brothers, six matters are proposed for our consideration: who suffered and for whom; how much he suffered; in what; how; and for what benefit to us.

**Who suffered?** God, impassible, incomprehensible, immortal. A wondrous thing, brothers, and unheard-of throughout past ages [Col. 1870D]: that the impassible One suffered, that the incomprehensible One was comprehended, that the immortal One died. Although these statements may appear contradictory, they are nevertheless truly predicated of the same person according to different natures. For in Christ there are not two persons, God and man, but one and the same person consisting of two natures.

The union of divinity and humanity in Christ is so great, without confusion, that whatever we say about the Word, we also say about that man, and whatever we say about that man, we also say about the Word. Hence, my brothers, we boldly proclaim that God died and that this man is the Creator of the world. The incongruous combination of words does not prejudice the truth of what is said.

**For whom did he suffer?** For human beings, for servants, for sinners. [Col. 1871A] Thus God suffered for human beings, the Lord for servants, the Holy One for sinners.

Behold, brothers, wondrous and unheard-of compassion; wondrous and unheard-of condescension. Let temporal lords who are inhuman and cruel toward their servants be ashamed—those who do not wish to show mercy toward the offenses of servants and the poor, nor to have compassion on their weaknesses, but rather afflict offenders inhumanely and allow the sick to perish from cold and hunger, grieving more over the illness of their animal than of their servant.

What is this? God had compassion on you, a wretched human being and sinner, and you, a human being, do not have compassion on another human being, a servant on a fellow servant. The One who needs nothing has shown mercy to you who are in need. And you, who are in need, do not show mercy to one who is in need.

**How much did he suffer?** Deprivations and injuries. He suffered deprivations both of material things—for example, bodily poverty and want [Col. 1871B], hunger, thirst, and weariness—and of the mind, such as sadness and grief.

He also suffered injuries, both from his own people and from strangers: exactions affecting his possessions, insults in words (Matthew 21), and afflictions in his body. He suffered exactions because, being required to do so, he paid tribute to Caesar; the soldiers divided his garments and cast lots for his tunic (John 19).

They also inflicted insults upon him, calling him the son of a carpenter, a glutton and a wine-drinker, a lover of prostitutes and tax collectors (Matthew 11). They called him a deceiver and reproached him, saying: “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matthew 27). He also suffered bodily afflictions: slaps, spitting, chains, scourging, and death.

My brothers, if God endured so many [Col. 1871C] and such unworthy things for us, who are unworthy, what ought we to do for him—or rather, for ourselves? The rich God became poor for you. And you, for the sake of your salvation, refuse to be poor? God suffered hunger, thirst, weariness, sadness, and such things for you. And you refuse to suffer these things for your salvation?

God and Lord of all endured subjection for your sake and paid tribute to Caesar. And you, for your salvation, refuse to submit and to pay tribute to earthly rulers? God endured insults and mockery from servants for your sake. And you cannot bear to have such things said to you by your equals? God suffered scourging and death for you. And for the redemption of your soul you cannot suffer what, whether you wish it or not, you will eventually have to suffer?

[Col. 1871D] Brothers, God endured every lowly and harsh thing for us, except sin. We wretched people, on the contrary, patiently endure subjection to sin and the devil, but refuse to endure human subjection, poverty, and affliction—which are medicines for souls. Why is this? Because we wish to live not by God’s law but by our own law, and to follow our own way rather than God’s.

**In what did he suffer?** On the wood. From eternity God had ordained that Christ would suffer on the wood, both because this kind of death was more degrading and because it was more fitting. It was more degrading because thieves and criminals were hanged on wood. Thus he wished to suffer these things because he wished to suffer what was more degrading for us.

It was more fitting [Col. 1872A] because the devil had tempted and overcome Adam through the wood. Therefore it was fitting that the one who had overcome humanity through the wood should be overcome by a human being through the wood. It was fitting that the human being who had sinned through the sweetness of the wood should be healed through the bitterness of the wood.

That the Lord would triumph over the devil had been foretold by the Psalmist: “Declare among the nations that the Lord has reigned from the wood” (Psalm 95).

[Note: The Vulgate does not have “from the wood.”]

**How did he suffer?** Willingly and innocently. Willingly, because he handed himself over to the one judging him unjustly (1 Peter 2). Hence he himself says: “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down, and I take it up again” (John 10).

Innocently, because “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2). Patiently, because “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered [Col. 1872B], he did not threaten” (ibid.). Indeed, he rebuked Peter and healed the ear that Peter had cut off.

We too, brothers, following the footsteps of our Teacher, should willingly endure the bitter and sorrowful things of this world, because just as a sick person does not attain health without suffering distress and tasting bitterness, so we, sick with sins, cannot attain true salvation without enduring hard and bitter things.

Let us suffer, as far as we can, innocently, following the example of our Lord, so that temporal punishments may not be punishments for guilt to us but merits for a crown. But if at times we are scourged for our sins, let us acknowledge in those very scourges, like the good thief, that we deserve them and thus become purer; let us not, like the wicked thief, become hardened in our iniquity and become worse through correction [Col. 1872C].

Let us also suffer patiently, without murmuring and without accusing God’s judgment, but giving thanks to God, who disciplines the son whom he loves more greatly (Hebrews 12), knowing that punishments either cleanse sins or increase our reward.

**For what benefit to us did he suffer?** For four reasons.

First, so that he might bear our sins, according to what Isaiah had foretold about him: “Truly he himself bore our infirmities, and he carried our sins” (Isaiah 55).

Second, so that he might show us the charity that he had for us and invite us to love him more fervently. Hence he himself says: “No one has greater charity and love than to lay down his life for his friends” (John 12).

[Col. 1872D] Third, so that he might leave us an example to follow. Hence he himself says: “Whoever serves me must follow me, and where I am, there also will my servant be” (John 12).

Fourth, so that he might call us back from error to the way of truth, from darkness to light, and from the worship of the devil to the worship of our Creator.

For previously, my brothers, we were like wandering sheep without a shepherd; we were blind, without the true light; we were servants of the devil, while ignorant of the true Creator. But now, my brothers, let us rejoice and give thanks to our Redeemer, because we have now been turned back to the Shepherd and Bishop of our souls (1 Peter 3). May the eternal almighty Father grant us to love him with our whole heart and follow him with all our strength—the God who, with the same Son [Col. 1873A] and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LVII. SECOND SUNDAY AFTER EASTER
Jesus said to his disciples: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John 10), etc.

The Lord and our Redeemer, dearest brothers, because he is meek and humble of heart, compares himself to lowly persons. For he does not say, “I am a good king, a good emperor,” but, “I am the good shepherd.”

Moreover, in the reading preceding this one, the Lord had spoken about the thief; consequently, he now speaks about the hired man and the good shepherd. There are therefore three: the thief, the hired man, and the shepherd, differing from one another in name, entrance, intention, work, and merit.

[Col. 1873B] The thief is the heretic, who steals Christ’s sheep from the unity of faith and the Church, drags them over to the devil’s side, and kills them. He is rightly called a thief because he loves theft—that is, darkness—in accordance with the saying: “Whoever does evil hates the light” (John 3). He is called a robber (*latro*) from hiding (*latere*), because he lies in hidden ambushes in order to kill the innocent. He does not dare preach his heresy openly before holy teachers, but secretly and furtively among the simple and ignorant.

Nor does he enter the sheepfold through the door, as the Lord testifies; rather, he climbs in elsewhere. For he does not enter through the humility of the door—that is, Christ—but through pride and empty glory, forcing himself into the number of the faithful and taking a name for himself. His intention, too, is not to benefit but rather to rule and harm.

Hence the Lord says: “The thief comes only [Col. 1873C] to steal, kill, and destroy” (John 10). He steals when he separates souls from the unity of the Church; he kills when he destroys them with the poison of treacherous heresy; he utterly destroys them when he ruins them completely by evil example.

His work is to corrupt the truth of the Scriptures by interpreting them perversely, to mix falsehood with truth, to attack, with the pen of the law, the head—that is, the divinity of Christ—, to cloak his wickedness under hypocrisy, and thus to deceive; then, to live off the possessions of those whom he deceives, and to destroy them through bad teaching and bad example.

His merit is utterly evil, because he is guilty not only of his own soul but of all the souls whom he destroys by bad example and teaching. As many souls as he destroys, so many condemnations will he suffer.

The hired man, however, is everyone who seeks to preside in the Church of God [Col. 1873D] not for the honor of God or the salvation of souls, but only for temporal payment. Such people are nearly all church prelates today—which is all the more lamentable—who do not eat in order to evangelize, but rather evangelize in order to eat; and, worse still, eat without evangelizing. They consume the offerings of the faithful and the sins of the people, yet do not correct or instruct them.

They seek a church not where the devotion of the faithful abounds, but where the abundance of revenues is greatest. They love more the multitude of wicked people who offer gifts than the church of the poor faithful who are unable to offer anything.

Why he is called a hired man is obvious: the name comes from the temporal payment for which [Col. 1874A] he preaches and when it fails, he ceases. Since he does not love the sheep but the profit he receives from them, he is not a shepherd, because he seeks to feed not the sheep but himself.

Hence the Lord says: “The hired man, who is not the shepherd and whose own the sheep are not…” (John 10). He does not make them his own through love, but makes them alien to himself through contempt.

The hired man’s entrance into the Church is not through Christ, the door, but rather through ambition, simony, and empty glory. Even if at times he enters without payment, and even if he has been called, nevertheless, because he seeks not what belongs to Jesus Christ but what belongs to himself, he enters not through Christ the door but through ambition.

The hired man’s intention, moreover, is vain and evil; whatever he does, preaches, or offers is unacceptable to God. [Col. 1874B] Hence the Lord speaks to them through the prophet Malachi, saying: “Who is there among you who will shut the doors and kindle my altar without payment? I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord, and I will not accept an offering from your hand” (Malachi 1).

The hired man’s work is to seek temporal honor and profit, to feed himself, to preach only in words, to corrupt by bad example, to neglect the care of the sheep, and to flee when the wolf comes.

“They love,” he says, “the first places at banquets, the first seats in the synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by men” (Matthew 23; Luke 20). And again through the prophet: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves! Are not flocks fed by shepherds? You ate the milk, clothed yourselves with the wool, but you did not feed my flock. [Col. 1874C] You killed what was fat, and you did not strengthen what was weak; you did not heal what was sick; you did not bind up what was broken; you did not bring back what had been cast away; you did not seek what had perished. Instead, you ruled them with harshness and power. And my sheep were scattered because there was no shepherd, and they became prey for every beast of the field” (Ezekiel 34).

It is as though he were saying: Although you fed yourselves on the prayers and sins of the people, you did not perform the shepherd’s office. You did not strengthen what had been broken by various tribulations with priestly assistance; you did not recall the erring to the way of salvation; you did not seek, with pastoral concern, the one lost in despair.

In the Gospel passage about which we are speaking, the Lord likewise says of the hired man: “He sees the wolf coming, abandons the sheep, and flees.” [Col. 1874D] The wolf is the devil, or his members, who lie in wait for Christ’s sheep.

If the devil tempts, drags away, and tears Christ’s sheep, the hired man flees because he refuses to watch over them. If an evil man oppresses the good, if he robs the orphan and widow, or if he disturbs the Church, the hired man flees, fearing to incur loss, because he refuses to exercise a stern judgment against the wicked.

And why does he flee? Because he is a hired man and has no concern for the sheep—that is, he loved the payment, not the sheep.

Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “You did not go up to confront them, nor did you set yourselves as a wall for the house of Israel” (Ezekiel 13). He goes up to confront them and sets himself as a wall for the house of Israel who rises courageously against persecutors and offers himself in defense of the Church.

[Col. 1875A] The hired man’s merit is temporal payment for whatever good he may have done; for the evil he has done by living badly and corrupting the sheep through bad example, it is spiritual condemnation. For what does a shepherd deserve who, through his negligence, allows the sheep entrusted to him to be torn apart and returns alone to the Lord?

Hence the prophet says: “Therefore, shepherds, hear the word of the Lord: Behold, I myself will come against the shepherds; I will require my flock from their hand, and I will make them cease from feeding my flock, so that the shepherds will no longer feed themselves” (Ezekiel 34). For, deprived in this life of every position of authority and subjected to every misery, they will no longer feed themselves as they used to on empty glory and the offerings of the faithful; rather, they will be fed by worms that do not die and by fire [Col. 1875B] that is not extinguished.

The shepherd, however, is the one who feeds the Lord’s sheep not for temporal payment but solely out of love for God and neighbor, seeking not what belongs to himself but what belongs to Jesus Christ (Philippians 2).

The one and supreme shepherd is he who, speaking by an antonomastic title of himself, says: “I am the good shepherd.” He is rightly called a shepherd because he feeds his sheep by his good example, good teaching, and his blood.

He is also, with the Father, the door and the doorkeeper—that is, the power through which he himself or his vicar enters to govern the sheep. Hence he says: “Whoever enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep; to him the doorkeeper opens” (John 10).

The intention of the supreme shepherd is not to rule over the sheep but to benefit them. He did not come to be served but to serve; he did not come here to reign but to suffer; he did not come to be fed [Col. 1875C] but to feed.

His office is to recognize his own sheep and call them by name; to lead and precede them; to feed and guard them; to oppose himself to the coming wolf; to lay down his life for his sheep; and to care for and gather them.

He recognizes his own sheep both through the election of predestination and through the approval of a good life. He calls them by name when he summons each one to himself through the particular virtue by which he knows that person: Abel through innocence, Job through patience, Moses through meekness, and David through humility.

He leads the sheep by bringing them out, guiding them along, and bringing them all the way. He brings them out of the pit of misery, guides them along the way of justice, and brings them to the pastures of life.

He goes before the sheep by his good example, showing them the way. He feeds them bodily and [Col. 1875D] spiritually, and finally eternally. He guards them from the snares of the devil, the contagion of sin, and the pit of hell, and no one can snatch them from his hand (Job 10).

He opposes himself to the coming wolf by exposing his snares, restraining his power, nullifying his efforts, and protecting the sheep from him. He lays down his life for the sheep because he redeems them from the power of the devil by his own blood.

He also cares for the sheep. Wherever he recognizes them as his own, he brings back and regathers those scattered by the wolf in the time of darkness, so that there may be one sheepfold and one shepherd.

Hence he says through the prophet: “Behold, I myself will seek my sheep. I will bring back what had been cast away; I will seek what had perished; I will bind up what had been broken; I will strengthen what had been weak; and I will guard what was fat and strong” (Ezekiel 34). This is what the great [Col. 1876A] and supreme shepherd does.

But we, his least shepherds and vicars, who ourselves also need a shepherd, should follow his footsteps as far as he grants us the ability. We are not hired men but shepherds. Seeking to feed not ourselves but the Lord’s sheep, let us enter the sheepfold not from elsewhere, like the thief and the hired man—that is, not through ambition, simony, or any vain and evil intention—but through the door, which is Christ, seeking his glory and the progress of his sheep.

Let us intend rather to benefit than to rule, seeking Christ’s glory, not our own. Let us imitate the zeal of the supreme shepherd. Let us recognize our own sheep: inwardly through confession, and outwardly through consideration of their life and conduct.

[Col. 1876B] Let us call the sheep by name, summoning each one according to his or her particular virtue to undertake the work. Let us lead the sheep out of the pit of sins. Let us guide them through the justice of good works and, as far as lies in us, bring them to the pastures of eternal joys.

Let us go before the sheep by the example of good works. Let us feed them spiritually, and also feed those who are in bodily need, so that at last we may be fed eternally with them.

Let us guard them as much as we can, through prayer and preaching, from the snares of the devil, the contagion of sin, and the punishments of hell. Let us oppose ourselves to the coming wolf—that is, the devil or an evil person—who wishes to rage against the sheep: driving away the devil through renunciations, and restraining the evil person by pastoral judgment.

For the sheep, if necessary, let us lay down not only our external possessions but also our life. For in this especially the good shepherd [Col. 1876C] is distinguished from the thief and the hired man.

Let us also seek out the scattered sheep and rescue from the devil’s power as many as we can, gathering them into Christ’s sheepfold. Let us bring back those cast away through error; seek those who have perished through sin; bind up those who are broken through repentance; strengthen those who are weak with consolations and exhortations; and guard those who are fat and strong so that they may persevere.

If we do this, our merit will undoubtedly be great, because we shall return to the Lord not alone but with the multiplied flock, receiving as many crowns as there are souls whom we have led to him. And, as it is written, “Those who have instructed many will shine like the stars of the firmament” (Daniel 12).

Behold, dearest brothers, you have heard our office [Col. 1876D] and our danger. Hear, in turn, your office and your danger.

The office of good sheep is to recognize the great and supreme shepherd through faith, love him, and lay down their lives for him through charity; to hear and follow him through obedience; and, together with him and under other shepherds, to become one sheepfold through love and communion in the sacraments.

Good sheep should also recognize the lesser shepherd, love him, hear him, follow him, and feed him. If they have any faults, they should cover them, and under him become one sheepfold with the others.

The sheep should recognize the shepherd—that is, observe and approve his good life and conduct. They should also love him as the spiritual father and guardian of their souls, and pray for him. For whoever does not love his shepherd despises hearing and following him.

[Col. 1877A] Good sheep should also hear their shepherd through obedience and follow him through imitation.

Since there are three—the hired man, the thief, and the shepherd—the thief, because he preaches badly and lives badly, should neither be heard nor followed. The hired man, because he preaches well but lives badly, should be heard but not followed. Hence the Lord says: “Whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not act according to their works, for they say things and do not do them” (Matthew 23).

The shepherd, however, because he preaches well and lives well, should be heard and followed. Hence the Lord says: “The sheep hear the shepherd’s voice and follow him; they do not listen to or follow a stranger, because they do not know the voice of strangers” (John 10).

[Col. 1877B] The sheep should also feed their shepherd—that is, provide him with temporal support—so that in his pastoral care he may be more watchful in proportion as he is freer from external concerns.

Hence the Apostle says: “Who feeds a flock and does not eat of its milk?” (1 Corinthians 9). And elsewhere: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your temporal things?” (ibid.).

The sheep should also not judge their shepherd. Rather, if he has any faults, they should cover and overlook them, remembering that Ham, who mocked his father’s nakedness, was cursed, whereas Shem and Japheth, who covered it, were blessed.

The sheep should also become one sheepfold under one shepherd through faith, charity, and unity in the sacraments, because the devil seizes solitary and wandering sheep.

[Col. 1877C] Let us therefore pray, brothers, that the Shepherd of shepherds, our Lord Jesus Christ, may grant us to fulfill the office of a good shepherd and to inspire in you the zeal of good sheep, so that both we and you may deserve to reach the pastures of eternal verdure: he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, God, forever. Amen.

# HOMILY LVIII. THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER EASTER

“I beseech you, as foreigners and pilgrims, to abstain from fleshly desires that wage war against the soul” (1 Peter 2), etc.

The Apostle does three things in this reading, dearest brothers. First, he exhorts us to live temperately within ourselves; second, to conduct ourselves well among the nations; third, to be subject and humble.

We attain the first by fleeing vices; the second by acquiring virtues; and the third by avoiding the pride that ordinarily arises from them.

[Col. 1877D] First, therefore, he exhorts us to live temperately and purely when he says: “I beseech you, as foreigners and pilgrims, to abstain from fleshly desires that wage war against the soul.” In these words, my brothers, he shows from what we must abstain, why we must abstain, and how.

From what? From fleshly desires—that is, from boastfulness, drunkenness, lust, sensual pleasure, greed, empty glory, and the other vices in which the flesh delights, and through which people become carnal by delighting in them.

Paul says of these: “Whoever sows in the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh” (Galatians 6).

Why must we abstain from them? Because they wage war against the soul. This is what Paul says: “The flesh desires against the spirit” (Galatians 5). Whoever is possessed by the vices and [Col. 1878A] desires of the flesh is emptied of spiritual virtues, because gluttony extinguishes temperance; drunkenness, sobriety; lust, chastity; sensual pleasure, discipline; greed, contempt for the world; and the remaining vices extinguish the remaining virtues.

Vices are called carnal because they arise from the flesh, the flesh delights in them, and through them a person becomes carnal. Virtues, however, are called spiritual because they arise from the pursuits of the spirit, the spirit delights in them, and through them a person becomes spiritual.

How, then, do I beseech you to abstain from fleshly desires? As foreigners and pilgrims.

All pilgrims are foreigners, but not all foreigners are pilgrims. For there are some foreigners—that is, people coming from elsewhere—who regard and love exile [Col. 1878B] as their homeland; they are also called settlers. Pilgrims, however, are so called from traveling and continually passing from place to place.

We too, brothers, are foreigners in the exile of this world, both because we were created in our first parent to be citizens of heaven, from which we were expelled into this exile through the first transgression, and because the greater part of us—the soul—is heavenly by origin, not earthly.

We are foreigners but not pilgrims if, having forgotten the heavenly homeland for which we were created, we love and cultivate the world as heaven, exile as homeland, and misery as blessed life.

Many among us are of this kind today—which is all the more grievous—brothers who, believing that there is no blessed life, cling to earthly things, quarrel, fight, and kill for earthly things, or erect [Col. 1878C] towers and construct costly buildings, as though they were going to live forever.

O wretched man! Every day you pass from childhood to youth, from youth to old age, from old age to death, and yet you consider yourself the possessor and citizen of the world! Why do people who are dying every day, why do the tombs and bones of the dead which you see every day, not move and warn you, so that you may understand that you are a foreigner and pilgrim in this world?

Believe your own eyes, therefore, and show that you are a foreigner and pilgrim in this world, and say with the prophet: “I am a foreigner and a pilgrim, like all my fathers” (Psalm 38). Weep and sigh, and say amid the miseries of this exile: “Woe is me, that my sojourning has been prolonged!” (Psalm 119).

A pilgrim does four things, brothers: every day he hastens toward the end of the journey; he follows the better [Col. 1878D] road; he is held back by no enticements; and he abstains not only from superfluous things but even from certain necessities.

We too, brothers, as true pilgrims, should hasten toward the end of this exile, toward our eternal homeland. Let us follow the better road: the straighter, smoother, and purer one.

Let it be straighter, as we turn neither to the right toward empty glory nor to the left toward disgrace. Let it be smoother, as we avoid the mountains of exaltation and the valleys of despair. Let it be purer, as we avoid the swamps of lust and sensual pleasures.

Let us also be held back by no enticements. Just as flowering meadows, clear rivers, and pleasant places do not hold back the pilgrim, so, brothers, let not the beauty of this age hold us back—not the luxury of riches, nor any pleasure, nor secular honor. [Col. 1879A]

Let us abstain, in the manner of pilgrims, not only from all superfluous things but also from certain necessities, avoiding an excess of cares, possessions, and riches. “Everyone who competes in the contest abstains from everything” (1 Corinthians 9); and, “Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content” (1 Timothy 6). Let us also, as far as we can, cut back and restrict even the necessities themselves, in the manner of a pilgrim.

The second part follows, in which the Apostle exhorts us to conduct ourselves well among the nations, saying: “Maintain good conduct among the nations.”

This is what Paul says: “Provide what is good not only in the sight of God but also in the sight of all people” (Romans 12).

There are three things, brothers, that shape good conduct: [Col. 1879B] living innocently, giving offense to no one, and seeking what is useful and pleasing for everyone.

Even if someone is good in himself, if he nevertheless scandalizes others by his words and example, he does not conduct himself well. Again, if he offends no one but refuses to benefit others, he does not conduct himself well among the nations. And again, if he offends no one and seeks to benefit others but does not know how to do so graciously and agreeably, he does not conduct himself well among the nations.

Therefore, whoever lives innocently, offends no one, and seeks what is useful and pleasing for all has good and gracious conduct among the nations.

What good does good conduct provide? It extinguishes infamy, closes the mouths of detractors, causes people to glorify God, and converts the wicked through good example.

Because of this manifold benefit, [Col. 1879C] good conduct should therefore be desired. Hence he adds: “So that, when they slander you as evildoers, they may see your good works and glorify God on the day of visitation.”

Therefore, brothers, let us pursue with every effort good conduct among the nations.

The third part follows, in which the Apostle exhorts everyone to the humility of submission. First he addresses free people, when he says: “Be subject.”

It is as though he were saying: Even if you are free by birth or by grace, do not become proud or contend for precedence, as lovers of this world do. Rather, be subject.

And because submission without merit is defective unless it is rendered as it ought to be, to whom it ought to be, and for the reason it ought to be, he adds: [Col. 1879D] “To every human creature for God’s sake.”

Submission must therefore be made not under compulsion but willingly. Forced submission is wretched. Again, even if it is made willingly, it is defective if it is offered to one to whom it ought not be offered; for serving the devil is defective.

Therefore he adds, “to every human creature”—that is, to every person—not only to those who are greater but also to equals and lesser ones. Following this, the apostolic lord calls himself the servant of the servants of God, in accordance with the saying: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclesiasticus 3).

Again, submission is not good if it is made in the proper manner and to the proper person but not for the proper reason. Whoever subjects himself improperly to another—for example, for the sake of temporal advantage, ambition, or greed—does not make a good submission.

Therefore the Apostle adds, “for God’s sake.” For [Col. 1880A] we ought to humble ourselves toward one another and submit to one another solely for his sake, since he himself did what he commanded: that we should minister to one another and wash one another’s feet.

“Whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by God for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of those who do good.”

This is what Paul says: “There is no authority except from God, and whoever resists authority resists the ordinance of God. Do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will receive praise from it. But if you do evil, be afraid, for it does not bear the sword without reason” (Romans 13).

For this reason, brothers, God established authorities in this world: to protect the good and restrain the wicked. Even if they sometimes abuse their authority by punishing the just and justifying the wicked, God nevertheless brings this about for the punishment of the wicked and the praise of the good.

[Col. 1880B] For this is God’s will: that by doing good you silence the ignorance of foolish people, who despise what they do not know and condemn what displeases them.

“As free people,” he says, “in mind, be subject to human beings—not as though you possessed freedom as a veil for wickedness, but as people free by birth or by grace.”

Here he touches upon certain people, brothers, for whom freedom becomes an occasion for sinning more—people who, the freer they are in body, are the more unrestrained in sinning. Because they are free by birth, they become slaves of sin and the devil.

But they should be like servants of God, who reject every servitude except servitude to sin, and desire no freedom more than freedom of mind.

“Honor everyone,” in accordance with the saying: “In showing honor, anticipate one another” (Romans 12). “Love the brotherhood,” both in affection and in action. [Col. 1880C] “Fear God,” with love, and love him with fear. “Honor the king,” in accordance with the saying: “To whom honor is due, honor; to whom tax, tax; to whom tribute, tribute” (Romans 13).

Finally, he exhorts servants to submit to their temporal masters in will just as in condition: “with all fear”—that is, not merely servile fear but filial fear—so that they may both fear and love them.

“Not only,” he says, “to the good and gentle, but also to the harsh”—that is, the severe and immoderate—“be subject.”

For this is grace: that the servants’ gentleness and patience may soften and moderate the masters’ lack of restraint.

Let us embrace the humility of voluntary submission with our whole heart, brothers, because it conquers the cruel by enduring patiently; it conquers the proud by humbling itself; it conquers the angry by showing gentleness; [Col. 1880D] it conquers the abusive by saying nothing in reply; it conquers the envious by fleeing glory; it conquers the greedy by being content with little; it merits the glory of human beings by submitting itself to everyone; it merits imitation of Christ by desiring not to be served but to serve; and it merits exaltation by God by always humbling itself.

May the almighty Lord grant us to attain this virtue in mind and body, through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

# HOMILY LIX. THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER EASTER

Jesus said to his disciples: “A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me, because I am going [Col. 1881A] to the Father” (John 16).

As our Lord and Redeemer was going to his passion, he foretold to his disciples what was going to happen to them. Why? For three reasons: to show that he was God, aware beforehand of all future events; to prepare his disciples in advance for adversity; and to teach them beforehand to hope for consolation amid adversity.

This reading has four parts. First, the Lord foretold to his disciples his departure and return. Second, the mutual questioning of the disciples, who did not understand this, is presented. Third, the Lord shows what was going to happen to the disciples either at his departure or at his return. Fourth, he explains it by means of a comparison.

As the Lord was therefore going to his passion, he first prepares them for his departure when he says: “A little while, and you will no longer see me.” But so that they would not despair because of his [Col. 1881B] absence, he promises them that after a little while they would see him again, adding: “And again a little while, and you will see me.”

And so that they would not cling only to his bodily presence, he says that after a little while he will ascend to the Father, so that they might desire to follow him to heaven.
