The Lord does something similar every day, dearest brothers, with his chosen ones, giving them consolation after adversity and adversity after consolation. If he always gave them adversity in this world, they would despair; and if he always gave them present prosperity, they would cling to it and would not desire the future.

Thus the kind and merciful Lord alternately turns his face toward and shows his face to his chosen ones in this world. He seems to turn his face away when, as though abandoning them, he allows them to suffer [Col. 1881C] persecution. He shows them his face when he causes them to advance in goodness.

But the Lord does both, brothers, through a great and beneficial dispensation. He allows them to be troubled so that they will not presume upon themselves; he causes them to prosper so that they will not fail.

Therefore, brothers, when we are placed in adversity, let us always hope for better things from God; in prosperity, however, let us always be afraid. In adversity let us hope in God, for, according to Solomon, “Who has hoped in the Lord and been put to shame?” (Ecclesiasticus 2).

In prosperity, however, let us fear, for “blessed is the one who is always fearful” (Proverbs 28). And blessed is the city that fears war while living in peace.

The second part follows, in which the disciples ask one another: “What does this mean that he says: ‘A little while, and you will not see me,’ etc.? We do not know what he is saying.”

But since those words of the Lord are not difficult, but rather clear to understand, what does it [Col. 1881D] mean that the disciples say, “We do not know what he is saying”? It means that although they believed him to be Christ, the Son of God, they did not believe that he would depart from them through his passion and return to them through his resurrection.

Although the Lord had often said that he would suffer and rise again, they did not believe that this would be fulfilled literally. Instead, they thought that some other mystery was signified by those words.

This is why they say: “We do not know what he is saying”—that is, we do not know from what meaning he is uttering these words.

They were inexperienced and still carnal, and by no means thought it fitting for the Son of God to descend to such a great humiliation of insults, to suffer and die in so disgraceful a manner. [Col. 1882A]

Hence Peter also said to him: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall never happen to you” (Matthew 16). But the Lord, rebuking this vain judgment of his, said: “Get behind me, Satan; you do not understand the things of God” (ibid.).

Because in this matter Peter was opposing the divine will, he is called Satan. He is invited to abandon what he judged wrongly and to follow the divine judgment.

Even today there are certain people like Peter and Christ’s still-inexperienced disciples who think that just people and ministers of God should in no way suffer poverty, disgrace, and affliction in this life, or be punished by the wicked with insults, injuries, torments, and death. They believe that those who do or suffer such things have been rejected by God in this life; conversely, they think that those who prosper [Col. 1882B] here are blessed and friends of God.

But to anyone who thinks in this way it must be said: “Get behind me, Satan; you do not understand the things of God.” For God tests his chosen ones here through much tribulation, as gold in a furnace, so that he may place them purer in his treasure.

The third part follows, in which the Lord confirms what he had foretold by the consequences that were going to befall the disciples, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you: You will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice.”

Because for a short time they did not see Christ, who had died and been placed in the tomb, the disciples wept, while worldly people, whose life the disciples had condemned, rejoiced. But because they saw him after the resurrection, the disciples’ sorrow was turned into joy, and the joy [Col. 1882C] of worldly people was turned into sorrow and fear.

And it is necessary not only for those people, brothers, but also for all the faithful to be sorrowful, weep, and lament in this valley of tears.

Why? For two reasons: both because of the grave consciousness of sins and because of the delay of the heavenly homeland.

When we remember what and how many sins we have committed, and how great a punishment has been prepared in hell for those sins, we must weep, because tears wash away the offense that one is ashamed to confess with the mouth.

Again, when amid the miseries of this exile we meditate on how great a blessedness has been prepared in heaven for the just, we must weep, in accordance with the saying: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered you, Zion” [Col. 1882D] (Psalm 136).

Therefore he brought forth this twofold weeping when he said: “You will weep and lament.”

We should all desire and love this twofold weeping, brothers, so that we may say with the Psalmist: “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God. My soul thirsted for God, the strong and living one; when shall I come and appear before the face of God? My tears have been my bread day and night” (Psalm 60).

If our heart is hard and dry, let us continually pray to the Lord that in his mercy he may grant us the grace of these two kinds of tears. Even if he sometimes delays, he will not always take away his mercy from us; rather, he will grant us the desired grace of tears. [Col. 1883A]

This is well signified by Achsah, the daughter of Caleb, who, seated on a donkey and going to her husband, wept, sighed, and said: “Give me a blessing, father. You have given me a southern and dry land; give me, I beg you, an upper and a lower watercourse.” And her father granted it to her (Joshua 15).

Our soul, too, while seeking the heavenly bridegroom in spirit, should sit upon a donkey—that is, restrain and govern the bestial movements of the flesh—sigh toward the heavenly Father and cry out to him, saying: “Give me your blessing, Lord. You have given me a dry and hard mind; give me, I beg you, an upper and a lower watercourse,” so that I may weep both for my sins and from longing for the heavenly homeland.

And the merciful Lord will at some time [Col. 1883B] hear our petition.

Let us therefore desire these holy tears, brothers, because they will undoubtedly be turned into joy when we rejoice over the complete remission of our sins and the attainment of the heavenly homeland, in accordance with the saying: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matthew 5; Luke 6).

Conversely, the joy of worldly people, who prosper in this life, spend their days in good things, and rejoice when they have done evil, will be turned into everlasting tears, in accordance with the saying: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn” (Luke 6).

The fourth part follows, in which the Lord demonstrates the foregoing points by means of a comparison, saying: “When a woman gives birth, she has sorrow, because her hour has come. But when she has given birth to the child, she no longer remembers the distress, because a human being has been born into the world.” This is what the Psalmist says by another comparison: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in rejoicing. Going, they went and wept, casting their seed; but coming, they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Psalm 125).

The Lord appropriately compares the soul of the righteous person to a pregnant woman. For just as a woman, through union with a man, conceives a child within, so the soul, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, conceives in the mind—through faith, hope, and charity—the reward of eternal fruit. He also appropriately compares the labor and suffering of the righteous in this life to the travail of a woman giving birth. For just as a woman patiently endures the pain in hope of the child who is to be born, so the righteous person patiently endures temporal labor and anxiety in hope of an eternal inheritance.

He likewise appropriately compares the reception of the eternal reward to the reception of a newborn child, since just as the awaited offspring is received only through labor, so the desired reward is received only through patience in temporal suffering. This stands against those who think they can reach the eternal homeland through temporal prosperity. Just as joy over a child’s birth makes the pain of childbirth forgotten, so the joy of eternal blessedness makes the labor of temporal tribulation forgotten, so that, compared with eternal joy, the temporal labor that preceded it seems to have been nothing, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Romans 8).

Conversely, the magnitude of the punishment of Gehenna among the reprobate will be so great that it will make them forget the joy of eternal prosperity, so that, compared with eternal punishment, temporal prosperity will appear to have been like smoke, or a dream.

Then, applying the preceding comparison, the Lord adds: “You indeed now have sorrow”—that is, over my departure—“but I shall see you again,” after the resurrection, “and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you.”

We too, my brothers, while we are tested and afflicted in this world, as though the Lord were abandoning us, have sorrow. But if we have endured adversity with equanimity and have given thanks to God amid our sorrow, then after the general resurrection he will see us again, and the Lord will be seen by us face to face; and our heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take our joy from us. May he grant this to us who, as perfect Trinity, lives and reigns, God. Amen.

# HOMILY LX

## FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER EASTER

“Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1), etc.

My brothers, in this reading the Apostle does four things. First, he says that every good thing is from God. Second, he shows that no evil comes from God. Third, he shows that God gives good things freely. Fourth, he exhorts us to pursue good things and flee evil things.

Thus, first showing that every good thing is from God, he says: “Every good gift,” etc.

There are, my brothers, four kinds of good things. Some good things are temporal, some natural, some spiritual, and some heavenly. Temporal goods are those possessed by us externally, such as property and possessions, wealth, powers, and honors. These are indeed good in their nature, since they were created by a good Creator, in accordance with the words: “God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good” (Genesis 1). For those who use them well, they are material for good action; for those who use them badly, they are an occasion of evil action. Temporal goods are worth no more to the wicked than a sword is to a madman.

Natural goods are those that God grants to each person at creation, such as the goods of the soul and the goods of the body. The goods of the soul include reason, memory, and foresight. The goods of the body include beauty, strength, speed, and things of this kind. Although these too are good in their nature, they become evil for those who use them badly, just as they are good for those who use them well.

Spiritual goods include faith, hope, charity, wisdom, justice, fortitude, temperance, and the other virtues, as well as the other gifts of the Holy Spirit. These are called, by excellence, gratuitous gifts, or graces, because they make people pleasing to God and good, and because they can neither be possessed nor abused by the wicked.

Heavenly goods are immortality, freedom from suffering, and the other goods that will be bestowed upon the elect in the resurrection. Of these it is said: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2).

There are therefore these four kinds of good things. The first two are common to both the good and the wicked; the remaining two belong only to the good, and are therefore more greatly to be desired. The temporal is merely a good gift; the natural is better; the spiritual is best; but the heavenly gift is a perfect gift.

Nevertheless, every gift—whether good, better, or best—and every perfect gift is from above. Therefore, my brothers, let no one deceive himself. Let no one attribute the good he possesses to himself; let no one ascribe it to his own strength, skill, or labor. Rather, let him give thanks to the highest and eternal Father, from whom every good thing descends.

Let him regard temporal and natural goods as small, since they are shared even by the wicked. Let him strive with all his strength to acquire spiritual and heavenly good, and let him ask for them from the heavenly Father with desires, prayers, and sighs. He is the Father of all lights: whether of the temporal light that he created at the beginning to illuminate the world; or of the spiritual light by which he illuminates sinners inwardly; or of the eternal light that he prepared in the heavenly realm for his angels and elect. He gives temporal light for consolation, spiritual light for merit, and eternal light as a reward.

Therefore, my brothers, we who see temporal light should use it in such a way that through it we may come to eternal light. But you who do not see temporal light should not take it heavily that you lack the light possessed by perjurers and unbelievers, serpents and toads. Let us all strive to possess spiritual light, through which we may deserve to reach the eternal light in which God will be seen.

The second part follows, in which it is shown that evils do not come from God, when it is added: “With whom there is no change, nor shadow of alteration.”

Therefore, my brothers, there is no change in him, because he is altered by no change. He is not changed through generation or corruption, since he has neither beginning nor end; nor through increase or diminution, since he cannot become greater or less; nor through alteration or change of place, since he is unchangeable and immeasurable.

Hence it was said of him by a certain wise man:

> Moving the world, you are not moved;  
> Holding a place, you are not held;  
> Changing time, you are not changed;  
> Establishing what wanders, you do not wander.

Thus the immutable God himself changes creatures, but does not transform them, since he does not corrupt them through vice beyond their natural goodness. This is explained more clearly when it is added: “Nor shadow of alteration”—that is, nor darkness casting its shadow in turn.

For, as John says: “God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all” (1 John 1). He illuminates; he does not darken. There are, however, different kinds of darkness: the darkness of night, the darkness of adversity, the darkness of eternal condemnation, and the darkness of sin.

God alternately overshadows the day through death. Hence it is said to him:

> Eternal Maker of all things,  
> Who govern night and day,  
> And grant the times their times,  
> So that you may lessen weariness.

God likewise alternately overshadows prosperity through adversity. Hence he also testifies concerning himself: “Forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evil” (Isaiah 45).

God overshadows the life of the reprobate through the darkness of eternal condemnation, since at the end he will cast them into the outer darkness. But God never alternately overshadows the human mind with inner darkness—that is, with the darkness of vices. He places the brightness of virtues in minds, but never places within them the darkness of vices.

If Pharaoh (Exodus 4) and other wicked people are said to have been hardened or blinded by him, he did this not by changing their evil disposition, but by withdrawing grace.

Therefore, my brothers, let us always say that we possess good things from God, not from ourselves. And let us always say that we possess evil things not from God, but from ourselves. Let us not excuse ourselves by accusing God, in the manner of the old Adam, saying: “I cannot fulfill God’s severe commands; I cannot resist vice, because by nature I am weak and powerless.” For this is as if we were to say: “This is not to be attributed to me, but to God, who created me such.”

Shame upon such wickedness! We attribute iniquity to the just, cruelty to the pious, and accuse the Lord of ignorance, as though he did not know what he had made and did not know what he had commanded. It is as though, forgetting human frailty—of which he himself is the author—he had imposed upon humanity commands that it could not bear.

But, my brothers, no one knows our strength better than the one who gave it to us. He who is just did not command anything impossible. Nor will he, being pious, condemn a person for what that person could not avoid.

The third part follows, in which it is shown that God gives us his good things freely, when it is added: “Of his own will he begot us by the word of truth, that we might be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures.”

What he says here about one grace he leaves to be understood of all the others. The first and greatest grace that God bestows upon us here is that he regenerates us—who were begotten through the desire of the flesh as children of wrath—through the grace of baptism as children of adoption and mercy. He makes children of election from children of condemnation, and children of God from children of the devil.

Thus God regenerates us by the word, that is, through the word of truth. He does not say “through baptism alone,” because the word also cleanses in baptism. For if you remove the word, what is the water of the baptistery except water?

God therefore regenerates us as his children through the word of truth—that is, through his Son, or through the word of faith that the Son himself preached to us. This is what John says: “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John 1).

He did this not on account of our merits, which did not exist, but willingly—that is, solely by his own gratuitous will. Hence John says: “In this the love of God appeared, not as though we had loved him, but because he first loved us” (1 John 4).

If it is asked why God chose us as his children, the true and complete answer is: because he willed it. This is especially clear because he was compelled by no necessity—for no one can compel him—nor was he moved by his own advantage, since he has no need of our good things; nor was he bound by our merits, since none had preceded.

But if some merits appear to follow, they are undoubtedly the result of his grace, since he himself works in us both the will and the accomplishment (Philippians 2).

Let us therefore give thanks to God, my brothers, because solely through his own gratuitous will he separated us from the number of the reprobate, chose us as his children, enriched us with his benefits, and prepared eternal blessedness for us—provided that we persevere in the grace of baptism and obey his commandments.

But why did he willingly beget us through the word of truth? So that we might be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures, namely, so that we might be restored to that dignity and primacy among creatures in which we were created.

Humanity is the beginning of creatures—not in time, but in cause and dignity. Humanity is not the beginning of creatures in time, because humanity was not created before the other creatures; rather, the other creatures were created before humanity. Humanity is the beginning of creatures in cause, because the other creatures were created for humanity, not humanity for the creatures. Humanity is also the beginning of creatures in dignity, because it surpasses the other creatures through the prerogative of dominion and reason.

Let us therefore reclaim, my brothers, with the help of divine grace, the prerogative and dominion over creatures that we had in the beginning. Let us not subject ourselves through avarice to temporal things, but rather rule over them. Let us not admire them, but rather despise them, spending them in the service of God and for our own and our neighbor’s needs.

The fourth part follows, in which the Apostle urges us to follow good things and avoid evil things, when he adds: “Let every person be swift to hear”—understand, the word of God.

We must not open our ears to hear empty talk, buffoonery, flattery, detraction, and blasphemies; rather, we must close them, lest poisonous words entering through them be able to suffocate the soul. Hence the Wise Man says: “Fence your ears with thorns, lest they hear an evil tongue” (Ecclesiasticus 28).

“Slow,” he says, “to speak and slow to anger.”

Because the Apostle was speaking to simpler people, he urges them to be swift to hear the word of God and slow to speak, since truth is heard more safely than it is preached. This is directed against those who become teachers before they have become disciples, presuming to teach what they have not learned.

But every person, my brothers, ought to use the ears more than the tongue; and when he speaks, he should speak with forethought, in accordance with the saying of the Wise Man:

> When you wish to say something to another, first say it to yourself.

Let us moderate this slowness, however, so that we neither speak before the proper time nor remain silent when the time is right. For just as excessive haste in speaking is vicious, so is excessive slowness.

It is written: “Woe is me, because I was silent!” (Isaiah 6.) The Prophet does not ask that a wall be placed before his mouth, but a door—one that is now closed and now opened—when he says: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth and a door around my lips” (Psalm 140).

The command to be slow to anger should not be understood in the same way as the command to be slow to speak. For it is not sometimes good to become angry, as it is sometimes good to speak; rather, we are commanded that, if we cannot always avoid anger, we should at least avoid it as much as we can and immediately restrain and delay the movement of anger as it arises. Delay and slowness are a remedy for anger, and when anger is delayed, it is softened.

“Anger,” he says, “does not produce the justice of God.” This is litotes: it says less and signifies more. For when a person’s mind is disturbed by anger, it produces injustice.

Therefore, brothers, learn to avoid anger and to be gentle and meek. For the more meek and tranquil you are, the more like and close to God you will be, in whom no agitation occurs.

To enable you to avoid anger and injustice, uproot their roots from yourselves: all impurity and abundance of wickedness. In this way, you will not be impure in yourselves in heart or malicious toward your neighbors. And so, with the meekness of obedience, receive the implanted word—that is, the word sown in you.

The order, my brothers, is fitting. Unless the thorns and thistles of impurity, wickedness, and the other vices are first torn out of us, the word will not be able to germinate in us. For it is written: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 16).

Therefore, my brothers, first tear the thorns of vices from your hearts, so that the word of God preached may firmly remain in you, take root in you through continual remembrance, be cultivated in you through frequent meditation, flower through good will, bear fruit through good works, and save your souls through perseverance—the word of God working in you. He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# HOMILY LXI

## FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER EASTER

“I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’” (John 16.)

About to go through his Passion to the Father, our Lord and Redeemer, my dearest brothers, foretold his departure to his disciples, lest, if he departed suddenly and unexpectedly, he should make them excessively sorrowful.

In this reading, as we have heard, he foretells four things: that he is going to the Father; that this will be beneficial for them; that he will send them a Comforter; and that the Comforter himself will bestow good things upon them.

First, then, he foretells that he is going to the Father, when he adds: “I am going to him who sent me.”

What is this, Lord, that you say? You are always with the Father, and the Father is always with you. How can you go to him with whom you are always one and the same? When you say this on earth, are you not with the Father in heaven, and is the Father not with you on earth?

My brothers, how did the Son of God descend from the Father to earth, and how did he ascend from the world to the Father? He descended humbled and ascended glorified; he descended through the humility of incarnation and ascended through the exaltation of glorification.

He descended through humiliation, dissimilarity, and obscurity of place. Through dissimilarity, because from Creator he became creature, and from impassible he became passible. Through obscurity of place, because he who is seen to exist more fully in heaven, through the purity of that place, appeared incarnate in the world, in which God seems to exist less fully because of the obscurity of the place.

He also ascended through the exaltation of glorification, in accordance with the words: “You crowned him with glory and honor” (Psalm 8). He ascended also through the withdrawal of dissimilarity, because from passible he became impassible, and from mortal immortal. He ascended also through the purity of place, because according to the flesh he ascended to that place where the divinity appears more clearly through the purity of the element.

“And none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’” For when you see me ascending into heaven, there will be no need for you to ask where I am going, since you will see that I am ascending to heaven. Whoever asks is doubtful.

But although you know that I am going to the Father—to whom, certainly, going is glory and joy—nevertheless sorrow will fill your heart. For if, my dearest brothers, we cannot help grieving at the departure of one of our friends and intimates, how could the disciples not grieve at the departure of their supreme teacher, our God and Lord, whom they loved so greatly?

It was therefore necessary that these things be told them and that the consolation soon to come be promised to them.

Moreover, my brothers, every action of Christ is instruction for the Christian. Just as Christ is the Son of God by nature, so the Christian is a child of God by grace. Just as he was ineffably begotten by the Father, so the Christian is invisibly regenerated through baptism by God the Father. Just as Christ was sent into the world to fulfill the Father’s dispensation, so the Christian is sent by God the Father into the world to fulfill his will.

Therefore, if, following Christ’s example, the Christian neither speaks nor acts from himself but from God and seeks the Father’s glory, then, having brought this life to a good conclusion, he can also say with Christ: “I am going to him who sent me.” No one should doubt or ask concerning such a departure of the righteous person, “Where are you going?”—as certain worldly people, being of little faith, are accustomed to say: “Who knows where the souls of the dying go?”

But the faithful person neither asks nor doubts. Rather, he knows without doubt that the soul of the righteous goes to the rest prepared for it by God. Although this is true, the faithful person still cannot look upon the death of the righteous without sorrow, since it is pious to rejoice for Martin, and it is pious to weep for Martin.

The second part follows, in which the Lord shows that his ascension to the Father will benefit the disciples, when he adds: “But I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go.” He then explains why it is expedient: “For if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you.”

What is this, Lord, that you say? Was not the Spirit, the Paraclete, inseparably with you and is he not so still? Did you not also give him to the disciples on earth? How, then, can the Paraclete not come, when he is essentially everywhere?

My brothers, for the Holy Spirit to come into us means nothing other than that his gift and grace come into us. The Lord had already given the disciples the grace of the Holy Spirit on earth, but not as fully as on the day of Pentecost.

But why, my brothers, would the Holy Spirit not come fully to the disciples unless the Lord went to the Father? Because, as long as the disciples saw the Lord bodily, they did not raise their minds more fully to contemplation of the divinity.

His bodily appearance therefore had to be taken away from them, and he had to be carried up into heaven before their eyes, so that in their minds they might follow the Lord to heaven and always sigh with desire for the place where they had seen the Lord ascend.

But even today, my brothers, unless the consolation of temporal prosperity is withdrawn from us for a time, our desire is not raised toward the joys of eternal consolation. Hence the bride in the Song of Love says:

> Flee, my beloved,  
> And be like a goat  
> And a fawn of the deer  
> Upon the mountains of spices (Song 8).

When a goat or a fawn of the deer happens to be seen by a person, how quickly it flees and suddenly withdraws itself from human sight! It is therefore as though the bride were saying: “If, Lord Jesus Christ, your temporal and bodily departure is thus necessary to me, flee through bodily departure upon the mountains of contemplation and virtue, so that our desire may follow you there.”

Let us also pray, my brothers: Lord Jesus Christ, if you know that it is beneficial for us, let the consolation of temporal prosperity be withdrawn from us, so that our desire may be directed more and more toward the joys of eternal consolation.

The third part follows, in which the Lord promises that he will send the Holy Spirit to the disciples, when he adds: “But if I go, I will send him to you.”

It is as though he were saying: “Do not grieve over my bodily departure, for I will not leave you orphaned; I will not leave you desolate. Rather, I will send you a Comforter.”

The Holy Spirit is called the Comforter because it is his work to inspire consolation in minds, a remedy for those who grieve, counsel for those without guidance, wisdom for the foolish, and joy for the sorrowful.

Hence the Prophet says: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Psalm 93 [citation as printed: Psal. XCXIII]). And again concerning the same Spirit: “He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds” (Psalm 146).

Since such great and useful consolation could not be given to the Apostles unless the Lord departed from them bodily, they had to pray that he might be bodily absent from them for a time, so that the surpassing consolation of the Holy Spirit might be given to them invisibly.

We too must pray, my dearest brothers, that although the consolation of temporal prosperity may be withdrawn from us for a time, the consolation of the Holy Spirit may be invisibly granted to us.

The fourth part follows, in which the four benefits that the Holy Spirit was to confer upon the disciples are shown: correction, teaching, prophecy, and power.

That he was to give them correction is shown when it is said: “When he has come, he will convict the world of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment.”

The Holy Spirit convicts worldly people either through the mouths of preachers or through inward inspiration. Through the mouths of preachers, as when he cries out through John: “Brood of vipers, who will teach you to flee from the coming wrath? Produce worthy fruits of repentance” (Matthew 3).

Through inward inspiration, as when he inspires compunction inwardly without a preacher. Hence David says to the Lord: “You have shaken the earth”—that is, the earthly mind—“you have shaken it,” so that, moved from its security, it might fear and be troubled (Psalm 59), so that it might distrust itself.

But since, Lord, driving someone to despair is diabolical and not your work, heal its wounds through grace, for it has been shaken (same passage).

The Holy Spirit convicts the world of three things. First, of the sin of unbelief, which he explains by adding: “Because they did not believe in me”—that is, when they saw me bodily present.

He also convicts it of righteousness, namely, the righteousness of faith. The righteousness of faith is to believe what you do not see. He explains this by adding: “Because I go to the Father, and you will no longer see me.” It is as though he were saying: “He will convict them because they were unwilling to believe either in me present in the flesh or in me seated at the right hand of the Father.”

He also convicts the world of judgment, that is, of condemnation, because he says: “The prince of this world has already been judged.” It is as though he were saying: “He will strike them with fear, lest they be condemned as the devil has been condemned.”

That he was to confer teaching is shown when he says: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. When the Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth”—understand, all the truth necessary for you.

In this the Lord gives teachers a model for judging the character of those to whom they speak: they should teach simpler things to the simple and more perfect things to the mature.

This is directed against certain people who preach subtler and more obscure matters to the simple, or obscure plain things with more obscure words, wishing to display to others how much they know rather than to benefit them. Yet the Teacher of teachers, the Lord Jesus Christ—in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Colossians 2)—taught simple people simple things in simple speech, leaving room for the Holy Spirit, who on the day of Pentecost suddenly made the uneducated wise.

The Apostle to the Gentiles likewise says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians 3).

“When that Spirit comes,” he says, etc.

Just as the Holy Spirit is called the spirit of counsel and the spirit of consolation, so he is called the spirit of truth. And why? He adds: “Because he will teach you all truth”—understand, all the truth necessary for you.

This distinguishes him from evil spirits, which are called spirits of error and falsehood, because they teach every error and falsehood. Even if they sometimes speak certain truths, they speak them in order to deceive.

Therefore, I marvel at the madness of those who do not fear or hesitate to consult the devil and believe him. It is utterly insane to consult the enemy of one’s salvation about one’s salvation.

To show that the operation of the Son and the Holy Spirit is the same, the Holy Spirit will teach nothing except what the Son would have taught if the disciples had been able to bear it. For he does not speak from himself, but just as he is from the Father and the Son, so he knows and speaks from the Father and the Son. For the Holy Spirit’s hearing from the Father and the Son means nothing other than his knowing from the Father and the Son.

That the Holy Spirit was also to confer prophecy is shown when he adds: “He will announce to you the things that are to come.” This was fulfilled in John the Evangelist, who through the Holy Spirit wrote the book of the Apocalypse, namely, a prophetic book; and in the prophet Agabus and the daughters of Philip, who foretold future things in the Spirit.

That he was to confer the grace of miraculous powers is shown when he adds: “He will glorify me.” He will glorify me when he makes my disciples shine with powers and signs in my name. He will glorify me when he makes my glory known throughout the whole world.

Therefore, my brothers, let us pray to that Paraclete, that spirit of counsel, spirit of consolation, and teacher of truth, that he may convict us inwardly of sin; that he may shake the rashness of our mind inwardly; that he may make our sins displeasing to us; that he may convict us and set us before our own face, so that, ashamed of our ugliness, we may accuse ourselves and weep over our sins; and that he himself may heal us through his mercy, he who heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds (Psalm 146).

To him be honor and glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# HOMILY LXII

## FIFTH SUNDAY AFTER EASTER

“Be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves” (James 1), etc.

In this reading, my dearest brothers, the Apostle James exhorts us not merely to hear the word of God but also to do it.

First, he shows what the person who is merely a hearer of the word of God resembles. Second, he shows what good the person who acts upon it gains. Third, he shows what false religion is. Fourth, he shows what true religion is.

First, then, concerning the hearer of the word of God who does not act upon it, he shows what such a person suffers: namely, that he is deceived by himself. His expectation is frustrated, because it is false; and his future hope is frustrated, because it will be empty. In the future it will profit him nothing to have heard the word of God when he refused to do it.

He shows this by a comparison, saying: “For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he shall be compared to a man observing the face of his birth in a mirror. He observed himself and went away, and immediately forgot what he had been like.”

Just as it benefited the person nothing to see his own face in a mirror if he immediately forgot it, so hearing the word of God benefits nothing the person who refused to do it; indeed, it harms him.

Hence the Lord says concerning the Jews: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin”—understand, not as much sin as they had, because they heard and did not act (John 15). And elsewhere: “The servant who knew the will of his lord and did not do it shall be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12). The Apostle Peter likewise says: “It would have been better for them not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back from it” (2 Peter 2).

Therefore, brothers, let none of you deceive himself by thinking that he will find mercy because he frequently hears Mass, the law of God, and preaching. The person who hears and does not obey binds and deceives himself all the more.

But for this reason no one should say, as some are accustomed to say: “I will not hear the word of God, because if I heard it and did not obey, I would become more guilty.” Let no one, brothers, say this, because “the ignorant person will be ignorant” (1 Corinthians 14). And again: “The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit; he refused to understand, so as to do good” (Psalm 35).

Ignorance that arises from contempt excuses no one; rather, it accuses him, especially in a matter that it was necessary to know. Thus, just as the person who hears the word of God and does not obey is guilty, so too is the person who refuses to hear when he could obey.

The Apostle appropriately compares Sacred Scripture to a mirror. Just as women who desire to please their bridegroom look at their faces in a mirror so that they may correct what is ugly and further adorn what is beautiful, so faithful souls who desire to please Christ look at themselves in Sacred Scripture, so that they may cleanse whatever is ugly in themselves and further adorn whatever is beautiful.

Let us therefore consider, brothers, the face—that is, the knowledge—of our birth in the mirror of this Scripture: “A human being, born of a woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries” (Job 14).

Here we can consider what a human being is: guilty through conception, ever fearful because of the brevity of life, and wretched through the miseries of guilt and punishment.

The second part follows, in which it is shown what good the doer of the word gains, when it is added: “But whoever looks intently into the law of freedom and perseveres in it, becoming a doer of the work and not a forgetful hearer, this person shall be blessed in his deed.”

Here the Apostle calls the Gospel the law of freedom, because it frees us from the slavery of the old law, from the slavery of sin, and from the slavery of the devil. Whoever looks intently into it by understanding it, perseveres in it by continually meditating upon it, becomes a doer of the work by obeying it rather than a forgetful hearer, and will be blessed in his deed.

There are, my brothers, certain people who look intently into the law, understanding it well, but do not persevere in it except as long as they perceive temporal profits in it, as is the case with certain preachers and priests.

There are also some who persevere continually in it by meditating, reading, and investigating, as do certain learned teachers, but not in order to practice it; rather, they do so in order to appear wise.

Neither the former nor the latter are blessed. Only the doer of the law will be blessed.

The third part follows, in which it is shown what religion is false, when he adds: “If anyone thinks that he is religious, but does not bridle his tongue and deceives his own heart, his religion is worthless.” In one example he shows what is understood universally. For that religion is universally false which, while avoiding the other vices, neglects to avoid one. Just as no one is healthy unless he has avoided every kind of illness, [Col. 1893D] so no one will truly be religious unless he avoids at least all kinds of grave vice.

For there are, as it is read here, some who frequent the church, fast, pray, practise continence, and give alms, yet, while avoiding the other vices, do not bridle their tongue alone. Rather, they deceive their own heart, because the more religious and freer from sin they think themselves to be, the more unrestrained they are with their tongue: judging the sins of others, slandering, cursing, and devoting themselves to empty and excessive talk. But their religion is worthless, because, as Solomon says: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. XVIII). And James likewise: “Just as a small fire sets a great forest ablaze, so also the tongue, though it is a small member, defiles the whole life” (James III).

Similarly, there are others in the Church who, although they have subdued the body, avoided lust, [Col. 1894A] bridled the tongue, and fled the other vices, nevertheless do not guard against greed. They say that they are providing either for their sons or daughters, or for their household, or for the poor, and thus they deceive their own heart, although it is written: “Every greedy person, which is the service of idols, has no share in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Eph. V). Therefore, my brothers, guard your heart with every vigilance. For what good is it to have watched over the other gates of a city if the enemy has entered through one? Therefore, my brothers, it is of no benefit to have avoided the other vices if one still remains.

The fourth part follows, in which it is shown what true religion is, when he adds: “Holy and undefiled religion before God and the Father is this: to visit …” As though he were saying: Truly religious is the person who is holy and undefiled before God [Col. 1894B] the Father and for the sake of God the Father. He shows in what respect such a person is holy when he adds: “To visit orphans in their tribulations.” In what respect he is undefiled he shows when he adds: “And to keep oneself undefiled from this world.”

Religion, my brothers, is the worship owed to God. It is called *religio* from *religare*, “to bind again,” because it binds and unites us to the one God. As James indicates here, it consists in three things: fear of God, purity of oneself, and love of one’s neighbour.

The fear of God is not servile but filial, so that fear may be joined with love, and love with fear. God is to be feared because he is God, and loved because he is Father. True religion therefore consists in fear and love of God, and in observance of his commandments. Hence Solomon says: “Fear God and observe his commandments; [Col. 1894C] for this is the whole human being” (Eccl. XII).

The observance of God’s commandments consists in two things: purity of oneself, so that a person keeps himself undefiled by the vices of this world; and love of one’s neighbour, so that he visits orphans, widows, and the needy in their tribulations.

Therefore, brothers, let us fear and love God together: out of fear, avoiding offending him; and out of love, striving to obey him. For love of him, let us keep ourselves undefiled by the vices of this world—by gluttony, lust, covetousness, greed, envy, anger, pride, and the other vices—and let us embrace the virtues opposed to them: abstinence, continence, contempt for the world, generosity, gentleness, love, humility, and the other virtues.

Let us also visit the needy in their tribulations: feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, offering hospitality to travellers, clothing the naked, visiting the sick and the imprisoned, redeeming captives, burying the dead, correcting those who go astray, giving counsel to the uninstructed, [Col. 1894D] and carrying out the other works of mercy.

For this, brothers—this is holy and undefiled religion. May almighty God grant us both its merit and its reward. Amen.

## HOMILY LXIII. THE FIFTH SUNDAY AFTER EASTER

“Jesus said to his disciples: Truly, truly, I say to you, whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John XVI), etc.

This reading, my brothers, is divided into four parts. First, the Lord instructs his disciples [Col. 1895A] to ask; second, he foretells when they will know how to ask rightly; third, he shows that at that time the Father will be ready to hear them; fourth, the disciples’ response is added.

First, while instructing his disciples to ask, he says: “Truly, truly, I say to you, whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you.” In these words the Lord instructs us, my brothers, that if we want what we ask to be given to us, we must ask for something, ask the Father, and ask in the name of Jesus Christ. If these three things come together, he confirms that it will be given to us by doubling the affirmative adverb *amen*.

The person asks for “something”—that is, for the one thing—which the Psalmist requests when he says: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. XXVI). And concerning this [Col. 1895B] the Lord says elsewhere: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness” (Matt. VI).

In comparison with temporal goods, that is truly “something,” because it is perpetual, unchangeable, and sufficient. Whatever is temporal, however, is not truly “something,” because it is changeable, fleeting, and insufficient. Hence none of those things satisfies those who possess them. Concerning them Solomon says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccl. I). For that which now is and presently is not does not truly exist.

Whoever therefore asks for such a thing asks for nothing. Hence the Lord adds here: “Until now you have asked nothing in my name.” Indeed, the disciples had asked the Lord for many things. James and John had asked that one sit at his right hand and the other at his left in his kingdom (Matt. XX). They had asked that fire come down from heaven and consume the Samaritans (Luke IX). The blessed Virgin had asked for wine at the wedding [Col. 1895C] (John II). The disciples had asked for the health of the Canaanite woman’s daughter (Matt. XV). Yet the Lord says to them: “Until now you have asked nothing.” Because they were seeking temporal things, they were asking for nothing.

But he shows what they ought to ask when he adds: “Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.” “And you will receive,” that is understood, if you ask the Father and ask in Jesus’ name.

In this life, my brothers, there cannot be complete joy, but only partial, insufficient, and brief joy. It is partial because, if things go well in one respect, they do not go well for this person in every respect. It is insufficient because, in the respect in which things go well for him, he wishes them to go still better. It is brief because, as Solomon says: “Laughter will be mingled with sorrow, and mourning takes possession of the end [Col. 1895D] of joy” (Prov. XIV).

In the future life, on the contrary, there will be complete joy, because it will be universal, sufficient, and eternal: universal, because everything will turn out well; sufficient, because no one will desire things to turn out better; eternal, because no sorrow will follow it.

Therefore, my brothers, taught by the Lord, let us not ask the Lord for evil things, as some do when they ask for harm to their neighbour or the death of an enemy. Nor should we ask the Lord for empty things, as some do when they ask for riches, glory, honours, pleasures, and worldly joys. Rather, let us ask for unchangeable good; let us ask that our joy may be complete.

Yet whenever we ask for temporal goods, let us ask for them on account of the kingdom of heaven and for the sake of attaining the kingdom of heaven. For I do not deny [Col. 1896A], my brothers, that temporal things should be requested from the Lord, especially since the Church prays daily for peace, health, and fertility. But these things must be requested with right intention as to their end and with discernment regarding the conditions.

Whoever asks for them for their own sake, and not for the sake of attaining the kingdom of heaven, asks wrongly and does not deserve to be heard. Hence James says: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (James IV), as he indicates, “so that you may spend it on your passions.”

Again, whoever asks for temporal things without discerning the conditions asks foolishly and does not deserve to be heard. Paul indiscreetly asks that the angel of Satan be taken away from him, although it was necessary for him to preserve his humility. Thus he is not heard, but is told: “Power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. XII). The same man says of himself there: “Lest the greatness of the revelations [Col. 1896B] should exalt me, a thorn in the flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan to strike me.”

Therefore, my brothers, let us ask for the kingdom of God for its own sake and as our chief concern. Let us ask for temporal things not for their own sake but for the sake of that kingdom, and with discernment regarding the conditions: namely, that he give them to us if it pleases him and if he knows that they are expedient for us—for he knows better than we do what is expedient for us.

He himself demonstrated this manner of asking by his own example. With a condition, he asked that the cup of his Passion be taken away from him, saying: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI). The dignity of heavenly and spiritual goods, however, is so great that we ask for them absolutely and without condition.

From whom should we ask? From God the Father. Although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one source and giver, the Church nevertheless directs almost all prayers to the Father, a few to the Son, and fewer still to the Holy Spirit. But at the command of our mediator Jesus Christ, let us ask the Father for all good things, since he is the source of the Son and [Col. 1896C] of the Holy Spirit, and of all good things.

Thus in the Lord’s Prayer we direct our speech to God the Father, calling him Father, because, like a father, he is gracious toward our just petitions—provided that through obedience and holiness we prove ourselves worthy sons of his. Otherwise, as degenerates and unworthy persons, he does not hear us at all.

For it is written: “Whoever stops his ear so as not to hear the law, his prayer is accursed” (Prov. XXVIII). And Isaiah says: “When you stretch out your hands toward me, I will turn my face away from you; and when you multiply [Col. 1896D] your prayers, I will not hear you. For your hands are full of blood” (Isa. I).

In what should we ask? In the name—that is, in the faith—of Jesus Christ. We do this if we, as true Christians, hold to Christ’s true faith and teaching. In Christ and through Christ our mediator, who is the source and accomplisher of our redemption, through whom we have access and who intercedes for us with the Father, we shall obtain salvation from the Father.

Hence almost all prayers conclude: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ.” For “there is no other name under heaven, nor on earth, in which it is necessary for us to be saved” (Acts IV). Therefore, since Jews, pagans, and false Christians do not ask in the faith of Christ, they cannot obtain eternal salvation.

Therefore, my brothers, if you ask for something, and ask the Father [Col. 1897A] in the name of Jesus Christ, the Father will undoubtedly give it to you.

He does not say, “For whom you ask.” For the perverse life of the reprobate often prevents the Lord from hearing prayers made for them. Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “And you, son of man, do not take up praise and prayer for this people, for I will not hear you” (Jer. IX). And elsewhere: “If Moses and Samuel were to stand before me, my soul would not be toward this people” (Jer. XV).

It is as though he were saying: I will not even hear those who are proved to have been powerful in obtaining through prayer, on behalf of these people. Yet, my brothers, even if what you ask will not be given on behalf of those reprobates, it will nevertheless be given to you, because you will not be without reward for your work of mercy, according to the Psalmist: “And my prayer shall return into my bosom” (Ps. XXXIV). And according to the Gospel: [Col. 1897B] “If a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; but if not, it will return to you” (Luke X).

This too should be noted: he does not say, “Immediately he will give it to you.” For even if the Lord delays, he does not take away your petitions but postpones them, so that you may ask more and thereby merit more. Nevertheless, after long persistence he will undoubtedly give it to you, because he wills it as Father and can do it as God.

Since the words of the Gospel mentioned above still seemed plain and clear to the apostles in their simplicity—and therefore, when they sometimes asked for something and did not obtain it, they might seem not to be true—the Lord shows that they must be examined more subtly than they sound, when he adds: “I have spoken these things to you in proverbs.” A proverb is a brief and [Col. 1897C] clear saying that must be understood more subtly than it sounds.

The second part follows, in which the Lord foretells to his disciples when they will know how to ask rightly, when he adds: “The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in proverbs, but will announce the Father to you openly.”

This hour, brothers, was after the Ascension and the sending of the Holy Spirit. Then those words which, because the disciples previously understood them less fully, had become proverbs, became clear and open to understanding. Through the Holy Spirit the Son also instructed them more deeply concerning the mysteries of God the Father. Concerning this hour he adds: “On that day you will ask in my name.”

For then, and only then, did they ask for eternal salvation or for what leads to it.

Would that the Lord might deign to teach both you and us inwardly and invisibly through his Holy Spirit, so that the words of sacred Scripture, which are for us like obscure proverbs, might become clear and open to us. Thus may we be able to understand more deeply the glory and sweetness of God and taste them through contemplation, [Col. 1897D] so that, spurning all temporal things, we may desire and seek that alone, saying with the Psalmist: “For what is there for me in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Ps. LXXII).

Let no one, brothers, presume to understand the Scriptures by his own intellect or by his own study, as some do. For unless the key of David opens them for us—the key “which opens and no one shuts, which shuts and no one opens” (Rev. III)—the book of the holy Scriptures will remain closed to us. The contemplation of divine sweetness will also remain closed to us, concerning which the Psalmist says: “How great is the multitude of your sweetness, [Col. 1898A] O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you” (Ps. XXX).

You have hidden it from the negligent and revealed it to those who fear you. This is what the Lord says: “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. II; Luke X).

This hour may also, brothers, be understood as the future life. Then the Lord will no longer speak outwardly through proverbs, but, with realities themselves speaking to us, he will announce the Father to us openly, according to what Paul says: “Now we see through a mirror and in an enigma, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know even as I am known” (1 Cor. XIII).

“In that day,” he says, “you will ask in my name.” For when the sun of the eternal day shines upon the souls of the saints, they will no longer know how to ask for temporal things, but only for the robe of immortality—while those who already possess one robe [Col. 1898B] will ask for another, and the faithful still labouring on earth will ask for both.

The third part follows, in which the Lord shows that the Father will be ready to hear the disciples when they ask in his name, saying: “And I do not say to you that I will ask the Father for you; for the Father himself loves you.”

As though he were saying: When you ask the Father in my name, I do not say that I will then ask the Father for you as though he were difficult to persuade to hear you. For the Father himself loves you, just as I do, and he will be gracious in hearing you.

It is therefore evident, my brothers, by contrast, that whoever asks the Father for riches, honours, or any temporal thing does not ask the Father in Jesus’ name—that is, for eternal salvation, [Col. 1898C] but rather to fulfil his own will. In such a petition he will undoubtedly find the Father hard and difficult to persuade. But if he should perhaps give him what he requested, he will give it in his anger.

But what does he mean when he adds: “The Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came forth from God”? Did the disciples love the Lord first in time or as a cause, and therefore the Father love them? No, my brothers; rather, as John testifies: “He himself first loved us” (1 John IV).

Because the Father loved the disciples, the disciples loved and believed in God. The causal conjunction *because* signifies there not the cause of being but the cause of understanding. The disciples’ loving and believing in God was not the cause that moved God to love them; rather, it was the reason by which they understood that God loved them. For they could not [Col. 1898D] have loved God unless God had loved them and inspired his love in them.

“I came forth,” he says, “from the Father, and came into the world; and again I leave the world and go to the Father.” As though he were saying: It is not enough for you to believe that I came forth from the Father through eternal birth, unless you also believe that I came into the world through temporal birth, that I again leave the world through bodily departure, and that I ascend to the Father through the bodily glorification of the Ascension. The Catholic faith requires us to believe these things, together with the other articles of faith.

The fourth part follows, in which the disciples respond to the Lord’s saying that he had spoken to them in proverbs and that an hour would come when he would speak to them not in proverbs but openly:

“Behold,” they say, “now you speak openly [Col. 1899A] and say no proverb.” Because the disciples understood the outward plainness of the Lord’s words, they thought that the words themselves were plain and contained no depth of subtle meaning. Even today there are people like them who attend only to the surface of sacred Scripture and think that it contains no mysteries of hidden things.

But sacred Scripture is so arranged that in it a child can walk and a giant can swim. Through its outward history or moral teaching, the inexperienced are nourished; through its inward allegory, the wise are exercised.

“Now we know,” they say, “that you know all things, and there is no need for anyone to question you. By this we believe that you came forth from God.” Since the Lord not only instructed them concerning all their doubts but also anticipated their questions [Col. 1899B] by answering them before they asked, and answered their hidden thoughts, they confess that he knows all things and came from God.

To answer hidden thoughts and doubts is divine, not human. Hence it is said to him through the Wise One: “You alone know the hearts of the children of men” (2 Chron. VI).

Therefore, my brothers, wherever we may hide, we are before the eyes of the divine majesty, which observes our works, words, thoughts, and pleasures, however hidden they may be. For this reason a great necessity has been imposed upon us to live honourably. If we are ashamed to say or do anything disgraceful before the eyes of an earthly king or prince, how much more ought we to be ashamed to do or say anything disgraceful before the eyes of almighty God?

Let us therefore wipe away, [Col. 1899C] my brothers, the filth of our sins with the tears of repentance; let us correct our life and cleanse our conscience. For “blessed are the pure in heart, for they alone shall see God” (Matt. V).

Let us therefore pray to him that he, who alone can do so, may cleanse our heart, so that we may deserve to see him within our heart, for ever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LXIV. ON THE GREATER LITANY

“Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (James V), etc.

In this reading, my brothers, the Apostle exhorts us to three good things: mutual confession, mutual prayer, and mutual correction. These three good things are great before God and very necessary for us. [Col. 1899D] Confession is necessary for ourselves; prayer and correction for ourselves and for others. Through mutual confession we cleanse ourselves, and through mutual prayer we assist one another. Through mutual correction each of us wins the other for God.

He urges us to confession when he says: “Confess your sins to one another.” Consider, my brothers, what confession is, from what it derives its name, how necessary it is, to whom it should be made, when it should be made, and how.

Confession is a sorrowful narration of one’s own sins. It must be sorrowful, because whoever recounts his sins for boasting or pleasure does not remedy them but increases them. This is directed, my brothers, against those who recount their sins not with a sorrowful manner but rather with laughter. Such people certainly do not confess their sins but instead proclaim them. [Col. 1900A]

Confession is called *confessio*, as though it were a common declaration, so that in heart, mouth, and deed we may confess that we have sinned: in the heart, let us repent; with the mouth, let us accuse ourselves; in deed, let us make satisfaction.

Confession is so necessary for us that through it our sins are forgiven, and without it they are not forgiven. That sins are forgiven through confession is evident in David. When the prophet Nathan accused him of adultery with Bathsheba and of killing her husband, using the example of the rich man who possessed a hundred sheep and seized the one little ewe belonging to his poor neighbour, David did not blush to confess his sin before everyone, saying: “I have sinned before the Lord” (2 Sam. XI). At once the Lord said to him through the prophet: “The Lord has taken [Col. 1900B] away your sin” (ibid.).

Behold, my brothers, who could adequately weigh the depths of divine mercy, by which he destroys such grave sins through confession alone? Hence David himself says: “I said: I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (Ps. XXXI).

That sins are not forgiven without confession when a person has the time and opportunity is shown by the prophet when he says: “First declare your iniquities, that you may be justified” (Isa. XLIII). And the philosopher says: “If you expect the physician’s treatment, you must uncover the wound.”

To whom should confession be made? Confession of grave sins should be made specifically to a priest, who alone has the power of binding and loosing, just as under the Law the judgment concerning leprosy was entrusted to priests alone.

Confession of venial sins [Col. 1900C], however, may be made mutually and to anyone, even to someone of lesser rank, because on account of venial sins a person is not separated from God unless through negligence he exceeds proper measure—just as under the Law no one was separated from the camp on account of scabies or an impetigo.

This confession is made not because the other person can absolve from sins, but because through our own humiliation, the accusation of our sins, and our brother’s prayer, we are cleansed from sins. Hence we do not say, “I forgive your sins,” but say in prayer: “May almighty God have mercy on you,” and so forth.

When should this confession be made? At every time when we recognize that we have sinned. Whether at home, in the field, or on the road, if I have sinned, I should immediately say to the brother who is with me: “I have sinned; pray for me.” If he is not present, I should confess to God [Col. 1900D], saying: “Lord, I have sinned; have mercy on me.”

Especially, brothers, at the first hour of the day we should confess what we did wrong during the night, and at Compline what we sinned during the day. Most especially, brothers, when we wish to approach Mass or to celebrate or receive another sacrament, we must cleanse ourselves through confession.

This confession is well signified by the bronze basin under the Law, which Moses placed at the entrance of the tabernacle, where those about to offer sacrifice washed their hands.

How should we confess? With contrition of heart, humility of countenance, beating of the breast, bodily supplication, and a sorrowful voice.

The Apostle urges us to mutual prayer when he adds [Col. 1901A]: “And pray for one another, that you may be saved. For the continual prayer of a righteous person has great power.”

Prayer is a devout affection of the mind toward God, which is sometimes stirred up by the voice when the mind grows sluggish. Prayer, therefore, is not the voice but rather the affection of the mind by which we desire to obtain something from God.

It must be devout, because through prayer we ought to ask for things pertaining to devotion. When our mind grows sluggish in prayer, we should stir it through the voice, so that the sound of the mouth, entering through the ears, may awaken the mind’s sluggishness.

Prayer performed only in the heart, even without the lips, is acceptable to God. Hence Susanna, remaining silent, is said to have cried out because of the intense concentration of her mind, and to have been heard by God (Dan. XIII). Prayer performed with the lips alone, however, is not acceptable before God. Hence he himself says: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” [Col. 1901B] (Matt. XV; Isa. XXIX).

The Apostle shows here for whom we should pray, what we should pray for, whose prayer has power, what kind of prayer is effective, and how great its power is.

For whom should we pray? For one another—that is, for our brothers. We are not bound to pray in the same way for heretics, unbelievers, and those who sin against the Holy Spirit. Hence John says: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (1 John V).

If we pray for such people, we ask not for their salvation but for their conversion, and we add a condition: “As you will and know, Lord, so deal with them.”

What should we pray for? “That you may be saved.” He does not say that you may be honoured, glorified, or delighted in this world. Concerning those who ask for such things, James says: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly,” as he indicates, “so that you may spend it on your desires” (James IV).

Rather, let us ask for what the Lord commands in the Gospel: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” [Col. 1901C] (Matt. VI).

Whose prayer has power? He shows this when he adds: “The prayer of the righteous.” For “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers; but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil” (Ps. XXXIII).

What kind of prayer has power? He shows this when he says: “Continual prayer”—that is, prayer possessing intensity and persistence. For lax and weary prayer ordinarily does not obtain what it seeks.

How great is its power? He shows this when he says: “It has great power.” Prayer obtains from God the forgiveness of sins, the bestowal of graces, the turning away of adversities, and the consolation of prosperity. Prayer drives away the devil, appeases God’s anger, directs our way, and leads us to the kingdom of God. [Col. 1901D]

Prayer has power both for the person who offers it and for the person on whose behalf it is offered. Even if it has no power for the one for whom it is offered, it can nevertheless have power for the one who offers it devoutly. For it is written: “And my prayer shall return into my bosom” (Ps. XXXIV).

The extent of prayer’s power is shown by the example of Elijah, and this is an argument from the lesser. If one human being, subject to passions like us, fleeing the threats of a little woman, yet enduring them and fearing death, turned away the rain by one prayer and again gave it to the earth (1 Kings XVII), what will the prayers of many righteous people, even continual prayers, accomplish?

He urges us to correct and convert sinful brothers when he says: “If anyone among you [Col. 1902A] has gone astray, and someone converts him”—that is, by word, example, or prayer—“he should know that whoever converts a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death.”

He shows how useful the conversion of brothers is both to the person converted and to the person who converts him. Its usefulness to the person converted lies in the fact that it saves his soul from death. Just as the soul is more precious than the body, so the almsgiving that saves a soul which will never die is greater than that which saves a body destined necessarily to die.

He shows how useful it is to the person who converts another when he adds: “And covers a multitude of sins,” understanding this to mean his own sins. For it is written: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Eccl. III).

The conversion of a brother not only covers the sins of the person who converts him; [Col. 1902B] it also obtains a crown for him. For as many souls as a person saves, so many crowns will he have. Hence it is written: “Those who have instructed many will shine like the stars of the firmament” (Dan. XII).

What almsgiving, brothers beloved, what victory could be greater than, in imitation of our Redeemer, to break the bars of hell, rescue the vessels of captivity, snatch the guilty from the jaws of the devil, and win them for Christ?

Therefore, my brothers, let us always keep before our eyes the death now threatening us and the severe judgment of God, and let us flee grave sins as though they were death. Let us daily remedy venial and daily sins through mutual confession; let us assist one another through prayer; let us bear one another’s burdens; and let us strive to win those who go astray for God.

Thus, if we cannot [Col. 1902C] arrive at the great day of judgment and eternal recompense with as many triumphs as Peter and Paul, let us arrive with one or two, or with as many as we can, through the generosity of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God for ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LXV. ON THE GREATER LITANY
Who among you, having a friend, will go to him at midnight and say to him: “Friend, lend me three loaves, because a friend of mine has arrived from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him” (Luke 11)?

This reading, dearest brothers, is divided into two parts by means of two parables. Since God and our Lord, [Col. 1902D] when we pray, often does not hear us immediately but delays, so that by praying more and more we may merit more and more, he therefore exhorts us through the first parable not to grow weary of prayer or despair of obtaining what we ask, but rather to persist in prayer at the fitting time, promising that those who ask persistently will unquestionably be heard by God at the proper time.

He therefore takes this parable from a man who turns to his friend in need. Although the friend makes excuses and says that he cannot help, nevertheless, if not by friendship, at least by persistence, he moves him to help him. As far as the literal meaning is concerned, then, two things are to be considered for us in this parable: namely, the negligence that we display toward ourselves, and the good will that God has toward us.

We display negligence toward ourselves [Col. 1903A] because we are negligent in seeking and obtaining eternal salvation, whereas we are fervent in seeking and obtaining temporal things. For if some temporal necessity overtakes us, we are anxious, unable to sleep, and, rising at midnight, we run about, exhausting friends and neighbors. With tears and sighs, prayers and promises, we do not cease knocking until we receive what we lacked.

But when the greatest of all necessities continually overtakes us—namely, escape from eternal death—and we are negligent about avoiding it, we sleep and do not rise before dawn in order to knock upon God and his saints with prayers and promises of amendment, so that, once our sins have been forgiven, we may be able to avoid eternal death.

If some secular king or prince [Col. 1903B] promised to give us the riches or honors of this world, with what desire would we follow him, and with what diligence would we serve him? At his command we would travel throughout the world, cross the seas, visit barbarian nations; we would not be held back by cold, heat, dangers, or swords. And all this would be so that we might obtain the false and fleeting riches and honors of this world—things which perhaps we will never obtain.

Yet now, when almighty and truthful God promises the blessed and eternal kingdom, we neglect to obey him and disdain to serve him; we are unwilling even to follow him amid prosperity itself. Why is this, brothers? Is it not because we fix our root in the love of the world, and either do not believe God when he promises the kingdom of heaven, or despise him?

Nevertheless, God the Father, [Col. 1903C] like a devoted father, has good will toward us. He rouses us when we are negligent, invites us by his promises, and commands us to ask. And certainly, brothers, he who commands us to ask desires to give. “Ask,” he says, “and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.”

In these words, my brothers, he shows us how we ought to ask in order to deserve to be heard. For we do not deserve to be heard if we ask with the voice alone. He himself says elsewhere: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father—he will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 7).

If, then, we wish to enter, let us ask with the heart, seek through action, and knock through perseverance. Let us ask by praying devoutly, seek by doing good, and knock by persevering [Col. 1903D] insistently. And let us not doubt, brothers, that we shall obtain what we ask, since, as Truth testifies, the one who asks in the manner just described receives; the one who seeks finds; and to the one who knocks it will be opened (Luke 11).

According to the mystical meaning, our friend, to whom we must turn in the night of necessity, is God the Father, who, as the Apostle says, because of the great love with which he loved us, sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh (Ephesians 2). The friend who comes to us from a journey is our mind, which departs from us whenever, having forgotten its own salvation and ours, it goes out to desire earthly things.

It comes to us from its journey when it returns from the tumult of earthly desires to meditate upon its own salvation and ours. It returns hungry, because in [Col. 1904A] earthly desires no satisfaction is found. Nor do we have anything to place before it, because divine grace, which is the food of the soul, is not in human hands.

Therefore, when hunger compels our friend, we must not delay, as do those who postpone the salvation of their souls. We must rise as quickly as possible from the midnight of sin and ignorance and hasten as quickly as possible to our one friend, God the Father, asking him for three loaves—that is, faith in the Trinity, or the threefold understanding of sacred Scripture: historical, moral, and mystical—by which the hunger of our souls may be satisfied.

For just as “the righteous person lives by faith” (Romans 1), so also by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God (Matthew 4).

The one inside then [Col. 1904B] answers and makes excuses, while, with the door of hearing closed, he pretends not to be able to offer help. From this it appears that the door of preaching is closed, and that the servants—namely, the holy preachers, already stripped of their fleshly clothing—are with God in the chamber of eternal rest. Thus it seems impossible that God should rise, either by himself or through his ministers, to instruct us.

This appears to have happened today, brothers, when the door of preaching seems already to be closed no less among preachers than among hearers, since both groups are failing alike. Nevertheless, brothers, if we persevere in knocking with prayers, sighs, and tears, I tell you that, moved by his love and by our crying out, he will provide us with spiritual bread.

Another parable follows, in which the Lord shows that God the Father gives only good things, and that he gives them [Col. 1904C] not because he is compelled by our merit or persistence, but immediately because of his paternal affection. He demonstrates this by an argument from the lesser: if earthly fathers, although they are not good in themselves but rather evil, know how to give their children who ask not evil but rather temporal goods—not because they are moved by the merit or importunity of their children, but by paternal affection—how much more will the heavenly Father, who is naturally good, give spiritual and eternal goods to his children who ask, moved solely by the affection that he possesses by nature.

According to the literal meaning, my brothers, let us consider in this parable how earthly and animal-like is the affection of fleshly parents toward their children, and how true is the love of the heavenly Father toward his children.

A fleshly father is more concerned to nourish his son’s body [Col. 1904D] than his soul.
