He is very anxious lest his son hunger, lest he grow cold, lest he be struck by a serpent, lest he die by some accident. He gathers a treasure for him, hastens by every means to enrich him and establish him as an heir, and trains him in the cunning of acquiring and preserving wealth.

But if he sees that his son is a liar, perjurious, deceitful, greedy and covetous, rapacious and violent, he despises him—or rather, he rejoices, calling him wise and respectable.

But what follows from this? After the wicked son, instructed by his wicked father, has grown up, he surpasses his father’s wickedness. First he rises up against the parent himself, hates his life, disinherits him, and pretends not to know him as he perishes from hunger.

O wretched father, [Col. 1905A] why do you accuse your son for this? He is doing what you taught him. If you wanted to find him devout, why did you not teach him to be devout? If you wanted to find him just, why did you not teach him to be just? What you handed on to him, he returns to you.

Such were the Israelites, whom John calls “offspring of vipers” (Luke 3)—that is, poisonous children of poisonous parents. And the Lord says through Ezekiel: “I am a jealous God, avenging the sins of parents upon their children” (Exodus 20)—that is, disciples of paternal wickedness.

[Note: [Col. 1905] Nothing of this kind is found in the Vulgate in Ezekiel; on the contrary, he says: “A son shall not bear the iniquity of his father” (Ezekiel 18).]

For just as parents are punished because of the perverse instruction of their children, so children are punished because of their evil imitation of their parents.

The heavenly Father, however, [Col. 1905B] loves his children with true affection—not only in that he chose them from eternity, redeemed them by the blood of his Son, and prepared an eternal kingdom for them, but also in daily correction and instruction. He hates them in evil and loves them in goodness and toward goodness, in which true love consists: “He who spares the rod hates his son” (Proverbs 13). And a father corrects the son whom he loves more.

Thus the heavenly Father recalls his children from evil through prohibitions, threats, and punishments. He draws them toward good through commandments, promises, and the gift of his graces.

Therefore, fathers and mothers of families, imitate the heavenly Father. Love your sons, grandsons, and all your friends in goodness, not in evil. Love them more in soul than in body, more toward God than toward the world. Desire and acquire for them spiritual riches rather than bodily riches, heavenly riches rather than earthly ones.

From the breast, instruct them in the fear of God [Col. 1905C], in faith, hope, charity, devotion, patience, humility, and the other virtues and good morals, remembering that “a wise son is the glory of his father, and an foolish son is the disgrace of his parents.” And just as a good son is the blessing of his parents, so an evil son is the curse of his parents (Proverbs 10).

For just as the goodness of children belongs to the parents who taught them, so the evil of children belongs to the parents who neglected to correct them. We have an example of this in the rejection of Eli and his sons.

According to the mystical meaning, bread signifies charity, by which the soul is refreshed. Conversely, the stone represents the hardness of a mind hardened in evil. The fish, which [Col. 1905D] lives hidden in the waters, signifies faith, which comes from hidden and invisible things.

Conversely, the serpent that appears signifies the poison of unbelief or heresy. The egg, in which there is the hope of offspring, expresses hope. Conversely, the scorpion, which strikes with its tail—that is, with the end of its body—denotes final despair.

If, then, my brothers, someone asks the heavenly Father for faith, hope, and charity, will the kind and merciful Father give him the vices opposed to these virtues—namely, unbelief, despair, and hardness of heart? Certainly not, because with him there is “no change or shadow due to alteration” (James 1).

Indeed, if someone through ignorance were to ask him [Col. 1906A] for something harmful to himself, he, who knows better than we do what is beneficial for us, would not hear him. Thus he did not wish to hear Paul when he asked that the thorn in his flesh be removed, although it certainly seemed harmful to him (2 Corinthians 12).

In this, brothers, he provides us with an example, so that we may hear our friends in good things, not in evil things. For whoever at times hears someone in evil shows himself to be that person’s enemy.

This is why, brothers, the devoted and merciful Lord does not hear us in many evil desires and in our ill-considered petitions; by this he shows himself to be our true father and true friend.

Let us therefore love him above all things and before all others. Let us embrace him with all our inward being. For his sake let us avoid every shameful thing and every vice; let us [Col. 1906B] flee from the fleeing world; and let us abandon all transitory things before we are abandoned by them.

Let us hasten with all desire toward eternal goods, so that we may deserve to see God the Father in his beauty. Amen.

## HOMILY LXVI. FOR THE VIGIL OF THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

“To each of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Ephesians 4), etc.

This reading, dearest brothers, must be examined carefully, because it contains a teaching without which salvation cannot exist. For here the Apostle speaks of the grace of God, through which alone, as the Apostle himself says, “we are what we are” (1 Corinthians 10).

Among the articles of our faith this too is necessarily included, [Col. 1906C]: we must believe that whatever good we possess, we possess freely from God. Whoever boasts that he possesses some good from himself or from his own merits will have no glory before God.

This reading therefore has five parts. First, the Apostle says that grace has been given to each person by Christ. Second, he proves this by the authority of Scripture. Third, he enumerates the graces themselves. Fourth, he demonstrates for what use they were given. Fifth, he makes clear what end they have.

The Apostle therefore says first: “To each of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift.” He says three things: that grace has been given to each of us, that it has been given according to a measure, and that it has been given by Christ.

Although by saying “to each of us” the Apostle [Col. 1906D] understands only ministers, nevertheless it is universally true that grace has been given by Christ to every human being. Since grace means whatever is given freely, whatever a person possesses—whether the good of nature, the good of fortune, as people commonly say, or the good of grace—may be called the grace of God, because it has been given freely by God.

Yet because the goods of nature and the goods of fortune are common to both the good and the wicked, virtues and their proper uses, since they belong only to the good, are characteristically called graces.

The Lord did not wish any of his creatures to be entirely deprived of some participation in his goodness, lest it should appear unseemly and unworthy of its creator. Rather, he endowed each of his creatures with some grace of his own.

Why? [Col. 1907A] For three reasons: so that every creature might possess something in itself by which it could display the abundance of divine goodness; so that it might have something for which to give thanks to God the giver; and so that it might have material by which it could merit before God.

Therefore, my brothers, let each person show himself worthy of the grace given to him, give thanks for it to God its author, and strive to merit greater things by ministering through it to his brothers.

Whoever has wisdom should instruct the inexperienced. Whoever has power should defend the Church, orphans, and widows. Whoever has wealth should use it to assist the needy. Whoever has influence with a prince should speak to him on behalf of the poor. Whoever has eloquence should use it to defend the uninformed. Whoever knows some craft should use it to help those in need.

Let each person beware lest, by hiding the talent entrusted to him by God, he thereby deserve to be deprived of it and of his other goods as well.

Grace has been given to each of us [Col. 1907B] according to a measure. The Lord did not wish to give all graces to one person.

Why? For three reasons: lest any creature should ever regard itself as equal to its Creator; lest anyone should think that he had no need of anyone else; and lest he should despise the other creatures.

Rather, he wished each of us to need another’s grace, so that, seeing that he needed the grace with which his brother shines, each person might prefer that brother to himself and seek his help. In this very way, he would learn, from the grace given to him, to minister to those in need, just as he wished others to minister to him from their graces.

Therefore, my brothers, let each of us [Col. 1907C] think that we lack much. Let us admire the graces of our brothers, so that we may become humble in our own eyes and place our brothers before ourselves.

And just as we wish them to minister to us from their graces, so let us minister to them from the grace given to us, so that through this we may also merit the graces that we do not possess.

This distribution of graces is made by Christ together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Just as they are one author, so they are one giver. Yet the graces are said to be distributed by Christ because he is the head of all the faithful, whose members are all believers.

In Christ, as in the head, [Col. 1907D] the fullness of all graces is contained. He possesses all graces—not only in the power to distribute them, as God, but also in their use, as man. He possesses all the graces that it is fitting for him to possess. And from his fullness, as John testifies (John 1), we have all received according to measure (Ephesians 4), from him who does not have the Spirit by measure.

This is well signified in the anointing of Aaron. When the fullness of the anointing was poured by Moses upon his head, it dripped down through his beard and the rest of his members to the very edge of his garment (Psalm 132).

So, my brothers, from the fullness of the graces with which Christ was invisibly anointed by the Father, grace drips first and more abundantly upon the beard—that is, upon the manly and more perfect—then upon the others, even down to the lowest.

Therefore, my brothers, let us pray to him with sighs and groans, so that from his fullness of graces—even if [Col. 1908A] not as much as upon the apostles and the other saints, at least a little—he may sprinkle us, as the last members of his Church.

The second part follows, in which he proves by the authority of the prophet that graces are given by Christ, when he says: “Therefore it says: ‘Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to human beings.’”

The force of the proof consists in this: the work in question could be accomplished neither by a mere human being nor by a mere God. A human being could not rescue captives from hell, lead them on high, and give the gifts of the Holy Spirit to human beings unless he were God.

He therefore first descended by assuming humanity; and this is what the Apostle adds in explanation: “What does ‘he ascended’ mean except that he had first descended into the lower parts of the earth?”

As if he were saying: How could he ascend unless he had first descended? He descended not only into the lower regions but also into the lower [Col. 1908B] parts of the earth—that is, into hell—breaking it and leading captivity captive out.

The people of the saints who were held in hell were not merely captivity; they were captivity that had itself been captured. In that they had been expelled through the devil’s deception from the homeland of paradise, for the attainment of which they had been created, and were exiled in the misery of this world, they were captivity.

Again, in that they had been taken captive by the misery of this life into the greater misery of hell, they were not merely captivity but captive captivity.

The Lord therefore led this captive captivity with him on high, in the manner of a triumphant conqueror.

For just as someone who is about to fight an enemy [Col. 1908C] first arms himself, then cautiously attacks the enemy and overcomes him through great labor, afterward binds him, destroys his fortress, leads out the captives, and, returning with the standards of victory to his own seat, distributes gifts among his attendants, so the Lord acted.

First, when he was about to fight the devil, he armed himself with humility. He attacked him through hidden wisdom, overcame him through patience, bound him through strength, broke hell, led out his own who were held captive there, and, ascending into heaven in triumph, gave the gifts of the Holy Spirit to his own.

This does not mean that he gave these gifts only on that occasion, since from the beginning he had always bestowed his grace upon his own. Rather, what had been hidden was that he visibly demonstrated himself to be the giver of heavenly gifts.

Holy Church [Col. 1908D] represents this victory of Christ through the processions that it customarily holds during these days. It proceeds in procession as the victor who was crucified in the flesh upon the cross, carrying the weapons with which he triumphed.

Holy water proceeds with him—that is, the grace by which he sprinkles and fortifies his own. The banners proceed as signs of his victory.

The dragon also proceeds, as the defeated one before the victor. It is alive only in its head and empty in its rear part, because it is able to suggest the first part of sin, namely, thought. But it cannot compel Christ’s servants to consent to the habit or completion of sin.

And certainly he is a weak enemy who cannot harm anyone unless that person consents to him.

The people of the faithful [Col. 1909A] follow the crucified one in procession, awaiting from him the gifts of his graces, as the liberated await their liberator.

Let us therefore follow him, my brothers. Let us follow him not merely with our feet but with true faith, firm love, and the fulfillment of his works and commandments. For those who follow him in this way will not lack his gifts; without doubt he will bestow upon them both the wages of his graces here and the blessedness of rewards in the future.

And lest anyone should think, as certain heretics have thought, that there are two persons in Christ, the Apostle shows that the one and same person is both the one who descended and ascended as man and the one who gave the gifts of the Holy Spirit as God. He adds: “The one who descended is himself also the one who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fulfill all things” that had been foretold about him through the prophets.

And the same one is he who “gave some as apostles, others as prophets,” and so forth.

This is the third part, in which the Apostle [Col. 1909B] enumerates certain graces of ministry that God bestowed upon the ministers of his Church, through which they might govern and instruct it in this world.

Among them the principal are the apostles, whom our Lord Jesus Christ sent from his side to announce the faith of salvation to those ignorant of it.

Others are prophets, who foretold future events through the Holy Spirit, such as Agabus and the daughters of Philip.

Others are evangelists, who received the privilege of writing the Gospel.

Others are pastors and teachers, who govern and teach the holy Church.

The Apostle [Col. 1909C] rightly says not only “pastors” but adds “teachers,” clearly demonstrating that the leaders of the holy Church must be not only pastors but also teachers, so that they may teach in word those whom they feed by example.

This plainly condemns those who assume the teaching office in the Church while being blind in sacred Scripture. For according to Truth itself: “If the blind lead the blind, will they not both fall into a pit?” (Matthew 15).

These ministries of the Church, if they are possessed together with the inward grace of charity and the other virtues, are certainly of great merit. Otherwise, they do not help those who possess them but rather harm them.

For what did apostleship profit Judas? What did prophecy profit Balaam and Caiaphas? What did writing the Gospel profit heretics? What did teaching profit wicked teachers?

Therefore, brothers, let us who have undertaken [Col. 1909D] ministry in the Church pray that God may bestow upon us inward grace, through which we may be able to administer outwardly in a worthy manner.

The fourth part follows, in which it is shown for what use the Lord gave the aforementioned graces to human beings, when it is added: “For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry.”

For what use did he give those graces? For the work of ministry. He gave apostleship to a person so that he might announce the Gospel. He gave prophecy to a person so that he might proclaim future events. He gave wisdom to a person so that he might teach.

This plainly condemns those who are sluggish in the administration entrusted to them: they hold the place of a shepherd and do not feed; they receive the wages of a preacher and do not preach; they wish to be called teachers and do not teach.

They rightly deserve to be cut down with the axe [Col. 1910A] of eternal damnation, because they occupy the ground and produce no fruit (Luke 13).

And what purpose does the work of ministry serve? It serves the perfecting of the saints and the building up of the body of Christ. Through the ministry of teachers, each of the elect may progress as he ought, and the whole body of Christ—that is, the Church—may be built up in its members, so that neither anything may be lacking to some members of the Church nor any member may be lacking to the Church itself.

When teachers fail in the Church, the elect are deprived of instruction, and the prophetic saying is fulfilled: “The children asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lamentations 4).

The Church itself is mutilated in its members, lacking a tongue with which to instruct and eyes with which to see the way.

The Church is called the body [Col. 1910B] of Christ because Christ is called the head of the Church by a certain likeness. Although the head and the members are of one nature, the head presides over, watches over, and governs all the members of the body from the innermost chamber of the brain, where the seat of the senses, wisdom, and strength is located. From there it diffuses through the marrow the benefits of vitality and sensation to the lower members joined to it by nerves and veins.

The members of the entire body obey and serve their head. They are joined both to the head and to one another, helping and ministering to one another.

So, my brothers—so Christ, in order to be our head, became human, sharing one nature with us. He presides over, watches over, and governs all the members of the Church. From the treasures of his wisdom, strength, and graces, [Col. 1910C] he pours them into his lower members, who are joined to him by faith and love.

These members of the Church—that is, all of us who are believers—must obey and serve Christ our head and be joined to him through charity. Otherwise, we lose the benefits of his grace and, becoming withered like useless members, are cut off from the unity of Christ’s body.

We must also, my brothers, be joined to one another by the bond of charity as members of one body, help one another, and minister to one another.

Does the eye see only for itself? No, it sees also for the other members. Does the foot carry only itself? No, it carries the other members as well. Does the hand defend only itself or draw only what is necessary for itself? No, it does so also for the other members.

Similarly, each believer must minister from the grace given to him by God not to himself alone but to the other members of the Church.

The wise person, [Col. 1910D] who is like the eye of the Church, should be wise and foresee things not for himself alone but also for the other faithful. The preacher, who is the tongue of the Church, should instruct not himself alone but also the others. The lower common people, who are like the foot of the Church, should sustain not themselves alone but the whole body of the Church through their labors. The prince, who is like the hand of the Church, should defend not himself alone but the whole Church.

The fifth part follows, in which it is shown what end the aforementioned ministries ought to have, when it is added: “Until we all attain to the unity of faith and the knowledge of the Son of God.”

Two ends are noted here: the end of purpose and the end of cessation.

The ministers [Col. 1911A] of the holy Church ought to administer the aforementioned ministries with this purpose—not to become rich here, not to become famous here, not to be honored here, not to satisfy their appetite and belly here, but so that, together with the peoples subject to them, they may be able to meet Christ without reproach when he comes to his judgment.

Then also, my brothers, every such ministry will cease. For then the saints will not need to be corrected, instructed, or governed by a human being; the presence of the divine majesty will illumine them.

Let us therefore strive, brothers; let us strive with all diligence so that we may be able to meet Christ without reproach when he comes, and this in the unity of faith and the knowledge of the Son of God.

Two things are placed here, in which the true blessedness of souls will be perfected: namely, the union of minds and the knowledge of the divine majesty.

Then [Col. 1911B] there will not be faith, which is shadowy, but rather complete knowledge of all things. Yet the Apostle said “in the unity of faith” because only those who here preserve the unity of true faith as far as they can will attain to that complete union of minds, where the saints will be united with God and by God in charity, so that they can will nothing other than one and the same thing in every respect.

Thus, if anything belongs properly to individuals, it will become common through charity.

The knowledge of the divine majesty and splendor will perfect the blessed life in the elect, according to what the Lord says: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17).

How great, brothers—how great do you think will be the sweetness, how great the blessedness, of seeing that majesty and that splendor into which the holy angels desire to gaze (1 Peter 1), whose vision and presence will drive away all ignorance, misery, stain, and weakness?

Just as iron, through its proximity to fire, [Col. 1911C] is so inflamed and made fiery that it no longer seems to be iron but entirely fire, so blessed spirits, through the presence of the divine splendor and heat, will be inflamed, so that they will no longer seem to be creatures but entirely divine.

This will happen in souls. In bodies, however, we shall attain to “a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.” Then we shall be perfect in our members, in beauty, in strength and virtues, and in age.

Hence he adds: “To the measure”—not indeed of bodily stature, but of the fullness of Christ’s age. We shall rise in the full age in which Christ was when he suffered.

Let us therefore, brothers, [Col. 1911D] strive with all desire toward the ineffable blessedness of that resurrection. In hope of it, let us hold the present life in contempt; in hope of it, let us despise all transitory things; in hope of it, let us embrace all harsh and adverse circumstances, flee vices, and strive to do good.

Let us desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, so that at last we may deserve to see him joyfully in his glory, through the one who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY LXVII. FOR THE VIGIL OF THE ASCENSION

“Jesus lifted up his eyes to heaven and said: ‘Father, glorify your Son’” (John 17), etc.

Our Lord and [Col. 1912A] Redeemer, dearest brothers, when his passion was already at hand, poured out to the Father the prayer that you have just heard.

Yet since the Son has the same authority and power as the Father and would equally give what he was asking, just as the Father would, why did he ask the Father, when asking appears to belong to a lesser and weaker person?

For three reasons: so that he might truly express in himself the humility and humanity assumed for our sake, in which he is less than the Father; so that in this, as in all other things, he might always defer to God the Father; and so that he might demonstrate to us an example and pattern of prayer.

We too, brothers, always following the example of God and our Lord, should always profess our humility and lowliness. Let us attribute everything not to ourselves but to God the Father. Let us always strive to defer to our brothers. Let us accustom ourselves to devotion and prayer, which is the unconquerable fortress of Christians.

This reading has two parts. [Col. 1912B] In the first, the Lord prays for his own glorification; in the second, for the preservation of his own.

As the Lord is about to pray, he first raises his eyes to heaven; then he invokes the Father, also names himself Son, and finally makes his request.

He could do this more truly than anyone, because he always raised the eyes of his heart to heaven, truly had God as his Father, and truly showed himself to be the Son. Hence the Father also said to him: “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 17).

Nevertheless, following him according to our limited capacity, when we are about to pray let us first raise to heaven the eyes [Col. 1912C] of our heart, our desire, our hope, and our intention. For those who have set their eyes on turning toward the earth (Psalm 16) do not deserve to be heard.

Let us also invoke God the Father, believing that he bears toward us a devoted and paternal affection: that he first created us, afterward re-created us through the blood of his Son, freely begot us as children of adoption, and prepared a heavenly kingdom for us; and that, as a devoted Father, he is ready to hear the petitions of his children.

Those who do not believe these things do not deserve to be heard.

Let us also, as far as we can, show ourselves worthy children of God the Father. Let us show ourselves so, I say, through love, obedience, and imitation. Those who through contempt, disobedience, and wicked conduct degenerate from God do not deserve to be heard.

If, then, brothers, [Col. 1912D] we raise the eyes of our intention toward heaven, firmly believe in God the Father, and, as far as we can, show ourselves to be worthy children of his, then we shall be able to ask him with confidence.

In praying, the Lord first explains his petition; second, its end; third, its manner; fourth, its benefit; and fifth, its merit.

He explains his petition when he says: “Glorify your Son.”

But since the Son of God, in his divinity, in which he is always equal to the Father, cannot be made greater, holier, or more glorious, he did not ask to be glorified in that nature. Rather, he asked to be glorified either in his humanity, in the glory of his works, in the faith of believers, or in the power of judgment.

And since he could not be deprived of the desire of his lips, the Father glorified him in these four [Col. 1913A] ways.

The Father glorified the Son in his humanity when he raised him from the dead and placed him at his right hand in glorified flesh.

He glorified him in his works when, either before or after the resurrection, he demonstrated through miracles and mighty deeds that he was truly the Son of God.

Hence he himself said through a voice from heaven: “I have glorified him, and I will glorify him again.”

He also glorified him in the faith of believers when he made those who believed in him illustrious in holiness and works.

Therefore the Son himself says in what follows: “And I have been glorified in them,” namely, in the disciples. In the power of judgment he will glorify him still more, when he shows him to be the judge of all—judge saving his own and condemning the reprobate.

He explains the end of his petition when he says: “That your Son may glorify you.” The conjunction “that” signifies not only consequence but also final cause. It signifies consequence because, since Father and Son, as correlatives, are simultaneously one in nature and knowledge, once the Son is known and glorified, it follows that the Father too is known and glorified. Again, since Father and Son are substantially alike, and the other is known in one who is like it, it follows that, once the Son is known and glorified, the Father also is known and glorified.

It signifies final cause because the Son asks to be glorified by the Father for this end: that the Father may be glorified in him. It is as though he said: “Father, glorify me for the praise and honor of your name.” In this, my brothers, he gives us an example: whatever we wish and ask, we should wish and ask not for our own praise but for the praise and honor of God, saying with the Psalmist: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Psalm 112).

The Son glorified the Father in three ways: by proclaiming his name to human beings; by performing signs and miracles in his name; and by attributing everything to him and referring everything back to him. Imitating him, dearest brothers, let us also glorify God’s name as far as we can: always proclaiming his glory; doing good in his name to the best of our ability; attributing all our good to him and referring it back to him.

He also explains the manner of glorification when he adds: “Just as you gave him authority over all flesh, so that he might give eternal life to all whom you have given him” [Col. 1913D]—understand: so that he might make this truth manifest to all. This has already been fulfilled in part. It is already manifest to the faithful that Christ has received from the Father authority over all flesh; and to the faithful who have departed from this age he has already given eternal life. At the end it will be manifest universally to all, when he appears as judge of everyone, giving eternal life to his own and punishment to the reprobate. Then the Father will be fully glorified in the Son, and the Son glorified in the Father.

Christ says that authority was given to him by the Father because what he possessed by nature insofar as he is God became his by grace insofar as he is human.

He explains the benefit when he adds: “And this is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” [Col. 1914A]. I say that the benefit is not his but ours. He himself does not need us, as another does who says to him through the Psalmist: “You are my God, for you have no need of my goods” (Psalm 15). He did not wish to be believed in or known by us for his own sake, but for ours. Although he was supremely blessed, he did not need to be known by the miserable or to approach the miserable. But when we were miserable, we greatly needed to recognize him who is supremely blessed and to approach him; otherwise we could not have eternal life. “For this,” he says, “is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.”

The knowledge of the Father and the Son with the Holy Spirit is twofold: the first is by faith, the second by direct vision; the first is on the way, the second in the homeland; the first is obscure and enigmatic, the second open and clear. Yet each can in its own way be called eternal life, because the first leads to eternal life. Knowledge by direct vision, however, is called eternal life because it bestows eternal life.

The knowledge and vision of the divine majesty and glory will drive all misery from the elect and bestow every blessedness upon them. The sight of a calm and cheerful sky makes a person glad. What wonder, then, if the incomparable delight of the divine majesty makes the one who sees it joyful? The sight of the sun’s light and heat illuminates and warms human beings. What wonder, then, if the immensity of the divine splendor and love illuminates and inflames those who are present? The presence of fragrant spices sweetly perfumes whatever is nearby. What wonder, then, if the inexhaustible wealth of sweetness and fragrance perfumes and delights those who are present? The melody of musical instruments delights those who hear it. What wonder, then, if the ineffable harmony of divine concord attracts and delights those who are present? The sweetness of honey and nectar delights those who taste it. What wonder, then, if the marvelous sweetness of divine goodness nourishes and delights those who taste it?

“Taste and see,” says the Psalmist, “that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33). And if these earthly, lowly, transitory things, dearest brothers, affect, nourish, and delight us in this way, how incomparably will that divine delight, that splendor, that sweetness, that sweetness of flavor affect, nourish, and delight its own forever? Indeed, there is no comparison between earthly things and eternity. But, as best we can, we stammer rather than express the great things of God, because “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him” (Isaiah 64; 1 Corinthians 2).

He explains the merit when he adds: “I glorified you upon the earth; I completed the work that you gave me to do.” Christ alone truly merited and could merit. For two conditions are required for someone properly to be said to merit: namely, that he be the author of his own work and that he have someone superior to him before whom he may merit. Unless he is the author of his own work, he cannot merit, because no one ought to be crowned or condemned for another’s work. And unless he has someone superior to him, he cannot merit, because no one merits unless there is someone from whom a reward may be awaited.

For this reason, a human being or an angel cannot merit. Even if such a being has someone superior to him, he cannot be the author of his own work, since he is not the author of all the good things he has done but only their minister, because “it is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish” (Philippians 2) [Col. 1915A]. Nor can God the Father or the Holy Spirit merit, because even though he is the author of his own work, he has no one superior to him before whom he may merit. Christ alone, therefore, is able, insofar as he is God, to be the author of his own work and, insofar as he is human, to have someone superior to him before whom he may merit. Thus Christ alone merited and could merit.

The saints, however, are said to merit because, although they do not perform good works by themselves, they cooperate with God. Therefore, although God crowns only his own work in us, they are nevertheless said to be crowned according to their merits. We call divine grace “our merits” only in a proper sense, even though the Apostle openly declares that God “saved us, not because of works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy” (Titus 3).

Thus our Redeemer, explaining his merit, says: “I glorified you upon the earth.” He does not say “in the earth,” because God is glorified especially in those who, through contempt for the world, are not in the earth but above the earth, while he glorifies them. The works by which God is glorified are themselves not earthly but rather above the earth.

“I completed the work entrusted to me,” but not from myself, because you yourself entrusted it to me and gave it to me to do. In this the pride of those who suppose that they have brought their work to completion by free choice and by their own powers is confounded. The Son of God says that it was given to him by the Father to do what he did. And you, insolent worm, say that you did from yourself what you did.

“And now,” he says, “glorify me, you Father, with yourself.” It is as though he said openly: “I have done what you commanded; give me the reward I have merited. Glorify me with yourself”—that is, glorify me through the resurrection and by seating me at your right hand.

“With the glory,” he says, “that I had with you before the world existed”—that is, declare to human beings that I possess the glory that I have always had and have with you. “I have manifested your name,” namely, the name of your fatherhood. For some had known the name of divinity, but it was not known that he had a Son consubstantial with himself.

To whom? To the human beings whom you gave me from the world—that is, those whom you separated from the mass of transgression and joined to me through faith [Col. 1915D]. “They were yours,” he says, “by election, and you gave them to me by vocation.” Although the Son possesses all things by the same authority as the Father, nevertheless, deferring to the Father in everything, he says that the Father gave them to him as a human being, or even as Son, because just as he is God from God by birth, so he possesses from the One who possesses.

The second part follows, in which the Son intercedes with the Father for the preservation of his own: first by displaying their merit, and afterward by praying for them. He displays their merit when he adds: “And they have kept my word.” In this he shows us, my brothers, that if we wish him to intercede for us with the Father, we must observe his word. For those who despise the Son’s word wait in vain for him to be their intercessor with the Father, since the Son’s word is from the Father.

Therefore he adds: “And they have understood that everything you have given me is from you.” This also allows us to understand that just as commandments are not observed unless they are first known, so they cannot be perfectly known unless they are first observed. By observing the Gospel, we merit penetrating to its inner understanding and recognizing that it comes not from a human being but from God. Hence the prophet says: “From your commandments I have gained understanding” (Psalm 118).

That is why those who neglect the Gospel do not understand it. Because of the simplicity of the evangelical message, they think that it did not come from God but was invented by simple human beings [Col. 1916B]. But lest the disciples flatter themselves by thinking that they had received either observance or knowledge of the divine word from themselves, he adds: “For the words that you gave me I have given them”—not merely to the ear of the body but also to the ear of the mind.

Moreover, by saying that he gave them not his own words but the Father’s, he confounds the presumption of those who presume to announce to the people not divine teaching but their own opinions, although the Lord says to the prophet: “And you shall announce to them from me” (Ezekiel 3).

“And they,” he says, “received them.” It is as though he said: “Although they were given to them entirely as a gift, nevertheless, because they received and retained them gratefully, they merited.” “And they have known,” he says, “that I came forth from you”—either through eternal birth or through the incarnation. And lest it appear that they had already attained that clear knowledge which will exist in the future, he explains by saying: “And they truly believed that you sent me”—that is, determined that I should become incarnate.

Afterward, praying for his disciples, he says: “I pray for them,” namely, for their preservation; “I do not pray for the world”—not only for them, as he explains later, but also for those who will believe in him through their word.

In this prayer, my brothers, he also prayed for us, if we follow the faith and teaching of the apostles. “I do not pray for the world,” he says—that is, for lovers of the world.

What is this, Lord Jesus, that you say? Did you not command us to pray for wicked people and for our enemies? Did you not pray for wicked people and lovers of the world—that is, for those who crucified you—so that they might not lose their place and nation (John 11), saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23)?

Indeed you did. But he prayed for those whom he knew would presently be converted from love of the world to love of God. But we, brothers, pray for any wicked people whatsoever, because although all may be converted, we do not know who will be converted and who will not.

“But for those whom you have given me,” he says—that is, those whom you have separated from love of the world and made mine through faith and charity. “And it is yours, my Father, to hear me praying for them,” because they are yours—not merely by possession, as it is said, “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Psalm 23), nor merely by ministry, as it is said, “The tribe of Levi belongs to the Lord” (Numbers 3), but also as your own by eternal predestination, election, and love [Col. 1917A].

And lest they seem no longer to belong to the Father because the Father gave them to the Son, he adds: “All that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine.” Nor is it surprising that they are one in dominion and possession, since they are one in will, majesty, and substance.

In this we are shown that earthly brothers, fathers, and sons ought also to be one not only by blood but by love and possession; and that an affluent father when his son is begging, or an affluent son when his father is begging, are alike to be condemned.

“And I have been glorified,” he says, “in them”—that is, in those whom you gave me, whom I glorified by faith, works, and life. Glorify us also, we beg you, Lord Jesus Christ, so that you too may be glorified in us. Sanctify us, I say, so that you too may be sanctified in us. Glorify your work, so that in it you may appear as a glorious craftsman. Sanctify your servants, so that in them you may appear as a glorious Lord.

“And now,” he says, “I am no longer in the world.” Why? Because through his passion, resurrection, and ascension he is coming to the Father. “And these,” he says, “are in the world”—that is, they will remain longer amid worldly tribulations, because they are necessary for preaching the Gospel. And therefore I pray you for their preservation.

Pray also to the Father, Lord Jesus Christ, for us, who are still in this wretched world; who here are harassed by evil spirits, overcome by our own desires, and shaken by worldly tribulations; who, already in peril, cry out to you, who are no longer in this world, who now sit equal with the Father at his right hand. You hold spirits, flesh, and storms in your hand. We always invoke you as our helper. May our eyes always be upon you, lest we perish. Command the spirits, restrain the flesh, calm the storms, and guide us to yourself, so that we may always deserve to see and bless you, the one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY LXVIII. ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

“I composed the first account, O Theophilus, of all that Jesus began to do and teach until the day when, after giving instructions through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen, he was taken up” (Acts 1), etc.

Dearest brothers, Luke the Evangelist wrote the evangelical and apostolic history at the request of Theophilus, a religious man [Col. 1917D]. Passing from one work to the other, he uses a transition in three ways: first, by continuing the words of the speaker in the first transition; second, by briefly recapitulating what was said beforehand; third, by beginning the history of the Apostle with the Lord’s Ascension.

Thus, using the first transition, he says: “I composed the first account, O Theophilus, of all that Jesus began to do and teach.” He calls the Gospel the “first account”—first both in the order of writing and in dignity. The Gospel surpasses all the Scriptures, both old and new, by the dignity of its subject matter.

The word “account” derives from *sero, seris* (“to sow”). The Gospel is called an account because it is sown in the hearts of the faithful. Hence, according to the evangelical parable, the word of God is called good seed. When it falls on good soil, it produces fruit—some thirtyfold, some sixtyfold, and some a hundredfold (Luke 8).

Would that, dearest brothers, Christ might today sow the seed of his Gospel in your hearts through our mouth and make it bear in you a hundredfold harvest, as only he can. “For neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3).

He shows what subject he treated when he adds: “Of all that Jesus began to do and teach.” The whole Gospel is composed of the works and teaching of Christ. Every action and instruction of Christ is food and formation for the Christian soul. When Christ was silent, he instructed by acting; and when he was not acting, he instructed and taught by speaking [Col. 1918A].

The order is also fitting. He first began to do and afterward to teach. What he had first shown by example, he later presented in words, giving his disciples and preachers an example of observing the same order. In this my presumption—and that of those like me—is confounded: I preach many things to you that I nevertheless do not practice. But would that, through your prayers, brothers, this very confusion might produce shame in me, shame correction, and correction amendment, so that what I did not do before, I might at least begin to do after I have preached it!

And what does the Evangelist mean, brothers? Why does he say that he composed an account of all that Jesus began to do and teach? Who could do this, especially since the Evangelist John says that if Christ’s works were written out individually, he does not think that the world itself could contain the books that would be written (John 21)?

But I think, brothers, that when he says “all,” this should be understood not of each individual item within each category but of the categories of individual things. Even if he could not write everything about everything, he could at least write something about everything. He wrote about Christ’s works, preaching, journeys, passions, and the other things necessary for human salvation.

He shows where he ended the first account when he says: “Until the day when, after giving instructions to the apostles.” And what did he instruct them? What the apostles were to do after his Ascension. The phrase “through the Holy Spirit” may refer either to the apostles’ election or to his Ascension. Both were accomplished through the Holy Spirit [Col. 1918D].

The second part follows, in which Luke recapitulates what was said beforehand, saying: “To whom he also presented himself alive.” Who are these? Only those whom he chose. For the others were not worthy to receive the Lord displaying himself risen again.

He presented himself risen again by the divine power that he possesses in common with the Father and the Holy Spirit, in accordance with what he had foretold: “I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again” (John 10). By this power he will present all the dead alive again, after his own passion, which was unlike that of all others. For he alone bore our sins, not his own, upon the wood (1 Peter 2).

“Appearing to them for forty days.” Why, dearest brothers, did Christ wish to ascend into heaven not immediately after the resurrection but after many days? So that, by appearing frequently, he might confirm the apostles’ faith in the resurrection. And why after forty days? So that he might gladden for as many days the disciples whom, while dead, he had saddened for forty hours, in accordance with his promise that their sorrow would be turned into joy (John 16).

At the same time, through the symbolism of the number forty—which is completed by multiplying ten by four—he signified that he would perfect in them, through the Gospel, the fulfillment of the Decalogue.

“He appeared with many proofs.” A proof is an argument that produces belief in something doubtful. He appeared with many proofs because through many demonstrations he confirmed their faith in his resurrection: namely, by presenting himself to be seen, heard, and touched; by going and returning among them; by speaking; and by eating and drinking.

Hence John speaks both boldly and openly: “What was from the beginning,” he says, “what we have seen and heard and what our hands have touched” (1 John 1). And what ambiguity about the resurrection, my brothers, could remain in the hearts of the disciples after so many proofs?

The following also contributes to this: “And speaking about the kingdom of God.” Just as he had always been accustomed to speak about the kingdom of God before his passion, so afterward he always spoke about the same kingdom. Hence he was recognized by two disciples at Emmaus through similar words, and through a similar blessing and breaking of bread (Luke 24).

In this he leaves an example for everyone, and especially for those who hold his place in the Church, so that they may speak never about empty, idle, or harmful matters, but always about the kingdom of God and the things that pertain to it [Col. 1919C].

The third part follows, in which he pursues the history of the Lord’s Ascension at greater length, adding: “And while eating with them he commanded them,” etc.

Let us consider, brothers, how great the sweetness of this final meal today must have been. It was a meal of charity, a meal of joy, and a meal of instruction. Just as a householder about to depart for a foreign land summons his friends and relatives to a final meal, celebrates it with them with special affection, and instructs them how they should arrange his affairs, so the supreme Lord celebrated his final meal with his own even more sweetly and tenderly, and instructed them what they ought to do [Col. 1919D].

Hence it is added: “He commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem.” They were not to depart either from the place or from what it signified: that is, they were not to depart from community and communion, nor from the vision and desire of peace, but were to await the promise of the Father. This promise is also mine, he says, because “you have heard it through my mouth.”

In this we too are warned, brothers, not to withdraw from the communion of the Church if we desire the grace of the Holy Spirit to come upon us. For the Holy Spirit cannot dwell in divided and restless hearts.

He subsequently shows what gifts they were to receive through the Holy Spirit: namely, the power of cleansing and the boldness of giving testimony. He speaks of cleansing when he adds: “For John baptized with water”—understand, with water alone. “But you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now,” namely, with the Spirit cleansing you from your sins and illuminating your ignorance.

But because certain Jews had heard him speak about the kingdom of God and the fulfillment of the Father’s promise, they ask him whether at that time he would restore the kingdom of Israel—that is, the temporal and worldly kingdom that the Jews still expect to come, not remembering that the Lord had answered Pilate that his kingdom was not of this world (John 18).

The Lord rebukes their simplicity, saying: “It is not yours to know the times,” etc.—namely, future times or moments, that is, the future changes of events—“which the Father has placed in his own power.”

In this he plainly condemns those who inquire into times and future events through omens, lots, and divinations. This is a great crime, prohibited in both the Old and the New Testament. Those who do it incur a double loss: deception in the present and condemnation in the future.

Then he shows the second grace that the Holy Spirit was to confer on them when he adds: “But you will receive the power of the Holy Spirit”—for a twofold use, namely, for your sanctification and for the display of signs and miracles.

He adds a third grace when he says: “And you will be my witnesses”: by living well, boldly proclaiming my name, working miracles, and dying bravely for me, “in all Judea and Samaria and to the end of the earth.”

It is as though he said: “You will preach the salvation that I accomplished in the midst of the earth first to those within your household, then to your neighbors, and afterward to those who are distant and at the ends of the earth.”

Would that, my brothers, the Holy Spirit also descending upon us might grant us cleansing from sins, sanctification in virtue, and strength and boldness to preach, so that, casting aside earthly desire and earthly strength, we might constantly proclaim the word of God before kings, tyrants, and the wicked.

“And when he had said this”—understand, and when he had led them out to the Mount of Olives. For this reason, brothers, a solemn procession is rightly held today in memory of the procession that our Redeemer made today to the Mount of Olives.

Leaving his disciples the dear kisses of peace and blessing them, he was lifted up before their eyes, so that they might testify to the Ascension they had seen.

But by whom was he lifted up? Surely, my brothers, the Lord did not, like one powerless, need someone else’s aid to lift him up, as Enoch, who is said to have been taken away (Hebrews 11), or Elijah, who is said to have been carried away in a chariot (2 Kings 2)? Certainly not.

Those men, being merely human, could not cross even the aerial heaven and enter the earthly paradise by their own power. But our Redeemer, as true God, raised himself to the empyrean heaven by his own power. Thus the man himself was raised by himself who is God.

“And a cloud received him from their eyes.” This cloud did not carry him as an aid but as a ministry. The elements serve their Creator. The marble of the mountain from which the Lord ascended preserves to this day the impressions of his feet, as though stamped in wax. Like a pavement, it does not allow iron to be placed upon it but repels it.

The cloud—that is, condensed air—received him like a bearer. The heavens of heavens received him as Lord. Rational creatures, namely angels and human beings, testify to and marvel at the Ascension of their Lord that they had seen.

Hence it is added: “And while they were looking intently into heaven as he went,” etc.

What was the reason, my brothers, that the disciples contemplated the Lord ascending with such attention? There were several reasons: love, sadness, joy, wonder, desire, and hope.

Love: for, as far as we can, we long for what we love. Just as friends watch a friend crossing the sea from a lookout for as long as they can, and when they can no longer see their friend, they watch the ship, so the disciples contemplated their most beloved Lord ascending for as long as they could. When they could no longer contemplate him, they contemplated the cloud. When they could no longer contemplate the cloud, they contemplated the road.

Sadness: because they could not help grieving over the bodily departure of the one they loved so greatly.

Joy: because they rejoiced ineffably at the glorification and exaltation of the one they loved so greatly.

Wonder: because they marveled beyond measure that human nature, previously so humbled, had now been exalted above all the heavens.

Desire: because they desired with their whole affection to follow him. Although their bodies remained on earth, they followed him into heaven with their minds and dwelt together with him in heaven.

Hope: because they hoped that, where their supreme Head had gone before them, they, his lower members, would ascend as well.

“And while these things were happening, behold, two men”—that is, angels in the appearance of men. Two, so that “every word might stand by the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19).

They stood there to show themselves fellow ministers. They stood beside them to demonstrate that through Christ’s Ascension human beings had now been made equal and joined to them. Henceforth they do not permit themselves to be worshiped by human beings.

And they said: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven?”—as though stupefied and carried away in ecstasy into heaven.

They are called men because they were manly in virtue. They are called Galileans because in hope and desire they were journeying toward heaven. They were standing because they were already prepared in mind to follow their Lord.

“Why do you stand looking into heaven?” This question is not asked by one seeking information or rebuking them, but rather by one instructing them. This is what follows: “This Jesus who has been taken up from you into heaven.”

It is as though he said: “Do not now expect him to return—or never. He will come, but not at present; he will come at the end for judgment. He will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven: openly, gloriously, with clouds, with the ministry of angels, and sweet and joyful to you.”

May we too, together with them, deserve to see him joyfully and securely. In the meantime, let us be like them: men in spiritual virtues; Galileans, journeying toward heavenly things in hope and desire; standing and prepared to follow him; and looking into heaven more with the eyes of the mind than of the body, despising all earthly things, avoiding every stain, and already dwelling with our whole mind with Christ in heavenly places.

Let us draw near to him as far as we can—by mind, life, desire, and works—so that at last we may hasten joyfully to him, guided by him who on this day ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father, living and reigning with him and the Holy Spirit forever. Amen.

## HOMILY LXIX. ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

“Finally, as the eleven disciples were reclining at table, Jesus appeared to them” (Mark 16).

Dearest brothers, Mark the Evangelist explains in the reading just heard the history of the Lord’s Ascension, which was celebrated on this day [Col. 1922B]. This reading is divided into six sections. First, the Lord appears to his disciples; second, he rebukes them; third, he instructs them; fourth, he promises them assistance; fifth, he ascends into heaven; sixth, it is shown that the disciples obeyed the Lord, while he cooperated with them.

The Evangelist first describes the Lord’s appearance when he says: “Finally, as they were reclining,” etc. “Finally” means on the final day of the forty days, namely, today. The Lord appeared to his eleven disciples as they reclined at table with the blessed Virgin and the others who were staying with them.

He appeared not only to them but, as another Evangelist testifies, he also ate with them (Luke 24). But why, my brothers, did the Lord eat when he was about to ascend into heaven and had no need to do so? For three reasons: to demonstrate through eating the reality of his flesh, which he was about to exalt into heaven; to provide his beloved with an abundant final experience of his desired presence before he departed; and to impress more deeply upon the hearts of his own the memory of his charity and sweetness through the intimacy of this final meal.

Let us therefore consider, brothers, how great the piety and sweetness of this final meal today must have been. Just as a householder about to depart for a foreign land and bid farewell to his own summons his friends and relatives, celebrates a final meal with them, shows them greater affection at the end, and orders his affairs, so today our Lord and Redeemer, about to ascend into heaven, celebrated a final meal with his dear mother and dear disciples [Col. 1922D]. At the end he showed them greater affection and commanded what they were to do after his Ascension, as what follows demonstrates.

The second part follows when it is added: “He reproached them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him after he had risen from the dead.”

To reproach is to cast a fault in someone’s face. Some reproach another publicly, though they do not love him, because of hatred and defamation. This is not good but a very great evil. But one who wishes to follow the Lord’s example should reproach the sinner for his fault privately, solely for the sake of charity and correction [Col. 1923A].

A public reproach, because it does not appear to flow from the fountain of charity but from hatred, usually does not reform the sinner but rather provokes him. A reproach made privately, however, because it appears to proceed from good zeal, makes the sinner our friend and reforms him.

Certainly, not everyone who fails to believe something is an unbeliever. A person can properly be called an unbeliever when he does not believe what he ought to believe, especially when he has sufficient testimony from someone to whom he ought rightly to give credence.

Such were certain disciples who did not believe that the Lord had truly risen, although the other disciples—who had already seen the Lord risen, touched him, and eaten and drunk with him—provided them with sufficient testimony to the Lord’s resurrection.

Such also are the wretched Jews to this day, who do not wish to believe in the Lord’s resurrection despite the testimony of their own prophets, of the apostles and evangelists, and of signs and miracles [Col. 1923B].

Such unbelief arises from hardness of heart, which wishes to believe no one except itself, supposing everyone else to be either deceived or false. But, my brothers, just as it is foolish credulity to believe everyone, so it is perverse unbelief to believe no one.

Hence John says: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (1 John 4). It is as though he said: “After you have tested whether the spirits are from God, give them your faith.”

But, my brothers, why did the Lord permit his chosen disciples to doubt his resurrection for so long? He permitted this not without reason but through a prudent and useful dispensation for our sake. Those who believed slowly and with difficulty benefited us more than those who believed immediately.

The credulous readily believe even a matter not yet proved. The unbelieving, by contrast, scarcely wish to believe a matter proved in many ways. Who, then, would not believe what even the unbelieving could not fail to believe?

Who would not believe that Thomas, the unbeliever, was compelled to believe by his own sight and by the careful touch of his hand? Who would not believe that Paul, an unbeliever and persecutor of the faith, was compelled to believe after being thrown to the ground and blinded by the Lord speaking to him, and afterward illuminated again by that same Lord? (Acts 9.)

Let us therefore believe, brothers, without hesitation what even unbelievers believed, and let us give thanks to God, who wished his disciples to doubt for this reason: so that we would not doubt. He wished them to be unbelieving for a time so that we would not be unbelievers [Col. 1923D].

The third part follows, in which the Lord instructs his disciples what they must do after his Ascension, saying: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature,” etc. The disciples, first chosen and instructed by the Lord, were afterward sent to preach. By this those are put to shame who, before they are taught, presume to teach and preach; before they are disciples, they become teachers. Those too are put to shame who, neither called nor sent, presume on their own authority to exercise mastery and preach, paying no attention to what the Apostle says: “How shall they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. X).

“Go,” he says, “into all the world.” [Col. 1924A] Behold, brothers, how great a field is handed over for cultivation to so few farmers. Indeed, the Lord says elsewhere: “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Luke X). For this reason they are forbidden to carry anything on the road and to greet anyone, so that they may proceed without encumbrance and without delay, and hasten to carry out the office of preaching entrusted to them. In this also an example is set before us, their successors in preaching: we must not burden ourselves with the honors of secular affairs, nor consume our time in conversation and empty words, but attend readily and promptly to the office of preaching.

“Preach,” he says, “the Gospel,” not another doctrine. By this those are put to shame who, abandoning evangelical doctrine, presume to preach to the peoples things devised by themselves or borrowed from elsewhere, although the Lord says through the prophet: “You shall announce to them from me” (Ezek. III).

“To every creature,” that is, to the human being, for whose sake every creature was made, and in whom every creature is contained through participation in its natures. For he has being with the stones, life with the trees, sensation with the animals, and discernment with the angels. Therefore, brothers, since we are called “every creature” because of our excellence, let us vindicate by our conduct the dominion which by nature we possess over creatures. Let us rule temporal things through right use and proper administration; let us not shamefully subject ourselves to them, as some do through greed and avarice. Of such people it is written: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. XLVIII).

What benefit those who heed the preaching obtain is shown when it follows: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved.” But someone says: “I believe and have been baptized; therefore I shall be saved.” You speak truly, brother, if you keep the covenant which you made in baptism. In baptism you promised that you would renounce the devil, his pomps, and his works. But if you have fallen back into the works of the devil, you have broken the covenant, and faith and baptism have become useless to you. For it is written: “What benefit is there for one baptized from the dead, if he touches him again, from his washing?” (Ecclus. XXXIV). Faith also, as James testifies, is dead without works (James II). Paul likewise says of those who believe but do not perform the works of faith: “They profess in words that they know God, but in their deeds they deny him” (Titus I).

Therefore, my brothers, if you truly believe and keep the covenant of baptism inviolate, without doubt you will be saved. But if you have broken the covenant of baptism and faith, hasten, brothers, hasten through the tears of repentance to renew it as quickly as possible, since divine mercy will not deny salvation even to those who, after falling, rise again through true repentance.

What those who do not heed the preaching obtain is shown when it is added: “But whoever does not believe will be condemned.” He does not say, “Whoever does not believe and has not been baptized,” because without faith neither baptism nor works are beneficial. Therefore, my brothers, three things are necessary for us adults to possess: faith, baptism, and works. One of these, without the others, can benefit us nothing. [Col. 1925A]

The fourth part follows, in which the Lord promises that signs will always confirm the preaching of the disciples, saying: “These signs will accompany those who believe: In my name they will cast out demons,” namely, from bodies possessed by them. “They will speak in new tongues,” that is, in various and unheard-of languages. Concerning these we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how is it that we hear each of them in our own language in which we were born? Parthians and Medes” (Acts II), etc.

“They will take up serpents,” as we read concerning blessed Hilary, that, when they saw him, serpents turned and fled, unable to endure his presence. “And if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them,” as we read concerning blessed John the Evangelist, who drank poison by which others had been killed; and he not only remained unharmed but also raised the dead whom it had killed. “They will lay hands on the sick, and they will be well,” as we read concerning blessed Peter, who healed the sick not only by his touch but also by his shadow (Acts V).

But surely, my brothers, are we who do not now perform these signs not believers? Or, if we are believers, why do we not perform these signs? Because signs and wonders were given for unbelievers, so that through them they might be brought to faith, as the teacher of the nations testifies: “Tongues are given as a sign, not to believers but to unbelievers” (1 Cor. XIV).

Since miracles were therefore necessary in the primitive Church, the Lord performed many miracles, even through certain people who were Christians in name only. When at the end they say, “Lord, did we not cast out demons in your name and perform many mighty works?” he will say: “I do not know you” (Matt. VII). But now, since faith has increased throughout the whole world, and signs are not necessary among believers, there are many who shine before God with inward virtues and yet do not perform miracles outwardly. We water newly planted shoots, but when they have grown we cease. Thus miracles nourished the young Church; once it had been strengthened, they ceased.

Nevertheless, brothers, although we do not now perform outward signs, yet, with God’s help, we can perform spiritual virtues, which do not have so much glory here and therefore are of greater merit. In the name of Christ we cast out demons spiritually if, through prayers, correction, and exhortation, we free a sinner from the dominion of the devil and of sin and win him for God.

We speak in new tongues if, stripped of the oldness of falsehood, slander, flattery, empty speech, and other vices, we praise God with new and pure praises, and rebuke and teach the ungodly with holy and new words. We take up serpents if, as far as we can, we drive the serpentine malice from the hearts of the malicious by reproofs, threats, and promises; or at least repel it so that it may not harm others. We drink something deadly and it does not harm us when, hearing slander and malice, we do not consent to them but rather repel and rebuke them. We lay hands on the sick, and they are well, when, placing upon weak and sorrowful souls the hand of counsel and assistance, we enable them to recover and be strengthened. [Col. 1926A]

Let us strive after such virtues, dearly beloved brothers, and desire to possess them. They produce holiness, whereas outward miracles do not produce holiness but merely display it. John the Baptist—than whom, according to the Lord’s testimony, no greater has arisen from woman (Matt. II)—performed no sign, as the Jews testify; yet he lacked no virtue.

The fifth part follows, when it is added: “And indeed the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them”—that is, after he had also led them out onto the Mount of Olives and given them the kiss of peace and his blessing—“was taken up into heaven.” He was not taken up by another’s assistance, as Enoch and Elijah were, but he himself, as man, was taken up by himself as God. Nor was he taken up merely into the airy heaven, as Enoch and Elijah, but into heaven, indeed above the heavens, above the cherubim and seraphim, and above every creature. Hence the Prophet says: “Sing praises to the Lord who ascended above the heavens of heavens toward the east” (Ps. LXVII).

For the Lord ascended above the heavens of heavens, having subjected every height to himself. He ascended toward the east because today, bodily, he came to that eternal and inaccessible light from which every light arises. “And he sits,” he says, “at my right hand.” To sit, my brothers, is the posture of one who rests, reigns, and judges. Therefore our Redeemer is rightly described as sitting after his passion and Ascension, because after labor he rests, after battle he reigns, and after he was judged he judges.

In this, brothers, an example is set before us: if here we labor and suffer in imitation of our Redeemer, we shall rest with him; if in imitation of him we fight against the devil, we shall reign with him; if here we are judged in imitation of him, we shall judge with him. Hence he himself says: “Whoever ministers to me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also will my minister be” (John XII). Therefore, brothers, let us share in labor if we wish to share in honor; let us be companions in punishment if we wish to be companions in glory.

But why does Stephen, after the Ascension, see the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God? (Acts VII.) Because Stephen was engaged in combat for his name, and therefore he sees him standing as though ready to be his helper. We too, my brothers, if we fight for his name, although he now reigns seated, shall nevertheless experience him standing—that is, ready to bring us aid.

Again, why is our Lord Jesus Christ described as sitting at the right hand of God, when God the Father has neither a right nor a left hand? The glory of eternal blessedness is represented by the name “right hand.” Hence the Lord says that at the judgment he will place the sheep at his right hand (Matt. II). Therefore our Redeemer is said to sit at the right hand of God because he reigns in the glory and majesty of the Father. By sitting at the right hand we also commonly understand equality. For when we make someone sit at our right hand, we make him, as it were, our equal in honor. Christ, therefore, is rightly said to sit at the right hand of the Father, because he reigns with him in glory and in equality of majesty. [Col. 1927A]

Therefore, as the Psalmist exhorts us, let us sing praises to the Lord who ascended above the heavens of heavens toward the east. Let us sing praises, I say, to the Lord, not to the world or to worldly vanity, whose joy will be turned into sorrow, but to the Lord who, just as he was born and suffered not for himself but for us, so also rose for us and ascended above the heavens for us.

Let us rejoice, brothers, because our nature, to which it had been said, “You are earth, and into earth you shall return” (Gen. III), has today been exalted above every height of heaven and placed at the right hand of God the Father. Let us rejoice, I say, because he who sits as judge in heaven is a participant in our nature and our advocate. Let us rejoice because the angels no longer despise us human beings as once they did, but rather venerate us and serve the nature that has been exalted above them. Let us rejoice because Christ has opened for us the entrance to the heavenly kingdom; and if we truly love him, without doubt we shall arrive where he has gone before us. [Col. 1927B]

The sixth part follows, in which the disciples are described as obeying the Lord, when it is added: “But they went forth and preached everywhere.” For, as had been foretold concerning them: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII).

But surely, brothers, could they do this by themselves? Hear what follows: “The Lord working with them and confirming the word through the accompanying signs.” The Lord, who commanded the disciples to go and preach, himself gave them both the will and the ability to do so; himself supplied the word to them as they preached; himself confirmed their preaching with powers and miracles; himself prepared the minds of their hearers and inclined them to believe, according to what he had said to them: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV).

This is plainly directed against those who ascribe what they understand shrewdly, what they argue persuasively, and what they do vigorously to natural talent and their own powers of eloquence, rather than to God, as though they were saying: “We will magnify our tongue; our lips are our own. Who is our lord?” (Ps. XI). In contrast, Paul cries out: “It is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX).

For he first works a good will in us without us; afterward he cooperates with us in the good work, which through his mercy he will reward in us as though it had proceeded from us alone. Would that he who today sent me to preach to you would work with me, giving a right and well-sounding word to my mouth, giving you also an understanding heart to comprehend, and confirming my word, so that what I have preached to you may be confirmed in me by conduct and deeds, and in you by signs of contrition and amendment. Thus may we deserve to ascend to those everlasting joys where our Lord Jesus Christ ascended on this day, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# HOMILY LXX. THE FIRST SUNDAY AFTER THE ASCENSION

“Be prudent and watchful in prayers” (1 Peter IV), etc.

In this reading, dearly beloved brothers, the Apostle Peter intends to instruct us in conduct. He urges us toward five things: prudence, prayer, charity, works of mercy, and always referring whatever good we do to the Lord.

Urging us first toward prudence, he says: “Be prudent.” Prudence is the leader and guide of all virtues. For just as someone who lacks light wanders and does not proceed, so anyone without wisdom can neither avoid error nor proceed rightly. Hence the Law also commands that no sacrifice be offered without the salt of wisdom.

Prudence is a virtue that weighs each matter with the truest judgment. It has three parts. The first wisely distinguishes not only between good and evil, but also between good and better, and between evil and worse. The second wisely chooses what has been discerned. The third wisely acquires what has been chosen.

The first part of prudence therefore teaches us, dearly beloved brothers, what is a lesser good, what is a greater good, and what is the highest good; what is a lesser evil, what is a worse evil, and what is the worst evil.

The lesser goods are riches, honors, powers, and whatever temporal possessions we hold. They are indeed good, because they were created and given by God, who makes nothing but good things; yet they are lesser goods, because even wicked people possess them, and when used badly by those who possess them, they become evil. Greater goods are virtues and the gifts of the Holy Spirit, because only the good possess them, and through them one goes toward the highest good. The highest good is eternal blessedness, which is God. [Col. 1928C]

By contrast, lesser evils are temporal miseries, needs, and afflictions. They are called evils, that is, punishments inflicted for evils. Yet they are lesser evils, because they are inflicted even upon the good, and when the good use them well, they become good for them. Worse evils are vices and sins, which make those who possess them evil and drag them toward the worst and highest evil. The worst and highest evil is eternal damnation.

Therefore, my brothers, we must desire above all and before all else the highest good and eternal blessedness, which is God. After that, the virtues and gifts of the Holy Spirit, which lead us to it, are to be desired more than anything else. Conversely, we must avoid damnation before all else, and after that we must flee vices and sins, which drag us toward it.

But lesser good and lesser evil—that is, temporal abundance or want, prosperity or adversity—we must neither desire nor avoid excessively.
