Since these become good for those who use them well and evil for those who use them badly, we should place them more in God’s will, so that he may grant us what he knows will benefit us most. For there are some who would be saved only through prosperity, and there are some who would be saved only through adversity.

Thus the first part of prudence instructs us. Opposed to it is the folly that does not distinguish evil from good, but rather takes evil for good or good for evil, falling under that curse: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil” (Isa. V). Or it regards a lesser good as a greater good, or a lesser evil as a greater evil.

With this folly—which is all the more grievous—many today are afflicted. They flee worldly poverty and afflictions more than vices and sins or eternal damnation, and desire worldly riches, honors, and little glories more than virtues and eternal blessedness. Thus they despise spiritual and eternal goods for the sake of temporal goods, calling someone wise who knows how to amass temporal goods by any art, fraud, or abomination. But such wisdom is certainly folly before God. Hence the Lord says: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the prudence of the prudent” (Isa. XXIX; 1 Cor. I). Why? “Because they will leave their riches to others, and their tombs will be their houses forever” (Ps. XLVIII).

The second part of prudence is, after discerning wisely, to choose wisely. For it is of no benefit to distinguish wisely between good and evil, and between lesser and greater good, unless you choose what ought more to be chosen.

This is plainly directed against us, teachers and pastors of peoples, who, although we distinguish well between good and evil and between lesser and greater goods or evils, and teach others what they ought to choose, nevertheless knowingly choose what is worse ourselves, hastening to become richer rather than more justified, and to be more honored in the world than before God. But what will happen to such people? They will descend alive into hell—that is, knowingly—because, rejecting the greater good, they chose what was worse for themselves. [Col. 1929B]

The third part of prudence is to acquire the chosen good wisely. One acquires the chosen good wisely when one strives to possess it as readily and easily as possible. This, my brothers, is directed against some of us who, although we have chosen to strive toward the highest good, nevertheless do not strive toward it readily, but delay ourselves through the cares of secular affairs and desires. We do not pay attention to the fact that “everyone who competes in the contest abstains from everything” (1 Cor. IX).

Hence, like Moses, we are reproved by Jethro—that is, by any secular person—because, neglecting divine matters, we wear ourselves out in foolish labor over secular affairs. Therefore, my brothers, let us heed the advice of the gentile and choose certain stewards who will carry the burden of secular cares for us, so that we may attend more freely to the things that belong to God. [Col. 1929D]

Second, he urges us toward prayer when he adds: “And be watchful in prayers.” What we have chosen through prudence to pursue or avoid, we obtain chiefly through prayer. Through prayer we both drive away the assaults of demons and vices and obtain the virtues and gifts of the Holy Spirit and eternal blessedness.

Moreover, since the demons never sleep but are always watchful in laying ambushes, let us, as far as we can, always be watchful in prayer, according to what the Apostle says elsewhere: “Be watchful in prayers, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter V).

Since the devil is chiefly defeated through prayer, he therefore tries as far as he can to hinder one who prays. He sends, as far as he can, laziness, sleepiness, and alien and empty thoughts upon the one praying. But let us, as the Apostle urges, be watchful and repel his evil attacks as far as we can, according to what is read concerning Abraham: “The birds of heaven descended upon the sacrifices, and Abraham drove them away” (Gen. XV).

We are then watchful in prayers, my brothers, when we are watchful not only in body but also in mind and in our actions. Whoever is watchful in prayer only in body, while sleeping in sin through his conduct or mind, should certainly be said not to be awake but rather to be sleeping in prayer. Minds reach the Lord’s ears more than voices, and deeds more than words.

Therefore, brothers, let us place before our eyes two people: one wicked, who prays while awake only in body; and another righteous, who, through the habit of prayer, prays even while sleeping. I say, brothers, that the former, while awake, sleeps in prayer, whereas the latter, while sleeping, is awake in prayer: although he sleeps in body, his good life and good purpose pray on his behalf.

I saw a certain priest who was dying. Although he had reached the point where he understood nothing in this world, nevertheless, because of the long habit to which he had become accustomed while alive, even as he died he did not cease frequently offering divine praises.

Let us therefore accustom ourselves, my brothers, to pray not only with the voice but also with mind and deed. Let us rise with the Psalmist at midnight to give thanks to the Lord (Ps. CXVIII). Let us also praise him seven times: at the morning praises, at Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline. Indeed, whatever we do—whether we leave the house, return, sit, rise, or do anything else—let us always arm ourselves with prayer, so that through long habit, even while sleeping or dying, we may be unable not to pray. For if it is not without sin when the wicked, through habit, swears even while sleeping, it is not without merit when the righteous prays even while sleeping. [Col. 1930C]

Third, the Apostle urges us toward charity when he adds: “Above all, my brothers, have continual mutual charity among yourselves.” The good which we choose through wisdom and request through prayer, we possess through charity. For whoever has the charity of God surely already has God, because “God is charity” (1 John IV), essentially in himself and causally in us.

Charity is the love by which we love God for his own sake, and ourselves and our neighbor for God’s sake. We must love God, brothers, for his own sake for three reasons: because he is naturally good in himself and worthy of love; because by loving us first he merited being loved; and because it is supremely beneficial to love him.

We must love our neighbor not for his own sake but for God’s sake: because he is God’s work; because God commanded us to love him; and because he is good, or so that he may become good. We must love either ourselves or our neighbor in what is good, not in what is evil. To love oneself or one’s neighbor in evil is not love but hatred.

We must therefore exercise great discernment in loving an evil neighbor, so that we love his nature without loving his wickedness, and hate his wickedness without hating his nature. For the one who loves the wickedness of his neighbor on account of his nature sins equally with the one who hates his nature on account of his wickedness.

We must have this charity continually. For just as the body cannot live without the spirit, so the soul cannot live without love of God and neighbor. No adversity, not even death itself, interrupts true love, because “love is strong as death” (Song VIII)—indeed, stronger than death. And in the life to come it will not perish but will be perfected.

We must also have this charity “among ourselves,” that is, rooted in our inmost hearts, so that we do not love in word or with the tongue, as some do, but in deed and in truth (1 John III). We must have it above all, because when it is possessed, everything is possessed, and when it is absent, nothing is possessed. Nothing has value without it, and through it everything has value.

It is the oil that cannot be pressed down but rises above all liquids. Therefore, if we cannot possess all virtues or all knowledge, let us at least possess charity, so that through it we may possess all virtues and knowledge in others.

Why we ought to possess charity he shows when he adds: “Because charity covers a multitude of sins,” etc.—those of the future, so that they may not occur, and those already committed, so that they may not appear for punishment. For by this, brothers, our sins are especially forgiven: when we forgive others, when we show compassion toward the suffering, and when through mercy we bear the burdens of others. [Col. 1931C]

Fourth, he urges us toward works of mercy when he adds: “Be hospitable to one another without murmuring.” Charity, once possessed, cannot remain idle but displays itself through works of mercy. Among works of mercy, brothers, hospitality is especially important. Because Lot and Abraham, and many other fathers in both the Old and New Testaments, received human beings into their homes, they were worthy to receive angels, indeed God himself.

This is one of the six works of mercy which the Lord will remember at the judgment: “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me” (Matt. XXV). The Apostle commands that this be done without murmuring. Whoever performs this or any other work of mercy with murmuring of the mouth or bitterness of mind loses both the deed and its merit.

This is directed against those who, when a guest arrives, mutter among themselves, become sad, darken their faces, and complain that their house is not spacious enough and that they lack sufficient beds and coverings. They say that much of the day still remains, so that they force their guests to leave.

What shall I say, by contrast, about those who invite guests into their homes in order to strip them of their possessions? They are thieves and robbers. Therefore, my brothers, let us devote ourselves to hospitality for God alone. Let us receive guests gladly; indeed, following the custom of the ancients, let us seek them out and compel them to enter. Let us gladly offer them what we can, for devotion pleases God more than the greatness of the service.

Next he urges us toward the other works of charity when he adds: “As each one has received a gift, administering it.” God grants particular gifts to each person for this purpose: so that each one may administer his gift not to himself alone but to those who do not possess it.

Therefore, let the one who has wisdom teach the ignorant; let the one who has riches support the needy with them; let the one who has power use it to defend the powerless. Otherwise, by hiding the light under a measure and concealing the talent, they will be deprived of them and rejected (Luke II; Matt. XXV).

“As good stewards,” he says, “of the manifold grace of God.” A good steward is not one who keeps his master’s goods for himself alone, but one who distributes them according to his master’s will. We, brothers, are not masters but stewards of the possessions entrusted to us by the Lord God.

If, therefore, we do not distribute the Lord’s goods to his needy children as he commanded, we are rightly convicted of being thieves of the Lord’s property and murderers of his poor. Let the rich fear this and reflect upon it—those who refuse to distribute their riches to the poor who are perishing from want. They are guilty of as many souls as they could have saved from hunger but refused to save. [Col. 1932B]

Fifth, he urges us to handle the work of God worthily when he adds: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God”—that is, if anyone speaks the words of God, let him speak them as the words of God.

A preacher does this when he attributes his sermon to God, refers it back to God, and delivers it worthily. He attributes the word to God when, if he says anything good, he ascribes it not to himself, as some do, but to God. He refers the word back to God when he directs it not toward temporal profit or glory, as some do, but toward God’s glory and the benefit of his neighbors. He delivers God’s word worthily when he does not destroy it by a bad example, and does not utter it negligently or sluggishly, as some do, but rather preaches the word of God with a good example, great devotion, and diligence.

“If anyone ministers,” he says—that is, if anyone is a minister—“let him do so as from the power which God supplies.” We do this when, if we minister anything well, we attribute the whole of it to God, refer it back to God, and, as far as we are able, minister devoutly, wisely, and diligently.

“So that in all things,” he says, “God may be honored.” For when we show ourselves to be good preachers, good ministers, and good sons of God, God is honored and sanctified in us—not because he becomes more holy through us, but because through him we become holier. This is through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be honor and glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# HOMILY LXXI. THE FIRST SUNDAY AFTER THE ASCENSION

“When the Paraclete has come, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me” (John XV).

As our Lord and Redeemer was about to withdraw from his disciples through his passion and ascend into heaven, he promised them, so that they would not grieve at being abandoned and desolate, that he would send them a comforter, namely, the Holy Spirit.

In this reading he foretells four things to them: first, that he will send them the Holy Spirit; second, what the Holy Spirit will accomplish in them; third, he shows that persecutions will come upon them; fourth, he explains why he foretells these things.

First, therefore, he foretells that he will send them the Holy Spirit when he says: “When the Paraclete has come, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father.”

But none of you, dearly beloved brothers, when you hear of the coming, sending, or descent of the Holy Spirit, should understand a local movement of the Holy Spirit. Since the Holy Spirit is one in substance with the Father and the Son, and just as he fills all things substantially, so he cannot come near or withdraw locally.

Rather, the Holy Spirit is said to come or descend to us when his gift and grace are sent into us, according to the figure called metonymy, namely, when what belongs to the gift is ascribed to its author.

In this sense John says that seven spirits of the Holy Spirit have been sent into the whole earth, because there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit which are distributed to the faithful throughout the world. But here we must consider, dearly beloved brothers, that the Holy Spirit is not said to be sent on account of every gift of his. If he gives someone knowledge, power, or something of this kind, which wicked people also possess, the Holy Spirit is not for that reason said to be sent into him. He is said to be sent on account only of those gifts which sanctify a person, such as charity, self-control, mercy, and the other virtues.

Therefore, my brothers, let us desire and strive to obtain not those gifts which the wicked also possess, but those which belong only to the good, and through which they deserve to have the Holy Spirit as their indwelling possessor.

“Whom I,” he says, “will send to you from the Father.” Of this same Spirit he says elsewhere: “Whom the Father will send in my name” (John XIV). From this it is plainly evident that the Holy Spirit is sent by the Father and is sent by the Son. But the Son’s sending of the Holy Spirit comes not from himself but from the Father. Hence he adds: “Whom I will send to you from the Father.”

Of him he further says: “Who proceeds from the Father,” namely, eternally and ineffably. Hence, brothers, a twofold procession of the Holy Spirit is understood. One is that by which the Holy Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son, as the third person in the Trinity and one substance with them; the other is that by which he proceeds daily and temporally from the Father and the Son to sanctify creation.

This same Holy Spirit is called by many names. He is called the Holy Spirit because he sanctifies creatures. He is called the Paraclete because he comforts the desolate, heals the sick, gives counsel to the ill-advised, and forgives the guilty.

He is called the Spirit of truth because he does not deceive like the devil, but faithfully fulfills his promises and makes people truthful: truthful in the confession of sins, truthful in the proclamation of truth, and truthful in the intention of their works.

He is also called Love, Concord, and Goodness, both because he is the bond of the Father and the Son, and because in human hearts he breathes and nourishes love, concord, and goodness.

Therefore, brothers, we must continually implore him with increasingly ardent desires, so that that desirable Holy Spirit may sanctify us from our impurities, make us truthful, and render us loving, harmonious, and kind.

Second, he shows what the Holy Spirit worked in the disciples when he adds: “He will bear witness concerning me.” In three ways, brothers, the Holy Spirit bears witness concerning Christ, namely that he is the Son of God: through the working of miracles and mighty deeds; through inward inspiration in people’s hearts; and through the testimony of preaching. For the Holy Spirit persuaded some to believe in Christ through miracles and mighty deeds, others through inward inspiration, and still others through outward preaching. The Holy Spirit bears witness to Christ metonymically, in that he makes human beings bear witness to him. Hence he also adds: “And you will bear witness.” [Col. 1934B] As though he were saying:

“You too, who are now timid—having abandoned me, fleeing, denying me at the voice of a single servant girl, and hiding for fear of the Jews—when the Holy Spirit, namely the Spirit of fortitude, strengthens you inwardly, will bear witness concerning me before every nation and every tongue, without daring to confess me even with one tongue because of the Jews’ opposition. And how will you do this? In four ways: by preaching me as the Son of God; by living rightly in me, since the holiness of ministers bears witness to the holiness of their master; by performing mighty deeds and miracles in my name, since the power of the name bears witness to its author; and by suffering for my name, since one who does not refuse to die for a cause bears excellent witness to it.”

[Note: [Col. 1933] Thus you, not for yourselves: Radulphus Ardens discovered it; B. Pascal is praised for it. See *Pensées de B. Pascal*, [lacuna], “Witnesses who have themselves slaughtered.”—ED. P.]

Would that, my brothers, the Holy Spirit might descend upon us also, giving us boldness and strength to bear witness to Christ. For what I cannot say without tears is that we, the teachers of the Church, are today more timid than Christ’s uneducated disciples were at the beginning of the nascent Church. When, because of fear of some secular person, we either deny or remain silent about the truth, we deny Christ, who is the truth. When a robber robs a poor man and we withdraw our assistance from him, we flee as though we had abandoned Christ. When a powerful man oppresses an orphan or a widow and we say nothing against him, we remain silent as though Christ were hanging upon the cross. When we do not oppose the persecutors of the Church through the rigor of justice, we hide ourselves as though for fear of the Jews.

“For you have been with me from the beginning.” As though he were saying: Since a person can rightly bear witness to what he has seen and heard, you can rightly bear witness concerning me, because you have been with me from the beginning, instructed in the truth about me through familiar companionship. Hence the apostles chose in Judas’s place not a novice, but one who had been instructed at length in Christ’s teaching. Thus Peter says: “It is necessary that one of these men who have accompanied us throughout the whole time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us become with us a witness of his resurrection” (Acts I). This is directed against those who choose an inexperienced novice as a teacher, and also against those who presume to teach and preach a doctrine in whose school they have not been nourished.

Third, he foretells three persecutions that will come upon them, namely expulsion, death, and disgrace. He speaks of expulsion when he says: “But I have told you these things”—that is, I have foretold them—“so that you may not be scandalized because they will exclude you from the synagogues.” Just as today, because of public crimes, we excommunicate some people and expel them from communion with the Church, so the Jews excluded Christ’s disciples from the synagogues as criminals, because of Christ.

He speaks of death and disgrace when he adds: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God.” As though he were saying: They will think so badly of you that they will believe you so hateful to God that, in killing you, they will suppose themselves to be performing a service for God and pleasing him by doing so. “And they will do these things,” he says, “because they have not known the Father, nor me”—because they have not known that God is my Father, nor that I am his Son. As though he were saying:

“Do not be distressed if you are expelled from the synagogues of those who do not know God. Do not be distressed if you are killed for God’s sake by those who are ignorant of God. Do not be distressed if you are judged hostile to God by those who have not known God. For to be excluded from the fellowship of the wicked is to be joined to God; to be killed for God’s sake is to live; to endure false disgrace for God’s sake is praise.”

From this, brothers, let us take an example of consolation whenever the wicked hate or despise our fellowship, whenever they persecute us to the point of death, or whenever they slander and judge badly those of us who live well. To endure these things patiently for Christ’s sake is to bear witness to Christ, and thus to be Christ’s martyr.

Fourth, he gives the reason why he had foretold these things to them: “I have told you these things,” he says, “so that when the hour comes, you may remember them, because I told you.” And what benefit resulted from this? Many benefits: so that they might understand him to be truthful in all things; so that they might confidently await the consolation he had foretold; so that they might arm themselves bravely against adversity; so that they might endure adversity courageously; and so that amid adversity they might rejoice in the hope of consolation. The benefit of these predictions to the apostles became clear when they went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been judged worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus (Acts V).

Let us therefore, my brothers, implore our Redeemer Jesus Christ with sighs and tears, so that he may give us the Holy Spirit, who will inspire in us repentance for sins; moderation in prosperity; courage in adversity; consolation in sorrow; contempt for earthly things; and love of heavenly things—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY LXXII. ON THE HOLY DAY OF PENTECOST

“When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, all the disciples were together in the same place,” etc. (Acts II). Today, dearly beloved brothers, we celebrate the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the disciples. Since the preceding reading explains it sufficiently, it is appropriately read in the Church today. Seven things are therefore shown in this reading: when, upon whom, where, with what signs, [Col. 1936A] and how the Holy Spirit descended; what he bestowed upon them; and how great an amazement followed from it.

First, then, we are shown when the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples, when it is said: “When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled.” Now the Holy Spirit is read as having been given to the apostles twice. First, on the very day of the resurrection, when the Lord breathed upon the apostles, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX). Second, on the day of Pentecost, namely on this present day.

On the day of the resurrection he was given to them for the remission of sins, so that, rising with the one who had risen, they too might rise from the sins into which they had fallen by fleeing, denying, distrusting, or doubting. But on the fiftieth day the same Holy Spirit was given to them for strengthening and confirmation, so that thereafter, firm in faith, they would yield to no persecution, but would rather preach the truth steadfastly before every authority.

Hence, at the first giving of the Holy Spirit, they are said to have received only the Holy Spirit, whereas at this one they are also said to have been filled with the Holy Spirit. Likewise, brothers, even today the Holy Spirit is given to the faithful twice: first in baptism or in penance, for the remission of sins; second in confirmation, for confirmation and strengthening.

This is aptly signified by the fact that the disciples are remembered as having received the Holy Spirit first on the day of the Lord’s resurrection and as having been filled with the Holy Spirit afterward, on the fiftieth day. For unless we first rise from our sins through the Holy Spirit, and labor toward the forty-day penance and the fulfillment of the Decalogue, we cannot be filled with the Holy Spirit.

We, therefore, my brothers, who lie in the tomb of sins, should pray to that most gracious Spirit to make us rise from our sins. But you who have already risen from sins through the Holy Spirit, and have labored through the forty days of satisfaction and the Decalogue of the law, pray also to that most holy Spirit that he may fill you with an increase of his gifts and confirm you in strength.

Second, we are shown upon whom the Holy Spirit descended, when it is said: “All the disciples”—that is, they were all waiting and prepared to receive the Holy Spirit, in accordance with what the Lord had commanded them: not to depart from Jerusalem, but to await the Father’s promise (Acts I). They waited and prepared themselves to receive the Holy Spirit by praying and fasting.

That they did so by praying is shown in the Acts of the Apostles, where he says: “They were persevering in prayer with the women and Mary, the mother of Jesus” (ibid.). That they did so by fasting we learn from the fact that, when the Jews asked why his disciples did not fast, the Lord answered: “The children of the bridegroom cannot mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them. But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast” (Matthew IX; Mark II; Luke V).

Whatever may be said about fasting from food, it is absolutely certain that they fasted, as far as they could, from every vice and sin, from every evil and vain thought, and from every evil and vain word, so that, having been purified, they might be found worthy to receive purely the Spirit of purity.

We too, my brothers, if we desire to receive the Holy Spirit, should make it our concern to be Christ’s disciples and to persevere in prayer and fasting. We are Christ’s disciples if we embrace his discipline and teaching in humility, in quietness, in fear, and in love. For the Holy Spirit undoubtedly rests upon such people. Hence he himself says through the Prophet: “Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah LXVI).

It is also necessary that we persevere in prayer, not merely with the lips, but from a pure heart. For, as the Wise Man says: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wisdom I). It is also necessary that we fast not only from food, but also from evil and vain thought, speech, and action. For it is written: “Wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body enslaved to sins” (ibid.).

Third, it is shown where the disciples were praying when the Holy Spirit came upon them, when it is added: “Together in the same place.” He says less but signifies more. For they were in the same place, in the same heart and love, and in the same sharing of possessions.

They were in the same place because they were in the same city, Jerusalem, on the same Mount Zion, in the same upper room of sacred Scripture and spiritual refreshment. They were also in the same heart and love, since it is written of them: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV). They were likewise in the same sharing of possessions, because no one said that anything he possessed was his own, but everything was common to them (ibid.).

The Prophet admires their unanimous dwelling together and communion in the Spirit, saying: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Psalm CXXXII); and elsewhere: “God is in his holy place: God, who makes those of one mind dwell in a house” (Psalm LXVII), that is, people of one accord.

No place is more holy or more favorable to God than the harmony and unanimity of holy souls, which he alone produces by his grace in holy assemblies. For where there is peace and concord, there, without doubt, are charity and God. But where there is discord, strife, and hatred, there most certainly is the evil spirit.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, if we desire the Holy Spirit to come upon us, let us remove quarrels, discord, envy, and hatred from our midst. And just as we assemble together in the same church, just as we share in the same sacraments, and just as we have one faith, one baptism, one God and Lord, so let there be in us one will, one charity, and one sharing of possessions.

Let the poor share material goods with us, just as they share spiritual goods. Let them share earthly things with us, just as they will share in eternal things.

But what shall I say about certain monks who, although they eat in the same refectory, rest in the same dormitory, keep watch in the same choir, live with the same common possessions, and serve in the same order, nevertheless quarrel with one another through envy and hatred? What shall I say also about married couples who, although they have one table, one bed, and, according to the Apostle, one flesh, nevertheless harbor inward hatred and discord?

Certainly, all who are such receive not the Holy Spirit—which is the more grievous—but Satan as their inhabitant.

Fourth, it is demonstrated by what signs the Holy Spirit revealed his coming upon the disciples, when it is added: “And suddenly there came from heaven a sound,” etc.

The coming of the Holy Spirit was demonstrated by two signs. One was a sound suddenly made from heaven, like that of a strong, rushing wind, which filled the entire house where the disciples were sitting.

This sound appropriately signified the coming of the Holy Spirit. Sound is invisible, and invisibly reaches the ears of each person all at once; it penetrates even to the heart and awakens it to understanding. Thus the Holy Spirit is invisible in his nature, and invisibly reaches all the faithful simultaneously; he penetrates to the innermost parts of their hearts and awakens them to understanding.

The sound appropriately came from heaven, because the Holy Spirit is sent by the highest Father, according to the saying: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James I).

It is also appropriately said that it was made suddenly and “like a strong, rushing wind,” because the Holy Spirit worked in the disciples suddenly and swiftly. He did not gradually but suddenly and quickly make them wise from being uneducated, fervent from being lukewarm, and bold from being timid, so that each of them could say with the Psalmist: “Now I have begun. This is the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Psalm LXXVI).

The adverb “like” may indicate an expression of truth, since that sound truly signified the coming of the Holy Spirit, who was rushing powerfully—that is, carrying them away from the mind and separating them from carnal effects. Or it may indicate only a comparison, since the sound was like a spirit, that is, like a strong wind. For the word *spiritus* is equivocal, referring both to spirit, wind, and song, just as among the Hebrews *Ruha* [], and among the Greeks *pneuma* [πνεῦμα].

The other sign was fire divided into tongues, which rested above each of them. Hence it is added: “And there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and one rested upon each of them.”

The Holy Spirit is appropriately signified by fire. For the Holy Spirit is love. Hence John says: “God is love” (1 John IV). The Lord also calls the Holy Spirit fire, saying: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke XII).

Just as there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, so there are seven properties of fire. Fire softens hard things, warms cold things, illuminates dark things, strengthens soft things, tests impure things, rises upward, and multiplies when divided.

So too the Holy Spirit softens hard hearts through the spirit of fear; warms the cold through the spirit of piety; illuminates the dark through the spirit of knowledge; strengthens the weak through the spirit of fortitude; tests the impure through the spirit of counsel; carries upward through the spirit of understanding; and, when distributed, enriches through the spirit of wisdom.

For wisdom is a noble possession: when distributed, it receives increase, but it disdains a miserly possessor and slips away unless it is made public.

The Holy Spirit therefore came upon the disciples in fire because he produced in them the properties of fire mentioned above. He had come upon Christ in the form of a dove because he had descended to gather sinners through the dove’s simplicity.

He came upon them in tongues because he made them eloquent in every language, so that they might both know and dare to speak in all languages the wisdom they had received from the Holy Spirit.

Would that, brothers, the Holy Spirit might also deign to descend upon us lowly preachers, and inspire us with wisdom, eloquence, and fortitude, so that we may understand the word of God and confidently dare to express what we understand, at least in the language we know!

Fifth, it is shown how the Holy Spirit is said to have descended upon the disciples, when it is added: “And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit”—that is, with the grace of the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit is not otherwise said to descend, come, or be given except because his grace is given, according to a figure of speech by which what belongs to the gift is attributed to the giver.

Let no one, therefore, suppose that the substance of the Holy Spirit appeared in the things heard or seen there. For the substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is invisible; and just as it fills all things, so it can neither approach nor withdraw locally.

The disciples are now said to have been filled with the Holy Spirit because, even if they are said to have possessed the Holy Spirit beforehand, they were nevertheless fearful: they fled, hid, and remained silent, and were therefore only half-filled with the Holy Spirit. But now, because they could no longer contain within themselves or silence the power conceived from the Holy Spirit, but, like a vessel filled with new wine, were bursting forth and overflowing, they are rightly said to have been filled with the Holy Spirit. Hence the Jews later said that they were drunk.

Sixth, what the Holy Spirit bestowed upon the disciples is shown when it is said: “And they began to speak in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance.”

O dearly beloved brothers, how swift a teacher the Holy Spirit is! No interpretation was needed for understanding, no practice for use, and no time for study. Rather, through the marvelous and unheard-of working of the Holy Spirit, the timid suddenly became bold, the uneducated wise, and the speechless speakers of every language.

The timid suddenly became bold, because those who previously did not dare to speak now began to speak publicly. The uneducated suddenly became wise, because those who previously, as the Lord testifies, were without understanding (Matthew XV), now understood and proclaimed the mysteries of Scripture and the mighty deeds of God. He suddenly made the speechless speakers of every language, because those who previously did not know how to speak even the one language of the Hebrews perfectly now spoke every language perfectly.

They did none of this through their own strength, intelligence, or learning, but only as, and in the measure and manner in which, the Holy Spirit gave them utterance, according to what our Lord had promised them: “When you stand before kings and governors, do not consider how or what you should speak, for it will be given to you in that hour what you should speak” (Matthew X; Mark XIII).

Beautifully, just as in the construction of Babel—the tower of confusion—one language was divided into many because of pride (Genesis XI), so now, in the building of the Church, the house of God, many languages are united because of humility. “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV).

Therefore, brothers, let us presume nothing about our strength, intelligence, choice, or merit, but rather about the grace of God, who “has hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matthew XI; Luke X), and “makes the tongues of infants eloquent” (Wisdom X).

Seventh, the great amazement that followed the mighty works of the Holy Spirit is demonstrated when it is added: “Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem religious men from every nation under heaven,” and therefore people ignorant of all the languages.

When the sound occurred—namely, when the various languages were heard—a multitude gathered as though for something marvelous and unheard-of. Their minds were confused by this event, whose cause and manner they could not investigate, because each one heard them speaking in his own language.

They were all amazed and wondered, saying: “Behold, are not all these who are speaking Galileans, of one language and nation? How is it that each of us hears our own language, in which we were born? [We are] Parthians and Medes and Elamites, etc.; we have heard them speaking in our own languages the mighty deeds of God.”

Why, my brothers, did the Lord give his disciples the ability to speak in various languages? For three reasons.

First, for the convenience of preaching, so that whenever they came to a people of any language, they would not need an interpreter, but could preach immediately.

Second, as a sign of divine power, so that, by observing that they spoke every language, people might recognize that they had been taught and sent by God. Hence Paul says: “Tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers” (1 Corinthians XIV).

Third, as a figure of the universal conversion, so that it might be signified by this that not only the Jewish people, but also, according to the Prophet, “every people, tribe, and tongue shall serve him” (Daniel VII). Hence Paul says: “Every tongue shall confess that our Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians II).

So that we may truly confess him, let us pray to the Holy Spirit that with his holy fire he may burn, cleanse, confirm in goodness, illuminate, and inflame our kidneys and our heart, so that, having despised all earthly things, we may strive with our whole desire toward heavenly things and endeavor to draw our neighbors there with us. Through Jesus Christ. Amen.

# HOMILY LXXIII. ON THE HOLY DAY OF PENTECOST

“If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John XIV), etc.

Since today’s solemnity of the coming of the Holy Spirit, dearly beloved brothers, has gathered us together today, we have thought it necessary to deliver to you at least a brief sermon on the Gospel reading.

This reading is divided into five sections. As the Lord was approaching his passion, first he exhorts them to love. Second, he promises them the Holy Spirit. Third, he gives them peace. Fourth, he consoles them so that they will not be afraid. Fifth, he shows them that, because of his obedience, he is about to suffer while innocent.

First, then, he exhorts the disciples to love, commended here by example and commandment, showing what true love does and to what it leads. He shows what it does when he says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word.”

The effect of true love is observance of God’s commandments. Therefore, brothers, if we truly love God, we observe his commandments. But if we do not observe his commandments, it is clear that we do not truly love him.

Let no one among you deceive himself, brothers. He deceives himself who says that he loves God but does not keep his commandments. Hence the same John says: “If anyone says that he loves God and does not keep his commandments, he is a liar” (1 John II).

Let no one excuse himself on the grounds of inability. Someone says: “I am weak and feeble by nature, and his commandments are burdensome and difficult. Indeed, I love God, but I cannot bear the difficulty of his commandments. I cannot renounce my own will completely; I cannot renounce my flesh; I cannot renounce the world.”

But the person who says this sins in two ways: first, because he accuses God of cruelty, saying that he gave a commandment which a human being cannot fulfill; and second, because he lies by saying that he cannot do what he himself can do. For God, who gave the commandment, knows what each person is capable of better than the person himself.

No one in necessity is unable to do for God what he is able to do. For the sake of bodily health you drink water, fast, endure iron and fire, and abandon your own will—and you cannot do these things for God? For worldly ambition you serve in armor, endure hunger, cold, toil, and misery, and expose yourself to dangers and death—and you cannot do these things for God?

And why is this? Is it not because we love the world more than God? For if we loved God more, or even as much as we love the world, then, with his help and with our conscience in agreement, we could endure more for God than for the world, while our conscience contradicted us.

The saying is indeed true, brothers: “For one who loves, nothing is difficult; for one who is unwilling, nothing is easy.” Therefore, when the Lord says: “The way that leads to life is difficult and narrow” (Matthew VII), this should be understood of the unwilling. But when he says: “My yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew XI; the source reads “II”), this should be understood of the willing.

But, my brothers, since God says: “If anyone loves me”—using the present tense—why did he likewise not say in the present tense, “he keeps my words,” rather than “he will keep them”?

Because, when someone begins to love God, he cannot immediately observe his commandments perfectly. Rather, as love grows, he gradually begins to accustom himself more and more to observing God’s commandments, so that what was initially burdensome because unfamiliar later becomes pleasant through habit. Hence the Psalmist says: “I ran in the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart” (Psalm CXVIII).

To what the love of God leads is shown when he adds: “And my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and we will make our dwelling with him.”

That we love God and keep his word is, as it were, our merit. But that the Father will love us and make his dwelling with us is, as it were, the reward.

But what does it mean here that, after we have loved God and kept his word, the Father will love us, when God’s love precedes our love, as John testifies: “He first loved us” (1 John IV)?

It should not be understood, brothers, that after we have loved God he then begins to love us. Rather, he who first loved us, once we begin to love him and observe his word, will increasingly show that he loves us by pouring out his graces upon us more abundantly.

Hence he also adds: “And we will come to him.” God is said to come to us when he grants us an abundance of his grace.

Who are the “we” who will come? The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For whoever has the love of God has the Holy Spirit, who is the love of the Father and the Son.

But because he comes to some through compunction—people who do not love finally, but grow cold or lukewarm in the time of temptation—he adds: “And we will make our dwelling with him.”

Let us consider, brothers, let us consider how great a dignity, how great an honor, and how great a sweetness it is to have the Trinity dwelling as a guest in the lodging of our heart. Certainly, through true love and observance of God’s commandments, we receive such a guest into our midst; through persevering purity, we retain him as a perpetual inhabitant.

If we were about to receive a temporal king, a prince, or one of our temporal friends, would we not clean our house so that no disgrace might offend the eyes of the one entering? Would we not also adorn it with festive decorations and prepare festive dishes, so that the person entering might delight in our hospitality?

How much more, brothers, when today we are about to receive through more abundant grace the Holy Spirit—or rather, the whole Trinity! Let us cleanse the lodging of our heart through true tears of repentance, adorn it with various virtues, and prepare for God among us a banquet through good pursuits and pure contemplation, so that he may be pleased to dwell in us and always delight in us. For he says: “My delights are to be with the children of men” (Proverbs VIII).

Since there are some who appear to observe certain commandments of God either from slavish fear or from natural goodness, but not from true love of God, he shows that no one can fulfill God’s commandments except through true love, when he adds: “Whoever does not love me does not keep my words.”

Therefore, brothers, the love of God and observance of his commandments are, as it were, equal things. Just as we do not truly love God unless we observe his commandments, so we do not truly observe God’s commandments unless we love him. Whatever is meritorious is meritorious solely through love.

Although the authority of the Father and the Son is the same in all things, because the Son is from the Father, honor is always given to the Father. Hence he adds: “And the word that you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me.”

In this the pride of certain people is confounded—those who think that they can of themselves do, know, or speak something good. They say: “Our lips are our own; who is our Lord?” (Psalm XII; the source reads “II.”) Blush, insolent worm! The Son of God says that he neither speaks, knows, nor can do anything from himself, and you, little man, presume that you can know or speak anything good from yourself!

The second section follows, in which he promises the disciples the Holy Spirit, saying: “I have spoken these things to you while remaining with you. But the Paraclete,” etc.

As though he were saying: “While I remain bodily with you, I have spoken these few things to you. I would still have many things to say to you, if you were able to bear them. But the Holy Spirit will supplement what I have said less fully, also giving you a greater capacity for understanding.”

He calls him the Paraclete, that is, the consoler, because he was going to console the disciples, who would be saddened by his departure, strengthen those who were less strong, and instruct those who were less learned—and not only them, but also all who would piously believe.

He also calls him the Holy Spirit because he inspires holiness. Whatever holiness or goodness a human being possesses, he possesses through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

“Whom the Father will send in my name.” Elsewhere he says: “Whom I will send to you from the Father” (John XV). From this it is shown that the Son sends the Holy Spirit, but that what the Son sends he has from the Father. The Father also sends him through the Son.

“He will teach you all things and remind you of all things.” My brothers, this was fulfilled today in the disciples, when the Holy Spirit suddenly and miraculously worked in them. Those who had previously been uneducated suddenly became wise; those who had previously known very little of the Scriptures became spiritual in their understanding of the Scriptures; and those who had previously known only one language suddenly knew all languages.

O my brothers, how powerful, marvelous, and swift in his works is the Holy Spirit, who accomplishes quietly and without meditation or delay in his own people what can scarcely be accomplished through labor, study, and a long period of time!

“And he will remind you of all things.” Many times, brothers, we know something but, when the occasion requires it, do not know it. But the Holy Spirit grants his own not only knowledge, but also the ability to know how to use it in the right place and at the right time.

But the Lord says elsewhere: “When you stand before kings and governors, do not consider how or what you should speak; for it will be given to you in that hour what you should speak” (Matthew X; Mark XIII). For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.

The Holy Spirit therefore supplied the disciples not only with holiness and wisdom, but also with eloquence, the opportunity and appropriateness for speaking, boldness, confirmation through miracles, and strength to resist.

Would that that holy and wondrous Spirit might deign to descend upon us, however inadequate we preachers may be, and inspire us with goodness and wisdom for living and thinking rightly; with eloquence, opportunity, and boldness for preaching well, appropriately, and courageously; with confirmation to establish our preaching through our works; and with strength to resist the persecutors of the world.

The third part follows, in which the Lord gives his disciples peace, saying: “I leave peace with you;” namely, in the commandment, “I give you my peace”—in the soul, that is, so that here also, insofar as possible, you may have peace, and may hasten by desire toward eternal peace. “Not as the world gives,” he says, “do I give to you.”

Now there is one peace of prosperity, another of goodness, and another of wickedness. The peace of prosperity is indifferent. For to one who uses it well, it is good; to one who uses it badly, it is bad. Abraham and the other patriarchs made good use of the peace of temporal prosperity. Of such people it is said in the Psalm:

“Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways. You shall eat the labors of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you. Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine within the walls of your house. Your sons shall be like young olive plants around your table” (Psalm 127).

On the other hand, the wicked make bad use of the peace of temporal prosperity. For instead of blessing God because of it, they forget him, become proud, grow soft, and become arrogant. Of such people it is said in the Gospel: “And indeed, in this your day are the things that are for your peace” (Luke 19), and so forth. David likewise says: “I was jealous of the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners. They are not in the labor of men, and they will not be scourged with men” (Psalm 72). And elsewhere: “Their sons are like young plants in their youth; their daughters are adorned, embellished like the likeness of a temple; their storehouses are full, overflowing from one thing into another” (Psalm 143), and so forth.

This temporal peace of prosperity, however, is not greatly to be desired or sought by us, my brothers, because for some people adversity is more useful in this world than prosperity. For many are saved in adversity who would not be saved in prosperity. Conversely, many weak people are saved in prosperity who would not be saved in adversity. Therefore, brothers, let us submit ourselves to the divine will, so that he himself may give us what he knows to be more useful for us.

The peace of goodness, however, is the agreement of many in what is good. This is the peace that Christ promises and gives us. Of it, it is said here: “I give you my peace.” Of it also it is said: “And his dwelling became established in peace” (Psalm 75). We ought to have this peace with God, with ourselves, and with our neighbor.

With God, so that we may agree with his will in all things, and thus be one spirit with him. With ourselves, so that the flesh may consent and agree with the spirit. With our neighbors, so that we may be at peace with all people, desiring and seeking what is good for everyone insofar as it depends on us—even if they themselves are hostile toward us, in accordance with David’s saying: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceful” (Psalm 119).

Nevertheless, for the sake of peace we must not consent to the wicked in wickedness; rather, we should correct them or separate ourselves from them. Hence the Lord says: “I have not come to send peace upon the earth, but a sword. For I have come to separate a son from his father” (Matthew 10).

The peace of wickedness is the agreement of many in what is evil—as when the spirit consents to the flesh in evil, or when several people are united in evil. Of this it is said that Herod and Pilate became friends in the death of Christ (Luke 23). This peace is the worst, because the more closely the wicked agree, the worse they become. This is the peace that the world gives, not God.

The fourth part follows, in which the Lord, foreseeing that his disciples would be troubled by his departure—for who would not grieve at the departure of so great and such a teacher?—prepares to console them, saying: “Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid”; that is, let it not be troubled because of fear. Because of the fear of my departure, let not your heart be disturbed from its tranquillity.

He shows why they should not be troubled when he adds: “You have heard that I said to you: I go away and I come to you.” I go away from you to the Passion, and I come to you through the Resurrection. Or, I go away from you by suffering and ascending to the Father, and I come to you by sending the Holy Spirit, from whom I cannot be substantially separated. This is what he says elsewhere: “I will not leave you orphans” (John 14).

Then he shows that his departure would not only do them no harm but would even benefit them, saying: “If you loved me”—that is, if you knew how to love me perfectly—“you would certainly rejoice because I am going to the Father.” And why? “Because the Father is greater than I”: not with respect to the substance of divinity, but with respect to the substance of humanity.

It is as if he said: “My ascension to the Father is exaltation for me and consolation for you, because the exaltation of the teacher ought to be the joy, consolation, and hope of the disciple.”

“This I have told you,” he says, “before it happens, so that when it has happened you may believe me to know future things as God, just as I know things that are past.” This too, my brothers, is today an argument for our faith: Christ is true God, who knows future things just as he knows past things, as well as the other things that belong to God alone.

The fifth part follows, in which he shows that he will suffer immediately in innocence, out of obedience, saying: “I will no longer speak much with you, because on this night I shall hand myself over to the members of the devil to be crucified.” For the prince of this world—that is, of those who love the world—comes through his members, “and he has nothing in me,” that is, no claim or jurisdiction.

In us, my brothers, who were conceived in sins and do not live without sins, the devil appears to have some claim. But in him whose conception and life knew no stain, he certainly had no claim at all. Yet if the devil dared to come against him in whom he had no claim, what do you think he will do to us wretched people, in whom he appears to have a very great claim through our sins?

What, then, shall we do except, insofar as we can, free ourselves from his power through repentance and cling by true faith and charity to him in whom he has no claim whatsoever?

“But so that the world may know,” he says, “that I love the Father, and that just as the Father has commanded me, so I do.” It is as though he said: “I do not hand myself over to the devil because he has any claim over me, but so that the elect from the world may know that I love the Father and obey his command in the redemption of the human race.”

Therefore, my brothers, since God loved us so greatly that he handed over his only-begotten Son to death for us, let us love God and observe his commandments, so that we may deserve to have him dwelling and remaining within us. Let us have peace with one another—not the peace of the world, but the peace of God. Let our entire hope, consolation, and desire be in God. For his sake, let us live innocently and patiently, seeking and doing his will in all things. He grants this, who in the perfect Trinity lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## PART TWO

[Col. 1945]

## FIRST HOMILY: ON THE DAY OF THE TRINITY

[Col. 1945C]

“May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the charity of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be always with all of you. Amen” (2 Corinthians 13).

Today, dearest brothers, we celebrate a solemnity in honor of the holy and undivided Trinity. It was fitting, indeed, that after the solemnity devoted especially to the Son—at his Nativity, Resurrection, and Ascension—and especially to the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, and especially to the Father on Sundays and on each day, we should today solemnize together the three, that is, the holy Trinity.

This is not because we divide in honor the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, whose honor and glory are the same, but because, just as the three have one substance in common, so each has its own special property.

Hence it is written [Note: [Col. 1945D] Preface of the Mass for the Sunday of the Holy Trinity.]: “In the persons, distinction; in the essence, unity; and in the majesty, equality is to be adored.”

There is distinction in the persons, because it is proper to the Father to beget, proper to the Son to be born, and proper to the Holy Spirit to proceed. The Father is distinguished from the Son and the Holy Spirit by paternity; the Son is distinguished from the Father and the Holy Spirit by birth; and the Holy Spirit is distinguished from the Father and the Son by his procession.

But no one, my brothers, when he hears that the Son of God is born from the Father or that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, should think—as happens in human generation or procession—that the substance of the Father is divided or diminished in the Son, or that the substance of both is divided or diminished in the Holy Spirit. For this reason, to remove such an idea, it is added that in the essence of the three persons there is unity. For they are one substance, one God, and one Lord.

Again, no one should think that, as happens in human birth or procession, so in the holy Trinity the Son is less than the Father, or the Holy Spirit less than both, whether in time, rank, or power. For this reason, to remove such an idea, it is also added: “In the majesty, equality is to be adored.” For the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of the same Trinity, the same majesty, and the same power.

From the eternal and supreme Father the co-eternal and co-equal Son is always born; and the co-eternal and co-equal Holy Spirit always proceeds from them.

In the sun there are three things: a fiery substance, radiance, and heat. From the fiery substance radiance, coeval with it, is always born. From both, heat, coeval with them, always proceeds. Although these three are distinguished from one another by their properties, they are nevertheless one sun, not three suns.

Yet no comparison drawn from temporal things is adequate to God. But with whatever examples we can, we stammer rather than speak forth what cannot be understood or expressed.

When, therefore, you hear “Father,” believe that he is Father. When you hear “Son,” believe that he is Son. When you hear “Holy Spirit,” believe that he is the Holy Spirit. How the Father begets the Son, or how the Father and Son breathe forth the Holy Spirit, do not investigate, if you do not wish to err. For, according to the prophet: “Who will declare his generation, or his procession?” (Isaiah 53.)

[Col. 1947B]

Since, then, today we celebrate the solemnity of the holy Trinity, the previously mentioned short reading, in which the three persons are named, is appropriately recited today. It is a kind of blessing in which the Apostle wishes three things for us: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the charity of God the Father, and the communion of the Holy Spirit.”

But since these three are equally common to the three persons, why is grace here specially attributed to Christ, charity to the Father, and communion to the Holy Spirit?

Grace is here appropriated to Christ because Christ not only bestows graces upon us but also freely gave himself to us. Hence Isaiah says: “A child is born to us, and a Son is given to us” (Isaiah 9). That he became human, suffered, died, rose again, and ascended into heaven was all for us, and all is grace.

The Apostle wishes this grace of Christ always to be with us. It is with the faithful in four ways: through effect, through remembrance, through gratitude, and through reciprocity.

It is with us through effect if what is generally true—that all human beings are redeemed by Christ—is accomplished particularly in us. Indeed, my brothers, Christ redeemed all human beings, insofar as it depended on him. He himself was a sufficient sacrifice for the redemption of all. But some, by living badly, withdraw themselves from the grace of their redemption.

Hence Paul exhorts us: “Let no one be lacking the grace of God” (Hebrews 12). For he does not say, “Let some be lacking the grace of God,” but “let no one be lacking,” to show that although grace is present to all through God’s goodness, human perversity nevertheless drives it away.

It is with us through remembrance if we continually and thoughtfully consider how lowly, disgraceful, and harsh were the things Christ endured for us. This is why the crucified Christ and other depictions of Christ are displayed for us in the church: so that through them the grace of the Lord’s dispensation may be recalled to our memory.

It is with us through gratitude if we continually bless him for the mercy he has worked for us and offer him thanksgiving with our whole heart, if we continually cause his holy name to resound in our mouth—not like the nine lepers cleansed by the Lord, who on account of their ingratitude were rejected by the Lord (Luke 17).

It is with us through reciprocity if we do for him what he first did for us, if, just as he died for us, we too die for him. Hence it is written: “When you sit down at a great table, know that you must prepare similar things for him” (Ecclesiasticus 31). And the Prophet says: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take the cup of salvation” (Psalm 115).

It is as though he said: “Since the Lord has bestowed so many and such great things upon me, what can I worthily render to him? Since I owe my whole self to him because he was made for me, what shall I render to him for having redeemed me—and redeemed me in such a manner? And even if I were able to repay myself to him a thousand times, what would such repayment or comparison be between me and him—so little compared with so great, so sinful compared with so holy? In whose sight not even the stars themselves are clean, how much less are we, whose life is nothing but temptation, and who dwell in houses of clay?”

Nevertheless, even if I cannot repay him, I shall at least do what I can; I shall continually acknowledge that I cannot repay him, and I shall offer him that sacrifice which I am able to offer.

Charity is here appropriated to God the Father because it belongs to the Father to love and always to hold the Son dear. But God the Father did not wish merely to love his only-begotten Son or make him his heir; through the blood of his only-begotten Son he also adopted us, unworthy servants, as sons, and, contrary to the custom of earthly parents, made servants co-heirs with his Son.

“As the Apostle says, we are heirs indeed of God, but co-heirs of Christ” (Romans 8).

The Apostle therefore wishes the charity of God the Father always to be with us—either that charity by which God loves us, or that charity by which we love God.

The charity by which God loves us is always with us if, through our manner of life, through the bestowal of greater graces, and through perseverance—may he himself deign to accomplish this through his mercy—he completes and confirms in us that love by which he called us and made us his faithful people.

The charity by which we love God, my brothers, is always with us if—may he himself grant this to us!—we continually love him with our whole being as our supreme and true Father; if we preserve his commandments inviolate; and if, insofar as we can, we imitate him as good sons in purity, mercy, holiness, and the other virtues.

Communion is likewise appropriated to the Holy Spirit because, since the Holy Spirit is love, concord, and goodness, it belongs to him to communicate his gifts by distributing his graces to the faithful.

The Apostle therefore wishes the communion of the Holy Spirit always to be with us—either that communion by which he communicates his gifts to us, or that by which he makes us communicate our good things to others. Both belong to him. And may that holy and gracious Spirit work both kinds of communion in us!

The first: that he may communicate to us the abundance of his graces, granting us true faith, hope, and charity; wisdom, justice, fortitude, and temperance; and his other gifts, both spiritual and bodily. May we be worthily adorned with these gifts and thereby deserve to have the Holy Spirit himself dwelling within us.

The second: that he may make us communicate to others the very graces bestowed upon us, so that we do not uselessly hide the talent entrusted to us, but rather distribute it for the benefit both of ourselves and of others.

Therefore, my brothers, let us pray with our whole heart that the grace of Christ, the charity of God the Father, and the communion of the Holy Spirit may always be with us, so that we may deserve to receive the gifts of God and communicate what we have received for the benefit both of ourselves and of others.

Then we shall not be condemned as useless servants because of the talents we have received, but rather may we deserve to be rewarded for the profit we have gained, through the generosity of God and our Lord, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, to whom belong one honor, one power, and one glory throughout infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY II. On the Day of the Trinity

[Col. 1949B]

“There was a man from the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews; he came to Jesus” (John 3).

This reading is divided into two parts, dearest brothers. The first part contains Nicodemus’s approach to the Lord and his confession; the second, the instruction given to him by the Lord.

First, therefore, Nicodemus is shown approaching the Lord. In this, five things are shown to us together: from what kind of people he came, who he was, how great he was, when he came to the Lord, and what he said to him.

From what kind of people did he come? From the Pharisees, that is, from that evil offspring whom John the Baptist calls a brood of vipers. “Brood of vipers,” he says, “who will teach you [Note: [Col. 1949D] The Vulgate has “showed” or “demonstrated.”] to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matthew 3; Luke 3.)

From an evil stock, therefore, something good was born, like a rose from a thorn, in accordance with what John himself says: “For God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones” (ibid.).

This is so, brothers, so that no one may claim that the wickedness of his parents prevents him from becoming good, just as the holiness of his parents does not benefit someone who lives badly, since the Lord says through the prophet that “the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezekiel 18), and so forth.

Who came? Nicodemus, that is, “victor over the people.” And he truly was a good victor over the people: when his people were unbelieving, he was believing; when his people were proud, he was humble.

Let us imitate him, my brothers, and let each of us strive to overcome the vice characteristic of his own people. If you are a Jew, strive to overcome the unbelief innate in Jews. If you are a Gaul, strive to overcome the pride innate in Gauls. If you are a Roman, strive to overcome the greed innate in Romans. If you are a Poitevin, strive to overcome the gluttony and talkativeness innate in Poitevins; and similarly with the others.

How great was he who came? He was a ruler of the Jews and a teacher in Israel. Yet although he was so great and such a man, he was not ashamed to become a humble disciple.

By this, rulers and teachers are refuted who would rather remain ignorant than humble themselves and be instructed.

When did he come? At night. And why at night?

If because of the urgency of necessity, this is something we should imitate, so that we do not delay in seeking the physician of our souls. If because of convenience, this too is something we should imitate, so that we choose a suitable time in which we may be instructed more intimately. If because of shame or fear of the Jews, it is a sign of imperfection. But even this is something we should imitate, so that, if we are still imperfect and unable to overcome shame or fear, we nevertheless strive to learn secretly rather than remain ignorant, and to do good secretly rather than do nothing.

What did he say? “Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher. For no one can perform these signs that you perform unless God is with him.”

He confesses three things about the Lord: that he has come from God; that his teaching is from God; and that this can be recognized through these divine works.

These three things, my brothers, ought to be present in each one of us if we are good shepherds and preachers. A shepherd must be sent by God, like Aaron. This refutes those who thrust themselves forward, of whom the Lord says: “They reigned, but not from me” (Hosea 8).

A shepherd must also teach not his own doctrine but God’s. Hence the Lord says: “And you shall announce to them from me” (Ezekiel 3).

He must also perform works unlike those performed by worldly people, works that no one can do unless the Lord is with him.

“We know that you have come from God as a teacher.” It is as though he openly said: “Since you have come from God as a teacher, teach us how we may attain the kingdom of God.”

The second part follows, in which the Lord teaches Nicodemus how we may attain the kingdom of heaven.

Three things are necessary for us to be able to ascend to the kingdom of God: baptism, the Lord’s ascension, and his Passion. Through baptism we are made worthy to ascend. Through the Lord’s ascension, heaven is opened to us. Through his Passion, a ladder is raised for us by which we may ascend.

He therefore instructs Nicodemus concerning baptism when he says: “Unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” It is as though he openly said: “Through baptism a person is made fit to deserve to attain the kingdom of God.”

Here he indicates that there are two births: the first, carnal; the second, spiritual. Through the first, a human being is born from a human being in sins, for death. Through the second, a person is born inwardly from God in the Holy Spirit, for eternal life.

Of the first, David says: “I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Psalm 50). Of the second, John says: “As many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name; who were born not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man, but from God” (John 1).

But Nicodemus, ignorant of spiritual birth, said like an uneducated person: “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter into his mother’s womb again and be born?”

What Nicodemus says about the first birth is also true of the second, because neither the first nor the second can be repeated.

He therefore explains to Nicodemus what he had said obscurely, demonstrating three things: from what the second birth comes, how it differs from the first, and what sort of person it produces.

He shows what it comes from when he says: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.”

In the Lord’s baptism there are an outward sacrament, the reality signified, and inward purification. The outward sacrament—that is, the external washing from external uncleanness—is performed with water, when a person is immersed in it three times in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen.

But inward purification from sins is performed by the Holy Spirit. Thus external washing accomplishes nothing without the interior washing—for example, when an adult approaches baptism deceitfully or without devotion. Yet neither can the interior washing occur without the exterior, except when the shedding of blood supplies the place of baptism.

Then he assigns the difference between the first and second births when he says: “What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the spirit is spirit.”

From a carnal human being, through carnal desire, a carnal human being is born. From the Holy Spirit, through baptism, a spiritual human being is born.

Through the first birth we are born children of the old man Adam; through the second we are reborn children of the new man Christ. Carnal birth also comes first in time, while spiritual birth comes later, because unless a person has first been born carnally from Adam, he cannot be born spiritually from Christ.

Hence the Apostle says: “The spiritual was not first; rather, the natural, and afterward the spiritual” (1 Corinthians 15). This is why an infant in its mother’s womb cannot be regenerated.

Afterward he demonstrates what sort of person spiritual generation produces when he adds: “The Spirit breathes where he wills,” that is, he enlightens the heart of whomever he wills. “And you hear his voice,” either through the Scriptures, which were written in the Spirit of God, or also through a person speaking in the Spirit of God.

“And you do not know where he comes from or where he goes,” that is, you, who are carnal, do not know from where that grace comes to a person, or toward what great good it leads him.

“So it is,” he says, “with everyone who is born of the Spirit.” For whatever the Spirit is like, he makes the person whom he inspires like that. Just as the Spirit is free, breathing where he wills, so he makes the person whom he inspires free, liberating his will by grace, so that whenever he wishes, he may be able to do good.

The wicked person, even if he has a will free from necessity, nevertheless does not have it liberated from sin through grace. Just as the Spirit makes himself known through a voice, so he reveals the person whom he enlightens to be righteous through good words and works and through other outward signs.

For just as the carnal person does not know where the Spirit comes from or where he goes, so he does not know that the spiritual person has been born from God and is journeying toward the kingdom of heaven.

Therefore, brothers, you who are spiritual, whose life is hidden with Christ in God (Colossians 3), should not be surprised if carnal people mock you, despise you, or regard you as nothing. “For the animal person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2). He tastes and seeks only earthly things.

When Nicodemus then asked how these things could happen, he heard: “You are a teacher in Israel, and you do not know these things?” By this the Lord showed that a teacher of the Church ought not to be ignorant of spiritual ministries.

For is it fitting for a shepherd to be beastlike, to walk bent over in the manner of a beast, rather than to stand upright as a human being and to understand the things that are above, not the things that are upon the earth? (Colossians 3.)

“Amen, amen,” he says, “I say to you, we speak what we know, and what we have seen in secret we testify openly” [Note: [Col. 1951D] The Vulgate does not have “in secret” or “openly.”] “and you do not accept our testimony.”

The same thing happens today, brothers, because when spiritual teachers teach the things they know spiritually and testify to what they have seen with spiritual eyes, beastlike people do not believe their testimony. They do not believe that anything exists except what they can see with bodily eyes.

“If I told you earthly things,” he says, “and you do not believe”—such as: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2)—“how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?”

This is an argument from the lesser. For someone who does not believe earthly things, which are not remote from human reasoning, how will he believe heavenly things, which exceed human reason?

The Lord then instructs Nicodemus concerning his Ascension when he adds: “And no one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.”

He speaks of himself as though of another, to give us an example of avoiding arrogance. It is as though he said: “If you wish to ascend into the kingdom of heaven, cling through the unity of charity to the Son of Man, who alone ascends with his members.”

Therefore, my brothers, if we wish to ascend into the kingdom of heaven, let us cling by faith and charity to our head, our Lord Jesus Christ, because whoever is not a member of Christ’s body cannot ascend to the kingdom of heaven.

Hence he himself says: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14). He himself is the door; he himself is the doorkeeper; he himself is our guide and lifter-up to the kingdom of heaven.

That the Son of Man ascends into heaven he proves from the fact that he is the same person as the Son of God who descended from heaven. But, more expressly, he says that the Son of Man, at the very time when he was speaking these words on earth, was in heaven.

Although the sequence of the expression would have required it to be said that the Son of God descended and the Son of Man ascended, the incongruous joining of the words does not prejudice the truth of what is said. Thus the same Son of Man is confusedly said both to have descended and to have ascended, both to speak on earth and to be in heaven, so that the heresy that attempted to divide Christ into two persons might be utterly rejected.

For the catholic faith confesses in Christ indeed a twofold nature, but only one person. Hence, although the expressions do not follow one another in a strictly consistent order, we nevertheless boldly and truly confess both that the Son of Man created the world, and that the Son of God was born from a Virgin—and, what is greater, that he died.
