He instructs Nicodemus concerning his Passion when he adds: “And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness” [Note: [Col. 1952D] The Vulgate has “desert.”] “so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

Beautifully, he instructs the teacher of the law concerning his Passion through a figure of the law, indicating that this and other things had gone before in the law as figures of him.

When fiery serpents were killing the children of Israel in the wilderness, Moses, at the Lord’s command, raised up a bronze serpent on a pole. Those who looked upon it were freed from the fiery serpents (Numbers 21).

Moses prefigured the Jewish people. The bronze serpent lifted up on a pole prefigured the exaltation of Christ upon the wood.

Christ is fittingly represented by a bronze serpent, because just as the bronze serpent had the likeness of a serpent but not its reality, so Christ had the likeness of sinful flesh, but not sinful flesh.

And just as the bronze serpent, although it appeared to be a serpent, was incorruptible and enduring, so the Lord, although he appeared to be a mortal human being, was nevertheless, according to his divinity, eternal and immortal.

Just as those who looked upon the bronze serpent were not killed by the fiery serpents but lived, so whoever looks upon Christ crucified with true faith and love is not killed by the serpent-like temptations of the devil but has eternal life.

It is therefore as though Nicodemus—or any believer—were told: “If you wish to be freed from the devil’s ambushes and to ascend into heaven with the Son of Man, look always upon him crucified.”

Look, I say, with faith; look with love; look through imitation. In accordance with what he himself teaches elsewhere: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9).

For this is the way, my brothers; this is the ladder by which we ascend to the kingdom of heaven. We do not go to the kingdom of heaven through riches, honors, or pleasures, but through true faith; through true love of God and neighbor; through renunciation of temporal possessions and even of one’s own body; through humility and patience.

May our Lord Jesus Christ grant us to follow him along this way and attain him—the one who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY III. ON THE FEAST OF THE HOLY TRINITY
Fear God and keep his commandments. This is the whole of man (Eccles. XII). In this brief conclusion, dearest brothers, the rule and instruction of the whole of human life are contained. For when Solomon had preached at length on the various judgments and opinions of different people, he finally concluded with this judgment, which was more true and more necessary for man. Therefore, brothers, if you cannot read many Scriptures, if you cannot retain many sayings, at least always retain this very brief maxim in your minds. Strive to fulfill it, since by doing this you will attain eternal life.

You must therefore see how God is to be feared, how his commandments are to be kept, and how this is the whole of man: “Fear God,” he says. It is as though he were plainly saying: Do not fear the loss of temporal things; do not fear temporal punishment or death; fear God alone. For fear of temporal loss is vicious. Only the person who loves temporal things excessively fears losing them. For it is written: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world; for if anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (1 John II).

Therefore, brothers, let us imitate the ancient Fathers, who did not desire earthly possessions and did not love what they possessed; for that reason they did not fear losing them, but rather abandoned them without resentment and gladly distributed them to the poor. Let us imitate blessed Job, who possessed such great riches without love, held them without fear, and lost them without sorrow. Let us therefore drive this worldly and vicious fear from ourselves; let us learn to despise earthly things and to lose them with laughter—or rather, to distribute them.

Fear of punishment or death, however, is natural, and therefore, unless it becomes excessive, it is not vicious. Hence the Lord, who possessed nothing but goodness, willingly assumed this fear for our sake: he feared death and was sorrowful because of it. Yet he exhorts his followers not to fear death: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. X). It is as though he were saying: Although it is human to fear death, nevertheless, because of the fear of God, overcome the fear of death.

Hence, although the apostles feared death as human beings, Paul nevertheless cries out: “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. I). And Andrew: “O longed-for cross!” For what nature feared in them, the will embraced. Therefore, brothers, even if our flesh fears punishment or death, let us nevertheless, while living rightly, desire to suffer or die for Christ. For if death is to be feared, it is to be feared because of what follows it.

Death itself, since it is momentary, is not a great punishment. But the punishments that follow death are great and eternal, and therefore more to be feared. Let adulterers fear death; let thieves, murderers, the greedy, perjurers, and all other wicked people fear death. We, brothers, if we live rightly, if we love God with our whole heart, if we keep his commandments, ought not to fear death. Indeed, awaiting it with confidence, we ought even to desire it, so that through it we may pass from exile to our homeland, from sorrow to joy, and from misery to blessedness.

Therefore, brothers, let us fear God alone. For he is to be feared in all things, and all things in him. Neither the devil, nor man, nor a wild beast, nor anything else can harm us unless he wills it. Hence the Wise Man says: “Whoever fears God has all things fearing him; and whoever does not fear God fears all things.”

The fear of God is threefold: servile, initial, and filial.

A person fears God servilely when, conscious of his sins, he does not love God as Father but fears him as Judge, like an evil servant who fears his master but does not love him. The devil and wicked people fear God with this fear. This fear, insofar as it is initial, is good; insofar as it is servile, it is evil. True love casts out this fear, because when an evil person is converted and begins truly to love God, he begins no longer to fear him servilely. Hence John says: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment. Whoever fears has not been perfected in love” (1 John IV).

Therefore, my brothers, if any one of us is conscious of guilt, let him be converted quickly, confess, and mourn his sins, so that he may cease to fear God servilely and begin truly to love him.

Initial fear exists when someone, turning to God, begins to love him, yet because he is not yet secure in his conscience, fears his judgment. Concerning this fear it is said: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. CX), because when someone begins to love God through fearing him, he begins to have right understanding.

Filial fear exists when someone fears God not because of an evil conscience but solely out of love, like a good son or a chaste bride, who love—the former his father, the latter her bridegroom—not because of a guilty conscience but solely out of love. David speaks of this fear: “The holy fear of the Lord endures forever and ever” (Ps. XVIII).

Therefore, brothers, let us fear God solely out of love: he who created us, who loves us as a father loves his children, who gave himself as the price for us, and who will give us his temporal goods here and heavenly goods in the future. When all our friends abandon us, he does not abandon us, but consoles us through prosperity and corrects us through adversity.

In observing God’s commandments, we must consider four things.

First, we must not trust in our own strength but in God alone. For this reason the Jews, who said, “There is no one lacking who might fulfill it; rather, what is lacking is someone who might command,” were unable to fulfill the law. But we, brothers, must trust that we can perform his commandments not from ourselves but through God’s help. For he gives both the will and the accomplishment. Hence the Apostle says: “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. III); and elsewhere: “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy” (Rom. IX).

Second, we must perform God’s commandments as they are to be performed: in what manner, to what extent, and in what order.

In what manner? We must perform God’s commandments out of love, not out of fear, nor out of carnal love. Out of fear, some people refrain from committing murder, adultery, and theft, but for that reason they do not fulfill these commandments: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal” (Exod. XX). For, as the poet says:

> The wicked hate sin through fear of punishment.  
> The good hate sin through love of virtue.  
> (Horace, *Epistles* I.16.52–53.)  
>   
> [Note: Compare Horace, “you will commit no offense against yourself,” etc.; and here the first verse does not precede but follows the next one.]

Some also do what God commands out of carnal love, because they love their children, wives, and parents carnally, not spiritually; and therefore they do not fulfill God’s commandments.

To what extent? We must perform God’s commandments according to our ability. Some, although they are able to give much to the poor, should not think that they fulfill God’s command concerning almsgiving merely because they give something. For God considers not how much, but from how much one gives.

In what order? We must perform God’s commandments in the order in which they are to be performed. For if I love myself or something else before God, or if I love strangers more than my parents, I do not fulfill the commandment concerning love.

Third, we must perform God’s commandments for the purpose for which they are to be performed. Whoever gives alms for the sake of empty glory does not observe the commandment concerning almsgiving, which must be done for God alone. Concerning such people the Lord says: “Truly I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI).

Fourth, we must not boast before ourselves about observing God’s commandments, but attribute everything to God, as he himself commanded, saying: “When you have done everything, say: ‘We are useless servants; we have done what we were obliged to do’” (Luke XIX). And the Apostle says: “Whoever boasts, let him boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. I).

After Solomon commanded us to fear God and keep his commandments, he adds the reason, saying: “For this is the whole of man”—that is, every person was made for this. The whole of man consists in doing these things. Every person was made for this, because man was made by God to fear and love him above all things, to observe his commandments, and, by doing this, to obtain a blessed and everlasting life.

This is plainly directed against those who fear or love a human being, or some other thing, more than God, or who obey a human command more than God’s. When they offer to a creature the fear, love, and obedience owed to the Creator, what else do they do but worship the creature in place of God? Whatever you worship and love more is your god. If, therefore, you place money before God, you make money your god. If you place a prostitute before God, you make the prostitute your goddess. If you place Bacchus before God, you make him your god.

The whole of man also consists in fearing God and doing his commandments. For the person who does not fear God and does not keep his commandments no longer truly exists. God alone, whose essence is eternal and immutable, is properly said to be. Hence he says to Moses: “Thus you shall say: ‘He who is has sent me.’” And: “I am who I am. This is my name” (Exod. III). It is as though he were saying: All temporal things, because they now are and now are not, do not truly exist.

Therefore, my brothers, the more we approach God’s goodness through imitation—so that we may be holy as he is holy, pure as he is pure, and merciful as he is merciful—the more we exist. The more we withdraw from God, who is true being, through the dissimilarity of wickedness, impurity, cruelty, and the other vices, the less we exist. Not because a human being can become nothing, but because it is better not to exist than to exist badly, and better to be nothing than to exist unhappily.

Hence the Lord says concerning Judas: “It would have been better for that man if he had not been born” (Matt. XXVI; Mark XIV; Luke XXII). For the reprobate will desire death in hell, but death will flee from them (Rev. IX); nor will they perish completely, so that they may always be able to perish. Since eternal punishment is therefore twice as severe as any temporal punishment, it would be better for the reprobate to perish utterly once than to endure forever by continually perishing.

Therefore, dearest brothers, having despised the world with its desires, let us fear God alone with love and love him with fear; let us strive to keep his commandments, so that with his help we may deserve truly to exist, live, and reign with him forever—he who, in perfect Trinity, lives and reigns as God. Amen.

## HOMILY IV. FIRST SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“God is love” (1 John IV), and so forth. These words are spoken, dearest brothers, by the apostle and evangelist John, beloved by the Lord, who also reclined at supper upon his breast. Because he was loved by the Lord more tenderly than the others, he spoke more deeply and excellently than the others about his beloved and about his love.

In this passage, therefore, he does six things. First, he shows how great a love God has had for us. Second, he exhorts us to love. Third, he demonstrates that what he has said about God’s love is true. Fourth, he commends love. Fifth, he urges us to love God. Sixth, he proves that God cannot truly be loved without the neighbor.

Wishing, therefore, to show how great a love God has had for us, he says: “God is love.” Certainly, if God loved not everyone, but only those who deserved it, he could not properly be called love—that is, love itself. But now, because he loves everyone, even those who do not deserve it, he may emphatically be called love and loving-kindness. For God so overflows with the entrails of compassion and love that he leaves no one without an experience of his goodness and love: “He makes his sun rise upon the just and the unjust, and rains upon the good and the evil” (Matt. V). “He gives food to the beasts and to the young ravens that call upon him” (Ps. CXLVI).

Hence it is truly said to him through the Wise Man: “You hate nothing of what you have made, O Lord” (Wis. XI). Nevertheless, divine love and generosity are by no means without order. They would be so if he loved all—the good as well as the evil—equally. But this is not the case. Rather, he grants lesser goods to the evil. Hence it is written: “You will save humans and beasts, O Lord” (Ps. XXXVI)—that is, temporally. To the good, however, he reserves the greatest goods, which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart” (1 Cor. II). Nevertheless, insofar as it depends on him, he will save everyone eternally.

Here the Apostle also shows four things: how greatly he loved us, for what purpose, when, and how.

He shows how greatly he loved us when he says: “In this the love of God has appeared among us, because he sent his only-begotten Son into the world.” God loved us greatly, brothers, since he handed over for us not gold or silver, not an angel or any other creature of his, but his own only-begotten and most beloved Son.

For what purpose? He shows this by adding: “So that we might live through him.” He did not love us so that he himself might become better because of us, but so that we might become better through him. And this, brothers, is true love: it seeks not its own advantage but that of another.

When did he love us? He shows this when he adds: “In this is love, not that we loved him, but that he first loved us.” He loved us, then, when we did not love him, but rather were his despisers and enemies. And this, my brothers, is true and perfect love: to love even one’s enemies.

How did he love us? He indicates this when he adds: “And he sent his Son as an atonement”—or, as another translation has it, “as a reconciler”—for our sins. He therefore loved us rightly: he did not love in us the evil that we ourselves had done, but rather the good that he himself had made in us or was going to make in us. Thus he loved us so that he might make us just from sinners, free from slaves, and holy from the polluted. And this, my brothers, is true love: to love the good in a person and hate the evil.

The second part follows, in which the Apostle exhorts us to love, saying: “Dearest, if God has loved us, we also ought to love one another.” This is an argument from the lesser: if God, who is not bound to love us, has loved us, much more ought we, who are bound to love one another, to love one another.

We are bound to love our neighbor for three reasons: because he is God’s work, and we are bound to love the Creator in his creature; because God commanded that he be loved, and we are bound to obey God’s commandments; and because God loved human beings, and we are bound to imitate his example.

Therefore, my brothers, let us love our neighbors following the example of our Creator, giving them and giving for them not merely what is of little value but even what is more precious to us. Let us love them not with a view to temporal recompense, nor toward temporal life, but toward eternal life. Let us also love them first, without waiting for them to love us first; rather, let us anticipate them and make lovers from those who do not love, and friends from enemies.

Let us love them and wish them good, loving the good that is in them, but hating and removing whatever evil may be in them.

Someone might ask: Why do you first urge us to love our neighbor, when you ought first to urge us to love God? He answers: “Because no one has ever seen God.” It is as though he were saying openly: Because God is invisible, and his love is invisible, I therefore first urge you to love your neighbor, in whom God alone is loved, and in whose love the love of God is more truly demonstrated.

Hence he adds: “If we love one another”—understand, for God’s sake—“God remains in us through the love and charity that comes from him, which is perfected in us”; that is, it appears in our true love of our neighbors, because God truly loves us, and we love him.

The third part follows, in which the Apostle shows by his own authority and that of the other apostles that what he had said about the love of God is true. First he shows that he and the others are people whom one ought to believe, and then he adds: “In this we know that we remain in God and he in us, because he has given us from his Spirit”—that is, from the gifts of the Holy Spirit, through which we have been instructed, sanctified, and purified.

We apostles saw by faith the divinity of his Son and with the eyes of the body his humanity. We testify by our conduct, preaching, and miracles that the Father sent his Son as the Savior of the world. We also testify that, for whoever confesses with heart, mouth, and deed that Jesus is the Son of God, God dwells in him through grace, and he himself dwells in God through love.

We apostles have learned by experience that this is true, and we believe in the love that God has for us; therefore we are compelled to love him. Unbelievers do not love God precisely because they do not know that they are loved by God.

Therefore, brothers, if we wish God to remain in us and us in him, let us confess that our Lord Jesus Christ is true God, the Son of the true God, and the Savior of the world. Let us confess this, I say, with heart, mouth, and deed, because one without the others is not sufficient, especially where it is necessary. Peter confessed the Lord in his heart, but nevertheless fell by denying him with his mouth. “With the heart,” as Paul says, “one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X).

There are also some false Christians who confess Christ with heart and mouth but deny him by their deeds. Concerning such people Paul says: “They profess in words that they know God, but in their deeds they deny him” (Titus I).

Therefore, brothers, let us believe Christ with firm faith, love him with ardent charity, confess him in preaching and action, and, if necessary, even in death, so that we may deserve to remain in him and he in us forever.

The fourth part follows, in which he commends love in five ways.

First, he commends it because it is so worthy that God wished to be called by its name. He shows this when he says: “God is love.”

God is called love substantially, causally, actively, and passively.

Substantially, God is called love—that is, loving-kindness—because his substance is love, just as it is wisdom, power, and the like.

Causally, he is called love because he produces love, peace, and harmony in his creatures. He brings it about that the four elements, although they have contrary natures, are joined together in one harmonious unity of love. He brings it about that the four humors in the body, although contrary, are united in one harmonious state of health. He brings it about that in the Church there is “one heart and one soul” among the multitude of believers (Acts IV). He also brings it about that different persons are of one mind and one way of life in a household (Ps. LXVII).

God is also called love actively because the Lord is kind and gracious toward all: loving some through election, as the elect; some through the bestowal of graces, as those who are presently just; and all through the preservation of their existence.

He may be called love passively because he is lovable in himself and sweet to love. The Psalmist had tasted his sweetness when he said: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII). And elsewhere: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you” (Ps. XXX).

Second, he commends love because it makes us worthy to remain in God and makes God remain in us. Hence he adds: “Whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him.”

Through love we remain in God, because if we love God, we remain in God in heart and desire; we do his commandments, prefer his will to our own, and hasten toward him with all our strength. Through love, God also remains in us, because if we truly love God, he dwells in us, filling us with his graces, sustaining us, protecting us, ruling us, and guiding us.

Third, he commends love because love makes us like God. Hence he adds: “In this love is with us, because as he is, so are we in this world.” That is: As Christ is merciful, holy, and good, and a lover even of his enemies, so we who are in this world, desiring through love to be made like him, should strive to become merciful, holy, and good, and even lovers of our enemies, in accordance with his command to us: “Whoever serves me, let him follow me” (John XII). He adds the reward when he says: “And where I am, there my servant will be also” (ibid.).

Here, fourth, he commends love because it gives us confidence at Christ’s coming. It is truly as the common saying goes: “He goes safely to court who has a relative as magistrate.” So too, brothers, if we have truly loved God, if we have imitated him as Father in holiness, mercy, and the other virtues, we will come with great security and confidence to his second coming.

Trusting in this security, the Prophet does not fear death or judgment, but rather prays that it may come: “Bring my soul out of prison,” he says, “so that it may confess your name” (Ps. CXLI). And Paul: “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. I).

Fifth, he commends love because it excludes fear, saying: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear.”

Which fear? Although there are five kinds of fear—worldly, human, servile, initial, and filial—perfect love entirely excludes worldly fear. Whoever perfectly loves God does not fear the losses of worldly things, but is rather prepared to leave without sorrow what he possesses without love.

It also excludes, for the most part, human fear, because whoever perfectly loves God does not tremble at temporal punishment or death, but rather awaits it confidently, so that through it he may reach the vision of God for which he longs.

It also entirely excludes servile fear, because whoever perfectly loves God, purified of sins through love, has nothing in his conscience of which to be afraid, but rather something from which to rejoice and become secure. Hence it is added here: “Because fear has punishment.” Whoever fears servilely on account of guilt is tortured in his conscience.

It also excludes initial fear. Hence it is added here: “Whoever fears”—understand, in his conscience—“is not perfected in love.” For whoever truly and perfectly loves God is not divided, as a beginner is, partly by fear and partly by love, but is wholly possessed by the security of love.

Perfect love does not, however, exclude filial fear, because even the person who loves God most perfectly here fears, while walking along the slippery road of this age, lest he fall and offend God. He fears like a chaste woman fears her bridegroom—not fearing his coming, but his departure.

In the blessedness of the future, love will be so perfect that it will entirely exclude fear, either so that fear does not exist at all or so that it does not make a person fearful but reverent. What is read—“The holy fear of the Lord endures forever and ever” (Ps. XVIII)—is to be understood either of the good to which fear has led or of reverence.

The fifth part follows, in which he urges us to love God, saying: “Let us therefore love God, because he first loved us.”

There are, my brothers, three principal reasons why we ought to love the Lord.

The first is that he is good and lovable in himself. He indicated this reason earlier when he said: “God is love.”

The second is that he has deserved to be loved. This reason is indicated here when it is said: “Because he first loved us.”

The third is that he will give the reward of eternal blessedness to those who love him. He indicated this reason earlier when he said: “So that we may have confidence at his coming.”

Why do such great incentives to love, dearest brothers, not awaken our minds to love God? And if we neglect to love him because he is good and lovable in himself, why do the benefits of his mercy, displayed to us daily in love, and the desirable rewards of eternal blessedness that he has prepared for us, not inflame us to love him?

The sixth part follows, in which the Apostle shows that God cannot truly be loved without the neighbor, saying: “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar.”

He does not say “his enemy” or “the wicked,” because we ought always to hate enmity or wickedness, but to love the brotherhood of nature. This is directed against those who either love a person’s wickedness because of their friendship with him, or hate a person’s nature because of his wickedness.

Then he proves by two arguments that God cannot be loved without the neighbor.

His first argument is taken from the lesser, when he says: “For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” It is as though he were saying: In no way. It is less to love our neighbor, whom we see every day, with whom we have been raised, and to whom likeness and familiarity bind us. It is greater to love God, whom we do not know through any sense but believe through faith alone.

Then he proves the same point by an argument drawn from the authority of the commandment, adding: “And we have a commandment from God, that whoever loves God should love his brother also.” No one can truly love God unless he fulfills his commandment. Hence the same Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John XIV).

Therefore, my brothers, if we wish to have confidence and security at the coming of the supreme Judge, let us meanwhile love God and neighbor: God for his own sake and above all things; our neighbor for God’s sake and as ourselves. Let us not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth (1 John III), feeding Christ in the hungry, clothing him in the naked, welcoming him in strangers, and visiting him in the sick, so that we may deserve to hear him say: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV). Amen.

## HOMILY V. FIRST SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“Jesus said this parable to his disciples: ‘There was a certain rich man,’” and so forth (Luke XVI).

Since in this parable, dearest brothers, the name of the poor man is also given, it is clear that it is not merely a parable but also a history. It is a parable because by means of a likeness it demonstrates what should be done and what should be avoided. It is also a history because it is confirmed as an actual event by the poor man’s being identified by his proper name.

But why, my brothers, is the poor man’s name given while the rich man’s name is withheld? Is it not because the poor man is known by God through election, whereas the rich man is unknown to God through rejection? Hence God says to the chosen Moses: “I know you by name” (Exod. XXXIII). And in the future the Lord will say to the rejected: “Truly I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. XXV).

Here, brothers, our perversity is put to shame: we remember the names of the rich and powerful, but neglect to know the names of the poor. And why is this, unless because we are respecters of persons? We know the rich, whom God does not know, but do not know the poor, whom God knows.

Nevertheless, we read of blessed Clement that he had the poor of the regions written down by name.

The proposed parable has six parts. First, the merit of the rich man is presented; second, the merit of the poor man; third, the reward of the poor man; fourth, the punishment of the rich man; fifth, the rich man prays for himself; sixth, he prays for his own people but is not heard.

First, then, the merit of the rich man is presented when it says: “There was a certain rich man.” Here it is shown that what the Lord says elsewhere is true: namely, that a rich man will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty, and that it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven (Luke XVIII).

Riches, when wrongly used, commonly generate many vices: empty glory, pleasure, excess, pride, and contempt.

That they generate empty glory is shown when it is added: “who was clothed in purple and fine linen.” That expensive clothing is sought for glory is clear from the fact that no one desires to be clothed in costly garments except where he knows that he will be seen by many. If there were no sin in the luxury of clothing, the Lord would never have praised John the Baptist for the roughness of his garments and reproved others for their softness, saying: “What did you go out into the desert to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses” (Matt. XI).

That riches generate pleasure and luxury is shown when it is added: “And he feasted splendidly every day.” He is reproved in two respects: both because he delighted in sumptuous banquets and because he did so daily. He also delighted in the expense, preparation, and gluttony of food, which the Lord forbade, saying: “Beware lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony, drunkenness, and the cares of this age” (Luke XXI).

He did this every day. Even if one may sometimes dine more splendidly and delicately, whether because of a feast, guests, or illness, to do so every day is nevertheless a great vice.

That riches generate excess is shown in both respects: he dressed excessively and feasted excessively. That they generate pride and contempt is suggested by the fact that the rich man exalted himself in his riches and despised the beggar who was perishing before his door.

The second part follows, in which the merit of the poor man is described when it is added: “And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, who lay at his gate, full of sores, desiring to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table, and no one gave him anything.”

Four aspects of Lazarus’s misery are shown: he was a beggar; he was sick; no one helped him in either respect; and, lying before the rich man’s door, he endured a great temptation through seeing the pleasures that were present there.

Just as the presence of the sick beggar was an occasion of greater condemnation for the rich man, so the presence of the rich man’s pleasures was an occasion of a greater crown for the beggar. If the rich man had not had the beggar before him, he might seem to have had an excuse for his riches. And if the sick beggar had been kept away from the sight of those pleasures, he would not have endured such a fierce struggle of temptation.

How many temptations, my brothers, do you think Lazarus endured? He was a beggar, yet daily saw before his eyes the rich man and his household overflowing with riches. He was sick, yet saw the rich man and his household rejoicing in their health. He was hungry, yet saw the rich man and his household belching from excessive satiety. Oppressed by so many miseries, he daily saw the rich man and his household flourishing in so many prosperities.

Great indeed was this Lazarus: pressed by so many calamities, yet not crushed; enduring so much suffering, yet remaining patient. Although so many scourges tortured him, they nevertheless did not wrench patience from him.

Following his example, let the poor and the sick learn not to murmur in their adversities, not to condemn the rich, but to bless God and attribute their scourges to their sins. “And no one gave him anything,” because just as the rich man was without mercy, so he had servants without mercy, in accordance with Solomon’s saying: “An ungodly ruler has all ungodly servants” (Prov. XXIX).

“But the dogs also came and licked his sores.” Where a human being disdained to minister to God’s servant, a beast served him as best it could.

The third part follows, in which the poor man’s reward is described when it is added: “And it came to pass that the beggar died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom.”

Dearest brothers, who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high and regards the humble in heaven and on earth, raising the needy from the dust and lifting the poor from the dung heap? (Ps. CXII.) Behold: the one whom man abhors, disdains, and avoids, the compassionate Lord, above all, visits and receives through the ministry of his holy angels, transferring a precious pearl from the dung heap and placing it in the blessed rest of his elect.

Abraham’s bosom is a tranquil place in the upper underworld, where those who died in Abraham’s faith rested while awaiting Christ, who would open the kingdom of heaven to them.

The fourth part follows, in which the rich man’s punishment is described when it is added: “But the rich man also died, and he was buried in hell.”

Behold: the one whom a crowd of servants and friends surrounded, comforted, and flattered is carried away through the harsh ministry of cruel demons and transferred into hell—from purple and fine linen into the harshness of darkness; from splendid banquets into perpetual hunger and thirst; and from the gentle hands of weeping friends into the hard hands of shrieking demons.

And why? Not because he is said to have seized or defrauded anything, but because he spent his own possessions excessively and gave nothing to the poor. If those who do not give what is theirs are condemned in this way, brothers, what will those who seize what belongs to others suffer?

Then, lifting his eyes while he was in torments, he saw Abraham from afar—far off both in place and in disposition, since one joined to God can desire nothing other than what God wills—and Lazarus in his bosom.

Now, since the just always see the reprobate in punishments, both to increase their joy and to glorify their own labor, the reprobate can see the elect only beforehand, but afterward they cannot; for it is written: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God.”

The fifth part follows, in which the rich man prays for himself but is not heard. Thus it is added: “And he himself, crying out”—more through feeling than through his voice—“said: ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me.’” He calls him “father,” whom he was unwilling to imitate as a son; and he who, while living in luxury and ignorant of misery, is now placed in torments begins to learn what evil misery has and what good mercy has. You rich, therefore, lest the same thing happen to you, learn through compassion, amid riches, both misery and mercy, because in the next life the one who has not shown mercy in this life will not find mercy. Hence James says: “Judgment without mercy will be made upon him who has not shown mercy” (James II).

“And send,” he says, “Lazarus, so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water to cool my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame.” Behold, brothers, how terrible God is in his counsels concerning the sons of men (Psalm LXV). The rich man, who did not wish to give Lazarus, when he was hungry, the crumbs falling from his table, was brought by a just judgment to the point of asking, while burning, for a drop of water from Lazarus’s finger—and not receiving it. If he had given him even crumbs out of mercy, he would have found some refreshment in his torments. Therefore, brothers, if you wish to find mercy, show mercy: invite the poor to your banquets, or at least give them the leftovers from your table; give even the crumbs that fall, lest, if you neglect to give these, you fail to find refreshment in the fire.

But why is the rich man said to have burned especially in his tongue, unless because he had devoted it to feasting and to the loquacity associated with it? And Abraham said to him: “Son, remember that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things. But now he is comforted, while you are tormented.” No one, dearest brothers, is so evil that he never does some good; nor is anyone so holy in this life that he never commits a sin. But God, the just judge, leaves no good unrewarded and no sin unpunished. Therefore, if the rich man had done any good amid his many evils, it was rewarded for him in the bestowal of the temporal prosperity that he loved. And if Lazarus had committed any evil amid faith, hope, steadfastness, patience, and the other virtues, temporal tribulation’s fire purified it all. Conversely, the rich man’s evils were punished in eternal suffering, while Lazarus’s good deeds were rewarded in eternal life.

From this let the rich learn to fear when things go well for them in this life, when they flourish and abound: lest, on account of that prosperity, their good deeds be rewarded in this world and their sins be reserved for eternal fire. Conversely, let the poor and afflicted learn to hope well when they are punished by poverty, affliction, and misery, because through that adversity their sins are cleansed, if they bear it patiently, while their good deeds are reserved for eternal reward.

“And between all this” [Note: [Col. 1965D] The Vulgate reads, “in all these things.”] “a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot, nor can they cross from there to us.” Certainly, if those who are in torments wish to cross over to rest, that is not surprising. But how can those who are in rest wish to cross over to those who are in torments, and yet be unable to do so? I think that, through the customary compassion and piety that the saints possessed in this world, they would wish, out of pity, to cross over to those who are in punishment, were they not so closely joined to divine justice that in no way could they will anything other than what God wills. For in eternal blessedness, where there is no pain, there can be no compassion, since compassion does not exist without pain.

The sixth part follows, in which the rich man prays for others but is not heard, when it is added: “Therefore I ask you, father, to send him to my father’s house, for I have five brothers, so that he may testify to them, lest they too come to this place of torment.” Frustrated in his prayer for himself, he prays for his brothers, and now begins to love the souls of others, although while alive he did not love his own.

Indeed, for the increase of his torment, knowledge, memory, and compassion are left to him. He is tormented more because he knows that Lazarus, whom he once saw miserable beneath him, is now glorified above him. He is tormented more because he remembers the happiness he once had in his father’s house with his brothers. He is tormented still more because he pities his brothers, whom he sees coming, through the same way of life, to the same condemnation.

And Abraham said to him: “They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them.” As if he were saying: “The Law and the prophets teach how eternal condemnation can be avoided.” “No, father Abraham,” he said, “but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent,” because he himself had despised the Scriptures.

There are many such false Christians today who, not believing the sacred Scriptures, say: “Who has returned from the underworld to bear witness to us?” In this they show themselves to be unbelievers, since they believe neither in the rewards of the righteous nor in the punishments of the reprobate. But it is then added: “If they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead.” Whether “to listen” here is understood as “to believe” or as “to obey,” it is plainly true today that the Scriptures bear witness concerning Christ. Those who do not wish to believe the Scriptures do not wish to believe Christ, who rose from the dead. Those who do not obey the Law or the prophets, which represent a lesser degree of perfection, do not obey the more perfect teaching of Christ, who rose from the dead.

Therefore, brothers, let us learn to despise riches, to observe moderation in clothing and food, to be more generous and merciful toward the poor, and from the goods entrusted to us to make the poor our friends and intercessors, so that, when we fail, they may receive us into the eternal dwellings (Luke XVI). Behold, every day we see many Lazaruses before our doors; they thrust themselves upon us importunately and ask, though they ought to have been asked. If, my brothers, we perhaps see certain things in them that need correction, let us not for that reason despise them, because the fire of tribulations expiates whatever in them needs expiation. If they are good, they should be received as our brothers and intercessors. If not, let us give them a double alms. Let us give them both bodily bread and the spiritual bread of the word, so that we may receive a double reward from them; so that, when the Poor One of the poor, our God and Lord Jesus Christ, comes, he may receive us into the eternal dwellings.

## HOMILY VI. THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

[Col. 1966B]

“Dearest, do not be surprised if the world hates you,” etc. (1 John III).

This reading, dearest brothers, has four parts. First, it says that it should not be surprising if the wicked hold the good in hatred. Second, it shows that those who have charity live, while those who lack it die. Third, by Christ’s example it urges us toward perfection in love. Fourth, it dissuades us from a false love of the world.

Thus, first, it says: “Do not be surprised if the world hates you,” that is, the lovers of the world. It says two things: that the world hates the righteous, and that this should not be surprising. And for what reason does the world—that is, the wicked—hate the righteous? For three reasons.

The first is that the life of the righteous is opposed to the life of the wicked. For just as there is as much opposition between fire and water, between light and darkness, so there is as much opposition between justice and injustice, between chastity and lust, and between the other virtues and the vices opposed to them. Therefore there can be no peace or harmony between those who practice these things and those who practice their opposites.

The second reason is that the good hate and condemn the life of the wicked. The third is that they rebuke and correct them, desiring to take them away from the devil and win them for God.

Thus, while the good hate the wicked with a good hatred, the wicked persecute them with an evil hatred, according to the saying: “With perfect hatred I hated them; they have become enemies to me” (Psalm CXXXVIII). Perfect hatred exists when we hate the vice of the wicked person in such a way that we love his nature. This is not hatred but rather love. Hence the Psalmist says: “They repaid me evil for good, and hatred for my love” (Psalm CVIII).

John the Baptist rebuked Herod, saying: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Mark VI). But for the very reason that Herod ought to have thanked John, he imprisoned and beheaded him. This is the recompense of the wicked.

The Wise Man encompasses the reasons why the wicked hate the good in these words: “The impious said among themselves, thinking wrongly: ‘Let us surround the righteous man, because he is opposed to our works. He claims to have knowledge of God; we are regarded by him as triflers, and he abstains from our ways as from impurities,’” etc. (Wisdom II).

It should not be surprising that the wicked hate the good, because they are lovers of the world; hence they are called “the world” here. But, as John testifies, “if anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” [Col. 1967A] (1 John II). It should not be surprising that the wicked hate the good, since they also hate themselves. “He who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Psalm X). How will he love another who does not love himself?

It should not be surprising that the wicked hate the good, because this is what they have always done: they do not do what the good deserve, but what they themselves are accustomed to do. Thus, from the beginning, the wicked Cain persecuted and killed his righteous brother Abel. Thus the wicked brothers persecuted the righteous Joseph; the wicked Saul, holy David; the impious Hebrews, the holy prophets; the wicked Jews, Christ; and unbelievers, the faithful.

Therefore, dearest brothers, do not be surprised if the lovers of the world hate and persecute you. For the Lord says to his disciples: “If they persecuted me, they will persecute you,” so that the Psalmist’s saying might be fulfilled: “Because they hated me without cause” [Note: [Col. 1967] In John, read: “so that the word written in their law might be fulfilled,” etc.] (John XV).

The second part follows, in which he shows that those who have charity live, while those who do not have it die, when he adds: “We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brothers.” As if he were saying: “As long as we were without love of God and neighbor, we were in the death of sins. But after we began to love God and our neighbor, we began to live—that is, the life of the virtues.”

For just as hatred and contempt are the source of all vices, so, conversely, love of God and neighbor is the source of all virtues. Through love we are joined to God and to our neighbor, so that we may be members of Christ’s body, which is the Church. But if we lack love, we are no longer members of Christ or part of the integrity of his body; we bear no fruit, but are dead and destined for condemnation.

The Lord showed this in the Gospel through the likeness of the vine and the branches, saying: “I am the vine and you are the branches. Just as the branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me. If anyone does not remain in me, he will be cast out like a branch and will wither; they will gather him up, throw him into the fire, and he will burn” (John XV).

Hence it is also added here: “He who does not love remains in death.” Let each one of us therefore examine himself to see whether he loves God and his neighbor. If he loves, let him know that he lives in God and is a member of Christ. But if he does not love, let him know that he is dead in sin and is not a member of Christ. Such a person should hasten to rise again through repentance and to cling to Christ through love, lest perhaps, like a branch cut off, he be cast into the eternal fire.

And if he is guilty who does not love, what is the condition of one who also hates? “Everyone,” he says, “who hates his brother is a murderer.” He does not say “an enemy” or “an evildoer,” because it is good to hate a person’s enmity or wickedness, but to hate the brotherhood of his nature is murder.

Therefore, brothers, great discernment must be exercised here: we must hate the vice of a person in such a way that we do not hate his nature, and love his nature in such a way that we hate his vice. This stands against those who, either because of friendship with a person, consent to his vices, or, because of hatred for his vices, hate the person’s nature. And you know that every murderer does not have eternal life abiding in him, just as a withered branch cut off from the vine does not.

The third part follows, in which he urges us toward perfection in charity by Christ’s example, saying: “By this we have known the charity of God: that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.”

As if he were saying: “Charity is known through the presentation of a work. Therefore, just as God showed us through his action the charity that he has toward us by laying down his life for us, so let us also show through our works the charity that we have toward our neighbors by laying down our lives for them.”

This is an argument from the greater. If God—who was under no obligation, who is so great and of such a nature, and who existed before us—laid down his life for us, who are such and so great, how much more ought we, who are under obligation, to lay down our bodily lives for our brothers, who are our equals?

Thus, if we see our brothers captured by pagans, wavering and uncertain in the faith, we are obliged to strengthen them in the faith by laying down our lives for the confirmation of their faith, lest they perish in soul through denial. But we are not obliged to lay down our lives for the bodily life of our neighbor.

Nevertheless, we read in the *Dialogues* that Saint Sanctulus pledged his life for a certain cleric captured by unbelievers, so that, in the morning, either the captive or Sanctulus himself would be handed over to them in his place. When he had compelled the captive to depart during the night, Sanctulus himself presented himself to the executioner in the morning. When the executioner wished to behead the saint with his sword raised, his right hand became stiff. Astonished at this miracle, the unbelievers asked his pardon and begged him, by his prayer, to restore the right hand to his executioner; they also asked him to request whatever gift he wished from them. But after obtaining by oath from the man that he would never again shed Christian blood, the saint restored his right hand to him, and he set free all the Christian captives whom they held.

[Note: [Col. 1967] Saint Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book III, chapter 47, volume LXXVII of Migne’s *Patrologia*.]

Behold, my brothers, how great is the power of charity: when one person exposes his body to death for another’s body, divine power is manifested. And not only are those two delivered, but many others also are freed from death.

The fourth part follows, in which he dissuades us from false love, saying: “If anyone possesses the substance of this world, and sees his brother suffering need, and closes his bowels against him, how does the charity of God”—which even lays down its life for its neighbors—“remain in him?”

As if he were saying: “If someone does not give his needy brother the worldly substance that he possesses, how will he give his life for him?” True love is distinguished from false love by this: true love cannot close the bowels of compassion, but does what it can. If it has much, it gives much. If it has little, it willingly shares even that.

To the thirsty person, if he has it, he gives wine; if he does not have wine, he gives at least warm water. If he lacks wood with which to heat it, let him give even cold water. He will not lose his reward, for the Lord says: “If anyone gives a cup of cold water in my name, he will not lose his reward” (Matthew X; Mark IX).

If he cannot do more, let him at least give consolation; let him give compassion, prayer, and good will, which suffices for one who can do no more. For it is written: “And on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II).

False love is that which, when it can offer help, pretends not to see, and loves not through deeds but through words alone and promises (praemissis). The Apostle dissuades us from this when he adds: “My little children, let us not love in word or with the tongue, but in deed and in truth”—that is, let us not love in word alone, as certain hypocrites do, but also in deed. Let us not love with a loquacious and flattering fiction, but with truth of heart.

Therefore, my brothers, let us have love that is not feigned but true. This will be so if we know how to love God alone in our neighbor; if we establish God alone as the sole cause of our love and our work; if we expect our reward not from a human being but from God alone; if we seek to please not human beings but God alone in all things; and if we strive to store up treasure not on earth but in heaven. May God and our Lord grant this, he who lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY VII. THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

Jesus said this parable to his disciples: “A certain man made a great supper and invited many” (Luke XIV).

In this parable, dearest brothers, seven things must be noted: the preparation of the great supper, the invitation of many, the summons to the supper, the excuses of some, the introduction of others, the compulsion of still others, and the eternal exclusion of those who make excuses.

The preparation of the great supper is the predestination of eternal blessedness from the foundation of the world. This blessedness is called by many names. Here it is called “a great supper”; elsewhere, “the kingdom of heaven”; elsewhere, “the heavenly homeland”; elsewhere, “eternal joy”; elsewhere, “rest”; and by similar names.

Why is this so? Because heavenly blessedness is so great and of such a nature that “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart” (Isaiah LXIV; 1 Corinthians II), etc. Just as the human mind cannot comprehend it, so human words cannot signify it. For just as understanding succumbs to the greatness of the thing, so words do not explain the thing as it truly is.

Yet because it was necessary for this blessedness to be signified to us in some manner—and because we human beings could neither understand nor speak of it except through human words—the same blessedness is named by many borrowed and improper names that signify temporal pleasure. It is signified by many names so that the particular quality of eternal blessedness, which cannot be signified by one name, may be signified by another. If it could be fully signified by a single name, it would not be necessary to designate it by many names.

They are borrowed because all these names—blessedness, supper, kingdom of heaven, heavenly homeland, and the like—have been transferred from temporal things to eternal things, although there is no true comparison between temporal and eternal things.

They are improper because they do not express the truth of the thing, but indicate it in some way through resemblance. They signify temporal pleasure so that, through temporal pleasures, which are brief and empty, that eternal pleasure may be signified which will be unfailing and true.

Because human beings take their greatest delight here in a splendid supper, the kingdom of heaven—where it will not be necessary to eat—is here called a supper, because there the saints, after the evening of this world, will be refreshed with eternal satiety. It is called “great” because it will be sufficient both for the number and for the capacity of all.

The invitation to this supper occurs when a person approaches his end. For when, brothers, we approach the faith and the sacraments, it is then promised to us. If we persevere in the faith, we shall share in that eternal blessedness.

Behold, brothers, we have all been invited to that eternal supper. Let us therefore hasten toward it in faith and desire, and make ourselves worthy of it through our works.

We are summoned to the hour of the supper by the servant when, through the order of preachers, we are admonished to hasten to come to eternal blessedness. Behold, brothers, I who speak—whatever kind of person I may be—am a servant who calls you to the hour of the supper. For the hour of the supper will be at the end of the world, or even at the end of each individual life. When we depart from this age, we enter that eternal supper, if we are worthy.

I cry out, brothers—I cry out to you: prepare yourselves as quickly as possible for the eternal supper while you can, lest you then begin to wish for it when you will be unable to do so. Wash your consciences through repentance. Put on the wedding garment. Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands (Luke XII). For only such people are admitted to the supper.

But behold, brothers: some are called and consent. Others are called and even compelled. There are, then, three kinds of people who make excuses.

One says: “I have bought a farm, and I must go out to see it.” He, my brothers, has bought a farm who acquires for himself, through the pride of domination, the pride of ruling. There are many such people today—which is all the more grievous—who, despising the eternal supper, purchase honors and dignities for themselves, paying money for them to human beings, and even selling their souls to the devil for them.

Alas, what a terrible exchange! What shall I say about those who are not even ashamed to commit a crime in the holy Church—those who sell or buy orders, churches, and the offices of ecclesiastical sacraments? With whom should these be counted, except Judas and the Jews who sold and bought Christ? Their money will be with them for their destruction, as Peter said to Simon Magus (Acts VIII).

These people must go out from the pursuit and love of spiritual goods and see, through their base love, the dignities they have bought: exalted outwardly but cast down within, conspicuous outwardly but dark within. Of them it is written: “An inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end” (Proverbs XX).

Another said: “I have bought five yokes of oxen, and I am going to test them.” The five yokes of oxen, which are joined in pairs, signify the five bodily senses, which are likewise joined in the members. For just as yokes of oxen cultivate and tend [read: plough] the earth, so the five bodily senses cultivate and attend to earthly things.

He has bought yokes of oxen who, at the price of his soul, acquires and purchases only temporal things subject to the five senses. His eyes are captivated solely by the beauty of bodily forms; his ears delight only in the sounds of empty melodies; his taste is enticed by the flavor of wines, foods, and seasonings; his nostrils are ensnared by the sweetness of luxurious scents; and his sense of touch delights in luxurious contacts.

Hence it is appropriately added: “And I am going to test them.” For through the five senses external things are tested. The eye tests what is more beautiful; the ear, what is more melodious; the nose, what is more fragrant; taste, what is more flavorful; and touch, what is more pleasant.

Although both this man and the one mentioned above despise going to the eternal supper, he nevertheless asks to be excused, saying: “I ask you to hold me excused.” For those who pursue and seek temporal honors and earthly riches, and purchase them through a most evil exchange, do not wish to abandon or despise what they love excessively; yet they ask religious people to excuse them before God and to pray for them. As if they were saying: “I cannot despise these things, but I ask you to excuse me and pray for me.” Their voice sounds humble, but their mind contains contempt and pride.

Another said: “I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.” By the name “wife,” carnal pleasure and lust are understood here—not because marrying a wife is evil, but because many marry solely for pleasure. Whoever therefore serves bodily pleasure is so entangled in the habitual vices of the flesh that he admits that he cannot go to God’s great supper.

These three kinds of people who make excuses are held back from going to God’s supper by the three vices that John sets forth in his Epistle, saying: “Do not love the world, brothers, nor the things that are in the world, because whatever is in the world is either the desire of the flesh”—that is, pleasure—“or the desire of the eyes”—that is, riches—“or the pride of life” (1 John II)—that is, ambition for honors. And he adds: “But if anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (ibid.).

Therefore, my brothers, let us turn our minds away from love of the age; let us restrain the love of pleasure; let us exclude the desire for riches from ourselves; and let us avoid pride and ambition.

Regarding the introduction of others to the supper, it is added: “Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in here the poor and the weak, the blind and the lame.”

By these people, my brothers, who neither make excuses nor are compelled to enter, are signified the humble, who presume greatly on God and nothing on themselves. Although they are in the streets and lanes—that is, amid the breadth and turmoil of secular life—they are poor in spirit. Considering themselves weak, they are also blind, confessing their ignorance; and they are lame, recognizing their imperfection.

When these people are called to the eternal supper, they consent all the more quickly because they despise earthly things all the more. The more they recognize their weakness, the less they desire earthly pleasure.

For it is impossible for anyone to love God and the world at the same time. The more someone loves God, the more he despises the age; and the more he loves the age, the more he despises God.

Therefore, brothers, let us not love what we shall soon leave behind. We shall either leave all worldly things or be left by them. Let us love those things that do not pass away, which make their possessors blessed.

Regarding the compulsion of others, it is added: “Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel whomever you find to enter.” These signify those who are farther away, who wander farther from the city of God along the roads and amid the business of this age.

Since they are hardened in their love of the world, they do not come to God’s supper unless they are compelled by adversities, poverty, illnesses, and afflictions. When they see that in this age they cannot find the rest and happiness they sought, they are compelled by adversities to turn to the Lord.

Concerning such people the Lord speaks under the figure of an adulterous woman, addressing Judea: “I will hedge in your way with thorns, and I will fence it with a wall, and you will not be able to find your path. You will seek your lovers and will not find them; you will seek them and will not catch them, and you will say: ‘I will return to my husband, because it was better for me then than now’” (Hosea II). And David says: “When he slew them, they sought him and returned” (Psalm LXXVII).

Therefore, my brothers, consider that when the Lord allows people to prosper in their evil ways and to fulfill their perverse desires, this is indeed a hidden judgment, but it is a sign of God’s great anger. Hence the Lord says through the Psalmist: “And I dismissed them according to the desires of their heart” (Psalm LXXX). And through the prophet: “I will no longer be angry with you; my jealousy has departed from you” (Ezekiel XVI).

Against this David prays: “Do not hand me over to my desire, to the sinner” (Psalm CXXXIX)—that is, to the devil.

But when God does not permit sinners to fulfill their evil desires, and instead obstructs them and afflicts them with adversities, this is a sign of God’s mercy. He strikes here so that he may not strike forever; he does not spare here so that he may spare forever.

Regarding the exclusion of those who make excuses from the eternal supper, it is added: “Amen I say to you, none of those men who were invited will taste my supper.”

Here, dearest brothers, the great severity of the eternal Judge must be considered. The very one who now flatters us with paternal affection, who invites us through promises, who now draws us through inward inspiration and now compels us through adversity; who now begs us, though he is the one who ought to be begged; who now sends us messengers and makers of peace; and who—what is more—recalls those who flee and invites those who despise him: he will appear terrifying in the judgment.

Hence he says through the prophet: “Your ears shall hear the voice of one admonishing behind you” (Isaiah XXX). And to those who now despise the one calling them, although then they cry out, “Lord, Lord, open to us” (Matthew XXV), he will say to them terribly: “Amen I say to you, I do not know you” (ibid.).

Therefore, brothers, while we have time, let us follow his calls. Let us not be delayed by ambition, greed, or pleasure. Let us receive his scourges and corrections with thanksgiving, so that, compelled if necessary, we may reach his eternal supper—the one who draws us, and who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY VIII. THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“Humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the time of visitation,” etc. (1 Peter V).

In this reading, dearest brothers, the Apostle does four things. First, he urges us to humble ourselves. Second, he urges us to place all our anxiety in God. Third, he urges us to be sober and watchful. Fourth, he promises that God’s help will be present to us.

First, then, he urges us to humility. Humility is a virtue that makes a person, through the truest knowledge of himself, regard himself as contemptible. Just as pride is the root of all evils or vices, so, conversely, humility is the foundation of all virtues. Whoever gathers virtues without humility carries dust, as it were, into the wind. For the other virtues without humility not only do no good but actually do harm, since they make a person proud.

Humility is so pleasing to God that a humble sinner pleases God more than a proud righteous person, as he himself demonstrates to us through the example of the humble publican and the proud Pharisee (Luke XVIII).

Our Lord Jesus Christ especially professed this virtue and invites us to it by his example, saying: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew IX). Following him, the blessed Mother of God, as though forgetting her virginity and the other virtues with which she shone, said: “Because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke I).

This virtue made Moses God’s intimate servant. It made David a man according to the Lord’s heart. The Apostle Peter therefore urges us to it when he says: “Humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the time of visitation.”

There are, however, some who are under the hand of God but are not humbled. Others are under the hand of God and are humbled. Still others humble themselves even before the hand of God.

Here, by the hand of God, we understand chastisement and scourging. Hence Job says: “Have pity on me, at least you, my friends, because the hand of the Lord has touched me” (Job XIX).

Those, then, are under the hand of God but are not humbled who are scourged by God, yet do not recognize their sins through humility of mind so that they may be corrected. Such was Herod; such was Antiochus; and such were the other perverse people who were scourged by the Lord but were neither humbled nor corrected.

Concerning such people the Lord says through the prophet: “I struck them, and they did not grieve” (Jeremiah V); and elsewhere: “We treated Babylon, but she was not healed” (Jeremiah LI). As if he were saying: “We did what ought to have been sufficient for her healing, yet she was not healed.”

Such people will be punished more severely than all others in hell, because here they were not corrected by scourges but made worse.

Those who are humbled under the hand of God are the ones who, recognizing their sins beneath their scourges, humble themselves and are corrected. Such was Paul, who, struck by the Lord, was humbled and corrected. Such were those of whom it is written: “When he slew them, they sought him and returned” (Psalm LXXIX).

Those who humble themselves even before the hand of the Lord are not worn down by any affliction or scourges; they humble themselves voluntarily in their prosperity and are corrected for the better. Such was Moses, and such also was David, who remained humble even in prosperity.

The first humility, therefore, because it occurs in the body alone, is useless. The second, because it occurs also in the mind, is good. The third, because it occurs in the mind and also voluntarily, is best.

But because some are humbled by God and held among scourges in such a way that they despair, the Apostle adds: “So that he may exalt you.” As if he were saying: “Humble yourselves under God’s scourges in such a way that you retain hope, because he himself will exalt you.”

And because some again humble themselves hypocritically so that they may be exalted in this life, he adds: “At the time of visitation”—that is, at his second coming. For those who seek to be exalted here will be worthy to be humbled in the next life.

The second part follows, in which the Apostle urges us to place all our anxiety upon God, in these words: “Casting all your anxiety upon him, because he cares for you.” As though he were saying: Do not think that, under the scourges with which God afflicts you, you are being neglected by God; rather, hope in him at that very time, because scourges are signs not of one who neglects, but of one who loves [Col. 1974B].

Moreover, we ought to place all our anxiety and hope in God in every matter, but in different ways according to the different matters. We ought to place our anxiety concerning the salvation of our soul in God in such a way that we ourselves are no less concerned about it, knowing that the kingdom of God comes not to those who sleep or are negligent, but to the concerned and those who labor. Hence it is also added: “Be sober and watchful,” and so forth.

We ought, however, to place in God our concern for those things that pertain to bodily life in such a way that, even if we do not have anxiety about them, we nevertheless have foresight concerning them. For the Lord forbids us to be anxious about these things, saying: “Do not be anxious, saying: What shall we eat, or what shall we drink, or with what shall we be clothed? For your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things” (Matthew VI). We are not, however, forbidden to exercise foresight concerning them. Hence the Apostle says: “Whoever does not work, let him not eat” (II Thessalonians III); and elsewhere: “Rather, let each person labor so that he may have something with which to give to one suffering need” (Ephesians IV). And Solomon says: “Because of the cold the lazy man did not wish to plow; therefore he will beg in summer, and it will not be given to him” (Proverbs XX).

When we are forbidden to think about tomorrow (Matthew VI), “tomorrow” is to be understood as the more remote future. It is not thinking about tomorrow to make provision in the present year for one’s grain supply. For, he says, “Sufficient for the day is its own evil” (ibid.), that is, it is enough to think about the present miseries, needs, and requirements of the body. Why should we be anxious about future miseries and shortages that perhaps we shall never see [Col. 1974D]?

We must likewise place our anxiety concerning dangers and uncertainties, and concerning matters in which human counsel fails, in God in such a way that our own anxiety is unable to provide for us. Yet by anxious prayer let us make God anxious, so that he may deign to counsel and provide for us—he who does not abandon those who hope in him. “For he cares for you,” he says, as a good head of a household cares for his family. Let us therefore be good servants to God, and he will be a good head of the household to us. If we serve him faithfully, he will likewise faithfully provide for us both present wages and eternal rewards.

The third part follows, in which the Apostle exhorts us to sobriety and watchfulness, saying: “Be sober and watchful in prayers, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls about, seeking someone to devour.”

The Apostle commands us to be sober not only from feasting and drunkenness arising from worldly desire. This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “See that your hearts are not weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness and the cares of this world, lest sudden calamity come upon you” (Luke XXI). But because it is not enough to be sober unless we are also fortified by prayer, he adds: “And be watchful in prayers.”

Moreover, he commands us to watch in prayer not only so that in prayer itself we may not wander in mind, but rather be attentive and watchful, but also so that we may remember to watch in prayer not only during the daytime hours but also during the night, according to what Jeremiah commands: “Rise and praise at the beginning of your watches” (Lamentations II). And David says: “Seven times a day I have praised you”; and: “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you” (Psalm CXVIII).

And why must one keep watch [Col. 1975B] in prayers? “Because,” he says, “your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls about, seeking someone to devour” (ibid.).

Four characteristics make the devil equipped to do harm: he never sleeps, but is always watchful in ambush; he is invisible, and therefore can do harm more easily; he is naturally skilled in cunning; and he is long-lived, and therefore, through long experience, more crafty. Since, then, our adversary is thus equipped, the greater necessity rests upon us to keep watch: “like,” he says, “a roaring lion.”

When the devil rages openly, he is called a lion; when he secretly injects poisonous temptations into us, he is called a serpent; when he deceives us through cunning, he is called a fox; when he deceives not at the beginning but at the end, he is called a scorpion or a dragon, and so forth. Hence it is written: “You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon” (Psalm XC).

Just as a lion, by roaring, sends terror and bewilderment among animals so that they cannot flee, so the devil, when he approaches, is accustomed to send a certain horror and stupor upon human beings, so that they are unable to guard themselves against him.

He also prowls around the fold of the faithful in the manner of a lion, so that, if he finds anyone wandering away from the unity of the others, he may kill him. He also circles around each individual believer, so that, if he should find some part in him less well defended, he may enter through it and destroy him.

Therefore, my brothers, let each person guard himself with greater force, lest he be separated from the unity of the faithful flock. Let him also, according to Solomon, guard his heart with all vigilance (Proverbs IV), lest through our negligence some entrance be found in us for the adversary [Col. 1975D].

He shows how he must be resisted by adding: “Resist him, strong in faith.” Join faith, therefore, to the sobriety and prayer that he mentioned earlier, and you have three means by which you can resist the devil. Through sobriety we keep watch; through prayer we conquer the devil; and through faith—faith working through love—we render his frauds and temptations powerless.

Hence Paul says: “In all things take up the shield of faith, with which you may extinguish the flaming darts of the evil one” (Ephesians VI). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain: Move from here and throw yourself into the sea, and it will happen” (Luke XVII).

Then, by the example of others, he urges us to resist the devil’s temptations, adding: “Knowing that the same temptation which is in the world is being inflicted upon your brotherhood.” As though he were saying: You alone do not endure the battles and temptations of the devil; all the faithful who are in this life also struggle against diabolical temptations—men and women alike, the old and the young alike.

Therefore, men, it should be shameful for you to be overcome by the temptations of the devil that even women have conquered. It should also be shameful for you, bearded and gray-haired men, to be overcome by the temptations of the devil that even boys and children have conquered. It should likewise be shameful for anyone to be softer and more effeminate, and not to resist temptations against which countless others resist.

The fourth part follows, in which the Apostle promises future divine assistance to the faithful who are fighting, adding: “But the God of all grace, who called us into his eternal glory in Christ Jesus after we have suffered a little, will himself perfect, confirm, and strengthen us” [Col. 1976B].

He is called the God of all grace because he is the giver of every grace: the grace of beginning, progressing, and perfecting; of confirming and strengthening. And he who called you through his initiating and perfecting grace will likewise, through his grace, perfect you in those things that are lacking in you, confirm you so that you do not fall, and strengthen you in the other life so that you cannot fall.

But he inserts this statement to show for what purpose he called us: namely, to his eternal glory; and through what means he called us: namely, through sufferings.
