This he indicates when he says, “after we have suffered a little.” He says “a little” because temporal sufferings are brief and insignificant in comparison with the future blessedness, in accordance with Paul’s statement: “I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans VIII).

And in whom has he called us? In Christ Jesus. This too can be referred to each individual clause, since they suffered in Christ Jesus, and in Christ Jesus he will perfect, confirm, and strengthen them.

“To him be glory and dominion throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

Glory belongs to him because, just as he is powerful here to give grace, so he is powerful in the future to give us glory. Dominion also belongs to him because, just as here he is powerful by his dominion to restrain the devil and his followers, so in the future he will be powerful by his dominion to condemn them.

Let us therefore, brothers, ask him to grant us perfect humility, hope and trust in him; to grant us sobriety, faith, and watchfulness in prayer, together with the other virtues through which we may be able to overcome the devil and attain everlasting glory. May he himself deign to grant this, the blessed God throughout the ages. Amen.

## HOMILY IX. THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“Tax collectors and sinners were approaching Jesus to hear him” (Luke XV).

This reading, my brothers, is divided into four sections. First, it contains the approach of penitents to Christ; second, the Pharisees’ murmuring on account of it; third, the proof that sinners ought not only to be received but also to be sought; fourth, rejoicing over one converted sinner more than over certain righteous people.

Showing, then, first that repentant sinners approached Jesus, he says: “Tax collectors and sinners were approaching Jesus.” And because they could have approached with a wrong intention, he adds: “to hear the word of God.” It is therefore clear that they approached him not only bodily but also mentally. They approached like sick people to a physician, like the accused to an advocate, like sinners to one who is merciful, like the unclean to a bath, like wandering sheep to a shepherd, and like the blind to one who gives light.

David urges people to approach God in this manner when he says: “Approach him, and be enlightened” (Psalm XXXIII). Following their example, you too, sinners, approach frequently to hear the word of God, because no one can willingly hear God’s word without beginning to dislike evil.

The second part follows, in which it is shown that the scribes and Pharisees murmured against Jesus, as it is added: “And the scribes and Pharisees were murmuring against him” [Col. 1977B].

Murmuring is neither an entirely hidden nor an entirely open reproach, but something midway between rebuke and detraction. The Pharisees, who do not know how to love what is good in another person but rather envy and distort it, could no longer completely conceal the excess of envy they had conceived, yet they did not dare to reveal it openly; instead, they murmured.

But let us, brothers, detesting envy, detraction, and murmuring, learn to love what is good in another, to incline doubtful matters toward the better interpretation, to rebuke a sinner openly, and not secretly to detract from or murmur against him. Detraction and murmuring arise from hidden malice. They do not wish to benefit, but only to harm. No one detracts or murmurs in order to improve another, but rather in order to defame and injure him.

Open rebuke, however, if it is offered kindly, benefits both the one who gives it and the one to whom it is given; and if it does not benefit the recipient, it cannot fail to benefit the one who gives it. Hence the philosopher says: “Rebuke me openly; do not bite me secretly.”

“Look,” they say, “this man receives sinners and eats with them.” They are lying: whoever receives sinners is himself a sinner, just as whoever receives thieves is a thief. To receive a thief or a sinner is to consent to his theft or sin.

To receive sinners, however, with the intention that they may be corrected is not to receive sinners, but brothers. The Apostle commands us to do this when he says: “If an unbelieving woman consents to live with a believing husband, let the believing husband not depart; for the unbelieving woman will be sanctified through the believing husband” (I Corinthians VII).

Therefore, according to the philosopher, “Take into your company the person whom you can make better, or who can make you better.” For the improvement of another among us, the Apostle commands: “Receive the weak brother” (Romans XIV). For our own improvement through others, the poet says:

“Now offer yourself to better men.”  
(HORACE, Epistles I, epistle 2, line 68.)

But if someone persists in being incorrigible, he should not be received; indeed, if he has been received, he should be excluded, lest the many be corrupted by the vice of one. Hence the Apostle says: “Remove the evil person from among you” (I Corinthians V); and elsewhere: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second correction” (Titus XXXIII [citation as printed]).

And the philosopher says: “Associate with yourself such companions that you will not be defamed by their companionship.”

“And he eats with them.” Following the example of our Redeemer, we too may eat with sinners for the purpose of correcting them through the opportunity of a meal, so that while they feed us bodily, we may feed them spiritually.

Because, then, the tax collectors and sinners were being corrected through the word of God, he received them and ate with them. But the Pharisees, distorting even good things, say that he receives them—that is, supports sinners. In this they show that they do not possess true righteousness.

For one who is truly just condemns no one, despises no sinners, but rather sympathizes with them; he does not distort the good deeds of others, but even interprets doubtful things for the better. In contrast, these arrogant righteous men reproach God for his mercy, disdain sinners, and even interpret good things as evil [Col. 1978A].

The third part follows, in which the Lord proves through a twofold parable that repentant sinners ought not only to be received but also to be sought.

Literally, this is a proof from the lesser to the greater. If a man searches with such concern for a lost sheep, or a woman for a lost drachma—temporal, irrational, and perishable things—carries them back on her shoulders when they are found, rejoices, and urges her neighbors to rejoice with her, how much more ought a human being to seek with greater concern for salvation a human being, his brother, who has been lost through sin—a rational being who will live forever—and, after finding him through his own labor, carry him back to the Church, rejoice in his correction, and urge others to rejoice with him?

In this, my brothers, our hardness is exposed—which I cannot mention without grief—for we grieve more over the loss of an ox, a sheep, or our money than over the loss of one or many souls. If a temporal possession is lost, we search for it with great concern, tiring ourselves and others, and we do not stop until we find it. But if a brother’s soul, for which Christ died, perishes through sin, we do not care; indeed, we neglect it, often ridicule it, or even consent to its sin.

Why is this so, except that we do not possess love of neighbor, to which we prefer a sheep or a donkey?

According to the mystical sense, however, the proof proceeds from the greater. Mystically, the man or woman is understood as Christ, the Wisdom of God. The sheep or the drachma, on which the image of the king was inscribed, is understood as the human being made in the image of God.

If Christ, God and Lord of all, loved the fugitive servant, the human being, so greatly that, in order to recover him, he left the ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness—that is, the nine orders of angels in heaven—bodily, sought the human being amid the various errors of the world, carried his sins upon the cross, brought him back to his homeland, and rejoiced in this, inviting the angels to rejoice with himself, not with the sheep—should not a human being love another human being, brother love brother, set aside every business in order to win him, seek his salvation, bear his sins, and bring him back to God; rejoice in his salvation more than in worldly profits; and urge others to rejoice with him [Col. 1978D]?

The fourth part follows, in which the Lord adapts the comparison, saying: “Thus there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of repentance.”

Indeed, my brothers, we are accustomed to rejoice more over the recovery of something lost than over something never lost. It is greater to restore a thing than to preserve it, and more wonderful to rise after a fall than to stand without ever falling.

Here it can also be observed that some people, the more grievously they have fallen, the more fervently they rise again. Because they know that they have committed unlawful things, they also cut themselves off from lawful things; they do more than has even been commanded; they never believe that they have done enough; they completely renounce the world; they strive toward heavenly things with their whole desire; they seek them with sighs and tears; and they readily accept any hardships for their sake.

In contrast, some, because they think they have committed no grave crime, remain lukewarm. They do not burn with desire, sighs, or tears for heavenly things, but live neither cold nor sufficiently hot [Col. 1979B].

There is therefore greater joy for God and his angels over the fervor of one penitent than over the lukewarm righteousness of many righteous people, because a king loves more the soldier who, after fleeing, returns and presses the enemy forcefully than the one who neither fled nor ever fought bravely.

Let us therefore, dearest brothers, avoid the hardness and false righteousness of the Pharisees. Let us sympathize with sinners, the poor, and the afflicted; let us seek the conversion of those who have turned away; let us correct those who wander and call them back to God. Nothing acquires mercy for us more than showing mercy to others.

Let those who have fallen return fervently to their former state, so that by their conversion they may cause grief to the devil and joy to God and his angels. Let those who are righteous never grow lukewarm, but always burn with love and compassion for their neighbor, and strive to carry back with themselves to God the spoils of captivity.

May our Lord Jesus Christ grant this, he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY X. THE FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans VIII), and so forth.

This reading, my brothers, is divided into three parts. First, the Apostle shows that the sufferings of the saints are not worthy of comparison with the greatness of their rewards; second, he says that although they do not wish to be subjected to sufferings, they nevertheless bear them patiently in hope; third, he says that all people groan amid sufferings, including the saints themselves, and therefore desire eternal glory more intensely.

First, then, he says: “I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the glory that is to come, which will be revealed in us.” As though he were saying plainly: Through no temporal sufferings can we merit in a manner worthy of the greatness of the glory that will be bestowed upon us in the future.

For our emperor, dearest brothers, is generous—indeed, he is generosity itself—and he does not wish to make his rewards commensurate with the smallness of our labors. Rather, from the abundance of his riches, he wishes to heap upon us beyond measure.

Our labors are small; our rewards will be immense. Our labors are brief and momentary; our rewards will be eternal. Our labors are earthly; our rewards will be heavenly. Our labors contain little bitterness in themselves; our rewards will contain ineffable sweetness.

As it is written: “Neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him” (Isaiah LXIV; I Corinthians II).

That the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us, he proves when he adds: “For the expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the children of God.”

Here he calls the faithful “creation” because in this life they appear to differ scarcely at all from the other creatures. They are from the earth, dwell on the earth, live from the earth, are changed and corrupted, and die like the other creatures. Hence the end of the human being and of the beast appears to be the same.

According to the state of eternal or future life, however, he calls them “children of God,” because then they will be like God in immortality, purity, glorification, and radiance, in accordance with what John says: “Beloved, we know that we are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. When it appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III).

He therefore says: “The expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the children of God.” As though he were saying: The faithful who are in the misery of this world await another life, so that in it they may be glorified as the children of God. Though they are now so very small, they await so great a thing: that those who are now like beasts may become like God.

His repetition of “expectation” and “awaits” signifies the certainty and desire of those who are waiting.

Here those people are condemned—which I cannot mention without groaning—who place their hope only in this life and do not even suppose that another life exists, saying: “Who has returned from the dead to testify to us that another life exists? Human beings are always born and die; a person passes away like a shadow and smoke and will exist no more.”

Therefore, they say, “while it is permitted, let us spend our days in good things; let us rejoice, feast, indulge ourselves, crown ourselves with roses, dress ourselves in silk, lie in softness, and do whatever our heart desires, since tomorrow we shall die.”

Certainly there are many such people today. Although they do not say this with their mouths, they nevertheless show by their deeds that they believe it. Of them it is truly said: “Because a human being, when he was in honor, did not understand, he was compared with foolish beasts and became like them” (Psalm XLVIII)—indeed, more miserable and worse than they, because it would be better for such people to die completely with the beasts than to live forever in death with demons [Col. 1980D].

The second part follows, in which it is shown that the faithful are subjected unwillingly to miseries, yet bear them patiently in hope, as it is added: “For creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope.”

My brothers, the human being is subject to a twofold vanity: the vanity of sins and the vanity of punishments. The wicked willingly serve the vanity of sins, but they are subjected unwillingly and with murmuring to punishments, which bring benefit by purifying sins. The faithful, however, are unwillingly subject to sins and resist them as far as they can.

As for punishments, although the will of the flesh does not wish them, the will of reason nevertheless endures them patiently because of their usefulness. What teacher is more patient than Christ? Yet, in accordance with the will of the flesh, he showed that he did not wish to suffer when he said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew XXIV; Mark XIV; Luke XXII).

Thus, my brothers, in this life the righteous are subject to vanity: the vanity of persecutions, needs, disturbances, deficiencies, and other punishments. But they endure all these things patiently for the sake of God, who subjects them to such vanities in hope of reward and deliverance.

The Lord also subjected the devil, because of his pride, to the vanity of sins, miseries, and disturbances, but not in hope. Why? Because, although the devil was of a spiritual and stronger nature and had sinned by himself, he did not merit hope of deliverance. The human being, however, being of an earthly and more fragile nature and having been deceived by the tempter, merited hope of being liberated.

From this it is clear that when some beings of a stronger nature sin, and sin more by themselves, they are less excusable.

Let us therefore, brothers, flee subjection to sins and vices. Let us patiently endure subjection to weaknesses, needs, persecutions, and other such things for the sake of God, who has subjected us to them in hope—a hope that will not disappoint.

Hence it also follows: “For creation itself will be liberated from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God,” when, as he himself says elsewhere, “this corruptible body will put on incorruption” (I Corinthians XV).

He does not say “any creation,” but “creation itself”: that which, as far as it can, shakes off vanity and strives toward God with its whole hope and desire. It alone will be liberated from the bondage of corruption, which he earlier called vanity, and will be received into the freedom of the children.

Then it will be liberated from the bondage of sin; from the bondage of punishment—that is, from suffering and dying; and from the bondage of the necessity of eating, clothing itself, sleeping, and such things.

Then, as John says, God will wipe every tear from the eyes of the saints, and death will be no more, neither mourning, nor crying, nor any pain, because the former things have passed away. They will no longer hunger or thirst, and the sun or any heat will not fall upon them (Revelation XXI).

The third part follows, in which it is shown that all people groan amid the miseries of this life, including the saints themselves, as it is added: “For we know that every creature groans and labors in childbirth until now.”

Every human being, brothers—both good and evil—groans amid the tribulations and miseries of this world, whether he wishes to or not; but only the good person labors in childbirth. To labor in childbirth is to labor in order to bring forth fruit.

The wicked therefore groan in this life but do not labor in childbirth, because their groaning and labor—being directed toward temporal things—will not have eternal fruit. The good person, however, both groans and labors in childbirth here, because his groaning and labor are not fruitless; rather, he will obtain the fruit of eternity.

The Lord shows this in the Gospel by comparison, saying: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow. But when she has given birth to the child, she no longer remembers her anguish, because a human being has been born into the world. So you also now have sorrow, but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John XVI).

“Groans and labors in childbirth until now,” he says—that is, from the beginning of the world until now and until the end, from Abel to the last righteous person.

“And not only that,” he says, “but we ourselves also, who have the first fruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly, awaiting the adoption of the glory of the children of God, the redemption of our body.”

As though he were saying: Not only do the lesser faithful groan amid the miseries of this world, but we apostles ourselves also, who first and more abundantly received spiritual gifts, although we are comforted, nevertheless groan inwardly as we consider the miseries in which we are now placed and await the adoption of the glory of the children of God.

He also adds “the redemption of our body,” showing that not only souls will be glorified in the other life, as certain heretics have imagined, but that our very bodies will also be redeemed from every corruption and enriched with eternal glory.

From the two things set forth here—the consideration of present misery and of future glory—arises in us compunction, that is, compunction born of desire for the heavenly homeland.

From two other things—the consideration of our sins and the consideration of the eternal punishments owed for them—arises in us penitential compunction.

Let us therefore, sinners, always keep before our eyes the shamefulness of our sins and the bitterness of the eternal fire owed to them, so that we may always repent and always groan and weep over our sins [Col. 1982C].

Let us also consider together the misery in which we now are and the eternal blessedness of heavenly joys, so that we may groan and weep out of desire for that blessedness and hasten toward it with our whole desire.

Now let us sow in tears what we may afterward reap with rejoicing, so that we may deserve to be numbered among those of whom the Psalmist says:

“Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds. But coming, they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Psalm CXXV).

By the bounty of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XI. THE FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“Jesus said to his disciples: Be merciful, just as your heavenly Father is merciful” (Luke VI) [Col. 1982D].

In this reading from the holy Gospel, dearest brothers, the Lord intends to instruct us to show mercy always, as much as we are able and know how.

First, therefore, he urges us to be merciful after the example of our heavenly Father. Second, he demonstrates how much mercy merits. Third, he shows that an ignorant or vicious person ought not to presume to teach.

First, exhorting us to mercy, he says: “Be merciful, just as your heavenly Father is merciful.” Elsewhere also he says: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus XIX).

These words clearly demonstrate that the Lord wishes us to be his imitators; he wishes us to act as children of our Father. Otherwise he does not count us among his children, but among rejected servants.

So, it is said, the eagle acts: it exposes its young to the rays of the sun, and it loves as its own the chick that, following the example of its father, looks upon the sun’s ray with unwavering gaze. But the one that does not do this it casts away as degenerate.

The raven likewise despises its young as unlike itself before it sees them becoming black. After it sees them black, it loves them as like itself.

A human being also loves the son whom he sees serving and obeying him, but hates the disobedient son.

Let us therefore, my brothers, imitate God and conform ourselves to him, so that we may deserve to be children of God. Let us be holy according to our measure, just as he is holy. Let us be righteous, just as he is righteous. Let us be merciful, just as he is merciful.

He is merciful to such an extent that he has left no creature without experiencing his mercy. “He gives food to the animals and to the young ravens that call upon him” (Psalm CXLVI).

He gives not only to his worshipers and friends but also to those who despise and oppose him; for “he makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust” (Matthew V).

Let us too, brothers, imitate his kindness insofar as we can. Let us give not only to those we know but also to those we do not know; not only to friends but also to enemies. Let us help one person materially, another by our word, another by advice, another by correction, another by admonition, and another by consolation. Let all feel our good example and our kindness, so that the name of God may thus be sanctified in us and we may be children by imitation of our Father who is in heaven.

Second, the Lord shows how much mercy merits. He sets forth four kinds of mercy, attaching to each its reward.

He sets forth the first when he adds: “Do not judge”—concerning doubtful matters or lesser faults. We are permitted to judge concerning manifest evils and manifest goods. Of these it is said: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matthew VII).

But we are forbidden to judge concerning doubtful matters and lesser faults, because we do not know with what intention they are done, and because they can be done by both good and evil people. Such matters include eating and drinking, speaking with a woman, eating with an evil person, and similar things, which we ought to interpret in the better sense.

If, for example, we see a priest speaking with a woman, we should say that he is giving her counsel concerning her soul, or something of that kind. Lesser faults too—such as occasionally breaking a fast, sometimes eating or drinking too much, or frequently associating with evil people—we ought to excuse on the grounds of dispensation, illness, or charity.

For just as it is characteristic of a malicious mind to distort even good things, so it is characteristic of a benevolent mind to incline even bad things toward the better interpretation.

He gives the reward of this mercy when he adds: “And you will not be judged”—understood, concerning rash judgment. Those who judge rashly here will be judged by the Lord for their rash judgment.

He sets forth the second kind of mercy when he adds: “Do not condemn,” even those who are openly evil; rather, await and pray for their conversion, because the person who is evil today may perhaps be good tomorrow or the day after.

It would be the height of folly to have condemned Mary Magdalene while she was still foolish, or Paul while he was still a persecutor—both of whom afterward shone before God with such great merits [Col. 1984A].

He gives the reward of this mercy when he adds: “And you will not be condemned,” namely, for foolish condemnation. Those who now rashly condemn sinners will be condemned by the Lord for their rash condemnation.

For these two kinds of mercy, Saint Martin is praised when it is said of him: “Judging no one, condemning no one.”

Hence Paul says: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master” (Romans XIV).

And the philosopher says: “See whether you are still evil, and spare those like yourself. But if you have ceased to be evil, why do you cut off from others the opportunity for amendment?”

In this, brothers, our presumption is exposed: we judge the sins of others. By one judgment we spare our own sins and condemn those of others; by another, we justify ourselves in our hearts. We judge ourselves by one standard and our neighbors by another, although it is written: “One weight and another weight, one measure and another measure—both are an abomination before God” (Proverbs XX).

He sets forth the third kind of mercy when he adds: “Forgive.” For it is a great almsgiving to forgive injuries to the one who inflicts them, to free a slave from servile condition, or to remit a debt owed by a poor debtor.

He gives the reward of this mercy when he adds: “And you will be forgiven.” Through this almsgiving our sins are forgiven us by the Lord.

Hence in the Lord’s Prayer we say: “Forgive us our debts, just as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew VI). In this condition we bind ourselves: if we do not forgive, neither will we be forgiven. Indeed, through the parable of the servant who was forgiven but refused to forgive, it is shown that the sins which seemed to have been forgiven return [Col. 1984C].

Therefore, brothers, let us lay aside hardness of heart. And if we wish God to forgive us, let us forgive others.

He gives a fourth form when he adds: “Give alms,” whether bodily—for example, food to the hungry, clothing to the naked, lodging to the stranger—or spiritual, such as correction, instruction, exhortation, and consolation, or practical assistance: help in adversity, counsel in danger, support in legal cases. He states the reward of this mercy when he adds: “And it will be given to you.” Here, grace; in the future, glory.

To show how generously the alms we give are to be rewarded by God, he adds: “A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing, they will pour into your lap” [Col. 1984D]. He calls eternal blessedness a measure because it will be measured out to each according to his merits. It will be good, for it will give us the supreme and eternal Good to enjoy. It will be pressed down, containing no emptiness or vanity, unlike earthly goods, which are empty, vain, and imperfect. It will be shaken together, that is, containing within itself all the goods necessary for us, since earthly things can satisfy no need completely. It will be overflowing in quality, quantity, and duration. In place of vain goods, it will give truly good things; in place of empty things, fullness; in place of insufficiency, sufficiency; in place of small things, greatness; in place of things that perish, eternal things.

Who will give these things? The poor, because they will be the reason for their being given. This is what is said elsewhere: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal dwellings” (Luke XVI) [Col. 1985A]. Why, then, brothers, are we hard-hearted about distributing these earthly goods to the poor, who are promised to us as the ones who will reward us with eternal goods?

“For with the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you.” By this he does not represent a strict proportion between rewards and merits, especially since elsewhere he says that the righteous will receive a hundredfold (Matt. XIX). Rather, it is to be understood in this way: whoever gives more will receive more, and whoever gives less, less, according to Paul’s statement: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows in blessings will also reap in blessings” (II Cor. IX).

Third, by means of a comparison he shows that one who is ignorant ought not to assume the office of teacher, adding: “If the blind lead the blind, will not both fall into a pit?” The blind leads the blind when an ignorant person presumes to govern another ignorant person. This is directed against those who, while not yet disciples, become teachers—those who do not know how to govern their own souls but presume to govern the souls of others [Col. 1985B].

But just as a blind man leading a blind man falls more heavily, falling upon another as well as himself, than he would if he fell alone, so an ignorant person who governs another ignorant person falls more heavily than if he had presumed to govern no one, because he falls on account of the souls he drags with him to destruction, and beneath the souls he drags with him.

That an ignorant teacher is to be punished more severely than an ignorant disciple, he shows when he adds: “A disciple is not above his teacher.” This is litotes: just as he is lower in rank, so he is lower in reward if he is good, and lower in punishment if he is evil. And why is this so? It follows: “But everyone will be perfect if he is like his teacher.” For the simple disciple imitates the teacher, thinking that he will be perfect if he can become his equal.

Thus nothing harms the peoples of the Church more than the perversity of their teachers [Col. 1985C]. For whatever they see their teacher doing, they wish to do, saying: “Am I better than my priest? ‘A disciple is not above his teacher.’”

Again, by means of a comparison he shows that a vicious person ought not to assume authority, when he adds: “Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not consider the beam that is in your own eye?” It is as though he said: How do you presume to rebuke others for a lesser fault when you yourself suffer from a greater one? How do you dare to rebuke your brother’s anger, which is like a speck in the eye of the mind, when you do not rebuke hatred, which is like a beam in your own mind?

“Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.” It is as though he said: First correct yourself if you wish to correct others; first cleanse yourself if you wish to cleanse others. For the hand that wishes to cleanse another must itself be clean, lest, if it is unclean, it pollute what it touches even more [Col. 1985D].

For this reason the Lord said of the woman caught in adultery: “Let him who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her” (John VIII). It is as though he said: Adulterers ought indeed to be judged, but by the chaste; the malicious ought to be condemned, but by the innocent; the guilty ought to be corrected, but by the just.

Therefore, brothers, if we wish to rebuke someone, let us first see whether we are like him. If we are, let us groan together with him, and let us admonish him not to obey us, but to be corrected together with us. If we are not like him, yet once were like him or could have become so, let us show him compassion; and let us rebuke him not out of hatred but [Col. 1986A] out of mercy. Rebukes should be administered rarely and only when great necessity requires it, with regard for God and with the beam removed from one’s own eye.

Therefore, my brothers, let us devote ourselves to works of mercy and avoid judging and condemning others. Let us forgive, so that we may be forgiven; let us give, so that it may be given to us; so that we may deserve to receive a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing—that is, eternal blessedness. May he grant this to us who is God, blessed above all things. Amen.

## HOMILY XII. THE FIFTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“Be all united in prayer, compassionate, lovers of the brotherhood, merciful, modest, humble, and so forth” (I Peter III).

This reading, my brothers, is divided into four parts [Col. 1986B]. First, the Apostle exhorts us to the six virtues that he enumerates. Second, he exhorts us to a better recompense. Third, he shows that no one can harm those who are zealous for the good. Fourth, he admonishes us to sanctify God within us.

First, then, he exhorts us to six virtues, saying: “Be all united in prayer.” Now some people cannot be united unless they are good and friends. The wicked cannot be united, because they serve opposing vices. How could a miser and a spendthrift be united? How could a cruel person and a negligent person be united? How could an impetuous person and a fearful person be united? But the good, because they cultivate virtues—which are never opposed but always harmonious and mutually uniting—can be united if they love one another affectionately.

All good people, in desiring common goods, are of one will. But concerning another person’s particular goods, one may sometimes grow cold. When, however, good people love one another so deeply that each desires the other’s goods as his own, they are undoubtedly united. “The multitude of believers,” he says, “had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV). They had one heart because they desired the same goods, and one soul because each loved the other as his own soul.

The Apostle therefore exhorts us to be united, especially in prayer—that is, in desiring and requesting what is good. For one prayer offered by a great number of the faithful cannot be ineffective if they are united in heart. Let us therefore, my brothers, be united in prayer not only with all the other faithful but also each person within himself [Col. 1986C].

For just as someone who asks wrongly and thereby disagrees with the unity of the Church is unworthy of being heard, so is the person who, through a reprehensible life, is at odds with the good he requested in prayer.

And because unity is especially recognized through compassion, the Apostle next exhorts us to be compassionate toward those who suffer—not falsely, as flatterers do, but with genuine affection of mind, making the sufferings and losses of our brothers our own, as Paul did when he said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (I Cor. X).

Through compassion let us show that we are truly members of Christ and of the Church. Just as, when one member of the human body suffers, the other members suffer with it, so let us suffer with the afflictions of our neighbors [Col. 1987A].

Nor, when we see our neighbors afflicted, should we despise them as inferior and miserable, as some do. Although they give much to the poor, they do so more from the compulsion of a command than from love of brotherhood. For this reason the Apostle adds: “Lovers of the brotherhood,” so that we may not proudly exalt ourselves above them, but rather descend to their level and regard them as our equals and brothers.

We should also be lovers of the brotherhood toward those who do not appear to need our assistance, sharing our possessions with them, offering them the services of charity, and loving them as brothers of Christ. Let us not belong to those who live only for themselves, showing familiarity to no one and the service of charity to no one, and who, as though other human beings did not exist, are bound by no affection to anyone [Col. 1987B].

The Apostle calls such lukewarm people “without affection, without covenant, without mercy” (Rom. I). Even brute animals condemn such people, for they customarily love animals of their own kind with a sort of brotherhood. A horse waits for its companion who is following; it more willingly follows the one going ahead; it longs for the absent one and neighs. What, then, ought a rational creature to do?

And because some people show compassion and brotherhood toward certain persons but are merciless toward those who have harmed them, he adds: “Merciful”—that is, merciful in forgiving injuries inflicted upon us. For the Lord binds us by this condition: if we wish to be forgiven, we must forgive. Otherwise, nothing will be forgiven us by God. Hence, in the Lord’s Prayer, the Lord commands us to ask under this condition, in these words: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI; Mark II) [Col. 1987C].

Then he continues, saying: “If you do not forgive your brothers’ sins from your hearts, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you” (ibid.). If, therefore, my brothers, we wish to find the supreme Judge merciful toward us, let us ourselves be merciful toward those who have harmed us. “For judgment without mercy will be shown to the one who has not shown mercy” (James II).

And because some people are excessively merciful toward subjects who sin, he adds: “Modest.” Modesty, my brothers, is the balance, seasoning, and temperance of the other virtues; without it they are not virtues but vices [Col. 1987D]. Modesty tempers mercy, preventing it from falling either into laxity or into harshness. It also tempers wisdom, preventing it from falling either into excessive cleverness or into dullness; it tempers courage, preventing it from falling either into boldness or into cowardice; it tempers justice, preventing it from falling either into credulity or into negligence; and it tempers generosity, preventing it from falling either into extravagance or into greed.

Let us therefore love modesty, my brothers, so that through it we may choose and hold fast to the virtue that lies between opposing vices.

And because, once the other vices have been driven away, pride finally attacks us, this passage at the end admonishes us to humility, when it adds: “Humble.” Humility is indeed the guardian of the virtues. Whoever gathers the other virtues without humility is like someone carrying dust into the wind [Col. 1988A].

For many people, having trampled down vices and acquired virtues, have found this an occasion for pride; and because they boast that they have conquered the vices, they are themselves conquered. This is well signified by Eleazar, who fell beneath the elephant he had killed. For the person who is lifted up by victory over the vices is struck down, as it were, beneath the enemy he has overthrown.

Therefore, my brothers, let us acknowledge our own weakness. We can do nothing good from ourselves, but only sins. If we possess anything good, let us attribute it not to ourselves but to God. Let us never trust in our own strength or merits, but only in God’s mercy. While we are on the slippery road of this age, let us always be afraid and remember how many great men have fallen before us.

The second part follows, in which the Apostle exhorts us to a better recompense, saying: “Not returning evil for evil, nor abuse for abuse, but, on the contrary, blessing” [Col. 1988B].

There are four kinds of recompense: returning evil for good; returning good for evil; returning evil for evil; and returning good for good. The first belongs to the devil and his members; the second to Christ and his members; the third to those who are moderately wicked; the fourth to those who are moderately good.

The Lord shows in the Gospel that it is not enough for us to return good for good unless we also return good for evil, saying: “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the pagans do this? But love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. LIII).

The Apostle says the same here, and proves that this is how we must act by adding [Col. 1988C]: “For you were called to this, so that you may possess a blessing as your inheritance.” It is as though he said plainly: Do not curse, but rather bless, because you have been called to eternal blessing. For no good harvest comes from bad seed, nor will a good reward be gathered from an evil merit. “Whatever a man sows,” as Paul says, “that he will also reap” (Gal. VI).

If, therefore, my brothers, we wish to attain eternal blessing, let us never curse but always bless. If we wish to attain eternal goods, let us never do evil but always do good. It is written of the reprobate: “He loved cursing, and it will come upon him; he did not desire blessing, and it will be far from him” (Ps. CVIII).

The Psalmist proves the same by his authority, saying: “Whoever desires to love life and to see good days”—that is, whoever loves and wishes to see eternal life—“let him restrain his tongue from evil,” namely, from thinking evil, “and his lips from speaking deceit” (Ps. XXXIII). “Let him turn away from evil,” understanding this as referring to action: let him neither think, speak, nor do evil. And because this is not enough, he adds: “And let him do good.” Living in this way, let him seek eternal peace.

And because that supreme peace cannot be possessed here, let him pursue it by maintaining peace with himself, peace with his neighbor, and, insofar as it lies within him, peace even with his enemy. In this way he will be able to attain everlasting peace, because “the eyes”—that is, the Lord’s merciful regard—“are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to hear their prayers” [Note: [Col. 1987D] The Vulgate does not have “to hear.”]. “But the face of the Lord’s anger is against those who do evil” [Note: [Col. 1988D] The Vulgate omits “of anger.”] (ibid.).

The third part follows, in which the Apostle shows that no one can harm those who are zealous for the good [Col. 1989A]. Those are zealous for the good who never imitate evil but always imitate good; who examine more carefully the lives of the good who are living, read the lives of those who have died, and imitate and strive to reproduce whatever they find best in them. This is most useful for those who are striving toward perfection. Hence we read of Saint Antony that, associating with earnest men, he imitated the lives of them all.

For this reason the Apostle says: “Be zealous for the better gifts” (I Cor. XII). He therefore says of such people: “Who is there who can harm you if you are zealous for the good?” It is as though he said: No one, because God does not wish this; indeed, he loves and protects such people.

Neither the devil nor any human being can harm them. Rather, even when either thinks he is harming them, he benefits them, because by persecuting, harassing, and even killing them, he makes them more glorious [Col. 1989B]. Thus the devil did so to Job, Decius to Laurence, and Decianus to Vincent: while each thinks to extinguish them, he makes them glorious.

For this reason David speaks to the Lord about the devil, saying: “This dragon whom you formed to sport with him” (Ps. CIII). The devil is truly mocked in this: when he intends to harm the elect, he harms himself and assists them.

Hence it follows: “But even if you suffer for the sake of righteousness, you are blessed.” Why? Because, as the Lord testifies: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). “Do not fear their fear,” he says, “and do not be troubled” (Matt. X).

Excessive fear commonly so disturbs the reason of some people that, stupefied and confused, they do not perceive what they ought to do [Col. 1989C]. But we, my brothers, should fear not any creature but God in his creatures. Let us fear him, I say, with love, and love him with affection—for this fear does not bring tribulation but rather counsel and consolation.

The fourth part follows, in which the Apostle admonishes us to sanctify our Lord Jesus Christ in our hearts.

How do we sanctify Christ in our hearts? By striving to sanctify our hearts in him. This is accomplished if we earnestly imitate his life and conduct and follow his teaching. Let us be pure, according to our measure, as he is pure; merciful as he is merciful; just as he is just; holy as he is holy [Col. 1989D], so that at last we may deserve to be where he is.

May he himself deign to grant this—he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XIII. THE FIFTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“When the crowds were pressing upon Jesus to hear the word of God, he was standing beside the lake of Gennesaret” (Luke V).

This reading, my brothers, is divided into five chapters. First, we are taught with what eagerness we ought to hasten to hear the word of God. Second, through the failure of the fishing, the frequent failure of preaching is signified. Third, the preacher is instructed by the Lord’s example. Fourth, through the catch of fish, it is signified that Peter and his companions would become fishers of souls [Col. 1990A]. Fifth, the Lord consoles Peter in his astonishment and promises him the office of preaching.

First, then, we are taught here, brothers, with what eagerness we ought to hasten to the word of God, when it is said: “When the crowds were pressing upon Jesus to hear the word of God.” For what else is it to press upon someone than to run with desire? With great desire, therefore, and great eagerness, those who pressed upon Jesus ran to hear the word of God.

This is especially shown by the fact, my brothers, that neither need nor time nor place could hold them back from following him. Hunger came upon them when they had already remained with him for three days, and yet they followed him. Night came, and yet they followed him. The narrowness of the place came, and yet they followed him, so much so that, because of the crowd pressing upon him, he was compelled to board a boat and go out onto the sea [Col. 1990B].

In this, my brothers—which I cannot say without groaning—our lukewarmness and slowness are put to shame. We scarcely gather to hear the word of God; when gathered, we scarcely listen; and when listening, we scarcely carry anything from it into practice.

Where, my brothers, is that hunger of which the prophet—or rather, God through the prophet—says: “I will send a famine upon the land, not a famine of bread or of water, but a famine of hearing the word of God” (Amos VIII)? Where is that sweetness of the divine word which, once tasted, makes the Prophet exclaim: “How sweet are your utterances to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth!” (Ps. CXVIII)?

The second part follows, in which the failure of preaching is signified through the failure of the fishing, when he adds: “And he saw two boats standing beside the lake” [Col. 1990C]. The Lord sees, in his mercy, two boats—that is, the churches of circumcision and of the uncircumcised—still empty of good fish.

And why were they empty? The fishermen had labored all night and had caught nothing, and therefore they were going down and washing their nets. What then happened to them in the fishing often happens in preaching. Fishermen—that is, preachers—often labor in preaching, and yet they catch no one with the sweetness of the word and win no one for God.

Why? Because they labor through the night and not in the word of Jesus. Two obstacles are understood to prevent preaching from catching its hearers: either the hearers are unworthy of benefiting, or the preacher is unworthy of producing benefit.

When the hearers are unworthy, the preacher labors through the night in vain, because, when the Sun of righteousness is absent, no one can be enlightened by a human being. Unless there is someone within who teaches, the teacher’s tongue labors in vain [Col. 1990D].

When, however, the preacher is unworthy of benefiting either himself or others, he often labors in vain because he does not preach in the word of Jesus—that is, in the word of salvation—but in the word of display: he does not preach in order to benefit but in order to appear impressive; he presumes upon his own eloquence rather than upon Christ’s grace; and, further, he does not preach in the word—that is, according to the commandment—of God.

For God keeps the unworthy away from preaching, saying: “Why do you declare my justifications and take up my covenant in your mouth?” (Ps. XIX).

Therefore, my brothers, when preaching does not take hold in you, you must weep, lest perhaps by God’s hidden judgment you have been rejected from grace. We preachers, too, must weep, lest perhaps we are unworthy to benefit either ourselves or you [Col. 1991A]. Then, according to what we read here, we ought to go down—that is, humble ourselves—and wash the nets: by reviewing our preaching, we should wash away with tears whatever we have exceeded through empty glory, through excessively harsh reproof, through excessive gentleness, or through ignorance.

The third part follows, in which the preacher is instructed by the Lord’s example, when he adds: “But getting into one of the boats, which was Simon’s, he asked him to put out a little from the land. And sitting down, he taught the crowds from the boat.”

Here the Lord instructs the preacher by his own example in five respects, showing namely what position the preacher ought to occupy, what he ought to preach, what he ought to request, how he ought to live, and from where he ought to teach.

What position he ought to occupy is shown when it says: “Getting into the boat.” The preacher ought to ascend, so that he may be elevated in rank, knowledge, and life. Hence the prophet says: “Ascend upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion” (Isa. XL).

What he ought to hold and preach is shown when it says: “Into one boat, which was Simon’s.” The boat into which he ascended is called both one and Simon’s—that is, belonging to the obedient—so that he may understand that he ought especially to hold and preach unity and obedience: the unity of the Church and obedience to the commandments [Col. 1991B].

What he ought to request is shown when it adds: “He asked him to put the boat out a little from the land.” The preacher ought to ask Simon—that is, Christ, who was obedient to the Father even unto death—to move the Church a little from land into the sea [Col. 1991C], so that it may be in such a condition that it has neither excessive repose and security amid earthly prosperity nor excessive anxiety and fear amid adversity. Thus it will not grow sluggish and fall apart through excessive security and repose, nor be disturbed and shattered through excessive fear and anxiety.

How he ought to live is shown when it adds: “And sitting.” For sitting is the posture of teachers. Sitting, he rests in the lower part and is raised up in the higher part. In the preacher likewise, the lower part of the inner person—that is, the senses—ought to rest from concern for temporal things, while the higher part, namely reason, ought through contemplation to be raised toward heaven.

From where he ought to preach is shown when it says: “He taught the crowds from the boat” [Col. 1991D]. Whether the preacher speaks to those outside or to those within, he must always teach from the boat. He himself must always be in the boat, not merely in number but also in merit and doctrine.

The fourth part follows, in which, through the catch of fish, it is signified that Peter and his companions would become fishers of souls, when Jesus says to Simon: “Put out into the deep, and lower your nets for a catch.”

To Peter alone, because he was to become the leader of the word, he says: “Put out into the deep”—that is, into the depths of worldly people. To him and to the others, because they were all to become preachers, he says: “Lower your nets for a catch.”

If nets are stretched rigidly, the fish spring away and are not caught. Nets stretched more loosely, however, can enclose and retain the fish. The disciples are therefore commanded to loosen the nets of preaching, so that they do not drive sinners away through excessive rigor and harshness but rather retain them through leniency and forgiveness [Col. 1992A].

For this reason a more relaxed way of life is first permitted to novices and beginners. But Peter, having learned by experience that he himself could draw no one to God, now presumes nothing from himself but everything from the word of God, saying: “Master, we have labored all night and caught nothing. But at your word I will lower the net.”

And when they had done this, they enclosed a great multitude of fish. See, my brothers, what it means to do everything by the word of God and to presume nothing from oneself. The one who by his command drew the fish to Peter’s net is himself the only one who, through his mercy, draws and catches sinners in the net of preaching. Hence the Lord says: “No one can come to me unless my Father draws him” (John VI) [Col. 1992B].

“But the net was breaking. And they beckoned to their companions who were in the other boat to come and help them. And they came and filled both boats, so that they were almost sinking.”

The net of preaching is broken when the unity of the Church is torn apart by heresies and schisms because of an excessive multitude. Yet no fish falls away, because none of the elect perishes.

Since the Church of the Jews was not sufficient, the Church of the Gentiles is filled in equal measure with the elect. Both boats are so filled with peoples that they are almost submerged amid the storms of this tumultuous world; yet they are not submerged, because the Lord governs them [Col. 1992C]. The multitude of evil people that grows within the Church beyond measure almost drags the righteous with it into perdition, unless the Lord extends to them the hand of his support.

The fifth part follows, in which the Lord consoles Peter in his astonishment and promises him the office of preaching.

Peter, astonished at the miracle of the fish, fell at Jesus’ knees, saying: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man.” Peter speaks imprudently: while acknowledging himself to be a sinner, he excludes from himself the source of forgiveness. It is as though a sick man were to say to a physician: “Withdraw from me, doctor, because I am ill.”

On the contrary, if you are ill, do not separate the physician from yourself. If you are a sinner, do not drive away from yourself God, the physician of sinners. There are still people today who resemble Peter in this illness. When they consider themselves sinners, they tremble to undertake the way of life, yet they do not fear lying in the idleness of their own torpor; and, as though they had no counsel amid their confusion, they die while fearing life. Such people are foolish and timid [Col. 1992D].

True humility, although it distrusts itself, nevertheless trusts that it can do all things in God.

But the Lord, consoling Peter in his astonishment, said: “Do not be afraid”—that is, do not fear my companionship, because it will not burden you but lift you up; it will not harm you but help you.

“From now on,” he says, “you will be catching human beings.” It is as though he said: From a fisherman you will become a preacher; in place of a boat, you will govern the Church; in place of a net, you will have preaching; in place of fish, you will catch human beings.

Peter and his companions, drawn by the miracle, drawn by the promise, and drawn by inward inspiration, immediately follow the Lord. For it follows: “And when they had brought the boats to land, they followed him.”

Following the Lord into preaching, they renounce everything, because the office of preaching is not rightly undertaken unless love of temporal things is abandoned [Col. 1993A].

Therefore, my brothers, although we are sinners and although we are weak, we ought not to shrink from the burden of the divine commandments. Rather, with hope in divine assistance, we should begin courageously, knowing that God gives both the ability and the accomplishment. As he made a king from a shepherd, a preacher from a fisherman, and a shepherd from a persecutor, so may he make us strong from the weak, obedient from the disobedient, and lovers of himself from those who despise him, so that from this we may bless him forever. Amen.

## HOMILY XIV. THE SIXTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“Whoever among us has been baptized into Christ Jesus has been baptized into his death” (Rom. VI).

In this reading, my brothers, the Apostle shows that we Christians [Col. 1993B], who have been baptized into Christ Jesus, ought, as we promised in baptism, to preserve purity and newness of life.

He does three things. First, he shows that those who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death. Second, he shows the purpose and benefit of this. Third, he explains what he had stated obscurely.

First, then, he says: “Whoever among us has been baptized.” But because there are baptisms of Jews, Gentiles, and heretics, which do not cleanse inwardly, he adds: “Into Christ Jesus”—that is, in the power of Jesus Christ, who alone possesses the authority to baptize.

Hence it was said to John through the Holy Spirit: “Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes” (John I). Others possess not the authority but only the ministry of baptizing.

Thus baptism is not imparted better by a good minister or worse by a worse one, because it is not they but God who baptizes: they pour the water, but God cleanses [Col. 1993C].

Moreover, when the Apostle says: “We have been baptized into Christ Jesus,” he does not intend to demonstrate the form of baptism, which the Lord promulgated in the Gospel in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Some, however, say that it can be performed in the name of Christ, because in Christ—that is, in the Anointed One—the Father who anoints and the anointing, namely the Holy Spirit, are understood.

“Into his death,” he says, “we have been baptized.”

We are said to be baptized into Christ’s death in three ways. First, into death understood as faith in his death, because without faith in Christ’s death baptism profits nothing. Just as the Israelites were not freed from the fiery serpents unless they looked upon the bronze serpent raised up on a pole [Col. 1993D], so neither are we freed from sins or from the devil unless in faith and hope we look upon the crucified one.

Or we are baptized into death understood as the efficacy of Christ’s death. For baptism received all its efficacy from Christ’s death. Unless Christ had died, the guilt of original sin would not have been washed away by the blood and water that flowed from his side, nor would the flaming sword have been removed from the entrance to paradise.

Or certainly we have been baptized into Christ’s death, that is, into the likeness of Christ’s death. Hence he adds: “For we have been buried with Christ through baptism into death.”

The Apostle assigns a likeness between our baptism and Christ’s death. Just as Christ was buried through death so that he would no longer live a carnal and worldly life but rather a spiritual and heavenly one, so through baptism we die and are buried to sin, so that thereafter we may no longer live a carnal and worldly life but rather a spiritual and heavenly one [Col. 1994A].

This is well signified by the fact that the person who is baptized is first stretched out in the manner of Christ hanging upon the cross. Then his hands and feet are, as it were, crucified when he confesses that he renounces the works and pomps of the devil. Afterward he dies wholly to sin and is, as it were, buried when, in imitation of Christ’s three-day burial, he is immersed three times in the font.

Thus, my brothers, when we are baptized, we are, as it were, buried with Christ into death—that is, in the likeness of his death—provided, my brothers, that we keep the baptismal covenant; provided that we have died to sin [Col. 1994B] and do not return to the works and pomps of the devil.

“For what benefit is there in the washing of one who has cleansed himself after contact with a dead person and then touches that person again?” (Eccles. XXXIV).

The second part follows, in which the benefit for which we are baptized is shown, when he adds: “So that, just as Christ rose from the dead to the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life.” For this benefit we are baptized into Christ’s death: so that, just as Christ rose from the dead and lives forever with the Father in a new and glorious life, so we too may rise through baptism from the death of sins and henceforth live for the glory of God in a new and glorious life of virtues. This is aptly signified by the fact that, after the child rises from the font—as from a tomb—he is clothed in a new white garment and illuminated by a burning candle.

And that this is conferred upon us through baptism, the Apostle proves by adding: “For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be in that of his resurrection.” It is as though he said: If we are like him in death, we shall be like him in resurrection; if we are like him in labor, we shall be like him in glorification. Therefore, my brothers, let us imitate, insofar as we can, the Lord’s labor and passion. Even if there is no one to crucify or kill us, at least let us crucify ourselves through fasting, labor, and abstinence; let us mortify our body together with its vices and desires. Let us kill vices and sins within us, so that we may deserve to rise—here in the soul to new life, and in the future, in soul and body together, to glory.

Moreover, he says beautifully: “Planted together in the likeness of his death.” For Christ, in his death and burial, was planted, as it were, in the likeness of a grain which, buried and dead in the earth, rises again, grows, and is renewed for the better. So also our Lord Jesus Christ was, as it were, planted in his death and burial; and from the very place where he seemed to perish, he was increased and renewed all the more. Hence, comparing himself to a grain of wheat, he says: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John XII). And elsewhere: “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed which, although it is the smallest among all seeds, when hidden in the earth grows into a great tree, so that the birds of the air rest in its branches” (Matthew XIII; Mark IV; Luke XIII).

Thus, my brothers, Christ, who was previously regarded as insignificant, “the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Psalm XXI), dead and buried, rose again as if planted; and his name grew throughout the whole world, so that spiritual men rest in his virtues and teachings. So also the holy martyrs, who in this world were considered worthless and almost refuse and scum, were planted, as it were, in passion and death, and were renewed for the better. Their name grew far and wide through their virtues and miracles, so that spiritual men also dwell, by imitation, in their conduct and virtues.

So too, my brothers, let us love being worthless, poor, and despised in this world for God’s sake, so that, planted as it were through baptism and repentance, mortifications and sufferings, we may rise, be renewed, and bear fruit, both here and in the future, so that lovers of heaven may delight even in the examples of our virtues.

The third part follows, in which he explains what the Apostle had said obscurely, saying: “Knowing that our old man was crucified together with Christ, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, so that we might no longer serve sin.” Our old man is called the antiquity of our man, that is, the desire and rebellion of the flesh. This antiquity is called old either because it has grown old within us from our ancient father Adam, or because it resembles old age. Old age does three things: it bends the body, dulls the senses, and draws one toward death. So too that original desire bends the soul away from its uprightness, dulls reason and the other powers of the soul, and draws the soul itself toward death.

This desire ought to be crucified within us, through the example and power of the Crucified One, by baptism and the mortification of the flesh. How? “So that the body of sin might be destroyed.” He does not simply say, “so that the body might be destroyed,” since the body is not to be broken but governed, so that nature may be sustained through moderation and vice destroyed. Therefore those sin equally who destroy the body through excessive mortification and those who nourish it in vices through excessive luxury. For we owe the body, as to a beast of burden serving the spirit, three things: food, the rod, and a burden—food for sustenance, the rod for correction, and the burden of divine service.

Thus, my brothers, let us feed our body so that it does not become unruly, and let us chastise it so that it does not fail. Therefore he says not that the body itself should be destroyed, but “that the body of sin”—that is, sin—“might be destroyed.” Explaining this, he adds: “So that we might no longer serve sin.” He does not say, however, “so that we may not sin,” since, as John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John I). Because man, although he could resist sin, was unwilling to do so, it was imposed upon him that, when he wishes to resist, he is unable. Hence the Apostle says: “I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive” (Romans VII), and so forth.

For this reason he says not “so that we may not sin,” but “so that we may not serve sin,” since the first movements of desire are not in our power; but if we resist them immediately, we do not serve sin. Whoever, although moved by the first movement of desire, immediately restrains it so that it does not descend either to pleasure or to consent, may safely say with the Apostle: “If I do what I do not wish, it is not I who sin [Note: [Col. 1995D] Vulgate: “It is not I who do it.”], but sin that dwells in me” (Romans VII). Therefore, my brothers, whenever we are moved to desire, let us immediately restrain that movement, strike our breast, and invoke divine assistance.

It follows: “For if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with Christ.” Some die in Christ, some also with Christ, and some for Christ. Those who, although they were sinners during their life, die in repentance and confession of Christ also die in Christ. Those who, during their life, were imitators of Christ and crucified and mortified their flesh with its vices and desires (Galatians V), die with Christ. Those who shed their blood for Christ die for Christ.

Therefore, my brothers, even if we cannot die for Christ as martyrs, let us at least die with Christ as confessors, mortifying our bodies to sin. For, as the Apostle says: “If we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him”—in this life spiritually, and in the future eternally.

“Knowing,” he says, “that Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies; death shall no longer rule over him”—just as it did, though by his will and not by necessity. “For in that he died to sin” (understand: to remove the sin of others), “he died once.” But in that he lives, he lives for God, that is, for the glory of God the Father.

So also you, my brothers, who have been baptized in Christ, consider yourselves dead indeed to sin, but alive to God—that is, to seek the glory of God and to do his will. Therefore, my brothers, if we are true Christians, let us imitate Christ’s death and life. Let us crucify our members with their vices and desires. Let us crucify our heart, so that it may never think evil but always good; our tongue, so that it may never speak evil but always good; our hands, so that they may never do evil works but always good ones; our feet, so that they may never walk an evil path but always a good one; our ears, so that they may never be open to evil words but always to good ones. Thus, renewed with Christ as the new man, may we be able to live happily with him.

May he deign to grant this, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XV. SIXTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

Jesus said to his disciples: “Amen I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew V).

This reading, my dearest brothers, is divided into three sections. First, the Lord shows that the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees is not sufficient for possessing the kingdom of heaven. Second, he supplies what the Law seemed to contain insufficiently. Third, he shows how an offering ought to be made.

He therefore says: “Amen I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees,” and so forth. At that time the scribes and Pharisees thought themselves righteous when they fulfilled the precepts of the Law by outward action alone, believing that judgment concerned actions only, not thoughts. They considered homicide, adultery, and theft to be forbidden by the Law only as acts. But homicide, adultery, and theft of the will they regarded as either no sin or a venial sin.

But this false righteousness was not sufficient for salvation. For just as a good will alone is sufficient for salvation to one who can do no more, according to the saying, “and on earth peace to men of good will” (Luke II), so an evil will alone is sufficient for condemnation to one who can do no more. An evil will, therefore, is condemnable both among human beings and before God. Among human beings, the man who wished to betray the king is guilty of death, even if he was unable to carry out the betrayal. Before God also, the man who wished to commit adultery or homicide is regarded as an adulterer or murderer, even if he was unable to carry it out.

Hence the Lord himself says: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew V). And the poet:

> “Even if the body is kept chaste, the mind is adulterous.”  
> (Ovid, *Amores*, Book III, elegy 4, line 5.)  
> [Note: [Col. 1997D] Ovid: “Even if you have now preserved it.”]

The Lord therefore requires from his people not only bodily innocence but also purity of mind. Hence the same Son of God and of man shows himself in John’s Apocalypse girded around the breasts with a golden belt (Revelation I). Why? Because in the Gospel the Lord commands not only deeds but also the wandering thoughts that arise from the breast to be restrained.

Therefore, my brothers, avoid not only evil deeds but also evil desires; mourn them and submit them through confession to the judgment of priests. Judge them before they are judged by him who searches the kidneys and hearts—that is, hidden pleasures and thoughts (Revelation II)—who, when he comes, “will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and will reveal the counsels of hearts” (1 Corinthians IV).

For, my brothers, how much better it is to be ashamed here for an hour before a priest than to be ashamed at the universal judgment before God, his angels, and his saints? How much better it is to weep and grieve here for an hour than to mourn and suffer torment forever!

The second part follows, in which the Lord supplies what the Law seemed to contain insufficiently, when he adds: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: You shall not kill. But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment.”

Since the letter of the Law seems to prohibit only homicide in deed, the Lord adds that homicide in the will is also condemnable. Nevertheless, my dearest brothers, these additions, and the other additions made by the Lord in the Law, may be called additions or supplements with regard to the letter and to those who follow the letter. With regard to the spiritual meaning and to those who understand spiritually, however, they are not additions but rather explanations.

The Gospel is nothing other than the Law understood spiritually. Thus, if you understand this command spiritually—“You shall not kill”—you understand that this command prohibits not only homicide in deed but also homicide in the will and the other kinds of homicide.

There are six kinds of homicide. The first is homicide in deed, which is openly prohibited in the Law. The second is homicide in the will. Hence John says: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John III). The third is homicide by bad example. Hence the Lord says: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be plunged into the depths of the sea” (Matthew XVIII; Mark IX).

The fourth is homicide through perverse teaching. Hence the Lord says: “If the blind lead the blind, will they not both fall into a pit?” (Matthew XV; Luke VI). The fifth is homicide through withholding bodily sustenance. Hence it is written: “Whoever can aid one who is perishing and does not, kills him.” The sixth is homicide through withholding the word of God. Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “If you do not announce to the wicked that he should turn from his evil way, he himself will die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezekiel III).

Here, therefore, the Lord shows that not only homicide in deed but also homicide in the will is liable to judgment, when he says: “But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment.”

It must nevertheless be known, my brothers, that not every anger is blameworthy, nor is every blameworthy anger condemnable. Whoever becomes angry not against his brother’s nature but against his vice, in order to correct him, has praiseworthy anger, provided he does not exceed the proper measure. Moses, Phinehas, Joshua, Peter, and the other saints were moved by this anger against sinners.

Hence the Lord calls those preachers who neither become angry nor rebuke the vices of sinners “mute dogs” through the prophet: “Mute dogs unable to bark” (Isaiah LVI).

When someone becomes angry against his brother without good zeal, if the first movement is immediately restrained, the anger is indeed blameworthy but venial, and it is called *propassio*. Of this it is said: “Be angry and do not sin” (Psalm IV). And: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Ephesians IV). Then, my brothers, the sun sets upon our anger when, because of it, the sun of charity sets within us.

But when the first movement of evil anger is not restrained and extends even to consent to harm, the anger is condemnable and worthy of judgment—that is, of accusation. If the inward anger is expressed against a brother through some word of indignation, it will be worthy of counsel—that is, of a sentence of condemnation.

Now *raca* is an interjection of one who is indignant among the Hebrews, just as *heu* is among the Latins, signifying indignation alone. But if the heat of that anger produces against one’s brother a word signifying a definite insult—for example, if he calls him foolish or insane—it will be worthy of the fire of Gehenna.

The degrees of sins therefore require degrees of punishments. For just as anger in the mind is less condemnable than anger aroused through a word of indignation, and anger aroused through a word of indignation is less condemnable than anger expressed through a word of insult, so here a lesser punishment and judgment must be understood through “judgment” than through “counsel,” and a lesser one through “counsel” than through Gehenna—just as accusation is feared less than a sentence, and a sentence less than punishment.

Therefore, my brothers, let us altogether avoid inflicting insults upon our brothers, and also avoid becoming indignant or angry against them. Let us learn to distinguish nature from vice; let us learn to love our nature in every human being and to hate vice; let us learn always to be peaceful in disposition and to become angry against vice, yet with moderation and gentleness. For gentle correction reforms sinners, whereas intemperate correction disturbs even those who ought to be reformed.

But even if it should sometimes happen, my brothers, that we become angry or indignant without reason, or even inflict insult or injury upon our brothers, let not the sun go down upon our anger. Let us humble ourselves before our brothers as quickly as possible and ask forgiveness and peace; otherwise, our daily prayers, offerings, and almsgiving cannot be acceptable to God.

Hence it is also added: “Therefore, if you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled with your brother; and then, coming, offer your gift.”

This is the third part, in which it is shown how an offering ought to be made. You must make it from what is yours, not from what belongs to another; for whoever offers sacrifice from the plunder of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son before his father’s eyes (Sirach XXXIV). Hence it says here also, “your gift,” not another’s.

You must also offer it at the altar, directing your entire intention toward the altar—that is, toward God. This is directed against those who offer without directing their intention toward God, but rather toward human eyes.

You must also make the offering with a clean conscience, so that you first offer your clean conscience to God. For it is not the one offering who pleases God on account of what is offered; rather, what is offered pleases God on account of the one offering. Hence: “The Lord looked upon Abel and his gifts” (Genesis IV)—as though first upon him, and afterward upon his gifts. But “upon Cain and his gifts he did not look” (ibid.). It is as though he said: Because Cain displeased God, his gifts therefore also displeased him.
