If, then, when you are offering, you remember that your brother has something against you—that is, if your conscience reproaches you for having injured your brother in some way, whether by anger, indignation, insult, injury, or something of this kind, and therefore he has a cause for complaint against you—leave your gift there before the altar and go first to be reconciled with your brother.

But if your brother happens to be far away from you, leave your gift there—that is, interrupt the act of offering, as it were—and promise that, once you have found your brother, you will make full satisfaction to him. Then, continuing what you began, you shall offer your gift.

But if your brother has nothing against you, while you have something against him, you are not commanded to leave your gift and ask him for forgiveness. You are commanded only to put aside the hatred and resentment you hold against him in your heart, and thus to offer your gift.

We read, my brothers, of Saint John, patriarch of Alexandria, that one day, while celebrating Mass and singing the Lord’s Prayer, he came to the petition in which we ask that our debts be forgiven us as we forgive our debtors (Matthew VI). He remembered a certain grievance that existed between himself and a cleric. Remaining silent, he summoned that cleric; after being reconciled with him, he returned to his place and sang: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.”

Therefore, my brothers, if we wish our prayers, offerings, and almsgiving to please God, let us make satisfaction to those to whom we owe it, and let us forgive those who owe us. Let us cleanse our heart from every evil will; let us humble our cleansed heart; and, once humbled, let us offer it to God with tears of heavenly desire and the ardor of devout love.

“For the sacrifice acceptable to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Psalm L).

May he grant us to make this sacrifice, who is blessed forever. Amen.

## HOMILY XVI. SEVENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“I speak in human terms, because of the weakness of your flesh” (Romans VI).

In this reading, my dearest brothers, the Apostle commands us to abandon sins and pursue righteousness, and he does so in this manner. First, he says that he commands human and easy things. Second, he commands us to abandon vices and practice righteousness. Third, he shows what follows sin. Fourth, what follows righteousness. Fifth, he shows that eternal death is justly owed for sin, while eternal life is given freely.

He therefore says first: “I speak in human terms, because of the weakness of your flesh.” As though he were saying plainly: Since you are still weak and carnal, I do not exhort you to more difficult and perfect things, but rather to easier and human ones. For I do not command you to abandon everything for Christ, give it to the poor, and follow Christ naked. Nor do I command you to confront persecutors and shed your blood for Christ, or to abandon marriage and profess chastity, or to do other things of this kind, which belong to the perfect.

For now I command you only to abandon your sins and vices and to perform works of righteousness, which also belong to the imperfect. Hence it is added: “Just as you presented your members to serve impurity and iniquity for iniquity, so now present them to serve righteousness for sanctification.”

This is the second part, in which he commands us to abandon sin and pursue righteousness. Here the Apostle briefly indicates how the sinner progresses from evil to worse and how the good person progresses from good to better.

First, the sinner accustoms himself to impurity of mind and body, such as gluttony, lust, and other forms of disgrace. Then, so that he may have the means to satisfy his impurity, he accustoms himself to works of iniquity. Impurity is directed against oneself; iniquity against one’s neighbor. Thus, in order to satisfy his gluttony, lust, and other disgraceful desires, he envies, covets, steals, snatches, deceives, and acquires by right and by wrong. Through these things he advances into iniquity—that is, he is perfected in wickedness.

Conversely, the good person first accustoms himself to works of righteousness: namely, to render to each person what is his—to God religious devotion; to himself purity; to parents honor; to members of his household care; to superiors obedience; to inferiors governance; to equals fellowship; to the good love; to the wicked correction; to the oppressed mercy; and to all equity. Through this habituation he progresses into health—that is, into the perfection of goodness.

Therefore, my brothers, in accordance with the Apostle’s command, just as you presented your members to serve impurity and iniquity, so present them to serve righteousness and holiness. God did not give or redeem the body and its members to us so that they might serve sin, but so that they might serve him.

Hence the Apostle says: “The body is not for fornication but for the Lord” (1 Corinthians VI). And again: “Do you not know that your members are Christ’s, and that you are not your own? For you were bought at a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (ibid.).

Alas, my brothers, how grave an injury we inflict upon our Creator when we misuse in the service of sin and the devil our body and members, which he himself created and redeemed to serve him. “Taking the members of Christ,” says the Apostle, “shall I make them members of a prostitute? Certainly not!” (ibid.)

Therefore, brothers, let it never be that we pollute our members, sanctified for God, with the devil’s impurity. For our members cannot in any way serve the devil and God at the same time.

Hence it is also added: “For when you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness.” And what, my brothers, what slavery is more wretched and pitiable than to serve sin and the devil? And what freedom is worse than to be free from righteousness, which is the Lord’s gentle yoke and his light burden? (Matthew XI.)

In this matter—for which there is reason to grieve—some people are confused, having “freedom” as a veil for wickedness. Because they are free by birth, they wish to be free from the yoke of obedience and righteousness, preferring to be subject to crimes rather than to their elders, and saying: “Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke from us” (Psalm II). But what follows? “He who dwells in heaven will laugh at them, and the Lord will mock them” (ibid.).

The third part follows, in which it is shown what follows sin, when he adds: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” As though he said: Evil; for the end of those things is death.

The fulfillment of an impure and wicked desire seems to sinners to be a kind of sweet fruit, because for a moment they take pleasure in its use. But the Apostle proves from what follows that such fruit is extremely evil, since shame and death follow from such fruit. For we necessarily blush not on account of what is good and honorable, but only on account of what is shameful and dishonorable.

This shame, therefore, is a witness to the disgrace committed. Impurity and iniquity are so condemnable that they are condemned even by the impure and wicked person himself. For within the mind of the wicked person there is an evil conscience that accuses him. Memory and shame are also witnesses who testify against him, as is reason itself, which judges and condemns him. There is also fear, which punishes and torments him.

Hence it is written: “No guilty person acquits himself when he is his own judge.”

There is, nevertheless, my brothers, a certain useful confusion of spirit: one who looks upon his sins, recoils from them as he looks, blushes as he recoils, and corrects himself as he blushes.

If iniquity is condemned here even by the person who commits it, and even in its fruit, how much, my brothers, do you think it will suffer in the future when condemned by the supreme Judge? For “the end of those things is death.”

Death, namely, is twofold. Hence the prophet says: “Crush them with a double destruction” (Jeremiah XVII). The first is the death of the soul buried in sins. The second is the death of soul and body together in Gehenna, in perpetual torment.

The end, therefore—that is, the completion—of those sins is the death of the soul, since through them it is deprived of the true good, the true light, and the true life. It is made brutish, blinded, mortified, wrapped and bound in the bonds of sins, buried in the tomb of vices, and weighed down beyond measure by the heap of a sandy habit.

Their end is also the death of Gehenna, since the death of those whose life has died and ended in guilt will live in punishment. For, according to the Psalmist, “death will feed upon them” (Psalm XLVIII); it will not consume them. For just as an ox does not eat grass by the roots but eats it in such a way that it can eat it again each day, so the reprobate will always be tormented by death and yet will not be annihilated, so that they may always exist and always die.

Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “They will desire to die, but death will flee from them” (Revelation IX).

They will be tormented by four kinds of punishment: shame, fear, repentance, and pain. But that shame will be without covering; that fear without hope; that repentance without usefulness; that pain without compassion and without death; death without end; and the end without cessation.

The fourth part follows, in which it is shown what follows righteousness, when he adds: “But now, having been freed from sin”—namely, through baptism and repentance—“and having become servants of God”—through righteousness, that is, through the righteousness itself—“you have your fruit in sanctification, and the end of those things is eternal life.”

From the works and practice of righteousness we progress into fruitfulness, because nothing better and nothing more beautiful can be possessed in this life. For what, my brothers, what is better and more beautiful than to be free from every disgrace and every vice; to be pure in mind and body; to have the devil beneath one’s feet; to despise all worldly things; to be content with little; to be kind to those in need and beloved by all; to hasten toward the heavenly homeland with complete desire; and not even to fear death, but rather to await it securely, and when others are afraid, to remain secure and joyful in God?

And if the fruit of righteousness is so sweet in this life, how much sweeter, my brothers, do you think its reward will be in the other life?

“The end,” he says, “is eternal life.” And truly that life will be life, in which there will be nothing mortal and nothing corruptible. The soul will no longer be corrupted by sins but will shine with every virtue. It will not be disturbed by upheavals but will always be joyful, always secure, always peaceful, and always harmonious. It will not be diminished by failings but will abound in every wisdom, every grace, and every perfection. The body will not be corrupted by vices but will be adorned with complete integrity, beauty, and dignity. It will not suffer want but will be filled with complete satiety and abundance. It will not be burdened by weakness but will be enriched with health, youth, strength, and agility.

The fifth part follows, in which it is shown that eternal death is justly owed for sin, when he adds: “For the wages of sin is death”—that is, death is owed as the debt of diabolical wickedness. Since the sinner did not wish the good from himself and committed sin, he deserved death from himself; hence death is owed to him as a wage.

The condemned person therefore has no ground for murmuring against the Judge, but rather has reason to rage against himself, since he voluntarily abandoned life and chose death, according to the saying: “God did not make death” (Wisdom I)—that is, he did not make the cause of death—but human beings summoned death to themselves with hands and feet.

Next, it is shown that eternal life is given only freely, when he adds: “But the grace of God is eternal life.” For man neither wished nor could nor did the good from himself, but only through the grace of God, which precedes and follows the human being, giving both the will and the accomplishment.

The grace of God, therefore, is both our righteousness and its reward. For God crowns only his own grace in us. The righteous therefore have no ground for boasting or attributing anything to themselves, but only to the grace of God, which freely predestined us, freely called us, freely justified us, and will also freely crown us through Jesus Christ our Redeemer, who with him and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XVII. SEVENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

When there was a great crowd with Jesus and they had nothing to eat, he summoned his disciples and said to them: “I have compassion on the crowd,” and so forth (Matthew VIII).

This reading, my dearest brothers, is divided into four parts. First, the hunger of those who were with Jesus is demonstrated; second, the Lord’s compassion; third, the disciples’ imperfection; fourth, the filling of four thousand people from seven loaves and the gathering up of what remained.

The hunger of those who were with Jesus is therefore demonstrated first, when it says: “When there was a great crowd with Jesus.” But why, my brothers, did the Lord, who is the bread of satiety, wish his followers to suffer hunger?

For two reasons: to strengthen their faith in their hearts, when he would satisfy them in a wondrous and unheard-of manner while they were hungry; and to provide his followers with an example, so that if they should ever suffer hunger, they would not despair but remember that those who followed Jesus Christ bodily had also suffered hunger and had suddenly been gloriously satisfied, and would hope that they too would be powerfully visited by him.

This very hunger is often exceedingly useful to the saints, since it compels them to despise temporal things and sigh for eternal ones; it cleanses their stains, nourishes their virtues, and makes them content with little. By contrast, daily abundance corrupts many. Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “This was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: fullness of bread and abundance” (Ezekiel XVI).

The second part follows, in which the Lord’s compassion is demonstrated, when he himself said to his disciples: “I have compassion on the crowd, because they have now remained with me for three days and have nothing to eat. And if I send them away fasting, they will faint on the way. For some of them have come from far away.”

When the Lord displays pity and compassion in himself, he instructs us in two matters: in faith and in conduct. In faith he instructs us because, by showing that he possesses human compassion, he shows that he truly assumed the weakness of our humanity. In conduct he instructs us because, by his example, he shows that we ought to be kind and merciful toward the afflicted.

Therefore he did not hide this compassion inwardly, but rather, after summoning his disciples, displayed it, saying: “I have compassion on the crowd.” It is as though he said: Remember to have the mercy you see me having toward the afflicted.

He shows, however, toward whom we ought especially to have compassion when he adds: “Because they have now remained with me for three days.” Although, my brothers, we ought to have compassion and provide assistance to everyone, we ought especially to do so to those who follow the Lord and labor by carrying his commandments. Hence the Apostle says: “Let us do good to all, but especially to those who are of the household of faith” (Galatians IV).

But in the fact that the Lord does not send them fasting to their homes lest they faint on the way, he also shows that he is kind and faithful toward his faithful, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Corinthians X).

Therefore, brothers, following the Lord’s example, let us always have a heart of mercy toward the afflicted, knowing that with whatever measure we measure for others, it will be measured back to us. If we are merciful, we shall find a merciful Judge. If we are merciless toward others, God will also be merciless toward us. Hence James says: “Judgment without mercy will be upon the one who has not shown mercy” (James II).

Therefore, brothers, I lament certain people who are Christians in name alone, who, as though they were made of iron or stone, are moved by no pity for the afflicted. And if they ever have to pass by a beggar, a leper, a naked person, or someone in misery, they turn their face away; they cannot even look at them, as though they had forgotten the condition of human frailty. Yet if they see their donkey or pig sick, they grieve, apply medicine, and weep over its dying. Why is this, brothers, except that they lack love of God and neighbor, preferring their own donkey or pig to their neighbor?

The third part follows, in which the imperfection of the disciples is shown, when, answering the Lord, they say: “From where could anyone satisfy these people with bread in the wilderness?” The disciples reveal their own imperfection when, in the Lord’s presence, they declare that it is either impossible or difficult for the crowd to be satisfied with bread. They also demonstrate that they have undergone human temptation when, in the Lord’s presence, they despair that seven loaves will suffice for the crowds. Indeed, we frequently suffer this greater and worse temptation, my brothers, when a hungry person cries out at the door and we complain that we have only a little grain in the granary, a little bread in the chest; through the avarice of our minds we diminish or deny the goods given to us by God, when by [Col. 2005A] generosity we ought to multiply them. Let us therefore lay aside, brothers, this faintheartedness and always trust in God’s generosity. For if he abundantly provides even for the faithless and wicked, how much more will he abundantly provide his faithful stewards with the means of doing good. Let us recall the generosity of the saints, who distributed to the needy beyond their own means and yet, through God’s providence, always had abundance, so that God seemed to contend with them—he by supplying, and they by distributing. Hence Solomon says: “Some are always taking away, and are always in need; some are always giving, and are always in abundance” (Prov. XI). And the Psalmist: “He scattered abroad, he gave to the poor; his righteousness [Col. 2005B] endures for ever and ever” (Ps. III).

The fourth part follows, in which the Lord feeds four thousand people with seven loaves and a few small fish, after seven baskets of fragments have been taken up. In this he instructs us in three ways: in faith, in mystery, and in conduct.

In faith, because, while he miraculously satisfies so many people with seven loaves—when, if the loaves had been divided into individual portions, scarcely one person would have received a single morsel—and while he multiplies the remnants so that seven times more is taken up than was set out, he proves that he truly possesses divinity, just as through his human compassion he showed that he truly possessed humanity. Thus, in this reading, he demonstrates himself to be true God and true man.

[Col. 2005C]

He instructs us in mystery, because through this deed he directs us toward the mystical meaning. The seven loaves therefore signify the totality of the holy Scriptures, in which the fullness of the sevenfold grace is contained. The few small fish signify the examples of the holy Fathers, who, in comparison with the wicked, are few and humble. For just as fish make bread more pleasant to eat, so the examples of the holy Fathers make the sacred Scripture easier to understand and follow. The loaves and fish are therefore distributed to those reclining upon the ground, because the mysteries of the holy Scriptures and the examples of the holy Fathers are received only by the humble. Hence the Lord says: “I give you thanks, Father, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and have revealed them to little ones” (Matt. XI; Luke [Col. 2005D] X).

The Lord first gives thanks over the loaves, then breaks them, and afterward gives them to the disciples to distribute. Likewise, the spiritual teacher, following the Lord’s example, ought to give thanks to the Lord for having obtained the nourishment of the holy Scriptures, then break it—that is, expound it—and afterward, by teaching, hand it on to his disciples, so that they may expound it to their hearers. Four thousand people are fed by them, that is, multitudes of people from the four regions of the world. And seven baskets of leftovers remain, because spiritual understandings exceed the capacity of their hearers, and more always remains from them than is grasped.

He also instructs us in conduct by this very act, because, while he has compassion on the hungry [Col. 2006A] and distributes among the multitude the loaves he possessed, he urges us by his example to do the same.

The Lord therefore commands the crowd to recline upon the ground, just as he himself often did with his disciples. In this he condemns the extravagance of those who do not know how to eat except on painted couches and elaborate tablecloths.

He gives thanks over the loaves, instructing us that, whether we are about to eat or about to give food, we should give thanks to God, who grants us either refreshment or the means—and likewise the will—to give alms, according to what Peter says: “If anyone ministers, let him do so as from the strength which God supplies” (1 Pet. IV).

The Lord breaks the loaves, teaching us that, if we cannot give whole loaves, we should break them and distribute the broken pieces. Hence he himself says through the prophet: “Break your bread for the hungry” (Isa. LVIII).

He gives the loaves to his disciples to distribute, instructing us to teach our children and household members to give alms and, by giving through them, to train them to give.

He feeds the crowds with loaves and small fish, and there is no mention of wine or seasoning, so that he might teach us to seek simple foods, simply prepared, and to be content with what is present. The hungry are satisfied, and more is taken up than was set out, to show that the grace of almsgiving always abounds: here, the Lord continually supplies those who give alms with an abundance of things to distribute; and in the future he will repay them with heavenly things for earthly ones, and eternal things for temporal ones. Hence Solomon says: “He who is merciful to the poor lends to the Lord” (Prov. XIX).

[Col. 2006C]

Blessed Nicholas, taking pity on the people who were perishing from hunger, after giving away what belonged to him, borrowed one hundred measures of grain from sailors and revived the hungry people; when the sailors measured it back, they found no less than they had lent.

There was also a charitable man named Sanctolus who was restoring the church of Saint Lawrence. When the workmen asked for food, he consoled them with words but had nothing to set before them. Anxiously going here and there, he came to an oven in which neighboring women had baked bread the previous day. Finding there a very large and white loaf, he carried it around to the neighboring women. When they denied that the loaf was theirs, he set it before the workers. After they had been satisfied, he gathered up more fragments than he had set out. He set them out again on the second day and gathered up a multiplied quantity. And so, for ten days [Col. 2006D], they were satisfied with that loaf, as though the bread grew by being eaten.

[Note: [Col. 2005] Saint Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book III, chapter 47, volume LXXVII of *Patrologia*.]

Let us therefore, my brothers, lay aside faintheartedness and, confident in divine generosity, accustom ourselves to giving alms. Let the one who has much give much; but let the one who has little also willingly share that little. For, as the Psalmist says: “The good man is merciful and lends; he will arrange his affairs with justice, because he will never be shaken” (Ps. III). And elsewhere: “All day long he is merciful and lends, and his offspring will be blessed” (Ps. XXXVI). May the God of mercies grant you both the merit and the reward of mercy. To him belong honor, glory, and dominion, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XVIII. EIGHTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

[Col. 2007A]

“We are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh” (Rom. VIII), etc.

This reading, dearest brothers, is divided into two parts. First, the Apostle urges us to live not according to the flesh but according to the spirit. Second, he shows that those who live according to the spirit are children and heirs of God.

In urging us to live not according to the flesh but according to the spirit, the Apostle says: “We are debtors”—understand, to the spirit, not to the flesh. As you know, dearest brothers, the house of a head of a family is well ordered when the man is subject and obedient to God, and rules and governs the entire household; when the wife, together with the whole household, serves and obeys him. Hence the Apostle says: “The man is the head of the woman; Christ, however, is the head of the man” (Eph. V).

But when the woman and the household are not subject to the man, but rather the man to them, [Col. 2007B] the house is badly ordered. This disorder existed in the dwelling of our first parent. He did not render to God the obedience he owed him; rather, he obeyed the deceived woman, to whom he owed not obedience but governance and correction. For this reason he fell into disorder within himself, because the sensuality of his own flesh, together with its senses, often does not obey its head—that is, the spirit—but rather contradicts it and drags it toward consent, not to its own head, God, but to its serpentine suggestions. Thus, abandoning God and heaven, for which he was created, it thinks about, desires, and seeks only lower things, namely earthly ones, and so lives not spiritually but carnally.

Since, therefore, brothers, so great and such disorder had passed from our first parent into all of us, [Col. 2007C] the Son of God came, made man, so that by his example and grace he might restore in us the order we had lost. He commanded that henceforth our mind should serve God and compel sensuality, together with its senses, to agree with it, so that we might live according to the spirit and not according to the flesh. This is what the Apostle means when he says that we are debtors to the spirit, not to the flesh.

And because we owe certain things to the flesh—such as correction, governance, and care—he explains in what respect we are not debtors to the flesh, when he adds: “To live according to the flesh.” Although, brothers, we live in the flesh, we must not live according to the flesh, that is, according to the will of the flesh.

For the one who lives according to the flesh [Col. 2007D] is the person who, as far as he can, satisfies both the will and the pleasure of the flesh—who is carried along without restraint, like an animal, into gluttony, lust, anger, unbelief, pride, and the other vices that partly arise from the flesh and make people carnal and animal-like. Such people perceive nothing spiritual, nothing heavenly, nothing divine, but only flesh and earth. Hence the Apostle says: “The animal person does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. II).

What such people will suffer, the Apostle shows when he adds: “For if you live according to the flesh, you will die.” Here this means the death of the soul in sins, and in the future the death of both soul and body in Gehenna.

Do we not see that even here [Col. 2008A] the one dies a bad death who, having lost the honor in which he was created in the image of God, has become brutish and bent down over the earth like a beast, so that it may rightly be said of him: “When man was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with foolish beasts and became like them” (Ps. XLVIII)?

Does not the one also die a bad death who is deprived here of life and the true light—which is God—and is enveloped in inner darkness? Will not the one die an exceedingly evil death in the future who will always suffer the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth; whom the fire that is never extinguished and the worm that never dies will torment forever?

“But if,” he says, [Col. 2008B] “by the spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.” The Apostle could indeed have said, just as he had said, “If you live according to the flesh, you will die,” so, conversely: “But if you live according to the spirit, you will live.” But because some think that they can live spiritually in this life without abstinence and mortification of the flesh, he says attentively: “If by the spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.” because, while he has compassion on the hungry and distributes among the multitude the loaves he possessed, he urges us by his example to do the same. The Lord therefore commands the crowd to recline upon the ground, just as he himself often did with his disciples. In this he condemns the extravagance of those who do not know how to eat except on painted couches and elaborate tablecloths.

He gives thanks over the loaves, instructing us that, whether we are about to eat or about to give food, we should give thanks to God, who grants us either refreshment or the means—and likewise the will—to give alms, according to what Peter says: “If anyone ministers, let him do so as from the strength which God supplies” (1 Pet. IV).

The Lord breaks the loaves, teaching us that, if we cannot give whole loaves, we should break them and distribute the broken pieces. Hence he himself says through the prophet: “Break your bread for the hungry” (Isa. LVIII).

He gives the loaves to his disciples to distribute, instructing us to teach our children and household members to give alms and, by giving through them, to train them to give.

He feeds the crowds with loaves and small fish, and there is no mention of wine or seasoning, so that he might teach us to seek simple foods, simply prepared, and to be content with what is present. The hungry are satisfied, and more is taken up than was set out, to show that the grace of almsgiving always abounds: here, the Lord continually supplies those who give alms with an abundance of things to distribute; and in the future he will repay them with heavenly things for earthly ones, and eternal things for temporal ones. Hence Solomon says: “He who is merciful to the poor lends to the Lord” (Prov. XIX).

Blessed Nicholas, taking pity on the people who were perishing from hunger, after giving away what belonged to him, borrowed one hundred measures of grain from sailors and revived the hungry people; when the sailors measured it back, they found no less than they had lent.

There was also a charitable man named Sanctolus who was restoring the church of Saint Lawrence. When the workmen asked for food, he consoled them with words but had nothing to set before them. Anxiously going here and there, he came to an oven in which neighboring women had baked bread the previous day. Finding there a very large and white loaf, he carried it around to the neighboring women. When they denied that the loaf was theirs, he set it before the workers. After they had been satisfied, he gathered up more fragments than he had set out. He set them out again on the second day and gathered up a multiplied quantity. And so, for ten days, they were satisfied with that loaf, as though the bread grew by being eaten.

[Note: [Col. 2005] Saint Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book III, chapter 47, volume LXXVII of *Patrologia*.]

Let us therefore, my brothers, lay aside faintheartedness and, confident in divine generosity, accustom ourselves to giving alms. Let the one who has much give much; but let the one who has little also willingly share that little. For, as the Psalmist says: “The good man is merciful and lends; he will arrange his affairs with justice, because he will never be shaken” (Ps. III). And elsewhere: “All day long he is merciful and lends, and his offspring will be blessed” (Ps. XXXVI). May the God of mercies grant you both the merit and the reward of mercy. To him belong honor, glory, and dominion, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XVIII. EIGHTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

[Col. 2007A]

“We are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh” (Rom. VIII), etc.

This reading, dearest brothers, is divided into two parts. First, the Apostle urges us to live not according to the flesh but according to the spirit. Second, he shows that those who live according to the spirit are children and heirs of God.

As you know, dearest brothers, the house of a head of a family is well ordered when the man is subject and obedient to God, and rules and governs the entire household; when the wife, together with the whole household, serves and obeys him. Hence the Apostle says: “The man is the head of the woman; Christ, however, is the head of the man” (Eph. V).

For the one who lives according to the flesh is the person who, as far as he can, satisfies both the will and the pleasure of the flesh—who is carried along without restraint, like an animal, into gluttony, lust, anger, unbelief, pride, and the other vices that partly arise from the flesh and make people carnal and animal-like. Such people perceive nothing spiritual, nothing heavenly, nothing divine, but only flesh and earth. Hence the Apostle says: “The animal person does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. II).

What such people will suffer, the Apostle shows when he adds: “For if you live according to the flesh, you will die.” Here this means the death of the soul in sins, and in the future the death of both soul and body in Gehenna.

Do we not see that even here the one dies a bad death who, having lost the honor in which he was created in the image of God, has become brutish and bent down over the earth like a beast, so that it may rightly be said of him: “When man was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with foolish beasts and became like them” (Ps. XLVIII)?

Will not the one die an exceedingly evil death in the future who will always suffer the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth; whom the fire that is never extinguished and the worm that never dies will torment forever?

“But if,” he says, “by the spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.” The Apostle could indeed have said, just as he had said, “If you live according to the flesh, you will die,” so, conversely: “But if you live according to the spirit, you will live.” But because some think that they can live spiritually in this life without abstinence and mortification of the flesh, he says attentively: “If by the spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.”

It is as though he said: If by the power of the Holy Spirit—or even by the power of your spirit, enlightened by the Holy Spirit—you put to death vices and sins in your flesh through abstinence, you will live: here with spiritual life, and in the future with heavenly life.

For since, brothers, spirit and flesh are always at war with one another, the weaker the flesh is, the stronger the spirit is; and the stronger the flesh is, the weaker the spirit is. Hence the Apostle says: “When I am weak, then I am stronger and powerful” (2 Cor. XII). And elsewhere: “I live, yet it is no longer I; rather, Christ lives in me” (Gal. II).

[Col. 2008C]

As though he were saying plainly: I do live, but not by the life of carnal vices [reading uncertain: *carealium*, evidently for *carnalium*], by which I formerly lived; rather, by spiritual life.

The second part follows, in which the Apostle shows that those who live according to the spirit are children and heirs of God, saying: “For those who are led by the Spirit of God are the children of God.”

Those who are led by the Spirit of God are moved toward thinking, speaking, and acting well not by the flesh or by an evil spirit, but by the Holy Spirit, who presides over the flesh. He does not say “are governed,” but something greater: “are led.” For the Spirit does not merely govern us as a rider governs a horse; by a hidden energy—that is, by an operation—he also works inwardly within us. He acts in us so that we may act. For, as the Apostle says, he works in us both to will and to accomplish (Phil. II).

[Col. 2008D]

This directly opposes those who think that they can accomplish something by themselves, when the Lord says in the Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV).

“For those,” he says, “who are led by the Spirit of God are the children of God” (John XV). Such ought you to be. For you did not receive in baptism and confirmation the spirit of slavery again in fear; rather, you received the spirit of adoption.

One and the same spirit, my brothers, is called by different names because of the different gifts it bestows. It is called the spirit of wrath among the Egyptians, because it brought upon them vengeance for sin. It is called the spirit of slavery and fear among the Jews, because in the law it instilled fear in them. Hence they served it more from fear than from love. It is now called the spirit of adoption among the faithful, because it grants them filial love, through which it adopts them as children.

Therefore, brothers, if you serve him not from consciousness of sin or fear of Gehenna, but from love, you have certainly received the spirit of adoption, in which you cry: “Abba, Father.” “Abba” is Hebrew; “Father” is Greek and Latin. All the faithful—Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins—if we love and imitate God with filial affection, confidently call him Father.

Behold, my brothers, how great is the piety and kindness of God. Although we were unworthy servants, in order to show us the depths of his compassion toward us, and to invite us not to fear him but rather to love him, he commanded us to call him Father rather than Lord, and to regard no father as his equal, saying: “Do not call anyone your father on earth; for one is your Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. XXIII).

An earthly father either abandons us, or does not love us, or loves us badly; but the heavenly Father cannot forget his own. Hence the Psalmist says: “My father and my mother have forsaken me, but the Lord has taken me up” (Ps. XXVI).

The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit—that is, gives confirmation to our spirit—that we are children of God. He does this in three ways: through the Scriptures, calling us children, as when he says, “Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. XXXIII); through the marvelous wonder of his works, manifesting us as children of God.

From these evidences, my brothers, the Holy Spirit securely confirms our spirit in faith, hope, and charity that we are children of God. For if we possess these things, we no longer fear God; rather, we love him as a Father, hope well in him, and confidently flee to him for refuge.

“And if children, then heirs.” Three things make a person an heir: birth, merit, and a will. These same three things, brothers, make us heirs of an eternal inheritance.

First, by his free will, God predestined us from eternity to be heirs. Second, the birth of spiritual baptism called us to the heavenly inheritance. Third, our merit, aided by grace, makes us worthy of it. Hence the Apostle says: “Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified” (Rom. VIII).

The heavenly inheritance differs from a temporal one in this respect: here an heir does not receive the inheritance until after the death of the testator. God, however, has made us heirs in such a way that we also obtain an eternal inheritance together with him.

Again, a temporal inheritance is diminished when it is divided among many heirs; but a heavenly inheritance suffers no diminution. Again, envy arises among co-heirs from a temporal inheritance. For, according to the poet, “Every power will be impatient of a partner” [Note: [Col. 2009D] Lucan, *Pharsalia*, Book I, verses 92–93]. But from that eternal inheritance all envy will be banished. For each person will rejoice in the glory of his neighbor as in his own. Hence the Father’s only-begotten Son himself did not wish to be the sole heir, but to have co-heirs with him.

Therefore, my brothers, rejecting the temporal and empty inheritance, let us strive with our whole desire toward that heavenly inheritance: eternal, without succession; distributed, without diminution; shared, without envy; sufficient, without need; joyful, without sadness; blessed, without any misery. May the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, lead us to it. To him belong honor and glory throughout the endless ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XIX. EIGHTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matt. VII).

Our Lord and Redeemer, dearest brothers, foreseeing the persecutions that would come upon his disciples, took care to foretell them and arm them against them. He foretold that two kinds of persecution would come upon them.

One would be open, of which he says elsewhere: “You will be handed over by parents, relatives, and friends to death, and they will put some of you to death” (Luke XXI).

The other would be hidden, against which he fortifies us here in the following manner. First, he warns us to beware of false prophets. Second, he shows generally and by means of a likeness by what signs they may be recognized. Third, he explains spiritually by what things they may or may not be distinguished.

He therefore says: “Beware,” that is, being watchful, guard yourselves against false prophets.

He particularly warns us to beware carefully of this hidden persecution, because it is worse than the open kind: first, because it does greater harm, even killing souls; and second, because it is more difficult to foresee. The one who hides fraud under the appearance of friendship and service more easily trips us up. For it is characteristic of deceit to conceal itself.

The poisoner hides poison beneath honey; the traitor, fraud beneath service; the hypocrite, wickedness beneath religion; the heretic, falsehood beneath truth.

Although here, by “false prophets,” we could understand any hypocrites who conceal one thing and pretend another, the statement refers especially to heretics. While they outwardly feign religion, inwardly they conceal a heretical rapacity by which they hasten to slaughter the souls of the simple.

By the clothing of sheep, therefore, we understand sheep-like simplicity, with which heretics and all deceitful people cloak their iniquity—through speech, clothing, service, food, and other such outward things.

Of the speech of such people David says: “His words are smoother than oil, yet they are arrows” (Ps. LIV). Of their clothing it is said here: “Beware of false prophets who come to you in sheep’s clothing.” And the Apostle says: “Satan disguises himself as an angel of light” (2 Cor. IX).

Of their service the poet says:

“By service the prostitute and every traitor prevail.”

Of simulated abstinence and continence, the Apostle says to Timothy: “The Spirit clearly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, paying attention to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, forbidding marriage and abstinence from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful, because every creature of God is good” (1 Tim. IV).

Such are today, my brothers, the Manichaean heretics who have stained the region of Agen with their heresy. They falsely claim to maintain the life of the apostles, saying that they neither lie nor swear at all. Under the pretext of abstinence and continence, they condemn the eating of meat and marriage. For they say that approaching a wife is as great a crime as approaching one’s mother or daughter.

They also condemn the Old Testament. Of the New, they accept some things and reject others. And what is more serious, they proclaim two creators of things, believing God to be the creator of invisible things and the devil to be the creator of visible things. Hence they secretly worship the devil, whom they believe to be the creator of their bodies.

They say that the sacrament of the altar is merely pure bread. They deny baptism and proclaim that no one can be saved except through their hands. They also deny the resurrection of bodies.

Avoid those devilish men, my brothers, because, as the Lord foretold, “They come in sheep’s clothing, although inwardly they are ravenous wolves” (Matt. VII). Therefore, to guard against their cunning, be “wise as serpents.”

The second part follows, in which the Lord shows generally and by means of a likeness how they may be recognized. He says: “You will know them by their fruits,” that is, by their works.

The Lord speaks metaphorically here. Just as the taste of a fruit reveals what kind of sap belongs to the tree’s trunk and root, so from outward works one may judge to what kind of will a person’s heart belongs.

The Apostle shows the fruits of the wicked in his Letter to the Galatians: “The works of the flesh are manifest, namely fornication, uncleanness, lust, avarice, service of idols, sorcery, enmities, contentions, rivalries, quarrels, dissensions, heresies, envies, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these, which I foretell to you, as I have already foretold, that those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God” (Gal. V).

He shows what the fruits of the good are when he adds: “The fruit of the spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, gentleness, faith, modesty, continence, chastity” (ibid.).

“Do they,” he says, “gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles?” That is: Can sweetness and kindness, and the fervent grapes of charity, come from sinners, wickedness, and thorny vices?

As though he were saying: No. A wicked person can pretend to perform a virtuous work, but he cannot truly perform it. But if he has pretended, how can he be distinguished? Because a pretender, although he can imitate some things, cannot imitate everything; because what is feigned is not firm, just as a changed color is not firm; and because simulation is exposed when challenged.

Therefore, whoever truly wishes to detect dissimulation should inquire not what the person does or says openly, but what he does or says secretly. Moreover, if you observe the pretender’s works carefully and continually, he will gradually become contemptible to you. But the more you observe a good man, the more you will admire him.

Thus, “a bad tree cannot bear good fruit, nor can a good tree bear bad fruit.” That is, a person who is evil cannot perform works pleasing to God and worthy of eternal reward; nor can a person who is good perform works that are evil and worthy of eternal condemnation.

Yet an evil person sometimes performs certain small good deeds, because, occasionally moved by natural compassion, he feeds the hungry, clothes the naked, and welcomes the stranger. This may serve to lessen his punishment, but not to gain eternal life. For he does not do good well; rather, good is done through him.

Conversely, a good person sometimes commits certain small sins, overcome by natural weakness. Through these he does not deserve eternal punishment but temporal punishment.

What the bad tree deserves, he shows when he adds: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.”

Take note, brothers; take note. He does not say, “Every tree that bears bad fruit will be cut down”—although that is certainly understood—but says: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down.” It is not enough for a person not to do evil unless he also does good. For it is written: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI).

In avoiding evil, you avoid punishment alone and do not acquire a reward. If you say to me, “I have not committed theft,” I reply: “You do not use straps” [the printed *loris* is contextually uncertain]. If you say, “I have not killed a person,” I reply: “You do not feed ravens on the cross.” The rich man clothed in purple is read to have been tormented in hell, not because he had seized what belonged to another, but because he did not give what was his. What, then, will happen to the one who has seized what belongs to another?

Therefore, my brothers, when you have avoided evil, do good, because the axe has already been placed at the root of the tree (Matt. III)—not only of the evil tree, but also of the barren one.

The third part follows, in which the Lord shows spiritually by what works the good are not distinguished from the wicked, and by what works they are distinguished.

He shows by what works they are not distinguished when he adds: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven.”

There are three kinds of works. One is proper to the good, such as love of God and neighbor; doing good even to enemies; preserving peace, concord, wisdom, justice, and the other virtues. Another is proper to the wicked, namely vices and their works. The third is common to both good and wicked people: certain intermediate works, such as praying, fasting, wearing sackcloth, giving alms, restraining lust, and similar practices. These take their character from the intention of the person performing them. In those who use them well, they are good; in those who use them badly, they are evil.

The Lord therefore shows that the kingdom of heaven will not be possessed on account of these common works when he says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven.” Similarly, not everyone who fasts, nor everyone who gives alms, and so forth.

Then he shows by what work the good are distinguished from the wicked, adding: “But everyone who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven.”

The one does God’s will who truly believes, rightly hopes, and firmly loves. The one does God’s will who does what God wills and does it as God wills. The one does God’s will who places it before his own will and before all others, saying: “Not my will, Lord, but yours be done” (Matt. XXVI; Mark XIV).

Therefore, my brothers, let us seek and do God’s will in all things, loving him with all our heart, with our whole soul, and with all our strength, more than ourselves. Let us love our friends in God and our enemies for God’s sake, not returning evil for evil but good for evil, a blessing for a curse, just as the Lord Jesus both did and commanded.

May he himself grant that we fulfill this. To him belong honor and glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XX. NINTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“Let us not desire evil things, as they also desired them,” etc. (1 Cor. X).

This reading, my brothers, is divided into four parts. [Col. 2013B] First, by the example of the ancients, it warns us against vices. Second, it demonstrates that the falls of the ancients were written as a figure and a warning for us. Third, it warns us not to be seized by temptation. Fourth, it says that God will not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can bear.

First, then, he dissuades us from five vices: namely, evil desire, idolatry, fornication, tempting God, and murmuring. He warns us away from evil desire when he says: “Let us not be desirous of evil things, as they also desired them.” He added “evil” because there is a good desire and there is an evil desire. For if good desire did not exist, the Prophet would not have said: “My soul has desired to long for your ordinances at all times” (Ps. 118). And if evil desire did not exist, the Lord would not have forbidden it in the Law, saying: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exod. 20).

The soul has, from its creation, the natural faculties of desire, anger, and reason. Therefore it is necessary that our soul desire something—either God or the world. But it cannot desire God without despising the world; nor can it desire the world without despising God. Let us therefore, my brothers, turn all our desire from the world toward God, from evil toward good: that is, let us desire God and every good thing, and flee the world together with every evil.

He warns us away from the desire for evil things by the example of the Israelites when he adds: “As they also desired them.” After crossing the sea, they grew weary of the manna in the desert and desired meat and the delicacies of Egypt; and in their longing they returned to Egypt. Therefore they were struck by a great plague from the Lord. In this it was prefigured that we too, if after baptism and nourishment with heavenly bread we return in longing to the desires of the world and the devil that we have renounced, will be struck by eternal punishment. [Col. 2013C]

He warns us away from idolatry when he adds: “Nor must you become idolaters.” An idolater is one who gives to a creature the worship owed to the Creator. There are two kinds of idolaters. Some are idolaters in opinion, such as those who, in their opinion, attribute divinity to the sun, the moon, or some other creature. Others are idolaters in conduct, such as those who place a creature before the Creator; for whatever someone loves more, he makes his god.

Thus whoever places gluttony of the belly before God makes the belly his god. Whoever places wine before God makes Bacchus his god. Whoever places his Venus before God makes Venus his god. Such people are numerous today—something I cannot say without groaning—serving their vices and sins rather than God. Although they say with their mouths that they believe in God, they deny him in their actions and conduct. Hence Paul says: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Tit. 1).

Here also, to warn us against becoming idolaters in either manner, he gives the example of the Israelites, adding: “As some of them did, as it is written: The people sat down to eat and drink”—that is, food sacrificed to the calf [idolothyta?; perhaps idolothyta?]—“and rose up to play,” that is, to sing psalms to the calf and worship it. Therefore, at Moses’ command, they were punished by the sword. In this it was prefigured that we too, if we become idolaters either in opinion or in conduct, will be punished eternally. [Col. 2014A]

He warns us away from fornication when he adds: “Nor must we fornicate.” Fornication is every sexual intercourse except the marital union of a man and a woman. It has many forms: simple fornication, between an unmarried man and an unmarried woman; moechia, between a married man and a married woman; adultery, between an unmarried man and a married woman, or between a married man and an unmarried woman; incest, which occurs with one’s mother, sister, or kinswoman; Sodomitic lust, between males or between females; and the unmentionable act, or abomination, which occurs when a man or woman has intercourse with a brute animal. All these forms of fornication are criminal and damnable.

The Apostle warns us away from all of them by the example of the Israelites when he adds: “Some of them fornicated with the Midianite women,” whom Balak had sent, on Balaam’s advice, with provisions to meet them and ensnare their souls; “and twenty-three thousand of them fell by the sword of Balak.” In this, brothers, it was prefigured that we too, if we fornicate in this or that manner, will perish eternally. [Col. 2014B]

He warns us away from tempting God when he adds: “Nor must we tempt Christ.” He tempts God who tests, by experiment, either God’s power or his love toward himself. Such temptation arises either from lack of faith or from vainglory. One tempts God in two ways: in order to test either God’s power or his love toward oneself, one either voluntarily throws oneself into dangers or demands that miracles be performed for oneself.

As we read in the *Lives of the Fathers*, a certain hermit threw himself into obvious danger through vainglory. The devil appeared to him in the form of a good angel and persuaded him that he was so holy and dear to God that, even if he threw himself into a very deep well, he would not be harmed but would be guarded by angels. He threw himself into the well and was pulled out by the brothers scarcely alive. And—what is worse—he could not be persuaded in any way that he had suffered a diabolical deception, and so he died most miserably.

The devil tempted the Lord in this same way when, placing him on the pinnacle of the Temple, he said to him: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down” (Matt. 4). The Lord, who knew him very well, replied: “It is written: You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (ibid.).

Unbelieving Jews in the desert demanded that miracles be performed for them in order to test God’s power. Hence the Psalmist says: “They tempted God in their hearts, asking for food for their souls. And they spoke evil against God and said: Can God perhaps prepare a table in the desert? For he struck the rock, and waters flowed, and torrents overflowed. Can he also give bread?” (Ps. 77). And they did not tempt God only once, but many times in the desert. Therefore they perished from fiery serpents, which killed them by their heat and thirst. In this it was prefigured that we too, if we tempt God, will perish eternally. [Col. 2014C]

It is not, however, tempting God, my brothers, if a believer, when danger threatens and human counsel fails, entrusts himself wholly to God amid the danger; nor is it tempting God if, for the praise of God and the benefit of one’s neighbor, when one sees that it is necessary, one asks God to perform miracles.

He warns us away from murmuring when he adds: “Nor must you murmur.” Murmuring is a reproach that is neither entirely open nor entirely hidden, occupying a middle place between detraction and rebuke. Properly speaking, it is the vice of an inferior who, through impatience, is unwilling to endure his superior, yet does not dare to rebuke him openly. It is a very great vice, generating seditions, disagreements, and quarrels.

It is characteristic of a good man not to murmur, but rather, if someone is blameworthy, either to correct him privately or to rebuke him openly. He warns us away from this vice by the example of the Israelites. Some of them murmured against Moses and Aaron about the priesthood, and also against God concerning the hardship of the journey through the desert; therefore they perished at the hands of the destroyer. Some were destroyed by fire, others by the opening of the earth, and others by the striking angel; thus they were exterminated from the land of the living. In this it was prefigured that we too, if we murmur against God or against our superiors—as some do—will be expelled from eternal life. [Col. 2015C]

The second part follows. In it the Apostle shows that the falls of the ancients occurred as a figure and were written for our warning, when he adds: “These things happened to them as a figure.” The temporal punishments by which the first transgressors were punished signified the eternal punishments by which all transgressors will be punished in hell.

God condemned the first gluttony and disobedience in our first parents by the punishment of mortality, to show that all gluttons and disobedient people would be punished by eternal death. God likewise condemned the first lust of the sons of God with the daughters of men by the Flood, signifying that all fornicators would perish eternally in waters of snow. God also struck the first Sodomites with fire and sulfur, signifying that all Sodomites would be punished by eternal burning and stench.

He likewise condemned Lot’s wife, who looked back toward what had been renounced, with the stony hardness and insensibility of salt, signifying that all who look back toward the renounced desires of the world will be struck with eternal hardness and blindness—and similarly in the other cases. [Col. 2015D]

“These things,” he says, “were written for our correction.” The falls of those who came before were written for the warning of those who came afterward. For a foolish person, my brothers, is one who sees someone before him fall and does not take care.

“Upon whom,” he says, “the ends of the ages have come”—that is, upon us, who were born at the end of the ages—and therefore, if we transgress, we deserve to be punished more severely. For the virtues, falls, and teachings of those who came before were written for our instruction. If, then, those who sinned without the Law and did not know the greatness of their sins were punished so severely, how much more severely will we be punished if we transgress, instructed as we are in the time of grace and through the Scriptures?

Therefore, he says, “Let anyone who thinks that he is standing take care lest he fall.” It is as though he were saying plainly: The road of this world is slippery, and many—both those who came before and those who come afterward—fall. Therefore let everyone who seems to himself to be standing fear while he is still able to fall.

The third part follows. In it the Apostle warns us not to be overcome by temptation when he says: “Let no temptation seize you except what is human.” He does not say, “Do not be tempted,” because it is necessary and useful for a human being to be tempted in this life; rather, he says, “Let no temptation seize you,” that is, let it not overcome you. And because this is impossible so long as we are in this life, he adds: “Except what is human.”

Human temptation is that which arises from ignorance, weakness, or necessity. Temptation arises from ignorance when someone sins unknowingly—for example, when someone thinks he is speaking the truth but speaks falsely, or when he thinks he is giving another good advice but nevertheless does not advise him well, and in similar cases.

Temptation arises from weakness when, after excessive thirst, we drink too much, and in similar cases. Temptation arises from necessity when we are tempted by the first movements that we cannot avoid. Human temptation is described in this way because it is human to be tempted in this manner, and because it was inflicted as a result of the sin of our first parents. [Col. 2016A]

But if, my brothers, we sin not through ignorance but deliberately, or through obstinacy, or if of our own free will we follow our desires, it is unquestionably not human temptation but rather diabolical temptation, and therefore damnable.

The fourth part follows. In it the Apostle shows that God will not permit us to be tempted beyond our capacity when he adds: “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear.”

God is called faithful—that is, truthful in his promises—because he is always present to his faithful, just as he himself promised, saying: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). Therefore, he says, “he will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear.”

Here he plainly refutes those who, excusing their sins and accusing God, say: “God abandons us and oppresses us with an unbearable burden of commandments and temptations, although he has given us a feeble nature incapable of resisting vices.”

Away with such sacrilege! God is accused of faithlessness, cruelty, and ignorance: of faithlessness, as though he abandoned us before we abandoned him; of cruelty, as though he had given us unbearable commandments that we could not fulfill and permitted temptations to come upon us that we could not resist; and of ignorance, as though he did not know what human nature could do or endure.

But, my brothers, God abandons no one first, because he is faithful; he imposes nothing unbearable upon us, because he is compassionate; and he does not fail to know the powers he has given us, because he is all-knowing. [Col. 2016B]

“But,” he says, “with the temptation he will also provide an advantage”—that is, a gain—“so that you may be able to endure it.” It is as though he were saying: With the temptation he will provide us with two things: the gain of progress and the power to endure.

Therefore, brothers, let us exclude diabolical temptations from ourselves with all our strength; let us restrain human temptations as far as we can; and let us redeem those we have committed through tears of repentance and works of mercy. Let us hasten with all our desire toward our eternal homeland, where there is no temptation. May the almighty and merciful God grant us to reach it, he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXI. THE NINTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

[Col. 2017B]

“Jesus said to his disciples: A certain rich man had a steward, and this man was accused before him of having wasted his goods” (Luke 16).

My brothers, we must not draw everything we have heard in this parable, taken according to the literal sense, into an example for imitation. We must not commit any fraud against a temporal lord; rather, his rights must be rendered to him, according to the Apostle’s saying: “To whom honor is due, honor; to whom tribute, tribute; to whom tax, tax” (Rom. 13). Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Render to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God” (Matt. 22). Therefore he himself, although he was King of kings and Lord of lords, rendered tribute to Caesar as an example of humility.

This parable is to be understood by contrast: if the man who, through the cleverness of fraud, provided for the future from the resources entrusted to him by his master is praised, then surely the man who, through true wisdom, provides for himself in the next life from the resources entrusted to him by God is to be praised by God all the more. [Col. 2017C]

We must also note what is said here: “The children of this age are more prudent than the children of light in their own generation.” This can be understood in two ways: either because the wicked are more prudent in worldly matters than the good, which happens because they are more attentive in those matters; or because the wicked are more prudent in evil than the good are in good.

But why? Why are the wicked more prudent in the works of the devil than we are in the works of God? Why do the love of God, the sweetness of the heavenly reward, and the security of a pure conscience have less power among us than the love of the world and temporal profit have among the wicked, together with the torment of a bad conscience? Let us therefore awaken, my brothers, from our sluggishness, and let us be ashamed if we see the wicked more watchful, more ready, and more clever in doing the works of the devil than we are in doing the works of Christ.

Mystically, five things are proposed for our understanding in this parable. First, that we are not lords but stewards of our possessions; second, how we mismanage the Lord’s possessions; third, how the Lord demands an account from us concerning his possessions; fourth, how useful fear is for discovering counsel; fifth, how we can make friends for ourselves from the possessions of the Lord our God.

First, then, my beloved brothers, this parable shows that God almighty, made man for us and rich toward all who call upon him, has a steward—namely, every human being to whom he has entrusted his goods. He has entrusted three kinds of goods to human beings: external, bodily, and spiritual. Of these goods he made the human being not the lord but the steward—that is, the guardian and dispenser—so that the person might guard and distribute them according to the will not of himself but of the Lord.

He also gave him a law and commandments concerning how, to whom, how much, and when he ought to distribute them for the profit and honor of his Lord.

But, as the second point in this parable demonstrates, a human being wastes his Lord’s goods when he neither uses nor distributes them according to his Lord’s will. He wastes external goods when he does not distribute them to the poor and the sick, does not honor the Lord, does not build churches or houses for the poor, and does not benefit his homeland, but either hides them untouched through avarice or scatters them luxuriously, vainly, and arrogantly through extravagance; and thus, instead of serving God, he serves vices and the devil. [Col. 2018A]

Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “I gave them wool and linen, grain, wine and barley, my silver and gold, which they made into Baals” (Hos. 2).

A person wastes bodily goods when he makes his body serve fornication rather than the Lord; when he misuses the tongue God gave him for blessing by using it for cursing, lying, perjury, and slander; when he misuses the eyes God gave him for good purposes by using them to covet a woman and to look upon vanity; when he misuses the ears given him for hearing God’s word by using them to hear lies, slanders, and vanities; when he misuses his nostrils to smell luxurious perfumes and prostitutes’ ointments rather than the fragrance of virtues; when he misuses his hands to strike impiously with the fist, shed blood, and cause harm rather than to do good; when he misuses his feet to run toward evil rather than to follow the way of the Lord; and when he misuses his sense of taste for feasting and drunkenness rather than for eating and drinking with sobriety of spirit.

He wastes spiritual goods when he misuses free will to choose evil rather than good, to serve the world rather than God, and the flesh rather than the spirit; when he misuses understanding to investigate how he can harm rather than benefit; when he misuses memory to remember evil rather than good; and when he misuses foresight to set a snare for his neighbor rather than to offer help.

The waste, misuse, and disgraceful habit of all these things, my brothers, brings the steward before his Lord God under an evil report. Therefore, as the third point in the parable demonstrates, the Lord calls the steward and says to him: “What is this that I hear about you? Give an account of your stewardship.”

The Lord God settles accounts with the human steward twice: first in this age, and afterward in judgment—but in different ways. Here he settles accounts with a person in order to inspire fear and correction; in judgment he will settle accounts with him in order to inflict punishment according to his merits. Here he does so to exercise mercy; there, to exercise justice.

Thus here the Lord settles accounts with his human steward, whom he wishes to correct rather than destroy. He calls him and summons him to answer when he inflicts some illness upon him, and he questions him either inwardly through divine inspiration, or outwardly through a priest, or through some correction that says to him: “Brother, the Lord is calling you and demanding an account from you for everything you have done against him. Make provision for yourself quickly, because you will no longer be able to act as steward. Through death the administration of temporal things will soon be taken away from you.” [Col. 2019A]

When these things have been inspired inwardly or said outwardly, the human steward is inwardly shaken and becomes afraid. This fear, shaking him inwardly this way and that, draws him to deliberate about what he should do, as the fourth point in the parable signifies when it adds:

“The steward said to himself: What shall I do, since my lord is taking the stewardship away from me? I cannot dig”—because in the other life there will be no time for earning but for receiving, no time for sowing but for reaping, no time for laboring but for resting. “I am ashamed to beg,” he says. In the other life the beggar will always suffer shame and will find no helper, as is shown in another parable of the Gospel, when the foolish virgins ask the prudent virgins for oil and do not receive it.

Hence Solomon says: “Because of the cold the sluggard would not plow; therefore he will beg in summer, and it will not be given to him” (Prov. 20).

“I know what I shall do.” Consider, brothers, consider how useful fear is. This steward would never have thought about his salvation if fear had not inwardly shaken him. But with fear pressing him inwardly, he deliberates, seeks, and finds counsel, according to the Prophet’s saying: “Because of your fear, Lord, we conceived, were in labor, and gave birth to the spirit of salvation” (Isa. 26). We conceived through good thinking, were in labor through effort, and gave birth through doing good.

The fifth point follows: how the steward can prepare friends for himself from his lord’s possessions. Hence he also says: “I know what I shall do, so that, when I am removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses.”

Calling together each of his lord’s debtors, he said to the first: “How much do you owe my lord?” He replied: “A hundred measures of wheat.” He said: “Take your bill, sit down, and write eighty,” and so forth.

Since everything we have, my brothers, belongs not to us but to our Lord, when we lend, we lend our Lord’s possessions; and those who owe us are debtors to the Lord. [Col. 2019D]

The steward therefore prepares friends for himself from his lord’s goods when he sympathizes with Christ’s poor and remits the debts of some either partly or entirely; when he gives extra assistance to another; when he helps one by praying, another by correcting, another by instructing; when he supports one with words, another with advice, another with patronage, and another with material resources; and when he shares temporal goods with others so that he may reap their spiritual goods.

When the Lord concludes the parable by saying, “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity,” this must not be understood to mean that one may give alms from riches acquired unjustly, especially since it is written: “Whoever offers sacrifice from the property of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son in the presence of his father” (Eccl. 34). Rather, it is to be understood of the riches of iniquity—that is, riches unjustly retained—because they make many people wicked, proud, and vain.

This, brothers, must always be committed to memory: the Lord added, “When you fail”—that is, when you fail through temporal death, and when you fail in your merits—“they may receive you into eternal dwellings.” He did not say, “You may be received because of them,” but “they may receive you.” [Col. 2020A]

Behold, brothers, how great is the dignity of Christ’s poor, who deserve to be judges and doorkeepers of the kingdom of heaven, so that they may receive or exclude whomever they wish.

Therefore, my brothers, let us venerate, cherish, and love Christ’s poor; and, despising everything else, let us strive to be Christ’s poor ourselves, so that through them and with them we may deserve to be received into the eternal dwellings. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

## HOMILY XXII. THE TENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY.

[Col. 2020B]

“Brothers, you know that when you were gentiles, you were led away, going to mute idols” (1 Cor. 12), and so forth.

The Apostle says this, beloved brothers, to the Corinthians who, although now converted by him, had previously been gentiles and had worshiped mute idols. He does three things. First, he shows that idolatry and blasphemy are induced by evil spirits. Second, he says that a true confession of faith comes from the Holy Spirit. Third, he lists the various gifts of God, asserting that they are all given by the same Holy Spirit.

Showing, then, first, that human beings are led by evil spirits to idolatry and blasphemy, he says: “Brothers, you know that when you were gentiles, you went to mute idols, being led by evil spirits.” [Col. 2020C]

Gentiles, my brothers, are so called from γῆ (*gē*), which means “earth,” or from *gignendo*, “giving birth,” because, not cleansed through some sacrament nor instructed through the Law, they remain as they were born. They were born unclean and remain unclean. They were born children of wrath and remain children of wrath. They know nothing heavenly, nothing spiritual, but only the earth from which they were born.

Without resistance they allow themselves to be led by evil spirits into various errors, so that, abandoning the one true Creator, they worship idols not merely of one kind but of many kinds: images of human beings, four-footed animals, and serpents. All these are mute, for according to the Psalmist: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths but will not speak; they have eyes but will not see. They have hands but will not touch; they have feet but will not walk; they will not cry out through their throat. Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. 113).

This is indeed true, because whoever makes idols, or attributes divinity to them, becomes like those idols. He has a mouth like a human being, yet does not reason; he has eyes like a human being, yet does not contemplate truth as a human being; he has ears like a human being, yet does not understand truth as a human being.

Some false Christians today are like such people—something I cannot say without groaning. Although they confess with their mouths that there is one Creator, they are nevertheless so deceived and dragged along by evil spirits that in their conduct and actions they worship and venerate not only idols but also—what is even worse—pleasures. [Col. 2020D]

One is led by the spirit of lust to worship Venus. Another is led by the spirit of drunkenness to worship Bacchus. Another is led by the spirit of mammon to worship money. All of them are more deserving of condemnation because, against their own conscience, they place a creature before the Creator. Even if not with their mouths, they deny Christ by their actions.

This does not happen through the Spirit of God but rather through an evil spirit. Hence it is added: “I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Anathema to Jesus.’” Idolatry, apostasy, blasphemy, and the other vices were introduced by evil spirits. Therefore, with the Apostle, I say to those who blaspheme, commit perjury, or swear by the name of Jesus, that no one speaking in the Spirit of God blasphemes, commits perjury, or swears by the name of Jesus, but rather does so while speaking in an evil spirit. [Col. 2021A]

The second part follows. In it the Apostle says that true confession comes from the Holy Spirit when he adds: “And no one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit.”

In saying this, the Apostle is not opposed to the Lord’s statement in the Gospel: “Not everyone who says, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7). For here he uses “to say” in the sense of “to confess.” The person who truly confesses is the one who confesses with mouth and deed what he holds in his heart. Such confession can in no way be possessed except from the Holy Spirit.

For we cannot think well, speak well, or act well from ourselves unless the Holy Spirit comes first to us, he who works in us both willing and accomplishing (Phil. 2). [Col. 2021B]

Those who boast either of their talent, eloquence, or strength are condemned in this matter, saying: “Our lips are from ourselves.
