Who is our lord?” (Ps. 11); and: “Our hand is exalted, and not the Lord, has done all these things” (Deut. 32). Yet the Lord says in the Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

The third part follows. In it the Apostle lists the diversity of gifts, showing that they are given by the Holy Spirit.

First, then, he sets out three kinds of God’s gifts: graces, ministries, and operations. He shows that each of these is subdivided into several forms when he adds: “There are divisions of graces.”

Although every gift of God is grace because it is given freely, here, by antonomasia, virtues are called “graces,” because they make the one who possesses them pleasing and gracious. Such are faith, hope, charity, wisdom, justice, fortitude, temperance, and the other virtues, which make people lovers of God and lovable to God and human beings.

These virtues possess such holiness and goodness in themselves that they are called not only gifts of the Holy Spirit but also the Holy Spirit himself, as Isaiah says: “The Spirit of the Lord will descend upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel,” and so forth (Isa. 11). And John says: “These are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth” (Rev. 5)—that is, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

The gifts are diverse, but the giver is one. Hence here too, after saying, “There are divisions of graces,” he adds: “But there is one Spirit.” [Col. 2021C]

These gifts accompany the Holy Spirit inseparably, so that no one can possess these gifts without possessing the Holy Spirit, nor possess the Holy Spirit without possessing these gifts. Let us therefore, my brothers, strive to acquire these gifts with every effort and vigilance, through which we may deserve to retain the Holy Spirit as a permanent inhabitant within us.

Next he sets out the second kind of gifts when he adds: “There are divisions of ministries, but one Lord.” There are many kinds of ministries in the Church serving one Lord, such as the ministry of preaching, the ministry of the priesthood, and similar offices. If these are possessed together with the virtues mentioned above, they are of great merit and usefulness in the Church of God. Otherwise, they not only do no good but even do harm.

This is directed against certain members of our order who desire the office of preaching or the priesthood more than merit. They desire more to be honored by people than to be honorable. Of them the Lord says in the Gospel: “They say and do not do. For they love the first places at banquets and the first seats in the synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by people” (Matt. 23). [Col. 2022A]

Next he supplies the third kind of gifts, saying: “There are divisions of operations, but there is one God who works all things in all.”

God gives human beings many kinds of operations, such as operations of miracles, operations of necessary labors, operations of almsgiving, and similar works. But since whatever is given by the Holy Spirit is given by the Father and also by the Son, why did the Apostle distinguish matters here in such a way that, when speaking of graces, he said “one Spirit”; when speaking of ministries, “one Lord”; and when speaking of operations, “one God”?

He did so to signify to us that graces are obtained only through the love of God, who is the Holy Spirit; that ministries come from the Lord and are offered to him; and that God is the author who performs operations through us. Hence, after saying “one God,” he added: “Who works all things in all,” distributing each thing to each person.

He shows why God grants us his gifts when he adds: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for usefulness.” He calls the gift of the Holy Spirit the “manifestation of the Spirit,” because through the gift of the Holy Spirit the Holy Spirit himself is shown to be present within us. [Col. 2022B]

Such gifts are given for our benefit, both our own and that of others. Those who receive God’s gifts uselessly, and therefore benefit neither themselves nor others, are condemned and are rightly deprived of the talent they uselessly concealed.

Next he gives examples from the three kinds of gifts, saying: “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom,” which concerns heavenly things; “to another a word of knowledge,” which concerns the proper administration of earthly things; “to another faith in the same Spirit.”

Wisdom, knowledge, and faith, if possessed together with charity, are graces of the virtues. Expressions of wisdom, knowledge, and faith, and teaching, are ministries. “To another, grace for conferring healing upon the sick”: this is indeed a ministry.

Next he gives an example of operations, adding: “To another, the operation of virtues,” that is, of miracles, or good works of virtue; “to another, prophecy,” that is, revelation of hidden things; “to another, discernment of spirits,” so that he may know which spirit is from God and which is from the devil; “to another, kinds of tongues,” so that he may speak in various languages; “to another, interpretation of obscure sayings.”

All these things, and similar things, are worked by one and the same Spirit. It is as though he were saying plainly: What you believed when you were led away to worship mute idols is not true—namely, that, according to the divinity of the gifts, there is a diversity of gods, so that Minerva gives wisdom, Pan medicine, Mercury eloquence, Mars courage, and so forth.

Rather, one and the same Holy Spirit works all these things, distributing them to individuals—not giving everything to one person, lest he become proud, nor giving nothing to anyone, lest he despair, but giving particular gifts to particular people, so that no one may despise another and each may learn to assist the other, whose help he needs.

He distributes them, he says, “as he wills, to whom he wills, and in the measure he wills,” bound neither by our merits nor compelled by any necessity, but guided solely by his free and gracious will.

Therefore, my brothers, since we have freely received the gifts of the Holy Spirit, let us freely share them with those who do not possess them. Let the one who has wisdom instruct the ignorant. Let the one who has temporal possessions support the needy. Let the one who has power defend the weak. Let the one who has eloquence offer himself as advocate for orphans and widows. Let the one who has the grace of prayer intercede for sinners, so that each person, gaining advancement both for himself and for others from the grace entrusted to him, may deserve to receive an eternal reward. Amen.

## HOMILY XXIII. THE TENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY.

As Jesus was drawing near to Jerusalem, seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: “For if you had known, even you” (Luke 19). Having prefaced the reading, dearly beloved brothers, let us examine first what pertains to the literal sense, and then what pertains to the mystical sense.

According to the literal sense, the Lord demonstrates in this reading that he possesses four things: true humanity, true divinity, true justice, and true charity. He shows that he possesses true humanity when he weeps like a true man. For weeping belongs to humanity. But what is it, my brothers, that the Lord is never read to have laughed, but is read to have wept, except that all laughter arises from vanity, whereas weeping is useful to us? Concerning laughter, Solomon says: “Laughter is always in the mouth of a fool.” And elsewhere: “Laughter will be mingled with sorrow, and mourning takes possession of the end of joy” (Proverbs 14). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Woe to you who laugh, for you shall weep” (Luke 6).

Weeping that arises not from the loss of temporal things, but from longing for the heavenly homeland, or from contrition for sins, or from compassion for another’s misery, is exceedingly useful to us, brothers. Hence Solomon says: “It is better,” he says, “to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” (Ecclesiastes 7). And the Lord says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5).

When Jesus was therefore drawing near, seeing Jerusalem—that is, foreseeing the evils that were to befall the city—he wept over it out of compassion. [Col. 2023D–2024A] He wept for three reasons: to demonstrate that he possessed true flesh; to show that he possessed genuine compassionate pity; and to set before us an example that we too should weep. If he, who had nothing in himself for which to weep, wept because of the sins of others, what ought we sinners to do, who have many things within ourselves for which to weep? And if he who is God so sympathizes with human misery, how ought we human beings to sympathize and show mercy to other human beings—brothers to brothers?

Therefore, brothers, let us weep for our own sins, and, following the Lord’s example, let us also weep for the sins of others. Let us not do as certain people do, who ridicule those who sin and mock another’s downfall, like the Pharisees, who are moved against sinners not through compassion but through derision or indignation. Those who never show compassion toward sinners never deserve forgiveness for their own sins.

Rather, let us imitate the philosopher Praeabus, who, as we read in the *Lives of the Fathers*, wept when he saw a theatrical woman. When he was asked why he was weeping, he replied: “Two things compel me to weep: one is the destruction of this sinful woman; the other is that I do not desire to please God as much as she desires to please the people.”

The Lord demonstrates that he possesses true divinity by seeing and recounting future events as though they were present. “For if you had known—even you,” he says; that is, if you had known the evils threatening you, you too would have wept. “And indeed on this your day, the things that belong to your peace”—as though he were saying: “At present you have your own day and your own peace; at present you rejoice and delight in the time of your prosperity and peace. But now the evils that are to come upon you are hidden from your eyes.”

He then adds: “For your enemies will surround you with a rampart; they will surround you on every side; they will throw you and your children who are within you to the ground; and they will not leave in you one stone upon another.” All these things, my brothers, which the Lord foretold, were fulfilled by the Roman leaders Titus and Vespasian, forty years after the Lord’s Passion. On the very solemnity during which they had crucified the Lord, the city was overthrown, and of its inhabitants one million were killed, some by the sword and others by hunger. The rest were taken captive throughout the nations and sold for thirty-one denarii—those who had sold Christ for thirty pieces of silver.

The very site of the city bears witness to this overthrow, containing within it the place of Calvary, which had previously been outside the gate. Why these evils befell them, the Lord shows when he adds: “Because you did not recognize the time of your visitation.” These evils were to come upon them because they refused to recognize Christ as their visitor and redeemer.

Hence the prophet says: “The kite in the sky knows its appointed time; the turtledove, the swallow, and the stork know the time of their coming, but my people have not known the judgment of God” (Jeremiah 8).

That this blindness came upon that people through the sin of their priests, the Lord shows when he adds: “And entering the temple, he began to drive out those who were selling and buying in it.” In this, my brothers, the Lord demonstrates that he possesses true justice. For he would not possess true justice if he never punished sinners.

Thus the Lord sometimes shows mercy and sometimes punishes, in order to teach us to have compassion together with justice and justice together with compassion: that is, we should be so compassionate toward human nature that nevertheless we do not spare people’s sins.

The Lord therefore drove the sellers and buyers from the temple, saying: “It is written: ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer.’” As though he were saying: “My house has been appointed for prayer, not for selling, buying, or conducting any other secular business.”

This is plainly directed against those who turn the church of God into a storehouse, placing granaries and wine-vats in it; or who turn it into a marketplace, setting up shops there for goods or conducting lawsuits; or who turn it into a dining hall, eating and drinking there, although the church is a place of spiritual nourishment, not bodily nourishment. Therefore, my brothers, let us avoid these practices and neither do nor say anything in the oratory except what pertains to prayer, from which it also receives its name.

“But you,” he says, “have made it a den of thieves.” The priests who, out of greed, allowed a marketplace to be established in the temple were thieves, since under the pretext of religion they secretly practiced greed. The sellers and buyers were also thieves, since in their business dealings each secretly deceived the other; for trade is scarcely ever, or perhaps never, conducted without fraud.

Hence the Apostle forbids anyone to overreach or defraud his brother in business, because God is the avenger of such things (1 Thessalonians 4).

The Lord demonstrates that he possesses true charity because he does not withhold the grace of preaching even from the unworthy. Hence it is added: “And he was teaching daily in the temple.” Those whom he had rebuked and driven outside the church through the severity of justice, he sought to recall to salvation through preaching. In this he gave an example to the teachers of Holy Church: although they excommunicate and rebuke sinners, they should nevertheless always love them inwardly and hasten by every means to recall them to the church.

What the Lord did once in history, he does not cease to do spiritually every day. Through his elect, who foresee with spiritual eyes the future rejection of the wicked, he mourns for those who do not know why they are being mourned—those who rejoice when they do evil and exult in the worst things (Proverbs 2). If they foresaw their damnation, they too would weep and mourn for themselves together with the elect. Here they have their day because here they spend their days in prosperity. Here too they have their peace because they prosper along their evil way, while the punishments to come are hidden from their eyes.

Since they refuse to foresee evils that would disturb their temporal joy, they hurry toward death as though their eyes were closed. For days will come when, as their souls leave their bodies, their enemy demons will surround them with a rampart, setting the evils they have committed before them. They will surround and hem them in on every side, repeating before their eyes the iniquities not only of their deeds but also of their words and thoughts. They will throw them to the ground when their flesh is reduced to dust.

Their children too will be thrown down, when on that day all their thoughts perish (Psalm 145). These thoughts are also signified by stones, when it is added: “They will not leave in you one stone upon another.” For when a perverse soul adds an even more perverse thought to a perverse thought, it is as though it places one stone upon another. When the perverse soul is carried away to damnation, this structure of thoughts is scattered—and this because it did not recognize the time of its visitation.

God visits the perverse soul sometimes with a scourge, sometimes with a miracle, but always with a commandment. Since it does not repent even through these means, it will finally be handed over to its enemies, with whom it will be tormented eternally.

If every secular soul is punished in this way, how much more an ecclesiastical person, who by living badly destroys not only himself but others as well? This is what follows: Jesus entered the temple and began to drive out those who were selling and buying in it.

In the temple, a person sells or buys when he gives or receives for a price ecclesiastical offices that ought to be given for God alone. In the temple, a person sells when he administers justice for a bribe. In the temple, a person buys when, in order not to do what he ought, he purchases exemption from judges by paying a price. In the temple, a person sells when he sells for human praise the good works he ought to perform for God alone. In the temple, a person buys when he purchases from flatterers, by means of gifts, the reputation of being called good.

To all such people it is said: “You have made my house a den of thieves.” For while the wicked occupy a place of religion, they kill there through malice, where they ought to give life through prayer.

But because the Lord continually instructs us through the Scriptures against every form of wickedness, it is rightly added: “And he was teaching daily in the temple.”

Therefore, my brothers, we who sin every day should always keep the punishments awaiting sinners before our eyes. For it is written: “In the day of good things, do not forget evils” (Ecclesiasticus 11). And elsewhere: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful” (Proverbs 28).

Let us therefore consider that at the departure of our souls the demons will surround us and demand an account from us of all our sins. If the devil came to Christ, who said, “The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 12), then if he came to Christ, in whom he had nothing, how much more will he come to us, in whom he has many things?

Therefore, brothers, let the sweetness of this life become bitter to us. Let the sins known by the devil to be within us be washed away by penitential tears. Let fasts, almsgiving, prayers, and the other good works redeem the evils we have committed, so that the more fearful we now are concerning our souls, the more secure we may be at the departure of our souls, through the generosity of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXIV. THE ELEVENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“I make known to you the Gospel that I preached to you, which you also received, in which you also stand, through which also you will be saved” (1 Corinthians 15).

This reading, my brothers, has three parts. First, the Apostle commends his preaching. Second, he affirms Christ’s Passion, burial, and resurrection. Third, he humbles himself.

In the first place, commending his preaching, he says: “I make known to you the Gospel that I preached to you.” As though he were plainly saying: “Not as the error and fickleness of false preachers usually do—preaching one thing to you now and something else later—but the same thing that I preached to you I now also make known to you: what I preached to you by voice, conduct, and virtues when present, I make known to you in writing while absent.”

The Apostle was so diligent in instructing the Gentiles that he confirmed not only those who were present through his voice, conduct, and virtues, but also instructed those who were absent and those yet to be born through his writing. In this the negligence of myself and of preachers like me is put to shame: we instruct neither the absent through writing nor even the present through words, concealing the talent of preaching entrusted to us. Even if we sometimes preach something good in words, we destroy it through our conduct and works.

The Apostle therefore commends his preaching to the Corinthians, to whom he writes, persuading them in many ways to persevere in it.

First, he commends it by its name when he calls it the Gospel, which means “good news”—concerning faith, namely, and conduct directed toward eternal life. And what news, my brothers, can be better than that which leads us into eternal life through the truth of faith and the integrity of conduct?

Next, he commends his preaching by the authority of his apostleship, since he had been sent by God to preach, when he says: “which I preached to you.”

He also commends it by the Corinthians’ reception of it—since they had abandoned their errors and received the truth—when he adds: “which you also received.” As though he were saying: “It would be shameful for you to apostatize from the truth once you have known it.”

He commends it by its power when he adds: “in which you also stand”—standing manfully in virtues, although previously you were flowing away through vices.

He commends it by its usefulness when he adds: “through which also you will be saved”—you who previously had been destined for eternal damnation.

And what, my brothers—what ought we to hear, retain, or love more than that message which has been sent to us by God through the apostles, which, once received, must not be altered, which makes us stand firm in virtue, and which leads us to eternal salvation?

Therefore, brothers, let us always grasp the Gospel with our ears, hold it in our hearts, practice it in our works, and preach it with our words. The damnation of those who abandon the Gospel and read and love fables and vanities is certain.

“In what terms I preached it to you, if you hold it fast—unless you believed in vain.”

There is one kind of reasoning belonging to nature and another belonging to faith. The reasoning of nature is that if a woman conceives, she has had intercourse with a man; that if someone is God, he cannot die; that if someone is human, he cannot walk upon the waters; and so forth.

The reasoning of faith, however, is that he who is the author of nature is not subject to nature, but can act contrary to the principles and courses of nature: that a virgin may give birth, that the eternal may become temporal, that the immortal may die, and that a human being may walk upon the waters, and so forth.

It is concerning this reasoning, then, that the Apostle speaks here when he says: “In what terms I preached it to you, if you hold it fast—unless you believed in vain.”

He believed in vain who first believed and afterward either doubts or does not believe. He believed in vain who contradicts faith by living badly. He believed in vain who either denies or remains silent when it is necessary to confess.

The second part follows, in which the Apostle confirms Christ’s Passion, burial, and resurrection, first by the testimony of the Scriptures and then by the testimony of the apostles and of himself.

He confirms them by the testimony of the Scriptures when he says: “For I delivered to you first of all what I also received—not from a human being.” Hence he says elsewhere: “I did not receive it from a human being, nor was I taught it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (Galatians 1): “that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures; and that he was buried; and that he rose again according to the Scriptures.”

Christ’s Passion, burial, and resurrection were signified in the Scriptures not only by words but also by events. They were signified by words because Isaiah foretold his Passion, saying: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter” (Isaiah 53). Likewise: “He was wounded because of our iniquities; he was crushed because of our crimes” (ibid.).

The same prophet foretold his burial in the person of the Father: “Because of the crime of my people I struck him, and he shall give the impious for his burial and the rich man for his death” (ibid.).

Hosea also foretold his resurrection: “He will revive us after two days, and on the third day he will raise us up” (Hosea 2).

And the Psalmist, speaking in the person of Christ himself, says: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp; I will arise at dawn” (Psalm 56).

These events were also prefigured by actions. Jonah’s being cast into the sea clearly prefigured Christ’s Passion; his being received into the belly of the sea-monster, Christ’s burial; and his being returned alive to the shore, Christ’s resurrection.

Moreover, my brothers, Christ’s Passion for our sins, his burial, and his resurrection not only redeemed us from our sins, but also instilled his love in us and gave us an example.

They redeemed us from our sins because neither original nor actual sins are counted against us for punishment if we hold the faith and sacraments of the crucified one.

They instill Christ’s love in us because, by willingly dying, being buried, and rising again for us, Christ showed us how greatly he loved us and invited us more fervently to love him in return. If such a great and glorious Lord did so many and such great things for us, his servants, what ought we to do for him?

They also gave us an example. Christ suffered for us on the sixth day, rested in the tomb on the Sabbath, and rose on the eighth day, thereby showing that we too ought to labor and suffer for him through the six days of this age. Thus, when we pass from this age, we shall have rest on the Sabbath—that is, in the seventh age: rest in the tomb according to the body and in paradise according to the soul. On the eighth day—that is, in the general resurrection—we shall rise into eternal glorification.

Next, he confirms the resurrection by the testimony of Christ’s apostles when he adds: “And that he was seen by Cephas,” that is, Peter, on the very day of the resurrection. Hence Luke says: “The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon” (Luke 24). “And afterward to the Eleven,” with the doors closed, as John and Luke show (John 20; Luke 24).

Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, some of whom remain until now, while others have fallen asleep. Then he was seen by James, and afterward by all the apostles.

We do not find these two appearances described in the text of the four Gospels. From this we understand that the Lord appeared more often than the four Evangelists record.

Blessed Jerome reports that the *Gospel of the Nazarenes* describes James, the brother of the Lord, as having vowed not to eat until he saw the Lord risen from the dead. Accordingly, on the very day of the resurrection, the Lord appeared to him and said: “Set the table and eat, for the Son of Man has risen from the dead.”

“Then,” he says, “he was seen by all the apostles”—in Galilee, that is, and on the Mount of Olives on the day of the Ascension.

Confirming the same resurrection by his own testimony, the Apostle adds: “And last of all he was seen also by me”—namely, on the road, when I was going to Damascus.

The third part follows, in which the Apostle humbles himself in four respects: in his compelled conversion, in his lowliness, in his unworthiness, and in his complete lack of self-confidence.

He humbles himself through his compelled conversion when he says: “Last of all, as to an untimely birth, he appeared also to me.” An untimely birth is something extracted imperfectly from the womb before the time of birth, whose life is despaired of. Such was the Apostle: at the time when the other apostles were created, he was not created as an apostle for the preaching of Christ, but was, as it were, violently drawn from the womb of the synagogue and converted. His salvation would have been despaired of had the grace of God not come to his aid.

Indeed, my brothers, voluntary conversion is more worthy than compelled conversion. Nevertheless, many perfect men have shone forth through compelled conversion.

He humbles himself through his lowliness when he adds: “For I am the least of the apostles”—that is, I am last in calling, since I was not present with the other apostles in Christ’s familiar companionship and conversation, but was added to them afterward.

He humbles himself through his unworthiness when he adds: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle.” And why? “Because I persecuted the Church of God.”

Behold, brothers: Paul, the vessel of election and teacher of the Gentiles, who labored more than all the others, does not consider his great merits, which he had acquired through gaining countless souls, writing the teaching of the Gospel, and enduring many labors and sufferings. Instead, he kept his eyes continually on the sin he had committed and on the merits of the other apostles, so that he might always remain humble before himself and place others above himself.

Imitating him to the best of our ability, dearly beloved brothers, let us never look within ourselves at whatever good we may possess. Rather, let us always place our sins and the good qualities of others before our eyes, so that we may always humble ourselves and place others above ourselves.

He humbles himself through complete lack of self-confidence when he adds: “By the grace of God I am what I am.” As though he were saying: “Of myself I was evil. By myself, or by my merits, I am neither good nor able to become good. I am what I am solely by the grace of God, through which I also possess what I am—namely, because his grace was not empty in me.”

God’s grace is empty in the person who is ungrateful to God, or who hides his talent, or who does not persevere. The Apostle was not such a person.

He was not ungrateful, for he said: “By the grace of God I am what I am.” He did not hide his talent, for he preached continually, both alive and dead. He persevered, for neither death nor life could separate him from the love of God.

Therefore, brothers, instructed by the Apostle’s example, let us attribute nothing to ourselves and never trust in our merits. Whatever good we possess, let us attribute to the grace of God. Let us always give thanks to God as its author. Let us expend the talent entrusted to us for the benefit of others, and let us always strive to persevere in goodness, so that we may be able to attain eternal blessedness, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXV. THE ELEVENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“The Lord spoke this parable to certain people who trusted in themselves as though they were righteous and despised the others: ‘Two men went up …’” (Luke 18).

In this reading of the holy Gospel, dearly beloved brothers, the evil contained in pride and the good contained in humility are demonstrated as follows: first, the pride of certain people is described; second, a parable is brought forward against them; third, what pride deserves and what humility deserves is demonstrated.

In the first place, describing the pride of certain people, the Evangelist says: “The Lord spoke to certain people who trusted in themselves …”

There are, my brothers, four kinds of pride.

The first occurs when someone believes that the good he possesses comes not from God but from himself. By arrogating divine authority to himself, he thereby makes himself both an idol and an idolater. Such was the apostate angel, who wished to claim divinity for himself. Such were the pagan philosophers, and also many false Christians, who presume upon free will and think that they obtained what they possess through their own intelligence, strength, and labor, saying: “Our hand is exalted, and not God, has made all these things” (Deuteronomy 32).

Such was Horace, who said: “I myself shall prepare an even mind.” Such were also those of whom David says: “Our lips are from ourselves; who is our lord?” (Psalm 11). This is properly called arrogance.

Opposed to this kind of pride is that humility which believes that it possesses no good from itself.

The second occurs when someone believes that the good he possesses comes from God, but on account of his own merits. Such people—though this is a matter for sorrow—are numerous today. When riches, honors, or dignities are bestowed on them by God, they think that they received these things from God because of their merits. This is properly called presumption.

Opposed to it is that humility which says: “By the grace of God I am what I am.”

The third occurs when someone boasts that he possesses a good that he does not possess. This belongs properly to hypocrites and is properly called boastfulness. Opposed to it is that kind of humility which never wishes to be called better than it is.

The fourth occurs when someone, despising the others, desires to appear uniquely to possess what he has. This is properly called pride. Pompey was proud because he did not want to have an equal; Caesar was arrogant because he could not tolerate having a superior.

Opposed to it is that humility which conceals and hides even the good it possesses, so that it may be regarded as inferior to the others. Thus we read of a certain nun who, although exceedingly religious, pretended to be almost foolish.

The Evangelist indicates that those against whom the Lord was speaking possessed these four kinds of swelling pride. For they trusted in themselves, not in God; they thought they possessed goodness not from God but through their own effort; and they were not righteous, but despised the others as though they were righteous.

The second part follows. To confound their manifold pride, the Lord introduces a parable about a proud righteous man and a humble sinner, saying: “Two men went up into the temple to pray: one a Pharisee and the other a Publican.”

“They went up into the temple,” he says, which was literally situated in a more elevated place. Morally, whoever wishes to pray correctly must abandon the depths of vice and ascend through desire toward higher things.

“They went up,” he says, “to pray.” Behold how right their intention was. If the work of each was good in its general character and right in intention, why was neither received? Because the work of one was corrupted by the leaven of pride, while the work of the other was commended by the seasoning of humility.

So great, brothers, is the stain of pride that no matter how good a work may be, pride corrupts it. This is that small amount of leaven that corrupts the whole lump (1 Corinthians 5). Conversely, so great is the good of humility that, no matter how bad a work may be, humility corrects it.

“The Pharisee,” he says, “standing, prayed these things within himself.” This Pharisee was righteous in name, righteous in deed, and righteous in intention—unless he had corrupted his intention through the vice of pride.

He was righteous in name because Pharisees were called certain religious people who, because of their observance of religion, separated themselves from secular life. Hence they were called Pharisees, that is, “separated.”

He was righteous in deed because he avoided vices—robbery, injustice, and adultery—and performed good works, fasting and giving tithes.

He was also righteous in intention because he performed the good things he did for God’s sake and attributed everything to him, not to himself; hence he also gave thanks to God.

Yet, although he had avoided the other vices, he did not guard himself well against pride alone, which usually conquers the righteous last. But what does it profit you to exclude enemies from every other side if you admit them through one opening? Hence Solomon says: “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Proverbs 4).

Ezekiel likewise writes that the living creatures were full of eyes on every side (Ezekiel 10), because the saints must always keep watch on every side.

“I give thanks to you, Lord,” he says, “that I am not like the rest of humanity: robbers, unjust, adulterers.”

Behold, brothers, how perversely this Pharisee spoke. If he had given thanks to God for the good things bestowed on him, he would indeed have acted well. But he gives thanks not so much for his own good as for another’s evil. He gives thanks not so much because he himself has acted well as because another has sinned. He gives thanks not so much because he is good as because he is alone.

He therefore sinned in many ways: because he took less pleasure in his own good than in the evil of others; because he despised others; because, comparing himself with them, he sought glory for himself from their degradation; because he praised himself; because he listed the vices of others not with compassion but with insult; because, from general vices, he descended into personal detraction; and because, whereas he ought through charity to have covered his brother’s multitude of sins by praying before God, he appeared to accuse him before God, saying: “Like this Publican as well.”

As though he were saying: “You ought not to spare this Publican, who is not like me.”

“And the Publican, standing far off, did not dare to raise his eyes toward heaven.”

By contrast, brothers, this Publican was a sinner in name, a sinner in deed, and a sinner in conscience.

He was a sinner in name because Publicans are those who involve themselves in public crimes or public business—activities that can scarcely ever, or perhaps never, be administered without sin.

He was a sinner in deed because he was as the Pharisee described him: a robber, unjust, and adulterous.

He was a sinner in conscience, bearing witness against himself concerning himself when he said: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”

Although he was such a person, nevertheless, because he despised and humbled himself, he deserved forgiveness.

The Pharisee, considering his own virtues and the vices of others, exalted himself and despised them. The Publican, by contrast, considering his own vices and the virtues of others, despised himself and placed others above himself. Separating himself from everyone and from the sanctuary, he stood far off, judging himself more contemptible than all and unworthy of the sanctuary.

He therefore possessed the greatest humility, and with it the shame and confusion that accompany it. Hence he did not dare to lift his eyes toward heaven.

He also possessed the greatest contrition of heart, which arose from the things mentioned above. Hence he beat his breast, accusing himself, judging himself, and punishing himself. Since our heart is in our breast, whoever beats his breast shows that his heart accuses, judges, and torments him.

He also possessed true confession when he said: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” Without excuse he accused himself; without reservation he humbled himself; without any presumption concerning himself he hoped for forgiveness from grace alone.

The third part follows, in which what pride and humility deserve is demonstrated when it is added: “Amen, I say to you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other.”

The supreme Judge, who can neither be deceived nor wishes to deceive, therefore publishes his judgment concerning the merits of the proud righteous man and the humble sinner, saying: “This man went down to his house justified rather than the other”—that is, in comparison with the other.

A similar statement is read in the prophet: “Sodom has been justified by your daughters, Jerusalem” (Ezekiel 16)—that is, “In comparison with your daughters, O Jerusalem, Sodom is righteous.”

Behold, brothers, the judgment rendered by God, who searches hearts and kidneys, and who does not judge according to human appearance. What human being would not prefer someone righteous in name, deed, and conscience to someone sinful in name, deed, and conscience? No one.

But “God is terrible in his counsels concerning the sons of men” (Psalm 65). He placed before the righteous man who boasted and preferred himself to the sinner a sinner who despised and humbled himself.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, let the righteous fear, no matter how righteous he may be, and let the sinner not despair, no matter how sinful he may be.

Therefore, brothers, when we gather in church and see before us someone of infamous reputation, let us not despise that person, nor consider ourselves good by comparison with him. Through God’s working, the enormity of his sins may become an occasion for greater humility and repentance, so that he may leave more justified than we do—who, secure as though our sins had been forgiven, are not sufficiently humble or repentant.

For without doubt, the more someone humbles himself, the more he is exalted before God. Hence the general judgment is added: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

He exalts himself who thinks himself above himself, who desires to be called or seen as greater than he is. Conversely, he humbles himself who restrains himself below himself, who does not consider himself greater than he is, and who does not desire to appear or be called greater.

Therefore, brothers, since pride is the ruin even of the righteous and humility is the exaltation even of sinners, let us always humble ourselves. Let us always keep our sins before our eyes; let us always consider our weakness. Conversely, let us always admire the good qualities of others, especially those we have not yet attained.

Let us not consider whom we are greater than, but whom we are less than. Let us also reflect that those who appear inferior to us may surpass us through humility. Thus let us always live humbly, timidly, and subject to all, so that, following the example of our Lord Jesus Christ, we may strive more to serve than to be served, more to be subject than to rule, more to obey than to command.

May we deserve to have grace and reward with the humble, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXVI. THE TWELFTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

[Col. 2033D]

We have such confidence through Christ toward God—not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God (II Cor. III), etc.

This reading, my brothers, has three parts. First, it shows what kind of confidence he himself and the other apostles have in God. Second, he commends the ministry entrusted to him by God. Third, he proves that the ministry of the New Testament ought to be glorified more than that of the Old Testament.

First, then, showing what kind of confidence he himself and the other apostles have in God, he says: “We have such confidence through Christ toward God.” He says three things: in whom he has confidence, through whom, and what kind of confidence. In whom he has confidence he shows when he says, “toward God.”

The Apostle says that he has confidence in God, and by his example teaches us to have confidence in God likewise, since God alone can save, truly loves, and is truthful. Kings, princes, parents, and worldly friends, however, can save neither themselves nor us. Hence the Psalmist says: “Do not put your trust in princes, nor in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation. His spirit will go forth, and he will return to his earth” (Ps. CXLV), etc.

Nor do they truly love us, since all worldly friends love us not for our advantage but for their own. God, however, loves us not for his own advantage but for ours. Again, they are not truthful, since it is written: “Every man is a liar” (Ps. CXV). But God is truthful.

Therefore, my brothers, let us place all our confidence in God alone, not in temporal things, since parents, friends, and all temporal things have deceived us. God alone does not abandon those who hope in him. Hence it is written: “Who has hoped in the Lord and been put to shame?” (Eccles. II). And David says: “For me, it is good to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God” (Ps. LXXII).

He shows through whom he has confidence when he says, “through Christ.” Through Christ alone we have access to the Father. He is the reconciler and mediator of God and human beings; he always intercedes for us insofar as he is human, and saves us equally with the Father insofar as he is God. Therefore, my brothers, let us love him with all our inward being, since, as the Apostle says, “there is no other name in heaven or on earth by which we must be saved” (Acts IV).

What kind of confidence he has in God he shows when he says, “not that we are sufficient to think anything from ourselves.” It is as though he were saying: “We do not place confidence in ourselves, either wholly or partly, as some do, but we place all our confidence concerning everything in God.” For we have such confidence in God that we do not have confidence from ourselves even to think, much less to speak or do, anything; our confidence comes from God.

Here he confounds those who presume upon their free will, their intelligence, their strength, or their riches, since it is written: “A king is not saved by great strength, and a giant will not be saved by the multitude of his strength” (Ps. XXXII). And elsewhere: “Whoever trusts in riches will fall” (Prov. II).

But because, according to ordinary usage, we sometimes say that we think something “from ourselves,” that is, by our own reasoning, without the assistance of another creature, the Apostle adds, “as though from ourselves,” with “as authors” understood. For even if we sometimes think something from ourselves, we are nevertheless unable to think anything by our own authority—especially since we possess neither reason itself nor the ability to think anything through reason from ourselves, but from God, as Paul says: “In him we live and move and are” (Acts XVII).

But our sufficiency is from God—in all good things, that is. For in no good things, whether bodily, spiritual, or heavenly, are we able to abound except through him. Unless he works through us, our labor toward obtaining temporal things, our striving toward spiritual things, and our merit toward obtaining heavenly things are ineffective.

Hence he himself says to his disciples: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV). And the Apostle says: “It is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX). And elsewhere: “Neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth” (I Cor. III).

The second part follows, in which the Apostle commends the ministry entrusted to him by God when he adds: “Who made us competent ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the spirit.”

Thus, in three respects, he commends his own ministry and that of the other apostles: when he shows by whom they were made ministers, what kind of ministers they were made, and of what they were made ministers.

By whom? By God. Here he condemns those who assume a ministry for themselves, not from God but from themselves. Concerning such people the Lord says: “They have reigned, but not from me” (Hos. VIII).

What kind? Competent. Three things make a minister competent: a good life, a good reputation, and good preaching. One of these is not sufficient without the others.

Of what? Of the New Testament, that is, of the Gospel.

Sacred Scripture is rightly called a testament for three reasons: because it is like a document testifying to the covenant made between God and humanity; because it testifies to the divine will that we ought to do; and because it is like a testament of the inheritance promised to us by God.

The Gospel, too, is called the New Testament for three reasons: either because it was given by the new human being, Christ; or because it contains a new teaching, in comparison with the Mosaic law; or because, when observed, it makes a person inwardly new.

“Of the New Testament,” he says—“of the one established”—“not of the letter but of the spirit.”

In sacred Scripture, my brothers, there are two things: the superficial, external meaning of the letter and the inward, spiritual understanding. The superficial, external meaning of the letter has led many into error, such as Jews and heretics, because they did not attend to the sense from which, or the purpose for which, the words were spoken, but only to what they appeared externally to signify.

Hence he adds: “For the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.” This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John VI), calling the flesh the external meaning of the letter, which sometimes not only does not profit but even harms.

For all the figurative passages of the Old Testament, when understood only according to the letter, are a letter that kills. Moreover, even the moral passages, if someone establishes the cause of his righteousness in them, are a letter that kills. Likewise, certain passages in the New Testament, if understood only according to the letter, are a letter that kills, such as: “Whoever does not have a sword, let him sell his tunic and buy one” (Luke XXII).

Therefore, let the ministers of the New Testament read and understand the sacred Scriptures not according to the meaning they produce, but according to the meaning from which they arise, attending to what is said historically, mystically, tropologically, and anagogically. Thus they may be worthy, with Paul, to be competent ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the spirit.

Here, my brothers, I lament certain members of our order who know how to read neither spiritual understanding—indeed, not even the crude surface of the letter itself—blind men and guides of the blind, who are answerable for so many souls, whom through the blindness of their folly they lead into perdition.

[Col. 2036A]

The third part follows, in which the Apostle proves that the ministry of the New Testament is to be glorified more than that of the Old Testament, saying:

“If the ministry of death, formed in letters upon stones, was glorious, so that the children of Israel could not gaze upon the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance, which is passing away, how will the ministry of the spirit not be more glorious?”

It is as though he were saying: If the ministry of the letter of the law that kills, written upon stone for a time, was followed by glorification, so that the Israelites could not look upon the face of Moses, how much more will glorification follow the ministry of the spirit of the life-giving letter? Indeed, it is as though he were saying: It will.

This is an argument from the lesser. The letter is lesser, whereas spiritual understanding is greater.

He subsequently says the same thing in different words: “For if the ministry of condemnation is glorious, much more does the ministry of righteousness abound in glory.”

He calls the law death and condemnation for three reasons: because, understood according to the letter, it kills; because, by forbidding sin, it more greatly provokes people to sin; and because, without mercy, it exacted life for life.

Hence the Apostle says: “I would not have known covetousness unless the law had said, ‘You shall not covet’” (Rom. VIII).

The Gospel, however, he calls spirit and righteousness because it gives life and justifies.

The law was given to the Jews written upon stone. This signified that, just as stone scarcely receives letters, and when it receives them it receives rough or unformed ones, yet does not easily lose them, so the Jews, hard and stony, scarcely received the habituation of legal ceremonies; having received them, they held them in a crude manner, and they were unwilling to abandon them even when the Gospel came.

Hence the same Apostle says: “But even to this day, when Moses is read, a veil lies over their eyes” (I Cor. III). This veil, however, was torn away from the apostles and other spiritual men in Christ’s passion.

Nor does the ministry of the Gospel excel only the ministry of the law; the teachers and executors of the Gospel themselves also excel the teachers and executors of the law.

I do not say this, my brothers, as though some teachers and executors of the law could not have been equal or even superior to certain teachers and executors of the Gospel—as some deacons may be equal or superior to certain priests—but the excellence of the ministry and of the matter ministered is being shown in general.

Let us therefore give thanks, brothers, to the Lord our God, who has granted us, living at the end of the age, the excellence of evangelical teaching. Let us pray that he may grant us, unworthy teachers though we are, both to understand the Gospel rightly and to teach it profitably; that he may grant you, the hearers, to hear and retain it well; and that he may grant both us and you to fulfill it in conduct, works, and life.

Thus may we deserve both to be justified in the present life and to be glorified in the future, through our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who in perfect Trinity lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY XXVII. THE TWELFTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

Jesus, going out from the borders of Tyre, came through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, within the region of the Decapolis (Mark VII).

In this reading from the holy Gospel, dearest brothers, five things are proposed to us according to the literal sense: the Lord’s solicitude, the misery of the deaf and mute man, the charity of those who petitioned on his behalf, the power of the Lord who heals, and the proclamation of the miracle contrary to his command.

First, the Lord’s solicitude for the salvation of the human race is demonstrated when it is said: “Jesus, going out from the borders of Tyre,” etc. He had great concern for the salvation of human beings, and therefore traveled through the lands, cities, and fortified places in which he knew he would benefit some people.

Imitating him, dearest brothers, let us not wait to be sought out; let us ourselves seek those whom we may benefit.

Second, the misery of the one to be healed is described when he is called deaf and mute. He was greatly wretched because he was both deaf and mute. One who is mute can neither make his misery known to another nor ask for advice or help. One who is deaf cannot hear the counsel by which he might be saved.

Thus he was greatly wretched and pitiable: he could neither ask for help in his misery nor, even if it were offered, hear it. For this reason the misery of the mute and deaf is especially deserving of compassion.

Other afflicted people, even if they suffer great misery, can nevertheless disclose it and ask for help. But the more insensitive the deaf and mute person is, the more pitiable he is.

Therefore the charity of those compassionate people has pity on him. They bring him to Jesus and ask on his behalf for what he himself could not ask. They could have refrained from bringing him and merely pleaded for him, but they bring him so that his manifest and present misery may move God more strongly to compassion.

They also show greater charity toward him by not merely asking for the wretched man but by bringing him himself and presenting him.

This stands against certain hard-hearted and merciless people who do not know how to sympathize with a brother’s misery but, worse still, mock and curse the deaf because he cannot hear, and place an obstacle before the blind because he cannot see, although Moses says: “You shall not curse the deaf, nor place an obstacle before the blind” (Lev. XIX).

Let us therefore, brothers, strip ourselves of all hardness and all inhumanity. Let us learn to have a merciful heart toward the needy and afflicted, to assist them according to our ability, and, in another’s misery, to mourn our own misery, which we have experienced or may experience.

Let us imitate God and our Lord, who is merciful not only toward the righteous but also toward the unrighteous. Thus here he is moved by compassion not only toward the misery of the mute and deaf but also toward the prayer of those who show compassion.

Hence it is added: “And taking him aside from the crowd.”

Fourth, the Lord’s power is shown in three things: in teaching, in humility, and in might.

It is shown in teaching when it is said: “And taking him aside from the crowd.” Here, by his example, he teaches us that when we wish to show mercy and give alms, we should flee the crowd and the gathering of people, so that our almsgiving may be more pleasing to God the more hidden it is from human eyes.

Hence the Lord says: “When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you as the hypocrites do in the lanes and squares. But when you give alms, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing, and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matt. VI).

And elsewhere: “Hide almsgiving in the bosom of the poor, and it will itself pray for you to the Lord” (Ecclus. XXIX).

The Lord’s power is shown in humility when it is added: “He put his fingers into his ears, and, spitting, touched his tongue.”

Behold the Lord’s great humility: he does not disdain to put his holy fingers into the deaf man’s filthy ears and to touch the mute man’s unclean tongue with his holy saliva, although he could have bestowed salvation by a single word.

In this he gives us an example: if he who is absolute purity and holiness did not shrink from human uncleanness and infirmity but treated it with compassion, then human beings should not shrink from touching human beings, nor worms from worms, nor decay from decay.

Again, the Lord’s power is shown in teaching when it says: “Looking up to heaven, he groaned.” By this he instructs us, my brothers, that when we pray, or do an act of mercy or any other good, we should always look toward heaven more with the mind than with the eyes, in accordance with the Prophet’s words: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains; from there my help will come” (Ps. CXX).

Let us attribute everything to God, hoping for everything from him and in him, while groaning over ourselves and within ourselves, since of ourselves we can do nothing good.

The Lord’s power is demonstrated in might when, at his command, the deaf man is given the use of hearing and the mute man the use of speech, when he says: “Ephphatha,” which means “Be opened.”

For immediately his ears were opened, the bond of his tongue was released, and he spoke correctly.

Here the Lord demonstrates that he is the same one who in the beginning merely spoke, and all things came to be.

Fifth, the proclamation of the miracle contrary to his command is demonstrated when it is added: “And he commanded them to tell no one what they had seen,” etc.

But why, my brothers, did the Lord forbid the things he had done to be proclaimed? As an example. He offered an example of avoiding vainglory, so that we likewise, when we show mercy to another, may demand secrecy concerning our deed, lest popular acclaim corrupt it. Rather, let the deed be more pleasing to God the more hidden it is.

But because they marveled at it all the more and spoke of it, saying, “He has done all things well,” etc., he showed that the virtue that seeks concealment is more wondrous when it cannot remain concealed.

For glory flees those who seek it and follows those who despise it.

But, my brothers, should those who did not remain silent after being commanded to do so be judged guilty of disobedience? Not at all, because they did this not out of contempt but out of love.

Virtue, even if it seeks to be concealed, ought nevertheless not to be concealed. If the one who performs it hides it, the one who receives it ought not to hide it.

Nor did the Lord command his miracles to be kept hidden because he wished to conceal them; rather, he wished them to be spread more widely for the salvation of many. He prohibited this only as an example.

In the mystical sense, Jesus’ going out from the borders of Tyre—which is interpreted as “narrowness”—and coming through Sidon, that is, “hunting,” to the Sea of Galilee, within the region of the Decapolis, occurred when, because of unbelief, he abandoned the narrow confines of Judea and, proceeding by the hunt of preaching through the Decalogue of the law, passed over to the sea of the Gentiles.

For this had been foreseen by the Lord: the Gentile people would be received into the faith only through the abandonment of Judea. Hence the Prophet says: “The bed is too narrow for one to fall, and the covering is too short to cover both” (Isa. XXVIII).

At that time the Gentile people were deaf to understanding the word of God. Many in the Church are like this today: through the vice of their sin and negligence, they have a deaf ear of the heart for understanding God’s word, in accordance with the saying: “He was unwilling to understand, so that he might do good” (Ps. XXXV).

They have a mute mouth for praising God, in accordance with the saying: “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. XV).

Since they cannot worthily pray for themselves, the devotion of the faithful ought to offer them to God in prayer for healing. In response to their prayers, God often heals them, making them understand and speak the word of God, though formerly deaf and mute.

When the Lord is about to heal the deaf and mute man, he takes him aside from the crowd, showing that anyone who wishes to be completely healed of his vices must avoid the crowd of vicious people and the occasion of sin.

For it is written: “With the holy you will be holy, and with the perverse you will become perverse” (Ps. XVII). And elsewhere: “Behold, I withdrew, fleeing, and remained in solitude” (Ps. LIV).

The Lord puts his fingers into the deaf man’s ears when he pours the gifts of the Holy Spirit into a deaf heart. Hence the Prophet says: “The Lord opened my ear” (Isa. L).

He touches the mute man’s tongue with saliva when wisdom, which flows from the highest head—that is, from God the Father—makes a mute person eloquent and fluent in preaching the word of God. Hence it is said of the same wisdom that it makes the tongues of infants eloquent (Wis. X).

He says “Ephphatha,” which means “Be opened,” when by his most powerful command he orders the heart to be opened for understanding and the tongue for speaking the word of God.

Hence these words are also spoken in the catechism of those being baptized, when their ears and nostrils are touched with saliva.

“And immediately his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was released, and he spoke correctly.” With God working visibly within, the one who had been deaf and mute immediately becomes understanding and eloquent in the word of God.

Recognizing his former deafness and silence, he understands and blesses his Creator.

Therefore, brothers, if by God’s grace we already have the ears of our hearts open for understanding and a mouth for proclaiming the word of God, let us magnify the divine goodness. Let us offer to the Lord our brothers who are still deaf and mute, so that he may heal them, begging him to place upon them the hand of his mercy and make them understand, proclaim, and carry out his holy word.

Thus, together with them, may we deserve eternally to contemplate and praise the divine majesty, by the favor of him who in perfect Trinity lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY XXVIII. THE THIRTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“Promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed” (Gal. III), etc.

In this reading, dearest brothers, the Apostle argues against certain Jews who thought that they possessed righteousness and salvation through the works of the law. There are also similar people today—which is cause for grief—certain false Christians who, because they avoid some vices and perform good works, think that they are righteous and will attain salvation.

The Psalmist confounds both groups when he cries out in prayer: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O Lord, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. CXLII). And the Prophet says: “All our righteousnesses are like a menstruous cloth before you, O Lord” (Isa. LXVI).

Therefore, my brothers, if we wish to be true Christians, let us hold firmly to this faith: we cannot be justified or saved by any of our works, but only by the grace of God, who freely justifies the ungodly.

We are not justified because we have done good things. Rather, because we are freely justified by God, we do good things, and by doing good we are saved.

The Apostle therefore shows three things: first, that salvation comes to us only by grace; second, that this grace comes through Jesus Christ; third, that it does not come through the law.

Showing that salvation comes by grace, he says: “Promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed.” It is as though he were saying openly: The promises were made to Abraham and freely given, not on account of works of the law or of any preceding merits.

These are properly called promises that are made entirely freely, especially if you consider by whom, what kind, and to whom these promises were made.

By whom? By God, who can be bound neither by any necessity, nor by his own advantage, nor by any debt.

He cannot be bound by necessity, because he is wholly free—indeed, freedom itself. He cannot be bound by his own advantage, because he needs nothing. Nor can he be bound by debt, because he is subject to no one.

Although he has promised, he is not bound by the obligation of his promise, since he promised only to those who are worthy—and no one can be worthy unless God freely wills to make that person worthy. Thus, in general, grace has accomplished everything: what he promised, what he makes worthy, and what he grants as promised.

What promises were spoken to Abraham by God is read in Genesis: namely, that all nations would be blessed in his seed. This is understood as a spiritual and eternal blessing more than a bodily and temporal one; and that he would give him a land flowing with milk and honey, signifying the land of the living, which remains forever, flowing with the milk of true wisdom and the sweetness of heavenly grace.

To whom were these promises made? To Abraham and to his seed—that is, to those who are fathers of many nations through faith, teaching, and example, and to those who imitate their faith, teaching, and example.

Therefore, my brothers, if we wish to share in the holy promises spoken to Abraham, let us be holy and imitate Abraham and the other holy fathers. Let us be strong in faith, obedient to God in all things, placing God before everything, instructed in spiritual and heavenly matters, distinguished in life, fervent in charity, outstanding in hospitality, fathers to others by our example, and, by our life and conduct, the light of the world.

Second, the Apostle demonstrates that grace has come through Jesus Christ alone when he adds: “He does not say, ‘And to seeds,’ as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: ‘And to your seed,’ which is Christ.”

That is, the Lord said to Abraham: “In your seed all nations will be blessed” (Gen. XII).

He says “seed” in the singular, not “seeds” in the plural, signifying that divine blessing would be brought to all nations not through several persons born from Abraham’s stock but through Jesus Christ alone.

For he did not say that all nations would be blessed in the patriarchs, or in the prophets, or in the priests, or in the Israelite kings, but in Christ alone, in accordance with what Jacob foretold: “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor the ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent, and he will be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX).

He, uniting the two peoples—the Jews and the Gentiles—in himself as head and cornerstone, conveyed to all from the fullness of the graces and blessings with which he was anointed without measure.

This was signified by the oil poured upon Aaron’s head, which descended upon his beard and even to the hem of his garment (Ps. CXXXII).

Would that Christ might also deign to let something of the fullness of his graces and blessings drip upon us, his final members, so that, just as he has given us the designation of his name in the name “Christian,” he might also grant us some share in the outpouring of his immense anointing and blessing.

“Now this I say: a testament confirmed by God.”

What testament? The testament of free promises—or of promised graces. I say that it was confirmed by God the Father in the time of grace through the death of the testator, Jesus Christ; this is called the New Testament.

If we truly follow and hold to it, dearest brothers, we are here pledged by the grace of new justification, and in the future we will inherit eternal blessedness.

Third, the Apostle demonstrates that salvation does not come from the law.

First, he proves this by the fact that when the promises of future salvation were made to Abraham, the law had not yet been given; indeed, it was not given until four hundred and thirty years later.

This is what he says: “The law, which was made four hundred and thirty years afterward, does not annul the covenant so as to abolish the promise.”

It is as though he were saying: If the law were necessary for obtaining the promised inheritance, it should have been given together with the promise, so that it might define the promise—namely, that the promised inheritance could not be obtained except through the law.

But this did not happen. After the promise had been made, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob died before the law was given, and yet they obtained the inheritance.

Therefore, from the fact that the law was given such a long time after the promise, it is clear that the law does not annul or abolish the promise—that is, the works of the law do not destroy the grace of the promise.

Likewise, my brothers, after we have been freely called to the faith, if afterward we perform certain good works, the grace of God is not thereby abolished, nor is God thereby compelled to reward us as though by debt. Rather, the one who freely calls freely justifies and freely rewards.

Second, he proves by indirect reasoning that salvation does not come from the law when he adds: “For if the inheritance comes from the law, it no longer comes from the promise.”

This is an argument from opposites, for merits and grace are opposites. It is therefore as though he were saying: If the inheritance is given on the basis of the merit of legal observance, then it no longer comes from the grace of the promise.

He immediately assumes this by destroying the consequent, adding: “But God granted it to Abraham through a promise.”

From these words the unspoken conclusion follows: Therefore the inheritance does not come from the law.

We may reason similarly: If salvation comes to us from our merits and works, then it no longer comes from grace. But it is certain that salvation is given to us by grace; therefore it is not given to us from our merits and works.

The question that the Apostle saw could be raised, he raises and answers, adding: “What, then, is the law?” It was set in place because of transgressions, so that they might be avoided and punished.

It is as though he were saying: The law was not established to abolish grace but rather to abolish and correct sin.

For the commandments of the Old and New Testaments were not given, my brothers, so that salvation might be given through their observance as through its cause, but so that through them we might be corrected and instructed in how we could attain salvation.

Many people were righteous before the law and attained salvation. Hence the Apostle says: “The law was not established for the righteous but for the unrighteous, the ungodly, and sinners” (I Tim. I).

“It was established,” he says, “not forever, but until the seed should come”—that is, until our Lord Jesus Christ should come, in whom God had promised that all nations would be blessed.

The law was ordained—that is, established in an orderly manner—in the intervening period between the time of the natural law and the time of grace.

First, my brothers, human pride had to be convicted by the natural and written law. Once a person understood that, by the powers of free will, he could be justified or saved neither by the natural law nor by the written law, he would flee to grace and, despairing of himself, place all his hope in God’s grace.

The law was ordained through angels—that is, through the ministry of angels, through whom the Lord spoke to Moses.

Or certainly, he calls Moses and Aaron and the other teachers of the law “angels,” that is, messengers of God. Yet they were only ministers of the law, not its authors, because the law was in the hand—that is, in the power and authority—of the mediator between God and human beings, Jesus Christ, who, as Lord of all, had the power to establish the law whenever he wished.

Through him alone—something that could not be accomplished through the law—grace, peace, and reconciliation between God and human beings are brought about.

This is clear from the statement: “But the mediator is not of one party; God, however, is one.”

It is as though he were saying openly: Since a mediator is properly one who, by participating in and coming between two opposing parties, brings them into agreement with one another, if Christ were only of the divine nature or only of the human nature, he would not be the mediator of God and human beings.

For, my brothers, you sometimes see among worldly people that when two tribes are hostile to one another, a man from one tribe is given in marriage to a woman of the other tribe, so that through that marriage the two tribes may be reconciled.

Thus, when there was hostility between God and humanity, it pleased the Most High to reconcile to himself the human being who had fled from him and was his enemy, joining his Son to human nature so that he might be both God and human being. Through him, God might be reconciled to humanity and humanity to God.

Since the law was established after God’s promise and only for a time, does this mean, Paul says, that the law is contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not!

The law would indeed be contrary to the promises of God if righteousness and life came from the law rather than from the grace of the promise.

But the Apostle shows that this is not so, saying: “For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would truly come from the law”—with “and life as its consequence” understood.

But this is not so.

For it is universally true, my brothers, that we cannot be justified or saved either by our free will, or by observance of the law, or by any of our works or virtues, but only by the mercy of God, which freely justifies the ungodly.

The law not only did not justify the Jews; it also increased sin.

Hence it is added: “But Scripture confined all things under sin.” For, by occasion, it provoked some people more strongly to sin, in accordance with the poetic saying:

> We always strive after what is forbidden, and desire what is denied.  
> (Ovid, *Amores* III, elegy 4, line 17)

As a sick man presses toward forbidden waters.

It also caused some people, by occasion, to boast and become proud of the works of the law.

But it confined all people under sin—that is, it showed that they were confined—by forbidding covetousness.

For since no one, however righteous, can at some time avoid coveting altogether, the law demonstrated that all were confined under sin and were transgressors of the law.

And why did it do this? “So that the promise might be given to those who believe through faith in Jesus Christ.”

It is as though he were saying: The Lord permitted all people to be confined under sin so that it might become evident that the promise of the eternal inheritance would be given to believers solely through the grace that is in faith in Jesus Christ.

Therefore, my brothers, let us lay aside all self-glorification and all pride of mind, and recognize that the evil within us comes from ourselves.

If we have any good, let us understand that we have received it not from ourselves but from God alone, and have received it freely.

And in accordance with the Lord’s command, when we think that we have done everything, let us say that we are “unprofitable servants” (Luke XVII)—unprofitable, indeed, of ourselves. If we are useful in anything, it is from God, who, when we were children of wrath and perdition, freely calls us to be his children, freely justifies those whom he calls, and freely blesses those whom he justifies—provided that we are not ungrateful for his grace, that we do not possess his grace idly but actively, and that we multiply the talent entrusted to us and return it to the Lord with manifold profit.

May he himself deign to grant this to us, who in perfect Trinity lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY XXIX. THE THIRTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY
Jesus said to his disciples: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see” (Luke 10). In this reading, dearly beloved brothers, three things are demonstrated. First, it is shown that those who see what the apostles saw are blessed. Second, the lawyer is presented asking and explaining how eternal blessedness may be attained. Third, in response to his question, the Lord shows who or what kind of person one’s neighbor ought to be.

The Lord therefore says to his disciples: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see.” Some, however, saw Christ only bodily, such as the persecuting Jews; others only spiritually, such as later Christians; and others both bodily and spiritually, such as the apostles and disciples. But the Jews, who saw Christ only bodily, were not blessed on that account; rather, they became worse. For although they saw Christ’s miracles and works and heard his preaching, they took care not to believe but to disparage him, and so they became more depraved. Hence the Lord says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15).

But we who follow him, seeing Christ only spiritually and with the eyes of faith, are undoubtedly blessed if we hold fast to the life of faith. Yet more blessed are the disciples, who saw, heard, and handled Christ simultaneously with the eyes of the body and the eyes of the heart, and ate and drank with him. What sweetness, what love, what strength, do you suppose, my brothers, Christ’s present bodily fellowship conferred upon the disciples? Perceiving the hidden divinity through his outward miracles, they believed and preached him all the more firmly the more clearly they saw him. Hence John says: “What was from the beginning, what we have seen, what we have heard, what our hands have handled concerning the Word of life, we announce to you” (1 John 1).

But you may say: Did not the Lord say to Thomas, “Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20)? And Gregory says concerning this: “Faith has no merit when human reason supplies the evidence.” Those who did not see Jesus in the flesh yet believed therefore seem to be more blessed. Indeed, if faith without sight were as great as the faith strengthened by bodily sight, it would plainly seem to possess not lesser but greater merit. Yet, brothers, it can scarcely happen that someone who has not seen the Lord except spiritually should have as firm a faith as one who saw him both bodily and spiritually. Things tasted are believed in one way; things merely smelled are believed in another.

For many kings and prophets wished to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it. How great, brothers, do you suppose was the desire of the ancient saints who knew in the spirit that Christ was to come; how great their sighs, how great their wonder! Their desires, sighs, and wonder are signified by the seven antiphons sung for seven days before the Lord’s Nativity. They begin with “O,” an adverb expressing desire and wonder, as when they are sung in the second tone, almost as if lamenting: “O Wisdom, O Adonai”—as though asking, “When will you come? When shall we see you? When shall we hear you?”

[Col. 2045A]
