The second part follows, when it is added: “And behold, a certain lawyer stood up, testing him, and saying: ‘Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?’” Although the lawyer’s eyes saw the Lord outwardly, they did not see in him the things the disciples saw. They did not see divinity in his humanity, majesty in his humility, or wisdom in what appeared foolishness. For he had a film over his eye—that is, pride in his knowledge. Such a person is rejected from God’s ministry. Humble knowledge sees; proud knowledge does not see.

The lawyer’s proud knowledge puffed him up but did not build him up. Thus he is shown to have been elevated, boastful, and contemptuous because of the knowledge he possessed without humility. He was elevated when it says, “he stood up,” for he should be understood to have raised himself more in mind than in body. He was boastful and contemptuous when he asked about what he already knew—not in order to learn or teach, but to flaunt his knowledge and mock another’s simplicity.

Such, sadly, are many teachers today. Inflated by their learning, they read and dispute not to benefit themselves or others, but to display themselves and confuse the simple. Although they may know many books, they certainly do not see the divine wisdom in humility, because they have a film over their eye. Of them it is said: “Claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Romans 1), since their words of wisdom have no taste of wisdom.

But the Lord, who knew that he had asked this in order to test him, said: “What is written in the law? How do you read it?” The Lord grants the lawyer an opportunity to play the teacher, knowing that this was what he most desired. For proud knowledge often presumes to teach even when it has not been questioned, but it rejoices especially when questioned, because it has found an opportunity to play the teacher and display itself—the very thing it most desired.

“You shall love,” he says, “the Lord your God.” This commandment shows why God should be loved and to what extent. Why should he be loved? For three reasons. First, because he is good in himself; this is implied by the word “God.” Second, because he has deserved to be loved by us, having created, nourished, and redeemed us; this is implied when he is called “Lord.” Third, because he gives himself as the reward to those who love him; this is implied by the word “your.”

The extent to which he is to be loved is shown when it says: “With all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength”—that is, with all that you know, with all that you live, and with all that you can. It is as though it said: Direct all your powers, strength, virtues, movements, and actions toward loving God.

But what, my brothers, is the purpose of such an insistence upon these words? Would it not have been enough to say simply, “With all your heart”? It was said for greater clarity; and if it could have been expressed more clearly, it would have been expressed more clearly, because what is never sufficiently done can never be sufficiently said. God can never be loved enough by us. No one will love him as much as he deserves and as much as he is worthy to be loved.

“And your neighbor,” he says, “as yourself.” He does not say, “as much as yourself”—for no one is required to do that—but “as yourself.” We ought not to love ourselves except for the sake of the good and toward the good, that is, so that we may become good. Likewise, we ought to love our neighbor only in the good and toward the good: in the good that he already possesses, or so that he may possess it—in other words, we should wish our neighbors to have the good that we wish for ourselves.

Let us therefore love both ourselves and our neighbors with discernment, my brothers. For just as one sins by not loving the good in one’s neighbor, so one sins by not hating the evil in him. “Do this,” he says, “and you will live.” It is as though he said: “It is not enough merely to know this, which is what you boast about.”

The third part follows. The lawyer, knowing that “neighbor” can be understood in several ways—by kinship, familiarity, faith, disposition, or location—asks who is meant by “neighbor” in this passage. He wished thereby to justify himself, that is, to display himself as a prudent and righteous questioner.

And Jesus, looking up toward heaven—thereby signifying that he was about to speak of great and spiritual matters—said: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among robbers,” and so forth.

In this parable, my brothers, the Lord shows who our neighbor is: everyone who shares our nature. He also shows what a neighbor ought to be toward another neighbor: kind and merciful through love and compassion. According to the mystical meaning, the Lord shows that he is nearer to the human race than all others, not only according to the flesh but also according to the love, compassion, and redemption that he bestowed upon us undeserving people. As he himself says: “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15).

Four things are shown in this parable: the fall of the human race, the devil’s persecution, the insufficiency of the law, and Christ’s mercy.

The fall of the human race is shown when it says: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among robbers.” This man is the human race, which, in the first man, descended when it tried to ascend through pride. For it is written: “The heart is exalted before destruction” (Proverbs 16).

He therefore descended from the heavenly Jerusalem, for which he had been created, into Jericho—that is, into the decline of this world. Jericho is interpreted as “decline” or “moon.” And by sinning he fell among robbers, that is, under the power of demons, who secretly concealed their snares under the guise of the serpent and of upright counsel.

The devil’s manifest persecution is immediately shown when it adds that they “also stripped him,” namely, of gratuitous goods such as virtues and their fruits. They also inflicted wounds—understand, in his natural goods, such as intellect, memory, and the like. They deprived him completely of his gratuitous goods; they did not deprive him completely of his natural goods, but they impaired them within him.

“And they went away”—not ceasing to harm him, but hiding themselves—leaving him half dead. From whom and to whom? From God, and to himself as man. For because of his sin he was deprived of divine assistance and abandoned to his own will. Yet he was not entirely dead, but half alive. The devil could not completely remove from man the spark of reason which, even when he sins, says to him, “You are doing wrong.”

The insufficiency of the law is shown when it says:

[Col. 2047A]

“And it happened that a certain priest went down the same road, and, seeing him, passed by. Likewise, a Levite, when he was near the place and saw him, passed by.”

The priest and Levite going down the same road are the priesthood and ministry of the law, whose ministers likewise fell into the same misery. When they were near him and saw him, they passed by, because the priests and ministers of the law knew the misery of the human race, and were near it through experience and compassion; but, unable to bring assistance, they passed by. The law displayed sins but did not remove them.

Christ’s mercy is shown when it adds:

“But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came near him.”

The Samaritan, whose name is interpreted as “guardian,” is Christ, the guardian of human beings. Journeying from heaven into the world, he became man’s neighbor through his humanity. Seeing the man’s miseries, he was moved with compassion.

And “coming near,” through compassion, “he bound up his wounds,” through correction and repentance, “pouring in oil and wine”—that is, sweetness and hope of pardon, and the severity of threats. He binds his wounds when he cries out: “Repent” (Matthew 3). He pours in oil when he adds: “For the kingdom of heaven is near” (ibid.). He pours in wine when he says: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (ibid.).

He “placed him on his own beast” when he carried the man’s sins in his own body upon the wood. He “brought him to an inn” when he placed him in the bosom of holy Church to be restored. He “took care of him” when he sends human beings prosperity at one time and adversity at another, as he knows will be beneficial.

“On the next day”—that is, after the Ascension—“he brought out two denarii,” giving the teacher of the Church knowledge of both Testaments and saying to him: “Take care of him,” by correcting, teaching, strengthening, and admonishing him. “Whatever more you spend”—by adding new interpretations, admonitions, and examples—“when I return, I will repay you,” when I return to repay each person according to his merits.

“Which of these three,” he asks, “seems to have been neighbor to the man who fell among robbers?”

“The one who showed mercy to him,” he says.

In this, my brothers, it is shown that kinship of race or flesh is nothing in comparison with the kinship that belongs to love and compassion. Since this was more abundant in Christ than in others, he is more truly our neighbor than all others and is more to be loved. After him, too, whoever is the greater imitator of him is more our neighbor and more to be loved.

Hence it is also added: “Go, and you do likewise.” That is, just as Christ acted for us, so let us act for him: loving him above all things; laying down ourselves and what belongs to us for him; showing love and compassion for every person for his sake; forgiving those who persecute us for the injuries they inflict; winning the wicked for God through word and example; comforting the afflicted; receiving strangers; clothing the naked; feeding the hungry; redeeming captives; and performing other similar acts of piety for Christ in his members, so that from him we may receive the final and eternal blessing. Amen.

HOMILY XXX. THE FOURTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY.

[Col. 2048A]

“Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh” (Galatians 5), and so forth.

Here the Apostle does four things, my brothers. First, he warns us not to live according to the flesh. Second, he demonstrates how great the conflict is between flesh and spirit. Third, he shows what the desires of the flesh are and what harm they cause. Fourth, he demonstrates what the desires of the spirit are and what benefit they confer.

First, therefore, warning us to live according to the spirit and not according to the flesh, the Apostle says: “Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh.” He is plainly saying: “You will not fulfill the desires of the flesh.” This is an argument from opposites. The desires of the spirit and the desires of the flesh are opposed, so much so that no one in this life can fulfill the desires of both simultaneously.

The desires of the spirit are to despise the world, to long for heavenly things with all one’s strength, to be content with little, to love fasting, sobriety, watchfulness, chastity, moderation, justice, and the other virtues. Conversely, the desires of the flesh are to love the world, despise heavenly things, abound in earthly riches, feast, become drunk, sleep, live in lust, live extravagantly and unjustly, and the like.

The Apostle does not say: “Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the necessities of the flesh.” For we can indeed both live spiritually and satisfy the necessities of the flesh—for example, by eating, drinking, and sleeping moderately, possessing things moderately, and doing similar things. Hence, when Paul writes to the Romans, he does not say, “Do not care for the flesh,” but says carefully: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Romans 13), allowing necessity and forbidding excess.

Again, the Apostle does not say: “You will not be moved by the desires of the flesh,” especially since our carnal movements are not in our power. Rather, he says: “You will not fulfill the desires of the flesh,” that is, you will not bring them to effect. We can therefore live spiritually and yet sometimes be moved by the desires of the flesh; but we cannot both live spiritually and bring the desires of the flesh to effect.

Therefore, my brothers, let us strive to live spiritually, so that, even if we cannot entirely remove the shameful desires arising within us, we may nevertheless restrain and bridle them. For blessed David says: “Blessed is he who will seize”—that is, restrain—“and dash his little ones against the rock” (Psalm 136), that is, against Christ.

The second part follows, in which the great conflict between spirit and flesh is shown when it adds: “For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do whatever you wish.”

The flesh often prevents us from doing the will of the spirit, and the spirit often prevents us from doing the will of the flesh. Here, dearly beloved brothers, five matters seem to require examination.

First: Why is the flesh said to desire against the spirit, when the flesh can do nothing except through the spirit?

In this passage, my brothers, “flesh” does not mean flesh alone but sensuality together with the flesh. There are two powers or faculties: the higher, which is the spirit, and the lower. The higher is reason, which contemplates and seeks heavenly things. The lower is sensuality, which desires and seeks only temporal things through the body’s five workshops—that is, its five senses.

The higher part is therefore called the spirit, or the inner person. The lower part, together with the flesh, is called the flesh, or the outer person, because it derives from the flesh alone the fact that it desires and seeks temporal things. Hence a person who lives according to sensuality is called a carnal person, indeed wholly flesh; conversely, one who lives according to the spirit is called a spiritual person, indeed even spirit.

Second: Whence comes such great opposition between spirit and flesh—that is, between reason and sensuality—that one desires against the other?

It comes from the fault of the first parent. Before the fault, God had created and ordered man so that he felt no rebellion within himself. The spirit was subject and obedient to its Creator, while the flesh, or sensuality, obeyed the spirit in everything without contradiction. But because the spirit became disobedient to God through sin, its lower part consequently and deservedly refused to obey it—that is, carnality together with its senses.

This is why Adam saw himself naked after the sin: he recognized that he had been stripped of the grace and dominion that he possessed over his members. This opposition in man therefore arises not from nature, but rather is a punishment inflicted because of sin.

Third: Why does the Lord not remove this opposition from his servants?

Because, my brothers, the Lord knows that it is useful to his servants in three ways. It makes them humbler, so that they do not presume upon themselves: when they see that they can overcome their inward rebellion not by themselves but only through grace. It makes them more merciful toward others, for from their own misery they learn how they ought to show mercy to others. And it makes them more victorious. The greater the battle they feel and overcome, the greater the crown they will obtain.

Fourth: How can we obtain victory in this inward and most familiar conflict?

Not through ourselves, my brothers, but through God’s grace alone. Hence the Apostle says: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?”—“The grace of God through Jesus Christ” (Romans 7).

But since God’s grace does not come to those who sleep, if we wish to overcome this rebellion within us, we must apply ourselves diligently to prayer and to the mortification of the flesh. We must continually watch over the movements of our heart and flesh, utterly extinguishing evil movements when they arise and correcting good ones even when they go too far.

Let us not be like certain carnal people who recognize no rebellion within themselves, but accept every movement that arises and resist no temptation. Let us also pray and seek help from above against our evil impulses, saying with the Psalmist: “Lord, burn our kidneys and our heart” (Psalm 25)—that is, “purify our inward parts with the fire of the Holy Spirit, so that they do not take pleasure in evil and the heart does not think evil.”

Let us also mortify the flesh with fasts, prayers, and labors, and compel it to serve the spirit, because among two rebels, the weaker one becomes, the stronger the other is. Hence the Apostle says: “When I am weak, then I am stronger and powerful” (2 Corinthians 12)—understand, according to the spirit.

Fifth: If, as the Apostle says, “we do not do what we want,” or “we do what we do not want” (Romans 7), how can these acts be counted to us for reward or punishment?

There are two contrary wills in a person: one belonging to reason, the other to sensuality or the flesh. We judge unwilling persons according to the will that prevails.

Every evil person wishes to be saved according to the will of reason, but according to the will of the flesh he does not wish this, since through it he performs actions contrary to that will. Because the will of the flesh prevails in him over the will of the mind, he must be judged more unwilling than willing to be saved.

Similarly, a good person may wish, according to the will of the flesh, to know another man’s wife; but according to the will of the spirit he does not wish this, and he restrains the will of the flesh. Such a person should be said to be more unwilling than willing to know the woman.

Because of this twofold will Solomon says: “The sluggard both wills and does not will” (Proverbs 13). Everything we do, my brothers, ought therefore to be counted to us according to the will that prevails, not according to the will that is overcome.

Let us therefore restrain the will of the flesh within us and nourish the good will of the spirit within us. “But if you are led by the spirit,” he says, “you are not under the law.” Carnal and sinful people are constrained under the law; spiritual people, however, have no need of the law, since they are governed by their own reason. Hence the Apostle says: “The law was not established for the righteous, but for the unrighteous and sinners” (1 Timothy 1).

The third part follows, in which the Apostle enumerates the desires of the flesh, saying: “The works of the flesh are manifest; they are fornication, impurity, immodesty, lust, the service of idols,” and so forth.

Fornication is every sexual union apart from the lawful one. Impurity is every sexual union contrary to nature. Immodesty is every shamelessness expressed in words, movements, or dissolute gestures. Lust is every extravagance in food, clothing, or any other excess.

The service of idols is twofold: first, that of those who offer to a creature the worship owed to God; second, that of those who place a creature before the Creator—for example, the greedy person who puts money before God, the lustful person who puts a prostitute before God, and the glutton who puts his belly before God.

Sorceries are those things performed through poisons or magical arts. Enmities occur when people hate not vices but the persons themselves. Contentions are verbal battles over something useless, or over something useful pursued uselessly. Rivalries are the envy of wicked people at another’s prosperity. David warns us against them, saying: “Do not rival the wicked, nor envy those who do iniquity; for like grass they will quickly wither” (Psalm 36), and so forth.

Anger consists of disturbances of the mind against a person rather than against a vice, or against a vice immoderately. Quarrels are alternating and insulting lacerations, like those of dogs; hence they are called *rixae* from *ringo, ringis*, “to snarl.” Dissensions occur when some stubbornly disagree with the truth or with common practice. Sects occur when some divide the unity of faith, love, or community.

Envy occurs when people burn with resentment over the good fortune of others. Concerning it the poet says: “Nothing is more justly condemned than envy, which immediately condemns and torments its own author.”

Homicides are spoken of in the plural because there are six kinds of homicide. Drunkenness consists of frequent and immoderate drinking. Revelries consist of frequent and immoderate feasting.

“And things like these,” he says—understand, the vices that I proclaim to you, as I previously proclaimed them—so that you may beware of them while you have time for repentance and amendment. For those who do such things—understand, finally—will not obtain the kingdom of God; that is, they will be damned. There is no middle state.

Therefore, my brothers, guard yourselves from such things with every care. And if perhaps you have sometimes done such things, remember, while it is permitted, to wash yourselves clean with the tears of repentance.

The fourth part follows, in which the Apostle enumerates the desires of the spirit, saying: “The fruits of the light are love, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, faith, gentleness, moderation, self-restraint, chastity.”

But why, when speaking of vices, does the Apostle say “works of the flesh,” while speaking of virtues he says “fruits of the light”? Because vices, like perishable works, quickly fall and pass away, whereas virtues, like fruits, multiply, enlighten the mind, and draw it toward eternal light.

He places love—that is, love of God and neighbor—before the other virtues because it is the source and origin of all virtues. Once it is possessed, the others are possessed as well; and whoever does not possess it has become guilty of everything.

The joy meant is not worldly joy, whose end is occupied by grief, but spiritual joy, which consists in hope or in the possession of spiritual and eternal good.

The peace meant is not that of which the Lord says, “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matthew 10), but the peace by which a person is reconciled to God, to himself, and to his neighbor.

Patience is equanimity in enduring adversity. Long-suffering is the virtue by which we endure adversity for a longer period without weariness and hope for rewards. Faith is the apprehension, with assent, of invisible things pertaining to salvation. Goodness is the virtue that detests every form of wickedness. Kindness is the virtue that is ready and prepared to do good. Gentleness is the virtue that makes us tractable and humble in obeying. Moderation is the virtue that restrains evil impulses within us and every form of excess. Self-restraint is the virtue that abstains even from things permitted. Chastity is the virtue that cuts away every lust within us.

And what benefit do these things confer? Freedom from the yoke of the law and from vices. Hence it adds: “Against such things there is no law”—that is, the law neither condemns nor oppresses such people as it does the Jews.

“But those who belong to Christ,” he says, “have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires.” That is, those who possess the virtues of Christ mentioned above have put their vices and carnal desires to death within themselves and live for God.

Therefore, let us put vices and the wantonness of the flesh to death within us through fasts, vigils, labors, and prayers. Let us devote ourselves to love, peace, patience, chastity, and the other virtues, so that, dead to the world, we may live for God—living here by spiritual life and in the future by heavenly life—through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

HOMILY XXXI. THE FOURTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY.

“When Jesus was going to Jerusalem, he passed through the middle of Samaria and Galilee. And as he entered a certain village, ten leprous men met him” (Luke 17).

In this reading from the holy Gospel, dearly beloved brothers, six things are first to be considered according to the literal sense: the Lord’s concern for human salvation; his ready compassion; his observance of the law; the lepers’ faith and obedience; the divine power possessed by Christ; how great a good gratitude is and how great an evil ingratitude is.

The Lord’s concern for human salvation appears in this: having descended from heaven to earth for the salvation of human beings, while he was on earth he was always concerned with the same matter. He went about amid labor and thirst, and, because of plots against him, traveled from place to place, going around cities, villages, and places where he knew he would find someone predestined to life. Thus he might gather the children of God who were scattered, as he himself says, into one body (John 11).

In this he gave the pastors of holy Church an example that they should do the same. Following him, the apostles did this, and so did the other Fathers. Setting aside their own rest, they went through labors, hardships, and dangers to win souls for God.

Alas! What shall I say about the laziness of modern pastors? They disdain the salvation of souls and never leave their leisure unless perhaps financial gain draws them out. If a poor person lying on a pallet should call them to him to ask their counsel concerning his soul, they become indignant and refuse to go when they know that there is no financial profit. Or, if they reluctantly go because they fear the authority of their superiors, they complain about the weather and the roads and curse the sick, for whom they ought to have prayed.

Such men are not to be counted among pastors, but among hirelings.

Christ’s compassion appeared in this: when he saw the ten lepers, he took pity on them, giving us an example that we should always have within us the bowels of mercy toward the affliction of the wretched. Hence elsewhere he says: “Be merciful, as your heavenly Father is merciful” (Luke 6).

This directly opposes those who, as though they were made of iron, are moved by no compassion toward the misery of others. But as James says: “Judgment without mercy will be shown to the one who has not shown mercy” (James 2).

Christ also demonstrates that he observes the law when, in accordance with what was written in the law, he sends the lepers to the priests.

If we examine the matter carefully, brothers, the Lord sent the lepers to the priests for three reasons. The first was to demonstrate thereby that he was not destroying the law but fulfilling it. The second was to honor the priests and to demonstrate that they ought to be honored and that offerings ought to be made to them.

Hence those who refuse to honor or defer to the Lord’s priests because of the baseness of their way of life are refuted. They do not consider that we honor not the minister in himself but God in the minister, and that we entreat and offer to the priest not for his own sake but to God in him.

The third reason was to signify that spiritual leprosy—that is, mortal guilt—must be disclosed to the priest through confession.

The lepers also testified that they possessed faith and hope when they cried out: “Jesus, have mercy on us.” Unless they had believed that he could bestow such mercy upon them, they would never have asked this of him; and unless they had hoped for it, they would not have asked him for healing.

They also displayed obedience to the Lord when, at his command, they immediately ran to the priests.

But let us consider, my brothers, how great is the power of faithful obedience. It is not written here that they reached the priests; rather, they were cleansed while they had begun and intended to go, and their will was counted as the deed.

Here, brothers, let us strive to possess the virtue of faith and obedience. If you have faith and obedience, even if you cannot do what you are commanded, do what you can, and it will be counted as the deed. For as Samuel says: “Obedience is better than sacrifices” (1 Samuel 15).

We read in the *Lives of the Fathers* that when a certain abbot wished to test the obedience of a novice, he commanded him to leap into a burning oven. When the novice had leaped into it immediately at his word, he came out unharmed.

Maurus also, at the command of Saint Benedict, walked upon the water like Peter when he drew the boy Placid from the waters.

Why say more? The goodness of obedience is demonstrated by the evil of the first parent’s disobedience.

The Lord also demonstrated that he possessed divine power when he healed the lepers while they were absent, without the aid of any action or word, by his will alone. He wished to demonstrate openly that he is the one of whom the Prophet sings: “But the Lord is in heaven; he has done whatever he has willed” (Psalm 93).

How great a good gratitude is, and how great an evil ingratitude is, is shown when it adds:

“But one of them, when he saw that he had been cleansed, returned, glorifying God with a loud voice. And he fell on his face at Jesus’ feet, giving thanks.”

Let us consider, my brothers, what is meant by the words, “When he saw that he had been cleansed,” and by the words, “glorifying God with a loud voice,” and by the fact that “he fell on his face at his feet, giving thanks.”

He saw that he had been cleansed—that is, seeing that he, who had previously been such through guilt, had by grace been made such a different person, he returned not merely in heart but also in deed to his cleanser. He magnified the divine power with a loud voice—not so much a noisy voice as a devout one. He fell on his face, recognizing that he had fallen from his merits, attributing his amendment to its sole author, and giving thanks to him for the gratuitous gift.

This Samaritan, whose name means “guardian,” was fittingly one who guarded in memory the benefit bestowed upon him. This was contrary to those who proved forgetful of the benefit.

How great an evil ingratitude is is shown when the Lord says: “Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine?” He is plainly saying: Because they did not return to give thanks as they ought, they fell through the evil of ingratitude back into their former leprosy—indeed, into one worse than the earlier condition.

“No one,” he says, “was found who returned to give glory to God except this foreigner.” It is as though he said: “My acquaintances and relatives, as usual, always prove ungrateful to me. Although many have experienced divine benefits, no one is found grateful to God except this one, a lover of love and unity. Even the Jews themselves are unworthily ungrateful to me for the benefits bestowed upon them, but this foreign Gentile, who was not instructed by the law to give thanks, alone proves grateful to me.”

“Your faith,” he says, “has saved you.”

[Col. 2054B] Why, then, was the Lord accustomed in such cases to say, “Your faith has saved you,” rather than, “Your hope,” or, “Your love”? For just as faith is necessary for salvation, so too are these. But at that time, when almost everyone was unbelieving, faith was sought first, since it is the foundation of all the virtues. Yet faith alone is not to be understood here, but faith together with hope and love. “Go,” he says, “in peace”—that is, advance toward peace of mind and onward to the peace of eternity.

According to the mystical meaning, four things are to be considered by us. First, where and by what road we ought to go. Where? To Jerusalem. By what road? Through the midst of Samaria and Galilee—that is, we ought to proceed by keeping God’s commandments in such a way that we turn neither toward what is too little nor toward what is excessive. We should maintain the mean of the virtues so that we approach neither the more remote nor the nearer vices. Thus let us hold to generosity without inclining either toward prodigality or toward avarice; thus to justice, without approaching either cruelty or laxity; and similarly in the other virtues. We must also journey by desire toward heavenly things and dwell above in our minds, so that we may say with the Prophet: “This is my portion in the land of the living” (Ps. 141); and likewise: “For what have I in heaven, and besides you what have I desired upon earth?” (Ps. 72). Those who dwell here in mind do not travel toward the heavenly Jerusalem.

Second, these ten lepers indicate to us how we ought to ask the Lord to cleanse us inwardly. They met the Lord, stood at a distance, raised their voices, [Col. 2054D] and said: “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.” The ten lepers signify those who, although they profess the Decalogue of the Law, are notorious for manifest crimes—people of the sort that many of us are, something I cannot say without groaning. If, then, brothers, we are leprous through sins, we ought, following their example, to meet the Lord who comes by grace, through our desire. Nor should we be slow to rise, as are certain people who scarcely wish to be corrected even by scourges and tribulations. Let us also stand at a distance: conscious, that is, of our own leprosy, let us humble ourselves and judge ourselves unworthy either to approach the company of human beings or to enter God’s sanctuary, as the Publican is recorded to have done. Let us raise our voice more through devotion than through loudness—not someone else’s voice, but one proceeding from the affection of our inmost [Col. 2055A] heart. And let us say with faith and devotion: “Jesus, Master”—that is, one for whom to command is to do—“have mercy on us,” washing us from the leprosy of sins.

Third, the Lord indicates to us how he himself cleanses sinners from their sins when he says: “Go, show yourselves to the priests.” Although daily and lesser sins are forgiven us through any slight satisfaction, even without explicit confession, the Lord commands us to show our leprosy—that is, our greater crimes—to the priests and to make satisfaction according to their instruction. But why, since the Lord could cleanse these sins by himself, did he command us to confess them to priests? For three reasons: so that no one would despair on account of sins, since he could find a physician of sins close at hand; so that each person might also gain merit by humbling himself before another human being, his equal; and so that each might bear the burdens of the other.

But what does it mean that the lepers are cleansed on the way, before they reach the priests, except that sinners, while they are going—or are willing to go—to confess to priests in penitence, are cleansed from their sins in that very purpose? Hence David: “I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the guilt of my sin” (Ps. 31). As if he were saying: “I resolved within myself to confess my sin, and you, Lord, forgave it.” Nevertheless, sinners must not therefore disdain to confess their sins to priests, since through contempt they would remain culpable. For although sins are forgiven in contrition of heart, it is not thereby shown that they have been forgiven with respect to the Church. God, as author, looses or binds; the priest, as minister, declares that someone has been bound or absolved. Hence the Lord commanded his disciples to loose Lazarus and let him go, although he himself had raised him from the tomb.

Fourth, we are shown how, while fleeing ingratitude, we ought to give thanks to God for cleansing or for the bestowal of graces. There are three kinds of ingratitude: first, that of those who do not return thanks to God for a benefit bestowed; second, that of those who return to their vomit; third, that of those who uselessly hide the talent entrusted to them. In all these cases, not only are graces withdrawn through ingratitude and vices restored, but they also become worse, as the Lord elsewhere testifies: “The last state of that man becomes worse than the first” (Matt. 12; Luke 11).

Let us, therefore, brothers, following the example of the tenth leper, consider what we were through our fault and what we are through grace. Let us return in heart to God our cleanser; let us praise his mercy with great devotion of heart; and let us fall at his feet—not backward, like Eli unto death, but forward, that is, in recognition of our own frailty, attributing our sins to ourselves and the good we possess to God, and therefore always giving him thanks. Nor should we give him thanks only for the good things bestowed upon us, but also for losses and scourges, saying with blessed Job: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not also receive evil things? The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” [Col. 2056A] (Job 1).

For even some wicked people give thanks in prosperity. Hence David: “He will give thanks to you when you have done good to him” (Ps. 48). But to give thanks in adversity belongs only to the truly good, who understand that adversities themselves are great gifts, through which a gracious father chastises the children whom he loves more dearly. Among such people, brothers, let us desire to be chastised by God, so that we may deserve to be consoled with them. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXII. THE FIFTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit” (Gal. 5–6), etc.

This reading, dearest brothers, has three parts. First, the Apostle exhorts us to spiritual life. Second, he shows what that spiritual life is. Third, he commands those subject to spiritual teachers to share all their goods with them.

Thus, first exhorting us to spiritual life, the Apostle says: “If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit.” My brothers, the word “spirit” is understood in four ways in sacred Scripture. Sometimes it is used to signify the human spirit, as when it is said that a human being consists of body and spirit. Sometimes it signifies a part of the spirit itself, namely the higher reason, as in: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26; Luke 24). Sometimes it signifies the interior meaning of the letter, as in: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 5). Sometimes it signifies the Holy Spirit.

According to the first meaning, therefore, the Spirit enables us to live bodily as well. According to the second, third, and fourth meanings, it enables us to live spiritually. The Apostle says, then: “If we live by the Spirit, let us walk by the Spirit.” As if he were saying openly: If we cannot live either spiritually or even bodily except from the Spirit, let us act according to the Spirit and not according to the will of the flesh. Let us not, therefore, my brothers, be like Adam, who “went in the counsel of the ungodly,” consenting to the suggestions of his wife and the serpent. Rather, let us repel the devil’s temptations and compel our flesh, through fasts and mortifications, to obey the counsel of the spirit.

The second part follows, in which the Apostle shows what the spiritual life is: namely, a life that flees vices [Col. 2056D] and follows virtues. Hence he adds: “Let us not become desirous of empty glory”—with “or of the other vices” understood. He places empty glory here especially because it usually attacks spiritual men in particular, who possess many good things in which they might glory. Empty glory exists when someone attributes, seeks, or accepts glory for some good that he has or seems to have—not to God, but to himself.

I said “that he seems to have” because a hypocrite also seeks human glory for a good that he merely pretends to possess. Others, if they glory in the good they possess—whether spiritual or bodily—glory and take pride in bodily good only when they are worldly and brutish people. But glory and self-exaltation often grow even in great and spiritual men from spiritual good. Among all these people, some attribute the glory of the good they possess to themselves, thinking that they have it from themselves or from their own merits. Others seek human glory outwardly, and if no one praises them, they are not ashamed to praise themselves. Others, although they do not seek human praise for their good, nevertheless accept praise offered by others. Although they blush at the praise offered to them and profess themselves unworthy of it, inwardly their spirit rejoices and glories when it hears the praise.

This glory is called empty or vain because it is cancelled by the true glory of eternal reward. Hence the Lord says of such people: “They have received their reward” (Matt. 5)—namely, the temporal glory they sought, not the eternal.

“Provoking one another,” he says, “envying one another.” It is characteristic of vainglorious people to provoke others to contention and rivalry, so that in the contest they may appear superior. If they cannot overcome them, they envy them and are tormented by their good.

Let us, therefore, dearest brothers, if we do any good, neither glory inwardly within ourselves nor seek outwardly the little breeze of human glory, nor accept it when offered. Instead, let us interrupt the words of the praiser by saying: “Do not praise a person during his lifetime. Praise him after death” (Ecclus. 11). Then neither does the one who praises flatter, nor is the one praised tempted.

But since it is not enough to avoid vices unless we also do good, the Apostle adds: “Brothers, if anyone is overtaken in any trespass, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. 6:1). Here he exhorts us to compassion and to the instruction of those who have gone astray. James testifies that this is of the greatest merit, saying: “Whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins” (Jas. 5).

The stronger and wiser are to be corrected differently when they sin, and the weaker and less instructed differently; differently those who sin deliberately and those who sin through being overtaken; differently those who sin in many things and those who sin in one; differently those who do what they ought not and those who do not do what they ought. The latter is a trespass. Whoever is stronger and wiser, or sins deliberately, or sins in many things, or openly acts against a commandment, must be reproved more severely.

But if a person—that is, a frail human being—is suddenly overtaken, not in many things but in some trespass, you who are spiritual, to whom the correction of sinners belongs, should instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness: not mocking or cursing them, or driving them to despair, as some do, but rather drawing them to repentance by the example of converted sinners and promising forgiveness.

“Keeping watch on yourself,” he says, “lest you too be tempted.” As if he were saying: When you consider other people, consider yourself also, since you are human and frail and can likewise be tempted—or have already been tempted. Learn from yourself what sort of person you ought to be among others. Nothing, brothers, moves a person more powerfully toward mercy and compassion than consideration of his own danger. Hence the Lord first allowed Peter, the chief of the apostles, to fall, so that he might learn in himself how he ought to show mercy to others.

“Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.” There is a burden of sins, a burden of necessities, and also a burden of troubles. Let us therefore, my brothers, bear the burdens of our neighbors’ sins by praying for them, reproving them, and calling them to amendment. Christ acted in this way: he not only bore our sins by praying, reproving, and calling us to amendment, but also bore their punishment in his own body. He is the Lamb who bore the sins of the world (John 1).

Let us also bear the burden of our neighbor’s necessities by having compassion on his needs and afflictions, giving counsel, and providing assistance. Christ both acted and taught in this way: he had compassion on human needs and afflictions, gave counsel, and helped. Let us also bear the burden of our neighbor’s troubles by enduring with equanimity the indignation, insults, and injuries inflicted upon us by them, and by praying for them with affection. Christ both acted and taught in this way: he endured and shared in the hatred, insults, and injuries of his persecutors, returning love for hatred, prayer for insults, and beneficence for injuries.

“If anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself.” In general, my brothers, this is true: if someone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he certainly deceives himself. If someone thinks he does not need the help of others, he deceives himself. If someone thinks he is something through his own merits or in comparison with others, he deceives himself—and so forth.

“Let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself alone, and not in another.” A work is good and approved when it is good in its kind, good in its intention, and undefiled by empty glory or pride. Many perform a work that is good in kind but distorted in intention, such as the person who gives alms with a vain intention. Many perform a work that is good in kind and right in intention, but corrupted by empty glory or pride, as when vainglory secretly joins itself to the act while it is being done or after it has been done.

When vainglory lies in the intention itself, the enemies have taken their position at the head; when it joins our right intention, “they have placed a stumbling-block beside the way” (Ps. 139); when it follows after the deed, “they have lain in wait for our heel.” Whoever therefore tests his work in its kind, in its intention, and in its preservation, “will have glory in himself alone,” he says. He does not say “from himself,” because true glory comes from God alone, but “in himself”—that is, in his conscience, not outside it.

Explaining this, he adds: “and not in another”—that is, not from comparison with the wicked or the less good, nor from the praise of flatterers, as many do when they attribute glory to themselves. Whoever glories in this way is deceived. But whoever glories in God concerning the good given to him by God acts well before himself. Hence the Apostle says: “Our glory is this, the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1).

Is the greater evil or lesser goodness of others our praise? Certainly not. “For each person will bear his own burden” [Col. 2059A]. This is not contrary, brothers, to what was said above: “Bear one another’s burdens.” This saying is directed against those who think that they are either praised or defiled by another’s sin. Each person will bear the burden—that is, endure the punishment—for his own sin, not another’s, unless he makes another’s sin his own through consent or negligence. The former saying is directed against those who are so hard-hearted that they do not know how to have compassion for the need or frailty of their neighbors.

Let us likewise, brothers, have compassion on sinners without becoming involved in their sins through consent; and let us flee involvement in our neighbors’ sins in such a way that we nevertheless draw near to them through compassion.

The third part follows, in which the Apostle commands those subject to share all their goods with their spiritual teachers, saying: “Let the one who is catechized”—that is, instructed in the word—“share all good things with the one who catechizes him.” The Lord also commands this in the Gospel.

Why? For three reasons. First, because it is a debt. Hence the Lord says: “Eat and drink what they provide, for the laborer is worthy of his food” (Luke 10). And the Apostle says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it too much if we reap your material things?” (1 Cor. 9). And the Lord says in the Law: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain” (Deut. 25).

Second, because it is expedient. If a spiritual teacher had to be concerned about bodily necessities, he would be hindered from reading, prayer, preaching, and the other spiritual pursuits in which he ought to remain vigilant for the sake of those subject to him. Therefore, so that he might be free for spiritual things, the Lord commanded him to receive necessities from those subject to him. Hence even an excess of hair and beard is cut away from him, lest they impede his sight, hearing, or the other senses, so that he may understand from this that the excess of external cares must be cut away from himself.

Third, because it is useful. It is useful for secular persons, by supplying temporal goods, to make themselves sharers in the merits of spiritual men. Hence the Lord says: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward” (Matt. 10). He does not say “a reward for receiving a prophet,” but “a prophet’s reward.” Whoever supports a prophet or preacher so that he does not fail in spiritual work in a certain sense makes the prophet’s reward his own.

Hence, by way of symbolism, the Lord even places the elm among useful or fruitful trees, saying through Isaiah: “I will place in the wilderness the cedar, the thorn, the myrtle, and the olive tree; I will set in the desert the fir, the elm, and the box tree together” (Isa. 41). Although the elm is barren, it usually supports a vine with its fruits. This signifies that among spiritual men in the Church of the Gentiles the Lord places secular persons who, although they do not possess the spiritual men’s fruit, nevertheless support spiritual men with their fruits through temporal benefits.

But because certain avaricious subjects are accustomed to excuse themselves by poverty, he adds: “Do not be deceived; God is not mocked.” As if he were saying: “By making excuses you can deceive a human being, but not God.” Therefore you must do the good that you can, because whoever does not sow good in this life cannot reap good in the other life. Hence he adds: “Whatever a person sows, that he will also reap.” For whoever sows in the flesh—that is, does carnal and evil works—will reap corruption from the flesh, that is, punishment. And whoever sows in the Spirit—that is, acts according to the will of the Spirit—will reap eternal life from the Spirit.

Therefore, while doing good, let us not grow weary. In due time we shall reap, if we do not fail. As if he were saying: Whoever does not fail in sowing will not fail in reaping. “Therefore,” he says, “let us do good to everyone”—understand: as much as we can, and to each person whom we see to be in need.

As for what is read, “Do good to the just, and do not give to the wicked” (Ecclus. 12), this does not deny assistance to a person’s nature, but to his wickedness. Although we ought to do good to everyone, nevertheless we should do so especially to those who are of the household of faith. Although we ought to do good both to Jews and to pagans, we should do so especially to Christians, and among Christians to those who are more closely joined to us by brotherhood, blood, or familiarity; for our love ought to be ordered.

Thus, brothers, let us have toward all the viscera of kindness and compassion, helping one person materially, another by word, another through protection, another by counsel, another through correction, another through admonition, and everyone by goodwill and prayer. In this way, having sown generously here, may we deserve to reap more generously in eternity, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXIII. THE FIFTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“No one can serve two masters” (Matt. 6).

As this reading from the holy Gospel, dearest brothers, suggests to us, there are three kinds of people. Some serve God, some serve the world, and some wish to serve both but cannot. Those serve God who cling to him with their whole heart and as their chief concern, and obey him. This service is blessed, desirable, and benedictional, for it is written: “To serve God is to reign.”

Those serve the world who cling to it as their chief concern and obey their desires. This service is unhappy and wretched. For it is written: “Whoever commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8). And to the extent that a sinner serves many vices, he is subjected to as many dominions of the devil.

Those wish to serve both God and the world at once who want to follow partly God’s commands and partly the desires of the age. Concerning such people Solomon says: “Woe,” he says, “to the person who walks on two roads.” A person walks on two roads who wishes to rejoice with the age and with God, who wishes to do what belongs to the world and what belongs to God. When I say “the world,” understand the world’s desire.

Against such people the Lord first shows here that no one can serve two masters. Second, he prohibits worldly anxiety. Third, he shows what we ought to seek.

He therefore says: “No one can serve two masters”—masters who are opposed. For either he will hate the one, that is, the devil or the world, and love the other, that is, God; or he will endure the one, that is, the devil, and despise the other, that is, God.

He expressed himself elegantly by saying “he will endure.” No one loves the devil, even though he does the devil’s will. Just as someone who loves a tyrant’s maidservant does not love the tyrant, but because of his love for the maidservant endures the tyrant’s harsh slavery, so worldly people do not love the devil, but because of their love for worldly pleasure endure his tyranny.

He does not say, “He will hate God,” because scarcely anyone’s conscience can hate God, from whom he has being, life, and understanding. Rather, because of his love for the world, he despises him.

He explains who these two masters are when he adds: “You cannot serve God and Mammon,” that is, riches. Mammon is said to be a demon who suggests to people the love of riches.

He does not say, “You cannot serve God and rule over riches,” for the faithful can do this. You, therefore, brothers, who possess worldly property, riches, wives, and children, take note of what is said here and weigh it in your minds. If you cling principally to God, placing him before riches, wives, children, and honors, preferring to lose everything rather than offend God, then you serve God and live rightly. But if—God forbid!—you place the love of riches, honors, marriage, and children before God, choosing rather to offend him than to abandon those things, then you serve not God but the world, having become wretched and pitiable slaves not only of the world but also of the devil.

The second part follows, in which the Lord prohibits anxiety over temporal things, saying: “Therefore do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will wear.” He does not say, “Do not be provident,” for it is not temporal provision but anxiety that is prohibited. Anxiety is what suffocates and extinguishes in us the love and concern for eternal things. Hence elsewhere, in a parable, he says that the thorns which sprang up choked the word of God (Luke 8).

To make provision according to God’s will for the necessities of ourselves, our families, and even the poor is good. When it is said elsewhere, “Do not think about tomorrow” [Col. 2061D] (Matt. 6), “think” means either the distant future or being anxious; it is directed against those who accumulate necessities for many years.

That we ought not to be anxious about food or clothing he proves from the greater, adding: “Is not life”—that is, the soul—“more than food, and the body more than clothing?” As if he were saying: God, who gave us greater things, namely life and the body, will give what is less, namely food and clothing.

Again, he proves from the lesser that we ought not to be anxious about food, when he adds: “Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth more than they?” That is, of greater value in God’s sight. As if he were saying: If God gives birds food without their anxiety, how much more will he give food to you, who are rational and made in the image of God?

Mystically, however, the birds signify the vain and wicked people of this world, who flit about through curiosity, are lifted up through pride, are brought down to the earth through greed, and do not live by their own labor but by the labor of others through rapacity. If the Lord gives food to these people, who despise him, how much more will he give it to his faithful?

Again, he proves from the lesser that we ought not to be anxious about clothing, saying: “Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither labor nor spin. Yet I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.” Literally, no purple or silk with which Solomon or any illustrious person in the world is clothed can be compared with flowers. For what is as white as a lily? What is as red as a rose?

“If God,” he says, “so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, people of little faith?” Understand: he will clothe you here with temporal clothing and in the future with the robe of immortality.

Mystically, the lilies signify the powerful and glorious people of this world. Born in the world’s material abundance, they grow in the world through the height of honors and bloom through temporal prosperity. They do not labor or spin, because they are not among those who labor, and they will not be scourged with ordinary people. Therefore, “pride held them fast; they are covered with their iniquity” (Ps. 72), etc.

If God thus clothes the proud and glorious people of this age, who are in fact grass—for “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field” (Isa. 40)—and tomorrow will be thrown into the furnace of eternal damnation, how much more will he clothe you, his worshipers?

But it must be considered very carefully, my brothers, that he calls those who are anxious about food or clothing people of little faith. Those who have great faith undoubtedly know that God will provide everything necessary. Therefore, brothers, if you fear that necessities will be lacking for you, you have little faith.

The third part follows, in which the Lord shows what we ought to seek, when he adds: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness.” First—that is, principally—we ought to seek the kingdom of God, which we ask daily in the Lord’s Prayer to come, as the prize and goal. And his righteousness—that is, the virtues and good works which are the road by which we go to the kingdom of God.

“And all these things,” he says—namely, temporal things necessary for the present life—“will be added to you,” as incidental matters. They are not to be sought for their own sake, but for the sake of eternal things. Just as the king’s soldiers do not count their military pay as the recompense for their labor, so neither should we, brothers, count the necessities of temporal life as the reward of the prize.

For who, as Paul testifies, ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? (1 Cor. 9.) If, then, brothers, we serve as soldiers for Christ, let us be concerned not with our pay but with earning the reward. Our Lord Jesus Christ, the King of kings, provides pay here for his soldiers and reserves eternal rewards for the future; with the Father and the Holy Spirit he lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXIV. THE SIXTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

[Col. 2063A]

“I ask you not to lose heart over my tribulations on your behalf, which are your glory” (Eph. 3), etc.

In this reading, dearest brothers, the Apostle exhorts the Ephesians, and through them each of us, to steadfastness and strength in faith, hope, and love, in the following manner. First, he begs them not to lose heart in his tribulations. Second, he shows that he prays for their strength and perfection. Third, he gives thanks to God, who is able to give his people something better than they themselves know how to ask.

The Apostle, therefore, placed in chains because of the Gospel, feared that the tribulations inflicted upon their teacher might become fear and weakness for the disciples, whom he could not strengthen by word; so he strengthens them in writing. In this, brothers, the Apostle’s remarkable love is certainly shown: he was more concerned about the steadfastness of his disciples than about his own chains.

He says, therefore: “I ask you—and I ask this concerning you—not to lose heart in my tribulations,” that is, on account of my tribulations, “which are indeed on your behalf,” that is, inflicted upon me because of the faith preached to you, “which are your glory”—that is, not losing heart in either my tribulations or your own is your glory. For soldiers who are brave in battle are glorious before God; conversely, the fearful and those who fail will be inglorious.

As a furnace tests gold, so tribulation tests the righteous. Therefore, my brothers, you ought not to wonder if the Lord allows his people to be troubled and scourged in the world. Gold cannot be pure unless the furnace has refined it.

Therefore I too, my brothers, beg you with the Apostle not to lose heart in tribulations, whether such things befall me, you, or even holier men, since the heavenly craftsman is accustomed to polish the vessels of election through great tribulation.

The second part follows, in which the Apostle shows that he prays for the steadfastness of his disciples, saying:

“For this reason”—namely, so that you may not grow faint—“I bend not one knee,” as the Jews did before Jesus, or as hypocrites do, who humble themselves in body but not in mind, “but my knees,” that is, I entreat with mind and body, “before the Father of our God and Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named.”

Although God is alone good, alone Lord, and alone King, he nevertheless willed that, by participation in his goodness, human beings should be called good, lords, and kings. Likewise, although he alone is Father, he nevertheless willed that human beings should be called fathers from him.

God is called Father for four reasons: by generation, creation, teaching or example, and adoption. By generation he is Father only of the Son. By creation he is Father of all creatures; by teaching or example, only of rational creatures; by adoption, only of the good. Whoever is called father in heaven or on earth—whether in the first, second, third, or fourth way—has this from God the Father.

In heaven, both the Son and the Holy Spirit are called Father with respect to the creation of all things, the teaching and example of rational creatures, and the adoption of the good; but they have this from the Father. For just as they are not from themselves but from the Father, so they are neither God nor Father except from the Father.

On earth, human beings are called fathers of their own children by generation, of their juniors through the authority of teaching and example, and even of the children of others through adoption. But whether in this way, that way, or the third way, they have it not from themselves but from the supreme Father.

Thus, from God the Father every fatherhood—that is, every manner of being called father—both exists and is named. For what reason, then, do you bend your knees to the Father? “So that he may give you,” he says, “according to the riches of his glory.” Although God possesses all the riches that are in heaven and on earth, the “riches of glory” here means the virtues and their works, because they make a person truly glorious and lead him to eternal glory.

And what is he to give? “That virtue may be strengthened in you,” that is, that you may be strengthened in virtue, and specifically that you may possess the virtue of strength and steadfastness in the inner person. Great bodily strength is not necessary for Christians, because great bodily strength and fatness oppress the soul. Since flesh and spirit are opposed to one another, the stronger one is, the weaker the other is. Hence the Apostle says: “When I am weak, then I am stronger and powerful” (II Cor. XII).

He explains what he had said: “Let him give,” I say, “virtue.” And what virtue? Christ, who is the virtue and wisdom of God, dwelling through faith in your hearts. Whoever possesses him possesses every virtue and grace.

Let him also grant that you be “rooted and founded in charity,” so that you may be unable either to be uprooted or moved from charity. Even the elect, if at some time they are moved somewhat, are nevertheless not uprooted. David, who sinned, was moved but not uprooted, and therefore he did not wither.

“So that you may be able,” he says, “to comprehend with all the saints.” For only the saints can comprehend—and theirs is the knowledge of the ministry of God’s kingdom. And what is it that they may comprehend? “What is the length, breadth, height, and depth.” For “charity is patient and kind; it believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (I Cor. XIII).

Charity itself is long in patience; it is broad in love, of both friend and enemy; it is broad in hope, namely, hope of eternal rewards; it is deep in faith and in the avoidance of eternal punishments. For whoever does not have charity rooted in him challenges others in patience, fails in love, grows languid in hope of eternal reward, and hesitates in faith concerning eternal punishment.

And because we cannot be steadfast in faith and in the charity of Christ, since we do not know how great a charity he had toward us, he adds: “Let him also grant you to know the charity of Christ which surpasses knowledge.”

Christ had a charity surpassing knowledge because he laid down his life for servants and enemies, in order to make them sons and friends. He also possessed both the charity of knowledge and the knowledge of charity—that is, he had wise love and loving wisdom.

Some possess charity, but not according to knowledge. Of such people the Apostle says: “They have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. X). Others possess knowledge, but not according to charity. Of such people the Apostle says: “Knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up” (I Cor. VIII).

Therefore, brothers, let us strive to know the charity of Christ that surpasses knowledge, so that, just as he loved us wisely, we may likewise learn to love him wisely.

“So that you may be filled,” he says, “with all the fullness of Christ.” That is, in this life, according to the measure of the way, may we possess the fullness of wisdom and virtue; and in the future, the fullness of eternal recompense, where we shall no longer know and love through a mirror and in a riddle, but fully.

The third part follows, in which the Apostle gives thanks to God, showing that he is powerful to do all things more abundantly than we ask or understand; for the power of God surpasses both our petition and our understanding.

Behold, brothers: when the Apostle supplicates and asks God, he first called him Father, because it belongs to a father to will what is good for his children. Second, he showed him to be rich in gifts, when he said, “According to the riches of his glory.” Now, third, he shows him to be powerful in all things, upon which the accomplishment of the petition depends.

For whoever wills to give, abounds in gifts, and is able to give will undoubtedly give. Therefore, brothers, let us ask God devoutly and steadfastly. Since he wills, abounds, and is able, he will certainly grant us what we rightly ask.

“According to the virtue,” he says, “that works in us, he is powerful to do all things”—that is, by that virtue through which he makes us just from unjust, wise from foolish, and powerful from powerless.

“To him be glory in the Church and in Christ Jesus,” that is, may he appear glorious in them, “through all generations,” that is, forever.

Therefore, brothers, just as the Apostle entreated certain Corinthians, so we now entreat you: do not grow faint in tribulations, whether ours or yours. For the stones that are to be placed in the heavenly building must here be squared and polished. Whoever is not here squared or polished by corrections and disciplines is not to be set among the stones of the supreme building.

This is well signified by the fact that the wood and stones of the temple were polished only on the outside, not within. For “the sound of a hammer or an axe was not heard in the temple” (III Kings VI). This signifies that the saints are struck in this world, not in heaven.

Therefore, brothers, as the Apostle did, let us bend our knees before God for the steadfastness of our faith. You too ought to do this for your salvation, so that both we and you may together be found worthy to reach eternal blessedness, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXV. THE SIXTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“Jesus went into a city called Nain. And his disciples and a great crowd went with him. When he drew near the gate of the city, behold, a dead man was being carried out, the only son of his mother” (Luke VII).

In this reading from the holy Gospel, dearest brothers, there is shown, first according to the literal sense, the solicitude, mercy, humility, and omnipotence of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ concerning the salvation of human beings.

His solicitude is shown when it says: “Jesus went into a city,” and so forth. He was solicitous for the salvation of human beings, going here and there wherever he foresaw that he would find an opportunity to do good for them. He went where he knew that gatherings of people were, so that he might announce to them the word of life. He went where he knew that the sick were, so that he might mercifully heal them. He went where he knew that the poor and miserable were, so that he might offer them consolation.

In this he also set an example of action for his own people, confounding the hardness of those who avoid places where they know that the poor and miserable are, lest perhaps they should be compelled by their presence and persistence to pity them and help them.

No one should think that it happened by chance that, as the Lord approached the gate, the dead man was being carried out. This was not arranged accidentally but by divine ordinance.

The Lord’s mercy is shown when he sympathizes with the widow, who was miserable and pitiable through a threefold misfortune: she was a widow, she was carrying out her dead son, and she had no other child. Because she was so pitiable, the city’s crowd, taking pity on her, accompanied her, consoled her, and attended to the funeral.

In this, my brothers, let us also learn to accompany and console those who mourn and to attend to funerals, since it is an act of humility and mercy to console the sorrowful and bury the dead. Tobias, because he buried the dead, deserved mercy and illumination from the Lord.

The Lord also, in order to give us an example of pitying and consoling the afflicted, moved by mercy, consoles the widow in word and deed: in word, when he says to her, “Do not weep”; in deed, when he returns her son alive.

The Lord’s humility is shown when he does not disdain to touch the bier of the dead man, whom he could have raised by a mere command. If we examine the matter more subtly, he touched it for three reasons: as an example of humility, for an understanding of the law, and because of the mystery of the figure.

As an example of humility, the Lord touched the bier so that, if he who is eternal life wished to touch a dead man, we, who are corpses and corruption, would not fear to touch, wash, and bury the dead. In this he confounds certain inhuman and hard-hearted people who, as though they themselves would not die, fear and abhor the dead.

For an understanding of the law, he touched the bier to show that the prohibition against contact with the dead in the law was to be understood not carnally but spiritually, especially since he himself, who is purity itself and cannot be defiled, touched the dead man. In the contact with the dead, consent to sin was spiritually prohibited.

He also touched the bier because of the mystery, to signify that, in resurrection from the sin of a criminal deed, satisfaction through a deed is necessary, as will be said later.

The Lord’s omnipotence is demonstrated when the dead man is raised at his sole command. In this he shows himself to be the same one who in the beginning merely spoke, and all things were made (Gen. I).

Wonderful is the power in the Lord’s word, at whose voice the underworld is immediately opened and the soul that it held comes forth; the cold man grows warm, and he who was dead departs from death.

Everyone was seized with fear, so that they both feared and loved the one whom they saw to be so powerful in deed and word, and they glorified God. Let us also, imitating them, learn to fear and praise God at the same time in his holy and wondrous works.

Mystically, however, the dead man signifies one dead in sin. Although the Lord raised many dead people, the evangelists mention only three, for a definite reason involving the mystery. The three dead signify three kinds of sinners among those dead in sins: one dead through the sin of the will, one dead through the sin of deed, and one dead through the sin of habit.

The Lord therefore first raised the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, privately in the house and with few words. This signifies that when someone sins only in the mind, as though in secret, he is more easily raised by the Lord and with less satisfaction.

Second, as we read here, the Lord raised the widow’s son at the gate, touching the bier and saying more. This signifies that when sin goes outside through the carrying out of a deed, greater satisfaction is required, both of deed and of prayer.

Third, he raised Lazarus, dead four days, from the tomb, weeping, crying out, and having the stone removed. This indicates that when someone is weighed down by habitual sin and already reeks through a corrupt life and infamy, he is so bound and oppressed by habitual sin that he is scarcely raised again. Nevertheless, through God’s great mercy when he regards him, he sometimes rises; but great tears, confessions, prayers, and the labor of great satisfaction are necessary.

A fourth dead man is announced to the Lord, but he is not said to have been raised by him. Instead, he says to the one who announced him: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Luke IX). A dead person buries a dead person when a sinner fosters and flatters another sinner.

The Lord does not raise this person, because when the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul and the wicked person is blessed (Ps. IX), he is bound on one side by the chain of habit and on the other is nourished by the oil of flattery, so that he does not rise to the pardon of amendment.

Therefore, my brothers, avoid flatterers. Love those who correct you. Beware lest you sleep in habitual sin. Make satisfaction quickly for the sin of deed or will, lest sudden death overtake you, because “at an hour when you do not expect it, the Son of Man will come” (Luke XII) to summon and judge you.

Therefore, brothers, let us always keep our death before our eyes. Let us constantly consider how terrifying the heavenly Judge will be when he comes. Let us wipe away the filth of our sins with sighs, tears, and good works, so that we may deserve confidently to see Christ the Judge when he comes, by the favor of him who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXVI. THE SEVENTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“I, a prisoner in the Lord, beseech you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called” (Eph. IV), and so forth.

In this reading, dearest brothers, he intends to strengthen the Ephesians, and through them all believers, in the unity of charity and in matters of this kind.

First, he beseeches them to persevere in the faith to which they had been called. Second, he urges them to possess the virtues that produce and preserve peace and charity. Third, he urges them through charity to be one body and one spirit.

He therefore says: “I, a prisoner in the Lord, beseech you.” My brothers, the Apostle was bound by a threefold chain: the chain of iron, the chain of the body, and the chain of charity.

The chain of iron bound him for Christ when he wrote these things. Hence he says elsewhere: “I indeed am bound, but the word of God is not bound” (II Tim. II).

He also recognizes that he is bound by the chain of the body—not only the Apostle, but every true Christian who understands that he is burdened in the body, exiled, and a pilgrim away from God. Hence the same Apostle says: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I). And the Psalmist says: “Bring my soul out of prison, that it may confess your name” (Ps. CXLI).

By the chain of the charity of God and neighbor, not only the Apostle but every believer must always be bound; otherwise he is not a believer.

The Apostle was bound to God and neighbor by love in such a way that, although placed both in the chain of iron and in the chain of bodily misery, he was more concerned for the salvation of souls and of his neighbors than for the twofold misery that surrounded him.

Hence he also beseeches them for their benefit, knowing that the progress of disciples is the joy and crown of the teacher. Thus he says elsewhere: “Therefore, my most beloved and most desired brothers, my joy and my crown, stand firm in the Lord, dearest ones” (Phil. IV).

What does he beseech them concerning? “That you walk worthily,” he says, “of the calling with which you were called.”

There is a twofold calling of the faithful. The first is the calling by which they are called to faith; the second is the calling by which, through faith, they are called to eternal life.

Therefore, a person walks worthily of the calling with which he was called when he rightly holds the faith and, through it, walks worthily by doing good works toward eternal life.

But many today—and this is all the more grievous—have been called to faith but do not walk worthily through it. They do not progress by doing good works but instead go backward; and although they confess God with their mouths, they deny him by their deeds.

The second part follows, in which the Apostle urges us to possess the virtues through which charity and peace are preserved and maintained, when he adds: “With all humility and gentleness and patience, bearing with one another in charity.”

Thus humility, gentleness, patience, and mutual forbearance are the virtues that produce and preserve charity and peace. This is evident from the vices opposed to them, which destroy charity and peace. These are pride, anger, impatience, and contempt for one’s neighbors.

That pride disperses peace Solomon shows when he says: “Among the proud there are always quarrels” (Prov. XIII). For where each person, through pride, wants to rule, charity and peace cannot exist.

Conversely, humility nourishes peace, because the humble person cannot quarrel but always seeks to yield and submit.

That anger destroys peace is evident from this: just as the movement of the sea or air disturbs tranquility and calm and generates a storm, so anger disturbs the repose of the mind and gives birth to agitation and fury.
