Hence the poet [Note: Horace, Epistles I, epistle 2, verse 62]: “Anger is a brief madness.”

Conversely, gentleness is peace of the air. Whoever is gentle and tranquil within himself can also make others peaceful.

That impatience disturbs peace is evident from this: whoever cannot bear himself will not be able to bear others. And whoever is discordant with himself will be in harmony with no one.

Conversely, the patient person, because he patiently endures the injuries of all, can have peace with everyone, insofar as it depends on him, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Having peace with all people, insofar as it is possible for you” (Rom. XII).

That contempt destroys peace and charity is evident because the contemptuous person does not fear giving offense. As the Wise Man says: “Where there is contempt, there is frequent injury.” And where there is frequent injury, there is frequent unrest and frequent disturbance.

Conversely, bearing the burdens and infirmities of others nourishes charity and peace; for service produces friends.

Therefore, brothers, pride contends over superiority; anger grows angry against one who refuses; impatience inflicts injury; contempt considers it beneath itself to have inflicted injuries.

Conversely, humility does not contend; rather, it willingly submits to the one who contends. Gentleness does not grow angry; rather, it calms the angry person. Patience does not strike back; rather, it bears calmly the one who inflicts injury. Mutual forbearance does not despise; rather, it helps those who are despised.

Strive, therefore, brothers, to possess these virtues if you wish to have true charity and peace among human beings.

The third part follows, in which the Apostle urges us through charity to be one body and one spirit, adding:

“Being diligent to preserve the unity of the spirit,” that is, the charity through which the Holy Spirit works in the bond of peace, so that we may be joined and bound together through a covenant.

“One body and one spirit”—understand, may you be—“just as you were called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in us all.”

The order of the text is: Just as you were called in one hope of your calling, just as you have one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God and Father of all, so be one body and one spirit.

We, my brothers, have been called through faith in one hope of the same eternal recompense.

We also have one Lord, who rules us both by the right of creation and by the right of restoration. Thus, although many lords are spoken of on earth, there is nevertheless one principal Lord in heaven and on earth. The others are not truly lords but are called *domni* in a diminutive sense.

We also have one and the same faith: that is, we all believe the same things about God, and the articles of faith are the same among all believers.

There is likewise one baptism among all the faithful, because it is celebrated among all in the same faith, in the same element, and in the same form. Similarly, the other sacraments are the same among all believers.

There is also one God and Father of all, namely, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Since he is God, he is to be feared and worshiped. Since he is Father, he is to be loved and imitated.

He is above all by presiding, through all by working, and in all by filling. He is substantially filling all things, but he is specially present in all believers by dwelling in them through grace.

Therefore, brothers, just as we are one in all these things, so let us be one body and one spirit.

All the faithful are metaphorically called one body, which is the Church. Christ is called the head of this body for three reasons.

Just as the head, although it is of one nature with the body, nevertheless excels it, so Christ, although he is of the same nature as the Church, surpasses it.

And just as the head, in which all the senses are located, watches over the safety of all the members, so Christ, in whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. II), provides for the whole Church.

Third, just as the marrow and strength descend from the brain of the head into all the members, so that the member into which this flow ceases withers and becomes useless, so all grace descends from Christ into all the faithful. If it does not flow into someone, that person withers in goodness and becomes useless.

The faithful are likewise called one body for three reasons.

First, because they are joined both to Christ the head and to one another by the nerves of charity; second, because, like members, they serve and help one another; third, because when one rejoices, the others rejoice, and when one suffers, the others sympathize, as members do.

All the faithful are also called one spirit, that is, one in spiritual love, and also because they have the same understanding and the same will.

Therefore, my brothers, just as we are one in faith and hope, one in the service of God, and one in receiving the reward of the same eternal blessedness, so let us be one body. Let us be like faithful members, joined through charity to Christ the head and to the other members; let us serve one another, helping one another and bearing one another’s burdens and infirmities; let us rejoice with one another in good things and sympathize with one another in adversity.

Thus, admonishing, supporting, helping, consoling, and exhorting one another, may we together be found worthy to reach the desirable blessedness of eternity, through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXVII. THE SEVENTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“When Jesus entered the house of one of the rulers of the Pharisees on the Sabbath to eat bread, they were watching him” (Luke XIV).

In this reading, dearest brothers, our Lord and Redeemer does three things.

First, he enters to eat among those plotting against him. Second, confounding them, he heals a man suffering from dropsy. Third, he shows where one ought to recline when invited, giving us great lessons in all these matters.

In that he does not shrink from turning aside to eat with the rulers and those plotting against him—in fact, he even corrects and instructs them—he shows the greatness of his goodness and mercy and makes known to us by his example what we ought to do: namely, that we should offer our enemies love in place of hatred, not hatred in place of hatred, and should strive to benefit them.

For this reason we should eat even among rulers and wicked people: so that we may offer them the spiritual bread of correction and teaching.

The Lord also sets forth in this meal an example of frugality and abstinence, since he eats bread in the house of a ruler and on the Sabbath. The evangelist specifies three things: eating bread, on the Sabbath, and in the house of a ruler.

He does not say that he ate meat, fish, or delicacies, but only bread, although, as Lord of all things, he could have had all these and greater things at hand if he had wished. By this he wished to show in himself what he commanded elsewhere when he said: “Do not make provision for the desires of the flesh” (Rom. XIII).

Let the gluttons therefore be ashamed, those who do not know how to eat unless they have delicacies and enticements. This is what they desire, and for this they labor, exhausting the air, forests, and waters by hunting.

He also adds that it was on the Sabbath, that is, on the feast day of the Jews, to confound those who, although they live sparingly on ordinary days, nevertheless provide themselves lavishly on feast days, not considering it a feast unless it is filled with meats and delicacies.

But it is foolish to honor the solemnities of God or of the saints with banquets when we know that they pleased God by fasts.

He also adds that it was in the house of a ruler, to reprove those who, although they live sparingly at home, are caught and enticed when they visit rulers by the luxurious foods of rulers.

Therefore, brothers, the Lord is sustained by bread, on the Sabbath, and in the house of a ruler, to show that we ought to be content with little both on feast days and among rulers.

Nevertheless, because envy does not know how to be softened by benefits, although the Lord offered the Pharisees love and teaching, they were still plotting against him. Hence it is added: “And they were watching him,” that is, they were watching against him—watching maliciously—so that if he healed the sick or did anything else on the Sabbath, they might accuse him.

The evangelist hints at this when he adds: “And behold, there was a certain man suffering from dropsy before him.” Thus, my brothers, thus the wicked always watch the pious, the unjust the just, so that they may find an opportunity to accuse them and corrupt their works. Hence it is written: “The sinner watches the just and gnashes his teeth at him” (Ps. XXXVI).

The second part follows, in which the Lord confounds their malice and heals the man suffering from dropsy, when it is added:

“Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?” But they remained silent.

Here the Lord shows himself to be the true God, since he responds to their evil thoughts, presses them in their hearts, and brings them to the point that, out of confusion, they remain silent.

They saw that, whichever answer they gave, they would be caught in a rhetorical trap. For if they said that it was lawful to heal on the Sabbath, the Lord would say to them: “Then you should not rebuke me if I heal on the Sabbath.” But if they said that it was not lawful, he would say to them: “Why, then, do you care for your animals on the Sabbath?”

They therefore remain silent, like defendants who see that their consciences have been exposed.

The Lord heals the man suffering from dropsy not only by a word, although he could have done so, but also by touching him, to show that on the Sabbath one must not abstain from every work—for one who refrains from good work keeps the Sabbath badly—but from servile work, which is understood above all as sin.

“Which of you,” he says, “if his ox or donkey falls into a pit, will not immediately draw it out on the Sabbath?”

The Lord shows that they themselves suffered from a more serious dropsy of avarice. According to their own opinion, they did not violate the Sabbath when caring for their animals; through their avarice, they preferred the care of animals to the care of human beings; and in both matters they transgressed the law and offended God.

Mystically, however, they themselves were both the man swollen with water through dropsy and the ox submerged in water. Through the flow of water, the flow of riches is signified.

Just as a person suffering from dropsy drinks more and thirsts more, so, the more they possessed, the more they thirsted. And just as an ox submerged and perishing in an excess of water is destroyed, so they perished, submerged in an abundance of riches.

Therefore, brothers, let us flee the vice of the Pharisees: let us not refrain from good works on feast days; let us not prefer the care of our beasts to the care of human beings, as many do—to our grief; let us not swell up with or be submerged in the hypocrisy of avarice.

The third part follows, in which the Lord, in reproving the Pharisees who loved the first places at banquets, shows where one ought to recline when invited, saying:

“When you are invited to a wedding, do not recline in the first place,” and so forth.

Although this parable is to be observed according to the literal sense, it is to be observed even more spiritually. All of us who are Christians have been invited to the wedding feast of the heavenly banquet.

No one in the Church should prefer himself to another either in thought or in rank, lest perhaps that other person be greater before God and be placed before him in holiness or dignity.

Behold, my brothers, how many kings, rulers, bishops, and persons of high standing in the world now place themselves before others in dignity, reputation, and power. But certainly, when he comes who alone discerns the merits of each person, he will place some widow, some poor person, or some person considered lowly in this world before them.

Then, not without a certain shame, they will begin to occupy the last place, having been put behind those whom they had placed before themselves in this world.

Therefore, brothers, let each person in the Church consider himself lowly and humbly place himself before all. Let him contend only in humility, so that when he comes who invited all the faithful to his eternal wedding feast, he may say: “Friend, go up higher, because the more humble you were than others for my sake, the higher you will be with me than others.”

We can possess this humility if we always place our sins before our eyes; if we consider the virtues of others, especially those that we lack; if we weigh our own frailty; and if we admire the holiness of others.

Thus we shall begin to become lowly in our own sight and to place others before ourselves.

May he deign to implant this humility in us who humbled himself for our sake, our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXVIII. THE EIGHTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY
[Col. 2073B] I always give thanks to my God for you all (1 Cor. 1), and so forth. In this reading, dearly beloved brothers, the Apostle shows how greatly he rejoices in the progress of the Corinthians, namely, his disciples. For the joy of true teachers is the progress of their disciples, and rightly so. For he knows that he is both the prompter and likewise a participant in his disciple’s merits. Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Therefore, my most beloved and most greatly desired brothers, my joy and my crown, stand firm thus in the Lord, dearly beloved” (Phil. 4). Conversely, the disciple’s ruin is the teacher’s grief. Hence the same Apostle says that he mourns those who have fallen. Elsewhere also he says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. [Col. 2073C] 11).

Therefore, brothers, if I am a true teacher, I ought not to be harsh and cold toward you, like certain mercenary and false teachers, who teach not for spiritual gain but even for temporal profit. Rather, through true love for your souls, I ought to seek gain and, if necessary, to spend not only what is mine but even myself for you. You also, if you are true disciples and true sheep, ought not to be harsh and cold toward your shepherd, like certain perverse disciples, but to love him as a spiritual father and, through charity, to share with him not only what you possess but yourselves as well. Thus there may be communion between you and your shepherd not only in spiritual goods but also in temporal goods—so that the teacher may regard the disciples’ progress or loss as his own, and the disciples may regard the teacher’s [Col. 2073D] progress or loss as their own.

Therefore, since the Doctor of the Gentiles shows that he rejoices in the progress of his disciples, first he gives thanks to God for their progress. Second, he shows what graces have been bestowed upon them. Third, he demonstrates what reward he expects from this. Thus he says: “I give thanks to my God.” To give thanks is to bless the author of graces for the grace bestowed. Since we possess nothing of our own with which we can repay God, at least we ought always to confess ourselves his debtors.

This, dearly beloved brothers, is exceedingly necessary. For if one who is always grateful to God for grace bestowed deserves not only to retain what has been given but also to obtain something greater, then one who is ungrateful for a benefit bestowed deserves to be deprived not only of benefits yet to be conferred but even of the benefit already received. Hence [Col. 2074A] we read that the ancient Fathers sang songs as though in thanksgiving for divine benefits, such as the Song of Mary, the Song of Moses, and the Song of Hannah. Hence the Hebrews relate that King Hezekiah, because he did not sing a song to the Lord for the victory given him by God, fell into illness. Hence also the nine lepers cleansed by the Lord, because they disdained to return with the tenth to give thanks to God, are unknown through their rejection, as the Lord says: “Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine?” (Luke 17).

Such people are numerous today—which is all the more grievous—who are ungrateful for divine benefits and attribute what they have either to their own prudence, their own strength, or their own labor, rather than to God. There are others who, although they give thanks to God in prosperity, are silent in adversity. Of them it is written: “He will give thanks to you when you have done good to him” (Ps. 48); but certainly contemptible is the voice of praise that proceeds from the joy of prosperity.

Therefore, brothers, let us give thanks for all good things—not only for prosperity but also for adversity. If we judge rightly, these are inflicted upon us by God for correction or testing, according to the saying: “By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night his song” (Ps. 41). For the Lord commanded that in the day of prosperity we should remember his mercy and his benefit, and that in the night of adversity we should sing him a hymn of thanksgiving. Hence Job: “The Lord has given, the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1). For it is philosophical [Col. 2074C] to fear in prosperity and to sing in adversity.

The second part follows, in which the Apostle shows for what he gives thanks when he adds: “In grace,” that is, “for the grace which has been given to us in Christ Jesus.” Grace is so called as something given freely. Therefore, brothers, since whatever we possess has been freely given us by God, everything is grace. Nevertheless, by a special designation, virtues and the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which belong properly to the good, are called graces. Temporal goods, however, because they are common to the good and the wicked alike, although they too are given freely by God, are not usually called graces.

Among graces, one is grace unto grace, another grace for grace, and another is grace for grace unto grace. Grace unto grace is only the first grace, [Col. 2074D] which is given entirely freely, not as a merit in return for some preceding grace, as faith is. Grace for grace is, according to John, eternal blessedness, which is bestowed in return for preceding graces as just merits, and for which no other grace is awaited. The intermediate graces between the first and final grace are graces for grace unto grace, because they are conferred in return for a preceding grace, as for a merit, in order to earn other graces.

Do not be surprised, brothers, if I call the merits of the righteous graces; for, according to the Apostle, we possess nothing that we have not received from God and received freely. But because through one grace we arrive at another, they are also called merits, though improperly. For, according to Augustine, God crowns only his own grace in us.

These graces are said to have been given in Christ Jesus, that is, in the faith of Jesus Christ. For faith is the first grace and the foundation of all graces. Then, explaining grace, he adds: “Because in all things,” he says, “you have been made rich”—namely, in all graces necessary for earning eternal life. Whoever possesses these has true riches and is truly rich.

Therefore, brothers, desire and seek these riches, which lead a person to true sufficiency and always accompany those who possess them. But if you do not have temporal riches, despise them; if you have them, distribute them to the poor. For in the Gospel the Lord calls these riches deceptive, because they deceive a person, since they make him neither happy nor self-sufficient, and because they cannot remain with him. Concerning them David says: “They slept their sleep, and all the men of riches found nothing in their hands” [Col. 2075B] (Ps. 78). Elsewhere: “And they will leave their riches to others” (Ps. 48).

Hence, although David abounded in temporal riches, because he did not possess spiritual riches as abundantly as he wished, he calls himself poor and needy, saying: “I am needy and poor; God, help me” (Ps. 61). Therefore, brothers, if you truly wish to be rich, love those spiritual and eternal riches and hasten toward them with your whole desire. If temporal riches overflow, do not set your heart upon them, but distribute them to the poor.

He shows in what things they are rich when he says: “In every word”—namely, of the preaching of the Old and New Testament—and “in all knowledge,” both of divine and of human things. This knowledge, certainly, if it is held together with charity, is a virtue, just as the Testament [Col. 2075C] of Christ was confirmed among you.

He calls Scripture a testament because it bears witness to an eternal inheritance. The Gospel, therefore, is the Testament by which Christ, dying, testified to us an eternal inheritance if we should love him. This Testament was confirmed among the Corinthians because they themselves were so strengthened in it through faith, hope, and charity that neither death, nor life, nor the sword could separate them from love of Christ the testator or from love of the inheritance.

“So that nothing,” he says, “may be lacking to you in any grace”—understand, any grace necessary on the way. Hence it is clear that some of the Corinthians were already perfect according to the perfection of the way.

Let us cast off, brothers, our imperfection and tepidity, daily entreating Christ the testator with sighs [Col. 2075D] to confirm us in his Testament and grace, so that we may in no way be separated from him.

The third part follows, in which the Apostle shows what the Corinthians expect through the graces mentioned above, saying: “As you await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ.” To await is to hope with desire. The Corinthians, then, hoped with desire and awaited the revelation of Jesus Christ.

But the wicked do not await it; rather, they fear Christ’s coming, like an adulterous woman who dreads her husband’s arrival. You can observe this in yourselves, brothers, because one who is conscious of no guilt and sincerely loves God awaits his coming with desire, as that of his Father and friend, grieving that amid the miseries [Col. 2076A] of this age he is delayed from seeing him, according to Paul’s saying: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1).

Therefore, brothers, let us prepare ourselves to be people for whom this world is an exile and the revelation of Christ desirable. Christ’s coming is called a revelation for three reasons: either because he will manifest himself in power, though he first came hidden, according to the saying: “As lightning comes out from the east and appears even to the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matt. 24); or because he will reveal the hidden things of hearts, according to the saying: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also bring to light the hidden things of darkness and will reveal the counsels of hearts” (1 Cor. 4); or because then it will be revealed who are the elect and who are the rejected, according to the saying: “Little children, it has not yet appeared what we shall be; but when he appears, then we shall be like him” (1 John 3).

But because we cannot confidently await Christ’s coming by our own virtue, he adds: “Who will also confirm you unto the end, without crime”—he does not say, “without sin.” For in this world we cannot live without at least venial sin. Hence John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1).

These venial sins, however, which occur daily—in an idle word, in laughter, in delaying to go to church or to give alms, and the like—are erased by daily acts of satisfaction, such as striking the breast, almsgiving, prayer, and similar acts. But he says “without crime,” that is, without mortal sin, such sins as separate a person from God. Thus, confirmed [Col. 2076C] by God, we shall be secure on the day of judgment.

It is called a day either because of great and continuous charity, or because of the revelation of Christ’s glory, or because of the revelation of hearts and the glorification of the righteous. Yet although that day will be day for the elect, who will be enlightened, it will be night for the rejected, who will be shut up in eternal darkness, so that they will be without the true sun, without the warmth of goodness, and without the opportunity to do good, according to the saying: “The night is coming, when no one can work” (John 9).

From that night may almighty God preserve us and grant us to see his eternal and blessed glory, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# HOMILY XXXIX. THE EIGHTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

[Col. 2076D] “The Pharisees gathered together, and one of them, a doctor of the law, questioned Jesus, testing him” (Matt. 22–23). Dearly beloved brothers, the text of this Gospel reading ought to be heard with all the greater eagerness because it contains teaching necessary for our souls.

It has four parts. First, the Pharisees gather and one of them questions Jesus. Second, Jesus answers them. Third, he refutes them. Fourth, he instructs the simple. The Pharisees therefore gathered together. The wicked, although they are divided not only from others but also among themselves—which happens because they serve contrary vices—nevertheless unite in persecuting the good.

Thus Herod and Pilate, although they were enemies, united in putting Christ to death. Likewise the Pharisees and Sadducees, although divided and discordant, united in accusing Paul. So too the powerful and malicious of this age, although they serve contrary vices, nevertheless assist and ally themselves against the righteous.

Let us strive, my brothers, to overcome their united wickedness through wisdom, patience, and prayer, saying with the Prophet: “Hurl them down, Lord; divide their tongues” (Ps. 54)—that is, so that just as the wickedness at the tower of Babel was hurled down through the division of tongues, so now it may be hurled down through division of hearts.

The Pharisees therefore gathered together against the Lord so that, since they could not overcome him by reason, they might overcome him by numbers. And they question him through one man, so that if he prevailed, all might seem victorious; but if he were defeated, only he might seem defeated.

“One of them,” he says, “a doctor of the law, questioned him.” A doctor of the law rises up against the Author of the law. Hence it is clear that knowledge without charity is harmful, according to Paul’s saying: “Knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up” (1 Cor. 8).

Many heretics today resemble this doctor of the law: they attack the truth with words of charity. Those who persecute God himself and the Church through riches, powers, and honors given them by God are also like them.

Since a question may be asked either for the purpose of learning—as when a disciple questions a teacher—or for the purpose of deceiving—as when a malicious person questions a simple one—the evangelist determines the intention with which the doctor of the law questioned Christ when he adds: “Testing him.”

He tested him, then, not in order to prove him, as God tested Abraham; nor in order to teach him, as a teacher tests a disciple; but in order to deceive him, as the devil tests a Christian, saying: “Teacher, which is the great commandment in the law?”

Under the appearance of simplicity in his words, he lays traps of ambush, according to the saying: “His words were smoother than oil, yet they were arrows” (Ps. 54). He questions not in order to instruct or to be instructed, but to display his own expertise and mock the other’s simplicity. Such people—something to be lamented—are numerous today: they seek and dispute about the Scriptures not in order to practice them but to appear learned, and, as the Philosopher says, “They wish to know in order to be known.”

The Teacher of truth, however, does not remain silent before one who tests the truth, showing that, whatever the intention with which truth is questioned, we should disclose it if the occasion is suitable.

[Col. 2077D] The second part follows, in which the Lord, answering the Pharisees, instructs us concerning love of God and neighbor and concerning the order of loving. Since the whole Law and the Prophets are fulfilled through this, he instructs us concerning love of God when he says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind.”

In this commandment he demonstrates why and to what extent God is to be loved. Why? For three reasons: because he is good in himself, which he suggests by saying “God”; because he has deserved to be loved by us by creating, nourishing, and redeeming us, which he suggests by saying “Lord”; and because he gives himself as the reward to those who love him, which he suggests by saying “your.”

He shows how greatly God is to be loved when he says, “with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind”—that is, with all that you know, with all that you live, and with all that you remember. For all our movements, just as they come from God, must likewise be directed toward God.

But, my brothers, what does this repetition of the words “with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind” mean? Would it not have been sufficient had he said “with all your heart”? Certainly. Yet so many words are repeated for greater emphasis, because what is never sufficiently practiced can never be sufficiently stated.

But who can fulfill this commandment? No one on the way. Why, then, was it given? So that a person may recognize that he is always imperfect on the way and strive toward the homeland, where he can fulfill it. Yet even in the homeland he will not be able to love God as much as God deserves.

He instructs us concerning love of neighbor when he says: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Here it is indicated in what respect, in what manner, and for what reason one’s neighbor is to be loved.

In what respect? In that he is our neighbor, joined to us by nature, faith, kinship, benefaction, place, or familiarity. We are therefore commanded to love every human being, whether known or unknown, friend or enemy, good or evil—not insofar as he is evil or an enemy, but insofar as he is our neighbor by nature, faith, or virtue, or, if he is not, so that he may become one.

How should you love your neighbor? “As yourself.” He does not say “as much as yourself,” but “as yourself”—that is, love yourself well and your neighbor well. For one who loves himself badly hates himself. Therefore let us love our neighbor as ourselves, wishing him as many good things as we wish for ourselves.

The reason why one’s neighbor should be loved is suggested to us by the fact that in the first commandment we are ordered to direct all the movements of our soul and body toward loving God. Hence it is clear to us that even the movements of love by which we love ourselves or our neighbors must be directed toward God as their cause and end, so that we love both ourselves and our neighbors only in God and for God.

He instructs us concerning the order of loving by calling that commandment “greatest” and “first,” and this one “second.” The commandment concerning love of God is greatest in dignity and first in order. We must therefore love God above all things; in second place, our own soul; in third place, our neighbor’s soul; and in fourth place, our own body.

The Lord shows that father and mother must be loved first among our neighbors when he gave the commandment concerning their love as the first commandment of the second tablet. After them, one’s wife is to be loved, since although father and mother are to be left bodily for the sake of one’s wife, they are not to be left in the mind. After one’s wife come children; after children, brothers; after these, grandchildren. Thereafter, the person who is more closely joined to us by blood, familiarity, or benefaction is to be loved more; and finally come enemies.

Hence the commandment of love is called by the Prophet: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 118), because it extends from love of God all the way to love of one’s enemy.

That the whole Law is fulfilled through these two commandments, the Lord shows when he says: “On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets.” Whoever loves God keeps his commandments. Whoever loves his neighbor does not wish to harm him in anything, but rather to benefit him. Thus he neither kills him, nor commits adultery with his wife, nor steals his property, nor does the other things that are forbidden.

Therefore, if you cannot know all the Scriptures, at least hold fast to the commandment concerning love of God and neighbor. For the person who holds charity in his conduct holds both what is evident and what is hidden in the divine words. Whoever has this has everything, and whoever offends against it has become guilty of all.

Hence the Prophet says: “I have seen the end of all perfection; your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Rom. 13). And the Apostle says: “Love is the fullness of the law” (ibid.).

Therefore, brothers, let us hold love above all things, because love preserves the law, brings God near to itself, makes neighbors into friends, reconciles enemies, overcomes the devil, disregards death, bears adversity with equanimity, wisely moderates prosperity, shares everything, never fails, makes the goods of others its own, and alone sees and knows God.

The third part follows, in which the Lord refutes the assembled Pharisees by questioning them in this way: “What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?” He questions them not so that he himself might be instructed by them—for he knew all things—but so that he might instruct them, though they did not wish to be instructed; so that, by exposing their ignorance, he might refute their pride, since they were puffed up with knowledge of the law; so that he might teach us about Christ’s eternal birth; and so that he might silence the Pharisees’ talkativeness.

He therefore refutes their pride when he shows that they do not know how Christ is called “Lord” by the prophet David. They thought—and the Jews still think—that Christ would be a mere human being descended from David’s seed. Therefore, according to their own view, the Lord rightly asks how David calls Christ his Lord, since, according to them, David is earlier in time and is his father by generation. For if Christ is David’s son, how is he his Lord? Or if he is his Lord, how is he his son?

The Lord, however, instructs us concerning his eternal generation through the words of the prophet, who introduces the Father speaking to the Son, as follows: “Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109). In the verses that follow it is immediately shown that Christ is coeternal with the Father, who says to him: “With you is the beginning on the day of your power” (ibid.), with “it is mine” understood; and that he was born from him, when it is added: “Before the morning star I begot you” (ibid.).

Therefore, my brothers, what the Jews do not know, we understand: Christ has two births. One is from the Father before the ages, according to which he is one God and Lord with the Father. Hence David calls him Lord. The other is in time, from the Virgin, namely from David’s seed; hence he is also called the Son of David.

He also imposes silence on the Pharisees, so that, being so clearly confounded over their ignorance of Christ’s birth, they would no longer dare to attack him concerning knowledge of the law, since they saw that he knew all the law’s secrets.

The fourth part follows, in which the Lord instructs the disciples and the simple crowd morally, saying: “The scribes and the Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat,” and so forth (Matt. 23).

As we gather from this and from other passages of the holy Gospel, my brothers, there are three kinds of leaders: the shepherd, the mercenary, and the thief, differing both in name and in intention.

The shepherd is one who feeds Christ’s sheep through charity, by example and by word. Concerning him the Lord says: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John 10). The mercenary is one who feeds Christ’s sheep by word, but not by example, for the sake of temporal things. Hence the Lord says: “The mercenary flees because he is a mercenary and does not care about the sheep” (ibid.). The thief is the heretic, who feeds Christ’s sheep neither by example nor by word; rather, he kills them while pretending that he is feeding them. Concerning him the Lord says: “The thief comes only to slaughter and destroy” (ibid.). He slaughters by evil speech and destroys by evil example.

In this Gospel reading, therefore, the Lord speaks about mercenaries under the name of scribes and Pharisees. He does so in this way: first, he describes what they are like and how they conduct themselves. Second, he shows what the people owe them. Third, he describes their vices. Fourth, he forbids the disciples to imitate them.

He shows what they are like when he calls them scribes and Pharisees. They are scribes because they know the law; they are Pharisees because through pride and empty glory they separate themselves from others, possessing knowledge without charity, which, according to the Apostle, puffs up rather than builds up (1 Cor. 8).

How do they conduct themselves? “They sit on Moses’ seat.” The seat of teachers is like the tribunal of judges and the throne of kings. The seat therefore signifies the teaching of the law or of the Gospel.

The good shepherd sits on the seat because he restrains himself within the teaching of the law and does not transgress it. The mercenary, however, sits upon the seat because by evil conduct he transgresses and tramples upon the teaching of the law. The heretic sits outside the seat because he keeps the teaching of the law neither in deed nor in word.

Second, he shows what the sheep owe the mercenaries when he adds: “Whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not act according to their works.” As though he said plainly: Since they preach the teaching of the law, they are to be heard; but since by their evil lives they transgress it, they are not to be followed.

The good shepherd, because he keeps the law both in teaching and in life, is to be heard and followed. Hence the Lord says: “The sheep hear his voice and follow him” (John 10). The mercenary, because he keeps the law not in life but only in teaching, is to be heard but not followed. Hence it is also said here: “Whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not act according to their works.”

The thief, because he keeps the law neither in teaching nor in life, is to be neither heard nor followed. Hence the Lord says: “The sheep did not listen to them, because they did not know the voice of strangers” (ibid.).

The Lord knew that some subjects would refuse to listen to teachers when they saw the depravity of their lives. For this reason he says here: “Whatever they tell you, observe and do.” He also knew that some would follow the depraved lives of teachers, saying: “Does not the priest do this and that? Does not my bishop do it too? How could I be holier than they?” Therefore the Lord adds: “Do not act according to their works,” because they are to be followed in teaching, not in life.

[Col. 2081A] Third, he adds six vices of the mercenaries: transgression, cruelty, laxity, empty glory, gluttony, and ambition for honor and glory.

He reproves them for transgressing the law when he says: “They say and do not do.” Concerning the supreme Shepherd it is written: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1). For teaching without life is not enough. If you speak and do not act, it will be said to you: “Why do you yourself not do what you command? Why do you preach against stealing and steal?” (Rom. 2.)

Hence the Psalmist says: “But to the sinner God says: Why do you recount my righteous deeds and take my covenant upon your lips? Yet you hate discipline and cast my words behind you” (Ps. 49). Hence the episcopal staff is bent back upon itself, so that what one preaches to others one may show in oneself.

Again, life without teaching is not enough. Hence the Prophet cries: “Woe is me, because I have been silent” (Isa. 6). Another says: “If you do not announce to the wicked that he should turn from his wickedness, he will indeed die in his wickedness because you did not announce it to him; but I will require his blood at your hand” (Ezek. 3).

Alas, my brothers, how few true shepherds there are today! For we who are called shepherds of the people stumble both in life and in teaching. As great as the difference is between a shepherd and a sheep, so great ought to be the difference between the life of the shepherd and the life of the subject, so that, in view of the shepherd’s excellence, the subjects may be called a flock.

A priest ought to be among the people like a light in darkness, like a star on a throne, so that by the brightness of his path the others may follow the way. Hence the Lord also says: “You are the light of the world; you are the salt of the earth” (Matt. 5), so that through the brightness of your life the people may be enlightened and through your wisdom the tasteless and ignorant may be instructed.

But—and I cannot say this without a groan—we who ought to have been the light of the world have become darkness, and “as is the people, so is the priest” (Hos. 9). We also stumble in teaching, both because we are slow to preach unless we are attentive to temporal gain, and because we show partiality, rebuking the poor more harshly while either flattering or remaining silent about the vices of the powerful. And why is this, brothers, except that we despise the poor and fear the powerful, falling on one side from charity and on the other from the strictness of justice?

He reproves the Pharisees for cruelty when he adds: “For they bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them on people’s shoulders.” That they impose heavy burdens belonged to austerity; that they impose unbearable burdens belonged to cruelty and impiety.

Certain false shepherds do this even today. Unable to have compassion on the weaknesses of their subjects, some impose the burden of fasting on bread and water throughout one’s entire life. Others require that one always lie upon the ground in sackcloth and ashes. Others require that one always live as an exile barefoot. Others require that one abandon everything and enter the desert.

When the weak regard these things as unbearable, they despair of forgiveness, abandon all satisfaction, and remain in their sins. For it is written: “The donkey following its mother, overloaded, turns aside.” Those who do such things do not consider that the Samaritan applied oil and wine to the wounded man: [Col. 2082A] the oil of mercy and the wine of correction.

Hence Paul also says: “If someone is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should instruct such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6).

Therefore the good shepherd should approach the sinner in the manner of the Samaritan and be moved with compassion for him. After being weakened through compassion, he should pour in oil by offering consolation and promising forgiveness. Third, he should pour in wine by correcting moderately. Fourth, he should lift him onto his own animal, bearing his burdens through prayers, sacrifices, and offerings, so that he may imitate the true Shepherd who himself took away our infirmities and himself bore our sins.

He reproves the Pharisees for excessive laxity when he adds: “But with their finger they do not wish to move them.” As though he said: They impose the heavier commandments on others, but they themselves do not even wish to undertake the smallest of them; and thus, while they are savage toward others, they are less [read: more] indulgent toward themselves.

By contrast, the duty of a good shepherd is never to indulge his own vices, but to judge and treat himself more harshly and to be more indulgent toward others. In this, my brothers, we sin greatly every day: imposing heavier burdens of satisfaction upon others while treating ourselves leniently, judging the vices of others and excusing our own.

We impose harsh and lengthy fasts upon others while devoting ourselves to feasting and drunkenness. We command others to practice chastity while indulging our own loins. We command others to dress in sackcloth and lie in sackcloth and ashes while we dress in soft garments and recline in comfort. We urge others to abandon everything and distribute it to the poor, while we, being greedy, store up treasures on earth—making a double judgment, one for our neighbor and another for ourselves. What we condemn in others we excuse in ourselves, although it is written: “A scale and a scale, a weight and a weight, both are an abomination before God” (Prov. 20).

He reproves them for empty glory when he adds: “They do all their works so that they may be seen by people.” But, as the Lord says elsewhere, “they have received their reward” (Matt. 5)—namely, the human praise that they sought.

Good shepherds also sometimes do good things publicly before people, but they do not seek their own glory from this; they seek God’s glory and their neighbor’s benefit, according to the Lord’s command elsewhere: “Let your works shine,” he says, “before people, so that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 6).

Then he explains the things in which the Pharisees sought empty glory when he adds: “For they enlarge their phylacteries and lengthen their tassels.”

The Lord had commanded in the law: “You shall have my commandments as something always hung before your eyes.” Adhering to the letter of this command, the Pharisees wrote the Ten Commandments on little painted tablets and hung them on their foreheads, so that they might appear more observant of the law than others. Hence he calls this little tablet here a phylactery, from *phylasse*, meaning “to observe.”

The Lord had also commanded that tassels be made on the corners of garments. The Lord therefore had them on his garments, one of which the woman with the issue of blood is read to have touched. But the Jews, lovers of empty glory, made larger tassels for themselves, [Col. 2083A] on which they tied thorns, so that by their pricking they might be reminded of the divine law.

Many of us today, my brothers, resemble these people. So that they may be seen by others, they dress more religiously, live more sparingly, murmur psalms more frequently, pray at greater length, bend their knees more often, begin first in the choir, and finish last. But all who are like this are undoubtedly wretched: for the sake of the wind of favor they sell the reward of virtue—wretched in this age, and more wretched in the age to come.

He reproves them for gluttony when he adds: “For they love the first places at banquets.” As though he were saying plainly: They wish to appear glorious so that they may be honored by people through invitations, the first place, and more lavish feasting.

We too are like this today, my brothers—which is grievous—when we rejoice if princes and powerful people invite us, place us in the first position, and set before us various dishes and wines. We eat the marrow of the earth, feast, and become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery, while the poor man perishes outside from hunger and thirst.

But the good shepherd should never go outside his own house to eat merely for the sake of eating, except for the sake of benefiting others: so that he may feed spiritually those who invite him and feed him bodily. At table, however, he should avoid pride in his seat, satiety in food, cheerfulness in drink, and frivolity in speech, so that he may build up his fellow guests not only by his words but also by the example of his gravity.

He rebukes them for ambition when he adds: “And they love the first seats in the synagogues.” Alas, how greatly this ambition for positions of authority has grown among us today! [Col. 2083C] They seek to become teachers before they have learned to be disciples; to command before they have learned to obey. Some pretend to holiness, others serve princes, others amass money, others frequent the court, so that what they do not attain by merit they may obtain by hypocrisy, bribery, violence, or entreaty—the dignity of the chair. But let him understand that he is not a bishop who prefers to rule rather than to benefit.

Let no one presume to defend his ambition with that saying of the Apostle: “Whoever desires the office of bishop desires a good work” (1 Tim. 3). For he says “work,” not honor; work, not wealth; labor, not repose; ministry, not domination; care, not glory; bearing the burdens of others, not being carried by others; seeking not one’s own interests, but those of Jesus Christ. [Col. 2083D] Whoever, therefore, desires the episcopate in this manner desires a good work.

But how rare such a person is today, dearly beloved brothers! Rather, almost everyone shows, when he reaches a position of dignity, with what intention he sought it: they ascend badly and live worse. They take for themselves a great number of horses, so that they no longer appear to be bishops but tyrants. They send ahead in carriages and pack animals a large and costly quantity of furnishings, as though they were transporting military camps. They proceed with purple-adorned reins and gilded trappings. There is no limit to their clothing, their food, their palaces, their silver dishes, or their golden cups. Exalted upon the chair, they forget that they are mortal; they assume the role of the rich, cast aside the poor, sell the orders of the Church and of justice, and desire to sell more dearly what they have bought at great cost. [Col. 2084A] Reading and contemplation are despised, and profitable lawsuits are pursued.

He rebukes them again for vainglory when he adds: “They love greetings in the marketplace and to be called rabbi by people.” When the devil has been unable to corrupt the works of some people either at the beginning of their undertaking or in its execution through an intention of vainglory, he later attacks them by offering favor and praise, in accordance with what the Lord said to the serpent: “And you shall lie in wait for his heel” (Gen. 3). He therefore brings upon them flatterers by whom they are greeted, praised as blessed, and deceived, according to Isaiah’s saying: “My people, those who call you blessed are themselves deceiving you” (Isa. 3).

Although outwardly they blush and declare themselves unworthy of praise, inwardly the soul rejoices and delights in praise, and is thereby stained. No one notices the battle with vainglory except the person who declares war upon it and investigates it carefully.

Fourth, the Lord forbids the disciples to imitate the Pharisees when he adds: “But you must not be called rabbi.” There is a difference, my brothers, between being called rabbi and wishing to be called rabbi. Wishing to be called rabbi is always a sign of ambition and vainglory; being called rabbi, however, may characterize both the good and the wicked. Being called a teacher does not harm a good teacher; indeed, it benefits him. For when a good man hears himself called a teacher, he understands from this that an obligation has been laid upon him: what he is called by name must also be true in reality. Therefore he strives and labors, by word and example, to show himself a true teacher to others.

But being called a teacher harms a wicked teacher. For when he hears himself called a teacher, he believes others more than himself, and is thereby driven not to correct himself, [Col. 2084C] but rather to become more proud. “For you are all brothers,” he says. As though he were saying: Although in office and excellence you are teachers to others, nevertheless, by charity and humility, equal those subject to you, and wish to be called brothers rather than teachers or masters.

Nor should you think that the spiritual brotherhood among you is inferior to bodily brotherhood. For no bodily brotherhood compares with spiritual brotherhood. Hence he also adds: “And call no one your father on earth, for you have one Father, who is in heaven.” A human being is called the father of a son not because he creates him, but because he is merely the minister of his generation. God, however, is himself the Creator of body and soul; he is the author of generation, both the first and the second; he is the nourisher, teacher, and savior.

And do not be called teachers, because “you have one Teacher, the Christ,” who alone teaches everyone, and without whom no one is taught. For he is teacher both by authority and by office. He teaches outwardly and inwardly: outwardly by word and example, inwardly by inspiration. Unless there is someone within who teaches, the teacher’s tongue labors in vain. A human being is called a teacher only with respect to external ministry.

“The one who is greatest among you,” he says, “shall be your servant.” As though he were saying plainly: Let there be no rivalry among you concerning teaching, but concerning service; not concerning precedence, but concerning humility. Just as the Son of God came into this world not to be served but to serve everyone and to lay down his life for all, so someone should approach pastoral office not to be enriched, [Col. 2085A] not to be honored, and not to be served, but rather to serve himself and lay down his life for the souls subject to him.

For “whoever exalts himself” temporally “will be humbled” eternally. Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, following the true and supreme Teacher, let us seek in this world not to be enriched, honored, delighted, or served, but rather to serve, teach, and benefit others, with poverty, humility, patience, and labor, so that in the heavenly kingdom we may deserve to be enriched, honored, and delighted.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XL. THE NINETEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who has been created according to God in holiness and the righteousness of truth” (Eph. 4), etc.

In this reading, dearly beloved brothers, the Apostle exhorts us to the newness of an innocent life. He does so in this way: first, he urges us to change from evil to good; second, he sets out the aspects of the old condition that we must flee and the works of newness that we must perform.

First, therefore, he urges us to change from evil to good when he says: “Be renewed,” etc. Renewal takes place when the old condition is stripped away and lost newness is recovered. We, brothers, were formed new in Adam, but when he sinned, we fell with him into the old condition.

Certainly, what is new is pure, firm, and strong. What is old, however, is corrupt, weak, and feeble. Adam was created new because he was pure, firm, and strong: pure, without sin; firm in resisting vice; strong in persevering in the good. But because he sinned voluntarily, he incurred the old condition and became impure, weak, and feeble. Impure, because he was corrupted by vice; weak in resisting vice. Since, although he could have avoided sin, he did not wish to do so, it was inflicted upon him that, when he wished to avoid it, he would be unable.

He was also weak in doing good, for by himself he cannot do good unless he is aided by God’s grace. Adam is therefore called the old man. His old condition is that corruption and weakness which he incurred by sinning, and which is called the sickness of nature, or the sting of the flesh, or the inclination to sin. This is original sin. It is also called “sinning sin,” because through it, whether we wish it or not, we sin.

On account of this the Apostle exclaims: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” “The grace of God through Jesus Christ” (Rom. 7).

Christ, by contrast, is called the new man because he was conceived not from desire but from the Holy Spirit. He was created and remained pure, firm, and strong. His innocence and holiness are called newness. Therefore, just as we are born from Adam’s corrupted mass, so we are born corrupted from the corrupted, old from the old. But through the grace of Christ, the new man, we are renewed when his original sin is forgiven us in faith and baptism, and innocence is bestowed upon us. According to the Apostle, by imitating Christ in holiness we make ever greater progress from day to day.

Renewed by this newness, the Apostle says: “I live, yet it is no longer I; Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2). In what this renewal takes place, how and through whom it occurs, and of what it consists, the Apostle subsequently explains.

He shows where it takes place when he says: “In the spirit of your mind,” that is, in your spirit and mind. By “spirit” he understands the soul’s lower power, namely sensuality; by “mind,” the higher intellect.

Sensuality is that power of the soul which comprehends bodily things through the body’s workshops. The Apostle therefore urges us to be renewed in our sensuality, so that our senses may no longer be directed as formerly toward old things, but rather toward performing the works of the new man: so that the eye may not look upon temporal things in order to desire them, but rather in order to despise them; and may look upon the poor not to scorn them, but rather to have compassion on them; so that the ears may not hear unlawful things, but the sacred words of the Lord; so that the nostrils may not smell the scents of prostitutes, but rather the sweetness of spiritual virtues; so that taste may not be ensnared by seductive flavors, but by fasting and every word that proceeds from the mouth of God; so that touch may not take pleasure in unlawful contact, but in chastity.

He also commands the intellect to be renewed, so that it may no longer devote itself to wickedness, deceit, fraud, evil counsels, and evil arts, but rather to spiritual studies and holy readings, to the wisdom of God and contemplation of heavenly things, so that the image of God, deformed in us, may be restored.

He shows how this restoration takes place when he says: “And put on the new man,” that is, the newness of Christ, the new man, so that, insofar as we are able, we may be innocent as he is innocent; holy as he is holy; merciful as he is merciful; and, to the extent he grants, imitators of him.

He shows through whom this renewal takes place when he adds: “who has been created according to God,” that is, his newness has been created according to God. As though he were saying: This newness cannot arise in us from ourselves, but from the one who says: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. 21).

Seeking this renewal of the mind from God, the Prophet says: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Ps. 50). And we also, my brothers, who possess nothing from ourselves except sin, should pray with groaning; let us pray daily with tears and sighs; let us pray, I say, with the Prophet: “Take away from me the oldness of sin, Lord, and renew a right spirit within me” (ibid.).

He shows of what this renewal consists when he says: “In holiness and the righteousness of truth.” In holiness toward ourselves, and in righteousness toward our neighbors; and so that both holiness and righteousness may belong to truth—that is, to the truth of the work and the truth of its end.

For there are some—an occasion for sorrow—who are pretenders: they are neither holy nor righteous in their deeds, but merely pretend. Others, although they possess works of holiness or righteousness, nevertheless degenerate in their purpose, when they expect secular glory from them.

The second part follows, in which the Apostle sets out the aspects of the old condition that he teaches us to flee, and the aspects of newness that he commands us to follow, saying: “Therefore, putting away all falsehood, speak the truth,” etc.

There are three aspects of the old condition: the oldness of the mouth, the oldness of the heart, and the oldness of conduct. Conversely, there are also three aspects of newness: newness of the mouth, newness of the heart, and newness of conduct.

He therefore commands us to cast away the oldness of the mouth when he says: “Therefore, putting away all falsehood.” Falsehood is a false expression by the voice with the intention of deceiving. To lie is so called as if it were “against the mind,” according to the saying: “They have spoken with deceitful lips and a double heart” (Ps. 11), that is, from duplicity of heart.

There are six kinds of lies. The first is one that benefits someone and harms no one, as when someone lies in order to preserve another person’s life. The second is one that benefits and harms no one, as when someone lies in jest. The third is one that benefits one person and harms another, as when a seller lies to a buyer. The fourth is one that harms someone and benefits no one, as when someone wishes to deceive his enemy. The fifth is a lie told solely from the desire to lie, which is a remarkable sin. The sixth is lying in matters of the faith, which is characteristic of heretics.

Detraction, flattery, whispering, and accusation are also included under falsehood. Although they may sometimes contain the truth of the matter, because they are spoken with an evil purpose, they are lies.

Every lie must be avoided. Hence he says here: “Putting away all falsehood.” And the Prophet says: “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Ps. 5). Therefore no one is permitted to lie. He may, however, remain silent about the truth or evade malice by means of a modal proposition.

As blessed Augustine relates, a certain bishop, firm in name and faith, hid a man who was accused before him. When the man was sought, he said: “It is not permitted me either to betray him or to lie.” Dragged before a pagan king, he persisted in this same course even unto death. He became renowned for truth and justice, and through his grace even the accused man was freed.

Behold, brothers, how truth and justice are admired even among unbelievers. It is permitted to evade an inquirer by means of a modal proposition, as when a gladiator asks, “Where is that man?” and we answer, “I do not know,” understanding, “I do not know for you.” We find such expressions in sacred Scripture, as in: “You shall die and shall not live” (Isa. 38), where the implied qualification is “unless you weep.”

This is a duplicity that deceives no one, but rather helps.

The Apostle invites us to the newness of the mouth when he adds: “Speak the truth, each one with his neighbor,” that is, with every person. Truth is a true expression by the voice with a proper end. The expression is indeed true when what is conceived in the heart is expressed by the voice, whatever the state of affairs may be.

Thus, when Paul promised that he would go to the Corinthians, because he spoke as he intended, he spoke the truth, even though he did not go. Conversely, if someone says, contrary to his mind, that he will do something and then does it, nevertheless, because he spoke against what he felt, he lied. But if he says what he feels and does so without a proper end—that is, not for God’s sake—he is a liar.

Thus, if a witness testifies to the truth for the sake of money, he is a liar. Behold, brothers—an occasion for sorrow—how rare truthful people are today. Even if there are some who say what they feel, almost everyone directs his intention not toward God but toward a temporal end.

What the Apostle added, “because we are members of one another,” should be understood in this way: all the faithful are members of Christ, and we ought to assist one another as members. When, therefore, a brother lies to his brother, what else is this than the left hand lying to the right? And when the left hand lies to the right, what else is it than acting against itself? Thus, without doubt, my brothers, whoever lies to another first harms himself.

He urges us to cast away the oldness of the mind and put on newness when he adds: “Be angry, and do not sin.” What the Apostle says here about anger he understands also of the other passions or disturbances of the mind: fear and sadness, desire and joy, anger and hatred.

These passions are natural, and good people use them well while evil people use them badly. Whoever fears offending God fears well, and whoever is saddened by having offended him is saddened well. Conversely, whoever fears that he may be unable to fulfill his evil desire fears badly, and whoever is saddened because he did not fulfill it is saddened badly. Similarly, whoever is angry against his own or another’s sin is angry well.

The Apostle therefore urges us—but in an inverted order—to put on newness of mind when he says: “Be angry,” with the implied qualification, “against vices.” He also urges us to cast away the oldness of mind when he says: “Do not sin,” with the implied qualification, “through anger or another movement of the mind.”

Or, as some wish, the first movement of anger, which is not within our control, is permitted to us when it says, “Be angry.” But anger after that movement, as a grave sin, is forbidden when it says, “Do not sin.”

“Let not the sun,” he says, “go down upon your anger.” This may be understood literally, so that anger should be so brief that it does not last until sunset. Hence in the *Lives of the Fathers* we read of two men: one had never seen the sun behold the other angry; the other had never seen the sun behold the first eating.

Or “the sun”—that is, the love of God and neighbor—must not set in your hearts because of excessive anger, so that we may be angry against a brother’s vice in such a way that we do not lose the charity owed to his nature. For when anger prevails, it disturbs the charity of the mind, so that the mind can no longer discern what is fitting.

Hence the poet says: “Anger is a brief madness” [Note: [Col. 2087D] See note 61]; and Solomon says: “The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (Prov. 21). This is a *litotes*, that is, it means: “It accomplishes unrighteousness.” For a person whom anger has disturbed does not know how to judge justly.

Therefore, when the emperor Theodosius, driven by a sudden fit of anger, had ordered more than ten thousand people to be killed, he was rebuked by blessed Ambrose. He then established a law that thereafter, whenever an emperor or judge became enraged against an accused person, he should not judge him immediately, but the accused should remain in custody for thirty days, so that the judge’s mind, having been calmed, might then judge better.

“Do not,” he says, “give place to the devil.” Whoever gives place to sin gives place to the devil, just as whoever gives place to virtue gives place to the Holy Spirit.

The Apostle commands us to cast away the oldness of conduct when he adds: “Let the one who was stealing steal no longer,” understanding by theft robbery, fraud, usury, and every form of extortion. Concerning these he says elsewhere: “Let no one defraud or overreach his brother in business, because the Lord is the avenger of those who do such things” (1 Thess. 4).

For if, my brothers, the person who does not give what belongs to him is condemned, what will become of those who seize what belongs to others?

He commands us to assume the newness of conduct when he adds: “Rather, let each one labor with his own hands at what is good,” that is, at an honest and useful occupation. By this he includes every kind of labor or honest craft, such as agriculture, shoemaking, carpentry, and other arts of this kind, by which a person can honestly provide for himself and others.

This is directed, my brothers, against certain people who live idly and meddlesomely, always looking to the hands of others, without considering that they thereby incur several vices: idle laziness, inexcusable begging, shameful shamelessness, and the deserved bearing of other people’s sins.

Against such people the Apostle says: “If anyone will not work, let him not eat” (2 Thess. 3); and the laws of the emperors prescribe that able-bodied beggars be consigned to servitude.

Conversely, my brothers, how honorable is a way of life sustained by manual labor, if it is carried out justly and with a right intention—and how many good things it contains! First, a person lives from his own just labor; second, from what he earns he renders God the offerings that are owed; third, he has something with which to redeem sins; fourth, according to what is said, he has something with which to give to one suffering need.

Let us therefore strive, dearly beloved brothers, to possess this threefold newness of mouth, heart, and conduct, so that we may deserve to be new members of Christ, the new man, by the gift of him who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XLI. THE NINETEENTH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“Jesus went up into a boat, crossed over, and came to his own city” (Matt. 9).

In the literal sense, dearly beloved brothers, the Lord shows in this reading of the holy Gospel that he possesses both true humanity and true divinity. He demonstrates that he possesses true humanity when, in the manner of human beings, he boards a ship, crosses over, and visits his earthly homeland.

The almighty and supreme Lord, to whom all the elements are subject, could indeed have divided the sea or, as he once did, walked upon the waters with dry feet. But he wished to demonstrate in himself the true signs of the humanity he had assumed. When we read that Christ hungered, thirsted, became weary, crossed over by ship, and had an earthly homeland and parents, we believe that he truly assumed our humanity and weakness.

Moreover, since we needed instruction concerning both his divinity and his humanity, at one moment he walks upon the waters as God, at another he crosses over in a boat as a human being; at one moment he feeds many thousands from a few loaves as God, at another he hungers and thirsts as a human being; at one moment he heals others as God, at another he suffers as a human being.

Here he demonstrates that he possesses true divinity in four ways. First, in his knowledge of another person’s faith. Hence it is said here: “When Jesus saw their faith.” They could have brought the paralytic to him not from faith but from temptation or mockery, but they could not deceive the Lord, who searches the kidneys and hearts.

Second, in the forgiveness of sins. Hence he says: “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you.” Here we should note, my brothers, that the Evangelist does not say, “Seeing the faith of the paralytic,” [Col. 2090B] but “the faith of those who brought him.” If another person’s faith had such power for the paralytic that he was healed in mind and body, how much power do you think each person’s own faith has?

But you will say: Did Christ forgive the sins of an unbelieving man? Certainly not. Rather, because of the faith of those who brought him, the Lord inspired faith in the paralytic, and thus forgave the sins of the one who believed.

Third, he shows that he possesses true divinity in his knowledge of the thoughts of others. When the scribes were saying within themselves, “This man blasphemes,” he said: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Mark 2).

Fourth, he shows it in the healing of the paralytic by a mere command. Here, my brothers, there are four signs belonging properly to God alone: knowledge of another’s faith, forgiveness of sins, inspection of the thoughts of others, and healing accomplished by a mere command. Yet when he wishes, he works these things through ministers as their author.

But since he was about to perform the first three invisibly, he confirmed them by the fourth, visible sign. Hence he said: “But so that you may know that the Son of God [of Man] has authority on earth to forgive sins”—with the implied addition, “and to know faith and the thoughts of hearts”—“behold, I demonstrate this to you by a visible sign.”

Therefore the Evangelist adds: “Then he said to the paralytic: Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house.” And he rose and went to his house.

In the tropological (moral) sense, this reading instructs us in four matters.

First, in the fact that the Lord boarded a boat, crossed over, and came to his own city, we are instructed by his example that we too should board the boat and cross over from the exile of this world to our eternal homeland.

The boat signifies the holy Church. Although in this world it is harassed by evil spirits, although it is shaken by waves of tribulation, although it is now lifted up by prosperity and now almost submerged by adversity, nevertheless, with God guiding it and the Holy Spirit driving it forward, it transports those who are in it, through the unity of faith and charity, to the harbor of eternal salvation.

But—and I cannot say this without groaning—there are many today who appear to be in the Church in number but are outside it in merit. They do not wish to cross over to that homeland; rather, they love to remain in the shipwreck of this world, and would not want the present misery to end, but to last here forever.

There are also many who, what is more grievous, attack and tear apart the very boat of the Church by heresies, contentions, plots, and persecutions—the boat by which they could cross over—and, insofar as it lies within them, submerge it. But they themselves are submerged as they deserve. The boat, however, reaches the harbor of salvation with its faithful.

Let us therefore cross over, brothers, in hope and desire, and let us hasten toward our city—our city indeed, since, as the Apostle says, “you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (Eph. 2), “heirs indeed of God, and fellow heirs with Christ” (Rom. 8).

Second, because we must seek not only our own salvation but also that of our neighbors, we are instructed by those who brought the paralytic, lying on his bed, to the Lord to be healed. We too should have compassion on the sick, whether in mind or in body, and offer them to the Lord for healing through prayer and desire.

Let us not belong to the number of those who, as though they were made of stone or iron, are moved by no compassion over the afflictions and pains of their neighbors. Rather, let us imitate the one of whom we speak, Jesus Christ, who continually overflows with compassion toward the sick and sinners, as the Prophet says of him: “Truly he himself bore our sicknesses, and he himself carried our sins” (Isa. 53).

Let us also imitate his imitator, Paul, who said of himself: “I became weak to the weak, so that I might gain the weak” (1 Cor. 9). And elsewhere: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11).

Third, in the fact that the Lord looked upon the faith of those who brought the paralytic, we are instructed that, if we wish the Lord to hear us when we pray for ourselves and for others, we should strive to possess perfect faith—that is, faith working through charity (Gal. 4).

It is impossible for prayer or anything else to please God without faith. Hence James says: “If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach anyone. But let him ask in faith, without doubting. For the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind. Let that person not think that he will receive anything from God” (Jas. 1).

If, therefore, neither the one who prays nor the one for whom prayer is offered is known to God, how are they heard? For we know that God does not hear sinners; but if anyone is a true worshiper of God, God hears him (John 9).

Rather, if someone who through unbelief or impiety is hateful to God presumes to intercede for an accused person, God is not only not appeased but is further provoked.

Therefore, my brothers, let us strive through true faith to make ourselves known and familiar to God, so that we may deserve to have a place of intercession before him.

Fourth, in the fact that the Lord forgives the paralytic’s sins not on account of his own faith but on account of the faith of those who brought him, he shows how much influence the faithful have in interceding with him—not only for themselves but also for others—and how inclined he is to hear their prayers.

You, therefore, brothers, who are truly faithful, who possess a place of intimacy and intercession before God, do not conceal or refuse the help of your intercession from the accused and sinners. Even if they do not ask you, do not disdain to ask on their behalf. Do not hide the talent entrusted to you, but pray for everyone; pray for each person.

For God cannot despise the prayers of his faithful. Through our prayers, may he in his mercy raise us who lie weak upon the bed of a tormented conscience; who are paralytics—that is, loosened in our limbs—and powerless; who are unable to will what is good, speak what is good, or do what is good. May he raise us to do good, so that we may lift the bed—that is, the flesh of our weakness—away from vice and carry it toward the heavenly gift.

May he deign to grant this, he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. [Col. 2092B] Amen.

## HOMILY XLII. THE TWENTIETH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“See carefully how you walk” (Eph. 5), etc.

In this reading, dearly beloved brothers, the Apostle exhorts us to walk carefully along the road of our worldly pilgrimage, so that we may deserve to reach our eternal homeland by it.

This reading has four parts. First, he urges us to walk carefully; second, to free and redeem ourselves from temporal impediments; third, to become intoxicated not with worldly but with spiritual intoxication; fourth, for Christ’s sake, to submit to and support one another.

Urging us to walk wisely along the road of this world, the Apostle says: “See carefully how you walk.” A person walks carefully, dearly beloved brothers, when he walks where he ought, by the way he ought, and in the manner he ought.

We walk where we ought if we hasten toward our eternal homeland with our whole desire, so that there we may see the God of gods in Zion, since, according to the Apostle, “we do not have here a lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come” (Heb. 13).

Therefore, brothers, let us always raise our eyes toward Christ, who went before us, and follow him along the road by which he went before us. “The eyes of the wise are in his head.”

We walk by the way we ought if we advance from good to better along the way of faith. Faith without works is of no benefit to one who has the opportunity to act, nor are works without faith. The Jews and Gentiles possess good works of piety, but because they do not possess faith, they cannot reach the eternal homeland through them.
