Some false Christians also possess, my brothers, the way of faith; but because they act badly, they do not walk along the way of faith; rather, they turn back. Therefore, brothers, if we wish to reach God through faith, let us stretch ourselves from good works toward better ones.

We walk in the manner we ought if we walk rightly, clearly, and moderately. We walk rightly if we do not turn to the right through prosperity or to the left through adversity. We walk clearly if we avoid the mountains of pride and presumption and the valleys of sadness and despair. We walk moderately if we go neither too quickly nor too slowly.

The person who hastens too much at the beginning becomes weary and fails before the proper time. This is what some do at the beginning of their conversion: they take on such a great burden that they must fail before the proper time.

The person who proceeds too slowly becomes sluggish and does not reach the goal at the proper time. This is what those do who make little or no progress in their actions.

Therefore, brothers, with moderation let us extend ourselves from lesser things toward greater ones, so that we may never fail but may advance toward perfection.

But because there are some who, under the pretext of almsgiving, involve themselves in cares and worldly affairs, the Apostle adds: “Not as unwise people, but as wise.”

This is the second part, in which the Apostle urges us to free and redeem ourselves from temporal cares, which some foolishly embrace, saying that they do so in order to have something to distribute to the poor. But the Apostle wishes the servants of God to be unencumbered.

Hence he says elsewhere: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs” (2 Tim. 2). Therefore here too he adds: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.”

A person redeems time when, in order to be able to pass through it peacefully and quietly, he leaves behind even what belongs to him. Thus the same Apostle, rebuking the Corinthians because they were contending in court, says: “Why not rather suffer injustice?” (1 Cor. 6). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone wishes to contend with you and take your tunic, give him your cloak also” (Matt. 5). And elsewhere: “If anyone takes what is yours, do not demand it back” (Luke 6).

This, however, is counsel, not commandment. For everyone is permitted to reclaim what belongs to him, but no one is permitted to do so contentiously. Under judicial procedure it is permitted for the less perfect to reclaim what is theirs; for the more perfect it is not permitted.

It is therefore divine counsel that, so that we may never fall into contention, we should yield to the one who contends and, my brothers, even relinquish what belongs to us.

“For the days are evil,” not in their essence, but because of the wickedness of those who use them badly—those who persecute people whom they see burdened with riches along the road of this world.

Therefore, brothers, let us be content with necessities alone, so that we may pass peacefully and unencumbered along a road infested with robbers and bandits.

Hence it follows: “Therefore be prudent, understanding what the will of God is.” For God wishes his servants to be despisers of the world and thus to hasten toward him unencumbered.

This is why God sets adversaries and impediments against those who desire to become rich, to glory, and to take pleasure in this world: when they see that they cannot prosper in this world, they may turn to God.

Hence the Lord speaks under the figure of a fornicating wife to Judea, saying: “I will hedge in your way with thorns; you will seek your lovers and will not find them. And you will say: I will return to my first husband, because it was better for me then than now” (Hos. 2).

The third part follows, in which the Apostle urges us, so that we may travel the way of God more cheerfully, to become intoxicated—not with worldly drunkenness, but with spiritual drunkenness—saying: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery, but be filled with the Holy Spirit,” and so forth.

There are three kinds of drunkenness: the first is wine-induced, the second worldly, and the third spiritual. The first [Col. 2094A] consists in immoderate wine-drinking, the second in immoderate desire, and the third in abundant charity. The first drunkenness, therefore, is evil, because it disturbs human perception, alienates the mind, and arouses people to dishonorable and shameful acts. Wine, after all, uncovered Noah’s private parts and caused Lot to lie with his daughters. “Woe to you,” says the Prophet, “who are mighty at drinking wine and strong at mixing drunkenness” (Isa. V).

The second drunkenness is exceedingly wicked, because through love of the world it disturbs the senses from the service of God, alienates the mind from wisdom and the love of God, and drags it toward crimes and evil deeds. This is the cup of Babylon, from which all the sinners of the earth become drunk.

The third drunkenness is most holy, because through love of God it withdraws the senses from evil works, alienates them from love of the world, and draws them by desire toward the heavenly homeland. [Col. 2094B] The saints become drunk with this. Hence the Prophet says: “They shall be inebriated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. XXXV). And elsewhere the Lord says through the Prophet: “My cup,” he says, “which makes drunk—how splendid it is!” (Ps. XXII).

Therefore, brothers, as we grow weary amid adversities on the road of this world, it is necessary for us to become drunk—not with worldly drunkenness, which makes us forget God and our neighbor, but with spiritual drunkenness, which makes us forget worldly things and hasten with our whole desire toward eternal things.

Be filled, then, brothers, with the Holy Spirit, who will provide us with many consolations and helps on the way of God, for, under his inspiration, you will speak to one another in psalms. Travelers do this, because by varied conversation they lighten the toil of the road. On the road of this exile, psalms ought to be the conversations and alleviations of the earth. Hence we sing in them: “Your testimonies were my songs in the place of my pilgrimage” (Ps. CXVIII).

Let us also sing with our voices and make melody in our hearts to the Lord, with hymns and spiritual songs, after the manner of pilgrims who, once a part of their labor has been overcome, sing. A hymn is praise of God accompanied by song. A song, however, is an exultation of the mind concerning eternal things, breaking forth into the voice.

Thus spiritual drunkenness grants the faithful, amid adversities, not only consolations in psalms, but also rejoicing in hymns sung aloud and in spiritual songs of the heart. It also makes them give thanks to God, as sailors do after a shipwreck, singing palinodies—songs of recantation.

The fourth part follows, in which the Apostle urges us, while we are on the road of this age, to be subject to one another in the fear of Christ, so that we may contend only in humility and service, supporting one another in the manner of travelers: the strong supporting the weak, the light the heavy, the swift the slow. Thus we fulfill the Apostle’s saying: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. VI), who himself “took away our infirmities and bore our sorrows” (Isa. LIII).

Because of fear and love of him alike, we too ought to bear the weaknesses of others. And if, my brothers, we walk cautiously in this way; if we free ourselves from worldly impediments; if, through spiritual drunkenness, forgetting temporal things, we hasten toward eternal things with our whole [Col. 2095A] desire; if, through charity, we bear one another’s burdens—we shall undoubtedly reach eternity in triumph, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XLIII. THE TWENTIETH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding feast for his son” (Matt. XXII).

This king, dearest brothers, is God the Father, who is King of kings and Lord of lords. He has a royal Son reigning as king together with him, as the Psalmist says: “Give the king your judgments, O God, and your justice to the King’s Son” (Ps. LXXI).

God the Father therefore made a wedding feast for his Son, because he determined that the Son should take our nature upon himself. He did this not because he himself was in need, but because we were in need. He did it out of his mercy, to lift up our misery.

Consider, then, three things: the cause of the wedding, the dowry, and the banquet. The cause is the reconciliation of humanity with God. For just as, my brothers, you often see that when there is hostility between two families, a marriage becomes the cause of reconciliation between a man of one family and a woman of the other, so it happened here. There was a great discord between God and humanity. Humanity, having been thrust into this exile through the first transgression, did not know God; indeed, through evil works it attacked him. But God, who is exalted, hated humanity because of its disobedience.

Yet because God does not forget to have mercy (Ps. LXXVI), it pleased him to reconcile his fugitive to himself, and he made his Only-Begotten Son the mediator of this reconciliation. By joining our humanity to himself, he reconciled humanity to God and God to humanity.

The Son of God also bestowed a dowry upon his bride, giving her here the ring of faith, the pledge of the other virtues and graces, and promising that, if she persevered in his love, he would give her the dowry of heavenly rewards.

God also prepared a banquet at the wedding of his Son in the Church through communion in the sacraments, setting out bread from heaven, “which strengthens” (Ps. CIII), and wine, “which gladdens the heart of man” (ibid.). He also set out, through the instruction provided by examples, bulls—that is, the holy Fathers of the Old Testament, who struck back with the horn of retribution—and fatted animals—that is, the holy Fathers of the New Testament, who, raised up by the richness of grace and lifted toward heaven on the wings of contemplation, would nourish the guests by their examples and words. [Col. 2095D]

At this wedding feast are set out for imitation the innocence of Abel, the justice of Noah, the faith of Abraham, the chastity of Joseph, the meekness of Moses, the gentleness of David, the patience of Job, the perfection of the apostles, the conscience of the martyrs, the sobriety of confessors, and the purity of virgins.

To this wedding feast, as the Lord testifies, many are called, but few are chosen. For many are invited and repeatedly called, yet they do not come. Many are also called and come, yet they are cast out. Few, however, are those who, in comparison with the others, will feast eternally with the bridegroom and the bride.

Behold three distinctions. Those who were invited and called repeatedly are the Jews. They were first invited through the patriarchs, and afterward called through the prophets and apostles, yet they scorned coming: one instead went to his estate—that is, into love of earthly possession, fearing to lose his place and nation; another went to his business—that is, preferring the assessment of his observances to the commandments of God. Against them the Psalmist speaks: “Because I have not known,” he says, “business”—or, according to another translation, “learning”—“I shall enter into the powers of the Lord” (Ps. LXX).

The rest seized his servants—that is, the apostles and their followers—and killed them after subjecting them to insults: one they stoned, like Stephen; another they beheaded, like John the Baptist and James son of Zebedee; another they threw down from a height, like James son of Alphaeus; and so forth.

God the Father, angered, sent out his armies through the agency of the Romans and destroyed those murderers and burned their city. Through the agency of the angels as well, he condemned their souls and their city—that is, their bodies—to be burned in everlasting fire.

Many are also called and come, yet some of them are cast out. These are the Gentiles, my brothers—that is, us. We were called from the crossroads, that is, from the various errors of idolatry and the other vices, and through preachers, both good and bad, summoned to Christ’s wedding, we came together. Hence the Psalmist says: “I announced and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number” (Ps. XXXIX).

For just as on a threshing floor the number of straw exceeds the number of grains beyond counting, so in the Church the number of the reprobate exceeds the number of the elect. In the Church they are contained by number, not merit; by name, not divine power. Nowhere are the good alone except in heaven, and nowhere are the evil alone except in hell.

In the world, however, the Lord willed the good and the evil to be mixed together for three reasons: the evil are with the good for purification, for testing, and for manifestation.

Through the persecution of the evil, the good are purified from sins. Hence it is written: “What the furnace does for gold, tribulation does for the righteous” (Prov. XVII). Through the temptation caused by the evil, the righteous are tested in patience and in the other virtues. Hence it is written: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested he will receive the crown of life” (Jas. I). Through comparison with the evil, the holiness of the righteous is manifested more clearly. Hence the bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters” (Song II).

Therefore, my brothers, endure the evil patiently, because the righteous must always have a Cain and a Judas. No one can be Abel whom the wickedness of Cain does not exercise.

“But the king,” he says, “entered to see those reclining.” This is what God does every day. For while we sit in the Church, while we share in his body and blood and in the other sacraments, he distinguishes and observes with what disposition and devotion we conduct ourselves, in accordance with the saying: “The Watcher stands above, who sees us every day and observes our deeds.”

“He saw a man,” he says, “not dressed in a wedding garment.” The wedding garment by which the worthy are distinguished from the unworthy is charity. It is called a garment because it excludes every coldness of evil and retains every warmth of goodness. It is called a wedding garment because Christ the bridegroom, coming to join the Church to himself, came clothed in it.

This is Christ’s seamless tunic, not divided by hatred or envy, nor torn by heresy or schism. This is Joseph’s long tunic—that is, enduring—for “charity never fails” (1 Cor. XIII). It is also multicolored because of the variety of virtues contained in it.

This is likewise the bride’s tunic, who “stood at the bridegroom’s right hand in a garment of gold” (Ps. XLIV), because true charity is adorned with the radiance of wisdom and surrounded by the variety of virtues.

Whoever possesses this garment reclines securely at the wedding feast. To the one who does not possess it, God says—whether through the Scriptures, through preachers, or through the inner reason: “How did you enter here among the faithful, when by your wickedness you are of a different color from them, and by hatred and envy you are discordant with them? How do you dare, being such a person, to approach the altar table and the other sacraments?”

But he was silent. The one whom his own conscience rebukes becomes silent. The one who remains silent about the confession and amendment of his sins becomes silent.

And the king said to his servants, namely, the angels: “Bind his hands and feet and cast him into the outer darkness.” And rightly so, because he refused to avoid the inner darkness. There will be “weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

Just as the individual members delighted in their particular vices, so they are tortured by particular punishments. The feet, which ran toward evil, and the hands, which committed crimes, are bound with fiery chains. The eyes, which abused divine light in order to do evil, are blinded externally by darkness; and those which rejoiced and delighted in the sight of desirable things will weep eternally.

The teeth, which delighted in gluttony, will gnash because of the excessive cold. The tongue, which delighted in slander and cursing, will burn eternally without any relief, as you read concerning the rich man clothed in purple. The sense of taste, which delighted in banquets and drunkenness, will suffer hunger and thirst eternally, as you read in the Gospel and in the Apocalypse.

The noses, which delighted in luxurious perfumes, will be afflicted eternally with an intolerable stench. In the Apocalypse you read about the lake of fire and sulfur into which the reprobate will be cast (Apoc. XX). The ears, which delighted in the sound of harps and wanton songs, will be tormented by the shrieking of punishments, the roaring of demons, and the wailing of the miserable, as you read in the Prophets and in the Apocalypse.

The members that delighted in wanton and pleasurable touches will be punished eternally by worms and burning. Hence you read in the Prophet and in the Gospel: “Their worm does not die, and the fire is not extinguished” (Isa. LXVI; Mark IX). Thus the bodies of the impious will be tortured according to all their senses and actions.

Nor will the soul remain untouched. Internally, according to its passions, it will be tormented eternally by blindness and ignorance, a bad conscience and useless repentance, pain and shame, anger and envy. Amid these and so many evils, as John teaches in the Apocalypse, the wretched will desire death, “and death will flee from them” (Apoc. IX).

Few, however, are the elect who will feast eternally at Christ’s wedding. Concerning them the Psalmist says: “Your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored; their authority has been greatly strengthened” (Ps. CXXXVIII). But when it is added, “I shall number them, and they shall be multiplied beyond the sand” (ibid.), how are they few? They are few because they are chosen, because they are precious, because they are beloved.

They are chosen from the multitude of the evil, like grain from the multitude of straw, gold from the multitude of sand, and a pearl from the multitude of stones. They are precious through the price of virtues, the price of holy works, and the price of eternal rewards. They are beloved because they are friends, because they are sons, because they are heirs of God and coheirs with Christ—coheirs, that is, of Christ’s glory, Christ’s honor, Christ’s blessedness, and Christ’s joy.

Therefore, brothers, let us strive to belong to the number of the few elect. Let us put on the charity of God and neighbor. Let us be united with the heavenly bridegroom and bride not only through participation in the sacraments, but also through the union of love and purity, so that we may always be able to recline securely at the eternal wedding feast, by the generosity of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XLIV. THE TWENTIETH SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“Be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might” [Col. 2098C] (Eph. VI).

In this reading, dearest brothers, the Apostle urges and teaches us how we may resist our enemies, and he does so in the following way. First, he urges us to be strengthened in God and to arm ourselves with his armor. Second, he shows against which enemies we must fight. Third, he shows with which weapons we can resist and attack them.

First, therefore, he urges us to be strengthened in God when he says: “Be strengthened in the Lord.” It is as though he were saying: Brothers, do not trust in yourselves or in anything temporal, but in God alone.

In this he confounds worldly people, who trust in their own strength or that of their friends, in their wealth, or in their wisdom, and who therefore are deceived and perish. You, however, brothers, if you are true Christians, should place your hope in God and no one else; do not trust in your own strength.

For it is written: “The giant will not be saved by the greatness of his strength” (Ps. XXXII). Do not trust in your wisdom, because it is written: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent” (1 Cor. I). Do not trust in your riches, because it is written: “He who trusts in his riches will fall” (Prov. II). Do not trust in human beings, for it is written: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm” (Jer. XVII).

Do not trust that, by the strength of free choice, you can fulfill God’s commandments. For it is written: “I swore and determined to keep the judgments of your justice” (Ps. CXVIII). Yet the speaker shows that he had presumed upon himself in this when he adds: “I have been humbled exceedingly” (ibid.).

He likewise says: “I said in my abundance: I shall never be moved. But you turned your face away from me, and I became troubled” (Ps. XXIX). Peter too presumed excessively upon himself, saying: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matt. XXVI; Mark XIV); yet he did deny him.

Judas Maccabeus, too, so long as he trusted in God alone, always proved victorious; but when he trusted in the Romans, he fell.

Therefore, brothers, let us place our hope and our strength in God alone, and let us say with the Prophet: “I will love you, O Lord, my strength; the Lord is my firmament, my refuge, and my deliverer” (Ps. XVII). And also: “But for me it is good to cling to God and to place my hope in the Lord God” (Ecclus. II), because, as it is written: “Who has hoped in the Lord and been put to shame?” For hope, according to the Apostle, “does not disappoint” (Rom. V).

Why we ought to hope in the Lord and be strengthened in him, the Apostle shows when he adds: “And in the power of his might.” Power is found in external things, whereas strength is found in internal things. In God, however, power and strength are the same.

Why, then, does he say, “in the power of his might”? Because many possess power without strength. They have power externally, but not internally. Externally they rule human beings, but internally they cannot rule themselves. Externally they are masters of people, but internally they are slaves of vices. Externally they conquer people, but internally they are conquered by anger, desire, pride, and the other vices.

Thus they rule externally, but without reason; they judge, but without justice; they command, but without discernment; they act with authority, but without moderation. Lest anyone suppose anything of this sort concerning God’s omnipotence, he added “strength,” because his omnipotence is strength. Whatever he does, he does wisely, justly, courageously, and moderately.

How we can be strong in God he shows when he adds: “And put on the armor of God.”

The second part follows, in which the Apostle shows against which enemies we must fight when he adds: “Against the snares of the devil.” For our struggle is not against flesh and blood only, as is understood. We have three enemies against whom we must fight: our flesh, the world, and the devil.

Concerning the flesh the Apostle says: “The flesh desires against the spirit” (Gal. V). Our struggle, therefore, is not against nature, but against the vices of flesh and blood. We ought not to destroy our nature, but to nourish it, whether in our own person or in our neighbor.

Hence the Apostle says: “No one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it” (Eph. V). This confounds those who persecute nature, whether in themselves through excessive mortification, or in their neighbor through hatred, as well as those who, conversely, indulge nature excessively, whether in their own vices or those of others.

Nature must be loved and nourished in such a way that the vices are destroyed; and the vices must be destroyed in such a way that nature is nourished. We overcome the vices of flesh and blood by fasting, laboring, and working.

The second enemy is the world—that is, the wickedness of worldly people. Concerning it the Lord says: “If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you” (John XV). And: “If you were of this world, the world would love what was its own; but because you are not of this world, therefore the world hates you” (John XV).

And John says: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world, because whatever is in the world is either the desire of the eyes, the desire of the flesh, or the pride of life” (1 John II).

The Apostle refers to this enemy when he says: “Against the rulers of this world.” By “this world” he understands the wickedness of worldly people, which is ruled by demons. We must fight against the wickedness of the world through patience, contempt for the world, and desire for the heavenly kingdom.

The third enemy is the army of evil spirits. Against it the Apostle Peter urges us, saying: “Be prudent and watchful in prayers, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour. Resist him, strong in faith” (1 Pet. IV).

The Apostle under discussion elaborates on this more fully, saying: “Against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in heavenly places.”

In these words, my brothers, the Apostle magnifies the wickedness of evil spirits, so that, the worse our enemies are in doing harm, the more ready we may become to resist them.

He calls them “principalities” because they do not persecute us singly or separately. Rather, following the example of the holy angels and archangels, some are greater princes and others lesser, and together with all their subjects they persecute us with one accord.

He also calls them “powers,” because by the nature of their origin they possess great vigor and power, and human beings could not resist them unless God restrained their wickedness. Hence we read that an angel killed the firstborn of Egypt in a single night (Exod. XII). But, as the same Apostle says, “God is faithful and will not allow anyone to be tempted by them beyond what he can bear” (1 Cor. X).

He also calls them “rulers of the world of this darkness,” not of the world’s structure, which God alone both created and rules, but of the darkness of this world—that is, of worldly wickedness, blindness, and ignorance, which they exercise in human beings and through wicked people.

Here he demonstrates their excessive cunning, since, both from their spiritual origin and from the practice of long experience, they possess a lively acumen by which they devise magical arts, incantations, deceptions, and snares for deceiving.

He also calls them “spiritual wickedness,” that is, spirits of wickedness. Because they are spirits invisible to us, they can deceive us more easily, since we guard more effectively against visible enemies than against invisible ones.

By adding “wickedness,” he indicates the demons’ innate malignity. A wicked person is one who is naturally malicious—not because malice is natural, but because vice has become ingrained in place of nature. The devil, however, by the demands of his own merits, has become so obstinate in his wickedness that he neither wills nor can do anything except evil. He always wants to harm—not because he hopes to gain anything from it, but because he has always been accustomed to doing harm.

The demons dwell in the heavenly places—that is, in the air—and hence they are also called aerial powers. Some of them, however, dwell in the waters, others in the woods, and others among us; and the nearer they are to us in place, the more they are to be feared.

The third part follows, in which the Apostle shows with what weapons we can resist and overcome the enemies mentioned above.

“Therefore,” he says, “take up the armor of God,” which is called God’s armor because it is bestowed upon us not by human beings but by God alone. “So that you may,” he says, “resist on the evil day,” that is, on the day of the wickedness of the depraved, who now have their day; “and stand perfect in all things,” that is, fortified on every side for resistance.

Just as the enemies are spiritual, so the armor must be spiritual. For evil spirits use the arrows of vices to contrive to corrupt and wound our nature; we, conversely, must fortify it with the protection of virtues.

They attack us invisibly either through illicit pleasure or through illicit thought. First they attack us through illicit pleasure, when they wish to wound us through pleasure, gluttony, and lust.

Against these the Apostle urges us to have abstinence and continence when he says: “Let your loins be girded.” For lust rules in the loins. Hence the Lord, speaking to Job about the devil, says: “His strength is in his loins” (Job XXXVIII). And in the Gospel: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke XIX).

When, therefore, he commands us to gird our loins, he orders us to restrain luxury through abstinence and continence.

Evil spirits also shoot arrows at us through temptations, so that they may wound us with wicked thoughts. Against these the Apostle urges us to put on the breastplate of justice, which will guard us so that we are not wounded by evil thoughts.

Furthermore, against these two vices the Lord commanded through Moses that the priest be equipped with white linen undergarments around his loins and with the breastpiece of judgment.

They also commonly shoot at us in the feet—that is, in our affections—so that they make us cling only to earthly things and not to heavenly ones. Against this the Apostle teaches us to put sandals on our feet, so that, fortified by the example of the righteous dead, we may not cling to earthly things but strive toward heavenly things, when he says: “With your feet shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace.”

Only those who have been shod in the manner described above are prepared to evangelize.

Evil spirits also commonly wound us through unbelief, making us doubt either the punishments of the reprobate or the glorification of the righteous, and thus causing us to grow weary in the labor of justice.

Against this the Apostle teaches us to have the shield of faith, with which we can extinguish the fiery darts of the enemy. The strength of faith, by which we firmly believe that God rewards the good and avenges the evil, extinguishes within us the arrows of lust and desire.

Yet they sometimes wound even those who believe firmly with the dart of excessive fear and despair. Against this the Apostle urges us to take up the helmet of the hope of salvation, so that our head—that is, the faith of Christ within us—and our unbroken justice may be preserved.

After the Apostle has armed us with weapons of protection, he also arms us with a sword, by which we may not only defend ourselves but also attack the enemy, when he teaches us to take up the sword of the Spirit, that is, the spiritual sword, which is the word of God.

The sword by which God the Father conquered the aerial powers is Christ. It consists of a hilt and iron—that is, of humanity, by which he is grasped through faith, and of divinity, which cuts on both sides, because it can kill both body and soul.

This is the axe laid at the root of the tree, which condemns not only fruitless human beings but also demons.

The word of the Gospel is likewise called a sword. If we hold it in our hand—that is, in our action—we can, through the word and in the name of Christ, cast out demons by exorcism and put their wickedness to death.

We can also kill wicked people by excommunicating them, or at least kill their wickedness, when through the Gospel we cause them to die to sin and live to God.

Thus, brothers, if we are fortified with such weapons, we shall be able not only to live securely but also to abolish the wickedness of demons and snatch captives from their jaws.

May God and our Lord grant this to us, he who in perfect Trinity lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XLV. THE TWENTY-FIRST SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“There was a certain royal official whose son was ill at Capernaum” (John IV).

From this reading of the holy Gospel, dearest brothers, you can observe how necessary temporal adversity is for a human being. For if the son of this royal official had not fallen ill, he would not have been compelled to approach Christ.

The kind and merciful Lord therefore willed the royal official’s son to become ill for this reason: so that he might compel the official to come to him. For it is written: “When he slew them, they sought him and returned” (Ps. LXXVII).

This reading has three parts. First, the royal official makes a request of the Lord, but indiscreetly. Second, he is justly rebuked by the Lord. Third, he is mercifully heard.

The royal official therefore approaches the Lord because of his son’s illness and makes a request of him, but indiscreetly. His request is indiscreet, first, because, setting aside the salvation of the soul, he asks only for bodily health for his son. If he had asked discerningly, he would first have sought the salvation of his own soul and that of his son. For it is written: “Seek first the kingdom of God” (Luke XII).

Second, he asks indiscreetly because he begs the Lord to come down to heal his son, as though the Lord were unable to grant health to anyone unless he were bodily present. By this he plainly demonstrates that he did not believe him to be the true God. For if he believed him to be the true God, he would know that he is present everywhere through his divinity.

Third, he asks indiscreetly because, after being rebuked by the Lord for his unbelief, he nevertheless persists in it, saying: “Lord, come down before my son dies,” as though the Lord were unable to raise the dead.

For this reason he is justly rebuked by the Lord. This is the second part, in which the Lord rebukes his unbelief, saying: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you will not believe.”

This is why elsewhere the Jews ask him to perform a sign, saying: “What sign do you perform, so that we may see and believe you?” (John II).

Although “wonders” and “signs” may refer to the same things, they are called signs from their signification and wonders from the amazement they produce. They were asking the Lord to perform works that would be wonders—that is, admirable works beyond the customary course of nature—and signs—that is, works signifying that he was God.

The Jews were hard-hearted and belonged to the number of those who are difficult to convert. There are four ways in which divine mercy draws sinners to itself.

One person it calls solely through inner inspiration, as with Mary Magdalene and the thief; another through preaching, as with the Samaritan woman; another through the manifestation of miracles, as with the centurion; another through the necessity of adversity, as with Paul.

Yet it draws them all through inner illumination, according to the saying: “No one comes to me unless my Father draws him” (John VI).

This royal official it called through both necessity and miracle: through necessity, because if his son had not fallen ill, he would not have come to Christ; through miracle, because, as the Lord himself says, unless the royal official had seen signs and wonders, he would not have believed.

It nevertheless happens that those who were more difficult to convert become firmer in faith, and the more difficultly they could be removed from unbelief, the more difficultly they can be removed from faith, as is evident in Paul.

The third part follows, in which the ruler is graciously heard by the Lord, when he is told: “Go, your son is alive.” The ruler had plainly asked two things of the Lord: that he should come down and that he should heal his son. In the matter, therefore, in which he had not asked rightly, the Lord does not hear him. But in the matter in which he had asked rightly, though not fully, he hears him more fully. For he did not wish to come down into his house, for three reasons: namely, to show that he is everywhere by the power of his divinity; to heal the absent sick man more wondrously; and to show that he is not a respecter of persons. For this reason he did not wish to go to the ruler’s son even when asked, although he freely promised that he would go to the centurion’s servant. In this, my brothers, he puts our perversity to shame: we honor the rich on account of their riches and despise the poor on account of their poverty, weighing secular honor in everything more highly than nature.

James also rebukes us concerning this very matter, saying: “My brothers, do not hold the faith of the glory of Jesus Christ with respect of persons” (James 2). “For if a man wearing a shining garment and having a gold ring on his finger enters your assembly, you say: ‘Sit here comfortably.’ But if a poor man in shabby clothing enters, you say: ‘Stand there,’ or, ‘Sit beneath my footstool.’” But if this is a sin, what is the meaning of Paul’s saying: “To whom honor, honor; to whom tribute, tribute” (Romans 13)? And elsewhere: “The good presbyters are worthy of double honor” (1 Timothy 5).

But justification is one thing, and respect of persons another. Justification is to give each person what is his because of God, so that, as the Apostle commands, one gives honor to whom honor is due, tribute to whom tribute is due, and tax to whom tax is due. Respect of persons, then, is an abuse of reverence for a private reason: for example, when someone honors a person not because of God but because of some temporal consideration.

Accordingly, all human beings, insofar as they are human beings, are to be venerated and loved equally. The good, however, are to be honored more than the evil. Just as people are not to be honored because of their riches and powers but because of God, so they are not to be despised because of their poverty, but are to be honored because of God.

But if one rich man and one poor man of equal goodness should come before me, ought I to venerate them equally? Certainly—if it can be done without giving offense to the rich man. But because the rich are more easily offended than the poor, and, as Saint Benedict says, “the fear of the powerful itself demands honor,” in order to avoid the sin of giving offense we prefer the rich man to the poor man, while nevertheless loving the poor man no less in our mind and showing him no less respect when apart from the rich man.

Therefore, my brothers, let us imitate our Redeemer as far as we can, avoid respect of persons, honor the poor, and visit the sick with devotion.

In this matter the ruler asked rightly, though not fully, and the Lord hears him more fully than he had asked. For he had asked only for the bodily health of his son, whereas the Lord also gives him the salvation of his soul, that is, faith—and not only to him, but also to the father himself and to the whole household. For when he saw the threefold miracle—namely, that the Lord had healed an absent man, that he had done so by a single word, and that he had healed the son at the very moment when he had spoken there—the ruler himself believed, and his whole household also.

Let us too believe firmly in him, my brothers, with faith working through love (Galatians 5): loving him with complete devotion, preferring his will to our own, doing his commandments, keeping ourselves unstained, loving our neighbors in God and our enemies for God’s sake, visiting the poor through compassion and almsgiving, despising all earthly things, and hastening toward heavenly things with our whole desire. He grants this, the God who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XLVI. THE TWENTY-SECOND SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“I am confident concerning you in the Lord, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1), etc.

In this reading, dearest brothers, the Apostle does three things. First, he shows that he trusts in God concerning our salvation; second, he shows what affection he has for us; third, he prays that we may make further progress, so that we may attain the fruit of the eternal reward.

Showing, then, that he trusts concerning our salvation, he says: “I am confident concerning you in the Lord.” He does not say, “I am confident in you,” because “cursed is he who trusts in man,” as we explained on the preceding Sunday. He demonstrates, however, in whom he trusts and concerning whom. In whom? In God. Concerning whom? Concerning you, that you may be brought to completion. In this, my brothers, he gives us an example, so that we may never trust in our friends, but in God. Let us never trust in ourselves because of our friends, but let us speak concerning ourselves to God with the Psalmist: “But it is good for me to cling to God and to place my hope in the Lord God” (Psalm 72).

“What is it, Paul, that you trust in God concerning?” “Because he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of Jesus Christ.”

The Apostle sets down three things: that he began a good work in you, that he brings it to completion, and that he does so until the day of Jesus Christ. By these three, three graces are signified. The first is initiating grace, the second perfecting grace, and the third saving and crowning grace. Through the first grace God freely justifies the ungodly, when he gives him contrition of heart; through the second he perfects him in goodness; through the third he gives him the reward.

The first is called operative grace. Hence the Apostle says: “God works in us both to will and to accomplish” (Philippians 2). The second is called cooperative grace. Hence the same Apostle says: “Not I alone, but the grace of God with me” (1 Corinthians 15). The third is called saving grace. Hence the same Apostle says: “Not from works of righteousness that we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Titus 3).

Thus the first, the second, and the third are all called grace, because they are given freely. But through the first God acts in us without us; through the second he acts with us; through the third God rewards in us what was in us from God, not from us. Hence Gregory says: “First God acts in us without us, so that afterward he may act with us; and through his immense mercy he rewards in us that which is as though it had proceeded from us alone.”

Therefore, my brothers, those who think they can abandon their sin by themselves, and those who think they can begin some good by themselves, are greatly mistaken. James speaks against them, saying: “Behold, you say: ‘Tomorrow we will go into the town and spend a year there.’ And what is our life? A vapor appearing for a little while,” instead of saying: “If the Lord wills, we shall do this” (James 4).

No less foolish are those who think that, once goodness has been bestowed upon them, they can stand or progress by themselves. Hence David says: “I said in my abundance: I shall not be moved forever” (Psalm 29). But, reproving himself for this, he says: “You turned your face away from me, and I became troubled. To you, Lord, I shall cry” (ibid.), etc.

For we are like a small child, my brothers, who cannot rise by himself unless he is lifted up by his tutor. Once lifted up, he still cannot stand by himself or set out unless he is supported by the tutor’s hand. So also, brothers, a person lying in sin cannot rise from sin unless he is lifted up by the prevenient grace of God. Once raised from sin, he can neither stand nor progress in goodness unless he is sustained by cooperative grace.

Therefore, my brothers, let us recognize our weakness and understand that of ourselves we can do nothing except sin. Let us pray, saying: “May your grace, Lord, always go before us and follow us, and may your mercy accompany me all the days of my life” (Psalm 58). And for what purpose? “That I may dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days” (ibid.). This is what is said here: “until the day of Jesus Christ.” The day of judgment is called the day of Christ because then he will manifest his glory, then he will reveal the secrets of hearts, and then he will glorify his faithful with eternal light.

The second part follows. In it the Apostle, showing his affection for them, proves by two considerations that it is right for him to trust concerning their salvation: namely, because he loves them and because he has them as companions in the defense and confirmation of the Gospel. For concerning those whom we love and whom we see in a good condition, we trust in God concerning their perseverance and salvation.

This is what he says: “Just as it is right for me to think this concerning all of you, because I have you in my heart, in my bonds, and in the defense and confirmation of the Gospel, as all of you are companions of my joy.” As though he were saying: “I trust in God concerning you as it is right for me to think concerning all of you”—that is, as I think concerning all of you, to trust that all of you are companions of my joy, whether eternal joy or even present spiritual joy.

“And why do you trust in God concerning us in this way?” “Because I have you in my heart through love, and this even in my bonds.” In this he shows that he loves them so greatly that he cannot forget them even in adversity; for adversity cannot extinguish true love.

He also has them in his bonds through compassion, and in the defense and confirmation of the Gospel, because they defend the Gospel with him against unbelievers, against heretics, and against sophistical quibbles, and because they also confirm it with him—by the authority of the prophets, the truth of arguments, the testimony of miracles, and the exhibition of a good example.

It is certainly right, dearest brothers, that those who are companions on the way in love, persecution, and preaching should also be companions in the eternal joy of the homeland.

Let us preachers take an example from this, and you subjects as well. Let us conduct ourselves toward you as Paul did toward his disciples. Even in bonds Paul held his disciples in his heart through love. We too, brothers, ought always to have you in our hearts, whether when we pray, when we give alms, or when we approach the sacrifice of the altar.

This is why the Lord commanded that the legal high priest should wear upon his breast the breastpiece inscribed with the names of the twelve sons of Israel when he sacrificed (Exodus 28). So too, when we offer the Son to the Father, we ought to have our names written in our hearts, praying that the faith of the imperfect may be strengthened, that the strength of the saints may increase, and that the sins of sinners may be forgiven.

Conversely, the disciples loved Paul as a father, assisted him in his bonds through compassion and service, and helped him as much as they could in the defense and confirmation of the Gospel. So you too, brothers, ought to conduct yourselves in your prayers and almsgiving: to have compassion on our weaknesses, to rejoice with our prosperity, and to defend and confirm our preaching by word and example.

But lest anyone should think that the Apostle said these things not truthfully but by flattery, he calls God as witness, saying: “God is my witness, how I long for you in the inward parts of Jesus Christ,” that is, in Christ.

Life is in the inward parts, and the inward parts are the innermost regions; moreover, we pass food into our inward parts. He, therefore, is in the inward parts of Christ who lives in him, who is intimate with him through love, and who is incorporated into him through union. This is especially signified through communion in the Eucharist. For when we receive the body of Christ, it is not Christ who is incorporated into us, but we who are incorporated into Christ.

The third part follows. In it the Apostle prays that they may progress until they receive the reward, saying: “And this I pray, that your love may abound more and more.”

Love cannot be idle or cold; like fire, it always tends upward and toward increase. But because some have love without knowledge, namely when they love a person in a way in which they ought not to love him, he adds: “in knowledge”—that is, knowledge of spiritual and bodily benefits, because in both respects the person who truly loves his neighbor ought to help him.

“So that you may be,” he says, “sincere and without offense.” Those are sincere whose life is corrupted by no admixture of vainglory or evil intention. Those are without offense who offend the weakness of their neighbor neither through sin nor through indiscreet goodness.

What he says here, “sincere and without offense,” is the same as what he says elsewhere: “Providing what is good, not only before God but also before all people” (Romans 12).

Living in this way, brothers, you will come safely to the day of judgment, and then you will be “filled with the fruit of righteousness through Jesus Christ, to the praise and glory of God.” Just as the wages of sin are death, so the fruit of righteousness is eternal life. The righteous will be filled with this in the future, because that little portion which each person will possess will sufficiently fill him—especially since, through love, the glory of each individual is shared by all.

And this is through Jesus Christ, its author and rewarder, to the praise and glory of God: either the glory by which God will glorify them in soul and body and praise his own, calling them blessed and also children; or the glory by which the elect will glorify and praise God forever, according to the saying: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm 8).

May he make us participants in this blessedness and praise, the God who lives and reigns in perfect Trinity, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XLVII. THE TWENTY-SECOND SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“The kingdom of heaven is like a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants” (Matthew 18).

Who is this king, dearest brothers, except the King of kings and Lord of lords, who creates, possesses, and governs all things? He is rightly called king, since he governs everything in such a way that he leaves nothing disordered. Even if he permits evil to occur either in the world or in hell, he nevertheless directs it toward the end of either his mercy or his justice.

What is read—“in hell there is no order”—is to be understood as referring to the order of restoration. For in hell, as in the world, rest does not follow labor, happiness misery, day night, or relief sorrow. Rather, there is continuous labor, continuous misery, continuous night, and continuous torment.

The servants of this supreme king are human beings, because he created them for this purpose: that they should serve him and do his will. All of them, however, are his debtors, because “we all offend in many things” (James 3). We ask that these debts be forgiven us when we say daily in the Lord’s Prayer: “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6).

This reading therefore shows us four things: how God settles accounts with his servants and threatens them; how readily he shows mercy to those who promise amendment; how great is the cruelty of our mercilessness; and how severe divine justice is against us.

God settles accounts with us, his servants, when he judges and distinguishes us. There are two judgments of God: one the judgment of distinguishing merits, the other the judgment of distinguishing rewards.

The first takes place daily in the Church, when God illuminates one through mercy and blinds another through justice, makes one ascend from virtue to virtue, and permits another to fall from vice into vice. The second judgment will take place at the end, when the wicked will go into eternal fire, but the righteous into eternal life (Matthew 25).

Of the first it is said: “Judge me, God, and distinguish my cause” (Psalm 42). Of the second it is said: “God will render to each according to his works.”

“And behold,” he says, “one was brought who owed him ten thousand talents.”

A person owes ten thousand talents to God when he owes God satisfaction for the Decalogue left unfulfilled. Such, my brothers, are nearly all of us. For who dares say: “I have fulfilled the law”?

Such a person is brought before God either by the angels, who are said to present the merits of each individual to God, or by the cry of the poor, whom he had not ceased to wrong.

“And since he had nothing with which to repay,” etc.

The sinner has nothing with which to repay when he has nothing within himself—no contrition or amendment—by which he might make satisfaction. The Lord commands that such a man be sold, together with his wife, his children, and all that he possesses, and that payment be made.

For when someone does not wish to make satisfaction for the sins he has committed, God commands that his spirit, his wife—that is, the flesh, whose softness he had enjoyed—and his children, that is, the senses begotten from spirit and flesh, together with all his members, be handed over to eternal punishment on account of his sins, and that a fitting vengeance be exacted from him.

Behold, brothers, how terrifyingly God threatens those who do not repent.

The second part follows. In it is shown how readily God has mercy on the penitent, when it is added: “But that servant fell down and begged him, saying: ‘Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.’ And the lord, moved with compassion for that servant, released him and forgave him the debt.”

The sinner, understanding that hell is being prepared for him on account of the sins he has committed, falls down and begs the Lord to have patience with him. He repays everything when, recognizing his sin, he humbles himself, asks that time for repentance be granted him, and promises full satisfaction.

If there is true humility and true contrition, God releases him so that he may live a better life and forgives his sins, according to what he himself says through the prophet: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live” (Ezekiel 18).

Who could sufficiently contemplate, my brothers, the depths of divine mercy? He threatens so severely for this purpose: that he may forgive more quickly. As soon as we promise him amendment, he grants us pardon.

The third part follows. In it the cruelty of our mercilessness is demonstrated, when it is added: “But that servant went out and found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii; and he seized him and was choking him, saying: ‘Pay what you owe,’” etc.

The sinner, having gone out from the humility of contrition and having become, as it were, secure, found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii.

As great as the difference between a hundred denarii and ten thousand talents is, both in quantity and in number, so great is the difference between the sins we have committed against God and the sins our neighbor has committed against us. For, in comparison with the sins we have committed against God, the sins our neighbor has committed against us are almost nothing.

“He found,” it says, “one of his fellow servants.” There is weight in these words, as though the man should have had greater mercy on him, because one ought to be more merciful toward the wretched when one has experienced wretchedness oneself. Conversely, the wretched person deserves to be reduced to misery if he has no mercy on the wretched.

“And he seized him and was choking him”—that is, he was demanding payment cruelly and violently. For one who chokes another takes away his voice, so that he cannot ask or implore mercy.

This is what certain hard and merciless people do. They not only deny forgiveness to those who have wronged them, but would also wish forgiveness to be denied them by God, fearing that their offenders might implore or obtain God’s mercy.

“And that fellow servant fell down and begged him, saying: ‘Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.’”

If we are bound to forgive all our wrongdoers, my brothers, then we are especially bound to forgive those who have humbled themselves, asked for pardon, and promised amendment. Therefore, whoever does not have mercy on such people will undoubtedly not obtain mercy.

“But he was unwilling. He went away and had him put in prison.”

He puts his debtor in prison who desires to send the person who wronged him into hell. Many people today are like this—which is all the more grievous: even if they cannot condemn their offenders by deed, they condemn them at least as far as they can, by desire and by cursing.

“When his fellow servants saw what had happened”—that is, the angels or religious people—“they reported with complaints to their lord what had taken place.” For there is nothing, my brothers, that exasperates the angels and saints of God against us more than our having stubborn hatred toward our neighbors.

The fourth part follows. In it is shown how severe divine justice is against the merciless, when it is added: “Then his lord summoned him.”

The Lord summons the sinner when he makes him pass from this life to another.

“Wicked servant,” he says, “I forgave you all that debt through baptism and repentance, because you begged me, having been humbled through contrition. Should you not also have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had mercy on you?”

The Lord will not reproach the reprobate in judgment for having sinned in this way, but for not having had mercy, through which they could have redeemed their sins; and because they were not toward their neighbors what God had been toward them. For these and similar words the Lord will address the reprobate in judgment:

“I satisfied you; why did you not satisfy me in my own? I clothed you; why did you not clothe me in my own? I had mercy on you; why did you not have mercy on me in my own?”

“And being angry, he commanded him to be handed over to the torturers until he should repay the entire debt.”

God is said to be angry, dearest brothers, not because of an agitation of anger—which never occurs in God—but because he inflicts punishment. The anger of God is called the infliction of punishment, by transferring the name of what precedes to what follows.

“He commanded him,” it says, “to be handed over to the torturers until he should repay the entire debt.”

This will happen, dearest brothers, when the Lord hands the wicked over to eternal punishment, to be tortured together with the devil and his angels, until they repay a fitting vengeance for all the iniquities they have committed—that is, forever. For those whose life was dead in guilt will have a death that lives in punishment.

“So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if you do not forgive your brothers from your hearts.”

But you may say: “Will the Lord, the just judge, demand again in hell sins forgiven in baptism or confession, when it is written: ‘The Lord will not judge twice for the same thing’” (Nahum 1:9, according to the Septuagint)?

But it must be understood, dearest brothers, that sins are not fully forgiven except to those who persevere in repentance and amendment. Hence it is written: “Go, and do not sin again” (John 5). For repentance is to lament the evils committed and not to commit again the evils that ought to be lamented.

Therefore, to those who do not persevere in repentance, all their sins return; or they are punished only for their ingratitude and negligence, as though all their sins had returned and been committed anew.

Let us think about this, my brothers; let us fear this. The condition of forgiveness has been set before us: if we do not forgive, we will not be forgiven. For, as James says, “judgment without mercy will be upon the one who has not shown mercy” (James 2).

We also bind ourselves to this condition daily in the Lord’s Prayer, when we pray: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6).

We read concerning Saint John, patriarch of Alexandria, that when a certain cleric had offended him, he was celebrating Mass one day. As he was chanting the Lord’s Prayer and came to the petition mentioned above, remembering the grievance he held against the cleric, he summoned him, reconciled him to himself through forgiveness, and then, returning to the prayer, said: “And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

Let us do likewise, my brothers. Let us forgive, so that we may be forgiven. Let us show mercy, so that we may find mercy. Let us be pious and gentle toward the offenses of our neighbors, so that we may deserve to find the supreme Judge, our Lord Jesus Christ, pious and gentle toward us. He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever. Amen.

## HOMILY XLVIII. THE TWENTY-THIRD SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“Be imitators of me, and observe those who walk in this way, as you see our example” (Philippians 3–4), etc.

In this reading, dearest brothers, the Apostle does five things. First, he urges those to whom he writes, and us together with them, to imitate himself and those like him; second, he urges them to avoid those who are contrary; third, he shows toward what we ought to strive and what we ought to hope for; fourth, he urges perseverance; fifth, he urges us to offer assistance to those who labor for the Gospel.

He says, then: “Be imitators of me, and observe those who walk in this way, as you see our example,” etc.

Three things must be noted here, brothers: the Apostle’s confidence, what imitation accomplishes, and in what it ought to consist.

The Apostle’s confidence appears in his commanding us to imitate him. In this he shows himself worthy of imitation. And truly, brothers, he was worthy of imitation, since he was a true imitator of Christ, as he says elsewhere: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 4; 1 Corinthians 11; Ephesians 5).

Such ought a preacher to be: one who expressly imitates Christ and whom his inferiors can follow without stumbling.

In this, brothers—something I cannot say without a groan—our presumption is put to shame. We want to be called shepherds, and yet we are not imitators of the true Shepherd. We love the honor but do not maintain the life. What results, then, except that we drag both ourselves and those who imitate us together to ruin?

For it is written: “If the blind lead the blind, will they not both fall into a pit?” (Matthew 15; Luke 6.)

Therefore, brothers, do not go astray through imitating us. Avoid what you see to be blameworthy in us, and strive to imitate what is worthy of imitation. For you have Jesus Christ as your head and leader, and Paul as his imitator; following them, you will never go astray.

Imitation is very effective, whether for good or for evil. For imitation is an assimilation arising from admiration and desire for an exemplar. First, brothers, we admire some virtue in someone; then we are inflamed with the desire to attain it, and we begin, as far as we can, to imitate that person.

Imitation exists both in good and in evil. Many admire the riches, honors, and glories of worldly people, and, inflamed by desire for such things, imitate the wickedness of worldly people, through which they acquire worldly riches, honors, and glories.

Against them David exhorts us: “Do not be envious of those who do evil, and do not be jealous of those who practice iniquity, for they will quickly wither like grass” (Psalm 36), etc. Likewise: “Do not be envious of the one who prospers in his way, or of the man who practices injustice” (Psalm 36), etc.

Therefore, brothers, do not admire temporal riches, honors, or glories. For if you do not admire them, you will not desire them.

Hence the poet:

> “Not to admire [temporal things] is almost the one and only thing …  
> that could make and preserve one blessed.”

[Note: [Col. 2111D] Supply: “temporal.”]

(Horace, *Epistles*, Book 1, Epistle 4, verses 1–2.)

Imitate only virtues, dearest brothers, good morals, and the good works of the saints. And, in accordance with the philosophical precept, sometimes take an honorable man as an example for yourselves, and order your conduct according to his example.

If you cannot now find someone who is wholly just and honorable, nevertheless imitate whatever you see to be praiseworthy in each person, and avoid whatever is blameworthy—like a painter who has many exemplary forms before his eyes and chooses whatever he sees to be most suitable in each one.

We ought, however, my brothers, to imitate in the saints not the excellence of honors and dignities, as Lucifer and the first man did, who sought to seize divine exaltation by robbery, nor as Simon Magus did, who wished to purchase the power of the apostles with money. Rather, we ought to imitate the virtues: humility, patience, love, and the other virtues that Christ left us as an example and that Paul and the other apostles imitated in Christ.

For the Lord did not say: “Learn from me to know everything,” or “to create the world,” but he said: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew 11).

“And observe,” he says, “those who walk in this way, as you see our example.”

The apostolic example is right faith and right conduct. Therefore, those whom we see keeping the apostolic form—that is, right faith and right conduct—let us follow. But those whom we see deviating either from right faith, as heretics do, or from right conduct, as false Christians do, let us avoid.

The second part follows. In it the Apostle teaches us whom we ought to avoid, saying: “For many walk”—understand, not according to our example, but badly—“of whom I often told you, and now tell you even with tears, when I was with you.”

He rightly says “many,” because there are many whose conduct we ought to avoid. But few are worthy of imitation.

“But now,” he says, “I tell you even with tears.” In this, brothers, the Apostle’s remarkable affection and love must be noted. He had love for everyone: he wept not only for sinful brothers but even for enemies, imitating his Master, who said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23).

They left this as an example for us; yet we keep it badly, cursing and calling down evil upon our enemies and rejoicing at their ruin, although Job says: “If I rejoiced over my enemy because evil had found him, let something such as this happen to me” (Job 31).

If people who lived before the Law, or under the Law, did this, what ought we to do, who live in the time of grace?

Let us therefore overcome, brothers, the hardness of our hearts, and learn to love our enemies—by “enemies” I mean their nature, not their vice—according to what David says: “I hated them with a perfect hatred” (Psalm 138). Perfect hatred is to hate not nature but vice.

“Enemies,” he says, “of the cross of Christ.”

The enemies of the cross of Christ are those who regard Christ’s cross as a stumbling block, like the Jews, or as foolishness, like the Gentiles. Those who, although they believe in Christ’s cross, nevertheless refuse to carry it may also be called enemies of the cross of Christ.

Sadly, we are like this today—Christians in name only. We preach the cross and wish to be saved through the cross, yet we do not wish to carry the cross. We do not crucify our flesh with its vices and desires. We seek not what is bitter here but what is sweet; not sorrow but prosperity. We do not patiently endure injuries inflicted upon us, but rather return evil for evil and curse for curse, although our Master says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16), and: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed” (Luke 9).

“Whose end,” he says, “is destruction, whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame—those who set their minds on earthly things.”

The order is: “Enemies of the cross, who set their minds on earthly things, whose end is destruction,” etc.

For those who either do not believe in the cross of Christ or do not carry it set their minds on earthly things, not heavenly things, and therefore their end is destruction. They do not believe in the resurrection or in a future judgment, but think that the end of human beings is the destruction of their souls.

For they say: “Who has returned from the dead to announce to us that there is another life? Human beings die and do not rise again. So it was, so it will always be: some die and others are born. The letter deceives us, promising who knows what future goods. But surely it is foolish to lose the present goods that we see and possess for the sake of certain goods that perhaps will never come. While we are alive, let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.”

Even if some do not say this in words, they nevertheless show by their deeds that they believe it, while they seek and love only earthly things and satisfy their appetite and belly.

“Whose god,” the Apostle says, “is their belly.”

For whatever someone loves more, he shows that he worships. The miser worships money instead of God, the lustful person Venus, the glutton his belly, and the drunkard wine.

Does he not worship his belly instead of God who obeys his belly more than God? Who does more for his belly than for God? Who visits the kitchen more frequently than the church? Who takes more pleasure in the smell of meats than in incense and prayers?

Let us therefore, brothers, flee this great vice. Let us satisfy not gluttony but nature, according to the philosopher’s saying: “Let feasts consist in having conquered hunger.”

“And glory,” he says, “in their shame”—supply: the glory they now have will be in their shame.

For the glory they now have in the fatness and splendor of the flesh, and in the abundance of beautiful and pleasant things, will then be in their shame. For, according to the Book of Wisdom, they will say in hell:

“We fools considered their life madness, and behold, how they are counted among the sons of God. We went astray, and the sun of righteousness did not shine upon us” (Wisdom 5).

Great, brothers, will be the shame of the reprobate when, having lost their temporal glory, they are without glory and see above themselves those whom they once held in derision, when all their sins and all their shameful thoughts are exposed.

The order must also be noted. Those who are enemies of the cross of Christ set their minds on earthly things; therefore they think that the end is destruction; therefore they indulge their belly and the glory of the flesh; and from these things will come condemnation in shame.

Source/review notes: One proposed edit is a no-op and should be replaced: “free of neither of these faults” reverses the source’s negation. Change it to “free of either of these faults” (or “subject to neither of these faults”).

The third part follows, in which the Apostle shows toward what we ought to strive and what we ought to hope, saying: “Our citizenship is in heaven.” As though he were saying: Let others love earthly things, but our citizenship by hope is in heaven. For if we are true Christians, in mind, speech, and [Col. 2114A] deed we strive toward heaven, and there we dwell in desire; and although at times necessity requires us to attend to earthly matters, nevertheless we always return in mind to heavenly things and dwell among them.

He shows through whom and how we shall reach them, adding: “For we await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will reform the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of his glory.” Would that we, brothers, could truly say with the Apostle that we await our Savior! For what else is it to await than to hope with desire? Therefore those await the Lord with sighs who have resolved to love him with all their heart here and to fulfill his commandments.

“He will reform,” he says, the body deformed [Col. 2114B] because of sins, restoring it to its original—or rather, to a greater—immortality. For what was created immortal, that is, capable of not dying, will be made by the Lord immortal, that is, incapable of dying. I say “the body of our lowliness,” that is, the body which is now vile and exposed to punishment and misery. Or the genitive may be causal, since, because we now humble ourselves voluntarily, we shall then be glorified.

“According to the power by which he is able to subject all things to himself.” For he who appeared subject and humble at his first coming will appear at his second coming to possess such power that he can subject all things to himself—that is, heavenly, earthly, and infernal things: restoring the heavenly, glorifying the earthly, and condemning the infernal. For then he will show that life and death have been subjected to him, granting life and [Col. 2114C] destroying death.

The fourth part follows, in which the Apostle exhorts them to perseverance. And because we receive the exhortation of a friend more readily than that of another, the Apostle first shows the affection he has toward the children of his preaching:

“Therefore, my most beloved and greatly desired brothers, my joy and my crown, stand firm thus in the Lord, most beloved” (Philippians IV).

He calls them “most beloved brothers” because he loved them most fervently, not only on account of nature, but also because of the abundance of brotherly love that was in them. He calls them “greatly desired” because he greatly desired their progress. He calls them his “joy” because the good that was in them was the cause of his own rejoicing. He calls them his “crown” because they were to be [Col. 2114D] the cause of his crown.

The last two designations are the causes of the preceding two. He held them dear because they were the cause of his joy. He desired their progress because they were to become the cause of his crown. For as the disciple advances, the teacher’s reward increases.

Let the pastors of the Church learn from Paul what they ought to be toward their subjects. Let them love their good most dearly; let them greatly desire their progress; let them greatly rejoice in their good; let them consider their progress their crown. Therefore, in correcting, instructing, and exhorting them, let them always keep watch as though they were acquiring their own crown.

“Stand firm,” he says; stand firm as I preached to you, as you received, and as you yourselves began. Stand firm as Moses stood before Pharaoh, and [Col. 2115A] as Phinehas stood resolute among the fornicators. Stand firm like a square stone which, whichever way it falls, remains stable.

Let pride not raise you upward; let despair not engulf you downward; let the wind of flattery not move you from the right, nor the wind of detraction from the left. Let hidden temptations not move you backward, nor open persecutions forward. And let all this be done not in yourselves but in the Lord, who alone raises up the fallen and strengthens those who stand upright.

“I urge Euodia,” he says, “and I entreat Syntyche to have the same mind in the Lord.” These two persons, because they disagreed either with the others or with each other in faith or charity, are therefore admonished by the Apostle by name, so that they may think and feel as one in faith and charity, both with the others and among themselves. For there can be no good where there is disagreement in faith and charity [Col. 2115B].

The fifth part follows, in which he admonishes one person by name, and through him the others, to bring help to those who labor in the Gospel, saying:

“I also ask you, my true companion, help those who labored with me in the Gospel, together with Clement and my other fellow workers.”

Certainly, although all those in need ought to be helped, the ministers of Christ especially deserve help: those who labor in Christ’s ministry and in the common salvation of all. For the preachers of the Gospel are ministers of Christ; the Gospel of Christ is also a ministry, and preaching is the common salvation.

Therefore, my brothers, you ought especially to help those who labor with Paul and, following Paul’s example, labor in the Gospel either by preaching or by suffering for it. Help them by receiving them, [Col. 2115C] supplying them with what they need, defending them, and commending them. For if our Redeemer is said to be received in every poor person for the sake of the cause, he is received especially in Christ’s ministers both for the sake of the cause, for the sake of their ministry, and for the sake of their holiness. Their names are inscribed in the book of life through predestination.

You, therefore, brothers, who do not know how to preach or teach, and do not devote yourselves to prayer, contemplation, or the other spiritual works, at least help those who can do these things; receive them and support them with temporal benefits. If you cannot be in the Church of God a vine, olive tree, or fig tree through spiritual fruitfulness, at least be an elm in the Church of God by supporting spiritual men, so that, just as you are their fellow helpers [Col. 2115D] here, so also in the future you may deserve to be fellow participants in eternal recompense.

May the one and true God, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, grant this to us. To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XLIX [printed: XLVIX]. THE TWENTY-THIRD SUNDAY AFTER TRINITY

“The Pharisees went away and took counsel in order to trap Jesus in his speech” (Matthew XXII).

There are two parts to this Gospel reading, most beloved brothers. First, the malice and cunning of the Pharisees are demonstrated. Second, how the Lord dissolved their plot is revealed.

First, then, the malice of the Pharisees is described when it is said: “The Pharisees went away and took counsel,” and so forth.

If we consider all the histories of the ancients and the entire course of worldly life, my brothers, we shall always find [Col. 2116A] that falsehood persecutes truth, malice goodness, and impiety piety. And since God is omnipotent and just, why does he permit this? So that the wicked, as their merits demand, may become worse, and the holy holier, according to the saying in the Apocalypse: “It is right that he who is in filth become still filthier, and that he who is holy be sanctified still” (Apocalypse XXII).

“For many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord will deliver them from them all” (Psalm XXXIII). Conversely: “The wicked will be caught in their own snares” (Proverbs XI). And again: “They dug,” says the Prophet, “a pit before my face, and they fell into it” (Psalm LVI).

Behold, brothers, how from the beginning Cain persecuted his brother Abel, to Abel’s glory and his own disgrace; Esau persecuted his brother Jacob, to Jacob’s glory and his own disgrace. [Col. 2116B] Saul persecuted David, to David’s glory and his own disgrace. Idolaters persecuted the prophets, to their glory and their own disgrace. The Jews persecuted Christ, to his glory and their own disgrace.

Thus we read here also that the Pharisees went away and took counsel in order to trap Jesus in his speech.

Where did they go away from, or where did they go? From goodness to malice, from truth to falsehood, from the counsel of the righteous to the counsel of the wicked. And since blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the wicked (Psalm I), these men, by contrast, are wretched because they went in the counsel of the wicked.
