For what purpose? “In order to trap Jesus in his speech.” Because they could find no fault with him in his life, conduct, or works, they tested whether they might be able to trap him in his speech.

Thus, [Col. 2116C] brothers, even today the wicked lie in wait for the good. When an orphan, a widow, or some simple person without a lawyer, speaking plainly in his own case, states the truth, the wicked lie in wait for them in order to trap them in their speech and so rob them of their possessions.

“And they sent,” he says, “their disciples with the Herodians.”

Why did they not come themselves? So that, exercising their malice through others, they might themselves appear innocent. Why do they not send either only their disciples or only the Herodians? They send both, so that if, out of fear of worldly power, he should say something against the law, he might be accused by the former; and if, out of fear of the latter, he should say something against secular authority, he might be seized by them.

“Teacher,” they say, “we know that you are truthful, and that you teach the way of God in truth, and that you care about no one. For [Col. 2116D] you do not regard the person of men.”

They praise Christ’s teaching not from the heart but deceitfully, and they encourage him to speak freely on behalf of the law against secular authority, so that he might thereby be seized by that authority. Although they describe it with a sinister intention, nevertheless they sufficiently set forth the perfection of a teacher’s office.

For the perfection of a teacher is contained in these four qualities. First, he must be truthful in the purity of his life. Second, he must be truthful in his instruction in the law. Third, he must not be concerned with anyone, that is, he must not be anxiously preoccupied with temporal affairs. Fourth, he must not be a respecter of persons.

But, my brothers, few today—something to be mourned—possess this perfection of the teaching office.

Some, although they preserve purity of life in themselves as an example, nevertheless do not possess the truth of doctrine with which to instruct. Of them the Prophet says: “The priests themselves [Col. 2117A] did not know understanding” (Isaiah LVI). Although they live purely in themselves, because they are blind in the Scriptures they presume to lead the blind, and together with them they fall into the pit (Matthew XV).

Others teach correctly but do not live correctly. Of them the Lord says: “They say and do not do” (Matthew XXIII). Such men—we are unworthy preachers today, something I cannot say without groaning—do not blush to commit the vices that they condemn with their voices. They are like a burning candle, which gives the benefit of light to others but suffers loss itself.

There are others who appear both to live and to teach in truth, yet they sin in being more concerned than they ought to be with secular affairs. Such are we today, something to be mourned, who devote little or no effort to prayer, reading, contemplation, [Col. 2117B] preaching, and the other spiritual pursuits, while occupying ourselves with secular lawsuits, business, and anxieties. We do not heed the Lord’s prohibition of this anxiety when he says: “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’” (Matthew IV), and so forth. And the Apostle says: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (1 Timothy VI).

There are still others who are free of neither of these faults, yet are respecters of persons, flattering the rich either gently or by never reproving them. They do this out of fear or favor. Hence the Prophet calls them mute dogs unable to bark (Isaiah LVI), while in the meantime they correct the poor with excessive harshness out of contempt. Therefore the Lord says through the [Col. 2117C] prophet: “You ruled them with severity and with power” (Ezekiel XXXIV).

“Is it lawful,” they ask, “to give tribute to Caesar, or not?”

With a horned sophism they intend to trap the Lord. At that time there was a dispute among the Jews about this matter: some said that tribute ought to be paid to the Romans because they fought for the peace and safety of all; others prohibited paying tribute to Caesar because the law commanded that service be given to God alone and that first fruits and tithes be offered to him.

If he affirmed that tribute was owed to Caesar, the teachers of the law would accuse him; but if he denied it, the Herodians would seize him. But Christ, the examiner of hearts, recognizing their wickedness, said: “Why do you put me to the test, hypocrites?”

This is the second part, in which the Lord dissolves their plot.

First, he reproves their duplicity [Col. 2117D] when he says: “Why do you put me to the test, hypocrites?” He calls them hypocrites because in their words they displayed simplicity, while in their hearts they concealed duplicity.

He dissolves their sophism when he adds: “Show me the coin of the tribute.” And when they had brought him a denarius, he said: “Whose image and inscription is this?”

He asks what he already knew, so that from their own answer [Col. 2118A] he might draw his conclusion against them. They say to him: “Caesar’s.”

“Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”

He so balances his answer that he says nothing either against the law or against secular authority. In this he commands that tributes be rendered to authorities, just as tithes and offerings are rendered to God. For he himself established authorities and the laws of kingdoms. Hence he also commanded Samuel to declare to the Israelites the right of kingship.

Indeed, he himself, together with Peter, paid tribute to Caesar—both to avoid scandal and as an example—showing that those who owe it do well to pay it, since he paid it who did not owe it.

And the Apostle says: “He who resists authority resists the ordinance of God” (Romans IX). And elsewhere: “Render to whom honor is due, honor; to whom tribute, tribute; to whom tax, tax” (Romans XIII).

[Col. 2118B] For it is the work of justice to render to each person what is his: religion to God, purity to oneself, honor to parents, care to members of one’s household, correction to children, love to brothers, submission to masters, kindness to subjects, and equity to all.

When we render to Caesar what is his for God’s sake, we also render to God what is his, since we do this because of his command.

Just as we render to Caesar his denarius, which bears his image, so we ought to bring and render our soul to God, since it was made according to his image and likeness.

There are three things in a denarius: the image and likeness of the king, the inscription of his name, and the form of its roundness. The soul likewise was created according to the image and likeness of God and inscribed with his name, so that it might be good from [Col. 2118C] the Good and Christian from Christ, according to the saying: “Having his name and the name of his Father written on their foreheads” (Apocalypse XXII).

It is round—that is, perfect—having been created without the fracture of vice and without the bending of sin. Hence the Prophet says: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Psalm IV).

The countenance of God is reason, through which God’s will is known; the light is divine grace, by which reason is illumined. This has been marked upon us because, the purer and holier we are, the more reason is illumined and the more like God we become.

Therefore, brothers, let us strive with all zeal and all our strength so that the image and likeness of God, deformed in us through vice, may be reformed through the practice of virtues. And with him working in us, let us be holy as he is holy; truthful as he is truthful; merciful as he is [Col. 2118D] merciful, so that with the Psalmist we may say:

“To you my heart has said: ‘My face has sought you’; your face, O Lord, I shall seek” (Psalm XXVI),

so that at last you may grant us to contemplate it face to face, you who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, live and reign as God forever and ever. Amen.

Chapter IV.—That they were deceived in measuring the sun and moon and in determining habitable regions; and that if anyone believes Macrobius on these matters, he will easily be endangered in faith. 154

Chapter V.—That according to the Apostle such things must be tested and cut back to the sobriety of the Christian rule. 155

Chapter VI.—Concerning their unsound confession and the fall of Origen, who was excessively influenced by their doctrines. 155

Chapter VII.—Concerning the Holy Spirit and his sound and moderate teaching: that he abandons the proud and permits them to be cut to pieces by the unclean spirit. 156

Chapter VIII.—That the philosophers, deprived of the blessings of the patriarchs, did not deserve to think anything worthily about the mystery of the Trinity. 157

Chapter IX.—That such things arose from an evil spirit, and that the author of division concealed idolatry under many arguments. 157

Chapter X.—That they are the Egyptians whom we must plunder, and that they have prepared for us treasures and adornments of eloquence. 158

Chapter XI.—Concerning God, whom we have as the subject of our speech; concerning right confession; and concerning the creation of angels and human beings, with regard to whose fall the Lord’s judgment has been mercifully tempered. 159

Chapter XII.—Concerning the commandments of obedience, by which the person who despises the commandment is restored; and concerning the fact that this restoration was signified in many ways, so that the fall of the first fathers was permitted to signify the greatness of grace, as in the case of David, from whose line the Author of forgiveness was born. 160

Chapter XIII.—Concerning the prophets who foresaw and desired the two comings. 161

Chapter XIV.—That, once the proper order had been established, God was born of a Virgin, the philosophers’ syllogism having been destroyed. 162

Chapter XV.—With what result he was born. 163

[Col. 2120]

Chapter XVI.—Concerning God who was born, from whom every truth of the Scriptures was disclosed; and concerning the raising of souls and the teaching of humility. 163

Chapter XVII.—Concerning the simplicity of the Apostle Peter and the merit of his faith. 165

Chapter XVIII.—Concerning the two sacraments of regeneration and nourishment, instituted before the Passion at the Supper. 165

Chapter XIX.—That on the cross of Jesus Christ there is forgiveness of sins and redemption for all, including the former saints. 166

Chapter XX.—Concerning the glory of the resurrection, and that the disciples were called not to philosophize but to announce eternal life. 167

Chapter XXI.—Concerning the coming of the Spirit, what he accomplished in them, and the fact that perfection is not present in this life but that the beginning of blessedness is. 168

Chapter XXII.—That these matters have been treated briefly in order to show how dangerous it is to assent to the writings of those who know nothing about the resurrection of bodies; and that their definition has been destroyed, since the spirit subjected to the flesh cannot grasp this. 170

Chapter XXIII.—That certain Teutons have fallen away from obedience to and unity with the Roman Church, saying that they have no pontiff except Caesar. 172

Chapter XXIV.—Concerning the letter they composed against Saint Pope Gregory, and the fact that this letter must be answered through the grace of God. 174

**Chapter I.**—Nazareth, Acre, Cana of Galilee, the Lord’s Leap, Mount Tabor and Hermon, Nain, Mount Endor, the Kishon torrent, Jezreel, the plain of Megiddo, the mountains of Gilboa, Scythopolis, Genunium, Dothan, Samaria, Shechem, Sychar, Luz, Mount Gerizim and Ebal, Diospolis, and Jerusalem are described briefly. 1055
